https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.text:
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.

India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.

That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.

Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.

Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.

Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.

Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.

The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.

In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.

Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.

Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.

Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.

Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.

Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.

Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.

"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.

"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.

"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."

Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.

In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.

The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.

Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.

Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.

Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.

The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.

She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.

An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.

Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.

That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.

The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.

Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.

Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.

India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.

With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.summary: Harmanpreet Kaur has been appointed captain of India's women's cricket team. The 37-year-old has been in charge for almost a decade. She helped India beat South Africa in the final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5zj.title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5zj.text:
As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.

It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.

The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.

"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.

The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.

Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.

And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.

"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.

Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.

For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.

Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.

"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."

"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."

Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies.

Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.

Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.

Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.

Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".

Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.

"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.

"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.

Yaakov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.

In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.

He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.

"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."

But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.

"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."

For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.

A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".

"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."

Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.

He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.

Netanyahu has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the attacks.

Col Richard Hecht was the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October. He told me the refusal of political leaders - including Netanyahu - to accept responsibility was part of the reason he resigned six months later.

"It's a disgrace," he told me. "When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military."

At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem on Monday, the father of one of those killed on 7 October stood up to challenge the prime minister.

"You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered," he said, before security guards led him away. "Shame! Disgrace!"

Three years on from the attacks, calls for accountability are growing. Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government into establishing a state commission of inquiry.

Yizhar Shai, a former minister and opposition politician whose youngest son Yaron, a soldier, was killed on 7 October, is part of that campaign.

"We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th," he told me during a protest in Tel Aviv last week. "Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything."

Netanyahu has consistently refused a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.

Before calling an election, his government proposed an alternative "national commission of inquiry", whose members would be appointed by political parties.

But despite passing a raft of other legislation before parliament ended its session in July, Israel's government said it ran out of time to pass a bill setting out its plans for the inquiry.

We approached several members of his Likud party for an interview, without success. We also requested that the party respond to their critics, and are waiting for their response.

Netanyahu's denial of responsibility has now become an election issue, as he prepares to run for re-election later this month.

A video game called Sleepy Bibi, released by the team of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, asks players to help the prime minister avoid responsibility by dodging warnings of an attack and "making it to bed safely".

Netanyahu has styled himself for decades as Israel's "Mr Security", and despite presiding over the worst security failure in Israel's history, is running on the same security platform again.

For the past three years, he focused on waging new wars against Israel's enemies - Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Polls suggest a close race, and that the 7 October attacks are central to many voters' decisions.

Yaakov Katz says the legacy of 7 October is a coin with two sides.

"There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion," he told me. "But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls."

The shadow of the attacks hangs over this election, dividing Israel once again along political lines.

For supporters, it confirms that Benjamin Netanyahu is still needed to keep Israel safe.

Critics say his political survival puts Israel at risk.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5zj.summary: The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. There are growing questions about what caused the country's intelligence failure. Israel's prime minister has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the 7 October attacks.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93.text:
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.

"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.

While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.

Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a US gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."

That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?

Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.

There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.

When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.

"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."

He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.

But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.

Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.

It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.

"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."

Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".

"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."

And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".

"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.

Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.

For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.

Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website.

It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself.

"Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!"

Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor.

"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor."

While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism.

Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries.

According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution.

"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic."

Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president.

The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short.

It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole.

"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job."

He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy.

In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.

"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.

According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most.

"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.

With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign.

That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.

"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"

Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.

He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.

However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike.

He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.

"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."

Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.

If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.

"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c962yz.title: Watch: Why was the sign at the British consulate in East Jerusalem removed?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c962yz.text:
Israel said in September it would shut the British consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the building ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.

Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission".

The BBC's Middle East correspondent Yolande Knell says the UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband "sees this as being a good outcome".

The consulate is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.

Omar al-Bayoumi has always denied being an extremist and a Saudi spy.

Washington announced what it described as an "economic D-Day" against Iran, widening current sanctions and targetting countries with business ties with the regime.

After the homeowners made their initial report to the Israeli army, the first soldiers who arrived at the scene were filmed praying with the settlers.

Republican Senator Lindsay Graham's funeral is bringing the two world leaders to town, where they'll separately visit the White House to discuss their region's wars.

Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques, as well as cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.

Mojtaba Khamenei hasn’t been seen in public since March - but AI-generated images of him continue to spread online.

The BBC's chief international correspondent looks at how Iran's new leadership will respond to several issues affecting the country.

The US has launched the strikes on Iran in response to attacks on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Huge crowds have lined the streets of Tehran for the funeral procession of Iran's late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.text:
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.

Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."

Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.

"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.

He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.

Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.

The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.

The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped at 85,000 per year.

A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.

Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.

The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.

She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.

According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.

"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.

Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.

Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved".

Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell.

Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.

Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.

"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.

He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.

Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating that grace period altogether.

Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.

None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.

The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.

The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.

During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

He also accused other firms of committing Fraud through the process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents. The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3zx.title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3zx.text:
Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.

One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.

The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know.

"What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.

With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."

The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.

On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.

The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.

Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".

The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".

With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.

In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".

Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.

The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.

Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.

Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.

But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.

"Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio.

"Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."

Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".

"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

Asos confirms data profiles were taken but says no bank details or passwords were accessed.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687.title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687.text:
Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.

The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings.

Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia.

Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.

The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be published at the end of October.

Some of South Korea's biggest companies release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports.

These forecasts are treated with much more credibility than estimates by external analysts as they are backed by internal company data.

There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology.

The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung, with its stock market valuation crossing $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year.

Investment in the industry has surged, with US tech giants including Google, Amazon and Meta pledging to pour more than $650bn into AI projects this year.

In June, South Korea unveiled plans for at least $880bn in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to build out the country's chip manufacturing capabilities in the coming years.

Rival Asian firms in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in chip plants as demand for AI soars.

A chip shortage driven by surging demand has led firms including Samsung to raise prices, making products such as smartphones and computers more expensive.

It is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2.text:
Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar.

From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme.

It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them.

It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time, which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross".

There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom.

Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96.

The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK.

Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones.

Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable.

"At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices.

"There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe."

She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time.

Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date.

"Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said.

The Petrol Retailers Association, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying.

Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0.title: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0.text:
OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.

The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.

On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.

However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.

When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens, it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".

Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."

The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.

OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.

In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.

The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.

But Common Sense Media's new research determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.

An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."

"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.

While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.

The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.

It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.

In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.

The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.

"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.

The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.

This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta, TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms.

OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT.

The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT.

OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0.summary: ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of artificial intelligence chatbot. But new research finds ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features often fail. The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.title: Rainmakers: The drones used to seed clouds
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.text:
On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered a start-up called Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company, based in El Segundo California, claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flares, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj3v.title: Braid-creator Jonathan Blow on making the 'biggest puzzle game ever'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj3v.text:
For ten years, Jonathan Blow has been working with a small team on what he believes is "the biggest puzzle game ever made".

The American developer is renowned as one of the fathers of the modern indie game movement, creating the genre-defining puzzle-platformer Braid in 2008.

Now, a decade on from his last project, The Witness, The Order of the Sinking Star is due to be released on Thursday - a game with roughly 1,500 puzzles that he estimates could take around 500 hours to complete.

So why make something the majority of players may never get even halfway through, let alone finish?

"Some people decide what to make based on what's practical or what makes business sense," Blow says. "It's never been the way that I think."

"I sort of make bad business decisions in a sense...because I let the design dominate that process. But then because we did that, we always have something unique," he says.

The blurb of the game - releasing on PC, Nintendo Switch 2, and PlayStation 5 - likens itself to a "game design supercollider".

The player travels through four worlds, viewed from overhead, which are built on the mechanics of four pre-existing free puzzle games from other designers (with their permission to do so).

These ideas are then "smashed together" to create hundreds of brand-new brainteasers.

For example, one world's mechanics, based on those from the free 2014 game Mirror Isles by Alan Hazelden, sees players use mirror reflections to swap places across islands.

When combined with the system of another free game created by Hazelden, Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes - where players throw stones into water to create paths - brand-new puzzle opportunities suddenly arise.

Taking a risk on making something more experimental is what appears to ultimately drive Blow, who says that as the industry has grown, the culture for developers has also changed.

"Somewhere along the way...this idea that the best designers were trying to always make new experiences...just sort of got dropped by the wayside," he says.

The outspoken designer is renowned for his frank takes on the industry - previously calling social media games such as Farmville "evil" and World of Warcraft's quest design "unethical".

In December 2025, Hazelden publicly distanced himself from Blow - writing in a post on Bluesky that he was "dismissive of diversity efforts" and "pro-MAGA".

Blow, who has not responded to these critiques publicly, tells me he instead decided to "sit down and focus on the games".

"What the players want from developers is good games," he says.

"They don't want us to be arguing, especially with each other, about political stances."

Blow says he is sceptical of AI, which was "not part of the pipeline at all" for Order of the Sinking Star, even though he recognises it as an "advancement" and an "interesting technology".

Of the benefits often cited by those who use the tech, such as increased productivity, he asks: "If you're saying you're ten times as productive and it's been 3 years, you should have been able to do thirty years of work."

"So where's this output of 30 years of work?"

Despite rejecting the tech, Blow says the industry faces an "uncertain time" in how it deals with AI, particularly with newer creators who may rely too heavily on it to code rather than learning the "weird glyphs" themselves.

"A danger is that not many people know how to program in the future," he says.

"And if AI can't really do everything, then the supply of programmers might not be enough to make good stuff."

Blow's refusal to compromise on any aspect of the Order of the Sinking Star transcends its core design.

The developer decided to make his own programming language, Jai, from scratch.

He then used this, alongside a custom engine, to make the game.

A game's engine is a piece of software that packs everything needed to craft a playable experience - including graphics rendering, physics simulation and scripting - into one place for creators.

Some developers turn to pre-built game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, rather than taking on the considerable challenge of building an engine from scratch.

For Blow, creating his own engine in this language meant he could build something "tuned and authored very specifically" to what he wanted to make.

It is yet another reason he gives for why this project, releasing on which started as a simple "design experiment", has taken ten years to finish.

"I do want the next project after this to be less on hard mode, or really it was nightmare mode, because we did so many things on hard mode at the same time," he reflects.

"But it's also been rewarding in a certain way. Because otherwise, what else are you in the industry for?"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj62.title: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notification to app users
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj62.text:
Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers.

Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app.

The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt.

Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed.

In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident.

The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach.

Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times.

The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets.

Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday.

Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history.

Shares in the company fell by around a tenth on Tuesday.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note".

But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts.

Users of the Asos app appeared to have received the alarming notification at around 10:00 BST on Tuesday.

Headlined "ASOS HACKED" and addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams, it said: "We have fully compromised the Snowflake instance."

"Engage with us, or we will leak it," it added, before linking to a Telegram channel.

The message left many ASOS customers confused.

"At first I thought it was an ad or a fun promotion like 'ASOS HACKED get 50% off everything for a limited time only'," Jodie, an analyst from Edinburgh, told the BBC.

"Then I read the rest of the message which clearly showed that it wasn't an ad and instead a message to IT."

"My main concern is that my information, such as bank information, home address, telephone number, has been compromised," said Erin, a student at the University of Sheffield.

She told the BBC that while her friends have expressed similar concerns about a potential data leak, her sister did not receive the notification on the Asos app.

"So the question is what is the extent? Are all customers affected even if they didn't get the notification? It's poor from Asos on all fronts."

Asos said in its statement that it took "immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms" on Tuesday - adding it was working with specialists within and outside the company, as well as relevant authorities.

It said it does not believe payment-card information or account passwords were impacted, and that its site and app are "operating as normal".

"Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate," it said.

The BBC understands the National Cyber Security Centre has offered assistance to Asos.

Meanwhile Snowflake - whose tools are used by dozens of firms to collect, analyse and store data - told the BBC its investigation was ongoing, but it had so far found "no compromise" of its platform.

The company's services have, however, been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years.

According to cybersecurity expert Jen Ellis, Snowflake collects data from multiple sources for analysis, and an "enormous" firm like Asos will have lots of data about how people shop globally.

However Dan Bird, from cybersecurity firm Horizon3, said the message implied the apparent hackers' access had gone beyond the Snowflake database.

"Sending a push notification to Asos's app users would require access to the company's notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised," he said.

"If both claims hold up, it suggests the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door."

The company has also shared a statement to the London Stock Exchange's Regulatory News Service, which provides updates to investors.

Cybersecurity experts, including Ellis, have told the BBC those behind those behind this incident are most likely trying to "apply pressure" to Asos to meet their demands, rather than target its customers.

While those who received this notification will undoubtedly be concerned, it is important to know that it does not mean your phone has been hacked.

We are still waiting to find out exactly what "basic personal information" may have been impacted in this incident, if any.

But for now, the advice is:

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvj6.title: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvj6.text:
Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago and described by the company as its largest single investment in Europe.

The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment and ordered measures that would "significantly alter the environment" to be suspended by 23 October.

Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance" and would follow the agency's guidance.

The orders relate to preparatory work carried out at the planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani.

According to LVV's head of environment Tommi Muilu, work at the sites included the removal of trees and topsoil, the construction of site roads and storage areas, and changes to ditches.

Tuike Finland, the company behind Google's data centre projects, has been asked to provide an explanation and set out how it intends to proceed by 14 October. The agency said it could begin "enforcement proceedings" if the company failed to comply with its demand.

Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, had previously told the AFP news agency that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been felled. The conservation group had previously called for work to be halted while the environmental requirements were examined.

In a statement to the BBC, Google said: "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance."

It said it had "acted in good faith under the Forestry Act", carried out nature surveys and put measures in place to protect areas of high environmental value.

"As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," the company added.

Google announced last month that it would invest at least €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) in Finland over 2027 and 2028. Its plans included new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, alongside investment in its existing facility in Hamina.

The company said the infrastructure would help it meet growing demand for services including Search, Maps and its AI assistant Gemini.

Google said the construction phase in 2027 and 2028 would support more than 37,000 jobs and contribute an average of €3.6bn a year to Finland's economy.

As part of its expansion, Google also signed a 22-year power purchasing agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum covering up to half the capacity of the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Fortum said the agreement would help support the plant's continued operation until 2050.

Finland has attracted growing interest in data centres, with its cool climate and low-carbon electricity among the factors making it attractive to developers. Lower temperatures can also reduce the energy required to cool facilities filled with computer servers.

Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres. The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly.title: Italian PM files to trademark her voice against AI threats
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly.text:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has applied to trademark her voice in a move to protect herself against artificial intelligence (AI) deepfakes.

The application to the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) was made on Monday and can be found on their website. The prime minister's office also confirmed the application.

As part of it, Meloni recorded a four-second audio where she says "Io sono Giorgia" - I am Giorgia Meloni" in Italian - twice.

Meloni is not alone in filing to protect her identity from unauthorised use by AI platforms. In January, US actor Matthew McConaughey led the way by trademarking his image and voice.

Singer Taylor Swift did similar in April, submitting three trademark applications in the US - one using a photo of herself on stage during her Eras Tour, and the other two being audio clips of her introducing herself while promoting her last album.

In August, more than 80 performers called on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice.

Actors including Matt Lucas, Hugh Bonneville and Nicola Coughlan were among those calling for greater protection against their voices being used by AI.

Voice clones are created by training AI on recordings of real people. Quick versions can be made from a few seconds of audio, but high-quality copycats tend to require hours.

Meloni's decision to trademark her voice comes ahead of Italy's general elections next year.

The phrase, "Io sono Giorgia", was the title of Meloni's 2021 autobiography and is associated with the prime minister's political campaigns.

In 2024, Meloni sought €100,000 (£84,920) in damages after deepfake porn videos of her were uploaded online.

A deepfake image is one where the face of one person is digitally added to the body of another. In recent years, deepfake porn has become commonplace on the internet and victims have spoken out about the trauma it has caused them.

More recently, in May this year, Meloni warned of the dangers of deepfakes as several AI-generated images of her wearing lingerie were circulating online.

In a post on social media, Meloni added: "The point, however, goes beyond me. Deepfakes are a dangerous tool, because they can deceive, manipulate, and strike anyone. I can defend myself. Many others cannot."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants feature
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.text:
Ofcom is investigating whether Meta breached its duties under the UK's online safety laws with the launch of its "Instants" feature on Instagram.

The tool - allowing users to take and share an instant image with close friends, that disappears once viewed - was launched on Meta's photo-sharing app in May as "a new way to share photos in the moment".

But the regulator said the social media giant had not properly assessed risks posed by the feature prior to launching it - something it is required to do under the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA).

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement that it "takes its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously".

"We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it," they said.

"We will of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation."

Ofcom said its probe would examine whether Meta breached OSA duties by not carrying out "a suitable and sufficient illegal content risk assessment and children's risk assessment before the launch of Instants".

Under the UK's sweeping online safety rules, platforms including Meta must carry out and update risk assessments to comply with a range of duties, including to tackle illegal content.

They must also show how they prevent children permitted to use their services from encountering content deemed harmful for them.

This spans material relating to pornography, or promoting self-harm or suicide - as "priority primary content" - alongside things like abusive, hateful or bullying content.

"Our online safety laws are clear – significant changes to platforms must be risk assessed before they're launched," said Ofcom enforcement director George Lusty.

"This is a vital step that tech firms must take to protect their users," he added.

"You wouldn't launch a new car without testing it properly, and it's the same for online services."

Instants rolled out to the app's users in May as a way for people to share spontaneous images - something that was once what the app was all about.

Images shared with Instants can be viewed by those who have been selected as "close friends" by a user, or those who they follow and are followed back by.

Meta says the feature has a range of built-in protections, including for younger users with Teen Accounts, including preventing screenshots, reshares or forwarding of Instants.

But disappearing messages and images have been singled out previously as posing particular risks for child or teen users of some apps.

"Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today's investigation shows we'll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply," Lusty added.

Ofcom's decision to launch an investigation into the platform comes as Meta, TikTok and X also seek to challenge the regulator's enforcement of the OSA through judicial review.

All three companies have appeared in court this week, arguing they should not need to provide so much information in response to Ofcom's formal requests.

Meta has separately also argued Ofcom should not be able to levy fines for breaches based on its global annual revenue.

It also contends that its messaging and image-sharing apps should not have to face additional requirements under the OSA, such as tackling paid-for fraud ads.
