https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86.text:
A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters.

The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said.

Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents.

The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said.

There were £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year.

At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024.

Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts.

"As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them."

Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers."

He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg".

One of the most notable fraudsters identified by the ABI last year was a man found by IFED to have fabricated reports of stolen high-value Lego sets.

The man's scam claims to Axa Insurance during 2021 and 2022 also included other high-value items such as MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles and fishing equipment, IFED said.

In 2023, IFED said it found collectible Lego sets matching the ones claimed to have been stolen displayed in the man's living room during a search.

Alongside his prison sentence handed down last year, he was also ordered to repay the £14,000 he had claimed.

Other cases highlighted by the ABI included a man jailed for 20 months for manipulating women he met on dating sites into participating in staged car crashes, and a man sentenced to four and a half years for submitting over £300,000 worth of fraudulent travel medical emergency claims.

In general, the ABI said motor insurance remained the area where insurers identified the most fraudulent cases, accounting for 55% of all scam claims.

Meanwhile, the ABI's figures found that exaggerated loss remains the most common type of insurance fraud, with 26,900 cases identified.

This is when someone deliberately attempts to increase the cost of a claim beyond its true value, the ABI said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5j9.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5j9.text:
The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.

The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday.

Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay.

Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.

It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.

A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.

The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported.

The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.

But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products.

When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.

Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.

As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI.

OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department

The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.

It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.

Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.

Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system.

"The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said.

"Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official.

The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.

Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran.

Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.

Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.

Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage.

The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.

Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.

Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration.

Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week.

After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI.

"How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".

Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

Inside a supercomputer: A Tech Life special

Available for over a year

Security researchers have got an AI model to break its own rules and give advice on terrorist attacks and assassinations. They talk to Tech Life about their findings. Plus, indie game developer Jonathan Blow on why he spent 10 years inventing his own coding language and game engine for his newest release. And Shiona McCallum takes us through the latest in birth tech.

Presenter: Chris Vallance

Producer: Imran Rahman-Jones

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy.title: More than 800,000 hours of sewage spills in Wales last year, report claims
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy.text:
New figures show sewage was released into rivers, lakes and the sea around Wales for more than 800,000 hours last year.

The charity Surfers Against Sewage, which has analysed data from Wales' water companies, said there were more than 100,000 sewage discharges in 2025 - or one every five minutes.

The figures are down on the year before when sewage was discharged for more than 970,000 hours.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had strengthened its approach as regulators through increased monitoring and tighter guidance, and had overseen "significant programmes of environmental investment" by water companies.

Surfers Against Sewage said part of the reason for the drop was the dry weather seen during the summer last year, but underinvestment and a lack of enforcement remained an issue.

In its annual assessment, it said since 2019 it had received 992 reports of sickness in Wales caused by sewage, with 215 of those coming in 2025.

It said the impact of those sickness reports led to more than 2,200 days off work.

According to the charity, sewage was discharged into Wales' designated bathing waters for a total of 35,669 hours over the year.

At Llyn Padarn, Gwynedd, despite the lake's designated bathing water being classified as "excellent" for water quality, discharges lasted 1,614 hours.

Rules allow a limited discharge of sewage in periods of excess rain, but environmental groups remain concerned the levels pose a threat to wildlife and a health risk to swimmers.

Giles Bristow, chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage, said last year's figures equated to a discharge every five minutes, which he called a "shocking statistic".

He pointed to 90 places that authorities have said are good places to swim, but said they'd "been impacted by over 4,000 hours of sewage pollution".

"It's a really terrible picture that we're seeing of continued underinvestment and a lack of enforcement to ensure that this isn't happening," he added.

"People's lives and their health are being put at risk when they go to enjoy these amazing places."

Welsh Water said it will invest a record £2.5bn over the next four years, and understood the concerns about sewage discharge.

"We take our responsibility to protect these waters seriously and recognise that we need to improve," it said.

"In line with Welsh government policy, we are prioritising the overflows causing the greatest environmental harm."

Laura Anne Jones MS, Reform Shadow Cabinet Minister for Food, Farming and Agriculture, said called the most recent figures a "disgrace".

"Our waterways and beaches are some of the finest in the world, and everyone in Wales deserves to enjoy them unpolluted," she said.

"Reform value our natural resources, we would review the current EU law and introduce a Welsh Rivers Act to protect our beautiful rivers and beaches."

Hafren Dyfrdwy - which operates in mid and north-east Wales - said it was "working tirelessly" to reduce the average number of spills but "we know more needs to be done".

"Which is why we're investing £11m at our storm overflows to reduce spills to fewer than 20 a year by 2030," it added.

The Welsh government said it was "taking full control of water in Wales" and would "apply the polluter-pays principle, including prosecuting serious and persistent offenders".

"Water reform demonstrates how Wales and the UK can work together to strengthen and simplify devolution, while keeping effective cross-border cooperation," a spokesperson added.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said water companies must "take responsibility" for record levels of sewage pollution.

It added: "Our strengthened Water Bill will deliver cleaner waters, stronger accountability and will create a powerful new regulator to hold companies to account."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.title: First Hurricane of the Atlantic season due to hit the Gulf coast
https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c.text:
Hurricane Isaias continues to strengthen in the Gulf of Mexico

Isaias has strengthened to the first hurricane of the Atlantic season this year and will make landfall over the coming days.

Early on Thursday morning it became a category one hurricane with sustained wind speeds in excess of 80mph (129km/h)

It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches have been issued.

Isaias brings an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season so far with development suppressed by the growing El Niño pattern.

Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak

Hurricanes: Inside the deadly storms

In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Hurricane Isaias will intensify further, reaching a strong category two by Friday morning with sustained winds of around 110mph (177km/h)

Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds.

Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast, most likely around the Florida Panhandle and Mississippi border in the early hours of Saturday local time.

After landfall it will head north into Alabama and more of Missouri. While it will weaken to a tropical storm, it will still bring some dangerous winds and flooding rains throughout Saturday.

Damaging winds, torrential rain and coastal flooding are the major risks from the developing hurricane

Between 3 and 6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to north-west Florida.

A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding.

The US National Weather Service has issued Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches along the Gulf Coast.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency across 25 counties over concerns about potential impacts.

Several major sporting events throughout the region have been cancelled or rescheduled due to the incoming storm. The highly-anticipated football match between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama - due to be attended by President Donald Trump in the city of Tuscaloosa - is still expected to take place on Saturday.

As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken. But it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather for large swathes of the south-east USA as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas.

Forecasters in the US had predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average citing the developing strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean.

An El Niño weather event can lead to more wind shear over the Caribbean and Atlantic, which tears storms apart before they have time to develop.

Whilst lowering the odds of hurricane formation, it does not make it impossible.

Isaias has managed to form in an area with limited wind shear and very high sea temperatures - currently 30 or 31C - giving it the fuel it needs to grow.

Forecasters expect it to encounter more wind shear as it moves northwards over the next few days which should limit its intensification somewhat - but exact forecasts are likely to shift over the coming days.

How do hurricanes and typhoons form and is climate change making them stronger?

'The tornado was inside our house' - Florida reels after Milton

El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69w.title: The bendy elm crowned UK Tree of the Year
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69w.text:
A "bendy" wych elm has been crowned the UK's Tree of the Year 2026 - the first time a tree in Northern Ireland has won the title.

The 150-year-old tree on the central promenade in Newcastle, County Down took more than 30% of the national public vote.

The theme of the Woodland Trust's annual competition was Against All Odds, with trees across the UK shortlisted for being impressive, beautiful and sometimes baffling examples of how nature can survive adversity.

The trust's Northern Ireland director John Martin said he had been rooting for the "whimsical" tree to win and said tens of thousands of people across the UK had clearly felt the same.

"It's a great testament to the resilience of nature."

The so-called Bendy Tree saw off competition from nine other entries, including a small yew growing from the masonry of a Devon church tower for 200 years, a Scottish ash that survived a lightning strike, and a Surrey yew, in which early 19th Century villagers found an embedded English Civil War cannonball.

The wych elm is the last remaining tree of a row that was planted along the original promenade in the 19th Century to shelter it from the sea breeze.

The rest of the trees were felled in the 1980s during redevelopment.

The wind it protected people from has made its trunk grow almost horizontal.

But its leafy rainbow over the path means it is still protecting people - just slightly differently.

"The council has put a bench underneath it where people can come and sit in the shade and enjoy views of the Mournes and of the sea," Martin said.

"I think the whimsical nature of it and the fact that it's showed a lot of resilience over 150 years has proven it the winner this year."

But it has survived more than the weather.

As a native elm tree, it also resisted Dutch elm disease, which destroyed most of the 30 million elms around the UK in the 1960s.

Martin said the tree had shown "remarkable resilience" to live as long as it has and it was great to see a tree of this age acknowledged.

The Ancient Tree inventory lead at the Woodland Trust, May Chemais, said it was an "astonishing and bizarre" tree that had endured a lot.

"The Bendy Tree has been blasted by extreme winds, over and over again, for well over a century.

"But it has continued to exist and remain rooted, adapting to its surroundings and flourishing into this unusual shape that is providing shade and joy to its community.

"We've all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are - I think that's why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people."

She added that older trees like the Bendy Tree are part of a community's culture, providing shade and stories.

Northern Ireland has one of the lowest rates of woodland cover in Europe (8.7%).

In UK terms, it lags behind Scotland (19%), Wales (15%), England (10%) and also the Republic of Ireland, which has 11% cover.

A tree-planting action plan has been launched, with a target of 12% woodland cover by 2050.

But tree-planting rates need to more than triple to get on track for that.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5rm.title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5rm.text:
Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters.

The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work.

However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970.

The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope.

"It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC.

The UK was once home to large tuna fisheries, but overfishing of both the tuna and the smaller fish it preys on meant that by the 1960s it had largely disappeared.

The report credits its recent recovery to a concerted international effort that included reducing catch quotas, size limits and protection of spawning grounds, which was backed by campaigns from consumers, chefs and retailers.

Hannah Rudd, head of marine at the Angling Trust, said the result of this effort was close to an "explosion" in the population of the species.

"I think bluefin tuna is a golden case study that fisheries management works," she said.

The WWF report highlighted other species recoveries around the world, including an increase of more than 70% in the number of wild tigers - from around 3,200 in 2010 to about 5,700 in 2025.

Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to have its protection status downgraded from "endangered" to "least concern", after 50 years of conservation work in about 80 countries.

Elephant numbers are stable or growing in parts of southern Africa, thanks in part to new laws that give local people a share of the income elephants bring, including tourism.

Barrett said these successes resulted from a clear goal with a credible plan and people who believed they could make a difference. The report calls it "the science of hope".

"Hope is not the same thing as wishful thinking," he said. "Hope is not passive. Hope's about action."

But despite the individual successes, the overall picture for nature remains stark.

Working with the Zoological Society of London, WWF tracks nearly 36,000 populations of almost 6,000 species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians.

It estimates global monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970.

The figure measures the average change in the size of those populations, not the number of animals lost. About half of the populations are stable or growing, but their gains are outweighed by losses elsewhere.

Dr Katie Collins, a senior curator at the Natural History Museum in London, also said the index misses out vast numbers of important species because it covers only vertebrates, missing plants, insects and other creatures they depend on.

"If you lose garden snails, you lose the song thrush," she warned.

WWF says conservation alone cannot reverse the decline but there must be efforts to tackle the causes.

The biggest pressures come from farming, which can destroy the habitats wildlife depends on, and burning fossil fuels for energy, which drives climate change.

The organisation says the money is flowing the wrong way. In 2023, about $7.3 trillion (£5.53tn) went into activities that harm nature, compared with $220bn spent protecting or restoring it, the report estimates – a ratio of roughly 33 to one.

Barrett has worked on seven Living Planet reports, but he said this was the first where the takeaway message was to focus on hope.

"The fact that the science is still telling us that we've got a way out is actually extraordinary," he said.

"So it's a closing window of opportunity, but it's still open, just, if we act now."

Additional reporting Kevin Church and Miho Tanaka

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9d.title: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9d.text:
Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.

Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.

According to the study, there were 63% fewer occupied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.

The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.

Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.

Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.

In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.

BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".

A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.

This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.

The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.

Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.

"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.

"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.

The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.

Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.

Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.

"It's like a penguin Mordor."

Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.

Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).

Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.

There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.

Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.

Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.

Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".

"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.

"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."

As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.

The research is published in the journal Current Biology.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9d.summary: Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world in 2011. Scientists say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival. The number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.title: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.text:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.

The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.

For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.

But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.

In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.

You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.

And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.

When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.

So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.

The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.

The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.

Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."

By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.

Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.

"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.

Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.

In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.

"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".

At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.

Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".

"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.

Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness".

"In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News.

This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right.

Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions".

He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab".

They discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule. The scientists worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of the molecule.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq98.title: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq98.text:
A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.

The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.

But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.

Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.

One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.

"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.

Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.

"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.

The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.

While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.

"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.

According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.

Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.

The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.

"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.

The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.

The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.

The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.

They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.

Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.

The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.

"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.

Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.

Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.

"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.

Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.

The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.

"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq98.summary: The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq20.title: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins physics Nobel
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq20.text:
Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.

Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said "his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory".

He first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.

Halzen, who is now a US citizen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, told a news conference that he was surprised his idea worked so well.

"I have to emphasise how lucky I was. Because when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself."

Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.

But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System — in distant galaxies.

It is composed of thousands of sensors on long cables that are drilled and frozen into a 1km cubic block of ice.

Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events.

At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light.

These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them — allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see.

"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," said Prof Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.

"His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy."

On the rare occasions when a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it produces fast-moving charged particles. It is these racing through the ice, which give off a blue glow, which sensitive light detectors can pick up.

The pattern and timing of that light allow scientists to estimate the direction the neutrino came from — helping them trace its origins in the cosmos. But these interactions are so rare that the observatory needed an enormous volume of clear ice.

Halzen's idea was to use a vast natural ice sheet in Antarctica. So began an audacious plan to build a neutrino observatory at the geographic South Pole, with thousands of light sensors embedded deep in the ice.

The neutrino's ghostly nature, the very thing that makes it so hard to detect, also makes it a powerful messenger from the distant Universe.

Neutrinos rarely interact with material in its way, so they can go right through dense regions that light cannot easily penetrate.

And because they have no electric charge, magnetic fields do not bend their paths through space. That means their direction of arrival can point scientists back towards their source.

Their energies carry further insight into the processes that created them - helping scientists investigate how exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes accelerate particles to extraordinary energies.

Louis Barson, director of science at the Institute of Physics in London, said the IceCube Observatory had enabled astronomers to investigate phenomena that conventional telescopes cannot see.

"The discoveries that have followed are helping us understand some of the most energetic and mysterious processes in the universe - and that's thanks to Professor Halzen's work," he added.

Prof Subir Sarkar, physicist from the University of Oxford, quoted the French novelist Marcel Proust in describing his assessment of Halzen's contribution to science:

"'The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is'.

"Francis Halzen has led the IceCube collaboration on just such a voyage of discovery and opened a new window on to our Universe".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.title: UK oil refinery broke toxic pollution limits dozens of times, documents reveal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.text:
One of the UK's biggest oil refineries spilled pollution into local rivers and the Mersey Estuary on dozens of occasions in 2023 and 2024, documents shared exclusively with the BBC suggest.

EET Fuels, formerly known as Essar, which runs Stanlow refinery, pleaded guilty this year to 12 charges of breaching environmental law between 2018 and 2020.

But documents obtained by investigative journalists from SourceMaterial describe other breaches from the refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, with toxic chemicals and oil regularly spilled into the waterways and even groundwater.

EET Fuels said it "takes its environmental responsibilities extremely seriously".

The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed that it is investigating the breaches.

The Stanlow oil refinery is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK and processes 10 million tonnes of crude oil each year - producing around 18% of the country's fuel for road transport like cars and trucks.

EET Fuels, which bought the refinery from Shell in 2011 for £842m, holds a permit to operate the site.

This says it can discharge controlled amounts of oil and chemicals into the air and waterways. However, it must make efforts to limit pollution to the environment and harm to humans.

But reports from the EA into activities at the refinery, uncovered by environmental journalists SourceMaterial, show that in 2023 and 2024 the permitted levels for chemical releases were exceeded hundreds of times.

The regulator has determined this meant EET Fuels broke its permit conditions 58 times over the two-year period - which could amount to an offence.

The documents show the spills included toxic chemicals such as cyanide, benzene, and heavy oils - into the air and local waterways like Thornton Brook and the River Gowy which connect onto the River Mersey Estuary.

The estuary is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and home to endangered species including dolphins and a breeding ground for rare birds.

"Species like dunlin, black-tailed godwit and redshank will travel all around the world to feed and roost in the land around the River Mersey," explained Charlotte Harris, chief executive of Cheshire Wildlife Trust.

Harris said this has only been possible because organisations, including the Wildlife Trusts, have undertaken years of pollution clean up from legacy industry in the area.

"We've seen the Atlantic salmon return to the river and also the critically endangered European eel makes its way up the Mersey and into the River Gowy to breed each year as well," she said.

EA documents detail how pollutants like sulphur dioxide were released into the air at seven times permitted levels, cyanide into waterways like the Gowy at more than eight times permitted levels, and oil at more than thirteen times the allowed levels.

In one incident in July 2023, the company breached its permit after rainwater containing oil leaked from the site - the EA classed the event as "significant".

In its report it said there were a "significant number" of complaints from locals about the smell and further investigations indicated the oil had contaminated groundwater supplies.

EET Fuels told the BBC that the oil lost was on a "low scale" and "was strictly localised to two boreholes, all well within the Stanlow site itself".

A year later on 12 September 2024, another EA report says that oil was spilled again from the site. More than a tonne of oil was released into Thornton Brook and spread to the Mersey Estuary.

EET Fuels reported the incident to the authorities, but it took nearly two weeks for the company to provide an estimate of how much oil was spilled - another breach of the regulations which requires this within 24 hours.

An emergency response team was organised including regulators the EA and Natural England, local port authorities and the Fisheries Authority - according to meeting documents.

Natural England (NE), which regulates SSSIs, said in one meeting: "What has gone in there is going to have some impact on the vegetation and salt marsh and there is probably still a risk of ingestion by birds."

A drone was sent up to survey the scale of the damage which revealed oil had spread for more than a mile down the river and "there was brown discolouration around the reedbed". The footage showed wading birds - including the red-listed Dunlin - in the area.

"Where we have chemical pollution the impact isn't just localised. When it enters the river system, that system is highly dynamic and high energy, which means that pollution spreads far and wide really, really quickly," said Harris.

A floating barrier was deployed to try and contain the spill.

The regulators decided that because the site was not easily reachable, the public health risk was low, but a decision was made to close local cockle beds in the estuary while the water quality was tested by the Food Standards Agency (FSA).

The beds were given the all clear, but were closed for five weeks whilst testing took place.

Mark Taylor, CEO of the Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority North West, told the BBC: "The incident led to a delay in the fishers being able to derive an income from the bed".

He added that they were able to make up this income later in the season.

The incident was later categorised by the EA as a "minor" breach of the company's permit.

EET Fuels told the BBC in a statement: "Selectively chosen, historical permit exceedances from prior years in no way represent the current operational status, improving environmental performance, or governance of the refinery today."

The Environment Agency has launched a separate criminal investigation into what happened in September 2024 and told the BBC it remained "ongoing".

It said it was yet to confirm what action to take in relation to the 2023 offences.

As well as the Environment Agency's investigation, Natural England began its own investigation after the 2024 incident.

It eventually dropped this, and told the BBC: "Our assessment found that, while it was regrettable that the incident occurred, the environmental impact on the SSSI was minor."

But in internal emails Natural England told the EA its reason for dropping the investigation was it thought the company's permit to operate did not set any limits for how much oil could be released - despite the pollution risks.

Its officers wrote: "Thank you for sending the permit…. which verify Stanlow's stance that the storm overflow is permitted and further with no limit set to the quantity of oil released. With this in place, Natural England have decided not to take any further action."

James Wallace, chief executive at charity River Action, said these documents suggest "we're seeing a downgrading of pollution incident[s]... where evidence is being ignored."

When asked about its reasons for dropping the investigation, Natural England said its role was to assess the impact on the protected site and that any questions about "compliance with the environmental permit are matters for the Environment Agency".

EET Fuels is due to be sentenced next month for the previous permit breaches between 2018 and 2020.

Wallace said the fact this case took up to eight years to reach the courts and the company appears to have breached environmental law repeatedly, calls into question the effectiveness of the regulators in deterring environmental pollution.

"We need to see consistent law enforcement, and we need to see the threat of punitive measures by all industries, whether it's the water industry or oil refineries," Wallace said.

Harris from Cheshire Wildlife Trust agreed the current regulations were "not solving the problem at source at the moment".

"So when a business does impact a river like this, it is absolutely vital that they're held to account. But going further than that, it shouldn't be happening in the first place. We really do need to get a grip of how we treat our river systems," she added.

EET Fuels, also told the BBC: "[It] has backed its environmental commitments with decisive action, investing over £24 million in major wastewater infrastructure alone and delivering a measurable, upward trend in Environment Agency compliance ratings, improving from an F rating in 2023 to an E rating in 2024 as major capital projects came online."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.summary: Stanlow oil refinery, formerly known as Essar, pleaded guilty this year to 12 charges of breaching environmental law. Environment Agency launches separate criminal investigation into what happened in September 2024.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.title: Why are there so many mushrooms around this year?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699.text:
Have you spotted more mushrooms than usual on woodland walks or in your garden this autumn?

The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) has predicted mushroom sightings across the UK could reach record levels this autumn, saying drought followed by wetter weather could help some species flourish.

Lancashire forager Colin Unsworth said some species had appeared in "bumper" numbers, although others had been harder to find.

But Unsworth, who leads foraging trips across Lancashire, warned people not to eat wild mushrooms unless they were certain they had identified them correctly, as some poisonous species can closely resemble edible varieties.

Unsworth, who runs Forest Horizons in Adlington, said fly agaric, the distinctive red mushroom with white spots, and blushers had been found in good numbers.

Porcini mushrooms, also known as penny buns or ceps, had been "a bit thin on the ground", he said. He added there was an EU-wide shortage of the edible fungi, which are prized by chefs for their "lovely, robust flavour".

However, he warned that some poisonous species, including the brown roll-rim, can be mistaken for edible mushrooms.

"You get look-alike mushrooms," he said. "They can be really dangerous."

The RHS said prolonged hot weather and drought, followed by a wet autumn, could help some fungi flourish.

Its advice team recorded a 43% rise in inquiries about garden fungi following the 2025 drought, compared with the previous year.

Some species benefit from extra dead plant material left by drought, while others respond to stress in trees by producing more mushrooms.

Jassy Drakulic, RHS senior plant pathologist, said gardeners could notice a "remarkable variety of mushrooms and toadstools" appearing in lawns, borders and around trees this autumn.

She said fungi were mostly a sign of a healthy ecosystem, helping to break down organic matter and support plant health.

For Unsworth, autumn is the highlight of the foraging calendar.

He said understanding mushrooms helped "join the dots" between different parts of the landscape and explain why species were found in particular habitats.

A typical forage at this time of year could produce 20 or 30 edible types of mushroom, he said.

"In the autumn time, mushrooms take centre stage and they're so beautiful and they're so varied," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9dr.title: 'The wood is alive': Ranger retires after 38 years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9dr.text:
A "passionate" woodsman who spent almost four decades caring for wildlife has retired.

William McLaughlin spent 37 years working as Forestry England wildlife ranger at Bourne Woods, in Lincolnshire.

The 68-year-old, who was responsible for conservation and deer management, said: "If your job is your hobby, you don't work a day in your life."

Scott Martin, Forestry England manager for Bourne Woods, said: "His passion, expertise and dedication have made a lasting difference to these forests and the wildlife that depends on them."

McLaughlin said his love of the outdoors stemmed from childhood.

"I just always loved being in the woods," he said. "It was my environment."

He moved to Lincolnshire in 1990 after spending 15 years as a gamekeeper in Scotland's Western Isles.

"I couldn't think of anything else I would have done.

"The wood is alive – why would you want to be anywhere else?"

Reflecting on his career, McLaughlin said: "I've traveled in the London underground, people do that daily, all their working lives, and I think why would anyone want to do that?

"My favourite thing is being out here in the woods."

Deer management was an "integral" part of his role.

"If you have an unmanaged deer population, they pretty much destroy it, grazing on young vegetation meaning trees can't grow, which has a knock-on effect to wildlife."

Martin said McLaughlin's "wealth of knowledge" had been invaluable in "helping us care for these special places".

"His work on deer management has played a vital role in supporting the natural regeneration of native tree species, while his collaboration with local conservation groups has helped deliver positive outcomes for wildlife across the area.

"His contribution leaves a lasting legacy and we thank him for his remarkable service and wish him a long, happy and well-deserved retirement."

Despite retiring, McLaughlin said he would remain a familiar face in the woods.

"I won't miss it, because I'm still going to be here. I will miss my colleagues and the friends I have made though."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c8p3gz.text:
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.

Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".

And in 2016, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor - the nation's highest civilian honour - by Barack Obama in a ceremony at the White House.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement announcing Hamilton's passing, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.

A thunderous lift off, rapid satellite deployments and a fiery ending. That's how SpaceX's 14th launch of its Starship rocket panned out today.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.title: How a scientist used Britpop to reach Mars
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckzd.text:
A series of plaques has been unveiled across the UK to celebrate the country's first spacecraft to reach another planet.

Yet the mastermind behind Beagle 2 was never your typical rocket scientist.

With his mutton-chop sideburns, West Country accent and infectious enthusiasm, Professor Colin Pillinger persuaded politicians, pop stars and the public to support what had seemed impossible: a British mission to Mars.

For years the story of this maverick scientist was synonymous with ambitious British failure. So what changed to make it worthy of nationwide celebration?

Pillinger was born in Kingswood near Bristol and completed his degree at Swansea University.

He gained international recognition for his lunar research before moving to Cambridge University, where he analysed meteorites found in Antarctica that were believed to have come from Mars.

By the 1980s, he had become one of the founders of the Planetary and Space Sciences Research Institute at The Open University in Milton Keynes.

It was here he conceived the idea of sending a lander, named Beagle 2 by his wife, to Mars, where it could study the red planet directly for signs of life.

Space exploration was dominated by international superpowers and agencies such as Nasa, which had the funding for such expensive work.

Britain had no dedicated space agency, so Pillinger proposed that Beagle 2 hitch a ride aboard Mars Express, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft already scheduled to travel to the planet.

When the ride was approved in 1999, the ESA did not guarantee funding or wider support for the project.

The scientist believed that capturing the public's imagination would help attract financial backing.

Pallab Ghosh, the BBC's science correspondent, recalled being sceptical when he was sent to meet a "bloke in Milton Keynes who is sending a spaceship to Mars".

Those doubts deepened when Pillinger placed a model of Beagle 2 on the lawn. According to Ghosh, it "did not look much like a spaceship".

On another occasion, Pillinger loaded a Beagle 2 replica into a supermarket trolley and wheeled it around The Open University's car park, demonstrating its compact size to cameras.

The footage was later ridiculed on Have I Got News for You, ensuring it reached an even wider audience.

Pillinger persuaded Britpop band Blur to compose a distinctive call-sign that Beagle 2 would transmit to Earth after landing.

Artist Damien Hirst created a spot painting to serve as a calibration target for the lander's onboard camera.

The project eventually won financial support from the UK government, academic institutions, industrial contractors and private sponsors.

Beagle 2 was reportedly built for about £50m; in comparison Nasa spent $25bn on the Apollo programme during the 1960s.

Mars Express launched on 2 June 2003 with Beagle 2 aboard; it was due to reach Mars on Christmas Day.

On Christmas Eve, excited scientists and celebrities gathered at The Open University's London headquarters.

Members of Blur drank mulled wine, singer Myleene Klass handed out jelly babies, and the crowd waited for Beagle 2 to confirm it had landed safely.

The signal never came.

Pillinger and his team believed it had descended too quickly after being caught out by Martian atmospheric conditions.

Official inquiries by the government and ESA criticised the project's finances and management structure.

Supporters argued the project had brought industries together behind a single planetary mission.

Pillinger, undeterred, proposed a successor, Beagle 3, which ESA rejected in 2004.

In his 2010 autobiography, My Life on Mars, he recalled a builder stopping him in The Open University car park to shake his hand.

He wrote: "There's nobody in the UK I didn't reach."

Pillinger died in May 2014 after suffering a brain haemorrhage and falling into a coma.

Eight months later, high-resolution images captured by Nasa revealed something surprising.

Sitting in the red dust, just 5km from its intended landing site, was the largely intact Beagle 2.

The images confirmed that much of its landing sequence had worked. Its parachutes and cushioning airbags had deployed as planned.

However, its petal-like solar panels had failed to open fully, trapping the antenna and preventing Beagle 2 from communicating.

For his son Nic Pillinger, the discovery meant an achievement that had been "on ice for many years" could finally take its rightful place in history.

Reflecting on the fact that his father died without knowing the mission succeeded, Nick added: "My dad always spoke of himself as being the frontman to the band that was behind this.

"It wasn't just a one-man project. It was a huge number of people working across different institutions coming together to make it happen."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c617.title: Plaque honours Mars mission scientist
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c617.text:
A museum plaque has been unveiled in honour of the scientist who developed the Beagle 2 probe - the first British and European spacecraft to land on another planet.

The tribute, at the M Shed in Bristol, recognises the space probe landing on Mars on Christmas Day 2003 and honours the contribution to the mission of the late Bristol-born scientist Professor Colin Pillinger.

"He was exceptional," said UK Space Agency former chief scientist Chris Lee who worked on Beagle 2 with Pillinger. "He managed to get everybody excited about space exploration."

Another 12 plaques were announced earlier this year to be installed at a number of sites linked to the historic landing.

Lee was one of the Filton space crew who contributed to the Beagle 2 mission before he became a leading scientist for the UK Space Agency.

"We were at the time the principal place for space exploration in the UK and Colin came to us because of our experience," Lee said.

"He was always very positive, one of those can-do figures. Where we would see problems, he would see solutions."

The unveiling of the Beagle 2 plaque, located in the People Gallery at the M Shed, took place on Monday.

Bristol City Council's Head of Culture Philip Walker said they wanted to celebrate the achievements of Pillinger, who grew up in Kingswood, and his team.

"It's great to be able to celebrate his contribution to the city," he said.

Pillinger, who died in 2014, passed away before pictures of the landing site revealed Beagle 2 did not crash-land on Mars as had previously been thought.

But although the landing of Beagle 2 was successful, it was branded as a failed mission as it was unable to connect back to Earth once it landed.

The mission landing is still regarded, however, as an historic success for the European Space Agency which has subsequently influenced future exploration.

In the years that followed the Beagle 2 mission, the UK contributed significantly to flagship space projects, including the Rosetta comet chaser and the James Webb Space Telescope.

"Beagle 2 started the UK down the line of being able to do planetary missions and knowing it could engineer them," said Professor Mark Sims, who managed the Beagle 2 mission.

A more recent example is the ExoMars Rover, Rosalind Franklin, which is due for launch in 2028 with the aim of finding out if life has ever existed on Mars.

"It's a European Space Agency mission but the rover was built in Stevenage and it will land on Mars hopefully in 2030 and look for signs of life which is what Beagle 2 was aiming to do," Sims said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq20.title: Students blast off to US for Nasa robotics competition
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq20.text:
Could a robot designed by young engineering students from Northern Ireland end up on the Moon?

A team, from Queen's University Belfast (QUB), are heading to Florida later this month to take part in a Nasa 'lunabotics' competition.

Lunabotics is a university-level competition for teams to use the Nasa systems engineering process to design, build, and operate a lunar robot.

The students created a lab-built robot that they will bring to the competition to find out how it would deal with future moon missions.

The robots will be expected to dig up lunar material, drive over obstacles and use the material to form a wall.

Jack Fitzpatrick, who's studying for a PhD in mechanical engineering, said "it's a great feeling" to have been invited and they're looking forward to the opportunity to take part.

The team of 10 QUB students made it to the competition following their win at the competition earlier this year.

They'll be competing at the University of Central Florida against university teams from Australia, India and the US.

Jamie Smith is a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student.

He explained that the team was divided into three groups for software, electronics and mechanical.

Jamie was the software team lead for this project. He said their main task was to control the rover then provide the autonomous capabilities towards it.

And, they had to build rover simulations to test their software before they actually got one.

Jack, however, is part of the mechanical side.

"We analyse that something is physically strong enough, it's well built enough to survive this environment, it's going to have the traction to drive in this environment," he explained.

Jamie explained they designed the 52 kg aluminium frame robot rover and took it compete at a competition in Milton Keynes.

"We got on very well. We ended up winning the competition and had great fun," he said.

Then a few weeks later, they were invited to compete at Nasa's international Lunabotics competition.

Jack said that being asked to go was a "great feeling" and "a real opportunity to demonstrate everything that you've learned".

"It's just a great opportunity to represent Northern Ireland, the UK and really Europe abroad as we are the only European team that will be there," Jack explained.

Both of the students said their success was a reflection of both themselves and also the university and the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.

Jamie explained that the main objective of the rover is that should be able to drive itself around a lunar-simulated room.

"That means it should start at a point, figure out where it is within this room, travel to an excavation point, so in that point, it will pick up then some sand which is meant to be lunar-simulant.

"It'll pick up the sand and then deposit it at another location, and it's meant to do this all by itself."

Jack explained that the purpose of this is to simulate how real rovers carry out these kind of tasks on the moon.

"It's being able to autonomously operate on the moon and build environments for humans to later habitat. And that's the real drive behind why this competition exists," he explained.

Jack explained that there have been several precursor competitions in different countries and this competition takes the top tier of those competitions and brings them together "to really showcase the talent" that there is internationally.

"We are the winning team from the United Kingdom competition and we will be representing the UK and, by extension, Europe at this competition."

"We may not win the competition this year but we're building a base upon which we can improve year on year and maybe come back in a few years and really come through with a winning design," he said.

Caolán Boyle, Head of Robotics at QPL, said the team is "exceptionally proud and excited".

He said "hundreds of hours have gone into making the rover mission ready for the event".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n9.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n9.text:
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.

More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".

They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.

The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.

There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.

But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.

Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.

"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.

Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.

And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.

Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.

That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.

"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.

"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.

Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.

Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.

Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.

The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.

"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.

"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."

The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer, affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.

One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.

Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.

"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.

Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.

But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.

"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.

"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."

Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.

Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.

This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.

"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.

"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levels… which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

Additional reporting by Dominic Bailey
