He promises to "break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path" He also promises to overturn Margaret Thatcher's 1980s reforms to give the public greater control over housing, water and energy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.title: Faisal Islam: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.text:
It was a significant announcement from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his plans for the triple lock after the general election. It will reverberate well beyond the hall.

For months, I have heard suggestions that Andy Burnham was warm to the idea that the triple lock as we know it had to go.

I had expected him to try to forge a political consensus on this thorny issue at this stage, but he has gone further than that. He has tried to take the sting out of the politics of his decision by tying it to funding a new national social care service.

The government calls it an "adjusted triple lock" as it is keen that pensioners are reassured. It is more like a double lock plus. The sensitivity over this political gamble is clear.

Under Burnham's plans, the state pension will go up by either the pace of price rises or 2.5%, whichever is higher. So, it will still keep up with inflation and go up every year.

The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time.

The policy would be to maintain the state pension as a share of earnings at the record level it is due to reach in 2030.

This change is sharper than expected. Not a review or a consultation. Ministers and MPs will have to back the plans in interviews and, at some point, MPs will have to vote on changing the historic annual earnings link to the state pension.

It seems far more significant than a mere "adjustment". This will save many billions in the coming decades, but not so much in the next few years.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank says that, had Burnham's tweak been in place since 2011, it would have more than halved the annual £16bn cost of the triple lock, a £9bn saving every year. Government sources said the decision to make the change now will save around £15bn a year by 2040.

The prime minister was repeatedly advised that bond markets would show some appreciation for a UK government capable of taking tough decisions. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves might have imagined the same reward for her decision to scrap the winter fuel allowance, which was one of her first acts and later reversed.

Part of the UK premium in bond markets has been an understandable perception that UK politics cannot have long-term debates. And the triple lock is only one of the debates started by today's speech – with significant further moves on energy and post-Brexit policy expected – that the prime minister and chancellor need the markets as well as the country to get behind.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.summary: Andy Burnham's plans for the triple lock after the general election will reverberate well beyond the hall. The government calls it an "adjusted triple lock" as it is keen that pensioners are reassured. The sensitivity over this political gamble is clear, says David Cameron.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.title: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants major reform of social care in England to create "a system that works on NHS principles" and where "everyone contributes, everyone is covered".

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same", he told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

The prime minister has asked Baroness Casey to conduct a review on the "best way of doing it" and she has been asked to report by April 2027.

Casey will also look at how to pay for any reforms.

BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching social care reform and how much they could cost.

Some people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life.

It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000.

One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold.

In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.

Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population.

The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations.

But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances.

In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care.

This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes.

It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan.

The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped.

In England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250.

This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings.

Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support.

Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000.

The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified.

The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down.

An alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use.

This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home.

Scotland has implemented such a system.

However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet.

But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing.

The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036.

Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay.

Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers.

Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses.

Some have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS.

This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria.

The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036.

When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service.

It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died.

But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further.

In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded.

And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028.

It's worth bearing in mind that the four approaches above are not mutually exclusive.

Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.

Burnham told the BBC that any changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".

One option - suggested by former Labour Treasury minister Darren Jones - is to get rid of the triple lock on the state pension. This guarantees that the pension rises every year by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%, to pay for a new system of social care.

But the long-term revenues from such a move are uncertain, because the cost of the triple lock depends on the future volatility of the growth of earnings and prices.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated that keeping it in place could cost "anywhere between £5bn and £40bn per year."

The Resolution Foundation think tank has estimated that scrapping the triple lock now and replacing it with a simple earnings link would save the government only around £650m a year by the end of the Parliament.

That would be well below the estimated annual cost of most social care reform options.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.summary: Andy Burnham wants major reform of social care in England to create a system that works on NHS principles. He has asked Baroness Casey to conduct a review on how to pay for any reforms. BBC has looked at four options for approaching social care reform.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmeq.title: Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmeq.text:
The key thing to understand about Andy Burnham's speech is these were the words and the delivery of both a new prime minister and a grieving son.

Burnham is living through two life-shaping, even life-defining moments right now – becoming and adjusting to being prime minister during the final weeks of his dad Roy's life, and preparing his speech while dealing with the grief of his loss.

The funeral will take place in a few days' time.

Reflections on his dad's life and influence formed the personal spine to this deeply political speech, which ranged far and wide.

Labour figures are enthused that they now have a leader with what they see as a clear sense of purpose that can be easily articulated.

The tacit, unflattering comparison with former PM Sir Keir Starmer is obvious.

What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.

The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.

The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like – the idea being that the argument is won in advance.

Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.

The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.

The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest.

But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.

Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock – note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals – it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.

Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and – after a review to come – the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union.

How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.

And from the longer term stuff to the here and now – including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.

There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.

His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.

It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.

The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?

And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?

You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.

Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.

His pitch could be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election. The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g4.title: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g4.text:
The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election.

Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down.

But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence.

The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented.

All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 – which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II – failed to give her party a boost.

We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term – even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office.

Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election.

That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election – and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling.

But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process.

But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls.

The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens – much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters – the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving.

When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%.

Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street.

Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring.

Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. But despite having overtaken Reform in the polls, the new Labour leader still has to prove he can win back the working class pro-Brexit voters that Labour once regarded as its core vote but who now form the heart of support for Reform.

To do this – and put Labour on course for victory in 2029 - Burnham needs to deliver on the policy challenges facing his government, which remain as formidable as those that beset Sir Keir. Labour's prospects at the next election will ultimately depend on whether voters have come to believe that what he has said he will do is actually happening.

John Curtice is a professor of politics at Strathclyde University and senior fellow at the National Centre for Social Research and The UK in a Changing Europe

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.text:
The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours.

The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings.

Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts.

The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI.

Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today.

Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together".

"By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement.

"That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations."

He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future."

Last month, director general Matt Brittin said the BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services.

Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".

In June, the BBC announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage in its plan to save £500m across the corporation over the next two years.

Staff were told of proposals including ending Radio 4's The World Tonight, and reducing the number of permanent presenters on Today from five to four, with a single anchor on Saturdays.

It was revealed that BBC One's Breakfast would no longer be shown on Sunday mornings, and that the production teams making Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg and Newsnight would merge.

It followed April's announcement that the BBC would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - or almost one in 10 - in an attempt to tackle "significant financial pressures".

Last week, an influential group of MPs said the BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV, and that the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent.

In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.title: Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn9.text:
Shaun of the Dead and Mission: Impossible films star Simon Pegg has revealed he has been diagnosed with ADHD, which he said "confirmed a lot of stuff that I'd been wrestling with".

Pegg, 56, who also co-created and starred in films Hot Fuzz, The World's End, and TV series Spaced, said "there was a lot of build-up and suspicion, and it just took a while actually to get there."

Speaking on the podcast I'm ADHD! No You're Not on Thursday, he said he pursued a diagnosis as he "just wanted to know".

ADHD symptoms focus on three main areas - inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity plus lack of concentration.

Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who are negatively affected on a daily basis.

Pegg said he had previously been putting his symptoms down to "just character fault".

The actor and writer also spoke about his mental health, including having clinical depression and struggling to control his drinking, which he said he initially thought had "caused" his diagnosis.

"I felt like it was something that had come on in later life because I wasn't a naughty child.

"I've had bouts of depression in my adult life since 18 and I thought maybe it had come on with that.

"Maybe over the years with therapy and medication - whatever - I've been treating the symptoms and not the cause of why I feel that way."

Pegg said: "I did feel different in a way I might not be able to put my finger on. Maybe everybody feels that way.

"I just assumed ADHD kids were kind of chaotic and difficult and didn't pay attention in school," he added.

"But there were other things that I did do as a kid – fidget or whatever – that made me think, 'Oh no, maybe I've had this longer than I thought'."

Pegg said his wife has been supportive and is "dealing with it as if I'd been diagnosed ages ago", adding: "It's just who I am, and it's just things that I do.

"She makes allowances for forgetfulness and and lack of concentration."

Pegg had previously said he felt his poor driving was down to undiagnosed ADHD.

The star, who has had several speeding convictions, told LBC last year that he felt an ADHD diagnosis would help explain his poor concentration when it comes to driving.

He reversed into a post while on holiday in Greece, which prompted him to look up the symptoms of ADHD.

"I looked up on the phone 'Do people with ADHD get into more car accidents than people who don't have it' and the answer was yes.

"And it's because of a lack of focus and ability to kind of totally focus.

"And that was the final straw that broke my ADHD camel's back. I need to speak to a psychiatrist and find out for sure if I have this thing."

Other celebrities who have been diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood include comedian and actor Johnny Vegas, comic and presenter Sue Perkins, presenters Ant McPartlin and Richard Bacon, comedian Rory Bremner and model Erin O'Connor.

ADHD is described by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) as "a behavioural syndrome characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention".

The NHS estimates that about 2.5 million people in England have ADHD, including those without a formal diagnosis.

Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand.

Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018.

Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest ADHD is actually underdiagnosed.

In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp8.title: Gaten Matarazzo on life after Stranger Things as he makes West End debut
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp8.text:
Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference.

You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience.

The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End.

He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous.

Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life".

The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next.

"It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo

"We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film."

"I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it."

Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in.

But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child.

He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds".

"My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says.

"Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time.

"I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane."

In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends.

It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now".

"What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says.

"That's really fun to sing in context of today."

When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis.

It was considered groundbreaking at the time for tackling social taboos and centering stories of LGBT people.

Writer Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its premiere.

Matarazzo's co-star, Travis Ross, who plays Roger, says the show's themes still "ring true" today.

The 25-year-old says having Rent tends to attract people who "care so deeply" about the show's message, resulting in a connection between actors and the audience.

He calls it a "really beautiful community-driven piece of art".

Both Ross and Matarazzo are keen to acknowledge their fellow cast members and point out Rent is "an ensemble" piece.

"In the same way we get our moments to tell the story there's also ten other people who get their moments to tell the story as well," says Ross.

Many of those in the audience will be there to watch Matarazzo, and he says he's determined to get the role right.

"I'm on stage for the majority of the show and singing the whole time," he says.

"It's not anything that's particularly high or out of my range, it's actually a part that I think fits nicely in my pocket.

"But it's just so much singing, and making sure I'm doing it correctly is essential," he says.

Matarazzo also plans to embrace his return to the stage.

"Once we're in the run it will be great," he says.

"I just always love the opportunity to start and finish a character arc and story in real time.

"You don't get an opportunity to do that when you're filming."

Speaking of which - if he ever got the call to go back to Hawkins and step into Dustin's shoes, would he take the chance?

"If that happens, that's great, and if not, that's completely fine.

"I've loved doing the show so much, it's literally the greatest honour of my life."

Rent is at The Tom Stoppard Theatre, London. Gaten Matarazzo is booked to perform until 10 January.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60m.title: Cavern Club sold to new owners after 35 years
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60m.text:
Liverpool's Cavern Club and Magical Mystery Tour have new owners after 35 years.

A group called 14 Collective have bought Cavern City Tours, which also includes the Cavern Pub and Restaurant.

John Lennon's sister, Julia Baird, who was one of the previous owners, said she felt "sad for me personally, yet positive for the future of this world famous, number one music club", adding that it was being left "in good hands".

The Beatles played at the original Cavern 292 times as they were on the road to stardom between 1961-63.

But the underground club was filled in after it closed in 1973.

A replica was built on the site in 1984 and now attracts a million Beatles fans every year.

Managing director Bill Heckle trained to be a Beatles guide in 1982 before forming the Cavern City Tours in 1983.

Alongside Dave Jones they organised their first Beatles convention, which evolved into the annual Mathew Street Music Festival.

In 1991, they acquired the Magical Mystery Tour - bus tours of Liverpool - and the Cavern Club venue.

Heckle said the decision to sell was "not taken lightly" but it was "time for retirement".

"It is an emotional day, but a proud day, for the four Scouse owners," he said.

"It was never about putting Cavern City Tours up for sale to the highest bidder and it has taken over five years to find a suitable and like-minded custodian.

"However, we leave with the confidence that the new owners will continue to follow the path we have forged over the last 43 years."

In a statement, the new owners, 14 Collective, said: "We look forward to working alongside the existing management team, with a real appreciation for what makes the Cavern so special and excitement about what comes next."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.title: Black and African cinema hub opens in London
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.text:
A new black and African cinema and hub has officially opened in south-west London.

EbonyLife Place, based near Nine Elms, was unveiled with a ceremony attended by the Mayor of London Lord Khan, and its founder Mo Abudu.

Abudu, a Nigerian media mogul who was born in London, explained that the project was born from a desire to showcase and celebrate stories that she felt previously lacked a home.

"I do think there is a younger audience of young people now that just want to see great storytelling," Abudu said.

She added: "We make great films, and I think we need to create experiences where people can come and they can see the great work that we do in black cinema, in African cinema.

"We don't have enough spaces to serve black cinema in the United Kingdom... representation is so important to us."

At the heart of the cultural centre is a 160-seat auditorium featuring a year-round film programme.

The screenings will primarily focus on Nollywood cinema from Nigeria alongside other movies connecting to the black experience.

In addition to film screenings, the venue will host masterclasses, industry panels, and live performances by established and emerging talent.

Beyond its cinema space, the multi-storey venue features a bar, a lounge called "Fàhinti" (a Yoruba word meaning to lean back and rest), a Nigerian restaurant, a boutique showcasing African and diaspora designers, and walls lined with African diaspora artwork.

The project, financed almost entirely by Abudu's media group, mirrors the upscale lifestyle complex she launched in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos, in 2019.

Speaking at Thursday's launch, Lord Khan said: "London is the number one place in Europe to film," adding that the capital sits just behind Los Angeles and ahead of New York in the global film production footprint.

"As long as I'm mayor, we'll invest in culture," he said.

The opening coincides with the London Film Festival.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmj6.title: Katie Price 'angry' when told of ex's rape claim
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmj6.text:
The mother of a teenage girl allegedly raped by Katie Price's then-husband said she felt the former glamour model was "angry" about the allegation and "didn't care" about her daughter, a court has heard.

Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against the then 13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

Giving evidence in court on Thursday, the complainant's mother said when she told Price about the allegations, "she was quite angry and I didn't feel she was particularly upset for [the complainant]".

She added: "I didn't feel she cared about my daughter."

The court heard the teenager told her mother a year after the alleged rapes that Hayler had "done everything to her" to which she was "shocked".

The jury was told she tried to ask her daughter to explain but she said: "I can't tell you any more."

Asked if she questioned her further, she replied: "I didn't because she was so distressed."

The mother told the court she told Price about the allegations because she felt like she "had to".

Asked how Price reacted, she said: "She was shocked and probably swore.

"I feel she was just angry and feeling revengeful towards Kieran."

But the alleged victim's mother said her daughter did not "want anyone to know" and they had to "respect her wishes".

In court she said she and her daughter had fallen out after she told Price.

Asked if this was because she felt she betrayed her trust, the mother replied: "Yes, she probably didn't want anyone to ever know and yes it did cause arguments."

The mother said she noticed changes in her daughter's behaviour including her becoming more "withdrawn".

"My main concern was her washing, she would shower about four times a day and scrub her skin and it really worried me," she said.

She told the court she asked her daughter why she was washing so often to which she replied: "I just feel dirty all the time."

The complainant contacted the NSPCC in 2021 about the allegations which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.

Her mother told the court about the day her daughter informed her she had reported it to the police, adding: "She still hadn't told me exactly what had happened."

The court heard after it was reported the two discussed the matter.

The mum said: "She said it made her feel sick and dirty thinking about it whenever she thought about what had happened.

"At the time she thought it was normal but looking back on it she realised it wasn't because of her age and then she just felt dirty."

Hayler has suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations formed part of this, the court heard.

He was married to Price at the time of the allegations, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.

The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j4.title: How boxing inspired a play about men's mental health
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j4.text:
For many athletes, years of training can provide a routine, a purpose and an identity - but what happens when it all stops?

That question is at the heart of a new play which explores men's mental health through the world of boxing.

The Corner Man follows a fighter forced to confront life outside the ring after spending years dedicated to the sport.

Through his story, the play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.

Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris said the idea grew from his own experience of boxing and conversations with fighters.

"What is a boxer after he retires really played on my mind," he said, adding that the same questions around identity and purpose can apply beyond sport.

The play follows Liam Casey, who has dedicated much of his life to boxing, from the age of about nine into his 30s.

For Ferris, the story is not only about leaving the ring, but about losing the routine that comes with it.

"The idea of structure and what life is like whenever you lose that structure definitely played on my mind," he said.

"There are people who work in jobs for 10, 12, 13-odd years and just decide to change industries.

"I think there's a lot of people who may not know what to do with themselves after."

Ferris grew up performing in amateur theatre in Belfast and Lisburn before going to drama school in London in 2012.

He said returning home had given him the chance to tell new stories about the place where he grew up.

"I'm a Belfast boy at heart, and it is great to tell stories from the city," he said.

Ferris said "the boxing community in Belfast is phenomenal" and that it played an important part in shaping the story.

Alongside boxing, the play also looks at how men talk - or sometimes do not talk - about their mental health.

"I think the old phrase is 'say nothing', and we know that all too well," Ferris said.

"As a man, it is definitely hard for myself to talk about these things, and I try to be a little bit more open."

In the play, Liam struggles with life after boxing, but it is the other men around him who help provide a support network - something Ferris said was an important part of the story.

"It is healthy to talk, so definitely if you're a man and you're struggling, at least speak to somebody," he said.

Director Emma Copeland said she knew relatively little about boxing before becoming involved in the production, but soon immersed herself in the sport.

"I got really into boxing and went to a load of boxing classes and I'm still going," she said.

Copeland said she also watched films, read books and autobiographies and listened to podcasts to make sure she knew the world she was portraying.

For her, one of the most important parts of the play is the support the men offer each other.

"The angle that I see is that men supporting men, and helping and talking and encouraging support with each other and encouraging that conversation," she said.

"Rather than shutting it down or locking themselves away in their own feelings."

For actor Gary Trainor, the experience Liam goes through is not something that only applies to boxers.

Trainor, who plays gym owner Marty as well as several other roles, said suddenly losing something which has been central to your life could happen in many different circumstances.

"He's been so engrossed in the world of boxing for his entire life, to lose it in one injury and to try and figure out his life after that is, I think, probably universal in a lot of men's lives," he said.

"That could be maybe losing a job, anything like that."

Trainor described the play as "full of heart and humour" and said he hoped it would "make a few lads think".

For him, its message is a straightforward one - that "men should talk to each other a bit more about what they are feeling and how they are processing things".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j4.summary: The Corner Man explores the world of boxing and the challenges of men's mental health. Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris says the idea grew from his own experience of boxing. The play follows a boxer who has dedicated much of his life to the sport.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckwy.title: Suffragette role 'a gift' says Beverley Knight
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckwy.text:
Singer Beverley Knight said she hoped audiences watching her latest musical would leave feeling "empowered" and with the belief that their voices can make a difference.

Sylvia the Musical tells the story of suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst and the family rift caused by the fight for women's voting rights.

The Wolverhampton artist, who plays Sylvia's mother and suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst at the Birmingham Hippodrome said she was a "history nerd" and described the part as a "gift of a role".

"It's an absolutely killer story, and the best thing is it's true," she said.

"I want everyone bouncing out of there because it's a joyful musical, even though there's some absolutely heartbreaking moments in it."

The soul singer, known for hits including Shoulda Woulda Coulda and Get Up, told BBC Radio WM the musical was telling a "huge part of British history" from 1903, all the way to 1928.

"So most people know who Emmeline Pankhurst was, leader of the suffragettes, she was determined to get women the vote," she explained.

"But she came up against her middle daughter Sylvia, who not only wanted to get wealthy property owning women the vote, which was the case with men in the country, [you] had to be rich and male to vote, she wanted everybody to be able to vote.

"But Emmeline was focused on just the women and that put her on a collision course with her daughter and both of them were on a collision course with the government."

Knight added the show, which also features Naomi Katiyo as Sylvia Pankhurst, was "musically up my street" and was being called a "hip-hop musical" because it included elements of R&B, funk, soul, garage, gospel and house.

"The engine of the show is the music," she said. The whole thing is either spoken or rapped or sung. Of course, I'm doing mostly singing because I ain't rapping anything."

The former Highfields School pupil explained the story also went beyond the Pankhurst family, with some people who attended the show likely to have relatives who were involved in the suffragette movement.

"It's not just the story of the Pankhursts, there are going to be loads of people who will come to this show who will be like... my grandma or my great-grandma, she was involved in the suffragette movement.

"I want everybody to leave like, let's go, oh my god, that feeling of I can effect change, I can use my voice and effect change. I feel empowered."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckwy.summary: Sylvia the Musical tells the story of suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst and her family rift. Singer Beverley Knight plays Sylvia's mother and suffragettes leader Emmeline Pankhursts. She said she was a "history nerd" and described the part as a "gift of a role"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpq.title: 'I won Gladiators - now I'd love to become one'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpq.text:
Having been bashed, bumped and bruised on his way to winning Gladiators earlier this year, you might expect Josh McDonald wants to put his feet up.

But the Glasgow fitness coach has not only signed up for another go on the famous Eliminator challenge - he fancies becoming one of the Lycra-clad stars.

The 29-year-old triumphed in the third season of the popular programme, which was filmed in Sheffield last year.

He is now getting the chance to go again on games like Duel, Gauntlet and The Wall as part of a live tour across the country.

Several new Gladiators have joined the show for the new season, including three-time World's Strongest Man champion Tom Stoltman.

And Josh admitted he wouldn't mind "turning to the dark side" and joining the likes of Viper, Legend and Scotland's own Sabre.

He said: "I'd love to be a Gladiator and I think I'd be fantastic at it, with the message I bring, the personality I've got and the athletic ability I have.

"The problem is that while the gladiators are the pinnacle, they can't actually win the show - only the contenders can do that, and I'm really competitive.

"So you're better off being a contender than a Gladiator in some ways, as I don't think you would get the emotional rollercoaster that a contender will get from it.

"But if the opportunity to be a Gladiator came up, then I'd be there."

Josh was actually edged out in the first round of the show, but returned in the next stage after an injury to another contestant.

He did not let his second chance slip away, storming through to the final and taking the trophy after beating Tyler Spence, a teacher from Wigan, in a closely-fought contest.

However while Josh was jubilant to win the competition, the victory also brought with it a mixture of emotions.

He first watched the show growing up alongside his mother Clare, a single parent who raised him and his two younger brothers.

But in 2024, a few months before he got the offer to appear on the programme, his mother died after a long illness.

Josh then became the guardian of his younger brother Max, who was 14 at the time.

"I used to watch the show growing up with my mum," he recalls.

"She loved Wolf [from the 90s version] and it was something you'd sit on the couch going 'oh I could do that, I'd love that' and then the opportunity came up.

"Just before the show [was filmed] I wasn't taking care of myself as much, as I had lost my mum and was taking guardianship of Max and having that extra responsibility.

"There was a motivation of trying to prove myself that I could still compete and give Max something to cheer about, so I got back in training again."

Now he is trying to get ready for the games again, this time for the live tour.

It starts in Aberdeen this weekend and includes four shows in front of a home Glasgow crowd later this month.

"You can't go into a gym and just practice Duel, so what I am trying to do just now is focus on staying fit and healthy in general," he says.

"I've been at the local climbing centre trying to prepare for the Wall as that was the game I struggled with the most.

"In training I had been one of the quickest, and I'd thought to myself 'oh I'll get 10 points here' and then I messed it up every single time.

"I don't know if it was the pressure that got to me, as it's different when you have a Gladiator behind you, or maybe I just had too high expectations.

"I'm determined to do better on the tour."

Getting back involved with Gladiators was not something Josh - who proudly displays the trophy from the show on a table in his living room - had to think twice about.

"I'd have Gladiators champion tattooed on my forehead if I could so I bit their hand off to do it," he said.

"Doing the TV show was one of the highlights of my entire life and something I'll never forget so having the opportunity to relive it in Scotland is so exciting."

But no matter what is thrown at him Josh said being a guardian to Max was the toughest challenge he faced in life.

He added: "I've always had big brother responsibilities, and my mum was a single parent so I always tried to support her.

"But as soon as I stepped into the guardian role it flipped everything on its head. It's not something you can prepare for."

Since winning Gladiators he has become involved in various charities, including raising awareness for kinship charities.

Josh hopes he can help highlight that there is support available for people in similar situations to himself.

He said: "I thought I was one in a million and I had to stumble my way through it.

"A lot of the information I obtained was just me sourcing it and I felt very isolated.

"But there are thousands of us out there and I want them to feel like they are not alone."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpq.summary: Josh McDonald won the third season of the popular programme earlier this year. The Glasgow fitness coach is now getting the chance to go again on games like Duel, Gauntlet and The Wall. He is part of a live tour of the show, which starts in Aberdeen this weekend.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.title: How a folk band, football club and Fifa 11 came together for an unlikely terrace anthem
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.text:
It's a tale as old as time. Take one 16-year-old video game, a rising indie-folk band and a League One football team and what do you get?

A new football anthem for Wycombe Wanderers, courtesy of the unlikely figures of Irish chart-toppers Kingfishr, whose singer was the special guest under the Tuesday night lights of the club's Adams Park stadium this week.

It's a strange musical connection that came about in a way avid fans of sports video games can understand - via Fifa 11, a game the band said they started playing while recording their second album.

The band adopted Wycombe Wanderers as their team in the game and eventually posted a song for the club, which has racked up more than 190,000 views on TikTok.

The club caught wind of the song, written in an Irish folk style and with a lyrical focus on "the Wycombe wanderer, wandering away" and replied to the original post by saying: "You can wander our way anytime."

So it came that lead singer Eddie Keogh took up the offer on Tuesday night, as first reported by Irish sports site Balls.ie, and attended the club's 4-1 EFL Trophy victory over Bristol Rovers.

The song was even playing over the tannoy as he arrived, to the singer's shock as demonstrated by his "what is going on?" post to TikTok.

The club invited him onto the pitch where he was presented with his own club shirt with 'Kingfishr 1' on the back.

In statement to BBC News NI, a Wycombe Wanderers spokesperson said discovering the song was "brilliant".

"As fate would have it, Eddie from the band was able to join us that evening to visit the stadium, watch a game, meet the players and learn a little more about the club he's adopted as his own.

"A lot of our players are massive fans of the band, and the song from the TikTok has gone down extremely well with supporters, so we hope it might become a terrace anthem."

The club spokesperson added that Kingfishr "are welcome back to Adams Park at any time".

It's not the first sporting connection for the band, who first broke big in Ireland due to their viral track Killeagh, a song that has topped the Irish charts on three separate occasions.

The track details a community's attachment to their local Gaelic games club.

The band also played in Londonderry earlier this year where they were presented with shirts belonging to local clubs.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8j.summary: Wycombe Wanderers adopted Wycombe Winger as their team in the game. The band posted a song for the club on the internet and it has racked up more than 190,000 views. The song was written in an Irish folk style and has a lyrical focus on "the Wycombe wanderer, wandering away"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8.title: Paul McCartney's key sells for double the estimate
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8.text:
A key to Sir Paul McCartney's childhood home has sold for thousands of pounds at auction.

During the 1950s and 60s, Sir Paul lived with his family at 20 Forthlin Road in Allerton, Liverpool, and composed some of the earliest Beatles' tracks with John Lennon there.

Sir Paul moved out in 1963, and his father and brother in the following year. In 1965, American superfan Kathy Salt wrote to then-occupant Ashley Jones, who enclosed a photograph of the house and a key, with a tag attached, in his letter back.

The three items were sold to a British private collector at Dominic Winter Auctioneers in the Cotswolds on Wednesday, fetching a hammer price of £5,000 - double the estimate.

With fees, the buyer paid £6,100, and a collection of four autographs from the band, each inscribed to "Kathy" - the fan to whom the key belonged - sold for a total of £5,124.

Chris Albury, director at Dominic Winter Auctioneers, said the level of competition during the bidding "demonstrates that the Beatles' popularity remains as strong as ever".

"What makes these particular pieces so extraordinary is the deeply personal links to the band and to the people and places that formed part of their story," he said.

"The 20 Forthlin Road key is an example; it has a remarkable provenance stretching back to 1965 and provides a tangible connection to Paul McCartney's family home and to one of the most important addresses in Beatles history.

"To see it sell for £6,100 for three times its low estimate after such strong bidding was a fantastic result."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8.summary: Key to Sir Paul McCartney's childhood home sold for £5,000 at auction in Cotswolds. Key was written to American fan in 1965, with a photograph of the house and key. The key sold for three times its low estimate at auction, double the estimate.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crly.title: Welsh actress follows in footsteps of Florence Pugh and Benedict Cumberbatch
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crly.text:
A Welsh actress named in a prestigious line-up that has previously featured the likes of Benedict Cumberbatch and Florence Pugh says the selection was "so unexpected" that she forgot she applied.

Leisa Gwenllian portrays Effi in the Welsh language film Effi o Blaenau, which follows a young woman as she grapples with unemployment in a north Wales town before a night out drinking dramatically alters her life.

She joins a host of Hollywood stars who have previously been part of Stars of Tomorrow, an annual showcase highlighting rising British and Irish acting and filmmaking talent.

Gwenllian said she was proud to receive the honour and that Welsh language cinema was currently "having a moment".

Previous actors named in Screen International's talent programme also include Jodie Comer and Paul Mescal.

The film magazine received over 350 applications this year and decided on 10 actors and 10 filmmakers for its 2026 list.

Gwenllian, from Llanrug, Gwynedd, joked that "the pressure is on now" and said the recognition was a "great opportunity" which will open doors for her.

"I've gained a little bit of following in Wales because of this, but what that also means is that I kind of feel like I don't want to let those people down now who are so supportive of me and expect great things," she said.

"I just want to make my country proud and make my family proud."

Effi o Blaenau (Effi from Blaenau) is an adaptation of Gary Owen's play, Iphigenia in Splott, but relocated from Cardiff to Gwynedd.

Directed by Marc Evans, whose previous work includes BBC's Mr Burton, the film follows Effi as she navigates being out of work, clubbing and hangovers.

"I absolutely would not be there had it not been for Effi and I just feel very grateful that I got to play her and that it's reached so many people," Gwenllian said.

"I'm so proud to receive that honour because it's not only a recognition of my work but it's a recognition of the film and it's a boost for Welsh language cinema."

The industry here is having "a bit of a moment", Gwenllian said with a laugh.

"A director that I worked with, Helen Jones, she always says, 'It's not a moment, it's a movement', and we have to make sure that this continues.

"What Effi has proven is that there's an appetite out there for Welsh language films."

She said it was exciting that filmmakers were starting to take Wales seriously, and that the Welsh language should not be viewed as a barrier.

"People are so happy to watch other films in other languages with subtitles, so why not do it with Welsh."

Time Out said Effi o Blaenau was a cross between Greek tragedy and "British social realism", calling Gwenllian "formidable", while The Guardian described the film as a "sensation".

Gwenllian has most recently been filming a dark comedy set in Swansea.

ITV and S4C series Santa Maria is about a "class divide" in the city, with both Welsh and English versions.

"What's exciting about it is that even in the English language version, there's going to be a lot of Welsh," she said.

"I love working in Wales and playing Welsh characters, I think it's where I feel most at home."

Charles Gant, from Screen International, said Gwenllian was "a great talent discovery".

"It's rare that you see a rising young actor playing a role that is not just the lead in a film, but also in every moment of the film," he said.

"Leisa is a phenomenal talent, and casting directors and filmmakers will be sitting up and taking notice. She has warmth and charisma and that magical but unquantifiable essence that confers star status," he added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crly.summary: Leisa Gwenllian is named in a prestigious line-up of Hollywood stars. She plays Effi o Blaenau in the Welsh language film Effi O Blaan. The film magazine received over 350 applications this year and decided on 10 actors and 10 filmmakers.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqze.title: Oscar-winning actress Eva Marie Saint dies aged 102
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqze.text:
Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-winning actress who starred in Hollywood classics such as On the Waterfront and North by Northwest, has died aged 102.

Saint won the Academy Award for best supporting actress for her movie debut in director Elia Kazan's 1954 crime drama, On the Waterfront; playing Edie Doyle, the moral compass of the film and love interest of Marlon Brando's conflicted boxer-turned-docker.

Five years later, she portrayed femme fatale Eve Kendall, dangerously seducing Cary Grant's entangled advertising executive in Alfred Hitchcock's spy thriller, North by Northwest.

She died on Tuesday of natural causes, surrounded by family and loved ones at her home in Los Angeles, family representative Jeff Sanderson confirmed.

Until her death, Saint was the oldest surviving Oscar winner and one of the last remaining stars of Hollywood's golden age.

Starting her career in live television in the late 1940s, she also won an Emmy Award in 1990 for her career-capping role as the rich widow Lil Van Degan Altemus in People Like Us.

Born in Newark, New Jersey in 1924, Saint had originally intended to become a teacher before developing a passion for theatre.

She trained in New York at the Herbert Berghof Studio and then the Actors Studio - the home of method acting - co-founded by Kazan.

Saint burst on to the Hollywood scene with her performance as the gentle but resolute Edie in Kazan's classic, On the Waterfront.

Her co-star Brando was an intense method actor and Saint admitted to having found him "adorable" but "a little frightening".

"I felt that he could see right through me," she told Turner Classic Movies (TCM) in a 2013 interview.

Accepting her Oscar trophy while nine-months pregnant, Saint quipped: "I may have the baby right here!".

She wasn't far off, having her son just two days afterwards.

She was considered a surprise choice, though, to play one of Hitchcock's cool and calculating heroines in his masterpiece, North by Northwest.

The English filmmaker was known for being very demanding of his leading ladies.

"He worked with me from the outside in," said Saint.

"My hair, my makeup, my shoes, my jewellery, my purse, my gloves, everything. And just from creating that exterior for me, he gave me the sense of a spy lady."

Critics have argued that her character helped to create the sophisticated, sexually confident and intelligent blonde-haired archetype that many "Bond women", as they have been known, later followed in the 007 films.

Saint also starred opposite Paul Newman in Otto Preminger's Exodus in 1960, and alongside Warren Beatty in John Frankenheimer's All Fall Down.

But she then scaled back her career while raising a family with her husband, director Jeffrey Hayden.

Half a century later, Saint made a big screen comeback as Clark Kent's adoptive mother in the 2006 blockbuster Superman Returns, while in her 80s.

And she later had parts in the supernatural fantasy Winter's Tale, alongside Colin Farrell and Russell Crowe, and the 2019 nun drama Mariette in Ecstasy.

This all followed her Emmy win in 1990 for her role in the TV miniseries People Like Us, which was set among New York's high society.

Saint, who has two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame for her movie and TV work, said her longevity in acting had given her work extra depth.

"The longer you live, the smarter you get, because you've been around, you've seen things," she told TCM.

"You've gone through different emotional experiences in your own life, and hopefully, you understand things better.

"And that makes you a better actress."

Saint's marriage to Hayden lasted for 65 years, until his death in 2016, and she is survived by their two children.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqze.summary: Eva Marie Saint died of natural causes at her Los Angeles home on Tuesday. She won the Academy Award for best supporting actress for her 1954 film, On the Waterfront. She also won an Emmy Award for her role in People Like Us in 1990. She was the oldest surviving Oscar winner and one of the last remaining stars of Hollywood's golden age

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy5.title: Jimmy McGovern claims young offender institution staff 'lazy'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy5.text:
Bafta-winning screenwriter Jimmy McGovern has said going into young offender institutions to research his new drama left him believing that keeping inmates isolated from each other for long periods allowed staff to "sit on their backsides all day and do nothing".

McGovern said he was shocked after visiting "appalling" facilities while researching the latest series of his BBC drama Time.

He told BBC North West Tonight those in young offender institutions (YOIs) were "banged up 23 hours a day" as part of a policy to stop offenders mixing, which gave officers an "excuse for being lazy".

The Prison Officers' Association (POA) said that criticism was "unfair" to call officers lazy - and the policy was essential due to a daily threat of serious violence.

Liverpool-born McGovern focused on adult prison estates in the first two series of BBC hit Time.

But his third series, which sees a young cast star alongside David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran, follows young offenders through a system which McGovern said had "got to be better".

In researching the series, which he wrote with Samuel Bailey, McGovern decided to get a behind-the-scenes look inside real-life YOIs.

He said what he witnessed left him "truly shocked".

"It is absolutely appalling," he said.

"There's young boys with enormous energy banged up 23 hours a day [and] not allowed out of the cells.

"They call them rooms, but they're cells.

"And that's because of the keep-apart system."

The keep-aparts policy is a method of separating young offenders in a bid to cut down on violence.

The separation of young people in YOIs has been a topic of debate for a number of years - with the most recent review from HM Inspectorate of Prisons finding some held in YOIs were not permitted to leave their cells at all on some days.

McGovern said he recognised a need for "regimentation" in YOIs, but said he believed keep-aparts had increased following lockdown measures imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He said he believed the policy had allowed officers to avoid their duties.

"It allows officers to sit on their backsides all day and do nothing," he said.

"This happened before Covid, but Covid gave them the excuse to keep them banged up even more.

"After Covid, they didn't want to see the kids, so it became worse."

He said he did not believe an increased use of the policy was due to staffing and funding challenges.

"I'm afraid they're lazy," he said.

"I've met wonderful prison officers, but I've seen some lazy ones and the keep-apart system enables them to be lazy with an excuse for being lazy."

He said officers should be able to handle fights among the offenders and described conditions as "feral".

"They're young boys bursting with energy [being] cooped up," he said.

"When they get out, they want to fight, but [the staff] are prison officers. They should be able to handle that."

He said he understood how "tough" the job was and that the young offenders in the facilities were "very, very difficult, so there has to be an element of regimentation [and] rules and regulations... but that's your job".

POA chairman Mark Fairhurst said the body shared some of the concerns raised by McGovern.

"I have the utmost respect for Jimmy's work [and] he is right to highlight the serious problems within young offender institutions," he said.

"YOIs are among the most violent prisons in the country.

"Prison officers routinely put themselves in harm's way to prevent serious injury and save lives.

"Many of my members have suffered life-changing injuries and been forced to leave the service following vicious assaults."

He said the young offenders were "not simply naughty schoolchildren".

"Keep-aparts are an essential safety measure in an environment where serious violence is a daily reality."

He said officers at YOIs were "paying the price" of a lack of investment and staffing and it was "unfair to suggest staff are lazy".

"They are stretched to breaking point by chronic under-staffing and unmanageable workloads," he said.

"Without serious investment in staffing, facilities and rehabilitation, we will continue to see violent and chaotic YOIs - and prison officers paying the price."

The Ministry of Justice said it did not "recognise these claims about our hardworking prison staff".

"Their dedication helps ensure young offenders are punished as appropriate while being supported into rehabilitation, and we will deliver on our commitment to give children in prison more time outside their room," a spokesperson said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm62.text:
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.

The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.

Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.

Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.

Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.

While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.

The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.

Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come.

While viewers will gain access to a broader catalogue, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes".

As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.

For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.

That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must be shown in cinemas.

The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.

If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.

Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.

"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.

"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".

Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.

As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.

Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.

For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.

Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.

Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".

"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."

A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.

The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.

Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".

She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."

Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.

"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.

To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.

The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.

Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.

Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".

"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.

Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.
