https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c800.title: Jeffrey Archer: bestselling novelist whose political career ended in scandal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c800.text:
As many have observed, Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, led a life as colourful as the plot in one of his novels.

He was, at one time or other, a senior Conservative politician, a best-selling author, a peer of the realm, and a convicted perjurer.

Possessed of huge drive, vast wealth and immense personal charm, Archer bounced back from disaster and, more than once, rebuilt a shattered life.

But for all his talents, he will be remembered as a man affected by a defective moral compass, whose public humiliation was entirely self-inflicted.

Jeffrey Howard Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940.

Within two weeks, his parents moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where they bought a house from John Cleese's mother.

Archer's mother Lola was the first woman journalist on the weekly paper, the Weston Mercury.

In later life, Archer insisted that his father William, who was some 40 years older than his mother, was a decorated hero of the First World War.

In fact, he was a convicted fraudster who, according to a US newspaper, spent the war years conning people in New York.

In 1951, the young Archer went to Wellington School in Somerset.

Some people mistakenly assumed he had gone to the somewhat more prestigious Wellington College in Berkshire, and he did little to correct them.

Archer's academic career was undistinguished, and he left school with three O-levels. He did, however, embark on a fitness regime designed to improve his physique after his originally skinny frame led to taunts from fellow pupils.

After school, he drifted. There was a brief spell in the army and then a short course in physical education in America.

On his return, he spent five months as a probationary constable in the Metropolitan Police, before quitting to become a physical training instructor at a small prep school in Hampshire.

It was while holding a similar job at Dover College that his resume moved into the realms of fantasy.

He styled himself Jeffrey Archer, FIFPC, BSc, leading people to assume he had obtained a degree during his time in the United States.

In fact, as his unofficial biographer Michael Crick later discovered, Archer's alma mater in the States was, in fact, a bodybuilding club.

However, Dover College was so impressed, it backed Archer's bid to go to Oxford as a mature student to do a one-year Diploma of Education course.

At Oxford, he excelled in athletics, winning a Blue, although it was doubtful whether his course qualified him to be a bona fide member of the University.

More importantly, it brought him into contact with fellow students who would go on to hold senior positions in politics, finance and the media.

He also married Mary Weeden, a chemistry student whose beauty had attracted a long list of suitors. "It was love at first sight for me," the future novelist recalled, "but I don't think it was for her."

His public profile had been considerably raised when he managed to persuade The Beatles to come and support a £500,000 fundraising effort for Oxfam, a charity which Archer supported.

After serving as a Conservative councillor in London, he was put on the selection list for the safe Tory seat of Louth in Lincolnshire.

A reporter on the Times, John Clare, discovered that another charity for which Archer worked alleged he had misused expenses with claims for meals at posh London restaurants.

Clare buttonholed Archer and, according to his own account, the would-be candidate burst into tears and asked that the story be quashed.

It eventually appeared in the paper but with many of the salient details left out.

Concerns about Archer's suitability were ignored by the party members in Louth who adopted him. In a by-election in December 1969, he won the seat with a handsome majority.

He and Mary set themselves up in an expensive Kensington house and he became a member of Lloyds. He also began to build up his profile in parliament where he was seen as a liberal member of his party.

But, in 1974, he suffered a blow after being persuaded to invest in a Canadian company which claimed to have developed a process to cut carbon emissions. It turned out to be a scam.

Archer had taken out a second mortgage, as well as borrowing large sums from elsewhere, to raise money for the investment. Threatened with bankruptcy, he was forced to quit his parliamentary seat.

However, he managed to secure an agreement with his creditors and wrote his first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less in 1976.

A gripping tale about four cheated men and their efforts to get back money stolen from them, it was inspired, in part, by his own financial problems and did much to solve them.

Despite being rubbished by many critics, it sold well in the US and then in Britain, earning Archer a considerable sum in royalties.

Three years later, Kane and Abel, a ripping page-turner about the roller-coaster financial fortunes of two men who initially shared nothing but a date of birth, flew off the shelves.

A third novel, published in 1984, First Among Equals, about a cutthroat competition to become Prime Minister, cemented Archer's position as one of Britain's best-selling and highest earning authors.

It enabled him to purchase the Old Vicarage at Grantchester near Cambridge, formerly the home of war poet, Rupert Brooke, as well as a penthouse in London.

There, he entertained the great and the good with legendary parties, serving them with champagne and shepherd's pie.

First Among Equals, with its political theme, had more than hinted at Archer's desperation to get back into politics.

He got his chance in 1985, when Margaret Thatcher, impressed by his drive and personality, gave him an unpaid job as Deputy Chairman of the Conservative Party with responsibility for fundraising.

It lasted just a year.

In October 1986, the News of the World published a picture of Archer's friend, Michael Stackpole, paying £2,000 to a sex worker named Monica Coghlan.

The money was supposedly a bribe to persuade her to go abroad, to avoid the prying eyes of the press.

And while the News of the World did not allege Archer had slept with Coghlan, the Daily Star was less reticent.

Archer resigned his party post and sued the Star for libel. In court, he claimed the payment had been a goodwill gesture to a woman down on her luck.

Friends also gave him an alibi for the night the Star had claimed he was enjoying the company of Ms Coghlan.

It was the evidence of Mary Archer that swung the case.

Her appearance in court so captivated the judge, Mr Justice Caulfield, that in his summing up, he asked why a man with such a fragrant wife would sleep with prostitutes.

"Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex," Caulfield asked, "in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?"

The jury duly found for Archer and he was awarded £500,000 in damages. The News of the World later settled out-of-court with him, admitting they too had libelled him.

He went back to writing his books which continued to sell. By this time, he was thought to be worth more than £50m.

In 1992, he was offered a peerage by Conservative Prime Minister John Major in recognition for his work with a charity set up to help Kurds who were being oppressed by Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

His wife, meanwhile, had joined the board of Anglia Television which, in 1994, was the subject of a takeover bid. The day after the move was discussed by the board, Archer bought 50,000 shares in the company on behalf of a friend.

When the news of the takeover broke, the shares climbed in value and Archer made a profit of nearly £78,000.

A subsequent investigation cleared him of insider dealing, but soured relations with the Conservatives who were mired in their own battle against allegations of sleaze.

Undeterred, Archer, with the support of new Conservative leader William Hague, was selected as the Conservative candidate for Mayor of London in 1999.

Once more, the threat of scandal forced his resignation when the News of the World printed an interview with Archer's former friend, Ted Francis.

Francis alleged that the politician had lied on oath in his 1987 libel action against the Daily Star and Archer resigned as Conservative candidate for Mayor the next day.

There would be no forgiveness.

"This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer," said William Hague. "I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party."

In 2000, Archer was charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice.

At the same time, his play, The Accused, opened in London.

It featured a murder in which the audience were the jury and decided the guilt, or otherwise of the protagonist at the end of each performance.

In May 2001, a month after Monica Coghlan's death in a road accident, Archer went on trial. This time, his wife's testimony failed to sway the court. He was convicted and sentenced to four years in prison.

Shortly after his conviction, police began investigating allegations of corruption.

These related to the Kurdish charity in which Archer had been involved. There had been complaints that much of the £57m he said he'd raised never reached the Kurds.

However, police concluded that Archer, in fact, had received very little of the donations himself.

First in HM Prison Belmarsh and then in HM Prison Wayland, Archer used his incarceration profitably - by writing a three-volume account of his time inside entitled My Prison Diary.

Two years later, he was released, having served half of his sentence. "I learned a lot from it," he said. "The British people are very forgiving."

He retained his seat in the House of Lords, as there was no mechanism to remove an errant peer. He remained a member of Britain's upper house until his formal retirement in 2024.

Writing well into his mid-80s, he continued to churn out at least one, if not two, novels a year.

In the last years of his life, there were several volumes of The Clifton Chronicles: detailing the turbulent life of former dockworker, Harry Clifton.

There were also seven novels about a fictional policeman, William Warwick, who rises from humble constable in the Metropolitan police to the very top of his profession.

In January 2026, the 85-year-old announced that his forthcoming novel, Adam and Eve, would be his last.

An epic tale inspired by Hitler's indecision about whether to invade Britain, Archer poured everything into it. "Everyone would like to run their last 100m at the Olympics and win the gold medal," he told BBC Breakfast in September 2026.

Few critics praised Archer's prose style, his sense of humour, or the emotional depth of his characters.

But none could match his talent for relentless, aspirational, rags-to-riches plots that, once started, could not be put down.

Lord Archer often appeared incapable of separating autobiographical fact from fantasy in his continuing drive for public recognition.

He died a wealthy man, albeit one whom very few trusted.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c800.summary: Jeffrey Howard Archer was born in north London on 15 April 1940. He spent the war years conning people in New York and was a convicted fraudster. He was a Conservative Party Deputy Chairman of the Conservative Party.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck4g.title: Potty training scheme to roll out to 20 more areas
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck4g.text:
The number of children who were toilet-trained before starting school this year has increased significantly in a city where parents were given potty training guides with their first school offers.

York was the subject of the city-wide pilot, which also put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff.

Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes to tackle the number of pupils starting school without being fully toilet-trained.

The government said the pilot's results were "encouraging", and confirmed they were committed to 75% of pupils reaching a good level of development at the end of their first year in school by 2028.

Since April this year, parents across York have been targeted via GP surgeries, pharmacies, family hubs, schools, nurseries and libraries with information and offers of support on how to potty-train their child ahead of starting school.

Potty training guides were sent out to all families across York who had a child starting reception in September - with the aim that all children could use the toilet independently by the time they started school, except those with medical issues or special educational needs.

The results from all 55 mainstream primary schools across the city, shared exclusively with BBC News, suggested there had been a 43% drop since last year in the number of children who were not fully toilet-trained when they started school.

Across York last September, 148 out of 1,364 reception pupils (11%) were recorded as not being toilet-trained when they started school. This year, that fell to 85 reception pupils out of 1,374 (6%).

Parents Natalie and Lucy, who both have daughters starting reception next year, have welcomed the extra support on offer.

Lucy said she had noticed the drop-in sessions on potty training in her local children's centre and thought it was a "really good idea".

"I think it's really important that children are more prepared for that aspect of starting school," she said.

Natalie said getting her daughter Freya potty-trained in time for school has been a priority, but feels there is a lot of pressure on parents to do so.

"I think going to school is hard enough for children," she said.

"But for me it was really important that she's confident enough to use toilets, to be independent, to be able to go without relying on the help of teachers perhaps in an environment where they've already got lots of children to look after."

Natalie said the popularity of disposable nappies might be a reason why parents often wait longer to potty train.

"When I was little, we still had the terry towelling nappies and they had to be washed and hung on the line. So I think with disposable nappies it's easier," she said.

Around one in four children started school in England and Wales last year not fully toilet-trained, and teachers said they have been spending over an hour a day changing nappies, according to the latest research from the children's charity Kindred Squared.

Felicity Gillespie, chief executive of Kindred Squared, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that children not being potty trained when starting school was "a real concern for teachers".

"They tell us that they're losing, on average across the country, a day a week of teaching time to dealing with potty-training issues."

Gillespie is keen to spread the message that "it's best for children to be coming out of nappies" when they are between 18 and 30 months old.

"When the teacher's leaving the class to change someone's nappy, the rest of the class is having their learning broken up. So everybody loses out,” she added.

Jo Mould, who teaches reception at Robert Wilkinson Primary Academy in York, said she has noticed an improvement in pupils being ready for school this year.

"We've spent more time teaching in these last three weeks than we have in previous years," she said.

"The children have come in so ready to learn, because they're more settled and regulated socially and emotionally. We've had a really, really positive start to the school year."

York councillor Bob Webb said the impact of the scheme had been "so positive" for both schools and families.

But he acknowledged a potential "gap in support" for parents between seeing health visitors with their toddler, and the child later arriving at school.

He said the key to the scheme's success was collaboration across health visitors, schools and other community settings, but that there was "always more that could be done at an earlier age".

Twenty local authorities across England have now committed to adopt York's model, developed by Kindred Squared, and use it to encourage earlier potty-training in their areas.

Just over two-thirds of children in England (68.3%) leave reception class with a good level of development - a key measure of school readiness which includes things like communication skills, as well as physical, social and emotional development - according to the latest government stats.

That means they were assessed by teachers on being able to complete tasks like going to the toilet and paying attention in class.

The government has said it is still committed to increasing that proportion to 75% by 2028.

Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said it was "encouraging to see this pilot helping more children develop the confidence and independence they need before starting school", stressing the importance of parents taking early steps towards toilet training.

In York, Mould said she hopes next year's parents will take on potty-training even earlier.

"Ideally we'd be at the point where [children] don't need that support when they get here, because they've already been trained by the time they get to us."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck4g.summary: York pilot put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff. Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.title: Badenoch unveils plan to end £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge' ahead of Tory conference
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.text:
Kemi Badenoch has said a Conservative government would scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, the Conservative Party leader said: "What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so."

The earnings limit means only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for 30 hours of government-funded childcare or tax-free childcare.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch, who arrived in the city on Saturday, has vowed the party was new and different from the one that lost the 2024 general election.

The Conservatives - who have been polling behind Labour and Reform UK over the past year - are expected to use the four-day event to lay out more of their policy agenda ahead of the next general election.

Ahead of the conference, the Conservatives produced a 100-page essay setting out their principles including a "central" belief that business, rather than governments, create growth.

It argues that governments should create the conditions for growth, particularly through the tax system.

In her interview with the BBC, Badenoch pitched herself as a "classic old-school Conservative" adding: "I believe in common sense - people working hard and being rewarded for that effort."

She insisted the Tories would keep the state pension triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to change if Labour wins the next election.

She said the policy, under which state pensions rise each year by the highest of inflation, average wages, or 2.5%, was "the right policy for pensioners".

She added: "What we don't want to see is people going after the elderly, chasing after vulnerable and disabled people, and then the extremely large cohort of people who can work, who are not working, are left alone."

The Conservatives have long called on the government to cut the growing welfare budget including by implementing tighter restrictions on claimants.

The party said its childcare announcement would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year, although all three and four-year-olds are eligible for 15 hours of free childcare, regardless of parental income.

The same £100,000 eligibility threshold also applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme, and has remained unchanged since it was originally set under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government.

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power, they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely for tax-free childcare and government-funded childcare hours.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

In her interview with Kuenssberg, Badenoch said: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1m a year getting free childcare under a Conservative government, the Tory leader responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

The Tories argue the threshold may mean some people may delay having children until their incomes change, or decide not to start a family at all, describing scrapping it as "both pro-family and pro-growth".

By providing an increased incentive to work, the Tories said the move would also boost economic growth.

They added that it would tackle the "unfairness" that the threshold is calculated on an individual earner's income rather then for the whole household.

The party said the policy would be funded by cutting the number of public servants working in "executive non-departmental public bodies" - organisations which have a role in the processes of national government but operate at arm's length from ministers, such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

It said this would save £1.6bn by 2029-30, covering the estimated £700m cost of removing the childcare "cliff edge".

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

The earnings limit means only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for 30 hours of government-funded childcare or tax-free

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq07.title: Woman deceived ex-partner that she had given birth to his babies, judge rules
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq07.text:
A woman convinced her former partner she had given birth to two children who most likely did not exist in what a High Court judge described as an "extraordinary" and "elaborate campaign of deceit".

The man, who has not been named but was referred to as John in the judgement, applied to the Family Court after he was told the woman had sold their two children for a combined £500.

The case heard that the man received messages and photos of the children and paid the woman around £30,000 over the course of two years.

But in a hearing in February, the woman, who was referred to as Jane, told the judge she had lied about the pregnancies for revenge, claiming the man had abused her.

The court heard the man believed he was the children's' father because in late 2022 his partner told him she was pregnant, sent pictures of an ultrasound image and had become "visibly pregnant" as time went on.

In May 2023, shortly before the first baby was due, the woman called the police alleging she had been assaulted by the man.

He was arrested and subsequently held on remand for several months, Mrs Justice Judd said in her ruling which was published on Friday.

Following this, the woman sent a message to his stepfather saying the baby had been born as well as sharing baby photos.

At one stage she is said to have sent voice notes to her former partner's mother in the middle of the night with the sound of a baby crying in the background.

Later, she told the man she was pregnant again and the baby was due in August 2024.

However, before the due date, the couple split up and did not reconcile.

The woman would go on to tell the man's mother the baby had been born.

The woman admitted to the court she had told him she was pregnant when they were together, and afterwards, but conceded she had told a series of elaborate lies and that there were, in fact, no children.

She argued she was menopausal at the time and could not have been pregnant and bank statements show she attended a tanning shop on the day she said she had given birth, Mrs Justice Judd said.

In her judgement, the judge concluded that the "factors that weigh against the children genuinely existing were very strong, stronger than the factors pointing the other way".

She said the man was the victim of a "sustained and elaborate campaign of deceit" which also impacted his mother and closest friend.

"Added to this, the behaviour was cruel, leading a man and his mother to believe they had children and grandchildren respectively.", the Judge said.

The judge added she was unable to conclude the woman's motive for her behaviour but said financial fraud was a "possibility" and that the "complex mental health problems" she suffered from may have also played a part.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2k.title: Employers should teach primary-age children about work, says Milburn
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2k.text:
Children should be introduced to the world of work at the start of primary school, says the author of a major report into youth activity in the UK.

Former minister Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be learning about different careers, with work experience placements made mandatory for 14- to 16-year-olds.

However, teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools and say practical considerations must ensure all schools have access to the support.

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK were not in education, employment or training (known as Neet), between April and June 2026.

Milburn told the BBC "in primary school, it's really about opening their eyes and giving them a sense about what is possible".

Despite a push towards apprenticeships and work experience in Years 10 and 11, for many the journey towards becoming Neet starts well before their 16th birthday.

As a result, Milburn says children should be introduced to the world of work much earlier in their school journey, with dedicated space in the curriculum to "broaden horizons".

He told the BBC this could be achieved by employers giving talks in primary schools and offering taster sessions to children.

"It'd be good if employers came into schools and said, 'Look, this is what's going on, these are things that are possible.'"

Milburn says that for Key Stage 4 pupils - aged between 14 and 16 - experience must be given in a real workplace with employer feedback.

"Work experience needs to be mandatory. It makes a big difference," he told the BBC.

Milburn also emphasised the difficulty some young people face when trying to find work experience placements.

"There are about four in ten people aged 14-16 who aren't getting any work experience at all," he said. "In other schools, students are told to go off and find their own work experience and that often relies on the network of Mum and Dad."

These recommendations are due to be published in the final instalment of his government-commissioned report into the issue, which is expected to be published in the autumn.

Education is devolved in the UK, so while Milburn's review looks at the picture in all four nations, his recommendations regarding education are specific to England.

Currently in England, careers guidance must be offered to students aged 11-18 and work experience is not statutory.

The government has said its vision is to "guarantee two weeks' worth of work experience for every young person" in England.

In both Scotland and Wales, career-based learning is already a requirement in schools for students as young as three.

Emma, from Kirklees, has grandchildren in Years 1, 2 and 4 and thinks primary school is too young to be introducing careers talks.

"In primary school, there is too much trying to get little kids to grow up too quickly," she says.

"Just let them be little kids. I know they have to learn and the world's changing, but still, give them a chance to be kids."

But Zoe, another parent, disagrees.

"I think it's a good idea," she says. "It's something that everyone has to do, so if you learn early, it's something they don't have to learn later on."

Teaching unions have responded positively to the idea of introducing career-based learning into schools at a younger age, but have warned about the burden this could place on primary schools in particular.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of school leaders' union National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), warns of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools.

"Whenever new mandatory requirements are proposed, it is important to be clear about what might have to give way to make room for them," he says.

Whiteman also highlights the value of existing programmes such as "Primary Futures", which bring in volunteers from different professions into schools to "challenge stereotypes and raise aspirations".

"The earlier young people can begin to make connections between what they learn in school and the possibilities that lie ahead, the better," Whiteman says.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL), says having someone come into the classroom can really "enlighten [children's] motivation... and give them that sense of passion for all the opportunities beyond the classroom". Although he acknowledges that finding opportunities in rural areas could be more challenging.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2k.summary: Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be introduced to work experience. He says children should be taught about different careers at the start of school journey. But teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm98.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm98.text:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk.title: Antisemitism on the rise at universities, charity warns
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk.text:
Cases of antisemitism affecting university students and staff in the UK increased in the last academic year, according to a charity that monitors antisemitic incidents.

The Community Security Trust (CST) said it had recorded 95 "university-related" incidents in the 2025-26 academic year - up from 83 the year before.

It said the number had fallen from its peak in the year after Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza began, but remains "substantially higher" than before that point.

Universities UK (UUK) represents more than 140 institutions and said its members needed to "protect Jewish students and staff", adding that the findings were a "serious concern".

Lucy Powell, education secretary in England, said the findings in the CST report were "deeply troubling".

"We expect universities to take a zero-tolerance approach to antisemitism, and are providing training to help university staff identify and respond to incidents swiftly," she said.

The CST defines an antisemitic incident as "university-related" if it concerns a student, member of staff or academic at a UK university "in their academic or student capacity" - including on campus and online.

In 2022-23, the last academic year before the 7 October attack, the CST recorded 53 incidents. That grew to 272 in 2023-24.

A report from the charity examining the past two academic years says reported incidents fell in 2024-25 and but grew again in 2025-26.

The most common type of incident recorded by CST over both years was abusive behaviour, including verbal abuse, comments made in person or online and antisemitic graffiti.

Its report said that, for the first time, there were two occurrences of extreme violence in 2024-25.

It said there were six reported assaults across both years, eight incidents of damage and desecration to Jewish property - five of which were in student accommodation - and ten threats.

Around two-thirds of reported incidents involved antisemitic language or targeting alongside references to Israel, Gaza, Hamas, the 7 October attack, and the subsequent conflicts in the Middle East.

The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

Israel launched a mass military offensive on Gaza in response which has killed around 74,000 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

The CST report said: "While criticism of Israel and Zionism is not inherently antisemitic, the data in this report continue to demonstrate that anti-Zionist language is frequently deployed in conjunction with hostility towards Jews and Jewish organisations."

Mark Gardner, CST's chief executive, said "Jews are still facing a very serious campus antisemitism problem" and it was "particularly troubling that a growing proportion of the anti-Jewish actions involve university staff".

He added that universities had "a duty to ensure that Jewish students and staff can study, work and participate on campus the same as anyone else".

Raphi Leon, president of the Union of Jewish Students, said the report "must be a shot in the arm to boost action to support Jewish students and tackle antisemitism".

Vivienne Stern, chief executive of UUK, said: "The rise in antisemitic incidents in the UK, including on university campuses, is a serious concern.

"Universities have a responsibility to protect Jewish students and staff from abuse, and to ensure that students and staff clearly understand where the expression of a strongly held view becomes antisemitism and harassment."

She said UUK had worked with organisations including the CST on guidance for universities, but added there was "more to do, particularly in building confidence in the effectiveness of disciplinary processes".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5k.title: How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5k.text:
Students and graduates across the UK have different student loan plans depending on when and where they studied.

Loan rules vary between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but most students still need to borrow to pay for their studies. The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500.

Student loans vary depending on where you live in the UK and when you started your course.

They are typically made up of:

Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course. Maximum fees vary across the UK:

The separate maintenance loan is intended to cover accommodation, food, books and equipment.

Maintenance loans are means tested, so the amount you get depends on your family's household income. You might get extra money if you are disabled, or have children.

If you are under 25 and have no contact with your parents, you might be able to apply as an "estranged student". This means your parents' financial situation is not taken into consideration.

Research by the Higher Education Policy Institute published in May 2024 suggested maintenance loans in England typically only covered about half the cost of living, and even less for students in London.

In April 2026, over 20,000 students were told they had been "mis-sold" their maintenance loans as their courses were ineligible, and were told to pay back the money they had received.

Students who took out a loan in England to start university between September 2012 and July 2023 have a Plan 2 loan. These loans are still issued in Wales.

Graduates with Plan 2 loans pay back 9% of everything they earn over the repayment threshold.

In the November 2025 Budget, Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the threshold would be frozen at £29,385 between 2027 and 2030, rather than rising with inflation.

That means students will start repaying their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries will lead to greater repayments.

Campaigners want to see that change reversed, and for the government to consider a lower repayment rate and a lower interest rate.

Plan 2 loans take on interest at the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3% depending on earnings.

It means many graduates with Plan 2 loans have struggled to make a substantial dent in the overall debt they left university with, which is often in the tens of thousands of pounds, despite making repayments for years.

The maximum interest rate charged on Plan 2 loans is capped. The cap is reviewed periodically and may change from one academic year to the next.

The amount of maintenance support available to new students varies across the UK.

The maximum maintenance loan for students from England living away from their parents outside London is £10,830 for the 2026-27 academic year.

The government is reintroducing maintenance grants of up to £1,000 per year for students from lower income households in England on courses that support its Industrial Strategy. They will be available from 2028 and the government is still drawing up a list of eligible courses.

Students from Wales studying away from home can borrow up to £11,570 in the 2026-27 academic year.

Welsh students may also be entitled to maintenance grants, which do not have to be paid back.

In Scotland, the maximum annual maintenance loan is £9,400 for under-25s. Students can also apply for a number of bursaries and grants.

Students from Northern Ireland studying away from home can borrow up to £8,352 for the 2026-27 academic year.

Tuition fee limits and maintenance loan amounts are reviewed by the government each year and can change.

The government has said only those universities which provide strong outcomes for students will be able to charge the maximum amount in England.

Universities which fall below the quality threshold set by the regulator in England, the Office for Students, may also face a cap on the number of students they can recruit.

The tuition fees are paid directly to your university or education provider.

The maintenance loan is paid directly to your bank account in instalments.

Payments are made at the start of each term in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and monthly in Scotland.

In order to be paid you'll need to register at your university or college. You'll usually do this in the first week of your course, and you may have to take along your student finance entitlement letter.

In England you should get a text from the Student Loans Company a few days before to let you know the maintenance loan is on the way.

You can apply for funding up to nine months after the first day of the academic year for your course.

Depending on where you live, you will need to apply through:

Interest rates on some student loans are reviewed regularly. For the 2026-27 academic year, interest on Plan 2 and Plan 3 loans in England is capped at 6%.

You are charged interest on the loan from the day you take it out, but the amount varies across the UK.

It is important to understand that the terms and conditions of the loan and repayments can change after you have borrowed the money.

Future interest rate rises apply to all student loans, not just new applications.

For students in England, the interest rate is normally set at the retail price index (RPI) measure of inflation. The rate usually updates every September, but can also change throughout the year.

It is currently 3.2% for anyone who started university in 2023 or later.

Rates for students in the rest of the UK are:

How much graduates pay back depends on how much they earn.

You make one payment to cover both your tuition fees and maintenance loans.

But you do not have to start repaying your loan until you earn a certain amount of money after graduation.

You generally repay 9% of the amount you earn above this threshold.

The threshold for students in England who started university in 2023 or later, and therefore have a Plan 5 loan, is £25,000.

In Wales it is £29,385, in Scotland £33,795 and in Northern Ireland £26,900.

Students who took out a loan in England to start university between September 2012 and July 2023 have a Plan 2 loan.

Plan 2 repayment thresholds rose from £28,470 to £29,385 in April 2026, before being frozen - instead of rising with inflation - for three years.

You do not have to start making payments until the April after you leave your course.

Payments are made automatically through the tax system.

Some people choose to make extra repayments to clear some or all of their loan early - there is no penalty for doing this.

In some cases graduates have had repayments wrongly deducted from their wages.

For example, they may have had money taken before the April when they become liable, or after their loan had been repaid in full.

Alternatively, their employer may have put them on the wrong repayment plan. Payments may also have accidentally been triggered when graduates earned more than the monthly threshold - perhaps as a result of working extra shifts or getting a bonus - but did not exceed the annual limit.

These incorrect repayments can be refunded.

In May 2024, the Student Loans Company introduced a digital refund service, which was accessed by more than 400,000 people in the first six months.

You can check whether you are entitled to a refund on the SLC website.

Any overpayments you have chosen to make cannot be refunded.

In England, students who started university in 2023 or later will see their loans written off after 40 years, regardless of how much they may still owe.

For students with Plan 2 loans, including in Wales, this happens after 30 years.

It is also after 30 years in Scotland, and in Northern Ireland it is after 25 years.

You still have to repay your student loan if you leave your course early.

The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.title: Everything you need to know about university costs
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwye.text:
Graduates in England leave university with more than £47,500 in student debt, according to the latest statistics.

Figures from the 2025-26 financial year suggest that the amount borrowers owe when they first become eligible to repay has, on average, fallen compared to the year before.

But is a university degree worth it? And can graduates still expect to earn sufficiently more than those without a degree to cover the cost of going in the first place?

Last August, the annual cost of an undergraduate degree in England and Wales went up to £9,535 a year. It rose again to £9,790 in 2026.

The increases came after universities expressed growing concerns about funding pressures in recent years, pointing out that tuition fees had been frozen at £9,250 since 2017.

They argued that inflation meant those fees were worth less in real terms and there had been fewer international students to help make up the financial shortfall.

In October 2025, the government said university tuition fees in England would go up every year in line with inflation from 2026.

They are expected to increase every year by an inflation measure called the Retail Price Index minus mortgage payment interest, or RPIx.

UK nations set their own fees.

In Northern Ireland, the maximum annual cost of an undergraduate degree is £4,855 for Northern Irish students or £9,535 for other UK students. That will rise to £4,985 and £9,790 respectively in 2026-27.

In Scotland, undergraduate tuition is free for the majority of Scottish students and £9,535 for other UK students - rising to £9,790 in 2026-27.

Student loans are made up of two components:

Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course.

Maintenance loans are means-tested, so how much you can borrow depends on your family's income, and may not cover your actual bills.

The maximum maintenance loan for students in England is also set to increase by inflation every year from 2026.

For example, the maximum maintenance loan for students from England who live away from their parents outside London will increase to £10,830 for 2026-27, up from £10,544 the year before.

You are charged interest on your total loan from the day you take it out, but do not have to start paying it back until your annual income reaches a certain level.

Once you reach that level, you make a regular payment which covers both your tuition fees and maintenance loans.

Repayment rules are also different across the UK. They changed in England in 2023, meaning current and future students are likely to pay back more, over a longer period of time, than those who went to university earlier.

Money saving expert Martin Lewis said the extended repayment period would increase "costs by thousands" for lower and mid-earners.

Graduates in England who became liable to pay back their loans in April 2026 had an average debt of £47,730, according to the Student Loans Company - down from £53,000 the year before.

That's partly because this was the first year that any students who took out Plan 5 loans – introduced in England in 2023 – became eligible to repay, and their loans accrue less interest than earlier Plan 2 loans.

Plan 5 borrowers accounted for more than 10% of the total number of borrowers in the 2025-26 financial year.

Student rents have risen sharply in recent years, alongside other living costs.

The Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi) says average weekly costs for a first-year student in 2023-24 were £260 without rent, or £418 when rent is included.

Average annual rent across 10 university towns and cities - excluding London and Edinburgh - rose from £6,520 in 2021-22 to £7,475 in 2023-24.

Separate figures for London found that the average rent for purpose-built student accommodation in the capital was £13,595 in 2024-25.

Hepi said last year that students needed £61,000 over the course of a three-year degree in order to have a "minimum socially acceptable standard of living" - and that's excluding tuition fees. In London, that figure is £77,000.

The think tank's 2026 student survey found the percentage of full-time undergraduates in paid employment during term time was 65% - a slight fall from the previous year, but much higher than the 45% in 2022.

Eligible students in Wales and Northern Ireland can claim maintenance grants which do not have to be repaid.

Full-time undergraduates normally resident in Wales are entitled to at least £1,000, rising to £1,020 in 2026-27. Students from the poorest backgrounds who choose to study in London can get up to £10,124, which will rise to £10,325.

In Northern Ireland the maximum grant is £3,475, rising to £3,569 in 2026-27.

The government in England is bringing back maintenance grants of up to £1,000 per year for students from lower income households on courses that support its Industrial Strategy. They will be available from 2028 and the government is still drawing up a list of eligible courses.

The Scottish government offers financial support to certain categories of students, such as those with dependants.

Across the UK, students in financial difficulty can apply for hardship funding and they may also be entitled to financial assistance from charities.

Recent research from Hepi and AdvanceHE suggests that 45% of undergraduate students think the value for money of their course is "good" or "very good", up from 37% last year and the highest proportion recorded in more than ten years.

Whether or not university can be considered "worth it" will vary from person to person, depending on what they want to get out of it.

When thinking about the financial cost, it's important to consider that, once graduates earn a certain amount, they are required to pay back student loans over a period of up to 40 years. MPs launched an inquiry into student loans in England this year amid "widespread dissatisfaction" over repayment terms.

In general, graduates can expect to earn more than non-graduates, according to government statistics from 2024.

Median pay for working-age graduates rose to £42,000 in 2024, ahead of the £30,500 earned by non-graduates - though this data does not account for external factors, like prior academic attainment.

However, the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) has said that when taking account of inflation, graduate wages have declined in real terms - and the level of the decline varies depending on which job you're in.

When measured against prices in 2015, graduates surveyed in 2022 were earning £448 per year less on average than their counterparts who graduated three years earlier.

Earnings also depend on the subject studied and university attended.

Research published in 2020 by the IFS think tank in England suggests that, on average, women who study creative arts and languages degrees earn the same amount in their lifetime as if they had not gone to university.

In contrast, women who study law, economics or medicine earn over £250,000 more during their career than if they did not have a degree.

Men who studied creative arts on average earn less across their lifetimes than if they had not attended university. Male medicine or economics graduates earn £500,000 more.

Attending university can help students from poorer backgrounds earn more than their parents might have done, according to 2021 research by education charity the Sutton Trust in England.

But it found that only a fifth of graduates who were eligible for free school meals went on to be in the top 20% of earners - compared to almost half of graduates who attended private schools.

The Sutton Trust says attending a selective university - such as those in the Russell Group of leading universities - gives young people the "best chance of being socially mobile".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv4g.title: When parenting advice becomes too much
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv4g.text:
Before Rosie Whitfield became a mum, she imagined herself parenting very calm children.

"Then I had two wild boys," she says with a laugh.

Following the birth of her kids, Rosie spent hours online looking for the best advice and was drawn to one particular approach to parenting: Gentle parenting, which focuses on empathy and mutual respect with little emphasis on punishment, albeit with boundaries.

But she constantly worried her choices, from sleep schedules to handling toddler tantrums, were "ruining their lives forever".

Rosie does not blame the gentle parenting philosophy itself but instead says the overall amount of parenting advice online was "overwhelming" and "made mundane parenting choices feel like the absolute end of the world."

"I felt like if I was choosing to put the TV on for 20 minutes while I did the dishes or had a coffee, I was choosing to destroy my children's brains," says Rosie, who is originally from Birmingham and now lives in Dubai.

Rosie believes her confidence and intuition were stripped away as she questioned every parenting decision. And she is not alone.

Government research suggests that around two-thirds of parents with young children feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available and struggle with conflicting advice, with many turning to social media for support.

And it's not just the early years.

Research from the charity Action for Children found that many parents of teenagers who initially contacted the charity for help with school avoidance, ADHD or mental health, often went on to describe their own anxiety, exhaustion and uncertainty of how to parent with empathy and patience when close to burnout.

Faced with an array of parenting philosophies, or "brands" to choose from, is all of this advice helping parents or making them more anxious? And is there really a best way to parent? Or, as we strive to become the perfect parent, are we losing our intuition?

Parents today are confronted by parenting styles including "helicopter parenting", which is focused on closely monitoring and protecting children from harm, and "tiger parenting", which involves strict parenting and high expectations for achievement. There are also "snowplough parents", who try to remove obstacles from their child's path, and "dolphin parents", who aim to be firm but flexible.

Author Matilda Gosling, who wrote Evidence‑Based Parenting, says many of the parenting fads or trends complicate what should be a straightforward relationship between a parent and child.

"Some parents think 'I need to be a snowplough parent and plough all of these obstacles out of the way'."

"But it really complicates what is actually a fairly fundamental part of being human, which is that you are warm and you love your children and you put in place some boundaries around them."

Gosling believes parenting trends often represent a pendulum swing, with one generation trying to correct what it believes the previous one got wrong.

"Throughout history, you get these swings from one extreme to the other," she says.

Gentle parenting is seen by some as the latest swing away from a strict, detached parenting style popular in the 1990s, which often relied on controlled crying, the naughty step and time out.

It is built around understanding, empathy and respect but also emphasises the importance of boundaries.

One of the most widely studied models of parenting comes from developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind.

Baumrind identified three parenting styles, later expanded to four: authoritative (high warmth and high control), authoritarian (low warmth and high control), permissive (high warmth and low control), and neglectful (low warmth and low control).

"Authoritative is the gold standard," says Gosling who has looked at more than 1,000 studies.

Research has found that children raised with an authoritative approach, combining warmth with clear boundaries, tend to achieve better academic results, have higher self-esteem and stronger social skills.

But where gentle parenting fits within that framework is disputed. Gosling believes that it falls on the permissive side.

"It's very much child-led. The child ends up having so much control that there's no sense of safety coming from the outside."

However, Sarah Ockwell-Smith, who is widely credited with coining and popularising the term 'gentle parenting', strongly disagrees.

"It [gentle parenting] is not remotely permissive," she says, putting it firmly in Baumrind's authoritative category. Clear boundaries are "super important".

Social media, however, is flooded with memes of exhausted parents calmly negotiating with a child having a supermarket meltdown, something Ockwell-Smith finds deeply frustrating.

"I have to step away from the Instagram reels and the TikToks because I just want to comment, 'This is not gentle parenting'".

"You have house rules, family limits, discipline and consequences. But the difference is we look at discipline as learning and teaching rather than punishing."

Toddler tantrums and teenage behaviour, she argues, should be viewed through a lens of ongoing brain development, not 'they're being naughty' or 'they hate me'.

But despite the term being popular, Ockwell-Smith believes that gentle parenting is still a fringe movement and that authoritarian parenting remains the dominant style.

Around 80 years ago, American paediatrician Dr Benjamin Spock published a book called Baby and Child Care, which went on to sell millions of copies and became the main source of advice for mothers for generations.

The opening line was "Trust yourself. You know more than you think..."

The book challenged strict parenting norms of the time and in the following decades parents were offered more advice from an increasing range of voices.

Research into parenting has increasingly focused on the early years - from pregnancy to the age of two when the building blocks for lifelong emotional and physical health are laid down. For parents, that means more advice to navigate competing messages about what is best for their children.

Professor Ellie Lee, the director of the Centre for Parenting Culture Studies, has studied parenting for more than two decades, including research into mothers' confidence and uncertainty around infant feeding.

She says a major shift occurred in the 1990s when parenting became an increasing focus of public policy.

"Politicians started to say 'Parenting's the hardest job in the world. Children don't come with a manual. We need to give parents guidance. Parents need more support. We need parent education'."

Advice began to emerge on almost every aspect of family life, from tummy time, to feeding, to the right buggy, she explains.

Prof Lee argues that while some public health campaigns were necessary, such as advice not to put babies to sleep on their front after research into cot deaths, the growing culture of advice began to make parents paranoid.

"Dr Spock's 'trust yourself' philosophy is now a very counter-cultural piece of advice," she says. "What we say instead is 'always seek help',"

She believes this has made parents more anxious about doing things "right".

"Some of the things that are now presented as really high stakes are not," she says, using examples like breastfeeding exclusively for six months or how much tummy time a child needs.

"It's terrible because parents become completely exhausted."

Ockwell-Smith says the volume of advice can be "deafening and confusing".

"Actually, parents should just learn themselves and go on intuition," she says.

Others point out that there is also a problem of advice being given that is altogether wrong. Ruth Watts is a health visitor who began sharing content on social media after becoming concerned about misinformation online.

She had seen "experts" advise parents to wean babies onto solids early, offer treatment advice for tongue tie or allergies without medical training, and tell parents to put babies in their own rooms before six months.

Many families, she argues, are working longer hours while at the same time health services are being stripped back, leaving more parents looking online for breastfeeding, behaviour and sleep support.

"We are looking for that kind of personable, conversational approach from people, rather than reading a website."

Many factors shaping family life remain outside parents' control. A child's temperament, special educational needs, family support, finances and their own upbringing can all influence family life.

While some say parenting hasn't got harder but expectations have, others argue that parents today are facing more complex challenges than in previous generations with growing concerns around young people's mental health.

There are also debates around children spending more time on screens and less time outdoors, while schools are reporting increasing behavioural challenges and lower respect for rules and authority. Prof Lee believes parental confidence is at an all-time low.

"I think parents feel very nervous about disciplining children now because they're worried about how it's going to make them feel," she argues.

The confusion around the "right" way to parent has led some parents to turn to courses for help.

Aymara Lamche-Brennan, who has a 22-year-old daughter, four-year-old son and six-month-old daughter, signed up for a course during the summer when another mother at the school gate mentioned she was attending.

"The flyer said 'it's the toughest job in the world' and I thought yes it is, how can you help?'" Aymara says from her home in London.

"When I had my daughter, I was 19 and I didn't really think much about parenting styles, she was with me everywhere and I just kind of rolled with it, but what I really want to know now is what simple wins are there with parenting?"

Aymara said the Circle of Security course she attended gave her practical tools so she could help her children organise their feelings, take charge when she needs to and recognise when she was becoming stressed.

"It's not telling you how to parent. It's helping you think," says Jennifer Peters, a former social worker and director of the charity Connected Lives which runs courses across London, Derbyshire and Cambridgeshire.

She says most parents want the best for their kids but they don't always know how to get there, and that guidance can be helpful.

"I don't think people need to be bombarded with information but the group experience helps you think, 'oh, it's not just me' and lets you take a step back from it all," Peters says.

Back in Dubai, Rosie says the arrival of her second child changed everything as she realised her sons were "polar opposites" and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

A recent trip home to Birmingham also provided some perspective. Her eldest son was throwing a tantrum, and Rosie found herself wrestling with a familiar worry.

"If I send him upstairs, am I damaging him emotionally? Is he going to develop an attachment disorder because of this?"

But her mum said, 'Just send him upstairs. He can't hit his brother over the head with a horse [if he is upstairs]. Follow through with your actions.'

Rosie is taking this "generational advice" on board and has started "venting on social media" to show other mums that they are not alone.

Looking back on her first few years of being a mum, she said she wished she had known one thing.

"There isn't the perfect parent."

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world.text:
Counterterrorism police said the men were found inside the perimeter of R.A.F. Molesworth, a base used by the United States, raising concerns about security.

Reporting from London

Two Latvian men were arrested Thursday inside the perimeter of a British air base used by the United States and are being investigated on suspicion of a national security offense, according to counterterrorism police.

The two men, aged 36 and 32, are Latvian citizens living in Britain, according to the police statement. They were arrested at around 2 a.m. on Thursday after being discovered inside the perimeter of the base, R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire.

Their ability to enter the base will underline concerns about security at military installations operated by the United States inside Britain and other countries, which have been on heightened alert after officials in Britain, the United States, Israel and Germany received evidence of threats against the bases from Iran.

Last month, five British men were arrested on suspicion of a plot targeting R.A.F. Fairford, the air base used by United States bombers in some strikes against Iran during their eight-month war, although they have not been charged and the details of the incident remain murky.

The British police said Thursday that they do not believe that the arrests at R.A.F. Molesworth, which is about two hours north of London, are connected to the incident at Fairford.

“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at R.A.F. Fairford last week,” said Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, in the statement. She added: “A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage.”

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world.title: U.N. Warns Against Technology Used to Read Citizens’ Minds
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world.author: Jonathan Moens
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world.text:
A report by the secretary general warned that new technologies could be used to access and criminalize people’s innermost thoughts.

The scenarios sound like science fiction: Police officers accessing data contained in suspects’ brains to forcefully extract information, or to predict if offenders might plan to commit future crimes.

But the secretary general of the United Nations warned on Thursday for the first time that neurotechnologies are advancing so rapidly that governments’ ability to access and manipulate people’s brains could one day pose a threat to fundamental human rights.

The abuse of future technologies, Secretary General António Guterres warned, could lead to arbitrary detentions, the alteration of people’s mental states and infringements on privacy.

“Neurotechnology, including new and emerging forms, raises profound human rights challenges when applied to the administration of justice,” the secretary general wrote. “Its expansion beyond clinical settings into investigative, judicial and correctional contexts introduces significant risks, alongside potential benefits.”

To address such threats, the report lists a number of recommendations, including establishing regulations consistent with international law, recognizing thoughts as “highly sensitive personal data” and requiring explicit consent for the use of neurotechnology in criminal justice settings.

Human rights officials said the document was an important step toward raising global awareness of the issue and that it could help countries develop laws to prevent the abuse of such technology.

Connections: Soccer Edition

A new mode includes a study tool, but it still does a user’s homework. And a children’s safety nonprofit says the chatbot flunked its tests.

Credit...
Derek Abella

Brian X. Chen is The Times’s lead consumer technology writer and the author of Tech Fix, a column about the social implications of the tech we use.

Last week, I gathered a set of math problems, chemical equations and essay prompts and, as many students do today, fired up a web browser to ask ChatGPT for help with homework.

I wasn’t going back to school. I was testing ChatGPT for Teens, a new version of the chatbot that OpenAI designed to address mounting concerns over the potential harms of artificial intelligence on education and younger people’s health.

Amid steep declines in reading and math scores all over the country, recent studies have found that dependence on A.I. chatbots, which can write essays and provide answers to homework questions, may stifle students’ abilities to retain information and learn to solve complex problems.

ChatGPT and other chatbots have also made headlines in recent years for concerns that they may be contributing to some teenagers’ unhealthy behaviors, including self-harm.

In response, OpenAI announced in August that ChatGPT for Teens would be a new mode for 13- to 17-years-olds that included safeguards to limit high-risk conversations involving self-harm, violence, eating disorders and graphic content.

Parents can set up accounts for their children using parental controls, or the chatbot may automatically predict a user’s age based on their conversations. The company also said the mode would detect when a teenager was doing homework so that it could offer help instead of solely giving answers.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/scien.author: Bill Wasik
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/scien.text:
Photo illustration by Jane Stockdale for The New York Times

Are you proud of your chin?

You should be. In fact, give it an appreciative rub right now, or admire it in the mirror: That bony protuberance jutting out past your teeth is a trait that distinguishes you from the rest of the animal kingdom. Even your extinct hominin cousins — those enigmatic Neanderthals and Denisovans who strode bipedally like humans and even sometimes mated with them — never belonged to the chin club.

But why just us? One human who has deep thoughts on that mystery is Daniel Lieberman, an evolutionary biologist at Harvard. It’s a question he loves to ponder in part because his students love to ponder it, too. When he poses it to them in class, he says, “it always gets them on the edge of their seat, even though it’s completely unimportant.”

Dr. Lieberman is one of 100 scientists to whom the writers and editors on The Times’s Science desk recently posed a query of their own: “What is a big unanswered question in your field?” Responses poured in from biochemists, quantum physicists, archaeologists, oceanographers, Nobel Prize-winning biologists, geoscientists, entomologists, you name it.

Scroll down and you can read the 100 questions they sent back — a list that demonstrates the fascinating range of the scientific mission and mind-set. Some questions aim at concrete, day-to-day mysteries (“How do ants work together to produce the collective behavior of colonies?” asks Deborah Gordon, a biologist). Others interrogate first principles: “What determines the laws of physics as they exist in our universe?” Katie Mack, an astrophysicist, wonders. Still others express an urgency about human problems that want solving — like “Can we make the wildlife trade sustainable?” and “Can the human aging process be safely reversed?”

And some, like Dr. Lieberman’s, express a pure curiosity for its own sake. Various hypotheses have tried to explain why chins might have helped our ancestors survive, he notes, but none really make sense. The only one left is sexual selection: Maybe chins made some hominins more attractive to the opposite sex, and the trait won out over time. But the theory is impossible to prove; testing it would entail “showing pictures of people without chins and asking if you would sleep with them,” which, Dr. Lieberman notes, is “a terrible experiment.”

The recipients of the six awards in science, literature, economics and peace work are being announced this week.

By The New York Times

The recipients of the 2026 Nobel Prizes are being announced this week, including the Peace Prize on Friday.

Every October, committees in Sweden and Norway name Nobel laureates in a variety of prizes related to science, literature and economics, as well as peace work. Six prizes in total are awarded.

Laureates will receive their medals, prize money and diplomas in Stockholm and Oslo in December.

Here is a quick guide to this year’s prizes.

Six Nobel Prizes are awarded every year, each recognizing an individual’s or an organization’s groundbreaking contribution in a specific field. Prizes are given for physiology or medicine, physics, chemistry, economic sciences, literature and peace work, the last of which often draws the most attention because of the fame of the people and groups nominated.

This year, there were 287 candidates for the Nobel Peace Prize — 208 individuals and 79 organizations, the Nobel committee said. Last year, the institute received 338 nominations. The highest number ever received was 376 candidates, in 2016. (Here’s how those nominations work.)

Previous Nobel Peace Prize recipients include Kailash Satyarthi and Malala Yousafzai (2014); President Barack Obama (2009); Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk (1993); the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso (1989); and Mother Teresa (1979).

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/clima.title: Inside a Data Center Industry Conference
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/clima.author: Hiroko Tabuchi
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/clima.text:
At Data Center World last week, public backlash, and how to deal with it, was a popular topic.

Reporting from Data Center World, an industry convention, in Dallas.

Rajiv Vohra, a private equity investor who develops data center infrastructure, recently reminisced about the good old days of a year ago. “Nobody knew what a data center was,” he said last week at a gathering of industry leaders in Dallas. “We’d put a data center in, and nobody cared.”

But in the past year, that’s changed, said Mr. Vohra, who previously spent a decade working at Google. Communities across the country are up in arms over new data centers, especially the large, hyperscale projects behind the artificial intelligence boom. “The whole industry has been caught on its heels,” he said.

Diane Sullivan, chief development officer at the power developer Hecate Energy, put it another way: offering modest benefits to the local community in exchange for hosting a data center is no longer enough. “We used to buy a fire truck,” she said. “Now we have to be more creative.”

At Data Center World, a meeting held Sept. 21 to 23 at a sprawling conference center, I got a peek inside an industry grappling with the sudden eruption of community objections to data center projects across the country.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott had just announced he was effectively pausing the development of new data centers amid growing opposition to the projects and concern over their environmental effects. At least a dozen other states have introduced or considered legislation imposing bans, moratoriums or heavy restrictions on new data center construction.

Under scrutiny is the strain these gargantuan projects have brought to local power grids, causing steep increases in local electricity demand and in some cases driving up residential utility costs. Cooling requirements for massive hyperscale centers draw millions of gallons of water daily, triggering opposition in drought-prone regions of the country. That’s on top of fears of the havoc A.I. itself could wreak.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/clima.title: The Coal Industry Asked for a Rescue. Trump Obliged.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/clima.author: Brad Plumer and Claire Brown
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/clima.text:
In a previously unreported letter, a top lobbyist floated the idea of using emergency powers to keep aging coal plants open.

By Brad Plumer and Claire Brown

Brad Plumer reported from Washington and Claire Brown from New York.

Early last year, a top coal lobbyist sent a letter to Energy Secretary Chris Wright with a dire warning.

Roughly one-third of the nation’s coal-burning power plants were scheduled to close within five years, according to the letter, dated Mar. 11, 2025, from a coal trade group. Many of the closures would occur during President Trump’s second term.

But what if the plants didn’t have to shut down? The trade group, America’s Power, proposed an unusual remedy: The Energy Department could deploy rarely used emergency powers to force them to stay open longer.

Two months later, the Trump administration began doing exactly that.

The letter, which has not been previously reported, reveals some of the earliest known discussions about a move that experts have called an extraordinary intervention into the nation’s energy markets.

Since May 2025, the Energy Department has repeatedly issued emergency orders to keep nine coal-burning units at six plants operating long past their scheduled retirement dates, saying the facilities are needed to prevent looming blackouts. The orders have sometimes come over the protests of the plant’s owners and are expected to cost ratepayers hundreds of millions of dollars. A federal appeals court has already struck down one order, ruling that it overstepped the law.

The letter from America’s Power was made public through a Freedom of Information Act request by the Environmental Defense Fund, an environmental group.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.
