https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.title: Medical debt is crushing hospital patients in LA. Health officials may have a fix
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.author: Noam Levey
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.text:
Naman Shah examines a patient at Monrovia Health Center, a Los Angeles County public health clinic in Monrovia, California. Shah says reducing medical debt in the community will depend on effective prevention strategies, just as stopping the spread of infectious disease does.

LOS ANGELES — Every Tuesday, Naman Shah sees tuberculosis patients at a small public clinic in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley. Shah, a physician and epidemiologist at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, pores over images of battered lungs, listens to labored breathing and checks medications.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

It's part of an initiative dating to the early 20th century to control infections so tuberculosis doesn't spread. "We like doing things upstream," Shah said, "meaning before they happen, not after the damage is done."

Today, Shah and his colleagues are applying the same principle to medical debt. A key part of that effort is a new system to allow every hospital in LA County to easily screen patients for financial aid. The goal: to stop low-income families from getting a bill that buries them in debt.

Shah estimates this system could prevent several hundred million dollars of medical debt every year.

Shah at Monrovia Health Center.

In the U.S., an estimated 100 million adults have some form of healthcare debt. In LA County, the nation's most populous, public health officials calculate that about 800,000 residents have medical bills they can't pay.

"The impacts of medical debt were staggering," said Shah, who used to staff a rural health clinic in India and, since 2023, has led a county initiative in LA to tackle the debt problem.

"People end up with credit card debt and then a vicious cycle of high interest rates and poverty," he said. "People forgo their prescriptions. People forgo appointments. And then you get into worse health."

Hospitals typically offer financial aid to patients with low incomes. But information about assistance is often hard for patients to get. Applying can be cumbersome. And many eligible patients never seek aid, research shows.

"Most people walk into the hospital and walk out without any knowledge of financial assistance," said Jared Walker, founder of Dollar For, a nonprofit that helps patients nationwide apply for aid, often called charity care.

"The impacts of medical debt were staggering," says Shah, who since 2023 has led a Los Angeles County initiative to tackle the debt problem.

That's fueling debt. It's also driving costly collection efforts that even hospital officials acknowledge pointlessly target low-income patients who are unlikely to be able to pay.

"They're turning their wheels trying to collect on debt that isn't collectable," said Adena Tessler, regional vice president for the Hospital Association of Southern California.

One potential solution is a system that automatically screens and qualifies low-income patients for financial aid without requiring an application. This is called presumptive eligibility.

Some hospitals already use such systems, which rely on software that checks patient eligibility based on publicly available information such as credit history.

The strategy can be very effective. Shah said hospitals that have deployed presumptive eligibility systems have reported as much as a 50% increase in the amount of financial aid they give patients.

Under a state law passed last year, all California hospitals will have to start doing presumptive eligibility screening by next July.

But the systems can be expensive and difficult for smaller hospitals to implement. Only about 1 in 5 hospitals in LA County currently use them, Shah said.

Public health officials wondered whether they could help more hospitals set up the systems.

The county, which, like many local governments, faces major fiscal challenges, couldn't pay for this, Shah said. But the public health department could bring together healthcare and hospital officials in the county to figure out another solution.

"The beauty of government is not when it always has to do the work," Shah said. "We have the ability to make sure that people cooperate."

The Hospital Association of Southern California, initially wary of the county initiative, came to see improving hospital financial aid programs as beneficial to hospitals, many of which were wasting money on collections. "The billing process is cumbersome and costly," said Paul Young, a senior vice president with the association.

The association agreed to procure a digital presumptive eligibility system and make it available to its members. This bulk-purchasing approach, which Young compared to "a Costco model," would lower the cost for individual hospitals, he said.

At the same time, L.A. Care, a nonprofit health plan that administers Medicaid coverage for more than 2.5 million low-income county residents, committed $2 million to set up the system.

The investment reflected the safety net insurer's mission to make medical care accessible to more people, said Melanie Fontes Rainer, who leads strategic planning for L.A. Care. "It's going to make Los Angeles County better," she said.

Getting the new system up and running by January, as the partners hope, faces challenges.

Hospital officials are figuring out how the system will be funded in the long term. And it's unclear how many of the county's 88 acute care hospitals will ultimately use it, even if it's cheaper and easier to access.

The partners are also working to improve the data that the system relies on to screen patients. One goal is to link the system to tax records maintained by the state of California. This would provide hospitals with more accurate information on patients' income than current systems, which often rely on estimated income.

Walker, the patient advocate at Dollar For, said he's heartened by the county's effort. "I'm optimistic that we can make a better charity care system," he said. "And the fact that hospitals in LA County are willing to be innovative and creative about ways we can do that is super encouraging."

For his part, Shah said county public health officials recognize that a better screening system at hospitals won't by itself eliminate medical debt. But he said the public health department couldn't ignore a problem that affects more county residents than asthma or tobacco use.

"Prevention is our bread and butter," he said.

This article is part of Hidden Help, an investigative series from Tradeoffs and KFF Health News about how hospitals can protect their patients from the life-altering harms of medical debt.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.title: New Maryland law requires radiologists inform patients of heart disease warning sign
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.author: Michel Martin
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.text:
NPR's Michel Martin speaks with radiologist Dr. Lisa Mullen about a new Maryland law requiring that patients be notified if mammogram results show calcium deposits in blood vessels.

October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, which comes with reminders for annual mammograms. You might've heard one of these. One state is now requiring radiologists to tell patients whether their screenings for breast cancer reveal a warning sign for heart disease. That warning sign is called arterial calcification. Dr. Lisa Mullen is here to help explain that. She is an associate professor of radiology at Johns Hopkins University who helped revise the draft of the new legal requirement that's now in effect in Maryland. Dr. Mullen, good morning. Thanks for joining us.

LISA MULLEN: Oh, thank you for having me.

MARTIN: So what is breast arterial calcification, and what can it tell you about someone's health?

MULLEN: So breast arterial calcifications are basically calcifications - so that sort of white mineral - deposited in the wall of arteries in the breast - or, you know, we're seeing it in the breast. And since calcifications appear white on a mammogram, they are visible to radiologists, and they can be distinguished from other types of calcifications that occur commonly in the breast tissue. And it's important to know that arterial calcifications are not related to breast cancer or breast cancer risk. So they're not a marker of breast cancer, but they are potentially a marker of other cardiovascular disease.

MARTIN: OK. So it's a side benefit of getting that mammogram, right? The initial - the point of the mammogram is the breast cancer, but then you get this other benefit for some sort of indication. But what should...

MARTIN: ...Clinicians and patients do if this calcification is detected?

MULLEN: So, you know, what we're - well, just to backtrack a little bit, the new law in Maryland is requiring radiologists to report breast arterial calcifications if they're present on a mammogram. So this really only applies to mammograms. And then the law also provides some required language that has been added to patient result letters. So the lay letter that the patient gets when they have a screening mammogram or a diagnostic mammogram will have some information about breast arterial calcifications, along with information that the patient does or does not have breast arterial calcifications themselves. But then there's some general information as well.

So that paragraph suggests that if these calcifications are present, that the patient should speak to her primary care provider about her cardiovascular risk. So that would be the first step, just talking to the patient's provider. You know, so the woman talks to her provider about her cardiovascular risk. And maybe together, they can discuss whether a more formal risk assessment needs to be performed for that patient, and that could be very individual, depending on the patient and her own risks.

MARTIN: Well, to that end, you know, two other breast radiologists at Johns Hopkins opposed this law in part because they said there's not a standard step for how to follow up. And they said that that just creates more anxiety for patients. So what's your take on this? Why do you think this is still, you know, a positive step to require this notification?

MULLEN: Well, I think one of the challenges that's faced with this is that radiologists were reporting it, but it was kind of optional. So there's no national guideline about reporting this and no agreement about whether it should be reported or how it should be reported or what should be done if calcifications are found. And I think the legislation in Maryland, which is mandating reporting - and it really is a binary reporting, so basically, you know, yes or no, present or not present. So we're not really looking at the grade, the amount of calcification or the number of arteries that are calcified. So it's not really quantified, but it's more just yes or no, you have it or you don't. And I think the - you know, the opposition comes from all of these uncertainties that we're not really sure what the best evaluation would be if this is detected, you know, or what it ultimately means for the patient.

MARTIN: So I think the point is that then this is something you should then follow up and talk to your doctor about.

MULLEN: Yes, correct.

MARTIN: That is Dr. Lisa Mullen at Johns Hopkins University. Thank you so much.

MULLEN: Thank you, Michel.

(SOUNDBITE OF TINY DESK CONCERT)

LOS TEXMANIACS: (Singing in Spanish).

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-594.title: Republicans and Democrats find a unifying target: Pharmacy benefit managers
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-594.author: Blake Farmer
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-594.text:
Republicans and Democrats, both patients and politicians, seem united in their disdain for the healthcare companies known as pharmacy benefit managers. Tennessee and Arkansas are regulating now them.

There's a lot about healthcare that Americans actually agree on. In our Common Ground project with KFF Health News, we're looking at issues with bipartisan backing. Blake Farmer at WPLN in Nashville reports on one thing that is uniting people - their collective disdain for the healthcare companies known as pharmacy benefit managers.

BLAKE FARMER, BYLINE: Pharmacy benefit managers, known as PBMs, handle the part of health insurance related to the cost of prescription meds. They were promoted as a way to keep drug prices in check, but the largest are now owned by giant conglomerates that also own insurance companies and pharmacies. All this consolidation has turned them into a punching bag for all the frustration patients have with the healthcare system, like high prescription prices. CVS is one of the big companies that also owns a PBM. It's taking heat in Tennessee.

AMYE JOSEPH: We hate CVS. I'm going to be straight up. You can't talk to a pharmacist. They're overstressed. And prices just keep going up.

FARMER: Amye Joseph is 62 and lives in the mountainous eastern corner of Tennessee with her husband.

A JOSEPH: You're going to find this interesting. We have a two-party household. I'm a Republican (laughter). My husband's a Democrat.

FARMER: He's equally frustrated. They have a list of gripes that could fill the famously long CVS receipt. For example, Charlie Joseph discovered his blood pressure medication was actually cheaper when they didn't use insurance.

CHARLIE JOSEPH: You know, the whole healthcare thing is just frustrating on a good day.

FARMER: PBM officials say their industry has been unfairly maligned and that they're the only link in the drug supply chain trying to lower drug costs. Dave Marin, president and CEO of the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, addressed Congress in February.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DAVE MARIN: Yes, drug prices are still too high. Without PBMs, they would be much, much higher.

FARMER: But state lawmakers aren't buying it. Tennessee is one of two states that have now made it illegal for a company to own both a PBM and retail pharmacies. CVS fought the proposals with a multimillion-dollar TV ad campaign.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED COMMENTATOR: A hundred thirty-four CVS pharmacies across Tennessee shut down, making healthcare less accessible for families like yours.

FARMER: Those ads aired just before the vote this spring. Nevertheless, Tennessee lawmakers moved forward. Republican State Senator Rusty Crowe told his colleagues before the vote that they should consider the fierce resistance a sign that they were onto something.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

RUSTY CROWE: I learned when I was in the Vietnam War, when you start taking on flack, you know you're over the damn target pretty quick.

FARMER: Business-friendly Republicans voted alongside Democrats who favor more regulation. State Representative Antonio Parkinson, a Democrat from Memphis, says he feels like he voted in favor of lower drug prices and ma-and-pa pharmacies.

ANTONIO PARKINSON: If there's a benefit to my people, I'm supporting it.

FARMER: The most vocal critics calling for regulation of PBMs are independently owned pharmacies and their trade groups. In Tennessee, State Senator Bobby Harshbarger, who sponsored the pharmacy ownership ban, is also a small-town pharmacist. His mother is a pharmacist, too, and a member of the U.S. Congress, who's proposed a similar ban on PBMs owning pharmacies at the federal level. That bill has bipartisan sponsors and has created unlikely bedfellows of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley.

Antonio Ciaccia is CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a nonprofit think tank that tracks drug pricing. He says this legislative push reflects a feeling - even in the GOP - that the market for prescription drugs is being gamed.

ANTONIO CIACCIA: Republicans are looking at this issue, saying, we know what competition is supposed to do, and it isn't happening. This is not a free market. This is a free-for-all.

FARMER: In a statement, CVS told NPR the new state laws will do the opposite of what they're intended to and drive up prices. It's unclear if these bans on PBMs owning pharmacies will hold up in court, or if they do, whether CVS will follow through on closing all of its pharmacies. Either way, PBMs aren't finding many friends in politics at the moment.

For NPR News, I'm Blake Farmer in Nashville.

CHANG: This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-599.title: The WHO seeks more details on the death of a plague research lab employee in Russia
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-599.author: Charles Maynes
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-599.text:
The World Health Organization says it wants more information on what caused the death of an employee at a Russian plague research lab. Russia says the woman died of pneumonia of unknown origin.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Russian authorities continue to insist there is no health emergency following the death of a 28-year-old lab technician at a plague research institute in Siberia last week. The case has created global concern over an outbreak of the plague or some other deadly pathogen. From Moscow, NPR's Charles Maynes reports.

CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: For nearly a week, Russia's consumer health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has insisted the death of a female lab technician at a Siberian institute focused on combating the plague and other infectious diseases was due to pneumonia of, quote, "unknown" origin. A subsequent state investigation found no pathogens in the woman's body linked to her lab research, just as it said there was no evidence of an outbreak of the plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia where the institute is based. Yet, in a press conference Wednesday, the head of the World Health Organization, Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said these Russian assurances were, at the very least, incomplete.

(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)

TEDROS ADHANOM GHEBREYESUS: We don't yet have the full picture of this event. And we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment. Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports.

MAYNES: Exiled Russian media with contacts on the ground in Siberia, in particular, have chronicled moments that at times seemed at odds with the official version of events. For example, reporting quarantines at some local hospitals or highlighting posts that later disappeared on social media by local government officials about health dangers. NPR has not independently confirmed the reports. The U.S., which withdrew from the WHO under the Trump administration, has also been pushing for more information.

Today, the State Department issued a formal request for Russia to provide more details on the case. And the U.S. embassy in Moscow published a health alert for Americans still in Russia to seek immediate medical assistance should they experience any adverse respiratory problems. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also weighed in. In a statement, the CDC reminded the plague is treatable with antibiotics and said there was no indication of a broader threat to the United States. Meanwhile, President Trump played down the possibility the incident could've been a mishap involving a bioweapon.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so. And if you listen to them, it's under control.

MAYNES: Trump will have his own chance to try and learn just how much when he holds a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, expected later this week. Charles Maynes, NPR News, Moscow.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/g-s1-1469.title: What is the pneumonic plague?
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/g-s1-1469.author: Michaeleen Doucleff
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/g-s1-1469.text:
The bacteria that causes bubonic plague.

The ancient word "plague" is back in the headlines.

NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes reported this week on what we know about a Russian researcher working in a lab studying the plague who died from pneumonia of an unknown origin last week.

Maynes reports that the employee was a 28-year-old woman who worked in a lab in Siberia, some 2,500 miles from Moscow. An investigation by Russia's consumer health watchdog concluded that no pathogens in her body were connected to her work with infectious disease.

But local media have raised concerns about the spread of pneumonic plague, which NPR has not independently confirmed.

It's one of the diseases studied at the lab in Siberia. It's airborne and can be fatal.

While noting that 200 "contacts" were in quarantine, Russia has denied that there are cases of plague in the area. But questions loom. In a press conference Wednesday, the head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said these Russian assurances were — at the very least — incomplete: "We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment."

In the meantime, here's what we do know about the bacterial disease of plague — and the variant known as pneumonic plague.

The plague comes in several versions, depending on which body part the bacteria invade. When a flea bites a person, the individual typically develops what's called bubonic plague. In this case, the telltale sign is one or more swollen and painful lymph nodes, known as buboes. (The word "bubonic" comes from the Greek boubon, which means groin, because some people have swollen lymph nodes in their groin.) Doctors can diagnose the disease by taking a sample from the person's blood or lymph nodes and then submitting the sample to a lab for testing.

But when the bacteria spread to the lungs, this can cause what's called pneumonic plague. In this case, there's often no telltale sign of the plague, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

This version is much more dangerous, says medical entomologist Adelaide Miarinjara at Emory University. "It transmits pretty easily between people because it spreads through droplets, almost like COVID spreads."

And people can die more quickly with pneumonic plague than other forms, she adds, because the disease progresses more rapidly. "The key here is early diagnosis. If people aren't expecting it or don't seek treatment, they can die."

Treatment involves antibiotics, often administered by IV infusion.

In 2017, Madagascar suffered a large outbreak of pneumonic plague when a person from a rural part of the country brought the disease to the coastal city of Toamasina. That city hadn't seen a case of the plague in nearly a century, says Miarinjara, who was in Madagascar at the time. "A person transmitted the disease on public transportation," she says.

The country recorded more than 2,400 suspected cases, including nearly 1,900 cases of pneumonic plague. One study estimated that about 25% of people with confirmed cases died in this outbreak.

As for the reports of Russian "contacts" of the lab worker under quarantine — that reflects a long-standing response to sicknesses like the plague.

The idea of isolating, or quarantining, sick people dates back at least 3,000 years. The Book of Leviticus in the Bible mentions how to isolate people with leprosy.

The word "quarantine" itself arose during the Black Death, when the city-state of Dubrovnik, now part of the country of Croatia, enacted what is likely the first state-imposed isolation.

At the time, Dubrovnik was a wealthy merchant city along the coast of the Adriatic Sea. City leaders wanted to keep the bubonic plague out. So they began to force visitors to wait for 40 days on a remote island outside the city before coming ashore.

They called the wait quarantino, from the Italian word for "40."

"The first quarantine was pretty much improvised," Ivana Marinavić, the head of educational programs at the Lazarettos of Dubrovnik, told NPR in 2021. The Lazarettos were the first buildings ever constructed for the sole purpose of quarantining.

If you broke the quarantine during the plague, the consequences were severe. "Torture, or cutting your nose or your ears off," Marinavić told NPR.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-581.title: Doomscrolling too much? Try these tips to put the phone down and plug into real life
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-581.author: Marielle Segarra
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-581.text:
NPR Life Kit provides tips to help you reduce your screentime.

Are you seeking freedom from the tyranny of your smartphone? I mean, your phone is supposed to work for you even if sometimes it feels like the other way around, right? Well, NPR Life Kit's Marielle Segarra has tips to better manage your screen time.

MARIELLE SEGARRA, BYLINE: All right, we're about to get into our feelings. The first step in cutting back on screen time is to tune into how scrolling makes you feel. When you find yourself reaching for your phone or thinking, I should check Instagram for the hundredth time today, notice how you feel and how your body feels, too.

SAMMY NICKALLS: For example, I noticed that whenever I was feeling bad about myself in some way, I would log on Twitter.

SEGARRA: Sammy Nickalls is the author of "Log Off: Self-Help For The Extremely Online."

NICKALLS: Ask yourself, how do I feel right now? And what can I do? And most times it's not scroll. Most times, it's like, take a nap, or talk to a friend, or do something that makes you happy.

SEGARRA: Another thing you can do when you get the urge to scroll is resist. I know it feels like you have to pick up that phone, but you actually don't. Clinical psychologist Diana Hill is the co-author of a book called "I Know I Should Exercise, But...: 44 Reasons We Don't Move And How To Get Over Them." And she says there's this term in addiction research called urge surfing.

DIANA HILL: What we know about urges is that they're a lot like waves. They rise up, they get bigger and bigger and bigger, and they come back down again.

SEGARRA: The goal with urge surfing is to learn to get on board, stand up and ride that thing out. Another tip is to increase friction. Make it harder to use your phone. Jose Briones is the author of "Low Tech Life: A Guide To Mindful Digital Minimalism." He says set up screen time limits and then make them hard to override.

JOSE BRIONES: If you want to go into your iPhone and you want to use the app, and you set up a screen time limit - maybe it's 10 minutes, maybe it's 15 - and you went to it, right now you probably can beat that with two taps. You say, yes, I want more time. Are you sure? Yes, I'm sure.

SEGARRA: Instead, give the password to a trusted friend, and then you'll have to ask them for it if you want to get on Pinterest when you're really supposed to be getting that housework done. You can also use a physical device that you need to tap to unblock your apps.

BRIONES: The more friction you introduce into your life, the harder you're making it to use all of these services and devices, your brain is going to say, it's not worth it.

SEGARRA: Our last takeaway - don't keep your smartphone, tablet or computer in your bedroom overnight. Jean Twenge is a psychologist and author of "10 Rules For Raising Kids In A High-Tech World."

JEAN TWENGE: That's for people of all ages. A ton of research shows that people do not sleep as well or as long if those devices are in their bedrooms overnight. So even if it's off, the technology is just too tempting.

SEGARRA: She says this means no scrolling before bed and no scrolling when you wake up in the morning and also no scrolling if you happen to wake up in the middle of the night. Get an old-school alarm clock, and if you want your phone nearby for emergencies, leave it across the room, out of reach. By the way, Sammy Nickalls made this change, and she says it makes bedtime feel luxurious.

NICKALLS: Have you ever been to a hotel, like, that's kind of nice, and you get into the sheets, and it just feels so nice to kind of, like, have this time to yourself and just feel very calm? And it's, like, a very specific, in my mind, hotel feeling. And that's what I felt when I put my phone outside of my room and just, like, kind of let myself, like, relax and, like, maybe take a bath or, like, read for a while, and just away from any screens. It's like I got that presence of mind back.

SEGARRA: And she really is sleeping better.

For NPR News, I'm Marielle Segarra.

CHANG: And for more tips from Life Kit, go to npr.org/lifekit.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-598.title: How to define a measles death
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-598.author: Maria Godoy
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-598.text:
Historically, the CDC relied on state health departments' determination of measles deaths. Now, it's working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to create a clear definition.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

How do you count a measles death? That question has become a point of controversy. In Pennsylvania, officials have reported five measles-associated deaths in recent weeks. But so far, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has acknowledged just two deaths. NPR health correspondent Maria Godoy is here to break it down. Hi, Maria.

MARIA GODOY, BYLINE: Hi. How are you?

PFEIFFER: Good. So we have a mismatch. Why does the CDC's official measles death count not match what Pennsylvania officials are reporting?

GODOY: Well, last month, the CDC announced it was changing how it counts measles deaths. Historically, the CDC used to rely on reports from state health departments. And you want that rapid notification in an outbreak situation to respond rapidly. Now, however, the CDC is looking to official death records confirmed by the National Center for Health Statistics. But that system is slower. And it's designed for more long-term, retrospective data gathering on deaths. And, you know, this change happened after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly questioned the Pennsylvania deaths, suggesting that measles might not have been the cause of death. And Kennedy is a long-term vaccine skeptic, which has led critics to accuse the CDC of making the change for political reasons, to downplay the severity of measles.

PFEIFFER: So that accusation that politics is distorting health data, how has the CDC responded to that?

GODOY: Well, a couple weeks ago, the new CDC director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, gave an interview to a local news station, Atlanta News First. And in it, she denied that the death count data was being changed for political reasons. She said the U.S. lacked a standardized definition for measles-related death. And she drew a comparison to arguments over how COVID deaths were counted early in the pandemic.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ERICA SCHWARTZ: If someone got hit by a bus and they happened to have COVID, often that was called a COVID-related death.

GODOY: Now, many public health experts would dispute that analogy. But even those who accept that some COVID deaths might have been overcounted early in the pandemic, say, that is highly unlikely to happen when it comes to measles.

PFEIFFER: And why? What would make measles different?

GODOY: Yeah, you know, I spoke to Dr. Jake Scott. He's an infectious disease specialist with Stanford University. And he says there are really two key differences between COVID and measles, prevalence and screening. He says, in early 2022, the U.S. was reporting hundreds of thousands of cases of COVID each day. And many hospitals were routinely screening everyone for COVID to protect vulnerable patients. By contrast, even though the U.S. is seeing a measles resurgence, it's still around 4,000 cases for the entire year.

JAKE SCOTT: No hospital screens every single patient being admitted for measles. That would be ridiculous. And so if someone's being tested for measles, there's a clinical suspicion that that person may have measles.

GODOY: So in other words, you're not going to have measles as an incidental finding. It's not likely. He says the measles virus itself can cause damage, but it also weakens your immune system, so you're vulnerable to other infections. So, for example, if a person's immediate cause of death is pneumonia, but they had measles, he says measles is still likely the underlying cause of death. In other words, if measles shows up on a death certificate, he says, it almost certainly played a role.

PFEIFFER: All right. So we obviously want accurate health data. We also want trust in our public agencies. Where do we go from here?

GODOY: Yeah, the CDC is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to create a standardized definition of measles deaths that can be used across the U.S. that's expected to be ready in the next two to three months. In the meantime, we might continue to hear discrepancies between what the states report and what the CDC has to say.

PFEIFFER: That is NPR's Maria Godoy. Maria, thank you.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.title: Discursive Verses: Vic Mensa and the rise of a rap manosphere counterculture
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.author: Rodney Carmichael
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.text:
Vic Mensa is on the vanguard of commentators reclaiming spaces for radical Black tradition in the spheres of hip-hop discourse.

In the middle of Vic Mensa's sit-down with Rapsody on the third episode of The Vic Mensa Show, the rapper-turned-podcaster recalled "one of the most quintessential moments in Black thought." He was paying reverence to a 1971 conversation between poet Nikki Giovanni and writer James Baldwin. Though that dialogue happened more than 50 years ago, the moment has become an ever-present meme in recent years for embodying the gender gap that can make Black love and Black survival feel like contradictory pursuits.

While ruminating over that classic exchange, Rapsody and Mensa stumble onto a new question: "Where do Black men go to cry?" To which Mensa admits he finds refuge alone in the shower. "You've been convinced that vulnerability is weak," he says. "And you grow and you realize that it was a damn lie — that having vulnerability is far stronger than having some false machismo masculinity."

In that moment, Rapsody casually rises and reaches over to wipe the tears streaming down Mensa's face. "I'm glad that you could cry my brother," she responds. And with that, I had to hit pause just to register what happened. It's got to be the most tender and vulnerable exchange on a podcast I've ever witnessed.

For at least a decade now, podcasts have felt like rap's final frontier. Or an early retirement home for rappers with no pension parlaying their onstage talents into sideshow hosts. The medium launched by the original hip-hop podcast Juan Ep and its contemporary The Combat Jack Show gave way to a generation that cooked down the original formula, like crack, and distilled it to its lowest common denominator. Longform interviews and deep liner notes mostly gave way to trash talk, street gossip and celebrity-driven opinions dredged from our broader cultural obsession with fame, power and success.

In a space currently overrun by chatty patties, as Dame Dash famously declared, the freshest podders on hot mics are offering a counterweight to rap's reigning manosphere of podcast bros. I like to think of them as the podcast bruhs — an ideological alternative to the moderately conservative mainstream. Like the difference between rage-baiting and righteously raging against the machine. If one end is ruled by two of the highest-paid podcasters ranked by Forbes, Joe Budden and Charlamagne tha God, the other side is propped up by the likes of everyman Deante Kyle, a relative newcomer who only quit his truck driving gig a year ago to host the Grits & Eggs Podcast full-time.

Still, content is big business. Even in a beleaguered industry, Charlemagne tha God secured a $200 million bag. His Black Effect joint partnership with iHeart Podcasts now counts nearly 50 titles among a targeted roster it rolls out with the pace of a deep-pocketed major label in the '90s. Podcasting has also become an extension of the art form. Or performance art, per se. When Jadakiss throws a flag on his co-host Fat Joe's flagrant fouls, we're all in on the gag. What cats like Mensa, Deante Kyle, and even scholar Marc Lamont Hill are delivering is a type of performance, too. (Detractors might even call them "performative.") But their roles are steeped in a Black liberation politic that is equal parts sensitive, radical and intersectional. Even if they're just a blip on the dial of toxic, misogynistic, materialistic content, they're a blip worth watching.

The Rapsody episode wasn't Mensa's first intimate moment with a guest. The first one happened when he confided through tears to his friend Chance the Rapper how much it hurt him — and his pockets — when Chance decided against inviting Vic on tour years ago. Chance didn't try to wipe away those tears like Rapsody, but he did take a beat to empathize with Vic and apologize.

Toxicity loves company, and corporations love cashing in on the contagion with zero regard for its harmful effects. Mostly what these pods provide is a critical voice in a field where anything other than mindless praise is viewed as knocking the hustle.

Like a Five Percenter with the delivery of a Southern preacher, Kyle's community-minded commentary is uncut and unforgiving. Black celebrities get zero passes. When Jay-Z's boycott-busting, exclusive vinyl deal with Target backfired this summer, Kyle pulled no punches. "I don't know too much about Jay-Z personally," he said. "I will tell you this. The n**** hates a protest." Even LeBron's recent $15 million Polymarket deal, which will keep him afloat more than his NBA paycheck this year, came under Kyle's crosshairs. "Essentially, what LeBron James does is he helps usher in the newest generation of junkies," he said on an episode titled "Polymarket Pimps."

Mensa's podcast is a spinoff of the heavily-parodied, viral "Orange Tree" shorts that found him kicking anti-capitalist ballistics in a tank-top surrounded by citrus. His lineup of guests highlight a cross-section of Black culture from rap-adjacent to queer-friendly, including like-minded podcaster Van Lathan and singer Durand Bernarr. Mensa has also spoken about the challenge of securing funding for his show while avoiding gambling's sweeping marketing push. Meanwhile, Joe Budden shows no shame in pitching his biggest sponsor, the prediction market site Prize Picks, during paid advertorials every episode.

But Budden clearly senses a shift, too. In 2024, he made the strategic move to add Hill to his show's panel of homies and industry cronies. Whenever the CUNY professor rushes to some notable woman's defense, his couch mates cringe so much that it's become a predictable JBP bit. Clearly, he challenges the pod — and its millions of monthly listeners and viewers — with his feminist, abolitionist views. While there's no metric to measure Hill's positive impact, the move itself suggests how much Budden recognizes that his weekly conversations — which he clearly sees as a microcosm of the culture — are in desperate need of more intersectional thought.

In an era of anti-wokeness, it's refreshing to find a few bruhs who refuse to sleepwalk.

These three figures alone are not the complete list, nor are they necessarily indicative of a trend. However, they make up a vanguard (along with leftist streamers and YouTube essayists) that seems to be rising up in meaningful corners of the Internet to help reclaim some space for the Black radical tradition. The younger audiences they serve are down to engage in the kind of dialogue and ideas that grounded forebears like Baldwin and Giovanni. Only once we start to have those conversations more freely and openly can we decolonize our minds, too.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/g-s1-1418.author: Felix Contreras
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/g-s1-1418.text:
Credit: Photo: Zayrha Rodriguez/NPR

From jazz and Tejano to norteño and ska, 'El Tiny' returns with a takeover from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 for Latin Music Month.

Los Texmaniacs' music is a living history lesson. The conjunto sound is driven by the button accordion, a mid-19th century instrument that made its way to the U.S.-Mexico border by way of German, Czech and Polish immigrants. But this music is also just perfect for twirling on the dance floor to songs about true love, heartbreak, folk heroes and reflections on life.

In this band, everything goes back to Flaco Jimenez, the late Tex-Mex accordion master whose rootsy sound came to define conjunto. Los Texmaniacs band leader and bajo sexto player Max Baca had a long-standing musical partnership with Jimenez — they played the Tiny Desk together in 2012. And accordionist Josh Baca, Max's nephew, studied at the feet of Jimenez.

As Los Texmaniacs kick into "Boom and a Bang" at El Tiny, we're reminded just how close conjunto is to both Cajun music from Louisiana and the blues-driven rock and roll of Texas. The polka that closes out this set, too, is just another example of how this musical hybrid of cultures became a cultural tradition on both sides of the border.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-588.title: On 'She's the Best,' Troye Sivan takes the party to unexpected places
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-588.author: Isabella Gomez Sarmiento
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-588.text:
Isabella Gomez Sarmiento

The pop star's new album, She's the Best, gives Troye Sivan more breathing room to dig into darker feelings.

Throughout the last two decades, Troye Sivan has taken on all kinds of titles in pop culture: Child actor. Teen vlogger. Model. Pop star.

The Australian singer-songwriter grew up in the spotlight, cementing his status as a new kind of 21st-century public figure when he came out as gay to his half a million YouTube subscribers in 2013. Shortly after, Sivan signed to a major label and began releasing dreamy, synth-pop anthems that climbed charts around the world.

His 2023 album, Something to Give Each Other, marked a turning point in his career. Sexy and sleek, it packed a punch of high-BPM earworms and sultry confessions that presented Sivan as a grown-up, self-assured auteur who could fully command center stage. The choreo-driven singles "Rush" and "Got Me Started" became viral hits, earned Sivan his first Grammy nominations and even spawned a Timothée Chalamet and boygenius spoof on Saturday Night Live.

Soon after came "Brat summer," the mainstream explosion of his friend and collaborator Charli xcx's hedonistic hyperpop. In 2024, riding that rush and releasing the joint single "Talk Talk" for the Brat remix album, Sivan and Charli co-headlined the Sweat Tour; it transformed arenas into sweaty, strobe-light-filled nightclubs. Sivan says it was a thrilling moment in his career, but it also didn't paint a full picture of what he was going through at the end of his 20s.

His new album, She's The Best (out Oct. 9 via Interscope), gives the now 31-year-old star more breathing room to dig into darker feelings. Sometimes glitchy, verging on gloomy, at other times bright and bombastic, Sivan's fourth studio LP still pays homage to a long lineage of queer dance floors — with music videos set in the medieval era and modern-day NYC drag shows — but it also excavates a deeper layer of the star's desires.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Isabella Gomez Sarmiento, NPR: You spent a lot of time — I believe it was around five years — working on your last album, Something to Give Each Other. What was the process for She's the Best like for you?

I should not have done this, but we started the day after the Grammy Awards. I think it was sort of a panic response, almost, to coming off of the wave of the last album and that high. I was like, "I'm ready, let's go." And then I started the next day and I was like, "I'm not ready." I took some time, and basically, I think the thing that was confusing to me in the beginning of making this album was [that] there's almost two sides to it. One is I was having these experiences of being on stage and feeling like this really self-actualized version of myself where I was feeling a real, genuine sense of confidence and connection to the world. I was on tour with Charli xcx. There was a lot of partying going on. I think there was almost a sense of bravado there, you know?

Then what started to happen was there would be this crazy tension because I didn't feel like that all the time. I would go home to the hotel or wherever I was staying, and I think that there was — and sort of still is — a very deep sense of longing and loneliness that maybe was a bit exacerbated by the experiences that I was having. So when I started making the album, I was like, "Well, I want to honor this side of myself, which feels very connected and confident. I also want to be honest about what's going on." Over time, I realized that the only way to make something really, really true is to acknowledge the tension in my life. So the album is this journey, and it's intentionally got this sort of whiplash thing that happens a little bit where you go from a very intimate song to all of a sudden this song called "Troye Meets World" and it's like, "I'm back!"

I was going to ask about that, because the singles and the top of the album — it feels like a little bit of a fake out, right? You have this really high energy, like Troye coming off the Sweat Tour, and then you start to peel back some layers as the album goes on.

I really do see albums as the most detailed, layered way for me to document my life and catalog chapters in my life. If I do it well, to me, there's so many layers of how you tell the story. There's the lyric, but then there's also the melody and then there's also the sonic production. And to me, [She's the Best] does sort of tell the whole story. It ends on a sort of hopeful note. It ends with this song called "Lost Time," which is essentially a manifestation song. It's to this guy who I haven't met yet. The first half of it is this sort of beautiful love song, and then later in the song it says, "Someday soon I wanna meet ya." It just kind of really accurately ties up the whole thing and looks to the future because a lot of the album is like a love album to someone I don't know.

I want to take it back to the first track, "She's the Best." This song, in particular, and I think a lot of the album, has this messaging around the women in your life. What do they mean to you? How have they impacted you?

I think I spend so much time thinking about myself because of the nature of my work. I would like to think that I'm not an insanely self-centered person, but a lot of my days are centered around me. And then I also spend a lot of my life, because I want a boyfriend, thinking about men. I feel quite tortured by both of those subjects.

I think that in writing "She's the Best," it was me saying something that I've wanted to say and not really known how to for such a long time, which is that in the times in my life where I haven't always felt safe or protected by men, women have always been there. Growing up in the closet, having basically only girlfriends and then in my professional life, I've always been super comfortable in the orbit of a woman. I just have such deep gratitude that I wanted to share, and I wanted to share it in a way that hopefully didn't ever feel patronizing or too grandiose. You know, that's why I think a lot of the lyrics are so specific in that song. It's this collage in my head of all of these women and feminine people in general that have provided me with a sense of safety, a sense of inspiration and empowerment. Also, in a way, it's a love letter to the feminine side of myself, which I fought so hard for so long, and now I really, really appreciate.

And in a weird way, I think it's been the biggest blessing of my life is that I've always felt a bit other.

It's interesting because I think so much of the discourse around pop music is about the "main pop girls," and there's not really as much of an equivalent in terms of like giant male pop stars, particularly ones that are experimenting with gender expression and doing drag and singing about queer love and sexuality. You're doing all of those things. How do you see your place in that pop landscape right now?

I sort of see it the same way that I [saw] myself socially, growing up. I never felt like one of the girls. I was always hanging out with the girls, but I was always like the girls plus Troye. I definitely didn't feel like one of the boys because there was this crazy masculinity thing that I did not feel a part of. And in a weird way, I think it's been the biggest blessing of my life is that I've always felt a bit other. Like, I'm a deeply, deeply uncompetitive person. I don't feel like I am looking over my shoulder to compare myself to anyone, you know what I mean? So I don't really know where I sit in the whole thing.

Sometimes maybe the reaction that I feel online is a little bit more in line with what the girls get. Then other times I'm like, no, because the discourse around "pop girls" is insane. It's absolutely insane. I'm grateful that I don't have it to that extent. It's sort of a weird middle ground.

On "She's The Best," Charli xcx does some of the backing vocals. You guys obviously have a long history of working together, you toured together. Her husband, George Daniel of The 1975, also worked on the song with you. What was that like? Is that song partially an ode to her in any way?

Yeah, I think you can feel Charli on this album in general. I think that the way that I feel her in this music is because it's impossible to be around her and not feel inspired. She's so focused and she really, really throws herself at everything that she does, and that's really infectious to be around. She made me feel like a superhuman version of myself, just by being around her.

To me a song like "Party" has an intentional wink towards a Charli-esque sort of song because it tells the story of this time in my life where I was experiencing being so closely in her orbit. She's definitely one of the characters that was in my head when I [was] writing "She's the Best," alongside my sister, and my mom, and my teachers at school and my two best friends. So then to be able to have her voice in the chanting at the end, it just felt like a really nice little nod to that. I know that for George, it's obviously very special because she's the best to him as well.

I want to ask about the Madonna sample. It rocks. How did you think about conceptualizing it in this song, "Party"? Did you come to the sample first or were you already building on the song?

It started with the moment before the sample, which in the song there's quite a lot of drums and things going on and then everything kind of cuts out for a bit before the sample comes in. And in my head — because I think super visually when I'm making the music — we're in like a top wide shot of seeing everyone in this club. Then all of a sudden, we're in this ultra close-up, tight on someone's face at the party. All the music cuts out, and it's just this heavy breathing, the sound of somebody really losing themselves in the moment on the dancefloor. So it's this heavy breathing and this like sub-bass kind of thing that happens. Then slowly but surely, "Music" by Madonna fades in, and she's talking about how music makes the people come together.

To me, that ascension where your eyes are closed and you can feel the heat from the lights on your face and you can feel the bass in your chest, and you can also feel the bodies around you — that feeling is the thing that I crave the most, and that's always what I'm seeking when I go out. I've had that moment to "Music" by Madonna on the dance floor. So in my head, it's almost like a sound design choice where it's a storytelling thing. It placed me in the room.

What's your relationship to partying like at this point in your life?

The first word that comes to my mind is grateful. I've never really said this before, but I don't do drugs and I barely drink, and I have a really deep appreciation for partying. I think that part of growing up was, you know, the first time I went out in Berlin, for example, realizing that there's plenty of sober people around who were all there for something greater than each of us. It sounds corny to say, but I just think there's something so beautiful about a group of people getting together to listen to music and move their bodies.

I have this weird thing where sometimes when I'm on the dance floor, I imagine everyone's skeletons in their bodies, and I'm like, "This is kind of a hilarious thing that we're all doing. Why are we all, like, moving like this?" I think about it when I see a baby dancing as well. I think that there's something so innate about the connection between the body and music and then how that also connects you to the people around you. That is such a beautiful thing to me, and it's sort of the guiding light in my life and always has been.

I'm hoping that people can hear the album and just be like, “You know what? This is a real person. This is not a product."

What were some of the musical references that you were pulling from on this album?

I felt a really natural pendulum swing from my last album. I was trying to make this sort of very perfect pop, which I still love to do and probably will want to do for the rest of my life. But I was also very curious about creating something that felt very alive and not too contrived or controlled. I was listening to a lot of music that felt like it was coming more spontaneously than being too considered. Everything from Arthur Russell to the Avalanches to the Radio Dept. to Cornelius. It was a bit all over the place. Then, of course, I'm forever listening to Janet [Jackson]. Again, all of these things being true at once. I'm hoping that people can hear the album and just be like, "You know what? This is a real person. This is not a product."

Even some of the vocal delivery — the choice to do the singles in spoken word. I feel like you got to hear these different sides of your voice that maybe weren't as fully on display on the last album.

Every album, I think, I find a new part of my voice that I'm exploring. For example, on this album, the two singles are sort of the main two spoken moments, but there was something really interesting about that to me. With a song like "She's the Best," with such a grand statement, the idea of singing this sweet melody with such a sweet message gave me the ick. I was like, I want this to feel genuine. I don't want anyone to feel like they're being patronized. I need to deliver this in the most genuine way possible, and that felt like spoken to me.

But then there's also moments where I'm really exploring my falsetto on this album in ways that I haven't felt confident enough to do in the past. Or I'm really singing out on a few songs, as well, and pushing myself. I recorded a lot of the vocals at home for the first time and learned how to produce my own vocals. I think that really freed me a lot as well, because when I'm home alone, I can sound absolutely dreadful trying something that I've never tried before. There's no embarrassment there. So, yes, I'm definitely exploring all aspects of my voice on this album.

It's very, very nice when you write an album that you can sum up in a single sentence, and this is not that.

This album also goes in a lot of different directions. I'm thinking of songs like "Le Boy" and "Sex Star." There's all of this yearning and romanticism. Where were those feelings coming from for you?

The yearning and romanticism was coming from yearning and romanticism. I have been single for a long time, and I'm 31. My older brother has two kids and a beautiful wife, who's like a sister to me. I grew up in Perth, in Australia. There's not really much of an entertainment industry there. It's the most isolated city in the world. So in my head, that is who I am, you know. And then everything that has happened post has almost felt like a layer on top of what lies underneath, the "real me."

I have had moments where I'm so thrilled with how things have gone in my work life, but there is so much more to me and so much more that I still desire. Sometimes it almost feels like one cannibalizes the other, and I'll have these moments where I'm like, "What am I doing? I need to service this other part of my life more than I do and respect it more than I do." I don't know how people have both, and that has left me feeling, I think, a little bit — I don't want to say hopeless — but definitely in my feelings. I knew that I couldn't just write the side of the album that I'm more comfortable people seeing, which is the idea of connection and music and dance and whatever. I love that. That's 100% true, but it's not the whole story. Then it's this other side of the album that you're talking about.

Was there a freedom or any sort of fear in putting that out there on this part of the album?

For sure. I mean, it's definitely less sexy. It's very, very nice when you write an album that you can sum up in a single sentence, and this is not that. It's super, super vulnerable. It's the kind of thing where you don't want to admit to anyone like, "Oh yeah, I'm like, kind of lonely." It's just not a nice thing to acknowledge. But I've always written my music very diaristically and I use it as a form of catharsis, so I knew that I had to just go for it.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-598.title: BTS frontman RM is showing his art collection. Fans are flocking to see it
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-598.author: Chloe Veltman
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/07/nx-s1-598.text:
RM of BTS performs during the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Festival in Las Vegas in September.

The gift shop at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art is expecting a huge rush over the next few months.

"This is hands down the most inventory that we've ever front-loaded for an exhibition," said the museum's director of retail, Shane Salvata.

The reason for the merch overdrive is K-pop band BTS — or, more specifically, its leader, RM. The popstar is showing art from his personal collection for the first time at a museum, and SFMOMA is packed with fans clamoring to see the works and buy souvenirs.

Among those there for RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me on the sold-out first day of previews are Bay Area twenty-somethings Joi Karra and Bre Walker.

The pair met each other a few months ago at one of the BTS-themed events Walker organizes locally. Karra similarly takes BTS fandom seriously. The college student has a side hustle making BTS-inspired pins and other accessories.

"I love art and museums," said Karra. "I've been to SFMOMA many times before."

"I am not an artsy person," Walker said. "This is my first time actually coming to an art museum. And it's all because of Nam-joon."

She's talking about Kim Nam-joon — RM's real name. (RM was once known as "Rap Monster," but has gone by the shorter version for almost a decade.)

BTS's global fanbase — collectively known as ARMY, an acronym for "Adorable Representative M.C. for Youth" — came up with a verb to describe the lifestyle associated with the K-pop star's interests: "Namjooning."

"Just doing all the things that Nam-joon loves doing as well," Karra said by way of definition.

Visiting museums and collecting art are key to Namjooning. RM began doing these things nearly a decade ago.

His passion for painting and sculpture inspired some of his songs, such as "Yun" (about the 20th century Korean abstract artist Yun Hyong-keun) and "Still Life" (inspired by seeing still life paintings by 19th century European masters in museums). His art collection focuses heavily on works by Korean artists, from ancient times to the present, including Yun, Kim Whanki and Chang Ucchin.

RM, who is 32, worked with two SFMOMA curators on RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me. Most of the works on display are part of RM's collection, with a few additions from SFMOMA's collection — like a Mark Rothko painting, side-by-side with one by Yun.

Left, Untitled 1986-90 by Yun Hyong-keun; right, No. 14, 1960 by Mark Rothko.

Chang Ucchin, Road, 1986.

Chusa Kim Jeong-hui, Orchid Paintings and Writings, 19th century, Joseon dynasty.

At a press briefing ahead of the opening, RM said it was important to him to make sure the art on display resonated with today's audiences.

"There were two questions that mattered most to me," RM said. "One was, does it move me, really? And another was, right now in 2026, does this artist and does this work still have something to tell us?"

RM also described the exhibition as "a pretty long introduction" to himself. Fans like Walker and Karra, whose encyclopedic knowledge about RM goes far beyond the introductory phase, see it as a way to get deeper inside his head.

"I really just want to be a part of something that RM treasures, and find out why he treasures it," said Walker.

"I want to know why he chose certain pieces and what they mean to him," Karra said.

At the museum, Walker and Karra try to make sense of several large abstract paintings in a section of the show entirely dedicated to the yellow-brown color umber.

"He's got this obsession with umber and its relation to earth," Walker said. "He's a very 'nature' guy."

"And I think he likes abstract pieces because they can be interactive, like meditative," added Karra. "You can look at one of these and get lost in it. Even though there isn't much going on, it invites your imagination to fill in the pieces.

Blue-Umber '79-C6 by Yun Hyong-keun is featured in the exhibition.

"In one of the eight sections of the show, titled "Friendscape" and focused on the natural world and animals, the pair are struck by a cluster of seven delicately-carved waterfowl made out of wood by an anonymous, long-dead Korean artist. "That has to allude to BTS somehow because of the seven members, right?" said Karra. "Most winters, he likes to make little snow ducks — seven of them for the members. So I think that might be a bit of a nod to that."

"We're on the seventh floor, and there are seven ducks," said Walker. "It's all symbolic."

Not all of the art on display is as easy for these fans to interpret. A rock with the word "candy" engraved on it in orange by the contemporary multimedia artist Wonwoo Lee leaves Walker and Karra baffled. Fittingly, it's in a section titled "I don't know … but I like it."

"Yeah, I don't know either," Walker said with a shrug.

Wonwoo Lee, Candy Valley.

There's a lot to take in, with more than 170 works on display. Progress through the museum is slow-going, not just because of the crush of people packed into the galleries, but also because Karra and Walker keep bumping into other fans. Many of them stop to chat as well as share their own artworks inspired by RM and BTS.

"Would you like a bookmark?" said museumgoer Sara Larios, offering Karra and Walker her miniature works of art. "I made these from fabric from my mom's sewing cupboard."

Larios said she had flown in to see the exhibition from Zambia. She said RM has motivated her to spend more time experiencing art. "Back in Zambia, on RM's birthday, I organized Zambian fans to go to the National Museum on an art walk," she said.

As a maker of BTS-inspired art herself, Karra said she is touched by the various little gifts other fans have pressed into her hands. "It's so cool that these are not just freebies. A lot of them are handmade. It's like you're making art in response to the art," Karra said. "So I think that's beautiful."

For Walker, the experience of visiting a museum for the first time in her life has been eye-opening. "I guess I always thought that you had to have some kind of knowledge when looking at art to resonate with it. But after going through it, I feel like I could get something out of museums," she said. "I'll be back."

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/g-s1-1418.title: Tim Bernardes: Tiny Desk Concert
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/g-s1-1418.author: Anamaria Artemisa Sayre
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/g-s1-1418.text:
Anamaria Artemisa Sayre

Credit: Photo: Elizabeth Gillis/NPR

From jazz and Tejano to norteño and ska, 'El Tiny' returns with a takeover from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 for Latin Music Month.

"I will no longer carry the weight and burdens that aren't mine," Tim Bernardes coos behind the Desk. The Brazilian singer-songwriter sits easily in the poetry of the cosmos and his country, but communicates every emotion with tangible complexity.

Like so many great Brazilian artists, Bernardes translates hope and tragedy with the airiness of a butterfly but the precision of a surgeon. And beyond that, he integrates all of that sadness into his guitar. It's a wonder to watch him quite literally dance as he strums.

By the time he's moved the feeling through, a revelation bursts through his chest: "I came here to live," he chants. There is always melancholy at the outset — Brazilians call this saudade — but in his confrontation and curiosity, Bernardes finds joy on the other side.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/05/nx-s1-593.title: With a voice as vast as the ocean, Beth Taylor has arrived
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/05/nx-s1-593.author: Tom Huizenga
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/05/nx-s1-593.text:
The up-and-coming Scottish mezzo-soprano's debut recital album is a compelling collection of songs about the sea.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

A deep-voiced mezzo-soprano from Scotland named Beth Taylor may be flying under the radar now, but not for long. NPR's Tom Huizenga reports that with Taylor's debut solo album, she's poised to become the talk of the opera world.

TOM HUIZENGA, BYLINE: Beth Taylor's voice is almost shockingly beautiful, especially when unspooling long lines of text, like in this old Irish tune.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "MY LAGAN LOVE")

BETH TAYLOR: (Singing) And often when the beetle's horn hath lulled the eve to sleep.

HUIZENGA: Taylor's stock has been rising since she wowed judges at the Cardiff Singer of the World competition in 2023, where she was a finalist. Last month in London, she made her Royal Opera House debut to glowing reviews. And now, another debut - her recital album called "The Deeps Have Music."

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "SEA PICTURES, OP. 37: NO. 4: 'WHERE CORALS LIE'")

TAYLOR: (Singing) The deeps have music soft and low, when winds awake the airy spry.

HUIZENGA: The album title comes from this song by Edward Elgar. It's part of "Sea Pictures," the cycle which anchors the smartly curated recital of songs about the sea. Almost every proud British mezzo-soprano has a go at "Sea Pictures." The lyrics might seem dated with craggy coves and elfin imagery, but Elgar's sweeping music endures. And no one today offers the majesty and dramatic insight of Taylor, whose version sets a new standard. Her voice seems to plunge as deep as the oceans she sings about.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "SEA PICTURES, OP. 37: NO. 1: 'SEA SLUMBER SONG'")

TAYLOR: (Singing) Hush thee, O my child. Hush thee.

HUIZENGA: Taylor is a 32-year-old native of Glasgow and labels herself a mezzo-soprano. But I'm not sure that's true. Her sturdy, burgundy colored lower register sinks comfortably into contralto territory. It's a plush instrument used with intelligence, especially her phrasing, every line delivered with utmost care without being fussy.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "THE BREAKERS: NO. 2, 'TWILIGHT'")

TAYLOR: (Singing) A long, long strange cry that reels through the glade (ph).

HUIZENGA: That's music from "The Breakers," written by Cameron Biles-Liddell for Taylor and her empathetic accompanist, Hamish Brown. Along with new music, this album spotlights neglected composers, especially women, like the forgotten Parisian Hedwige Chretien. Her set of songs for "The Water's Edge" are at least a hundred years old, but they sound tailor-made for Taylor, who savors the open French vowels and subtle coloring.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "PETITS POEMES DU BORD DE L'EAU: NO. 2, LA BARQUE")

TAYLOR: (Singing in French).

HUIZENGA: Blessed with uncommon vocal beauty, the intellect to back it up and now a thoroughly satisfying debut album, Beth Taylor is at the doorstep of stardom.

PFEIFFER: The album by Beth Taylor is called "The Deeps Have Music." Our reviewer is NPR's Tom Huizenga.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "SEA PICTURES, OP. 37: NO. 2: 'IN HAVEN. CAPRI'")

TAYLOR: (Singing) Closely let me hold thy hand. Storms are sweeping...

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/05/nx-s1-590.title: DJ_Dave's 'Hardcore Software' is code you can dance to
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/05/nx-s1-590.author: Kai McNamee
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/05/nx-s1-590.text:
DJ_Dave writes and performs dance music with code. Her debut album, Hardcore Software, combines tech optimism with the open source spirit of an algorave.

(SOUNDBITE OF DJ_DAVE SONG, "HARD REFRESH")

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Sarah Davis first learned what an algorave is when she was in art school and saw a flyer for an unconventional music class.

DJ DAVE: And it was just like, music plus coding equals algorave. And I was like, music and coding? I love that. Like, I'm going to take the class.

PFEIFFER: That introduced her to something called live coding. It's where performers write code live on stage to create art.

DJ DAVE: It just, like, combined these, like, niche interests of mine that I almost didn't even know I had that much of a passion for. And I was just like, this is so perfect. Like, I need to make this my whole life.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "HARD REFRESH")

DJ DAVE: (Vocalizing).

PFEIFFER: Now, Davis writes and codes dance music under the name DJ_Dave. Her debut album, "Hardcore Software," is out now. NPR's Kai McNamee reports.

KAI MCNAMEE, BYLINE: It starts with just a few lines of text.

DJ DAVE: So I have kick, colon, space, S, open parentheses.

MCNAMEE: DJ_Dave taps out some code, and you get a drum pattern.

DJ DAVE: I'll write, like, X...

(SOUNDBITE OF TAPPING KEYS)

DJ DAVE: (Imitating musical beat).

(SOUNDBITE OF DJ_DAVE SONG, "GIVE IT 2 ME")

MCNAMEE: She adds a vocal sample and, with a few more keystrokes, tells the computer what bass notes to play.

DJ DAVE: E1, exclamation point, three. B1...

MCNAMEE: Those lines of code make up the track "Give It 2 Me."

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "GIVE IT 2 ME")

DJ DAVE: (Singing) What I want, I told you that I need your love, so give it to me. Running up my currents, I can't get enough of this feeling, baby.

MCNAMEE: DJ_Dave uses an open-source program called Strudel to make music. About a year ago, she started sharing her process online, livestreaming her coding sessions and posting video clips.

DJ DAVE: I would just, like, start a song and stream the process of making it and, like, ask people questions, let people give me suggestions. Like, I would, like, make, like, a chorus of a song and then be like, OK, I'm done and, like, move on. So with this album, I was like, I kind of want to finish these projects out.

MCNAMEE: The album is the result of a lot of collaboration. She'd get input from her social media followers, gauge the audience when she'd perform a new track.

(SOUNDBITE OF DJ_DAVE AND SWITCH ANGEL SONG, "ALWAYS LEARNING")

SWITCH ANGEL: Every time we sit down to work together, we just have, like, a million ideas.

MCNAMEE: Live coder Switch Angel worked with DJ_Dave on the track "Always Learning." After playing a show together in Los Angeles, the two of them hopped on a computer to jam.

SWITCH ANGEL: It's like, oh, I have this idea. Let me take over the keyboard. And it's just, like, leaning over and just, like, typing, you know, in the Terminal. And then she's like, oh my gosh, but what if we did this?

(SOUNDBITE OF DJ_DAVE AND SWITCH ANGEL SONG, "ALWAYS LEARNING")

MCNAMEE: Switch Angel is also one of the creators of Strudel, l the program DJ_Dave uses to make music. She says Dave finds new and creative ways to visually present the code.

SWITCH ANGEL: You know, she's got that mind for, like, fashion and design. We're always, like, learning from each other.

MCNAMEE: In a way, that idea of always learning from each other is core to the album.

DJ DAVE: It feels like it goes along with, like, the open-source nature of live coding in general. Like, I'm like, I don't gatekeep any part of my process. I tell people, you can go on my TikTok and, like, steal my song. Like, (laughter) it's right there. Like, the code is right there.

ALEX MCLEAN: It's like a real kind of ecosystem. It's just, like, a free flow of ideas.

MCNAMEE: Alex McLean has been live coding since the early 2000s. He's one of the artists who helped to build the live-coding community by writing and sharing software, hosting events.

MCLEAN: Events which were just based on making parties for people to dance to code. And that's when I coined this word with my friend - algorave - like a portmanteau of algorithm and rave.

MCNAMEE: And algorave usually features coders writing dance music live. And there's a visual element, which can be a projection of the coder's screen, graphics generated by another live coder.

MCLEAN: I'm working in this world of abstract symbols, but there might be people dancing in front of me. I might feel the subwoofers, like, shaking me while I'm writing the code. It's a really kind of strange full-body experience, really.

(SOUNDBITE OF DJ_DAVE SONG, "AIRGLOW")

MCNAMEE: The first time DJ_Dave went to an algorave in New York, she was blown away. She doesn't remember who the artists were, but there were three coders...

DJ DAVE: Wearing full-blown suits, button-down, tie, jacket and a headset, and they were just cooking. It was, like, so cool, and the music was really high energy, really cool the whole time. And it was so exciting.

MCNAMEE: You can still feel that excitement in her music today. DJ_Dave describes "Hardcore Software" as a hopeful album.

DJ DAVE: I feel like I have, like, obviously a lot of, like, tech pessimism in the modern landscape of things, but I also consider myself just, like, generally an optimist. And there's, like, a lot of things about tech that really excite me. And that was kind of, like, just how I felt making this album. I wanted to make songs that, like, make you feel like the future can be good.

MCNAMEE: DJ_Dave's "Hardcore Software" is out now. Kai McNamee, NPR News.
