https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-598.title: Medium Build's Nick Carpenter on growing up and finding his way back to fun
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-598.author: Henry Larson
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-598.text:
Nick Carpenter, who makes music as Medium Build, talks about his new album "King of Having Fun" and finding moments that make him feel like a kid again.

ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST:

I found out about singer songwriter Medium Build through his dog. This summer at the Newport Folk Festival, I was at a charity baseball game. And as I watched one songwriter after another strike out, this dog ran up to me.

NADWORNY: I learned that his name was Stanley and that he belonged to Nick Carpenter, who makes music as Medium Build. So during the festival, I went to Nick's set, and I thought, thanks, Stanley.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "HOME DEPOT")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) He's at the Home Depot, buying all the stuff to build a house. He's storming into plumbing, talking with a toothpick in his mouth.

NADWORNY: Nick Carpenter's new album is called "King Of Having Fun."

NICK CARPENTER: So you met Stanley without me.

NADWORNY: That's right.

CARPENTER: Were you - OK, I - he - you know, he wanders off, so I can't always record what he gets up to, but I love that he was making a good impression.

NADWORNY: (Laughter) Wait, does he wander off and make friends for you? Like, is that a thing?

CARPENTER: I mean, I have three dogs. Stanley is the newest. He's a puppy. He kind of made a splash at Newport. He's opening doors in my career. I mean, this is - I knew it - I knew he was doing good stuff, but this is proof.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "HOME DEPOT")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) Hey, Steve, been building walls since you were seventeen. Hey, Steve, hammered watching movies on repeat. Hey, Steve, is this how you pretend to keep it cool in a world so mean?

CARPENTER: That's why I love the dogs. They remind me - you know, you wake up, and you think it's all about you. And they're like, hey, I have needs. And that's good for me. I actually do better when I'm working. You know, I'd rather be serving than be served.

NADWORNY: Ooh. I want to go back to a pretty big decision that you made. You were in Tennessee, studying music. You were engaged. You ended the engagement. You left school. You moved to Alaska. Why Alaska?

CARPENTER: My older brother moved there when I was 18, and we grew up, you know, in a pretty suburban, kind of, like, conservative bubble of North Atlanta. And I had never been anywhere. You know, I'd been on, like, mission trips, but I'd never really traveled. And so when my brother moved to Alaska, I went up for six months when I was 18, and it changed my entire worldview. First time I'd seen non-Christians, like, living in community.

And, like, the suburban bubble I grew up in was so one thing. To go and find out that the world was completely spinning for 1 million other types of people, I was just like, oh, my goodness. This, like, godless, lawless, beautiful, like, connected-to-nature place will help me find whatever is really clicking inside of me.

(SOUNDBITE OF MEDIUM BUILD SONG, "PERCEIVED")

NADWORNY: You have a song on the new album called "Perceived." I wonder if we could listen to it together.

CARPENTER: Yeah, let's do it.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "PERCEIVED")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) Overall, its been a decent winter. I've been laying low, working on my heart. But the crippling weight of my own thoughts keeps me up at night.

NADWORNY: Tell me a little bit about that song and what was going on when you wrote it.

CARPENTER: Winters in Alaska are really grounding. I remember that lyric of, like, everything's going as normal, right? Like, the town hall is still happening on Twitter. Like, the day cook at the diner is still outside smoking a cigarette after his shift. Like, everything in Anchorage is so kind of, like, dependable. Everything's going fine. It's been a decent winter. But my brain, my brain is the enemy here - like, not the darkness, not the snow, not the temperature, not my job not giving me enough hours. It's like, my brain is the thing, like, the crippling weight of my thoughts.

And this career that's happening for me - now I'm on stage, and these people want to know all my thoughts and want to hear all my takes. And I just - I had a mental breakdown. I really - I had, like, a panic attack on stage. Here's all my dreams of playing music. And then you get in the business of making yourself consume, right? Like, I objectify myself. I made a product of myself. Like, you become the suit. You become the evil guy selling you. And that's a hard thing to realize.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "PERCEIVED")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) And I don't want to be right. And I don't want to be wrong. No, I don't want to be anything at all. And I don't want to be here.

CARPENTER: Do you really want this? Do you really want this? What would you give? Would you give up your privacy? We give up your friendship? Would you give up your relationships? That's been my biggest struggle with the career thing is trying to go back to being the servant.

NADWORNY: That's got to weigh on you.

CARPENTER: We're at a rehearsal studio, and I'm in this office, and there's all these posters of these bands, Santana and Aerosmith and Guns 'N Roses. Yeah, Steven Tyler in 1985 - like, could he go anywhere? I don't know, but now he's fine. No one's going to stop him. No one cares. We have this idea that these people are gods or demigods. No one cares.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "PERCEIVED")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) And I don't want to be right. And I don't want to be wrong. No, I don't want to be anything at all. And I don't want to be here. But I don't want to be gone. No, I don't want to be perceived. No, I don't want to be perceived. No, I don't want to...

NADWORNY: I want to listen to a little bit of "King Of Having Fun."

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "KING OF HAVING FUN")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) I used to be the king of having friends over Friday night, pet snake, black light, DVD, PSP, GTA, GTG. Sick stuff, stuffed crust, Mountain Dew, sugar rush. Now and then, now and then, I wish I could go back again.

NADWORNY: Wow. There is a whole childhood in that song - pet snake, video games, stuffed crust pizza - oh, the best.

CARPENTER: I remember when stuffed crust came out. That was a crazy day.

NADWORNY: Have you done anything lately that gave you that feeling of being a kid again?

CARPENTER: It takes more now. I've been riding my bike a lot this year. And, like, the other day, I rode my bike downtown for a concert, and everyone, when I walked in, was like, are you OK? Like, what are you - are you kidding? And I don't know why it just felt like - it felt so playful. It was like, there's something childlike about being like, these two wheels will get me there.

And you know when the wind gets in your hair and the salt and the - like, almost feels like you're flying, where if you're not in pain - if, like, you're not thinking about the pain or you're not thinking about your lungs, like, you just almost feel like you're just floating? That's kind of...

CARPENTER: ...Why it's so sweet for me

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "KING OF HAVING FUN")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) And half of me is fully jealous of the younger me, a kid who saw the light in little things, hadn't had a reason yet to run.

NADWORNY: Nick Carpenter makes music as Medium Build. His new album is "King Of Having Fun." Thank you so much for talking to me, and thank you to Stanley.

CARPENTER: Wow, he really got our friendship off the ground here. Thanks, Stanley.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "KING OF HAVING FUN")

MEDIUM BUILD: (Singing) But half of me wonders if I'll ever get the chance to be...

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-594.title: The record-breaking, genre-melting, career-redefining evolution of Miranda Lambert
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-594.author: Jewly Hight
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-594.text:
In the two decades since her breakthrough single, the revenge-fueled "Kerosene," Lambert has achieved just about every kind of success an artist can in the country music industry. With her new album, Crisco, she says her sights are set on new levels of stardom.

Miranda Lambert came out of the gate with a me-against-the-world attitude. In the video for her 2005 single "Kerosene" that established her early image, the scrappy, young Texas singer-songwriter wore a steely-eyed glare and a fitted "Mama Tried" tank top, in tribute to Merle Haggard, as she played the role of a woman exacting revenge on her cheating lover by torching his property.

In a way, she was also sending a message to the country music industry: No one should expect cheerful compliance from her. "Forget your high society," she sang caustically, "I'm soakin' it in kerosene."

Last year, Lambert marked the 20th anniversary of "Kerosene" on the Academy of Country Music Awards show by reframing her song as a duet with Ella Langley, an ascendant superstar a decade-and-a-half her junior. Sporting a replica of Lambert's tank top for the occasion, Langley swapped lines with her predecessor. The two of them sang the hook in unison, leaning into each other and playfully bumping hips. And all the while Lambert, no longer registering as such an intractable individualist, couldn't stop grinning.

She's had even more to smile about in 2026, not least because she had a hand in helping Langley create the biggest song of the year in any genre. "Choosin' Texas" is a throwback ballad that nods to early '80s Urban Cowboy sleekness, and Lambert co-wrote and co-produced it. The massive country hit has also broken pop-chart records, to Lambert's delight.

In the well-appointed basement sitting room of her managers' offices just off Music Row, she took a moment to reflect on the boundless popularity of a song that registers as unambiguously country: "If this is what brings people to country music and they can stay a while and understand that we've been cool the whole time and they just figured that out, let's go! I love that."

Her own new album Crisco summons the sensibilities of past eras when, in a spirit of expansiveness, country music absorbed pop production techniques such as sleek, propulsive grooves and lush orchestration. "A country disco record," Lambert laughs, "that wasn't on my bingo card."

That may be a tossed-off line, but the tone of her delivery implies plenty. I've interviewed Lambert a number of times over the years, and had never heard her sound so relaxed and amused by the unlikeliness, at least on paper, of her own current career moves.

Continuity is one of country music's central values, and few of its luminaries have undergone the notable evolution that Lambert has, both as an artist and a citizen of the industry community, across the last two-plus decades. For years, Lambert was single-minded in her drive to succeed in the country mainstream while upholding her artistic standards, holding the line on her hard-edged approach of undiluted twang, wiry, rocking energy and salty wit. Gradually, though, she fine-tuned her approach enough to achieve her goals: winning over country radio, headlining arenas, and earning numerous Grammy, CMA and ACM awards, platinum sales and critical acclaim on the strength of her albums. She managed to become a superstar without shedding her riveting idiosyncrasies.

What didn't interest her in the slightest was pop crossover. But she did begin admiring the expanded musical reach of some of her iconic predecessors when she partied at a New York drag bar during World Pride in 2019 with her brother and his husband. "All they were playing was, like, Reba and Dolly and Loretta and all these remixes on the video screens, and everyone was dancing their ass off," she recalls. "I always say I want to be [like] them, but I haven't done that."

Lambert took the step of commissioning a Nashville producer named Jesse Frasure to remix one of her songs. Frasure, a veteran specialist in bridging country and pop who uses the DJ name Telemitry, transformed her modern honky-tonk number "Tequila Does" into a tropical house track.

That kicked off Lambert and Frasure's unlikely songwriting partnership. "I hate to call her ballsy," Frasure says at the suburban ranch-style house where he does much of his music-making, "but it's a ballsy move to do these kinds of pivots and work with somebody like me."

Lambert had always relied on guitar as her primary songwriting instrument, and had to get used to programmed tracks and loops. "I've started to love it, but 10-years-ago-me would be like, 'I'm not doing that,'" she muses, adopting an exaggeratedly stubborn tone.

During one of their writing days, she and Frasure invited Chris Stapleton to come over and join them in creating what became "A Song to Sing," a feel-good duet inspired by Kenny Rogers and Dolly Parton's early '80s classic "Islands in the Stream." "It feels natural," Lambert marvels, "which is kind of shocking to me, too. It's not 'three chords and cry in my beer' — that's my norm — or 'burn your house down.'"

She took to the post-disco soft rock feel so readily that she and Frasure explored further down that path, ultimately writing the rest of the songs for this new album, Crisco, except for its lone cover, Jim Croce's "I'll Have to Say I Love You in a Song." To guide them, Frasure created a playlist that he titled "Mirandapolitan." He pulls it up on the desktop computer in his studio, places his cursor on the 1975 Glen Campbell classic "Rhinestone Cowboy," and scrolls. "I really loved when country music was playing around with pop sounds and arrangements in the '60s and '70s, even early '80s. So you had a lot of Glen Campbell. You had even Marty Robbins, his later stuff playing with string arrangements, or Lee Hazelwood or Nancy Sinatra playing with kind of pseudo western disco moments."

"So it's not all countrypolitan," he goes on, "but some stuff we put on this list was just to kind of help us live in the melodic sensibilities in the chord changes of that era."

At Blackbird Studios, a top-flight Nashville facility where Lambert has recorded several other projects, Frasure made it part of his production duties to arrive early and install disco balls and colorful, swirling accent lighting. "I've never done that before," he emphasizes. "No one does that. You usually go in and it feels like a [regular] recording studio and you do your thing."

Lambert and Frasure each thoroughly enjoyed getting swept up in this aesthetically exacting creative process, one that yielded extravagant, silken textures, sweeping string arrangements and supreme polish.

One of Lambert's great gifts as a singer and songwriter is her mastery of tone of voice and inflection, her way with a wisecrack or a bit of vinegary, well-placed emphasis. But all of that listening to lush, vintage sounds shifted Lambert's attention towards a different aim: crafting romantic, wide-screen melodies she hadn't attempted before. "Not with this much intention and drama," she notes.

For Lambert, conjuring dance floor fantasies is, in part, a way to follow in the lineage of Dolly Parton and other female country stars by reaching out to her LGBTQ+ fans with this club-ready music. And like Parton before her, Lambert relishes the thought of inspiring drag performances. "If I make it into drag shows and I'm a staple there," says Lambert, "I feel like that's a different level of iconic, and I'm chasing it for sure." During CMA Fest this past June, she showcased some of her new songs at a rooftop Crisco Disco drag brunch, an event that shared its name with a storied NYC after-hours gay club of the '70s and early '80s.

In "Snakeskin Boots," the glistening, cinematic opener of the Crisco album, Lambert cast Langley opposite her in a glamorous, diamond heist scenario set in vintage Los Angeles. At the same time that Lambert's been retooling her aesthetic, she's also been helping Langley, her protégé in a loose sense, achieve a true pop culture breakthrough. Lambert contributed mightily to Langley's hit album Dandelion as writer and producer. And as Langley weathers the whirlwind that comes with its blockbuster single, "Choosin' Texas," topping the all-genre Billboard Hot 100 chart longer than any other song in history, Lambert's cheering her on. "I want to sit here at home on my porch with a glass of wine and FaceTime her wherever she is in the world and hear about all of her journeys," Lambert says of the younger artist, "because I went on some of those already — and I'm a little bit tired."

Having any sort of presence on the pop chart is as new for Lambert as dabbling in disco influences. "You don't get many firsts when you're 23 years in," she observes. "You just don't." At her career's midpoint, she's really gotten into assisting new artists — not just Langley — in finding their footing. Lambert signs rising Texas talent like Dylan Gossett to Big Loud Texas, the record label imprint she co-founded with close collaborator and fellow Texan Jon Randall, and packs her schedule with songwriting sessions for others' projects. "I didn't really have other artists writing songs with me," she observes about her early years in the industry, "or sowing into my life in a mentorship way. I feel like I'm supposed to do it."

Frasure, who's spent nearly a quarter-century working in the Nashville publishing world, has seen how rare it is for a big name like Lambert to embrace a supporting role. He explains that when a previously unreleased song by a country star shows up on another artist's album, it's usually "because something [they wrote] didn't make their record and one of the publishers is pitching the song around," he says. But Lambert has become one of the seasoned pros that he regularly calls on to do co-writes with newer acts. "The amount of intimidation if you write with a young person [who's fixated on the fact that] Miranda Lambert's in the room …" Frasure begins. "[But] she has the ability to make them feel comfortable. She doesn't speak over them. She doesn't make them feel steamrolled in some sort of 'I know more than you' way."

Which says a lot about Lambert's mentality these days. "I mean, I feel like I'm the same exact person," she chuckles, "just calmed down a little bit."

And not opposed to smoothing things out musically for a change.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/nx-s1-599.title: Wildfire smoke affects animals in unique ways. Scientists are trying to understand it
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/nx-s1-599.author: Ari Daniel
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/06/nx-s1-599.text:
Olivia Sanderfoot of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology is trying to understand how the smoke billowing off of wildfires is bothering birds — and what can be done to prevent that harm.

Olivia Sanderfoot stands on a flower-freckled hillside in Amherst in Western Massachusetts. She listens for a moment — and a volley of birdsong flutters forth.

An Eastern Wood-Pewee. A goldfinch. A downy woodpecker.

"It's just magical," she says with an air of reverence. There are birds foraging among the flowers. Fluffy fledglings are darting about, learning the ways of the world.

"Every day that I get to start birding is a good day," she says. "If you want to get the widest range of species and hear the most songs, you want to be out here in the morning."

For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.

Sanderfoot, a global change ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, knows that for the birds that live here, not every morning is this idyllic. Over the summer, this area was suffused with toxic smoke from distant wildfires in Canada. It's an increasingly common problem, even in places untouched by flames. Fire season is starting earlier, lasting later, burning more land — and as a result, producing far more smoke.

"Smoke can blow hundreds to thousands of miles away from that burn site," Sanderfoot explains. "That means that the footprint of a smoke event greatly exceeds that of any fire. How do birds deal with that?"

This is the central question animating Sanderfoot's desire to form a new field of study called "smoke ecology." The goal, she says, is to understand how the smoke billowing off of wildfires may be disturbing wild places and creatures — and whether anything can be done to prevent possible harm.

Sanderfoot's curiosity about how birds cope with smoke emerged in 2018 when she was living in Seattle and wildfires blazed in Eastern Washington. "The air smelled acrid," she recalls. "The city was just blanketed in this sickly yellow, gray haze."

She was told it was a one-time event — yet the same thing happened two years later.

"I remember walking outside and my eyes were just burning," Sanderfoot says. "And I thought, 'What on earth are animals doing? Are they OK?'"

An adult bluebird sits atop a nesting box containing its chicks at the Mass Audubon's Drumlin Farm Wildlife Sanctuary.

Very little was known apart from anecdotes — like the absence of birdsong or the arrival of droves of birds to a backyard, famished and parched.

"Smoke is a toxic soup of substances," she says. "It's not just about what [birds are] inhaling, which is inevitably bad for them. It's also about how the cues that they use to navigate their world are upended when it gets smoky outside."

To puzzle out what was going on, Sanderfoot realized that she needed to collaborate with researchers from a range of other disciplines, including conservation biology, statistics, ecophysiology, and atmospheric chemistry.

"Real-world problems don't map cleanly onto the same academic silos that have been set up for decades," says Tracey Holloway, an atmospheric chemist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the lead of NASA's Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team, and a colleague of Sanderfoot's. "We need to be tackling new problems with new partnerships."

For instance, in order to understand what birds are inhaling, one has to know what's moving through the air in time and three-dimensional space. "It depends on which way the winds are blowing," says Holloway, "what chemical processes are happening in the air, and also patterns of rainfall and where the emissions are coming from." The science depends on air quality monitoring, satellite data, and evermore sophisticated computer modeling.

Birds are especially sensitive to smoke in large part because of how they breathe. A human being has soft lungs that allow inhalation and exhalation of air. By contrast, birds have rigid lungs surrounded by a collection of air sacs that act like bellows, pushing air continuously through the system.

"This allows birds to take up about twice as much oxygen with each breath that they inhale compared to us," says Sanderfoot. "This means that they're vulnerable to all the other things that are in the air, too."

Morgan Tingley, an ecologist at UCLA, is another member of the burgeoning smoke ecology cohort. "What we're trying to do is getting smoke to be recognized as a disturbance in and of itself distinct from fire that is worthy of our concentrated attention," he says.

For much of his career, Tingley has studied wildfires — events with a clear start and stop, and defined borders. But the smoke produced by those wildfires can present its own unique set of problems, as it can spread far from the original blaze.

"Smoke is extremely hard to predict and it's highly variable," he says. "It can be there one day, one hour, and gone the next. Which means that it's hard to actually disentangle what its impacts are because you can't really control it."

This means that it's not possible to anticipate where smoke will appear, or when. Scientists also prefer not to subject animals to smoke intentionally.

So when it comes to studying wildfire smoke and birds, the trick is to gather data everywhere. To do so, the researchers rely on legions of amateur birders and professional conservationists and ornithologists across the country who are already on the ground collecting data when smoke happens to blow in.

One such individual is Pam Sowizral, the bird project coordinator at Mass Audubon's Drumlin Farm Wildlife Sanctuary in Lincoln outside of Boston. On a sunny morning in late August, she walks up to a bluebird nest box and gently raps on the outside.

Pam Sowizral is one of the legions of birders and conservationists across the country who are already on the ground collecting data about birds when smoke happens to blow in.

"Always give a little knock first," she advises quietly. "Let them know you're coming." When she lifts the side panel, she reveals two feathery puffballs huddled on a bed of pine needles. These baby bluebirds are the last of the season here.

Sowizral says that nearly every year for the last 20 years, three times a week in spring and summer, she and her volunteers check the bird boxes here and count the nests and the eggs and how many chicks fledge. They check when the weather's good, when it's bad (within reason) — and when the smoke rolls in.

"Those periods of time when the smoke was here, the air somehow felt a little different," she says. But "that didn't stop us from doing our usual monitoring of our boxes."

That's key. Nationally, counts like this one, which is part of Cornell University's NestWatch project, provide a portrait of bird activity and behavior before, during and after smoke events.

Two feathery puffballs huddle on a bed of pine needles in a nesting box. These baby bluebirds are the last of the season.

Sanderfoot of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology says she's using these kinds of observations, alongside observations of breeding behavior, to help her understand how birds are coping with wildfire smoke in a variety of places.

She's revealed three distinct strategies, depending on the species and the individual birds. They either hunker down and stay put, fly away, or shift their behavior — by not vocalizing as much or venturing out less often, say.

"This could be an attempt to mitigate their exposure," says Sanderfoot. "It might also be how they are forced to respond if they feel unwell."

In addition, she and her colleagues have observed that repeated exposure to smoke appears to impair the body condition of a variety of birds, leading to lower weight overall.

"They all respond in different ways," she says. "And we need to figure out what those ways are and how effective they are in order to design effective conservation strategies for a rapidly changing world."

This is one of Sanderfoot's top priorities: determining what might constitute what she calls smoke refugia for birds — safer spots where they can hunker down until conditions improve. "I want to know where birds are going when it's smoky," she says, "what resources they're seeking out, and what we could provide to help them during a risky time" — like water and perhaps shelter or food.

"I would like to be able to give people something they can do to help," she says.

Sanderfoot's personal experience with wildfires didn't end in Seattle. "I almost feel like the smoke is following me," she says.

In early 2025, she and her family fled the fires in Los Angeles where they were living at the time. And this summer, she watched as a blanket of smoke descended upon parts of the U.S., including Ithaca where she lives now, blowing off the remote Canadian infernos. She says she doesn't think it's a coincidence.

"Let's put it this way," she says: "We can expect that the future will be smokier."

It's a fact that's true for birds and people, which means that what Sanderfoot and her colleagues learn about smoke ecology may reveal a clearer way forward — for us all.

"By learning more about birds," she says, "I think we might learn something about how we can take care of ourselves and each other."

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/01/nx-s1-598.title: New rules for sharing the Colorado River start today
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/01/nx-s1-598.author: Alex Hager
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/01/nx-s1-598.text:
Environment Story Of The Day
                
                    
                    NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Oct. 1 is when new federal rules for sharing the Colorado River start. It's going to be messy and courts will likely have to weigh in.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Starting today, California, Arizona and Nevada will get a lot less water. That's because of new federal rules for the seven states that share the Colorado River. Those states are still scrambling to figure out how they'll bear the pain of those reductions, as KJZZ's Alex Hager reports.

ALEX HAGER, BYLINE: After 20 years under the old rules, the new ones reckon with an uncomfortable reality - there just isn't enough water in the Colorado River to supply the nearly 40 million people who've come to expect it. After years of failed negotiations between the seven states that use the river, the federal government is forcing Arizona, California and Nevada to take about 20% less. But how exactly they'll cut back is still an open question.

TOM BUSCHATZKE: So we want to make sure that all of the water users who are going to be impacted have all of their plans in place to deal with the cuts.

HAGER: That's Tom Buschatzke, Arizona's top water negotiator. His state is hit the hardest by the new cuts. So he's working with allies in California and Nevada on a deal to spread out the pain of the reductions. But even with federal money as an incentive to use less water, getting cities and farms to tighten their belts is easier said than done.

JOHN BERGGREN: That's the real challenge because that's - you're actually talking to people about using less water and getting cut.

HAGER: John Berggren is a researcher with the environmental group Western Resource Advocates.

BERGGREN: The people negotiating these agreements, they reached a kind of high-level agreement of here's what we're willing to do, and then they have to go back and shop it around their state and make sure they can get their water users on board with what they are tentatively agreed to.

HAGER: Also complicating things, Nevada sued the federal government over the new river plans, which slowed down talks about that three-state deal. Another potential lawsuit could complicate things further. Arizona has set aside $9 million to sue other states or the federal government over the river and says it reserves the right to take its water complaints to court. For NPR News, I'm Alex Hager in Phoenix.

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-598.title: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-598.author: Geoff Brumfiel
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-598.text:
A Valar Atomics microreactor is seen on a C-17 aircraft, without nuclear fuel, at March Air Reserve Base in California on Feb. 15. The reactor was transported from March Air Reserve Base to Hill Air Force Base in Utah.

A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed exclusively by NPR.

Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators.

In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts).

The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028.

Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands.

The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state.

"It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands.

"The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it."

In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company.

"We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added.

In a statement, Valar said it was committed to a public engagement. "No construction begins before permits and approvals, and the public process leads along our internal targets set the pace," the company wrote.

Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build.

Valar Atomics CEO Isaiah Taylor (right) and Energy Secretary Chris Wright (left) stand behind President Trump as he makes an announcement on American nuclear innovation on July 24. Valar has been both an advocate of reforming nuclear regulations and a beneficiary of changes made by the Trump administration.

Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft.

The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive.

At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip.

"Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd.

The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build.

Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032.

In its statement Valar said it was fully committed to giving the public a say. "This is home, and we've spent eighteen months answering our neighbors' questions before being asked. We'll keep earning that trust one answer at a time," it wrote.

But Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project raises even larger questions. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used."

NPR's Shannon Bond contributed to this report.

Contact Geoff Brumfiel on Signal at gbrumfiel.13

https://www.npr.org/2026/09/29/nx-s1-597.title: The race to protect Santa Rosa Island's rare, damaged Torrey pines
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/29/nx-s1-597.author: Kendra Hanna
https://www.npr.org/2026/09/29/nx-s1-597.text:
Environment Story Of The Day
                
                    
                    NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

In May, a fire damaged 80% of the trees one of the only two naturally-occurring groves of Torrey Pines in the world. The National Park Service is trying to help them recover.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

In May, a wildfire swept through a grove of rare trees on an island off the coast of California. Those trees on Santa Rosa Island, called Torrey pines, grow naturally only in two places. The fire not only damaged the trees but also made them more vulnerable to erosion. Now, with the possibility of more rain this winter due to El Nino, scientists on the island are racing to put protections in place. From member station KCBX, Kendra Hanna has more.

(SOUNDBITE OF WAVES CRASHING)

KENDRA HANNA, BYLINE: To get to Santa Rosa Island, you have to take an hours-long boat ride from mainland Southern California. Santa Rosa is part of the Channel Islands National Park, and it's full of beaches, grassy hills and island foxes. But for restoration ecologist Michelle Gados, what's most exciting are the plants.

MICHELLE GADOS: Yeah, I mean, it's incredible to see, like, some of these plants that occur out here and nowhere else on Earth. I think there's, like, a total of five that are - just occur on Santa Rosa, none of the other islands. So yeah, it's pretty special.

HANNA: One very special plant that grows here is the Torrey pine. It's a wide, twisty tree that sometimes grows sideways like a bonsai. Gados is with the California Institute of Environmental Studies, which works with the National Park Service on Torrey pine restoration. Here's how she describes them.

GADOS: Majestic. Magical. Gorgeous. Glorious.

HANNA: According to the National Park Service, the species is vulnerable to extinction. That's because its limited genetic variability means it can't adapt well to environmental changes like drought. Plus, they only grow here and in San Diego, which is why the National Park Service is so concerned about helping them recover from a wildfire in May. More than 24,000 Torrey pines live on the island, and Gados says the fire damaged a portion of them.

GADOS: Some could be completely consumed and black to skeletons and others are just partially damaged. Some are still retaining. It's just a big mixed bag right now at this point.

HANNA: The Park Service estimates that between 60 to 80% of the Torrey pines on the island could die from burns. But Gados says it might not be that many. Some of the burned pines have started growing new needles, which is promising. Unfortunately, the trees are now facing a new threat - El Nino. It could mean more heavy rain on the island that can erode the soil around the tree's roots.

GADOS: Previously, you know, we had inches of, you know, years of accumulated pine needles.

HANNA: But the fire burned all of those needles, leaving behind bare dirt.

GADOS: If you get some heavy rain events, it's going to disturb the soil. If you get too much too fast, then all that soil could, you know, slide down the slopes.

HANNA: That soil is important for the health of the trees, but it's also full of the seeds that could be the next generation of Torrey pines. The National Park Service is trying to address this in two ways - protect the trees and plant new ones. Gados and her colleagues are working on both projects at the island's native plant nursery.

GADOS: Let's just go step into the seed shack.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOOR CREAKING)

HANNA: We walk into a small shed that Gados calls the seed shack.

(SOUNDBITE OF PLASTIC RUSTLING)

HANNA: Cradled in Gados' palm, Torrey pine seeds look a bit like almonds. The restoration team will use them to propagate hundreds of new trees. They're also installing erosion protection.

(SOUNDBITE OF SCISSORS CUTTING)

HANNA: A volunteer cuts up hemp and jute nets, which will be rolled into long tubes and then nailed into the ground around the Torrey pine grove. They catch debris and slow the rainfall as it rolls downhill. Gados says she's optimistic about the future of the grove but will have to wait and see how the pines react to the challenges of this year. For NPR News, I'm Kendra Hanna on Santa Rosa Island.

(SOUNDBITE OF NAS SONG, "2ND CHILDHOOD")

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: South West News Service
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme

A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Rachel Savage and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.

Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.

Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.

In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.

Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.

Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”

The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.

Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize.

Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.

Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.

In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”

Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”

Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”

While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight.

“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”

Associated Press contributed to this story

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Rachel Savage and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday

Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.

This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.

The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.

Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.

He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).

Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.

He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.

Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.

Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.

After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.

The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.

The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.

“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”

The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.

Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”

North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Lucy Kassa
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again

As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.

Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.

The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.

Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.

Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.

“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.

“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”

In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.

Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.

“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”

Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.

“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.

The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.

Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”

Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.

Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.

An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.

* Names have been changed to protect their identities

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Mohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu

On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.

After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.

Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.

“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.

“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”

On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.

She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.

“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.summary: Marian Haji Abdi Guled's son, 7, was seriously injured in a US drone strike in Somalia. She had no money for surgery and was unable to afford it for 10 months. After investigation, readers from across the globe raised money for his surgery.

The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, to address court before a Mexican judge hands down verdict

A Mexican judge is expected to hand down his verdict in the high-profile murder trial of three men accused of killing two Australian surfers and their American friend in 2024.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in an alleged robbery.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States. The prosecution is seeking 150 years in prison for each of the accused.

The prosecution and defence were expected to present their closing arguments from 1pm Thursday (6am AEDT on Friday), after which the judge was expected to announce his verdict.

If convicted, the three will be sentenced on Friday.

Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, will address the court. Both travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 8 September.

Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his widow, Natalie Weirtz, will also participate in the hearing in a video call from the United States.

The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ alleged murders as “hell”.

“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.

Authorities allege the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.

Jesus Gerardo is accused of leading the alleged attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. His girlfriend was sentenced at a separate trial in November to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Victoria Bekiempis

Ousted Venezuelan president and Cilia Flores have been in jail in New York since early January

The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.

The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism”-related charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Charging documents at the time alleged that Maduro spearheaded a “corrupt, illegitimate government that, for decades, has leveraged government power to protect and promote illegal activity, including drug trafficking”.

Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them. CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.

The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly wielded untold horrors to suppress opposition and maintain their control.

Maduro, Flores and other Venezuelan leaders “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the just-released charging document said.

Maduro and Flores, the superseding indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”. They allegedly “developed and facilitated the systems which they and their co-conspirators used corruptly to amass immense wealth and power, rewarding allies with ill-gotten funds and terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence”.

Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”.

The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.

“One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.”

Maduro and Flores also put pressure on Venezuela’s judiciary to make legal decisions that supported their efforts to thwart opposition, charging papers alleged. When one official resisted, Venezuelan intelligence agents arrested and tortured their family members, charging papers stated.

“For example, one family member … was forced to drink latrine water; assaulted with tear gas in Victim-1’s cell; threatened that Victim-1 would be killed at gunpoint; and placed in a cold room known as the ‘Freezer’ in which a bright light was left on at all times of day and night and music was blared on repeat,” the superseding indictment said.

This official “ultimately … relented and blocked the opposition figures from running for political office”.

During another alleged torture incident, authorities allegedly abused the friend of a suspected opponent by “asphyxiating him with a bag, applying electric shocks to his testicles and knees, and kicking and beating him with a blunt object”, court papers said.

One torture victim, who was repeatedly interrogated, endured numerous threats “including that his daughter would be kidnapped and raped if he did not confess and name his supposed confederates”, court papers state. “On one occasion, interrogators produced women’s underwear, claiming it belonged to his daughter.”

Shortly after this indictment surfaced, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release in an already scheduled proceeding, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities.

Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population.

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

“I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.”

Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said.

Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lbs and lost two teeth since her detention.

“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest.

Flores wore dark jail scrubs during her court appearance. She listened to the proceedings with headphones through a Spanish-language interpreter.

The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, which is prosecuting this case, opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. Prosecutors have argued that Flores was a flight risk. Prosecutors also maintained that she had received appropriate medical care.

Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid on Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!”

After Maduro’s forced ouster, Trump worked swiftly to gain access to Venezuela’s expansive oil reserves. In August, Trump announced a new oil agreement with Venezuela – claiming that the US would have “majority” control over 65bn barrels of proven reserves.

Venezuela boasts approximately 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves – the largest in the world. The White House has tried establishing a consistent flow of Venezuelan crude oil to US refineries while boosting US investment into the country’s flagging petroleum industry.

Trump has faced mounting pressure over skyrocketing gas prices in advance of November’s midterm elections. Greater access to cheaper oil and broadened output could help lower costs.

A Guardian investigation found, however, that Trump’s proclaimed “biggest oil deal in world history” is likely to fail due to legal and logistical problems.

They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas. Venezuela boasts approximately 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves – the largest in the world.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Emma Loffhagen and Leyland Cecco in Toronto
