Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red

‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson

Where to start with: Anne Carson

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.

The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The Nobel prize, regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, is awarded for a lifetime body of work. The winner receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000).

Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had told Carson of the award on the phone shortly before the news broke. “She had time to tell me that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world. She has been a professor of classics at various institutions including Princeton, New York University and McGill University in Montreal. She is the 19th woman to win, out of 123 literature laureates.

Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986 and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.

Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.

In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize, for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.

The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, congratulated the poet on X after the announcement. “With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, adding that it was a “proud moment for Canada”.

David Leonard, the executive director of the Writers’ Trust of Canada, said: “Anne is such a brilliant writer. Her work is broad, but also extremely smart.” Calling Carson’s work “intoxicating”, he said her four-decade career had resulted in a peerless collection of poems and essays. “They’re beautiful, they’re smart, they’re true and they are humane. It’s exactly what we need in our writing.”

Carson’s work has attracted praise from fellow writers including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”

Anders Olsson, the chair of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel Committee for Literature, praised Carson for work that had “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”. He said: “This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.”

Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera.

Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avant-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.

In a Guardian review of Red Doc>, Sarah Crown wrote: “To engage so fluidly, so originally and compellingly, with a story first told more than 3,000 years ago, is astonishing: her ambition is one thing; the fact that it is so completely achieved is, frankly, something else.”

Much of Carson’s work has emerged from her fascination with language itself. The Swedish Academy noted: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” adding that Carson had identified the etymology of words as “the starting point for all her work”.

Asked why she continually moved between forms, Carson said in an interview: “Boredom, I guess. There is a restlessness. There are a lot of forms to try.”

She has acknowledged the difficulties that come with her experimental style. “[My work] does fall apart a lot,” she said in a 2018 interview. “It gets just too weird for anyone to care about reading, or else it gets diluted into a sort of parody of itself.”

Ira Wells, the president of PEN Canada, said Carson’s win felt “particularly significant at a moment in which Canada and Europe are strengthening cultural ties amidst broader global disruption”. He added: “On an aesthetic level, Carson’s verse vibrates on profound human frequencies, at a moment in which more and more language is formulated by machines.”

Carson has generally kept her personal life out of interviews. However, in an August 2024 article for the London Review of Books, she disclosed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.

Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.

To browse works by Anne Carson, visit guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.summary: The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Author is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jonathan Watts
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not led to success at polls

M
ore fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.

This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.

The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%.

But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won.

Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.

If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.

Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest.

He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (690 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs.

Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Flávio’s brother, Carlos, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies.

Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff.

As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns.

That inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target.

Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife.

Lula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chafe at environmental limits.

Tied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalry between the US and China and amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries.

In the past two years, Donald Trump has ripped apart environmental regulations in the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right.

Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election.

That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election.

Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself.

This article was amended on 7 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly said that Jair Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate. It was Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, Carlos, and his stepmother, Michelle, who were elected.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Legislation is an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted death

Canada’s federal government said on Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death.

Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying (Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the justice minister, Sean Fraser, said his government would indefinitely bar people whose sole condition is mental illness from accessing the program. He said that while there was no “perfect consensus” on this issue, upcoming legislation reflected the “correct” approach.

Earlier this year, a government committee concluded the government should expand access to Maid and should “indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from eligibility for medical assistance in dying”. That report also flagged the need for “increased and more equitable access” to mental health services.

Canada’s Maid laws, drawn up after a 2015 supreme court decision, initially only permitted those who are terminally ill to be eligible for the procedure. But in 2019, a Quebec judge ruled that restricting access to those who had a “reasonably foreseeable death” was unconstitutional, forcing federal lawmakers to amend and expand the existing laws.

In 2021, the law was updated so adults could receive an assisted death if two doctors confirmed an irremediable physical condition causing immense suffering that cannot be relieved. Given the uncertainty surrounding mental illness, lawmakers in 2021 initially put a temporary exclusion in place for people who suffer solely from a mental illness. They renewed that pause in 2023 and 2024.

According to the latest government figures, the vast majority of Maid deaths – 95.6% – involved people whose natural death was considered “reasonably foreseeable”. Only 4.4% were cases in which death was not considered reasonably foreseeable. Those include people with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and incurable neurological disease that can causes profound disability and immense suffering.

The Liberal party’s legislation is also an effort to ward off a private member’s bill that would amend the section of the criminal code covering Maid so that “a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition”.

Advocates for expanding Maid to include mental illness alone say the current rules violate their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. Fraser acknowledged to reporters that a federal case – led by the advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada – challenging the government’s previous decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness could affect the upcoming bill.

Fraser said lawmakers would also work to decriminalize what are known as advanced requests, effectively giving people suffering from some illnesses such as Alzheimer’s the chance to choose Maid before their illness deprives them of the capacity to consent.

At present, Quebec is the only jurisdiction that permits the use of these requests. Fraser gave no specifics on the timing of the legislation but said that provinces will decide whether to provide advance requests. While the province of Alberta has already said it will not permit advance requests, the justice minister said the bill attempts to ensure “the doctors who provide the services will not be treated as criminals for doing so”.

In Canada, Crisis Services Canada can be contacted at any time on 1.833.456.4566, or via text on 45645 from 4pm-12am ET. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Under current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Responding to a Guardian report that revealed thousands of tonnes of fuel was transported to Russia, Seoul said it was investigating the cases

South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.

The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.

Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.

Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”

Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.

Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.

“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.

The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.

It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.

The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.

It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.

The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.

The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.

An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.

On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.

Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.

Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

Seoul, which has also been at loggerheads with Ukraine since Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, on Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Kyiv.

“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. “The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”

Government says it is ‘checking additional information’ about the loading cases reported by the Guardian. In July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market

Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.

Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.

The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.

Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.

Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%

The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.

Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.

The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries. They are suspected of violating anti-monopoly law. They have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires and

The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.

The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.

“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.

Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.

Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.

The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.

The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.

The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth.

Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”

He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.

A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.

The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires. Indonesian government accused of ‘gross negligence’ in class action suit over wildfires. Case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.

Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.

In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.

The airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.

Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.

The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.

In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.

Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.

Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa.

The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.

After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.

US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.

After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.

“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.

China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.

The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.

It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.

Reuters contributed to this report

China opened what it said was a joint ‘ support and training center’ at Ban Keun on 29 September.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Flydubai attack investigation widens as alleged hijacker’s training in New Zealand scrutinised
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Eva Corlett in Auckland and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne

New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Hammami, an Omani national, had allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air, the United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said. Israeli and other officials in the region suspect he originally planned for such an attack in July, but postponed it.

The New Zealand police assistant commissioner, Michael Johnson, on Tuesday confirmed the man was in the country on a student visa for 175 days, from 30 November 2018 to 23 May 2019.

“Police can confirm the co-pilot was in New Zealand to complete a portion of his flight training for a UK-based company, no longer operating in New Zealand,” Johnson said in a statement

The police are now investigating his time in the country, Johnson said.

New Zealand joins multiple countries scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted alone.

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree, RMIT University in Melbourne confirmed.

On a now deleted social media profile believed to belong to Hammami, the then student appears in a selfie with other teenagers in a shopping centre food court in Melbourne’s CBD.

The UK’s Telegraph reported on a post on a now deleted X account that appears to be linked to Hammami that described his years studying overseas as “the golden years of my religious commitment”, and claimed he became less observant when he returned to Oman.

On Wednesday, Australia’s peak Jewish body, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, called for a thorough investigation of Hammami’s associations in the country.

“We have seen over the years the availability of extremist literature in religious bookstores, the presence of preachers of hate and violence and the capacity for those living in Australia to fall under the sway of recruiters and nefarious street preachers,” the council’s co-chief executive, Alex Ryvchin, said in a statement.

“We have to understand who associated with this [alleged] terrorist, who influenced him and what vestiges of his murderous ideology remain.”

The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who also trained in New Zealand for a time, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.

In a phone call on Saturday with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation. Police confirm he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Jonathan Barrett Business editor
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Firmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.

A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.

“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”

Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.

But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.

Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.

The lack of demand means Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.

The polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.

This prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.

The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.

Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going to use retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.

The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.

The anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, who has spent time in prison for insider trading, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Donna Lu
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’

A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe.

Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does in months or years. These mysterious pulses were first discovered in 2007 and have puzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have an alien origin.

In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”.

The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record.

The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope (JWST).

Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”.

Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”.

There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field.

“Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said.

More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”.

Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen.

“[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said.

This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe.

Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists who first discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”.

Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes.

Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].”

The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.

It is believed to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded. The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed. It is thought to be more than double the previous distance record.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Queensland literary awards: ‘stunning’ debut inspired by segregated shantytown wins top prize
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Sian Cain
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Lenora Thaker wins $30,000 prize for ‘a work of state significance’ for The Pearl of Tagai Town, which draws on her family’s history in Cairns-Malay Town

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

A “stunning” debut novel described as “unambiguously and distinctively Queensland” has won the $30,000 top prize at the Queensland literary awards (QLAs).

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Meriam and Wagedagam author Lenora Thaker won the Queensland premier’s award for a work of state significance for her historical novel The Pearl of Tagai Town, which was inspired by her ancestors’ lives in an unmapped shantytown known as Cairns-Malay Town. The town once housed Indigenous Australians, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, Malaysian and Sri Lankan residents who had been segregated from the white population; it existed from the late 1800s until the late 1950s.

The QLA judges praised Thaker’s “accessible and deeply enjoyable” book for its “vivid sense of place”.

Sign up for our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning

“Warm, richly drawn characters and an innovative integration of Ailan languages come together in a rich, cohesive whole, bringing new insight and fresh imaginative life to a far north Queensland community. The Pearl of Tagai Town is a stunning debut novel,” the judges wrote in a joint statement.

The winners were announced at a ceremony on Thursday night at Brisbane Powerhouse, as part of Brisbane writers festival.

Claire Thomas won the $15,000 fiction category for On Not Climbing Mountains, which follows a woman on a trip in Switzerland, who distracts herself from grief with research on famous names who had connections to the country.

The $15,000 nonfiction prize went to Find Me at the Jaffa Gate: An Encyclopaedia of a Palestinian Family by Australian-Palestinian writer Micaela Sahhar, about how her family’s story was shaped by the Nakba, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel during the country’s founding in 1948. Sahhar won the same category at the Victorian premier’s literary awards in February.

The $15,000 children’s book category was won by Once I Was a Giant by Zeno Sworder, which has also won book of the year at the Australian Book Industry awards and the children’s category at the Victorian premier’s literary award. Illustrated and written by Sworder, the book tells the tale of a tree transformed into a pencil that then writes its own story.

Julianne Negri won the $15,000 young adult category for her book The Belly of a Wolf, Helena Pantsis won the $15,000 short story category for her collection Mother Salad and Eunice Andrada won the $17,500 poetry category for her collection Kontra.

The $15,000 people’s choice category was won by Sita Walker’s debut In a Common Hour, a novel that takes place across a single hour at a state high school. Walker has been a teacher for more than 20 years, and currently teaches English at a high school in Brisbane’s south-east.

Founded in 1999, the QLAs were previously known as the Queensland premier’s literary awards until 2012, when they were abolished by then premier Campbell Newman. Queensland’s literary community intervened to keep the awards alive.

The QLAs were administered by the State Library of Queensland from 2014 until 2025, when the awards were embroiled in controversy over the arts minister John-Paul Langbroek’s intervention to stop the library awarding a $15,000 fellowship to First Nations author K A Ren Wyld, over a social media post about the dead Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar.

Wyld said she had posted the comment in an “emotional moment”, and that her winning manuscript had nothing to do with Gaza.

Twelve QLA judges resigned in protest of Wyld’s treatment, leading to last year’s awards being delayed. Langbroek eventually handed their management over to the Brisbane writers festival from this year.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ben Smee
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Court hears police attended Wood’s Victorian home over a similar allegation about three years ago, but Snezana Wood had not complained then out of ‘fear of retribution’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The wife of former Bachelor star Sam Wood told police she “thought she was going to die” after he allegedly choked and assaulted her, a Queensland court heard on Thursday.

The court also heard that police in Victoria had attended Wood’s home in relation to a similar incident about three years ago, but that his wife, Snezana Wood, had not wanted to make a complaint at that time out of “fear of retribution”.

Sam Wood, a 46-year-old wellness influencer from Melbourne, was denied bail in a Queensland court on Thursday and will be held in custody indefinitely awaiting trial, after police argued his behaviour was “escalating” and that he posed an unacceptable risk.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Wood appeared in court via video link from the Maroochydore police watch house cells, where he had been held for about four days. He was arrested at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast on Sunday and charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.
 In outlining the prosecution case, police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris said the brief of evidence included a triple zero call made by a family member and photographs of Snezana Wood’s injuries.

Grigoris said Snezana Wood was supportive of the charges proceeding.

Sam Wood’s lawyer has indicated the reality TV star will fight the charges.

The court heard that Snezana Wood alleges she was choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”.

“She articulates the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” Grigoris said.

“She thought she was going to die.”

Grigoris said Snezana also detailed a previous matter in Victoria “being of a similar nature” and “involved choking”.

Sam Wood denied that any previous incident had taken place in Victoria.

Grigoris said there was body-worn camera footage of police attending his home and a police report in relation to that incident.
 Grigoris said Snezana Wood “did not make any criminal complaints on that occasion, she was in fear of retribution of the defendant.”

Grigoris also raised concern that Sam Wood, during his police interview, minimised his part in the alleged offending, and minimised the injuries suffered by his wife.

“He’s essentially victim blamed,” she said.

Sam Wood’s lawyer, Matthew Cuskelly, sought bail and said his client denied the allegations. He cited a psychologist’s report that said Sam Wood was suffering from “severe depression”.

“He ought to be given the opportunity to engage with mental health professionals,” Cuskelly said.

“And also try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment.

“Ultimately, as all families have, there was problems. And my client had been enduring the hardship of attempting to quarantine those problems from his family for some period of time. It was agonising.”

Cuskelly cited a psychologist’s report that describes ‘the difficulty that my client has been enduring in respect of the deterioration of his psychological state”.

“His depression is regarded as extremely severe.”

Cuskelly said Sam Wood had no prior criminal history and if granted bail would reside in Victoria with his father, Andrew Wood, who attended the court in support of his son.

Acting magistrate Janelle Boegheim said she was not satisfied by the defence argument that the case against Sam Wood was weak.

“The strength of the evidence against the defendant is … relatively strong at this juncture.”

Boegheim said it was likely the charges, if proven, would attract a term in prison.

Sam Wood was stood down by his own fitness empire, 28 by Sam Wood, on Monday, a day after he was charged.

“We have all been shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood,” said Mark Watkin, the group’s acting chief executive.

“We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties.

“Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.”

He is due to face court again on November 23.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: NSW police commissioner made last-minute bid to hold closed-door hearings into Sydney anti-Herzog protest
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Penry Buckley and Jordyn Beazley
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Police watchdog says Mal Lanyon’s timing in raising the issue was ‘regrettable’ and led to delays

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales police commissioner made a last-minute bid to hold hearings into Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest behind closed doors, delaying the inquiry, the police watchdog has revealed.

The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) has said that its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall, launched after widespread allegations of police brutality, would go ahead this month with a mix of public and private examinations, saying the timing of issues raised by police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was “regrettable”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Lecc launched an investigation after the protest on 9 February, during which numerous protesters – and 10 officers – were injured, including demonstrators in their 70s and 80s. Viral video footage showed police punching multiple protesters, and grabbing Muslim worshippers while they undertook their sunset prayers.

Thirty people were charged in the months after the protest, but four have since had their charges dropped. More than 20 of those charged are due to face a joint hearing next July.

In a decision made public on Thursday, the Lecc chief commissioner, Peter Johnson SC, revealed that legal representatives for Lanyon had indicated for the “first time” on 9 September that he wished to be heard on the issue of public and private examinations. The bid was made less than two weeks before the public hearings between September and November were due to start. Some hearings were also expected to be heard in private.
 “The timing of these issues being raised by the Commissioner of Police is more than regrettable given its impact on the orderly progress of the investigation, the preparation for examinations and the efficient and effective use of public resources by both the Commission and the NSWPF and the associated cost and disruption flowing from the delay,” Johnson said.

Johnson said the start date of public hearings, 21 September, was subsequently delayed to “a date to be fixed” to allow a private hearing for submissions on the issue.

Lawyers acting on behalf of Lanyon submitted that Lecc’s opening address and the examination of witnesses should occur in private and not be livestreamed. They argued that the Lecc Act does not have the power to hear “broad ranging open submissions” and said Lecc should not take the “unconventional approach of hearing opening submissions in public part way through an investigation that is already underway”. 
 But Lecc argued that it does have the power to decide when public examinations are appropriate. The counsel assisting submitted that public examinations were necessary because “there was already significant information concerning the events of 9 February 2026 in the public domain, including footage of use of force by police” and that senior police officers had advanced in public an “official narrative of what took place”. 
 “Public comments made by senior police increase the need for independent scrutiny,” the commissioner wrote.

The counsel assisting had pointed to specific features of the investigation as reason for why only private examinations were not appropriate. This included the “significant public concern” after the protest, including in parts of the Islamic community in Western Sydney.

On Thursday, the watchdog said its inquiry into the protest would begin with a public address by counsel assisting on 19 October, followed by five weeks of private hearings. Lecc expects senior officers will then appear at public examinations.

It said its Operation Makalu inquiry would analyse the use of OC spray, as well as the “improper use of arrest powers and the police use of force” at the protest. It will consider police planning ahead of the protest and “any opportunities for improvement in the policing of protests”.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

In his decision, the commissioner determined that private examinations would be held on “issues of fact” while public examinations would be held to deal with systemic issues, but only after the private examinations have been held.

In September, Palestinian Australian Eyad Shadid launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall. He alleged in his statement of claim that NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.

In a statement, NSW Greens justice spokesperson, Sue Higginson, described the push to hold hearings in private as “an extraordinary attempt by the police to suppress the public examination of allegations of serious misconduct by uniformed police officers, and to prevent public scrutiny of the political decisions and command structures that led to police violence against protesters”.

At a NSW parliamentary inquiry in May, Johnson said police had become “overly defensive” in response to requests for information in its investigations, describing the relationship between the agencies as “difficult”. He said the Lecc had received a record number of complaints, more than 800, as part of its investigation into the Herzog protest.

In a statement following Johnson’s comments, NSW police said it “complied with the requirements of the LECC Act in a cooperative manner”.

NSW police said in a statement it acknowledged the decision to hold private hearings and awaited the findings.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: French ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Education minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across France

High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education system in the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured.

Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise.

As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads.

Eliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.

The education minister, Édouard Geffray, told TF1 television on Thursday night that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to about 100 high schools identified as having particularly acute teacher shortages “between tomorrow and Tuesday”.

Geffray said he would also authorise the recruitment of “several hundred” new teachers. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would propose amendments to the 2027 budget to “translate some of the students’ demands into concrete measures, particularly regarding teacher replacements”.

Students earlier said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, the president of one high school students’ union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.

Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest, over teacher shortages, long school hours and dilapidated buildings, would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table”, the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.

According to an Elabe poll ​for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.

The education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the country’s high schools were at least partly open.

But more than 71,000 protesters took to the streets on Thursday, the interior ministry said. The demonstrations, backed by many teachers, parents and unions, involved further clashes with police around some school barricades in Paris. In Rennes riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.

A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened ​to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.

after newsletter promotion

Over the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.

At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers have been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days.

The government on Wednesday suspended the use of stun grenades by police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.

The protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investment in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.

The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.

Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighting the damage to schools and calling for parents ⁠to foot repair bills.

Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Thousands march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis

About 20,000 people took part in a march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her flat in the capital a fortnight before her death triggered mass protests over Spain’s housing crisis.

The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis before her death in hospital on Wednesday night.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election, to be held on 29 November.

Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”.
 Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.”

For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home, fending off three eviction attempts before the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.”

Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.”

Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.”

He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now, there were 44 people a day being forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.”

The Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat.

“Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said in a post on social media. “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.”

Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office.

Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”

after newsletter promotion

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences.

“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.”

The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office.

PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday to veto attempts to hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silence was thwarted by opposition parties.

Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmen would have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa, while one commentator had opined that “Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction” to become a leftwing saint.

At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with one even suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved. Another wrote: “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”
