https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell and Anna Bawden
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
England-focused mental health review returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system

Explainer | What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?

Analysis | No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real

The NHS in England is heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.

The stark warning was made in a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

It found there was an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and urged ministers to toughen the regulation of the private clinics to which many people are turning because they cannot get assessed quickly by the NHS.

The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.

The review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.

The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.

The evidence shows that sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles, the 607-page report found.

“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.

The report’s conclusions may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.

Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London, dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes” who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.

He lamented that an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”

The explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity has left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms, Fonagy said. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than were doing so in 2019. Another 254,000 people were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total number waiting to more than 800,000. Almost all – 90% – had been waiting for at least three months.

The number of six- to 11-year-olds being diagnosed with autism has also soared. It jumped 20-fold to 4.58% between 2000 and 2025 and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years, from 0.1% to 4.06% – a 40-fold jump. And the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years and more than 15-fold in 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively.

While 4 million children already suffer from “high psychological distress’’, if current trends continue, that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report warned. The number of under-18s who self-harm could also rise from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.

The exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition, Wessely warned.

The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.

The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.

The 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.

Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.

Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61% of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57% had ADHD symptoms.

The report said their needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health backed Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who received care.

“Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime,” said Dr Ronny Cheung, its officer for health services.

The NHS moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations in putting together the forthcoming mental health strategy, which is due by the end of the year.

In her response, she promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care. She has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.

She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”

She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated but did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.summary: Report led by Prof Peter Fonagy into sharp rise in demand for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions. Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services, report says. Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Nine in 10 school heads who responded say inspections still ‘negatively affected’ staff mental health

School inspections in England continue to damage the mental wellbeing of teachers and senior leaders, according to a survey commissioned by Ofsted that casts doubt on efforts to reduce the stress caused by inspectors’ visits.

The independent survey of school leaders who had undergone the revised inspections since last year found that 88% said it had “negatively affected” the mental wellbeing of school staff, including 29% who said it affected them “a lot”.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

School leaders called the results a “damning indictment” of Ofsted’s attempts to reform after a coroner’s finding in 2023 that an Ofsted inspection contributed to the mental health deterioration and death of headteacher Ruth Perry.

The Guardian reported last week that education secretary Lucy Powell wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after hearing complaints that the new format was stressful and damaging to teachers’ mental health.

Martyn Oliver, Ofsted’s chief inspector, said: “The data published today shows that we are on the right track. We are inspecting first and foremost in the interests of children and maintaining high standards, while at the same time improving the experience for the hard-working professionals in our nurseries, schools and colleges.

“I know that workload and wellbeing in education continue to be challenging, and I don’t take that lightly. We will keep listening to feedback from professionals and parents alike as we continue to improve what we do.”

But Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “It is extremely serious that the health of so many educators is being undermined and we do not understand how [Ofsted’s] chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver can then say the system is on the right track. This is clearly not the case.

“The feedback that we receive from our members shows a devastating toll on wellbeing and several have told us they will leave the profession before undergoing another Ofsted inspection. These are highly experienced and resilient professionals who will be lost to the education system.”

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the wellbeing and workload findings “should stop everyone in their tracks”. He urged Ofsted to release the full survey data rather than a summary.

“Ofsted is once again trying to put a positive spin on a truly terrible situation, showing the profession why it cannot be trusted,” he said.

“The evidence is clear that the framework is still creating unacceptable levels of pressure, workload and stress. It is a damning indictment – certainly not a vindication.”

Fewer than one in four schools agreed to be surveyed after their inspections, leading the authors, IFF Research, to note that its findings had limitations.

Ofsted highlighted the results from all categories, including childminders and further education providers, showing that six out of 10 respondents said their inspection would help them improve.

More than three-quarters of those inspected under the new approach said it had been conducted respectfully, collaboratively and empathetically, while a similar proportion said the inspections “successfully identified” their best elements.

But Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, described the overall results as “rose-tinted,” and added: “Lucy Powell has indicated a readiness to review.

“We want to see a new system that is more supportive, but also fair and effective. It is what the profession is crying out for.”

Nine in 10 school heads who responded say inspections still 'negatively' affected staff. Ofsted chief inspector Martyn Oliver says the data shows that we are on the right track.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Aletha Adu and Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Contest seen as test of Andy Burnham’s ability to unite Labour voters amid threat from Green party’s Zack Polanski

Polls have closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a test of whether Andy Burnham can unite Labour’s voters or whether Zack Polanski can peel off support from the party’s progressive flank.

Labour is seeking to retain Keir Starmer’s former north London seat, where he won a majority of more than 11,000 votes in the 2024 general election.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The byelection is seen as a measure of the political landscape under Burnham, almost three months into his premiership.

It is a significant first electoral test for Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, as part of a wider battle for younger leftwing voters who became disillusioned with the party under Starmer’s leadership over issues such as housing, the climate crisis and the war in Gaza.

Polanski has sought to run an energetic campaign involving thousands of activists, leaving the Green party conference early after his speech in an attempt to prove he and the Greens are a serious rival to Labour, despite the latest polling.

The Greens are hoping to reproduce their byelection victory in Gorton and Denton in February where they overturned a Labour majority.

However, the political landscape has shifted since then. Shortly after their byelection win in Greater Manchester, YouGov polling put the Greens on 21%, a few points ahead of Labour.

But the latest YouGov survey put the Greens 16 points behind Burnham’s Labour, which was on 27%. The poll came as Burnham proposed a more ambitious pitch to progressives at his first Labour conference as prime minister.

Holborn and St Pancras has a large number of students, younger voters and renters, with almost half of residents aged between 18 and 34, while about 45% were born overseas.

Polanski has argued that electing him would increase pressure on Labour to deliver more radical policies, including stronger rent controls, greater action on the climate crisis and public ownership of Thames Water.

But the leader of the Greens has faced questions about his own authority and was accused of being unable to articulate his thoughts on motions that became policies at his party’s conference.

In an interview with the Guardian last Friday, Polanski described the contest as “probably 50/50” and that it was “really on a knife-edge” while also insisting his leadership did not depend on victory.

Asked whether losing the byelection would undermine his position, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.”

Senior Green figures privately fear a defeat could severely damage his reputation amid concerns the party’s increase in members has not translated into an advantage in campaigning.

Labour has fielded Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in Britain as a child refugee after her family fled civil war in Somalia.

She has emphasised her longstanding connections to the area, presenting herself as locally rooted, and with experience of community work, homelessness and housing policy.

The closing days of the byelection campaign were overshadowed by a row within the Green party after members voted at their conference to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813 despite opposition from four of the party’s five MPs.

Polanski, who is Jewish, left the conference early to campaign in north London and did not participate in the vote.

As polls closed on Thursday, Burnham said the Green party’s Zionism motion was “completely wrong”.

Speaking to journalists on a trip to Berlin, the prime minister said it showed “terrible judgment on behalf of the Green party” and “shouldn’t be supported in any way, shape or form”.

The Labour leader called on Polanski “to say that it will be reversed and it won’t be Green party policy”, adding: “In my view, all political parties in the UK should do everything they can to support the two-state solution between Israel and Palestine.”

The byelection result may provide some insight into whether Burnham’s recovery in national support is translating into Labour’s inner-city strongholds, and into whether the Greens can continue to attract younger and progressive voters.

It will also offer a test of Polanski’s argument that the Greens can put pressure on the government from the left, even as Labour seeks to reclaim voters it lost under Starmer.

Polls closed at 10pm on Thursday and the result is likely to be announced between 2:30am and 4am on Friday.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Andy Burnham's byelection is seen as test of his ability to unite Labour voters. Green party's Zack Polanski Polls have closed in Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Burnham succeeded Keir Starmer in July as Labour leader in north London.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Curtis Flowers, US man wrongfully imprisoned for 22 years, dies aged 56
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Flowers, tried six times over 1996 murders of four people, faced execution before supreme court tossed his conviction

Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the US supreme court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died. He was 56.

Flowers’ family confirmed that he died on Wednesday at his home in Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told the Associated Press on Thursday.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers’ legal team.

Flowers was 26 when he was arrested several months after the July 1996 shooting deaths of four people inside a furniture store in Winona, Mississippi.

At the time, prosecutors described him as a disgruntled former employee who sought revenge against the store’s owner because she fired him and withheld most of his pay to cover the cost of merchandise he damaged. Nearly $300 was found missing after the killings.

Flowers was tried in the killings six times. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the high court’s 7-2 decision in 2019 that the removal of Black prospective jurors deprived Flowers of a fair trial.

During the sixth trial in 2010, Flowers was sentenced to death. There were 11 white jurors and one Black juror who considered the case after district attorney Doug Evans struck five Black prospective jurors.

Flowers remained in prison for six months after the supreme court ruling because he was still under indictment. He finally was released in December 2019 after a judge set bond.

Mississippi dropped charges against Flowers in September 2020.

“Today, I am finally free from the injustice that left me locked in a box for nearly 23 years,” Flowers said in a statement. “I’ve been asked if I ever thought this day would come. I have been blessed with a family that never gave up on me and with them by my side, I knew it would.”

He was sentenced to death in 2010 after a jury struck five Black prospective jurors. He spent 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the US supreme court threw out his conviction and death sentence.

Agents surrounded the man and child in his car before firing multiple rounds, according to Zohran Mamdani

A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in New York City on Thursday afternoon, according to the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

Early reports indicated that agents had surrounded the man and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds, the mayor said in a statement on Thursday evening. The child was physically unharmed, according to Mamdani.

The individual who was shot was conscious and taken to a hospital, the NYPD said in a brief statement.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Thursday evening.

The shooting took place at roughly 4pm in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx. The NYPD said they were not on the scene at the time of the shooting.

“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani wrote in an X post. “I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city.”

Witness video appeared to show several agents in the middle of the street in the aftermath, with one armed and another restraining a man on the ground, the New York Times reported. The City Reporter, a local news outlet, said video showed chaos after the shooting, with a crowd gathered and NYPD officers appearing to carry a man into the back of a vehicle.

Kathy Hochul, New York’s Democratic governor, said in a short statement that she had been briefed on the shooting, writing: “We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why.”

Mamdani expressed outrage in his post, saying: “I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities. Our thoughts are with the injured New Yorker and his family tonight. We are praying for his recovery. Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Hegseth says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Nidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December

Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad would carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.

Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.

Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.

In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.

But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.

The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in his second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five states in the United States allow for firing squads – Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah.

Abroad, Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.

Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Thousands turn out to welcome weary USS Lincoln sailors after record-breaking deployment
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Amanda Ulrich in San Diego
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Military families admit ‘mixed emotions’ as aircraft carrier finally returns to San Diego after grueling stretch at sea that took severe toll

USS Lincoln arrives at San Diego base – live updates

By 4am on Thursday, the sky still pitch black, 19-year-old Pvt Grayden Monroe and his mom had already arrived to the naval base in San Diego, California, the very first military family members huddled on a set of metal bleachers overlooking the dark water. They were waiting for Monroe’s 21-year-old sister to step off the USS Abraham Lincoln, the embattled aircraft carrier that has been at sea for the better part of a year.

Monroe, a soldier stationed at Fort Campbell, was wearing his army uniform for the occasion. “I hope she’s proud of me,” he said of his sister, “and I hope she knows damn well that I’m just as proud of her.”

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

As the sun rose over Naval Air Station North Island, thousands of people flooded on to the base for the USS Lincoln’s long-awaited return. The atmosphere was like a de facto festival, with a live band, performers on stilts, therapy dogs, handmade signs, giant cutouts of sailors’ smiling faces. People cried, laughed, screamed with joy.

When the Lincoln appeared in the middle distance around noon, rounding the corner past downtown, cheers erupted from around the bay. Sailors flanked the edges of the ship in uniform, waving to the crowd and making phone calls to loved ones. Below American-flag bunting, rust stains were visible on the sides of the carrier. The massive, city-like ship had finally reached land.

Military families and friends had longed for this moment for months.

The Lincoln first left San Diego last November, with an expected return date sometime in the spring. But as the US and Israel launched a war with Iran, the aircraft carrier was diverted to the Middle East, extending the deployment for the roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard for a then-unknown amount of time. The Lincoln’s deployment ended up spanning 321 days, including 264 consecutive days at sea without a port call, a record in modern naval history, the Department of Defense said.

For months, sailors have reported hazardous living conditions onboard the Lincoln: shortages of food and basic supplies, a spate of suicide attempts and a general sense of deteriorating mental health and declining morale. The reports immediately set off a political firestorm, with Democratic lawmakers calling for an investigation, even as Donald Trump and the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, sought to downplay the situation. The US navy confirmed last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group had attempted suicide since the start of the deployment.

After the Lincoln’s return home was officially announced in August, it took the carrier almost two long months to get back to San Diego, making a brief port call in Thailand and then tracing a route east across the Pacific Ocean.

But on the naval base on Thursday, the scene wasn’t completely euphoric.

An infant in a stroller was positioned with a sign that read “I have waited 234 days to hug my daddy!” The baby’s mom, Brenda Rivas, said she was five months pregnant when her husband deployed. He missed the birth, and the first time he was able to see his daughter over a video call was six months later.

“It’s mixed emotions,” Rivas said. “I’m more sad than excited because he did miss so much.”

And an emotional reunion on the pier wasn’t in the cards for everyone, especially for the many military families that are spread across the country.

Dawn, a mother who requested that only her first name be used because she feared retaliation from military officials, anxiously watched a live feed of the ship’s arrival from a small town in Texas, her eyes “glued to the TV” for hours. Her son is a service member on the Lincoln.

“I couldn’t sleep. Tossed and turned,” she texted early on Thursday morning. “I’m feeling so happy for my granddaughter to see her daddy!”

Imagining that the scene in San Diego would be too chaotic, Dawn is instead flying to California next week to reunite with her son and his five-year-old daughter. She’s planning to help him “get everything back in order”: make sure his house is clean, whip up some home-cooked meals.

Over the past 11 months, one thing has been keeping her son sane and tethered to a reality off the ship, she said.

“He said that all he could think about was his daughter,” she said. “That’s what got him through all this.”

As the sailors floated around the globe for the past year, their relatives sat at home and waited, wondering what could be happening thousands of miles away on the ship.

Dawn’s son sent her updates via WhatsApp whenever he got service. This past spring, he told her, the conditions were dire.

“Like 3rd world …” he wrote in a message. “We couldn’t get soap or toothpaste.”

He sent her pictures of mold dripping down the walls, of dwindling daily rations: sectioned cafeteria trays with only a few of the compartments full. Two hard-boiled eggs and watery soap. A scoop of grits and a few limp noodles.

The extended deployment, long working hours and supply shortages seemed to be taking their toll across the ship, especially on the younger sailors, Dawn said. Nearly half of all active-duty military members are 25 years old or younger. She could imagine her son, who’s now in his 30s, being like a father figure to some who were really struggling. The reports of some sailors attempting to jump overboard were true, her son told her.

“My son’s a tough kid, so he could take it,” she said during a phone interview last week. “But for those 19-year-old kids that go on a first deployment, it’s scary for them.”

One of the worst parts for Dawn was the unsolicited commentary, on Facebook and Instagram and in real life, saying that even if the ship’s conditions were rough, the sailors probably just couldn’t hack it.

“That’s exactly what people were saying about the people in the military: that they’re babies, and that back in 1969, or whenever they were [serving], it wasn’t like that,” she said. “I couldn’t even read the comments. I’m still upset about it.”

Those sentiments even came from Trump, who told reporters this summer that the Lincoln’s deployment was “not nearly long enough”.

That type of remark changed everything about how Dawn viewed the president.

“I like President Trump. I voted for him. But I don’t really think he understands,” she said.

“Let his son be out there, just for a couple days, and see how it goes. If he really would tolerate that, if his son could really take it – I’m sure he couldn’t.”

In a brief press conference on the naval base Thursday, Capt Daniel Keeler, the commanding officer of the Lincoln, answered several questions from journalists about the consistent reports of poor conditions on the ship.

“[Most of those issues] occurred in March and April, while we were engaged in active combat operations against a very determined foe,” he said. “Immediately once combat operations started, we were, I would say, a little bit challenged to get the normal fill of things. But I had enough food, I had all the supplies I needed to conduct combat. We never missed a mission. I also never missed a meal.”

Meanwhile, Hegseth again played down those same issues on Wednesday, saying instead that “a few folks in the media” aimed to “turn” the ship’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”

Keeler focused most of his comments this week on the success of the mission.

“For most of my sailors, this was their first time away from home, their first deployment, their first experience with combat,” he said. “I understand the anxiety that might have caused, but I can tell you this: our team of professionals on the ship led every single one of those sailors through that experience. And the great majority responded how sailors always do, with honor, courage and commitment.”

Now that the Lincoln has returned home after an unexpectedly grueling and high-profile deployment, sailors are left to determine what’s next.

Some of those next steps are immediate. Monroe, the 19-year-old, said his family was excited to take his sister out to dinner tonight – but then she’s back on duty tomorrow.

After the trials of the past year, a more serious takeaway for Monroe is his sense of what could happen during a deployment, and just how tough that isolation could be.

“When shit hits the fan, everything just kind of sucks. Especially when they’re out there on their own. It’s really just you and the guy next to you,” he said. “So getting stuck there and being able to push through something like that – I don’t think I could have done it, honestly.”

His sister, he added, was “probably one of my biggest role models”.

For Rivas, the wife whose husband missed their daughter’s birth, she’ll have to switch from being a single parent for a year to parenting as a team again.

“It’s gonna be different, teaching him how to take care of her,” she said. “But she’s good with people, so I’m sure she’ll adjust.”

For Dawn, as a Texan and someone who says she still wouldn’t vote for a Democrat, she walked away from the USS Lincoln experience with a very different outlook on Trump. The majority of those in her small town and in her family are lifelong Republicans, but the controversy surrounding the Lincoln has cut jaggedly across traditional party lines.

“It’s really hard for me because I just wanted [my son] to be OK. And I just, I don’t know …” she said, her voice trailing off over the phone. “I’m just not real happy with President Trump right now. At all.”

As for what her son thinks about the fraught deployment, she said, it’s probably too soon to tell how this experience will shape his life and career. But it has put some things into perspective.

“He just wants to live for his kid,” she said. “He wants to see his daughter grow up.”

Production of Pawn Shop allowed to go on despite concern about disruption and portrayal of immigration crackdown

A Daily Wire film production that appears to re-enact elements of Renee Good’s killing has been allowed to continue filming in a rural Montana town.

Production of Pawn Shop, the conservative media company’s upcoming movie, was temporarily halted earlier this month after residents of Livingston complained about inconvenient road closures, as well as the film’s portrayal of the Trump administration’s ongoing immigration crackdown.

The project, which reportedly stars Danny Trejo and Harvey Keitel, follows an ICE agent’s arduous effort to escape an angry mob seeking to free an immigrant he has detained, according to its logline.

During a Livingston city commission meeting last week, several residents took the podium to air a slew of grievances about Pawn Shop’s presence in the town. Little to no public notice was given, they said. Street closures were impeding access to a food pantry. The sound of gunfire was unsettling.

In one video of the shoot that surfaced online, a female protester can be seen driving a beat-up car into a flock of law enforcement agents, knocking one officer down, as another fires his weapon. Then, the car abruptly lurches back.

That scene drew backlash – and protesters – over its resemblance to an ICE agent fatally shooting Renee Good in January.

“A production can hijack our downtown with hired guns and re-enact mob beatings while blocking the entrance to a beloved non-profit,” area resident Bex Frucht said at the commission meeting. “They are simulating a highly controversial murder in our streets.”

The project’s filming permit was temporarily revoked amid the outcry, before being reinstated with new parameters around noise and any depictions of violence.

The Daily Wire co-founder Ben Shapiro blasted the city commission for deferring to what he described as “radical leftwing protesters”.

“When you put together a film it takes a lot – a lot in terms of production. You have to get the permit, which we did. You have to get everybody there, which we did. Every single day costs you hundreds of thousands of dollars to film. All these people decided to show up and disturb the filming,” he said in a video posted to X on Wednesday.

Livingston city commissioner Melissa Nootz did not immediately respond to an inquiry about Shapiro’s remarks.

Pawn Shop was originally set to wrap up production in Livingston on 10 October, according to town officials. It’s unclear if the temporary shutdown has pushed back that date.

Kaya Patten-Fusselman, executive director of the Livingston Food Resource Center, voiced support for the new conditions attached to the filming permit in a Wednesday statement posted to social media.

“This was about access. Having blocked access to the entrance of our one-way parking lot didn’t and doesn’t work for some of our clients,” Patten-Fusselman said. “I’ll keep working with the city so the next non-profit, business, or neighbor gets notice well before a street has multi-week closures.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump hosts awards party for tech billionaires, almost as if he doesn’t care about ordinary Americans
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Amid a cost-of-living crisis, with US midterms a month away, the president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords – again

H
e stands accused of being out of touch, enriching himself and his family, building a lavish White House ballroom and, with elections looming, neglecting the hardships of the voters who brought him to power.

Time for Donald Trump to show he still has the common touch? Nope.

On Thursday, the US president went to a building he named after himself, dished out awards to the world’s richest person – his old frenemy Elon Musk – and other tech billionaires and even received an award that belonged to his late uncle.

Given Trump’s gold fetish, the event was naturally entitled the Golden Age of American Innovation summit, which will be news to the many agencies and academies suffering billions of dollars in cuts to scientific research on his watch.

“We have an extremely high-IQ audience for a change,” the president told about 300 invited guests at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington, a compliment he never pays to the crowds who line up for hours to attend his campaign rallies.

Standing on a podium with a white backdrop and series of US flags, the president gave a perfunctory speech, sticking unusually close to his teleprompter. He made references to artificial super intelligence but steered clear of the datacentres these tech overlords are erecting all over the country and, in the process, achieving the unique feat of getting Democrats and Republicans to agree on how much they hate them.

Michael Kratsios, director of the White House office of science and technology policy, then treated Trump to a video about his uncle, Dr John Trump, an electrical engineer and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who received the National Medal of Science in 1983.

The short film’s claims that John Trump’s research produced X-ray generators “used for the first radiation treatments for cancer” and that “his radars jammed German defences” on D-day in 1944 owe something to his nephew’s fondness for “truthful hyperbole”.

Six years ago, the president, who believes in “good genes” and “racehorse theory”, suggested that his uncle’s legacy would help him fight the Covid-19 pandemic: “He was a great super genius. Dr John Trump. I like this stuff. I really get it. People are surprised that I understand it. Every one of these doctors said: ‘How do you know so much about this?’ Maybe I have a natural ability. Maybe I should have done that instead of running for president.”

Kratsios had a surprise for the boss. He presented Trump with his uncle’s National Medal of Science in a handsome frame as the audience clapped. He looked happy enough, though it was clear this won’t displace the gaudy Fifa peace prize from his trophy cabinet.

Among the six tech leaders who came up on stage to receive an award for scientific and technological achievement, five were immigrants.

The “America first” president gave the National Medal of Science to SpaceX chief executive Musk (born in South Africa); Google co-founder Sergey Brin (Russia); Jensen Huang (Taiwan), whose AI chip maker Nvidia is the world’s most valuable company; and Lisa Su (Taiwan), head of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices.

Trump also handed the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft supremo Satya Nadella (India) and Dell Technologies chief executive Michael Dell (Texas). Hours earlier, JD Vance had announced Microsoft’s suspension from a programme allowing companies to sponsor foreign workers for green cards.

Sign up to How we win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

The trillionaire Musk was wearing a dark suit, white shirt and white tie. Trump gave him a pat on the back, handed him the medal and gave him another pat, then showed him a certificate and patted him once more. In earlier remarks, the president called Musk an “industrial titan”, “brilliant engineer”, “national treasure” and “modern-day Thomas Edison”. He observed: “It all works out well for Elon, right?”

These guys’ relationship is more complicated than Rhett Butler and Scarlett O’Hara. Musk helped buy the 2024 election for Trump and found Doge a useful vehicle to gut the federal agencies investigating his companies. The president considered Musk’s Grok chatbot ingenious after it accurately predicted that ordinary Venezuelans would celebrate the removal of leader Nicolás Maduro, according to Time magazine.

Then came their explosive falling out, with Musk tweeting on his own X platform: “Time to drop the really big bomb: [Trump] is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.” It turned out both men were in the files.

Vance reportedly brokered a truce between the two titanic egos. The bromance has never been fully rekindled, but Thursday was proof that power and wealth can’t live without each other – especially with elections less than a month away and Trump’s approval rating in the doldrums.

When the ceremony was over, however, it was AI king Huang who remained on stage alongside Trump as the familiar strains of the Village People’s YMCA blasted from loudspeakers (“Young man, when you’re short on your dough,” did not resonate with this crowd). The pair were pointing and directing people, presumably for a photo op, and looking pleased with themselves. It was a fitting closing image of two men who rule the world and may yet find a artificial super intelligent way to destroy it.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords with a cost-of-living crisis. He dished out awards to the world’s richest person – his old frenemy Elon Musk – and other tech billionaires.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Chris Murphy says Pentagon blocked him from military base in Qatar and Iran strike on US embassy in Riyadh far worse than public led to believe

Senator Chris Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from a major US base in Qatar, yet saw enough damage on the US embassy in Saudi Arabia to conclude that an Iranian strike would have been deadly had it happened during the day.

The Connecticut Democrat, who sits on the Senate foreign relations and appropriations committees, described the destruction he witnessed in Riyadh as “extraordinary” and much more damaging than the public has been led to believe.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“Had that attack happened during the daytime, there’s no doubt that there would have been many, many Americans killed,” he told reporters on a call after returning from Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also accused the Pentagon of trying to prevent Congress from seeing the costs of the war first-hand, saying the Pentagon secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”.

Two drones hit the compound in the early hours of 3 March, days after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, setting off a fire and sending black smoke over the district. The building was reportedly empty at the time and no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry initially described the damage as minor.

But, according to Murphy, the drones caused extensive damage across several floors. The strike, he explained, hit “an area of the embassy in which there are a lot of people” and said that “part of that space is uninhabitable and will likely remain uninhabitable”. Murphy said some of it would not be repaired because the embassy is moving soon.

In Qatar, the senator visited Ras Laffan, the gas complex where Iranian drone strikes halted LNG (liquefied natural gas) production early in the war. Murphy said 17% of Qatar’s exports had been eliminated, probably for at least three years of repairs. He also said he saw just one LNG tanker in port, compared with the usual six, and about one a day leaving rather than 10.

Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from seeing more. He said he gave notice of his visit weeks in advance and submitted a written request for access to Al Udeid air base, the largest US military installation in the region. He also said he raised it with Adm Brad Cooper, the commander of the US Central Command, who appeared surprised that military leaders had also been barred from speaking to him. On arrival, Murphy said, he was told he would not have access to the base and no contact with military leadership.

In response, a senior Pentagon official told the Guardian that Murphy’s office “was informed before his trip” that he would not receive department support to access Al Udeid air base, as per Hegseth’s 3 March directive on travel restrictions in the region.

“That decision was communicated in advance by the office of the secretary of war for legislative affairs,” the official said in a statement. “The department applies the secretary’s guidance evenly.”

Murphy said he would draft language in the coming days requiring the Pentagon to give members of Congress access to overseas bases, which he would seek to include in next year’s appropriations and defense authorization bills. If the war is still going by early next year, he said Congress should withhold defense funding unless it includes a provision to end the conflict, and vowed accountability and investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers in next month’s midterm elections.

The administration, he said, was “giving its middle finger to the Congress, pretending as if we are totally irrelevant”.

“We will potentially have power of both the House and the Senate,” Murphy said of Democrats, “and we should make the end of the war a priority.”

In a brief news conference on Thursday afternoon, Captain Dan Keeler, the USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer, addressed widespread reports of mental health challenges faced by his crew during their long deployment.

“For most of my sailors, that this was their first time away from home, their first deployment, their first experience with combat,” Keeler said. “I understand the anxiety that that might have caused, but I can tell you this: our team of professionals on the ship led every single one of those sailors through that experience, and the great majority responded like sailors always do - with honor, courage, and commitment.”

“They are fantastic, fantastic sailors and marines, and they’re going to be cared for continuously on the next coming few months,” he added. “I deployed with five chaplains and a very well staffed mental health team. We got our sailors any care they needed and got them back in the fight when it was appropriate.”

Near the end of the news conference one reporter asked: “Were there some sailors who did try to commit suicide or jump overboard?”

“The key number that I like to focus on is zero; there were no suicides on board. There were no lost lives on on board,” Keeler replied.

“The suicide attempt number,” he went on. “You know, the secretary of the navy put out a number that encompassed the entirety of the strike group,” Keeler said, referring to a letter to Congress from acting navy secretary Hung Cao last month in which he wrote that there had been a total of eight suicide attempts across all the ships in the strike group led by the Lincoln.

“I think that key point has been lost when he, the secretary of the navy, put out the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group, that encompasses several thousand more sailors than what’s on board behind me,” Keeler added.

“We want the suicide attempt number to be zero. Having done this many, many times with the demographics that I have on board and the, you know, the stressful mission that we conduct, that’s unrealistic,” he continued. “That’s why I go to sea with a very, very well staffed mental health team. And when we had acute mental health cases, they immediately get seen by that mental health team and evaluated.”

At a preliminary injunction hearing, a federal judge said he would decide by Tuesday whether the temporary block he placed on Trump’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House would remain in effect. After almost a year at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier has officially returned to San Diego after a record-breaking deployment. Families and friends, clutching signs and holding flowers, welcomed many service members who have been away from home for more than 320 days. Conditions on the ship became the subject of intense concern and scrutiny, along with deployment extensions to support the Iran war. In September Hung Cao, the acting navy secretary, acknowledged that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group attempted to take their own lives.

Also today, the Trump administration announced it would block Microsoft from a program sponsoring foreign workers for green cards – which grant permanent residency in the US. These workers are already in the US on H-1B visas, a temporary work visa that allows US companies to hire skilled foreign workers for specialized jobs. However, the administration said it was suspending Microsoft from the so-called Perm program, the first step employers must complete when sponsoring workers for employment-based green cards. “You’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants,” said vice-president JD Vance at a press conference.

Families of service members have been eagerly awaiting the return of their loved ones at Naval Air Station North Island.

The president also presented the award to a number of other tech executives, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Donald Trump is currently hosting a science summit to honor top tech leaders including Elon Musk amid growing concerns over the risks of artificial intelligence.

At the US Institute of Peace on Thursday, Trump honored Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, AMD CEO Lisa Su, as well as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang – all of whom will receive the National Medal of Science.

“I recognize so many of you for an important summit on how we can revitalize the scientific enterprise in the coming years, and so we’re going to have lots of meetings and other things,” Trump told the audience.

Other industry leaders honored at the event include Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, both of whom will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

The event comes amid growing ties between the Trump administration and the AI industry as concerns mount over the technology’s rapid development and potential risks.

In a statement on Thursday, the justice department said it is targeting “the aging network of tankers the regime relies on to move billions of dollars’ worth of petroleum and petroleum products to foreign markets.”

Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said that the US will “continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales,” adding: “No enabler of Iranian sanctions evasion is safe from the full force of Treasury’s authorities.”

The US has imposed sanctions on 17 shadow fleet vessels that are responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil and petroleum and petrochemical products to a variety of South and East Asia markets, the treasury department said.

Eric Leventhal knows he’s going to vote for a Democrat in Congress when he goes to the polls in Missouri this November – the problem is he has no idea which candidate is going to be on his ballot.

In the state’s August primary, he voted for Fred Wellman, a Democrat running in the state’s second congressional district. But after a long and complicated legal battle sparked by Donald Trump’s desire to gain every advantage in the upcoming midterm contest, the districts have changed for the general election that will determine which party controls Congress. Leventhal said he lived right near the border of the first and second congressional district, so now he’s not sure which one he’s in.

“It is dizzying and embarrassing, frankly,” said Leventhal, a 35-year-old stay-at-home father.

Leventhal’s experience crystallized the mix of anger and confusion felt in Missouri, where an effort by Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map devolved into a saga that seemed to have as many twists and turns as the gerrymandered districts themselves.

Eric Deters says US ambassador to Greece asked him to pay off American Express credit card bill in return for access

A Trump donor accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, of engaging in a “quid pro quo” by asking him to pay off her $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials.

Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate and lawyer, told MS Now on Thursday that Guilfoyle had “ambushed” him last year with an offer to provide access to government officials if he paid her American Express credit card bill, before her US Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters told the network in response to a Wall Street Journal report that she had pushed him for the money.

“Kimberly Guilfoyle is a grifter,” he added.

The Guardian has asked Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment.

Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages, but that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance.

The report is the latest allegation about Guilfoyle’s conduct as a US official. Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador to Greece promised him “ride or die” access to Trump administration officials if he wired American Express $100,000.

Asked about the report during a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said he would not address the allegations. He reaffirmed his support for the US embassy in Greece adding, “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” Asked again about the reports on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment.

The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador.

A spokesperson for the Democratic staff of the Senate foreign relations committee confirmed to the Guardian that they were requesting further information and continuing to investigate.

JD Vance similarly expressed hesitation, similar to Rubio, on Thursday when asked to respond to a US ambassador offering access to government officials in exchange for money to pay off debts.

“With that hypothetical, Jen, obviously I don’t love that,” the vice-president replied. “But I don’t know exactly who you’re talking about. I don’t know the full details. What I find with these stories is you never want to comment in a purely abstract way because a lot of times the details really matter,” he added.

Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday, asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle.

“Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece, I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.”

Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist.

“If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote.

Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece.

But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express.

Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”

Deters said Guilfoyle had promised him thatshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment.

In other messages, Guilfoyle reportedly raised concerns about her communications with Deters becoming public and reprimanded him for not being discreet. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal,” she is said to have written in one message.

“What a nightmare, you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle reportedly wrote in another message.

A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal.

It is unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador promised him ‘ride or die’ if he wired American Express $100,000. Guil foyle

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: DoJ seeks to charge ex-Trump aide who gave key testimony on January 6 attack
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Cassidy Hutchinson told panel she had been told Trump lunged for wheel of SUV to try to join mob at Capitol

Prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division are seeking criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former top Trump White House aide who gave explosive testimony to the committee that investigated the US attack on the Capitol, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The potential charges involve lying to Congress, the person said.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Hutchinson, a former top aide to the White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, told the panel among other things that the deputy chief of staff for operations told her that Trump did not want to return to the White House on January 6 and at one point grabbed the wheel of his SUV to try to join supporters at the Capitol. Republicans have long disputed this account.

The justice department’s efforts to indict Hutchinson were first reported by Punchbowl News on Thursday.

“The department does not confirm or deny the existence of investigations, or the lack thereof,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.

In April, the New York Times reported that prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division, which handles investigations into civil rights crimes, had been tapped to investigate Hutchinson. It was seen as a highly unusual move at the time since the investigation would typically be handled by the US attorney for the district of Columbia. Hutchinson also said she was under investigation by the Department of Justice in filings in an unrelated case.

The case is the latest example of how Trump has used the justice department to prosecute his enemies. Last year, the justice department indicted former FBI director James Comey on charges of lying to Congress and Letitia James on mortgage fraud. Both indictments were dismissed after a judge ruled the prosecutor overseeing them had been unlawfully appointed. The department has since filed a new indictment against Comey for posting a picture of seashells arranged in a formation that said “8647.”

Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

The Trump justice department has also filed charges against the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center and the journalist Don Lemon.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency

Microsoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed through a US visa program for high-skilled workers, JD Vance announced on Thursday.

The US vice-president accused the tech company of abusing the H-1B system, which allows those on the visa to work while they apply for and are in the process of obtaining a green card.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“Our message to Microsoft is, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a press conference announcing the suspension. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

Microsoft said the vast majority of its workers were American and 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last year were for extensions or status changes for people who already worked for the company.

“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote in a statement. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.”

The US labor department also said Adobe had been similarly suspended.

“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” said Keith Sonderling, the US labor secretary, in a statement.

Microsoft applied for H-1B visas for nearly 3,700 workers in 2026, making it the fifth largest employer of workers on the visa. Tech companies are the biggest employers of H-1B workers across the industry. Amazon topped the list with more than 9,300 petitions this year. Sonderling said since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe had received about 230,000 approvals for H-1B visas and 100,000 “permanent labor certifications”, a step towards an employment-based green card.

“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.

The Trump administration has set its sights on the H-1B program for some time, arguing that it is rife with abuse. Vance said that, on average, workers hired through the H-1B program were making $20,000 less than US workers in the same position.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

“So I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played,” Vance said. “You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with.”

Immigration advocacy groups have long called for reforms for the H-1B program, though for different reasons. Those in the program are often beholden to their employer because their visas are tied to the company that applied for them, making it difficult to switch jobs if things aren’t going well or if they want to find a job with a higher salary.

These groups, like the National Immigration Forum, largely disagree with Vance. They argue that competing for specialized talent from around the world benefits the US economy.

“The United States has long benefited from its ability to attract talent from around the world, particularly in STEM, higher education, research, and innovation,” the National Immigration Forum wrote in a September 2026 blogpost discussing proposed changes to the H-1B program. “As countries increasingly compete for highly skilled workers, policies that make the United States less attractive could strengthen global competitors.”
