The US labor department also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high- skilled workers to apply for US residency.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.title: Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.text:
Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage

Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.

The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Theodore J Boutrous, who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues, said the president made abundantly clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar the three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. (Under binding court precedent, news organizations cannot be removed from the White House for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.)

Asked by Time for the “impetus” for the ban, Trump replied: “It’s just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I’ve got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it’s not only CNN, and it’s not only MSDNC [sic]. It’s a lot of other people.” He made no mention of national security concerns, one of the primary reasons that has been given by government lawyers as a rationale for the ban.

“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge, citing what he said was “a confession of viewpoint discrimination and retaliation”. He added: “It’s really just absolutely clear … President Trump, to give him credit – he’s not hiding it.”

While the judge didn’t give a strong indication of which direction he was leaning, he accepted Boutrous’s argument when questioning the lone lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik.

“The decision-maker seems to have said I’m taking this action because of X and Y, and the government is saying: ‘No, it’s Z,’” the judge said. “It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one around.”

Velchik, who began his argument by saying “the White House is a sacred place,” said a failure to adhere to basic standards of journalistic conduct was also one of the precipitating factors in the decision, something he said was in line with Trump’s comments criticizing the way that these three specific news organizations operate.

He also faulted the media companies for not responding to post-hoc letters giving the plaintiffs a chance to rebut the charges against them, something that Boutrous later described as a “sham process”.

In his ruling granting a TRO for the media plaintiffs, Kelly said the White House had violated constitutional requirements for due process by not giving the companies adequate notice for what the standards for acceptable conduct are and not giving them a chance to protest against the potential sanction in advance.

Nothing from Thursday’s hearing seemed to indicate that the judge had changed his thinking on that important standard, suggesting he is likely to adhere to his earlier decision-making and extend the lifting of the ban.

The judge told the government’s lawyer that they “still have a notice problem, it seems to [him], or at least a notice issue”. Kelly said the standards for adequate advance notice laid out in a binding circuit case involving a similar White House access issue “are probably the biggest hurdle you have”.
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.summary: CNN, MS Now and Politico are suing the White House over their coverage of Donald Trump. The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order he issued on 24 September. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but a judge said he would extend it until Tuesday.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: With no Pulisic and good results, have the USMNT moved on from their savior complex? | Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be over

Sign up for our free newsletter here

I
n 1990, then-United States men’s national team manager Bob Gansler made a critical and somewhat controversial choice. He left three of the program’s laureled veterans at home and brought a young and little-tested team to the World Cup in Italy, the USA’s first in 40 years.

As Gansler recalled later: “I was thinking not only for ’90, but I was thinking about the 90s.”

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

In 1998, Steve Sampson was looking to the future as well. He had lucked into the USMNT’s managerial gig and had barely clung on to it going into that year’s World Cup, but he nevertheless made a confident proclamation. “In 10 to 15 years, we’ll win the title, there’s no doubt about it,” he told the Washington Post. “When we Americans decide to do something, we’ll see it through.”

A sense took hold sometime during that period, while never really acknowledged or said out loud, that the USMNT were the team of the future.

They never really stopped being that. And this bullishness on the hazily outlined not-right-now-but-definitely-sometime-later-on tended to coalesce around one player, maybe two. The USMNT made their modern World Cup breakthrough powered by the energy and unfettered talent of 20-year-olds Landon Donovan and DaMarcus Beasley in 2002. When those two foundered at the 2006 World Cup, another young player, Clint Dempsey, emerged. That year, a 16-year-old Freddy Adu made his USMNT debut.

And so a pattern formed: the US soccer community waited to be lifted to the next plane by a savior. The next kid. Or maybe the one after that. He’ll do it for us. Or else the next one will.

Dempsey outlasted Donovan and faded just as Christian Pulisic emerged. Because even as a golden-ish generation coalesced around him, Pulisic was seen as the player expected to make something happen at the 2026 World Cup, the culmination of an eight-year project of rebuilding the national team. He was expected to activate Hero Mode, the way he briefly had in Qatar in 2022, throwing himself in front of a cross at the expense of a pelvic contusion but bundling the make-or-break winner into the Iranian goal.

He never did it in 2026. Aside from a great first half in the tournament opener, Pulisic’s home World Cup was a bust, and the USMNT’s campaign ended with a whimper.

On its face, it felt odd that Mauricio Pochettino should launch a youth movement in the first camp after the World Cup. The core of his team had hardly aged out; all but defender Tim Ream are comfortably on the right side of 30. All the same, he called in 13 debutants and eight teenagers.

If results in the months after a World Cup count for anything at all, they have vindicated the Argentinian’s decision to freshen things up. The kids, sprinkled in among a robust base of veterans, reeled off 4-1 and 4-2 victories over Peru and Chile, respectively, before dispatching Mexico in a merciless 3-0 walloping. On Tuesday, they concluded this jumbo-sized international window with a mature 1-0 win over Canada in a scruffy, scrappy game, vanquishing a team whose fierceness and physicality had given the US a great deal of trouble in the recent past.

What was startling, however, wasn’t just how much young talent is waiting down the depth chart – or now, perhaps, very much on the surface of it – but how little Pulisic, the latest savior, was missed in his absence. You easily might have forgotten that he wasn’t even there while watching a composed and polished team reel off four straight wins. The same was true for Weston McKennie, one of the USMNT’s load-bearing players for the last half decade. They both stayed with their Italian clubs, either hoping to use the time off to get back in favor with their manager (Pulisic at Milan) or to heal up an injury (McKennie at Juventus).

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

In their absence, so many players carried the load, contributing in ways big and small, taking turns coming up with the big play, that the burden was never on any one player. Cavan Sullivan may well be next in line in the succession of the USMNT’s star players – or maybe it will be Julian Hall, or Adri Mehmeti, or Zavier Gozo, or Justin Ellis, or Mathis Albert – but there was no intimation that this was his ship to propel under his own power. This was not Sullivan’s team now, as then-manager Bruce Arena told Pulisic after the US failed to reach the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

The big takeaway from this mega-pack of an international break – which encompassed more games than the USMNT’s run at several big tournaments – is that this team may, at long last, no longer be so dependent on one player, or even a small handful of them.

If this program is entering into a post-savior age – moving on from Pulisic-pendencia, as it were, or whoever-pendencia – that’s a clearer sign of progress than the emergence of some new prodigy, or indeed a cluster of them.

What this team, and this soccer country writ large, appear to have grown instead, is the kind of depth US fans used to envy in other, more developed soccer nations. If at the 2030 World Cup, the US TV commercials don’t all feature the same player, in the way Pulisic largely hogged the commercial blocks this past summer, it will represent another step forward.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I’m the attorney general of Washington state. Here’s how we’re protecting the midterm elections | Nick Brown
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nick Brown
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A coalition of Democratic attorneys general is working to make sure voters across the spectrum have their voices heard

Elections have consequences. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them.

Voters will be confident in their choices, but less certain whose voice will count in the face of myriad intrusions by the executive branch. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their say.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Led by the attorneys general of Washington, California, Massachusetts and Nevada, 24 states sued to block President Donald Trump’s US Postal Service plot to interfere with voting by mail. Last month, the supreme court upheld our lower court victories and blocked the administration’s unconstitutional power grab, at least for this election.

The law says states decide who receives a mail ballot. The USPS has never had the final say and, according to the American Postal Workers Union, until this year had never in its 250-year history tried to put such arbitrary restrictions on what mail it will deliver.

The case we brought was an important victory in every state, and particularly Washington, where more than 99% of voters cast their ballot by mail. States such as Colorado, Hawaii and Oregon have similarly high mail voting rates. But mail voting is not confined to blue states; it is widely used in red states as well, particularly those like Nebraska and the Dakotas, with large rural populations. It’s also the president’s preferred way to cast his own ballot.

The case of the postal service is just part of the multi-pronged federal attack states are pushing back against. The administration has abandoned the federal government’s traditional role of supporting election security and defending voting rights, work I participated in first-hand as a US attorney.

Recall, in 2020, Trump’s own administration – and particularly the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency – worked to protect the vote and defend the election. Then, efforts to misuse the Department of Justice were thwarted, and Trump relied on insurrectionists to do his bidding. In return for serving honorably, many public servants were sent packing upon Trump’s return to office, and the convicted insurrectionists were pardoned.

Now we have a US solicitor general who described the postal service’s attempt to deprive the rights of millions of eligible voters as only a “modest” use of federal authority.

The Trump administration is not known for its discretion or consistency. While the administration was in court purportedly concerned about election integrity, the president publicly demanded his supporters “cheat like hell” in midterm voting. I don’t think Republican voters want that any more than Democrats do.

We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters. Democratic state attorneys general are prepared, and have undertaken the largest multi-state effort to protect the vote in modern American history.

Recent rulings keep state elections on track and show the law is on our side. If Trump attempts to intimidate or discourage eligible voters, or to obstruct the counting of votes or certification of the election, Democratic state attorneys general will take swift action. States have decades of experience countering these threats when lodged by private actors, and they are just as illegal when attempted by the federal government.

Voters can do their part by exercising the right to elect their representatives. The president’s scheming benefits from public doubt and uncertainty. Democracy depends on the participation of its citizens, and every eligible voter should have the opportunity to render a verdict on their elected representatives.

That verdict is unlikely to favor President Trump, who ran on lowering costs, preserving peace, and economic stability, but instead delivered higher prices, hollowed out critical public services, engaged in unprecedented self-dealing, and began a globally destabilizing war with no end in sight.

Presidents don’t decide elections. State attorneys general and the millions of eligible voters we represent will exercise our constitutional powers to help keep it that way.

Nick Brown is the attorney general of the state of Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their voices heard. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them?

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation | Margaret Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Margaret Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day

When you hate the mainstream press as much as Donald Trump does, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy.

Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

And certainly not any awareness of how the first amendment is supposed to function in American democracy.

This week, his revenge tour took yet another turn.

He barred one of his most disfavored media organizations – Politico – from boarding Air Force One, where it was supposed to provide “pool coverage” to the rest of the press corps as Trump traveled to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon.

That move was met with a strong show of solidarity by several media outlets, who decided not to fill the Politico spot.

And the White House was defiantly delusional, claiming that Trump will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press”.

This latest chapter came with the usual blast of venom at the mainstream media, though not specifically aimed at Politico.

“The New York Times and many other Artificial Media Outlets should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” he posted on Truth Social.

The episode follows Trump’s effort in mid-September to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. Those organizations quickly sued, charging that Trump’s action was unconstitutional.

Trump-appointed judge Timothy Kelly came down on the side of the media, issuing a temporary restraining order that ordered the White House to reinstate the press badges that had been taken away.

And since then, CNN has been kept off Air Force One repeatedly, using the rationale that access to the White House is one thing, but access to the president’s plane is another.

“The law is absolutely clear,” Ted Boutrous, the first amendment lawyer who is representing the three news organizations said in a statement. “The harm to our clients, the first amendment and the public as a whole is profound.”

The Trump administration’s position is that traveling with the president is a privilege not a right.

The fight is not over, since Kelly will conduct a hearing later this week over the media outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction – a stopgap measure to protect press access in advance of a possible trial.

Trump, of course, has been picking fights with individual journalists and entire news outlets for years. At this very moment, there are court fights involving the Associated Press, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Disney, which owns ABC News and a number of local ABC affiliates.

So far, there’s been a rare display of support among news organizations that are normally each other’s competition. Columbia Journalism Review called it “a striking and heartening show of solidarity from the White House Press Corps”.

When the three outlets were kicked out of the White House last month, the other networks in the press pool decided not to replace CNN in the rotation, thus suspending coverage for a time.

Peter Baker of the New York Times noted that for the first time in his 30 years covering the White House, “the president will not have a network TV camera covering his everyday official actions and travels”.

What’s more, about 50 media organizations backed up the lawsuit by the three who had been singled out by filing an amicus brief.

It’s hard to understand exactly how less coverage and this constant squabbling benefits Trump, but apparently, he is making a different calculation.

His anti-press actions get a lot of attention, which is the very oxygen he requires to breathe. It doesn’t matter that much of the attention is negative.

Meanwhile, he has entered a phase of saying and doing ever more outrageous things, like his statement this week at a rally that his war in Iran was necessary to protect the world. Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it develops a nuclear weapon which prompted California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, to call the president “deranged and dangerous”.

Trump exudes a sense of desperation these days, with the midterm elections only weeks away and his approval ratings underwater.

His war against the press is something of a reflex for him – it’s what comes naturally, especially when he doesn’t like the shape of reality.

The press corps’ newfound solidarity is encouraging. It’s been a long time coming from a group that, in the past, has responded to this president’s constant abuse with deference and dinner invitations.

Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day.

Standing together will be a necessity in the weeks and months ahead.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.summary: Trump has been trying to ban three media outlets from the White House since September. The three were sued by the media, claiming that the action was unconstitutional. The White House has denied the media's request for a preliminary injunction.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa Bayoumi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Moustafa Bayoumi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
AI is already implicated in violent deaths and nearly started world war three. Those bad things? They only happen to other people

Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.

“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Yikes. This statement – and the approach it represents – is, well, problematic, to say the least. It’s also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.

Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to put non-toxic glue on pizza so the cheese will be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.

But culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.

OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT for homework help. The family’s lawsuit alleges that the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimed Raine misused the platform.)

And Raine’s action is hardly the only one. OpenAI is facing multiple lawsuits filed by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.

Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. In February of this year, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in the city of Minab, killing at least 120 children. (A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the US was probably responsible for the strike.)

In a recent investigation into the attack, Bloomberg News reported that an AI-linked system was used to target the school. In this case, the system is called Maven, and it is made by Palantir.

Unnamed defense officials told Bloomberg that “inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System”. The report also adds that “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus”.

AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen, I guess.

Or there’s the little detail that the US may have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.

In September, CNN reported that an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military decided that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. According to CNN, US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship.

Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.

Also found in CNN’s frightening story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things, I suppose.

Why does it seem that these technologies, which, in the words of Trump’s White House, are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor”, get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?

And isn’t it true that the more we rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? And why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?

Could it be that what’s behind the artificial intelligence revolution may be less about the utopian or dystopian future (take your pick) that’s just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?

AI may be the only thing keeping Trump’s economy afloat right now. And it’s paying dividends. According to the New Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet”.

Those bad things? They only happen to other people.

Meanwhile, we are being warned almost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they’ll end humanity.

But maybe the real worry here is not that the machines are taking over.

It’s that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good at taking jobs away from people, stealing the intellectual property of others, writing some piss-poor undergraduate essays, spying on you and your license plates and bringing us to the brink of world war three because God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines. Or the makers of those machines.

What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used. And despite what you may hear, China already regulates its AI companies quite aggressively.

Instead, Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia believe that the AI companies should simply regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.

Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI and OpenAI, the accords ask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models”, among other things. “Over time,” the agreement states, “it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”

I’m not holding my breath.

Trump, who has ordered the term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence”, posted the accord on social media on 29 September. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen on his account and the White House’s official account. It’s signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of the Unites States.”

Super intelligence, indeed.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Indiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularity | Howard Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Howard Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity

I
t’s over for now, but no professional sports team spent more time receiving and drawing attention to itself than did the Indiana Fever this season. The Fever has broken, the team eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces for the second straight season, but Indiana succeeded in being the WNBA’s canary in the coal mine, embodying both the obvious and unintended consequences of rapid growth, while also allowing themselves to be a season-long distraction: part-time professional basketball team, part-time right-wing culture war centerpiece. Less than a decade ago, Atlanta and Minneapolis were praised for their unified political stances. Today, Trumpism has replaced social justice as the defining characteristic of the league – and as the curtain closed on the 2026 WNBA regular season, Indiana stood at its epicenter.

The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports, known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity as a Black/queer league into its current climate of political divisiveness – a calculated and dangerous path to popularity. This season, there was the basketball of the WNBA, and then there was the Indiana Fever, the league’s Maga-friendly option.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Their two most recognizable players, Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, were in a constant state of churn, always in the news, always embroiled against an other, symbolizing and pandering to America’s fractures. Their best and longest-tenured player, Kelsey Mitchell, hasn’t been able to concentrate fully on basketball the past two seasons as the Clark-Cunningham sideshow devours the oxygen and may end her time in Indiana that began as the second overall pick in 2018.

Clark remains the league’s biggest name and its chief avatar – mildly reluctant or willing pawn, but an avatar nevertheless. She is an avatar for the money at a time when broadcasters and venture capitalists are making their bets on women’s sports. She represented a certain type of hope, that the day had arrived where women’s team sports would enjoy the same visibility as female stars such as Serena Williams and Lindsey Vonn.

She was an avatar of weaponization, the speculator’s proof that the WNBA is doomed by its own hand for not recognizing her overall importance to its future, a future bizarrely framed as bright only if Clark succeeds – an odd framework for sports, where the final score and holders of the trophies determines who wins.

Most obviously and explosively, Clark was an avatar for whiteness, a Christian, hetero whiteness that holds the pervasive belief that it is straight, white America – already the overwhelming and unchallenged dominant cultural and financial force in this country – that is under assault. Any struggle Clark showed on the court – a foul call, a non-call – was treated as if it were an urban crime statistic, unmistakable proof that Black people had even turned basketball lawless. The opportunistic and racist White House and the Trump administration repeated this fiction. Republican members of Congress earlier this season insinuated Clark was being discriminated against by the league because she is white. The Congressmen threatened the WNBA with a Department of Justice investigation if the league did not take steps to protect her. Clark and the Fever did little to dispel the notion.

Whenever Clark did succeed, her partisans saw it as proof of how much better the league would be if only it stopped persecuting her. Through Clark, and how she navigated playing basketball in a league largely comprised of Black women – even as Breanna Stewart, Paige Bueckers and a host of other white women thrive without incident – was how the government (as well as many fans and journalists) framed the state of women’s professional basketball. She is half of what all the fuss has been about.

The other half is Cunningham, who spent much of the season building the scaffolding for her second act by driving a wedge into heart of the league, positioning herself at the center of the attention-fueled culture war against trans women, being the blonde, blue-eyed foil to the league’s unruly Black women, and providing an entry point for the bros, their money and misogyny to show up, for men such an Enes Kanter Freedom to do what they have always done to women’s sport – find a way to denigrate it and be rewarded with attention. While it was all very tired and calculating, framed as speaking her truth, designed to reach the very group of white male sports fans that have either criticized or ignored women’s sports but are now bringing their toxicity to the tent under the guise of “growth,” Cunningham has been the subject of more attention than she’s ever had in her decade-long career, with public appearances and lengthy profiles. She knows exactly to whom she is talking, and why.

The Fever carrying these burdens – or wearing them proudly until having to answer for them – is how Clark’s career has shifted from starting her first season a phenom joining a team that hadn’t had a winning season in seven years to ending her third in daily controversy, with her as the signature, aggrieved face of Maga’s team.

With the avatars mercifully tabled, Clark emerged as an excellent player with enormous upside and serious deficiencies. She is a volume scorer but not yet a great one – her career field-goal percentage is just 42.3, below the league average, and for all her dazzle, her career three-point percentage is a below-average 34.2. She shot 36.1% from three this season, below the Fever team average of 38.6%. She is an adept playmaker whose true skill may be less in creating offense for herself and more in controlling the tempo of the game and involving her teammates. She was second in the league in assists and first in turnovers, fitting considering she constantly has the ball – similar to James Harden in a way. She is an apathetic defender.

As a basketball presence, she is wholly unlikeable. She does not play the game with her teammates as much as beyond them – a common affliction of many superstars that in victory is touted as a virtue but looks selfish following first-round defeats. She does not appear to play the game with joy or intensity, but carries a childish outrage, not only confronting officials on virtually every trip downcourt, but sprinting to berate them in dead-ball situations. Clark plays with grievance, an entitled grievance that recalls the White House grievance, the same grievance shared by much of the white electorate that uncoincidentally claims her as their champion – they’re all unfairly under attack.

For all the criticism, WNBA officials have actually shown remarkable restraint toward her. She exaggerates most calls and outwardly flops on others to steal calls – call it European gamesmanship, but the true nature of flopping is to receive something undeserved and is the worst example of immoral basketball. Even during timeouts Clark finds a way to spar with someone, be it a cameraman or an assistant coach.

Like Cunningham, however, Clark has mastered the key component of the so-called attention economy – she sees to it the camera is always on her. A more professional Clark, with fewer outbursts and deeper concentration on basketball would lower the temperature on the league, her team, herself, and would probably win her more trips to the foul line – but there was virtually no evidence this season that is what she wants.

Superstar petulance is nothing new, and if Stephanie White doesn’t return as coach, it won’t be the first time a star player will be accused of getting the coach fired. Nor is it the first time a sports team has reflected a national political mood or been pulled into its vortex. Usually reflection marks triumph – Black and Jewish America loved the Dodgers because of Jackie Robinson and Sandy Koufax just as the Yankee teams of Tony Lazzeri, Frankie Crosetti, Joe DiMaggio, and Phil Rizzuto made them beloved in Italian-American homes.

A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.

after newsletter promotion

Teams have also symbolized division. In the 1980s, the Boston Celtics were often considered white America’s team because of Larry Bird, the high number of white players the Celtics routinely signed, and the perception that the Celtics did not play with the flamboyant Blackness that defined the rest of the league, which allowed white fans to see themselves in their no-nonsense, blue-collar ethic.

Despite the presence of James White, Dont’a Hightower, the McCourty twins and Stephon Gilmore, the late-stage Brady/Belichick Patriots were adopted by certain white supremacists because the Patriots were led offensively by a handful of white players – Tom Brady, Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman. The supposedly colorblind whites had found their ideal.

None of those examples, however, have existed within the combination of today’s dark political intensity where the federal government has positioned itself as the legal guardian of whiteness and the precarious political footing of the league. The nation has effectively closed its borders to everyone except white South Africans, while Cunningham encourages the right to use the WNBA for anti-trans fodder and the DOJ believes Clark needs its protection.

In a feeble attempt to distance itself from the obvious racism, the Fever periodically made bland, unconvincing statements – there’s no room for hate in the game – but their actions undermined their sentiments. Cunningham knows exactly who her fans view as the enemy, which fires to stoke on her podcasts, which dog whistles to sound. As does Clark, for her constant on-court histrionics elicit the right sympathy from the right people. They both know exactly what they’re doing.

The season over, the Fever closed 2026 not by celebrating their best record since 2015, or by marking the first time since the 2009-2012 season the franchise posted three-straight 20-win seasons and have momentum as a potential title contender, but with more grievance. General manager Amber Cox read a ridiculous, gaslighting statement blaming outside media for the odious reputation of Fever fans. “The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and must stop,” she read from the podium. Mitchell’s own words painfully contradicted Cox, as did rival players around the league.

Maybe they just want it this way.

This article originally appeared on Howard Bryant’s Substack. You can subscribe here.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.summary: The Indiana Fever have been eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces. The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports. The team was known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency

F
or once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates.

Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That would require flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remain unpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of a red undertow rather than a blue wave.

Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populist James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such as Maine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with $700m of advertising booked since the start of September.

Mr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasingly distancing themselves from the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as “elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him are changing their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing.

Outrageously, Mr Trump has used taxpayer-funded adverts to laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts to restrict mail-in voting – used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it.

Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But should Democrats manage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible | Ted Widmer
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ted Widmer
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad

D
onald Trump was in Nebraska on Monday, and though his long rally speech had elements of a performance, this was no Bruce Springsteen album. He offered another dark meditation on a world spiraling out of control, one in which the destruction of American cities is increasingly a possibility, unless Americans trust him to use the vast powers of the presidency to annihilate his foes.

The president drew fury when he suggested that Iran could launch a nuclear attack and “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego. California leaders reacted with scorn at Trump’s alarmism.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Governor Gavin Newsom denounced Trump as “deranged and dangerous”, while the mayors of Los Angeles and San Diego, Karen Bass and Todd Gloria, objected strenuously to putting their cities in harm’s way, even if only in his feverish imagination.

Perhaps the worst problem with Trump’s speech – and there were many – was not that it vividly daydreamed about Armageddon-on-the-Pacific. It was just so delusional that it had almost no basis in fact at all.

It is inherently destabilizing when a nation’s leader cannot be trusted to make an accurate statement, and the situation is especially troubling when the nation is the United States, the defender of the rules-based order since 1945.

First, the claim itself. When read inside the transcript, the words don’t make a great deal of sense. It’s almost like scat singing as the president goes into his famous “weave”, his word for the way he lurches from one half-formed thought to another, like a rodeo clown on a bucking bronco.

“[Kamala] stole a lot of things that didn’t work out too well. But I want, I wanna see, I wanna see a tremendous victory. You wanna see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the word, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.

“They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s, this is a very small price to pay, and it’s gonna be over very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.”

If he was talking about the war as being “almost over with”, then he’s certainly wrong, as the conflict drags into its eighth month with no sign of resolution. But if he was talking about the midterms, then he’s correct that it will end soon, and not well for him.

In effect, he now has to go into the reddest part of a red state to sustain his vanishing popularity. Monday night’s rally was held at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds, in Hall county, Nebraska, which had a population of 62,895 in 2020. Even farmers are wary of this war, which has raised the price of fertilizers and diesel.

The language about LA and San Diego was to be fair, quite vague. Presumably, he was worried that Iran’s nuclear program might be able to target LA or San Diego. But by saying “let them …” it almost sounded like he was encouraging them to, as when John F Kennedy, in Berlin, held up that city as a model of courage and said: “Let them come to Berlin,” in both English and German).

In either case, there is no possibility of it happening, as his military advisers know, and as even he must know at some level. Iran does not have a nuclear weapon, nor can its missiles reach the United States, on either the east or west coast.

Furthermore, it is the height of irresponsibility to even discuss such an unimaginable threat. All foreign leaders understand that any attack on the United States with a nuclear weapon would result in an overwhelming counterattack. It’s called deterrence.

It is that knowledge – and the cautious way in which previous American presidents have talked about nuclear weapons – that has helped to preserve the peace all these years. We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad.

The rest of the speech was also a mess. There was a lot of red-baiting, despite the fact that the cold war ended in 1991. There were the usual schoolyard insults, in this case lobbed toward the Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (“I call him Alfred E Neuman”) and Georgia senator Jon Ossoff (“he looks like Pee-wee Herman to me”).

And more pot-stirring, with no basis in fact. Often, his claims undermined each other, as Trump claimed both that Iran has been rendered toothless (“we’re kicking Iran’s ass”) and that it remains a lethal threat, capable of destroying our second- and eighth-largest cities. Which one is it? Over and over, we have heard that Iran’s nuclear program has been “obliterated”. But if so, why are we still at war?

The rest of the speech was the usual farrago of distortions and lies, as the most casual effort to factcheck shows. “We want honest,” Trump said at one point, confusingly. Yes, we do.

But whether we are going to get it, is another question entirely.

Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why are the Democratic Socialists of America so successful? | Akin Olla
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Akin Olla
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There’s an unsung reason for the organization’s success even as other leftwing groups face a bumpy road

A lot has been written recently in an effort to understand the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and how we’ve risen to such prominence in a short time.

It is clear that we reflect a growing disillusionment with the Democratic party, and a further radicalization of the American population. But many leftwing social movement organizations, such as Black Lives Matter and the Women’s March, have risen in the last decade or so, and many groups, from MoveOn to the Sunrise Movement, have attempted to absorb large numbers of people, influence the Democratic party and enter the public consciousness with lower levels of success.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

It may just be that we happened to be the organization that had the name closest to the ideology of Bernie Sanders, the man arguably most responsible for reintroducing democratic socialism to the popular American lexicon. But name recognition alone can’t explain both our rapid growth and the ability to sustain that growth. Sanders has also talked about the need for a “political revolution” – but his own organization, Our Revolution, is politically irrelevant.

What is missing from the discussion is the DSA’s structure.

Unlike all of the groups I’ve named, it is a thoroughly democratically run organization that allows its members to set its goals, elect its leaders and amend its constitution. None of the other organizations even have constitutions to be altered. Instead, they have corporate bylaws and unelected executive boards to maintain their tax status with the IRS.

While the DSA is primarily operated and funded by its growing membership, the other organizations rely on foundation funding and have a deeper reliance on professional staff. While local chapters of most of these groups have almost no control over the national structure, the DSA functions as a federation in which the national office is beholden to its constituent parts.

The DSA is not succeeding because of a good name. It is growing because it treats its members like adults capable of managing their own affairs and that of the organization, and they reward it with monthly dues and a long commitment that supersedes the natural highs and lows of uprisings.

This idea isn’t new; in fact it is foundational to the success of the American project (well, OK, success is a bit of a stretch, isn’t it?). Writing in the early 19th century, the French philosopher Alexis de Tocqueville described these kinds of membership-driven organizations as the “free schools” of democracy that serve as the bedrock of America’s political system.

They prepare Americans to lead and give them the political vehicles in which they can work with their neighbors to steer the country. This model is dying, but we still see it alive through organizations like the NAACP and the US Student Association, which I was a member of in my youth.

The NAACP is more than a hundred years old and the US Student Association will be 80 next year. While the DSA was created in 1982, it can trace its full history as a faction within larger organizations going back well over a century.

It is doubtful that the conflict-ridden Black Lives Global Network Foundation, the 501(c)3 organization that took the reins of the BLM movement, will survive the decade.

BLM chapters have dissolved, broken away or become relatively dormant across the country. The network helped oversee the largest protest in US history, but it is doubtful that there are more than a handful of chapters functioning in the country. The Minneapolis chapter, arguably its most successful, reconstituted itself as Black Visions, and then sunsetted after years of misalignment and the forcing out of its original leadership.

The Green New Deal-championing Sunrise Movement has fared better, but not by much. It too has faced internal power struggles between leadership, who are paid staff members, and its base.

According to one former member, the organization went from having more than 500 chapters in 2021 to probably fewer than 90 by 2023. It has made efforts to become more democratic but could only muster 700 votes for an internal decision, despite counting more than 80,000 members years prior.

While some of this must be the natural attrition of social movements – the DSA’s membership also ebbs and flows – founders of the Sunrise Movement have publicly recognized the internal conflict built into their model.
  And this is why the DSA will continue to succeed where most groups fail. It has clear mechanisms for its membership to change the direction of the organization without engaging in backroom schemes and internal coups. Clashes still happen, but they are facilitated by clear guidelines that allow factions – called caucuses – to vie for power, and leaders have clear term limits.

Sign up to How we win

Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.

after newsletter promotion

I joined the US Student Association (USSA) with a desire to learn from it and steal members for my own organization, in the vein of the Québécois student unions. But the USSA was so democratic and full of meaningful deliberation that I realized I could change it from within instead of splintering it.

Over a decade later, I’m a dedicated alumnus who has volunteered dozens of hours out of sheer love for the organization. There is evidence that participating in a thoughtful deliberative process increases satisfaction with the outcomes of a decision and trust of institutions.
  I joined the DSA after sitting through one meeting and realizing that my voice actually mattered. I did not need to become a staff member or somehow be appointed to the board of directors. I could make the DSA what I want it to be, while being transformed by it in turn.

I hadn’t experienced that since my days at the USSA’s national student congress. And that is because the new model of social movement organization has long become dominant.

According to the Harvard sociologist Theda Skocpol, grant-funded, staff-run, low membership participation models became popular in the 1970s. They create an incentive model that I believe is deleterious to long-term social change.

Foundations force organizations to become constant money-chasing machines, applying for annual grant after annual grant, and to adopt a model of centralized control that maximizes efficiency – having tens of thousands of decision-makers can be messy, after all.

This model can still bring in a lot of members, but they tend to be temporary participants, or paper members, like the millions of members of MoveOn, who donate monthly but do little to operate between mobilizations, and have no clear role in determining the future of the organization as a whole.

I supported the development of a new generation of organizations through my work as a trainer with the Momentum Community, but the groups I advised, many of which are named in this article, still suffered from this top-down non-profit model. These groups can absorb thousands of people in moments of public frustration, but they are structurally unable to keep them.

The DSA is growing not only because it reflects frustration over the status quo; it is growing also because it gives people a voice within a vehicle that promises to change that status quo.

Akin Olla is a contributing opinion writer at the Guardian US

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called Trump | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home

T
he US midterm elections are a month away and it’s looking rough for the Republicans. I wouldn’t discount devious schemes behind the scenes, but, on the face of it, the president and his entourage seem to be flailing. Donald Trump is desperately dangling money in front of voters and promising “a big surprise”. Meanwhile, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the GOP senator Ted Cruz seem more concerned with fighting over who will be Trump’s heir than with the midterms.

If the polls are to be believed, Vance is the frontrunner for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But while he may have great name recognition, Vance is also unlikable. According to the CNN analyst Harry Enten, he is one of the least popular vice-presidents in history. He’s also apparently made enemies within his own party, largely because of his scepticism about the Iran war. His detractors include Cruz, who told MS Now in August that Vance wasn’t a shoo-in for the nomination. The party, Cruz said, was still figuring out the best candidate and needed “to decide who we are, what do we believe”.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

These remarks did not go unnoticed by the ever-observant vice-president. “It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said in an interview with NBC News on Friday. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans.”

Cruz, in turn, denied he was thinking about 2028 yet and suggested Vance may have a chip on his shoulder. “In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure,” Cruz told Politico on Saturday. “So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes.”

Yes, please continue making whatever comments you like, JD! In fact, I’d strongly suggest you take it up a notch and remind people of Cruz’s greatest hits. There was the time he fled to Cancún on holiday when his state, Texas, was facing deadly, record-breaking freezing temperatures, for example. And the time his official Twitter account “liked” a pornographic tweet (apparently it was “a staffing issue, and it was inadvertent”). And there’s the longstanding joke, which started with a meme in 2013, that Cruz is the Zodiac killer. Obviously, this was baseless, but it went viral because apparently it is believable. Indeed, a 2016 poll found that 10% of voters in Florida thought Cruz was the Zodiac killer and an additional 28% said they were not sure.

That said, Vance should be careful about what he dishes out: he’s been the subject of a few memes himself. Who can forget the (completely unfounded) viral rumours about the vice-president having sexual relations with a couch?

While Vance and Cruz may be butting heads now, I suspect they’ll eventually kiss and make up. They are pragmatists, which is a polite way to say soulless opportunists. They had similar journeys when it comes to Trump, for example. In 2016, Cruz called Trump, who nicknamed him Lyin’ Ted, a “serial philanderer” and a “pathological liar”. Around the same time, Vance wondered if Trump was “America’s Hitler” and called him “the most-raw expression of a massive finger pointed at other people”. Now, of course, it’s a very different story. Vance is veep and Cruz has become such a staunch Trump ally that the president calls him Beautiful Ted.

With the news as grim as it is, you’ve got to find satisfaction where you can. And it’s certainly satisfying to watch Vance (who absolutely does not fornicate with furniture) and Cruz (who is definitely not the Zodiac killer) feud. Ultimately, though, it may turn out that we don’t have to worry about either man come 2028. MS Now’s Rachel Maddow thinks the president may follow the authoritarian playbook and install a family member as his successor.

“If he wants [his family] to not end up in jail or prosecuted or having their … gains investigated … he’s got to make sure that the next president is also a Trump,” Maddow opined on a recent podcast. Potus himself has said “there could be” a Trump dynasty and seemed to suggest his daughter-in-law Lara may be his successor. Take a seat on a comfy couch for this one, JD: you’re going to have a tough time trumping a Trump.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: NFL today: How to watch Buccaneers v Cowboys, TV channels & live stream Thursday 8 October
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Alex Kirshner
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
How will the Buccaneers and Cowboys fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options

The bad news for the Buccaneers: Their 0-4 start has been an unmitigated disaster that, in normal circumstances, would have already evaporated their playoff chances. The good news for Tampa Bay, however, is that they play in the NFC South, meaning they’re still just two games out of a tie for the lead in what is often the worst division in the NFL. All is not quite lost yet.

If the Bucs want to join the 1992 Chargers and become the second team to make the postseason after an 0-4 opening, they’ll need to stop the bleeding on Thursday night in north Texas. They’ll have to do it without Baker Mayfield, who continues to nurse an injury to his throwing thumb.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

They’ll face a challenge against the Cowboys, who are just 2-2 but look like slim favorites in the NFC East while the Eagles struggle to get out of neutral. The Cowboys have gotten an excellent first four games from Dak Prescott, who has paced one of the most efficient offenses in football. No team is scoring more than Dallas’ 3.4 points per offensive series, and it’s been Prescott and the passing game doing most of that work. (Nearly 75%t of Dallas’ yards have come through the air, compared to a league average of two-thirds.) A big outing against Tampa Bay would solidify the Cowboys’ path to a division title.

Time: 8.15pm ET/1.15am BST (Friday)

Stadium: AT&T Stadium (Arlington, Texas)

United States: Stream on Prime Video

Canada: Stream on DAZN and Fubo

United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN.

Jerry Jones loves a splashy deal, and he made one before last week’s win over the Texans. The Cowboys sent out a package built around a second-round draft choice to bring in Steelers cornerback Joey Porter, who didn’t make a Pro Bowl in his first four seasons but established himself as one of the league’s tougher man-to-man cover players all the same. The next touchdown Porter surrenders as the primary defender on a target will be the first of his career. Dallas made the deal without giving Porter the new contract that had eluded him in Pittsburgh, suggesting Jones saw his acquisition as a win-now endeavor.

The Bucs will ride for another week, at least, with rookie QB Jalon Daniels. The Kansas product made his debut in Week 4 and finished 27th of the league’s 32 QBs in passer rating that week, and dead last in yardage per attempt. He sprinkled in a pair of interceptions — not an ideal start for a rookie who is about to turn 24 and whose six years of collegiate experience might have suggested a less rocky debut. Will Daniels find it hospitable to go up against the team that is dead-last in the NFL in net yards allowed per passing attempt (8) through the first four weeks? Tampa Bay’s last flickers of hope depend on it.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Senegalese college basketball player freed from ICE as another is detained
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Aminata Seck released on $2,500 bond after two months

Chinese player Qingfang Pang detained since September

Mississippi Valley State express concern for player

A Kentucky State University women’s basketball player from Senegal who was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been released after spending two months in custody.

At a hearing on Tuesday, a judge granted Aminata Seck a $2,500 bond, which was posted on Wednesday after ICE declined to appeal, according to Hishem Alsalman, managing attorney of Alsalman Law Office.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Meanwhile, a men’s basketball player from Mississippi Valley State University has been taken into ICE custody. Qingfang Pang, who is from China, was detained on 29 September and is being held at the Richwood Correctional Facility in Richwood, Louisiana, according to ICE’s detainee database.

“Mississippi Valley State University is aware of the situation involving one of our students and is deeply concerned for the student’s well-being,” the school said in a statement. “The student is registered as a full-time student at Mississippi Valley State University. University officials are closely monitoring the situation and are committed to providing appropriate support as circumstances develop.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said in an email that Pang entered the US legally on 17 November 2023, with authorization to remain until 5 September 2024, but stayed beyond that date.

“He accepted voluntary departure and will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson said. “This administration will not ignore the rule of law.”

Pang spent the past two seasons at Monroe University in New York before transferring to Mississippi Valley State. The 6ft 9in forward averaged 7.3 points and 3.8 rebounds per game at Monroe.

In Seck’s case, the judge found that she was neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk, Alsalman said on Thursday. The judge also ruled that she could continue working toward her degree and praised her academic and athletic achievements.

Seck, 26, was detained on 7 August at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport as she prepared to travel with her team to a tournament.

DHS previously said in a statement that Seck legally entered the US in 2019, then “chose to overstay her welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The agency said an immigration judge had ordered her removed a year earlier after she failed to appear at an immigration hearing.

Alsalman previously said an immigration judge had found that Seck did not receive notice of those proceedings.

Seck, who is from Dakar, Senegal’s capital, was named to the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference (SIAC) all-conference third team last season after leading Kentucky State with 11.7 points and 7.3 rebounds per game.

The 6ft 4in center recorded five double-doubles and scored a season-high 30 points against Lane College on 14 January.

Seck also received the SIAC Women’s Basketball Elite 16 award, the conference’s highest academic honor, which recognizes student-athletes who demonstrate exemplary achievement in both athletics and the classroom.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Victor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency run
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Exclusive by Matt Hughes and Nick Ames
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Confederation president clarifies his intentions to staff

Canadian was eyed as potential rival to Gianni Infantino

Victor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job at Fifa.

The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Montagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members.

At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region.

Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff.

The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years ago after the corruption scandal that culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”.

Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit.

It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total. That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa role

Montagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich.

Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March.

after newsletter promotion

Montagliani, Ceferin and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, are expected to use the council meeting to demand an independent review of FFE and call for broader governance reforms of Fifa, which would give a greater voice to stakeholders and formalise the council’s role in decision-making.

Previous calls from the trio, expressed in letters sent to Infantino last month, for Fifa to allocate a portion of its $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to members will also be discussed.

Delegates at Uefa’s Berlin meeting discussed a framework for Fifa reform, whose key points were made public during the afternoon. Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”.

Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.
