Meanwhile, every week about 300 families shop for free produce and pantry staples at a bus-accessible marketplace hosted by community non-profit Connecting for Children and Families, where Johansen volunteers – although the need is much greater than organizers can accommodate. In the past, “you had a lot of choice”, said Johansen, “so you could shop around for good prices”. She recognizes more local supermarkets jockeying for customers would make provisioning more convenient and affordable.

Restrictive covenants, however, have long stymied that competition. Chains such as Stop & Shop and Walmart often write these provisions into a grocery building’s deed or lease. Commonly, they disallow food from being sold in that spot, sometimes for decades, when the company vacates that store. The company may have opened another location a few miles away and wants customers to travel there; it most assuredly wants to prevent rival grocers from siphoning off shoppers. Supermarket restrictive covenants have flown largely under the radar for half a century, even as they’ve made lingering food deserts out of the communities they presumably serve.

Woonsocket has at least three restrictive covenants that severely limit grocery access for this community – including on the space vacated by Stop & Shop back in 2004. Walmart quit town in 2011, leaving behind yet another restrictive covenant that barred both grocers and pharmacies from moving into its abandoned space.

In attempt to improve the grocery landscape, in July, as part of Lieutenant Governor Sabina Matos’s Fair Price Grocery Agenda, Rhode Island became the second state to ban these so-called “scorched-earth” covenants, a small but growing wave of food security-focused legislation meant to ease the soaring expenses walloping Americans at the supermarket checkout. So far, these covenants have been banned in Chicago; Washington, DC; Madison, Wisconsin; and Bellingham and Seattle, Washington, and then the whole of Washington state. As of this writing, the California state senate was getting ready for a floor vote on its own ban – the last legislative stop before the desk of the governor, Gavin Newsom. Meanwhile, four US senators have requested that the Federal Trade Commission assess its ability to regulate the grocery industry’s use of restrictive covenants, indicating interest in pursuing a federal ban.

Lawsuits claiming that restrictive covenants violate US antitrust law have been brought against grocery companies over the years. Judges have tended to side with the grocers. “[A]ntitrust law exists to prevent reduced output, decreased product quality, or higher prices from harming consumers – not to achieve other ‘multiple goals’ (such as promoting fairness, improving income inequality, or preserving the job market),” one legal scholar wrote.

Laurie Beyranevand, director for the Center for Agriculture and Food Systems at the Vermont Law and Graduate Center, believes vaguely written antitrust laws need redefining. She explained that part of the problem with trying to use these laws to regulate grocers is that they require plaintiffs to “show that there’s a monopoly. But if regionally there are still other grocers that are available, it could be a challenge to demonstrate that there’s some sort of monopoly that they’re holding.” That’s left states and municipalities to figure out their own fixes, piecemeal.

Unearthing restrictive covenants requires extensive sleuthing through state business listings, municipal databases and hundreds of pages of real estate documents. No one has any idea of how many there are. Rhode Island has dug up seven so far, including a 75-year-term one that was buried in a 128-page condominium agreement (although, per earlier state law, it would have been invalid after 30 years). In California, their extent is “the million-dollar question”, said Beth Smoker, policy director at the California Food and Farming Network, an advocacy group that sponsored that state’s bill.

“Hunger is only increasing in California, then at the same time the cost of food is skyrocketing,” Smoker said about the urgency around passing these bans. “The pandemic and tariffs and inflation are contributing to that, and corporate profiteering in the large-scale grocery industry is also a hidden cause. It just became time that we start addressing hunger from multiple angles.”

Matos, the Rhode Island lieutenant governor, only learned about restrictive covenants when she invited the National Supermarket Association (NSA) of independent grocers to sniff out where a new grocery store could be built in Woonsocket. Discovering a covenant on the former Walmart, “I was in disbelief; I couldn’t believe that this was legal,” she said. Such a tailor-made space – a full-size supermarket needs at least 30,000 sq ft that can support massive amounts of plumbing and electricity – should represent a great opportunity for an independent grocer such as Michael Fernandez. He owns a mini chain called Brigido’s Fresh Market and is vice-president of the NSA’s New England chapter. But a covenant means “we can’t even look at it”, he said.

Restrictive covenants leave residents to scratch their heads about why a wealth of grocery choice has dwindled to no choice at all. These agreements, along with high costs and dynamic prices that change based on demand (another target of Matos’s food agenda, meant to protect Snap recipients from a surge just as their benefits arrive), are “slowly strangling us”, said one senior citizen waiting to shop at the non-profit discount Hope Market in East Providence, an area with poor food access and at least two active restrictive covenants. Fernandez calls the Rhode Island ban a “gamechanger for us in our business”.

That’s because bans have worked in other communities. New Zealand passed a country-wide ban in 2022, and since then independent and specialty grocers have begun to thrive. Washington DC saw 20 new grocery stores open in the five years after its 2017 ban, although it’s unclear how strong the correlation is between ban and boon.

Matos admits Rhode Island’s ban is just the first step in improving grocery access. It has no retroactive provision, meaning existing covenants will remain in effect until they run their contractual course; Matos said this was necessary to push some legislation through before Stop & Shop, which controls 42% of the state’s grocery market, had a chance to slap more restrictive covenants on properties as it closes more and more of its stores. Some food security experts, while broadly supportive of the ban, are concerned that, alone, it won’t move the affordability needle much. And few if any municipalities currently have the resources to do what DC did a few years back: pay Safeway almost $4m to release a grocery space from a covenant.

California, on the other hand, wrote into its pending ban a retroactive provision – already used in the state’s housing industry – that allows a would-be grocer to ask the county to void a restrictive covenant. In low-food-access Eureka, this would allow the 15 remaining years on a 50-year covenant to vanish practically overnight.

“Hunger is happening now – we can’t wait 15 years. That’s an entire childhood,” said Smoker. (A spokesperson for the California Grocers Association said that the organization supported efforts to expand food access but that there are “scenarios where lease restrictions are still appropriate for grocers looking to relocate within close proximity to an existing store, in order to invest in and improve its offering for the community”.)

Still, there are other challenges to getting supermarkets up and running in the communities that need them. One of these is a dearth of capital for smaller operators, which Mohammed Zameeruddin has experienced first-hand. He’s the owner of Daily Stop, a grocery store in Providence, with another being constructed in Woonsocket.

Determined to offer culturally relevant foods to Woonsocket’s Muslim, Latino, African and other populations, Zameeruddin leased the only truly viable space in a city with multiple restrictive covenants – a former Sears that requires an extensive and costly retrofit. Financing, however, has been bumpy and has led to delays in opening. “We thought the cost would be $3m or $4m. But it’s costing more than double,” he said. “You’re a small guy but the building, the contractor, the cost of everything is high.” Nevertheless, he hopes to open by December.

Across the road from the future Daily Stop, a restrictive covenant on a site now housing a military recruiting office won’t run out until 2034, so it will be a few years before that can be freed up for another potential grocery space. But in Richmond, south-east of Providence, a lease held by Stop & Shop on a supermarket-ready property recently expired after being vacant for 30 years. The new ban ensures that a restrictive covenant cannot be added to the new lease. (Stop & Shop did not immediately respond to a request for comment on restrictive covenant legislation.) Fernandez hopes all this means things are looking up for independent grocers, who he believes are more responsive to community needs.

“These big stores, they don’t care so much about the neighborhoods that they’re serving. They just respond to shareholders,” he said. “One hundred per cent, we’re a voice, we’re ears, we listen, and we cater the store to the area we’re in.”

At least one resident of Woonsocket is ready for this kind of grocery turnaround. “It’s big,” Johansen said about the competition to Shop Rite that the pending opening of Daily Stop represents. “If they open, it’s huge.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Rhode Island is the second state to ban a full-service supermarket. The state is down to one full-size supermarket serving 45,000 residents. The National Supermarket Association of independent grocers were asked to sniff out where a new grocery store could be built in Woonsocket.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘The silence was the worst part’: after culling his entire flock, US poultry farmer now fears bird flu
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Alissa de Chassey
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
As bird flu reshapes agriculture, small farms operate under strict rules. Just a single case could tank their business

Joshua Beebe often starts his day by cleaning the tires of trucks and cars entering his poultry farm.

“We spray them off and scrub them with a brush. It’s a precaution; the goal is to eliminate as many potential avenues for a pathogen to enter as possible,” said the owner of Tardif Poultry Farm, located in the Connecticut countryside east of Hartford.

Fear of avian influenza, specifically the HPAI subtype A (H5N1) virus, has been tormenting poultry farmers such as Beebe ever since the current wave of bird flu was detected in eastern Canada in 2021 and began spreading. The north-east US is not a high-risk region for on-farm outbreaks, but the possibility is always there. For Beebe and his workers, vigilance comes at a high cost: in time, money and mental strain.

Beebe has already gone through the trauma of being ordered to destroy his entire flock, 5,000 birds in all. In mid-2024, state-mandated testing detected salmonella in some of his birds. The bacterium can spread through eggs, and certain strains can infect and sicken humans.

The normal cacophony of the farm disappeared. “It was emotionally draining,” Beebe said. “I haven’t gone a day without seeing birds when I walk out my door in over 10 years. The silence [was] the worst.” Eight long months of mandatory quarantine on the farm finally ended the following February, and Beebe has been gingerly rebuilding his flock ever since.

Today, the farm is filled with a constant, low noise of about 3,000 birds clucking, chirping and moving. Beebe raises chickens, turkeys, pomeranian geese and a wide variety of ducks, including different breeds of mallards and welsh harlequins. “I really like the toulouse ducks. They’re a French breed,” he said. The farm sells its products directly to customers.

A fifth-generation resident of the town, Beebe bought Tardif Poultry Farm in 2020 after spending 12 years learning the business at a nearby farm. Now he finds himself doing more than just raising animals; he’s also constantly managing risks.

At first glance, the vibe at Tardif seems bucolic enough. At the entrance, a shop in a charming little wooden house displays products from other farms, crafters and artists. Milk, homemade spices and candles are carefully arranged.

Clients and friends can visit the shop, but “no one is allowed in the back where the birds are. Period,” Beebe said.

To guard against an outbreak, the farm strictly segregates the birds by age: from the hatchery to chicks, juveniles, and finally adults. “We have different boots for each station,” he said. Sick animals come last – although “we try not to keep sick animals around at this point”. His three employees follow the same flow, avoiding contact with younger birds, with their weaker immune systems, after handling older ones.

If employees have their own chickens at home, they have to wear a set of shoes specific for Beebe’s farm and come with laundered clothes to avoid extra risk.

Every new bird is placed in quarantine for 21 to 35 days after arrival. When birds die for any reason, their bodies are disposed of by burial or composting. In the event of larger die-offs, carcasses may be sent off-site for incineration, through the Connecticut Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory or the University of Connecticut. “Everything is very organized,” Beebe said.

The risks don’t only come from on-the-ground transmission from bird to bird, or from worker to bird. The overwhelming majority of avian flu introductions into domestic poultry have been traced to contact with infected wild birds – not spread between farms, according to a US Department of Agriculture (USDA) spokesperson.

“The virus is so abundant in the wild bird population,” said Richard Webby, who studies host-microbe interactions at the St Jude Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences in Memphis.

When these wild birds stop near the farm to drink the water, eat the feed or come into contact with domestic birds, the virus spreads. But they don’t even have to land to pose a risk.

When birds fly over farms, “even one gram of bird droppings can contain billions of viral particles”, said Ilaria Capua, an Italian virologist known for her research on avian influenza. And even if the birds are kept indoors, a cat or a mouse walking around could spread the virus.

To prevent direct contact between wild and domestic birds, Beebe uses a lot of netting. He’s also hung reflective ribbon high in the trees and placed fake owls around the farm to scare wild birds off.

The climate crisis may also complicate biosecurity efforts. Studies have shown that warming conditions can change how much migratory waterfowl move, with some wild birds reducing movement and others altering the timing of their migration as temperatures rise, according to Diann Prosser, research wildlife biologist at the Eastern Ecological Science Center. “These behavioral shifts mean birds may stay longer in certain areas,” she said.

Even within the farm, Beebe has to contend with extreme heat. Mixing different bird species in the same coop can create biosecurity risks. Yet during a particularly hot day last year, one of the coops became so overheated that he had to move the ducks in with the chickens. “I’d rather combine them for a day than have them die,” he said.

According to Prosser, this could be a concern. “We know that different [types of poultry] have different likelihoods of infection, such as ducks having more than chickens based on biosecurity practices and individual host responses.”

For some farms, even strict measures haven’t been enough. The virus has affected more than 174 million commercial birds since 2022, and there have been 71 confirmed human cases in the US since February 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

But even in regions where poultry farms are smaller, including New England, avian flu has struck. “I’m following the cases very closely,” Beebe said. Indeed, Connecticut is bordered by states with reported cases, including Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island.

The consequences of having even one confirmed case on a farm are dire. “Once you have one bird positive, you have to depopulate the entire flock. It’s sad, but that’s a mandatory USDA rule,” Indu Upadhyaya, a poultry and food safety expert at the University of Connecticut, said.

Beebe knows all too well what it means to depopulate an entire farm.

On 6 June 2024, state personnel showed up for routine mandated animal testing for bird flu and other diseases. Every three months, they collect samples from 30 birds per species, and once a year they draw blood from 300 birds of each species. They also conduct a swab test for 10% of each species.

A week later, on a sunny afternoon, the results arrived: 11 birds tested positive for suspected salmonella. The state quickly placed the farm under quarantine. “That means no birds out, no birds in,” Beebe said. The farm had to cancel orders with its suppliers, damaging those relationships. “Some rumors were going around locally, saying the farm had diseases, and I didn’t say anything. I wish I had been more educational in being open and in telling people what happened,” he said.

At that point, the farm had no money coming in. It also costs about $800 each day to keep the birds alive. After 30 days, another round of testing showed that a couple of the suspected birds had lower salmonella levels but were still positive.

In July, the state gave the farm two choices: depopulate the flock or retest every single bird. The testing costs $6.50 per bird, a price Beebe couldn’t easily cover. “At the time, we had 5,000 birds,” Beebe said.

Tardif Poultry Farm ultimately had to depopulate. The Thanksgiving turkey season – traditionally an important source of income for the farm, selling between 50 and 100 turkeys – was a total bust.

“I didn’t know what was happening to us,” Beebe said. They began by euthanizing the oldest birds, gassing them with carbon dioxide, double-bagging the bodies and getting rid of them in their own dumpster.

Eventually, they had to cull all the birds. “We caught all of them, we put them in a crate, and we have a chamber, like a box that the crate will fit in. We just turn the gas on for so long; it’s pretty quick,” Beebe said.

It took them about 10 days. “It’s probably longer than it should have been, but it was just so depressing,” he said. “It was eerie.”

The farm was still in quarantine until February 2025. The state finally gave the farm permission to repopulate only after testing almost everything the birds touched, including bedding, fences, coops and dirt. This time, the testing cost was shouldered by the Connecticut department of agriculture. Recovery has been slow. “I worked on the bloodlines of some of the birds for 10 years, and it’s all gone,” Beebe said.

Tardif Poultry will never know where the bacteria came from. Was it from someone driving in? From a wild bird? Something on the clothes of an employee?

The expenses continue to mount as Beebe slowly rebuilds his flock. “We’re still collecting birds back, but they’re not cheap. I think we spent $14,000 just on chickens,” Beebe said. He estimated that the total cost of repopulating his farm is now close to $50,000.

All of these recovery costs fell on the farm alone. Beebe sought indemnity payments from the USDA through the Connecticut department of agriculture but was told the farm was ineligible because the depopulation was considered voluntary. Retesting the birds was an option, officials said, even though it was unaffordable for Beebe.

Bryan Hurlburt, commissioner of the Connecticut department of agriculture, said that farmers bear the responsibility of testing for diseases other than bird flu (in the case of Beebe, the further tests after the first salmonella positive test) on their own.

In terms of depopulation and the financial burden it causes for farmers, “we do not have a program at the current time that would offset any of the losses”, said Hurlburt. The USDA does have indemnity programs that Hurlburt encourages farmers to pursue, but these are tied to specific disease-control programs – most notably for avian influenza – and typically do not apply to other infections, which are treated as a private business risk.

For Tardif Poultry Farm, salmonella turned out to be the wrong disease to have.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: HPAI subtype A virus has been tormenting poultry farmers since the current wave of bird flu was detected in eastern Canada in 2021. The virus has affected more than 174 million commercial birds since 2022. There have been 71 confirmed human cases in the US since February 2024.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Tents, night-vision goggles and bear tracking kits: America’s first nature library opens
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Donna Ferguson. Photographs by Kevin Mohatt
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
As well as books, the new facility in Colorado offers equipment to help connect people with the natural world. We asked five of the first visitors what they thought of it

M
ark Fink knows exactly why he opened the first public nature library in the US. “There are a lot of barriers for people to access nature here. We want people to learn about the birds and the plants in their own back yard and to appreciate that you don’t need a three-day camping trip in the mountains to experience nature.”

The library offers people in Colorado’s Adams county the opportunity to borrow books and equipment to help them to engage with the natural world – for free.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

While most of the 40,000 items in the library’s collection are books, members can also check out 850 nature-focused “try it” kits – anything from birdwatching equipment, gardening tools and wildlife cameras to hiking gear, microscopes and hammocks.

“In the US, as more information has come out about climate change and global warming, there’s been a lot of pushback on those scientific studies and their validity,” says Fink. He is executive director of Anythink Libraries, which opened the Nature Library in August and is funded by a local property tax levy.

“We want to let people make up their own minds. We want to provide opportunities for them to learn more about the climate, the human impact on the Earth and how we can help reduce climate change and make our environment more sustainable,” he says, adding that spending even 20 minutes in nature has physical and mental health benefits.In addition, research suggests that people who have more experience with nature are more likely to be inspired to help protect it.

Built using local stone, the library has 370 solar panels on the roof and a sustainable geothermal heating and cooling system. It sits on a 6-hectare (15-acre) site – a former ranch – with a hiking trail and eight different types of garden, including sensory and pollinator gardens, and two focusing on plants that thrive in Colorado and the nearby Rocky Mountains.

Inside, children can play in a boulder field made up of rocks from a local quarry, plus there are free workshops to help people build their confidence in activities such as birdwatching, gardening and hiking.

We asked five of the first people to visit the library what they thought of it.

I heard about the library on Facebook. I decided to take my mom.

It’s hard for an 88-year-old to go up to the mountains and connect with nature. I work full-time – I’m a pharmaceutical shipping specialist – and although my mom’s pretty independent, she mostly stays home when I’m at work.

There was a peaceful little rock garden outside, and she was able to walk around in there with her walker. At her age, it’s very important to get out of the house and do that.

Then we sat down by the mud pit. That was really cute to see – all these little children running through it and making mudcakes.

My mom loves reading and doing puzzles, and she was surprised to discover she could borrow a wooden puzzle and a Danielle Steel book. She told me it would be too expensive. I said: “Mom, it’s a library.” It was such an impressive building and she couldn’t quite believe that everything was free. It made her so happy.

We’re having a water shortage in Colorado, so when I go back, I’m planning to borrow a book about how to design a drought-friendly garden, like the one I saw there.

I’m a scientist for a science education company – I write curriculum for college students, for labs. I love nature and I love libraries and thought a nature library sounded like a cool place to go, especially with a child.

Asha is growing up in a world where we have to care about and protect our environment. And with the current people in power, it feels like we’re going backwards, and that’s scary. I think she’s going to be forced into making tough decisions to protect the natural world – I think we all are – and I would rather she do that from a love of nature than a sense of doom.

What’s exciting about the library is that it makes nature more accessible to her. She can touch it and interact with it in ways that she can’t when we’re out elsewhere. Also, when I’ve had a stressful week, I want to be able to go outside where I can hear birds and touch grass.

We’re thinking of replacing our lawn, which died over the summer, with plants that can support pollinators, so we borrowed a pollinator-garden planning kit and a couple of bird guides from the library. We live near a lake that the birds of the Rocky Mountains visit – if I can learn to identify them, I can teach Asha their names.

The next time we go, I’d like to borrow a stargazing kit so we can take Asha up into the mountains and look at the stars together.

During our visit, Asha had a great time climbing on the boulders and playing in the mud pit. It was such a fun way for her to connect with nature on a very physical, sensory level and it made me realise that she doesn’t get many opportunities to actually touch some dirt in her everyday life.

We’ve since created a little mud patch in our own garden, which she has really enjoyed playing in. Being in the library has made me recognise that this kind of activity is a good experience for her, it’s building the love of the natural world that I want to foster and nurture in her. It’s worth the mess.

I’m a freelance photographer, videographer and content creator, focusing on outdoor family adventures, so the Nature Library sparked my interest. Camping gear can be expensive and a lot of people don’t know if they want to invest in it. Having tents and hammocks available to borrow is a phenomenal idea.

We borrowed an outdoor camera with a macro lens, which encouraged my son to go out in nature and photograph bumblebees and flowers, and a GPS gadget. We used that to go on an adventure along a very scenic alpine trail, Santa Fe Peak. I didn’t have to convince my son to come with me – he was excited to go because of this gadget. He was able to use it to plan our route and guide me. We picked a spot we had never been to before and explored. It was a perfect all-day adventure.

That gadget would have cost me $300 or $400, and the camera $500, so to be able to check them out without buying was brilliant.

We also borrowed a digital wind-speed meter, and talked about that, too. We watched a whole YouTube series about windmills and wind-power plants, and how the energy is produced and stored.

I think visiting a nature library is a good way to teach children about nature and encourage them to care about the environment and wildlife. Whether my son was climbing on the boulders or playing in the mud pit, time flew by. The trail around the library is also very beautiful and I noticed that in the garden, they have hoses so children can water the plants.

We’ve gone back twice because there’s so much to do, and I’m excited for the winter when I’m thinking of borrowing some snowshoes and micro spikes, and going on hikes to test them out.

In this economy, with families struggling, I love that people are able to go to this library for a few hours and share community resources that can help us build a better future and learn to explore the great outdoors.

We live in Nebraska and decided to go to the library while we were on a trip to the Rocky Mountains. My wife is an architecture designer, so she wanted to see the building and I love the idea of a nature library.

The countryside in the US is beautiful. But I’m from Cuba and when you go into nature there, there is a feeling that it is wild and untouched. There are so many trees and so much wildlife. Here, by comparison, it is quite built up.

My son and I are interested in books about bugs at the moment and enjoyed reading about insects at the library, what they do, how they live and why they are important.

We get a lot of insects in Nebraska and my son doesn’t always realise they aren’t dangerous, especially if they are big and buzzing around. Like every kid, sometimes he gets scared. I think if he knew more, he would probably just say “oh look at this”.

I grew up much closer to nature in Cuba than he is growing up. I’d like to encourage him to go out and do more. I wish there was a nature library near us in Nebraska.

I’m a professor at the University of Colorado in Boulder – I study kids, learning and technology. I do a lot of community engagement work with libraries and I decided to visit because I was curious about what it meant to have a nature library. I also grew up visiting libraries and want my son to do that.

When we arrived, Miles gravitated towards the “try it” equipment and the natural disasters section – he has been interested in tornadoes, tsunamis, earthquakes and wildfires since he was about three.

He grabbed a book on wildfires and decided to borrow a fire sensor. He thought it could sense fire, but actually it’s a tool that measures humidity, temperature and wind velocity and direction, so you can understand if there’s a risk of a wildfire nearby. But we decided that next time we will try to borrow night-vision binoculars and hike one of our favourite trails at twilight.

We also borrowed a bird-watching book and a brochure about animals, insects and trees that can be seen here in Colorado.

I was born in the Philippines, and emigrated to Los Angeles when I was young. I don’t know much about the wildlife of Colorado, although I’ve lived here for 10 years. Until we borrowed that book, I didn’t know what a Steller’s jay was. But because of that book, we were talking about it – and today I saw one. I can’t wait to tell Miles.

We’re not a very outdoorsy family and as someone who grew up in a big city, I feel a bit intimidated by the idea of camping in the mountains. But Miles is always asking to go, and being able to borrow camping equipment from the library makes it easier for us to try it.

I hope going to the library can help me and other transplants to Boulder to feel that the wild open spaces of Colorado are ours, too – that they are there for everyone and we all need to take care of them.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown

T
he mother’s hands were peeling from walking on the torched ground. Her eight-month-old baby, which clung to her side, was dehydrated and thin. The pair, named Mama Abu and Abu (“ash” in Indonesian), were found in an oil palm subsidiary estate, rescuers say.

The orangutan pair were saved last month from wildfires that are devouring Indonesia’s forests and peatland, unleashing thick smog, and destroying the habitat of some of the planet’s most vulnerable species.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Primate specialists from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have called for urgent international assistance to help control the fires, warning this week that thousands of orangutans could be killed, injured or displaced.

Wildfires happen every year in Indonesia, where fire is often used to clear land to make way for palm or pulp plantations. But the arrival of a supercharged El Niño has brought especially dry conditions, causing blazes to spread rapidly across parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan (the Indonesian part of Borneo) and Papua.

The fires have also taken hold across peatland, which is extremely hard to extinguish as it smoulders underground. In its natural state, it should be waterlogged, but over recent decades, vast areas have been drained by industrial agriculture, leaving it highly flammable.

Habitat containing 52% of the total Bornean orangutan population is now affected by the fires, according to a statement from the IUCN’s primate specialists.

They are not the only animals affected, however. Blazes have also spread into the habitats of five gibbon species, all of which are listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List. Geopix, an environmental NGO, warned earlier this month that 4,500 fires had been detected across 21 Sumatran elephant habitats over recent months.

“I believe that the toll on wild animals being burned, dead, because of the fires is huge,” says Dr Karmele Llano Sanchez, a veterinarian and co-founder and CEO of Yiari, a non-profit focused on primate and habitat conservation, which rescues orangutans and other species from torched forests.

Even animals that survive the catastrophe can face long-term consequences. Food availability falls in the aftermath of fires as forests struggle to recover, and the risk of conflict between animals can rise if they are displaced and forced to live closer to each other. Experts believe that, as with humans, there will also be health impacts for animals that have lived with months of dense smog.

So far, more than 20 orangutans, as well as other species such as pangolin, have been evacuated from the fires by Yiari, which is working alongside West Kalimantan’s Natural Resources Conservation Agency, searching the forests for animals in need and responding to reports from the public.

One of the rescued orangutans died, probably due to smoke inhalation.

Others have been found with burns on their hands after touching the scorching ground, or are hungry and dehydrated.

“It hasn’t rained in 80 days here, and everything is dried and burned,” says Sanchez. “[There are] no leaves and no fruits – nothing they can eat.”

Animals that are evacuated are given sedatives through a dart, which can be fired as high as 30 metres into the trees. A team of about 10 people will hold a net to catch the animal as it tumbles from the branches. An adult male orangutan can weigh about 70kg.

If a mother is carrying very young offspring, they usually fall together, with the baby clinging to its mother.

Such evacuations are a last resort, says Sanchez, undertaken when the area of forest is destroyed: “Otherwise they will for sure die.”

There are many animals in peril that simply can’t be reached: proboscis monkeys, which are endangered, Sunda pangolin and snakes – including a python and king cobra – have all been found dead, according to local media reports.

Forestry ​minister Raja Juli Antoni told media the wildfires could continue until early November, with the rainy season expected to arrive late. An estimated 600,000 hectares (1.4 million acres) were damaged by fire in August, according to the environmental group YKAN.

Researchers have observed that large fire events have been followed by unusually high litterfall, where leaves and small branches drop from trees. This is probably because smog has blocked sunlight, preventing photosynthesis, says Dr Susan Cheyne, co-director of Borneo Nature Foundation International, which has conducted studies on the trend.

“Even though the fires are out at this point there is still a knock-on effect on food,” says Cheyne, who is also vice-chair for the International Union for Conservation of Nature primate specialist group section on small apes.

Such die-offs of leaves occur just as dry season returns, just when species such as orangutan need to eat more, as they rely on flowers and leaves rather than the sugary fruits and pulp that are abundant during the rainy season.

Erin Vogel, professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey, says the forest can take years to recover, with trees producing less fruit afterwards, possibly due to a decline in pollinators.

In the longer term, tree diversity across burned peat forests can remain suppressed even 12 years on, research has shown. If fires recur, this risks trapping forests in a permanently degraded state.

The full extent of the long-term impact of the fires on surviving orangutans’ health is unknown. During smoky periods orangutans show ketosis, a sign of increased fat breakdown. It’s believed this is because the smoke raises energy demands, probably by forcing the immune system to work harder.

Research published after the 2015 fires found orangutans called less in heavy smoke, and that they had reduced vocal quality. Most vocal changes persisted for two months after the smoke had cleared and probably signalled changes in health, researchers concluded.

Gibbons, which rely on song to attract mates, cement bonds and defend territory, have also been found to sing less when exposed to heavy smoke.

“We know how [smog] impacts humans in the long term – it can lead to medical problems, breathing problems, asthma, cancer, infections, future lung capacity issues,” says Vogel. “So, I think, there’s no reason to predict that it wouldn’t affect them the same way.”

Further studies are needed, but for now, research sites themselves are threatened by the flames. Both the Tuanan orangutan research station in Central Kalimantan, and Rangkong research station in West Kalimantan, have been threatened by fires in recent weeks. Staff and local people have worked to halt the spread, setting up improvised sprinkler systems and clearing the ground cover. Localised rains have brought some relief at Rangkong, though staff fear this may only be temporary. At Tuanan, where there is still no rain, the fire fighting continues day and night.

Decades of research are at risk, says Vogel, who is co-director of the Tuanan orangutan research programme. Academics there have studied the same trees, 2,500 in total, and the same individual orangutans for 23 years, accumulating a crucial body of long-term data.

The IUCN says “urgent technical and financial support” are needed, but that the emergency response must be followed by greater investment in re-wetting peatland, addressing deforestation, and ensuring burned forests are restored, not converted into plantations.

For now, rescuers continue to search the forests for wildlife at risk. The mother and baby rescued last week are now being held at a quarantine centre run by Yiari.

When it is safe, they will be released in a new location – one with enough food and no other orangutan populations that might compete with them for territory. “We need to look for a location that is safe, that is a good forest,” says Sanchez. “It is not easy. But we are trying to do our best to find a place that is suitable for them.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populations
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Matthew Pearce
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Indigenous communities play crucial role, as ‘genetic bank’ area of wetland offers hope for critically endangered reptile

I
n the 1990s, conservationists in Cambodia feared the Siamese crocodile had disappeared for good. Fishing and hunting had devastated the species throughout the 20th century, leaving populations across its native south-east Asia on the brink of extinction.

But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the remote Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them. Passing this knowledge to researchers surveying the area in 2000 led to an official recording of the species – and bolstered the mission to revive the population.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“[The Chorng] share a spiritual relation between nature, sacred species and the forest,” says Sony Oum, the country director for Conservation International in Cambodia. “They believed that [the crocodiles] were there, and they helped the scientists and researchers to spot the sites.”

Now, more than a quarter of a century on from the initial sighting, a 315-hectare (778-acre) wetland in Pursat province at the northern end of the Cardamom mountains has been formally declared a genetic conservation area to protect the habitat of one of the world’s last wild populations of Siamese crocodiles.

The area, formally designated by Cambodia’s environment ministry on 22 July, will be home to at least 40 Siamese crocodiles that are thought to live there, making it a crucial site for a species still classed as critically endangered​ on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list.

Habitat destruction, poaching and cross-breeding with crocodiles kept on farms have left few genetically intact wild populations of Siamese crocodiles. With small, isolated groups in the wild vulnerable to inbreeding, conservationists say preserving genetic diversity can improve the animals’ ability to reproduce and withstand disease.

Oum describes the site as a “genetic bank” for the species – a population that, if it remains healthy and expands, could one day help support crocodile recovery in Malaysia, Myanmar and Indonesia, where the reptile is thought to have become extinct.

The new protection area is the latest stage in a conservation effort that has undertaken an extraordinary task.

In 2011, the conservation charity Fauna & Flora International set up a Siamese crocodile breeding facility to boost numbers of genetically pure Siamese crocodiles for release into protected rivers.

The charity has released 246 Siamese crocodiles into the wild since then, with 100 of those released since 2024.

“Natural recovery of this species takes a long time,” says Vanny Lou, who manages the Siamese crocodile programme in Cambodia for Fauna & Flora. “This is one of our approaches to boost the species’ recovery from the brink of extinction.”

“We have 648 individuals [at the breeding centre], including the parents,” he says. “Seventy-one of those are breeding parents – 54 female and 17 male.” Lou says it takes three to four years to get a baby crocodile to the appropriate age and size to release back into the wetlands.

Before release, some crocodiles are fitted with acoustic tags, allowing conservationists to track where they move and target protection efforts. Local community wardens then help monitor the animals and their habitats.

The wardens help the conservation organisations by identifying potential nesting sites, monitoring rivers, patrolling for illegal fishing and poaching, and reporting threats to government officials. And who better than the people who put the species back on the map – the Chorng.

Oum says the fact that Chorng communities have lived alongside the crocodiles for generations and regard them as sacred guardians of the rivers and forests makes them the perfect people to assist the conservation.

“The Indigenous people have a strong belief in the connection to nature,” says Oum. “They do some cropping and farming alongside the river, and when the Siamese crocodiles come to destroy the crops, [the Chorng] smile happily and feel blown away. They’ve been coexistent for a long time.”

In 2024, five wild Siamese crocodile nests containing 106 eggs were found in the Cardamom mountains. Community wardens monitored them and saw 60 hatchlings emerge – the species’ largest recorded breeding event in the wild this century.

“Without active involvement from the community as the frontline, our programme would not be successful,” says Lou.

Sim Khmao, a Chorng community warden, says they are happy to do it. “They are not afraid of the crocodiles,” he says. “They understand them – because they have been here since our ancestors’ period.”

But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: This is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Daniel Shailer in Vevring, Norway
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it

S
hortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said.

The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

These feelings of elation were short-lived. While Førsund and others celebrated, a government lawyer appeared on a television debate show to set out plans for a new temporary permit, and to allow the mine to continue to release waste directly into the fjord in the meantime. Four days later, the mine applied for fresh permission, and in late September, it was granted by Norway’s climate and environment ministry.

“When we heard the pollution would continue, it was like they snatched the carpet from under us,” says Førsund. “We have answered every letter, commented on every consultation, complained whenever we could. We have been knocked down so many times and this could have been the opportunity for change.”

While the government insists that it is acting lawfully, critics say the dumping threatens to foul one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. Others worry that the decision heralds a new wave of permits to pollute Norway’s fjords in the race to secure critical minerals.

“This is not only about the fjord and us and our lives,” says Førsund. “This is about principles. When you have a government that doesn’t respect the supreme court you’re changing the system itself.”

The move comes just as a wider spotlight is being shone on the issue of polluted waters in Norway. A recent report showed that Norwegian fish farms are filling fjords and other coastal waters with nutrient pollution equivalent to the raw sewage of tens of millions of people each year.

Meanwhile, populations of Atlantic salmon are at a historic low in the country – 155 of Norway’s 450 or so salmon rivers were closed to fishing at the start of the season this year.

Submarine tailings deposition (STD) – known colloquially by Norwegian critics as “fjord dumping” – is the process of pumping crushed rocks and chemical waste into the sea through pipelines hundreds of metres underwater. Proposed as an alternative to disposing of waste on land, the Norwegian government’s own Institute of Marine Research (IMR) warns that STD releases fine particles of toxic waste that can accumulate in smaller sea life and disrupt ecosystems at large.

STD is outlawed in all of North America, Australia, Russia, Brazil, China and most of Europe. The few countries that still permit the practice include Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Turkey.

The Engebø titanium mine, on Førde fjord near Vevring, was first proposed by Nordic Mining in 2006 and the government awarded a permit to release waste into the fjord less than 10 years later. In response, Friends of the Earth Norway launched legal challenges that worked their way up the country’s legal system, arriving at a week-long supreme court hearing in spring 2026. Meanwhile, the mine came online and began releasing waste late in 2024.

Nordic Mining is financed by investors including Japan’s Iwatani Corporation and the British offices of the international banks Morgan Stanley, UBS and Goldman Sachs. Other banks, including Standard Chartered and Citigroup, explicitly ban financing projects using STD.

Nordic Mining did not respond to repeated requests for comment from the Guardian, but said in a social media post shortly after the supreme court decision that it would continue with how it disposed of waste, with the encouragement of Norwegian officials.

“It has been said that our operation is illegal, that we have to close, that our work must stop. That is not the situation,” Nordic Mining said, adding that it was continuing “with the ambition to act responsibly, with respect for the fjords and mountains, and for the local community around us”.

Legal wrangling over the permit came to focus on the EU’s water framework directive (WFD), which applies to Norway as a member of the European Economic Area. The WFD allows industrial activities to pollute water bodies only when there is an “overriding public interest”.

The supreme court ruled that the reasons given when the permit was first awarded were not strong enough. However, the government argues they have grown stronger since the EU added titanium to its list of “critical minerals” in 2020.

“The Norwegian government considers the Engebø project to be of significant importance for Norway and Europe,” a ministry spokesperson said, because “the Engebø mountain contains one of the world’s largest known deposits of rutile, a titanium-bearing mineral. Within Europe, Norway and Ukraine are the only countries with significant resources of this kind.”

Legal scholars have questioned this logic. “That’s wrong. A permit exists or it doesn’t, and the supreme court decision is quite clear: the permit is illegal,” says Tarjei Ellingsen Røsvoll, associate professor of administrative and constitutional law at the University of Inland Norway.

“The government is then openly allowing a company to dump a bunch of stuff in a fjord illegally. That is unprecedented; it damages trust and undermines a fundamental structure of constitutional and administrative law. They should take responsibility for having made an invalid and illegal decision, morally and legally.”

While Nordic Mining awaited its new three-year permit, it continued to dispose of waste into Førde fjord. Økokrim, Norway’s central office for white collar and environmental crime, is now considering whether to investigate the dumping for illegality.

While there have been few comprehensive studies of the impact of STD on marine ecosystems, scientists have linked heavy metal pollution now present in some fjords to STD decades earlier.

The impact is particularly damaging when the waste is milled into small pieces, according to Terje van der Meeren, a research professor at the IMR, who co-authored the institute’s response to the Engebø mine application and testified during the supreme court hearings.

“It’s like flour,” says Van der Meeren, adding that waste from Engebø includes a chemical that degrades into carbon disulphide, a neurotoxin. “Our concern is that this fine dust will pass into the rest of the fjord. What will happen with the [fish] spawning in this fjord? We don’t know.”

In 2016, Van der Meeren and other IMR researchers travelled to the Arctic Repparfjord, in Hammerfest in the far north of the country, where a copper mine dumped waste for six years in the 1970s. Decades later, they found haddock with higher levels of lead, arsenic and chromium in their muscles than those in nearby waters, according to research published this year. Other Norwegian studies have found historic STD contamination in plankton, crabs and fish eggs.

Back in Vevring, Førsund and other campaigners are now preparing for a fresh legal battle over the temporary waste permit – though dumping is likely to continue for as long as it takes for a new decision to be reached.

She looks back on the first protests against the mine with nostalgia. In one photograph, taken more than a decade ago, protesters gathered for a meal on the banks of the fjord; Førsund’s daughter, now an architect, was only a child. “So many of these people are dead now,” she says.

“The fjord is bigger than us. It has given us food and income and meaning and music and fish and birds for thousands of years. Now it gives us the energy to keep fighting.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Norwegian government gives permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord. Decision comes despite 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it S. The EU added titanium to its list of ‘critical minerals’ in 2020.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Annaliese Smith in Greenland
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
As trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood species

‘W
hen I accidentally catch a shark, I bring it to my dogs,” Henrik Jensen, a 27-year-old from Greenland’s west coast, says casually. “I don’t let it back down because [the sharks] bully me and cut my lines.”

Jensen has fished for halibut in Ilulissat, Greenland’s third largest town, for a decade. He works an hour north of the town’s main iceberg-laden fishery, which sustains the livelihood of nearly 400 fishers. There, the halibut are bigger and more plentiful, but so are the Greenland sharks.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“This year I’ve lost around 6,000 hooks in total. Sometimes we lose 30,000 Danish krone [£3,440] a day,” says Jensen.

The Greenland shark is one of the least understood species on the planet. As well as being the world’s slowest shark, it is the second-largest carnivorous species, after the white shark, according to the Shark Trust. Reaching about six to seven metres in length, they can live for more than 400 years. For a long time they were thought to be completely blind, although scientists have recently discovered this may not be true.

The sharks inhabit a vast range across the deep and cold waters of the north and west Atlantic, but their attempts to feed on the northern fisheries’ main catch – Greenland halibut and Atlantic cod – often see them tangled in gear and brought in as bycatch.

This acrimonious coexistence has been documented ever since targeted fishing for the sharks’ liver oil ceased in the 1960s, but it came to a head earlier this year. The Avannaata municipality, of which Ilulissat is the administrative seat, approved a controversial plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering 300 krone for every heart of a Greenland shark.

Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of the municipality, says: “We need to safeguard the income of fishermen and the catch so that we can continue to eat the foods that we have relied on for generations.”

For many fishing inshore, working in small teams on dinghies, it brought a longstanding issue to a head. Timotheus Petersen, chair of the fishing association in Kullorsuaq, says: “Our longlines are expensive – one costs 1,599 krone. When the sharks cut our lines, we cannot finish fishing. We have to spend more money and buy new gear.”

The plan was eventually dropped after the government questioned its legality, but the prospect of a future cull remains.

In its decision to approve the cull, Avannaata council cited a similar scheme from the early 2000s in the former Aasiaat municipality, where a bounty of 200 krone was offered. According to a 2007 report from the Danish Technical University, another scheme between 1986 and 2001 in the former Uummannaq municipality brought in 19,697 hearts.

But the marine conservation group Oceans North Kalaallit Nunaat (ONKN) argues that culls do not resolve the issue, highlighting the migratory nature of the species, which can swim up to 1,200 miles (2,000km) a year. “Sharks removed in north-west Greenland would quickly be replaced by individuals arriving from other regions,” ONKN warned.

Many fishers also do not consider 300 krone worth the effort of hauling a shark onboard. “It’s difficult to catch them,” Jensen says. “You need bigger hooks and chains for the lines, so I don’t think anyone wants to try.”

But the debate around a possible cull is alarming conservationists. “If somebody says, ‘I’m going to cull a couple of thousand Greenland sharks’, that’s a disaster in my opinion,” says Prof Nick Dulvy, a marine conservationist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia.

The Greenland shark is believed to become sexually mature at 150, which means the species replaces itself extremely slowly and will not rebound from a cull quickly. It is still recovering from targeted fishing throughout the 19th and mid-20th centuries, when, at its peak in 1948, 58,000 were landed.

“They are probably – biologically – the most sensitive species in the ocean to overfishing,” Dulvy says. Globally, it is estimated that 3,500 sharks are caught every year as bycatch and the population remains in decline.

Greenland’s fishing community highlight their longstanding problem with the sharks, but do not say why it has suddenly escalated. Jenseeraq Poulsen, the director of ONKN, suggests it is due to mounting pressures within a fishing industry that accounts for about 25% of Greenland’s GDP.

“If every Greenland shark in Baffin Bay vanished tomorrow, the inshore fishery in Avannaata would still face too many boats working a quota under pressure, rising costs and no alternative employment,” he says. “When margins are narrow, a longstanding nuisance becomes intolerable.”

Even though the price of halibut continues to rise, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the average size of the fish is decreasing annually. While Jensen maintains he can still make a good living from fishing, he describes putting fewer hooks out and bringing in fewer fish, suggesting this is due to overfishing by offshore trawlers.

For some of those fishing these waters, however, the shark is not the leading cause of losing gear. “There are more and more ‘ghost lines’ and they are too heavy to pull up by the machine we use,” Jensen says. Ghost lines are discarded or lost gear that can get entangled with new lines, breaking equipment and trapping marine life.

Halibut Greenland, a cooperatively owned fish-processing company in Ilulissat, provides funds to clean up ghost gear in the area, which ONKN views as more effective than a shark cull. Poulsen also proposes a gear-loss compensation scheme, as well as funded trials of acoustic shark deterrents.

Rebekka Nygård Bak, an adviser to Greenland’s Ministry of Fisheries, Hunting, Agriculture and Self Sufficiency, suggests new bycatch-friendly equipment regulations could be a solution. She says a campaign for better bycatch reporting will also be key to any next steps.

For Poulsen, the sharks and those fishing these waters are two components of the same ecosystem, facing growing pressures in changing seas. “The shark is the visible, tangible version of a problem whose real drivers are structural,” he says.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Karen McVeigh
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Fish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline

I
nside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west of Scotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs.

It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The coastline here, a metallic grey seen through the bothy’s windows, is dotted with beds of one of the UK’s most biodiverse and carbon-rich habitats, a 9,000-year-old pink seaweed called maerl, two of which are a mile long. This rare, fragile and threatened seaweed produces hard, chalky, coral-like skeletons that provide nurseries for scallops and fish.

Now, 10 years after local people, divers, activists and creel fishers ran a successful campaign to have scallop dredging banned by law in a 600 sq km (150,000 acre) zone now designated a marine protected area (MPA), they say they have already witnessed a dramatic revival of marine life. The transformation of a seabed damaged by decades of dredging has allowed the recovery of scallop populations and ended the fractious territorial battles between the industrial dredge fishing boats and the smaller, more sustainable creel boats, local people say.

The community rowing club and nearby tour operators report increased sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. A large spawning ground for herring, once plentiful here but since overfished, has been spotted nearby and in prawn and lobster creels, or pots, which are laid on the seabed.

Diyanne Ross, 65, the local artist who made the lanterns, is part of the Blue Hope Alliance (BHA), a coalition of groups using citizen science to protect marine ecosystems in the north-west Highlands. She says the community’s achievements in protecting underwater habitats was the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles. It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”

As a child, Ross remembers going out to sea for “boxes” of haddock, ling, pollack and cod – before populations declined. But she has seen recent signs of recovery. “There is more variety of fish being caught here than before,” she says. – anglers are catching haddock and cod.”

Outside on the pier, a hardy angler on holiday from Glasgow who has braved the wind to catch what he can, is rewarded by three fresh mackerel.

The recovery of scallop stocks, says Alasdair Hughson, a scallop diver, Scottish Creel Fishermen’s Federation (SCFF) chair and one of the BHA’s founders, has been “massive” and the seabed transformation like “night to day”. A decade ago, a boat supplying hand-dived scallops to his company, Keltic Seafare, would spend just two weeks in the Summer Isles.

Hughson, whose firm supplies shellfish to UK restaurants, admits his business stands to gain from the dredge ban, but says hand-diving is more sustainable, a claim backed up by research from Open Seas. The marine conservation organisation found low-impact fishing methods, such as diving and creeling, are not only more sustainable than dredging or trawling but that more of the revenue generated stays in the local economy.

Now, the Donna Marie creel boat, skippered by Ullapool-based Gary Lewis, runs to the Summer Isles almost all year. Lewis, who used to have to travel farther, to Skye and the Western Isles, before the dredge ban, says: “It’s not just the catch that’s improved, but the general health of the seabed.”

Central to the weekend-long Maerl-Herring festival celebrations, which includes storytelling, artworks and film, is the public launch of a BHA report spanning a decade of citizen science studies.

Jason Hall-Spencer, a professor of marine biology at Cyprus University of Technology, who wrote the report, says it shows the dredge ban in Wester Ross’s MPA, set up to protect the slow-growing maerl habitats and other marine features, has done its job. It has “protected the maerl to a massive extent” he says.

Author of the Conservation Status of Maerl Habitats in north-west Scotland, partly funded by NatureScot, Hall-Spencer has carbon dated the maerl in the bay as 9,000 years old.

“If scallop dredgers had spent the last 10 years going up and down here, the habitat would be obliterated,” he says. A single pass of heavy towed gear such as that used by scallop dredgers can crush or bury up to 70% of maerl. “The seabed is now incredibly rich. Maerl is a very important habitat, chock full of bivalves which provide food for skates and rays.”

Peter Drake, 73, a retired prawn fisherman from Polbain, a hamlet that is part of Achiltibuie, was part of Sea Change Wester Ross, a campaign group supported by SCFF, which grew into BHA. “It’s good to remember what we have achieved here” says Drake. “There’s already an improvement in fish populations, but it will take time.”

Orfhlaith McDevitt, 25, who has lived here for two-and-a-half years and runs Coigach Community rowing club, says: “People from the club say they see more minke whales, dolphins and porpoises than they did 10 years ago.”

Years before Ocean, David Attenborough’s documentary, sparked outrage by showing footage of scallop dredgers bulldozing the seabed, causing damage that could be seen from space, Sea Change and the SCFF compiled a body of evidence of the devastation scallop dredgers were doing to fishing grounds and seabeds in Wester Ross.

The dossier was presented to Scottish ministers in parliament. In 2016, despite fierce opposition by the dredging lobby, scallop dredging was forbidden by law in the Wester Ross MPA, now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl. Prawn trawling is permitted in designated areas, while hand-diving for scallops and creel fishing by local boats under 150 gross tons, is also permitted.

The maerl’s three-dimensional structure allows high levels of oxygen, essential to scallops, and emits a chemical that attracts them.

But threats to the ecosystem remain: the BHA surveys, also highlighted damaged maerl in some locations – from illegal dredgers and from invasive algal growth that scientists believe could be caused by nutrients from salmon farms.

“We know that salmon farms put more nutrients into the water,” says Sara Nason, a journalist and documentary maker who founded Sea Change, which later became the BHA and organised the Maerl-Herring festival.

The BHA has now launched a three-year project with more than £153,000 of support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional funding from members of the North & West District Salmon Fishery Board, to continue its work.

Elsehere, the battle for Scotland’s sea rages on. The Scottish government, which was criticised in June by the independent watchdog Environmental Standards Scotland for not fulfilling its legal duty to restore and protect the seabed, has launched a public consultation on improving protections for marine habitats and species inside and outside the MPA network.

Theresa Ross, who runs Achiltibuie Stores for the community of about 250 people living along this stretch of coastline, says the MPA is “fully supported” by local people as it “ensures fishing is more sustainable”.

But for a rural coastal community, where the sea supports livelihoods and few jobs exist, there are competing concerns, she says.

“There are more people working on the fish farm here than fishermen,” says Ross, whose husband is one of about six fishers in the village, while her son is one of 10 working on the farms.

“I support the status quo. But the fish farms are full-time jobs, guaranteed employment and well paid,” she says. “They are not weather dependent, like fishing.”

Nevertheless, Nason is one of many who are delighted that the end to dredging has been such a success, describing the protection of the maerl beds as “beyond priceless … We’ve achieved recovery of the whole ecosystem.”
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Scallop dredging has allowed the recovery of scallop populations and ended the territorial battles between industrial dredge fishing boats and the smaller, more sustainable creel boats. The Wester Ross MPA is now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Can hope save the planet? An endangered parrot that is beating the odds can help us find out | Helen Pilcher
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Helen Pilcher
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key

The new Living Planet Report is out. Published every two years, it assesses the health of the natural world and, historically, it’s made for gloomy reading.

Take 2024’s report, which showed global wildlife populations had plummeted by 73% in 50 years and that ecosystems were being pushed toward collapse.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

After reading it, I retired to a dark room and drank gin, but every time I popped my head out, there was more bad news: heatwaves, floods, wildfires and mass coral bleaching.

So, when this year’s edition dropped, I braced myself. But there was a plot twist. Biodiversity is still being pummelled, but not everywhere. According to the new report, conservationists have prevented the extinction of 32 birds and 16 mammals since 1993, and the numbers of wild tigers, elephants and sea otters are stable or growing. The energy sector has historically been extremely damaging to the planet, accounting for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the report notes we have passed a positive tipping point in the energy system, with the transition to renewables snowballing and coal use declining in many wealthy countries.

I can therefore see why the report is titled The Science of Hope.

But pegging it on hope is a bold move. People who write about the natural world, myself included, face a difficult choice. Focus on the bad news, and risk shouting into a void where people simply don’t want to listen. Focus on the good news and risk peddling “hopium” – stories that dull the pain briefly but do little to spur action.

The report, however, isn’t talking about your average kind of hope. It’s talking about a geeky kind of hope rooted in psychological research.

The American psychologist Charles “Rick” Snyder spent decades studying hope and came up with a surprisingly practical definition. Hope, he argued, starts with a goal but also requires pathways, or ideas about how to get there, and agency: the belief that you can make a difference. To this, the Living Planet Report adds another ingredient: resilience – the capacity to keep going when progress stalls. Or, as British anarchist punk band Chumbawamba famously put it: you get knocked down, but you get up again.

We can illustrate this point by looking at New Zealand’s kākāpō, the world’s fattest, greenest, least-able-to-fly parrot. When non-native predators drove the kākāpō to the brink of extinction, conservationists didn’t waste time wishing its numbers back up. In the mid 1990s, they moved the remaining birds to predator-free islands, and when recovery was slow, they changed tack.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

They experimented with hand-rearing, foster mothers and artificial insemination. They fitted the birds with smart transmitters and monitored them almost obsessively. When new technology came along, they embraced it: the genomes of every living bird have now been sequenced to inform decisions about who should breed with whom.

This is what real hope looks like. It’s not the same as optimism – the expectation that things will work out. Nor is it wishful thinking. And it’s certainly not “hopium”, which can make the problem seem smaller than it is. Real hope has its sleeves rolled up and is prepared to get messy. It leaves room for uncertainty and failure but refuses to believe that there’s nothing left to do. That’s why the opposite of hope isn’t despair. It’s inaction.

Scientists who have studied hope have found it matters what we’re hopeful about. A 2023 meta-analysis found that people who felt hopeful about their ability to make a difference were more likely to engage with the climate crisis – from seeking information and supporting climate policies to taking everyday action to reduce their environmental impact. Those whose hope rested on the belief that the climate crisis wasn’t really a problem were less likely to engage.

In other words, useful hope needs to be grounded in reality. And that requires knowing what we’re up against. This was why the Starmer government’s decision not to publish the full national security assessment on global biodiversity loss is so frustrating. The public has since seen an abridged 14-page version. But the detail – and any devil within it – likely remains hidden.

Produced by the Joint Intelligence Committee, it asks a stark question: what would ecosystem collapse mean for the UK?

The answer is bleak: threats to national security and prosperity, havoc wroughtwith food and water supplies, a surge in irregular migration and even more geopolitical instability around the world.

To find a way through the climate crisis, we need both a clear view of the problem and the determination to tackle it. How can we find the right pathway if we don’t have the full map?

In 1995, there were just 51 kākāpō. Today, there are 324, a remarkable turnaround for such a slow-breeding bird. Conservation plans are still evolving, and the species isn’t out of the woods yet. But at least it has a fighting chance.

That’s the kind of hope we need: pragmatic, resilient and open to revision. We need our governments to be honest about the scale of the challenge we face. Because when they withhold information, they don’t just rob us of knowledge. They also rob us of hope.

Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects
