Not signed in before? Continue with Google

On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.

Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day.

Their unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026.

Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-west England. However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.”

Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.”

Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.”

Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’”

Even those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.”

The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault.

Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”.

Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.”

The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP.

But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not.

Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.”

The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said.

She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident.

“I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.”

Edward, a trans man, was travelling home to Staffordshire with his partner, a trans woman, after a weekend in Wales. On a packed train from Aberystwyth, a man began loudly making homophobic comments and became confrontational.

“Normally in that situation I just walk on, but I physically couldn’t, we were so crammed,” Edward said. He finally yelled back, repeating: “You’re shouting homophobic abuse in front of your children.”

A railway worker eventually intervened and told the assailant and his family to move to another carriage. Edward chose not to report the incident to police, dissatisfied with the response to previous incidents. He now tries to avoid public transport: “I felt tearful, angry and scared afterwards.”

A fraction of passenger reports end up with arrest or prosecution. Last year, Sam was travelling north from London on a train packed with football supporters. As she tried to reach her reserved seat, a drunken man confronted her and pushed her backward.

She instinctively pushed him back. “Then I thought, what have you done?” she said. Other men began throwing beer cans while one held her by her rucksack. “I was being pushed and shoved … they were throwing punches as well.”

Amid the assault, one man deliberately grabbed her breasts. “I realised: ‘Oh no, I’m trapped on here with them for the next two hours’,” she said. “There’s nowhere to go. There’s nowhere to get off.”

Two BTP officers on the train got through to take a statement from Sam. The investigation was later dropped after police were unable to identify her assailant.

The experience had a big impact, leaving her “not doing a lot of things I used to do. It’s put me off trains massively. I think if faced with a train like that, I would just not board it.”

The BTP assistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us.”

He noted that when staff had body-worn recording, police brought offenders to justice in about 85% of incidents. “Anyone who witnesses violence or abuse on the railway should report it to us by texting 61016, or call 999 in an emergency,” he said.

The Department for Transport said the rise in assaults was “deeply concerning and unacceptable”. It has awarded a £63m increase in BTP funding by 2028-29, allowing more than 200 additional officers to be recruited, and investments in better CCTV and body-worn video. Dozens of new BTP officers will be specialised in tackling violence and intimidation against women and girls.

* Names have been changed

The headline of this article was amended on 4 October 2026 to correctly refer to Great Britain rather than the UK.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Alex Daniel
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports

Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.

The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.

In a translated document released on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet.

“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.

The alert follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.

Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.

Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’s bestselling car in March.

MPs have raised concerns that China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.

The UK Ministry of Defence has said it is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.

This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, including RAF Wyton in Cambridgeshire and the Dorset headquarters of Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS.

The AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.

The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.

It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.

On Wednesday, MI5 issued a rare public warning to UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.

The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: When her ‘soul cat’ died, she was bereft. Now she designs memorial jewelry to help others with pet loss
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Ashley Stimpson
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
A layoff and a leap of faith convinced Katie Teixeira she had what it takes to run her own business

I
n 2010, Katie Teixeira adopted a kitten found all alone in an abandoned house. The kitten – so tiny she fit in the palm of Teixeira’s hand – needed to be bottle-fed every few hours. For weeks, Teixeira set her alarm for middle-of-the-night feedings and drove home on her lunch break to care for the kitten she named Milo. As the cat grew, so did the connection between them.

“We just bonded,” Teixeira says. “Like mother and daughter.”

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

Eventually, Teixeira and her husband adopted four more cats, but Milo, a tabby with white toes, maintained a special place in Teixeira’s heart. “People talk about soul animals,” she says. “Milo was my soul cat.”

When Milo died in 2021, Teixeira was bereft. She wanted a way to commemorate her. While Teixeira, who was working as a procurement analyst for CVS Health at the time, had seen pet memorial jewelry online, keepsakes that sometimes included the animal’s ashes or fur, “it just didn’t speak to me”, she says. “I’ve always been artistic and very crafty. So I was like, let me try doing something myself.”

It took a few years for inspiration to strike, but in 2023, Teixeira made a ring using a few of the whiskers Milo had shed while she was alive, crisscrossing them over a shimmering silver resin.

What happened next, she says, “happened very fast”.

When Teixeira wore the ring to her next volunteer shift at PawsWatch, the cat shelter near her home outside Providence, Rhode Island, she was inundated with requests from people who wanted their own. Soon, Teixeira was making dozens of pieces, which she began posting on her social media accounts. When one of her Instagram reels went viral, her inbox swelled with questions and requests. So Teixeira took two days off from work and built a website. Just three months after she made her first ring, Fallen Whiskers was born.

For a while, the business was Teixeira’s side hustle, a passion project that filled her nights and weekends and allowed her to support the shelter, where she donates a portion of her proceeds. But then, in 2024, she was laid off from her job of 20 years.

Friends and family encouraged her to make her side hustle a full-time gig.

“I remember saying to her, and I know it’s cliche, that when one door closes, another opens up,” says Donna Lilla, the operations manager at PawsWatch. “It just felt meant to be.”

But Teixeira wasn’t so sure.

“I was terrified,” she remembers. Her husband’s work as a heavy equipment operator could sustain the family only for so long. But her startup costs would be minimal; all she needed was a small stockpile of ring and necklace settings, the mica powder she used to create the resin backgrounds – and the whiskers, teeth and claws of pet owners who put their trust in her. She decided to test the business out, only for a few months.

Two years later, Teixeira fills about 15 orders a week for pieces that sell for $125 to $150. She has more than 100,000 Instagram followers. Her customers speak about her in adoring terms.

“She’s doing God’s work,” says Rebecca Snyder, a non-profit professional from Westchester county, New York, who remembers the day she lost her cat Emma as “literally the worst day of my life”. The pain was so overwhelming, the 40-year-old sought grief counseling.

Snyder says the matching teardrop ring and pendant necklace that Teixeira designed, with whiskers laid over a pearlescent green resin that matched the Maine Coon’s eyes, provided tremendous comfort: “I felt like I had done Emma justice by honoring her in such a beautiful way.”

Teixeira has incorporated whiskers, ashes, fur, teeth, claw sheaths, reptile skins, horse mane, hedgehog quills, bones and bits of favorite toys and blankets into cufflinks, bracelets, earrings and necklaces. (All materials must be shed naturally or collected after death, she said.) She has made a pendant of lion whiskers for a zookeeper mourning the big cat and another pendant of tiger whiskers for the sanctuary worker who cared for the rescued animal.

Fallen Whiskers is a part of a broader shift in how Americans view their pets. According to the Pew Research Center, 97% of owners consider their animals to be part of the family; more than half say their pet is as much a part of their family as a human member. Also on the rise: the amount of money pet owners are willing to spend on their animals, during their lives and afterwards, including on things like cremation, burial, memorial services and the kinds of bespoke consumer goods Teixeira produces.

Americans spent $157bn on their pets in 2025, up from $90bn in 2018, according to the American Pet Products Association.

“I’m still kind of wrapping my head around the fact that I am where I am right now,” Teixeira says of being able to earn a living from her passion project. “I guess I’ve made it.”

But “making it”, she’s learned, is very much a job that never ends.

When she started out, Teixeira tried to do her own accounting using QuickBooks but soon became overwhelmed. She decided to hire a part-time bookkeeper, the only individual on her payroll besides herself. “It’s just one thing I don’t have to worry about, and I can focus more on my customers and my orders,” she says.

Balancing her books has gotten much trickier in the last year. In April 2025, the Trump administration announced a 10% minimum tariff on almost all jewelry-related imports (with some countries and products facing much higher rates), a policy that affects Teixeira, who imports materials she can’t source in the US. A shaky market, meanwhile, has pushed investors into assets like precious metals, a trend that has essentially tripled what she pays for silver and gold.

“I have to extend that cost on to the customers,” she says. “It sucks – period.”

According to the Jewelers of America, an industry group that represents retailers and suppliers, these market shocks “pose a grave threat” to small jewelers like Teixeira, who rely on imported materials and operate on much thinner margins than big box stores. “The uncertainty of an escalating trade war can … potentially jeopardize the livelihoods of small retailers who form the backbone of the US jewelry market,” the group said in a position statement.

Teixeira says she is constantly monitoring her material costs, and, “as needed, adjusting on my side”, a time-consuming chore that takes her away from her workbench.

But according to Teixeira, managing costs isn’t the most difficult part of running Fallen Whiskers – it’s managing her emotions.

“The biggest challenge is the emotional weight of the work that I do,” she says. “Every day, I’m just diving into other people’s grief.”

That’s because Teixeira doesn’t just ask her clients for the fur and ashes they want included in their jewelry. She asks them to tell her the story of their bond with that animal. “And I’ve been there,” she says, “so it stirs up a lot of my own grief.”

While not a requirement, Teixeira says learning about the pet is a part of her creative process, as well as her way of helping other people through the pain of losing a companion.

“I was high-peak grieving, so writing was therapeutic for me,” says Natacha Hein, a clinical research contract specialist at Children’s hospital in Denver. “She helped me get over the hump.”

Hein stumbled upon Teixeira’s work online when she was looking for a way to memorialize Zazu, the “spicy” tabby that transformed the self-professed dog person into a cat person. “I wanted to feel like he was always around me,” Hein said.

The other shops she looked at “didn’t have that interaction piece. Their content felt scripted. There wasn’t a lot of warmth.” The conversations she had with Teixeira made her feel safe to send the jewelry maker precious, irreplaceable materials like fur and ashes. The day Hein received her ring, a smoky green the color of Zazu’s eyes, “was emotional as all hell”, she says. “I give Katie so much credit. It is a beautiful thing she is doing.”

So far, Teixeira has relied solely on word of mouth and daily posts on Facebook and Instagram to market Fallen Whiskers. Demand is growing, but Teixeira – who works on one piece at a time – isn’t in a rush to scale. “I don’t ever want it to feel transactional,” she says. That’s not to say the small-business owner doesn’t have aspirations.

“One day, I’d like to start my own cat sanctuary,” she says. “That’s my big, big dream.”

She and her husband adopted four more cats, but Milo, a tabby with white toes, maintained a special place in Teixi's heart. The Trump administration announced a 10% minimum tariff on almost all jewelry-related imports.

https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.title: Financial bullying can ruin a marriage: first-person stories
https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.author: Jana Kasperkevic
https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.text:
When partners consider finances, when is it ‘my’ money, and when it is ‘our’ money? Guardian readers shared their experiences

A survey of about 1,000 Americans found that one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully. Our readers, however, insist that that might be a label easily assigned to a partner who is simply being financially responsible.

When we put out a call to out readers last week to see if any of them had similar experiences, we found that many of you wouldn’t define the actions described as financial bullying. Instead, quite a number of you insisted that keeping track of your partner’s expenses was simply budgeting and being financially responsible.

Adam: “Having disagreements about spending in a relationship is hardly bullying, it is natural and unavoidable and has happened since the dawn of money.”

Rebecca: “I thought it was called teaching financial responsibility.”

Sean: “Families should work together to maintain a budget, often one spouse is more reckless than the other, that’s not bullying, that’s being responsible.”

Sarah: “Financial bullying?! Sharing a life together and a bank account means both parties get to be involved in spending decisions.”

Nicole: “My husband knows how much money I spend. From a certain amount, I always ask him, if he’s OK with it. I won’t call it ‘financial bullying’, I call it ‘living together’. Someone has to keep an eye on the family’s money.”

Okay... but in all fairness, if you have a joint back account, and a budget, and one member of the party goes out and spends $250 unannounced on some superfluous item, then that's worthy of a conversation. And monitoring how much both people are spending is good practice.

There's nothing wrong with checking in, making sure that both parties in a relationship know how much they can spend on XY or Z.

I often look at charges and ask my husband what they are. Mostly, to make sure that anything unusual is not fraud. Secondly, if there is a huge charge for something we didn't discuss, to make sure he knows what our budget is and to stay within it. My husband often does not know what is in our bank account, flies off on work, spends a large amount of money on dinner and drinks, and then leaves me scrimping on grocery bills.

Does that make me a bully if I check our balance and warn him if his spending is going over the budget? You know, we also have rent and food to pay for, and only one bank account between us, of which I am the larger earner. My husband should feel ashamed if he blows our budget on expensive meals or jeans. Just as I should feel ashamed if I go out on a shopping spree that prevents us from buying food. Where does necessary budgeting and monitoring end, and bullying begin?

double quotation markMy ex-husband routinely spent our rent/bill/food money on restaurants, taxis and other things we really didn’t have the budget for. Finally I got sick of being behind on rent and always running out of money for food, and put my foot down. He refused to sit down and do a budget with me, saying “Why don’t you just do it?” So I did.

I made a budget of all his personal spending, and finally I had to make him choose between taxis to work and lunch at restaurants, which felt bizarre and incredibly uncomfortable for me. He chose taxis over lunch, and after that, whenever colleagues would ask him why he wasn’t joining them for lunch, he’d tell them that his wife wouldn’t allow it.

So my question is, who was the financial bully in this situation, me or him?

A reader from Arkansas says she was financially bullied by her then-husband for years:

double quotation markBut not the way you mean: when I suggested he cut back on his credit-card use on the card held in my name, he sharply increased his use, increasing our debt to $23,000 in a matter of months. That’s what I call financial bullying.

Even checking the accounts doesn’t stop financial ruin:

double quotation markA few years after we were married, my ex-husband developed a drug abuse problem. I was balancing the checkbook every month. He would take money out of our accounts to buy and sell drugs and not tell me. When the accounts wouldn’t match up, he would berate me for not being accurate. He spent all of our money and ran the credit cards up to the max.

When we got divorced we had two credit cards, one for the home and one for his “business” that never got off the ground. The agreement was that I would pay off the family card and he would pay off the business card. Of course, he never did and the creditors came after me – I wound up paying both of them off. My credit was wrecked for seven years.

double quotation markReading the comments here I guess none of the commentators has experienced this.

I have and it certainly was bullying. Talking about finances together is very different from keeping a tight eye on your partner’s spending and questioning every last penny. In my situation, this was coupled with a wholly one-sided approach to discussing joint spending which characterised what I suggested as ‘spending on me’ while what they wanted as ‘spending on us’.

Unless you’ve been in that sort of relationship, I recommend that you aren’t so quick to judge.

double quotation markBeen there too. Money I earned was “our money”, money she earned was “her money”. She was serious. She would get hysterical whenever I bought a magazine yet she felt she could blow hundreds in one shopping spree on whatever she felt like having.

A female reader living in New York wrote:

double quotation markI am in an arranged marriage, to a man who is self-made after a struggled childhood, with disregarded needs, as defined above. However, unless purchases are made to his own liking, he is extremely tight with money. For many years into my marriage – around five – I had no say in the type of food I ate or clothes I wore. My request for a choice of three types of breakfast cereals was seen as “an attempt to cremate his money”. My clothes came from Walmart or Value City.

When we went out, I was expected to eat at home, and could not have a $1 coffee or $1 hot dog in case I got a little peckish under the guise of ‘saving money’ and ‘aggressive savings targets’. If an eggplant spoiled in the refrigerator, the spoiled part was taken and smeared across my face and down my arms, to teach me the value of money. The rear of the television set was checked for warmth on arrival home from work to prove I had been watching TV all day and therefore ‘wasting electricity’. My grocery shopping was severely monitored, as I ‘made it my mission to waste money’.

I think it is important to note I had no earnings of my own during this period.

Fast-forward many years. Now I have my own earnings. My favorite shops are Nordstrom and Anthropologie [where I shop] on the regular and hide [purchases] in the closet. [I] accuse [my] better half of a bad memory when the clothes, bags and shoes make an appearance – with no apologies or regret whatsoever for my behaviours!

However, I think it’s fair to say that we have a sizeable bank balance and the mortgage is a year from being paid off in full.
https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-mon.summary: Survey of 1,000 Americans found one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully. Guardian readers insist that keeping track of partner's expenses was simply budgeting and being financially responsible.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/ja.title: ‘I ain’t goin nowhere’: Gullah Geechee people fight off developers with a historic referendum
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/ja.author: Timothy Pratt in McIntosh county, Georgia
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/ja.text:
A citizen referendum, only the second of its kind in Georgia history, seeks to block a zoning amendment

I
re Gene Grovner stood behind his house on a recent morning, between chicken pens on one side and rows of winter collard greens on the other, holding a knife and skinning a raccoon splayed across a wood post.

“The meat is good roasted,” Grovner said. He pointed to the collards, a burst of green in the winter cold, and the chickens, with their eggs. “If you ain’t lazy, you can live good here,” he said, referring to Sapelo Island off the coast of southern Georgia.

Then he waved in a broad circle, pointing out the nearby modest homes of family members, all bearing the same last name as him, which Grovner, who is 70, says stretches nine generations back on Hogg Hummock.

The community is home to the Gullah Geechee people, descendants of enslaved west Africans who worked on cotton, indigo and rice plantations from North Carolina to Florida. In places like South Carolina’s Hilton Head Island, the Gullah Geechee population was nearly wiped out by development starting in the 1960s.

On Sapelo Island, post-enslavement, freed Black folks were granted land in Hogg Hummock in part because it was seen as marshy and less desirable than the rest of the island. It is the only remaining sea island community of Gullah Geechee people in Georgia.

“All that’s family,” Grovner summed up. “All those people who want to build houses here ain’t gonna close me in.”

Outsiders building large vacation houses was what was at stake in Tuesday’s election in McIntosh county, where Sapelo is located – only the second citizen referendum on a county plan or policy in Georgia history. (Nearby Camden county voters defeated a county plan to build a rocket-launching pad through a referendum in 2022.)

The referendum, brought about after more than 2,000 registered voters in the county signed petitions, allowed residents to vote on whether they were for or against a zoning amendment increasing the amount of residential square footage permitted in Hogg Hummock from 1,400 to 3,000.

Unofficial results released on Tuesday evening showed that nearly 85% of 1,869 county voters opposed the zoning increase.

Allowing larger houses to be built on the island would have opened the door to developers – “all those people” Grovner named – which then would raise taxes, making it harder for Gullah Geechee people to continue living on Sapelo, and potentially changing the island’s cultural and environmental landscape forever.

The number of Gullah Geechee people living on Sapelo has dwindled to between 30 and 40 residents, down from about 500 in the early 20th century. Dozens of the residents’ children and other family members have moved to the mainland over time. Nonetheless, many of these family members maintain ties to the island; some still own property and plan on retiring there.

“Every county in the state of Georgia is looking at” Tuesday’s results, said Kathleen Russell, editor of the Darien News – because any county’s residents can now mount a referendum and challenge zoning rules, she said.

The referendum made history in the region as well, as referendums “are incredibly rare in the majority of the south”, said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. The reason: “States where formerly enslaved people lived, the state governments did not want those people to exercise their power,” Fields Figueredo said.

The ability to stage a referendum in Georgia comes from provisions in the state’s constitution. First, a certain percentage of a county’s registered voters signs a petition indicating they want to vote on a policy from the county’s elected representatives. The percentage varies based on the county’s population.

Once the threshold of confirmed signatures is reached and a referendum is authorized, it is “a form of holding power accountable, where systems of governance are challenged”, said Fields Figueredo.

The Gullah Geechee people who were leading the effort to hold the referendum first had to defeat the county’s legal challenges, based on assertions that zoning rules weren’t covered by language in the state’s constitution. It took a September state supreme court decision to give the green light to Tuesday’s election.

The Guardian spoke to a handful of the nearly 1,000 county residents who cast ballots during a two-week early voting period ending Friday. All had ties to Sapelo Island and Hogg Hummock, and felt strongly about the need to protect the community from unchecked development.

The unspoiled qualities that allow Gullah Geechee people to live close to nature also make the island a prime location for natural science; in the 1950s, Sapelo was the site of foundational research in the nascent field of ecology.

After casting his ballot on Thursday, Nick Macías described Sapelo as “an ecologically important island you don’t find anywhere in the world”. Macías, who works as assistant operations director at the island’s University of Georgia Marine Institute, pointed out that Sapelo was the only Georgia sea island with healthy communities of marsh grass – a keystone species, or one that other animals and plants in an ecosystem depend on for survival.

after newsletter promotion

Allowing larger houses and increased development in Hogg Hummock “would put stress on the carbon footprint” of the island and displace Gullah Geechee people, he said: “When it comes to preserving the [Gullah Geechee] culture, it comes down to the next generation being able to live there.”

Also voting last week, Samuel – who didn’t want his last name used – had gotten off his job early as a trucker to cast a ballot. He has ties to Hogg Hummock through his wife, who has family there. “It’s a unique place,” he said. “You go there … and they treat you like family. They take you in.”

The trucker remembers first visiting as a teenager. “They showed me medicine for toothaches, using plants,” he said. As for the community’s ongoing struggles, he said, “I’ll fight for it till the end. They deserve it. It’s their place.”

One of Ire Gene Grovner’s relatives in Hogg Hummock is his brother, Bobby Gene Grovner. He’s renovating his home on the island, with plans of leaving it to his two daughters. “These ones who come with a pocketful of money, it ain’t gonna work,” he said, referring to developers with interest in the community’s land.

Still, Bobby Gene, who turns 67 later this month, said “it’s tiring” to have to fight in courtrooms and government halls for his community.

“I ain’t got but 40 years left!” he said, laughing.

His brother Ire Gene is involved in another unresolved legal battle, laying claim to several dozen acres of land that a 2024 lawsuit asserts was taken from his family by the state of Georgia in nearby Raccoon Bluff, a 698-acre plot of land on the island formerly inhabited by Gullah Geechee people. The lawsuit includes land deed records in Grovner’s family dating to 1875.

An ongoing case involving the subject of Tuesday’s referendum, filed by the Southern Poverty Law Center, asserts that the proposed zoning amendment was discriminatory. “The people in [Hogg Hummock] feel like they’ve been shut out,” said the SPLC attorney Miriam Gutman. “[They] want to pass their land onto their children and grandchildren. They want to be part of the conversation” about the community’s future, she said.

But even the immediate future after Tuesday’s result is unclear, as the McIntosh county attorney, Adam Poppell, recently stated that voters rejecting the county’s attempt to increase the maximum square footage allowed on the island doesn’t mean conditions will revert to what they were before: a limit of 1,400 sq ft. Instead, Poppell said, the election’s result leaves Hogg Hummock with “no zoning” – meaning anything could be built.

The county attorney did not answer a request for comment.

Dana Braun, attorney for the Hogg Hummock residents who mounted the referendum effort, said another lawsuit would be likely if the county insists on Poppell’s interpretation of where things stand. “The county apparently loves paying lawyers for losing battles,” he said.

After cleaning off his knife and preparing the raccoon on Friday, Ire Gene turned to face the chicken pens and the morning’s eggs. His position on the future of Hogg Hummock: “I ain’t planning on goin’ nowhere.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: What would make your life easier? Martin Lewis asks public for ‘small ideas’ to improve UK
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Finance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panel

Every day, people run into what the finance expert Martin Lewis calls “the life-potholes of unintended consequences” – clunky systems and poorly conceived rules that make life harder than it should be. His latest project, the Small Ideas Initiative, will attempt to address that, with a cross-party panel of politicians and policymakers crowdsourcing ideas for everyday fixes to take to government.

The ideas could cover anything from health and schools to policing, tech and money. Lewis is encouraging people to submit ideas for “practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK” before 12 November.

“If we can fix some of those frustration points, we can make people’s lives easier, save time and help everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy,” said Lewis.

“There’s just a sense that there’s so many little things to fix,” said Polly Mackenzie, who worked with Lewis to come up with the idea. Mackenzie, who was director of policy to Nick Clegg during his deputy premiership, says the initiative could be an avenue to regaining trust in public institutions.

“I think this is about rebuilding confidence in the idea that government can sort stuff out, rather than rebuilding confidence on any one political party having the right ideas,” she said.

Mackenzie will sit on the panel, which will choose about 50 ideas to take to the government, councils and regulators. Alongside Lewis, the initiative is run by the innovation charity Nesta and the public participation charity Involve.

The Reform MP Danny Kruger, the former Conservative MP Penny Mordaunt, and the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, are among those sitting on the panel alongside Mackenzie. She said the group had “a real interest and capability in getting involved and sweating the small stuff”.

The ideas they are looking for will be “no-brainers” that are not party-political and would be easy fixes. Mackenzie said a good example was when she and Lewis first set up the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute and discovered through a survey that GPs had been charging to fill out debt and mental health evidence forms.

“People in debt crisis were having to pay 80, 100, 150 quid to get forbearance for their debts, which is just wrong-headed,” she said. In 2019, two years after the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute started its campaign, the law changed.

Before the initiative’s launch, people in north London shared the policies they would consider submitting. Clare, a railway worker, suggested the government should increase rubbish collections during heatwaves, saying her bins had been “a buffet for flies” this summer. Mark, who works on a market stall, said he would ask the government to put more bins in and around train stations. “There are no bins. I know it’s for security reasons, but I think they could find a way,” he said.

Kwajo Tweneboa, a social housing campaigner who will also sit on the deciding panel, said relatively small changes could make a “massive difference”.

“One small change I’d like to see is housing providers aiming to fix repairs properly, rather than repeatedly applying plaster fixes that don’t address the underlying problem and prolong the misery for tenants,” he says. “I’ve seen how something that should be a straightforward repair can drag on for months, with residents having to repeatedly chase their landlord while the problem gets worse.

“It’s about listening to those everyday experiences and turning simple, practical ideas into policy that can make a tangible difference to people’s lives.”

The finance expert calls life-potholes of unintended consequences 'life-pOTHoles of consequences' The initiative is run by the innovation charity Nesta and the public participation charity Involve.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Campaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send overhaul
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Kiran Stacey Policy editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Exclusive: Letter to government says changes will unfairly remove legal protections for children in England

Letter: Legal rights must be retained for children with Send

Campaigners are calling on Andy Burnham to abandon the core elements of the government’s overhaul of special educational needs provision in England, arguing they unfairly remove children’s legal protections.

A group of children, parents and experts, led by the broadcaster Chris Packham, have written a letter calling for the prime minister to gut the plans laid out under his predecessor Keir Starmer.

Starmer and Bridget Phillipson, the former education secretary, announced the sweeping changes this year, aiming to curb the increase in legally mandated education, health and care plans (EHCPs) and save money in the long term.

Now campaigners are hoping the change of prime minister and education secretary may bring a change of heart from the government – even though officials say it is unlikely.

In the letter, published in the Guardian, the campaigners say: “The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat.

“The government’s proposed … reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable EHCPs, parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.”

They add: “We … urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.”

The letter is signed by 36 people, including Packham, the actor Sally Phillips, the clinical psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen and the Guardian columnist John Harris.

The changes were announced in February after lengthy consultation by ministers with experts and Labour MPs.

Under the plans, instead of legally enforceable EHCPs, millions of pupils will be given individual support plans, which will be agreed between parents and schools but will not be subject to independent legal appeal.

These support plans will be administered by schools rather than local authorities, and parents who are unhappy with them will be asked to appeal to the school rather than being given recourse to an independent tribunal.

Schools will be given more resources to help support Send children, but the overall package is designed to curb the rapid escalation in costs under the current system, which has left councils in England facing a projected £6bn financial black hole in two years’ time.

However, the Guardian revealed on Thursday that the projected savings risk being undermined by a flood of new applications for EHCPs, as parents look to secure legal protections before the new system takes force.

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

The campaigners say they want significant changes to the proposals, including keeping the current threshold for EHCPs, allowing parents to appeal against decisions at a tribunal and scrapping the assessment system proposed for individual support plans.

Ministers are consulting on the measures and are expected to recommend some changes to Phillipson’s proposals.

However, those close to the process say Burnham and Lucy Powell, the new education secretary, are likely to adopt more minor modifications to reinforce legal protections rather than the wholesale changes called for by the campaign group.

A spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain. Our once-in-a-generation reforms will change that.

“Legal duties on schools to identify and support children’s needs are getting stronger, not weaker. And we will never leave parents without a route to challenge decisions about their child’s support.

“We have consulted on our proposals to make sure we get these reforms right, and in the meantime we’re investing in schools to improve inclusion.”
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: Campaigners say changes will unfairly remove legal protections for children with special educational needs. They want Andy Burnham to abandon the core elements of the government's overhaul of special educational provision.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.title: UK politics: Polls open in Holborn and St Pancras byelection – as it happened
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.author: Taz Ali and Tom Ambrose
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text:
Good morning and welcome to our UK politics live blog.

Polls have opened in Keir Starmer’s old seat in Holborn and St Pancras, where the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is hoping to break Labour’s longstanding grip in the north London constituency.

He might have his work cut out for him. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali is projected to retain the seat in today’s byelection, but the party shouldn’t take victory for granted. As the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker, reports, Polanski has mounted an intensive campaign, but the scale of the challenge is clear from the numbers. Starmer won the seat by 11,500 votes in 2024, after Labour majorities of nearly 28,000 in 2019 and more than 30,500 in 2017.

You can read Peter’s report from this morning here:

Andy Burnham is in Berlin today where he will hold meetings with German chancellor Friedrich Merz. On the agenda is a new joint security partnership to counter sabotage, cyber-attacks and other hybrid threats, as well as support for Ukraine, instability in the Middle East, and disruption to global trade routes. We’re expecting to hear from the prime minister this afternoon.

The diplomatic row between Britain and Israel is escalating over the UK’s consular presence in East Jerusalem. Israel said the British consulate has “ceased to function” with 20 diplomats due to leave, but the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the building will remain open and renamed the “UK Mission”.

That’s all from us on the UK politics blog. Here’s a quick recap of the day’s events:

Voters in Holborn and St Pancras have been casting their ballots in today’s byelection to replace Keir Starmer in the north London constituency. Join us again tomorrow as we bring you the results, the latest developments and reaction.

Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel, with only seven to remain in the building. Patrick Wintour has the full report here:

Andy Burnham held talks with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in Berlin, where the prime minister said he was “very committed to securing deeper cooperation” with the EU. Burnham said he wanted to see “if we can bring the UK closer to Europe, particularly in the interest of economic growth and collaboration on irregular migration”.

Ed Miliband announced new sanctions against Russia targeting oil companies, shadow fleet tankers and military supply chains. The foreign secretary made the announcement during a trip to Ukraine, where he met the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Andy Burnham said the Green party’s decision to back a declaration that Zionism is racism was “a completely wrong decision”, PA reports.

Speaking to reporters in Berlin, the prime minister said:

I think it was a completely wrong decision, a terrible judgment on the part of the Green party of England and Wales.

In effect, ruling out a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, and for that reason it shouldn’t be supported in any way, shape or form.

I would call on the leadership of the Green party to say that it will be reversed and it won’t be Green party policy.

In my view, all political parties in the UK should do everything they can to support the two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, and that certainly will remain the government’s position.”

Adrian Ramsay, a former Green party co-leader and MP for Waveney Valley, said he has “no intention of leaving the Green party” over the Zionism is racism row.

During the party’s conference in Brighton, the Greens voted in favour of a policy motion that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion, including Ramsay, who described it as an “unhelpful distraction” and “wrong in principle”.

He has responded to speculation that he could quit the party, saying on X:

To be clear, I have no intention of leaving the Green Party. I am urgently working with colleagues who share my concerns about recent developments to get the party back on track.

I have been a party member for nearly thirty years, was elected as a Green councillor in my twenties, have served as Deputy Leader and Co-Leader and was proud to be elected as an MP for the Green Party in 2024.

I am proud to represent the views of the vast majority of party members and my constituents in Parliament as a strong advocate for the Green Party’s core purpose: protecting and restoring the natural environment in the wake of major threats to society from environmental decline.

The need to push these core Green issues up the political agenda has never been greater.”

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to give us your support. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Ed Miliband announced new sanctions against Russia targeting oil companies, shadow fleet tankers and military supply chains.

The foreign secretary made the announcement during a trip to Ukraine, where he met the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The pair visited the site of a Russian strike that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The attack yesterday killed 22 people, including five children.

Miliband condemned the “appalling atrocity”, saying: “There can be no clearer sign of [Vladimir] Putin’s evil intent and evil strategy in this conflict.

“Because I heard from the governor that the vast, vast majority of people killed in this region, affected in this region, are civilians, the buildings targeted are civilian.

“And we know what international law says about this, that when you target civilians, it is war crimes, and that is the evidence that I see here.”

Speaking alongside Zelenskyy, he said: “I believe I speak on behalf of the British people that we stand with you, Mr President. We stand with you as we have stood with you since 2022 and indeed since 2014. We stand with you in this conflict.

“We are your brothers and your sisters in this conflict. And we are going to be with you as long as it takes.”

There are 100 tagging breaches a day in London “and rising”, the Metropolitan Police commissioner has said.

Mark Rowley warned many offenders are being bailed back into the community on the same conditions with “zero sanction”. He also said the force is arresting “two or three early release offenders a week”.

The first wave of the latest early prison releases began last week, with nearly 5,000 prisoners set to be freed in stages over the next year as the Sentencing Act 2026 comes into force.

It follows a previous scheme launched in 2024 and is intended to address prison overcrowding. Speaking on LBC today, Rowley said:

I’m worried about the number of offenders being released into communities. At the moment we’re arresting two or three early release offenders a week who are being recalled to prison or doing further offending.

That’s been since the start of August we’ve been capturing that data. We’re getting increasing numbers of tag breaches to enforce that probation is sending to us – it’s now over 100 tag breaches a day in London… and rising.

Back to Berlin, Germany’s Merz and UK’s Burnham have issued statements after their talks.

Burnham talked about rebuilding the UK’s relationship with the EU after Brexit. Their meeting in Berlin came ahead of the UK-EU summit later this year – expected in late November – as he said he is “very committed to securing deeper cooperation” with the EU at the summit.

He wanted to see “if we can bring the UK closer to Europe, particularly in the interest of economic growth and collaboration on irregular migration,” he said.

You can read more of his statement, and that of Merz, over on the Europe live blog:

We have some comments (via the Common Wealth thinktank) from Labour MP Alex Sobel and the general secretary of the University and College Union (UCU), Jo Grady, in response to the Transition Security Project report on the government’s military strategy.

As Peter Walker reports, the study warns the UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste

Sobel said: “At this time of global instability, it is critical that we spend every pound carefully ensuring our troops are well looked after and that procurement supports UK industry and provides best value.”

Grady added: “Working people are repeatedly told there is no money to properly fund our colleges, universities and public services, whilst billions of pounds are poured into maintaining the capacity to fight wars around the world.

“This report exposes the enormous costs to taxpayers and the huge amounts of waste involved. Real security means decent jobs, strong public services and social security, not ever-increasing spending on weapons and war.”

The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned.

According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents.

Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions that have often made the world less safe, the report says ministers should prioritise changing their approach rather than immediately increasing spending, with resources shifted from overseas commitments to domestic defence.

The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and a defence investment plan (Dip) was unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.

Starmer’s then defence secretary John Healey resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that Healey is chancellor that target has been shelved for now.

It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre that was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham.

Prime minister Andy Burnham has arrived in Berlin, where he was welcomed by German chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Their meetings today will focus on tackling cyber-attacks and hybrid threats in the form of a new security partnership. My colleague Jakub Krupa will have more over on the Europe live blog here.

A serving member of the Royal Navy has been charged with spying, police have said.

Teddy Young, 24, will appear today at Westminster magistrates’ court after he was charged with obtaining protected information that could benefit a unnamed foreign power.

He was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on 6 October after an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London (CTPL). He had now been charged with a number of offences under the National Security Act, the Metropolitan police said on Thursday.

Cmdr Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.”

Ed Miliband is in Kyiv this morning. There’s scant information about what he’s actually doing there, other than “make clear the UK’s unwavering support for Ukraine”, as the Foreign Office says. We shall, as ever, bring you more when we get it.

Away from the byelection, research has found Brexit, Liz Truss’s mini-budget and other “shocks” over the last 10 years have led to a serious and lasting deterioration in the UK population’s mental health.

The findings come as Prof Peter Fonagy prepares to publish the report of his long-waited government-commissioned inquiry into the dramatic increases in recent years in diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism. It will be published on Friday amid concern that those conditions help explain why a record 2.8 million Britons are too sick to work and almost 1 million young people aged 16 to 24 have become “Neets” – not in education, employment or training.

Researchers led by Dr Annie Jeffery of University College London used data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study of 87,857 people aged 16 and older, which was collected every year between 2009 and 2024, to estimate the mental health impact of those five “systemic shocks”.

The past decade or so has been tumultuous, shaped by multiple overlapping shocks and ongoing uncertainty and instability that have impacted mental health in Britain,” said Jeffery.

We have shown that major government decisions and current global events can have substantial impacts on people’s mental health.

Here are some of the latest images from the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, which the Guardian’s head office is just on the boundary of:

Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.

The Institute for Government (IfG) thinktank says the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.

The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”.

The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future.

The Guardian recently reported that councils and schools have reported a surge in applications for EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.

Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.

The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​will not be closing but will ⁠be known as a UK mission, remaining independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people.

Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to close ‌on Thursday over the UK’s plans to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank.

Miliband said that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks, it would now work to build up its presence.

He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, ‌following speculation it ​could expel some Israeli diplomats from Britain.

Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.

The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians.

Israel had threatened to close it in protest at the UK’s decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused the governing Labour party of being hostile towards his country.

The French finance minister, Roland Lescure, said the UK could rejoin the EU “anytime” after Andy Burnham indicated a major review of Britain’s relationship with the bloc.

Lescure said it was up to the British public whether to return to the EU, telling the BBC that “if they’re willing to come back, they will have to decide”.

“But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime,” he added. Ben Quinn has the full report here.

As our political correspondent Aletha Adu reported last week, the prime minister opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way” as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
More research into the troubling rise in early onset cancers is needed. But we already know that food is among the culprits

T
he latest findings about the rise in cancers in people under 50, from the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), are extremely concerning. While a cancer diagnosis is bad news at any time, it is a particular blow for those in younger age groups where most people are in good health. Overlapping trends observed in England, the Netherlands and the US include a troubling rise in the incidence of colorectal (or bowel) cancer. Other diseases that have increased in England include uterine and kidney cancers.

These diseases are still rare in young people: 10 times more adults in their 50s, 60s and 70s are diagnosed than those in their 20s, 30s and 40s. Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients. Diagnosing more cancers sooner is an explicit policy goal in England, where late diagnosis and lower uptake of screening are two reasons for mortality rates that are higher than elsewhere in Europe.

But diagnostic improvements are unfortunately not the main reason for increased cases. While research is ongoing and many questions remain, evidence points to obesity and poor diet causing cancers as well as heart disease and type 2 diabetes. The Prospect-UK trial is currently seeking 250,000 participants for a longitudinal study into early-onset (under-50) bowel cancer. It will scrutinise information about nutrition in more detail than has been done previously, including what people are eating less of.

The success of international efforts to cut lung cancer through targeting smoking set a powerful precedent for public health campaigning. This took longer than it should have done, due to tobacco industry lobbying. But it remains the gold standard of regulation combined with messaging, to bring about behaviour change. The WCRF data shows that lung cancer rates in under-50s have continued falling.

So far, efforts to cut obesity have had nothing like the same impact. The patterns are not the same everywhere; one recent study found that in some countries a rapid rise had been replaced by a levelling-off. But English-speaking countries have some of the worst records, and the lack of strong action in the UK is among the big disappointments of health policy in the last decade.

Politicians from Boris Johnson to Wes Streeting have committed to obesity action plans, only to water them down in the face of opposition from the food and drink industries. Last year, scientists wrote to Mr Streeting to protest that the government had done “virtually nothing” to alert consumers to the carcinogenic properties of the nitrites added to bacon and ham.

There is a grim irony in dramatic advances in cancer research and treatment coinciding with the rise in early-onset cancers. For many doctors and patients, this a period of hope. But politicians and health bosses must guard against a situation in which some groups have improved prospects, while others face increased risks linked to socioeconomic disadvantages.

In relation to obesity and diet, the close link with poverty points to the need for ministers to view public spending holistically, and to recognise that the NHS is not the only institution with the capacity to improve health. While more research into early-onset cancers is needed, existing data tells us a great deal. Governments should be as bold in tackling the causes of obesity as they once were in confronting big tobacco.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Kemi Badenoch’s personal brand is not strong enough to revive a party that so thoroughly lost the trust of the British people

F
or a party that keeps losing elections, the Conservatives have enjoyed a remarkably upbeat conference in Birmingham this week. A party with a strong regicidal impulse is united behind Kemi Badenoch. Opinion polls show the leader’s personal ratings, while not spectacular, outperforming the wider Tory brand. Mrs Badenoch exuded confidence in her keynote speech on Wednesday, setting out what she believes is a path back to power.

The strategic focus is the economy. The Conservative leader expects Andy Burnham’s honeymoon to come to an end when his chancellor delivers a painful budget later this month. A spending review will then compound the pain, forcing grim trade-offs on a prime minister who has a reputation for deferring hard choices.

Mrs Badenoch presents herself as made of sterner stuff. By that she means she is prepared to say that an overgrown state does too much for too many people. What the Tory leader imagines to be fiscal courage is really ideological complacency pitched at her party’s comfort zone. The Conservative conference generated multiple commitments to cut taxes, mostly for upper-middle- and high-income families, alongside pledges to boost spending on defence and prison places, while also reducing the national debt. This is affordable, according to Mrs Badenoch, thanks to £70bn of “savings” the Conservatives claim to have identified in cuts to the civil service, regulators and working-age benefits.

It is a phoney equation that doesn’t account for the increase in costs to government once the social consequences of austerity become apparent. But the proposed reallocation of resources from mythical undeserving benefit-claiming idlers to enterprising but overtaxed middle-class families is a trusted campaign device.

Mrs Badenoch presents this agenda as “something for everyone”. In reality, she is trying to reach two particular audiences. The Tories need to attract voters in their former “blue wall” heartlands, now held by Liberal Democrats, and people who backed Boris Johnson in 2019 and then switched to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. These groups have very different attitudes, crudely represented by the polarised political identities that coalesced into leave and remain blocs – one nationalistic, the other more liberal – on the question of Brexit.

Mrs Badenoch spent two years courting the former camp with hardline positions on immigration and hostility to net zero climate policy. She has belatedly noticed the existence of people who are appalled by Mr Farage’s agenda. A significant passage in her speech on Wednesday rebuked Reform UK politicians who use a narrow ethnic definition of Englishness.

But mostly the Conservative leader talked about tax cuts, because she believes they appeal across the spectrum. That is often a reliable assumption, although the same plan didn’t help the Tories in 2024. Reckless pre-election giveaways succeeded only in poisoning the fiscal well for Keir Starmer.

The problem for the Conservatives then was that people didn’t trust them to govern responsibly or competently. This hasn’t changed. Mrs Badenoch thinks victory is available by attaching her personal brand to a classic Tory formula, unrevised for decades. Judging by the mood in Birmingham, her MPs and members agree. This is what happens when a party speaks to itself. A much harder test awaits when they have to speak to a country that remembers Conservative government well enough to be disinclined to listen.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/nil.title: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash | Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/business/nil.author: Nils Pratley
https://www.theguardian.com/business/nil.text:
Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills

South West Water owner taps investors after sewage spills

W
ater is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told the Labour party conference last week, reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England.

And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride.

But the idea that shareholders never lose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners of Thames Water have been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances).

Meanwhile, the owners of Southern Water have been obliged to shove in cash on dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issue to fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures.

The new-ish Pennon chief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place.

Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”.

Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism.

The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low.

For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine.

One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point.

If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper.

Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: All hail the Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives | John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: John Crace
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
The Tory leader is now too big for the party to allow her to fail, so everything she does is acclaimed a work of genius

W
here’s AI slop when you need it? It could all have been so much simpler. Just ask ChatGPT to write me a leader’s speech in the style of Kemi Badenoch. Make it an hour and 10 minutes long, so plenty of room for padding. Go heavy on the slogans, cliches and the obligatory crap politician jokes. Ones we’ve all heard many times before. Not least at this conference.

Make the usual digs at Labour and put the boot in to Reform. The main aim of the speech is to try to reposition a party that is tanking in third place on 20% in the polls as the main opposition to the government.

And just to give everyone a reason to go home with a feeling of mild optimism, chuck in a retail offer at the end. An uncosted tax cut for people who are rich but don’t feel quite rich enough. The new multimillionaire common-or-garden lower middle classes.

Unfortunately, Kemi made the schoolgirl error of trying to write the speech for herself. And it was much the worse for it. What’s the point of having AI if you don’t use it? It was too long, too flabby. No real argument, just a collection of random thoughts. Andy Burnham in Liverpool it wasn’t.

Parts of it even seemed to bore Kemi herself. As if she was going through the motions. Lazy, even. That it was still by far and away the best speech of the entire conference is not really the point. More of a reflection of how dire the others have been. Four days of the Tories in Birmingham is a trial for anyone remotely sentient.

On the surface, the Tories have seemed a happy tribe this week. There has been a soporific tranquillity to the proceedings. Few members attending, nonexistent queues and above all no Robert Jenrick. Or even Liz Truss. How we miss her.

But the unity feels very fragile. The Tories are now Kemi and Kemi is the Tories. The party has bet the bank on her. Kemi even now calls herself the captain, coach and owner of the Tories. Everyone else is an also-ran.

This comes at a huge risk. Because Kemi has become almost too big for the Tories to allow her to fail. So they daren’t question her. Anything she does has to be acclaimed as a work of genius. Just walking on stage is enough to secure her a standing ovation. No one has ever quite walked like that before.

The party has been captured by the Kult of Kemi. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy that could lead them to oblivion. They have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless. They are out of other options.

Just don’t stop to ask why nothing the Tories seem to do is cutting through. Why the polls are stubbornly flatlining. Why it’s odds-on that beyond the few hundred people in the hall, no one will pay a blind bit of attention to her speech. It will be forgotten within a day.

Wednesday morning’s proceedings began with the Tory chair, Kevin Hollinrake. Kev’s dog got a bigger cheer than Kev. Next up was the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, a one-man cluster of antimatter. No man can suck the energy out of the room like Nick. The only thing that would cheer him up is a public execution.

Then the Philpster. The UK’s self-proclaimed superhero. The vigilante who took on the French. Endearingly, he still thinks the French navy knows who he is. Chris, most of the UK don’t know who you are. Nor do they care.

After this, things began to get surreal as each member of the shadow cabinet was announced and applauded as they took their seats. A bit like a third-rate talent show. The presenter still didn’t know who Nick Timothy was, despite having introduced him moments earlier. She also got Helen Whately’s name wrong. And there was one empty chair. Tom Tugendhat had invented an unmissable trip to India to get out of the embarrassment. Wise choice.

A spot of Elgar and then it was Kemi. There was a fight for the soul of the country. There’s always a fight for the soul of the country as far as the Tories are concerned. They don’t seem to realise that it was them that ripped the soul out of it.

“What a great conference we’ve had,” she said. It was hard to know if she was being ironic. Other than the fact that everyone has been wandering round in brain-dead surprise that the Tories still exist, it’s been a disaster.
