After that things went weird. As if we were entering a weird dystopia. Being asked to believe the unbelievable. Like when she said that her shadow cabinet was a united team that listened to one another. This after Kemi had literally said she was the party and that anyone who disagreed with her could go fuck themselves. The whole point of Kemi is that she listens to no one.

She also had a pop at Labour for putting all their faith in one man. Pots, kettles. As for Reform, she had nothing but contempt. You’d like to think that would rule out a possible coalition.

The one moment when Kemi became truly passionate – believable even – was when she talked about race. This was Kemi at her best, talking about something she really cared about. Even if she did imagine there was no racism in football in the 1970s and 80s. But this bit was all too short and the speech began to feel like it was dragging into eternity. We’d still be trying to stay awake well into the afternoon.

Finally the reveal – the inheritance tax reduction that would be funded by as-yet-unspecified welfare cuts. There would be no inheritance tax on anyone leaving their home to their children. With an extra million-quid freebie thrown in, in case you needed to do it up after your parents had let it get tatty. You could hear the cheers from the country’s stately homes echo around the hall.

Here was a party that really got it. Which was prepared to do something about the cost of living for the mega-rich. Even as Kemi was speaking, millions of ordinary citizens were phoning their brokers to liquidate their stock market assets so they could upgrade their £1m homes to something far more palatial. The property market in mega-homes had just gone wild. The people’s earl, Charles Spencer, could breathe easy. Althorp was safe. Let them drink champagne.

There was just time for Kemi to pay tribute to Jeffrey Archer – the Tories have a soft spot for a convicted conman who ruined several lives – and then came the extended standing ovations. An echo chamber is going to echo.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10 | Henry Hill
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Henry Hill
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Conference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for power

O
n paper, the traditional role of the journalist at a British party conference boils down to some simple questions: what was the mood of the assembled activists? Did the leader give a good speech? In practice, the changing nature of conferences and the media makes this superficially simple task more complicated than it may initially appear.

Any journalist covering the leader’s speech, for instance, will have watched it in full. But it will reach the vast majority of its intended audience in fragmentary form, through clips – and speeches are increasingly written with that reality in mind. The conference hall is not really the audience, or the full speech really the product. This adds a layer of complexity to the reviewer’s task.

Likewise, it is less meaningful than once it was to talk about the mood of the conference. Thirty years ago, when our political parties were much more robust social institutions than they are today, millions of Britons were party members through thick and thin, and thousands attended annual conference whether they liked the leadership or not.

It was this democratic culture that gave us the spectacular showdowns at Labour conferences in the 1980s, or Tory activists cheering Norman Tebbit’s excoriation of the European Union in the 1990s. But it is unthinkable now: most people disaffected with a party – especially the Conservatives – are simply not members of it; they certainly don’t take time off work and spend several hundred pounds to attend conference.

Even with that caveat, however, there is no doubt that the mood inside the Conservative party is considerably improved on last year’s. Manchester proved that Kemi Badenoch can make good use of a spotlight, even in otherwise extremely challenging conditions, and her position has improved markedly since then. Her personal ratings are up, her party’s polling has recovered (a little), her only real rival for the leadership has defected to Reform UK, and Reform has its own problems.

The policy side of things is helping, too. I was very critical of Badenoch’s decision to go as slowly as she did on policy, and do think that first year of near-radio silence did the Tories serious damage. But the eventual policy announcements have, so far, been generally well-considered; if they still tend to err too much on the side of caution, it is at least better than the alternative, the wild promises of an opposition which has abandoned all hope of office.

Birmingham has also confirmed that the Conservatives have recognised the need for a strategic pivot. Badenoch has come under fire from some quarters for returning to the party’s “comfort zone” on tax cuts and deregulation, rather than trying to reassemble Boris Johnson’s 2019 coalition and go blow-for-blow with Reform.

But that analysis fundamentally misunderstands the current state of play. As much as the gladiatorial spectacle of the “fight on the right” appeals to journalists, so long as the Tories and Reform are polling where they are, they are not really each other’s primary opponent. Reform’s immediate front lies through Labour; of the 98 seats where it placed second in 2024, 89 are held by a Labour MP.

The Conservatives’ front, in contrast, is much more southern, affluent and Liberal Democrat-facing. Many commentators, both inside the party and out, too quickly assume this means “liberal”, because they assume such voters should be Tory by default. This ignores the fact that, by 2024, the Conservatives did not actually have an attractive economic pitch to those voters. Badenoch’s bet is that a substantial number of these voters – both those who defected to the Lib Dems and a large share who party strategists identify as simply having stopped voting – can be wooed back with a strong economic offer on things such as childcare and inheritance tax.

It remains to be seen whether she gets the polling bounce that is the traditional marker of a successful party conference. But based on what I saw over the past few days, I would say this was broadly a positive event for the Tories.

I worry, however, that the party itself is over-reading it. Yes, its situation has improved – but that is clearing the extremely low bar set by two sets of catastrophic local elections in 2025 and 2026. Yes, Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved – but she remains in truth the second least unpopular leader, rather than a particularly popular one.

Tory loyalists can be perhaps forgiven, meanwhile, for playing up the “Kemi bounce”, which has lifted their party from about 17.5% to about 20% in the current polling average, while ignoring the “Kemi slump” that preceded it (she took the leadership when the party was at 26% on that same average). But you would not guess, reading the room in Birmingham, that the Conservatives are still several points shy of their disastrous vote share at the 2024 election.

Yet perhaps this is again a problem of the chimerical nature of conference. The party strategists I spoke to seemed quite realistic about their task at the next election: avoid extinction and remain the largest rightwing party. But the party leadership could hardly make that their top line: it would simply demotivate their remaining troops and be severely punished by the press.

It is therefore their difficult task to consistently strike an optimistic note without entirely falling for it themselves – and ours to try to work out if, or when, they have.

Henry Hill is political editor of the Critic

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour? | Andy Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins

O
nly a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching to the Greens in huge numbers, Green candidates were winning across the country, and the party was second behind Reform UK in some national polls.

Like Reform, the Green party presented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.

After an unprecedentedly hot summer, some of that authority and momentum remains. Last week, at the party’s bustling conference in Brighton, impressive-sounding statistics about the party’s growth this year – along with modern icons of Green success, such as Hannah Spencer, victor of February’s Gorton and Denton byelection – were presented to determinedly cheering delegates in crammed halls.

This week, in the high-profile London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, where Polanski hopes to succeed Keir Starmer in Thursday’s byelection, the usual cheery squads of Green activists have been striding back and forth between wealthy streets and council estates, distributing thick bundles of a party newspaper with the front-page headline “Greens close in!”. Given the party’s recent election record, Polanski’s populist appeal and the possibility that some of the many local leftwing voters may see the contest as a low-risk way to warn Andy Burnham not to follow Starmer’s premiership rightwards, a Green win is not impossible.

But, even if it happens, the problems the party has accumulated since the spring will not have gone away. For some voters, the novelty of Polanski’s leadership has faded. For others his style, more radical and provocative than previous Green leaders, has allowed the party to shift to extreme positions, particularly on Israel, with the Brighton conference passing a motion (which the Jewish Polanski neither supported nor opposed) that “Zionism is racism”.

Meanwhile, Burnham’s confident, sometimes iconoclastic start as prime minister has removed Polanski’s unique selling point as a good communicator who does not accept the usually conservative terms of British political debate. In his conference speech, Polanski admitted: “Now I get asked, isn’t your job done?”

The idea that one of the Greens’ main purposes is to shift Labour leftwards and towards bolder climate policies, and that that approach is yielding results, was everywhere at Brighton, from mutually encouraging chats between activists in the queues to upbeat contributions from the main stage.

It’s not a role that should be dismissed as minor. The Greens’ influence over Labour – both undermining Starmer in record time by taking so many votes from his party and creating political space for Burnham’s coup and governmental refresh – has arguably been a sign of Britain belatedly catching up with other European democracies, such as Spain, where centre-left parties have long been forced to be bolder by more leftwing ones. After decades of Labour paying most attention to forces to its right, the Greens’ important place in Labour’s calculations makes a refreshing change.

And yet, being an influence rather than a definite national rival – the Greens are now about 20 points behind Labour in some polls – is undeniably a comedown. During Polanski’s first months as leader, he regularly said he wanted the Greens to “replace” Labour. Partly because of that apparent possibility, the Greens attracted respected leftwing strategists such as Michael Chessum and James Meadway, who had worked under Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership and became disillusioned by Labour under Starmer.

At some leftwing gatherings last spring, those who hadn’t switched to the Greens could feel a bit over-cautious and old-fashioned. It’s possible that the rightwing media even encouraged this shift, giving Polanski plenty of coverage, in order to divide the left and prevent Labour from ever holding sole power again.

With Labour’s electoral future now looking more promising, one of the Greens’ leaflets in Holborn and St Pancras modestly presents Polanski as “a strong voice … to keep Labour in check”. In his Brighton speech, Polanski said: “Vote Green and watch Labour move.” It’s a typically pithy and clever line: explaining the mechanics of politics to voters, and treating them like grownups, in ways that party leaders rarely do.

But it may not be an inspiring line for more tribal Greens who decided decades ago that Labour, and alliances with Labour, were not for them. Another Green conference theme was “Real hope. Real change.” It sounded defensive, and too similar to Labour’s conference theme the previous week: “Hope again”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The Greens do still hold the initiative on some issues: advocating rent controls, wealth taxes, an end to fiscal conservatism, and more radical climate policies, with Labour expected soon to allow a limited expansion of oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. There are also signs of the Greens positioning themselves as the party of the most disadvantaged, such as asylum seekers, benefits claimants and transgender people – groups that Burnham’s less judgmental government may treat better than Starmer’s did, yet probably within limits set by Labour’s considerable number of socially conservative supporters.

“We will always stand with … everyone who is under attack,” said Polanski in Brighton, a statement that could be seen as too vague, impractical and idealistic. Yet if this country is to become a more truly representative democracy – a possible upside of the current political fragmentation – why shouldn’t the most vulnerable effectively have their own party? The most privileged have had the Tories for centuries.

The astute political analyst Rob Ford suggests that the Greens’ poll decline “may not matter much” if the party still campaigns effectively and attracts strong support from the dozens of relatively youthful, highly educated and diverse urban constituencies. Thursday’s byelection will test that theory.

Yet either way, there is something disturbing about a party with such a crucial cause having to face a reduction in status. The Greens’ drift back towards the political margins reflects not just their own mistakes, but the reluctance of many Britons to face up to climate realities. As with Extinction Rebellion, it’s more comfortable to call them extremists and ignore what they say.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Ben Quinn with photographs by Graeme Robertson
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Little if any sign Bury Park is a place where any group might fear to tread, despite Tory MP’s comments to the contrary

F
rom behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people.

“The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton.

Outside, on the day after a shadow Conservative Home Office minister had claimed there were “no-go zones” for white people in Luton, there was a hum of activity on Dunstable Road, a thoroughfare lined with restaurants, jewellery stores and shops selling pakoras and other snacks. Further along, shoppers of different races trundled trolleys through the car parks of Sainsbury’s and Lidl.

Blake Stephenson, the MP for Mid Bedfordshire, who lives in a village 15 minutes away from Luton, had claimed at the Tory party conference on Monday that the town was “a very dangerous place” where some communities “live in ghettoes”. “There are parts where white people won’t go,” he said. “They are like no-go zones.”

His comments have been roundly condemned in Luton, but they echo the longer-term far-right framing of the English town as a poster child for the supposed dangers of Islamism and multiculturalism.

As the home town of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, it is also where the English Defence League (EDL), the street movement he used as a springboard to semi-celebrity status in likeminded circles, was launched. International far-right figures have eagerly seized on his depiction of the town. The Australian senator Pauline Hanson joined him there in July for a walkabout filmed by a major Australian TV network.

The 2021 census found that 54.8% of Luton’s population were non-white, making it one of four places outside London at that time where the majority of the population was from minority groups.

A day after Stephenson’s comments, there was little sign if any that Bury Park was a place where any group might fear to tread – even those giving out parking tickets.

Among a smattering of white faces on Dunstable Road was a traffic warden, who declined to give their name but said: “I’ve always felt perfectly safe, and if ever there has been a minor incident, generally a member of the public or a shopkeeper has come to my aid.”

Joshua Bozier, 36, a homeless man, said: “To be honest, I feel safer here in Bury Park than in the town centre. I know everybody here, whereas I’ve been spat at and urinated on in the centre. I’ve lived all over and Luton’s not what it’s made out to be.”

He said Robinson “spilled a lot of shit”, but he did point to the past conduct of some Islamist activists in the area, who in 2009 demonstrated against the Royal Anglian regiment’s homecoming parade from Afghanistan.

Only a tiny proportion of the town’s Muslim community were involved, but the incident became a useful symbol for the far right.

Dr William Allchorn, an associate professor at Richmond American University and an expert on the far right, said the relationship between the EDL and the Islamist activists “was mutually reinforcing and for people looking for a European example of the supposed consequences of multiculturalism, Luton came with an unusually ready-made set of images, personalities and stories.

“A series of confrontations occurred at exactly the moment when a new anti-Muslim form of street politics was developing, and an unusually effective political entrepreneur in Tommy Robinson was able to turn those local events into a national and eventually international story.”

Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, accused Stephenson of pushing the same “rightwing nonsense” as Robinson. The police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire, Labour’s John Tizard, wrote to the Tory MP to say: “These statements are not supported by evidence and bear a troubling resemblance to far-right agitators seeking to divide communities.”

Luton’s independent mayor, Javed Hussain, said he was baffled by Stephenson’s claims as he strolled through Bury Park, pointing out Christian, Sikh and Muslim places of worship and emphasising local regeneration.

“I’m at a loss to know why he is saying this because Luton is a very multicultural, diverse town, as well as very vibrant one, so it’s disheartening,” he said.

“Yes, in this area there may be a large number of people from an Asian background, but people from all over do travel here for all sorts of reasons, whether to shop or eat.”

Research by the council has also found that cohesion was strong enough for the town to avoid the fractures that led to violence in other English towns in the past, though there were warnings that more needed to be done, such as broadening cultural experiences for school pupils.

Not unsurprisingly, community relations are never far from the lips of local policymakers. While proud of the aspirational ethos among second- and third-generation British Asians in Luton, including his own family, Hussain said: “Look, if there was something I wish we could do more of, it would be to support children from council estates that are predominantly white. There is always more to do.”

It is also home to the English Defence League (EDL) and the English Defense League ( EDL) The town is home of a number of far-right activists, including the far- right activist Tommy Robinson.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense | Heather Stewart
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Heather Stewart Economics editor
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy

Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election.

In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early.

So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it.

The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall, underlined how unpopular it is.

But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be.

The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24.

And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax.

Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain.

Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return.

Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that.

Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC .

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move.

And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available.

As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive.

He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs. Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. By staying put, they will in turn make it harder for school leavers and university/college graduates to move to the area for work. This is bad for growth,” he said.

Indeed, he points out there would even be an incentive for those who can afford it to “upsize” – moving to a larger house, which would then effectively shelter the asset from inheritance tax.

If Badenoch and her party want to shovel an additional £6bn of taxpayers’ money to the already-wealthy in the hope of winning back votes in the stockbroker belt, so be it – but she should not be able to claim the policy would be anything but bad for economic growth.

But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London

T
he UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.

The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.

Not signed in before? Continue with Google

The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK considering a retaliatory expulsion of 27 Israeli diplomats from London.

It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel and Palestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.

“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.”

Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank.

Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives.

“I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue, wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.

It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967 has experienced its fair share of political upheaval.

The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967.

By the time the new consul-general moved into the premises, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before John Henry Lewen was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces.

Lewen assumed his post at the consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.

As the UK foreign secretary told parliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.”

Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb was placed under the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound.

Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah. In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration.

This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60 years on the site. The neighbourhood, mostly made up of diplomatic missions and UN and other international organisations’ offices, was quiet.

Residents in the area expressed disappointment over what they saw as a lack of international support for the Palestinian people in recent years.

“We have seen very little but studies and words, no action from the international community,” said Abu Abdo.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: UK consulate in East Jerusalem to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure. It is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which remains open. Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank.

n a previous life, if I ever went missing, you could reliably find me at the gym. But since getting these Bowflex SelectTech dumbbells that replaced 15 pairs of weights during the pandemic, I haven’t felt the need to leave my at-home setup.

When I earned my personal training certification in 2021, I was on a quest for a compact set of weights that would fit into my modest space, feel intuitive to use for beginner clients and still challenge veteran fitness buffs. These bells punch well above their weight in helpful specs, offering a solid range of five to 52.5lb in just one package. And as a ubiquitous pair of bells that boast a devoted following, I was surprised to find this generous Prime Day deal for up to 18% off.

As a certified personal trainer with a specialization in orthopedic exercise and senior fitness, I could talk about the benefits of strength training forever. Injury reduction, disease prevention, a boost in bone density and a better shot at longevity are just some of the ways weight training can drastically improve your quality of life.

What we don’t talk about nearly enough are the numerous barriers to entry associated with strength training, many of which the Bowflex SelectTechs lift: they are a relatively affordable one-time expense when you consider the price of a gym membership (a recent study clocked $65 per month as the norm, but I used to pay nearly double that). Their compact 17in x 8in footprint replaces an entire bulky weight rack. Switching between weight levels is easy, thanks to straightforward adjustment dials that allow me to more effectively achieve my hypertrophy goals without losing momentum or de-load as I approach muscular failure or as my form starts to slip to avoid injury. And unlike other bells I’ve owned, the included grooved storage trays help protect my floors and toes, a perk I appreciate given the number of times a rolling weight against my bare foot has unleashed a stream of expletives.

The dozens of other free weights in my home gym have rounded discs that won’t support me in plank-forward movements like renegade rows or weighted push-ups. The Bowflex set does, thanks to the discs’ stabilizing hexagonal shape. I’ve wrapped my sweaty palms around hundreds of barbells over the years, and can confidently say these feel most natural against my grip. Neither too traction-heavy (which causes callouses) and neither too forgiving (which can promote slipping), these weights allow me to see an entire movement through, contributing to proper form and a fair shot at endurance.

When shopping for your pair of Bowflex SelectTech bells, I implore you to buy new. Like I called out in my guide to the best at-home gym equipment, older models have been recalled due to weight plates unexpectedly dislodging from the handle. Mine have so far shirked a misfortune of this nature in their half a decade of use, but I anticipate their demise is coming soon enough.

The good news is that you’ll be in much better shape with the latest edition of these dumbbells, as they now have a new safety mechanism that positions the metal locking disc directly onto the handle to better reinforce each weight. I’ve thus never felt more confident recommending this new model both as a longtime shopping writer and fitness professional, and at this new low price, they are going in my cart too.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: John Musenze
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
With cancer cases rising fastest in poorer countries, Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu, president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control, says Africa needs investment in research, diagnosis and prevention

W
hen Dr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu last saw Gloria in Abuja, the young breast cancer patient was so ill that she was in hospital. The cancer had spread to her bones and lungs, and she was struggling with complications from the disease.

Then, at a global conference on cancer thousands of miles away in Hong Kong last month, Bagudu saw her again. Gloria was walking with a stick because of the cancer in her hips, but she was attending sessions, speaking about her experience and advocating for other patients.

“I saw her hopping on the corridor here. I was shocked,” Bagudu recalled.

Bagudu was recounting this story on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong, attended by more than 2,000 people from 124 countries.

A Nigerian paediatrician and advocate for cancer patients, Bagudu is president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) – the first African to lead the organisation. She takes up the role as cancer cases and deaths are projected to rise sharply, with the greatest increases expected in poorer countries.

“The fact that it [the election of a black person] took so long is a reflection of the inadequacy of cancer care along the entire spectrum in Africa and other low- and middle-income countries,” Bagudu says.

Her election comes as countries across the global south face a growing cancer burden while also struggling with shortages of diagnostic equipment, medicines, radiotherapy services, trained specialists and financing.

According to the most recent figures from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 20.6 million people were diagnosed with cancer and 9.8 million died from the disease in 2024.

The IARC forecasts an annual rise in cases of 67% to more than 34m by 2050, while deaths could reach 17.5 million, an increase of 79%. Most of the additional deaths are expected to occur in low-income countries.

According to Bagudu, the forecasts reinforce the need to reorientate global cancer policy towards countries where health systems are already under pressure.

“Cancer is tripling and is going to keep on increasing, and the people affected by it most are those from the global south,” she says.

Her ambition is to use the UICC, which represents more than 1,100 member organisations across more than 170 countries, as a bridge between countries with limited cancer services and the research, technology and treatments being developed elsewhere.

“I have this opportunity to be able to bring forth a lot of the problems that the low- and middle-income countries are facing to the global north,” she says.

But Bagudu says access to cancer care cannot be solved simply by building more specialist hospitals. “We keep building cancer centres and we keep seeing that it’s not enough,” she says.

Cancer centres need to be supported by screening, early diagnosis, radiotherapy, medicines, trained health workers and systems that prevent families from being pushed into financial hardship by treatment, she says.

“I’m trying to reduce financial toxicity for the woman in the village,” she says.

That gap is already visible in basic cancer services. UICC chief executive Cary Adams told delegates that less than half of the world’s population has access to diagnostic services, while many patients in low- and middle-income countries pay for care out of pocket.

Only 14% of the estimated 73 million people who need palliative care each year have access to it, according to figures presented at the congress.

Bagudu’s own work in Nigeria has focused on some of these gaps. A paediatrician and founder of the Medicaid Cancer Foundation, she helped establish Kebbi state’s first cancer-control plan and registry during her time as first lady of the Nigerian state from 2015 to 2023.

Sign up to Global Dispatch

Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team

after newsletter promotion

Her foundation has also worked on cancer awareness and access to treatment for vulnerable patients. She has campaigned for cervical cancer prevention, including the introduction of the single-dose HPV vaccine into Nigeria’s routine immunisation programme in 2023.

In 2024, she became senior adviser to Nigeria’s coordinating minister of health and social welfare with a brief that included women’s health and cancer advocacy. Bagudu now wants to take some of those lessons to the international level, including pushing for new approaches to cancer financing.

She says cancer has never received the kind of global treatment financing mechanism that HIV, tuberculosis and malaria have benefited from. “Cancer has never directly been a beneficiary of global funding for treatment,” she says.

She will support efforts to develop a global cancer financing platform modelled partly on the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria, to mobilise resources from governments, donors and other sources to strengthen cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

The proposal comes as African governments face competing demands on health budgets, and international development financing is under pressure with significant cuts to foreign aid.

Bagudu also wants greater attention paid to cancers that can be prevented or reduced through interventions already available. She plans to focus particularly on childhood cancers and liver cancer linked to hepatitis.

That prevention must go alongside investment in diagnosis and treatment, particularly as cancer risk is shaped by factors including tobacco use, infections, alcohol, diet and obesity, she adds.

She wants Africa to have a greater role in cancer research, rather than remaining primarily a recipient of discoveries and training from richer countries.

“Research is a little bit more difficult because you have to have the human capacity, you have to have the interest and then you have to have the right environment,” she says.

She points to emerging research centres in Nigeria, Rwanda and Kenya, as well as training programmes that bring African health workers to countries including China to develop skills in radiation therapy, cancer technology and other specialist areas.

The UICC has set targets including reducing cancer mortality by 25% by 2035, reducing exposure to major cancer risk factors by 30% and ensuring that 60% of cancers are diagnosed at an early stage.

Bagudu says the ultimate test of her presidency will be whether the global commitments made in conference rooms reach people far beyond them.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Nadeem Badshah

Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow

The family of a student who took his own life after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate have said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.

Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.

However, his family said that in September that year, the university told him he had not been awarded a grade for one course and would therefore not be eligible to graduate with an honours degree.

His family said as a result, he took his own life on 13 December 2024, the day he should have been graduating.

He was found dead in his bedroom by his mother, Tracy Scott, that morning.

Scott, who collected her son’s degree posthumously, has called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death.

The university has said it is “profoundly sorry” and is implementing a series of recommendations after a review.

The university’s internal inquiry found “systemic” errors in the way Brown’s degree had been graded, and that he had enough marks for a 2:1 honours degree. It also found that although Brown had told staff that he had concerns about his mental health, they had failed to offer him support.

On Tuesday it was reported that the family had settled a civil court action with the university. The sum of the settlement has not been disclosed.

On Wednesday, the family met the Scottish education secretary, Màiri McAllan, at St Andrew’s House in Edinburgh.

Speaking after the meeting, their solicitor Aamer Anwar said they had placed “the University of Glasgow on notice that they will be held to account”.

Anwar claimed that in its drive to become a global institution, the university had “forgotten its soul”.

He added: “Their failures were catastrophic and systemic. They failed not just in their duty of care to Ethan, but to many other students over the years.

“Today’s meeting with the minister was important and was welcomed. The minister offered to ask the QAA [Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education], who are investigating the university, to meet with the family.

“The family welcomed the apology by Ms McAllan for her predecessor’s statement in September 2025 which implied an acceptance of the university’s position that Ethan’s case was an isolated incident.”

Anwar added that the university’s governance process was “not fit for purpose”.

A spokesperson for the University of Glasgow said: “The university is profoundly sorry that Ethan tragically took his own life and fully understands the deep distress this has caused his family. We repeat our sincere apology as well as our deepest sympathy.

“Following an internal investigation into assessment regulations, the university self-referred to the Scottish Funding Council.

“The Quality Assurance Agency subsequently carried out a targeted peer review, which resulted in a series of recommendations for action.

“The university fully accepted the recommendations and is on track to implement them.”

A spokesperson for the Crown Office said the circumstances of Brown’s death were being investigated by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, adding that the family would be kept updated on any developments.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: LA officials document first case of a rabid raccoon in more than 50 years
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dani Anguiano
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Four people and a dog may have been exposed to rabies from the animal, Los Angeles public health officials say

Los Angeles county recently documented its first rabid raccoon in more than 50 years, and health officials are urging residents to never touch wild animals.

The county’s department of public health announced in a statement this week that four people and a dog may have been exposed to the animal at a backyard work site in the city of Westlake Village. The raccoon appeared in ill health but was not aggressive.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Rabies is spread through a bite or scratch from an infected animal. It kills tens of thousands of people each year, mostly in Africa and Asia, and is almost completely fatal once symptoms appear. The US sees fewer than 10 deaths annually “due to robust prevention efforts”, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Health officials in Los Angeles county told residents they should “always keep a safe distance from wildlife and contact your local animal control if you encounter an animal that appears sick, injured, or is behaving unusually” and ensure pets are up to date on their vaccines.

“The detection of rabies in a raccoon is an important reminder to never touch, handle, or feed any wild animals, even when they appear healthy,” said Dr Muntu Davis, the Los Angeles county health officer.

The group of people who were possibly exposed to rabies in Los Angeles county were receiving follow-up care, which includes a series of vaccines. The dog was up to date on its rabies vaccine and is “doing well” under quarantine, according to the health department.

It is not yet known which rabies variant the raccoon was infected with, although officials believe it was probably rabies from a bat. The county has not had a documented case of a rabid raccoon since 1973, according to the public health department, and the last known animal, aside from bats, to have rabies was a skunk in 2014.

This year, the county has seen the highest number of rabid bats it has ever recorded, the public health department said last week, with 69 documented cases. The sick animals have been found in every part of the county and nearly a third of all bats submitted for rabies testing were infected.

“Rabid bat detections can vary year-to-year, but Los Angeles county has seen a steady upward trend for more than a decade,” the public health department said.

World Health Organization detects no sign of further outbreak since Darya Shipilova died last week

The World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after the sudden death of a lab technician who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia.

Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested she may have become infected after an accident at her workplace, where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied.

Russian authorities have downplayed the incident and say Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals.

Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All ‌of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for ‌illness, and none to date have shown ​symptoms of illness,” he said.

Russian ⁠officials were still ​investigating whether viral pneumonic plague caused Shipilova’s death but the WHO had assessed the health risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for the rest of Russia and “very low” for Europe, he said.

WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia on Tuesday to be transparent about Shipilova’s death.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he wrote on X.

According to Russian media, 60 of Shipilova’s colleagues have been locked in the institute where she worked since Friday, sleeping on the floors and chairs while tests are carried out. Similar measures have been imposed in five hospitals, with relatives forbidden to see patients.

The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, urged people on Tuesday not to listen to rumours but to rely on statements from Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. It said the situation in Irkutsk was stable, with no new infectious disease cases reported among institute employees.

Washington has been watching developments closely. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called on Moscow on Tuesday to release more details about the case. “I think it’s incumbent upon ⁠Russia to obviously share more information with ​the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour ‌by hour.”

The Wall Street Journal reported that the US state department had sent Russia a confidential diplomatic communication known as a demarche warning Moscow that failure to disclose details runs counter to its international health obligations.

Trump said on Tuesday that he was due to speak shortly with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the technician’s death.

“I have a call scheduled, yes,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen “very soon”.

Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters.

In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.

“The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.

More than 1 million people in Great Britain now vape despite having never regularly smoked, ONS data shows

More than 1 million people in Great Britain now vape despite never having been regular smokers, with rates nearly doubling in just four years, according to figures that health experts describe as concerning.

About 5.4 million people aged 16 and above in England, Scotland and Wales (9.9%) used e-cigarettes daily or occasionally in 2025, Office for National Statistics data showed. Vaping was highest among those aged 25-34 (16.4%).

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

However, the ONS also found about 2.9% (1.1 million) of Britons who had never smoked cigarettes reported using an e-cigarette daily or occasionally.

The proportion of never-smokers now vaping has increased sharply, almost doubling, since 2021, when 1.5% of people who had never smoked reported that they currently used e-cigarettes.

Estimates published in the Lancet Public Health journal in 2024 suggested there were 1,006,000 people in England who vaped despite never having smoked.

But the data published on Tuesday was the first time official ONS figures had confirmed that the figure for England, Scotland and Wales had topped 1 million. The 2025 figure for Great Britain (1.1 million) was up from 940,000 in 2024, the ONS said.

Justin Webb, an associate professor of physical activity and health at London Metropolitan University, said it was “somewhat concerning that 1.1 million people who have never smoked reported using an e-cigarette”.

He added: “Vapes can help adults stop smoking, but they are not risk-free and their full long-term effects remain unclear. We need to preserve their value as a quitting aid while strengthening protection against uptake among children and non-smokers.”

The ONS data showed 25-34 was the only age group in which there was a rise in e-cigarette use, increasing from 12.9% in 2024 to 16.4% in 2025.

That made the age group the most common users of e-cigarettes in the UK, overtaking 16- to 24-year-olds, who were the most common users between 2021 and 2024.

Meanwhile, separate ONS figures covering all four nations of the UK showed about 4.9 million people aged 18 and over (9.8% of the population) smoked cigarettes in 2025. This was a decrease from 2024 (10.6%) and continues a long-term downward trend.

David Mais, from the ONS, said: “Fewer than one in 10 adults now smoke. This is the lowest proportion on record and continues the long-term decline in smoking.

“At the same time, e-cigarette use remains more common than smoking and has followed an overall upward trend since 2020.

“E-cigarette users are also getting older, with those aged 25 to 34 now overtaking 16- to 24-year-olds as the age group most likely to use them. This may reflect existing users getting older, growing popularity among this age group or a combination of both.”

When it comes to smoking, men were more likely to smoke than women in the UK in 2025, continuing a trend observed in previous years. About 2.8 million men (11.3%) and 2.1m women (8.2%) were thought to be current smokers.

The largest reduction in smoking prevalence between 2011 and 2025 was among the 18-24 age group, from 25.7% to 7.2%, the ONS found.

Hazel Cheeseman, the chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “For the first time, fewer than one in 10 people in the UK smoke. This is really encouraging progress and shows what can be achieved through sustained action to reduce smoking.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Russia has denied that Darya Shipilova died from plague after becoming ill at work but experts say there are still questions to answer

After a 28-year-old lab technician died last week reportedly after an accident at an anti-plague research laboratory in Russia, we take a look at what we know about the incident.

The exact details remain unclear but reports from Russia have suggested Darya Shipilova, an employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, died on 2 October, two days after becoming unwell at work.

According to Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.

However, there are other accounts: Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the neighbouring Buryatia region, initially said Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his social media post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.

Russian authorities have denied this to the World Health Organization (WHO), stating: “No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, ​Russian Federation.”

We are talking about a disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, typically found in small mammals and the fleas that feed on them. It is the same organism that was behind the bubonic plague or “black death” that swept Europe in the 14th century.

However, the bubonic form is different from the pneumonic plague that some have suggested caused Shipilova’s death.

The former is more common, results in swellings called buboes and is spread by the bite of infected fleas, whereas the latter is lung-based. Pneumonic plague has a higher mortality rate and can be spread between people.

One report in the media is that Shipilova was admitted with the disease after returning from Thailand, while another is that she became infected after breaking a test tube in the laboratory. Rospotrebnadzor has denied any such accidents have occurred at the institute.

It is worth noting that the plague is not a disease of the past.

“There are a few hundred cases of plague reported each year globally usually in geographically restricted areas, particularly in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo – although there are a small number of cases in the western United States, central Asia, Mongolia, etc,” said Dr Malick Gibani at Imperial College London.

That might not seem reassuring, but we no longer have to rely on medieval medicine.

Dr Simon Clarke at the University of Reading said: “Unlike many viral respiratory diseases, plague is caused by bacteria, and antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides work well against this pathogen if administered early enough and are often given prophylactically, post-exposure.”

However, Prof Brendan Wren at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said there were multi-antibiotic-resistant strains emerging, “and if the laboratory is working on such a strain, then treatment options may be limited”.

There have also been reports that almost 200 people with whom Shipilova may have had contact are now under medical observation, and that quarantines have been imposed in a number of hospitals.

“Isolation and monitoring are sensible strategies,” Wren said.

Prof Alice Hughes at the University of Melbourne added the incubation for pneumonic plague was only one to three days and, as yet no one has shown symptoms.

Prof Ian Jones at the University of Reading also offered reassurance. “This case here seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further.”

However, Clarke said there were still unknowns. “Until more details emerge, it is difficult to assess whether this represents an isolated case, an occupational exposure, or evidence of wider transmission,” he said.

The UN health agency’s spokesperson Christian Lindmeier has said the risk to others is low. “The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region,” he said.

Dr Zania Stamataki, an associate professor of viral immunology and academic lead for containment level 3 laboratories at the University of Birmingham, said the control systems used in the UK for hazardous organisms work, meaning laboratory-acquired infections are rare.

But, she added: “They are not impossible, and this is why an incident warrants a full account of what happened. That account matters beyond Russia.”

Other experts also stressed a need for transparency. “I think it’s important that we see how this pans out, and ideally, there’d be good communication between the public health authorities and the wider global health community,” said Gibani.

“I think this emphasises the need to be aware of ongoing outbreaks of serious bacterial pathogens and highlights the need for investment in biosecurity, particularly for preventing biological risks,” he added. “This could include developing medical countermeasures like better diagnostics or vaccines.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The deadly outbreak in Pennsylvania is its largest in more than three decades, and confirmed cases in New York are up

The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency on Monday in response to a dramatic spike in measles cases in the state.

Hochul’s administration said the emergency declaration was in response to a “growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states”, including Pennsylvania, which has been grappling with a deadly outbreak that is its largest in more than three decades.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The declaration expands the pool of people who can administer vaccines against measles and allows more individuals to order testing.

It comes as there have been 108 confirmed cases of measles in New York so far for the year, up from just one reported case in 2023. In Pennsylvania, which neighbors New York, five people have died after contracting the disease, and there have been 198 hospitalizations.

The state surpassed 1,000 measles cases on Monday while Ohio has also seen an increase.

New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio have sizable Amish populations, which tend to be undervaccinated. And undervaccination has been a driving factor in measles spreading after its domestic US spread had been eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates.

“After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York state, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said.

“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.”

The US is experiencing its worst year for measles since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with nearly 3,900 cases reported.

Of New York’s 108 measles cases, 101 have been reported outside of New York City, the state said. Since 15 July, 92 cases have been reported in underimmunized rural communities.

It is a stark increase from previous years. Beside the one reported case in 2023, there were only 15 in 2024 – and in 2025, there were a total of 48 measles cases.

The Trump administration health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has been criticized for his response to the measles outbreak. Before his appointment as health secretary, he was best known as an anti-vaccine activist.

Kennedy headlined an anti-vaccine conference in Washington DC in mid-September, as measles cases surged. He told the crowd there that they had a “strong and steadfast friend at the White House”.

Meanwhile, the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and the two men have clashed over how to classify measles-related deaths.

“The concerning rise in measles cases is due to a decrease in childhood vaccines driven by misinformation and is causing a public health emergency,” said state senator Gustavo Rivera, who chairs the senate’s health committee.

At least 95% of a community must be vaccinated against measles to prevent outbreaks.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Experts looking at UK, US and Dutch data found ‘significant increases’ in early onset cases of seven cancers, prompting warnings about lifestyle choices

Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.

The number of people under 50 diagnosed with prostate cancer in England has quadrupled since 2001, while early onset bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses more than doubled.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Analysis of English, US and Dutch cancer data by World Cancer Research Fund identified “significant increases” in early onset cancers for seven cancer types in England, five types in the US and four in the Netherlands.

Although cancer has been increasing across all age groups globally, the rate rise in early onset cases is greater than other ages.

Experts said the figures reflected the growing global obesity epidemic, poor diets and insufficient exercise, as well as growing awareness of cancer and earlier diagnosis.

Cancer among the under 50s is still uncommon, with the median age at diagnosis above 60, but the trend is worrying, the authors noted.

Commenting on the findings, Mark Lawler, professor of digital health and the chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, called the problem “a ticking timebomb that we need to [defuse] as quickly as possible, otherwise the numbers will undoubtedly continue to grow”.

He went on: “The overall trend is also particularly worrying as it comes on the backdrop of lifestyle factors contributing to thousands of deaths.”

In England, of the 12 tumour types studied, incidence rates of prostate cancer among men under 50 jumped from one in every 100,000 people in 2001 to 3.6 in every 100,000 in 2023. Over the same period, rates of bowel cancer among the under 50s leapt from 3.9 in 100,000 people in 2001 to 8.4 in 100,000 in 2023, while early onset uterine and kidney cancers also doubled to 3.9 and 3 per 100,000 people respectively.

The rate of breast cancer among the under 50s increased, albeit less sharply, from 42 to 47.5 per 100,000 in 2023, while there were also increases in the incidence of early onset pancreatic and liver cancers.

In the US, analysis of official data since 2000 found that among patients under 50, incidence rates of kidney cancer more than doubled from 2.5 in 100,000 people in 2000 to 5.3 in 2023, while bowel, uterine and pancreatic cancers all increased by more than 50% and breast cancer by about 20%.

For the Netherlands, the researchers found significant increases in early onset bowel, kidney, liver and cervical cancers.

In contrast, rates of lung cancer among the under 50s declined in all three countries, reflecting continuing declines in smoking in those countries.

Dr Giota Mitrou, the executive director of research and policy at the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), called the trajectory “concerning”, and added: “Behind every figure is a person facing cancer earlier than they, their family and often their doctor would expect. While cancer is still much more common in older adults, these changing patterns among younger generations need to be treated as a serious research and cancer prevention priority.”

WCRF said risk factors such as growing obesity levels, poor diet, insufficient exercise, alcohol consumption, smoking and environmental exposures (such as pollutants, chemicals, plastics, water and air pollution) could be contributing to the trend. About 40% of cancers are linked to these kinds of modifiable risks. However, greater awareness of cancer symptoms also means that people are more likely to be diagnosed earlier.

“While we don’t completely understand why more cancers are occurring in people under 50 years of age, it is likely that risk factors related to cancer – for example, overweight and obesity, diet, alcohol, consumption and smoking – play a role,” said Dr Vanessa Gordon-Dseagu, research translation manager at WCRF.

“At the same time, the public are increasingly aware of the risk factors relating to cancer and the signs and symptoms of the disease to look out for, so are more likely to seek out healthcare when they experience them.”

While more cancers are being diagnosed at an earlier stage, “increased diagnosis does not explain the whole story and more research is needed to understand early-onset cancers” she added.

King’s College London has announced a new trial of 250,000 people, funded by Cancer Research UK, to investigate the increase in bowel cancer cases among younger adults.

The study will seek a clearer understanding of the balance between worsening risk factors and better detection in the rise.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “These findings underline why early diagnosis is at the heart of our national cancer plan. To help catch cancer sooner, we’re investing in new technologies to speed up diagnosis, expanding genetic testing, and supporting research to better understand the causes of cancer and who may be most at risk.

We’re also prioritising research into less-survivable and rarer cancers, and our ambition is for three-quarters of people diagnosed by 2035 to be cancer-free or living well with cancer, saving 320,000 lives.

“Our newly announced national cancer board has a specific representative for children and young people, as we’re aware of the devastating impact of getting cancer at an earlier stage of life.”

Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country

Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.

Pennsylvania’s health department said on Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents ⁠have died ⁠after ​contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Lancaster county, with sizable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.

The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, over how to classify measles-related mortality.

Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.

Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.

“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”

In New York state, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.

Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.

The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.

In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.

Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.

According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s. That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters.

The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.

In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
More than half of US students surveyed said the problem damaged their ability to do academic work, study finds

Procrastination is the biggest problem that can harm students’ academic performance at university, according to a study of more than 65,000 young people who placed it above issues such as ADHD, anxiety or financial worries.

The study found that nearly half of the students surveyed named procrastination as the thing damaging their ability to do academic work, more than twice the number who named depression, while the same proportion said procrastination caused them significant distress above any other problems including family pressures or bullying.

Itamar Shatz, the author of the study and an affiliated lecturer at the University of Cambridge, said that while he expected the survey of US students would show that they experienced harm from procrastination, he was surprised by how strongly it affected them.

Shatz said: “Pretty much all of us procrastinate but it’s not a huge impediment for all of us. For the people that it is, it can be huge. It’s not just something we occasionally run into but, as we can see in these findings, it can be a major obstacle.

“It’s an obstacle that can interfere with academic success, with success in the workplace, it can cause issues in relationships, it can cause stress, it can cause health issues and stop us reaching out for help.”

The study, published in the journal Plos One, also suggests that procrastination could be a factor in a “vicious cycle” that can cause or exaggerate other issues such as stress.

“An example of such a feedback loop is a student procrastinating on a task, which causes them to feel stressed, which interferes with their sleep, which causes them to procrastinate on the task further,” the study said.

Fuschia Sirois, a psychology professor at Durham University and a co-editor-in-chief of the British Journal of Health Psychology, who was not involved in the study, said: “The salience of procrastination in students’ lives and its harms has been a topic of research for almost 30 years, with the first studies on the impact of procrastination on health and wellbeing conducted in the late 1990s and early 2000s. So this is an issue for which there is an established evidence base that clearly highlights the negative impact of procrastination on students’ lives.

“This descriptive study with a large sample provides some additional insights into the relative impact of procrastination with respect to its range of harms. But it is just a snapshot, so limits the conclusions we can draw.”

Sirois said myths about procrastination “being a character flaw” have persisted despite the existing research.

“People procrastinate to avoid the difficult emotions associated with a task, which affords them short-term mood repair. But in the long run the feelings of guilt, shame and stress from procrastinating catch up to them and take a toll on health and wellbeing,” she said.

Shatz, who has recently published a guide to overcoming procrastination, said that procrastination should not be compared with laziness, because procrastinators can often be highly motivated to tackle a task only to be derailed by other distractions such as perfectionism or burn-out.

Universities should be aware that many of their students are likely to be hampered by procrastination.

“They should understand that procrastination isn’t just a time management flaw that they can fix with a flyer, but it is one of the biggest obstacles that students face and needs to be treated with positive interventions. The good thing is that research shows that interventions can help,” Shatz said.
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: Study of 65,000 young people found procrastination is biggest problem that can harm students' academic performance. Nearly half of US students surveyed named procrastinating as the thing damaging their ability to do academic work. The same proportion said procrastinations caused them significant distress above any other problems including family pressures or bullying.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal with Angelique Chrisafis, produced by Tom Glasser, Saskia Collette and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli
https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2.text:
Angelique Chrisafis on the pupils and students who are taking to the streets and closing down schools in France

Thousands arrested, hundreds injured. It’s been a shocking week for France. Schools have been closed and ransacked. Some have simply been burned down.

The pupils are fed up with the status quo. And they’re furious about a school system that they say is failing them.

It began with outrage over shoddy school conditions in the banlieue, the deprived suburbs on the outskirts of Paris. But the movement has grown into something much bigger, fuelled by a feeling that no one cares about them – and that their lives are only going to get worse, explains the Guardian’s Paris correspondent, Angelique Chrisafis. She tells Nosheen Iqbal that a boy has already lost an eye, and another has lost a hand. So how will the protests be resolved?
