FORGET THE SPENDY flagship smartphone. Every year, we test a dozen or more devices to find the best cheap phones that perform where it counts and aren’t annoyingly slow. Wireless carriers in the US go out of their way to make expensive smartphones seem affordable. AT&T will advertise a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra for just $36 a month, but don’t let that fool you. With over 36 monthly installments, you spend more than a thousand bucks on a phone. Your pricey device may also keep you locked into the network, unable to switch wireless carriers until the phone is paid off.

Get a seriously great, affordable smartphone instead. Our top pick, the Google Pixel 10a, costs $499 and is as good as almost any flagship device. Our other recommendations strike a great balance between price and luxury. There’s even a folding phone in this guide! But it’s currently very tough to find phones worth considering under $400, since manufacturers slapped an extra $100 on most of their phones in response to the memory shortage.

Check out our many other mobile guides, including Best Android Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Best Phones With a Headphone Jack, Best Google Pixel, Best Moto Phones, and Best iPhones.

Updated October 2026: We added the Motorola Moto G Power 2026, Samsung Galaxy A37, and Motorola Razr 2026, refreshed the Samsung Galaxy S25 FE and Nothing Phone 4(a) Pro, added mentions for the TCL P80 Ultra and Nothing Phone (4b), and updated the FAQ.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

The Pixel 10a disappointingly may not change much from its predecessor, the Pixel 9a, but it remains the best smartphone on the market, especially for anyone trying to curb their spending.

It’s not the cheapest phone, but it has the best suite of features for the price, from an excellent dual-camera system to a sharp, 120-Hz screen, and performance that can run most apps and games perfectly fine thanks to the Tensor G4 chip. It’ll even get software updates for seven years, and Google says the battery is slightly easier to replace than the older model.

The biggest changes from the Pixel 9a are a brighter screen, faster wired and wireless charging (still no Pixelsnap magnets for Qi2 charging), and a tougher glass protecting the display. The plastic ring on the camera module is also gone, so the back of the Pixel 10a is even flatter than before—great for anyone who hates bulky camera bumps. These updates are still fairly minor, so if you happen to catch the Pixel 9a on sale, it’s still worthwhile if it means saving $100 or $150 bucks. However, the Pixel 10a will almost definitely also go on sale during major sale events like Prime Day and Black Friday, if you can be patient.

It’s nice to have faster charging speeds, but battery life overall is OK. It adequately lasts a full day with average use and then some, but folks who spend a lot of time on their smartphone during the day—whether it’s for navigating, music streaming, or reading fanfic—will likely find themselves hunting for an outlet in the afternoon.

The dual-camera system is versatile. The main 48-MP camera can snap pleasing photos, in low light and daytime, whereas the 13-MP ultrawide lets you capture sweeping scenes or group photos. Even the 13-MP selfie camera is pretty reliable. Naturally, with all the smart software features that Google is known for on its Pixel phones, there are some new AI perks here. Camera Coach lets you ask Google’s AI to give you suggestions on how to take a better photo, and Auto Best Take for group photos will automatically snap multiple pictures when you tap the shutter button and choose the best of each person, like fixing someone’s blinking eyes.

Speaking of, software is the top reason why I heartily recommend Pixel phones. I’ve detailed many of them here, but you can use Add Me to make sure everyone is in the group photo, including the photographer. Audio Magic Eraser lets you strip out unwanted sounds from your videos, like sirens. And Google’s Call Screen technology nips spam calls in the bud. I used the Hold for Me function to not have to listen to Delta’s terrible hold music for four hours after my flight was canceled.

Other perks include secure face unlock and fingerprint unlock—both work with sensitive apps that require biometric authentication, so you have multiple unlocking options. Secure face unlock is virtually nonexistent for every other Android phone at this price. There’s also NFC for contactless payments and an IP68 rating that protects it from the elements.

Apple’s cheapest iPhone—the iPhone 17e—is a better value than its predecessor, the iPhone 16e. MagSafe is the biggest addition here (one of the strangest omissions last year), so now you can take advantage of the large accessory ecosystem, whether you want to use a magnetic wallet that sticks to the back of your iPhone or a magnetic tripod to snap selfies on your travels.

Like the rest of the iPhone 17 lineup, the iPhone 17e also uses the same Ceramic Shield 2 glass mixture to protect the display, which is more durable and scratch-resistant and matches what’s on the pricier iPhones—always a plus. It’s no iPhone Mini, but this is Apple’s smallest phone in the lineup, which is nice for anyone who hates big-screen handsets, though you’re stuck with the old-school notch design instead of the Dynamic Island found on the rest of the iPhones. (There’s still Face ID!)

It’s powered by the latest-generation A19 chip, like the iPhone 17, though there’s one less graphics core, so there’s a minor hit to performance. I still had no trouble running all my usual apps and games, even Genshin Impact at its max graphical settings. Battery life is also solid, comfortably lasting me a full day, though extreme users will likely need a top-up before bed. I suspect the improved and energy-efficient C1X 5G modem is what helps extend battery life despite the small size of the phone.

Where this iPhone doesn’t quite feel like its $599 price is the camera. You can snap perfectly good photos with the 48-MP sensor, but that’s it; that’s the only camera on the back. Now compare it to the Pixel 10a and its dual-camera system, or the Samsung Galaxy S25 FE and its triple-camera module (often on sale for under $500). Apple should really have added an extra camera here for versatility, as the lone camera is too limiting.

Generally, camera performance is also a little lackluster in low light, especially if you’re trying to capture a moving subject like a pet. It may sound like it has the same 48-MP camera as the iPhone 17, but the sensor is smaller, so you’re not getting the same image quality. The selfie camera is also OK, but it can struggle with high-contrast scenes.

There’s no ultrawideband chip on the iPhone 17e, so you can’t precisely track AirTags—this iPhone will only give you the general vicinity of the tag’s location. And the screen is still stuck on a 60-Hz refresh rate when nearly every phone that costs this much has moved on to 120 Hz.

These concessions make the iPhone 17e feel a little overpriced, but it’s sure as heck better value than the iPhone 16e. If you don’t find the flaws off-putting and don’t care much for the camera experience, this smartphone will satisfy anyone looking for a good, reliable, and price-friendly iPhone. Apple also sells the iPhone 16 for $100 more, but I don’t think it’s worth paying more for less storage and slightly lesser performance, even if it has perks like a dual-camera system.

Want a Samsung phone but don’t want to pay the flagship prices? Samsung’s FE series is exactly that (FE stands for Fan Edition). Despite testing this year’s Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, we’re still recommending last year’s S25 FE, and that’s because very little has changed and the price has gone up. With the S25 FE hovering around $500, it would cost you an extra $200 to get the 26 FE and it’s simply not worth it. The S25 FE is very similar to the Galaxy S25 series, but think of it as a “lite” version. Certain elements are just a few notches below what you’d find in a flagship, like the screen, which doesn’t get as bright, and doesn’t feature an adaptive refresh rate that can go from 1 to 120 Hz. This phone’s MSRP was $650, but it has been steadily dropping in price and has been as low as $450—that’s the price that makes it worthwhile (and also worthy of consideration for this guide).

You still get a sharp 6.7-inch AMOLED screen with a 120-Hz screen refresh rate, a 4,900-mAh battery that generally lasts a full day with average use, and a triple-camera system with a 3X optical zoom lens. The results from the camera are surprisingly strong, though I did find that the phone has trouble autofocusing in low light, and nighttime images can be a little blurry if there’s a lot of movement. Like the two phones above, this Android phone will get some of the longest software support compared to competitors in this bracket.

I used it for more than a week, and the Exynos 2400 chipset didn’t cause me any strife. I booted up the very demanding Genshin Impact mobile game and maxed out the graphics—there certainly were stutters during gameplay, but it was totally playable. Almost all the Galaxy AI features are available on this phone, if that’s something you care about, too. (Read our Best Samsung Phones guide for more details about that.)

It maintains all the other flagship perks you’d want, from Qi wireless charging (Qi2 Ready if you have a magnetic case) and IP68 water resistance. It may look a little plain, but it’s a great all-rounder—just make sure you catch it on sale.

Midrange and budget phones usually don’t experiment too much with design, so they’re rarely exciting, but London-based Nothing has been trying to fix that for a few years with its attractive, stylish, and unique handsets. The latest iteration is the Nothing Phone (4a) and Phone (4a) Pro, though only the latter is available in the US.

It looks nothing like its peers. The Pro has a fresh camera module with a unique camera layout and the Glyph Matrix that the company debuted last year on the Phone (3). This tiny display has some fun functionality, like seeing an outline of your head so you can snap a selfie picture with the rear cameras (and still be in the frame). The triple-camera system boasts a 50-MP main camera, an 8-MP ultrawide, and a 50-MP telephoto zoom offering 3.5X zoom. Photos look natural and detailed, with pleasing colors and good exposure, but low light performance is a weakness.

This is a solid midrange phone with good performance, a nice screen, reliable battery life, and unique software design. Nothing’s retro take on Android is a pixel art aesthetic you won’t find anywhere else, with a lovely interface and fun widgets. There’s also the Essential Key, which you can press to capture a screenshot and dump the data into the Essential Space app, or press and hold to record a voice note.

The Phone (4a) Pro is competitive compared to the Google Pixel 10a, offering a triple-camera experience, a 144-Hz AMOLED screen, and speedy charging. However, software support isn’t anything special (three Android OS upgrades and six years of security updates), water resistance is a little lackluster (IP65), and carrier support can be a little wonky. But if you want a smartphone that will turn heads, the Nothing Phone (4a) Pro will do it.

The ongoing memory crisis driven by AI has led most smartphone makers to increase their prices by $100 across the board. Sadly, that means the Moto G Stylus (2026), which would have occupied this spot, now costs $500 and isn’t worth buying over the Pixel 10a or Nothing Phone 4(a) Pro above unless you are desperate for a stylus. It’s slim pickings for phones under $400 that are worth considering. Dropping below $500 (outside of sale events) is currently where you’ll feel the step down the most, which brings us to the Moto G Power 2026. Originally released at a much more reasonable $300, Motorola has jacked the price to $400.

While it’s less stuttery than its predecessor, the Moto G Power 2026 still has a MediaTek Dimensity 6300 processor with 8 GB of RAM. This improvement likely comes from performance optimizations and the latest Android version. The roomy 6.8-inch LCD is sharp and bright. There’s a reliable fingerprint scanner, a headphone jack for those of you who prefer to plug in when listening to music, and a microSD card slot. It’s also IP68/69 rated, so it will handle heavy rain or even brief submersion in fresh water.

Compared to last year’s Moto G Power, the selfie camera is now 32 megapixels, and the battery capacity is slightly higher at 5,200 mAh. As the name suggests, battery life is stellar, and you can get two full days of average use out of this phone. But Motorola has also made some unwelcome changes this year: the fun colors are gone, and it removed wireless charging.

The 50-megapixel main camera isn’t terrible, but colors can look washed out, and the image processing adds some over-sharpening. There’s also an 8-MP ultrawide that’s not great, and even the upgraded selfie camera is a bit disappointing. They all struggle with high-contrast scenes, and you must stay still to avoid blurry photos. If you’re patient, you can get decent images, but cameras are not the Moto G Power’s strong suit.

The Moto G Power 2026 gets two Android OS upgrades, alongside three years of security updates. That’s poor compared to its peers above, but Motorola has historically poor software support. The key thing is that Motorola phones go on sale often. It’s not a great deal at $400, but if you can get it near its original $300 release price or below, it’s a bargain. —Simon Hill

The Galaxy A37 does a good job of aping Samsung’s more expensive phones, and it’s a decent alternative to the Moto G Power 2026 above. It regularly dips to $375. You get a nice big AMOLED display, an IP68 waterproof rating, great battery life, and a good main camera. Sadly, the plastic frame feels a bit cheap, and it’s very easy to smudge the shiny gloss back.

The processor is limited, and the RAM starts at just 6 GB. Despite a few dropped frames in Asphalt Legends and some delay coming in and out of the camera, I didn’t find the performance to be too bad. The 5,000 mAh battery will see you through busy days and maybe stretch to two with light use. Like the Moto G Power, there’s no wireless charging.

I had low expectations, so was pleasantly surprised by the photos I shot with the main 50-megapixel camera, and the selfie camera is fine. The 8-MP ultrawide and 5-MP macro lenses are very poor. I’m not convinced the macro lens is worth including.

Samsung does offer a few other budget phones, but the A57 is only a teeny bit better than the A37 (not enough to justify an extra $100), and there is no A27 this year. If you can find last year’s Galaxy A26 for at least $100 less than the A37, it’s still worth considering for folks on a tighter budget. —Simon Hill

While $800 isn’t really anyone’s idea of cheap, the Motorola Razr 2026 is relatively affordable for a folding phone! It’s a flip-style phone, but the exterior screen is still large enough to see widgets, notifications, and even a few apps without opening the whole thing. Flip phones are great because they feel like normal handsets once opened, but they fold down to be super compact.

The slightly improved MediaTek chipset is fine. Expect an occasional slowdown, but nothing too frustrating. Motorola has also increased the battery capacity, so you might even squeeze two days out of it with light use.

The camera system is nowhere near as strong as the Razr Ultra, especially in low light and high-contrast scenes. But a 50-MP main camera is good enough to snag some pleasing photos, and the 50-MP ultrawide is handy for taking group shots. You can use the external screen as a viewfinder so everyone can make sure they’re in the frame. The selfie camera is solid.

You also get wireless charging (not Qi2), a decent fingerprint sensor, and better software support than Motorola’s lesser budget phones (three Android upgrades, five years of security updates).

We highly recommend you stick with the phones above, but here are some alternatives worth considering.

Samsung Galaxy A36 (left) and Galaxy A26 (right).

Samsung Galaxy A26 for $300: If you want a Samsung phone but don’t want to spend much, I think the Galaxy A26 is the best bang for your buck. Performance is solid, battery life lasts a full day, there’s an IP67 water resistance rating, and the camera is OK. It even has expandable storage (though no headphone jack), and Samsung promises six years of software updates, which is unparalleled at this price. It seems to no longer be available from Samsung, but there was no A27 this year, so snap it up if you can find it.

Samsung Galaxy A36 for $400: With a higher price, you’d think the A36 would be even better than the A26, right? Wrong. The Galaxy A36 hits many highs, including a brighter display, good battery life, and solid cameras, but storage is not expandable, and performance was bizarrely more choppy. The six years of software support are nice, but if the phone is already annoying to operate, I can’t imagine what it’ll be like in six years. It’s an OK phone, but you can do better. (It’s a better buy at its sale price of $230.)

TCL 60 XE Nxtpaper 5G for $200: TCL’s 60 XE has an anti-reflective matte screen called Nxtpaper to limit the blue light entering your eyes for better sleep and reduced eye fatigue. There’s no evidence to suggest that blue-light blockers work, but if you ignore those claims, this is still a great budget phone with a pleasing matte screen. There is a switch on the side that lets you flip between different display modes that turn the screen closer to a monochrome or color E Ink experience, great for fans of e-readers. Performance is good, the camera is decent, and there are extras like a headphone jack and microSD card slot. The only problem is that the screen is hard to read in direct sunlight. Folks in the UK might consider the more premium TCL P80 Ultra (£480), which has the same E Ink display party trick, but a much faster processor, better and brighter display, more versatile triple-lens camera, and a few other upgrades. Sadly, there’s no word on a US release for it yet.

Moto G 2026 for $200: The Moto G 2026 comes in this gorgeous pink! It’s a pretty-looking phone, and a decent $200 handset. Performance is sluggish, which is why I think you’re better off buying the Moto G Power 2026 when it goes on sale. The cameras are barely passable, but you can make contactless payments, access 5G connectivity, and perform day-to-day tasks with a bit of patience.

Moto G Play 2026 for $180: Motorola’s new Moto G Play 2026 adds 5G connectivity for the first time. However, performance is still quite sluggish, with apps and webpages taking several seconds to load. If you want to pay very little money, this will do the job, but I think you should buy the Moto G Power 2026 instead, especially when it inevitably goes on sale. While the Power’s performance isn’t amazing, it’s much better than the Play’s and has stronger cameras and more features.

Minimal Phone for $450: Want to reduce your reliance on a smartphone? The Minimal Phone has an e-paper touchscreen and a physical keyboard, but it runs Android. That means you can still access every app you’d want via the Google Play Store, but the experience is going to be inferior due to the phone’s low refresh rate (good luck watching videos on this thing) and the tiny monochrome screen. Still, this is a decent alternative (or maybe even a second phone) if you just want to get away from doomscrolling.

Samsung Galaxy A17 5G for $200: The new Galaxy A17 doesn’t change much from its predecessor—it’s still frustrating to use, perhaps even more so this year. The paltry 4 GB of RAM constantly slowed down everything. If I were in an emergency, I would not trust the A17 to help reliably. The good news is that the camera is decent, there’s a long software update window, and the AMOLED screen is nice—not to mention the expandable storage. But you need a lot of patience with this phone, so it’s only for someone whose needs are very minimal.

Nuu N20 for $130: Right after I tested the Galaxy A16 last year, I moved on to the cheaper Nuu N20. Color me surprised. Yes, it can still be sluggish, but performance on this nearly $100 phone is far better and manageable. I used it for a week with no major problems. Well, except one: GPS on this device isn’t great. The few times I used it for navigation, it struggled to find my location and was slow to update the map. Another big problem? The N20 runs Android 14, so it’s already out of date, and the company tells me there is no “exact schedule for software updates.”

Sonim XP Pro 5G for $550: This rugged phone is sold through Verizon only, but I tested it on Google Fi and didn’t have any connectivity issues. (Fi is powered by T-Mobile’s network.) I have dropped this Android phone multiple times on the sidewalk (on purpose), and the screen has not cracked. It's quite durable, and that’s largely the reason to buy it. On its own, it’s not wholly impressive—you can buy more powerful, feature-rich phones for the money. The camera is especially bad, consistently delivering blurry shots unless you stay as still as a statue. But performance is decent. It comes with 256 GB of storage with a microSD card slot, and there’s a customizable button you can set to trigger a shortcut or open an app.

Nothing Phone (3a) Lite for £249: Nothing’s Phone (3a) Lite is a confusing smartphone in its lineup. The CMF Phone 2 Pro exists and is similar in price (CMF is Nothing’s sub-brand), and in general, there are better phones you can buy for the money. The cameras are lackluster, and there’s a lot of bloatware, which feels like the opposite of Nothing’s philosophy. Performance is decent, as is its battery life. There’s also the very similar, but newer, Nothing Phone (4b) for £299. It adds the Glyph bar and some minor upgrades, like a better IP64 rating and stereo speakers, and drops the useless macro lens, but it’s an extra £50. Neither phone launched in the US.

If you’re eyeing a cheap phone, try to stick to name brands. There are several smartphones you’ll find for dirt cheap on Amazon, but you’re about to load up whatever you buy with your personal information and photos—it’s important to make sure it’s a reputable brand with good security practices (or at least some kind of record that it does issue security patches).

Outside of that, we generally recommend avoiding the previous generation (unless otherwise mentioned above). It may not get updates for much longer (if any), and prices aren’t usually that different. That’s why I don’t recommend Motorola’s Moto G series phones from 2024 or older—you may want to skip some of the 2025 models too, like the Moto G 2025, since its successor is already here.

We also don’t recommend you buy any HMD devices anymore. Sadly, the company has ceased its operations in the US market.

For the most part, yes. Cheap phones typically launch in the first half of the year. Google’s Pixel 11a, Apple’s more affordable iPhones, and releases from Nothing and others likely won’t land until the spring of 2027.

Consider Last Year’s Flagship Phones (or Used)

If none of these phones have the features you want or they aren’t as powerful as you’d like, your best option is to look for a previous generation flagship smartphone, which might be steeply discounted. Sometimes they’re easy to find, but manufacturers may stop selling them. Keep in mind that you’ll lose a year of software support, but that’s often still better than the software support available on cheap phones anyway. Prices fluctuate, so purchase accordingly.

Alternatively, consider buying a used smartphone. (We have some tips here.) You’ll need to research, but sites like Swappa, Gazelle, and Back Market have a good reputation and are solid places to buy a used or refurbished device. Look for the current top models on Android and iPhone from the past year or two, and see what they're going for in mint or good condition.

5G Smartphones, Explained

5G is the current cellular network generation, and it’s widespread enough that you should try to stick to phones that support it. It’s not replacing 4G LTE entirely, so you’ll see 4G in your status bar as you roam the country. You can read more about it here, but in short, 5G comes in two major types: sub-6 and millimeter wave (mmWave). The latter is usually only available in flagship phones and allows you to access superfast speeds, but you’ll rarely encounter mmWave (think select areas in major cities and certain venues, like stadiums and airports). Sub-6 isn’t much faster than 4G LTE, but it has a broader range and is more widely accessible. Most of the smartphones we recommend here support sub-6 5G, even those as low as $180.

Check Network Compatibility

If you buy an unlocked phone on this list and try to take it to one of your wireless carrier’s retail stores, they may tell you it isn’t compatible with the network. It likely is. Just use a paper clip or SIM ejection tool to pop the SIM card out of your current phone, then slide that SIM into your new phone. If it doesn’t work at first, reboot the phone. (Most cheap phones support eSIM technology, too.)

If you need a new SIM, try ordering one online from your carrier or see if they’ll give you one when you activate a line in the store (if you’re starting coverage). Tell them you have a phone. Often, reps will want to sell you a phone; that’s one reason they might hassle you into buying a different device in the store. Having said that, please make sure whatever phone you buy will work on your wireless network. Listings on retailers like Amazon should state clearly which networks a device will be compatible with. Also, make sure the listing says the phone is being sold “unlocked.”

In this guide, we’ve listed whether a phone works with a major US carrier. But what if you’re not on AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon? If we note that a phone works on T-Mobile, for example, that means it’ll likely work on smaller carriers like Metro by T-Mobile and Mint Mobile, both of which utilize T-Mobile’s cellular network. If you’re nervous about compatibility, look up the specifications of the exact model you’re considering. Make sure it has the LTE or 5G bands it needs to run on your carrier.

Warning for Verizon users: There’s a higher chance an unlocked phone will not work on your network. Make sure it is labeled to work on Verizon, or that it says the phone is CDMA-capable. If something strange is going on, like you don’t get any texts, you may also need to contact customer service and ask them to enable CDMA-less roaming. AT&T and T-Mobile are GSM carriers, which is the standard for most of the world; most unlocked phones are compatible with them.

https://www.wired.com/story/the-man-behi.title: The Man Behind a West Bank Telegram Channel Trying to Keep Palestinian Drivers Safe
https://www.wired.com/story/the-man-behi.author: Lama Rabah
https://www.wired.com/story/the-man-behi.text:
THE FIRST TIME we were supposed to meet Anas Hattab, he canceled at the last minute: There was no way to make it from his hometown in Tulkarm, in the northern West Bank, south to Ramallah, where we were meeting, and back before it got dark. That trip, which used to take him an hour, now often takes two to three hours—and some days far longer—because of Israeli military checkpoints on the way. This was one of those days.

This story was produced in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ), Lighthouse Reports, and Evident.

At 30, Hattab’s life now revolves around these checkpoints—perhaps more than any other Palestinian in the occupied West Bank. But he has also transformed his community’s approach to them: Nearly 350,000 people follow his traffic Telegram group, which has closed a gap left open by major navigation apps that fail Palestinian users. Local radio stations build their hourly road segments off his dispatches. A routing system used by West Bank companies and a new local app pull his data into their own.

It began in 2019. Hattab was working during the day as a digital designer at a newspaper in Ramallah. When one shift ended, he started another, this time as the paper’s delivery driver. That meant that most nights, Hattab had to drive all around the West Bank. After loading the fresh editions into his car, he would drive north, looping through the cities of Nablus and Jenin, eventually reaching his home in Tulkarm by dawn. He found himself dodging Israeli military raids, settlements he had to route around and, most of all, unpredictable checkpoints, which could cause hours-long delays and where armed Israeli soldiers could search him or his car.

For decades, Israel has restricted or barred Palestinian vehicles from many of the main arteries through the West Bank, while Israeli vehicles pass freely. Popular navigation apps like Google Maps don't account for any of it. They do not mark the 942 checkpoints, gates, and other barriers that now fragment the territory, and they default to what their algorithms deem the fastest routes, many of which run through settlements and areas under Israeli control. A Palestinian driver who follows their directions risks being arrested, fined, or shot.

Israeli checkpoints frequently make it difficult to travel even short distances in the West Bank, often blocking traffic for hours at a time.

Navigating these uncertain roads, night after night, wore on Hattab. He knew he wasn't the only one. “People were scared to leave their governorates,” he says. At the core of that fear was an information void. So he began devising a way to fill it, for himself and every other Palestinian in the West Bank.

Seven years ago, Hattab launched a Telegram group called “Road Conditions.” The idea was that people would share information with each other about movements at checkpoints—warn each other about delays or closures, about settler or military presence and violence. Hattab posted the link in local news groups, and waited. They came in a trickle, at first, and then, as checkpoints began to multiply in 2022 and delays got worse, they came in a flood.

As more people joined Road Conditions, the pressure on Hattab mounted. When checkpoints locked down major cities, the number of users could spike, sometimes by thousands at a time. Dozens of commuters would ask about the same checkpoint, and answers would pour in at once. “Clear,” “open,” “closed.” All three could be true within the same hour. "Ten minutes is a long time," Hattab says. "Things change instantly." The questions landed on him, thousands of messages a day. “In the beginning,” he says, “I barely slept.”

When Hattab started Road Conditions, his odometer read 70,000 kilometers. Within four years it read 274,000, inside a territory barely 130 kilometers from tip to tip. It is the equivalent of driving around the Earth more than five times, without ever leaving the West Bank.

What began as a crowdsourced tool for people to help each other navigate the occupied West Bank was becoming an essential utility. To keep Road Conditions reliable, soon after launching the group in 2019, Hattab closed the public chat and asked the most active contributors to become moderators. More than a dozen volunteers now run the feed. Drivers from every corner of the West Bank send them reports, usually with a photo or video. Moderators check these updates by asking others on the ground, cross-checking other local pages, or driving the roads themselves.

As Road Conditions grew, users asked about roads in cities Hattab had never been to. Nothing goes out until he or the moderators have checked it. Before posting a checkpoint is closed, they need to know where it is, whom to ask to verify the update, and what route a driver can take instead. So for six months, Hattab spent his days off driving with no destination. "I'd get in the car, get lost, wherever I ended up, I ended up," he says. He stopped to ask locals for the name of every checkpoint and bypass road until he held the whole map of alternative routes in his head.

A view of the “Road Conditions” Telegram channel Hattab created.

After October 7, 2023, a situation that was already dangerous became a crisis. An investigation we published in September, in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism, and Lighthouse Reports, found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent since then. Our analysis found that the average commuter in the West Bank now loses about 77 hours every year taking roundabout routes to avoid checkpoints. Towns that were once quick, 10-minute drives apart have been severed by gates and other obstacles that turn those trips into hour-long voyages. To arrive at our analysis, we went searching for data about checkpoint delays, about when they are open and closed. No official data exists. So our reporting team looked to the Telegram group that Hattab built, scraping the updates that originated from Road Conditions to produce a comprehensive database of the way checkpoints work.

Not long after October 2023, Hattab was driving home at 2 in the morning when a soldier at a checkpoint near the city of Qalqilya stopped him and took his phone. The soldier scrolled through some 20,000 photos Hattab had received on the group of traffic around checkpoints. “You photographed a military site!” the soldier said, then stepped aside to speak with an officer on his radio. The soldier came back and ordered Hattab to delete everything. “I started deleting, in all naivety,” Hattab says. He had erased thousands of photos before the soldier walked back over and told him to go.

“I make sure not to show the military jeeps, not to show one soldier,” Hattab says.

Hattab quit the newspaper and took a job as a sales representative for a construction equipment company because it would put him on a different road every day. “My point is not sales,” he said. “It's Road Conditions.”

Israeli settlers, living in the nearly 150 official settlements and an additional 185 new “outposts” established in the West Bank since 2023—all of which are illegal under international law—have in recent years become a daily threat. In March 2025, at the Yitzhar junction on Route 60, near Nablus, Hattab watched a settler cut off a coffee bean delivery truck directly ahead of him, get out, and beat the driver in the middle of the road. “He was screaming and cursing, armed, beating the driver, grabbing him, punching him, grabbing him again,” he says. Hattab posted the update to the group. That year, the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented nearly 5,443 settler attacks. In the first eight months of 2026, it recorded about 4,766.

At 4 o’clock one January morning in 2025, news was circulating about Israeli troops on the road out of the city of Tulkarm. By 7, no one knew if they were still there, and no one wanted to be the one to find out.

Hattab was heading from his home in Tulkarm to Ramallah that morning. He started the car. He turned onto the road that people had been asking about and drove slowly, watching the road ahead.

The path was clear. He posted it to the group. “By the grace of God, it was easy this time,” he says.

Hattab knows the roads better, he would wager, than almost anyone now. When a major junction closes, he can predict the closures that follow across a whole corridor, “like dominoes,” he says. “Think of ants. You set their path with a toothpick on the ground.”

Anas Hattab, creator of “Road Conditions.”

With no institutional support and two young children, Hattab sometimes doubts if he can keep going: “You’re supposed to give your family the best life, not give up stable income for a Telegram group.” To him, it's already more than that.

Other innovators have stepped into the fray, launching new apps and groups to help drivers manage traffic. In 2025, for instance, computer engineers Musab Nuirat and Ahmed Gharib launched A Ween Rayeh (Where Are You Heading?). It’s a Palestinian application that aggregates data to produce a real-time heat map of traffic. It was, by Nuirat’s count, the seventh local attempt to build a functional navigation system in the West Bank. And like nearly all the other efforts, A Ween Rayeh relied on Hattab’s data to update its map.

Hattab knows how important what he’s built has become. So he continues. Hattab knows the operation should be 10 times the size. And he knows he should be able to compensate the moderators. But as a volunteer himself, he has no way to pay them. “I can't give them more than a thank you,” he says.

Hattab considers it his duty. “You know how a taxi driver has souls with him in the car, and he has to drive carefully? Same principle.” Mistakes happen, no one can verify every update in real time. “In the end,” he says, “aren't we living in this country at our own risk?”

AMAZON PRIME DAY is one of the easiest times of year to save on Apple devices. Many Apple gadgets go on sale often, but Prime Day Apple deals frequently drop prices down to as low as we’ve seen—if not exceeding previous best discounts entirely.

You won’t find deals on the brand-new iPhone, but if you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple Watches, iPads, MacBooks, and third-party accessories, you’re in the right spot. But only hours remain as Prime Day comes to a close, so jump on it quick.

For more savings, be sure to check out all the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals we've found so far.

Updated 10:00 pm ET October 7: We've added a new deal and double-checked the existing discounts. Sign up for Prime here to unlock exclusive deals.

The Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds for iPhone users. They fall to this price quite frequently, but WIRED readers continually purchase them, and this deal is still better than paying full price. They have detailed sound, great noise cancellation and transparency modes, a built-in heart rate sensor, and live translation.

The AirPods Max 2 are sleek, stylish, and on sale for a match of the second-best deal we've seen. They've dropped to $399 a couple of times, but this deal is still worth considering if these are the headphones you want. The battery life could be better, and we wish there were custom EQ options, but we like them overall.

The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are some of our favorite workout earbuds thanks to their comfortable fit, appealing style, and punchy sound. They’ll stay put even if you’re sweaty, and the transparency mode and noise cancellation mean you can hear exactly as much of your surroundings as you want to.

The MacBook Air remains the best laptop we’d recommend for most people. It strikes a great balance of features, power, and price, offering enough performance for both work and play. The portable, sleek design and excellent battery life make it an easy recommendation for just about anybody. And in terms of price, this is the best deal we’ve seen on the M5 MacBook Air since June.

The standard 11-inch iPad avoided a price hike this year and remains a great tablet for families. It’s perfect for kicking back with a movie, game, or book, and it can be relied upon to keep the kids amused.

The new M6 Mac Mini is very fast and can easily serve as a local, agentic AI machine. But it also has a more mainstream appeal as a starter computer, complete with 16 GB of RAM, the powerful M6 chip, and 512 GB of storage. Amazon has the best deal on the very latest model, bringing the price to a new low since its release. The Mac Studio is also on sale, if you really want to dive in deep on running local AI models.

These are the best trackers for folks with an iPhone, and you can use them to keep tabs on your keys, travel luggage, bike, or whatever else you worry might go missing. The location of each AirTag is marked clearly in the Find My app. They also make great stocking stuffers.

AMAZON (GPS + CELLULAR)

The GPS-only version of this Apple Watch is a very solid deal if you don't need cellular connectivity or the large band. The Apple Watch SE is our top budget-friendly pick; it costs less than the higher-end models but leaves out some of their features. I'm surprised that every version isn't discounted, but we hope to see other configurations drop in price over the event.

AMAZON (NO NUMERIC PAD)

Unlike the Magic Mouse, Apple's Magic Keyboard is a beloved Mac accessory. Mechanical switch enthusiasts won't appreciate the shallow travel, but the tick-tack typing of the keyboard makes it a fast and comfortable keyboard to type on. And importantly, it gives you the macOS layout right out of the box. The non-Touch ID model is on sale for Prime Day, which makes it $70 cheaper than the version with a fingerprint reader.

As Apple purges the ports on its MacBooks, you might want to plug in a handy USB hub. This Plugable device is our favorite because it offers 140 watts of power delivery, every port you need, including 10-Gbps USB-C, and can support a secondary screen, up to 4K resolution at 60 Hz. It also boasts a robust metal chassis with clearly labeled ports.

BACKBONE (USB-C OR LIGHTNING)

I loved the Backbone One when I reviewed it, and I still think it’s the best mobile gaming controller. It makes it very easy to play games on my iPhone for hours at a time. I especially love it for traveling, whether on a plane or to my parents’ house for the holidays. It has a solid app and excellent controls, plus pass-through charging. This price is close to the best we’ve seen.

This slots into the bottom of your iPhone via the rotating USB-C connector and provides enough power to charge it up at least once. It’s a good alternative to a MagSafe power bank if you want something faster and more efficient than wireless charging.

The best MagSafe power bank has a built-in kickstand and can charge your phone wirelessly or via the included USB-C cable. The capacity isn’t massive, but it’ll still fully charge most phones at least once. The display lets you know how much juice is left at a quick glance.

Top pick in our guide to the best Apple 3-in-1 wireless chargers, this classy-looking tree has a lovely weighted base and spots to charge your iPhone (with support for StandBy mode), Apple Watch, and any AirPods with a wireless charging case.

This is the best Apple 3-in-1 travel charger because it is so compact when folded. It can charge your iPhone or Qi2-certified phone at up to 15 watts on a magnetic pad that can adjust to your preferred angle. A second pad charges AirPods or other wireless earbuds, and there is a fold-out Apple Watch charger.

This hard-wearing, fast-charging pick from the best USB-C cables can deliver 240 watts to charge any Apple gadget. It also has a tough, braided nylon exterior made from 100 percent recycled plastic, and comes with a lifetime warranty.

This neat little Apple 3-in-1 charger has space for your Apple Watch, AirPods, and iPhone (in any orientation, including StandBy mode). It also comes with a wall adapter, travel adapters, and a cable, all of which are unfortunately rare inclusions in this product space.

One of our favorite MagSafe wallets, the stylish Smartish Side Hustle clings to your iPhone magnetically and has a cutaway to make it easy to pop out your cards, saving time at the register. This price is the lowest we’ve seen.

I especially like the version of this MagSafe wallet that has Find My compatibility, but the basic version is good as well. Nearly every iteration is on sale. The wallet has space for two cards comfortably and can double as a kickstand or tripod for your daily fit checks.

Bandolier’s elegant, classy products feel a lot more luxurious than most iPhone accessories. This case turns your iPhone 17 into a crossbody device, and I especially like it for dinner or shows when I don’t want to set my phone down, or my outfit doesn’t have pockets. My Bandolier accessories show no sign of wear after three months of continuous use.

Our favorite silicone Apple Watch band has a pebbled leather look, but it’s softer, and it’s waterproof. Durable enough for workouts and water sports, but also smart enough for the office, the two-tone design is reversible.

TIMES ARE TOUGH. That's why I've assembled these great Amazon Prime Day Deals under $100 that are still around. You don't have to spend big to bag a necessity, level up a little, or treat a loved one. These deals are on devices we have road-tested and recommend year-round—just a bit cheaper than usual.

For the best of the best deals this Prime Day, check out WIRED's Absolute Best Prime Day Deals before the sales pass you by.

A good power bank will save you from that frantic dash to find an outlet. This compact beauty is our top power bank for good reason: ample 25,000-mAh capacity, fast charging for phones or laptops and two devices at the same time, a retractable 2-foot USB-C flat cable plus another 1-foot USB-C cord that doubles as a carry loop.

This is our favorite 3-in-1 charger for Apple devices. It can charge your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch at the same time.

This power bank is credit-card-sized and fits in basically any bag. Great for phone charging on the go.

These Soundpeats H3 wireless earbuds hit the sweet spot where value meets lossless audio, detailed sound, and clear voice audio for phone calls. No frills like heart-rate tracking. Just great sound and a low price.

You can't find a Kindle for under $100 anymore during Prime Day thanks to Amazon's price changes, but that doesn't mean you can't get a different e-reader instead. Not many are on sale for Prime Day, but this tiny, adorable pocket reader from Xteink that's small enough to magnet onto some smart phones is.

The best personal blender on the market, bar none. This 1,200-watt Nutribullet Ultra is perfect for smoothies, protein shakes, and pestos or salsas. It's easy to clean and stow away, so it doesn't take up counter space. When you're done blending, put the lid on the jug, and it's now a drink cup that'll fit in most car cup holders.

Our favorite basket air fryer keeps temperature better than some thermometers. It crisps wings and fries without blasting them. If you want a great air fryer without spending a lot, this is it.

Most vacuums under $100 aren't worth your time. But this little handheld model is a favorite of ours for cleaning cars, thanks to the long hose and handle. Regardless of what you're cleaning, it's easy to move around and get to hard-to-reach places like corners or deep trunks. There's also a useful charging stand that holds attachments and keeps the vacuum charged, which you'll want since it only holds a 15-minute charge (unfortunately normal for small vacuums like this).

This is our favorite budget indoor gardening system, and it doesn't require expensive subscriptions or proprietary pods. It's great for growing greens or tomatoes indoors, and there's an optional companion app.

Here's an affordable way to add some outdoor lighting to your apartment or house. You can use the app to add a splash of color to your exterior, or set up seasonal lighting for the holidays.

This mini speaker offers better sound quality than some of Amazon's other small models, and it works with Alexa+, naturally. It's the most affordable gateway into an Alexa-based system.

The sound quality is really best for casual listening since there isn't much bass, but the screen is super handy, showing your alarm, weather, songs, and calendar details when you ask Alexa.

Amazon's Echo Dot Max is powerful, with better sound than the rest of the range, and a built-in smart home hub. This deal isn't quite as good as it may seem, since Amazon recently increased prices on many of its products (the MSRP used to be $100). But Prime Day is still the best time to save on Amazon devices.

While our favorite portable Bluetooth speaker has been cheaper, we still think this is a decent deal. It delivers huge sound for its size and stays small and durable enough to sling in just about any bag. It offers IP68 water resistance, an easy-release strap, and a two-hour battery boost (or four if you reduce the bass). The Flip 7 also supports Auracast to sync with other new JBL models like the Clip 5 and Charge 6.

This gaming headset is a favorite of WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe. She's found it comfortable and lightweight for long gaming sessions, paired with surprisingly clear sound. It also comes in a couple of fun colors to add a little pop of fun to your desk (and head!)

If you want a screen-free gift for any kid, the Yoto Player is a great choice. It's ideal for kids between 3 and 12, with physical cards that slot into the top of the device to trigger stories and music. It also has a cute pixel-art display on the front, a built-in night light, and even a thermometer.

This is a play stage and kids speaker that has a great discount for Prime Day, and a fun gift for kids three and up. Kids can put a wooden cartridge into the slot and wooden character pieces on the soundstage to control the audio it plays.

My son got several gifts when he turned four, but this one is the big winner. He loves to build, take apart, and rebuild the pieces into the biggest shape he can (he calls it his planet) and I even got him a second set in another color. I wish I'd waited until now when it was on sale, though!

SwitchBot is better known for robot vacuums, but it has been steadily building a smart home range. This lovely fan has a brushless motor, a rechargeable battery for cordless operation, and rare Matter compatibility with the add-on SwitchBot Hub 3 bridge ($120).

Arlo's Pro 6 tops our best outdoor security cameras guide. It can record 2K video with a wide 160-degree field of view, and pairs with a swift-loading app that offers rich notifications, and supports two-factor authentication. The pricey catch is the subscription ($10 per month or $96 a year for a single camera, $20 per month or $216 a year for unlimited cameras).

Smart plugs are useful for turning non-smart things, like lamps, into connected smart devices you can remote control and schedule. The three-piece set is on sale for a good price, and they’re Matter-compatible.

TP-LINK TAPO (FOUR-PACK)

This pack of smart bulbs uses the same app as the smart plugs above, and is a well-priced set even when it's not on sale. If you're looking to set up multiple lights and devices in your home, get these on-sale TP-Link packs.

Apple HomeKit users may like these Matter-compatible color smart light bulbs from Meross, as they are natively compatible with Siri and the Apple ecosystem. They'll also work with Alexa and Google.

That includes phones, laptops, headphones, cameras, tablets, and much more. These are all products we've tested ourselves and stand by in terms of quality and value.

But they won't last forever. You have until tonight to pull the trigger. If you haven’t found the deal you want yet, browse our roundup of the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

Updated on October 7 at 7:15 pm ET: Added some new tech deals and checked through the current products on sale.

Sign up for Prime here to unlock exclusive deals.

The flagship Apple AirPods Pro 3 are its best wireless earbuds, and they're at the lowest price since June. Music sounds great, noise cancellation works well, and they offer excellent call quality. Apple added more ear tips for a better fit for small ears, new tools like heart rate sensing and live translation, and enhanced support for folks with hearing loss. If you use an iPhone, these are the wireless earbuds for you.

The Nothing Headphone (1) is one of our favorite pairs of over-ear headphones. With an attractive and distinctive design that combines a transparent look with tactile controls like a volume wheel and media control paddle, these headphones make a real statement. They also boast top-notch battery life. This is the best discount we’ve seen on them so far.

Prime Day is a great time to pick up older models at deep discounts. The Sonos Beam Gen 2 is a great example, having coming out originally in 2021. It's since been supplanted by the Sonos Beam Ultra, but that model is hundreds of dollars more (even while on sale!), and the Sonos Beam Gen 2 has never been cheaper. Our own audio expert, Harry Rabinowitz, used this model in his own home as his primary soundbar and found it to be a particularly good fit for smaller homes.

Speaking of deals on older models, if you've always fancied one of those picture-style TVs, this 2025 Samsung model has a matte finish to make paintings and photos look more real, for when you're not using it as a TV. The magnetic bezels are customizable, and some folks love the look. To be honest, these aren't best TVs, sadly, Amazon doesn't have any Prime Day deals on them.

It's rare to find a brand new OLED TV on this big of a discount, but that's exactly what this Bravia 6 deal is. While this is definitely Sony's entry-level OLED option, I'm still surprised to see this big of a price cut this early. We tested the Sony Bravia 8 II a few months back, which is this TV's “True RGB” older sibling, and while the Bravia 6 is missing some of those bells and whistles, it still delivers excellent color contrast and deep blacks where it counts.

Available in dazzling hibiscus, the Google Pixel 11 stands out, and also happens to be the best option in Google’s new lineup for most people. It boasts an excellent camera, long battery life, and decent performance, alongside Qi2 25W support for magnetic charging and accessories, and super slick contextual AI features.

The Samsung S26 Ultra was the pick of the bunch this year, with a cool privacy screen, blazing performance, long battery life, and an excellent camera, but all three of Samsung’s S26 phones are on sale right now. These are the lowest prices they’ve been so far.

The Moto G Stylus is our pick of the best cheap phones under $400, and is is as low as it has ever been right now. If you miss a headphone jack and microSD card slot, this could be a winner. This is the 2025 model, but Motorola increased the price by $100 for the 2026 Moto G Stylus, and, apart from the upgraded active stylus, there’s little to justify the extra cost.

AMAZON (41 MM AND WI-FI)

GOOGLE (41 MM AND WI-FI)

The Google Pixel Watch 5 is the best smartwatch for Android phone owners. It tracks your activity, sleep, heart rate, and more automatically, and works seamlessly with Gemini. You can also get insights and coaching from Google Health if you subscribe.

This is a solid smartwatch, and an especially great choice if you have a Samsung Galaxy phone. You can save yourself a significant sum by opting for last year’s model and Samsung’s Galaxy Watch9 is only a modest upgrade over the Watch8, considering it’s $120 more expensive.

Anyone with a trio of Apple gadgets (iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods) will benefit from snagging one of the best Apple 3-in-1 wireless chargers for their nightstand, and this is my top pick. The wide base keeps it steady, enabling you to remove your iPhone from the magnetic wireless charging pad one-handed, the Watch pad lets any strap dangle, and the base has a spot for AirPods, too.

This power bank does it all. I love the translucent design, offering a peek at the electronic innards. https://www.wired.com/story/tropical-sto.title: Tropical Storm Isaias Set to Be First Atlantic Hurricane of 2026 Season
https://www.wired.com/story/tropical-sto.author: Brian Kahn
https://www.wired.com/story/tropical-sto.text:
THE 2026 ATLANTIC hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.

El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.

Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.

The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)

Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.

Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.

Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.

The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.

For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.

Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.

None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

https://www.wired.com/story/how-a-weirdl.title: Shaq Got Hacked. Now He’s Pitching for a VPN
https://www.wired.com/story/how-a-weirdl.author: Lily Hay Newman
https://www.wired.com/story/how-a-weirdl.text:
AT A PROMOTIONAL event in Times Square on Wednesday for the security company NordVPN, brand ambassador Shaquille O’Neal said he is eager to raise awareness among regular people about the importance of digital security and personal privacy.

“I have a video of me beating up Charles Barkley, and I wouldn't want the world to see that. That was a joke,” O'Neal says. “But everybody needs to have control of their own information.”

After being targeted by scammers who claimed that he was trying to buy a house and they were working on the transaction, O’Neal says, he realized he needed to learn more about cybersecurity and digital defense.

“I was hacked for the first time, not a bad hack, and I didn't know what to do,” he told reporters. “So I had to look into it. Once that happened, I really had to start paying more attention, because I would think nothing like that could ever happen to me, but it could happen to anybody.”

O'Neal, of course, is not just anybody. Still, the four-time NBA champion and media personality says that he doesn't have particularly sensitive data on his devices and tries to live a normal life as much as possible. When WIRED asked, though, whether he worries that he needs to take extra precautions to protect himself and loved ones as a result of his high profile, O'Neal said, “Yes, I think about it all the time, but I don't let it consume me, because if you let it consume you you can go crazy. But you have to be able to have great reactionary skills if something happens.”

A prolific tech investor who was early to AI, O'Neal emphasizes that the goal of his relationship with NordVPN is to inform the public and help people protect themselves. NordVPN is, well, known for its VPN. But the company has other offerings, including antivirus, threat detection, and scam-defense products that are geared toward accessibility for consumers. Marijus Briedis, the company's chief technology officer, says he was surprised by the findings of a recent NordVPN poll showing that 73 percent of Americans have an overconfidence in traditional antivirus and believe it can protect them against anything from identity theft to online tracking.

“The weakest link is between the computer and the chair, and I've been thinking so much about how to solve that problem,” Briedis told WIRED. “So the thing we are doing right now is focusing on education. It's a really interesting problem, how to do it in the best way. It's still haunting me in my dreams.”

https://www.wired.com/story/the-science-.author: Fernanda González
https://www.wired.com/story/the-science-.text:
THE KAROLINSKA INSTITUTE awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine to researchers Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. Their discoveries led to the development of optogenetics, a technique where scientists can turn individual nerve cells on or off using beams of light.

According to Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Medicine, “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of.” No other technique allows for such precise study of a living brain, helping researchers better understand the functions of our nervous systems as well as various neurological diseases and disorders.

But this prize is not just a celebration of neuroscience. It also serves as a triumphant example of what can happen when different disciplines of biology converge, as the findings that served as the basis for the development of optogenetics emerged from research in microbiology.

At the end of the last century, Peter Hegemann began a series of studies to understand how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. Previous research documented that Chlamydomonas has an “eye spot,” a small orange dot on its surface that contains a light-sensing molecule called retinal.

Hegemann used tiny electrodes to measure the electrical signals generated by the alga and to expand our understanding of this structure’s rapid response. The scientist discovered that the organism was capable of producing an electrical impulse about 0.5 milliseconds after receiving light. This response time is 20 times faster than that of the human eye, whose light detection process takes at least 10 milliseconds.

Hegemann suggested that light detection in the alga must be the result of a much simpler process than that identified in the human eye. In the early 1990s, he proposed that the eye spots contained a protein that both detected the light and responded to it, likely opening as a channel to let ions through. At the time, this hypothesis sparked controversy. Many ion channels had been documented up to that point, but none could respond to light on their own.

To test his theory, the scientist attempted to isolate the light-sensitive proteins from the eye spot. However, when removed from their natural environment, these proteins became unstable. Later, a group of Japanese researchers sequenced the complete DNA of Chlamydomonas, which allowed Hegemann’s team to identify two genes that would create proteins with the expected characteristics of a possible light-sensing channel.

Georg Nagel took the next step of verifying the function of the genes. He introduced copies of each of the identified genes separately into different groups of frog eggs. The eggs began to produce the corresponding proteins, which eventually localized to the cell membranes. Nagel then turned on the lights.

Both proteins functioned as ion channels that opened when exposed to light. He named the genes channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2. Further experiments showed the protein produced by this second gene—called ChR2 for short—opened especially quickly, the flow of ions occurring in just 0.2 milliseconds. It explained the extraordinary speed of the light reaction originally observed in Chlamydomonas.

When the researchers introduced the gene into mammalian cells—which do not normally respond to light—the cells generated an electrical signal when illuminated. This is what got the neuroscientists particularly excited.

Ion channels are important across many types of cells, but they do some especially heavy lifting in our nervous systems. The electrical impulses that neurons use to communicate with one another, as well as other tissues in our body, are mediated by the flow of ions in and out of the cell. If you can control the ion channels, you can control the neuron.

This is where Karl Deisseroth comes in. Deisseroth was searching for a method that would allow him to toggle the activity of specific nerve cells in a living brain. In his view, this tool could expand our understanding of brain functions and open new avenues for treating conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.

Following the discovery of ChR2, he asked Nagel for the DNA sequence so he could introduce it into rat nerve cells. The neurons, growing in dishes, produced ChR2 and, when illuminated with blue light, reacted immediately—sending an electrical impulse that propagated to other neurons. This result, obtained in 2005, was decisive in establishing ChR2 as a tool for neuroscience.

In the following years, Deisseroth, Hegemann, and Nagel collaborated to identify other proteins capable of activating or deactivating neurons using different wavelengths of light. With this toolkit, researchers can now design experiments where one group of neurons is turned on by one wavelength of light and another set of neurons is controlled by a different wavelength.

The term optogenetics was coined in 2006 and has since been implemented in a variety of studies. “Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute stated in a press release.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

They discovered that single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. They used tiny electrodes to measure electrical signals generated by the alga.

https://www.wired.com/story/meet-the-ven.title: Meet the Vendors Selling ‘Cornell Seven’ Merch
https://www.wired.com/story/meet-the-ven.author: Ej Dickson
https://www.wired.com/story/meet-the-ven.text:
LAST WEEKEND, THE clothing brand Cherrykitten published an Instagram post promoting T-shirts, crop tops, and sports bras with the slogan “I Am Jane Doe” emblazoned on the front. “ALL OF US ARE UNTIL NONE OF US ARE,” the company wrote in the caption, adding that it would donate 5 percent of the net sales proceeds to the National Organization for Women.

A reference to the “Cornell Seven” case, in which an anonymous woman accused seven Cornell University fraternity members of sexual assault, among other counts, #IAmJaneDoe started going viral last week. Many sexual assault survivors used the hashtag in solidarity with the alleged victim after trolls attempted to dox her on social media. (All seven of those accused have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.)

The message, while powerful, may have been ill-suited for appropriation by Cherrykitten, a brand perhaps best known for selling tank tops and crop tops with slogans like “Pls do not give me a cigarette no matter what I say” and “AI cannot generate tits like these.” The company received immediate backlash on social media for selling the shirts, with many accusing it of tastelessly capitalizing off of a grisly sexual assault case. “Using the cornell seven sexual assault as a merch idea and then donating ONLY 5% to a womens charity.. oh cherrykitten.. you’re fucked,” one tweet with 2.2 million views read.

The brand removed the post, issuing an apology for “turning a real and deeply serious situation into a product,” according to a screengrab of a now-deleted Instagram post. (Cherrykitten did not respond to WIRED’s requests for comment.) But Cherrykitten is far from the only brand attempting to market apparel around the Cornell Seven case, which has garnered outrage around the world.

On Amazon, there are more than 6,000 results for “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts; on platforms like Etsy and Redbubble, there are hundreds of sellers promoting such merch, including T-shirts, sweatshirts, hats, bracelets, mugs, and bumper stickers. The listings, which include keywords like “feminist,” “true crime,” “protest,” and (weirdly, on Redbubble) “lizzieborden,” often feature AI-generated photos of women with shiny hair and broad grins modeling the merch.

One such seller, who requested her name be withheld to protect her privacy given the sensitive nature of the case, is the owner of a three-year-old shop on Etsy which sells T-shirts with progressive slogans. Her “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirts in shades like ash, dark chocolate, and purple cost between $19.53 and $27.93; she’s sold 21 since October 1.

An assault survivor herself, the seller tells WIRED via email she came across the Cornell Seven story on social media, and was “deeply moved” by the #IAmJaneDoe movement. “I wanted this shirt to be a small but visible way of saying: we see you, we believe you, and we stand with you,” she says.

“[When] I came across the Jane Doe story on social media, I saw yet another woman who had been failed by people and systems, and I felt really strongly about that. That we need to stand up for her. That she deserves justice ... For me, ‘I Am Jane Doe’ was not about turning anyone's pain into a trend,” she says. “It was my way of saying that I see her, I believe her, and I stand with her.”

It’s not uncommon for Etsy vendors to sell items inspired by current events. It happened after the murder of George Floyd in 2020 and during the 2022 Johnny Depp/Amber Heard defamation case, where much of the merch was pro-Depp and featured quotes from Depp on the stand. As WIRED has previously reported, the rise of mass-produced print-on-demand goods, as well as Etsy’s relatively lax policies toward AI-generated listings, allow vendors to rapidly create, design, promote, and sell such items in accordance with the news cycle.

Yet there are often ethical questions associated with commodifying social movements for a quick buck, and it can be difficult for consumers to vet the motives of those selling such products.

“If [people are] raising money to support survivors, that’s OK,” Simintha Esson, chief development officer for RAINN, the country’s largest anti-sexual-assault organization, tells WIRED when asked about the recent onslaught of Jane Doe merch. “We know the need is there—calls to RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline are up 73 percent in the last week. But if it’s just exploiting Jane Doe’s name and case for profit, people are better off giving to an organization that is trying to make things better.”

Even those who purport to be financially supporting survivors are worthy of skepticism. The website I Am Jane Doe Merch, for instance, includes such bestselling items as an “I Am Jane Doe” baby tee, an “Educate Your Sons” crop top stenciled with a butterfly, and a “Dead Men Don’t Rape” T-shirt featuring the serial killer Aileen Wuornos. (According to website data, more than 700 Aileen Wuornos T-shirts have sold.)

The website, which was created on October 2, according to the domain reverse-search tool WhoIs, includes a description stating that an unspecified percentage of the proceeds will go directly to Jane Doe herself, “to help her legal expenses and related costs.” “Any contribution, no matter the amount, can help lessen that burden and support Jane in accessing support, advocacy, and/or justice and accountability,” the description reads.

When reached for comment, however, Thomas P. Giuffra, the attorney for Jane Doe, tells WIRED that there are no authorized fundraising sites for Jane Doe. While she has requested that all donations go to RAINN, other efforts such as I Am Jane Doe Merch are “not affiliated with us, and we urge the public to use caution before contributing to one,” he says in a statement. (Though WhoIs data has kept the identity of the owner of I Am Jane Doe Merch anonymous, WIRED has reached out to an email address associated with the website for comment.)

Some influencers selling “I Am Jane Doe” merchandise are donating all or most of the proceeds to organizations benefiting sexual survivors. Justin Kralemann, a content creator and activist who goes by the handle the Woke Ginger, says he was inspired to sell shirts after women flooded to his comments section to share their own experiences with sexual assault and trauma.

“Their stories broke my heart,” he says. “I’m a cisgender man and can’t directly speak to women’s lived experiences, but I wanted to do something beyond sharing news updates to help those fighting sexual violence against women.”

With EQNQ Studio, a company that makes “progressive apparel that celebrates equality, community, and the courage to speak up,” according to its website, Kralemann is selling “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts in teal (the color associated with Sexual Assault Awareness Month) and dark heather for $24.95 a pop. He says approximately 67 percent of the proceeds will support the national organization End Rape on Campus, and approximately 33 percent will go to EQNQ Studio, the small business producing, hand-making, and shipping the shirts. Per EQNQ, they have sold 255 shirts thus far.

A few days after we started corresponding, the Etsy vendor selling sweatshirts provided an update: she had decided to stop selling the “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirt and to donate the remainder of the profits to RAINN. She didn’t think that she or those who purchased the sweatshirt had bad intentions—“we all know how difficult it is to change things as individuals, [and] at the very least, we can show our support with a shirt,” she says. But she said that she has come to understand the potential ethical issues raised by “turning a story like this into something that is sold, even when the intention behind it is solidarity.”

“Even though we don't know who Jane Doe is, and we don't need to know, this is still her story,” she says. “I have decided that stepping back from this particular design is the right thing for me to do.”

https://www.wired.com/story/openai-chatg.title: The New ChatGPT Is More Show Than Tell
https://www.wired.com/story/openai-chatg.author: Reece Rogers
https://www.wired.com/story/openai-chatg.text:
WHEN YOU ASK a chatbot a question, you’ll often get a wall of text back, maybe with an image or two pulled from the web. That may no longer be the case soon, as OpenAI overhauls how ChatGPT answers prompts.

On Wednesday, OpenAI unveiled an “Intelligent UI” update for ChatGPT that generates visual, custom elements—when helpful—for answering a user's questions. The company's new experience is powered by its recent GPT-6 model, which rolls out to paid users today and to free users tomorrow.

I got a quick test of the user interface before launch, and these visual elements felt like a welcome change. When I asked for a diagram of a slug, ChatGPT generated an anatomy-focused visual with buttons I could press for each different part, from the upper tentacles to the muscular foot. I also generated a San Francisco apartment affordability calculator with movable sliders to adjust income and other expenses, showing what percentage of my take-home pay different units would cost.

My favorite part of this quick hands-on with ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI was an airplane seat explorer. I’m not a fan of sitting in the exit rows, so I asked ChatGPT to generate a custom tool to compare the cabin layouts between four different Alaska and Delta planes. In its output, I could tap any seat on the map for more details, and ChatGPT highlighted the exit rows in green.

While useful in some results, every ChatGPT answer won’t suddenly include a chart or graphic. “We have a design team that spent a lot of time figuring out when adding a diagram, chart, or buttons adds value versus when it's starting to feel cluttered,” says Aarush Selvan, a product manager at OpenAI. If a user isn’t interested in visuals, they can tell ChatGPT to generate fewer of those outputs.

These visual results are similar to what Google announced earlier this year for Search when it expanded the bespoke results users may see. Google’s version is called “generative UI.” One example: If you want to better understand deep space, Search can output an adjustable graphic that breaks down how black holes work, using multiple sliders.

Chatbot experiences have increasingly become multimodal, meaning that text, images, and voice blend into one user experience. OpenAI's launch of an updated ChatGPT that's easier on the eyes and more interactive for over a billion users signals that the multimodal era is here. However, a larger shift toward generative user interfaces may spark an identity crisis for designers, as AI dictates more of what software looks like for individual users.

With AI tools now able to quickly generate custom software, the future of chatbots is further personalized and attuned to what I want to see, and what I want to see is slug diagrams. Good riddance to walls of text.

An aesthetician we spoke to also scanned her skin before and after the treatment, and they found less inflammation and hyperpigmentation and an improvement in fine lines.
