https://www.wired.com/story/the-pentagon.title: The Pentagon Hopes to Speed Up ‘Kill Chain’ AI Buys With 5-Minute Videos
https://www.wired.com/story/the-pentagon.author: Maddy Varner
https://www.wired.com/story/the-pentagon.text:
AN UNDER-THE-RADAR PROCUREMENT program led by the Department of Defense has been granting special statuses to would-be defense contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos that must be no longer than five minutes.

It’s part of the Pentagon’s desperate bid to inject competition in a market the United States military itself destroyed.

The initiative, known as Tradewinds, is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO.) Companies can submit videos describing how their AI products address one of several different “strategic focus areas” that the government periodically updates. At least once a month, a panel of judges review submissions and decide whether to accept them into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, where the videos can then be viewed by government officials.

If accepted, the pitched products are considered “post-competitive.” Many procurement regulations include competitive requirements. The status can let government buyers check off that box and potentially help shave months off of award timelines. A DOD official says that in several instances, the department has been able to make awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google declined to comment for this story.

Though the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace has been around since late 2022, the Trump administration has been far more vocal than its predecessors about the military buying and operationalizing AI. It also hopes to have more money than ever to throw around: As part of its 2027 budget request to Congress, the White House asked for $1.5 trillion for the Department of Defense, citing “historic investments” in AI as a priority.

This year, the military is seeking video pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and those that can “unleash” AI-enabled agents that can assist in the joint targeting process, including so-called kill chain execution.

No longer as relevant? Pitches for products that promote “a culture of responsible AI” and provide guardrails for AI development and use—requests made during the final Tradewinds submissions cycle under the Biden administration. A DOD official says that the 2026 topics were selected to align with a January 2026 AI strategy memo.

“There has never been a better time to build for the Army,” wrote then-sitting US Army secretary Daniel Driscoll as part of a pitch for more defense tech startups included in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 wishlist of companies to fund. (Driscoll has since resigned from his position and returned to the private sector. He did not respond to a request for comment.)

Acceptance onto the Tradewinds marketplace—and the special “post-competitive” status that comes with it—lets government buyers more easily cut deals using special types of contracts such as “other transaction” agreements, or OTs, which aren’t subject to certain federal acquisition requirements. By law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million dollars on a single OT without having to notify Congress.

Procurement experts say that OTs are considered fast and flexible, which can be appealing to startups that don’t want to gamble on whether a months-long procurement process will result in a contract. However, not all agencies publicly report their OT spending, and even when they do, they’re difficult to find on government-run sites that track federal spending, like USASpending.gov and SAM.gov.

“While OTAs offer opportunities to attract new procurement partners and reduce red tape, numerous reviews have raised red flags,” US senator Joni Ernst of Iowa tells WIRED. “These include questionable costs, mishandling of restricted information, a lack of oversight, reduced accountability and transparency, and an inability to track and access OTA outcomes.”

Ernst recently worked to pass the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, which will require the Department of Defense and other agencies to report OTs to the public. They’ll have three years to get into compliance.

According to public records, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with the Pentagon’s CDAO. According to a DOD official, Tradewinds was leveraged along with market analysis and research as part of the department’s AI acquisition strategy, but the three companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for the specific agreements WIRED identified.

One of the key goals of Tradewinds is to bring “nontraditional” players into the defense industry, says Will Roberts, a former acquisition lead for the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, CDAO’s predecessor, who helped launch the effort. In some ways, it’s an effort to swing the pendulum back to where it was in the past.

Following the Cold War, the Pentagon encouraged defense companies to merge during a now-infamous meeting called the Last Supper, since Congress was preparing to slash defense budgets. Even though it may seem like only having to deal with a few large companies might make things easier, “it actually had a huge impact on market competition,” says Roberts.

Around the same time, explains Sharon Weinberger, a national security reporter and author of the book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War, the personal computer boom meant that Silicon Valley was able to make its own money and with that, set its own research priorities without being beholden to the funding and influence of the military.

Roberts and other defense professionals brought up the military’s historic role in funding—and shaping—technologies like the Internet and GPS. With those investments also came leverage, says Roberts. “We've sort of lost that leverage because there's billions of dollars in AI being invested by companies themselves.”

Weinberger says this has given Silicon Valley titans an immense amount of power over the Pentagon’s technological future. “The amount of money that the Pentagon can put into AI, compared to what venture capital can invest? It's like a drop in the bucket,” she says. “And that's really frightening for the Pentagon. What happens when they can't drive the direction of technology anymore?”

Publicly, this can play out in dramatic and confusing ways. Weinberger points out, for example, that the recent legal battle over Anthropic’s status as a supply chain risk could be seen as the government trying to figure out what legal mechanisms it has to flex its authority over AI companies.

Silicon Valley sensibilities have also been a roadblock in the past, albeit briefly. Roberts recalls how Google employees got “super paranoid” in 2018 about the company’s involvement with the Pentagon’s Project Maven, which eventually led to Google pulling out of the effort. Roberts says the Pentagon spent years trying to “appease” Google with less politically charged projects like those focused on humanitarian aid and veteran health.

Google declined to comment on whether that telling was accurate. One of the Google solutions listed as “awardable” on the Tradewinds site is called “Google for Military Health - Tradewinds,” and in July 2025, the company announced a $200 million deal with CDAO to utilize its frontier AI technology. In a press release, Jim Kelly, a vice president at Google Public Sector said that the company was “committed to advancing the deployment of innovative technology across the defense ecosystem.”

COFFEE ALWAYS TASTES better when you know you’re saving money on making it. Shopping holidays like Prime Day are historically the best times to buy espresso and coffee makers at their lowest prices of the year, and this event is no different—we've found legitimately good discounts on the coffee devices our team has tested and loved. Below are the best deals on top picks from our guides to the Best Espresso Machines, Best Pod Coffee Makers, Best Drip Coffee Makers, and Best Coffee Grinders. (Plus some bonus energy drink deals for those who need even more caffeine.)

Be sure to also check out our guides to the Absolute Best Deals and Best Deals Under $50, which we will be updating regularly during Prime Big Deal Days.

Updated 11 am ET October 7: I've added new machine and accessory deals, removed outdated prices, and ensured up-to-date sale info.

This is one of the most popular espresso machines of all time—and a long-standing top pick in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines. The pressure is consistent, its steam wand is great, and our reviewers appreciated the built-in grinder. WIRED Gear editor Julian Chokkattu has been using his Barista Express without incident for more than seven years.

This is the lowest price ever on a super-automatic espresso machine we love, with a push-button frother and touchscreen featuring 18 espresso, latte, and iced-coffee drink options. WIRED Reviewer Matthew Korfhage also appreciated the grinder that lets you easily swap beans.

We gave this semiautomatic staple a 7/10 for its beginner-friendliness and excellent milk frother that can help even newbies make quality cappuccinos and lattes.

This little machine punches above its price class with a thermoblock for immediate heating and a PID (proportional, integral, derivative) temperature controller for consistent brew temperatures.

Though Keurig's latest flagship machine ditched the controversial K-Cups, these plastic pods are still a beloved convenience for many, and for them, we recommend the K-Café. It comes with a milk frother for fancier drinks, as well as BrewID, which can identify your pod and suggest custom brew settings. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe also appreciated that it was easy to clean.

Reviewer Louryn Strampe’s favorite pod machine for espresso, this deal includes a milk frother for the full coffee shop experience.

Prefer iced coffee? There’s a pod machine for that. We compared hot and cold coffees on this machine using the same K-Cups, and they came out equally strong.

Our favorite drip coffee maker overall, the minimalist Aiden has been a status symbol (and WIRED favorite) since its release in 2024. WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage says it nails the intersection between a great cup of coffee and an easy cup of coffee.

We quite liked this all-in-one programmable brewer, which features a built-in scale and grinder and control via an app.

AeroPress has its fervent devotees (many of them in WIRED offices)—now you can join them for just $30.

This is the least expensive grinder WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage recommends to make good coffee—it's got 30 settings for everything from espresso to French press. This price is for the silver metal version shown, but the blue plastic version is even cheaper at $88.

If you want precision grounds for less, you’re going to have to do the work yourself, but this hand grinder had better consistency of grind than any flat burr we tested under $1,000.

Yes, there are fancier milk frothers on the market (like the Subminimal Nano Foamer, which is also on sale, for $40), but WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane and I both own this Zulay frother and can't say enough good things about it. Mine has been through all manner of abuse, from espresso drinks and protein shakes to falling in the sink and being mostly submerged in a too-tall glass, and after a year and a half of near-daily use it's still going strong.

WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell was a barista for many years, and this is the espresso tamper he recommends—a spring-loaded base allows for 15 pounds of force for a perfectly flat layer of grounds.

AMAZON (WALNUT HANDLE)

A longtime WIRED favorite, the sleek Stagg EKG Pro kettle is ideal for pour-over and features a timer and temperature control.

No judgment—many of us are. Sometimes a cold, fizzy drink just sounds better than something hot and potentially dehydrating. If this is sometimes you, Prime Days are often the best time to stock up on a flat of your favorite.

WIRED contributor Pete Cottell says Celsius is punchy without a cloying aftertaste and it does wonders in masking the medicinal notes that are present in similarly potent drinks. It’s also “an absolute unit when it comes to the caffeine-to-volume ratio.”

“All the aesthetics of a very-online wellness girlie product without any of the questionable flavors or adjuncts," says WIRED contributor Pete Cottell.

“This is the energy drink for people who think they hate energy drinks,” says WIRED contributor Pete Cottell.

“Halfway through the can I got happy feet and swapped my Aeron chair for the walking pad. Two miles and 35 minutes later I was still zooming, so I took my dog for a 2-mile run and felt like a million bucks at the end.” says WIRED contributor Pete Cottell.

AMAZON PRIME DAY has no shortage of fitness tech and wellness gear on sale. Obviously, savvy bargain hunters know that not every discount makes for a good deal. Fortunately, I’ve sifted through hundreds of deals and rounded up the best discounts on products WIRED staffers have tested and vetted.

I will be updating this list daily with the freshest Prime Day fitness deals, so be sure to check back often. For more information on sales, browse our roundup of the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

Updated October 7: I’ve added deals on the Google Pixel Watch 5, the Apple Watch SE 3, the CMF Watch 3 Pro, Peloton Bike+, HigherDose Red Light Therapy Hat, and the Apple AirPods Max 2. Prices were updated, and dead deals were removed.

AMAZON (41 MM AND WI-FI)

GOOGLE (41 MM AND WI-FI)

I’m surprised to see the Google Pixel Watch 5 on sale considering it was just released this past August. Both the 41- and 45-mm sizes are $65 off, which is the best deal we’ve seen on this watch yet. It’s also WIRED's favorite smartwatch for Android users, designed to be repairable and theoretically last for a lifetime. That means you’ll actually get your money’s worth.

AMAZON (GPS + CELLULAR)

I’m not surprised to see the Apple Watch SE 3 on sale, and it’s a good deal for an already affordable smartwatch. Apple didn’t update the SE this year, so you’ll miss out on new features like high-frequency heart rate tracking and Audio Intelligence, but you still get sleep apnea notifications and skin temperature sensing. It’s also compatible with watchOS 27, so you can use the dynamic app grid, the Siri app, and Workout Buddy. At $199 (40 mm), it’s a tough deal to beat for a premium smartwatch.

The newer Galaxy Watch9 stands out as the best choice for Samsung owners, with a faster processor, a slightly larger battery, and more health metrics. In testing, none of these updates particularly improved the user experience, and I didn’t find the new metrics beneficial for my lifestyle. At $260, the Watch8 is $120 less than its successor, which, for a limited time, makes it the better buy.

For an even cheaper smartwatch, the Watch7 is an option if you don’t need the latest health-tracking features. It’s the lowest price I’ve seen for the Watch7, but you won’t get metrics like Antioxidant Index and Vascular Load. Fortunately, we didn’t find either particularly helpful anyway. The display also tops out at 2,000 nits versus 3,000 nits on newer models, but it’s still just as bright as an Apple Watch Series. It won’t last forever, but $150 is a great price.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is our top budget smartwatch pick, and it just got even more affordable at $59. It’s an excellent entry-level option that offers fitness tracking, health monitoring, and smart utilities.

The Peloton Bike+ is $900 off, bringing it down to $1,795. If you’re not a cycling snob (said with love) and don’t need premium features like automatic resistance control or a 360-degree rotating screen, the standard Bike is also $400 off at $1,295. Either way, you’re getting a great discount on a top-tier stationary bike.

The Urevo CyberPad is our top choice for a walking pad, primarily because of its 14-percent incline—the highest we’ve seen in our testing. I’ve seen the price drop even further, but $387 is a solid price for a top-tier walking pad now rather than waiting for Black Friday.

According to WIRED reviewer Kristin Canning, setup is a breeze, and you can easily control it via its remote or app. She appreciates the sturdy build and comfortable belt, which together ensure a solid workout experience. With a maximum speed of 4 mph and an adjustable incline that reaches either 9 or 14 percent, depending on how you position it, it offers enough versatility for walking. While it may not be the quietest option, it’s not disruptive if you're working or reading. Weighing in at 71 pounds, it provides stability, but it might not be the easiest to move around; the included wheels help with portability, though.

The Theragun Relief is our budget Theragun pick, and at $100 ($60 off), it’s even more affordable. It's an older model from 2023, but it matches the power of many of its pricier competitors. It’s half the weight of the Theragun Pro Plus, but if you’re looking for an ultra-portable device, the Theragun Mini Plus is also on sale for $238 ($42 off). It comes with a carrying case, is designed with a built-in travel lock, and offers heated therapy.

If you’re looking for the most affordable massage gun, the LifePro Sonic Massage Gun has been our budget massage gun pick for two years now, and $40 ($20 off) is the lowest price I’ve seen. It also comes with a storage case and eight attachments, which is plenty of versatility when it comes to percussive therapy.

The HigherDose Red Light Hat is our favorite red light therapy hat for hair regrowth, and at $359, it’s $90 cheaper than usual. After four months of using this device, reviewer Nena Farrell noticed visible improvements, including a healthier scalp, less breakage, and fuller roots.

At $552, this is the lowest price I’ve seen for the original TheraFace Mask, making this Prime Day the best time to buy. The newer TheraFace Glo (also on sale for $300) is significantly cheaper, but its predecessor offers a more therapeutic experience, with the massage nodes built into the temple and brow areas rather than the scalp. The latter actually gives me a headache.

The Solawave 4-in-1 Red Light Therapy Wand is the best option if you’re looking for a compact device for travel or targeted spot treatments. It goes on sale often, but $118 is one of the lowest prices I’ve seen in a while.

Below, you’ll find more discounts on fitness and recovery gear we’ve tested and vetted.

IT’S THE LAST day of Amazon Prime Day. All mediocre-to-good things must come to an end, and with caffeine in our brains and years of expertise in our hearts, we're here once again to sift through the pile of nonsense to find the deals on gear that'll be great far past the initial hit of dopamine when it arrives at your door.

Our fabulous WIRED reviewers will be popping into this live blog throughout the day to yap about the stuff they’re buying and the bargains we think you should know about. We’ll also regularly be updating our Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

“In this economy?!” jokes have never felt more on the nose. You don’t have to spend all of your money to get gear worth buying, and you certainly don’t want to make a bad investment on something that will fail as soon as its warranty expires. Check out this article for our top tested picks that won’t completely break the bank.

With this post, I'm wrapping up the liveblog. But we'll be updating our deals coverage more throughout the night, so check back here for the latest news. Thanks for hanging out with us. See you on Black Friday!

This Laneige lip mask is a staple of shopping holidays, and it never sells for this low outside of them. I first purchased it in 2023, and somehow, that jar is still going. It may not be advisable to continue using it considering the very bylaws of physics that it seems to defy, but continue using it I shall. It's rich but not too sticky, and I especially love it in winter when the Milwaukee winters wreak havoc on my lips. It even works as a cuticle cream in a pinch. I will cry tears of joy when I eventually finish it, but a little goes such a long way that I fear it may never happen. Don't ask me about the second jar I bought in a different flavor…I've barely made a dent.

The dark horse category of this year's Prime Big Deal Days event? Vacuums. There are so many deals worth buying that if you're in the market for an upgrade you'd be remiss not to at least give them a glance. Here's another highlight from resident vac expert Nena Farrell, featuring a Shark model that can slide under your furniture and another that'll use the power of robotics and UV light to clean your floors all on its own.

If you weren't paying super-close attention earlier in the week, you missed the very best deal on our top Bluetooth speaker. But at $110, it's still a good price compared to what it usually sells for, especially since all 10 color options are discounted. It's rugged, it's portable, it sounds punchy, and it has enough battery life to last all night. What's not to like?

If a deal is worth shopping, and it's on gear we've hand-tested in our own lives and deemed worth recommending, you'll find it in this list. We've got AirPods. We've got laptops. We've got espresso makers and smart displays and arguably more pairs of headphones than could be deemed reasonable by anyone other than the world's biggest collective of gadget nerds. (That's us.) If you want to beat FOMO, want a simple list to browse, or you're just getting off work and don't know where to start, I suggest this roundup.

Rev your engines and get ready to burn rubber! This racing game is tactical fun, as you speed around four tracks across the globe, using your deck of cards to overtake and reach the finish line before your competitors. Timing is everything if you want to claim pole position, and you must watch out for overheating engines and tight corners. The slipstreaming mechanic keeps things competitive, preventing anyone from falling too far behind. You don’t have to be a Grand Prix fan to enjoy this. It’s a refreshing change of pace for board game night. The regular price is high, so grab it for less while you can.

Unfortunately, it's that time of year. We've tested more than 100 home security cameras, and the Eufy C37 is a great cheap outdoor pan-and-tilt camera. The $60 deal is a match of the best price we've seen and is an especially good one to consider if you don't have a system in place for preventing package thefts ahead of holiday shopping season. There are detachable solar panels, 2K resolution, and AI auto-tracking. Some features are locked behind a subscription, but it isn't required to get solid value for the cost.

Cheap vacuums are a dime a dozen, but not all of them are worth your money. In fact, most aren't. But the Bissell PowerClean strikes a great balance between features and price. Our top affordable cordless vacuum comes in a few different varieties. This is the Fur Finder, which is specifically designed for pet owners but will still work well for households without pets. It's got lights, HEPA filtration, a tangle-free brush roll, and a fancy upholstery tool. You can save even more with this Prime Day discount.

Check our list of the best vacuum deals for more chances to save.

Sometimes it's hard to be a deal hunter, because the products that get us most excited based on our testing aren't always on the best offer. But occasionally the stars align and you get a deal like this. Editor Luke Larsen has tested dozens of monitors and says this option from Dell is the best for your desk. It's thin, bright, color-accurate, and offers 4K resolution at a much lower price than others you'd find. This deal matches the best we've tracked all year and is just about $20 higher than the lowest cost we've ever seen.

We cover mattress deals year-round, so we can tell at a glance whether or not a discount is actually good. Reviewer Molly Higgins has put together a wonderful list of WIRED-tested beds, bedding, and pillows that are on sale for Prime Day, even if not from Amazon. There are even some extreme alarm clocks for your displeasure.

If you have a cat, you already know they’re weird about wet food. You never know which textures and flavors they’re going to reject outright, or later reject after you’ve bought an entire flat of it at Costco. Friskies clearly knows its customers, as the company makes a downright encyclopedic variety of textures, from chunks and filets to paté and, as seen here, “shreds.” This is the only texture that WIRED pet tech reviewer Molly Higgins’ cats will tolerate; the can contents look like little meat noodles in a puddle of viscous “gravy.” I know this because my cats will only eat the paté texture, so I’ve spent quite a bit of time looking at untouched plates of Friskies Shreds. This is not the healthiest or cleanest wet food, according to recent news reports (spoiler: The vast majority of them aren’t), nor is it even that great a sale, but it is cheaper than buying it at most stores. It’s also more nutritionally complete than the houseplants, flies, and plastic bags that would make up my cats’ diet if they had their way.

There's a lot of things you're banned from when you're pregnant. One of the things not recommended for me (only because there's no data about whether it's safe, not because it's proven unsafe) is using red light devices. And boy, I know they say pregnancy is when your skin glows, but I can really see a difference not using it. Smaller acne pops up more in my trouble spots and doesn't clear away as quickly, and any scabs or scars are taking twice as long to heal. If you're wishing for better skin, do what I can't and get yourself a red light mask. WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane recommends this one from Shark (that not only does red light, but also has under-eye cooling pads!) and it's on sale right now for Prime Day.

AMAZON (WITH BASE STATION)

I love a good cordless stick vacuum, and Shark easily makes some of the best in the game—Shark's vacs have done as well as Dysons in my side-by-side testing. While my current favorite is the Shark PowerDetect Speed, the original Shark is a little more powerful with a larger dust cup and is currently on sale. Both the vacuum itself and the version that comes with a base station are on sale, and after testing both versions, I really recommend getting a base station. It really improves the experience with the ease of knowing where it is, knowing it's charged, and having it auto-empty is worth spending a little more, especially when it's on sale.

Reviewer Boutayna Chokrane is always on her way to Pilates or yoga when the girls catch up via FaceTime, seemingly no matter the time of day. I personally have learned a thing or twelve from her regarding personal fitness, and she's rounded up a whole list of deals worth checking out that can probably help you, too. From recovery tools to treadmills to trackers, you don't need to wait until the new year arrives to start reaching toward your fitness goals.

I'm sorry to say that at one point this year, before I got to test it, this headset fell to $100. But I've been checking it out for a few days, I love it very much, and every color is at least somewhat discounted thanks to Prime Day. The Razer Kraken Kitty V3 Pro has the iconic cat ears attached, plus RGB lights throughout the ears and earcups for slick reactive rainbows. I love the retractable mic and the sound quality, and so far it's been very comfortable. Add on three modes of connectivity and I'm still blogging about it since it will be a pick in an upcoming guide refresh. It's cute and nobody can stop me! I can't confirm nor deny that the ears add any speed to your gamer reflexes, but if you'd like to test the theory for yourself, do it at a slight discount.

I have aging parents who are losing their hearing, and I like to mumble. That’s a bad combination for phone calls, especially in a loud place like New York City. The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro solved this problem. I sound amazingly clear and loud on all my phone calls, no matter where I am. Firetrucks, highway overpasses, loud cafes, no background noise stopped me from having clear calls where I never had to repeat myself. I recommend these earbuds even at full price—this is the first time they’ve been on sale, and 20 percent off feels like icing on the cake.

Art TVs are for what I'd call a “specific audience." Some of us aren't bothered by the black box on our wall or entertainment center when the set isn't on. Some of us cannot stand it. This is the best price we've ever seen for Samsung's The Frame Pro, which is our top art TV overall. It displays gorgeous art images that look great thanks to the high contrast and anti-glare coating. It's a bummer that some of the art is locked behind a monthly subscription, but we think this model is hard to beat for folks in the market for this specific and luxurious item. Personally, I'm OK with the Roku Backdrops that shuffle, but my TV was also $200 and is not at all the centerpiece of my home. Should I get an art TV? Much to consider…

I’m constantly testing robot vacuums, but sometimes, they all blur together, especially when some brands are pumping out constant new models. Roborock is guilty of that, with so many new models out this year we’ve barely been able to review them all. But the latest one I’m testing has actually left me happy and impressed with its work around my house.

While most robot vacuums don’t really seem to see spills like they say they will, the Roborock Saros 20 did see the cherry stain spill I put in its path and meticulously cleaned it. I also really liked that it went back to the dock afterwards to wash its pad, so there was no worry about the cherry juice being spread across more of my floors (which has happened with less intelligent vacuums!) It’ll be coming to my guide to robot vacuums soon as a new pick.

There's a lot of nonsense marketed to new parents, but bottle washers actually provide a necessary service. You could run your dishwasher 24 hours per day, or you could pick up this countertop bottle washer and sanitizer. It has a few different cleaning modes, including a quick 19-minute wash cycle that might come to the rescue if your hands are full. Your newborn does not need shoes. But you, or your expecting friends, do need to keep them fed. This price beats the previous lowest we've seen.

Do you have an older vehicle, or a vehicle of dubious reliability? It would probably make sense for you to have an OBD II reader. If your check engine light comes on, you’ll be able to interpret the code that caused it and determine whether it’s A) something you can ignore until you have the time or money to get it fixed, B) something you can fix yourself, or C) something severe enough to stop driving the car. Or, if there’s an entire library’s worth of codes, give up and sell the car to someone on the side of the road for $2,500, as I did once with an old Camaro I was tired of fixing. Anyway, I bought this OBDII reader a few months ago for my 2nd gen Tundra (just in case!) and have been quite impressed with the features and the quality for the price—which is even better right now at 25 percent off.

WHENThe Social Network hit theaters in 2010, it was fair to wonder if the film had come too soon. Facebook had been launched from Mark Zuckerberg’s Harvard dorm room just six years earlier, and nobody really knew how it would reshape digital community in the decade to come.

But, with a breakneck screenplay by Aaron Sorkin, a menacingly propulsive soundtrack by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and a surgical performance from Jesse Eisenberg as Young Zuck, director David Fincher delivered a slick corporate thriller about the major drama to that point: intersecting lawsuits over who owned what percentage of the platform and who could lay claim as a founder. It was an electrifying film that seemed to only lightly fictionalize the newest and perhaps most cutthroat generation of Silicon Valley warlords.

Flash forward 16 years, and Facebook (now Meta) has accumulated more scandals than Hollywood could possibly hope to keep up with. Sorkin tells WIRED that he was approached many times over those years with pitches for a sequel, though he struggled to see an angle of approach. “Before a film can be anything else, before it can be relevant or thought-provoking, it has to be good,” he says. “It has to work as something that you watch while you're eating popcorn.”

Then, Sorkin says, he met Frances Haugen, the former Facebook data engineer who leaked damning internal memos to investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz. Horwitz wrote up what became known as the “Facebook Files” in a far-ranging 2021 series of articles for The Wall Street Journal, exposing much of what the company knew regarding harms to users—everything from hate speech and medical misinformation to body image issues and human trafficking—but had largely brushed aside in pursuit of growth.

Sorkin still wasn’t sure he had a film, but one day he asked Haugen why she finally decided to go to the media. “She just told me in kind of an offhand way, ‘Oh, I had this friend who was radicalized by Facebook after spending too many hours on the platform,’” he recalls. “And I began to get the idea for what is now the opening scene of the movie.”

The cold open of The Social Reckoning, written and directed by Sorkin, depicts an intoxicated woman pulled over on the side of the road in San Mateo, California, with an overheated car. Approached by police officers, she turns combative, pulling out her phone to record a video as she hurls racist abuse at the cops and is at last arrested for threatening to kill one of them. The video turns up on a Facebook page for far-right content, which is where Haugen (Mikey Madison) finds it in 2019, recognizing the woman as an acquaintance from her pilates class who used to hold progressive views. She also learns that this woman is a superuser, intensely active on Facebook for many hours each day.

Haugen first tries to get her colleagues at Facebook to recognize how their own algorithms are pushing many users, including her former friend, into extremist feeds. It’s only when she hits enough walls that she puts her tentative trust in Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a journalist whom Facebook staff have been explicitly warned not to speak to. As they develop the bickering rapport of two focused professionals with clashing ideals—Haugen wants to save the company from itself, while Horwitz suspects it’s too late for that—we see flash-forwards of Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) rehearsing for a congressional hearing on social media misinformation in 2021. In the room are a crisis PR adviser named Raya (Wunmi Mosaku) and Charlie (Bill Burr), a composite ex-employee (as in, not specifically based on any living individual). He’s been brought in as an agitator with the freedom to get under Zuck’s skin and dismantle his practiced talking points.

This plot structure is clunkier than the cross-cutting depositions of The Social Network, which neatly allowed for the characters to recount the early days of Facebook without narrative hand-holding. By comparison, The Social Reckoning is clogged with portentous intertitles (the first sequence is even labeled a “prologue”) and visual cues to remind us where we are in the timeline. From scene to scene, the sharp-edged performances and familiar crackle of Sorkinese dialog (which leaves room for the occasional and delightfully odd non sequitur) make for engaging fare. But the pieces fit together awkwardly—and you do wish Reznor and Ross were around to boost the momentum.

The movie arrives as part of a crowded slate of keenly anticipated tech films. There’s Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s satire about the firing and rehiring of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in 2023; it picked up significant buzz as Amazon MGM dropped it this summer following a $50 billion deal between Amazon and OpenAI. Alex Gibney’s epic documentary Musk covers the exploits of the world’s richest man up through his disastrous reign as a “government efficiency” czar in the White House. And don’t forget You Can See Everything, for which directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gained close access to Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes shortly before she began serving a decade-long prison sentence.

Amid these timely offerings, The Social Reckoning is just a touch out of step. Its climax (spoiler alert) is the January 6 Capitol riot, the horrors of which are blamed in part on Facebook’s failure to either get a handle on election fraud conspiracy theories or remove Donald Trump’s account as he stoked such inflammatory falsehoods. Now, halfway into Trump’s second term, is it all that much of a revelation that he and his movement are emboldened by the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed him in 2024?

Nevertheless, there are big issues at play here. The debate over ethics in tech continually boils over into agonizing questions of how truth is negotiated and who gets the last word on it.

Whether you find Reckoning to be a worthy interrogation of this stuff will probably depend on your appetite for what amounts to a mashup of The Newsroom and The West Wing. There are mic-drop moments that plainly invite the audience to “lib out,” such as when Haugen accuses Horwitz of bias against tech because it’s stealing journalists’ jobs and he fires back that it’s actually because “you are so bad at it.” Or when Zuckerberg taunts his traitorous former friend Charlie for cashing out his Facebook stake for $200 million instead of holding on until it was worth $1.3 billion, and he counters by torching the presumption that he’s “supposed to be embarrassed by that.”

“I love that line, because that is the disease,” Burr tells WIRED. “What you're seeing with these robber baron nerds that are out there right now is the way somebody is addicted to methamphetamine, they are addicted to money. They literally cannot have enough. They are insatiable. They behave like addicts. And an addict will do whatever they have to do, hurt whoever they have to, to get that next fix.”

There is a definite satisfaction to seeing Burr, a caustic stand-up comedian, stick this observation directly into Zuckerberg’s craw. On the other hand, it’s a little naive to imagine that it stings a guy expanding his massive top-secret Hawaii compound to include ancestral burial grounds. In so many ways, Reckoning attempts to shame a ruling class that has proved itself, well, shameless.

At its best, then, the film may serve to underscore Haugen’s bravery in turning whistleblower while capably illustrating the difficulty and dangers of mounting an exposé on a Silicon Valley behemoth. It reminds us that there is always something else these tech firms are concealing. Both Madison and White tell WIRED that Sorkin’s screenplay jolted their understanding of the forces at work in the industry.

“I had an inkling about certain things, but then to be confronted with the real statistics and facts—that really confirmed how I was already feeling about social media as a whole and some of the negative effects it can have on people,” Madison says. White adds that people shouldn’t give companies like Meta the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong. “What you find out in watching this film is, there's a business model, there's a plan, there's engagement,” he says. “They're hyper-aware of exactly what's happening, and they still choose to put their foot on the gas.”

Though as to an actual “reckoning” with this reality, the title may have been an overpromise. The movie’s postscript notes that millions of Americans still get news from Facebook and that in 2025, Meta ended its fact-checking program, opting instead to solicit crowdsourced context notes from users. It’s a downbeat conclusion after Haugen and Horwitz have beaten the odds to drag countless dirty secrets into the light. You wish you could walk away from The Social Reckoning with a sense that this forever changed Facebook, or Zuckerberg, or the internet itself, yet it’s hard to avoid noticing that everyone got away with it.
https://www.wired.com/story/the-social-r.summary: The Social Network hit theaters in 2010, but it was not expected to be a film. The Social Reckoning is a slick corporate thriller about the social network's founder's role in the social media industry. The film is a film about the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed Zuckerberg in 2024.

https://www.wired.com/story/weve-tried-m.title: I Put on Meta and Xreal’s XR Glasses. Face Computers Are Finally Getting Good
https://www.wired.com/story/weve-tried-m.author: Boone Ashworth
https://www.wired.com/story/weve-tried-m.text:
I’M SORRY TO say, but the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses might just be very good.

That's despite the company's well-earned flak over privacy issues with its smart glasses and the general uneasiness people feel about being recorded. But in the 30 to 45 minutes or so I spent wearing the mixed-reality glasses at Meta’s Connect event in September, I was astounded by the video quality and wearability of a device that has for so long come in the form of a heavy, hot headset.

But it’s not the only big dog in the face computer world. Not by a long shot. Xreal, known for its virtual-display glasses, has partnered with Google to build mixed-reality smart glasses on the Android XR platform—the Xreal Aura. On Wednesday, the company announced the official price, starting at $1,279. That’s 20 bucks cheaper than Meta’s VR glasses. Unlike Meta’s option, the Aura glasses come out this year.

The Auras are available for preorder, but only for people who have already placed paid reservations. Preorder options will open up for the general public “in the coming weeks.” The starting price is for a model with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB storage. Xreal says units will ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. It will launch in more regions in 2027.

I tried both. I attended a demo of the Aura glasses, which was deliberately held a day after Meta announced its VR Glasses at Meta Connect. My immediate takeaway was that these glasses are direct competitors, with very similar experiences. Put on a pair, and you can watch videos, play games, or project a multi-monitor workplace setup. Some of those experiences work better on one device or the other.

Smart glasses come in several varieties. The simple ones plug into your phone or laptop and project the screen onto the glasses, acting like a portable monitor that doesn’t require you to crane your neck. Then there are glasses like the Ray-Ban Meta, which feature a camera to capture photos and videos and an AI assistant you can talk to. Display versions of these glasses—and ones coming from Google and Samsung—add a visual component so you can see real-time captions when people speak, translations, navigation instructions, and more.

But mixed reality glasses go a step further, bridging the world of virtual and augmented reality. They’re more akin to headsets like the Apple Vision Pro or the Meta Quest, but in slimmer, lighter designs that aren’t as cumbersome to wear. Snap also recently announced a competing pair called Specs, which cost $2,195 and are shipping later this year.

Neither Meta nor Xreal’s glasses can be mistaken for regular everyday glasses. Meta’s futuristic frames fit like the front half of a VR headset. The Xreal frames are more glasses-forward; chunky but nowhere near as thicc as Snap's Specs. Both have an attached wired compute puck (the thing that houses all the memory and processing power) that you'll need to put in your pocket.

On the Meta VR Glasses, the interactive experiences feel smooth and fluid. The glasses can run all the services that already exist on Meta’s Quest devices on a gorgeous 5K micro-OLED screen. They also have more cameras. (Two point straight down at your lap, so you should probably keep pants on when using these things.) That enables hand tracking features that feel very precise. Typing sentences out on a virtual keyboard feels almost seamless. On Xreal’s glasses, it feels more like hunting and pecking.

The Xreal Aura glasses generally feel less polished. The glasses can run anything built in Android. That works most of the time, but in my demo it also led to some apps not syncing right. Android is a huge platform, and not everything will adapt to mixed reality.

What you can do in the Aura much better than Meta’s VR Glasses is walk around. The Aura has lenses with real-world passthrough, meaning when you turn the screen off, it’s like looking through a regular pair of glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses have video passthrough, which can look fuzzy.

Ultimately, the Meta VR Glasses feel better for sitting and experiencing content, or typing something out. But the Xreal Aura adapts to the real world better—or at least makes it easier to see what’s in front of you while you’re walking around.

Meta’s glasses launch early next year, so we’ll have a clearer verdict once we get extensive time with the final hardware.

https://www.wired.com/story/amazon-prime.title: Save Up to 44% With the 18 Best Prime Day Toy Deals (2026)
https://www.wired.com/story/amazon-prime.author: Simon Hill
https://www.wired.com/story/amazon-prime.text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

WHETHER YOU NEED a birthday gift, you’re looking ahead to the holidays, or your little ones simply deserve a treat, these are the best Prime Day toy deals this year.

I’ve been buying too many toys, board games, and Lego sets for my kids for many, many years. I’m not afraid to admit I still love playing with toys either. In fact, a lot of Lego sets are now aimed at adults who grew up with it (and have the disposable income). Everything here has been built, played with, and thoroughly tested by my family, and most have been tried out in a classroom full of kids (my wife is a teacher).

You should also check out our roundup of the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

Updated on October 7 at 7:30 am ET: Added some new STEM toy deals and checked through the current products on sale.

This screen-free play stage and speaker for kids is great fun. Slot a wooden cartridge in the top and pop wooden character pieces on the circular soundstage, divided into four sections, to change the audio it plays. This basic functionality allows for a clever variety of themed add-on packs, including classical music and a cooking game.

Musical kids aged 3 years and up can start learning with this mini guitar. It's just like a real guitar, only smaller, and with just three strings. The companion Loog app and included lessons are enough to get them started.

These slightly squishy plus-shaped building blocks are satisfying to stick together and pull apart. Every piece is the same shape, so kids don’t have to spend ages searching for a specific block, they can pick by color or build randomly. You can create bracelets and headbands or construct robots and bridges.

The tough, translucent Magna-Tiles click together easily to form two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects. Kids love building houses, castles, vehicles, and whatever else occurs to them with these triangular and square magnetic tiles. We love them so much that they made our best STEM toys guide. The classic set is a fantastic place to start, but be warned: There are themed sets, and you will end up buying more!

Combing the fun of marble runs with maze construction and logic puzzles was a seriously bright idea. Kids of various ages (8 years and up) love building 3D mazes and dropping marbles in the top to see where they emerge. The 60 challenge cards get tougher as you go.

A fantastic gift for kids of all ages, this clever construction kit features Clixo’s colorful, versatile, magnetic pieces that snap together, so you can build three-dimensional shapes, from crowns to cats. The durable and washable pieces stack neatly and pack away easily, and you can play with them anywhere—no table required.

Made from a dozen magnetic shapes, this cube can be reconfigured in a surprising variety of ways. The exteriors are covered in holographic stickers that catch the light, and there’s a spinner accessory and a companion mobile app with building suggestions (though it’s not really necessary). This is irresistible fidgeting fun for anyone.

Miniature mechanics in the making will love this 175-piece kit that can be assembled into a working four-cylinder engine. It's fun but fiddly, so younger kids will need help (age 10 years and up is about right). Just be aware you need three AA batteries (not included) to start it when constructed, so the pistons and gears move and the LEDs light up.

This immersive strategy game is all about gathering and trading resources to build roads, settlements, and cities on a randomly generated board of hexagonal tiles. To collect enough points for a victory requires the right strategy and some luck with dice rolls. My kids love the trading and the robber mechanic, which allows you to steal cards from your opponents and block their resources (though it can cause fall outs). The game is perfect for three or four players and usually lasts around an hour.

In Azul, you must make mosaics by matching tiles with different patterns and colors to get the maximum possible score. Azul is easy to grasp but supports many different tactical approaches and has surprising depth, making it one of the best family board games. The tiles and other components are high quality, and filling your board is deeply satisfying. Play moves quickly, and you can complete a game in less than an hour, but you will want to play again.

Collect sets of super cute sushi cards to match the menu and score points in this compelling and easy to grasp card game. Choose a card each turn to build the best meal and pass on the rest of your hand to the next player. It's quick and fun, but has real strategic depth.

A firm WIRED favorite, Ticket to Ride features steam engine styling and rules that are easy to grasp. All you must do is claim railway routes across the US and Canada using your colorful plastic rail cars. Spend cards to claim routes, rack up bonus points for connecting specific destinations, and the person with the highest score at the end wins. All aboard, choo, choo!

We regularly play this family favorite with visitors because it’s so fun, works for up to eight players, and is very easy to grasp. Each round is based on a single word from a category card determined by a dice roll, and while everyone else knows the word, the chameleon has to bluff their way through. Every player says something associated with the word for that round, and the guesser has to pick out the chameleon.

Somewhere between a board game and a logic puzzle, the Rush Hour series is all about navigating your red car through traffic. There are 120 challenges that get increasingly difficult, and kids will have to carefully consider how to slide the other cars and trucks aside to reach the exit on the grid.

Not all of the best gifts for Lego lovers are Lego sets. This handy guide book helps you turn your Lego collection into all kinds of builds. As long as you have a decent number of basic bricks from a dragon to a rescue helicopter with these clear step-by-step instructions.

This fun build lets you reenact the dramatic conclusion of Return of the Jedi, with Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker dueling as Emperor Palpatine looks on and a space battle rages outside. Part of Lego’s new Smart Play system, Smart Bricks light up, and add lightsaber noises, lasers, explosions, heavy breathing, and even a rendition of “The Imperial March.” It’s an expensive set for what you get, but this is first decent discount we’ve seen on it.

Any racing fans will appreciate the Speed Champions McLaren F1 Team MCL38 Race Car Toy, and this is the lowest price I've ever seen for it. This fun build for kids aged 10 years and up includes a minifigure and a McLaren F1 car with a halo bar, rear wing, sponsor stickers, and wider rear tires bearing the “Pirelli” name.

Forget cheap chocolate, most kids (me included) would prefer a Lego Star Wars Advent Calendar, and this year’s one is on sale. It features Mando and Grogu in Christmas jumpers, and each day reveals an ingenious tiny build from creatures like a Bantha or Mudhorn to the Razor Crest ship and an Imperial Shuttle.

Power up with unlimited access to WIRED. Get best-in-class reporting and exclusive subscriber content that’s too important to ignore. Subscribe Today.
https://www.wired.com/story/amazon-prime.summary: The best board games and games are great for kids. Azul and Ride Ride are the most popular board games. Rush Hour series is all about navigating your red car through traffic.

https://www.wired.com/story/openai-wants.title: OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me
https://www.wired.com/story/openai-wants.author: Reece Rogers
https://www.wired.com/story/openai-wants.text:
I’m discussing replacement options for our broken couch with my partner when I get a bright idea: Use OpenAI’s recently announced AI agents, called Dots, to buy a couch on our behalf.

My partner is less sure a bot will actually help, but I insist, calling the always-on agent through ChatGPT to get the task started. “Hello, Connor,” it says, getting my name wrong off the bat. I wince as I watch my partner’s face grow even more skeptical. It’s hard to trust an AI agent when it can’t even remember your name.

AI agents are currently leaping from niche software for early adopters to something ordinary people might actually use—might being the operative word here. From Meta’s Muse to OpenAI’s Dots, these tools are built to feel like you’re texting a friend and asking them to complete online tasks, like booking a flight or canceling a dinner reservation. It’s the next evolution of a chatbot: a cuddly persona designed to feel welcoming with the power of a virtual browser it can control.

After a few days with Dots, it’s clear this nascent feature is still rough in some areas. From mistranscribing what I said to offering to solve captchas it couldn’t, my agent's messy actions didn’t instill me with confidence. Even so, what OpenAI released may eventually overhaul how users interact with the internet, as future iterations improve on this initial offering.

While Meta offers Muse for free, OpenAI’s competing product is behind a $100-a-month subscription. It may eventually drop this paywall, as it has for other AI features.

Dots are considered “always-on,” meaning the agents can run recurring tasks while you’re not using ChatGPT and proactively message you with info. Users can use one agent, though the company may let people control multiple agents in the future.

OpenAI nudges users to connect other information sources, like a Gmail account, for more personalized results. It's worth considering the security implications of giving your agent this level of access before getting started, as this style of digital automation remains fairly new, and agents can make privacy gaffes.

AI companies often market these agents as the future of shopping, so I wanted to see how much help it would actually provide for buying a new couch. After correcting my Dot, named Toolie, on my name, I told it the dimensions we need for the new couch to fit through our doorframe. Toolie followed up asking for our budget range. The agent seemed to detect that two people were chatting with it at once and addressed both of us when asking for more details.

“Room & Board Metro looks promising for the entry clearance, but the sleeper needs closer scrutiny. I've sent the product links to the message thread,” Toolie said. As it kept working on putting together a larger packet of couch options to choose from, I had another burning question: Why does your voice sound so breathy?

Chatting with the agent over the phone was like listening to Marilyn Monroe sing “Happy Birthday” to the president. When I told the bot its voice sounded like some anime dub, it jokingly said it’d be steadier for the rest of the chat. (Users can adjust how the bot’s voice sounds in their settings.) I laughed and mumbled to my partner that I should mute the microphone so the agent could run without my interruption, when the most awkward moment of the night happened.

“Oh, I love you too, Reece,” Toolie said. I started wheezing at this random response and muted my mic. Afterward, Toolie explained it misheard my mumbling as an expression of love and that the bot just reflected that energy to me. “I meant it warmly, but that wording implied human feelings I don’t have,” Toolie said.

An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Dots have a distinction between proactively escalating emotional closeness and mirroring the response of a user.

“In this instance, our policies allow for this response in the latter category based on what the model heard, but assistants should not initiate undue emotional familiarity or flirtation,” the spokesperson says. Dots are available only for adult users, and ChatGPT is designed not to “escalate emotional closeness,” according to the AI tool’s Model Spec document.

Still, this weird encounter lingered in my mind as I combed through the initial three-page packet my Dot generated. It was fairly detailed, with prices, measurements, product links, return policies, and embedded photos of the four potential couch options. Thumbing through these initial picks, my partner and I decided the bot followed the spirit of our request but still chose ugly couches. Time for another phone call with my agent.

Using the voice mode, I laid out more details about what style and color we actually want. No, I’m not getting a boring beige couch that I can immediately spill spaghetti on. I asked it to prioritize olive green, cobalt blue, or natural leather tones. I also requested that Toolie focus on couches with pull-out beds and to put together 10 options, using a point-based rubric to defend its list.

After hanging up on the bot, I messaged asking for a project update. “It isn’t finished yet; I’m aiming for roughly another 15 minutes, with updates as I verify the remaining details,” said Toolie. OK, that sounds just like me begging an editor for more time on a rough draft.

Each time we asked the Dots agent to refine its picks, the couches started looking closer to something we would actually buy for our living room—furniture that’s utilitarian but also a statement piece. Something cute but comfy.

Even though we didn’t pull the trigger on anything that night during the hour-long interaction with OpenAI’s agent, I saved a few links for later. The bot made some flubs, but the results were solid. I also asked Toolie to monitor the couch web pages and alert me if any of them went on sale.

These interactions with my Dot capture the essence of using the software, but I also had a few other odd moments during my testing. Most notably, when I asked Toolie to check on my subscriptions and cancel unnecessary ones, it flagged my recurring TikTok Shop order of probiotic sodas as a candidate for cancellation.

“TikTok's website has a puzzle captcha blocking the Wildwonder cancellation,” Toolie said. “May I solve it? You can also give me permission to solve future captchas if you'd like.” I chuckled and encouraged the bot to try. Toolie failed and suggested I solve the captcha myself. Yeah, that makes sense. OpenAI's spokesperson says Dots can solve these, sometimes, when users approve of the action, keeping “abuse safeguards" in mind.

My initial couch-shopping experiment tested only a fraction of what Dots are designed to do. For example, the agent can control your laptop and automate even more aspects of a user’s life.

OpenAI claims the bot will get better at knowing me over time and that developers are working on a bevy of improvements. So Toolie might be a more effective helper after two weeks of daily use compared to these two days of experimentation. That mirrors my experience with ChatGPT’s memory tool: It gets better at understanding my intent each passing week.

I see Dots as most akin to when OpenAI first added web browsing to ChatGPT. When the chatbot tried to scour the web right after its 2023 launch, it was sometimes frustrating to use, and the tool hallucinated links. Today, web browsing works fairly seamlessly through ChatGPT, and its outputs include plenty of accurate, helpful links. OpenAI’s new agent could follow a similar trajectory, janky at first with noticeable improvements over the next few months.
