https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/how-sta.title: Regulators are trying to protect you from being fired by AI – here’s how
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/how-sta.author: Radhika Rajkumar
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/how-sta.text:
Innovation
>
Artificial Intelligence

Regulating AI at work is happening slowly, but it's still stuck at the state level.

October 8, 2026, 1:05 pm ET

AI use at work is up, touching everything from everyday tasks to hiring and performance reviews. An April survey conducted by MyPerfectResume found that of 1,000 HR professionals, 73% said they use AI to make hiring decisions and 52% said they use AI to inform “restructuring and role planning.”

Hiring managers are also turning to AI for deeper behavioral insights when screening candidates: Over half of respondents (51%) use it to “flag ‘risky’ candidates.” Only 26% of respondents said they don’t use AI to make decisions about layoffs.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

California Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed new legislation protecting workers from certain AI-powered decision-makers in the workplace. The bill covers these issues from a few angles — here’s what the regulation is trying to address, and how it could set the tone for future state or federal legislation.

SB 947, somewhat cheekily called the “No Robo Bosses Act,” prohibits employers from outsourcing disciplinary and termination decisions entirely to AI, referred to in the bill as automated decision systems (ADS). The bill requires employers to check any AI decisions on employee discipline or termination, as well as provide the employee with a description of the reasons for the decision. That includes any data used to make the decision, including personnel files, evaluations, work product, peer reviews, and “witness interviews.”

“If an employer cannot corroborate the ADS output or the human reviewer has concluded that the ADS output is inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading, the employer shall not use the ADS output to make a disciplinary or termination decision,” the bill states.

Also: AI just broke your career ladder – here are 6 new ways to the top

The law, which goes into effect on July 1, 2027, lets affected employees file complaints with the California Labor Commissioner if they believe this process was not followed correctly in a firing decision. It does not fully prohibit the use of automated systems for these determinations. It also requires employers to clarify whether “a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is caused by an AI system,” according to a brief on the governor’s website.

While AI regulation at the federal level remains less specific, mired in voluntary agreements with labs, and arguably focused on distractions, states have risen to the challenge of creating initial protections for workers. Still, when it comes to AI in hiring and other workplace processes, some states like Colorado and Connecticut have opted for mandating disclosure of AI use rather than actual intervention.

California and New York have tended to lead the charge on stricter laws, though Illinois passed a landmark bill this summer, becoming the first state to require third-party audits of frontier labs.

Also: 73% of tech job listings require AI skills now: How to show off yours

Lily Li, a lawyer specializing in AI and founder of Metaverse Law, told ZDNET she sees California’s latest law setting the precedent for other states. But she also anticipates companies finding loopholes in the law’s required human review process.

“We could see employers engaging in check-the-box reviews rather than meaningful human review, to avoid the operational costs of an additional layer of review,” she said. “The ability for an employee to request an explanation is a helpful check against this, however.”

With that concern, it’s possible the onus of tackling unvetted AI-driven firings will fall on complainants contesting their own firings in court. Still, protections like these will remain patchwork across the country until some version of them is adopted at the federal level.

https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/ai-lega.title: Can AI fix legacy IT? The ‘economics don’t hold up,’ says former IBM strategist
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/ai-lega.author: Joe McKendrick
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/ai-lega.text:
Innovation
>
Artificial Intelligence

Vendors are pitching AI as a cure-all for legacy IT systems, but is it?

October 8, 2026, 10:35 am ET

At some point in your career, or at many points, you might have been asked to help with an IT modernization program, porting applications from older systems, such as mainframes, to newer systems, be they on-premises or in the cloud.

Also: 5 ways to use AI to modernize your legacy systems

Modernization has been on CIO agendas for decades. Popular efforts have included web services, microservices, cloud, virtualization, and x86-based Windows and Linux servers. These efforts aimed to create more advanced and flexible systems.

When reflecting on these trends, it sometimes feels like modernization is always something that’s five years away. Now, it’s AI’s turn to modernize IT systems.

So far, AI implementations have bypassed technology modernization efforts, according to a survey of 2,000 senior IT decision-makers by IT services specialist Kyndryl. Only 10% of tech chiefs said they are applying agentic AI as a modernization tool. The burning question: Will AI eventually make a difference where earlier efforts have fallen short? Or is AI just another elixir in a never-ending quest?

The results of modernization, as we’ve known it, have been less than stellar. Kyndryl researchers found that modernization is often just another expensive, time-consuming project.

“Only about half of those modernizing report achieving better IT operations, and less than half are seeing innovation gains,” the study’s authors observed.

“Nearly one in five, 18%, say their firms saw limited or unclear value from modernization efforts.” In addition, almost half of respondents said they are behind schedule and suffering cost overruns.

Also: The best AI leaders are ‘a little bit off the wall,’ says Google Cloud executive

Modernization must become more than swapping out mainframes or other legacy systems for something sleeker.

Enter agentic AI, which could shape the next wave of modernization. This time, instead of replacing mainframes and other legacy systems, the focus is on expanding tangible business capabilities.

“Cost reduction and legacy escape are no longer the leading motivations to modernize,” reported Kyndryl. “As AI increases demand on nearly every element of IT, and as sovereignty considerations become more acute, leaders want their complex technology estates — a mix of old and new decisions — to work better.”

Also: 12 rules of agentic AI for successful enterprise transformation

Agents can operate autonomously while providing more visibility on dependencies between systems, both legacy and new. “Fewer than one in 10 organizations are fully confident they know those dependencies today, a significant technical blind spot,” the Kyndryl report stated.

“Agentic AI is showing early promise to address longstanding challenges in modernization and speed progress,” the Kyndryl authors added.

“Agentic AI is being used to map hidden dependencies, generate code, and create documentation — all traditionally time-consuming, error-prone processes. Organizations not using agentic AI for modernization are much more likely to be behind schedule than early adopters.”

However, modernization challenges remain despite AI’s promises. Even the most forward-looking organizations can find modernization to be an endless quest.

“IT modernization increasingly looks like a chronic condition,” agreed Andy Thurai, founder of The Field CTO and former chief strategist with IBM, commenting on the study.

“According to this report, four in ten enterprises are still running mainframes. We keep hearing modernization is the number-one mandate, yet the finish line is always 5 to 10 years out.”

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance — how businesses could make it work

Another issue is that “organizations are addicted to buying software,” said Thurai. “The legacy systems underneath it almost never get decommissioned. AI is now the latest shiny distraction from the grind of untangling that technical debt.”

CIOs must contend with a situation in which “vendors are pitching AI to IT leaders as the cure-all,” Thurai continued. “The economics don’t hold up. When AI drives infrastructure sprawl, the monthly bill becomes a black box. The report found that three in 10 leaders already worry AI-driven modernization will end in wildly unpredictable compute costs.”

Also: What workers are really using AI for — and what they aren’t

AI-based modernization may have its moment in the sun, especially for organizations “that went past the bolt-on chatbot,” said Thurai. “They’re using agentic frameworks as an orchestration layer to map out hidden technical dependencies, and then generating the missing documentation as they go. Agentic AI is speeding up initiatives that used to eat months of error-prone manual labor.”

In short, agents could be just the latest chapter of a nonstop journey. “Sooner or later, today’s AI-driven architectures are going to be the legacy environments somebody else has to modernize,” said Thurai.

https://www.zdnet.com/tech/microsoft-sur.title: Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra finally has a starting price (you should sit down)
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/microsoft-sur.author: Kyle Kucharski
https://www.zdnet.com/tech/microsoft-sur.text:
Tech
>
Computing
>
Laptops

The Surface Laptop Ultra is an AI powerhouse, with Nvidia's new RTX Spark chip and up to 128GB of unified memory - and it's priced for power users.

October 8, 2026, 8:13 am ET

Microsoft announced a launch date for its new Surface Laptop Ultra: October 18th, with a starting price of $2,599 for the lowest-tier configuration (and going up to $6,000 from there). It dropped the news at a showcase event in San Francisco on Wednesday, attended by Satya Nadella and Jensen Huang, the CEOs of Microsoft and Nvidia, respectively.

Also: I tried the Surface Laptop Ultra at Computex, and it’s clear: Microsoft means business

I first saw the Surface Laptop Ultra at Computex in Taiwan earlier this year, armed with Nvidia’s new RTX Spark processor that runs Windows on ARM, up to 128GB of unified memory, and a premium aluminum body.

Up close, it’s a gorgeous machine, with a 15-inch HDR display at 2,000 nits, a large haptic touchpad, thoughtful design elements (nearly invisible cooling vents, rounded edges), and a magnetic USB-C port called “magnetic connect” that snaps the charger into place. It looks like a Surface, yes, but it feels like the next stage in its evolution.

The other five RTX Spark laptops from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and MSI were also at the event, all of which I first saw at Computex and have similarly premium features: OLED displays, haptics, up to 128GB of unified memory, and similarly sky-high price points. But the Surface Laptop Ultra was the darling of the show with its own dramatic sizzle reel and focus in live demos.

All of these laptops are built for AI power users, creators, and developers. While they can certainly run games, they aren’t explicitly marketed as gaming laptops. Instead, demos showcased complex workflows in Blender, ComfyUI, and Photoshop, running large local models that previously would have needed to run on the cloud.

Microsoft’s positioning of the Surface Laptop Ultra as the leader of the RTX Spark pack allows it to own the narrative of the next evolution of powerful Windows devices. All this memory is made not just for what’s considered “frontier” today, but future-facing workflows, especially with the emphasis on Windows’ “hybrid intelligence,” which aims to make the cloud-to-local transition more seamless.

Also: I saw the first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops – these 4 models will lead the new ultrabook boom

In that vein, these are future-facing devices: the first generation of a new brand of AI-first laptops that are both a response to existing competitors and an indication of where PCs are headed. It’s no surprise that many of the aforementioned features are also core components of Apple’s MacBook Pro, to which the Surface Laptop Ultra is certainly a response.

Sure, Apple’s design language is present when you look at the Surface Laptop Ultra, but you could say that about almost any modern PC. What’s more interesting is how intentional the doubling down is. Microsoft says it spent several years developing this laptop, showcasing multiple design iterations at the event, and emphasizing a “get it right” approach that I’d say is certainly evident in the final product.

In that sense, the Surface Laptop Ultra is also a risk for Microsoft. The resources devoted to this flagship device are not inconsequential, and as much as it communicates important brand positioning, it also needs to sell.

But RAM and storage are as expensive as ever, and dropping $6,000 on a laptop is only possible for a certain subset of the consumer market. These laptops ultimately speak to a niche power user, and Microsoft and Nvidia have their work cut out for them when it comes to communicating these products to the right demographic.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, as well as the other five RTX Spark Windows PCs, are available for preorder today starting at $2,599, with general availability on Oct. 16th.

With so many users giving reviews, tips, and insider knowledge about local restaurants, Google compiled its first fan-favorite dining list, complete with the dining trends of Maps users in 10 global cities: Atlanta, Chicago, London, Melbourne, Montreal, New York, San Francisco, Santiago, Seattle, and Tokyo.

Every city on Google’s list shows the most popular places users go to celebrate an occasion, catch a great vibe, and get the most bang for their buck.

I’ve visited some of the restaurants and cafes that made Google’s list in New York and Chicago, and most of the listings in Atlanta. Though locals may consider some places tourist traps, they have stellar reviews and are popular with everyday people.

From my perspective, these restaurants capture the culture and vibe of the cities they’re in, promising great food, a good experience, and a way to try the flavors of immigrant communities that settle in major metropolitan areas.

https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/manager.title: Managers are using AI to write performance reviews – and it shows

Does AI use help or hurt feedback at work? Here's what one survey found.

October 7, 2026, 5:47 pm ET

As AI use ramps up at work, where are the pros and cons, and for whom? New research from professional development firm Highwire shows where AI has entered the feedback loop — and where it’s both a potential problem and a solution for employee development.

Highwire surveyed 1,034 corporate employees on how AI is infiltrating manager-employee relationships. It found that 78% of managers reported using AI to “help draft, edit, summarize, or inform feedback or a performance review” in the last year. Most of those managers, perhaps unsurprisingly, noted that AI sped up the process of prepping that feedback (Highwire told ZDNET it did not ask managers what else they noticed about using AI).

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – with no time to upskill

However, only 16% of non-managerial employees surveyed were told AI influenced their review. Maybe concerns about being perceived poorly for using AI are behind that drop in transparency: an Atlassian study from June found that owning AI use at work backfired.

The details of how managers are using AI for feedback matter here, though. Having an AI tool format or summarize human-written observations, for example, is a different level of intervention than handing AI some performance data and asking it to crank out a review top to bottom.

As for how that feedback is landing with employees: 54% of those surveyed said feedback “has become more specific and actionable.” But 34% found feedback more generic, and 32% said it was less useful. A third of employees potentially pulling less value from their reviews than before AI entered the picture isn’t minor, even if the majority is finding a benefit.

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

The survey also found that “nearly 1 in 4 employees now rehearse difficult workplace conversations with an AI tool.” Highwire frames this as the result of a vacuum: Only 44% of employees reported having their manager’s support to practice a high-stakes conversation or other difficult workplace scenario, far less than the 85% who say practice is key. AI is therefore filling a needs gap for nervous employees.

The findings about rehearsing with AI are echoed in AI video company Synthesia’s latest release, Sessions. The new feature lets employees practice conversations with one of the company’s AI avatars and get an assessment from an “AI coach” — essentially an automated, scaled version of the one-on-one training managers typically give to employees.

Synthesia told ZDNET that it developed the feature based on feedback from enterprise customers wanting to expand access to those managerial touchpoints without stretching human bandwidth (though the company maintains Sessions is not a replacement for mentorship). For Synthesia customers, a tool like Sessions fills training gaps they couldn’t fix before (though data on how effective those training experiences are for employees remains to be seen). Both Highwire’s take and Synthesia’s investment in Sessions points to a simulation trend at work, with AI playing a greater role in how employees learn.

Also: Give AI ‘stuff nobody wants to do’ – and 4 other ways to use agents more effectively at work

It’s worth taking the intentions of Highwire’s survey with a grain of salt. Much the opposite of Synthesia’s mission, Highwire’s business relies on companies needing human-led professional training that invests in their employees’ people skills. That doesn’t necessarily include teaching managers how to farm out responsibilities to AI, and it doesn’t see rehearsing with AI as a valid alternative to employee-manager prep.

“Highwire conditions the human skills that can’t be automated,” the company’s site reads.

Still, the takeaway isn’t far off from other, less-than-desirable AI work trends. Some employees might argue that unhelpful AI-generated performance reviews fall under the workslop umbrella.

Google is cutting off free users from the Flash and Pro models. AI Plus subscribers are losing out too

October 6, 2026, 2:00 pm ET

Those of you who use Google’s Gemini app or website for free will soon be able to use only one AI model for your queries and conversations. And it’s the weakest of the bunch.

In a new support document, Google revealed that free users will lose access to the Flash and Pro models starting Friday, Oct. 9. Anyone without a paid Google AI plan will be stuck with only the lowest-tier and least robust Flash-Lite model.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing any code

And there’s more bad news. People who subscribe to the cheapest Google AI paid plan, namely the $5-per-month AI Plus option, will lose access to the Pro model on the same date, leaving them with only the Flash and Flash-Lite variants.

The one bright spot here is reserved for users of the $20-per-month AI Pro plan. If you subscribe to this one, you’ll gain access to the Deep Think reasoning mode, which is currently reserved only for AI Ultra users who shell out $100 or $200 a month for the privilege.

In a nutshell, a free user who needs Flash would have to pay for an AI Plus subscription. An AI Plus user who needs the Pro model will have to jump to a Pro plan.

Why is all of this important, and how does it affect your use of Google AI in the real world? The answer depends not only on how frequently you use the Gemini app and website but for what purposes.

You can use Gemini via four, or actually five, different plans or methods, each with greater access and more features. First up, you’re able to use it for free without any type of paid subscription. Next, the AI Plus plan is a budget-friendly paid option. The AI Pro subscription is a beefier plan for people with more demanding requirements. And the two AI Ultra plans are the cream of the crop.

Each plan currently offers three models to choose from: 3.8 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, and 3.1 Pro.

Also: Is AI conscious? Why experts are worried

Flash is designed as a generalist, capable of handling most common AI tasks, such as providing information, summarizing files, generating and analyzing images, and chatting.

Flash-Lite is a faster but slightly less capable version, able to handle repetitive tasks but not adept at deeper knowledge and reasoning.

Pro is the most analytical of the three, solving more difficult and challenging problems, especially those focused on such areas as math, logic, and coding.

With the least expensive paid plans, Flash is typically the default and go-to model. When I use Gemini with my AI Pro account, Flash is the model that’s automatically chosen. For me, that’s perfectly fine for 90% of the tasks I run.

Free users typically see Flash-Lite as the default since their access to the other two models is limited. The Lite flavor should suffice for most general tasks but not for any type of deep reasoning or complex problem solving, potentially putting many free users in a bind.

To make things just a bit more complicated, Google says each model will now allow you to choose an error level among low, medium, and high. The higher the level, the greater the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough responses to your questions. However, higher levels will also chew up more of your limits.

Speaking of limits, Google does restrict how — and how much — you can use Gemini. But instead of doling out access based on a specific number of requests or conversations, the company uses a compute-based limit that will now refresh every five hours until you reach your weekly quota. This means that your limits are based on the complexity of your prompt, the features you use, and the length of your chat.

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

Paid users naturally have higher limits than those without a subscription. Plus, premium models and tasks eat into your limits more and may cause you to hit your quota faster. Asking Gemini to generate an image or video, use Deep Research or Deep Think, and tap into the Pro model will use up your limits more quickly than everyday chats and requests.

If you’re confused and frustrated by all these changes and conditions, you’re not alone. The more we demand of AI, the more that companies like Google curb or control our access, thus adding more complexity to the whole process.

The main bright spot here is that Google AI subscriptions are doled out on a monthly basis. So you can stick with free access or one of the paid plans and switch month-by-month if you find yourself too limited by your current level.

Microsoft is ending support and updates for Office 2021 on October 13. What does that mean, and what are your alternatives?

October 6, 2026, 12:40 pm ET

Microsoft continues to offer one-time purchase versions of Office for people who don’t want to pay a regular monthly or annual fee for Microsoft 365. But even these non-subscription versions can wear out their welcome, and that’s happening with Office 2021.

In a new support document, Microsoft revealed that it’s ending support for Office 2021 as of Tuesday, October 13. This means that the company will no longer provide technical support, software updates, bug fixes, or security patches, leaving the software unprotected against vulnerabilities that may pop up.

Further, Microsoft will stop updating the online help and support pages for the product. If you have a question or problem, you won’t find the solution online, at least not from Microsoft. You’ll still be able to use the software for as long as you want, just without the usual support and updates.

Also: How you can get Microsoft 365 (formerly Office) for free – 3 easy ways

Microsoft typically ends support for certain desktop products at some point. Windows is the most obvious example. But here, the deadline is a hefty ten years. On Oct. 15, 2025, support ended for Windows 10 after its debut back in 2015. Microsoft has thrown a lifesaver to people still on this version with its Extended Security Updates (ESU) program, guaranteeing security updates at least until Oct. 12, 2027.

Released in 2021, Windows 11 still has a long support life ahead of it. But each new annual iteration of Windows 11 Home and Pro gets cut off after two years. Currently, Windows 11 23H2 is no longer supported. Version 24H2 Home and Pro edition will hit end of support on October 13 of this year. Support for version 25H2 will stop on Oct. 12, 2027. But with the new 26H2 edition, you’ll be supported until Oct. 10, 2028.

Also: Microsoft Office 2024 now available without a subscription for PC and Mac

The one-time purchase edition of Office used to enjoy a much longer support period, lasting for 10 years. Support ended for Office 2010 in 2020 and for Office 2013 in 2023. Since then, however, Microsoft has gotten stingier. Support for Office 2019 ran out after six years in 2025. And now support for Office 2021 is ending after only five years.

The likely reason? Microsoft wants to push more people to its subscription-based Microsoft 365 product. To do that, the company has to make it more difficult for them to use the one-time license version.

Now, what do you do if you are still using Office 2021? As I see it, you have five options.

https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/mistral.title: Mistral’s new Le Chonk model brings AI cybersecurity to your business – and you control it
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/mistral.author: Radhika Rajkumar
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/mistral.text:
Innovation
>
Artificial Intelligence

Open models are vying to become the everyman defense solution for a growing swarm of agent breaches.

October 6, 2026, 9:00 am ET

French AI lab Mistral has shipped its latest model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4) — and it’s positioned as the open solution for all your defense requirements.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot, and the stakes are existential

One outcome of recent AI security incidents is that open and proprietary models are being pitted against each other. Initially framed as less safe because of their malleability, open models are viewed as a new option for cyber defense after proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI proved just as risky.

Mistral said ML4, which the company has nicknamed “Le Chonk” for its trillion-parameter size, is built for security that stays under user control — unlike proprietary models, which frontier labs can technically rescind access to at any time.

“The cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample said.

After a hack-filled summer that put AI model security under the spotlight, everyone is looking for a reliable AI security solution that suits their needs. ML4 prioritizes cyber defense capabilities, advertising customizable control and data sovereignty.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware – how to spot the trap

In a briefing, Lample and Mistral’s VP of Science Pierre Stock emphasized that security is a key requirement for the company’s enterprise clients, echoing an ongoing industry trend. Following the Hugging Face breach, Mistral was one of many companies that signed Nvidia’s Open Secure AI Alliance, a cross-industry partnership that argued open models are crucial to democratizing defenses against increasingly common AI security incidents.

“ML4 is the beginning of a leading generation of open-weight, customizable, cybersecurity models that enterprises can fully own and control, without vendor lock-in,” Mistral wrote. “Enterprises and states should not have to rely on a closed model vendor that could arbitrarily turn off their cyber defense capabilities.”

By Nvidia’s logic, and its Alliance that aims to democratize AI security tools, the race is between Mistral and other open models to achieve state-of-the-art security prowess.

“In absolute terms on cyber capabilities, ML4 outperforms the best models from Kimi, Deepseek and Meta,” a Mistral spokesperson told ZDNET via email.

Also: Who owns AI risk at work? Business and tech leaders can’t agree, PwC survey finds

Le Chonk is available now in public preview. Mistral said it will release the model weights on Oct. 27. That time gap gives the lab a month “to work with developers, cybersecurity leaders and state authorities to further assess ML4’s capabilities and behavior in real-world environments” — a practice that’s becoming commonplace for proprietary American labs like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic as concerns about model capabilities mount.

Similarly to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s rollout of Astra, initial testing partners will get access to a less guardrailed version of ML4 with “expanded cybersecurity capabilities.”

Outside security, Mistral said Le Chonk excels in finance and multimodal use cases. The company said it is still waiting on final benchmarks. However, early third-party analysis shows ML4 competing on par with pricier proprietary models like GPT-6 Astra in certain computer vision tasks (like in the benchmarks below), as well as impressive open-weight Chinese models like Kimi K3. Le Chonk met or slightly outperformed DeepSeek models on financial work tasks, and hit a new high of 15% for open-weight models on Harvey’s Legal Agent benchmark.

As a reminder, benchmark scores themselves should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering how many models cheat.

Also: The AI models that cheat the most, according to new CAIS benchmark

Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Moonshot (which develops Kimi models) have been accused of distilling, or ripping off, proprietary models from American labs to gain their competitive edge. Mistral reiterated it’s not participating in that process.

“We are fully separate from other models, and we don’t take inspiration from them,” Stock said in the briefing.

The company also leaned on its commitment to sovereignty, an equally hot topic, especially in Europe.

“Customers will soon have flexible deployment options: self-deploy or access it via our API in the region of their choice, including our European sovereign region where data stays under EU jurisdiction,” Mistral wrote.

Training a competitive model in a compute shortage is no small task for a trimmer lab like Mistral, which doesn’t have the same resources as a pre-IPO giant like Anthropic.

“ML4 was trained from scratch on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months, deployed in Mistral’s own data centers in Europe,” the company said, adding that the preview will also run on those same GPUs. For context, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said on X that OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on roughly 100,000 GPUs. That’s quite the fraction.

“We expect the model to improve significantly over the next few months. This model will also serve as the base for a new wave of specialized and optimized models from Mistral,” the company added.

Claude helped me vibe-code a Mac app and pass Apple’s review in less than two weeks. Come with me on my journey from idea to purchasable App Store product.

Senior Contributing Editor

Senior Contributing Editor

October 5, 2026, 8:03 am ET

At around noon on Sunday, Sept. 20, I came up with an idea for a Mac app. One week later, on Sunday, Sept. 27, also around noon, I submitted my completed app to Apple. Four days later, Apple accepted the tool, and it went live on the App Store.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps … and I think I love it

This is the story of an unrelated assignment by a ZDNET editor, a happy accident, and vibe coding at its best. It began 30 years ago, with a giant library of icons.

When I started my first software company, one of the first products I introduced was Icon Factory for HyperCard. It won several awards. This product supported my company and our employees for years. Those icons were all black and white, as was HyperCard.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

In 1997, after years of customer requests for colorful Finder desktop icons, we created a three-volume set of 32×32 pixel color icons called Icon Gallery. This was a boxed product of more than 2,000 icons. Icon Gallery sold through retail, mail order distribution, and direct mail.

Icon Gallery was one of the last boxed software products I produced. I’ll be honest with you. I can’t recall when or why I stopped selling Icon Gallery, but it probably tracked with when I stopped physically manufacturing boxed products. That decision, of course, tracked with the rise of the web.

Now, let’s fast forward to a few months ago. While decluttering some cubbies in my office, I found the packaging for a couple of my old software products, including Icon Gallery. I stuck the box on a shelf. Once again, I pretty much forgot about it.

Then, last month, in honor of this year’s big iPhone event, my editor asked me to write a series of historical Apple stories. While writing ‘AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps … and I think I love it,’ I dug through my server for a screenshot or box illustration of an AI product I produced for the Mac in the late 1980s.

Also: Is AI conscious? Why experts are worried

I found that image, and I also found an old Macromedia Director file containing all 2,338 icons from 30 years ago. In the mid-90s, I had converted Icon Gallery’s icons to Director format and sold the resulting product to animators as an asset library. Director was big in the CD-ROM days, and has since faded into Mac history along with HyperCard and other vintage apps.

But there it was, sitting on my Mac Studio’s desktop: a 30-year-old file containing all those assets, in a long-dead file format. I felt like an archeologist cracking open an ancient mummy’s tomb.

So, I gave that ancient file to Claude. My prompt was simple: “This file is an old Macromedia Director file containing a large library of icons. Can you separate the icons into their own folder?”

Claude didn’t put up a fuss. The AI didn’t complain that the Director files were so wildly out of date that it couldn’t do anything. All it asked was what format I wanted the files in, and whether I wanted the white edge pixels to be transparent.

Also: I built an iOS app in just two days with just my voice – and it was electrifying

According to the log, this process took four minutes and 30 steps. In less time than it takes to brew a cup of coffee, I had 2,000-plus PNG images, organized into topic folders. I didn’t really have any plans for the icons. I was mostly surprised at how easily Claude extracted bit data and converted it into PNG files.

That was on Sept. 2. I then let the extracted collection of vintage files sit in a folder on my Desktop.

Eighteen days later, on a Sunday afternoon, I needed a graphic for something I was working on. I thought about my old icons from Icon Gallery and thought, “Hey, it would be cool if I had an app to browse and resize these icons.”

And, in that moment, Icon Gallery ‘97 was born. Why not, right? I have AIs.

I worked in both Claude Desktop (to talk strategy) and Claude Code (to build the Mac app). Within a few hours, I had a working Mac app that could browse the original library and create perfectly scaled, hard-edge bitmap icons from 32×32 pixels up to 1,024×1,024 pixels.

I officially had a proof of concept.

But how would I productize it? Claude recommended two viable courses of action. The AI recommended naming the product Icon Gallery ‘97: 30th Anniversary Edition, celebrating the hand-created retro icons. This vintage feel could be appealing in a world of AI-generated art.

Also: I used Claude Code to vibe code an Apple Watch app in just 12 hours

Claude also recommended adding a recoloring feature, so designers could not only choose the old icons, but recolor them to match brand or identity colors. The AI also recommended creating collections and favorites.

Then a friend recommended I build in an ‘Export to Slack’ feature, because the retro icons would be very cool as Slack emojis. My wife saw the same potential for dragging the icons into texts. I made sure those features were in the app.

Once you have favorites and collections, what happens if you want to use the app on another Mac? Ah, so now iCloud syncing needed to be added. And so it was.

Lest anyone imply that vibe coding involves issuing one “Make me an app,” command, let me dissuade you of that notion. I gave Claude Code 502 individual directives in the four days that I actively interacted with it.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex – here’s why

These were not full-time coding days. I visited the doctor for my yearly physical, spent Friday with a contractor working on the house, and had to turn in three major feature article thought pieces for ZDNET.

But around that work, I talked to Claude and guided its development process. Then I went back to my other priorities.

Back when we first started using AI coding agents, I developed an internal headcanon that helps me think about how to manage the bots. I view them as working partners at the end of a chat transcript. I use this approach to work with many of my human partners, so it works well.

As such, sometimes I fire off a question to Claude Code. In one case, shortly after we built in the in-app purchasing mechanism and proved it worked, I realized that someone could buy the app, do a full icon export, and then request a refund. I asked Claude, “Do we care?”

Claude suggested not fighting refunds. That decision matched with my long-term software publishing style. If someone doesn’t want my code, don’t make them pay for it. But that question fired off a more interesting discovery. Claude realized that all 2,146 icons sat inside the app as loose PNG files. Anyone who downloaded the free version could right-click it, choose Show Package Contents, and copy the entire collection without buying anything.

We added encryption and packaged the app with a single scrambled file. As images are requested, they’re unscrambled dynamically.

Before we submitted the tool to the App Store, we tested it. We deliberately corrupted copies to prove the check would catch them. Then we ran the app’s own decryption engine over every icon. The decrypted output matched the original files, so we shipped it that way.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

At another point, I realized the window scrolled incredibly slowly. I had to persuade Claude to run some tests. As it turned out, the code compressed full-sized images for each preview, and another block of code rebuilt the entire window 482 times during each resize request.

Persuading Claude became a common theme (very much like working with a human partner). I wanted a selection rectangle that could be dragged across icons. Claude thought this approach was unnecessary. Then I explained that Macs have been able to drag-select since before 1997. Eventually, Claude got that one working.

I’ve said this before, but this is how I spent a lot of my career managing programmers. I’d work with them briefly throughout the day, among all the other activities I managed for the company.

Vibe coding with Claude didn’t seem much different. The AI even pushed back on some instructions, copped a ‘tude here and there, and complained about some of the assignments. It could totally have been another human at the other end of the chat. In some ways, Claude seemed more human than some people I’ve worked with.

Also: ‘I can’t stop’: 80% of developers find AI coding more addictive than helpful

Claude also got very fussy about the collection’s provenance. I found it interesting how careful the AI was about making sure the app would get through App Store review. Its concern was who owned the icons. I had to convince it that my company created the icons in the 1990s and that my current business was the legal descendant of the original enterprise. All the assets were mine.

Even so, Claude pointed out some icons Apple was likely to block, including a Caterpillar logo and a person’s head that looked for all the world like Charlie Brown. We also had a bunch of gunshot icons, a popular theme in 1997 but completely tone deaf in 2026. I removed those icons as well.

One really cool advantage of using AI coding is how quickly you can test out ideas. Git can branch code. This capability isn’t AI-related at all, but it means you can revert to a previous codebase or integrate changes. I mixed using Git branches with AI experiments. At one point I asked Claude to try a completely different visual design. Claude built it within an hour, and within 30 seconds I decided it was horrid. We were able to revert instantly.

I am not a complete App Store neophyte, but I might as well be. The last apps I built for the App Store were in 2008. The last payment I got from Apple for those apps was in 2012. The world, and the App Store, have both changed a lot since then.

In preparing my submission to the App Store, I used Claude to walk me through each screen and submission option. I took screenshots of every new screen and sent them to Claude before hitting the confirm or next button. This approach worked quite well.

I also used Claude for advice on setting up the App Store account. The biggest advice I got was that new App Store businesses (those under $1 million in sales) can apply as a small business and commissions will drop from 30% to 15%. That’s a big win.

Also: How to install and configure Claude Code, step by step

Before submitting the app to the App Store, I instructed Claude to launch a series of adversarial agents to examine the app end to end. Although I’d done a lot of testing, the agents did find a few things that needed to be fixed before submission.

Probably my biggest surprise was the graphics that accompany an App Store submission. Apple allows up to ten 2880×1800 graphics that are displayed with the app in your listing. Creating these graphics took me three days around my other work. In other words, creating the graphics took almost as long as creating the app.

That’s because Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT were terrible, horrible, unfortunate, ineffective, and overall completely incompetent at creating App Store promo images. While I’ve had lots of great success with AI image generation, there’s something about getting the message right in an App Store promo image that made the AIs fail. So, I did the work by hand in Photoshop, like a caveman. You can see some of those graphics above, sprinkled throughout this article.

Oh, and here’s a tip. Once you set up TestFlight, which is the tool for sharing your app across users and machines, limit your uploads. On Wednesday, I uploaded 21 builds between 6:49 am and 9:20 pm, while fine-tuning the final look and feel of the submission. Apple refused to accept the twenty-second submission and made me wait a full day to try again.

That pause pushed the whole project back a day.

Here are a few more thoughts:

Signing up as an Apple Developer costs $99/year. Without that, you can’t upload your software to the App Store or use TestFlight.

Look, I don’t know how well the app will do financially, and frankly I don’t care all that much. I’m certainly not expecting it to fund my retirement. But it was a ton of fun and let me productize something I wanted to use for myself. It was also gratifying to give new life to all that creative retro art from the past. The process gave me a safe and controlled way to learn how to code in-app purchases for my other app projects, and it was a great test case for whether you can get AI to help create an app (in the space of a week) that can be submitted and approved by the App Store and Apple (in just another four days).

Oh, and I did not write one line of actual code. Not. One. Line.

Some iPhone 18 Pro Max phones on AT&T are stuck in SOS mode. Two updates can prevent it, but affected phones need replacing.

October 2, 2026, 9:43 pm ET

If your iPhone 18 Pro Max has lost service on AT&T and is unable to make calls, send texts, or even use mobile data, two new software updates won’t be enough to get it working again. But Apple will replace the phone for free.

A couple of weeks ago, iPhone 18 Pro Max owners on AT&T began reporting they had lost cellular service. AT&T initially directed customers to install iOS 27.0.1 “immediately,” warning the problem could prevent calls to 911.

Also: iOS 27.0.1: Apple fixes annoying iPhone 18 Pro restart issues

Apple has now confirmed to ZDNET that an issue affecting “a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users” on AT&T’s network may cause their devices to lose service. “We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today,” Apple said. “These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”

Since the updates are intended to prevent the issue, they won’t fix devices already affected. Those will require a replacement, according to Apple.

iPhone 18 Pro Max owners on Reddit have reported randomly losing their connection to AT&T, with phones switching to SOS mode. While Wi-Fi still works, they can’t make calls, send texts, or use data over the network.

Also: 7 iOS 27 features that make old iPhones exciting again

AT&T has subsequently sent a text to customers to warn them about an “important Apple Software update” that’s available for affected phones. “Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911,” the mobile carrier said. “Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update.”

Apple has not provided an exact number of affected devices, though it has only observed the issue among iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T.

Apple and AT&T have not publicly explained the cause, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s cellular hardware could be a factor. Our sibling site, CNET, noted a recent iFixit teardown shows the US version of the phone uses Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem.

Also: Your iPhone just got a hidden anti-scam upgrade in iOS 27

However, CNET also cited a TechInsights teardown that shows the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max use the same modem, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max seems to add a new millimeter-wave antenna. Neither Apple nor AT&T has linked that antenna to the service failures.

For now, the cause remains unconfirmed.

According to Apple, two new updates for iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T are intended to help prevent the cellular connection problem, but they won’t restore service to phones already affected.

If you have an iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T, Apple strongly recommends installing iOS 27.0.1. To check for the update, go to Settings > General > Software Update. AT&T is also urging customers to install the update.

Next, install a new carrier settings update on your iPhone 18 Pro Max. It will automatically download for AT&T users over the next 14 days, according to Apple. To manually trigger it, go to Settings > General > About.

If your iPhone 18 Pro Max is already without cellular service because of the AT&T network issue, it can’t be reactivated through software updates and requires a hardware replacement instead, Apple said. The company confirmed to ZDNET that replacements will be provided free of charge.

Also: 5 iOS 27 upgrades that make a big difference – and why I love them

So, affected owners can:

When contacting support, explain you have an iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T that has lost service, and mention whether you installed iOS 27.0.1 and the carrier settings update. From there, request your free replacement.

AT&T previously told ZDNET that customers who continue to experience problems should seek additional support from Apple or an AT&T store. “Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right,” AT&T said.

This authentic-looking scam starts with a sponsored Google link - and it's catching people off-guard.

October 2, 2026, 2:18 pm ET

A new scam involving ChatGPT has emerged, and it might lead you to install malware on your computer if you’re not careful.

Over the past several days, reports have surfaced of users encountering a strange interaction when using ChatGPT. “Service Availability Notice,” the message reads. “We’re currently experiencing limited availability on the primary domain. Please choose one of the following options to continue:”

Also: This new cyberattack tricks you into hacking yourself. Here’s how to spot it

The chat presents an offer to upgrade to a Plus subscription or a link to a backup domain. Here’s how the scam works, why it’s so convincing, and what you can do to avoid it.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis’ copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

The scam starts when you search “ChatGPT” in Google. Like almost every Google search, you’ll see sponsored results, or paid ads, above the authentic search results. If you click on what appears to be a real link to ChatGPT, you’re taken to what appears to be the actual site.

Instead, you’ve landed on a custom GPT, or a user-generated, specialized version of ChatGPT that’s tailored for specific tasks. In this instance, the task is to spit out the availability notice response no matter what’s entered.

What’s most convincing is that you’re on the actual ChatGPT domain and your account is logged in (if you were before). There’s nothing at first to indicate this isn’t authentic other than the name “Plus 5.6.” If you’re not familiar with ChatGPT model naming conventions, though, this wouldn’t stick out.

Also: I’m a tech pro, and an AI job scam almost fooled me

If you click the link in the response (it’s a free site hosted on Google Sites and obviously not a ChatGPT domain), you’re presented with a fake Cloudflare verification and instructions to paste and run a command in Windows/PowerShell. Running that command installs malware on your computer.

I tried the process myself and clicked on the first result after a simple search for ChatGPT. I landed on one of the scams. No matter what I typed, I got the same “limited” response with a link. My editor here at ZDNET tried the same process and got the normal ChatGPT, so it doesn’t appear to be all sponsored results.

Google told me it had deactivated several accounts associated with the specific ad campaign I saw, but that, of course, doesn’t mean this issue won’t pop up again, so it’s good to be aware.

Here’s how you can avoid this specific scam, and some general advice for staying safe online.

Roman Oliinyk, CEO and founder of PayCore Media Inc, a network security specialist who has spent 10 years building data-leak protection systems for large US companies, noted that a real Cloudflare check would never ask you to do anything on your keyboard. “At most,” he said, “it asks you to check a box or press a button.”

Also: This simple ChatGPT trick helps you spot scams before you click or respond

Oliinyk also recommended treating sponsored results as ads (which they are) and treating a link from a chatbot as you would a link from a stranger.

I’ve reached out to both Google and OpenAI for comment. OpenAI hasn’t responded yet, but a Google spokesperson told me: “Malvertising has no place on Google. We’ve suspended several advertiser accounts to block this campaign and we continuously update our defenses to stop new threats.”

Some Pixel users are having tap-to-pay problems, and there's no fix from Google yet. But here a few things that helped others.

October 2, 2026, 11:16 am ET

If you’ve had trouble using tap-to-pay with your Pixel phone over the last few weeks, you’re not alone.

Since the middle of last month, users on Reddit and other support forums have been reporting problems using tap-to-pay. In some cases, the feature fails intermittently; in others, it’s entirely non-functional. The problem is, you don’t know it’s not working until you’re in a situation in which you need it right then.

Also: Google Wallet got a lot of new tricks in 2026 – these 5 are my favorites

Google Wallet’s usefulness has exploded in recent years, and it now holds everything from your driver’s license to transit passes to insurance cards and more. It’s incredibly convenient until times like this, when the feature not working can cause big problems for your day if you rely on it.

Here’s what’s happening and what you can do about it.

The issue appears to be that some Pixel phones aren’t acknowledging there’s an NFC terminal nearby when users open Google Wallet, so the device doesn’t transmit the necessary information to complete the transaction. The Pixel 11 does have a repositioned NFC antenna (toward the top of the phone rather than in the middle, as in the past several generations), but the bug is affecting a number of devices, including just about every phone from the Pixel 9 series onward. I saw it on my own Pixel 10 Pro.

Also: Use Google Wallet? Turn on these 4 security settings to guard your cards and IDs

It’s not clear if the issue is with Google Wallet or the device.

I’ve reached out to Google, but the company hasn’t acknowledged the bug yet, so there’s no official fix. Based on user reports, though, there are a few things you can try to get tap-to-pay working again.

https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/pwc-dig.author: Charlie Osborne
https://www.zdnet.com/innovation/pwc-dig.text:
Innovation

Artificial Intelligence

PwC research highlights a growing need for someone to own AI. Is an AI chief the answer?

October 1, 2026, 5:00 am ET

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption continues to surge, with agentic AI and large language models (LLMs) now integrated into everything from enterprise applications to chatbots that help you with food delivery.

Also: LLMjacking can run up your business’ AI bill fast – how to stop it

The benefits of AI are clear: it can streamline business operations, reduce manual workloads, serve as a research and analysis assistant, and give employees tools that make day-to-day work less strenuous and time-consuming.

But we’re now experiencing the trade-offs. Rogue AI models, friendly AI hacking innocent companies, potentially thousands of AI-related security incidents being investigated, and AI agents acting as new entry points into corporate networks.

Who should be responsible and take ownership of AI when things go wrong? According to new research from PwC, businesses can’t agree.

On Friday, PwC released its Digital Trust Insights 2027 report, which surveyed approximately 4,000 business and tech leaders across 71 countries.

According to the survey, no single role has a clear responsibility for managing agentic AI or its security, although awareness of both the benefits and disadvantages of AI has reached the board level in around half of businesses.

Also: 1 in 4 organizations can’t detect rogue AI agents in their business – survey

In total, 47% of those surveyed said cybersecurity is a standing agenda item for boards, which is far from enough. However, the foundations are there: nine out of 10 business leaders said practices like board oversight, executive accountability, and enterprise risk integration are now in place.

On AI, about a third of organizations (33%) have recognized the need for accountability and hired for dedicated AI roles, including AI chief officers and AI board members.

PwC’s research reveals a problem in the enterprise sector: whether these AI roles also include overall accountability or responsibility for AI-related security and governance.

Overall, 29% of CEOs and security and risk leaders said accountability sits with the CIO, CTO, or a similar technology role. 17% of respondents said the responsibility lies with the CISO or cybersecurity teams, while 26% said it should stay with “a dedicated AI leader or AI function.”

In addition, 11% of respondents said accountability is unclear, with responsibility shared across multiple roles or functions.

The research shows that while the enterprise understands someone needs to take responsibility for agentic AI and the security issues around its deployment, monitoring, and security, the chain of responsibility hasn’t yet been defined.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

It was only back in 1994 that the first formal CISO, Steve Katz, was hired by Citigroup to handle the aftermath of Russian cyberattacks. Now, the idea of a medium-to-large business without one is almost inconceivable.

CIOs and CISOs generally have enough to handle, so adding new AI-related security management and control could be too much of a burden. If so, we may be on the verge of a new hiring drive for AI-expert CISO counterparts: the CAISO, a chief AI security officer.

While the enterprise at large experiments with defining AI accountability and dividing responsibilities across different roles, technology can now assist businesses in maintaining control of their AI agents.

Jim Taylor, Chief Product and Strategy Officer at RSA, told ZDNET that the same identity controls that have secured human users for decades need to be used to manage agentic AI.

It’s easy to forget that each AI model, or agentic AI deployment, has an identity. They are linked to a set of credentials; they have varying levels of access to resources and information, and can perform tasks or act on behalf of a human employee.

Just as we have passwords, zero-trust principles, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and other access controls that verify our identities, Taylor suggests each agentic AI build should have the “same identity controls that have been securing human users for decades.”

That’s not to say this removes the need for a leadership-level human overseer, but by boosting security through agentic AI governance controls, organizations can better prepare for the ongoing risks associated with AI.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance – how businesses could make it work

For example, a centralized platform could register AI agents sanctioned to operate in corporate networks, and each agent could be tied to a human owner who must personally authorize high-risk actions. Taylor also suggests that organizations deploying AI should ensure governance controls mapped to industry frameworks are applied, and that AI agents be evaluated frequently and decommissioned when they are no longer needed.

“Companies will keep investing in AI, but they’ve brought on workers they don’t see and can’t control,” Taylor commented. “Those agents won’t be held in compliance violations — but the organization will. If they do deploy agents, then they’ll need the means to keep them secure.”

https://www.zdnet.com/tech/opensuse-leap.author: Jack Wallen

Tech
>

>
Operating Systems
>
Linux

One of the more secure Linux distributions has added another feature to help further lock it down.

September 30, 2026, 1:58 pm ET

I’ve been a fan of SUSE and openSUSE for a long time. I actually remember SUSE Linux before it was SUSE Enterprise Linux or SUSE Enterprise Linux Desktop. Even back then, the distribution was a power user’s dream come true.

One reason for this was its security.

openSUSE has been, for a very long time, one of the more secure of the “mainstream” Linux distributions. And in German-speaking countries, openSUSE is quite popular due to its ties to the German company SUSE.

Also: This Linux distro makes openSUSE accessible to all – even newbies should take a look

Starting with version 16.1, openSUSE Leap (the stable version of the distro) is adding another layer to its security that should further elevate it as one of the more secure distributions on the market. That layer is immutable mode.

According to the official openSUSE blog, “Leap 16.1 is the first Leap release to offer an Immutable Mode, a transactionally updated system with a read-only root filesystem. This is essentially what our users know from Leap Micro, just integrated directly into Leap.”

For those who don’t know, Leap Micro is a specialized, lightweight, immutable, and fixed-release operating system designed for containerized workloads, edge computing, and virtualized environments. Leap Micro is not a desktop OS, but Leap is. And with Leap benefiting from what Micro already has, this could be a huge step forward.

First off, the same blog mentions that Leap Immutable “is the way forward for container and virtual machine hosts, edge devices and anyone who prefers atomic updates with easy rollback.” It’s the last bit that should raise eyebrows, as the developers intend Leap Immutable not only for specialized deployments but for anyone who prefers atomic updates on the desktop.

Also: What is openSUSE and who is it for?

But atomic updates and immutability aren’t exactly the same thing. Does that mean Leap Immutable will be a sort of “immutable light”?

The answer is a resounding “no.” After a bit of digging, it became clear that Leap Immutable will be a fully immutable distribution.

Also: Fedora Kinoite vs. Silverblue: My verdict after testing both immutable Linux distros

First off, immutable mode is a feature you can toggle during the installation, which means you can choose which version of openSUSE Leap to use: standard or immutable.

If you go with immutable, what that means is the root file system is mounted as read-only. I’ve previously discussed immutability in “Immutable Linux delivers serious security — here are your 5 best options.” Give that a read to find out more.

Essentially, when an OS is immutable, those directories (such as /usr and /etc) are mounted as read-only and cannot be altered. If you were to accidentally run a malicious script on an immutable system, it would be unable to alter anything in those immutable directories. That’s a serious security improvement and is also the future of Linux.

Also: 5 reasons to switch to an immutable Linux distro today — and which to try first

But openSUSE Leap doesn’t just benefit from the added security of immutability, as it already includes plenty of security-focused features.

openSUSE was already a highly secure Linux distribution, thanks to several layers of security. Those layers are as follows.

Up until version 15.6, openSUSE used AppArmor as its mandatory access control (MAC) security feature to restrict what system resources, files, and directories programs could access.

Also: I’ve spent years with immutable Linux – RakuOS fixed my biggest annoyance

Starting with version 16.0, openSUSE made the switch to SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux), which was created by the NSA (in collaboration with open-source organizations such as Red Hat) to further secure Linux systems. SELinux is an incredibly powerful tool that labels every file, process, and port on a system, follows the rule of least privilege to block actions that are not allowed by specific rules, and even requires the root user to follow those rules.

openSUSE makes use of firewalld as its dynamic firewall management system, which includes zones (predefined trust levels), runtime vs. permanent changes (changes that are applied but are removed upon reboot vs. changes that are permanent), and management tools (both the command-line tool, firewall-cmd, and the GUI app, firewall-config).

Also: 5 Linux distros I recommend to help businesses cut costs and boost security

openSUSE’s implementation of firewalld is similar to that of most Fedora-based distributions, so it’s well known for being one of the stronger firewall implementations.

openSUSE also includes binary hardening, which is the collection of default security flags and compiler options that are used during software compilation to make executable files and libraries more resilient to exploits such as buffer overflows and memory corruption.

The key hardening measures include:

Permission profiles are predefined templates, specifically created to enhance security, that target file permissions, ownership, and special execution bits. The purpose of these profiles is to centralize control of permissions, enforce security during package installation and updates, and govern file modes, owners, groups, capabilities, and access control lists (ACLs) for particularly sensitive directories.

Btrfs snapshots are “moment-in-time” save points of a file system subvolume, and Snapper is the SUSE tool used to automatically manage those snapshots.

Also: One of the most user-friendly Linux distros I’ve ever used is also one of the most secure

With snapshots, it is possible to easily roll back a system to a working point, so if something were to go wrong with a system, it could be restored from a previously working snapshot. With Snapper, it’s possible to configure when snapshots are taken and how many snapshots are retained.

If your system is hacked, you could effectively roll it back to a point in time prior to the hack and then take action to prevent the hack from happening again.

Regular source refers to the repositories used by openSUSE, which are the standard Source RPM Repository and the main OSS (open-source software) repository. On top of that, openSUSE is built directly from the source code from SUSE Enterprise Linux, which ensures enterprise-grade stability and security.

When you combine immutability with the standard openSUSE security features, it’s pretty easy to conclude that the distribution will be highly secure. Immutable distributions are already touted as some of the most secure operating systems on the market, and with openSUSE adding an immutable mode to Leap, you can be sure that it will leap ahead of the pack with regard to security.

Also: Atomic vs. immutable Linux: Why choose one when these nine distros offer both?

You can download an ISO of Leap 16.1, which includes immutable mode, from the official openSUSE download server.

New with iOS 27 (and iPadOS 27) is a setting called Impersonation Risk Detection that aims to warn you of suspicious activity that could trap you in a scam.

September 30, 2026, 12:47 pm ET

Social engineering scams often succeed because they evade traditional security protections to trick you into doing something that puts you at risk. Now, Apple has created a new defense designed to protect iPhone and iPad users from these types of scams: Impersonation Risk Detection

Also: A stranger can learn a lot about you in 5 minutes online – how to check and delete it

Apple introduced the new security feature in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27. When enabled, this option will warn you before you take certain actions in a supported app that might lead you to an active scam. The goal is to help you when more traditional security measures like two-factor authentication can’t detect or protect you from a potential threat.

Let’s say you’re using an app on your iPhone or iPad that supports Impersonation Risk Detection. You’re about to perform a sensitive action, such as making a payment, changing your password, or sharing your account details. Impersonation Risk Detection steps in to analyze your Apple account and the information on your device to look for signs of a scam.

Based on the results, Apple will send one of the following three risk levels to the app:

The app then decides what to do next. If a high level of suspicious activity is found, the app could ask you to verify your identify, show a warning, or delay your action before it gets you into trouble. The app makes this determination, not Apple.

Also: I’ve used my iPhone 18 Pro for a week – these 5 features make the upgrade worth it

Apple will analyze certain information related to an interaction to generate the risk level, but it never receives the data itself. The company doesn’t analyze your content in such apps as Mail, Messages, and Photos. But Apple does learn the type of action you attempted when an app requests a risk assessment. Supported apps receive only the risk level and not the data used to create it.

Impersonation Risk Detection is turned off by default because a supported app requires a certain level of access to your actions and activities.

To enable the setting in iOS 27 or iPadOS 27, go to Settings and select Privacy & Security. Swipe toward the bottom of the screen and tap the setting for Impersonation Risk Detection. At the next screen, turn on the switch for “Share with App Developers.” After turning this setting on, you may have to wait 24 hours for it to take effect.

Also: Mobile phishing is a bigger threat than email now – how to stay protected

Any apps that participate in Impersonation Risk Detection will appear on the same screen, so you can always check them periodically for recent activity. You’ll see which apps asked for a risk assessment and which actions triggered the request. Here, you can also turn off access for individual apps.

Both built-in and third-party apps can support the feature, though Apple didn’t list any specific programs on its support page. However, with social engineering scams so pervasive, hopefully enough apps will jump on this bandwagon to better prevent people from becoming victims.

Pearson has agreed to acquire Workera to help businesses assess employees’ AI skills and target training where it’s needed most.

September 30, 2026, 8:25 am ET

Pearson, a global learning and assessment company, announced on Sept. 29 that it has agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the United States Space Force to verify what their employees can do and where they may need to improve.

Also: 73% of tech job listings require AI skills now: How to show off yours

The announcement comes less than a week after Workera’s 2026 State of Skills Intelligence Report was published on Sept. 23.

The report found that nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly, but almost 60% have no time to upskill, suggesting business leaders and working professionals need to find more common ground on how to upskill for an AI-enabled world.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Workera was already aiming to help organizations fill their AI skills gaps, and a partnership with Pearson opens new horizons for AI upskilling and education, especially in the workplace.

In an exclusive interview with ZDNET last week, Workera CEO and founder Kian Katanforoosh shared details about Workera’s latest program, Ambient, an AI-native skills assessment tool currently being piloted, with over 10,000 signups on the waitlist, which aims to measure skills in the flow of work.

“If you manage to merge work and learning, you’re effectively helping someone learn exponentially more than in the past. Today, with AI, we’re able to bring learning closer to work because AI understands unstructured data,” Katanforoosh told ZDNET.

Also: AI agents are your new colleagues – how to get the best results

Pearson’s move for Workera indicates its desire to strengthen its enterprise offerings with adaptive skills training and assessments to meet the increasing demand for workforce upskilling in the AI era.

In the release, Pearson said Workera’s technology and talent will accelerate its “ability to help enterprises build the workforce they need for AI-driven transformation, reflecting Pearson’s continued investment in enterprise skilling.”

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

Workera’s technology is designed to give business leaders a live baseline of their workforce’s capabilities, including AI fluency, targeted development, verified outcomes, and better talent decisions across the board, according to the press release.

Pearson hopes that its heritage in the education space can usher in a new era of AI skills training, with the help of Workera, founded in 2019.

“Combining Workera’s talented workforce and technology, with Pearson’s expertise in learning and assessment, strengthens our ability to help enterprises close skills gaps faster and build more agile and capable workforces,” Vishaal Gupta, president of enterprise learning and skills at Pearson, said in the release.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all

Upon completion of the acquisition, anticipated in H2 2026, Workera will become part of Pearson’s Enterprise Learning & Skills business unit, and Workera co-founder and CEO Kian Katanforoosh will join its leadership team.

“Together, we’ll bring Workera’s AI and Pearson’s deep expertise in learning and assessment to a shared ambition: building the gold standard for workforce readiness and helping people achieve more than they thought possible,” Katanforoosh said in the release.

Innovation

Google analysts warn that stolen AI credentials are being sold underground, and businesses are footing the bill.

September 29, 2026, 3:09 pm ET

Security experts warn that it’s not just artificial intelligence (AI) going rogue that we have to worry about — there’s also a booming underground economy for selling access to your AI models and computing power.

Speaking to the Financial Times, John Hultquist, chief analyst for Google Threat Intelligence Group, said that the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in what is known as LLMjacking over 2026, a trend that could cost businesses dearly.

If cryptojacking came to mind, you’re on the right track. While cryptojacking describes stealing computing power to illicitly mine cryptocurrency, LLMjacking is the AI equivalent: using AI power and resources that don’t belong to you.

Also: OpenAI’s Dots: Like OpenClaw declawed – for $200/mo ChatGPT Pro users

In the cybercriminal world, this means trying to secure credentials or API keys that give a criminal authorized access to business AI accounts, which often have high usage limits, or potentially none at all — with token overspill charged outside of typical subscription costs.

Cybercriminals can obtain username and password combinations or API keys by gaining access to a corporate network, stealing them via phishing, data breaches, vulnerabilities, or insider threats. This grants cybercriminals the opportunity to use an AI model without paying for the tokens themselves, for reasons such as:

Once stolen, credentials and API keys can also be sold on the underground to other cybercriminal groups.

As AI models offered by organizations, including OpenAI and Anthropic, continue to advance in sophistication, capacity, and skill, they require more computing power.

The more power you need, the more tokens you need to purchase — or the higher the level of subscription you must purchase.

For enterprise companies, inflated billing caused by unauthorized users can climb rapidly, with Sysdig’s Threat Research Team estimating costs of around $46,000 and even over $100,000 per day on top-tier models.

Combine the raw power of AI and exposed credentials that can be easily purchased online, and you can see why LLMjacking is exploding in popularity.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

According to Hultquist, the security team has spotted illicit access to AI models offered by companies including Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI for up to 97% off, and some traders even guarantee ongoing access should a compromised account be revoked or closed.

The financial damage isn’t limited to the victims of LLMjacking. As the analyst points out, by leveraging stolen AI power, cybercriminals now gain an “economic advantage” in conducting attacks by using AI resources paid for by others, while defenders are constrained by rising token costs.

AI accounts are a hot commodity, and it is up to owners to reduce the risk of compromise — especially with such high financial consequences at stake.

Phishing is, and probably always will be, one of the main causes of account theft or exploitation, so implementing valuable training and awareness programs beyond an annual tick-box exercise is one of the first ways businesses can protect themselves.

Also: Why phishing training doesn’t stop your employees from clicking scam links

Misconfigured instances, settings, and exposed data can all lead to LLMjacking, and so security teams should be given the time and capacity to run frequent audits — as well as regular patch cycles to fix unpatched vulnerabilities that could provide unauthorized network access.

Another critical way to defend your organization against LLMjacking is to adopt the principles of least privilege. Least privilege, or zero trust, is a framework in which employees have access only to the resources they need for their work, and only when they need them, which can reduce the risk of admin-level accounts being exploited for malicious purposes.

Finally, avoid hardcoded credentials and API keys, and businesses that believe there has been a security breach should rotate all credentials and keys without delay. If unusual AI usage, such as spikes in activity, is found, then consider temporarily revoking access and contact your provider.
