https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Number of known species of giant waterlilies almost doubles
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Michael Le Page
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Giant waterlilies are not exactly inconspicuous plants. But in the past few years, we have discovered no fewer than three new species, taking the total to five. The latest species to be described was identified with the help of social media, satellite photos and a mad jungle dash in the dark.

“I think it’s incredible that we find something so new, which is so large, in this world where we think everything is already known,” says Maarten Christenhusz at the Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, who has helped describe two of the new species.

Why rediscovering extinct species can actually be a bad thing

Giant waterlilies are famed for their massive leaves, which grow up to 3 metres wide. For many decades, just two species were known: Victoria amazonica and Victoria cruziana. Then in 2016, Carlos Magdalena at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew, London, noticed that giant waterlilies grown from seeds from Bolivia were a bit different, with even larger leaves. In 2022, Magdalena and his colleagues published a paper showing that this was a new species, Victoria boliviana.

Magdalena hasn’t stopped there. In 2021, Jeremiah Harris, who runs a carnivorous plant business in the US, posted pictures online that he took while swimming near the Inírida river in Colombia next to what he assumed was V. amazonica.

Magdalena was struck by the photos because scientists had thought there were no giant waterlilies in this region. “This river is geographically completely separated from the Amazon, and has been for millions of years, and that is why this is such an interesting find,” says Christenhusz.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their team examined satellite photos and found telltale green dots confirming there really were giant waterlilies growing there. They then organised an expedition to the region. The team found two plants but neither was flowering – and analysing the flowers is a crucial step in establishing whether a waterlily really is a new species.

At 11pm on the last night of the expedition, with the plane due to leave at 9am, the researchers seemed to have failed. Then one of the guides, Gustavo Melo from the Indigenous Tucano community, said he knew where some more giant waterlilies were growing. The team set off by boat in the dark, and found five plants in a small lake just before sunrise, including some that were flowering.

Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues have now published a paper describing the new species, which they have named Victoria colombiana. It differs from V. amazonica in the orientation of the spines beneath the leaves, and in the shape of its flowers and fruits. The spines are a defence against manatees and plant-eating fish, Christenhusz says, so they vary between species depending on which herbivores are most prevalent.

Botanists have finally proved what Charles Darwin was unable to nail down – that a genus of plants known to catch insects also digests them, suggesting the extent of plant carnivory has been underestimated

As far as the team is aware, V. colombiana is found in only one small area. A single event, such as a pollution spill, could wipe out the entire species, says Christenhusz. But the team is planning to try to collect seeds to help ensure the species survives.

Meanwhile, Magdalena also realised that the giant waterlilies growing in the Pantanal region of South America, hundreds of kilometres to the south-east of Colombia, must have been isolated from other populations for a very long time. Sure enough, genetic studies revealed that they are another distinct species, despite looking very similar to V. cruziana. Magdalena, Christenhusz and their colleagues will publish a paper soon to describe this fifth species, which they have decided to name Victoria mattogrossensis.

Phytotaxa

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: The big unanswered question about Russia’s ‘plague’ death
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Michael Le Page
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
The recent death of a lab worker at a plague research institute sparked fears of another pandemic. But on 7 October, Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it was ending precautionary measures and that most of the nearly 200 people put under quarantine have been released, after tests found no dangerous pathogens.

Was this all much ado about nothing? After all, we still don’t know what caused the pneumonia that killed the lab worker, nor, if it was plague, how she became infected. And the most pressing question of all: why did Russia respond so dramatically to her death? The measures taken went beyond what would be expected for a case of plague. There are two broad possibilities: conspiracy or colossal screw-up.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: AI or ‘super intelligence’? Trump isn’t the only one who is confused
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Jacob Aron
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
In the decades since the field began, most of the debate surrounding artificial intelligence has been about the intelligence part: can machines really think like we do? But in recent weeks, US President Donald Trump has kicked off an argument about the other part – and joined a long tradition of shifting the goal posts when it comes to AI.

“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing,” said Trump during a speech at the UN General Assembly on 22 September. He is calling for artificial intelligence to be rebranded as “super intelligence”, backing this move with an executive order signed on 29 September and the launch this week of a body called the Super Intelligence Force for coordinating US AI policy.

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

Putting aside the fact that “Super Intelligence Force” sounds like a Saturday morning cartoon, what are we to make of this attempted rebrand? Trump isn’t actually alone in seeking to distance modern AI systems from the original conception of AI in the 1940s and 50s. Last year, Meta CEO Mark Zuckberg published a note declaring that “superintelligence” (one word) is now in sight. Reaching further back, the word was originally popularised by philosopher Nick Bostrom as the title of his 2014 book.

For me, Trump’s super intelligence and Bostrom’s superintelligence have distinct meanings that are worth preserving. Trump’s rebrand is an effort to cement US dominance in the field of AI – his executive order states that “the term ‘Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies”. But superintelligence as envisioned by Bostrom goes far beyond the capabilities of our current AI systems. To understand why, we need to dig into history a bit more.

Long before the birth of ChatGPT, AI researchers distinguished between weak AI and strong AI, terms first defined by philosopher John Searle in a 1980 paper titled “Minds, brains, and programs”. Loosely speaking, he considered weak AI to be a computer simulation of a human mind, but not an actual mind itself, whereas he felt strong AI describes actual cognition emerging from software. Searle dismissed this latter idea as ridiculous: “No one supposes… that a computer simulation of a rainstorm will leave us all drenched. Why on earth would anyone suppose that a computer simulation of understanding actually understood anything?” Decades on, I find it hard to disagree.

In the wake of Searle’s influential paper, weak and strong AI underwent their own Trump-style rebranding, as people began to discuss differences in AI capabilities rather than AI consciousness – perhaps because the former is much easier to measure and moves the arena of debate from the philosophy department to the computer science lab. Weak AI merged with another term, narrow AI, to mean a system capable of human-level performance at a specific task. We have been living with narrow AI for decades, depending on how you want to define it, encompassing everything from spam filters to chess playing to driverless cars. In some sense, once something becomes achievable by narrow AI, it is just software – a phenomenon known as the AI effect.

Strong AI, meanwhile, gave way to general AI – a system capable of human-level performance at any task. A general AI is a highly desirable goal because it means that, rather than having to build a new system for every possible task, the AI would be able to transfer learning from one domain to another, just as a human can. In 2002, general AI morphed into “artificial general intelligence”, or AGI, largely due to Shane Legg (who would go on to co-found the firm DeepMind) popularising the term.

Most of the big AI companies, including DeepMind and OpenAI, were founded with the stated goal of achieving AGI. In the 2010s, this was seen as a slightly wacky and sci-fi research goal. Today, it is a business model, with trillions of dollars of investment riding on building an AGI in the near-future.

Despite this, definitions of AGI are woolly. OpenAI’s charter defines it as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. An agreement between OpenAI and Microsoft that was leaked in 2024 defines it as a system capable of generating $100 billion in profit. OpenAI isn’t yet profitable, with expenditure far exceeding revenue, but that didn’t prevent its president, Greg Brockman, from saying “welcome to the AGI era” with the release of its Astra model in September.

However you define AGI, it isn’t the same thing as superintelligence. Bostrom defines this plainly in his book as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest”. In other words, a superintelligence must be more cognitively capable than any human scientist, artist, philosopher or other cognitive performer that ever lived. It isn’t enough to be better than Albert Einstein or Marie Curie – you must also beat William Shakespeare, Leonardo da Vinci, Steve Jobs, Jane Austen and many, many others. Clearly, we haven’t achieved superintelligence. A real superintelligence would probably transform the world in ways we can’t imagine.

There is one problem running though all of these definitions, though, and it lies in the second part of AI: what actually is intelligence, and how do we measure different levels of it?

The standard answer is intelligence quotient, or IQ. Attempts to measure the IQ of various high-end AI models (by having them produce answers to IQ test questions) give ranges of 130 to 150 IQ, although this is complicated by the fact that the tests themselves may have formed part of the models’ training data. Human IQ scores have reached over 200, often in young children because the scores depend on age, but higher scores are increasingly difficult to measure reliably. More pressingly, IQ is now widely considered to be a flawed measure of intelligence, rooted in eugenics, that ignores many aspects of human capability. Attempting to apply it to AI feels fairly fruitless, then.

As an alternative, some computer scientists have tried to come up with AI-specific intelligence tests. One of these is ARC-AGI, which looks not only at the capabilities of a model, but also at the cost of running it, meaning that less computationally intensive models can score higher. The test is now in its third iteration, and one of OpenAI’s latest models, GPT-6.1 Sol, scores 96.2 per cent, completing the test at a reasonably cheap $3800. Does that make it AGI? I don’t think so, and I would expect a fourth version of the ARC-AGI test to come along soon, resetting the bar that models must exceed.

Does this mean we will never achieve AGI, and then superintelligence? Despite the certainty of the AI firms that we will – which is probably half real belief and half marketing – I think at this point, it is impossible to say. The meanings of these terms and our methods for evaluating them are constantly shifting. What seemed liked magic in 2022 – a computer that could answer you back – is now an annoyance in 2026, with Google’s AI Overviews often producing confidently incorrect information at the top of your search results.

Today, the most impressive achievements in AI seem to come from mathematics, but perhaps that will soon become passé. My feeling is that, if AGI ever comes, there won’t be one moment in which we declare it has arrived, but rather a gradual realisation that it is already here and we’ve just started calling it something else.

OpenAI appears to have made a subtle error when publishing its proofs of the Navier-Stokes problem, a team of mathematicians has claimed. The error doesn’t mean that the proofs are incorrect or that OpenAI hasn’t correctly solved the problem, but it does call into question whether mathematical results generated by AI models can always be relied on.

“What has to be done with all of these large language model-generated proofs is that they will have to be read by humans, and this creates an enormous extra burden on mathematicians,” says Anders Hansen at the University of Cambridge.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Climate satire Digger – with Tom Cruise on top form – is full of surprises
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Bethan Ackerley
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Things aren’t looking good for Digger Rockwell, the ageing oligarch behind the crisis in Alejandro Gonzalez Iñárritu’s new climate change satire Digger.

Nor is the prognosis rosy for the film itself – panned by critics and passed over by global audiences, it is poised to become one of the biggest flops of 2026.

But don’t let that negativity fool you. Pretentious, bombastic and sometimes painful, it is nevertheless a brutal takedown of the forces and failures behind planetary degradation. Held together by a terrific performance from Tom Cruise, Digger is more than worth your time – even if you end up hating it.

Imagine a world where ruthless capitalists set their sights on Greenland’s natural resources, with the express support of the US government. Now, if your brain isn’t addled from such flights of fancy, imagine that years of extraction have led to potentially world-ending consequences.

Must-watch documentary shows how Bush Senior failed the climate

That’s the situation in which Rockwell finds himself after an explosion at one of his oil rigs dislodges an iceberg the size of Maryland, sending it straight towards Europe. What follows is a Dr Strangelove-esque send-up of our current political morass that, to be frank, is rarely very funny.

There’s a moment early on in Digger that sums up the problem: President Compson (John Goodman) and his hawkish advisers meet with Rockwell to discuss the impending disaster. In so doing, one of Compson’s cronies uses invective of a sort that can’t be published in respectable science magazines. “Please,” Compson warns him, “there are women present.” The lackeys – all pale, stale and male – look around confused. A better comedy might have left the joke hanging as a burst of welcome absurdity, but Digger ploughs on. Compson and his cronies fall into peals of laughter at the mere thought of women entering the halls of power. In service of what looks like a tired old trope, Digger cuts itself off at the knees.

But oddly enough, that’s part of the point. It’s hard to, er, dig into what Digger is all about without spoiling the film entirely, but it is concerned with how we tell stories about “real” issues.

And in fact, some of the most appealing moments of Digger come when it plays with scale – the value of one death over hundreds of thousands, or of a single man’s influence over the crowd.

But as time goes on, you begin to see why Iñárritu lets the artifice peek through, and then the film’s true nature unfolds.

With the potentially catastrophic, record-smashing El Niño still peaking in the Pacific Ocean, scientists are warning of a fundamental ecological shift that would see swathes of the Great Barrier Reef become dominated by seaweed instead of coral.

During El Niño events, warmer ocean waters pool in the eastern and central Pacific. However, the phenomenon also dramatically disrupts the usual monsoon troughs, low-pressure zones that bring cooling clouds and rain to the Great Barrier Reef region.

This is why the worst Great Barrier Reef coral-bleaching events have coincided with past El Niños, such as the devastating reef mortality that occurred in 2024.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Leah Crane
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
The floodgates of AI mathematics have opened. On 7 October, OpenAI released 722 mathematical papers using an AI model to examine an astonishing range of topics, from longstanding mathematical mysteries to small improvements in rarely considered curiosities.

Of course, there hasn’t yet been time for mathematicians to comb through all of these results, let alone to actually check them: some of the papers are hundreds of pages long, dense with complex computations. Many of them have not been formalised – reduced to steps that can be checked by a computer – meaning there is little assurance that they are accurate. Three have already been retracted. Nevertheless, even a preliminary comb through the thicket of papers turns up some that are likely to make a splash.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Neanderthal Europe was as much a wooden age as a stone age
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: James Woodford
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Wooden tools, weapons, building materials and domestic items discovered in a Spanish cave challenge the assumption that Neanderthals’ technological life was based primarily on stone.

The finds have given an unprecedented glimpse into everyday Neanderthal life and are a rare opportunity to recover part of their missing world, says Josep Vallverdú at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution in Spain.

“Neanderthal technology was not only made of stone; it was also made of wood,” he says.

Before the Stone Age: Were the first tools made from plants not rocks?

“The archaeological record gives us a very biased picture of prehistoric technology. We see the stone because it survives, while a huge part of their material culture has simply disappeared.”

Vallverdú and his colleagues have now completed the first systematic review of nearly 600 wooden objects, all between 40,000 and 62,000 years old.

The finds have been collected by generations of archaeologists since the 1980s, excavated at a rock shelter site called Abric Romaní near Barcelona. They include timber imprints in travertine – a rock rich in calcium carbonate that precipitates out of water in certain environments. The rock preserves the patterns of the wood grain even though the timber long ago rotted away. Charred artefacts and actual preserved timber have also been found at the site.

See Alice Roberts at New Scientist Live 2026

The researchers’ first job was to determine exactly which pieces were used or made by Neanderthals. Only 13 qualified. Most of the remainder consist of trunks, branches, twigs, roots and firewood accumulations.

Maria Gema Chacón, also at the Catalan Institute, says the researchers have been surprised at how “complex Neanderthal woodworking could be, and how well they understood the properties of wood”, with the two spears being especially striking to her.

“Producing long, straight shafts and shaping them deliberately into pointed weapons required planning, skill and careful selection of the raw material,” says Chacón.

The technological behaviours preserved at Abric Romaní are comparable to those documented for Homo sapiens, she says.

Stick shaped by ancient humans is the oldest known wooden tool

Other finds included a mysterious wooden tripod, as well as timber trays reminiscent, in terms of likely utility, of the coolamons traditionally used by Indigenous Australians to carry food and water. Some of the wooden objects appear to be structural poles.

But perhaps the item that has most surprised the team is a “club-like” object that has no precedent from any other palaeolithic site.

Palmira Saladié, also at the Catalan Institute, says the club-like object is “not simply a stick with a thicker end”.

“There is a distinct narrow handle and an enlarged, asymmetrical head, giving the object a much more complex and deliberate form,” she says. “This particular configuration is what we have not been able to find a convincing parallel for in the prehistoric record.”

Vallverdú says the site shows that wood was a normal and important part of Neanderthals’ everyday life.

Why early humans radically changed their toolkits 200,000 years ago

“We have evidence of woodworking across many archaeological levels and over thousands of years, and the objects are associated with very different activities: hunting, domestic tasks, containers and the organisation of living spaces,” he says.

Chris Stringer at the Natural History Museum in London says the archaeological record of wooden artefacts has been “severely constrained” by the generally poor preservation of organic materials.

The finds reveal a much wider technological repertoire of woodworking skills, he says.

An analysis of ancient human artefacts finds that the container, a simple but critical tool, may have originated 500,000 years ago. Columnist Michael Marshall explores how slings, ostrich eggs and wooden trays helped our ancestors survive

“This is of course evidence from only one site, in one area, and one time span,” says Stringer, “so it’s just the tip of the iceberg in terms of a whole and mostly hidden technology that ran in parallel with the much better-known stone tools of the Palaeolithic.”

“Wood, plant fibres, hides, bone and other organic materials must have been central to daily life, but they normally disappear,” says Mariana Nabais, also at the Catalan Institute. “So when a site like Abric Romaní preserves wooden imprints and charred wooden objects, it is almost like suddenly seeing the missing half of the toolkit.”

Naoki Morimoto at Kyoto University in Japan describes the wooden objects as “remarkable”.

“Preserved organic materials are truly rare, and they reveal a ‘hidden’ aspect of Neanderthals that we have been missing,” says Morimoto.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: 194-year-old tortoise has exceptional DNA repair systems that fight off ageing
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: James Woodford
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
The world’s oldest known land animal – Jonathan the giant tortoise – has had his genome probed for the first time. This has revealed that parts of his genome to do with mitochondrial function are as efficient as those of a 5-year-old member of his species. Efficient mitochondria may give his DNA repair systems more energy to fight off the effects of ageing, enabling him to live to an estimated age of 194.

What’s more, some of his genetic changes seem similar to those of supercentenarians. “This study adds to the body of evidence that the mechanisms of ageing may be conserved across species,” says Stephen Clark at the Kallel Foundation, a non-profit organisation focused on interventions to extend human healthspan, in Nashville, Tennessee.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea), and Napoleon Bonaparte are the two most famous residents of St Helena island in the South Atlantic. Napoleon arrived at the remote British territory after he was exiled in 1815, while Jonathan is thought to have been shipped there, possibly from Aldabra Atoll, in 1882. Jonathan arrived as a fully grown adult that was thought to already have half a century under his belt, putting him at around 194 years old today.

The researchers calculated that Aldabra tortoises have an average lifespan of around 80 years, but they can live much longer. To understand the mechanisms behind Jonathan’s extraordinary longevity, Clark and his colleagues have studied his genome.

“I firmly believe we can learn about the global mechanisms of ageing by looking at the exceptions,” says Manel Esteller at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute in Barcelona, Spain, who led a study into a 117-year-old woman, once officially the world’s oldest person.

Esteller and his team found that the woman had exceptionally efficient mitochondrial function, which led Clark and his colleagues to suspect Jonathan similarly had “very efficient and very young” mitochondria, says Clark.

They had to study his genome via saliva samples and cheek swabs. This was because St Helena authorities refused their requests to draw Jonathan’s blood, given his fame and the risk of infection.

This was a major limitation, because it meant the researchers were unable to isolate large pieces of DNA, which are more stable in blood. Instead, they had to assemble fragments from Jonathan’s saliva, where DNA is more prone to bacterial contamination, and fill in the gaps using DNA from another Aldabra tortoise.

Once they had made the best possible composite of his genome, they compared it to the DNA of four other Aldabra tortoises. “We found 287 genes that had changes in them that were unique to him,” says Clark.

A clinical trial to reverse age-related vision conditions using stem cell treatment could finally deliver on the promise of a major discovery in ageing and regeneration made 20 years ago, says columnist Graham Lawton

Of these genes, 41 are though to be functionally significant, meaning they actively contribute to an organism’s biology, survival and regulation. A dozen of them were also found in ageing databases of the genes of other long-lived animal species.

Parts of Jonathan’s genome to do with mitochondrial function were as young as a 5-year-old Aldabra, says Clark. “This, in turn, has helped him manage the effects of ageing by giving the DNA repair systems more energy from the mitochondria to fight off the effects of ageing.”

Kousuke Hashimoto at the University of Osaka, Japan, says the work is “fascinating”, but notes that Jonathan’s genome was compared against that of only a few other tortoises, which may have unique genetic changes themselves.

Science Advances

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Women are talking about menopause — health systems must listen
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Hala Zahreddine Fahs
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Hala Zahreddine Fahs is a senior consultant in drug discovery and development at New York University, New York City, USA, and a women’s health science communicator in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

In Arabic, menopause is still commonly called sin al-ya’s, which translates as ‘the age of despair’. The term describes the end of menstruation as something to endure rather than to openly discuss.

Menopause research is underfunded and care for it is uneven across the world. In the Arab region, the problem is compounded by gaps in physicians’ training and the widespread belief that menopause is a private and natural transition that does not require medical intervention.

Things are slowly changing. Social media has helped to make discussions of menopause less taboo in Arab nations. Specialist services are beginning to emerge. Health systems must now capitalize on this growing awareness to provide better training, clear communication and accessible care.

The new science of menopause: these emerging therapies could change women’s health

Some Muslim people value their ability to fast and pray without interruption from menstruation, but poorly managed menopausal symptoms can disrupt individuals’ health, careers and ambitions. Yet efforts to improve care in Arab countries are constrained by a thin evidence base.

Take hormone replacement therapy (HRT), which can relieve menopause symptoms. Concerns about breast cancer became a barrier to its use after a broadly misinterpreted 2002 report linked the two (J. E. Rossouw et al. JAMA 288, 321–333; 2002). Nuanced conversations with physicians can help to weigh up the benefits and risks, which vary with the timing, formulation and route of treatment — but these are often lacking. And local data are sparse. A 2026 review of 22 Arab countries found only 15 studies of HRT use from seven countries (N. Al Zadjali et al. Front. Glob. Womens Health 7, 1722268; 2026).

Cultural and religious beliefs can contribute to concerns. As a researcher engaged in public-health communication across the Arab region, I’m often told ‘We were created this way, so why change what is natural?’ And women’s questions are often dismissed, or their disparate symptoms treated separately. A survey of 254 physicians across the Middle East and Africa found that fewer than 30% correctly identified the diagnostic criteria for menopause (S. A. Beshyah et al. Climacteric 26, 455–464; 2023).

How menopause reshapes the brain

I saw the consequences in my own family. For two decades, my mother experienced hot flushes that affected her work and quality of life, and later developed osteoporosis. Yet her symptoms were dismissed. I eventually turned to the scientific literature myself and questioned why HRT had not been discussed with her. No one should need to have a scientist in the family for their symptoms to be taken seriously.

Where trusted clinical guidance is difficult to obtain, social media and commercial wellness providers sometimes fill the information gap, potentially amplifying poor advice. I encounter individuals who have been encouraged by online wellness influencers and firms to buy extensive, unnecessary hormone-panel measurements, repeated cortisol tests and ‘hormone-balancing’ supplements — counter to advice from national guidelines, such as those in the United Kingdom.

Action is needed at three levels.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: US proposes $100,000 charge for international students to do post-graduate work
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Dan Garisto
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Universities in the United States would have to pay as much as US$100,000 for one of their graduates to work at a US job after their education under a new federal proposal. Credit: Getty

International students in the United States would face a US$100,000 price tag to work a science job in the country after graduation under a proposal made public yesterday by the administration of US President Donald Trump.

The proposed rule would require academic institutions to foot the bill for a work programme called optional practical training (OPT), which allows overseas students to work in the United States for up to 3 years after finishing an undergraduate or graduate degree.

Some 420,000, or roughly one-third, of international students participated in OPT in the 2025–26 academic year, making it the largest pipeline of global talent into the US workforce.

International PhD students to face strict limits on time in the US

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposed rule, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”. The DHS projected that if the rule were finalized, OPT enrollment would drop by as much as 44% and universities would pay between $8.4 and $16.5 billion annually.

An unpublished analysis of the rule’s effects on OPT enrollment by Michael Clemens, an economist at the Johns Hopkins School of Government & Policy in Washington DC, projects that the number of students who enroll after a bachelor’s degree would be halved, and that enrollment by those with master’s degrees would be virtually eliminated. Clemens also noted that OPT is especially important for international PhD graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields, drawing roughly 70 percent of them in 2022.

The proposed rule is the latest in a series of Trump administration attempts to restrict immigration, which have already limited the country’s ability to recruit scientific talent. In 2025, for example, Trump announced a $100,000 levy on a visa reserved for researchers and other highly skilled foreign workers. As a result, new applications for those visas plummeted by 90%, according to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

If the new proposal and related restrictions are implemented, the combined measures “will obliterate the pipeline” of talent, says Clemens. In a separate analysis commissioned by the US National Academies of Science, he and his colleagues found that the size of the entire US STEM workforce would drop by 6–11% over a decade if all the administration’s proposals were implemented.

A spokesperson for the DHS said that the $100,000 charge “would strengthen program oversight while addressing concerns of fraud and abuse”, but did not respond to questions about the impact to the international STEM talent pipeline.

The OPT programme has expanded dramatically over the past decade, as international students have taken advantage of it to work at top tech companies such as Google and Amazon. Last year the number of recent graduates enrolled rose by 14%, even as the number of new international students dropped, notes Violet Buxton-Walsh, an immigration policy researcher at the Institute for Progress, a non-profit think tank in Washington DC. Despite restrictions on immigrants, “[t]here are very few who have better options than staying in the U.S.,” she says.

Canada recruits dozens of US scholars — including several science stars

The administration’s proposal, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, would require graduates to pay a $70,000 charge for their first year of OPT; STEM graduates would pay an additional $30,000 for a two-year extension.

Without the lure of OPT, the number of international students in the United States is likely to drop sharply, multiple scholars told Nature. As a result, Clemens projects that US colleges and universities could lose a combined $2.5 to 4.2 billion each year in tuition and other revenue.

Ina Ganguli, an economist of science and innovation at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says the impact goes beyond numbers and finances. “It will change the type of students who are going to come to the US”, she says, because top prospects have the freedom to look elsewhere.

By introducing and tracking mutations as the cells of a mouse embryo divide, researchers have mapped relationship between cells. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library

‘Cell recorders’ based on gene editing have captured mouse development in unprecedented detail.

Two independent teams of scientists published the findings today in Science and in Cell. One team recorded the cell-by-cell development of a two-week-old embryo from a single fertilized egg1, and the other captured most of the cell divisions in embryos as organs formed2.

Both studies were inspired by a landmark early-1980s effort: the first — and still only — full map of animal development. Using only a microscope, UK biologist John Sulston observed each cell of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans as the animal grew from an egg into an adult with precisely 959 somatic, or fully differentiated, cells.

Tracing the lineage of most other animals in this way, particularly mammals, isn’t possible, says Jay Shendure, a genome scientist at the University of Washington in Seattle, who led the Science study. C. elegans is transparent, and each worm develops in precisely the same way, with the same 959 cells having followed an unvarying pattern of cell divisions.

But in mammals such as mice — in which development is hidden and cells number in the billions — external cues such as growth factors influence whether a cell's fate, for instance, whether it will end up in the lungs or liver.

Bizarre CRISPR enzyme kills cancer cells by shredding their DNA

A key question in biology, says Shendure, is how such randomness can give rise to individuals of the same species that have broadly the same form. “Twins look the same, humans kind of look the same, yet even twins develop through very different sets of cell divisions,” he says.

Shendure first tackled this question around 2016, when he and his team developed a method based on the gene-editing technology CRISPR that introduced ‘barcodes’ — gene edits at particular locations — into the cells of developing zebrafish (Danio rerio)3. The team then used DNA sequencing to check which barcodes were present in various cells, and inferred relationships between them.

But these CRISPR-based 'lineage recorders' can harm cells if too many edits are introduced during development, says Jonathan Weissman, a molecular biologist at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who led the study in Cell.

To circumvent these issues, the teams led by Shendure and Weissman used a more precise and less damaging technique, called prime editing, to introduce edits as cells divided during embryo development.

Shendure’s team took a fertilized mouse egg and applied a technique they have named DNA Typewriter, which adds sequential, indelible genetic marks to specific spots in the genome as cells divide. The egg was then implanted into a mouse. After two weeks, when the embryo had formed major organ systems, the researchers read the DNA Typewriter edits and were able to reconstruct the relationships of 1.3 million edited cells —about 10% of the embryo’s total.

As permafrost thaws in the Arctic, a company wants to use blankets to prevent erosion of the landscape.Credit: Jeff Vanuga/Nature Photo Library/Science Photo Library

A Canadian start-up firm is developing a way to prevent greenhouse-gas emissions from permafrost by stabilizing the soil with an insulating ‘blanket’ of woody materials. If the method works, it could be the first tool to directly forestall green-house gas emissions that are escaping from permafrost as the Arctic heats.

“Our goal is to make sure the carbon in the soil remains buried,” says Cansu Culha, co-founder of PermaC and a natural-hazards researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada.

Earth’s frozen environments are thawing as temperatures rise in response to human emissions. The only reliable way to slow that melting on a global scale is to slash emissions from the burning of fossil fuels. But some researchers are exploring methods to prevent the thaw directly, ranging from placing reflective mats on glaciers to pumping water onto sea ice to thicken it.

Researchers say that PermaC’s approach is the first they know of to focus on preventing permafrost thaw and its associated emissions, which are estimated to be equivalent to those of Japan.

The company just completed the first test of its insulating blankets in Canada’s Northwest Territories at an area of rapidly eroding permafrost known as a retrogressive thaw slump. These slumps occur when a hill of permafrost thaws and collapses, enabling erosion to take big bites out of the landscape. This exposes deeper layers of soil to warming, forming hotspots of CO2 and methane emissions. One estimate suggests that these areas of rapid erosion could amplify permafrost emissions by as much as 40% compared to models that only account for gradual thaw.

The company’s approach is to stabilize the edge of the slumps with a layer of wood shavings, soil and native seeds, and a burlap-like mat of coconut husks. Culha says she got the idea after hearing about Indigenous communities in Alaska that prevent permafrost degradation by planting trees along the edges of slumps. Similar erosion-control blankets are used in temperate areas, but they haven’t been used to insulate or stabilize permafrost until now, she says.

PermaC has yet to release results from this year'stest. But the blanket seems to have halted erosion: over the Arctic summer, the edge of the slump without the blanket retreated by 5 metres, whereas the blanketed area saw no measurable retreat, Culha says.

“That’s very promising,” says Christina Schaedel, a permafrost scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Falmouth, Massachusetts, who has been advising the company. However, the result is from only one slump over one summer, she adds.

One challenge is calculating how much CO2 the blankets prevent from being emitted. Measuring the CO2 emissions from slumps is not straightforward and remains an active research question, says Mark Lara, a biologist who studies permafrost landscapes at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. “There definitely are slumps that are spewing out carbon,” he says. But there are “lots of minutiae that could dramatically impact the results”, he adds. For instance, the emissions from any given slump depend on its geometry, the amount of carbon in the soil and how much of that carbon ends up as CO2 or methane after erosion.

So far, Culha has only rough estimates for the emissions that the blankets might prevent. Extrapolating from research on erosion rates and soil carbon in the Arctic, she thinks that about 2,200 tonnes of CO2 a year might be prevented from being emitted at the average carbon-rich slump. If those calculations are accurate and the blankets can be installed at 20,000 slumps across Canada and Alaska — the company’s ambitious goal over the next decade — she estimates that they might prevent about 40 million tonnes of CO2 emissions a year, roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of Hungary.

Culha says the company is developing a detailed methodology that a third party could use to verify prevented emissions, which would be necessary for the company to sell carbon credits for emissions the blankets prevent. People could purchase those credits to offset emissions elsewhere. The firm aims to issue credits as soon as next year, and has so far raised Can$1.4 million (US$1 million) from investors, says Culha.

As AI agents’ scientific prowess grows, some scientists worry about getting scooped not just by human rivals, but also by bots. Credit: Getty

As AI agents’ ability to do science autonomously continues to improve, scientists are facing a once-unthinkable question: will I get scooped by a bot?

At least twice in the past five weeks, researchers have said that they had been working for an extended period on a particular research question, only to learn that artificial-intelligence companies had either answered the question before them or announced results before they were ready to do the same. In response, researchers who are worried that AI tools might scrape their unpublished work and scoop them are limiting their use of such tools.

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Nevertheless, some AI researchers, although not all, say that AI agents are increasingly likely to reach conclusions before scientists can do so. Researchers are “going to be scooped, but not because they’ve uploaded a manuscript”, says Geoffrey Irving, chief scientist at Resolution, an AI-safety research organization in Berkeley, California. “They’re going to get scooped because the AIs are very good at solving problems, and they’re going to get better and better.”

On 7 September, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University in New York City, posted online that he and a collaborator had made progress on the Navier–Stokes problem, a long-standing open question in fluid dynamics. According to Buckmaster’s account, he and Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic, based in San Francisco, California, whose work with Buckmaster was a personal project, had been pursuing the problem for a year. Buckmaster’s 7 September post also included a paper with the solution to a simpler version of the problem. The next day, 8 September, OpenAI, also in San Francisco, announced that its agents had solved the puzzle — a timing that Buckmaster has publicly questioned.

Who gets credit in the AI era? OpenAI maths bombshell sparks debate

Buckmaster raised the possibility that information that he and Alpöge had uploaded to an OpenAI tool could have been used to train the company’s models. OpenAI disputed this scenario. The company said in a statement that an investigation had confirmed that Buckmaster’s “prompts” in the two months before the 8 September announcement “could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training”. The statement also said that OpenAI’s researchers and agents “did not see any of their [Buckmaster and Alpöge’s] work through any means until they released it publicly”.

Two weeks later, Anthropic announced that agents running on its Claude large language model (LLM) had discovered that certain viruses have a pattern of repeated DNA segments similar to the pattern seen in CRISPR gene-editing systems. After the announcement, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a PhD student in computational biology at the University of Copenhagen, told The New York Times that he has been studying the same DNA patterns for several years, often using Claude, but has not published the work. Mestre also raised the possibility that information his team had uploaded to Anthropic’s tools could have been incorporated into Claude’s training data. Anthropic told the Times that its model was “not trained on any user transcripts”.

Despite these reassurances, some scientists are now re-evaluating how they use AI. Sandra Laurentino, a reproductive epigeneticist at the University of Münster in Germany, says she no longer trusts AI systems. She now uses AI only to check why her code fails, and before doing so changes all of the parameter and variable names to generic labels such as “group A has feature X” to avoid giving the system information about her experiments. “I am quite careful when it comes to AI,” she says, but the recent controversy has “made me even more paranoid”.

The AI discoveries have also made Samuel Mehr, an auditory cognitive scientist at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, even more hesitant to use commercial AI models than he already was. He has created an AI-use policy for his laboratory that forbids students from uploading protected information to commercial LLMs and warns against using the models for any part of the research process. “I think it’s incredibly risky to hand out your intellectual property to third parties when you don’t know what they’re going to do with it,” he says.

The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis (shown here in an electron microscope image) circulates naturally in some parts of the world in wild rodents.Credit: Eye Of Science/Science Photo Library

The death of a 28-year-old researcher at a Siberian laboratory, possibly from pneumonic plague, has triggered international alarm over whether the incident could spark a wider outbreak. Biosecurity specialists have been assuring the public that this is highly unlikely. Their concern about the incident is the lack of transparency around it.

Although news sources have reported that about 200 people at the lab might have been exposed to the researcher and quarantined, Russia’s public-health regulator has insisted that there was “no emergency” at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk, and that the researcher died from pneumonia of “unknown” origin.

Black Death bacterium has become less lethal after genetic tweak

The Russian government’s sparing disclosures combined with unverified rumours of a lab accident have fuelled demands by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the US government for epidemiological data. Only on 7 October — five days after the researcher’s death — did Russian officials reveal that the researcher had been vaccinated against the plague, and that “thousands of tests” revealed that neither she nor others who might have been exposed had tested positive for dangerous pathogens.

Russia has dismissed the concerns over secrecy, with Kremlin officials telling news outlet CNN that it has kept the WHO informed “in accordance with established practice”.

Although the risk of a wider epidemic is minimal — the Yersinia pestis bacterium that causes the disease is treatable with antibiotics — the incident exposes vulnerabilities in global biosurveillance, says Gregory Koblentz, a biosecurity-policy specialist at George Mason University near Washington DC, who studies lab safety.

Nature spoke with Koblentz about why pandemic fears are misplaced and the dangers of government secrecy when responding to this type of incident.

Gregory Koblentz studies laboratory safety at George Mason University near Washington DC.Credit: Rod Lamkey/Abaca Press/Shutterstock

There is a reason the Black Death happened 600 years ago, when we didn’t have sanitation, hygiene or modern medicine. Today, we are much better prepared to handle plague than back then.

Post-COVID-19 pandemic, there is this speculation: “Is this going to be COVID-26?” SARS-CoV-2 was a novel virus for which we didn’t understand the immunology, and didn’t have antivirals or vaccines. In contrast, Y. pestis is a very well-studied, well-characterized bacterium for which we have lots of different antibiotics and for which there are vaccines available.

The WHO [which held a press briefing on 6 October] characterized it well: there is a low risk for people who live in Irkutsk, an even lower risk across Russia, and an extremely low risk for Europe and the world.

Plague is endemic in that part of the world, so there is a legitimate public-health reason to do research on Y. pestis to develop diagnostic and detection methods at such a lab.

I’m not aware of any historical evidence linking this institute to the Russian bioweapons programme. Russia has at least three known military facilities that do research on biological weapons, so those would be where the programme is mostly located. Conflating this accident with Russian bioweapons research activities is not helpful because this was a public-health lab where this accident happened. The idea that all public-health labs are secretly working on bioweapons is just nonsense.

Separately, Russia inherited the world’s largest bioweapons programme when the Soviet Union fell apart, and for the last 10 years or so, they have been modernizing that programme. That is a major concern, because it’s a violation of the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention [which internationally banned the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons].

Just you wait: big dogs tend to age more quickly than small ones, which might be attributed to differences in the chemical tagging of the genome.Credit: Jacob King/PA Images/Alamy

A chihuahua might be at a disadvantage in paw-to-paw combat with a Great Dane, but being little has its benefits: a sweeping analysis of dog breeds has found that small pooches tend to age more slowly than large ones, and big dogs might have rogue ‘jumping genes’ that hop around the genome to blame.

The study1, which encompassed nearly 900 dogs representing about 120 breeds, found that ageing in dogs is accompanied by changes in certain chemical groups added onto DNA that can control gene activity. These marks on DNA are part of a cell’s epigenome, and the loss or gain of these groups is sometimes used as a biological marker of ageing.

Big dogs tended to accumulate epigenetic changes at a faster rate than small dogs, the study found. And male dogs amassed them faster than female dogs, even if the male dogs had been neutered at a young age.

“It’s fascinating,” says Borbála Turcsán, who studies dog cognition and behaviour at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, and was not involved in the study. “It provides a molecular background for something we also observe at a behavioural level.”

The work appears today in Science1.

Some of the largest dog breeds, such as Irish wolfhounds, live an average of ten years or less. In contrast, Brianah McCoy, who studies ageing at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, recalls her grandmother’s pet chihuahua: “That dog lived for like 20 years,” McCoy says. “And she was not nice.”

Dogs might have evolved to read your emotions

McCoy, then working at Arizona State University in Tempe, and her colleagues are members of the Dog Aging Project, which, so far, has enrolled about 55,000 participants. Some of their loyal humans periodically fill out surveys about their pet’s health and environment and submit blood samples.

To learn more about how breed and sex affect ageing in dogs, the team analysed the placement of chemical tags called methyl groups on DNA in 894 dogs, and combined this with genetic sequencing and other data.

The researchers then used these data to develop a molecular clock based on correlations between methylation patterns and chronological age. The resulting clock could predict a dog’s age to within a year based on its epigenome. Those dogs whose epigenetic age was older than their chronological age also had a higher risk of dying in the next two years.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is on course to become the fourth space power to touch an asteroid, according to scientists and engineers involved in the country’s space programme. On 1 October, they announced the completion of a probe that is expected to career into the reddish rock known as Justicia in 2035.

The probe was designed and built in the UAE. It will now be shipped to the University of Colorado Boulder, where collaborators will integrate it with the main MBR Explorer spacecraft before a launch scheduled for March 2028.

The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid belt (EMA) will observe six asteroids using an array of cameras and spectrometers, which can analyse material composition remotely. It will also observe Venus and Mars, before the MBR Explorer spacecraft dispatches the tiny 10 kilogram probe to its final destination, the asteroid Justicia.

Justicia’s unusual red colour suggests that the asteroid contains materials more commonly found further out in the Solar System than its current orbit between Mars and Jupiter. If it originated in the outer reaches and migrated inwards, that makes it an ancient “traveller from the past” that could give clues as to how the Solar System formed and the origins of its water, said Elias Tsoutsanis, chief researcher for the Propulsion and Space Research Center at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi. The TII is a government-backed research agency that designed and developed the probe. Tsoutsanis was speaking at an event in the city on 1 October marking the probe’s completion.

The asteroid mission will be the country’s second interplanetary venture, building on the success of its Hope orbiter, which reached Mars in 2021 after six years of development.

The UAE’s relatively quick ascent into the club of space-faring nations has come through a programme of hiring international partners who have helped to design and build their various spacecraft while also training Emirati researchers and engineers.

The progress on the latest mission shows the UAE’s growing independence in space science and technology, said computer scientist Najwa Aaraj, chief executive of the TII, at the 1 October event. Whereas every part of Hope was a collaboration, the UAE built the probe component of the EMA on its own. “I’m very confident that in the next mission, we don’t need Colorado,” she added. “Everything can be done end-to-end here.”

The country’s activities in the skies seem to be having an impact on the ground. Since the UAE announced its plan to send a mission to Mars in 2014, there has been a 30% rise in students enrolling in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, said Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi, chair of the UAE Space Agency, at the event. Between 2015 and 2025, the number of UAE universities offering aerospace engineering and space-related degree programmes has roughly doubled, he later told Nature.

Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen captures images during the lunar flyby.Credit: NASA

Planetary scientists have fresh ‘Moon joy’ to explore. On 7 October, NASA released more than 800 gigabytes of images, audio recordings, written notes and other data gathered by the Artemis II astronauts on their historic flight past the Moon in April.

An accompanying report chronicles observations made by the first human eyes to view the Moon up close since 1972, such as the astronauts’ description of the colours of the lunar surface and the flashes of light seen by the crew as micrometeorites pelted the Moon.

But the report also details some of the challenges of sending humans to explore the surface of the Moon, which both the United States and China plan to do. As lighting conditions changed, the Artemis II astronauts’ perceptions of the lunar surface also changed, showing how difficult it is to assess the Moon’s terrain accurately. At times, sunlight overwhelmed the crew’s vision. Understanding such issues is important for future astronauts trying to avoid hazards such as craters and boulders as they navigate onto and across the Moon.

Artemis II, which launched on 1 April and returned to Earth on 10 April, carried four astronauts around the Moon and back. The journey took the crew as much as 406,771 kilometres from Earth — the farthest that humans have ever travelled from their home planet. The goal was to test how well the mission’s Orion capsule could keep humans alive in deep space. But the astronauts also did some science, including more than six hours of lunar observation collectively dubbed ‘Moon joy’, during their 6 April flyby.

First photos from Artemis II: see stunning ‘Earthset’ and more

With today’s information release, “I’m really excited for the community to just take this and run,” says Marie Henderson, a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland Baltimore County in Baltimore, who is one of the mission’s deputy lunar-science leads. “A whole bunch of new eyes is just going to make a huge difference.”

The new lunar dataset adds to those gathered by multiple orbiters and flyby probes over the years, from many nations. Comparing and contrasting the Artemis II observations, made in situ by human eyes, with those from robotic spacecraft can enrich understanding of the Moon, scientists say.

For instance, the astronauts’ descriptions of the colours of the lunar surface are valuable for providing a record of human perception, says Elisha Jhoti, a planetary scientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, who plans to work with the data. “The images we see from the Moon are not exact representations of what our eyes would see,” she says. The astronauts reported colours including brown, tan and green in various places on the Moon, including a shade like “mould growing on sandwich bread” in one spot, according to astronaut Christina Koch.

I was with Artemis II’s scientists during the Moon fly-by. Here’s what I saw

The new data also detail how astronauts’ perception of the degree of darkness in some craters varied as the spacecraft travelled past the Moon and lighting angles changed. That’s important information if future missions send astronauts to navigate in areas such as those near the Moon’s poles. “It’s going to be hard to be in those low-light conditions,” Henderson says.

Manuel Spitschan is a professor at the Technical University of Munich in Germany and a research-group leader at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tübingen, Germany.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Manuel Spitschan and his team meet monthly to discuss memos prepared by members of the laboratory.Credit: Translational Sensory & Circadian Neuroscience Unit

Every month, the members of my laboratory gather for a video call that starts in silence. For 20 minutes, the whole group sits and reads a memo written by one of us. Then, we discuss it for the remaining 70 minutes.

Since we started doing this in April 2024, we have written around 50,000 words between us — the length of a short novel — on topics ranging from the design of a particular experiment to a postdoc’s uncertainty about her scientific focus. And all of them were covered in a memo no longer than six pages.

The ‘memo meeting’ format comes from industry. It was introduced by the technology company Amazon in 2004 after the firm’s leaders argued that the information density of text is higher than that of presentations, and that meeting time is better spent discussing a written document. Whether the six-page narrative beats alternative ways of sharing information has never been tested empirically, but it is well embedded in Amazon’s corporate practices and is discussed in shareholder letters.

I wanted to experiment with this format in another domain: our scientific discussions. By using memo meetings to supplement weekly check-ins focused on logistics and fine-grained scientific topics, I hoped that the lab would become more efficient. What I did not anticipate was that this format would change what topics people were willing to bring to the table.

My neuroscience research group investigates how the environment influences human circadian rhythms and sleep across a wide range of biomedical-research areas, including laboratory, field, intervention and modelling studies. Our monthly meetings bring together our diverse methods, unifying our various strands of work. And the memo method puts everyone on equal footing.

Presentations can act as a crutch when the speaker is uncertain about something. For example, if you’re discussing a research design, you can put something like ‘n = 40, fully counterbalanced assignment of conditions’ on a slide without discussing how counterbalancing is being done and what happens if it fails. Writing in full sentences requires exacting precision, and any gaps in understanding will become apparent to the author as they draft the memo. Those gaps will also be visible to the reader if not addressed. Writing six pages might seem like a lot more work than throwing together a slide deck, but it is time better spent: a memo still provides an update for other lab members, but it also develops the writer’s thinking.

Twenty-two easy ways to power up your lab meetings

Because reading time is set aside during the meeting, everyone has the same opportunity to engage with the material. This levels the intellectual playing field. We are not allowed to drift away, as might happen during a presentation; if people finish reading early, they generally spend the rest of the allotted time taking notes. It is understood that during the session, distractions should be kept to a minimum.

Sometimes, I have had to ensure that people don’t exceed the six-page limit. Most memos end up being about 1,900 words (five to six pages), including figures and tables. But the page limit isn’t really the constraint; the 20 minutes are. If we can’t read the document in the allotted time, it is too long.

When I suggested that we start using this technique, I did not enforce a specific template. However, a common format has stuck: the memo starts by posing the problem or question it discusses and ends with questions that the author hopes will be answered after the discussion.

E. J. Kavounas lives in Los Angeles and works in media. His near-future fiction has appeared in Infinite Worlds and Uncharted Magazine. More at ejkavounas.com.

I always start with my hair. Scalp, eyebrows, the fuzz on my upper lip. I swear if I make it out of here, I’ll never touch tweezers again. In the shower, I scrub every flake of dead skin. A single cell could give me away.

Next, make-up. Luckily, newer bots have lab-grown skin with humanizing blemishes, so I can leave the mole on my chin. The wig’s nylon fibres used to itch but I barely notice now. Body heat is the tough one. We run hot. The yellow jumpsuit passes for a standard uni, but aerogel-infused lining makes it stiff in all the wrong places. When I check the mirror, I’m a mannequin version of me. Talons of guilt hook into my gut. I never used to lie. Now it’s my whole life.

A strip of text slices my reflection. My lenses parse a few words from their endless updates. Our code embedded in theirs. I open the map with an eye-swipe. My pulse kicks up. The rendezvous is clear across town. The only way to make it is mass transit.

In the maglev, I’m shoulder to shoulder with bots, swaying as we bank. The trick is to smile while focusing on nothing. I’d feel lonely if it weren’t so terrifying. I dwell on the absurdity: a train filled with bots in matching unis. Yellow for logistics. Blue for repairs. Green for horticulture. Like the old ads. Ubiquitous companions ushering in an era of clean abundance. Which they did — once we were out of the way.

The city scrolls by. Bullet holes patched. Blood scrubbed clean. We pass a gutted skyscraper. Floor after floor of hydroponic racks. We glide over avenues once choked with traffic, now lush greenways. Their city is both garden and ghost town.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

One day, I’ll ride this train to the end and simply walk away. Into the desert where there are no bots. But today, I’m to meet a conductor of a different line. It’s taken months to get the invite and I’m late.

“Can you help me?” The voice is glitchy. A courier bot stares at me with foggy eyeballs. It lurches forward, gears grinding, blocking the exit. “I am lost.”

I could push it out of the way and reach the doors before they shut. But bots don’t push each other. I miss my stop.

I press my tongue to the roof of my mouth. Nano-gel coats my throat like syrup. If the bot’s sniffer catches a droplet of DNA, this car will flood with red-suits. “Where are you going?” I ask with genuine-sounding concern.

During the war, old models were the easiest to hack. We’d rip off their plastic skulls and mine them for intel.

“I m-m-m-missed the last update.”

“Three more stops,” I say like the helpful little bot it thinks I am.

“Thank you.” It pushes sagging features into a smile, then ambles away.

I get off at the next station, several blocks from where I need to be. I have to hurry, but I remember not to run.

I walk through a part of the city the bots haven’t fixed yet. Under an abandoned freeway. Past mouldy mattresses and crates of decaying fruit, black with flies. I’d almost forgotten what rot smells like.

“Late,” a voice says from the shadow of the underpass. As he steps into the light, it’s obvious. He’s in yellow, like me. Logistics gets fewer questions. But it’s his walk. The worry in his voice. For all their sniffers and scans, I’m still better at spotting fakes. “Almost left without you.”

“Why didn’t you?” I ask, because I would have.

“Worth the risk.” He steps closer. It’s hard to see what he really looks like under the make-up, but there’s something about his eyes. A fire. For a split second I believe he’s different from the others. He might have a shot. But then I remember what’s out there. The odds stacked against us. “Were you followed? We think they have a spy.”

“I was careful.” I can’t meet his gaze. Sometimes it’s harder to be a person than a bot.

He nods. “The others are waiting.”

“Others?” I ask, trying to mask the guilt. One is bad enough.

“Don’t worry, there’s a seat left.” He gestures to a utility door behind him. To the labyrinth of ancient tunnels and sewers. “Let’s go.”

“Wait,” I say. “Tell me how to get there.” I blink twice so the cameras in my lenses can record. “In case we’re separated.”

He walks me through it. Step by step, ending at the port where the ship waits.

“I’m sorry,” I tell him.

“For what?” he asks, just before a drone blasts into the alley, kicking up dust and garbage.

A phalanx of red bots rushes in. They surround him and raise their rifles.

He curses at them, but saves his worst for me.

Now it’s hard not to meet his stare. I force myself to look away.

“Wait,” I tell one of the security bots.

Semiconductors are materials that have an electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator. They are ubiquitous in modern technology, enabling the controlled flow of electricity in everything from solar cells to smartphones. The properties of a semiconductor are governed, in part, by its electronic bandgap — the energy needed to promote an electron to a conducting state. Semiconductors with large bandgaps are sought for electronic devices that must operate at high voltages or high temperatures, but such materials have been difficult to produce. Writing in Nature, Steele et al.1 report a semiconductor with the biggest bandgap recorded so far, which exceeds 7 electronvolts (eV). This demonstration pushes semiconductors into a regime that has long been reserved for insulators.

For decades, the most precise timekeepers have been atomic clocks. The mechanism of these clocks relies on the transition of electrons between the energy levels of atoms or ions. But some applications require even more precise timepieces — such as nuclear clocks, which depend on transitions that occur in the nuclei of atoms. Writing in Nature, Toscani De Col et al.1 and Huang et al.2 report the first implementations of a nuclear clock, a milestone in the field of metrology. Toscani De Col et al. also demonstrate that their clock shows promise for detecting a possible form of dark matter — the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the Universe.

Strawberry contains the letter ‘r’ three times, but when asked, many large language models (LLMs) answer that the letter appears twice. This happens because most LLMs encode words as ‘tokens’ that represent sequences of letters. LLMs that operate in this way can achieve excellent performance, but they cannot access the individual characters in each word, which are encoded as binary sequences called bytes. Writing in Nature, Minixhofer et al.1 now report an approach called byteification that retrofits token-based LLMs to operate at the byte level. The authors show that byteified models can achieve competitive performance while retaining the ability to read individual characters.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Melissa Hobson
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Melissa Hobson is a freelance marine-science journalist based in Hastings, UK.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Polina Brangel is using tools such as artificial intelligence to strengthen pandemic preparedness.

More than five years after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers continue to try to anticipate the next global disease outbreak that could cost millions of lives and cause economic chaos. Polina Brangel, a research-and-development data-innovation lead at the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), headquartered in Oslo, is trying to prevent this.

Brangel began studying biotechnology engineering at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev in Israel in 2007, graduating from her combined programme with both bachelor’s and master’s degrees in 2012. Later that year, she began her PhD in bioengineering and biomedical engineering at Imperial College London.

Nature Spotlight: Infectious diseases

Her role was originally focused on biosensor development for oncology diagnostics, but Brangel became involved in developing rapid diagnostic (lateral flow) tests to detect various cancer biomarkers. When Ebola broke out in West Africa in 2014 and the World Health Organization (WHO) called for rapid, simple and accurate tests for the disease, Brangel realized that she had the right tools but was using them for a different purpose.

The decision to repurpose her work to tackle Ebola led to a career in pandemic preparedness, and she joined CEPI in 2023. She has developed tests to understand the immunological biomarkers found in people who have recovered from Ebola, has studied the immune response elicited by COVID-19 and now focuses on protecting people from ‘Disease X’.

Brangel spoke to Nature about her work in the field, what she has learnt from the COVID-19 pandemic that could help prevent future pandemics and the part artificial intelligence is playing in preparedness efforts.

Disease X is the term, coined by the WHO in its 2018 Research & Development Blueprint for Epidemics, for a hypothetical pathogen that infects humans. The WHO created a list of priority pathogens deemed likely to cause a pandemic that have no available countermeasures, such as vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics. The list includes the viruses that cause Ebola, Lassa fever and Rift Valley fever.

As serology technical officer at the WHO, I was trying to understand the immune response elicited by COVID-19. With infectious diseases, you do a sero-epidemiology study: drawing blood from a small cohort of people, looking at immune-response antibodies to work out how many individuals had been infected and extrapolating to derive the prevalence in the population.

The infection numbers we estimated went from almost zero to around 90% between different countries because we had so many different tests that could look for these antibodies. The problem is that the tests were all accurate, but the different set-ups were not comparable. We worked with the former agency Public Health England to introduce an international standard for benchmarking assays1. Before this, each laboratory would choose its own assay and the results couldn’t be compared.

This taught me the importance of harmonizing data if we are to use them as evidence for decision-making. Sound, strong science isn’t enough.

CEPI has a methodological programme focused on Disease X. We’re working with the 25 known families of virus that can infect humans, most of which come from animals. These include filoviruses (the family that includes Ebola), coronaviruses (such as SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19) and orthoflaviviruses (including those that cause dengue, yellow fever and Zika). We can’t develop vaccines for all 25 so we prioritize the pathogens considered most likely to infect humans, then generate as much knowledge as possible about their genomic sequence.

Pathogens must mutate to jump from animals to humans, so we use computer simulations to predict which ones will undergo mutation. Feeding the most likely ones into AI tools enables us to start developing and testing vaccine sequences and designing clinical trials.

AI models are being used to track zoonotic diseases. Will they prevent the next pandemic?

AI gives us three things: speed (extremely important in a pandemic response); the ability to integrate data from disparate sources; and federated access that enables us to learn from source information even when it’s retained by the owner, whether that’s a government agency or commercial company.

CEPI’s Pandemic Preparedness Engine for Disease X is our idea for a collaborative scientific tool that will integrate fragmented knowledge bases — such as information on genomic sequences from various sources — and enable researchers around the world to build vaccines and medical interventions. It will be a bit like a chatbot. Imagine that a researcher in Malaysia identifies a new Nipah virus and wants to build a vaccine. They could input the genomic sequence of the virus and its location, and the AI agent could suggest how to create or tweak specific molecules (antigens) to trigger the correct immune response.
