Antiretroviral medication is used to both control HIV and prevent its transmission, helping to reduce the incidence of AIDS.Credit: Arlette Bashizi/For The Washington Post via Getty Images

The year 2016 was one for the history books. It saw Donald Trump winning the US presidential election, the United Kingdom voting to leave the European Union and the declaration of Zika virus — a mosquito-borne and sexually transmitted virus that causes severe birth defects — as a global public-health emergency.

It was also the year that the United Nations committed to eliminating AIDS.

AIDS was first defined in 1983 as a disease caused by HIV, which is thought to have jumped into humans — most probably from chimpanzees or monkeys — in the early to mid-twentieth century. The virus destroys immune cells responsible for fighting off infection. Since then, more than 44 million people around the world have died of AIDS or HIV-related diseases, as a result of their immune system no longer being able to defend against even common infections. An estimated 41 million people are currently living with the virus.

Nature Spotlight: Infectious diseases

Antiretroviral drugs are highly effective at suppressing HIV to undetectable levels, transforming what was once a death sentence into a manageable chronic condition. People with undetectable viral levels also can’t transmit the virus, and those same antiretroviral drugs can prevent infection in healthy individuals who are exposed to the virus. But despite decades of research, a complete cure or an effective vaccine have proved elusive.

In January 2016, the UN’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) — a global initiative to address poverty, inequality and climate change — came into force as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Among them was SDG target 3.3, a strategy targeted at ending the AIDS epidemic, along with epidemics of other communicable diseases, by 2030. The initiative aimed to reduce the number of new infections by 90%; from 0.24 infections per 1,000 people in 2016 to 0.025 infections by 2030. Later that year, at the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on Ending AIDS in New York City, member states set a goal to reduce both new HIV infections and the number of deaths from AIDS-related illnesses to fewer than 500,000 by 2020, and made a commitment to end AIDS as a public-health threat by 2030.

Only one human disease has ever been completely eradicated. In 1980, after a 13-year vaccination campaign by the World Health Organization, smallpox — a deadly infectious disease caused by the variola virus — was eliminated worldwide, in what has been described as humanity’s greatest public-health achievement. At the time of its creation, SDG target 3.3 seemed bold but achievable.

By 2020, the world had made major gains towards achieving this aim, which included the targets of having 90% of people living with HIV diagnosed, 90% of those diagnosed being on antiretroviral therapy and 90% of those on antiretroviral therapy being virologically suppressed. The ‘90-90-90’ targets were then raised to 95-95-95 by 2030.

Seventh patient ‘cured’ of HIV: why scientists are excited

Today, however, the 2030 goal is looking increasingly unattainable, despite new HIV infections globally declining by 40% since 2010. “Unless we have some dramatic changes to the way we are doing things, then it’s highly unlikely that we are going to meet that goal,” says Kenneth Ngure, president of the International AIDS Society (IAS) and a public-health researcher at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology in Nairobi.

The problem is not scientific or medical; it’s political. According to a 2026 report by the Joint UN Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), the big barriers to overcome are funding cuts to essential treatment and prevention services and a lack of health-infrastructure investment to enable access to them; stigmatization of people with HIV; and the high cost of new, more-effective medications1.

Speaking at the 2026 IAS conference in July in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, warned that the HIV pandemic was far from over and could resurge without urgent action. “When prevention disappears, infections rise; when treatment is interrupted, people die,” Byanyima said during a press conference. “We’ve seen this before; we know how this story ends if we fail to act.”

Funding from high-income nations around the world for HIV-related projects in low- and middle-income countries dropped from nearly US$8.3 billion in 2024 to $6.2 billion in 2025, according to one report2.

Much of that decline was the result of cuts to US funding, which decreased from $6.7 billion to $4.6 billion. The Trump administration shut down the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cut support for the long-running President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) — an initiative that has saved around 26 million lives since its creation (see go.nature.com/4avmfao). Instead, the administration launched the America First Global Health Strategy that promised fundamental changes to the structure of HIV funding and support, shifting the focus to the United States and reducing funding to other countries.

Angeli Achrekar speaks at the AIDS 2024 Conference in Munich, Germany. Credit: UNAIDS

The funding cuts have hit community-based prevention services the hardest. For instance, in sub-Saharan Africa, which currently accounts for around half of all new HIV infections, programmes providing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) — involving antiretroviral drugs being taken to prevent infection rather than to treat it — greatly declined in 2025. Cameroon, Nigeria and Zambia all reported that the number of people receiving PrEP that year had fallen by at least half1. Multiple countries have also seen major declines in HIV testing, condom programmes and programmes designed to increase access to prevention services through changes to laws, regulations and policies that stigmatize or criminalize service users.

New infections have continued to increase in some Asian countries — such as Bangladesh, the Philippines, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, for example — and other nations including Brazil, Venezuela, Egypt and Fiji1,3.

“There are countries that, over time, they had gotten to a point of relative control of their epidemics, and then the minute you take your eyes off of it, you see these outbreaks,” says Angeli Achrekar, deputy executive director and global practice lead at UNAIDS.

“They may be small numbers, but the issues are still very real because when the virus continues to spread faster than we’re getting population-based viral suppression, we’re in a real bind,” she adds.

The goal of eliminating a disease as a public-health threat provides “a sort of escape clause”, says John Kaldor, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute at UNSW in Sydney, Australia. “We’re not actually trying to rid the earth of this condition,” Kaldor says. Elimination as a public-health threat means that new and existing cases are managed as an individual clinical problem, rather than requiring population or community-level responses such as mass screening, testing and treatment programmes. If those larger programmes are still needed and cost-effective, then elimination as a public-health threat hasn’t been achieved, Kaldor says.

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now

To end AIDS as a public-health threat, no groups or communities can be left behind. The idea of ending AIDS is problematic, says sociologist Jaime Garcia Iglesias, at the University of Edinburgh, UK, “because AIDS has always been defined … by the inequalities at a global scale, as well as inequalities in countries at the level of different communities. If we don’t tackle that, we’re not going to end AIDS — or we may end talking about AIDS but not actually end the epidemic and the conditions that made it possible.”

For example, Fiji had very few cases of HIV/AIDS for many years, but now has the fastest growing epidemic in the world, with a 14-fold increase in infections since 2021. A survey of those starting HIV treatment in 2024 found that nearly half reported injecting drugs as the main behaviour that puts them at risk of HIV infection3, suggesting that people who inject drugs are a group that needs targeted prevention and treatment interventions.

By most researchers’ definitions, superintelligence is an aspirational category of systems, not a reality.Credit: Andrzej Wojcicki/SPL

‘Superintelligence’ has arrived — at least by one definition of the term.

Will AI really kill us all? The science behind the hype

In an executive order issued on 29 September, US President Donald Trump declared that humanity is in “a new era of Super Intelligence”. The term artificial intelligence is outdated, the order said: “[T]oday’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence.” The order also directed federal agencies to use the phrases “Super Intelligence” and “SI” instead of “artificial intelligence” and “AI”.

Trump’s declaration has had a mixed reception. A post by billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk on the social-media platform X said: “No more AI. SI. It’s better,” adding that his company SpaceXAI will change its name to SpaceXSI. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, however, continues to use the term AI in his posts.

Trump’s order defines ‘Super Intelligence’ as “the technologies and systems encompassed by the term ‘artificial intelligence’”. But researchers were using the term superintelligence to refer to hypothetical, highly capable technologies long before the executive order. The word was popularized in science philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 book Superintelligence, which defined it as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest”.

A 2025 petition in which a host of AI researchers and others called for a slowdown in the development of superintelligence, similarly describes it as a system “that can significantly outperform all humans on essentially all cognitive tasks”.

But the term is still not completely defined, says Melanie Mitchell, an AI researcher at the Santa Fe institute in New Mexico. For instance, the components of human-level intelligence remain undefined. “None of this has rigorous meaning. People can use these terms to mean what they want,” she says.

Name changes are not a new practice for Trump. In August, when the United States and Canada were feuding over tariffs, Trump ordered federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America. The change reflected the lake’s importance to the United States, Trump’s order said.

Trump explained his reasoning behind the SI change to the United Nations last month. It “is much more accurate” than the term artificial intelligence, which “makes it sound fake”, Trump said, “And it’s not fake.”

Too dangerous to release: is Mythos the start of the restricted-AI era?

Darrell West, who researches AI policy at the Brookings Institution in Washington DC, sees the president’s renaming of AI as an effort to rebrand the technology as public sentiment turns against it. About 8 in 10 of those surveyed in a US poll last month were worried about the pace of AI development, and nearly 9 in 10 said they’re more concerned than excited about the prospect that AI might exceed human intelligence.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed worries about AI, for example posting on social media: “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” He has also criticized AI leaders who have called for regulation.

“The hope is that changing the name improves public acceptance of the technology” so that “the AI revolution will go forward”, West says. “But I think that is fanciful thinking.”

Asked about West’s assertion, the White House referred Nature to Trump’s public statements on the need for a new term.

Humans have never travelled alone. When our ancestors spread out of Africa and across the other continents, they carried their microorganisms with them. Writing in Nature, Carter et al.1 compare the community of gut microbes (also known as the microbiota) from the Indigenous Hadza people of Tanzania with that of the Tsimane of Bolivia, whose populations diverged during human migrations that occurred tens of thousands of years ago. The authors report that, despite these dispersals, hundreds of microbial species are present in both groups. Furthermore, genetic differences between strains of the same microbial species in Hadza and Tsimane populations were broadly consistent with the timescale of prehistoric human migrations. Many of these shared microbes are now rare or missing in populations from industrialized regions.

The winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Henri Kagan (left) and Kenso Soai, were announced on 7 October.Credit: Académie des sciences, Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty

Chemists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have won this year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on a long-standing mystery: how can living organisms create molecules that are just one of two possible mirror-image variants? In the 1980s, Kagan showed how catalysts can amplify a small asymmetry in handedness. And in the 1990s, Soai demonstrated that a one-handed molecule, produced in a reaction, can become its own catalyst, driving even greater asymmetry. Together they provided clues as to how natural reactions in living organisms might overwhelmingly produce just one type of mirror-image molecule.

I watched today’s chemistry prize announcement with a bevy of colleagues from the Nature chemistry journals, and the consensus in that room was that the winning work was a surprise, but a good one. Across the chemosphere, there was a lot of appreciation for the fact that we don’t have to debate, this year, if the work was ‘really biology, rather than chemistry’. And I heard several admiring mentions of chemist Donna Blackmond. Her work explores the mechanistic details of asymmetric organic catalysis and many thought she would also have been a worthy winner. And of course we were all delighted that Kenso Soai’s seminal 1995 paper, on what’s today known as the Soai reaction, was published in Nature (especially after seeing our beloved rival Science get a special mention in yesterday’s physics prize announcement).

Flora Graham, chief editor, Nature Briefing

Seventy-one percent of people with cancer in the United States live for at least five years after diagnosis, up from 49% in the late 1970s, says a new report. Highlights include huge strides against lung cancer and childhood leukaemias. In some cases, the numbers tell a nuanced story: the five-year survival rate for prostate cancer is now nearly 98% — a figure so high that it suggests some of the tumours were not malignant to start with, says cancer epidemiologist Rebecca Siegel.

Blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) can hear and respond to sounds up to 74 metres away — beyond the radius that scientists thought the animals’ hearing was restricted to. Researchers found that the sharks often turned sharply away from speakers playing certain frequencies of noise, which suggests they could tell where it was coming from. A response at this distance “suggests that they are detecting the particle motion associated with sound”, which hasn’t been observed in sharks before, says zoologist and study co-author Stephen Kajiura.

A patient is tended to by two nurses using a CUBE mobile isolation unit.credit: Elie BIGABA / ALIMA

In hospital isolation wards, health workers who treat people with Ebola must don time-consuming and uncomfortable protective suits. Intensive-care physician Richard Kojan and his colleagues developed the CUBE (emergency biosecurity chamber for epidemics), which allows them to treat highly contagious people in the field without the stifling suits. The 9-metre-square room can be set up in 90 minutes. “When we introduced the CUBE, we invited patients’ relatives into the facilities to see their family members through the plastic walls of the unit,” says Kojan. “It had never been possible to see and spend time with their loved ones before. This has had a huge social impact and helped to resolve tensions.” (Nature | 9 min read)

Read more in Nature Spotlight: Infectious diseases. (Elie BIGABA / ALIMA)

A growing body of evidence hints that the human brain can produce new nerve cells throughout a person’s life, challenging the long-held belief that people are born with all the neurons they’ll ever have. If that’s true, our brains could have an enduring ability to repair and regenerate. But neuroscientists remain divided, and influential papers have come down on both sides of the argument. Still, some think that the evidence is strong enough to shift focus onto potential applications of neurogenesis, such as treating neurodegenerative disease.

Earlier this year, a team of nanoscientists visited a local primary school to give a lesson on their work. To give the kids a sense of just how small ‘nano’ is, a teacher wrote 0.000000001 on a whiteboard. The children quickly adorned the number with a face, antennae and legs — the ‘nanopillar’ was born. The student “made the science their own”, the team writes. The group uses these visits both to inspire young children and to test themselves: “if we cannot explain our research to a second grader, then we probably do not understand it as well as we think we do”, they say.

Nature Nanotechnology | 5 min read

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Can your brain grow new neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Mariana Lenharo
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

Illustration by Klara Gryglicka

For a long time, it was a truism in science that the human brain is born with all of the neurons it will ever have. But truisms can crumble, and this one is looking shaky.

The brain struggles to make new neurons in people with depression

A tantalizing body of evidence suggests that the human brain produces new nerve cells throughout a person’s life. If that’s true, then our brains could have an enduring ability to repair and regenerate.

That concept sounds very appealing to neuroscientist Arturo Alvarez-Buylla at the University of California, San Francisco, who has spent years investigating this topic. “If someone shows it clearly, I’ll be the first to be super happy and say, well, I didn’t waste my life studying a mechanism that is not present in humans.”

The problem is, when he looks at the data, he just doesn’t see it.

The question of whether the human brain can generate nerve cells after childhood has been controversial for decades. Influential papers have come down on both sides of the argument over the years, and the concept has captured public interest well beyond academia.

Part of the reason for the prominence of the debate is that it involves the giants in the field, says Hongjun Song, a neuroscientist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. “The people who have positive and negative data are the top researchers,” he says, “and they are all doing good science.”

Some researchers think the evidence for neurogenesis is strong enough that it’s time to focus instead on understanding what these neurons do and, ultimately, on whether this process can be used to treat diseases that involve neurodegeneration. But at the same time, questions remain about the methods used to detect neurogenesis, which today rely mostly on genetic markers associated with it and provide only indirect evidence of its existence.

Gerd Kempermann, a neuroscientist at the German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases in Dresden, says that, despite the continuing debate, the field is now moving to what he calls a consolidating phase. “Yes, there are some gaps to be closed,” he says. “But at the same time, there’s just an explosion of opportunities.”

Santiago Ramón y Cajal, who is considered one of the founding fathers of modern neuroscience, famously wrote in the 1910s that, in the adult brains of mammals, “everything may die, nothing may be regenerated”. For many years, this was a central dogma of the field. The first to challenge it was neuroscientist Joseph Altman, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, who found signs of adult neurogenesis in the brains of rats and cats1 in the 1960s.

Some think that the finding cost him his job. “The fact is that he really didn’t get tenure at MIT as a result of this,” says Rusty Gage, a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California. “It was just hard for people to believe that there could be new cells being born in the nervous system of the adult.”

But in the 1980s, neurogenesis was discovered in adult birds2, where it was thought to play a part in song learning. Evidence in many other animal species followed, and the idea became more widely accepted.

New neurons being produced (red) in the hippocampus of middle-aged mice.Credit: Michael Fatt

A typical method for detecting newly generated neurons in animals is to inject them with a chemical called bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU). Because of its structure, BrdU is incorporated into DNA when a cell divides, and researchers can then tell which neurons are newly generated by using a marker that recognizes the molecule.

In the 1990s, Gage and his colleagues were wondering whether this process happened in humans. They were specifically interested in the hippocampus — a brain region involved in memory and learning — because neurogenesis had been observed there in other adult animals. At the time, BrdU was sometimes used as a diagnostic tool in people with cancer to check how rapidly their tumours were dividing. The researchers theorized that if they investigated the brains of these individuals soon after their deaths, they could check whether neurogenesis had occurred in the time since BrdU had been administered.

Brains of ‘super agers’ are strong producers of new neurons

“So, we were able to do it,” Gage says. The researchers could see cells that had incorporated BrdU, meaning that they had originated from dividing cells. Some were non-neuronal cells, but the team identified others as neurons. “We knew this was important,” Gage says. So, the group brought in scientists from other laboratories to look at the samples and check whether they agreed with the team’s interpretation. The researchers also sent tissue to collaborators in Sweden, who analysed the samples and came to the same conclusion. The findings, based on brain tissue from five people, were published3 in Nature Medicine in 1998. The paper was accompanied by a light-hearted Editorial4 that declared that there was no longer a reason to lose sleep over the thought of “the inevitable, gradual loss of our precious and predetermined 100 billion neuronal quota”.

The case had been settled, it seemed. Twenty years later, a paper5 would throw the field into turmoil.

One of the authors of that controversial paper was Shawn Sorrells, a neuroscientist who is now at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania. Back in the 2010s, as a postdoc in Alvarez-Buylla’s lab, he was studying the amygdala, a brain region involved in processing emotions. Because neurogenesis had been established in the hippocampus by Gage and other groups, Sorrells’s project was to probe the amygdala for signs of proteins that are indicative of cell division and immature neurons, to check whether these two stages of neurogenesis could be found throughout life in that area, as well.

When a lab technician was sectioning a sample of human brain tissue, Sorrells asked him to take sections from the hippocampus as well. That way, the tissue could be used as a positive control; given the findings from other groups, Sorrells thought that newly generated neurons would definitely be found there.

He was confused when none showed up. The focus of Sorrells’s project shifted to investigating why that was. He collaborated with another neuroscientist in his group, Mercedes Paredes, who now has her own lab at the University of California, San Francisco, and with researchers at labs in Spain and China. Altogether, they analysed 59 brain samples from people of various ages and tested several methods to detect new neurons. Their findings suggested that the number of young neurons in the hippocampus drops sharply during a person’s first year of life, to a tiny number later in childhood, with almost none appearing in any samples from people above age 13. “We did this independently in three different labs, because I really wanted to be convinced,” says Alvarez-Buylla.

Many studies looking for new neuron growth in the human brain have included the hippocampus (cell nuclei shown in blue), a hotspot for neurogenesis in animals.Credit: Cell Applications Inc./Science Photo Library

All of the checking and rechecking took time. “You start to realize it’s not just you, it’s not just the antibodies, it’s not just your protocol, it’s not just that sample,” Sorrells says. “This takes years and years of us working together to decide that it was clear enough that we needed to say something.”

When the results were finally published in Nature in 2018, the push-back was immediate, with some scientists saying that the evidence was not strong enough to support the researchers’ conclusion.

Kempermann thinks that the controversy sparked by the paper drained a lot of energy from the field. “It was really a drawback, it has killed careers and we know that people in the field had a hard time getting grants” after that, he says. In the years between the 1998 and 2018 papers, other influential work had supported the existence of human adult neurogenesis, with the paper by Sorrells and his colleagues being an outlier. “It was unclear to us why everybody was jumping on the one negative finding.”

The uproar prompted researchers to investigate why some scientists were seeing these young neurons and others weren’t. The next year, María Llorens-Martín, a neuroscientist at the Autonomous University of Madrid, argued that the difference in findings might come down to how the human brain tissue was preserved and processed. Using her own preservation methods and some of the same markers that Sorrells and his colleagues had used, her team found “abundant” neurogenesis in healthy people between 43 and 87 years of age6. Alvarez-Buylla says that he tried her technique, but it did not change his conclusion. He says that although some cells display markers for immature neurons, they don’t have the shape of a young neuron, and there’s no good evidence that they are generated in the adult, as opposed to being cells that haven’t matured since infancy.

The latest studies in the field identify adult neurogenesis using gene-expression techniques. The idea is that, if scientists know which genes are expressed in cells at various stages of neuronal development — from neural stem cells to intermediate progenitor cells and neuroblasts (the precursors to neurons), all the way to immature neurons — they can look for them in the cells of the adult human brain using single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Most studies use post-mortem samples; if they find cells bearing these genetic signatures, it suggests that neurogenesis was ongoing at the time of death.

When the technique was first used, it initially seemed to suggest that adult neurogenesis was not present in humans. Research led by scientists at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, used gene-expression signatures that had been identified in newly generated mouse neurons and searched for the same signatures in brain tissue from several species. Although they spotted cells with these signatures in pigs and monkeys, they failed to find them in people7.

Brain-cell growth keeps mood disorders at bay

The problem, says Song, was that different species seem to use distinct genes to control the process of neurogenesis. To solve this, he and his team used data from human infant neurogenesis as a reference. His lab also pioneered an approach involving an artificial-intelligence model to identify the molecular signature of young neurons in infants and look for them in adults. With that method, the team was able to find cells with the characteristics of immature neurons in people of various ages8.

But critics argued that they couldn’t tell for sure whether the immature neurons had really been produced in the adult brain, or if they had existed in their immature state for decades. “There was a possibility that these immature cells were generated right after birth, or even before birth, and they just stayed immature for a long period of time,” Song says.

Last year, a paper in Science addressed that gap. Using a similar technique involving single-nucleus sequencing and machine learning, stem-cell researcher Jonas Frisén at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm and his team found dividing cells — neural progenitors — in adult human brains9. “That’s one step further,” says Song. Now, it’s clear that “in the human adult brain you actually have cells that can divide with a potential to give rise to neurons”.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: James Dinneen
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Search author on:

Controlled fires burnt at Mount Solitary in the Blue Mountains range in Australia in 2018.Credit: lovleah/Getty

The suppression of Indigenous burning practices in Australia after British colonization probably transformed swathes of the southeast into dense, flammable forests that contribute to bigger, hotter bush fires today, according to a reconstruction of fires in the region over the past 1,000 years published in Nature1.

The researchers suggest that restoring Indigenous approaches to forest management could lower the risk of devastating fires, particularly as the climate warms. “It gives us another variable when we’re trying to tackle this problem, rather than just focusing on climate change,” says Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a Wiradjuri scholar and palaeoecologist at the University of Melbourne, Australia.

The team set out to understand why southeastern Australia is experiencing larger, more-destructive fires, such as the unprecedented Black Summer fires in 2019–20, which burnt more than 8 million hectares of land of forest in that region.

In 2022, a team that Fletcher was part of used pollen records to show that forests in the region tended to be more open and grassy before British colonization at the end of the eighteenth century2. Soon after the colonization, forests changed, says Fletcher. “You can see right across the landscape there was an increase in woody fuels following the British invasion,” he adds.

To investigate this pattern in more detail, Fletcher and his colleagues collected a sediment core from a lake at the southeastern tip of Australia in Croajingolong National Park, part of the traditional lands of the Gunaikurnai people. Reconstructions of the landscape as well as historical evidence show that they regularly burnt the land until their violent removal by the British in the mid-nineteenth century.

Like in the 2022 work, the researchers analysed pollen in the extracted sediment to reconstruct the make-up of plant species and the structure of the surrounding forest over the past 1,000 years. This record showed an open woodland, with grasses and few trees for 800 years. Then, around 1840, the researchers found that the coverage of eucalyptus (Eucalyptus spp.) had doubled and woody shrubs had spread across the area.

The team also analysed charcoal in the sediment to estimate the temperature of fires over the study time frame. They identified molecules produced by burning plants at different temperatures in the laboratory, then searched for those molecules in the sediment samples. They found an increasing fraction of high-temperature charcoals from the mid-nineteenth century onwards, suggesting more-intense fires.

The researchers say that the changing vegetation and fire regime are linked: hotter fires spur the growth of more-flammable vegetation, more fuel and a denser canopy, creating what they call a “catastrophic wildfire loop”. Eucalyptus trees rapidly sprout after a blaze clears out other competing plants, says Fletcher.

The authors attribute this change to the end of regular, small fires ignited by Indigenous people to protect certain areas from burning or to promote vegetation growth in other areas for animals to eat.

On 15 May this year, an Ebola disease outbreak caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus was declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. This species was named after the Ugandan district in which it was first recorded in 2007. In the two previous known Bundibugyo virus outbreaks in these countries, the fatality rate was between 30% and 50%. By 23 September, the number of cases in the DRC had reached 7,890 and around 3,799 people had died — a death rate of around 48%.

There is no licenced vaccine or cure for this species of Ebola virus. Two of four potential Bundibugyo vaccines — which aim to train the body’s immune response to the virus — are currently in clinical trials, as are a number of drugs that could be given to people who have potentially been exposed to the virus but do not yet have symptoms.

Nature Spotlight: Infectious diseases

Richard Kojan, an intensive-care physician at The Alliance for International Medical Action (ALIMA) in Paris, has been working on the frontlines of the response in the DRC. Health-care workers such as Kojan face many challenges. The symptoms of Bundibugyo infection are very similar to that of the more-deadly Zaire species: fatigue, headaches, fever, bleeding and severe diarrhoea and vomiting. Many people with these diseases arrive at treatment centres in circulatory shock and ultimately die from multi-organ failure.

Kojan has more than two decades of medical experience. He has worked as an anaesthetist in public and private hospitals since 2002, after graduating as a specialist in intensive care and anaesthesiology from the University of Kinshasa. He joined ALIMA in 2010.

We don’t have vaccines for many of the viruses in the filovirus family, which includes the Ebola viruses. As well as this, health systems in low-income countries such as the DRC are not well prepared for epidemics like these, and we tend to discover outbreaks late: that is why death rates are often very high at the beginning of an outbreak. While we’re running diagnostic laboratory tests, the virus continues spreading. Low resource levels also mean that health-care workers aren’t well prepared with measures for infection prevention and control, such as isolating patients, and they might not have the required medical equipment.

Ebola is not a health-care worker’s first thought when someone presents with symptoms. For example, fatigue is one of the first symptoms, but lots of people in this region are working incredibly hard, many of them are fatigued. No one sees a person with that symptom and immediately thinks they might have Ebola, which makes it hard to spot the early stages of an outbreak.

Better diagnostics could have limited this Ebola outbreak

Also, Ebola symptoms are very similar to those of many other tropical diseases, including malaria. Even when people seek medical treatment quickly, other diseases must be ruled out before Ebola is considered. As this is happening, time is being lost because the virus is still multiplying inside the person’s body.

It’s very difficult. Many people arrive at our treatment facilities with metabolic disorders, electrolyte imbalances from loss of fluids, unstable blood pressure and blood flow to vital organs, and in shock or respiratory distress. Health-care workers need to urgently correct electrolyte imbalances with intravenous potassium and treat respiratory issues with oxygen. Antibiotics are given to prevent bacterial infection — one of the major complications of Ebola — and adrenaline is used to counter shock.

All of this is challenging because people with Ebola are kept in separate rooms in the hospital in an area known as the red zone. To enter it, health-care professionals must put on full personal protective equipment (PPE), which takes time. This makes it difficult to monitor patients continuously and to intervene quickly when there is a problem. The PPE makes you sweat so much that it’s hard to stay inside the red zone for more than 30 minutes. After 20 minutes, you start to feel bad. But all of our facilities are full of patients. So, you can’t go inside for just 30 minutes. You would never be able help everyone in that time.

Atherosclerosis involves the build up of fatty plaque (yellow) in the walls of arteries, limiting the flow of blood (red blood cells shown).Credit: Kateryna Kon/SPL

A gut microbe that’s commonly found in humans manufactures a molecule that is capable of slashing cholesterol levels and shrinking plaque in arteries, according to a study published today in Nature1.

Baffling chronic pain eases after doses of gut microbes

When given to mice, the compound, from the gut bacterium Bacteroides uniformis, reduced the animals’ arterial plaque by about half. It achieved the feat, researchers found, using the same biological action as that of statins, drugs that are prescribed to hundreds of millions of people worldwide to ward off cardiovascular disease.

The findings underline new ways in which people’s collection of gut microorganisms, known as their microbiome, might be harnessed to protect the heart, says study co-author Wenjing Zhao, a microbiologist at Sun Yat-sen University in Shenzhen, China.

The study provides “valuable evidence that the gut microbiome can influence vascular health”, moving beyond a simple link between heart disease and the microbiome, and towards “evidence for a potentially causal biological mechanism”, says Ben Chen, a cardiovascular specialist at Monash Victorian Heart Institute in Melbourne, Australia.

Diseases caused by atherosclerosis, the progressive build-up of inflammatory plaques in the walls of arteries, remain the leading cause of death globally. Although daily doses of statins have reduced the number of deaths, this alone fails to reduce cholesterol sufficiently in nearly half of people with advanced heart disease. And some people can’t tolerate high doses of the drugs.

Memory loss is fuelled by gut microbes in ageing mice

To find an alternative, Zhao and her colleagues analysed the gut flora present in stool samples from people with and without cardiovascular disease. One species stood out: B. uniformis. That’s because levels of the bacterium were often depleted in those with heart disease compared with in healthy individuals.

Next, researchers genetically engineered mice so that they developed atherosclerosis and fed them a high-fat diet to simulate the conditions in some people with heart disease. When the scientists administered live B. uniformis to the animals, it shrunk the plaques in their main arteries by about one-third, compared with the untreated mice. The bacterial dose also led to a drop in the levels of fatty substances in the blood, including total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein (LDL), sometimes called ‘bad cholesterol’. Moreover, it reduced the amount of inflammatory immune cells infiltrating the rodents’ arterial walls.

Zhao and her colleagues isolated the molecule driving this protection: pentadecanoic acid. Further analyses showed that the molecule inhibits a liver enzyme involved in cholesterol production that is also targeted by statin medications. Blocking the enzyme triggers the liver to generate more LDL receptors, which in turn yank excess cholesterol out of the bloodstream.

The 3D and line structures of pentadecanoic acid (carbon, grey; oxygen, red; and hydrogen, white).Credit: Chromatos/Shutterstock

To see whether the animal findings would translate to people, Zhao’s team examined blood and stool samples from more than 200 human donors. People with abnormally high concentrations of fatty molecules such as cholesterol in their blood had lower levels of pentadecanoic acid than did healthy individuals. Stool analyses also showed that people with heart disease carried fewer bacterial genes dedicated to manufacturing the molecule than did people in the control group.

More than 700 preprints in various fields of mathematics were posted simultaneously by OpenAI.Credit: Monty Rakusen/DigitalVision via Getty

The research community is in uproar after OpenAI released a trove of more than 700 mathematical preprints entirely generated by AI on 6 October. The San Francisco, California-based maker of ChatGPT posted the preprints on the software repository Github.

Although some mathematicians celebrated the solution of longstanding problems, others took to social media to complain about being scooped. Some were incensed at what one physicist called a ‘slopocalypse’, even if the mathematical content could end up being formally correct.

The sheer number of papers posted at the same time is “staggering”, wrote Alvaro Lozano-Robledo, a number theorist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs, on the social-media platform X. “Why is OpenAI trying to solve hundreds of math problems to be released all at once?”, he added.

In an e-mail to Nature, a spokesperson for OpenAI wrote that the company’s goal is to provide tools for mathematicians and scientists. “To accomplish this, we evaluate and develop our models against difficult frontier problems in all sciences.”

Who gets credit in the AI era? OpenAI maths bombshell sparks debate

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at rival company Anthropic, also in San Francisco, commented on X that there will be “sad stories” for some researchers who might find their projects pre-empted by the OpenAI release. “We should put that aside for today though. It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history,” he wrote, because it shows how quickly the technology has become useful to mathematicians.

The large batch of preprints did not include any solutions to the five remaining ‘Millennium Prize Problems’, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which has its scientific headquarters in Oxford, UK, at the turn of the twenty-first century. (OpenAI’s preprint on the Navier-Stokes equation, released in September, solved one of the original seven problems. Another one was solved by mathematicians in the early 2000s.)

Still, some of the preprints were on problems related to those five, including the Hodge conjecture on complex algebraic varieties and the Riemann hypothesis on the statistical properties of prime numbers. The spokesperson for OpenAI said, “We will leave it to the broader community to assess [their] significance.”

The winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Henri Kagan (left) and Kenso Soai, were announced on 7 October.Credit: Académie des sciences, Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty

Two scientists who solved the mystery of why some chemical reactions create molecules that are just one of two possible mirror-image variants have won this year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Henri Kagan, at the University of Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Kenso Soai, at Tokyo University, share the 12-million Swedish kronor (US$1.2-million) prize, announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on 7 October.

Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light

“I am very excited to receive the very nice news about the Nobel prize. This is one of the most exciting days in my life,” said Soai, speaking to the Nobel committee after the prize was announced, adding that he was out shopping near his house when he received the call.

Although they could occur in either form, life’s building blocks are one-handed or ‘homochiral’ — for example, DNA is right-handed whereas amino acids in humans are left-handed. The prize-winning discovery relates to the key question of how this chemical asymmetry emerges in nature.

In experiments conducted in the 1980s, Kagan showed how a small asymmetry in the handedness of a catalyst can be amplified in the reaction products1. Then in 1995, Soai designed a reaction in which a chiral product was also itself a catalyst, driving even greater asymmetry in handedness2. Together, this research suggests how natural reactions in living organisms might overwhelmingly produce just one type of mirror-image molecule.

“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, in a statement. “The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular.”

“Kagan is a very, very modest person with a real passion for chemistry, he didn’t care about being famous,” says Olivier Riant, an organometallic chemist at the University of Louvain in Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium, who as a PhD student in Kagan's lab at the University of Paris-Sud.

Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of cosmic neutrinos

Today, the discoveries are essential for chemists when designing reactions to create drugs, materials and even perfumes. The winners’ discoveries “challenge what we thought we knew and open up entirely new ways of thinking about, and designing, chemical reactions”, says Mónica Pérez-Temprano, a mechanistic chemist at the Institute of Chemical Research of Catalonia in Tarragona, Spain.

Chemists have long known that some molecules come in two mirror-image or chiral forms, known as enantiomers, and that life often operates using just one of these. But when chemists carried out reactions that created such molecules, they usually obtained an even mix of the two types. How living organisms create just one mirror-image was therefore a conundrum.

Catalysts — substances that drive a chemical reaction but are not used up — soon emerged as the key. If the catalyst itself is chiral, this can boost the creation of just one mirror-image molecule. In 1953, Charles Frank, a theoretical physicist at the University of Bristol, UK, suggested that if chemical reactions could produce their own chiral catalyst, it would have a self-reinforcing effect and cause one mirror-image to dominate3.

The winners of the 2001 Nobel chemistry prize, William Knowles, Ryoji Noyori and Barry Sharpless, designed reactions that used a chiral catalyst to steer reactions into creating just one version of a molecule. This year’s prize recognizes Kagan and Soai for going further and realizing Frank’s vision by designing chemical reactions that create their own chiral catalyst.

“Kagan showed how it could be done in principle and then the Soai reaction gave us the first actual real example,” says Jonathan Clayden, an organic chemist at the University of Bristol, UK.

Soai “did a remarkable job of tuning autocatalytic reactions”, says Stephen Fletcher, a synthetic chemist at the University of Oxford, UK. In a chemical mixture, “sometimes you could have one million molecules of one handedness on one side, and one million and one molecules of the other handedness on the other side, and Soai worked on how to amplify the imbalance — that’s remarkable”.

The work of Kagan and Soai has attracted a lot of interest from researchers seeking to explain why molecules of life, such as amino and nucleic acids, tend to be present in only one chiral form, says Furkan Öztürk, a geochemist at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena who studies the chemistry of the origins of life.

Since the discovery of the Soai reaction, Öztürk says, scientists have sought to determine whether or not a similar reaction could have occurred on ‘prebiotic’ Earth, before life emerged. “The catch is that the [Soai] reaction requires conditions — famously, it cannot run in water — and reagents that are not so compatible with prebiotic Earth conditions and its chemical inventory,” he says. “But I think there is a lot to learn from its fundamental principles to understand the prebiotic origins of homochirality.”

“A lot of people are trying to work on biological relevance to the Soai reaction. I can see this prize being a spark” to rekindle this research, says Fletcher.

Kagan first discovered a reaction in which an initial slight imbalance in the chirality of the catalyst amplified over the course of the experiment, creating a much larger imbalance in the presence of each type of chiral catalyst. Soai then looked for other reactions with this asymmetric effect and, crucially, ones in which the catalyst forms part of the reaction, known as autocatalytic reactions.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Peter Wieczorek
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature 
volume
 658, 
pages
337–341 (2026) Cite this article

The seventh row of the periodic table of the elements has been completed with the discovery of the five heaviest elements from flerovium (Fl, Z = 114) through oganesson (Og, Z = 118)1. Chemical properties of the superheavy elements (SHE, Z ≥ 104) are unique owing to the strong influence of relativistic effects on their valence electron shells2. The stability of the metal–ligand bonding in carbonyl complexes is a property that is predicted to be affected by such effects3,4. Here we present an experimental gas chromatography study on the stability of the Sg(CO)6 complex. The measured formation yields of Sg(CO)6 and W(CO)6 enabled determining the first bond dissociation energy (FBDE) of Sg(CO)6, which is 4(2) kJ mol−1 lower than that of W(CO)6 and corresponds to a value of 188(9) kJ mol−1. Thus, the trend of increasing FBDE values of hexacarbonyls within group 6 of the periodic table is reversed from W to Sg. Our result agrees with state-of-the-art theoretical calculations, which predict a decrease in the FBDE from W(CO)6 to Sg(CO)6 owing to the relativistic destabilization of the 6d atomic orbitals (AOs) in Sg (ref. 4). Also, the adsorption enthalpy value of Sg(CO)6 on gold of \({45}_{-6}^{+4}\,{\rm{kJ}}\,{{\rm{mol}}}^{-1}\) is reported.

Man-made SHE (atomic number Z ≥ 104) are produced in nuclear fusion reactions by irradiating Pb, Bi or actinide targets with heavy ions. The rates of those reactions substantially decrease with increasing Z, reaching production rates of single atoms per week for Og. Also, extremely short lifetimes of SHE isotopes limit the number of chemical systems that can be studied experimentally5,6,7. SHE heavier than seaborgium (Sg, Z = 106) were chemically investigated only in the gas phase8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15.

Investigations of chemical bonding in compounds of the heaviest elements are of particular interest because strong relativistic effects influence their valence AOs. The 7s and 7p1/2 AOs are relativistically contracted and stabilized, leading to the closed shell (6d107s2) and quasi-closed shell (7s27p1/22) configurations in copernicium (Cn, Z = 112) and flerovium (Fl, Z = 114), respectively, and thus to high volatility and inertness of these elements8,9,10,11,12. The stabilized 7p1/2 AO also leads to a weaker reactivity of nihonium (Nh, Z = 113) and moscovium (Mc, Z = 115) with respect to their lighter homologues Tl and Bi, respectively (ref. 13). In the elements of the 6d series, the valence 6d and 7s AOs participate in chemical bonding. The indirect relativistic effect is the destabilization and expansion of the 6d AOs, screened from the nucleus by the spherical inner s and p1/2 AOs. This effect is expected to influence properties of the 6d element compounds2, albeit to a lesser extent, as the central metal atom is surrounded by ligands6.

Among the known SHE compounds, the hexacarbonyl complex of Sg, Sg(CO)6, in which the Sg atom is in the zero-valent state and surrounded by six neutral carbon monoxide (CO) ligands, has attracted much attention14. In particular, the value of the FBDE, that is, the energy needed to detach one CO ligand from Sg(CO)6, is a measure of the compound stability and is expected to be influenced by relativistic effects3,4. Bonding in the hexacarbonyls of lighter homologues of Sg, that is, Cr, Mo, W, was originally investigated theoretically using the density functional theory (DFT) approach16,17,18. Two types of electron density transfer process were shown to be involved in the formation of the metal–CO bond: the σ-forth donation from the molecular orbital Φσ(Eg) of the CO ligands to the d(Eg) AO of the metal atom (M) and the π-back donation from the d(T2g) AO of M to the Φπ(T2g) of CO (ref. 16). The influence of relativistic effects on the M–CO bond strength in hexacarbonyls was shown to increase from Cr to Mo and to W (ref. 18). Nash and Bursten calculated the FBDE of W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6 using the relativistic effective core potentials (RECPs) and suggested that the FBDE value should increase from 46(2) kcal mol−1 for W(CO)6 to 47(2) kcal mol−1 for Sg(CO)6 owing to the stronger d(M) → (π)CO back donation overcompensating the weaker σ(CO) → d(M) donation from the CO ligands3. However, those calculations were unable to reproduce the experimental FBDE values for carbonyls of Mo and W and the FBDE of Sg(CO)6 has been obtained by normalizing the calculated values for the lighter complexes to the experimental ones3. The most recent FBDE calculations for Mo(CO)6, W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6 were performed by Iliaš and Pershina4 using several non-relativistic and relativistic DFT approaches, as well as ab initio Dirac–Coulomb (DC) correlated methods, including  coupled cluster with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations (CCSD(T)). The best agreement with the experimental FBDE value of Mo(CO)6 and W(CO)6 was achieved by the Amsterdam Density Functional (ADF) spin–orbit (SO) and DC-DFT methods. These calculations for Sg(CO)6, at both the scalar relativistic (SR) and SO levels, predicted the FBDE of Sg(CO)6 to be about 10 kJ mol−1 smaller than that of W(CO)6. This decrease in the M–CO bond strength in Sg(CO)6 compared with W(CO)6, which is unexpected given the increasing trend from Cr to W, is ascribed to the reduction in the electron density transfer processes, that is, both in the σ-forth donation from the Φσ(Eg) of CO to the d(Eg) AO of Sg and the π-back donation from the d(T2g) AO of Sg to the Φπ(T2g) of CO (ref. 4). The relativistic destabilization of the 6d(Sg) AOs is responsible for this effect (for details, see Methods section ‘Relativistic effects on the d(M) AOs’). The non-relativistic FBDE values were, by contrast, increasing from Mo to Sg, that is, Mo < W < Sg (ref. 4). These controversial predictions for the stability trend of the hexacarbonyls in group 6, along with a general desire to study the influence of relativistic effects on bonding in the 6d element compounds, sparked interest in related experimental studies.

The Sg carbonyl complex, Sg(CO)6, was synthesized in 2014 and its adsorption on a SiO2 surface was studied in comparison with hexacarbonyl complexes of Mo and W (ref. 14). Almost identical interaction strengths with the SiO2 surface, that is, adsorption enthalpy (\(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Si}}{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\)) values, were reported for all three compounds14. Follow-up studies performed by different groups aimed at increasing the efficiency of such carbonyl complex studies19,20,21,22,23. These studies focused on determining the FBDE of the Sg hexacarbonyl complex and synthesis of carbonyl complexes of elements heavier than Sg. They also include the study of the chemical speciation of carbonyl compounds on a one-atom-at-a-time level performed using the laser ablation method in combination with time-of-flight mass spectrometry23. Before the present work, a first experimental attempt to measure the FBDE value for Sg(CO)6 was reported; however, no FBDE value for Sg(CO)6 has been given24.

As described in Methods section ‘Experimental’, 259Sg nuclei were produced by means of the nuclear reaction 208Pb(52Cr,1n)259Sg (ref. 25) and isolated in the gas-filled separator TransActinide Separator and Chemistry Apparatus (TASCA). Nuclear reaction products were flushed from a gas-filled recoil transfer chamber (RTC), installed at the TASCA focal plane, into the combined gas chromatography and detection set-up. The latter consisted of two detector arrays, connected in series, in which the 161,162W and 259Sg species were deposited according to their volatility (see Fig. 1 and Methods section ‘Experimental’ for details). All products of the multistep process of the carbonyl complex formation and decomposition, which occur inside the RTC, are extracted as cations or neutrals by the gas flow into the first detection channel, miniCOMPACT13, except for those that adsorbed on the surface inside the RTC owing to finite extraction yields. The miniCOMPACT array, kept at room temperature, was directly connected to the RTC to detect non-volatile species, for example, unreacted atoms/ions and carbonyl complex fragments, M(CO)n (1 ≤ n ≤ 5), extracted from the RTC by rapidly flowing gas and deposited in miniCOMPACT by diffusion-controlled deposition. The second array, COMPACT, was similar to that used in previous studies on the in situ formation and adsorption of W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6 (ref. 14) but had a Au layer on the detector surface.

Experimental set-up behind the second quadrupole magnet (Q2) at the end of the TASCA separator. Fusion products recoiling from the target, 259Sg (161,162W), produced in the nuclear reaction of the 52Cr ion beam with the 208Pb (112Sn) targets, were separated with TASCA and entered the RTC through a 6-μm-thick Mylar window. They were thermalized inside the RTC in a He + CO gas mixture and flushed out to the gas chromatography set-up. The first gas chromatography and detection channel, miniCOMPACT, is covered with a SiO2 layer and connected directly to the RTC exit. A negative temperature gradient was maintained along the second detector array, COMPACT, which has a Au layer on the detector surface. It was connected to miniCOMPACT with a 30-cm-long polytetrafluoroethylene capillary.

The presence of the 161,162W and 259Sg species inside the two arrays was determined by registration of their nuclear decay (see Methods section ‘Experimental’). As expected, the 161,162W and 259Sg species were found to be distributed between the two arrays. The species deposited in the first miniCOMPACT array (Fig. 2, left panel) were assigned to non-volatile metal atoms and carbonyl fragments M(CO)n (1 ≤ n ≤ 5; M = 161,162W, 259Sg). These unsaturated carbonyl complex fragments are highly reactive and react very quickly with other molecules or surfaces they encounter20,26. Thus, on first contact with a solid surface in the first detector array, they readily adsorb on the SiO2 surface. The hexacarbonyl complexes, 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg(CO)6, known as volatile and non-reactive species, pass through the miniCOMPACT array and reach the COMPACT array, in which they adsorb on Au at lower temperatures according to their known volatility (Fig. 2, right panel).

The distributions of events registered in the miniCOMPACT detector array (left panel) and in the COMPACT detector array (right panel) originating from: 259Sg (green bars), sum of 259Sg and its daughter 255Rf (red bars) and 161,162W (black line histogram). The decay chains from 259Sg observed in COMPACT and their positions, as well as the temperature gradient in COMPACT (dashed grey line), are shown in the right panel, together with the experimental distribution pattern of 161,162W(CO)6. The known decay properties of the decay chain from 259Sg are shown to the left of the graph27. Colour coding in the decay chains: α decay (yellow) and spontaneous fission (SF) (green). The α-particle energies are given in MeV. The black triangles represent the decays observed during beam-off periods.

In the miniCOMPACT array, 126 chains were detected. Of these, 72 chains were assigned to decay chains starting from 259Sg and 54 chains/spontaneous fission events to 255Rf, the α-decay daughter of 259Sg. Thus, about 40% of all chains were registered without the leading 259Sg decay, which is the result of the decay of short-lived 259gSg (T1/2 = 402(56) ms) and 259mSg (T1/2 = 226(27) ms)27 inside the RTC. The ratio between the total number of chains (126 events), starting from either 259m,gSg or 255Rf, and the number of chains starting with the 259m,gSg decay (72 events) allows estimating the flush-out time to about 250 ms. Three extra decay chains starting from 259Sg were observed in COMPACT and assigned to the deposition of 259Sg(CO)6. No further decay chains, with missing 259Sg, were registered in COMPACT. Only the events that started with 259Sg were used for the calculation of the ratio of chains between the two detectors. Using Poisson statistics for uncertainty quantification, the three observed Sg events in COMPACT translate to 1.43–6.27 events at the 68% confidence level28. About 20% of all 161,162W events were found in COMPACT forming a deposition peak of 161,162W(CO)6, whereas the main 161,162W fraction was found in miniCOMPACT, deposited as non-volatile species (Fig. 2). Thus, the ratio between volatile, M(CO)6, and non-volatile species, M(CO)n (0 ≤ n ≤ 5) (M = 161,162W and 259Sg), registered in COMPACT and miniCOMPACT, respectively, was determined as 0.20 ± 0.01 for 161,162W and \({0.04}_{-0.02}^{+0.05}\) for 259Sg. These ratios indicate a rather low chemical yield of the hexacarbonyl complex formation. On the basis of Monte Carlo simulations29, the probability for nuclear decay in flight of volatile 259m,gSg(CO)6 was estimated to be about 16%. Given the three detected events from 259m,gSg(CO)6, this would add fewer than one event, which would be among the 72 259m,gSg events registered in miniCOMPACT. This would change the ratio of volatile and non-volatile for 259m,gSg fractions to 0.05, which lies within the statistical error bars of the value \({0.04}_{-0.02}^{+0.05}\).

On thermalization in the carrier gas (He:CO = 1:1) inside the RTC, the 259Sg and 161,162W ions (or atoms) undergo collisions with He atoms and CO molecules, leading to subsequent chemical reactions, predominantly with neutral CO molecules. They can also react with gas impurities, for example, water molecules. Such adducts of metal ions (Ac2+ and No2+) with water and nitrogen molecules were recently observed behind the Berkeley Gas-filled Separator30. We kept the concentration of such impurities below about 1 ppm, so that formation of complexes with CO molecules was highly favoured over that of adduct formation.

Shorter-lived isotopes of Sg and W were used in the present study compared with the first study by Even et al.14, in which only volatile hexacarbonyl complexes could be registered. Still, the chemical yields of 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg(CO)6 observed in the present experiment are similar to the 10–20% for 164W and about 5% for 265Sg reported from the first study24. This allows concluding that the chemical equilibrium between carbonyl complex fragments can be reached on a very short timescale, as it was also observed in dissociation studies of the hexacarbonyl complexes of the lighter homologues with short-pulsed lasers31. Thus, the shorter half-lives of the Sg and W isotopes used in the present experiment did not lead to a reduction of the chemical yield.

Only the hexacarbonyls have an enhanced chemical inertness and volatility and can reach the COMPACT detector array. The experimental distribution of 161,162W(CO)6 and the position of the three 259Sg events in COMPACT were compared with deposition distributions obtained by a Monte Carlo simulation code based on the model of mobile adsorption29. Similarly low adsorption enthalpy values on the SiO2 surface for both W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6, determined in the previous study14, allow for a rather simple ratio determination between the volatile (M(CO)6) and non-volatile (M(CO)n (1 ≤ n ≤ 5; M = 161,162W, 259Sg) fractions. The analysis of the simulated distributions in both detector arrays suggests that the probability for the decay in flight of 161W and 162W in the miniCOMPACT is low and can be statistically neglected. Thus, the ratio between the sums of the 161,161W and 259m,gSg events registered in COMPACT and miniCOMPACT, respectively, can be taken as the ratio between volatile and non-volatile fractions. The ratio between two W isotopes with different half-lives was determined by the analysis of the alpha energy spectrum from the first strip of the miniCOMPACT detector array as 161W:162W = 25:75. The Monte Carlo simulations of the distribution pattern were performed for the individual W isotopes. The final distribution for both isotopes, 161W and 162W, was obtained by weighted summation. For the simulation of the distribution pattern of 259Sg, an averaged half-life value of 320 ms was used, as obtained by Folden et al.25 in the experimental study using the same nuclear reaction 52Cr + 208Pb. This value is in agreement with the averaged half-life value for two states 259m,gSg observed by Antalic et al.27.

The patterns of the experimental and simulated distributions of W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6 on Au are shown in Fig. 3. The simulated ones, which describe the experimental distributions well, correspond to their adsorption enthalpy values, \(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Au}}}({\rm{W}}{({\rm{CO}})}_{6})=40(5)\,{\rm{kJ}}\,{{\rm{mol}}}^{-1}\) and \(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Au}}}({\rm{Sg}}{({\rm{CO}})}_{6})={45}_{-6}^{+4}\,\,{\rm{kJ}}\,{{\rm{mol}}}^{-1}\), respectively. The error bars were evaluated on the basis of statistical considerations—the simulated distributions at the given limits reproduce the experimental ones at the 68% confidence level. In the present study, the COMPACT detector surface was covered with Au, in contrast to the first experiment with Sg(CO)6, in which a SiO2-covered COMPACT detector array was used14. The \(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Au}}}\) value of W(CO)6 on the Au surface determined in the present experiment is close to that from previous studies on Au, \(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Au}}}({\rm{W}}{({\rm{CO}})}_{6})={41}_{-4}^{+3}\,{\rm{kJ}}\,{{\rm{mol}}}^{-1}\), obtained by Even et al.32. Notably, we find that the \(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Au}}}\) values of Sg(CO)6 and W(CO)6 on Au are several kJ mol−1 lower than the \(-\Delta {H}_{{\rm{ads}}}^{{\rm{Si}}{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) values on a SiO2 surface14,33. The values indicate that the deposition of volatile hexacarbonyl complexes well below room temperature on both surfaces occurs owing to physisorption. However, the interaction with the surface can be potentially influenced, for example, by CO molecules adsorbed on the cold Au surface34 or by the level of hydroxylation of the SiO2 surface35.

In the multistep decomposition–recombination process, the rates of the recombination reactions with CO ligands are close to zero under vacuum conditions and reach equilibrated values at a CO gas pressure of several tens of millibars36. The carbonyl complex formation in the present study was favoured by a high CO partial pressure. However, the decomposition process is facilitated by intense fluences of neutrons, electrons and photons as well as fast He ions from the He filling gas37. Thus, chemical interactions between the Sg and W ions or atoms with CO molecules inside the RTC are multistep decomposition and recombination processes, which result in a variety of metal–carbonyl species in a dynamic equilibrium.

The relation between the rate constant and the FBDE was commonly applied in the decomposition studies of carbonyl complexes. This method, described in Methods section ‘Determining the stability of the complex’, was used for the determination of FBDE values of several carbonyl complexes relative to the known FBDE value of the reference complex, Cr(CO)6 (ref. 38). Applying this method, the measurement of the 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg (CO)6 fractions under identical conditions allows for the direct determination of the FBDE value for Sg(CO)6 relative to the known value for W(CO)6. The formation of the carbonyl complexes of 161,162W and 259Sg was studied under identical conditions, that is, equal reaction times and CO concentration. Furthermore, the concentrations of all metal carbonyl species are negligibly small compared with the concentration of the other reactant, CO gas. Therefore, the ratio between the concentration of 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg(CO)6 can be described as the ratio of their rate constants (see Methods section ‘Determining the stability of the complex’ for details):

in which AW and ASg are values of the Arrhenius pre-factor for W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6, respectively. In our study, we used the value for the Arrhenius pre-factor of 1015.6 for both hexacarbonyl complexes, which was used also for Mo and W hexacarbonyls in ref. 38. A smaller Sg(CO)6 fraction compared with W(CO)6 should result in a lower FBDE value of the Sg(CO)6 complex. Using the obtained ratios of volatile and non-volatile fractions of 0.20(1) for 161,162W and \({0.04}_{-0.02}^{+0.05}\) for 259Sg, an energy difference of 4(2) kJ mol−1 between the FBDE values of W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6 was calculated. By subtracting this difference from the experimental FBDE value of W(CO)6 of 192(8) kJ mol−1 (ref. 38), the FBDE value for Sg(CO)6 results in 188(9) kJ mol−1. The error bar was obtained by mean squared summing and is dominated by the large error of the experimental FBDE value for W(CO)6. A more precise determination of this value would reduce the error bar of the value of Sg(CO)6.

Figure 4 shows the experimental FBDE value obtained for Sg(CO)6 along with those for the lighter homologues from ref. 38, in comparison with the theoretical data obtained at the different levels of theory3,4. We can see that the calculations using the non-relativistic ADF method (ADF-NR) predict an increasing trend in FBDE from Mo to W and Sg (ref. 4). The calculations using the RECPs-CCSD(T) method also give a 4 kJ mol−1 higher FBDE value for Sg(CO)6 compared with that of W (ref. 3). However, those calculations were unable to reproduce the experimental FBDE values for lighter homologues (Fig. 4). Our experimental data revealed a 4(2) kJ mol−1 decrease in the FBDE from W(CO)6 to Sg(CO)6, being smaller than that predicted by Iliaš and Pershina4 (about 10 kJ mol−1 using the ADF-SO and DC-DFT methods and 15 kJ mol−1 using the X2c-CCSD(T) method), however, in full agreement about the decreasing trend.
