The stability of the Sg(CO)6 complex was investigated in the present work. This was done by a comparative study of carbonyl complex formation with the short-lived isotopes 161,162W and 259Sg on a single-atom-at-a-time level. The formation of carbonyl complexes was performed in situ on thermalization in a He + CO gas mixture. Products of the multistep chemical interactions, the non-volatile metal–carbonyl fragments and the volatile hexacarbonyl complexes 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg(CO)6, were detected individually in two detector arrays. Three out of 75 registered events from 259Sg were found in the second detector array and were assigned to the 259Sg(CO)6 complex. This allowed for determining the fractional yields of the hexacarbonyl complexes and a ratio of the rate constants for the last step of the hexacarbonyl formation. On this basis, the FBDE of Sg(CO)6 was found to be 4(2) kJ mol−1 lower than that of W(CO)6. This trend reversal in the increasing FBDE values of the group 6 hexacarbonyls from W to Sg is in agreement with the results of the latest relativistic calculations4. According to these calculations, the predicted Sg–CO bond weakening is a result of a decrease in both the σ-forth and π-back bonding in Sg(CO)6 caused by the relativistic destabilization of the 6d(Sg) AOs (ref. 4). Thus, the FBDE of a SHE compound, Sg(CO)6, was measured for the first time and is found to be in excellent agreement with modern theory. Our study presents a sensitive method for investigating the influence of relativistic effects and opens a new pathway for determining physical observables in the chemistry of the heaviest elements.

The synthesis of 259Sg(CO)6 and 161,162W(CO)6 was performed at the gas-filled separator TASCA at the GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung GmbH, Darmstadt, Germany39, and was similar to that in the first study of the 265Sg(CO)6 carbonyl complex at the RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science, Wako, Japan14. At RIKEN, the isotope 265Sg was produced by irradiating 248Cm targets with a 22Ne beam, separated with the gas-filled recoil separator GARIS. Only volatile hexacarbonyl complexes Mo(CO)6, W(CO)6 and Sg(CO)6 were transported through a 10-m-long Teflon capillary to a SiO2-covered chromatography column. Here a negative temperature gradient was applied14. This column also served as a radiation detector for the identification of the studied radionuclides. In separate experiments, the behaviour of Mo and W carbonyl compounds was also studied.

In the present work, the isotope 259Sg, which has two states, 259gSg (T1/2 = 402(56) ms) and 259mSg (T1/2 = 226(27) ms)27, was produced in the cold nuclear fusion reaction 208Pb(52Cr,1n)259Sg (ref. 25). Short-lived radioisotopes of W, a chemical homologue of Sg, were produced by the nuclear reaction 112Sn(52Cr; 2-3n)161,162W (T1/2(161W) = 409 ms; T1/2(162W) = 1.19 s). 52Cr2+ ions, provided from a Penning ionization gauge (PIG) ion source, were accelerated by the UNIversal Linear ACcelerator (UNILAC) at the GSI Darmstadt to energies of 4.95(2) MeV u−1. A pulsed (5 ms beam-on, 15 ms beam-off) 52Cr14+ ion beam (average beam intensity of 6 × 1012 per second) irradiated the 112Sn and 208Pb targets. Targets were made from 208PbS and 112SnO2 and mounted on a rotating target wheel40. The target material was thermally evaporated onto carbon foils with an average thickness of 100(5) μg cm−2. Each target wheel contained four segments of 208PbS or 112SnO2 with an average thickness of 0.80(5) and 0.60(5) mg cm−2, respectively. In total, 4.0(2) × 1018 52Cr14+ ions impinged on the 208Pb targets during the two-week experimental Sg run. The W isotopes were produced in a 2-h run, during which a beam integral of 4.4(1) × 1016 was collected.

The nuclear fusion–evaporation products were separated from the intense primary beam and from unwanted products of multi-nucleon transfer reactions with the gas-filled recoil separator TASCA. TASCA, consisting of one dipole (D) and two quadrupole (Q) magnets in a DQ1Q2 configuration, was operated in the high transmission mode39. A He filling gas at a pressure of pHe = 0.8 mbar was used in TASCA. The 259Sg and 161,162W ions, recoiling from the target, were guided through TASCA, in which the magnets were set to rigidities of 2.16 and 1.64 Tm for Sg and W, respectively.

The formation process and volatility of carbonyl complexes were investigated by applying a gas–solid chromatography method5,6. Adsorption studies were conducted on two surface types, SiO2 and Au, in the temperature range from room temperature to T = 110 K. Evaporation residues reaching the RTC (diameter: 60 mm, depth: 20 mm) were thermalized in a 1:1 gas mixture of He and CO gas at 1 bar (Fig. 1), similarly to the first Sg(CO)6 study performed at RIKEN, Japan14. The gas chromatography and detection set-up consisted of two detector arrays in series and was similar to the set-up used for the chemistry studies with Nh and Mc (ref. 13). The first array (miniCOMPACT) was 16 cm long and was directly attached to the RTC exit. The second array (COMPACT) was 32 cm long and was connected to the first detector array by a 30-cm-long polytetrafluoroethylene capillary with an inner diameter of 2 mm. Both detector arrays consist of two panels facing each other, each divided into 32 positive–intrinsic–negative diodes mounted in a row. These radiation detectors registered α particles and fission fragments emitted by nuclear decays occurring inside the detector channel. The distance between opposite detector panels is 0.6 mm, thus, they form a narrow gas channel with a cross-section of 10.0 × 0.6 mm2. The silicon photodiodes were covered with a 30–50-nm-thick layer of SiO2 (miniCOMPACT) or Au (COMPACT)10,12,13. The detector pair 15 of miniCOMPACT and the bottom strip 23 of COMPACT lost functionality during the experiment. The gas mixture of 50% He (99.9999%) and 50% CO (99.997%) circulated in a closed loop at a flow rate of 2.5 l min−1. Less than 100 ms are required to flush out the whole detection set-up. The gases were further purified of water impurities using MC400-202FV (SAES) cartridges installed in a closed loop. These cartridges had internal particle filters that efficiently removed aerosol particles down to a size of 3 nm. The water content in the carrier gas was on a level of about 1 ppm.

It is known that the decomposition products of the hexacarbonyl complexes, that is, the residual fragments, formed by means of removal of one (or more) CO ligand(s) on contact with a hot metal surface, are substantially less volatile and more reactive than the hexacarbonyls41. The thermal decomposition of hexacarbonyl complexes on a metal surface was proposed as a method of choice to determine carbonyl compound stabilities on a one-atom-at-a-time level20,26. For this, in situ-formed volatile hexacarbonyl complexes are transported by a gas flow through an isothermal column made of metallic silver, placed upstream of a detector array and kept at elevated temperatures. Thus, hexacarbonyl complexes decomposing on the metal surface do not reach the detector. The breakthrough yield through the decomposition column measured at different temperatures is indicative of the stability of the hexacarbonyl complex—a higher stability, that is, FBDE, translates to a higher temperature, at which a certain fraction, for example, 50%, decomposes inside the column20. This approach was validated using Monte Carlo simulations for the evaluation of the FBDE of Mo(CO)6 and W(CO)6 and laid a basis for the expected behaviour of Sg(CO)6 (ref. 26). However, an earlier attempt to determine the FBDE value of 265Sg(CO)6 was unsuccessful, probably because of limited statistics, because a much larger number of Sg atoms is required to measure the breakthrough curve in the isothermal regime24.

In macrochemistry, the stability of carbonyl complexes with 3d, 4d and 5d transition metals is commonly studied by infrared laser absorption spectroscopy or by mass spectrometry of the fragments following the dissociation of the complexes induced by thermal dissociation, photo-dissociation or particle impact42,43,44. These studies showed the relation between the fragmentation pattern and individual bond energies. Mass spectra of positively charged products of the M(CO)6 complex dissociation (M = Cr, Mo, W) show the existence of all M(CO)n (0 ≤ n ≤ 6) fragments, from metallic ions up to hexacarbonyl ions, even after interactions at low energy and for very short (several microseconds) interaction times31,45.

The mass spectra obtained by electron impact decomposition include all fragments already at low electron energies. From roughly 70 eV on, the fragment ratios become fully equilibrated43. The measurement of the fragmentation pattern and of ionization energy thresholds (appearance energies) for all fragments allows for evaluating the bonding energy between the metal atom and the last bound CO ligand for the individual fragments with different numbers of ligands43. These branching ratios carry substantial information on the thermochemistry and photodissociation dynamics of metal carbonyls and allow for the unambiguous determination of the individual CO bond dissociation energies46. The abundances of individual fragments in the equilibrated state reflect their thermochemical and kinetic behaviour (Extended Data Fig. 1). Thus, the individual CO bond dissociation energies can be determined from a measurement of the individual fragment concentrations46.

All of the separation processes of CO ligands from carbonyl complexes and their fragments are concurrently accompanied by recombination processes, in which a free CO molecule attaches back to a carbonyl fragment, especially at non-negligible CO partial pressure47. Summarizing the previous studies on the decomposition of the hexacarbonyl complexes, we conclude that the decomposition is a multistep and reversible process, in which the equilibrium is reached on a microsecond timescale. Thus, the method, which is based on the determination of fractional yields and their relationship to the corresponding binding energies, can also be applied to carbonyl complexes produced at the single-atom level.

The activation energy for a certain decomposition or recombination step is equal to the bonding energy for that specific CO ligand with the central metal atom. In the last step of the hexacarbonyl formation, M(CO)5 + CO ↔ M(CO)6, that is, the first step of the hexacarbonyl decomposition, which is especially interesting for the present study, the rate constant depends on the value of the FBDE, which replaces the activation energy Ea in equation (4) for the first decomposition step26.

The relation between the rate constant and the FBDE was commonly applied in the decomposition studies of carbonyl complexes. Therefore, the decrease of the M(CO)6 concentration in the laser-induced decomposition was determined as a product [M(CO)6] = kτr, in which k is the rate constant and τr is the reaction time38,48. The method described here was applied to determine the experimental FBDE values in carbonyl complexes with Mo, W and Fe, relative to the Cr carbonyl complex, measured by laser-induced photodissociation. In group 6, the FBDE values of hexacarbonyl complexes, and, thus, the stability, increased from Cr to Mo and further to W (ref. 38).

In the present work, the formation of the carbonyl complexes of 161,162W and 259Sg was studied under identical conditions, that is, equal reaction times and CO concentration, similarly to decomposition studies with lighter homologues, Cr, Mo and W (refs. 38,48). Furthermore, the concentrations of all metal carbonyl species are negligibly small compared with the concentration of the other reactant, the CO gas. Therefore, the measured M(CO)6 fractions can also be determined as a product [M(CO)6] = kτr (M = 161,162W and 259Sg) and the ratio between the concentration of 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg(CO)6 can be described as the ratio of their rate constants:

Combining equations (4) and (5), we can conclude that the measured ratio between the concentration of 161,162W(CO)6 and 259Sg(CO)6 yields the difference between the corresponding FBDE values.

Applying the proposed method and determining fractional yields of specific carbonyl complexes by a mass analysis method, bond dissociation energies can be determined for individual carbonyl fragments identified in future experiments on the single-atom level. The chemical speciation is especially important for carbonyl complexes with odd-Z elements, in which, unlike in macroscopic amounts, only mononuclear species can exist23,49. The exact nature of the latter has not been identified experimentally and cannot be inferred through comparison with classical macroscopic systems.

In a recent study4, performed at a higher level of relativistic theory than in ref. 3, Iliaš and Pershina concluded that the trend reversal in the FBDE from W to Sg is a result of the weakening of both the σ-forth and π-back donations. This is because of the relativistic energy destabilization of the 6d AOs in Sg. Generally, the (n − 1)d AOs expand when going down in group 6, see the maximum radial values, Rmax[(n − 1)d5/2/(n − 1)d3/2)] Mo(1.398/1.384 a.u.) < W(1.516/1.496 a.u.) < Sg(1.793/1.675 a.u.). However, the negative energies of those orbitals, E[(n − 1)d5/2/(n − 1)d3/2], increase from Mo to W and then decrease from W to Sg, that is, Mo(0.294/0.301 a.u) < W(0.324/0.348 a.u.) > Sg(0.257/0.297 a.u.)50. Because the group 6 M–CO bonding was shown to be of preferentially electrostatic nature4, the trend in the FBDE is defined exclusively by the trend in the AOs energies. The steady expansion of the (n − 1)d AOs of the metals, overlapping with molecular orbitals of the ligands, does not influence the trend in the FBDE.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Yun-Xing Wang
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The dynamic interplay between RNA structure and its associated Mg2+ ions is central to RNA function yet remains poorly understood at a near-atomic level1,2,3,4. Here, using a heterogeneity-focused protocol for cryo-electron microscopy data analysis of conformationally flexible RNA particles, we determined the structures of RNase P RNA ensembles composed of 76 coexisting active and inactive conformers that differ in a transient tertiary interaction that is critical for activity. The binding of the accessory protein does not change the local structure but induces thermodynamic allostery that enhances catalysis by altering the dynamics of the tertiary interaction. Four distinct classes of Mg2+ ions have critical roles in the structure, dynamics and catalysis of the conformational ensembles. Together, these findings establish a new paradigm in which catalysis is regulated through multimodal communications coupled with the dynamics of RNA–Mg2+ conformational ensembles, rather than a single static catalytic structure in a single action mode.

RNA structure and dynamics are crucial to its function. Despite decades of development in structural biology, the structural dynamics of RNA and its associated Mg2+ ions have never been directly visualized at near-atomic resolution. High-resolution techniques, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), have largely emphasized resolution over dynamics, averaging vast numbers of particles or molecules in lattices, often stabilized in non-physiological Mg2+ environments, to obtain a single consensus structure. The NMR approach largely relies on probabilistic inference models that satisfy measurements5,6,7. Conversely, computational methods describe atomistic motions using force fields that remain approximate, particularly in modelling electrostatic interactions and Mg2+ coordination8,9. As a result, the conformational ensembles of RNA and dynamics of Mg2+ ions in its native ionic conditions remain unresolved. Recent efforts to visualize RNA heterogeneity, including atomic force microscopy combined with machine learning (AFM–HORNET)10,11, have revealed the breadth of conformational sampling but not the distinct structures with associated Mg2+ ions, in the presence or absence of accessory proteins, at near-atomic resolution. Thus, the structural basis and mechanistic relationship between the conformational dynamics of all components and their functions or activities are unclear. In particular, Mg2+, a central determinant of RNA folding and catalysis, has been studied only in the context of static structures or through molecular dynamics simulations, and, to our knowledge, its dynamic trajectories within flexible RNA frameworks in the absence and presence of protein factors have not been experimentally mapped, so its roles in RNA conformational dynamics are poorly understood.

Cryo-EM is particularly well-suited for large protein assemblies with a large rigid structural core, but it also holds promise for exploring conformational dynamics12,13,14,15. Nevertheless, its full capability has yet to be demonstrated for the structure determination of highly heterogeneous RNA conformational landscapes that contain less populated but functionally important conformers. The bacterial Geobacillus stearothermophilus RNase P RNA (GstRPR) exemplifies this problem. It is an especially informative test case, because the RNA itself provides much of the structural scaffold. Accordingly, the conformational plasticity resolved here is likely to reflect intrinsic properties of the RNA scaffold that are more protein-constrained in other lineages. It has a specificity domain (S-domain) (residues 87–249) and a catalytic domain (C-domain) (residues 1–86 and 250–417). Although well-folded, more than 80% of its residues remain flexible under physiological Mg2+ concentrations11, and the mechanistic coupling between its conformational sampling, roles of Mg2+ and catalytic activity remains unknown. This RNA enzyme is responsible for a universally required step in tRNA maturation and thus is essential to all life. Our previous study shows extensive conformational heterogeneity of the component of this ribozyme under physiologically relevant Mg2+ concentrations, but the structural basis of the biological relevance of heterogeneity and protein component rnpA is not entirely clear without a description of the conformational space at near-atomic resolution. Here we demonstrate that a heterogeneity-focused cryo-EM strategy can overcome some of the challenges in visualizing heterogeneous RNA conformational landscapes, resolving the structure dynamics of the ribozyme component in the presence and absence of rnpA at near-atomic resolution, including numerous structural and catalytic Mg2+ ions. Our strategy establishes a practical workflow to guide the analysis of cryo-EM data from highly heterogeneous molecules and reveals biological principles that are more complex than simple action models based on the static snapshots of structures. Thus, our study as a whole provides a framework for visualizing the structural dynamics of flexible RNA and associated Mg2+ ions, and for bridging RNA conformational dynamics and activity.

In cryo-EM data analysis, the applicability of the Fourier slice theorem critically depends on accurately classifying projections into conformationally and orientationally homogeneous subgroups. This is directly affected by the inherent low signal-to-noise ratio of cryo-EM images of molecules, and especially relatively small molecules by cryo-EM standards, making it difficult to determine whether variation between projections arises from differences in conformation or orientation16,17. Using our large-scale simulation framework, EMCrafter18, we simulated realistic noise and explored the empirical estimation of the minimum number of particles required to determine a 3D volume at a given resolution for G. stearothermophilus RNase P (GstRNase P) (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Methods). In our experimental setup, we estimate that at least 50,000 particles are required to obtain a volume with a resolution of around 3 Å for RNase P RNA, provided the particle stacks are homogeneous. This number is useful as a reference for evaluating feasibility and estimating the total time required to record data for mapping the conformational space of heterogeneous GstRNase P (Supplementary Methods).

To facilitate the cryo-EM data analysis, we developed an iterative workflow that moves away from the focus on attaining maximal resolution by prioritizing the capture of heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 2). Our analysis protocol consists of four steps: data processing, particle pruning, heterogeneity determination, and 3D refinement, among which heterogeneity determination and its iterations with particle pruning are the most critical procedures (Supplementary Methods). Within heterogeneity determination, there are four sub-steps (Extended Data Fig. 2) aimed at identifying the major conformational states present in the dataset (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Methods). This step used the expectation-maximization algorithm with a full solvent mask, revealing broad heterogeneity across the entire particle volume. The input was generated using local refinement with a focal mask applied to the rigid core. In the subsequent stage, additional structural variability, particularly in peripheral regions, was explored using focal and solvent masking strategies. When these approaches produced well-resolved volumes containing sufficient particles for further subclassification, additional rounds of 3D classification were performed to identify distinct conformational states. If classification produced only similar volumes, the input particle stacks were treated as a single conformational class, which then served as a reference for final 3D refinement. Particle stacks that provided incomplete volumes, typically due to extensive continuous motion, were considered unsuitable for discrete classification. These subsets were instead analysed using continuous heterogeneity methods, including 3DFlex12 and 3D variability analysis17 (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). In the final step, the resolved homogeneous particle stacks were re-cropped to the nominal pixel size (0.732 Å per pixel). Reference-based motion correction and/or non-uniform refinement were performed in CryoSPARC12 to maximize the final volume resolution. Further details on these analyses are provided in Supplementary Methods.

We determined 55 and 21 conformationally distinct volumes of GstRPR in the apo and holo states, respectively (Fig. 1a,b, Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4 and Supplementary Table 1). The individual volumes are well defined at a global resolution of around 3 Å, as estimated by the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation at the 0.143 criterion, with average resolutions below 2.6 Å for the core and 5 Å for the peripheral regions (Fig. 1c). The 76 volumes can be broadly described as two major conformer classes based on the absence (open) or presence (closed) of the tetraloop–tetraloop receptor (TL–TLR) interaction involving P10.1 and P12 in the S-domain. Conformational heterogeneity in both apo and holo states becomes obvious in the superimposed volumes (Fig. 1d). Moreover, the S-domain, consisting of P9, P10.1, and P12, also shows continuous motions in both the apo and holo states, as indicated by the analysis using 3DFlex in CryoSPARC (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Video 1).

The 417-nucleotide GstRPR consists of more than fifteen structural elements (Fig. 2a) and can adopt multiple conformations in both apo and holo states (Fig. 2b,c, Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 1). Conformational heterogeneity, especially in peripheral structural elements, including P1, P19 and L15 in the C-domain and P9, P10.1 and P12 in the S-domain, is readily visible. Comparison of the atomic movement similarity matrix (AMSM), indicative of concerted motion correlations of the structural elements derived from the cryo-EM data and those from the AFM–HORNET approach, shows a correlation of the matrices of 0.897 (Fig. 2d,e), suggesting a remarkable similarity in movement correlations derived from two orthogonal approaches. Nevertheless, the major difference between the two correlation maps lies in P19, with the AFM–HORNET models suggesting that P19 shows less motion correlation with P10.1 and P12 than those in the cryo-EM models (Fig. 2f). This difference is due to the higher resolution of the cryo-EM volumes, by which discrete conformers with relatively subtle correlated motions, such as P19 with P10.1 and P12, could be detected. By contrast, the AFM–HORNET approach selects visibly distinct conformers with large amplitudes, which outweigh those with relatively small amplitudes, as if the small motions were uncorrelated. Thus cryo-EM provides structures of dominant conformers at near-atomic resolution, whereas AFM–HORNET captures a broader conformational space by capturing rare structural states that are otherwise averaged out in the cryo-EM approach.

Analysis of the holo AMSM (Fig. 2g) shows a correlation pattern nearly identical to that of the apo state, with a Pearson correlation of 0.96 (Fig. 2d,g). Nevertheless, the difference AMSM between holo and apo models reveals that most of the structural elements are overall more correlated in the holo models, indicated by red and orange, than those in apo models (Fig. 2h). However, two small dark blue areas between P10.1–P12 in the S-domain and P19 in the C-domain are less motion-correlated upon rnpA binding (Fig. 2h, dashed outlines). Further analysis using the root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) correlation between the apo and holo ensembles reveals the divergent behaviour of residues in P12, primarily involving those in the interdigitated T-loop motif (IDTM)19, compared with the other residues (Fig. 2i), suggesting a significant conformational change in IDTM upon rnpA binding.

We then examined the motion amplitudes of various structural elements. Averaged pairwise root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) per residue in the apo and holo conformers by cryo-EM shows an overall motion pattern similar to that derived using AFM–HORNET11 (Fig. 2j), with RMSD observed by cryo-EM as large as 30 Å in the S-domain. However, this amplitude is much smaller than that observed by AFM–HORNET. The difference in amplitude reflects the fundamental distinction between the two techniques for the same reason described in the previous section. More importantly, both cryo-EM and AFM–HORNET show that one of the largest motions involves P10.1 and P12. Furthermore, the largest amplitude change observed in the plots of per-residue RMSDs averaged over all permutation pairs between the conformers in apo and holo cryo-EM ensembles also involves P10.1 and P12, where IDTM resides (Fig. 2j–l). Detailed principal component analysis of the cryo-EM conformers shows that rnpA binding alters the orders, motion directions and distributions in the top four principal motion components involving these two peripheral structural elements in addition to others (Extended Data Fig. 5, Supplementary Videos 3 and 4 and Supplementary Fig. 17). IDTM is a general structural element and has important roles in RNA–RNA recognition19. However, the synergistic relationship between P12 and P10.1 is not clear.

Together, rnpA binding appears to exert an allosteric effect that results in distal remodelling of the P12 and P10.1 regions. Before establishing this causal relationship, however, it is essential to determine whether rnpA binding also leads to structural remodelling of the binding and catalytic sites. The RNase P RNA component has been shown to be responsible for catalysis in non-physiological Mg2+ concentrations20. However, the question of whether RNase P possesses a preformed catalytic structure among all conformers under 1 mM Mg2+ concentration, independent of the presence of the protein cofactor or substrates, remains unclear.

Our previous low-resolution analyses identified a structurally invariant region (IR) encompassing both the catalytic centre and the rnpA-binding site11. Nonetheless, some experimental evidence suggests that in the absence of rnpA, the active site may be only partially ordered, with structural Mg2+ ions stabilizing the RNA fold but leaving the catalytic geometry incomplete21,22. In the present study, with an average Q-score exceeding 0.7 (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13) and a local resolution of approximately 2.3 Å (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21), the IR structures are well defined in both apo (Fig. 3a,b) and holo conformers (Fig. 3c,d). The overall IR volume undergoes little change across all conformers detectable at the current resolution (Supplementary Fig. 23), regardless of rnpA presence (Fig. 3b,d–f). The average correlation among conformer volumes in both apo and holo ensembles exceeds 0.93 (Fig. 3b,d), and the IR structures within each ensemble are superimposable with root-mean-square fluctuations within 0.6 Å. Moreover, the IR structures of apo and holo conformers are nearly identical upon superposition (Fig. 3g,h), supporting a preformed catalytic architecture and a lock-and-key mode of interaction between rnpA and GstRPR. Notably, in the presence of rnpA, the base-stacking interaction between A334 and G335 exhibits more stable behaviour than in its absence. These results underscore the primary role of GstRPR in both structure and catalysis, similar to protein enzymes23. The rigid IR thus appears to be catalytically ready even in the absence of rnpA, consistent with our previous finding11. This rigidity of the catalytic and rnpA-binding sites resembles that of protein enzymes23, in stark contrast to the ligand-induced ordering and conformational plasticity characteristic of many cis-acting ribozymes24. Therefore, the enhancement of activity by rnpA does not arise from structural remodelling at the catalytic or rnpA-binding sites.

Multivariate cluster analysis was performed to further characterize conformers in both the apo and holo ensembles, revealing two distinct classes of conformers (Fig. 4a,b). The minor conformers comprise approximately 13% of the apo ensemble but increase to 43% in the holo state. Structural comparison of these conformers shows that their primary differences lie in the TL–TLR interaction and the IDTM region (Fig. 4c–f). In the absence of the TL–TLR interaction between P12 and P10.1 (open), the IDTM adopts a quasi-helical structure (Fig. 4c,e), whereas formation of the TL–TLR interaction (closed) stabilizes a properly folded IDTM (Fig. 4d,f). Thus, rnpA binding shifts the population from around 13% closed conformers in the apo ensemble to 43% in the holo ensemble (Fig. 4g), reflecting an allosteric mechanism that favours TL–TLR formation and correct IDTM folding without structural remodelling at the binding or catalytic sites. Consistently, mutations that disrupt the TL–TLR interaction and IDTM nearly abolish catalytic activity (Fig. 4h), indicating that this interaction is required for proper IDTM folding and that the closed ensemble represents the active conformation. Under 1 mM Mg2+, both TL–TLR and IDTM regions exist in a dynamic equilibrium, in contrast to the static structure observed under high Mg2+ conditions19,25. Examples of the secondary structural layouts of the IDTM region in open and closed conformations are shown in Extended Data Fig. 6f. Notably, one holo conformer, a captured transient intermediate state, exhibits a formed TL–TLR interaction but an unformed IDTM (Fig. 4i), suggesting that TL–TLR formation may precede IDTM folding. The IDTM sequence is highly conserved across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes26,27,28. Whereas the active IDTM structure in GstRNase P depends on the TL–TLR interaction, in archaeal and eukaryotic systems, which do not have an equivalent of P10.1 for the equivalent interaction, the IDTM structure is maintained by the Rpp21, Rpp29, and Rpp38 heterotrimer26,27,28. Furthermore, our interpretation of active and inactive conformers based on the conformational analysis of the TL–TLR interaction and the proper formation of IDTM is consistent with the ternary complex of the GstRNase P with pre-tRNAGly (Fig. 4j,k). Collectively, these structural results indicate that rnpA binding allosterically shifts the conformational equilibrium toward the active, closed state, characterized by a stabilized TL–TLR interaction and properly folded IDTM.

Mg2+ ions have long been characterized by their positions and occupancies in static RNA structures; however, the relationship between ion motion and RNA conformational dynamics and function, which is critical for understanding their roles in RNA folding and catalysis, remains poorly defined. The ability to resolve conformational ensembles now enables direct visualization of ion movements and changes in occupancy across distinct RNA conformers. At an average local resolution of 2.3 Å within the IR, Mg2+ positions and occupancies are clearly resolved across all conformers (Extended Data Figs. 6, 7a,b, 8 and 9 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). In total, we identified 2,147 and 648 Mg2+ ions in 55 apo and 21 holo conformers (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Methods), respectively, corresponding to an average of approximately 39 Mg2+ ions per apo conformer and 31 per holo conformer. Notably, rnpA with pI of 10.8 is likely to displace an equivalent of approximately 8 Mg2+ ions overall (static or transient), resulting in a total absence of Mg2+ at the interface without a discernible change in Mg2+ distribution elsewhere.

Using standard distance-geometric-based criteria for ion identification29,30,31,32, we observed Mg2+ ions either directly coordinated or hydrated (Extended Data Fig. 7c–f, Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Methods). Notably, atoms participating in Mg2+ coordination are predominantly OP1, OP2, N7 and O6 of purine (A or G) bases, with static Mg2+ coordination consistently involving OP1 and/or OP2 (Extended Data Figs. 7a,b,8 and 9). Whereas prior reports identified Mg2+ association with purine bases4,30, our results reveal the dynamic nature and mechanistic relevance of these interactions. Coordination of static Mg2+ ions consistently involves phosphate OP1/OP2 and, less frequently, purine N7 and O6, underscoring their architectural role.

On the basis of motion trajectories and appearance score, we found four classes of Mg2+ that are static, transient, hopping or companioning (Fig. 5). Mg2+ ions with appearance score of 1.0 and dynamically confined within a narrow spatial displacement range <1 Å were classified as static (Extended Data Figs. 7c–f,  6a,b, 8a and 9a). A total of 1,100 and 231 static Mg2+ ions were identified in the apo and holo ensembles, respectively (Supplementary Table 2). Some of those ions show positional fluctuations, probably reflecting local thermal motion within the inner coordination sphere, even though they are coordinated by relatively rigid regions of the RNA structure (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Video 5). The positional RMSF of these Mg2+ ions is within 0.7 Å (Supplementary Methods), reflecting their structural stability.

The first subclass of static Mg2+ is located at or near the catalytic site, namely, M1 and the hydrated ions Mh1 and Mh2 (Fig. 5a, Extended Data Fig. 6b,c and Supplementary Video 5), with positional RMSFs of less than 0.2 Å across all conformers (Extended Data Fig. 7f). The catalytic Mg2+ ion, M1, is directly chelated by the phosphate oxygens of A50, A389 and A390 (Fig. 5a), consistent with its established catalytic role and the presence of a preformed catalytic site geometry, regardless of rnpA binding or peripheral conformational state (Fig. 3b,d). The hydrated Mg2+ ion Mh1 is coordinated by OP1 of A49, O6 of G51, N7 of G394 and O6 of G395, among the closest to the catalytic Mg2+ (Fig. 5a). Clear density corresponding to an outer-sphere water molecule interacting with A50 and A51—the two key catalytic residues—is also observed (Extended Data Fig. 6c). A second hydrated Mg2+, Mh2, is also positioned near the catalytic pocket (Fig. 5a), with well-resolved hydration water visible in the density map (Extended Data Fig. 6c). Mh2 is coordinated by O2 of A49, N3 of G389 and N6 of A330. These findings are of interest regarding the role of polarized water molecules in RNase P catalysis22,33,34,35. A second subset of static Mg2+ ions functions primarily in structural stabilization, as they are primarily located within the pseudoknot, base-stacking, kissing-loop and base-triple motifs, where they chelate surrounding phosphate groups to maintain local tertiary architecture (Fig. 5b). The RMSFs of these stabilizing Mg2+ ions are all within 0.7 Å with an appearance score of 1.0, indicating complete conservation across all conformers.

Beyond these static ions, three additional dynamic classes were identified, each defined by distinct occurrence patterns and motion trajectories (Fig. 5c–e). Transient Mg2+ ions (RMSF > 1 Å, appearance score < 1.0) (Fig. 5c) show conformer-dependent localization and occupancy, in contrast to the static ions. These ions are typically averaged out and not visible in crystallographic or conventional cryo-EM analyses. These ions could represent distinct ion binding sites correlated with RNA conformation or underlying uncertainty in the data due to diffuse and extended density, probably representing a mixture of occupancy states. Notably, these ions are localized within an open channel along the expected tRNA-binding path at the catalytic core, suggesting a possible role in stabilizing intermediate charge distributions (Supplementary Video 6). These transient hydrated ions are thus likely to participate in the transition to a catalytically competent multi-metal configuration, consistent with cooperative multi-ion catalysis observed in other ribozymes. Indeed, those transient ions are located within 2–3 Å of those ions seen during enzyme–tRNA complex formation and promoting catalytic activation upon substrate binding24 (Extended Data Figs. 8d and 9d).

Hopping Mg2+ ions (appearance score = 1.0) exhibit coordinated movement along networks of binding sites (Fig. 5d, Extended Data Figs. 6d, 8b and 9b and Supplementary Video 7). Although they were predicted by molecular dynamics simulations36,37,38, this represents, to our knowledge, their first direct visualization. These ions shuttle between neighbouring coordination sites involving phosphate OP1/OP2 and purine N7/O6 over a distance of about 10 Å. This behaviour, primarily observed in the major groove of a G-rich motif, highlights a mechanism by which Mg2+ ions dynamically redistribute charge without inducing large-scale structural changes, underscoring the dynamic yet structurally coherent nature of RNA–metal interactions. Finally, companion Mg2+ ions move synchronously with their coordinating residues (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Figs. 6e, 8c and 9c), maintaining local rigidity through stable coordination within globally flexible elements. These ions preserve local structure while permitting global motions. One such ion anchors an A–A stacking interaction that stabilizes docking of the P12 helix between P9 and P10.1 (Extended Data Fig. 6e), exemplifying Mg2+-mediated synergistical coupling between local rigidity and global flexibility.

Our approach to the cryo-EM data analysis enabled us to estimate a more realistic signal-to-noise ratio from experimental cryo-EM datasets using EMCrafter (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 10) and approximate the minimum number of particles required per conformer as a benchmark to achieve a given target resolution, important to the feasibility of heterogeneous structure determination at near-atomic resolution. Our cryo-EM analysis workflow, focused on resolving heterogeneity within a dataset, also offers a range of possibilities, capturing the motion trajectories of flexible structures and Mg2+ ions as well as those of water molecules and substrate-recognition intermediates.

The structural analysis of the conformational ensembles reveals a possible novel interaction mode. We speculate that allostery is communicated not by local structural remodelling through an induced fit at either the binding or catalytic sites, but by redistribution of pre-existing conformers through long-range thermodynamic coupling within the RNA structure. This type of dynamic allostery was first proposed for protein structures39. Thus, as one possible model in this case, changes in Mg2+ distribution in apo versus holo structural models are local at the rnpA-binding interface, where rnpA might act as a polycation by replacing an equivalent of eight overall and approximately four Mg2+ sites at the binding interface, and the coupling might occur as a result of the change in electrostatic landscape39 (Supplementary Fig. 15). The validity of this model needs to be further tested. Thus, our findings potentially define a hybrid model that unifies lock-and-key recognition with conformational selection40,41 and extends the principle of population-shift allostery42 to RNA catalysis. rnpA, which might act as a thermodynamic controller of the GstRPR conformers, may introduce a new regulatory principle for ribozymes, redefining protein-assisted ribozyme catalysis as thermodynamic, rather than structural, control. The observation of a population shift driven by protein cofactors that results in catalytic activation may directly connect conformational dynamics to function and unite classical and statistical models of biological recognition. This multimodal, dynamical allostery recognition relay spans three molecules: rnpA, GstRPR and the substrate.

Traditional descriptions of roles of Mg2+ in RNA catalysis, ‘inner-sphere’ and ‘outer-sphere’, or ‘structural’ and ‘diffusive’36,37,43,44,45 derive largely from static structural or thermodynamic models. Here the four Mg2+ classes establish a dynamic, semi-quantitative framework linking ion motion and occupancy to RNA function, whereas RMSF and appearance score metrics provide measurable parameters that connect ion dynamics to structural and catalytic behaviour, replacing the simplistic ordered–disordered dichotomy. The transient Mg2+ class may interplay with conformational transitions, revealing how transient ions stabilize electrostatic potentials during the conformational transition. This dynamic interplay provides a mechanistic explanation for how ribozymes achieve catalytic precision without losing structural adaptability, resolving the longstanding paradox between rigidity at the catalytic and protein-binding sites and the peripheral flexibility required for binding non-canonical substrates. The discovery of hopping Mg2+ ions introduces the concept of dynamic electrostatics, in which ions migrate among adjacent coordination sites to maintain energetically favourable states in a flexible structure. Our experimental observation supports the presence of dynamic Mg2+ ion coordination, which was previously proposed on the basis of molecular dynamics calculations3,46. Finally, companion Mg2+ ions demonstrate that local electrostatic compensation persists within flexible peripheral regions, providing a structural basis for conformational sampling without destabilization.

In summary, catalytic competence of RNase P arises from changes in active conformer population in the ensembles and the redistribution of Mg2+ ions, which function not as static cofactors but as dynamically coupled electrostatic stabilizers. The concept of the four Mg2+ classes in RNA may also redefine how metal ions are treated in both experimental and computational RNA studies. It challenges the conventional practice of modelling Mg2+ as fixed or averaged sites in molecular dynamics simulations, cryo-EM density fitting and crystallographic refinement. Thus, our findings may motivate the use of ensemble or trajectory-based representations of Mg2+ binding, rather than static placements, for accurate electrostatics. The framework presented here provides a unified physical basis for interpreting ion densities in high-resolution RNA structures and for improving the representation of metal ions in mechanistic models of RNA catalysis. This dynamic view may also suggest a practical criterion for targeting Mg2+ sites in RNA engineering or drug design: static, high-occupancy sites as potential druggable targets versus inherently labile sites.

Continuous RNA flexibility revealed by 3DFlex analysis. The video illustrates conformational variability derived from 3DFlex analysis in cryoSPARC4. The 3DFlex model was trained with a rigidity weight of 1, using a mesh generated after resampling the particle box size to 128 × 128 pixels. A density threshold of 0.012, soft padding of 2, and z-clip of 0.9 were applied during mask rendering. The resulting deformation field highlights continuous motion in the peripheral RNA regions, which are more flexible relative than the RNA core. This flexibility explains the lower local resolution observed in the periphery of the reconstruction and supports the dynamic nature of these RNA segments in the TL–TLR open state.

3D Variability Analysis reveals TL–TLR conformational transition within the S-domain of RNase P RNA. This video illustrates conformational dynamics identified through 3D variability analysis in cryoSPARC, performed using a filter resolution of 6 Å. The analysis resolves a continuous motion corresponding to a tertiary interaction transition between the tetraloop (TL) and tetraloop receptor (TLR) regions within the S-domain of the RNase P RNA. Across the principal variability component, the TL–TLR pair undergoes a conformational change from an open, unpaired state to a closed, interacting configuration, consistent with dynamic tertiary contact formation. This motion highlights the intrinsic flexibility of the S-domain and provides structural insight into the molecular basis for conformational rearrangements that modulate RNA folding and stability.

Morph trajectory illustrating conformational variability obtained from PCA and clustering for apo ensemble. Structures from apo ensemble were used to generate the corresponding main directional morions observed in cryo-EM using PCA, after alignment of all models against the invariable region. Clustering analysis (k-means) was then performed on the PCA coordinates to identify major conformational states. For visualization, ChimeraX’s morph function5 was used to interpolate between the cluster-representative structures, producing a continuous trajectory of the motion, highlighting the structural differences that underlie the separation of conformational states shown in Extended Data Fig. 5.

Morph trajectory illustrating conformational variability obtained from PCA and clustering for Holo ensemble. Same approach as Supplementary Video 3, applied for cryo-EM derived ensemble for holo sample. Supplementary Videos 3 and 4 illustrate the conformational dynamics of RNase P RNA in the absence (apo, rnpA-free) and presence (holo, rnpA-bound) of its protein component. Each ensemble, that comprises 55 models for the apo and 21 models for the holo form, was subjected to the same morphing protocol to visualize the collective motions captured within each structural ensemble. The morphs were generated in ChimeraX5 by interpolating atomic coordinates between consecutive models, providing a continuous trajectory that reflects the predominant conformational fluctuations within each state. All structural elements are coloured according to secondary structure motifs, following the scheme shown in Fig. 2a–c of the main text, enabling direct visual correlation between the video and the figure. Together, these morphs highlight the effect of rnpA binding on RNase P RNA, revealing how protein association modulates RNA flexibility, stabilizes specific structural regions, and contributes to active form.

Morph trajectory illustrating examples of rigid Mg2+ ions. This video shows representative trajectories for rigid Mg2+ ions, highlighted by zooming into specific regions of interest. Directly coordinated Mg2+ ions are shown as blue spheres, while hydrated Mg2+ ions are shown as green spheres. Case 1: Catalytic region. Catalytic residues are shown in red, and the catalytic Mg2+ ion (M1), and the two hydrated ions (Mh1 and Mh2). Cases 2 and 3: Local structural stabilization by Mg2+ ions. In case 2, an Mg2+ ion stabilizes a base-stacking interaction that precedes formation of the pseudoknot within the catalytic core. In case 3, an Mg2+ ion stabilizes the kissing-loop region.

Sequential visualization of the structural ensemble highlighting a transient Mg2+ ion in the catalytic core. This video displays each model of the structural ensemble in a stepwise manner using ChimeraX. Beginning with Model 1, each structure is shown individually while the previous model is hidden, progressing sequentially through the entire ensemble. The visualization focuses on the catalytic core to reveal the transient presence of an Mg2+ ion (red sphere), whose appearance varies across models. Catalytic residues A50, A389, and A390 are shown in red; the catalytic Mg2+ ion (M1) is represented as a blue sphere; and the hydrated ions (Mh1 and Mh2) are shown as green spheres. This visualization highlights the dynamic, model-dependent ion occupancy within this region

Visualization of hopping Mg2+ ions along coordinated RNA binding sites. This video illustrates the dynamic hopping behaviour of Mg2+ ions as they transition between neighbouring coordination sites within a G-rich RNA motif. Using Chimera5, the trajectory highlights ion movement along a network of phosphate (OP1/OP2) and purine (N7/O6) coordination sites over a distance of ~10 Å. The Mg2+ ion (green sphere) is shown relocating between adjacent positions without inducing detectable large-scale structural rearrangements in the RNA. This visualization provides direct structural evidence of Mg2+ ion hopping, previously predicted only by molecular dynamics simulations, and demonstrates how RNA maintains structural rigidity while enabling dynamic redistribution of charge through transient ion coordination

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: T. Schumm
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The laser-accessible nuclear transition in the thorium-229 isotope has been identified as a candidate for realizing an optical nuclear clock1 that might outperform current optical clocks based on electron-shell transitions in atoms or ions2. It is expected to be more robust against external perturbations3,4 and to provide enhanced sensitivity in clock-based tests of the fundamental principles of physics5,6. Here we realize a thorium-229 nuclear clock by stabilizing a continuous-wave laser to the 148-nm nuclear transition with rapid feedback based on absorption spectroscopy7. The thorium-229 nuclei are embedded in a millimetre-sized, room-temperature calcium fluoride crystal. A subharmonic of the 148-nm radiation is continuously compared with a Yb+ single-ion clock. The nuclear clock shows a shot-noise-limited fractional frequency instability of \(3\times 1{0}^{-12}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\) where τ is the averaging time, approaching 10−15 instabilities over 1 day of operation. Improvements to the instability by several orders of magnitude are projected for future devices. We use the nuclear clock to constrain models of ultralight dark matter by searching for periodic fluctuations and slow drifts in the nuclear transition energy, on timescales between 20 s and 1 day. Benefitting from the enhanced sensitivity of the thorium-229 transition, these constraints compete with the best atomic clocks concerning dark matter coupling to photons and go beyond previous measurements regarding coupling to the strong force.

Over the last 70 years, atomic clocks based on microwave and optical electronic transitions have successfully served as frequency standards based on their high levels of stability and accuracy2,8,9,10. To elevate these atomic timekeeping devices to the next generation, in 2003, Peik and Tamm1 proposed a nuclear clock based on the extraordinarily low-energy isomeric state of the thorium-229 (229Th) isotope at 8.4 eV. With a lifetime approaching 1 h for a bare nucleus in vacuum, this transition offers a potential resonance quality factor of the order of 1019 (ref. 11). Additionally, the nucleus couples only weakly to perturbative fields12, which allows the construction of an optical clock implemented in a solid material at room temperature13. By doping microgram amounts of 229Th into a crystal host, an experimentally simple and robust clock can be created, offering a large gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared with approaches based on a single or a few isolated nuclei, while only moderately degrading the resonance quality factor1,4,11,14.

A clock based on the 229Th nuclear transition is of great interest for testing theories beyond the Standard Model of particle physics that indicate that the fundamental constants vary over time5. The low energy of the 229Th isomer transition originates from a coincidental near-cancellation of the mega-electronvolt-scale Coulomb and nuclear contributions to the binding energies of the 229Th ground and excited states, making the transition frequency highly sensitive to fluctuations in the coupling constants of the interactions involved5,6,15. As a result, a solid-state nuclear clock in its development phase would already be competitive with or may even surpass the sensitivity of advanced comparable atomic clocks in the search for dark matter.

The realization of a nuclear clock builds upon half a century of scientific discoveries. See the reviews in refs. 12,16. In a research stream initiated by Kroger and Reich in 1976 (ref. 17), the energy of the 229Th nuclear transition was narrowed down from an originally conjectured value of below 100 eV to −1(4) eV (ref. 18), 3.5(1.0) eV (ref. 19) and then 7.8(5) eV (refs. 20,21) using gamma spectroscopy. Using the internal conversion decay channel, the existence of the 229Th isomer was proven in 2016 (ref. 22) and the energy value refined to 8.28(17) eV (ref. 23). An optical detection of the 229Th radiative nuclear decay was realized in 2022, which determined the isomer energy to be 8.338(24) eV (ref. 24) in the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) range. Thereafter, resonant laser excitation in Th:CaF2, Th:LiSrAlF6 crystals and ThF4 and ThO2 thin films was reported in 2024 and 2025 (refs. 25,26,27,28), quickly followed by the resolution of the nuclear quadrupole structure in Th:CaF2 (refs. 13,29).

The development of 148-nm continuous-wave laser systems in 2025 (refs. 30,31), in combination with highly doped 229Th:CaF2 crystals32,33, has enabled the measurement of the nuclear transition with absorption spectroscopy7. With this technique, it became possible to probe the 229Th nuclear transition continuously, without being limited by the long isomeric state lifetime of approximately 10 min. Moreover, absorption provides a higher detection efficiency, yielding three orders of magnitude more signal photons per second compared with fluorescence.

An optical clock is based on an atomic transition with a narrow linewidth, which is probed by a clock laser with a long coherence time. By stabilizing this laser to the atomic resonance, it can inherit the desired stability and reproducibility from the atom. Aiming for millihertz resolution and accuracy, the feedback times in this process typically extend to several seconds, requiring a pre-stabilization of the laser for higher-frequency noise to an optical cavity that has a suitable short-term stability. With the combination of these two control loops, very stable laser frequencies can be generated and then converted into a time signal through a frequency comb acting as an optical clockwork34.

Here, we transfer this concept from an atomic to a nuclear reference transition. Although previous studies7,13,14 demonstrated that it is possible to excite the 229Th nucleus using VUV lasers stabilized to external frequency standards, it has not yet been possible to construct a system in which the laser interrogating the 229Th nuclei is steered by the nuclear transition itself. Our system is a nuclear clock that operates as a stand-alone device.

The nuclear clock is composed of a cavity-stabilized laser for short-term stability (referred to as the clock laser) and a 229Th interrogation system providing long-term stability (Fig. 1a). We use a continuous-wave VUV laser source to interrogate the 229Th nuclei7,30. This laser source comprises a 1,187-nm frequency-quadrupled commercial laser (the seed laser in Fig. 1) and a single-pass second-harmonic-generation stage using a randomly quasi-phase-matched strontium tetraborate (SBO) crystal. The frequency and linewidth of the 1,187-nm interrogation laser are determined by an offset phase lock to the clock laser. We modulate the offset lock frequency to perform absorption measurements. For the clock laser, we use a high-finesse cavity-stabilized external-cavity diode laser operating at 1,187 nm. The stabilization of the clock laser to the cavity uses a Pound–Drever–Hall scheme on a sideband generated by an electro-optical modulator, allowing us to shift the frequency of the clock laser independently of the cavity resonances.

The 148-nm laser enters a vacuum chamber containing the Th:CaF2 crystal and the detector. We use a segment of the X2 crystal; other pieces of the same ingot were used in refs. 13,14,25,29,35,36,37,38,39. The temperature of the crystal is monitored throughout all measurements; without active stabilization it remains within an interval of plus or minus 0.5 K around 294.7 K. The detection is based on a photomultiplier tube (PMT) with a CsI photocathode, operating in photon-counting mode, placed behind the crystal for the absorption spectroscopy of the nuclear transitions7.

The beat frequency fb for clock comparison and diagnostics is measured between the 1,187-nm output of the clock laser and the nearest mode of a stabilized infrared-frequency comb (Fig. 1b). The repetition rate of the comb is stabilized by locking the respective nearest comb mode to a high-finesse cavity-stabilized external-cavity laser at a wavelength of 1,542 nm. The absolute frequency of the comb is calibrated with radiation from an external-cavity laser at 1,542 nm, provided through a Doppler-compensated fibre link from the Austrian Federal Office of Metrology and Surveying (Bundesamt für Eich- und Vermessungswesen or BEV), where it is referenced to a Yb+ single-ion clock. We use this for comparison measurements between the Yb+ ion clock and the 229Th nuclear clock. Using the beat signal between the clock laser and the comb, we characterize the clock laser cavity drift and compensate for the dominant linear component of approximately 200 mHz s−1.

In clock operation, the clock laser is stabilized to the interrogated nuclear transition frequency with the help of a feedback loop that corrects for residual instability or drift of the cavity. To obtain the error signal of the 229Th absorption line, we modulate the interrogation frequency between two frequencies separated by \({f}_{{\rm{FWHM}}}/\sqrt{3}\), with fFWHM the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the measured absorption peak, and we record the difference between the signals. Scanning is then done by moving the centre frequency over the scan range. The resulting curve has a zero crossing at the absorption peak and a near-linear slope around it. For a detailed description and an example of the error signal shape obtained, see Methods.

We can neglect absorption saturation effects as we are operating in a regime where the number of 229Th nuclei in the excited state is much lower than the ground-state population at any time. Therefore, the fractional absorption amplitude A is constant in time. The \({\rm{SNR}}\,\approx \frac{A}{\sqrt{1-A}}\sqrt{\phi }\), where ϕ is the number of photons detected per second. With 65 pW of VUV laser power reaching the PMT, which has a detection efficiency of 10%, and 0.75% absorption on the 229Th 5/2 → 3/2 transition, this equation yields SNR ≈ 17 after 1 s of measurement.

In each clock cycle, we perform a measurement at the centre frequency determined in the preceding cycle for a given integration time T. The result is a point on the previously measured error signal function, which we then invert to get the actual frequency deviation from the zero crossing. This deviation, expressed as an infrared frequency, is then added to the current driving frequency of the electro-optical modulator in a single adjustment step to shift the laser back to the 229Th resonance. The actuation of each adjustment step takes about 1 s. The size of the step depends on the integration time T and the stability of the high-finesse cavity used in the clock laser.

If T is short, the noise in the detected PMT counts will result in a high uncertainty in the estimated line centre. If T is long, the residual drift of the cavity during the measurement also increases this uncertainty. We can choose T such that the SNR of the error signal is high enough to avoid degrading the short-term stability of the clock laser inherited from the cavity. For T = 30 min, the feedback signal of the nuclear resonance barely impacts the fractional frequency instability at 1 s, which is then comparable with the measured cavity instability of approximately 10−15. In contrast to fluorescence measurements, absorption spectroscopy also enables us to use feedback times much shorter than the isomer lifetime. With T = 20 s, the short-term stability deteriorates more strongly from the level obtained with the cavity alone, but the laser is locked to the 229Th frequency on a shorter timescale. This enables faster comparison of the 229Th and Yb+ transition frequencies, which extends the accessible mass range for ultralight dark matter searches.

The standard metric for characterizing the stability of a clock is the Allan deviation, the square root of the two-sample variance of consecutive measurements of the normalized clock output frequency. In Fig. 2 we show the overlapping Allan deviation σy (ref. 40) plotted versus the averaging time τ. For τ > T, the instability is determined by the shot-noise-limited interrogation of the 229Th nuclear transition \({\sigma }_{y}(\tau )\approx (\varGamma /{f}_{0})(1/\mathrm{SNR}){(\tau /{\rm{s}})}^{-1/2}\). Here f0 = 2.0204 × 1015 Hz is the nuclear transition frequency7 and Γ is the measured linewidth of approximately 100 kHz.

The fractional frequency instability for different averaging times τ is shown for two clock operating modes. One mode stabilizes to the 5/2 → 3/2 transition with T = 20 s between adjustment steps (red curve), the other with T = 30 min (blue curve). For τ > T, both curves follow the calculated shot-noise trend of the 5/2 → 3/2 interrogation.

The current state of the power stability of the VUV laser system allows us to operate the nuclear clock without any intervention for 1 day. The clock operation is not affected by fluctuations of the crystal temperature of approximately 0.1 K, consistent with the temperature dependence of the 5/2 → 3/2 transition (1.8 kHz K−1 at 295 K) reported in ref. 37.

Although the clock reaches fractional frequency instabilities in the low 10−14 range within a continuous clock run, we observed that the reproducibility between runs on different days was limited to approximately 5 × 10−13. Before each clock operation run, it is necessary to realign the laser system. In our current set-up, this necessarily leads to a small change in the axis and location at which the VUV laser traverses the crystal. Therefore, each clock operation probes slightly different local regions of the X2 crystal, as the laser beam has a diameter of approximately 0.5 mm and the crystal has a diameter of 3.1 mm. To test whether this explains the reduced reproducibility, we used an x–y translation stage to perform measurements on four different crystal positions.

We determined the respective line centres through T = 20 s measurements over a total duration of ttot = 20 min on each of the probed crystal positions. As visible in Fig. 3, the deviations δfi of the line centres from the frequency average of all five measurements differ by up to 1.7 kHz between datasets, which is well above the 0.13-kHz spread expected from statistical fluctuations in our measurement but within the uncertainty reported in previous studies of the line-centre reproducibility14. Remeasuring at the same crystal position (scans 2 and 4 in Fig. 3) yields a reproducible line-centre frequency. We conjecture that local strains induced by structural inhomogeneity causes these frequency shifts. In future implementations of the Th:CaF2-based clock, constraining the optical path through the crystal to a reproducible volume or improving doping homogeneity and minimizing strain through optimized growth conditions may enhance reproducibility.

To address some of the most pressing open questions in fundamental physics, such as the origin and properties of dark matter, a variety of theories predict the existence of new ultralight scalar bosons41. Even if these bosons only have feeble interactions with the known matter particles, their influence might still be observable in high-precision experiments. For example, couplings to the electromagnetic force, strong force or quarks would lead to an apparent oscillation of the fine structure constant α, the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) scale parameter ΛQCD and quark masses mq, respectively, with a frequency corresponding to the mass of the new boson. Because the transition energies in atoms and nuclei depend on these fundamental constants, their values would oscillate too42. Here the 229Th nuclear transition offers a big advantage: the extremely low energy of the isomer state is a result of a coincidental near-cancellation of mega-electronvolt-scale electromagnetic and strong nuclear force effects. This makes the transition very sensitive to changes in α, ΛQCD and mq. Owing to unknown nuclear parameters, precise values of these sensitivity factors cannot at present be calculated15,43, but it is predicted that they will exceed those of the most sensitive atomic clock transitions by several orders of magnitude5,6,43,44. Thus, even if the 229Th nuclear clock does not yet reach the same level of frequency instability as the best atomic clocks, it already yields competitive results in searches for fundamental physics.

We searched for periodic signals in the 229Th transition frequency in the data from the T = 20 s clock operation shown in Fig. 2 (red curve). We related the variation in the infrared beat frequency fb to the variation in the ratio between the Yb+ and 229Th transitions \({f}_{{\rm{Th}}}/{f}_{{{\rm{Yb}}}^{+}}\) through \({\partial }_{t}\,\log ({f}_{\mathrm{Th}}/{f}_{{\mathrm{Yb}}^{+}})=8({\partial }_{t}\,{f}_{{\rm{b}}})/{f}_{0}\). To search for possible oscillations of this ratio, we compute the best-fitting amplitudes \({{\mathcal{A}}}_{{\rm{f}}}=\sqrt{4{P}_{{\rm{f}}}/{N}_{\mathrm{tot}}}/{f}_{0}\) using the Lomb–Scargle method (Methods). Here Pf is the power spectrum of the beat frequencies converted into the VUV, and Ntot is the total number of statistically independent measurements. This result is sensitive to oscillations with frequencies between 1/ttot and 1/T, where ttot is the total measurement time of approximately 23 h.

To identify the statistical significance of the peaks in the Lomb–Scargle periodogram, we used Monte Carlo simulations of the clock feedback loop to calculate a 5% detection threshold. As no amplitudes exceeded this detection threshold, we established an upper limit for the amplitude of oscillations in the investigated frequency range (Fig. 4a and Methods). The upper limit can further be used to restrict possible couplings to scalar dark matter. The size of the coupling constant de for the interaction between a scalar boson ϕ and photons relates to the measured power spectrum Pf as follows (Methods):

The first factor contains the 229Th-specific enhancement through the large sensitivity factor \({k}_{{\rm{Th}}}^{\alpha }\) and transition frequency. The second factor indicates how the uncertainty decreases with reduced noise and higher statistics. The final factor leads to the decreasing sensitivities for higher boson masses mϕ and contains a suppression factor that is the same for any clock measurement, where c is the speed of light. For variations of the fine structure constant α, which corresponds to a scalar coupling to photons, the nuclear clock presented in this work imposes limits like those of the best comparable atomic clocks (Fig. 4). The transition frequencies of atomic clocks are less dependent on nuclear properties, even for those clocks that are based on hyperfine transitions, like the Cs clock. Thus, their sensitivities to variations of ΛQCD and mq are lower. The nuclear clock presented in this work reached a factor of 10 to 1,000 deeper into the parameter space than earlier experiments with atomic clocks. Compared with ref. 44, in which measurements of the 229Th line position and shape over 10 months were analysed, our measurement offers an improvement of around one order of magnitude in the accessible frequency range. The fast feedback of the absorption scheme allowed us to directly probe masses that could previously only be restricted through a line-shape analysis44,45. In future clock measurements, further enhancements in sensitivity can be expected. The frequency limits of the Lomb–Scargle periodogram are given by 1/ttot and 1/T. Therefore, lower frequencies could be reached by operating the clock for longer, whereas higher frequencies are accessible by reducing the cycle time. The sensitivity over the whole frequency range scales with the square root of the number of statistically independent measurements Ntot.

Apart from searches for oscillations, we analysed the frequency ratio \({f}_{{\rm{Th}}}/{f}_{{{\rm{Yb}}}^{+}}\) data for possible slow drifts. A linear fit of the T = 20 s and ttot ≈ 23 h data gave a slope of (2 ± 4) × 10−14 d−1, consistent with 0. Using the same sensitivity constants introduced above, this corresponds to linear drifts of \(\log \alpha \), \(\log \,{\varLambda }_{\mathrm{QCD}}\) and \(\log \,{m}_{q}\) of (2 ± 4)/kTh × 10−14 d−1. The aforementioned line-centre reproducibility will be a limiting factor when extending this search to months or years.

The performance of the 229Th clock could be straightforwardly improved by increasing the VUV laser power. The power limitation of the laser source used in our experiment is defined by the spontaneous domain-inversion structure of the SBO crystal. Only a fraction of the domains contributes to the frequency upconversion of the 297-nm radiation.

One order of magnitude gain in the VUV power could be achieved by using the presented randomly quasi-phase-matched SBO in an enhancement cavity, which is limited due to optical losses at 297 nm. Further enhancement of the VUV power to the hundreds of nanowatts level could be reached by using commercially available 3-W ultraviolet lasers.

Higher VUV power levels could be obtained using four-wave mixing in Cd vapour31, for which 300 nW has already been reported, or by fabricating patterned SBO46 and BaMgF4 crystals47. For a first-order periodically poled nonlinear crystal, a VUV power of at least 1 μW can be expected. However, this has not yet been demonstrated due to technical challenges in the submicrometre periodic poling.

The shot-noise-limited clock instability scales with \({\sigma }_{y}(\tau )\approx (\varGamma /{f}_{0})\) \((1/\mathrm{SNR}){(\tau /{\rm{s}})}^{-1/2}\). Beyond increasing the laser power, there are two other ways to improve the clock performance: increasing the absorption and decreasing the linewidth Γ. We operate in a low-saturation regime, where the fractional absorption amplitude A does not change with time. This will be the case as long as the number of photons that are absorbed during the lifetime of the isomeric state is much lower than the number of 229Th nuclei in the beam path. In the current experiment, approximately 3 × 108 photons were absorbed in 10 min, although there were approximately 1016 229Th nuclei in the beam path. Therefore, absorption measurements are expected to operate far from saturation, even if the available laser power increases significantly with further laser developments.

In ref. 14, it was found that Γ increases with the 229Th density ρTh. The absorption A also depends on ρTh and increases as \(A=1-\exp (-\bar{\sigma }L{\rho }_{{\rm{Th}}}\,\chi )\). Here L is the length of the light path through the crystal, χ quantifies the percentage of Th atoms that are in a D centre (for X2, 58.6%; ref. 29) and \(\bar{\sigma }\) is the absorption cross section, which itself scales with Γ−1. These scalings imply that an optimal ρTh exists for which σy is minimized. The shot noise limit resulting from this theoretically optimal doping density and χ = 1 is only a factor of 2 lower than that of our current crystal, X2. Therefore, no large improvements in σy can be expected by modifying ρTh in future Th:CaF2 crystals. It should be possible with longer crystals and VUV cavities to increase the path length L by a factor of 10, resulting in an order of magnitude higher SNR. With this, and a laser power of 1 μW, 229Th-doped CaF2 crystals could reach a fractional frequency instability of approximately \(1{0}^{-15}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\).

Going beyond Th:CaF2, there are other possible host crystals. We expect crystals containing Th as part of the stoichiometric crystal structure, such as ThF4, to have reduced linewidths. In such crystals, 229Th is not a dopant and, thus, does not distort the crystal structure, presumably reducing the inhomogeneous broadening of the nuclear transition. This is also expected to improve the line-centre reproducibility.

Another relevant contribution to the linewidth is the magnetic interaction with neighbouring F-19 nuclei, which causes broadenings in the range 0.1–1 kHz (refs. 4,27). Even smaller linewidths might become accessible with spinless solids48. To benefit from these improvements, the linewidth of future VUV lasers needs to be narrowed down equivalently. Using a conservative linewidth estimate of Γ = 1 kHz, a crystal with similar doping density and dimensions as the one presently used would yield an optical depth \(\bar{\sigma }L{\rho }_{{\rm{Th}}}\,\chi \approx 1\). With this, and using a 100-pW laser with a high stability cavity, a fractional frequency instability of approximately \(1{0}^{-16}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\) could be reached. This would bring the frequency instability of the nuclear clock to the same level as state-of-the-art optical atomic clocks49,50,51 while still maintaining the form factor and simplicity of a solid-state clock. Compared with the nuclear clock introduced in this work, this would enable a four orders of magnitude increase in sensitivity to the variation of the fundamental constants.

In the 229Th interrogation system, a commercial laser (FHG-TA Pro, TOPTICA) provides an output power of approximately 500 mW at a wavelength of 296.8 nm, frequency-quadrupled in two doubling stages and one amplification stage from a diode seed laser at 1,187 nm. The final second-harmonic-generation process is based on nonlinear frequency conversion in an SBO crystal kept under a high-purity N2 atmosphere (purity 5.0). Fundamental radiation still present in the beam after the final second-harmonic-generation step is separated using three dielectric-coated mirrors. For the absorption measurements, we used a head-on type PMT (R6835, Hamamatsu) mounted inside the vacuum chamber and operated at 2.5 kV. We used the same segment of the X2 sample60 as in ref. 7. The segment in use has a cylindrical geometry with a diameter of 3.1(1) mm and a length of 4.2(1) mm and was oriented such that the beam traversed along the centre line of the piece. The measured average concentration of 229Th in the segment was 6.6(5) × 1015 mm−3.

The seed laser of the FHG-TA was locked to the clock laser (CLS, TOPTICA) through an offset frequency phase lock. A fast photodiode with a bandwidth of 10 GHz measured the beat frequency between the two lasers, which was then mixed with a reference frequency. The fast loop of this lock actuated on the seed laser diode current, and the slow loop was used to steer the grating of the laser diode. The laser was scanned by modulating the reference frequency.

Like the actuators of the offset lock, the Pound–Drever–Hall lock of the clock laser to the cavity was also configured such that the fast feedback loop actuated on the laser diode current, whereas the slow feedback signal of the Pound–Drever–Hall scheme controlled the position of the grating for optical feedback to the laser diode.

For clock comparison measurements and drift rate measurements of the cavity, the beat frequency fb of the clock laser with the frequency comb (FC1500-250-ULN, Menlo) was recorded using a dead-time-free frequency counter (K+K FXE) operated in Π-type counting mode61,62 at a gate time of 1 s. Our method of comparing the thorium clock at TU Wien with the Yb+ clock (TOPTICLOCK, TOPTICA)63 at BEV follows the scheme described in ref. 7. The Yb+ clock was based on the 435.5-nm E2 transition of a single 171Yb ion.

All frequency synthesizers and counters in the 229Th clock system and the frequency comb were referenced to the 10-MHz signal of a commercial Rb clock (FS725, SRS).

To perform an absorption measurement at a specific frequency, we modulated (square wave) the offset lock frequency between the seed laser diode and the clock laser with 10 Hz between the target frequency and an off-resonance frequency. Each modulation cycle was also reflected in a synchronization signal connected to a time-resolved pulse counter (TimeTagger Ultra, Swabian Instruments). The modulation ensured that power fluctuations in the laser output did not affect the measurement. The detection set-up consists of a PMT, a radiofrequency amplifier and the pulse counter, which binned the arriving pulses from the PMT relative to the last synchronization edge. The absorption was then calculated by subtracting the on-resonance counts from the off-resonance counts and dividing by the off-resonance counts.
