Both Treg populations were significantly enriched in HGLs compared with normal tissue. By contrast, no CD4+ Tconv cell or CD8+ T cell populations were increased in HGLs, highlighting the selective enrichment of Treg cells before invasion in patients at high risk of LUSC. This pattern was seen in abundance analyses informed by cluster (BATF+ Treg cells, false discovery rate (FDR) = 0.014; TCM-like Treg cells, FDR = 0.018; Fig. 1d) and neighbourhood (BATF+ Treg cells, 70 out of 101, median log2[fold change (FC)] = 3.15; TCM-like cells, 132 out of 197, median log2[FC] = 5.16; Fig. 1e,f), including bootstrapped miloR models (BATF+ Treg cells and TCM-like Treg cells enriched in 10 out of 10 and 4 out of 10 miloR iterations, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 1b). Compositional changes were reflected in pseudobulk analyses of CD4+ T cells, in which BATF+ Treg cell genes (for example, FOXP3, IL2RA, TNFRSF4, CCR8 and BATF) were among the most differentially expressed in HGLs relative to normal lung (Fig. 1g).

We validated these findings by deriving a BATF+ Treg gene signature from scRNA-seq data (Supplementary Table 2). This signature intensified during LUSC tumorigenesis in bulk transcriptomic data from 122 bronchial biopsy samples13 (HGLs versus normal tissue, P = 0.0012; Fig. 1h). Integration of UCLH and external large-scale scRNA-seq datasets20,21,22,23 formed an expanded object (461 samples from 271 patients; Extended Data Fig. 1c–e), in which we confirmed that BATF+ Treg cells were significantly increased in both preinvasive and invasive LUSC (P = 2.25 × 10−10 and P = 4.45 × 10−9, respectively) and LUAD (P = 1.34 × 10−2 and P = 2.8 × 10−28, respectively), in models accounting for study and total T cells24 (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). We further verified preinvasive enrichment of BATF+ Treg cells in this integrated dataset using a sliding scale of sample sizes (Extended Data Fig. 1h) and neighbourhood analyses (Extended Data Fig. 1i). TCM-like Treg cells were also more abundant in preinvasive and invasive LUAD and LUSC than in normal tissue (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g), although to a lesser extent than BATF+ Treg cells in neighbourhood analysis (HGLs versus normal tissue: 73 out of 145 of BATF+ Treg cells and 8 out of 39 of TCM-like Treg cell neighbourhoods enriched, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 1i).

The preinvasive BATF+ Treg cell program from HGLs showed strong transcriptional similarity to highly suppressive eTreg cell signatures6,25,26 associated with NSCLC disease progression (for example, TNFR+ tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) Treg cells26, normalized enrichment score (NES) = 2.28, adjusted P = 8.19 × 10−23; Fig. 1i) and those which associate with a lack of major pathological response to neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 (for example, OX40hiGITRhi TIL Treg cells6, NES = 2.21, adjusted P = 4.49 × 10−15; Fig. 1i). To confirm this relationship using our own signature, we leveraged an external study of patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy27,28 wherein a high relative BATF+ Treg cell score defined failure to respond to PD-1 blockade (n = 59, odds ratio (OR) = 0.24, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.1–0.61, P = 0.003, accounting for CD8+ T cell infiltration and tumour mutational burden; Fig. 1j).

These data suggest that an eTreg cell population associated with lung cancer progression and immunotherapy failure emerges in premalignant airway lesions of patients at substantial risk of NSCLC. These results provide a potential basis to target and track early pulmonary tumorigenesis via Treg cell-directed immune interception.

We next considered that BATF+ Treg cells may partially derive from circulating precursors4,7, which could enable noninvasive tracking of early tumorigenesis to cue lung cancer interception.

scRNA-seq and T cell receptor sequencing (TCR-seq) analyses of CD4+ T cells in HGLs highlighted that 28.9% of BATF+ Treg cells were expanded. Expanded BATF+ Treg cells preferentially shared clonotypes with local progenitor phenotype TCF7+ CD4+ Tconv cells and TCM-like Treg cells, which implied ongoing Treg cell differentiation in HGLs (Fig. 2a–c and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). Notably, 17.6% of all BATF+ Treg cell clonotypes in the lesion were shared with CD4+ T cells in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs; Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 2a), which suggested that BATF+ Treg cells could derive from local and/or systemic precursors. To refine this model, we assessed BATF+ Treg cell transcriptional heterogeneity according to clonal origin. Blood-shared BATF+ Treg cells retained an increased expression of progenitor and recirculation markers (LEF1 and KLF2), and Tconv-related cells expressed increased levels of effector transcripts (for example, IFNG). By contrast, unshared BATF+ Treg cell clones displayed an activated, tissue-adapted regulatory program (CXCL13, TNFRSF8, HLA-DQA1, HLA-DPA1 and HLA-DQB2), and an elevated antigen presenting cell (APC)–T cell contact signature29,30 (P = 0.04; Fig. 2d,e). To analyse BATF+ Treg cell crosstalk in situ, we conducted interactome and abundance analyses of all cells in HGLs and in normal tissue. We observed significant increases in APCs expressing major histocompatibility complex class II (MHCII) molecules, and predicted MHCII signalling to BATF+ Treg cells from dendritic cells and CD86–CTLA4 and TNFSF9–TNFRSF9 interactions in HGLs (Extended Data Fig. 2c–i). Together, these data suggest a model in which preinvasive BATF+ Treg cells are partially derived from newly infiltrated clones in the circulation while also being supplied and/or maintained via APC-driven differentiation, activation and expansion in HGLs.

To discern which circulating T cells might supply BATF+ Treg cells, we clustered blood CD4+ T cells. We identified seven clusters, including a blood eTreg cell population (hereafter termed circulating eTreg cells) that partly resembled BATF+ Treg cells. This population was characterized by the highest levels of FOXP3, BATF, IL2RA, CTLA4, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18 and ENTPD1 (encoding CD39) in the circulation and enrichment of the BATF+ Treg cell signature from HGLs (Fig. 2f,g and Extended Data Fig. 2j). Circulating eTreg cells were the dominant blood CD4+ T cell population that shared clonotypes with BATF+ Treg cells, which occurred at levels significantly greater than expected by chance (88.7%, OR = 38.49, P = 2.43 × 10−12; Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 2k). Clonotype-aware cross-tissue pseudotime analysis predicted a blood (circulating eTreg cell) to lung (BATF+ Treg cell) differentiation trajectory, which was mirrored by the dynamics of the key state-defining marker genes BATF (BATF+ Treg), TCF7 (progenitor) and FOXP1 (memory) (Fig. 2i,j).

Given the overlap between BATF+ Treg cells and circulating eTreg cells, we considered that the latter may rise during preinvasive LUSC progression and track tumorigenesis. To test this, we collected all evaluable PBMCs from patients with low-grade lesions or HGLs in the UCLH bronchoscopy surveillance cohort (129 samples from 47 patients; Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b) and performed unsupervised flow cytometry analyses31 (Fig. 2l,m and Supplementary Table 3). Patients with HGLs displayed significantly increased frequencies of activated and effector memory CD4+ T cells (TEM cells), including two clusters of CD45RA−CD39+ eTreg cells: CD39hiCD38int eTreg cells (q = 0.036) and proliferating eTreg cells (q = 0.036) (Fig. 2m,n and Extended Data Fig. 3c–f). This result was confirmed by manually gating CD45RA−CD39+FOXP3+ cells (Fig. 2o,p and Extended Data Fig. 3e) and adjusting for age, smoking history and previous cancer diagnosis (P = 0.033; Fig. 2q). Extended phenotypic analysis of the CD39+ eTreg cell population revealed preferential co-expression of the eTreg cell markers GITR and OX40 alongside HELIOS, PD-1 and Ki-67 (Extended Data Fig. 4).

These data suggest that a clonally coordinated blood-to-lung eTreg cell axis emerges during LUSC development, which may inform tracking and targeting of preinvasive immune regulation for lung cancer interception.

We next examined whether the preinvasive eTreg cell circuit was detectable in patients diagnosed with NSCLC during CT screening. PBMCs from patients with screen-detected NSCLC (90% of which were stage I) in the UCL study ‘analysis of screen-detected lung cancers’ genomic traits’ (ASCENT study32, n = 57) were analysed by flow cytometry alongside PBMCs from age-matched hospitalized individuals assessed for malignancy, infection and autoimmunity, as well as healthy platelet donors (n = 29; Fig. 3a, Methods, Extended Data Fig. 5a–c (cohort 1) and Supplementary Fig. 1). Circulating CD39+ eTreg cell frequencies were significantly increased in early-stage NSCLC compared with healthy individuals (P = 0.0092; Fig. 3b,c and after adjustment for clinical covariates, P = 0.030; Extended Data Fig. 5d). To validate these observations, we compared PBMCs from an independent sample set of 77 early-stage LUAD cases from the ASCENT study (84% of which were stage I) with those from 67 individuals undergoing CT screening in the ‘assessment of novel biomarkers in participants undergoing targeted lung health checks’ (ALPINE) study33 who fulfilled screening entry criteria but showed no signs of disease on imaging (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c, cohort 2). Circulating CD39+ eTreg cells were once more significantly enriched in early-stage LUAD, including after adjustment for clinical variables (P = 7.10 × 10−5; Extended Data Fig. 5e).

To measure nascent intratumoural Treg cell enrichment, we analysed CD4+ T cells in TILs from patients with early-stage NSCLC (n = 16; Extended Data Fig. 5f). Two CD45RA–FOXP3hi eTreg cell clusters expressing BATF+ Treg cell markers (OX40+GITR+4-1BB+CCR8+CTLA-4+) distinguished by intermediate or high activation state were the only populations significantly enriched in NSCLC TILs compared with paired normal tissue (Fig. 3d,e; P = 5.85 × 10−4 for the 4-1BBhi subset, P = 5.83 × 10−4 for the 4-1BBint subset), with results verified by manual gating (Fig. 3f).

To assess the clinical relevance of this coordinated increase in local BATF+ Treg cells and circulating eTreg cells, we quantified the BATF+ Treg cell signature in tumour bulk RNA-seq data and circulating CD39+ eTreg cells by matched peripheral blood flow cytometry in all patients with clinical follow-up and sufficient material in the ASCENT study (n = 89 (76 with stage I disease); Fig. 3g). Stratification by the median of either metric alone showed that high circulating or intratumoural eTreg cells associate with shorter disease-free survival (DFS; Extended Data Fig. 5g). Notably, patients with a combined high tumoural BATF+ Treg cell signature and elevated circulating CD39+ eTreg cell frequency experienced a more marked reduction in DFS (hazard ratio (HR) = 3.91, 95% CI = 1.53–9.99, P = 0.0044; Fig. 3h), independent of clinical or technical covariates (HR = 2.99, 95% CI = 1.06–8.42, P = 0.038; Fig. 3i). These data indicate that cross-tissue amplification of eTreg cells can identify patients with CT screen-detected NSCLC who are at increased risk of rapid recurrence or death and may benefit from earlier intervention.

To better define preinvasive Treg cell dynamics, we leveraged longitudinal samples from patients who developed LUSC during CT surveillance and in whom blood was sampled at 3–12-month intervals from enrolment to diagnosis in the ASCENT study and the UCL SUMMIT study (‘cancer screening study with or without low-dose lung CT to validate a multi-cancer early detection blood test’)34 (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 6a). We generated longitudinal pre-diagnosis TCR-seq repertoires from blood DNA and annotated the phenotype of each clonotype via patient-matched scRNA-seq and single-cell TCR-seq (scTCR-seq) of PBMCs isolated at diagnosis, which were pre-enriched for non-naive CD25hi CD4+ T cells. Clustering identified three major blood Treg cell subsets. This included a cluster of eTreg cells expressing BATF, CTLA4, TNFRSF4 and TNFRSF18, which were enriched for the BATF+ Treg cell and circulating eTreg cell signatures from patients with HGLs (Fig. 3k). Longitudinal clonotype analysis demonstrated a marked increase in eTreg cell clonotype frequency from baseline to diagnosis (P = 4.45 × 10−6), a smaller increase in naive-like Treg cell clones (P = 0.002) and no change in TCM-like Treg cell clonotypes (P = 0.829; Fig. 3l and Extended Data Fig. 6b). These results establish that circulating eTreg cells map tumour development in CT-surveilled NSCLC, and suggest that eTreg cell dynamics may inform methods to guide patient selection and timing for NSCLC interception or early intervention in CT screening programmes.

To experimentally test the hypothesis that early lung tumorigenesis induces a tractable eTreg cell circuit, we used a carcinogen-induced mouse model. We have previously shown that N-nitroso-tris-chloroethylurea (NTCU)-driven carcinogenesis recapitulates molecular and histological features of LUSC, including progressive squamous dysplasia descending a tracheal–bronchial path marked via aberrant KRT5 expression35. Accordingly, NTCU induced low-grade (week 15) then both low-grade and high-grade (week 18) tracheobronchial preinvasive squamous lesions. At week 24, all mice developed HGLs and 83.3% had early invasive lung squamous carcinomas (Fig. 4a). We observed significantly increased Treg cell abundance at the bronchial tree in NTCU-exposed mice compared with age-matched control mice (Fig. 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). By contrast, no increase in CD8+ T cells or CD4+ Tconv cells was seen in the bronchial tree, and all T cell lineages remained unchanged in the distal lung parenchyma. This result highlights a spatially restricted and selective pattern of Treg cell enrichment during preinvasive pulmonary carcinognesis (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). Furthermore, 72.4% of Treg cells in proximity to the bronchial tree were OX40+, consistent with BATF+ Treg cell identity (Extended Data Fig. 7d,e).

scRNA-seq of mouse lungs identified seven CD4+ T cell clusters, including three Foxp3+ Treg cell populations. The first population was an eTreg cell cluster labelled as BATF+ Treg cells. This cluster was defined by high Foxp3 expression and strong co-expression of BATF+ Treg cell orthologues (for example, Batf, Tnfrsf18, Tnfrsf4 and Tnfrsf9).s The second and third populations were defined by the expression of a TCM-like module (Foxp1, Bach2 and Satb1) in the presence of either intermediate (TCM-like Treg cell 1) or low–negative (TCM-like Treg cell 2) Foxp3, eTreg and lymph node-homing (Ccr7 and Sell) gene expression (Fig. 4d,e). BATF+ Treg cells (log2[FC] = 1.48, FDR = 0.017) were significantly increased in NTCU-treated mice compared with control mice (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 8a–c) and displayed strong transcriptional similarity to human BATF+ Treg cells from patient HGLs identified via AFB (NES = 2.28, FDR = 4.86 × 10−7; Fig. 4g).

We next conducted scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq analyses of lungs and blood at 18 weeks after NTCU initiation, when the dominant preneoplasias are HGLs and invasive disease is yet to form. BATF+ Treg cells in the lungs of NTCU-exposed mice contained significantly more expanded clones. These expressed a tissue-adapted, terminal effector Treg cell program (for example, Il2ra, Dusp4, Ccr8, Cxcr6, Itgav, Tnfrsf8, Havcr2, Lag3, Pdcd1 and Il10), alongside activation markers (Tnfrsf9), and were enriched for signatures of APC engagement, IL-2 signalling and tissue chemotaxis (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8d–f). By contrast, BATF+ Treg cells in lungs from control mice were predominantly unexpanded and expressed genes marking a quiescent progenitor state (for example, S1pr1, Lef1, Klf2 and Slamf6; Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 8d–f).

BATF+ Treg cells shared clonotypes with TCM-like Treg cells and progenitor CD4+ cells in lung samples taken 18 weeks after tumour induction (Extended Data Fig. 8g,h). They also shared clonotypes with circulating eTreg cells expressing mouse orthologues of human circulating eTreg cells (for example, Foxp3, Batf, Ccr8, Helios, Il2ra, Ctla4, Tnfrsf4, Tnfrsf18 and Entpd1; Fig. 4j,k and Extended Data Fig. 8a,i). Circulating eTreg cell clonotypes preferentially overlapped with BATF+ Treg cells in NTCU-treated mice but not control mice (P = 0.013 in NTCU, P = 0.925 in control; Fig. 4k and Extended Data Fig. 8i).

These data suggest that before invasive disease, carcinogen-driven in vivo tumorigenesis promotes activation, differentiation, clonal expansion and accumulation of pulmonary BATF+ Treg cells that are partly seeded from the circulating eTreg cell pool. The results also support the contention that cross-tissue eTreg cell amplification is a species-conserved feature of early LUSC tumorigenesis.

Consistent with clonotype sharing, pseudotemporal modelling placed circulating eTreg cells upstream of pulmonary BATF+ Treg cells along a trajectory marked by loss of Tcf7 and S1pr1 expression and acquisition of Batf, Irf4 and Tnfrsf18 expression (Fig. 4l). This pattern mirrors the blood-to-lesion Treg cell transition inferred from observations in human preinvasive disease.

We postulated that the preinvasive eTreg cell axis would originate from upstream remodelling of T cells and/or myeloid cells in the lymph nodes. Flow cytometry analyses revealed significantly elevated PD-L1 expression on migratory cDC1 cells in the dLNs (mediastinal) of NTCU-treated mice at week 18. This change was absent in the non-draining lymph nodes (ndLNs; inguinal), which indicated that development of high-grade preneoplasia is accompanied by a locally modulated priming environment conducive for T cell regulation36,37,38,39 (Fig. 4m,n and Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Concurrently, we observed an increased abundance of total, effector (CD44+OX40+GITR+CD39+) and TCM-like (CD62L+) Treg cells in the dLNs but not ndLNs of NTCU-exposed mice (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 8j,k).

To assess whether NTCU-driven carcinogenesis induced an increase in circulating eTreg cells, we longitudinally analysed tail vein blood at 3–6-week intervals during preinvasive progression (weeks 12–24) via flow cytometry. Compared with age-matched controls, eTreg cells were significantly increased in the circulation of NTCU-exposed mice throughout early tumorigenesis (P = 7.39 × 10−4; Fig. 4q,r). To functionally interrogate the dLN–blood–lung axis, we blocked lymph node egress in NTCU-treated mice at week 18 for 72 h using the S1P receptor 1 antagonist FTY720. Total Treg cells (13.7-fold, P = 0.0043) and eTreg cells (gated as CD62Llo 8.5-fold, P = 0.0043) were significantly reduced after FTY720 administration in NTCU-treated mice. This result confirms the partial dependence of circulating eTreg cells on lymph node output and provides evidence of systemic and local CD4+ T cell contributions to the BATF+ Treg cell pool (Fig. 4s).

These data indicate that carcinogen-driven in vivo LUSC tumorigenesis triggers preinvasive skewing of migratory dendritic cells in the dLN and amplifies a clonally coordinated systemic–pulmonary Treg cell network that is partially dependent on lymph node egress. These findings corroborate observations in preinvasive clinical samples, identify the eTreg cell axis as a conserved feature of lung tumorigenesis across species and establish the NTCU model as a translational platform to explore Treg cell-directed interception.

We next sought to identify clinically relevant strategies for LUSC interception. Pathway analysis of CD4+ T cells in the lungs of NTCU-exposed mice highlighted that PI3K signalling was significantly elevated in BATF+ Treg cells (Extended Data Fig. 8l). We have previously shown that genetic inactivation of the leukocyte-enriched PI3Kδ isoform in Treg cells improves solid tumour control40. Accordingly, PI3Kδ inhibitors already in clinical use for B cell malignancies41 preferentially inhibit trafficking and maintenance of Treg cells over other T cell populations and have entered clinical trials for solid tumours, in which Treg cell contraction seems to drive antitumour activity42,43. Thus, we leveraged the PI3Kδ inhibitor PI-3065, which demonstrates anticancer potential independent of cancer-intrinsic antiproliferative activity40,44. Consistent with this, PI-3065 did not have a significant effect on the proliferation of NTCU-induced squamous (epithelial) cell organoids (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We therefore administered PI-3065 from 15 weeks, when preinvasive disease emerges, until the 24-week end point (Fig. 5a). As a control, we dosed mice with BYL719 (also known as alpelisib)45, which inhibits the ubiquitously expressed PI3Kα. Systemic administration of both inhibitors was well tolerated (Extended Data Fig. 9b–d), and characteristic PI3Kδ-dependent activity was evident in the spleen, including a reduction in marginal zone B cells46 (B220+CD21+CD23−) (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f).
