Of note, we observed unambiguous RNA density in the active site of the RNA helicase AQR, locally resolved to 3.9 Å resolution (Fig. 2a–c and Extended Data Fig. 4b). On the basis of reports of AQR binding approximately 40 nucleotides on either side of the intron BP14,28,29, a proposed low-resolution RNA path3 and the relative positions of the RNA elements in the ILSAQR, we assigned this RNA as the circular portion of the intron–lariat. The intron–lariat is enclosed in an RNA-binding channel of AQR formed by its RecA1, RecA2 and Stalk domains, resembling the RNA-binding mode of the structurally related RNA helicase Upf1 (ref. 30) (Fig. 2a–c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Unlike RNA-free AQR in the preceding ILS complexes, in the ILSAQR, the AQR RecA2 domain shifts position to close over the bound intron–lariat RNA (Extended Data Fig. 4d,e). The PPIE RRM domain sits at the entry of the AQR active site, suggesting that it guides the intron–lariat towards AQR (Fig. 2a–c and Extended Data Fig. 4b). AQR is an Upf1-like SF1 family helicase with single-stranded nucleotide translocase activity of 5′-to-3′ polarity26,31. Our structure suggests that AQR translocation along the intron–lariat would be poised to unwind the U2–intron branch helix and pull on the intron–lariat BP adenosine (Fig. 2c,d). This is reminiscent of the role of AQR in spliceosome activation, where it is thought to pull the intron to extract the branch helix from the SF3B complex, allowing the BP to participate in branching26,27. AQR could therefore assist both spliceosome activation and disassembly, as previously proposed32. Because the termination factor C19L2 occludes the buried intron–lariat BP in the ILSAQR, AQR translocation may also dissociate C19L2 from the spliceosome (Fig. 2b). Overall, our ILSAQR structure supports a role for AQR in extracting the intron–lariat BP from the spliceosomal RNA network during termination.

In the ILSAQR, we also observed the RNA helicase DHX15, bound in the same position as in previous ILS structures2,3,4,5 (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4f). DHX15 is a DEAH-box RNA helicase that unwinds the U2–U6 helix II in the ILS by translocating on U6 snRNA with 3′-to-5′ polarity2,13. Our structural data suggest that DHX15 and AQR may both act during spliceosome disassembly, either sequentially or simultaneously, to unwind different RNA elements: U2–U6 helices II and I, and the U2–intron branch helix, respectively (Fig. 2d). We hypothesize that this remodelling may further allow refolding of the internal U2 snRNA branch stem loop33, promoting U2 snRNA dissociation from the spliceosome (Extended Data Fig. 4g). Overall, these data suggest a model in which two RNAs pulled in opposite directions initiate dismantling of the RNA network of the spliceosome and extraction of the intron–lariat BP during ILSAQR remodelling. The dependence on AQR probably varies across introns14, and we do not exclude AQR-independent routes to BP exposure for debranching.

Debranching of the intron–lariat is critical for intron turnover and nuclear RNA homeostasis6,12 and has been proposed to occur on the spliceosome14,15,16, although molecular evidence has been lacking. The DIS complex contains a debranched intron and forms after the ILSAQR (see the section ‘ILSAQR is remodelled into the DIS’), suggesting that debranching precedes intron ejection. In the ILSAQR, AQR is poised to extract the intron–lariat BP from the RNA active site, exposing it for debranching. This would, however, require the debranching enzyme DBR1 to be tethered near the extracted BP (Fig. 2e).

DBR1 was absent from the ILSAQR mass spectrometry data, probably reflecting its transient interaction with the spliceosome. To identify candidate spliceosomal interactors of DBR1, we immunoprecipitated overexpressed GFP-tagged DBR1 from human K562 cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a). This enriched the known DBR1 interactor MPLKIP34 and ILS-specific termination factors, consistent with previous results12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 2). Moreover, proximity labelling of DBR1 fused to the biotin ligase TurboID35 enriched MPLKIP, the termination factor C19L1 and the NTR complex (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table 4). A reciprocal experiment using C19L1–TurboID enriched DBR1 and MPLKIP, supporting their proximity in spliceosomal complexes (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table 4).

To investigate the molecular basis of DBR1 binding to the spliceosome, we performed AlphaFold2 Multimer36,37 screens of DBR1 and MPLKIP against the proteins present in the ILSAQR (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We obtained high-confidence predictions only for DBR1 with the termination factor C19L1 and the NTR protein SYF1, involving two conserved peptides in the DBR1 C terminus (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5d,e). Peptide I (DBR1 residues 420–434) was predicted to bind to the metallophosphatase (MPP) domain of C19L1, and peptide II (residues 524–532) to the helical repeats of SYF1 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 5d). These predictions agree with our DBR1 proximity labelling data (Fig. 2f) and previous biochemical data15,16. Both peptides could simultaneously engage with the ILSAQR and would be compatible with the predicted DBR1–MPLKIP interface (Fig. 2e). Peptide I is particularly well conserved and would tether the catalytic domain of DBR1 to the C19L1 MPP domain through a 30-residue linker, placing DBR1 near the intron–lariat BP after its extraction (Fig. 2e). The NTR subunit SYF1 carries a similar motif (SYF1 residues 812–824), which may indicate exchange between the two peptides at C19L1 during termination (Extended Data Fig. 5f).

We confirmed the predicted DBR1–C19L1 interaction with recombinant proteins, where wild-type DBR1 peptide I, but not its scrambled version, bound the C19L1 MPP domain in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Furthermore, we have shown that overexpression of wild-type DBR1 rescued the cell growth defect caused by acute depletion of endogenous DBR1–dTAG38, whereas DBR1 lacking peptide I did not (Extended Data Fig. 5h), demonstrating the cellular importance of the DBR1–C19L1 interface.

Together, we established a direct DBR1–ILS interaction that may facilitate intron–lariat debranching on the spliceosome after DHX15 and AQR extract the intron–lariat BP from the ILS RNA network.

The remodelling of ILSAQR by DHX15 and AQR would be expected to rearrange the RNA network for debranching, dissociating the ‘early’ termination factors C19L1, C19L2, GCFC2, TFIP11 and DHX15, and exposing surfaces for binding of the ‘late’ termination factors DHX35, GPATCH1 and WDR83 (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1a). The essential and highly conserved protein YJU2B (Extended Data Fig. 6a) is ideally positioned to guide this exchange. In the ILSAQR, the YJU2B zinc-finger domain binds the PRP8 linker and finger-palm domains, otherwise inaccessible in catalytic and post-catalytic spliceosomes (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 6b). The YJU2B helical domain displaces a CDC5L α-helix (residues 357–382) from the ESS2–SNW1–PRP8 interface in the preceding ILS″ (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 6b), and runs along SYF1 and SYF3 to help position the C19L1 MPP domain and thereby DBR1 (Fig. 2e). Although WDR83, GPATCH1 and DHX35 were not detected in the final purified ILSAQR sample, low levels were present before gradient purification, indicating transient association (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Consistently, using purified proteins in in vitro pulldowns and gel filtration assays, we confirmed the interactions predicted by AlphaFold3 between YJU2B–WDR83, WDR83–GPATCH1 and GPATCH1–DHX35 (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Figs. 1b,c and 6c–e). DHX35 and GPATCH1 were also enriched in proximity labelling experiments using both YJU2B and C19L1 as bait (Fig. 2f, Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 4). We therefore propose that YJU2B may aid the recruitment of DHX35, GPATCH1 and WDR83 during ILSAQR remodelling.

To probe the ILSAQR-to-DIS transition in the human system, we used an in vitro remodelling assay using human nuclear extract expressing GFP-tagged YJU2B (Extended Data Fig. 7a). ATP treatment caused the depletion of the ILS-specific termination factors (TFIP11, C19L1 and C19L2) from anti-GFP-purified spliceosomes (Extended Data Fig. 7b). Given the low abundance of endogenous DIS factors, we supplemented the assay with a recombinant heterodimer of catalytically inactive DHX35(K83A) and a minimal GPATCH1 construct (residues 1–440; Extended Data Fig. 7b). DHX35(K83A)–GPATCH1 was recruited to the remodelled ILSAQR in an ATP-dependent manner, consistent with the formation of a DIS-like intermediate (Extended Data Fig. 7b) and our C. elegans assay (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These results support a model in which ILSAQR is remodelled into DIS, possibly involving additional short-lived intermediates.

To understand the molecular consequences of ILSAQR remodelling and the roles of DHX35–GPATCH1–WDR83 (Fig. 3a) in termination, we next analysed the DIS structure (Figs. 1c and 3b). Its protein and RNA composition resembled the 35S spliceosomal complex, which accumulates at the end of pre-mRNA splicing in vitro18,19. The DIS contained the NTR, the NineTeen complex (NTC), the U5 snRNP and the DIS-specific termination factors DHX35, GPATCH1 and WDR83 (Fig. 1c), but lacked the six ILS-specific termination factors (TFIP11, GCFC2, C19L1, C19L2, DHX15 and YJU2B), the U2 snRNP and ESS2 (Figs. 1c and 3d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1g). The DIS RNA network was almost completely dismantled, with only a partial U6–intron–5′ SS duplex remaining (Fig. 3c–e and Extended Data Fig. 7c). Remodelling of the ILSAQR by AQR and DHX15 thus causes major compositional and conformational changes without complete disassembly of the spliceosome.

In the ILSAQR, AQR would extract the intron–lariat BP for debranching by the C19L1-tethered DBR1. As C19L1 is absent from the DIS, which forms after the ILS, we reasoned that introns bound to the DIS are probably debranched. As we observed no cryo-EM density for the intron BP in the DIS (Extended Data Fig. 7c), we used an RNA sequencing assay to determine the branching status of the DIS-bound introns. RNAs from purified ILSAQR and DIS complexes showed high read coverage across introns that sharply dropped at the 3′ SS–3′ exon boundary, confirming that both complexes primarily contained excised introns (Fig. 3f–h). Because reverse transcription often terminates at the tripartite RNA junction around the BP of a branched intron–lariat39, branched introns can be identified by a drop in read coverage upstream of the BP relative to downstream, where reverse transcription initiates at the 3′ SS (Fig. 3f). Individual introns associated with the ILSAQR showed a sharp decrease in read coverage upstream of the predominant BP, whereas the same introns bound to the DIS showed more uniform read coverage (Fig. 3f). We observed the same trend globally across all excised introns detected (Fig. 3g). The vast majority of DIS-associated introns are therefore debranched. We confirmed this using an orthogonal long-read RNA sequencing approach, analysing deletions introduced during reverse transcription around branched BPs40,41 (Extended Data Fig. 7d–f). A subset of DIS-associated introns showed signs of branching in both experiments (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 7e), suggesting that debranching largely occurs on the spliceosome but is not a prerequisite for the ILSAQR-to-DIS transition. These branched introns may represent complexes in which debranching is delayed or AQR independent.

To test whether the ILSAQR-to-DIS transition represents a general pathway for human introns, we analysed the overlap among the excised introns associated with each complex. If the ILSAQR is remodelled into DIS, introns detected as branched lariats in the ILSAQR should be detected as debranched, linear species in the DIS. Indeed, the vast majority of ILSAQR-associated introns were detected in the DIS sample (Fig. 3i), indicating that sequential passage through ILSAQR and DIS is the predominant spliceosome termination pathway.

These combined biochemical and structural data support intron–lariat debranching on the spliceosome and reveal a new spliceosome state containing a debranched intron.

To disassemble and recycle the spliceosome9,10, the debranched intron must be ejected from the DIS, which may require the correct positioning and activation of the DIS-specific RNA helicase DHX35. In the DIS, DHX35 is anchored primarily through its contacts with GPATCH1 and the PRP17 WD40 domain (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). GPATCH1 interacts with DHX35 through several regions, including its regulatory G-patch and I-patch domains that bind across the RecA1 domain and the C-terminal domain of DHX35 (Extended Data Fig. 8a) similar to how other co-factors interact with their cognate DEAH-box RNA helicases42,43. The DHX35-interacting segments of GPATCH1 are interspersed by PRP8-binding regions that wind around the endonuclease, RNaseH and finger-palm domains (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). A C-terminal GPATCH1 motif tethers WDR83 (Fig. 3a,b). Of note, the surfaces that bind to DHX35 and GPATCH1 are available in the DIS but occluded in earlier on-pathway spliceosome states, which could prevent premature termination (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Moreover, DHX35–GPATCH1 binding to PRP8 in the DIS would clash with C19L2, the RNA active site and the intron–lariat BP in the ILSAQR (Fig. 3d,e), rationalizing why ILSAQR remodelling is required to form the DIS with correctly positioned DHX35.

To understand how DHX35 may act in the DIS, we examined its RNA network. In the preceding states (from pre-Bact to ILSAQR; Extended Data Fig. 8c), U6 snRNA forms an internal stem loop and pairs through its ACAGA region with the intron 5′ SS, forming the U6–5′ SS helix44,45,46. This tethers the 5′ SS to the RNA active site through approximately 2.5 helical turns (Fig. 3e). In the DIS cryo-EM density, however, the U6 internal stem loop is not visible, suggesting that it is mobile or unwound, and only one helical turn of the U6–5′ SS helix remains (Fig. 3d). Although we did not resolve RNA density in the DHX35 active site, the U6 snRNA regions 3′ of the ACAGA sequence are well positioned to dock into it. DHX35 could then translocate along the U6 snRNA in the 3′-to-5′ direction, unwinding the remaining helical turn of the U6–5′ SS helix to eject the intron and disassemble the spliceosome (Fig. 3c,d).

This predicts that the DIS can disassemble without additional factors. We therefore immobilized the purified DIS on beads via GFP-tagged DHX35, supplied ATP and analysed the released proteins (Extended Data Fig. 8d). Indeed, the U5 snRNP, NTC, NTR, but not DHX35, GPATCH1 or WDR83, were released upon ATP addition (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f and Supplementary Table 5). To probe the role of DHX35 in this assay, we also purified DIS complexes using the catalytically inactive GFP–DHX35 mutant (K83A). These spliceosomes were compositionally indistinguishable from the wild-type DIS (Extended Data Fig. 7g and Supplementary Table 2), indicating that the DIS forms before DHX35 action. Adding ATP to the immobilized DIS containing DHX35(K83A) did not release spliceosome proteins, supporting a role for DHX35 in disassembly (Extended Data Fig. 8e and Supplementary Table 5). These data indicate that DHX35 may translocate along U6 snRNA to unwind the partial U6–5′ SS duplex, ejecting the debranched intron for decay and freeing the spliceosome for recycling.

In addition to successful pre-mRNA splicing, defective spliceosomes erroneously assembled on aberrant pre-mRNA introns must also terminate during spliceosome quality control (SQC)47,48,49. How such defective human spliceosomes are recognized and terminated has remained unclear, although both DHX15 and DHX35 have been implicated50,51,52,53,54. Recent structures of Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Chaetomium thermophilum spliceosomes5,23 revealed both helicases in the same SQC complex, corresponding to a defective B* spliceosome (B*D) stalled before branching on introns with an aberrant 5′ SS5,23. In these structures, DHX15 and DHX35 are poised to act on U6 and U2 snRNAs, respectively, to terminate the defective complex and reject the pre-mRNA. Given the structural homology between S. pombe and human splicing machineries8,23,53 and our ILSAQR and DIS data, DHX15 and DHX35 may be central to ejecting both excised introns and aberrant pre-mRNAs from the spliceosome.

To explore the parallels between regular and defective termination, we revised the cryo-EM structure of the S. pombe defective B*D complex (also named Bd-II)23 (Fig. 4a). We identified the S. pombe protein Saf4 as the functional orthologue of YJU2B23 (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6a) and assigned several unidentified densities (Fig. 4a,b), including an uncharacterized protein: LENG1 (S. pombe C5E4.10c; Extended Data Fig. 9a). LENG1 runs along the C-terminal domain of CWC22, a catalytic-stage spliceosome subunit absent from ILS and DIS complexes (Fig. 4a). LENG1 is a paralogue of the essential branching factor CWC25 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). AlphaFold3 predicts a high-confidence YJU2B–LENG1 complex for both human and S. pombe orthologues, homologous to the YJU2–CWC25 heterodimer in the regular C complex55,56 (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). In the ILSAQR, the position of the YJU2B zinc-finger domain is incompatible with the predicted LENG1 interaction (Extended Data Fig. 9e) and TFIP11 occupies the CWC22-binding site2, which could explain the absence of LENG1 from regular terminating spliceosomes (Fig. 2e).

Given the role of YJU2B in guiding DHX35–GPATCH1–WDR83 to the ILSAQR, we explored whether YJU2B–LENG1 may recruit these factors to the B*D. Supporting this, LENG1 is confidently predicted to bind to GPATCH1, WDR83 and YJU2B20 (Extended Data Fig. 9f), through interfaces compatible with the B*D structure (Fig. 4b). These factors and DHX35 have been previously detected by mass spectrometry in the human C complex57,58,59,60 and rank among the top LENG1 co-dependencies in human CRISPR–Cas9 screens24,25 (Extended Data Fig. 9g). Moreover, GFP-tagged LENG1 co-immunoprecipitated multiple spliceosome factors from human cells, including CWC22 and the SQC-related factors YJU2B, DHX35, GPATCH1 and WDR83, corroborated by LENG1 proximity labelling data (Extended Data Fig. 9h,i and Supplementary Tables 4 and 6). LENG1 may thus act with YJU2B to guide DHX35 via GPATCH1–WDR83 towards SQC complexes. Consistently, our RNA sequencing from native DHX35–GFP pulldowns revealed reads spanning intron–exon junctions (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7d,f). The native DHX35 purification could thus be heterogeneous. Although the regular DIS represents the predominant state, DIS-like states could have arisen from defective spliceosomes stalled either before, as in the B*D, or after branching. The roles of these SQC factors, and the full scope of states they target, await further investigation.

The involvement of DHX15 and DHX35 in both regular and defective spliceosome termination highlights mechanistic parallels between these pathways. Both helicases bind simultaneously to the defective B*D complex5,23 (Fig. 4a), whereas in regular termination, they are distributed across two sequential states: the ILSAQR and the DIS (Fig. 5a,c). DHX15 occupies the same position in B*D as in ILS complexes2,3,4,5, loaded onto the U6 snRNA 3′ end. The DHX35–GPATCH1 interfaces are indistinguishable between the DIS and B*D (Fig. 5a,c), but owing to their different RNA network configurations, DHX35 would act on U2 snRNA in the B*D and on U6 snRNA in the DIS. In the B*D, DHX35 might also act sequentially on U2 and U6 snRNAs. Moreover, C19L1 and C19L2, which are critical for regular termination, are absent from the defective B*D. Conversely, LENG1 would act only in defective spliceosomes, contributing to their recognition for SQC, although the precise mechanism remains to be determined.

We propose that these different RNA network configurations may explain the differences between regular and defective termination. During regular termination, the U2–intron branch helix is stabilized by the ILS-specific C19L2, which buries the branched intron BP in the RNA active site and occludes the PRP8 surface needed for the subsequent binding of DHX35–GPATCH1, thus necessitating ATP-mediated remodelling to form the DIS. This stepwise dismantling may be necessary for debranching on the spliceosome, providing a window in which C19L1-tethered DBR1 can act on the extracted intron–lariat BP (Fig. 5b). By contrast, in the B*D during defective termination, the U2–intron branch helix has already been disrupted23 and the intron has not yet undergone branching. Therefore, temporal separation of DHX15 and DHX35 activities would be dispensable, allowing single-step disassembly during SQC (Fig. 5c).

Together, we have captured native human spliceosomes during termination, revealing how three RNA helicases—AQR, DHX15 and DHX35—and their co-factors orchestrate the gradual dismantling of the spliceosomal RNA network, coupling intron–lariat debranching and ejection to regular spliceosome disassembly. We extended this paradigm to defective termination, in which DHX15 and DHX35 are aided by an overlapping but distinct set of factors to reject aberrant introns. Our results show how both regular and defective spliceosomes terminate specifically and efficiently, sustaining the processing of protein-coding mRNAs and the fidelity of gene expression.

Total nematode extract was prepared from a C. elegans strain expressing endogenously 3×FLAG-tagged PRP19 (ref. 2).

Disassembly assays in the presence and absence of ATP were performed in technical triplicates. A total of 500 µl nematode extract was supplemented with either 5× splicing buffer with ATP (50 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 175 mM KCl, 10 mM ATP, 20 mM MgCl2, 100 mM creatine phosphate, 250 µg ml−1 creatine kinase and 15% PEG 8000) or 5× splicing buffer without ATP (50 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 175 mM KCl and 20 mM MgCl2). The supplemented extracts were incubated at 20 °C for 1 h with gentle agitation. Of magnetic anti-FLAG bead slurry (Sigma) equilibrated in detergent wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 150 mM KCl, 1 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.05% Igepal 630 and 10% glycerol), 20 µl was then added to each reaction. The samples were transferred to 4 °C and incubated with the beads for 2 h with gentle rotation. The beads were washed four times with 1 ml detergent wash buffer, transferred to fresh tubes and then washed an additional four times with detergent-free wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9 and 150 mM KCl). The washed beads were resuspended in detergent-free wash buffer, transferred to fresh tubes and submitted to the Vienna BioCenter Mass Spectrometry Facility for on-bead tryptic digestion and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) analysis.

The resulting raw MS data were processed for protein identification and label-free quantification. To identify the proteins that were depleted from the beads upon ATP treatment, protein abundances in the samples with and without ATP were compared. Proteins were considered significantly enriched based on statistical tests (moderated t-test in limma, P < 0.05) and an arbitrary log2 fold change cut-off of 1 (twofold enrichment over control on a linear scale). The data were visualized in GraphPad Prism 10.

N-terminally EGFP–3C-tagged DHX35 and YJU2B overexpression cell lines were generated using a lentivirus system. Lenti-X 293T cells (Takara) were polyethylenimine transfected with lentiviral carrier plasmids containing either pRRL-SFFV-EGFP-3C-DHX35 or pRRL-SFFV-YJU2B-3C-EGFP. These were transfected alongside viral helper plasmids pCMVR8.74 (Addgene #22036) and pCMV-VSV-G (Addgene #8454). After 2 days, supernatant containing the lentiviral particles was collected. Wild-type K562 cells (DSMZ) were infected at limiting dilutions and EGFP-expressing cells were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting using a BD FACSAria III instrument (BD Biosciences). Integration and expression of the constructs were confirmed by in-gel EGFP fluorescence and immunoblotting for DHX35 (CAS HPA062700, Sigma; dilution 1:250) or YJU2B (CAS OAAB02156, Aviva SysBio; dilution 1:1,000). All cultures were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination.

To generate inducible cell lines, C-terminally 3C–EGFP-tagged DBR1 and N-terminally EGFP–3C-tagged mutant DHX35(K83A) constructs were cloned into a PiggyBac transposon donor plasmid containing a doxycycline-inducible TRE Tight promoter. Wild-type K562 cells (DSMZ) were electroporated with equal amounts of transposon donor and PiggyBac transposase plasmids using a Neon NxT Electroporation System (NEON1S, Thermo). Cells were selected using blasticidin (R21001, Invitrogen). Expression of the transgene was induced using 0.1 µg ml−1 doxycyclin (D9891, Sigma-Aldrich) for 18 h and EGFP+ cells were isolated using fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Expression of the constructs was confirmed by in-gel EGFP fluorescence and immunoblotting for DBR1 (CAS PA5-30616, Invitrogen; dilution 1:500) or DHX35 (CAS HPA062700, Sigma; dilution 1:250). All cultures were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination.

HEK293T cells were endogenously tagged at the C terminus of DBR1 with GGGS3-FKBP12(F36V)-V5-IRES-lox5171-mScarlet3/mNeonGreen-lox5171, where FKBP12 is the protein that brings DBR1 to the cellular ubiquitination machinery in the presence of the dTAGV-1 compound, and lox5171 is a Cre recombinase target site. An sgRNA targeting the DBR1 C terminus was designed using CHOPCHOP61 and cloned into a modified plasmid #217659 (Addgene), in which the mCherry coding sequence was replaced with a puromycin resistance cassette. The sgRNA plasmid was co-transfected with two donor plasmids. The donor plasmids contained the repair template with the desired tag followed by either mScarlet3 or mNeonGreen and flanked by the DBR1 homology arms. Five days after transfection, cells co-expressing mScarlet3 and mNeonGreen, which indicated homozygous tagging, were sorted by flow cytometry and then allowed to recover for 4 days. The cells were then treated with homemade recombinant Cre recombinase for 2 h at 37 °C in serum-free medium to excise the coding sequences of the fluorescent protein markers from the DBR1 loci. After 3 days of recovery, mScarlet3/mNeonGreen double negative cells were single-cell sorted into medium supplemented with extra 25% of FCS. The selected clones were expanded and genotyped by Sanger sequencing. The homozygous clones were selected, and protein depletion upon addition of the dTAGV-1 compound was validated by western blot using an antibody to DBR1 (CAS 66951-1-IG, Proteintech; dilution 1:10,000).

To generate HEK293T DBR1–dTAG cell lines that also inducibly overexpress various DBR1 constructs (wild type, catalytic mutant (H85A) and deletion of peptide I residues 420–434 (Δpep1)), the coding sequences of DBR1 were cloned into the PiggyBac transposon donor plasmid under a doxycycline-inducible TRE Tight promoter. The DBR1 constructs were tagged on the C terminus with a P2A self-cleaving peptide followed by mScarlet. The DBR1-P2A–mScarlet expression cassettes were inserted into the HEK293T DBR1–dTAG cells by electroporation, and the successful clones were selected by fluorescence-activated cell sorting, as described above for the DHX35(K83A)–GFP and DBR1–GFP K562 overexpression cell lines. All cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination.

To generate stable inducible cell lines for proximity labelling experiments, HEK293 Flp-In T-REx parental cells at approximately 80–90% confluency were co-transfected with a pcDNA5/FRT/TO plasmid, which carried the coding sequence of DBR1, C19L1, YJU2B, LENG1 or nuclear localized EGFP fused on the 3′ end to the TurboID-V5 tag, and the pOG44 plasmid (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 1:5 mass ratio (donor:pOG44) using the JetOptimus transfection reagent (Polyplus-transfection). For a 24-well plate format, 350,000 cells were seeded per well onto the transfection complex. Twenty-four hours after transfection, cells were expanded into a six-well plate. Forty-eight hours later, selection was initiated. The cells were seeded to achieve 25–30% confluency and allowed to attach for approximately 2 h. The medium was then replaced with selection medium containing 100 µg ml−1 hygromycin B and 15 µg ml−1 blasticidin S HCl. The selection medium was refreshed every 3–4 days. The selection process was monitored using the parallel wild-type cell culture, and selection was continued until all wild-type cells had died (approximately 10–14 days), at which point the pooled colonies of resistant cells were expanded without antibiotics. Successful integration was confirmed by western blotting using an antibody to the V5 tag (CAS R960-25, Thermo Fisher Scientific, dilution 1:3,000). All cultures were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination.

cDNA corresponding to LENG1 was amplified from cDNA by PCR and inserted into a PGK-EGFP-N1-IRES-PURO plasmid, thereby tagging LENG1 at its C terminus with EGFP. The annealed double-stranded DNA fragment of NLS (GGTGGTCCTAAGAAGAAGAGAAAGGTT) was similarly cloned into PGK-EGFP-C1-IRES-PURO as a control.

The plasmids expressing the tagged proteins were transfected into RPE-1 cells62 using polyethylenimine reagent (Brunschwig Chemie) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Two days after transfections, antibiotic selection of cells was initiated by adding 1 μg ml−1 puromycin to the growth media. The selection medium was replaced every second day until the cells reached confluency. The expression of tagged proteins was verified by western blot using an antibody to GFP (CAS 11814460001, Roche, dilution 1:1,000) and fluorescence microscopy. All cultures were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination.

The nuclear extracts for cryo-EM, RNA sequencing and biochemical assays were prepared from the human K562 cells stably overexpressing EGFP-tagged DHX35 or YJU2B as previously described2,63. To prepare nuclear extract from the K562 cells overexpressing EGFP-tagged DHX35(K83A) or DBR1, expression of the tagged protein was first induced by addition of 0.1 µg ml−1 doxycycline. The cells were cultured for 48 h before collecting and preparing nuclear extract as previously described2,63.

Approximately 25 ml of the nuclear extract of K562 cells stably overexpressing DHX35–EGFP was applied to approximately 1.5 ml of GFP-Trap Agarose beads (Chromotek) equilibrated in wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.05% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 8% v/v glycerol). The beads were incubated with the nuclear extract for approximately 3.5 h at 4 °C with gentle rotation. The beads were then washed five times in 10 ml wash buffer. The washed beads were incubated twice for approximately 1 h at 4 °C with gentle rotation in 0.5 ml elution buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 3% w/v sucrose and 0.1 µg ml−1 3C protease). The eluted samples were then applied to a GraFix64 15–30% w/v sucrose gradient containing 0.05% glutaraldehyde in the heaviest fraction in a gradient buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP and 2 mM MgCl2). The gradient samples were spun in an SW60 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter) at 22,000 rpm for 16 h at 4 °C. The gradients were fractionated manually, and each fraction was quenched with 45 mM lysine. The sedimentation coefficients were estimated using the CowSuite software, and the peak spliceosome fractions were further confirmed by SDS–PAGE. The peak spliceosome fractions were pooled and concentrated using Amicon Ultra 0.5-ml concentrators with 100-kDa molecular weight cut-off (Sigma). During concentrating, the sample was buffer exchanged to a cryo-EM buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 0.5 mM TCEP, 100 mM KCl and 2 mM MgCl2) to remove sucrose and excess glutaraldehyde.

Approximately 25 ml of the nuclear extract of K562 cells stably overexpressing YJU2B–EGFP was incubated overnight with 2 µg ml−1 benzonase before proceeding to anti-GFP affinity purification and gradient ultracentrifugation as described above for DHX35-containing spliceosome.

The purified spliceosome samples were incubated with a 2-nm continuous carbon film (prepared in-house) for either overnight (DIS), approximately 7 h (ILSAQR; dataset 1) or approximately 3 h (ILSAQR; dataset 2) in a homemade humidity chamber at 4 °C. The carbon film was picked up with a glow-discharged R3.5/1 holey carbon grid (Quantifoil). Of ice-cold cryo-EM buffer, 3 µl was applied to the grid before blotting at 4 °C and 80% humidity and plunging into liquid ethane using a Leica EM GP2 instrument.

Two datasets of ILSAQR were collected using a Titan Krios G4 equipped with a Falcon 4i direct electron detector (Vienna BioCenter). Dataset 1 contained 26,091 movies, whereas dataset 2 consisted of 27,327 movies. The energy filter was set to a width of 10 eV. The C2 aperture was set to 50 µm, whereas the objective aperture was retracted. In both datasets, the movies were collected at a total dose of 40 e− Å−2 in EER format with a pixel size of 0.951 Å per pixel. The target defocus of both datasets ranged from −1.0 µm to −2.5 µm.

A dataset of 12,277 micrographs was collected using a Titan Krios G4 equipped with a Falcon 4i direct electron detector (Vienna BioCenter). The energy filter was set to a width of 10 eV. The C2 aperture was set to 50 µm, whereas the objective aperture was retracted. The movies were collected at a total dose of 50 e− Å−2 in EER format with a pixel size of 0.951 Å per pixel. The target defocus ranged from −1.25 µm to −2.25 µm.

Pre-processing (gain correction, motion correction and contrast transfer function estimation) of both datasets of the ILSAQR was performed in cryoSPARC live65.

For dataset 1, 931,992 particles were picked on-the-fly using the Blob picker in cryoSPARC live with a minimum and maximum particle diameter set to 250 Å and 450 Å, respectively. The picked particles were extracted with a box size of 128 pixels at a binned pixel size of 4.01 Å per pixel. A 2D classification was performed to select the particles representing 2D class averages with clear internal features. The selected particles were subsequently used to generate three 3D ab initio models. Three rounds of heterogeneous refinement were performed using the ab initio models as references. Only the particles from the best class were carried over to the next round of refinement, resulting in the final subset of 232,423 particles. Particles in dataset 1 were also picked in Warp66 using a model trained on manually picked particles with an expected particle diameter of 350 Å. The 1,172,730 Warp-picked particles were processed the same as above, resulting in a subset of 294,689 particles. Upon removal of duplicate particles, the combined Blob-picked and Warp-picked particles were re-extracted with a box size of 448 pixels at a binned pixel size of 1.15 Å per pixel and further processed by reference-based motion correction in cryoSPARC. In the end, 310,532 particles were obtained from dataset 1.

For dataset 2, particles were picked in Warp66 using a model trained on manually picked particles with an expected particle diameter of 350 Å. The picked 1,068,365 particles were extracted with a box size of 128 pixels with a binned pixel size of 4.01 Å per pixel. The three ab initio models from dataset 1 were used for three rounds of heterogeneous refinement with only the best class being carried over to the next round of refinement. The selected particles were then re-extracted with a box size of 448 pixels at a binned pixel size of 1.15 Å per pixel and further processed by reference-based motion correction in cryoSPARC. In the end, 197,936 particles were obtained from dataset 2.

The particles from both datasets were combined, resulting in a complete set of 508,031 particles. A non-uniform refinement generated a consensus map of the ILSAQR (map 1) at a global resolution of 2.40 Å. By performing a local refinement with a mask around the core of the spliceosome, we obtained map 2 at a resolution of 2.34 Å. To further improve the resolution of specific spliceosome regions, we performed local refinements with masks around the zinc-finger domain of YJU2B (map 3 at a nominal resolution of 2.32 Å), the helical bundle of the NTR subunits PRP19–CDC5L–SPF27 (map 9 at a nominal resolution of 3.83 Å), the helical repeats of the NTC subunits SYF1–SYF2 (map 10 at a nominal resolution of 2.59 Å) and the U5 Sm ring (map 11 at a nominal resolution of 2.88 Å).

The GCFC domains and the coiled-coil interaction interface of TFIP11 and GCFC2 were poorly resolved in map 1, probably due to their flexibility and potentially their partial occupancy. To better resolve these termination factors in the ILSAQR, we performed two rounds of 3D classification with a mask around TFIP11–GCFC2 on the combined 508,031 particles. First, we performed a hard 3D classification in cryoSPARC. The 139,130 particles from the best 7 out of 50 classes were selected for a 3D classification in RELION5 with Blush regularization67 with a T value of 40. The resulting best class containing 6,794 particles was locally refined in cryoSPARC with a mask around TFIP11–GCFC2 to generate map 8 at a nominal resolution of 7.37 Å.

For certain spliceosomal regions, combining particles from two datasets did not result in significant improvements in density quality. Specifically, to produce ILSAQR maps 4–7, only the 310,532 particles from dataset 1 were used.

To improve the resolution of the termination factor C19L2, we performed a local refinement with a mask around C19L2, resulting in map 4 at a nominal resolution of 2.84 Å.

To better visualize AQR within ILSAQR, we performed a hard 3D classification on the particles from dataset 1 with a mask around AQR. Particles from 3D classes with the best-defined AQR density were used in a local refinement with a mask around AQR before proceeding to 3D variability analysis in cryoSPARC with the same mask. The 46,099 particles from the best cluster out of 10 were used for another local refinement with a mask around AQR, generating map 5 at a nominal resolution of 3.92 Å.

The region of ILSAQR containing the helical repeats of SYF1, the MPP domain of C19L1 and the interacting helix of YJU2B appeared to be flexible and, hence, poorly resolved in map 1. To better visualize this region, we performed 3D variability analysis of the 310,532 particles from dataset 1 after homogeneous refinement with a global mask. One out of 10 clusters with the best-defined region of interest containing 26,265 particles was selected and further locally refined with a mask around SYF1–C19L1–YJU2B. This produced map 6 at a nominal resolution of 6.32 Å.

To better resolve DHX15 that appeared to be flexibly tethered to the ILSAQR, we performed several 3D classification jobs varying the class similarity values with a mask around DHX15. The best classes from several classification jobs were combined, duplicate particles were removed and locally refined with a broad mask around DHX15 and the surrounding regions, and further 3D classified with the same broad mask. The 9,659 particles from the two best classes were further locally refined with a mask around DHX15, resulting in map 7 at a nominal resolution of 8.62 Å.

Pre-processing (gain correction, motion correction and contrast transfer function estimation) of the DIS dataset was performed in cryoSPARC live65.

Particles were picked on-the-fly using the Blob picker in cryoSPARC live with a minimum and maximum particle diameter set to 250 Å and 350 Å, respectively. The picked particles were extracted with a box size of 256 pixels with a binned pixel size of 1.90 Å per pixel. A 2D classification was performed to select the particles representing 2D class averages with the best internal features. The selected particles were subsequently used to generate three ab initio 3D models. Three rounds of heterogeneous refinement were performed using the ab initio models as references. Only the particles from the best class were carried over to the next round of refinement, resulting in the final subset of 140,678 particles. DIS particles were also picked in Warp66 using a model trained on manually picked particles with an expected particle diameter of 350 Å. The 514,099 Warp-picked particles were processed the same as above, resulting in a subset of 130,283 particles. Upon removal of duplicate particles, the combined Blob-picked and Warp-picked particles were re-extracted with a box size of 448 px with a binned pixel size of 1.19 Å per pixel, resulting in the final dataset of 153,470 particles.

We used all 153,470 particles to perform a non-uniform refinement and obtained the overall consensus map of the DIS (map 1) at a global resolution of 3.14 Å. Although the core of the DIS in map 1 could be visualized at high resolution, many peripheral spliceosome regions were poorly defined and required further 3D classifications and local refinements to obtain high-quality cryo-EM densities.

To improve the density of the intron–U6 snRNA duplex, we performed a 3D classification with all 153,470 particles with a mask around the RBM22–intron–U6 snRNA region. The best class from this classification was further refined using non-uniform refinement, resulting in map 2 at a nominal resolution of 4.67 Å.

To improve the density quality of the WD40 domain of PRP17, we performed a local refinement around this domain and obtained map 3 at a nominal resolution of 3.97 Å.

To improve the density quality of DHX35–GPATCH1, we imported all 153,470 particles to RELION5 and performed a 3D classification with Blush regularization67 with a mask around DHX35–GPATCH1 and a T value of 150. The best class from the 3D classification containing 63,636 particles was imported back into cryoSPARC. After homogeneous reconstruction, a local refinement with a mask around DHX35–GPATCH1 was performed, generating map 4 at a nominal resolution of 2.90 Å.

We performed a 3D classification on all 153,470 particles to assess the homogeneity of the dataset. Although we did not observe multiple distinct spliceosome complexes in the dataset, we identified 45,958 particles that yielded a DIS map with the highest quality peripheral densities. We performed a non-uniform refinement on these particles to obtain a more complete DIS map at a nominal resolution of 3.62 Å with better peripheral density quality than map 1. We used the same subset of particles to perform local refinements with masks around two NTC regions—the PRP19–CDC5L–SPF27 helical bundle and the RBM22–PPIL1–PLRG1 region—resulting in map 5 at a nominal resolution of 5.35 Å and in map 9 at a nominal resolution of 4.04 Å, respectively.

To better visualize AQR within the DIS, we performed a hard 3D classification with a mask around AQR, producing a class with the best AQR density with 15,913 particles. After homogeneous reconstruction, a local refinement with a mask around AQR was performed, generating map 6 at a nominal resolution of 7.34 Å.

We consistently observed a low-resolution density near DHX35 that appeared to be shaped like a WD40 domain. Given our biochemical data and in silico protein interaction predictions (Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1), we assigned this density as the GPATCH1 interactor WDR83. To improve this cryo-EM density, we performed multiple rounds of 3D classification. Specifically, we performed five 3D classification jobs with variable values of class similarity with a mask around the putative WDR83 density in cryoSPARC. The best classes from all jobs were selected. After removing duplicate particles, the selected particles were used in two rounds of 3D classification in RELION5 with a mask around WDR83 at T values of 80 for the first round and of 40 during the second round. The best class containing 1,826 particles was reconstructed using homogeneous reconstruction in cryoSPARC, generating map 7 at a nominal resolution of 9.65 Å. Given the limited resolution of map 7, we could not explicitly assign the orientation of WDR83 in the DIS.

In maps 1 and 2, the helical repeats of the NTR subunits SYF1–SYF3 and the Sm ring of the U5 snRNP were not well resolved, probably due to the inherent flexibility of these spliceosomal regions. Therefore, we performed focus refinements with masks around SYF1–SYF3 and the U5 Sm ring, resulting in map 8 at a nominal resolution of 5.19 Å and map 10 at a nominal resolution of 3.35 Å, respectively.

We generated the composite map of the human ILSAQR from ILSAQR maps 1–11 as previously described2.

To prepare a model of the human ILSAQR, we started from our previously published model of the human ILS″ (PDB 8RO2)2. First, we removed the following protein segments that were not observed in the cryo-EM density of the ILSAQR: SDE2, SYF1 residues 791–824, CDC5L residues 57–111 and 357–382. To model the zinc-finger domain of YJU2B (residues 43–118), we predicted its structure together with a Zn2+ ion using AlphaFold3 (ref. 36) and rigid body fitted the predicted model of this domain. To model the helical region of YJU2B (residues 163–233), we predicted the structures of the YJU2B–SYF1–SYF3–C19L1 and YJU2B–PRP8 complexes in AlphaFold3. Both models were rigid body fitted. We also added BRR2 residues 39–57 (as in PDB 8Q7X)9, PPIE RRM residues 1–80 (as in PDB 9FMD)2 by rigid body fitting. We also modelled additional ESS2 regions (residues 65–87, 178–189, 211–234 and 240–254) guided by AlphaFold3 predictions and ModelAngelo68. The RNA in the active site of AQR was modelled as an unknown RNA sequence. The position of DHX15–TFIP11 G-patch was adjusted by rigid body fitting into map 10. PAXBP1 was replaced with GCFC2 by first deleting the TFIP11–PAXBP1 dimer from the model and then fitting an AlphaFold3 prediction of the TFIP11–GCFC2 dimer into map 6. We truncated side chains for non-proline residues to their Cβ atoms in map regions where side-chain density was lacking.

We modelled the RNA in the active site based on the structure of the human ILS assembled on the MINX pre-mRNA (PDB 6ID1)3 but only assigned a sequence for a consensus 5′ SS and a BP adenosine, whereas all other nucleotides were modelled as uridine and truncated to their ribose moiety. The portion of the intron bound to AQR and PPIE was modelled based on AlphaFold3 predictions.

All models were manually adjusted using ISOLDE69 in ChimeraX. The final model was real-space refined against the composite map in Phenix70. We generated base-pairing and stacking restraints in Phenix to stabilize nucleic acid geometry. We further used the input model to generate reference model restraints. The non-bonded weight parameter was set to 1,000 and rotamers were fitted for side chains with poor density that were also outliers.

We generated the composite map of the human DIS from maps 1–10 as previously described2.

To prepare a model of the DIS, we started from our previously published model of the human ILS″ (PDB 8RO2)2. First, we deleted DHX15, TFIP11, PAXBP1, C19L1, C19L2, SDE2, ESS2 and U2 snRNA, which were not resolved in the cryo-EM density of the DIS. We also truncated U6 snRNA to residues 1–35 and the intron to 10 residues, six of which were base paired with U6 snRNA. Given that a mixture of introns is present in the endogenous DIS sample, no sequence was assigned to the intron.

To model DHX35 and GPATCH1, we predicted the structures of DHX35–GPATCH1, GPATCH1–PRP8 endonuclease domain and the GPATCH1–PRP8 finger-palm domain using AlphaFold2 Multimer37. The regions of GPATCH1 that were predicted with low confidence were truncated, and the predicted models were rigid body fitted into map 7. The segments of GPATCH1 towards its C terminus that were confidently predicted to interact with DHX35 but lacked experimental cryo-EM densities were also removed. The fitted models were adjusted using ISOLDE69 in ChimeraX. The segments of GPATCH1 that were not confidently predicted but were present in the cryo-EM density were manually built in ISOLDE.

The RNaseH domain of PRP8, which was relocated in the DIS compared with the ILS″, was rigid body fitted into the DIS map. BRR2 residues 39–57 (as in PDB 8Q7X)9 and the RRM domain of PPIE (residues 1–80; as in PDB 9FMD)2 were added by rigid body fitting followed by manual adjustments in ISOLDE.

We also modelled the WD40 domains of PRP17 and of WDR83 bound to GPATCH1. The orientation of the PRP17 WD40 was assigned based on its position relative to the PRP17 N-terminal domain that anchors the protein on the surface of BUD31. We rigid body fitted the predicted AlphaFold2 Multimer model of WDR83–GPATCH1 into map 9. Owing to the low local resolution of map 9, we could not unambiguously assign the orientation of WDR83–GPATCH1. The resolution of map 9 was also not sufficient to unambiguously determine whether WDR83 was bound by GPATCH1. However, our biochemical data (Extended Data Fig. 6d) and AlphaFold predictions (Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1) strongly indicate that WDR83 is anchored by GPATCH1 in the DIS. We truncated side chains for non-proline residues to their Cβ atoms in map regions where side-chain density was lacking.

The final model was real-space refined against the composite map in Phenix70 as described above for ILSAQR.

To revise the structure of the defective fission yeast spliceosome B*D (PDB 9ESI)23, we first focused on identifying the protein chains that were originally modelled as ‘unknown’. We compared the published model to our models of the human ILSAQR and DIS. We noted that all but one of the unidentified chains were modelled in our new human spliceosome structures. We predicted the structures of the S. pombe proteins and their interactors in AlphaFold3 (ref. 36) and rigid body fitted them into the published map (EMD-19942)23. This allowed us to add CDC5L (S. pombe name Cdc5) residues 456–476, CCDC12 (Cwf18) residues 101–142 and GPATCH1 (C20H4.06c) residues 260–280.

We also identified an unassigned density on the surface of PPIL1 in the B*D spliceosome that was modelled as an N-terminal domain of SNW1 in our previously revised human P complex spliceosome (PDB 9FMD)2. We predicted the structure of S. pombe SNW1–PPIL1 (S. pombe names Prp45–Ppi1), rigid body fitted the model into the published map and further adjusted it manually using ISOLDE69. This allowed us to add SNW1 (Prp45) residues 42–83 to the model of the S. pombe B*D spliceosome.

To identify the unknown density on the surface of CWC22 (S. pombe name Cwf22), we examined the previously published spliceosome structures for proteins modelled in the same location, as well as searched the human predicted interactome database20 for CWC22 interactors. The S. pombe orthologues of the proteins that were identified as potential CWC22 interactors were then further tested for their predicted interaction with S. pombe CWC22 using AlphaFold3. This narrowed down the list of potential candidates to three proteins: CWC25 (S. pombe name Cwf25), SLU7 (Slu7) or LENG1 (SPCC5E4.10c). As described in the main text and in Extended Data Fig. 9a, in the published map, we observed a segment of four residues with unambiguous side-chain densities: P-Y/F-W followed by an amino acid with a side chain of at least two non-hydrogen atoms. Only the sequence of LENG1 matched the unambiguously resolved side-chain density (Extended Data Fig. 9a). The S. pombe CWC22–LENG1 prediction was rigid body fitted into the published map and then manually adjusted in ISOLDE, using a more confident prediction of the human proteins as a guide.

We also adjusted the RNA network of the B*D spliceosome. Specifically, we noticed implausible base-pairing geometry in the 5′ SS–U6 snRNA region, and adjusted the model based on an earlier S. pombe spliceosome structure (PDB 3JB9)71. Finally, we truncated intron nucleotides that were poorly resolved and outside of known consensus sequences to their ribose moiety.

We truncated side chains for non-proline residues to their Cβ atoms in map regions where side-chain density was lacking. The final model was real-space refined against the published map (EMD-19942)23 in Phenix70 as described above.

Pulldowns with nuclear extracts from both induced and uninduced (negative control) K562 doxycycline-inducible DBR1–EGFP cells were performed in technical triplicates. Of nuclear extract, 1 ml was added to the GFP Trap beads slurry (Chromotek) equilibrated in wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 50 mM, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.05% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 8% v/v glycerol). The beads were incubated for 3.5 h at 4 °C with gentle rotation. The supernatant was removed, and the beads were washed five times with 1 ml wash buffer. After removing residual buffer, bead-bound proteins were eluted by addition of 150 µl SDS loading dye. All three replicates of the pulldowns from extracts of both induced and control cells were run for 3 min at 180 V on a Novex Tris-glycine 4–12% 1.0 mm WedgeWell gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and submitted to the Vienna BioCenter Mass Spectrometry Facility for in-gel tryptic digestion and LC–MS/MS analysis. Protein abundances in both DBR1–GFP and control samples were compared, and the data were visualized in GraphPad Prism 10.

Cell pellets were solubilized in EBC-1 (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 2 mM MgCl2, with protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails (Roche)) supplemented with 500 U benzonase for 1 h at 4 °C on a rotator. The lysates were cleared from insoluble chromatin by centrifugation and were subjected to immunoprecipitation with GFP Trap beads (Chromotek) for 1.5 h at 4 °C under rotation. The beads were then washed five times with EBC-2 buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40 and 1 mM EDTA) and boiled in Laemmli buffer for 10 min at 95 °C.

After the pulldown, the GFP beads were washed three times with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, followed by overnight digestion using 0.5 μg trypsin at 37 °C under constant shaking. Digested peptides were separated from the beads using a 0.45-µm filter column (Merck) that was pre-washed with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate. Trypsin activity was quenched by acidifying the sample with trifluoroacetic acid to a final concentration of 1%. Peptides were desalted and concentrated using in-house-assembled triple-disc C18 stage-tip columns (66883-U; 3 M) as previously described72. In brief, the columns were first washed with methanol, then with buffer B (80% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid in water), followed by buffer A (0.1% formic acid in water). The samples were loaded using vacuum centrifugation. Finally, peptides were eluted with 32% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid in water, lyophilized and dissolved in 0.1% formic acid in water. All solvents were LC–MS/MS grade.

Mass spectrometry data were acquired at the proteomics facility of the Andalusian Center for Molecular Biology and Regenerative Medicine (CABIMER) using a Vanquish Neo liquid chromatographer (Thermo Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer. Mass spectrometry RAW data were analysed using DIA-NN (v2.3.2 Academia)73. Protein abundances in both LENG1–GFP and control samples were compared, and the data were visualized in GraphPad Prism 10.

For proteomic analysis, each stable HEK293 Flp-In T-REx cell line that can inducibly overexpress a TurboID-tagged protein of interest (DBR1, C19L1, YJU2B or LENG1) and a control cell line (nuclear EGFP–TurboID) were processed in biological triplicates. Three million cells per 10-cm dish were seeded. After 24 h, TurboID expression was induced with 100 ng ml−1 doxycycline for another 24 h. This was followed by biotin labelling with 500 µM D-biotin for 15 min. After labelling, the reaction was stopped by placing dishes on ice. The medium was removed, and the cells were washed once with PBS. The cells were then collected by scraping them off in 5 ml ice-cold PBS and transferred to a fresh tube. The cell pellet was washed for a total of four more times by centrifugation at 300g for 4 min at 4 °C before getting resuspended in 1 ml ice-cold PBS. The final pellets were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

The thawed cell pellets were lysed by addition of 120 µl ice-cold RIPA buffer with Halt protease inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific), followed by vigorous vortexing and incubation on ice for 20 min. The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 20,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. Protein concentration in the supernatant was determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Of total protein, 300 µg from each lysate was incubated for 3 h at 4 °C with 30 µl of the MagReSyn Streptavidin MS magnetic bead slurry (ReSyn Biosciences) equilibrated in ice-cold RIPA buffer. The beads were washed three times with RIPA buffer supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a 10-min rotation for each wash. This was followed by one wash in MS-grade PBS, during which the bead slurry was transferred to a fresh low-bind tube to minimize detergent carryover. Finally, five additional washes were performed with MS-grade PBS. After the final wash, all residual PBS was removed, and the dry bead pellets were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

The final washed bead pellets were submitted either to the Vienna BioCenter Mass Spectrometry Facility or to the Max Perutz Labs Mass Spectrometry Facility on dry ice for on-bead tryptic digestion and analysis by LC–MS/MS. The resulting raw data were processed for protein identification and label-free quantification. To identify high-confidence proximity partners, protein abundances in each bait-TurboID sample were statistically compared against those from the control samples (nuclear-localized EGFP–TurboID). Proteins were considered significantly enriched based on statistical tests (moderated t-test in limma, P < 0.05) and an arbitrary log2 fold-change cut-off of 0.75 (approximately 68% enrichment over control on a linear scale). Data visualization was performed in GraphPad Prism 10.

The recombinant human C19L1 MPP domain (residues 1–278), which carried an N-terminal His10-MBP tag followed by a 3C protease cleavage site, was expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 DE3 in LB media at 18 °C overnight using a pOPINB+ plasmid.

The cell pellet was resuspended in lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 500 mM NaCl and 5% glycerol) supplemented with cOmplete protease inhibitor tablets (Roche). The cells were lysed by sonication, and the lysate was cleared by centrifugation. The lysate was then applied to a 5-ml MBP Trap HP column (Cytiva) equilibrated in lysis buffer. The column was washed with lysis buffer before elution of the protein with a step gradient of 12 mM maltose. The eluate was diluted fivefold with buffer A (25 mM HEPES-NaOH and 5% glycerol) to reduce the salt concentration in the sample to 100 mM NaCl. The diluted sample was applied to a 5-ml HiTrap Q anion exchange column (Cytiva) equilibrated in buffer M (25 mM HEPES-NaOH, 100 mM NaCl and 5% glycerol). The column was washed with buffer M before elution of the protein over a linear gradient of 100–800 mM NaCl. The peak fractions were concentrated using a Sartorius centrifugal concentrator with a 50-kDa molecular weight cut-off (Sigma) and subsequently loaded onto a HiLoad Superdex 75 16/60 size-exclusion column (Cytiva) equilibrated in size-exclusion buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM dithiothreitol and 5% glycerol). The peak size-exclusion fractions were pooled, concentrated and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen.

Human DHX35 was cloned into a pGB10 plasmid with an N-terminal His10−3×FLAG tag followed by a 3C protease cleavage site. The plasmid was introduced into E. coli DH10EMBacY cells to generate bacmids74. The purified bacmid was transfected into Sf9 insect cells to produce a baculovirus that was then further amplified in Sf9 cell. The resultant virus was used to infect Hi5 insect cells at a volume ratio of 1:400. The cells were grown for approximately 72 h before collecting by centrifugation.

The cell pellet was resuspended in lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol and 20 mM imidazole) supplemented with cOmplete protease inhibitor tablets (Roche) and DNaseI (Sigma). The peak fractions containing DHX35 were pooled and diluted fivefold in buffer A (25 mM HEPES-NaOH and 5% glycerol) to reduce the salt concentration in the sample to 100 mM NaCl. The diluted sample was then loaded onto a 5-ml HiTrap Q anion exchange column (Cytiva) equilibrated in buffer M (25 mM HEPES-NaOH, 100 mM NaCl and 5% glycerol). The column was washed with buffer M before elution of the protein over a linear gradient of 0.1–1.4 M NaCl. The peak fractions were concentrated using a Sartorius centrifugal concentrator with a 50-kDa molecular weight cut-off (Sigma) and subsequently loaded onto a HiLoad Superdex 200 16/60 size-exclusion column (Cytiva) equilibrated in size-exclusion buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM dithiothreitol and 5% glycerol). The peak size-exclusion fractions were pooled, concentrated and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen.

The eluate was diluted fivefold with buffer A (25 mM HEPES-NaOH and 5% glycerol) to reduce the salt concentration in the sample to 100 mM NaCl. The diluted sample was applied to a 5-ml HiTrap Q anion exchange column (Cytiva) equilibrated in buffer M (25 mM HEPES-NaOH, 100 mM NaCl and 5% glycerol). Human full-length WDR83 carrying an N-terminal His10-3×FLAG-3C tag and its binding region of human GPATCH1 (residues 560–651) were cloned into a pGB10 plasmid. The plasmid was then used to generate a baculovirus and to express the complex in Hi5 insect cells, as described above for DHX35.

The cell pellet was resuspended in lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 5% glycerol and 20 mM imidazole) supplemented with cOmplete protease inhibitor tablets (Roche) and DNaseI (Sigma). The cells were broken open by sonication. The lysate was cleared by two rounds of centrifugation and subsequently applied to a 5-ml HisTrap column (Cytiva) equilibrated in lysis buffer. The column was washed with lysis buffer, and the protein was eluted over a linear gradient of 20–350 mM imidazole. The peak fractions containing WDR83–GPATCH1 were pooled and diluted fivefold in buffer A (25 mM HEPES-NaOH, 0.5 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol) to reduce the salt concentration in the sample to 100 mM NaCl. The diluted sample was then loaded onto a 5-ml HiTrap Q anion exchange column (Cytiva) equilibrated in buffer M (25 mM HEPES-NaOH, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol). The peak fractions were concentrated using an Amicon centrifugal concentrator with a 30-kDa molecular weight cut-off (Sigma). Of the WDR83–GPATCH1 complex at 79 µM, 2 ml was subsequently loaded via a 5-ml loop onto a HiLoad Superdex 200 16/60 size-exclusion column (Cytiva) equilibrated in size-exclusion buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 200 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol). SDS–PAGE analyses of each chromatographic run showed that WDR83 and GPATCH1 co-purified throughout the procedure, indicating the formation of a stable protein complex.
