Full-length human DHX35 carrying a K83A mutation and an N-terminal His10-3×FLAG tag, and the GPATCH1 construct encompassing the binding regions to both DHX35 and PRP8 (residues 1–440) were cloned into a pGB10 plasmid. The plasmid was then used to generate a baculovirus and express the complex in Hi5 insect cells.

The 3×FLAG–DHX35(K83A)–GPATCH1(1−440)–TwStrep complex was purified as described for the WDR83–GPATCH1 complex above, except for the size-exclusion step, in which the DHX35(K83A)–GPATCH1(1−440) complex was loaded onto a HiLoad Superdex 200 16/60 size-exclusion column (Cytiva) equilibrated in size-exclusion buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 250 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol).

The peptides used in in vitro pulldown assays were synthesized at the Vienna BioCenter Peptide Synthesis facility as previously described2. In brief, the peptides were synthesized with an N-terminal fluorescein and a C-terminal biotin tag on a Liberty Blue peptide synthesizer (CEM) using Fmoc chemistry. The lyophilized peptides were dissolved in 25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9 to a concentration of 1 mg ml−1. The following peptides were synthesized: DBR1 peptide I (420–434) wild type: fluo-ALSSINPDEIMLDEE-biotin; DBR1 peptide I (420–434) scrambled: fluo-EEIEMISLADDLSNP-biotin; YJU2B wild type (134–178): fluo-EHEKKQKLETDAMFRLEHGEADRSTLKKALPTLSHIQEAQSAWKD-biotin; YJU2B(M146A L149K E150K) (134–178): fluo-EHEKKQKLETDAAFRKKHGEADRSTLKKALPTLSHIQEAQSAWKD-biotin.

Of MBP-tagged C19L1 MPP, 5 µM was mixed with 50 µM of either wild-type DBR1 peptide I or its scrambled version in the final reaction volume of 50 µl. Reactions containing either MBP–C19L1 MPP alone or the DBR1 peptides mixed with MBP as background binding controls were also prepared. The salt concentration in all reactions was adjusted to 100 mM NaCl. Of each sample, 5 µl was removed for SDS–PAGE analysis as input. The binding reactions were incubated for 40 min at 4 °C while rotating. Subsequently, the samples were added to 30 µl of amylose bead slurry (NEB) equilibrated in wash buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 0.1% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 5% v/v glycerol). The beads were incubated for 2 h rotating at 4 °C. The supernatant was removed, and the beads were washed five times with 500 µl wash buffer. Upon removal of residual buffer, 50 µl elution buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 50 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 5% v/v glycerol and 20 mM maltose) was added to each sample and incubated at 4 °C for 30 min while rotating. The eluates were collected, mixed with SDS loading dye and ran on a Novex Tris-Glycine 4–12% 1.0 mm WedgeWell gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 20 min at 180 V. The DBR1 peptides were visualized by fluorescence signal at 488 nm on a ChemiDoc imager (Bio-Rad), whereas MBP–C19L1 MPP and MBP were stained afterwards with Coomassie blue (Vienna BioCenter Molecular Biology Service).

Of DHX35, 4 µM was mixed with 1 µM of either wild-type or mutant (M163K V171R L236E) GPATCH1 G-patch domain (residues 137–247) in the final reaction volume of 50 µl. Reactions containing individual proteins were also prepared as background binding controls. The salt concentration in all reactions was adjusted to 50 mM NaCl. All samples were incubated at 4 °C for 35 min while rotating. Of each sample, 5 µl was removed for SDS–PAGE analysis as input. Subsequently, each sample was added to 40 µl of amylose bead slurry (NEB) equilibrated in wash buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 50 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 0.03% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 5% v/v glycerol). The proteins were incubated with the beads for 1.5 h at 4 °C while rotating. The beads were then washed five times with 0.5 ml wash buffer. After removing residual wash buffer, 50 µl of wash buffer supplemented with 40 mM maltose was added to the beads and incubated for 1 h at 4 °C while rotating. The eluates were collected, mixed with SDS loading dye and ran on a Novex Tris-Glycine 4–12% 1.0 mm WedgeWell gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min at 180 V. The gel was stained with Coomassie blue (Vienna BioCenter Molecular Biology Service).

Of either wild-type or mutant (M146A L149K E150K) YJU2B peptide (134–178), which was predicted to interact with WDR83, 80 µl was added at 25 µM to 80 µl StrepTactin Sepharose bead slurry (IBA) equilibrated in wash buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.9, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.05% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 10% v/v glycerol). The beads were incubated with the peptides for 1 h at 4 °C while rotating and then washed four times with 0.4 ml of wash buffer. The washed beads containing the immobilized peptides were split into two samples and incubated either with or without 80 µl of the WDR83–GPATCH1(560–651) complex at 29 µM. The WDR83–GPATCH1(560–651) complex was also incubated with the beads lacking immobilised peptides as a background binding control. The salt concentration in all samples was adjusted to 50 mM NaCl and incubated at 4 °C for 2 h while rotating. The beads were then washed five times with 0.5 ml wash buffer. After removal of residual wash buffer, 80 µl of wash buffer supplemented with 50 mM biotin was added to each reaction and incubated for 1 h at 4 °C while rotating. The eluates were collected, mixed with SDS loading dye and ran on a Novex Tris-Glycine 4–12% 1.0 mm WedgeWell gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 25 min at 180 V. The YJU2B peptides were visualized by fluorescence signal at 488 nm on a ChemiDoc imager (Bio-Rad). The gel was then stained with Coomassie blue (Vienna BioCenter Molecular Biology Service) to visualize WDR83. The band corresponding to GPATCH1 in a Coomassie-stained gel could not be unambiguously identified, because its band overlaps with the bands of the YJU2B peptides.

HEK293T homozygous DBR1–dTAG-V5 cells containing the doxycycline-inducible mScarlet-tagged DBR1 constructs (wild type, catalytic mutant (H85A) and deletion of peptide I residues 420–434 (Δpep1)) as well as a control line lacking DBR1 overexpression were mixed 1:1 with wild-type HEK293T cells that constitutively expressed GFP. Cells were split into two wells: one well was treated with the 500 nM dTAGv-1 compound, whereas the other well was left untreated to serve as a control. Expression of the DBR1 constructs was induced using 1 µg ml−1 doxycycline. Cells were split at a ratio of 1:3 every day to prevent them from reaching confluency. The percentage of GFP+ cells was measured using an iQue Screener Plus high-throughput cytometer (Sartorius AG) immediately after mixing and again after 8 days. The average percentage of GFP− cells per line was calculated from technical triplicates across three biological replicates and served as a proxy for cell growth phenotype.

Relative expression levels of the inducible DBR1 constructs were measured as the mScarlet signal in each well after 1 day, when the GFP signal, and hence, cell viability, did not differ across conditions. The average mScarlet signal was then normalized to that of the wild-type DBR1 construct.

Of nuclear extract prepared from K562 cells stably overexpressing EGFP-tagged YJU2B, 120 µl was incubated with the recombinant 3×FLAG–DHX35(K83A)–GPATCH1(1−440)–TwStrep complex at various final concentrations (0, 0.5 µM or 4.5 µM) either in the presence or absence of 5 mM ATP. The reactions were incubated at 37 °C for 40 min before being applied to 45 µl GFP Trap bead slurry (Chromotek) equilibrated in wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.05% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 8% v/v glycerol) supplemented with 2 mg ml−1 BSA. The binding reactions were incubated for 1.5 h at 4 °C. The beads were then washed three times with wash buffer and twice with harsh wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 200 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.1% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 8% v/v glycerol). The proteins immobilized on the beads were eluted in 60 µl detergent-free wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 8% v/v glycerol) supplemented with 0.1 µg ml−1 3C protease for 1 h at 4 °C.

The eluates from all samples were then analysed by western blot using standard protocols with the antibodies to spliceosome proteins YJU2B (CAS OAAB02156, Aviva Systems Biology; dilution 1:100), PRP8 (CAS AB190347, Abcam; dilution 1:1,000), BRR2 (CAS AB241589, Abcam; dilution 1:1,000), AQR (CAS A302-546A, Bethyl Laboratories; dilution 1:1,000), TFIP11 (CAS PA5-49275, Invitrogen; dilution 1:1,000), C19L1 (CAS 31700-1-AP, Proteintech; dilution 1:5,000) and C19L2 (CAS 24872-1-AP, Proteintech, dilution 1:200). 3×FLAG–DHX35(K83A) and GPATCH1(1−440)–TwStrep were detected using antibodies to FLAG (CAS F3165, Sigma-Aldrich; dilution 1:500) and Strep (CAS 2-1509-001, iba; dilution 1:10,000) tags, respectively.

For RNA sequencing, endogenous human DIS was purified by anti-GFP affinity purification and gradient ultracentrifugation as described above for cryo-EM sample preparation, except that no glutaraldehyde was added to the gradient and that the pooled spliceosome-containing gradient fractions were not concentrated.

Endogenous human ILS″ for the deletion rate experiment and endogenous human ILSAQR for the read truncation experiment were purified from K562 cells stably overexpressing TFIP11–GFP or YJU2B–GFP, respectively, using anti-GFP affinity purification and gradient ultracentrifugation as described above and previously2, except that no glutaraldehyde was added to the gradient and the peak gradient fractions were not concentrated.

The pooled spliceosome fractions were incubated with 0.4 mg ml−1 proteinase K in 2 mM EDTA and 0.04% SDS for 1.5 h at 37 °C with gentle shaking. A 0.1 volume of 7.5 M ammonium acetate was added to the sample and mixed thoroughly. One volume of phenol-chloroform solution (ITW reagents) was added to the sample and briefly vortexed. The sample was spun down at 20,000g for 5 min. The top aqueous layer containing nucleic acids was transferred to a fresh tube, mixed with 2 volumes of isopropanol and 0.002 volumes of GlycoBlue co-precipitant (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and incubated overnight at −20 °C. The sample was then centrifuged at 20,000g for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was removed, and the remaining pellet was washed in ice-cold 70% ethanol. The washed pellet was briefly air dried and resuspended in 10 µl nuclease-free water.

For each sample, 3 µl of RNA was polyadenylated by incubating in a reaction containing 2 µl 5×SSIV reaction buffer (Invitrogen), 0.25 µl E. coli polyA polymerase (NEB), 0.25 µl RNasin (Promega), 0.25 µl 0.1 M dithiothreitol (Invitrogen) and 0.5 µl 0.5 mM ATP (Invitrogen) at 37 °C for 15 min. The samples were placed on ice, diluted with 9.25 µl water, then heated at 95 °C for 4 min to fragment the RNA. To anneal reverse transcription primers, 1 µl of 10 mM dNTPs and 1 µl of 10 µM dT(22)V-P7 primer were added, and the samples were heated to 65 °C for 5 min before cooling to 42 °C. To initiate reverse transcription, 2 µl of 5×SSIV reaction buffer (Invitrogen), 0.5 µl 0.1 M dithiothreitol (Invitrogen) and 0.5 µl SSIV enzyme (Invitrogen) were added to the samples, and the reactions were incubated at 42 °C for 20 min. The reactions were cooled to 37 °C and incubated with 2 µl exonuclease I (NEB) for 15 min to remove excess reverse transcription primers. To further remove excess RT primers, the samples were size selected using SPRI beads with a final PEG8000 concentration of 7.5% and a final isopropanol concentration of 22.5%. The samples were eluted from the beads, then RNA was hydrolysed by the addition of 1 µl 1 M NaOH and incubated at 95 °C for 10 min. The pH of the samples was then neutralized by the addition of 1 µl 1 M HCl and 10 µl 1 M HEPES pH 7.9. The cDNA was then purified using 2 volumes of SPRI beads and 3 volumes of isopropanol. The cDNA was eluted in 5.3 µl water, to which 1 µl DMSO and 2 µl 10 µM L01clip2.0 adapter was added. The mixture was heated to 75 °C for 2 min and then placed on ice. Adapter ligation was initiated by the addition of 2 µl 10× T4 RNA ligase reaction buffer (NEB), 0.2 µl 100 mM ATP (NEB), 9 µl 50% PEG 8000 (NEB) and 0.5 µl T4 RNA ligase 1 high concentration (NEB), and the reactions were incubated overnight at room temperature. The reaction was size selected using 20 µl SPRI beads and 13.33 µl isopropanol (final concentration of 25%). The resulting cDNA was amplified in a 50 µl quantitative PCR using Illumina-compatible i5/i7 indexed primer pairs and NEBNext Ultra II Q5 (NEB) according to the manufacturer instructions until the libraries appeared to amplify linearly. The resulting libraries were purified using 1.5 volumes of SPRI beads, then sequenced using a NovaSeqX 10B XP 2 × 150bp flow cell (Illumina) at the VBCF Next Generation Sequencing Facility.

Complete reproduction of all data analysis from the raw sequencing data to the final plots can be performed by executing the Snakemake pipeline (https://github.com/rfara/spliceosome_disassembly). In brief, all read pairs were trimmed of adapter and polyA sequences using cutadapt (v4.9) and UMI sequences were extracted using UMI-tools (v1.1.5) pre-mapped against the full human rDNA repeat sequence and GENCODE (v44) basic snRNA sequences using bowtie2 (v2.5.4). Unmapped reads pairs were mapped using STAR (v2.7.11b) against the GRCh38 primary assembly and GENCODE (v44) basic annotation. Uniquely mapping reads were deduplicated using umitools (v1.1.5). Introns and exons were defined using MANE Select transcripts from GENCODE (v44). Branchpoint locations were obtained from publicly available CoLa-seq data75, and the highest scoring branchpoint per intron was used for analysis. Read pairs for which the 3′ end mapped to the 3′ SS were considered to be derived from excised introns.

Of RNA, 5.5 µl was poly-adenylated by addition of 7 µl of the poly-adenylation reaction mix (4 µl 5X SuperScript IV RT buffer (Invitrogen), 1 µl 10 mM ATP, 1 µl 100 mM dithiothreitol, 0.5 µl RNasin (Promega) and 0.5 µl E. coli polyA polymerase (NEB)) and incubation at 37 °C for 20 min. To begin primer annealing, 1 µl of 25 mM dNTPs and 1 µl of 10 µM barcoded reverse transcription primer were added to the reaction, and the reaction was heated to 65 °C for 3 min. The reaction was cooled to 42 °C, and reverse transcription was initiated by the addition of 5.5 µl of the pre-heated reverse transcription mix (4 µl 5 M betaine, 0.5 µl 40 µM template switching oligo, 0.5 µl 200 mM MgCl2 and 0.5 µl SuperScript IV (Invitrogen)). The reaction was incubated at 42 °C for 1 h, then purified using homemade SPRI beads at a ratio of 1.8X. Library amplification quantitative PCR was performed using PCR mix (NEBNext Ultra II Q5 Master Mix, 1X EvaGreen (Biotium) and 500 mM partial P5 and P7 primers) with a long extension time (98 °C for 10 s, 69 °C for 20 s and 72 °C for 3 min 30 s). Samples were removed when linear amplification was observed and subsequently purified with 1.5X SPRI beads. The resulting libraries were quantified using the Qubit HS DNA kit, and the distribution of fragment sizes was quantified using the Fragment Analyzer. The libraries were sequenced using a Nanopore R10.4.1 Flow Cell.

The raw Nanopore data were base called using Dorado (v0.9). The libraries were demultiplexed and trimmed of adapter sequences and polyA sequences using cutadapt (v5.0). The reads were then mapped sequentially with minimap2 (v2.29)76 to rRNA sequences, snRNA sequences, spliced transcriptomic sequences and the genome, with the unmapped reads from mapping to each reference being passed to the next mapping. All reference sequences were derived from the hg38 human genome and the GENCODE (v44) annotation.

Branchpoint locations were annotated by CoLa-seq75. Deletion positions within reads were identified, with the value of a deletion being divided by the length of the deletion, and metaprofiles of the deletions were calculated relative to these branchpoint positions by summing the deletions at every position and dividing by the number of input reads. For the proportion of spliced transcripts to intronic reads, the total number of transcriptomic mapping reads and intron mapping reads was used.

Of nuclear extract from K562 cells expressing either wild-type DHX35 or mutant DHX35(K83A), 3 ml was applied to 500 µl GFP Trap bead slurry (Chromotek) equilibrated in wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.05% v/v Igepal CA-630 and 8% v/v glycerol). The beads were incubated for 3 h at 4 °C with gentle mixing. The beads were then washed five times with 3 ml wash buffer, transferred to fresh tubes and washed five more times with 1.5 ml detergent-free wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.9, 100 mM KCl, 0.5 mM TCEP, 2 mM MgCl2 and 8% glycerol). A small volume of both wild-type and mutant DHX35 bead samples was removed, incubated with 180 µl detergent-free wash buffer supplemented with 0.1 µg ml−1 3C protease overnight at 4 °C to elute the bound DIS complexes that represented an assay input. The rest of the beads of the wild-type and mutant DHX35 samples were both distributed across six fresh tubes each, resulting in three technical replicates per sample. After removing residual wash buffer, 120 µl detergent-free wash buffer was added to each tube and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C to allow temperature equilibration, which may cause nonspecific dissociation of various proteins from the beads. The supernatant was then removed and 120 µl detergent-free wash buffer supplemented with 20 mM MgCl2 and either 10 mM ATP or 10 mM ADP was added to three tubes each of both the wild-type and mutant DHX35 samples. The assays were incubated for 30 min at 37 °C shaking at 800 rpm. The samples were then spun down, and the supernatants containing the proteins released from the beads were collected, run for 3 min at 180 V on a Novex Tris-glycine 4–12% 1.0 mm WedgeWell gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and submitted to the Vienna BioCenter Mass Spectrometry Facility for in-gel tryptic digestion and LC–MS/MS analysis.

The resulting raw MS data were processed for protein identification and label-free quantification. We found that one replicate of the DHX35(K83A) ADP sample had not been injected correctly for LC–MS/MS, leaving two instead of three technical replicates for this condition. To identify the proteins that are released from the beads upon ATP treatment, protein abundances in each ATP sample were compared with protein abundances in the corresponding ADP samples. The samples of wild-type DHX35 and DHX35(K83A) were compared separately to account for potential differences in the starting protein amounts on the beads. Proteins were considered significantly enriched based on statistical tests (moderated t-test in limma, P < 0.05) and an arbitrary log2 fold-change cut-off of 1 (twofold enrichment over control on a linear scale). Data were visualized in GraphPad Prism 10.

Release assays were also analysed by western blot using standard protocols to validate that DHX35 that could not be detected by MS was not non-specifically released from the beads. Input samples as well as the released protein samples form a single replicate of wild-type DHX35 and DHX35(K83A) each were probed with the antibodies to the spliceosomal proteins DHX35 (CAS HPA062700, Sigma; dilution 1:250), WDR83 (CAS PA-60143, Invitrogen; diluted 1:500), BRR2 (CAS AB241589, Abcam; dilution 1:1,000), PRP19 (CAS AB228694, Abcam; dilution 1:1,000) and CWC15 (CAS 25293-1-AP, Proteintech; dilution 1:1,500). The primary antibodies were incubated with the milk-blocked membranes overnight at 4 °C. A horseradish peroxidase-coupled goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (CAS 31466, Invitrogen; dilution 1:10,000) was applied to each membrane before developing with Pierce ECL reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

a. C. elegans ILS remodeling assay in whole nematode extract. Top: Experiment schematic of the assay. Bottom: Results of the remodelling assay measured by quantitative mass spectrometry and shown in a volcano plot. Nematode extract was incubated with ATP, after which spliceosomes were purified by a pulldown on the endogenously 3xFlag-tagged NTC subunit PRP19 (ref. 2). Although PRP19 is generally common to all catalytic and post-catalytic spliceosome states, the ILS is the dominant spliceosome state in C. elegans extract. In the experiment, the known termination factors are released after the ATP treatment (DHX15, PAXBP1, C19L1, C19L2, TFIP11), while the later termination factors (DHX35, GPATCH1) associate. Other spliceosomal subunits do not significantly change in abundance. This suggests that in extracts the ILS remodels but does not completely disassemble upon ATP treatment. Differences between groups were statistically evaluated using limma with a moderated two-sided t-test. The multiple testing correction used the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. The horizontal dashed line marks a threshold of p-value of 0.05, the vertical dashed lines denote a log2-fold change threshold of one (two-fold change on a linear scale). b. Predicted alignment error (PAE) plot of the DHX35–GPATCH1–WDR83–YJU2B complex prediction from AlphaFold3. Each binary interaction was confidently predicted in five out of five models. c. Model of the DHX35–GPATCH1–WDR83–YJU2B complex prediction from AlphaFold3. d. Table of the co-dependency rankings of DHX35, GPATCH1, WDR83 and YJU2B in each other’s CRISPR-Cas9 knock-out viability screens, according to the DepMap database24 (as of June 2026). Co-dependency means that the four proteins are required for growth in the same set of cancer cell lines, indicating that they may function in a common cellular pathway. e. Experiment schematic for the endogenous purification of DHX35- and YJU2B-containing spliceosomes. f. SDS-PAGE analyses of the immuno-purified samples of the YJU2B- (top; ILSAQR) and DHX35- (bottom; DIS) containing spliceosomes. The bait protein for either experiment is written in bold. The molecular weight in kilodalton (kDa) of the molecular weight marker is indicated to the left of each gel. a. Close-up view of the RNA active site of the ILSAQR showing how the intron-lariat branch point (BP) is occluded from the solvent by both protein and RNA components of the spliceosome, making it inaccessible to debranching. b. Cryo-EM density of AQR and its surrounding proteins in the map of ILSAQR. The RNA density is observed in the active site of AQR, resolved at a nominal resolution of ~4 Å (left). Upon low pass filtering, further RNA density is observed extending from the AQR active site towards the RRM domain PPIE, which may guide the intron-lariat towards AQR (right). The density is coloured according to the protein and RNA it represents. c. Comparison of the RNA-bound AQR structure in the ILSAQR (left) and the crystal structure of the RNA-bound UPF1 core (PDB 2XZ0; right)30. Protein domains of both helicases are indicated and coloured based on the scheme in Fig. 2a. d. Comparison of RNA-bound (top left) and RNA-free (top right) human Upf1 crystal structures30 with AQR in the human ILSAQR (middle left), C. elegans ILS″ (middle right)2, and DIS (bottom) cryo-EM structures, showing that AQR adopts a closed RNA-bound conformation in the ILSAQR but remains in an RNA-free open conformation in the ILS″ and DIS. The silhouette of the respective RNA-bound conformation of Upf1 and AQR is shown underneath the coordinate models of the different states. Arrows depict the direction of movement of the RecA2 domain upon RNA binding. e. Cryo-EM densities of AQR and its surrounding proteins in the ILS″ from C. elegans (EMD-19399)2 and in the human DIS, showing that RNA density is absent from the AQR active site in both complexes. The map of Ce ILS″ was gaussian filtered to match the density detail of the AQR density in the human ILSAQR. Despite the low local resolution of AQR in the DIS, its active site is empty. After intron-lariat BP extraction and debranching on the ILSAQR, AQR would likely run off the linearized intron RNA owing to AQR’s 5′-to-3′ polarity. This would leave AQR unable to further contribute to RNA remodelling, consistent with the absence of RNA density in the AQR active site in the DIS. f. Cryo-EM density of DHX15 after extensive image classification, revealed DHX15 relative to NTR components of the ILSAQR at a nominal resolution of 9.5 Å from 9,659 particles (see Extended Data Fig. 2 for classification tree). The density is consistent with a model of DHX15 in complex with U6 snRNA and TFIP11 G-patch, as also seen in other ILS structures2. Both the model and the map are colored according to the protein they represent. The DHX15 domains were defined in ref. 43. g. Comparison of U2 snRNA conformation in the ILSAQR (right) and in the free U2 snRNP (left; PDB 6Y5Q)33. The region of U2 snRNA corresponding to nucleotides 25-45 (light green) is base-paired with the intron-lariat forming U2/U6 helix I and the branch helix in the ILSAQR. The same region forms an internal branch point stem loop (BSL) in the free U2 snRNP. Remodelling of the ILSAQR RNA network by the RNA helicases DHX15 and AQR, and specifically the dissolution of the branch helix by AQR, may thus allow the BSL to reform. This could further promote U2 snRNP release from the spliceosome.

a. Immunoprecipitation (IP) experiment of doxycycline (Dox) inducible GFP-tagged DBR1 from the nuclear extract of human K562 cells. Left: Experiment schematic. Right: SDS-PAGE analyses of the anti-GFP nanobody pulldowns from the nuclear extract of either uninduced (−; left lane) or doxycycline-induced (+; right lane) DBR1-GFP K562 cells. The pulldown was performed five times. The molecular weight in kilodalton (kDa) of the molecular weight marker is indicated to the left of the gel. The band corresponding to GFP-tagged DBR1 and the bands corresponding to spliceosome components PRP8 and BRR2 are labelled to the right of the gel, indicating the purification a DBR1-containing spliceosome complex. b. Heatmap of the quantitative mass spectrometry data of the DBR1-GFP immunoprecipitation experiments described in panel a. The data were normalized for protein abundance in the pulldown from the uninduced cells. The heatmap shows specific enrichment in the DBR1-GFP pulldown of the known DBR1 interactor MPLKIP and of the ILS components, especially the disassembly factor C19L1. The experiment was performed in technical triplicates. c. Pairwise AlphaFold2 Multimer36,37 protein interaction screens of DBR1 (left) and MPLKIP (right) against spliceosome factors identified by mass spectrometry of the ILSAQR complex. Proteins with both a high iPTM score37 and a high PEAK score78 were selected as putative interactors. DBR1 and MPLKIP were additionally included in each other’s screens as respective positive controls. Although MPLKIP was previously proposed to recruit DBR1 to spliceosomes34, we did not find confident predictions for a binding interface between MPLKIP and any of the ILSAQR proteins. The predicted interfaces of DBR1 with MPLKIP, SYF1, and C19L1 are fully compatible with each other and could occur at the same time. d. Predicted alignment error (PAE) plot of the DBR1–MPLKIP–C19L1–SYF1 complex prediction from AlphaFold3. The plot shows that DBR1 could bind to all three interactors simultaneously. Each binary interaction was confidently predicted in five out of five models. e. DBR1 interacts with the spliceosome via two conserved peptides. Top: Average predicted pathogenicity score per residue of DBR1 according to AlphaFold Missense79. Mutations in the catalytic MPP domain of DBR1 appear to be universally pathogenic, while the disordered C-terminal region of DBR1 contains two stand-out regions of increased pathogenicity, corresponding to peptides I and II. Bottom: Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of DBR1 peptides I and II. Peptide I displays a higher degree of sequence conservation across eukaryotes than peptide II, suggesting that peptide I might be more functionally important. Peptide II may overlap with the nuclear localization sequence of DBR1 (ref. 80). Each residue was coloured according to its BLOSUM62 conservation score. f. Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of the human DBR1 peptide I with a highly similar peptide in the spliceosomal protein SYF1 from various eukaryotic species. This SYF1 peptide may also bind the C19L1 MPP domain, suggesting that DBR1 peptide I may displace SYF1 to associate with the spliceosome, potentially explaining why DBR1 associates transiently with ILS complexes at steady state. The SYF1 peptide, which is predicted to bind C19L1, lies adjacent to an I-patch motif that may inhibit the nearby DHX15 (ref. 42) (Fig. 2b). Displacement of SYF1 from C19L1 by DBR1 peptide I could release this inhibitory motif, promoting DHX15 activation and physically coupling ILS remodelling to DBR1 binding. The biological significance of these observations remains to be determined. Each residue in the MSA was coloured according to its BLOSUM62 conservation score. g. In vitro pulldown experiment with purified recombinant proteins demonstrating a direct and specific interaction between DBR1 peptide I and the MPP domain of C19L1. MBP-tagged C19L1 MPP (residues 1-278) was immobilized on amylose beads and incubated with either wild-type (wt) fluorescein-tagged DBR1 peptide I or a scrambled (sc) version of the same peptide. Only the wild-type peptide showed an interaction with C19L1 MPP. Amylose beads with immobilized MBP were used as a control to assess the background binding of the DBR1 peptides. The pulldown was performed three times. The molecular weight in kilodalton (kDa) of the molecular weight marker is indicated to the left of the gels. h. Depletion-rescue experiments show that the DBR1–C19L1 interaction via DBR1 peptide I is needed for normal cell growth. DBR1-dTAG HEK293T human cells were mixed at a 1:1 ratio with GFP-expressing HEK293T cells. The small molecule dTAGV-1 was added to the culture to deplete endogenous DBR1 only in the GFP negative cells. Expression of various DBR1 rescue constructs was simultaneously induced by adding doxycycline. The proportion of GFP negative (DBR1-depleted) cells was assessed by fluorescence-activated cell sorting after eight days. Wild-type DBR1 (wt) overexpression was significantly more effective at rescuing cell growth than overexpression of either the catalytic mutant DBR1 (H85A) or DBR1 lacking peptide I (Δpep1). This indicates that peptide I contributes to normal DBR1 function in cells. The fluorescence signal of the mScarlet-tagged DBR1 constructs was measured by FACS one day after the start of doxycycline induction. The mScarlet levels relative to wild-type DBR1 are indicated underneath the plot. The wild-type DBR1 was expressed at the lowest level out of the three constructs, demonstrating that measured growth defects of the two mutants are not explained by low expression levels. Average values from three biological replicates measured in technical triplicates are plotted, and the standard deviation is indicated.

a. Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of the N-terminal extension and the zinc finger domain of YJU2B and YJU2A. A comparison of the consensus sequences of YJU2A and YJU2B is also shown in the middle. Comparison of the YJU2B binding site in the ILSAQR with the equivalent regions in other spliceosome states2,56, where the YJU2B binding interfaces are occupied by other state-specific factors. a. Experimental scheme of the in vitro ILSAQR-to-DIS remodelling assay. b. Western blot analyses of the ILSAQR-to-DIS remodelling assay. The proteins in the treated extract before the pulldown (Input) are shown on the left, while the proteins bound to the anti-GFP beads (GFP elution) are shown on the right. The proteins were eluted by 3C protease cleavage of the GFP tag from YJU2B. The DHX35K83A-GPATCH11−440 construct included the minimal region of GPATCH1 required to bind both DHX35 and the spliceosome but lacked the region binding WDR83 (GPATCH1 residues 574-654) to prevent alternative means of recruitment to the spliceosome, for example, through the YJU2B-WDR83 interaction. DHX35 and GPATCH1 were detected using anti-Flag and anti-Strep antibodies, respectively. The experiment was performed two times. c. Comparison of models (top), cryo-EM density maps (middle) and models of proteins and RNAs fit into the corresponding maps (bottom) of the RNA-based active site of the ILSAQR (left) and DIS (right) complexes. The cryo-EM densities of both complexes were low pass filtered and clipped to highlight each RNA active site. The cryo-EM densities corresponding to RNA elements are coloured according to RNA identity, while the rest of the spliceosome is coloured in grey. Proteins in the bottom panels are coloured by identity in cartoon representation. The cavity of the active site is empty in the cryo-EM density of the DIS, demonstrating that the RNA network of the DIS has been almost completely dismantled, excepting the partial U6-5′SS duplex and the U6 5′-end. d. Normalized read coverage at pre-mRNA intron 3′-ends, contained within ILS″ or DIS complexes, representing 533,004 reads in the ILS″ and 16,207 reads in the DIS. Read coverage at the annotated 3′SS was set to 1. The nucleotide distance from the 3′SS is indicated on the x-axis and explained with a pre-mRNA schematic underneath. e. Normalized deletion rates of excised introns contained within DIS or ILS″ complexes, aligned at the branch point adenosine, representing 452,677 reads in the ILS″ AQRand 13,224 reads in the DIS. Deletions are caused by error-prone reverse transcription through a branched intron-lariat, illustrated in the diagram on the right. Intron-lariats of the purified ILS″ produced a sharp peak in deletion rate around the annotated BP as expected. In contrast, introns of the purified DIS displayed a more uniform deletion rate with a significantly reduced peak at the annotated BP, providing additional evidence that DIS-associated introns are predominantly debranched. Owing to the low frequency of reverse transcription errors, the observed deletion rate significantly underestimates the absolute percentage of branched introns. Deletion rates are calculated per position and normalized to the deletion rate across all read positions. The nucleotide distance from the branch point is indicated on the x-axis and explained with an intron schematic underneath. f. Bar chart showing the proportion of intronic and exonic reads among the pre-mRNA reads detected in the ILS (ILS″ in the deletion rate experiment or ILSAQR in the BP truncation experiment) and DIS complexes in the branch-point deletion rate experiment depicted in panels d and e (left) and in the branch point truncation experiment shown in Fig. 3 (right) (see Materials and Methods for details). The majority of pre-mRNA reads in both samples in both experiments come from introns, which, together with the intronic read coverage plots in panel d and in Fig. 3h, suggests that both the ILS and the DIS are associated primarily with excised introns. The higher percentage of exonic reads in the DIS sample compared to the ILS may indicate either contamination or that some defective catalytic spliceosomes were also purified in the DHX35-GFP pulldown in addition to the DIS complex, consistent with the role of DHX35 in spliceosome quality control5,23. We cannot exclude that a fraction of particles in our DIS cryo-EM reconstruction originates from SQC complexes that assembled prior to pre-mRNA branching or after branching and debranching. However, we consider this unlikely owing to (i) the lack of cryo-EM density for the 5′-exon in the exon channel, (ii) the absence of LENG1 and CWC22, which would be expected in a B*D SQC complex, and (iii) the predominant association of excised and debranched introns with the DIS in the two RNA sequencing experiments.

a. Close-up view of GPATCH1 and its interactions with PRP8 and DHX35 within the DIS. PRP8 and DHX35 are coloured according to their protein domains, respectively. Comparison of the interactions between DHX35, GPATCH1 and PRP8 in the human DIS (left) and the defective B*D spliceosomes from S. pombe23 (middle) and C. thermophilum5 (right). DHX35 and GPATCH1 bind through similar and conserved interfaces in both regular and defective spliceosomes. PRP8 and DHX35 are coloured by their domains with the domains of the S. pombe and C. thermophilum proteins assigned based on their structural similarity to the human orthologues. c. Comparison of the DHX35–GPATCH1 binding site in the DIS to the equivalent regions in earlier state spliceosomes. The DHX35–GPATCH1 binding surface on PRP8 is occupied by other spliceosomal factors in all earlier spliceosome states: the SF3B complex of the U2 snRNP in the Bact complex56, the RNA helicase DHX38 in the C complex56, and the state-specific factors Cactin and C9orf78 and the branch helix in the P complex2. d. Experimental scheme of the DIS release assay. e. DIS release assay coupled to mass spectrometry of DIS complexes purified on either wild-type (wt) DHX35 (top) or catalytic mutant (K83A) DHX35 (bottom), DIS-associated proteins are released upon ATP-treatment in the presence of wild-type but not mutant DHX35. DHX35, GPATCH1, WDR83 are not released and remain on the beads (Extended Data Fig. 8f). These data indicate that DHX35 could catalyse spliceosome disassembly. Differences between groups were statistically evaluated using limma with a moderated two-sided t-test. The multiple testing correction used the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. The horizontal dashed line represents a significance threshold of p-value = 0.05, the vertical dashed line marks a log2-fold change threshold of one (two-fold change on a linear scale). f. Western blot analyses of the DIS release assay. One replicate of each sample from experiment in panel e was analysed by western blotting. BRR2, PRP19 and CWC15 were specifically probed and released from the bead-immobilized DIS complex in the presence of wild-type (wt) DHX35 upon addition of ATP, consistent with the quantitative mass spectrometry data. In contrast, DHX35 and GPATCH1 were probed and not released, consistent with neither protein being detected among the released proteins by mass spectrometry. This shows that the release of the spliceosomal proteins is not caused by non-specific dissociation of DHX35 from the beads. Two independent experiments were performed. g. Heatmap of the mass spectrometry data of the immuno-purified spliceosomes containing either wild-type (wt) DHX35-GFP or catalytic mutant (K83A) DHX35-GFP. Both wild-type and catalytic mutant DHX35 co-purify essentially identical spliceosome complexes, which match the composition of the DIS. This shows the suitability of the DHX35K83A-containing DIS as a negative control in DIS release assays and strongly suggests that the DIS represents a spliceosome state before DHX35 RNA helicase action.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A 7-eV bandgap semiconductor based on silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Darrell. G. Schlom
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

In rectifying power electronics, wider-bandgap (Eg) semiconductors allow higher efficiency and power density with the Baliga figure of merit proportional to Eg5.5 (refs. 1,2). Unfortunately, the unique ability of semiconductors to have their conductivities controllably modulated over orders of magnitude by equilibrium doping methods becomes increasingly elusive as the bandgap increases. Increasing demand for wider-bandgap semiconductors has led to many materials previously considered insulators—including GaN, SiC, AlN, Ga2O3 and GeO2—to emerge as useful semiconductors after decreasing defect densities and finding appropriate dopants. Here we report silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3 films with bandgaps exceeding 7.0 eV grown by suboxide molecular-beam epitaxy, surpassing that of cubic boron nitride, the next-widest-bandgap semiconductor known3,4,5. In the colossal-bandgap regime, >6 eV, our silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3 films have room-temperature conductivities over 100 million times higher than all previous reports6. We fabricate a Schottky diode and a field-effect transistor (the AlphaFET) with colossal-bandgap channels. These α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3 films and devices use sapphire, an abundant, inexpensive substrate with excellent quality that is produced at massive scale, facilitating the development and adoption of colossal-bandgap electronics. Our achievement breaks the trend of increasing synthesis difficulty, cost and small size of ever-wider-bandgap semiconductors, for example, diamond and cubic boron nitride.

D.B. managed mask design, patterning of devices onto the thin films and measurement of device behaviour. P.S. handled the ellipsometry measurements with assistance from U.K. M.R. assisted D.B. with measuring the breakdown voltage of the AlphaDiodes. M.K.I.S. and M.D.W. carried out the SIMS measurements. V.-A.H., N.P. and F.G. calculated the theoretical mobilities as a function of x using density functional theory (Fig. 2e). I.S. performed focused-ion-beam specimen preparation and APT measurements. S.D. performed APT measurements and data analysis. B.M. supervised the APT experiments and data analysis. M.S. oversaw the ellipsometry measurements. D.A.M. oversaw the STEM measurements. H.G.X. and D.J. helped design the devices, assisted in analysing the results and edited the paper. D.G.S. oversaw the MBE growths, helped conceive of the experiments, assisted in the analysis of the results and was the primary editor of the article drafts.

This carrier density is then used to fit the donor density ND and donor activation energy ED. b, A plot of the electron concentration ne as extracted from temperature-dependent Hall measurements as a function of T. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Overcoming key challenges in the evolutionary transition to multicellularity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: William C. Ratcliff
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature 
volume
 658, 
pages
327–336 (2026) Cite this article

Dozens of independent origins of multicellularity have profoundly shaped Earth’s evolutionary and ecological history. These transitions have given rise to massive radiations encompassing thousands to millions of species and the evolution of increasingly complex bodies. Multicellular taxa now constitute the majority of Earth’s biomass and have fundamentally transformed global ecosystems, underpinning diverse biomes from forests and grasslands to coral reefs. While these macroevolutionary patterns have long been recognized, the microevolutionary processes driving the transition to multicellularity have remained unclear. Questions remain on how solitary cells form cohesive groups, how these groups become evolutionary units capable of adaptation at the multicellular level, and how novel cell types and developmental patterns emerge. Recent discoveries of previously unknown multicellular species and the development of experimental models have provided important insights into these questions. This work reveals that seemingly insurmountable evolutionary hurdles are often readily overcome either through the repurposing of ancestral unicellular traits or through emergent properties of multicellular collectives that arise spontaneously. Here we review key breakthroughs in our understanding of the microevolutionary processes that underpin the evolution of increasingly complex multicellularity, focusing on mechanisms through which single cells can evolve into functionally integrated multicellular organisms.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: tRNA dosage regulates lineage dependency and resistance in prostate cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Andrew C. Hsieh
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Lineage plasticity underlies therapeutic resistance in cancer1,2, yet the translational mechanisms that enable this phenotypic flexibility remain largely unknown. Here using prostate cancer as a model of lineage dependence, we performed unbiased small RNA sequencing and identified tRNA1Arg(UCU) as a regulator of lineage transitions and therapy resistance. tRNA1Arg(UCU) is capable of reprogramming lineage dependence, which can be tuned to restore sensitivity to therapies that target the androgen receptor. We identify TARDBP and ZSCAN29 as DNA-binding proteins that directly engage the genomic locus of tRNA1Arg(UCU) to regulate its expression, a result that highlights the importance of non-canonical tRNA-specific gene regulation. Mechanistically, tRNA1Arg(UCU) controls a translational program centred on SWI/SNF chromatin remodellers, which is necessary to maintain lineage fidelity. In patients, tRNA1Arg(UCU) is downregulated in neuroendocrine prostate cancer and its loss is associated with accelerated metastasis and poor survival. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized tRNA-specific regulatory axis that links codon biology to lineage dependence and therapy resistance in prostate cancer.

Lineage plasticity is a cellular property that enables development and stress adaptation3,4. It is characterized by the ability of cells to differentiate into alternative identities that take on new epigenetic states, transcriptional programs and morphologies5,6,7. However, in the context of cancer, lineage plasticity is often co-opted as a response to therapies, pulling cancers away from their lineage-specific dependencies to drive drug resistance8. This is especially apparent in lineage-dependent cancers1, in which effective inhibition of the driver lineage factor9,10,11,12 can induce cellular reprogramming to promote cell survival. Like its tissue of origin13, prostate cancer requires the androgen receptor (AR) for growth14,15. However, genetic loss of TP53, PTEN or RB or treatment with second-generation AR pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) has been shown to drive lineage independence from the original AR-dependent lineage through neuroendocrine (NE) differentiation or alternative cell states16,17,18,19,20,21. Despite progress in defining the epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms that underlie lineage dependencies and transitions in cancer1,2, the role of mRNA translation in controlling cell fate remains largely unexplored despite its substantial implications for therapy resistance and patient outcomes.

tRNAs are the crucial mediators of mRNA decoding that supply amino acids to growing polypeptide chains through the ribosome during protein synthesis22. tRNAs are organized into isoacceptor families—molecules that carry the same amino acid but differ in the anticodon—and are further subdivided into isodecoders that share anticodons but differ in their body sequences23 (Extended Data Fig. 1a). In mammals, approximately 300 unique isodecoders exist24. The advent of methods to quantify tRNA have revealed that tRNA dosage can vary significantly between different cell types and tissues25,26,27,28,29. This result suggests that tRNA abundance may be an important catalyst for distinct cellular functions in physiology30. Indeed, inherited mutations in various components of RNA polymerase III, the macromolecular complex responsible for tRNA synthesis, lead to tissue-specific diseases rather than a complete loss of cellular functions31. tRNA dysregulation has also been implicated in cancer, which highlights its broader impact on human disease32. Altered tRNA pools were first discovered in cancer in 2009 through microarray profiling of breast cancer33. Since then, growing evidence has shown that specific tRNAs can actively contribute to distinct cancer-promoting functions. Overexpression of the initiator tRNAiMet has been linked to increased proliferation in breast cancer and metastasis in melanoma34,35. Moreover, specific tRNAs can drive metastasis by promoting the translation of mRNAs enriched with their cognate codons36. These findings underscore the regulatory role of tRNA dosage in cancer cell behaviour. However, important questions remain, including the mechanisms that underlie tRNA dysregulation in cancer and how tRNA abundance is linked to lineage dependence. Addressing these questions will provide a unified framework in our fundamental understanding of translation dynamics and their role in shaping the phenotypic diversity of cancer.

Using prostate cancer as an archetype of lineage dependence, we report here that a single tRNA species, tRNA1Arg(UCU), is a key regulator of lineage conversion and therapy resistance. We show that tRNA1Arg(UCU) changes can promote lineage transitions, and its restoration sensitizes tumours to therapies that target the AR pathway. We identify TARDBP and ZSCAN29 as DNA-binding proteins that regulate the expression of tRNA1Arg(UCU) by directly interacting with its genomic locus. Functionally, tRNA1Arg(UCU) governs lineage dependency through translational control of a SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling component, SMARCC2. Clinically, tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression is significantly reduced in NE prostate cancer and correlates with reduced overall survival. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism of tRNA dosage regulation, with implications for lineage dependence and plasticity in lethal prostate cancer.

To map tRNA dynamics during lineage plasticity, we conducted multiplex small RNA sequencing (MSR-seq)28 to profile full-length tRNAs, their fragments and selected chemical modifications during the transition from prostate adenocarcinoma (AD) to a lineage plastic (LP) state defined by decreased AR activity and increased NE features. We used an in vitro model, whereby LNCaP AD cells were engineered to undergo lineage plasticity through knockdown of RB1 and overexpression of TP53R175H, MYCN, ASCL1, SRRM4, NR0B2, BCL2 and KRASG12V. This combination reproducibly generates a phenotype with reduced AR expression, increased NE markers and resistance to AR-targeted therapies37 (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Among 49 isoacceptors, only tRNAArg(UCU) was significantly downregulated during lineage transition in two separate analyses (DESeq2 analysis, log2 fold change (log2[FC]) = –0.338, false discovery rate (FDR) = 2.42 × 10–25 in Fig. 1a; and edgeR analysis, log2[FC] = –0.336, FDR = 1.02 × 10–4 in Extended Data Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 1).

Among the five tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoders, tRNA1Arg(UCU) was the most abundantly expressed (Extended Data Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1). Moreover, tRNA1Arg(UCU) was the sole tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoder that was substantially decreased in the context of lineage plasticity (DESeq2 analysis, log2[FC] = –0.336, FDR = 1.55 × 10–6 in Fig. 1b; and edgeR analysis, log2[FC] = –0.357, FDR = 1.626 × 10–3 in Extended Data Fig. 1e). Notably, this reduction was not accompanied by changes in fragmentation or chemical modifications (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g), which indicated that there was a specific reduction in mature tRNA1Arg(UCU). Downregulation of tRNA1Arg(UCU) was further confirmed by quantitative PCR (qPCR) and northern blot analyses in both LNCaP and C4-2B (a cell line that is a LNCaP metastatic derivative38) AD and LP cells (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1h–j).

To investigate the association of tRNA1Arg(UCU) and lineage identity, we profiled nine prostate cancer cell lines and observed a strong positive correlation between tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels and AR activity (Pearson’s r = 0.85, P = 0.0034; Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1k). Conversely, there was a strong negative correlation between two NE marker genes (ENO2 and SCN3A) and tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression (Pearson’s r = –0.72, P = 0.03 and r = –0.72, P = 0.027, respectively; Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1l). We next examined tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression in the LTL331 patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model, a well-established PDX derived from prostate AD tissue that transdifferentiates to NE prostate cancer (NEPC) after castration39 (Fig. 1f). We found a stepwise reduction in tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance from pre-castration to post-castration to relapse samples (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2a), and this coincided with the loss of AR signalling and acquisition of NE features (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

To further validate these findings, we developed an in situ hybridization assay that enabled us to specifically quantify tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression in patient tissue samples (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e). Analyses of 56 patients from the University of Washington (UW) prostate cancer rapid autopsy cohort18 revealed that AR+ tumours express higher levels of tRNA1Arg(UCU) than NE+ tumours (Fig. 1h,i), which correlated with the MSR-seq quantification results (Spearman’s correlation coefficient r = 0.41, P = 0.045; Extended Data Fig. 2f) and not with tRNA chemical modifications at the probe-binding site (Extended Data Fig. 2g). Furthermore, only tRNA1Arg(UCU) was downregulated in both LNCaP LP cells and NE+ patient tissue samples (Extended Data Fig. 2h,i and Supplementary Table 2). tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance positively correlated with AR activity (Spearman’s r = 0.37, P = 0.018; Fig. 1j). Conversely, there was a negative correlation between the NE marker gene ELAVL4 (ref. 18) and tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels (Spearman’s r = –0.36, P = 0.019; Fig. 1k). These observations across multiple model systems and patient tissue samples collectively establish tRNA1Arg(UCU) as a lineage-associated isodecoder, the abundance of which decreases with the transition from AR-driven AD to a LP state in prostate cancer.

It remains unclear whether tRNA1Arg(UCU) is simply a marker of lineage transitions or has a functional role in driving them. To address this gap in knowledge, we engineered doxycycline-inducible short hairpin RNA (shRNA) expression constructs targeting tRNA1Arg(UCU) (shUCU) or a non-targeting control (shScr) and stably expressed them in LNCaP and C4-2B cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We observed a 25–50% reduction in tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels, as measured by northern blotting (Fig. 2a) and qPCR (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Knockdown was specific for tRNA1Arg(UCU) and did not affect other tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoders (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Silencing of tRNA1Arg(UCU) led to a decrease in AR pathway genes at both the transcript (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 3d–f and Supplementary Table 3) and protein levels (Fig. 2c), alongside increased expression of genes in neuron-related pathways (Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3e–g). Furthermore, these changes were specific to tRNA1Arg(UCU) because knockdown of tRNA2Arg(CCG) and tRNA3Arg(UCG) did not alter AR pathway gene expression (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i). Together, these findings indicate that reducing tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage promotes phenotypic plasticity in androgen-responsive cells.

Our findings raise the question of whether this phenotypic switch can affect cellular responses to therapeutics that target the AR, which are commonly used in patients with prostate cancer. To this end, cells transduced with shScr or shUCU were treated with the following ARPIs approved by the US Food and Drug Administration: enzalutamide, apalutamide or darolutamide40,41,42. Notably, shUCU-transduced cells were significantly more resistant to these ARPIs across multiple concentrations in both LNCaP and C4-2B models than shScr-transduced cells (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 3j). Conversely, tRNA1Arg(UCU) knockdown increased sensitivity to the AURKA inhibitor, alisertib, which has been shown to have activity in NEPC43 (Extended Data Fig. 3k). These results demonstrate that decreasing tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage is not only phenotypically relevant but also reprograms AR dependency.

To explore the functional impact of tRNA1Arg(UCU) depletion in a physiological context, we generated a prostate cancer mouse model haploinsufficient for n-Trtct2 (also known as n-Tr22), which encodes tRNA1Arg(UCU). Hi-Myc44 mice that develop prostate tumours were crossed with n-Trtct2 knockout mice (n-Trtct2–/–)45 to produce mice with only one copy of the tRNA gene (Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/–). We derived Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/+ and Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/– organoid lines from these mice (Extended Data Fig. 4a) and assessed lineage dependence (Fig. 2g). MYC protein levels were equivalent between the two genotypes, and Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/– organoids had reduced tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Reduced n-Trtct2 dosage significantly increased resistance to ARPI treatment by threefold (Fig. 2g). To evaluate the in vivo consequences on lineage dependence, Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/+ and Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/– mice were aged for 9 months and subjected to surgical castration to mimic AR pathway inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 4d). We focused our analyses on ventral and anterior prostate lobes because Hi-Myc mice exhibited strong MYC expression in these lobes (Extended Data Fig. 4e). No differences were observed in uncastrated controls, whereas castrated Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/– mice displayed significantly enlarged prostate glands (Fig. 2h). At a histological level, 25% of castrated Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/– mice exhibited large high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) glands compared with 0% of castrated Hi-Myc;n-Trtct2+/+ mice (Fig. 2i). Together, our observations demonstrate that reduced tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage promotes lineage transitions and confer resistance to AR-targeted therapies.

Next, we asked whether restoration of tRNA1Arg(UCU) could reverse lineage transition and restore sensitivity to ARPIs. Re-expression of tRNA1Arg(UCU) in LP cells (UCU cells) was confirmed by northern blotting, and increased tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance did not affect expression levels of the other tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoders (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). We first performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on LNCaP AD, LP and UCU cells to compare expression of AR-regulated genes. AR pathway genes19 that significantly decreased in the context of lineage plasticity were restored after addback of tRNA1Arg(UCU) (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 4). This result was supported by qPCR data and further validated at the protein level (Fig. 3c,d). Conversely, NE marker gene expression decreased after tRNA1Arg(UCU) re-expression (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Lastly, overexpression of genes encoding tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoders 2–5, tRNA1Arg(ACG), tRNA2Arg(CCG) and tRNA4Arg(CCU) in LNCaP LP cells did not lead to increases in AR pathway genes, which is in contrast to what we observed with tRNA1Arg(UCU) addback (Extended Data Fig. 5d–h and Supplementary Table 4).

These findings raise the question of whether the restoration of an AR-activated phenotype is functionally relevant. To this end, we treated LNCaP and C4-2B AD, LP and UCU cells with the ARPIs enzalutamide, apalutamide or darolutamide. Relative to AD cells, LP cells were resistant to AR inhibition. However, addback of tRNA1Arg(UCU) was sufficient to restore sensitivity to ARPIs (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). By contrast, AD and UCU cells were less sensitive to alisertib treatment than LP cells (Extended Data Fig. 6c). Next, we sought to determine whether restoration of lineage dependence could be observed in a prostate cancer model in which treatment resistance naturally evolved. LNCaP-abl is a subline of LNCaP cells that developed androgen insensitivity after 87 passages in androgen-depleted medium46. Despite expressing the AR, it has a low AR activity score, reduced tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression and is resistant to AR-targeted agents46 (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1k). We generated LNCaP-abl cells in which tRNA1Arg(UCU) was overexpressed. This model had enhanced expression of AR pathway genes at the mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). Moreover, expression of tRNA1Arg(UCU) was sufficient to improve the sensitivity of LNCaP-abl cells to enzalutamide (Fig. 3h).

Our findings prompted us to investigate the physiological relevance of increasing tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage on lineage dependence. We used the transgenic AD of the mouse prostate (TRAMP) model, in which mice develop PIN that progresses into poorly differentiated NE tumours47,48. These mice were crossed with n-Trtct2 transgenic mice (n-Trtct2OE), which overexpress tRNA1Arg(UCU) by eightfold49, to generate TRAMP;n-Trtct2OE mice. After 5 months, corresponding to the emergence of PIN, mice were castrated to deplete androgen levels (Extended Data Fig. 6f). One month later, prostate tissues were collected and analysed. Notably, TRAMP mice had a higher incidence of PIN glands than TRAMP;n-Trtct2OE mice. This result provides support for the concept that increasing tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage promotes AR dependence (Fig. 3i). Together, these findings reveal that lineage dependency in prostate cancer can be modulated by a single tRNA species.

We next sought to determine how tRNA1Arg(UCU) is downregulated in the context of phenotypic transition. Previous studies have shown that tRNA dosage can be regulated by neighbouring RNA polymerase II activity50,51 and by co-occupancy of RNA polymerase II and transcription factors51. This led us to ask whether there are transcription regulators that specifically occupy the TRR-TCT1-1 (also known as tRNA-Arg-TCT-1-1) gene locus. We analysed the ENCODE transcription factor ChIP–seq (chromatin immunopreciptation with high-throughput sequencing) database52 and identified 11 DNA-binding proteins that interface with the TRR-TCT1-1 gene locus (Fig. 4a). As transcription factor binding has been shown to buttress tRNA levels51, we next asked whether any of these factors are decreased in the context of lineage transition. The COMPASS complex component ASH2L gene53, the DNA and RNA binding protein TARDBP gene54, the zinc-finger protein ZSCAN29 gene and the telomere-associated protein ZBTB40 gene55 were all downregulated in LP cells compared with AD cells (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 5).

To determine whether these factors regulate tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression, we individually silenced ASH2L, TARDBP, ZSCAN29 and ZBTB40 and quantified tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance. TARDBP and ZSCAN29 silencing led to a significant decrease, but their combined knockdown did not further reduce tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels (Fig. 4c,d and Extended Data Fig. 7a–d). ASH2L and ZBTB40 knockdown did not reproducibly affect tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression (Extended Data Fig. 7e–h). Consistent with these findings, nuclear TARDBP and ZSCAN29 protein levels were reduced in LP cells relative to AD cells (Extended Data Fig. 7i). Moreover, TARDBP and ZSCAN29 expression correlated with tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance in specimens from patients with prostate cancer (Spearman’s r = 0.4, P = 0.0092 for TARDBP; Spearman’s r = 0.31, P = 0.05 for ZSCAN29) (Fig. 4e). Given the role of tRNA1Arg(UCU) in regulating prostate cancer lineage plasticity, we next investigated whether TARDBP and ZSCAN29 are associated with lineage states in patient tumours. TARDBP and ZSCAN29 expression was inversely correlated with NE and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) gene signatures (Extended Data Fig. 7j–m). These findings extend our experimental observation to human disease and establish that TARDBP and ZSCAN29 are associated with lineage plasticity in patients.

Next, we performed CUT&RUN profiling of TARDBP and ZSCAN29 across all tRNA genomic loci in LNCaP AD and LP cells. Among all tRNA genes, TRR-TCT1-1 was the only locus that exhibited coordinated reductions in TARDBP and ZSCAN29 occupancy together with decreased mature tRNA abundance during lineage plasticity (Extended Data Fig. 8a–c). In the six TRR-TCT isodecoder loci, only TRR-TCT1-1 showed significantly reduced occupancy of both TARDBP (log2[FC] = –4.811, FDR = 0.006) and ZSCAN29 (log2[FC] = –3.858, FDR = 0.015). Although TRR-TCT2-1 (also known as tRNA-Arg-TCT-2-1) also exhibited reduced TARDBP occupancy (log2[FC] = –3.573, FDR = 0.038), ZSCAN29 occupancy was increased in LP cells (log2[FC] = 0.532, FDR = 0.015). No significant differences in TARDBP or ZSCAN29 occupancy were detected at TRR-TCT3-1 (also known as tRNA-Arg-TCT-3-1), TRR-TCT3-2 (also known as tRNA-Arg-TCT-3-2), TRR-TCT4-1 (also known as tRNA-Arg-TCT-4-1) and TRR-TCT5-1 (also known as tRNA-Arg-TCT-5-1) loci (Fig. 4f, Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 6).

Given that TARDBP occupancy was reduced at both TRR-TCT1-1 and TRR-TCT2-1 loci, whereas ZSCAN29 occupancy was reduced only at TRR-TCT1-1, we sought to determine why only tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels decreased during lineage plasticity (Fig. 1b). Because H3K4me3 is associated with active RNA polymerase II and III transcriptional activity51,56,57,58, we examined H3K4me3 enrichment across TRR-TCT loci. Notably, the TRR-TCT1-1 locus exhibited substantially higher H3K4me3 enrichment than any of the other TRR-TCT loci (Fig. 4g,h). Moreover, H3K4me3 abundance was decreased selectively at the TRR-TCT1-1 locus following lineage conversion, whereas no significant changes were observed at the TRR-TCT2-1 locus (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 8d). Consistent with these chromatin changes, POLR3A CUT&RUN demonstrated a selective reduction in RNA polymerase III occupancy at the TRR-TCT1-1 locus during lineage plasticity, with no corresponding changes at the other TRR-TCT loci (Extended Data Fig. 8e).

On the basis of these findings, we tested whether TARDBP and ZSCAN29 preferentially regulate expression of the H3K4me3-enriched TRR-TCT1-1 locus compared with all other TRR-TCT loci. Knockdown of TARDBP or ZSCAN29 in LNCaP and C4-2B cells selectively reduced tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression, whereas the remaining tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoders were unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 8f,g). Consistent with these findings, depletion of TARDBP or ZSCAN29 significantly reduced RNA polymerase III occupancy only at the TRR-TCT1-1 locus in both cell lines (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Together, these findings demonstrate that TARDBP and ZSCAN29 preferentially maintain RNA polymerase III occupancy at the H3K4me3-enriched TRR-TCT1-1 locus, which in turn selectively promotes tRNA1Arg(UCU) transcription.

tRNA levels can regulate mRNA-specific translation through codon optimality59. We reasoned that tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage may influence the translation of AGA-enriched mRNAs to induce lineage dependence. To test this idea, we generated AGA-specific translation reporters in which mCherry is fused to a DHFR degron sequence via a series of in-frame AGA codon linkers60 (Fig. 5a, top). Efficient translation through the AGA linker leads to translation of the DHFR degron and degradation of mCherry, whereas inefficient translation results in mCherry accumulation. After transduction of AD, LP and UCU cells, LP cells exhibited a fourfold increase in the mCherry-to-EBFP2 signal compared with AD cells, which indicated that there was reduced translational capacity at AGA codons (Fig. 5a, bottom). This effect was highly specific because addback of tRNA1Arg(UCU) reduced the fluorescence intensity back to the level of AD cells (Fig. 5a, bottom). We repeated the assay with different combinations of AGA codon repeats (2×, 4× or 6×) and observed the same trends (Extended Data Fig. 9a). These findings demonstrate that tRNA1Arg(UCU) dosage can influence AGA codon translation in a lineage plasticity model.

We next performed polysome RNA-seq to see whether we could observe a similar effect on endogenous mRNAs. Polysome RNA-seq is a technique in which ribosome-bound mRNAs are fractionated by density and sequenced to determine the translation efficiency (TE) of each mRNA transcriptome-wide (Extended Data Fig. 9b). We compared codon usage among AD, LP and UCU cells by assessing the codon composition of mRNA with the highest and lowest significant TEs (FDR < 0.05). In AD cells, the Arg-AGA codon was one of the most significantly abundant codons in high TE mRNAs along with Lys-AAA and Glu-GAA. This result indicated that there is efficient translation in the AD model (FDR = 0.0002) (Fig. 5b). However, in LP cells, Arg-AGA codons were no longer enriched (FDR = 0.62) (Fig. 5c). Notably, addback of tRNA1Arg(UCU) restored AGA codon translation (FDR = 0.0002) (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Table 7).

To identify candidate translational targets of tRNA1Arg(UCU), we analysed the 2,193 mRNAs that were translationally upregulated following tRNA1Arg(UCU) restoration (Fig. 5e, left, and Supplementary Table 8). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed enrichment for transcriptional programs, including gene expression (R-HSA-74160, FDR = 0.0023) and RNA polymerase II transcription (R-HSA-73857, FDR = 0.00481) (Extended Data Fig. 9c). Notably, of these mRNAs, five components of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex were among the enriched transcripts: ACTB, BCL7B, BCL7C, SMARCB1 and SMARCC2 (Fig. 5e, right). Given the central role of SWI/SNF in sustaining AR signalling in prostate cancer61, we focused subsequent analyses on the core SWI/SNF subunits SMARCB1 and SMARCC2. Of these, only SMARCC2 protein abundance decreased during lineage transition and was restored by tRNA1Arg(UCU) addback (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 9d), whereas SMARCC2 mRNA levels were unchanged (Fig. 5g).

To determine whether SMARCC2 sensitivity to tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance is mediated by encoded AGA codons, we generated a codon-switching reporter in which Arg-AGA codons in SMARCC2 were replaced with Arg-CGC codons. Wild-type and codon-switched reporters were introduced into AD, LP and UCU cells. LP cells transduced with the Arg-AGA reporter showed reduced SMARCC2 protein abundance compared with AD and UCU cells (Fig. 5h). By contrast, the Arg-CGC reporter was insensitive to lineage state changes (Fig. 5h). These findings indicate that efficient SMARCC2 translation depends on tRNA1Arg(UCU) availability through AGA codon usage.

We next examined whether SMARCC2 mediates the lineage effects of tRNA1Arg(UCU). Silencing of SMARCC2 in LNCaP UCU cells reduced AR pathway activity at both the mRNA and protein levels, which led to a reversal of lineage features induced by tRNA1Arg(UCU) re-expression (Fig. 5i,j and Extended Data Fig. 9e,f). Next, we asked whether this reduction in AR activity alters sensitivity to AR inhibition. Notably, LNCaP UCU cells became resistant to enzalutamide treatment following SMARCC2 knockdown (Fig. 5k). Together, these data reveal that tRNA1Arg(UCU) regulates the translation of SMARCC2 to modulate lineage state, AR signalling and sensitivity to AR pathway inhibition.

Last, we sought to determine the correlation between tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression and patient survival. Per cell tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance and mean expression were calculated for each tumour sample and correlated with clinical features. Patients with the lowest tRNA1Arg(UCU) abundance had a significantly shorter time from diagnosis to first bone metastasis (Spearman’s r = 0.34, P = 0.045), start of androgen deprivation therapy to death (Spearman’s r = 0.36, P = 0.033) and androgen independence to death (Spearman’s r = 0.44, P = 0.011) (Fig. 5l–n). Together, these equated with a shorter overall survival (Spearman’s r = 0.38, P = 0.023) (Fig. 5o). These data reveal that low tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression is associated with substantially more aggressive disease and shorter survival.

On the basis of these correlations and the observations that tRNA1Arg(UCU) depletion increases metastasis-associated genes (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f), we performed an in vivo metastasis assay using luciferase-expressing C4-2B cells transduced with shScr or shUCU (Extended Data Fig. 9g). Following intracardiac injection (Extended Data Fig. 9h), tRNA1Arg(UCU) depletion led to a fourfold increase in metastasis (Extended Data Fig. 9i,j). These findings demonstrate that tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels not only affect AR dependence and therapy response in prostate cancer but also metastatic progression in vivo.

Our study highlights the role of tRNA1Arg(UCU) as a regulator of lineage dependency in prostate cancer. Specifically, we uncovered a marked specificity in tRNA dysregulation during lineage transitions. Rather than observing a broad alteration in tRNA abundance, we found that only tRNA1Arg(UCU) was consistently decreased when cells underwent a lineage switch from an AR-dependent to an AR-independent state. This specificity was further validated by tRNA1Arg(UCU) knockdown and overexpression experiments, which demonstrated that prostate cancer lineage dependence could be toggled by modulating a single tRNA. Notably, this programmable lineage conversion also had significant therapeutic implications. Specifically, conversion to an AR-low activity state with NE features conferred resistance to ARPIs. It is intriguing to consider why the reduction of tRNA1Arg(UCU) drives ADs to adopt a LP cell fate with NE features. Notably, a comprehensive analysis comparing tRNAs in neurons and non-neuronal cells revealed that tRNA1Arg(UCU) exhibited the most significant decrease among all isodecoders45,49. This finding indicates that low tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression could be a common feature of neuronal gene expression programs. It remains to be determined how tRNA1Arg(UCU) controls neuronal expression networks.

Another important question raised by our findings is what distinguishes tRNA1Arg(UCU) from the other tRNAArg(UCU) isodecoders. Although tRNA4Arg(UCU) is highly divergent from tRNA1Arg(UCU), tRNA1Arg(UCU) differs from tRNA2Arg(UCU), tRNA3Arg(UCU) and tRNA5Arg(UCU) by three base pairs (Extended Data Fig. 10a): one in the acceptor stem (C6-G67 versus U6-A67) and two in the T stem (C49-G65 versus G49-C65 and C50-G64 versus U50-A64 and C50-U64). These positions contact eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1A (eEF1A), which mediates aminoacyl-tRNA delivery into the ribosome, as well as the ribosome itself in the A, P and E sites (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). We speculate that these differences influence interactions with the translation machinery to provide a potential structural basis for tRNA1Arg(UCU) specificity.

Our study underscores the importance of isodecoder-specific regulation of tRNAs, extending it beyond canonical RNA polymerase III-mediated transcription. We identified the DNA-binding proteins TARDBP and ZSCAN29 as previously unknown regulators of tRNA1Arg(UCU) expression with significant implications for lineage state in prostate cancer. Although the upstream signals that govern TARDBP and ZSCAN29 expression remain to be defined, integrative analysis identified Notch signalling as a candidate regulatory pathway, consistent with the established loss of Notch activity during NEPC progression62,63 (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). These findings complement emerging evidence that transcription factors contribute to the regulation of tRNA abundance. For instance, RNA polymerase-III-bound loci can colocalize with active chromatin regions and engage general transcription factors such as ETS1 and STAT1 to promote tRNA synthesis51. Although this study provides mechanistic insights, we are unable to link these regulatory mechanisms to disease phenotypes. Nevertheless, our study directly implicates tRNA gene regulation in cancer, offering one of the first demonstrations of isodecoder-specific control as a crucial determinant of a malignant state. Consistent with this view, recent large-scale tRNA expression profiling and network analyses have identified ZZEF1, a sequence-specific transcription factor, as a key regulator of the TRK-TTT3 (also known as tRNA-Lys-TTT-3) locus and metastasis in breast cancer64. These studies highlight an emerging paradigm in which context-specific transcriptional control of tRNA genes has a fundamental role in cancer biology and underscore the need to fully dissect the regulatory logic underlying RNA polymerase-III-dependent transcription.

Our study also revealed the clinical significance of tRNA1Arg(UCU) in prostate cancer. Analyses of patient specimens demonstrated that reduced tRNA1Arg(UCU) levels are associated with decreased overall survival in the setting of AR pathway inhibition. However, these clinical associations are derived from retrospective analyses, and prospective studies will be required to assess the predictive utility of tRNA isodecoders as biomarkers of AR-targeted therapy resistance. Beyond its potential as a biomarker, there is growing interest in the therapeutic application of tRNAs. Notably, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated delivery of suppressor tRNAs has been used to restore protein function in models of mucopolysaccharidosis type I65, and lipid nanoparticle-based tRNA delivery has enabled re-expression of CFTR in epithelia derived from patients with cystic fibrosis66. These emerging technologies offer a potential framework for restoring tumour-suppressive tRNA isodecoders such as tRNA1Arg(UCU) to reprogram lineage dependency and re-sensitize tumours to therapies in patients with prostate cancer.
