Milo42 identifies condition-associated changes in cell abundance across transcriptionally similar neighbourhoods defined on a single-cell k-nearest-neighbour graph. Applying Milo to euploid and T21 cells revealed substantial transcriptional divergence in cardiomyocytes (Fig. 5b). T21-enriched vCM neighbourhoods had reduced scores for maturation and compaction signatures derived from the euploid trajectory (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 7i). This result was further supported by a decreased proportion of compact cardiomyocytes in T21 hearts compared with euploid hearts (Fig. 5d), and a lower activity scores of common and compact maturation GRNs in T21 compact cardiomyocytes than in euploid cells (Extended Data Fig. 8b).

To determine whether the reduced abundance of compact vCMs observed in the human T21 dataset is accompanied by structural alterations in ventricular architecture, we analysed a mouse model of Down’s syndrome (Dp1Tyb)43 using high-resolution episcopic microscopy (HREM)44, which enables three-dimensional reconstruction of cardiac morphology (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). Heart samples were analysed at embryonic day 15.5 (E15.5), a stage at which CHDs, including ventricular and atrial septal defects, are readily detectable. This analysis revealed a reduction in the thickness of the compact myocardial layer in Dp1Tyb hearts relative to wild-type (WT) littermates (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 7), consistent with impaired ventricular compaction at the structural level. Notably, stratification of Dp1Tyb embryos by CHD status revealed a further reduction in compact myocardial proportion in CHD-positive embryos compared with those without CHD (Extended Data Fig. 8e and Supplementary Table 7). This result suggests that the severity of compaction defects is associated with structural cardiac abnormalities in this model. In parallel, spatial transcriptomic analysis of human T21 heart samples showed a reduced estimated abundance of compact vCMs (Extended Data Fig. 8f), in agreement with the single-nucleus analysis (Fig. 5d). Although direct structural quantification in human fetal tissue is limited by the availability of two-dimensional sections, these complementary analyses across species consistently support the idea that there is impaired ventricular compaction in the T21 context.

To further explore why T21 hearts exhibit reduced compact vCMs, we performed cell–cell interaction analysis using CellphoneDB, comparing human euploid and T21 cells. This analysis revealed broader rewiring of intercellular signalling involving vCMs as both signal senders and receivers (Extended Data Fig. 9a). As signal senders, vCMs in T21 cells showed reduced VEGF signalling across multiple target cell types, alongside increased ephrin and teneurin signalling. As signal receivers, vCMs exhibited increased neuregulin signalling, a key pathway that regulates ventricular trabeculation and compaction, and reduced IGF and VEGF pathway activity. These changes were observed consistently across multiple interacting partner cell types, which indicated that there was a coordinated shift in signalling environment rather than isolated pathway perturbations. Among these altered signalling axes, the semaphorin–plexin pathway showed a particularly marked and structured perturbation. Specifically, semaphorin ligand genes were upregulated across multiple cardiac cell types in T21 hearts, including SEMA3C (Extended Data Fig. 9b). This was accompanied by downregulation of PLXNA4 and upregulation of PLXNA2 in cardiomyocytes. Given previous work showing that SEMA3C–PLXNA2–PLXNA4 signalling is required for myocardial compaction9, this receptor–ligand mismatch may impair semaphorin responsiveness, which in turn leads to reduced numbers of compact vCMs.

To better understand the differences between the two karyotypes, we performed differential gene expression analysis using cellular neighbourhoods identified by Milo as biological replicates (Fig. 5f). Neighbourhoods enriched for T21 or euploid cells were analysed separately in each cell type. This analysis revealed that pathways related to myogenesis, hypoxia response and oxidative phosphorylation were disrupted in T21-enriched neighbourhoods. Furthermore, gene signatures associated with apoptosis and cellular senescence were upregulated in T21-enriched neighbourhoods, particularly in the cycling vCM population. Endocardial cells, previously implicated as major contributors to the cardiac phenotype in Down’s syndrome, exhibited alterations in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition signatures. To investigate conserved gene program perturbations between humans and mice, we generated scRNA-seq data from the hearts of E13.5 WT and Dp1Tyb mice (Extended Data Fig. 9c). We integrated the data using scVI (Extended Data Fig. 9d) and performed cellular neighbourhood-based differential expressed gene analysis and gene set enrichment analysis. The analysis revealed shared enriched gene sets between humans and mice, such as impaired oxidative phosphorylation and heightened activation of apoptosis pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f and Supplementary Table 8).

To explore potential upstream regulators of the apoptosis-associated program in T21 vCMs, we performed SCENIC+ analysis using matched snRNA-seq and snATAC–seq data from T21 and age-matched euploid samples. To focus on the T21-associated cell states most relevant to this phenotype, we restricted the analysis to Milo cellular neighbourhoods enriched in cycling vCMs and pruned the inferred GRN to apoptosis-associated target genes. This analysis highlighted several candidate regulators, including NRF1, FOXO3, SP3, MAZ and SMAD5, connected to target genes involved in intrinsic apoptosis, including BCL2L11, CASP3 and CYCS (Extended Data Fig. 9g). Notably, these candidate TFs are not encoded on chromosome 21, which suggests that the apoptosis-associated transcriptional program in T21 cardiomyocytes probably reflects downstream regulatory consequences of T21 rather than direct dosage of TFs encoded in chromosome 21.

Survival and anti-apoptotic signalling are closely associated with the proliferation, compaction and maturation of cardiomyocytes45. Increased levels of apoptosis have been linked to CHDs and the impairment of myocardial compaction46. To assess the impact of T21 on apoptosis sensitivity, we differentiated human T21-induced pluripotent stem cells and their isogenic counterparts into cardiomyocytes. Using TUNEL staining, we evaluated the proportion of apoptotic cardiomyocytes in these cultures and found an increased proportion of apoptotic cardiomyocytes in T21 cultures (Fig. 5g), which indicated that that these cells have an increased susceptibility to apoptosis.

Thus, increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis may contribute to impaired ventricular compaction in T21.

We present a multimodal atlas of human cardiogenesis across the first and second trimesters, integrating gene expression, chromatin accessibility and high-resolution spatial profiling. The atlas captures cellular niches, including the SAN, supports cellular niche annotation through TissueTypist and can be used to identify early perturbations of compact vCMs in T21. TissueTypist transfers hierarchical niches across Visium SD, Visium HD, MERFISH, Xenium and non-cardiac data without previous cell segmentation. The bundled model is optimized for the fetal heart, although custom models can be trained for other tissues. As a supervised classifier, TissueTypist cannot discover new tissue types, but low-confidence predictions may highlight uncharacterized structures.

Fetal pacemaker cells colocalize with parasympathetic neurons, but not sympathetic neurons, in early development. Consistent with parasympathetic innervation preceding sympathetic innervation47, this finding confirms that the first trimester is a critical window for establishing SAN parasympathetic innervation. This developmental period coincides with the transient decrease in fetal heart rate48, which raises the possibility that early parasympathetic activity contributes to functional modulation of pacemaker output. Predicted GRNs governing axon guidance programs in pacemaker cells highlighted canonical pacemaker TFs, including TBX3, TBX18, SHOX2 and ISL1, as central regulators, which extends their established roles to control this innervation process18,49,50. This result suggests that axon guidance is not a secondary feature but an integral component of pacemaker cell identity during human development. We further defined the spatial organization of these interactions using high-resolution spatial transcriptomics. Notably, parasympathetic neuronal cell bodies were positioned in close proximity to the core pacemaker populations, which provides direct spatial evidence for neuropacemaker coupling. Interestingly, this organization seems to emerge progressively. That is, at earlier stages (5–6 PCW), parasympathetic neuronal signals are sparse or not clearly localized, despite robust expression of axon guidance genes in pacemaker cells. This temporal offset suggests that pacemaker cells may establish a permissive molecular environment before neuronal recruitment. By later stages, the combined spatial proximity and region-specific activation of guidance pathways (including SLIT–ROBO, semaphorin and ephrin signalling) support a model in which neuropacemaker interactions are organized into spatially restricted niches in the developing SAN, which are defined by specific cellular composition and signalling programmes.

T21 heart samples showed fewer compact vCMs, downregulation of myogenic, oxidative phosphorylation and hypoxia-response programs, and increased apoptosis. Cell–cell communication analysis revealed a broader rewiring of signalling interactions involving vCMs in T21. Reduced VEGF signalling from vCMs was notable, given the genetic evidence linking VEGF pathway perturbation to congenital heart defects in T21 (ref. 51). Conversely, increased neuregulin–ERBB signalling, an established regulator of trabeculation and ventricular compaction52, may reflect compensatory or dysregulated maturation programs. Moreover, reduced IGF signalling further supports this interpretation, in line with reported systemic IGF deficiencies in Down’s syndrome53 and the established role of IGF1 in cardiomyocyte proliferation and survival45. These observations suggest that T21 disrupts a network of signalling pathways that govern cardiomyocyte maturation, survival and tissue organization, rather than a single dominant axis.

Increased apoptotic activity during cardiac development may reduce the cardiomyocyte pool available for maturation and compaction. This result is consistent with Dp1Tyb mouse studies linking chromosome 21 gene dosage to cardiomyocyte proliferation and mitochondrial function40. The precise molecular mechanisms that link T21 to apoptosis remain to be fully elucidated. Nevertheless, these observations raise the possibility that altered cardiomyocyte survival and maturation pathways represent early, potentially targetable processes in T21 cardiac development. Previous reports have indicated that T21 disrupts multiple cardiac lineages, which together contribute to structural malformations40. Cardiomyocytes showed greater transcriptional divergence than endocardial and cushion cells, although endocardial epithelial-to-mesenchymal-transition signatures were also altered (Fig. 5b,f). The functional significance of this upregulation, however, remains to be determined.

The T21 hearts analysed here were sampled at 11–14 PCW, a time period during which septation defects cannot be determined confidently from the two-dimensional sections. We therefore interpret the molecular and cellular changes as early T21-associated perturbations that may increase CHD risk, not as evidence that they cause septal defects. Therefore, future studies incorporating volumetric imaging will be needed to capture the full range of structural anomalies.

Overall, this atlas advances our understanding of human heart development and its perturbation in T21, with implications for disease modelling and regenerative medicine.

All tissue samples were obtained after Research Ethics Committee approval and written informed consent from mothers. The embryonic and fetal heart samples corresponding to the donor IDs BRC2251, BRC2253, BRC2256, BRC2260, BRC2262, BRC2263, C82, C83, C85, C86, C87, C92, C94, C97, C98, C99, C104, C194, BRD2757 and BRC2758 were provided from terminations of pregnancy from Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust under permission from the NHS Research Ethical Committee (96/085). The donor IDs Hst32, Hst33, Hst36, Hst39, Hst40, Hst41, Hst42, Hst44, Hst45 and Hst48 were from the MRC/Wellcome Trust Human Developmental Biology Resource (University College London (UCL) site REC reference: 18/LO/0822; www.hdbr.org; registered project title: ‘A multi-omics analysis of fetal cardiac development and the impact of T21’, registered project numbers 200556 and 200747). Donor IDs and other information are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Samples used for single-nucleus isolation and spatial transcriptomics were flash-frozen (unembedded) or frozen in OCT and stored at −80 °C, or formalin-fixed and subsequently embedded in paraffin blocks. All tissues were stored and transported on ice at all times until freezing or tissue dissociation to minimize any transcriptional degradation. Single nuclei were obtained from flash-frozen tissues using sectioning and mechanical homogenization as previously described23. In brief, 5–10-mm thickness frozen tissues were first sectioned with a cryostat in a 50-μm thickness sections. All sections from each sample were homogenized using a 7 ml glass Dounce tissue grinder set (Merck) with 8–10 strokes of a tight pestle (B) in homogenization buffer (250 mM sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 1× protease inhibitor, 0.4 U µl–1 RNaseIn, 0.2 U µl–1 SUPERaseIn and 0.05% Triton X-100 in nuclease-free water). The homogenate was filtered through a 40 μm cell strainer (Corning). After centrifugation (500g, 5 min, 4 °C), the supernatant was removed and the pellet was resuspended in storage buffer (1× PBS, 4% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 0.2 U μl–1 protector RNaseIn). Nuclei were stained with 7-AAD viability staining solution (BioLegend) and filtered through a 20 μm cell strainer (CellTrics). Positive single nuclei were purified by FACS using a MA900 multi-application cell sorter (Sony) and its proprietary software (Cell Sorter Software v.3.1.1) (Supplementary Fig. 1). Nucleus purification and integrity were verified by microscopy, and nuclei were manually counted on the basis of Trypan blue exclusion. The suspension of nuclei was adjusted to 1,000–3,000 nuclei per microlitre and loaded on a Chromium Controller (10x Genomics) with a targeted nucleus recovery of 5,000–10,000 per reaction. 3′ gene expression libraries and ATAC libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions of Chromium Multiome ATAC+Gene Expression kits (10x Genomics). Libraries were sequenced using NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina) at the Wellcome Sanger Institute with a minimum depth of 20,000–30,000 read pairs per nucleus.

For fresh-frozen (FF) samples, samples were frozen and embedded in OCT medium using a dry-ice-cooled bath of isopentane at −45 °C. OCT-embedded samples were sectioned using a cryostat (Leica CX3050S) and were cut at 10 μm. For FFPE samples, fresh samples were fixed in >5 times their volume of 4% v/v formalin at ambient temperature for 24 h before processing with paraffin on a Tissue-Tek Vacuum Infiltration Processor 5 (Sakura Finetek). FFPE blocks were sectioned at 5 μm using a microtome (Leica RM2125RT). RNA integrity number (FF samples) or DV200 (formalin-fixed) was obtained using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. CytAssist FFPE Visium Spatial Gene Expression (10x genomics) was performed following the manufacturer’s protocol. For FF samples, the Tissue Optimization protocol from 10x Genomics was performed to obtain a permeabilization time of 45 min, and the FF Visium Spatial Gene Expression experiment was performed as per the manufacturer’s protocol (10x Genomics). H&E-stained Visium Gene Expression slides were imaged at ×40 on a Hamamatsu NanoZoomer S60. After transcript capture, the Visium Library Preparation Protocol from 10x Genomics was performed. Eight cDNA libraries were diluted and pooled to a final concentration of 2.25 nM (200 μl volume) and sequenced on 2× SP flow cells of an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. For Visium HD, the tissue section was prepared in the same manner as the standard Visium samples. H&E staining and tissue preparation were performed following the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Handbook (CG000684), and samples were imaged on a VS200 microscope (Olympus). Samples were then processed and sequenced following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent kits user guide (CG000685). The Xenium In Situ Gene Expression with Morphology-based Cell Segmentation Staining user guide (CG000749) was used with the Xenium Prime-5K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel (5,001 genes).

After sequencing, samples were demultiplexed and stored as CRAM files. Each sample of single-nucleus data was mapped to the human reference genome (GRCh38-2020-A) provided by 10x Genomics using CellRanger software (CellRanger ARC v.2.0.0) with default parameters. Each sample of Visium was mapped to the human reference genome (OCT, GRCh38-3.0.0; FFPE, GRCh38-2020-A) with SpaceRanger software (OCT, v.1.1.0; FFPE, v.2.0.0; Visium HD, v.3.0.1) with default parameters. For Visium samples, SpaceRanger was also used to align paired histology images with mRNA capture spot positions in the Visium slides. Part of the single-cell samples were mixed with different donors after nucleus isolation for cost-efficient experimental design (Supplementary Table 2) and were computationally demultiplexed (Soupercell, v.2.0)54 based on genetic variation between the donors.

Single-cell data analysis was performed in Python 3 using standard scientific-computing and single-cell analysis packages, including pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and Scanpy; package versions used for individual analyses are provided in the code repository and environment file. For the single-cell transcriptome data, the CellBender algorithm (remove-background; v.0.2)55 was applied to remove ambient and background RNA from each count matrix produced using the CellRanger pipeline. Downstream analysis was performed using the Scanpy package. Doublets with a score of >0.15 were removed using Scrublet (v.0.2.1)56. We performed quality control and filtering based on the following settings: number of genes > 500, total counts > 1,000, per cent mitochondrial < 5 (nuclei), per cent mitochondrial < 20 (cell), per cent ribosomal < 5 (nuclei), per cent ribosomal < 20 (cell), red blood cell score < 1 (nuclei) and red blood cell score < 2 (cell). For the multiome ATAC data, the data processed using CellRanger ARC were further analysed using ArchR (v.1.0.2)57. Quality control was performed, considering, among other factors, transcription start site enrichment, nucleosomal banding patterns, the number and fraction of fragments in peaks, reads falling into ENCODE blacklist regions as well as doublet scores computed by ArchR. For high-quality cells, reads were mapped to 500-bp bins across the reference genome (hg38; TileMatrix). Gene scores based on chromatin accessibility around genes were computed from TileMatrix using the createArrowFiles function to check their consistency with measured expression values. Before peak calling, pseudo-bulk replicates were generated (addGroupCoverages) for each fine-grained cell state annotated using the paired gene expression data. Peak calling (501 bp fixed-width peaks) was performed for each cell state, and the peak sets were merged to obtain a unified peak set (addReproduciblePeakSet). A cell-by-peak count matrix was obtained using the addPeakMatrix function. For the Visium data, histological tissue annotation was performed based on the H&E image, and the Visium spots on the irrelevant regions (‘out of tissue’ and ‘cavity’) were removed. Spots of each sample were further filtered for more than 500 UMI (OCT) or 5,000 UMI (FFPE) counts and 300 (OCT) or 1,000 (FFPE) genes.

For Visium HD data, Bin2cell (v.0.3.3)16, which is a tool to reconstruct cells from the 2-μm bin data by using H&E image and gene expression data, was performed to identify each single cell. Initially, the data were pre-processed by removing uninformative genes and bins (genes expressed in fewer than three cells and bins with no counts). For nucleus segmentation using H&E images, the input image resolution was controlled by the ‘microns per pixel’ (mpp) parameter (mpp = 0.3). We applied the b2c.destripe function with quantile = 0.99 to correct the striped appearance. Nucleus segmentation was performed using StarDist, an efficient segmentation algorithm with a pretrained HE model: b2c.stardist with prob_thresh=0.05. To capture transcripts in the cytoplasm around the identified nuclei, the b2c.expand_labels function was used (max_bin_distance=2). To detect cells with missing nuclei in the H&E image, Bin2cell performed segmentation on a representation of total expression per bin. The total counts (destriped counts) per bin were converted into an image using the b2c.grid_image function (mpp = 0.3, sigma = 5). Segmentation was then performed on the converted image with the pretrained StarDist fluorescence model: b2c.stardist with prob_thresh=0.05 and nms_thresh=0.5. The cell segmentations obtained from the H&E image and gene expression data were merged using the b2c.salvage_secondary_labels function. Counts of bins assigned to each cell were grouped using the b2c.bin_to_cell function to generate a cell-by-gene matrix. Using the reconstructed cells, we conducted quality control and filtered the cells according to the following criteria: number of genes > 30, number of bins > 3 and number of bins < 60. The thresholds were arbitrarily chosen on the basis of the distributions to exclude outliers. For Xenium data, a multimodal cell segmentation algorithm was applied to generate a cell-by-gene matrix (Xenium instrument software (v.3.1.3.1) Analysis version, xenium-3.1.0.4). For both Visium HD bin2cell cells and Xenium original cells, the segmented cell data were further processed using TACCO17 to perform reference-based compositional annotation and to resolve mixed-cell signals. A matched scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq dataset was used as reference, supplemented by high-confidence singlet profiles identified in the spatial dataset. For each bin2cell cell, TACCO was applied using its optimal transport-based framework to infer fractional contributions of reference cell types (coarse-grained) in a shared gene expression space. The resulting compositional annotations were retained as continuous cell-type fractions. For categorical analyses, each bin2cell cell or Xenium cell was assigned a dominant coarse-grained cell type based on the maximum fractional contribution. To obtain cell-type-resolved expression profiles, the object-splitting procedure of TACCO was applied to partition gene expression counts into cell-type-specific components based on inferred compositions. These decomposed profiles were used for subsequent fine-grained cell-type annotation, based on batch-aware data integration (scVI58,59 and Harmony60), followed by unbiased clustering and marker-driven approaches. This resulted in a dataset containing 213,873 Visium HD cells (5 sections from 3 donors) and 362,277 Xenium cells (2 sections from 2 donors). We note that cardiomyocytes at the fetal developmental stages analysed here are predominantly mononucleated, with binucleation emerging mainly during the perinatal period61. As a result, segmented units in both Visium HD (bin2cell) and Xenium data are expected to correspond closely to single cells, and multinucleation is unlikely to represent a major confounding factor for segmentation or downstream compositional annotation in this study.

For the low-resolution Visium SD data, we used the cell2location (v.0.1)15 method to spatially map fine-grained cell types of the developing heart (defined using single-cell transcriptomics data11) in the Visium data. In brief, we first estimated reference signatures of cell types using scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq data and a negative binomial regression model provided in the cell2ocation package. The inferred reference cell-type signatures were used for cell2location cell-type mapping that estimates the abundance of each cell type in each Visium spot by decomposing spot mRNA counts. The mapping was performed per group of sections of each time point (4, 5, 7, 13, 16 and 20 PCW). The H&E images of the Visium slides were used to determine the average number of nuclei per Visium spot (n = 20) in the tissue and used as a hyperparameter in the cell2location pipeline. For the T21 Visium data, we used snRNA-seq data from T21 heart samples as the reference for cell2location mapping, following the same workflow. For the immature aCM versus mature aCM comparison, a temporary (that is, used only for this analysis) annotation was made whereby the scFates milestones before the divergence of the principal graph were labelled as AtrialCardiomyocytesImmature (all other fine_grain annotations remained) (Extended Data Fig. 7d). These signatures were mapped in the Visium data using cell2location. The per spot cell-type abundances were extracted for spots with the structural annotation ‘atria’. For each of the 4 labels (immature/mature for each of aCML and aCMR) a proportion was calculated as follows: the abundance of that label divided by the combined total of the immature and mature abundances for the corresponding cell type. For instance, proportionaCML immature = abundanceaCML immature/(abundanceaCML immature + abundanceaCML mature). This process enabled a comparison between the mature and immature versions of the same cell type.

scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq data were processed as described in our accompanying study11. In brief, after pre-processing and removal of low-quality cells and nuclei, single-cell transcriptomic data were integrated using scVI58 (v.0.19.0) accounting for categorical covariates of donor, cell or nuclei and kit 10x, as well as continuous covariates of total counts, percentage of mitochondrial reads (%mito) and percentage of ribosomal reads (%ribo). Neighbourhood identification, high-resolution Leiden clustering and further dimensional reduction using UMAP were performed based on the scVI latent space. Cells and nuclei of extra-cardiac origin were removed based on the following marker gene expressions: lung epithelial cells (IGFBP2, EPCAM, SOX2 and NKX2-1); hepatocytes (ALB, APOA1 and TTR); hepatic stellate cells (CRHBP, FCN3 and OIT3); parathyroid cells (PTH, MAFB and GATA3); and further erythrocytes (FTH1, HBA1, HBA2 and HBB). The remaining data were integrated using scVI with the same variables, followed by the downstream processing. To annotate cell types, cell barcodes comprising major clusters were subsampled from the initial raw count matrix for subclustering analysis and processed separately through the same downstream analysis as described above.

Subclusters were annotated on the basis of immunohistochemical validation and literature evidence.

For ATAC data, post-quality-control data were integrated using cell-by-peak count matrix peakVI62 accounting for batch variation (donor). Neighbourhood identification and dimensional reduction using UMAP were performed based on the peakVI latent space.

To assess concordance between transcriptional and chromatin accessibility landscapes across fine-grained cell types, we computed pairwise distance matrices in gene expression (GEX) and gene accessibility score (GAS, ArchR) spaces. scRNA-seq and multiome-derived gene accessibility data were first restricted to a shared set of genes present in both modalities (21,369 genes). For each modality, counts were library-size-normalized to a total of 10,000 per cell and log-transformed using a log1p transformation. Cells were grouped according to fine-grained cell-type annotations, and for each cell type, median expression (GEX) or accessibility (GAS) profiles were computed across all cells, which resulted in one representative profile per cell type for each modality. Pairwise Euclidean distances between these cell-type-level profiles were then calculated separately for GEX and GAS, which produced two symmetric distance matrices (cell type × cell type). To quantify concordance between modalities, we computed the correlation between the two distance matrices using a Mantel test with Spearman’s correlation and 999 permutations.

Low-resolution Visium spatial transcriptomic datasets (OCT and FFPE; 4, 5, 7, 13 and 16 PCW) were integrated using spot-level cell-type abundance estimates derived from cell2location. The resulting spot × cell type matrix was used to construct a batch-corrected neighbour graph using BBKNN, followed by Leiden clustering and UMAP visualization. Cellular niches were defined using a multistage clustering strategy, in which initial clusters capturing broad anatomical compartments were iteratively subclustered to resolve finer spatial niches. At each stage, clusters were annotated on the basis of the relative enrichment of structurally informative cell types (including atrial and vCMs, pacemaker cells and vascular populations), combined with known anatomical context. For anatomically distinct structures not fully resolved by transcriptional composition (for example, lymph node, atrioventricular ring, coronary and great vessels), annotations were further refined using manually curated regions from matched H&E images.

For high-resolution Visium HD data, cellular niches were identified using CellCharter20, which integrates transcriptomic similarity with spatial neighbourhood structure. Segmented cells (bin2cell) were embedded in a scVI latent space, which served as input for CellCharter. Neighbourhood aggregation was performed using multiple configurations of spatial layers (n layers = [0,1], [0,1,2], [0,1,2,3]) and clustering resolutions (k = 5–20). For each parameter combination, clustering stability was quantified, and the optimal configuration (n layers = [0,1,2,3], k = 8) was selected based on maximal stability. Each cluster defined by the initial round of clustering was subsequently subsetted and re-clustered (n layers = [0,1,2,3], k = 8) to resolve fine-grained niches, which enabled hierarchical decomposition of tissue architecture. To systematically characterize cluster identity, enrichment of each cell type in each cluster was quantified using an odds-ratio-based framework. For each cell type–cluster pair, a 2 × 2 contingency table was constructed comparing cells of the given cell type inside versus outside the cluster and relative to all other cell types. Odds ratios were computed with Haldane–Anscombe correction (+0.5) and log2-transformed. Significance was assessed using two-sided Fisher’s exact tests, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing. Clusters were annotated based on significantly enriched (FDR < 0.05) structural cell types, such as aCMs and vCMs, pacemaker cells, vascular, epicardial and endocardial populations.

To enable consistent annotation across datasets and modalities, we constructed a hierarchical cellular niche ontology integrating Visium SD and Visium HD annotations. Niches identified independently in Visium SD and HD datasets were matched on the basis of concordance in anatomical correspondence. When necessary, terminology was harmonized across datasets. Niches were organized into a two-level hierarchy (Fig. 2c) as follows: (1) coarse-grained anatomical compartments (for example, atrial myocardium, ventricular myocardium, conduction system, vasculature and epicardium); and (2) fine-grained spatial niches representing substructures in each compartment (for example, SAN head, SAN tail and trabecular versus compact myocardium).

This structure was defined using transcriptomic similarity between niches, supplemented by anatomical knowledge and manual curation. The resulting hierarchical labels were used to train the TissueTypist model, which enabled both coarse and fine-grained niche prediction across spatial transcriptomic platforms.

TissueTypist is a hierarchical classifier for cardiac tissue niches in spatial transcriptomic data. It jointly leverages Visium SD 3 prime, Visium SD FFPE and high-resolution Visium HD FFPE training references, and it produces both a coarse-grained (7-class) and a fine-grained (21-leaf) niche annotation per spot or window. The package is implemented in Python and is distributed with a unified tissuetypist command-line interface and three pre-trained weight presets covering the cardiac hierarchy. All the functions and documentations are available from the GitHub repository (https://github.com/Teichlab/TissueTypist).

Three reference modalities were used: 19,179 spots of Visium SD 3 prime, 19,633 spots of Visium SD FFPE and 215,913 single cells from Visium HD FFPE. These were summarized into 9,583 sliding-window pseudobulk windows (sum raw counts per window, then normalize_total (target_sum=1e4) and log1p). All three references carry expert annotations stored in niche_coarse_Apr2026 (7 coarse niches: ventricle, atrium, pacemaker conduction system, vasculature, epicardial region, AV junction and lymph node) and niche_fine_Apr2026 (21 fine-grained niches plus the explicit intermediate node ‘sinoatrial region’). The niche hierarchy is shown in Fig. 2c.

For each modality we compute a per-niche differentially expressed gene (DEG) set with scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups (t-test_overestim_var, one-vs-rest, restricted to the shared-gene catalogue produced by the phase 0 build-catalogue step). DEGs were filtered by adjusted P < 0.05, log fold change ≥ 0.5 and minimum mean log-expression ≥ 0.5. Per-niche DEGs were then unioned across modalities and across niches per sub-model. We added the union of the top 4,000 highly variable genes (HVGs, ‘seurat’ flavour) per modality, requiring HVG status in >2 modalities for the coarse model and >1 for fine sub-models (relaxed to 1 when a single reference is present). This DEG \(\cup \) HVG strategy was the default; a DEG-only mode was also exposed. Each sub-model received three feature blocks: (1) the spot’s own log-normalized expression of the selected genes; (2) per-gene neighbourhood-max features built per section (k = 6 hexagonal neighbours for SD, k = 8 square neighbours for HD windows); and (3) a single distance-to-tissue-edge feature derived from the annotate_edge function. Spatial features were computed once on the full reference and then on the row-subset and column-subset for each sub-model, which ensured that the tissue-edge geometry was not distorted by niche subsetting.

A single weighted logistic regression pipeline was fitted per sub-model. The own features passed through StandardScaler, the neighbour features passed through StandardScaler then a multiplicative weight (default 0.3), and and the distance-to-edge feature passed through a multiplicative weight (default 5.0). The classifier was LogisticRegression (solver = “lbfgs”, C = 0.01, max_iter=500, class_weight=None). We provided three weight presets: default (0.3/5.0), own_only (0.0/0.0) and neighbour_heavy (1.0/5.0).

At inference, query data were normalized in the same gene space used during training and passed through predict_adata. The coarse model produces tt_coarse_label and tt_coarse_score. Spots assigned to a terminal niche were returned as-is, whereas non-terminal spots were routed through the corresponding sub-model chain. Each stage emitted a label and a softmax probability, gated by a tunable confidence threshold θ—when the confidence falls below θ, the chain falls back to that stage’s low_confidence_route (for example, ‘atrial myocardium’ or ‘great vessels’), which preserves an interpretable annotation rather than forcing a low-confidence leaf call. Output columns included tt_coarse_label / tt_coarse_score, tt_fine_label / tt_fine_score, tt_joint_score (product of stage confidences), tt_final_label, and tt_low_conf.

Because normalize_total(target_sum=1e4) distributes counts across all genes present in the AnnData, the normalization denominator differs between full-genome reference data (around 14,745 shared genes) and a targeted query panel (for example, about 232 MERFISH genes or around 5,000 Xenium-5K genes). Direct prediction would therefore see a systematic scale mismatch. We addressed this issue through panel-specific re-training (tissuetypist train-panel). The reference AnnDatas were subset to the intersection of the query panel and the shared-gene catalogue, normalized in that reduced gene space, and the entire hierarchy was re-fit using the same chain walker. Three gene-selection strategies were supported: fresh DEG \(\cup \) HVG on the panel-normalized data (default), a user-supplied curated marker list applied to every stage (custom) or the per-stage gene lists from a previous full-genome run intersected with the panel (pre_computed). For Xenium and MERFISH, query cells were first aggregated into pseudobulk windows in micrometre coordinates with sliding_window_pseudobulk_cells, after which prediction followed the same two-stage routing as for Visium queries.

We benchmark accuracy with leave-one-section-out (LOSO) cross-validation across the 14 reference sections (7 SD 3 prime, 2 SD FFPE and 5 HD), refitting DEG \(\cup \) HVG independently per fold and per sub-model so the evaluation matches production training behaviour. Metrics are reported as weighted, macro and micro F1 for both coarse and fine label levels, overall and per modality, together with per-class precision–recall and per-sub-model confusion matrices. All fine-level metrics used the resolution-aware scoring mode, which maps the following: (1) intermediate-level ground-truth labels (for example, ‘sinoatrial region–non-terminal category’) to their canonical intermediate class and evaluates the corresponding spots at that level; and (2) excludes spots for which predictions fall back to a non-leaf intermediate label when the hierarchical traversal confidence is below θ = 0.5.

We first obtained a latent space based on both the RNA-seq and ATAC–seq data using multiome data and MultiVI63. The latent space was used for obtaining two-dimensional embeddings and a series of trajectory analyses using scFates64. For vCMLs, multiome data of compact and trabeculated cardiomyocytes were integrated with accounting for categorical covariates of the donor and sampled region, as well as continuous covariates of total counts, %mito, %ribo and cell cycle scores (S and G2/M phase). Multiscale diffusion space was obtained using the MultiVI latent space and the Palantir algorithm. The neighbourhood graph was obtained using the Palantir diffusion space and was used for force-directed graph embedding. The Palantir diffusion space was also used for obtaining a principal graph with the SimplePPT algorithm. Pseudotime calculation and the assignment of milestones and segments were performed by setting the youngest milestones as the root. The genes for which expression levels were associated and upregulated along the pseudotime were selected either by subsampling compact or trabeculated populations or by using all nuclei. For aCMs, multiome data of left and right cardiomyocytes were integrated with multiVI, accounting for the same covariates as before. To avoid an over-representation of either cell type, data for which the whole heart had been processed were used. The downstream steps were performed in the same was as for the analysis above. Two trajectories, consisting of milestones leading from the root to terminal milestones in the aCML and aCMR clusters, respectively, were defined. Association of gene expression with pseudotime was tested along each of these two trajectories independently, as well as across the whole embedding. For monocyte and macrophages, both the cells and nuclei samples with region = =’whole heart’ were integrated with accounting for categorical covariates of donor, cell or nuclei, and kit 10x, as well as continuous covariates of total counts, %mito, %ribo and cell cycle scores (S and G2/M phase). The downstream steps were performed in the same way as the analysis above. Pseudotime calculation and the assignment of milestones and segments were performed with setting two milestones (29: YS-derived macrophages, 2: monocytes) as roots (scf.tl.roots, scf.tl.pseudotime). To explore genes involved in LYVE1+ macrophage maturation, the segments belonging to the trajectory (that is, which formed a contiguous path) were subsampled, and the genes for which expression levels were associated and upregulated along the pseudotime were selected (scf.tl.test_association, sc.tl.rank_genes_groups). The pathway enrichment analysis was performed using the selected genes and GSEApy65.

The gene expression profile of SAN pacemaker cells (‘SinoatrialNodeCardiomyocytes’) were compared to that of other cardiomyocytes, and 675 DEGs were obtained (scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups, log fold change > 1, mean expression > 0.1). For the fetal-specific gene signatures, the fetal SAN pacemaker cell population was compared to the adult counterpart (SAN P cell23). For each cell type, donors were treated as replicates by making pseudo-bulk data (mean). Groups that had fewer than ten cells were removed from the analysis. Wilcoxon rank-sum test was performed to identify DEGs (620 genes; log fold change > 1, mean expression > 0.1). Intersection of the two DEGs were used as fetal-specific pacemaker cell signatures (143 genes) in the downstream analysis. The gene signatures of the vCML populations were selected as follows. For compact or trabeculated cardiomyocyte-specific signatures, genes associated with and upregulated along the pseudofime (calculated per population) and expressed higher in one population compared with the other (either compact versus trabeculated or trabeculated versus compact) were selected (compact, 130 genes; trabeculated, 107 genes). For the common signature, genes associated with and upregulated along the pseudotime of both populations were selected (336 genes). Pathway enrichment analysis was performed for each gene signature using GSEApy.

The SCENIC+ pipeline22 (v.1.0.0) was used to predict TFs and putative target genes as well as regulatory genomic regions harbouring TF binding sites. For each analysis, gene expression and chromatin-accessible region (peak) counts of multiome data were used as input. For the analysis of pacemaker cells, all the cardiomyocytes were used as input and metacells were created by clustering cells into groups of approximately ten cells based on their RNA profiles and subsequent aggregation of counts and fragments. For the maturation analysis of atrial and left ventricle cardiomyocytes, the same multiome data used for the trajectory analysis were used as input. Metacells were created using SEACells66 (ten nuclei per metacell) based on the MultiVI latent space and subsequent aggregation of counts and fragments. For monocyte and macrophage populations, multiome data were subsetted from the data used for trajectory analysis, and metacells were not created because of the small nucleus number. CisTopic was applied to identify region topics and differentially accessible regions from the fragment counts as candidate regions for TF binding. CisTarget was then run to scan the regions for TF-binding sites and GRNBoost2 was used to link TFs and regions to target genes based on co-expression and accessibility. Enriched TF motifs in the regions linked to target genes were used to construct TF-region and TF-gene regulons. Finally, regulon activity scores (AUC) were computed with AUCell based on target-gene expression and target region accessibility. Networks of TFs, regions and target genes (eGRNs) were constructed by linking individual regulons. TF–region–gene links for all analyses can be found in Supplementary Tables 4–6. The constructed network was further pruned for downstream analysis and visualization. For the SAN pacemaker cells, GRNs that target SAN pacemaker cell gene signatures, ion channel genes or axon guidance genes were first selected. For each TF–region–gene interaction, either TF (log fold change > 1, mean expression > 0.1, proportion of expression > 0.1) or region (log fold change > 0, proportion of accessibility > 0.01) being SAN pacemaker cell-specific (compared with other cardiomyocytes) were further selected. For the vCMLs, GRNs that target ‘compact’ and ‘common’ gene signatures were selected similarly to the GRNs of SAN pacemaker cells (compact cardiomyocyte GRNs). In silico TF perturbation analysis was performed using CellOracle32 (v.0.20.0) for the aCM and vCML analysis. A CellOracle object was made using the genes included in the SCENIC+ regulons of each population. Input baseGRN was also prepared using the same regulon (only activator regulons). The cluster labels were generated by combining fine-grained cell types and binned chronological age (n bin = 3). TFs that govern the pruned GRNs were tested for in silico perturbation.

The spots that belong to left ventricle regions were manually selected (Extended Data Fig. 2g). The inner (endocardial side) and outer (epicardial side) most layer were manually annotated. Using the OrganAxis algorithm12, we calculated the relative distances of each spot from the two manually annotated layers. We calculated the L2 distance of all spots to the closest corresponding points in each annotation by number of k-nearest neighbour (kNN) points (dist2cluster, kNN parameter = 4). To construct an axis anchored to the interface between two structures (‘transmural axis’), we fitted a normalized signoidal curve to the relative distances of each spot and placed spots in relative positions in respect of the two structures (axis_2p_norm). The gene expressions and cell-type abundances were aggregated per bin along the transmural axis and clustered along the transmural axis and visualized (seaborn.clustermap). The cell-type abundance was normalized for each individual sample (age) to account for potential technical variability related to different heart sizes. This normalization enabled us to analyse the transitions of cell-type localizations across the transmural axis. For gene selection, transmural axis was binned into three parts (outer, middle and inner) and DEGs for each part (compared with the rest) were selected (log fold change > 0.5, mean expression > 0.01). Pathway enrichment analysis was performed for the genes upregulated in the outer or inner part. Nucleus segmentation of the H&E images of Visium sections was performed using Cellpose67 implemented in Squidpy68 (squidpy.im.segment, method=cellpose_he, flow_threshold=0.8, channel_cellpose=1).

For the analysis of scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq data, we performed CellPhoneDB25 (v.5) analysis using all cells in the dataset to infer cell–cell interactions among fine-grained cell types: ‘statistical_analysis_method’ with the default parameters and selected ligands and receptors, all of which were expressed in at least 5% of the cells. The ligand–receptor interactions were further selected on the basis of mean expression levels and the biological questions as indicated in the main text and the figure legends. For the analysis using Visium HD data (Fig. 3j), we performed CellPhoneDB (v.5) analysis using cell types and ligand–receptor genes, constrained by their spatial localizations in the identified SAN niche, as determined by TissueTypist. The ‘statistical_analysis_method’ with the default parameters and selected ligands and receptors, all of which were expressed in at least 5% of the cells, were used. For plotting, the ligand–receptor interactions and the cell types were further selected on the biological questions as indicated in the main text and the figure legends.

FFPE fetal heart tissue sections (5 μm) were placed onto SuperFrost Plus slides. Staining was performed using a RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent kit v.2 assay (Advanced Cell Diagnostics, Bio-Techne), automated with a Leica BOND RX, according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Automated pretreatment included baking at 60 °C for 30 min, dewaxing, heat-induced epitope retrieval at 95 °C for 15 min in buffer ER2 and digestion with Protease III for 15 min. Following probe hybridization, tyramide signal amplification with Opal 520 and Opal 650 (Akoya Biosciences) and TSA-biotin (TSA Plus Biotin kit, Akoya) with streptavidin-conjugated Atto 425 (Sigma Aldrich) was used to develop RNAscope channels. All nuclei were DAPI stained. Stained sections were imaged using a Perkin Elmer Opera Phenix High-Content screening system with a ×20 water-immersion objective (NA of 0.16, 0.299 μm per pixel). The following channels were used: DAPI (excitation, 375 nm; emission, 435-480 nm); Opal 520 (excitation, 488 nm; emission, 500–550 nm); Opal 650 (excitation, 640 nm; emission, 650–760 nm); and Atto 425 (excitation, 425 nm; emission, 463–501 nm).

To identify condition-specific shifts in cell populations between euploid and T21 heart samples (or WT and Dp1Tyb mice), we performed neighbourhood-level differential abundance testing using Milo42. Milo detects differential abundance of transcriptionally similar cell populations by first constructing a kNN graph from the single-cell latent space (here derived from scVI integration). Rather than testing predefined clusters, Milo defines a large number of overlapping local neighbourhoods on the kNN graph, each representing a small, transcriptionally coherent region of cell-state space. These neighbourhoods therefore capture subtle and continuous cell-state variation without requiring hard clustering. For each neighbourhood, Milo counts the number of cells originating from each biological sample and performs a negative binomial generalized linear model to test whether neighbourhood abundance differs between conditions while accounting for sample-level replication. P values were corrected for multiple testing using spatial FDR, which accounts for overlap between neighbouring graph regions. This neighbourhood-based framework increases sensitivity to detect condition-specific shifts in cell states, particularly when differences are gradual or confined to subregions of a broader cell type.

Post-quality-control T21 snRNA-seq data from four hearts (11–14 PCW) were further curated by removing non-cardiac cells and non-reproducible (across samples) cells. Coarse-grained and fine-grained cell-type annotations were assigned using a label-transfer approach (CellTypist), referencing euploid snRNA-seq data. The T21 dataset was then integrated with age-matched euploid samples (12–14 PCW, 3 hearts), referred to as ‘T21 + Euploid’ in the associated web portal. Using the integrated dataset, the proportions of compact cardiomyocytes in the left and vCM and right vCM populations were quantified. To generate a shared latent space for comparative analysis of T21 and euploid samples, and to assess T21-associated changes in cell population using Milo42, we performed donor-balanced subsampling across cell types (referred to as ‘T21 + Euploid, subsampled for Milo analysis’ in the web portal). Integration of the subsampled data was performed using scVI, accounting for donor identity and continuous covariates, including total transcript counts, %mito and %ribo. The shared latent space generated by scVI was used to generate two-dimensional UMAP embedding (Fig. 5a) and to construct a KNN graph (with n neighbours = 20), which formed the basis for identifying overlapping cellular neighbourhoods using milo.make_nhood. Differential abundance testing was then conducted between T21 and euploid samples, and significantly altered neighbourhoods were identified (spatial FDR < 0.1). To perform differential gene expression analysis using cellular neighbourhoods as replicates, significantly enriched neighbourhoods (FDR < 0.1) associated with either T21 or euploid were used. For these neighbourhoods, we refined cell-to-neighbourhood assignments to ensure that each cell was uniquely assigned to a single neighbourhood, avoiding overlap across neighbourhoods. Gene expression data were then aggregated in each refined neighbourhood to generate pseudo-bulk expression profiles. These pseudo-bulk data were used as input for differential expression analysis using edgeR69, comparing T21-enriched neighbourhoods to euploid-enriched neighbourhoods in each cell type. The resulting lists of differentially expressed genes were subjected to pathway enrichment analysis using GSEA using blitzgsea package70 to identify pathways associated with T21-related transcriptional changes.

Embryonic hearts were collected at E15.5 and processed for HREM44. Three-dimensional image stacks were acquired at 2.5 µm voxel (x,y,z) resolution. To ensure consistent orientation across all samples, hearts were aligned in the transverse plane using the great vessels as anatomical landmarks. Specifically, image stacks were oriented such that the aortic and pulmonary valves appeared in the same transverse plane when viewed from proximal to distal. This standardization enabled reproducible cross-sectional analysis across WT and Dp1Tyb hearts. The measurement region was defined in the ventricular part of the heart distal to the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) and papillary muscles. Beginning at this reference plane, measurements were acquired over 250 µm at 25 µm intervals, which produced 11 measurements per heart. At each measurement plane, the following regions of interest were manually traced using Fiji: the total outer heart area and the inner trabecular area, including the trabeculated myocardium and ventricular lumen. Both left and right ventricles were included in all measurements. The compact myocardium area was calculated by subtracting the inner trabecular area from the total outer heart area. To account for variation in heart size, the compact myocardium proportion was expressed as a ratio of compact myocardium area to total outer heart area. The 11 measurements per heart were averaged to generate a single value per specimen for statistical analysis. Compact myocardium proportions were compared between WT and Dp1Tyb groups using two-sided Mann–Whitney t-test. P < 0.05 is considered as significantly different. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Samples were not randomized to experimental groups. Investigators performing the manual image segmentation were blinded to genotype.

Mice carrying the Dp(16Lipi-Zbtb21)1TybEmcf (Dp1Tyb) allele have been previously described43 and have been deposited into The Jackson Laboratory (strain 037183). Dp1Tyb mice were backcrossed on a C57BL/6J genetic background for more than ten generations. Mice were maintained in independently ventilated cages in a specific pathogen-free facility and given food and water ad libitum. All animal experiments were carried out under the authority of a Project Licence granted by the UK Home Office and were approved by the Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body of the Francis Crick Institute. To generate embryos, Dp1Tyb female mice were crossed with C57BL/6J males. Hearts from five Dp1Tyb and nine WT mouse embryos at day 13.5 of gestation (E13.5) were dissected and subsequently dissociated into single cells using a Neonatal Heart Dissociation kit and gentleMACS Octo dissociator (Miltenyi Biotec). Cells were resuspended in PBS, 0.04% BSA, filtered through a 40 µm FLowmi cell strainer and kept on ice until loaded. Approximately 20,000 cells were loaded on a Chromium Chip and partitioned in nanolitre-scale droplets using a Chromium Controller and Chromium. Next, GEM Single Cell reagents (CG000315 Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits User Guide (v3.1 - Dual Index)). In each droplet, the cells were lysed and RNA was reverse transcribed. All of the resulting cDNA in a droplet shared the same cell barcode. Illumina-compatible libraries were generated from the cDNA using Chromium Next GEM Single Cell library reagents in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions (10x Genomics, CG000315 Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits User Guide (v3.1–Dual Index)). Final libraries were subjected to quality control using an Agilent TapeStation and sequenced using an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. The sequencing read configuration 28-10-10-90 was used.

Each sample was mapped to the mouse reference genome (refdata-gex-mm10-2020-A) provided by 10x Genomics using CellRanger software (CellRanger v.6.1.2) with default parameters. Downstream analysis was performed using the Scanpy package. Doublets with a score of >0.15 were removed using Scrublet. We performed quality control and filtering based on the following settings: number of genes > 200, per cent mitochondrial < 20 (cell) and red blood cell score < 2. After pre-processing and removal of low-quality cells and nuclei, the coarse-grained and mid-grained cell types were annotated by transferring cell-type labels from the human dataset (CellTypist). Single-cell transcriptomic data were integrated using scVI58,59, accounting for continuous covariates of total counts, %mito and %ribo. Neighbourhood identification, high-resolution Leiden clustering and further dimensional reduction using UMAP were performed based on the scVI latent space. For differential abundance testing, overlapping cellular neighbourhoods were identified using Milo42 and the calculated neighbourhood graph based on the scVI (n neighbors = 10) latent spaces (milo.make_nhoods). Differential abundance testing was performed between genotypes (WT and Dp1Tyb), and significantly enriched neighbourhoods were identified (spatial FDR < 0.25). Data have been deposited into the Gene Expression Omnibus (accession number: GSE240137). Differential gene expression analysis and GSEA analysis were performed similarly to the human T21 data, as described above. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Samples were not randomized to experimental groups. Blinding was not performed for the scRNA-seq experiment.

This study used the T21 human iPS cell line WC-24-02-DS-M and its isogenic euploid control WC-24-02-DS-B (WiCell Research institute). The iPS cells were maintained in feeder-free conditions on Geltrex (Thermo Scientific) in mTESR1 (Stemcell Technologies). Cells were passaged as aggregates every 3–4 days at a ratio 1:6 using a combination of enzymatic and mechanical dissociation. Karyotype and pluripotency were confirmed via Karyostat+ and Pluritest assays (Thermo Fisher Scientific), respectively, and genetic stability was monitored via routine low-pass sequencing (Genomics STP, Francis Crick Institute). The identities of the WC-24-02-DS-M and WC-24-02-DS-B iPS cell lines were confirmed by short tandem repeat profiling during initial cell banking, with routine authentication testing performed during culture by the Cell Services STP at the Francis Crick Institute. Mycoplasma testing was performed by the Cell Services STP at the Francis Crick Institute.

An adaptation of the standard WNT modulation protocol (PMID: 24930130, PMID: 23257984) was used to differentiate human iPS cells into cardiomyocytes. Cells were dissociated into single cells and seeded on 12-well plates at a density of 5.7 × 104 cells per cm2 in mTESR1 and 10 µM Y-27632 (Tocris). Medium was replaced daily with mTESR1 until cells reached 70–85% confluency (day 0), at which point the medium was switched to RPMI 1640 (Thermo Scientific) supplemented with B27-insulin (Thermo Scientific) and 12 µM CHIR99021 (Selleck Chemicals). The medium was replaced with RPMI + B27-insulin after 24 h and then with RPMI + B27-insulin supplemented with 1 µM IWR-1 (Sigma) and 65 µg ml–1 L-ascorbic acid (Sigma Aldrich) after a further 24 h. Routine medium changes occurred every 48 h thereafter with RPMI + B27-insluin + L-ascorbic acid until day 6, switching to RPMI + B27 + L-ascorbic acid from day 8 onwards. Between days 10 and 13 cultures were subjected to a 72-h period of ‘metabolic selection’ consisting of 24 h of incubation in DMEM(–glucose/–glutamine) (Thermo Scientific) followed by 48 h of RPMI1640 without glucose, 4 mM lactate and L-ascorbic acid. Cardiomyocytes were re-plated routinely between days 14 and 16 and before relevant assays using a cardiomyocyte dissociation kit (Stemcell Technologies) as per the manufacturer’s guidelines.

TUNEL staining was performed on iPS-cell-derived cardiomyocytes at days 30–35 of differentiation. Before analysis, iPS-cell-derived cardiomyocytes were re-plated onto 96-well imaging plates (Greiner Bio-One) at a density of 4.5 × 104 cells per cm2 and allowed to adhere. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature. TUNEL staining to detect apoptotic cells was performed using a Click-iT Plus TUNEL assay (Invitrogen) per the manufacturer’s instructions. Subsequently samples were stained with mouse anti-cardiac troponin T (Invitrogen, MA5-12960) overnight at 4 °C, followed by donkey-anti-mouse-568 secondary antibody (Invitrogen, A10037) for 60 min at room temperature and DAPI (Sigma-Aldrich) for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were imaged using an Operetta CLS high-content analysis system (PerkinElmer) and analysis of TUNEL-positive cardiomyocytes (cardiac-troponin-T-positive cells) was performed using Harmony (v.5.2) software. Nuclei were segmented based on DAPI staining and cardiomyocytes were identified using a threshold for cardiac troponin T (Alexa568) intensity in the cell area surrounding but not including the nucleus (‘surrounding region’). TUNEL-positive cells were identified using a threshold for TUNEL stain (Alexa 647) intensity in the nucleus region. Cells meeting the threshold for both ‘cardiomyocyte’ and ‘TUNEL-positive nuclei’ were identified and quantified as TUNEL-positive cardiomyocytes.

A doxycycline-inducible PRDM16 overexpression line was generated using a piggyBac-based system as previously described36. A piggyBac-based doxycycline-inducible PRDM16 construct was assembled using In-Fusion cloning (Takara Bio). PRDM16 was synthesized by Genewiz from Azenta Life Sciences and PCR amplified (Cloneamp Takara, 639298), after which it was inserted in the PB-HS4-DOX-T2A-mCherry-bGHpA-HS4-EF1a-TetO-T2A-Puro-HS4 vector (a gift from J.-P.N.-B.) using In-Fusion Snap Assembly master mix (Takara, 638948), resulting in PB-HS4-TRE3G-PRDM16-T2A-mCherry-bGHpA-HS4-EF1a-TetO-T2A-PuroR-SV40pA-HS4 (PB-Dox-PRDM16-mCherry). PCR-amplified fragments were gel extracted using a Monarch gel extraction kit (NEB, T1120). NEB stable competent Escherichia coli (NEB, C3040H) were used for heat-shock transformation for 30 s at 42 °C and grown overnight on an ampicillin selection plate. The following day, three successfully grown colonies were picked and grown overnight in 4 ml LB medium with ampicillin (100 mg ml–1, Merck, A9518-5G). PB-Dox-PRDM16-mCherry plasmid was purified using a QIAprep Spin Miniprep kit (Qiagen, 27104) validated with Nanopore sequencing (Oxford Nanopore Technologies) by Source Bioscience. Transgenic Dox-PRDM16 was created using the REUS2 human embryonic stem cell line (The Rockefeller University). REUS2 cells were seeded at 6.5 × 105 cells per well in a Martigel-coated (Corning, 354277) 6-well plate in mTeSR 1 basal medium (Stemcell Technologies, 85850) with Rocki (1:1,000). The following day, cells were washed with PBS and incubated in 1 ml Opti-MEM medium (Gibco, 31985070) with Revitacell supplement (1:100, Fisher, 15317447) and 400 µl transfection mix which included Super piggyBac Transposase expression vector (Stratech, PB210PA-1-SBI) (500 ng), 2 µg PB-Dox-PRDM16-mCherry plasmid DNA and 3.5 µl Lipofectamine Stem transfection reagent (Life Technologies, STEM00003). DNA–lipofectamine mixtures were incubated at room temperature for 20 min and then added dropwise to cells followed by 3 h of incubation at 37 °C. After incubation, medium was replaced with 3 ml mTeSR supplemented with Revitacell supplement, the following day medium was replaced by 3 ml mTeSR. Two days after transfection, cells were clump-passaged at 1:3 split ratio and incubated in 2 ml mTeSR medium supplemented with Rocki (1:1,000) and 0.5 µg ml–1 puromycin for selection. Media were refreshed with selection media every 2–3 days thereafter. When 80% confluency was reached, one well of heterogenic cells was passaged in a 24-well plate to check doxycycline dose–response based on mCherry signals, a second well was single-cell passaged at 1:500 split ratio to select single colonies. Twenty isogenic colonies were picked and transferred to a 96-well plate to expand and duplicate. One isogenic duplicate was used to check doxycycline responsiveness (at 0.1 µM) based on mCherry signals. The brightest isogenic clone not treated by doxycycline (duplicate) was selected to expand and use for further experiments. PRDM16 overexpression levels were validated using RT–qPCR. The RUES2 human embryonic stem cell line was obtained from an established source and was not independently authenticated in our laboratory. Cell identity and quality were routinely assessed based on characteristic colony morphology and expression of pluripotency markers. Mycoplasma testing was performed by the Tissue Culture Facility at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute during culture and remained negative throughout the study.

Cardiomyocyte differentiation was performed using the generated doxyccyline-inducible PRDM16–mCherry RUES2 line together with the parental wild-type RUES2 control line, following our established cardiomyocyte differentiation protocol (GiWi protocol). After differentiation, cardiomyocytes were enriched by metabolic selection in lactate-containing medium from day 13 to day 17, as indicated in the experimental design (Extended Data Fig. 7k). For the overexpression experiment, lactate-selected cardiomyocytes were dissociated and replated at a density of 1.5 × 105 cells per well in 48-well plates (day 21). Experimental conditions comprised genotype (PRDM16 Tet-ON or wild-type RUES2), doxycycline treatment (with or without doxycycline; day 27 onward), and collection time point (day 10 after treatment initiation). For each condition, four independent wells were processed as technical replicates for bulk RNA-seq. Doxycycline hyclate (Sigma, D9891) was prepared as a 2 mM stock solution in nuclease-free water, aliquoted and stored at –20 °C. For induction, doxycycline was added to culture medium at a final concentration of 1 μM. Medium was replaced every other day with fresh medium containing doxycycline for the +Dox condition, whereas matched –Dox controls were cultured in parallel without doxycycline. At collection (day 37), cells were washed once with PBS and lysed directly in RNA preservation–lysis buffer (Zymo buffer, Plasmidsaurus) and processed as independent technical replicates. Bulk RNA-seq was performed at Plasmidsaurus, and induction efficiency was monitored by mCherry fluorescence imaging. To quantify cardiomyocyte maturation, we defined a maturation gene signature based on genes identified in Extended Data Fig. 7i, comprising compact cardiomyocyte-specific and shared maturation-associated genes (n = 466). To exclude doxycycline-induced transcriptional effects independent of PRDM16 overexpression, DEGs between WT +Dox and WT –Dox conditions (P < 0.05, log2 fold change > 2) were removed, resulting in a refined doxycycline-independent maturation gene set (n = 236). Gene expression values were z-score normalized across samples, and a maturation score was computed for each sample as the mean z-scored expression of genes in the signature. Downstream analyses compared control and PRDM16 Tet-ON cardiomyocytes under +Dox and –Dox conditions to evaluate the effect of PRDM16 overexpression on maturation-associated transcriptional programs. The inclusion of matched WT +Dox and –Dox controls enabled separation of doxycycline-dependent effects from PRDM16-specific effects. Statistical comparisons were performed using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.

a: Heatmap showing log2-transformed odds ratios (log2(OR)) for enrichment of each cell type (columns) within each cellular niche (rows). Enrichment was calculated using a 2×2 contingency table comparing the frequency of a given cell type within a cluster to its frequency across all other clusters, relative to all remaining cell types. A Haldane–Anscombe correction (+0.5) was applied to avoid zero counts. Positive values (red) indicate enrichment, while negative values (blue) indicate depletion relative to the global cell type distribution. Asterisks denote statistically significant enrichment (two-sided Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction, FDR < 0.05) and are shown only for positive log2(OR) values. b: Representative comparison between cellular niches identified from Visium HD data using CellCharter and manual histological annotations across multiple developmental stages (5–9 PCW). For each section, H&E images, manually annotated anatomical regions, and computationally derived cellular niches are shown. Visium HD-derived niches recapitulate major anatomical compartments, including atrial myocardium, atrioventricular junctional regions, and ventricular layers. c: Quantitative comparison between obtained cellular niches and histological annotations. Heatmap shows the proportion of histological labels within each predicted niche (row-normalised confusion matrix), demonstrating strong correspondence across anatomical compartments. For quantitative evaluation, computationally derived niches and histological annotations were harmonised to a shared anatomical label set to account for differences in annotation granularity. Agreement between Visium HD-derived niches and histological annotations was high (Cohen’s κ = 0.76, accuracy = 0.81, macro-F1 = 0.70). Statistical significance was assessed using a permutation test (n = 1000), confirming that the observed agreement exceeded that expected by chance (p < 0.001).

Performance was evaluated using 14-fold leave-one-section-out (LOSO) cross-validation across all spatial modalities: 7 Visium SD (3-prime) sections (4 donors), 2 Visium SD (FFPE) sections (1 donor), and 5 Visium HD sections (3 donors), with a maximum of two sections per donor included in training. a: Weighted F1 scores at the coarse (7-class) and fine (21-niche) hierarchy levels, stratified by modality and pooled across all evaluable spots (SD) or count-aggregated windows (HD)(n indicated below each modality). b: Per-niche fine F1 score plotted against the number of training sections containing each niche (out of 14). Plot size scales with the number of ground-truth spots per niche and colour denotes the parent coarse niche. The dashed line indicates a linear fit (Pearson r = 0.58). The lymph node class (present in a single section) yields F1 = 0 under LOSO due to complete absence from training data. c: Row-normalised confusion matrix at the fine-niche level, aggregated across all LOSO folds. Rows represent ground truth and columns predicted labels; diagonal values correspond to per-class recall. Labels are grouped by parent coarse niches (indicated by coloured text), with grey lines marking block boundaries. Overall classification performance at the fine level shows strong agreement between predicted and reference annotations (Cohen’s κ = 0.75, permutation p < 0.001; accuracy = 0.81; macro F1 = 0.64; weighted F1 = 0.80). d: Heatmap showing correspondence between TissueTypist-predicted anatomical niches and original niche annotations from the MERFISH dataset9. Each row represents a TissueTypist-predicted niche and each column represents the original annotation. Values indicate the proportion of original labels within each predicted niche (row-normalised confusion matrix). Predicted and original annotation labels were harmonised to a shared anatomical label set to account for differences in annotation granularity. Agreement was moderate across anatomical compartments (Cohen’s κ = 0.51, accuracy = 0.62, macro-F1 = 0.49), with statistical significance confirmed by permutation testing (p < 0.001). e-g: Application of the TissueTypist framework to an independent human lung Visium SD dataset21. (e) Representative spatial comparison between original annotations21 (left) and TissueTypist predictions (right). Each spot is coloured by its assigned fine-grained niche label. (f) Per-niche fine F1 score plotted against the number of sections containing each niche (out of 11) in a LOSO evaluation. Point size scales with the number of ground-truth spots per niche. The dashed line indicates a linear fit (Pearson r = 0.88). (g) Row-normalised confusion matrix at the fine-niche level, aggregated across all LOSO folds. Rows represent ground truth and columns predicted labels; diagonal values correspond to per-class recall.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Australia’s current wildfire crisis linked to colonial land-use change
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Russell Mullett
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The global wildfire crisis1 is often attributed to climate change, a framing that overlooks crucial historical drivers. Biomes at the forefront of this crisis, such as the temperate eucalypt forests of Australia, have seen alarming increases in large, intense wildfires in recent decades. Yet evidence of how colonial land-use change and the disruption of Indigenous fire use altered vegetation structure and fuel dynamics remains scarce. Here we reconstruct 1,000 years of vegetation and fire change in a temperate eucalypt forest in southeastern Australia. Before the British invasion (from 1788 CE), fire use by the Indigenous Gunaikurnai people maintained stable, open woodlands through frequent, fine-grained, low-temperature cultural burning. Colonial disruption drove cascading changes: increased fire temperature, a fourfold rise in eucalypt cover, a shift from open woodland to forest and increased soil erosion. These transformations preceded anthropogenic warming, indicating that the vulnerability of these forests to wildfire is shaped by colonial land-use legacies. By creating more flammable landscapes, colonial land use amplified the influence of climate change, suggesting a reinforcing feedback (the ‘catastrophic wildfire loop’) in which high-intensity wildfires raise fuel loads and further increase the likelihood of climate-driven fire. Integrating Indigenous knowledge into fire management is therefore essential to restoring resilience and mitigating future wildfire risk.

The archaeological radiocarbon determinations underlying the summed probability density analysis are available from the SahulArch radiocarbon collection of the OCTOPUS database v.2.3 (https://octopusdata.org/). Precise archaeological site coordinates are withheld, as they are in the source database, to protect Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property and Indigenous Data Sovereignty. The radiocarbon determinations required to reproduce the analysis are provided in full. Previously published datasets used in this study are available as follows: the Australasian temperature reconstruction from the PAGES 2k Consortium global multiproxy database40; the FFDI reconstruction29; the colonial frontier massacres in Australia, 1788–1930 dataset42; relative pollen productivity estimates for southeastern Australia9; Victorian ecological vegetation class mapping138,139; Victorian fire history records from the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action38; and the National Vegetation Information System12.

Vegetation cover was reconstructed using the publicly available DISQOVER R package (REVEALSinR function; https://github.com/MartinTheuerkauf/disqover). Age–depth modelling used rbacon v.3.5.2; radiocarbon calibration used SHCal20 in OxCal v.4.4; Bayesian growth models used nimbleCarbon v.0.2.5; change-point analyses used changepoint v.2.3 and envcpt v.1.1.3; pollen zonation used rioja v.1.0-7; FTIR analogue matching used analogue v.0.18.1. a, Pre-1750 (pre-colonial) vegetation map138. b, Extant (2005) vegetation map139. Victoria’s Ecological Vegetation Class (EVC) system provides spatial classification of native vegetation into discrete types based on floristic composition and structure. Two primary datasets are referenced: a pre-European reconstruction (pre-1750) and a present-day map (2005) compiled from field surveys, aerial photography, satellite imagery, and vegetation plots. The pre-1750 layer is constructed from biophysical modelling of potential natural vegetation (the vegetation predicted under prevailing climate and soils), supplemented by historical records, explorer accounts, early surveys, and ecological inference. Because this approach models climate-driven vegetation potential rather than the vegetation that existed under active Indigenous land management, it cannot recover the open woodland maintained through millennia of cultural burning. Consequently, the pre-1750 and 2005 layers are effectively identical at this site: both map the dense eucalypt forest and shrubland that characterizes the landscape following colonial disruption of cultural burning. This equivalence is not an artefact of data quality; it reflects a foundational assumption embedded in the national vegetation baseline that treats post-colonial vegetation as the natural reference condition. Our palaeoecological record demonstrates that this assumption is incorrect at Purghagoolah, where the pre-colonial landscape was an open woodland, not the closed forest mapped by either dataset.
