Figure 4a schematically illustrates the nucleation-growth decoupling strategy for 2D MoS2 with programmed shape. The EF-SCN system allows control over single, multiple and zero nucleation, all tunable by Lgrowth. Therefore, by integrating a large-size nucleation zone with a small-size only growth zone where nucleation is suppressed, the positions of nucleation and growth can be spatially decoupled. The SEM image in Extended Data Fig. 8a confirmed that a MoS2 flake nucleated in the nucleation zone penetrated the only growth zone, resulting in a line-shaped single-crystal MoS2 (Extended Data Fig. 8b). We further extended the strategy to fabricate a single-crystal stripe 2D MoS2–MoSe2 heterostructure (Extended Data Fig. 8c), which is confirmed by non-contact-mode phase mapping (Extended Data Fig. 8d). Collectively, these observations demonstrate that the nucleation–growth decoupling strategy is not limited to enlarging crystal size but also enables deliberate shape engineering of single-crystal 2D TMD beyond the conventional triangular morphology.

To evaluate the quality and device potential of the line-shaped 2D TMD channel, we fabricated FETs with the structure shown in Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 8e with an average channel length of 6.8 μm and width of 0.83 μm, using 10-μm-long single-crystal MoS2. As shown in the transfer curve in Fig. 4c, the line-shaped single FET exhibits typical n-type behaviour, with an on-current density of 12 μA μm−1. Importantly, a high field-effect mobility of 117 cm2 V−1 s−1 was achieved, surpassing previously reported values for selectively grown MoS2 FETs, indicating the excellent electrical properties of single-crystal MoS2 grown by EF-SCN8,9. In Fig. 4d, the mobility distribution across a total of 16 single FET arrays reveals an average mobility of 74 cm2 V−1 s−1 with an RSD of 21.8%, demonstrating a performance variation comparable to that of previous 2D TMD single-crystal FETs. In addition, to evaluate the large-area uniformity of the EF-SCN system, we analysed the performance of 50 back-gated FETs fabricated using single-crystal MoS2 channels grown across a 2-cm substrate. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 9, the devices exhibited RSDs of 10.45% in mobility and 14.66% in on-current density, supporting the superior uniformity of the EF-SCN system over a large area. Further details are provided in Supplementary Note 8.

Meanwhile, the long single-crystal channels synthesized via the nucleation–growth decoupling strategy render high-density and low-variation device layouts feasible within a confined footprint. We therefore propose single-crystal multiple FETs, in which multiple transistors are defined along a single channel (Extended Data Fig. 8f). As shown in Extended Data Fig. 8g, the single-crystal multiple FETs consist of 4 active channels, each with a length of 0.31 μm and a width of 0.87 μm, integrated within a 10-μm-long single-crystal MoS2. Comparing the relative deviation and RSD of field-effect mobility, single-crystal single FETs (4 sets, 16 devices) showed an overall RSD of 21.8%, whereas single-crystal multiple FETs (4 devices) showed a markedly lower RSD of 7.8%, which is a 65% reduction in variation (Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). This indicates that fabricating multiple channels within a single crystal enables lower variation than defining a single channel in a single crystal, suggesting that the single-crystal scaling capability of EF-SCN holds strong potential for low-variation device architectures.

Conventional selective-growth approaches, although effective in producing high-quality single-crystal TMDs, are inherently limited to applications using homogeneous channel or vertical heterostructure formation, leaving in-plane lateral compositional control less accessible8,9. However, lateral heterojunctions are important for device engineering, as they enable direct modulation of electronic properties along the channel direction. In this regard, the EF-SCN system offers a distinct route to the in-plane alignment of lateral heterostructures through precise spatial regulation of nucleation and lateral growth, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 10a–d. We successfully synthesized 2D MoS2–MoSe2 lateral superlattices with precise positional and orientational alignment at the array level. As shown in the HAADF-STEM image in Extended Data Fig. 10e, these lateral heterostructures exhibit sharp interfaces with an intermixing width of less than 2 nm. Such spatially programmed growth introduces contact engineering strategies via strain modulation at the 2D TMD heterojunctions, enabling selective metal contact formation via ALD on the MoSe2 region in MoS2–MoSe2 lateral heterostructures38 (Extended Data Fig. 10f).

Figure 4e presents a schematic illustrating the fabrication of self-aligned ALD contact FETs. Ruthenium (Ru) ALD on the MoS2–MoSe2 lateral heterostructures grown by EF-SCN selectively deposits on the MoSe2 region owing to local strain distribution (Fig. 4g). As shown in Fig. 4f, a well-aligned 2D/3D hybrid structure is achieved at the array level, and AFM measurements confirm the formation of 15-nm-thick Ru film. Using this Ru film as a contact, self-aligned ALD contact FETs were fabricated with a conformal Ru layer at the contact region on the TMD surface where monolayer MoS2 is preserved in the channel region, as verified by HAADF-STEM (Fig. 4h). The device with a channel width of 2.5 μm and length of 1.4 μm exhibited a typical n-type behaviour under drain voltages ranging from 0.01 V to 1 V (Fig. 4i). The maximum electrical performances include a field-effect mobility of 4.3 cm2 V−1 s−1 (Vds = 0.01 V), an on/off ratio exceeding 107, an on-current density of 2.0 μA μm−1 and a subthreshold swing of 170 mV dec−1. Despite the harsh conditions of Ru ALD (oxygen exposure at 220 °C) expected to degrade electrical properties of the channel, the device delivers meaningful performance considering previous reports on direct ALD contact-based 2D TMD FETs39,40.

Collectively, these results demonstrate that the deterministic nucleation control and precise crystal orientation alignment of EF-SCN facilitate expansion towards advanced device applications that remain inaccessible with conventional approaches (see Supplementary Note 9 and Supplementary Table 4 for a detailed comparison with conventional confined growth). This is evidenced by high-performance and low-variation FETs fabricated through large-size, shape-controlled single-crystal growth, as well as self-aligned ALD contact FETs enabled by spatially controlled lateral heterostructures. Therefore, the EF-SCN system serves as a foundational platform for advanced 2D material devices, ranging from homogeneous single-crystal channel applications such as high-density logic circuits to heterostructure-based applications, including spatial doping for rectification, heterojunction design for optoelectronics, strain modulation in 2D materials, edge contacts via lateral growth and anisotropic 2D materials41,42,43,44,45,46,47,48.

We demonstrate that the EF-SCN system establishes a physical framework for selective growth by enabling deterministic control over nucleation position for effective single-crystal growth and multifunctional 2D TMD architectures. Unlike conventional 2D TMD ASG, reactive species released from the etching-flux barrier create a non-uniform nucleation probability distribution and localize a single-nucleation site at the pattern centre, enabling spatially controlled MoS2 single crystals up to 10 μm. The platform also exhibits broad process compatibility, including low-temperature growth, amorphous substrates and large-scale implementation. Nucleation-rate modelling further establishes a quantitative design rule for zero, single and multiple nucleation as functions of growth-region size, process time and MOCVD conditions. Extending this concept, nucleation–growth decoupling produces line-shaped single-crystal MoS2 and programmable stripe heterostructures, enabling field-effect mobilities up to 117 cm2 V−1 s−1 and multiple FETs within a single crystal with low device-to-device variation. Precise positional and orientational control also enables self-aligned ALD contact FETs through spatially programmed 2D/3D heterostructures with Ru AS-ALD. More broadly, the in-plane regulation of nucleation and growth provides a route to strain modulation, contact engineering and other complementary-metal–oxide–semiconductor-relevant functions within a selective-growth sequence. These capabilities highlight EF-SCN as a versatile platform for translating channel design, stressor formation and doping strategies into the 2D materials regime.

The monolayer MoS2 was grown in a home-made horizontal hot-wall quartz tube, with MHC (Sigma-Aldrich), DES (Sigma-Aldrich), hydrogen (H2), potassium chloride (KCl) (Sigma-Aldrich) and argon carrier gas. The flow rate was controlled by the mass flow controller. The MOCVD process was conducted at 430–800 °C and 1–20 torr for 200–3,000 s. The EF-SCN behaviour was controlled by adjusting the MOCVD conditions, with DES flow rates of 0.5–20 sccm and MHC flow rates of 2–5 sccm, depending on the nucleation type. The monolayer MoS2–MoSe2 lateral superlattice was grown by alternating supply of DES and dimethyl selenide (Alfa Aesar). The MoS2 MOCVD process was mainly carried out on c-plane sapphire (Madelab), c/a miscut sapphire (0.5–5°, MTI Korea) and amorphous SiO2 (Waferbiz) patterned with etching-flux barrier. To compare the MoS2 growth behaviour, not only c-plane sapphire but also a-Al2O3, a-SiO2 and a-HfO2 deposited on Si(100) by an electron-beam evaporator (Atech) were used as substrates.

The etching-flux barrier was mainly fabricated on a sapphire substrate using electron-beam lithography (VEGA3 LMH/ELPHY quantum lithography system). Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA; 1000 HARP PMMA eB 0.7, KemLab) was spin-coated on the substrate at 4,000 rpm and baked at 180 °C for 3 min. Subsequently, a conductive protective coating solution (AR-PC 5092, Allresist) was spin-coated at 2,000 rpm and baked at 90 °C for 2 min. After patterning process by electron-beam lithography and removing the AR-PC with deionized water, the electron-beam-exposed region was developed by methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK) and isopropyl alcohol (IPA) solution (MIBK/IPA 1:3 positive radiation resist developer, KAYAKU) for 15–20 s, followed by cleaning in IPA for 20 s. Finally, the etching-flux barrier was fabricated by depositing 5–20 nm of HfO2 (or ZrO2) using an electron-beam evaporator, after which a lift-off process in acetone at 70 °C for 30 min was conducted. For the large-scale demonstration, photolithography was used to fabricate the barrier patterns. AZ 5214E photoresist (Merck Performance Materials) was spin-coated at 4,000 rpm and baked at 115 °C for 60 s. The photoresist was then exposed for 10–14 s using a mask aligner (Midas MDA-600S) and developed in AZ 300 MIF solution (Merck Performance Materials) for 45 s. Subsequently, the barrier material was deposited using an electron-beam evaporator, followed by lift-off in dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma-Aldrich).

The 2D TMD EF-SCN results were mainly measured with a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Hitachi S-4800). The MoS2 thickness was confirmed by AFM (NX10, Park Systems) in non-contact mode, and non-contact-mode phase mapping was also performed with the same instrument. The Raman and photoluminescence spectra of MoS2 were measured using a confocal Raman spectroscopy system (LabRAM ARAMIS, Horiba) equipped with an argon ion laser of 514.5 nm wavelength. Photoluminescence mapping was performed using a confocal Raman spectroscopy (XperRAM C, Nanobase) with a 532-nm laser, 2,400 grooves per mm grating and a reference peak at 680 nm (1.82 eV). HAADF-STEM images of single-crystal MoS2 and self-aligned ALD contact FETs were obtained using FEI Titan3 G2 60-300 (FEI) operated at 200 kV and 300 kV. Atomic-resolution AFM measurements were performed in ultrahigh vacuum (5.0 × 10−10 mbar) at room temperature using contact mode. In second-harmonic generation (SHG) measurement, the wide-field SHG images were obtained using a femtosecond laser system (Light Conversion PHAROS). The excitation pulses were generated using an optical parametric amplifier (ORPHEUS) providing a wavelength of 1,300 nm at a repetition rate of 100 kHz. The polarization-resolved SHG signals were measured using a femtosecond titanium:sapphire laser operating at a central wavelength of 800 nm with a repetition rate of 80 MHz. To generate contour mapping images for nucleation probability and density, SEM images were converted into a binary image using ImageJ. Then, each growth region was divided into evenly spaced subunit areas and flake centres were counted within each subunit area.

To investigate the oxygen emission from the HfO2 etching-flux barrier, 50-nm HfO2 deposited on Si(100) substrate by an electron-beam evaporator was thermally annealed at 750 °C for 2–360 min under vacuum with argon gas. The compositional analysis of HfO2 was evaluated by XPS (Nexsa G2, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The XPS measurements were operated at room temperature under high vacuum (<2 × 10−8 torr) in constant analyser energy mode with a pass energy of 50.0 eV, a step size of 0.05 eV and a beam diameter of 400 μm. The XPS peaks were fitted using Thermo Avantage software. To examine the phase and crystal structure changes of HfO2 depending on annealing temperature (350–850 °C), grazing incidence X-ray diffraction (Ultima IV, RIGAKU) measurement was performed with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.541 Å). The X-ray diffraction data were analysed using PDXL software. For analysis of the MoS2 etching behaviour by HfO2, MoS2 flakes were first grown on Si/SiO2 (90 nm) substrates via MOCVD and subsequently dry-transferred onto sapphire substrate patterned with 20-nm HfO2 barrier. PMMA was spin-coated onto the MoS2-grown substrate at 8,000 rpm for 40 s and baked at 180 °C for 10 min. The PMMA/MoS2 flakes stack was dry-transferred onto a HfO2-patterned sapphire substrate using a thermal release tape and polydimethylsiloxane. PMMA was then removed using acetone, and the sample was rinsed with IPA. Finally, the transferred samples were thermally annealed at 750 °C for 1 h under vacuum with argon gas.

Ru films were deposited using a travelling-wave-type ALD with (ethylbenzyl)(1-ethyl-1,4-cyclohexadienyl)Ru(0) (EBECHRu, Hansol Chemical) as the precursor and O2 as the reactant gas. The EBECHRu precursor was stored in a stainless-steel canister and heated to 100 °C to obtain sufficient vapour pressure, and the delivery lines were maintained at 10–15 °C higher than the bubbler temperature to prevent condensation. The ALD process was conducted at a stage temperature of 220 °C, and each unit cycle consisted of an EBECHRu pulse (3 s), nitrogen (N2) purge (45 s), O2 pulse (3 s) and N2 purge (45 s). High-purity N2 gas (99.999%) with a flow rate of 200 sccm was used for purging residual gas molecules and by-products.

Hybrid diffusion–reaction process emulation was used to test whether spatially separated precursor supply and oxygen etching flux can reproduce the zero–single–multiple nucleation behaviour of EF-SCN. The emulation domain was defined as a simplified triangular growth template on a hexagonal lattice, with a precursor reservoir positioned above the template and an oxygen reservoir placed along the template boundary to mimic HfO2-derived etching species. Diffusion and reaction steps were alternated using a cellular-automaton-based scheme35,36,37, in which the reaction step included the essential events required for EF-SCN: precursor adsorption, nucleus formation, lateral growth and oxygen-mediated etching.

Process-condition effects were represented by varying schematic parameters corresponding to template size, adsorption and nucleation probability, lateral-growth probability, and etching-flux supply. These parameters were used to capture the experimental effects of Lgrowth, DES-controlled nucleation density and MHC-controlled lateral-growth rate. The resulting outcomes were classified as zero, single or multiple nucleation according to the number of surviving nuclei, and the spatial distribution of nucleation events was used to identify NAR and NSR formation. Complete lattice definitions, update rules, parameter values, seed statistics, and NAR and NSR quantification procedures are described in Supplementary Note 7.

A top-gated FET based on single-crystal line-shaped MoS2 was fabricated using electron-beam lithography. A gold (Au) layer (40 nm) was deposited via electron-beam evaporation to form the source, drain and top-gate electrodes. The top-gate dielectric was prepared by depositing a 0.7-nm Si seed layer via electron-beam evaporation, followed by 8 nm HfO2 using ALD. The dielectric capacitance of 6.2 × 10−7 F cm−2 was confirmed by employing capacitance–voltage measurements on metal–insulator–metal capacitors. A back-gated FET array was fabricated using photolithography. Source and drain electrodes were formed by thermal evaporation of a 40-nm Au layer. For encapsulation, a 1-nm Si seed layer was first deposited by electron-beam evaporation, and a 10-nm HfO2 layer was subsequently deposited by plasma-enhanced ALD. For a 2D TMD FET with Ru AS-ALD contact, a source–drain isolation process was required to separate the continuous Ru film formed outside the superlattice region. The Ru layer was etched using inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching with a mixed gas of O2 (24 sccm) and carbon tetrafluoride (CF4, 6 sccm), using PMMA as the etching mask. The source, drain and top-gate electrodes were deposited by electron-beam evaporation of Au (30 nm). The top-gate dielectric was prepared by depositing a 0.7-nm Si seed layer, followed by 30-nm HfO2. The dielectric capacitance of 8.5 × 10−7 F cm−2 was confirmed by using capacitance–voltage measurements on metal–insulator–metal capacitors. Electrical measurements of the back-gated FET array were performed at room temperature under vacuum using a semiconductor analyser (B1500A, Keysight), and those of the other devices were performed at room temperature under ambient conditions using a semiconductor analyser (4200A-SCS, Keithley).

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A split attractor design for rapidly writing a navigational goal
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Katherine I. Nagel
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Recurrent attractor networks are widely thought to form the basis of working memory1,2,3, but how they can be rapidly switched on and off is unclear4,5,6,7. Here we investigate stability and switching in a recurrent circuit of the fly navigation centre8. h∆K and PFG neurons are recurrently connected in a ring structure and exhibit shared persistent bump activity that turns on with odour and terminates at the end of a goal-directed run. Using whole-cell recordings, we show that persistence in h∆K depends on recurrence, and that h∆K receives slow recurrent excitation and fast inhibition from its synaptic partners. Computational modelling reveals that these synaptic dynamics yield persistent attractor dynamics over a range of synaptic strengths. Next we examine the mechanisms of rapid switching. We find that whereas both populations show similar activity during runs, they become decoupled during turns and rest. We can reproduce these differential dynamics in our model by using inhibition to dynamically uncouple activity in h∆K from PFG. When h∆K is inhibited, PFG neurons follow their inputs from the compass system; when h∆K is disinhibited, recurrent interactions lock this input into place, forming a heading memory. Consistent with this model, we find that inhibitory inputs onto h∆K increase during turns and are suppressed during odour and goal-directed runs. Our work reveals how disinhibition can serve as a gate to rapidly write an ongoing measurement to a recurrent circuit.

Distributed networks of recurrently connected neurons are widely thought to form the substrate for short-term working memory1,2,3. During working memory tasks, neurons in the prefrontal cortex and elsewhere exhibit persistent activity that turns on with cue presentation and terminates with behaviour9,10. The duration of persistence in these neurons is much longer than their intrinsic membrane time constants, arguing that persistence arises from network interactions3. Computational models that feature local recurrent excitation and global inhibition can recreate the types of persistent activity that are observed experimentally1,11 (Fig. 1a). However, such networks exhibit a fundamental trade-off between stability and flexibility1. Networks configured to generate stable attractor dynamics are difficult to shut off once activated5. Computational models therefore often implement gates to control the timing of attractor dynamics4,6,7,12. How such gates might be implemented at a circuit and synaptic level is unclear.

The Drosophila brain offers a unique opportunity to study the function of recurrent circuits at a cellular level13,14,15. Connectomics describes the architecture of fly networks with synaptic and cellular precision8,16,17, and precise genetic tools enable functional interrogation of the same networks18. The fan-shaped body (FB) is a highly recurrent part of the fly navigation centre called the central complex, and is thought to compute and encode allocentric goals8,19,20,21,22,23,24,25. The FB contains about 30 types of local neuron that interact through complex patterns of feedforward and recurrent connectivity8. Several FB local neuron types have been shown to encode goal direction signals for navigation as positionally stable bumps of activity across the columns of the FB22,23,24,26,27,28. FB output neurons compare these goal signals to an internal compass, computed in the ellipsoid body29 to drive egocentric steering19,24,25. How goal signals in local neurons are dynamically regulated, and the function of local recurrent connections, are both unclear.

Here we investigate how stable activity and rapid switching are combined in a discrete recurrent microcircuit within the FB. When flies navigate towards food, brief encounters with odour drive persistent goal-directed runs that are biased in the upwind direction26,30. In a previous study26, we showed that a group of FB local neurons called h∆K exhibit a stable bump of activity that turns on with odour and persists while the fly maintains a stable heading. Sparse activation of h∆K neurons caused flies to walk in repeatable directions relative to wind22, whereas silencing led to less persistent trajectories after odour loss26. Together these data support the idea that bump activity in h∆K neurons represents a persistent goal signal for navigation.

h∆K neurons are embedded in a recurrent network reminiscent of classic models of working memory (Fig. 1a,b). First, h∆K neurons are tightly recurrently connected in a ring structure with a second group of FB local neurons called PFGs (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1a–d,f). Second, PFG neurons receive direct structured inputs from compass neurons in the ellipsoid body, which represent heading as a bump of activity13,29. Each PFG neuron receives heading inputs tuned to a different segment of the world8 (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1d). Finally, h∆K and PFG neurons both receive global input from several types of broadly projecting tangential neurons (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1e). The similarity of this network to classic working memory models suggests that this architecture might function to store heading representations and transform them into short-term goals.

Here we show through imaging, whole-cell physiology, genetic manipulations and computational modelling that persistent goal representations in h∆K are likely to emerge through recurrent interactions. We show that excitation and inhibition onto h∆K have distinct dynamics that promote tuneable persistent attractor states across a range of excitation and inhibition weights. Finally, we examine the mechanisms that allow h∆K activity to be rapidly turned on by odour and off when the fly turns. We observe that even though h∆K and PFG are tightly anatomically coupled, they show similar activity only during runs, and diverge during turning and rest. We can reproduce these dynamics in a model by using feedforward inhibition to dynamically decouple h∆K from PFG in a stimulus and behaviour-dependent manner. Imaging from inhibitory inputs onto h∆K supports this model, showing that h∆K neurons are inhibited during turning and disinhibited during odour and goal-directed runs. Our data and models introduce a circuit motif—disinhibition of a split recurrent network—that allows stable attractor dynamics to be rapidly switched on and off by either sensory input or ongoing behaviour. We propose that this motif may represent a general solution to the problem of combining stability and flexibility in recurrent circuits.

h∆K and PFG neurons are strongly and reciprocally connected within columns of the FB (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). Reciprocal connections between h∆K and PFG are the most numerous of any recurrent connection in the central complex (Extended Data Fig. 1h). h∆K neurons express the fast excitatory neurotransmitter acetylcholine, whereas PFGs express tyramine, myoinhibitory peptide and diuretic hormone 31, but no classical fast transmitter18. To test the hypothesis that these recurrent connections contribute to persistent bump activity previously observed in a broad h∆K line26 (VT062617-Gal4), we imaged from each population using cell-type-specific split-Gal4 lines18. We recorded neural activity during closed-loop odour- and wind-guided navigation26 (Fig. 1c). In this paradigm, a tethered fly walks on an air-supported ball that controls the orientation of a wind stimulus in closed loop to simulate wind from a fixed direction. During each 50 s wind trial, we presented odour (0.5% apple cider vinegar, ACV) as either a 15 s step, or as 1–10 500 ms pulses at 1 Hz. In response to odour, flies selected a heading trajectory that was biased upwind (Extended Data Fig. 1i–k) and persisted for several seconds after odour offset (Extended Data Fig. 1j,k).

Both h∆K and PFG neurons showed a localized bump of activity that was preferentially activated during odour (Fig. 1d–g and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c) and persisted while the fly maintained its trajectory (Fig. 1h–m and Extended Data Fig. 2d). In both populations, the probability and amplitude of bump activity grew similarly with pulse number (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). In h∆K, the distribution of bump persistence times was very similar to the distribution of goal-directed walking times (Fig. 1i), whereas in PFG the neural distribution was slightly longer (Fig. 1l). To test whether neural persistence predicts behavioural persistence, we detected all bump offsets that occurred after the odour stimulus, and compared trajectories associated with bump offset to those associated with maintained bump activity (Fig. 1j,m). In both h∆K and PFG neurons, bump offset was associated with a significant deviation of heading from the ‘goal’ direction adopted during odour, compared with periods when the bump remained on. Bumps were also weakly associated with higher forward velocities, and a greater probability of orienting upwind (Fig. 1j,m). Together, our results argue that h∆K and PFG neurons show similar odour response dynamics and similar persistent activity associated with maintaining a goal heading, consistent with the hypothesis that recurrence between these populations contributes to persistent activity.

We next investigated whether persistent activity might arise in part from intrinsic properties of h∆K neurons. We performed whole-cell patch clamp recordings from h∆K neurons (labelled by VT062617-lexA) and injected positive or negative current. We observed rapid responses to current injection (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b) with no persistent excitation. We conclude that intrinsic conductances alone do not generate persistent excitation in h∆K.

We next explored whether input from tangential neurons could drive persistence (see Fig. 2b, which shows connectivity and predicted neurotransmitters8,31). To test this, we recorded from h∆K neurons using VT062617-lexA (Fig. 2c) and stimulated tangential neurons that had been previously shown to encode odour and drive upwind running22 (65C03-Gal4, labelling 17 tangential neurons including FB6A and FB6D (FB6A/D); Extended Data Fig. 3c). We observed a brief inhibition that switched to slow and persistent excitation later in the stimulus (Fig. 2c). Persistent excitation grew with duty cycle (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e), and was strongly reduced by the nicotinic antagonists curare (10 µM) and imidacloprid32 (100 nM; Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3f). These tangential neurons express markers for both acetylcholine18,22 and glutamate18 (usually an inhibitory transmitter in the fly brain33) which might account for the biphasic effects of stimulation. To test whether recurrent signalling is required for persistent h∆K activity, we performed the same experiment while blocking recurrent signalling from h∆K using tetanus toxin (Fig. 2e). Blocking recurrent signalling abolished persistent excitation and switched the response of h∆K from excitation to weak inhibition (Fig. 2e,f). We conclude that h∆K neurons can generate persistent activity in response to synaptic input, that persistence requires cholinergic excitation, and that it depends on recurrent signalling by h∆K neurons.

To determine whether PFG neurons excite h∆K neurons, we used the same genetic strategy to stimulate PFGs and record from individual h∆K neurons. PFG stimulation drove excitation in some cells and inhibition in others (Fig. 2g), perhaps because optogenetic stimulation unrealistically depolarizes all members of the class. h∆K neurons that responded with excitation showed slow and persistent dynamics. Of note, we also observed slow persistent excitation in h∆K when we stimulated a serotonergic recurrent tangential neuron34 (ExR3; Fig. 2b,h and Extended Data Fig. 3g,h). We could reduce this persistent excitation using the broad serotonin receptor antagonist methysergide (50 µM; Fig. 2h,i and Extended Data Fig. 3i). These data argue that multiple recurrent excitatory inputs onto h∆K drive slow and persistent dynamics.

In most computational models of recurrent attractor networks, broad inhibition is required together with local recurrent excitation to prevent runaway excitation1,11,35. We therefore tested whether some tangential inputs provide global inhibition onto h∆K. Using connectomic predictions of neurotransmitter phenotype16,31, we identified two putative inhibitory tangential neuron types that synapse onto h∆K, called FB5V and FB6M (Fig. 2b), and made or identified lines that label each type (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To test whether these neurons provide functional inhibition onto h∆K, we stimulated each neuron type and recorded from h∆K using the same genetic strategy. In all lines we observed strong and rapid inhibition that depressed over time (Fig. 2j,l and Extended Data Fig. 4c). For both neuron types, stimulus-evoked inhibition was converted to excitation by 5 µM picrotoxin, a concentration that is known to block type A (GABA) γ-aminobutyric acid receptors33 (Fig. 2k,m and Extended Data Fig. 4d). We conclude that some tangential inputs provide broad and rapid inhibition to the h∆K–PFG circuit, consistent with computational models of attractor network design.

Imaging, physiology and connectomics indicate that the h∆K–PFG circuit contains the local recurrent excitation and broad inhibition required to form an attractor network. However, our experiments also revealed distinct dynamics for synaptic excitation and inhibition: excitation is slow, whereas inhibition is fast. Slow excitation might arise from peptides and modulators expressed by PFG and other FB neurons in addition to or instead of fast neurotransmitters18. To understand how synaptic dynamics contribute to recurrent network function, we developed a connectome-based computational model. In our model, the firing rates of individual h∆K and PFG neurons, and a single global inhibitory tangential neuron, depend on both external input and recurrent signalling between these neurons, as well as a leak term (Fig. 3a and  Methods). The connections between the 30 h∆K and 18 PFG neurons were specified by a Gaussian function fit to the structure of recurrent connectivity between h∆K and PFG observed in the hemibrain connectome8 (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). The tangential neuron receives input from all h∆K and PFG neurons and provides global inhibition to both populations. The global strength of excitation and inhibition could be scaled through two free parameters (Fig. 3b).

We first explored whether this network could reproduce the persistent bump activity that we observed experimentally. We provided spatially structured input to h∆K and PFG neurons (Fig. 3c) and examined activity after this input was removed. We found that any asymmetric input to the network was transformed into a localized bump of activity with a profile resembling recorded bump activity (Fig. 3c,d). The width of the attractor bump grew and plateaued exponentially with the width of the Gaussian function describing local recurrent connectivity (Extended Data Fig. 5f,g). We also tested whether an attractor bump could be generated with real connectivity values. Using real weights from the hemibrain connectome16, we could generate a bump at most locations in the FB, although bump amplitude and duration varied across locations (Extended Data Fig. 6a), whereas with Gaussian connectivity, we could generate a bump of equal magnitude and duration anywhere around the ring (Extended Data Fig. 6b). We conclude that the recurrent architecture of h∆K, PFG, and inhibitory tangential neurons supports persistent ring attractor dynamics even with noisy biological variation in connectivity strength36.

Next, we investigated how differential synaptic dynamics contribute to network function. To model synaptic dynamics, we filtered the synaptic output of each population by a second-order differential equation to generate an alpha function (Methods). We fit the two time constants of these alpha functions to our synaptic physiology data (Extended Data Fig. 5c–e). When all synapses were fast, we observed that small changes in global excitation or inhibition strength rapidly transitioned the network from a regime with transient responses (decay <0.1 s) to a regime with non-decaying responses (Fig. 3e). Slow decays similar to those we observed experimentally were only observed for a narrow band of excitation and inhibition weights. By contrast, when recurrent excitation was slow, we observed a large regime of slowly decaying persistence (Fig. 3f). Within this regime, small changes in global excitation or inhibition strength gradually modulated the duration of persistence (Fig. 3g,h). By incorporating trial-by-trial noise in excitation and inhibition strengths, the slow model—but not the fast model—produced a distribution of decay times approaching the ones we observed experimentally (Fig. 3i). We conclude that the combination of slow excitation and fast inhibition allows the recurrent architecture of h∆K and PFG to produce persistent activity using a broad range of excitation and inhibition strengths, and further allows the duration of persistent activity to be tuned through small changes in these strengths.

Finally, we tested whether the effects of slow excitation on stability and tuneability are specific to the h∆K–PFG circuit architecture, or a more general property of recurrent circuits. We generated a simplified recurrent network with one self-recurrent excitatory unit and one bidirectionally connected inhibitory unit (Extended Data Fig. 7). By assuming that the membrane time constant and synaptic onset kinetics were much faster than synaptic offset kinetics, we created a dynamical system with only two variables: recurrent excitation and inhibition (Methods). Similar to our full model, this simple network showed persistent activity that depended on the speed of recurrent excitation: fast excitation led to a narrow band of excitation and inhibition strengths with decaying persistent activity (Extended Data Fig. 7a), whereas slow excitation led to a much larger regime of tuneable decay durations (Extended Data Fig. 7b). This regime deteriorates rapidly with excitatory synaptic speed but is relatively insensitive to the kinetics of inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). We conclude that slow excitation promotes stable and tuneable persistence independent of network configuration.

Our imaging, electrophysiology and modelling support the hypothesis that recurrent interactions between h∆K and PFG generate a shared persistent activity bump during odour-evoked goal-directed runs. However, this model does not address how the bump is turned on and off (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Close examination of our imaging data revealed that PFG and h∆K neurons showed distinct bump dynamics depending on the fly’s behaviour. In PFGs, a low-amplitude bump was present at most times, and translated across columns during turns, becoming brighter during straight goal-directed runs (Fig. 4a). By contrast, h∆K only showed detectable bumps of activity during straight runs, and the bumps that appeared were generally fixed in place (Fig. 4b), consistent with our previous observations26. To test whether these differences in bump dynamics held across trials and flies, we measured how far each continuous bump deviated laterally across the FB (Fig. 4c). We found that both the maximum and cumulative lateral deviation were significantly smaller in h∆K compared to PFG (Fig. 4d). We further divided trajectories into periods of rest, turns, and straight running (Methods), and plotted the probability of observing a bump and its average amplitude during each behaviour. In both populations, bump probability and bump amplitude were highest during straight running (Fig. 4e,f). During turns and rest, PFGs showed a low-amplitude bump, whereas h∆K rarely showed a bump (Fig. 4e,f). These data argue that h∆K and PFG show similar dynamics during straight goal-directed runs, and that their activity must be functionally uncoupled at other times by some external mechanism.

In many parts of the central complex, lateral movement of a bump has been shown to encode a change in heading13,29, whereas in some local neurons, bump movement reflects travelling direction20,21. To test whether lateral shifts in PFG or h∆K bump position encode heading changes, we identified large shifts in heading (between 45–130°), and plotted bump position associated with these turns. We found that PFG bumps reliably shifted across columns during turns, similar to EPG neurons of the heading compass29 (Fig. 4g). By contrast, h∆K activity largely disappeared during turns, but could reemerge at a new position following the turn (Fig. 4h). In single trails, we could observe a positive correlation of PFG bump position with heading (Extended Data Fig. 8b,d). By contrast, h∆K neurons showed discrete jumps in bump position, with bumps appearing only during periods of relatively fixed heading (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). Correlations with travel direction were weaker than those with heading for both populations (Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). We conclude that both PFG and h∆K can track heading changes, but that PFG encodes continuous changes in heading, whereas h∆K exhibits punctate encoding only during straight runs.

Our observations suggest that PFG neurons might be able to switch between tracking heading (at low amplitude) and holding a goal signal (at high amplitude), when h∆K neurons turn on as well. A goal signal should not shift with heading23,24, and in a previous study, we found that h∆K bumps (labelled by the line VT062617-Gal4) did not shift when the wind was rotated during odour, driving compensatory turns26. To test whether PFG activity can switch between tracking heading and encoding a goal, we performed similar experiments in which we shifted the wind direction by 90° during either wind or odour while imaging from PFG neurons. We found that movement of the PFG bump depended on its amplitude (Fig. 4i,j). When PFG bump amplitude was low, bump position often shifted with heading (Fig. 4i, left), whereas when bump amplitude was high, bump position tended to remain fixed (Fig. 4i, right). To quantify this, we computed a rotational gain (ratio of bump movement to heading change) such that 1 indicates perfect encoding of heading and 0 indicates a positionally stable bump (see Methods). The rotational gain of the PFG bump was negatively correlated with bump amplitude on a trial-by-trial basis (Fig. 4j, left and Extended Data Fig. 8g). Rotational gains above 0.75 were only observed when the PFG bump had a low amplitude, and were almost never observed in h∆K (Fig. 4j, right). We also observed a significant drop in rotational gain following odour onset by using a sliding window to compute rotational gain over time (Fig. 4k and Methods). We conclude that whereas h∆K shows a fixed bump position when present, PFG can switch from following heading to maintaining a stable goal-like bump position, in a manner that depends on bump amplitude and sensory input.

Our analysis suggest that the h∆K–PFG circuit can switch between a mode where PFG alone follows heading and a mode where both PFG and h∆K show stable goal-like bumps. To identify a mechanism underlying this switch, we revisited the connectome and our computational model. In published connectomes, only PFGs receive direct input from the compass system (EPG and ∆7 neurons that track fly heading, Fig. 5a; although h∆K does receive input from PEN neurons that encode angular velocity and rotate the heading bump37,38). This input is significantly weaker than the recurrent connections between h∆K and PFGs (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). We investigated whether this difference in input could be combined with gating of recurrent connectivity to produce the dynamics that we observed in our imaging. If recurrent connections were shut off, PFGs should follow their compass input, whereas if recurrence were switched on, their activity would be locked in place at the location of the last compass input. To test this idea, we provided a moving compass input to PFG neurons, and gated recurrent connections between h∆K and PFG OFF or ON (Fig. 5b). Consistent with our prediction, we found that when recurrent excitation was gated OFF, PFG bump position followed the compass signal with low amplitude bumps, whereas h∆K was silent. By contrast, when recurrent excitation was gated ON, both PFG and h∆K showed a localized high-amplitude bump that remained in place despite shifting input, similar to our experimental observations (Fig. 4a,b,i–k).

Seeking a more physiological mechanism to rapidly gate connectivity between h∆K and PFG, we explored whether strong inhibition of h∆K could serve the same decoupling function. We repeated our simulation but replaced gating of recurrent connections with strong inhibition of h∆K (Fig. 5c). We found that when h∆K was inhibited, PFGs followed the compass with a low-amplitude bump, whereas when h∆K was disinhibited, both populations showed a localized high-amplitude bump. Consistent with the observation that recurrent connections between PFG and h∆K are several-fold stronger than feedforward input from the compass system across connectomes (Extended Data Fig. 9b), we found that in order for disinhibition to stabilize bump position, recurrent excitation strength must significantly outweigh feedforward heading input (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d).

Finally, we tested whether this disinhibitory mechanism could be used to rapidly write an ongoing heading signal into memory. We simulated time-varying heading trajectories and removed inhibition when the fly was oriented in different directions (Fig. 5d), or sequentially removed inhibition after an update in heading (Fig. 5e). We observed that disinhibition rapidly stabilized bump position at the location of the compass input when inhibition was first removed (Fig. 5f). We conclude that disinhibition could serve to functionally gate recurrent interactions between anatomically connected partners, rapidly switching the circuit from following an input to storing a pattern in memory.

Our model results suggest that disinhibition could support the divergent dynamics we observed in PFG and h∆K neurons. If this model is correct, we would expect inhibitory inputs onto h∆K to be tonically active, and to show inhibition during sensory stimuli that promote goal-directed running. We would also expect higher activity during turns, when we observe suppression of h∆K relative to PFG. To test these predictions, we imaged from the two inhibitory tangential neuron types we previously identified through electrophysiology– FB5V and FB6M— as flies performed our olfactory navigation task.

Activity in these inhibitory inputs to h∆K strongly supports our disinhibition model. We first imaged from FB5V neurons (Fig. 6a), a group of nine neurons per side that provides feedforward inhibition only onto to h∆K, similar to the inhibitory input that we modelled above (Fig. 5c). We observed tonic activity that was strongly supressed during odour, and continued its suppression during maintained trajectories after odour offset (Fig. 6b). Across flies, we observed weak inhibition by wind and strong inhibition by odour (Fig. 6c and Extended Data Fig. 10a). On a moment-to-moment basis, we found that FB5V activity was negatively correlated with upwind velocity, and positively correlated with angular speed, exactly as predicted by our disinhibition model (Fig. 6d,e). These encoding features might reflect the dendritic inputs to FB5V, which are found in regions encoding both odour (crepine (CRE)39) and pre-motor activity (lateral accessory lobe (LAL)40,41,42; Fig. 6a). To examine the encoding of turns in more detail, we detected large turns (∆heading > 130°) and plotted average activity associated with these (Fig. 6f). We observed strongly increasing activity during large heading changes (Fig. 6f,g). To examine encoding of goal-directed walking, we detected deviations from the goal direction adopted during odour (>90° from goal direction) and plotted activity associated with these deviations (Fig. 6h). We observed that FB5V activity increased when the fly deviated from its goal (Fig. 6h,i). Our imaging data thus support a role for FB5V suppression in enabling h∆K activity and goal-directed walking, and a role for FB5V elevation in decoupling h∆K from PFG during turns.

We also examined the activity of FB6M neurons. This group of two neurons per side provides input to both h∆K and PFG and receives feedback from h∆K (Fig. 6j). We observed tonic activity with suppression only in response to wind (Fig. 6k,l and Extended Data Fig. 10b). FB6M activity during wind was positively correlated with angular speed, but showed no correlation with upwind velocity (Fig. 6m,n). Similar to FB5V, FB6M showed increased activity during turns (Fig. 6o,p) and when the fly deviated from its goal direction (Fig. 6q,r). The wind encoding of FB6M might reflect its inputs in mechanosensory regions, which are known to encode the presence of wind (wedge (WED)43,44; Fig. 6j). In our model, we find that inhibition of both h∆K and PFG does not decouple their activity but instead shuts off both populations (Extended Data Fig. 9e). We conclude that FB6M also plays a disinhibitory role, but may permissively regulate the activity of PFG and h∆K together, rather than serving to decouple these populations.

Attractor networks composed of recurrently connected neurons contribute to many neural functions, including gaze stabilization45,46, spatial working memory9, motor control and decision making10, navigation13,47 and emotional states48,49. By forcing diverse patterns of input onto a limited set of stable states, attractor networks offer many advantages for computation2, such as de-noising50, evidence integration51,52,53 and short-term information storage1. In computational models, recurrent networks with realistic fast units often fail to reproduce the slow persistent activity dynamics observed in experiments35,48. Attractor networks with fixed weights also do not generate activity restricted to particular behaviours, sensory inputs or internal states10,49. How biological recurrent networks are structured to generate stable dynamics that can be rapidly switched on and off by sensory input or behaviour is unclear.

One solution to generate robust slow dynamics is to make recurrent excitation slow35,48. A common mechanism for generating slow excitation is through N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors35, although other mechanisms, such as synaptic facilitation51 and peptide signalling48 have also been proposed. Conversely, many network models use gates to control the onset and offset of attractor dynamics4,6,7. Disinhibition is a common motif for gating or regulating the gain of neural activity. In cortical circuits, a canonical disinhibitory circuit from VIP interneurons to PV interneurons to pyramidal neurons has been shown to regulate neuronal gain54, contrast sensitivity55 and learning56. Disinhibition also contributes to skilled motor actions coordinated by the basal ganglia in mice57 and HVC in songbirds58. Despite the prevalence of disinhibition, the interaction of disinhibitory gating mechanisms with recurrent circuits has not been investigated in detail.

Here we took advantage of fly connectomes8,16 and genetics18 to investigate the relationship between anatomical connectivity and dynamics. Our results largely support the idea that recurrent connections between h∆K and PFG give rise to persistent activity bumps. We observed similar dynamics in both populations during goal-directed runs. We found that h∆K neurons exhibit persistent activity in response to synaptic input that was abolished by blockade of recurrent signalling. We built a connectome-based computational model of this circuit and found that it could stabilize activity at any location. However, some of the persistence we observed may arise upstream of this circuit, as inhibition in FB5V inputs to h∆K also outlasted the odour. A recent study identified MBONs upstream of FB5V that modulate movement timing following odours and might contribute to dynamics that we observed in FB5V59. The architecture of this network bears a marked resemblance to classical models that are proposed to underlie working memory in the prefrontal cortex1,60. However, the accessibility of the fly circuit also reveals several design features that enable this circuit to combine stable representations with rapid gating.

First, slow excitation in the h∆K–PFG circuit appears to be achieved through multiple biophysical mechanisms. PFG neurons do not express any fast transmitter, and instead express only neuromodulators and peptides18. Consistent with this expression profile, when we observed excitation in h∆K on stimulating PFGs, this excitation was slow and persistent (Fig. 2g). Our model indicates that slow recurrent excitation from local PFG neurons can generate attractor dynamics over a range of excitation and inhibition strengths and can make the duration of persistent activity tuneable. Our work expands on the classical idea that NMDA receptors are critical for building a stable working memory circuit1,35, and recent results arguing that neuropeptide receptors are required for a persistent aggressive state in mice48,61, suggesting that any slow signalling mechanism can serve to stabilize persistent activity.

Second, the h∆K–PFG recurrent network is split into two parts. In most attractor models, recurrent excitation occurs within a uniform population of excitatory neurons. Here instead we find that the network is composed of two morphologically8 and transcriptomically18,62 distinct neuron types that receive distinct inputs. PFG neurons receive a heading direction signal from the compass system, whereas h∆K neurons receive inhibition from FB5V. In our model, this allows PFGs to encode the content of memory, while FB5V gating of h∆K controls the timing of memory formation. By separating input from timing control, our model enables rapid gating of recurrent activity. h∆K and PFG also receive common input, for example from travel direction-encoding h∆B neurons20,21, which might allow the circuit to perform additional computations. The separation of the circuit into two halves may also facilitate proper wiring of the network. Future studies might investigate the molecular signals that allow h∆K and PFG to wire together in a ring structure, that establish the necessary ratio between recurrent and feedforward synapses, and that allow h∆K and PFG to wire to both distinct and common inputs.

Finally we show through modelling that inhibition of one half of such a split attractor network can allow a circuit to rapidly switch between two modes: information following and information storage. Our model functions similar to a latch in digital logic63. When one half of the circuit (h∆K) is strongly inhibited, the recurrent circuit becomes functionally decoupled, and the other half (PFG) can follow their inputs freely. Disinhibition can rapidly turn on the recurrent circuit and lock the current input value into place. This model is consistent with several pieces of experimental data shown here. It reproduces the observed dynamics of both h∆K and PFG neurons during ongoing navigation and wind shifts, as well as the activity of FB5V during odour and turns. Our model is also consistent with causal experiments shown in our previous studies. In Matheson et al.22, we showed that sparse activation of h∆K neurons (labelled by VT062617-Gal4) could drive movement in a reproducible goal direction, and in Kathman et al.26, we showed that optogenetic silencing of h∆K neurons reduced the persistence of odour-evoked runs. A rigorous test of our computational model will require additional causal experiments. For example, activation and silencing of FB5V should switch the circuit between information following and information storage, with predictable changes in the amplitude and rotational gain of both PFG and h∆K activity. Writing a bump into h∆K or PFG using laser activation24 should also produce predictable changes in the activity of the other population and behaviour.

Gated recurrent networks have been theorized to initiate intrinsic dynamics, such as persistent activity, and to coordinate more complex forms of dynamics, such as the manipulation of information in working memory and motor preparation and control3,6. Similar types of gates are used extensively in machine learning64, including as a solution to rapidly reset memory traces65. Here we describe a biological form of gating that allows a recurrent anatomical circuit to dynamically alter its function on fast behavioural timescales. If integrated into recurrent networks with different connectivity structures2,66,67,68,69, disinhibition could be used to rapidly alter the function of other types of attractor networks, allowing for flexible use of line attractors, rotations, sequences or bistable attractors in a stimulus- and behaviour-dependent manner.

Female flies were raised on standard cornmeal-agar medium at 25 °C on a 12-h light cycle. For optogenetics experiments, the food was supplemented with 50 µl of 35 mM all-trans retinal (Sigma, R2500, dissolved in ethanol) mixed with ~1 teaspoon of hydrated potato flakes. Experimental flies were aged to 1–3 days for electrophysiology experiments or 9–14 days for imaging experiments. A list of fly genotypes is shown in Supplementary Table 2 and a list of fly reagents is shown in Supplementary Table 3.

Calcium imaging was performed as described in our previous study26. In brief, we anaesthetized flies over ice and a chilled (4–10 °C) aluminium sarcophagus and then glued them onto custom 3D-printed holders. We minimized movement of the brain by stabilizing the proboscis and head, and glueing the eyes, head and anterior tip of the thorax to the holder. To access the FB for imaging, we removed a small piece of the surface cuticle, trachea and air sacs over the back of the brain using sharpened forceps. We positioned flies over an air-supported ball (9 mm diameter General plastics FR-7110, painted with black spots, supported by 0.4 l s−1 air) using two cameras (30 fps, FLIR Blackfly, Computar 8.5 mm 1:1.3 adjustable lens) at the front and side of the fly. A third camera (100 fps, Grasshopper, 94 mm/0.5× InfiniStix Proximity Series lens, Edmund Optics Focal Length Extenders, working distance 15 cm) was used to track the ball using Fictrac software70. We illuminated the fly and ball using two infrared LEDs (M850F2) and T-cube LED Drivers (LEDD1B) coupled to fibre optic cables (Thorlabs M118L03 flat cleave patch cables). We continuously perfused (1 ml min−1) the brain with extracellular saline (103 mM NaCl, 3 mM KCl, 5 mM TES, 8 mM trehalose dihydrate, 10 mM glucose, 26 mM NaHCO3, 1 mM NaH2PO4H2O, 1.5 mM CaCl22H2O and 4 mM MgCl2.6H2O, pH 7.1–7.4, osmolarity 270–274 mOsm) bubbled with carbogen (5% CO2, 95% O2) and warmed to 33 °C.

We performed all imaging under a 20× water objective (Olympus Plan Fluorite XLUMP 20×/1.0) using an infrared laser (SpectraPhysics MaiTai HP or Coherent Axon 920) at 920 nM and 25–35 mW (measured at sample) using a galvo-galvo scanner. Simultaneous fluorescence emission from GCaMP7f and tdTomato were separated by bandpass filters (Semrock, FF01-525/50-32 for green and FF01-607/70-32 for red) and detected using two GaAsP photomultiplier tubes. We captured volumes consisting of three 192 × 96 µm optical sections, separated by 15 µm, taken at 8 volumes s−1 with a 1.2 µs dwell time.

In all imaging experiments, flies walked on a floating ball and received wind (25 cm s−1) and odour (0.5% apple cider vinegar, 0.3 l min−1) stimuli controlled by custom Python code. The wind direction was set by a rotary union (Dynamic Sealing Technologies, LT-2141-OF-ES12-F1-F2-C2) controlled by a stepper motor (Oriental PKP566FMN24A, with controller CVD524-K) and microcontroller (TeensyDuino +USB), and was controlled in closed loop by the flies’ heading measured by ball movement as we described previously26. The starting wind direction was randomly selected from 0°, 45°, −45°, 135° or −135°. Wind was on from 5–60 s of each 65 s trial. The odour signal was randomly selected between five possible patterns on interleaved trials: odour step (15 s) or odour pulses of 1, 4, 7 or 10 pulses (1 Hz, 0.5 s pulse width). When the odour was turned off, a compensatory air valve was opened to maintain total air speed. Air to all lines (wind, ball support, odour, compensated air) were passed through a pressure regulator (Cole-Parmer MIR2NA) and charcoal filters (Drierite 26800 Drying column, with desiccant replaced by activated charcoal). Wind and compensated air were also humidified. Airflow for the wind line was controlled by a mass flow controller (Aalborg Model GFC17), while airflow for odour, compensated air, and ball support were controlled by flowmeters (Cole-Parmer PMK1-010608). We controlled the timing of wind stimuli using a solenoid valve (Cole-Parmer Masterflex 01540-11), and the timing of odour and compensate using high-speed three-way solenoid valves (Lee company, LHDA1233115HA).

During wind-shift experiments, the wind was rotated by 90° across 2.2 s either in the presence of odour (10 pulses at 1 Hz) or without odour. The onset of the shift was set to occur 4 s after odour onset. We also included control trials where wind was not shifted in the presence or absence of odour. The data from non-shift control trials were included in all analyses that did not depend on the precise odour stimulus.

For electrophysiology, we anaesthetized flies over ice, glued them to custom 3D-printed holders, and then removed their two front legs. To access dorsal cell bodies, we removed a large piece of the cuticle, trachea, and air sacs from the back of the brain, then manually detached the sheath using fine forceps. We minimized brain movements by removing the muscles on the brain and stabilizing the proboscis with glue. Starting at the dissection, and maintained throughout the entire experiment, we continuously perfused extracellular saline (same recipe as above), bubbled with carbogen, over the brain. Using a 40× objective (Olympus, LUMPLFLN40XW), an LED source (Cairn Research MONOLED), and a filter (U-N19002 AT-GFP/F LP C164404) we visualized GFP-positive cell bodies for recordings. Prior to recording, we cleaned the area around the target cell using fine-tip glass pipettes filled with extracellular saline.

For patch clamp recordings, we pulled glass pipettes with a Sutter P-1000 puller, pressure polished the pipettes (final resistance of 3–5 MΩ), and then filled them with intracellular solution (140 mM KOH, 140 mM aspartic acid, 10 mM HEPES, 1 mM EGTA, 1 mM KCl, 4 mM MgATP, 0.5 mM Na3GTP, and 13 mM biocytin hydrazide). We amplified the voltage signals using an Axonpatch 200B amplifier with a Brownlee Precision 410 preamplifier and then digitized the signals at 10 kHz. We delivered 73 µW mm−2 red light (625 nm, measured at light source) for activating CsChrimson using a Thorlabs LED (M625F2) and T-Cube LED Driver (LEDD1B) coupled to optical fibres cables (Thorlabs M118L03 flat cleave patch cables) positioned below the head.

To better observe a mixture of excitation and inhibition, we depolarized cells to −38.1 ± 7.1 mV (mean ± s.d., n = 37 cells) using a small amount of positive current. Cells that did not spike were discarded. In all experiments, we randomly looped through 11 stimuli: seven optogenetic light stimuli (4 s of 12 µW mm−2 low power; 4 s of 23 µM mm−2 medium power; 4 s of 73 µM mm−2 high power; 1 Hz pulses with 0.2 duty cycle; 1 Hz pulses with 0.5 duty cycle; 1 Hz pulses at 0.8 duty cycle; and a light plume stimulus), three current stimuli (4 s of −4 pA; 4 s of 0 pA; and 4 s of 4 pA), and one wind or odour stimulus (wind on for 20 s, 5% apple cider vinegar on for 4 s). We constructed the light plume stimulus by filtering the odour encounters of a fly navigating in a virtual olfactory plume26 with a positive derivative filter. The stimuli were looped five times in all cells, and then five times per drug condition. While we only report the results of light pulse stimuli in this paper, the voltage changes we observed—such as fast inhibition or slow persistent excitation—were seen across all optogenetic temporal patterns used.

In several experiments, we perfused drugs onto the brain to block neurotransmitter receptors. In these experiments, drugs were mixed with extracellular saline and perfused onto the brain for at least five minutes before resuming stimulus presentation. Since picrotoxin generated large excitatory responses to synaptic input, we often hyperpolarized the cells to −50.3 ± 10.2 (mean ± s.d., n = 10 cells) to minimize depolarization block. If cells did enter depolarization block, we paused the experiment until the cell recovered. The list of drugs, their sources and the final concentrations used are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

To perform immunohistochemistry, dissected brains were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (dissolved in PBS) for 15 min, washed 3× in PBS, incubated in 5% normal goat serum (dissolved in PBST) for 60 min, incubated overnight in primary antibody solution (dissolved in 5% normal goat serum), washed 3× in PBST, incubated overnight in secondary antibody solution (dissolved in 5% normal goat serum), washed 3× in PBST, and washed 3× in PBS. The primary antibody solution contained chicken anti-GFP (Fisher Scientific RRID:AB_1074893) 1:50, mouse anti-nc82 (DSHB RRID:AB_2314866) 1:50, and rabbit anti-dsRed (Clontech 632496) 1:500. The secondary antibody solution contained Alexa488-conjugated goat anti-chicken (Fisher Scientific RRID:AB_2534096) 1:250, Alexa633-conjugated goat anti-mouse (Fisher Scientific RRID:AB_2535719) 1:250, and Alexa568-conjugated goat anti-rabbit (Fisher Scientific RRID:AB_2576217) 1:250. For imaging, the brains were mounted on microscope slides, immersed in Vectashield (Vector Labs H-1000), sealed with coverslips, and then imaged using a 20× objective (Zeiss W Plan-Apochromat 20×/1.0 DIC CG 0.17 M27 75 mm) on a Zeiss LSM 800 confocal microscope at 1.25 μM depth resolution.

To compare hemibrain neuron morphology to R65C03-GAL4 (Extended Data Fig. 2c), we warped a stain of R65C03 (from Flylight71) and hemibrain skeletons of layer 6 tangential neurons using the 2018 Janelia female template brain72. We overlaid the warped stain and warped skeletons and identified neurons with high overlap.

Data from the hemibrain connectome16 were obtained from neuprint explorer (http://neuprint.janelia.org, hemibrain:v1.2.1) and analysed using custom Python code. Prior to visualizing the weight matrices (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 1f), we sorted each cell type by their FB or protocerebral bridge x position (that is, columns), with h∆K positioning determined by their axons. To count the fraction of FB6M or FB5V synapses onto h∆K axons, we sorted synapses by their x position on a h∆K cell-by-cell basis. To calculate the ratio of recurrent synapse to EPG synapses (Extended Data Fig. 9b), we also examined data from the FAFB (https://codex.flywire.ai, FAFB v783) and male CNS (http://neuprint.janelia.org, male-cns:v0.9) connectomes. For each PFG neuron, we calculated the total number of synapses from h∆K neurons, the total number of synapses to h∆K neurons, and the total number of synapses from EPG neurons. The recurrence was the average synapses to and from h∆K neurons, and this was divided by the total inputs from EPGs to calculate the ratio. Since the FAFB data was less curated, and occasionally contained PFG neurons with 0 connectivity to EPG or h∆K neurons, we only included PFG cells that had a total recurrence strength and heading strength both above 10. Neuron and brain visualizations in Extended Data Fig. 1a,b were made using Flywire data17,73 in Codex (https://codex.flywire.ai/?dataset=fafb&data_version=783)74.

We used fictrac software70 to transform the x, y and z rotations of a custom-made ball into 2D walking trajectories. The forward velocity and angular velocity were directly calculated as rotations around the x and z axes, respectively, which were then used to calculate heading (motor position, calculated as the integral of angular velocity), position (x = integral of forward velocity × sin(heading); y = integral of forward velocity × cos(heading)), and upwind velocity (vy = forward velocity × cos(heading)). The rotation around the y axis (side velocity) was additionally used to calculate travel direction (heading + tan−1(forward velocity/side velocity)). For data analysis, the position, angular velocity, angular speed, upwind velocity, and forward velocity were smoothed using a running average of 1 s width.

We used custom Matlab software to pre-process our calcium imaging data (see ref. 26 for details), including motion correction, fluorescence extraction (across eight hand-drawn regions of interest (ROIs) across the FB), and alignment with fictrac behavioural data. To detect activity bumps in h∆K neurons, PFG neurons, and neurons labelled by VT062617-Gal4, we lowpass filtered bump amplitude data (Butterworth filter (sampling rate (fs) = 100 Hz, cut-off frquency (fc) = 2 Hz)) and then established a threshold on a trial-by-trial basis according to the minimum ∆F/F value of that trial and the ∆F/F s.d. across all trials. For most analyses, this threshold was set at minimum(∆F/F) + 1 × s.d., but to identify large PFG bump onsets and offsets for Fig. 1k–m, the threshold was increased to minimum(∆F/F) + 1.75 × s.d. A minimum bump duration was set at 3 s, and any above-threshold activity within 3 s of bumps was merged. To calculate bump position, the raw ∆F/F values across all 8 ROIs were smoothed (running average, width ~2 s) and then fit with a von Mises distribution at each time step using the Matlab function fminsearch. To aid fitting, we used the previous bump position or the ROI with the maximum ∆F/F (if the previous time step did not have a bump) as the initial search values. These bump positions were reported as a phase angle, where −180° is the left side of the FB and 180° is the right side of the FB.

During calcium imaging of FB5V and FB6M neurons, the calcium signal showed an artefactual decay from trial start to trial end. This artefact was removed by fitting an exponential decay using the beginning (first 5 s) and end (last 5 s) of the ∆F/F signal, and then subtracting this fit from the ∆F/F signal. Therefore, all ∆F/F signals reported for FB5V and FB6M are changes from this baseline.

In Fig. 1i,l, and Extended Data Fig. 1k, we calculated the persistence of walking direction following odour. To calculate the persistence of walking direction, we first defined a goal direction as the mean heading direction adopted in the first second after odour offset (post odour) or after trial start (baseline control), and then identified the time when flies stopped walking (forward velocity under 0.5 mm s−1 for at least 1.5 s) or deviated from the goal direction by at least 45°. In Fig. 1h,i,k,l, we calculated the persistence of neural activity following odour. To calculate the neural persistence, we calculated the time between odour offset and bump offset. To better compare neural and behavioural persistence, we only considered trials where the bump activity turned on before odour offset and turned off after odour offset.

In Fig. 1j,m, we aligned bump amplitude and behavioural data to bump offset. We only included trials where the bump activity turned on before odour offset and turned off after odour offset, and we removed any data before bump onset. In control bump ON data, we took the same trials, but only included data between bump onset and bump offset, each aligned by the midpoint of the bump. For goal deviation, the ‘goal’ was defined as the mean heading during the first 1/6th (between 0.18 and 4.46 s) of the bump ON or bump offset data. The durations of bump ON and bump offset data were matched for each trial.

In Fig. 3d, we calculated the mean bump width of h∆K activity. To do this, we isolated periods with bumps, aligned the raw ∆F/F calcium signals (across 8 ROIs) to the column with the highest signal, and then normalized the activity by the maximum activity.

In Fig. 4d, we calculated the maximum bump deviation and cumulative bump deviation. To quantify maximum bump deviation, we calculated the difference between the minimum and maximum unwrapped bump position between each bump onset and offset. To quantify cumulative bump deviation, we calculated how much the unwrapped bump position changed at each time point between bump onset and offset, summed the absolute value of these changes, and then divided the sum by the total length of the bump period.

In Fig. 4e–g and Fig. 6f,g,o,p, we identified discrete periods of turning. To identify turns, we identified segments of data where the unwrapped heading shifted by at least 90°. We then identified the beginning and end of each turn by searching backwards or forwards in time, respectively, until the heading stabilized (the maximum change in heading over 0.25 s was smaller than the 80th percentile of heading s.d. across all bins of the same duration). Since this algorithm isolated periods of turning with different durations, when turns were aligned in time (Figs. 4g and  6f,o), the data were time warped such that all turns were equal in length. In cases where small turns were compared to large turns (Fig. 4g), turns were classified as small if the total change in heading was less than 130°, and large otherwise.

In Fig. 4e,f, we further classified behaviour as ‘rest’ or ‘straight running’. Rests were defined as periods of low movement (v < 0.5 mm s−1) for at least 3 s. Straight running was defined as movements with high walking speed (v > 50th percentile of speed for given fly) and stable heading (∆heading < 90°). Short straight running bouts (under 3 s) within 1 s of larger bouts were merged, and large bouts (over 3 s) within 3 s of each other were merged. Any turns that had overlapping sections with straight running bouts were removed.

In Fig. 4h, we calculated discrete shifts in h∆K bump position following turns. To do this, we identified pairs of h∆K bumps separated in time. For each bump pair, we calculated the change in wrapped heading from the end of the first bump to the beginning of the second bump, and then classified the pairs as left turns (0° > ∆heading) or right turns (0° < ∆heading). Since these data were wrapped, we centred the wrapping around the bump position or heading taken at the end of the first bump.

In Fig. 4i–k, we selected trials where a bump was present for the entire duration of the wind-shift stimulus and the fly walked for at least 20% of the bump period. We then calculated the rotational gain across these bump periods by dividing the cumulative change in unwrapped bump position by the cumulative change in unwrapped heading. Therefore, each data point in Fig. 4i represents a single bump from a single wind-shift trial. As both bump position and heading are represented by angles (see above for bump position), a rotation gain of 0 indicates stable bumps and a rotation gain of 1 indicates perfect tracking. The average bump amplitudes were calculated across the same time periods as the rotational gains. We ensured that the bump position and heading data were pre-processed equivalently by filtering both data sets using the same filters (moving average with a width of 13 samples at 100 Hz) and downsampling the data to match the original imaging sampling rate (downsample from 100 Hz to 6.37 Hz). To test the robustness of the correlation between bump amplitude and rotation gain, we bootstrapped the data (with replacement) 10,000 times and calculated s.d. error on the fit, R2 and P values. For Fig. 4k, we analysed all trials that contained an odour stimulus. For each time point, the rotation gain was calculated by comparing the cumulative change in bump position to the cumulative change in heading within a 2 s window beginning at that timepoint. To avoid timepoints where the bump was mostly absent or the fly heading was stationary, we excluded timepoints if the total window did not contain sufficient bump data (<50%), if the cumulative delta heading was too low (<0.4°), or if the rotational gain was too high (>5).

In Extended Data Fig. 8b–f, we correlated bump position with heading or travel direction for each trial. We only excluded trials if the trial contained no bump activity.

In Fig. 6e,n, we cross-correlated FB5V and FB6M ∆F/F signals with angular speed or upwind velocity. Prior to cross-correlating, we mean subtracted the fluorescent and behavioural signals. To remove wind-coupled activity fluctuations in FB6M data, we only used data from 5 s after wind onset and 5 s before wind offset.

In Fig. 6h,q, we aligned FB6M and FB5V activity to deviations from goals. We first defined a goal direction as the mean heading adopted in the first second after odour offset, and then aligned neural and behavioural data to the time when flies deviated from this goal by at least 45°.

For analysis of electrophysiology data, the voltage traces were lowpass filtered using a Butterworth filter (fs = 10,000 Hz, fc = 5 Hz), downsampled by a factor of 10, and then baseline subtracted. We calculated persistent excitation (Fig. 2d,f,i and Extended Data Fig. 3e,h) by summing the baseline-subtracted voltage signal between light offset and trial end, and then normalizing by the length of this period. For visualizing voltage signals across trials (for example, Fig. 2c), the voltage signals were sorted by persistent excitation (Fig. 2a,c,e,g,h and Extended Data Fig. 3a) or inhibition during the stimulus (Fig. 2j,l and Extended Data Fig. 4c).

All statistics were ran using GraphPad Prism 10 and reported in Supplementary Table 1. Non-parametric statistical tests were used if the data were not normally distributed (see Supplementary Table 1). An alpha value of 0.05 was used to determine significance, with *0.01 < P < 0.05, **0.001 < P < 0.01, ***0.0001 < P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001 reported on figures. For imaging experiments, flies were only included for further analysis if they reliably oriented upwind on at least 50% of trials, which was identified by a convergence of heading values towards the upwind direction (0°) and an increase in mean upwind velocity around wind or odour onset. For electrophysiology experiments, cells were only included for analysis if they showed visible spiking activity, defined as rapid deflections above 10 mV. Other than these criteria, all data and replications were included in the manuscript. Sample sizes (number of flies or cells) were selected based on previous experiments. Stimuli were randomized within each experiment. Experimenter was not blind to genotype but all analyses were applied programatically to all datasets without regards to genotype.

To model the FB recurrent network, we created a rate-based dynamical system model consisting of 30 h∆K neurons, 18 PFG neurons, and 1 global inhibitory neuron. We approximated all dynamical systems using Euler’s method of integration with a time step of 0.001 s. To generate ring recurrence between h∆K and PFG neurons, we gave each neuron a relative position in the FB, indicated by an angle from 0 to 2π, and then connected the populations with local excitation that was maximum at overlapping positions and decayed with distance. This was done explicitly using a Gaussian equation fit to the real connectivity from the hemibrain connectome (Figs. 3 and  5) or using the connectivity directly from the connectome (Extended Data Fig. 6). The local spread of the Gaussian connectivity was set by the local connectivity width (σ, Gaussian s.d.), which establishes how quickly the connectivity decays as the distance (in radians) between h∆K and PFG neurons increases (σPFG>h∆K = 0.25, σh∆K>PFG = 0.25, in radians). The best fit Gaussian connectivity was found by searching for the local connectivity width (σ) that minimized the absolute error between the fit weight matrix and real weight matrix. Each column of the real weight matrix (the connectivity of each PFG neuron to all h∆K neurons) was normalized to ensure fits were based on the local connectivity width rather than variability in synaptic strength across the FB. Although real h∆K neurons have a 180° shift across the FB, for simplicity, we only show connectivity and activity simulations from the ‘axons’ of h∆K neurons. The weight matrices between h∆K or PFGs and the global inhibitory neuron were either one-to-all or all-to-one.
