Phase shifts were stochastic, occurring with a 0.1% chance at each time step, and when they occurred, they were randomly drawn from a Gaussian distribution with µ = 0 and σ = 50° and then smoothed over time according to:

Where \(\tau \)smooth equals 1. To account for the differences in synaptic strength between EPGs>PFG and h∆K<->PFG synapses, we decreased the amplitude of the sinusoidal input to 1/6 of the recurrent excitation strength. We controlled the gate in Fig. 5 by either externally changing the excitation strength (exc in equations (1,2), increased from 0 to 7) or changing external input to h∆K (\({\overrightarrow{I}}_{{\rm{h}}\Delta {\rm{K}}}\) in equation (1), inhibition corresponded with a value of −5, and disinhibition corresponded with a value of 0). In Extended Data Fig. 9e, we additionally attempted to gate bump dynamics by adding external input to h∆K and PFG neurons (\({\overrightarrow{I}}_{{\rm{h}}\triangle {\rm{K}}}\) and \({\overrightarrow{I}}_{\mathrm{PFG}}\) in equation (1), increased from −1 or −2 to 0).

To calculate the network decay rate in Fig. 3, we calculated the maximum difference in h∆K output at each time step following external input offset and then fit this difference with an exponential decay function.

In Fig. 3d, we expanded the model simulations to predict how each simulation would appear if the neurons were recorded using population imaging, such as calcium imaging. Calcium imaging captures activity throughout each active neurons’ axons. Therefore, we calculated how much each model neuron should spread across the FB to synapse with its postsynaptic partners. This spread was then applied to the model simulation to get a better prediction of how far activity of the active neurons would spread across the FB. In Extended Data Fig. 5f,g, to keep the neuron size the same across simulations we used real connectome data to estimate the width of real h∆K neurons, and then used this spread to estimate the width of FB activity. We fit the relationship between local connectivity s.d. and FB activity percentage with an exponential equation.

In the parameter space in Extended Data Fig. 7c,d, for each pair of parameters (ainhibition and aexcitation), we first calculated the decay tau of the excitatory neuron across each excitatory strength value, removed all values above 30 s, and then we summed these values to get the total ‘sum’.

In Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 6, we calculated the bump position by finding the relative position (as an angle) of the neuron with the maximum activity.

This means that the variables uexc and uinh instantaneously follow the synaptic dynamics. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Cryo-EM structure of a methanogen nitrogenase–PII protein supercomplex
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Edwin Antony
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Nitrogenases are metalloenzymes that catalyse the reduction of atmospheric dinitrogen to ammonia, sustaining the global nitrogen cycle1,2. Although bacterial nitrogenase has been extensively characterized, the architecture and regulation of archaeal nitrogenases have remained unknown despite longstanding evidence of nitrogen fixation in methanogens. Here we report a cryo-electron microscopy structure of a native nitrogenase–PII protein supercomplex from Methanosarcina acetivorans. The structure reveals an assembly of three NifDK heterotetramers bridged by six NifI1,2 heterotrimeric PII complexes, which sterically block NifH association and lock the enzyme in an inactive state. The PII complexes show asymmetric binding of ADP and 2-oxoglutarate, coupling nitrogenase inhibition directly to cellular energy and nitrogen status. Addition of 2-oxoglutarate and ATP releases the NifI complexes, stimulating a threefold increase in NifDK activity in vitro. This higher-order architecture identifies a regulatory strategy in methanogens in which PII proteins drive nitrogenase oligomerization to control activity. The finding that nitrogenase activity may be modulated through direct assembly into higher-order structures indicates future directions for the exploration of nitrogenase evolution, regulation and biotechnological applications.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A Jurassic mammaliaform swimmer and transformation of the mammalian pharynx
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Z.-X. Luo
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The discovery of a well-preserved mammaliaform fossil from the Middle Jurassic period of China reveals evidence on the evolutionary transformation of the feeding apparatus and the ecological diversity of Mesozoic era mammals. Mammaliaforms are evolutionary predecessors to modern Mammalia1,2,3, and their morphologies provide primary insights into the evolutionary origin of mammals. The rare preservation of a therian-like pharyngeal vault (throat passage) and hyoid skeletal anatomy (throat bones) in this mammaliaform suggests that critical soft-tissue anatomy for therian-like swallowing, drinking and suckling behaviours had evolved in the common ancestors of Docodonta and Mammalia, long before the rise of modern mammals. This fossil exhibits a wealth of features specialized for swimming, filling in a major gap of anatomical knowledge of pelvis and hindlimb for early mammals. It is characterized by highly distinctive canines and pseudo-carnassial sectorial teeth for a faunivorous diet. We interpret that this mammaliaform was semiaquatic, swimming and foraging in water, with a lifestyle analogous to the extant platypus. This species is the largest of Jurassic mammaliaforms. It expands the body size range of docodontans, and adds to a growing body of evidence that multiple docodontans exploited diverse niches with semiaquatic and other ecomorphotypes. Docodontans are an early example of replicated evolution of the semiaquatic and other ecomorphotypes in the Mesozoic ecosystem dominated by dinosaurs, long before the diversification of extant mammals.

Megacauda shows taller and more reclined cusps than Castorocauda. d, Differences of molars in lingual view between Castorocauda (line drawing) and Megacauda (grey shading): m2: cusp g large and distinct in Castorocauda but absent in Megacauda; m3: cusps b and g are large and distinct in Castorocauda, but are reduced in Megacauda; m4: entoflexus is narrow and distinct in Castorocauda but wider and shallower in Megacauda; cusp c smaller in Megacauda than in Castorocauda. e, Differences of molars in occlusal view between Castorocauda (line drawing) and Megacauda (grey shading): m2 is bilaterally compressed more at the mesial and distal ends in Megacauda, in contrast to the more rectangular mesial and distal ends, and a fully formed distal basin in Castorocauda. m3-m4: cusps b and g are larger in Castorocauda than in Megacauda. Development of distal occlusal basin on m2-m3-m4: present in Castorocauda (plesiomorphic for docodontans) but absent in Megacauda (absence of distal basin is related to bilaterally compression, an apomorphy, as compared to most other docodontans). a, Plesiomorphic features of the mammaliaform Morganucodon in which the pterygoid transverse process (plesiomorphic equivalent to hamulus) is more anteriorly placed, closer to the edge of the palatine and the upper tooth row, and also laterally aligned with the mandible. This plesiomorphic configuration lacks any required space for the muscles of the medial pterygoid group (Morganucodon: original graphics by Luo, modifed from ref. 1, previously re-interpreted from SI Ref 138). b, apomorphic configuration of Megacauda, in which the pterygoid hamulus is already therian-like: presence of a hook, placed more posteriorly and away from the palatine border, and also shifted medially from the corner of the palatine pyramidal process, such that the pterygoid hamulus is widely separated from the mandible. This apomorphic configuration has a saddle (concave area) of palatine for the passage of the M. tensor veli palatini to the soft secondary palate. The concave area lateral to the hamulus and posterior to the palatine pyramidal process is the space to accommodate the medial pterygoid muscle in extant therians, and for the M. tensor veli palatini and the levator veli palatini that are developmentally associated with the medial pterygoid muscle. The hook-like shape also indicates the pterygopharyngeal muscle that originates anteriorly from the hamulus in extant therians and is linked to the superior pharyngeal constrictors. c, interpretive reconstruction of soft secondary palate, with M. tensor veli palatini and M. levator veli palatini curving around the pterygoid hamulus, and with M. pterygopharyngeus originating medial to the pterygoid hamulus to connect with the superior pharyngeal constrictor. d and e, marsupial Didelphis virginiana with the derived musculoskeletal characters of the palatine, the pterygoid hamulus, and the hyoid apparatus with the ptergygopharyngeus muscle and the tensor veli palatini. f, Didelphis – visualization of diceCT scanning of the musculoskeletal structure of the palate and pharynx in the region of the pterygoid hamulus and the hyoid apparatus, to illustrate the muscle attachment of the tensor veli palatini and the ptergyopharyngeus muscle (=the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle). These palatopharyngeal musculoskeletal features of Didelphis provide the comparative evidence for reconstructing the soft secondary palate, the tensor veli palatine and the levator veli palatine for the docodontan Megacauda.

a, Megacauda pelvis (in anterolateral view with strong pectineal (pubic) tubercle and large notch for the M. iliopsoas as part of the hypertrophied pelvic-femoral muscles for rotation and adduction of the femur. b, Megacauda: disarticulated hindlimb and pes: femur in anterior view, tibia and fibula in anterolateral view, pes in ventral (plantar) view. c, Castorocauda: disarticulated hindlimb and pes: both Megacauda and Castorocauda show a specialized ankle joint capable of hyper-abduction and eversion. These semi-aquatic docodontans also show an elongation of the lateral pedal digit rays (4 and 5), more robust medial metatarsals, a strong lateral curvature of the phalanges resulting in asymmetrical feet, for paddling function of the hindlimb and pes in swimming, also with abducted foot posture as seen in Tachyglossus. d, land-living Agilodocodon hindlimb in anterolateral view and pes in dorsal view, showing far less elongation of the lower hindlimb and relatively shorter pes, and more symmetrical pedal digit rays10, all of which are plesiomorphic by contrast to specialized limbs of semi-aquatic docodontans.

a, Main-part (PMOL-AM00026A) XRF photograph, inset (b) of the posterior region of the rib cage. b, magnified area of the posterior thorax to show the broad and overlapping ossified costal rib plates, in both the left side of the ribcage (b-2), and the right side of ribcage (b-3) on either side of the sternal series (b-1). c, rib 6 shows a flattened and expanded distal plate, in stereo pair (c1 and c2). d, rib 7 shows a flattened and expanded distal plate, in stereo pair (d1 and d2). e, Monotreme Ornithorhynchus: ribcage with calcified costal rib plates that are so broad as to overlap each other, forming an imbricated series of costal plates in thoracic rib 6 through rib 13. Monotremes (both Ornithorhynchus and Tachyglossus) are also unique in exhibiting a fully calcified sternal segment of the thoracic ribs and forming a distinct joint with the intermediate costal rib segment (SI-Ref Gasc 1967). Outline of Ornithorhynchus skeleton in ventral view (e1) (new drawing, differing from previous illustrations of SI-ref 133, SI-Ref 241), and the ribcage in detail (e2) based on new observations of museum specimens). f, schematic reconstruction of thorax of semi-aquatic docodontans, to show the estimated positions of the broad and calcified costal plates in imbricated series (grey). Both Megacauda (Extended Data Fig. 10a–c) and Castorocauda13 show imbricated costal plates and plate-like distal thoracic ribs, as seen in monotremes. g, Land-living docodontan Microdocodon8 (original drawing by Luo, re-labeld from Ref-8 SOM Fig. S10) is characterized by thin, rod-like costal cartilages linking the thoracic ribs to the sternal series, a similar plesiomorphic pattern observed in other docodontans preserved with ribcage such as Agilodocodon10 and Docofossor12. All docodontans lack the ossified and jointed sternal rib segments of rib 1 to rib 5 as seen monotremes.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Human lung organoid modelling of tissue-resident antiviral T cell responses
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Calvin J. Kuo
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Tissue-resident immunity constitutes a first line of defence against pathogens and enables rapid innate and adaptive memory responses1,2,3. However, experimental studies have been hindered by a lack of holistic human in vitro models that enable epithelial infection in the context of tissue-resident immune subsets. In lung, differing notions of transient versus sustained residency of tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM cells) have challenged the extent to which anamnestic recall immunity to respiratory pathogens occurs locally or in concert with secondary lymphoid organs4,5,6. Here we generated long-term adult human distal lung organoids from intact tissue fragments in 3D air–liquid interface culture, which co-preserved epithelial and stromal components with endogenous lung-resident immune cells (T cells, B cells, natural killer cells and myeloid cells). The organoid T cells expressed residency and memory markers and preserved T cell receptor repertoires of cognate fresh tissue. SARS-CoV-2 infected the organoid lung epithelium, stimulated inflammatory cytokine production and, crucially, induced SARS-CoV-2-specific, tissue-resident T cell responses. Furthermore, boosting T cells within intact organoids with SARS-CoV-2 peptide pools blunted subsequent SARS-CoV-2 infection, consistent with a component of virus-specific protective TRM cell function in the absence of secondary lymphoid tissues. Overall, this immunocompetent lung organoid system demonstrates functional control of viral infection by lung-intrinsic memory T cell responses, provides a rationale for local vaccination strategies and validates a general platform for investigation of human tissue-resident immunity in health and disease.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A gut microbial odd-chain fatty acid alleviates atherosclerosis in mice
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Wenjing Zhao
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

The gut microbiota plays a pivotal part in human health, yet the molecular mechanisms that underlie its effects are largely unexplored. Bacteroides, a dominant genus in the human gut microbiota, is depleted in patients with atherosclerosis1, but its causal relationship with disease remains unclear. Here, using a mouse model, we show that administration of Bacteroides uniformis alleviates atherosclerosis through the upregulation of hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor expression. Bioactivity-guided screening revealed pentadecanoic acid (PA, C15:0), a saturated odd-chain fatty acid, as a principal bioactive metabolite. PA supplementation reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden by around 50% and significantly improved plasma lipid profiles, a result that underscores its therapeutic potential. Mechanistically, PA enhances cholesterol clearance by directly inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, suppressing hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis and promoting plasma low-density lipoprotein cholesterol removal. Analyses of 100 gut bacterial strains revealed that PA production occurs across multiple Bacteroidota genera. Notably, PA is markedly depleted in patients with dyslipidaemia. In summary, a Bacteroidota-derived odd-chain fatty acid regulates gut–liver crosstalk, and modulation of the microbial–metabolic axis has atheroprotective potential.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Observation of critical topological phase transition
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Baile Zhang
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:

volume

358–364 (2026) Cite this article

Phase transitions are traditionally understood within two seemingly incompatible theoretical paradigms. Landau–Ginzburg phase transitions1,2 are continuous, occurring at critical points where microscopic details become irrelevant and universal behaviour emerges, driven by gapless fluctuations with scale-invariant correlations3. By contrast, topological phase transitions connect gapped phases characterized by quantized topological invariants4,5 and, in doing so, necessarily pass through gapless phase boundaries where such invariants become ill-defined6,7,8,9. Here using an acoustic metamaterial platform, we experimentally demonstrate a unifying scenario—a critical topological phase transition—in which topology becomes well-defined at criticality10,11,12,13, overcoming this conventional incompatibility, and reorganizes critical behaviour by driving a phase transition along critical phase boundaries14. This transition gives rise to a topology-enforced multicritical point at an isolated intersection of critical boundaries with distinct topology. Along these boundaries, we observe topological edge states and diagnose criticality by means of logarithmic entanglement-entropy scaling15,16,17. At the multicritical point, the entanglement entropy shows additive logarithmic scaling given by the sum of contributions from adjacent boundaries, directly evidencing topology-enforced multicriticality. These findings establish a hierarchical organization of phase transitions, in which topology shapes criticality beyond the conventional Landau–Ginzburg paradigm and standard topological phase transitions.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: 5-oxoETE links redox control of epithelial damage detection and resilience
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.author: Philipp Niethammer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.text:
Nature (2026) Cite this article

Organisms harness oxidative stress to rapidly attract white blood cells to wound sites and to kill pathogens1,2,3. To this end, host tissues increase their own oxidative stress resilience and repair capacity via adaptive redox signalling4,5,6. Here, using live zebrafish and human cells, we identify a metabolic redox signalling mechanism that integrates oxidative immune defence with tissue adaptation. We demonstrate that DHRS7, an orphan short-chain fatty acid dehydrogenase–reductase, generates or consumes the pro-inflammatory lipid 5-oxoETE as a function of cytoplasmic NADP+/NADPH ratio. At wounds, where oxidative stress and NADP+ are high, 5-oxo-eicosatetraenoic acid (5-oxoETE) production by DHRS7 rapidly alerts antimicrobial white blood cells through the G-protein-coupled receptor OXER1. In undamaged tissue, where NADP+ is low, DHRS7 quenches unnecessary inflammation. Notably, we find that 5-oxoETE also supports epithelial redox resilience; OXER1-deficient zebrafish exhibit intestinal apoptosis, barrier disruption and microbial inflammation. Mechanistically, 5-oxoETE induces the expression of NUDIX hydrolases, which protect the cytoplasmic nucleotide pool from oxidation and prevent apoptosis in zebrafish and human intestinal cells. Thus, our data reveal a conserved mode of redox sensing and signalling—beyond classic thiol oxidation—that leverages NADPH metabolism to orchestrate the antimicrobial and pro-resilience functions of oxidative stress.

Oxidative stress is a hallmark of inflammatory, cardiovascular, fibrotic, infectious and neurological diseases1. Although in excess it can cause toxic damage to biomolecules, oxidative stress also serves fundamental innate immune functions. For example, NADPH oxidases (NOX proteins) of integumental surfaces and white blood cells produce large amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) to kill intruding microbes. Oxidative stress also marks potential sites of pathogen entry, such as wounds, to bring in immune reinforcements2,3. Concomitantly, non-lethal oxidative stress confers host resilience against ROS-induced bystander damage by upregulating antioxidant circuits or triggering regenerative responses4,5. The latter may include the polarization or recruitment of repair leukocytes (N2 neutrophils or M2 macrophages), stimulation of growth factor signalling and upregulation of antioxidant defences (for example, glutathione peroxidases)5. To serve as diffusible immune and resilience signals, ROS can reversibly modify cysteines of signalling proteins6. In addition, oxidative stress may trigger redox-mediated metabolic signals. For instance, at zebrafish wounds, NOX-mediated ROS generation locally alters the NADP+/NADPH cofactor balance in vivo7. Animals and humans that lack epithelial or myeloid NOX activity are prone to infection, for instance, during chronic granulomatous disease, a hereditary NOX2 deficiency8. The NOX-deficiency phenotypes cannot be solely explained by a lack of microbicidal ROS function and seem to involve aberrant redox signalling. Most current research on redox signalling focuses on the posttranslational modification of kinases and phosphatases by reversible thiol oxidation, whereas the contribution of ‘metabolic’ redox cues remains largely unexplored.

Zebrafish is a powerful animal model for the study of redox biology and rapid wound responses by intravital imaging. Their innate and adaptive immune repertoire and their responses to infection or wounds largely mirror those of mammals9. In zebrafish larvae, Ca2+ influx at the wound margin activates the epithelial NOX Duox. This enzyme produces H2O2 while consuming NADPH to mediate rapid leukocyte recruitment2. Acute neutrophilic wound inflammation via Duox and H2O2 was shown to involve both reversible Lyn kinase oxidation and production of 5-oxoETE3,10,11. 5-oxoETE serves as a potent leukocyte chemoattractant in fish and primates and is linked to allergic inflammation, infection defence, colitis and possibly cancer11,12,13. During oxidative stress, 5-oxoETE is formed from arachidonic acid by non-enzymatic lipid peroxidation or by 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5) and NADP+-dependent 5-hydroxyeicosanoid dehydrogenase (5-HEDH) activity14. Research into the oxoeicosanoid pathway has been hampered by the unknown genetic identity of 5-HEDH and the lack of obvious OXER1 orthologues in rodents. Here we set out to identify the 5-HEDH enzyme to better understand its regulation by oxidative stress and its physiological function.

Earlier work14 characterized 5-HEDH as a microsomal lipid dehydrogenase–reductase that interconverts 5(S)-HETE and 5-oxoETE in an NADP+/NADPH-dependent manner15 (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a), without identifying its genetic identity. We confirmed reversible 5-HEDH activity in human lung and intestinal epithelial cancer cells (A549 and Caco-2) using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) to detect product formation after supplying 5(S)-HETE or 5-oxoETE as substrates (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1b). Consistent with a low cytoplasmic NADP+/NADPH ratio in unstressed cells, there was a pronounced bias towards 5-oxoETE consumption. Based on the known cofactor dependence, subcellular localization16 and evolutionary conservation of 5-HEDH, we compiled a high-priority shortlist of 5-HEDH candidates and tested it using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) knockdown in A549 cells. Only knockdown of DHRS7, which encodes a short-chain dehydrogenase–reductase (SDR)17, significantly reduced 5-oxoETE or 5-HETE below wild-type control levels (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). Although knockdown of LMNA, HSD17B2, PECR and CBR1 also reduced 5-HETE levels, the effects were less pronounced than those observed with DHRS7 knockdown, and none of these knockdowns decreased 5-oxoETE levels (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

The DHRS7 nucleotide and protein sequences are conserved from fish to humans (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). Zebrafish and human DHRS7 proteins are approximately 58% identical. Although there are no available experimental DHRS7 structures, the superposition of AlphaFold predictions for DHRS7 orthologues points to high structural conservation (Extended Data Fig. 2c). DHRS7 features a NADP(H)-binding Rossman fold, and localizes to intracellular membranes, including those of the endoplasmic reticulum18,19, nucleus and mitochondria (Extended Data Fig. 2d–f). Based on co-localization metrics (Pearson’s r, Manders’ M1 and Manders’ M2), DHRS7 overlaps stronger with endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear markers than with mitochondrial markers (Extended Data Fig. 2f). Its cofactor preference and localization (endoplasmic reticulum)16 are consistent with those reported for 5-HEDH. Whereas DHRS7 was initially proposed to face the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, subsequent studies demonstrated its cytoplasmic orientation20,21 (Extended Data Fig. 2d). DHRS7 is broadly expressed in immune cells (for example, macrophages) and non-immune cells (for example, epithelial and glandular cells and fibroblasts) in various tissues including the prostate, liver and digestive tract19. Zebrafish single-cell RNA sequencing resources suggest that the overall expression pattern is relatively conserved22. In vitro, DHRS7 possesses reductase activity towards dihydrotestosterone, benzil and 4,4′-dimethylbenzil23. More recently, DHRS7 was identified as an acyl–alkyl-glycerone phosphate reductase that generates a distinct subset plasmalogen species compared with DHRS7B24. However, its physiological substrates and broader biological functions remain largely unknown. Of note, dehydrogenase activity was not previously described for DHRS7. Furthermore, the previously described conversion of 5α-dihydroxytestosterone to 3α-androstanediol also reflects reductase rather than dehydrogenase activity21.

To independently confirm our shRNA knockdown results, we generated DHRS7-knockout A549 cell lines using two different single guide RNAs (sgRNA1 and sgRNA2) (Extended Data Fig. 1e). 5-oxoETE and 5-HETE synthesis was significantly reduced in three independent DHRS7-knockout clones compared with the wild type (Fig. 1c). Similar results were obtained in CRISPR–Cas9-mediated DHRS7-knockdown Caco-2 cells (Extended Data Fig. 1f). In line with the previously reported endogenous subcellular localization, doxycycline (Dox)-induced DHRS7–eGFP localized to endomembranes (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 2d–f) and rescued 5-oxoETE and 5-HETE production (Fig. 1e). Dox alone (that is, without DHRS7 induction) had no such effect (Fig. 1f). DHRS7 overexpression also increased 5-oxoETE production of Caco-2 cells (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Overall, our data show that DHRS7 reversibly mediates the conversion of 5(S)-HETE to 5-oxoETE. In both unperturbed lung- and intestinal-derived epithelial cells, the reaction is biased towards the reverse (reductase) direction, suggesting that DHRS7 functions as 5-oxoETE sink at baseline.

To delineate whether or how oxidative stress affects 5-oxoETE production (Fig. 1g–i and Extended Data Fig. 1h), we exposed A549 DHRS7-knockout cells with or without Dox-induced DHRS7 expression overnight to RSL3 (Fig. 1g), which facilitates lipid peroxidation by inhibiting GPX4, or imidazole ketone erastin (IKE), which impairs cellular cystine import and glutathione (GSH) production. Alternatively, cells were briefly subjected to H2O2, which—unlike RSL3 and IKE—can directly initiate lipid peroxidation in the presence of iron25. H2O2 also increases the NADP+/NADPH ratio (Extended Data Fig. 3a), most probably because the rapid oxidation of GSH to glutathione disulfide (GSSG) drives NADPH consumption through glutathione reductase and other NADPH-dependent antioxidant systems. This compensatory response helps to protect cells against irreversible lipid and protein oxidation.

Pointing to additional enzymatic or non-enzymatic production routes, H2O2 exposure of cells increased 5-oxoETE levels in the absence of DHRS7 (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 1h, left). In the presence of DHRS7, these levels were substantially increased (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 1h, right). Hydrophilic (Trolox) and lipophilic (liproxstatin-1 (LPX1)) ROS quenchers completely abrogated H2O2-dependent enzymatic and non-enzymatic 5-oxoETE production, presumably by buffering oxidative stress (that is, limiting NADPH consumption by antioxidant circuits) and scavenging reactive oxygen intermediates that are involved in non-enzymatic 5-oxoETE formation. RSL3 and IKE significantly stimulated 5-oxoETE production in the presence of DHRS7 or after H2O2 pretreatment (Extended Data Fig. 1h), suggesting that DHRS7 sensitizes 5-oxoETE production to oxidative stress. Lipid peroxidation quenchers (LPX1 and vitamin E) curb rapid neutrophil recruitment to larval zebrafish wounds in vivo26. At least in part, this anti-inflammatory effect might derive from inhibition of 5-oxoETE production. Together, these regulatory relationships (Fig. 1i) suggest that DHRS7 mediates inflammatory redox sensing.

5-HEDH activity was often studied in microsome suspensions, where redox cofactor concentrations can be freely adjusted, and the reaction monitored via an NADPH fluorescence readout27. As mentioned above, previous studies suggest that the DHRS7 faces the cytosol20,21 (Extended Data Fig. 2d)—that is, the enzyme is exposed to the cytoplasmic cofactor pool. By western blotting and NADPH fluorescence monitoring, we detected endogenous DHRS7 protein and activity in nuclear, granular (mitochondria and lysosomes), and microsomal fractions of HEK293T cells, but not in the cytosol (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). To generate DHRS7-deficient microsomes, we depleted DHRS7 in HEK293T cells using CRISPR–Cas9 (Fig. 2a,b). Compared with wild-type microsomes, the DHRS7-deficient microsomes were severely impaired in converting 5(S)-HETE to 5-oxoETE and vice versa (Fig. 2c). Overexpression of human DHRS7 (HsDHRS7) or zebrafish Dhrs7 (DrDhrs7) restored both the forward and reverse reactions (Fig. 2d–g and Extended Data Fig. 3d,e). 5-HEDH activity was retained after purification of the Flag-tagged protein. Compared with the purified HsDHRS7, purified DrDhrs7 exhibited pronounced dimerization along with lower enzyme activity, possibly caused by sub-optimal purification conditions (Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 3h–m). Collectively, our cell, microsome and purified protein experiments establish the evolutionary conserved 5-HEDH function of DHRS7.

On microsomes, the dehydrogenase reactions of HsDHRS7 and DrDhrs7 showed similar pseudo-first order kinetics when varying 5(S)-HETE or NADP+ and measuring NADPH product formation using the same amount of microsomal DrDhrs7 or HsDHRS7 (Michaelis constant (Km) ≈ 0.5–1.5 μM, maximal velocity (Vmax) ≈ 15–50 nmol min−1 pmol−1 enzyme; Extended Data Fig. 3f,g). By contrast, the related SDR enzymes DHRS7B, DHRS7C, DHRS9, RDH11 and 15-PGDH28 showed no significant 5-HEDH activity (Extended Data Fig. 4a–h), suggesting that 5-HEDH activity is specific for DHRS7. As expected, NAD+ was a less efficient cofactor than NADP+ (Extended Data Fig. 3f, middle). Besides 5(S)-HETE, DHRS7 also oxidized 5(S)-HEPE, 6-trans-12-epi leukotriene B4 (LTB4) and 5S,15S-dihydroxy-6E,8Z,10Z,13E-eicosatetraenoic acid (5S,15S-DiHETE), but not 5(R)-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (HETE), LTB4 or 12S-HETE (Extended Data Fig. 4i–n), consistent with previous findings obtained using whole microsomal fractions15,29. Thus, the allylic 5(S)-hydroxyl group seems to be required and (R)-hydroxyls are preclusive for 5-HEDH dehydrogenase activity, in line with previous reports on 5-HEDH. Assuming a cytoplasmic NADP(H) pool size of about 3 μM (ref. 7), the micromolar Km of DHRS7 would be expected to function well as a cytoplasmic NADP+/NADPH sensor29,30.

Informed by previous studies of the catalytic31 and cofactor-binding sites32 of SDR family proteins, we generated five site-directed mutants of HsDHRS7 (K207E, Y203F, S190A, N162L and R82E). Although none of the mutations altered the subcellular localization of the enzyme, the K207E, Y203F and S190A mutations abrogated DHRS7 activity, whereas the N162L and R82E mutations had a stimulatory effect (Fig. 2i). When microsomes were provided with 5(S)-HETE, human, zebrafish and bovine DHRS7 showed similar rates of NADPH generation, but rat and mouse DHRS7 were much less active towards the same substrate (Fig. 2j). Species-dependent differences in the substrate selectivity among highly homologous enzymes or transporters are not uncommon33. Despite their conserved catalytic centre and similar secondary structures, SDR enzymes are known to display high catalytic plasticity34. Sequence alignment of the human, bovine, zebrafish, mouse and rat DHRS7 protein sequences indicates various amino acids as differentially conserved between the rodent or non-rodent orthologues (Extended Data Fig. 5). Probing their functional significance by systematic mutation may further explain the structural basis of species-specific 5-HEDH.

Overall, the above experiments underlined the redox-regulated bidirectionality of the Dhrs7 reaction (Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 6f). In unstressed tissue, where the cellular NADPH/NADP+ ratio is high, the reductase direction of the enzyme (5-oxoETE → 5-HETE) is thermodynamically favoured, that is, DHRS7 functions as a metabolic sink for 5-oxoETE at baseline conditions. The removal of this sink from uninjured tissue should give rise to 5-oxoETE accumulation from DHRS7-independent sources. 5-oxoETE accumulation was indicated by our DHRS7-knockout cell line experiments (Fig. 1h, −Dox). Using CRISPR–Cas9, we generated dhrs7 mutant fish (Extended Data Fig. 6a–e) and subjected their uninjured tail fins to LC–MS lipidomic (LIPID MAPS) analysis. As predicted from the enzymology of DHRS7–5-HEDH, the samples from dhrs7 mutant adults showed a significantly higher 5-oxoETE baseline along with decreased levels of select prostaglandin-related lipids (for example, bicyclo-prostaglandin E2 (bicyclo-PGE2)) (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 1).

Given the highly transient and localized dynamics of oxidative stress at zebrafish wound margins2 as well as the tissue quantities needed for LC–MS lipid measurements, a matching analysis of wounded tail fins was impractical. As we previously established that early leukocyte chemotaxis to injured tail fins requires 5-oxoETE along with Hcar1-4 (refs. 10,11), we instead decided to harness the leukocyte wound response as a proxy readout for 5-oxoETE generation at larval wound sites10,11. To this end, we counted the number of neutrophils (lyz+), macrophages (mpeg+) or both (transmitted light) at the injury site after triggering the wound response by hypotonic shock as previously described10 (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 6g–i). Similar to our previously published hcar1-4 mutants (hcar1-4mk214/mk214)11 and morphants10, homozygous dhrs7 mutants (dhrs7mk224/mk224 and dhrs7mk225/mk225) showed significantly impaired leukocyte recruitment to tail fin wounds (Fig. 3c,d, Extended Data Fig. 6g–i and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Consistent with previous findings12,35, macrophage chemotaxis was also inhibited (Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Videos 3 and 4).

Bath isotonicity blocks rapid wound closure, biomechanical cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPla2) activation and arachidonic acid release at zebrafish wound margins. The underlying osmo-responsive mechanotransduction mechanism has been extensively studied and reviewed elsewhere11,36. Since rapid leukocyte migration to zebrafish wound sites depends on 5-oxoETE, this response is diminished by isotonic bathing. Notably, leukocyte migration can be reconstituted either by switching to hypotonic bathing solution, which activates endogenous arachidonic acid production by cPla2 (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 6g–i), or by adding pure arachidonic acid (or 5(S)-HETE or 5-oxoETE) to the isotonic bath10.

If Dhrs7 mediates the conversion of arachidonic acid or 5(S)-HETE into 5-oxoETE at wounds, rapid leukocyte chemotaxis to externally provided arachidonic acid or 5(S)-HETE should be significantly impaired in dhrs7 mutant but not wild-type larvae. Indeed, dhrs7 disruption significantly blocked arachidonic acid- or 5(S)-HETE-dependent leukocyte chemotaxis to isotonic wounds (Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). The less complete inhibition of leukocyte migration to 5(S)-HETE-perfused, isotonic wounds aligns with the notion that 5(S)-HETE itself can act as a low-affinity agonist for the OXER1 receptor37. As expected, neutrophil chemotaxis to 5-oxoETE-perfused, isotonic (that is, ‘open’) wounds was unaltered in the dhrs7 mutants. Of note, 5-oxoETE-mediated macrophage migration was significantly affected (Extended Data Fig. 6l–n). Single-cell RNA sequencing data suggest strong Dhrs7 expression in macrophages22. Macrophages could potentially harness Dhrs7 as an adaptive chemoattractant sink to steepen shallow 5-oxoETE gradients ‘on the go’. This idea is fully consistent with the known redox-dependent enzymology of Dhrs7 and the concept of self-generated chemotactic gradients38. Although it may elegantly explain the above observation, more work is required to validate this idea.

dhrs7/hcar1-4 double mutation impaired acute leukocyte recruitment akin to the individual mutations, confirming that Dhrs7 and Hcar1-4 operate within the same acute, leukocyte recruitment pathway (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). Tail fin regrowth after amputation was slightly impaired in hcar1-4mk214/mk214 but less so in dhrs7mk224/mk224 mutant larvae (Extended Data Fig. 6q,r). As both mutants exhibited similar leukocyte recruitment defects, these defects were unlikely to mediate this subtle regeneration phenotype. Whether it instead reflects trophic 5-oxoETE signalling functions remains to be investigated.

DHRS7 and OXER1 mRNA and protein are expressed in the human digestive system, with highest mutual overlap in the small intestine19. In our previous work, we demonstrated that zebrafish Hcar1-4 is functionally orthologous to human OXER111. According to single-cell RNA sequencing resources22,39, their orthologues are expressed in the zebrafish digestive tract. However, the role of Dhrs7 in the zebrafish digestive tract is unknown. Consistent with a loss of 5-oxoETE sink function under homeostatic (that is, unstressed) conditions (Fig. 3a), dhrs7 mutants exhibited increased baseline neutrophil infiltration into their intestinal linings (Fig. 3g), which was sensitive to antioxidant treatment (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 7c). As intestinal apoptosis was unchanged in those fish (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a for representative images) and because the phenotype was insensitive to broad-spectrum antibiotics (Extended Data Fig. 7b), intestinal barrier defects with opportunistic microbial infection are unlikely to have contributed to it.

Hcar1-4 mutation (hcar1-4mk213/mk213 and hcar1-4mk214/mk214) increased baseline neutrophil infiltration (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7d), as in dhrs7 mutation or dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-mediated damage of wild-type guts. Of note, hcar1-4 and alox5a26 mutations abrogated the DSS-induced inflammation, implying its dependence on 5-oxoETE (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Figs. 6f and 7e). In mammalian animal models and human patients40, 5-LOX inhibitors such as Zileuton and MK-866 are known to improve colitis- or asthma-related symptoms, arguing for the physiological relevance of these zebrafish findings.

Whereas the sterile inflammatory dhrs7 mutant gut phenotype was consistent with non-enzymatic 5-oxoETE accumulation, it was difficult to reconcile the pro-inflammatory effect of hcar1-4 mutation with the established chemotactic role of 5-oxoETE10,11,14. As our previous work had shown increased expression of cell death-related transcripts (for example, casp6a and casp6l1) in hcar1-4 mutant larvae11, we investigated whether the pathway might have anti-apoptotic effects on epithelial cells. Indeed, we observed a pronounced increase in intestinal apoptosis in hcar1-4, but not in alox5a or dhrs7, mutant fish (Figs. 3h and 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Application of 5-oxoETE at a concentration lower than that used in the tail fin wounding experiments had no effect on intestinal neutrophil counts but reduced intestinal apoptosis in an hcar1-4-dependent manner (Extended Data Fig. 7h,i). Furthermore, hcar1-4 mutation significantly increased gut barrier permeability as measured by fluorescent dextran leakage from the gut lumen into the adjacent interstitial space (Fig. 4c). Pharmacological inhibition of apoptosis normalized the baseline neutrophil numbers in hcar1-4 mutant intestines (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 7j,k).

ROS are cytotoxic and can cause cell death of host cells as well as pathogens. These highly reactive and diffusive molecules may be generated when immune or intestinal epithelial cells become exposed to gut microbes, and have been ascribed both microbicidal and pro-repair functions41. However, hosts only benefit from ROS-mediated signalling and defence if they can effectively protect themselves against their toxic effects by increasing their own redox resilience. We conceived that Hcar1-4 signalling might contribute to such resilience.

Scavenging of hydrophilic ROS with Trolox rescued both apoptosis and neutrophilic inflammation (Fig. 4e) in hcar1-4 mutant intestines, whereas blocking lipophilic ROS with LPX1 had little effect (Extended Data Fig. 7l,m). Thus, Hcar1-4 selectively suppressed the toxicity of hydrophilic ROS. To test whether neutrophils are the source of the ROS, we chemogenetically ablated nitroreductase (NTR2.0)-expressing neutrophils in hcar1-4 mutants by bathing the larvae in metronidazole. Neutrophil depletion did not reduce intestinal apoptosis (Extended Data Fig. 7n). By contrast, treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics rescued both the apoptosis and neutrophilic inflammation phenotypes in hcar1-4 mutants (Fig. 4f). Together, these data suggest that hcar1-4 deletion impairs the tolerance of intestinal linings towards microbiota-linked ROS in vivo, which in turn increases apoptotic damage, chronic barrier leakiness and inflammation.

To test for phylogenetic conservation of the anti-apoptotic effects of OXER1, we silenced the human receptor in monolayer cultures of Caco-2 cells using either small interfering RNA (siRNA)- or CRISPR–Cas9-mediated knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 8a,c,d). OXER1 knockdown, but not non-targeting control (NTC) oligonucleotides, increased baseline apoptosis in serum-starved cells (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 8b). This was prevented by Trolox, but not LPX1, treatment (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b), mirroring our results in zebrafish. Furthermore, pretreatment with a physiologically relevant concentration of 5-oxoETE (1 μM) blunted H2O2-induced apoptosis compared with the vehicle control in an OXER1-dependent manner (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). These experiments suggested that baseline OXER1 signalling protects Caco-2 cells against baseline ROS toxicity.

Again, we sought clues for the putative resilience mechanism in our previously published hcar1-4 mutant transcriptomics data11. Those data revealed a strong repression of nudt15 transcription in hcar1-4 mutants (Extended Data Fig. 9e), whereas other antioxidant systems showed little change. NUDT15 (also known as MTH2) is one of several NUDIX hydrolase enzymes (NUDT1, NUDT15 and NUDT18, also known as MTH1, MTH2 and MTH3, respectively) involved in the elimination of oxidized purine nucleotides, which have been shown to protect cultured cells from oxidative stress42. Silencing of NUDT1, but not NUDT15, increased apoptosis in Caco-2 cells compared with NTC (Extended Data Figs. 8g and 9f), highlighting NUDT1 as the relevant functional isoform in human cells. OXER1 and NUDT1 knockdown blunted NUDT1 protein expression as assessed by β-actin-normalized NUDT1 band densitometry (Extended Data Figs. 8e,f, 9g and 10a–d) or immunofluorescence (Extended Data Fig. 10e,f). Conversely, pretreatment with 5-oxoETE enhanced NUDT1 expression in wild-type, but not in OXER1-silenced, cells (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 10g–i). Notably, the anti-apoptotic effect of 5-oxoETE pretreatment was lost in NUDT1-silenced cells (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Together, these experiments argue for a mechanism in which NUDIX hydrolases (Nudt15 or NUDT1) mediate anti-apoptotic functions of OXER1 in zebrafish and human cells by protecting against the genotoxic effects of oxidized nucleotides.

To further test this idea in vivo, we used two complementary approaches: First, we knocked down NUDIX hydrolases in wild-type zebrafish with an F0 CRISPR approach (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 11a–f). Second, we overexpressed NUDIX hydrolases in the gut epithelium of hcar1-4 mutant larvae using the intestinal epithelium-specific cldn15la promoter (Fig. 5h). F0 CRISPR of nudt15, but not nudt1, increased neutrophil counts (Fig. 5f) and apoptosis in the intestine compared with NTC (Extended Data Fig. 11g). F0 CRISPR larvae for both nudt1 and nudt15 were grown to sexual maturity without overt developmental defects. F0 CRISPR of nudt15 increased intestinal neutrophil counts and intestinal apoptosis in wild-type larvae but not in hcar1-4 mutants (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 11h). As the hcar1-4 and nudt15 mutant phenotypes were not additive, both proteins are likely to form part of the same genetic pathway. Expression of zebrafish Nudt15 or human NUDT1 in the gut epithelium using the intestinal epithelium-specific cldn15la promoter reduced neutrophil counts in hcar1-4 mutant guts back to control levels (Fig. 5h), underlining the functional redundancy of both enzymes and highlighting the need for a more detailed study of the physiological role of different NUDIX hydrolase enzymes.

Here we uncovered DHRS7 as a conserved, redox-regulated enzyme of the oxoeicosanoid pathway and find that oxoeicosanoid signalling protects intestinal linings from oxidative bystander damage, orchestrating its microbicidal, innate immune functions with epithelial resilience.

Owing to their pleiotropic chemical reactivity, ROS damage a broad range of known and unknown pathogens, along with nearby host cells that are not properly protected. Both the oxidant (NOX proteins) and antioxidant (such as reduced GSH–GSSG glutathione peroxidase–reductase) systems that manage immune-related oxidative stress require NADPH. If metabolism43 cannot resupply NADPH sufficiently quickly, the NADP+/NADPH and GSSG/GSH ratios increase. The temporary collapse of these antioxidant ‘floodgates’ permits membrane and protein oxidation44. Transient thiol oxidation of signalling proteins promotes the recovery of tissue homeostasis, in part through DNA protection, growth factor signalling, organelle remodelling, wound repair and regeneration6,30.

DHRS7 epitomizes a different, metabolic redox signalling paradigm in which the formation or degradation of a paracrine redox signal (5-oxoETE) depends directly on redox cofactor mass action, not protein oxidation. Like many other arachidonic acid-derived mediators, including prostaglandins, leukotrienes, lipoxins and specialized pro-resolving mediators, 5-oxoETE exerts its biological functions through a cognate G-protein-coupled receptor37,45, allowing changes in its metabolic production to be directly translated into cellular responses. DHRS7 metabolically couples innate immune cell recruitment to the respiratory burst activity of epithelial (Duox) or myeloid (NOX2) NADPH oxidases that often indicate pathogenic threats. Suppression of the sink function of DHRS7 by oxidative stress or by genetic deletion promotes 5-oxoETE accumulation, attracting leukocytes to damaged tail fins or intact intestinal linings. In addition, the OXER1 pathway prevents apoptosis of zebrafish and human intestinal cells by inducing DNA-protective NUDIX hydrolases42. Thus, oxoeicosanoid signalling not only triggers an innate immune response, but can also selectively protect the host against the damaging consequences of immune-linked ROS by increasing the redox resilience of mucosal barriers. Along with transient thiol oxidation of tyrosine kinases, this integrated mechanism may coordinate the pro-inflammatory and trophic functions of H2O2 at epithelial damage sites2,3,30.

The lack of clear OXER1 orthologues in rodents has severely impeded preclinical research into this pathway for the past 30 years. Although its causes are unknown, this conservation gap is no evolutionary oddity. Various biomedically relevant genes are conserved in fish and humans, but not in rodents—for example, human adenosine deaminase 2 (ref. 46). For studying specific, disease-relevant traits it is not sufficient to consider an organism’s mean evolutionary distance to humans, because the distance of its individual traits, such as, OXER1-mediated immune regulation, may markedly diverge from this average47. Combining alternative models with human cell culture approaches can thus help illuminating the ‘blind spots’ of mouse genetics. This approach led us to the identification of 5-HEDH activity as DHRS7. Although human and mouse and rat DHRS7 are more similar (78% amino acid identity, one-to-many comparison) than the human and zebrafish protein (58% amino acid identity, one-to-one comparison), mouse and rat DHRS7 showed little 5-HEDH activity in our microsome assay, unlike zebrafish, bovine and human DHRS7. Given the limited number of species and the unclear structural cause of this intriguing divergence, one must be cautious of overinterpretation. Nevertheless, the concomitant loss of OXER1 and DHRS7-dependent 5-HEDH-activity from rat and mouse seems to be notable and may point to the taxon-specific disappearance of an entire pathway. Using a systematic mutational approach and by modelling lipid ligand binding, we are currently seeking to identify the residues responsible for 5-HEDH substrate selectivity and activity. Once those are known, the question of whether the loss of OXER1 preceded the loss of the 5-HEDH function of DHRS7 or vice versa will become more approachable.

Because the catalytic direction of DHRS7 depends on cytoplasmic redox state and because DHRS7-independent production routes for 5-oxoETE exist, the inflammatory roles of the enzyme may vary depending on whether it generates or degrades 5-oxoETE. In undamaged tissue, when the NADP+/NADPH ratio is low, DHRS7 reductase function may limit the accumulation and diffusion of basal 5-oxoETE, the enzyme may have an anti-inflammatory function, in line with our observation in the zebrafish gut. However, when the NADP+/NADPH ratio is high, for example, at wound sites, DHRS7 boosts 5-oxoETE without limiting its diffusion, and the enzyme may have an overall pro-inflammatory function. When target cells, such as macrophages, express DHRS7, they may become their own 5-oxoETE gradient-shaping sinks. By dissipating the very signal that attracts them, DHRS7 expressing cells may both amplify the gradient they are following and contribute to the removal or the enhancement of the inflammatory cue at its source—that is, provide positive or negative feedback depending on whether oxidative stress at the source persists or has been resolved. Furthermore, OXER1 modulates inflammation in opposite ways: by protecting epithelial barriers from oxidative damage, it indirectly prevents barrier disruption and infection; and by recruiting leukocytes, OXER1 directly supports infection defence11. Thus, depending on redox state, DHRS7 can have anti-inflammatory or pro-inflammatory functions.

The integrated, pro-inflammatory and pro-resilience functions of 5-oxoETE may contribute to mammalian pathophysiology. Namely, tissue abundance of 5-oxoETE seems to correlate with mucosal health in patients with inflammatory bowel disease13, consistent with a mucoprotective role. Pharmacological OXER1 inhibition in primates not only inhibits leukocyte infiltration of bronchial linings, but is also linked to the disappearance of bronchial mucus-producing cells12, perhaps through apoptosis. Furthermore, 5-oxoETE was reported to promote the tissue-protective N2 polarization of neutrophils48. Pro-migratory function was previously shown for OXER1 in cultured cancer cells in vitro49, and deletory OXER1 and DHRS7 frameshift mutations occur in gastrointestinal and endometrial tumours50. OXER1 expression also appears to be prognostic for colorectal, pancreatic and renal cancer outcomes19. Future studies should determine whether or how these observations are linked to metabolic redox signalling and NUDIX-dependent mucosal protection.

Adult wild-type and transgenic reporter casper52 zebrafish were maintained at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) Zebrafish Core Facility53, and all experiments were conducted in accordance with institutional animal healthcare guidelines, with approval from the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of MSKCC. Generation and genotyping of alox5a and hcar1-4 mutants used in this study were described previously54. Both the leukocyte and apoptosis phenotypes were more robust in the hcar1-4mk214/mk214 line (this line has a large truncation and a mutation at an upstream part of the hcar1-4 coding region, whereas the mk213 line is mutated at a more downstream genomic region), so we used this line for the majority of the experiments. For wounding assays, larvae aged 2.5 to 3 days post-fertilization (dpf) were anaesthetized in isotonic E3 medium (145 mM NaCl, 0.17 mM KCl, 0.33 mM CaCl2, 0.33 mM MgSO4) containing 0.2 mg ml−1 ethyl 3-aminobenzoate methanesulfonate (Tricaine/Syncaine, Sigma, E10521). Oxoeicosanoid signalling in the intestines was studied in 6 dpf larvae. At 2.5-6 dpf, the sex of zebrafish larvae cannot be determined, and it is unlikely to influence the biological processes under study. For the adult lipidomics studies, both male and female fish were used (three biological replicates for each sex and genotype).

For wounding experiments, the tail fin tips of anaesthetized 2.5–3 dpf larvae were carefully removed with a surgical microblade (Fine Science Tools, 10318) at the boundary of the notochord, ensuring the notochord remained uninjured55. For regeneration assays, the regenerated fin length was measured 3 days post-amputation, from the notochord to the distal edge of the regrown tissue56.

For the chemical colitis experiments, DSS was obtained from Sigma (42867). On the day of the experiment, a 10% w/v stock of DSS was made in embryonic E3 medium as described previously57,58. DSS was further diluted to a working concentration of 0.25% w/v in E3. Larvae at 5 dpf (wild-type or mutant) were randomly distributed to E3 with or without DSS for 24 h. The fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS or PBSTX before further processing. ZVAD-FMK was obtained from ApexBio (A1902) dissolved in DMSO and stored as a 300 mM stock solution at −20 °C. The drug was used at a working concentration of 300 µM in E3 as described59,60. Larvae at 5 dpf were randomly distributed to E3 with ZVAD-FMK or 0.1% DMSO for 24 h. The fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS before further processing. Z-DEVD-FMK was obtained from MedChemExpress (HY−12466) dissolved in DMSO and stored as a 300 mM stock solution at −20 °C. The drug was used at a working concentration of 150 µM in E3 as described61. Larvae at 5 dpf were randomly distributed to E3 with Z-DEVD-FMK or 0.05% DMSO for 24 h. The fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS before further processing. NS3694 was obtained from MedChemExpress (HY-108356) dissolved in DMSO and stored as a 10 mM stock solution at −20 °C. The drug was used at a working concentration of 10 µM in E3 as described61. Larvae at 5 dpf were randomly distributed to E3 with NS3694 or 0.1% DMSO for 24 h. The fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS before further processing. Metronidazole was obtained from Sigma (PHR1052-1G) dissolved in DMSO and stored as a 100 mM stock solution at −20 °C. The drug was used at a working concentration of 150 µM in E3 as described by us and others54,62. hcar1-4mk214/mk214 tg(lyz:QF2 × 5×QUAS:NTR2.0) larvae at 5 dpf were randomly distributed to E3 with metronidazole or 0.15% DMSO for 24 h. The fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS with 0.05% Triton-X (PBSTX) before further processing. Ampicillin (BP1760-25) and kanamycin (BP906-5) were obtained from Fisher, dissolved in distilled water and stored at −20 °C. Antibiotics were used at a working concentration of 50 µg ml−1 and 15 µg ml−1 in E3 for ampicillin and kanamycin, respectively. Larvae at 4 dpf were randomly distributed to E3 with either ampicillin/kanamycin or 0.1% distilled water. Larvae were transferred to fresh E3 with or without antibiotics after 24 h. Fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS or PBSTX before further processing. Trolox was obtained from Selleck chemicals (S3665), dissolved in DMSO and stored as a 50 mM stock solution at −20 °C. The drug was used at a working concentration of 50 µM as described63. LPX1 (SML1414-5MG) was obtained from Sigma Aldrich dissolved in DMSO and stored as a 100 mM stock solution at −20 °C, and used at a working concentration of 20 µM as described26. For experiments with 5-oxoETE, the lipid was obtained as an ethanol-based solution (Cayman Chemical, 34250) and was used at a working concentration of 300 nM. Larvae at 5 dpf were randomly distributed to E3 with 300 nM 5-oxoETE or 0.1% ethanol for 16 h. The fish were euthanized and fixed using 4% formaldehyde in PBS or PBSTX before further processing.

Intestinal neutrophils were visualized by Sudan Black staining as described11,26,64. In brief, Larvae were fixed in 4% formaldehyde in PBS overnight at 4 °C, washed 3 times with PBS and stained with Sudan Black (Sigma Aldrich, 199664) for 1 h. Larvae were washed 3 times with 70% ethanol and rehydrated in PBS with 0.1% Tween (PBST) for 5 min. Larvae were then treated with depigmentation solution (1% KOH, 1% H2O2 in water) for 5 min followed by 2 PBST washes before imaging.

Active caspase-3 was visualized using the protocol described with minor modifications65. Larvae were fixed in 4% formaldehyde in PBSTX overnight at 4 °C. Larvae were then washed with PBSTX and blocked for 2 h at room temperature in a blocking solution (PBSTX supplemented with 2 mg ml−1 bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 1% DMSO). Primary antibody (anti-active caspase-3 (BD Biosciences Product: 559565 and 570524)) was diluted 1:100 (for 559565) or 1:500 (for 570524) in blocking solution and larvae were incubated overnight at 4 °C. Larvae were washed with PBSTX and incubated with secondary antibody conjugated with Alexa Fluor 488 or 555 (Abcam, ab150077 or ab150078, respectively) diluted 1:1,000 in blocking solution overnight at 4 °C. Finally, larvae were washed with PBSTX and mounted for imaging.

Microgavage was performed as described66. 4 kDa molecular weight FITC-labelled dextran (Sigma Aldrich FD4-100MG) was dissolved in PBS to obtain a 10 mg ml−1 solution. This solution was then loaded into a microinjector needle. Before gavage, 6 dpf zebrafish larvae were anaesthetized with 0.2 mg ml−1 MS-222 (Fisher Scientific, NC0589195) dissolved in E3. After verifying proper depth of anaesthesia, the larvae were positioned laterally, ventral side towards the vertical wall of an agarose mold. Afterward, the needle was gently manoeuvred down the oesophagus and into the anterior intestine. The dextran was then injected into the lumen (typically, volumes of 5–10 nl were used). The needle was then gently but firmly removed from the fish. Larvae were then transferred to E3 to recover from the anaesthesia and kept in E3 for 60 min and then used for imaging experiments.

Two independent guide RNAs (gRNAs) (dhrs7-sgRNA-1 and dhrs7-sgRNA-2) of zebrafish dhrs7 (ENSDARG00000003444) were designed and ordered from IDT (integrated DNA Technologies). The Cas9–gRNA ribonucleoprotein complex (single dhrs7-sgRNA-1 or a combination of dhrs7-sgRNA-1 and dhrs7-sgRNA-2) was injected into the cytoplasm of 1-cell-stage zebrafish embryos. After the injected F0 larvae matured (2–3 months post-fertilization), individual F0 adults were crossed with wild-type adults to produce F1 progeny. These F1 larvae were then grown to sexual maturity, and genomic DNA was isolated from their tail fins for genotyping. Tail fins were partially amputated, suspended in 250 μl of 50 mM NaOH, and incubated at 95 °C for 10 min. Samples were then cooled on ice for 10 min, neutralized with 25 μl of 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8), and vortexed. The genotyping primers are listed in Supplementary Table 2. PCR products from F1 dhrs7-sgRNA-1 adult fish were incubated with FastDigest PvuII (Thermo Fisher Scientific; FD0634) enzyme at 37 °C overnight. The reaction mixture was then separated by agarose gel electrophoresis. F1 heterozygous adults were identified by the presence of three DNA fragments (404, 340 and 68 bp). The 404 bp product represents a mutant allele where the PvuII site has been disrupted by Cas9-induced mutation. This 404 bp band was isolated from the agarose gel and sequenced via Sanger sequencing. F1 heterozygous adult zebrafish with the frameshift mutation of interest (4 bp deletion, dhrs7-1; Extended Data Fig. 6) were bred to achieve homozygosity.

PCR products from F1 dhrs7-sgRNA-1 and dhrs7-sgRNA-2 injected heterozygous adult zebrafish were also separated by agarose gel electrophoresis. The PCR products using the dhrs7-sgRNA-1 primers, digested with PvuII, revealed an in-frame mutation with a total 12 bp deletion (8 bp deletion and 4 bp deletion). Meanwhile, the PCR products using the dhrs7-sgRNA-2 primers, digested with BseLI (Thermo Fisher Scientific; FD1204), showed a frameshift mutation with a 2 bp deletion. The digested PCR products of dhrs7-sgRNA-2 were identified by the presence of three DNA fragments (252, 147 and 107 bp). The 252 bp product represents a mutant allele where the BseLI site has been disrupted by Cas9-induced mutation. This 252 bp band was isolated from the agarose gel and sequenced via Sanger sequencing, confirming the 2 bp deletion. F1 heterozygous adult zebrafish with the frameshift mutation of interest (14 bp deletion (8 bp deletion, 4 bp deletion and 2 bp deletion), dhrs7-2; Extended Data Fig. 6) were bred to achieve homozygosity.

Potential gRNA target sites were identified using the web program CHOPCHOP (http://chopchop.cbu.no/index.php). All gRNA target sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Two independent gRNAs for nudt1 (ENSDARG00000030573) and four independent gRNAs for nudt15 (ENSDARG00000113961) were designed and ordered from IDT (for sequences see Supplementary Table 2). As a negative control, non-targeting guides were ordered from IDT (1072544,1072545 and 1072546). The target-specific or non-targeting Alt-R CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and common Alt-R trans-activating CRISPR RNA (tacrRNA, IDT 1072532) were dissolved in nuclease-free duplex buffer (IDT; 11-01-03-01) to obtain a 100 mM stock solution. To prepare the crRNA:tracrRNA duplex, equal volumes of 100 mM Alt-R crRNAs (1:1) and 100 mM Alt-R tracrRNA stock solutions were mixed to obtain a final concentration of 10 mM each. The mixture was heated to 95 °C for 5 min and then cooled down to room temperature. ALT-R SpCas9 Nuclease (IDT, 1081058) was diluted to 1 mg ml−1 with Cas9 working buffer (20 mM HEPES, 150 mM KCl, pH 7.5). The Cas9–gRNA ribonucleoprotein complex was assembled by combining the crRNA:tracrRNA duplex and Cas9 protein solutions at a 1:1 ratio, incubated at 37 °C for 5 min and then placed at room temperature. Cas9–gRNA ribonucleoprotein complex solution (2.3 nl) was injected into the cytoplasm of 1-cell-stage zebrafish embryos. At 2.5–3 dpf, genomic DNA was isolated from individual F0 larvae for genotyping. Each specific target sequence of interest was PCR amplified from the genomic DNA samples with the primers listed in Supplementary Table 2. Next, PCR products were incubated with the FastDigest (Thermo) restriction enzymes BccI (NEB, R0704S) for nudt15-g1, BseLI (FD1204) for nudt15-g2, MvaI (FD0554) for nudt15-g3, Cfr10I (FD0184) for nudt15-g4, BstXI (FD1024) for nudt1-g1, or in the case of nudt1-g2, BtsI-v2 (NEB, R0667S) for at least 2 h at 37 °C. Then, samples were separated by agarose gel electrophoresis (see Supplementary Table 2 for primers) and guide efficiency was evaluated (Extended Data Fig. 11).
