Quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) was performed using Maxima SYBR Green/Fluorescein qPCR Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific; K0242) on a Bio-Rad real-time PCR machine. Relative OXER1 expression was normalized to β-actin and calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method70. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 2.

DHRS7 orthologues from Homo sapiens (ENSG00000100612), Danio rerio (ENSDARG00000003444), M. musculus (ENSMUSG00000021094), R. norvegicus (ENSRNOG00000005589) and B. taurus (ENSBTAG00000020729) were cloned to pSBtet vector containing a C-terminal eGFP–6×His sequence. Human DHRS7 point mutations (K207E, Y203F, S190A, N162L, R82E) were generated and inserted to the pSBtet vector. All the pSBtet-DHRS7 constructs were co-transfected with the pCMV(CAT)-T7-SB-100 transpose vector into A549 cells (for co-localization assays) or HEK293T DHRS7-KO1 cells (for microsome experiments). Stable cell lines were selected for one week with 10 μg ml−1 blasticidin S hydrochloride, induced with 1 μg ml−1 Dox for 1-2 days, and subsequently screened by flow cytometry for eGFP-positive cells. For DHRS7 overexpression in Caco-2 cells, human DHRS7-eGFP was cloned to the pCW57-tet vector. Lentiviral production and infection were performed as described above. Stable cell lines were selected with 600 μg ml−1 G418 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10131035) for 7-10 days, induced with 1 μg ml−1 Dox for 1-2 days, and subsequently enriched by flow cytometry sorting for eGFP-positive cells.

DHRS7 from H. sapiens (UniProt ID: Q9Y394) and D. rerio (UniProt ID: Q0P3U1) was expressed in HEK293S GnTI− cells (ATCC, CRL-3022), using the inducible stable cell line system. Briefly, the HsDHRS7 and DrDhrs7 cDNA sequences were cloned into the pSBtet vector containing a C-terminal 3C–eGFP–3×Flag–10×His sequence. The stable cell lines were generated by co-transfection of pSBtet-hsDHRS7 (or pSBtet-drDhrs7) and the pCMV(CAT)-T7-SB-100 transpose vector, followed by 1 week of selection with 10 μg ml−1 blasticidin S hydrochloride. All plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

The stable cells were grown in suspension at 37 °C in FreeStyle 293 Expression Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 12338026) with 2% (v/v) FBS under 8% CO2. When the cells reached a density of 2.0–2.5 × 106 cells per ml, 1 μM Dox and 10 mM sodium butyrate were added, respectively, and the growth temperature was lowered to 30 °C to boost protein expression. After 48 h of treating Dox and sodium butyrate, the cells were collected by centrifugation at 550g and resuspended in lysis buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% (v/v) glycerol supplemented with cOmplete protease Inhibitor Cocktail tablet EDTA-Free (Roche, 04693132001). The cells were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored in −80 °C.

All protein purification steps were performed at 4 °C. Thawed cell pellets were processed for microsome extraction as described above, then solubilized with 1% (w/v) n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM) for 1 h. Insoluble materials was removed by centrifugation at 33,745g for 1 h. The supernatant was subsequently incubated with prewashed anti-Flag M2 resin (Sigma Aldrich, A2220) for 1 h and washed with 10 column volumes of washing buffer (microsome purification buffer containing 0.1% (w/v) DDM). The HsDHRS7 or DrDhrs7 proteins were eluted using 5 column volumes of elution buffer (washing buffer containing 0.2 g l−1 3×Flag peptide (Sigma Aldrich, F4799)).

To remove the affinity tags, 3C proteases were then added to the eluted proteins to remove the eGFP and 3×Flag–10×His tag before the elution was concentrated by a 50-kDa MWCO spin concentrator. The sample was then purified by size-exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 28-9909-44) equilibrated with washing buffer containing 0.003% (w/v) DDM. Peak fractions were pooled and used for the further activity assays.

Stable cell lines were established by fluorescence-activated cell sorting of eGFP-positive cells at the MSKCC Flow Cytometry Core on BD FACSAria (Aria5/Aria6), FACSymphony S6 and FACSDiscover S8 instruments. Cells were gated sequentially: intact cells on FSC-A/SSC-A (P1); single cells by two successive doublet-discrimination gates (P2, P3); and eGFP-positive cells on the eGFP channel versus a second fluorescence channel to exclude autofluorescence (P4), with the positive gate set relative to a GFP-negative control (0% in P4). The gating and sorting strategy is shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. Flow cytometry was used solely to enrich fluorescent protein-expressing cells during line generation; no flow-cytometric data are presented as experimental results.

HEK293T DHRS7-knockout and DHRS7-overexpression cells were plated in 96-well plates, 1 mM H2O2 was added to the cells for 20 min. Then the NADP+/NADPH ratio was detected using the NADP/NADPH-Glo Assay (Promega, G9082). In brief, each well of cells was washed with 50 μl PBS, followed by homogenization with 50 μl of base solution containing 1% DTAB. Next, 50 μl of each sample was transferred to an empty well and mixed with 25 μl of 0.4 N HCl. The plate was covered and incubated at 60°C for 15 min, then cooled down to room temperature. To neutralize the acid, 25 μl of 0.5 M Trizma base was added to each well containing acid-treated cells and add 50 μl of HCl–Trizma solution was added to each well containing base-treated samples. Finally, an equal volume of NADP/NADPH-Glo Detection Reagent was added to each well, and the plate was gently shaken and incubated for 30 min at room temperature. Luminescence was recorded using Gen5.

For the A549 cell culture LC–MS lipid detection, 1,000,000 cells were plated to 6-well plate and incubated at 37 °C overnight. The next day, cells were washed three times by PBS. Then, 1 μM 5-oxoETE or 1 μM 5(S)-HETE was added to 1.5 ml of Leibovitz’s L15 medium (Thermo fisher Scientific; 21083027) and introduced to each well. The cells were incubated at 37 °C for 20 min. The supernatant was collected for the LC–MS analysis.

For the LC–MS lipid detection in HsDHRS7-knockout A549 cells under different treatments, 500,000 cells were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated at 37 °C overnight. The next day, 0.2 μg ml−1 Dox was added to induce DHRS7–eGFP expression for 24 h. On the third day, cells were treated with either 1 μM RSL3, 1 μM or 5 µM IKE, 20 μM LPX1 or 50 μM Trolox overnight (18 h). After RSL3 or IKE treatment, 1 μM 5(S)-HETE was added for 20 min. For H2O2 treatment, 1 mM H2O2 and 1 μM 5(S)-HETE were added to the medium, with or without 20 μM LPX1 or 50 μM Trolox for 20 min.

Before lipid extraction, 10 μl of a standard solution (0.5 μg ml−1 5(S)-HETE-d8 and 0.5 μg ml−1 5-oxoETE-d7) was added to each sample. The eicosanoid extraction was performed with some modifications of an earlier method71. Samples were extracted using Sola Solid Phase Extraction Plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific; A00707). In brief, the columns were conditioned with 3 ml of 100% methanol and then equilibrated with 3 ml of double-distilled H2O. Samples were loaded onto the columns, and the sample flow throughs were reloaded to ensure efficient binding. The columns were washed twice with 1 ml of H2O: Methanol (90:10 by v/v) to remove impurities. Metabolites and lipids were eluted with twice 500 μl of 100% methanol. Prior to LC–MS analysis, samples were evaporated using a SpeedVac and reconstituted in 50 μl of H2O: acetonitrile:acetic acid (60:40:0.02 v/v/v).

For LC–MS lipid detection in HEK293T microsomes, cells from 10 plates of each genotype were collected by centrifugation at 3,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The pellets were resuspended in 50 ml NTE buffer (150 mM NaCl, 15 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 7.5), and centrifuged again at 3,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting pellets were resuspended in cold cell lysate buffer (0.1 M potassium phosphate buffer pH 7.5, 250 mM sucrose, 50 mM KCl, 1.1 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM DTT, 1:1000 protease inhibitor cocktail (Millipore Sigma, 11873580001)). The cell suspension was lysed using a Dounce homogenizer with 50–60 strokes. To remove unbroken cells, cellular debris, nuclei and mitochondria, the lysate was centrifuged at 12,000g for 20 min at 4 °C. Microsomes were isolated by ultracentrifugation at 186,000g for 1–2 h and resuspended in cold resuspension buffer (0.1 M potassium phosphate buffer pH 7.5, 50 mM KCl, 1.1 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM DTT, 20% (v/v) Glycerol, 1:1000 protease inhibitor cocktail). Protein concentration was determined by the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific, PI23227). The concentration of HsDHRS7–eGFP and DrDhrs7–eGFP was quantified using eGFP standard.

The enzyme assay was performed as follows: 1 ml reaction buffer (90 mM potassium phosphate, 40 mM KCl, 0.1 mM DTT, pH 7.5) containing microsomes from HsDHRS7-KO1 (20 μg) and HsDHRS7-overexpression (20 μg, containing 4.39 pmol HsDHRS7–eGFP), or HsDHRS7-knockout (16 μg) and DrDhrs7-overexpression (16 μg, containing 4.39 pmol DrDhrs7–eGFP), 10 μg microsomes (HEK293T, DHRS7-KO1, DHRS7-KO2, DHRS7-KO3), 100 μM NADP+ or 100 μM NADPH, 1 μM 5(S)-HETE or 1 μM 5-oxoETE was incubated at 37 °C for 20 min. The reaction was stopped by placing the tubes on ice and adding 10 μl of a reference standard solution (0.5 μg ml−1 5(S)-HETE-d8 and 0.5 μg ml−1 5-oxoETE-d7), followed by 4 ml hexane. The aqueous phase was acidified to approximately pH 3.0 by adding 20 μl of 4 N HCl to facilitate the extraction of carboxylic acids. Samples were vortexed and centrifuged at 3,000g for 10 min at 4 °C to ensure phase separation and remove precipitated materials. The organic phases were collected, evaporated using a SpeedVac, and reconstituted in 150 μl buffer A (water/acetonitrile/acetic acid, 60/40/0.02, v/v/v).

Whereas absolute 5-oxoETE/5-HETE baseline levels often varied between individual lipid extractions (for example, Fig. 1b versus Fig. 1c), within the same extraction–LC–MS session, the relative differences were consistent (for example, Fig. 1b, − versus + 5(S)-HETE or 5-oxoETE, or Fig. 1c, WT versus KO). To account for these technical variations, each analytical batch was processed with its corresponding wild-type controls, and absolute lipid concentrations were not directly compared between batches.

All samples were analysed using a Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Scientific 8362543) coupled to an ID-X Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific FSN30160) equipped with a heated electrospray ionization (HESI) probe. For eicosanoid analysis, reversed-phase separation was performed on an Acquity UPLC BEH Shield RP18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 µm; Waters) as previously described72. The mobile phase consisted of (A) acetonitrile/water/acetic acid (60/40/0.02, v/v) and (B) acetonitrile /IPA (50/50, v/v). The stepwise gradient conditions were carried out for 10 min as follows: 0–5.0 min, 1–55% of solvent B; 5.0–5.5 min, 55–99% of solvent B, and finally 5.5–6.0 min, 99% of solvent B. The flow rate was maintained at 0.5 ml min−1, with an injection volume of 10 µl. Samples were kept at 4 °C during analysis, and the column temperature was set to 50 °C. Mass spectrometer parameters were as follow: ion transfer tube temperature, 300 °C; vaporizer temperature, 275 °C; Orbitrap resolution MS1, 120,000, MS2, 30,000; RF lens, 60%; maximum injection time MS1, 50 ms, MS2, Auto; AGC target MS1 and MS2 were Auto. Samples for analysis were run in both negative and 2,500 V used for negative ion voltage; Aux gas, 10 units; sheath gas, 40 units; sweep gas, 1 unit. HCD fragmentation was performed using stepped collision energies of 15%, 25%, and 35%. Full-scan mode with data-dependent MS2 (ddMS2) was applied across a mass range of m/z 200–600. Internal calibration was performed using EASY-IC. A scheduled targeted inclusion mass list was used for the analysis, including 5-HETE, 5-oxoETE, 5-HETE-d8 and 5-oxoETE-d7. Peak identifications were performed using Excalibur 3.1 (Thermo Scientific, OPTON-30965). The retention time, precursor ion mass/charge, and fragmentation patterns of 5-oxoETE, 5-HETE, 5-oxoETE-d7, and 5-HETE-d8 were confirmed using purchased standards. The following transitions were monitored: 5-oxoETE: 317.2122 > 203.1806, 5-HETE: 319.2280 > 115.0402, 5-oxoETE-d7: 324.2563 > 210.2242, 5-HETE-d8: 327.2783 > 116.0463. For quantification, the area under the curve (AUC) for 5-HETE and 5-oxoETE was normalized to the AUC of the corresponding internal standards (5-HETE-d8 and 5-oxoETE-d7, respectively).

For the adult tail fin lipidomic analysis, 0.1 g of tail fin tissue from 3–6-month-old of dhrs7wt/wt and dhrs7mk224/mk224 zebrafish were collected. The samples were sent to the University of California, San Diego Lipid Maps facility for LC–MS analysis. The tail fin tissues were homogenized in 1 ml 10% methanol in water using a Bead Mill 24 (Fisher Scientific, 15-340-163). Internal standards were added to 100 μl homogenate. Eicosanoids were extracted using solid-phase extraction with Phenomenex Strata-X polymeric reversed-phase columns. The samples were dried and reconstituted in buffer A (water/acetonitrile/acetic acid, 60/40/0.02, v/v/v). Analysis was performed with a Water Acquity UPLC interfaced with an AB Sciex 6500 QTrap instrument. Chromatographic separation was achieved with a step gradient from 100% buffer A to 100% buffer B (acetonitrile/isopropanol, 50/50, v/v) over 5 min. Standard curves were generated under identical conditions. Data analysis was conducted using Analyst and MultiQuant software packages73. The raw lipidomic data output are presented in Supplementary Table 1. Sex-associated differences were assessed separately for each lipid after log2 transformation with a lipid-specific pseudocount equal to one-half of the smallest positive concentration, using an exact balanced permutation test that preserved genotype and the allocation of 3 females and 3 males within each genotype (20 assignments per genotype; 400 joint permutations); the overall sex effect was defined as the average within-genotype male-minus-female contrast, genotype-by-sex interaction as the difference between mutant and wild-type contrasts, and Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied separately to each family of P values, with q < 0.05 considered significant74,75,76,77,78.

For each lipid species, wild-type and dhrs7 mutant groups were compared using six biological replicates per genotype, comprising three females and three males. Fold change was calculated from the untransformed concentrations as the mutant group mean divided by the wild-type group mean, such that values greater than 1 indicate higher concentrations in mutants and values below 1 indicate lower concentrations. For heat map visualization, concentrations were standardized separately for each lipid across the 12 samples by subtracting the row mean and dividing by the row standard deviation. Consequently, heat map colours represent relative within-lipid abundance across individual fish and do not indicate absolute concentration differences between different lipid species. Sex effects and genotype-by-sex interactions were evaluated separately using the exact balanced permutation analysis described above and were not used to select the lipids displayed in the genotype heat map (Fig. 3a).

HEK293T cells from 10 plates were collected and lysed as previously described. The nuclear pellet was collected by centrifugation at 1,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was then transferred to a new tube, and the granule pellet was collected by centrifugation at 15,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was transferred again to a new tube, and the microsome pellet was collected by high-speed centrifugation at 186,000g for 1–2 h at 4 °C. The supernatant was used as the cytosol.

For the NADPH production assay using different cell components, 10 μg of nuclear, granule, microsome and cytosol fraction were incubated with 1 μM 5(S)-HETE and 100 μM NADP+.

For the microsomal NADPH detection extraction experiments, HsDHRS7 (human), DrDhrs7 (zebrafish), DHRS7B, DHRS7C, DHRS9, RDH11 and 15-PGDH were cloned and ligated to the pSBtet-eGFP vector. These constructs were transfected into HEK293T cells and selected using 10 μg ml−1 blasticidin S hydrochloride. Blasticidin-resistant cells were then treated with 1 μg ml−1 Dox for 24 h, GFP-positive cells were sorted via flow cytometry to establish stable cell lines.

The enzyme assay was performed in a total volume of 100 μl containing reaction buffer (90 mM potassium phosphate, 40 mM KCl, 0.1 mM DTT, pH 7.5), the indicated amount of microsomes, 100 μM NADP+ or 100 μM NAD+, and 1 μM 5(S)-HETE. NADPH (NADH) fluorescence was detected using Gen 5 plate reader with excitation at 340 nm and emission at 445 nm. The assay was conducted at 37 °C with readings taken every minute for 60–90 min.

Reactions were initiated by the addition of substrate immediately before placing the plate into the gen5 reader. Consequently, the first fluorescence measurement was acquired after an unavoidable delay between reaction initiation and data acquisition.

The first 20 time points of the NADPH kinetics were fitted with a line to approximate initial velocities (v0). The R2 values of each of these fits were averaged to yield an overall R2 value. Next the v0(NADP+) and v0(5(S)-HETE) isotherms were fitted with a Michaelis–Menten model v = Vmax × [S]/(Km + [S]), with [S] being the substrate concentration, Vmax being the maximal enzyme velocity, and Km the Michaelis constant (indicating half-maximal enzyme saturation). Fitting and figure plotting was performed in MATLAB 2024b (Update 4,24.2.0.2833386, 64-bit, win64, MathWorks) using the base functions and the optimization and statistics and machine learning toolboxes (v24.1; lsqcurvefit). For better readability, the corresponding live script MMcalculation.mlx was edited/annotated using ChatGPTo1 (OpenAI). This script obtained all numerical NADPH(t) data from a formatted Excel file (MichaelisMenten.xlsx), in which the NADPH concentration data was provided (in μM) in replicates as columns for each substrate concentration. For more details, please refer to the annotated MATLAB script.

Cells were grown in six-well plates to confluence, washed once with ice-cold PBS and collected in RIPA buffer (Cell Signaling, 9806) containing protease inhibitors (Roche, 11836153001). Lysates were centrifuged at 18,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C and protein content was determined using the BCA assay (Thermo Scientific, A65453) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Lysates containing 10 µg protein were treated with reducing agent (50 mM DTT, Thermo, NP0009) and sample loading buffer (NP0007, Thermo), boiled for 10 min and subjected to SDS–PAGE on precast gradient gels (NP0322, Thermo) at 120 V for 120 min. Proteins were transferred to nitrocellulose membranes using standard procedures. Membranes were blocked in 5% skimmed milk dissolved in TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBS-T) for 2 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies were diluted in TBS-T containing 3% BSA and rocked at 4 °C overnight (anti-NUDT1 (abcam, ab200832), 1:5,000; anti-β-actin (Sigma, A5441), 1:5,000, anti-DHRS7 (Abcam, ab156021), 1:1,000, anti-eGFP (Abcam, ab184601), 1:1,000). Afterwards, blots were washed 5 times with TBS-T at room temperature and incubated with secondary antibodies conjugated to HRP (anti-mouse (Cell Signaling, 7076S), 1:4,000, anti-rabbit (Cell Signaling, 7074S), 1:2,000) diluted in TBS-T containing 2.5% skimmed milk for 1–2 h at room temperature. Blots were washed 5 times in TBS-T and signals were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescent detection reagent according to manufacturer’s instructions (Cytiva, RPN2235). For quantification, images were background subtracted and the respective band intensities were quantified using the straight line tool and mean grey value function in ImageJ. Full-length, uncropped images of all western blots and gels are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

For experiments, cells were trypsinized and seeded into 8-well precoated imaging dishes (ibidi, 80826) at a density of 8,000 cells per well and grown to confluence for experiments. Trolox was used at a working concentration of 50 µM and LPX1 was used at a working concentration of 20 µM in serum-free EMEM. For experiments with 5-oxoETE, the lipid was obtained as an ethanol-based solution (Cayman Chemical, 34250) and was used at a working concentration of 1 µM in serum-free EMEM. Cells were treated with the compounds or the appropriate vehicle control overnight. For H2O2 treatment experiments, a 1 M stock solution was diluted from 30% H2O2 on the day of the experiment. Cells were treated with 1 mM H2O2 or vehicle control diluted in serum-free EMEM for 2 h.

Immunofluorescent staining of fixed Caco-2 cells was performed as described previously with some modifications79. In brief, cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde in PBS at room temperature for 15 min, washed 3 times with PBS, permeabilized with PBSTX for 15 min and blocked with 5% goat serum (Jackson Immunoresearch, 005-000-121) in PBS at room temperature for 1 h. Cells were incubated with primary antibodies (anti-active caspase-3 1:200 BD Biosciences Product: 559565 and 570524, anti-NUDT1, (Abcam, ab200832) 1:100) diluted in blocking solution at room temperature for 1.5 h. Cells were washed 3 times with PBS and then incubated with secondary antibodies (1:500) diluted in blocking solution at room temperature for 30 min. Cells were washed twice with PBS and stained with DAPI (1:5000) in PBS for 15 min. Cells were washed 2 more times with PBS before imaging.

A549 cells were stained as detailed above, with the exception that the A549 cells were incubated at room temperature for 1.5 h with primary antibodies diluted in blocking solution: anti-Calnexin (endoplasmic reticulum marker, 1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 2679), anti-Cox4 (Mitochondria marker, 1:400, Cell Signaling Technology, 4850S) and anti-lamin A/C (Nucleus marker, 1:100, Cell Signaling Technology, 4777).

For live imaging80, 2.5-3 dpf anaesthetized Tg(lyz:pm2-mKate2) and Tg(mpeg1: eGFP) larvae were amputated in Isotonic E3 tricaine, and immobilized in ~200 μl of 1% low-melting agarose (Gold Biotechnology, A-204-100) dissolved in Isotonic E3, placed in glass-bottom dishes (MatTek Corporation, P35G-1.5-20-C). After solidification of the agarose, the larvae were covered with 2–3 ml Isotonic E3 Tricaine to prevent and maintain anaesthesia during imaging. After 5 min of imaging, the buffer was replaced with the indicated medium for 1 h imaging sessions. The medium used included Isotonic E3 tricaine with 7.5 μM arachidonic acid (Sigma, A3611), 5 μM 5(S)-HETE (Cayman, 34230) or 1 μM 5-oxoETE (Cayman, 34250). Neutrophils are counted once they had exited the blood vessels.

Imaging was performed at 28 °C in a heated imaging chamber (TOKAI HIT, WPI inc) using an inverted Nikon Eclipse Ti microscope. The microscope was equipped with a CFI Plan-Apochromat Lambda D 10× objective lens (NA 0.45), a motorized stage, a Yokogawa CSU-W1 Spinning Disk unit, a Photometrics Prime BSI Scientific CMOS camera (2 × 2 binning), and NIS imaging software (Nikon, 5.11.01). Fluorescence emission was excited using 488 or 561 nm diode lasers (Nikon). Channel acquisition intensities/exposure times were set at 50%/100 ms for the 488 nm laser power or 80%/100 ms for the 561 nm laser power to detect either macrophages or neutrophils, respectively. Emission was collected using 525/36 (green) or 605/52 (red) bandpass filters with a high-sensitive sCMOS camera using bandpass dichroic mirrors (Chroma Technology Corp., 89100bs) for filtering two separate fluorescence emission spectra (525/36 and 605/52, Chroma Technology) placed in front of the detector for isolated detection of green and red fluorescence, respectively.

To determine the subcellular localization of HsDHRS7–eGFP (green), we quantified its spatial overlap in A549 cells with organelle-specific immunofluorescence signals, including mitochondria (Cox4), endoplasmic reticulum (calnexin) or nuclear (lamin A/C). For pixel-wise co-localization analysis, SIM-phase (phase = 5–9, 27.5 µm G5) images were acquired using a 63× objective (Plan-Apochromat 63× NA = 1.4∞/0.17 WD = 0.19 mm Oil, 420782-9900-000 Zeiss) oil immersion lens and the Zeiss Elyra 7 microscope and reconstructed in SIM2 for 60 nm super-resolution microscopy. The samples were excited with OPSL lasers (488, 561 nm), red fluorophores were excited by 561 nm (4% power) and eGFP by 488 nm (4% power) laser lines, respectively. The light path is equipped with reflector turret mounted with FW1:LBF (405/488/561/642-nm laser blocking filter) beam splitters and filters for isolated 2x pco.edge sCMOS (v4.2 CL HS, innovate LCS-BU) isolated camera detection for red (TV1: LP570) or green (TV2:BP 495–550) emission. The acquisition of individual z-stacks takes about 12–20 s and 50–80 ms exposure time for both colours. The multiphase SIM data were recorded in apotome- or lattice- 3D leap modes with an FOV of 80.14 μm × 80.14 μm (1,280 × 1,280 pixels), 0.063 μm pixel size, 0.110–0.329 μm z-step, stack 5–10 μm and collected at 16-bit resolution (pco.edge sCMOS, Sensor Temperature, Air 7 °C).

SIM and Lattice-SIM reconstruction is performed with the SIM processing Tool of the ZEN 3.0 SR FP2 (64-bit, 16.0.20.306 black) software for applying SIM2 Image reconstruction. The advanced filter is set with best fit and Gauss (sectioning = 100), no detrending is used for either channel or scale to raw image. The set regularization weight is set to 0.015, with proc.Sampling and Out.Sampling set to ×2 or ×4 and ran the algorithm for at least 20 iterations. After image reconstruction, the voxel size decreased to 0.016 × 0.016 × 0.110–0.329 µm (Out.Sampling). The reconstructed SIM2 images were subsequently loaded into custom Fiji java macro for obtaining maximum-intensity-projected images that were automatically saved as.TIFF output and analysed in a custom Python script (https://github.com/zazadovv/Redox-DHRS7_subcellular.git). The obtained files were then analysed for region of interest with image segmentation on intensity thresholds and Pearson’s correlation coefficients as well as Manders M1/M2 coefficients. Co-localization analysis was performed using custom Python (v3.9.23) scripts built on NumPy (v1.25.281), SciPy (v1.9.382), scikit-image (v0.24.083), tifffile (v2023.2.2884), matplotlib (v3.7.585) and the napari image viewer (v0.4.1986) with magicgui (v0.10.187) extensions and QtPy (v2.4.3). GPU acceleration (when available) was provided by CuPy (v13.6)88.

Larvae were embedded in 200 µl 1% low-melting agarose in a glass-bottom dish (MatTek Corporation; P35G-1.5-20C). Larvae were oriented as shown in the schematic in Figs. 3g, 4b, 5e and Extended Data Fig. 7a (Larval zebrafish graphic was sourced from Scidraw.io (courtesy of L. Petrucco51)). For the experiments with live fish, E3 medium with tricaine was added to the top of the agarose after it solidified to prevent desiccation of the sample and maintain anaesthesia over the course of the imaging. Transmitted light images were acquired at room temperature (~25 °C) using NIS imaging software (Nikon, 5.21.03-build 1489). on a Nikon Eclipse Ti microscope equipped with a 10×, Plan-Apochromat NA 0.45 air objective lens, and an Andor Clara charge-coupled device (CCD) camera. Alexa 488 and FITC fluorescence was excited using an LED light source (Lumencor 7; Light Engine) with an internal 475/28 bandpass filter, and Alexa 555 fluorescence was excited using an internal 549/15 bandpass filter. The emission of Alexa 488 and FITC was sampled using a 525/50 bandpass filter (Chroma; 525/50 m), while the emission of Alexa555 was detected using a 632/60 bandpass filter (Chroma; ET632/60 m). z-stacks were acquired with a 5 µm step size with a total imaging depth of 80 µm.

Caco-2 cells were imaged on the same setup detailed previously for imaging active caspase-3 immunostained zebrafish larvae. DAPI fluorescence was excited using an LED light source (Lumencor 7; Light Engine) with an internal 390/18 bandpass filter and detected using a 460/50 bandpass filter (Chroma; ET460/50 m). Images were acquired in a single z-plane.

AlphaFold2.PDB files of DHRS7 orthologues were retrieved from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database from the listed species in Extended Data Fig. 2a. Mammalian models comprised H. sapiens (AF-Q9Y394-F1-v6), Pan troglodytes (AF-A0A6D2X0S6-F1-v6), Macaca mulatta (AF-A0A5F8AVE4-F1-v6), Callithrix jacchus (AF-F7IQ82-F1-v6), M. musculus (AF-Q9CXR1-F1-v6), R. norvegicus (AF-D4A0T8-F1-v6), Mustela putorius furo (AF-M3Y4J4-F1-v6), Equus caballus (AF-F6ZYE1-F1-v6), Sus scrofa (AF-A0A4X1W7G7-F1-v6), B. taurus (AF-Q24K14-F1-v6), Bos indicus (AF-A0A6P5CGV6-F1-v6), Bos mutus (AF-L8IVK0-F1-v6) and Myotis brandtii (AF-S7N8T4-F1-v6); avian models comprised Meleagris gallopavo (AF-G1NLG0-F1-v6) and Columba livia (AF-A0A2I0MNT2-F1-v6); the amphibian model was Xenopus tropicalis (AF-Q5FW40-F1-v6); and teleost models comprised D. rerio (AF-Q0P3U1-F1-v6), Oryzias latipes (AF-H2MM26-F1-v6), Oryzias melastigma (AF-A0A3B3D589-F1-v6), Nothobranchius furzeri (AF-A0A1A8UQ61-F1-v6) and Nothobranchius pienaari (AF-A0A1A8MMP9-F1-v6). Models ranged in size from 262 to 340 residues; C. livia (262 amino acids) and M. brandtii (289 amino acids) are partial gene models lacking the complete N-terminal region, whereas all remaining orthologues were full-length (334–340 amino acids). The PDB files are superimposed in UCSF chimera (1.18)89 using MatchMaker structural comparison tool with default settings90; simultaneously fetching the structures and running Needleman-Wunsch alignment and homology matching algorithm with best-aligning pair of chains91,92. The parameters for secondary-structure scoring included at 30% weight (secondary structure computed where absent; helix, strand and coil gap-opening penalties of 18, 18 and 6, gap-extension penalty 1), and iterative pruning of atom pairs until none exceeded 2.0 Å, fitting one α-carbon per residue with the human DHRS7 (AF-Q9Y394-F1-v6) as reference. The resulting DHRS7 superimposed model (Extended Data Fig. 2c) was visually processed in UCSF Chimera (1.18).

The predicted structure of HsDHRS7 was obtained from AlphaFold2 (ID:AF-Q9Y394-F1-v6), and the PDB file was used for membrane protein system assembly, and six steps were followed to assemble the hypothetical model using CHARMM36m and CHARMM-GUI Membrane Builder (v3.7)93. The AF2 pdb structure was first converted to CHARMM topology with standard charged termini and the default protonation states for physiological pH (~7.4), giving a net protein charge of +4. The protein orientation within the bilayer is determined using PPM 2.094. The system size for lipid bilayer was projected to heterogeneous lipid composition resembling that of endoplasmic reticulum membranes95. The bilayer was symmetrical, with an identical lipid complement in each leaflet (154 lipids per leaflet, 308 in total). Phosphatidylcholine was the dominant class (59.1 mol %), comprising 1-stearoyl-2-oleoyl-PC (SOPC, 18:0/18:1; 40 lipids per leaflet, 26.0 mol %), 1-palmitoyl-2-linoleoyl-PC (PLPC, 16:0/18:2; 27 lipids, 17.5 mol %) and 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-PC (POPC, 16:0/18:1; 24 lipids, 15.6 mol %). Phosphatidylethanolamine accounted for a further 22.1 mol %, as 1-palmitoyl-2-stearoyl-PE (PSPE, 16:0/18:0; 12 lipids, 7.8 mol %), 1-stearoyl-2-oleoyl-PE (SOPE, 18:0/18:1; 10 lipids, 6.5 mol %), 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-PE (POPE, 16:0/18:1; 8 lipids, 5.2 mol %) and 1-stearoyl-2-linoleoyl-PE (SLPE, 18:0/18:2; 4 lipids, 2.6 mol %). The remaining lipids were cholesterol (7 lipids, 4.5 mol %), N-palmitoyl-sphingomyelin (PSM, 16:0; 6 lipids, 3.9 mol %), 1-oleoyl-2-linoleoyl-phosphatidylserine (OLPS, 18:1/18:2; 5 lipids, 3.2 mol %), 1-stearoyl-2-arachidonoyl-phosphatidylinositol (SAPI, 18:0/20:4; 5 lipids, 3.2 mol %), 1-stearoyl-2-linoleoyl-phosphatidylinositol (SLPI, 18:0/18:2; 4 lipids, 2.6 mol %) and 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-phosphatidic acid (POPA, 16:0/18:1; 2 lipids, 1.3 mol %), giving 5.8 mol % total phosphatidylinositol. In brief, grouped by lipid headgroup, each leaflet contained 59.1 mol % phosphatidylcholine (PC), 22.1 mol % phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), 5.8 mol % phosphatidylinositol (PI), 4.5 mol % cholesterol, 3.9 mol % sphingomyelin (SM), 3.2 mol% phosphatidylserine (PS) and 1.3 mol % phosphatidic acid (PA). The environment was hydrated with TIP3P water molecules, added as a 22.5 Å water slab beyond the protein on each side of the bilayer. Counter-ions were added to neutralize the system and to reproduce a physiological ionic strength of 0.15 M KCl, with ion positions generated by a Monte Carlo procedure using a 20 Å ion-exclusion zone centred on the membrane to prevent ion insertion into the hydrophobic core. The final system contained 92 K+ and 64 Cl− ions (156 ions in total). The bilayer lateral dimensions were determined from the number of lipids per leaflet after correcting for the protein cross-sectional area (59 × 50 × 77 Å), comprising of rectangular unit cell 101.04 × 101.04 × 124.79 Å. The assembled model (Extended Data Fig. 2d) is visually processed in UCSF Chimera (1.18) and rendered in UCSF ChimeraX (1.10.1).

The AlphaFold-predicted structures of DHRS7 orthologues from M. musculus (AlphaFold DB:Q9CXR1, AF-Q9CXR1-F1-v6), R. norvegicus (AlphaFold DB:D4A0T8, AF-D4A0T8-F1-v6), B. taurus (AlphaFold DB:Q24K14, AF-Q24K14-F1-v6), D. rerio (AlphaFold DB: Q0P3U1, AF-Q0P3U1-F1-v6) and H. sapiens (AlphaFold DB: Q9Y394, AF-Q9Y394-F1-v6) were retrieved from a pipeline implemented in Python (v3.10.20). The DHRS7 orthologues were retrieved from Ensembl (release 116)96 through its REST interface using the requests library (v2.33.1). The one2one and one2many 253 orthologues were sampled across vertebrates. 187 orthologues within ±30 amino acids of the human reference length were aligned with MUSCLE (v5.3. build d9725ac)97,98. The AlphaFold-predicted structure of human DHRS7 (UniProt Q9Y394; model AF-Q9Y394-F1) was used to generate molecular surface from the atomic coordinates using a 1.4 Å probe radius, corresponding to a water-sized solvent probe. residues of interest were highlighted in yellow with 4.0 Å mapping radius, with the remaining DHRS7 surface rendered in grey molecular surface and molecular surface slice (Extended Data Fig. 5a) in UCSF Chimera (v1.18). Residues were selected from the cross-species MUSCLE alignment described above as positions at which H. sapiens, D. rerio and B. taurus DHRS7 share an identical residue that is substituted in both rodents (M. musculus and R. norvegicus). The human reference positions map directly onto the model. These 15 positions (human numbering)—L18, C147, D149, E160, P198, R218, S230, I232, C233, F291, W306, N310, G323, V324 and A326—were coloured yellow on the molecular surface of HsDHRS7. Per-species the secondary structure was assigned from the AlphaFold predicted structure models and overlayed on MUSCLE alignment, the secondary structure relies on backbone φ–ψ torsion angles of the model coordinates from AlphaFold. Conservation followed the Clustal convention and columns were scored by exact residue identity across the select species (Extended Data Fig. 5b).

DHRS7 orthologue protein sequence analysis and multiple-sequence alignment was performed with Python (v3.10.20). Sequence alignment and input/output and pairwise sequence-identity calculations were performed with Biopython (v1.87)99, tabular data were handled with pandas (v2.3.3.)100, numerical operations with NumPy (v1.24.4)81 and auxiliary panels were rendered with Matplotlib (v3.10.8)85. Sequences were aligned under default parameters (standard affine gap penalties) and pairwise identities to the human reference were derived from global (Needleman-Wunsch), BLOSUM62 alignments (gap-opening, −10; gap-extension, −0.5). The environment (Python v3.10.20) is provided as bundle.yml and multiple species sequence alignment output with protein.pdb model and the Extended Data Fig. 5b reproduction pipeline is available on GitHub (https://github.com/zazadovv/Redox-DHRS7_subcellular.git).

No statistical methods were used to determine the sample size, which aligns with those reported in previous publications10,11. Statistical analyses were performed by using GraphPad Prism 8 (v8.3.0) or MATLAB 2024b (update 4,24.2.0.2833386, 64-bit, win64, MathWorks). Outliers were identified and removed using the Rout method in Prism. Shapiro–Wilk test was used for measuring normal distribution for each dataset. Only if the data were normally distributed, a parametric unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-test was applied to the dataset. If the data were not normally distributed, nonparametric unpaired two-tailed Mann–Whitney U test was used. For datasets with small sizes (n = 3 or 4), Welch’s t-test was used even when the Shapiro–Wilk test indicates a departure from normality (Fig. 1c, right and Fig. 2c, right), because such small sample sizes are insufficient for reliable assessment of the underlying distribution. For multiple comparisons testing of normally distributed data ordinary one-way ANOVA followed by post hoc testing (uncorrected Fisher’s least significant difference post hoc test or Tukey’s post hoc test for comparing all experimental groups and Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test for comparing experimental groups to common control groups) were used. For normally distributed data with unequal variances, the Brown–Forsythe ANOVA was used followed by Dunnett’s T3 multiple comparisons test. For multiple comparison of non-normally distributed data, the Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA followed by Dunn’s post hoc test was used. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Exact P values for Welch’s t-test and Mann–Whitney U test reported by prism as P < 0.0001 were independently calculated using the Real Statistics Resource Pack for Microsoft Excel (v9.9, C. Zaiontz). For ANOVA based multiple-comparison tests, P values reported by Prism as P < 0.0001 are presented as such because exact numerical P values were not provided by the software. For adult zebrafish tissue lipidomics, sex-associated effects were assessed for each lipid in 12 independent biological samples (n = 3 females and n = 3 males per genotype) using an exact, two-sided balanced permutation test. Concentrations were log2-transformed after addition of a lipid-specific pseudocount equal to one-half of the smallest positive concentration. Sex labels were permuted within each genotype while retaining three females and three males, producing 20 possible assignments per genotype and 400 combined permutations. The overall sex effect was defined as the average within-genotype male-minus-female contrast, and the genotype-by-sex interaction as the difference between the mutant and wild-type sex contrasts. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied separately across the 84 lipid-specific P values for the overall sex effect and genotype-by-sex interaction analyses; an adjusted q value < 0.05 was considered significant. For genotype comparisons, six independent biological samples per genotype (three females and three males) were analysed. Normality was assessed separately within each genotype using the Shapiro–Wilk test. When both groups were consistent with normality (P > 0.05), a two-sided Welch’s t-test was used; otherwise, a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test was applied. Fold change was calculated from untransformed concentrations as the mutant group mean divided by the wild-type group mean. Lipids with a nominal genotype-comparison P < 0.05 were included in the heat map and ordered by decreasing fold change. All error bars represent the s.d. Detailed sample sizes are listed in the figure legends. Animal experiments conducted on different days were aggregated. Experiments were not randomized, and investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments or outcome assessment. For each treatment, both treated and control embryos were sourced from the same egg spawn. Animals were not reused across experiments. Larvae were selected based on normal morphology, a beating heart, and circulating red blood cells. All images in the figures represent typical phenotypes and expression patterns for their respective conditions. All detailed statistical tests are presented in the Source Data.

(a) CRISPR design for dhrs7 mutant zebrafish using single guide RNAs (sgRNAs). For dhrs7mk224/mk224, sgRNA1 was designed to target exon 2. Target disruption is predicted to occur at a PvuII restriction site (CAG^CTG) (highlighted by orange text) in the genomic DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) sequence. For dhrs7mk225/mk225, two different sgRNAs were used together. Specifically, sgRNA2 was designed to target exon 6. Target disruption is predicted to occur at a BseLI restriction site (CCGTGTG^AAGG) (highlighted by orange text) in the genomic DNA sequence. (b) dhrs7 mutant alleles. The mutant dhrs7mk224/mk224 allele was generated by sgRNA1 and has a 4-base pair (bp) deletion resulting in a frameshift and the destruction of PvuII restriction site. The mutant dhrs7mk225/mk225 allele was generated by co-injection of sgRNA1 and sgRNA2 and has a 12 bp deletion leading to the destruction of a PvuII restriction site, as well as a 2 bp deletion and the destruction of a BseLI restriction site, resulting in a frame shift. Purple text, mutant sequence (insertion) that differs from the wt sequence. Red text, deletion sequence that differs from the wt sequence. (c) The mutant dhrs7mk224 and dhrs7mk225 alleles both have premature stop codons in the coding sequence. Red text, mutant dhrs7mk224 and dhrs7mk225 sequences that differs from the wt sequence. (d-e) Genotyping of progeny from heterozygous dhrs7mk224 or dhrs7mk225 zebrafish crosses by PCR, restriction digestion and agarose gel electrophoresis. (f) Oxoeicosanoid pathway. cPla2 is activated by physical stress (specifically, osmotic nuclear deformation) to release arachidonic acid (AA) from nuclear membrane phospholipids (PL). ALOX5 (5-lipoxygenase) metabolizes AA into 5-hydroperoxy-eicosatetraenoic acid (5(S)-HpETE). The catalytic site of ALOX5 is primed by free lipid peroxides (i.e., oxidative stress). 5(S)-HpETE may be either used for LTB4 production or reduced by a glutathione peroxidase (GPX) into 5-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (5(S)-HETE). The respective oxidized glutathione (GSSG) is converted back to reduced glutathione (GSH) by glutathione reductase (GR) under consumption of NADPH and generation of NADP+. Under oxidative (=high NADP+) and physical stress (=high 5(S)-HETE), 5-oxoETE is generated from 5(S)-HETE. Under unstressed conditions, the reverse reaction is preferred. 5-oxoETE exerts its physiological effects through the OXER1 receptor (or its zebrafish ortholog Hcar1-4). Francis Halzen, who today won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, was the driving force behind IceCube, the pioneering kilometre-sized neutrino observatory at the South Pole.

But Halzen, whom I have had the fortune to interview multiple times over the years while covering this field, never saw neutrino detectors such as IceCube as working in isolation.

The dream for many neutrino researchers — and the ultimate story for some reporters such as myself to tell — is to spot phenomena simultaneously with other types of observatories, in a feat of ’multi-messenger astronomy’.

Ever-more sophisticated telescopes allow astronomers to observe the Universe with electromagnetic signals beyond visible light: with everything from γ-rays down to long-wavelength radio.

Neutrinos — and high-energy cosmic rays, which are mostly protons — add a whole other ‘sense’. They enable researchers to observe and even build images with particles of matter instead of radiation. The idea is that ordinary, or ‘electromagnetic’, astronomy is only one of the many dimensions that can give a fuller picture of the Universe. Cosmic phenomena such as the supernova explosions of stars or the sudden flares of activity around supermassive black holes should spew out electromagnetic radiation but also neutrinos and other particles.

IceCube made its first ‘multi-messenger’ discovery in 2017, when it detected the neutrino labelled TXS 0506+056, also known as ‘Texas’. It was the first time that a high-energy neutrino was successfully traced back to a source — in this case, a blazar, a galaxy with an intense source of γ-rays.

That year, astronomers experienced an equally momentous multi-messenger event called a kilonova, the collision of two neutron stars. The kilonova was first spotted using yet another sense — the detection of gravitational waves, which are perturbations in the geometry of space. I was lucky to cover both the Texas event and the kilonova.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Xiaoying You
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Engineering graduate students from Egypt, Yemen, Indonesia and Niger watch a demonstration of a smart construction system at Southeast University in Nanjing, China. Credit: Heng Jiang

Every weekday, Fatma Satyani, an Indonesian PhD student in China, gets up at 7.30 a.m. to get ready for her day.

She usually eats a youtiao (fried dough stick) or a couple of baozi (steamed buns) with warm soya milk, a traditional Chinese breakfast, before heading out to classes at the Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology in eastern China.

“I love studying here,” says Satyani, who is doing a PhD on big data and business intelligence. “Chinese people are friendly, the food is delicious and getting around Nanjing is very convenient.”

Satyani is one of a fast-growing group of students from low- and middle-income countries — especially nations in Asia and Africa where China has made large investments in development — who are seeking a postgraduate education in the Asian superpower.

The number of international university students in China has climbed steadily since the nation lifted its strict COVID-19 pandemic lockdown rules in late 2022. According to the latest official statistics reported by China Daily, a state-run newspaper, 380,000 international students were studying in the country during the 2024–25 academic year, up by 15% from the previous year. Even so, these students made up less than 1% of the 48.5 million students in China’s higher-education system in the 2024–25 academic year. And the proportion of international students in China represents just a fraction of the share studying in the United States and the United Kingdom (see ‘A small fraction’).

Sources: HESA; IIE; NCES; Ministry of Education of China; ChinaDaily

In China, 61% of international students come from Asia, with most of the rest coming from Africa and Europe, at 16% each. About 71,750 of those are in master’s or PhD programmes, according to statistics from the government. Although on the rise, the number of international students is still lower than China’s 2018 pre-pandemic record of nearly 500,000 students, according to QS Quacquarelli Symonds, a UK-based company that analyses global higher-education institutions.

On the move: why PhD students study abroad in 2025

International PhD students based in China say that they were attracted to the programmes by generous scholarships, the opportunity to learn Mandarin and make Chinese connections and China’s rising capabilities in frontier technologies, such as artificial intelligence and data analytics. However, they also face several obstacles. Mandarin is a difficult language to master, and students often have limited options to stay in China after their courses end. Moreover, some countries consider a Chinese degree to be less competitive.

“In the past, we saw that America was the global first in science, technology and education. Looking ahead, I think China will be the global first in those areas, including attracting and training students and researchers from around the world,” Satyani says.

Satyani is in the second year of her PhD programme, having completed a two-year master’s in business management at the same university. She moved to China to study in 2023 because her university in Indonesia, Universal University in Batam, suggested that she do so after completing her bachelor’s degree there.

“I would like to work for Universal University as a professor in the future, so the university assisted me to come to China to study so that I can bring the knowledge I learn in China back to Indonesia and teach the students there,” Satyani says.

After her master’s, Satyani decided to pursue a PhD in China because she had enjoyed her life there and she “wanted to study something that would be useful for the future”. For her, China is a perfect place to learn how companies and governments use big data — large data sets that can be used to assess trends and patterns — and AI tools to improve efficiency. “You’ve got to learn futuristic knowledge in a futuristic country,” Satyani says.

Similarly, meteorology PhD student Aminu Dalhatu Datti was drawn to study at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology because, he says, it is a leading institution for meteorology and its advanced computing systems enable him to use complex models for data analysis. Datti, who is from Nigeria, says that he “had heard a lot of good things about China”, including the fact that it has a fast-growing economy and provides strong support for international students. “So, I wanted to come here and see the country with my own eyes.”

Chairina Hanum Siregar (third from left) introduced people to Indonesian tea and snacks at a cultural exchange event at Sichuan University in Chengdu, China, where she’s studying a PhD in management science.Credit: International Office of the School of Business, Sichuan University

Datti says that he’s been able to attend international meteorology conferences in China and that the knowledge and connections he’s gained from those will be valuable to him when he finishes his PhD and returns to his post at the Nigerian Meteorological Agency in Abuja.

For others, such as Chairina Hanum Siregar, it was lifestyle factors and scholarships that made China attractive. “As a woman, safety is very important, and I really like that the city of Chengdu is safe.” Siregar, who is from Jakarta, is a third-year PhD student in management science and engineering at Sichuan University in Chengdu.

Siregar also applied to universities in the United Kingdom and Australia but did not receive any scholarship offers. She says that she did not apply to universities in the United States at all because of concerns about public safety there.

In 2010, China launched a national campaign called Study in China to attract more global students and to “cultivate a batch of high-quality international students who understand China and are friendly to China”. In 2016, it announced that it would incorporate its international strategy for higher education into the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), its global infrastructure and development strategy. The initiative has projects in more than 140 partner countries, most of which are low- and middle-income nations. In a statement made at the time, the government described education and trade as the “two wings” that would propel the BRI forward.

All of the students interviewed by Nature’s careers team hold government scholarships. The exact level of sponsorship varies, but for a PhD student, the awards usually include tuition fees and medical insurance, as well as a monthly stipend and free or subsidized housing.

China’s generous scholarships play a key part in attracting international students, says Tu Mengwei, a sociologist at Swansea University, UK. For example, Satyani is a recipient of the Chinese Government Scholarship, which provides her with 3,500 yuan (around US$520) per month and free housing.

China’s effort to make its higher-education system more international has also involved strategies to attract post-PhD researchers from overseas, including people with Chinese ancestry, to work in China. “All of that is a part of a bigger scheme of expanding China’s soft power and global influence,” Tu says.

“Although the total number of international students in China has bounced back since the pandemic, the demographics have changed dramatically,” says Wen Wen, a higher-education specialist at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

In 2018, South Korea was the largest source of international students in China, followed by Thailand, Pakistan, India and the United States, Chinese government figures show. But in 2024, the five nations sending the most students to China were Thailand, Pakistan, Vietnam, Russia and Indonesia, according to QS (see ‘China’s student sources are changing’).

Alice Wei, a consultant at QS, isn’t surprised. China has always been a popular destination for students from Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam because of the close political ties and frequent trade activity between the nations, Wei explains. The rapid economic growth of countries in southeast Asia has also driven a demand for talent, leading young people to seek a high-quality education abroad, she says.

Sources: Ministry of Education of China; QS Quacquarelli Symonds

In Tu’s view, the influx of international students from Pakistan and other BRI nations in 2018–23 — when she was doing field work on the experiences of international students in China1 — was not only driven by China’s targeted policy, but also the applicants’ own plans and desires. For example, as China has strengthened its transport and infrastructure links with Pakistan, students there “gradually discovered that they would have better job opportunities if they learn to speak Mandarin or have connections in China,” Tu notes. “It’s a two-way street.” China has been building the Pakistan Economic Corridor2 since 2015, a $62-billion flagship project under the BRI that aims to construct a series of transport and infrastructure facilities linking Pakistan’s Gwadar Port on the Arabian Sea to western China’s landlocked Xinjiang autonomous region.

By contrast, the number of South Korean and US students in China has dropped. According to data from South Korea’s education ministry, South Korean student numbers plummeted by nearly 80% between 2017 and 2023, and the number of students from the United States in China shrank from around 24,000 in 2017 to just 400 in 2023, according to QS. The large drops are mostly due to China’s strict lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical tension and worsening public sentiment towards China in these nations, researchers say.

International students in China mostly study dedicated, predominantly English-speaking courses set up by universities. Few students live, study or do research alongside their Chinese peers. China has a long tradition of managing international students separately from their Chinese counterparts owing to immigration and public-security rules, Wen says.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: How digital breakdowns affect supply chains — and endanger the global economy
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Dabo Guan
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Dabo Guan is a professor of climate change and low-carbon transition at Tsinghua University, Beijing, China, and at University College London, UK.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Software-related problems have caused massive delays at transport hubs. Credit: Hesham Elsherif/Anadolu via Getty

Global supply chains depend on flows of information as much as they do on flows of goods1. Digital designs for products are shared across continents. Inventories and production schedules are managed using algorithms. Payments and logistics are orchestrated through data platforms.

Why we need an International Panel on Inequality

When these data exchanges fail — because of outages, congestion or cyber incidents — the ensuing disruption propagates among suppliers and customers2. Huge economic losses can result, even if there is no physical damage.

For example, in 2024, a faulty software update from cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike crashed millions of Microsoft Windows devices and triggered a global information-technology outage. Flights, hospitals and payment systems were halted, and firms on the Fortune 500 list of the biggest US companies by revenue lost US$5.4 billion. Digital downtime costs the world’s 2,000 largest businesses $400 billion each year, according to analytics firm Oxford Economics.

Yet, information flows are not tracked systematically. Nor are they included in the core instrument used by national statistical offices to map supply chains in the economy: the monetary input–output table3. This matrix traces the value of material inputs flowing between industries, but doesn’t capture energy, data or computational resources. Similarly, firms account for what they spend on information technology, but not for the data, computation and electricity on which their operations depend.

This omission is becoming a growing problem as digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, reshape economies, and as threats to energy grids, digital connectivity and cybersecurity escalate. For instance, in April 2025, a massive electricity blackout across Spain and Portugal that took half a day to fix cut Internet traffic to 17% of normal levels and froze electronic payments, at a cost of €1.6 billion (US$1.8 billion). Around one dozen subsea telecommunications and power cables in the Baltic Sea have been damaged in suspected sabotage incidents since late 2023.

Here I set out how firms and nations can build a practical statistical tool to track essential digital data.

Energy, computation and information flows are intertwined (see ‘Hidden connections’). Businesses, especially those with high power requirements such as data centres, increasingly choose where to locate themselves on the basis of access to clean, cheap and reliable sources of electricity. In the United States, Microsoft signed a 20-year agreement in 2024 to restart the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania to power its data centres. In China, the national East Data, West Computing programme is steering data centres towards western provinces, which are rich in renewables5.

Sources: Epoch AI; Ref. 4; go.nature.com/4YNESPH; TeleGeography, Global Internet Geography.

Global value chains and payment systems also need access to computational resources — such as processing power and memory — to produce, analyse and share data. The resources needed to train cutting-edge AI models have grown four- to fivefold each year for more than a decade (see go.nature.com/3tpemjh), and the largest AI-focused supercomputers now combine some 200,000 processors and draw as much power as 250,000 households (see go.nature.com/3tmh73s).

Furthermore, most economic transactions and markets are now digital. They are increasingly managed through digital tokens, which encode ownership rights, compliance requirements and how financial arrangements are to be settled.

Projections suggest that such tokens could become a major ‘commodity’ of future trade, from around $600 billion today to between $2 trillion and $9.4 trillion by 20305.

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations

Central banks and their umbrella body, the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland, are exploring tokenized platforms for cross-border payments, and many financial exchanges and regulators are moving towards tokenized markets for trading assets such as stocks, bonds and derivatives6.

Together, these resources reinforce one another through a feedback loop. Increasing use of AI and tokens drives demand for more computing power. Having more computing platforms and data centres raises electricity demand, which accelerates deployment of energy infrastructure and investments in the grid. All of this increases data generation, movement and storage. And value derived from the data — traded and settled using tokens — feeds back into investment in energy systems and digital infrastructure.

Thus, this chain, from watts to kilowatt-hours, floating-point operations per second (FLOPs), megabytes, tokens and dollars, captures an emerging driver behind modern growth that is not being tracked. The International Energy Agency projects that global electricity consumption by data centres could more than double from 415 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2024 to around 945 TWh by 2030, underscoring how rapidly this loop is scaling4.

Failing to track these dependencies has real costs. And when supply chains fail, the factors that made the network brittle go unaddressed.

For instance, in March 2025, a fire at a single electricity substation shut London Heathrow Airport for a day, cancelling around 1,300 flights and disrupting travel for more than 200,000 passengers. The official review found that a transformer fault, which was known since 2018, had gone unaddressed — and that the energy networks were unaware of the airport’s dependence on that single supply point7. No accounting framework linked the substation to the airport and the supply chains downstream; the dependency became visible only when it failed.

Accounting frameworks often fail to track dependencies on crucial infrastructure.Credit: Tatsuya Suzuki/Getty

Likewise, when a cyberattack halted production at the UK carmaker Jaguar Land Rover for five weeks in 2025, the damage — estimated at £1.9 billion (US$2.5 billion), making it the costliest cyber event in UK history — spread to more than 5,000 firms in the supply chain. No statistical instrument had recorded their dependence on a single manufacturer’s digital systems.

The chain of energy–data–computation interconnections is crucial for resilience because it represents constraints, not correlations. Conventional accounting can track who pays whom, but cannot trace where the physical and operational bottlenecks sit, how they shift over time or how a constraint in one layer (grid congestion, data-centre capacity, network disruption, transaction frictions) propagates into production losses elsewhere.

The difficulty is how to measure and assess these factors in a way that is consistent, comparable across countries and auditable by statistical offices, rather than being left to proprietary corporate dashboards.

Current statistical systems can describe the value of digital activity, but they do not yet provide a coherent way to quantify and attribute the throughput that determines supply-chain resilience. That is: the volume of computational resources supplied and used, the amount of data generated and transferred, how those flows propagate across domestic and cross-border production networks, and how they interact with electricity constraints and difficulties in settling transactions.

Since 2018, national accounting methodologies have taken a step towards making the digital economy visible, with the addition of a tool that was developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in Paris. Digital supply–use tables track the production of, trade in and consumption of digital goods, services and transactions. Canada and Australia published their first such estimates in 2019; the OECD released a handbook on their compilation in 20238; and the 2025 revision of the United Nations System of National Accounts includes a dedicated chapter on digitalization. But these tables remain based on economic values, not physical constraints.

How to measure a good life — tips for moving beyond GDP

In a fast-moving economy, it’s not monetary value that changes first, but technical quantities such as data-centre efficiency, what data and energy are used for, and the relationship between computation and data flows. These quantities have macroeconomic consequences. The International Monetary Fund estimates that AI-driven demand could raise US power prices by 8.6% if renewables cannot keep pace9. Measuring them exposes vulnerabilities — such as dependence on a single data centre, cable or settlement channel — and identifies successes worth replicating.

What’s needed is a more comprehensive instrument that would allow analysts to trace computation, network traffic and settlement exposure back to the sectors and demands that drive them10, creating a basis for targeted interventions. With such a map, resilience spending can go where the dependencies are deepest, rather than falling back on blanket measures11. Governments or companies might prioritize reinforcing a facility on which many crucial sectors rely, fast-tracking grid connections in computation-constrained regions or opening alternative payment-settlement channels if one goes down.

Such a tool must be practical — something that a national statistical office can compile, audit and update, rather than a one-off research data set. It should be built on the backbone of existing systems by adding a small number of layers that make information dependencies observable in the same accounting logic.

There are precedents in other areas. When tracking water, energy and carbon became a binding requirement for businesses and economies, supply-chain tracking systems added the appropriate extensions while remaining consistent with those for measuring gross domestic product.

However, each of those extensions tracked its resource as a separate input to production.

The IceCube Neutrino Observatory building sits above a vast cubic-kilometre array of photo detectors buried deep below the ice. (Ilya Bodo, IceCube/NSF)

Physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work in founding the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos that come from deep in space. More than 1 billion neutrinos pass through your hand every second, but they are hard to detect because they are unaffected by magnetic fields and rarely ever interact with matter. IceCube detects once-in-a-blue-moon interactions between atoms and neutrinos that have been emitted by cosmic events such as supernovae and γ-ray bursts. “This reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in this project”, Halzen said, “when really no respectable conservative physicist would have joined me.”

After decades of planning and construction, “there was no guarantee we would ever see anything”, said Halzen. But it took only two years for the collaboration to detect particles from outside our Solar System, establishing the new field of neutrino astronomy.

Reference: Science paper (from 2013)

Francis Halzen’s essay ‘Antarctic Dreams’, about IceCube’s precursor, the Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array, was featured in The Best American Science Writing 2000. In it, he says that, as a “superfluous theorist”, he has never made the journey to see his project in person. “But even now, on the nights when drilling goes on there, I can never sleep,” he writes. “To have your career on the line half a world away is hard enough. But to know that you have embroiled so many others in the same improbable adventure, that your funders and colleagues expect results, and that you are totally powerless to affect the outcome, is a form of exquisite torture.”

Exploratorium archive | 20 min read

Neutrinos are cool — that’s the first reason I’m so excited about this Nobel. When the Nobel committee made its announcement, several physics folk in our team grinned at each other. And I’d go so far as to put my money on neutrinos being the thing that finally breaks open the standard model of particle physics. The simplest version of the model says that neutrinos have no mass, but experiments show they do — we just don’t know exactly what it is. Or whether they are their own antiparticles, or if they have something to do with the great mystery of why there’s more matter than antimatter. IceCube’s purpose isn’t to study neutrinos themselves, but it has revealed more about them — such as how they interact with matter. Understanding neutrinos could mean understanding the Universe — whether that’s through IceCube’s successor, or one of the many other experiments racing to probe this particle du jour.

Lizzie Gibney, Nature reporter

“Theorists write two kinds of papers. One kind to explore the physics they really believe in, and another kind just to show how smart they are. And my initial neutrino papers were certainly in the second category. I had never any intention of ending up doing this, but then things got out of hand.”

Francis Halzen says that being “naive and ignorant” when he started working on the proposal for IceCube helped him to succeed, because he didn’t know all the ways that it could fail. (Jot Down | 28 min read, from 2014, free registration required)

Flu season might have come earlier than expected in the Northern Hemisphere, with the percentage of positive influenza tests in places such as the United Kingdom and west coast of the United States unusually high for this time of year. “An early start doesn’t necessarily mean a more severe season,” says epidemiologist James Hay. But it could prompt a rethink of when people should get their annual vaccines. Specialists are also concerned that the subtype responsible for most US cases so far, H1N1, is carrying a mutation that could help it to evade some people’s immunity.

A new analysis of notes made by X-ray crystallographer Rosalind Franklin further debunks the myth that she failed to grasp the significance of the data she herself generated. In his autobiography, biologist James Watson wrote that an image Franklin produced — known as Photograph 51 — triggered his ‘eureka’ moment about the helical structure of DNA. But Franklin had in fact already recognized and analysed the helical structure in an earlier image: Photograph 49. “She reused the same DNA sample for Photograph 51 to create a better-centred but otherwise identical diffraction image that would be suitable for publication,” write science historian Alistair Sponsel and crystallographer Brian Sutton.

Reference: Journal of the History of Biology paper

The rapid rollout of AI-powered wearables, such as smart glasses with cameras, could expose millions of people to non-consensual surveillance at an unprecedented scale, argues AI ethicist Joy Buolamwini. Policymakers must act now to update regulatory frameworks before this technology becomes ubiquitous, Buolamwini writes. This should include the introduction of spaces, such as schools and hospitals, in which covert recording is illegal.

A universal accounting system is needed to track how global supply chains could be disrupted by energy, data and computation failures, argues climate-change economist Dabo Guan. For example, in 2025, a fire at a single electricity substation — caused by an issue that had been spotted in 2018 — shut London Heathrow Airport, cancelling around 1,300 flights and disrupting travel for more than 200,000 passengers. “No accounting framework linked the substation to the airport and the supply chains downstream; the dependency became visible only when it failed,” Guan writes.

A technique called cell-free protein expression is helping synthetic biologists to design and manufacture scores of potentially useful proteins without the need to tinker with and grow microorganisms. The method enables researchers to produce proteins that would be toxic to living cells or get chewed up by a cell’s enzymes. The tech’s flexibility shortens the design–build–test–learn cycle from days or weeks to hours, says synthetic biologist Wilson Wong.

Today I’m celebrating a new candidate for the world’s loudest bird — the bare-throated bellbird (Procnias nudicollis). Males flaunt their wares with a 130-decibel mating call, louder than a jackhammer.

Let me know your favourite bird calls — or least-favourite loud sounds, plus any feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

The visible Universe owes its existence to the brief moments after the Big Bang when many of the laws of physics that hold the current Universe together were broken, allowing an imbalance between visible matter and antimatter to emerge1. One of these laws is the conservation of a quantity called baryon number, which is assigned to all protons and neutrons. Protons and neutrons are a type of particle called a baryon, which is made up of three fundamental particles known as quarks. Writing in Science, the STAR Collaboration2 reports the strongest experimental evidence yet that baryon number is carried not by the quarks themselves but by structures called baryon junctions, which bind them together.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Joy Buolamwini
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Joy Buolamwini is a senior fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, UK, founder of the Algorithmic Justice League in Boston, Massachusetts, and the author of Unmasking AI.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive of Meta Platforms, spoke about his company’s advances, including their latest smart glasses, at a conference in California in September.Credit: Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty

In an egregious example of the growing risks posed by camera-equipped wearables, an August 2026 Boston police report alleges that a registered sex offender used smart sunglasses to film children at a public spray pool (see go.nature.com/471zlwm). The incident illustrates how such devices can subject bystanders to intrusive surveillance without their knowledge or consent. The scale of the problem will only be compounded as the devices become integrated with artificial intelligence and the market expands.

Don’t sleepwalk from computer-vision research into surveillance

Technology firms are rapidly turning smart glasses from a niche gadget into a mass-market product, selling eyewear fitted with sensors as a tool for convenience and a platform for AI integration. They are the fastest-growing wearable category. More than eight million smart glasses were shipped in 2025, and by June 2026, sales of AI-equipped smart glasses had reportedly risen by more than 700% compared with the previous year. As someone who has spent a decade studying the potential harms associated with AI-powered biometric technologies, I urge policymakers to prepare for the major privacy-related crisis that is brewing.

Even at this nascent stage of adoption, media reports of bystanders expressing worry about ‘pervert glasses’ show why camera-equipped wearables pose a distinct problem: they can be more discreet than phone cameras and more portable than security cameras. These devices also mark a decisive shift from AI being confined to screens to it being embedded in consumer products that can continuously capture the physical world around us. AI-enabled wearables, including glasses, headphones and pendants, could thus expose millions of people to surveillance at an unprecedented scale.

Policymakers must therefore act now to update regulatory frameworks, before ambient AI becomes ubiquitous. They should include the creation of ‘consent-conscious spaces’ — such as schools, hospitals, courts and swimming pools — in which covert recording is prohibited by law and meaningful penalties are introduced to deter violations.

Halt the use of facial-recognition technology until it is regulated

A 2024 project by students at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which anticipated the current wave of wearable devices, showed the inherent risks in pairing AI with smart glasses (see go.nature.com/3tapz0y). In the demonstration, smart glasses live-streamed video to social media, on which an AI-powered facial-recognition system analysed the feed. The students said their aim was to show how existing tools can be combined with discreet recording devices to uncover sensitive personal information. A faceprint — a digital map of a face — created from a person’s image can be matched against databases of previously collected faces. Once it is linked to a name in a database, other personal details, including home addresses, can also be exposed.
