In September, “Baywatch” star Pamela Anderson opened up about her hepatitis C diagnosis in the 1990s. “It was a death sentence,” she said while accepting the Award of Courage from amfAR, an organization supporting HIV/AIDS research and advocacy. When she was diagnosed, she said, her doctor told her that she might only live another 10 years.

Her story is a good reminder of the amount of global progress that has been made in preventing and treating hepatitis C in just the last decade — and how far the U.S. has to go to catch up to our European neighbors.

Hepatitis C is a serious, bloodborne infectious disease that primarily impacts the liver. While some people can clear the infection on their own, the majority are at major risk of developing chronic, potentially fatal conditions like cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease. Hepatitis C infections are among the most common causes of medically necessary liver transplantations, second only to alcohol-associated liver disease.

Of all the factors that can increase a person’s risk of breast cancer, age is among the most significant. Almost half of people diagnosed with breast cancer are at least 65, and about 20% are 75 or older. Despite these rates, older women are frequently excluded from clinical trials; one study of breast cancer trials found that only 9% of participants were 65 or older, leaving physicians with a poorer understanding of how drugs behave in older adults and fewer guidelines with which to treat them.

There’s increasing evidence that these patients could benefit from more tailored treatments. Neil Carleton, a cancer biologist and first-year resident physician at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, said that breast tumors can develop and grow differently in older patients than in younger ones because of hormone levels and inflammation.

“It can be a very heterogeneous disease,” Carleton said. But “historically, we’ve kind of treated all breast cancer the same,” he added — in a way that’s “age-agnostic.”

https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/07/trum.title: Trump administration proposes $70,000 fee for popular international student work program
https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/07/trum.author: Jonathan Wosen
https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/07/trum.text:
As part of its ongoing bid to more tightly regulate international students, the Trump administration on Wednesday announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience.

The Department of Homeland Security said the fee would help combat alleged fraud and abuse in the work program, known as Optional Practical Training, which allows students to get hands-on work experience related to their field of study while still on a student visa. The department also said the restrictions would help U.S. citizens compete against international applicants in the job market.

“Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” said a department spokesperson in a press release. “American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”

This transcript has been edited for clarity.

Benjamin H. Levy III, MD: Welcome to this special Medscape video discussion about a groundbreaking new study that was just published in the September 2026 issue of the International Journal of Cancer. This was a study by Keren Papier, who is an epidemiologist at Oxford University, and some other colleagues that pooled two very large UK cohorts, close to 1 million patients in the UK, and tested whether drinking extremely hot beverages could cause an increase in esophageal cancer risk.

I'm Benjamin Levy, a gastroenterologist at the University of Chicago, and today I'm joined by Dr Emil Lou, who is an oncologist at the University of Minnesota. Dr Lou also has PhDs in microbiology and immunology, and I'm super excited to dive into this topic with you.

What's interesting about this paper is that there were prior studies and meta-analyses that found an association between drinking hot liquids in certain areas of Asia, Africa, South America, and the Middle East. We're talking temperatures above 70 ° C, so really, really hot beverages. For those of you in America, that's approximately 158 ° F. However, there was not an association seen so far in European studies except for the UK Biobank, which was used in the meta-analysis for this study.

Now, the International Agency for Research on Cancer does class hot beverages as a Group 2A carcinogen, which means it's probably carcinogenic. There was a 2025 UK Biobank analysis that found that very hot beverages could raise esophageal squamous cell carcinoma risk but not esophageal adenocarcinoma risk. Combined, there was a total of 2348 incident esophageal cancers detected on follow-up in these patients. Now, the breakdown was 1045 squamous cell carcinoma patients and 1303 patients who had adenocarcinoma.

This important journal article showed a significant increase in the relative risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with increasing temperature of drink consumption. It did not find an increase in adenocarcinoma risk, and it's important to note that they did not notice a distinction between what kind of hot beverages people were drinking. This is really applicable to our patients. It didn't matter whether it was coffee or hot tea.

Now, Dr Lou, could you tell us a little bit more about this newly published paper and why it grabbed your attention?

Emil Lou, MD, PhD: Yes, definitely. This is a really interesting study from a number of standpoints from an oncologic perspective. We know that in general, historically, squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus was more prevalent, but that's been on the downturn in terms of prevalence over at least the last decade or two. There’s been an increase in adenocarcinoma due to the risk factors that we'll certainly go into. There have been case-control studies in the past about this concept about hot beverages, maybe even scalding hot beverages, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer had set a cutoff of 65 ° C, which for those of us in the Western world is approaching 150 ° F, so it's pretty hot.

In the parts of the world where drinking hot beverages is really very common, and though many of these case-control studies were done in those areas of the world, namely in the Middle East and in Africa, this study was really prominent in that it was done in the Western world. We don't know much about how we can extrapolate findings from the earlier case-control studies that started to link hot temperature to potential causative factor of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus specifically.

Here, with this large cohort study over a very long period of follow-up time, being able to associate that in a Western population — and certainly in the United Kingdom that's well known for drinking a large amount of hot tea historically, but also coffee use is on the rise — helps us to distinguish a factor that from the cancer-causing standpoint or carcinogenesis, we always think about genomic drivers. We think about actionable issues, things in society, or behaviors that can modify or increase the risk of developing cancer, whether that be tobacco or alcohol use. No it's actually a factor that's separate from the actual content, but it's actually, in this case, temperature. That's really fascinating and certainly a modifiable factor.

It's interesting on a number of standpoints. It really expands our knowledge, and that's really what grabbed my attention. Dr Levy, could you tell us more about the Million Women Study population that was studied?

Levy: In the Million Women Study, or MWS, between 1996 and 2001 — those were the years I was in college approximately — the MWS recruited one 1.3 million women in England and Scotland through the National Health Service (NHS) breast screening program. Women aged 50 to 64 were sent a questionnaire with an invitation for routine screening and asked about sociodemographic, anthropometric, lifestyle, and health factors, and they were surveyed for approximately 3- to 5-year intervals afterward. The women were basically evaluated for deaths, cancer registrations, and hospital administrations.

Dr Lou, could you tell us a little bit more about the other analysis that was performed for this study in the UK Biobank group?

Lou: Two large cohorts, with the United Kingdom Biobank group comprising over half a million men and women in this case, and their age range was approximately 37 to 73 years of age. These were people who had registered with the NHS in England, Wales, and Scotland. They were recruited about two decades ago, between 2006 and 2010, by attending an in-person baseline assessment, and the subsequent follow-up was by questionnaire and survey. The information that was gathered was about lifestyle, sociodemographic factors, and health overall. It was collected at recruitment via touchscreen questionnaire, and the subsequent follow-up of participants was for determining and reporting of their health-related outcomes via electronic link, via age to routinely collected NHS data.

Before we get into the details of thermal injury, let's first talk about our current knowledge of esophageal cancers. Dr Levy, could you tell our audience about what we already knew about the risk factors for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma specifically?

Levy: One of the biggest reasons I went into medicine is to try to get people to quit smoking. Right off the bat, let's just emphasize that tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption are definitely the largest contributors. What's interesting is that there's some synergy between the two. I should use this opportunity to point out that the surgeon general, in January 2025, released a warning to the public about the GI risk of alcohol overuse, and esophageal cancer was one of these cancers. We've already been talking about alcohol consumption, so I just want to further emphasize this point.

There's actually synergy when patients use a combination of alcohol and tobacco. There can be up to a 12-fold increased risk in men and a 19-fold increased risk in women. It’s a very high risk factor, and so we should encourage our patients to decrease alcohol and tobacco use.

Other risk factors include red meat and processed meat, eating nitrosamine-rich foods, and foods that are preserved with sodium nitrite. When we barbecue or grill foods, especially red meat, it can release polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are potentially carcinogenic. Mate tea, which we'll get to in a second, is important for this study, and betel nuts. Also, processed meats can carry a relative increased risk of 1.59 per 50 g/day, so we really should try to encourage our patients to cut back on eating processed meats, so less sausage, bacon, hot dogs, and even deli meats.

Micronutrient deficiencies from vitamin A and E, selenium, zinc, and riboflavin can also increase your risk. There are also some genetic polymorphisms, such as people who don't process alcohol the same way. Mucosal injuries, and we see this in GI where someone intentionally drinks bleach as kind of a suicidal ideation, that's one of the big injuries we sometimes see. Achalasia, patients who have received prior radiation to the thoracic area, can increase risk, and in certain cases, HPV can also be a contributing factor in certain populations.

There are some inherited syndromes as well, just to round out all this for those physicians out there, that tylosis and Fanconi anemia dramatically increase the risk of esophageal cancer in these patients. There's even some research that I find really interesting being conducted to investigate whether poor oral hygiene can also contribute to risk.

Dr Lou, would you mind reviewing for us the known risk factors for esophageal adenocarcinoma? I was reviewing the squamous cell carcinoma. There are two main types of esophageal cancers, and we wanted to review all the risk factors for all kinds of esophageal cancer.

Lou: You might find this from the gastroenterology perspective as well, but certainly from the oncologic perspective, we've historically just lumped gastroesophageal together. Even here, it really magnifies the issue that esophageal cancer can be quite different, including in the driving causes, and we know much more about the genomic factors, the driver and passenger mutations associated, so everything from the biology to the potential causes. There's some overlap, but definitely with the continued rise of adenocarcinoma over the years as a specific subtype of esophageal adenocarcinoma, with increasing truncal obesity and sometimes concurrent with that, acid reflux, so GERD, gastroesophageal reflux disease, certainly is a risk factor and a driving issue that could potentially lead, with long-term exposure, to acid over time, especially with the reflux from the stomach into the lower part of the esophagus, Barrett esophagus.

Certainly overlap, as you said, Dr Levy, tobacco smoking, males more than females, just being male and even Caucasian populations over others. Age over 50 is associated with higher risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma. When people have a family history of Barrett esophagus or actual full-blown diagnosis of esophageal cancer of any kind, but especially adenocarcinoma, that poses a risk factor. There are some germline alterations with familial disease that can be associated with it, and some just yet to be discovered. Also, we know in terms of diet, diets that are low in fruits and vegetables and high in meats, as you said, in-depth, the ultra-processed foods and red meats certainly are part of that category, all pose risks for developing either a precursor like Barrett esophagus and/or actual full diagnosis of Barrett esophagus developing into esophageal adenocarcinoma.

On that note, Dr Levy, can you tell us more about, as a gastroenterologist and expert in this field, how do you normally screen via upper endoscopy or EGD for Barrett esophagus and esophageal cancer in general?

Levy: Anyone with a family history of esophageal cancer or Barrett esophagus are at increased risk. It's people with a family history, but also people with long-standing GERD symptoms, that we know are at risk. What's interesting is that we also know that there are many people that can develop Barrett esophagus who don't have any symptoms at all. As a GI field, we're trying to fine-tune the patient populations we are screening, and coming down the pipeline, there are some alternative methods in addition to endoscopy.

If patients have new-onset heartburn in the middle-age group, that kind of raises our suspicion that there may be something going on. People that have all of a sudden worsening heartburn symptoms. People, when we do an EGD, frequently when we take biopsies, if we see some abnormalities in the distal esophagus, sometimes it comes back as what we call Barrett esophagus, where there are some precancerous changes in the esophagus, and then we would do surveillance endoscopies over time because those patients are at slightly increased risk.

We would encourage weight loss and better management of their reflux symptoms to try to prevent progression. Some of the big-alarm features when we do upper endoscopies, or EGDs, are unintentional weight loss and dysphagia, trouble swallowing, or painful swallowing because we're trying to make sure that there's not a mass. Some atypical chest pain or heartburn symptoms would also encourage us to look.

When we do the EGD, we go through the esophagus, and we look at the stomach and in the small bowel. We examine the mucosa very carefully, and we'll take biopsies from different areas of the stomach if there's any kind of gastritis. Then we take time to focus at the GE junction, the distal esophagus, and we're very careful to examine the area. If we need to take biopsies, frequently we'll take four quadrant biopsies in different areas of the esophagus to really capture tissue for the pathologist to analyze.

We go over the results with the patient after the pathology comes back. I would encourage primary care doctors to ask questions about any kind of alarm symptoms.

What I find fascinating now with the GLP-1 medications is that hopefully some of these patients with obesity that have had chronic heartburn may be able to finally get it under control, because we have just so many patients that are just chronically on PPIs (protein pump inhibitors). Maybe with some of this weight loss, we're going to be able to improve patients' GERD, sleep apnea, and all kinds of other comorbidities that these patients carry with them. Hopefully we'll be able to try to prevent esophageal cancer from forming from this chronic reflux. Again, it's this reflux that's washing over distal esophagus and causing the mucosa to change to be able to protect itself, and that can predispose to premalignant changes over time.

Whatever we can do to try to prevent this reflux and weight loss is, especially in America, a major factor with patients being obese. I also encourage patients not to eat late at night because that can cause reflux.

Lou: As we alluded to earlier, we mentioned the betel quid nut or, as an example, where you had mentioned that as a risk factor for squamous cell and, I think, of oropharyngeal cancer. That's a type of product where it induces DNA damage, and it's very similar to tobacco smoke, alcohol, and some of the risk factors. Whereas here, very similar to what you were describing earlier, in the lower esophagus, the reflux. What it causes is what I would describe as a caustic reaction. It's an influence. It's based on acid. It's caustic. It causes injury.

The thermal injury for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus that we normally associate with the upper third or two-thirds of the esophagus, I kind of see as very similar, just a different mechanism. Nonetheless, even though it's not an actual product, it's actually the temperature in this case that's the modifying factor. I think of very much the influence of the pure heat of the substance, whether it be the tea or a cup of Earl Grey, coffee, mate, or other type of product, independent of that, as shown in this study, that the thermal injury really disrupts the mucosal membrane.

Anytime the mucosal membrane and squamous cells are disrupted, we think of it generally in medicine as a nice, very clear lining, which may be oversimplifying it, but there's always turnover of cells throughout our body, and squamous cells in the esophagus specifically are no different. If you're accelerating that repair and injury cycle, and basically a wound repair occurring internally in the lumen of the esophagus, that's going to make the turnover more prone to getting DNA damage and DNA damage that will accumulate over time to lead to an injury that will lead to premalignant states and eventually into actual carcinoma.

When there's an added factor of chronic inflammation, that also is a state that is predisposing at the cellular level and at the cellular neighborhood level, so to speak, of a recipe for a higher risk for cancer. All of those, whether it be at the DNA level or just the cellular proliferation level, and the inflammation are multipronged, but they're all adding up to thermal injury causing a risk factor that we think may be associated with the findings here, regardless of the actual product ingested, the tea, coffee, or others.

From your perspective, Dr Levy, from what we know from a global oncology and global health perspective, what are the esophageal cancer belts of the world where people are more prone to getting esophageal cancer? Does there seem to be a link between hot drinks and esophageal cancer in these geographic areas?

Levy: What's really interesting is some of the prior research that’s already been done, and one of the biggest studies or most important studies was in Northeast Iran. There was a cohort called the Golestan Cohort, where they found the temperature of drinking hot tea over 60 ° C carried a 41% higher risk. If patients reported a preference for very hot tea, that carried a 2.4-fold risk.

There are some other populations in North Central China, the Taihang Mountain region, where many people consume very hot soups and boiling hot food or drink. There are several other East Asian populations that showed increased risk of drinking hot beverages with squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus. I find this fascinating that in South America, where they drink mate, there's a huge squamous cell carcinoma burden in countries like Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and the Gran Chaco region of Argentina. The cause of this is people drinking large volumes of mate at very high temperatures, a drink very popular there. In a Paraguay study, the mate had an attributable risk factor of 53%.

There are also some regions of Africa where there are increased incidences where people drink very hot beverages, in certain countries such as Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia, Mozambique, and Zambia. In Tanzania, the recorded temperature of some beverages that people were drinking was above 70 ° C. I think, globally, we need to do a great job of teaching people about the dangers of drinking hot beverages, and this is something we don't get taught in medical school.

I think that's one of the main reasons we should pay attention to this study. We should've been paying attention, as physicians, to all these studies before, but this is really kind of like sounding the alarm bells in the oncology and GI communities that we need to teach patients not to eat or drink hot beverages and to wait a little bit and let it cool so that we can minimize any injury to their mouth, esophagus, or even stomach. This kind of begs the question that maybe we should look in the stomach to see if these hot foods are causing any kind of gastritis or damage there, too.

Dr Lou, are there specific cutoffs for temperature for elevated risk of squamous cell carcinoma?

Lou: It was very interesting, and as I mentioned, the International Agency for Research of Cancer had defined very hot as 65 ° C or above. For this study, they used a range of 60-65 ° C, so as we said, it's above 140-150 ° F. It's not a boiling temperature, but whether it be coffee or water, they associated the temperature cutoffs, and then also with increased cancer risk in squamous cell carcinoma esophagus, but not necessarily adenocarcinoma.

What's interesting is that they also examined, as an independent risk factor, the frequency of how much they were drinking. The investigators used the survey self-reported information, and they defined in this study as a cutoff six drinks per day, which sounds like a lot, but I think there are many cultures that do drink [that much], part of the social aspect of living, culture, and habit and everything, all of the above, whether it be tea or coffee, the UK or otherwise.

Since this was a Western study in the UK, they looked at people who had more than six drinks per day of the very hot variety, and they defined a relative risk of 1.71, and they interpreted that as a 71% higher risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma for the people who drank more than six of these very hot drinks per day than the ones who drank fewer than six per day.

It's interesting in that it's more of a consistent, almost like a pulse-like effect, so it's not just how much and how hot it is, but more of a combination of the factors, interestingly. Definitely, there is more to look at, and as you mentioned, in the stomach. We could easily extrapolate or imagine hot foods beyond just drinks would be future subjects for investigation to determine whether or not thermal ablation carries over to lower in the GI tract, including the body of the stomach.

Dr Levy, now that we have new data from the study in the September 2026 issue of the International Journal of Cancer that we've been discussing, what are some things that you think we should be doing to reach and teach the public about this potential risk for cancer?

Levy: The authors estimated in the study that approximately 14% of squamous cell carcinoma cases of the esophagus could be prevented if we shifted very hot drinkers to just drinking hot. I think that really drives home the point. We should be encouraging patients not to drink extremely, extremely hot beverages. What I find is that there are certain people who just like hot soup and hot beverages. We just need, from a public health perspective, to do some education nationally and internationally.

I've thought a great deal about this over the past couple of days since this article came out. One of the things we can do from a public health perspective is to try to encourage coffee spots to lower the temperature of their coffee. What's interesting, we're reading about microplastics, and research is being done. Separately from this issue of causing esophageal cancer, we should probably lower the temperature of hot beverages in any kind of cup that's lined by plastic or even in Styrofoam cups so that we can prevent the microplastics from melting off and entering the coffee, as well as when people make coffee at home through their single-use plastic cups. If we are able to lower the temperature of the coffee even in that and maybe try to get manufacturers to lower the temperature of coffee just slightly.

One thing that patients can do, is, if people like cream in their coffee, make sure that they have some milk, creamer, oat milk, or whatever kind of additive they want to add. We also should drive home the point that coffee is good for you in regards of hepatic steatosis of the liver. We do encourage patients who have fat in their liver to drink three cups of coffee per day. We're not trying to scare people away to not drink coffee, but it should be at a temperature that's not burning their mouth or esophagus.

Sometimes we order coffee out in restaurants and it's scalding hot. Do you think we can convince coffee restaurants to decrease the temperature of the drinks they're serving?

Lou: That’s an interesting question. It calls to mind more in media and even in pop culture, and it's been made light of where restaurants that I won't name, which have been sued in past years for selling scalding hot coffee, and then even in sitcoms, they made a plot line. One serious aspect this paper sheds light on is the potential damage it can do. We're looking at a system-wide change. It might be challenging, but it's worth a try to really put it in the domain of public health and educating the companies, and then it filters down to their individual franchises and their stores.

Really having an impact in saying that coffee is good for you, and there are so many studies, cardiovascular, even cancer risk, and so many other issues. Please, everyone listening, we're not discouraging coffee or tea. There are actually many health benefits, and they're enjoyable drinks. I think moderation in terms of the temperature. Again, if international agencies are labeling extremely high temperatures as an actual carcinogen, it's not the product itself, again, it's an actual temperature, then that's something that's very much modifiable. Whether restaurants can do it, the restaurant industry, if we get them on board, would be great.

You mentioned micro- and nanoplastics, which is a research interest of mine also, and we know that micro-and nanoplastics leach off at extremely high temperatures. Entering yet another mix that may be a future study that's performed we can review in this context. Whether it's a system-wide error, we know that at the individual level, if each individual takes to heart, anyone listening to this and physicians who are listening to this to educate their patients, maybe waiting just an extra couple of minutes to get it down from the very hot down to the less hot, but still hot-enough-to-enjoy level and temperature, might be the happy medium here.

Dr Levy, are there any preventive strategies from the food intake standpoint that we could teach our patients?

Levy: I think the key to this is fruits and vegetables, and we should encourage people to eat that. Fiber can help prevent colon cancer. It's just good for you. There's a relative risk of 0.84, so it can be very helpful. Beyond that, as we talked about earlier, I really want to drive home this point that we should encourage our patients to quit smoking and to dramatically reduce their alcohol intake. I think that's going to be a huge issue going forward. We've done a great job in America, getting people to quit smoking, but we still have work to do.

During the pandemic, there was a huge spike in alcohol consumption. It's a little bit better now, and some of the younger generations drink less. We have a large amount of data to support that. In America and worldwide, we really need to encourage our patients to cut back. It can reduce their risk of esophageal cancer.

Maintaining a healthy diet, maintaining a healthy weight, and trying to encourage people to eat at least three servings of fruits or vegetables per day. I have many patients who are very healthy, but there are certain areas of our country where it's much harder to buy fruits and vegetables. There aren't as many grocery stores around certain patient populations. We need to make fruits and vegetables cheaper and change this culture where instead of people, when they want a snack, reaching for chips, that they reach for a fruit or vegetable.

I find many of my patients are constipated because they're not eating enough fruits and vegetables or they're not drinking enough water or fluids. I think eating at least three servings of fruits or vegetables per day is a great, super easy start. I counsel my patients to try to have a piece of fruit or vegetable with each meal. If you do that three times a day, you don't even have to think about it.

Dr Lou, what do you think should be the future areas of research into this link between hot drinks and esophageal cancer?

Lou: It’s fascinating. You made a very good point about the fruits and vegetables because we know we have food deserts in this country, and it's not always accessible. At the same time, it is a modifiable risk factor. When we have access, we can definitely control the intake and the avoidance of the other factors like tobacco and alcohol.

When it comes to research, this really, again, coming back to that idea of a temperature as a potential carcinogen, not the actual product, and regardless of the product, is a really fertile area for research that I hope in this era of challenging times for research funding. This is an important area. There are more areas and opportunity in the lab and then in the translational aspect of from bench to bedside to be able to examine this.

One thing that comes to mind is organoids and other things where we can kind of mimic the human condition outside the actual human body to examine products, and then also examine, in this case, temperatures and in combinations to determine what is the mix or maybe the fatal mix that will be most likely to spur early DNA mutations, the thermal injury that leads to mucosal lining disruption, and then cellular proliferation changes in a lab. That's definitely something that's really a ripe opportunity that I hope will take off.

We mentioned a little bit about micro- and nanoplastics, and that might play into it, but really just focusing on the thermal injury and temperature aspect, there is more opportunity. This study is two cohorts combined and over a million patients over a long follow-up time. I think research, while the temperatures are defined, the survey results did depend on basically a relatively subjective reporting. People in one part of the world might define something as very hot, whereas people in another part of the world, whatever drink that they're consuming, might consider that moderate to somewhat hot. There is some subjectivity in the actual self-reporting, and some of that can't be avoided.

I know the investigators really parlayed the large body of data over time the best they could. Hopefully more studies like this that represent Western populations are conducted for us to determine what is applicable to a global health, global population, what might be region-specific, regardless of the type of drink that's being consumed. More studies like this would be really helpful and provide more depth. If we can unravel that at genetic level as well as the epigenetic level, that would be extremely fruitful for the field. I hope some of that will be forthcoming in the years to come that we can come back and discuss.

Levy: That would be awesome. Thanks for joining us for this conversation about this very large UK study examining whether consuming very hot beverages might place individuals at risk for esophageal cancer, especially from repeated thermal injuries. This has been so much fun, Emil. Thanks for joining us, and good luck with all your research.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Finding meaning in tragedy: What clinicians can learn from Pike’s execution attempt
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Christa Pike was sentenced to death for murder in 1996. On Sept. 30, she was injected with two 5 mg doses of pentobarbital but survived.

During the execution attempt, witnesses reported that Pike said she was in pain and then appeared to be snoring before she was transported to a hospital.

Pike’s attorneys said she gained consciousness and the ability to speak on Oct. 6, although she is unable to eat, swallow or move her swollen hands and arms, and has pneumonia and “cognitive confusion,” according to reporting from Reuters.

Lewis Nelson, MD, MBA, dean and chief of health affairs at Florida Atlantic University Charles E. Schmidt College of Medicine, told Healio that “assuming no long-term damage occurred due to having low oxygen levels while the drug was active,” Pike should not experience long-term adverse effects.

“The drug itself is not ‘toxic’ in that sense,” he said. “It’s unclear about the extent of the skin damage, but that usually heals with proper treatment.”

Theories have emerged about why the execution did not go as planned. For example, Nelson said it is also possible that the pentobarbital “was improperly made since it was not likely a commercial preparation.”

Another potential reason is that pentobarbital did not fully enter the bloodstream, Amit Bahl, MD, MPH, a professor of emergency medicine at Oakland University William Beaumont School of Medicine, told Healio.

“If an IV catheter is improperly positioned or the vein has been damaged, medication can leak into the surrounding tissue rather than entering the circulation. This is called infiltration, or extravasation when the medication causes tissue injury,” he said. “The result may be unpredictable absorption and reduced or delayed systemic drug delivery. However, without procedural and clinical details, we cannot determine whether this occurred in this particular case.”

Bahl explained that infiltration and other vascular injuries are potential complications of any needle puncture.

“Repeated attempts can produce multiple defects in the vein wall. A catheter may also become partially or completely displaced outside the vein,” Bahl said. “Even when the catheter remains within the vessel, significant vein wall injury can compromise medication delivery.”

Infiltration can happen “even with experienced clinicians, but appropriate vein assessment, insertion technique, and confirmation of catheter function are critical to reducing this risk,” Bahl said.

Nelson agreed, saying “many people have learned this skill but, depending on who was doing the procedure and the difficulty of finding an acceptable vein, it can be challenging.”

“That said, there are fairly easy ways of assessing whether the IV catheter is in the vein or under the skin, such as withdrawing a small amount of blood or injecting nontoxic normal saline using a syringe,” he said.

According to Nelson and Bahl, symptoms of infiltration or extravasation can include pain, tenderness, swelling, and changes and damage to the skin around the site.

“These effects occur because the medication is accumulating under the skin under pressure, which is distending the tissue,” Nelson said.

Bahl noted that vascular complications are not always immediately apparent, “particularly in patients who cannot communicate discomfort.”

“Importantly, the absence of obvious swelling does not guarantee that an IV is functioning properly,” he said.

When infiltration or extravasation is suspected, “stop the infusion and attempt to withdraw some of the extravasation medication, if possible,” Nelson said.

“Oftentimes, warm compresses can be placed to help speed movement out of the area due to enhanced blood flow, leading to more rapidness, but still slow compared to IV absorption,” he said.

Bahl said the IV catheter “should not be flushed” when infiltration is suspected, “and the site should be assessed for tissue injury and vascular compromise.”

“Depending on the medication, aspiration through the existing catheter and other drug-specific interventions may be indicated before catheter removal,” he said. “Alternative vascular access should be established when continued treatment is necessary.”

To avoid complications, Bahl said clinicians should perform vascular assessments before IV placement to identify patients with difficult access.

“When traditional access is unlikely to succeed, clinicians should escalate early to technologies such as ultrasound guidance rather than repeatedly attempting unsuccessful insertions,” he said. “Ultrasound can help identify suitable vessels and guide catheter placement.”

Bahl underlined that patients “are not pincushions.”

“Difficult IV access should trigger a change in strategy, not simply another needle stick,” he said. “We have effective technologies and evidence-based approaches to vascular access, yet repeated unsuccessful attempts remain common.”

A successful IV placement is not getting the needle in the vein, Bahl said, but “establishing reliable vascular access that safely delivers the intended therapy.”

“What happens during insertion can have significant consequences for everything that follows,” he said.

Amit Bahl, MD, MPH, can be reached at amit.bahl@corewellhealth.org.

Lewis Nelson, MD, MBA, can be reached at lnelsonmd@gmail.com.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Kidney disease often overlooked in women
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Kidney disease in women may be often underdiagnosed and undertreated due to lack of sex-specific research and recognition of reproductive health as an important variable, according to a scientific statement published in Circulation.

The American Heart Association issued a scientific statement calling on greater recognition and treatment of kidney disease in women; assessment of reproductive health during kidney care; and increased enrollment of women in clinical trials to improve knowledge of sex-specific treatment outcomes.

The authors reported that approximately one in 10 women globally have chronic kidney disease (CKD), and women with CKD often go undiagnosed for a variety of reasons.

One example cited in the statement was that based on the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation for estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a creatinine level of 1 mg/dL in a 50-year-old man indicates an eGFR of 92 mL/min/1.73 m2; however, similar levels for a women the same age is indicative of an eGFR of 69 mL/min/1.73 m2, or stage 2 CKD.

“One important challenge is that kidney disease may be underrecognized in women. Kidney function is commonly estimated using creatinine, a waste product generated by muscle,” Eman Y. Gohar, PhD, MS, FAHA, assistant professor of medicine in the division of nephrology and hypertension at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, and chair of the scientific statement writing group, told Healio. “Because women generally have less muscle mass and may produce less creatinine, kidney dysfunction may sometimes appear less severe than it actually is, which can contribute to delayed recognition or referral.”

In addition, women receive less CKD surveillance, and evidence-based recommendations are more slowly adopted for women, according to the statement.

“The statement was needed because women experience unique biological and life-stage factors, including pregnancy and menopause, that can affect kidney health in ways that are not fully reflected in current care models or research. The writing group aimed to bring attention to these gaps and identify opportunities to improve kidney care for women throughout their lives,” Gohar told Healio. “Kidney health is not one-size-fits-all. A woman’s menstrual health, pregnancy experiences, menopausal status and other sex-specific factors can provide important clues about current and future kidney health. The statement points out that CKD is closely connected to heart health, overall CV-kidney-metabolic health as well as reproductive health. Earlier recognition, equitable access to care and research that better reflects women’s experiences could help improve outcomes for millions of women worldwide.”

The writing committee stated that during pregnancy, renal changes include a 40% to 65% increase in eGFR attributed to increased renal blood flow, thereby reducing serum creatinine, urea and uric acid. However, for women with baseline CKD, creatinine levels of more than 1.4 mg/dL increase risk for progression of CKD and adverse pregnancy outcomes, according to the statement.

“Beyond diagnosis, women experience risk factors that men do not, including pregnancy-related complications such as preeclampsia, early menopause and conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome,” Gohar told Healio.

“During the reproductive years, certain conditions and autoimmune diseases may increase kidney disease risk. Pregnancy creates physiological changes that can reveal underlying kidney disease. Complications such as preeclampsia are recognized as important warning signs for future problems,” Gohar said. “For women living with CKD, pregnancy requires careful planning and management because kidney function and BP can affect both maternal and fetal outcomes.”

Safe and effective contraceptives are available for women with CKD, despite longstanding concerns, and should be offered regardless of CKD stage to avoid unplanned pregnancies, according to the study.

The authors noted that contraception efficacy in people with CKD is similar to that in the general population.

Among women who are postmenopausal, declining renal function is hypothesized to be caused by estradiol loss; however, there is a paucity of studies evaluating whether menopausal hormone therapy could prevent the progression of CKD, according to the statement.

The authors added that confounding risk factors such as greater prevalence of obesity, diabetes and hyperlipidemia among postmenopausal women compared with premenopausal women may contribute to later risk for kidney disease.

“Managing well-established risk factors such as high BP, diabetes and obesity remains critically important. But women should also discuss pregnancy history, menopause status and other reproductive health factors with their healthcare team because these may offer valuable insights into kidney health,” Gohar told Healio. “At a broad level, increasing participation of women in clinical trials and incorporating reproductive health assessments into routine kidney care are all important steps toward better health outcomes for women.”

Several opportunities to improve women’s kidney care at the clinical research levels were identified in the scientific statement, with a call to action for clinical trials designed to:

“We have made tremendous advances in understanding kidney disease; however, women continue to face unique challenges that are not always recognized in research or clinical care,” Gohar told Healio. “By recognizing these differences and designing research studies and health systems that better reflect women’s experiences, we have an opportunity to improve both kidney and CV health for future generations of women.”

Eman Y. Gohar, PhD, MS, FAHA, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Gohar EY, et al. Circulation. 2026;doi:10.1161/CIR.0000000000001471.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Q&A: ACP updates guidance on ethical AI use
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom; Jan K. Carney, MD, MPH, MACP, FRCP
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

In a new position paper, ACP detailed key principles for ethical, responsible AI use in healthcare.

AI — when implemented thoughtfully — has the potential to strengthen clinical decision-making, advance patient care “and preserve the central role of the patient-physician relationship,” according to an ACP press release. However, the technology is being adopted rapidly and “there has not been consensus on guidance around issues” like disclosure, fairness and privacy, and both “physicians and patients need practical ethical guidance to help ensure these technologies are used responsibly, equitably, and in ways that support high-quality, patient-centered care.”

Healio spoke with ACP president Jan K. Carney, MD, MPH, MACP, FRCP, to learn more about ACP’s position, the reasoning behind it, deskilling and more.

Healio: Why did ACP publish this position paper? Why is it important to address ethical AI use in medical practice?

Carney: ACP published this paper to address potential benefits and risks of the rapid acceleration of AI use in healthcare from an ethics and professionalism perspective. This position paper updates one from 2024 that first made recommendations in 10 areas. The current paper considers AI as augmented intelligence, meaning that it is a tool to assist physicians and patients, noting that there are at least 200 guidelines emerging in the literature, but no consensus on key issues such as patient privacy, disclosure of AI use and equitable use of AI to help patients.

Healio: What are the potential benefits and consequences of AI use in medicine?

Carney: AI can help physicians in diagnosing disease, identifying treatment alternatives, and making preventive care recommendations. It is particularly helpful, based on current literature, in helping physicians improve diagnostic accuracy in finding skin cancer and interpreting mammograms.

Healio: What are the key components of ACP’s position paper? What values is this policy grounded in?

Carney: ACP’s paper is grounded in the patient-physician relationship as the foundation for the best possible healthcare outcomes. This ethical foundation addresses the core responsibilities of physicians in the patient-physician relationship, including always doing what is in the patient’s best interests, doing no harm, respecting patient autonomy and, in the setting of limited resources, providing care for as many patients as possible.

Patients trust physicians for their evidence-based knowledge, as well as the judgement and trust that defines the patient-physician relationship, especially over time. This trust comes from ongoing communication, considering the clinical evidence and judgement for each patient, and considering patient values and preferences. Physicians are trusted sources of health information and advice, based on science and evidence, and applied to each patient. This patient-physician relationship along with accountability and trust requires the human elements essential to the practice of medicine, elements never reproducible through chatbots.

Healio: The policy paper mentions a hot topic, deskilling . Is there a way to prevent deskilling and ensure AI is used as a way to augment physician intelligence instead?

Carney: I think about deskilling as letting AI think and reason for you, leading to less rigorous or less intensive critical thinking. Automation bias suggests that something from a machine may be more accurate or reliable. In fact, with AI, you must be cautious because AI has varying rates of hallucinations — what I call confabulation — where the material sounds very convincing but is totally wrong. Rates of hallucinations and confabulation vary by how complicated the task or question is, with rates often 5% or lower for simple questions. For scientific questions or medical literature reviews, rates of confabulation can be over 90% in some studies. Confabulation about clinical guideline questions or tasks requiring clinical reasoning vary widely. Teaching physicians — at all levels of their medical education — how to generate questions that minimize this risk, called “prompt literacy,” is essential. Another good practice is to verify the references when asking a question, and to consider the AI response against your expert judgment as a physician for the individual patient.

Healio: Is this an area where regulation should be considered? Why or why not?

Carney: Rather than calling for specific federal regulations, ACP supports oversight and governance of AI’s use in healthcare, outlining key areas in its 2024 position paper. The most recent 2026 paper outlines three ethical guideposts for AI use in healthcare and medicine. The first is termed relationality, reinforcing the principle that AI supports, not weakens, the patient-physician relationship. Self-governance, the second guidepost, refers to physician integrity and independent clinical judgment. Competence means physicians using their expert medical knowledge to help patients, uniquely for each patient, fairly, equitably and without bias.

Healio: Are there any policies that primary care providers should put in place? Any best practices they should know about?

Carney: PCPs, whether in health systems or independent practice, should develop habits and best practices that minimize documented AI risks, such as bias and confabulation, and maximize potential benefits from AI use, using skills of prompt literacy. ACP’s three ethical guideposts provide a practice framework in the context of the patient-physician relationship.

Healio: What is the take-home message here?

Carney: I would love readers to read the paper! The three ethical guideposts provide a practical framework to think about AI use in clinical practice. One of the recommendations in the paper says it best, “when physicians use AI to support medical decision making, that use should respect and promote — not replace — physician-independent clinical judgment and recommendations based on the patient’s individual needs and values.” AI use is changing rapidly. Our goal is to minimize risks to patient care and safety, and maximize potential benefits to patients and to clinical practice. ACP has also developed an AI Resource Hub.

Healio: Is there anything else you would like to add?

Carney: ACP’s four positions in this paper are particularly helpful, emphasizing the patient-physician relationship, physician education in the appropriate use of AI, AI’s use in supporting, not replacing, physician independent clinical decisions and promoting health equity by mitigating bias in AI use. https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: US heart death declines slow, but decades of disparities remain
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Cardiovascular disease deaths in the U.S. continued to decline, but progress has slowed and disparities in CVD-related mortality persist, according to research published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology.

Total CVD mortality from 2000 to 2019 remained highest among the Black population in the U.S., followed by Indigenous, white, Hispanic and Asian individuals, researchers reported.

“For clinical practice, these findings point to the value of integrating local epidemiology into risk assessment, outreach and care delivery,” George A. Mensah, MD, FACC, director of the Center for Translation Research and Implementation Science at the NHLBI, said in a press release. “Health systems and clinicians need to align prevention strategies with the dominant local causes and the populations experiencing the greatest burden.”

Mensah and colleagues used death certificate data from the U.S. National Vital Statistics System and small-area models to calculate age-standardized mortality rates among Indigenous, Asian, Black, Hispanic and white individuals across more than 3,000 counties and 21 causes of CV death from 2000 to 2019.

The researchers estimated that the age-standardized mortality rates of total CVD in the U.S. in 2019 was 237.8 per 100,000 population (95% uncertainty interval [UI]; 237.2-238.4).

Yearly decline in total CVD deaths were markedly larger between 2000 and 2011 (3.2%; 95% UI, 3.2%-3.2%) vs. 2011 to 2019 (0.8%; 95% UI, 0.8%-0.9%), according to the study.

In 2019, researchers observed age-standardized total CVD mortality was highest among Black individuals in the U.S. (304.8 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 302.7-306.9), followed by Indigenous (256.7 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 228.9-288.2), white (240.9 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 240.2-241.7) Hispanic (178.3 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 174.5-182) and Asian individuals (140.3 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 136.2-144.2).

Age-standardized total CVD mortality continued in this ordering from 2000 to 2019, according to the study.

Among the Indigenous population, states with the highest number of counties with the highest age-standardized total CVD mortality rates were Oklahoma followed by North Carolina, Montana and Kansas, according to the researchers. The researchers reported that Neshoba County, Mississippi; Cumberland County, New Jersey; and Sedgwick and Shawnee counties in Kansas all had total CVD mortality rates exceeding 600 per 100,000 population in 2019.

Among the Asian population, states with the highest number of counties with the highest age-standardized total CVD mortality rates were California followed by Wisconsin, Texas and Oklahoma. Researchers reported the counties with the highest mortality rates in 2019 were reported in Washington County, Arkansas (328.8 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 262.7-397.9); Sheboygan County, Wisconsin (274 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 220.4-332.1); and Brown County, Wisconsin (257.9 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 208-313.6).

Among the Black population, states with the highest number of counties with the highest age-standardized total CVD mortality rates were Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Tennessee, and the counties with the highest mortality rates in 2019 were Martinsville City, Virginia, (665.6 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 552.7-797.2) and Webster County, Mississippi (532.6 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 454.5-615.3), according to the study.

Among the Latino population, researchers reported states with the highest number of counties with the highest age-standardized total CVD mortality rates were Texas followed by New Mexico, Michigan and Colorado, and the county with the highest mortality rates in 2019 was Honolulu County, Hawaii (466 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 417.9-517.4).

Among the white population, states with the highest number of counties with the highest age-standardized total CVD mortality rates were concentrated in the South and Appalachia, and the counties with the highest mortality rates in 2019 were Martinsville City; (643.1 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 561.5-731.8); Petersburg City (541.3 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 473.1-609.8); and Covington City, all in Virginia (483.2 per 100,000 population; 95% UI, 414.5-560.4), according to the study.

“Detailed knowledge of county-level variation is important for all racial and/or ethnic populations,” Mensah said in the release. “It can inform appropriate local-level clinical and public health practices, policies and strategies needed to have a sustained effect on reducing or eliminating racial, ethnic and place-based cardiovascular disease disparities.”

Mensah GA, et al. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2026;doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2026.07.010.

https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.title: Governance key to balancing AI augmentation, risk for deskilling
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.author: Octavia Feliciano
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

An aircraft’s autopilot can guide every aspect of a flight, from takeoff to landing. But it is expected, and reassuring to know, that a pilot has the skills to intervene and assume manual control at any time, especially during an emergency.

There is a similar expectation for healthcare professionals, who increasingly encounter AI’s expansion in practice to aid clinical diagnoses, documentation and decision-making. The concern? That overreliance on AI could eventually erode clinical skills and competencies, a phenomenon dubbed “deskilling.”

“Research is showing that there is a fine line between augmentation and deskilling, and there’s a slippery slope between the two,” Ron Keren, MD, MPH, senior vice president and chief medical officer at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, told Healio.

Public-facing AI became mainstream with the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, but the technology’s impact is already felt across medical specialties.

A 2025 observational study published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology found that adenoma detection rates during colonoscopies performed without AI fell from 28.4% in the 3 months before AI was introduced into practice to 22.4% in the 3 months afterward.

“Because adenoma detection correlates with interval colorectal cancer risk, that could translate to approximately 18% more missed cancers,” Maxim Topaz, PhD, RN, MA, Elizabeth Standish Gill Associate Professor of Nursing at Columbia University Medical Center, told Healio.

He emphasized an urgent need to monitor AI’s impact on care quality, as well as to develop oversight strategies to address deskilling concerns.

“We still have hundreds of trials asking whether AI improves care and almost none measuring what happens when it is switched off,” Topaz said.

“There’s no doubt AI is here to stay in some form,” Amy Oxentenko, MD, MACP, MACG, AGAF, professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic College of Medicine and Science and vice dean of practice and chief patient experience officer for all Mayo Clinic sites, told Healio. She also noted it is easy to imagine “a day in the life” in which these AI systems may fail.

As healthcare becomes more reliant on AI, clinicians may be less prepared to function when those systems are unavailable: Algorithms can go offline, vendors can fail and hospitals can get hit by cyberattacks, Topaz cautioned.

Disruptions are not the only concern. Anxieties about deskilling are shared by healthcare professionals and patients alike. In a Wolters Kluwer survey, 77% of doctors, 70% of nurses and 68% of patients expressed concern about AI-driven deskilling.

“AI helps augment clinicians’ capabilities, but the core judgment about a clinical scenario should always be made by the clinicians themselves,” Deepti Pandita, MD, FACP, FAMIA, chief AI officer and vice president of clinical informatics and chief medical informatics at University of California Irvine Healthsystem, told Healio.

“What AI helps with is pattern recognition, documentation, triage support, decision support and suggestions — or what I call AI nudges — but ultimately, clinicians themselves are always responsible for the final diagnosis, the final output and final accountability,” she added.

Human oversight is critical to ensure AI tools support quality patient care and preserve clinical skills.

Topaz advised healthcare systems to identify frontline practitioners, including nurses and other clinicians, to serve on governance boards.

“Deskilling is a workforce and patient safety issue, not an IT issue,” he said.

Keren also encouraged clinicians to become involved in AI governance at their practices and institutions, regardless of whether they personally embrace AI or are skeptical of it.

“[Clinicians] should play an active role in helping us design how AI tools are integrated into clinical care,” Keren said. “They will know best what’s going to help them, and what’s going to potentially negatively impact their performance.”

The clerical areas of practice — where AI tools are being applied at the fastest rate — raise fewer deskilling-related concerns, according to Keren.

“Wisely, both the developers of AI technologies, as well as the health systems that are implementing them, have started with these clerical tasks, like documentation, note-taking, coding and billing, facilitating communications with patients through portals, and scheduling,” Keren said. “In that setting, errors are consequential, but less likely to cause serious patient harm.”

Oxentenko concurred, noting AI tools that handle clerical and administrative tasks can save time and give clinicians more bandwidth to connect with their patients. However, she did highlight an important caveat.

“It’s still incumbent on [the clinician] to review notes that AI has generated,” Oxentenko, who also serves on the Healio AI advisory board, said. “You can’t get complacent and assume it’s going to be accurate. An incorrect medication or dosage could have grave consequences.”

On the other hand, AI tools that perform clinical care tasks — summarizing patient records, interpreting medical images, generating differential diagnoses and providing clinical decision support — require the greatest oversight from clinicians and governance boards, Keren emphasized.

In these areas, “errors have the potential to really harm patients,” he said.

When it comes to tackling governance of AI tools, Topaz advised healthcare systems and practices to “start with measurement, because you cannot govern what you do not measure.”

Topaz proposed several metrics that health systems and practices could employ including, “periodic unassisted performance assessments in quality programs, manual-mode protocols where a defined share of cases — for example, one in five — is completed without AI, and monitoring of automation bias signals such as override and agreement rates.”

Developing a governance structure does not necessarily require new hires.

“In a resource-constrained environment where you don’t have a green light to hire new [full-time employees] all the time, I think the best process is to reskill or upskill current roles and fit them into the governance process,” Pandita said.

When budget and resources are tight, governance initiatives monitoring clinical skills also can be scaled appropriately.

“Smaller practices can run a lighter version and pick one core skill each quarter and audit it without AI assistance,” Topaz said.

In addition to deskilling, Topaz raised concern about “never-skilling,” the risk that medical students may rely too heavily on AI tools during training and never fully develop clinical competencies necessary for practice.

Keren said he is optimistic about the future of medical education if AI-assistive tools are thoughtfully designed and receive proper oversight.

“Trainees are coming into those programs more savvy with AI and digital tools than ever before, which is great,” Oxentenko said. “However, we need to balance that with making sure we’re teaching trainees the fundamental baseline skills.”

Keren encouraged educators to adopt or develop AI tools with features that protect the development and maintenance of clinical skills. That might include AI tools that carefully explain their own “reasoning” or provide references to primary sources that trainees or clinicians can interrogate and evaluate.

He also suggested that clinical care AI programs only provide diagnoses or treatment plans after a student or clinician submits their own. Users of the tool can then compare their conclusion with the AI output and see where they align or conflict.

Keren emphasized further study in this area is critical.

“The research we need should evaluate optimal AI implementation design features that minimize the deskilling phenomenon, which is measured in terms of errors of omission or commission,” he said. “If you can solve the problem with one design feature, there’s no point in adding the second one, because it’s more cost and more potential inconvenience.”

While it may be impractical to unilaterally ban trainees from using AI tools, Keren said it may be valuable to introduce “AI-free zones” — time periods or locations where AI is not available — to promote self-reliance.

“Education should require demonstrated competence without AI before granting competence with it,” Topaz said. “Practically, that means shadow-mode training where learners form their own assessment before seeing the AI output, simulation that exposes trainees to AI failures and hallucinations, and AI-free components in board certification.”

According to Pandita, medical education should retain its emphasis on clinical reasoning, differential diagnoses, and interpretation of history and exam features, but also expand to comprehensively address AI proficiency.

“AI literacy should be a required competency,” she said.

Pandita emphasized that students should understand what AI is and how it works. For this education to be thorough, it should include knowledge of how to identify bias in AI, how data can drive good or bad output from AI and how to avoid automation bias, as well as address data governance.

Oxentenko expressed concern that the absence of AI tools in underserved areas might compound challenges related to healthcare deserts.

“It may be harder to attract clinicians to come to those areas if they don’t have the AI resources that people have been trained with,” she said.

Overreliance on AI in medical training might undermine care in rural or resource-constrained regions in other ways, as well.

“If a trainee trains in a program that’s very AI supported, and then goes out to provide care in a rural community where they don’t have those resources, are they going to be able to have the same level of disease recognition and the same quality outcomes?” Oxentenko asked.

The specialties and areas of practice most vulnerable to AI-driven deskilling include endoscopy, radiology, pathology, dermatology and cardiology, according to Topaz.

A narrative review of research on clinical deskilling found that available data, while limited, indicate the presence of AI-driven deskilling across these specialties, with particular concern for endoscopists, computational pathologists and breast-imaging radiologists.

Topaz said the study highlights that “performance can drop when AI is removed, and automation bias affects clinicians at every experience level.”

These specialties carry the greatest risk for automation bias, according to Keren, because many cases fit obvious patterns. If clinicians in these specialties are not vigilant, they may miss a “curveball” that slipped past the AI.

Pandita noted similar areas of concern.

“High-volume specialties with very standardized workflows are ones that are very amenable to readily accept AI outputs,” she said.

However, the risk for AI-driven deskilling is not limited to those areas of medicine.

“Everyone’s potentially at risk,” Keren said. “Regardless of your role, being a healthcare provider is going to require some level of vigilance, and some level of slow, deliberate and reasoned thinking at some point in your day.”

The risk for harm to patients may be most pronounced in critical care settings.

“High-stakes environments concentrate the risk because they have no slack,” Topaz said.

He pointed to AI systems that detect early warning signs of sepsis as an example.

“Recognizing deterioration in an intensive care unit or triaging in an emergency department is a minutes-matter skill, and skill decay surfaces exactly when time pressure peaks,” Topaz said. “A nurse who has spent 2 years deferring to an early-warning score must suddenly spot the septic patient without it, and that moment tends to arrive at 3 a.m. during a downtime event.”

While system-level solutions are key to mitigate risk for deskilling, Oxentenko encouraged clinicians to consider what they can do as an individual to maintain their skills.

“Within your institution or practice, what are you doing to continue to make sure that your eyes, hands and thinking stay sharp in times without those AI tools?” she asked.

As AI evolves, governance boards and committees will have to keep pace with new tools and technologies.

“Currently most governance programs are about AI implementation, guardrails and security evaluations,” Pandita said. “As we move forward from implementation to maintenance, we have to evolve governance into a long-term process.”

Pandita emphasized that AI governance is different than oversight for other healthcare technologies.

“AI changes very rapidly,” she said. “You have to constantly monitor models — whether they are your own or vendor-delivered — and that should be looped into your governance ecosystem.”

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Potent P2Y12s show no benefit in patients with AF, ACS
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — Potent P2Y12 inhibition plus direct oral anticoagulation did not cut ischemic risk and raised bleeding risk vs. clopidogrel and direct oral anticoagulants in patients with atrial fibrillation and acute coronary syndrome, data show.

The results of the EPIDAURUS trial that evaluated the optimal antithrombotic regimen in patients with AF and ACS undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention were presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress and simultaneously published in Nature Medicine. The trial was prematurely terminated after enrollment due to safety concerns from the data and safety monitoring board.

Play Video
Leslie Cho, MD, discusses the results of the EPIDAURUS trial presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress.

This is a modal window.

“In patients with atrial fibrillation and acute coronary syndromes, current ESC guidelines recommend short triple antithrombotic therapy, followed by dual antithrombotic therapy based on clopidogrel and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). This class I recommendation is primarily based on the results of four randomized controlled trials, one for each DOAC,” Konstantinos D. Rizas, MD, professor and head of the heart failure outpatient clinic at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, said during the presentation. “These trials showed that a dual antithrombotic therapy, based on DOACs, significantly reduced bleeding complications compared to a triple antithrombotic therapy based on vitamin K antagonists.

“However, a pooled meta-analysis of these trials also showed that the dual antithrombotic therapy significantly increased stent thrombosis and also showed a trend for more myocardial infarctions compared with triple antithrombotic therapy,” Rizas said. “Based on these facts and lack of evidence, we stated the hypothesis that in patients with atrial fibrillation and acute coronary syndrome, dual antithrombotic therapy based on DOACs, in particular factor Xa inhibitors, and prasugrel or ticagrelor for 1 month, followed by DOACs and clopidogrel, could reduce ischemic complications without significantly increasing bleeding events compared to the standard therapy recommended in the guidelines.”

EPIDAURUS was an open-label, randomized controlled trial for which researchers enrolled 602 of the anticipated 1,474 patients with AF and ACS undergoing PCI (median age, 78 years; 26% women). Participants were randomly assigned to a DOAC plus prasugrel or ticagrelor, switching to clopidogrel after 1 month, or to a DOAC, clopidogrel and in-hospital aspirin.

The trial was halted after the data and safety monitoring board, in its third meeting, concluded that it was unlikely to show superiority, and that the number of deaths, ischemic strokes and bleeding events was elevated in the DOAC/prasugrel or ticagrelor group, Rizas said during the presentation.

The primary endpoints of the trial were assessed via hierarchical testing at 6 weeks. For the primary efficacy superiority endpoint, the order of hierarchy was death, definite or probable stent thrombosis, MI, ischemic stroke, systemic thromboembolism and urgent revascularization, and for the primary safety noninferiority endpoint, the order of hierarchy was death, Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) type 3c bleeding, BARC type 3b bleeding, BARC type 3a bleeding and BARC type 2 bleeding, Rizas said.

At the time the trial was stopped, the DOAC plus prasugrel/ticagrelor strategy failed to show superiority for the primary efficacy endpoint (win-loss ratio, 1.19; 95% CI, 0.61-2.32; P = .61) or noninferiority for the primary safety endpoint (win-loss ratio, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.39-1.11; P = .115; P for noninferiority = .713) compared with the DOAC plus clopidogrel strategy, according to the researchers.

In time-to-event analyses, risk for the efficacy endpoint was not significantly different between the experimental and control groups at 6 weeks (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.44-1.66; P = .639) or at 6 months (HR = 1.14; 95% CI, 0.72-1.8; P = .57), the researchers found.

The researchers reported significantly higher risk for BARC type 2 or higher bleeding events at 6 weeks in the experimental group compared with the control group (HR = 1.87; 95% CI, 1.01-3.47; P = .048).

Regardless of treatment group, compared with patients who had no clinically relevant bleeding, those with BARC type 2 or higher bleeding had a twofold greater risk for subsequent ischemic complications (HR = 2.18; 95% CI, 1.16-4.11; P = .016), Rizas said.

“Within the limitation of premature termination of the trial, there was a consistent signal for more bleeding complications without a sign of benefit with respect to ischemic complications in the experimental group,” Rizas said during the presentation. “The results of EPIDAURUS do not support the routine combination of drugs with prasugrel or ticagrelor.”

This year I’m taking home from ESC 2026 the EPIDAURUS trial. It was an interesting trial looking at patients with AF and MI, and whether we should be using the potent P2Y12s like prasugrel and ticagrelor plus apixaban (Eliquis, Bristol Myers Squibb/Pfizer), or whether we should be using clopidogrel and DOACs.

The study had to be terminated early because of the significant increase in bleeding in the potent P2Y12 plus DOAC arm.

For our patients who have AF and MI, we should be putting them on apixaban or rivaroxaban plus clopidogrel, and not doing potent P2Y12s.

Rizas KD, et al. Hot line 3. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.
