https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.title: Q&A: How women physicians can find joy in personal finance
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.author: Jill Rollet; Brittne Halford, MD, MPH
https://www.healio.com/news/nephrology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Brittne Halford, MD, MPH, paid off $138,000 in medical school debt in 2 years and 9 months without feeling (terribly) deprived of the good things in life.

“I am from a family that’s rich in culture and community and support, but not as far as passing down wealth. My parents could not afford to send me to college, but I was able to acquire enough scholarships to pay for undergrad and matriculate to medical school,” Halford, an internal medicine physician and financial coach, told Healio. “Like many individuals, I had a lot of graduate school debt, and I saw how it was impacting me personally. So, I committed to paying it all off aggressively, and while doing that I also realized that there’s a lot more that I could do with my finances if I educated myself.”

She began to share what she learned on social media and eventually founded More Joy More Wealth, a company that helps clinicians understand finances.

Ahead of her presentation, “Creating financial systems not just goals,” at the Women in Medicine Summit, Halford spoke to Healio about student loan debt, using nonfinancial resources to avoid “retail therapy” and the importance of financial literacy.

Healio: You’re speaking at the Women in Medicine Summit, is there advice you give specifically to women in medicine, as opposed to men or people in other professions?

Halford: There are some specific challenges women in medicine face that other people in medicine or in other professions do not. Women in medicine still face a gender pay gap that over the course of a career could be $2 million. That’s substantial not only in terms of the amount of money, but in what that money can afford, the opportunities it presents. Compared with men, women in medicine also have fewer investments and more student loan debt. They also tend to manage the household and carry the mental load of caring for kids. Other literature shows that women in medicine, women physicians, don’t have the same longevity benefit over men as women in many other types of professions.

All these things impact how a woman, and particularly a woman in medicine, experiences her career and her financial stewardship. If you’re dedicating time to your patients and to your family, there might be little time to engage in your finances and attain that financial literacy that makes you feel confident to navigate this portion of your life well. Women often defer to someone else to manage their money. There’s an assumption that a financial advisor is doing the right thing on their behalf, but there’s a lack of awareness and confirmation.

Healio: Your website is called More Joy More Wealth. How do you think about joy connecting to wealth?

Halford: There’s literature that shows when you focus on joy, you actually have more wealth. Wealth can be defined as the numbers in the bank account, but it also includes other forms of wealth: emotional, physical and social wealth. I want women to think about what wealth means from a holistic perspective and how they can get there.

When I was paying off my student loan debt, it felt like a cloud around me. But when I decided to pay it off aggressively — $138,000 in 2 years and 9 months — I also decided I would do it without completely depriving myself of everything else that brings me joy for this one goal. I can have joy and experience life while achieving this goal.

I want women to know that they have permission to experience joy while seeking wealth and to understand that if they do, they will actually have more wealth. There’s an opportunity cost there. If you focus on the things that matter for you, you won’t feel deprived and you won’t be unnecessarily spending on retail therapy. You can invest that money and pay down your debt or achieve other life goals.

Healio: What is the main takeaway of your presentation?

Halford: The main takeaway is to spend on systems. When we think about money, we think about what money can do and also about spending. Spending is the use of money, but also the use of other types of resources — time or mental energy or other types of resources. Instead of just spending on trying to get yourself to a specific goal, I want women to invest in the systems that will help to create sustainability for themselves, to prevent burnout and to sustain their abilities to achieve goals. We set new goals all the time, but we don’t want to have to recreate the financial system for every goal. You can invest in systems — whether that’s the people or resources around you, the schedule that allows you to monitor your resources, invest in yourself by spending time with a therapist so you can understand some of the fears and things you might be trying to put a bandage on by using your money.

That’s the big picture. I walk people through a feedback loop to look at their inputs, the process, the outputs and the feedback, and how they can apply a familiar framework to their finances.

Healio: Do you have an easy example of that?

Halford: One easy example: An input can be your income. Depending on the person, they may have income from various sources or one source, but then it goes through a process, what you do with your money when it comes in. Part of what I teach is to have a four-part bank account system that allows you to have an output where managing money feels good, you have the freedom to spend while also accomplishing your goals and you have enough for uncertainty that protects your peace.

You create four different accounts: one for your fixed needs, one for your variable wants, one for your emergency fund and one for those goals. You can do all four at the same time. They require different levels of monitoring, but the system ensures that you have all your financial needs met by having that structure in place.

Healio: What is the most common concern women in healthcare have about their finances?

Halford: For women in healthcare, the biggest concern is student loans. We have large loans and often that’s the first major expense we must pay regularly. It is also something we experience a lot of negative emotions about because it is such a large amount and can limit our lives. I have a colleague who did not get married — she had a fake wedding ceremony, but they legally were not married — because of their student loans. They had to think about all their assets and all their calculations for repayment. That is extreme, but it reflects a sentiment of putting your life on hold because of this financial burden. Yes, student loans are something I see women in healthcare often facing.

Healio: What is the biggest financial mistake you see women in healthcare committing?

Halford: The mistake I see is deferring financial literacy to someone else. Financial literacy has two components: understanding and use. Often women might read a book or listen to a podcast, but then from there, there’s no action, they don’t engage more meaningfully with their finances after acquiring that information, which then does not allow them to build their financial confidence. And so they defer to a financial advisor or to their tax professional or someone else with this assumption that everything is being done correctly. I know from personal experience that that is not always the case.

What I want women to do instead is to engage more meaningfully. Mastery comes from practice and from honing that skill so they can build financial confidence. If they choose to delegate the responsibility of investing to someone else and they understand the cost of that decision, that’s fine, but I don’t want you to defer because you feel disempowered.

Healio: Are there a few things that readers can act on right away?

Halford: The first thing is to believe. It sounds cliché, but everything we do starts with a thought. If we have this negative talk, “I’m not good with money,” “the financial advisors are better,” “money is just stressful,” we don’t engage. Whatever you hope to attain with your money, you have to believe that it is possible.

Belief then is often followed by curiosity. Then you start to act on it. So, the second piece is: Don’t wait. Often I hear people waiting for the best opportunity, the best time — “I’m going to start investing when I pay off my student loans, get married, finish residency.” Fill in the blank. I’m saying you are only going to get there by doing it. Women often make up excuses for why they are waiting. Just don’t wait, start engaging now.

Brittne Halford, MD, MPH, can be reached at morejoymorewealth@gmail.com.

Disclosures: Halford reports she is founder of More Joy More Wealth.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: ASCVD risk from high Lp(a) persists into old age
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Dan Beck
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

MUNICH — The risk for atherosclerotic CVD in adults with high lipoprotein(a) levels is similar between older and younger adults. However, the absolute risk is highest for older individuals aged 70 to 100 years, according to study findings.

The results of the Copenhagen General Population Study were presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress and simultaneously published in Circulation.

The connection between high Lp(a) and ASCVD has been proven, but there was not much research available on high Lp(a) levels as a risk in individuals older than 70 years — and specifically those aged up to 100 years, researchers reported.

Researchers analyzed data from 103,341 participants from Denmark aged 20 to 100 years (median age, 58 years; 56% women) from 2003 to 2015. Overall, 9,091 patients were diagnosed with ASCVD after a median follow-up of 12.5 years.

High Lp(a) increased ASCVD incidence with the same relative risk across age groups, with age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratios ranging between 1.12 and 1.18, showing no evidence that age had any bearing on risk, the researchers reported, adding that the findings were similar for both men and women.

“For all the age groups, all the way up to 80 to 100, it’s exactly the same hazard ratio. At all ages, Lp(a) is very important,” Børge G. Nordestgaard, MD, DMSc, a cardiology expert from Copenhagen University Hospital in Denmark, said during a presentation.

The relative risk for ASCVD in individuals with 50 mg/dL higher Lp(a) was similar for older and younger individuals, but the absolute risk for ASCVD “increased with stepwise higher lipoprotein(a) and stepwise higher age,” Nordestgaard and colleagues wrote in the simultaneous publication.

The total population showed an absolute increase in the incidence of ASCVD of 1.2 per 1,000 person years. For adults aged 20 to 49 years, the incidence increase was 0.3; for those aged 50 to 59 years, the incidence increase was 0.8; for those aged 60 to 69 years, the incidence increase was 1.5; for those aged 70 to 79 years, the incidence increase was 2.7; and for those aged 80 to 100 years, the incidence increase was 4.5.

“The older (groups) have an enormous risk, so certainly, even though we don’t get evidence immediately, it seems like the elderly would have the most benefit of reducing Lp(a),” Nordestgaard said.

The finding is, according to the researchers, “not entirely surprising given that age is the predominant driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.”

“If you’re old and you survived to a certain age, Lp(a) is much more important,” Nordestgaard said.

The findings of this study emphasize the importance of Lp(a) as a risk factor across the lifespan.

In particular, the relative increase in risk for a given Lp(a) level is similar across age groups, while the absolute risk rises with age, likely related to cumulative Lp(a) exposure as well as increased prevalence of other risk factors. This highlights why all adults should have Lp(a) testing at least once — Lp(a) is associated with increased cardiovascular risk regardless of age.

Importantly, findings were also consistent regardless of sex. Given the greatest absolute risk in those of older age, the authors argue these may be the best candidates for Lp(a)-targeted therapies. This may be a particularly relevant finding with the recent announcement of the negative topline results for the Lp(a)HORIZON trial of pelacarsen (Ionis/Novartis).

These findings help us understand the contribution of Lp(a) to risk across the spectrum of age and help further our understanding of where to target more aggressive preventive efforts addressing modifiable risk factors.

Nordestgaard B, et al. Lipoprotein(a) and cardiovascular disease in individuals aged 70-100 years. Presented at: European Society of Cardiology Congress; Aug. 28-31, 2026; Munich.

https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.title: ACP: Use hormone therapy as first-line treatment for menopausal vasomotor symptoms
https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades
https://www.healio.com/news/womens-healt.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

American College of Physicians, or ACP, issued new clinical guidance in Annals of Internal Medicine, recommending hormone therapy as a first-line treatment for menopausal vasomotor symptoms.

Menopause has received increased attention in recent weeks, with a Senate committee holding the first-ever congressional hearing on the condition. During the hearing, witnesses voiced support for the FDA’s updates to hormone therapy labeling, where warnings for CVD, breast cancer and probable dementia were removed from six products following an FDA panel discussion in July 2025.

Experts previously told Healio the updates are in line with current evidence and may help reassure clinicians and patients about the safety of hormone therapy.

According to Amir Qaseem, MD, PhD, MHA, MGIN, MRCP, FACP, ACP chief science officer and senior vice president of clinical policy at the Centers for Evidence Reviews, and colleagues, vasomotor symptoms like hot flashes or night sweats are the most common symptoms during perimenopause, impacting up to 80% of women, “and can last into the postmenopausal time period.”

ACP developed its guidance using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach, along with systematic reviews on the effectiveness, harms and public and patients’ values and preferences of pharmacological treatments for vasomotor symptoms.

ACP strongly recommends estrogen in combination with progestogen in women with a uterus or estrogen monotherapy in women without a uterus as first-line treatments for vasomotor symptoms.

The organization suggests serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors — desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine — as second-line treatments in women with contraindications to or who do not tolerate first-line treatment.

In women with contraindications to or who do not tolerate first- or second-line treatments, ACP recommends selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, including escitalopram or paroxetine; gabapentin; or neurokinin receptor antagonists, including elinzanetant (Lynkuet, Bayer) or fezolinetant (Veozah, Astellas Pharma), as third-line treatments.

Clinicians should use informed shared decision-making “and discuss benefits, harms, contraindications, comorbid conditions, values and preferences, financial burden, and access to and availability of treatments” when determining a treatment, Qaseem and colleagues wrote.

The authors highlighted several considerations for clinicians. For example, clinicians should ask patients about their experience with vasomotor symptoms, “as they may not initiate these discussions,” and provide information about the course of symptoms to normalize conversations.

Qaseem and colleagues noted that it is common in clinical practice to avoid initiating estrogen treatment (alone or alongside progestogen) in women aged older than 60 years “or more than 10 years after their final menstrual period and to limit treatment duration to 3 to 5 years.”

They also advised that a history or higher risk for CVD, endometrial or breast cancer, stroke and venous thromboembolism may affect the overall balance of benefits and harms of treatment.

Clinicians should additionally inform patients that estrogen treatment “may lead to changes in vaginal bleeding pattern and abnormal withdrawal bleeding or flow, which may require further evaluation,” the authors wrote.

In an accompanying editorial, Regina Castaneda, MD, a postdoctoral research fellow at Mayo Clinic, and Stephanie S. Faubion, MD, MBA, medical director at The Menopause Society, said ACP’s guidance “is timely given the rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape in the management of menopause symptoms.”

Castaneda and Faubion praised several parts of the guidance, including its consideration of outcomes like quality of life, adverse events, patients’ values and endometrial safety, assessments of certainty of evidence and its emphasis for clinicians “to proactively initiate conversations about menopause and provide education.”

They acknowledged that questions of when to initiate and how long to continue hormone therapy remain, as “women who experience menopause at a later age may be older than 60 years while still within 10 years of their final menstrual period.”

“Thus, age over 60 years should not be used as an absolute contraindication,” they wrote. “Additionally, while a 3- to 5-year duration is commonly referenced, the available evidence does not allow definition of a duration beyond which the balance of benefits and harms changes.”

Castaneda and Faubion concluded that ACP’s guidance “offers a strong foundation for individualizing treatment of menopausal women and clarifies evidence gaps that remain.”

Qaseem A, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2026;doi:10.7326/ANNALS-26-01205.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Nearly one in four US adults projected to develop heart failure
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Nearly one in four U.S. adults are projected to develop heart failure in their lifetime, and the overall prevalence of the disease is expected to keep rising due to an aging population with increasing comorbidities, researchers reported.

Cost-effective guideline-directed medical therapy use remains low among patients with HF, and healthcare costs for HF are estimated to increase to up to $858 billion annually by 2050, according to the latest iteration of the Heart Failure Society of America’s HF statistics report published in the Journal of Cardiac Failure.

“HF is moving in the wrong direction on several fronts at once, even though we have more effective, affordable therapies than ever before,” Eiran Gorodeski, MD, MPH, director of the Advanced Heart Failure and Transplant Center at the University Hospitals Harrington Heart & Vascular Institute and 2026 chair of the report writing committee, told Healio. “Age-adjusted HF-related mortality has risen about 37% since 2010, which undoes more than a decade of earlier progress, and early 2024 data suggest the rise is continuing.

“The landscape of HF in the U.S. has changed, especially among younger adults — aged less than 65 years,” Gorodeski said. “HF is no longer just a disease of grandparents. Cardiometabolic HF [with preserved ejection fraction], driven by obesity, hypertension, diabetes and kidney disease has emerged as the predominant new disease in this younger population. It tracks closely to areas in the U.S. where obesity is highly prevalent, including areas with lower socioeconomic status and rural areas.”

Gorodeski and colleagues reviewed contemporary data, recent publications and validated data sources to produce the present fourth iteration of the HF statistics report. The researchers identified 12 principal findings.

The researchers estimated that approximately one in four U.S. adults (24%) will develop HF during their lifetime, and among those who are asymptomatic, one-third already meet criteria for stage A HF.

The current prevalence of HF among U.S. adults is estimated to be approximately 3% and is expected to increase to 3.8% by 2050 due to an aging population and growing prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors, according to the report.

HF mortality among younger adults rose between 2001 and 2020, increasing 121% among U.S. adults aged 25 to 44 years and 96% among U.S. adults aged 45 to 64 years, the authors wrote, noting that this represents “a fundamental shift in the epidemiological landscape of HF.”

As of 2023, HF mortality represented 14.6% of total all-cause deaths among U.S. adults, and between 2001 and 2023, age-adjusted HF mortality rates rose approximately 37%, according to the report.

Reported disparities in HF hospitalization and mortality persist, with Black U.S. adults experiencing rates more than twofold higher compared with white U.S. adults and more than threefold compared with Asian U.S. adults.

Reported geographic disparities in HF burden persist, with rates varying from 8% in Hawaii to 15% in Oklahoma, and the highest burden occurring in the Deep South, Appalachian and lower Midwest states.

“Data in HF Stats 2026 show where to direct resources,” Gorodeski told Healio. “Black adults have the highest incidence, hospitalization and mortality rates. HF prevalence varies nearly twofold across states, with the highest burden in the Deep South, Appalachia and the lower Midwest. Rural patients receive less optimal therapy and follow-up. These patterns reflect differences in access and care delivery, which means they can be changed.”

Quadruple guideline-directed medical therapy, consisting of a beta-blocker, renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor, is estimated to be utilized in only 18% of patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction, according to the study.

“A sobering finding is that despite the availability of highly effect medical therapy, it is underutilized,” Gorodeski told Healio. “Only about 18% of patients with HFrEF are on all four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy. Fewer than 1% reach target doses. Full implementation could save roughly 95,000 lives a year in North America. So the gap is not mainly a gap in knowledge or in drugs. It is a gap in implementation, access and care delivery.”

A broad estimation showed healthcare costs related to HF are $312 billion annually, 40% of which is attributable to HF hospitalizations, and the researchers projected costs to reach $858 billion annually by 2050.

“The cost-effectiveness of GDMT in HFrEF has improved tremendously over the last year,” Gorodeski told Healio. “The argument that there is a cost barrier for optimal GDMT in HFrEF is no longer valid in 2026.”

The prevalence of cardiomyopathies including transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and genetic causes of HF is increasing, yet likely underestimated due to continual underdiagnosis, according to the report.

HF uniquely impacted certain vulnerable populations, such as older U.S. adults with HF who experience comorbidities including frailty, cognitive impairment and depression, and cancer survivors who experience a 1.4- to 1.6-fold higher relative risk for incident HF compared with adults without cancer. The researchers also noted that pregnancy-related HF was attributable to more than 10% of pregnancy-related deaths, and peripartum cardiomyopathy occurred in approximately one in 1,000 to one in 2,230 live births.

Advanced HF and cardiogenic shock surpassed acute MI-cardiogenic shock as the leading shock etiology in contemporary registries, according to the report.

The researchers reported that healthcare systems often lack the infrastructure for advanced HF care. End-of-life care for patients with HF is poorly integrated; match applications for advanced HF and transplant cardiology physicians has declined since 2020; and many programs lack psychology staff, dietitians, social workers and dedicated pharmacy support, according to the report.

“In the midst of these important epidemiological observations, we have a simultaneous workforce crisis,” Gorodeski said told Healio. “Interest in advanced HF fellowship training has declined since 2020, and specialists are concentrated in the North and Northeast, while the burden is heaviest in the South and Midwest. Team-based care with advanced practice providers, pharmacists, dietitians and social workers is associated with fewer admissions and deaths, but many programs still lack these roles.”

Eiran Gorodeski, MD, MPH, is director of the Advanced Heart Failure and Transplant Center at the University Hospitals Harrington Heart & Vascular Institute. Gorodeski can be reached on LinkedIn and on X at @EiranGorodeski.

Gorodeski EZ, et al. J Card Fail. 2026;doi:10.1016/j.cardfail.2026.07.009.

https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.author: Andy Tau, MD, FACG, FASGE; Robert Stott
https://www.healio.com/news/gastroentero.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in medical practice are not just about reaching underserved communities but should also influence who is recruited to care for them.

According to Andy Tau, MD, FACG, FASGE, chair of recruiting at Austin Gastroenterology in Texas, DEI is helping shape the qualities the practice looks for in its next generation of gastroenterologists.

“It is my overt mission statement to try to recruit people in our group who are excellent gastroenterologists, but I also want them to be people who will be willing, as part of their mission statement as gastroenterologists, to go out in the community and take care of people who may not look like themselves,” Tau told Healio. “The recruiting effort has to attract excellent gastroenterologists first and foremost, but I’m not satisfied with just that.”

This philosophy extends beyond recruitment, according to Tau. Physicians at Austin Gastroenterology participate in outreach across Austin’s cultural communities, including health fairs, community clinics and cultural festivals, where simple conversations with passersby at their booths can translate into patients getting screened and potentially save lives.

The practice also has a longstanding partnership with People’s Community Clinic of Austin, providing colonoscopies at no cost for underserved patients, including many non-English speakers and those without insurance.

Tau noted that these efforts reflect what he believes DEI should mean, particularly in a state like Texas where the term itself has become politically charged.

“Kindness and goodness to one’s neighbor is a Texan value, and so in some ways it just needs to be relabeled, put in a different way,” Tau told Healio. “Whether you want to label that as DEI or whatever you want to say that is, the spirit of charity and spirit of caring for one’s neighbor and being inclusive is my goal when I try to recruit.”

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: Fasting duration minimally affects most routine blood tests
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Andrew (Drew) Rhoades
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Fasting fewer than 8 hours or more than 12 hours before a routine blood test did not significantly impact the results, new observational data in JAMA Internal Medicine show.

The practice of fasting before blood tests is intended to reduce variability in measurements, but recommendations for fasting durations are inconsistent, according to Sunghwan Shin, MD, PhD, from University of Ulsan College of Medicine in Seoul, Korea, and colleagues.

They added that evidence needed to determine optimal fasting time is limited by multiple factors, including:

The researchers aimed to address these gaps by assessing the effects of fasting durations of fewer than 8 hours, 8 to 12 hours and more than 12 hours among 101,148 people (57% men) aged 18 years or older in the Republic of Korea.

The main outcome was whether differences in test results exceeded established analytical performance specifications (APS).

“A fasting-related difference smaller than the APS is therefore unlikely to be clinically important, whereas a difference exceeding the APS may be large enough to alter clinical interpretation or decisions,” Shin and colleagues wrote.

The final dataset included 9,755,547 test results across 372 test items.

The researchers reported that 27 of 121 routine analytes exceeded APS — but just 10, mostly with “recognized postprandial physiology” — were “confirmed in paired within-person analyses, suggesting confounding.”

Triglycerides (20.1%; 95% CI, 17.4%-22.8%), gamma-glutamyl transferase (14.8%; 95% CI, 3.9%-25.7%), lipase (36.4%; 95% CI, 15.7%-57.1%) and glucose (10.8%; 95% CI, 10%-11.6%) were higher when participants fasted fewer than 8 hours. However, lactate and glucose were 27.9% and 15.4% lower, respectively, from 0.5 to 4 hours of fasting. Lipids “showed no significant short-term trend within this window,” they wrote.

For those who fasted more than 12 hours, total bilirubin (17%; 95% CI, 18.2% to 15.9%) and 25-hydroxyvitamin D (9.9%; 95% CI, 14.4% to 5.4%) were higher.

No analyte exceeded APS between the 8- to 12-hour and over 12-hour groups.

The findings suggest reconsidering rigid fasting recommendations “in favor of a more nuanced, analyte-specific approach to pretest preparation,” the researchers wrote.

“Adequate fasting (8 or more hours) should be maintained when glucose or precise lipid measurement is the goal, whereas greater flexibility may be reasonable for many other routine tests,” they wrote. “Prolonged fasting beyond 12 hours conferred no measurable advantage for any analyte, including triglycerides, and represents an avoidable burden for patients.”

According to Leigh A. Frame, PhD, MHS, RYT, a board member at Johns Hopkins Medicine Alumni Association who was not a part of the study, several limitations, as well as differences in dietary patterns between Americans and South Koreans, “are relevant to interpreting these findings.”

She explained recent national surveys, though from different timeframes, suggest South Koreans consume more energy from carbohydrates than Americans (58% vs. 51%) and less from fat (23% vs. 33%), and the analysis did not account for what meals were eaten prior.

“Meal size, carbohydrate quality, fiber and fat content, along with a person’s metabolic health, influence the response after eating,” she told Healio. “A higher-fat meal could produce a larger triglyceride response, while carbohydrate quantity and quality influence glucose.”

Because the median age of the cohort was 61 years, “applicability to younger adults, including premenopausal women, is also uncertain,” she said.

But “the overall principle is applicable to U.S. practice and consistent with current lipid-testing guidance,” Frame said. “The exact numerical differences across the broader range of tests would benefit from confirmation in more diverse populations.”

Frame said the take-home message is that “fasting instructions should depend on which tests are ordered and what clinical question they are intended to answer.”

She noted fasting glucose still requires fasting, as “diagnostic criteria specify at least 8 hours without caloric intake. A glucose result obtained after eating should not be interpreted using fasting diagnostic thresholds.”

HbA1c does not require fasting, she said. “It reflects longer-term glucose exposure, although conditions affecting red blood cells or hemoglobin can complicate interpretation.”

A lipid panel does not need fasting immediately, although it is recommended “in selected circumstances, including known or suspected triglyceride disorders, a family history of dyslipidemia or premature atherosclerotic CVD, or nonfasting triglycerides of at least 400 mg/dL,” Frame said.

Unnecessary fasting, according to Frame, has “safety and access costs.”

“For patients taking insulin or sulfonylureas, skipping a meal without appropriate medication guidance can increase hypoglycemia risk,” she said. “Requiring morning appointments can complicate testing for shift workers, caregivers and people with transportation constraints. This is where social drivers of health come into laboratory practice.”

She recommended that clinicians “give clear instructions tied to the ordered tests, document fasting status and time since eating, and consider collection conditions when interpreting unexpected results.”

“When following a sensitive measurement over time, consistent preparation and collection timing can make the trend more informative,” she said.

Shin S, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2026;doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.4718.

Disclosures: Shin and colleagues report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.title: Transient ischemic attack associated with higher dementia risk
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.author: Shawn Arrajj
https://www.healio.com/news/neurology/20.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

People who experienced transient ischemic attack had a higher risk for developing dementia than those who did not have one, and dementia rates in these patients were three times higher than stroke rates over the long term, according to researchers.

The results indicate that long-term follow-up for patients who experience a transient ischemic attack (TIA) should take cognitive and brain health into consideration, along with stroke prevention, said Raed A. Joundi, MD, DPhil, assistant professor in the department of medicine, division of neurology, at McMaster University.

“It would be important to inquire about changes in memory, thinking, or the ability to manage daily activities during follow-up, particularly when concerns are raised by the patient or family,” Joundi told Healio.

The population-wide cohort study examined data from 113,081 patients who experienced a TIA in Ontario, Canada, between 2002 and 2022 (mean age, 70 years; 50% female).

Past research into the associations between TIA and dementia risk has largely been in the form of prospective cohort studies. Using population-wide administrative data may help overcome biases of inclusion, sample size and missing data, according to the researchers.

Roughly one in five study participants, or 19.3%, were diagnosed with dementia over a mean follow-up period of 7.11 years, compared with 15.2% of a matched control group, Joundi and colleagues wrote. A total of 20% of participants who experienced a stroke were diagnosed with dementia over that time.

The overall rate of dementia among those with TIA was 2.71 per 100 person-years after 20 years, compared with a dementia rate of 2.03 per 100 person-years in the control group.

“It is important to put the one-fifth number into context because the average age of the population was about 70 years, so dementia is expected to occur in some people regardless of having a TIA,” Joundi said. “However, 15% of the matched comparison population developed dementia ... despite the similarity of age and other factors, showing a higher risk after TIA.”

After matching to age, sex and major vascular risk factors, a person who experienced a TIA had increased risk for developing dementia than someone who did not experience a TIA (HR = 1.34; 95% CI, 1.31–1.36).

The risk for dementia was highest in the first year following a TIA (HR = 1.75; 95% CI, 1.66–1.85). Within 5 years, the HR was 1.46 (95% CI, 1.42–1.5), and within 10 years it was 1.38 (95% CI, 1.35–1.41).

Joundi and colleagues also examined risk for dementia after stroke.

Compared with risk for dementia following stroke, risk following TIA was lower within the first year (HR = 0.67; 95% CI, 0.64–0.7). However, risk rates became similar after 5 years, researchers wrote.

Over the 20-year period following a TIA or a stroke, dementia occurred about three times more often than a subsequent stroke, Joundi said.

“I was surprised by the magnitude of the risk over the long term,” he said. “That really highlighted for us how important cognitive decline may be as a long-term complication of TIA.”

There is some overlap between the kinds of stroke prevention recommendations physicians emphasize after a TIA and general brain health recommendations, including controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes, avoiding smoking and being physically active, according to Joundi.

However, he said those measures need to be maintained for the long term.

“This is key because we know that secondary prevention measures are less intensive after TIA compared to stroke,” he said.

Moving forward, Joundi told Healio that research should dig into what specifically is driving the increased risk for dementia.

Prospective studies that follow people after they experience a TIA and administer cognitive assessments, MRI scans and blood biomarker tests would be useful in helping to distinguish dementia types and analyze patient symptoms, he said.

Identifying which mechanisms are preventable could help inform interventions and reduce risk, Joundi said.

“This could help determine the contribution of genetics, small vessel strokes, brain atrophy, neurodegeneration and potentially inflammation,” Joundi said. “It could also help us understand whether TIA itself contributes to these processes or is primarily identifying people who already have a brain that is more vulnerable to cognitive decline.”

Raed A. Joundi, MD, DPhil, can be reached at Raed.Joundi@phri.ca.

Joundi RA, et al. Neurology. 2026: doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218554.

Disclosures: Joundi reports holding a National New Investigator Award from the Heart & Stroke Foundation of Canada and the Anne Marie Brune/PHRIChairin Vascular Dementia. Please see the study for all other authors' relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.title: AMA opposes change to airline emergency medical kit regulation
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.author: Emma Bascom
https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The AMA is urging the Federal Aviation Administration to rethink its proposed changes to requirements for emergency medical kits on commercial airlines.

Allowing each airline to determine its own medical supplies could compromise the safety of passengers during an in-flight emergency, according to an AMA press release. But some experts have said that a new focus in the rule could be an innovative approach.

FAA has proposed eliminating the list of required items for commercial in-flight emergency medical kits to be replaced with “a performance-based requirement to ensure contents are practical and sufficient to allow crewmembers to address the most common medical emergencies that occur onboard commercial aircraft,” according to the proposed rule.

The nine most common medical emergencies (and treatment options) the FAA addressed are:

“FAA seeks to increase flexibility for operators while maintaining predictability for operators to equip their onboard medical kits,” according to the rule. “This action is necessary to address requirements in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024.”

In a comment letter to Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford, AMA’s CEO and Executive Vice President John Whyte, MD, MPH, strongly supported updating the 2-decade-old onboard medical kit requirements but opposed the proposal to entirely eliminate federal minimum standards — meaning individual airlines would have “broad discretion to decide which medications, diagnostic tools, devices and quantities are ‘adequate’ for the emergencies they must be prepared to address.”

That is an important consideration because physicians who respond to an in-flight emergency have the daunting task to “assume responsibility for a patient” while in an environment they cannot control and did not design, Whyte wrote.

“We do not expect an aircraft to function as an emergency department. We do expect a physician who stands up when that call is made to be able to rely on one basic assurance: regardless of which commercial airline the patient happened to board, the essential tools needed to determine what is wrong, provide evidence-based emergency treatment, monitor the patient’s response, and protect the people providing that care will be there when they reach for them,” Whyte wrote.

AMA called for an evidence-based national standard that is consistent and informed by recommendations from the Aerospace Medical Association, “which convened a working group to examine emergency medical kits and develop suggested guidelines,” according to the AMA press release. The organization additionally warned that “leaving these decisions to individual airlines, without a common clinical standard,” could lead to inconsistent access to critical materials — diagnostic tools, medications and other equipment — when physicians treat passengers in the air.

Douglas H. Jones, MD, medical director at Bateman Horne Center for Excellence and president of Food Allergy Support Team, as well as a columnist for Healio, said “the current requirements need to be modernized, but modernization shouldn’t mean eliminating a consistent national minimum” standard.

“I agree with the AMA that there should be an evidence-based standard that is regularly updated, with airlines free to go beyond it. Flexibility should exist above the safety floor, not instead of one,” he said. “In-flight medicine is an unusual environment: an unfamiliar patient, limited space, unfamiliar equipment and potentially hours before definitive medical care. That’s exactly where standardization matters most.”

So, variability in that setting is a major concern for Jones.

“The same emergency could occur on two different airlines with very different resources available to treat it,” he said. “When a clinician volunteers to help at 30,000 feet, there should be a reasonable expectation of what medications and equipment will be available. The cost and effort required to maintain these basic resources are small compared with the potential consequences of not having them when they are needed.”

William Brady, MD, FACEP, FAAEM, a professor of emergency medicine, executive vice chair and The David A Harrison Distinguished Educator at the University of Virginia Health System, told Healio that “a standardized approach is most appropriate across airlines, so that if a healthcare provider does need to access the kit, then they’re going to find the same materials, supplies, medications” — but that does not mean that one size fits all.

“If you think about planes and routes and coverage areas where you’re flying over a continent with multiple airports and multiple hospitals that you can land and divert to, that kit could be a little more basic vs. some of the long-haul flights where there’s nothing but water underneath the plane for many, many hours and, therefore, no place to divert to or land or anything and, therefore, no hospital,” he said. “That type of plane might have the standard kit plus some modifications that would be appropriate for a longer time in the air, but that would be the only variation that I think would be medically appropriate.”

Additionally, “a revision of the existing kit is sorely needed,” Brady said, because “the kits are configured based on older medical science, and things have evolved considerably” since they were initially developed. However, he said it is unrealistic to expect a completely comprehensive kit to have the tools any provider would need for any condition.

“These kits can be revised in a rational way. They should be consistent across one plane to the next, one airline to the next, with the alteration capability for an increased set of supplies for truly the long-haul flights — the overwater flights without ability to land,” Brady said.

Paulo M. Alves, MD, global medical director of Aviation Health, told Healio that regulations can move more slowly “than the progress of medicine,” so he believes “focusing on the conditions to treat, instead of how to treat them, is an innovative and progressive approach,” especially considering that most of the kits carried by major airlines in the U.S. have “significantly more items than the current regulations.”

“In fact, one of the problems is that because of the prescriptive framework, items lacking any support evidence such as ammonia inhalants are mandatory,” Alves said. “The question becomes how the FAA will enforce that the nine conditions identified will be properly addressed by the individual airlines. I believe that more than ever, the medical input will be needed, both from the airline's and the regulator's perspectives.”

Alves said the identified conditions “came from the best available evidence in the published medical literature.” He noted two studies in particular: one published in The New England Journal of Medicine, which evaluated the outcomes of medical emergencies that occurred on a commercial airline flight, and another in JAMA Network Open that analyzed the characteristics of in-flight medical events on a commercial flight and factors linked to aircraft diversion, transport to a hospital or in-flight death.

“A specific dataset was prepared and analyzed for the sake of this effort, which is a subset for the U.S.-based airlines from the one published at the JAMA Network,” he said. “The prescriptive approach utilized until now creates the odd situation of requiring medications that are obsolete, or subject to shortage, keeping in mind that a complete emergency medical kit is an item required by law for the aircraft to take off.”

Alves also said that he hopes “the methodology followed will be published soon” but noted “the different conditions were identified and their incidence calculated against passenger and operational data obtained from the Bureau of Transport Statistics for the same period of data collection; the severity of each condition was estimated by the multiple specialists on the panel; [and] a risk matrix: severity versus frequency was built and served as the basis for the recommendations.” Priority, naturally, “was given for the most severe and the most frequent.”

“I believe that the AMA maybe could have a different perspective if aware of the process followed by the panel. The evidence about in-flight medical events is available and published rather recently in one of their own journals,” he said. “Having worked for many years helping the airlines in the U.S. and abroad, I can affirm that data collected by the so-called ground-based medical support (GBMS) providers, though not perfect, is the best source one can utilize.”

GBMS providers are outsourced telehealth companies with emergency medicine physicians who offer remote assistance to flight crews in medical emergencies, according to a study in Digital Health. Alves said virtually every airline in the U.S. has a contract with those providers, “and the level of utilization has grown over the past few years, making this sample even more representative.”

Alves also highlighted that this debate centers around a unique situation for the medical profession, because, ultimately, a “medical volunteer is primarily another passenger and is not on board to work.”

“The solution of trusting a medical volunteer to address in-flight events has become an industry practice but is far from being a consistent professional one. GBMS services became a widely utilized resource, which is not fully known by the traveling public, including the medical sector,” he said

Some advocates have argued that the national standard should also include epinephrine autoinjectors (EpiPen, Viatris).

The Federal Aviation Administration has required epinephrine to be present in in-flight medical kits since 2003, “but most airlines today only stock vials of the drug” rather than “the easy-to-use autoinjectors,” according to the Food Allergy Research & Education organization.

In a video posted to his LinkedIn account, medical social media mogul Mikhail Varshavski, DO — more commonly known as Dr. Mike — described an emergency that happened on a flight when he was onboard. The patient had an allergic reaction, but because the plane did not carry EpiPens, Varshavski had to “do some rough calculations” with the epinephrine in the kit, which is meant to be used during cardiac arrest.

The patient survived, and Varshavski has since lobbied with senators to ensure EpiPens are present on planes. On Sept. 18, in response to the proposed rule, Senator Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Aviation, called for every passenger airline based in the U.S. to guarantee that their in-flight medical kit include epinephrine “in delivery methods designed that can be easily self-administered by individuals without medical training.”

Jones said “we don’t need to turn an airplane into an emergency department” for proper care.

“We do need a consistent, evidence-based minimum for predictable, life-threatening emergencies that applies across airlines,” he said. “For anaphylaxis specifically, if an airline is expected to be prepared to treat it, epinephrine should be immediately available.”

Brady said that, although EpiPens expire and are expensive, he has “no problem with saying” they should be present on planes. But he also pointed out that epinephrine is already there, just not in an easy-to-use method.

“It does require some degree of expertise [to administer], which then circles back to my comments ... that every healthcare provider that opens that kit, frankly, doesn’t have the expertise to understand and use some of the equipment and some of the medications appropriately. Many do, but some don’t, and it’s not their fault. That’s the area of the medical world they work in, and they don’t use those tools,” he said.

Jones said that, because “anaphylaxis is a time-sensitive emergency, and epinephrine is the first-line treatment,” he favors “adult and pediatric epinephrine autoinjectors, which simplify administration and reduce opportunities for dosing errors in an already challenging environment.

“For passengers with food allergies, there is an additional challenge: food served in the air may not provide the same allergen information patients are accustomed to seeing on packaged foods on the ground. That uncertainty makes preparedness for an allergic emergency even more important,” he added.

Alves said that “auto-injectors like the Epi-pen are nice-to-have items, as well as nasal sprays and oral dissolving medications,” but “it should be noted that flight attendants are not allowed to administer injections, including the auto-injectors.”

“Given the public interest about auto-injectors, a separate discussion is warranted.” Alves said. “Epinephrine is available today and is obviously included in the recommended list of medications. The decision of having it in a different, easier, form of administration depends on a cost-benefit analysis, as they are not inexpensive items. A relatively recent study concluded that an in-flight medical emergency requiring epinephrine administration is rare with an incidence rate of 1 event in 12.5 million passengers. With that said, most of the major US airlines are carrying auto-injectors already, despite the lack of regulatory requirement. The same [can be said] about naloxone in nasal spray.”

Brady, who is also medical director of Albemarle County Fire Rescue and editor-in-chief of American Journal of Emergency Medicine, said “it’s important for everyone to realize that a commercial airliner is just that. It’s not a flying medical clinic. It’s not an ambulance. It’s not a medical entity. It’s a means of transportation where people can, hopefully, safely and comfortably go from point A to point B.”

“Passengers, whether they become the patient or they’re the volunteer healthcare provider, really shouldn’t expect comprehensive medical care” in a commercial flight, Brady said. Still, he said airlines have a responsibility with basic safety.

“You don’t expect that on a subway or a bus or a train,” he said. “With that being said, airlines do need to have basic medical equipment on board, with the ability to give that equipment to appropriately trained healthcare providers to use. Clearly, an AED is important. Flight attendants need to be trained in basic first aid and CPR. Pilots need to be aware of these emergencies and have a lower threshold for diverting when life- and limb-threatening problems happen.”

Alves agreed that “the aircraft is not a hospital.”

“The recommendations provided by the panel to the FAA which appear in the draft advisory circular are the product of extensive research and debate,” he said. ‘The resources on board should be geared to address life-threatening situation and to stabilize less severe events. We also believe that assessment tools should be present to better evaluate the severity of the specific condition.”

The process of the FAA’s proposed rule is still ongoing, Alves said.

“In the meantime, I think the traveling public should be reassured that most U.S. airlines go above and beyond the regulatory requirements regarding the management of in-flight medical events,” he said. “All large airlines contract services of GBMS. Those, through periodic reviews of their casuistic, have been making recommendations to update and upgrade their kits according to what is truly happening in the air for many years.”

Additionally, there is hope in rapid advances in air-to-ground communication, like “the introduction of on board wi-fi and apps specifically designed to help the management of in-flight medical events,” which are already dramatically changing things, “allowing for the medical volunteer to speak directly to a well-trained colleague on the ground,” Alves said.

Paulo M. Alves, MD, and William Brady, MD, FACEP, FAAEM, can be reached at primarycare@healio.com.

Douglas H. Jones, MD, can be reached at rmaaimd@gmail.com.

Disclosures: Brady and Jones report no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: FDA approves pediatric pulmonary valve that grows with patients
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

The FDA announced the approval of the first size-adjustable pulmonary valve replacement designed for children with congenital heart disease.

The device (Autus Size-Adjustable Valve, Edwards Lifesciences) is designed to be expanded to keep pace with a child’s growth and could reduce the need for repeat surgeries, according to the FDA press release.

The valve can be surgically implanted as small as approximately 13 mm in diameter and can expand up to 22 mm via transcatheter balloon dilation, according to the release.

In addition, the FDA said this is the first approved heart valve designed with polymeric material instead of animal-derived tissue for its inner leaflets.

“For children born with congenital heart disease, valve replacement timing has always been a difficult decision — wait too long and you risk harm to the child, but intervene too early and they may need multiple open-heart surgeries as they grow,” Michelle Tarver, MD, PhD, director of the FDA’s Center for Devices and Radiological Health, said in the release. “The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve gives doctors the option of far fewer trips to the operating room, which may result in better quality of life for these children and their families.”

Approval was based on data from the Autus Valve pivotal study, a prospective, single-arm, multicenter study, which included 62 patients across 12 sites in the U.S. aged 18 months to 16 years who needed pulmonary valve replacement.

The study met its primary safety and effectiveness endpoints, with all patients free from device-related complications at 30 days and favorable valve performance with no reinterventions at 6 months, according to a company release.

Outcomes were consistent through 1 year, with a reported mean right ventricular outflow tract gradient of 40 mm Hg or less, less than moderate regurgitation and no reinterventions, according to the release.

Longer-term studies are underway.

This device addresses a very real and important unmet need in congenital heart disease. One of the challenges we face when replacing a pulmonary valve in a young child is that we are implanting a fixed-size prosthesis into a patient who is going to grow. Even when the valve itself continues to function well, the child may simply outgrow it, potentially leading to another open-heart operation.

What is particularly exciting about the Autus valve is that it was designed specifically with the pediatric patient in mind. It can be implanted at a relatively small diameter and subsequently expanded in the catheterization laboratory as the child grows. If that strategy proves durable over time, it has the potential to reduce the number of open-heart surgeries some children require.

The available evidence is very encouraging, but it is important to distinguish what we know today from what still needs to be demonstrated with longer follow-up.

The pivotal study provides reassuring evidence regarding initial procedural safety and short-term valve performance. At the same time, this is a relatively small, single-arm study, and the most important questions for a pediatric valve are inherently long-term questions. We still need to understand durability over many years, the performance of the polymeric leaflets and, perhaps most importantly, how the valve performs after serial expansion as children grow.

There is reasonable evidence supporting safety and effectiveness for approval, particularly given the significant unmet need in this population, but approval should be viewed as the beginning rather than the end of evidence generation. Long-term follow-up will be extremely important.

This approval is important beyond this particular valve because pediatric congenital heart disease has historically been an area where device development has lagged behind adult structural heart disease.

The concept of designing a valve around the fact that a child will grow is exactly the type of innovation we need. If long-term results demonstrate that the valve can be safely expanded multiple times while maintaining good function, the impact could be significant — not simply in terms of valve performance, but in potentially reducing cumulative surgeries and the overall burden of treatment on children and their families.

Disclosures: Tarver reports being an employee of the FDA.

https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.title: Q&A: Protecting your career and family as a surgeon and mother
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.author: Vaninder Dhillon, MD; Scott Buzby
https://www.healio.com/news/cardiology/2.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

Communication of needs at home and in clinic to build a manageable work schedule is essential to balancing motherhood and a career as a surgeon, a speaker reported.

At the Women in Medicine Summit, Vaninder Dhillon, MD, associate professor in the department of otolaryngology, head and neck surgery at Johns Hopkins Medicine, highlighted the five points, or “truths for the surgeon-mom:”

Healio spoke with Dhillon, who is a mother of three children, about the balance of being a surgeon and a mother, the importance of communicating your needs in clinic and at home and advice for female medical students in training who may want to become mothers themselves.

Healio: What motivated you to give this specific presentation at the Women in Medicine Summit?

Dhillon: When the submissions came out about topics, one of them was motherhood and being in this profession. I’m an otolaryngologist and our society meetings don’t have huge talks on this subject, so I thought it would be interesting at a Women in Medicine Summit to have that panel. I submitted it as an abstract and it was accepted.

That was the impetus for doing that, as well as a literary search-excuse to look at what’s been done, what’s been talked about and what’s been written about on this topic.

Healio: Could you summarize what your literary search revealed on this topic?

Dhillon: On PubMed, there are a lot of papers on surgical residencies and motherhood, barriers to motherhood or barriers to completing a surgical residency for trainees that are moms-to-be. A lot of those have been published because the cohort is easy to follow, and they came to a lot of conclusions about what barriers there are for trainees in terms of becoming moms or even going through pregnancy, but I didn’t see a lot about surgeons who became a mom after training and what that experience was like in the workforce.

What is written out there is heterogeneous. The discussions are more survey-based, and everyone’s experience is just so different, and so I tried to tie common threads and outlined that in my five points.

Healio: When you decided to start a family, how did your timeline fit with your residency or practice?

Dhillon: I did not have children in residency. I was post-fellowship, so motherhood for me started at a later point in my career, which I know is not uncommon for a lot of women.

My first child was born 3 years into my practice. I relate now that I’m mid-career in my practice to trying to find the balance at this point with what is possible with my career. I have an academic career, which is different than other models of practice like private practice. In my talk, I’m hoping to relate the things that, in hindsight, I found to be helpful in terms of perspective as a mom and as a surgeon. What has evolved for me in my practice in relationship to being a mom, and what my goals are now 11 years in.

It’s still evolving for me. But the things I’ve learned in the past decade have been a combination of experience, mentorship and things that I’m hoping to relate as if you’re planning on starting family, maybe after training or even during training.

Healio: Did you face any explicit or hidden biases when you announced your pregnancy in the surgical field?

Dhillon: I didn’t have biases or barriers to starting a family when I was in practice.

But the maternity leave at my institution is a certain amount of time and I had to decide if I was going to accept just 6 weeks of maternity leave. For me, that wasn’t enough, so I had to do extra legwork to file for short-term disability, which wasn’t frowned upon, but it’s just more time away from practice.

I also take call on top of my own individual practice, and that is something that you have to plan, because obviously you’re not part of the call pool when you’re gone, and it affects everyone else’s schedules, especially availabilities, and so that was something that I had to communicate.

Once I had my children, finding the appropriate amount of time and appropriate place to breastfeed or pump at work was something I had to navigate.

Now that my kids are past the infant stage, I’ve shifted my clinical template and I’ve modeled it so that the time that I’m at work, I’m as productive as possible. It’s a nontraditional template in the time that I’m there compared with other colleagues, which wasn’t necessarily accepted at first. But once I implemented it and showed that I was able to do more work in a shorter amount of time to make up for not being there as long, it was OK with the institution.

It was a lot of navigating my needs, my kids’ needs and my family needs with the time that I spend at work, and the amenities that I needed to go through pregnancy and postpartum.

Healio: What support did you receive from your program or colleagues during your pregnancy and maternity leave?

Dhillon: My coordinator and my clinical staff were supportive once I communicated what I needed. My colleagues were supportive about my call schedule and during my second pregnancy, I communicated early on that I was going to be gone. I helped with the call load in the earlier part of my pregnancy when I was more mobile and not concerned about any late pregnancy issues like being on my feet so my partners would be able to manage the amount of time we were on call equally.

My colleagues were supportive during my maternity leave to not have any clinical patient care-related issues directed to me because my practice was on hold. People were covering for me. I know that doesn’t always happen if you own a practice. Sometimes patient care is still on you, but that was nice to not have to worry about that. Other support I’ve received at my hospital was a later start in the operating room when I had to get my children to daycare. They gave me an extra hour to get to the hospital so I wasn’t behind in my case start.

There were a lot of little areas here and there where I received support, and a lot of it had to do with me being communicative early on.

Healio: What advice would you give on managing unpredictable or long hours in the office or operating room with childcare pickups and family life?

Dhillon: Every surgeon is different. I’m, fortunately, in a practice where I don’t have long surgeries. That doesn’t mean there aren’t other examples of where I have long days. But if that’s the case, where you can’t be front and center for the family, you probably need to establish some proxies. It’s certainly not easy for everyone, but establishing either with a partner, family or friend a pickup/drop-off schedule. Also, talking to whoever you work for if you’re not self-employed. Maybe I can do one long day out of 5 days of the week, but not two or three, because I have childcare needs. Find out the balance of what the expectation of productivity is with what your time can allow. It’s doable, but you have to plan ahead.

Healio: Can you describe a time when your work-life balance failed, and how you managed to emotionally recover from that?

Dhillon: There have been plenty of times. The most common scenario is my kids getting sick. My husband is full time, and I’m full time, so we don’t have a point person if the children are sick.

There have been plenty of days where I wake up at 4 a.m. with a sick child, have a full day in clinic, and I have to cancel. It’s not necessarily a failure. But it certainly doesn’t help me in terms of my productivity. There’s a lot of rescheduling. Patients aren’t happy, but it’s the necessary thing that has to be done because that day is just for the children.

Other examples are when I’ve tried to go to work meetings with my whole family. We quickly realized that the burden of going to a work meeting at this point in my career with little kids, and it goes the same for my husband, who’s not in medicine, is too much for the other person. We’ve decided that if we have to go to work meetings, we make it short and sweet, and the other person is home with the kids and with that point person.

There have been moments where I’ve not been able to balance work and family. Sometimes I just have to focus on one, and that’s the way it is.

Healio: What advice would you give on handling the mental transition from a potentially high-risk surgical case to then being fully present at home?

Dhillon: It’s not easy. There definitely have been bad days for me at the hospital, and it could be a morbidity or even a mortality, where a patient of mine passed away and I was home and had to come in. It’s difficult, but the best thing I could advise is, if you have a supportive partner at home, communicate as soon as possible that it’s going to be one of those days. Explain the context of what’s going on before you get home, so the other person can take over. You can’t necessarily be apart from the children and you’re going to have to manage. But if someone can take over 99% of it, or 80% of it, it’s just mentally easier. It’s better than coming home and breaking down in front of the whole family. It’s hard sometimes to compartmentalize completely, but communication with your partner or your point person is probably the best advice.

Then also figuring out what kind of self-care you need at some point in the near future, because those days are not easy to get over, even if you don’t have kids. Sometimes talking to a colleague, or if you have a mentor, picking up the phone and having a conversation about what happened helps. People in your space understand what’s happening, and it might be easier than having that conversation at home.

Healio: Do you feel that motherhood has changed your approach to patient care, or made you a more empathetic surgeon?

Dhillon: Yes. It’s definitely made me patient and has slowed me down. I am not as rushed to get through a day or try and be more productive than I can be. I’ve certainly also formatted my schedule so that if I have a day where I have a lot of complicated patients, I’ve increased the amount of time I can spend with them in clinic.

I don’t follow a cookie cutter template in the sense of the amount of time ascribed to seeing a patient. So if I can foresee it’s going to be a complicated kind of day, I outline it for myself or I move other patients to another day.

If my surgical patients are still in the hospital after hours, it’s good for me sometimes to go round on my patients after I put my kids to bed. Motherhood changes the sense that you’re not in control of anything, and that time is not necessarily on your side, so you just slow down and be mindful of things.

Healio: What systemic changes do hospitals still need to make to retain women in surgical specialties?

Dhillon: There should be an open policy, if a woman is either a mom or new mom, regarding their needs for time in the office or in the hospital vs. time they need at home.

Having a forum for women, either online or maybe every 6 months, to sit down and have a discussion with staff about needs and ability to carve out time in the office for what you need to get home on time. It’s an important way of retaining women in the field.

Having resources available, like if you recently moved to this area and need childcare, these are some childcare options and potential subsidies. These are not just givens when you join a practice, but if you’re showing up at work and you don’t have the resources to deal with stuff at home, it’s hard to be at work mentally or physically. Having those resources is important.

At Johns Hopkins, we now have a Women’s Professional Advancement Council that’s institution-wide, which developed in the past decade, and has been great about providing resources, communication, forums, fireside chats and mentorship about how to navigate this. Again, it’s not perfect within every institution, but having an internal resource center would be important when you start somewhere to help navigate motherhood and practice.

Healio: What advice would you give to female medical students who fear they cannot be both a mother and a surgeon?

Dhillon: I would assure them that they certainly can.

If medical students have a timeline for what they want in terms of starting a family, it’s important they look into the resources at an institution. Based on my literature search, there are some places in the country that publish their written policies online. For example, when are your research years? When are your no-call blocks? There are times during where the program is shaped so that women planning on having children can be in those blocks during their pregnancies so that they can have more time off during that time and then get back to their other blocks afterward.

During residency interviews, you can talk to program residents about what the family lifestyle is like for their surgical trainees. There is more transparency on that now than even when I was going through this.

I would certainly encourage medical students to look into being a surgeon if that’s what their heart’s set on, and they want to be moms. I don’t think that there’s a barrier there.

Vaninder Dhillon, MD, can be reached at cardiology@healio.com.

Disclosures: Dhillon reports no relevant financial disclosures.

https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.title: GLP-1 use associated with nail detachment, hair loss
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.author: Gabrielle M. Grasso
https://www.healio.com/news/dermatology/.text:
Purpose-built for physicians

GLP-1 receptor agonist users experienced higher rates of nail disorders and hair loss than those with no exposure to the medication, according to a presentation at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venerology Congress.

While the association of hair loss with GLP-1s has been increasingly outlined in studies, the evidence suggesting a link with nail disorders is new, according to Charles Taïeb, MD, executive master in health policy at Sciences Po in Paris.

“Until now, nail changes associated with the use of GLP-1 receptor agonists had essentially been anecdotal and isolated to a handful of adverse event reports,” Taïeb told Healio. “But we found a strong and consistent nail signal in this study.”

The researchers evaluated the prevalence of hair loss and nail disorders among 575 GLP-1 receptor agonists users and 1,329 controls with no GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure from Brazil, France, Mexico and the United States. All participants had type 2 diabetes and/or obesity with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher.

The hair and nail disorders assessed included unusual hair loss, loss of hair volume or density, dandruff and scalp erythema, nail fragility, dyschromia, changes in thickness, onycholysis, and ridges or grooves. Weight loss was measured over a 3-month period, according to the study. The mean duration of GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment was 18.5 months.

Results showed that GLP-1 receptor agonist users reported weight loss over 3 months more frequently than controls at 76.3% vs. 47.3% (P < .001). More than 66% of GLP-1 receptor agonist users reported at least one nail disorder during those 3 months compared with 52.8% of controls (P < .001).

Nail detachment was the most common nail disorder reported, with a prevalence that was nearly seven times higher in the GLP-1 receptor agonist group vs. the control group (39.3% vs. 8.7%; OR = 6.84, 5.3-8.81; P < .001). GLP-1 receptor agonist users also reported higher rates of dyschromia (45.6% vs. 17%; OR = 4.09, 3.29-5.08; P < .001) onycholysis (49.2% vs. 29.7%; OR = 2.29, 1.87-2.8; P < .001), fragility (58.3% vs. 51.1%; OR = 1.34, 1.09-1.65; P = .005) and ridges or grooves (46.8% vs. 31.8%; OR = 1.89, 1.55-2.31; P < .001).

“What surprised us most is that these differences persisted when we looked only at participants who had lost weight, suggesting that weight loss alone does not seem to account for them,” Taïeb said. “And these controls were not drawn from the general population but from people with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity who had never taken the drugs, so the two groups share the metabolic background.”

The researchers believe that these nail changes are influenced by multiple factors associated with GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment, according to Taïeb.

“Our working hypothesis is that the nail matrix, like the hair follicle, is a rapidly renewing keratinized structure and may be sensitive to the same metabolic and nutritional changes that accompany these treatments, possibly with a direct effect of the drug on top,” Taïeb said. “Which of these contributions dominates, and whether the changes are reversible, is exactly what our planned prospective study is designed to answer.”

Taïeb told Healio that, due to the study’s design, the findings do not establish that GLP-1 treatment caused the changes. In fact, half of GLP-1 receptor agonist users reported nail problems prior to starting treatment. However, after adjusting for preexisting dermatologic conditions and nutritional deficiencies, nail detachment and discoloration remained approximately two to three times more frequent among GLP-1 receptor agonist users compared with controls.

In the same study cohort, researchers found that the prevalences of hair and scalp involvement was 50.4% in the GLP-1 receptor agonist group and 33.5% in the control group — a more than 4-fold difference (OR = 4.49, 3.62-5.56; P < .001). The risk for experiencing new onset hair loss was more than double among GLP-1 receptor agonist users vs. controls (26.1% vs. 11.6%; OR = 2.67; 2.03-3.5; P < .001). GLP-1 receptor agonist users were also more likely than controls to report a loss of hair volume/density (42.4% vs. 19.3%; OR = 3.23, 2.61-4; P < .001) and scalp erythema (OR = 3.05, 2.34-3.99; P < .001).

Most cases of hair loss in the study were accompanied by scalp itching, redness or scaling with scalp redness — an important clue for why hair loss may be occurring in this cohort, according to Taïeb.

“The classical explanation, telogen effluvium after rapid weight loss, does not predict an inflamed scalp,” Taïeb said. “So, our hypothesis is that an inflammatory component is involved, in addition to the shedding linked to weight loss. Scalp inflammation was the rule rather than the exception, which clinicians do not currently look for and which may be treatable.”

Because GLP-1s are increasingly prescribed to a large and growing population, dermatologists will continue to be involved in these patients’ ongoing care, according to Taïeb.

“Ask about hair, scalp and nails before starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist and during follow-up and examine them,” Taïeb said. “Look for treatable contributors, including pre-existing dermatological conditions and nutritional deficiencies, and keep in mind that not everything that happens during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment itself.”

According to Taïeb, hair loss and nail changes may prompt patients to stop their GLP-1 treatment on their own. Physicians should encourage them to continue their prescribed regimens and seek dermatologic care, Taïeb said.

“The message we want to pass on is awareness rather than alarm: These changes are frequent, usually benign and are not a reason to discontinue therapy on one's own initiative,” Taïeb told Healio. “Anyone who notices them should mention it to their doctor. The next step is prospective research following patients from the start of treatment, with standardized dermatological examinations and biological monitoring, to establish when these changes develop, why they occur and whether they are reversible.”

Charles Taïeb, MD, is executive master in health policy at Sciences Po and managing director of the European Market Maintenance Assessment. Taïeb can be reached at dermatology@healio.com.

Piraccini BM, et al. AS-1799. Presented at: European Academy of Dermatology and Venerology Congress; Sept. 30-Oct. 3, 2026; Vienna.
