https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/spacex-n.title: Apollo, banks in talks to finance SpaceX's $40 billion Nvidia GPU purchase
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/spacex-n.author: Seema Mody
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/spacex-n.text:
Apollo Capital and several banks are in talks with SpaceX to facilitate the $40 billion purchase of Nvidia GPUs, a source told CNBC.

The deal will primarily rely on the investment-grade debt market.

Discussions are preliminary and details have yet to be finalized, including key lenders.

Apollo Capital Management
 and several banks are in discussions with SpaceX
 to help facilitate the company’s purchase of $40 billion worth of Nvidia
 graphics processing units, according to a person familiar with the talks who asked not to be named to discuss the matter.

The deal will primarily rely on the investment-grade debt market, which SpaceX just tapped four months ago, the person said.

Two weeks after its record-breaking IPO in mid-June, the space exploration company raised $25 billion in bonds at different durations. CNBC was told at the time that SpaceX’s bond sale saw incredibly high demand, highlighting strong interest from fixed-income investors.

But since then, artificial intelligence-related bonds have sold off, while credit spreads have widened.

SpaceX’s $40 billion debt deal will likely use GPUs as collateral and Apollo Capital is said to be playing a leading role in facilitating the financing, the person said.

Apollo declined to comment. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The market is still operating under the expectation that GPUs hold their value for about seven years, according to a person in the credit industry who asked not to be named to discuss the matter. Computing power is scarce and the shortage is not expected to abate anytime soon, which supports the value of high-performing GPUs.

The Financial Times was first to report on the financing talks.

While a bond deal of this size is notable, it follows a series of bond issuances from Meta
, Amazon
 and Google
 as the cost to fund the AI buildout gets more expensive.

Both sources told CNBC that more debt sales are expected, fixed-income investors are demanding a higher yield to service the debt, a sign that participants are becoming more selective about their AI exposure.

SpaceX is already running a massive load of Nvidia AI chips and has plans to add to it.

CEO Elon Musk said in a Sept. 24 post on X that his company’s Colossus data center in Memphis, Tenn., was running 230,000 Nvidia AI chips, while Colossus 2 had 550,000. Musk said the company would more than double the number of chips by late December to reach 1.21 million, “If we get lucky.”

For the SpaceX bulls, the company has inked compute deals with Google, Anthropic
, Reflection AI and Cursor, which it later bought, and bringing more capacity online could boost revenue quickly.

On the flipside, the company reported nearly $40 billion in debt in its second-quarter financials, and its existing debt trades near junk bond levels, as credit markets have, overall, been more skittish.

However, to make SpaceX’s ambitions a reality, it needs to keep spending — and on more than just chips.

—CNBC’s Morgan Brennan contributed to this article

This is CNBC’s Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox.

Happy Wednesday. Even the Television Academy is cutting the cord. Starting next year, the Emmy Awards will stream on Amazon Prime Video under a six-year exclusive deal announced yesterday.

 closed at a record yesterday.

Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day:

Stock investors have officially climbed yet another wall of worry. The S&P 500 ended yesterday’s session above 7,800 for the first time, marking its first record close in nearly two months.

President Donald Trump has directed federal immigration officers to descend on major U.S. cities in his second term. A growing body of research shows that where Immigration and Customs Enforcement conducted raids, an economic chill has tended to follow.

A University of Pennsylvania study found that communities subject to ICE raids saw pullbacks in spending and foot traffic, which University of Pennsylvania professor Zeke Hernandez said can result in “recession-like conditions.” The Brookings Institution reported last month that employment fell in cities most impacted by ICE raids.

CNBC traveled to Minneapolis, where the Department of Homeland Security conducted Operation Metro Surge — what it billed as the largest-ever immigration enforcement event. The city estimates it lost almost $700 million in economic activity between December and April, and the state has seen its unemployment rate spike, outpacing the national average for the first time in nearly two decades.

In an effort to improve the experience of doing business with an artificial intelligence bot, Meta
 is teaming up with Walmart

The protocol will be an open standard intended to clarify how AI agents can interface with businesses, CNBC’s Kate Rooney reports. Sierra co-founder Bret Taylor, who’s leading the initiative, told CNBC that without such a rulebook “it is kind of chaos.”

The expansion will open the program to more companies, and members will get access to thousands of dollars’ worth of products and credits.

Shares of Nasdaq-listed Webull are down nearly 30% in premarket trading this morning. The CNBC and SurveyMonkey Quarterly Money Survey released this week shows that Americans feel stretched by shelter costs — especially if they’re renting. The data comes as mortgage rates climb at a faster clip and housing prices keep rising.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/google-f.title: Google ordered to halt work on two data centers in ‘Texas of Europe’
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/google-f.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/google-f.text:
Google has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it’s developing in Finland until environmental impact assessments have been completed.

“We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance,” a Google spokesperson told CNBC.

Finland has emerged as a key location for data centers amid the AI boom.

Google
 has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it’s developing in Finland, a month after the tech giant committed to investing $15 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure in the country.

Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency, or LVV, on Tuesday issued a notice to Google subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend building work for data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani until the environmental impact assessments have been completed.

The suspension request applies, among other things, to the removal of trees, removal of topsoil, excavation, quarrying, crushing, transfer of soil masses, ditching, and the construction of roads and storage areas, according to a Google translation of an LVV press release.

“We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance,” a Google spokesperson told CNBC, adding that it would follow the LVV’s guidance.

“We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas,” the spokesperson said. “As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares [320 acres] at Muhos.”

The LVV ordered Google to halt work no later than Oct. 23. The request does not apply to planning, measurements, soil surveys, or other measures with minor impacts that can be easily restored.

“In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure,” Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at the Finnish licensing and supervision authority, said in the statement.

Finland has emerged as a key location for data centers amid the AI boom, with hyperscalers and developers eyeing its available land and power, which is in short supply throughout most of Europe.

Several data center projects with potential capacities of hundreds of megawatts have recently been announced in the country.

The rise in demand has led to Finland being dubbed the “Texas of Europe.” The U.S. state has become one of the leading locations for AI data centers globally, with a number of huge projects announced by hyperscalers and AI labs, including Google, Meta, Microsoft and Anthropic.

Google’s $15 billion plan for Finland will mark its largest investment in Europe. The capital will be deployed through 2028 into data centers and other supporting investments like energy projects, the company said in a statement at the time.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/economy-.title: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/economy-.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/economy-.text:
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said the growth needed to shrink debt without budget cuts or tax increases looks out of reach for now, with global public debt heading past 100% of GDP.

Investment in AI is on track to match or exceed the sums that went into building railroads, power grids and telecom networks.

But if earnings disappoint, heavy borrowing by AI hyperscalers and large foreign holdings of U.S. stocks could turn a letdown into a wider shock.

SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.

Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is “rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy.”

But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already “underwhelming” growth this decade.

“Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here,” Georgieva said.

Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a “negative energy supply shock” from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a “positive demand shock” from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is “highly uneven across the world.”

On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.

The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. “Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy,” Georgieva said.

But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, “increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she said.

The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. “The AI building boom is inflationary,” she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.

Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.

That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades. Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.

Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the “worst offenders,” Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had “a relatively easy ride” because interest rates stayed below growth rates. “Higher interest rates now put an end to that.”

The interest-to-growth differential is now “much less favourable” and “set to climb higher,” she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now “out of reach in the near term.”

The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.

After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries’ fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, “fiscal space is crying out for replenishment,” Georgieva said.

Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but “should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock.”

Citing Amara’s Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is “somewhere in the transition between today’s AI building boom and tomorrow’s arrival of AI’s benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk.”

Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. “Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” she said.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/economy-.summary: International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva says growth needed to shrink debt looks out of reach for now. She urges policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt. Investment in AI is on track to match or exceed the sums that went into building railroads, power grids and telecom networks.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/singapor.title: Singapore's Temasek warns of the ‘biggest risk’ facing markets right now
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/singapor.author: Lee Ying Shan
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/singapor.text:
A reversal in the AI trade could be triggered by several factors, including safety concerns that lead to tighter regulation: Temasek

AI has been one of the key forces keeping U.S. stocks near record highs even as Treasury yields have surged.

SINGAPORE — An unwinding of the artificial intelligence trade poses the biggest risk to markets, according to Singapore’s state-owned investment giant Temasek.

“We don’t see that as imminent, but will you have bumps in 2027? Yeah, possibly yes,” Rohit Sipahimalani, Temasek’s chief investment officer, said at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore.

AI has been one of the key forces keeping U.S. stocks near record highs even as Treasury yields have surged, Sipahimalani said, pointing to the earnings strength of major companies tied to the technology.

The S&P 500 has remained around record territory despite the rise in borrowing costs, supported by “AI and the earnings momentum around the key players,” he said.

But the strength at the index level masks weakness beneath the surface. Sipahimalani noted that roughly half the stocks in the Russell 3000 were at least 20% below their June highs, highlighting the degree to which the market’s resilience has depended on a small group of winners.

A reversal in the AI trade could be triggered by several factors, he said, including safety concerns that lead to tighter regulation or signs that customers are failing to generate sufficient returns from their spending on the technology.

Temasek, however, remains bullish on AI over the longer term and has continued to increase investments into the sector. About half of the investment firm’s AI exposure is currently in publicly traded assets, a proportion it would ideally increase to around 70% to 75%, Sipahimalani said.

That would give Temasek greater ability to adjust its investments as the industry evolves, compared with private assets that can be harder to exit quickly.

“One of the things we recognize is that AI is such a fast-changing environment that things could change quite easily, and you have to be able to pivot,” he said.

Temasek has invested in private AI model developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, but “the size of exposure there would be different compared to some of the other areas where we have more flexibility” Sipahimalani said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/flop-ai-.title: Trillions are being ‘wasted’ on the AI boom, Arthur Hayes says. He’s betting on what comes next
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/flop-ai-.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/flop-ai-.text:
Humanity is “wasting multi-trillion dollars” on AI data center build-up, according to former BitMEX CEO Arthur Hayes.

A key test could come in late 2027 or 2028, when new data center capacity is delivered and customers face their compute commitments.

Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies could benefit from the excess liquidity that follows a bailout, Hayes said.

Former BitMEX CEO Arthur Hayes is betting that the artificial intelligence boom will eventually produce a familiar outcome: too much investment, a crash and, ultimately, a bailout that sends crypto higher.

Hayes, co-founder and chief investment officer of crypto investment firm Maelstrom, said in response to questions from CNBC at the Gamma Prime Investing Conference in Singapore that humanity is “wasting multi-trillion dollars” on building AI data centers.

The massive data center buildout would ultimately make computing power “extremely cheap and extremely plentiful,” Hayes said.

The bet runs against the massive investment pouring into AI infrastructure, as technology companies race to secure the computing power needed to develop and run increasingly advanced AI models. Hayes sees that buildout eventually becoming overcapacity, setting the stage for a downturn that he expects will ultimately benefit crypto.

“If you study financial history and you study every single major technological rollout, it always is overbuilt. There always is a crash, and there always is a bailout,” Hayes said.

Investors who position for those bailouts stand to benefit, Hayes said, pointing to the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and other episodes over the past two decades.

“Thankfully, we have bitcoin and other crypto to soak up that excess liquidity, and so we know the asset that’s going to perform the best when the bailout comes,” Hayes said, adding that “you just have to be patient.”

SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic are among the end users driving demand for computing power, and none of them makes money, Hayes said. Once the data centers currently under construction are completed, infrastructure providers will seek payment for the compute those companies have committed to, he said.

That could come in late 2027 or 2028, when much of the new data center capacity is delivered, according to Hayes.

The bull case is that AI becomes “so useful” over the next 12 months that demand grows enough for AI companies to become profitable, Hayes said.

Some companies supplying the AI boom are already making money, Hayes said, pointing to memory chipmakers and Nvidia. The question for investors is whether they are paying the right multiple for those companies’ forward earnings, he added.

Hayes also said he does not like betting on falling prices or shorting AI companies, calling it “not really a great investment opportunity,” but added that major technological rollouts have historically been overbuilt.

The abundance of computing power created by the AI buildout is also behind Hayes’ latest crypto venture, Flop, an AI-agent payments project expected to launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Cheaper and more plentiful computing power would allow AI agents to proliferate, Hayes said.

His new project, Flop, aims to create a spot market for computing power, where participants are rewarded with Flop tokens for providing GPUs and performing AI inference.

There is currently no payments network for AI agents, Hayes said. Flop aims to create a spot market for compute.

“If agents can convert a currency directly into compute, which is what they eat and consume, then they will use this currency,” Hayes said. “That’s our bet.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/jim-cram.title: Cramer says these blue-chip stocks are among the best ways to invest in the AI boom
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/jim-cram.author: Alexa LoMonaco
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/jim-cram.text:
Jim Cramer said established tech giants with strong businesses and multiple ways to benefit from AI are some of the best places to invest in the boom.

He remains diversified but is overweight AI, arguing those stocks offer more opportunities for growth as higher rates weigh on much of the rest of the market.

CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Tuesday that some of the best ways to invest in the artificial intelligence boom are established tech giants with multiple opportunities to capitalize on the technology.

The “Mad Money” host acknowledged concerns about stretched AI valuations and comparisons with the dotcom bubble. Rather than backing away from a trade that continues to drive much of the market’s gains, Cramer said he favors blue-chip companies with strong businesses and management teams that can find new ways to benefit from AI.

“Because I think that a lot of things can possibly go right, I want to stick with the AI data center plays,” Cramer said.

He pointed to Meta
 and Microsoft
 as two examples. Cramer’s CNBC Investing Club owns both stocks.

While Meta shares had a rocky start to 2026, Cramer said he trusted CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team to figure out how to monetize its AI spending, which the Facebook and Instagram parent is expected to do with Muse. The stock now trades around $738.

“I didn’t think, ‘what a bunch of chowderheads, they don’t have anything AI,’” Cramer said. “I thought that Mark Zuckerberg and his dream team are brilliant and they’ll figure something out.”

Cramer had a similar view of Microsoft when shares traded at a 52-week low of $350 in June. “I didn’t think their best times were behind them,” Cramer said, despite at times expressing frustration in the stock’s performance. Ultimately, though, Cramer retained the Club’s shares because of his trust in the veteran leadership team of CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood.

“I thought, ‘They’re going to figure out this Copilot, and with their Azure web services business they’re going to make a ton of money.’” Shares now trade around $529, as the market has grown more confident in Microsoft’s plan for Copilot. Also, in late July, the performance and guidance for Azure also surpassed Wall Street expectations, leading to a stock rally.

Cramer also highlighted Advanced Micro Devices
 and Intel
 in semiconductors, Marvell Technology
 in chips and fiber, and CrowdStrike
 and Palo Alto Networks
 in cybersecurity.

The strategy looks particularly attractive to Cramer as higher interest rates make growth harder to find elsewhere. AI-related companies, by contrast, are among the relatively few businesses that can continue delivering strong growth in this environment, he said.

“When I query about 80% of the S&P 500
 about what can possibly go right, I can’t even think of anything for most of them,” Cramer said. “Sure, that can change when the war ends. Until then, though, the AI-related stocks give you the most opportunity for something to go right.”

That doesn’t mean the AI trade is without risk. Cramer acknowledged that enthusiasm can become excessive. He also stressed, “I want to be diversified, and I certainly run a diversified” portfolio for the Investing Club.

Cramer’s Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC’s Investing Club, owns shares of META, MSFT, INTC, CRWD, PANW.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/meta-joi.title: Meta joins with group of companies to tame ‘chaos’ of doing business with AI bots
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/meta-joi.author: Kate Rooney
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/meta-joi.text:
Walmart, Meta and OpenAI Chairman Bret Taylor’s startup Sierra are building a set of tech standards to make it easier to do business with AI bots.

As Meta’s Muse and other buzzy AI agents like Instinct see a boom in popularity, some companies have struggled to figure out what’s happening inside their walls.

“It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists,” said Taylor.

A month after Meta’s
 launch of Muse, the personal agent that quickly turned into a viral sensation, a group of companies is coming together to try to simplify the process of bringing the technology into the business world.

Meta, Walmart
, Stripe and a handful of other companies are publishing what they’re calling a “personal agent protocol.” It’s an open standard meant to dictate how artificial intelligence agents can interact with businesses.

Enterprise AI startup Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce
 co-CEO Bret Taylor, is part of the group. Taylor, who’s also chairman of OpenAI and is leading the initiative, told CNBC in an interview that companies have a lot of work to do to figure out how and when personal agents are able to access information.

“Companies will know when it’s a personal agent versus an actual person. For a lot of companies there’s a risk: you don’t want just a random bot that isn’t acting on behalf of a person to have access to this service,” Taylor said. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists.”

Meta’s Muse has become the most popular and buzzy version of personal AI agents since hitting the market in early September. It soared to the top of Apple’s
 App Store and remains there, ahead of ChatGPT. However, Amazon
 is among the companies that have blocked Meta’s agents, citing worries of website scraping.

Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent and sued the startup in November, alleging the company took steps to “conceal” its AI agents so they could continue to scrape Amazon’s website without approval. Perplexity called the lawsuit a “bully tactic.”

For the new standard, Taylor compared it with the experience of logging into other websites with Google
 or Facebook credentials, technology he worked on when he was tech chief at Facebook. He said the practice will help with authentication so that businesses know if they’re dealing with a bot, and will provide visibility into what personal agents are actually doing through these websites.

David Singleton, vice president of engineering and consumer products at Meta Superintelligence Labs and former technology chief at Stripe, highlighted security. In order for agents to work well, he said, customers need to share credit card and personal information, and the new standard creates some level of visibility and control.

“We’re defining rails that we hope personal agents and business agents can run over for the future,” Singleton said, comparing it to email. “If you think about email, it works great because it is a standard that everyone can use to talk to each other, and we think this is going to be quite similar.”

Singleton said Muse already has millions of users in the U..S and it’s “growing rapidly.”

“What we’re finding is that people love using Muse for all kinds of things, things like signing their kids up for classes, finding and buying the best gifts, scheduling that dentist appointment that you have been putting off for six months,” he said. “We need a mechanism to have it go faster and smoother.”

While OpenAI and Anthropic aren’t on board now, Taylor said he expects the AI giants to participate, and indicated he will be “really disappointed” if it’s not being used by competitors.

“The whole point of this is to be an open standard,” Taylor said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/anthropi.title: Anthropic expands Claude Startups program in bid to snag founders and fast-growing companies
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/anthropi.author: Ashley Capoot
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/anthropi.text:
Anthropic announced it’s expanding its Claude Startups program, which gives members access to thousands of dollars’ worth of Anthropic’s Claude products and credits.

The expansion marks the AI company’s latest push to deepen its ties to founders and fast-growing companies.

Anthropic said startups that were founded within the past five years or funded within the past two years are able to apply.

Anthropic
 on Tuesday announced it’s expanding its Claude Startups program, the artificial intelligence lab’s latest push to deepen its ties to founders and fast-growing companies.

Claude Startups initially launched in May, and thousands of companies are already participating, according to Anthropic. The company is opening up the program to more organizations, and members will get access to thousands of dollars’ worth of Anthropic’s Claude products and credits to help them build.

“Startups are often the first to push Claude to its limits,” Beth Robertson, head of startups at Anthropic, told CNBC in a statement. “When a new model ships, they’re ready that same day to take on projects that used to seem out of reach. Claude Startups gives founders credits, tools and direct time with our team, so more companies can build this way from the start.”

The vast majority of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its business customers, and it has spent much of the last year trying to fend off rivals like OpenAI
 and Google
, which both offer their own programs for startups. As it gears up for what is widely expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering, Anthropic is working to ensure that the next generation of businesses will be built using its products.

Claude Startup members can receive up to $45,000 worth of discounts and credits through the Claude Startup Stack, which Anthropic described as a “set of benefits for the tools a startup runs on.” Additionally, eligible organizations can access a one-time $1,000 application programming interface, or API, credit, as well as a free year of Claude Team for up to five premium seats.

Anthropic said members can also meet with the company’s applied AI team through virtual office hours and connect with other members of the Claude Startup community at events.

Startups that were founded within the past five years or funded within the past two years are able to apply, Anthropic said.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/anduril-.title: Anduril lands $2.9 billion Navy submarine shipyard contract days after Luckey joins Pentagon weapons group
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/anduril-.author: Samantha Subin
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/anduril-.text:
Anduril landed a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to support submarine production.

The company said it will build components for the Virginia-class submarine.

Co-founder Palmer Luckey, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk were named to the Pentagon’s Project Meridian.

Anduril won an up to $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy on Tuesday to boost submarine production, days after co-founder Palmer Luckey was named to a Pentagon future weapons task force.

The company is also investing $3.7 billion to scale a new shipyard at Sparrows Point, outside Baltimore, Maryland, slated to start operations in 2030 and create about 3,100 jobs.

Anduril said the 2 million-square-foot facility will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Some parts, including torpedo tubes, will be manufactured at a 160,000-square-foot facility in Orange County, California.

“This is about putting more food on the table and being able to meet the requirements that our country has to produce more submarines,” said Anduril President and Chief Strategy Officer Chris Brose in a press briefing.

President Donald Trump thanked Luckey by name in comments Tuesday afternoon to mark the investment, calling him a “friend” and “very brilliant guy.”

The deal comes days after the Department of Defense tapped Luckey to join a new initiative called Project Meridian to identify and develop capabilities for future U.S. conflicts, raising questions over defense tech’s growing sway in Washington as the companies compete for government contracts.

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX
 CEO Elon Musk are also part of the project. Both SpaceX and Anduril are actively working with the U.S. government.

Department of Defense Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael addressed Luckey’s involvement with the Pentagon in comments to CNBC on Tuesday, dismissing any concerns about a potential conflict of interest.

“There’s really nothing to see here,” he said.

Michael said the collection of academics, former military and industry leaders in Project Meridian is “exactly the right kind of mix that you want” to prepare for any future conflict.

Defense tech companies and their leaders have seen their influence grow in Washington in recent months as Trump seeks to bolster U.S. military capabilities, including shipbuilding.

Marc Andreessen, whose venture firm Andreessen Horowitz pours billions into defense tech firms, including Anduril, was named to the Pentagon’s defense policy board this summer, alongside Thiel Capital’s Blake Masters.

Anduril is widely known for building autonomous drones and crafts. Over the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was reportedly in talks to build drone boats on the site.

Brose said the facility will focus on the Virginia-class submarine program, illustrating a push into conventional shipbuilding by the growing defense contractor.

“Our goal here is to be a critical, and hopefully, over time, much larger and growing part of the supply chain for our lead shipbuilders,” He said. “And over time, we hope that’ll grow up to very large sections of the ship.”

Trump made several references to autonomous submarines and drones during his remarks.

The massive Virginia-class vessels are built by General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries. This summer, General Dynamics won a $76.6 billion Navy award to build submarines.

“This is an opportunity to really reimagine how a shipyard is built and how this work is done, and that’s just not something that our current industrial base has the luxury of doing,” Brose said.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.title: Wildlife Populations Have Plunged Globally, But Some Buck the Trend
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.author: By Kiley Price
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.text:
A new report paints a dark picture of the state of global wildlife—but also highlights flickers of light where some populations are on the upswing.

Over the past half-century, populations of thousands of vertebrate species across the globe have decreased in size by 73 percent on average, according to the “Living Planet” report published Wednesday by the nonprofits World Wildlife Fund and the Zoological Society of London. A number of factors contributed to this precipitous decline, including habitat loss, overexploitation and climate change.

However, a closer look at certain regions and biomes offers reasons for hope, the report’s authors say. Roughly half the populations they studied are stable or even increasing. Though these gains are outweighed by the greater magnitude of losses elsewhere, they show that concerted conservation efforts have made a difference for species such as green sea turtles and bluefin tuna, according to lead author Rebecca Shaw, the chief scientist at the World Wildlife Fund.

“The report focuses on hope because even though the headline statistic is really, really stark … what we see underlying the statistic is some real movement in some species,” Shaw said.

Despite these successes, the report stressed the importance of tackling biodiversity loss at a global scale by changing the three major systems driving extinction: food, energy and finance.

The “Living Planet” reports are released roughly every two years. The latest taps into data from tens of thousands of populations of 5,790 vertebrate species across the animal kingdom—from Laysan albatross to ring-tailed lemurs.

Rather than tallying the total number of animals lost or gained, the researchers measured changes in relative abundance of populations. That means a small population of monkeys that has dropped from 200 to 100 would have experienced the same 50 percent loss as a large colony of 20,000 bats that has dipped to 10,000.

This method allows researchers to compare data from different populations and better track overall trends, said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London who works on the Living Planet Index that informs the report.

“The reason we do that is so that we can get a good picture of what is happening across different species by giving them equal weight within this index,” she said. “We’re getting a better signal of the health of the environment.”

So while the new report does not mean there are 73 percent fewer wild vertebrate animals in total today than in 1970, it does show populations the report monitored are plummeting on average. However, diving deeper into the numbers reveals the varied stories playing out for wildlife around the world.

By geography, monitored species populations have faced the most significant decline in Latin America and the Caribbean, with an average 95 percent decrease from 1970 to 2022. In that same timeframe, North America and the combined regions of Europe and Central Asia have seen around 25 percent declines, though the authors pointed out that development in those areas had already had large-scale impacts on nature prior to 1970. Declines in Africa and the Asia and the Pacific region were 80 percent and 49 percent, respectively.

The researchers also broke the numbers down by biome. Freshwater species were the clear losers, seeing an overall decline of 85 percent—significantly more than terrestrial or marine species, though these vertebrates are also seeing major losses.

The report attributed the nosedive in freshwater species to a number of factors, including pollution, overharvesting and habitat loss caused by infrastructure such as hydropower dams. Impacted species included in the report range from migratory fish such as Chinook salmon in the Western United States to the Amazon pink river dolphin in Brazil, which plummeted by 65 percent between 1994 and 2016 alone in the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve in the state of Amazonas.

For terrestrial species, habitat loss and degradation drove much of the biodiversity decline, while marine life faced major threats from overfishing.

Viorel Popescu, an associate research scientist at Columbia University who wasn’t involved in the report, said it’s valuable to bring these “huge amounts of data” that are largely invisible to most of the public “to the forefront.” But he added that the report may be an underestimate of total biodiversity losses, given that it only focuses on vertebrate species the authors analyzed. Other scientists have echoed this critique.

Popescu pointed to the collapse of many populations of insects, which make up roughly three-quarters of all known animal species on Earth. In fact, beetles alone account for 25 percent of all animal species.

“Those declines could be even more drastic,” Popescu said.

The report also pointed to bright spots around the world. For example, in 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to be downlisted by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature, which means populations increased enough around the world for the animal to no longer be considered endangered.

But this recovery didn’t happen overnight. According to the report, a roughly five-decade coordinated conservation effort launched across more than 80 countries helped populations rebuild through protecting nesting females and eggs, beach management, lighting regulations, turtle excluder devices and other bycatch reduction measures to help reduce sea turtle entanglements in fishing gear.

Researchers have also documented population increases for species such as tigers, Southern African elephants and Atlantic and bluefin tuna following conservation initiatives and stricter industry regulations.

However, efforts to help pull species from the brink are struggling to secure the necessary funding to meet the accelerating global extinction crisis, experts say. In the United States, the Trump administration has made deep cuts to conservation programs, both domestically and internationally.

“[D]evelopment aid budgets from national governments and international agencies have historically formed the majority of global conservation funding, with a focus on supporting the communities living alongside wildlife,” Andrew Terry, the chief conservation officer at the Zoological Society of London, said in an emailed statement to Inside Climate News. “Cuts to these aid budgets by governments across the northern hemisphere have had widespread impacts on people and nature alike.”

Even if additional funding emerges, the new report argues that ensuring the long-term future of the world’s biodiversity requires fundamental shifts to society, particularly in the food, energy and finance sectors. Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and a major contributor of climate-warming greenhouse gas emissions alongside fossil fuels.

Experts say accelerating clean energy uptake can help decrease emissions that fuel global warming, avoiding climate threats to biodiversity. Credits: Jason Houston/WWF-US and Pand P Studio/Shutterstock/WWF

According to the report, accelerating solar uptake around the world illustrates how systems can change to reduce their impact on biodiversity. However, financial systems are still pumping money into development that hurts biodiversity, with one estimate suggesting that $7.3 trillion flowed into activities that harm nature in 2023, more than 30 times the money spent on efforts to protect or restore it.

Shaw said the new report shows countries must simultaneously increase conservation funding to restore wildlife populations, while reducing investments in the activities that undermine them.

“Go after the root causes, don’t do this species by species,” she said. “Focus on the food system, the energy system and the finance system, and the connections between the three. That’s a recipe for really turning around the loss of wildlife and the loss of species that we’re seeing at a global scale.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.title: To Block Solar Energy Projects, One Community Lumped Them in With Junkyards and Adult Bookstores
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.author: By Dan Gearino
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.text:
In Montgomery County, Indiana, utility-scale solar projects appear on an official list of undesirable land uses that also includes “adult-oriented businesses.”

So it wasn’t surprising that the county Board of Commissioners unanimously rejected a 200-megawatt solar project on Sept. 28.

But it still stings for renewable energy advocates. It shows a huge challenge lurking right behind the debate over a U.S. Senate energy permitting bill. Even if the federal government eases the permitting process, much of the country is off-limits for wind and solar development because local residents and their elected officials oppose it.

One person who repeatedly defended the Indiana project at public meetings was John Smillie, a solar power supporter who lives in Crawfordsville, the county seat. He works as a finance manager for an industrial lighting company and does charitable work, written about by Canary Media, to help nonprofits install solar.

I spoke with Smillie this week to explore how Montgomery County and the country are supposed to move into the energy future when a seemingly beneficial project gets smacked down in such a fashion.

“Hearing the disinformation is very difficult,” he said.

For example, people opposing the project said China doesn’t use solar panels, it just sells the panels to the United States.

“That’s radically untrue,” Smillie said. Indeed, China has installed more solar power than any other country.

Video of the meeting shows more than an hour of testimony, including repeated claims that solar is a danger to human and animal health. Such concerns are widely debunked, but they are repeated at government meetings as if they were true.

Commissioners said they were swayed by testimony that the project may reduce nearby property values and change the character of the area.

“This is a large agricultural area,” said Commissioner Jim Fulwider.

Solar will “change the looks and the surroundings of that community for years to come with the size of that project,” he said.

Researchers have looked at how solar and wind projects may affect property values. A 2023 study from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory—which did not include data from Indiana—showed small effects in some states, but nothing close to the drastic changes that opponents have claimed.

Much of the world of environmental and clean energy advocacy is now focusing on the permitting bill in the U.S. Senate, announced on Sept. 30.

Supporters of the bill, including clean energy industry groups, say it would unleash a building boom for interstate power lines, wind, solar and battery projects. Opponents, including many environmental advocacy groups, say the measure would accelerate construction of fossil fuel infrastructure and lock in decades of emissions that contribute to climate change.

I think what happened in Montgomery County and similar communities across the country must be part of the discussion. Even if federal permitting gets easier, developers will struggle to build if local residents and elected officials are not on board.

By the end of 2025, there were 888 state and local laws restricting renewable energy across 48 states, according to Columbia Law School’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. The center’s database shows restrictions in more than 30 of Indiana’s 92 counties.

Notably, Montgomery County is not one of them. Its limits are indirect, stemming from a comprehensive planning process in 2024 that includes wind and solar as undesirable land uses, based on focus groups with residents. The county’s list of undesirable uses also has junkyards, landfills and adult-oriented businesses, among others.

Researchers at Ball State University in Muncie, Indiana, released a policy brief in April showing that county-level restrictions on wind and solar are associated with a decrease in economic activity, while Indiana counties without restrictions saw a net gain. The limits on development also contributed to a net loss of jobs, mainly in manufacturing and transportation, that were partly offset by small gains in agricultural jobs.

I reached out to Engie North America, developer of the solar project, and the Montgomery County Board of Commissioners, and didn’t hear back from either.

The project would have paid more than $40 million in local taxes during its lifespan and generated enough electricity each year to meet the needs of about 32,000 households, according to Engie North America. The company planned to spend more than $300 million to build the solar farm.

It’s not every day that Montgomery County has a company wanting to invest $300 million.

And the project was to be in a location with few houses within view, with greenery planted to partially block the view, Smillie said.

“Most people going through Montgomery County would never have noticed it was there,” he said.

I don’t have a solution to the problem playing out in Indiana and so many other places.

Ideally, developers would get better at connecting with local residents and elected officials, while local officials would find ways to use revenue from renewable energy projects to reduce taxes and fund community priorities.

States could also step in to limit the ability of local governments to block projects, as Illinois, Michigan and others have done. That approach may lead to more projects being built, but it can also deepen resentment from rural communities and probably isn’t a long-term solution.

I asked Smillie how he felt walking out of that meeting.

“Pretty doomy,” he said.

Other stories about the energy transition to take note of this week:

Supreme Court Hears Landmark Climate Deception Case: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments this week in Suncor v. Boulder, a case that affects dozens of lawsuits accusing fossil fuel industries of deceiving the public about climate change, as my colleague Nicholas Kusnetz reports. The sides focused on procedural issues regarding whether the case should be allowed to proceed. Oil companies are seeking protection from courts and lawmakers from liability related to climate change, and the outcome of those efforts has major implications for the trajectory of the shift away from fossil fuels.

Tandem Solar Cells Could Be a Leap Forward for U.S. Manufacturers: Tandem solar cells, which use several layers of solar material to produce additional energy, offer U.S.-based solar manufacturers a chance to catch up with competitors in China, as Ivan Penn reports for The New York Times. Tandem PV, First Solar and Hanwha Qcells are among the companies working to develop the products.

Solar Program Grantees Seek Damages: Organizations that stood to benefit from the federal government’s Solar for All program have already won a judgment that will restore funding from the Trump administration, and now they are asking a court for damages related to the disruption of the funding, as Diana DiGangi reports for Utility Dive. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is still weighing whether to appeal the Sept. 18 ruling that restored the program. Solar for All was a Biden administration initiative aimed at expanding access to customer-owned solar, but it became caught up in the Trump administration’s push to claw back funding from clean energy programs.

New Chevrolet Bolt Has Extremely Limited Run: General Motors had touted the return of the Chevrolet Bolt as an affordable electric vehicle. But the subsequent cancellation of federal EV incentives may now be prompting the company to scale back production to just 35,000 units in the model’s one-year run, according to a union official cited by Kalea Hall of Reuters. The Bolt went on sale this year with a starting price of $27,600. The model may be a casualty of a shifting market in which entry-level EVs are getting hurt by last year’s removal of consumer tax credits.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.title: Maryland Demands Answers as Fuel Leak Persists From Joint Base Andrews
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.author: By Aman Azhar
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.text:
Maryland environmental regulators say jet fuel continues to seep into Piscataway Creek from Joint Base Andrews more than six months after the spill was reported, despite the base’s assurances that it has isolated the damaged fuel system and stopped the leak.

“MDE remains deeply concerned about the ongoing environmental impacts and continues to observe signs of jet fuel coming from the site,” the Maryland Department of the Environment said in a written response. “Jet fuel continues to flush into the creek, particularly after heavy rain.”

In its response to Inside Climate News, the installation acknowledged that they continue to “actively contain and recover” spilled fuel trapped in soil that flushes into the creek during storms.

Piscataway Creek connects Joint Base Andrews, located in Prince George’s County, to the Potomac River near Fort Washington Park. The adjacent Piscataway Park provides public access points to the creek and the river for fishing and boating.

The initial incident drew criticism from lawmakers and environmental advocates over the base’s delay in reporting the spill. The fuel system failed a tightness test on Dec. 11, according to the MDE, which said the base’s leak detection system failed multiple times between January and March, spilling roughly 32,000 gallons of jet fuel into the creek.

The agency said it was not notified until fuel odors and a sheen were seen near the creek’s headwaters on March 23, and the base did not report the full extent of the discharge until April 8. The MDE, which has enforcement authority under state environmental regulations, then ordered the military facility to carry out an emergency soil investigation, install monitoring wells and remediate contaminated soils.

Differing estimates of how much fuel has spilled has complicated the mitigation work. A May letter nine members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation sent to U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink described approximately 32,000 gallons leaking across multiple dates and locations. Approximately 10,000 gallons from January and February incidents were reportedly contained within the fuel infrastructure and approximately 22,000 gallons were discharged into the environment.

The lawmakers asked for an accounting of how much fuel had entered the creek and how much remained underground, along with plans to prevent further contamination during rain events.

In its June 22 reply, the Air Force said the pressure-test failure on Dec. 11 was caused by a faulty valve that did not release fuel into the environment but distorted pressure readings. It said the anomaly delayed leak detection until the fuel was detected in the waters on March 23.

“JBA did not notify MDE of the failed pressure tests,” the Air Force said, adding that the matter is part of an ongoing internal investigation.

The Air Force did not provide the exact volume of the spill, saying it was “not yet possible” to determine how much fuel remained in soil, groundwater and the creek, and said it had recovered more than 35,000 gallons of a fuel-water mixture from the creek, a value the MDE has yet to verify.

“Over six months since the jet fuel leak was reported, JBA has yet to identify the exact location of the leak, diagnose the cause of the failure, or take appropriate action to fix the problem,” MDE representatives told Inside Climate News in the latest response.

In background interviews, agency officials vented their frustration that despite repeated requests over months, the base continues to stonewall requests for site-specific information, such as a basic site model displaying a map of fuel lines, creeks and environmental assets nearby, or the precise location of the crack in the underground fuel line. It has also not carried out standard subsurface probing to map the contamination plume under the tarmac. Under state oil control rules, agency officials noted, handlers of jet fuel are expected to account for every drop and quantify spills and the installation has not met that basic requirement.

The base did not respond to allegations that the MDE’s requests for information have been rebuffed. It offered a different assessment of the situation on the ground.

“The compromised section of the hydrant system was identified, isolated, and completely drained to eliminate any residual risk of fuel contaminating a water source,” a JBA spokesperson said in emailed comments. They did not say when this correction took place.

Asked whether its assertion that “the active leak has been stopped” meant the spilled fuel was no longer entering the creek, the spokesperson clarified that the assessment applied specifically to “fuel escaping from the infrastructure.”

The base further stated that its June testing could not conclusively determine the location and cause of the leak, and a pressure test is planned within the next few weeks. “The exact timeline for repairs will be dependent on the test results and subsequent engineering assessments,” it said, and that the affected sections would remain drained and isolated until repairs and retesting were completed.

In a follow-up response, the base said pressure readings on the isolated line remained stable and that it was conducting MDE-approved tightness testing of the remaining active infrastructure.

Asked whether the MDE had independently reviewed and concurred with its conclusion that the fuel leak had stopped, the base said the agency “concurred with the immediate isolation and draining of the affected loop.” It did not specify whether MDE independently verified the outcome or what evidence the agency had reviewed.

The base’s subsurface investigation has also left unanswered questions about groundwater contamination. The spokesperson acknowledged that the first phase of investigation “did not definitively define the plume.”

Meanwhile, surface-water testing by the base and MDE continues to detect fuel-related chemicals in the sampling done through Aug. 26, the most recent results MDE published. Both agencies tested water from three regularly monitored locations located within the base perimeter.

The results are listed under Diesel Range Organics (DRO), which typically include diesel fuel, motor oil, jet fuel and mineral oils, but also can include non-petroleum compounds, such as raw sewage, cooking grease by-products and yard enhancement chemicals.

The testing shows that levels at all three locations for petroleum compounds are well below levels in April, when testing began, ranging from 269 to 944 parts per billion. However, the more recent results show mixed trends.

Between Aug. 12–13 and Aug. 26, readings fell from 116 to 94.7 ppb at one site and from 96 to 60.5 ppb at the third location in the table. At the second on-base site, they rose from 67.6 to 157 ppb, similar to levels recorded in that same location in June and July.

Both the base and MDE said the results showed an overall downward trend across the locations. The elevated reading on Aug. 26 complicates that picture, but does not directly point to the faulty infrastructure at the base or indicate an active leak.

It is also unclear how to read the levels. MDE’s table lists 47 ppb as the “surface-water action level” for the fuel-related chemicals, and every numerical result in that category, including the three from Aug. 26, are above that action level.

But MDE said it judges the data against 470 ppb, a value drawn from Maryland’s groundwater cleanup standards, “because no one is drinking directly from Piscataway Creek and no drinking-water supply wells are located adjacent to the base.” The 47 ppb entry, the agency said, “is correct” and reflects the laboratory’s most conservative drinking-water benchmark, reported as received for consistency.

Six earlier sampling results exceeded the 470 ppb level, including 622 ppb in MDE’s own sample from May 18. Four of the six came from the location that showed a spike in August sampling, including 8,840 ppb JBA reported on May 18. The same day MDE recorded 622 ppb in the same location, and 1,350 ppb on July 6. MDE said the results showed the continued presence of petroleum compounds in the creek “and triggers further monitoring and investigation requirements of JBA.”

Rain also continues to be a cause for concern.

MDE said in April that the base’s contamination prevention system had failed twice early that month, when a containment dam collapsed during heavy rain. In their May letter, lawmakers wrote that initial containment measures had been insufficient during moderate rainfall until they were improved in mid-April. The Air Force subsequently told lawmakers in its June letter that the upgraded containment “successfully held fast” during an April 19 rain and subsequent storms, based on visual observations.

But an MDE inspection on Aug. 5 documented submerged underflow dams and all but one absorbent and hard boom, a barrier placed to contain the contaminated water, disconnected after the heavy rain.

The base acknowledged the failure, saying a heavy storm in early August triggered rapid flooding and the creek rose over 6 feet, which overwhelmed and displaced containment structures.

Asked directly whether petroleum escaped downstream, the base said subsequent inspections found no sheen, odors or distressed vegetation, and said the large volume of stormwater had diluted residual fuel.

The base did not identify where the vacuum-truck recovery took place or provide storm-specific chemical sampling results.

As Inside Climate News reported earlier, the spill has further imperiled the creek. In their May letter, lawmakers wrote that legacy pollution from the base had already caused PFAS contamination in Piscataway Creek. MDE noted in April that fish-consumption advisories related to PFOS, a PFAS compound, predated the spill.

The latest sampling table marks PFAS results “NA,” or not analyzed, beginning July 29 at all the three monitoring sites. MDE defended discontinuing PFAS testing, saying initial testing served as a precaution for working conditions and that PFAS was unrelated to the fuel spill. It said it had sampled the creek’s surface water for PFAS on a number of occasions and continues working with the Air Force on separate PFAS sampling and remediation plans.

Dean Naujoks, an investigator with the Potomac Riverkeeper Network, called on the EPA and MDE to take enforcement action and require remediation to address environmental contamination from the spill. “When is the EPA and the Maryland Department Environment going to bring an enforcement action against Andrews Air Force Base for this ongoing jet fuel contamination, and what are they going to do to remediate the problem?” he asked.

The agency officials said each day that fuel continues to discharge into the environment can trigger civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day, on top of any final fine for the total volume spilled into the waterway. There will ultimately be significant violations, fines, penalties and cleanup requirements, once the spill volume and duration are fully established, they said.

Meanwhile, the Air Force arranged a staff-level briefing for Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen’s office in late September, Congressional sources confirmed to Inside Climate News. The senator was not satisfied with the responses the Air Force has provided so far, they said, and his office will be requesting more information in the coming weeks.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.title: In Harrisburg, Advocates Rally for Tougher Rules on Fracking
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.author: By Marie Cusick
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/08102.text:
Environmental groups and citizens are urging Pennsylvania regulators to increase the minimum amount of protective buffer space between gas wells and homes, schools and water sources. The issue has taken on new urgency as the AI data center buildout spurs more demand for natural gas.

On Wednesday, a coalition of environmental and community groups held an event at the state capitol to draw attention to their concerns. They complain they’ve been waiting two years for the Department of Environmental Protection to move forward with a petition they filed in 2024, urging the agency to increase minimum setback requirements.

Katie Weber lives in Hanover Township, Washington County and went to Harrisburg because she’s concerned about plans to build a large cluster of data centers powered by an on-site natural gas plant near her home.

“We are united and our message is clear,” Weber said. “We do not want data centers, and we do not want fracking anywhere near our homes, our schools or our daycares.” The day before, activists argued for a three-year moratorium on data centers in another rally at the capitol.

Gov. Josh Shapiro had been an early proponent of the AI buildout in the state, but shifted his stance earlier this year as public opposition mounted. He has signed executive orders aimed at putting some limits on data centers, including having them “build, bring online, or buy incremental electric capacity” to power their facilities. The goal is for data center builders to foot the bill for the increased power demand instead of Pennsylvania ratepayers.

Environmental advocates, like Lisa Graves-Marcucci of the Environmental Integrity Project, worry Shapiro’s efforts will push data center builders to rely more heavily on natural gas to power the facilities—leading to more pollution on site and negative environmental and health impacts from increased shale gas production.

“We’ve realized now that fracking will fuel the data centers,” said Graves-Marcucci.   “Communities that already have a lot of fracking could see an increase, or communities that don’t have fracking may get some. It’s all the more reason we need these protective setback distances.”

Environmental groups argue a growing body of peer-reviewed research shows more space would provide more protection from potential health harms, including chronic stress, excessive noise and light, poor air quality, vehicle accidents, explosions and chemical spills.

Two years ago, the coalition of groups filed what’s called a petition for rulemaking with the state Department of Environmental Protection’s Environmental Quality Board— asking regulators to evaluate whether the existing setback requirements could be expanded. For example, under current law, a gas well could be 500 feet from a home.

“We are looking for a common-sense protective setback of one kilometer, which is a little over 3,000 feet,” said Gillian Graber, executive director of Protect PT, a community group for Westmoreland and Allegheny counties. “The current setback is very old and out of date.”

Their petition also calls for greater distances between gas wells and buildings serving vulnerable populations like schools or hospitals. David Hess, a former secretary of the Department of Environmental Protection, who authors a blog covering state environmental issues, views the push to increase the setbacks as reasonable.

“We’ve been shale gas drilling here in Pennsylvania for more than 20 years, and to not look at those kinds of issues, like setbacks and other things, would be a huge oversight,” Hess said. “We’ve learned a lot from these operations and how they impact people living next to them. If anyone thinks 500 feet is adequate to deal with any of the issues, I think they’re kidding themselves.”

In 2018 Colorado expanded its oil and gas well setback requirements to be 1,000 feet from schools. A 2020 grand jury report about fracking in Pennsylvania led by then Attorney General Josh Shapiro recommended 2,500 foot setbacks for buildings and 5,000 feet for schools and hospitals.

DEP spokesman Neil Shader said the agency is continuing to review the petition.

“DEP thoroughly reviews all petitions submitted, along with the other associated materials submitted with the petition, before delivering a recommendation to the EQB,” Shader wrote in an email. “This particular petition included several scientific studies, which DEP is reviewing using in-house experts (including a toxicologist) to be able to deliver a fully informed recommendation to the EQB.”

The Marcellus Shale Coalition, a natural gas industry trade group, argues the DEP lacks the legal authority to increase the setback requirements via this rulemaking petition, because those limits are already spelled out in state law, and any changes would have to go through the legislature.

Patrick Henderson, vice president of government affairs and communications at the Marcellus Shale Coalition, previously worked in Republican Gov. Tom Corbett’s administration and helped update the state’s oil and gas law in 2012, in response to the drilling boom.

“That process Governor Tom Corbett put forth was the product of an advisory commission that he appointed with environmental, industry, local government officials and academia to develop,” said Henderson. “Those setback requirements derived a lot from that input.”

Lisa Graves-Marcucci of the Environmental Integrity Project, said the environmental groups are hopeful DEP will respond to them before the end of the year.

“There is no draft rule,” she pointed out. “We’re just waiting for the formality for them to say they’ve reviewed the petition. We believe it merits the full process of rulemaking.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102.title: Compounding Climate Impacts Drive Tropical Forest Decline
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102.author: By Bob Berwyn
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102.text:
Ozone pollution from fires, along with extreme heat and drought, is further weakening the Amazon rainforest’s ability to absorb carbon dioxide, new research shows.

The Amazon and other forests absorb more than a quarter of human-caused CO2 emissions each year, more than 11 billion metric tons. But in recent decades, increasingly larger areas of forests have begun releasing more CO2 than they absorb, especially during droughts and heat waves.

One study, published Monday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, documents how smoke from wildfires, agriculture and forest-clearing burning contributes to leaf-damaging ozone formation far from the flames.

This means fires in the Amazon have a double impact on the climate. They directly release climate-warming CO2 as vegetation burns and reduce the ability of remaining trees to absorb and store CO2. The reduction is equal to about 24 percent of the carbon released by the fires.

That “hidden effect is a significant loss to the Amazon’s carbon budget that hasn’t previously been considered,” said lead author Flossie Brown, an atmospheric chemist at ETH Zürich, a university in Switzerland.

The second study, published Monday in the American Geophysical Union journal Earth’s Future, found that the extreme heat and drought that gripped the Amazon and other tropical forests in 2023 and 2024 during El Niño conditions could occur nearly every year within 20 to 30 years, cutting CO2 uptake severely and even disrupting the self-regulating forest-to-atmosphere moisture cycle.

Repeated extreme heat events can “trigger self-perpetuating rainfall losses,” warned

lead author Johanna Van Passel, an ecologist at Ghent University in Belgium. “You have this feedback loop,” she said. “If the forest is suffering, it will cause less rain to fall in other parts, and those forests will also start suffering.”

All tropical forests stayed unusually hot for an 18-month period overlapping with El Niño conditions, on average, and 80 percent of the forests were drier than average. The Amazon rainforest was particularly hard-hit. After a full two years of drought, water levels at the port of Manaus sank to the lowest level in more than a century of record-keeping. Globally, three-quarters of tropical forests endured extreme heat and drought simultaneously for an average of six months, the study found.

Even if human carbon emissions are eliminated or neutralized by 2075, extreme heat and drought will still be six times more likely across tropical regions by the end of the century than they have been over the past 25 years.

Under any higher-emissions climate scenario, the extreme, forest-damaging conditions seen in 2023 and 2024 are projected to become the annual norm across most tropical regions by the 2040s, with or without El Niño. It’s a “very striking” projection for the near future, Van Passel said.

Brown, the lead author of the ozone study, said the research offered a way to connect the often-invisible atmospheric chemistry of the atmosphere with real-world effects “that felt really relevant and important to me.”

Some of the data came from enclosed growth zones at TropOz laboratory “where we can control conditions like ozone concentration and really measure the trees,” she said. Other measurements used to understand ozone’s effects come from satellites that track vegetation reflectivity and from flux towers installed in the rainforest canopy that detect changes in the air’s chemistry.

One surprising result was that, during the 1997 to 2024 study period, there was “on the whole, a decline in ozone damage, coming from increasing CO2 concentrations,” Brown said. One reason is that, as the concentration of CO2 rises, trees can photosynthesize more efficiently, so they take up less air, and less ozone, through their stomata.

But the overall decline was outweighed by the effects of extreme events. Fires, smoke-driven ozone, drought and heat are becoming more frequent and more damaging, with impacts far greater than similar events would have had in a cooler climate.

The next cycle of extremes is already beginning, with a powerful El Niño driving drought in the region and the season for agricultural burning starting in the coming weeks.

The fires are not intended to become huge or burn the forest, but during droughts, they often escape control and release significant amounts of nitrogen oxides that can be carried distances and combine with other reactive organic molecules to form ozone.

Brown said ozone damage is just one of many pressures on the Amazon, as drought and high temperatures are “already moving the Amazon into conditions that it didn’t grow to withstand.” Limiting the damage requires changes in the way agricultural fires are managed, including using practices other than burning, and slowing deforestation and other degradation, she added.

Her biggest single concern is extreme drought. The Amazon evolved as an environment that is always wet, “and now, this isn’t the case,” she said. “A natural rainforest shouldn’t burn. It’s too wet. So even the fact that we create and see these fires that spread into the Amazon is already some kind of tipping point.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102.title: The American Livestock Industry’s Main Lobbying Group Treated Climate Change as a PR Problem
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102.author: By Georgina Gustin
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/07102.text:
In 1991, Random House published a picture book called “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: ABC’s for a Better Planet,” in which the masked cartoon turtles trade in their signature nunchucks for signs bearing environmental slogans.

For “A,” the turtles explain the sources of acid rain. Under “B,” the concept of biodegradability.

“Don’t Pollute Dudes!” the turtles exhort under “D.” They designate the letter G for “Green Power!”

Then the book reaches the letter “M”—for meat.

“A lot of the world’s cereal crop is fed to cattle, when it could be used to feed to starving people instead,” the book says. “And cattle expel methane, a gas that makes the greenhouse effect worse.” Underneath is a drawing of one of the turtles, Donatello, eating a salad.

“What can you do?” Donatello says, instructively. “How about not eating so much meat in the first place?”

This message and its potential to harness the power of early-’90s “Turtlemania” did not sit well with the meat industry. Its top lobbying group, then the National Cattlemen’s Association, now the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), publicly called for Random House to cease publication.

This example of meat industry pushback is one of many that Jennifer Jacquet, a researcher with the University of Miami, and her colleague Loredana Loy unearthed while researching the association’s influence, much of it in archives at the University of Wyoming. On Wednesday, they published a new paper in the journal PLOS Climate, in which they document a string of instances of the NCA attempting to tamp down messages and distort facts about the climate impacts of livestock, the researchers say.

“What we found in the archives really reveals the lack of concern about global warming,” Jacquet said, “and yet an incredible concern about the public’s view of the role of livestock in global warming.”

Jacquet and others have long researched the industry’s attempts to downplay its greenhouse gas emissions. Some of Jacquet’s recent research documents that the industry knew about its climate impacts long before the public became broadly aware of them, but worked to obstruct policies and campaigns meant to reduce emissions and consumption.

If those dietary or policy shifts had happened, they could have significantly lowered emissions: Jacquet and her colleagues calculated that lowering meat consumption in the United States by 50 percent per capita could have been up to 80 times more effective in reducing methane emissions than all the efforts to limit methane from the oil and gas industry over a 30-year period, starting in the early 1990s.

The latest paper adds details to the record, citing more examples of the industry’s efforts and specifically homing in on the National Cattlemen’s Association.

The NCBA did not respond to requests for an interview or for comments.

Jacquet said she wanted to look at the period immediately after 1986, when researchers published a major paper estimating the significant emissions of methane from enteric fermentation—the burps of ruminant animals. In 1988, NASA’s James Hansen famously testified about the “greenhouse effect” before a U.S. Senate subcommittee, saying that “non-CO2” gases, including methane, were also warming the atmosphere.

In the years that followed, as a new wave of environmental action arose and governments across the world started to act on climate, influential books advised people to eat less livestock-based food for both health and planetary reasons. “Diet for a New America” by John Robbins advocated a shift toward vegetarian diets and “Beyond Beef: The Rise and Fall of the Cattle Culture” by Jeremy Rifkin traced the long history of beef production, railing against intensive factory farms.
