As New York City hosted global leaders for the United Nations General Assembly last week, Washington was consumed with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit on Sept. 24. Artificial intelligence loomed large in both cities, with New York the epicenter of AI talks involving a wide range of global leaders, while Washington narrows its geopolitical lens to one bilateral relationship. The dichotomy is stark and raises a question: How would specific bilateral commitments between China and the United States impact each nation’s broader, existing foreign affairs strategy for AI?

Washington and Beijing have developed clear—and sharply divergent—diplomatic strategies to influence how other nations will develop, deploy, and govern AI systems and establish global AI leadership in the coming decades. Washington has emphasized strategic competition and American market dominance, bundling access to advanced chips, cloud services, AI models, compute power, applications, and financing into a “full-stack” AI export package that features U.S. industry and would be available to favored nations.

Beijing has promoted a vision for widespread collaboration based in AI as a development priority, with a focus on offering AI models that can be locally owned and operated, adapted for local needs, and supported by access to training and capacity building, a new multilateral AI body, and Chinese applications. Washington’s strategic partnerships have been designed to position the United States as the undisputed winner of an AI race with China. China’s partnerships have been designed to emphasize multilateral inclusion and equitable access to the benefits of AI, particularly for middle- and low-income countries.

China has been taking steps to move its foreign policy from rhetoric to practice, even though announcements still outpace implementation. On the eve of China’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in July, representatives from 29 countries signed an agreement establishing the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO) as an “independent” intergovernmental organization headquartered in Shanghai. (Additional countries are now reported to have signed on, according to Chinese media outlets.) The following day, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged 5,000 AI training and seminar opportunities for developing countries over five years. He also announced plans for international AI application centers with leading regional organizations such as BRICS, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the African Union, and the Arab League, as well as assistance for 30 countries to use China’s AI-powered Mazu meteorological early-warning system.

It remains unclear exactly how WAICO’s commitments would play out in practice. The July announcement described its status and aims but did not clarify a financing mechanism, offer a delivery structure for its commitments, or clarify how the organization’s independence would be protected and assured. It is clear that WAICO is designed to help China realize its stated AI strategy. For example, China’s July AI cooperation and development action plan called for accessible computing services for developing countries and support for adapting open AI models to local needs, a sentiment Xi echoed in his speech at the WAIC. (Open-weight models allow developers a model they can copy and adapt for their own purposes, without requiring them to train a model from scratch. This can make AI systems cheaper and more affordable and can be particularly useful for nations that need to build systems to operate across highly specific, local environments.)

Meanwhile, China’s existing cooperation with ASEAN may illustrate how regional partnerships would operate in practice: The ASEAN-China Artificial Intelligence Industry Innovation Center, inaugurated in Beijing on May 24, forms part of the two sides’ digital cooperation agenda. Its planned work pairs practical demonstrations of AI applications in sectors such as healthcare and agriculture with training for ASEAN officials, company employees, and students, connecting access to AI technologies with the skills needed to use them. With more than 3,000 exhibits from over 1,100 companies, the WAIC displayed the industrial breadth that could underpin Chinese AI applications.

Washington has begun implementing its own competing multilateral AI offer through Pax Silica, which seeks to secure the supply chains needed to build and power AI systems and has garnered support from approximately two dozen U.S. partners and allies. Efforts like the American AI Exports Program support U.S. consortia selling systems abroad, giving members priority access to federal financing and export-license processing. The departments of commerce and state have announced a range of new programs aimed at strengthening ties between American technology companies and foreign markets, including mechanisms to connect U.S. suppliers to foreign buyers, credential AI supply chains, and finance commerce-designated export packages.

While the U.S. approach offers components of an AI ecosystem strategy, no U.S. program creates a soft-power offering similar to China’s development offerings. The U.S. has also expressly rejected proposals for any form of independent multilateral body that would support broader AI governance or cooperation.

After the WAICO announcement, Washington indicated that it might even go a step further toward isolationism by positioning Pax Silica as an all-or-nothing proposition for its signatories. Reuters reported a draft letter from the State Department announcing that membership in Pax Silica “[could not] be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own.” While Reuters could not establish if or when such a letter would be sent, it did quote an unnamed U.S. official who said the letter was drafted to clarify that governments “​can’t have it both ways.”

China, meanwhile, has publicly defended countries’ right to choose AI partners according to their development needs, allowing Beijing to present its assistance as compatible with keeping other partnerships open. That stance aligns more closely with what other governments are seeking when it comes to AI. On Sept. 21, Finland and Norway, along with 19 other nations and the European Commission, issued a joint statement urging global collaboration to address emerging frontier AI risks. The signatories included members of Pax Silica, WAICO participants, and nonaligned states.

Nations are not only aligned in seeking more multilateral mechanisms; they are also aligned in their desire to avoid dependency on any individual nation’s technology stack. On Sept. 14, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde warned that reliance on foreign AI raises questions about whose laws govern sensitive data and whether access to essential services could be withdrawn or used as leverage in political negotiations. Governments weighing those risks lose nothing by increasing collaboration with Beijing, and pressure from Washington to forgo alternative partnerships and deepen dependencies on the U.S. as a technology partner seems increasingly foolhardy in a geopolitical environment where partners’ and allies’ trust in the U.S. has hit all-time lows.

Beijing may talk about safety, but its model of AI diffusion is made to go rogue.

It is hard to see how the U.S. can “win” any AI race by forcing governments around the world to choose between the two leading powers. Governments need support that fits the systems they already use and leaves them room to adopt AI on their own terms. They will want, and need, to build systems that incorporate both American and Chinese AI technologies as they seek to harness the benefits of AI transformation. They may also look for broader support than the limited offerings that the U.S. currently provides.

WAICO gives Beijing a standing organization through which it can organize this cooperation. Its appeal to partner governments is the prospect of practical help as their needs change, with membership in an institution devoted to AI development. A government could begin with one public service application and return for support adapting it to another language or extending it to other agencies. Whether WAICO can provide that assistance, and how much influence members will exercise over its priorities, remains unclear.

In addition, governments seeking to import and scale AI systems need to know whether a system will work with their data, meet local requirements, and remain affordable to operate—requirements that China has named explicitly in its technology diplomacy strategy. AI export packages that meet those needs early in adoption will secure a critical first-mover advantage for the nation (or companies) behind them.

Training programs will shape local engineers’ familiarity with specific software or hardware tools, and procurement rules built to support early purchases will determine which technologies can be deployed, how, and by whom.

First-mover advantages won’t go to the AI leader with the most cutting-edge models. It will go to the country that can best support partner nations in connecting infrastructure, models, applications, financing, capacity building, and operational standards into a coherent offering that allows leaders to scale AI adoption while maintaining their right to mix and match systems as needed.

The world is waiting to see what, if any, agreements the U.S. and China might strike on managing AI risks. For the United States, any agreement undercuts its ability to demand that partners and allies refrain from collaboration or trade with China regarding their own AI needs. For China, a stated commitment to openness and inclusion will be challenged by a singular agreement with the United States that excludes all other nations from access to critical information sharing on AI risks and safety standards. If the U.S. and China can agree to cooperate on critical AI safety risks, world leaders will breathe a collective sigh of relief. And then, with their next breath, they will ask, “Where do we come in, and what does this mean for us?”

At the moment, Beijing is far better positioned to answer that question than Washington.

Kenton Thibaut is a senior China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Democracy + Tech Initiative and the Indo-Pacific Security Initiative.

Kat Duffy is a senior fellow for digital and cyberspace policy and the director of LEAD AI at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Ethiopia’s military forces rebel fighters out of Tigray’s capital of Mekelle, Kenya confirms its first-ever recorded Ebola case, and the United States waives human rights restrictions to send military aid to Egypt.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Ethiopia’s military forces rebel fighters out of Tigray’s capital of Mekelle, Kenya confirms its first-ever recorded Ebola case, and the United States waives human rights restrictions to send military aid to Egypt.

Sign up to receive Africa Brief in your inbox every Wednesday.

A week and a half into renewed fighting in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, pro-government forces seized the Tigrayan capital of Mekelle, the country’s third-most populous city, from rebel fighters over the weekend.

The Tigray Peace Force, a militia allied with the federal government, entered Mekelle on Saturday, followed by the Ethiopian military. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) has since retreated from the city, though it said its fighters would continue to “operate from somewhere else” as they seek to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

Nearly four years after the end of a 2020-22 civil war, major conflict resumed in Tigray on Sept. 23, when the TPLF seized three airports in the region and launched attacks into the Afar and Amhara regions. It had formed an alliance with six other rebel groups a few days prior to the offensive. By the end of September, the renewed fighting had displaced an estimated 150,000 people.

While Ethiopia’s government appears to have the upper hand in the latest round of fighting, at least for now, the conflict has worsened a growing rift between Addis Ababa and regional powers.

Before the fighting, Ethiopia’s diplomatic relations with Eritrea, Egypt, and Sudan were already frosty. But the situation deteriorated last month when Ethiopia accused the three nations of backing the anti-Abiy alliance. All of them deny involvement.

“We are not party to the domestic crisis facing Ethiopia now. It has nothing to do with us,” Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told Reuters on Sunday.

Tensions are especially fraught between Ethiopia and Eritrea. On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it would close its embassy in Eritrea’s capital of Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Addis Ababa within 48 hours. This prompted Eritrea to cut all diplomatic ties, accusing Ethiopia of a three-year “agenda of incessant hostility” in order to gain “sovereign Eritrean ports and coastal areas.”

Abiy has increasingly sought access to the Red Sea via Eritrea in recent years. Ethiopia became landlocked in 1993, after Eritrea gained independence from Addis Ababa, and Abiy has repeatedly framed direct sea access as an existential pursuit for his country. “Ethiopian civilization cannot be realized without a sea outlet,” Abiy told parliament on Monday as he was sworn in for a new five-year mandate following elections in June.

Addis Ababa also ordered a senior Egyptian diplomat to leave Ethiopia on Thursday; Egypt responded by expelling a counsellor at the Ethiopian Embassy in Cairo.

Meanwhile, the leaders of all three nations, along with Somalia, held a summit in Egypt on Sunday in which they called for “peaceful solutions to conflicts” in the region, according to an official statement. They also demanded compliance with international law on waterways. (Both Egypt and Sudan harbor grievances over Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which they say restricts their water access.)

On Monday, the Ethiopian Foreign Ministry reaffirmed Addis Ababa’s “legitimate” interests in the Red Sea and the Nile basin in response to the regional summit. Political “rhetoric, coercive measures, and acts of destabilization will not alter Ethiopia’s geographic and historical realities,” it said in a statement.

For now, regional hostility is unlikely to escalate beyond rhetorical attacks, especially if the Ethiopian military can contain the fighting and Djibouti’s port remains accessible to Addis Ababa and free from Houthi attacks. (Djibouti handles around 97 percent of Ethiopia’s import and export cargo.)

With conflict ongoing in Somalia, Sudan, South Sudan, and Yemen, no party wants another war—and the subsequent economic impact—in the region.

So far, regional instability in recent years has significantly impacted Egypt in lost Suez Canal revenue. An attack against Eritrea would similarly erode Ethiopia’s double-digit growth and thwart Abiy’s foreign investment plans.

Still, there has been a lack of third-party mediation in Tigray while the Iran war has captured international attention. Without active, international diplomacy, long-simmering tensions could once again lead to widespread fears of an all-out proxy war in the Red Sea region.

Wednesday, Oct. 7: The African Union launches the Africa Credit Rating Agency in Mauritius.

Thursday, Oct. 8: The Court of Arbitration for Sport hears Senegal’s appeal against being stripped of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title.

Friday, Oct. 9: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi visits Malaysia for talks to strengthen ties with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

Monday, Oct. 12: Ethiopia starts hosting the 65th session of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

Ebola spreads. Kenya confirmed its first case of Ebola on Tuesday. A Kenyan national who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo for seven years tested positive for the virus after landing in Nairobi on Saturday. He was taken from the airport to the hospital, where he later died. Kenya’s Ministry of Health is tracing 57 other people who came into contact with him, including those on his flight.

Africa’s current Ebola epidemic, which is centered in Congo, is the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record. The Kenyan case follows new figures from the Congolese Health Ministry, which show that the outbreak had killed more than 4,000 people out of 8,500 recorded cases as of Oct. 3.

Over the weekend, France pledged to increase its funding and support for the Ebola response in eastern Congo. It also held a national humanitarian conference in Paris on Oct. 6 that aimed to draw wider international resources to containment efforts.

Fraught relations. U.S.-South Africa tensions have deepened in the wake of heated public exchanges between South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola and the U.S. ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III.

In a recent interview with South African newspaper the Sunday Times, Lamola said that Bozell should “get out of the kitchen” if he no longer believes in dialogue after the ambassador said that Washington had “run out of patience” with South Africa. “You can’t have a diplomat who says the time for talking is over,” Lamola added. Bozell responded on X, “Another Minister Lamola personal insult aimed at an American leader (this time me).”

The animosity follows Washington’s announcement last month of targeted visa restrictions against unspecified South African individuals who enact or enable discrimination against white Afrikaners. Bilateral relations have deteriorated over the past year and a half as the Trump administration has peddled false claims of a white genocide in South Africa.

In the 2026 fiscal year, the United States admitted just 13,000 refugees, compared with around 100,000 in 2024. Nearly all of those admitted in 2026 have been white South Africans.

U.S. military funds. On Thursday, the U.S. State Department waived restrictions concerning Egypt’s human rights record to release more than $300 million of military aid to Cairo. An internal memo sent to lawmakers highlighted Egypt’s “helpful role” amid the U.S. war in Iran.

The Biden administration issued a similar waiver in 2024, citing Egypt’s assistance during Israel’s war in Gaza. Egypt has received around $1.3 billion annually in U.S. military aid since the late 1980s. Seth Binder and Kristina Biyad argued in Foreign Policy in May that no U.S. administration has applied sustained pressure on Egypt, “sending a clear signal to Cairo that U.S. red lines are negotiable.”

Minerals deal backlash. The African arm of the International Trade Union Confederation has criticized a framework agreement that Abuja and Washington signed last month that aims to bring U.S. private investment to Nigeria’s critical-minerals industry.

The organization said that details about the agreement were “scanty” and that questions remained over how it would benefit Nigerians. “Nigeria cannot replace dependence on crude oil exports with dependence on exports of lithium, rare earths or other unprocessed minerals,” it said in a statement, adding, “Agreements of this strategic importance warrant legislative scrutiny.”

Following U.S. strikes against Islamist militants in Nigeria in December, some Nigerian observers questioned whether the intervention was genuinely motivated by counterterrorism, believing that it might instead be part of the Trump administration’s bid to access Nigeria’s mineral wealth. The minerals agreement has heightened those concerns.

The Alliance of Sahel States (AES), comprising Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, has launched a television channel with support from Russia. Tafouk TV, which began broadcasting on Sept. 16, seeks to counter Western media narratives about AES nations and share information about the junta-led governments’ war efforts against Islamist insurgencies.

Tafouk signed a cooperation agreement in July with RT (previously Russia Today), Moscow’s state-funded broadcaster. All three nations have largely kicked out French media outlets in recent years as they have severed diplomatic and military ties with France, their former colonizer.

Russia’s risky gambit. In Foreign Policy, Taiwo Hassan examines the shifting security dynamics in Niger following a coup attempt in August, which failed in part because of the support that Russia’s Africa Corps gave to the country’s ruling junta.

He argues that “while Russia’s strategy of regime protection has proved successful in expanding its footprint across the Sahel, it also contains the seed of its own exhaustion.”

Algeria-Tunisia ties. In the New Arab, Abdelkader Cheref argues that Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s recent pledge to protect Tunisia from external threats is an attempt to limit Emirati influence in the country that will also help shield Tunisian President Kais Saied from democratic accountability.

Both Algiers and Tunis “have stifled democracy by altering constitutions, demonising opposition, and ramping up the criminalisation of critics,” Cheref writes.

U.S. President Donald Trump stood in front of the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 22 and made two explicit threats. He threatened to use military force in Latin America in service of U.S. interests, and he threatened annihilation for both the Iranian government and the Iranian people. The actions he proposed contravene both the international laws prohibiting war and the international humanitarian law that protects civilians in conflict. What’s more, the U.N. Charter prohibits even threats of aggression, while the laws of war, themselves part of U.S. law, prohibit indiscriminate threats against a civilian population. Accordingly, Trump’s public deliberations about who to invade and who to annihilate were themselves crimes, committed in full view of thousands of diplomats and heads of state.

Ongoing reports and analysis

Trump is accustomed to asserting the primacy of force over law and clearly anticipates no punishment for doing so in front of a body dedicated to saving humanity from the scourge of war. Indeed, his administration is bent on shrinking the U.N. and dismantling the International Criminal Court (ICC)—“brick by brick, if necessary,” in the words of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

U.S. President Donald Trump stood in front of the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 22 and made two explicit threats. He threatened to use military force in Latin America in service of U.S. interests, and he threatened annihilation for both the Iranian government and the Iranian people. The actions he proposed contravene both the international laws prohibiting war and the international humanitarian law that protects civilians in conflict. What’s more, the U.N. Charter prohibits even threats of aggression, while the laws of war, themselves part of U.S. law, prohibit indiscriminate threats against a civilian population. Accordingly, Trump’s public deliberations about who to invade and who to annihilate were themselves crimes, committed in full view of thousands of diplomats and heads of state.

Ongoing reports and analysis

Trump is accustomed to asserting the primacy of force over law and clearly anticipates no punishment for doing so in front of a body dedicated to saving humanity from the scourge of war. Indeed, his administration is bent on shrinking the U.N. and dismantling the International Criminal Court (ICC)—“brick by brick, if necessary,” in the words of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The administration’s hostility to the principle and mechanisms of international legal accountability makes eminent if cynical sense in light of its many transgressions. These include, but are not limited to, the crime of enforced disappearance by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) against both U.S. citizens and foreign nationals; the deaths of people in ICE custody via neglect; the rendition of refugees and asylum-seekers to foreign prisons and hostile third countries; the bombing of civilian targets in Iran; the United States’ ongoing campaign of murder on the high seas against unspecified and unknown individuals in Latin America and the Caribbean, at least some of whom have been identified as civilians, most of whom have not been identified at all; and the dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development and its downstream consequences, which, according to epidemiological models, “has already caused the deaths of six hundred thousand people, two-thirds of them children,” and by 2030 is projected to result in more than 14 million additional deaths, a figure that includes between 4 million and 5 million deaths among children under the age of 5.

Many in the United States and around the world are desperate to see Trump and his top advisors held accountable for all this lawlessness but are at a loss for how to do so. Both the domestic power that accrues to the American president and an international balance of power dominated by U.S. military and economic might obstruct easy pathways toward justice. But there are still meaningful steps that both America’s domestic opposition and the international community can take. These steps include supporting the ICC, enabling international investigations into enforced disappearances and civilian deaths, and rebuilding America’s foreign aid architecture.

For the U.S. domestic opposition, the clearest pathway toward accountability is pledging to join the ICC when the Democratic Party takes office and vocally supporting the ICC as it is repeatedly targeted for destruction by the Trump administration. Joining the ICC, as scholars Beth Simmons and Allison Danner argue, allows states moving through violent periods to make credible commitments that human rights violators will be prosecuted. This is a strategy that helps build trust with both foreign governments and with domestic publics reeling from abuses, who do not have to trust that the government itself will hold perpetrators to account if it has bound itself to an institution that will undertake investigations and prosecutions if it does not.

A frequent U.S. argument against joining the ICC has been that U.S. domestic institutions are strong enough to impose accountability on American officials. But while lower courts in the U.S. have demonstrated their fidelity to the law, the U.S. Supreme Court has established presidential immunity as the law of the land. Joining the ICC is no bar against domestic prosecutions, since the court operates on the principle of complementarity, only beginning its work if domestic courts have indicated they cannot or will not pursue accountability.

Another common concern is that joining the ICC would increase the risk that U.S. nationals would face prosecution. But the ICC can already investigate crimes committed by Americans against foreign nationals regardless of whether the U.S. is a party to the ICC. Accordingly, joining the ICC and cooperating with its investigations would be an extra measure of good faith, and a strong way for the domestic opposition to signal it will not hold the U.S. above international law.

Foreign governments play a key role here as well. Last month, U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen argued European countries and other signatories to the ICC should sanction Rubio and Trump for obstructing the ICC’s investigations into Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. This is a classic pathway for enforcing international law: domestic opposition calling on other countries to help discipline their governments into compliance.

The Trump administration is reportedly preparing an extensive sanctions regime against the ICC, ramping up the measures that have thus far only targeted individual court officials, and ultimately forbidding most transactions with the ICC for companies, banks, and individuals. These actions would effectively collapse the court and even potentially set free those standing trial for or already convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

A formal coalition of countries has emerged to challenge Israeli violations of international law. A similar coordinated effort to diplomatically isolate the U.S. officials attempting to break the ICC will be necessary to ensure the international community’s continued ability to prosecute the highest crimes against humanity.

Pursuing prosecutions at the ICC is not the only international tool available to Americans who object to the Trump administration’s actions. The U.N.’s human rights bodies also provide avenues toward subjecting state treatment of civilians to scrutiny. Panels of independent experts and researchers operating under a multilateral mandate can investigate how governments treat those within their borders or at the receiving end of their actions. The U.S. domestic opposition can draw on these tools, and foreign governments can support them.

In 2016, for example, the U.N. General Assembly established the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism. Its mission was to “assist in the investigation and prosecution of persons responsible” for the most serious crimes against the Syrian people beginning in 2011 and gather evidence at a standard designed to facilitate thousands of prosecutions at any court that has standing to bring a case, and it was established without the involvement of the Syrian government at the time. Beyond laying the groundwork for legal accountability, investigations of this kind can also simply help people learn what happened to loved ones, with truth serving as a kind of remedy in the absence of any other.

An investigative mechanism like this one might help U.S. opposition leaders and concerned foreign governments in their quest to learn who is being murdered in the United States’ boat-bombing campaign in the Caribbean. U.N. experts have condemned the killings; highlighted the complex, multilayered nature of the violations; and said they are in touch with the U.S. government on the issue. If Democrats take the House, investigations into the campaign and the decision-making process that produces will be vital. But even absent that, congressional Democrats can partner with international experts to help determine who was killed and for what ostensible reason. Support from the international community could provide vital access and funding, as victims might be of many nationalities, and regional governments might be less likely to undertake independent investigations themselves.

                Dismantling the ICC Doesn’t Serve U.S. Interests            


    
    	The Trump administration’s campaign against the court is transparently cynical.

    Janine di Giovanni, 
    Christopher “Kip” Hale

Rodrigo Duterte’s prosecution at the International Criminal Court shows why U.S. officials should be worried.

The Trump administration’s campaign against the court is transparently cynical.

The U.N.’s standing committees on human rights can also help U.S. domestic actors to track down and repatriate the people ICE has disappeared. Civil society groups, nongovernmental organizations, reporters, and individual elected officials are doing remarkable work to try to find those who have vanished into ICE’s detention facilities. Reporters have tracked individual removal flights. Elected officials have attempted oversight of nearby detention facilities at sometimes great personal cost, and Rep. Joaquin Castro has tried to find those who have disappeared into the Dilley detention center in his district in Texas and secure their release. Some U.S. groups are already working with the U.N.’s Committee on Enforced Disappearances as part of an effort to locate those kidnapped by ICE. A coordinated effort by elected Democrats to back these tools would signal their substantive interest in addressing the harms the United States’ immigrant apparatus has inflicted.

Indeed, we can gauge the importance of these multilateral mechanisms from the steps criminal actors take to escape their oversight. When the Committee on Enforced Disappearances requested information about Venezuelan migrants the U.S. sent to CECOT in El Salvador, for example, the government of El Salvador took great pains to argue that the chain of responsibility under international law implicated only the U.S. government in crimes.

The Trump administration cannot carry out its plans without the assistance of other willing governments. These other leaders may be able to envision a world where there will be repercussions for their actions, even if Trump can’t. This makes these U.N. committees important. Both international and U.S. domestic human rights advocates can work with these international experts to build bodies of evidence that might later help establish justice or facilitate repatriation.

Finally, recommitting the U.S. to meaningful foreign aid is a mode of accountability. Nothing can bring back the lives cut short when the U.S. suddenly slashed foreign aid. The people Elon Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency betrayed weren’t passive recipients of U.S. charity, however—they were active partners in implementing international programs addressing HIV/AIDS, infant mortality, maternal mortality, food insecurity, cholera, and conflict-related death, among others. Their work warrants renewed support.

Foreign aid is not a winning electoral issue, but most voters do not make their decisions based on foreign aid, either. Accordingly, there is ample space for Democrats to build new, more just pathways for projecting power in the world. Future iterations of foreign aid will have to be more just, less sensitive to changes in U.S. leadership, and even more anchored in community-led projects and partnerships. In practice, this may mean the U.S. funding and supporting programs that are designed, led, and facilitated by local experts through long-range, multilaterally managed funds that cannot be easily terminated.

Accountability is core to building the world these partnerships promise. The Trump administration has been proceeding as though there will never be justice for its crimes and making foreign-policy decisions as though military power can substitute for reliability, consistency, and credibility. U.S. opposition leaders should act now to embrace a different path. This means pledging to join the ICC, cooperating with U.N. bodies investigating war crimes, and making plans to restore U.S. foreign aid. These measures will signal that the United States still seeks to be a good international partner and hold the Trump administration accountable for slashing foreign aid, abusing human rights, and threatening war.

This post is part of FP’s ongoing coverage of the Trump administration. Follow along here.

Anjali Dayal is an assistant professor of international politics at Fordham University. She is also a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Institute for Women, Peace, and Security.

In 1957, Washington went all-in on the development and production of intercontinental nuclear missiles for fear that Moscow was pulling ahead in the arms race. Using estimates of what Soviet factories could produce, the U.S. Air Force projected that the Soviet Union was on track to possess 500 intercontinental missiles by 1960—hundreds more than the United States planned to deploy.

Decades later, Washington’s approach to the race in artificial intelligence rests on a similar logic: If U.S. labs do not double down, China will pull ahead and be the first to reach the holy grail of artificial general intelligence—that is, cognitive abilities that match or go beyond human abilities. Maybe. In the 1950s, the U.S. count of Soviet missiles ended up being wrong. This time, Washington could be measuring the wrong thing altogether with its focus on technological benchmarks. Beijing instead measures the success of its AI rollout in terms of adoption and diffusion across its economy and beyond. This has a key safety implication: Beijing’s version of the AI rollout has no off switch.

In 1957, Washington went all-in on the development and production of intercontinental nuclear missiles for fear that Moscow was pulling ahead in the arms race. Using estimates of what Soviet factories could produce, the U.S. Air Force projected that the Soviet Union was on track to possess 500 intercontinental missiles by 1960—hundreds more than the United States planned to deploy.

Decades later, Washington’s approach to the race in artificial intelligence rests on a similar logic: If U.S. labs do not double down, China will pull ahead and be the first to reach the holy grail of artificial general intelligence—that is, cognitive abilities that match or go beyond human abilities. Maybe. In the 1950s, the U.S. count of Soviet missiles ended up being wrong. This time, Washington could be measuring the wrong thing altogether with its focus on technological benchmarks. Beijing instead measures the success of its AI rollout in terms of adoption and diffusion across its economy and beyond. This has a key safety implication: Beijing’s version of the AI rollout has no off switch.

Today, China lags behind in frontier AI but not by much. Since 2023, all frontier models have been American, but the best Chinese models, such as Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8 Max, and GLM-5.3, are just a few months behind the leading U.S. ones, according to Epoch AI. For U.S. labs, that is fuel to advance faster. The idea that the United States is still ahead rests on a single premise—that the decisive battleground for AI is the frontier. China, however, may well be running another race.

Whereas the U.S. AI ecosystem fixates on top-notch models, Beijing likes to see AI a bit like the internet: a technology to embed in the economy and means to an end. In August 2025, China released its “AI Plus” action plan, borrowing its name from the 2015 “Internet Plus” plan. This blueprint makes for an enlightening read. While Washington focuses on the supply side—chips, data centers, and frontier models—Beijing treats AI as a tool to achieve broader long-term objectives, such as boosting manufacturing productivity, tackling a dire demographic outlook, supporting innovation, and fostering the diffusion of Chinese technology standards abroad. The plan targets a “penetration rate”—whatever that means—of 70 percent for AI agents and smart devices by 2027 and 90 percent by 2030.

At home, China’s AI plan rests on three pillars. The first is collecting industrial data. In 2020, Beijing formally designated data as a factor of production in a bid to make the most of the data points that Chinese factories, logistics networks, and smart cities generate. China’s bet is simple: Crunching all of this data with AI at scale—using small-scale, specialized models that operate far from the frontier—will boost production, further cementing China’s standing as the world’s top manufacturing power. Work on this front is already underway. In March, for example, a U.S. congressional commission reported that a firm in Guangdong was using data from intelligent cameras to feed into an AI model that improved quality inspection, saving the company more than $140,000 per year.

The second pillar involves developing industrial applications for AI. U.S. consultancy IDC estimates that nearly half of China’s industrial firms had deployed specialized models or agents by mid-2025. That data is from more than a year ago—an eternity in the AI world—suggesting that the share of Chinese firms using AI is likely to be even higher now. Looking ahead, Beijing has even bigger goals. In January, China announced that it was aiming for 1,000 industrial AI agents, 500 application scenarios, and 1,000 showcase firms by 2027. Again, the focus is on applying AI widely and quickly, rather than top-notch benchmarks.

The final pillar is embodied AI—physical robots controlled by AI models. On this front, the latest annual report of the International Federation of Robotics is sobering. Last year, Chinese firms installed 354,000 industrial robots, more than all other countries combined. According to data from MERICS, China also produced 12,800 humanoid robots last year, about 90 percent of the worldwide total. It is not far-fetched to imagine that many of these robots could soon take orders from AI models that learn from their own factories’ data.

Abroad, China’s AI strategy relies on developers adopting Chinese models because they are cheap and good enough for many use cases. Crucially, Chinese AI models are often “open-weight,” meaning that their core parameters are available for anyone to download, fine-tune, and run on their own server. U.S. firms such as Meta and Nvidia release open-weight models, too, but Chinese ones are proving much more popular. According to OpenRouter, seven of the nine most popular AI models in mid-September were Chinese. This popularity fuels a self-reinforcing cycle. When firms download China’s AI models to build on them, they absorb Chinese technical assumptions and help make them industry standards. This further fuels the diffusion of Chinese AI tools.

This fast and wide diffusion has critical implications for the AI safety debate. The U.S. conversation about AI safety focuses on creating a kill switch if things go wrong. Closed U.S. models come with such a panic button because they run on their makers’ servers. In June, for example, Anthropic suspended global access to frontier models Mythos 5 and Fable 5 in order to comply with the U.S. government’s sudden imposition of export controls. In July, U.S. Reps. Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran introduced the AI Kill Switch Act in the House, and in September, Sen. John Kennedy’s AI Emergency Button Act reached the Senate floor before stalling. Both would require developers to design ways to shut down AI models. The proposals also highlight growing concern about recursive self-improvement, or AI’s ability to self-improve and autonomously create new, more powerful models.

The catch is that these safety debates are irrelevant in the Chinese AI ecosystem. No developer can recall every single copy of an open-weight model that runs in thousands of Chinese factories or on servers across the globe. In August, Chinese AI lab Zhipu held off on publishing the weights of GLM-5.3 for two weeks because of concerns about the model’s cybercapabilities. The company knew that there would be nothing left to recall once the weights were out. Since the weights were finally released later that month, developers have downloaded GLM-5.3 more than 1.4 million times on the Hugging Face platform.

Developers have put these downloads to good use: In just over a month, they released some 80 variants of GLM-5.3. Most such versions tweak the model so it runs faster or on less powerful servers. Others are more intriguing; just a few days after Zhipu released GLM-5.3’s weights, a developer posted a version—billed as a security-research tool—that removes the model’s safety guardrails. Even flagship U.S. firms are not shying away from getting their hands on Chinese models and rejiggering them. U.S. chipmaker Nvidia published a compressed version of GLM-5.3 that optimizes disk space and memory use.

Cutting-edge U.S. models are too expensive for much of the world.

The issue goes deeper: Nobody can see what users do with open weights once a user stores them on their own computer. The AI safety incidents that are making the news, such as the recent hack of Australia’s Medicare statistics portal by OpenAI agents, are public largely because they involved closed models that record interactions. In November 2025, Anthropic announced that it had reason to believe that a Chinese state-sponsored group had used Claude Code against roughly 30 global targets. (Some experts questioned Anthropic’s account, noting that sophisticated attackers would never use a closed-source model from a U.S. firm that logs all messages instead of using an open-weight model that evades such detection.)

In 1961, the U.S. panic over Soviet intercontinental missiles came to an end after Washington finally found a way to actually count them, thanks to the new Corona spy satellites. At 25 at most, the count of Soviet intercontinental missiles was no higher than the United States’. The problem today is that no satellite can track China’s AI successes if they hinge on widespread diffusion into factories and onto foreign servers, regardless of where the models stand compared with the technological frontier. China’s AI advances could well be as invisible as they are hard to stop. Washington may have to rethink what the global AI race really looks like.

Agathe Demarais is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a senior policy fellow on geoeconomics and technology at the European Council on Foreign Relations, a visiting professor at the College of Europe, a former global forecasting director at the Economist Intelligence Unit, and the author of Backfire: How Sanctions Reshape the World Against U.S. Interests. Bluesky: @agathedemarais.com

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: China opens a new military base in Laos; a rumor that Trump will attend the next ASEAN summit spreads; and the hairy rhinos of Sumatra are expecting babies.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: China opens a new military base in Laos; a rumor that Trump will attend the next ASEAN summit spreads; and the hairy rhinos of Sumatra are expecting babies.

What Does China’s New Military Base in Laos Mean?

China has established a military base in Laos. It is its third overseas military base and its second in Southeast Asia; the other two are in Cambodia and Djibouti.

The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy are situated at an airport about 30 miles from Laos’s capital, Vientiane, according to an announcement last week from Beijing’s Defense Ministry.

Satellite imagery shows that work started last year, according to Reuters. This will be China’s first overseas air force base.

The ministry said that the facilities exist to help Laos train its air force pilots. Data on the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force is sketchy, but open-source intelligence firm Janes reckons that it operates five SAIC LE500 basic trainers and four Yakovlev Yak-130UTS advanced jet trainers.

China’s global military presence is dwarfed by that of the United States. But in 2017, it opened its first acknowledged overseas military base, a logistics base in Djibouti, where it has a permanent presence.

In 2025, it opened a joint training and support center at Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, located on the Gulf of Thailand. However, Cambodia has insisted that there are no permanently stationed Chinese personnel or warships based there. And vessels from other navies, including the U.S. Navy, have visited Ream.

If China now develops a meaningful presence in Laos, what does this change?

China-focused military commentator Rudy Lu suggested that the base would allow China to shape Laos’s air force and encourage Laos to purchase Chinese equipment. The base could also be used in annual joint aviation drills with Thailand. The commentator quoted a Chinese military analysis account that said this would make the training “closer to actual combat.” Last and not least, the account said the base could let China “exert influence in the Indochina Peninsula in the future.”

Vietnam will likely be most concerned, as it has long viewed Indochina as its backyard, not China’s. In 1978, it invaded Cambodia to topple the pro-China Khmer Rouge government. When China then invaded Vietnam in 1979, Laos vocally backed Vietnam.

Now, though, China has—at the least—a peripatetic presence in both countries, in addition to its growing bases in the South China Sea. In a crisis, this could give China serious leverage over Vietnam, Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told Bloomberg.

Taiwan is also concerned. In the event of conflict over the South China Sea or Taiwan, the base could help China intercept U.S. Air Force assets flying across Indochina from their Diego Garcia base in the Indian Ocean, said Su Tzu-yun, a defense expert at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, in an interview with the Taipei Times.

However, a number of experts have suggested that the base might not add much to the power projection capabilities already provided by military bases in southern China.

The only government to comment thus far has been Thailand. It is a U.S. treaty ally and has a long border with Laos, but it also cultivates warm ties with its neighbor and with China.

A Thai Defense Ministry spokesperson told Reuters that Thailand is a close partner of both Laos and China and that the former had a sovereign right to decide to host a Chinese base.

“Nevertheless, Thailand will ​continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter ​proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” he ⁠added.

Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, who visited Laos just before the opening of the base was announced, told media that the United States had warned Thailand in advance, but that Thailand could not interfere. He had not raised the issue with Laos during his visit but said he would at a later date.

Sihasak also said that the growing involvement of superpowers in the region made Thailand more important, as Bangkok “does not choose sides.”

Myanmar nationals deported. Myanmar Navy vessels carrying 1,476 Myanmar nationals deported from Malaysia docked at Thanlyin port, near Yangon, on Sunday.

Footage from AFP showed the returnees wearing shirts emblazoned, in English, with the phrases “I [heart] Myanmar” and “Happy Voyage Back to Motherland.”

The returnees were the first batch of the 5,000 migrants that Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that Myanmar has agreed to take. It was unclear if any of those returnees included minority Muslim Rohingya, who were subject to a genocide at the hand of Myanmar military.

A Myanmar Foreign Ministry official told The Associated Press that only “genuine citizens” were repatriated. Myanmar’s junta has denied that Rohingya are citizens, instead claiming that they are illegal immigrants from Bangladesh.

Regardless, the United Nations has raised concerns that Myanmar is not a safe country to return migrants to.

Malaysia, however, has insisted that these are all voluntary repatriations, with persons held in immigration detention facilities agreeing to go home. But conditions in said facilities are grim.

These arrivals are part of a wider deportation push by Malaysia and other countries in the region. More than 8,000 migrants have been returned from Malaysia by air this year and nearly 2,000 have returned from Cambodia, according to Myanmar state media.

Rising anti-immigrant sentiment has helped shift Malaysia from a resolute opponent of the Myanmar junta within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to seeking an accommodation in the name of facilitating deportations.

Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing is due to visit Malaysia later this month.

Cabinet reshuffle. On Thursday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto launched a major reshuffle of his cabinet, his seventh and largest to date since he took office nearly two years ago. This comes on the heels of Prabowo appointing his third finance minister last month.

The move looks like an attempt by Prabowo to both inject some technocratic competence into the system in the form of veteran bureaucrats to cement his power.

Foreign Minister Sugiono, a young protégé of Prabowo widely seen as failing to handle his brief, was kicked upstairs to become coordinating minister for human development and cultural affairs. He has been replaced by veteran diplomat Arrmanatha Nasir.

This move somewhat parallels how former Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, an experienced economist but also a political outsider seen as Prabowo’s man, was replaced by powerful bureaucrat Suahasil Nazara in September.

Politics saw police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo given a pointless promotion to become the head of the presidential office. Listyo was a loyalist of former President Joko Widodo. He served in Surakarta when Widodo was mayor there, and his national ascent tracked Widodo’s.

Replacing him is Suyudi Ario Seto, the former head of the national narcotics agency, who was also a province police commander in Banten in 2024, when the gubernatorial election swung dramatically in favor of a pro-Prabowo candidate.

Suyudi has hit the ground running, replacing all regional police chiefs on the island of Java.

Trump to ASEAN summit? U.S. President Donald Trump is planning to attend the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines, which runs Nov. 16-18, according to an exclusive from the South China Morning Post (SCMP). These may then be followed by bilateral talks with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. First lady Melania Trump may also join him, and I will be there too.

The trip would dovetail with Trump’s planned attendance of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, which runs Nov. 18-19.

SCMP reported that Southeast Asian countries including the Philippines had been lobbying Trump to come, hoping that it would signal U.S. commitment to region. Trump did attend the second of last year’s ASEAN summits in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and the summit in Manila in 2017.

Since SCMP reported this, there has been no other official information confirming or denying the story.

Since Trump’s ascendancy to the White House, U.S. standing in Southeast Asia has declined sharply. The last ASEAN conference, in Cebu, Philippines, was dominated by the still-ongoing energy shock unleashed by Trump’s Iran war.

Egy Vikri of Indonesia celebrates with the FIFA ASEAN Cup trophy after the team’s victory in the FIFA ASEAN Cup final between Indonesia and Thailand at Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Oct. 5.Robertus Pudyanto/FIFA via Getty Images

Congratulations to Indonesia on their Monday night victory over Thailand in the final for the first FIFA ASEAN Cup, hosted in Gelora Bung Karno Main Stadium in Jakarta.

A slow nil-nil game took a sudden dramatic turn with a Thai player sent off in the 80th minute. The subsequent Indonesian free kick deflected off a Thai player Iklas Sanron for a goal. But Thailand swiftly equalized with a screamer from none other than Iklas.

Thailand then drew ahead with a goal in extra time, but Indonesia swiftly equalized. The game settled on penalties, where Indonesia won 4-2.

FP’s Most Read This Week

How the Trump administration got the pro-MAGA head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar out of jail, and what might it mean for U.S.-Myanmar relations, by Gabriele Steinhauser, Alexander Ward, and Patricia Kowsmann in the Wall Street Journal.

Why leave an oil-rich sultanate to pick bananas in Australia? Asif Ullah Khan looks at the problem of Brunei’s unemployed youth in the Diplomat.

The “Land of Smiles” is feeling fed up with badly behaved foreigners. Patpicha Tanakasempipat takes a look at Thailand’s tourism industry for Bloomberg.

In Focus: Sumatran Rhino Double Pregnancy

On Sunday, the Indonesian government announced that two Sumatran rhinos, the world’s most endangered rhino species, had fallen pregnant. Ratu and her daughter Delilah, residents of the Way Kambas National Park on the island of Sumatra, are both due to give birth in May next year.

Just 34 to 47 Sumatran rhinos are thought to still be alive in the wild, spread through four isolated populations.

The world’s smallest rhino is solitary by nature, living in dense tropical forests. Covered with long hair, they are the closest living relative of the woolly rhinos of the Ice Age.

The population may have long been small. Genomic research suggests that changing climate and rising seas meant that 9,000 years ago, the population may have already fallen to just 900 breeding individuals and remained low since.

But in the 19th and 20th centuries, the species still ranged into the Asian mainland, including Malaysia, Thailand, Myanmar, eastern India, and Bhutan. However, poaching and habitat loss have devastated its numbers.

Now only isolated pockets remain in Sumatra and Borneo. The latter island is home to the Bornean rhino, a subspecies thought to be extinct before being rediscovered in 2016. Two Bornean females in captivity are now being subjected to an attempt at in vitro fertilization via semen from a Sumatran male.

This, plus the breeding facility in Sumatra, represent a last-ditch effort to keep the species alive. Happily, there has been no evidence of this rhino species being poached in more than a decade.

Meanwhile, the Javan rhino is in a perilous state. Its range—which once encompassed Java, Sumatra, and mainland Southeast Asia—has been reduced to a tiny pocket in western Java.

In 2025, it was reported that its numbers had dropped by more than a third, from 76 to 50, after a wave of poaching. The poachers were eventually arrested.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Jakarta. X: @rachman_joseph

Whatever happens in the coming months, the prospects for a lasting peace between the United States and Iran are dim.

Iran’s nuclear program, missile and drone arsenal, and proxy groups still stand; control of the Strait of Hormuz remains contested; and perhaps most important, Russian and Chinese support is facilitating a rapid Iranian reconstitution. Meanwhile, the war has exposed fundamental vulnerabilities in the United States’ Middle East posture and munitions inventories, and U.S. forces have exited the conflict exhausted and depleted.

Whatever happens in the coming months, the prospects for a lasting peace between the United States and Iran are dim.

Iran’s nuclear program, missile and drone arsenal, and proxy groups still stand; control of the Strait of Hormuz remains contested; and perhaps most important, Russian and Chinese support is facilitating a rapid Iranian reconstitution. Meanwhile, the war has exposed fundamental vulnerabilities in the United States’ Middle East posture and munitions inventories, and U.S. forces have exited the conflict exhausted and depleted.

The White House and Department of Defense should expect a more difficult Iran in the months ahead.

In seven months, Iran has validated the utility of its drone and missile arsenal, successfully driven a wedge between Israel and its Arab neighbors, and degraded U.S. forces. Simultaneously, Iran’s mines, small boats, drones, and missiles have largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, holding global energy markets hostage. Rather than isolate Iran from Russia and China, the conflict appears to have only increased their defense industrial cooperation. Buoyed by these successes and motivated to deter future U.S. and Israeli interventions, Iran has every incentive to reconstitute its missile and drone arsenal, learn from this war, and continue its bid for regional dominance.

The question for the United States is therefore not just how to end the current conflict, but how to avoid a new disaster that dwarfs the losses and damage of recent months. We recently ran two war games exploring what a future round of fighting might look like. The results were grim. An honest appraisal suggests that Washington must change its approach to missile and drone defense in the region or risk major losses.

Set in late 2027, our war game was based on a scenario in which an Israeli attempt to “mow the grass” sparked a new round of fighting. By this point, both Russia and China had helped rebuild and upgrade Iran’s drone and missile arsenal—an activity already underway—and Iran had incorporated Russian strike tactics to make its attacks more deadly. In other words, the Islamic Republic had more offensive tools and a sharper sense of how to use them.

We also assumed that at this point the U.S.-led regional coalition possessed more numerous and advanced drone defenses. More generously, we assumed that U.S. and regional actors had replenished their Patriot, THAAD, SM-3, and SM-6 stockpiles (a process that will likely take until at least 2029), and that they were able to rapidly reposition defenses as the crisis boiled into conflict.

Despite these optimistic assumptions, things still ended badly for the U.S. side. In both war games, the Red team (Iran and its proxies) inflicted substantial initial damage on its chosen targets. One Red team retaliated against U.S. military bases, while the other focused on Israeli critical infrastructure and air bases. In both scenarios, ballistic missiles cratered runways while drones and cruise missiles targeted warehouses, fuel, aircraft, and air defense radars, rendering U.S. bases inoperable. Israeli air bases were temporarily closed, though extensive hardening limited the damage. Red also launched hundreds of ballistic missiles and drones at Israel’s electric grid and a desalination facility, knocking out power and forcing water rationing.

Strains on the U.S. inventory were no less significant. In both games, the Blue team expended hundreds of its high-end Patriot, THAAD, and Standard Missile interceptors, rapidly depleting newly restored supplies in just days. Counter-drone systems occasionally offered useful point defenses, with air-launched APKWS rockets from defensive counterair patrols offering the most flexible drone protection. But even these improved capabilities were overwhelmed by Iran’s layered, multiwave drone and missile salvos.

A major insight that emerged from our war games was the dangerous potential for Iran to increase the scale of its attacks while focusing on a handful of targets. After the first few days of the 2026 war, Iran launched an average of 30 to 50 missiles and 100 drones a day, spread across the region. In sharp contrast, the Red teams in our war game typically fired 150 to 300 weapons at just one target. Larger salvos, concentrated on fewer targets, exhausted defenders’ ready interceptors and delivered scores more missiles and drones before batteries could be reloaded. Red’s inventories were large enough to sustain attacks of this size and scale continuously for weeks—if not months—while Blue only had several reloads’ worth of missile defense interceptors and struggled to destroy Iran’s dispersed mobile launchers.

This threat is not far-fetched, and the United States’ current approach will not be enough to counter it. Despite significant effort, U.S. industry cannot replace the high-end missile interceptors fired in the 2026 war fast enough to be ready for a near-future conflict. Should full-scale fighting resume against a reconstituted Iran in the near term, coalition forces will run out of Patriot, THAAD, and Standard Missile interceptors in days, not weeks. Though offensive counterattacks are sometimes seen as a solution, “shooting the archer” has proved difficult: Combined U.S. and Israeli offensive airpower has failed to totally eliminate the Iranian drones and missiles that hold the Middle East at risk. Moreover, U.S. aircraft increasingly operate from distant bases in Jordan, Israel, and beyond to limit their vulnerability to attack, making it even harder to hunt for small, mobile Iranian launchers.

The fight has offered Iran and other adversaries a clear picture of U.S. weaknesses.

To prevent this scenario from becoming a reality, several things need to change.

Most glaring, the Gulf needs a more integrated sensing and shooting network. With only minutes to react to Iranian drone and missile salvos, early detection buys critical time to communicate and avoid mistakes. The United States has historically taken a leadership role in intelligence-sharing among Gulf countries, but it faces challenges from partners’ hesitation to participate and share information. The time has come to break these silos and unlock increased air domain awareness over the Persian Gulf.

Equally important, the United States and its regional partners not only need more air defense interceptors, but also a more selective approach to using them. Highly capable PAC-3 missiles have become stopgap tools in the absence of more cost-effective solutions. But this is not a sustainable arrangement. These missiles should be conserved for high-end threats and not fired at drones except when the intended target is of sufficiently high value. Deploying a more robust and layered set of interceptors will help ensure that high-end missiles can be used more selectively. This, in turn, also requires fielding more cost-effective drone and cruise missile defenses. Senior Pentagon leaders must develop, test, procure, and deploy new systems as quickly as possible.

Finally, Washington must make its regional assets harder to find and destroy. This requires hardening bases, deploying decoys, and dispersing assets in order to complicate Iranian targeting. Economic infrastructure will likewise require greater redundancy and resilience, including by embedding spare capacity and burying key assets, so that commercial hubs can absorb future strikes without halting operations. With Washington facing long lead times for interceptor deliveries, these forms of passive defense are particularly important in the short term.

U.S. efforts to deter and defend against a future Iran will ultimately depend on a larger strategic question: What should U.S. objectives and posture in the Middle East be? The United States cannot be everywhere, and some bases within range of numerous short-range Iranian weapons may be indefensible. The White House and Congress must measure these emerging risks and decide whether American forces will simply defend transportation and sea lines, or whether they will also defend and deter against future attacks on regional allies. These questions directly weigh on the types of air defenses the United States needs and how urgently they are needed.

War games are not predictive, but they provide a safe environment to fail and learn. If the United States does not reevaluate its approach to air defenses in the Middle East, it will risk catastrophic losses in the future. The question for U.S. leaders now is whether they can adapt before time runs out.

Stacie Pettyjohn is a senior fellow and director of the defense program at the Center for a New American Security.

Philip Sheers is an associate fellow in the defense program at the Center for a New American Security.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/06/sau.author: Alexandra Sharp
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/06/sau.text:

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at joint efforts to counter Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the potential future of nuclear weapons in Lithuania, and espionage allegations against a former German spy chief.

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey triggered a mutual defense pact on Monday in response to repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure. The joint deterrence measures, which appear to include the “rapid deployment” of Pakistani and Turkish troops to the Persian Gulf kingdom, mark the first time that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement has been invoked since it was signed in August.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at joint efforts to counter Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the potential future of nuclear weapons in Lithuania, and espionage allegations against a former German spy chief.

Sign up to receive World Brief in your inbox every weekday.

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey triggered a mutual defense pact on Monday in response to repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure. The joint deterrence measures, which appear to include the “rapid deployment” of Pakistani and Turkish troops to the Persian Gulf kingdom, mark the first time that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement has been invoked since it was signed in August.

The Houthis have yet to comment on the activation of the mutual defense pact.

Under the trilateral, NATO-style agreement, “any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” Although military cooperation among the three Sunni Muslim-majority nations is nothing new, the timing of the pact’s creation was particularly notable, as it came less than one month after Yemen’s Houthi rebels began launching attacks on Saudi Arabia.

In recent weeks, fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government has only worsened. Houthi forces seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait, and targeted critical energy infrastructure and Muslim holy sites in Saudi Arabia. This week, the Houthis also claimed to have launched attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Aramco-associated Petro Rabigh refinery, and other locations.

In response, Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen launched a counteroffensive on Monday in an effort to retake the coastal territory. Yemeni officials said the forces successfully recaptured several key towns near Bab el-Mandeb.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has doubled down on the defense of its own territory by bringing Pakistan and Turkey further into the fold. A joint statement released by the three countries following Monday’s emergency meeting in Riyadh did not explicitly name the Houthis as the rationale for activating the pact, though it did cite recent attacks on the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

It is unclear to what extent Islamabad and Ankara will aid Riyadh. The trio announced on Monday that they will “move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.”

However, Pakistan said it will not release the details of its deployment, though Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said on Monday that Islamabad and Ankara were already aiding Riyadh in a “supporting role,” including in the form of reconnaissance. And the Turkish parliament has yet to ratify the mutual defense pact.

Still, even the threat of joint involvement could dramatically shift the Saudi-Houthi conflict. The members of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement boast a combined military strength of nearly 1.4 million active troops. That doesn’t include their 3,400 aircraft, 6,000 tanks, and more than 340 naval assets. Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority nation in the world, and Turkey has NATO’s second-largest armed forces.

Risks of new escalation. Lithuania’s parliament voted in favor of a constitutional amendment on Tuesday that would lift a ban on nuclear weapons being stationed on the country’s soil. “With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” opposition leader Laurynas Kasciunas said. “Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of all deterrence, this decision is strategically important,” he added. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas echoed that rationale, arguing that if “Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions that we are having today.”

Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution prohibits the country from hosting nuclear weapons or foreign military bases on its territory. Tuesday’s amendment would only reverse the nuclear weapons ban, though U.S. President Donald Trump has recently proposed building a U.S. military base in Lithuania. Two ballots are required to pass for any change to take effect; the second vote is scheduled for Jan. 12.

Moscow did not take the news lightly. On Tuesday, Russia warned Lithuania that altering Article 137 to allow for nuclear weapons or a NATO base deployment would spark greater conflict in the region. “Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday. “On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions.”

Espionage allegations. German police arrested former spy chief August Hanning on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason, and working as a secret service agent. It is unclear which foreign government German authorities believe that Hanning allegedly helped. A former chief of staff to one of Hanning’s successors was also arrested on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state.” Germany’s federal prosecutor’s office alleges that the man, identified only as Manfred D., provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 government documents, many of which were classified, in the years after Hanning had left his post.

Hanning served as the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, from 1998 to 2005, after which he worked for the Federal Interior Ministry and eventually moved into the private sector as a consultant. He is the first former head of Germany’s intelligence agency to be accused of espionage. Hanning, who has denied the allegations, and Manfred D. are expected to appear before a judge later this week; Manfred D. has yet to comment on the charges.

Tuesday’s revelations come amid another scandal for Hanning. Evidence of the spy chief’s alleged actions was only discovered during a separate, unrelated investigation into a German steakhouse heiress who is on trial for the attempted kidnapping of her children from her estranged husband. Prosecutors in that case allege that Hanning helped connect the woman to the Israeli spy firm that is accused of carrying out the abduction; Hanning has denied any involvement in the kidnapping. His work as a consultant has also come under scrutiny in the past.

Growing Ebola outbreak. Kenya recorded its first case of Ebola on Tuesday, expanding the deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo into East Africa. According to local authorities, the man—a Kenyan national who had lived in Congo for the past seven years—became ill last month, traveled into Uganda via road, and then flew to Nairobi on Saturday. He died at a private hospital in the Kenyan capital late Monday.

Congo confirmed its first case of Ebola’s rare Bundibugyo strand on May 15. Since then, more than 8,400 cases have been reported, making this year’s outbreak the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in the country’s history. Already, Ebola deaths in Congo have surpassed 4,000. Uganda and France have also recorded Ebola cases, though only three deaths have been confirmed outside of Congo—the third being this week’s incident in Kenya.

Congo’s neighbors have implemented strict travel restrictions to prevent the virus’s spread. Uganda closed its border with Congo in May, and Kenya has required all travelers from Congo to fill out an online questionnaire about their potential exposure and health status before being granted entry. This week’s case in Nairobi “underscores the importance of sustained preparedness across the region,” the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement.

This year’s Nobel Prize in physics went to Francis Halzen on Tuesday for his work pioneering a new type of astronomy known as neutrino astronomy. In the late 1980s, Halzen conceptualized using light sensors embedded deep within the South Pole’s ice to detect high-energy neutrinos originating from the distant cosmos. That work eventually led to the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, where Halzen and more than 400 researchers from around the world use the information from the telescope to understand more about the inner workings of phenomena such as supermassive black holes.
