Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

It’s Golden Week, China’s fall national holiday period, so as the Chinese public heads to Southeast Asia for vacation or simply enjoys a break from work, we’re doing one of our periodic deep dives.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

It’s Golden Week, China’s fall national holiday period, so as the Chinese public heads to Southeast Asia for vacation or simply enjoys a break from work, we’re doing one of our periodic deep dives.

This week, we’re talking about childbirth in China—and how social stress and family pressures contribute to one of the world’s lowest birth rates.

Sign up to receive China Brief in your inbox every Tuesday.

Fertility almost always declines as countries get richer, but China has seen one of the sharpest drops of any nation, especially since 2017.

It’s a credit to public stubbornness that during many of the one-child policy years, from 1979 to 2015, the average Chinese couple had close to two kids anyway. Now that the government wants them to have two, the average couple has only one. It was a shock to officials that loosening the policy to two children in 2015 and then to three in 2021 produced no uptick in births.

Commentary tends to focus on cost: China is the second-most expensive place in the world to raise a child. The biggest expenses come later, when education costs soar. The government tried to solve this problem by banning private K-12 tutoring in 2021, but that only created a gray market where parents pay even more for tutors.

Yet in talking to Chinese parents, I’ve found that pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care are major reasons why having a kid is a one-and-done choice for most.

First, there’s the career cost for women. On paper, China has generous, universal maternity leave. (Paternity leave is much shorter and exists only as a patchwork of local rules.) But because of weak enforcement and widespread informal employment, many women do not or cannot take it—particularly those without a college degree.

Even urban, professional women face a real risk of being replaced or sidelined in their careers after having children. Gender discrimination is illegal in China, but firms regularly advertise men-only roles or say that they will hire only married women who already have children. Government messaging on the topic, which has sometimes stressed that child-raising is women’s natural role, has only made matters worse.

This gap between policy and reality follows women into the delivery room. The price of childbirth in Chinese public hospitals is supposed to be low, and the government is pushing to make it free. But the medical system is rife with graft, and parents usually have to pay bribes at every stage of the birthing process.

China’s cesarean section rate, like that of many countries, is far above the 10 percent to 15 percent that the World Health Organization considers normal, reaching an overall rate of 44.5 percent in 2020. One of the reasons why doctors push C-sections is because parents are expected to pay more in bribes and the hospital can bill more; during anti-corruption campaigns, the C-section rate drops significantly.

The birth experience in China is also very old-fashioned. Parents have little say in medical decisions, mothers are often treated like children by hospital staff, and fathers are rarely allowed in the delivery room. Follow-up on issues such as postpartum depression is minimal, and family members are expected to care for the new mother—even in the hospital.

That family presence is a primary source of stress for many Chinese parents. Grandparents are widely expected to move in and help, and when they live nearby, this can be a great support. But many young couples live far from their hometowns, and having parents or in-laws sleeping on the sofa in a one-bedroom apartment can be very stressful for the parents and a considerable burden on the grandparents.

That’s compounded by the near-universal insistence on “sitting the month,” a roughly 30-to-40-day postpartum confinement for mothers. Once common worldwide, the practice protected new mothers from the strain and disease exposure of agricultural work. Since the 1950s, medical advice has tended against it because it increases the risk of problems such as postpartum depression and deep vein thrombosis.

In China, however, the 1980s brought a revival of this practice, largely because it was often banned under Mao Zedong and women were forced back into the fields soon after giving birth. Women of that generation tend to blame their own health problems on not having been able to rest during this time and passed that belief down to their daughters, along with even stricter rules.

Young urban middle-class families are also encouraged to hire a live-in nurse for this month, which is both expensive and adds yet another person to a crowded home. I know families where the new parents, both sets of grandparents, and a nurse were crammed into a small Beijing apartment.

Surrogacy is banned in China but increasingly common anyway. There are ongoing attempts to legalize it, especially since babies born via surrogate can have trouble getting a hukou, the vital residency document that determines access to public services. (Until 2022, single mothers faced the same problem.)

For now, those seeking surrogacy in China must turn to a market that runs from gray to black. On one end of the spectrum are private arrangements and well-organized, if illegal, matching services; on the other are more concerning arrangements where parents have no contact with the surrogates, who may be themselves be trafficked.

On top of the surrogate’s fees, parents usually bribe a hospital for fake documents showing a standard pregnancy and birth. Chinese couples will endure all of this for the sake of a child. But the numbers show that they’re very reluctant to go through it twice.

James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/06/us-.title: What’s Freezing the U.S. Housing Market?
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/06/us-.author: Cameron Abadi and Adam Tooze
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/06/us-.text:
Your all-access pass to FP

The annual rate of home sales in the United States recently fell to 3.98 million, its lowest level since June 2025. The stagnant housing market may be because of the country’s elevated interest rates, with the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate now past 7 percent. That makes it more than just a housing story, because the interest rate is partly determined by competition for capital from the booming artificial intelligence industry.

What are the dynamics in play in the U.S. housing market right now? Are high U.S. interest rates mostly due to broad economic growth? What role is the AI industry playing in the frozen housing market?

The annual rate of home sales in the United States recently fell to 3.98 million, its lowest level since June 2025. The stagnant housing market may be because of the country’s elevated interest rates, with the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate now past 7 percent. That makes it more than just a housing story, because the interest rate is partly determined by competition for capital from the booming artificial intelligence industry.

What are the dynamics in play in the U.S. housing market right now? Are high U.S. interest rates mostly due to broad economic growth? What role is the AI industry playing in the frozen housing market?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: What exactly is going on in the housing market? How would you describe the dynamics at play right now?

Adam Tooze: The term that seems to be commonly used by analysts is “freezing up” or “frozen.” The mortgage rate is over 7 percent, which is lower than the 7.7 percent rate in 2023 when inflation spiked. But the crucial point is that as recently as 2022, you could get a mortgage for as little as 3 percent; during COVID, it fell even lower than that.

An increase in interest rates from 3 percent to over 7 percent is a huge financing shock to what is the largest single asset class in the world. By comparison, U.S. Treasurys is a $40 trillion asset pool; American domestic real estate, so housing, is $55 trillion, of which owner-occupied is $48.7 trillion. This is flat-out the single largest element of the U.S. economy. If you add in commercial real estate, it’s $26 trillion.

For the financing costs on a market that large to shift as much as this is a story that ought to rank alongside the Treasurys in terms of its macroeconomic implications. Because it impacts households and therefore impacts consumption, it in some senses is a more direct impact on people’s lives.

Another way of describing this is that this is another aspect of the cost-of-living crisis and conversation going on in American society, as it has in so many others in recent years. It’s also a K-shaped story about the division within American society at its most elemental level—namely, what do you pay and how do you finance your home? American mortgages are very peculiar beasts by global standards. They offer fixed rates for very long periods of time but with the one-sided advantage to the borrower that they can refinance whenever they like, essentially, for relatively modest cost and it’s a normal thing to do.

So what happens is that when interest rates fall, people who are well-organized financially refinance their mortgages. Currently, about 50 percent of American mortgage holders are locked in on 30-year interest rates that are less than 4 percent—incredibly good financing, given that the inflation rate in the U.S. is currently ticking along at 3 percent. Half of that population is locked in, and for them to consider moving, they would have to refinance—presumably if they’re moving up the chain—more money at a rate that is not 4 percent but 7 percent. So it’s incredibly off-putting.

But even if you had taken out a mortgage 12 months ago, over the lifetime of a 30-year mortgage your interest costs would be tens—if not hundreds—of thousands of dollars lower than they are right now.

So, you can see why from that side there is a real freezing pressure going on. What’s happening is precisely what you described: a contraction of the overall market. A market economist would say, the way this works is if demand falls, the price should fall. But the problem with the U.S. housing market right now is that structurally, if you look at household formation compared to new construction of buildings, there’s a fairly substantial deficit, so prices are remaining stuck high.

But even at those prices, not many people are actually willing to sell because of the refinancing costs when they move into a new property. The entire market is in this sort of frozen state. There were periods in the early 2000s during the real estate frenzy before the 2008 crash where house sales were running at the rate equivalent to 7 percent of households, so real considerable churn. Not all of those were properties that people lived in, but nevertheless it suggested a very large mobility.

That rate is half or less than half that currently—so we really are talking about a kind of deadlock.

CA: There’s a lot of talk about the Iran war leading to inflation, leading to the need for higher interest rates. But this doesn’t seem to be an oil story, because the price of oil is steady right now and yet interest rates are continuing to go up. Is this about a broader economic growth story in the United States that is producing increased interest rates?

AT: There are a variety of contending stories about these interest rates. This is one of the things that folks maybe outside the financial markets don’t appreciate. Mortgages are ultimately refinanced through bonds, which are issued by banks—mortgage banks or Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac overwhelmingly. This then becomes part of the pool that sits directly alongside U.S. Treasury debt.

What determines those interest rates, those yields—in other words, the relationship between the price that you pay for the bond and the underlying flow of income you derive from it—is determined by this complex array of factors that provide the stuff of endless conversation about the economy much more than, say, chat about how Apple is doing or Nvidia, which is really the stock market story. The macro story is dominated by the questions you’ve just raised.

There is the possibility that this is to do with particular supply shocks and therefore pressure on prices, which one could generalize to a story about a tendency in the modern economy to supply shortage—which tends to drive prices up, right? It could be, on the other hand, a growth story, an excess of demand story—which would be AI in the American case, with huge volumes of new debt being issued and rapid growth.

Of course, there’s the fiscal conversation. Is the problem ultimately that the American government is issuing too much debt? Then there’s drama of the Federal Reserve and who’s in charge of the Fed and what we think Fed policy is going to be. Because the Fed has a huge say in the development of long-run interest rates in particular. All of those narratives are out there right now.

I think the smart money currently is to say: Yes, there’s structural pressure from price shocks; yes, there is also structural pressure from very large government issuance; but the more likely force driving this right now is some story about the relative robustness of the U.S. economy, which is sustaining a lot of economies in an updraft. We’re not in a deflationary moment by any means.

Then, furthermore, there has been a substantial shift in the market’s assessment of the likely reaction function of the Fed. Last year, the markets were still betting that we would see multiple rate cuts by the Fed to address a slowdown in most of the American economy. Now, after the display of bravery by [Fed chair Kevin] Warsh and the Fed leadership, markets are pricing in to increases in interest rates from the Fed side for the rest of this year. That’s a huge shift.

When you put all of those factors together, some people will say this is really alarming, and this may produce instability as hedge fund strategies unwind, and we’re back to the Treasury market story. But a calmer assessment would simply be: This is exactly what you would expect to see interest rates doing in an economy with 3 percent inflation that seems to be running hot and where all of the taps are on.

This is exactly what fixed-income markets ought to be doing, and mortgages are part of that giant pool. It is the logic of this lock-in effect that generates particular issues and the fat that has been under construction of housing. But it’s not in and of itself a sign of anything disastrous happening here.

CA: Are AI data centers pushing up the cost of capital that could go toward financing mortgages? Is that part of the reason that the housing market is freezing, as you mentioned it?

AT: The way I would think about this is not through a kind of piggy bank of money that has to go either to houses or to AI, and then say AI is somehow crowding out housing. The volume of debt issuance by AI is now large enough to be up there with Treasury issuances in certain categories. So, it’s certainly a big factor. But an awful lot of that is being generated essentially by credit creation within the financial system.

That’s the connection: This boom in finance-leveraged investment in AI is creating a hot economy to which the Fed then responds by raising interest rates.

Within the kind of undulating, quite baggy economy—which isn’t tightly constrained by a pot of money but is this expanding, kind of liquid balloon structure of credit—as the hot bit drags the entire economy forward and the Fed responds, the slower-moving bits are squeezed. That is what we are seeing. The equilibrium interest rate for the housing market would probably be lower than it would be for the AI-driven economy. The Fed is caught between one and the other.

We’re seeing this very severely in the supply side, in the construction of everything other than data centers. Since the end of 2023, data center construction has increased at an annualized rate, adding up what they do per month and multiplying it by 12. We’ve seen a $50 billion increase in spending on data center construction and a $120 billion collapse in the construction of absolutely everything else. That’s exactly what you would expect in this ooze model of the economy, where the bit that’s growing fastest is dragging policy into a higher interest rate level—which the AI sector has to absorb because they’re so obsessed with speed, they have to move forward on this.

Everyone else in every other bit of the construction economy is just going, well, in due course we’ll do that project, but now at 7 percent-plus interest rates is not the moment to do it. So that all gets deferred.

I would put it in that kind of way. It’s more a macro crowding out—and it’s not even direct competition for workers, because the people who build data centers are not the people necessarily that are building housing. But it’s in effect by way of the interest rate, which is being set to suit the AI economy and slow it down but is squeezing the more fragile bits of the economy.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi

Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/06/chi.author: Michael Poznansky and Ian Easton

There is fierce debate about whether the United States should, would, and could defend Taiwan in the event of a military assault by China. But there is another way events could play out that doesn’t involve a dramatic blockade or amphibious invasion: nonforcible realignment or, in a worst-case scenario, bloodless annexation, whereby an elected government in Taipei concludes a treaty effectively ceding Taiwan’s territory to the People’s Republic of China. Such a strategy, known by euphemisms like “winning without fighting” or “peaceful reunification,” is Beijing’s preferred outcome. And Washington is unprepared for it.

The threat of nonforcible realignment or annexation presents distinct obstacles from an openly violent military conflict. Reversing a covert and coerced, yet seemingly voluntary, political decision in Taipei to capitulate would also be exceedingly difficult, putting a premium on prevention. With Taiwan’s next presidential election approaching in a little over a year, and the leading candidates still uncertain, the time is ripe to address this vulnerability.

But there is another way events could play out that doesn’t involve a dramatic blockade or amphibious invasion: nonforcible realignment or, in a worst-case scenario, bloodless annexation, whereby an elected government in Taipei concludes a treaty effectively ceding Taiwan’s territory to the People’s Republic of China. Such a strategy, known by euphemisms like “winning without fighting” or “peaceful reunification,” is Beijing’s preferred outcome. And Washington is unprepared for it.

The threat of nonforcible realignment or annexation presents distinct obstacles from an openly violent military conflict. Reversing a covert and coerced, yet seemingly voluntary, political decision in Taipei to capitulate would also be exceedingly difficult, putting a premium on prevention. With Taiwan’s next presidential election approaching in a little over a year, and the leading candidates still uncertain, the time is ripe to address this vulnerability.

Many experts believe it is unlikely Taipei would readily comply with any attempt at forced unification. In 2022, a Taiwanese public opinion poll found that 70.2 percent of respondents were willing to defend Taiwan if China took military action. Another found that over 60 percent of Taiwanese between 20 and 39 said they were willing to defend Taiwan; the same poll showed that 72 percent of respondents between the ages of 40-49 said they would fight. What happens, though, if the order to fight never comes?

“Peaceful reunification” is a Chinese Communist Party (CCP) euphemism coined in a 1979 “Message to Compatriots in Taiwan.” It is a seemingly benign phrase that conceals a massive, state-orchestrated campaign of psychological and political pressure that the CCP hopes might result in the destruction of a democratic nation.

China has long claimed Taiwan’s territory and has been conducting a sophisticated global effort to isolate and weaken its neighbor, laying the groundwork for a potential future takeover. The goal of subduing the enemy without fighting is pervasive in Chinese strategic thought.

The most extreme scenario would be a formal unification agreement. This is a high bar. As of 2019, it requires a supermajority of Taiwanese legislators followed by a national referendum. Yet below this are more gradual scenarios of realignment. A pro-Beijing government could erode Taiwan’s security partnership with the United States by evicting trainers, rolling back conscription laws, and allowing arms sales to lapse. CCP-friendly leaders could ink wide-ranging economic and so-called peace frameworks that would bind Taiwan and mainland China in ways that would be difficult to reverse later.

Nonforcible realignment or annexation seems unlikely, but it is a growing possibility. In recent years, several of Taiwan’s leading politicians have openly embraced cross-strait policies that closely align with the CCP’s preferred direction. Cheng Li-wun, a former Taiwan independence advocate and the new head of the Kuomintang (KMT, or Chinese Nationalist Party), visited China in April and explicitly called for a more open orientation towards Beijing. A few weeks after the lunch, she told a staff writer at the Atlantic that “everything is possible, because we’re just one big family.” Cheng reaffirmed her position in a Foreign Affairs article, “Taiwan Doesn’t Have To Choose.” This followed her controversial presence at a November 2025 memorial event honoring Wu Shi, one of the most dangerous CCP spies in Taiwan’s modern history. Former President Ma Ying-jeou has publicly claimed that Taiwanese self-defense efforts are futile, and Taiwan should trust Xi Jinping.

To be sure, Taiwanese political figures like Cheng and Ma may well be conducting exchanges with Xi in good faith and with peaceful purposes. Nevertheless, the CCP is not motivated to seek peace and stability. History shows that anything masquerading as CCP acceptance of a cross-strait consensus is a dangerous gamble.

When the British ceded formal control of Hong Kong to China in 1997, the CCP agreed to a “one country, two systems” model, offering political autonomy for 50 years. But by the early 2020s, China passed a national security law enhancing its ability to suppress dissent and subsequently changed the electoral system by requiring by “that only ‘patriots’ who ‘respect’ the Chinese Communist party can run in elections,” according to the Council on Foreign Relations, alongside other moves.

The danger extends beyond a handful of politicians. Over the last five years, there has been a stark increase in prosecuted spy cases in Taiwan. The island’s military, legislature, and executive branch have seen a dizzying array of espionage and infiltration cases, with defendants from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party, as well as the opposition KMT and Taiwan People’s Party—which together hold a majority coalition in Taiwan’s legislature. While the sheer volume of prosecutions suggests Taiwan has robust counterintelligence capacity, it also suggests the CCP has been effective at exploiting vulnerabilities.

Recruiting spies is the tip of the iceberg. The CCP’s political warfare and influence efforts include funding local Taiwanese officials to travel to China and amplify pro-unification messages, sophisticated AI-enabled disinformation surrounding elections, and allegedly paying several Taiwan media groups for pro-CCP coverage. None of these tactics are decisive on their own. Rather, they are aimed at bolstering China’s image, undermining faith in the United States, and eroding confidence in continued resistance.

It’s time for the U.S. to embrace strategic clarity.

Given the extraordinary scope of the CCP’s covert influence and political interference campaigns, Taiwan faces the ever-present possibility of a winning candidate stepping into Beijing’s camp after a national election. It is no longer unimaginable that the people of Taiwan could elect a leader secretly controlled by the CCP, or even simply one that pursues strategic realignment towards China in the hopes of forestalling a military showdown. While there is always the possibility that the election of a very Beijing-friendly government that failed to end Taiwan’s democratic system could usher in a more pro-U.S. government in follow-on elections, it would be risky to bank on such an outcome.

Nonviolent realignment or unification might at first blush appear to solve several thorny issues for Washington. Most obviously, it would spare decision-makers the need to prepare for a costly war with China. Further, some might argue that it is official U.S. policy to accept any election outcome that reflects the will of Taiwan’s people, functionally tying Washington’s hands. Neither argument stands up to scrutiny.

First, while the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 does rest “upon the expectation that the future of Taiwan will be determined by peaceful means,” it also requires the United States to “maintain the capacity … to resist any resort to force or other forms of coercion that would jeopardize the security, or the social or economic system, of the people on Taiwan” (emphasis ours). In theory then, Washington is plausibly bound as a matter of policy to oppose Taiwan’s subjugation through the pursuit of so-called peaceful reunification which would invariably occur amid an environment of intense coercion.

In practice, the devil is in the details. Unambiguous coercion of the Taiwanese public, wherein the CCP gave Taiwan an explicit ultimatum between surrender or war, would fall squarely within the type of coercion covered by the Taiwan Relations Act. So too would coercion of individual political figures through schemes like legal intimidation, blackmail, or bribery—if it could be readily proven. The situation would be considerably more challenging, however, if realignment occurred against the backdrop of a seemingly democratic decision, even one made possible by years of political warfare and manipulation. Even if the United States could marshal conclusive proof of such tampering, it might open itself up to allegations of tampering in the democratic process.

Apart from the question of any legal obligations, nonforcible realignment or annexation would technically free the United States from having to weigh whether to confront China militarily—but the strategic damage would be enormous. Washington will have lost a small but powerful partner, and a linchpin of postwar U.S. security architecture in the Pacific.

If Xi achieves his goals without firing a shot, it would deny the United States a legitimate basis to militarily contest Taiwan’s realignment towards, or absorption by, China. This is one of the greatest challenges posed by winning without fighting. Given U.S. commitments to sovereignty and self-determination, leaders would be hard-pressed to forcibly reverse the popular will of the Taiwanese people, even if that choice was made possible by political warfare.

Yet the loss would be enormous. If Taiwan’s democracy ended with a whimper rather than a war cry, it would leave whole the entire Chinese army. China would have little need to deploy a large garrison force and wage costly pacification campaigns, freeing its military to undertake global operations from a position of strength. At the same time, China would capture Taiwan’s world-class chip ecosystem intact.

While Taiwan’s situation is distinctive, history offers clues about the difficulties Washington has confronted when facing strategic realignment, actual or feared, by allies and partners absent forcible action by adversaries. During the Cold War, the United States found it exceedingly hard to stymie the election of leftist leaders—including ones who were willing to sell their own democracy to Moscow—without incurring blowback. This left decision-makers with limited options, usually covert.

In some cases, the United States helped safeguard democracy. During Italy’s 1948 elections, policymakers feared that major gains by communist politicians would provide the Soviets a strategic outpost in the heart of Europe. A National Security Council report at the time warned that the ascension of the People’s Bloc would enable “a pattern made familiar in Eastern Europe,” namely allowing communists to “take over complete control of the government and transform Italy into a totalitarian state subservient to Moscow.” To forestall this, the CIA secretly provided support to non-communist parties and politicians. The U.S. government continued to quietly fund centrist politicians and labor organizations in Italy into the early 1960s.

In other cases, like Chile in the 1960s and 1970s, U.S. efforts took a darker turn. For years, Lyndon Johnson, and later Richard Nixon, tried to quietly blunt the electoral prospects of Marxist leader Salvador Allende. When it became clear in the fall of 1970 that Allende could win the presidency, the CIA unsuccessfully tried to engineer a coup. For years afterwards, the U.S. waged a secret campaign of economic warfare and coup plotting until Allende’s ouster in 1973. Augusto Pinochet, a brutal dictator, took over. Exposure of the operation, along with a host of other covert actions in this period, created a scandal that produced sweeping intelligence reform.

China has shown it will not hesitate to use every tool at its disposal, including economic links, cultural exchanges, and even alleged vaccine blockades, to undermine Taiwan’s government. Winning without fighting is especially appealing if the military balance continues to confront Xi with the prospect of a highly uncertain war. At the same time, the United States lacks a clear plan for what it would do if this approach yielded a major strategic realignment or potentially annexation.

U.S. planners and strategists should do more to prepare for the worst, using all instruments of national power at their disposal. That begins with revisiting and enhancing Taiwan policy. While Cold War-era tactics to covertly undermine any future pro-CCP regime in Taipei would obfuscate a flagrant violation of sovereignty norms, they would likely be exposed and hand Beijing a pretext for harsher crackdowns. Overt efforts to reverse the situation on the ground might cause escalation and engender local resentment.

Because post-realignment options are fraught, Washington must proactively develop a strategy to strengthen Taiwan relations. Arms sales alone are not enough. Investing in public diplomacy; countering China’s political warfare campaign; aiding Taiwan with counterintelligence to uncover united front work; and providing robust reassurance must all be prioritized to ensure that China’s winning without fighting scenario never comes to pass.

The Trump administration, growing increasingly fretful of high fuel prices just a month before the U.S. midterm elections, issued late Monday a novel executive order meant to make diesel fuel a little cheaper for beleaguered truckers and farmers. It almost certainly won’t help.

(That tax revenue, like the gasoline tax, helps pay for highway maintenance.) The Trump administration, growing increasingly fretful of high fuel prices just a month before the U.S. midterm elections, issued late Monday a novel executive order meant to make diesel fuel a little cheaper for beleaguered truckers and farmers. It almost certainly won’t help.

U.S. President Donald Trump authorized the deferral, through the end of the year, of federal taxes on diesel fuel used to power vehicles on roads and highways. (That tax revenue, like the gasoline tax, helps pay for highway maintenance.) His solution is to temporarily legalize the use of so-called red-dye diesel—a tax-free diesel flavor normally earmarked for off-road uses such as agriculture, mining, and logging—for use by truckers.

There is no difference between red-dye diesel and regular diesel except the addition of red dye, which is put into the fuel to make it easier for inspectors to see if potential violators are using tax-exempt fuel where they shouldn’t; the fines and penalties are steep. Trump’s measure would, in theory, shave 24 cents off the price of a gallon of diesel, which last week was at record levels and remains very high, at $6.31 a gallon. If states follow suit with their own tax breaks, diesel could potentially be back under $6 a gallon.

But there are a lot of problems with the hail-mary measure. For starters, it is only a deferral of those federal fuel taxes, not an outright suspension. Unless Congress passes legislation, at some point those deferred taxes will come due, which simply means storing up bigger bills and bigger accounting headaches for truckers down the road.

“It’s one thing to waive a tax and another thing to simply defer it. This just looks like a mess, but then again, it’s all a circus,” said Tom Kloza, the chief energy advisor at Gulf Oil and a four-decade veteran of petroleum product markets.

More importantly, while the measure could, if taken up by both sellers and buyers of red-dye diesel, slightly lower prices for some highway users, it won’t add any supplies to a very tight market. The reason U.S. diesel prices are high is because supplies of diesel are strained, and there is little relief on the horizon. U.S. refiners can’t produce any more than they already are, and other global exporters have voluntarily or involuntarily curbed their own supplies.

“This doesn’t move the needle in any way on diesel availability,” Kloza said. “It almost seems silly.”

There is another risk in potentially robbing Peter to pay Paul, beyond the prospect of lost tax revenues needed to keep highways operable. Farmers who operate tractors, combines, and other off-road vehicles are also suffering from high diesel prices, and the new measure could open up their privileged red-dye diesel to much broader use by the trucking industry. That may be why Trump, in his executive order, stressed the need for the Department of Agriculture to ensure availability of red-dye diesel for farmers, who are in harvest season.

Finally, the measure doesn’t address the fundamental reason for the high fuel prices, which is a combination of stubbornly high crude oil prices and a shrunken global refinery complex that produces things such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel.

Ukraine will redouble its long-range strikes on Russia’s oil refineries in reprisal for Moscow’s stepped-up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure ahead of winter, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said over the weekend. Ukraine’s “long-range sanctions” have already struck most of Russia’s oil refineries at least once, and the Ukrainian Defense Ministry says it has taken out about half of Russia’s refining capacity. Industry experts suspect the long-term damage to Russian refineries is less than such headline estimates suggest, but since Russia was the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the United States, the offensive still affects global supplies.

The Middle East has still not recovered its refining capacity that was damaged or constrained by the Iran war that began in February, even though crude oil flows out of the Persian Gulf have in recent weeks rebounded. That lack of refined product exports from the region is likely to persist, as Iran has intensified its anti-shipping campaign in recent days, with at least 11 attacks on tankers and other vessels just in October. Most analysts figure at least 3 million barrels of formerly exported Middle East refined products remain absent from the market.

Kyiv’s energy war on Russia may hurt on the margins, but the real culprit is Trump’s war on Iran.

But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.

And the United States, despite deferrals on tax and scheduled fall maintenance at big refineries, cannot squeeze much more out of facilities that were operating at a near-record 95 percent capacity in the third quarter. Many refiners have put off scheduled seasonal maintenance to keep producing at record margins, but that means more will have to go offline early next year.

And just to keep things interesting, a tropical depression-cum-tropical storm-cum-hurricane is forming in the Gulf of Mexico, with a projected path that will take it right toward the U.S. Gulf Coast refining complex.

Trump’s executive order is a “cosmetic measure. It’s the whole world, not just the United States, that looks like it could have a pending diesel crisis this winter, especially Europe. If you get a cold winter in the U.S. or Europe, or that Gulf storm develops, diesel could be $10,” Kloza said.

That Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto skipped the annual inaugural proceedings of the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) this year is not so unusual—after all, so did the leaders of China, Germany, India, Mexico, South Africa, and a host of other nations. Nonetheless, Prabowo’s absence has prompted speculation that he intended to send a message by avoiding a visit to the United States. Although Jakarta officially cited Prabowo’s need to address domestic priorities, some Indonesian experts see his absence as reflecting growing frustration with Washington following Jakarta’s attempts to align with Trump administration priorities.

Ongoing reports and analysis

At last year’s UNGA, Prabowo publicly offered considerable Indonesian resources in support of a Gaza settlement, pledging a financial contribution and potentially “20,000 or even more” peacekeepers in the territory. He also took the notable step of promising Indonesian recognition of Israel once Israel recognized a Palestinian state. In February, Prabowo participated in President Donald Trump’s inaugural Board of Peace meeting and linked Indonesia’s troops commitment to a U.S.-led stabilization force for Gaza. During the meeting, Prabowo declared that Indonesia “completely agree[d]” with and was “fully committed” to Trump’s 20-point plan, praised Trump’s leadership, and expressed optimism that the plan could achieve “real peace.”

That Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto skipped the annual inaugural proceedings of the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) this year is not so unusual—after all, so did the leaders of China, Germany, India, Mexico, South Africa, and a host of other nations. Nonetheless, Prabowo’s absence has prompted speculation that he intended to send a message by avoiding a visit to the United States. Although Jakarta officially cited Prabowo’s need to address domestic priorities, some Indonesian experts see his absence as reflecting growing frustration with Washington following Jakarta’s attempts to align with Trump administration priorities.

Ongoing reports and analysis

At last year’s UNGA, Prabowo publicly offered considerable Indonesian resources in support of a Gaza settlement, pledging a financial contribution and potentially “20,000 or even more” peacekeepers in the territory. He also took the notable step of promising Indonesian recognition of Israel once Israel recognized a Palestinian state. In February, Prabowo participated in President Donald Trump’s inaugural Board of Peace meeting and linked Indonesia’s troops commitment to a U.S.-led stabilization force for Gaza. During the meeting, Prabowo declared that Indonesia “completely agree[d]” with and was “fully committed” to Trump’s 20-point plan, praised Trump’s leadership, and expressed optimism that the plan could achieve “real peace.”

At home, Prabowo’s support for Washington’s Gaza initiative was hardly cost-free. His willingness to contemplate recognizing Israel had already generated controversy in overwhelmingly pro-Palestinian Indonesia, but opposition intensified after Jakarta joined Trump’s Board of Peace and committed to deploy troops. Indonesian Muslim organizations and civil society groups questioned whether the initiative would genuinely advance Palestinian statehood or only subordinate Indonesian foreign policy to the United States and Israel. Public opinion was similarly skeptical. For example, a March 2026 survey found that 50.9 percent of respondents opposed Indonesia’s membership in the Board of Peace, while 44.9 percent opposed deploying Indonesian troops in Gaza, compared with just 33.8 percent who supported the deployment. The controversy eventually reached Prabowo’s own governing coalition as several politicians called for Indonesia to reconsider its involvement.

The Iran war has significantly worsened Prabowo’s domestic headaches over supporting Washington in the Middle East. His government suddenly found itself uncomfortably associated with a warmongering United States targeting another Muslim-majority state. In response, Prabowo froze Indonesia’s Board of Peace engagement and suspended its planned troop deployment to Gaza. Prabowo also placed explicit conditions on any reinstatement of Indonesia’s troop commitment, stressing that Indonesian forces would not disarm Hamas and would participate only with the explicit consent of Palestinian leaders—presumably including Hamas—and key Muslim-majority states, including Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. In response to reports that Indonesia could contribute $1 billion to the Board of Peace, he said that he never committed any money to the body—in contrast to his earlier U.N. pledge to help finance peace in Gaza. Jakarta’s retreat complicates the White House’s portrayal of the Board of Peace as an international success story. To make matters worse for Prabowo, the war has driven up energy costs, creating additional concerns for Indonesia’s economy and consumers.

Coincidentally, on the same day Prabowo attended the Board of Peace meeting in February, his country also signed a new tariff agreement with the United States. Jakarta was shocked when Trump slapped U.S. imports from Indonesia with an extremely high 32 percent tariff in April 2025. The two sides eventually negotiated the rate down to 19 percent, but Indonesia made enormous concessions that arguably compromised its sovereignty; Jakarta had to agree to restrictions in its economic relations with its other major partner, China. The deal requires, for example, that Indonesia aligns with U.S. export controls on sensitive technologies and avoids entering trade agreements with other nations that could compromise “essential U.S. interests.” Nevertheless, Prabowo attempted to spin the deal to his population, arguing: “We finally reached a mutually beneficial agreement based on mutual respect. I think the outcome is good.”

Washington’s new strategy is little more than a euphemism for unpredictability.

Prabowo would have rather moved on from the issue, but just one day later—on Feb. 20—the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Trump’s tariffs illegal, unleashing a torrent of criticism that Indonesia should have just waited before signing a negotiated deal. A commentary published by the Jakarta Post called the timing “disastrous,” arguing that Prabowo’s team should have anticipated the ruling and postponed the signing.

Compounding the situation further, the Trump administration opened a Section 301 investigation into alleged Indonesian manufacturing overcapacity just three weeks later, followed the next day by another investigation into Indonesian imports of products allegedly made with forced labor. Jakarta responded to the latter by introducing a new prohibition on imports produced with forced labor, but Washington nevertheless slapped Indonesian goods with a 10 percent tariff in July. Meanwhile, the U.S. investigation into excess capacity continues to hang over the relationship.

As if these bilateral irritants weren’t enough, another emerged in April when it was revealed that Prabowo had approved a new agreement to give the U.S. military precleared access to Indonesia’s sovereign airspace for crisis responses and other contingencies. The Indonesian Defense Ministry later denied that a binding commitment had been made, suggesting that Prabowo was forced to backtrack. Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin nevertheless acknowledged that he had signed a letter of intent with his U.S. counterpart, Pete Hegseth, while Indonesia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs warned that blanket U.S. access risked entangling the country in a South China Sea conflict. Once again, Prabowo’s effort to move closer to Trump had created political backlash at home. And once again, his government was forced into defending itself against accusations that it was compromising Indonesian sovereignty.

Despite these troubles, the U.S.-Indonesia partnership has continued to progress in several key areas. The annual Super Garuda Shield military exercise—organized by the Indonesian and U.S. militaries and involving various partner countries—has expanded in both the number of participating countries and the depth of cooperation. U.S.-Indonesian critical minerals cooperation is also growing, and the two countries have announced tens of billions of dollars in new commercial deals.

Yet some of the biggest advances in the relationship, whether on security or trade, have produced new and unintended political consequences for Prabowo at home and abroad. Still, he has invested heavily in both his personal relationship with Trump and the broader U.S.-Indonesia partnership, suggesting that he is unlikely to reverse course quickly. Instead, Prabowo is more likely to make some marginal adjustments—this week, for example, he appointed an experienced diplomat, Arrmanatha Nasir, as his new foreign minister, who may scrutinize Indonesia’s international commitments more heavily before they are signed. So far, at least, Prabowo hasn’t absorbed enough blowback to conclude that closer ties with Washington are more trouble than they are worth.

For those of us growing weary of the predictions made by Silicon Valley CEOs about artificial intelligence possibly leading to the extermination of the human race, the new Israeli documentary NAZA is a counterpoint, even if that wasn’t the filmmakers’ intention.

The nearly 80-minute film takes us far away from the tiresome tech doomers (who keep racing ahead with the technology despite their apocalyptic concerns) and transports us to the nighttime rooftops of Tel Aviv, where Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor interview 24 anonymous members of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) about their role in the relentless military strikes on Gaza over the past three years.

For those of us growing weary of the predictions made by Silicon Valley CEOs about artificial intelligence possibly leading to the extermination of the human race, the new Israeli documentary NAZA is a counterpoint, even if that wasn’t the filmmakers’ intention.

The nearly 80-minute film takes us far away from the tiresome tech doomers (who keep racing ahead with the technology despite their apocalyptic concerns) and transports us to the nighttime rooftops of Tel Aviv, where Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor interview 24 anonymous members of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) about their role in the relentless military strikes on Gaza over the past three years.

NAZA, which takes its name from the Hebrew acronym for “collateral damage,” focuses heavily on the AI systems that became an integral part of the war in Gaza after the Hamas attack of Oct. 7, 2023. “‘You have to trust the system,’” one soldier recalls an officer telling him. Otherwise, “‘everything will fall apart.’”

The soldiers talk about the role they played in Israeli programs such as Lavender, an AI system that identifies enemy targets, and the unfortunately named Where’s Daddy, which involves using children’s cellphones to track when a Hamas target—their father—returns home. In the case of Where’s Daddy, the resulting strikes, as one soldier recounts, would kill the suspected Hamas member but typically also his family, including the child whose phone was hacked.

Some of the concerns expressed by soldiers in NAZA are not new, such as modern warfare being akin to a video game, a sentiment frequently expressed since the advent of armed drones and push-button warfare. In fact, there are no major revelations in the film—the filmmakers published many of the details about these AI systems previously in the Guardian, which co-produced the film; +972 Magazine; and the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call. But that’s perhaps beside the point: The immense power of the film is derived from the firsthand testimony of the soldiers who took part in this AI-driven system of destruction and now wrestle with the consequences of their actions, including many thousands of dead civilians.

So, what then does their testimony tell us about AI and war? In NAZA, no one is worrying about rogue AI killing us off—that’s more a concern for Silicon Valley companies looking to raise capital. Rather, the film is rightfully concerned about the way that AI allows the military to justify killing ever more people, even as these systems absolve humans of the moral responsibility for choosing targets.

“My role is entirely technical,” says one IDF member, describing his part in the Gaza war.

In this sense, AI gives soldiers a certain remove from the decision-making and even imbues such systems with virtue, since machines aren’t driven by hatred. “Having AI decide who lives and dies is better than leaving the decision to someone whose friend was killed by Hamas last week,” a soldier says.

Yet the film quickly reveals the hollowness of this sentiment, since we learn that in targeting a Hamas operative, the Israeli military sometimes knowingly allowed dozens of noncombatants to be killed as collateral damage—as many as 50 civilians per strike.

Yet if AI is supposed to transfer responsibility for killing from humans to computers, and thus absolve humans of moral responsibility, it doesn’t quite work. The humans who appear in NAZA clearly feel responsible—or at least responsible enough to risk their careers and potentially their freedom to give interviews to the filmmakers. (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened to strip the filmmakers of their citizenship.)

Even as NAZA is, in some respects, an indictment of AI, in the end it’s more an indictment of humans and, in particular, humans born in a country traumatized by the Holocaust and then traumatized again by the attack of Oct. 7. On that day, fighters from Hamas and other groups brutally killed some 1,200 people and abducted another 251, holding many of them hostage for months or years. The film’s message is that Israelis, the victims of so much suffering, lost their moral core that day and created a system that has allowed for the killing of extended families and the destruction of entire city blocks, including hospitals and schools, in pursuit of Hamas militants.

A conversation with Nobel laureate Maria Ressa.

Like nuclear weapons, AI was born of human ingenuity. But its challenges are unique.

A conversation with the multilateral institution’s top tech envoy.

The war has also clearly led to another form of trauma for at least some Israelis: soldiers who lament their role in a campaign that has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza, according to numbers tracked by local health authorities. One Israeli soldier interviewed in NAZA describes hearing the screams of children through his headphones as they were killed in airstrikes. Another says he saw video of stray dogs consuming dead bodies in Gaza.

The anonymous Israeli soldiers who appear in the film understand a complexity that is difficult for many observers of this polarizing conflict—those partial to one side or the other—to absorb: that the horror of Hamas’s attack, which did not distinguish between soldiers and civilians, was followed by another horror—an Israeli war whose operators ostensibly targeted combatants but also knowingly civilians.

Where does this leave us with AI and warfare? Can AI actually improve the way wars are fought, or will we use it merely to absolve ourselves from blame when innocents are killed? And turning back to the doomers wringing their hands while simultaneously fundraising to build AI faster: If AI is so powerful, why then, after three years of war, is Israel still carrying out strikes against Hamas in Gaza?

That last question reminds me of an interview I did with a Pentagon scientist at the height of the war in Afghanistan, when the military was using advanced algorithms—the predecessor of AI—to predict insurgent attacks on U.S. and coalition forces. In a moment of frustration, the Pentagon official admitted that the Taliban appeared to be holding their own in the war, without fancy algorithms or even computers.

A decade after we spoke, the United States pulled out of Afghanistan, allowing the Taliban to quickly seize power. Now, the computers have grown exponentially better, AI is generating targets, yet U.S. and Israeli victories remain elusive, whether in Gaza or now in Iran.

As for the morality question, there is so far no evidence that AI is better at selecting military targets and avoiding civilian deaths, only that it chooses targets faster and that it gives the veneer of legitimacy. That perhaps is the inadvertent message of NAZA: It’s not that AI is all powerful but that it provides a technocratic justification for strikes that often end up killing innocent people.

Hollywood long ago recognized this folly, even when it was theoretical. In many movies about AI, the real danger is not necessarily the computers devoid of empathy that lead us to near self-destruction but the deluded humans who gave them that power in the first place.

In NAZA, the AI systems are the tools of death, but the real problem is the humans.

In the end, AI may or may not kill us all, as the CEOs of companies rushing to build the technology warn us. Or, as NAZA demonstrates, it may just spit out more names than humans could possibly gather on their own and let us do the killing ourselves. We seem to be good at it.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/palestini.title: The End of Gaza
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/palestini.author: Khaled Elgindy
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/palestini.text:
KHALED ELGINDY is a Senior Research Fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft and the author of Blind Spot: America and the Palestinians, From Balfour to Trump.

A Failing Peace Process Leads to Only One Outcome

Ayear after the Trump administration negotiated an agreement to end the war in Gaza, Palestinians are still waiting for the “day after” to arrive. The October 2025 cease-fire plan freed the last remaining Israeli hostages and ostensibly ended hostilities, but Israel continues to constantly strike targets in Gaza, often killing civilians, including some 300 children in the past year. The deal also envisioned a phased political process that would help reconstruct the devastated territory. Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and the point person for the Middle East, promised in January this year that restoration of core services and infrastructure—including water and sewage systems, electricity networks, hospitals, and bakeries—would begin within 100 days. And yet, nine months later, Gaza has seen no reconstruction, no restoration of basic services, or even an end to daily violence. Instead, the vast majority of its inhabitants remain packed into squalid and sprawling tent cities along a tiny—and ever-shrinking—strip of coastline, plagued by disease and rodent infestations, enduring extreme shortages of food, medicine, clean water, and access to basic sanitation.

Gazans may not be in the grip of famine as they were in prior years, but the humanitarian situation remains catastrophic—and it is not sustainable. The intolerable conditions could very well lead to a further explosion of violence. They are also enabling the endgame that many Israeli leaders want: the eventual eviction of Gaza’s over two million Palestinian residents.

Indeed, the status quo seems to suit the Israeli leadership. In a recent interview, Nikolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat serving as the high representative of Trump’s Board of Peace, which is overseeing the Gaza peace plan, revealed where the main obstacle to progress lies. On Israel’s commitments, Mladenov gently noted, is “where we are little bit stuck right now.” Kushner has also blamed Israel’s “crazy elections” later this month, which he says have made the Netanyahu government “a little irrational” in regard to Gaza.

Although electoral considerations are undoubtedly a factor—Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight and, for him, existential reelection campaign—the totality of Israeli words and actions point to something deeper and more alarming: ultimately, the Netanyahu government’s strategy has less to do with stabilizing Gaza or even disarming Hamas than with rendering the territory uninhabitable and ejecting its population.

Whether or not the Trump administration shares this goal, its extraordinary deference to Netanyahu’s far-right government and general indifference to the plight of Palestinians is facilitating just such an outcome. Unless the United States and its allies and partners are prepared to force Israel to abide by its commitments, it may only be a matter of time before Gaza is lost forever.

It is hard to overstate the scale of death, destruction, and suffering inflicted on Gaza and its roughly 2.2 million inhabitants over the past three years. In the wake of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, terrorist attack on Israel, Israeli military and political leaders vowed to “flatten” Gaza and turn it into a “city of tents,” promising that “Gaza will never go back to what it was.” They have delivered on those threats. The 223,000 tons of explosives dropped on Gaza—roughly equivalent to 15 times the power of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima—have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the vast majority of them civilians, and reduced most of Gaza to rubble. Israel’s assault, over which it is currently on trial for genocide at the International Court of Justice, has wiped out some 92 percent of Gaza’s housing stock, 95 percent of its farmland, all 12 of its universities, and nearly half of its 36 hospitals—in other words, the very institutions and infrastructure that sustain life.

After such devastation, last year’s cease-fire came as an undoubted relief. Under the first phase of Trump’s Gaza plan, the parties agreed to an immediate end to all military attacks, the exchange of hostages and prisoners, the restoration of basic services, and a massive surge in humanitarian aid. Apart from Hamas’s release of Israeli hostages, however, most of these commitments have been only partially fulfilled. Phase two, formally launched in January even though Israel had yet to meet its phase one obligations, envisioned the stabilization of Gaza through the deployment of an international force and the establishment of a Palestinian technocratic governing body, known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, coupled with the gradual disarmament of Hamas and the phased withdrawal of Israeli forces. Those last steps together serve as prerequisites for the long-term reconstruction of the Gaza Strip as laid out in phase three.

A full year after the cease-fire was announced, Israel continues to block the entry of Palestinian governing and policing bodies that would allow Hamas to relinquish power and reconstruction to begin. Hamas and Israel are still at loggerheads about the sequencing of the group’s disarmament in relation to an Israeli withdrawal. Although the food situation has improved since last year’s famine, Israel continues to restrict humanitarian aid, allowing only a fraction of the daily 600 truckloads required in the cease-fire deal to enter the territory. More than 90 percent of Gaza’s inhabitants are internally displaced. Moreover, since the cease-fire, the Israeli army has unilaterally expanded its control from just over half of Gaza’s territory to around 65 percent of it. Frequent airstrikes by Israel have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians since the cease-fire was declared. That the death toll continues to mount during a cease-fire is a testament to the dystopian reality that has become Gaza’s new normal. As the UN’s Middle East envoy Sigrid Kaag put it, Gaza’s “living conditions are hell on earth with no prospect of significant change in sight.”

Israel is not solely responsible for the persistence of hellish conditions in Gaza. Hamas bears some of the blame. The Hamas leadership spent months stubbornly resisting calls for disarmament, as required by the Trump plan, ultimately agreeing to do so only under intense pressure from Egypt and other mediators. The Trump administration also bears significant blame. It has let the political process stall, gives Israel tremendous latitude, and is highly lopsided in its enforcement of the terms of the cease-fire. It has effectively allowed Israel to continue the war in Gaza, albeit on a smaller scale.

Only a few months ago, it seemed as if the impasse had been finally broken. In late July, Trump announced a breakthrough on implementing the second phase of his Gaza plan. After seven months of intense and highly fraught negotiations, Hamas and the Board of Peace reached a deal on the disarmament of the Palestinian militant group, paving the way—theoretically, at least—to start the desperately needed recovery and reconstruction work as well as the entry of new Palestinian governance and policing mechanisms. The plan’s success hinged on a carefully crafted sequence of events: Hamas would disarm in parallel with an Israeli military withdrawal, a scheme designed to ensure progress and prevent either side from exercising a “veto” over the process.

That Hamas, a group founded on armed resistance, had agreed to any form of disarmament was unprecedented and rightly hailed by Trump as a “historic” achievement. Even so, Netanyahu categorically rejected this road map, insisting that there could be no Israeli withdrawal until Hamas was fully disarmed and that Israel remained free to continue military operations in Gaza. In other words, Israel is insisting that Hamas meet all its phase two obligations even before Israel has met any of its phase one obligations—a position that renders the plan unworkable.

The process is once again stuck. Without progress on either Hamas’s disarmament or Israel’s withdrawal, the Palestinian governing committee (currently marooned in Cairo) and police force cannot enter Gaza; neither can any international force. The Trump administration and the Board of Peace have tried to fudge the issue of sequencing since the summer—publicly embracing the Israeli position that Hamas must be fully disarmed first while privately assuring Hamas and others that the road map has not changed. But ambiguity typically plays to the advantage of the stronger party; such hedging from Washington was as good as an explicit endorsement of the Israeli position. Having already given Israel an effective pass on most of its phase one obligations by refusing to condemn Israel’s near-daily cease-fire violations, the Trump administration was now effectively relieving it of second phase obligations as well. Gaza’s reconstruction and rehabilitation remain on hold indefinitely.

The dangers of the current impasse were best outlined by Mladenov in an interview in September. He warned that the absence of any meaningful progress in Gaza was foreclosing the future of the territory and the possibility of a two-state solution, with grave consequences for the wider region. “If we allow for Gaza to continue in the situation that we have now,” Mladenov cautioned, “Gaza will be gone. It will be gone for good.” He continued: “If the international community does not focus on the situation in Gaza, where you have two million Palestinians who live in terrible conditions, we will not be able to find our way back to a credible path to resolving the Israeli-Palestinian question.” At the same time, “we are putting the seeds of a next security, military crisis that is going to emerge.”

Left unsaid by Mladenov, however, is that Netanyahu is quite content for the process to remain stuck in this way. Israel’s prime minister, who only reluctantly acceded to Trump’s 2025 Gaza cease-fire, has managed to continue waging war in Gaza without incurring significant costs. The ongoing military operations and the humanitarian crisis in Gaza don’t incite meaningful outrage in Israel, while even Netanyahu’s main election rivals have felt compelled to trash the U.S.-backed Gaza road map. International outrage over the carnage in Gaza, meanwhile, has largely subsided, with many countries preferring a failing peace process to none at all.

For Netanyahu, ongoing violence at this level—just enough to prevent Gaza’s meaningful recovery and reconstruction but not enough to trigger a major international outcry—has become an end unto itself. Much as he insisted on the implausible goal of “total victory” during the first two years of war, he insists now on the equally unachievable objective of Hamas’s “total disarmament.” It is one thing for Hamas to give up its rockets, missiles, mortars, and other heavy weapons, but it is unrealistic to imagine that the group will surrender every last rifle or handgun, particularly when Israeli forces continue to operate in the territory. Netanyahu’s uncompromising stance helps placate his extremist coalition partners, justify permanent Israeli military control over Gaza, and indefinitely forestall any political accommodation with the Palestinians.

More crucially, keeping Gaza in a kind of political, military, and humanitarian limbo—with neither a real cease-fire nor a return to full-scale war, limited short-term relief but no long-term reconstruction, and a population consumed with the imperatives of survival but lacking any real hope for the future—serves the broader vision harbored by many Israeli hard-liners: making Gaza uninhabitable to the point that its residents are forced to leave. For Netanyahu and his far-right government, the immiseration of Gaza is not ancillary but central to Israel’s strategy. Israeli leaders, including Defense Minister Israel Katz, have vowed to remain in Gaza indefinitely and not withdraw. More tellingly, in the two-thirds of Gaza now under direct Israeli control, the Israeli army has wiped out virtually all traces of Palestinian life, systematically razing thousands of structures and flattening entire neighborhoods and agricultural lands, while erecting military bases and other permanent infrastructure.

Members of the Netanyahu government have made no secret of their desire to remove Gaza’s population and allow the territory’s eventual settlement by Israeli Jews. Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, among the most vocal and notorious proponents of expelling Palestinians, recently unveiled a seven-year plan for the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from Gaza, including moving 250,000 Palestinians out of Gaza in the first year. Ben-Gvir is not the only government member to say the quiet part out loud. Katz has called for facilitating the emigration of Gazans “by any means,” adding that “there is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration.” Netanyahu himself has advocated for the same, privately confirming in 2025 to a group of lawmakers that Israel has been “destroying more and more houses” in Gaza so that Palestinians “have nowhere to return.” “The only obvious result will be Gazans choosing to emigrate outside of the strip,” observed Netanyahu.

The Trump administration may not be averse to such an outcome. In January 2025, Trump proposed that the United States “take control” of Gaza and “clean out” its more than two million inhabitants as part of an ill-conceived vision of turning a depopulated Gaza into a “Riviera of the Middle East.” Although Trump backed off the idea following an immense international outcry, the administration’s laissez-faire attitude toward Israeli violations suggests it can tolerate prolonged Palestinian suffering.

The consequences of perpetuating Gaza’s misery are dreadful. As Mladenov has warned, continuing along the current path is likely to produce two outcomes: inducing growing numbers of Palestinians to leave the Gaza Strip and increasing the likelihood of violent escalation, including a return to full-scale war. In both cases, once again, the costs would be borne overwhelmingly by Palestinians in Gaza, although others would also pay a price, as the wider region grows more unstable and as Israel’s and the United States’ international standing further erodes.

As life in Gaza does not meaningfully improve and as deadly Israeli attacks continue, the likelihood of an explosion grows. Hamas, which has been decimated but not yet unseated, has so far shown relative restraint and a willingness to absorb regular hits, including a series of assassinations of its members and regular airstrikes by Israel. Its current pragmatism will probably not hold forever. Netanyahu, who thinks that keeping Israel on a constant war footing will allow him to retain power, may welcome the opportunity to wage what is in effect a forever war in Gaza. A prolonged occupation in Gaza, however, is unlikely to produce tangible military benefits while sapping Israeli resources and public morale, deepening Israel’s international isolation and foreclosing the possibility of normalizing ties with more Arab states. Likewise, the prospect of a Palestinian exodus from Gaza might fuel the fantasies of those in Israel who want to see the creation of a “Greater Israel,” but it would also confirm Israel’s pariah status and condemn Israelis and Palestinians to further decades of conflict.

For the United States, meanwhile, continued violence and an increasingly farcical peace process could lead to the unraveling of one of Trump’s few concrete foreign policy achievements while keeping the region in a state of perpetual turmoil. With the Iran war casting the United States as unreliable and encouraging Washington’s regional allies to pursue alternatives to a collapsing U.S. security umbrella, failure in Gaza would cement the impression of the United States as a superpower has-been.

There is little doubt that both Trump’s Gaza plan and the mechanisms created to oversee it, including the Board of Peace, are deeply flawed. The process they outlined is intensely lopsided in Israel’s favor, does not demand any accountability for past (and ongoing) atrocities, denies Palestinian agency and self-determination, and for several reasons, including its bypassing of the stipulations of the Geneva Conventions, is inconsistent with international law. But in the absence of a more serious and equitable peace process, the current road map for Gaza offers the best chance for bringing desperately needed relief and recovery to the territory’s suffering population—as long as it is implemented fairly.

Assuming the Trump administration genuinely supports the plan and wants to see its fruition, a way forward through the current impasse still exists. The United States and its partners must do three things. The first is to recognize that Israel’s interests in Gaza are not the same as, and in many ways run directly counter to, those espoused by the Trump administration and the broader international community. Whereas the latter is focused on the long-term stabilization and the rehabilitation of Gaza, the former seems bent on making it impossible for Palestinians to continue living in the territory. Second, improvements in the daily lives of ordinary people in Gaza should be insulated, if not totally delinked, from the political process. The safety and dignity of more than two million civilians cannot continue to be held hostage to the decisions of Hamas, much less the machinations of internal Israeli politics. The well-being of Palestinians should not be a bargaining chip used by Israel, or for that matter the Board of Peace, to extract political or military concessions from Hamas.

Finally, the United States and the other mediators must work to ensure that both sides abide by their obligations under the October 2025 cease-fire and should be prepared to impose consequences for noncompliance. This includes ending armed attacks by both sides, allowing a massive influx of unconditional humanitarian aid, and restoring basic services, clearing debris, and helping revive local livelihoods as required in phase one of the Trump plan. Likewise, Hamas’s disarmament, Israeli withdrawal, the installation of a new administration in Gaza, and the territory’s reconstruction are not separate issues but parallel ones. They must be pursued in parallel, as laid out in the Board of Peace’s original road map, for the process to work. Finally, for any of these to be possible, the United States and the Board of Peace must press Israel to allow Palestinian technocrats and the newly trained Palestinian police force to enter Gaza as soon as possible.

These measures will be a tough sell in Washington, particularly given Trump’s close alignment with Netanyahu and the latter’s commitment to his extremist coalition partners. But there is no way around them, regardless of the outcome of October’s election in Israel. Although many observers expect a Netanyahu victory would give the prime minister the space to move ahead with Trump’s Gaza plan and the road map, the evidence of the last three years and the nature of the current government suggest he will not. A radical coalition under Netanyahu with a renewed mandate will likely spend the next four years working to finish destroying Palestinian life in Gaza, to say nothing of the West Bank, where Israel’s de facto annexation is proceeding at a breakneck pace.

Trump may well want to consider whether it is worth sacrificing his Gaza peace plan, on which he has staked considerable political capital, for an Israeli government that may be on its way out. The fallout from Gaza’s destruction and the suffering of its people will be felt for generations. Only Israel and its chief enabler in the White House can determine whether the years to come will be a time of rebuilding and healing or one of perpetual violence and instability.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/middle-ea.author: Alan Boswell
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/middle-ea.text:
ALAN BOSWELL is Project Director for the Horn of Africa at the International Crisis Group and host of The Horn, one of the organization’s podcasts.

Conflicts in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa Have Become Inseparable

On June 3, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the U.S. Congress that the fighting that had raged for three years in Sudan was now a “proxy war” and blamed Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) for frustrating American efforts to bring the conflict to an end. Rubio was saying out loud what many observers already knew: what started as a domestic power struggle has morphed into a wider regional war, drawing in outside powers and spilling across Sudan’s borders.

The spread of the conflict in Sudan is part of a larger geopolitical transformation. For much of the past century, policymakers have treated the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula as separate strategic regions divided by the Red Sea. That distinction is now evaporating. Wars on one side of the sea increasingly alter the military calculations on the other. This entanglement is only deepening in the wake of the United States’ and Israel’s decision in February to launch a war on Iran, driving a deeper wedge between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh (which were already at odds), weakening the American-anchored security order in the region, and underscoring the importance of securing the Red Sea for shipping.

For the past decade, the UAE has been the most aggressive outside player in the Horn of Africa, establishing ports and military bases, offering large financial packages to key allies, and involving itself extensively in Sudan’s civil war. But the recent war in Iran, along with the breakdown of the Emirati-Saudi security partnership in Yemen last December, made Riyadh less confident of Washington’s protection, more anxious about the UAE’s security ties to Israel, and more intent on controlling the Red Sea’s security picture. And so as Saudi Arabia has leaned into an alignment with Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan, it has also brought that alignment to bear to strengthen key partnerships in the Horn. It is trying to counter factions in the Horn that are backed by the UAE or Israel even as it struggles to manage threats from Iran and its allies—including the Houthis, who have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

At the same time, the risk of conflict is increasing between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), backed by Saudi Arabia and its allies, and Ethiopia, an ally of the emirates, as well as the chance that another direct war could erupt between Ethiopia and Eritrea. A new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the Red Sea would likely turn into a regional conflict that overlaps with the one in Sudan. And it would not only be aggravated by the existing Emirati-Saudi rift—it might well deepen that divide.
