https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Trump envoys, European officials to discuss ‘new ideas’ for Ukraine peace in Miami
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
President Donald Trump's envoys will meet Ukrainian and European officials in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" and seek a unified proposal to end the war with Russia, two US sources told AFP.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the talks after a day in which a Russian strike on buses killed 30 people in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, one of the deadliest attacks in weeks.

"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelensky said Thursday. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."

Zelensky said his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, as well as Ukraine's top officials: Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia will take part in the talks in Florida.

READ MORE
Black sea and black ops: How exposed is Europe to Ukraine war spillover?

The US-led peace efforts to end the Ukraine war have been largely stalled, with Washington focused on its conflict with Iran despite Kyiv saying Russia has ramped up aerial attacks.

But US officials said they were making a fresh effort in an enlarged format, following visits to Moscow and Kyiv by last month by Witkoff, Trump's business friend-turned-roving envoy, and the president's son-in-law Kushner.

"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region," one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.

"The American negotiators also invited national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union."

US officials said the envoys would discuss "security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan, and other aspects of the conflict."

READ MORE
More than 30 killed in Russian strike on buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk as Kyiv targets data centre

They added that the Europeans had expressed "frustrations" to Washington about energy costs -- which Trump has blamed on Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel refineries, rather than his Iran war.

"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.

"So, the United States is trying to mediate with the sides with the goal of creating a unified proposal."

Zelensky said last week that the United States wanted to revive peace efforts by trying to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia and hold it by the end of October.

The Kremlin said last month that three-way talks on ending the war could take place in October.

Previous rounds of talks have failed to yield tangible progress towards peace, with Moscow unwilling to drop its maximalist conditions to end the fighting.

Trump said earlier this week that he had a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although it was expected to focus on the reported death of a researcher at a Russian plague lab.

In a sign that Ukraine was under discussion, Witkoff was seen by AFP reporters traveling with Trump on Air Force One on Wednesday on a campaign trip to Texas for the US midterm elections.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/the.author: François PICARD
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/the.text:
With the United States in drawdown mode - and reports its president's entourage is coveting commercial deals with Moscow - what’s Europe’s to do? The same Europe that’s still grappling over whether the closing of a few Russian consulates is strong enough of a response to the August drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig, Germany. So... how far will Russia push Europe? How equipped are Europeans both for hybrid warfare and war on the cheap… what with the Ukraine war illustrating how easy it is to mass produce the drones that can pummel cities and sap morale? Is the threat real or exaggerated, particularly in the minds of the tens of millions who will be called on in the coming months to cast ballots in Spanish, French and Italian elections?

Produced by François Picard, Rebecca Gnignati, Juliette Laffont, Ilayda Habip, Charles Wente.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Students barricaded a high school in northeastern Paris with garbage bins on Thursday before police moved in with tear gas, as France’s nationwide protests showed few signs of ending.

The Hélène Boucher high school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests Thursday. Riot police gathered in side streets as students converged on the school. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid being recognized.

READ MORE
Live: French government vows to boost teacher numbers in bid to ease school crisis

At least a dozen demonstrations supporting the high school students’ movement were planned across France later in the day, including a rally at Place de la Bastille in Paris, where tear gas and a water cannon were fired at protesters.

Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when students, most of them under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, according to the interior ministry. The education ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed Thursday.

While the number of school closures was down compared to Tuesday, pressure is mounting on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.

The protests against the underfunding of schools – many of them struggling with dilapidated facilities and insufficient staff – have drawn troublemakers not concerned about the aims of the protest movement as well as unions and political groups.

In a TV address, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults”.

He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles”. France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth”, Lecornu said.

At the lycée, 18-year-old university student Emma Khelil came to offer support to those at the barricades at her former high school. She told The Associated Press that she’s really concerned about police violence.

“We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” Khelil said. She also said that she had noticed insulation problems and water leaks in the school building and had even seen rats on occasion. Other students confirmed that they’d seen rats too.

READ MORE
'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing

She was not convinced by Lecornu’s efforts to calm the situation.

“I don’t think the movement is going to lose momentum. As long as things don’t change, we’re going to see the movement grow stronger, and potentially a convergence of struggles, especially with the next presidential election coming up,” she said.

Not long after she spoke, police surrounded a nearby square. The crowd surged, and tear gas was fired.

Smoke from burning garbage nearby hung in the air at Place de la République as hundreds of high school and university students prepared to march toward Place de la Bastille, the demonstration’s focal point.

Some carried signs bearing their schools’ names; others held placards reading “More money for repression than for our education”, and “Who protects us from the police?”

“We’re here, we’re demonstrating, and we won’t stop. Until October, November, December if necessary. Nothing will stop us,” said Sofia Ferdials, 18, a student at Paris 8 University.

Dounia Gergeon, a 39-year-old school librarian, said she joined the demonstration at Place de la Bastille because she shared students’ concerns and worried about a broader crisis facing young people anxious about their futures. At the middle and high school where she works, time was set aside for students to discuss their demands.

“They do not feel supported,” she said. “They feel cornered and forced to work under these conditions.”

Authorities deployed tear gas and a water cannon at the protesters, some of whom hurled projectiles at riot police.

READ MORE
What France's student protesters want – and what the government is offering

France is not the only country to be dealing with student-related protests.

In Belgium, Willy Demeyer, the mayor of Liege, issued a ban on public gatherings until midnight on Oct. 16, citing a “real, serious and imminent risk” of further clashes and vandalism.

City police said they used water cannon and tear gas on Wednesday to hold back several hundred protesters. Authorities sent emergency text messages advising shopkeepers to close due to rioting.

Nearly 90 people were arrested and several police were injured. Police reinforcements were sent from the capital, Brussels, and from Antwerp, and more are coming. Smaller protests have been held in Mons and Charleroi.

Belgium’s Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said on social media that the “perpetrators will have to answer for their actions before the courts”.

The Belgian protests, organised through online chat groups, include demands for more teachers and smaller classes as well as complaints about education reform in Belgium, but are also likely inspired by events in France.

Student protests have spread to several Italian cities, though on a much smaller scale and over a broader set of domestic grievances. Activists have explicitly invoked the French movement with the slogan “let’s do as they do in France”, while organising school occupations, assemblies and marches.

In Turin, students occupied several high schools over building conditions, education funding and increased military spending. In Rome, students occupied one high school and walked out of another, while students in Naples added opposition to a planned migrant detention centre to their demands.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Two Latvian men arrested at UK base housing US and NATO intelligence hubs
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
UK police said Thursday they had arrested two Latvians inside a military base in southeast England housing US and NATO intelligence hubs after the perimeter fence was breached.

The incident comes days after an incident near another military base in southwest England.

Counter-terrorism police said the two men, age 36 and 32, were arrested at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire, southeast England.

They are being held on suspicion of trespass and suspicion of entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK", said police.

Both are Latvian nationals residing in the UK.

The arrests come after a major incident at RAF Fairford on September 27 that led to the arrest of seven men, all in their 20s, who have since been released on bail. One is a dual UK-Iranian national.

Following that incident, the United States withdrew its B-1 bombers stationed at the Fairford base.

READ MORE
US withdraws B-1 bombers from British military base RAF Fairford amid security concerns

"At this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week," said counter-terrorism policing head Helen Flanagan

But the authorities were "keeping an open mind", she added in a statement.

RAF Molesworth, formerly a World War II airbase, is now a non-flying facility managed by the US Air Force.

It also hosts the NATO Intelligence Fusion Centre, whose website says it has a workforce of more than 200; and Washington's intelligence operations in Europe and Africa, according to the CIA website.

Police said a security patrol had spotted an abandoned vehicle near the base and police found a "small breach" before arresting the men in the early hours of Thursday.

The nature of the threat at RAF Fairford is still not clear but police were called to the site after three white vans were spotted acting "suspiciously" in its vicinity.

Last June, pro-Palestinian activists broke into another airbase, RAF Brize Norton in southern England, posting video showing them spraying a plane with red paint.

Police say perimeter fence was breached after a "small breach" at the base. The two men, aged 36 and 32, are being held on suspicion of trespass and suspicion of entering a prohibited place.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: French, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.

SpaceX brought the US, French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.

NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.

They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.

“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet”.

READ MORE
Exclusive: French astronaut Sophie Adenot recounts her ‘miracle’ mission from orbiting ISS

Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them – NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired – fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.

The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.

Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.

In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.

Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy moustache – a space rarity – groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style moustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honour his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew moustaches in solidarity.

Will his moustache disappear now that his mission is over?

“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”

Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the US, Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/peo.title: How long will the global energy crunch last?
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/peo.author: Kate MOODY
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/peo.text:
Jim Burkhard, Vice President and Head of Research for Oil Markets, Energy and Mobility at S&P Global, says elevated oil prices are here to stay. "It's the new normal until flows are normalised out of the Strait of Hormuz. There's no replacing the Middle East as a source of supply."

He says damaged infrastructure and high shipping costs are also part of the medium to long-term challenge. "You also have a refining issue, which is not confined to the Middle East (...) you've gone from $60,000 as the daily rate for one of these [oil] tankers to over a million. So the transportation costs have gone up – it's really stunning."

Burkhard says that after two energy crises in less than five years, governments are looking at different ways to ensure their energy security. "How does a country become more resilient in terms of safeguarding its energy supply? And the answer is not going to be the same around the world. Some countries may say, look, we want to produce more oil and gas in or nearby our country. Others are saying we want to move away from oil and gas. So it's a mixed response, it's not a uniform response, and it depends on the resources and options that a particular country or region has at its disposal."
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/peo.summary: Jim Burkhard says high shipping costs and infrastructure are also part of the challenge. He says the Middle East is not a source of supply for oil and gas.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Search warrants for former prince Andrew's homes were unlawful, UK court rules
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
British police on Thursday said that search warrants it secured to search properties linked to King Charles III' younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been incorrectly granted and must be quashed.

King Charles' younger ​brother was arrested on ‌suspicion of misconduct in public office in February and searches carried out at properties in Sandringham, eastern England, and Windsor.

Andrew was suspected ‌of leaking confidential government documents to the late convicted sex-offender ⁠Jeffrey Epstein when Andrew was a British trade representative, between 2001 and 2011.

Police have not charged him and Andrew, ​the second son of the late Queen Elizabeth II, ‌has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, also saying he regrets their friendship.

WATCH MORE
Epstein, Andrew's arrest and a royal crisis

The arrest of Mountbatten-Windsor, and the anger over his relationship ‌with Epstein, left the British royal family facing one of its worst crises in ​90 years.

Mountbatten-Windsor applied for the search warrants to be quashed and Thames Valley Police said it accepted that they had not been properly granted.

"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed," a Thames Valley Police spokesperson said.

"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."

It said its criminal investigation which began after the release of millions of documents by the US Department of Justice relating to the late US sex offender Epstein was still ongoing.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Ten people were injured after the car crashed near a procession of Knights fans at Wallsend on October 3. (ABC News)

The 18-year-old P-plater who allegedly struck a crowd of Newcastle Knights fans at Wallsend on grand final weekend has been granted bail after a hearing in Newcastle Local Court.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe did not apply for bail at his first court appearance on October 4, and has spent six nights in custody.

Mr Samarasinghe is due back in court at the end of the month.

The 18-year-old accused of driving a car that hit and injured 10 Knights fans in Newcastle has been granted bail at a review hearing, after spending six nights in custody.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe is facing a total of nine charges, including three counts of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, three counts of negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and three counts of causing bodily harm by misconduct.

He appeared via audiovisual link in Newcastle Local Court today, after his lawyers lodged a bail review application earlier this week.

Thousands of fans had lined the streets of Wallsend to wave the Newcastle Knights off to their first NRL grand final in 25 years, before a car rammed into the crowd at a roundabout on Link Road.

Ten people were hospitalised after the incident and two victims, including a 5-year-old girl, were left in a critical condition at the time.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe faced a bail review hearing today. (Source: Facebook)

The court heard Mr Samarasinghe, a P-plater, was seen driving erratically before the crash.

He was arrested soon after the incident and faced court less than 24 hours later.

In his first appearance on October 4, Mr Samarasinghe did not apply for bail, which was formally refused.

He has since undergone a medical assessment in custody.

Hunter New England Health confirmed the conditions of the 10 patients had improved since the incident, and three remain in care in a stable condition.

Calls have been growing for a state-led trauma response to assist the thousands of potential witnesses to the crash.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.title: Nurse says hospital parking fix needed after being chased to her car
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.author: Clancy Balen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Nurse Audrey McAllister says she was followed by a group of men while walking to her car after a shift. (ABC News)

A Royal Hobart Hospital nurse says she was chased to her car by a group of men on Queens Domain after a shift.

The nursing union says it wants to see better parking solutions and more safety measures introduced for hospital staff.

The Tasmanian government says it is undertaking "occupational violence prevention risk assessments" of all entrances to the hospital.

A Hobart-based nurse who was chased by a group of young men while she walked to her car after work says a lack of parking options in the city continues to put health workers at risk.

The incident occurred on Monday night when Audrey McAllister had just finished her shift at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

It was late, just past 11pm, but not an unusual time for the nurse to clock-off.

"I don't want to park up there again": Nurse approached by group of men after shift

However, as Ms McAllister walked to her car, which was parked at Queens Domain — a roughly one-kilometre walk from the hospital — she was chased by a group of about seven young men who began to yell at her as she walked past.

Ms McAllister ran to her car and locked the doors, before calling the police.

While she made it back to her vehicle safe and physically unharmed, Ms McAllister said the experience had left her shaken.

"I don't ever want to park up there again," she told 936 ABC Hobart.

The area around Queens Domain is where many nurses, midwives and other shift workers park their cars to save money on expensive inner-city car park fees, or where they are forced to park due to the lack of options close to the hospital.

There is no dedicated parking for hospital workers in Hobart's CBD.

While only a short walk from the city centre, the Queens Domain area is poorly lit and predominantly bushland.

Securing safe and affordable parking for health staff is an issue that the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Union (ANMF), of which Ms McAllister is a delegate, wants to see addressed.

"Unfortunately, that's not an isolated incident," ANMF Tasmania branch secretary Emily Shepherd said of Ms McAllister's experience.

"We don't want to wait until one of our members has some serious adverse outcome or, worse, loses their life in this type of scenario."

The Royal Hobart Hospital is centrally located in Hobart's CBD and is the largest hospital in the state.

Often, however, staff are unable to access nearby parking.

The closest option, Argyle Street car park, closes at 10pm.

Emily Shepherd says the union is extremely concerned about Audrey McAllister's experience. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The nearby Market Place car park is open 24/7 but can quickly become expensive or unaffordable if access is needed several times per week.

Ms McAllister said she would like to see private car park providers create dedicated and safe hospital staff parking for shift workers.

"There's no subsidised rates for healthcare workers," Ms McAllister said.

The ANMF said it had put up a raft of requests to the Tasmanian government to try and encourage it to provide better safety measures for health staff as part of ongoing enterprise agreement negotiations.

These included introducing a shuttle service or security to escort staff back to their vehicles after their night shifts, and for a roof to be built over the bike storage area at the hospital so that staff can ride to work without fear of theft.

A Tasmanian government spokesperson said any violence or threatening behaviour towards health staff was completely unacceptable, "regardless of whether they are on duty, or travelling to and from their place of work".

The spokesperson said "violence prevention risk assessments" of all entrances to the hospital were being undertaken, and the government remained committed to delivering fair pay rises and improved conditions for nurses and midwives.

"We are continuing to negotiate in good faith," they said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.title: Students run hairdressers and cafe at remote Indigenous school
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.author: Vanessa Jarrett
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Teacher Alison Cope with students Juu'garr Bamboo and Jahlaila Beckett. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

New VET training spaces have opened at the Wadja Waja High School, with a cafe, hairdressers and recreation facility.

It allows the 110 students at the independent school in Woorabinda to access more education and training closer to home.

Principal Cherie Blinco says attendance at the school has improved, as the new opportunities give the students a reason to come.

There is more than meets the eye when you look inside the collection of green buildings nestled at the rear of the Wadja Wadja High School.

The front donga has been kitted out as a cafe, with a counter space for taking orders, a coffee machine and a dining area.

Just next door is a hair salon, complete with mirrors, wash basins and styling tools.

Across the corridor, fishing rods hang on the wall, with tables arranged into a study room.

Student Lataya Skeen taking coffee orders in the training cafe. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

The services might be commonplace in other communities, but for the 1,000 people who call Woorabinda home, these spaces are a rarity.

"We looked at the community and what we needed in community," school principal Cherie Blinco said.

The Aboriginal community, 170 kilometres south-west of Rockhampton, only has a handful of shops, with the nearest place to order a coffee about 40 kilometres away.

The new facilities allow the senior students at the school to study vocational certificates that also go towards their year 12 graduation.

"These spaces are about much more than training; they are about creating opportunities for our young people here in Woorabinda, building confidence and employment skills," Ms Blinco said.

Wadja Wadja High School principal Cherie Blinco with former teacher Hector Costello. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

The idea to offer vocational education and training (VET) subjects at the school was the brainchild of retired principal Hector Costello, who did advisory work at the school in 2019.

"What I discovered was the standard curriculum they were delivering just wasn't working for the kids here," he said.

"In VET you can achieve much more tangible things and it's got much greater real-life applicability for students here.

"A lot of schools are doing it but for this community it has worked perfectly. "

Enrolments at the Wadja Wadja High School have grown over the past 12 months to now 110 students. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Attendance rates at the school have "skyrocketed" over the last few months since the VET programs were introduced, principal Cherie Blinco said.

"It gives them a purpose to come to school … learning something that they can use within their community and it means that they don't have to leave to get that education," she said.

Future hair salon students Juu'garr Bamboo, Jahlaila Beckett, Virginia Finlay and Carol Oakley. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Kuku Yalanji woman and year 10 student Jahlaila Beckett plans to study a certificate in salon services next year.

"I was pretty excited … The commitment we want to put into doing hairs and stuff. I think it's a big opportunity to go out there and explore more," Jahlaila said.

Wadja Wadja woman and year 11 student Juu'garr Bamboo is also enrolled next year and said she had already learnt some things that might help her to become a hairdresser in the future.

"We've just been practising hairstyles and how to start a conversation with some of the locals here in Woorabinda," Juu'garr said.

Kulgoodah Dancers, led by Terrence Adams Snr, performing at the grand opening ceremony for the new VET training spaces at the Wadja Wadja High School. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

An official grand opening of the space was held this week.

Students opened the cafe for trial runs over term three, before an official grand opening of the space this week, which welcome community members.

Community members of Woorabinda supporting the new cafe. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

"Now that we've got it in Woorabinda, it's going to be so great," local Woorabinda resident Renee Hill said.

"It's so wonderful seeing the kids having a go at everything.

"We don't put the kids down, we encourage them so it's really good to come and pop in and have a coffee and just see their smiling faces."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.title: State government takes control of Sydney Town Hall Square project
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Urban Development and Planning

Designs for the proposed public square were unveiled in August. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

A planned $94 million plaza in front to Sydney Town Hall has been deemed a State Significant Development.

The City of Sydney council project will now be subject to another development approval process.

The Independent Planning Commission found it could deliver "significant" public and economic benefits.

The NSW government has moved to take control of the City of Sydney's Town Hall Square project.

Planning Minister Paul Scully last month forced a pause on work to create a 4,500-square-metre civic plaza outside the CBD's Town Hall, while the Independent Planning Commission (IPC) provided advice on the proposal.

Plans for the square were put on display for community feedback in August after council unanimously resolved in February to move ahead with the design and construction of the square.

The council has said the plaza, which will require the demolition of several buildings the city has obtained since the 1980s, was necessary to create a gathering point for community events, music events and markets.

Mr Scully said he accepted an IPC recommendation the proposal be declared a State Significant Development (SSD), a development approval process reserved for large or sensitive projects, paving the way for a council development application.

"This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application before its determination by the IPC," he said in a statement.

The City of Sydney has allocated $150 million to the project. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

The IPC assessment only considered whether the project should be declared a SSD and did not grant development approval.

In advice to the minister, IPC member Richard Pearson said the square could deliver "significant" public and economic benefits and given state-owned public transport infrastructure, its significance extended beyond the council area.

The City of Sydney council has been contacted for comment.

The council has previously said while the project would be delivered in coordination with the state government and a SSD designation could lead to "unnecessary costs or delays".

Council has estimated the project would cost $94 million with $150 million allocated to allow for cost overruns.

The house and street in Orelia have been cordoned off after the man's death. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Homicide detectives are investigating the death of a man at a house in Perth's southern suburbs.

WA Police say they were called to a residence on Nye Way in Orelia about 2:20pm yesterday after "reports of a serious incident".

Officers found the man dead at the house.

In a statement, police said another man "known to the deceased" was found inside the house and taken into custody.

Detectives and forensic pathologists were among those sent to the scene.  (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

The investigation is being led by the Homicide Squad and remains ongoing.

The street was still blocked off this morning, with three police vehicles on the scene, along with a forensic van.

Officers appeared to be working in the backyard of the property.

Earlier, police said detectives and forensic specialists were among those at the scene.

"The incident is contained; there is no threat to public safety," they said in a statement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.title: Powderfinger confirm reunion, 16 years after breaking up
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.author: Dan Condon
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

After days of cryptic clues, Brisbane rock icons Powderfinger have confirmed they are getting the band back together. (Supplied: Ian Jennings)

Powderfinger, one of the most celebrated acts in Australian music history, have confirmed they are reforming, 16 years after breaking up.

In a video posted to the band's social media this morning, frontman Bernard Fanning said they would "do some shows all around Australia from September next year".

"We always said that if we were going to get back together to do some shows, that you guys would be the first to know," he said.

"We're going to build something pretty special just for you guys," guitarist Darren Middleton said. "We'll see you from the stage."

The video confirmed what fans had already suspected: They were behind a series of cryptic teasers that had appeared around the country over the past week.

Internet sleuths took no time figuring out Powderfinger's connection to the posts.

They identified references to the band embedded in opaque imagery shared via a new account named The Return of the Electric Horsemen, and projected onto landmarks across the country.

The rumour mill has been in overdrive ever since, with some fans predicting a full-scale reunion, while others are picking something less dramatic, like reissues of classic albums.

Yesterday, the band's official account, which had recently been wiped clean, posted the tease for the first time.

"Add enough time to enough variables and something extraordinary happens…" the caption read.

Formed in Brisbane in 1989, Powderfinger spent their first few years as just another local rock band, until their second album, 1996's Double Allergic, brought them their first taste of national acclaim.

Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

By the time they released Odyssey Number Five in 2000, they were one of the biggest bands in the country.

That record peaked at the top of the charts and won six ARIA awards, including Album of the Year and Record of the Year for My Happiness.

They are an especially decorated act in the triple j Hottest 100, winning the 1999 and 2000 countdowns, making the annual polls 22 times, and picking up three entries in last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, including a spot in the top 10.

There have been two semi-reunions over the years. Four members played together at Splendour in the Grass in 2017, and the band's virtual performance during 2020's COVID-19 lockdowns raised more than $450,000 for Support Act and Beyond Blue.

The band confirmed they would head back on the road from September next year, but stopped short of sharing further details.

Whenever and wherever those shows take place, Powderfinger will not be the only Australian legacy act fans have been clamouring to see this year.

The news comes just a week after Powderfinger's peers Silverchair responded to calls for them to reform for the NRL grand final.

"Thanks to everyone who's asked if we're playing before the game. We're way too rusty, so sorry, no can do," the statement read.

Powderfinger embarked on a mammoth farewell tour of the country before splitting in 2010, selling more than 200,000 tickets across 34 shows.

Topic:
Urban Development and Planning

The foreshore redevelopment at Cable Beach in WA's Kimberley continues to remain a construction site as its opening date approaches.

Originally slated to be complete mid-to-late this year, the project's timeline and opening has blown out to next year.

Broome locals remain frustrated but not surprised by the extended delays.

One of Australia's most-famous beachfronts continues to remain a construction site with a timeline for the multimillion-dollar redevelopment of Cable Beach blowing out.

The landmark beach in Broome, 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, is a major state and national tourists drawcard with its famous camel rides and sunsets a feature of West Australian tourist campaigns.

But the long-term redevelopment of the precinct, which will see a water park, amphitheatre, new beach access and other features added, has left access to much of the area restricted since 2023.

Keen tourists and locals were promised the final stage of the project would be complete by the mid to late-2026.

Camel rides are a staple of Cable Beach tourism.  (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

But as that deadline approaches the Shire of Broome says the project's official opening will not occur until 2027.

They were unable to confirm whether construction work would be complete by the end of this year.

The development has drawn a mixed reception from locals, with many frustrated by the ongoing restrictions to parking and beach access.

Jemma Vincent and Giles Fresher grew up in Broome, enjoying everything Cable Beach has to offer.

Ms Vincent said she was not surprised to hear about delays to the opening.

"Sounds about right, everything takes a long time to do here," she said.

Jemma Vincent and Giles Fresher grew up in Broome and say the redevelopment delays impact the lifestyle. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Among Ms Vincent's circle of friends, being denied car access via ramp to the northern side of Cable Beach was the biggest concern.

"People didn't really care about [the construction] as long as you could get down onto the beach and have car access," she said.

But fellow Broome local Grant Garrett said he believed the redeveloped foreshore would be great for tourism.

Grant Garrett has lived in Broome for two decades and is supportive of the project. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

"Any kind of progress for Broome is good, but I think it's come along very slowly, unfortunately," he said.

"Overall, when it's all done, it will be a great improvement for the community and tourism industry."

While supportive of the redevelopment overall, Spinifex Brewing chief executive Leanne Andrews said the road closures had reduced foot traffic and spontaneous visits to its Cable Beach venue.

"Probably the biggest thing is not knowing when it's going to finish and the prolonged staffing impacts," she said.

"I've no doubt it will be positive in the end but it would be good to know when it's actually going to finish."'

The chief executive of Broome's Spinifex Brewing said road closures had impacted their Cable Beach business. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Ms Andrews said a lack of communication around progress and timelines had proven disruptive for Cable Beach businesses.

"It's still on the website as mid to late-2026. It's been one of those developments that's just kept on keeping on," she said.

"We're one community and I guess we all just want to see each other succeed."

Cable Beach is known for its four-wheel drive access. (ABC News)

A Shire of Broome spokesperson said it was committed to providing updates as key milestones were confirmed.

"We know there is strong community interest in the redevelopment," they said.

"The shire is working closely with the contractor and reviewing the latest project information to ensure the information we provide to the community is accurate and up to date.

"Planning is also underway for an official launch event which is expected to take place next year."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.title: Michael Robotham's latest novel sat in his bottom drawer for 35 years
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.author: Nicola Heath
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Michael Robotham is a two-time winner of the CWA Gold Dagger for Best Crime Novel. (Supplied: Hachette Australia)

Michael Robotham was a 22-year-old journalist working for a Sydney newspaper when he began writing his first novel in the early 1980s.

"[It] was going to be my great Australian novel … [and] win me every prize in the world," Robotham tells ABC Arts.

He finished it six years later, when he was living in London. It came very close to being published.

Set in a small country town based on his hometown of Gundagai in the Riverina region of NSW, the novel had the working title Blessed Are the Meek.

"I missed out by a single vote in an acquisitions meeting for a major publisher," Robotham says.

"I was told that it was really the setting … They just felt it was a little bit too hard for them to market, because this was obviously well before Jane Harper and Liane Moriarty and few Australian-set books had ever done well internationally."

He consigned the manuscript to his bottom drawer and spent the next decade working as a journalist and then as a ghostwriter.

ABC Radio National's annual Top 100 Books countdown is on! Tune in on October 17-18 to hear how the nation voted.

Robotham returned to Australia in the 90s, but when he eventually began writing a new novel he recalled the advice he'd been given and set it in the UK.

That book, The Suspect — the first instalment of what would become the popular Joe O'Loughlin series — triggered a bidding war at the London Book Fair before it was published in 2004. It has since sold more than 1 million copies worldwide and was adapted for television in 2022.

Now, two decades later, Robotham has finally set a book in Australia.

Tell Me Something True, Robotham's 20th novel, is a "seriously rewritten and re-imagined" version of that first manuscript.

"All the story and the characters remain the same, but it's been in the bottom drawer since the 1980s," he says.

Robotham wrote the first version of Tell Me Something True on a Remington typewriter, so the first step of the rewriting process was transferring it to a computer.

When he cast an appraising eye over the original story, he recognised both strengths and weaknesses in his work.

"I read some sections and thought, 'Wow, that guy could really write! Whatever happened to him?!' And then I read other sections that I thought, 'Oh, that's so naive. That was a 20-year-old … who was very self-indulgent and full of himself.'"

Robotham says his latest novel, Tell Me Something True, leans into the tradition of small-town mysteries. (Supplied: Hachette Australia)

He also found that the world had moved on in many ways.

"There was no such thing as a sensitivity reader all those years ago," he says.

"It's amazing how you'd put things in books 20 years ago that you wouldn't put in a book today."

But the most significant change was structural. The original story unfolded chronologically.

"Back then, it was the story of Arlo Hackett and his brother Luke … and into their life I dropped this very feisty, opinionated teenage girl, Saxon, who arrives in a stolen car," he says.

In the published version, Robotham created a second storyline set in the present as Arlo returns to his hometown of Yulara after his release from prison.

To contemporary readers, Tell Me Something More belongs to a well-established tradition in Australian publishing of mysteries set in the bush, also known as outback noir, kicked off by Jane Harper's 2006 novel, The Dry.

But, as Robotham good-humouredly points out, his novel predates the trend by decades.

"I did this first," he says. "Well before the others did it, I'd done it."

Robotham describes Tell Me Something True as his most autobiographical work.

"It's my most personal book in a sense," he says. "There are scenes in it that are lifted straight out of my childhood."

Robotham's father was a teacher, and the family moved often when he was a child.

His primary school years were spent in Gundagai, a town of 2,000 people on the Murrumbidgee River known, among other claims to fame, as the resting place of 19th-century bushranger Captain Moonlite.

Robotham says the novel's protagonist, Arlo Hackett, "pleads guilty because he believes he should have stopped the crime happening". (ABC Radio - Conversations)

While Robotham says the town is easily recognisable to anyone familiar with its geography and history, he chose not to use its name in print, renaming it Yulara instead.

"In small towns there is only one high school and one high school principal and only one senior police officer," he says.

"I didn't want people playing a guessing game as to whether I based any of this on real-life characters."

As the popularity of outback noir attests, a small town is a fertile setting for a fiction writer.

"Small country towns are very slow to forgive," Robotham says.

"They're full of secrets and yet they're places where it's almost impossible to keep a secret."

There's a literary crime spree underway in Australia thanks to authors such as Jane Harper and Chris Hammer.

In Tell Me Something True, the newly freed Arlo attempts to resume life in Yulara, but encounters hostility from the town's residents, many of whom he's known his whole life.

His mother is in a nursing home and the house he grew up in is in disrepair.

With nowhere else to go, he sets about fixing up the house.

As he reflects on his past, told in flashbacks, he begins to question the events that led to his imprisonment.

"Initially you're asking readers to accept a narrator who spent 12 years in prison for being an accessory to a terrible rape and murder," Robotham says.

"And you're thinking, 'How am I going to go along with this? Do I want to spend time with this man?'

"But as his story unfolds, you realise how badly wronged he's been."

Robotham says he can see his early literary influences in Tell Me Something True, from John Irving's The World According to Garp (1978) and Hotel New Hampshire (1981) to John Steinbeck's 1937 novella, Of Mice and Men.

Also an enthusiastic reader of Australian fiction, Robotham's number one choice in the Top 100 Australian Books was Illywhacker by Peter Carey.

Shortlisted for the 1985 Booker Prize, the novel tells the story of the memorable and idiosyncratic Herbert Badgery.

"He's a 139-year-old con man who relates the story of his life, and you can't believe a word of what he says … and I loved that," Robotham says.

Robotham is also an admirer of Year of Wonders by Geraldine Brooks, his former colleague-turned-fellow novelist.

"It's an astonishing piece of research," he says.

"I'm in awe of people who write historic fiction. The idea of capturing that period of history of the plague years in that tiny, isolated village in Britain — I thought she did a remarkable job."

The latest new releases from some of the world's biggest literary stars, including Emily St John Mandel, RF Kuang and Kate Atkinson, are among this month's best books.

Robotham acknowledges we're at a crucial moment in global publishing thanks to the encroachment of AI.

"There was something like a million extra books published in the last year because they've been generated by AI. There's going to be a tsunami of AI slop," he says.

"But I'm a realist … It might make mistakes now, but AI will get better."

Robotham is currently part of a lawsuit in the US accusing tech companies of stealing authors' work to train their language models.

"I hate the idea that we're going to probably cave into the AI companies and give them some sort of right to Australian copyrighted material," he says.

"To me, it's like someone robbing your house and then saying to you, 'Don't worry about it, I'll give you your toaster back'."

Michael Robotham will be at Sydney Writers' Festival's Homegrown at the State Library of NSW on October 10.

ABC Radio National will count down the Top 100 Australian Books on air on October 17 and 18.

Topic:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art

Mr Yumbulul's 1983 mosaic graces the floors of Sydney's famous Bondi Pavilion. (ABC News: Tamsyn Buckle)

Community leaders, Mr and Mrs T and C Yumbulul both died late last month.

Mr Yumbulul was an Arnhem Land clan leader and world-renowned artist.

Mrs Yumbulul was an Italian migrant who moved to Arnhem Land as a young woman.

Indigenous leaders around Australia are paying their respects to Arnhem Land elders Mr and Mrs T and C Yumbulul, following their deaths last month.

Aboriginal and Torres Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names and images of people who have died, used with the permission of their family.

Mrs Yumbulul migrated from Italy with her family as a child, before moving to Elcho Island off the coast of north-east Arnhem Land as a young woman.

She went on to marry Mr T Yumbulul, the son of legendary philosopher and diplomat David Burrumarra.

Mr Yumbulul was a world-renowned artist whose work features as a mosaic on the floor of Sydney's Bondi Pavilion and in galleries around the world.

Mr and Mrs Yumbulul are being remembered by Indigenous leaders across Australia. (Supplied)

Marina DeJurnett (Wangurra) was raised by the Yumbululs and described them as "once in a lifetime people".

"He wouldn't have been able to live without her and she couldn't and wouldn't live without him either."

Family member Marina DeJurnett (Wangurra) described Mr and Mrs Yunbulil as "once in a lifetime people". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mrs Yumbulul was born in the city of Trieste in northern Italy and migrated to Adelaide with her family as a 12-year-old.

She travelled to Arnhem Land as a young woman where she met Mr Yumbulul in the community of Galiwin'ku on remote Elcho Island.

After marrying Mr Yumbulul in 1982, she spent the rest of her life with him, learned the local language and became an integral part of the community.

Prominent academic and Aboriginal activist has been friends with the Yumbululs since the 1990s. (Supplied: Potter Museum of Art)

Long-time friend and colleague, academic Marcia Langton, described her as "a delight to speak to".

"She always maintained her own very strong personality, but she was also beautifully integrated into Yolŋu culture," she said.

One of Mr Yumbulul's artworks featured on the world's first plastic banknote, a special edition $10 note commemorating the bicentenary of European settlement in 1988.

Mr Yumbulul contested the reserve bank's use of his art in the Federal Court. (ABC News)

The image depicted the "highly sacred" morning star poles, which Professor Langton said were "only seen at ceremonies".

It was used without Mr Yumbulul's permission and he sued the Reserve Bank of Australia over it.

While he was unsuccessful, the judge's comments set a new legal precedent.

Top End historian Mike Owen said Mr Yumbulul played an important role in identifying and recording historical artefacts from around the world.

Mike Owen said the Yumbululs life stories were "just extraordinary". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"His parents and grandparents grew up in a pre-iron world … so I was able to ask him about artefacts that he would have heard about as a kid," he said.

Mr Owen said Mr Yumbulul's ability to "engage with all sorts of people" meant he helped identify ancient artefacts from around Australia and as far away as Scotland.

"I was over in the Ness of Brodgar, an important archaeological site in the Orkneys, in 2019," Mr Owen said.

Mr annd Mrs Yumbulul were passionate about preserving and sharing the history of Arnhem Land. (Supplied)

"[Archaeologists] found these artefacts and they didn't know what they were for.

"So I asked [Mr Yumbulul] and he said, 'oh, they're for getting the meat out of crab's legs'.

"To be able to go to someone and talk to them about what we as humans were doing and using in the Stone Age is remarkable."

Ms DeJurnett said while art and culture were big parts of the Yumbululs' lives, they "didn't sit in one bucket," and their work with remote communities throughout northern Australia had a big impact.

"They both worked in health," she said.

"[Mr Yumbulul] led the regionalisation of health services.

"This was basically returning back control over health services across the region to Aboriginal control."

Mr and Mrs Yumbulul were married for nearly 45 years. (Supplied)

Former federal minister for Indigenous Affairs Nigel Scullion first met Mr Yumbulul when he was working as a fisherman off the Arnhem Land coast in 1984.

He described him as "a great Australian".

He said Mr Yumbulul was "a very fine negotiator and a great diplomat" who regularly gave him advice during his time in politics.

Nigel Scullion first met the Yumbululs in 1984 and they became close friends. (Supplied)

"He had me on speed dial and he used to, from time to time, let me know what he thought about particular matters," he said.

"He made sure that his voice was heard, not by the activist sort of yelling, always through diplomacy."

Councillor Louise Elliot has been suspended two times during this term, and is now appealing a third suspension. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Hobart councillor Louise Elliot is appealing a decision handed down by an independent panel which found she had harassed fellow councillor Ryan Posselt.

The complaint is from May last year and has only been made public following changes to the Tasmanian Local Government Act.

If the appeal is unsuccessful, it would give the Minister for Local Government the option to remove her from council, even if she is re-elected in the current local government elections.

A Hobart councillor who is running for deputy mayor could be removed from council if re-elected if her appeal against a third suspension is unsuccessful.

A code of conduct panel found councillor Louise Elliot had committed four breaches by harassing fellow councillor Ryan Posselt on multiple occasions.

It determined Cr Elliot be suspended from performing and exercising the functions and powers of her office for a period of one month, and for her to apologise to Cr Posselt.

Cr Elliot was found to have harassed a fellow councillor on multiple occasions. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

She has appealed the decision, meaning the suspension has not come into effect.

The findings had previously been kept confidential, with all code of conduct determination reports unable to be disclosed until they were placed on the council agenda, following the conclusion of appeals.

LISTEN: Council code of conduct process being used for 'nonsense', former mayor says

But local government law reforms earlier this year mean they are no longer considered confidential once they are provided to all relevant parties.

Local government elections are currently occurring in Tasmania, with voting to close on October 27.

Cr Elliot is running for councillor and deputy mayor of Hobart.

If she is re-elected and her suspension is upheld, she will serve the suspension in the next term of council and the minister has the option of sacking her.

The complaint was submitted by Cr Posselt in May 2025 and outlined five instances in which he argued Cr Elliot had breached the code of conduct, four of which were upheld.

The panel found Cr Elliot harassed Cr Posselt on three of these occasions, all of which she disputed.

Councillor Ryan Posselt's complaint included a lack of moderation of social media comments intended to embarrass him. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The breaches were described as similar in nature to previous breaches.

The panel's report said Cr Elliot "considered that by continuing the kinds of behaviours which had already been shown to breach the Code of Conduct, this would highlight a need for change to the Code itself".

The panel said "this civil disobedience is a political strategy. However, it is not and cannot be a defence to a charge of breaching the Code as it now exists.

Cr Elliot was also found in breach by not moderating comments on her Facebook page under a post she had made about a previous code of conduct matter with Cr Posselt.

The panel described the resulting comments as "unfair, embarrassing, and offensive".

"Allowing material to be published on her Facebook page which would be considered offensive and embarrassing to a reasonable person, as determined objectively by the Panel, is a breach of the Code," the panel wrote.

Cr Elliot told the panel she "can't be moderating comments 24/7".

A further complaint about an email Cr Elliot sent to councillors in which she said she was "disgusted" at a decision they made was not upheld.

Cr Elliot described the complaints as being related to "hurt feelings".

"If I was to lose my seat, if I was to lose my office, I'm not going away, I'd just get louder, with less restrictions," she said.

Her previous two suspensions related to similar breaches of the code of conduct.

She was suspended for seven days over social media posts in 2023, including posting an image of Hobart councillors beneath a headline stating "Hobart hates women" after they rejected her push for a third type of public bathroom for transgender people.

A code of conduct panel described this as "inflammatory, attention-grabbing, wholly unobjective and essentially child-like".

LISTEN: Speed date the Hobart lord mayor candidates

She was also suspended for two months in relation to publicising information regarding a parent of lord mayor Anna Reynolds, which a panel described as having "no purpose other than as an attempt to cause political harm to Cr Reynolds by association".

The Local Government Act says the minister "may remove the councillor from office" for a third suspension if they occur in one term of office, or if they are serving the second of two consecutive terms.

Local Government Minister Kerry Vincent was contacted for comment.

A government spokesperson said it wasn't appropriate to comment on individual matters.

"Tasmanians deserve to have confidence in their councillors; they're leaders in our community. The local government elections underway provide an opportunity for Tasmanians to elect their preferred councillors."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.title: Turtles found buried in metres of mud returned to rejuvenated wetland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.author: Zaarkacha Marlan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Paul Keyte releasing turtles into the Gingham Wetlands. (Supplied DCCEEW)

The first turtles rescued from a dried-out Gingham Waterhole in the Gwydir Wetlands near Moree are back in the wild.

Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo helped rehabilitate the rescued turtles and is now incubating more than 250 eggs laid by the reptiles.

The remaining adult turtles will be progressively released, while hatchlings are expected to be returned to the wild by the end of next year.

The first turtles rescued from a dried-out wetland in north-west NSW are back in their natural habitat, with a new generation of turtle hatchlings expected to join them later this year.

Ten broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles were released at Gingham Waterhole in the Gwydir Wetlands in September by the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW).

They were among 39 rescued from the waterhole after it dried out in April, and taken to Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo for rehabilitation.

Turtles covered in mud, saved from the Gwydir Wetlands by UNE ecologists in April 2026 (Supplied: Debbie Bower)

Senior keeper James Witcombe said seeing the first reptiles return to a refilled wetland after months in care was a significant moment.

"It's the kind of moment that we as zookeepers and conservationists live for, to see something that's a pretty devastating reality turn into a much better future," he said.

"To see that first group of 13 returning to their wetland and seeing photos of the wetland full of beautiful water and invertebrates returning to that space, it really is a special moment."

The 13 turtles were returned to Gingham Waterhole as part of a staged release in September. (Supplied: DCCEEW)

The turtles were found burrowed deep in the mud, after Water NSW temporarily suspended environmental water flows to the wetlands earlier this year.

Turtles buried in mud at the Gwydir Wetlands. (Supplied: Greens MLC Cate Faehrmann)

Mr Witcombe said the 39 reptiles arrived in Dubbo covered in thick mud and underwent comprehensive health assessments, while keepers quickly adapted the purpose-built platypus conservation centre to accommodate them.

"They were all covered in dense, filthy mud, so we set up a bit of a production line to get them all cleaned off and identified," he said.

Keepers and veterinarians monitored the turtles' recovery, regularly weighing them and providing plenty of food to improve their condition after they experienced stress in the drying wetland.

Once the turtles were healthy enough, keepers lowered the water temperature to mimic winter conditions and provided UV lamps and basking areas to give the light they needed.

The rescued turtles spent several months in care at Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo. (Supplied: DCCEEW)

The initial health checks also revealed 14 female broad-shelled turtles were carrying eggs.

Because broad-shelled turtles usually lay their eggs during rainy conditions, keepers instead induced egg-laying.

Now more than 250 turtle eggs are sitting in an incubator at the Dubbo zoo.

Most of the female broad-shelled turtles arrived at the zoo carrying eggs. (Supplied: DCCEEW)

"We will still see a very large percentage of those make it to hatching stage," Mr Witcombe said.

The hatchlings could provide an important boost to the population, with foxes and other feral pests known to dig up the subterranean turtle nests at the Gingham Waterhole.

The young turtles are expected to be released into the wild by the end of next year.

Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition

Environmental flows resumed in late May and refilled Gingham Waterhole, allowing the staged return of the turtles to begin.

DCCEEW executive director of conservation programs Ingrid Emery said the reptiles were being selectively released.

"They are being returned progressively over the coming months as the conditions allow and as they're healthy enough to do so," she said.

"We are seeing the ecosystem recover out there," she said.

Environmental water deliveries had been suspended earlier this year amid concerns about inundation of neighbouring private property.

Wildlife specialists rescued the turtles as Gingham Waterhole dried out earlier this year. (Supplied: DCCEEW)

Ms Emery said the department was working with landholders and an environmental water advisory group to plan future water deliveries.

"We're planning to use our environmental water to maintain refuge habitat, because we know we are going into a dry period," she said.

The released turtles will not be individually tracked, but Ms Emery said ongoing ecological monitoring would help the department assess the health of the wetland and plan future water management.

Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja has told his autobiography will come out after the South African Test series. (Getty Images: Albert Perez, file photo)

Australian captain Pat Cummins says the team has "moved on" from the infamous Sandpapergate incident.

Usman Khawaja, who played in the 2018 Cape Town Test that saw three players suspended over ball tampering, is preparing to release an autobiography.

Khawaja's book will be released next month, a week after Australia's Test tour of South Africa.

Pat Cummins says he is not fazed by the prospect of the so-called Sandpapergate incident being raised in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which will be the first from any Australian player who played in that 2018 Cape Town Test.

Cummins confirmed today Khawaja had called to inform him he was writing the book, which will be released days after the end of Australia's first Test tour of South Africa since the infamous match.

How much will be written about the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket remains to be seen.

Khawaja is a childhood friend of former opening partner David Warner, who copped a 12-month ban for the ball-tampering scandal.

In 2018, Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket to its very core. Here's how a febrile atmosphere colluded with a team persistently testing the limits of acceptability to change the game.

At the time, Warner was painted as the architect of the ploy, with captain Steve Smith also suspended for a year and Cameron Bancroft nine months.

There was a report at the time that Khawaja had suggested the team should take joint responsibility for the incident, rather than just the three players.

However, a Cricket Australia investigation found no other player had knowledge of the plan to apply sandpaper to the ball, a point that has long been maintained.

Australia's bowlers have also previously issued a statement saying they did not know a "foreign substance" would be taken onto the field.

There is no suggestion Khawaja's autobiography, which has been penned without a ghost writer, will suggest anything other than what the investigations found.

Usman Khawaja's (left) upcoming autobiography book may mention the 2018 South Africa tour and Sandpapergate. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney, file photo)

Cummins was asked ahead of Friday's first Test in Durban if Khawaja had specified how much detail he would go into and if he would agree with his former teammates' version of events.

"You would have to ask him," Cummins responded.

"It's obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times.

"It was dealt with then. All I can say is as a group we've moved on. [I'm] very happy with the last eight or nine years, how we've been as a group and evolved.

"He didn't go into too much detail … As always, it was, 'No worries. You can tell your story. That's fine.'"

It has been hard to escape talk of the 2018 series in the lead-up to the first Test.

South Africa is going in with two spinners for the first Test in Durban, but the Australian line-up is still unclear with illness and pitch questions still to be answered.

Cummins noted on Thursday there was a larger-than-normal media turn-out in Durban, with this also the battle between the world's top-two sides.

Beyond the ball-tampering scandal, the 2018 series was littered with clashes between the two teams from the middle of the pitch to dressing-room stairwells.

But tensions have thawed significantly since, with neither side expecting similar dramas.

"It was quite a big series that 2018. It was pretty full on," Cummins said.

"After that, I think pretty much every Test team in the world felt like they'd made some adjustments.

"This group is quite a different group in how we approach playing and I'm really proud of how the guys have been since that 2018 series."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/h.author: Annabel Bowles
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Nidal Hasan was an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major when he carried out a shooting in 2009. (AFP: Bell County Sherriff's Department)

The US says it will live stream its first firing squad execution by the military since World War II.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, was sentenced to death in 2013.

The execution is set to take place on December 3.

The United States's first execution by a military firing squad since World War II will be live streamed, the Pentagon has said.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people and injuring dozens more in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, would happen on December 3.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Mr Hegseth told conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News.

"People need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things."

When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Mr Hegseth replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on December third."

The execution is set to take place at the Texas military base where Hasan committed his crimes.

The Pentagon official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not offer more information and said details would follow.

It comes days after US President Donald Trump approved the execution by firing squad, set to be the first execution carried out by the US military since 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was hanged.

Psychiatrist Nidal Hasan is set to become the first person to be executed by the US military in more than six decades.

Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist at the time of the Al-Qaeda inspired mass shooting, was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.

He chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.

In November 2009, the US-born man opened fire at a medical facility on the Fort Hood base, which served as a staging point for soldiers later deployed to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Thirteen people were killed and 32 injured, most of them soldiers.

During Hasan's trial, it was revealed he spent weeks planning the deadly attack.

Nidal Malik Hasan was found guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder. (Reuters: Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)

The court heard he videoed a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol he purchased, and went to a gun range outside Austin where he asked for advice on how to reload with speed and precision.

Soldiers later testified that Hasan's rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting.

Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims.

The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.

Soldiers held a vigil at Hood Stadium in November 2009. (Reuters: Jessica Rinaldi)

Mr Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action.

Experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution.

"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," said Eugene R Fidell, a military law expert and visiting lecturer at Yale Law School.

This week authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched the execution of death row inmate Christa Pike, making headlines around the world.

Days after receiving two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, Pike woke up, becoming the first person to survive the administration of such drugs.

On Thursday, local time, Pike was walking around in her hospital room and speaking, according to her lawyer.

The botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner in which the US puts criminals to death.

As death row inmate Christa Pike remains in hospital following a failed lethal injection, we take a closer look at the track record for botched executions in the US.

Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and the vice-president of the National Institute of Military Justice, said at a time when many states were having difficulty carrying out lethal injections, firing squads were being seen as a more humane alternative.

"Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner," he said.

But Professor Fissell said: "I don't think that's what's motivating this [decision to execute Hasan by firing squad]."

"There's a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasise, the 'lethality culture'," he said.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Mr Hegseth's announcement raised a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns about Hasan's dignity.

"This is a president who's about spectacle and that's, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver," Professor Semel said.

At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Last year, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.title: Data centre operator Firmus pulls blockbuster ASX float after lacklustre demand
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.author: Nassim Khadem and Lin Lin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. (Supplied: Firmus Technologies)

The mega float of data centre operator Firmus has been pulled.

It follows poor interest from investors amid concerns about the company's debt and a lack of detail.

The company says it will pursue private funding.

AI data centre company Firmus has withdrawn its application to list on the ASX, scrapping what was set to be one of Australia's biggest share market floats.

The company cited recent market volatility and conditions, saying the offer would not appropriately reflect its long-term growth prospects.

Firmus said it would now pursue private market funding while considering other options.

"We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said in a statement.

Firmus, the AI factory builder backed by chip-making giant Nvidia, was set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997.

The company's founders, co-chief executives Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield, targeted a $44 billion valuation, but prospective investors pulled back based on the high sale price of $11 a share and concerns over an AI bubble.

Yesterday, reports emerged that Firmus and its advisors were considering reducing the size of the initial public offering (IPO) and lowering the per-share price from $11 to $8.25.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield at Firmus's St Leonards, Launceston site. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Many investors were also focused on Mr Curtis's criminal background — he is a former investment banker who served one year in prison a decade ago for insider trading.

With AI infrastructure demand accelerating across the Asia-Pacific, Firmus's website says its broader portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries: Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia.

It said two sites were operational in Australia and Singapore and five were "under development, targeting ready-for-service over the next 24 months".

Its website also spruiks its relationship with US chip giant Nvidia, which has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus.

Ahead of Firmus's announcement this morning, UniSuper chief investment officer John Pearce released an investment update detailing potential investors' doubts about the AI company and why the super fund would not directly invest in it.

The company is reportedly having to price its shares lower as it closed its books to potential investors abruptly overnight.

"Firmus is a neo-cloud company, and that means it provides cloud services, in very simple terms, to AI companies," he said.

"The capital raise will be about $7 billion and that will give Firmus a total market value of around $44 billion."

Mr Pearce said even though UniSuper was not directly investing in Firmus, UniSuper would own some shares if the float proceeded "because we have index strategies in our portfolios and Firmus will ultimately be a part of the major indices".

He said the reason UniSuper was doubtful about investing was the high valuation.

"At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation.

"Furthermore, we're quite concerned that Firmus will have to keep coming back to the market for a lot more debt and more equity to fund its expansion plans."

Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway yesterday raised concerns over the company's debt levels.

Lochlan Holloway is not convinced by the Firmus float. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"The neo-clouds are heavily geared," he wrote in an economic note.

"The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans."

Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about $US30 billion ($43 billion) of debt, about six times the $US5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028.

"Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," Mr Holloway said.

Why Firmus float hangs in the balance (Alicia Barry)
