https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/g.title: More young men than ever are gambling, but not to win
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/g.author: Madigan Landry and Neve Brissenden
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Fans cheer Fremantle on Cappuccino Street. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

Australians spend an eye-watering $30 billion each year on gambling. We are, comfortably, the world's most profligate punters.

It is a challenging figure to quantify, but observing the front bar of your local pub can help to understand who, and where, that 10-figure sum comes from.

As the AFL and NRL finals played out, venues across the country were packed to the brim, most in attendance in varying stages of desperation for their team to score.

While all were focused on the game, most kept one eye on their phones, hoping one or more legs on a bet had come off.

While winning money would seem like the obvious goal, it is increasingly no longer the only one.

Win or lose, having a bet on is increasingly part of the social life of thousands of men across the country.

The ABC visited a pub in Bunbury, WA's largest regional city, during the recent finals series, where almost every table of men had a bet on.

Roy, who was having a casual Thursday night drink with his friend, had two multi-bets on, despite not supporting either team.

"[I have a bet on] for all games, regardless of who's actually playing," he said.

Across the room, sitting together at a small table, eyes darting between the 90-inch screen on the wall and the smaller one in their hands, Adam and Dylan spoke about how gambling applications on their phones had impacted their habits.

"I had multiple apps, but I've deleted most of them," Adam said.

"I used to be pretty bad, but I've slowed down now."

Punters at a pub in regional WA speaking with ABC about how gambling shows up in their lives. (ABC South West: Neve Brissenden)

Dylan said inducements from his application of choice, Sportsbet, were frequent.

"Sportsbet loves me … I don't get any messages aside from them," he said.

The ABC also spoke to a table of women who were not gambling.

Tanika said that while she did not bet, it was something that surrounded her.

"A lot of my friends gamble … my brother and my dad do it as well," she said

"I think it's just like one of those things, like the social, the footy club, everyone's doing it."

In January, the federal government's gambling reforms will come into effect, including an opt-out service for online betting advertising.

Experts are pushing for public access to the data collected by gambling companies, in a bid to allow more targeted research and support.

But they are also pressing the government to address the social drivers of gambling's rapid growth among young men.

Vincent Mancini, a senior research fellow at The Kids Research Institute, said a growing number of young men considered betting part of their identity.

"The gambling industry has built sports gambling participation into the expression of manhood," Dr Mancini said.

Sports betting sits alone in this sense, with poker machines and horse or greyhound racing lacking the same cultural cachet.

Vincent Mancini says that for young men, gambling is about socialisation rather than winning. (Supplied: The Kids Research Institute)

Dr Mancini said gambling had become so synonymous with socialising, it was no longer about the win.

"When we speak to a lot of young boys, they realise that they're eventually going to lose the money," he said.

The 12 months to March this year saw participation in online gambling surpass venue-based gambling, like poker machines or casino gaming, for the first time in Australia's history.

Again, WA provides an interesting case study, boasting both the nation's most restrictive betting laws and its second-highest rate of gambling, according to the Australian Gambling Research Centre.

That is despite WA banning poker machines in 1962, limiting their use exclusively to Perth's Crown Casino, in an attempt to curb gambling losses.

As other states look to introduce stricter controls on poker machines, data shows online gambling will likely undermine reforms.

Despite strict gambling laws, Western Australia remains the state with the second-highest proportion of gambling in the country. (ABC News)

It is a trend and discussion that is front of mind for football clubs like the Busselton Magpies, and others all over the country.

"In our club rooms, we've got probably seven TVs that run every game of football while we're playing and training," club secretary Ray Gannaway said.

"Of course there's every betting agency in our face at every break, at every change."

Ray Gannaway says consuming gambling advertisements is an unavoidable part of watching live sport. (ABC SOuth West: Neve Brissenden)

He said the club has been working with the AFL to run mental health programs for younger players across all age groups, with gambling forming a big part of those conversations.

"We just aim to make sure our players are well informed about the ramifications if gambling becomes an addiction," he said.

"We're well aware that the boys will team up and have a punt on special occasions."

Mr Gannaway wants gambling advertising banned, and understands why young men get addicted.

"Exposure is what gives conversation, so take the exposure away, we stop talking about it," he said.

Ray Gannaway at a Busselton Football Club training session. (ABC South West: Neve Brissenden)

The other key factor is the prominence of gambling in Australia's cultural life, from two-up and its links to Australia's mining and wartime history, through to the national status of events like the Melbourne Cup.

Legalised casinos took gambling from back rooms and SP bookmakers to social and commercial hubs in every major city.

Curtin University gambling researcher Louise Francis said the industry had traded on that history to legitimise near-universal access to electronic betting.

A punter spins the pennies in the two-up ring in Kalgoorlie. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"We're talking, like, highly sophisticated gambling machines, highly sophisticated wagering, the multi-bets," she said.

"And how they know that they can send things, you know, inducements to one person, not another — they can latch on to people.

"That's not tossing up two coins in a two-up ring; we can't compare the gambling of 200 years ago to today."

Louise Francis says marketing has made gambling synonymous with Australia's cultural identity. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Dr Francis said the federal government's most recent reforms should have been a "blanket ban."

"I think they find it increasingly difficult to stand up to an industry that is so pervasive and powerful, and it is not just a gambling industry.

"We are talking about a sporting industry, we're talking about broadcasters that rely on that advertising revenue … it's a whole ecosystem."

One million Australians either suffer from, or live with someone suffering from, severe gambling harm.

Dr Francis said the industry's resistance to advertising restrictions showed how important marketing is.

"Sometimes you see industry say, 'Oh, advertising is not that big, people would do it anyway if we didn't advertise,'" she said.

"It's a huge component of how they engage with the population … if it's not that important, don't advertise."

Independent Senator David Pocock said the Albanese government's reforms were too "weak" to have a meaningful impact.

"The parliament recommended a complete advertising ban and an end to all inducements for a reason," Mr Pocock said.

"The changes won't drive the deep cultural change we need to stop Australians being the biggest losers in the world when it comes to gambling losses per capita."

But Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government's reforms struck the appropriate balance.

"Children should be able to know the players and follow their team and celebrate a goal without gambling being an inextricable part of that," she said.

"These reforms also introduce choice; if you do not want to see gambling ads online, you will not have to."

The gambling industry body Responsible Wagering Australia warned against further reform.

"We risk pushing Australians towards illegal offshore websites where they lose the safeguards Australians rightly expect," they said.

"The industry has already taken significant action to reduce wagering advertising, voluntarily cutting free-to-air television advertising spend … on top of the federal government's new restrictions from 1 January 2027."

The Brisbane Lions are on the verge of being out of finals contention with a loss this weekend. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Brisbane enters its round nine match against Hawthorn in an uncomfortable position.

Already two games out of the top eight, a loss would make a finals series mathematically impossible for the perennial contender.

Across AFLW history the Lions have missed finals just once, 2019, and made seven of nine grand finals.

So the come-down this year with just two wins from eight starts across the opening two months seems like a stark fall.

They have been caught in the eye of a perfect storm, making the 2025 Grand Finalist a bottom-eight side, and maybe that's not such a bad thing.

Across the opening decade of the AFLW the Lions have been durable, with coach Craig Starcevich regularly enjoying his pick of the list each week.

High-performance manager Matt Green has been a driver of this.

This year things have been different. Two-time premiership forward Taylor Smith was traded to Sydney over the off-season, as were premiership duo Poppy Boltz and Ellie Hampson to Greater Western Sydney and Port Adelaide, respectively.

The Lions lost plenty of talent in the off-season, including Taylor Smith to the Sydney Swans. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Metcalfe)

All-Australian forward Courtney Hodder has been unavailable this year due to pregnancy, stalwart Ally Anderson missed the opening four rounds of the season, her first ever absence, with a hamstring concern.

And throughout the year a number of other players have spent time on the sidelines nursing injuries.

This all adds to an aging playing list with a heavy reliance still on those senior players to set the tone.

For the first time in its history, Brisbane has been challenged for depth and player availability and it has exacerbated already emerging issues in its game style.

Brisbane has always been a hard-running, super fit team, relying on that to plug any holes that its game style might offer.

Unfortunately, this is the growth area for most other clubs in recent years, closing the gap on Brisbane at the top of the pack.

AFLW games are becoming faster, higher-scoring and more entertaining, and the stats and numbers behind the scenes prove it.

No longer will long bombs toward the front half into space for its runners beat the best teams. The increasing defensive strategy and organisation across the competition plans for this attacking style.

The Lions have struggled to establish more nuance across their ball movement.

Many of their players have been recruited based on their athletic attributes given the game style they were expected to play, but are struggling to adapt toward more of a precise ball movement game.

The area of the ground where this hurts most is with the Lions' forward 50 entries. 82.8 per cent of their entries turn into opposition rebounds, the fourth-highest rate across the AFLW this year.

The only sides conceding higher rebound rates are Port Adelaide (85.1 per cent), Collingwood (85.6 per cent), and St Kilda (87 per cent).

Blazing away through the middle of the ground and either kicking to an outnumber, or putting the ball out of their forwards' advantage, has been a common theme of the Lions this year, but it's not a brand-new problem.

Brisbane's goal efficiency, goals per inside 50, has been steadily dropping since its premiership season of 2023, hitting a club-low of 15.1 per cent this year.

It simply isn't getting bang for buck up forward and hasn't for a while.

Some of this can be the result of personnel with no Smith, Hodder, or Neasa Dooley. But more of this is due to haphazard attacking movement.

The club boasts the second-lowest disposal efficiency in the AFLW this year, using the ball at just 59.0 per cent, ahead of only contested beasts Port Adelaide, and this is another metric that has steadily dropped for the Lions over recent years.

Their ball use is getting more panicked, less considered, and less effective over time.

Where the Lions have typically been strongest is in defence. They've prided themselves on squeezing the ground, minimising opposition inside 50s, and making life hard for forward lines when they do get into attacking positions.

This has been another steady shift, now conceding a club-high 36.1 inside 50s per game. While some of this has been due to the aforementioned poor ball use and, therefore, turnovers, another large piece has been weakening control around stoppage.

The Lions are losing clearance by 6.3 per game this year, the second-greatest average deficit behind 2017. They are giving up 20.6 points from the source per game. This is an increase of more than a goal compared to its 12.0 points conceded from stoppage on average last year.

They are being burnt at stoppage, and burnt badly.

It means more pressure on the back line to defend more inside 50s and ultimately greater scores conceded each week.

All of this has contributed to an unfamiliar feeling for the Lions: not being considered a contender for finals.

But it's not necessarily a bad thing as it's a chance to regenerate, get some rare games into the kids.

Claudia Wright, Marlo Graham, Sophie Peters, Evie Long, and Asher Fearn-Wannan have all played a lot more footy than they would have expected and load up with their highly-rated academy prospects in December's draft.

Before that, however, they'll be considering Sunday's clash with the Hawks as one last throw at the stumps.

Against former midfield coach Daniel Webster, and as inaugural Lion Kaitlyn Ashmore brings up game number 100 wearing the brown and gold, they will be hunting a win to remain a narrow chance at yet another finals series.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, has spoken of grappling with his mental health at several points throughout his life. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

Prince Harry says he spent years grappling with his mental health following the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales.

The Duke of Sussex has spoken of falling into depression in 2019, weeks after stepping back from royal duties and relocating to North America.

The revelation comes about a month after Harry, his wife Meghan and children Archie and Lilibet returned to Britain.

Prince Harry has spoken of impacts to his mental health through his life, including during his step back from royal duties to relocate to North America, and after the death of his mother.

The Duke of Sussex revealed on Thursday he felt "emotionally numb" in the wake of the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, and spent years trying to cope.

"I couldn't remember my mum's laugh, couldn't remember what she looked like," he said in a video posted online for a mental health learning platform.

"I felt like I had to be sad in order to prove to her that I missed her.

"In my 20s I went to war twice thinking I could outrun my feelings, but that's not what happened.

"I'd spent so long emotionally numb, to a large extent because nobody told me that joy was still allowed — that it wasn't betrayal."

Harry says he began to forget his mother's appearance and the sound of her laugh following her death in 1997. (Georges De Keerle/Getty Images)

Harry served for 10 years with the British Armed Forces, including two deployments to Afghanistan as an air controller and helicopter pilot.

Harry also revealed in the video that he "slipped into depression for about two weeks" in 2019 after he chose to move to Canada with his wife Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in a high-profile split with the British Royal Family, according to a BBC report.

The prince was just 12 years old when Princess Diana died. (WireImage via Getty: Anwar Hussein)

"Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I'd never experienced before," the duke said.

"It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house."

Harry, Meghan and their children, seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet, returned to Britain from California in August, six years after stepping away from their royal duties.

Harry spent 10 years serving the British Armed Forces as a helicopter pilot and was deployed to Afghanistan twice. (AFP/Clarence House)

In September, the children were stalked by "certain European paparazzi" while at school in the English countryside, according to Harry's spokesperson.

The spokesperson said photographers walked the perimeter of the children's new school before stopping to look in the grounds and monitor the children there.

Prince Harry's children have been stalked by "certain European paparazzi" while at school in England.

Security issues have plagued the family's return to the United Kingdom, despite them seeking to keep the location of their new home and the children's school private.

Harry has long blamed the press for the death of his mother, who was killed in 1997 when the car she was travelling in crashed as the driver sped away from chasing paparazzi.

He has compared the press's treatment of Meghan to what his mother suffered.

The couple became private citizens in 2020 and organised their own security team, but want the British government to provide their family with automatic police protection, as it does for other senior members of the royal family.

The Western Bulldogs lodge the paperwork for Zak Butters ahead of the free agency deadline as teams continue to jostle for Nick Blakey's services.

Follow all the news and debate from the AFL trade period in our live blog.

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Mama mia, the news is coming thick and fast now.

Cal Twomey and Tom Morris have both reported that the deal, involving a stack of players of and draft picks, has just been approved by the AFL and will now go ahead.

I will bring you the full details of the deal in the next post. But it's happening.

The decision is in. Nick Blakey wants to become a Kangaroos.

Cal Twomey of AFL.com.au reports Blakey toured the facilities at Arden St this morning and completed a medical with the club before officially selecting them as his chosen destination.

Over to North Melbourne and Sydney now to get a deal done.

Hey Chris How likely is it that Gold Coast will offer pick 7 and a future first rounder for Schubert and Butler

I'll field this one for Chris. There is more chance of the Hawks chucking in Nick Watson to sweeten the deal than those picks going back Hawthorn's way.

We'll be dealing in future seconds and future thirds for Aidan Schubert and Sam Butler.

AFL.com.au's Cal Twomey reports that the Zak Butters paperwork is in. The Western Bulldogs have taken a big step towards securing the superstar midfielder.

Port Adelaide now have three days to match the contract offered to Butters by the Dogs. It is highly unlikely they will do so.

I wonder if this means the AFL is close to approving the rest of the mega-deal, giving Port and the Dogs the confidence to go ahead with the free agency play.

Following on from Essendon's likely draft with the first pick, what's the current thinking for Richmond with the second? Earlier in the year all the hype around Richmond circles was for Harry Van Hattum, but given he's dropped on some mock drafts and the tigers now signing Briggs, who are they likely to target instead?

In many ways the Tigers will shape the top five or six picks in this draft with their selection. Like Chris, I expect Essendon will take Ethan Drever with the first pick in the open pool, leaving Richmond with a strong group to pick from.

I certainly wouldn't be counting out Harry van Hattum with that pick. He may not have had the season he had hoped for and has slipped in some rankings around the place, but not in mine. He remains a unique and exciting ruck prospect, and he has spent a fair bit of time talking with Richmond already, going so far as sitting down and discussing ruck craft with Ivan Maric.

If van Hattum gets past Richmond, I don't think the Eagles take him as they went with Cooper Duff-Tytler early last year (even though I think HVH is more likely to be a leading AFL ruck than CDT), so he could end up a steal for someone like Melbourne, depending on how the top 10 shakes out after trades.

If not van Hattum, Richmond would look closely at Arki Butler. I would wonder if he is not a little too similar to the style of player they have taken early in previous years already.

Heath Mellody should come under strong consideration too, as I think he would balance out the young Richmond midfield really well. There's more than a little Trent Cotchin in Mellody.

Hey trade bloggers, nice to be here alongside Chris again.

Got to be honest, I've not got a single clue what any of you are talking about. Seems to me that we BADLY need some trades, you're all losing your minds a little bit.

I'm expecting Zak Butters and Ben King news today at the very least, and hopefully some Nick Blakey progress too. There's still well over a dozen deals still in the balance, many of which are waiting for the big dominos to fall before they start moving too. It's all ahead of us.

Hate to add fuel to the fire, but you have yet another LW! But I'm an east-coast, Doggies supporter, so you know...less of a headscratcher? Maybe I don't even count!

- Lily...as in another LW

If the saints get blakey i will give up football. Silvangni is running the club into the ground and is allowing disgusting behaviour from players

Obviously Nick Blakey has the police investigation hanging over his head, which is no doubt leading to mixed feelings.

I'd love to know how Saints and Roos fans are feeling about him potentially joining your club.

Hey Chris, cheers for keeping me busy through two very slow days at work. With Geelong falling back in the race for Lizard, where does that leave Freo and Lawson Humphries? Has an offer been made there?

Very quiet on the Lawson Humphries front, Matty.

I'd say he stays at Geelong now that the Nick Blakey ship has sailed.

Humphries is out of contract in 2028, I'd say he might be more of an option for Freo (and maybe West Coast) next summer.

Stuff this trade talk, get the three LW's on a call and have them work out the future of West Coast

To LW1, LW2 and LW3 (and LW ad nauseam) I know this ages me, but "I am Spartacus" comes to mind.

Who could LW really be? In all seriousness though, regarding Zak Butters, is there a live realistic chance where a trade can't be reached? What could happen then? I presume all hell would break loose for one.

Hey Chris, what is the status with the Ben King Trade to Hawthorn? When does the 48 hours expire for Suns to match the offer? Could the King compensation pick be traded to the Hawks for Schubert and Butler?

The Suns have until 4:15pm this afternoon to match Hawthorn's contract offer to Ben King if they want to force a trade.

The general consensus is that this will not happen and they will accept a compensation pick from the Hawks.

Given they have no other picks of value, it wouldn't shock me if they split this pick in order to get the Schubert and Butler deals done, but they certainly won't be sending 7 to Hawthorn.

Hi Chris, If I can further add to the drama, I am yet ANOTHER LW that is Perth-based. However, I do support the Dockers.

What on earth is going on over there in Western Australia folks?

I can't be having more LWs than completed trades right now.

G'day CDS, huge fan of your work mate. Quick draft question for you - Who do you see the Bombers taking at 1 and what other needs to they need to address with the haul they've got?

- Liam 'Chalkie' MacLeod

Thanks for the love, Liam!

My gut feel is that they go with Ethan Drever. He tested really well at the draft combine and has speed and athleticism, two attributes the Bombers really lack.

Mark McVeigh made a point to mention that he wanted to add speed to the list, and I think Drever fits really well with the likes of Dyson Sharp, Sullivan Robey and co as the inside-outside midfielder that the Dons don't quite have yet.

In terms of what they need, it is still just about everything.

I'd love to see them add some more pressure forwards and I think the backline needs a lot of work as well with Ridley gone and McKay a shell of his former self.

They'll be hoping for a clean bill of health for Lewis Hayes after a wretched run with injuries.

So the plot thickens - I think there's at least three LWs. Neither The LW and the Luke w sniping each other yesterday after noon were me, I'm completely different and commented twice yesterday completely separately. Whats even weirder is that we all seem to be disgruntled eagles supporters. At this point I'm questioning my grip on reality. Have I been cloned? Am I real? Am I forgetting making comments here and then arguing with myself. Can you help me?

Do you think the Bulldogs would give up all their draft picks to get Butters? And would the AFL even allow that?

I'll be honest, Coco, I've got absolutely no idea with this one.

I'm not even sure Port is going to accept the compensation pick, and if they do, what does that mean for a trade?

Do the Dogs send some young players Port's way?

Honestly, anything could happen with that one. It doesn't seem like a cut and dry transaction.

Essendon has signed NGA product Jayden Nguyen to a one-year deal as a Category B rookie.

That means Nik Cox, Kayle Gerreyn and Tom Edwards are the players that remain unsigned for the Dons.

"Jayden's constant application to improvement has been terrific in his first couple of seasons and we're excited to see that roll on into next year," Bombers list boss Matt Rosa said.

"He's got a willingness to take the game on and use his speed but also has a real competitive streak in him which has translated well to his VFL performances as a pressure forward.

"We're confident Jayden can continue to develop his game and be an asset as he continues to develop his forward craft."

My two cents on the LW situation yesterday. You can absolutely love the club’s history and be a proud Eagles fan (as I am) while acknowledging how badly they’ve fallen away. They’re conservative to a fault at the trade table and consistently get outperformed by rival clubs at this time of year. Trading pick three and missing out on Jagga is another example. If two wooden spoons in three years, and the second half fall off in 2026 isn't a wake-up call heads need to roll from the board down.

It seems as though the LW beef was a major talking point out of day four's blog.

Any substance behind the rumblings of Bobby Hill meeting with Freo? He'd be the perfect replacement for Switta. If the motivations there, which clubs are in the running to get the norm Smith medallist back on a list?

I think there will be a bit to play out on the Bobby Hill front, Ed.

A healthy and engaged version of him would definitely be helpful for the Dockers, or any time, for that matter.

However, it has been a while since we've seen that version, so I'd say that one is very firmly a wait and see for now.

Chris, Freo are absolutely going to regress outside the top 4 if they don't move some magnets this offseason, especially with the types of moves Geelong and Hawthorn have made. Geelong probably overcome them in the semi if it's Marshall v Jackson not Edwards v Jackson.

I'm going to actually push back on you here, Georgia, I think the Dockers are absolutely fine to run it back.

Let's be honest, they probably should be premiers. They've got one of the most stacked lists in the competition.

Sometimes it's a case of if it ain't broke, don't fix it!

Is there still a chance blakey nominates gold coast or geelong

It appears as though that ship has sailed, Ge.

I think it'll be either St Kilda or North from here on for Blakey.

Nicole and Zach Miller and their son Cohen at their home in Farleigh. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

The Australian College of Midwives says up to a third of Australia's privately practising midwives may leave the profession when an insurance exemption ends in January.

Only midwives with a qualification requiring 5,000 hours of clinical experience are eligible for a Commonwealth-funded insurance product.

Medical professionals warn it could lead to more homebirths without qualified health practitioners.

Nicole Miller gave birth to her son Cohen at her home in Farleigh, North Queensland, in February.

She remembers the day fondly: "It's the best feeling ever, really," she said.

"Being in the comfort of your own home is second to none."

But within months, midwives, including Ruth Davison, who delivered Cohen, may no longer be able to practise.

An exemption that has allowed privately practising midwives to attend homebirths without insurance covering claims of error or negligence will end on New Year's Eve.

Nicole Miller says she preferred not to give birth in a hospital setting. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell )

All midwives outside of a hospital setting will need a Commonwealth-funded product from the Medical Insurance Group Australia (MIGA).

The insurance is available only to "endorsed" midwives, a qualification that requires additional study and 5,000 hours of clinical practice, which may be accrued over the last six years.

As part of the changes, the federal government has covered the total cost of eligible claims made against endorsed midwives performing homebirths since July 1, 2025.

Ruth Davison has been practising in Mackay since 2021. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

In Australia, a second practitioner is required to attend each homebirth.

Mackay midwife Ms Davison, who is endorsed, said that requirement would be difficult in regional areas.

Ms Davison said the other insured midwife in the region was often out of town, which meant it would be "difficult" to continue her service.

"I can [currently] have a registered midwife, I can have a registered nurse, a doctor or a paramedic.

"But come the first [of January], I'm not going to be able to have that."

Jessica McGair has been assisting Ruth Davison during homebirths, but is not yet endorsed. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Midwife Jessica McGair splits her time between the Mackay Base Hospital and assisting homebirths.

"I only work part-time, and that would look like about six years before I would even be eligible to be endorsed, plus also further study as well," she said.

In 2023, the number of home births had more than doubled, from 923 in 2019 to 2,081, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said the insurance requirements would provide "important safeguards for practitioners, women and families".

The Australian College of Midwives (ACM) warned up to a third of Australia's 500 private-practice midwives could leave the profession by January.

Kelley Lennon says the insurance requirements could affect an already stretched workforce in regional and rural areas.  (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Chief midwife Kelley Lennon said endorsement allowed a midwife to prescribe medication and order tests.

She said while the qualifications helped midwives provide a "full suite of care" for mothers before and after labour, they were not necessary for a second midwife assisting a birth.

"The concern is that if women aren't able to access a midwife, they may consider to birth without a registered health practitioner, which we know of as a freebirth," she said.

Ms Lennon said she had met with government to advocate for a more accessible insurance product for homebirths.

The Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA), which regulates private and public practitioners, said in a statement the changes were not about limiting homebirths.

"This protects the public from financial and safety risks resulting from a negligent act, error, or omission in a practitioner's conduct."

It said all midwives would need to be appropriately covered by January 1, 2027.

The NMBA said it was reviewing public feedback on its registration process for midwife endorsement, including the 5,000-hour clinical practice requirement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.title: Special edition coins continue Live Aid legacy 41 years on
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.author: Mietta Adams
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Live Aid concert was watched by an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries. (Supplied: Live Aid)

The Perth Mint is releasing special edition Live Aid coins to raise money for projects in Africa.

Midge Ure says the collectible coins will help continue the legacy of the legendary concert and its associated charity Band Aid.

The coins will be released in December.

When Scottish musician Midge Ure began planning a musical fundraiser in 1985 to help victims of famine in Ethiopia, he anticipated it would be a six-month project.

That legendary concert was Live Aid, a 16-hour international pop music telethon featuring megastars like David Bowie, Madonna and Queen that ended up being one of the biggest television broadcasts of all time, watched by an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries.

Freddie Mercury performs with Queen at Live Aid in 1985. (Supplied: Live Aid)

More than 40 years later, the concert and its associated charity Band Aid is still raising money for Africa — and now there's a Perth connection.

This week the Perth Mint unveiled plans to release special edition Live Aid collectible coins in December, each with an original vinyl single of Do They Know It's Christmas, signed by the song's creators, Ure and Sir Bob Geldof.

Midge Ure performing with Ultravox at Live Aid in 1985. (Supplied: Live Aid)

Ure, who teamed up with Geldof to organise Live Aid, is happy to still be fundraising for charity.

"That coin is something special because long after Bob and I are dust, that coin will carry on telling the story as well as generate a huge amount of income to support the charities that we've been supporting for the last 40 years," he said.

Scottish musician Midge Ure at the Perth Mint, which is producing special edition coins to pay homage to Live Aid. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

The 72-year-old could be forgiven for putting his feet up after a hugely successful music career, having played a key role in well-known bands including Ultravox, Thin Lizzy and Visage.

But it's unlikely he'll fade to grey.

As he reflected on Live Aid four decades on, Ure told the ABC he was still heavily involved in the charity that continues to harness the power of music to help some of the world's most vulnerable people.

"It's one of these things that once you get involved in it, you can't walk away," Ure said.

"It's very difficult to hang up your spurs and just hand it across to someone else."

Around 72,000 people attended the Live Aid concert at Wembley Stadium in July 1985. (Supplied: Live Aid)

While Live Aid garnered a worldwide audience in 1985 at a time when music was a powerful way to generate donations, Ure said the digital age and a distracted audience would make it impossible to recreate on that scale today.

"But it'd be a much better planet if we could organise things like that. There are many, many good causes out there that deserve that break.

"Maybe now you would have to do some kind of TikTok thing."

While an original, signed vinyl of Do They Know It's Christmas would be a coveted addition to any music collection, the 1984 song has attracted controversy amid criticism that it perpetuates negative stereotypes about Africa.

Ghanaian-English musician Fuse ODG said lyrics such as "there won't be snow in Africa this Christmas time" and "where nothing ever grows" made people less likely to travel to Africa or invest in businesses there.

Band Aid performing Do They Know It's Christmas during the Live Aid concert in London. (Supplied: Live Aid)

Ure defended the song and said it had been made in a very short time frame.

"Yes, there's snow in Africa, we know that. We're not stupid. But we just knocked it out, it's a song, simple."

Ure said the release of the vinyl record alongside the collector's coin was a new way of ensuring the song was enjoyed for generations to come.

"You can only do so many remixes or so many new recordings of that song and people just get fed up hearing it," he said.

The coins will be accompanied by a signed vinyl of Do They Know It's Christmas. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Another driver for Band Aid's revenue is the Live Aid Musical — with 10 per cent of all ticket sales donated to the charity.

The musical debuted at The Old Vic in London where it became the theatre's fastest-selling musical ever, and is set to come to Australia late 2027.

Remembering Live Aid 40 years on

Ure said it was all about generating new ideas for new audiences to raise money for an age-old problem, as Ethiopia continues to face a hunger crisis.

These days, Live Aid and its associated charity Band Aid administer funds to projects across the continent that solicit its help.

Since 1984, the trust's website states it has raised more than $275 million towards projects in Ethiopia and other countries.

"We're like a drawdown facility at a bank," Ure said.

"There are many, many good causes out there that deserve that break.

"We have to think about how the legacy will continue. So we're in the process of doing that now."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.title: Officials forced to break law to keep mentally impaired man in prison
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.author: Keane Bourke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A prisoner was denied appropriate psychiatric care while detained at Hakea Prison (Supplied: Office of the Inspector of Custodial Services)

A man was kept in jail illegally because of a severe shortage of beds at WA’s only facility for mentally impaired prisoners.

A Supreme Court judge found officials were being forced to break the state's own rules due to a lack of beds at the Frankland Centre at Graylands Hospital.

Planning is underway to expand the capacity at Graylands, but there is no timeline.

A mentally impaired man was kept in jail illegally and denied suitable mental health care because of a chronic lack of beds in Western Australia's only psychiatric facility caring for prisoners.

That is the scathing assessment of a Supreme Court judge ruling in the case of a man, known only by the pseudonym 'SJQ', who was denied appropriate psychiatric care for about two months while detained at Hakea Prison in Perth's south.

A magistrate had previously found the man, who is in his 40s, unfit to stand trial to face an assault charge because of his treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia.

He was ordered to be sent to the Frankland Centre at Graylands Hospital for treatment

But that was not possible because the state's only facility for mentally impaired prisoners does not have enough beds to cope with soaring demand.

WA's prison population has quadrupled since the Frankland Centre opened in 1994.  (ABC Radio Perth: Alicia Bridges)

The 30-bed facility opened in 1993 and has not increased its capacity since, despite WA's prisoner population growing four-fold over that period, according to the judgment.

Justice Terence Palmer last week found officials were being forced to break the law by keeping people like SJQ in prison until a bed becomes available.

He rejected arguments from the government's lawyers that staff had "done their best" with the "limited resources available to them".

The practice of giving criminals lighter sentences because of poor conditions in Western Australia's jails should stop in most cases, the state's Court of Appeal rules.

"Those charged with the care of mentally impaired people involved with the criminal justice system should not be placed in a position where a lack of resources forces them to act unlawfully," he wrote.

While SJQ was eventually moved to the Frankland Centre after an appeal was lodged, Justice Palmer said it was in the "public interest" to call out the treatment, which "reveals a systemic failure that should be decried".

State governments have been warned for years about a lack of beds at the Frankland Centre.

In 2018, WA's Inspector of Custodial Services warned the number of beds "has been inadequate for over a decade", and four years later found "inhumane" conditions amounted to breaches of human rights.

The facility operated at 99 per cent occupancy last financial year and had a waitlist of 18 people immediately before SJQ was ordered to be sent there, including another person in a similar position.

At one point, the waitlist ranged from 6 to 212 days, according to the judgement.

Debra Zanella runs community service provider Ruah, which operates the state's only mental health law service.

Debra Zanella says people experiencing mental illness can live long lives if they are properly cared for.  (ABC News: Cason Ho)

She said the judgment was not a surprise to anyone involved in the sector and argued the stigmatisation of mentally impaired prisoners resulted in the systemic failure identified by the judgement.

"In any other part of our health system we would not deny anybody that care," she said.

Ms Zenalla acknowledged the government was working towards expanding the capacity of Graylands, with a nearly $200 million project including plans for 32 sub-acute male forensic mental health beds.

Advocates say mentally ill prisoners are stuck in conditions that "breach human rights"

"I'd want to make sure that … we use the correct data to tell us now what we need, what we'll need into the future, and we make sure we have a timeline," she said.

A state government spokesperson said a contractor had been appointed in April as part of early planning work, which would allow the government to confirm a timeline soon.

"The state government is considering the judgement and will continue working across the justice and health systems to ensure people are accommodated in the most appropriate setting as soon as practicable," they said in a statement.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.title: Taxpayers could be on hook for ATO tax bill from bungled accounting
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.author: Lucy MacDonald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Government

Treasurer Eric Abetz is overseeing another wave of public sector redundancies, but these are not affected by the tax classification bungle. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Tasmanian state service employees who took voluntary redundancies stretching back over a decade could be on the hook for a tax bill after successive state governments bungled their tax arrangements.

The government has self-reported the issue to the ATO, which centres on the way in which the redundancies were classified for tax purposes.

After pressure from Labor and questions from the ABC, a Tasmanian government spokesperson on Friday said "no past employee will be affected" and that the "employer will deal with any financial implications".

Tasmanian taxpayers could be on the hook if the Australian Tax Office (ATO) chases payments going back decades relating to voluntary redundancies for state service employees.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) reported last Friday that the state government had made a voluntary disclosure to the ATO after discovering it had been incorrectly classifying its voluntary redundancy payouts for tax purposes.

The redundancy payouts had been classified as "genuine redundancies", meaning they were tax-free up to a limit and then taxed at a reduced rate, but according to the ATO, genuine redundancies are not voluntary.

Tasmanian Education Minister Jo Palmer's office claimed there were no proposals to cut a specialist team that works with teachers. A week later, the team is being cut by a quarter.

The state government has now conceded that its many voluntary redundancies should have been classified as employment termination payments, which are usually taxed at a reduced rate, up to a certain limit.

This means the workers should have paid more tax on their redundancies.

It's been able to sort out the current round of redundancies, covering the tax for those who have already been paid out so that people get what they expected.

But it estimates the incorrect practice has been in place since Labor was in government under premier Lara Giddings, potentially even further back than 2011.

That era was also marked by significant job cuts, many in the form of voluntary redundancies.

The ATO now has to work out if it wants to recover the money it's owed.

After pressure from Labor and questions from the ABC on Thursday, a Tasmanian government spokesperson on Friday said that "no past employee will be affected".

The Tasmanian government will slash 1,700 jobs through natural attrition and negotiated voluntary redundancies, as Treasurer Eric Abetz unveils his second state budget.

Labor Workplace Relations spokesperson Ella Haddad had earlier called on the government to give workers certainty.

She was critical of the government's focus on the fact the incorrect practice likely started under a Labor government.

"No matter how far back this stretches … the truth is, they've been in power now for almost 13 years.

"They've had 13 years to get it right, but under [Treasurer] Eric Abetz everything is getting worse."

She has also questioned if the government could face fines from the ATO.

On its website, DPAC said that no action is required from former employees "at this stage".

"Further information will be provided as advice becomes available, including any contact with former employees as needed."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.title: Fears backpacker ballot will leave coastal towns short-staffed
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.author: Caitlan Charles
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

There are concerns about how to fill jobs when the backpacker ballot begins.  (Flickr CC BY-NC-ND 2.0: Jo Christian Oterhals)

Hospitality experts say the backpacker ballot could create significant workforce shortages in holiday towns that rely heavily on seasonal workers.

North Coast Hotel Group director Harry Barry says his business hires backpackers because of a local workforce shortage.

Business leaders along the NSW coast are looking to negotiate a federal agreement to help fill roles in the regions.

For publican Harry Barry, backpackers are the lifeblood of his business.

But he says many of his employees are considering returning home after the federal government announced a backpacker ballot, which would effectively cap second-year backpacker visas.

"The incentive was a guarantee they could extend their visas by another 12 months," he said.

"A lot of them are deciding that there is no guarantee that [they're] going to be earning enough money to pay [their] way.

Harry Barry says a designated area migration agreement could help the Coffs Harbour region.  (ABC Coffs Harbour: Claudia Jambor)

The new backpacker ballot will cap annual places at 45,000 for second-year visas if the standard 88 days of regional work are completed.

Even fewer third-year places are available.

About 57,000 people qualified last year.

Mr Barry is among a number of business owners concerned about how the cap will impact their staff.

The director of the North Coast Hotel Group runs pubs from Grafton to Taree that employed 80 backpackers over the past two years, with 20 still on his books.

"If we're employing 80 backpackers, we're doing it for a reason, and the reason is we can't find local workers to fill the slots," he said.

Harry Barry believes the new backpacker ballot will negatively affect the Mid North Coast.  (ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor)

According to jobs website Seek, there were more than 130 vacancies in the Coffs Harbour region in the industry on Wednesday.

To fill the gap left by backpackers leaving, Mr Barry is backing a push to establish the region as a priority area for semi-skilled migrants, also known as a Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA).

The DAMA is an agreement between the federal government and a state or regional authority that assists regional areas to fill roles that would otherwise remain empty.

It allows skilled migrants, in industries of need, to move to the area for work. Industries include skilled roles in hospitality, agriculture, engineering and more.

The agreements are usually in place for five years before they are reviewed.

Backpackers help pick fruit across regional NSW.  (ABC Rural: Stephanie Anderson)

There are 13 DAMAs in place across Australia, with one operation in New South Wales; two in South Australia; five in Western Australia; one in the Northern Territory; two in Victoria; and two in Queensland.

Regional Development Australia Mid North Coast CEO Madeleine Lawler said the DAMA was not about filling jobs with migrants that could have otherwise employed locals.

"The DAMA requires businesses to be able to substantiate that they have been seeking Australians for a long period of time and have not been able to fill these positions with Australians or people locally," she said.

A similar agreement in Townsville, in Northern Queensland, brought in an additional 480 workers over three years to fill a skills shortage.

Holiday hotspot Cairns has held a DAMA for the past seven years.

The agreement, according to the Cairns Chamber of Commerce, was key to keeping the region thriving.

CEO Patricia O'Neill said there was a hotel on Thursday Island, which was included in the Cairns agreement, that would shut down without DAMA workforce.

Patricia O'Neill says the DAMA has been a lifeline for the Cairns region.  (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

"Government go to [Thursday Island] regularly; there is only one hotel in the place. If they weren't able to apply to attract a chef, that hotel would need to close [because] it can't feed anyone," Ms O'Neill said.

"That's how critical a DAMA is to certain parts of an economy up here.

"Without having the Far North Queensland DAMA, we would not have a thriving economy; we would not have a workforce to take up jobs."

Each area with an agreement has a list of specific jobs, tailored to the region's needs, that can be filled by overseas workers.

There is already a DAMA in place in the Orana region, which includes Dubbo, and is open to agricultural workers — including berry pickers, chefs and cooks, mechanics, truck drivers, hospitality and retail managers, and waiters.

A spokesperson for Steve Whan says the government is investigating whether NSW could include more DAMAs. (ABC South East NSW: Floss Adams)

A spokesperson for Skills, TAFE and Tertiary Education Minister Steve Whan said the NSW government had conducted a feasibility study into state-led DAMAs.

"Consultation with key stakeholders is underway and will inform a proposal to the Department of Home Affairs," they said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.title: Snowtown killer's outing from prison 'sickening', victim's nephew says
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.author: Jordanna Schriever  and Rachael Merritt
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

James Spyridon Vlassakis was granted parole last month. (ABC News)

The nephew of one of the victims of the Snowtown murders says seeing serial killer James Vlassakis out in public gave him "flashbacks".

Vlassakis was filmed leaving the Adelaide Pre-release Centre yesterday morning.

Vlassakis will spend about 12 months in the centre, which allows prisoners transition from custody into the community.

The nephew of one of the "bodies in the barrels" murder victims says seeing images of convicted serial killer James Spyridon Vlassakis out in public is "sickening".

Ron Lane, the nephew of victim Barry Lane, said the images of Vlassakis leaving the Adelaide Pre-release Centre yesterday brought back dark memories and a fear of inadvertently running into him in public.

"Seeing the photo for the very first time of him now is a shock to the system and gives flashbacks on why he was in [prison]," he said.

"It's just a memory of everything that has happened.

Ron Lane was about seven when he last saw his uncle. (ABC News)

Vlassakis, the youngest of the perpetrators involved in the notorious serial killings, was jailed for life in 2001 and given a 26-year non-parole period, backdated to his arrest in 1999.

His testimony helped authorities to convict John Bunting and Robert Wagner, who were jailed for 11 and 10 murders, respectively.

His testimony also helped to convict murder accomplice Mark Ray Haydon, who was released into the community in after serving a 25-year sentence.

Vlassakis pleaded guilty to the murders of Fred Brooks, Gary O'Dwyer, David Johnson and his half-brother Troy Youde.

Last year the Parole Board granted Vlassakis parole, but the state government tried to block the decision.

It was subsequently upheld in a ruling handed down by the Parole Administrative Review Commissioner last month.

The old Snowtown bank building, where eight bodies were found in 1999. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Vlassakis will spend up to 12 months at the pre-release centre while the Parole Board monitors his progress and decides on the conditions for his release into the community.

Vlassakis walked through the centre's car park yesterday, accompanied by another man, before driving off in a car and returning later in the morning.

Parole Board chair Frances Nelson KC previously said Vlassakis would be subject to the "standard conditions" of parole, including a curfew, restricted movements and drug and alcohol testing.

Mr Lane told the ABC he was worried about stumbling across Vlassakis while out in public.

"As we all know, Adelaide is very small and you can just about bump into anybody," he said.

"You could go down the shops, not knowing that he's out as well, and you're coming towards him, you could just be frozen solid."

Barry Lane was one of the 12 victims of the murders. (Supplied)

Mr Lane was about seven years old the last time he saw his uncle, who was killed by Bunting and Wagner in October 1997.

Some of his fondest memories of his uncle included going on drives and to get fish and chips.

"We'd go to a playground and he would push you on the swing," Mr Lane said.

Snowtown killer James Vlassakis's image can be revealed after South Australia's highest court lifted a suppression order made 25 years ago.

He said Vlassakis's transition back into the community was "a failure"of the justice system, and felt uncertain the parole conditions were adequate enough to keep the community safe.

"Knowing that someone like that is out here sends a sickening [shock] to the body," Mr Lane said.

"I didn't expect him to be out this quick to be adjusting to life on the outside when he should be locked up like the other two in there.

"This guy should have got 100 years behind bars for killing four victims.

"It doesn't make anything right that he can be out there like nothing's happened.

In a statement released yesterday, a government spokesperson said Vlassakis would be "subject to strict conditions for the remainder of his life", with any breach bringing the possibility of his return to custody.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The float of AI company Firmus has been scrapped, throwing into chaos plans to list a company estimated at one point to rocket into the Top 20 most valuable firms in the nation.

Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.

Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.

Prices current around 11:24am AEDT.

Live updates on the major ASX indices:

Choose what information you see below by using filters

Im a shareholder in Firmus as a private investor. Does this mean it will never perform IPO or is it still possible later down the track. There is a clause that allows for larger share in company if it doesn’t list by November ?

There are examples of companies having to try multiple times to get listed on the stock market.

The most recent I can think of is Latitude Financial, which finally got there — third time lucky! — in 2021.

It had two failed attempts to list and given the share price has cratered -69% in its five years as a public company, was it a good idea?

If you really are a private investor in Firmus, we're keen to speak to you. Please drop me a line at ziffer.daniel@abc.net.au

Firmus's decision to abandon its ASX float has been devastating for investors who've already poured their money into the data centre operator.

Maas Group, founded by ex-NRL player Wes Maas, is a perfect example.

The company owns a 3.2% stake in Firmus and has $1.2 billion worth of contracts to do the electrical fit-out for its yet-to-be-built data centres.

Yesterday, Maas's share price fell by a massive 22.4%. Basically, it lost nearly a quarter of its value (roughly $500 million) in one day!

I covered this in my finance report on yesterday's 7pm News:

Now its shares are in a "trading pause" pending a further announcement, as my colleague Daniel Ziffer mentioned a little earlier.

Mr Maas sold his construction materials division (which was half his company) in order to fund that 3.2% stake in Firmus.

He has essentially gone "all in" when it comes to the AI investment boom and is surely hoping Firmus recovers from this huge setback quite soon.

If you're puzzled as to why we're so focussed on the failed float of AI company Firmus today, it's because of the explosive way it was set to debut on the stock market.

Priced by its proponents at $44 billion, that would make it the 16th most valuable company in the nation, above the current market capitalisation of companies like toll road operator Transurban Group ($40b), QBE Insurance and supermarket group Coles.

To put it another way, the only companies bigger in Australia would have been our Big Four banks (CommBank, ANZ, NAB, Westpac) and Macquarie, our mega-miners (BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue), gas giant Woodside Energy, retailers Wesfarmers and Woolworths, blood products company CSL, telco Telstra and construction behemoth Goodman Group.

Then, just below all these established names: Firmus.

It's starting to look more obvious in hindsight, isn't it.

If there have been big questions about Firmus' valuation and eventual falling over of it being floated, surely this gives Big Tech a reminder that Australia does not trust/want data centres in it's backyard?

Many communities in Australia are angry about the imposition of data centres in their area, or future plans to do so.

But that disquiet pales into insignificance to the US, where the rapid expansion has had immense impacts.

In many areas, imminent elections are being fought with AI/data centre issues at the forefront. States like New York have put in a moratorium (temporary ban) on new centres.

Part of the attraction of the Firmus float, its proponents put, was that its plans in Australia and Asia weren't as contentious as the difficulty US developers were finding.

As we weigh the failure of Firmus to float on the Australian stock exchange, it's worth remembering that SB Energy in the US has hit a similar hurdle.

Here's Filip Tortevski, Senior Analyst at Wealth Within, on the similarities:

"With US data-centre developer SB Energy also delaying its float, I believe investors are looking harder at the gap between today’s price and tomorrow's profits. For years, technology companies could grow without constantly building expensive physical assets. AI has changed that. Billions must be spent on chips, power and data centres before the expected cash arrives.

"But what happens if a competitor delivers comparable AI using far less computing power?

"China's DeepSeek has already demonstrated methods to make AI training and operation more efficient, while delivering competitive results across a range of benchmarks. The competitive threat is real. Cheaper AI could encourage more use, so this does not automatically mean fewer data centres, but if usage growth fails to offset those efficiency gains, developers could be halfway through construction when demand forecasts are cut.

"Existing contracts may offer protection. However, future expansion becomes harder to justify, while construction costs and debt still need to be paid. Demand does not even need to fall. It simply needs to grow less than investors have already priced in. AI may change the world and still disappoint shareholders.

"The danger is paying for tomorrow’s revolution at a price its profits cannot support."

In unsurprising news, a few minutes before trading opened, the ASX announced that "trading in the securities of the entity  (Maas Group) will be temporarily paused pending a further announcement."

The company is deeply enmeshed with Firmus.

Yesterday its shares fell more than 22% as concern grew about the likelihood the float would be pulled.

The flagship ASX 200 index that tracks the value of our 200-largest listed companies is up 36.3 points or +0.4% to 8,696.7 points in the opening minutes of trading.

Before we get going on the markets, here's a recap from around the world overnight via Daniela Hathorn, Senior Market Analyst at capital.com.

These are the key bits:

"Markets have turned more defensive this morning as renewed Middle East tensions, rising oil prices and persistently elevated bond yields put pressure on risk appetite. Wall Street finished lower on Wednesday, while Asian and European equities have extended the weakness today. The broader equity rally remains supported by strong earnings expectations and AI investment, but the increasingly narrow leadership is leaving markets exposed to shifts in the rates outlook.

"Meanwhile, Brent has surged towards $US104 as attacks on commercial vessels around the Strait of Hormuz intensify, including a tanker strike off Qatar. Reports that Washington is considering further military action against Iran have added to the uncertainty, while Hurricane Isaias is threatening production in the Gulf of Mexico.

"Furthermore, Wednesday's Fed minutes reinforced the central bank's hawkish bias, although the key takeaway is seemingly a lack of appetite for continued rate hikes. Most policymakers still anticipate another rate hike before year-end, despite softer employment data suggesting the labour market is losing momentum, but these are seen as an insurance against sticky inflation rather than the start of a new tightening cycle.

"Europe is facing an additional layer of pressure from sovereign debt markets. Borrowing costs remain elevated amid fiscal and political uncertainty, highlighting the increasingly difficult environment for governments already struggling with weak growth and expensive debt servicing.

"The rise in energy prices is particularly problematic for Europe, where it threatens household purchasing power and corporate margins while limiting central banks' ability to support growth. This creates a more challenging backdrop for European equities, especially domestically exposed and highly leveraged businesses."

Firmus blames “market volatility and market conditions”. With all due respects, it is my personal view that broadly speaking, the business plan falls short of instilling the level investor confidence for the IPO to succeed.

That's a pretty solid summary Peter, not just of potential small investors but apparently the large ones as well.

...but our focus is understandably on the collapse of the much-hyped float of AI data centre company Firmus.

Keep up to date on this blog and at our breaking article here.

Just yesterday, listed construction firm MAAS was answering a call from the stock exchange, which gave it the equivalent of a speeding fine.

The company is a shareholder in Firmus and a key partner in building its data centres.

The stock fell 22% yesterday and the ASX asked: why?

Here is the response, .

"MGH notes that there has been significant market speculation and commentary concerning whether the proposed IPO of Firmus will be proceeding.

"As previously disclosed, MGH is both an investor in Firmus and, through its subsidiary, JLE, a supplier to Firmus.

"MGH considers that such speculation has influenced investor sentiment towards MGH and contributed to recent trading in its securities. MGH is not aware of any undisclosed information that would explain the recent trading."

Shares in the company will be one to watch when the market opens shortly.

It was going to be as big as Woolies.

Depending on the different valuations mooted for AI data centre company Firmus, when it listed on the Australian stock exchange its "value" would have been akin to that of our largest supermarket chain, Woolworths Group.

Now Firmus has decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX, after big investors baulked at the price and questions arose about the ability of the nascent company to expand rapidly and still return the profits it promised.

Mark your diary, the failure of this initial public offering (IPO) will be one of the biggest business stories of the year, with ramifications for our market, AI and how investors feel about risk.

There's a lot more to come.

A statement from Firmus has just been published.

The AI company has scuppered its float, which would have made the company "public" and allowed investors to trade shares in it.

Here's the statement:

"Firmus has decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX.

"Having considered recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions, the Board determined that the terms on which the Offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the Company's business and long-term growth outlook.

"The Board therefore concluded that proceeding with the Offer was not in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders.

"Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options.

"We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress."

AI data centre company Firmus has confirmed it has withdrawn its application to list on the ASX, scrapping what was set to be one of Australia’s biggest share market floats.

The company cited recent market volatility and conditions, saying the offer would not appropriately reflect its long-term growth prospects.

Firmus says it will now pursue private market funding while considering other options.

People have lots of thoughts. The chief investment officer of UniSuper, John Pearce, put out an investment update just before recent news on Firmus that explains some of the doubts potential investors have about the AI company.

"Speaking of the share market, I'd like to make a few comments about a very exciting development on the Australian Stock Exchange, and that's the IPO or Initial Public Offering of a company called Firmus.

"Firmus is a neo-cloud company, and that means it provides cloud services, in very simple terms, to AI companies. The capital raise will be about $7 billion and that will give Firmus a total market value of around $44 billion.

"That's a big company by Australian standards, well within the top 20, so not surprisingly, it's getting a lot of publicity. And UniSuper has also got some publicity over this because I've been quoted as saying that we're not going to be investing in Firmus."

But he makes a key point here. Essentially all investors, particularly superannuation accounts, will end up investing in the company.

"A couple of points of clarification. UniSuper will end up owning some shares in Firmus because we have index strategies in our portfolios and Firmus will ultimately be a part of the major indices.

"Furthermore, we outsource some of our funds to external managers and they might buy Firmus shares. However, it is true to say that we will not be participating in this IPO in any meaningful sense."

So why didn't UniSuper want in, directly?

"It all comes down to valuation. We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation. At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation. Furthermore, we're quite concerned that Firmus will have to keep coming back to the market for a lot more debt and more equity to fund its expansion plans.

"Having said that, I'm delighted that the founders of Firmus are listing on the Australian Stock Exchange and I really do hope that other founders take their lead."

Mr Pearce notes that between the recording and release of his note, "there have been reports that the Firmus IPO has not been well received. Reports indicate that unless the deal is materially repriced, it may be shelved".

Timing is everything.

As markets in the US and Australia focus on the potential jittery returns on the mega-build-out of AI, the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is about to start hearings again.

From 10:30, we'll hear from Monash AI Institute, the Director of eResearch and Monash University and then the RMIT Enterprise AI and Data Analytics Research Hub.

Then it's CDC Data Centres, who recently ended a relationship with yet-to-list Firmus.

There are tech and business groups on the list, before three of our "Big Four" banks discuss issues relating to AI:

We'll bring you highlights during the day.

Surely, there's few greater compliments than leaving a listed company and the stock tanking.

(Although maybe if the market was assured about succession planning and the team you'd left in place that wouldn't happen, but anyway…)

The upshot is that yesterday jeweller Lovisa announced its chief financial officer Chris Lauder had resigned.

And the "value" of the company dropped 10%.

Here's some of the statement.

"Chris will serve his six-month notice period, with his final day on Wednesday 7 April 2027, fully supporting an orderly transition.

"Lovisa has a very strong global finance team, and the Board will appoint a successor following a global search process."

Lovisa Global CEO John Cheston went on to say "we would like to thank Chris for his significant contribution to the group over the last nine years and wish him well for the future."

What was all of that?  We'll find out when the market opens today.

Lovisa stocks ended the day 9% lower at 22.44

A good point made by Salt Funds managing director Matt Goodson in the New Zealand Herald about how rising bond yields had put the AI and data centre sector under pressure.

This is what he told the paper.

"If you look at the broader sector over the last few weeks, the quality listed players like Goodman Group, Infratil and Next DC have all been quite weak, chiefly under pressure from rising bond yields.

"Effectively these are very-long-duration property assets in many ways with very attractive yields on development, so rising bond yields has been the thing weighing on the sector."

Bond yields are the returns on what is generally considered the safest investment — the debt of large governments like the US and Australia.

My colleague David Taylor wrote a great explainer recently about how the rising price of an "I-O-U" note is changing the shape of global markets.
