https://www.dw.com/en/how-a-multibillion.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
https://www.dw.com/en/how-a-multibillion.text:
Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.

However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."

He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.

"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."

Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."

However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.

"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.

However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.

"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.

While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.

"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.
https://www.dw.com/en/how-a-multibillion.summary: Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Argentina has laid claim to the islands for two centuries. The Falklands is home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean.

https://www.dw.com/en/nobel-prize-in-lit.title: Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson
https://www.dw.com/en/nobel-prize-in-lit.text:
Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."

Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.

The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson moved with her family among several small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.

Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regard translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.

Carson is also heavily influenced by the King James Bible and more modern writers including Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov Award.

Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did revealed in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease.

Canadian poet, essayist, translator and scholar Anne Carson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," noted the Swedish Academy, who praised the author for her "desire for new meaning" as a poet and her "obsession with words" as a philologist.

The Hungarian novelist and screenwriter has produced a "compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art," noted the Swedish Academy, who has awarded Krasznahorkai the Nobel Prize in Literature for 2025. His debut novel "Satantango" (1985) was adapted into a legendary 7.5-hour film by Bela Tarr.

Han Kang is the first South Korean author to win the Nobel Prize in literature, recognizing "her intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life." Her publication debut came as a poet in 1993; the Man Booker International Prize for fiction, awarded to her in 2016 for her novel "The Vegetarian," marked her global breakthrough.

The Norwegian playwright has had 1,000 productions of his plays staged in more than 50 languages. He is also the author of novels, poetry and children's books. The Nobel Prize committee selected the writer "for his innovative plays and prose which give voice to the unsayable." He is shown here at the National Book Awards in 2022, where he was a nominee for "A New Name: Septology VI-VII."

The French author, born in 1940, is renowned for her autobiographical prose works that go "beyond fiction in the narrow sense," said the Swedish Academy. Among others, her 2001 book "Happening" deals with her illegal abortion from the 1960s. She was selected "for the courage and clinical acuity with which she uncovers the roots, estrangements and collective restraints of personal memory."

Tanzanian novelist Abdulrazak Gurnah won the Nobel Prize in literature in 2021 "for his uncompromising and compassionate penetration of the effects of colonialism," said the Swedish Academy. "His novels recoil from stereotypical descriptions and open our gaze to a culturally diversified East Africa unfamiliar to many in other parts of the world."

Crowned with the Nobel Prize in literature in 2020, the American poet and essayist had already won major awards in the US, including the Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award, as well as the National Humanities Medal, which was presented by Barack Obama in 2016. Her most notable works include "The Triumph of Achilles" (1985) and "The Wild Iris" (1992).

The Austrian author born in 1942 became famous with experimental plays such as "Offending the Audience" in 1966. He also co-wrote Wim Wenders films, including "Wings of Desire." The decision to award Handke the Nobel Prize was criticized since he is also known for his controversial positions on the Yugoslav wars. In 2014, he had also called for the prize to be abolished, dubbing it a "circus."

The Polish writer was actually awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in 2019, since it had been postponed for a year following scandals affecting the Swedish Academy, the body that chooses the laureates for the award. A two-time winner of Poland's top literary prize, the Nike Award, Tokarczuk was also honored in 2010 with the Man Booker International Prize for her novel "Flights."

Japan-born British novelist, screenwriter and short story writer Kazuo Ishiguro won the 2017 award. His most renowned novel, "The Remains of the Day" (1989), was adapted into a movie starring Anthony Hopkins, while his latest novel, "Klara and the Sun" (2021), has been made into a film with Jenna Ortega in the titular role. His works deal with memory, time and self-delusion.

An atypical but world famous laureate: US songwriter Bob Dylan was awarded the Nobel Prize in literature in 2016. The Swedish Academy selected Dylan "for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition."

Calling her work "a monument to suffering and courage in our time," the Swedish Academy honored the Belarusian author and investigative journalist in 2015. Alexievich is best known for her emotive firsthand accounts of war and suffering, including "War's Unwomanly Face" (1985) and "Voices from Chernobyl" (2005).

The French writer's stories describe a universe of haunted cities, absentee parents, criminality and lost youths. They are all set in Paris with the shadow of World War II looming heavily in the background. The Swedish Academy described the novelist, whose work has often focused on the Nazi occupation of France, as "a Marcel Proust of our time."

Canadian writer Alice Munro, who died in 2024, was no stranger to accolades, having received the Man Booker International Prize and the Canadian Governor General Literary Award three times over. The Swedish Academy called her a "master of the contemporary short story."

Guan Moye, better known under his pen name Mo Yan, was praised by the Swedish Academy as a writer "who with hallucinatory realism merges folk tales, history and the contemporary." The decision was criticized by Chinese dissidents like artist Ai Weiwei, who claimed Mo Yan was too close to the Chinese Communist Party and did not support fellow intellectuals who faced political repression.

The academy chose Tomas Gosta Transtromer (1931-2015) as the winner in 2011 "because, through his condensed, translucent images, he gives us fresh access to reality." In the 1960s, the Swedish poet worked as a psychologist at a center for juvenile offenders. His poetry has been translated into over 60 languages.

The Peruvian novelist, who died in April 2025, received the Nobel Prize "for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual's resistance, revolt, and defeat." In Latin America, he was famous for stating "Mexico is the perfect dictatorship" on TV in 1990, and for punching his once-friend and fellow Nobel laureate, Gabriel Garcia Marquez, in the face in 1976.

The German-Romanian author was awarded the Nobel Prize as a writer "who, with the concentration of poetry and the frankness of prose, depicts the landscape of the dispossessed." She is noted for her work criticizing the repressive communist regime of Nicolae Ceausescu in Romania, which she experienced herself. Müller writes in German and moved to West Berlin in 1987.

The Swedish Academy called J.M.G. Le Clezio an "author of new departures, poetic adventure and sensual ecstasy, explorer of a humanity beyond and below the reigning civilization." Le Clezio was born in Nice, France, in 1940 to a French mother and a Mauritian father. He holds dual citizenship and calls Mauritius his "little fatherland."

The 11th woman to win the award since its creation in 1901, British author Doris May Lessing (1919-2013) wrote novels, plays and short stories. The Nobel Prize recognized her for being a writer "who with skepticism, fire and visionary power has subjected a divided civilization to scrutiny." She also campaigned against nuclear weapons and the apartheid regime in South Africa.

The winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The winner also receives a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, and is expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.

On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, followed by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.

Edited by: Rob Turner

https://www.dw.com/en/south-korea-recall.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine ambassador amid POW dispute
https://www.dw.com/en/south-korea-recall.text:
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine. Seoul is upset about a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war being made public knowledge at the UN and had demanded — but not received — an apology.

South Korea said on Thursday that it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine amid a deepening diplomatic rift over making the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul public last month.

The two countries have been at loggerheads since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's speech at the UN General Assembly, during which he spoke about the capture and later the transfer of two North Korean soldiers who had been fighting against Ukraine alongside Russian forces.

South Korea has called for an apology from Ukraine, saying the comments breached a confidentiality agreement and could put the POWs' families still in North Korea at risk.

Kyiv, meanwhile, has said no such agreement existed and voiced a desire to smooth over a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of apologizing.

"The govenment has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine," Seoul's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday.

"The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and wil continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end," it said.

Last week, President Lee Jae Myung called for a "public apology" from Kyiv and said South Korea would take "additional measures" if one was not forthcoming. He said that during the prisoner swap, "the Ukrainian side demanded confidentiality and agreed to it, but unilaterally disclosed it."

When challenged with what Myung described as "utmost courtesy," he said Kyiv instead denied the existence of a confidentiality agreement, making him out to be a liar, and spoke of the prospect of war on the Korean peninsula.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, had spoken of a "diplomatic misunderstanding" that he said "we sincerely hope to resolve."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bilateral tensions also emerged this week amid the publication of an investigative report in The Guardian claiming that fuel was being shipped to Russia from South Korea via sanctioned tankers, alleviating the strains on diesel supplies amid Ukraine targeting Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure.

South Korea has walked a fine line on Russia's war in Ukraine, providing humanitarian and non-lethal equipment to Kyiv, as well as financial assistance, but also seeking to maintain cordial ties with Russia, which has a small stretch of border with North Korea near Vladivostock.

North Korea, meanwhile, sent troops to help Russia reclaim the border region of Kursk that Ukraine was able to partially occupy, and has since celebrated this deployment at home with much fanfare, while seeking closer ties to Putin's Russia.

https://www.dw.com/en/as-russia-steps-up.title: As Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian data centers, could Ukraine soon be offline?
https://www.dw.com/en/as-russia-steps-up.text:
As Russia targets Ukraine's data centers more and more, experts say the country's internet system is too robust to shut down entirely. However, services could become more expensive.

Hackers and power outages were once the largest threat to Ukraine's data centers. Now, it is the buildings themselves that are in the cross hairs.

Since early September, Russia has been  targeting these centers, which house the physical infrastructure needed to store digital information, systematically.

Digital infrastructure in and around the capital Kyiv was already affected but after the attacks, several television channels and streaming services were temporarily unavailable. Subscribers to several cable networks also reported that they had difficulties connecting.

The servers and computer systems needed to store data and keep online services operating smoothly are a crucial target because if they are damaged, it can have a nationwide effect. All online systems, ranging from news portals, state registries, banking and finance, need functioning data centers to operate smoothly.

Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said Russia had targeted major Ukrainian data centers to disrupt the flow of information. "As Russia isn’t achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite widespread damage caused by Russian attacks, experts do not believe the country risks having a complete internet blackout. Telecommunications expert Oleksandr Glushchenko told DW that this was because the entire sector was quite decentralized.

"The industry was never regulated in Ukraine, and no multi-million licenses were required,” he explained. "Entering the market was very affordable, which is why thousands of businesses started offering their services."

He added that Ukrainians could choose between multiple providers — and in some cases up to 10. This competition, he said, meant that Ukraine had "some of the best internet provider services in the world."

At the same time, he noted, damage caused by kinetic attacks could cause certain providers to "go dark" while repairs took place.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksandr Fediienko, who is a member of the parliamentary Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, posted similar sentiments on the social network Facebook: "Will the internet disappear in Ukraine? Of course not. The infrastructure will be restructured, and alternative sites will be established." He added that the Russian attacks made no sense because Ukrainian providers were able to restore service so quickly.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor on defense technology, said that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers were part of a wider campaign. "They've already been scaring us with claims that there won't be food or fuel, and now they're scaring us with the prospect of losing internet access," he wrote on Facebook.

Glushchenko said that even if a server was destroyed, its data would be available from other data centers where it was stored, including abroad. "The system can automatically switch to a different data center," he explained.

He pointed out that telecommunications companies also stored copies with cloud services offered by providers such as Google and Amazon.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Oleksandr Olshanskyi, the founder of the Ukrainian web hosting provider MiroHost and also the head of the leading Ukrainian IT service company Internet Invest, told the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine that his data center had been almost totally destroyed but that this had not made a major difference. He said that the vast majority of his clients remained unaffected, as they could fall back on operation capacities in Poland and the Czech Republic. "I'm only left with about 150 out of 20,000 to 25,000 clients, who for some reason did not shift, duplicate or secure their data," he explained.

Tech experts have recommended that Ukrainian data centers place a higher priority on decentralization, saying they should be as spread out as possible geographically, and also that data should be cloned and secured in other data centers abroad. Moving infrastructure into underground spaces could also be a solution, but this would translate into extra costs for customers.

"We've grown accustomed to having the fastest and cheapest internet in Europe, and the best technical support," Fediienko said but pointed out that this was "about to change."

Beskrestnov also expected the price of internet services to rise soon, to cover the costs of repairing damage to infrastructure.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-bundeswehr-.title: German Bundeswehr: A new naval port in Emden aims to enhance Germany's defense capabilities
https://www.dw.com/en/german-bundeswehr-.text:
Citing the escalating security threat, Germany's Navy has decided to establish a second port on the North Sea coast. Emden was chosen as the location.

After months of evaluating different locations, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced that the Bundeswehr's new naval port will be built in Emden, on the North Sea coast of Lower Saxony.

"Emden offers ideal conditions, such as quick access to the Atlantic Ocean and the far north," Pistorius said. He added that a second port is needed to accommodate the growing German Navy: New ships and boats require berths, and additional service members need housing. Furthermore, he said, "this will enhance the deterrence capabilities of both Germany and NATO."

The commercial port of Emden is the economic heart of East Frisia. Not only does it dominate the cityscape, but it also provides thousands of jobs. Directly adjacent to the port is the large Volkswagen plant, from which cars are exported by ship to destinations around the world. The port also serves as a shipment hub for large components for wind farms in the North Sea. Now, a naval base with up to 2,000 military posts will be built by the early 2030s. Emden hosted a Bundeswehr base until 1997, but it was no longer needed after the end of the Cold War and was consequently decommissioned.

Coastal land is tough to come by in Germany, but that's not the case in Emden. The port city has "the great advantage of having a lot of available space where a new port can be developed," says Johannes Peters, an expert on maritime security at the Institute for Security Policy at the University of Kiel.

"Emden offers the opportunity to build a dedicated naval port that complies with the latest requirements, including those for security and port protection," Peters emphasizes in an interview with DW. Pistorius estimates that up to 450 hectares of land will be needed — equivalent to about 630 soccer fields.

The only naval port currently on the German North Sea coast is located in Wilhelmshaven. From a strategic perspective, it doesn't make sense to have just one port and nothing to fall back on, security expert Peters emphasized. "If some kind of scenario where conflict breaks out were to actually occur and this infrastructure were to fail, then you'd have a real problem. That's why they want to diversify their options here now."

Pistorius said there was a strategic advantage to a second naval port on the North Sea: "This makes us harder to predict in an emergency and expands our operational capabilities."

The planned port in Emden is intended to complement and provide relief for the Wilhelmshaven naval base. This is where Operational Flotilla 2 is stationed, a large formation consisting of frigates and supply ships. The Wilhelmshaven naval base is also being expanded as the fleet grows and personnel levels increase.

In reference to Wilhelmshaven, Pistorius said the "smallest navy in the history of the Bundeswehr" now had more responsibilities than ever before. "So the navy must grow, and it will," P{istorius said. "We have laid the groundwork for this in all areas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bremerhaven was also on the shortlist. Although it will not be getting a naval base, the German government is investing a great deal of money there as well. The port will be expanded into a logistical hub that could be used to deploy large troop contingents and heavy equipment from NATO allies in the event of an emergency.

That is the plan outlined in "Operation Plan Germany," Germany's defense plan in the event of a crisis or threat to alliance security. The federal government is allocating up to €1.35 billion ($1.51 billion) for the expansion.

Although Emden has been officially chosen as the site, so far this is only a memorandum of understanding between the Defense Ministry, the state of Lower Saxony and the city of Emden. Construction of the naval port is likely to take years. "There are still major hurdles to overcome," says Defense Minister Pistorius.

"You can't just walk into a home improvement store and buy a new naval base," Pistorius said. "Marine engineering, transportation links, the barracks — we need to get started on these right away."

The city, with its approximately 50,000 residents, is expected to benefit from the construction of the port, especially since the future of the local Volkswagen plant is uncertain because of ongoing economic trouble for the automaker.

Mayor Tim Kruithoff was all the more delighted. "This is a great day for Emden," he said. He called the planned naval base "an extraordinary opportunity" for jobs and for the economic development of the entire region.

This article was originally written in German.

The Bundeswehr's new naval port will be built in Emden, on the East Frisia coast of Lower Saxony. The commercial port of Emden is the economic heart of East Fr is the cityscape of EastFrisia.

https://www.dw.com/en/middle-corridor-ca.title: Middle Corridor: Can Bulgaria be a safe gateway for Asian imports to the EU?
https://www.dw.com/en/middle-corridor-ca.text:
The EU wants more trade via the Middle Corridor, which could bring big benefits for Bulgaria. But Tuesday's drone attacks on commercial ships off the Bulgarian coast are a stark reminder of the security risks involved.

On the morning of October 6, drones hit two commercial ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, sinking one of the ships and causing alarm and outrage in both Bulgaria and the European Union.

The drone attacks come at a time when the EU is pushing for Bulgaria to become a key entry point for goods imported from Asia to the bloc via the trade route known as the Middle Corridor.

The Middle Corridor, which the EU also refers to as the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, connects Europe and Asia. It begins in China and runs through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey before reaching the EU.

Although it is mostly made up of railways and roads, short sections of the corridor cross the Black and Caspian Seas.

The EU has this year declared its intention to bet big on this trade route, a move that could affect Bulgaria's railways, roads and ports.

Bulgaria's land border crossing with Turkey, Kapitan Andreevo, is already one of Europe's busiest, trucks frequently lining up at the checkpoint.

The country also has two strategic ports on the Black Sea — Varna and Burgas — and a new section of a railway line between Istanbul and the Bulgarian border is set to open this fall.

In September, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos called Bulgaria "Europe's Connectivity Gateway" due to its strategic location on this route.

A few months earlier, Kos said the Middle Corridor could considerably cut transport times from Asia to Europe from 45 days to just 15 days and is safer than the two traditional routes for goods being transported to Europe from Asia.

One of these was an overland route via the Northern Corridor through Russia. Trade along this route dropped sharply after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The other route, sometimes referred to as the Ocean Route, sees goods traveling by ship through the Red Seaand the Suez Canal. But fears of disruption caused by wars and instability in the Middle East mean that many goods are now being shipped all the way around Africa — a journey that takes around 45 days. That results in delays and costs for businesses and consumers alike.

All of this explains why the Middle Corridor suddenly seems so attractive — a fact confirmed by Vessela Tcherneva, deputy director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, who is based in Sofia, Bulgaria.

"The Middle Corridor is a project that basically avoids both war theaters that we have near Europe," Tcherneva told DW. "It avoids the route through Russia, and also it avoids the route through the Middle East."

As promising as it sounds, a lot needs to change before the Middle Corridor can really compete with the Ocean Route.

"You have, first and foremost, security limitations," said Tcherneva. "The security situation in Central Asia needs to really have improved enough so that one can make long-term plans for constructing big projects."

Tcherneva also stressed that weak institutions and bureaucracies in countries along the Middle Corridor are an issue. Russian involvement cannot be ruled out.

"We have seen infrastructure projects in the past not happen because they were not perceived as being in Russia's interest, and the Russians seem to have quite a bit of leverage in the countries along the route," she said, adding that "the outcome of Russia's war in Ukraine is going to have an impact on the success or failure of the Middle Corridor."

Tuesday's drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea are a stark reminder that security on the route could well remain a problem.

In addition, the water level in the Caspian Sea, which is situated on the Middle Corridor, is falling, with climate change as a key driver. This means there is no guarantee that ships will be able to cross it in the future.

Then there is the problem of infrastructure: Ports and railways along the route lack capacity for big increases in trade volumes.

Despite these risks and limitations, the EU clearly wants to see more trade coming through the Middle Corridor, even if it cannot replace existing routes.

In her recent State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU wants to improve what it calls "connectivity." It wants to diversify trade routes, increase trade flows and reduce freight transit times.

To do so, it aims to raise €12 billion ($13.5 billion) in public and private investment.

Bulgaria could benefit from this in a number of ways.

"The Bulgarian railways have been underinvested in for many, many years now — for decades. Bulgarian ports would also benefit greatly from investment," Tcherneva told DW. "Developing better road connections from the Mediterranean up, but also east-west, would help, especially the north of the country, which is currently not very well connected. So, there are clear benefits."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
https://www.dw.com/en/middle-corridor-ca.summary: The EU wants more trade via the Middle Corridor, which connects Europe and Asia. The Middle Corridor is a key entry point for goods imported from Asia to the EU. The EU has this year declared its intention to bet big on this trade route. The route could cut transport times from Asia from 45 days to just 15 days.

https://www.dw.com/en/gerhard-schröder-v.title: Gerhard Schröder visits latest Russian employer, Hyperglobus
https://www.dw.com/en/gerhard-schröder-v.text:
Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder visited a Moscow supermarket in his new role on the supervisory board. Schröder is no stranger to retirement stipends in Russia — or the scandal that accompanies them.

Gerhard Schröder visited one of the Moscow branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain on Wednesday, a few days after being named a member of its supervisory board.

Russian TV footage showed employees at the branch greeting the former German chancellor and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, with sustained applause.

Schröder has current or recent links to a series of Russian businesses and to President Vladimir Putin, issues that have become increasingly contentious in Germany in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The new Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus was spun off from Germany's Globus Holding last year.

Last week, Hyperglobus announced that Schröder had been appointed to the supervisory board. The supermarket confirmed that the former chancellor and Social Democrat had visited a branch on the western outskirts of Moscow on Wednesday.

"I'm very pleased to be here, to see this wonderful hypermarket, to see the results of your work and to meet you, my wonderful colleagues," RBC television in Russia quoted Schröder as saying.

Schröder also reportedly called last week for the continuation of remaining trade ties between Russia and countries like Germany amid the sanctions imposed since the start of the war in Ukraine.

"It is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow us to hear each other and look for ways forward," newspaper RBK reported him as saying last Friday.

Schröder's close ties to Putin came under scrutiny even while he was still in office, notably in 2004 when Schröder responded to a question from a reporter by saying that, yes, he believed Putin was a "flawless democrat" or lupenreiner Demokrat.

Even 22 years ago, this assertion strained credulity in many eyes — not least among opposition groups or in war-torn Chechnya.

On leaving politics, Schröder kept close ties to the Kremlin and took up a series of senior roles, perhaps most famously on the board of the Rosneft energy giant and before that on the board of the Nord Stream gas pipeline project that was majority owned by Gazprom.

In 2014, not long after the annexation of Crimea and as a Russian-backed civil war brewed in Ukraine, Schröder was Nord Stream's guest of honor in St. Petersburg, where he celebrated his 70th birthday in lavish style.

Four years later, after an election many in the West decried as bordering on a sham, Schröder took a prominent place at the 2018 swearing-in ceremony for Putin's fourth presidential term at the Kremlin (pictured above).

Now-deceased Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny once said Schröder was Putin's "errand boy."

In 2024, Schröder was stripped of a state-funded office and staff — typically provided to former chancellors — on the basis that he was no longer fulfilling any obligations tied to his previous role in government.

His party, the center-left Social Democrats, tried on several occasions to eject him as a member. Each attempt failed to clear the high legal bars required, and he remains a member, having joined in 1963.

Putin has often suggested him as a possible peace mediator between Russia, Ukraine and Europe — with Schröder also expressing a willingness to take on the role — even though the reality is he would likely be entirely unacceptable as a mediator to all parties other than Russia, and particularly to Ukraine.

SchröDer has been named a member of the supervisory board of the supermarket chain. He has been linked to a series of Russian businesses and to President Vladimir Putin.

https://www.dw.com/en/transgressive-edgy.title: Transgressive, edgy DIY: What the 90s meant for British art
https://www.dw.com/en/transgressive-edgy.text:
The 1990s are remembered for Britpop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the familiar icons.

The 1990s in Britain are often remembered through a haze of nostalgia consisting of rave culture, Britpop and provocative art and fashion by the likes of Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen.

Undeniably, the decade was a time of major change in British society — the long reign of Margaret Thatcher had come to an end and the West entered a period of relative post-Cold War stability.

Meanwhile, British cultural icons like Oasis, the Spice Girls and Vivienne Westwood garnered international fame.

But Tate Britain's new exhibition "The 90s: Art and Fashion," which opens on October 8 and runs through February 14, 2027, urges viewers to look beyond the familiar names and images.

Even though now prominent artists such as Damien Hirst and Juergen Teller are among the show's 70 contributors, the exhibition also aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities which were left out of the mainstream discourse.

After all, says chief curator Edward Enninful in the exhibition's program, "the energy of the 90s was not concentrated in a single movement, but distributed across communities, disciplines and geographies that have not always been equally represented."

For Enninful, the exhibition is personal: The Ghanaian-born British fashion editor, stylist and creative director became the youngest-ever fashion director of i-D Magazine in the 90s at age 18, helping shape the diverse and experimental London fashion scene of the 1990s. He later became editor-in-chief of British Vogue in 2017.

Enninful writes that he and his co-curators aimed to present a body of work which "reflects a broader landscape of practices and voices that shaped the period, many of which operated beyond the structures of visibility at the time." The exhibition pays special attention to artists of color and women whose work was not necessarily showcased as prominently at the time.

Black masculinity became "a site of cultural negotiation" in Britain in the 90s, writes co-curator Helen Little in the program text: "Figures such as Chris Ofili, Steve McQueen, Keith Piper, Koto Bolofo and Ozwald Boateng reimagined the Black masculine, challenging the racist specter of Black men, who had been defined as part of a masculinity crisis linked to post-industrial decline and excluded from the narrative of 'Cool Britannia.'"

Just like "Swinging London" in the 1960s, "Cool Britannia" became a widespread phrase to refer to the 1990s as an era during which British youth culture, pop music, art and political optimism boomed.

The 90s also offered artists plenty of chances to create without waiting for support from traditional gatekeepers. Britain entered the decade in recession, but that economic uncertainty also left artists free to do what they wished.

Empty buildings and industrial spaces were turned into informal venues. A 23-year-old Damien Hirst orchestrated "Freeze," a self-organized student exhibition in 1988 in a disused London warehouse. It became a landmark early art exhibition for the generation of artists known as the "Young British Artists" or YBA.

Artists Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin opened The Shop, a temporary art gallery and social space in 1992, as a place where exhibitions could develop outside established galleries. Lucas and Emin also paved the way for women artists thanks to their deeply personal works and their edgy expressions of female liberation.

While the Spice Girls helped make feminism accessible to a younger generation of Brits in the 90s by popularizing the "girl power" slogan and shaping "identity through agency power and resistance," as Tate curator Helen Little argues, Emin and Lucas meanwhile "presented a new visual language of clothing as art to tackle societal taboos around female sexuality, vulnerability and desire" — from t-shirts with provocative slogans to a grunge look of scuffed Dr. Martens boots with razor blades. Their work "held a mirror up to gender, behavior and identity," Little writes.

At the same time, the British fashion industry came into the international spotlight.

In a feminine sensuality counter to the gender stereotypes dismissed by Emin and Lucas, waif-like Kate Moss came to represent the feminine ideal of the 1990s. Dubbed "heroin-chic," the style was an antithesis to the glamorous, athletic physiques of the supermodels who preceded her. Corinne Day's photographs of the model led to the raw aesthetic to be labelled "grunge" after the anguished style of rock music hailing from Seattle and led by Nirvana.

The trend has undergone significant cultural reexamination since then: "Along with the look also came criticism that the strung-out look of drug or alcohol addiction was glamorized while encouraging serious eating disorders in a generation of young women," points out Alex Farquharson, director of the Tate Gallery in his foreword to the exhibition.

The 1990s were also an exciting era for Britain in haute couture, as legendary designers John Galliano led Dior, while Alexander McQueen started directing Givenchy at the age of 27.

McQueen's runway presentations were more akin to performance art than commercial fashion shows — and they often included historical critiques. Among them was the famous finale of his Fall/Winter 1998 collection at a London warehouse, during which the model stood in a circle of flames. Titled "Joan," the show was a reference to the killing of Joan of Arc.

McQueen designed several other runway shows that reflected on British history, with topics of conquest and punishment repeatedly coming to the forefront. His 1995 presentation "Highland Rape" referenced the history of Scotland's subjugation, with the designer describing it as "England's rape of Scotland."

As co-curator Jessica Vaughan points out in her exhibition text: "Art, fashion and photography were not simply transgressive reactions … but reflected a genuine public unease with Britain's global identity and its past."

In a world that can now feel increasingly mediated by screens, algorithms and established platforms, the artwork of the 90s offers a reminder of the value of physical spaces and fresh DIY creativity of the last smartphone-free decade.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier
https://www.dw.com/en/transgressive-edgy.summary: "The 90s: Art and Fashion" urges viewers to look beyond familiar names and images. The show aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities left out of the mainstream discourse.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.title: Germany news: Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.text:
Political extremism threatens Germany's existing social order, Chancellor Merz has said. The Transport Ministry has proposed a five-year plan to improve Germany's ailing railroad infrastructure.

This blog has now closed. Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 7, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has begun a three-day state visit to neighboring France. He landed at Paris' Orly airport on a damp evening and made his way to the German Embassy.

He said Europe needed to face its various security and political challenges with a mixture of the head's reason and the heart's emotion.

"Reason and heart, that's what Europe needs again today, in a time of wars and crises, in which our democracies are under attack to an extent not seen since the second World War," Steinmeier said.

He said it was a mixture of reason, or head, and heart that had made the Franco-German reconciliation after the war possible.

Steinmeier was playing on a quote from French writer Victor Hugo, who in the 19th century said that in Europe, Germany was the heart and France was the head or the reason. Steinmeier said he would leave it open to debate whether the modern-day French or Germans might agree with this particular division of anatomical labor.

What mattered, he said, was that there could be only one response to the current circumstances: "Europe must, now above all, stand up confidently and in unison for the values that made us what we are: respect for human dignity, peace, freedom, democracy."

On Thursday, Steinmeier will visit the Pantheon monument in Paris with President Emmanuel Macron, to honor the Jewish historian and resistance fighter Marc Bloch, who was murdered by Nazi Germany.

Steinmeier also intimated that a new deal on Franco-German youth cooperation might be signed amid the visit, speaking of a "promise for a new generation of German and French youth, who want to learn to understand, value and love each other."

The visit coincides with considerable  political unrest among French young people in the form of ongoing school funding protests.

Steinmeier also said prior to leaving Berlin that his state visit would be "something of a farewell tour with a truly committed European and a good friend."

Both he and French President Macron took office in 2017, and both will be leaving their posts early in 2027.

Steinmeier's post, however, is far more ceremonial and removed from daily politics than that of the French president.

Immediately following its initial parliamentary session on Tuesday, Saxony-Anhalt state legislators from the far-right AfD and far-left BSW called for the federal government in Berlin to drop sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, as well as demanding an end to all arms deliveries and financial aid for Ukraine as Kyiv defends itself from a nearly five-year Russian invasion.

Both parties are known for their Russia "friendly" stances and their ties to the Kremlin.

They have also latched onto Moscow's claim that Berlin and other EU and NATO governments are the true "war mongers" in Ukraine, baselessly claiming that Russia is a peace-loving nation forced to defend itself against hostile neighbors.

BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht echoed AfD co-chair Alice Weidel in labeling the initiative "a signal for peace."

"Economic sanctions against Russia must end immediately," a statement said.

Germany's federal leadership, under two chancellors, has shown steadfast — if at times cautious — support for Ukraine and demanded Russia end its killing of civilians before entering into further dialogue.

Beyond dropping sanctions, the AfD and BSW insist Germany must normalize relations with Moscow, and stop "financing the war," arguing instead that money spent helping Ukraine defend its democracy would be better spent in Germany.

State governments in Germany have no say in federal foreign and energy policy, but the parties say they launched their effort in an attempt to force change in Berlin.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday addressed the threat of political extremism to the existing social order, accusing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and far-left BSW parties of wanting to wipe out "the DNA of our democracy."

"Extremism," said Merz, "is forcing its way into our state legislatures with a vengeance."

Merz, speaking in Berlin, called this week’s election of an AfD politician as speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament — the first time a far-right politician has been tapped to lead a statehouse since 1945 — a "historic break."

Moreover, Merz slammed politicians — potentially from his own conservative CDU party — for casting ballots in favor of Tobias Rausch in the Saxony-Anhalt vote, saying he was "deeply concerned and somewhat appalled" when the AfD's candidate was elected to the speaker position.

Rausch received 48 votes but the AfD and BSW only have 44 between them. It is unclear from whom Rausch picked up four extra votes — he was elected in a secret ballot.

Observers assume these came from within the CDU, but Merz said "false flag" attacks also occur in politics, implying the Social Democrats, the Left party and the Greens, all of which are also represented in the state's parliament, could be attempting to weaken or sow division in the CDU.

"Anyone ‌who ​casts their vote for the AfD is ​playing the extremists' game and undermining ⁠credibility," ​said Merz. "In any ‌case, this is incompatible ​with ⁠the values of my party, ⁠the ​CDU."

The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D., is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

Read all about it in this article by DW's Ben Knight: German spy scandal threatens national security

Police in Oberding, Bavaria, on Wednesday warned residents in Notzinger Moos near Munich airport to remain vigilant and urged them to keep children and small animals indoors amid a spate of puma sightings.

"According to initial expert assessments," a spokesperson for the local government said, "it could be a puma."

Authorities say it is unclear where such a cat would have come from, adding that no circuses are currently operating in the area.

It is unclear what actions — if any — local police will take.

Police have reportedly received one photo of the animal, though they have not yet published it.

Authorities encouraged anyone with information on the animal, its location or origin to contact police in the city of Erding.

The Frankfurt Book Fair opened with the Czech Republic as guest of honor. The program ranges from presentations of literary works to political debates. In addition, Latin America's 50th anniversary as the first guest of honor at the fair will be commemorated on a special stage, and Chile will present its plans as the guest country for 2027.

"Our future guest country, Chile, will have a strong presence, contributing to the program with 14 authors and illustrators," said Ines Bachor, the fair's director of public relations, at a press conference. "In addition, there will be a truly broad program featuring works from a wide range of countries, from Argentina to Guatemala, including comics."

The fair will be attended by prominent literary figures, such as the French-British essayist, lawyer and novelist Philippe Sands, who will receive the German Booksellers' Peace Prize on Sunday. On Saturday, he will participate in a roundtable discussion on the possibilities of prosecuting war crimes and the destruction of ecosystems.

The organization Writers in Exile will present some of its scholarship recipients who have found refuge in Germany, such as the Chinese philosopher Zhang Xiaomao and the Afghan writer Maryam Kishawarz, who will speak about the situation of women in her country.

Belarusian Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ales Bialiatski will also take part in a debate on the repression of critical literature in his country.

Another key topic will be the impact of artificial intelligence on issues related to intellectual property and historical memory.

The "Frankfurt Calling" program of the 78th Frankfurt Book Fair will feature 120 cultural events.

On Friday and over the weekend, the fair will open its doors to the general public, with authors signing books and presenting new releases.

The arrest of August Hanning, the former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency, on charges of espionage and treason has sent shockwaves through the country.

He has now been sent to prison awaiting trial.

DW looks at the latest developments surrounding Hanning in this article:  Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges

The question of which lawmakers besides those of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and populist BSW voted to elect the AfD's Tobias Rausch as parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday continues to fuel speculation — and outrage.

The choice of a far-right figure to preside over a state parliament for the first time since World War II has been described as a "breaking of taboos" by the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

Most observers suspect that politicians from the center-right Christian Democrats are the most likely to have backed Rausch, despite their party's official adherence to the "firewall" principle rejecting cooperation with the AfD.

DW looks at the growing mystery surrounding the affair in this article: Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?

As mentioned at the start of this blog, railroad woes are one major theme in our  Germany coverage.

But here is some very positive news for once: The parliamentary transport committee has finally endorsed a plan by railway operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) to build a new line linking Hannover and Hamburg by 2050.

The project for what is one of Germany's most important transport routes is planned to cost at least €9 billion ($10 billion) and had prompted years of wrangling.

It still requires backing by the full Bundestag, or lower house of parliament, on Thursday, but that is likely to be a formality.

The new two-track line will be designed for speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour (155 miles per hour), cutting journey times between the two cities by 18 minutes.

However, it will be some time before construction begins: The preliminary planning report that forsees submitting approval documents in 2034, with construction to start in 2036.

Renovation of the existing line between the two cities is also planned for 2029 under the agreement.

According to DB, that route is already heavily congested, carrying up to 147% of intended capacity.

The agreement was reached despite opposition from lawmakers representing constituencies affected by the new construction, including Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil of the Social Democrats (SPD).

US group the Backstreet Boyswill play their final of 10 concerts in Düsseldorf tonight, capping off a week of street parties and sing-alongs to celebrate the band.

"We'll take you on a trip back in time," member Howie Dorough promised.

To the rhythm of "Larger Than Life", Nick, Howie, Brian, AJ and Kevin appeared floating above the venue, crossing the Merkur Spiel-Arena on hoverboards each night.

Against the backdrop of a giant screen displaying futuristic graphics, accompanied by pyrotechnics and a laser show, the American stars have almost finished their short German residency.

The five musicians had already presented the show, Into The Millennium, at the Sphere in Las Vegas.

According to Live Nation, the event organizer, around 450,000 tickets have been sold for the performances. These 10 concerts are the only shows the band will perform in Europe on this tour.

The concert series carried the subtitle Homecoming: Live in Germany, because the band have enjoyed a loyal fan base since their early days in Germany, as the singers emphasized in Düsseldorf.

"Germany, you were our first love. You loved us before everyone else, and we loved you," Kevin Richardson said. "So many years, so many memories," Nick Carter added.

The boy band was founded in 1993 in Orlando, Florida and was part of the pop boom of the late 1990s.

The German government has said the acquisition of a majority of shares in Hamburg logistics company Zippel by China's state-owned shipping giant Cosco could pose a security threat and has blocked the sale.

The purchase of 80% of shares in Zippel by a Chinese company "would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of Germany’s and the EU’s supply chains," an Economy Ministry spokesman said.

Speaking after a Cabinet meeting in Berlin, the spokesman said that although Germany welcomed foreign investment in general, "there may be investments that threaten the country's security."

Reports at the end of April said that the BfV domestic intelligence agency already had reservations about the takeover, which had been approved by the Cartel Office in February.

The business daily Handelsblatt reported at the end of September that the government was intending to block the sale, though this was not confirmed by Berlin at the time.

Cosco already holds a 24.99% stake in the Hamburg container terminal Tollerort.

That deal prompted a debate at the time about China's participation in critical infrastructure in Germany.

Most people in Germany consider that Chancellor Friedrich Merz is not up to the job, a new survey has shown.

In all, 67% of respondents in the survey by the Ipsos institute were either wholly or fairly in agreement with the statement "The chancellorship of Friedrich Merz has failed."

A whole 48% completely agreed on Merz's insufficiency as leader, according to the survey published in the Spiegel news magazine.

There were regional differences in assessment's of Merz's performance, with 80% of people in eastern states completely or somewhat dissatisfied compared with 64% in the west.

However, there was much less agreement on which conservative politician could replace him if he were to step down or be ousted.

The survey gave a choice between the leader of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), Markus Söder, his party colleague Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt or the premier of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, Hendrik Wüst.

Altogether 43% of those surveyed said none of those named came into question, while some 14% responded with "Don't know."

Söder was, however, the favorite with 20% support, followed by Wüst on 16%.

Dobrindt lagged far behind on just 5%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The co-leader of the Social Democrats (SPD), Lars Klingbeil, says coalition partner the Christian Democrats (CDU) has questions to answer after the election of Tobias Rausch, a politician from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), as parliamentary speaker in  Saxony-Anhalt.

"The fact that the candidate of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, which is classified as 'confirmed right-wing extremist,' was elected as state parliament speaker with considerably more than just AfD votes raises very urgent questions," said Klingbeil, who is also deputy chancellor and finance minister.

"Electing right-wing extremists to such positions breaks with a taboo," he said.

"Not just the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could happen."

The SPD federal parliamentary party staged a march through Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Tuesday to protest at the election result.

The state chapter of the AfD, which won a landslide victory at September elections, is classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rausch was elected speaker with 48-29 votes, though just 44 votes for him would have resulted if only his party (39 seats) and the populist BSW (five seats), which had pledged to back him, had voted in his favor.

The CDU parliamentary leader, Sven Schulze, had recommended that the 15 parliamentarians in his party abstain from voting, but there were only five abstentions altogether in the secret ballot. One CDU member was absent.

The other three parties represented in the legislature — the SPD, the Left Party and the Greens — had all declared their opposition to Rausch.

Schulze said he could not believe that the four extra votes for Rausch came from the ranks of the CDU, although there has been widespread speculation that this was the case.

All mainstream parties in Germany have so far officially stated that they reject any form of cooperation with the AfD in keeping with the so-called "firewall."

August Hanning, the former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service (BND), who was arrested on suspicion of espionage, is due to appear on Wednesday before an investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe, who will decide whether he should remain in custody pending trial.

Hanning, who stepped down as head of the BND in 2005, is under investigation on suspicion of espionage-related offenses, including high treason, obtaining state secrets, attempted high treason, and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reaffirmed Germany's support for Israel in remarks on the anniversary of the deadly October 7, 2023 attacks led by the Palestinian militant group Hamas.

"Germany stands firmly by Israel's side. Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime is never repeated," Merz said.

"We stand for the security and existence of Israel — this is a lesson drawn from the Shoah [Holocaust] and part of German identity," he said.

Merz said Germany believed that the two-state solution was the best way to establish peace in the region.

He also said the German government would do all in its power to combat rising antisemitism, adding that Jews had to be able to live in Germany without fear.

Merz said his thoughts on the anniversary were with the victims and their families, survivors and former hostages.

"And we hope that the deep pain and wounds inflicted by this day — by these monstrous, barbaric acts — can heal," he said.

Several events are being held in Berlin to mark the anniversary.

The Palestinian militant group Hamas led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023 in which some 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 others abducted.

The attacks triggered the ongoing war on Hamas in Gaza, which left some 74,000 Palestinians dead, most of them civilians.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-enlargement-eur.title: EU enlargement: European Commission tables reforms to prepare bloc for new members
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-enlargement-eur.text:
The European Commission is proposing earlier access to EU markets for candidate countries, new voting rules to reduce vetoes and extra safeguards for a bigger bloc. But is the reform fair — or even feasible?

The European Commission wants to inject new momentum into its enlargement process, which has seen some candidate countries waiting for decades to join.

Albania, Montenegro, Moldova and Ukraine are currently the frontrunners to join the bloc, with EU officials expressing the hope that Montenegro could do so as early as 2028.

"A larger union is a long-term investment in Europe's peace, security and prosperity," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told journalists in Strasbourg on October 6.

One key question is how the EU can take in more countries in the near future without becoming harder to run or running the risk of democratic backsliding in new member states.

The Commission's answer to this question is to simultaneously require candidate countries to meet EU standards and get the bloc itself to reform by removing obstacles in the accession process and protecting its democratic values.

One of the main stumbling blocks in accession negotiations so far has been the need for unanimous decisions across all 27 members. In the past, individual states have often blocked a candidate's progress because of bilateral issues.

The delays caused by Hungary's blocking of Ukraine's negotiation process are a prominent example.

Now — and not for the first time — the Commission is recommending that member states move away from the principle of unanimity for decisions like the opening of negotiation clusters, replacing it with qualified majority voting.

"Every cluster that you open is subject to three individual decisions, and every single decision is subject to unanimity. It's mind-blowing, and I think this clearly needs to go," a Commission official, who wished to remain anonymous, told journalists on Tuesday.

The catch is that a shift to qualified majority voting would itself require a unanimous decision.

"I have some reservations as to whether there will be unanimous agreement from the member states to move to qualified majority voting," Tinatin Akhvlediani, head of the enlargement program at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS) told DW, pointing to previous attempts to change voting rules that were shot down by member states.

To incentivize reform in candidate countries, the Commission is proposing gradual integration, which means that these countries could be granted some of the benefits of membership before joining — as long as they meet the EU's criteria.

"Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership. It is the accelerator for enlargement," Kos said on Tuesday, underlining that the process would stay merit-based.

This could have a motivational effect on candidate countries, Nina Vujanovic, a research fellow at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, told DW: "Reforms are important, but it is also important to reward that process a little bit earlier, ahead of accession," she said.

Earlier access to EU benefits is not entirely new: Montenegro, for example, already participates in the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) even though it is not yet a member.

The Commission now wants to give candidate countries such early access more systematically and link it to strategic alignment.

"This is not something that will be available [to candidate countries] unless they really orient themselves on the EU," a Commission official told journalists.

Making strategic alignment a condition is new and reflects the EU's efforts to adjust to the geopolitical tensions members and candidates are facing.

"The EU is trying to keep candidate countries out of the hands of Russia," Heather Grabbe, a senior fellow at Bruegel, told DW. "Strategic alignment is aimed very squarely at politicians like Aleksandar Vucic in Serbia, who has clearly promoted Russian interests," she said.

The new procedures would demand alignment not only with the EU's foreign and security policy, but also with its standards on economic security. "Trading gas with Russia is simply not something that builds trust with the European Union," said Nina Vujanovic.

To prevent breaches of democratic rules by new member states, the Commission proposes a 15-year period within which it would be easier to sanction new members by cutting financial support or restricting voting rights.

In an interview with The Guardian and other European media, Commissioner Kos made it clear that the EU had learned its lesson from the democratic backsliding it saw in the past in countries like Poland or Hungary: "No more Viktor Orban. We have to have quicker mechanisms than only Article 7."

Critics point out that this safeguard would create unequal conditions within the union.

"It is inherently unfair," says Heather Grabbe. "In the 2040s, why should Montenegro face different conditions than, say, Slovenia?"

Many current candidate countries have a shaky record when it comes to democratic norms, as Tinatin Akhvlediani points out: "They are actually fragile democracies. So, this approach vis-a-vis these countries can be very much justified."

Experts say that while it might be desirable to apply similarly strict rules to all members, it is not realistically feasible as it would have to be approved unanimously and, as Grabbe says, "it's very hard to get turkeys to vote for Christmas."

Although the Commission's push for new rules in relation to enlargement is likely to move the debate forward, it is ultimately up to member states to decide how much of it becomes reality.

The European Council, which is made up of the heads of state or government of the 27 EU member states, the European Council president and the president of the European Commission, is expected to discuss the proposals at its upcoming meeting on October 15–16.

The outcome of those talks will determine how quickly the Commission's new enlargement agenda can move forward.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
