https://www.dw.com/en/trust-in-the-germa.title: Trust in the German Constitutional Court is eroding — how can this be stopped?
https://www.dw.com/en/trust-in-the-germa.text:
Germany's top court, which turned 75 this year, is losing the population's trust, surveys show. Some say reforms in the way it picks candidates would help, to also accept candidates nominated by the far-right AfD.

The Federal Constitutional Court — Germany's equivalent of the US Supreme Court — still enjoys the most trust among the population of any branch of government, but that trust is slipping, according to recent surveys.

A new survey by the pollsters YouGov, commissioned to mark the 75th anniversary of the founding of the court, found that about two-thirds (66%) of Germans trust the Federal Constitutional Court. This was significantly more than the other major branches of the country's government system: The Bundesrat, the upper house of the German parliament, scored 47%, the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag 38%, and the Federal Government itself 29%.

But other surveys show those figures were significantly higher just a few years ago: One study from 2025 by the Allensbach Institute found that trust in the court was as high as 81% in 2021.

Exactly why this has happened remains a matter of conjecture: As a possible explanation, some analysts have pointed to the decisions the court made to allow the government to curtail certain freedoms during the COVID-19 pandemic — which precipitated many protests.

That period also saw an overall drop in trust in all the branches of government, and this decision, some argued, showed that the court was not an independent arbiter after all.

Christine Landfried, former professor of political science at Hamburg University, thinks the criticism that the court can be too political doesn't really make sense. Its purpose was always ultimately to make political decisions — but ones based on a legal argument, rather than a political debate.

"A constitutional court always deals with political questions," she told DW. "But the way that decisions are arrived at should follow legal arguments and legal methods. That's different from politics."

The court was founded in 1951, in the aftermath of World War II, to make sure that the laws of the newly founded West Germany adhered to the constitution, or Basic Law, which came into effect in 1949. Over the years, it has had to interpret the tenets of the Basic Law (democracy, human dignity, the rule of law) into many political questions: What happens to citizens' data? Should the government protect the climate? How much money should unemployed people be paid?

Former Constitutional Court judge Gertrude Lübbe-Wolff thinks that the problem is not that the court is too political, but that its composition does not reflect new political realities in Germany.

As things stand, there is an agreement in the two houses of the German parliament, the Bundestag and the Bundesrat, that the main parties each propose a certain number of candidates for the court's two chambers, or senates. The Bundestag and the Bundesrat each pick half the judges for the two eight-seat senates.

That agreement was fractured, however, last year thanks to a campaign against the candidate Frauke Brosius-Gersdorf, nominated by the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) whose position on decriminalizing abortion and other issues were deemed by some as too liberal. The campaign — driven by populist and unproven claims on social media — caused some parliamentarians from the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to withdraw their support, before Brosius-Gersdorf herself withdrew her candidacy.

Though this affair may have damaged trust in how the court's judges were selected, Lübbe-Wolff argues that maintaining the court's plural composition is "extremely important for sensible and balanced decisions that are broadly accepted by the public," she told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unlike US Supreme Court judges, many of whom are familiar names whose opinions and party affiliation are widely known, the people who sit on Germany's Constitutional Court are not famous at all. But they are nominated by different parties in parliament, and their political affiliations are usually known to those who care to follow the nominations.

But a key difference to the US Supreme Court, Landfried points out, is that while in the US, the judges only have to agree on a decision, but each can write their own reasoning, the German Constitutional Court makes an effort to produce a joint reasoning for each decision, or a majority reasoning if some judges disagree. "The Federal Constitutional Court acts much more as an institution," she said. "It's considered very important that this or that senate made a decision, and not that individual judges are in the foreground."

Lübbe-Wolff's new book, entitled "Does the Federal Constitutional Court need (more) Reform?" contains a few ideas for how the court could be improved to make it less dependent on the choices of the political parties. One suggestion: Instead of having the different parties in the parliamentary committee propose candidates, the seats on the Constitutional Court would be advertised like any other job, and people would apply, and then have the committee decide on who to accept. This would, Lübbe-Wolff argues, maintain the democratic principles behind the court selection while reducing the influence of party politics. Austria and Switzerland both already have similar systems.

Landfried likes this idea. "That would mean party politics is not such a big part of the selection," she said. "Very good people could apply who haven't been chosen by the party."

Lübbe-Wolff also believes that, for the sake of plurality, the Bundestag should allow candidates put forward by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be considered for the Constitutional Court. Germany's domestic intelligence agencies consider some sections of the AfD extremist and hostile to the constitution.

Indeed, the recent YouGov survey found that, among supporters of the major political parties, AfD supporters had by far the least faith in the court: Only 34%, compared to around 80% for both the CDU and SPD.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nevertheless, some constitutional courts at the state level have already accepted AfD nominees into their ranks, notably Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

Now Lübbe-Wolff believes that the wider array of parties in the German parliament mean that the AfD and the socialist Left Party should also be allowed to propose candidates. "It used to be that the CDU and the SPD could simply decide between themselves which judges to elect," she said. "Today they always need votes from the Left Party too, because the AfD has become so big." She calls this imbalance a "structural problem."

But she believes that there are enough safeguards in the selection processes to ensure that no candidate for the Constitutional Court would hold views that were directly hostile to the constitution. "I think there are people who I believe are close enough to the AfD that the party could put them forward, but at the same time stand reliably on the foundation of the constitution," she said. "I think there are people of a younger generation in that category, but they don't want to out themselves."

Landfried is not sold on the idea. "For me, sections of that party are hostile to the constitution, it is partly right-wing extremist," she says, though she doesn't believe that all AfD voters are far-right. "But I have my reservations, and I wouldn't agree with that proposal."

Landfried is concerned that, because of Germany's Nazi history, the federal constitutional court should be especially wary about allowing people who potentially have far-right sympathies a place on the body that is, more than any other, meant to safeguard German democracy.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Germany's Stuttgart Airport saw the temporary suspension of all departures and arrivals due to a bomb threat that turned out to be a hoax.

Police looked into a claim a man had made to an employee that he had been carrying a bomb in his luggage, which resulted in the terminal being evacuated and all air traffic being stopped.

Germany's Federal Police said no threat was detected, and the airport's operations resumed shortly after the threat was found to be not true.

The 24-year-old man who claimed to be carrying a bomb is under investigation for allegedly disturbing the peace by making threats of criminal offenses.

The 2026 German Book Prize has been awarded to Shida Bazyar for her novel "Die Lücken" (which could perhaps be translated as "The Gaps"), with the jury describing her book as "a novel against ambivalence."

The book is set in fictional community, Heimesbach in Hunsrück, "in which 90 years of German history have nested themselves in the walls and the biographies," as the prizegivers put it.

"The novel leads us through the years and the heads of those who shaped the village: from Jewish families who lost everything, via Nazi profiteers, who later reinvented themselves as innocent hangers-on, through the Sharifi and Karimpour families, who fled from Iran decades later," the book prize writes. "Shida Bazyar succeeds in providing a virtuoso storytelling mosaic about the burden of history, the lie of the new start, and the desire to finally find a home."

The jury praised Bazyar's storytelling format in particular, saying it was an ideal vehicle to convey disparate and yet interconnected ideas.

"The author chooses compelling literary strategies: The view of an omniscient narrator, and the caleidoscopic structure of the text make it possible to jump between times and to create both closeness and distance at the same time," they wrote in their explanation for the award.

The 38-year-old Bazyar was born in Germany to Iranian parents who fled in the 1980s.

"It's not so easy for me to truly experience joy, I have to say," Bazyar said in her acceptance speech. "Because it is quite a strange feeling when you write a novel about people who were persecuted, terrorized and murdered. To then be truly happy about its success, that doesn't seem quite right to me." Therefore, Bazyar said, she'd like to dedicate the accolades to the people the book is about.

Bazyar also made this year's shortlist for the International Booker Prize for her debut novel from 2016, "The Nights are Quiet in Tehran," which became a hit when translated into English in 2025.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have written to the EU's Ursula von der Leyen, saying the bloc needs tougher — and faster — means to respond to unfair trade practices by third countries.

Their appeal names no names but it seems most likely to have China in its crosshairs, or just maybe the US under Donald Trump's erratic trade policies.

This comes days before the EU trade commissioner heads to Beijing for talks, and just over a week before this month's EU leaders' summit, where the issue might well come up again.

Read the full story here.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has returned to his former high school on a visit marking the school's 100th anniversary, telling pupils they should aim for better grades than he managed.

Merz graduated from the Friedrich-Spee-Gymnasium in Rüthen, western Germany, 51 years ago.

"Do a slightly better Abitur than I did," the chancellor told pupils, referring to Germany's school-leaving qualification that allows students to attend university.

Merz has kept his exact final grade a closely guarded secret. Last year, he joked that his school certificate was locked in a safe at home.

He did, however, suggest that his overall grade was somewhere around 3.8 — a relatively poor result in Germany's grading system.

Merz has previously said he lacked discipline and motivation at school and at one point had to repeat a year.

"I didn't have difficulties with school; the school had difficulties with me," he joked on Monday.

He said things improved after he changed schools and moved to Rüthen, where mathematics and physics eventually became two of his favorite subjects.

Hundreds of pupils greeted Merz on his return, with some calling out "Hello, Chancellor" as he arrived.

The visit came less than a week after Merz presented the German School Award in Berlin, where he said he wanted to focus more personally on education policy and visit schools more frequently.

Germany plans to build a new naval base in the northern city of Emden as it expands its armed forces.

The federal government and the state of Lower Saxony signed a declaration of intent for the project on Monday, the Defense Ministry said.

Germany currently has only one North Sea naval base, in Wilhelmshaven. The ministry said it would not have enough capacity to accommodate the navy's planned expansion.

"New ships and boats need berths. Our soldiers need accommodation and training facilities," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said.

Pistorius said the new base could create up to 2,000 military posts and that Emden's access to the Atlantic made it an ideal location.

Lower Saxony Premier Olaf Lies said the aim was for the base to be operational by the early 2030s.

High-tech goods from China, such as electric vehicles or even robot vacuum cleaners, could represent a security risk, the BfV domestic intelligence agency has warned.

BfV head Sinan Selen told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin that the issue was of "great concern" to him.

"I already see substantial shortcomings that create potential for abuse," he said.

Data collected via the products could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products."

"In terms of resilience and availability (this) could confront us with problems," he said.

The warning comes as sales of high-tech products to Germany are growing and Chinese manufacturers compete ever more strongly with their German counterparts.

Deutsche Telekom plans to use artificial intelligence and automation to cut annual costs by around €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) by 2030.

The target covers the German telecommunications giant's operations outside the United States.

Deutsche Telekom is already using AI for repetitive tasks in network operations, customer service, software development and administration.

Its "Frag Magenta" chatbot handled around 2.6 million customer service calls in the first half of 2026, the company said.

At T-Mobile US, in which Deutsche Telekom holds a majority stake, AI agents now handle 40% of customer contacts.

Outside the US, Deutsche Telekom expects savings from AI and automation to reach €1.1 billion by 2027 and €2.5 billion by 2030.

"AI is fundamentally changing Deutsche Telekom," CEO Tim Höttges said. He said the technology was improving networks and customer service while opening up new business models."

The German football team has had its first four international matches under its new coach, Jürgen Klopp — a mixture of success, failure and in-betweens.

DW analyzes Klopp's methods and relationship with the team as shown over the past couple of months in this article: Klopp's first Germany internationals: What did we learn?

Grassroots groups within the Social Democrats (SPD) — the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government — have spoken out against plans to "flexibilize" the working week in a position paper.

In question is a paragraph in the coalition agreement that speaks of "the possibility of a weekly rather than a daily maximum working time."

The conservative Christian Democrat (CDU)-Christian Social Union (CSU) bloc has pushed to have a maximum number of hours that can be worked per week rather than the current daily standard limit of eight hours.

Although the four SPD groups fundamentally accept the idea, they are calling for strict controls, among other things wanting collective labor agreements under which both parties work out details as "a necessary prerequisite."

They also say exceptions should made in certain sectors where illegal employment is prevalent.

Employers' associations in June objected to the idea of collective labor agreements as a coercive measure when it was put forward by the Labor Ministry, leading to its retraction, with the CDU saying that it went against the coalition agreement.

The position paper submitted by the SPD groups could thus lead to a new split in the coalition, stating as it does: "It is not in keeping with a modern reform of working hours regulation or a better compatibility of work and family when bosses can decide alone when employees can knock off work."

Germany's Federal Court of Justice (BGH) has ruled that a person facing deportation cannot be detained as a flight risk simply because their past behavior suggests they might try to avoid being deported.

The case concerned a stateless Palestinian man who sought asylum at a police station in Germany in April 2023. Austrian authorities had already issued a decision requiring him to return.

A court in the German city of Duisburg ordered the man detained while his transfer was being arranged.

The courts argued that his previous actions indicated a risk that he would try to evade deportation. He had lived in Austria since 2020, where two asylum applications had been rejected, and had also applied for asylum in Belgium and Germany.

But the man had never explicitly said that he intended to avoid deportation.

The BGH ruled that his behavior alone was not enough to establish this particular ground for detention.

A person's words do not necessarily have to state the intention literally, the judges said. But it must be "clear and unambiguous" from what the person says and the circumstances that they intend to evade deportation.

The court found that the man's detention from May 7 to June 6, 2023 had therefore violated his rights.

German immigration law provides several other grounds on which people can be detained pending deportation.

Peter Hegemann from Germany's Humbolt University and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg have won this year's Nobel Prize in medicine alongside their US colleague, Karl Deisseroth.

You can read more about their achievements in this article: German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine

Germany is facing a growing risk of a violent confrontation with Russia as Moscow continues a campaign of hybrid warfare with other countries in Europe, the head ‌of ⁠Germany's BND ⁠foreign intelligence service warned on Monday.

Speaking before the Bundestag at ​the ‌annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs, Martin Jäger said: "The confrontation we are facing with Russia has ​taken on a new, more dangerous dimension."

"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled ‌in a violent conflict with Russia — the ‌attempted ​attack in Leipzig is just one example," he said.

"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," he added.

Jäger was referring to a drone attack at Leipzig airport in August that the German government has blamed on Russia.

Russia has repeatedly denied any intention of attacking ​NATO
countries, with President Vladimir Putin, however, saying on Thursday: "But if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond."

The Justice Ministry has put forward a draft bill making it easier for domestic abuse victims to leave joint tenancy contracts and obliging perpetrators to pay for any ensuing costs.

"The path to a self-determined and safe life after domestic abuse is often still a long one," Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig told newspapers from the Funke media group.

"We want to make it a bit easier," she added.

She said the draft bill aimed to give domestic abuse victims clear legal rights against their abusers, including being able to demand that the latter pay any costs arising from the premature termination of the joint lease.

The bill also envisages increased protection for children and relatives of victims.

Under current German law, family courts can impose bans on domestic abusers taking up contact with or approaching their victims but not other members of the same household.

Hubig said the draft law foresaw such protections being extended to other people dependent on the abuser without any separate application being made.

According to police statistics, nearly 266,000 people in Germany were affected by domestic abuse in 2024, 70% of them women and girls.

The Justice Ministry has said the real figure is likely to be much higher, estimating that 95% of cases go unreported.

Since May, the German government has paid out subsidies to 100,000 households wanting to procure an electric vehicle, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper on Monday.

Schneider, from junior coalition partner the Social Democrats (SPD), said the program, worth €3 billion ($3.36 billion), had "far exceeded our expectations."

He said that every additional electric vehicle protected households from high fuel prices and made the county less dependent on expensive oil imports and international conflicts.

According to the Bild article, half of households applying for the subsidy had a maximum annual income of €45,000 and three-quarters of them €60,000.

Schneider said he found it particularly important that this graduation of payments according to income functioned properly.

Preliminary assessments have shown that less than 15% of households that applied for the subsidy were looking to buy vehicles from China, contradicting expert views that Chinese automakers would profit the most.

The Left Party is taking a row about a remark made by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche to the Constitutional Court after Reiche failed to give a declaration to cease and desist on time.

Reiche had posted a remark on the official Instagram site of her ministry saying: "Antisemitism and expropriation endanger Germany and the economy."

The comment refers first to the unproven accusation that the Left Party is antisemitic in its ideology and then to the Left Party's plan to socialize apartments from corporate landlords in a bid to reduce skyrocketing rents in the capital.

Reiche doubled down on her criticism of the socialist party in comments she made during a visit to Ukraine over the weekend, telling the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild she feared a national loss of growth if a leftist coalition took power in Berlin.

"What the Left Party represents here in Berlin and the people that it represents is dangerous not only for Berlin but for our country," she said.

The Berlin branch of the Left Party has accused the Christian Democrats (CDU), to which Reiche and Chancellor Friedrich Merz belong, of carrying out a "large-scale campaign" against its top candidate, Elif Eralp, who won recent state elections in Berlin.

It has taken legal action over similar statements on CDU interior ministry websites in various states, criticizing the use of official government channels to denigrate another party.

The ministries in Saxony and Schleswig Holstein withdrew the statements, but those in Baden-Württemberg, Brandenburg and Hesse have so far not done so.

https://www.dw.com/en/jürgen-klopp-faces.title: Jürgen Klopp faces myriad of issues after rough start with Germany
https://www.dw.com/en/jürgen-klopp-faces.text:
Jürgen Klopp has done things a little differently since becoming Germany coach. Casting a wider net for talent and trying to connect with players and country haven't made an immediate impact, but he is not bowed.

Four games, three goals, two draws, one loss and one win. Jürgen Klopp would have hoped for better results from his first international break as Germany coach. But though the comfortable win over Serbia (2-0), draws against the Netherlands (1-1) and Greece (0-0) and a shock loss to Greece (0-1) in Germany leave them third out of four in their Nations League group, Klopp saw mostly positives.

"Everyone showed what they're made of; everyone earned their place. We've shown signs that we can do some things better than people gave us credit for. I wanted to get something going, and I definitely saw that happen," he said after Sunday's 0-0 draw in Thessaloniki.

For all the positivity of the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach, the four matches have, in reality, been a mixed bag for Germany.

Having fallen in the last 32 of the 2026 World Cup and exited in the group stage in 2022, Germany's footballing stock has never been lower.

Klopp tried to address this by casting his net wider, announcing a 44-man squad that split over the matches. He then said this would be a one off, but that his strategy of trying to find a diamond in the relative rough who could adapt to the international game had given him valuable insights.

"Hard work, lots of information — these guys are brimming with talent," he said of those given a surprise opportunity.

"People were saying that German soccer was at rock bottom and that there was no talent. ... They're not lacking in talent."

While Klopp may have seen potential, and has credit in the bank from his past work, he will need to turn that into results before too long.

While much has been said about Klopp's success in imprinting his trademark Gegenpressing (counter-press) style early on, he is also a coach who places a high value on connection. Throughout the international break, he has worn a cap emblazoned with the slogan "Einer von 83 millionen” (One of 83 million) in a reference to the German population and an attempt to unify in a country divided by the rise of the far-right AfD party.

He addressed the issue in his opening press conference and then reiterated his position after some social media users branded the team "not white enough" after their loss to Greece.

"There is no reason to give these people any thought. They aren't getting any of my attention. I have little time for stupidity in real life and none on social media either," Klopp said in answer to a question posed by DW.

As well as speaking honestly about his country, Klopp has been open with his new players.

"He has a very good rapport with every player. He tries to reach out to every player and make them feel good, that they're important and that they deserve to be here," said Florian Wirtz, who went on to label his coach as a "master" at managing relationships.

With limited time together, forming bonds between player, coach and country can elevate a national team. It may prove to be more important than any tactical plans.

One of the key men in the more senior squad that started the opener against the Netherlands, Kai Havertz limped off after 29 minutes. He was replaced by Eintracht Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib while Nick Woltemade (on loan at Juventus from Newcastle) and Jonathan Burkhardt, also Frankfurt, were also tested up front over the four games.

None of the replacements scored, with Woltemade guilty of a particularly bad miss against Serbia and Burkhardt having a goal disallowed against Greece on Sunday. While all have potential and have enjoyed strong patches of form in their careers, none is tried and tested at the top level, and none is playing in the Champions League. With Havertz being somewhat injury prone, Klopp needs someone to emerge as a viable backup.

Injury is also, sadly, beginning to be a major feature of Jamal Musiala's career. He picked up a thigh injury in the warmup to the Netherlands game that may keep him out for a month. He's also missed games this season due to a neurological condition and missed the first half of last season with a broken leg, which came soon after another lengthy spell out. At his best, he is probably Germany's brightest attacking spark, but it's been a while since that level has been seen.

For Wirtz, the issue is slightly different. He was excellent in the win over a limited Serbia team, scoring one and creating the other. It was a reminder of a talent that has been largely dormant at Liverpool where he's shown his creative best only in glimpses. He followed it up with a decent display against Greece but saw Burkahrdt inadvertently block his goalbound header. There were signs Klopp's system may suit him.

"He's really gotten us on board with his philosophy," said Wirtz of his coach. "I enjoy it myself, too. I get to show my strengths when we have possession."

Klopp will need more of the same from Wirtz, who captained the side in Greece, if Germany are to move forward.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

https://www.dw.com/en/bosnia-election-ne.title: Bosnia election: New steps to prevent electoral fraud, but nationalist parties remain on top
https://www.dw.com/en/bosnia-election-ne.text:
New technology has stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead or absent voters, and turnout has fallen to a record low. But it was a case of deja vu in Bosnia's elections with the same parties winning.

Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the polls on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging.

Chief among the abuses was the casting of ballots in the name of deceased voters who had lingered for years on outdated voter rolls.

At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked.

In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher.

The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this.

This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks.

This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate.

Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community: the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats.

The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted.

For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps: The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority.

A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member.

That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat.

For Milorad Dodik, the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection.

In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative, the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska.

Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD.

The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side."

Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next.

He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step.

"That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik.

The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message.

Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine.

That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out.

If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before.

The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same.

The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law.

Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well.

The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat.

So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created.

"The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory.

The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader.

"HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote.

Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country.

The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point.

Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton.

The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller.

So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it.

All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia, the EU and the US. Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory.

Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
https://www.dw.com/en/bosnia-election-ne.summary: Bosnian election was a case of deja vu in Bosnia's elections with the same parties winning. The election was held on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging. BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party.

https://www.dw.com/en/hundreds-of-french.title: Hundreds of French schools shut, teen loses hand in protests
https://www.dw.com/en/hundreds-of-french.text:
The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. A teenage boy lost his hand, seemingly while trying to pick up a police tear gas grenade.

Several hundred schools in France closed totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said.

The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation.

A 15-year-old boy in the northern town of Lens sustained a severe injury to his hand amid one of the protests on Monday. French news agency AFP cited a police union source as saying he appeared to have picked up a sting ball grenade, another term for a type of tear gas grenade also often called a blast ball, and it exploded in his hand.

The demonstrations have started to dominate France's political debate just a few months before presidential elections that will choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, who is approaching term limit.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended in some 400 to 500 high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled."

According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday.

Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons."

He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began.

"There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said.

"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added.

Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday.

The protesting teenagers at French upper high schools, called Lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities.

They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning.

Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.

He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition.

Since Friday, teenagers have been taking to the streets outside various schools in Lille, Lyon and Saint-Denis. The students are protesting dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms, a shortage of teachers and stressful exams. Local blockades have given rise to a nationwide movement that is increasing pressure on the French government. And discontent continues to grow across the country.

The protests are taking a more serious turn. Education Minister Édouard Geffray says 76 people were injured, including students and police officers. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez reports about 440 arrests during Tuesday’s demonstrations, most involving minors. Authorities also say that in seven incidents, hydrochloric acid was allegedly thrown at police officers during clashes.

Students are complaining about oversized classes and a shortage of teachers. While the government describes the blockades as irresponsible, it acknowledges that the difficulties at the lycées must be taken seriously. OECD data show that the share of the French budget allocated to education has recently declined.

The unrest comes at a delicate time for France. On Thursday, the government plans to present its 2027 budget. Spending cuts are expected to ease the strain on public finances. Student protests and a public-sector strike are increasing the pressure. The debate over funding for education is thus becoming part of a broader conflict over France’s austerity measures as a whole.

Education Minister Édouard Geffray has reacted strongly to the riots and announced legal consequences. "This violence is unspeakable," he said. Anyone who legitimizes or calls for further blockades is endangering students as well as public service employees. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also warned against escalation and called the protests irresponsible.

Anger is particularly intense in Seine-Saint-Denis. Hundreds of students are gathering in front of the Lycée Paul-Éluard. Many young people there feel they are at a disadvantage when it comes to education and resources. Sixteen-year-old Victoire describes the conditions at her school as dire. Her complaint: "We, the children of the suburbs, are abandoned and neglected."

In Paris, Marseille, Lille, and other cities, thousands of civil servants and public-sector employees demonstrated for higher salaries. They warned of the consequences of years of austerity measures. Firefighters also participated en masse in the rallies. According to union figures, about 8,000 firefighters took part.

France's national debt has reached a record high, forcing the government to take action. But any austerity plan is politically explosive. Lecornu must cut billions without sparking new social protests. At the same time, President Emmanuel Macron's camp does not have a majority in Parliament. The budget thus threatens to become yet another political test.

As with the previous budget, Lecornu is seeking support outside the government camp. The prime minister is particularly keen to find common ground with the Socialists in order to get the budget through Parliament. However, there is little room for maneuver: The presidential election is coming up next spring. Radical cuts could further exacerbate the social discontent that is already palpable.

The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters.

More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.

On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat.

Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort.

The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate."

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

https://www.dw.com/en/nationalists-top-b.title: Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
https://www.dw.com/en/nationalists-top-b.text:
Bosnia-Herzegovina's three-member presidency is set to be dominated by nationalists from the three major ethnic groups, including Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, backed by disqualified Serb secessionist leader Milorad Dodik.

Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday vote, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters taking part in the general election in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency.

With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities.

Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik, who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska.

With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote.

Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote.

Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS).

Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat.

Between 1992 and 1995, more than two million people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war. Despite the country being peaceful for decades, ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive as a way to hold on to power. Many voters, however, say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric.

The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges.

There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them.

The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.

Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months.

The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district.

These entities are further split into several cantons and communities.

The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia.

In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot.

Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022.

After the vote, Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, thanked Putin and also credited "Donald Trump's magnificent victory" for keeping his political camp alive.

He added that "now, thanks to the new environment, we are political winners."

Dodik, wants close ‌ties to Serbia and Russia and secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.

In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.

The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.

Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.

Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.

Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.

But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws.

https://www.dw.com/en/uk-remands-2-irani.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
https://www.dw.com/en/uk-remands-2-irani.text:
The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism  against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.

The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England.

He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.

The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.

Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.

He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.

The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.

One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.

The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.

Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.

Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.

The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.

Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.

UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.

Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.

The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.

Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.

Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

https://www.dw.com/en/bosnia-and-herzego.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina is still shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
https://www.dw.com/en/bosnia-and-herzego.text:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is governed by a system established after the Bosnian war — more than 30 years ago. Ethnic divisions, a complex administration and European integration all shape the country's political reality.

To call Bosnia and Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east.

This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights.

Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews, or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages.

The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency, made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle.

This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process.

This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups.

During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide, in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces.

By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad.

The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995.

Although Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent.

The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995.

The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions.

The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader. Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions.

With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs.

A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia.

A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors.

Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies.

https://www.dw.com/en/german-reunificati.title: German reunification: How inequality is shaping a new East German identity
https://www.dw.com/en/german-reunificati.text:
A new study highlights persistent structural disparities in wealth and leadership positions between East and West Germany, 36 years after reunification.

German reunification may be 36 years in the past, but when it comes to wealth, the divide between East and West Germany is far from history. East Germans still earn less on average, receive smaller pensions and own less property, according to Elisabeth Kaiser, the Federal Government Commissioner for Eastern Germany.

Kaiser, born in the state of Thuringia in the socialist German Democratic Republic (GDR) in 1987, has put the enduring wealth gap at the center of the debate. A study she presented in Berlin points to decades in which private entrepreneurship and opportunities to invest in one's financial future were restricted in the East. That meant, Kaiser said, that "families have not been able to acquire or pass on as much wealth." The consequences, she argues, have had a profound impact upward mobility.

But it is not only East Germans who see fewer chances of upward mobility these days. Kaiser pointed to the latest "Deutschland-Monitor," an annual survey she commissioned to make her point. Although this year's survey is still being analyzed, early findings reveal that about two-thirds of respondents across the country believe that financial and social mobility depend crucially on wealth, personal connections and social background.

This perception is reflected in the numbers. Even though the percentage of East German executives in the highest federal agencies has risen from 13.9% in 2022 to 16.3% today, Kaiser says, "The further up the management ladder you go, the lower the percentage of East Germans you find."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Based on these findings, the Commissioner for Eastern Germany calls for greater equality in decision-making. "And that is why I would like to see East Germans sitting at the table wherever decisions are made in the country," she said, "in the ministries, in government agencies, in business, academia, the judiciary, culture and the media."

With just under 20%, East Germans are significantly underrepresented in all sectors relative to their share of the population. To back this up, Kaiser cited the "Elitenmonitor,"  another study commissioned by her office. With over 3,000 top positions examined across twelve sectors over a long period of time, the Elitenmonitor study, conducted by the universities of Jena (Thuringia), Leipzig (Saxony), and Zittau/Görlitz (Saxony), can offer more than just a snapshot.

According to the report, the percentage of East Germans in leadership positions in both the public and private sectors only increased from 10.9% to 12.1% from 2018 to 2024. And in the business and cultural sectors, the percentage of East Germans has actually declined.

Most striking of all is that among the 100 largest German companies, all executives are from West Germany — and the same holds true for the military. East Germans are also severely underrepresented in top positions in the judiciary and the media.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The insufficient representation of East German perspectives in nearly all areas of society also appears to have consequences for how East Germans are viewed. Kaiser says that her generation, born around the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, did not feel East German for a long time. It was only in school and during vocational training that she realized there were differences between East and West that would sometimes put her at a disadvantage.

This has also shaped stereotypes about East Germany, both past and present. "An East German identity is also being created politically to some extent because people are looking for some way to orient themselves, because they're looking for a common bond," Kaiser knows from her many experiences and conversations.

As an example, she cited the symbolic power of the Simson moped, produced in the millions during the GDR era — a symbol of mobility and freedom for many young people at that time.

Leading representatives of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party classified in part as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency, frequently make public appearances riding on Simson mopeds. One of them is Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate who recently won state elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Without specifically mentioning the AfD by name, Kaiser lamented the exploitation of cultural symbols for political purposes."It creates a very powerful emotional connection," said Kaiser regarding the use of the Simson brand.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As for the AfD and its recent electoral successes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, Kaiser said that these elections send a dangerous signal. She believes that international investors and skilled workers will ask themselves: Should I go there or not?

Kaiser specifically mentioned sectors that have played an important role as drivers of economic growth and innovation in eastern Germany, such as the semiconductor industry, battery cell research, healthcare, biotechnology and renewable energy. Her concern is that the economic upswing in these sectors could suffer as a result.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/spain-s-parliament.title: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue
https://www.dw.com/en/spain-s-parliament.text:
Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to the bid.

Spain's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing.

Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through.

Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week, including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus.

Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate.

Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think."

One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures.

The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172.

The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166.

Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply.

Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government.

The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike.

"The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike."

The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life.

The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs.

Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30.

"People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday.

The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament.

https://www.dw.com/en/naza-israeli-milit.title: "NAZA": Israeli military issues statement on film
https://www.dw.com/en/naza-israeli-milit.text:
The award-winning documentary "NAZA" continues to spark controversy in Israel. The Israeli military has now published a multi-page statement calling the film's portrayal "distorted."

When it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in mid-September, "NAZA" received a 25-minute-long standing ovation and the Special Jury Prize. But in Israel, the documentary has fueled heated debate.

Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar described the work of filmmakers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham "treason against the state" and urged that their citizenship be revoked. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also sharply criticized the documentary.

Now the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has also rejected the film's allegations about its conduct during the war in Gaza. In a multi-page document, the military accuses the filmmakers of presenting a "distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture." The film, it says, is based on "substantial factual errors" resulting from "manipulative misrepresentations of reality."

The 80-minute documentary examines the Israel Defense Forces' operations during the war in Gaza. It is based on interviews conducted with 24 anonymous military and intelligence personnel, who describe internal procedures and decision-making processes involved in selecting targets in the Gaza Strip. According to the interviewees, high civilian casualty estimates were, in some cases, deliberately factored into these decisions.

The IDF rejects those claims. It says it has never planned or carried out attacks while anticipating hundreds of civilian deaths. It also disputes the film's claim that artificial intelligence selected targets without human oversight, saying people have always made decisions about targets and attacks.

The military also accuses the filmmakers of omitting important facts. According to the IDF, the film fails to show the role of military legal advisors and commanders in reviewing and authorizing attacks or the measures it says it takes to protect civilians. It also argues that the film does not adequately address the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, in which over 1,200 people were killed and 250 people were taken hostage.

Several human rights organizations and a UN commission have accused Israel of committing acts of genocide in Gaza. According to health authorities in Gaza and other sources, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began.

Speaking at the awards ceremony in Venice in mid-September, co-director Yuval Abraham said: "We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist. That is why it's really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film."

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham also worked on the film "No Other Land," which won an Oscar for Best Documentary Feature in 2025.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"NAZA" comes from the Hebrew term "Nezek Agavi," meaning collateral damage. According to a soldier interviewed in the film, the acronym is used within the military to refer to the estimated number of civilians who could be killed in an attack.

Numerous human rights organizations, including the Israeli group B'Tselem, have expressed their support for the filmmakers. After its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, "NAZA" is now showing in theaters worldwide.

This article was originally published in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-franz-re.title: Germany's Franz Reindl elected new IIHF president
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-franz-re.text:
Franz Reindl has been elected president of ice hockey's world governing body. The former forward was a member of West Germany's Olympic bronze medal-winning team.

Franz Reindl came from behind to narrowly beat Petr Briza of the Czech Republic in a run-off vote to become the International Ice Hockey Federation's new president on Friday.

Reindl had trailed Briza 48-36 in the first round of voting but picked up crucial votes after Aivaz Omorkanov of Kyrgyzstan was eliminated. He then beat Briza 60-57 in the runoff held on the Spanish island of Tenerife. Six of a total of nine candidates had withdrawn prior to the election.

The 71-year-old German, who had been a member of the IIHF Council since 2016, succeeds Canadian-born Frenchman Luc Tardif, who had announced in March that he would not seek a further term in office. Reindl's election comes 5 years after he had finished as runner-up to Tardif. His term runs until 2030.

Reindl has done it all in German ice hockey, having been a player and coach, as well as serving as the first CEO of the top-flight professional league, the Deutsche Eishockey Liga (DEL), from 1994 to 19<96. He also headed the organizing committees for three World Championships — in 2001, 2010 and 2017. From 2014 to 2022 he served as president of the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB), overseeing an upturn in the fortunes of the men's national team, which won the silver medal at the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics in 2018.

"Franz Reindl has shaped German ice hockey for decades—as a player, but above all through the various key roles he has held within our federation," the current DEB chairman, Frank Lutz, said.

"The fact that the international ice hockey family is now entrusting him with the leadership of the IIHF is a great tribute to his work."

Like Briza, who was a goalie for the Czechoslovakia team that won bronze in Albertville in 1992, Reindl was also an Olympic bronze medalist, having been a member of the 1976 West Germany team who beat the United States and Finland to finish third in Lake Placid.

Domestically, Reindl played 669 games and scored 423 goals for SC Riessersee and SB Rosenheim over 16 seasons in the Eishockey-Bundesliga, the predecessor to the DEL.

Tardif's years as IIHF president were marked by two major events: the return of National Hockey League players to the Olympic tournament in Milan Cortina this year, and the exclusion from international play of Russia in 2022 over the country's full-scale war on neighboring Ukraine.

Reindl is the second German to be elected IIHF president after Günter Sabetzki, who held the post from 1975 to 1994.
