https://www.dw.com/en/climate-leaders-ca.title: Climate leaders called for solar energy for 'everyone, everywhere' by 2030, but with three years to go, is that goal attainable?
https://www.dw.com/en/climate-leaders-ca.text:
Prominent climate leaders have called on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to make a push for solar power before the decade is out, repowering the world with cheap, clean energy. Is that possible?

In a world "set ablaze by war and  warming," with ever-worsening climate disasters such as wildfires in Europe and collapsing glaciers in Nepal, solar energy provides a solution in the form of clean, affordable power, prominent climate leaders wrote in an open letter.

Signed by author Bill McKibben, former UN Climate Secretary Christiana Figueres and Canada's former Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna, the letter makes a clear call. It urges governments, businesses, institutions and the public to come together to provide clean, affordable energy to "everyone, everywhere by 2030" — from the close to one billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.

With just a little over three years to go until the decade is out, how realistic is this push?

"It's an ambitious target, but we've blown away in terms of where we thought we would be on solar and renewables," McKenna told DW. "So let's just keep on going."

According to global energy think tank Ember,solar power has grown at its highest rate in eight years. In 2025, it increased by a record 30% over the previous year and has risen more than tenfold since 2015.

Solar is the cheapest form of electricity in the history of the world, said McKenna, who founded the climate advisory firm Climate and Nature Solutions, and the global coalition Women Leading on Climate.

"It is scaling way faster than anyone ever imagined."

As is battery technology used to store excess renewable energy.

"The cost of batteries have as well come down as the cost of solar modules," said Eicke Weber, a physicist and former director of Germany's Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems who went on to found the European Solar Manufacturing Council, among other things.

"We have the technologies available and we have enough money to finance it," he said, of a transition to widespread solar access.

In 2025, for the first time in 100 years, renewable energy sources overtook coal power in the global electricity mix, Ember's most recent analysis showed.

At the moment, installed solar capacity around the world stands at 3 terawatts. 1TW equals 1000 gigawatts, and a single nuclear power plant has a capacity of 1GW.

Currently, the world produces about 1TW of new photovoltaic capacity each year, most of it in China. Weber says in order to fully change global energy supply to renewables, we would need about 50TW, adding that "we have more production capacities than we are selling."

Roughly 655 million people still lack accessto electricity.

"The pace of electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa has to triple to achieve universal access by 2030," McKenna said, pointing out how quickly this gap could be closed with solar.

Areas without electricity have the opportunity to leapfrog straight into clean technologies, she says, bypassing the fossil fuels that are heating the planet. Rising global temperatures are fueling extreme weather events such as drought, storms and flooding around the world.

"And there's a misunderstanding, which is often propagated intentionally by fossil fuel companies, that it's expensive, it's hard, it's unreliable. And that just isn't the case anymore," she said. "To be honest, the most unreliable thing is if you're trying to pass fossil fuels through the Strait of Hormuz."

Hans-Josef Fell is used to the argument that certain things cannot be done. Widely known as a pioneer of renewable energy, he drafted Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act, which established feed-in tariffs that catalyzed clean energy growth at home and beyond.

"The Renewable Energy Sources Act unleashed exponential growth that shattered every assumption about what was achievable. It overturned the scenarios and projections that policymakers and experts had considered realistic. In the end, reality outperformed all expectations," said Fell, who now heads the think tank Energy Watch Group.

Fell, who has lived off grid for five years, said achieving a global energy transition requires political and societal will that is "currently lacking around the world because public debate is dominated by fossil fuel interests."

According to calculations by his think tank, if global energy demand were met entirely by renewables, solar energy would account for roughly 60-70% of the supply. The rest would come from wind power, and other sources, such as bioenergy and hydropower.

Countries like China and Pakistan have already pushed ahead.

"It is in our hands right now in the year 2026 to say we drop everything, we concentrate on this problem. We don't need to wait for new research," Weber said.

"It is possible to achieve this, but it would require a very kind of moonshot program," he added, saying it would need serious political backing.

He says while it might be possible for Germany to pull off such as transition in two or three years, if the political will were there, it would likely take longer to achieve on a global scale. "We would need probably till 2040 to say that we have a goal of a worldwide 80%, 90% electricity from renewables."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"I would sum it up this way: If we as a global society tackle this properly, we might actually be able to make it happen," Fell said. "And even if we achieve only 90% of that goal, it would still be a remarkable accomplishment."

McKenna pointed to the need for blended finance, calling on governments, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the private sector to put in money.

"What is irrational is continuing down the road of fossil fuels," she added. "That's irrational on the costs, the risks, the impacts. It's an old technology."

https://www.dw.com/en/manchester-city-pr.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
https://www.dw.com/en/manchester-city-pr.text:
Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City has become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.

Manchester City has won the English Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. Whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high-profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs." These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report, used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Der Spiegel, a German magazine, and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continues to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a club statement. "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

On Friday, the club issued a further statement saying it had lodged a "comprehensive Appeal."

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off the books, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. The report says all this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Although the Premier League, the world's most commercially successful football league, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point out that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to take action. The report shows that Manchester City, which had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour, fronted the takeover. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds several government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation-state ownership of this type is controversial in European football. Manchester City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain, which Qatar owned and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United, which is owned 85% by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.

The club immediately started splashing out on big-money transfers after the UAE investment arrived. At the time, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA introduced its Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules for the 2011-12 season, while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relatively low commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club was handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with these financial rules, City set up a system they called "Project Longbow" in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine, but one arm of it was an agreement with a third party called Fordham that was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money into their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.

That's the question on everyone's lips. So far, no sanctions have been imposed on City, and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile, the club, which is top of the Premier League, faces Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have previously fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5 million breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the Premier League does not operate England's second-tier league, the Championship.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.

This article was originally published on September 30, 2026. It was updated on October 2, 20206 with Manchester City's statement confirming that it had lodged an appeal.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

https://www.dw.com/en/ard-deutschlandtre.title: ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey: Germans unite in frustration over the government
https://www.dw.com/en/ard-deutschlandtre.text:
On the 36th anniversary of reunification, Germans are dissatisfied with the country's political leaders. They don't believe they'll be able to handle the challenges posed by AI, Russia and Donald Trump.

Ahead of October 3, which marks the reunification of West and East Germany in 1990, pollster infratest dimap asked 1303 eligible voters to assess their personal situation. Twenty percent of those identifying as East Germans, but 44% see personal advantages. Only a quarter said reunification had no major impact on them personally.

More than half of West German respondents said reunification had no major impact on their personal lives. The remaining half is split: 19% said reunification had a positive impact, while 18% said it had a negative one.

Germany held three state elections in September, two of them in eastern states. They were seen as a test of nationwide voter sentiment. The results were particularly devastating for the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

In Saxony-Anhalt and the city-state of Berlin, where it had been in government, the CDU dropped by 10% compared to the previous election and lost its hold on power. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the party even failed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in parliament. This has never happened before in Germany's history.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Merz has long been unpopular and has seen his support fall even further in the aftermath of the elections. The coalition he leads, comprised of the CDU, the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), is unpopular. Only one in 10 respondents in the survey said they were satisfied with the federal government's work and the chancellor's performance, a historic low. Only 40% of CDU supporters say they are still satisfied with Merz.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the domestic intelligence agency has classified as, in part, far-right extremist, continues to benefit from the voter dissatisfaction with the centrist parties.

If a general election were held now, the CDU/CSU alliance would win only 20% of the vote. That is one of the lowest figures in the party's history and a far cry from the 43.8% it won in the first election after reunification in 1990. The SPD polls at only 13%. This means that the ruling parties together would not even win one-third of the vote and would lose their majority in parliament.

The AfD would remain the strongest political force. It has been polling steadily at 27% nationwide. The environmentalist Greens are up slightly, reaching 16%, while the socialist Left Party has dropped by the same margin, landing at 11%. With this result, it would be a Herculean task to form a majority in the national parliament.

The overall situation in Germany gives only one in eight people cause for optimism, while nearly nine in 10 express concern. Voters for the AfD and the Left Party are particularly worried.

Two-thirds of respondents said they're worried that humans could lose control over artificial intelligence, and just as many are worried about the consequences of US President Donald Trump's policies for Germany. Six in 10 expressed concern about climate change, and just over half said they are worried that Russia could attack other countries in Europe.

About one in two respondents fear they will not be able to maintain their standard of living in the future. A similar number are concerned about immigration to Germany.

By far the biggest source of concern for Germans, however, is that political parties cannot find common answers to key political issues.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany is a rapidly aging country. Fewer working people must support an ever-increasing number of retirees.

The aging society also strains the health care system. Since 2015, the number of people in need of long-term care has risen from about 2.8 million to about 6.5 million — and the trend continues to rise.

According to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, only one in six eligible voters believes that the federal government will succeed inmaking the social security systems sustainable for the future.

Not all respondents said they are willing to dig into their own pockets: Voters who tend to support left-leaning parties would be more likely to accept higher social security contributions than benefit cuts. Among AfD and CDU/CSU voters, the opposite is true.

Three-quarters of respondents view the government's proposed reform measures as contradictory. They complain about an ever-increasing burden, even though the government had promised relief.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sixty-one percent say that cuts should be scaled according to individual financial capacity, even if this would place a heavier burden on some people.

One in two would be more willing to accept cuts if the necessity were explained in a way that made sense. The message to policymakers is clear: reforms require explanation and social balance; otherwise, they lose acceptance.

The welfare state and the health care system are regarded as key achievements in Germany. When asked what works particularly well in Germany compared to other countries, survey respondents most often cited social benefits and medical care. Education, schools, vocational training and universities came in last place.

High energy prices continue to burden citizens and the German economy. The ongoing crisis in the Persian Gulf is driving oil prices even higher. This is impacting fuel and electricity prices in Germany.

Respondents to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey found that the government is not doing enough to address high energy prices. Three-quarters of them said the government's efforts are insufficient.

A "Tankrabatt" (fuel discount) has again come into effect on October 1: Through the end of the year, the federal government is reducing the energy tax on gasoline and diesel by about 17 eurocents ($0.19) per liter. A similar discount was already in place from early May through the end of June. That cost the government €3.4 billion.

Some of that money ended up in the pockets of oil companies and gas station operators because they did not pass on the full discount. Experts view the measure critically.

Added to this is the fact that fossil fuels are being made cheaper despite shortages, which is controversial from a climate policy perspective. The new fuel discount has received only a lukewarm reception among the public; half of those surveyed in the ARD Deutschlandtrend poll believe it is the wrong approach.

This article was originally written in German.

Only one in eight people say they're optimistic about the future of Germany. A "Tankrabatt" (fuel discount) has again come into effect on October 1.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-south-kore.title: Ukraine, South Korea clash over transfer of 2 North Korean prisoners
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-south-kore.text:
A diplomatic scandal has erupted over two North Korean prisoners of war, with South Korea demanding an apology from Ukraine. What's been the reaction in Kyiv?

Speaking at the UN General Assembly on September 23, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sparked a diplomatic dust-up with South Korea.

In his speech, Zelenskyy mentioned that Ukraine had recently "sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea" — men who had been captured by Ukrainian forces during fighting in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025. Both had expressed a wish to resettle in South Korea, he said.

The reaction from Seoul was swift: South Korea's Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador to Seoul, Andrii Vieshkin, and demanded an explanation for what it described as Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the prisoners' transfer, despite a prior agreement to keep the matter confidential, along with an official apology.

Responding to Zelenskyy's speech, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war was a sensitive topic with wide-ranging consequences for diplomacy and national security on the Korean Peninsula.

Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's spokesperson, wrote on Facebook that no such confidentiality agreement existed between the two countries, adding that it was wrong to keep secret where such prisoners were being transferred.

Soon after, South Korean presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan called Lytvyn's denials false, according to news agency Reuters. Kim said Ukraine had asked for confidentiality — allegedly over concerns there might be criticism at home if the North Korean prisoners weren't swapped for Ukrainian prisoners being held in Russia.

Seoul had agreed to the secrecy for diplomatic reasons, he added, but also to protect the prisoners and their families who were still living in North Korea.

Nataliya Butyrska, an Asia-Pacific expert at the New Europe Center in Kyiv, told DW that Ukraine and South Korea lacked a continuous, trust-based dialogue, especially under the current government in Seoul.

"We should actually be natural partners — we should be standing shoulder to shoulder, with North Korea fighting against Ukraine," she said. "But that's not the case, due to a lack of trust."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The prisoner transfer has been a hotly debated topic in South Korean media in the last week — not least because, according to South Korea's constitution, North Koreans are considered citizens of South Korea. It's also been instrumentalized by opposition lawmakers, while President Lee, aiming to ease tensions with the North, has taken a more measured approach.

"The prisoners could have been used by Ukraine to improve bilateral relations between Kyiv and Seoul," said Butyrska, adding that no one in South Korea was now thinking of thanking Ukraine for transferring the prisoners.

Butyrska pointed out that Russia, which usually doesn't express any interest in foreign prisoners, had actually demanded the return of these two North Koreans. "There was even a period of six months when the Russians refused to release any Ukrainian prisoners of war," she said. "They were not prepared to undertake any swap, because they wanted the North Koreans."

For some observers, the diplomatic crisis can be linked back to domestic conflicts in South Korea. The opposition wants to know why the president agreed to keep the prisoner transfer secret, and have accused Lee of trying to gain favor with the North.

"President Lee Jae Myung was surprised by the incident, and now wants to shift the blame in part on Ukraine," said Mykola Polishchuk, a Korea expert based in Ukraine. He believes the transfer would have become public knowledge sooner or later, and that Seoul knew that Kyiv was going to comment on it. Reports that Ukraine had asked for secrecy were, he added, a way for a frantic politicians in Seoul to come up with an explanation.

"Ukraine has ended up mired in a scandal which it neither wanted nor planned for," said Polishchuk.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"South Korea has been pursuing the transfer of the prisoners for a long time. And now everybody seems to be happy that those Korean prisoners are in custody," said Shim Sangmin from the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul. "But what really complicates the matter is the fact that the South Korean government is trying to make new ways to reconcile with the North Korean regime." He said Seoul was now worried that this transfer of North Korean prisoners could hamper efforts to reestablish communication between the North and the South.

In his view, the Lee government is "more open to the idea of reestablishing ties" with Russia, rather than continuing to cooperate with Ukraine. "That's possibly one of the reasons why this government is skeptical about containing military cooperation with Ukrainian military forces, even though there would be a definite military advantage for South Korean military forces," he added.

Butyrska said the latest developments indicate a likely further cooling of ties between Kyiv and Seoul.

"The South Korean government wasn't particularly friendly toward us to begin with, and will now likely keep its distance," she said, adding that it would have been better for Kyiv to have stayed quiet.

In return for a gesture of goodwill and "quiet diplomacy," she added, Ukraine might have seen support from South Korea in another form — technology, for example, especially via third countries. While South Korea isn't directly selling weapons to Ukraine, it does deliver to Poland, Finland, the Czech Republic and Romania, and it's pursuing further integration with the European military equipment supply chain.

For Polishchuk, any cooperation on military technology between Ukraine and South Korea is out of the question, now and in the future. He believes trade and humanitarian help would continue, however. South Korea, he said, is highly unlikely to side with Russia, especially given Seoul's many obligations toward the United States.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

Ukraine's president sparked a diplomatic dust-up with South Korea over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war. South Korea isn't directly selling weapons to Ukraine, but it does deliver to Poland, Finland, the Czech Republic and Romania.

https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-stock-marke.title: Turkey: Stock market scandal hits half a million investors
https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-stock-marke.text:
Asset managers are alleged to have artificially inflated the value of their funds. Turkish authorities have made multiple arrests, and a leading AKP lawmaker has resigned.

Investors in Turkey want one thing above all else: for their money to retain its value. Given inflation of around 30%, that is not exactly easy. As a result, many people are buying gold, foreign currency or stocks and increasingly, mutual fund shares that promise high returns.

But the stock market has become a trap for around half a million Turkish investors. In mid-September, the benchmark BIST 100 index plummeted by 6% in a single day and lost about 12% within just a few trading days.

This sharp drop in stock prices was triggered by a major market manipulation scandal. Approximately 455,000 investors have been affected, more than 45 people have been arrested and a high-ranking politician from the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has resigned.

Everything started when some investment fund providers had trouble making timely repayments to investors. Among those affected were funds managed by the companies Pusula Portfoy and Tera. Two Tera funds alone held assets totaling around €6.5 billion ($6.37 billion).

In response, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) intervened and shut down the funds of seven asset managers, including Tera, Pusula and Atlas. According to the state-run news agency Anadolu, a total of 131 funds are set to be liquidated.

The Istanbul Public Prosecutor's Office is now investigating charges of fraud, violations of the capital markets law and the formation of a criminal organization, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced.

The suspicion: The fund companies are alleged to have artificially inflated the value of their funds, while in reality their funds contained worthless "junk stocks."

Among the 45 people arrested so far are executives from investment firms. In addition, the assets of 42 individuals and 46 legal entities have been frozen, according to Gurlek on X.

The Istanbul Stock Exchange has also taken action: it excluded 27 stocks from the BIST 100 benchmark index as of October 1.

The funds are being liquidated: Their assets will be sold and the proceeds distributed to investors in proportion to their fund shares. The deadline for this has been extended from three to six months. According to Aysel Gundogdu, an independent financial advisor in Istanbul, this is intended to reduce selling pressure so that stocks are not sold at fire-sale prices. However, this does not mean that the liquidation of each fund will take six months. Depending on market conditions, it may be completed more quickly.

Only, there is no guarantee. An investment fund is not a savings account and any loss in value affects the investor. Gundogdu expects that money market funds will largely be redeemed. With hedge funds and equity funds holding "junk stocks" that are virtually untradeable, however, the situation could prove more difficult.

It is important to distinguish between market losses and damages resulting from potential irregularities.

Economist and columnist Guldem Atabay emphasized that a distinction must be made between price losses and manipulation: Investors bear the market risk, but they do not have to accept false information, artificially inflated prices, or a lack of oversight.

If funds are closed or liquidated, the shares and other securities in the portfolio can be sold. The question is how much they are worth and how easily they can be sold.

Financial expert Gundogdu believes that the fund's assets will not cover investors' claims. Furthermore, she says there have been structural failures. "The crisis is far greater than a simple liquidity crisis. There are flaws in management and oversight."

She therefore considers it possible that the assets of the fund founders and managers could also be tapped to make up for the shortfall.

Economist Atabay calls for those responsible to be identified and for the damages to be recovered from them. Following the liquidation of the funds, it must be clarified who is responsible for any legal violations. "Liquidation is no substitute for accountability," Atabay said.

The crisis has already led to the resignation of a high-ranking female politician in the ruling AKP party. Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, deputy party chair and former minister of family affairs, asked Turkish President and AKP leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan to "relieve her of all her posts." This has been a phrase frequently used within the AKP for years when someone is forced to resign.

She was facing allegations regarding stock transactions by her and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, in connection with the fund crisis. Political responsibility, she wrote on social media, goes beyond legal responsibility. She said her position should not hinder the investigation.

The opposition now intends to bring the issue before Parliament. Selcuk Ozdag, deputy leader of the Yeni Yol parliamentary group, announced that as soon as Parliament reconvenes, he will submit a motion for a parliamentary investigation. The investigation is intended to determine whether politicians are involved in the manipulation scandal.

This article was originally published in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-stock-marke.summary: Turkish authorities have made multiple arrests and a leading AKP lawmaker has resigned. The stock market has become a trap for around half a million Turkish investors. The crisis has already led to the resignation of a high-ranking female politician in the ruling AKP party.

https://www.dw.com/en/eu-ministers-mull-.title: EU ministers mull new ways to curb irregular migration
https://www.dw.com/en/eu-ministers-mull-.text:
The proposals include setting up so-called return hubs outside the EU and strengthening the border agency Frontex. Greece has even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations.

The interior ministers of European Union countries met in Luxembourg on Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen border controls and curb undocumented migration into the 27-member bloc.

Following the talks, they approved a new regulation to boost deportations of irregular migrants.

It will allow member states ​to establish so-called return hubs outside the EU for migrants who are legally required to leave the bloc but cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

Countries including Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands have been exploring options to change migration policy and set up such migrant centers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"When it comes to return hubs," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters, "it's progressing very well."

"We are moving in the right direction," he said without providing further details.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said there were "preliminary" talks on return hubs but declined to say which countries were involved.

More work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits, he said.

"These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term," Dobrindt noted, adding that he was nevertheless hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.

Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said a technical mission already visited a potential host country in early September.

Supporters of the policy say return hubs could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.

But critics question their legality and argue that they violate migrants' fundamental rights.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Thursday, Greece even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations. The right to seek asylum is guaranteed by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.

Athens argued that current rules are inadequate to handle mass arrivals as in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.

The Spanish government estimates over 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While most of them have since returned, some 10,000 remain, reinforcing calls in some EU capitals for a tougher approach. The Spanish government has said only minors and small groups of the people who entered Ceuta were brought to mainland Spain.

Greece's proposal appeared to draw support from some member states.

"We have to find a legal way not to bring them into the asylum procedure," said Dutch Migration Minister van den Brink. "In situations like Ceuta, it should be treated as ​a border management issue rather than an asylum issue."

Asked whether he saw a suspension of asylum as possible under the new emergency law, ​Magnus Brunner, EU commissioner for migration, said: "Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times," while stressing that "we will always comply with fundamental rights and values."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The interior ministers' talks come as undocumented migration remains high on the EU's political agenda, with far-right parties increasingly gaining support across the bloc.

The situation has pushed many governments towards tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this month that the Commission will propose an emergency tool for countries to better deal with mass migration movements.

But details are still being worked out.

There are also plans to strengthen the EU's border agency, Frontex, with many stressing the need for the organization to have a rapid intervention force that could intervene in border crises.

Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands have been exploring options to change migration policy.

https://www.dw.com/en/klopp-wins-first-g.title: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
https://www.dw.com/en/klopp-wins-first-g.text:
It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the victory over Serbia.

After 47 days, three matches and 44 squad players, Jürgen Klopp has a first win as coach of Germany's men's fotball team. A straightforward 2-0 victory over Serbia in the Nations League on Thursday meant the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach avoided becoming the first Germany boss to win any of his first three games.

"I'm really happy today," Klopp told German public broadcaster ZDF. "We were outstanding when defending and when we had the ball. We simply played wonderful football."

Klopp had raised a few eyebrows by naming two squads for the four fixtures in this extended international window. But after a somewhat fortunate draw against the Netherlands and a shock loss to Greece with the more senior of the squads, it was left to those lower down the pecking order to get things going Thursday in Munich.

That meant a completely new starting XI and debuts to ‌goalkeeper Jonas Urbig ⁠and ⁠winger Derry Scherhant. Such players should "develop without the top dogs" Klopp said before the game. And while Urbig was untroubled by Serbia, his Bayern Munich teammate Tom Bischof made his mark by turning in the opener after Florian Wirtz, one of the sprinkling of senior players, hit the post. It was Bischof's first goal for Germany in only his second national team game.

"It's indescribable," said Bischof after the game at Bayern's Allianz Arena. "The stadium was on fire. I let it all out and was overjoyed." Unfortunately, he said, "my knees hurt a little from sliding on my knees. But that doesn't matter."

After a string of tournament failures, the latest new dawn for Germany comes with a little more patience. As well as Klopp's track record, there is a general acceptance from inside the country and abroad that Germany are no longer a top tier side.

"We're not the Bayern Munich of European football," Klopp said prematch. "We're a team that needs to find its footing."

While one win against a limited Serbia side will not change that, the emphatic nature of the performance impressed the new boss.

"I liked everything — the opening phase, the middle section, and the end. Our counter-pressing was off the charts," said the man whose Gegenpressing (Counter-pressing) tactic became his trademark at Dortmund. "We can afford to take all the liberties and risks we want when we win the ball back together. Everyone was there during our pressing moments."

Jürgen Klopp played professional football for 15 years, spending 11 of them in Mainz. He only reached the second division in Germany. beginning as an attacking player but ended his career as a defender. He retired midway through the 2001-02 season to fill the coaching vacancy at Mainz after the club sacked Eckhard Krautzun.

During Klopp's playing career, Mainz frequently fought against relegation to the German third tier. That changed when he took the helm at the club. In Klopp's third season, Mainz earned promotion to the Bundesliga for the first time in club history. Klopp enjoyed three seasons in the top flight before Mainz were relegated again in 2007. He left the club a year later to join Borussia Dortmund.

Klopp's appointment was part of a broader strategy change at Borussia Dortmund: to develop football stars instead of buying them. He committed to 20-year-olds Mats Hummels and Neven Subotic as his center back pair — the youngest in the Bundesliga. Dortmund finished in sixth place and fifth place in his first two seasons at the club.

From 2010 to 2012, Klopp led Dortmund to their most successful two-year stretch in club history. They won their first Bundesliga title in nearly a decade in 2010-11. Klopp followed that accomplishment up by leading BVB to their first domestic double in club history the next season.

It didn't take long for Dortmund fans to fall in love with Klopp. His press conferences became a weekly spectacle and his energy on the touchline became contagious. On the pitch, he implemented an active, high-pressing system that brought BVB, a club that was only a few years removed from near-insolvency, back to the pinnacle of German football.

Klopp did not secure domestic silverware after that two-year run, but he did lead Dortmund to the Champions League final in 2013 — their first final since their 1997 title. His side ultimately came up short against Bayern Munich, losing 2-1 late on to hand their German rivals a piece of their treble that year.

Klopp's last season with Dortmund in 2014-15 was far worse than any other. His side were second-to-bottom at the winter break, though Klopp wound up leading them to a seventh-place finish. He did manage to get BVB to the German Cup final before losing to Wolfsburg. Dortmund and Klopp decided to part ways after the season, ending his seven-year stint with the team.

It didn't take long for Klopp to land back on his feet. Liverpool appointed the German coach in October of 2015, less than five months after he parted ways with Dortmund. In his first press conference, Klopp dubbed himself "The Normal One" — after being asked how he fitted in compared to the likes of Jose Mourinho, who notoriously once called himself "a special one."

Liverpool fans took to Klopp's highly animated coaching approach, but it didn't initally lead to success. The Reds finished eighth in the Premier League in his first season, though he did lead them to the Europa League final before losing to Sevilla. But he guided Liverpool to the Champions League with a fourth-place finish the following season.

Much like he was in Dortmund, Klopp became a club favorite at Liverpool. His passionate personality and the attractive attacking football enabled by players like Mohamed Salah and Sadio Mane proved a real hit in the stands.

In 2018, Jürgen Klopp guided Liverpool to the brink of the biggest title in European club football. However, an injury to Mo Salah and two blunders by German goalkeeper Loris Karius put paid to Liverpool's hopes of winning the Champions League as Real Madrid made history at their expense.

A year later, Klopp got his revenge as Liverpool won the Champions League final against Tottenham. The European run was one for the ages, and included one of the greatest European comebacks of all time as Liverpool overturned a three-goal deficit against Barcelona to make the final. Liverpool lost the Premier League title by one point.

The following year, Klopp won the Premier League title with Liverpool. They also won the Club World Cup. In 2022, after a trophyless season, Klopp helped secure Liverpool a domestic double as they won both the FA Cup and League Cup. In January 2024, Klopp announced he was leaving, saying he had run out of energy. He left the club having won 8 major titles.

In a surprise to many, Klopp started a new role at Red Bull as "Global Head of Soccer" in January 2025. He was criticized for the move as the organization stood in opposition to much of what German football's traditions stand for and for having a multi-club model. In the role he provided strategic support to Red Bull clubs.

After Julian Nagelsmann's departure as Germany head coach has been named his successor – a job many believe he had long coveted. With Euro 2028 being hosted by the UK and Ireland, Klopp stands to get the chance to coach Germany in the familiar place where he had his greatest success to date as a coach.

The second half brought more debuts for players who may not have made a traditional 26-man squad. Cologne winger Said El Mala and Brentford's Vitaly Janelt made their Germany bows while Celtic's Mika Baur became the country's 1,000th men's international.

It was "surreal," Baur said. "Today was a highlight for everyone, not just for me with my debut."

While Klopp may have seen enough from a few of the second string to afford them opportunities in the future, the performance of Liverpool midfielder Wirtz, who scored Germany's second goal, may be the most critical of the night.

Wirtz, 23, has struggled to find his best form in the Premier League and has blown hot and cold in his 47 caps for Germany. A cool and composed finish suggested that the player who was so highly regarded at Bayer Leverkusen can be coaxed to life by Klopp.

"It was loads of fun. Every single one of us gave it our all on the field. We stuck to the game plan and did almost everything right," said Wirtz, who took the captain's armband later in the game. "The players around me made it easy for me. We had a lot of movement in the middle. We were all fired up."

The challenge now for Klopp is to work out which of his wide pool of players are the ones he can rely on to take Germany to Euro 2028 and beyond. The next step is a chance for revenge against Greece in Thessaloniki on Sunday.

https://www.dw.com/en/weakened-us-fuel-e.title: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could see drivers pay higher running costs while also increasing carbon emissions.
https://www.dw.com/en/weakened-us-fuel-e.text:
Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could yet see drivers pay higher running costs while increasing planet-heating emissions.

As part of its "Freedom Means More Affordable Cars" initiative, the US Department of Transportation this week rolled back fuel efficiency rules under the guise of lowering vehicle prices.

The Trump administration's transport agency says US taxpayers will save $138 billion (€122 billion) over the next five years — new vehicles will be $1,300 cheaper on average — since automakers will no longer have to invest in more fuel-efficient fleets.

But this does not account for soaring gas prices as Middle East conflicts choke global supply.

"Any savings on the front end get eaten up and spat out by excess costs of fuel… Fuel economy standards have saved drivers hundreds of billions of dollars," said Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island in a social media post.

Under the revised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rules, vehicle fleets only require an average fuel efficiency of about 35 miles per gallon (14.7 kilometers per liter) by 2031, down around one-third from 50 miles per gallon.

Implemented by then-President Joe Biden in 2024, the updated efficiency rules aimed to incentivize the production of low emission electric vehicles and hybrids. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates the standards would have saved 70 billion gallons (265 billion litres) of fuel over 25 years.

Meanwhile, nonprofit advocacy group the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) says an earlier version of CAFE regulations has saved US consumers about $321 billion at the gas pump since 2010.

As the world's biggest petrol consumer, the US burns through 20 million barrels of oil per day, which is 20% of global consumption, notes Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the US-based nonprofit environmental group Center for Biological Diversity.

"Transportation is the biggest consumer of that oil, making strong auto standards the most effective way to cut pollution and oil use," Becker said in a statement.

The rules that have been diluted this week would have prevented more than 710 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050 — the equivalent of running 165 million gas-powered passenger vehicles for a year.

"With transportation representing nearly 28% of US greenhouse emissions, rolling back fuel economy standards is a dangerous setback for near-term climate goals," said Ben Scott, head of Energy Demand at UK-based climate think tank Carbon Tracker.

"It risks keeping inefficient combustion engines on the road much longer than climate science demands," he told DW.

But following President Donald Trump's elimination of greenhouse gas emissions standards for light- and heavy-duty vehicles last year, Dave Cooke, senior vehicles analyst for the UCS Clean Transportation Program, said the rollbacks merely compound "a much more significant step backwards."

He said the trend sends "a specific signal to automakers," adding that "the United States is seeking to maximize oil usage to increase oil company profits."

This will be to the detriment of climate targets, with high-polluting oil contributing one-third of global fossil fuel emissions that continue to rise — along with temperatures.

The world just had the hottest August on record as severe heatwaves in Europe caused more than 16,000 excess deaths in Germany alone.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sales of low emission EVs are down in the US in 2026, especially after Donald Trump scrapped the $7,500 tax credit for new electric vehicles.

American automakers also continue to push back against regulations that would incentivize a switch to EVs, arguing there is a lack of consumer demand.

"It's highly unlikely that the United States will suddenly become awash in electric options when neither the auto industry nor regulators seem interested in providing such choices for consumers," said Cooke.

But Ben Scott believes that while softening US fuel economy standards "will create temporary headwinds", it won't stall an inevitable transition to electric vehicles.

"With EVs delivering vastly lower running costs, electrification becomes a clear-cut economic choice," he said of cars running on "cheaper, domestically secure energy that will drive the transition forward, regardless of short-term politics."

As less efficient cars and trucks consume more oil that's more expensive and in shorter supply, "the fragility of oil-dependent transport" is set to be exposed, he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/germans-biggest-fe.title: Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living, an annual study finds
https://www.dw.com/en/germans-biggest-fe.text:
What do Germans fear most in 2026? Wars? Global crises? Wrong. Their biggest concern is the cost of living, which keeps rising.

People in Germany are more politically engaged than they have been in a long time. This was also evident in the high voter turnout in the September state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Germans are passionately debating immigration, the upcoming reforms to pensions, healthcare and long-term care, as well as democracy and the rule of law.

But by far their greatest fear is the cost of living in Germany, which is becoming increasingly expensive. At least, that is the finding of the 2026 study on "Germans' Fears," which the insurer R+V presented in Berlin.

From early May through late July of this year, researchers surveyed some 2,400 German-speaking citizens aged 14 and older.

The cost of living is again their top concern, as it has been in the survey for many years in a row. This study has been conducted annually since the early 1990s.

Last year, 52% of those polled cited the rising cost of daily life as their greatest concern; in 2026, that figure has risen to 59%.

At a press conference in Berlin, Isabelle Borucki, a political scientist from Marburg who served as a consultant on the study, explained why.

"The price of key items — energy, housing and food — has risen noticeably. This reduces the financial leeway for leisure, vacations and purchases. People can afford less and less."

The study also shows that people are well aware that Germany's social security systems are in a serious crisis. Both the state pension fund and long-term care insurance are chronically in the red.

Most people also seem to realize that taxes and contributions will rise. That is why the fear of higher taxes is stronger than in previous years.

"Behind the fear of higher taxes and benefit cuts lies the question of fairness, with people wondering who will bear the costs of modernization," Borucki said. "And they worry, 'Can I still rely on getting benefits I am entitled to?'"

But what about the issues that are also dominating the headlines in Germany? What about immigration and the increasing polarization of society? Or global upheavals?

A narrow majority of 52% of those surveyed fear that the number of refugees is overwhelming the German state. This fear ranks third among all concerns.

But when it comes to global upheavals, Germans are not so concerned.

Only 45% of respondents fear that US President Donald Trump's policies are making the world a more dangerous place, researcher Grischa Brower-Rabinowitsch said.

"That's significantly fewer than during his first term."

In 2018, during Trump's first term, 69% responded to the same question by saying that this made them very afraid. "After years of constant geopolitical alarm bells, people are starting to get used to it," Brower-Rabinowitsch said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This trend also seems to hold true for other areas of concern: Germans are looking to the future with considerably less anxiety than expected. Only 34% now fear a war involving Germany, down from 41% last year.

Since 1992, the study has asked people if they are afraid of losing their job? Currently, only 20% of the surveyed members of the working population answered "yes." That is the lowest figure ever recorded.

However, the assessment of politicians — both those in the government and those in the opposition — is sobering: Respondents were asked to grade politicians with one being the best and six the worst (the grading system used at German schools). The result was an average score of 4.1, which is barely a passing mark.

Political scientist Borucki places the primary responsibility on the current government of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz which came to power in May 2025.

After the end of the previous coalition government, many associated the new coalition with hopes for more leadership, less conflict and a rapid economic turnaround.

"That has not come to pass," says Borucki. "There is now a gap between the grand announcements and tangible results. People are disappointed and losing confidence."

This article was originally written in German.

The cost of life is again their top concern, as it has been in the survey for many years in a row. Only 34% now fear a war involving Germany, down from 41% last year.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.title: Germany news: Merz lauds NATO with Westphalian Peace Prize
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-news-merz-.text:
At a ceremony to honor NATO, the German chancellor warned that Russia will threaten the rest of Europe if it isn't stopped in Ukraine. In other news, the German military will set up its first drone regiment.

These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.

Below, you can review a rundown of the stories from and about Germany that hit the headlines on Thursday, October 1, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Germany's 2-0 home win over Serbia in the UEFA Nations League marked Jürgen Klopp's inaugural victory as national team coach.

Florian Wirtz and Tom Bischof both scored goals as a youthful Germany team easily defeated a lackluster Serbia team in Munich.

The win eased the pressure on Klopp, who started his tenure with a 1-1 draw against the Netherlands and a shocking 0-1 loss to Greece last weekend.

A loss or tie would have made him the first German coach in history not to win any of his first three games.

Germany will conclude the international window on Sunday with a match against Greece in Thessaloniki, while Serbia will travel to the Netherlands.

Read more about Germany's win over Serbia here: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'

The German military will establish its first drone regiment next year, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Thursday evening. This comes as Berlin draws on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.

"We will establish the Bundeswehr's first drone regiment in the course of 2027," the minister said, describing the regiment as "an independent unit for unmanned systems."

According to Pistorius, the unit will consist of up to 600 members and have a range of up to 500 kilometers.

"Anyone who wants to prevail on land simply has to master the use of unmanned systems," the minister said.

Germany has been looking to ramp up its military's use of drones, partly as a result of lessons learned from the war in Ukraine, where drone warfare plays a key role in fighting Russian invasion.

In June, German army chief Christian Freuding announced his intention to rapidly expand the use of drones and unmanned weapon systems during a visit to the Freedom Shield 2026 military exercise in Lithuania.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a keynote speech on foreign policy, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz issued a stark warning against reducing aid to Ukraine in its defense against Russia.

"If we waver in Germany, then Europe wavers. If Europe wavers, then Ukraine wavers as well," he cautioned at the ceremony in Münster where the Westphalian Peace Prize was awarded to NATO.

Merz specifically warned that Russia could attack Germany and NATO if Ukraine falls. "If we fail to stop Moscow, then sooner or later, the Russian war machine will turn against us, against NATO itself. We must not turn a blind eye to this danger," he stressed.

The German chancellor emphasized that without German aid, the war against Ukraine would result in an "imposed peace." This would lead to mass migration toward the West and the destabilization of the Ukrainian state, according to Merz.

He touched only briefly on the meeting between Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York last weekend.

Merz said it was yet another example of how diplomatic efforts fell on deaf ears in Moscow. Russia understands only the “language of strength” and must be brought to the negotiating table through this approach, he stressed.

Merz said that "unity and strength remain prerequisites for successful negotiations with Moscow. And this can only encourage us to keep the United States of America by our side in our policy regarding Ukraine."

Merz said that a united front is also needed in Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has seen significant success in recent state elections and currently leads in nationwide polls.

"We in Germany, too, will not allow ourselves to be divided," Merz said. "Not by hybrid attacks, not by social media agitation driven by Moscow-controlled bots, and... not by the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers."

The AfD wants Berlin to stop providing military and financial support to Ukraine, lift sanctions against Russia, and restore dialogue.

The Westphalian Peace Prize is awarded every two years by the Economic Society for Westphalia and Lippe (WWL).

The award commemorates the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, which was concluded in the town halls of Münster and Osnabrück.

It brought an end to the Thirty Years’ War and is regarded as a contribution to the European peace order among states with equal rights.

This year, NATO was honored for its contribution to the European peace order.

Damen, a Dutch defense and shipbuilding conglomerate, is seeking €4.7 billion (about $5.30 billion) from the German government after it cancelled plans to produce F126 warships.

In June, the German Defense Ministry announced that it would terminate the multi-billion-euro project to build F126 frigates.

The ministry said it would instead buy eight MEKO A-200 frigates from TKMS (Thyssen Krupp Marine System), which is headquartered in Kiel, northern Germany.

The amount sought by Damen comprises the contractually agreed payment and compensation for what the Dutch company says was a breach of contract by the German government, according to a letter sent to two parliamentary (Bundestag) committees and seen by the Reuters news agency.

Damen is also exploring potential additional claims for damages, the letter said.

The Dutch company said the German government was responsible for delays to the project.

Low water levels in Lake Constance have forced boat services in one section of the waterway to be suspended, the municipal utility company in the southern German city of Konstanz said on Thursday.

The ferry operator, Bodensee-Schiffsbetriebe (BSB),  has suspended services on the Untersee region until further notice, it said.

In a statement, BSB chief Frank Weber was cited as saying: "We have kept the ferry service running right down to the last centimeter. We have now reached the point where the risk of getting stuck in the harbor entrance has become too great."

The service had to be suspended to protect passengers and the ships, it continued.

The lake, which is known as the Bodensee in German, borders Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

The water gauge for the lake is currently measuring 251 cm (99 inches), 108 cm under the mean level of 359 cm for this day of the year as measured over many years.

A long period of dry weather has forced tourist and cargo ships in other waterways across Germany to reduce or suspend services.

Cargo shipping on the Rhine has been particularly affected, with negative consequences for several industries that depend on river-borne supplies of raw materials.

An insurance company has carried out a survey to discover what people in Germany are most scared of.

And it is neither fascism, nor the climate crisis, nor spiders, nor Elon Musk, but — the cost of living.

Read our article to find out more: Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living, an annual study finds

The German government has so far not granted entry to any Afghan nationals on a humanitarian list drawn up by the previous government, despite examining more than two dozen individual cases in keeping with a ruling by the Constitutional Court.

In response to a parliamentary question by Left Party politician Clara Bünger, the Interior Ministry said 25 cases had been examined since the court ruling on July 22, but all had been rejected.

After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan in August 2021, the previous coalition government of Social Democrats (SPD), Greens and Free Democrats (FDP) had promised to grant entry to Afghan nationals who had worked for German institutions there or who were seen as endangered.

The current conservative-led government paused that program in May 2025 and in December 2025, the Interior Ministry rescinded all entry permissions that had been given under the scheme, saying there was "no political interest" in taking the people in.

The Federal Constitutional Court however ruled in July that Germany could not revoke the scheme en masse and that admission requests had to be considered on a case-to-case basis.

Bünger called on the government "to take in the some 500 people still in question immediately and in an uncomplicated manner."

She said the fact that these Afghan nationals had been forced to live for years in fear and uncertainty was unjustifiable.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Poland says it will extend controls along its border with Germany by six months until March 30 next year.

The Polish Interior Ministry said it would also be extending the measure, introduced in July 2025, on the border to Lithuania.

"Border controls are an effective tool ​for ⁠curbing illegal migration. Extending them will make ⁠it ​possible to manage migration pressure and strengthen border security," the ministry said in a statement.

Since the reintroduction of border controls, nearly 1,300 people have been denied entry into the ​country at ⁠the Lithuanian ​border and nearly ​1,200 at the German border, ​the statement said.

Germany has also had additional border controls in place at all its entry points since September 2024.

The border controls have been imposed even though Poland and Germany are members of the EU's Schengen Area, in which borders are theoretically meant to be open to allow seamless travel between EU members.

Under the Schengen Borders Code (SBC), member states are allowed to only temporarily reintroduce border controls in the case of security threats.

Both Poland and Germany have cited the threat of illegal immigration as having prompted the reinstatement of the controls.

A three-month fuel tax cut went into effect in Germany at midnight on Wednesday, with motorists now likely to pay prices for gas and diesel that are lower by 16.7 cents (18.9 US cents) per liter in the coming weeks.

Prices before the cut went into effect were well over €2 per liter in most places, with September the most expensive month on record at the pump.

The same measure was introduced in Germany in May and June to give relief to motorists as fuel prices spiral largely as a result of the war in the Middle East.

The tax cut technically applies only to fuel leaving storage facilities or refineries, with gas stations not directly required to lower their prices.

However, prices at most filling stations are expected to fall quickly, as happened in May and June.

Critic of the measure say it reduces incentives to save fuel and will potentially not be passed on in full to all consumers.

Supporters say it is currently the best way to relieve the burden on motorists.

NATO is to be awarded with international Westphalian Peace Prize, worth €100,000 ($113,350), on Thursday afternoon, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz set to give the laudatory address.

The prize, which is expected to be received by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the ceremony in Münster, honors the military alliance for its contribution to the European peace order.

The award is being presented to NATO at a time when its role as guarantor of Europe's security has been cast into some uncertainty by US ambivalence under the Trump administration.

The Westphalian Peace Price, which commemorates the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, is awarded every two years by the Economic Society for Westphalia and Lippe.

The 1648 peace agreement, concluded in the city halls of Münster and Osnabrück, ended the Thirty Years' War and is considered by many as a milestone in establishing the principle of national sovereignty.

The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has officially dropped its founder's name from its title to become the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason.

However, it will retain the abbreviation BSW.

Secretary general Oliver Ruhnert said Wagenknecht's name had initially been used because of her popularity but that the party had now succeeded in establishing itself as a brand in its own right.

Wagenknecht, a former parliamentary leader of the Left Party, founded the BSW in 2024, stepping down as its leader in November 2025.

Although the BSW advocates economic policies that are left-wing, it also has a nationalist and anti-migration stance that are more typical of the right-wing political spectrum, making it hard to classify in conventional terms.

It also favors closer ties with Russia.

Federal police arrested a suspected member of the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group in central Germany on Wednesday morning.

Prosecutors allege that the man joined the group in Iraq at the latest by early 2016, fighting in its ranks until early 2017.

He was detained in the Waldeck-Frankenberg district, north of Frankfurt, and is now being held in pre-trial detention after appearing at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe.

Politicians from the socialist Left Party, the environmentalist Greens and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) in Berlin are set to meet on Thursday to talk through several contentious issues before embarking on possible coalition negotiations.

Among other things, the talks will focus on accusations of antisemitism leveled at the Left Party, which won recent elections.

The party has also been accused of cultivating links to organized crime.

The accusations were fueled by the attendance of a well-known local figure with alleged criminal ties and a controversial pro-Palestinian activist at an election night event held by the Left Party in the Neukölln district of the city on September 20.

The Greens and the Left Party have said reaching agreement on these contentious issues is a "basic prerequisite" if formal exploratory talks on a coalition are to begin.

If the Left Party were to end up leading a coalition in the German capital, its lead candidate and parliamentary group co-leader, Elif Eralp, could become the first female governing mayor of Berlin.

A hearty guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn as the new month gets underway!

We will be looking at the pre-preliminary talks between the Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) on possibly forming a coalition in the capital, Berlin.

The parties are approaching the matter with great caution amid accusations that the Left Party, which won recent elections, is antisemitic and maintains contacts with organized criminality.

This comes as another party, the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), changes its name to the catchy "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason", while retaining the BSW abbreviation.

Meanwhile, motorists should be seeing prices at gas stations take a sudden fall as a fuel tax cut goes into effect.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-debates-al.title: Germany debates alleged antisemitism in the Left Party
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-debates-al.text:
The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?

The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election on September 20. This means there's a good chance that the party's top candidate, Elif Eralp, could become Berlin's next mayor — making her the first member of the Left Party to hold that office.

Preliminary talks with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the environmentalist Green Party are scheduled to take place on October 1. If the talks are successful, it would represent a major step toward forming a coalition government.

Securing a clear commitment from the Left Party against antisemitism within its own ranks is seen as a prerequisite for successful cooperation. Yet doubts still persist about whether the party and its representatives can adequately protect Jewish life in the city.

During the election campaign, a performance at a Left Party event by the rapper Dahabflex made headlines and sparked outrage when he used slogans seen as antisemitic during his performance. And later, at an event held by the Left Party to celebrate its election victory, an appearance was made by Ibrahim Ibrahim — a supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is on the EU's list of terrorist organizations. The leaders of the Left Party have repeatedly distanced themselves from both incidents, both at the federal and state levels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, thinks these statements are mere lip service.

"In the fight against antisemitism, which is tolerated and allowed to run rampant within the party's ranks, the Left Party no longer has any credibility," reads a press statement released two days after the election. Schuster explicitly appealed to the SPD and the Greens not to form a coalition with the election winner.

High-ranking members of the federal government have also spoken out. Wolfram Weimer, government commissioner for culture and media who has no party affiliation, accused the Left Party of "openly flaunting antisemitism" and called into question the €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in funding for the capital's cultural sector for the coming decade — a deal that had already been agreed upon with the Berlin state government. Weimer claimed that many figures in the cultural sector are alarmed by the prospect of a government led by the Left Party.

Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also voiced concern. A video titled "Antisemitism and Expropriations Threaten the Economy" is available on her ministry's Instagram account, in reference also to the Left Party's plans to nationalize large private housing companies.

Reiche describes the Left as a party "that openly embraces antisemitism, that instills fear in the Jews of this city, that opposes Jewish life and that cheerfully welcomes organized crime at election parties."

The Left Party is now seeking an injunction to compel the Minister of Economic Affairs to delete the video.

"Reiche is using taxpayer money to spread propaganda against the Left Party on the Economy Ministry's official channel," said Left Party Federal Co-Chair Ines Schwerdtner.

In an open letter, a group of 150 prominent Jews from various social backgrounds has voiced support for the Left Party. Among those who signed it are the author Eva Menasse and the former director of the Einstein Forum in Potsdam, Susan Neiman. They advocate for a "social and safe city" and emphasize the importance of voting for different parties.

They explain their motivation as follows: "We are writing this letter because, over the past few weeks, we have heard the same claim time and again: that the Left is dangerous for Jews, and that a coalition involving the party poses a danger to our safety. We reject this claim not because we downplay concerns about our safety, but because we actually take them seriously."

Without naming the party directly, the signatories of the letter wrote that they believe that the greatest enemy of Jewish life is the Alternative for Germany (AfD): "At a time when an in-parts openly fascistic political party is marching towards power across Germany, it is an abdication of responsibility on the part of mainstream media and elements of our own community to continue to pretend that the Left presents the largest threat to Jewish safety."

In light of this, the letter states: "The constant accusations of antisemitism against the Left are not only cynical political weaponization, but they also conflate nearly any criticism of Israel with antisemitism."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Left Party is the only party in the German parliament that opposes arms deliveries to Israel due to the military operation in the Gaza Strip following the terrorist attack by the radical Islamist group Hamas on October 7, 2023. Based on a resolution passed at its party convention, the Left Party classifies the ensuing war as a genocide.

Human rights organizations and a United Nations (UN) commission have also classified Israel's actions in Gaza against the Palestinian people as a genocide. The Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has invoked Israel's right to self-defense.

The intensifying debate over antisemitism within the Left Party is complicating the formation of a government in Berlin. At a party congress convened on short notice, Elif Eralp, the potential future mayor of Berlin, emphasized that her party has a duty to bring people together and build bridges.

"And in doing so," Eralp said, "it must be absolutely clear that there must never be any calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people must never be made from our platforms."

With these remarks, Eralp once again criticized the antisemitic rapper's performance during the Berlin election campaign. Jewish people must be able to feel safe in Berlin, said Eralp.

"I will strengthen Berlin's diverse Jewish community and combat antisemitism. And Palestinian and Muslim people must also feel seen and safe," Eralp said.

Outside the building where the special party convention was held, about 20 Jewish people expressed their solidarity with the party. A poster in Hebrew and German lay at their feet, reading, "Mazel Tov to the Left," congratulating the party on its September 20 election victory in Berlin.

One of the demonstrators was Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York.

"Antisemitism is real — we know that," Grabell told DW. "But three years of genocide are also real, as are illegal occupation, forced destruction and displacement in the West Bank — that, too, is real."

Grabell emphasized that they were there to support the Left Party in its efforts to advance progressive policies. "We also want to show the diversity of Jewish life in German society. Everyone talks about the different sides — we are also part of Jewish life."

This article was originally written in German.
