https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protest
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.

Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of ⁠voter lists.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.

A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.

Police authorities ⁠didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.

The CJP said that ‌among those detained was a group ‌of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being ‌taken away in a bus to an unknown location.

The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.

The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.

The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.

The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.

The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the ​resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.

In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.

Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.

“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who ⁠actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture ​student who attended the Bengaluru protest.

There were also protests over ​police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.

On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of ​using “brute force” to briefly detain ‌party leader Rahul Gandhi, his ​sister Priyanka Vadra, and other ​lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.

Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.

BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.

Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

Here’s a fuller rundown on Labour’s win in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection that has been a high-stakes battle for the left of British politics.

The byelection, called after the former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Zack Polanski.

Abdi-Wali recieved 12,292 votes to Polanski’s 8,928, Sammy Gecsoyler reports.

Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4% down from 2024.

The Greens conceded defeat shortly before the result was announced, with a party spokesperson saying “taking the fight to Labour in one of its safest seats shows just how far the Greens have come”.

Labour’s victory will be a relief for Andy Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.

While Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Greens leader, the party put a bright spin on what it called an “incredible result” with the increased vote share he brought the party in the byelection.

“Achieving a huge swing in one of Labour’s safest seats – an increase of 22% in vote share since the general election – is an incredible result for the Green party, and during a honeymoon period for the new PM,” a Greens spokesperson quoted by PA Media said.

We are disappointed to miss out tonight but any ideas of a return to the cosy two-party system is just wishful thinking on the part of the establishment. We are here to stay and just getting started.

The voters have delivered a message to the Labour government today. They want real change.

Zack Polanski has said he definitely intends to stay on as leader of the Greens despite his byelection defeat.

Asked on Sky News if he would continue as party leader, he said: “Yes absolutely, that’s what leaders do.”

He also said after the poll result that it had not been a mistake standing in the north London seat, saying he was happy to stand in elections.

I don’t think it was a mistake at all, I think it has been an opportunity to present Green party values, to talk about rent controls, tackling the climate crisis, nationalising Thames Water. It’s been amazing to speak to people in Holborn and St Pancras, I’ve really enjoyed that.

Here’s a fuller rundown on Labour’s win in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection that has been a high-stakes battle for the left of British politics.

The byelection, called after the former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Zack Polanski.

Abdi-Wali recieved 12,292 votes to Polanski’s 8,928, Sammy Gecsoyler reports.

Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4% down from 2024.

The Greens conceded defeat shortly before the result was announced, with a party spokesperson saying “taking the fight to Labour in one of its safest seats shows just how far the Greens have come”.

Labour’s victory will be a relief for Andy Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.

See the full report here:

Labour campaigned hard in this byelection, fielding the 42-year-old leader of Camden council as the party’s candidate. Sagal Abdi-Wali arrived in London in the early 90s – speaking no English – after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia.

In a pre-poll message to byelection voters, prime minister Andy Burnham said:

This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.

Returning to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s acceptance speech, the newly elected Labour MP said that whether people voted for her or not, “I promise that I will work every day to do whatever I can and all I can to improve your life”.

This moment means something deeply personal to me – to represent the place that gave me a home, and my family a home, gave me opportunity and helped shape the person I am today.

Camden gave me a community and instilled in me a belief in social justice, in equality and in fairness. And to now have the privilege of representing this same community in parliament is something that I will carry with enormous pride and humility.

I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong. For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place, and know that their path too belongs here.

This is Camden, and this is Britain.

Sagal Abdi-Wali is speaking and saying she is “deeply honoured” to be chosen by her constituency and that her commitment to it “runs deep”.

From the bottom of my heart I want to say thank you.

Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali has been declared the byelection winner with 12,292 votes. Zack Polanski came in second for the Greens with 8,928, while the Conservatives’ Ewan Cameron polled third with 1,922.

The byelection candidates have gathered in the vote tally room at Camden Council headquarters in north London and it appears a declaration of the results is imminent.

Circling back to Caroline Lucas, the former Green party leader said shortly after the byelection polls closed that Zack Polanski had made a “mistake not to show leadership” over the Zionism policy vote, but she declined to say if he should resign over it.

“He should have been there and he should have voted,” she told BBC Newsnight.

I would’ve hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom, in my view.

Lucas said she expected he would face a lot criticism from fellow Greens now the byelection was over. But asked if he should resign, she said:

I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks ... obviously he has been completed taken up with this byelection. I want him to speak now about what’s happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. I think the jury is out about whether or not he will do that but I very much hope he will.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Victory by Sagal Abdi-Wali in north London seat will be a relief for Andy Burnham in high-stakes battle for the left of British politics

Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a high-stakes battle for the left of British politics.

The byelection, called after the former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. Abdi-Wali recieved 12,292 votes to Polanski’s 8,928.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4% down from 2024.

The Greens conceded defeat shortly before the result was announced, with a party spokesperson saying “taking the fight to Labour in one of its safest seats shows just how far the Greens have come.”

Labour’s victory will be a relief for Andy Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.

While Starmer won a 11,572 majority in the constituency for Labour at the 2024 general election, victory in the byelection was not guaranteed. Andrew Feinstein, a leftwing independent, came second in 2024, and the Greens peeled off some Camden council seats from Labour in May’s local elections.

Abdi-Wali, the leader of Camden council, is a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s.

Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, was accused by Labour of “straightforward racism” after he said she was being “foisted” on voters in the constituency and suggested she was not British.

The Greens ran a strong ground game, dispatching thousands of members to knock on doors in the constituency, even before Polanski was selected as the party’s candidate.

Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his eco-populist party, which fell into turmoil after it voted on Sunday to adopt a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism. The motion passed in a vote by Green members at the party conference despite opposition from four of its five MPs.

The motion said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. The head of the Jewish Greens condemned the motion and said she may leave the party, although it was supported by some Jewish Greens.

Even members who supported large parts of the motion were unhappy about its narrow conception of Zionism which some fear could brand those in favour of the idea of a Jewish homeland, but not specifically the modern-day state of Israel, as racist.

Polanski missed the debate on the motion and did not cast a vote, which left some members frustrated over his lack of leadership on the matter. Shortly after polls closed, Caroline Lucas refused to say whether Polanski should stand down. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, the former Green leader said: “I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday,” when the motion was voted on. Polanski was campaigning in the constituency instead.

The Greens’ standing in the polls, and Polanski’s personal approval ratings, had already fallen in recent months, after a peak in popularity last summer, exemplified by the Greens’ seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February.

Midway into the race, George Galloway, running in “self-exile” out of outside the UK, put his name on the ballot in a move that many Green supporters warnedsaid could pull votes away from Polanski. He received 314 votes.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Millions on alert as Hurricane Isaias set to bring dangerous storm surge
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Residents in areas from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Florida urged to ‘evacuate if told to do so’

Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida were under hurricane warnings on Thursday as Hurricane Isaias heads toward the US Gulf coast, with weather officials warning of dangerous storm surge, hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall and flooding.

Isaias intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, and has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, as well as evacuation orders and school closures in several Florida counties as officials urge residents to prepare for its arrival.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Thursday evening that Isaias, now a category 2 hurricane, has sustained winds of 100mph (160km/h). It is expected to make landfall in the northern Gulf coast late Friday or early Saturday.

The NWS warned that Isaias was “expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf coast on Friday” and that it was expected to bring a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast.

Storm surge warnings, issued when there is a “danger of life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland from the coastline”, are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas have been urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so.

The NWS further warned that “preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds in the warning area should be rushed to completion today”.

Hurricane warnings were in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf county line in Florida, with the NWS warning that “damaging hurricane force-winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern Mississippi”. Residents were being urged to prepare for possible “long-duration power outages”.

Tropical storm warnings were in effect from parts of Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and from east of the Bay/Gulf county line to Aucilla River in Florida. Gusty winds were also possible across parts of the Yucatán peninsula on Thursday.

Isaias was expected to bring heavy rain to the central Gulf coast and much of the south-east from Friday into the weekend, with 3-7in of rain expected from south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region.

The NWS warned that localized rainfall totals of up to 15in were possible, and noted that flash and urban flooding was possible, along with isolated river flooding.

Isolated tornadoes could also develop on Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far south-western Georgia, the NWS said, adding that “the tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida”.

On Thursday afternoon, the Georgia governor, Brian Kemp, issued a state of emergency ahead of Isaias, for all 159 counties, enabling emergency management teams to “make necessary arrangements and position needed resources ahead of the storm’s impact”.

“As we always do with weather events, we’re hoping for the best but preparing for the worst,” Kemp said. “I encourage all Georgians to take this storm seriously and prepare now by stocking up on food, batteries, flashlights, water, and other necessities in case of severe weather impacting communities Friday night through Saturday.”

It came as Alabama governor, Kay Ivey, declared a state of emergency in 40 counties on Wednesday, saying the order would allow officials to take “any needed steps ahead of landfall”. A flood watch is also set to take effect for all of central Alabama from 7pm local time on Friday through 7am local time Saturday morning.

The Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, also declared a state of emergency this week for 25 counties.

At a news conference on Thursday afternoon, DeSantis said that the hurricane was “expected to make impacts with the winds as early as Friday afternoon” and said “landfall is projected at this point to be late Friday night into the wee hours of Saturday morning. It’s moving pretty quickly.”

He added: “Execute your plan now if you’re in that area, execute it, it’s something that we’re going to have to get through, we’re going to have impacts, and I’ve pretty much said that from the outset, there will be impacts.

“We are assuming that this could reach category 3 status.”

Several counties in Florida have issued local emergencies and evacuation orders. Officials in Okaloosa county declared a local state of emergency on Wednesday and ordered some residents in coastal areas to evacuate.

On Thursday, Florida’s Walton and Franklin counties issued mandatory evacuation orders for some areas. Officials in Escambia county issued an evacuation order for residents in areas including Perdido Key, Innerarity Point, Pensacola Beach and other low-lying areas.

DeSantis said on Thursday that the Florida division of emergency management was coordinating with all local counties to address resource requests and to position equipment before the storm. He also said that 900 personnel with the Florida department of transportation were conducting pre-storm preparations.

Several school districts in Alabama and Florida have announced closures, while Florida State University’s Tallahassee campus announced it will be closed on Friday.

The hurricane is also expected to disrupt travel. Destin-Fort Walton Beach airport said it would close all operations at 9pm local time on Thursday, and remain closed until further notice.

Meanwhile, Pensacola airport announced it would be closing to commercial operations at 10am CT on Friday, with the reopening date and time to be determined.

The Federal Aviation Administration warned on Thursday that “Hurricane Isaias may lead to oceanic route closures in the Gulf” and that thunderstorm delays are possible in Orlando, Tampa, Miami and Fort Lauderdale. The Southern Rail Commission said Amtrak’s Mardi Gras service along the Gulf coast will be suspended through the weekend.

Additionally, starting Friday, the Crescent service between New Orleans and Atlanta will be suspended until Monday.

In Tennessee, the NWS office in Morristown warned that “remnants of Hurricane Isaias will bring heavy rain and strong, gusty winds to our area this weekend”. The office said that “high winds could top 60–70+ mph in the eastern TN mountains and foothills, with isolated flash flooding possible in heavy rainfall areas”.

In Ohio, the NWS office in Wilmington cautioned that Isaias would hit the Ohio valley this weekend, with strong winds expected, with possible “widespread rain” and storms.

In Pennsylvania, the NWS office in Pittsburgh said “moisture from Hurricane Isaias is forecast to reach our region this weekend” and that they were expecting “soaking rain, but risks of significant flooding are low”.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Execution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new low | Paul Daley
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Paul Daley
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity

M
ore fool me! Here I was thinking nothing that America’s Trump administration could do or say, no matter how politically and morally bankrupt, no matter how venal or violent, was capable of shocking me any longer.

Then I woke to today’s news that one of the Trump cabinet’s bigger boofheads – the uber Christian nationalist, crusader-fantasist and “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth had announced that America would have a public firing squad execution of murderer Nidal Hasan.

Reckless global militarisation including a threat at the UN to annihilate Iran, a litany of sexual misconduct allegations against the commander in chief, claims of blatant presidential corruption … they have all ceased to surprise and shock us, so inured has the world become to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration.

But now we have execution TV. Tune in to the livestream on Thursday 3 December to watch a military firing squad shoot the life out of Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a US army base in 2009.

State-sanctioned killing as entertainment! Yes, the world’s supposedly greatest (or formerly greatest) democracy has arrived at an horrific new moral nadir.

The fact that America remains Australia and the west’s most relied-upon and trusted ally despite the global wrecking ball the second Trump administration has proved to be, was already cause for deep concern.

But being so closely allied to a country that now wants to turn the execution of a human being – no matter what their crimes – into a live entertainment event, promises to redefine depravity.

Given that American states continue to execute so many convicted criminals, where might the United States ultimately draw the line? No doubt the ilk of Hegseth in American society – and elsewhere – will count down the days until they can tune in to the live coverage of Hasan’s execution in droves. Might the audience cry out for more – for livestream cameras in the death chambers across the land of the free?

How would this populist administration respond? If you think it’s a fanciful question, consider how far American governance and presidential values have slid in the moral murk in the past two years alone.

Meanwhile, it’s hard to contemplate a more audacious appeal to American society’s darker angels than this looming entertainment event.

But there we are. We have arrived.

Pass the popcorn, Don and Pete!

It would be heartening today to hear political leaders the world over condemn Hegseth and Trump’s planned introduction of Ghoul TV.

But let’s please start in Australia, where federal governments have for a long time opposed capital punishment – let alone turning it into a public spectacle. Will the prime minister and his senior ministers stand up and condemn without qualification this depraved plan for America to livestream an execution? What about the leaders of other political parties here, some of whom have, after all, supported capital punishment?

Meanwhile, how much further into the moral quagmire must America wallow before Australia rethinks its craven military dependence on Washington – not least via the reckless shackling of our strategic reliance to the US via the $368bn (and counting) Aukus submarine deal?

Announcing America’s decision to turn killing into a form of entertainment, Hegseth said: “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

America’s defense department later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.

This represents a significant lurch in the US from civilisation towards savagery.

You can’t choose your family. But you can choose your friends and allies. And you can also tell them firmly when they’ve careened off the ethical rails.

Actions speak louder than words.

And this planned livestreamed execution says it all about what is happening in America today, opening the window ever wider on the Trump administration’s moral vacuity and its paucity of human decency.

Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: LeBron James shines in pre-season debut for revamped Philadelphia 76ers
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
James scores 10 points in 18-minute Sixers debut

Jaylen Brown leads Philadelphia with 18 points

Nets pull away in third quarter for 114-108 victory

NBA superstar LeBron James delivered a solid first-half performance in his first pre-season game for Philadelphia on Thursday, but the new-look 76ers fell 114-108 to the Brooklyn Nets.

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, announced in July that he had signed a two-year, $8m deal with the 76ers, ending weeks of speculation over where the four-time NBA champion would land as a free agent after eight seasons and one title with the Los Angeles Lakers.

The 41-year-old, entering a record-extending 24th NBA season, won two titles with Miami, another with Cleveland and a fourth with the Lakers. He is aiming to help the Sixers win their first championship since Julius Erving led the team to the title in 1983.

Thursday’s game marked his first chance to play alongside new teammates Joel Embiid, VJ Edgecombe, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, who arrived from the Boston Celtics.

James scored 10 points, making his only shot from the field and all eight of his free-throw attempts. He added four rebounds, five assists and a steal in 18 minutes and four seconds, all in the first half.

Brown led all scorers with 18 points. Julius Randle had 14 for the Nets, who outscored the Sixers 37-23 in the third quarter to take control.

But all eyes were on James, starting with his signature pre-game chalk toss, performed for the first time in a 76ers uniform.

James smoothly directed the Sixers’ offense during his time on the floor, recording all five of his assists in the first quarter and combining effectively with Maxey.

“I think there was some really good things happening, you know, right off the bat,” 76ers coach Nick Nurse said after seeing his starters together for the first time.

“A bunch of back cuts and good passing et cetera ... there were segments where obviously we turned the ball over a lot ... just the little clunky segments, too. But, again, it’s pre-season, first time they’re together.

“I think you look at it as what’s good and what are the learning experiences, things that we can improve.”

The 76ers have two more pre-season games, both against Boston, before opening the regular season against the defending champion New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on 20 October.

James’s arrival has already left the 76ers contending with distractions away from the court.

The superstar took to Instagram to dispute a claim made by a play-by-play announcer during the team’s first pre-season game on Monday that he had admonished Embiid for arriving late to practice.

“He ain’t been late, so stop the lie,” James posted.

James acknowledged at the team’s media day last month that the attention surrounding the 76ers would be “doubled, tripled and quadrupled now that I’m here.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: OpenAI’s Jason Kwon gave even-toned, reassuring answers to the Australian government. Did … ChatGPT write this?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Kwon’s answers were provided in a helpful, quiet and calm manner, but his mea culpa left the audience not much the wiser

Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare.

Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey parliamentary committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making.

In other words, just like ChatGPT.

Even the content of his responses evoked the AI assistant he was there to defend.

Asked by the senator David Pocock “why did you send an email to an arbitrary department email?”, Kwon replied: “In retrospect, we should have done what you’re suggesting.” Asked why Open AI’s CEO Sam Altman wasn’t informed before his meeting with Australia’s deputy prime minister Richard Marles, and why the company didn’t fess up there, Kwon said: “I agree the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better”.

One couldn’t help but be reminded of the way the chatbot responds when pulled up on a mistake: “Good catch. You’re right to push back. My bad, that one’s on me.”

In Kwon’s parlance, the models – built from the ground up by OpenAI, which reportedly wants to value itself at $1.4tn – “accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to.” He tried to explain that the “novelty” of this incident meant the company had “learned our lesson”, which was that it should inform victims of such incidents much earlier, rather than waiting.

Kwon again apologised for the company only sending a casual email to the federal government disclosing that its agent had inappropriately accessed Medicare statistics, but tried to explain to Tuesday’s parliamentary hearing that it was sometimes “difficult” to figure how to make such notifications to a big sprawling public service.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Pocock helpfully offered: “I assume someone in your government relations team has mobile phone numbers of ministers and various people?”

There was a similar air of post-facto contrition as Kwon – OpenAI’s chief strategy officer – could offer few answers about why Altman didn’t inform Marles about the incident when they met face-to-face in San Francisco on 1 September. That was nine days before the company emailed Services Australia, and nearly a whole month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.

Kwon said Altman wasn’t aware of the incident before the Marles meeting. After Tuesday’s committee hearing, it’s still unclear why.

Sign up to Politics, really

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

after newsletter promotion

It’s a big government, and maybe Kwon is right that it’s “difficult” to find the right person to talk to. But some could also argue that your boss shaking hands with Australia’s deputy prime minister would be something of a useful window.

At least, we learned, he said the company didn’t use AI to write the infamous email. Small blessings that they managed to ask a human to write it – even if it went to an obscure inbox.

But with Australia striving to become a tech capital for datacentres and AI – as the revolving door of big tech companies told the inquiry, from Anthropic to Microsoft and Google – then setting the basic rules of the road for these firms, about how they must act and respond to this country and its government, is critical.

Kwon said OpenAI was committed to providing future notifications “very quickly”, and that there were no further incidents they were aware of. But he casually dropped in one staggering fact: OpenAI was still trawling through the activity logs for the agents involved in the Services Australia breach, with those logs totalling 50 petabytes of data.

A petabyte is 1,000 terabytes, or 1m gigabytes.

Kwon made the mind-boggling claim that it would take a human 66m years – never sleeping, never resting – to go through that data by hand.

The team tasked with checking Services Australia’s email inboxes must be hoping there aren’t any more dramas lurking in there.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: ICE agent shoots man in car with five-year-old child in New York: Mayor
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent has shot a man in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, calling the incident an “unconscionable and incredibly serious situation”.

In a statement he published on X, Mamdani said early reports on Thursday indicated agents surrounded the man and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds.

The child was believed to be physically unharmed, he added.

Mamdani said he had called President Donald Trump and would demand that he end all ICE enforcement actions in the city. “I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities,” he said.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said ICE officers were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” in the Bronx at about 4pm to arrest a man it described as a Dominican national with a criminal conviction.

It said an officer “discharged his weapon” and the man was injured.

DHS said the incident remains under investigation.

According to a statement by the New York Police Department, the man remains conscious and is receiving medical treatment at a nearby hospital.

The shooting comes after months of mounting criticism of the agency.

In January, federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens in Minneapolis: Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, killed by an ICE agent on January 7, and Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, shot by a US border agent.

After Good’s killing, Trump officials labelled her a “domestic terrorist” even as video of the shooting cast doubt on claims she had tried to run over an agent.

The federal government removed local authorities from the investigation, rejected calls for a civil rights probe, and sent hundreds more agents to Minnesota, bringing the total to 3,000, as protests spread to hundreds of US cities.

Trump blamed the shift in American opinion about the immigration agency on unfair media coverage, urging DHS and ICE to publicise the “violent criminals” they arrest.

ICE has been tasked with a target of one million deportations a year.

The agency doubled in size to more than 22,000 agents by January and is now the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency, with about $75bn allocated to it over four years under a tax bill Trump signed last year.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Christa Pike case underscores prevalence of botched executions in US
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Brian Osgood
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The botched execution of Christa Pike has sparked debate about the death penalty in the United States, where lethal injections, experts say, are frequently marred by mishaps and incompetence.

The attempted execution of Pike, a woman sentenced to death for her participation in the murder of a classmate when she was 18 years old, was called off after two doses of pentobarbital failed to kill her on September 30.

Witnesses reported that she continued to breathe, snore and lift parts of her body off the gurney to which she was strapped even after the lethal injections were administered. Pike’s lawyers said that she had regained consciousness at the hospital on October 6 but faces a long path to recovery.

Governor Bill Lee announced a pause on executions in the state and promised a “comprehensive, third-party review” of the incident, the second case this year in which Tennessee authorities have called off an execution after a failed lethal injection attempt.

The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment when asked by Al Jazeera why the execution attempt failed and whether it planned to try to execute Pike again.

While the case has attracted nationwide attention, experts say that botched execution attempts, largely carried out through lethal injection, are a disturbingly common feature of capital punishment in the US.

“This is an opportunity for everyone to stop and really carefully examine all of the ways in which this execution went wrong and to make good decisions about how to move forward, if we’re going to move forward with this method of execution,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit research group based in Washington, DC.

Of the various methods of execution in the US, lethal injection is by far the most common. It is also among the least reliable.

States such as Tennessee, Idaho, Alabama, Arizona, Texas and Oklahoma have all recorded at least one botched execution via lethal injection since 2022, and a survey of executions in the US between 1890 and 2010 found that lethal injections were botched at more than twice the rate of all other methods.

Researchers attribute the poor record of lethal injection to a number of factors, including the difficulty of carrying out what amounts to a medical procedure in a prison setting without access to qualified staff.

Major medical organisations bar members from assisting in executions on the basis that it violates their mandate to do no harm, meaning that prisons rely on staff members or officials with dubious credentials to carry out the procedure.

“Lethal injection has all of the delicacies of a medical procedure: all of the error-prone qualities, all of the need for precision. But it has been warped to fit the needs of execution settings,” said Corinna Barrett Lain, a professor at the University of Richmond School of Law and author of a book on lethal injection.

She explained that she has witnessed botched executions that drag on for hours and include prisoners being punctured with needles more than a dozen times. “It’s this really bad combination of a delicate procedure that is not performed in a delicate way.”

Pharmaceutical companies also restrict the use of their products in executions, meaning that some states acquire drugs used in lethal injection through facilities called compounding pharmacies.

Such pharmacies often prepare medications not manufactured commercially, and the drugs they produce are not as extensively scrutinised as mass-produced medications. Some states have also sought to stretch existing stockpiles of drugs used in lethal injections, though they can become expired or faulty.

The risks are compounded by the people the lethal injections are administered to.

Those on death row often spend years or even decades waiting for their execution. Since many are of an advanced age, they are more likely to have health issues that can further complicate the procedure.

Botched executions often feature failed attempts to locate a vein or set an IV line.

While state officials have yet to offer an explanation of why Pike’s execution failed, her lawyers had previously argued that she had small veins and a blood condition that were likely to complicate a lethal injection effort.

After the lethal injections, Pike’s lawyers described her arms as swollen and burned.

Maher, the head of the Death Penalty Information Center, said those symptoms suggest the injection may not have properly reached her bloodstream.

“Everyone has speculated that the drugs were administered to her but did not enter her bloodstream in sufficient amounts to kill her,” she said. “It’s likely that her veins were blown, or that the needle went through the vein.”

When the lethal injection drugs fail to be properly administered, executions can be drawn out and, in some cases, unnecessarily painful for prisoners.

After the first dose of pentobarbital was administered to her, Pike reportedly stated that she felt her arm was “about to burst open”.

In May, Tennessee also called off the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff struggled for more than 90 minutes to establish a backup IV line.

In February 2024, the state of Idaho likewise suspended the execution of Thomas Creech, a man in his 70s, after an execution team failed to properly insert an IV after eight attempts in his arms, legs and feet.

Despite such incidents, lethal injection has become the primary method of execution in 28 of the 29 states that still allow capital punishment, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The first execution via lethal injection occurred in Texas in 1982.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, 39 people were killed by lethal injection in 2025, compared with five by lethal gas and three by firing squad. The last electrocution of a prisoner took place in 2020, and older methods such as hanging have not been employed since the 1990s.

Michael Radelet, a professor of sociology at the University of Colorado who has tracked botched executions, says that lethal injection has taken the place of older forms of execution that came to be seen as outdated and draconian.

Such methods also resulted in grim spectacles that distressed observers. Prisoners being electrocuted sometimes caught on fire or disturbed witnesses with the smell of burning flesh.

“Lethal injection is relatively new, but it’s part of a long-term trend going back hundreds of years in search of a more ‘humane’ method of execution,” Radelet told Al Jazeera.

But he added that the method’s promise of a more peaceful and clinical procedure has been belied by its poor record.

He also pointed to autopsies that show that, despite the relative sterility of the procedure, prisoners still experience pain.

Critics say such information calls into question the widespread use of lethal injection and whether it should be discarded altogether.

“Lethal injection, from the very start, was about a humane-looking execution, not a humane execution,” said Lain, the law professor. “There’s a big difference.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Christa Pike was sentenced to death for her involvement in the murder of a classmate when she was 18. Pike's lawyers said she had regained consciousness at the hospital on October 6. Pike faces a long path to recovery. The first execution via lethal injection occurred in Texas in 1982.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Key takeaways from US Senate debate in Michigan between El-Sayed, Rogers
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The leading candidates in Michigan’s heated Senate race have faced off in their first televised debate, with less than a month remaining before the United States midterm elections.

Thursday’s hour-long debate was a microcosm of how tense the toss-up race has become.

Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, formerly the health director for Wayne County, repeatedly sought to paint his Republican adversary Mike Rogers as a yacht-owning millionaire out of touch with ordinary voters.

For his part, Rogers, a former member of the US House of Representatives, lobbed accusations at El-Sayed that he was soft on “terrorism” and had foreign sympathies.

The Michigan-born El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks while on the campaign trail, with Republican President Donald Trump labelling him an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer” whose history “goes back to the days of the Jihad”. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate.

The two candidates spent much of their hour onstage together speaking over one another, as they exchanged pointed barbs.

“He can’t condemn a terrorist act that happened on our soil in the state of Michigan. He can’t bring himself to condemn –,” Rogers began, referencing a March attack on a synagogue.

“I did condemn it,” El-Sayed said, jumping in. “No, you did not,” Rogers replied, with El-Sayed quickly responding, “You make stuff up. You make stuff up.”

The Senate race in Michigan is considered key to the battle for control of the US Senate. Democrats are seeking to flip both chambers of Congress, but shifting control of the Senate will be a tougher prospect, given that only a third of its 100 seats are on the November 3 ballot.

Host Rick Albin at times struggled to keep the debate on track, as tensions rose.

“We’ve got dozens of questions we want to get to. You can’t litigate all of these with 14 different rebuttals, so please work with me,” Albin told the two candidates at one point.

Here are the key takeaways from the evening’s debate.

The ferocity of the debate was underscored by the high volume of ad hominem attacks the candidates deployed against each other.

But Rogers repeatedly pushed a series of attacks that seemed to centre on El-Sayed’s identity as a Muslim.

In response to a question about healthcare, Rogers said that El-Sayed has “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.

Later, when asked about his position on surveillance by Flock cameras, Rogers argued that such technology has helped catch people suspected of terrorism. He then implied that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras were suggestive.

“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked El-Sayed. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list …”

El-Sayed interjected, seeming to dare Rogers to continue his thought.

“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”

Muslim and Arab candidates in the US have frequently been subjected to Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, accusing them of support for “terrorism” and Islamic fundamentalism.

There were issues, however, on which both candidates found a measure of common ground.

Both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed the US-Israeli war against Iran should end, but they had opposite views on Washington’s relationship with Israel and its role in the conflict.

High gasoline prices and inflation, El-Sayed said, were directly caused by the Iran war, and he blamed the Trump administration for Iran’s decision to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a critical trade route.

“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said. “We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”

Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, but he also justified the conflict, saying that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been “set back twenty years”, echoing a frequent White House talking point.

The Trump administration has argued that the war was necessary to prevent Iran from creating a nuclear weapon, a goal Tehran has long denied.

Rogers’s position led El-Sayed to accuse him of “cheerleading” for the war and the Trump administration.

As part of the debate about US foreign policy, the candidates were also pressed on their positions about the US alliance with Israel.

The country is considered the largest overall recipient of US aid since World War II. From the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 through September 2025, experts estimate that Israel received nearly $21.7bn in military aid.

El-Sayed has openly called for ending aid to Israel, and he has repeatedly denounced the conflict in Gaza as a genocide, in line with evaluations from United Nations experts and human rights watchdogs.

During the debate, he indicated he preferred US taxpayer dollars to be spent on domestic concerns like education and healthcare, rather than Israeli aid.

“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”

He also blamed Israel for the US military action in Iran. “I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.

Rogers, meanwhile, has joined most of his fellow Republicans in continuing to support aid for Israel. He argued that the country had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”.

“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” the debate host asked.

“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.

Another hot-button issue during the debate was Trump’s crackdown on immigration.

The Republican leader has pledged to carry out the largest mass deportation effort in US history, and his campaign has spurred human rights concerns.

When asked how they would approach the crackdown, both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed on tempering the militarised nature of the campaign.

In several cities, including Minneapolis, Minnesota, immigration authorities have been accused of racial profiling and using excessive force against immigrants and protesters, as well as violating their rights to due process.

Multiple fatal shootings have occurred during immigration enforcement operations, including the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

Rogers indicated he would not have supported such confrontational operations, but he repeated a Trump claim that the raids were taking dangerous criminals off the streets.

“I think the public efforts in Minnesota were probably not appropriate,” Rogers said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighbourhood for less problems. So that, to me, was something that they could have done differently.”

He later claimed that, under Trump, the country had seen “the largest decrease in murders ever recorded”.

El-Sayed, meanwhile, has previously voiced support for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a key agency in Trump’s deportation campaign. He defended that stance on the debate stage.

“ICE right now is not about immigration enforcement. ICE is about terrorising our streets,” he said.

Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, felt acutely in neighbouring Michigan, was another key topic of conversation.

El-Sayed depicted Rogers as an uncritical backer of Trump and his tariffs and tied him to past free trade deals such as the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which paved the way for companies to shift manufacturing facilities out of the US – though Rogers did not enter Congress until 2001, eight years after NAFTA passed.

“You did that, man. That was your policy. NAFTA, that was your policy,” said El-Sayed.

Rogers sought to distance himself from the current trade war but expressed support for a deal with Canada that would loosen some of Ottawa’s tariffs on US goods.

“I would like to see the deal made,” said Rogers, adding that high Canadian tariffs for US goods “should be eliminated”.

Both candidates tried to strike a balance between criticism of the economic fallout of the trade war and qualifying their support for more selective tariffs, favoured by some industries and labour unions as a means of protecting domestic jobs.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Republican Mike Rogers has accused El-Sayed of being soft on 'terrorism' and had foreign sympathies. Rogers and El-sayed agreed on tempering the militarised nature of the campaign.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Protests, debate follow death of Maricarmen, 87, Spain protest symbol
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Thousands of Spaniards protested outside Spain’s parliament after the death of Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction ignited nationwide protests and sparked a snap general election.

Meanwhile, tributes to Abascal were debated within the legislature as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election.

Maricarmen Abascal died on Wednesday after being hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on a stretcher from her Madrid home on September 23.

While in the hospital, she reached a deal to return to her home but died before she could return. No cause of death has been announced.

“They killed her through heartbreak,” Diana, a demonstrator, told Al Jazeera. “Taking an 87-year-old woman out of her home after she had lived in the same house for 70 years, that is killing someone.”

Diana joined thousands of protesters outside Spain’s parliament.

Outside Abascal’s building, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children’s drawings.

“They’re not deaths; they’re murders,” protesters chanted as they walked from a protest camp in the central Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s former home on Thursday.

Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for November 29 after parliament failed to pass emergency housing measures.

Tributes to Abascal in the Madrid region’s legislature caused arguments as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative opposition People’s Party (PP), accused Sanchez and the Socialists of trying to exploit the housing crisis for political gain ahead of the election.

“We will not allow this attempt to manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people; all of this has happened during their eight years in government. It won’t fly,” Feijoo said.

The PP, which holds absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to observe a minute of silence in her honour. Instead, hard-left deputies staged one outside City Hall and gave Abascal a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms.

Left-leaning parties criticised conservatives for rejecting legislation in parliament aimed at curbing soaring rental prices.

A survey carried out in June and published by state pollster CIS on Thursday found that 76.3 percent of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79 percent believed the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity.

Ombudsman Angel Gabilondo said addressing the housing crisis would require greater commitment from all levels of government.

He said his office was preparing a housing report and reiterated proposals to expand public housing, restrict tourist rentals, increase rent assistance and strengthen protections against evictions for vulnerable households.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Maria del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday after being hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion. Protesters outside Spain's parliament protested outside the Madrid region's parliament. Tributes to Abascal were debated within the legislature as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: UN extends Darfur arms embargo, blocks broader Sudan sanctions proposal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The United Nations Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region by two months but failed to agree on a US proposal to widen it to the whole country, after permanent members Russia and China opposed it.

The 15-member council unanimously adopted Resolution 2830 on Thursday, extending the sanctions regime until December 11 to allow more time for negotiations.

It also extended the mandate of the panel of experts that monitors the measures until January 11, 2027. The UN described the text as a short-term “technical rollover”, after the regime was last renewed for one month on September 11.

The sanctions were first imposed in 2005 under Resolution 1591.

The council set up an arms embargo on armed actors in Darfur, a travel ban and an asset freeze on designated individuals and entities, and a five-member panel of experts to monitor them.

Despite weeks of discussion, the United States failed to secure approval to expand the embargo. Russia and China have argued for keeping the existing regime.

“The current sanctions regime is over 20 years outdated, and is insufficient to address the realities of the war today,” US Ambassador Jeff Bartos told the council last month, urging it to “expand the arms embargo across the entire territory of Sudan”.

Russia’s deputy UN ambassador, Anna Evstigneeva, said at the time: “We will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions by the council on Sudan.”

Sudan’s UN ambassador, Al-Harith Mohamed, argued that a total embargo goes against the UN Charter’s guarantee of the right to self-defence.

The war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has killed at least 59,000 people, though aid groups warn the toll could be far higher.

It has also displaced about 13 million people and pushed parts of the country into famine.

The army holds central and eastern Sudan, while the RSF controls Darfur in the west and parts of the south.

Darfur, a region about the size of Spain, has seen some of the worst violence, with displacement camps attacked and repeated ethnic massacres killing thousands at a time.

It extended the sanctions regime until December 11 to allow more time for negotiations. The UN described the text as a short-term ‘technical rollover’ after the regime was last renewed for one month on September 11.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: USS Lincoln returns to US after long deployment supporting war on Iran
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The United States aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has returned to its home port after a 322-day deployment, including a record 265 consecutive days at sea, during which it helped wage the US-Israel war on Iran.

The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, on Thursday, where members of its crew were greeted by family and friends.

“It feels amazing,” 20-year-old Abel Ramirez told The Associated Press news agency, adding that his parents had driven from Texas to meet him. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.”

The record-setting deployment of the USS Lincoln became a symbol for larger criticisms of the US war effort, which has dragged on since February with no clear end in sight and has strained US military stockpiles.

The prolonged deployment prompted a series of news reports calling attention to deteriorating conditions, food shortages and a series of reported suicide attempts by crew members.

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth praised the sailors on Wednesday in remarks that accused the media of trying to turn the ship into “a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.

President Donald Trump and members of his administration have frequently lashed out at the news media for critical reporting on the war on Iran. Trump himself has called the reporting about the USS Lincoln “fake news”.

“The Lincoln has been out there for a period of time, a good period of time,” he said at an Oval Office meeting on August 17. “I know people on the Lincoln, and they say it’s beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.”

Earlier that month, when confronted with the amount of time the USS Lincoln had spent at sea without a port stop, Trump quipped that its deployment was “not nearly long enough“.

The reports of mental health strain on the USS Lincoln come as public opinion polls show low approval ratings among US voters for the war against Iran.

On Thursday, the Pew Research Center released a poll that found 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the war, compared with 33 percent who approved.

The war has also fuelled concerns about the cost of living ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Since the war began, Iran has hindered commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the trade of fuel, fertiliser and other goods.

Sailors returning home on the USS Lincoln said that they were looking forward to fresh meals and spending time with their families.

Alma Solano Velez said that her husband, one of the US service members on board, shared a list of foods he had been craving over his 10-month deployment: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas, among others.

She added that he had spoken about “the lack of food and showers” and was looking forward to seeing their four-year-old daughter.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Will Ethiopia’s neighbours intervene as Tigray war escalates?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – After nearly two weeks of fierce fighting, Ethiopian federal forces entered the Tigrayan capital of Mekelle as forces from an alliance of rebel groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), withdrew from the city.

The fighting that erupted late last month has effectively ended the 2022 Pretoria ceasefire and the fragile peace that followed the devastating Tigray war.

But Mekelle’s capture may mark the end of conventional warfare rather than the end of the conflict. Fighting has continued elsewhere in Tigray, while reports of Eritrean troops entering northern Tigrayan towns have added a potentially more dangerous regional dimension.

Ethiopian federal forces used air power and ground forces to advance across Tigray. After suffering successive defeats around the towns of Alamata and Kobo, rebel forces withdrew into the surrounding countryside. They have pledged to continue fighting.

“We will confront the enemy on our terms and where we choose,” TPLF leader Debretsion Gebremichael said.

There are echoes of the war that began in 2020, when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government declared victory after federal forces captured Mekelle. Tigrayan forces subsequently regrouped in the mountains, retook much of the region and recaptured the capital, prolonging the war for nearly a year and a half.

The renewed conflict could follow a similar trajectory, particularly if the TPLF and other armed groups succeed in turning the mountainous terrain into a prolonged armed rebellion. Ethiopia is already fighting insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia, raising the prospect of its federal forces being stretched across multiple fronts.

But the battlefield reversals suffered by the rebels could have implications well beyond Tigray. They have raised concern in Egypt and among other Ethiopian rivals, according to Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an African analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute.

“Egypt views the Renaissance Dam, and any Ethiopian [army] move towards the Red Sea, as a strategic threat, so it has allied with Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia against any Ethiopian unilateralism,” Ibrahim told Al Jazeera.

“Ethiopia is seeking a sea outlet; Eritrea sees this as an existential threat.”

Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea won its war of independence in 1991, leaving Addis Ababa heavily dependent on neighbouring countries for access to international trade.

Abiy has increasingly made access to the Red Sea a strategic priority since 2023, raising concerns in Eritrea over Ethiopia’s ambitions, particularly over the port of Assab.

Ethiopia currently relies heavily on Djibouti for maritime trade, while also pursuing alternative arrangements, including through Kenya and Somaliland.

After being sworn in on Monday for another five-year term following his party’s victory in the June 1 election, Abiy again put the issue at the centre of his parliamentary address.

“Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea,” he told parliament.

The issue has increasingly become part of a wider regional contest.

In recent months, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia have found themselves sharing concerns over Ethiopia’s regional ambitions. On October 4, the leaders of the four countries met for a quadrilateral consultative summit in New Alamein, Egypt, where they discussed regional issues and pledged to strengthen political, economic and trade cooperation as well as consultation and coordination.

The meeting does not amount to a formal military alliance, and the four countries have different interests in their dealings with Addis Ababa. The summit’s joint declaration also called for respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, noninterference in internal affairs and the peaceful resolution of disputes.

But their concerns increasingly overlap around Ethiopia’s ambitions in the Red Sea, the Nile and the wider Horn of Africa.

Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have also deteriorated sharply since the Pretoria ceasefire. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats on October 1, accusing Asmara of hostile acts and involvement in the renewed fighting. Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic ties, while denying that it supported the opposition alliance. Egypt and Sudan have also denied Ethiopian accusations that they are backing the alliance.

The Ethiopian army’s advance into Tigray has added another layer to that rivalry.

“The [Ethiopian army’s] advance in Tigray directly threatens [Eritrean President] Isaias [Afwerki] and the Eritrean state,” said Etana H Dinka, an assistant professor of African history at the University of Miami.

Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian troops during the 2020–22 Tigray war, but relations between Abiy and Isaias have since deteriorated. Eritrean troops have reportedly been seen in towns in northern Tigray, adding a potentially significant new dimension to the conflict. The Associated Press news agency reported Eritrean troops entering Adigrat and Idaga Hamus after crossing into Ethiopia, while Eritrea has neither confirmed nor denied the troop movements.

For Eritrea, the location of the fighting matters as much as its outcome.

A prolonged conflict in Tigray could keep Ethiopian forces tied down and limit Addis Ababa’s ability to pursue its Red Sea ambitions. But a decisive Ethiopian victory could leave the federal government with greater freedom to turn its attention towards regional rivals.

“With reports that Eritrean troops are moving into Tigray, Eritrea seems keen on boosting TPLF forces withdrawing northwards, so that the engagement between Ethiopian and Eritrean soldiers takes place in Tigrayan territory, and not in Eritrea,” said Mohamed Kheir Omer, a researcher focused on the Horn of Africa.

That could create an incentive for Eritrea to support forces capable of keeping the Ethiopian army tied down, without necessarily entering a direct confrontation of its own.

Sudan’s war adds another dimension to the regional rivalry.

Egypt has provided political backing and logistical and technical support to Sudan’s army, according to the Reuters news agency, while the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been accused of atrocities in Darfur.

Ethiopia has faced accusations of facilitating support for the RSF. A Reuters investigation reported in February that Ethiopia was hosting a camp in its western Benishangul-Gumuz region where thousands of fighters linked to the RSF were being trained. Reuters cited eight sources, including a senior Ethiopian government official, who said the United Arab Emirates financed the camp’s construction and provided military trainers and logistical support. The UAE denied the allegations, and Reuters said it could not independently verify the UAE’s role.

Those competing relationships are part of a broader contest over the Nile, Sudan, the Red Sea and access to trade routes.

For Egypt, its dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains a major strategic concern. For Eritrea, Ethiopia’s search for a Red Sea outlet is viewed through the lens of national security. For Sudan’s neighbours, the conflict threatens to reshape regional power balances.

The shared interests of Ethiopia’s regional rivals do not necessarily translate into direct intervention.

Egypt has its own calculations over the Nile and Sudan. Eritrea has a direct security interest in developments in Tigray. Somalia is dealing with its own security challenges and a complicated relationship with Addis Ababa. Sudan remains consumed by its devastating civil war.

At the same time, Ethiopia’s federal forces now face the possibility of fighting on several fronts.

The TPLF, Amhara Fano and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) have each sought to challenge the federal government in different parts of the country. If they can maintain pressure on the army while retreating from major population centres, the fall of Mekelle could prove to be only the first phase of a much longer conflict.

For Ethiopia’s rivals, the question is whether to exploit that vulnerability or avoid being drawn into another regional war.

The extent of any regional involvement may ultimately depend on whether the TPLF can keep federal forces tied down in Tigray, and away from the Eritrean border.

“It isn’t difficult to understand Cairo’s commitment to prevent Ethiopia from succeeding in the current warfare, whatever its army’s intended goals, including Abiy’s acclaimed access to the Red Sea, are,” University of Miami’s Dinka said.

The question now is whether those regional calculations will remain largely diplomatic or spill into the battlefield.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Ethiopian forces enter Tigrayan capital of Mekelle as forces withdraw from city. Fighting has continued elsewhere in Tigray, while reports of Eritrean troops entering northern Tigrayans have added a potentially more dangerous regional dimension. Egypt has provided political backing and logistical and technical support to Sudan's army.

OpenAI says it disrupted an Iran-origin influence operation that used fake journalist identities to place articles about the US-Iran conflict in online publications around the world.

The company said the network, which it dubbed “Bogus Bylines”, used seven fake personas to pitch long-form articles to small and medium-sized outlets focused on international affairs, geopolitics and the Middle East. OpenAI said it identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under those names across roughly a dozen outlets.

According to OpenAI, the operators used ChatGPT to refine articles and pitches, generate social media comments and prepare internal reports. The accounts originated in Iran and used VPNs to obscure their location.

The company said most of the articles and comments focused on the US-Iran war, while some social media activity dealt with US politics. The operation also generated comments designed to portray the US as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally and Iran as a resilient victim.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8.title: Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8.text:
Preliminary laboratory results from a Kenyan patient who was suspected of contracting the Ebola virus have come back negative.

Fears of a second case of Ebola in the East African country were allayed on Thursday after the governor of Wajir County, where the patient is being treated, revealed the test results.

“I am pleased to report that the preliminary laboratory results indicate that the sample is NEGATIVE for Ebola Virus Disease,” the Wajir county governor said in a statement.

The suspected patient is a 20-year-old man with a travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda to Kenya.

The other Kenyan patient who tested positive for the virus and subsequently died had travelled the same route.

Kenya had reported its first-ever Ebola case on Tuesday after a citizen who became sick in the DRC died in Nairobi.

The deadly strain of the Ebola virus has spread widely, starting in the DRC earlier this year. The DRC officially declared an outbreak in May.

Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record. The ongoing outbreak in the eastern DRC has killed at least 4,205 people out of more than 8,700 reported cases.

The outbreak spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July.

The strain behind the latest spread has been dubbed the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), believed to have spread from animals to humans through a new transmission route. No vaccine currently exists for Bundibugyo.

The first case in Kenya drew scrutiny over the status of the virus in neighbouring Uganda and exposed lapses in Kenya’s border screening systems. The patient who died was able to pass through multiple airport temperature checks.

The World Health Organization (WHO) is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and strengthen checks for travellers entering the country.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8.title: Hegseth says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be ‘public’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8.author: Evan Semones
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8.text:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the execution of a former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in Texas will be publicly available to watch.

In an interview with the media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Hegseth was asked about President Donald Trump’s recent order to use a firing squad to execute Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of the 2009 shooting.

The secretary said he approved of the decision, calling it a “no-brainer”.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth told interviewer Jack Posobiec. “Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Hegseth added that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (19:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place.

Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for the shooting.

The former Army major walked into an army processing centre on the Texas base, shouted “Allahu akbar” (God is greatest) and opened fire on fellow military members waiting to get medical attention.

Hasan’s execution required approval from Hegseth and Trump, who authorised the use of the firing squad on Monday.

An official with the Defense Department told Al Jazeera that Hasan’s execution would be “livestreamed”, adding that more details would come soon.

It is not clear from Hegseth’s remarks whether troops, spectators or US military officials would be present in person for the execution. US Army regulation states that at least two media outlets should be selected as witnesses.

No state or federal execution has ever been televised in the US. The last public execution in the country took place more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky, on August 14, 1936.

The last time a US military execution was conducted by firing squad was in 1945, for desertion during World War II.

When asked to comment on Hegseth’s remarks – and whether Trump would view the execution – the White House referred Al Jazeera to the Pentagon.

The Trump administration announced it would add death by firing squad as an acceptable method for federal executions in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.
