https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Man City charges: Mourinho jokes Premier League case will outlast him
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.author: Kevin Hand
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho joked that he may not live to see the end of Manchester City’s legal battle with the Premier League after the club appealed against a ruling that found it guilty of serious financial rule breaches.

An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, as well as three of four charges relating to failures to cooperate with the investigation. City have denied wrongdoing and lodged an appeal.

The Premier League said that City used “sham” commercial agreements to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.19bn) over nearly a decade, resulting in inaccurate financial reporting and breaches of spending rules.

Mourinho managed Manchester United from 2016 to 2018 and led them to a second-placed Premier League finish behind Pep Guardiola’s City in 2017-18.

“I would rather laugh about it,” Mourinho said when asked about the case in an interview with Italy’s Corriere dello Sport.

“I think we will eventually get an ending, but we are both in our 60s, and we’ll need to be lucky enough to still be around when the final verdict arrives.

“There will be a verdict, then appeals, then more appeals.”

Mourinho has long maintained that one of his greatest achievements in football management was finishing second behind Guardiola’s side, given their spending power at the time.

The Portuguese manager, now 63, said in 2024 that he had not given up on being awarded a winner’s medal for the 2018 season.

“I think we still have a chance to win that league because maybe they punish Man City with points and maybe we win that league,” he quipped at a press conference ahead of a Europa League match against United with his then-club, Fenerbahce.

“Then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal.”

The appeal process will be conducted in private, and it remains unclear whether any sanctions would be imposed before it is heard, or whether any punishment would take effect immediately.

City, seeking a sixth successive league win, are top of the Premier League with 15 points from five matches and travel to Liverpool on Sunday.

Holders Arsenal entertain Leeds on Saturday, while United host Tottenham later the same day.

Mourinho’s Real Madrid trail fierce rivals and La Liga leaders Barcelona by six points, with five wins and two defeats from their seven league matches this season.

Both Barca and Real are in action on Saturday, with Getafe and Villarreal visiting, respectively.

https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/sp.title: SpaceX calls for better coordination in orbit after near-misses with Starlink
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/sp.author: Stephen Clark
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/sp.text:
“These led to conjunctions of tens of meters to hundreds of meters. Way too close to comfort.”

Space has plenty of room for more megaconstellations, but only if all operators are willing to share information about where their satellites are and where they’re going, a top executive at SpaceX and its AI subsidiary said this week.

Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s vice president for Starlink and president of Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, used a presentation Tuesday at the International Astronautical Congress in Turkey as a clarion call for improved data-sharing among satellite operators.

SpaceX’s Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites, about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit. Radars and telescopes routinely track thousands more pieces of space junk.

Starlink is, by far, the largest satellite constellation in operation today. But if you buy the buzz, Starlink is just the tip of the iceberg. SpaceX has revealed plans to launch up to a million satellites for a new constellation, called Starmind, to deploy AI computing capacity in low-Earth orbit. Amazon is in the early stages of launching a network of thousands of satellites to compete with Starlink, and two Chinese megaconstellations are now in full-scale deployment.

All of this raises the question of how to mitigate the risk of a collision in orbit, an event that could create thousands more pieces of space junk, potentially triggering a self-perpetuating cycle of debris generation. The risk of a collision on any given day is fantastically low. Space is vast and empty, and low-Earth orbit is a long way from filling up. SpaceX and most other Western operators de-orbit their rockets and satellites at the end of their missions to prevent additional debris in orbit.

“That said, the law of large numbers says that if it can happen, it will happen,” Nicolls said.

There’s still a long way to go to improve tracking, awareness, and coordination in orbit. This is sometimes called space traffic management. No global treaties or regulations require satellites to broadcast their locations and maneuvers or mandate coordination among satellite operators. Without rules of the road, it is up to governments and companies to set norms of behavior.

“Once you can track this debris, and if you can track it well, these are like obstacles on a road. If you can measure them, you can predict where they’re going to be, and you can avoid them,” Nicolls said. “What you can’t avoid is other operators who maneuver without telling you where they’re going to go. We have many examples of this on Starlink, unfortunately.”

Nicolls presented several examples of satellites from other operators closely approaching Starlink satellites as they zip around the Earth at 5 miles per second. The examples did not suggest nefarious intent, such as spying or an attempt at striking a Starlink in orbit. Instead, the other satellites conducted maneuvers and changed their trajectories without their owners informing anyone.

“Either they were not publishing their ephemeris to us, or they were not considering the ephemeris of others when they were maneuvering, and these led to conjunctions of tens of meters to hundreds of meters,” Nicolls said. “Way too close to comfort.”

An ephemeris contains information about a satellite’s location and movement. Some operators may not want to share this information, believing secrecy might provide a competitive or strategic advantage. But if spaceflight is to be sustainable, it is vital to err on the side of openness rather than secrecy.

“The minimum standard in low-Earth orbit needs to be that you know where your satellite is, and you know where it’s going. You need to be able to predict where your trajectory is, and that prediction needs to be reliable,” Nicolls said.

SpaceX lauds itself as the benchmark for orbital stewardship. It pretty much has to be, with so many Starlinks in orbit and so much of its business relying on space.

The company has lowered the altitude of the entire active Starlink constellation below 500 kilometers (310 miles), an adjustment that provides three benefits. It moved the network away from other heavily trafficked regions in low-Earth orbit, expedited reentry for any failed Starlink satellites, and improved service for Starlink customers. All of SpaceX’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which began launching on the company’s Starship rocket last month, will fly even lower, at about 350 kilometers (217 miles).

SpaceX also publishes ephemeris data for its Starlink satellites and has asked other operators to share their data, too. Without ephemeris sharing, operators rely on tracking data or their own satellites’ collision avoidance capabilities.

Starlink satellites, for example, use onboard navigation cameras to detect other objects in orbit. SpaceX calls the system Stargaze, and it now tracks about 90 percent of maneuvering satellites that intersect Starlink orbits, Nicolls said.

That is good, but it would be better if all operators agreed to be more open about what their satellites are doing. It is now a “fairly common occurrence” that Starlink satellites detect an upcoming close encounter and autonomously maneuver out of the way, Nicolls said. If there’s not enough to steer away from a close encounter, Starlink satellites can hunker down at the time of greatest danger. These “ducking maneuvers” involve pointing the satellite to minimize the chance of a collision, Nicolls said.

Starlink satellites perform about 1,000 collision avoidance maneuvers per day to get out of the way of functioning satellites or bits of space debris. In the last few months, Nicolls said Starlink satellites have steered clear of about 650 active satellites from other operators. Only half of those 650 come from operators that participate in ephemeris sharing with SpaceX, he said.

“In particular, it’s been very challenging to share data with international operators,” Nicolls said. “There has been good progress here. There have been some good stories here on how we’ve begun to share data. For example, we share data closely with the Chinese space station as well as some other Chinese satellite operators, but there are many that we do not, and we have no information about where those satellites are or where they’re going.”

A chart in Nicolls’ presentation suggested the problem largely lies with Chinese and Russian satellites. But some in the United States, Europe, and Japan also decline to share.

“My fundamental ask here is that we need to make headway here and begin sharing data across all vehicles, from whatever country you are, with us and with others, to promote a safe operating environment,” Nicolls said.

What do SpaceX’s competitors think? Ars asked the head of Amazon Leo, Rajeev Badyal, about coordinating with Starlink, his chief competitor in the satellite broadband market. Amazon has 396 satellites in orbit today, with hundreds more awaiting launch when their rockets are ready to take them to orbit.

“Space safety is paramount to us as well,” Badyal said. “Every launch we do, we actually coordinate with SpaceX. We coordinate with others who have satellites. We let them know where we’re going to drop them off, how we’re going to orbit raise, etc. So we have regular meetings with companies like SpaceX to exchange data.

“So, for us, sharing ephemeris or sharing the information necessary for space safety is a non-issue,” Badyal said. “We’re big proponents of making sure that all of us operate in this domain in space in a coordinated fashion because [the] consequences of not doing so are significant for everybody, and there’s no reason not to.”

Amazon Leo’s first-generation constellation will consist of 3,232 satellites, and the Federal Communications Commission in February approved Amazon’s request for a 4,504-satellite second-generation network. Amazon has filed for FCC approval for an additional 5,105 satellites for direct-to-device connectivity, but the company is still far from matching the size of the Starlink fleet.

“Obviously, SpaceX is the largest constellation out there,” Badyal said. “We work with them hand in hand. In terms of China and adversaries, that’s something I can’t comment on at the moment. At some point, we will have to coordinate, or it’ll end up being a negative thing for everybody, especially if they get to scale.”
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/sp.summary: SpaceX's Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites. The risk of a collision on any given day is fantastically low, says Michael Nicolls.

https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.title: Judge weighs if Trump can charge $100K for early access to Truth Social posts
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.author: Ashley Belanger
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.text:
Judge questioned if Trump delaying access to Truth Social posts by a second harms the press.

Likely in the next few weeks, a federal judge will decide if Donald Trump can become the first president to personally profit from selling early access to government information in his social media posts.

At a hearing Wednesday, Department of Justice civil attorney Brantley Mayers argued that there was no conflict whatsoever with Trump charging up to $100,000 monthly for instant API access to Truth Social posts that often break news from his administration.

Trump is the largest stakeholder and majority owner of Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company that owns Truth Social, and the value of the API access comes largely from Trump’s role as president.

News groups suing have argued that Trump’s exorbitant API fees violate the First Amendment and the Presidential Records Act by creating tiers of access to government information in social media posts that Trump doesn’t technically own. Additionally, Trump’s exorbitant API fees undermine the Fifth Amendment. That prohibits the government from “charging unreasonable sums that cannot be justified to offset the cost of the government benefit, and granting preferential access to crucial government information for arbitrary and irrational reasons,” news groups argued.

However, Mayers likened Trump’s Truth Social posts—which have announced military strikes, ceasefires, tariffs, immigration policies, and major changes in his administration—to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s evening radio addresses known as “fireside chats,” Courthouse News reported. His personal feed acts as an unvarnished public service, not a greedy profit grab, the DOJ argued.

It’s clear, though, that Trump could potentially make $1.2 million per subscriber annually by selling government information that is not Trump’s property. Before Mayers could proceed, US District Judge Paul Oetken “cut him off,” Courthouse News reported.

“Well, President Roosevelt didn’t charge money for his fireside chats, did he?” Oetken asked.

Responding, Mayers suggested that although Roosevelt didn’t charge for his broadcasts, there were similar “barriers to entry” keeping every American from tuning in. Just as some news groups today can’t afford to pay $60,000 to $100,000 for Truth’s API, some Americans in the ‘30s and ‘40s couldn’t afford radios, he argued.

Nikhel Sus, chief counsel for a group representing news plaintiffs called the Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), told Ars that the judge was right to push back on the DOJ’s comparison. During the hearing, the judge acknowledged that the Truth API could be discriminatory by creating “two classes of people,” Courthouse News reported. Sue said that he also clearly recognized the “symbiotic relationship” between Trump and Truth Social.

Criticizing the comparison to FDR’s fireside chats, Sus told Ars that the DOJ “can throw out these hypotheticals that have absolutely nothing to do with this situation until the cows come home, but they’re not persuasive.”

At the hearing, Oetken asked “tough questions” of both sides, Sus told Ars. No elected official has ever owned a media company where they can profit off presidential announcements, and the judge took time to remark that “there hasn’t really been anything like this case.”

Talking to Ars, Sus argued that the lack of precedent should trigger alarm bells, not excuse the conduct, as the DOJ has suggested. “Just because no prior president had the gall to try to do something so flagrantly corrupt and illegal doesn’t mean that it is legal,” he said.

Initially, Oetken approached claims that the API scheme violated the First Amendment with skepticism, Courthouse News reported. At one point, he wondered if Trump delaying the general public’s access to information by potentially as little as a fraction of a second would meaningfully harm the free press. Although it’s easy to see how an algorithmic trader would benefit from getting information just a little bit sooner, “It’s a negligible delay to a human being,” Oetken suggested.

But the conflict isn’t only about timing, nonprofit news organizations have argued. TMTG has confirmed that large news groups are already in talks to buy API access because there is immense value in the service that goes beyond getting instant access to Truth Social posts. For example, the API “provides a machine-readable feed and a historic archive of all of President Trump’s Truth Social posts,” Sus told Ars. With that access, even if Trump deletes posts—which he frequently does—any news group can maintain a more reliable log of all posts.

“It is absolutely worth something,” Sus told Ars. “And it’s not just the algorithmic traders. News outlets use APIs too.”

The judge sees the case as complex and did not rule from the bench, instead promising a written ruling on whether to enjoin Trump from selling API access while he’s in office at a later date. Sus told Ars that courts typically treat requests for preliminary injunctions urgently and that he expects a decision in the next few weeks.

Until then, news groups remain optimistic that the court’s ruling will swing their way, Sus said.

“All we’re asking for is that when the president chooses to make government information available to the public, he has to do so on equal terms,” Sus said. “He cannot discriminate based on who’s willing to pay the president’s personal company hundreds of thousands of dollars. That is obscenely corrupt and unconstitutional.”

Defending Trump’s scheme, Mayers asked the judge to look at Trump’s interests as wholly separate from the media group that bears his name. He claimed Trump had nothing to do with the decision to charge for API access to his posts, branding them as a “completely private commercial decision” made exclusively by TMTG.

Nonprofit news groups suing, however, have argued that the expensive API pricing is “corrupt,” ignoring America’s long history of providing equal access to presidential records. On Wednesday, David Schulz, an attorney representing The Intercept, argued that the scheme gives a “direct advantage” to newsrooms that can pay the high price for previously free access.

“Trump Media specifically is courting the largest news organizations in the country to get them to subscribe to Truth API,” Sus told Ars.

If Trump’s gamble pays off and the judge approves the API sales, Sus warned that the press would suffer, as more politicians could follow his lead and access to even more government information would be delayed behind paywalls.

“If the president is allowed to do this, it sets a very dangerous precedent for enabling public officials to profit off of their office and specifically profit off of government information,” Sus told Ars.
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.summary: Donald Trump is the largest stakeholder and majority owner of Trump Media & Technology Group. The DOJ says Trump's exorbitant API fees violate the First Amendment and the Presidential Records Act.

https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.title: Trump Mobile hack and apparent lack of FCC authorization raise security alarms
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.author: Jon Brodkin
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.text:
After hack and data breach, senator asks why Trump Mobile lacks some FCC filings.

Trump Mobile apparently failed to obtain necessary authorizations to operate the international calling portion of its phone service, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) wrote in a letter to the company today.

Her letter said Trump Mobile also doesn’t appear to have submitted a required plan for fighting robocalls. Trump Mobile’s key business partner, Liberty Mobile Wireless, did make a robocall database filing, but it was not complete, Hassan said.

Hassan’s letter raised questions about Trump Mobile’s security related to a report that hackers stole personal data of 3,615 customers and Trump Mobile’s previous confirmation that a vendor it uses exposed customers’ personal data on the Internet. Hassan alleged that Trump Mobile failed to follow multiple FCC filing rules that are supposed to help ensure the security of mobile services.

“The apparent absence of authorization for Trump Mobile international services raises questions about who is providing or reselling the international telecommunications services advertised by Trump Mobile, the authority under which those services are being provided, and the company’s commitment to complying with requirements designed to safeguard national security,” Hassan told Trump Mobile CEO Patrick O’Brien.

Referring to the recent data breach, Hassan said it’s worrisome that a ransomware group “claimed that when it notified Trump Mobile of the breach, the company responded that ‘[w]e have no team to handle this.’” Trump Mobile also seems to lack a robust customer authentication process and offers “streamlined service activation that can make it easier for scammers to obtain US numbers,” Hassan wrote.

Trump Mobile, which has a trademark and name licensing deal with the Trump family, advertises that its customers can call more than 230 countries and territories. “Yet a search of the FCC’s International Communications Filing System suggests that Trump Mobile does not hold the necessary authorization for these services under Section 214 of the Communications Act of 1934,” wrote Hassan, the top Democrat on the US Congress Joint Economic Committee.

Hassan said the authorization process requires disclosure of foreign ownership so the FCC can assess potential national security risks. These FCC filings are required both for carriers that operate their own networks and Mobile Virtual Network Operators (MVNOs) like Trump Mobile, which resell other carriers’ mobile service, Hassan’s letter said.

Hassan’s letter cited a 2012 ruling against a different carrier, in which the FCC said “international telecommunications carriers that fail to obtain Section 214 authority may endanger important public interest considerations involving national security, law enforcement, foreign policy and trade policy.” She also cited the 2021 revocation of China Telecom Americas’ authorization, in which the FCC said that a carrier controlled by a foreign government could be used to “access, monitor, store, disrupt and/or misroute US communications” for the purpose of espionage.

Hassan asked questions about Trump Mobile’s ties to Liberty Mobile Wireless, an MVNO based in Florida. Trump Mobile officials told The Verge in February that Liberty Mobile is the “enabler” and “backbone” of Trump Mobile, and that Liberty Mobile handles much of Trump Mobile’s technical, legal, and financial operations.

Trump Mobile officials’ statements to The Verge indicated that Trump Mobile and Liberty Mobile are run by the same people. Hassan’s letter asked whether Trump Mobile owns, operates, or controls Liberty Mobile.

Trump Mobile emerged last year, claiming it would sell a phone made entirely in the US. Trump Mobile quickly abandoned that claim but couldn’t deliver the promised phone on time. Preorders shipped nearly a year late, and the phone’s price increased from $499 to $749. Hassan’s letter noted that the phone itself is reportedly “a near exact match for the HTC U24 Pro, a phone launched in 2024 and manufactured in China.”

Hassan said she found evidence that Trump Mobile and Liberty Mobile both failed to submit required information about efforts to verify customer identities. Hassan wrote:

Concerningly, Trump Mobile and Liberty Mobile also seem to have weak scam prevention efforts. They do not appear to have included “a description of their ‘know-your-customer’ [KYC] processes in their robocall mitigation plan,” which is required in annual Robocall Mitigation Database (RMD) filings. Liberty Mobile’s most recent filing does not appear to include KYC information, and a search for Trump Mobile and T1 Mobile LLC, its operational business name, in the database yielded no filings under those names.

Failure to comply with RMD rules can be punished with fines, removal from the database, and an order requiring other phone companies to block the offending carrier’s phone traffic. Hassan quoted an FCC enforcement advisory issued in February of this year, which she said “made it clear that compliance by MVNOs like Trump Mobile and Liberty Mobile is especially important because ‘[r]esellers of voice service that serve end-users are often in the best position to identify customers that are the source of apparently illegal traffic.’”

Hassan’s letter asked O’Brien a series of questions related to the data breach, Trump Mobile’s ownership structure, its relationship with Liberty Mobile and other carriers, its systems for subscriber verification, compliance with various legal obligations, its FCC filings, device sales, and which countries supply parts for Trump phones. She requested a response by October 29.

We contacted Trump Mobile, Liberty Mobile, and the FCC today and will update this article if we receive any comments.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has proposed stricter Know-Your-Customer rules, but that doesn’t necessarily mean he would be quick to investigate Trump Mobile. Carr is an enthusiastic Trump supporter and backs Trump’s claim of power over historically independent agencies like the FCC. Carr recently refused calls to take action on a complaint that Trump commercials violate laws against using taxpayer funds for propaganda.

https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/10/fed.title: Feds get ready to rewrite car headlight rules
https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/10/fed.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
https://arstechnica.com/cars/2026/10/fed.text:
Reducing glare and allowing modern light technologies will be two goals.

One of the regulations that make vehicles in the US different from those in Europe or Japan is our headlight rules. They’re laid out in the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), and changing them is—or used to be—a lengthy, laborious process, which is a major reason automotive lighting technology has lagged in the US. But the current administration says it’s time for “bolstering driver safety, slashing red tape, and embracing new technologies,” so it’s going to start a negotiated rulemaking process to rewrite the regulations to suit 2026.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Jonathan Morrison said. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”

While it is fair to be skeptical of the government’s efforts to streamline bureaucracy, it is also fair to say US headlight regulations really could use an update.

When Ars started covering cars, automakers like Audi, BMW, Mercedes, Toyota, and Volvo were trying to import adaptive headlight technology. At the time, the FMVSS only allowed for “dumb” high- and low-beams, nothing else. Meanwhile, lighting technology evolved, adopting first lasers and then LEDs with addressable pixels that can block out those that would otherwise illuminate oncoming cars.

In 2013, in response to Toyota’s petition, NHTSA said it would start the rulemaking process. It took another five years before a rule was published for consideration; in the interim, the NHTSA was considering adopting Europe’s rules before deciding that if a car with adaptive beam lights “does not have a long preview of another vehicle, such as in an intersection scenario or when two vehicles are oncoming on a curved road, ADB does not have enough time to react to adapt its beam pattern.”

One key difference is how vehicles are regulated. In Europe, cars are homologated for type approval; manufacturers submit examples to authorities for testing to ensure they conform to the rules, and then the authorities approve the car for sale. In the US, OEMs tell NHTSA their cars comply with the FMVSS, or face sanctions if that turns out to be false later. At the time, NHTSA felt that Europe’s glare tests were too subjective for a self-certification regime and decided instead to write its own.

In 2022, that final rule was ready. Since then, cars with active beam matrix LED headlights have gone on sale in the US; Audi’s big new SUVs are a good example, although they are limited in functionality compared with the same technology fitted to European-spec cars.

Among NHTSA’s goals for an updated FMVSS 108 are harmonizing US standards with their global counterparts, updating the rules for technologies like LEDs, ambient light sensors, automatic high beams, and replaceable light sources, improving test procedures for lenses and optics, understanding how to better aim headlights, and making sure that none of this blinds anyone else on the road with glare.

Join a subscriber-only conversation with one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35.

Available only for MIT Technology Review subscribers.

Friday, October 16, 2026

Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. Join senior AI reporter James O'Donnell as he interviews King about his work, being named one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35 and new ways of seeing biology.

Going live on October 16th at 18:30 BST / 1:30pm EDT / 10:30am PDT

Speakers: James O'Donnell, AI Reporter, and Samuel King, Bioengineering PhD Candidate, Stanford University/Arc Institute

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems.

Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

Meet the new kids nipping at the heels of the AI giants.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/07/college-s.author: Chris Park
https://fortune.com/2026/10/07/college-s.text:
Last fall, I stood at the center of what would have been one of the biggest deals in sports: a $2.4 billion public pension fund investment in the Big Ten Conference. In the end, it failed. Congress fired off letters, and trustees balked. The deal was an attempt to provide schools with the capital to compete like professionals; its collapse was one data point in a season of upheaval. That same fall, Lane Kiffin walked out on an 11-1 Ole Miss team weeks before its first playoff game, lured to LSU by a war chest the Rebels couldn’t match.

A month into the new season, last winter’s transfer portal jumpers are starring in new colors, Coach Kiffin’s latest exploits have put LSU at odds with its own league, and administrators are chasing lawsuits, lifelines, and someone to blame. Everyone agrees the sport is in crisis. Most are wrong about why. The turmoil doesn’t stem from a shortage of money or rules. It stems from the fact that universities haven’t learned how to run their most valuable franchises.

If the histrionics coming out of Washington are any indication, the discord won’t abate soon. The Protect College Sports Act, from Sens. Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell, has cleared the Senate and now awaits consideration in the House. Mr. Cruz says the PCSA, the latest of a half-dozen other college sports fixes Congress floated in the past year, is  “the last train leaving the station.” House Majority Leader Steve Scalise says the bill “need[s] to be fixed,” a task the House likely won’t get to until after the midterms.

Whatever and whenever Washington decides, the courts have already established that athletics departments have to pay near top dollar for top talent. Student athletes now earn more than $2 billion a year in revenue sharing and marketing deals. Top college football coaches command NFL-caliber salaries; fired head coaches alone have collected over $1 billion in severance since 2015. These sums fuel a wilder free agency than any pro league would tolerate: one in five football players transfers each year, and the most brazen riders of the coaching carousel swap schools midseason.

The Cruz-Cantwell bill would tighten restrictions on athlete pay and transfers, bar in-season coach poaching, and dangle antitrust exemptions before Power Conference schools willing to pool media rights with smaller colleagues. None of it would alter the sport’s long-term cost structure. College football is the nation’s second most valuable sports media property. The market for players (and coaches) will inevitably settle closer to NFL and NBA rates than schools pay today.

University leaders sprinting to Capitol Hill should heed the warning of McDonald’s founder Ray Kroc, who famously eschewed government intervention: if we have to bring in “government to beat our competition, then we deserve to go broke.” The truth is that college athletics is now subject to genuine market forces, but schools have barely begun the sorts of investments that will be required to adapt, let alone win.

What might those investments look like? Ask the pros. 25 years ago, Billy Beane’s Oakland A’s proved that an innovative franchise outgunned on payroll in a hidebound industry could out-maneuver its competition; “Moneyball” is now standard operating procedure across pro sports. The strongest NFL organizations invest relentlessly in the competitive infrastructure that players and coaches don’t control: player development, capital allocation, data analytics, and sports science that buoy an organization even as its talent comes and goes.

College programs neglect that groundwork, and it shows. The Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks employ nearly three times as many non-uniform football operations personnel as the College Football Playoff champion Indiana Hoosiers. After a last-second win over the Colts last season, coach Mike MacDonald awarded a game ball not to a player but to Brian Eayrs, the team’s Director of Football Analysis and Special Situations, whose timeout strategy preserved the clock for Seattle’s winning drive. (Microsoft now features Eayrs in its national ad campaign for Copilot.) Even the best college programs subscribe to a nonproprietary printed manual for in-game strategy — and coaches are praised for using it at all.

The most storied coaches in college sports were institution builders whose regional, relationship-driven networks of high school coaches functioned as proprietary talent pipelines decades before teams used spreadsheets. As recruiting migrates from Friday Night Lights to the transfer portal, that old infrastructure has crumbled. No one in higher education has built its modern replacement.

The pros have. The Oklahoma City Thunder employ the NBA’s largest operations staff from the league’s third-smallest market, and woo talent with distinctive offerings like concierge health care for players’ families. Major athletics departments instead spend toward sameness, waging arms races to build lookalike weight rooms.

Modernizing raises two harder questions.

First, who is leading our schools? NFL general managers have the owner’s ear; university presidential tenure has declined for two decades. As power migrates from the head coach’s office, universities must relocate it —to the president, elsewhere in the athletics department, or the board.

Second, what is the point of a college education? As public trust collapses and Washington moves to fund the individual scientist over legacy institutions, universities would be wise not to assume that exceptional students need them—whether they wear lab coats or shoulder pads.

The moment this season ends, the multi-billion-dollar college bidding war will resume. NIL payments for promising players will rise; so will severance checks for failed coaches. Most universities will keep chasing the quick fixes in hiring and firing that Colorado coach Deion Sanders likened to Brazilian butt lifts. With or without Congress, the fix isn’t more politics. It’s college leaders who start competing and investing, like the pro owners who do this for a living.

The bill would tighten restrictions on athlete pay and transfers, bar in-season coach poaching, and dangle antitrust exemptions. The market for players and coaches will inevitably settle closer to NFL and NBA rates than schools pay today.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/nvidia-a.title: Nvidia-backed Aussie AI firm Firmus withdraws historic IPO, citing market volatility
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/nvidia-a.author: Jenny Lee
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/nvidia-a.text:
The company said the proposed offering terms did not adequately reflect its business strength and long-term growth outlook, and it will instead pursue private funding options.

Firmus had reportedly sought to raise $5 billion through the IPO, which would have valued the company at about $30.6 billion, nearly triple its valuation in August.

Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia
, has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.

Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.

“The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders,” Firmus said in a statement. “Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” it added.

Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which would have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia’s history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion.

In August, the company announced a $2 billion funding round backed by Nvidia, Coatue Management, Blackstone and Jane Street, bringing its total equity raised over the preceding year to more than $3 billion and its valuation to over $10.5 billion.

Firmus also announced agreements with Meta last month to provide GPU computing capacity at its AI data centers in Southeast Asia, built on Nvidia’s DSX platform, to support Meta’s AI research, model development and training.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/taiwan-t.title: U.S. East Asian envoy says investors are overpricing Taiwan conflict risk
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/taiwan-t.author: Anniek Bao
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/taiwan-t.text:
Investors are overestimating the risk of conflict across the Taiwan Strait, according to Michael DeSombre, U.S. assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs.

Beijing has sought to increasingly solidify its military presence near the island, with reports revealing an unprecedented sighting of a military vessel off the coast.

SINGAPORE – Investors are overestimating the risk of conflict across the Taiwan Strait, a top U.S. East Asian diplomat said, stressing that deterrence and “substantial consequences” would keep Beijing from taking the island by 2027.

While the U.S. government has often indicated Beijing’s directive for the People’s Liberation Army to be ready for military action in Taiwan by 2027, Beijing has never publicly confirmed the timeline.

“I actually think the most mispricing is with regard to Taiwan, where actually I think people are overpricing the risk of something happening across the Taiwan Strait,” said Michael DeSombre, assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told CNBC on Thursday.

“Both China and the U.S. don’t want conflict, and we’re able to deter conflict,” he told CNBC’s Sri Jegarajah in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Milken Institute Asia Summit. “Concerns of that perhaps are priced at too high a level.”

Beijing claims Taiwan as its territory and hasn’t ruled out force to bring it under its control. The democratically governed island’s government rejects Beijing’s claims.

China has also sought to push Washington for a change in its longstanding diplomatic stance on the island to formally “oppose” Taiwan independence. However, the summit last month between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping did not yield any public agreement on Taiwan.

The U.S. President has held back approval of a new package of arms sales to Taipei worth $14 billion after an earlier package of $11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan had drawn a sharp response from Beijing in December.

Days after the leaders’ summit, Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Arizona for the opening ​of a new de facto consulate in ‌Phoenix.

Beijing has sought to increasingly solidify its military presence near the island in recent months. A Chinese military boat was spotted along with two vessels off Taiwan’s Pacific coast for the first time in August, Reuters reported, citing a surveillance report. It has also been courting Taiwan’s opposition party, the Kuomintang, since last year to pull the island into its orbit as it prepares for the presidential election in 2028.

Asked whether plans to “reunify Taiwan” by 2027 were a cause for concern, DeSombre said that Xi is “a very rational actor ... To the extent that he realizes that it can’t be done, or it can’t be done without substantial consequences, it won’t happen.”

DeSombre played up the importance of keeping deterrence credible. “That’s why it’s important … ensuring that we have the deterrence in place with our allies and partners to make sure it does not happen.”

Taiwan is the world’s leading ​manufacturer of cutting-edge computer chips and TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, has invested tens of billions of dollars in facilities in Phoenix. The projects have received ​significant U.S. subsidies as Washington seeks to revive domestic semiconductor manufacturing.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro wins third-place candidate’s support against Lula
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
Right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Thursday gained the support of Augusto Cury, the third-place candidate in Brazil's presidential election, bolstering his chances against incumbent leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

"My support is not a blank check," Cury said in a statement, after winning nearly three percent of the vote in Sunday's first round of voting, compared to Bolsonaro's 47 percent and Lula's 45 percent.

Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest for plotting a coup after losing Brazil's last election in 2022.

Prior to the announcement, the younger Bolsonaro was leading in polls on Thursday, which gave the senator 52 percent compared to Lula's 48 percent, according to the Datafolha institute.

READ MORE
Thousands protest Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, fearing far-right return

Lula, 81, downplayed the polls as he sought to secure a fourth term.

"I don't assess polls, I don't work like that. I work knowing that I need to have more votes than Flavio to win the election. I have 17 days to do that," he said at a press conference Thursday.

While Bolsonaro is hoping to bank on his allegiances in the final stretch of the campaign, Lula has been strengthening his presence on social media, where the right has an upper hand.

Thousands of people demonstrated on Thursday in Sao Paulo and other cities against the return of the far right to power in Brazil, a day after a similar march in Rio de Janeiro.

Renan Santos, the fourth most popular candidate with 2.6 million votes, has refused to support either leading candidate.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.author: Will Hunter
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Healthcare Facilities

Ginny Chalmer was diagnosed with a chronic lung condition earlier this year. (Facebook: Ginny Chalmer)

An Adelaide woman says she spent four hours on the floor of the Noarlunga Hospital when seeking treatment for a chronic lung condition.

Ginny Chalmer, 71, attended the hospital by ambulance on Wednesday.

SA Health has apologised to Ms Chalmer and says it will conduct a review of the matter.

A woman has detailed how she spent four hours on the "cold floor" of an Adelaide public hospital while seeking treatment for a lung condition, calling her experience "totally wrong".

Ginny Chalmer, 71, lives with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a condition which causes shortness of breath and impacts her oxygen levels.

The former nurse of 10 years was diagnosed earlier this year and attended a doctor on Wednesday, when her symptoms worsened after catching a virus.

She was advised her oxygen levels were low and was sent in an ambulance to Noarlunga Hospital for further treatment.

Ginny Chalmer says she does not want others to have the same experience she did at Noarlunga Hospital. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Ms Chalmer said when she arrived, she was placed in a wheelchair and taken to a waiting room where a paramedic deemed her "fit to sit" despite telling staff she thought she was not.

She said she "felt so unwell" while sitting that she made the choice to lay down on the floor.

"I said, 'no, I need to stay lying down, could you get me a blanket so I could lie on it?' and so they got me a blanket."

Ms Chalmer said she was quickly seen by a "lovely doctor" who told her she wanted to start treatment quickly — but was told the hospital did not have any beds available to put her in.

"They did bloods, they did nasal swabs and things like that [on the floor] — it wasn't that invasive, it just shouldn't happen," she said.

Ginny Chalmer was treated on the floor at Noarlunga Hospital. (ABC News: Chris Lawless)

She was also "horrified" about the privacy of other patients in the waiting room after overhearing details about people's conditions and outcomes.

"I just thought, 'wow, what about the confidentiality?'" Ms Chalmer said.

"Now, I know everything about this man that's actually sitting there, I just couldn't believe it was actually taking place."

SA Health said it had apologised to Ms Chalmer and would undertake a review of her experience.

"We do not put patients on the floor for treatment," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"On occasion, we do commence some treatment for eligible patients in the waiting room to ensure treatment can start as quickly as possible.

"The safety of our patients and staff is a key priority, and this helps reduce the time people need to wait and reduces the time people need to stay in hospital."

Jack Batty says Ginny's experience was unacceptable. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Liberal Opposition Health spokesperson Jack Batty said he was shocked to hear about Ms Chalmer's "floor care" experience and labelled it "entirely unacceptable".

"Having a 71-year-old woman lying on the ground in a public waiting room for four hours, being treated … with no privacy, is totally unacceptable," he said.

"These sorts of conditions are absolutely disgraceful — they should never take place in a system in South Australia."

Acting Health Minister Joe Szakacs said there was no mandate or practice "to treat people on our floors".

"The individual felt the need to lie down, that's entirely appropriate for her to choose to do," he said.

"Our nurses and doctors provide the care they have to provide, often in circumstances which are far from linear and far from easy.

"I think in this circumstance, the doctors and nurses involved did so in a way we should commend."

Joe Szakacs says nearly 500 people are waiting on an aged care bed in SA. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Mr Szakacs said South Australia's hospital network remained busy for a number of reasons, including a lack of available aged care beds and rising presentations from flu cases.

"Nonetheless, the local health network is taking a look at this, I think that's also appropriate and where things can be improved or done differently ... [it] is always committed to doing that," he said.

He added that patient confidentiality was "non-negotiable" and would form part of the review.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/y.author: Eva Blandis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/y.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Ashton Friend was behind the wheel of a fatal hit-and-run at Hillcrest in 2025. (ABC News: Jordanna Schriever)

A man has been given a suspended sentence over a road crash that killed 20-year-old international student Samia Malik.

Ashton Friend had pleaded guilty to causing death by careless use of a motor vehicle and leaving the scene of an accident.

The court heard today CCTV showed Ms Malik's hands were in what looked like a "praying motion" but no explanation was given as to why she was on the road.

A young driver who hit and killed a woman kneeling, with her hands in a praying motion, on a road in Adelaide's north-east has avoided jail.

Ashton Friend, 20, of Banksia Park, previously pleaded guilty to causing death by careless use of a motor vehicle and leaving the scene of an accident after causing the death of 20-year-old international student Samia Malik.

South Australia's District Court previously heard Ms Malik had been kneeling on North East Road at Hillcrest for around four minutes before she was hit by Friend's car about 11pm on May 6, 2025.

In sentencing Friend on Tuesday, Judge Anne Barnett said CCTV vision showed Ms Malik's hands were in what looked like a "praying motion".

No other explanation has been given as to why the 20-year-old was on the road.

It also heard that Friend had not seen Ms Malik nor realised he had hit her when he was driving home from his girlfriend's house.

"He was absolutely at a loss about what had just happened. He hadn't been aware that there was something on the road. He heard this noise," defence barrister Jane Abbey KC had submitted to the court.

"What he hoped was that it had been an animal, or something like that."

CCTV captured Samia Malik being struck by Ashton Friend's vehicle. (Supplied)

Ms Abbey added that there was "relatively little" damage to Friend's car.

The court had heard that in the days following the collision, Friend saw a news report about what had happened but was in a "state of paralysis".

Friend also previously read an apology to the court in which he said he was "deeply sorry".

"I will have to carry my failures with me for as long as I live," he said.

Judge Barnett sentenced Friend to one year, three months and 29 days with a non-parole period of eight months.

The sentence was suspended upon the 20-year-old entering a bond to be of good behaviour for two years.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.author: Giselle Wakatama
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Anthony Nugent was shot dead at his Hamilton South unit in September 2022. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Drug dealer Anthony Nugent was shot dead at the front door of his Newcastle unit in 2022, a day after selling a fake gun.

Mohamad Raad, Tyrone Tuli and Mohd Azlan Latham-Aznan were found guilty of murder.

Raad, the shooter, was sentenced to a maximum of 23 years in jail, Tuli to 20 years and Latham-Aznan to 15 years.

Three men have been sentenced to hefty jail terms over the payback murder of a Newcastle drug dealer which stemmed from a fake gun deal.

Hamilton South heroin dealer Anthony Nugent was shot dead at his apartment front door on September 6, 2022, as payback for selling a fake gun.

Police searched a garden near the unit block after Anthony Nugent was killed. (ABC Newcastle: Blake Doyle)

In May, Mohamad Raad, 46, Tyrone Tuli, 30, and Mohd Azlan Latham-Aznan, 29, were found guilty in the Supreme Court in Newcastle of murder.

They were sentenced today by Justice Peter Hamill, who noted the men sought out Mr Nugent, angry over the $22,000 sale of a fake gun.

Raad, who was the shooter, was sentenced to a maximum jail term of 23 years, with 17 years and six months non-parole.

Police made arrests after the shooting. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Tuli was sentenced to a maximum term of 20 years and four months, and Latham-Aznan to a maximum term of 15 years and three months, reflecting his lesser role.

A jury accepted Raad was the shooter, and that Tuli and Latham-Aznan were both present and part of a joint criminal enterprise.

Justice Hamill said witnesses described talk about the gun deal before Mr Nugent was shot through his screen door.

"A witness spoke about returning the money relating to the phoney gun supply," Justice Hamill said.

Raad argued the gun went off accidentally.

Justice Hamill rejected that, saying the double-barrelled shotgun was fired with an intention to kill.

"The firearm was discharged from a very close range to Mr Nugent's chest," he said.

"I am satisfied beyond reasonable doubt at the time Mr Raad discharged the shotgun into Mr Nugent's chest,  he intended to kill him.

"The trigger was pulled deliberately."

The men stood trial in Newcastle District Court. (ABC Newcastle: Robert Virtue)

In sentencing the men, Justice Hamill took into account the harm caused to Mr Nugent's wife.

In her victim impact statement, she told the court she was unable to afford a private rental, forcing her to stay in the same public housing unit where Mr Nugent was killed.

"Offences like these make people in the community feel less safe and secure, and the impact on friends and relatives is devastating," Justice Hamill said.

"His partner has had no choice but to reside at the very unit where the murder occurred, making it extremely difficult and stressful.

"She is constantly reminded of the murder and does not feel safe in Hamilton South."

Justice Hamill said the case was "a serious example of murder" and the men needed to be punished for their joint roles.

"The offence was committed in company, committed in the victim's home, the offence involved use of a weapon being a loaded double barrel shotgun," he said.

Police investigate the shooting death of Anthony Nugent in 2022. (ABC Newcastle: Blake Doyle)

"Mr Nugent was impaired and affected by drugs and relaxing at home, with the blast from the gun heard in the nearby area."

At the end of sentencing proceedings, Justice Hamill again offered his condolences to Mr Nugent's family.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Sam Wood appeared in a Sunshine Coast court via video-link on Thursday. (Supplied: @scottbreton)

Sam Wood will launch a new fight for bail in the state's highest court after he was remanded in custody yesterday.

Mr Wood's legal team says it has been instructed to file a bail application with the Supreme Court of Queensland.

Mr Wood remains in police custody to return to court on the Sunshine Coast on November 23.

Online fitness trainer and former reality TV contestant Sam Wood will take his fight for bail to the highest court in Queensland.

Mr Wood, who is facing domestic violence charges, spent his first night in prison since his application for bail was rejected by a magistrate on the Sunshine Coast.

If you need help immediately, call emergency services on Triple Zero.

The 46-year-old has since been moved from the police watch house in Maroochydore to the high-security Brisbane Correctional Centre in Wacol.

Police allege Mr Wood became involved in a family argument that ended with him assaulting his wife Snezana at a Noosa property on Saturday night.

He is charged with the domestic violence offence of assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.

Police allege Mr Wood became involved in a family argument in Noosa on Saturday night before he assaulted and strangled his wife.

Mr Wood's legal team confirmed it had been instructed to make a bail application to the Supreme Court of Queensland, which would happen "imminently".

His legal team is expected to visit the prison early next week.

At yesterday's bail application in the Maroochydore Magistrates Court, the accused appeared via video-link from the police watch house.

Police prosecutor Sergeant Jeanette Grigoris told the court the alleged assault left Ms Wood fearing for her life.

Sergeant Grigoris also referred to a video supplied by the complainant in which she described being "choked", having her head banged on the floor and being unable to breathe.

Snezana Wood, left, and her daughter Eve Markoski-Wood, with Sam Wood. (Supplied)

The court heard it was Mr Wood's stepdaughter who made a Triple Zero (000) call to police that led to the fitness influencer's arrest.

The prosecution opposed bail yesterday, telling the court Mr Wood had "the resources to essentially flee the jurisdiction".

Sergeant Grigoris told the court about an alleged previous domestic violence incident in Victoria.

Mr Wood was moved from the police watch house to Brisbane Correctional Centre after his bail application was denied. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

She told the court the alleged incident also involved Mr Wood throwing his wife against the wall and strangling her.

The prosecutor said Ms Wood did not file a police complaint at the time because she was "in fear of retribution of the defendant".

"[Mr Wood] is at an unacceptable risk of committing further offences having regard to his escalation in behaviour, the previous matter in Victoria, and the nature and seriousness of the offences before the court," Sergeant Grigoris said.

The prosecutor said Mr Wood denied the Victorian incident.

Sam Wood's father Andrew Wood (left), solicitor Mathew Cuskelly and barrister David Cole arrive for the bail hearing. (ABC News: Nykayla Dux)

Mr Wood's lawyer, Mathew Cuskelly, argued his client should be released, given his lack of criminal history.

He also cited comments by a forensic psychologist who found Mr Wood was suffering from "extremely severe" depression.

Acting Magistrate Janelle Boegheim denied Mr Wood's bail application and remanded him in custody until November 23.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.title: McLaren driver clocked allegedly doing 259km/h on WA highway
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Traffic Offences

The McLaren MA3 was allegedly clocked speeding well above the limit along Forest Highway in Binningup.  (ABC South West WA: Bridget McArthur, file photo)

A speed camera detected a McLaren MA3 coupe travelling at 259km/h on Forrest Highway in Binningup.

Police have charged the 21-year-old alleged driver after executing a search warrant at a home in Shenton Park in Perth's western suburbs.

A total of 553 people were charged with reckless driving offences and 3,075 vehicles were impounded between July and September following a crackdown on speeding in WA.

A 21-year-old man has been charged after he was clocked allegedly travelling at 259 kilometres per hour while behind the wheel of a high-performance car in Western Australia's South West.

Police say the orange McLaren MA3 coupe was pinged doing 149km/h above the 110km/h speed limit along Forrest Highway near Noble Street in Binningup, about 140km south of Perth, on August 12.

After conducting "extensive inquiries" to identify the driver, police executed a search warrant yesterday at a home in Shenton Park in Perth, where they seized several items.

The young man was one of several drivers charged for allegedly driving recklessly on WA roads. (ABC South West WA: Bridget McArthur, file photo)

It led to the young man being charged and the McLaren car, which has a top speed of around 325km/h and the ability to accelerate from 0 to 100km/h in just 3.2 seconds, has been impounded.

WA Police Commander Mike Peters said the alleged speeds reached by the young driver were alarming.

"At 259km/h, there is no margin for error. A momentary lapse in concentration, a vehicle entering the roadway, or an unexpected hazard would have catastrophic consequences," he said.

Commander Mike Peters says police have zero tolerance for drivers using WA roads as a racetrack. (ABC News)

Police Minister Reece Whitby described the driver's alleged behaviour as "unbelievably stupid" and said innocent people were at risk of paying the ultimate price.

In recent months, police have investigated a number of incidents involving excessive speed and reckless driving on WA roads.

A total of 553 people were charged with reckless driving offences and 3,075 vehicles were impounded between July 1 and September 30.

More than 3,000 vehicles were impounded as part of the blitz. (ABC South West WA: Bridget McArthur, file photo)

Among those charged was a 26-year-old Waikiki man who allegedly reached 197km/h — 127km/h above the 70km/h speed limit — on Ennis Avenue in Port Kennedy in Perth's south.

A 23-year-old woman from Beechboro was pinged allegedly doing 133km/h in a 70km/h zone in her Land Rover in a residential area on Marshall Road in Malaga in Perth's north on September 26.

"If you treat our roads like a speedway, expect WA Police to come after you. Our officers will use every tool available to identify you, take your vehicle off the road and hold you accountable," Mr Whitby said.

The 21-year-old alleged driver is due to face Bunbury Magistrates Court on October 15.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/r.title: Rider safety behind attempt to halt MotoGP, game developer tells court
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/r.author: Stephanie Richards
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Stephanie Richards

The future event has been slated for Victoria Park in Adelaide's east. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Joshua Hogan is seeking a permanent injunction against the proposed Adelaide MotoGP street circuit works, including any tree removal.

The Queensland game developer told the Federal Court he loved motorsport, but it was his view rider safety concerns should be considered.

A judge has ordered Mr Hogan and the SA government — which says track safety is "paramount" to the design — to file written submissions later this month.

A Queensland man who is taking legal action to halt the South Australian government's plans for a MotoGP circuit has told a court he is concerned about rider safety on the proposed track.

Joshua Hogan is seeking a permanent injunction against the proposed MotoGP street circuit works, including any tree removal, in the Adelaide parklands.

Appearing in the Federal Court for the first time on Friday, a self-represented Mr Hogan said he was a game developer who loved motorsport, but it was his view rider safety concerns should be considered.

"[They could possibly be] killed in a situation if the track itself is not adequate to a Grade A safety standard in the FIM (Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme)."

The Adelaide MotoGP event is slated to start next year and would be the only street circuit in the MotoGP World Championship.

Former MotoGP world champion Wayne Gardner and motorsport journalists have previously raised concerns about rider safety on the proposed 4.13-kilometre-long circuit, which revives elements of Adelaide's old Formula One track, including the straight down Rundle Road and a corner near the Stag Hotel.

The design for the Adelaide MotoGP street circuit released in August. (Supplied: SA Government)

An SA government website states the proposed circuit design was informed by "detailed collaboration" between the SA Motor Sport Board, FIM, MotoGP and Supercars Australia, and included safety elements such as run-off areas, air fences and marshals.

"There are no compromises when it comes to rider and driver safety," the website states.

In a statement after the hearing, an SA government spokesperson said safety had been "paramount in the proposed circuit design, which has been informed by detailed collaboration".

"Experts in engineering, circuit design and motorsport safety have been engaged to guide the design," the spokesperson said.

"In addition, specialist input has been provided by former 125cc and 250cc World Champion and current MotoGP Safety Advisor Loris Capirossi and five-time Supercars champion Mark Skaife."

Mr Hogan told the court on Friday he had spent six months researching the Adelaide circuit and had found "a lot" of inconsistencies.

"I understand the timeline for a motorsport event is very tight, particularly with a circuit with this amount of importance to it, but I also feel that it's also down to rider safety," he said.

An artist's impression of the Adelaide MotoGP track in the East End.

Court documents released to the ABC earlier this month showed Mr Hogan's challenge was based on similar legal arguments to those previously dismissed by the Federal Court in relation to the North Adelaide golf course upgrade.

Mr Hogan argued that the execution of plans for the MotoGP development, without being referred to the Federal Minister for the Environment, would be a breach of federal conservation laws.

Alison Doecke KC, representing the SA government, told the court on Friday that the development had been referred to the federal minister.

She said the state government anticipated "a response to the first step of that referral" between October 21 and 23, after which "early works" on the circuit would commence.

Justice Erin Longbottom ordered Mr Hogan and the SA government to file written submissions later this month.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.title: Federal government backtracks on disaster funding split
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.author: Emma Johnson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The federal government will not go ahead with a proposed 50-50 funding split for disaster recovery with states. (ABC News: Glen Ingram)

The Commonwealth government will no longer pursue a plan to split disaster recovery funding 50-50 with states and territories.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the decision came after consultation with councils and other community groups.

Queensland's government and councils, which pushed for the changes to be dropped, have welcomed the announcement.

The federal government has abandoned its proposed changes to disaster recovery funding, following pushback from states and councils.

In June, the government announced plans to split disaster recovery funding 50-50 with states and territories, having previously contributed up to 75 per cent in some areas.

Queensland would have felt the biggest impact — it received $1.3 billion under the current framework in 2024-25, the highest proportion in the country.

An open letter to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese claims the proposal will "bankrupt" councils, while the federal government urges their state counterparts not to "stoke fear".

Queensland's disaster recovery minister Ann Leahy this week wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, calling for Canberra to abandon the proposed changes.

The letter, signed by all Queensland mayors and peak industry groups, said the changes would leave communities to fund the shortfall.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers confirmed today the federal government would keep its current cost-sharing arrangements.

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government wanted to provide "certainty" during disaster. (ABC News)

"This is about ensuring that the Commonwealth government is providing certainty and providing funding when disaster hits," Mr Chalmers said.

"We do take seriously all of the consultation that has happened between the government, local councils, and with other organisations to make sure that we get this right."

"Our goal here is to make sure that disaster funding can be faster, that it can be adequate and that we get the funding where it is needed as quickly as possible."

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain thanked councils across the country for their input on the proposal.

"I want to ensure our reforms reflect the varying experiences of communities across Australia, and these changes to the reforms will ensure no community is left behind," Ms McBain said.

"The reforms will also help ensure the system is fairer, and it's easier for councils to access funding when they need it."

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli pushed the Commonwealth to scrap the funding changes. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

In a statement, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said the prime minister had listened to Queensland's concerns and made a "commonsense decision".

"We now wait to see further details, and ensure this is delivered and funding arrangements are maintained in full, so Queenslanders can have certainty and confidence in their hour of need during disaster season," the statement said.

"Today's decision diverts disaster for the most disaster-prone state.

"We look forward to strengthening our preparedness and response ahead of disaster season, in the knowledge that there will be no changes to a formula that has worked for decades."

The Local Government Association of Queensland (LGAQ) also welcomed the announcement.

"Thank you to the Commonwealth for running consultation and responding swiftly to the concerns raised by Queensland local government," LGAQ president Matt Burnett said.

"We also welcome its confirmation that councils can continue to claim costs under Counter Disaster Operations and that funding activation thresholds will be revised to ensure all communities get the support they need."

Six Queensland mayors protested a meeting about disaster funding in Melbourne in July. (ABC News)

Western Queensland Alliance of Councils [WQAC] executive officer Greg Hoffman said "it would have taken an awful long time to repair roads, bridges and other important council infrastructure" if the proposed changes had been implemented.

"The implications of the change to 50-50 from the previous 65-35 [funding split] were disastrous for the local communities if the federal government was going to walk away from that level of support,' Mr Hoffman said.

Nick Dal Santo has announced he will take charge for one last game, against Collingwood.  (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Nick Dal Santo will coach one final game with St Kilda's AFLW side, stepping down from the post after eight winless games in 2026.

The Saints are bottom of the ladder, and narrowly avoided becoming the first AFLW side to fail to score in a game in a 30-point loss to the Bulldogs.

St Kilda will undertake an independent review of its AFLW football program, with Brad Lloyd appointed to lead the review.

St Kilda's disastrous AFLW season has led to coach Nick Dal Santo stepping down after six seasons in charge, ahead of an independent review of the football program.

With four rounds to go until the end of the regular season, the Saints sit at the bottom of the AFLW ladder with eight losses from as many games.

St Kilda's percentage is a league-worst 37.2. The team is averaging 23 points per game in attack, while conceding an average of 62 points a game.

St Kilda were 90 seconds from failing to score in their AFLW clash against the Western Bulldogs, as Essendon's first win of the year leaves the Saints as the only winless team in the league.

The situation reached a critical point after last weekend's game, where the Saints lost by 30 points to the Western Bulldogs in Ballarat.

Ashleigh Richards kicked a point at the 17-minute mark of the final term, for what proved the team's only score of the game.

This meant the Saints avoided becoming the first team in AFLW history not to score in a full game.

In a club announcement on Friday, St Kilda confirmed Dal Santo's decision.

Saturday's (home) match against Collingwood will be Dal Santo's final game as senior coach.

"Nick has made a significant contribution to our AFLW program across six seasons and will always be an important part of our football club," St Kilda CEO Carl Dilena said.

"His care, commitment and leadership have been unwavering, and we thank him for everything he has given to the program, including leading the team to its maiden finals appearance last season."

Umpiring, teams without a win and big risers: These are the topics fans are talking about midway through the AFLW 2026 season.

Dal Santo was quoted in the statement saying he was proud of "where we've been able to take this program", but that he had been giving thought to whether continuing was the right decision for him and the club.

"It's been a privilege to coach this group and help shape its formative years in the competition.

"I have a strong love for this club. I wanted to contribute to women's football, and with a daughter of my own, it's great to see a pathway for young females with football ambitions.

"I'm looking forward to finishing my time as coach alongside the group this weekend and wish them every success for what comes next."

St Kilda confirmed that football administrator and executive Brad Lloyd from Apogee Sports would lead an independent review into the program.

Lloyd has previously led reviews at AFLW clubs Richmond and Carlton.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/g.title: Gippsland registers nine earthquakes in six days
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/g.author: Danielle Pope and Lily Kristanto
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Geoscience Australia produces maps which show where across the state "felt" reports are submitted after an earthquake. (Supplied: Geoscience Australia)

Geoscience Australia has recorded nine earthquakes in Gippsland in the nine days to start October.

A magnitude-3.2 earthquake was felt in Leongatha on Wednesday evening, days after a magnitude-4.9 quake hit near Leongatha.

Emergency services are encouraging residents to be prepared in the event another quake hits the region.

An earthquake scientist says there is nothing unusual about the number of earthquakes recorded in Gippsland in the past nine days.

Gippsland has been hit by nine earthquakes in the nine days of October, starting with the magnitude-4.9 quake that rocked the region on Saturday.

That earthquake came one week after a magnitude-3.9 earthquake was recorded at Ensay, in eastern Victoria, which at the time was labelled the most powerful recorded in the area in more than a decade.

Eight aftershocks have been recorded since Saturday's quake, including two tremors overnight of magnitude-2.5 and 1.5.

Geoscience Australia said it received more than 2,000 reports of people feeling Wednesday's tremor, which hit at a depth of 10 kilometres.

Seismology Research Centre chief scientist Adam Pascale said the recent aftershock activity is expected, and there might be more to come.

"We do see this type of activity regularly, just sometimes they're clustered a little bit closer together and other times they're not," he said.

Adam Pascale says earthquakes do not need to be big to cause damage. (Supplied: Adam Pascale)

Mr Pascale said he expected there would be more aftershocks.

"Whether there's larger events is impossible to tell but again we need to be prepared."

Monash University seismologist and Australian Earthquake Engineering Society president, Dee Ninis, said Gippsland had a history of earthquakes.

"Korumburra is an area that gets quite a few earthquakes; they probably experience an earthquake large enough to be felt a couple of times a year," Dr Ninis said.

The region had two magnitude-4.6 quakes in 2009 only a few weeks apart, and also a magnitude-4.4 quake in 2011.

Dr Ninis said even though Australia was not along an edge of a tectonic plate boundary like New Zealand or Japan, it could feel the impact of distant plate movement.

The largest earthquake on record in Victoria was the magnitude-5.9 magnitude quake near Woods Point in 2021, which was felt 130 kilometres away in Melbourne.

Dee Ninis says Gippsland has a significant history of earthquakes. (Supplied: Dee Ninis)

Mr Pascale said Australia had the potential to register large earthquakes.

"We haven't recorded one of that magnitude [7], we've gotten into the high sixes before in Australia in the last 60-odd years that we've been doing the monitoring, but there is a potential for quite a large earthquake," he said.

Victoria's State Emergency Service will run earthquake drills in Gippsland in schools, workplaces and with community groups next week.

Dubbed the Great Shake-Out, the event will teach people how to remain safe during an earthquake.

Victoria SES assistant chief officer Cameron Rothnie said preparedness was key.

Cameron Rothnie says Gippsland is well prepared for earthquakes.  (Supplied)

"We're promoting drills where people are encouraged to practice three safety steps if you feel the ground shaking, which is drop, cover and hold on," he said.

Mr Rothnie said the SES had been closely monitoring the aftershocks.

"Aftershocks are likely to fade away from here, although we can't rule out another big one," he said.

"Gippsland is very well prepared for earthquakes.

"We have a really strong and robust regional earthquake plan … and we have increased staff availability this week and over the weekend."
