https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.title: Mass evacuations, cars washed away in Chilean flooding disaster
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.author: Luke Cooper
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Chile's San Carlos de Apoquindo was flooded by mudslides.

Parts of central Chile have been inundated by flash flooding that swept away vehicles and damaged buildings at the foot of the Andes mountain range.

A disaster zone has been declared for the regional commune of Las Condes, and at least six people have been injured in the flooding.

The Chilean Army has been deployed to Las Condes to assist in the emergency response and clean-up efforts.

Raging floodwaters have caused major damage to buildings and vehicles and led to a disaster declaration in a regional Chilean commune at the foot of the Andes mountain range.

Parts of the Las Condes town, in the western outskirts of the Chilean capital Santiago, became inundated on Thursday, local time, according to the country's meteorological authorities.

Cars were swept away or destroyed and infrastructure uprooted by the flash flooding. (Reuters: Pablo Sanhueza)

A central weather station located near Santiago has recorded more than 60mm of rain in the past four days, the national meteorological agency reported.

A "red alert" warning has been issued by the Chilean disaster agency Senapred for at least 10 regional areas spanning an area of about 50 kilometres, encouraging people to leave immediately.

The agency also confirmed at least six people had been reported as injured in the flash flooding and taken to various medical centres.

At least 11 aged care residents and the staff and clients of a university health clinic in Las Condes were evacuated, while 60 children were sheltering inside a technical college, Senapred said.

Mudslides in Santiago, Chile.

Newly-elected Chilean President José Antonio Kast Rist later announced that the government's disaster management committee had met to discuss the flooding.

After the meeting, a "zone of catastrophe" was declared for Las Condes in a bid to "allocate all resources to address the emergency", Mr Kast said in a post on X.

"We are facing an emergency of rapid activation in Las Condes with grave impacts to vehicles and homes in some streets, produced by flooding of water and mud," he said.

Mauricio Lorca, the national director of Chile's Geology and Mining Service, said authorities were calling the flooding a "flash flow" phenomenon.

A public bus became trapped in floodwater and debris after being washed down a major street near the capital Santiago. (Reuters: Pablo Sanhueza)

"[It] means a rapid flood of water that is generated in a very short time, and that drags a large amount of sediment and materials that can affect riverbeds, rivers or slopes."

The Chilean Army also announced it had deployed specialist vehicles, infantry soldiers and emergency response teams to parts of Las Condes to help with clean-up and rescue efforts.

Some residents sought to escape the rising floodwaters on foot. (Reuters: Pablo Sanhueza)

Videos shared online by residents impacted by the disaster showed dark floodwater rapidly flowing through General Blanche, one of the largest roads in Las Condes.

In one of the clips, several people could be seen clinging to an open escape hatch on the roof of a red public bus as it was washed away.

Chilean police doorknocking residents during evacuations also helped some people cross floodwaters. (Reuters: Pablo Sanhueza)

The Chilean Meteorological Department also issued a thunderstorm alert warning for regions between an area north of San Felipe, through Santiago, to south of the town of Linares.

All school classes were suspended on Thursday, local time, according to Santiago's regional metropolitan transport body, which also strongly advised against personal travel in nine of the impacted areas.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.author: Jean Bell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Road Accidents and Incidents

Victoria Police said the woman was found on Remembrance Drive in Cardigan with critical injuries. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

A woman has died after she was found with critical injuries on a road near Ballarat in the early hours of this morning.

Victoria Police said the 42-year-old woman, who has not been identified, was found by a passer-by on Remembrance Drive in Cardigan at about 2:10am.

The woman was flown to hospital, but later died.

Police said she may have been lying on the road at the time she was struck by a truck or another vehicle.

The two-lane road where the incident occurred has a speed limit of 80 kilometres an hour.

Officers found debris at the scene that they said could indicate a truck was involved in the incident.

Anyone who drove through the area in the early hours of the morning is being urged to come forward, police said.

The circumstances of the incident remain under investigation.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

Members of Australia's Test squad from the infamous 2018 South Africa tour have enjoyed mixed fortunes in the years since. (Getty Images: Lee Warren)

The members of Australia's touring party from the 2018 South Africa series have endured various fortunes in the eight years since.

Some have seen their careers go to new heights, while others struggled to recapture their form from before the ball-tampering saga.

Others never featured for Australia again.

As Australia plays its first Test in South Africa since 2018, here is a look at where everyone from the previous tour ended up in the years that followed.

Steve Smith is no longer Australia's Test captain, nor is he at the peak of his powers, but he still remains the best batter in the team. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

It is somewhat of an indictment on where Australian cricket has gone since the last South Africa tour that Smith is still by far the team's best batter.

Although, a glass-half-full view might suggest that it is a sign of Smith's incredible longevity.

While he is not at the peak of his powers like he was on the last tour, Smith is still the trump card in the line-up and will be the wicket South Africa's bowlers most covet.

Smith has retired from all white ball formats and is primarily a Test cricketer at the international level.

David Warner was not quite able to recapture his best form at the Test level following his suspension in 2018. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Arguably Australia's main antagonist in 2018, Warner last represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in mid-2024.

Following his ball-tampering suspension, Warner never quite recaptured his form, particularly in the Test format.

Warner averaged 48.63 in Tests prior to the 2018 South Africa tour and finished his career averaging 37.28 in 38 Tests afterwards.

He is now a T20 gun for hire in various competitions around the world.

Cameron Bancroft (left) famously fronted the press conference alongside Smith where Australia admitted to tampering with the ball using a piece of sandpaper. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Bancroft's international career suffered the most out of the three players banned from the 2018 tour, having been the man caught by the Supersport cameras trying to hide a piece of sandpaper from the umpires.

The right-hander has played just two Tests since. The last of those came in 2019, and his Test career looks just about done.

Still just 33, Bancroft remains a prolific domestic run scorer, and ranked third in terms of runs in the Sheffield Shield last year. He has 33 first class centuries to his name.

Joe Burns enjoyed a few more years of Test cricket for Australia before going on to represent Italy. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Burns was one of the players drafted into the Australian XI for the final Test in 2018 after the suspensions of Smith, Warner and Bancroft.

He enjoyed a productive 2019 at the Test level before playing the last of his Tests for Australia on Boxing Day in 2020.

Burns later became a T20 specialist for Italy, averaging 45.16 in eight matches across 2024 and 2025 to help the Italians qualify for their maiden T20 World Cup this year, but was left out of Italy's World Cup squad.

Pat Cummins has gone on to captain Australia in multiple formats since the 2018 series, where he was only just returning from a series of back issues. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cummins's Test career was in its infancy in 2018, having just returned to the side following years of injury issues.

Since then he has become one of the finest all-format bowlers as well as Australia captain.

Under Cummins's tenure, Australia has won an ODI World Cup and the ICC Test Championship, both in 2023.

He has been named in the Test Team of the Year on four occasions, and was named Test Cricketer of the Year in 2019.

Peter Handscomb has played fleetingly in Australia's Test side since 2018, and is seen as somewhat of a spin specialist. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Another player who came in for the final Test in 2018, Handscomb has forever been on the periphery of Australia's Test side.

Handscomb was famously the man who told the Australian team that they'd been caught ball tampering, after chatting to then-coach Darren Lehmann on a walkie-talkie while flipping an Aussie rules football in between his hands.

Considered a specialist in spinning conditions, Handscomb has added just seven Tests to his career since the 2018 series, but is an outside chance to feature again in India next year after recently being added to the Australia A side.

He was the leading scorer in the last Shield season, scoring 724 runs at an average of 34.47 in very bowler-friendly conditions.

Josh Hazlewood is one of the few Australians who has seen his career have an uptick following the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Hazlewood enjoyed some of his best years as a Test bowler following the 2018 tour.

The right-arm paceman averaged 25.77 with the ball prior to that series and has seen that average dip to an elite 21.17 in the years that have followed.

Hazlewood is still prolific when he is able to get on the park, but his body has given him problems over the last few seasons.

The 35-year-old was restricted to just four Tests last year, but still took 16 wickets at an average of 17.93.

Jon Holland played just two Tests for Australia after not featuring at all during the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Holland was one of the players who didn't play a single Test during the last South Africa tour, and has mostly remained on the outer since.

His two Test appearances following the 2018 tour yielded just four wickets at an average of 75, and he was unsurprisingly surpassed in the spin pecking order.

Nevertheless, Holland continued to enjoy his time in domestic cricket, helping Victoria claim a Sheffield Shield title in 2018–19.

Holland's first class career ended in 2023 when he was let go by Victoria after 95 Shield appearances.

Usman Khawaja completely reinvented his Test career as a prolific opener before retiring from international cricket at the start of this year. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Khawaja played all four Tests as Australia's number three in 2018, but his struggles in that series were no indicator of what was to come.

After being left out of the Test side in 2020 and 2021, Khawaja returned for the New Year's Test in 2022 and had an incredible stint as one of Australia's openers.

Khawaja scored eight of his 16 Test centuries after his return in 2022 and averaged 48.05 as an opener, one of the best marks by an Australian.

He retired from Test cricket following Australia's Ashes triumph against England last summer and is now a T20 specialist for domestic leagues after also retiring from Shield cricket.

Nathan Lyon still has a stranglehold on the sole spinner spot in Australia's full-strength Test XI. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Lyon remains a mainstay in Australia's first-choice Test XI, just as he was in 2018.

Despite being the oldest player in Australia's team, no spinner has been able to claim Lyon's spot as the non-pace bowling option alongside Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins.

Lyon's body has slowly begun to show signs of aging in the past few years, and he played just two of the five Tests against England in last summer's Ashes.

His performances in the Bangladesh Tests suggest he won't be an automatic selection in South Africa.

Mitch Marsh retired from Test cricket after last featuring in the 2024 Boxing Day Test, but is now Australia's T20 captain. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Marsh played all four Tests against South Africa in 2018, but struggled to kick on from that series in the years that followed. He was the man with the ball in hand when the ball-tampering storm erupted.

He had a strong 2023, scoring a century and four 50s to end the calendar year with an average of 67.50, but managed an average of just 18.86 the following year and saw his Test career come to an end after Boxing Day.

Marsh has since retired from Test cricket but remains in Australia's ODI and T20 sides, captaining the country in the shortest format.

His name gets mentioned with regards to a Test return every once in a while, but that ship appears to have sailed with Australia well-stocked with all-rounder options.

Shaun Marsh did not feature again in Australia's Test XI once Smith and Warner returned from their suspensions. (AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts)

The other Marsh brother also played all four Tests in the 2018 series, but struggled thereafter.

Marsh was relied upon heavily during the suspensions to Smith, Warner and Bancroft, but did not play another Test once the trio were cleared to return.

He played his last first class match in 2023 and his last T20 in the BBL at the end of 2024.

Marsh is one of 10 former international cricketers involved in the CLT10, India's first luxury-format indoor cricket league.

Despite being a key member of Australia's white ball teams, Glenn Maxwell never played another Test match after 2017. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Maxwell has not played a single Test since 2017 but remains a white ball superstar.

He played a key role in Australia's T20 World Cup and ODI World Cup wins, in 2021 and 2023 respectively.

He retired from ODIs in 2025 but still plays for Australia in the T20 format and is considered one of the most dangerous short-form players in the world.

With less international cricket on his plate, Maxwell is a gun for hire for domestic T20 leagues around the world.

Tim Paine captained Australia after the ball-tampering scandal, before being forced to resign under controversial circumstances himself. (Getty: Ryan Pierse)

Paine was thrust into centre stage following the sandpaper debacle on the 2018 tour, captaining Australia in the final Test of the series in Smith and Warner's absence.

The Tasmanian keeper retained the captaincy even when Smith returned, and eventually led his country in 23 Tests.

Paine's reign as captain came to an end when he resigned in November 2021 after explicit messages he'd sent to a co-worker in 2017 resurfaced.

He ended his playing career at all levels in 2023 and took up coaching. Currently he is the head coach of Pakistan Super League side Multan Sultans.

Matt Renshaw has only recently returned to Australia's Test side after spending years in the wilderness. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Renshaw was among those drafted into the Australian side for the final Test of the 2018 series in Johannesburg.

He played three more Tests in 2023, including one against South Africa, but managed just nine runs in four innings.

Renshaw received a Test recall earlier this year against Bangladesh, but managed just eight in his sole innings at the crease.

The left-hander has been most effective for Australia at the T20 level, where he averages 38.83 at a healthy strike rate of 125.94.

Jhye Richardson's body has stopped him from enjoying the Test career many believed he was destined to have. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Richardson has been the nearly man of his generation of Australian cricketers.

He did not feature in the 2018 Tests, but made his debut the following year, shining with six wickets in two Tests.

However, repeated injury issues halted his once-bright career, allowing him to play just two Tests in the last seven years.

He currently features in Australia A's Tests against India A. If his body holds up, he should be back in Test calculations in the not too distant future.

Chadd Sayers's one Test appearance came during the final Test of the 2018 South Africa series. (Getty Images: Lee Warren)

Sayers was another one of Australia's inclusions for the Johannesburg Test in 2018, and it wound up being the only Test he would ever play.

A prolific Shield performer in the lead-up to the South Africa series, a knee injury ruined his 2018–19 season.

Sayers continued to play for South Australia and eventually retired from first class cricket at the end of the 2020–21 season.

Following his retirement, Sayers spent some time as a runner for SANFL side Woodville-West Torrens.

Mitchell Starc remains the spearhead of Australia's bowling attack despite approaching 37 years of age. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Starc's career has gone from strength to strength since 2018, and he remains one of the most feared new ball bowlers in world cricket.

Nearly 37, Starc is as fast as ever and remains an integral part of Australia's Test line-up.

At the end of the 2018 series, Starc had taken 182 wickets at an average of 28.17 in 43 Tests.

Since then, he has taken a further 263 wickets at an average of 24.70 in 64 Tests, and his career mark of 445 Test wickets is the most by any left-arm bowler.

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

Ukrainian children's rights advocate Mykola Kuleba has pioneered a campaign to return children deported by Russia. (AFP: Getty Images)

While US President Donald Trump is again lobbying to win the Nobel Peace Prize, a number of frontrunners have emerged who experts say are far more likely to win the award.

This year's winner will be announced in Oslo later today and the Norwegian Nobel Committee has 287 nominations.

The prize is awarded annually to people or organisations who have done the most to promote peace between nations.

Nominations are not public but the acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, Haakon Gjerløw, who is considered a top analyst of the Nobel Peace Prize, has tipped five leading contenders.

A Ukrainian mother embraces her 13-year-old son, Bohdan, who was taken to Russia from a Russian-organised summer camp. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

A Ukrainian children's rights advocate, Mykola Kuleba has devoted much of the last two decades to saving kids in his country from threats like human trafficking and cyberbullying.

Tens of thousands of Ukrainian kids are believed to have been taken by Russia. We joined a rescue mission to bring four home.

Since Russia's invasion of Crimea and Donbas in 2014, he has led efforts to deliver emergency aid and evacuation assistance to Ukrainians deported by Russia from the occupied territories.

Mr Kuleba co-founded rescue charity Save Ukraine, later concentrating on the return of vulnerable civilians including children, orphans and families after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

He previously led efforts to recognise and expand the rights of minors in Ukraine, serving as the country's children's ombudsman, head of the Kyiv Children's Service and co-founder of the Ukraine Without Orphans Alliance.

Mr Gjerløw said both the work of Mr Kuleba and Save the Children emphasised the need to protect children in war.

Alsanosi Adam from Emergency Response Rooms in Stockholm ahead of an award ceremony in 2025. (AFP: TT News Agency)

Civil war-hit Sudan is in the midst of a major humanitarian crisis, with food, water and medical supplies in short supply.

Community-led initiatives like the Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) have stepped in to fill the gap and deliver essential humanitarian assistance to millions.

Led by a grassroots network of Sudanese civilians, the ERRs have been instrumental in setting up communal kitchens, supporting evacuations, fixing vital communications infrastructure and supplying essential resources like clean water, fuel and medical supplies.

Most aren't legally registered but receive funding from Sudanese residents, charitie, and international development agencies. Mr Gjerløw said awarding this year's peace prize to Sudan's ERRs would highlight the power of everyday people to serve humanity in difficult times of conflict.

British journalist and CPJ chief executive Jodie Ginsberg during this year's International Four Freedoms Awards ceremony in Middelburg. (AFP: Nicolas Tucat)

This US-based watchdog group has continued to defend the rights of journalists in an increasingly hostile global environment.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)  keeps an annual register of the number of journalists and media workers killed around the world.

In 2025, that number hit a record 129, the highest since they started compiling records more than three decades ago.

Gaza became the deadliest war zone for reporters in modern history, according to the CPJ.

Mr Gjerløw said awarding this group a Nobel Peace Prize would send the world a reminder that peace and democracy were threatened if journalists were prevented from doing their jobs.

A European astronaut during a spacewalk on the International Space Station's truss structure. (Supplied: NASA)

Perhaps an outsider for the award, both literally and figuratively, Mr Gjerløw believes there's some merit to this one.

Orbiting about 400 kilometres above Earth, the ISS represents a rare symbol of global cooperation amid crumbling multilateralism and narrowing national interests, according to Mr Gjerløw.

It was November 20, 1998, and a rocket wasn't an unusual sight in this remote part of Kazakhstan. But today's cargo was a piece of history that would have seemed impossible just years before.

The product of space agencies from the US, Russia, Canada, Japan and the European Union, the ISS launched in 1998 and has since been visited by 222 astronauts from as many as 18 countries.

It has been continuously occupied since November 2000.

A Nobel Peace Prize for the ISS would celebrate what humanity could achieve when working together, Mr Gjerløw said.

Hearings at the International Court of Justice over Israeli actions in Palestine territory. (Getty Images: Nikos Oikonomou/Anadolu)

Multilateral collaboration was the underlying theme in Mr Gjerløw peace prize picks. This one is no different.

He said both institutions remained crucial for maintaining global order in an increasingly fragmented world.

Established in 1945, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) settles legal disputes between states from its headquarters in The Hague.

While its rulings can be difficult to enforce with no formal enforcement mechanism, the ICJ remains a globally accepted system for dispute resolution.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) is also based in The Hague and has the power to prosecute individuals for international crimes including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

Mr Gjerløw said both organisations would be deserving of the peace prize as they represented the importance of holding states and leaders accountable to international law.

Maria Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025 for promoting democratic rights in Venezuela. (Reuters: Heiko Junge)

Mr Gjerløw is only the acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, so did not put forward his own list in 2025.

Then-director Nina Græger's predictions were largely similar but did not include eventual winner Maria Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who gifted her peace prize to Mr Trump.

Ms Græger's picks were limited to organisations and included Europe's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, and The Carter Center, a human rights organisation founded by former US president Jimmy Carter.

She also tipped the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom, the CPJ, Sudan's ERRs and both the ICJ and the ICC.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee is due to announce this year's peace prize winner at 8pm AEDT tonight.

Topic:

Yvonne Weldon said on social media she was the complainant at the centre of Mick Mundine's historical abuse charges. (ABC News: Chantelle Al-Khouri)

Prominent Indigenous elder Mick Mundine has been accused of child sexual assault by City of Sydney councillor Yvonne Weldon.

Ms Weldon revealed in a social media post on Friday that she is the now-adult complainant at the centre of the charges.

Mr Mundine was granted police bail on Thursday and is due to face a Sydney court next week.

City of Sydney councillor Yvonne Weldon has come forward as the complainant at the centre of prominent Indigenous elder Mick Mundine's child sexual assault charges.

Mr Mundine was arrested on Thursday by the Sex Crimes Squad over the historical allegation involving a 15-year-old girl, which is alleged to have taken place in Redfern in 1986.

The Aboriginal Housing Company chief executive, 79, was charged with sexual assault, and sexual assault of a person under the age of 16.

Ms Weldon made the announcement in a social media post on Friday, writing that it was "never too late to speak up".

"I have carried this for 40 years. It is time to no longer carry it," she said.

"I came forward for the children who are here now and to break the culture of silence that allows abuse to continue.

"To other survivors of abuse in its many forms, you are not alone.

"It is never too late to speak up and seek support."

Mr Mundine was granted police bail after being charged on Thursday. (LinkedIn)

Elected in 2021, Cr Weldon is the first Aboriginal councillor to sit on the City of Sydney council.

Mr Mundine was granted bail by police to front the Downing Centre Local Court next week.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.author: Charlie Gore and Tahlia Roy
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ACT emergency services were called to a massage parlour across from Cooleman Court in Canberra's south. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

Five people have been taken to hospital after a car drove into a shopfront in Canberra's south.

Emergency services used an airbag to free three people, all workers at the store, from under the vehicle.

Of the five people injured two were in a serious but stable condition, one in a stable condition, and the other two had minor injuries.

ACT emergency services have freed three people who were trapped underneath a car after it was driven into a shopfront in Weston in Canberra's south.

Authorities say five people were injured in the crash, including the three workers who were trapped, the vehicle's driver, and a fifth person who was in the store.

Emergency services are still on scene and the car remains deep inside the building. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

The car remains deep inside the building, which houses Harmony Tree Therapeutic Massage and Day Spa, and sits across from Cooleman Court shopping centre off Brierly Street.

ACT Ambulance Operations Manager Chris Tyrrell said the five people treated at the scene were all taken to the Canberra Hospital.

Mr Tyrrell said two of those people were in a serious but stable condition, one was in a stable condition, and another two had minor injuries.

Paramedic Chris Tyrrell says it is "astounding" the victims were not more severely injured. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

"The patients had to be removed from under the vehicle," he said.

"It's frankly astounding that the injuries weren't more severe.

"The fact that we're only dealing with lower limb injuries, albeit serious lower limb injuries, is quite fortunate."

ACT Fire and Rescue Commander Jeff Dau said crews arrived on scene shortly after 11:45am to "a scene of chaos and confusion".

"The vehicle's gone from the parking area [outside the shopfront] straight into the commercial premises," Commander Dau said.

ACT Fire and Rescue's Jeff Dau says airbags were used to raise the vehicle off the trapped people. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

"We were confronted with three persons trapped, and we also had one person in the vehicle."

He said it took about 45 minutes to free the people who were trapped.

"We used airbags to raise the vehicle, and with that we were able to release the entrapped patients," Commander Dau said.

One other person, who was in the store at the time, walked out of the business with only minor injuries.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash where three people were trapped under the vehicle. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

ACT Policing Detective Sergeant Jonathan Turkich said the driver, an 84-year-old woman, was assisting with enquiries.

He said she had tested negative to drugs and alcohol, and there was "no suggestion" the crash was a deliberate act.

Detective Sergeant Turkich, who leads ACT Policing's Major Collisions Team, said multiple police units attended the scene to assist.

"Our hearts go out to the victims, go out to the wider community impacted by this — because, as you can see from the response and the people around, it affects everyone," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.author: Jamie McKinnell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A jury has been shown crime scene exhibits in the Lamarre-Condon double murder trial, including a car rental card found at the property. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

Dozens of photographs of items located where the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were found have been released.

Jurors in the Beau Lamaree-Condon double murder trial were shown the exhibits this week.

The 31-year-old is accused of shooting the couple using his service pistol in 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder.

High-visibility clothing, a helmet, white bloodstained overalls and a rental car card with the name "Beau L-C" were amongst a collection of items at the location where the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were found south of Sydney in 2024, a jury has heard.

The scene, near a monastery at rural Bungonia, was photographed and documented after the discovery on February 27, 2024, eight days after the alleged murders of the young couple.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon is facing a three-month trial in the NSW Supreme Court, where he has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and his lawyers have indicated an argument of self-defence.

The location of where the bodies of Mr Davies and Mr Baird were found. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The 31-year-old is accused of shooting Mr Baird and Mr Davies using his service pistol in Mr Baird's home in Paddington, in Sydney's east.

The court on Friday released dozens of photographs shown this week as jurors heard evidence from a retired crime scene specialist, Greg Moon, who attended the Bungonia site.

Gravel at scene where the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were found. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

Concrete bag packaging found at the property. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The bodies of Mr Davies and Mr Baird were found inside surfboard bags near mounds of gravel on a fence line, partially covered by rocks, sticks and branches, the court heard.

Police found and photographed a fired gun cartridge and there was a wheelbarrow and spade also in the area.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder. (Supplied: Liam Mendes)

Black garbage bags and piles of discarded property included clothing, a weight, cable ties, gumboots, and packaging of supplies such as concrete, tarpaulins and overalls.

The Crown alleges that Mr Lamarre-Condon initially attempted to sink the couple's bodies in a dam using quick-set cement and weights, before returning later to move them.

A shovel and a wheelbarrow were found with cement mix residue on them. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

Overalls stained with blood were recovered. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The jury has seen CCTV footage of a person in high-visibility clothing dressed as an Uber Eats delivery driver on the morning of the alleged murders.

The Crown says Mr Lamarre-Condon waited for Mr Baird's housemates to leave that morning, and during an opening address Crown Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC said he would invite the jury to infer the defendant spent time "steeling" himself on the street for what he was allegedly about to do.

Jesse Baird (left) and Luke Davies were allegedly shot dead in February 2024. (Instagram)

The Crown's case is that Mr Lamarre-Condon developed a jealous infatuation with Mr Baird after the end of a somewhat casual romance in parts of 2023, and had allegedly stalked him leading up to the deaths.

But the defence has flagged an alternative version of what took place inside the terrace, saying Mr Lamarre-Condon went there to collect belongings, was surprised that Mr Baird was home, and that two separate struggles involving the gun resulted in two tragic deaths.

John Stratton SC, representing Mr Lamarre-Condon, has previously told jurors that his client tried to clean the scene out of panic and knew how the situation would be perceived.

A pair of gumboots. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

A black helmet found at the property where the bodies were found. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The collection of exhibits released on Friday, at the end of the third week of the trial, include photographs of two keys found at the Bungonia monastery site.

In a video also released by the court after it was played to jurors, a detective later tests the keys at Mr Baird's Brown Street terrace and confirms they unlock the front door and a security door.

The jury has heard that before arriving at the monastery, police had scoured a dam at a farm about 15-minutes away and found other evidence including more cable ties, weights, and concrete residue.

Detectives located that farm after taking an induced statement from a witness who said she had been with the defendant days after the alleged murders, on a drive to Goulburn in a white van, and that they had been to a farm.

That witness, who has been given the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy during the trial, also said they had stopped at Bunnings to buy an angle grinder.

The trial, before Justice Natalie Adams, will continue on Monday.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/l.title: Victorian language charity with $16m kitty has links to white nationalists
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/l.author: Ruby Jones, Michael Workman, and Matt Martino
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The ESU's Victorian branch is under investigation by the charity's national branch following revelations of funding provided to white nationalists. (ABC NEWS Verify/ESU)

An ABC NEWS Verify investigation has found the English-Speaking Union's Victoria branch provided a $2,000 grant to white nationalist publication The National Observer.

The charity also has ties to a far-right white nationalist organisation, the British Australian Community.

The Australian English-Speaking Union has launched an investigation into the Victorian branch following questions from ABC NEWS Verify.

A national charity has launched an internal investigation into its Victorian branch after ABC NEWS Verify uncovered funding for far-right, white nationalist organisations.

The investigation began after the ABC alerted the Australian English-Speaking Union to a $2,000 grant ESU Victoria made to a white nationalist online publication called The National Observer (TNO).

In a recent anonymous article titled "Australian Remigration — What it would look like, and how it could be achieved tomorrow", TNO called for the "accelerated removal of non-citizens" and for incentivising the permanent "departure" of some Australians who hold dual citizenship.

Another recent TNO article was titled "Are White Australians being replaced? The media says it's a conspiracy theory, the data says otherwise".

The ESU is a registered charity dedicated to promoting stronger ties between English-speaking peoples. (ESU Victoria)

The National Observer also has its own weekly podcast hosted by the organisation's founder, who goes by the name "John Lawson".

In November 2025, TNO published an interview by Lawson with Eric Orwoll, founder of US "whites only" enclave Return to the Land, about how their ideas could be used in Australia.

Australian white nationalists have also appeared as guests on the podcast and aired racist and antisemitic views during their interviews.

John Lawson does not show his face on the podcast's videos, instead using this image. (The National Observer)

Representatives of far-right European political parties have starred as guests on The National Observer's podcast, sharing lessons on pro-nationalist politicking.

During an episode with a campaigner for German political party Alternative for Germany, or AfD, one of the Australian hosts confessed that the purpose of The National Observer was to "try and build a young elite who have these right-wing ideas", a movement they said they hoped could replicate the AfD's electoral success.

In a statement to ABC NEWS Verify, ESU Victoria defended awarding the grant to TNO.

"The National Observer's application relied on its provision of independent podcasts promoting Australian culture, heritage and language. That application sought funding for the purchase of media equipment (lapel microphones) and website development.

"While the content of the National Observer's podcasts are that organization's responsibility, we support the common law freedoms available to all Australians, including freedom of expression," the statement read.

ESU Victoria's defence appears to be out of step with the national charity parent body, ESU Australia, which told ABC NEWS Verify it took the matter seriously and had launched an internal investigation.

"AESU is a non-partisan, non-political organisation. We do not engage in political advocacy, nor do we support donations to political organisations or to any organisation that does not uphold the ESU's purpose and mission," a spokesperson told ABC NEWS Verify.

The global English-Speaking Union exists across 50 countries and was founded more than 100 years ago by British journalist Sir Evelyn Wrench, who, according to the organisation, "envisioned a world where shared language could bridge cultural divides and foster peace".

The English-Speaking Union's first branch was founded in London in 1918 by Sir Evelyn Wrench. (ESU)

The Victorian branch's activities, many of which are aimed at young people, include rhyming poetry competitions and supporting schoolchildren to practise public speaking.

It has significant sums of money at its disposal: according to financial documents, ESU Victoria has more than $16 million in cash and assets.

The ABC does not suggest that all ESU Victoria members share or support white nationalist views.

ESU Victoria shares a building with white nationalist organisation, the British Australian Community. (ESU Victoria)

ABC NEWS Verify can reveal ESU Victoria also has ties to a far-right political interest group called the British Australian Community (BAC).

The BAC says it exists to "promote and defend the interests of Anglo-Celtic Australians".

The group has engaged in white nationalist rhetoric, including advocating for remigration, which is the deportation of those of non-European heritage.

In a post on X in 2024, the BAC referenced Australian Anglo-Celtics being "under siege" by the "threat" of "mass indiscriminate immigration".

The BAC has talked about demographic replacement in its social media content. (X: British Australian Community)

In a 2024 press release, the group referred to itself as "immigration patriots" and called on then-opposition leader Peter Dutton to "initiate the orderly remigration of recent arrivals wishing to return to their homelands".

It then explicitly called for the creation of a race-based immigration system, asking for the adoption of "immigration policies designed to cap and reduce ethnic diversity in Australia".

It also wanted a government department created to deport people.

"The British Australian Community recommends establishing a Department of Emigration responsible for managing the diplomatic and logistical dimensions of mass negative migration," the release said.

Company documents reveal the BAC and ESU Victoria share a building in Ascot Vale in Melbourne's inner North-West.

ESU Victoria president Robert Furlan was previously a secretary of the BAC.

According to a post in a BAC group on social media, since 2016, all BAC members are automatically associate members of the ESU in Victoria.

When asked about this, ESU Victoria said the BAC was historically a corporate member of ESU Victoria, but that as of 2016 all its corporate membership and associated benefits had ceased to operate.

In the past, ESU Victoria has provided funding for a BAC campaign opposing the renaming of places and monuments to recognise Indigenous heritage. It also sponsored an annual BAC event called "Britfest".

ESU Victoria told the ABC it has no current financial relationship with the BAC.

"ESU Victoria Branch and the British Australian Community are separate entities. ESU Victoria Branch has no comment to make about the BAC's website content or media statements other than to reiterate our support for common law freedoms, including freedom of expression," the ESU Victoria statement said.

Company records show that the current secretary of the BAC is Frank Salter.

Dr Salter co-founded an organisation in the 1970s called the Australian National Alliance (ANA).

Reports at the time described it as an anti-immigration group with a focus on recruiting young people.

Dr Salter later moved into academia and has written extensively on ethnicity, genetics, and "mass immigration".

In 2023, the ESU Victoria announced the awarding of a grant to Dr Salter supporting a publication titled "Collected essays on the national question".

Federal election candidates and elected officials are sharing content from The Noticer, a news site regularly publishing articles promoting white supremacist and neo-Nazi ideologies.

Dr Salter's books are also advertised via Amazon affiliate links hosted on the far-right website The Noticer.

The Noticer also has published Dr Salter's opinions on race, describing him as a representative of the BAC.

ABC NEWS Verify understands Dr Salter has also been a member of ESU Victoria in the past, though it is not clear if he still is.

Dr Salter did not respond to a list of questions sent to him by ABC NEWS Verify.

On its website, the ESU Victoria says it adheres to a definition of English-speaking people that is defined as "people of the British Isles and their descendants who settled in countries such as Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States of America".

Extremism researcher Josh Roose, from Deakin University, told ABC NEWS Verify that the ESU Victoria branch appeared to share some of the more "traditionalist pseudo-intellectual elements" of the far right or the extreme right.

"They believe that the English-speaking peoples, which appears to be quite narrowly defined to white countries, are people who are losing their heritage and need some sort of support to maintain that in the face of overwhelming odds," he said.

Dr Roose said some of ESU Victoria's activities — like its grant to The National Observer — risked crossing the line into funding political activism.

"When you're platforming white nationalists … there's a very, very thin line here as to what's acceptable and it certainly warrants further investigation."

Dr Roose called on the Australian government to initiate a thorough review into ESU Victoria, to investigate their stated aims, mission, and their actual activities.

"When a charity is being used and cloaked effectively in a certain language to allow it to use tax breaks … at times to achieve a political purpose, then it's moved well beyond its remit."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.title: Hollard insurance fined $2m for handling of claim that destroyed home
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.author: Adelaide Miller
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Federal Court has ordered Hollard insurance to pay $2 million. (Supplied)

Insurance giant Hollard has been fined $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable.

The corporate watchdog ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof.

The Federal Court ordered Hollard to pay $2 million for failing to promptly assess the damage, delaying rectification work and for failing to properly protect the property from further damage.

It was also found to have taken too long to find temporary accommodation for the couple, failed to consider expert reports, and not clearly communicate with the couple throughout the claims process.

Hollard has also been ordered to pay ASIC's legal costs.

In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for Hollard said the insurer acknowledges the Federal Court's findings initiated by ASIC.

"We extend our deepest apologies and sincerely regret the impact of this experience on the customer," the spokesperson said.

Hollard is a privately owned insurance company and one of the largest in Australia, underwriting insurance for motor, home, contents, bicycle, pet, and business products.

It is the company behind brands including CBA's insurance product, Everyday Insurance, Real Insurance, Australian Seniors and Steadfast.

In 2024, the company had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion.

Hollard initially accepted the couples' claim, before repeatedly delaying inspections, reports and repair work, only to then reject the claim in April 2023.

ASIC said the rejection was based on a non-expert opinion, despite prior expert reports outlining the damage.

ASIC alleged the combination of delays in decision-making, poor communication and ignoring expert advice exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm.

Sarah Court says Hollard's delays mean the home in regional Victoria needs to be demolished. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Its chair Sarah Court said the outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith.

She said it was a warning to insurers about the devastating impact poor claim-handling and prolonged delays can have on consumers.

"Hollard's serious claim handling failures left a family in limbo for years and living in a home that was uninhabitable," Ms Court said.

"When Australians make an insurance claim they are often facing some of the most difficult times in their lives.

"This decision confirms that insurers must act fairly, communicate clearly and make decisions without unnecessary delay, and must put their customers first."

The family was initially offered $1,000 from Hollard as a goodwill payment in late 2022 to settle their claim.

Once Hollard denied the claim, the couple then lodged a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which determined the storm caused structural damage to the roof.

Hollard had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion in 2024. (Supplied)

Hollard then agreed to pay the couple a cash settlement of more than $1.5 million for the total loss of the building, as well as temporary accommodation.

ASIC sued Hollard after the cash settlement. The penalty Hollard has been ordered to pay goes to the Commonwealth of Australia, to be paid within 28 days.

In delivering the judgment the judge said: "The saga experienced by the insureds was extended and must have been stressful and traumatic."

"They were given the run-around in more ways than one and lived in their ever-deteriorating home as the saga wore on."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.title: Piastri hopes for better in Singapore as fading challenger promises 'all-out' attack
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.author: Michael Doyle
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Oscar Piastri is taking a positive attitude into this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix. (Getty Images: Formula 1/Anni Graf )

Oscar Piastri is hoping McLaren will be more competitive during the Singapore Grand Prix weekend after a disappointing round last time in Malaysia.

George Russell will start from the back of the grid after taking a penalty following last weekend's power unit failure for the Mercedes driver.

The Singapore Grand Prix will be held at the Marina Bay circuit on Sunday night.

Following a difficult weekend in Malaysia, Oscar Piastri is hoping McLaren will enjoy better results and have a more competitive car in Singapore.

Piastri finished sixth at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, after his team sent him out on slick tyres in wet conditions to start the race, forcing the Australian into the pits as the race began.

The McLaren driver was able to fight his way back through the field, at times showing strong pace, but said sixth was the best result the team could hope for.

Max Verstappen's long wait for another Formula 1 race win is finally over, and the drivers' championship race might be over, too.

"We know we've not been as competitive as we would have liked the last couple of weekends,: Piastri said in Singapore ahead of this weekend's racing.

"In Malaysia, I think sixth was more or less what we could've done."

McLaren enjoyed a mid-season resurgence, with Piastri's teammate claiming back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Norris won those races from pole position, and then again was fastest in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix in September.

But the reigning constructors' champions were not realistically in contention for wins, but did show promise at times.

It is that inconsistency during weekends which has hurt McLaren in 2026, and something Piastri is hoping can be improved to end the season, starting in Singapore.

"At certain points in [Malaysia], we looked very quick. On my second hard [tyre] stint, and Lando as well on his soft [tyre], we were more or less the quickest cars on the track at one point.

"It's in line with the rest of the year — if you can get the car into the right window, it's very quick.

"But we've struggled to get it there for a lot of the last two weekends. Hopefully we can make things a bit easier this weekend."

George Russell's dream of a maiden F1 world title is hanging by a thread, after the Briton suffered a power unit failure with five laps remaining last weekend in Malaysia.

Following his retirement, Russell is now 84 points adrift of teammate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli, with a maximum of 183 points left in the championship.

If Antonelli is able to outscore Russell by 16 or more points this weekend, then he can mathematically win the title as early as the following round in Austin, Texas.

To make matters worse for Russell, he will start Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid, after being forced to take on new power unit components which exceed the yearly limit for a driver.

This comes directly on the back of last weekend's power unit failure which ended his race early.

With an improbably steep mountain to climb to maintain a glimmer of hope in the title race, and starting from the back of the field for Sunday's race, Russell has promised to throw everything at this weekend.

"All-out attack; just trying to enjoy the weekend," he said.

"Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this [track] would be probably the second bottom of the list after Monaco. But unfortunately, just with how things have panned out, we have no choice but to take it here."

Antonelli started 19th for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza after taking on new power units, but drove one of the finest races in recent memory to claim a remarkable victory.

Hopes for Russell to replicate that are slim, with the Marina Bay street circuit tight, slow, and notoriously difficult to overtake on.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/h.title: Harry Connick Jr pens tribute to mother he lost as a 13yo
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/h.author: Mawunyo Gbogbo
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Harry Connick Jr has written a book about his mother to accompany his Carnegie Hall tribute performances. (Supplied: Georgia Connick)

These days, Harry Connick Jr is well known as a Grammy and Emmy Award-winning musician, singer, composer, actor, and a legendary live performer.

But the multi-platinum best-selling artist was also once a young boy whose mother believed in him.

Their time with each other was tragically cut short when Anita-Francis Livingston Connick, who was affectionately known as Babe, died when Connick Jr was just 13.

When his mother was diagnosed with ovarian cancer, Connick Jr, who was then a young piano prodigy, tried to immediately make her wish — that he would one day perform at Carnegie Hall — come true, so that she could be there in the audience.

"I called Carnegie Hall to see if I could play there," Connick Jr told ABC News.

Harry Connick Jr stepped out on stage at Carnegie Hall for the first time when performing on May 22, 2026. (Supplied: Harry Connick Jr)

So, Connick Jr waited.

He waited a long, long time.

Earlier this year, on May 22 and 23, Connick Jr made his Carnegie Hall debut.

The earlier date would have been his mother's 100th birthday.

It meant so much to Connick Jr to fulfil his mother's dream in this way that he rehearsed off site, so that the moment he walked onto the stage would be his first time performing there.

"It was probably the most unusual performance I've ever done only because it's been a place that I've wanted to play for almost 50 years," Connick Jr said.

Connick Jr penned the tribute Babe: Elaboratio. (Supplied: HarperCollins Publishers Australia and New Zealand)

"I first knew about it because my mum had a vision for me to play there.

"She always wanted me to perform there since I was a little kid.

"I had never been inside that room because I wanted to wait for a special occasion.

"And then on May 22, I walked out, never having been in there, and I walked out on the stage for the first time and played and it was just magical."

The performance is now an album available on streaming services, CD and vinyl, and he's written a book with the same title.

Connick Jr wanted Babe: Elaboratio A Tribute to My Mother to be written as he remembers her.

It isn't a biography, he says, it's a tribute.

Harry Connick Jr (right) with his sister Suzanna and mother Anita. (Supplied: Harry Connick Jr)

"It was important for me to speak from only my perspective because that's what the music was," Connick Jr said.

"It wasn't about other people's memories.

"It was all about an elaboration based on the memories that I had.

"Otherwise, it wouldn't have been as personal.

"I could have talked to my sister and compared stories with her, but it wouldn't have been my memory.

"I think there's something really special about how we all experience things and remember things.

"And it's so interesting how different people have different perspectives of things.

"So, if I wanted this to be my perspective, then I had to keep it within the confines of my own memory."

His mother was a trailblazing judge in New Orleans, and while her career milestones are categorically impressive, it's clear she also applied her determination and wisdom in motherhood.

In the book, Connick Jr paints a scene in which he packs his bags as a young boy with the aim of running away from home.

His mother, too, packs her bags, indicating she was going with him.

It's a beautiful, tender moment between mother and son that made Connick Jr realise he didn't want to run away after all.

"She was a great believer in the discovery process," Connick Jr said.

"And so, if there was an opportunity for me to learn something, experientially as opposed to her explaining it to me, then she would take advantage of that.

"So, when I was wanting to run away, she went and got her suitcase and said, 'let's go'.

Anita-Francis Livingston Connick was one of the first female judges in New Orleans. (Supplied: Harry Connick Jr)

"And it put me in a position of realising that I really didn't want to run away, and I was just upset about something.

"And she allowed me to figure that out for myself.

"And that's who she was.

"She was a big believer in that sort of way of raising kids."

Babe: Elaboratio is out now.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.title: ATO delays credit card ban as government backs down after business backlash
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.author: Clare Armstrong, Jane Norman, and Holly Tregenza
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

The government will foot the bill to delay the ATO credit card ban until the end of the financial year.  (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The Australian Taxation Office will delay the implementation of its controversial credit card ban until the end of the financial year.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has announced the government will cover the cost of the delay.

The tax office had justified the move by saying it would cost $200 million a year to absorb the fees.

A ban on credit card payments to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) will be delayed until next year, with the federal government agreeing to temporarily cover the cost of card surcharges after pressure from businesses.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the funding would allow the ATO to accept credit cards until June 30, giving them "more time" to consult with businesses and "get it right".

"We take very seriously the feedback ATO and the government have received in relation to implementing this surcharge ban," he said.

The ATO announced last week it would stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from December in response to the Reserve Bank's ban on surcharges.

The tax office had argued it would cost taxpayers about $200 million a year to absorb the fees and noted only 5 per cent of small businesses used a credit card to pay their tax bill.

But the decision sparked widespread backlash from small businesses, with several Albanese government ministers also raising concerns about the impact of the ATO's ban.

The government said the ATO had explored a number of options, including engaging with credit card companies to negotiate lower fees, but was unsuccessful.

Mr Chalmers said the government was aware the tax office was "grappling" with the issue before it made the decision in late September.

"But I don't know the specific timing," he said.

The treasurer said the government insisted on a transition period and the ATO initially landed on a two-month period, with the ban to take effect in December.

"Today we are substantially extending that period so that the ATO has the opportunity and the time to consult more, particularly with small business, on their implementation," he said.

Surcharge bans are supposed to save consumers money but retailers say they're being forced to put prices up and are finding ways around the reforms.

The ATO's credit card ban was announced after the RBA, which is independent, banned credit card surcharges across the board, a move hailed by Labor as a cost-of-living win for taxpayers.

Earlier in the week, Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar had called for a "clear message from government" in support of small business.

Mr McKellar welcomed news of the extension and said the organisation would continue engaging constructively to find a long-term solution.

"This announcement provides some much-needed breathing space for small business. Now there must be genuine consultation with business on this," he said.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor demanded the credit card ATO ban be scrapped altogether, claiming it was "screwing business".

"Today they've decided they're going to screw them tomorrow, or at least in nine months time," he said.

"No-one should be thankful to the treasurer for doing that."

Greens leader David Shoebridge said the delayed ban would offer some relief for small businesses, but argued the government had failed to tackle the underlying issue of price gouging by the major banks.

"Who wins again? The banks. This time, being funded by taxpayers in order to subsidise an incredibly profitable part of their business," he said.

"The answer here is to prohibit the banks from putting these charges on businesses."

Andrew McKellar welcomed the extension. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Yesterday, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil defended the Reserve Bank's decision to scrap the credit card fees, but argued the government had "real concerns" about what the ATO was proposing.

"We really want the ATO to go back and talk to business about what they have decided to do here and think about how they can find a solution that works for everyone," she said.

Members of the crossbench had also raised concerns about the change, with independent Kate Chaney calling on the ATO to reconsider or grant businesses a longer grace period to adjust.

"Credit cards are one way businesses manage cash flow when a tax bill lands. Removing that option with around eight weeks' notice makes things harder," she said.

The treasurer said costs for the extension would be finalised in the mid-year budget update, or MYEFO, due in December.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Nvidia-backed Lumentum sold out of AI server parts till 2029
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Lumentum Holdings’ optical components are “completely sold out” through early 2029 on demand from tech companies clamoring for faster artificial intelligence data centers, according to its chief executive officer.

Lumentum is unable to meet about 70% of demand for some products through next year, and won’t be able to address 30% of demand for some other products through 2028, Michael Hurlston said in an interview in Tokyo on Friday. Just six months ago, Hurlston said Lumentum was on track to sell out its capacity by 2028.

The company, which received an investment of $2 billion from Nvidia earlier this year along with rival Coherent, supplies advanced indium phosphide devices that help enable high-speed cloud computing and data transmission. Analysts on average expect Lumentum’s sales to more than double this year.

“We are really trying to catch up, add capacity as fast as we can, but we are very, very far behind what customers want,” Hurlston said. “We are completely sold out, so there’s no end in sight.”

That’s as some investors are becoming more cautious about rising costs and debt levels around a global rush to build data centers and other AI infrastructure. To allay concerns from key suppliers, big tech providers have been offering guarantees for long-term agreements.

The sector is bracing for further supply constraints as the U.S. reportedly considers a ban on new Chinese optical transceiver models. Lumentum and Coherent would not be able to fill the vacuum left by Chinese makers such as Innolight, according to Counterpoint Research.

To meet runaway demand, the San Jose, California-based company has ramped up capacity 12-fold at its key factory in the Tokyo metropolitan area over the past two years. It plans to invest at least $350 million in the site and a neighboring facility. It’s also expanded capacity at its plant in Caswell, England.

To expand its product lineup, however, the company will need to consider an acquisition, Hurlston said.

“I think probably in the next year, we’d like to add additional capability to what we currently have,” he said.

It takes three to five years for companies like Lumentum to build new production capacity. But hyperscalers have agreed to take on some of the capital spending risk, Hurlston said. “These hyperscalers are willing to put money behind it.”

Silicon photonics, which uses light to transmit data, is expected to replace copper-based interconnects in data center clusters as advanced AI hardware demands faster transmission. Optical networking also helps systems generate less heat and consume less power.

Japan is home to a broad base of companies with expertise spanning indium-phosphide semiconductors, optical fiber and silicon photonics, including Fujikura, Sumitomo Electric Industries, Furukawa Electric, Hamamatsu Photonics, Mitsubishi Electric and Hitachi High-Tech.

Lumentum acquired some of its technology via Japan through its 2018 purchase of Oclaro which had inherited Hitachi’s optical research. Today, its facility in Sagamihara, Kanagawa Prefecture, is one of the world’s most advanced indium phosphide device production sites, capable of delivering stable, high-quality output.

Earlier this year, Israeli silicon-photonics foundry operator Tower Semiconductor took full control of a 300-millimeter factory in Uozu, Toyama Prefecture, with plans to expand photonics shipments.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Lumentum Holdings is unable to meet 70% of demand for some products through next year. The company supplies advanced indium phosphide devices that help enable high-speed cloud computing and data transmission. Analysts on average expect Lumentums sales to more than double this year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Dozens protest in Tokyo after U.S. Marine accused of murder in Okinawa
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Dozens of protesters lined up in front of the Foreign Ministry on Thursday after a U.S. Marine was accused of killing a woman in Okinawa Prefecture, with many holding signs decrying crimes by U.S. service members.

The case is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fueled unease over the large U.S. troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China, with U.S. officials warning it could undermine ties vital to security in East Asia.

Public reaction to Anna Yagi’s killing, however, has been muted compared with the mass demonstrations that followed the rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three U.S. servicemen in 1995.

Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha last weekend and taking her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said.

Leaders of Thursday’s protest spoke over loudspeakers about abuses by U.S. service members and called on the government to respond, with others in the crowd rattling noisemakers in assent.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called the killing “extremely brutal and heinous,“ and Tokyo said it had strongly protested to the U.S. and demanded measures to prevent a repeat of such incidents.

Japan hosts the largest overseas contingent of U.S. forces globally. Most of the 18,000 Japan-based marines are stationed in Okinawa, which the U.S. held from the end of World War II until 1972.

That presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel.

The U.S. on Wednesday began a 48-hour pause of military operations and a ban on alcohol while troops undergo training on standards and discipline. Service members have also been given a monthlong curfew for a “period of reflection.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Dozens of protesters lined up in front of the Foreign Ministry on Thursday after a U.S. Marine was accused of killing a woman in Okinawa Prefecture. The case is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fueled unease over the large U. S. troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Alcohol makers in Japan tap into U.S. ready-to-drink market
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
NEW YORK – Japanese alcoholic beverage makers have entered the growing U.S. market for ready-to-drink (RTD) products, including those known as canned chūhai in Japan, but not canned beer.

While U.S. consumers are steering away from alcohol amid the soaring cost of living and rising health consciousness, RTD beverages are increasing their presence.

According to British beverage market research firm IWSR, yearly alcohol consumption in the United States fell by 1%, on average, between 2015 and 2025, with beer and wine seeing significant declines in recent years.

On the other hand, the consumption of RTD products, mostly canned beverages that are premixed and ready for immediate consumption, grew by an average of 14% per year during the same period.

The popularity of RTD products was ignited by the introduction of hard seltzers, which are carbonated alcoholic beverages that are not as sweet as other RTD options. According to IWSR President Marten Lodewijks, hard seltzers became a hit among U.S. consumers looking for an alternative to beer.

Last year, RTD products accounted for 8% of all alcohol servings in the country, up from 2% in 2015. The market size reached $22 billion.

In light of the growing popularity of RTD products, Japanese companies have introduced U.S. versions of popular RTD products in Japan.

In 2023, Suntory Holdings started selling its -196 Vodka Seltzer series in some U.S. states. The drinks became available nationwide in 2025.

Asahi Group Holdings released Zeitaku Shibori products tailored to the U.S. market last December, while Kirin Holdings started selling some Hyoketsu products in March.

Although RTD products currently hold only a small share of the U.S. alcoholic beverage market, Japanese makers believe that these products are promising and are rushing to establish foundations for sales in the United States, at a time when alcohol consumption in Japan continues to decline.

IWSR’s Lodewijks, however, highlighted fierce competition within the RTD market, saying that although there are a lot of RTD brands in the United States, only a few have been successful.

He also warned that the growing presence of RTDs could cause sales declines for beer and other makers.

Lodewijks added that Japanese beverage makers have “done very well” by associating their RTD products with Japanese food but added that they “haven’t really gone beyond that.”

Citing the rise of tequila as a symbol of Mexican culture, he added that Japanese beverage makers’ success hinges on whether their products can represent Japanese culture as a whole, including movies and music, because a simple link to Japanese cuisine has limited effects.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Japanese alcoholic beverage makers have entered the growing U.S. market for ready-to-drink (RTD) products. Last year, RTD products accounted for 8% of all alcohol servings in the country, up from 2% in 2015. The market size reached $22 billion.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan deal drought cuts IPO fundraising to lowest in 14 years
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Yasutaka Tamura
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Fundraising through initial public offerings (IPOs) in Japan is drying up, in contrast to a dealmaking boom across Asia, after regulatory changes and a dearth of artificial intelligence related companies depleted up the listings pipeline.

The number of first-time offerings fell to 32 this year through the end of September, the lowest nine-month tally since 2012, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. The amount of funds raised by companies including taxi app provider Go slid to a four-year low, even as fundraising surged in the rest of Asia.

While companies along the AI supply chain have driven dealmaking around the world, Japan is yet to match the wave of startups that can capture the imagination of investors, like in China. Some IPO hopefuls were also deterred by the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE)’s plan to raise the bar for companies to remain listed in its startup section, as part of its effort to attract more quality issuers.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: The number of first-time offerings fell to 32 this year through the end of September. The amount of funds raised by companies including taxi app provider Go slid to a four-year low.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Aces star A’ja Wilson collects record fifth MVP award
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
OCTOBER 9, 2026 – Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson became the first five-time MVP in WNBA history Thursday, extending her record with another selection as the league’s top player.

Wilson received 65 of 74 first-place votes, becoming the first player to win three straight MVP awards. Prior to the current streak, she also won in 2020 and 2022.

Wilson, 30, averaged 26.2 points to lead the league in scoring for the third straight season. She also averaged 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.9 blocked shots and 1.4 steals in 41 games.

Wilson (713 points) also received nine second-place votes. Minnesota rookie point guard Olivia Miles (442) earned six first-place votes to finish second, while Indiana Fever guard Kelsey Mitchell (287 points, two first-place votes) finished third.

Indiana guard Caitlin Clark finished fourth with 212 points and one first-place vote, followed by New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart with 171 points.

Wilson was very emotional when she was informed of the award on the Aces’ practice court.

Later, she reflected on an earlier segment of her life where she never would have guessed “five-time MVP” or “three-time champion” would be labels attached to her name.

“When you dream as a young girl, you dream so big and you write your goals out and you just never imagine you will be able to check them off,” Wilson said in a press conference. “And when you’re able to check them off — small wins, big wins — it truly means a lot. I think that’s why I cried a little bit harder on this one because 15-year-old A’ja wasn’t sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP, she wasn’t dreaming about being a three-time champion, she was dreaming about surviving this world.

“For me to sit up here surrounded by these trophies and to be able to play the game of basketball every single day, it just means a little bit more to me and it’s something I won’t take for granted.”

Wilson, an eight-time All-Star, scored at least 20 points in 33 games, the third-highest single-season streak in WNBA history behind Mitchell’s 35 this season and Wilson’s 34 in 2024.

Wilson also tied the WNBA single-season record she set in 2025 with 13 games of at least 30 points.

The Aces, winners of three of the past four WNBA championships, face elimination Friday night when they host the Golden State Valkyries in Game 3 of their best-of-five semifinal series. Golden State holds a 2-0 lead.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson becomes first five-time MVP in WNBA history. Wilson, 30, averaged 26.2 points to lead the league in scoring for the third straight season. She also averaged 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.9 blocked shots and 1.4 steals in 41 games

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Global financial institutions are beefing up their debt capital market teams in Japan, hiring bankers and relocating staff, to capture a boom in fundraising driven by mergers, acquisitions, and artificial intelligence capital.

In July, Goldman Sachs Securities hired Dai Kitatani, former head of debt capital markets at Citigroup Global Markets Japan, as head of DCM operations, and UBS Securities appointed Takehiro Sakuramoto, formerly of Goldman Sachs, as its first dedicated DCM head in four years.

At UBS, the DCM head role had been held concurrently by a banker covering financial institutions for the past four years. Sakuramoto’s appointment marks the return of a dedicated DCM head as the firm steps up its focus on debt capital markets.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office said Thursday that it has requested that Dutch authorities hand over Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the Netherlands, who has been convicted in Russia.

The office also requested the handover of eight others, including former ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan, from relevant countries.

In 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin for his country’s invasion of Ukraine. In retaliation, Russian authorities placed ICC officials, including Akane, on its wanted list.

In December 2025, a Moscow court sentenced Akane and others to prison terms of three years and six months to 15 years for issuing arrest warrants for those including the Russian president.

The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, which has criticized the ICC over its war-crimes investigation of U.S. military personnel, sanctioned Akane, a Japanese citizen, in August this year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Jennifer A. Dlouhy
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump accused Microsoft, Adobe and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a U.S. worker visa program and suspended them indefinitely from a longstanding immigration initiative that has served as a crucial talent pipeline for Silicon Valley and Wall Street.

The suspensions, announced Thursday by U.S. Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, also targeted information technology services giants Cognizant Technology Solutions, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Those firms, either based in India or with large operations there, are often called outsourcers for their role offering contract IT work to other businesses.

At a briefing in Washington, Sonderling said there were multiple federal investigations underway into the use of a system that allows U.S. employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency. Vance singled out Microsoft, the world’s third most-valuable company, for what he characterized as exploitation of the program.

SAN DIEGO – The USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier whose lengthy deployment in the Persian Gulf supporting U.S. President Donald Trump’s war on Iran sparked fears for its large crew’s welfare, arrived back at its home port on Thursday.

Families of service members lined the quayside in San Diego to welcome home loved ones they have not seen for almost a year.
