https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: France to fight student unrest by dispatching thousands of teachers
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Albertina Torsoli
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
France’s government has pledged to dispatch thousands of additional teachers to understaffed schools throughout the country in an effort to rein in student protests that have led to clashes with riot police.

Newly deployed software “helped identify schools facing situations I would call highly problematic,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray said in a TF1 television interview Thursday, unveiling details of an “emergency plan” to address student grievances. “Starting tomorrow, we will be deploying teachers to these schools.”

Some 3,000 substitute teachers that currently have no students “because the past assignment processes were inefficient” will be dispatched to classrooms “in the coming hours, in the coming days,” Geffray said. The minister will also allow recruitment of “a few hundred more teachers than normally permitted,” he said. The measures will cost “several tens of millions of euros” between now and year-end, Geffray said.

French students prolonged their protests on Thursday after Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said his policy response would only come at the end of October.

The government counted more some 71,500 demonstrators nationwide, including some 24,500 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry. While that’s well below the numbers on Tuesday, urban riots are on the rise with several “grave incidents” reported in cities such as Poitiers, Toulouse and Saint-Etienne, leading to more than 500 detentions, according to the ministry.

In a speech late Wednesday, Lecornu confronted concerns over energy prices, saying France would release diesel reserves as part of a recent agreement among Group of Seven nations. He didn’t address the student complaints that have fueled about two weeks of demonstrations.

The government faces a wide range of demands from farmers, fishermen, truckers and construction companies, as well as nurses and people who rely on cars for work and are being hit by high fuel prices. It has suspended the use of some weapons by police after a student lost a hand due to an explosive, further fueling students’ complaints about police violence.

Another day of demonstrations is planned for Oct. 13.

The student unrest is fueling investor concerns about France’s deficit targets, parliamentary gridlock over the government budget and uncertainty surrounding the presidential election and the fiscal policies of the candidates.

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whose party has never held the presidency, is leading in polls. French political uncertainty has roiled the bond market since President Emmanuel Macron’s failed gamble to call early elections in 2024, which resulted in a hung parliament.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan’s household spending falls again despite wage gains
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Yoshiaki Nohara
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Japan’s household spending fell for a ninth month even as wages continued to climb, showing consumers remain cautious as persistent inflation squeezes purchasing power.

Outlays by households adjusted for inflation declined 3.1% in August from a year earlier, the internal affairs ministry reported Friday. Economists had forecast a 3.6% drop. Spending rose 0.1% from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis.

The latest evidence of fragile spending complicates the Bank of Japan’s communications as authorities stay on track for further interest rate hikes. Real wages, adjusted for inflation, have risen every month this year, but that hasn’t translated into stronger consumer demand. A growing number of pensioners in the aging nation doesn’t benefit from wage growth.

“Government measures have kept a lid on inflation to a certain extent, but everyone can feel firsthand that food prices are rising in their daily shopping, so I think there’s a deep-seated sense that high prices are continuing,” said Harumi Taguchi, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “Even though wages are rising, the number of retirees is increasing, too, and they do not benefit from wage increases.”

BOJ Gov. Kazuo Ueda has repeatedly warned about upside risks for inflation, and many market participants are betting that the BOJ will raise the benchmark interest rate again by the end of the year. Friday’s data indicate that inflation and domestic demand aren’t rising hand in hand. Raising interest rates too fast or too high could weigh on the economy.

Slumping outlays on education and entertainment, food, home maintenance and rents and utilities led the overall index lower. The only component of the index that didn’t decline was transportation and communications, as spending related to cars edged higher.

The drop in outlays for education and the 5.2% year-on-year decline in spending on utilities reflect the impact of subsidies and other steps rolled out by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi as part of her campaign to rein in the cost of living.

The premier is also set to cut the sales tax on food to 1% from the current 8% starting in April in a bid to further help households with inflation. She has pledged to return the tax rate to the original level after two years.

“As for the sales tax cut, I don’t think it will have much of an effect. Rather than boosting consumption, I believe it will merely put a floor under it,” Taguchi said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Outlays by households adjusted for inflation declined 3.1% in August from a year earlier. Economists had forecast a 3.6% drop. The latest evidence of fragile spending complicates the Bank of Japan’s communications.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.K.’s Burnham says he is open to Germany joining joint fighter jet program
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Sam Tobin
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. was open to Germany joining a partnership between Britain, Italy and Japan — known as the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) — to build a new fighter jet, after he met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Thursday.

“I’ve indicated to the chancellor ... our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham told a news conference. “That is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan.”

There has been mounting speculation that the founding GCAP countries could open the door to Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter program collapsed in June.

A German official said no decision had been taken on participation in a new fighter jet program but reiterated that Merz favored a European option over Germany going it alone.

“We’re in a very early stage with the reevaluation of our options,” the official said. “Germany hasn’t taken a fixed decision, it’s looking in various directions.”

The GCAP has been set up to allow differing levels of involvement and it expanded for the first time in July, when Canada signed on as an observer, which could pave the way for deeper engagement in the future. Saudi Arabia has long been touted as another country interested in joining.

Germany is viewed by some defense experts as a suitable partner given its growing military budget and the fact that it already works on the Eurofighter Typhoon with the U.K. and Italy.

From Britain’s point of view, adding another country at a time when its military budget is under strain would help share the cost burden, but Japan may need convincing. Italy has also said in the past it would be open to new countries joining to help share the cost.

Japan is particularly focused on the 2035 target for the program given the security threat from China and the fact that it is due to start retiring its F-2 fighters in the middle of the next decade.

Some executives have warned that adding new partners could lead to delays. The GCAP is being led by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the U.K. is open to Germany joining a partnership between Britain, Italy and Japan. The Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) has been set up to allow differing levels of involvement. The GCAP has been led by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.

The death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal on Wednesday produced tears and anger in the Spanish capital’s emblematic Puerta del Sol square, the epicenter of the movement where hundreds are camping in protest.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the U.S. of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Maduro faces new charge of torturing U.S. citizens in custody
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Bob Van Voris
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife face a new criminal charge that they are responsible for the alleged torture of U.S. citizens detained in the South American country.

Prosecutors in New York filed the new criminal count Thursday, adding to existing charges against Maduro, 63. The government specifically said that Maduro conspired in the torture of nine people, three of whom were U.S. citizens.

Venezuelan officers detained an American identified only as “Victim-7,” who was tortured over two or three days, then transferred to a prison where he endured beatings, electric shocks, asphyxiation, forced injections and deprivation of food and water over 8½ months, according to the new court filing. At least two other U.S. citizens allegedly suffered similar torture and injuries.

The government says Maduro conspired in the torture of nine people, three of whom were U.S. citizens. At least two other U.s. citizens allegedly suffered similar torture and injuries.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.S. military to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: W.g. Dunlop
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
WASHINGTON – The execution by firing squad of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, a Pentagon official said Thursday, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said it would be carried out in “public.”

Hasan, a U.S. Army psychiatrist, shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. His execution will be the first by the U.S. military since 1961, and the first it has carried out by firing squad since World War II.

“It will be livestreamed. Details will follow,” the Pentagon official said on condition of anonymity.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Nidal Hasan shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. His execution will be the first by the U.S. military since 1961.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Mike Fu
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
OK, film buffs, time to do some finger calisthenics and ready your devices: Tickets for the Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) go on sale Oct. 17.

The 39th edition of TIFF brings more than 200 films from 112 countries and regions to screens across central Tokyo. The festival opens Oct. 26 with “Sukiyaki,” Takahisa Zeze’s dramatization of the story behind the 1961 song of the same name that became a surprise global hit, and closes Nov. 4 with Yeon Sang-ho’s action-horror flick “Colony.”

Under the theme “Connecting — Cinema Connects Us to the World Beyond,” TIFF invites attendees to cross geographical, cultural, linguistic and temporal borders through film. If you’re new to the festival, we’ve put together a guide to the basics, from buying tickets to choosing what to watch.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: Elvis comes back as a ghost in a noh theater play
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Kenji Kurabayashi
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
The king of rock ’n’ roll, Elvis Presley, has had many reimaginings in popular culture, but Japanese noh theater might be one of his most unexpected contexts yet. Nonetheless his ghost will be on stage in Tokyo on Oct. 10 and 11.

Theatre Nohgaku will bring its original noh play “Blue Moon Over Memphis” to the sophomore edition of Autumn Meteorite Tokyo, one of Japan’s largest performing arts festivals that takes place at the Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre in Ikebukuro. Although the play was previously performed at Waseda University’s Okuma Auditorium and Kyoto’s Kongo Noh Theatre in 2024 and at Tokyo’s Kita Noh Theatre in 2025, Autumn Meteorite contextualizes the work in the constellation of world theater and brings it to wider audiences. This time, the venue will be a contemporary theater stage instead of a traditional noh stage with four pillars and the show is just one of the festival’s international offerings.

“Blue Moon,” slated for the festival’s opening weekend, is a prime example of the artistic possibilities of cross-cultural exchange.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.summary: The play will be on stage in Tokyo on Oct. 10 and 11. The play was previously performed at Waseda University’s Okuma Auditorium and Kyoto’'s Kongo Noh Theatre in 2024.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.title: Former Greentown China head charged for taking bribes over stake in real estate project
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.author: Cannix Yau
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-.text:
Hong Kong corruption watchdog charges Zhang Yadong for taking HK$20 million in bribes from mainland Chinese developer for stake in latter’s project

Hong Kong’s corruption watchdog has charged the former head of a listed company for allegedly accepting HK$20 million (US$2.5 million) in bribes from a mainland Chinese property developer in exchange for acquiring a stake in the developer’s real estate project.

Zhang Yadong, 58, who was chairman of Greentown China Holdings from 2019 to 2025, faced a count of conspiracy to accept advantages, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said on Friday.

The case was mentioned at Eastern Court on Friday.

Prosecutors alleged that between January 2020 and March 2023, Zhang conspired with his son, a middleman, a shareholder of an estate developer in Dailian, Liaoning province, and others to accept bribes totalling HK$20 million from the shareholder in exchange for Greentown China acquiring equity interests in the developer’s project.

An ICAC investigation revealed that the shareholder had been pitching a Dalian real estate project to Greentown China since 2019.

Zhang allegedly solicited bribes from the shareholder through the middleman to facilitate Greentown China’s acquisition of the project for 440 million yuan (US$65.6 million).

“The bribes were suspected to have been deposited into the bank account of the defendant’s son in multiple payments through the middleman,” the watchdog said.

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-europe-us-.title: Ukraine, Europe, US to meet in Miami for talks on ending war
https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-europe-us-.text:
Officials from Ukraine, Europe and the US are meeting in Miami to discuss ways to break the deadlock in the war. The meeting comes as Russian strikes on Ukraine killed more than 70 people this week.

Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.

Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.

More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.

"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."

Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.

"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.

"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.

Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.

"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at ‌the negotiating table," he said.

Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.

"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.

Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.

"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on ​the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.

Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.title: Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.text:
A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting on Fort Hood has said that while he supports the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he is concerned about it being livestreamed.

Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times, told the BBC that the "method is befitting" for Nidal Hasan because other methods like lethal injection would be "doing him a favour".

Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers in a medical building at Fort Hood, in Texas, in 2009.

But while Lunsford agreed with the method of execution, he said it was "not something you should view for entertainment purposes".

Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, he said: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief."

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public will be able to view a livestream of the execution, saying it is important for people to see the consequences of this kind of crime.

If it goes ahead, and legal experts told the BBC it might not ever happen, it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.

Lunsford explained that while he is concerned about the "effect" and "message" a livestream would send to younger people, when it comes to the survivors, their families and the families of the victims, they "should be able to look at it".

"I'm gonna be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude you failed, I'm still here,'" he said.

"I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," the former sergeant explained.

"I think the method is befitting for him because the lethal injection - that's doing him a favour. Gas chamber? Is doing him a favour."

But Lunsford said that as a Christian, he has forgiven Hasan because "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him".

"We're taught that with your last breath you can ask for forgiveness and I think that's what he [Hasan] should do," he added.

Telling his account of what happened that day, he said Hasan got out of his chair and jumped onto a counter, before pulling out a weapon and discharging rounds.

Lunford said he was looking for an exit via the back door, which was "two or three strides" away from him when he was first shot above his left eye and then "hit two more times in my back" as he crawled behind a desk.

"At that point I played dead," he said. When Hasan moved on, he grabbed a nearby wounded soldier and went outside, where Lunsford said Hasan came up behind them and shot him again.

One memory he said that "bothers" him from the day was of a woman who told Hasan she was pregnant.

"We heard a gunshot and the last thing that girl was saying was: 'Oh my god, my baby, my baby.'"

Lunsford said personnel don't carry weapons in medical facilities, and that Hasan "took the coward's way out" to attack them there.

"And then for him to say he is fighting for his cause? I've read the Quran, and everything that he said he was doing that was in the Quran is not supported by the Quran," he explained.

Hasan's execution was announced by the Pentagon earlier this week, in what will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

Legal experts have told the BBC there are a number of hurdles around the livestreaming of this which could mean it is successfully challenged in court.

Some politicians have been vocal in their opposition.

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN it was "disgusting" while Republican Senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what "oppressive dictators" did.

"It should not be happening in America," he added in a post on X.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1w.summary: Alonzo Lunsford says he supports Nidal Hasan's execution by firing squad. He says he is concerned about the "effect" and "message" of the execution. Lunsf says he has forgiven Hasan because he doesn't have the same compassion for him. He said he was shot seven times and played dead

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.title: France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.text:
The French government has made its first sign of giving ground to teenage protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday evening, at the end of another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.

The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18, since protests began centred around demands for more resources in secondary education.

In what unions have billed as Act Four of the three-week movement, some 71,000 people staged protests across the country on Thursday, with 24,000 gathering at the Bastille in Paris.

Police once again intervened with tear-gas to disperse groups who attacked them with paving stones and homemade fireworks.

In Bordeaux, a lycée, or high school, was ransacked by protesters, and in Marseille a deputy-head was beaten up.

On Friday, some 140 lycées - out of 3,500 - were totally or partially closed, a big drop on previous days. But another day of action has been called for next Tuesday.

Geffray's announcement was the first material concession to the protesters' complaints.

It has long been recognised by all concerned in French education that too many school hours are being lost because of absent teachers and their non-replacement by available supply staff.

The minister said that thanks to new software coming online at the ministry, it would be possible to direct 3,000 supply teachers to the 500 or so lycées identified as being in the greatest need.

Many of these schools are likely to be in high-immigration city suburbs, where the lack of teachers is most acute.

Geffray also said that more money would be made available under an already existing scheme for those teachers who want to work overtime hours in order to plug gaps.

And he promised that students' grievances would be taken into account in forthcoming discussions on the education section of the 2027 state budget.

But the offer contained no major promise of new investment on a scale likely to appease protesters.

The government is wary of appearing to buy social peace because it knows France's precarious debt situation is being followed closely by international money markets.

Reaction from student leaders has been guarded to say the least.

Nathanaël Combary, who represents the most moderate of the three main lycée unions Renouveau Lycéen (Lycée Renewal), said students were waiting to see how the promise was carried out in practice: "We've had some announcements which correspond to part of our demands. But obviously people want to see the money and more concrete results."

"As long as we do not have €10bn on the table, we will continue our action," said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Etudiante (Student Union), which is close to the radical-left France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Mélenchon praised Thursday's demonstrations, saying on X that the students had "retaken the Bastille".

But at the other end of the political spectrum, a spokesman for the hard-right National Rally (RN) condemned the government's concessions.

"The message is: if you break things, you get given stuff," said Laurent Jacobelli. "When you burn cars, attack police, you gain something in return. It's the legitimisation of violence."

The movement is the most serious student unrest in France in many years, and comes against a backdrop of rising tension in the country - with anger over rising fuel prices and distress in the farming sector also liable to trigger protests.

Next Saturday, 17 October, has been earmarked as a day of demonstrations by a revived "yellow vest" movement.

In addition, the approach of presidential elections in April and May - in which both hard right and hard left are expected to perform strongly - is exacerbating the mood of confrontation.

The government is hoping that the approach of half-term holidays at the end of next week - as well as the arrival of colder and wetter weather - will take some of the sting out of the protests.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.summary: Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday. It comes after a day of protests by students demanding more resources in secondary education. The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.title: Thieves steal 30,000 wine bottles worth €5m in Italy, reports say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.text:
Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media reports.

Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad.

At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds.

Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy.

"A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said.

He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine.

"Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras; perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us."

He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen."

The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between €150 and €500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge.

The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made.

Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of €263m (£223m) last year.

There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken.

Seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c59v.title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c59v.text:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien".

In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital.

New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation".

"Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said.

The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.

Late on Thursday evening, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting and had expressed "outrage on behalf of New Yorkers".

"I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."

Trump has not yet commented publicly on the shooting.

The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession".

He was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS statement.

It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.

Mamdani, meanwhile, said he would ask Trump to end ICE enforcement actions in the city.

"I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities," he wrote on X on Thursday evening.

New York, which is a Democratic stronghold, is one of several American cities that bars its police officers from assisting with federal immigration enforcement.

A group of protesters gathered at the scene on Thursday evening, chanting "we want justice" and "ICE off our streets now".

There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one which caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

The man was arrested by police officers in December 2023 and released "a few days later" New York Governor Kathy Hochul says she has spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.title: Crazy Rich Asians to return as TV show with original film's stars
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.text:
Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name.

The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor.

"It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.

The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its £110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance.

Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.

It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.

Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.

He said the film had "changed his life", calling the cast and crew the "most creative and hilarious group of people I've ever known".

"Since then, this cast has become movie stars, superheroes, arena-filling performers and even an Oscar winner, so bringing everyone back together feels like coming home."

Lim added: "Our writers room is humming and we can't wait to share what we've come up with."

The series, co-produced by HBO and Warner Bros Television, will start production next year.

"Constance, Henry, Ronny, and Michelle are global superstars, and we know the passionate fans of the film and megahit novels can't wait to see more," said said Casey Bloys, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y.summary: Constance Wu and Henry Golding will return to lead roles in new TV series. The show will be made by HBO and will be produced by the same company. The series will be based on the hit film, which topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.title: Doctor accused of 1994 Rwanda genocide offences to face trial in UK
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy.text:
A doctor accused of a number of offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide is set to face trial in autumn next year.

Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He is the first person in the UK to have been charged over the genocide.

Brown, of Islington, north London, is charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.

A judge has now set his provisional trial date to begin in October 2027. He denies wrongdoing and has not yet entered a plea.

The defendant appeared via video link from Belmarsh prison on Friday for a pre-trial hearing at the Old Bailey during which Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb set a provisional eight to 12-week trial from October 4 2027.

A plea and case management hearing has also been set for 15 January.

He has indicated he will plead not guilty to the charges against him.

An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were killed during the 1994 Rwanda genocide which lasted for 100 days.

Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.

Between April 6 and 13 1994, he was allegedly a party to six murders and was later charged following a seven-year British investigation into the killings.

The court heard on Friday that a £100,000 bail condition, imposed earlier in October, had not yet been met.

Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC told the court the events in 1994 were "the most devastating wave of mass killing in modern history".

Jones said: "One hundred thousand were murdered in Kigali especially in the first days and weeks of the genocide."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz7.title: Three Saudi nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz7.text:
Three Saudi nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said after Yemen's Houthis said they targeted the facility.

The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X.

It said the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second one struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia.

One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement.

Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said.

Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two missiles, reports said.

The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks.

The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on October 6 and 7.

Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport.

The latest attacks come amid mark an escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.

The Houthi military spokesperson said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".

The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.

But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade, and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz7.summary: Yemen's Houthi group says it has attacked the airport with two missiles. The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities" The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zj.title: Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zj.text:
As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold.

"It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.

With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far.

"There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."

Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand.

"Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said.

"Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."

After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation".

The attacks, he said, were "tearing Kyiv apart".

Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too.

"I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says.

Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision.

A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided.

"People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter."

Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding.

For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent.

Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope.

"Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK."

The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties.

"We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says.

The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation.

Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking.

"Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling."

Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland.

"Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says.

For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside.

Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.

"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains.

"Everything that can be a Russian target."

On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door.

In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home.

The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation.

At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most.

"After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good."

Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her.

"She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains.

Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad.

Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before.

The authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens – the elderly and women with young children – are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts.

Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid.

The plants, constructed in fortified bunkers and protected from drone attack by huge steel cages, are each capable of providing electricity and heat to several hundred of the city's high-rise apartment blocks.

But with energy companies already talking about scheduled power cuts and supermarkets experiencing periodic shortages of some goods, the pressures to leave are growing.

Evgeniya Blyznyuk says she does not expect to see a mass exodus from the capital and says most people have yet to make up their minds, reluctant to jeopardise their jobs or take children out of school.

"They will postpone it until conditions become really unliveable," she says.

Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk and Anastasiia Levchenko.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6zj.summary: Ukraine's power grids are under attack by Russia's drone and missile strikes. The country's power grid is under attack with prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2.title: Cars torched and shops looted as anti-migrant violence erupts in South Africa
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2.text:
At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say.

Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast.

The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum.

This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details.

The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged".

It said that the new policy would still abide by the Constitutional Court ruling.

South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.

Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban.

Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said.

In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications.

Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors.

"There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC.

"At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added.

Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers.

Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property.

In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals.

Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported.

Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence.

The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction.

The latest unrest follows a July ruling by Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines.

The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents.

This prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration.

Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status.

Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa.

Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks.

Earlier this year, anti-immigration groups staged weeks of demonstrations demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country by 30 June.

The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments.

South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.

The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.

Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.

Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.

Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6dx.title: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6dx.text:
Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said.

"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.

The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said.

Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.

They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".

Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".

Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.

Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.

The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.

She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.

Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.

Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvly.title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvly.text:
Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm.

"I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees.

On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures".

OpenAI repeated these claims on Friday morning in a note from research leaders.

"We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said.

"Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment."

The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society.

The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company.

Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI".

Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote: "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.

"I believe that was why I was fired."

OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks.

"We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X.

"Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5n4.title: Meet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5n4.text:
When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student.

Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years.

But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses.

Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained.

Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral.

In a recent BBC Bangla interview, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving.

"I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening."

The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.

There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India.

Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation.

Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate.

Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings.

After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).

Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms.

Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him.

"It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview.

While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed.

After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital, Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg.

Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right."

After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences.

But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP".

And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats.

Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man.

The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter.

"The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla.

"If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said.

Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.title: Why Elon Musk is taking on India's richest man over Starlink
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.text:
Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.

The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.

India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.

Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment

The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.

The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel.

In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment.

Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers.

"You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".

On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.

"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.

Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries.

"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.

Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.

The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.

Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.

Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.

Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."

Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.

SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.

Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.

Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.

Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.

India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.

Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday.

The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.

In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

The remark comes a day after Musk accused powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqe8rn.title: Watch: Fleeing Kyiv for the countryside ahead of winter
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqe8rn.text:
Kyiv resident Olena Konoplia has decided to move to Ukraine's countryside, as Russian attacks on the city have intensified and the prospect of another cold winter looms.

Russia has been targeting Ukraine's power grid leaving locals without electricity and heating, and they will soon face prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures.

Olena told the BBC she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.

"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explained.

Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France amid a wave of protests by high-school pupils.

The BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from a large demonstration in northern France.

The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases.

The demonstrators are calling for better government investment in high schools.

A series of measures to tackle the housing crisis were defeated in parliament on Friday

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says the situation in Catalonia remains "very complicated".

The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is in Madrid, where a series of marches have been scheduled, after Spain's Congress rejected measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.

The BBC's Hugh Schofield is in Paris as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages spreads across France.

More than 400 people, mainly minors, were arrested on Tuesday, the country's interior minister says.

Turner’s early 19th century painting - Rome, from Mount Aventine - will be on display in the Italian capital for the first time ahead of an auction in London in December.

The BBC's religion editor Aleem Maqbool explains what Pope Leo's visit means for France.

All 29 people aboard the ship were safely evacuated using lifeboats, the Hellenic Coastguard said.

The BBC's Hugh Schofield looks at why the visit is met with enthusiasm the Church attributes to growing spirituality among the French.

The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay her rent set after it was increased by an investment firm.

Thousands turned out to witness Céline Dion perform in Paris on Saturday, her first show after a six year illness-induced hiatus.

Crowds have been flocking to the British Museum to see the Bayeux Tapestry as it's on public display in the UK for the first time since it was created nearly 1,000 years ago.

Tens of thousands of people lined the streets to pay their respects after 13 days of national mourning.

Thieves stole four Renoir paintings and abandoned two in garden as they fled, according to the local mayor.

The 70m (230ft) tapestry, which tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066, will be on display the British Museum.

Norway's new King takes the first major step of his reign as his father, the late King Harald V, lies in state at the Royal Palace.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9d.title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9d.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings.

The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests.

Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn).

One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation.

"Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said.

Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta.

It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region.

The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street.

Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment.

The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear.

UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO.

"We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors.

He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans.

"It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC.

This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research.

Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said.

"It's more like a bet on a dream", he added.

Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment, thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability.

OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to.

There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more.

That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create.

In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public.

The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each.

AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought.
