https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjzx.title: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjzx.text:
Warning: This article contains strong language.

Meredith Whittaker has little patience for the AI doom that dominates headlines - she thinks warnings of AI turning on humanity is a fear "not anchored in science".

"The risk is very real," says the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app of the same name, "but it's not the shiny ghost stories the wild-eyed boys are talking about".

Instead, she believes the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly.

She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material, reportedly leading the US to prepare a military response.

"We almost went to war with China," she tells BBC Global Women.

"A system that produces faulty intelligence and almost gets us into a war with China should not be considered super-intelligent by any standards."

Signal has an estimated 40-70 million users - a drop in the ocean next to WhatsApp, which has billions.

But it is renowned for its tough stance on protecting users' privacy - it hides who is sending a message from its own servers, limiting the data available to outside observers or hackers.

Time magazine named Whittaker one of the most powerful people in AI. She moves through the rooms where its future is discussed, from Silicon Valley boardrooms to Downing Street, Davos and the Vatican.

She studied literature at university and joined Google in 2006 as an entry-level temp with no computer science degree.

In late 2017, she made her name when a colleague told her about Project Maven, a secret Google contract with the US Department of Defense to build AI for drone targeting.

She understood what it meant to "compress the kill chain": to shrink the time between a machine flagging a target and someone deciding to fire, reducing deliberation. With thousands of colleagues, she pushed back.

"This is going to launder bad intelligence and bad data," she remembers arguing publicly.

The following year Whittaker helped organise a walkout, in which some 20,000 staff protested against the company's handling of several issues, including what they felt was the rushed introduction of new technology. Google dropped the contract and Palantir picked it up.

She draws a direct line from Maven to the US missile attack on a school in Iran this year, which she says relied on the system and on outdated intelligence that identified the school as a military target.

"This is exactly what we were warning about in 2017," she says.

In response, Palantir told Global Women there was "no evidence that Palantir's software was at fault in this terrible tragedy".

It added that "Palantir is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies". And earlier this year it's UK and Europe boss, Louis Mosley told the BBC that "there's always a human in the loop, so there is always a human that makes the ultimate decision".

The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".

Governments, including the UK's, argue for more access to conversations on messaging apps. They say this is to protect women and children.

At London Tech Week 2026, then Prime Minister Keir Starmer said technology companies would be expected to detect and block nude images on children's devices, or face legislation.

Whittaker argues children would be able to circumvent any such measures, calling the government's approach "an unprecedented regime of communication and information controls".

The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology told the BBC it is preparing legislation.

Would Signal leave any country, the UK included, that forced it to weaken its encryption?

"Yes! My God, I have a backbone," she says. "It doesn't change based on mood. It doesn't change based on consultants."

Faced with exposing people "who rely on us, sometimes in the context of life or death, to surveillance that could be weaponised against them", she says, "we would leave the market".

The app is fully or partially blocked in Russia, China and Iran.

Rani Govender, Head of Child Safety Online at the National Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children, told the BBC it hears from children who have been groomed and moved on to end-to-end encrypted platforms, where they are coerced into creating child sexual abuse material.

"Tech companies are responsible for the design choices they make, and they cannot ignore the risks those choices can create for children."

But Signal does have support from some women's groups, often those from the Global South who use the app themselves.

"In a time of state surveillance and cyber-attacks, Signal is a tool for survival," says Hera Hussain, founder of the gender abuse charity Chayn, which is active throughout South Asia.

"With any platform, it can be used by bad actors too, and we have to hold that truth too."

I put to Whittaker a case from Canada, where police officers shared racist and misogynistic messages in a Signal group which leaked only when one of them passed it on to the media.

A lawyer for one officer said the men believed Signal was as private and safe as their own home.

"If they had that conversation in the kitchen and their bro snitched, would it be: 'What are we doing about kitchens?'" she asks.

"It has to work for everyone or it works for no-one. This is the principle of fundamental rights. They apply even to assholes."

She points to a US woman jailed after Meta handed over messages showing she helped her daughter access abortion in a state where it had been criminalised.

Private communication, she says, protects people from many kinds of harm - "an abusive spouse, a misogynist law enforcement officer with access to a database, or an authoritarian government that doesn't think women should get educated".

What would she want to say to a woman who wants to enter the tech field but is intimidated by the gendered aspect of the profession?

"Do you love it?" she says.

"Do you sit down at a terminal and feel a rush of energy? Do you enjoy playing with and defining AI systems?"

Then she pauses and says: "Are you able to navigate interesting and gnarly environments where not everyone is going to be chill? Because there's nothing more dangerous than being a coward in front of a bully."

I ask her if these environments are full of bullies.

Her colleague says, "I think that's 2pm" - the time we agreed to end the interview.

Meredith smiles. "I'd say don't be a simp," she says, using a term for someone who shows extreme deference to authority figures.

"It's not going to help you. Don't laugh at the joke if you don't think it's funny."

Additional reporting by Katie Roberts
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjzx.summary: Meredith Whittaker is the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app. She says the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly. She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq98.title: £15m spent cleaning illegal waste supersite in ancient woodland
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq98.text:
The clearance of a notorious illegal waste "supersite" in Kent has been completed after 15 months at a cost of £15m to the taxpayer.

The dump at Hoads Wood, near Ashford, which is on a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) known for rare plants and wildlife, was targeted by criminals who dumped nearly 40,000 tonnes of waste over six months in 2023.

It was the first supersite in England to have central government money spent on its clear-up, with work at two other sites bringing the total taxpayer's bill to £26m.

The government said the completion of works on Friday showed "just how serious" it was about tackling waste crime and restoring affected countryside.

The Environment Agency-led clean-up operation began in June 2025 and has seen 2,500 lorry loads of waste removed from the woods by specialist contractors to a landfill site in Essex.

The countryside charity CPRE Kent, residents and Kent Wildlife Trust joined forces in 2024 to campaign for the clearance of the waste, which was piled up to 15ft (4.6m) in places.

They welcomed the work's completion but some are concerned the criminal gangs may return to dump waste.

One of the organisers of the 'Rescue Hoads Wood' campaign said the cleared site would now be "catnip" to both organised gangs and opportunist fly-tippers.

He told the BBC: "Our biggest fear now is people are going to be able to access this site and start dumping on it again and unless the authorities are quick it will happen again."

The Environment Agency (EA) said it was extending the current restriction order in place that prohibits access and had dug ditches to make the site inaccessible to waste trucks.

Matthew Higginson, the EA's area environmental manager, said the regulator, police and local authorities had a joint "trigger plan" in place.

"That will bring all law enforcement partners to work together closely and much more quickly to stop anything like this happening in the future," he said.

Meanwhile, there remain conservation concerns over the future of the countryside site.

Ian Rickards, area manager for Kent Wildlife Trust, said it would take decades for ancient woodland species to return.

But he added: "It won't recover as it was but there are benefits to this. You've now got open space within the woodland. You've got wet bodies. You've got ponds. You've got these piles of dead wood as well.

"All of this will start creating, collecting and attracting wildlife back into here so it'll be fascinating to see how the site recovers."

The Hoads Wood illegal waste site is one of hundreds across England that include a number of so-called "supersites" - those that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish - that were exposed by the BBC earlier this year.

As well as the £15m spent on clearing Hoads Wood, another £6m has been spent on the clearance of an illegal supersite in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, and a further £4.8m of taxpayers' money has been allocated to the clear-up of a third site near Wigan.

In August, the government launched a national action plan to tackle waste crime, which it estimates costs the country more than £1bn every year.

But Hoads Wood campaigners have criticised the authorities for not acting quickly enough when the illegal tipping was first reported at the Kent site.

At the height of the activity in the summer of 2023, locals said there were as many as 20 to 30 trucks per day dumping waste at the ancient bluebell woodland.

The EA's Matthew Higginson said the agency did respond quickly to reports of the dumping but had to spend time investigating "to make sure we had a robust case to take to court in order to get a restriction order which closed the site".

Investigations into who was behind the dumping are ongoing, with three arrests made in February 2025.

Environment secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "This government is taking action on the illegal waste sites that have blighted communities.

"Handing this ancient woodland back to local people, alongside our nationwide clean-up of waste sites, shows just how serious we are about restoring the places people love."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5n4.title: Data centre raises noise and wildlife impact fears
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5n4.text:
A huge data centre planned in a village near a nature reserve would generate "very high noise levels" without extensive measures to block it, experts have said.

Plans have been submitted to South Norfolk Council for a 150 megawatt facility in Keswick on the edge of Norwich, which includes assessments of its potential environmental impact.

The scheme is causing concern, with thousands of people signing a petition against it, due to fears it could harm neighbouring wildlife sites.

But Norwich Apex Data Centre has defended the scheme, claiming assessments showed it would not harm protected areas like Marston Marshes.

The data centre is also causing concern over its potential water usage, noise pollution and the scale of the facility harming the landscape.

Assessments of the noise it could create found it has the "potential to generate very high levels of noise to the surrounding area" and would require extensive mitigation measures.

The majority of noise would come from the 72 chiller units on the roof.

A spokesperson said: "Our environmental assessments conclude the data centre will not harm nearby designated wildlife sites.

"The data centre will use air-cooling technology, meaning no water will be required for cooling. Water will only be needed for everyday uses, such as toilets and staff facilities, with none taken from nearby rivers or marshes.

"The facility has also been designed so that operational noise levels at surrounding sensitive locations are in line with existing background levels."

The firm also said the facility could create up to 150 permanent jobs and that it would create planting and landscaping to screen the development and reduce the visual impact.

It would also be located close to an electrical substation for offshore wind farms in the North Sea, from which it could draw power.

The project has already been met with opposition, with thousands signing a petition against it.

Daniel Elmer, the Conservative leader of South Norfolk Council and county councillor for Keswick, said he will formally object to the proposed facility.

He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "My personal view, is that it is just too damned big for the site it would be on.

"It is right next to the marshes and the southern edge of Norwich, while it is near a listed church.

"That's the southern gateway into the city of Norwich. I think you have to think, in terms of the Norwich 'brand', what visitors to the city would see when they travel down that road.

"What they see needs to be aesthetically pleasing and I am not sure that is what they will get, given the application which has been submitted at the moment."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c209.title: How cleaning up the air is speeding up global warming - and revealing a bigger problem
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c209.text:
This July, during Britain's record-breaking hot summer, a curious row broke out on X over climate science.

Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice shared a Telegraph article headlined: "Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution." He said cleaner air, rather than carbon dioxide, was behind higher temperatures and claimed the public had been "gaslit".

He was wrong to suggest that carbon dioxide is not the primary driver of global warming. But the science he was distorting is real - and much more interesting than his original claim.

The fossil fuels that we've been burning for more than a century produce two very different kinds of pollution. As is well known, carbon dioxide warms the Earth. But less well-known is sulphur pollution, which forms vast numbers of tiny particles in the air and reflects sunlight back into space, partly counteracting the warming effect of carbon.

Thanks to clean-air policies around the world - like the US's Acid Rain Program in the early 1990s, that reduced gas pollution from power plants - sulphur emissions are falling sharply while carbon dioxide emissions remain near record highs.

Scientists increasingly believe the loss of that cooling effect is slightly speeding up global warming.

The past three years were the three warmest ever recorded, and the Met Office says 2027 is "very likely" to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record.

And away from social media, the argument over Tice's tweet raised an even more interesting - and worrying - question. Is it possible that our planet is actually more sensitive to greenhouse gases than we imagined?

And if so, might the climate be changing more rapidly than we feared?

Global temperatures jump around naturally from year to year. El Niño, for example, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean, can temporarily push them higher. So a run of record hot years does not necessarily mean the underlying rate of global warming has increased.

Reto Knutti and his team at ETH Zurich have tried to strip out the effects of El Niño and other natural fluctuations to reveal the underlying trend.

"It's pretty clear that the rate of warming has accelerated," says Knutti, a professor of climate physics at the Swiss university and a former co-ordinating lead author for the IPCC - the UN-backed body that produces the world's most authoritative assessments of climate science.

A separate study published this year reached a similar conclusion after accounting for several major natural influences.

And it seems aerosols are playing a role.

Burning coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which forms tiny particles known as sulphate aerosols. These particles are bright and reflect some sunlight before it can reach and warm the planet's surface.

You've probably heard the greenhouse analogy used to explain global warming. Gases like carbon dioxide make it harder for heat to escape from the Earth, rather like the glass windows of a greenhouse.

Well, sulphur pollution acts a bit like dust on the greenhouse windows. The more dust that gathers on those windows, the less sunlight gets inside, and the slower the greenhouse heats up in the first place.

Dr Øivind Hodnebrog, a principal researcher at Cicero, the Norwegian climate research institute, has studied how falling aerosol pollution affects the climate. "Sulphate aerosols, they are really small particles, but they are bright particles," he says.

As well as reflecting sunlight, aerosols also cool the planet by changing the formation of clouds. Aerosols act like tiny seeds around which water vapour can condense, making some clouds brighter or longer-lived. Pollution from ships can even create bright trails through marine clouds visible from space. So more aerosols mean brighter clouds and more reflection, and so less warming.

But sulphur pollution also damages human health (it can get into our lungs and make it harder to breathe), and causes acid rain, which can destroy forests and kill fish - and so countries have spent decades cutting it. Emissions have fallen sharply in Europe, North America and China, while new rules have also reduced sulphur pollution from shipping.

In our greenhouse analogy, it's as if we've wiped some of the dust away from the windows of the greenhouse, allowing in more sunlight.

And while carbon dioxide remains in the climate system for centuries, sulphate aerosols survive in the atmosphere for just days or weeks. So when sulphur emissions fall, their cooling effect disappears almost immediately.

The effect is strongest where sulphur pollution has fallen fastest. One study estimates it has added around half a degree to summer warming in western-central Europe since 1980.

Prof Piers Forster, a climate scientist at the University of Leeds and another senior author of the IPCC's most recent assessment, estimates that declining aerosol pollution may now be adding around 0.05C to 0.1C of warming per decade.

But aerosols can only explain part of the recent acceleration in warming. Greenhouse gases remain much more important.

Forster estimates they are currently adding around 0.2C of warming globally per decade. "It is a very significant contribution," he says of the aerosol effect, "but it is not as important as the greenhouse gas contribution by quite a long way."

"The aerosols have masked some of the greenhouse gas warming from earlier," is how Hodnebrog explains it.

"Masked" - that's an interesting word he uses. What he means is cleaner air is not causing the underlying warming; it is removing some of the cooling that had been holding that warming back.

So if cleaner air is only responsible for part of the recent acceleration in global warming, what else is at work?

To see what else might be going on, scientists zoom out and look at the Earth as a whole: how much energy it absorbs from the Sun, and how much heat it loses back into space.

Scientists call the difference Earth's energy imbalance.

Cleaner air is part of that picture. Fewer sulphate particles mean less sunlight is reflected away - in our greenhouse analogy, the windows are cleaner.

For a long time, the Earth has been absorbing more energy than it loses. That surplus is what warms the planet. And Knutti says that imbalance has roughly tripled over the past two decades - although the precise increase depends on which years are compared.

Greenhouse gases principally work by making it harder for heat to escape out into space. That's what we're all familiar with. But when you look at Earth's energy imbalance, you find that there's also more sunlight getting in (and therefore more heat that can be absorbed).

So what else might be letting more sunlight in?

Much of that change appears to involve something we have already encountered in this story: clouds. We saw how sulphur pollution can make some clouds brighter and longer-lived, reflecting more sunlight away. But global warming itself can also change clouds. As some parts of the ocean warm, low cloud cover can diminish. That matters because clouds are bright, while the ocean beneath them is dark. Remove some cloud and more sunlight reaches the sea, where much of it is absorbed as heat.

That can create a feedback: warming reduces some cloud cover, which allows more sunlight in, which produces still more warming.

And the oceans are certainly heating up. The World Meteorological Organization says the oceans have warmed more than twice as fast over the past two decades than they did between 1960 and 2005.

Dr Paulo Ceppi, a climate physicist at Imperial College London, says his research suggests this feedback loop between climate change and clouds is more important than sulphur pollution in explaining the recent decline in low clouds.

But there's still lots of uncertainty. Scientists say the impacts of cleaner air, natural variations and the effects of warming itself are all tangled together. And, when I asked Knutti how much of the cloud change came from each, his answer was simple: "We don't know."

And this is where the story takes an even more worrying turn.

That uncertainty matters because clouds are one of the hardest things to represent in the computer simulations scientists use to project future warming. Some models show more warming than others for the same amount of greenhouse gas emissions.

Scientists call this variability "climate sensitivity": how much the climate responds to gases like carbon dioxide.

And the recent observations give Knutti and his colleagues a new way to test those models. They found that models which best predicted the recent warming, as well as the rise in the Earth's energy imbalance, are also the ones with a more sensitive climate.

In other words, the models that predict more warming are looking like the most accurate.

His team's analysis suggests that the same emissions could produce about 25% more warming than we previously thought.

And a study published in the journal Science last year points in a similar direction. Models which projected relatively little warming struggled most to reproduce the observed rise in Earth's energy imbalance.

Under policies governments currently have in place, the world is estimated to be heading for around 2.8C of warming by the end of the century. Forster says that if this new evidence proves correct, the same broad emissions path could instead produce warming closer to 3.5C.

It sounds serious - but there are important reasons for caution.

Warming appears to have accelerated, but Forster says that does not mean it will keep doing so. He points out that the recent observations that underpin these estimates cover a relatively short period.

"We have to be very cautious of how we go about interpreting observations that last for one or two decades," he says.

The satellite record is short, natural variations are large, and these new studies do not overturn previous estimates.

But still, some scientists are alarmed.

So - is cleaning up the air making global warming worse?

In one narrow sense, yes. Removing sulphate pollution takes away some of the cooling that had been counteracting greenhouse warming. That really has contributed to the recent acceleration. But cleaner air has not caused climate change.

The aerosol story may help explain part of that acceleration. But the wider evidence raises a more worrying possibility: that the climate responds more strongly to greenhouse gases than central estimates have assumed.

If that's correct, the same emissions could produce more warming than we expected. Climate risks increase with every fraction of a degree of warming, with the potential for more severe heatwaves, floods, droughts, and wildfires as temperatures rise.

Some of the science we have explored here is complex and important questions remain unresolved. But on the central point, the science is clear: the more greenhouse gases we emit, the warmer the planet will become.

And, if the climate really is more sensitive than previously thought, cutting emissions quickly becomes even more important.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw80.title: Fund launched to back community wellbeing projects
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw80.text:
A charity has launched a new fund aimed at improving health and wellbeing in Jersey.

The Island Health Fund will create a dedicated way for individuals, families, businesses and charitable trusts to support projects such as medical equipment, research, clinical innovation, community health initiatives and specialist training, the Jersey Community Foundation said.

Chief executive Anna Terry said: "This is not about replacing government funding. It is about what additional philanthropic support can make possible."

An independent panel would be set up to oversee funding decisions and help shape priorities, the foundation said.

Tom Binet, health minister, welcomed the initiative "and the opportunity it creates to attract new philanthropic support for health and wellbeing in Jersey".

"This is a new opportunity for individuals, families, businesses and others who want to contribute to the future of health in our island," he said.

Jersey Community Foundation said it would now work with healthcare providers, charities, government and businesses to identify areas where extra funding could make a difference.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv2d.title: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv2d.text:
Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America.

Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down.

The question is: what is he able to do with just a few weeks to go before election day - and will it work?

Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues.

The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US.

Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months.

While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline.

David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices.

"Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says.

Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates.

"The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says.

While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel.

"A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said.

The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies.

Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself.

"The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained.

The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said.

"The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion."

The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product.

"If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said.

But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts.

Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns, following pressure from Trump to do so.

De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree".

Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution.

"As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears."

Earlier this week, Trump said he was "thinking about" suspending federal tax on gasoline.

De Haan said the president has also been imploring states to cut state taxes on gasoline and several have done so, including Ohio and Georgia.

State taxes form a "moderate portion" of what consumers pay at the pump, and those reductions have helped reduce prices and national averages, he said.

However, suspending or reducing the federal levy on gasoline would require the cooperation of Congress.

"That may be difficult to obtain ahead of the midterm elections," said De Haan.

It is also a costly measure.

De Haan estimated that in Indiana, which cut its tax on gasoline in May, it has cost the state government $1bn (£760m) in lost revenue.

Trump has also previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

While that would provide partial relief in the Gulf and Midwest, according to Pearce, he adds it would be of "little benefit" to the Northeast and West Coast.

"The policy risks backfiring because it would result in stockpiling of diesel, and as that storage runs out, refineries would need to cut back on production," he said.

"That would raise prices of other energy products, including gasoline."

De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated".

"The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said.

That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.

Even if those conflicts are resolved, Ruisard said that due to damage to facilities in the Middle East caused by military strikes it would still take production four to six months to return to normal.

"The message to consumers and industry is that regardless of what happens and whether the president is able to successfully negotiate that kind of a deal," he said.

"High prices are here to stay for a little while at least."

Additional reporting from Daniel Bush

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.text:
A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire.

Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year.

West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs.

Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said.

Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it.

"So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight."

The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car.

At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise.

Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars.

"Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added.

The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund, which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry.

West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year.

Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow.

"They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car."

Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car.

"So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art.text:
Everton are currently seventh in the Premier League after seven matches

Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.

The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m.

In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter".

"The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said.

"When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters.

"With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton."

TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window.

In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025.

Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.

Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong.

Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after.

The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry.

TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward".

"Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued.

The decision of Everton's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times.

A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players.

The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG.

It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League.

Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners.

TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis.

Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers.

This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure.

Speaking on 5 Live Breakfast, former Everton goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis described TFG's plans to sell the club as a "shock".

"It's come as a bit of a shock. They have stabilised the club. There was so much financial uncertainty when they arrived, it's felt like a turbulent time," said Brown-Finnis.

"We [Everton] have a stadium to be crazily proud of, it's going to generate revenue from a commercial point of view.

"If the Friedkin Group sells up tomorrow, they have left the club in a much better place. I just hope that they do their due diligence.

"I hope the new owners want to drive the club forward. Everton fans have spent too much time in a financially turbulent era."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.text:
More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy.

Jersey's high value residency programme grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals.

One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island.

However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling".

About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme.

O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes.

"They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals.

"So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy."

High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income.

They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax.

O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way.

"First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income.

"And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand.

"High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off."

Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them.

He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy.

"If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said.

"So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%.

"We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax.

"We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions."

John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme.

He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly".

"I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community.

"As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all.

"I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally.

"And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work.

"They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmew.title: Polanski vows to stay on as Green leader as criticism mounts
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmew.text:
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.

The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he "should resign", adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Lichtenstein's comments come after former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.

Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that.

The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year.

Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.

In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with – it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee."

Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.

The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom".

Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told BBC Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election."

She later appeared to mollify her criticism slightly, posting on X that Polanski's leadership had "transformed the party" and she hoped he would now "help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures".

Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.

However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".

Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.

On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist.

"I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."

Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."

In private, plenty of longstanding Green figures remain frustrated and accuse Polanski of being "missing in action" over the motion.

They say the result is an untenable situation where he leads a party whose policy on the Middle East he disagrees with.

"He is in danger of losing the confidence of both wings," one critic pointed out, referring to how some supporters of the motion have now been left irritated too by Polanski's refusal to publicly back them.

But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.

Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit.

"I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now from the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".

The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.

Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons between her party's previous antisemitism scandal, telling BBC Breakfast she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.

Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.title: Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.text:
Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, seeing off a challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski.

Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali held the north London seat for Labour, but the party's majority was reduced from 11,572 to 3,364.

At a victory rally, Abdi-Wali told supporters: "People voted for hope and now we're going to be able to deliver for them."

The by-election, which was triggered after former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP, had been seen as a key test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can win over voters who have switched to the Greens.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast after his defeat, Polanski said the result proved his party was "more of an electoral threat in these seats than we've ever been before".

"This is the foundation we're looking to build on," he added.

He insisted he would stay on as leader despite the result. Polanski is under pressure over his response to a policy motion passed by members at his party's conference that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Labour's Abdi-Wali secured 45% of the vote, followed by Polanski on 33%.

However, the Green Party's vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.

The inner London constituency has been Labour since it was created in 1983, with the party taking at least 40% of the vote at every general election.

In her victory speech at the count in Camden, Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a testament to the success of diversity in the borough.

Later, speaking at a rally alongside Labour Party deputy leader Lucy Powell, she thanked voters for making her the MP "for this constituency that has given me so much".

"It gave me a community, gave me a home, gave me an opportunity, gave me an education, gave me so many of my friends - everything I am today has been shaped by it."

She told supporters that as an MP she would campaign on ending homelessness and taking Thames Water into public ownership.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham congratulated Abdi-Wali on a "fantastic campaign" while Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir said she was "a brilliant champion for our communities".

Asked what had gone wrong for his party, Polanski said the Greens had increased their vote share in the seat since the last election, describing the result as "our second best by-election result in Green Party history".

"I'm not going to sit here and pretend I'm not disappointed. No politician runs in a by-election and doesn't want to win," he told BBC Radio 4's Today.

"But at the same time, to see the growth in what was supposedly a safe Labour seat since 1983 [and] is now a marginal Labour seat, that's clearly growth and next time we can get it over the line."

Speaking to broadcasters earlier in the day, Polanski dismissed suggestions his leadership was under threat, saying: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."

He said voters had been "excited about our plans for rent controls, tackling the climate crisis and nationalising Thames Water".

The Greens had hoped they could overturn Labour's substantial majority in the constituency after the party made gains in local elections in the area in May.

It saw a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned.

Earlier, former party leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC Polanski had failed to show leadership over the motion, passed by party members, which said Zionism was a form of racism.

Speaking after polls closed but before the result of the by-election was announced, Lucas criticised Polanski for not taking part in the debate or voting on the motion at the Green Party's conference in Brighton on Sunday, describing the motion as "dangerous" and "divisive".

Asked if Polanski should stand down, she said: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks.

She continued: "I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.

"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."

The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Polanski was not present for the vote on the motion, after leaving the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.title: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm70.text:
In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.

Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has quite the story to tell.

She arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s, grew up locally in Camden, became a councillor four years ago, the council leader in May and is now Sir Keir Starmer's successor as the MP.

But in the offices of Camden Council at three o'clock this morning, the focus of the press pack, me included, was on Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, as we waited for the result.

This constituency has long been a safe Labour seat – the political home of the former prime minister and before that the former cabinet minister Frank Dobson. So a Labour victory here falls in the column marked "relief" for Downing Street rather than "jubilation".

Nonetheless, the Greens did very well in local elections in London in May, riding the crest of a political wave which began shortly after Polanski became the party's leader just over a year ago.

His failure to win here will prompt questions from some about stalling momentum, but the party can and does point to the big swing to them since the general election and a result that was by a long way the second best ever result for them at a Westminster by-election.

Incidentally, in finishing third the Conservatives have beaten Reform UK for the first time in an English by-election since the general election. It seems likely that Reform's result was hampered by Restore Britain, who managed almost half as many votes as Reform did, in a constituency not very favourable to either party.

But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election – and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.

Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And he repeatedly declined to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.

But this morning he did speak to journalists.

He told BBC Breakfast that if he had he been there for the vote he "would have voted for the amendments".

Asked if he would have voted against the motion in the hall on that day, Polanski said: "the motion as amended I would have voted for, the motion unamended I wouldn't have voted for."

He added: "I think it's an imperfect motion, there's parts I disagree with and parts I agree with."

Some in the party are furious about what has happened in recent days, with one figure telling me: "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control."

Green Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.

Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.

And – significantly – the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.

Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".

He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people".

"I believe that is clearly racist," he added.

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

And asked if he believed in a two-state solution – an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other – he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".

He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together".

"No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.

But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.

The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.title: Alison Hammond: 'I thought I was having heart attack on air'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y.text:
Alison Hammond has said she feared she was having a heart attack on air when she had to rush off ITV's This Morning midway through the programme last week.

The presenter appeared to clutch her chest as she left the show last Friday, and was taken to hospital to have a heart check-up.

She turned out to have suffered a panic attack, and said the experience was "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through".

Returning for her weekly slot on Friday, she told viewers: "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack. I'm so glad I'm here. I feel so grateful. I feel so thankful to God, to everything in life."

She added: "It felt like a heart attack. It was very real."

Alongside co-host Dermot O'Leary, Hammond introduced the programme by thanking him for holding the fort after her dramatic early exit, and also thanking everyone who sent good wishes.

She added: "It was the first time I've ever experienced anything like that. Secondly it was live on TV so I thought, oh my gosh, my son might be watching.

"So I just ran. I ran off TV. I would never do that normally but I just couldn't catch my breath."

The panic attack came on very quickly, she explained.

"It just was like a wave, something which I've now found out is adrenaline. That came into my body. I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack."

The experience has given her a new perspective on life, she continued.

"I'm so happy that I'm here, and I'm so happy to see you," she said, putting both hands on Dermot's cheeks before hugging him.

"You were absolutely wonderful. And I'm so glad we're alive, and if anything it's made me look at life so much differently. Taking stock, look after my health. I'm drinking a lot of water."

The 51-year-old compared the feeling of the panic attack to crossing into a "surreal" place like the otherworldly Upside Down in TV show Stranger Things.

"I felt like I went into the other world - what's that show that I loved? Stranger Things. You know when you go into the Upside Down world? I felt like I went into the Upside Down world.

"I couldn't grasp my breath, and it was a panic attack."

Hammond and O'Leary also spoke further about panic attacks with former BBC Breakfast host and psychologist Dr Sian Williams, who has written a book about anxiety.

Hammond said she had been unsure about returning to This Morning - but felt that if she didn't come back this week, she may never do so.

"I'll be honest with you, I was anxious about coming back. But I thought, if I don't come back today, I probably wouldn't come back... because then I would have made a thing that it's This Morning that's causing the panic.

"But it can happen anywhere. It comes in ebbs and flows."

She and Williams also discussed the pressure of presenting live TV. "I do live TV all the time, I didn't realise it was having - I don't know if it was having an impact - the fact that you have to be 'on' in order to do it. I don't know," Hammond said.

She concluded the segment by telling viewers: "I'm back, babes. Keep rolling."

Following her departure from last Friday's episode, Hammond posted a video from a hospital bed saying she was "getting my old ticker checked out" after what she described as "a little bit of a palpitation", which she hoped "was just a little panic attack".

She missed the Attitude Awards on Wednesday, where she won the The Honorary Gay Award.

The Birmingham-born presenter also hosts TV shows including This Morning and For the Love of Dogs.

Also known as anxiety attacks, panic attacks can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or whether they have a history of anxiety.

According to the MIND mental health charity, panic attacks are an extreme anxiety response. They can develop quickly, and come with very intense symptoms.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cry4.title: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cry4.text:
It has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com.

And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release.

Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction.

"No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said.

"But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking."

The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village.

Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker.

Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before.

As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture.

And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women.

Wicker has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor.

The film has had mixed reviews from critics, with the Telegraph giving it just one star and calling it "a mortifying adult fairy tale", but the Times awarded four stars, mainly for Colman's "astonishing performance".

But since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz from audiences online - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes.

Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”.

When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for.

"And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?"

She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it.

"You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said.

Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet.

"I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see."

But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says.

He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot.

"We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said.

"But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great."

The film is based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones.

After its premiere at Sundance film festival earlier this year, The Guardian awarded it two stars, praising the "eye-catching premise" but cautioning that there was "too much wood but not enough fire".

But The Hollywood Reporter was more positive, calling it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure".

Away from the social media buzz, the film's stars say it also taps into deeper themes, from gender roles to breaking societal rules.

"It's very funny and strange and wonderful, but I find it very moving. And it's a good one to discover beyond the Ikea memes," said Debicki.

"It touches on a lot of stuff. Hierarchy, social structure," said Skarsgård. "But it's done with such a light touch."

"It's about love, and it is funny, but it's also a romance, and it very gently laughs at the sort of traditions we have in marriage and community," said Colman.

"I think it's something that you will come out and discuss a lot."

Wicker is released in UK cinemas on October 30.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60e.title: Video game Cyberpunk 2077 to get live-action movie adaptation
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60e.text:
A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures.

The Hollywood studio is working with producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura, known for his work on the Transformers films, and CD Projekt Red (CDPR), the developer of the sci-fi role-playing game.

CDPR's joint-chief executive Michał Nowakowski said in a statement the company was "excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise".

Details of the film's story, potential release date and casting information are yet to be revealed.

Despite a troubled launch in 2020, the Cyberpunk 2077 video game, which stars Keanu Reeves, has sold more than 40 million copies worldwide.

The John Wick star plays rockstar Johnny Silverhand, a terrorist whose consciousness is stored on a chip inside the body of main character V.

Set in Night City, a fictional metropolis in a dystopian version of California, players work to uncover a conspiracy involving the shady Arasaka megacorporation.

An expansion, Phantom Liberty, starring Idris Elba was released in 2023 and has sold more than 15 million copies, according to CDPR.

Cyberpunk has already been successfully adapted into a popular animated series - Edgerunners - with a second season due to premiere on Netflix later this month.

The streamer also produced The Witcher, an adaptation of CDPR's massively popular fantasy role-playing series.

It originally starred former Superman actor Henry Cavill, but he was replaced by Liam Hemsworth in the show's fourth season.

Multiple video game series have been adapted for TV and film in recent years, with more due to follow.

Two Super Mario movies, a big screen version of Minecraft and a series of Sonic the Hedgehog films have each seen global box office takings of about $1bn.

PlayStation game The Last of Us was made into a hit series by HBO, and Prime Video says its adaptation of post-apocalyptic role-playing series Fallout is one of its most-watched programmes.

Xbox maker Microsoft announced this week it had created a new "XP" division to focus on licensing its games for films, theme parks and other tie-ins.

Earlier this week, Paramount Skydance completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.

It's promised to release 30 films annually for the next two years, but also prompted fears over job losses and price rises for streaming services such as HBO Max and Paramount+.

Additional reporting by Peter Gillibrand.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.title: Music group with learning difficulties fulfils late MP's Broadway dream
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.text:
A music group with learning disabilities received a standing ovation as they fulfilled a dream of the late MP Sir David Amess.

The Music Man Project is a charity based in Southend-on-Sea, Essex, that teaches children and adults with learning disabilities to sing, sign and play original music.

They have performed for the King, at the Royal Albert Hall and London Palladium, but a trip to perform in New York was the dream of their former president and Southend West MP Amess before he was murdered in 2021.

The project's founder David Stanley said: "Following his death, I just made it my mission to fulfil that promise, really, in his memory."

"So that we remember Sir David for all of the work he did for championing people with learning disabilities in Southend, and then obviously across the country, through the Music Man Project's expansion."

Stanley, who wrote, produced and featured in the show, paid a tribute to Amess during the performance.

With a crack in his voice, he spoke into a megaphone - one of Amess' signature accessories on the political campaign trail - the words: "We promised we'd get them to the Broadway and we did it my friend, we did it."

The morning after, Stanley told the BBC he was "exhausted" and "overwhelmed with emotion".

"We got a brilliant standing ovation," he said.

"It's nothing short of what the students deserved.

"To be fair though, they've got a standing ovation from the King at the Royal Albert Hall before, so this was expected really with something like this."

They performed at the Town Hall in New York with a full house of almost 1,500 people, and a venue known for its historic significance.

It was founded in 1921 by suffragists and one of the only venues in New York to openly welcome Black artists.

Stanley said his group were "perfect" and "incredible" on the night.

He said it proved what he has always said about people with learning difficulties.

"We give them the opportunities and you believe in them and you have high expectations of what they can achieve, then they will always come through, they surprise you.

"Decades ago we would have hidden certain parts of society away, now they're performing on Broadway."

Their performance told the story of the group's journey, from its beginnings 27 years ago to where they are now with 200 members.

Stanley told BBC Essex presenter Sonia Watson that their visit would also include a performance at the United Nations.

"I get to make a speech at the UN. So it's full of pinch me moments this tour."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9y7.title: Why did Dolly Parton record a song in Welsh?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9y7.text:
A Welsh language collaboration between Dolly Parton, her niece Jada Star and singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis might not have been on your bingo card for this year.

But their cover of smash-hit Jolene, with Welsh and English lyrics, has been released on Friday.

The song, recorded before Parton's death on 25 August, is her second posthumous single.

A teaser video released last week shows how Parton spent some time understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation and recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville in early 2025.

Lewis, a proud Welsh speaker from Neath, started translating some of her favourite tunes in 2024, landed on the Parton classic and recorded a video of herself singing it.

"I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada," Lewis said.

Star, also a singer-songwriter, came over to Wales from Nashville and bonded instantly with BBC Radio Wales' Lewis.

The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, and she would get her aunt involved too.

Star and Lewis said Parton, who has links to Machynlleth in Powys, was "proud" to sing in Welsh.

On the track, Parton recites that "heartbreak sounds the same in every language".

Fans across the world reacted to the news of the new single.

"Really looking forward to hearing this version," one commented

"Cannot wait for this," another said while another fan commented "anghygoel", which translates to amazing.

This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language.

She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011.

Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046.
