They are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six were charged with terrorism offences. They have told lawyers they were forced to film false confessions. The interior ministry has denied the allegations of torture or ill-treatment.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it

A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.

But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.

Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.

Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.

He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.

Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.

They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.

“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.

“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”

The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.

Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.

“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.

Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”

The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.

Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”

The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.

Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens.
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.summary: Giant waterlilies are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture. They are extremely rare and at risk of extinction.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Adam Morton in Nadi, Fiji
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji

Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.

But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether the world’s countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month. Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia – which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31 – pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.

Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific. But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and Europe, representatives from big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.

On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.

In a powerful speech, the 13-year-old Melelusi Sokotia told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.

Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.

“This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight,” Tabuya said. “Our responsibility does not.”

The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C goal of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.

Through the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for the poor and vulnerable who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.

Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31.”

Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk. Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”

“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”

Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%.

But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.

Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels.

Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel, but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.

Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.

Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.

Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout. “This means no new projects,” she said.

“You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”

Australia pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to World is ‘already in a transition’ and ‘ready in transition” says Kurum.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Nino Bucci Courts and justice reporter
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Employee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hears

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.

The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop.

They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”.

Graham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week.

He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia.

He provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment.

Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied.

Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”.

Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place.

Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this.

He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas.

Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable.

The company was not swayed and on 2 December last year sent him a termination letter that stated it had carefully reviewed his written submissions and found that he had not provided flight screenshots with his name, medical evidence that showed his partner was unable to travel, an adequate explanation for not telling his manager he was in Singapore, and had previously complied with “absence and approval processes”, demonstrating that he was familiar with them and had instead made “a conscious choice not to follow” them.

after newsletter promotion

“Your conduct represents a serious breach of company policy, a failure to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, and an irreparable breakdown of trust and confidence,” it said in the letter.

Graham told the commission he worked remotely twice before November 2025: the previous year from Townsville, and in April and May 2025 from Bali. He had been employed by Xe for 20 months.

But his manager said she had not been aware he had ever worked remotely from overseas.

A Microsoft Teams message from Graham to his manager was included in evidence before the commission that detailed his claim he was working from home as he had a plumbing issue during one of the days he also told the commission he worked from Bali.

Matheson found that she was satisfied that the dismissal of Graham was unreasonable because while there was a valid reason for his dismissal, the process followed was procedurally unfair.

This was because Xe failed to fully raise the matters it was relying on in making the decision to dismiss Graham, Matheson said.

She found that reinstatement was inappropriate but also decided against awarding compensation.

This was, she said, in part because his misconduct contributed to the decision to dismiss him, and he was paid four weeks in lieu of notice.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Adidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe branding
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Australian Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Global sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ design

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark.

Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims.

During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months.

He pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers.

“There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said.

Adidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013.

It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted.

“This is a pretty simple matter,” he said.

White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.

He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.

“Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said.

“Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.”

The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

He noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing.

Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products.

Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027.

It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013.

Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand.

The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025.

Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success.

The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany.

The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Israel condemns Nobel peace prize award for ICJ judge Navi Pillay - live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Martin Belam (now) and Jakub Krupa (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Navi Pillay has begun giving a press conference after the declaration that she has won this year’s Nobel Peace prize. She began by saying she dedicates the award to “survivors of international crimes”.

She called on people to stand together in the defence of rule of law.

Reuters is carrying a few more of Navi Pillay’s words upon her receipt of the Nobel peace prize. It quotes her warning that mounting political ⁠attacks on international law risked returning ⁠the world to a ​system ‌in which “power ‌rather than law ‌determines whose suffering matters.”

This award strengthens my conviction that we must stand together in ‌defence of the rule of law, ​in defence of independent courts, and an international legal order ⁠based on principle.

Navi Pillay has said that she hopes world leaders will take note of her award, and it will remind them that they have a legal obligation to uphold human rights. She said it was wrong that states where attacking the institute of the international criminal court.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to give us your support. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

Navi Pillay has begun giving a press conference after the declaration that she has won this year’s Nobel Peace prize. She began by saying she dedicates the award to “survivors of international crimes”.

She called on people to stand together in the defence of rule of law.

For what its worth, the Nobel Committee was also asked about the question of Gaza earlier – and said it was not taking a stance on whether Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

“It’s her report, the Commission’s report, and of course we have great faith in her professionalism, in her integrity, but that work is of a UN inquiry commission,” Jørgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, told AFP when asked to comment.

He said it was up to international courts to rule on the issue, stressing that the Nobel Committee “is not the court”.

But not everyone is happy with Pillay’s Nobel win; well, Israel is not.

The Israeli foreign ministry said in an angry statement on X:

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner.

Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes.

Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

As mentioned earlier (11:06) – and referenced by Pillay herself (12:02) – she worked last year on a UN report which called the situation in Gaza an ongoing genocide.

Southern Africa correspondent

South Africa’s president Cyril Ramaphosa has offered his congratulations to Pillay.

“Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally. She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place.

The honour bestowed on her reminds us to build a society where every person, whatever their circumstances, can develop their abilities and contribute fully to our nation and the world.”

He noted that Pillay joined former African National Congress president Albert Luthuli, Archbishop Desmond Tutu and former presidents Nelson Mandela and FW de Klerk as South African winners of the Nobel peace prize.

He concluded:

“We congratulate Justice Pillay and wish her well as she continues to participate in various platforms to secure the rights and dignity of all people.”

Spain’s Pedro Sánchez is the latest European leader to offer his congratulations.

In a post on X, he said:

“Navi Pillay is a renowned South African jurist who has devoted her life to pursuing impunity and defending the weak against the powerful. From her country, from the UN, and from the International Criminal Court.

Today, she has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. From the Government of Spain, we join in the recognition, applaud her work, and reiterate, now more than ever, our support for international organisations tasked with safeguarding peace.”

European Council’s António Costa said:

“Heartfelt congratulations to judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay on being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

A truly deserved honour at a very timely moment, as international law faces mounting pressure.

Her lifelong commitment to human rights, justice and international law reminds us that peace can only endure when dignity, accountability and the rule of law are upheld. The EU stands firmly for these values.”

The Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay is especially important given current attacks on international law, the president of the ICC said.

“At a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law, this recognition carries particular significance,” said Tomoko Akane in a statement quoted by AFP.

The United States has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick-by-brick”, furious at the court issuing arrest warrants for Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the military campaign in Gaza.

Washington has sanctioned top ICC officials and has threatened to slap sanctions against the court as a whole, which would cause the institution significant operational difficulties.

“This is an important recognition of the vital role that international justice plays as a cornerstone of lasting peace,” said Akane in her statement.

Southern Africa correspondent

Dire Tladi, a South African judge serving on the International Court of Justice, where both he and Pillay are judges on the case brought by Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya minority, said:

“I am extremely pleased for Navi and very proud of her. This is absolutely well deserved for a lifetime dedicated to making the world a better place.

As a South African currently serving with Navi in Gambia v Myanmar where she serves as ad hoc judge, I feel particularly privileged and proud.”

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s Truth & Reconciliation Commissions, said:

“I congratulate our beloved Navi Pillay on her richly deserved Nobel Peace Prize. She follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity.

From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war—a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice.

At the ICC, as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable.

For those of us who have benefited from her leadership and commitment to human rights, democracy, and the rule of law, she has been a generous mentor and trusted adviser. I cannot think of anyone more deserving of this extraordinary honour.”

UN human rights chief Volker Türk joins in congratulations for Pillay on the award.

He says “if you walk about this building, there is emotion, there is happiness, there is a great joy that one of ours has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.”

“To say it is well deserved is a total understatement, and especially at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wields enormous power.

This award is particularly poignant. It is an award to all those who around the world, dedicate their lives to the defence of human rights, often at great risk to their security.”

Türk says it is “a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything – to peace, and security, and prosperity.”

He says the award for her is great “not only [because of] what she embodies, but also of her as a person, as a very warm person, as someone who has touched many of the lives of my colleagues.”

“The fact that the Nobel award committee decided to give this to Navi Pillay is a collective win for human rights, but also for the for seeking justice and accountability in this world.

And it’s clear that we need the international criminal accountability mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court.

And it’s clear that this is a very strong signal that this is absolutely critical in today’s world. And we see so many violations occur everywhere.”

Southern Africa correspondent

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, who is also known for his activism for LGBTQ+ rights and people living with HIV/Aids:

“The award is richly earned and lavishly justified.

It comes at a painful time in our national life. As elsewhere, we have been wrecked by anguish about cross-border migration. This has led to hate-filled anti-migrant xenophobic movements distributing toxic untruths about cross-border migration. The result is that families, mothers, babies, traders, workers, have been terrorised, and many forced to flee.

The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the Prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country (Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay) are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa.”

Looking visibly amused by the decision in the video, Pillay repeatedly asks if that’s even true, as she says someone called her up and she thought it was a joke.

(She gets reassured that it’s on the BBC, so it must be true.)

“Your applause means victory, really. You don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this. So that. That’s how I appreciate your applause today.”

“But being a lawyer and a judge I still want to verify,” she laughs.

She says it is “very appropriate” that she is with her “good friends, all of whom support human rights,” as she references her last big thing, the delivery of the UN inquiry report on Gaza, which called it an ongoing genocide.

“One of the main reactions to that … was paying tribute to me for my courage.

And you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision making.”

“So right now, I’m still involved as ad hoc judge in the case brought by the Gambia against Myanmar. So everybody says when you going to stop, when are you going to stop? I just turned 85 just last month. I can’t obviously stop my work in support of the Nuremberg Principles, because of the people we meet here.”

She ends laughing: “You know, I hope this is not a joke!”

In a hilarious video posted by Amnesty International’s secretary general Agnes Callamar and showing the moment Pillay found out about the award, her associates applaud her as she walks into the room in disbelief, before joking:

If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said “few have devoted their lives to justice, peace, and human dignity” like Navi Pillay, as she congratulated her on the win.

“Congratulations to lawyer and human rights activist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay on her Nobel Peace Prize.

Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did.

From the violence of apartheid in South Africa to the horrors of the Rwandan genocide, she has confronted some of humanity’s darkest chapters.

She has looked the brutality of injustice in the eye and never looked away. She is the defender of the persecuted, the vulnerable, the voiceless and the excluded. Of the rule of law over the right of might.

In a world that needs justice more than ever, her courage and moral clarity are a precious compass.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Gang broke into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loaded two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getaway

Thousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind in Italy.

A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Among the bottles targeted were those most prized by wine collectors and consumers, including Solaia, Guado al Tasso and Tignanello, notable as one of the first red wines in the Tuscany region to be produced without white grapes. All the stolen bottles, ranging in price between €120 and €400 a bottle, are from the firm’s 2023 vintage.

The theft occurred on Saturday as the company based in the hilltop town of Cortona prepared for a major shipment to buyers abroad. However, the robbery was only discovered when staff arrived for work on Monday morning.

“The gang was very prepared,” Renzo Cotarella, chief executive of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere della Sera. “A theft of this scale and value has never happened before in Italy.”

He said he had “great confidence” that investigators would trace the stolen wine, which included 3,000 bottles, some of them magnum-sized, of Barolo Ginestra.

“Two trucks full of merchandise can’t just disappear into thin air,” he added. “The Tuscan roads are full of cameras. Perhaps with a bit of luck we’ll be able to recover at least some of the bottles.”

There have been several thefts at wineries in Italy in recent months, including one in Alba in the northern Piedmont region in mid-September.

But Cotarella, who suspects the same gang could have been involved, never imagined a theft of such scale would happen to his firm. Unfortunately, the company’s insurance policy does not cover the robbery of wine at such huge value.

“We had always considered the possibility of having a few cases of wine being stolen during their transportation, but certainly not that two trucks manage to enter the cellar and make off with such a huge haul,” he told Corriere.

Such large wine robberies were usually meticulously prepared and would probably be carried out by those with an intimate knowledge of wine themselves, Corriere suggested, with the target destination possibly collectors, bars or restaurants. However, a sudden increase in the supply of such wines could raise suspicion.

As the investigators continue their search, Cotarella said the company, which was established in 1385, has warned customers to be wary of any offers of its wine outside official channels.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in Montenegro
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Pjotr Sauer
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Founder of influential Rybar blog detained after warnings of attempts to destabilise Balkan country, officials say

A leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested in Montenegro, after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.

Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.

The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.

Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.

“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.

Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.

The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.

Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.

Sign up to Headlines Europe

A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day

after newsletter promotion

Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.

The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, allegations Moscow denied.

Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and is seeking membership of the EU, imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Sarah Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Online retailer’s 26% jump sharpens focus on exemption letting cheap parcels into the country duty-free

Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos.

The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before. The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before.

Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London.

The strong trading figures are likely to increase pressure on the government to bring forward action to change the “de minimis” rule that has underpinned the rise of the fast-growing online specialists Shein and Temu.

Fears about China’s retailers and manufacturers dumping goods in the UK have grown since the US last year revoked its own de minimis exception for Chinese-made goods, crimping Shein’s expansion there.

The retailer’s model is based on shipping orders of cheap clothes from Chinese factories to homes so that each order is low enough in value to avoid import duties.

Under the US exemption, which was scrapped last year, parcels with a value of less than $800 (£600) shipped to individuals had been spared from import tax.

The EU is also phasing out its exemption on customs duties for low-value parcels. It began in July by replacing the €150 de minimis relief with a flat €3 customs duty.

The former UK chancellor Rachel Reeves said she would get rid of the UK’s rule, which allows overseas sellers to send goods valued at £135 or less direct to British shoppers without paying any customs duty, by 2028. However, major retail bosses have said the government should move sooner.

Investors’ concerns about global government regulatory changes meant Shein’s value was far lower when it listed on the stock market than had been expected several years ago.

Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at the start of 2022 and has recently begun manufacturing in other countries including Turkey and Brazil.

After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.

Last week, Shein reported a 67% fall in group quarterly profits to £173m in its first results since the float, blaming higher oil prices and freight rates linked to the war in Iran.

Former prince surrendered lease on home within its first 25 years after public outcry about the rent he paid

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been granted £302,000 in compensation after the lease on his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor was officially surrendered.

A crown estate spokesperson said the former prince paid £1.8m in repair and restoration costs, and the lease was handed back more than 50 years early.

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Andrew was entitled to compensation because, as per the terms of his lease, he surrendered it within the first 25 years.

The crown estate spokesperson said: “The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return.”

The former Duke of York moved out of the Windsor mansion this year as the US Department of Justice released files related to the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein.

He was forced to move into Marsh Farm on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, amid public outcry about the rent he paid on the Royal Lodge.

In June, a National Audit Office investigation revealed that the late queen’s second son received an unknown amount of private income from subletting three cottages on the Royal Lodge estate while paying a peppercorn rent – a small, symbolic payment – for more than two decades.

The crown estate spokesperson said the property would now be marketed by two nationally recognised agents for its proposed future use.

On Thursday, Mountbatten-Windsor won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him.

The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.

Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.

The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.

The arrest followed information that emerged from the Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender. Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.

Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Leader of Jewish Greens calls for Zack Polanski to resign after byelection loss
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Vivien Lichtenstein says party leader should stand down over ‘Zionism is racism’ policy

UK politics live – latest updates

The leader of the Jewish Greens has called for Zack Polanski to step down as pressure increases on the Green leader to acknowledge anger within the party over a new policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for the state of Israel to be abolished.

The comments by Vivien Lichtenstein come after Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, criticised Polanski for a lack of leadership in missing the debate and vote at the weekend that resulted in the policy being passed.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Lichtenstein had said she was considering quitting the Green party of England and Wales following the vote at the party conference to adopt the policy, which states that Zionism is racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.

Polanski was not at the conference on Sunday when the motion was debated; instead he was campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which he finished second to Labour.

In post-byelection interviews Polanski, who is Jewish himself, said he would have voted against the motion had he attended. Two amendments he supported, including one that called for a two-state solution rather than a single Palestinian state, were voted down.

Lichtenstein, speaking to Times Radio, said that even though Polanski was campaigning, he should have spoken and voted for the amendments online, which was an option. “He should have done that. And I think that was a big mistake on his part.”

She said she was surprised to hear Polanski say he had been working with Jewish members of the party, adding: “I don’t know which Jewish members of the party he’s been working with. It certainly hasn’t been with the Jewish Greens committee.”

Asked if Polanski should continue in his role, she replied: “No, I think he should resign.”

Lucas, who remains one of the Greens’ best-known and popular figures, said on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.

Speaking to Newsnight, before the byelection result, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”

Asked if Polansksi should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.

“Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection. I want him to speak now about what’s happened. I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. I think the jury is out about whether or not he will do that, but I very much hope he will. But that is a long way from full-throated support.”

Jonathan Bartley, who was formerly the Green co-leader with Lucas, and is now a councillor in Lambeth, south London, called on Polanski to “put his hands up” and apologise.

“I think [the policy vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now from the Green party,” he told the BBC.

There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Kiran Stacey Policy editor

Exclusive: Abena Oppong-Asare urges chancellor to unlock billions of pounds, as housing associations say they could build 41,000 homes in 10 years

The Labour chair of the Commons housing committee is urging John Healey to bring forward billions of pounds of planned spending on social and affordable homes in England, after housing associations said they were ready to build tens of thousands more.

Abena Oppong-Asare called for the chancellor to allocate money from the £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) as soon as possible, rather than after the election as planned.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Housing associations have said they could build an additional 41,000 homes outside London over the next 10 years if they had more government funding.

They said the extra units would help the government get closer to its target of building 1.5m new homes across this parliament – though the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, recently admitted that it would be difficult to achieve.

Oppong-Asare said: “The government should use the upcoming budget to increase the building of social homes by ensuring a significant proportion of the Social and Affordable Homes Programme is allocated during this parliament.

“Families stuck on social housing waiting lists need to see action now. I urge the chancellor to ensure a significant sum of the £39bn SAHP is allocated during this parliament and that truly affordable social rent homes are prioritised as part of this package.”

Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, announced the £39bn 10-year fund last year, having changed the government’s borrowing rules to allow her to borrow more for capital projects.

The money was due to be spent on a mix of council houses and a number of other types of affordable housing, including affordable rents and shared ownership schemes.

Before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had said the scheme should be reallocated entirely to social rent housing.

But when the first £10bn was allocated under his government in August, it went to a mix of councils and housing associations outside London to spend on a variety of types of subsidised homes.

Ministers said the money would help build 70,000 new homes. But housing associations said they could have built an additional 41,000 – including 25,000 for social rent – if the government had given them all the money for which they bid.

They said they could start construction work on 15,000 of those in the next three years – though some associations have come under fire for selling their homes to the private sector.

The National Housing Federation (NHF), which represents housing associations, said ministers would have to allocate an additional £5.3bn from the programme to build the extra homes.

Ministers have said they are planning to allocate £6bn to London immediately. But of the remaining £13bn, they said they planned to hand out “significant sums” in the second half of the scheme, which would come after the next election.

Kate Henderson, the chief executive of the NHF, said: “Housing associations submitted bids with plans to build tens of thousands of affordable homes, but many organisations with sites ready to go and proven track records did not receive the funding needed to deliver these homes.

“With additional investment now, it is possible to help transform the lives of families in urgent need of an affordable home.”

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing said: “We’ve already announced nearly £10bn of allocations from the Social and Affordable Homes Programme so we can start building more than 70,000 council, social and affordable homes across England.

“Our record investment will help families trapped in temporary accommodation or stuck on housing waiting lists into safe, secure homes.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Alexandra Villarreal in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034

Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.

Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“When the Trump administration says things, it’s not always data-driven. And we wanted to see what the data shows, and what other people have found the data shows,” said Michael Ettlinger, one of the report’s authors. “Turns out that refutes what the US president primarily is asserting.”

The blowback on the economy from Donald Trump’s crackdown is wide-ranging, even as the federal government’s aggressive mass deportation campaign quietly ramps up further.

“We are just beginning to see the harms in terms of what is happening here domestically. But the impacts of these policies, of these efforts, are going to be long-lasting. And I think that is by design,” Vanessa Cárdenas, executive director of the pro-immigration reform organization America’s Voice, told the Guardian.

The report, Economic Impacts of Trump Administration Immigration Policy, was commissioned by America’s Voice and conducted by researchers at Economic Insights and Research Consulting, a firm focused on economic analysis.

Its conclusions underscore how recent federal policies revoking immigrants’ legal protections or targeting them for enforcement have had dire effects on the nation’s affordability crisis and job market, especially in regions and industries that rely disproportionately on foreign-born workers.

In the US agricultural sector, where 42% of crop workers are undocumented and 68% are foreign-born, farmers across the country are warning that the vast majority or in some cases all of their workforce has disappeared overnight, leaving produce to fall to, or rot in, the ground and go to waste.

Food products heavily reliant on immigrant labor have experienced much sharper price increases than food overall since Trump retook the White House, according to the report.

Examples of immigrant-reliant food price increases that have exceeded the average increase in grocery prices over the last 19 months, compared with the 19 months before Trump returned to office in January 2025, are: fresh whole milk up by 5.7%, canned vegetables up by 6.3%, and apples up by 7.2%, the report found.

In that period before Trump’s inauguration, the vast majority of foods that principally depend on immigrant labor for production saw prices rise more slowly compared with other foods and some prices even fell outright, according to the report.

“One thing that changed was the [immigration] policy. Before, the trend for all those goods was a lower inflation rate. And afterward, the trend was higher inflation. So the trend was reversed, and that was quite striking,” said Robert Lynch, one of the report’s authors.

The construction industry, where foreign-born workers fill almost a third of all occupations, has also been severely affected. States more dependent on immigrant labor have seen costs for new single-family homes soar 10.9% in 2026, compared with the first eight months of 2024, bringing building projects’ monetary value from an average of $305,752 to $338,752.

And the issuance of housing permits to build single-family homes has dropped 10.6% nationwide since January 2025, with higher declines in regions more reliant on foreign-born workers, the research found.

Meanwhile, native-born Americans are missing out on potential income in hard-hit states like California, Nevada, New Jersey, Florida and New York, where construction employment is on the decline – because when there are no immigrant roofers to build a home, American electricians and plumbers lose that project, too.

“It’s not like someone can go work in construction and just not have any skills. And we’re losing people who have been here for decades working in construction. That could be fixed, but it’s going to take time,” Ettlinger said.

Other industries with soaring costs and severe labor shortages include healthcare, including home health care, nursing homes, adult daycare, lawn care, landscaping and groundskeeping, where immigrants have historically comprised a disproportionate share of the workforce and expertise.

By September 2025, less than nine months into the second Trump administration, native-born workers had already lost an estimated 51,000 to 297,000 jobs because of changes to US immigration policy, the report said. The labor force shrunk by an estimated 919,000 people during the 18 months of Trump’s second term, while job growth has slowed to roughly a third of the rate it was before he retook office.

The federal government risks losing a large segment of the $26bn in payroll taxes from unauthorized immigrants who help to support the US social security fund that pays out to American seniors – while not being able to access those benefits themselves. Now, social security trustees, including the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, labor secretary, Keith Sonderling, and social security commissioner, Frank Bisignano, are warning that lower net immigration than expected is threatening worse finances for the flailing retirement benefits system, which could mean cuts to Americans’ entitlements.

“The share of that annual loss due to the Trump immigration policy would be $2,152 [per person on average]. Thus, the Trump immigration policies, if continued, would reduce projected average annual Social Security benefits by 8.6% in 2034, and every year thereafter,” the report’s authors write.

They told the Guardian that if the administration’s immigration agenda continues as expected, the implications for the US economy could get even worse.

“We would expect higher prices,” Lynch said. “We would expect more job losses, slower economic growth and the affordability crisis getting worse – partly because prices are higher, partly because people are losing their jobs and their incomes and they can’t afford as much.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034. Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Shrai Popat (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
A decision by US officials to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan would amount to torture, the UN said.

US defence officials said US Army psychiatrist Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at a military base in 2009, would face a firing squad and the execution would be broadcast live, adding that details would come later.

“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.

The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

While there has been bipartisan backlash to Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the Department of Defense plans to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution in December – some hard-right Republicans have welcomed the news.

“Public execution is what this terrorist deserves,” said Andy Ogles, a GOP congressman from Tennessee. “We will be watching.”

While there’s limited research about support for public executions, according to a recent Pew survey, 66% of Americans favor the death penalty for those convicted of murder. Digging into the numbers, there is also a partisan split too – with 51% of Democrats supporting the death penalty compared to 84% of Republicans.

However, only 39% of Americans said that capital punishment actually deters people from committing crimes.

Apologies for the brief interruption. We hope you’re appreciating these factual, verified, up-to-the-minute news updates provided by our expert reporters.

You won't find a paywall around our live blogs – or any of our news, because the Guardian believes that access to trustworthy information is vital for democracy.

In a time of increasing misinformation spread by bad actors, extremist media and autocratic politicians, real, reliable journalism has never been more important – and we’re proud to be able to make ours free thanks to the generous support of readers like you.

By helping fund the Guardian today, you can play a vital role in combating the bad faith and self-interest of a powerful few who spread lies to undermine our democracy, enrich themselves, and stoke division between Americans.

Before you get back to reading the news, we would be grateful if you could take half a minute to give us your support. We value whatever you can spare, but a recurring contribution makes the most impact, enabling greater investment in our most crucial, fearless journalism. Thank you.

According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 – six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.

The Death Penalty Information Center says that 135 soldiers have been executed by the US military since 1916.

“Secretary Hegseth’s comments may be simply aspirational,” the center said in a statement.

“There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be live streamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public.”

Amnesty International ‌Australia has urged the country’s prime minister ​Anthony Albanese to press the US ​to reverse its decision over the Pentagon’s livestreamed execution plan.

“The suggestion that an execution by firing squad should be livestreamed for public viewing is an appalling disregard for human dignity,” said Kyinzom Dhongdue, a campaign manager at the rights group.

“Turning a state-sanctioned killing into a public spectacle only compounds the cruelty of the death penalty.“

A decision by US officials to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan would amount to torture, the UN said.

US defence officials said US Army psychiatrist Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at a military base in 2009, would face a firing squad and the execution would be broadcast live, adding that details would come later.

“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.

The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year.

A defence department official later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.

In an interview with the rightwing channel Real America’s Voice, the defence secretary said the firing squad would carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas on 3 December. It would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

US voters are about to deliver their first national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.

Today, the Guardian launches its 2026 midterm voter panel. Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about the issues that matter to them, from the cost of living, immigration and healthcare to the war in Iran and whether they trust their political leaders.

The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood with less than a month to go until election day. The Guardian will return to its voter panel before the final votes are cast.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

The Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, has received fierce criticism from across the political spectrum.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, defense secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed, prompting condemnation across the political divide.

Speaking on CNN, Democratic senator Chris Murphy said:

I mean, that’s disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions? I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public execution is medieval. It’s frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups, and the fact that the United States is doing it - I just learned this.

That is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That’s what America has become? Um, that’s, that’s pretty extraordinary.

Republican senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what “oppressive dictators” did. In a social media post, he said:

Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.

Meanwhile, Democratic senator Patty Murray commented:

We can seek justice in this country without glorifying violence and turning an execution into a grotesque public spectacle. What this criminal did was abhorrent and must be punished – but we as a country cannot condone livestreaming a man’s death for entertainment.

We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square. Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing? The Pentagon must revoke this decision immediately.

And the Democratic representative Betty McCollum said:

Secretary Hegseth’s desire to conduct a public execution is disturbing and should be stopped. The Army has not conducted an execution by firing squad since World War II and the U.S. has not had a public execution since 1936. Nidal Hasan has been found guilty of his crimes and should be held accountable for them but turning a federal execution into a media spectacle is appalling and unbecoming of the U.S. military.

The Pentagon’s announcement also drew backlash from human rights groups, while New Zealand’s national censor said on Friday it would be unable to block the ⁠planned livestreamed execution.

Speaking about the prospect of the execution being livestreamed, Hegseth had said:

It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.

Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.

In other developments:

In a televised Maine Senate debate Democrat Troy Jackson said that, in addition to Brett Kavanaugh, Republican Susan Collins has voted to confirm dozens of anti-abortion judges.

Republican Mike Rogers continually used Islamophobic attacks on Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in a Michigan Senate debate, accusing the Muslim candidate of being “bought off by Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaida”.

Donald Trump claimed that the US will not strike Iran “at any time prior” to the midterm elections on 3 November.

Why is Hegseth being criticised over the Iran war? The Democratic senator Chris Murphy said Hegseth was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Murphy claimed the Pentagon blocked him from visiting a military base in Qatar and that an Iranian strike on the US embassy in Riyadh was far worse than the public were led to believe.

What has Donald Trump said about the US war on Iran? The US president has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran.

Billionaires across the US are spending vast sums to support California’s Proposition 39, a measure that would require voters to show identification before casting their ballots. The measure is being promoted amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state. Various out-of-state conservative donors have given millions of dollars in support.

Why are some voters calling Missouri’s elections ‘dizzying and embarrassing’? Thanks to a protracted legal battle over an effort by Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map, some voters are no longer sure which congressional district they live in or who will be on their ballot paper for the midterms.

What happened in last night’s crucial midterm debates? Rachel Leingang, George Chidi and Auzzy Byrdsell have rounded up the key takeaways from debates in the battleground states of Michigan, Georgia and Maine.

A lawyer who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues has told a court that Donald Trump’s own words are one of the strongest parts of their case, after the US president made clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him.

CNN, MS Now and Politico were asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. The district court judge Timothy Kelly – a Trump appointee – said he would extend it until next Tuesday. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until then.
