https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Hurricane Isaias ‘biggest test’ for Fema since Trump cuts, experts warn
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sara Sneath in New Orleans
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Gulf officials say they are ready for storm but concerns raised about restructured agency’s ability to respond effectively

Gulf state officials say they are prepared for Hurricane Isaias, but the storm could be the first major test of Fema’s ability to deploy a large surge workforce after the Trump administration’s sweeping cuts and restructuring of the agency, emergency management experts say.

The Trump administration has said it wants to eliminate, or drastically downsize, Fema, putting more burden on states. More than 4,300 employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, about 17% of the workforce, according to a recent US government accountability office (GAO) report. The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO.

“It’s not whether Fema is going to respond. They’re going to respond. It’s more about the depth,” Currie said.

One of the ways that staff was reduced at the agency was through early retirement, meaning many of those who left were more experienced people. From January 2025 to January 2026, 58 senior executive service employees left Fema, according to the GAO report. In the prior three fiscal years, the agency reported about 13 senior executive service separations on average per year.

Among the top officials who left the agency last year was the region four administrator, who oversees eight states, including Florida and Alabama, where Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Deanne Criswell, who led Fema under the Biden administration, said it was less about the number of people who left the agency and more about the loss of experience. “My biggest concerns are always the loss of institutional knowledge. You lose that knowledge. You lose the people who had been through these big disasters in the past,” she said.

In a written statement, Fema said the agency is actively monitoring and preparing for Hurricane Isaias.

“Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, the safety of the American people is DHS’s top priority,” the agency said. “Fema incident management assistance teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and Fema personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. Fema is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell air force base in Montgomery, Alabama, to supplement state resources if requested.”

Governors of Florida, Georgia and Alabama have declared states of emergency for counties projected to be affected by Hurricane Isaias. State emergency management personnel in Louisiana and Mississippi said they have been in regular contact with Fema and received full support from the agency earlier this year during Tropical Storm Arthur, which brought flash flooding and tornadoes across the Gulf coast.

At a news conference on Thursday, Jared Perdue, the Florida division of emergency management executive director, said the state has had very close coordination with their federal partners at Fema. But Currie warned that the agency could quickly find itself stretched thin if it has to respond to more than one natural disaster, a possibility that could become quickly consequential as El Niño strengthens and the agency heads into the fall and winter months.

“The bigger risk is how big it is and a second disaster happening and their ability to staff those,” he said. For example, In 2024, Hurricanes Helene and Milton made landfall in Florida less than two weeks apart. In response, Fema deployed 13,500 employees, straining staff capacity. “Fema has struggled to have the right number of people with the right qualifications, even before these cuts,” Currie said.

In June, Fema had active recovery efforts for over 1,000 open emergency disaster declarations. If the agency is forced to deploy personnel to multiple new disasters, as it did in 2024, Fema would likely have to marshal staff from these other active recovery efforts, putting those efforts on hold, Currie said. “Even though it’s been said that it’s been a quiet hurricane season, it could still be a busy disaster season,” he said.

Last month, a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration’s plan to cut Fema staff by 50% was unlawful. The administration has been slow to approve major disaster funding this year, according to an analysis by the Texas Tribune. Most major disaster declarations by Fema in 2026 came a month after the initial request, about three times longer than average, according to the report.

Ginny Goldman, the founder of Rebuild: the National Disaster Survivors Association, a member organization of climate disaster survivors, said those who went through the flooding in Texas Hill Country this summer still have not received FEMA individual assistance. In a Truth Social post, Donald Trump said the federal government would send $50m for disaster recovery assistance.

“Where is it at? What about the folks struggling to get back on their feet?” Goldman asked. Hurricane Isaias would be the “biggest test of Fema” since the Trump administration’s staffing cuts, she said. “And it’s coming at a challenging time because there are so many other compounding factors that are making life hard for people in America.”

While Gulf state officials have not expressed concern that Fema’s staffing cuts could impact the agency’s ability to respond to Hurricane Isaias, Goldman said disaster survivors are likely to notice. “If you’re a disaster survivor that is trying to navigate a system that is already broken, versus a civil servant in a government agency that is used to navigating a broken system day-to-day, you will have a different perspective on whether it’s broken or not,” she said.

Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before

Business live – latest updates

OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.

The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.

However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.

Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.

OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.

News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.

The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July.

Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.

Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI.

Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks.

Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race.

Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The Democrats taking the fight to Republican strongholds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ankita Rao
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In Florida, Kansas, Iowa and Texas, Democratic candidates are outperforming the predictions, but both parties may struggle to consolidate gains

This was originally published in The Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inbox

The most valuable education I received for becoming a political editor was growing up in Florida. During the entirety of the 18 years I lived there, it was a purple state that voted for Barack Obama twice, and while I would not say my community was diverse, the spectrum of political ideology was vast. I had a close friend who kept a life-sized cutout of George W Bush in her bedroom, and another who helped organize Amnesty International fundraisers against landmines. When the state turned deeply Republican in 2016, and remained that way, I continued to harbor a suspicion that it wasn’t the whole story.

Even so, nothing could prepare me for the sheer surprise when Angie Nixon – the state legislator who joined the Democratic Socialists of America running against Alex Vindman, a centrist with national name recognition – won the Democratic primary for Senate in Florida. That shock has continued in the months after, as we see the Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly running neck-and-neck with Republican Byron Donalds, who seemed like a shoo-in just weeks ago. And while Nixon is polling behind her Republican opponent, Ashley Moody, the race is much closer than anyone following Florida politics expected. So much so that the senior progressive senator Bernie Sanders has newly poured millions of dollars from his campaign funds into the state, and the popular congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez went to campaign with Nixon last month.

This trend is not limited to Florida. Democrats are overperforming in several Republican-held areas and states across the country, whether it’s Kansas, where a Democratic Senate candidate newly has the edge, or Iowa, where both the governor’s seat and congressional districts could flip. In deep red Texas the focus has been on the Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, but more recently the party’s candidate for governor, Gina Hinojosa, has turned heads, too. Around the country, voters seem eager to wield their political power at a time when Donald Trump sees historic lows in his approval rating.

The deep dissatisfaction Americans have with the current government is coming into sharp relief as we get closer to election day. Our reporters have heard the frustration at gas stations, at schools and at rallies. People are fed up with the status quo and looking for a way out, even if, as is true in Kansas, it means choosing a party that hasn’t won the seat in almost a hundred years. It doesn’t help that Republicans have chosen a number of openly corrupt and problematic candidates, like Roger Marshall who is running for Senate in Kansas, a doctor who sued thousands of patients, or Texas’s Ken Paxton, a state attorney general with a long record of personal and financial scandal.

This can all be true at this current moment, but there is still a longevity question that both parties will need to answer in the coming years. Midterm elections almost always serve as a check on the White House, but neither party has turned that momentum into long-term gains. In fact, many surveys show that both the Republican and Democratic parties are deeply unpopular. The upcoming election seems to be far more reliant on specific candidates in specific places with the exact right message for their voters – whether that means inviting Barack Obama to rally, or avoiding Kamala Harris altogether. Even if there is a “blue wave” in November, it will require much more work to sustain enthusiasm through the presidential election in 2028 with a unifying message.

With just under four weeks left to go, it remains to be seen whether the Democratic advantage holds, and how decisive a victory the party has if it does. But as a Floridian, I’m reminded by this election that although Americans might be polarized and stratified in filter bubbles, we are still exceedingly capable of making ourselves heard.

It’s a sign of the times when several high-profile Republican candidates are speaking in direct opposition to Donald Trump.

While the entire top of this newsletter was focused on Democrats performing well in Trumpland, it’s important to note that there are places where Republicans have surprised people too. One of those is Minnesota, where my colleague Rachel Leingang has extensively covered state races. While the Democratic Senate candidate, Peggy Flanagan, is still holding the lead, some have noticed that Republican Michelle Tafoya is making gains in the otherwise Democratic state.

Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, is positioning herself as conservative with some asterisks, such as supporting some abortion rights and criticizing Trump’s actions in the Iran war. It’s notable that national Republicans haven’t invested in her race.

Minnesota has seen deep political turmoil in the past few years, from the federal immigration enforcement raids that killed two American citizens to the murder of a beloved state leader. It is also one of the targets of the Trump administration, which capitalized on a recent statewide fraud investigation. While indicators suggest Flanagan will hold on to the vote, we’ll be watching what impact rural Republican voters have in the state.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘It could have been any one of us’: Black college students march for Nolan Wells
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adria R Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Recent death of the student in Mississippi is just the latest in a long string of unsettling deaths of young Black people

O
n Wednesday afternoon, hundreds of students gathered on the Jackson State University (JSU) campus for a rally to call for transparency in the mysterious death of young Black people and to encourage student engagement in politics and the fight for voting rights.

As the sun began to set, the students, many of whom wore black, marched through the historically Black university’s plaza chanting: “Nolan Wells, Trey Reed, Tasia Fortune, Kohen Wiley, Jaylen Lewis – Black Lives Matter!” All five were young Black Mississippians – the youngest, Wiley, was one-year-old while the eldest, Fortune, was 29 – who either died under suspicious circumstances or were killed by police.

The students wound through the campus, with school police and others looking on, continuing their chants until they made it to the Cofo Civil Rights Education Center. The building was significant: it was the organizational home for the Mississippi Freedom Summer of 1964, a largely student-organized movement that aimed to increase Black voter participation during the Jim Crow era, and the statewide headquarters for the Council of Federated Organizations, a coalition of the Mississippi branches of the NAACP, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, the Congress for Racial Equality and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

“This is the first step of advocacy,” Camrynn Wimberly, a JSU student and one of the organizers of the march, said. “This is the first step of collective action and political power. The more this spreads, the more we continuously advocate for the same thing and let them know that we will not stand idly by as rights are stripped from us, as parents grieve, as we wonder whether or not we will be next – that is the first step to something greater.”

The students at JSU are part of a larger movement of students at historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) who are calling for justice and transparency in the cases of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old Black student whose disappearance and death have received national scrutiny, and other young Black people who died in mysterious or suspicious circumstances.

Also this week, students in the Atlanta University Center Consortium (AUC), which includes Spelman College, Clark Atlanta University (CAU) and Morehouse College, as well as Langston University, Prairie View A&M University and other schools, marched to demand answers about the cause and manner of Wells’ death, which remain undetermined, and other suspicious deaths of young Black people.

On 1 October, students in the AUC held a march in solidarity with Nolan Wells and his family. Thousands of students participated.

“We’ve seen time and time again the mistreatment of cases involving young Black Americans,” Barhn Gadson, president of CAU’s chapter of the NAACP, said. “There’s not so much of an attention towards it until we do things like having to march and having to riot. We’ve gotten to a point where we are tired of having to fight for young Black males or young Black females or any Black individual for our lives to mean something.”

A’Nija Hughley, president of Spelman’s NAACP chapter, said that it was important for all students, but specifically those at HBCUs, to speak up.

“As HBCU students, we’re in a unique position where we are allowed to learn how to be critically conscious, and we learn how structures are built to work against us,” she said. “As students who are legacies of those who started the civil rights movement and the Atlanta student movement, it’s kind of our job to speak up and then also show our support for [Wells’] family.”

Hughley said that the idea for a solidarity march came from a student in her chapter who wanted to know what they could do for Wells. Though the students are in Atlanta, they said that they marched in solidarity with Wells and other young Black people who have died in suspicious circumstances.

“To us, it’s we either speak out or we just shut up,” Gadson said. “Just because we may not be in the same city or the same state doesn’t mean that we can’t speak out on it. And just because there is a one ruling here doesn’t mean that we aren’t going to protest, doesn’t mean that we are not going to advocate for our community. I mean, we are the NAACP. This is what we’ve been doing for years.”

Hughley said that, instead of a larger protest where they marched to the capitol building or otherwise engaged the larger community, she wanted to keep the march AUC-wide. “We cannot sit and look at injustice and not say anything about it,” she said. “It honestly could have been any one of us. This one hits close because he’s around our age. He looks like us.”

Wells’ similarities to the students in age and appearance were also noted by the JSU students who rallied on Wednesday afternoon. As they made their way across the campus, they chanted: “Our lives matter. That could’ve been me. They look like me. Say their names!”

Jakari Holland, an organizer of the rally and founder of the Mississippi Access Project, said that the school’s location in central Mississippi made it particularly important for students to speak out. “Multiple people have passed away inside Mississippi under suspicious circumstances,” Holland said. “Jackson State University, being a public institution and bringing in public funding, but also at the centerpiece inside the capital in Mississippi, we have to take a stance. We have to bring awareness and transparency in light of what’s happening. This could be any one of us. We’re young people inside Mississippi, and we’re seeing what’s going on in the backyard of our home.

Like the students in Atlanta, Holland was keenly aware of the historical significance, not only of JSU, but of Jackson and Mississippi, in general. “Our HBCUs have a long history of people being advocates and standing against things,” he said. “The Greensboro Four, when they were at North Carolina A&T and sat down in Woolworth’s lunch counter. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. The students at South Carolina State that were shot. The people that our Gibson-Green plaza is named for. It’s crazy to see that people love talking about and celebrating Black history, but when you’re living through it, that’s when the issue comes about because you don’t like people that challenge the societal norms.”

They are part of a larger movement of students at historically Black colleges and universities who are calling for justice and transparency in cases of Nolan Wells.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: After the strongest storm in a generation, Hawai’i residents take recovery into their own hands – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Noelle Fujii-Oride and Akasha Rabut on Kaua'i
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
On Kaua‘i, neighbors repair each other’s roofs, teens deliver meals and locals use their own equipment to clear roads

I
t was a few hours after the sun rose over the verdant valleys and clear waters of Hā‘ena on Kaua‘i’s North Shore. Michael Olanolan was already in his excavator, clearing the main highway where a wall of fallen trees had blocked access. Other neighbors joined him, moving debris so electric crews could reach utility poles downed by Hurricane Lowell.

The 76-year-old father of nine and grandfather of 26 did this every day for weeks after Lowell hit the Hawaiian islands of Kaua‘i and Ni‘ihau on 7 September. His generational home lost part of its roof to Lowell’s winds, but family and friends helped him repair it, freeing him up to also help his community. Clearing out roadways became his full-time job while residents were getting back on their feet.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“That’s the way we are up here,” said Olanolan, who owns a landscaping and excavating business. “We help each other.”

The strongest storm to impact Kaua‘i in 34 years, Lowell brought heavy rains, winds and coastal waves to the island, knocking out power to roughly 90% of the island’s 36,000 electric utility customers. Rural North Shore homes suffered flood damage and went without power for nearly three weeks; on the South Shore, Lowell’s storm surge devastated beachfront properties and roads. So far, Hawai‘i governor Josh Green’s office reported 10 destroyed homes and 67 with significant damage.

Past storms, like one in 2018 that damaged hundreds of North Shore homes and cut off the community from the rest of the island, have taught communities to take disaster response and recovery into their own hands because federal government aid – such as financial and cleanup assistance – will take time to come through. Some don’t put hope in government aid at all. They know they need to rely on one another.

After Lowell, residents islandwide cleaned flood-damaged homes, tarped roofs, cooked hot meals and conducted door-to-door checks of neighbors. When the power was out, communities created systems to deliver ice and gas to those in need. Their efforts persisted even as two more storm systems passing south of the Hawaiian islands brought more winds and rain.

Hawaiian culture is steeped in mālama, or care, of each other and the land, even encouraging newcomers to help out, said Megan Wong, a Wainiha resident who coordinates the Kaua‘i Resilience Team, which ran a community hub where nearby residents could get supplies, meals and other help in Lowell’s immediate aftermath.

“I think it comes from this innate place of, like, seeing your community as family and ‘ohana’,” said Wong. “If everyone steps to the table and does their part, then we can all make it through together.”

The island, with its 73,000 residents, is still waiting on federal aid. Hawai‘i has taken damage from six storm systems this year – five of which occurred within the last two months and were driven by a strong El Niño. So far, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has approved nearly $21m in household and individual assistance for a set of storms in March.

In the coastal town of Kekaha on Kaua‘i’s west side, residents weren’t waiting for the government to rescue them.

Dennis Eguchi, a Kekaha resident who is part of area nonprofit E Ola Mau, said when he went outside the morning after Lowell hit, he already saw 18 people assessing damage or cleaning up yards in the neighborhood. Two others went down nearly every road with chainsaws cutting damaged trees. Dozens of others were asking how they could help.

Before the state could clear the coastal highway, another group was removing sand and boulders in the early morning hours. The volunteer crew grew to a handful of residents who brought out their backhoes, skid steers, loaders and other machines. The road was clear by 1pm.

“That’s because the community, they’re resilient enough to know what the issues are and they just do it,” Eguchi said.

Born out of the sugar plantations that were Hawai‘i’s economic engine for more than 150 years, Kekaha is home to a tight-knit, multi-ethnic community. Eguchi said plantation laborers took care of each other through activities like building a community pool and handing out gift bags during the holidays.

Chris Faye, whose grandfather was a manager for Kekaha Sugar Company for decades, said the plantation mobilized its people and machinery to help clean up after Hurricanes Iwa, which damaged over 11,000 buildings on Kaua‘i and O‘ahu in 1982, and Iniki, which damaged or destroyed 14,000 homes in 1992.

Those efforts instilled a sense of giving that continues today.

“On the Westside, no one takes credit for what we do,” Eguchi said. “We do it because we love Kekaha.”

North Shore residents learned lessons from the 2018 storms, which left its main highway closed for over a year. For example, one community hub wasn’t enough for all residents affected, especially if areas only accessible by crossing single-lane bridges got cut off by landslides or flooding. So after Lowell, a second hub was created at Wainiha Country Market, near the mouth of the Wainiha River.

In the weeks after the storm, community members and nonprofits dropped off food, water, gasoline, ice, baby food, shovels and other supplies. The hub’s team also sent kids on bikes to deliver food to residents who were cleaning their flood-damaged homes. Now, it focuses on helping residents connect with other resources, like financial assistance.

Megan Fox, executive director of local food production nonprofit Mālama Kaua‘i, said she’s seen community-based disaster response improve since the 2018 North Shore floods. Different groups know their roles and are better at avoiding duplicating efforts. Wainiha Country Market operates a community hub, for example, while Wong’s group coordinates volunteer crews.

There’s also a way for everyone to help. Kūpuna, or elders, have done wellness checks of other kūpuna, helped sort through flood and rain damage, and cleared homes from mud and other debris.

“Everyone is giving what they got,” Fox said.

In rural communities like Hā‘ena and Wainiha on the North Shore, some residents were first reluctant to accept help because they believed others needed it more. In the days after the storm, Wong had trouble getting neighbors to accept donated ice even though the area didn’t have power or running water.

“You really need to be in touch with your community to say, like, ‘it’s OK to say that you need something. We’re here to help, and we’ll help all the people that need something,’” she said.

In the town of Kīlauea on the North Shore, Raina Bautista and her family cooked as many as 220 meals a day for utility and county workers and neighbors, even while they waited for their own water and electricity to be restored. They relied on their camping stove and stored water before switching to collected water from a water buffalo sent by the county. Meals were simple, such as spaghetti, chowder, pasta and adobo, based on items from their church’s food pantry before community members began donating food.

Her 15-year-old niece Kale Sambrano was the face of the operation, standing on the side of the road each day to hand out meals and toiletries to passing cars. She also waved down buses and postal workers to feed them, too.

“I was 11 when Iniki hit, and that was all we did was go up and help with the Red Cross, you know, pack bags and give meals,” Bautista said. “And it’s kind of ingrained, so we’re passing it on to this next generation.”

Myra Kanahele, who grew up on the private island of Ni‘ihau and now lives in Kekaha, said it’s been inspiring to see so many community members jump in to help. Many were struggling before the hurricane, as Hawai‘i’s cost of living, which was already 84% higher than the US average, has increased. The storm has reminded many of the importance of checking in on one another and giving whatever help they can.

Kanahele, who has been helping other Ni‘ihau descendants and Kekaha residents through her nonprofit, Hi‘ianelani o Ni‘ihau, mentions the ‘Ōlelo Hawai‘i, or Hawaiian, phrase “kōkua aku, kōkua mai”: Help others, and help will be given to you. Kanahele hopes that spirit will continue even as Kaua‘i’s recovery ends.

“At that little point of time, just seeing everybody working together in the neighborhood, I was like: ‘Wow, maybe we need this,’” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘People are feeling the real impacts’: influencers use humor to make fun of the private equity industry
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Heather Timmons
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Skits and parodies making fun of the trillion-dollar industry have taken over social media, racking up millions of views

J
ohnny Hilbrant Partridge kept getting stuck next to the same kind of finance guy at weddings – the one bragging about his family’s full-time nanny and lavish vacations while name-dropping elite club memberships and private schools.

To Partridge, a former fitness instructor, their shameless knack for self-promotion felt ripe for comedy. Using a filter that puts an exaggerated sneer on his face, Partridge donned a puffer vest and created “The PE Guy”, a caricature of the men who work in the private equity industry.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“All we did is acquire some youth hockey complexes, implement dynamic pricing and put some people on recurring revenue subscription models,” Partridge scoffed in a video after lawmakers introduced a bill this year to ban private equity from youth sports. “This country used to reward innovation, and suddenly it’s wrong to charge $11,000 for a development lacrosse weekend … give me a break.”

Since he first debuted the character last year, “The PE Guy” has racked up millions of views on Instagram and TikTok, becoming the most popular player in a fast-growing ecosystem skewering private equity. The multi-trillion-dollar industry has turned into a catch-all online for the ills of modern capitalism, inspiring “a day in the life” skits and parody rap music videos.

For many viewers, the draw is the dark humor, something that even the finance guys are embracing. Partridge said he gets invited to speak at insurance and private equity conferences and finance companies’ annual meetings as comic relief.

But it’s also been a way many Americans are learning how the industry, which often operates out of view and without the same oversight or regulation as publicly traded corporations, is affecting their lives.

Every business has bad actors, Partridge said, but he chose to focus on private equity because it is changing everyday things like health care so radically that “people are feeling the real impacts from it”, he said.

Private equity has found its way into everything from funeral homes to family dental offices. Once they were acquired by private equity firms, beloved chains like JoAnn Fabrics and Toys “R” Us faced bankruptcies, and many name-brands taken over by the industry have degraded in quality.

“When people say private equity, they don’t just mean the exact technical term,” said Hojung Kim, whose August Instagram post on how private equity is changing veterinary care got a million views in just two days. The term has come to represent “leveraged buyouts, hard cost-cutting in order to ruthlessly profit maximize and saddling the business with debt in order to self-enrich”.

Struck by the response, Kim, co-founder of an affordable LSAT prep business, started a series on other industries changed by private equity and built Grass, an app that helps users find independent American businesses.

“We hit a nerve. A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it,” Kim said. “As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.”

TikTok and Instagram are awash in pro-business content too, of course, as companies overall have spent  $37bn on influencer marketing in 2025, one advertising trade group estimates, and private equity companies are even buying up influencer tools like Uscreen.

But the private equity criticism continues to grow. Journalist Pablo Torre and comedian Stavros Halkias have gotten hundreds of thousands of views on a YouTube video railing about Blackstone’s takeover of Jersey Mike’s Subs and financial investors in sports teams.

“If they fucking destroy the Lakers, guys with Kobe [Bryant] back tattoos are going to start the proletariat revolution,” Halkias said in Why Private Equity Shouldn’t Exist, going off news that the Los Angeles basketball team was acquired by Bob Iger and Josh Kushner for $12.5bn in August. “The closest we’re getting to class consciousness is fast food and sports teams.”

Natalka Burian, owner of Elsa, a bar in Brooklyn, is among the food industry experts who are chronicling private equity’s takeover of restaurants and bakeries.

They can pay outrageous rents and snatch up the best locations, she said, which drives out businesses like her own.

“That’s money that should be going to local businesses,” Burian said. “I think there’s something about this blandness that takes away from our communities.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: A national verdict on Trump 2.0 is coming. Nine midterm voters share where they stand
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Rachel Leingang, George Chidi, David Smith, Fabiola Cineas and Ed Pilkington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
From cost of living to the Iran war, these are the issues that matter most to US voters across the political spectrum

US voters are about to deliver their first national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.

Today, the Guardian launches its 2026 midterm voter panel. Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about the issues that matter to them, from the cost of living, immigration and healthcare to the war in Iran and whether they trust their political leaders.

The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood with less than a month to go until election day. The Guardian will return to its voter panel before the final votes are cast.

Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

So, I’m an economics student, and one of the things I’ve noticed more and more is, we work more, but we seem to be getting further and further behind. Why is it that my grandfather could work an eight-hour union job and have enough to take care of five or six kids, and yet I work the same job and I’m struggling to get by? That makes no sense to me. I don’t understand why so many CEOs are saying companies are making record profits while people have to have two and three jobs.

Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter

My biggest hit that I’m having right now is labor. I don’t have labor. I don’t have workers that can, you know, finish the houses as fast as we used to. It causes a ripple effect when it comes to supply and demand – houses taking longer, interest rates going higher, so everything is just going up in value.

Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

It would be likely ICE. I feel like that right now is having the largest, most powerful negative impact on people in this country. And it’s very blatant, and I feel like stopping that would be a good touchstone for how we all move forward.

Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

His recent deal to establish or re-establish American hegemony in Greenland is a really big deal. Making sure that America has access to Greenland, and China does not, is a very important thing that Donald Trump has done. Also, with the Iran war, it is very important what we’re doing there, and I hope for as quick and decisive a success as can possibly be reached.

Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

I’m going to say the assault upon not only the immigrant community, but every community that he sees as being vulnerable. Giving the American people or a certain sector within the American population permission to be cruel and to exalt in this public display of cruelty – we are going to spend a long time recovering from that.

Morgan Akin 85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderate

There’s a number of things, but destroying public structures, buildings and so forth in Washington DC, and then building new ones that have no relevance whatsoever to democracy or the people of the country. He is benefiting from his office, increasing his income [by] billions of dollars, while Americans are suffering with high gas prices and food prices and so forth. I just filled my car up, just before you called. I have a Honda CRV, which is not a big car, and it cost me $78 to fill it up.

Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

My life is better. Myself and my husband, we are both retired. I’m retired from the education field. I was clerical; I was not in a teaching role. My husband was assembly line. He was a blue-collar worker. He worked for General Motors. But I’d say that we’re better off because I feel safer. I feel more hopeful for the future. The economy, of course – things could be better with gas prices, but I think that that’s a temporary problem right now.

Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

Economically, much worse. It’s worse than it was two weeks ago. I have a pickup truck. Filling my gas two weeks ago, two months ago, was $80. Now, it’s $120. I’m expecting it to be $150. And not only that, is my [utilities] bill going to go up. What else is going to go up? Groceries are going to go up just because shipping is going up. I’m not getting a raise yet, again, we’re making record profits. Who are those profits going to? Not you and me, not the people who need the money.

David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

My parents went out of business during Trump 2. My parents started a business, like, 20 years ago in the auto industry. They were very, very lucky because neither of them have college degrees. What sort of started in Trump’s disastrous Covid response, that was one of the first times that my parents had to take out a big loan that they weren’t sure about. In their industry, the tariffs have completely shaken up everything. It has caused them to have a lot less certainty, and eventually that built up, and they couldn’t go on any longer. They’ve got a new business in the works. We’re doing OK, but that was something that did personally affect me.

Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate

I never thought, in 32 years, as a Venezuelan American, that I had to carry my passport with me everywhere I go. I never thought that I will live in fear in the United States, even though I’m an American citizen.

Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

I’m very optimistic. This country’s been through worse and she’s always came out on top. I don’t think that there’s a better country in this world. I don’t think there’s a more powerful country in this world. As far as the best in leadership, I think we have it. As far as goals and policies that this country should strive for, I think Donald Trump has those in place.

Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

I’m not very optimistic. Thirty years ago, I would have said yes. We were the shiny new penny that everybody loved after World War II. Now we see the reverse: European countries have gotten their footing and are passing us. China is the worry. Xi is a smart man, a benevolent dictator. If we continue down this path of electing the Trumps of the world who do not embrace science, education or long-term economic stability and infrastructure, this country will continue to decline.

Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

Oh, I think America’s future is behind it. I believe we’re starting to witness the collapse of the American empire, sad to say, but just understanding how economics work and how everything is based on the petrodollar. I understand why Trump wanted to get away from EVs [electric vehicles], because if EVs took over, then less oil would be needed and the US dollar would be needed less and less. But what good is being the richest person on an ash heap? All the water is dehydrating. As the earth gets hotter and hotter, water is not sitting on the planet’s surface anymore, it’s in the air. It’s just going to be more storms, more lakes drying up, and what’s going on right now? Oh, we need all the fresh water for datacenters. What do you need datacenters for if nobody’s going to be here?

Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

I take great encouragement from some of the voices of the Black community, the immigrant community, people who have been involved in activism for decades – I do have optimism. It’s hard to balance sometimes, because there are certainly times when I feel like, oh, who even cares? And why is our country so special that we wouldn’t fall down the hellscape of authoritarianism? But there is a large movement, there is a large resistance, and it’s growing week by week. And I think we have a long tradition in this country of believing that we do have rights. We have these incandescently beautiful founding documents.

David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

I see movements domestically – obviously, the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] that has been killing it in the primaries. They’ve already done more damage than the Tea Party or Occupy Wall Street ever did, and it feels like this is just the beginning. So I’m very, very optimistic, and I think the world that we can accomplish, a world where everyone’s needs are met, at least in the wealthiest nation in the history of the planet.

Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter

Let’s be realistic: war is created for money to be created. I just feel everything just needs to end. Everybody, every country, needs to focus on themselves, and the United States needs to focus on the United States’ people.

Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

I want it to end with the least amount of death. I’m a mother of five children. I have three sons and two daughters. I have one grandson. I don’t want any kind of war because war brings death. But I think that the person that’s able to end this conflict is in leadership today.

Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

I don’t think a peace deal can be reached with the existing regime. Regime change in the Middle East has been very hard to master, so it really would have to be a move of the people in Iran. The propaganda war may be the most important front for a truly lasting peace to be achieved.

Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

At this point, we just need to walk away. There’s no winning; they are winning. We need to cut our losses and move on. I’m a little shocked that with our trillion-dollar military, one little country like Iran has somehow managed to deplete our resources. To reasonably manage a war and win, we have shown ourselves incapable. At this point, to save face, we need to spin some PR and walk away.

Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

I’m a veteran, so I’m trying to choose my words very carefully on that. With the conviction of Donald Trump. With the conviction of Benjamin Netanyahu of war crimes. With the conviction of Pete Hegseth.

Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

When you have a leader that is confident in his ability and he says what he means and he means what he says and he leads with confidence, I think people respect that. So I think that we’re being respected a lot more than we were in the last administration.

Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

You know how a lot of families have those old, racist grandpas that you just leave in a corner and you don’t bring them to family gatherings? That’s who the US is right now. It’s sad, but I don’t know who our allies are. And the allies Trump has have been the enemies of the United States for generations.

Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate

No good … We roll a red carpet for [Putin]… for [Xi Jinping] a week or two ago. We are doing business with [Delcy] Rodríguez in Venezuela, who is a criminal dictator.

Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

The most concerning section, especially in this election cycle, is that democratic socialist alliance. What they seem to be fighting for isn’t just a better safety net; it has become the dismantling of America as a concept, the dismantling of the west as a concept, and of reality itself as a meaningful concept in public discourse.

David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

I think what’s going on in the Democratic party is very productive. I think even the hard conversations over ‘DSA outsiders’ and: ‘Are these extreme ideas what we stand for?’ I think it shows that we’re expanding the conversation to policies that will help people’s lives in a real material way, and that we don’t have to only stop the worst of the Trump administration. We can also make healthcare work significantly better for everyone in the country. That’s a real consideration.

What’s the way that we can actually win and hold on to what’s most important? I think we’re seeing that there’s a route that we can both win more and hold on to our values. The whole basis of the logic that shifts the Democrats right is that ‘at least it’s what’s good for elections’ or ‘at least we’ll win, and then we can think about all the considerations and all the reform afterward. But first we have to win.’ Well, Kamala didn’t win, so what now? Plenty of moderate Democrats did not win. Hillary didn’t win. That logic is not as sound as they think it is.

Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

I am going to be in the air force. The president is the commander-in-chief of the armed forces of the United States, and as such, I will serve him honorably. If that’s a Democrat, then I will serve a Democrat honorably, because he will still be my president – or she.

Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

If I imagine a Democrat in the White House in 2028, being elected in 2028, inaugurated in 2029, I have to make the assumption that a lot of things take place that are no longer guaranteed. Trump has been threatening the midterm elections. If a Democrat were to be inaugurated in 2029, the popular resistance needs to hold firm and ramp up its pressure. There are some solid people out there. Adam Kinzinger, he’s solid; he was a Republican, but he’s kind of gone over, gotten over that. I have a lot of respect for Pete Buttigieg, probably because he’s able to speak very cogently, very decisively, with people who disagree with him.

Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate

Let’s not talk about 2028 until after [the] midterms. I think Andy [Beshear] and Gavin Newsom will be my two top choices if I were to think about 2028 right now, which I’m not.

Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

This country doesn’t vote for Democrats because they love Democrats … It’ll be because Trump has ruined things so poorly, and made things so bad, that people will turn around and come back again and vote again, just like they did when Trump was in office the first time and elected a Democratic president. Now, who it is … that’s the joke in the room. Because our best candidates are those who a lot of the American public are racist or bigoted against. I’m a Mayor Pete [Buttigieg] fan. I think he’s brilliant, he’s a brilliant man, he is. Just mentally, historically, in terms of what he’s accomplished in his lifetime, he’s brilliant. He’s gay. Can he win?

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them | Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat

The most basic function of government is to protect people from harm. Two growing phenomena – the climate crisis and AI – pose escalating risks of extraordinary harm.

The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Yet Donald Trump and his Republican enablers, backed by big money from big oil and big AI, refuse to do a thing about either risk. In many ways, they’re worsening both.

But there’s another way to reduce these risks: through liability law.

I have no more faith in the supreme court than you do, but I was struck by the responses of at least half the justices who will be considering an important case that opened the supreme court’s new term, Suncor v Boulder.

The case was brought by several Colorado localities against Suncor and ExxonMobil – one of about three dozen filed around the country in which cities and states are demanding that big oil reimburse them for the escalating costs of climate disasters brought on by the burning of fossil fuels.

On Monday, at least four justices (Samuel Alito has recused himself) expressed skepticism about big oil’s argument that the Clean Air Act explicitly prevents such lawsuits against polluters. “It’s like, wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” asked justice Elena Kagan.

Chief justice John Roberts drew parallels between Boulder’s claim and prior lawsuits against the tobacco and opioid industries in which states and localities won significant damages. “I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” said Roberts.

In 1998, the leading US tobacco companies agreed to pay $206bn to cover public health costs and smoking-related expenses. When translated into current dollars, this is more than $423bn.

And recall the $20bn paid by BP in 2010 to cover environmental and economic damage to the Gulf Coast after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Or the $7.4bn paid by the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma to resolve liability for the opioid crisis.

Such liability lawsuits – the last resort when the public is harmed by corporate malfeasance or nonfeasance – are also relevant to the risks posed by AI.

If AI agents escape super-secure environments to release dangerous toxins, or destroy critical water, electricity, transportation, or health infrastructure, AI companies and the tech giants behind them could be on the hook for tens if not hundreds of billions of dollars in payments to those who are harmed.

No way major investors in AI – or the insurance companies backstopping AI – are going to ignore this potential liability. The current dollar value of the tobacco settlement – as I said, $423bn – is comparable to what the tech giants spent on AI chips, servers, and datacenters last year.

This gigantic financial risk will weigh on the values of AI companies and the tech companies unless or until they become far more serious about protecting the public against such harms.

I expect political demands from the AI industry to limit such liability through federal laws that set caps on it and that establish industry-funded “trust funds” to pay for big liability judgments. A sane Congress (we may yet have one) wouldn’t agree without specific industry steps to dramatically increase safety.

In all likelihood, the AI industry will also seek government regulations it could use as partial defenses against such massive liability, just as pharmaceutical companies use certification by the Food and Drug Administration that their drugs are safe and effective to defend against lawsuits claiming their drugs cause harm.

The big AI investors and insurers will force this issue. More than 200 cases already in the courts involve cyber-liability and AI-related product liability. Follow the money. Insurers are already demanding more effective means of controlling AI risks, and big investors are demanding better means of limiting them.

Both the climate crisis and AI pose existential risks to human life on this planet. Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start.

The fact that liability for the climate crisis is already in the supreme court and that four justices seem sympathetic suggests how significant a role liability can play as an incentive for both fossil fuel and AI giants – and their insurers and major investors – to clean up their acts.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Christa Pike’s botched execution is a reminder of the horror of the death penalty | Moira Donegan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Moira Donegan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Lethal injection was a way for us to deny the reality of capital punishment. Pike’s experience shows us what it is

C
hrista Pike had asked to be hanged. In the weeks before her botched execution by lethal injection on 30 September, in which she survived two lethal doses of barbiturate pentobarbital and had to be hospitalized, Pike and her legal team had challenged Tennessee’s execution protocol.

The state’s lethal injection regimen had failed before. In May, Tony Carruthers was also sent to Tennessee’s death chamber, only to leave alive after prison officials struggled to find a vein.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

In Pike’s case, her lawyers argued, the lethal injection protocol was likely to fail again.

She also had vein issues, they said; if she was subjected to an ordeal like Carruthers’, in which prison officials punctured their prone prisoner more than a dozen times over the course of an hour in an attempt to administer the drug, Pike’s history of trauma, which is lengthy and acute, would serve to make the experience unconstitutionally torturous.

Pentobarbital, the drug that was set to be used to kill Pike, also risked a needlessly painful death.

“The drug supposedly burns very bad,” Pike said in a taped interview just weeks before her scheduled execution. “And so that sounds scary to me because they used the word Draino in speaking about this drug, and the thought of suffocating and drowning on my own bodily fluid and blood isn’t very appealing to me.”

It was to avoid this ordeal that Pike requested to be hanged by the neck until dead instead. Her request was denied. From the execution chamber during Tennessee’s failed attempt to kill her, witnesses said that they could hear Pike complaining about a burning pain in her arm, which felt, she said, like it was about to burst.

After nearly a week of being unconscious and intubated at a Nashville hospital after her failed execution attempt, Pike is now awake and talking. Her arms are severely injured from her execution attempt and not fully usable, but she’s still shackled to her hospital bed anyway. She still remains “foggy” from the effects of the state-administered overdose, and it’s unclear whether she will recover full cognitive function as doctors assess the state of her brain damage.

But she remembers the moments when Tennessee tried and failed to kill her. She is reportedly very angry.

We should be angry, too. In our name, a woman was tortured.

In many death penalty cases, there are real questions about the factuality of a condemned person’s guilt or the fairness of their trial and appeals process.

That is less true in Pike’s case: there is no factual doubt that in 1995, when she was 18, Pike, now 50, lured her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer into a wooded area, and with an accomplice, Pike’s 17-year-old boyfriend, tortured her for about half an hour before finally killing her by smashing her skull in with a piece of concrete. Slemmer’s mother has been a particularly vocal advocate for Pike’s execution, and is reportedly furious that her daughter’s killer has survived.

The wishes of victims and their families should be crucial to what our understanding of justice means. No one knows better the meaning and significance of violence than the people who it is inflicted on.

But it is also true that Pike’s criminal trial did not take into account factors in her life that might have explanatory, if not mitigating, power – such as the reality that she committed murder at the end of a childhood that had been marked by horrific, repeated, and severe sexual and physical violence.

And it is true, too, that when we assess what justice looks like, we must ask not only what would be most meaningful and satisfying for victims but also what best reflects our values and meets our obligations as a state. By that metric, the death penalty has always failed. It does not mete out justice so much as lower the collective community to the level of its worst perpetrators.

Lethal injection used to be a way for us to deny this. The protocol was developed in the US and first adopted for executions in the late 1970s. It was meant to replace older methods of state killing, such as gas chambers, electric chairs and firing squads, offering what was positioned as a more dignified and civilized, and supposedly less painful, way of murdering a human being.

What lethal injection did instead was medicalize the death penalty’s brutality, allowing its proponents a kind of polite denial of what the punishment actually is.

Pike shows us what it really is. It is violent, brutal and cruel. It is painful, no matter how much medical science is used to deny or obscure this; it is superfluous and contrary to the needs of justice, and it degrades those who engage in it.

For a long time, I thought of the death penalty as dangerously final, opening up the possibility of innocent people irretrievably lost, of mistakes that can’t be taken back. And it is true that this happens: America has executed innocent people.

But Pike’s experience shows us that this is not the end of execution’s horror. There is something worse.

Tennessee has issued a temporary moratorium on executions, and the governor has called for a review of what went wrong in Pike’s execution. But he should know what went wrong: the problems with the lethal injection protocol, as well as with the death penalty more broadly, were not mysteries even before the state of Tennessee failed to kill Pike.

It is still possible that Pike will have to fight not to be sent back to the execution chamber again. And this is another harm of the death penalty: the repetitiveness of its injustice, the way it keeps us from learning from our mistakes.

Rarely do we get a second chance to do right by someone like Pike. The state of Tennessee should not get a second chance to try to kill her.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Zavier Gozo: ‘You have to be uncomfortable to get to the highest levels’
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Crystal Palace’s American import had never lived anywhere but Utah before moving to London. Now, he’s aiming for more Premier League minutes

Much has changed in Zavier Gozo’s life since May.

Back then, Gozo was a day removed from learning that he wasn’t among Mauricio Pochettino’s 26 selections for the World Cup, having just made what proved to be his third-to-last appearance with boyhood club Real Salt Lake.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Gozo had only ever lived in Utah at that point. He would watch the World Cup from home, where he lived with his mother.

Today, less than five months later, he lives half a world away, is getting Premier League minutes and, as of a week ago, his first cap with the senior US men’s national team.

“It’s a big change to go from Utah to London,” said this master of understatement, stationed on a sofa in the lobby of the team’s downtown Minneapolis hotel in shorts, slippers, and a pristine white hoodie.

He has joined a familiar face there, at least, in his new international teammate – Chris Richards. The center-back has become a stalwart for club and country since joining Palace in 2022. He’s an every-minute option along the back, arguably their lead defender following the recent exits of Marc Guehi and Maxence Lacroix. Gozo has evidently endeared himself to Richards’ young daughter, too..

Then again, landing alongside a compatriot was far from the biggest hook that helped Gozo opt for Palace.

“I think I knew more [about them] than maybe the average [club],” Gozo says before listing their recent triumphs in the FA Cup (in 2025), the Conference League, and the Community Shield (both in 2026). “They were in a good run of form, and they have been for the last couple years, and have been showing it on the European stage.

“I’ve known them from [Wilfried] Zaha, and being a very good club that develops wingers and forwards in general. It seems like they always have a player that’s coming through their system that’s either sold for a lot or just becomes a very good player. And obviously, when Chris was there, I was just following them, and him, and their success. I feel like I knew a fair amount.”

Given Gozo’s ambitions, Palace’s track record of developing players from both their own academy and players brought in from other clubs was a significant reassurance. Their trophy cabinet and its rapidly waning open shelving was another boost, and their place in the Europa League offered even more games for Gozo to make his mark.

By the end of his time in MLS, Gozo hardly showed a flicker of fear. On one occasion, against Atlanta, he collected a ball at the edge of the final third near the right touchline with minimal attacking support. Rather than wait for support, he swiftly put the defender marking him through the spin cycle, cleverly dribbling infield and uncorking a curler to the far post. Four weeks later, against Kansas City, a split-second at the edge of the box was all he needed to execute a bombastic self-volley.

Rather than taking an incremental step up in difficulty, he’s now contending to make the bench in the world’s most competitive league.

“I think the coaching staff believes in me and is bought into developing me and the talent that I have,” Gozo said. “I think it’s a perfect environment for me to learn, but also be thrown into the fire a little bit. When you’re at RSL and you’re starting to become their best player, or one of their best players, and you go to Crystal Palace, sometimes you can lose confidence. Because it’s like, ‘oh wow, I can’t do the things I used to be able to do.’

“You just kind of have to figure out how you can become effective again, and yeah, obviously it can be hard at times, but also it’s what you want. You have to be uncomfortable to get to the highest levels.”

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

Beyond the sheer culture shock of switching from Salt Lake City to South London, Gozo has also seen his status on the roster switch. Gone are the days of being the boy wonder, the homegrown hero that fans have watched develop into a leading forward in MLS. Now he bears the pressure that comes with arriving on an eight-figure transfer fee, one of many promising American upstarts determined to thrive at the sport’s highest levels.

“It’s very different. Obviously, you don’t feel the connection with the fans as much. But also, you want to be able to do something for the fans, for them to be able to connect with you,” Gozo said. “[You want to] bring them happiness and bring them joy with what you do on the field. It’s more trying to prove yourself to the fans; I feel like with the fans of RSL, it’s kind of like they’re bringing you up, like giving you confidence while you’re coming up.”

He’s made three appearances from the bench for Palace in all competitions thus far, giving him a sense of the newly raised bar. The rate of play has increased considerably. Those defenders meeting him on the wing, like the aforementioned poor soul in Atlanta, are better supported by their teammates. Those spaces at the edge of the box, like the plot of grass afforded to him by Kansas City, are in far shorter supply.

Asked what he aims to improve after his Premier League introduction, Gozo said “physicality and not even being necessarily strong, but using your body in a way to either win a foul or protect the ball, and knowing when to take two touches, or take one touch, or turn and go dribble. Those are all things that you just have to have kind of perfect.”

Further refining those skills should also help him stick around Pochettino’s rejuvenated United States project. This past international window saw Gozo debut along with 11 rising upstarts, including fellow wingers Cavan Sullivan and Mathis Albert. Gozo appeared in just one of the four friendlies, logging nearly half an hour against Peru.

Gozo may be new to the senior team, but past camps and tournaments at the youth international levels are especially relevant given the program’s young sea change. He’s one of five members from the 2025 U-20 World Cup squad to debut in this window, having played with some since his first call-up to the U-15 level in 2022.

“I feel like the vibe at the national team has changed, especially since Pochettino has come here,” Gozo said, “Even just since the World Cup, I think a lot of people are more involved and paying attention.…It’s just an elevated energy, almost. It feels good to walk in and to be a part of this group.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Bucky Irving runs riot as Buccaneers stun Cowboys for first win of season
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Irving rushes for career-high 165 yards and two TDs

Rookie Daniels impresses in second NFL start

Prescott throws two picks as Dallas fall to 2-3

Bucky Irving already had his first 100-yard game since his rookie year in 2024 when the Tampa Bay running back finished off the Dallas Cowboys with a run that gave him a career high.

Jalon Daniels, the undrafted rookie filling in for franchise quarterback Baker Mayfield, enjoyed the view while doing plenty himself to get the Buccaneers their first win of the season in just his second start.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Irving ran for 165 yards, including a 72-yard run to set up the touchdown that put Tampa Bay ahead for good while scoring twice himself, and the Buccaneers beat the Cowboys 24-16 on Thursday night.

Daniels threw a TD pass to Irving in the first half while directing a turnover-free offense and amid several Dallas miscues, finishing an efficient 19 of 25 for 189 yards as the Bucs piled up 241 yards rushing.

Daniels is filling in for Baker Mayfield, who’s expected to be sidelined at least one more game with a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand.

“Six months ago, if you would have told me that my first win would have been on a Thursday night, [Amazon] Prime football game, I don’t know what I would have told you,” said Daniels, who threw three interceptions in a 17-14 loss to Green Bay in his debut. “Like I keep saying, through all the highs and lows, the bads, the goods, go through every single emotion because at the end of the day, it makes you better and prepares you for any situation that comes down the line.”

Irving had 21 carries and a 7.9-yard average while scoring on a 5-yard pass and a 1-yard plunge as the Bucs (1-4) finally found some footing in a season that started with expectations of winning the NFC South.

“We lost the first quarter of the season,” Bucs coach Todd Bowles said. “We didn’t lose the second, third or fourth. We’ve still got to play those. So we started the second quarter tonight. It’s a long way to climb out, but at the same time, we’re upbeat and if we played as hard and played as effective, we’ll be OK.”

Dak Prescott led a 99-yard drive and threw a 13-yard TD pass to George Pickens in the fourth quarter before his second interception off a tipped pass helped Tampa Bay clinch the win in the final two minutes.

The Cowboys (2-3) continued an up-and-down start to the season, this time with an offense that was at times as sloppy as the defense has been in both seasons under coach Brian Schottenheimer.

“I didn’t plan on being 2-3, disappointed by that for sure,” Schottenheimer said. “But we’re just getting started. There’s a lot of football left and we’re gonna play better. We know that.”

After Irving’s long run on the first play of the second half was followed by receiver Emeka Egbuka’s 14-yard TD run on a jet sweep, Prescott threw his first interception and the Dallas defense left Tez Johnson wide open on a 64-yard grab that led to Irving’s 1-yard plunge for a 21-10 lead.

KaVontae Turpin’s fumble on the subsequent kickoff led to a Tampa Bay field goal, but only after the Bucs converted a third-and-21 from the Dallas 48-yard line with Daniels’ 21-yard pass to Egbuka.

The Cowboys were missing one of the pieces they recently added to try to fix a porous defense. Cornerback Joey Porter Jr was a late scratch in what was supposed to be his second appearance since arriving in a trade from Pittsburgh last week.

Prescott was 24 of 42 for 316 yards in his first two-interception game of the season – his first picks since the opener.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Jamie Grierson
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns

Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts.

Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer.

Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has provided AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS.

The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m.

Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices? Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one.”

He added: “I think we are very targeted by the people that are targeting Israeli companies. We’re not an Israeli company, but because of our work in Israel we found ourselves in the middle of the row of the Gaza protests.”

Watson told the podcast he would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns if the situation arose, saying: “We don’t actually work in that sector, but yes, of course we would.”

He called Palantir “the most interesting company on the planet” as he announced his new role last month. The company said his job would be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”.

Watson was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, he has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir.

after newsletter promotion

Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while he worked for the company in London.

The Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the science, innovation and technology committee, which has raised concerns about Palantir, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “Tom is not the first politician to be blinded by tech hype. The key issue is we can’t be so dependent on one company. It’s a US company, subject to US legislation regarding access to our data.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Anthropic bans users from ‘needless abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
A spokesperson behind the tech company’s AI chatbot has not yet specified what counts as abusive or cruel content

Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness.

The Verge first reported the change in policy.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”.

In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”.

Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct.

The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare.

“We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website.

The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said he cannot rule out the possibility.

Meanwhile, Sam Altman, CEO of rival OpenAI, has appeared averse to the idea.

“I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue,” he wrote in an X post, days after the New York Times reported on Anthropic leaders’ extensive conversations with religious scholars.
