https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.title: The best sunrise alarm clocks in the UK, tried and tested for gentler mornings
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.author: Pete Wise
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter/20.text:
Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Our reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to Dreamegg

The best eye masks to help you sleep better

T
o wake each day in darkness is a plight you wouldn’t wish on your worst enemy, yet that’s what many of us do routinely throughout winter. Getting up in the dark decouples our life from our circadian rhythm (our body clock), with bodily processes such as cognition and metabolism put to work before they’re fully prepped.

Thank heavens, then, for sunrise alarm clocks. These “dawn simulation” devices glow with gradually intensifying brightness as your wake-up time approaches, kickstarting your circadian rhythm before you get out of bed. For many users, this results in a happier, healthier start to the day.

Sunrise alarm clocks can differ vastly – for instance, only some are bright enough to be medically certified as light-therapy devices for Sad (seasonal affective disorder) and other disorders. We’ve indicated the two alarms that have this certification in their specs below.

I tested 10 wake-up lights from Lumie, Beurer, Philips, Dreamegg, Blueair and Lexon to find out which would make the most difference to my mornings, and these are the eight I recommend. As a lifelong reluctant riser, I’ve found the experience of testing these devices a gamechanger – in fact, I’m now using one daily. Perhaps mornings aren’t so bad, after all …

Best sunrise alarm clock overall
Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150

Best budget sunrise alarm
Lumie Sunrise Alarm

Best sunrise alarm clock for heavy sleepers
Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100

Best sunrise alarm for late-night reading
Philips SmartSleep

Best mini sunrise alarm clock
Lexon Mina Sunrise

Best sunrise alarm clock for couples
Beurer Wake-up Light WL50

Mornings, eh? I’ve often felt lousy first thing, after waking up to a minutes-long medley of smartphone alarms.

When, at last, I drag myself out of bed, I frequently spend the day reviewing all kinds of gadgets, from Sad lamps to electric heaters. It’s a freelance job I’ve been privileged to do since 2017 – and as we tumbled dimly into 2025, the Filter gave me one of my most quietly life-improving assignments yet: reviewing sunrise alarm clocks. I tested three additional models in winter 2025/26, and one of these has emerged as my favourite of all.

The extent to which these gadgets have improved my mornings has surprised me – although it was greater in some cases than others. Frankly, I’d like other groggy wakers to feel the same benefit, and my reviews are written and ranked with this in mind.

Some brands did not want the sunrise alarm clocks I sourced for testing back, so those will be donated for fundraising to Cat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.

The only proper way to test a sunrise alarm clock is by using it to wake up each morning – so that’s what I did.

I used each model for at least two nights, testing out multiple light and alarm sound settings, and assessing the quality of wake-up for each device. I considered the brightness of each alarm, how close the glow felt to real sunlight, and the audio quality. Above all, I reflected on how lively and refreshed I felt after waking up with each one.

Many sunrise alarm clocks also have a sundown function, so I used this where available too. I also tried using each sunrise alarm clock as a reading light, to help me finish the day – as well as start it – smartphone-free.

Some sunrise alarm clocks go even further, with additional features such as app operability, multiple alarm profiles and mood lighting. To ensure a thorough review of each sunrise alarm clock, I played around with every possible customisation option and functionality.

Lumie is the brand that pioneered consumer-grade sunrise alarm clocks in the early 1990s, and that pedigree still shines through.

Equipped with a comprehensive set of wake-up sounds and medical-grade sunrise simulation, the Bodyclock Glow 150 is the best sunrise alarm clock of the many I’ve tested. It comes at a premium price, but could pay dividends for your sleep cycle.

Why we love it
The sunrise effect is among the most convincing I’ve experienced, rivalling the less fully featured (but slightly cheaper) Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100, which is reviewed below. It feels like waking to daylight, or emerging into a clearing after walking through dense woodland.

I found this model easy to control and configure via the five buttons surrounding the digital display. All of the personalisations that really matter are available, including sunrise light intensity and duration.

Crucially, there’s a great selection of alarm tones to choose between – not always the case with Lumie models – ranging from the wonderfully gentle to the brusquely rousing. I preferred “tropical birds” and “waves” to “beep” or “steam train”, although I enjoyed imagining a train enthusiast waking contentedly to the latter.

It’s a shame that … there’s only one colour available: black (with a white lamp). This will suit some bedroom design schemes better than others.

Certification: UK MDR 2002 and EU MDR 2017/745 medical classification
Modes: sunrise alarm, sunset, bedside light
Footprint: W19 x D12cm
Features: light-sensitive auto-dimming display
Brightness settings: five
Sunrise duration: 20, 30 or 45 minutes

Read our full Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150 sunrise alarm clock review

Imagine telling one of your ancestors that you were awoken this morning by your lamp, which was purring at you. I’m not pulling your leg, you might say, it’s all thanks to the Lumie Sunrise’s “kittens purring” alarm tone, which sits sweetly alongside four other natural sounds, including goats bleating and birdsong.

Why we love it
In all seriousness, this is an excellent sunrise alarm clock, and it comes at a standout price. Its sunrise light subtly brightens during the minutes leading up to your chosen alarm time, producing a lovely awakening that really did remind me of natural light.

I found it easy enough to set the Sunrise Alarm’s time and alarm, although pressing some of the buttons can be fiddly. Do keep the instruction manual handy, as there are lots of options and buttons to get your head around.

It’s a shame that … it lacks a little bedside table appeal. But having said that, this sunrise alarm clock has incredible performance for the price.

Certification: none
Modes: sunrise alarm, sunset, mood, bedside light
Footprint: W17 x D9cm
Features: mood lighting (six colours)
Brightness settings: 10
Sunrise duration: 30 minutes

I woke up feeling great when I used the medical-grade Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100, which bathes the room in gradually intensifying, sun-like light for a set period before the alarm goes off.

Why we love it
The device is supposed to realistically imitate the lightening shades of a sunrise – and it does so more convincingly than any other brand’s sunrise alarm clock. Depending on your chosen light intensity setting, it can get very bright.

The Spark 100 also has a sunset feature that graduates through the same red, orange and white light colours used with the sunrise function, but in reverse order. After the sunset cycle, the light can either switch off entirely or remain in a gentle night-light mode, whichever you choose.

Besides performing brilliantly as a wake-up light and sunset simulator, the Spark 100 is simply a nicely designed, well-made thing. I appreciated its soft-edged yet robust construction and handy features such as the cable organisation in the base. It’s a pleasure to have on the bedside table.

It’s a shame that … the alarm tone sounds piercing at the higher three of its five volume levels. I found myself settling for a 2/5 – though very heavy sleepers may prefer (or even relish) the louder options.

Certification: UK MDR 2002 and EU MDR 2017/745 medical classification
Modes: sunrise alarm, sunrise, sunset, bedside light
Footprint: W19 x D12cm
Features: tap to snooze, auto-dimming display, adjustable sunrise/sunset duration, adjustable digital display brightness
Brightness settings: five
Sunrise duration: 30 minutes

This lamp soon felt like part of the furniture on my bedside table. In typical Philips fashion, it’s a good-quality, dependable product, with a solid middle-of-the-road design that won’t look out of place in many bedrooms.

Why we love it
Setup is slick – I was able to set my alarm time, sound and brightness by following the simple prompts on the device’s display, without having to consult the manual. Subsequently tweaking your alarm(s) takes practice, but you’ll master all the controls you need after a few days.

The SmartSleep’s wake-up capabilities are impressive, combining brilliant light with a diverse choice of alarm sounds. It also has FM radio and 3.5mm auxiliary audio input options for the user who has tired of Alpine and gong bath soundscapes. There’s a 5V USB charging outlet at the rear of the lamp, too, which could free up a valuable bedside power socket.

I loved using this model as a reading light, as well as a sunrise alarm. Even when a bright setting is selected, the light seems relatively mellow and restful, which helped me get to sleep after reading pulpy detective novels late at night. The light can be deactivated with a press.

It’s a shame that … it costs such a lot. The SmartSleep has a hefty price to match its impressive performance.

Certification: none
Modes: sunrise alarm, sleep mode with sunset simulation, bedside light
Footprint: W22 x D12cm
Features: FM radio, Aux audio input, “RelaxBreathe” breathing exercises, adjustable sunrise duration, snooze, up to two wake-up profiles (with separate alarms)
Brightness settings: 25
Sunrise duration: 20, 25, 30, 35 or 40 minutes

My only general gripe with sunrise alarm clocks is that many of them are an aesthetic downgrade on a conventional bedside lamp – but this charming mini model from French brand Lexon is a stylish exception.

Why we love it
The obvious draw here is the design, which comprises a cute, mushroom-shaped light and colourful metal base with a wraparound digital display. It fits very neatly on to a small or well-utilised bedside table.

The sunrise light function roused me gently before the alarm tone (also gently rousing) sounded, and I got up feeling alert. Even though this isn’t a very bright light, it evidently did the trick, and it was suitable for bedtime reading, too.

You can choose from five alarm tones, all of which sound pleasantly full and rich. These include birdsong and water sounds, as well as some loud, piercing alarms that will suit particularly heavy sleepers. Beautifully finished and stoutly made, the Mina Sunrise is a cut above the rest in terms of build quality.

It’s a shame that … the control buttons are on the base, and can’t be seen in the dark without a secondary light source such as a smartphone torch. You’d struggle to adjust the settings in the middle of the night.

Certification: none
Modes: sunrise alarm, sunset, bedside light
Footprint: W11 x D11cm
Features: mood lighting (nine colours), snooze, cordless operation
Brightness settings: five
Sunrise duration: 30 minutes

Thanks to its capability to save two alarms for different times (each with its own sound and light settings), the Beurer WL 50 is a great choice for couples who get up at different times. That’s a rare feature in any sunrise alarm clock – let alone in such a reasonably priced model.

Why we love it
The sunrise mode itself is gentle yet effective, and it’s easy to activate the device as a reading light with a simple, groggy tap. I really liked the alarm sounds you get with the WL 50 too – which is just as well, as there are only two.

Perhaps that narrow choice of alarm tones sounds a little stingy, but it seems less so when you explore the WL 50’s alternative audio options. It doubles up as an FM radio, with space to save up to 30 station presets, which you can listen to throughout the day or use as a livelier alternative to an alarm tone. Bluetooth connectivity and an AUX input expand your listening options further.

Curiously, this sunrise alarm clock can be unplugged (when fully charged) and used on the go for up to three hours. It’s hard to imagine a situation wherein this would be useful, but I appreciate the gesture.

It’s a shame that … the sound quality isn’t great (but it’s good enough for the half-awake).

Certification: none
Modes: sunrise alarm, sunset simulation, bedside light, radio/speaker
Footprint: W11 x D11cm
Features: FM radio, AUX audio input, Bluetooth audio, portable use (up to three hours), LED mood light
Brightness settings: adjustable
Sunrise duration: 10, 20 or 30 minutes

Best for: an air-purifying sunrise alarm clock

Most of us spend around a third of our time in bed, so a sunrise alarm clock that also purifies your bedroom air seems like a good idea. This model, the Blueair Mini Restful, is heralded as the world’s first.

By sunrise alarm clock standards, it isn’t really mini. I found myself resting it on the floor, where I could see the digital display on the top, rather than putting it on my bedside table.

The sunrise function proved effective, waking me reliably with warm, increasingly bright light before the alarm sounded. As for the purification, the Mini Restful certainly made my air feel fresher after a windowsill-sanding session had kicked up untold volumes of dust. The fan works exceptionally quietly, although I still preferred to run it only during the daytime (this can be automated via the Blueair app’s schedule feature).

It didn’t make the final cut because … the sunrise alarm feature is only accessible via the Blueair app, and I feel that users should have the option to activate it manually. With that said, the app is a pleasure to use.

Certification: none; modes: night light, sunrise alarm; footprint: W17 x D17cm; features: air purification, app control, alarm schedule; brightness settings: scale of 0-100%; sunrise duration: 15-30 minutes

Best for: soothing sleep sounds

This compact, great-looking device offers something different, with a selection of 29 ambient sounds that can be used as white noise to help you fall asleep. There are also five options for rousing you in the morning, including birdsong, a campfire crackling and, my favourite, waves breaking on a shore. For me, perhaps the only issue with this approach was that the sounds did a better job of putting me to sleep than they did of waking me up.

The Sunrise 1 is a beautifully designed alarm clock, with a softly textured front and foolproof dimmer controls on either side to adjust the light level and digital display brightness. Reluctant risers will be pleased to note there’s a prominent snooze button at the top of the device – though, personally, I’ve rarely felt the need to use this feature while testing sunrise alarm clocks.

It didn’t make the final cut because … its light is a little too dim for my taste.

Certification: none; modes: sunrise alarm, white noise/sleep sounds, bedside light; footprint: W15 x D7.3cm; features: sleep sound timer, nine light colours, five wake-up sounds; brightness settings: adjustable; sunrise duration: Up to 60 minutes

A cursory glance at Google Trends search data – or perhaps at your chosen social media platform – will tell you that interest in sunrise alarm clocks has grown sharply in recent years. You may wonder: is this overdue recognition for a useful technology, or is it a murkier wellness trend to file alongside mouth taping and stuffing onion slices into socks?

While there hasn’t been a great deal of academic research into sunrise alarm clocks, some studies suggest they may benefit our sleep health. For instance, researchers from Ohio University found that trial participants had significantly better sleep scores and lower perceived stress and burnout after spending two weeks waking with a sunrise alarm clock while also avoiding smartphone use in bed.

The ultimate test of whether sunrise alarm clocks are a fad will be time. I’m still using mine, as I approach a third winter.

Sad bright-light therapy involves the use of intense light (in the region of 10,000 lux) to mimic the effects of bright sunlight. Sunrise alarm clocks tend to be far less bright than the average Sad lamp. With that said, light exposure around dawn and in the early morning can influence our circadian rhythms, so even a relatively dim sunrise alarm may still have benefits.

If you’ve been diagnosed with seasonal affective disorder and are looking for a light-therapy device, it’s best to ask your GP which product to use and how to get the most benefit. Sunrise alarm clocks that are classified as medical devices (indicated in the specs each product above) are more likely to suit users seeking a therapeutic effect than models with no medical certifications.

Getting up in the dark can feel awful, which makes a lot of sense because light helps our bodies wake up properly.

Humans are diurnal, which means we’ve evolved to be more wakeful, energetic and capable of chasing mammoths over vast distances during daytime. When the brain recognises increasing light at dawn, it sends signals around other regions of the brain and to other organs to calibrate bodily processes including temperature regulation, hormone secretion and metabolism. And when darkness falls, the brain prepares us for sleep – a helpful effect that many of us compromise by looking at bright smartphone or laptop screens.

These processes follow roughly 24-hour cycles known as our circadian rhythms. The term is derived from the Latin words circa (approximately) and diem (day), meaning around a day.

So, the sun is the original and best alarm clock – activating our minds and bodies with light, rather than startling us awake with sound. Think of your sunrise alarm as a plucky stand-in to rely upon during the star’s shorter winter shifts.

Some users find the light from their sunrise alarm clock more rousing than others do. If you’re a heavy sleeper, there’s a heightened chance that the artificial sunrise will not wake you (although it might still help you feel more alert on waking).

How you configure your sunrise alarm clock makes a difference. We all sleep more deeply during certain periods of our sleep cycle – and this includes particularly heavy sleepers. So, by setting your sunrise alarm clock to do a relatively long dawn simulation cycle (30 minutes is an option on several models), you give the gradually increasing light more time to rouse you. You’ll often have a choice between multiple light intensity settings, too, so select the brightest one available.

If you’re worried about waking up on time, all of the sunrise alarm clocks featured in this guide can conclude their sunrise cycle with an audio alarm tone. So, they could serve perfectly well as a wake-up alarm, even if they don’t successfully start rousing you before the beep. To be on the safe side, I’d recommend choosing a louder model, such as the Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.title: End Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.author: Alex Spencer
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.text:
PlayStation 5 (version played), Xbox, PC; Epic Games Publishing
This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition

A
small band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.

End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

This combination of cute and eerie immediately marks End of Abyss as part of the Scandi-chiaroscuro style pioneered by Limbo and Inside (from Playdead, in Copenhagen) and Little Nightmares (from Malmö-based Tarsier Studios, where the founders of End of Abyss developer Section 9 cut their teeth). Those games, though, were all puzzle-platformers. End of Abyss is a survival-horror game in the mould of PS1-era Resident Evil, which took a similarly zoomed-out approach, using fixed, CCTV-reminiscent camera angles. It’s a great way of controlling each scene’s composition for maximum aesthetic value – and, of course, to set up scares.

End of Abyss delights in lovingly decorated dioramas, with bodies and viscera laid out just so, illuminated by the flickering light of a CRT screen and some orange-glowing item (a valuable key or weapon upgrade) dangling just out of reach. As you’re studying these details, trying to figure out how you might reach that desirable object, at the edge of your vision a monster will peel itself from the darkness and attack before you can consciously register its presence.

What follows is a dance of backpedalling and firing your pistol, praying that it’s loaded with enough ammo to finish off the advancing assailant before it can catch up to you. Or, worse, your retreat carries you into another nest of monsters. These are foundational thrills of the genre, and End of Abyss keeps them intact as it shrinks them down to dollhouse size. They might be scarier still, in fact, because manually aiming a gun from a top-down perspective can be fiddly, and End of Abyss’s control scheme is so confounding (who puts reload on the right thumbstick?) that you’re fighting muscle memory as much as the monsters.

On top of this survival-horror foundation, though, End of Abyss layers elements of Dark Souls, Metroid and Hollow Knight – and here it overextends. This facility is big and complex enough for you to get lost in, filled with doors that only open from the other side and seemingly separate zones that join up in unexpected ways. These can be some of video games’ finest pleasures, when done right, but they make for an uncomfortable fit in a game that relies on a character so slow-moving that they can be threatened by a shambling zombie.

That striking gloomy style, meanwhile, is something of an achilles heel when you’re trying to tell one room from another. It’s not helped by a pause-screen map that struggles to convey the interlocking territory, and, at the time of playing, is prone to getting confused over questions as fundamental as which doors are locked.

This leads to a lot of unnecessary backtracking and, with every repeat visit, those carefully staged scenes lose some of their sheen. A composition that had you gawping the first time can’t hope to maintain that effect on the dozenth visit, while the shadow-peeling scares turn out to run on the clockwork logic of a fairground ghost train. Reaching the final boss after 12 hours, with much of the map still greyed out and other stretches tromped over endlessly, I’m left feeling exhausted, with little inclination to explore the other half of the game that (according to the completion percentage) remains unseen. Contrary to its fetchingly diminutive presentation, End of Abyss might be just too big for its own good.

End of Abyss is out now; £22.69

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Devi Sridhar
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

I
n the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.

Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.

While there were slight variations among the three countries, larger patterns are clear. Among women who are under 50 in England, breast, bowel, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreatic and stomach cancers have increased. For men under 50 in England, there were increases in bowel, kidney, liver, pancreatic and prostate cancers. This is the opposite of what we would hope to achieve in public health – and no, it isn’t only because we have better diagnostic tools, or are doing more testing. While this explains some of the increase, it doesn’t account for it all. The data indicates that younger generations are experiencing a higher incidence of some cancers than previous generations at the same age. Put more simply: you have a higher chance of cancer at a younger age than your parents.

Scientists are now working to unpick what has changed between generations that might be driving this uptick, especially trying to find things people may have been exposed to during childhood or adolescence in the 1990s that they wouldn’t have been in the 1950s.

Here are some potential explanations: what we eat has changed significantly over the past 50 years, with the rise in ultra-processed and fast foods as well as sugary drinks. We also are more sedentary as a population. These changes are linked to rising levels of excess weight and obesity. Body fat, especially around the vital organs and waist, is a risk factor for chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction, all of which are linked to higher cancer incidence. Globally, obesity rates have more than doubled among adults and quadrupled among adolescents since 1990. Data collected in 2024 found that about 66% of adults in England were either overweight or living with obesity.

But diet, physical activity and excess body weight doesn’t fully explain the rise of certain cancers – such as breast cancer – in young people. Studies have shown that for women before menopause, a higher BMI is, in fact, linked to a slightly lower risk of cancer (which is in contrast to older women, where a higher BMI significantly increases risk of developing breast cancer.) Going further, scientists are looking at the health impact of sustained exposure to environmental toxins like air and water pollution, chemicals and plastics that have become widespread and almost impossible to avoid over the past 50 years.

It has been scientifically challenging to identify one toxin that explains the global increase in cancers. Cancer can develop long after exposure to a toxic chemical, and over our lives we encounter a range of chemicals and pollutants. Saying which one, or whether it was during childhood, in utero, or adulthood, is difficult to pin down.

On the positive side, one area that we have made progress with in young people is lung cancer, largely driven by anti-smoking campaigns and widespread awareness of the links between smoking and lung cancer. So not everything is getting worse.

None of the continuing research into risk factors for early onset cancer should mean attaching blame to patients. One of the first human impulses when getting a diagnosis is to think “what caused this?”, and even further, “what have I done?” – and this isn’t helpful. In addition, scientists estimate that only 40% of cancers at a population level are because of an “individually modifiable” behaviour like smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity, or weight. The other 60% is a mix of ageing, genetic susceptibility, infection, possible environmental factors, and sometimes just bad luck.

With the research and investment continuing into scientific research, we will eventually learn what’s driving the rise in cancer in younger people. But for now, that mystery is still to be uncovered.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Gordon Brown
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

T
he coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies?

While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home to four of the world’s top 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, the UK produces 6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Our research expertise is one of the many reasons we have been at the forefront of recent inventions: from AlphaFold, which predicts how proteins behave, to viral-vector vaccine technology and AI that detects cancer as reliably as radiologists. Britain already sits at the intersection of AI, quantum computing and synthetic biology. The question then is: why, having led the first Industrial Revolution, should the UK not be the world’s great innovation nation once again?

We know the public have an entrepreneurial spirit, and back this vision. New polling for this week’s conference finds that 75% of people agree that innovation is essential for creating UK economic growth.

But it is disappointing that only 36% of the British public believes the country is a world leader in science. It is time for innovation to move to the forefront of government policy and the 10-year plan the government is preparing. If we were to raise Britain to Swedish or Japanese levels of innovation intensity we would, over time, leave every household £5,000 better off (according to my calculations), and increase our national income by £150bn a year as higher investment in research and development feeds through into productivity. And a jobs plan on the scale that Our Scottish Future has proposed for Scotland would mean about 3m new jobs across the UK.

We can identify the major hurdles to overcome. While the UK is good at startups and spin-outs, we are slow to turn startups into scale-ups, and even slower to turn scale-ups into global success stories. Per head of population, the US has double the number of $1bn companies and nearly three times as many $10bn-plus companies than the UK. And even when we do scale up at home, three-quarters of venture capital investment comes from overseas.

Turning this around will require a government to keep tackling the bottlenecks that are inevitably created from innovation. Speakers from future-facing companies at today’s conference will set out the steps that we need to consider. These will range from making sure firms can access the money they need to grow from UK investors, to new incentives for investors, to public-private partnerships – as happens in Germany, France and Italy – capitalised by the British Business Bank and the national wealth fund. Competition policy must favour new entrants against vested interests and be aligned with a favourable tax regime, such as through research and development credits that favour companies of all sizes.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Research for the conference has identified 127 innovative clusters covering every region and nation of the UK, many of which will succeed if we are willing to give long-term support to the infrastructure, skills training and research and development support from UK Research and Innovation they need to grow. In order to harness this potential, more power needs to be devolved to enable mayors and regional authorities to act locally while ensuring access to global markets.

Britain does not lack genius or great assets. Every nation, including ours, must do more to find its “lost Einsteins” – the young people in lower-income areas who have the talent but not yet the opportunity to show their creative genius. What we need now is to create a chain of hope that connects all people to intellectual discovery and deployment, to startups and scale-ups, and to global leadership – all aligned around a shared national purpose.

Sixty-four years ago, John F Kennedy declared that the US would lead a nationwide effort to be first on the moon. But the space initiative was not his first choice. He had wanted a national project that everybody could feel part of, and revealed he would have preferred to have chosen a project on Earth – if he could have found one with the same power to inspire a national mission that the whole population could enthusiastically embrace.

Today, we can choose to be the innovation nation. “This generation does not intend to founder in the backwash of the coming age,” said Kennedy of the US. And this generation of Britons has no intention of being left behind as the age of AI accelerates. Today’s event, spearheaded by the prime minister in Manchester – itself a city of innovation – will send a message that we mean to be in the global vanguard; not because, as Kennedy said, it is easy to do, but even though it is hard. For the challenge now is to do more than invent the future. We must invest in it, manufacture it and, wherever possible, own it here in Britain.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Exclusive: Badenoch’s flagship conference policy document cites £957bn estimate, twice the total in climate advisers’ data

Kemi Badenoch’s flagship party conference policy document overestimated the cost of net zero by nearly £500bn, seemingly after someone accidentally double-counted figures on a spreadsheet.

The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech.

Justifying the Conservatives’ decision to scrap the target of the UK reaching net zero emissions by 2050, introduced under Theresa May, the document says that estimates of how much this would cost the economy “have varied enormously”.

It goes on: “In 2020, the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated that its route to net zero would cost £957bn.” It cites the Sixth Carbon Budget produced by the CCC, the government’s climate change advisers, saying the report put gross economic costs at £1.4tn, falling to £957bn when savings were taken into account.

However, the figures in the report in fact total £478bn, half of what the Tory document said. The error appears to have arisen because a tally of all the costs in a CCC spreadsheet from the document also included the row showing totals for each individual column, thus doubling it.

A CCC spokesperson said: “We don’t recognise this number. The committee has previously offered to meet with Ms Badenoch and talk her through our advice. That offer is, of course, still open.”

The committee’s most recent analysis puts the expected cost of achieving net zero by 2050 at about £110bn, or about £4bn a year – 0.2% of GDP.

The error was spotted by the publication Carbon Brief, which informed the Guardian.

It is possible the Conservatives copied the figure without checking it. It appears to have been published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator.

The Conservative document says it is intended to be a precise diagnosis of the UK’s problems. It is modelled in part on The Right Approach, produced by Margaret Thatcher’s Tory party in 1976, which set out some of the economic ideas later used in the 1979 election.

In a foreword, Badenoch notes that “as an engineer”, she is used to correctly diagnosing issues so they can be addressed. A later part of the report says: “To fix a problem we must first have an accurate understanding of what is causing it.”

The Conservatives and Badenoch’s office were contacted for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Revealed: the ‘black box’ wastewater trade that rakes in millions for UK utility companies
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Rachel Salvidge
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Exclusive: Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutants

Water companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland.

Water companies in England are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

However, no independent regulator oversees the trade-effluent process and there is no central register, so Watershed Investigations, the Guardian and the campaign group River Action compiled a database of 26,000 consents, providing the first ever national picture of the system.

The investigation found an annual total of up to 608bn litres of industrial wastewater entering sewage works from sites such as power stations, pharmaceutical plants, food factories, hospitals, abattoirs and waste facilities.

The permits are issued and enforced by the water companies themselves, with environmental regulators having no direct role. “It’s a bit of a black box,” one industry expert said.

Most sewage works only have biological treatment facilities, which are not designed to remove industrial chemicals, including flame retardants, Pfas, solvents and pharmaceuticals. Some permits on the database feature chemicals such as cyanide, chromium, cadmium and mercury. Watershed has mapped every sewage treatment works and the industrial companies permitted to send waste to each one.

Pollutants that survive treatment are discharged into rivers, lakes and seas as “treated effluent”, while those captured in sewage sludge are spread on farmland as fertiliser. The waste also adds to the overloading of sewer networks that triggers raw sewage spills, which have caused outrage, community protests and calls for the industry to be nationalised so that profits can be reinvested in improving the system rather than going to shareholders.

United Utilities made the most revenue from industrial waste last year, at £61.6m, followed by Yorkshire Water at £48.8m. However, these companies included revenues from tankered waste in their figures, while some others did not. Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water, Scottish Water and Wessex Water said they routed commercial tankered waste through separate companies within their groups.

Thames Water has the largest volume of permitted industrial sewage, at 113bn litres, followed by United Utilities at 105bn litres and Severn Trent Water at 79bn litres.

Across the sector, revenues from receiving industrial and commercial wastewater have risen sharply in five years, with Anglian Water’s increasing by 62%.

The industry expert said water companies had “a financial incentive to accept far more toxic material than they should”.

The permit regime was very old and not fit for purpose, they added. “Currently the Environment Agency doesn’t know exactly how much of this waste is going into waterworks each year.”

Waste handlers also drive tankers carrying industrial effluents, landfill leachate and other liquid wastes to sewage works. An Environment Agency (EA) officer said landfill leachate was its “greatest concern” because of the harmful chemical cocktail it can contain.

Both the officer and the industry expert identified Davyhulme wastewater treatment works in Manchester, operated by United Utilities, and Avonmouth, operated by Wessex Water, as big receivers of tankered waste. “Carriers will drive [long distances] to dispose of their wastes here … You can see lines of tankers queueing outside Avonmouth,” the expert said.

Checks by water companies across the sector can just involve taking a sample and carrying out basic pH and metals analysis, but even more advanced testing does not always pick up a wide range of potentially harmful substances, “and by the time you’ve identified [that] it had something nasty in it, it’s already gone”, the EA officer added.

But “ignorance is no defence”, said the officer. “They should be seeking sufficient information from the producer of that waste to satisfy themselves so they can treat it properly.”

The industry expert said the UK needed a dedicated liquid-waste treatment sector rather than relying on a “dilute and disperse” model.

Amy Fairman, the head of campaigns at River Action, said: “Industrial pollution must not become a lucrative business for water companies … Polluters must be held to account and made to pay, rather than passing the costs and consequences down the line.

“The public has a right to know what is being put into our sewage works and where those pollutants ultimately end up. The government has promised to clean up [England’s] rivers through the clean water bill – it must confront this hidden industrial wastewater trade and address the serious failures exposed by this investigation.”

“Water companies should never profit from pollution,” said a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. “We know the water industry hasn’t been working in the public interest for far too long and that’s why we are reforming it, including how wastewater is disposed of.”

An EA spokesperson said the trade-effluent framework was “developed over 30 years ago”, before many of today’s concerns about Pfas were fully understood, and that it was working to improve how contaminants in wastewater were managed.

A spokesperson for the trade association Water UK said: “Water companies [in England] are legally obliged to accept trade effluent and charges are set by Ofwat. The Environment Agency sets the permit conditions, but they make no account of the fact that sewers are not designed to treat a range of toxic substances such as forever chemicals and mercury, which is still, sadly, used by many dentists.

“That’s why we have long called for the government to ban these toxic substances and to force the manufacturers to pay the costs of removing them from the environment.”

A United Utilities spokesperson said it had “strict consent and control processes” operating under “regulatory requirements designed to protect public health and the environment” and that it “assesses, monitors and treats wastewater”. It added that tankered waste, including landfill leachate, was accepted only at specifically permitted sites.

NI Water said applications involving “priority substances” were referred to the Northern Ireland Environment Agency, and dedicated teams sampled sewer and tanker effluent to “oversee compliance”.

Scottish Water said it assessed trade-effluent applications based on factors including sewer and treatment capacity, protection of infrastructure and staff, and compliance with environmental standards. All water companies included in this article were contacted for comment.

Companies can also discharge industrial wastewater directly into rivers and seas, but this is subject to permits issued by the environmental regulators.

In England, water companies are regulated by Ofwat and the Environment Agency, with policy set by Defra. Ofwat also covers Wales, but environmental regulation sits with Natural Resources Wales and policy with the Welsh government. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regulators and publicly owned water companies, with policy set by their devolved governments.

This article was amended on 9 October 2026 to add context on the policy and regulatory framework within the devolved administrations of the UK; to note that the cited figure of 608bn litres of trade effluent is a maximum annual total based on applied consents; and to clarify a reference to the types of substances that can be missed by most routine water analysis.

Pollutants that survive treatment are discharged into rivers, lakes and seas as ‘treated effluent’ The Environment Agency sets the permit conditions but they make no account of the fact that sewers are not designed to treat toxic substances such as forever chemicals and mercury.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Digested week: Don’t worry about the plague, go and read some Anne Carson
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Emma Brockes
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
The world may be going to hell in a handcart, but at least now I get to say I know a Nobel prize winner

“Anyone worried about pneumonic plague?” This is a friend – a medic – texting me after reading reports at the weekend of the 28-year-old Russian woman who died while working at a “plague research lab” in Siberia. Relying on details from the famously open Russian state guaranteed the presence of a certain dark subtext to the tantalisingly short news item. Namely: lab-grown disease cultivated for reasons unknown and with a 100% mortality rate escapes Russian facility into general population, eight hours’ flying time from London. In other words, we’re all going to die.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

My first thought was: is this better or worse than the time that guy who’d been exposed to Ebola took the subway to go bowling in Brooklyn? The answer to which of course is that post-Covid, it’s worse: we know exactly how these things go, how they start small, with a news in brief buried 20 pages deep in the paper, moving glacially up the news list every few days until a lonely death in a Siberian laboratory leads, step by incremental step, to the zombie apocalypse.

Meanwhile, the word “plague” remains outlandishly unrelaxing, despite the best efforts of the New York Times to contextualise it. Elucidating the various different types of plague that can kill you – pneumonic, septicemic and bubonic – I have to say my money would have been on bubonic as the worst, what with the Black Death and all. Apparently, however, the most virulent form of plague is the one in question, pneumonic, spread by a cough or a sneeze and causing “a severe rapid-onset lung infection” that can kill within a few days. Advice from my medic friend in New York: “Get antibiotics for everyone.” Alternatively, invest in a sense of proportion.

I did not have “let’s have more firing squads” on my bingo card of talking points this week, but that is the serious discussion under way in the US after the horrific, botched execution of Christa Pike, the convicted murderer on death row who regained consciousness and started talking on Tuesday after the state of Tennessee failed to kill her.

This was the second botched execution by the state this year, and one of the apparently 7% of all executions in the US since 1972 that have not been effective, among the most common reasons cited being expired drugs and untrained executioners, but also malfunctioning electric chairs that set fire to their occupants.

As a result, the single method of executing a prisoner in the US that has resulted in no failed attempts whatsoever is the firing squad, a phrase that raises images, incomprehensible in a supposedly modern world, of a semicircle of shooters, none bearing sole responsibility, firing in the direction of the condemned’s head. For the first time in the US military since 1945, one such execution is due to happen at Fort Hood, Texas, in December, which this week Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, promised to livestream in defiance of anything resembling normal human behaviour.

There’s likely a joke about the failure of the Tory party to lie down and accept its fate after so many lethal injections, but I can’t quite bring it home. Instead, at party conference this week in Birmingham, we saw a chipper-seeming Kemi Badenoch step out on stage to perform her pantomime version of common sense, smartly referring to the Reform party as “that” – as in “we are not uniting with that”. The Tory leader does an extremely good job of appearing to be a plain-spoken and regular human in contrast with Reform, on the one hand, and what might delicately be called the unusual makeup of the Greens on the other.

It’s worth remembering what Badenoch looks like when the mask slips. If Boris Johnson’s real face was the rictus of an underbriefed, overconfident man white-knuckling his way through government while chuckling to himself like a toy in a horror movie, Badenoch strikes me as someone who is stuck on the gimlet-eyed setting of victory at all costs. Meanwhile, footage of Young Conservatives partying at conference never gets old, offering a strong rival for most embarrassing moment to the 30,000-word policy document the Tory leader – hide your face – has self-christened “Kemistry”. Someone tell her you can’t coin your own nicknames.

Anne Carson has won the Nobel prize for literature and, forgive me, but very occasionally when life gives you the opportunity to be insufferable, you can’t not take it. So, in response to this news, I would like to say that when I went hiking with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson in Iceland last year the thought struck me …

There was no thought; I just wanted to get it on the table about the hike – OK, it was a short walk up a rocky incline – it was with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson, who I have loved forever and have known since we met in Michigan many years ago. She is brilliant and funny and wise, and I could cite so many lines from her poetry but one of my favourites is this, from the poem Lines in her 2005 collection Decreation: “To my mother / love / of my life, I describe what I had for brunch.” I feel the same way about this line that Madonna used to say she felt about Frida Kahlo’s self-portrait, which is that if you don’t feel it vibrate through your system, I can’t ever really be your friend. (I’m aware most people would be fine with that.)

Sublime to ridiculous, Carson to Elon Musk, who is the subject of Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary that launched this week and which I can’t wait to see. Pre-publicity has focused on the contributions to the film of Justine Wilson, Musk’s ex-wife, who along with MacKenzie Scott (formerly Bezos) is part of the tech titans’ first wives club via which one can measure the journey taken by very rich men from marriage to regular women to women with no apparent interior lives. “He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” said Wilson, who also told Gibney her ex-husband once said to her: “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” No amount of money in the world, am I right?

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: A promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps | John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dear

A
s ever, among all the noise triggered by Labour holding the seat of Holborn and St Pancras, the most plain-spoken and undeniable analysis was provided by that sage and national treasure John Curtice, of Strathclyde University. The result, he said, echoed national opinion polls and reflected two undeniable facts: that the Greens are in need of a period of contrition and reflection, and Labour ought to be slightly less than ecstatic.

Andy Burnham’s party, with a majority of 3,364, he said, showed they “are in a much better position than they were six months ago, but still not as popular as they were in 2025”. The Greens, meanwhile, remain “a more significant player than historically they have ever been”, but have lost much of the ground they gained during Zack Polanski’s first year as leader, when the serial failures of the local MP – one Keir Starmer – provided him and his party with such a glorious succession of political opportunities.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Do not forget: the Greens’ success earlier this year in Gorton and Denton played a massive part in Starmer eventually leaving the political stage, and the man he barred from being the Labour candidate snatching his job. But now? Publicly, Polanski seems largely unrepentant about the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at his party conference, and confident he can resume where he left off. But his party’s claim that it tripled its previous vote share in the seat is very specious indeed: as the pollster Peter Kellner puts it, “the leftwing vote two years ago was divided between the Greens’ 10.4% and an independent, Andrew Feinstein’s, 18.9%. Together, they won 29.3%.” The true increase in the leftwing anti-Labour vote, therefore, is only 3.5 percentage points, and Polanski has thus taken such a significant blow that his experience of the next few weeks and months could be very choppy indeed.

Over the last week, I spent two days in the constituency, filming another episode of the Guardian’s Anywhere But Westminster video series, and got a deep sense that our politics remains in a state of unpredictable flux. So many people and the conversations we had come to mind. The young people of colour in the pinched neighbourhood of Somers Town – the urban village right next to Euston station – who were all voting Green, and talked of Gaza and the impossibility of living in our capital. The woman in upmarket Primrose Hill who told us she no longer told people she was Jewish for fear of instant uproar and upbraiding about Israel, a country she had last visited 15 long years ago. But most of all, a 24-year-old trainee teacher called Tom, who reluctantly still lives with his parents, and has no idea how he is going to hold down a job in his home city. He had once been an enthusiastic Green member and activist, he told me, and had every intention of voting for them, until the Zionism motion suggested a party perfectly happy to inflame the UK’s sense of division and polarisation. He decided to switch to Labour.

The searing summer should have provided the Greens with another boost, and a real chance of another byelection win. But now? Polanski – who endorsed the idea that Zionism is a form of racism eight days before his party’s conference began – looks not just morally questionable, but distinctly weak: one central bit of symbolism in this whole affair, let us not forget, was his absence from the Zionism debate and vote at his party conference.

And so to a geographical jump to a few other parts of the country. As I may have written once or twice in the past, I live in Frome, in Somerset: a 25,000-population settlement whose affinity with the Greens has been deepening for the last decade or so. They provide four of the six councillors who represent the town on our new unitary council. The rurality and climate-fear in the villages that surround us chimes with Ellie Chowns’s seemingly out-of-the-blue election two years ago as the Green MP for North Herefordshire and Adrian Ramsay’s success in the East Anglian seat of Waveney Valley. But there are also elements of the maverick, future-facing attitudes that waft down into our neck of the woods from Bristol Central, the seat held since 2024 by Carla Denyer, the former Green party co-leader. I think I know what was holding those two elements together, and partly powering the Greens’ resurgence: a mixture of radical, empathetic social democracy and urgency about the fate of the planet that also seems to have taken root in some of England’s suburbs.

With the possible exception of Bristol, if you wanted to completely wreck the Greens’ successes in all those places, you would bin that approach and accelerate exactly what Polanski has facilitated: not just a politics of no-surrender and provocation, but the entry into the party of embittered former Jeremy Corbyn supporters and assorted ultra-leftists, bringing with them a flimsy, pious gesture politics.

The party’s former leader Caroline Lucas and the longstanding Green activist Rupert Read are about to publish a mini-manifesto titled Climate Popularism: a guide to “breaking the grip of rightwing populism through a new politics of crisis resilience”, to be formally launched on 15 October. Written before the antisemitism meltdown, it rather minces its words about Polanski’s project, but makes it pretty clear why things have now gone wrong. “Some observers have wondered whether this new eco-populism has at times been a little too quiet about the ‘eco’ part,” Lucas and Read write. “On the doorstep, at least, this may be an understandable strategy … [But] as recent heatwaves have made abundantly clear, the salience of climate impacts will make adaptation concerns a doorstep issue before long.”

Lucas and Read make the case for “centrally funded, locally appropriate action to adapt neighbourhoods, infrastructure and ways of life, to prepare for the broad, cascading impacts of human-triggered climate change”. They propose a domestic retrofit programme that would entail a lot of “secure green jobs”. They also write, very perceptively, about an “exhausted majority” tired of our shrill politics, and suggest the “depolarisation” of the climate issue in the face of plain facts – which sounds like the direct opposite of how Polanski operates. There is talk of a politics of “courage, hope, love of place” – and, crucially, a decisive turn into the use of citizens’ assemblies. This is the kind of turn the Greens should undoubtedly take – but even if they do, they will now be starting in a deeply troubled and weakened state.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Burnham, meanwhile, still has no end of work to do. For what it’s worth, many of us have long believed that the substantial presence in British politics of a radical party free of Labour’s pussyfooting around the climate crisis and the harsh realities of inequality was an absolute necessity, and the Greens’ fitful growth was nothing but a good thing. Now, by contrast, as the fallout from Polanski’s sudden crash only deepens, they have a massive amount of self-questioning and reinvention to do. Whether they will even have the inclination is another question entirely.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Bragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losers
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
While the Labour and Conservative leaders will be delighted with their showing, Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zach Polanski have less reason for cheer

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Even his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anything but a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after his deeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”.

The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to “rip the plaster off” and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe.

A YouGov poll after the conference showed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises. Burnham’s success at the Labour conference was capped by a victory at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection a few days later seeing off a challenge by the leader of the Green party Zack Polanski.

This time last year, Kemi Badenoch was hanging on to her role as leader of the opposition by a thread. But in the past 12 months her personal favourability ratings have continued to improve, according to More in Common research. This was a conference where she tightened her grip over the Conservative party and leaned hard into her own brand, telling GB News’s Christopher Hope: “We are under new management. There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively, which is all me.”

While Badenoch’s speech lacked the emotional firepower of Burnham’s, she was assured and disciplined in her focus on the economy – not mentioning small boats or other elements of the culture wars which have energised her in the past. Promised giveaways to wealthy individuals, such as free childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and abolishing inheritance tax on family homes for the 5% of households that pay it, were designed to appeal to the Conservative’s traditional base, one of the first indications of a resolve to win back the “blue wall”.

The most powerful moment of the speech came as she drew a line in the sand between the Tories and Reform, thunderously telling her audience there would be no uniting the right: “I don’t want to live in a country run by people who threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English.” Whether she will reject any deal with Reform if the electoral circumstances dictate remains to be seen.

Both the Conservative and Labour communications teams can congratulate themselves on a job vigorously done in the past few weeks. The coup of the conference season came in the guise of a 27-metre (88ft) graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics in the style of the Bayeux tapestry, as seen through Conservative eyes. Senior party figures and members alike enjoyed the “Birmingham tapestry”, for its pointed jabs at defector Robert Jenrick, but the canniest move was including depictions of high-profile journalists, most of whom duly posted images of the propaganda to their sizeable social media followings.

The team at the Labour party conference successfully projected the “hopey-changey” vibes they had intended, mainly by producing as many posters and placards declaring there was “hope again” as there were participants at the conference. But special mention should also be given to the socials team at Labour HQ, whose snipes during their rivals’ conferences (“Who was less sure whether he’d finished, the shadow chancellor or the audience?”, they asked after Andrew Griffith’s less than assured end of speech exit) was a masterclass in side-eye.

This conference season saw the most sharply defined battle lines between right and left in a generation. Burnham used his speech to attack neoliberalism, saying: “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialisation. Deregulation. Privatisation. Austerity. Brexit.”

He was instantly accused by the Conservatives of indulging in a “socialist fever dream” of the 1970s. They went on to proclaim a love of Thatcher while simultaneously belting out the national anthem. In her speech, Badenoch pitched the fight against Labour as “a battle for the soul of this nation”, trotting out the well-worn Tory treatise that “what people earn belongs to them, not government”.

Ed Miliband lolloped through Liverpool’s conference centre with the ease of a man who appears to be very much enjoying his time as foreign secretary. In a lineup easily swallowed by the gravitational pull of the leader’s speech, Miliband delivered a deft piece of politics, telling assembled members they were “right” to be moved by the plight of the Palestinian people.

Over at the Conservative conclave, the Conservatives’ candidate for mayor of London, James Cleverly, also had a jolly time away from the main stage. “[Kemi Badenoch] knows, as I do, that our best bet of getting her into No 10 is getting me into City Hall,” he told a panel convened by the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS).

Reform UK billed its largest ever gathering at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Its leader, Nigel Farage, wanted to use the conference to outline a series of policy pledges for a Reform government’s first 100 days in office.

Instead the opening was overshadowed by the suspension of his close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr, after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim. Reform UK cleared them of breaking laws that ban foreign donations on Wednesday, but the matter remains under police investigation.

Farage’s own speech was interrupted by protesters, who appeared to be roughed up as they were thrown out of the hall. A man was later given a police caution after footage appeared to show one woman having her hair pulled and being hit with a walking stick.

Zack Polanski started his run in to the Green party of England and Wales’s conference by asking, unsuccessfully, if it could be delayed so he could focus on campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. He may now wish it had been cancelled altogether.

The party’s gathering in Brighton was consumed by controversy, after members voted in favour of an official policy stating that Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, is a type of racism. Polanski absented himself from the most toxic internal debate the party has faced for years, choosing instead to leave to campaign, and the party is still reeling from the fallout.

Shortly after the Greens’ triumph in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection it was polling above 20%; it now stands on 11%.

At first it seemed as if the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, had come through his party’s conference in Brighton relatively unscathed, despite going unexpectedly viral for a speech in which he enthusiastically, if not entirely successfully, attempted to rally a chant of “We care! We fight!”. But his opposition to Labour’s proposals to change the pension triple lock was met with opposition by senior and backbench Lib Dems, with one saying his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.

The chancellor used the word hope 21 times in his personal conference speech that, while warmly welcomed by Labour party members, managed to say very little about actual policy over quite a long period of time. In the days that followed, senior Labour figures privately voiced unease about Healey’s approach to his crucial first budget this month, noting it lacked detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises.

Among all the gaffes, the spills, the wrong names and forgotten policy details of this season of party conferences, one performance really did stand out.

Griffith, the shadow chancellor, was described by Badenoch as having “more business experience than the entire Labour cabinet combined” – attenders at Conservative party conference were left wondering if any of it had involved public speaking. After an address variously described as “an historic clunker”, “curious” and “the worst speech ever heard”, Griffith’s speech appeared to simply peter out and the shadow chancellor wandering awkwardly off stage, leaving the audience not knowing whether to clap, or simply follow him out of the room.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
It may sound odd to think Zack Polanski would be happy with second place, but after his most challenging week in politics, it could have been worse

Labour’s Abdi-Wali fends off Polanski and Greens

Holborn and St Pancras byelection – live updates

Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief.

For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Retaining a constituency formerly held by your last leader, Keir Starmer, and which has been overwhelmingly Labour since it was created in 1983, is in normal political times not that notable an achievement, but these are not normal times.

A low turnout of 38.7% and Abdi-Wali’s numerically modest 3,364 majority that resulted might not appear the greatest endorsement of the government, but it is also likely to have been in part due to the widespread assumption that Labour would win.

And what of the Greens, and particularly Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England and Wales, who decided to go for the high-profile seat himself? Again, it may sound curious to think he would be happy with second place, but after the most challenging week of his political life, it could have been worse.

Polanski got just under 33% of the vote, well above anyone else apart from Abdi-Wali, a proportion which shows that in an another election, and up against a Labour party not enjoying a Burnham bounce, the Greens could still be highly competitive in seats like these.

When Polanski said he wanted to stand, the hope was for another wave of enthusiasm and publicity of the sort that propelled Hannah Spencer to victory in February in another supposedly safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton.

He will nonetheless be quietly pleased that the result does not seem to have shown much of a shedding of Green votes after criticisms of, and deep divisions in, the party since it adopted a highly controversial policy on Zionism and Israel last weekend.

The new policy, decided by members at the Greens’ annual conference, equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism, and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. It is publicly opposed by four of the party’s five MPs, with numerous councillors distancing themselves as well and a handful resigning.

Polanski’s decision to not take a side, and even to absent himself from Sunday’s debate so he could campaign in the byelection, has prompted deep unease among some Greens, who termed it a failure of leadership. It was notable that after the result, Polanski had to state that he intended to stay as Green leader. “Yes absolutely, that’s what leaders do,” he said.

While some in the Greens had questioned Polanski’s decision to contest a seat in north London, rather than east London, where he lives, his allies make the point that Nigel Farage took eight tries to become an MP.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Either way, the result has not made Polanski’s position any worse. Had the Green vote collapsed he would have been under very intense pressure. As it stands, he must try to reassure sceptics in the party before seeking re-election in a year from now, under the party’s policy of two-year terms for leaders.

And what of the others? The Conservatives will be quietly happy with beating Reform UK to take third place, their 7.1% being almost exactly the same proportion of votes as they took in 2024. This might not seem like much of an achievement, but the party’s national poll ratings remain stubbornly below 2024 levels, and thus stasis will most likely be claimed as more evidence of a Badenoch bounce.

Down in fifth place, the emotions are different. While they are byelection specialists, the Liberal Democrats were never going to win here, but they had put in at least some effort to boost their vote, with MPs going out this week to knock on doors. Coming behind Reform on just over 3% of the vote will be a disappointment.

Amid the noisy debates over the leadership of Labour, the Tories and Greens, it can be easy to overlook the disquiet among some of Ed Davey’s MPs that the Lib Dems do not appear to be cutting through. He will not be feeling relief this morning.
