The Conservatives will be quietly happy with beating Reform UK to take third place.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Second UK health body drops Israeli drug firm after activist pressure
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Decision by Royal College of Pharmacy to end sponsorship comes after concerns over Teva Pharmaceuticals’ ‘activities’

A second major UK health body has cut ties with an Israeli drug firm after coming under pressure from pro-Palestine campaigners.

The Royal College of Pharmacy has dropped Teva UK, the British arm of the global medicines producer Teva Pharmaceuticals, as a sponsor of and exhibitor at its annual conference next month.

Its decision comes after that of the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) last week to cut its longstanding ties with Teva UK. The RCN, which represents 500,000 UK nurses, dropped Teva as a sponsor of both the union and an event on headache and migraine.

The Royal College of Pharmacy has 34,000 members and is the professional body for Britain’s pharmacists and pharmaceutical scientists. Teva UK was due to be an exhibitor at four of its events as part of a £15,000 deal, the college said.

A spokesperson said it had taken its decision after realising that unspecified Teva Pharmaceuticals’ “activities”, uncovered by a “due diligence review”, did not align with its values.

“The Royal College of Pharmacy has decided to end Teva UK’s current sponsorship and exhibition presence for our forthcoming annual conference with immediate effect.

“This follows a further due diligence review which has brought to our attention the possibility of certain Teva Pharmaceuticals activities which do not align with our values”, the spokesperson said.

It did not explain which activities it had concerns about but said the move was decided by its executive team after it became a charity in April, which led to it reviewing its policies. But Teva, which specialises in producing generic rather than developing new drugs, has a poor track record of corporate malfeasance.

Teva said it was “disappointed” at being dropped and that healthcare should not become “politicised”.

The college’s move comes after the circulation of an open letter by campaigners including UK Healthcare Petitions to Royal Colleges (UKHPRC) and signed by individual pharmacists and other health professionals.

The letter highlighted that the Royal Pharmaceutical Society – the Royal College of Pharmacy’s predecessor – had responded to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 by no longer investing any of its money in funds that involved Russian firms. It urged the Royal College of Pharmacy to “apply the same ethical scrutiny to its investments and commercial partnerships in relation to Israel”.

UKHPRC welcomed the RCN and Royal College of Pharmacy’s decisions. “We hope this reflects the ethical concerns that the public expects from healthcare professionals”, it said.

Medical royal colleges are the bodies that represent different types of doctors in the UK professionally, such as GPs and surgeons. UKHPRC is now urging other royal colleges which have or have previously had commercial relationships with Teva to shun the company. They include the royal colleges representing GPs, psychiatrists and hospital doctors, which have had sponsorship arrangements with Teva in recent years.

“These victories should reverberate beyond the royal colleges, into NHS boardrooms and pharmacy purchasing decisions. They have shown that a sponsor’s cheque need not come with the college’s conscience thrown in.

Dr Barrak Almoosawi, an NHS doctor and an organiser of the letter, said: “Nursing and pharmacy have acted; those still taking Teva’s money can no longer shelter behind the excuse that nothing can be done. A royal crest carries standing. It should never serve as a fig leaf for a failure of moral courage.”

In 2024 the European Commission fined Teva €462.6m for blocking rival firms from competing with Copaxone, its treatment for multiple sclerosis, in seven European countries for between four and nine years.

In 2023 Teva agreed to pay $225m in fines imposed by the US Department of Justice as an alternative to prosecution after it was charged with fixing the price of three drugs.

Previously, in 2016, it struck a deal with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Department of Justice to pay $519m (£393m) to settle civil and criminal charges involving its bribery of government officials in Russia, Ukraine and Mexico.

Teva Pharmaceuticals said in a statement: “We are disappointed by the Royal College of Pharmacy’s decision, and firmly believe healthcare is at its best when it remains focused on patients rather than being politicised. While we respectfully disagree with this decision, we will continue to act with integrity and remain focused on what matters most: helping patients access the medicines they need.

“We are humbled by the opportunity to serve more than 150m patients every day around the world and remain steadfast in our dedication to positively impact those we serve, guided by international laws, local regulations, and our shared values. Teva does not make donations to political parties, political organisations, or military entities in any country.”

This article was amended on 9 October 2026. An earlier version suggested that there were 34,000 pharmacists in Great Britain; in fact, this number referred to the membership of the Royal College of Pharmacy.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Alexander Hurst
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation

W
hen adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France may have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”

But the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECD education rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to over 30 today; half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year – many of them with no substitutes or replacements.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minutes each way between Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only 56% of what they are in Germany – even as over €200bn in public subsidies finds its way annually to businesses.

So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.

They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds more have been injured in some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week, almost half the number of arrests made during the months of gilets jaunes chaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges.

“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response.

Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.”

I can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancet found that 75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workers actively dislike AI and feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere.

For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.

A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences and more law and order. But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.

Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own. On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté (“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday.

after newsletter promotion

Responding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area – reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff.

But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.

As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.

Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Saudi Arabia reopens Riyadh airport after Houthi attack kills three
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Saudi Arabia has reopened Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport following attacks by the Houthis that killed three people and injured several.

In a statement on social media on Friday, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said attacks the previous day had hit airport facilities and an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia.

The Houthis have hit Saudi airports in several attacks this week as the armed group continues to face an offensive by the Riyadh-backed internationally recognised Yemen government.

The strikes on Thursday caused injuries ranging from minor to severe, as well as material damage, GACA said. Airport operations have now resumed and air traffic has returned to normal.

Saudia Airlines said one of its pilots was killed and an aircraft was damaged.

“It is with profound sadness that Saudia announces the passing of Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami,” the flag-carrier said in a statement, citing an “incident” at the Riyadh airport.

Saudi Arabia has seen several attacks by the Houthis in recent days, with the airports appearing to be the primary target.

GACA said Wednesday that attacks earlier in the week had killed three civilians and injured 36 at Abha and King Khalid airports. At least three people were also wounded in other attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemen border.

A Houthi military spokesperson said on Thursday that the armed group had launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid airport, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.

The campaign appears to be a revival of a tactic seen last month.

On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards King Khalid airport.

A day later, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area.

The Houthis have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating in there, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target.

The return to the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports comes as Yemeni forces continue a counteroffensive against the Houthis.

The push was launched after the Iran-aligned rebel group last month seized a broad swath of territory along the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, in a sudden push.

The Yemeni government forces this week claimed key gains around the Bab al-Mandeb coastline, but intense fighting continues.

The conflict, which was frozen for some years until it was brought back to life by the United States’ war on Iran, has stoked further upheaval in a region already destabilised by Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon.

It now threatens to draw other states into the conflict, with Pakistan and Turkiye having agreed to deploy troops under a mutual defence pact signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year.

A spokesman for Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that the country now has a “substantial number of forces as well as resources … in Riyadh”.

Pakistani military personnel “would not be crossing the borders of the other side for an attack on the Houthis, but of course (are acting) in the defence of the territory”, he noted.

The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government said on Friday that it had destroyed three rocket launch platforms that were used by the Houthis “to threaten regional security”.

Spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki declared that all Houthi attacks on civilians and civilian facilities “will be met with resolve” by the Saudi-led coalition.

On Thursday, the coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles heading in the direction of Riyadh, and one missile in the direction of the city of Khamis Mushait, close to the Yemeni border.

Earlier in the week, its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers, it added.

The Houthis have hit Saudi airports in several attacks this week. The strikes on Thursday caused injuries ranging from minor to severe, as well as material damage.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Real Madrid’s Mourinho lashes out at ‘ridiculous’ criticism of Mbappe
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho has slammed criticism of star striker Kylian Mbappe, calling the attacks “ridiculous”.

The French captain has come under fire for spending his time recovering from a left knee injury in France and Switzerland rather than Madrid. He suffered a hyperextension of the joint while playing in a Nations League match against Turkiye on September 25.

The 27-year-old was also pictured at the entrance of a Parisian nightclub and photographed on a bicycle when he was in Switzerland.

Some fans claimed it was a deliberate snubbing of Mourinho, who only days before had said players should avoid skiing or riding bicycles to avoid injury.

“Are these criticisms over the top? They are ridiculous,” Mourinho said at a news conference on Friday on the eve of Real’s La Liga home match with Villarreal.

“All the players who were obliged to be present every day for their recovery were here.

“Mbappe came, like the others, to undergo scans in order to be diagnosed.

“He then went to see a specialist in France because he has history with his knee, which we cannot ignore.”

Mourinho, whose side lost to Atletico Madrid in their last match and already lag six points behind bitter rivals Barcelona, is never one to shy away from a confrontation and tackled each of the criticisms against Mbappe.

“Problems involving football are not sufficient for you,” the 63-year-old Portuguese coach told reporters.

“Therefore, you have raised the issue of the discotheque, which in fact was not one because it was used for a private event for Fashion Week.

“As for the bicycle in Switzerland, it was in a hotel made up of small houses which makes them available so guests can ride to the communal areas, and you would have us believe he was competing in the Tour of Switzerland.”

Mbappe, who returned to training on Wednesday, could feature on the pitch as early as Saturday. Mourinho shrugged off the potential of a hostile reception for Mbappe against Villarreal, reiterating that he was “certain” the all-time World Cup record goal scorer has fulfilled “his obligations to Real Madrid”.

It is not the first time this season that Mbappe has been subjected to attacks by fans.

The Ultras Sur, a Real Madrid supporters group linked to the far right and banned from the Santiago Bernabeu, took issue with him last month.

They were furious that before a Real Madrid match, Mbappe, alongside Vinicius Jr and fellow Frenchman Ibrahima Konate, partially rolled up T-shirts bearing the words “We are all Ceutans“, which was intended to be a message of support for people in the Spanish territory bordering Morocco.

Ceuta, a Spanish North African exclave, has been grappling with a migration crisis.

Mbappe was also criticised earlier this season over his choice of a location for recovery from a previous injury, which led to an online “Mbappe Out” campaign by some Real fans.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.summary: Jose Mourinho has slammed criticism of Kylian Mbappe. The Real Madrid coach has been criticised for spending his time recovering from a knee injury. Mbappes has been pictured at the entrance of a Parisian nightclub and on a bicycle.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Manchester City charges: Maresca says Premier League club will win appeal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca says he has absolute faith the club will win its appeal after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.

In his first news conference since the bombshell announcement last week, the Italian on Friday also rejected any suggestion that City’s haul of silverware over the past 15 years was now tainted.

“I completely trust the club,” said Maresca, who was appointed manager in June but also previously worked at City as part of Pep Guardiola’s coaching staff.

“I trust the club because I trust the people, and this is also the reason why I joined the club. … There is not another club in the world where I would like to be.”

An independent commission found that City had arranged “sham” contracts with a number of their commercial partners to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) over nine seasons from 2009 to 2018.

The 10-time English champions, who continue to deny any wrongdoing, are appealing against the judgement.

They likely face a severe points penalty that could lead to relegation or even expulsion from the Premier League if they fail to overturn the verdict.

“The reason why I joined this club is because I completely trust 100 percent the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don’t have any doubt about that,” Maresca said.

“I spoke with the club for sure, and we all [have] trust, and the right moment to speak about that is when we win this appeal.”

Since an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008, City have become the dominant force in English football.

They have won eight Premier League titles, the Champions League and multiple other trophies over the past 15 years.

Maresca, whose side have won all five of their Premier League games this season, rejected the suggestion that those previous successes were now tainted.

“Absolutely not,” the former Chelsea boss said. “I know the effort from the players, from the club, from the manager in that time that was Pep.

“So I know exactly the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target.”

Guardiola stepped down at the end of last season after a trophy-laden decade at the Etihad Stadium.

City travel to Liverpool on Sunday for their first outing since the guilty finding, and Guardiola is set to attend their next home game against Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday.

“After 10 years here, he can come at any time he wants,” Maresca said. “I think it would be nice for him. It would be nice for the fans, for everyone.”

Maresca had spoken to City’s in-house media on Thursday and said the current players “don’t care too much about the noise” currently surrounding the club.

The new head coach and his players, however, are set for a hostile reception when they travel to Anfield, the home of their fierce rivals, but Maresca said his players would stay focused on the match.

“Probably [it] will be even more warm in terms of environment. But the reason why I decided to be manager is for this kind of game,” he said.

“I’m not worried at all. Again, the environment is from the players. It’s nice.

“In this moment, we are top of the league, so the players have all the reasons to be happy and excited.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.summary: Enzo Maresca says he has absolute faith the club will win its appeal. The Italian also rejected any suggestion that City's haul of silverware over the past 15 years was now tainted. City have been found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: ‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Stephen Quillen
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The United States government has moved to exclude some of the world’s top tech companies from a programme that allows them to sponsor skilled foreign workers for permanent residency.

Vice President JD Vance said the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of US workers.

It comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration continues efforts to clamp down on immigration – both legal and undocumented – and make it harder for immigrants to get residency or citizenship.

But the latest move also potentially impacts thousands of foreign workers, many of whom have spent years waiting for a backlog in applications to clear.

Here’s what to know about the latest policy:

The suspension concerns the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, which enables a US-based employer to sponsor a foreign worker’s green card — as the permanent residency is commonly known. To qualify, the employer is supposed to demonstrate that there are insufficient US workers for a needed job role and that bringing a foreign worker will not impact the pay or conditions of US workers in the industry.

PERM is a key step in the green card process for many skilled foreign workers. Major tech companies often hire workers on temporary visas, such as the H-1B, before they transition to permanent residency through the PERM process.

Vance on Thursday accused major companies of fraudulently using the current visa regime to displace US employees and bring in lower-paid foreign workers who amount to “indentured servants”.

“The programme has become rife with fraud,” said Vance at a White House news conference. He claimed that many workers who start off on temporary H-1B visas and later apply for permanent residency under the PERM programme are “being mistreated by their employers” and “used to undercut the wages of American workers”.

“You’ve got to hire great American workers,” the US vice president said. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling used similar language, saying the US would “shut down the pipeline of systemic fraud that has flooded our country”.

“The fraud doesn’t end with getting the job,” said Sonderling. “That job becomes a pathway for foreign workers and their families to stay in America permanently and eventually (become) US citizens.”

“And who pays for it all? The American worker,” he said.

Vance singled out Microsoft as a major offender and said it would be suspended from the PERM programme.

Other companies whose PERM applications will no longer be processed include US software firm Adobe and some of the world’s top IT firms, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Of these, Capgemini is French, Microsoft and Adobe are American, and the rest — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL — are all Indian.

“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” said Sonderling.

Vance said the suspensions would continue “as long as it needs to”.

Other companies that rely heavily on H-1B visas such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet’s Google will not be affected.

Critics of the H-1B visa and PERM green card process argue that some employers use the system not to fill legitimate skills shortages, but to reduce labour costs, gain leverage over workers and make it harder for US employees to compete for jobs. They say companies do this by hiring foreign workers at lower wages and manipulating recruitment conditions to keep out qualified US workers.

Vance said Microsoft last year let go 6,000 US workers, while also securing 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.

“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vance.

Sonderling said companies being suspended from PERM had received more than 230,000 H-1B visas and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications since 2009.

“That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.

The H1-B visa system has also emerged as a lightning rod for many of the most vocal backers of Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, some of whom have married criticism of the programme with anti-immigrant stereotypes  — particularly against Indians — to demand that the scheme be scrapped.

Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented new hires replacing US workers. In a statement, the company said that 80 percent of the roughly 6,000 H1-B visa applications it issued last year were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees”, not for new employees, and that the other filings were for “individuals already legally in the United States”.

The company also said that it only files applications for people who “meet the rigorous standards of this visa category” and that such employees are paid equally to any others who do similar work.

The suspension could make it harder for foreign workers in the tech industry to obtain permanent residency in the US. Many of those affected are likely to be Indian nationals, who account for a large share of the country’s skilled foreign workforce in the technology sector.

Each year, there are only 85,000 slots for new H-1B visas (not including filings for renewals), but hundreds of thousands of applications. Many H-1B visa holders work in technology-related jobs: 62 percent of the beneficiaries in the 2025 fiscal year worked in computer-related occupations.

Indian nationals account for roughly 70 percent of existing H-1B visa holders.

The Trump administration has already tried to crack down on the H1-B scheme, and in August proposed a new $103,000 fee for H1-B applications, after an earlier pitch for a similar fee was struck down by a federal court. The fee, the government argues, would help provide revenue that could be used to service the vast US immigration system, while reducing the incentive for companies to attempt to misuse H1-B visas.

But the new move to restrict the pathway to a green card for foreign workers already in the US, legally, could impact not just those who might have dreamed of working or living in the US — but thousands already in the country.

The US typically issues around 140,000 employment-based green cards every year. But it also has a strict country-based cap — applicants from any one country cannot receive more than seven percent of green cards issued in a year.

Yet, because the employment-based green card application system is largely used to convert many H1-B visa holders into permanent residents, applicants for permanent residency are disproportionately Indian.

The result: Nearly one million Indians legally in the US on work visas are currently stuck in the employment-based green card backlog. They represent 79 percent of the total green card backlog of around 1.25 million people.

Even before the latest move, Indian green card applicants in certain employment categories would have needed to wait for decades, according to a 2025 analysis for the Congressional Research Service.

Sonderling’s statement that the US will no longer process “any pending permanent labour certification applications” from the blacklisted companies has raised fears that tens of thousands of foreign workers in the country legally — most of them Indian — who have waited for years might suddenly no longer be eligible. For others, the wait could get even longer.

Yes. India’s Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement saying the US’s suspension does not “advance the shared ambitions of both countries”.

The ministry said that “talent mobility adds value” to both the Indian and US economies, including providing US companies “with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation”.

The ministry also criticised comments by Vance comparing foreign workers to indentured servants as “unwarranted” and “deeply offensive”, saying his words recalled “painful historical and colonial legacy connotations”.

Colonial powers — the British, Dutch and French — took more than 1.6 million Indian workers as indentured labourers to work on plantations and build railways in their other colonies: in Malaysia, Mauritius, South Africa, Kenya, Uganda, Fiji, Suriname, Guyana and other Caribbean countries.

India’s foreign ministry said Vance’s descriptions also “ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem”.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: suspension concerns the Permanent Labour Certification programme. It allows a US-based employer to sponsor a foreign worker’s green card. The suspension is a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Labour fends off the Green party in closely watched UK by-election
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The Labour Party has won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer, fending off a challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister.

Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader who came second.

The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was recently installed by lawmakers fearful that Starmer’s unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election.

After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result that triggered more questions about Polanski’s leadership, who had promised to make his party “an eco-populist” movement.

There are now five Green MPs, compared with one in 2023.

But Polanski, 43, came under fire after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference.

The move, which called for “the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers. Polanski did not vote on the motion.

Labour has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983.

Labour’s Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the United Kingdom as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for “those who seek to divide us”.

“We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built and pass it on,” she said.

After conceding defeat, Polanski, who is not an MP, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of “Andy Burnham’s honeymoon”.

Polanski congratulated Abdi-Wali, but said, “One in three voters backed us here, and we know that many more considered it.”

Al Jazeera’s Sonia Gallego, reporting from London, said, “The constituency has been going through what some people have been calling ‘the Burnham bounce‘ … so far there is a deep sigh of relief (among Labour) that they’ve managed to hold on.”

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has changed voter habits during the past three years. The Greens, far more critical of Israel’s conduct than any other party, got a boost in the 2024 general election.

Back then, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein, a pro-Palestine independent candidate, came second, with 19 percent.

Polanski has raised the “progressive vote” while “reducing the Labour vote”, Feinstein said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali won seat in Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes. Green Party leader Zack Polanski came second with 8,928 votes. The victory will buoy Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was recently installed by lawmakers.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
United States President Donald Trump has said that he does not intend to bomb Iran again until the November midterm elections, even though several US media outlets have reported that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to relaunch attacks before that vote.

Trump has been accused of misdirection on the issue in the past. The US launched its initial attacks on Iran on February 28, as talks with Iran were ongoing and despite Trump saying just the day before that he had not made any decision. One year previously, the US struck Iran towards the end of Israel’s June 2025 12-day war, despite Trump saying he would announce a decision about attacks “in two weeks”.

Still, striking Iran ahead of the midterm elections would be risky for the administration as the war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.

Resuming the war afterwards may have less of a negative impact on Trump, who is not eligible to run for another term as US president anyway.

Here’s what we know about Trump’s plans.

In the past two days, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and other publications have reported claims by unnamed officials that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to attack Iran before the midterms, if authorised to do so.

On Wednesday, US publication Axios cited US and Israeli officials saying the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for imminent major combat operations. The Atlantic also reported along similar lines.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social media platform that he will not order a resumption of strikes on Iran before November 3, when the US midterm elections will be held.

“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition…we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” he said.

The president added that the US is presently “having productive discussions” with the Iranian side. However, that was also the case on February 28, the day the US and Israel first struck Iran, triggering the war.

Trump did not make any reference to preparing for potential military operations, nor did he provide more details on the state of talks.

Trump and Republicans are worried about a voter backlash against the war at the polls. The US war on Iran is intensely unpopular domestically as Americans have had to grapple with surging prices of gas, food and other basic commodities because of the crisis in the Middle East.

Since the start of the war, surveys have shown that large numbers of Americans did not approve of striking Iran.

Now, about 65 percent of Americans say they “disapprove” of the way in which Trump has handled the Iran war overall, according to a Pew Research Center poll released on Thursday. Trump stated at the start of the war that it would go on for just a few weeks, however, it is now into its eighth month.

According to Pew, most Americans now believe the war will continue for at least another year. Even Republican or more conservative-leaning voters are growing more negative about the war, its poll found.

The conflict has also severely affected Trump’s personal ratings and eroded support for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll on Thursday found that only 30 percent of his supporters were enthusiastic about voting in the midterms, compared with 48 percent of Democratic voters.

About 13 percent of those who voted for Trump in 2024 say they are not sure who to vote for in the congressional elections.

Delaying attacks until after the elections could potentially shield Republican candidates from voter backlash, analysts say.

While analysts say Trump will see a good performance at the polls as approval for renewed strikes, a Republican defeat at the polls could equally further incentivise him to hit Iran again as he will calculate that he has little to lose at that point.

While that could further affect Trump’s ratings, the president is not eligible to run in the next presidential election in any case.

In recent weeks, the US president has threatened to “end” the war with force after the elections as talks with Iran have dragged on.

At a Republican convention in September, he accused Iran of trying to affect the outcome of the midterms and said that conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”.

In an interview with Time magazine two weeks ago, he also said it would be “possible” to ramp up bombing in Iran after the elections, but declined to elaborate. Analysts say his comments were designed to calm voters, while at the same time warning Iran of potential aggression after the vote.

Last week, the US military dispatched about 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines aboard several ships now sailing to the Middle East amid threats of new attacks from Trump. The vessel formation included the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group.

The deployment increases the number of US troops in the region to 20,000, alongside hundreds of aircraft and at least three carrier strike groups.

In the past, US troop build-up in the Middle East and the Caribbean has subsequently resulted in military action.

In June, Washington and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement that quickly broke down over control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump has repeatedly said that the US has the upper hand in the strait, citing more oil exports and Iran’s weakened economy. He has also voiced aversion to a deal with Tehran over management of Hormuz, but said he might consider it because “they’re willing to offer us anything to stop”.

Washington rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the strait based on certain conditions it wants the US to meet, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and guaranteeing an end to attacks. Last week, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran was considering a counterproposal from the US.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: The Pentagon has drawn up plans to attack Iran before the midterms. The US launched its initial attacks on Iran on February 28. Washington rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the strait.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Ex-OpenAI staff say they were fired for raising safety concerns
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: John Power
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Three former OpenAI employees say they have been fired due to their efforts to ensure the safety of artificial intelligence.

Safety researchers Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang levelled the accusations on Thursday after their dismissals last week. The trio warned of a “chilling” effect on other staff concerned about the frontier technology’s risks.

OpenAI said they were let go due to misconduct involving the mishandling of company information.

“I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation,” Balesni said in a post on X.

Korbak voiced a similar sentiment, expressing his belief that he had been terminated for raising concerns that OpenAI was “losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave”.

In an open letter published in tandem with their social media posts, Balesni, Korbak and Wang expressed concerns that their dismissal would make their former colleagues “afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI”.

“We could raise safety concerns and disagree openly, and were encouraged to draw on the expertise of independent safety organizations,” they said in the letter. “This is part of what made OpenAI special, and why we are immensely proud to have been part of the team.”

The three added that “if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties”, then AI could not be developed safely.

“It is that culture we are writing to defend,” they stated.

The trio denied violating company policy, saying any engagement with external safety experts had been in line with the mandate of their roles.

“Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they said.

“Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.”

In a statement, OpenAI said it had uncovered “a significant breach of trust” by the former researchers that went beyond what was described in their letter and said it stood behind the decision to fire them.

“We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the San Francisco-based company said.

“Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes.”

OpenAI added that it was saddened by the outcome.

“We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas,” the company said.

“We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.”

The ex-employees’ intervention comes as OpenAI and other AI companies are at the centre of intense debate about how to ensure the rapidly evolving technology does not expose humanity to catastrophic harm.

The risk of cutting-edge AI models escaping human control has been in the spotlight since July when it emerged that autonomous agents generated by OpenAI had hacked the software start-up Hugging Face.

OpenAI and its chief rival, Anthropic, have urged the international community to work together on a coordinated slowdown in AI development.

However, that suggestion has been rebuffed by the two leading AI powers, the United States and China.

Last month, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceXAI and Nvidia endorsed a voluntary accord calling for stronger internal safeguards and the engagement of external auditors to better manage safety risks.

The accord, announced by US President Donald Trump, drew a mixed response from AI safety advocates, many of whom criticised its nonbinding nature.

OpenAI has announced a number of steps to mitigate risks in the absence of formal regulation, including scrapping the planned release of its latest-generation model, GPT-6.1 Astra.

The ChatGPT creator said it decided not to go ahead with the release after its model failed to meet company standards for acting in accordance with human wishes.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.author: Lina Ghassan Abu Zayed
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.text:
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work.

For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems.

Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems.

She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities.

Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom.

“I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.”

In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling.

They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame.

The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead.

Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began.

Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended.

Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard.

Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires.

On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled.

Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them.

It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace.

“I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.”

Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams.

Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years.

The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another.

When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up.

In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone.

The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared.

There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam.

"These are my girls," she says again.

Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk.

Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks.

The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become.

Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings. Their futures still seemed to turn on exams, marks, university places and what their families could afford.

Maha remembers Sara Rayan laughing, and Ghaida, she says, is in Egypt now, studying dentistry.

Then, she reaches Lina al-Hour.

Here, she pauses, enlarges Lina’s face on the screen and falls silent. Her smile has disappeared. When she speaks again, her voice is quieter and catches slightly.

“This is my well-mannered student, Lina,” she says softly. “She is a martyr.”

On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. She was 18.

For a moment, the girls wrap their arms even tighter around one another in silence.

The photograph stays open on her phone.

Standing in the same schoolyard three years later, they tell one another they wish they could return to those days.

But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion.

Aya takes out her phone and holds it at arm's length, trying to recreate the selfie Sara took three years earlier.

“Sara should have been here to take it,” she says.

But Sara cannot come. She now works for an NGO, using her wages to help pay her university fees and contribute to her family's income.

Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders.

Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon.

Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women.

Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours.

“It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.”

After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology.

When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent.

But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees.

Aya turned to her older brother Yasser.

Seventeen years her senior, Yasser was a lawyer with his own practice, a wife and three children: Adnan, nine, Ahmad, seven, and three-year-old Ilaf. He helped support their parents and hoped one day to teach law at university.

“I used to always tell him, ‘You're a second father to me,’ because he was so kind to me, just like my father,” Aya says.

Aya remembers a summer's day in August 2023. Yasser, still dressed in his smart work clothes, came to take her from Nuseirat to the Islamic University of Gaza.

"Together, we went from department to department, trying to find a course that was affordable and that I would enjoy," she says.

Professors suggested engineering. But when they came out, Aya told Yasser she couldn't imagine herself studying computers or becoming an engineer.

“I could picture myself wearing a white coat, that's all,” she told him.

They tried health sciences next.

“Maybe I could study something in the medical field,” Aya suggested. “I really liked medical laboratory sciences.”

Yasser knew that his sister was giving up the version of university she had imagined. But he refused to let her see the decision as the end of something.

"Perhaps it's for the best," he told her. "Maybe one day you'll become a doctor in the field you choose to specialise in. You don't have to be a medical doctor; you could become a university professor with a PhD."

Then, he offered her a thought that has stayed with her. "He told me, 'Sometimes what is withheld from us can be better for us than what is given to us,' and I believe him."

Afterwards, he took her to Al-Taboun restaurant for lunch, while they kept talking about university and the choices available.

Aya enrolled in medical laboratory sciences, and Yasser bought her books and supplies. University had barely completed its first week when the war began.

A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house.

The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted.

She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to.

Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there.

On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food.

On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32.

Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation.

When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one.

“I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says.

Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained.

After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things.

"My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me."

She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat.

Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader, known as “the tall one”, had also imagined becoming a surgeon.

At school, she had loved Turkish dramas and anime and had a habit of doodling on her desk, much to the annoyance of her biology teacher. Those interests have since fallen away.

She graduated with 98.3 percent and enrolled in medicine at the Islamic University of Gaza on September 10, 2023.

Less than a month later, the war brought her studies to a halt.

Her father, Yunis Abd al-Qader, works as a paramedic with the Palestinian Red Crescent. During the war, he worked 24-hour shifts and returned home only for brief rest.

Lina worried each time he left.

“I would wonder if he would come back the next day," she says. "I wished I could be there with him, to help him through the difficult things he was seeing.”

Usually quiet and reserved, her father tried to spare the family the details of what he encountered. But sometimes, he came home exhausted, and the strain showed.

One account he shared stayed with Lina. After an Israeli strike, he had been recovering human remains. Initially, he believed they belonged to seven people. As he continued working, he realised there was an eighth.

Having witnessed the scale of amputations, fractures and other injuries, she wants to specialise in orthopaedic surgery.

As she continued her medical studies, Lina became close to another student, Shams Majdi.

Their friendship was still new when Lina struggled with a physiology problem and messaged Shams on WhatsApp for help.

Shams lived in northern Gaza, where internet access was unreliable. With Israeli quadcopters overhead, she travelled several kilometres to find a connection so she could help solve the problem with Lina over the phone.

Lina remembers the trouble her new friend took to help her.

Later, the two sat the same exam remotely, from different parts of Gaza.

Shams had again travelled away from home to find an internet connection.

After finishing the exam, Lina opened WhatsApp.

“Shams, did you get home?”

Lina says Shams was usually quick to respond, when she could. So she waited.

About 45 minutes later, a message appeared in their medical college group announcing that Shams Majdi had been killed.

Lina stared at the name.

For about 10 minutes, she says that she struggled to comprehend that it was the same Shams whose reply she had been waiting for.

She opened their conversation again.

“Shams, where are you?”

“Tell me this is a lie.”

She kept sending messages throughout the day. None was answered.

Shams had been killed in an Israeli strike on her home, alongside members of her family.

For the following week, Lina says, she cried whenever she opened her medical books.

There had been another Lina in Maha's classroom.

Lina al-Hour, the quieter girl who loved novels and wrote letters to her friends, had also enrolled in medicine. She had attended her first week of university before the war began.

On November 17, 2023, an Israeli air strike hit her family's home. Lina was killed alongside her parents, siblings and other relatives.

With no surviving parent or sibling for Al Jazeera to interview, her former classmates and teacher helped piece together memories of her life.

Maha remembers the way she listened in class. The girls remember how easily they could make her laugh.

Lina Abd al-Qader remembers the strangeness of sharing a name with a friend who is now gone.

“I and my friend who was killed had the same name,” she says. “But my friend was killed, and I still cannot get over it.”

Ghaida Zaqout is now in Egypt, more than 300km (186 miles) from the schoolyard where she once posed with her classmates. Speaking to Al Jazeera by phone, she recalls how she used to fill her schoolbooks with drawings of the wooden houses she admired in Japanese anime, and dreamed of becoming an architect.

On October 20, 2023, Ghaida turned 18.

By then, her sister Asmaa, her husband and their two children had moved in after losing their home in an Israeli air strike. Her maternal uncle's family was staying with them, too. About 15 people were living under one roof.

Ghaida decided to make herself a small birthday cake.

She found eggs, flour and baking powder and began arranging the ingredients in the kitchen, joking with her sister's children as she worked.

Then, her aunt called with news that her cousin Majdi, 33, had been killed.

He had always made Ghaida laugh. At family birthdays, he liked to scoop cream from the cake and smear it across her face. A natural storyteller, he could turn even the simplest anecdote into something funny.

They had last seen each other on October 5, when the family went to Roots Cafe on Gaza's seafront.

Ghaida left the ingredients on the kitchen counter and went to check on her mother. She doesn't remember who eventually cleared away the eggs and flour.

Her mother had previously undergone surgery for breast cancer and was receiving follow-up treatment at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, including medication and radiotherapy. As her mother's treatment became harder to continue inside Gaza, because of the genocide, the family decided Ghaida would accompany her out.

Leaving presented a problem she had never imagined having to solve. "I thought, how can I fit 17 years of my life into one bag?" she says.

Ghaida began with paper. She gathered every certificate she could find, going all the way back to kindergarten: school results, awards, certificates from courses she had taken. She packed photographs of friends and family and the little gifts her friends had given her, keeping the messages and notes that came with them.

There were practical things too, like her charger, Lyon potato chips and Al Awda’s crackers, and her pair of white wool pyjamas, speckled with red cherries, that she particularly loved.

Then, there was the family archive.

They had an old camera that had been used to document their lives since before Ghaida was born, along with CDs and a box of photographs accumulated over generations. There were pictures of her grandparents, her mother as a student, her parents before they married, their wedding and the announcement of their marriage.

Ghaida wanted to take the box, but there wasn’t enough room for it.

What she remembers most clearly about packing was deciding what she could bear to leave.

"I wished I could carry the whole house with me," she says, "not the material things, but the things that had meaning for us. You know what I mean? The things that touched our hearts."

The photographs were among the things that stayed behind. Later, certain they would not be able to return, the family asked a relative to go back to the house. There were too many photographs for him to carry away, and they did not want their family pictures falling into other hands.

They asked the relative to burn them.

She crossed through Rafah with her mother and 16-year-old brother Abdul Rahman and eventually settled in Madinaty, in the east of Cairo.

That first day, they ate fried chicken. For the first time in months, the things that had become difficult in Gaza were suddenly easy. Food was available. There was electricity. She could sleep without hearing shelling or drones overhead.

Her friends were still in Gaza. Ghaida would call and hear about the difficulty of finding food and water. Then, she would look at what was available around her in Egypt.

She lost her appetite and her weight plummeted by more than 10kg (22 pounds).

"My soul is in Gaza," she says.

It was not until September 2025 that Ghaida finally began university. She was 19, a month short of 20, sitting among students two years younger.

And she was no longer studying architecture. She chose dentistry to help people in Gaza when she returns.

"If the crossings open permanently," she says, "I will return immediately."

Yasmin Abu Zaid had grown up as "the pampered one", in the words of her older sisters, and something she admits to herself.

She is the youngest of three sisters and remained the family's youngest child for 10 years, until her brother was born. She had few household responsibilities. If she asked for something, her family usually found a way to get it for her.

Her grandfather was particularly indulgent. Whenever he went to the market, he would return with something for Yasmin, food, sweets, whatever had caught his eye and made him think of her.

Within days of the war beginning, Yasmin's life changed.

Her family lived on the third floor of the Ain Jalut towers in Nuseirat, in an apartment along Salah al-Din Street. When a nearby mosque was bombed that October, their home was badly damaged. The family temporarily moved into her grandmother's nearby flat. But by December, Yasmin was fleeing shelling again with her sisters and other relatives. Eventually, they drove south to Rafah, where they found temporary shelter.

Their old apartment was bombed again on January 4, 2024. On a different floor of the same building, her father's goldsmithing workshop, where he worked with gold brought into Gaza from the occupied West Bank, Egypt and Dubai, was destroyed. He has not worked as a goldsmith since.

Then, on June 8, 2024, the apartment they had been displaced to was hit by Israeli fire.

Yasmin was near a window with her sisters and other relatives when a shell struck.

She remembers the explosion, although it was not as loud as she would have expected. Then, the room filled with white dust.

Yasmin could move her arms. She knew she was bleeding, but could not tell where she had been injured. Shrapnel had entered her chest, and she struggled to breathe. Through it all, she could hear the screams for help from her sisters, until one of them passed out.

“I kept closing my eyes because I was so exhausted, and I couldn’t breathe properly,” Yasmin says. “Every time I closed my eyes, I remembered my life before the war. I felt like what was happening was just a nightmare that I wanted to wake up from.”

As her breathing became more difficult, she says, “I genuinely felt like I was going to die.”

Her father managed to find and rescue her and her sisters, but Yasmin says many weren't as lucky. "During the war, I lost about 30 members of my extended family, killed by Israeli forces."

Her education stopped for roughly a year and a half.

When she returned, she chose psychology, the subject that had interested her when she was still the pampered schoolgirl worrying about exams. But now she encountered the material differently.

As Yasmin learned about trauma and children's behaviour, she began recognising some of what she was studying at home.

Her sister would wake crying after hearing explosions. Her younger brother would wake frightened and run. Yasmin had her own response to bombardment.

"I used to look at the wall and feel that it was going to explode in my face," she says.

Her studies have changed the work she imagined doing, too. The girl who had once thought about helping children with disabilities is now particularly interested in children living with trauma.

The subject has also given her a way of thinking about what happened to her own family.

"It had a big impact on helping me accept the bombing of our home, my father's workshop, and everything we have lost," she says.

Back in her classroom, Maha continues teaching mathematics, just as she did before the war. But much has changed.

With classrooms damaged and teachers killed or displaced, the school is struggling to accommodate its pupils. Maha now teaches classes of up to 45 girls, far more than before the war.

Many of her students have been displaced, some repeatedly. Others have lost relatives and classmates. Maha herself is less strict now, she says. "Attendance and rules once mattered. If a student failed to turn up or didn't keep up with homework, I wanted to know why."

Now, she may already know. A girl might have been displaced. Her parents may be afraid to let her travel to school because of shelling. She may have had little to eat.

During periods of severe hunger, Maha watched students trying to follow lessons after barely eating the day before.

"I can see it on their faces," she says. "The girls aren't smiling. Their expressions have changed. They look sad and exhausted."

One of the strongest students in another class began sitting at the back. Maha noticed that 10 or 15 minutes before the end of lessons, the girl would fall asleep. She asked her what was happening.

Both of the girl's parents had been killed. She was caring for her younger sisters while trying to continue her own education.

Although the war had kept formal education largely suspended, some teachers, like Maha, were trying to keep pupils learning where they could, squeezing in classes and exams.

Maha remembers a particular student who would always get top marks. In February 2025, the girl came to her, disappointed with her score of 14 out of 20 on a mathematics exam.

"I told her not to worry. I'd overlook this result and that she should focus on the next exam, and I'm sure she will do better. I said I'd use that mark instead," says Maha. And the girl left happy.

A few hours later, the girl's home was bombed. She was killed. Maha would place two photographs of the girl in the classroom. One on the back wall. Another hung beside the blackboard: a selfie of her smiling, both hands raised in V signs.

"Every time I looked at the photograph, it shook me," Maha says. "I would always remember that moment before she was killed, when she was sitting there worried about her grade."

One thought kept returning. "Thank God, I didn't disappoint her. I kept my promise to her and let her leave that day happy."

Now, the students at their desks finish the problems Maha has set for them.

In the corner by the window, a girl looks up from her desk.

“Miss, I’ve finished. Can you come and check my answers?”

Maha looks once more at the photograph from June 2023, before putting her phone away.
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.summary: Al Jazeera finds 15 girls who were taken in a photo in Gaza in June 2023. They were 17 and 18 when Israel's war on Gaza began. They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: A’ja Wilson wins her third straight WNBA MVP and record fifth overall
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
A’ja Wilson fine-tunes her shooting touch after every practice. That extra work has defined her greatness since being drafted first overall in 2018.

On Thursday, she received a voice message from former Vice President Kamala Harris congratulating her on redefining greatness leaguewide after she was named the WNBA’s MVP for a third straight year and for the fifth time overall.

“Obviously, that is an honour,” Wilson said. “A woman of our history, and I’m so appreciative to be able to share that moment with her through the phone call and the message of her delivering that I won my fifth MVP.”

In addition to becoming the first player to three-peat, Wilson won the award in 2020 and 2022.

Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, Aces owner Mark Davis and team President Nikki Fargas accompanied Wilson’s mother, Eva, who presented her daughter with the trophy.

“Each one of these has not been taken lightly,” Wilson said while flanked by all five of her MVP trophies. “In my heart, they’ve always been so special. But this one here, I cried a little bit harder. This one here is just a little bit different. … When you dream as a young girl, you dream so big and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off.

“And when you’re able to check them off – small wins, big wins – it truly means a lot. And so I think that’s why I cried a little bit harder on this one, because 15-year-old A’ja wasn’t sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn’t dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world.”

The 30-year-old Wilson once again led the league in scoring with an average of 26.2 points per game while shooting nearly 53 percent from the field. She averaged 9.4 rebounds per game, a career-best 3.2 assists and 1.9 blocks.

Wilson has the defending champion Aces back in the WNBA semifinals for the eighth consecutive season although Las Vegas is down 2-0 in the best-of-five series against Golden State. Game 3 is on Friday.

“This is great. I love it, not going to take for granted, shine her up, let’s do it,” Wilson said on Thursday. “But tomorrow, when it comes to hoisting it in front of the fans, I love the fans, … but I doubt I will be doing that. I’ll be warming up with my team. … Everyone in this room knows the competitor that I am. Everyone knows what my main focus is, and that is to get a game.”

Wilson received 65 first-place votes and nine second-place votes for a total of 713 points from a national panel of sportswriters and broadcasters. Minnesota’s Olivia Miles received six first-place votes and 40 second-place votes (442 points) while Indiana guards Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark followed with 287 and 212 points, respectively.

No WNBA player besides Wilson has more than three MVPs. Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each have a trio. On the NBA side, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar has six, and Michael Jordan and Bill Russell each have five.

“A’ja Wilson is one of one,” Fargas said. “She’s now standing in a category that no other WNBA player in the history of the league has accomplished. She’s in the conversations with the Michael Jordans and the Wayne Gretzkys of the world – where she belongs.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Everton’s owners, The ‌Friedkin Group (TFG), are open to selling a controlling stake ⁠in the club ⁠as part of efforts to attract new investment, the Premier League club said on Friday.

The announcement comes less ⁠than two years after the US-based group acquired Everton from former owner Farhad Moshiri in December 2024, taking control of the ⁠club grappling with financial difficulties and a prolonged period of instability.

Since then, TFG has overseen Everton’s move into the Hill Dickinson Stadium and worked to improve the club’s financial position.

“When TFG became custodians of Everton, ‌the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch,” the owners said in a statement.

They said the immediate priority had been to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club’s future, including bringing the stadium to completion.

“With that foundation now safely in ⁠place, the time is right to consider the ⁠next chapter for Everton.”

TFG said it would only consider proposals from parties it believed could build on the progress made since its takeover and added that it ⁠would continue to support the club on and off the pitch throughout the process.

TFG’s decision follows ⁠a summer transfer window that, according to ⁠British media reports, drew criticism from supporters. Everton generated significant income through player sales but made only limited additions to their squad before the deadline.

TFG, which also ‌owns Italian club AS Roma and French side AS Cannes, said it had retained investment bank Moelis & Company to advise on the ‌process.

The ‌group and Everton said they would make no further comment while the process was under way.
