https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: 2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.

The committee’s announcement of the 125th Nobel Peace Prize, made on Friday in Oslo, said the award would go to the South African jurist for her work to promote peace and international law.

The committee said in a statement that Pillay, a former United Nations high commissioner for human rights, had been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.

“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” the statement read.

Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. It is judges, he continued, “who guard the thin red line between order and chaos”.

A South African of Indian Tamil origin, the 85-year-old Pillay was the first woman to start a law practice in what was then the province of Natal in 1967.

She was a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela, who previously won the peace prize, and other antiapartheid activists and was the first woman of colour to serve on South Africa’s High Court.

She later served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court and as the UN’s rights chief.

The committee highlighted her role during her time on the Rwanda tribunal in establishing that rape and sexual violence can constitute crimes against humanity and genocide.

Pillay chaired the UN Independent International Commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory, which concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

“We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,” she declared in a presentation to the UN General Assembly.

The conclusions found that Israel’s president, prime minister and former defence minister had “incited the commission” of genocide.

Pillay currently sits on the International Court of Justice in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide against the Rohingya.

Ashok Swain, a researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden said that while the prize won’t deliver any concrete change on the ground, the messaging of the award to Pillay is key in the current climate.

“International law … was never perfect, but at least some rules were there. Now it has become a free-for-all, and everyone interprets it the way they want,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have not seen this many conflicts in the world in the last half-century.

Reacting to the award, Pillay said she thought at first it must be a joke. “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this,” she remarked.

“The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what’s happening there as genocide,” she continued. “One of the main reactions to that report is paying tribute to me for my courage. And you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth?”

The prize, which is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), will be presented in Oslo ‌on ‌December 10 on the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.

Four other prizes were announced earlier this week for medicine, physics, chemistry and literature.

The Nobel committee received nominations for 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize. Other contenders included the International Space Station, emergency teams in Sudan, children’s advocates in Ukraine and two top international courts.

United States President Donald Trump has long coveted the prize and repeatedly said he deserves it despite starting the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.

Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, handed her medal to Trump after the US deposed former President Nicholas Maduro in January.

Pillay joked that she might share her prize with the US leader.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said in a video posted on social media by the secretary-general of Amnesty International that showed Pillay being applauded after the announcement of the award.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: The award will go to the South African jurist for her work to promote peace and international law. Pillay was a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela and was the first woman of colour to serve on South Africa’s High Court. She later served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International criminal Court.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: NBA star Wembanyama to French students: ‘I hear you’
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
France’s ‌basketball star Victor Wembanyama voiced his support on Thursday ⁠for French ⁠teenagers protesting conditions in the country’s schools.

The Ministry of the Interior said 71,500 people took part in Thursday’s demonstrations, ⁠including 24,500 in the main Paris march centred on Place de la Bastille.

“These are systemic inequalities – problems so deep-rooted ⁠that, in fact, I’m glad that high-school students and young people in general are speaking up,” Wembanyama told a news conference on Thursday night.

“I hear them, and I support them, and ‌I hope the people all over there will do the same.”

The San Antonio Spurs player had previously replied “I would love to” when a fan asked him in an Instagram post to join the protest with the French teenagers.

“I have a lot of interest. I meant it,” Wembanyama ⁠added at the news conference. “I was in ⁠that position not so long ago.

“I’ve had the chance to escape this system, to escape these problems. But it’s chance, it’s luck. So I ⁠want to show my support.

“It’s not something that’s completely unfamiliar to me. I went ⁠to high school in Nanterre, which was ⁠already a stronghold of ‘blocages’ back then,” he said, referring to student-led school blockades.

Concerns about state schools have helped prompt a number of France’s most significant protests ‌in decades.

They began last month at high schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, where anger over teacher absences ‌and ‌shabby facilities quickly evolved into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Japan’s Okinawa calls for review of US forces pact after killing
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The prefectural assembly of Okinawa has called for a review of an agreement overseeing the stationing of United States military forces on the Japanese island.

The assembly adopted the resolution on Friday. The vote came after a US Marine was accused of robbing and killing a local woman.

The call to adapt the Japan-US Status of Forces Agreement to urge the US military to prevent such incidents will be sent to the US embassy. The assembly also passed a statement to the same effect addressed to the Japanese government.

Ryotaro Odo, who heads the assembly’s special committee on US military bases, said the US military was “not functioning as an organisation”, pointing to failures in training and discipline.

He called the killing “extremely heinous and despicable” and urged the military to cooperate with investigators and discipline those responsible.

Some of the assembly’s members opposed the resolution because it failed to demand the dismissal of the US military chief in Okinawa, Japan’s Kyodo News agency reported.

Lance-Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, has been accused of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha on Saturday. He has denied the allegations.

The case has sparked a series of demonstrations in Tokyo and Okinawa.

The island hosts the majority of the 54,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drink-driving incidents by US personnel have long sparked protests.

The US military paused its operations for 48 hours from Wednesday and also imposed a 30-day curfew from midnight to 5am starting on Friday.

Tokyo has called in the US ambassador and the US forces commander in Okinawa to protest the incident, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the “heinous” crime.

Okinawa, which was under US control from 1945 to 1972, still hosts many facilities used exclusively by US forces.

The island’s assembly passed a similar resolution in 2024 after a series of sexual assaults by US servicemen came to light with the municipal assemblies of Naha, Ginowan, Miyakojima and Motobu filing protests.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: LeBron James stars in NBA preseason debut but Nets defeat 76ers
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
NBA superstar LeBron James delivered a solid first half in his first preseason game for Philadelphia, but the new-look 76ers fell 114-108 to the Nets in Brooklyn.

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, announced in July that he had signed a two-year, $8m deal with the 76ers, ending weeks of speculation over where the four-time NBA champion would land as a free agent after eight seasons and one title with the Los Angeles Lakers.

The 41-year-old superstar, entering a record-extending 24th NBA season, won two titles with Miami, another with Cleveland and a fourth with the Lakers, and is aiming to help the Sixers win their first title since Julius Erving led the club to the crown 43 years ago.

Thursday’s game marked his first chance to line up alongside new teammates Joel Embiid, VJ Edgecombe, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown – a new arrival from the Boston Celtics.

“It felt a little different,” James said. “Obviously, just wearing a new uniform, but the game is the game.

“We’re still trying to put each other in a position to be successful and complement each other the best way we can out on the floor,” he added. “But it’s going to take some time. Tonight was a good sample size for us to build on.”

James scored 10 points, connecting on his lone shot from the floor and making all eight of his free-throw attempts. He added four rebounds, five assists and a steal in 18:04 minutes in the first half.

Brown led all scorers with 18 points. Julius Randle had 14 for the Nets, who outscored the Sixers 37-23 in the third quarter to take control.

But all eyes were on James, starting with his first signature pre-game chalk-toss in a 76ers uniform.

James smoothly directed the Sixers’ offence in his time on the floor, making all five of his assists in the first quarter and combining effectively with Maxey.

“I think there was some really good things happening, you know, right off the bat,” 76ers coach Nick Nurse said after seeing his starters together for the first time.

“A bunch of back cuts and good passing, etc, there were segments where obviously we turned the ball over a lot … just the little clunky segments, too. But, again, it’s preseason, first time they’re together.

“I think you look at it as what’s good and what are the learning experiences, things that we can improve.”

The 76ers have two more preseason games, both against Boston, before opening the NBA regular season against the defending champion New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on October 20.

James’s arrival has already found the 76ers battling outside “noise”.

James took to Instagram to refute a report from a play-by-play announcer during the team’s first preseason game on Monday that James had admonished Embiid for being late to a practice.

“He ain’t been late, so stop the lie,” James posted.

James had acknowledged at the team’s media day last month that such outside hubbub around the 76ers would be “doubled, tripled and quadrupled now that I’m here”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: US ICE releases Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh from custody
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency in the United States has released Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh from custody after he was detained on September 24.

The award-winning filmmaker was released on Thursday, two days after he was granted bond, according to a statement by a campaign of his friends and relatives to free him.

However, ICE’s deportation case against Sheikh continues with the next hearing set for October 27, the campaign said.

Sheikh, whose work has explored conflict in his native India-administered Kashmir, was detained by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as he disembarked from a plane at Dulles International Airport outside Washington, DC, after arriving from California.

The 42-year-old, who lives in Alexandria, Virginia, entered the US on a student visa in 2019 to pursue graduate studies in film at Georgia State University and filed for asylum in 2020.

The campaign said he had a pending asylum application and was authorised to work and live in the US.

The DHS confirmed on Wednesday that Sheikh had been arrested on September 24 and said he “legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance”.

A pending application does not confer legal status in the US, the DHS said, adding he ⁠will receive due process.

Sheikh’s first feature film, Saffron Kingdom, garnered multiple honours, notably best feature film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, Los Angeles Film and Documentary Awards, Melbourne Independent Film Festival, Wake Forest Film Festival and Anatolian International Film Awards.

In 2025, Sheikh was also recognised with the emerging filmmaker activist award at the Teaneck International Film Festival.

His detention came amid a surge in the number of ICE arrests across the US, which hit record levels over the summer. About 50,000 arrests were recorded in July and August.

President Donald Trump’s administration said in August that it was ‌working “to identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Three years after October 7, prolonged war takes its toll on Israelis
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Caolán Magee
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
As Israel marks the third anniversary of the 7 October Hamas-led attacks, the psychological toll on its society remains visible, with an increase in PTSD among children, more adults struggling with everyday life amid mental health issues, and a rise in suicides among soldiers, experts have told Al Jazeera.

About 1,200 people died in the attacks on villages and army outposts in southern Israel, while Israel’s assault on Gaza has since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Gaza has been left almost uninhabitable amid a wave of destruction that a UN commission of inquiry has concluded amounts to genocide. Meanwhile, Israeli society continues to function, but beneath the surface, the attacks, war and missile strikes have compounded the psychological strain among its people.

New research has found that one in five Israelis reports severe difficulties with daily functioning because of their mental health, according to the National Mental Health Barometer, conducted by Clalit Health Services’ Research Institute and the Myers-JDC-Brookdale Institute.

Among children and adolescents, separate Clalit research shared with Al Jazeera recorded a 121 per cent increase in psychiatric emergency visits compared with the period before the war. Behind those figures are families living with bereavement and fears about what comes next.

During a webinar for journalists organised by Clalit Health Services to mark the anniversary, Irit Ben Arye recounted how her husband, Haim Ben Arye, drove south to help evacuate survivors from Kibbutz Be’eri. It was one of the communities attacked by Palestinian fighters on 7 October 2023.

The 52-year-old bus driver returned home crying, she says. About two weeks later, he died by suicide.

The couple were married for 30 years and had eight children. Irit worries about the lasting effects on them. Recounting to journalists what she told her children following the death of her husband, she said: “You have to ask for help, if something is bothering you, if you’re in pain, in the dark, you feel that you are alone.”

“Cry, ask, break something. Make yourself noticed, make us notice that you are in pain.”

The Ben Arye family are not the only ones experiencing mental distress. In fact, one-third of the Israeli population felt they needed mental health treatment, according to the National Mental Health Barometer report. Half reported that their leisure activities had been affected, while 35 per cent said they had difficulty forming and maintaining close relationships.

Israel’s attacks on Iran and retaliatory missile strikes have brought further periods of fear and interruption to civilian life. With missiles and airstrikes raining down on Israel at various times since 7 October, everyday activities can become calculations about access to shelter and the possibility of another attack.

Eric Vermetten, a professor of psychiatry at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands, told Al Jazeera that this type of repeated exposure to danger can lead to long-lasting psychological issues. “Repeated attacks, warning sirens and displacement turn ordinary decisions – where to sleep, whether to send children to school, how to plan tomorrow – into questions of safety,” he said.

“Maintaining that vigilance is exhausting: sleep becomes deeply fragmented, concentration falters and anxiety, irritability or withdrawal can seriously strain relationships,” he added.

Drawing on records from about five million members, Clalit Health Services’ assessment has found that psychiatric emergency visits among children and teenagers more than doubled over this period.

Edgar Jones, professor at King’s College London’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, told Al Jazeera that people respond differently to prolonged conflict. Some do adapt and develop ways of coping.

But if people experience the destruction of their home or the death of a relative, they may develop post-traumatic illness or depression, he said. “Many of those in this group will become war-weary should their daily lives continue to be disrupted and threatened.”

“Everyone has a breaking point,” Jones said.

The effects of prolonged warfare are also apparent among those carrying out Israel’s military attacks. Soldiers, including young conscripts, have been deployed to Gaza, where a United Nations commission of inquiry concluded that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians.

“For reservists, moving repeatedly between combat and civilian life may leave little to no time to reconnect with family or make sense of their experiences – loss, guilt, shame, anger, despair – before returning to duty,” Vermetten said.

Jones added: “They may, when reflecting on what they have been ordered to do, or failed to do, experience moral injury”.

“This arises when their actions challenge their view of themselves, sometimes leading to guilt, shame and anger against themselves.”

Israeli parliamentary data recorded 279 suicide attempts among serving soldiers between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 per cent of military suicide deaths in 2024. The figures exclude veterans who died by suicide after leaving service.

Vermetten cautioned against treating suicide as an inevitable consequence of prolonged war, but said that “conflict, loss and isolation can increase vulnerability” among soldiers who go on to take their own lives.

The psychological consequences of Israel’s military campaigns extend far beyond its own population. Since 7 October 2023, its assaults on Gaza and Lebanon, as well as attacks on Iran have brought death, destruction and displacement across the region, leaving children particularly vulnerable to lasting trauma.

UNICEF estimated that in Lebanon, 770,000 children have experienced psychological distress, while almost two-thirds of households reported that their children were anxious or nervous. The conflict has also compounded years of economic crisis, leaving families struggling to meet basic needs as well as support their children.

In Gaza, the scale of destruction and displacement has eroded the foundations on which psychological recovery depends, with hospitals and homes destroyed across the enclave.

UNICEF estimates that more than one million children are in need of mental health and psychosocial support, while much of the population is suffering from hunger, amid bombardment that has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire” last October.

“Children know trauma does not end when the bombing stops,” Jonathan Crickx, UNICEF’s chief of communication in the State of Palestine, said in February.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Iraq is set to ban the popular navigation app Waze, which was founded in Israel.

Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad announced the move on Tuesday. It has prompted discussions in Iraq over whether the country can build its own alternative and whether banning one app protects users’ location data.

The Ministry of Communications plans to block the use of Waze by the end of December, according to the Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada.

Sanad told the broadcaster Rudaw that it would take effect some time at the start of 2027.

He made the announcement on the sidelines of the Hitex 2026 technology exhibition in Erbil, the capital of the semiautonomous Kurdish region in northern Iraq.

“Because it comes from the entity [Israel] and is Israeli-made, we will ban it at the beginning of 2027,” he said.

Waze is a widely used navigation app. Hundreds of motorists, including taxi drivers, use it to get around. The service relies on users to report traffic jams, accidents and police checkpoints as they happen.

It was developed in Israel, and Google bought it in 2013 for nearly $1bn.

Waze’s privacy policy lets it collect users’ locations, routes, destinations, search histories and device details, depending on their settings.

Pooled across many users over time, such data have security value because they can reveal movement patterns, peak times and unusual changes.

Rudaw reported that the app has been the subject of security discussions in Iraq over its alerts being used to avoid checkpoints although Sanad did not link the ban to that issue.

Iraq does not recognise Israel or have diplomatic relations with it and has formally been at war with it since 1948.

A 2022 law criminalises any diplomatic, political, military, economic or cultural ties with Israel. Its penalties include life imprisonment and the death penalty. It was passed by 275 votes in the 329-seat Council of Representatives.

The law applies to all Iraqi citizens, state institutions and media as well as private companies and foreign entities operating in the country, including the Kurdish region.

Sanad has not specifically said Waze must be blocked under the antinormalisation law.

Distrust of Israel has been bolstered by the US-Israel war on Iran. The United States and its allies have targeted Iraq’s Iran-aligned militias with air strikes and economic measures.

During the war, Iraq also faced a serious case of Israeli infiltration. In May, US media reported that Israel had built two secret military outposts deep inside Iraq’s desert to support its war on Iran.

One post was nearly exposed by a local shepherd who stumbled upon it and was killed.

Sanad said users could switch to Google Maps or Iraqi navigation apps.

Communications Ministry spokesman Omar al-Amiri said in remarks carried by Al-Mada that Waze would be replaced by a yet-to-be-named Iraqi app.

He said the app would run without technical problems.

Al-Mada also quoted Iraqi technology researcher Mustafa Kamel al-Sharif as saying a national alternative would take more than an app with an Iraqi map and logo.

It would need accurate geographic databases, a constantly updated road network, routing systems and live data on traffic, accidents and closures, he said.

He also told the newspaper that the crux of the issue lies in how Iraq regulates its citizens’ data and other services may also collect sensitive data similar to Waze.

The ministry has not said how the block will be enforced or whether it will cover the Kurdish region. It has also not set out the ban’s legal basis or said when the Iraqi app will launch.

Another unknown is why Google Maps, owned by the same parent company, Alphabet, would remain available or serve as an alternative.

The government has also not answered why Waze is being banned now when its Israeli roots have been long known.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Waze is a widely used navigation app for motorists. It was developed in Israel and bought by Google in 2013 for nearly $1bn. The Ministry of Communications plans to block the use of Waze by the end of December.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Who is Dov Lando, the Israeli rabbi criticising Zionism?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
One of Israel’s top ultra-Orthodox rabbis, Dov Lando, has become the centre of controversy in Israel after comments emerged in which he denigrated Zionism.

In a recently released video recording, the 96-year-old rabbi is heard saying the ideology of Zionism caused the Jewish people to suffer “disasters”, and that Jewish Israelis may have been better off without a state.

The remarks have drawn rebukes from Israeli politicians weeks before landmark legislative elections, in which the role of the country’s growing ultra-Orthodox community – particularly over military service – is a major issue. The political alignment of ultra-Orthodox parties could also prove crucial to the formation of the next government.

So, who is Lando and why are his comments significant?

Dov Lando is a 96-year-old rabbi regarded as the leader of Israel’s Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community. Born in Poland and raised in the Lithuanian-style ultra-Orthodox tradition, Lando heads a yeshiva – a traditional Jewish academy – in the Israeli city of Bnei Brak.

He is a member of Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah, a council of senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis that offer religious guidance to the community, as well as the spiritual leader of Israel’s Degel HaTorah party. That party is part of the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance, which is a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition.

Earlier this week, Israeli media released a video of Lando making year-old comments that harshly criticise Zionism, military service and secular Israelis.

Lando, who has made similarly critical remarks before, is heard in the video saying that Zionism “caused the Arabs to hate us” and brought physical as well as spiritual “disasters” on the Jewish people.

“It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state,” Lando said, adding that international or Palestinian rule would have been “the best situation” for Jews.

Lando went on to castigate soldiers who adhere to Religious Zionism – a strand of Orthodox Judaism that upholds Zionism – saying “they are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah.” Many military operations, he said, are carried out “not for saving lives, but for the honour of the state”.

The veteran rabbi also had harsh words for secular Israelis, who he said have “no connection to Judaism at all”. He described them as having built “a state of apostasy and heresy”.

Lando’s remarks have drawn fierce criticism from numerous Israeli politicians, including all major figures that have joined an opposition alliance challenging Netanyahu.

Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party who is viewed as the opposition bloc’s most likely candidate for prime minister, said Lando’s “outrageous statements” were “the embodiment of anti-Zionism”.

Yair Lapid, the head of Israel’s opposition in the Knesset, called the comments “a disgrace to every Jew”.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance co-founded with Lapid, said Lando’s remarks are “anti-Semitic, anti-Zionist” and against the Israeli military.

Netanyahu has not commented on Lando’s latest reported remarks, but he publicly condemned earlier statements by the rabbi in July, when Lando accused the Religious Zionism movement of “incitement to murder” for its support for drafting religious seminary students into the military.

Members of the anti-Netanyahu opposition bloc have called for the UTJ, which Lando’s party is part of, to be cast out of any future government, and criticised Netanyahu for staying aligned with the group.

Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, said Netanyahu is “silent because without Rabbi Lando and his emissaries, he has no government”.

Netanyahu’s “political survival is more important to him than Zionism, more than equality in service, and more than the blood of our soldiers”, Golan said.

But breaking with the UTJ would come at a huge political cost to Netanyahu, whose coalition is already in for a tough election battle on October 27 and is polling well below the 61-seat threshold needed for a majority.

UTJ is projected to win 8 seats in parliament, according to an October 5 poll by Israel’s Channel 12.

“If Netanyahu attacks Lando forcefully, he pays a price with the Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) he needs to form a government,” said Ehab Jabareen, a researcher on Israeli affairs. “If he stays silent, he hands his rivals material to tell right-wing voters that the man who speaks of Zionism and security depends on a religious leadership that doubts Zionism itself.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Afghanistan’s emerald miners struggle with tools but attract global buyers
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Rob McBride
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Panjshir, Afghanistan — At a packed hall in the offices of the Panjshir provincial government, an auction is under way and the bidding is brisk.

The buyers, many from Kabul and some from overseas, have already closely examined the small piles of roughly cut green stones, shining their phone flashlights through them to check their quality.

Bidding for the best stones is competitive.

“Panjshir emeralds have many buyers around the world because of their very high quality,” gem merchant Ghulam Mustafa Habibi told Al Jazeera. “This is why their price is higher compared with other emeralds around the world.”

By the end of the auction, nearly 3,000 carats of the precious stones were sold – the 23rd sale of its kind so far this year. The value of emeralds sold to date in Afghanistan is estimated to be nearly 400m Afghanis ($6.12m), a steep rise compared with last year.

For a country impoverished by years of war and burdened by international sanctions, the trade in precious minerals is a valuable resource, especially in the remote corner of northeastern Afghanistan.

“Thankfully, more than 15,000 people are currently employed in Panjshir’s mining sector,” says Muhammad Aman Rezaii, a mining official responsible for overseeing the operation of many small artisanal mining operations dotting the Panjshir valley.

On the valley’s steep hillsides, miners toil for hours underground to make a living. In the otherwise barren and rocky landscape, which yields little, the precious stones are a lifeline.

“There are hardly any companies or manufacturing factories here. The main source of employment is the mining sector,” said Rezaii, adding that they have identified more than 2,000 other mining sites which could be developed.

Since taking power in 2021, the Taliban say they have signed deals with dozens of investors, mainly Chinese, Russian and Iranian, to mine gemstones and other valuable minerals.

According to the World Bank, state revenues rose 22 percent year-on-year in April and May, boosted by the auction of mines and other resources such as oil and precious minerals.

But Afghanistan’s gemstone mining sector is still lacking in international investment and expertise.

“There have been various proposals to establish an international market for Afghanistan’s precious minerals, particularly in Kabul,” Hafiz Muhammad Agha Hakim, the Governor of Panjshir province, told Al Jazeera.

“Processing machinery could be brought in so that these minerals can be processed and standardised here before being exported to markets around the world. At the moment, there is no standardised centre or proper processing facility.”

Back in the dusty confines of his mine, working in near-total darkness, miner Mahdi wields a crowbar while his friend beside him hits the surface with a hammer. He bemoans their lack of modern equipment.

“There are many challenges because we don’t have advanced equipment,” he says, taking a break from the digging. “We work only with basic tools such as shovels, pickaxes, drills and similar equipment.”

Rezaii said the miners need proper equipment that can make their work easier and safer, while also allowing the minerals to be extracted in a more professional manner. This would benefit the people of Afghanistan and particularly the miners,” he said.

“The area is vulnerable to landslides, avalanches, flooding and falling rocks. People here are working under extremely difficult and demanding conditions.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
United States President Donald Trump has said the US will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.

The US president said late on Thursday: “we are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” in a post on Truth Social. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”

Oil prices fell early on Friday as Middle East supply concerns eased somewhat after tensions in the energy-rich Gulf region had mounted in recent weeks.

The possibility of renewed fighting had appeared to drive up oil prices in trading on Thursday. Some analysts believe Trump’s comments were an attempt to try and bring prices back down.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is reviewing the US response to its seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran will respond within the “next few days”.

He added that negotiations are continuing through mediators, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported.

Iranian media reported “massive explosions” in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Friday, with Fars citing unnamed military sources as saying tankers using “unauthorised” routes may have struck sea mines.

On Tuesday, US Vice President JD Vance said Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity as part of an agreement to end the war. Experts say this demand may signal a softening of Washington’s earlier insistence that Tehran abandon enrichment altogether.

On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said negotiations with Washington were “futile”, accusing the US of using negotiations to attack Iran.

Russian President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian that Russia will “do everything” to help end the US-led war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported on Thursday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Brazilian Supreme Court judge issues arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
A Brazilian Supreme Court justice has issued an arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro, brother of presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, a move likely to heat up the hard-fought race.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the arrest warrant on Thursday, weeks before a runoff election for the country’s presidency between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, the favourite to win.

In June, the Brazilian Supreme Court convicted Eduardo Bolsonaro on charges of lobbying the US to interfere in the trial of his father, former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro.

Eduardo Bolsonaro has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration, accompanying him to a May meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House.

Both sides of Brazil’s deeply polarised partisan divide have long accused each other of corruption and lawfare as political drama reaches a crescendo in the buildup to the October 25 runoff.

In March 2025, Eduardo Bolsonaro pledged he would move to the US full time to “focus 100 percent” of his energy on freeing his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The move cost him his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator.

The 42-year-old former lawmaker lives in Texas and is a green card holder.

He was convicted of lobbying to impose sanctions on members of the Brazilian government and to implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father.

De Moraes, whom the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced in September 2025 to 27 years in prison for plotting to stage a coup.

The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his four-year sentence immediately.

“The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” de Moraes said.

De Moraes also cancelled Eduardo Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and instructed the country’s federal police to arrest him if he returns to Brazil.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Brazil's Supreme Court has issued an arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro. The arrest warrant was issued weeks before a runoff election for the country's presidency. Eduardo has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/xonas-.title: Xona’s commercial GPS alternative is about to go live
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/xonas-.author: Tim Fernholz
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/xonas-.text:
The first precision commercial alternative to GPS is preparing to go live when six satellites designed by the startup Xona Space Systems launch into orbit this month.

A service that competes with free signals provided by governments around the world may seem foolhardy, but Xona is hoping to add navigation and timing to the list of de facto government space monopolies disrupted by venture-backed startups.

Xona was founded in 2019 by a team of five engineers who originally met at Stanford University’s aerospace engineering graduate program. One, Tyler Reid, went on to earn a PhD, writing his thesis on the possibilities of using satellites in low-earth orbit to improve navigation.

GPS and analog satellite networks built by Europe, China and Russia provide huge value, but are also easy to jam and aren’t precise enough to be used alone for applications like farming robots or self-driving cars. Over “pizza and beer chats,” the friends mulled whether fixing those problems could be a business.

“My knee jerk was like, this is dumb,” Xona CEO Brian Manning told TechCrunch during a recent visit to the company’s headquarters. “Why would anybody replace GPS? It’s free, right? And I started digging into it. People think of GPS as a free service, but the market isn’t the service. The market’s the hardware, and you have billions of devices being sold every year; those things aren’t being given away for free. There’s an immense market that is desperately looking for better performance.”

That didn’t mean the road to delivering such a service was simple. Improving GPS with a stronger signal that offers more precise timing and location data remained a technical challenge. The company needed to develop a unique architecture that would allow its satellites to keep time without expensive atomic clocks onboard, taking advantage of the spacecraft’s proximity to Earth and close communication with ground-based sources of truth.

The other technical challenge the company solved was making sure its signals could be received by existing GPS receivers with a relatively simple software modification. That gives Xona immediate access to the market and smoothes the way through the regulations for broadcasting navigation signals.

Later this month, a SpaceX rocket is scheduled to launch six satellites for Xona. Four are similar to a prototype the company launched last year that proved its technology; those satellites are built around a satellite platform from Aerospace Labs. The other two satellites were built entirely by Xona at its Burlingame, California headquarters, and are intended to be the foundation of the company’s 258-satellite operational constellation, called Pulsar.

Pulsar will offer centimeter-level precision for geolocation, instead of the meter-level precision provided by GPS, and its signal is strong enough to be detected inside buildings and in urban environments. Manning also believes its signal is powerful enough to deter would-be jammers and spoofers, too.

Xona can begin beta-testing Pulsar with real customers once its satellites are in orbit and passing overhead the mid-latitudes about eight times a day.

Ian Gough, the CEO of TimeBeat, a company that specializes in electronic timing, says the initial pilot will allow his engineers to check and correct the timing provided by its devices around the world. By 2028, Xona hopes to offer full coverage in the U.S., Europe, Japan, and South Korea.

Xona has raised just over $300 million from venture investors since its founding, including $20 million from the U.S. Space Force. While the company is focused on offering a commercial service, the U.S. government is clearly interested in the technology, as jamming and spoofing of satellite navigation services become increasingly common in conflicts.

While there are literally billions of potential users for a new precision timing signal, Xona is also looking ahead to a world of growing autonomy. Reid, whose thesis inspired the company and who now serves as its CTO, worked on self-driving cars at Ford and saw that a service like Pulsar would be needed to realize the potential of autonomous vehicles of all stripes.

Xona’s headquarters boasts an incredible view of planes landing at San Francisco International Airport. Watching the jets come in, Manning points out that among “all the forms of mass transportation, the gold standard for safety is civil aviation. We see Xona and what we’re building being able to play a big part in that … to provide the service to a car, so you can feel as safe taking your hands off the wheel as you are laying back in an airliner.”
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/xonas-.summary: Xona Space Systems is launching six satellites this month. The company is hoping to add navigation and timing to the list of de facto government space monopolies disrupted by venture-backed startups. The service will compete with GPS and analog satellite networks built by Europe, China and Russia.

OpenAI said an internal investigation uncovered breaches “beyond what’s outlined in the letter,” but did not provide details.

The safety of frontier systems has become an increasing concern for staff inside AI companies following a series of high profile breaches this year, most notably OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face. Many staff are now calling for companies to slow down and do more to guard against the potential consequences of building self-improving systems.

https://www.wired.com/story/dunking-on-d.title: Dunking on Dating App Profiles Is Content Gold. People Are Getting Sick of It
https://www.wired.com/story/dunking-on-d.author: Jason Parham
https://www.wired.com/story/dunking-on-d.text:
Evangelizing to his 512,000 TikTok followers occasionally requires that dating coach Chad Franklin post the private communications of his clients, who pay upwards of $5,000 for his services.

In September, Franklin shared a DM conversation in which a woman implied she couldn’t afford an Uber with the text overlay “Don’t date POOR women!!!” That same month, he uploaded a video of a client’s successful text exchange on Hinge where they talked about the need to “flirt over some margaritas.” In the clip, Franklin can barely contain himself, noting that it was the type of tête-à-tête that gets his “dick hard”: “This is what men are looking for. We lead, you follow.”

Franklin posts under the alias @DefundSimping, and has made it his mission to help straight, career-driven guys in their “post-breakup, post-divorce” era undo their “simp” behavior, which he defines as putting women on a pedestal or giving them too much attention.

I reached out to the 30-year-old content creator because I wanted to talk about Hinge’s decision to start testing screenshot protection in India. The announcement set off a firestorm of reaction across social media last week, rekindling a debate around digital etiquette, privacy, and shame.

“​​Everyone who’s downloaded the app has seen the debauchery and the drama,” Franklin says, explaining that being online in 2026 simply means there is a chance you will become the day’s main character whether you intended to or not. “People are aware that they could be the next haha moment, but that doesn't mean they deserve it.”

TikTokers, X accounts like @hingestrange, and other online creators have built entire brands out of screenshotting and sharing bizarre dating profile prompts, cringe pickup lines, or red flags found while swiping. But critics of the trend argue it’s a form of public humiliation that should end.

In response to news of Hinge revoking profile screenshotting ability in India, some responded with relief.

“People on here kinda turned being on a dating app into both an extension of the panopticon and a window into their own personal penchant for cruelty,” writer Tres Dean noted on X. “I actually think this might be the first ethical development in online dating in years if not ever.”

X user @randy_mossad added, “Better for a million cheaters to go unpunished than for one regular person looking for love to get humiliated by leaked chats.”

In a TikTok video, Florida-based creator Kiara said she understands the change despite having posted screenshots to shame men who were hypersexual or “super disrespectful” in their profiles. “But I’ve noticed now that we’re in an ‘I hate men’ apocalypse ... women are posting men’s profiles simply because they’re not just not attracted to them,” she continued, describing the latter as being “wrong” and “mean.”

At a moment when the apps feel broken for so many people, there seems to be a desire for more private, less performative forms of dating and communication.

While apps like Raya and Grindr already include screenshot protection, the India pilot is the first iteration of it for Hinge, which will block screenshots on surfaces containing personally identifiable profile information, including Discover, Likes You, and Standouts.

The company confirms to WIRED that testing in India is part of an initiative to help singles build trust among other users and with the platform. The insights will determine whether and how Hinge introduces the feature in additional markets, but there are no current plans to greenlight screenshot protection in US or other regions.

A 2025 study in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication suggested that screenshots create “privacy turbulence” by allowing a recipient to permanently store and redistribute private conversations without the original sender's knowledge or consent, noting that the screenshot feature eliminates a shared boundary of control and strips away context.

But for some women in particular, screenshotting profiles has become a necessary precaution when vetting potential suitors. “Privacy’s in tension with safety. Screenshots can document inappropriate behavior or allow someone to check in with a friend before meeting a stranger,” says Lizzie Li, a communications researcher, who adds that communities like Are We Dating the Same Guy? grew partly out of women sharing screenshots to address safety concerns.

Asked whether the company has an obligation to prevent users from having their profiles turned into public content—30 million people currently use the app—a Hinge spokesperson tells WIRED that screenshot protection, along with Comment Filter and Did This Bother You?, is “another way we’re exploring how to help daters control how and where personal details are shared.” Singles will still be able to screenshot their messages with other matches if they want to report an account for potential safety concerns, affording women an extra layer of defense on dating apps where they disproportionately experience harassment and privacy violations. According to Hinge’s community guidelines, harassment, bullying, and intimidation are prohibited.

“When you are a bystander, it is fairly obvious that a privacy violation is occurring and most people would not want it to happen to them. At the same time, discomfort has not stopped the behavior,” says Alexis Ingber, an assistant professor at Syracuse University whose research focuses on privacy and emerging tech. “Dating-profile dunking reflects a broader sense of entitlement to others’ data.”

But Franklin, who has a knack for speaking in clip-ready one-liners, doesn’t believe dating apps have a duty to protect users from becoming a punch line on social media. “If you enter the dragon’s den, you may get bit by the dragon,” he tells me.

Still, with 20 clients on his roster, he says he does his best to block “every name, lip, face, and eye, trying to keep people private” when posting screenshots, because he understands that people are “scared of getting hit-pieced.” Before ending our Zoom call to meet with another client, he tells me there is actually one way to completely sidestep the problem. “If you don’t want to be potentially doxed, just don’t get on a dating app. Go talk to a girl at a dog park. Go to a farmer's market. Do it the old-fashioned way.”

MACBOOKS HAVE TAKEN most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.

But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.

Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.

Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.

The Mac Mini isn't the ultra-cheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.

The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.

I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.

Shipping times on the M6 Mac Mini have improved to the point where you can buy one and pick it up today from an Apple Store. The M5 Pro models, however, may take up to four weeks to ship.

Like with the Mac Mini, there are really two distinct versions of the Mac Studio. The base configuration comes with an M5 Max (the same chip in the MacBook Pro), sporting some really impressive GPU performance in particular. And that's the main thing to consider when deciding between the M5 Pro Mac Mini and the M5 Max Mac Studio. Like choosing between those two chips in a MacBook Pro, the main upgrade is in graphics performance. Going with the M5 Max also lets you configure it with up to 128 GB of unified memory, which matters if you plan to run heavy local AI models. On the other hand, this puts you over the $5,000 price point rather quickly.

And then, there's the M5 Ultra. This massive chip is literally two M5 Max dies stitched together, and to my surprise while testing, it sometimes resulted in double the performance, such as in GPU performance. But look, don't even bother considering this unless you know exactly what you intend to use it for. Just so you know what you're getting into, the model I tested had 256 GB of memory and cost over $11,000. You read that right. It's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk.

But I downloaded and started running on the M5 Ultra some of the largest and most powerful AI models I could find, and soon enough I had a foundation-tier LLM running completely on-device—no cloud needed. That means direct access to your computer for a powerful agentic AI to run wild with, all without the privacy and security concerns. Some simple agentic tests I ran on the M5 Ultra took minutes, whereas it took five times as long on my M5 Max MacBook Pro.

Size comparison between the Mac Mini (top) and Mac Studio (bottom).

And while this thing is clearly not intended for gaming, I was pretty blown away by how fast games like Cyberpunk 2077 ran. I've definitely never seen games play this smoothly on a Mac before.

Unfortunately, shipping times on the Mac Studio are still dicey. If you want anything with 128 GB or more of memory, you'll be waiting up to a month and a half for the M5 Max models. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, will take up to four months to ship at this point.

The iMac has been downplayed in recent years. The once-iconic all-in-one computer, which comes with the display, stand, and accessories, used to be an affordable go-to choice for students, families, businesses, and even content creators. But as Apple has shifted focus, the iMac seems less and less of a focus, with sporadic updates over the years. It hasn't been updated since 2024 and still uses the M4 chip.

It's not a bad computer, though. The screen is brilliant, and the performance is solid, even by today's standards. Its age, however, isn't reflected in the price you'd pay right now: $1,499 gets you 16 GB of RAM, 256 GB of storage, the M4 chip with an eight-core GPU, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a 4.5K IPS display. A second M4 model with a 10-core GPU and four Thunderbolt 4 ports starts at $1,699. (Like nearly all Apple products, the iMac got a price increase.)

The main issue for me is that there's currently only a 23.5-inch model, which is smaller than what most people will probably want. Until Apple releases a 27-inch model (as it has in the past), perhaps with an option for a “Pro” M-series chip, I can't see the iMac as a good choice for most people. The simplicity will be a draw, especially if researching and buying a separate monitor and peripherals sounds daunting.

Interestingly, it is also the only desktop-size Mac monitor that isn't at least 5K (it's 4.5K). So, while it's cheaper than buying a Studio Display paired with a new Mac Mini, the iMac also locks you into a one-time purchase you can't upgrade later. And as the focus on local AI only grows, I can't imagine the iMac regaining the relevance or attention it once had. On the plus side, it's the only Mac desktop available in seven colors.

At the very least, I hope it gets a refresh to the M6 in the next couple of months. It'll have been long overdue! Either way, now's not a good time to buy an iMac.

Why Is Everyone Buying a Mac Mini?

Before the launch of the M6 model, Mac Minis had been sold out for most of this year. Orders for Mac Studios were similarly backlogged for months before you could get one. The reason? Well, according to Apple on an earnings call, both computers are “amazing platforms for AI and agentic tools,” and that “customer adoption of that is happening faster than we expected.” In other words, they were caught off guard. AI frameworks released in 2026, such as OpenClaw, run best on a dedicated machine that never turns off and has lots of available RAM—such as a Mac Mini.

What Happened to the Mac Pro?

The last incarnation of the Mac Pro was one of Apple's most short-lived Macs. The most recent design was relaunched in 2019, alongside the Pro Display XDR. When it was unveiled, it was an exciting re-entrance for the Mac, focusing not only on Pro-level performance but also on upgradability. Unlike the current Mac Studio, the Mac Pro had modular components you could swap in and out—or upgrade. The design was much more akin to a traditional tower PC. For a company that had been moving in the opposite direction for so long, it was a breath of fresh air.

But it wasn't meant to last, and it survived only a few upgrade cycles. With the advent of Apple silicon and the rapid scaling of these system-on-a-chip (SoC) designs, the Mac Pro's focus on modularity made less and less sense. Apple didn't officially discontinue the Mac Pro until March 2026, but by then it had been almost three years since the Mac Pro was last updated. The Mac Studio with the “Ultra” chips has since fully replaced the Mac Pro.

M6, M5 Pro, M5 Max, or M5 Ultra?

Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio have two configurations to choose from, which gives a clean delineation between the two in terms of performance. When you move from the base chip to the Pro and Max chips, the main differences are GPU cores and, in some cases, the maximum amount of RAM you can upgrade to. Certain applications and tasks benefit greatly from stronger GPU performance, speeding up things like video rendering, 3D modeling, gaming, and AI inferencing. These are the same chips that are available in the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.

The jump between the Max and Ultra chips, however, is much more significant. This is where you enter performance territory not possible on a MacBook. It has twice the CPU and GPU cores of the standard Max chips, delivers far stronger performance, and lets you configure it with up to 512 GB of unified memory.

The iMac is still holding onto the M4. For most people, the chip is more than capable, but considering the age and the price of the iMac today, it's outdated for a new machine.

Here's a list of the different Apple silicon available for the Mac Mini, Mac Studio, and iMac.

MacOS famously doesn't scale well with 4K resolutions, which is what makes the BenQ MA270S such a great option for the Mac Mini or Mac Studio. It costs $600 less than the Apple Studio Display, and while it lacks features like a built-in webcam or excellent speakers, the BenQ MA270S delivers image quality and compatibility where it counts.

Most people won't fully utilize the Studio Display XDR's capabilities. But it really does achieve levels of HDR that no consumer monitor has ever attempted. Thanks to its startling number of local dimming zones (2,304, to be exact), the Studio Display XDR delivers professional-level HDR that's on another level—even compared with all the OLED monitors out there.

The Mac Mini has decent port selection, but it's missing two obvious ones: USB-A and an SD card slot. This accessory adds these ports, forward-facing as if they are part of the Mac Mini. It's a genius stand—perfect for photographers and videographers.

Here's one product that no one makes quite like Apple. While many people prefer a mouse, I always miss the MacBook's Magic Trackpad. If you use macOS gestures as much as I do, you'll get why.

I don't mind the standard Apple Magic Keyboard, but if you want a more tactile typing experience, I recommend this Keychron keyboard. Its classy look and use of wood contrast nicely in an all-metal Apple ecosystem, and the typing experience is second to none.

The Logitech MX Master 4 has the perfect combination of ergonomic comfort and precision. The thumb rest offers far more support than the laughably bad Magic Mouse, and the scroll wheel and extra buttons make you feel much more productive.
