Digger joins the ranks of these unsubtle, borderline noxious films; it features fiery accidents, signs of planetary collapse, bumbling bureaucrats, casual sexism, decaying pet animals, and bouts of senseless violence. But it also stars Tom Cruise in one of his weirdest roles ever, which is truly a delight to watch.

Digger revolves around a morally unsound man named Digger Rockwell, an oil tycoon (played by Cruise) who ignores warnings from climate scientists that he should stop drilling in the Arctic. A crack has formed in the ice sheet and is leaking methane into the atmosphere — and it’s only likely to get bigger, they say, posing a massive threat to life and property. When their warnings come to pass and an explosion at Rockwell’s oil operation in Greenland triggers a monstrous ice shelf to break off and drift toward Europe, Rockwell and the president of the United States (played by a ghoulish John Goodman), who helped facilitate the drilling, start to panic. These cartoonish men are, clearly, avatars for the real-life architects of the climate crisis: the companies that knew what they were doing, and the powerful governments that delayed meaningful action to correct such oversights.

Iñárritu takes pleasure in portraying them as howling windbags, targets of both ire from Ganesh, the film’s noble climate scientist played by Riz Ahmed, and of laughter from the audience. The way Rockwell and President Compson stumble through their hubris is often funny, but the laughs are closely followed by discomfort. Uncanny shots of trees falling in the background (only to be propped back up again?) begin to disorient the viewer. You think you’re watching a satire about the bad guys who started this mess, and then a crack in the movie’s narrative world appears.

At its heart, Digger presents the problem we have with climate change as one of narrative: What is the story about how things went wrong, and who gets to tell it? Its answers might get Iñárritu called a doomer, but I found the way he intellectualizes our current predicament too compelling to look away from. (Spoilers start here!)

Iñárritu pulls back a curtain, and reveals that Cruise is not actually Digger Rockwell; he’s an actor named Curtis Markson, and he’s playing Rockwell in a stage play. More specifically, Markson is an actor struggling to understand his character’s internal motivations. Here is where Cruise really shines: not as a laughable villain, but as a tortured artist trying to tell the story of the greatest crisis of our time. Goodman and Ahmed are, likewise, actors in supporting roles in this play-within-a-movie.

As the movie goes on and more details of the theatric production are slowly revealed, this structure offers up more complicating questions for the viewer. Why stage a play about climate change in the first place? Isn’t it bad enough to have to live through global warming without figuring out what to say about it? These questions are aimed at Iñárritu as much as they are at Hannah, the “hip” theatre director (played by the wonderful Sophie Wilde) tussling with a pedantic Markson. These two cannot agree on the nature of what they’re doing onstage. Is the story of climate change a farcical comedy or a devastating tragedy? What would be the point of telling it either way?

The answers offered by Digger will certainly alienate some audiences. During tech rehearsal, Hannah explodes at Markson, saying the purpose of art is to comfort the dispossessed, especially those whose families were lost or displaced by climate change. The point, she argues, is to laugh at Markson as Rockwell, and the sooner he gets onboard, the better. At this point, the viewer learns that an iceberg really did take untold lives throughout Europe, and the play is a cult classic detailing how the Rockwell family attempted to profit off of disaster.

Exactly why and how the play is being staged 25 years after these horrific events is a juicy twist I won’t share here. Suffice to say, Digger is concerned with legacy, and Iñárritu, the first and only Mexican filmmaker to have won the Academy Award for Best Picture twice, clearly is too. “The movie is not perfect,” he told the New York Times in a recent interview. He did it anyway because, as he put it, “I like taking risks.” Digger feels like the director’s latest bid to cement himself as an auteur, and it also feels like a vehicle for a potentially unpopular idea. Maybe art can’t change the world and maybe we shouldn’t expect it to — at least not when a tsunami is approaching.

https://www.carbonbrief.org/factcheck-uk.title: Factcheck: UK Conservatives double the ‘cost of net-zero’ after spreadsheet blunder
https://www.carbonbrief.org/factcheck-uk.author: Simon Evans
https://www.carbonbrief.org/factcheck-uk.text:
A booklet published by the UK’s opposition Conservative party includes a “cost of net-zero” that appears to have been doubled by a spreadsheet error.

The “common sense” policy document argues that “what people ultimately want is a government competent enough to solve the problems for which it takes responsibility”.

In a section that says “sophisticat[ed]…modelling” should not be a substitute for “political judgement”, the “Right Way” document disparages various estimates of the cost of net-zero.

The Conservative document then claims – incorrectly – that the government’s official adviser, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), had put the cost of net-zero at close to £1tn. It says:

“In 2020, the CCC estimated that its route to net-zero would cost £957bn.”

In fact, the CCC’s 2020 estimate was exactly half this amount – £478bn – and last year it published a revised figure of £108bn, largely as a result of the falling cost of electric vehicles (EVs).

The Conservative party’s erroneous claim appears to stem from another report that had accidentally added up numbers twice, using a spreadsheet published by the CCC in 2020.

The 2020 spreadsheet contains a table listing the additional investments that would be needed to build a net-zero economy, from low-carbon electricity generation through to heat pumps and EVs.

These extra capital expenditures, listed as “CAPEX”, add up to a total of £1.38tn over the 30 years of 2020-50. They are set against operational savings, listed as “OPEX”, of £0.90tn.

Added up over 2020-50, the combined CAPEX and OPEX figures come to a total of £478bn.

In addition to the annual sectoral CAPEX and OPEX figures, the CCC’s 2020 spreadsheet also has a line giving combined totals for each year. It appears that someone has added all of these numbers together, resulting in the savings and costs being counted twice.

This double-counted total for the cost of net-zero amounts to £957bn – as shown in the image below – and it appears to be the source of the claim in the Conservative booklet.

At the time of publication in 2020, the CCC said that the £478bn net cost of net-zero amounted to less than 1% of GDP over 30 years – and that the large investment needed would not only result in savings due to lower fossil-fuel imports, but that it would boost GDP overall, by around 2%.

In 2025, the CCC revised its estimates for investment costs and operating savings to £670bn and £562bn respectively, giving a net total of £108bn over 2025-50, or less than 0.2% of GDP.

Earlier this year, the committee said that cutting emissions to net-zero would cost less than a single fossil-fuel price shock and that doing so would have benefits worth £110bn per year.

The erroneous claim in the Conservative document is referenced to the CCC’s 2020 advice on the UK’s sixth “carbon budget”, which, as explained, does not contain the £957bn figure.

The earliest online use of the £957bn figure found by Carbon Brief is a 12 January 2026 article in the Spectator, by retired engineer and self-described “accidental energy analyst” David Turver.

A day later, Turver repeated the mistaken number in a report for the free-market Institute of Economic Affairs. His report cites figure 5.3 of the CCC’s 2020 advice.

However, as set out above, the CCC spreadsheet containing the data for figure 5.3 only adds up to £478bn, half the figure claimed by Turver.

It appears that Turver accidentally added up all of the numbers in the CCC spreadsheet, without noting that it already included a line for the annual total. This results in double-counting the cost.

(Turver’s report also triggered a slew of inaccurate headlines stating that net-zero would cost £7.6tn – or even £9tn. These figures, which came from Turver’s report, were based, among other things, on the implicit assumption that fossil fuels and the cars, boilers and power plants that use them are all free.)

After Turver’s report and article in January 2026, the erroneous £957bn figure was repeated in March by the Great British Think Tank. The organisation has the tagline “data, not vibes” and says of its work: “Every figure [is] sourced from official public bodies.”

The £957bn figure then appeared in the Conservative “Right Way” document in October 2026.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Brazil’s far right sweeps general elections, the Organization of American States ups the pressure on Nicaragua, and K-pop group BTS lands in South America.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Brazil’s far right sweeps general elections, the Organization of American States ups the pressure on Nicaragua, and K-pop group BTS lands in South America.

Sign up to receive Latin America Brief in your inbox every Friday.

Brazil’s general elections last Sunday unleashed a right-wing wave at the polls. Though most surveys projected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva narrowly leading in the first-round presidential race, right-wing Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro instead beat Lula by around 2 percentage points.

Bolsonaro and Lula are now headed to an Oct. 25 runoff, after knocking out 10 other candidates. Analysis by Felipe Nunes of pollster Quaest suggests that many Brazilians who initially intended to support less prominent right-wing candidates voted for Bolsonaro on Sunday, hoping to propel him to a first-round victory.

They almost succeeded: At one point early on Sunday night, it looked possible that Bolsonaro could win outright by earning at least 50 percent of valid votes.

By the time all votes were counted, Bolsonaro had earned 47.03 percent to Lula’s 45.16 percent. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won the most governorships in elections that were settled on Sunday—rather than also proceeding to a runoff—and grew its numbers in both houses of congress, maintaining its status as the largest party in each.

Though it is numerically possible for Lula to win the runoff, history stands against him. No presidential candidate since Brazil’s redemocratization in the 1980s has won a runoff election after losing in the first round. What’s more, the candidates who placed third, fourth, and fifth on Sunday were all right-wing, and many of their supporters will now likely back Bolsonaro.

Sunday’s results show that bolsonarismo is a movement “that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” Brazilian journalist Bernardo Mello Franco told the Guardian. The Liberal Party booted several center-right lawmakers out of office Sunday, furthering its takeover of the Brazilian right.

Offering another hypothesis for the results, Lula himself said on Wednesday that his campaign “was the least organized I’ve participated in since 1989 and we reaped what we sowed.”

As the Lula camp soul-searched, they reached at least one consensus: Their messaging needed a reboot, both in style and in substance. Campaign leaders quickly summoned Millennial and Generation Z congresswomen-elect with large social media followings to Brasília to teach them how to make better selfie videos.

Ahead of first-round voting, Lula’s campaign leaned on his history as an organizer in the 1970s and 1980s, but he debuted a more future-oriented slogan on Wednesday: “For working people, protection; for criminals, jail.” This new, tough-on-crime motto is an implicit acknowledgement that the right has dominated messaging around insecurity, even as Lula’s government has made some progress on the issue.

Nevertheless, Sunday’s results reveal deep voter rejection of Lula, even among groups that he purports to favor in his policies. Demographic data shows he performed worse on Sunday among lower-middle-class Brazilians than among the richest. (He won among the poorest.)

Brazil’s lower middle class includes many people who live on the outskirts of big cities, who are evangelical, and who work gig jobs such as driving for Uber and making motorcycle deliveries. In 2024, Felipe Krause wrote in Foreign Policy that Lula did not understand this growing lower middle class, even though he helped create it with anti-poverty policies during his previous tenure as president.

Krause pointed to the fact that in 2024, Lula was pushing a law to regulate gig work that some gig workers opposed because they feared it would decrease their income.

“The problem is that [Lula’s Workers’ Party]—and its associated unions—are unable to see these workers as anything other than exploited labor, even though they prize their autonomy,” Krause wrote, arguing that the lower middle class was looking for less red tape, more protection from violence, and respect for their religious beliefs.

Now, Lula has thrown his energy behind legislative efforts to outlaw standard work contracts that allow six-day workweeks. It’s a policy that some 70 percent of Brazilians support—but it doesn’t cover gig workers.

Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has continued to base his messaging around broad ideas of being pro-change, pro-business, and pro-security. His lack of details hasn’t turned off voters—so far. But both candidates will be under a closer microscope as the runoff approaches.

Monday, Oct. 12: The United Nations Security Council discusses Colombia.

Monday, Oct. 19: The Security Council discusses Haiti.

Sunday, Oct. 25: Brazilians vote in runoff presidential and gubernatorial elections.

Panama’s mining politics. In Panama, a giant copper mine that was shuttered after nationwide protests in 2023 moved closer to reopening last week after a government panel recommended conditions for doing so—with a catch. The panel called for a “reopen to close” plan that includes the phaseout of the plant’s activities with environmental monitoring.

Such a phaseout could reasonably take 25 years, analysts familiar with the panel’s report said. Environmental groups responded with skepticism to the plan but did not immediately stage protests, suggesting that it could be a viable way for Panama to reactivate a commercial asset that accounted for around 1.5 percent of global copper production prior to its closure.

The phaseout plan is designed for Panama’s government to recoup some of the lost revenue from the mine’s abrupt closure. It could put the country back on the global map of critical minerals suppliers. Although the government has studied how it might replace its mining revenue in the future, its energy transition plans are vague.

Chileans disapprove of Kast. Chile joined U.S. President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas militaristic, anti-crime initiative in September. Far-right President José Antonio Kast, who took office in March, made the decision—but polls show that many Chileans don’t agree with it. A survey conducted last week found that among Chileans familiar with the measure, 47 percent reject it, while 31 percent support it.

The numbers come amid high overall discontent with Kast. Only seven months into his term, he has a 60 percent disapproval rate, according to the same poll. High fuel prices triggered by the Iran war have worsened the pain of his cuts to public spending for households.

Amid the dissatisfaction with Kast, former left-wing Presidents Gabriel Boric and Michelle Bachelet are trying to reassert themselves in Chile’s political arena. They released a joint declaration last month criticizing Kast’s decision to join Shield of the Americas, saying that it was in Chile’s best interests not to pick a side in great-power competition.

Though Bachelet withdrew from the U.N. secretary-general race a few weeks ago, her latest moves suggest she is not bowing out of politics.

Fans of the K-pop group BTS pose for a photo ahead of a concert in Bogotá on Oct. 2. ANDREA ARIZA/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

BTS in Bogotá. A global cultural phenomenon has landed in South America. K-pop band BTS is visiting the region, and their itinerary is extensive. Their tour underscores the rise of Korean music in a neighborhood that has traditionally looked to the United States or Europe for its overseas cultural references.

The current BTS tour is visiting more Latin American countries and cities than Taylor Swift’s 2023-24 Eras Tour, one of the largest global concert runs in history. After a handful of shows in Mexico City in May, BTS landed back in the region last week, playing in Bogotá’s largest soccer stadium.

The concert in Colombia is part of a 14-show run that also takes BTS to Peru, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil—some of the countries that most streamed the band’s new album and most watched BTS-related videos on YouTube after its release in March, Yonhap reported.

Latin American fans are also remixing K-pop culture to intertwine with their own musical and political habits. In Peru, artist Lenin Tamayo—who sings in the Indigenous Quechua language—has created crossover songs in a genre that he dubs “Q-pop.”

K-pop fans have encouraged one another to attend political demonstrations in multiple Latin American countries in recent years; they called for participation in Brazil’s 2024 municipal elections, for example. It should come as no surprise that struggling Lula supporters have embraced the help of “K-pop warriors” to campaign for him online in recent days.

BTS played its first South American concert in Bogotá’s El Campín Stadium. That’s the home of which soccer club?

Independiente Santa Fe

The club shares the stadium with their rival, Millonarios.

The Organization of American States headquarters in Washington on Sept. 22, 2023. DANIEL SLIM/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

Last Friday, the Organization of American States (OAS) held a rare foreign ministers’ meeting to discuss how to respond to autocracy in Nicaragua. Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega’s July declaration that there would be no more elections in the country in part triggered the meeting.

At the meeting, OAS countries unanimously announced eight things they wanted to see change in Nicaragua, from releasing political prisoners to moving toward elections. They pledged to seek dialogue with the Ortega regime and, if nothing changes, to reconvene in up to 120 days to consider applying unspecified punitive measures (excluding military force).

The punishments could include economic penalties, Inter-American Dialogue political scientist and longtime Nicaragua observer Manuel Orozco told Confidencial. Last Friday’s move amounted to an escalation by the OAS and not “more of the same” verbal condemnations, he said.

What was especially striking was that the Trump administration seemed to be on board with a collective regional approach toward Nicaragua—unlike the unilateral moves it has made toward other left-wing autocracies in Cuba and Venezuela. The United States captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January; he faces U.S. criminal charges in New York that have now grown to include torture.

Nicaragua, however, does not loom as large as Cuba in U.S. domestic politics, nor does it hold major oil reserves like Venezuela.

“There is a pro-Trump majority today at the OAS, so letting the organization deal with the Nicaragua issue doesn’t take much political investment and can even free up [U.S. Secretary of State Marco] Rubio to deal with other things,” said a senior OAS official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive subject.

The OAS move sparked some optimism among Nicaragua’s exiled opposition. Several OAS delegations asked members of that group if they would be open to returning to the country if there were a pressure campaign to allow it, U.S.-based Nicaraguan democracy activist and professor Félix Maradiaga told Confidencial.

There is an opposition delegation “ready to enter the country the moment international pressure opens the doors” for them to be able to work there, Maradiaga said.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.title: Trump Is Gutting America’s Core Geopolitical Advantage
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.author: Robert B. Zoellick
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-st.text:
ROBERT B. ZOELLICK served as U.S. Trade Representative from 2001 to 2005, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State from 2005 to 2006, and President of the World Bank from 2007 to 2012. He is the author of the forthcoming book The World Economy in Practice.

The Strategic Costs of Antagonizing Canada and Mexico

The Trump administration’s attack on Canada and Mexico is cracking the foundation of the United States’ global power. Friendly relations with neighbors enhance security, promote mutual economic gain, and make it easier to handle transnational challenges. Weak neighbors export trouble. Today, Canadians perceive U.S. President Donald Trump’s high tariffs and belittling of their country as the “51st state” as assaults on Canada’s economy and independence. In Mexico, Trump’s economic coercion and threats of military intervention have revived deep historical anxieties about gringo hegemony.

The North American partnership took generations to forge. During the nineteenth century, the United States’ foreign policy concentrated on its home continent, where it competed with France, Mexico, Russia, Spain, the United Kingdom, and indigenous peoples for dominance. As the United States became a global power in the twentieth century, U.S. strategists took North American relations for granted. Washington turned its attention to Europe, the Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East. Since the closing years of the Cold War, however, U.S. presidents have recognized the need to invest in North America. Ronald Reagan laid out the strategic rationale clearly when he launched his presidential campaign in 1979: “The key to our own future security may lie in both Canada and Mexico becoming much stronger than they are today,” he explained. “It is time we stopped treating our nearest neighbors as foreigners.”

Geopolitics begin with geography, and the United States’ geography gives it an enormous advantage over the world’s other major powers. China and Russia each have to manage relationships with 14 neighbors, many of which are unfriendly or carry resentments from histories of conflict. India must deal with six, including a nuclear-armed rival. All three powers’ access to the world’s seas depends on passage through maritime chokepoints. In contrast, the United States borders two benign neighbors and enjoys open sailing on two vast oceans. Close cooperation with Canada and Mexico enhances homeland security, attracts investment, promotes innovation, creates a huge market rich in resources and talent, and helps all three countries deal with criminal networks, illegal immigration, and threats to clean air, water, and wildlife.

A safe, resilient, and adaptive North America is the starting point of U.S. global strategy. Washington is best positioned to navigate an uncertain world when the United States, Canada, and Mexico present a common front. Yet Trump’s bullying is driving the United States’ natural partners away. The president is destroying a precious geopolitical asset: a strong continental base from which Washington projects power.

Our editors’ top picks, delivered free to your inbox every Friday.

* Note that when you provide your email address, the Foreign Affairs Privacy Policy and Terms of Use will apply to your newsletter subscription.

William Seward, who served as U.S. secretary of state from 1861 to 1869, first appreciated that good relations with the United States’ neighbors would boost the country’s global influence. He asserted that to have “control of this continent is to be . . . the controlling interest in the world.” When he was negotiating the U.S. purchase of Alaska in 1867, Seward observed that Alaska and the Aleutian Islands “extend[ed] a friendly hand to Asia.” He also tried to buy Greenland, Iceland, the Hawaiian Islands, and islands in the Caribbean, hoping that the purchases would help secure the United States’ oceanic approaches.

Seward recognized, however, that the United States could also boost its power by strengthening economic links, not just by adding territory. He abhorred European imperial conquests of foreign lands. He had also opposed the 1846–48 U.S. war with Mexico. At the end of the U.S. Civil War in 1865, Seward prevented Generals Ulysses Grant and Philip Sheridan from invading Mexico to depose the Habsburg archduke who the French had installed as emperor. He reasoned that an invasion would arouse Mexican hostility and that the Mexicans could depose the interloper themselves—which they did, in 1867.

Seward dealt diplomatically with the United States’ northern neighbor, too. In 1867, the British government united its North American colonies to form the Canadian Confederation, in part to deter Washington from invading Canada in retaliation for London’s assistance to the Confederacy during the Civil War. Seward responded by choosing the peaceful path of arbitration to resolve wartime claims against the United Kingdom.

Seward envisioned a North American union created through free choice, not coercion or conquest. He believed in the attractive power of the United States. Commerce, he maintained, would be the new “god of boundaries” that would redraw borders and pull countries together. Ernest Paolino, his biographer, termed this idea Seward’s “law of imperial gravity.”

The restoration of Mexican President Benito Juarez in 1867, the same year the Canadian Confederation was formed, offered the prospect of a democratic North America with closer economic ties. The neighbors did establish peaceful relations. But Seward’s vision faded in later decades as Americans focused their sights westward, paying less attention to their neighbors to the north and south.

By the early twentieth century, the United States had come to take continental harmony for granted. The Mexican Revolution of 1910 ended that sense of security. In the decade of violent conflicts that followed, attacks on border towns and seizures of American property by revolutionaries and bandits prompted the United States to send two military expeditions into Mexico. Washington narrowly avoided a quagmire. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson’s reelection campaign slogan in 1916, “He kept us out of war,” referred as much to Mexico as Europe. Still, the instability on its doorstep made the United States vulnerable. In 1917, imperial Germany sent the new Mexican government a secret proposal of alliance—a message intercepted by the British—that promised German assistance in recovering Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas if Mexico were to side with Germany in the event the United States entered World War I.

The United States was able to stabilize relations with the one-party authoritarian state that consolidated control in Mexico in the 1920s. As the political scientist Pamela Starr explained, Washington accepted its neighbor’s autonomy, but “within limits.” As long as Mexico did not threaten U.S. security, the United States would not interfere. Mexico’s stability was more important than challenging its stunted democracy, prickly nationalism, and closed economy. This arrangement lasted about 50 years, during which the two countries found ways to cooperate. Between 1942 and 1964, for instance, the United States’ Bracero Program offered some 4.6 million Mexicans guest worker permits, filling labor gaps in the agriculture, railroad, and other industries.

The twentieth century also saw Canada transition from British dominion to sovereign North American partner and ally. During the 1920s and 1930s, the United States and Canada built bridges and tunnels to boost economic exchanges. U.S. Secretary of State Cordell Hull negotiated important reciprocal trade agreements with Canada in 1935 and 1938. After World War II, Canadians fought beside Americans in the Korean War and vigorously supported the establishment of NATO, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the United Nations, and other institutions that made up the postwar order. During the 1950s, the United States and Canada constructed the St. Lawrence Seaway. The two countries also established a vast radar system to monitor possible missile attacks over the Arctic. In 1965, they signed a pact creating a duty-free integrated automobile market.

The pace of North American integration picked up during the Reagan administration. Reagan’s outreach to his Canadian counterpart, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, encouraged Mulroney to propose an expansive free trade agreement in 1985. Mulroney ran a big risk: Canadians were wary of becoming economically dependent on or dominated by the United States, but they also wanted rules to discipline U.S. trade practices and encourage investment. The two countries concluded the agreement in 1987, and the U.S. Congress approved it the following year. The 1988 Canadian elections effectively became a referendum on the trade deal—one that Mulroney won.

Carlos Salinas, who assumed the Mexican presidency that year, recognized that a similar agreement would open up his country’s economy and attract investment. Mexico was struggling with debt crises, declining energy revenues, and the related breakdown of the ruling party’s half-century-old corporatist model, which had fostered a centralized, closed economy. Looking to escape stagnation and to spur reform, Salinas took the bold step of proposing a free trade agreement to President George H. W. Bush in 1990.

Canada joined the negotiations in 1991, and together the three countries signed the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1992. For Washington, NAFTA was about much more than trade. It was a big step toward historical reconciliation with Mexico, which had remained wary of the United States since losing half its territory in the war ending in 1848. Mexico was now looking to the United States to help it accelerate an economic, social, and political transformation. Mexican negotiators hoped to import the rule of law through protections for investment, competition, and intellectual property. And reformers sought inspiration from U.S. and Canadian institutions as they built a multiparty democracy and a more open society.

Bush saw NAFTA as a cornerstone of U.S. post–Cold War strategy, explaining in 1992 that the agreement was “the beginning of a new era,” part of “a new world order” that would help let the United States “prepare for the challenges and opportunity of the next century.” His administration believed that the partnership could both deliver economic benefits and ease the way for continental cooperation on foreign policy, the environment, immigration, and drug smuggling. Unlike the European Union’s model of shared sovereignty, economic integration through NAFTA was supposed to respect national sensitivities about independence and sovereignty.

Bush’s successor, President Bill Clinton, faced the challenge of getting NAFTA approved by Congress, which Clinton accomplished with strong Republican support. Clinton deepened Washington’s commitment to the North American project, extending a large loan to Mexico during the 1995 peso crisis to prevent economic instability from spilling over into the United States. And after the 9/11 attacks, amid fears that terrorism would disrupt trade, President George W. Bush launched initiatives to ensure safe, fast transit for commercial vehicles across the Canadian and Mexican borders.

Opponents of NAFTA asserted that Americans would lose many jobs to Mexican workers willing to accept lower wages, but these concerns were not borne out. The agreement was an economic and a strategic success. In 2000, six years after NAFTA came into effect, U.S. unemployment dipped to 3.8 percent, its lowest level in decades. Inflation fell, productivity rose, and real wages grew, with notable gains for low-wage workers. The pact encouraged investment in railroads, pipelines, electricity grids, and border systems that made supply chains more efficient, especially in manufacturing. U.S.-Canadian trade in goods and services grew from $169 billion in 1988 to about $900 billion in 2024. U.S.-Mexican trade neared $1 trillion, up from less than $100 billion before NAFTA.

Cross-border investment has powered this growth. U.S. direct investment in Canada rose from $61 billion before NAFTA to about $750 billion, and Canada’s investment in the United States increased from $27 billion to about $500 billion. American direct investment in Mexico rose from $15 billion to around $130–150 billion, while Mexican enterprises’ investments in the United States jumped from $1 billion to $40–50 billion. The United States is the source of as much as 60 percent of Canada’s and roughly 40 percent of Mexico’s imports—so when their economies grow and their companies and households buy more, the U.S. economy gains, too. Growth in more distant economies does not boost U.S. sales as much. When China imports more, for example, the United States receives only six to seven cents of every additional dollar it spends.

NAFTA’s architects also hoped that the agreement would create economic opportunities within Mexico, enabling people to find jobs at home rather than moving north. Because of Mexico’s economic difficulties, the number of Mexican-born immigrants in the United States had risen from about 760,000 in 1970 to nine million in 2000. But by 2010, Mexican immigration had fallen to net zero; most people arriving at the southern border came from Central America and beyond, and Mexico became an essential partner in helping the United States enforce its immigration laws.

Trump wanted to scrap NAFTA during his first term, but by then it had become too valuable to abandon. His administration settled for a renegotiation, replacing NAFTA with the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement in 2020. The new accord modernized provisions for digital trade and added procedures for labor complaints, but its complex terms to protect regional auto producers undermined that sector’s global competitiveness. The agreement also reduced protections for foreign investors in Mexico, weakening confidence in the rule of law.

The accord does not expire until 2036, but the North American idea is already on life support. The Trump administration declined this year to approve an extension of the trade pact to 2042, and uncertainty about its future now discourages investment in Canada and Mexico. An even bigger problem is that the Trump administration wants the freedom to ignore the agreement whenever it wishes. In 2025 and 2026, it placed high tariffs on Canadian autos, steel, aluminum, iron, metal-intensive equipment, lumber, and pharmaceuticals, claiming that these imports were a threat to U.S. national security. Given that the United States has supported the integration of those sectors for 70 years and that Canada has been a close military partner for more than a century, it is no surprise that the designation shocked and insulted Canadians.

The weakening or even breakup of U.S. ties with Canada and Mexico would be a strategic disaster. The three countries’ combined assets make North America a formidable global player. The continent stretches from the Arctic almost to the tropics. The three democracies together are home to almost a half billion people, and unlike most economies, their populations are still growing. They have a skilled labor force and an integrated infrastructure that fosters highly competitive agriculture, mining, manufacturing, and services. North Americans also have access to cutting-edge technologies, abundant financial capital, energy self-sufficiency, and the capacity to expand their production of oil, gas, and renewables.

This is an enviable hand to play, not one that Trump should fold. Washington must stop antagonizing Ottawa and instead cooperate with its northern neighbor on Arctic and maritime security, mineral extraction and trade, and technological innovation. Canada’s artificial intelligence talent, research capabilities, and energy resources complement those of the United States, just as its resources and manufacturing did in the twentieth century.

Washington also needs to help Mexico realize its potential. NAFTA helped Mexico create world-class economic institutions and a freer society, but corruption still pervades its state and local governments, legal institutions, police forces, and schools. Many Mexicans are stuck working in the informal economy. Drug and other criminal enterprises have taken advantage of the government’s weaknesses. With U.S. intelligence and technological support, however, Mexico can improve security and the rule of law. Building stronger, more trustworthy institutions will boost growth and make the country a better partner.

From Seward to Reagan, the Bushes, and Clinton, U.S. leaders have recognized that a strong North America offers the United States a strategic anchor in an uncertain world. Trump’s need to dominate, his zero-sum approach to economics, and his transactional instincts cast him outside this circle of strategic leaders. But the next U.S. president will have an opportunity to change course. The United States needs to revive its powers of attraction and treat its neighbors with respect to restore and expand a constructive continental partnership.

https://www.foreignaffairs.com/iran/iran.title: Iran’s Theory of Victory
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/iran/iran.author: Narges Bajoghli, Vali Nasr
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/iran/iran.text:
NARGES BAJOGHLI is an anthropologist and Associate Professor of Middle East Studies at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies. She is the author of Iran Reframed: Anxieties of Power in the Islamic Republic.

VALI NASR is Majid Khadduri Professor of International Affairs and Middle East Studies at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies and the author of Iran’s Grand Strategy: A Political History.

Tehran’s Fight for Great-Power Status in the Post-American Middle East

Narges Bajoghli and Vali Nasr

When it comes to Iran, the Trump administration has a decidedly dismal record. It failed to wear down the Islamic Republic with months of intense bombings. It could not bend Iran’s will at the negotiating table. Yet despite seven months of setbacks, U.S. officials believe that they have turned the page. They have implemented fresh sanctions while maintaining the existing American blockade of the country’s southern coast, throttling its access to outside commerce. As a result, they have concluded that the Islamic Republic will soon either concede or be downed. “We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared on September 1.

There is no doubt that Washington has dealt significant damage to Iran. But the Islamic Republic does not believe it is unraveling. In fact, Tehran thinks that it will defeat the United States—and it isn’t hard to see why. The Iranian government did not merely survive the U.S.-Israeli bombardment. It retaliated ferociously, damaging American military bases and obstructing the Strait of Hormuz. Its people are paying a hefty economic price thanks to damage caused by the war and Washington’s cutoffs, but much of the population has rallied around the flag and seems to accept that hardship is necessary if Iran is to defend itself. As a result, Tehran has been emboldened. Its officials may not see eye to eye on each tactic. But they share the same ambitions: evicting U.S. forces from the Persian Gulf, forcing Washington to remove all its sanctions, and getting the United States to accept that Iran is a great power.

This agenda might sound overly audacious, given that Iran has been materially weakened. But the Islamic Republic thinks its aims are within reach. It believes its military can drive U.S. troops from the Persian Gulf by continuing to strike American bases directly and by getting Arab countries to push the United States to leave. It thinks that by wreaking havoc on energy markets, it can force Washington to lift economic restrictions, as well. Tehran’s theory of victory, in other words, is that it can hold out and inflict enough pain that the United States will end its containment of Iran.

No one doubts that Iran has been battered by war. Months of American and Israeli bombs have damaged the country’s industries and infrastructure, spiking unemployment and pushing more Iranians into poverty. Washington’s sanctions and naval blockade have caused rampant inflation. And the American and Israeli militaries can count many tactical successes, including the assassination of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

But strategically, the conflict has been disastrous. U.S. officials believed that punishing aerial bombardments and sweeping efforts to degrade the Iranian economy would bring the Islamic Republic to its knees. They didn’t. Washington hoped that assassinating Khamenei would prompt a mass antigovernment uprising. That scheme also failed. Instead, Khamenei’s death brought out the Islamic Republic’s ardent supporters. They marched every night in the country’s main cities and were eventually joined by Iranians of other political hues, who rallied in support of their homeland. When the war started, Turkey planned to accommodate 70,000 Iranian refugees. But few people fled. In fact, as the war progressed, many Iranians living abroad returned home, including long-exiled cultural figures, journalists, and politicians, such as the singers Mohsen Namjoo and Bijan Mortazavi.

This surge in nationalism is not an endorsement of the Islamic Republic. Many Iranians remain deeply unhappy with the country’s leadership. But the anger at their government has been subsumed by their anger at Washington. Previously, most Iranians were skeptical of the Islamic Republic’s claim that the United States was bent on their country’s destruction and in fact hoped Tehran would seek better relations with Washington. But the bombings of Iranian cities and U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to annihilate the country’s civilization (saying, for example, that he might “blow the entire nation up” and drive it “into hell with no chance of survival”) have changed attitudes. Iranians across the political spectrum now do think that the United States wants to obliterate their country—or at least make it capitulate to every American demand.

This conclusion was apparent in our lengthy conversations with Iranians of all ideologies, which we started conducting when Washington first bombed Iran, in June 2025, and have continued to the present, tracing their political attitudes over that period. The vast majority expressed deep distress and anger at their government after the massacres that took place in response to January’s mass protests. But we found that political opinions have shifted drastically as the war has dragged on and as Trump has upped his annihilatory rhetoric. “We believed so much in the American promise,” Ali, a 45-year-old long-time dissident who has spent years in prison for his activism on social and political issues, told us. “Yet with this war and everything that Trump and his administration have said and done, it’s obvious the Americans sold us a false bill of goods. They want nothing but Iran’s total submission, and that’s not acceptable to us.” Mahsa, a writer and artist in her 30s, relayed similar sentiments. “Everything we believed the [United States] stood for, freedom and respect and democracy, I now see as lies,” she said. “As angry as I’ve been at our state over the years, this is our homeland, and no outside country has the right to kill our leaders and drop bombs on our children and attempt to destroy us.”

Little wonder, then, that Khamenei’s July funeral procession drew millions of mourners, even though the country was in the midst of conflict. At the event, people handed out red flags, symbolizing their desire for bloody vengeance. Shortly after, Iran attacked commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz, unraveling the precarious cease-fire the country had struck with the United States three months earlier.

Many U.S. officials seem to think that stiff economic pressure will ultimately prompt a shift in opinion—that if they suffer enough, Iranians will decide to try overthrowing their government or that the Islamic Republic, fearing for its survival, will submit to American demands. But this is magical thinking. Iran has spent the past 15 years developing an economy specifically designed to withstand American economic warfare. Iranian officials, for instance, have forged strong relations with neighboring traders and made the country nearly self-sufficient when it comes to food. As a result, even though Iran’s economy is hurting and inflation is high, cities and towns have had no shortages of important goods or services to date. “It’s incredible how well-run everything has been inside of the country,” Hamid Reza, an engineer who regularly travels between Isfahan and Tehran for work, said. “Things are expensive, but there have been no shortages whatsoever across the country. Everything has been managed internally with a lot of care.”

That is not to say that Iranians feel optimistic about their country. They are anxious about the future, and they yearn for a return to calm and economic relief. But they do not see the U.S.-Israeli war as liberating. Instead, they see it as gratuitous aggression, and the resulting nationalism has blurred the lines between political factions and diminished the likelihood of another political uprising. The war, then, has strengthened the Islamic Republic.

Much like its population, the Iranian government has adopted a more hostile view of Washington since the conflict began. The country’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has moved trusted lieutenants to key roles (even as he himself remains in hiding), and they are largely hard-line figures tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. These people, including Mohsen Rezaei, the national security adviser, and Hossein Taeb, the commander of Iran’s main domestic paramilitary forces, think deterring further attacks requires a decisive, aggressive response to any provocations. They are skeptical that Washington is serious about diplomacy. They point out that the United States has twice attacked Iran amid negotiations and then walked away from the memorandum of understanding it signed with Iran in June—and thus argue that it cannot be trusted. In fact, they believe that if the United States shows interest in talks, it might even be planning for renewed attacks, as it was in June 2025 and February 2026.

Iran’s relative moderates feel somewhat differently. These elites, which include Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Speaker of Parliament Muhammad Bager Ghalibaf, former President Hasan Rouhani, and former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, have consistently argued that Tehran should keep looking for a diplomatic solution to the conflict. Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf have highlighted the economic hardships facing ordinary people. But the distance between them and the country’s hard-line leaders is not as great as it might seem. As one analyst familiar with these figures told us, “No one is saying Iran should surrender.” They may see economic relief as a top priority, yet their solution is to force the United States to implement the memorandum of understanding it signed in June. That deal, in Iran’s view, committed Washington to unfreezing all of Iran’s assets, lifting all sanctions, never striking the country again, and paying reparations in exchange for nothing more than a cease-fire and renewed commerce through the Strait of Hormuz (on which Iran could still charge fees). Since the end of summer, Rezaie and Ghalibaf have declared that diplomacy must start with the United States returning to the memorandum. As the same analyst told us after recent UN meetings in New York, these figures think that “Trump is not ready” for real talks. Instead, they believe that Trump will return to this deal only if he comes to terms with Iran’s victory, and that means increasing the war’s costs for the United States.

Iran’s behavior will therefore be unrestrained and disproportionate. If the war resumes, it will attack across the whole region, not just in the country’s immediate vicinity. The dominant view in Tehran is that prudence and predictability will only invite greater U.S. pressure and will do nothing to advance its main military goals: making Washington pull all its troops from the Persian Gulf and accept Iran’s primacy. Iran’s repeated attacks on American military bases and facilities in Jordan, Syria, and across the Persian Gulf are already aimed at this objective. To an extent, they have succeeded. The strikes have seriously damaged several U.S. assets, forcing the United States to move many of its operations and military resources to Israel and Jordan and rely on a base in the central Indian Ocean for logistical support. The threat of Iranian attacks has even pushed Washington to withdraw all its B-1 bombers from a base in the United Kingdom.

Tehran is simultaneously trying to get Washington’s Gulf partners to close U.S. military bases in their countries. To do so, it has openly declared that peace and security in the Persian Gulf will depend on pushing out the American military and has repeatedly bombed Gulf states it suspects of aiding the U.S. war effort. Iran is ultimately unlikely to end the United States’ military presence in the Gulf region. But it has done enough to make Arab states think twice about relying on the American security umbrella, which could mean a smaller U.S. military footprint in the region.

Iran, of course, could force the American military out of its neighborhood without obtaining economic relief. In fact, the Trump administration announced “economic D-Day” in part because the military was fatigued and because Iranian attacks on the U.S. Navy have forced Washington’s ships farther away from Iranian shores. But Iran believes it can coerce its adversary into some kind of economic understanding by causing sufficient financial suffering. To that end, Tehran has worked to drive up the price of oil, gas, diesel, jet fuel, and other oil derivatives by attacking several energy facilities in the Gulf region, including Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas field (in retaliation for an Israeli attack on Iran’s South Pars gas field) and oil facilities in the United Arab Emirates’ Fujairah port. Iran is also striking tankers ferrying oil and natural gas. And it is trying to consolidate its control over the Strait of Hormuz, which it sees as sovereign Iranian territory. Washington has fought back hard against this effort, and has recently succeeded at helping tankers pass through the chokepoint. But these operations have required enormous naval resources, and the United States cannot sustain them forever.

Iran’s regional partners are also lending it a hand. Iranian-backed Iraqi forces have attacked a vital oil pipeline carrying Saudi Arabia’s oil to facilities on the Red Sea, which will markedly reduce global oil supplies for months. Its Houthi allies in Yemen have also consistently attacked Saudi oil facilities. The Houthis have even captured vast new territory and reached the Bab el Mandeb Strait, helping them menace the Red Sea—through which 12 percent of world trade passes. These attacks also showed that, although Iran’s network may be battered in Lebanon and Syria, it remains quite capable overall.

The United States may think that it has cornered Iran. But Tehran disagrees. It does not see itself on its heels or as out of options. Instead, it believes that it has won great-power status. It is proud of its military performance and feels as if it commands newfound international respect. Officials in Tehran cheered images of Iran’s delegation being enthusiastically received by member states at the September meetings of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the non-Western BRICS consortium.

Iran is still facing monumental challenges, and it has not found a way to turn what it has won in the war into enduring, peacetime gains. But it is ready to fight on, if and when it needs to. The government believes, as one Iranian senior analyst close to the country’s policymakers put it, that the Iranian people “are willing to endure economic pain and the suffering, if it means that [they] are going to win.” And its elites have coalesced around a shared strategy. Tehran, in other words, is confident that it can prevail by staying the course. No compromises are necessary.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tru.title: No, the French army did not deploy tanks against protesting students
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tru.author: https://www.facebook.com/FRANCE24.English
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tru.text:
France's student protests continued on Thursday, blockading schools and marching through cities across the country against underfunding, poor school conditions and a lack of teachers. The demonstrations have been violent in places, with hundreds of students, law enforcement officers and teachers injured. The violence has triggered discourse surrounding some protesters' use of violence, as well as accusations of heavy-handed riot police, as rights groups accuse them of using excessive force against children.

But alongside the protests, a wave of misleading content has been circulating online, including claims that the French army has deployed armoured vehicles against students.

One TikTok video, viewed more than 2 million times, appears to show an armoured vehicle driving past a group of protesting high school students. Captioned: "They brought back the tank", the video prompted outrage among internet users who believed the army was being deployed to suppress the demonstrations.

Whilst the video is genuine, its context is misleading.

The FRANCE 24 Observers geolocated the footage to a car park opposite Bernard Palissy High School in Gien, central France. The location matches details visible in the video, including the school building, a dividing wall and a nearby house with several chimneys.

But if it's not linked to the student protests, why was a French army vehicle passing directly outside the school?

Around 500 metres from the school's campus are the barracks of the 12th Equipment Support Base, a military unit responsible for maintaining armoured vehicles for the French army. The vehicle in the video was travelling back to the nearby barracks. There is no evidence that it was deployed against the students or that its presence was connected to the demonstrations.

The French Ministry of the Armed Forces confirmed this to FRANCE 24, describing the journey as a "routine journey with no connection to current events at the school".

The misleading video is part of a broader wave of content circulating around the protests, including old footage, images taken out of context and AI-generated material.

One viral post, for example, claims to show protesters "seizing" the Paris Stock Exchange, describing the footage as the beginning of a "global revolution".

But the video predates the current student protests. It has been online since 2023 and shows protesters entering the offices of Euronext, the company that operates financial markets including the Paris Stock Exchange.

The footage was filmed during protests against the French government's decision to raise the retirement age and predates the current student demonstrations by several years.

AI-generated imagery has also been presented as authentic footage from the protests.

One Facebook post claimed to show a policewoman being chased and beaten during a high school blockade. The image attracted thousands of comments and likes.

However, the image was generated using OpenAI tools, with its digital watermark indicating that it was AI-generated.

As international aid to Africa dries up, what does it mean for women and children on the ground? https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/rep.title: India's dowry curse: Outlawed practice remains deeply entrenched
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/rep.author: Khansa JUNED
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/rep.text:
Dowry refers to the transfer of money, property, vehicles, jewellery or other valuables from a bride's family to the groom or his family as part of a marriage arrangement. The practice was outlawed under India's Dowry Prohibition Act in 1961, but demands for cash and goods continue to be made before and after weddings.

This transfer is specifically done from the bride's side. India has long dealt with deep-rooted gender bias, where being born a woman is often seen as a disadvantage. Despite a legal ban on prenatal sex determination, research shows that between 2000 and 2019, nearly 9 million female foetuses were aborted in India. The preference for sons stems from rooted social attitudes: men are viewed as future breadwinners, while women are seen as financial burdens whose primary role is to be married off. And in exchange for marrying the woman who is considered a burden, men and their families demand luxury items.

In some communities, dowry demands can function like a market, with families negotiating according to the groom's education, occupation and income. Government employees and men with secure, well-paid jobs can command particularly high demands. Even families that reject the word "dowry" may accept expensive gifts presented as voluntary offerings to the bride or groom.

These demands often do not end with the wedding. Many women face pressure to continue bringing additional money, property or luxury goods from their families. Those who cannot meet these demands may face harassment, physical violence, abandonment or, in the most extreme cases, death.

Dowry is also linked to India's enormous wedding economy. Indian weddings are estimated to generate around $130 billion a year, with families spending heavily on ceremonies, jewellery, clothing and gifts.

For many families, the societal pressure is immense. Some borrow money or sell assets to meet wedding expenses and dowry demands.

Official crime data recorded 35,493 dowry-linked deaths between 2017 and 2022. Police also register tens of thousands of cases each year involving cruelty and harassment linked to dowry demands. But activists and researchers say the true scale of the problem is difficult to measure because many cases go unreported.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Renoir paintings stolen from French Riviera museum recovered, six suspects arrested
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Two paintings by French master Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been recovered a month after they were stolen from a museum in southern France, the town's mayor said Friday.

In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionist painter, abandoning two others as they fled.

"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history," said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer.

"Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief."

There has not yet been any statement from the police and Masson did not give any details regarding where the works were found or their condition.

The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum's tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, Masson said at the time of the robbery in early September.

READ MORE
French police hunt Renoir thieves after lightning museum heist

The theft took place in just a matter of minutes, shortly before 6:00am (0400 GMT).

A source close to the probe told AFP earlier this week that police had arrested five people as part of the investigation.

According to Masson, the museum alarm and police sirens forced the burglars – which he described as "well equipped and well informed" about the museum – to hurry.

They made off with a portrait titled "Madame Colonna Romano" and the depiction of a woman at a well called "Jeune femme au puits", his office said.

The paintings dropped during their escape include "Madame Pichon" and "Coco lisant", a portrait of Renoir's young son Claude reading.

The police said at the time of the robbery that it was clear that they were not first-time offenders, and that they had scoped out the premises before the crime.

The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir's last home before he died aged 78 in 1919.

Its collection comprises nine paintings by Renoir, according to the museum.

It also includes several sculptures by him, as well as objects and furniture that belonged to the painter, such as his easel and wheelchair.

A spate of heists at French museums – including at the Louvre – has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.

WATCH MORE
The Louvre heist: Security flaws and deeper cracks at France’s top museum

Crown jewellery valued at around $100 million was stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris last year.

The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the jewels they are accused of grabbing in the seven-minute heist have still not been found.

Italian police in August said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth over $10.4 million that were stolen in a three-minute heist from a museum in March.

And earlier this week, a book featuring a cover made of bronze and designed by Spanish surrealist painter Salvador Dali was stolen from an art museum in central France.

The paintings were stolen from a museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer in September. The thieves broke into the museum and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionists.

https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.title: Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of provoking war as Tigray rebels retreat
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20261.text:
Ethiopia and Eritrea each accused the other of starting a war of aggression on Friday as an internal Ethiopian conflict threatened to escalate into a regional war.

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing rebels in its northern Tigray state, who launched attacks against federal forces last month.

The two countries severed diplomatic relations, and over the past week, Eritrean troops have been seen in northern Tigray with Ethiopia launching drone strikes against their forces.

A foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP they estimated 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in Tigray.

Eritrea's conduct is "a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos wrote in a letter to diplomats.

Eritrea's information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, responded on X that it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from Ethiopia.

WATCH MORE
Ethiopia and Eritrea break diplomatic ties over conflict

Over the past week, the Ethiopian army has pushed back the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and seized their capital city, Mekelle, with Ethiopian Airlines saying flights to the city would resume from October 11.

There are also signs that federal forces have pushed back the Eritrean troops with heavy drone strikes.

Witnesses told AFP on Friday that the rebels had lost two other cities in Tigray: Shire and Adigrat.

An aid worker in Shire said TPLF fighters and the local administration left on Wednesday.

"Looters are operating in the city, and four people were killed and 11 injured in an exchange of gunfire related to the looting," he said, adding that pro-government forces were yet to enter the city.

Eritrean forces were seen in Adigrat in recent days before being targeted by Ethiopian drone strikes, according to a conflict monitor and witnesses.

The rebels were retreating to Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, according to a Tigrayan official from a TPLF dissident faction.

Kjetil Tronvoll, regional specialist at Oslo New University College, told AFP that the TPLF was "withering", with low morale and frustration with their leaders.

"Many are defecting and going back to their villages," he said.

"I do not believe (Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed) will stop at the border," Tronvoll said.

Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab.

"The hysterical infatuation with the Red Sea must also be seen with previous intentions to wage a war of invasion against Eritrea," the Eritrean information minister said.

Authorities in both countries have not responded to AFP requests for comment.

Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and fought a brutal border war from 1998 to 2000.

Relations improved with the rise to power of Abiy in 2018 and Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia during the latter's 2020-2022 civil war against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

But relations deteriorated after the war, with Eritrea angry over the way it was concluded and fearing an Ethiopian invasion.

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.author: Dheepthika LAURENT
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/pre.text:
The Italian parliament approved an electoral reform on Thursday that's dividing the press along political lines. The reform will introduce a prize for the majority-winning alliance, awarding it bonus seats in both houses of parliament if it wins at least 42 percent of the national vote. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says this will reduce the post-election bargaining that often results in shaky governments. The centre-right paper Il Giornale hails this reform, which it says restores more power to Italian citizens via a preferential voting system and declares Italy's "Third Republic". The conservative daily Il Tempo's editorial attacks the "nervous left". There are two ways to examine electoral law, it says: the first is suited to career politicians and aspiring candidates, and involves "obsessing over technicalities and dissecting every clause." The other way tries to take the long view, giving the system a strong push towards a bipolar structure, which is what the Meloni government has done, it says approvingly.

The Italian left has struggled to build a united alliance ahead of next year's elections, and the left-wing press are furious about the reform. Centre-left daily La Repubblica calls it the "law of power" and in its editorial deplores the "ultimate betrayal." It says through a "political makeover worthy of a magician, Meloni forced her own majority to approve an electoral law that only she and her inner circle wanted". La Stampa says Meloni has changed the rules while Il Fatto Quotidiano says Italian President Sergio Mattarella can veto this "latest piece of garbage" – but wonders if he will do so.

French paper La Croix has an interesting article about Saudi Arabia. It looks at how the kingdom has poured money into state-of-the-art weaponry, but its army is badly lacking skills. La Croix's correspondent in Saudi Arabia reminds us that Yemen's Houthi rebels have launched several brazen attacks against the kingdom in recent weeks, including strikes on Saudi airports. How is it possible that Saudi Arabia spends billions on military equipment but cannot thwart attacks from a tenacious but underequipped rebel group, the paper asks. According to La Croix, there are several reasons: internal struggles between Saudi's national guard and regular army, both of which are affiliated with different powerful families. The central command is also very hierarchical and paralyses any initiative on the ground.

We turn next to the US where Nidal Malik Hasan, an army psychiatrist found guilty of a mass shooting in Fort Hood, Texas in 2009, will be executed by firing squad. As the Washington Post tells us, if it goes ahead, it would be the first such military execution since April 1961, when an army sergeant was hanged for rape and murder. On Thursday, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution will be public and livestreamed. Hegseth said he wants people to watch the execution, so they understand "there are serious consequences for these types of things". If this goes ahead, the US would be added to a notorious list of countries in the world that hold public executions. Last year, of the 17 public executions, six were in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.

We end with the biggest shakeup of internet addresses in more than a decade. ICANN is a US non-profit organisation that controls the application approvals for domain names. It has unveiled new trends in IP addresses. Applications for more than 1,600 new addresses have been made. ICANN last expanded web domains in 2012, the Times of London tells us. At the time, new domains like .app, .web, .babysitting and .pizza were approved. This time around, AI is a big drawcard. AI companies are seeking to grab domains like .superintelligence or .chatgpt, while Meta has applied for .wearables. There are many novelty ones too. Among some new domain name applications are ".fart", ".bro", ".maga" and ".trump" and ".god". A Belgian LGBT non-profit wants to own .meow, which it says will be for the community but also cat lovers!

You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: South Africa's Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to South Africa's Navi Pillay, the judge who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal and who last year presided over a UN commission which accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.

Pillay, currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in a case where Myanmar also stands accused of genocide, has been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.

Pillay headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which does not speak on behalf of the world body, and which last year found that genocide was occurring in Gaza.

READ MORE
Israel is committing 'genocide' in Gaza, UN investigators say

Pillay told AFP at the time that her team had shared "thousands of pieces of information" with prosecutors at the International Criminal Court.

The UN said the prize for Pillay was testimony to the "value" of rights.

But Israel on Friday slammed the announcement saying that awarding Pillay legitimised "anti-Israel hatred" and that Nazi propagandist Joseph Goebbels must be "applauding from hell".

The Nobel committee denied it was taking a stance on whether Israel is committing genocide in Gaza by honouring Pillay.

"It's her report, the Commission's report, and of course we have great faith in her professionalism, in her integrity, but that work is of a UN inquiry commission," Watne Frydnes told AFP adding that it was up to international courts to rule on the issue.

The Nobel jury said it was honouring Pillay at a time when "the system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack".

"At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity," Watnes said.

"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," the committee said.

The prize – the ultimate diplomatic and humanitarian accolade – is sure to irk US President Donald Trump, whose administration has repeatedly attacked international justice institutions.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," Pillay said to a standing ovation captured by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard in Nuremberg and posted on the social network X.

'If you clap a little more I may share this prize with Trump': Pillay reacts to Nobel Peace Prize win

Last year, the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who subsequently gave her Nobel gold medal to Trump.

READ MORE
Venezuela's opposition leader Machado presents Trump with her Nobel Prize at White House meeting

The prize comes with a gold medal, a diploma and a prize sum of $1.2 million.

The award will be presented at a formal ceremony in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of the prizes' creator, Swedish inventor and philanthropist Alfred Nobel.

The Peace Prize is the only Nobel awarded in Oslo, with the other disciplines announced in Stockholm.

On Thursday, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Canadian poet Anne Carson for her modern twists on Greek mythology and antiquity that have inspired new forms of writing.

The 2026 Nobel season winds up Monday with the economics prize.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/l.author: Mietta Adams
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

Luci, now features Fiona O'Byrne's daughter. (Supplied: Lester Prize)

Melbourne-based artist Fiona O'Byrne has won the $50,000 Richard Lester Prize for Portraiture for an oil-on-linen painting of her daughter.

O'Byrne has been painting her children for more than a decade and her winning work — titled Luci, now — depicts her 20-year-old daughter sitting on a stool with a neutral expression on her face.

"Sitting together, you really see time move, and you see how the relationship changes," O'Byrne wrote about the piece.

The Lester Prize is held at WA Museum Boola Bardip. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

"It's an opportunity for me to stop and spend time observing her in this moment of her life.

Judges Alan Dodge, John McDonald and Bryony Nainby said they were captivated by the softness and tenderness of the portrait conveyed through an "unlaboured handling of paint".

They highlighted the intimacy between the sitter and artist reflected through the apparent ease in the subject's expression, the way light was captured in the work, and the details of the jacket and nail varnish.

O'Byrne picked up a paintbrush for the first time at 36 and has spent the past 10 years dividing her time between painting and landscape architecture.

Perth-based artist Yasamin Khadembashi won the $10,000 Ashurst Emerging Artist Prize for her two-metre long re-imagined self portrait Immoral Warrior.

Yasamin Khadembashi's Immoral Warrior is inspired by Iranian folklore. (Supplied: Lester Prize)

The judges commended Khadembashi's bold and adventurous use of materials, including rhinestones, synthetic eyelash extensions and metal leaf.

"The artist did not play it safe, but their bravery paid off," the judges said.

Sky Parra's Portrait of Scott Austic, Sharon Billinge's painting titled Celeste 3, Kim Harding's Kim with Black Cockatoo and Dapeng Liu's Guido were also awarded prizes.

The Lester Prize is one of Australia's most lucrative portraiture prizes, with a total prize pool of $140,000.

It received more than 1,100 submissions this year, the most in the prize's history.

Founding partner of The Lester Prize, Russell Lester, said this reflected the impact the prize had on the arts community.

"Our ongoing stewardship of Australian talent and creativity is of utmost importance," Mr Lester said.

The exhibition of the 40 finalist pieces is on display at Perth's WA Museum Boola Bardip until November 29.

The Lester Prize had more than 1,100 submissions in 2026. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano by Renoir was stolen in September. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

Two Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in southern France last month have been found, and six people arrested, local authorities said on Friday.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the town that hosts the Renoir Museum, Bryan Masson, issued a statement praising investigators who tracked down the paintings and suspects.

"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history, our heritage," Mr Masson said.

Mayor Bryan Masson addressed the press outside Musée Renoir after the heist. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The statement did not elaborate on how the paintings were tracked down.

The two missing paintings were Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well.

Police officers patrolled the front entrance of the Musée Renoir after the early-morning heist. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The thieves sliced through a fence, climbed through a window and initially stole four valuable Renoir paintings in the heist last month, but abandoned two of the artworks as they fled, authorities said.

Thieves sliced through a fence, grabbed 9 million euros worth of art, dumped half of them in a garden and escaped in under three minutes.

The whole operation took less than 3 minutes and targeted the most valuable works in the Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the regional prosecutor’s office said.

Investigators launched a national search for the perpetrators.

The theft conjured up painful memories of the spectacular heist of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and revived calls for better security and better funding for the many cultural sites large and small that dot France’s landscape.
