Litchfield's quick fire 50 helped the Australians to a commanding victory in Brisbane. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Australia defeated Bangladesh by seven wickets to take a 1-0 lead in the ODI series in Brisbane.

Opening batter Phoebe Litchfield struck 77 from 57 deliveries as the hosts chased down their target of 167 in just 25.4 overs.

The series will continue on Sunday and then finish on Wednesday, with both the second and third ODIs also to be played at Allan Border Field.

A Phoebe Litchfield masterclass has ensured Australia remains undefeated in 22 ODIs at Allan Border Field after seamer Megan Schutt joined an elite club of bowling greats.

Opener Litchfield's 77 off 57 deliveries ensured Australia polished off the meagre 166 all out set by Bangladesh in just 25.4 overs for the loss of three wickets.

Litchfield combined ramps, glides, clips, exquisite drives, lofted pitching wedges, reverse hockey thumps and thunderous wallops in another knock that confirmed she is unique in world cricket and an absolute joy to watch.

The left-hander was unstoppable in racing to her 12th ODI half-century.

All-rounder Annabel Sutherland, player of the match, finished the chase with 26 not out after earlier taking four wickets.

Australia pace bowler Schutt earlier snared her 150th ODI wicket in a probing opening spell to put the hosts on top.

Stand-in captain Tahlia McGrath invited the visitors to have first use of the surface and Schutt struck with the first ball of the innings, a vicious lifter that had opener Fargana Hoque edging to slip.

A Schutt inswinger trapped Sarmin Sultana (four) in front and from that moment the bowlers kept a vice-like grip on the run rate and picked up steady wickets to dismiss Bangladesh with the fourth ball of the final over.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport?

Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The wicket of Sultana was the milestone 150th for Schutt. Only legendary speed demon Cathryn Fitzpatrick (180) and current all-rounder Ellyse Perry (166) have more wickets for Australia in the format.

Schutt finished with 2-19 from her 10 overs with medium pacer Sutherland (4-30) proving a handful when she hit the pitch hard.

Spinners Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham and Alana King bowled with class.

The visitors had several cameos but nothing substantial. No.3 Sharmin Akhter made a classy and breezy 24, captain Nigar Sultana (29 off 86 balls) was brave but stodgy.

Veteran all-rounder Ritu Moni (45 off 63) showcased her experience and nous and was the best of a mediocre bunch.

Schutt has relished playing at AB Field throughout her career, where she now has 20 wickets.

The quick was initially left out of the ODI side in February against India before a quad injury to Kim Garth opened the door for a recall.

Schutt took 5-19 at AB Field on that occasion to provide a timely reminder of her talents.

McGrath, usually a vice-captain, has been elevated to lead due to injury to regular skipper Sophie Molineux and rotated her bowlers with panache.

The opener of three ODIs at the same venue, Friday's clash is the first match of the summer on home soil for Australia's victorious T20 World Cup side since lifting the trophy in July.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.title: Couple jailed for torturing 14-week-old puppy to death
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.author: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Gabrielle Becerra Mellet

Topic:
Animal Cruelty

Isabel Busher and Nathan Dekkers were sentenced in Bunbury Magistrates Court. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Isabel Busher and Nathan Dekkers have been sentenced to jail terms for the torture of their bull terrier puppy, Douglas, in 2024.

The court heard that a neighbour recorded audio of the puppy being beaten and tormented on multiple occasions.

The pair have been prohibited from owning another animal and will be eligible for parole after serving half of their sentences.

A West Australian couple who fatally tortured a puppy have been jailed.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of animal abuse, which some readers may find distressing.

Nathan James Dekkers and Isabel Maree Busher, both 26, admitted to torturing the bull terrier, Douglas, in Busselton in late 2024.

Facing the Bunbury Magistrates Court on Friday for sentencing, Dekkers was handed an 11-month jail term, and Busher was jailed for eight months.

The pair have also been permanently banned from owning another animal.

Both Dekkers and Busher had previously pleaded guilty to more than a dozen animal cruelty charges, including beating and tormenting the puppy and lying to RSPCA investigators.

They were due to be sentenced in May, but that was adjourned for Busher to undergo more psychiatric assessment.

The court heard the pair purchased the eight-week-old bull terrier puppy from a breeder in November 2024.

A neighbour overheard the couple abusing the dog on multiple occasions between December 8 and 23 and recorded audio of the incidents, which they later handed over to authorities.

While the tapes were not played in court, they were said to have captured the puppy's terrified whimpers and yelps as he was beaten and taunted.

Busher and Dekkers tortured and killed 14-week-old puppy Douglas in 2024. (Supplied: RSPCA)

On one occasion, an audio recording captured Douglas being strangled, while Busher taunted the puppy by growling and yelling at him.

On December 23, the couple was observed by neighbours driving off in a vehicle, returning about an hour later, with Douglas never seen again.

RSPCA inspectors and police attended the property that day, where they observed a yard that was small and fully paved, with a build-up of dog faeces and dried blood on the pavement.

The court heard the pair at first told authorities they had taken the puppy to a family member's farm; however, the relative later denied the claim.

Busher's defence lawyer Michelle Huber submitted there was no planning that had gone into Douglas' harm, but acknowledged the poor behaviour.

RSPCA prosecutor Ruby Harris described the offending as callous and wicked.

"The conduct was unwarranted, sadistic and cruel," she said.

The pair were sentenced at the Bunbury Magistrates Court. (ABC South West: Gian De Poloni)

In his decision, Magistrate Stephen Butcher said that while Dekkers was the one to strangle and slap the dog on at least one occasion, both were equally culpable in their offending.

He said he took into account intense community backlash toward the pair, including harassment they faced while attending court.

He also acknowledged a psychiatric assessment of Busher; however, he said it did not explain her offending.

"Her psychological profile explains some of the circumstances that have arisen here, but it doesn't excuse it," he said.

Outside court, RSPCA inspector Genna Haines welcomed the decision.

Genna Haines spoke outside court in Bunbury. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Ms Haines said it was one of the worst cases of animal cruelty she had seen in her career.

"We're pleased with the sentencing; the court has recognised the level of cruelty here," she said.

"The pain and terror Douglas was experiencing throughout the seven recorded beatings is evident."

Busher and Dekkers will be eligible for parole after serving half their sentences.

The Perth Bears are set to be the first team from WA to join the NRL since 1997. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

Anthony De Ceglie, the inaugural chief executive of the Perth Bears, has decided to step down, the rugby league club announced today.

Mr De Ceglie, a former Seven West media executive, was appointed in May 2025 to help put the club together ahead of its entry into the NRL next year as the 18th team in the competition and the first from Western Australia since 1997.

"I'm extremely proud of what the hard-working Perth Bears team has achieved in the past year," Mr De Ceglie said in a statement.

"I have no doubt that the Perth Bears will continue to grow and grow, and become a behemoth of the national sporting stage."

Anthony De Ceglie held several senior roles at Seven West Media before joining the Bears. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

The Perth Bears have not said why Mr De Ceglie is leaving.

It had been reported that the board was seeking to have him replaced.

Mr De Ceglie's decision to leave the club comes after the departure of former head of football David Sharpe, who quit in April.

Club chair Ben Morton thanked Mr De Ceglie.

This weekend marks the final NRL game in Perth before the city has its own team in the big league and as the beginning of forever looms, rugby league in the west is ready for its close-up.

"I thank Anthony for his leadership of the Perth Bears in our startup phase and we will now turn our attention to the leadership of our organisation as we enter the next phase of our story," he said.

Perth Bears general manager of football Gareth Holmes will act as chief executive until a permanent appointment is made.

Mr De Ceglie was previously the director of news and current affairs at Seven West Media, a role he held after overseeing Western Australia's flagship newspaper.

Channel 7 holds the rights to the AFL, while rival Channel 9 has the rights to the NRL.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Judge Navi Pillay
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

Navanethem "Navi" Pillay reacts to being awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

The South African-born former UN human rights chief was recognised for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee described her as a source of hope for all those who seek a more peaceful world.

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay for significantly enlarging the scope and impact of international law.

The South African-born former UN human rights chief was recognised for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

Ms Pillay, 85, served as a judge at the International Criminal Court, the High Court of South Africa and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

She was the first non-white woman to serve on South Africa's High Court.

Navi Pillay visits the Nazi death camp at Auschwitz, Poland, during her tenure as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. (Reuters: Mateusz Skwarczes via Agencja Gazeta)

She was also chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that last year found that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous".

Her work "is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world," Mr Watne Frydnes said, announcing her win.

Navi Pillay is holding onto hope (and the rule of law).

When the committee first announced the recipient, it had not yet been able to reach Ms Pillay to inform her she had received the peace prize.

Ms Pillay later joked that she might "share the prize" with US President Donald Trump.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," Ms Pillay said while being applauded at an event in Nuremberg.

Navi Pillay on a visit to Sri Lanka when she was UN Human Rights Commissioner in 2013.  (Reuters: Dinuka Liyanawatte)

The award is often considered the most prestigious honour on the planet.

"At a time when the number of wars and conflicts is rising, and when judges and institutions of international law are under political attack, the Nobel Committee wishes to issue a reminder that the ability to resolve conflicts without force or violence is dependent on the international rule of law," the committee wrote in a news release.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo received nominations for 287 candidates for this year's prize.

Experts say the committee typically focuses on the durability of peace, the promotion of international fraternity and the quiet work of institutions that strengthen those goals.

Former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay has won the Nobel Peace Prize. (Fabrice Coffrini, Getty Images)

Chris Sidoti, a human rights lawyer who worked together with Ms Pillay on the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, described her as "a modest, unassuming lovely and very funny person".

"There has never been a Nobel Peace Prize recipient more deserving of it than Navi," he told the ABC.

"She's not running a political agenda. She never has.

"She is entirely focused on the law.

"And as an unassuming dedicated, highly committed but extraordinarily intelligent person, what she does has always carried weight, whether it's in the courts in South Africa, in the apartheid period, or as High Commissioner for Human Rights or in international criminal tribunals or as chair of our Commission of Inquiry on Palestine and Israel."

UN human rights chief Volker Turk described Ms Pillay's award as "a collective win for human rights and for all those seeking justice and accountability".

"It's clear that we need international criminal accountability mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court, and it's clear that we have a very strong signal that this is absolutely critical in today's world," he said.

Navi Pillay was a former UN Human Rights Commissioner. (Reuters: Ruben Sprich)

"At a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law, this recognition carries particular significance," said ICC President Tomoko Akane in a statement congratulating Ms Pillay.

The Hague-based ICC has been the target of an escalating campaign by US President Donald Trump, who last month urged countries to leave it.

Acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo Haakon Gjerloew said the committee was not directly criticising Mr Trump by rewarding Ms Pillay, a former judge on it.

"I think it's generally rather a promotion of an international legal world order. Of course, he might react to someone who has been part of the ICC, but it's not a direct attack on Trump," he said.

The Nobel Peace Prize, often considered the most prestigious award, was announced in Oslo, Norway. (AP: Angela Weiss/Pool Photo File)

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness".

Ms Machado gave Mr Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-president Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: the Nobel Committee has said the honour itself cannot be transferred.

Four of this year's Nobel prizes were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

The physics award recognised a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare type of neutrino.

The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling the mystery of mirror-image molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.718 million).

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/i.title: Person of interest given alibi in schoolgirl's disappearance
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/i.author: Bryn Wakefield
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/i.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Person of interest Noel Morris (left) leaves court with his legal team. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

A coronial inquest has heard that a person of interest in Marilyn Wallman's disappearance, Noel Morris, was seen working at a coalmine when she went missing on March 21, 1972, in Mackay.

Mr Morris's uncle, Barry Morris, said he remembered seeing Noel twice that day at the Goonyella coalmine, around 145 kilometres from where Marilyn disappeared.

The court heard that Noel's wife, Ann Morris, had given birth to their daughter, Jodie, five days prior and was staying in Mackay at the time.

A person of interest in the disappearance of schoolgirl Marilyn Wallman was seen working more than 100 kilometres away at a Queensland coalmine on the day she went missing, a court has heard.

The 14-year-old's bicycle was discovered by her brothers on March 21, 1972, after she left to catch a school bus in Mackay, north Queensland, at 7:42am.

A fragment of her skull was found two years later at McGregor Creek, about 40km from where she was last seen.

At the time, Marilyn's brother, Rex Wallman, recalled hearing a young girl's voice behind a cane field near the bike and then a man speaking.

During a coronial inquest this week in Mackay, the girl's relative Noel Morris — who has not yet appeared before the inquiry — was named as a person of interest in the investigation.

On Friday, Noel's uncle, Barry Morris, told the inquest that his nephew had been at work on that day 54 years ago.

Noel Morris was the husband of Marilyn Wallman's cousin, Ann Morris. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Barry told the court via video link that he remembered seeing Noel "hauling coal from the coal face" at Goonyella mine where they worked about 145km south-west of Mackay.

The 81-year-old said he also saw his nephew playing cards in a break room, though he did not speak to him.

"[There] was sort of no need for me to have any recollection on it, except that Noel told my wife, which she told me when I got home, that Marilyn had been missing," he said.

Barry Morris said he could not remember where Noel was on the days before and after March 21 and did not know anyone else alive who could have seen his nephew at work that day.

The court heard Noel had been "like a brother" to Barry, but in the years following Marilyn's disappearance there had been friction in the wider family group.

Barry said he recalled his brother, Lionel Morris, telling family members at a gathering, "Noel done it", referring to Marilyn's disappearance.

Questioned by counsel assisting the coroner, John Aberdeen, why he did not defend his nephew, Barry said: "I knew it was crap."

Witness Jenny Goode told the court she had known Lionel Morris, her uncle, to be a heavy drinker who "always exaggerated things".

Ms Goode said family often visited her house at Bucasia, including Noel and his wife, Ann Morris.

Leslie Goode and Jenny Good leaving Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The court heard Ms Morris had been staying at the home before and after she gave birth to her daughter, Jodie, on March 16, 1972 — five days before Marilyn Wallman went missing.

Ms Goode said she could not recall if Noel had visited them in Mackay that week.

"I know Ann definitely stayed with me, and I would assume that Noel would have come down from time to time," she said.

"He was still working out at Moranbah."

Mr Aberdeen read evidence on Friday from Noel's wife, Ann.

In the statement, Ann said she had been told by Noel's uncle, Robert Morris, known as "Squizzy", that he and his nephew had been drinking together at the Bucasia home the night before Marilyn disappeared.

"Squizzy also says that they drank on till the early hours of the morning," Mr Aberdeen said.

Ms Goode and her husband, Leslie, said that no party had taken place that night.

Mr Goode told the court they had "never" had a party there at that time of the morning, on a working day.

The inquest, which is to determine the cause of Marilyn Wallman's death and whether any person was involved, will continue on Monday.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.title: More than 65,000 Canberrans are waiting to see a medical specialist
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.author: Annabel Whitehouse
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Annabel Whitehouse

Canberran Billie Spencer says her granddaughter would have to wait more than three years for a publicly funded specialist appointment. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

About 65,000 Canberrans are on a waitlist to see a publicly funded specialist to find out if they need to join another waitlist for surgery.

The figure, publicly disclosed for the first time, means more than 10 per cent of Canberrans are currently waiting.

Canberra Health Services is undertaking a review of outpatient services and referral pathways to better understand demand.

Canberra grandmother Billie Spencer says her five-year-old granddaughter will have to wait more than three years for a publicly funded specialist appointment, joining thousands on an invisible waitlist ahead of another inevitable waitlist.

Ms Spencer said her granddaughter suffers from excessive fatigue and struggles to keep her eyes open at school and concentrate.

"She needs to be assessed by a specialist, and we've had to wait months," she said.

Billie Spencer says she is frustrated that the health system forces patients to choose between long waits for public care and costly but timely private care. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The family concluded they had no other choice but to choice private healthcare.

"I believe in quality healthcare access for everybody regardless of your financial status, and I feel it's so disgusting that this is where we're at," she said.

"[I can't] believe that children are having to wait, or parents, grandparents are having to pay huge amounts of money to have their health needs met.

Michael Hickey says he did not expect the wait time for a public specialist appointment to be so long. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Michael Hickey knows this story all too well.

He has already waited more than four years to see a specialist and was "gobsmacked" when he was told he would have to wait another two and a half years.

Mr Hickey has been living with a genetic hand condition which gradually leads to a loss of function if not treated.

He joined the public specialist waitlist expecting a fairly smooth process, but the reality did not align with his expectations.

Michael Hickey says a known public waiting list would ensure patients could make more informed decisions about whether to seek private care. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"There's nothing but an acknowledgement to say, 'Thank you, we've received your note, your call is important to us, we'll get back to you,' and then crickets," he said.

Mr Hickey said he did not think the wait time would be so long.

"Why aren't the figures made known up front? Why isn't there a known waiting list so I can decide to go private if I wished to," he asked.

Mr Hickey said his injury was not debilitating, but was frustrated that it made hobbies and everyday activities "just that little more difficult".

Michael Hickey says that without treatment for his genetic hand condition, engaging in his hobbies is made more difficult. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Mr Hickey and Ms Spencer's granddaughter are among about 65,000 people who are waiting for outpatient appointments across public hospitals in the ACT.

The figure, which Canberra Health Services (CHS) has disclosed publicly for the first time, means more than 10 per cent of Canberrans are currently waiting.

That is despite nearly 18,000 elective surgeries completed in Canberra last financial year, according to government data.

This week, CHS launched a review of specialist and outpatient services. The review follows an independent inquiry into the territory's health system, which proposed 49 recommendations.

CHS said its review will examine outpatient services and referral pathways to better understand demand.

Alison Derrett acknowledged that the current waitlist to see a specialist through the public system was "not acceptable". (ABC News: Mark Moore)

CHS chief operating officer Alison Derritt said demand for outpatient services had been growing with a "big number" of people waiting for appointments.

"We do know that this is a problem," she said.

"It is not an acceptable position for us to have people on a wait list for an extended period of time, and our clinicians take this very seriously, and I take this very seriously.

"It's going to be one of those things that is a constant challenge for us … this is not something that will be done in a couple of weeks.

"This will be something that will take us weeks, months, and possibly up to 12 months."

The health body said patients would be contacted in the next couple of months to assess their conditions and confirm whether they still required an appointment.

For people like Mr Hickey and Ms Spencer's granddaughter, the wait for an appointment could hardly feel longer.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.author: Olivana Lathouris
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The NT government has flagged reforms that would remove the requirement for accused sexual offenders' names to be suppressed until committal. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The Northern Territory government has flagged changes to laws that protect the identities of people charged with rape and other sexual offences before they are committed to trial in the Supreme Court.

The changes would bring the NT in line with the rest of the country, with advocates saying the reforms are "well and truly overdue".

The changes are expected to be introduced to NT parliament before the end of the year.

The Northern Territory could soon become the last jurisdiction in the country to allow accused rapists and child sex offenders to be publicly named before they are committed to stand trial, under reforms flagged by the NT government.

Under Territory law, the names of people charged with serious sexual offences, including rape and child sex crimes, cannot be made public until they are committed to the Supreme Court — a process that can take well over a year.

The NT is currently the only jurisdiction in Australia that maintains the anonymity of people charged with these crimes before the committal stage.

After Queensland passed new legislation, the Northern Territory is now the only jurisdiction in Australia where alleged sexual offenders cannot be publicly named until they are committed to stand trial.

But NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro this week flagged changes to the laws, saying the reforms would be introduced by the end of the year.

"We as a government have already been doing the work, and the attorney-general has been doing the work, to change the laws to lift these suppressions, these gag orders, on these horrendous types of offences, and we look forward to bringing that to the parliament," she said.

The announcement comes after the identity of a man who raped a four-year-old girl at a Darwin town camp was made public earlier this week, after being suppressed for almost a year.

Nathaniel Farrell pleaded guilty in the NT Supreme Court to one count of rape following the June 14 attack, during which he lured the child away while she was playing before violently digitally raping her.

A suppression order preventing the publication of Farrell's name was made in the Darwin Local Court last year and was extended after the 34-year-old was committed to the Supreme Court.

The order also included the suppression of the names of the victim and witnesses involved in the case.

Last week, Chief Justice Michael Grant lifted the order allowing Farrell's name to be published and sentenced him to 10 years in prison with a seven-year non-parole period.

Chief Justice Michael Grant lifted the supression order on Nathaniel Farrell's name. (ABC News: Tiffany Parker)

Ms Finocchiaro said the government had since urged the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) to investigate any possible avenues to appeal the sentence.

"We as a government will be looking into the sentence and whether or not there's an opportunity for them to appeal," she said.

The DPP would not confirm whether an appeal was under consideration.

"Any decision regarding an appeal is to be made independently by the Director of Public Prosecutions following consideration of the relevant legal and evidentiary issues," a DPP spokesperson said.

Lia Finocchiaro says her government will change the laws that temporarily protect the identity of sex offenders by the end of the year. (ABC News: Tilda Colling)

Sexual assault survivor and creator of the #LetHerSpeak campaign, Nina Funnell, who has advocated for the NT to change its laws for years, said the reforms were "well and truly overdue".

Ms Funnell said laws that protect the identities of accused sex offenders can have unintended consequences.

Nina Funnell is a sexual assault survivor who has long advocated for the NT to reform its laws. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

"Many survivors come forward in the first place to protect others in the community," she said.

"Justice done in the dark is not justice.

"If we want survivors to keep coming forward to protect the community, the least we can do is ensure their efforts to make us all safe aren't being thwarted by decisions which prioritise the feelings of offenders over the principle of open justice."

Communications law expert from Melbourne University, Jason Boslan, said the underlying justification for suppression orders protecting the identities of people charged with sexual offences was to offer defendants "a level of protection" while the court considered whether there was enough evidence to proceed to trial.

Mr Bosland said the publication of a person's name before committal had the potential to cause reputational damage, however he said that should be weighed against community expectations.

Jason Bosland says ultimately Australia's justice system is based on the principle of "open justice". (ABC News)

"It's really about meeting those community expectations around transparency," he said.

"Our whole justice system in Australia is based on this system of open justice — the idea that everyone should know what's going on in the courts.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Consumer Goods

Mundella yoghurt was established in Western Australia in 1974. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Emerging processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets of collapsed Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company.

The companies were put into liquidation in August, leaving creditors owed millions of dollars.

Yoghurt production is expected to start near Margaret River before the Christmas period.

A late rescue deal and sale is set to keep two landmark West Australian dairy brands on supermarket shelves.

Mundella Foods and the Margaret River Dairy Company went into liquidation in August, with creditors owed millions of dollars.

Local processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets, including processing facilities in Perth and Margaret River, for an undisclosed sum.

Mundella Foods' operations near Mundigjong will not be used for processing by the new owners. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Artisanal Market managing director Kevin Sorgiovanni founded another well-known WA dairy and juice brand, Harvey Fresh.

He said he had been interested in buying the companies back in 2023, when they were sold by Chinese-owned Manassen Foods to The Cheeky Cow, which has since collapsed.

"We saw the Mundella and Margaret River business as a great opportunity for the South West and also to add some value back to the WA dairy market."

Mr Sorgiovanni said both brands of yoghurt would be manufactured at the export-approved Metricup processing facility near Margaret River.

Artisanal Markets will mothball Mundella's original manufacturing facility at Mundijong, near Perth, because of its poor condition.

Artisanal Markets is jointly owned by PenAgri Group and Research Corporation.

Mr Sorgiovanni told the ABC the new ownership had plans to target the Asian market for broader sales.

There are hopes to export Mundella yoghurt to Asia. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

"We want to do more than just the WA market," he said.

Mr Sorgiovanni said production at the Metricup facility would start at 2 million litres a year, but it had the capacity for 10 million litres.

The revival is welcome news for dairy farmers across southern WA, but challenges remain.

WA Farmers Dairy Council president Ian Noakes said he was keen to see how Artisanal Market would secure milk supply.

Ian Noakes has welcomed the sale. (ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia)

"Most of the milk in WA is contracted, and the main companies are not very good at letting a bit of milk go to somebody else," he said.

"So it would be a matter of waiting probably until somebody comes out of contract to get a milk supply."

Mr Noakes hoped the additional competition would improve the price points for local dairy farmers.

Temba Bavuma likes what he sees from Simon Harmer as he tries to spin it away from Renshaw's outside edge, but Renshaw hits with the spin and takes a single through cover.

No major issues for Cummins either.

He's around the wicket to left-handed Renshaw and still finding enough seam movement away to draw a false stroke outside off.

After a couple of miscues, Renshaw whips away through the leg side, finding the gap between mid-wicket and mid-on. Temba Bavuma tracks it down before the rope, so it's just three, but very nicely played.

The cloud cover has arrived, the wind has whipped up and the artificial lights are starting to have an impact as Simon Harmer starts his 11th over.

A couple down leg almost yield results as Cummins nearly overbalances and falls out of his crease, but manages to keep his toe down in the end.

Top edged by Cummins on the sweep, and it sails over leg slip and out of reach for two runs. A lot of luck in that one, but credit the skipper for hitting towards where fielders aren't stationed, even if it took an unconventional route.

Four! Beautifully played by the Aussie skipper as Mulder strays too wide and Cummins opens the face and runs a ball past gully and to the rope.

He tries again, but makes better contact this time and hits it straight to point.

Both batters manage to work off their bodies and take a couple into the deep.

And Pat Cummins gets low to guide a ball down to third man.

Cummins drives to mid-off and takes a quick single to end the over. So he will have to face the seamer, but Mulder is a little more comfortable than Nortje or Jansen.

And Matt Renshaw continues as he left off, leaving wide ones and working off his body into the leg side.

Good application from the rangy number five.

Another disappointing session comes to an end for the Australians, who lost Steve Smith (25), Alex Carey (14) and Beau Webster (4) after lunch.

Anrich Nortje, on his return to the Test match arena, has been simply scintillating for the South Africans.

Pace, fire, accuracy — it has been far too much for the once-again feeble Australian middle order.

The tourists well and truly teetering as we head to tea.

A teaser from Harmer, flighted and wide, and Renshaw is leaving it alone.

Quicker from the offie and Renshaw works a single.

Cummins has three balls to survive.

Four! Short and wide and pretty rank, and Cummins lashes it to the fence.

The Australian captain sees out the final two balls of the set.

There'll be no late heartbreak for the Australians in this session.

Close! Cummins is pushing forward violently and the ball thuds off his bat, just evading the close-in fielder on the on-side. The batters run a single.

Reverse! Renshaw is down and reverse-sweeping Maharaj into the ground. The ball bounces up and it's stopped at head height by the slipper.

Renshaw tries the same shot and this time gets it squarer, with the batters running a single.

There's a slip either side of the wicketkeeper as Renshaw defends into the off-side.

A bit of width from Harmer has Renshaw pushing a single into the off-side.

Cummins has a man either side of his helmet, but is looking assured as he earns a single through cover.

Marco Jansen hasn't quite found his rhythm since returning to the attack, and he begins his latest set with a wide one outside off.

Renshaw is shouldering arms.

Straighter from Jansen and Renshaw is back and prodding it into the off-side. No run.

Four! Ooft, that's not great from Jansen. Something goes wrong in his release and Renshaw is presented with a loopy full toss. The Australian flicks it behind square for a boundary.

Renshaw works a single, Cummins defends, and that, my friends, is over.

The off spinner has a single slip and an off-side bat pad to work with.

Cummins is defending.

The clouds are beginning to roll in, and it has suddenly gotten a whole lot darker in Durban.

An on-side bat-pad comes in for the final ball of the over, which Cummins prods back towards Harmer.

The left-armer is coming from around the wicket and angling in to the right-handed Cummins.

Three slips and a gully in wait.

Cummins tries to cut a ball that was far too straight — the ball jams down off his under edge and the batters run a streaky single.

Renshaw advances and plays a cute flick back past the bowler for a single.

Cummins gets one on his ribs, swivels and works a run behind square.

Renshaw is shouldering arms to end the over.

Three good balls to start the over from Harmer.

Flighted and tempting, Renshaw is defending.

Slightly quicker from the offie and Renshaw is beaten. The ball spins past his edge and is through to the keeper.

A loose one to end the over — Renshaw works it off his pads and the batters do well to return for a couple.

The Australians breathe a sigh of relief as Nortje is given a spell.

It's the towering Marco Jansen back to the bowling crease.

Renshaw pushes a single into the off-side and Cummins returns the favour.

Renshaw gets one on the pads and flicks attractively, but his shot is well-stopped at mid wicket. No run.

Cummins works a single off his body and that's over.

This is a good spell from Harmer.

A bit of fire from one end and water from the other at the moment. Both destructive in their own way.

Play and miss! Harmer prises some turn and Renshaw can't get bat to ball outside off.

Quick single! And Cummins dives into his crease as Bavuma arrows his throw in. The Australian captain is home — just.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The police operation targeted the Lone Wolf network across Australia and New Zealand. (AAP: Paul Miller)

An outlaw motorbike gang police say puts "profits ahead of public safety" has been targeted by Australian and New Zealand authorities in a bid to undermine its criminal control.

The Lone Wolf Outlaw Motorcycle Gang has been assessed as posing a "very high threat" in organised crime in Australia.

Police say this is driven by its alleged involvement in illicit drug importation and trafficking, money laundering and violence.

A national day of action by a specialised task force on Thursday ended in 20 arrests and 69 charges laid.

Investigators identified Rebels members allegedly wearing vests with the subdued or blacked-out patches of the gang's insignias in public.

Across Australia and New Zealand, Taskforce Morpheus conducted 18 search warrants, 10 firearms compliance checks and seized cocaine, MDMA, illicit tobacco and vapes.

The task force brings together all Australian state and territory police and Commonwealth law enforcement agencies.

Queensland Detective Superintendent Troy Pukallus said Lone Wolf used violence, intimidation and organised offending for financial gain.

"They have no regard for the impact their actions have on the safety and wellbeing of the community," he said.

Detective Superintendent Pukallus said police were sending a clear message that no matter how well-connected criminal gangs believe they are, authorities are committed to identifying, disrupting and dismantling organised crime networks.

Australian Border Force Commander Graeme Campbell said the illicit tobacco trade was a significant source of revenue for organised crime groups.

"With proven links between OMCG's (Outlaw Motorcycle Gang's) and illicit tobacco retail premises across Australia, profits are used to fund other serious criminal activity," he said.

Commander Campbell said authorities would continue to target groups that "exploit legitimate businesses", including tobacco shops, to "conceal and facilitate organised criminal activity".

Brad Abdy says outlaw motorcycle gangs should expect to be targeted "wherever they operate". (ABC News)

NSW Police Force Raptor Squad Commander, Detective Acting Superintendent Brad Abdy said outlaw motorcycle gangs should expect to be targeted "wherever they operate".

"By combining intelligence and resources across jurisdictions, we're making it increasingly difficult for organised crime groups to profit from their criminal activity," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.title: Court hears teen under drug influence during attack on woman
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.author: Eva Blandis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The woman was assaulted near the Mitcham Memorial Library, where she was sleeping rough. (ABC News)

A youth was under the influence of a "cocktail of drugs" when he assaulted a woman outside an Adelaide library, a court has heard.

He previously pleaded guilty to causing harm with intent and serious criminal trespass.

His sentence will be handed down next month.

A woman sleeping rough in Adelaide's inner south fell victim to a "sustained, malicious and intentional" attack at the hands of a teenager who was under the influence of a "cocktail of drugs", the Youth Court has heard.

The now-18-year-old, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously pleaded guilty to causing harm with intent over the attack on the woman in the vicinity of the Mitcham Memorial Library, on Belair Road at Hawthorn, on November 13, 2025.

The 64-year-old suffered serious injuries and was rushed to hospital.

The youth, who was 17 at the time of the offending, also previously pleaded guilty to serious criminal trespass in relation to a series of break-ins after the attack.

During a pre-sentence hearing today, defence barrister Patrick Dawes said a toxicology report identified a "cocktail of substances" in the teenager's system following his arrest.

"It's [his] memory and [his] position that he didn't voluntarily consume methylamphetamine, MDMA and benzodiazepines and other semi-synthetic opioids on the night of the 12th into the 13th," he told the court.

Mr Dawes told the court the then-17-year-old was in a state of "dysregulation" at the time of the offending after he was "seemingly assaulted" by peers in the hours before.

He added that, since the offending, his client has been diagnosed with autism and severe ADHD and that a cognitive assessment found his "overall intellectual function" is in the "low-average range".

Mr Dawes said that a psychological report prepared before the hearing deduced that there was a "nexus" between the teenager's mental health conditions and the substances he was influenced by.

The court also heard that the teenager has been diagnosed with alcohol use disorder but that he is "now in remission".

"He was admitted to the Women's and Children's Hospital within two or three days of his arrest due to severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms and spent six nights in hospital," he said.

The teenager previously pleaded guilty to causing harm with intent and serious criminal trespass in the Youth Court. (ABC News: Gary Rivett)

Mr Dawes said his client was in a state of "overwhelm" at the time of the offending and had "loss of control… which he takes responsibility" for.

He said a letter of apology by the teenager to his victim demonstrates his client's remorse.

"He's really sorry for hurting her and wishes he could take back what he did," he said.

Mr Dawes read an excerpt from the apology letter in which he said "it really hurt" to see the video recording of the offending.

"I can't remember why this all took place but when I rewatch the footage it really hurt me seeing myself act and treat a person in such a terrible way and you can understand how sorry I am," it read.

The court also heard that the psychological report concluded that the 18-year-old is at "moderate risk of reoffending of offences of violence".

A prosecutor asked the court to sentence the youth, who has been in detention since November last year, to a "further period of detention".

Mr Dawes conceded that a further period of detention would be appropriate.

Magistrate John Wells said he would sentence on the basis the attack was "intentional" and co-existed with the teenager's "meltdown".

Magistrate Wells added that the victim can be seen putting up her umbrella to protect herself.

"She cowers behind the umbrella," he said.

The 18-year-old will be sentenced next month.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.title: Man hit with angle grinder during attempted e-bike robbery
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.author: Rachael Merritt
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Mr Hoy is recovering after he was hit in the head with an angle grinder during an attempted robbery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

A man has been left with head injuries after he was hit with an angle grinder during an attempted robbery.

Stephen Hoy, 60, was staying at a caravan park in Adelaide when the incident happened in the early hours of Friday morning.

Police are still looking for the offender.

A man has been left with head injuries after he was hit with an angle grinder while trying to fight off an offender during an attempted e-bike robbery in Adelaide's inner-east.

Queensland man Stephen Hoy, 60, had been staying at a caravan park in Hackney after travelling to Adelaide to watch his son's band perform on Friday night.

Mr Hoy said he initially heard voices outside his caravan about 1:30am on Friday morning and was woken up hours later about 4:30am to the sound of machinery.

He stepped outside and saw a man allegedly trying to steal his e-bike which was locked to his motorhome.

Mr Hoy said he's feeling "lucky" his injuries were not more severe.  (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

"They had the grinder and they were just grinding through the lock on my bike, it happened in seconds," Mr Hoy told ABC News.

"I jumped out of bed and ran around the front way and he went around the back and then we ... had a fight."

"He had the grinder going and he swung it and hit me in the head with the grinder while it was going. That was the scary bit, I ended up on the ground, I didn't want him to pinch my bike.

Mr Hoy said he chased the offender to the curb where there was a second fight between the pair and the man ran away, dropping a number of his belongings.

Paramedics treated Mr Hoy at the scene and he later received stitches.

A police car at the Hackney caravan park on Friday.  (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Police said the e-bike was abandoned a short distance from the caravan and that the angle grinder was left at the scene, but the man was yet to be arrested.

The offender has been described as Caucasian and about 191cm tall.

Despite the incident, Mr Hoy said he was feeling "lucky" his injuries were not more severe.

"I'm feeling pretty good ... could have been anything when you've got a grinder that's going and a guy swings it at you and hits you in the head," he said.

Anyone with information or CCTV of the attempted robbery is urged to contact police.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/d.title: Premier says new information on Hawke children deaths should be considered
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/d.author: Amy Rossbach and Kimberley Putland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Tributes left for the three Hawke children following their deaths in 2022. (ABC News: Amelia Searson)

The WA Ombudsman has released a statement on his review into the murder of three children in the state's Pilbara region.

The review was completed in November 2025.

WA's premier says the new information could open the door for a coronial inquest.

Western Australia's premier says new information on the deaths of three children in the Pilbara released by the Ombudsman could be an opening for a coronial inquest.

Amid growing scrutiny over events leading to the deaths of the Hawke children in 2022, the state ombudsman has released new details of the case.

The children, aged 10, seven, and four months old, were murdered by their mother Margaret Hawke in South Hedland.

Following the deaths, the children's grandmother Dorothy Papertalk called for an inquest, but this was denied by then Coroner Phil Urquhart in 2025.

WA Ombudsman Bevan Warner said although information on individual deaths is not usually published, media coverage on the case meant it was "important for public confidence to report on the work undertaken."

Bevan Warner has released details on the investigation. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

Following Mr Warner's statement, Premier Roger Cook said while it was potentially new information, he would not ask the Attorney-General Tony Buti to call for a coronial inquest.

"I don't know if it was part of the evidence that the coroner considered, but if it wasn't, that again provides the opportunity for further consideration," he said.

"If there is fresh evidence — and that would appear to me that that is the case — well then that is an opportunity for the attorney-general to speak with the coroner."

Dorothy Papertalk sits by her grandchildren's grave in South Hedland. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Extensive evidence was examined during the review, including police body-worn camera video, and more than 1,700 pages of key agency records.

The review looked at police reports from 17 emergency calls and six family violence incidents.

Mr Buti has repeatedly said he was unable to order an inquest into the killings, even going as far as publishing private legal advice on the matter.

He was challenged in an open letter by former Governor Malcolm McCusker KC and former president of the Children's Court Denis Reynolds.

"That letter says that the attorney-general does have the power to direct the state coroner or coroner, the Act (Coroners 1996) says, to conduct an inquest," Mr Reynolds told 102.5 ABC Perth.

In answer to the letter, Mr Buti said he accepted the advice provided by the solicitor-general on the matter.

Tony Buti says he needs fresh evidence to ask for a coronial inquest. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"If new evidence is provided to me about this case that wasn't considered by former Coroner Urquhart, I will be able to consider exercising my power to order an inquest," he said.

WA Liberals leader Basil Zempilas questioned why Mr Cook had not called an inquest in light of the ombudsman's statement.

"I don't think anybody is satisfied with any of the explanations or any of the reasons that the premier or attorney-general have given for why an inquest has not been called," Mr Zempilas said.

"If there is fresh evidence, what are we waiting for? What is the attorney-general doing? Why has an inquest not been called?

"Have the details of the ombudsman's report been considered by the coroner? Why don't we know?"

At the same time as the ombudsman released the information on the Hawke children's case, terms of reference on the review into child protection in the Pilbara have been announced.

National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter visited Port Hedland last month after reports of children living unsupervised in squalid conditions earlier this year created a political firestorm.

Sue-Anne Hunter says a coordinated response for children and families is needed. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Ms Hunter said the WA government needed to make improvements that were not band-aid solutions.

"Governments must be held accountable for delivering material improvements in the lives of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families, not simply the level of activity they report," she said.

Ms Hunter said the review would examine how agencies responded to children and families, whether they worked together effectively, and what actions would improve those responses.

"The focus is the Pilbara, but the review will address a question that matters nationally: how government agencies turn their separate responsibilities into a coordinated response for children and families," she said.

The scope of the review will include children from the Pilbara who have been relocated or placed outside the region, including in out-of-home care, and young people aged 18–24 who have left care.

Ms Hunter said the review would not examine individual cases but could consider themes from significant cases.

"We won't be looking into cases that are currently under investigation or with coroners, but could possibly have a look at this one," she said of the Hawke case.

"I have spoken with the grandmother and hopefully I can get to speak to her again so she can feed into this review."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.title: Sister of 13yo critically injured in alleged arson pleads with other teens
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.author: Olivia Jenkins and Antonia O'Flaherty
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Emergency services were called to the home in Taylors Hill around 5am on Monday. (ABC News: Kate Meade)

The sister of a Melbourne 13-year-old clinging to life after an apparent botched firebombing earlier this week has urged other Victorian children not to accept money in exchange for carrying out crimes.

The ABC can also reveal new details about how one of the boy’s co-accused admitted to his involvement in the Taylors Hill incident, apologising to the 13-year-old’s family and offering them cash.

It was previously revealed that the group was tasked with lighting the fire by middlemen over WhatsApp.

The sister of a boy clinging to life after an alleged botched arson is pleading with Victorian children to resist cash offers to commit crimes amid a spate of firebombings wreaking havoc across Melbourne.

Warning: This story contains details that may distress some readers.

The 13-year-old was among a group of people allegedly involved in the firebombing of two cars in Melbourne's north-west in the early hours of Monday morning, which backfired when the boy himself caught fire, leaving him with burns to almost his entire body.

Speaking to the ABC as the schoolboy remains in a critical condition, the boy's sister said falling in with the "wrong crowd" could cost him his life.

"It's not just a crime, but a life on the line.

"He's fighting for his life."

Despite the boy undergoing a 12-hour skin graft surgery at the Royal Children's Hospital, police yesterday told a court it was "very possible" he could die from his injuries.

The 13-year-old boy was left with burns to almost all of his body. (Supplied)

The youths allegedly inadvertently covered themselves in petrol while dousing the vehicles before setting them alight.

They allegedly then tried to flee in a stolen car but crashed it moments later, running away and "leaving the child engulfed in flames, fighting for his life", according to prosecutors

Two 16-year-old boys, including one out on bail at the time, are behind bars after police laid a raft of charges over the incident.

Despite having no prior criminal history, one of the boys failed in his bid for freedom yesterday afternoon in a children's court.

A third 15-year-old boy was arrested and released without charge.

A detective yesterday told the court that the 13-year-old was "screaming for help before collapsing" in the aftermath of the incident.

"It breaks my heart," his sister told the ABC.

"I cannot imagine how scared he would've been burning alive."

The ABC can reveal new details about how one of the accused teens contacted the 13-year-old boy's family admitting to his involvement, offering them cash and apologising for the injuries the boy suffered.

After her brother was rushed to hospital with burns to 90 per cent of his body, his sister pleaded for information about the blaze, prompting one of the accused teens to contact her, the court heard.

In Snapchat messages obtained by the ABC, the boy admitted his involvement and apologised to the family.

"I am so deeply sorry for everything and please believe me when I say this, I'm not asking for your forgiveness and don't expect you to like me at all but I am so sorry for what happened to [him] and it's my fault this all happened," one message read.

"I've sent $1'000 [sic] to a friend to give to you guys and [the boy] when he recovers hopefully that helps you guys out.

"And I did not mean to leave [him] behind I didn't leave on purpose or any of that the news makes fake shit."

The boy vowed to "change my life around and start going to church and get into boxing".

Two cars were destroyed and a home was damaged during the arson attack. (ABC News)

It was yesterday revealed that the group of youths was tasked with lighting the fire by middlemen on WhatsApp.

The boy's sister said youths such as her brother were at higher risk of being targeted by older offenders with organised crime links through friends already engaging in criminal behaviour.

"Walk away. Speak up. Tell someone. Protect your life," she said.

Police allege the teens were promised a $3,000 payment to commit the arson.

The wounded boy's sister described her brother as sweet, insisting he would not want to hurt anyone.

"He was there for others and was a genuine, sweet soul," she said.

"I love that he will fight for the people he loves, even if that meant suffering."

The incident on Monday is among a string of similar arson attacks reported across Melbourne over consecutive nights this week.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.author: Jack Hislop
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Parliament

Luke Gosling says he will "absolutely be running for preselection" in his seat of Solomon at the next federal election. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Darwin-based Labor MP Luke Gosling, who is facing charges of assaulting the NT administrator and breaching bail, says he will again seek preselection ahead of the next federal election.

Mr Gosling denies all the charges, and says Territorians will look back on his arrest and prosecution and "shake their head[s]".

Mr Gosling is due to return to court later this month.

Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling says he will seek preselection again ahead of the next election, despite unresolved assault and breach of bail charges hanging over his head.

The Darwin-based Member for Solomon has been charged with two counts of assaulting Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly at the NT Thai Grand Festival in July.

Mr Gosling was subsequently charged with breaching his bail in August.

He denies all the allegations and his lawyer, Marty Aust SC, told the Darwin Local Court last month he would write to prosecutors requesting the charges be withdrawn due to "insufficient evidence".

David Connolly is the NT administrator, the equivalent of a state governor. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

Speaking at a press conference this morning alongside three Country Liberal Party (CLP) members of the NT parliament, Mr Gosling reaffirmed his view that his arrest had been politicised.

"I'll absolutely be running for preselection to keep representing the people of Solomon through our normal party processes," he said.

"I've been so encouraged by the support from not only my party members here in the Northern Territory, but everyday Territorians who see very clearly what is happening here and are wishing me all the best and all the support they can possibly give me.

In September, Mr Aust told the court in relation to the assault charges there was "not a single eyewitness to any event, nor a witness that gives opportunity for an event to occur".

Luke Gosling says future Territorians will "shake their head" when reflecting on the charges against him. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Save except for [Mr Connolly's wife] who puts it at a different place, at a different time and a different description," he said at the time.

"It has all the hallmarks of confusion or collusion."

Mr Gosling said in the future, Territorians would look back on his arrest and prosecution and find it hard to believe.

"This will in the future go down as something that the Territory will look at, shake their head, but ultimately move on from, as I have already, because the job that I have never stopped doing every day is delivering for the people of Darwin and Palmerston," he said.

A former president of the NT Cattlemen's Association, David Connolly was appointed to the role of NT administrator by the CLP government in December.

The NT administrator serves as the Crown's representative in the Territory, in a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.

In the lead-up to Mr Connolly's February swearing-in, there were calls for his appointment to be rescinded after past social media posts emerged from his deleted X (formerly Twitter) account.

David Connolly apologised to anyone who had been offended by his past social media activity before he was sworn in in February. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Some of the posts were labelled as "racist" and "denigrating of women".

The night before he was sworn in, Mr Connolly apologised to people who may have been hurt by the posts, saying he deeply regretted them.

Asked today if there should be renewed scrutiny over Mr Connolly's appointment if the charges against him were thrown out, Mr Gosling said the saga had been "a real education [and] eye-opener as to some of the dynamics going on here in the Northern Territory".

"It is obviously an issue for others to reflect on different appointments that have been made at different times," he said.

Luke Gosling says Anthony Albanese's federal Labor government doesn't do "captain's picks". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"In the federal Labor team, we believe in strong cabinet processes, we believe in Caucus members having a say, and I think that is the way of good government.

Responding to Mr Gosling's comments at the press conference, the CLP's Youth, Seniors and Equality Minister Jinson Charls said the NT government had already provided responses about Mr Connolly's appointment.

He said if Mr Gosling's charges were dropped, the NT government would provide a further response about the appointment "if that question is still relevant at that point in time".

Territory Labor president Clare Martin said preselections for the next federal election were not yet open either in the NT or nationally.

She said the timing would be determined by Labor's federal executive.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.title: Families of men killed on Mexico surf trip call for maximum sentences
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.author: Kamin Gock and Elissa Fitzgerald
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Callum (left) and Jake Robinson were killed while on a surfing trip in Baja California in 2024. (Supplied: Instagram)

Debra Robinson has asked for the maximum sentence to be given to three men accused of killing her sons and their American friend in Mexico.

Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad were shot dead during a surfing and camping trip.

A verdict in the case will be delivered tomorrow.

The mother of two Australian surfers who were shot dead in Mexico has called for their accused killers to receive maximum prison sentences, as the court prepares to deliver its verdict.

West Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, as well as their American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, were shot dead after being robbed while on a surfing trip in Mexico in April 2024.

Their bodies were found at the bottom of a well along Mexico's Pacific coast after they were reported missing.

Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús are charged with aggravated homicide, aggravated robbery, violent robbery and grand theft auto.

Ángel Jesús has been in custody in a local jail. (Supplied)

Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", faces a possible sentence of 378 years.  (Supplied: Mexican police handout)

Irineo Francisco has links to the Sinaloa cartel, according to court documents. (Supplied)

Closing arguments in the trial were heard in an Ensenada courthouse on Thursday, local time.

The defence cast doubt on the credibility of the investigation into the trio's deaths, as well as the testimony prosecutors relied on.

The families of the victims then addressed the court ahead of a verdict due to be delivered on Friday.

"Callum and Jake were our only children," said Debra Robinson, who has attended most of the trial with her husband, Martin.

Ms Robinson cried as she read her statement and requested the judge hand down "a maximum sentence of imprisonment on those responsible".

"No sentence can bring Callum and Jake back; nothing can undo what has happened, but accountability matters," she said, adding that the protection of other families should also be considered.

"We never want another family to experience the devastation and suffering that has been inflicted on ours."

Jake and Callum Robinson and Carter Rhoad were killed near a remote beach in northern Mexico.  (Supplied)

Jake, a 31-year-old doctor from Perth, had travelled to California to meet up with Callum, 32, who had been living in the US for 12 years after moving over to play lacrosse.

They then travelled south with Mr Rhoad to Mexico to go camping and surfing.

"We struggle to understand how three young men who showed kindness and trust, even in their final hours, could have been treated with such cruelty," Ms Robinson said.

"We understand that they gave up their keys and wallets, then begged for their lives and asked not to be killed.

Ms Robinson previously asked for a timely verdict, as she and her husband are due to leave Mexico on October 9.

Debra and Martin Robinson are in Mexico after their sons Jake (left) and Callum (right) were killed.  (Facebook: Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation)

The three accused looked uncomfortable in their seats as they listened to Ms Robinson's statement via a translator.

Mr Rhoad's fiancée, Natalie Weirtz, spoke on behalf of his family.

She described Mr Rhoad as an "incredible person" who dedicated his time to helping youths.

He had previously volunteered on humanitarian trips to South Africa, Guatemala and Mexico.

"I believe the accused are guilty and justice should be served in the highest degree," she said.

All three defendants previously rejected plea deals that would have seen them serve jail terms between 47 and 52 years.

A verdict is expected to be handed down on Friday. (ABC News: Timothy Myers)

Ari Gisell, the ex-girlfriend of Mr Gerardo, was sentenced to 20 years behind bars in November for her role in the robbery.

She was also fined 54,285 Mexican pesos ($4,323).

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/q.author: Janelle Miles
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Ambulance Service

Queensland Health data shows 42 per cent of patients arriving by ambulance are waiting longer than 30 minutes to be transferred to an ED.   (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Queensland Health data for August shows 42 per cent of patients who arrive at hospitals across the state by ambulance are waiting more than 30 minutes.

The figures are worse than in July, and only slightly better than in August 2024, before the LNP came into government.

A spokesperson for the Acting Health Minister says the recent data is the lowest August figure in five years.

Queues of long-wait ambulance patients outside many of Queensland's major hospital emergency departments have barely budged in the last two years.

The latest Queensland Health performance data for August shows statewide ambulance ramping is sitting at 42 per cent across Queensland's 26 top public hospital emergency departments (ED).

That means 42 per cent of patients who arrive at those hospitals by ambulance are waiting longer than 30 minutes to be transferred off a stretcher into an ED.

In July, ambulance ramping across the same hospitals stood at 38.7 per cent — 3.3 percentage points better than the August figures.

Ambulance ramping figures have barely budged in the last two years. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

The numbers are only marginally better than the August before the Crisafulli Government came to power in 2024, when ramping stood at 43.9 per cent.

In 2025 — Queensland's worst flu season on record — August ramping rates were at 45.6 per cent under the LNP Government.

The latest August data comes just ahead of the halfway mark in the Crisafulli Government's first four-year term and on the back of a late flu season.

It puts in serious doubt the Premier's commitment ahead of the 2024 election to get ambulance ramping down to under 30 per cent before the 2028 poll.

Health Minister Tim Nicholls is under pressure to get ramping under 30 per cent before 2028. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The latest figures pile more pressure on Health Minister Tim Nicholls after Premier David Crisafulli tied his cabinet future to cutting ambulance ramping to below 30 per cent before the next election.

Opposition leader Steven Miles predicted ramping figures would continue to worsen.

"You can't fix ramping while not delivering growth funding to our hospitals, not having a workforce plan, and not building the new beds that are needed," he said.

"The government still hasn't delivered a workforce plan to deliver the staffing those hospitals need and of course, they've delayed the build of new beds that would provide some relief to the bed block that is choking our emergency departments."

Opposition leader Steven Miles said ramping figures were likely to worsen. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

August ramping figures show hospitals in the Metro South Health region are particularly struggling.

Logan Hospital, south of Brisbane, recorded ramping levels at 61.8 per cent and at the Princess Alexandra Hospital, more than half of the patients arriving at the emergency department by ambulance were ramped for more than half an hour.

Topic:
State and Territory Government

Topic:
Indigenous Culture

In the regions, Cairns Hospital ramping was 45.6 per cent in August, Bundaberg Hospital was only marginally better at 44.7 per cent, and at Rockhampton Hospital, it was 39.1 per cent.

Gold Coast University Hospital just snuck in under the 30 per cent target, recording 28.9 per cent — a huge improvement on when the Miles Government was in power when ramping was at 48.2 per cent in August 2024 — two months before the Queensland election.

Ambulance ramping at Ipswich Hospital has been cut to 34.5 per cent since August 2024. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Ambulance ramping at Ipswich Hospital, west of Brisbane, has also turned around in the past two years.

In August 2024, a whopping 63.5 per cent of patients arriving by ambulance to the hospital, were ramped for more than the recommended benchmark of 30 minutes.

That has been cut to 34.5 per cent on the back of the Mater Springfield Hospital opening in May.

A spokeswoman for acting Health and Ambulance Services Minister Dale Last said the 2026 August ramping data was the lowest August figures in five years.

In August 2021, ambulance ramping was 38.7 per cent at Queensland’s major public hospitals.

This year’s data comes amid a record high 211,664 presentations to Queensland public hospital emergency departments in August.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.title: How the card surcharge ban could change our relationship with cash
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.author: Dannielle Maguire
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Personal Finance

Some small businesses may start offering discounts for cash payments after the card surcharge ban.  (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

With the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) ban on card surcharges now in effect you might start seeing local businesses offering discounts if you pay in cash.

Cash payments in Australia are much less common than they were a decade ago, but the RBA's latest data showed a slight uptick in cash use in 2025.

How could the ban on card surcharges impact how cash is used in Australia?

This graph from the RBA's 2025 Consumer Payments Survey tracks the percentage of Australians who use cash in a typical week.

As you can see, 2025's figure of 50 per cent is much lower than the 97 per cent in 2007.

But it's slightly higher than 2022's figure of 47 per cent.

John Hawkins, a senior economic lecturer at the University of Canberra, doesn't expect cash use to skyrocket.

"From January the government has required most grocery stores and petrol stations to accept cash, which may see some modest increase in its use," Dr Hawkins says.

"On the other hand, about 20 per cent of consumers say they used cash to avoid card surcharges.

"As these no longer apply we could see some drop in cash use."

Card surcharges have been scrapped under reforms by the Reserve Bank of Australia. (ABC NewsRadio)

Angel Zhong, a finance professor at RMIT, says she would be surprised if the surcharge ban reverses the long-term trend of card payments.

"I expect a modest uptick [in cash use] mostly at the margins: the café, the barber or the tradie offering a few per cent off for cash," Professor Zhong says.

"Australians moved to cards and mobile wallets mainly because of convenience, speed and record keeping, not because of price.

"A small discount at a handful of businesses is unlikely to change entrenched habits for most people."

The federal government will temporarily cover credit card surcharges after businesses warned that losing the payment option would put them under pressure.

Data from the RBA's 2025 survey showed people aged 65 and older were the most likely to use cash.

Cash might also still be preferred by people in regional areas with limited bank access or poor internet signal, people managing tight budgets, and people who have privacy concerns.

Professor Zhong says the goal should be to continue offering people the choice of using cash or paying by card.

Professor Zhong sees cash discounts as a sign of how much pressure small businesses are under.

"The RBA paired the ban with a cut to interchange fees, which was meant to soften the blow by lowering what businesses pay to accept cards," she says.

"But interchange is only one part of the cost.

"Small businesses typically pay their payment service provider a bundled rate, and there's no guarantee that the interchange savings flow through to that rate."

Card payments are much more common than they were in 2007.  (AAP: Dan Peled)

While big businesses could leverage their bargaining power to negotiate savings in their contracts, smaller businesses don't have that option.

And that means losing the ability to surcharge while missing out on a drop in costs.

"Against thin margins and rising operating costs, offering a discount for cash is one of the few ways a small business can steer customers toward a cheaper payment method," Professor Zhong says.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) says businesses can offer discounts to customers paying via particular means such as cash or PayID, but there are a few rules.

Cash use has dropped by more than 50 per cent in almost 20 years. But there has been a slight increase in cash payments since 2022.

Discounts should be clearly disclosed before payment and they have to advertise the non-discounted price.

They're not allowed to display the discounted price more prominently than the full price.

Yes, but there are rules about how businesses label these price hikes.

"They must not mislead consumers about prices, including about the reasons for any price increases," the ACCC says.

An example of this might be a nursery that used to apply a 1 per cent credit card surcharge for its products.

Price hikes are legal, but businesses have to be careful with their labelling.  (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

To compensate for that cost, they might increase the cost of a $10 pot plant to $10.10.

But let's say the nursery owner decides that, while they're setting new figures, they'll increase the pot plant's price to $12 to cover the rise in their electricity and water bills.

That's totally legal too.

But they aren't allowed to say the price increase from $10 to $12 is because of the ban.

"This will be misleading because the price increase also reflects other business costs, not just the cost of accepting card payments," the ACCC says.
