https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.title: The fruit and vegetables to look out for this month
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.author: Anna Chisholm
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Food and Drink

Asparagus will peak this month, Jo Toscano says.  (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Asparagus is "absolutely sublime" at the moment, according to green grocer Jo Toscano.

Snow peas are also in season during spring. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Asparagus, snow peas and garden peas are increasingly prominent on shelves as spring sets in.

While no-one doubts the convenience of frozen peas, Effie Ramos from organic market garden Remi's Patch in Naarm/Melbourne says there's something special about the ritual of slowing down and popping the pods open yourself.

University of Newcastle nutrition professor Clare Collins says shopping seasonally can help us to introduce variety into our diets.

"If you eyeball all the veggies and fruit, look at what hasn't visited your trolley for a few weeks," she says.

Asparagus is expected to peak in mid-to-late October, Ms Toscano says.

People tend to avoid the thick asparagus spears, but she says they're "juicy and full of flavour".

From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these easy recipes will put spring asparagus on your weeknight menu.

White asparagus doesn't offer the "great value" of green asparagus, Ms Toscano says "it is divine". She recommends peeling it as the exterior can be "quite fibrous".

Dr Collins says asparagus works well in an omelette, quiche or with a simple cheese sauce.

Garden peas are also in season.

"Fresh peas sort of stay elevated in price but when they're good they're really good and it's worth it," Ms Toscano says.

When garden peas are fresh and young, she suggests using the pods (after they've been shelled) to flavour homemade vegetable stock or blitzing and sieving that mixture to make an intense pea-flavoured cooking liquid.

Broad beans are also "awesome" right now, Ms Toscano says.

Ms Ramos says the leafy green tip of the broad beans have been popular and are "really good, fresh in a salad".

Effie Ramos says there is nothing as good as peas when they are at their peak. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm )

Broccoli and cauliflower "are pretty good value" and Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli are another good buy, Ms Toscano says.

Dr Collins says brassicas, including cauliflower, broccoli and cabbage, can be divisive because they can taste bitter to "super tasters" — people with a more sensitive sense of taste.

"But the good news, especially for parents, is that [through] repeated exposure you increase your tolerance," she says.

Avoid overcooking the produce and try roasting it or masking the flavour with something like a cheese sauce if someone you are cooking for finds it bitter, she suggests.

Jo Toscano says carrots are available year-round, but they are "unbelievable at the moment as well". (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Ms Toscano says lots of red capsicums are coming from Queensland and that there are "bargains to be had" over the next couple of weeks.

Dr Collins says you can use affordable capsicums and Asian greens in stir-fries.

Ms Ramos says it's a good time for beetroot, which can be added to salads, raw or cooked.

"A lot of people sort of underestimate the power of the leaves of the beets. You can have them raw, or I just blanch them with a little bit of olive oil," she says.

Ms Ramos expects an abundance of spring onions, coriander, parsley, which will decrease prices.

Grapes have started but they're still very expensive, Ms Toscano says, and the first stone fruit will begin appearing this month.

"With the confluence of WA and Queensland mango seasons in a few weeks, prices are expected to fall," she says.

Cathy Senn from Sensational Berries in Naarm/Melbourne says supplies of Victorian berries will increase as the month continues, adding to those coming from northern Australia.

A hot pudding doused in cream is always welcome in cooler months.

"Starting with the strawberries and then we'll go on to raspberries and then later on we'll have the blueberries come on and then the strawberries, the blackberries after that," she says.

Citrus varieties are "diminishing", Ms Senn says, pointing to her "about finished" blood oranges, cara cara oranges and ruby grapefruits.

Dr Collins says at this time of year you can often buy bags of great value lemons and oranges. If she's got people coming over, she likes to cook her lemon-and-orange delicious.

"You use the rind, the more rind the better," she says.

Separating the egg white from the egg yolks is "the tricky bit", but it's also a good opportunity to teach kids or grandkids how to do it.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.title: Man accused of deliberately injuring sheep at Canberra property refused bail
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.author: Harry Frost
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The sheep were allegedly injured at a rural property in Canberra. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

An 18-year-old man has faced the ACT Magistrates Court on a string of charges over an alleged incident of animal cruelty last month.

Police say several people broke into a rural property in Canberra's south and deliberately injured multiple sheep and ransacked a house.

Memphis Auld, 18, was refused bail, while police expect to lay charges against another man who is already in custody for other matters.

An 18-year-old man accused of breaking into a rural property in Canberra's south and injuring several sheep last month has been refused bail.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Police were called to the property adjacent to the Monaro Highway in Tuggeranong on September 17, after the owner arrived and found multiple injured sheep in a holding pen.

It is alleged several people went to the property the night before and used dogs to round up eight sheep and herd them into the pen.

Police said several of the sheep were deliberately injured with both firearms and what they called "edged weapons".

ACT Policing seized a large knife during a search warrant at the Richardson property. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

One sheep died, and another had to be euthanased.

The home on the property was also allegedly ransacked.

Police raided a home in Richardson yesterday and arrested Memphis Auld, 18, and seized a number of items including cannabis and a large knife.

A 16-year-old was also arrested but released pending further investigation.

Investigators say a 27-year-old man, who is currently in custody for other matters, is also expected to be charged over the incident.

ACT Policing says it seized cannabis from the Richardson property. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Mr Auld faced the ACT Magistrates Court today charged with four counts of joint commission aggravated animal cruelty causing death and one count of joint commission aggravated animal cruelty causing serious injury.

He was also charged with committing aggravated burglary with intent to damage property, possession of a prohibited firearm, trafficking cannabis, and multiple motor vehicle and driving offences.

Mr Auld applied for bail, with the duty lawyer telling the court Mr Auld's partner relied on his Centrelink payments to make ends meet, and his family were willing to support him to meet any conditions.

But the prosecutor opposed his release, arguing police held concerns that a firearm — believed to have been used in the incident — was yet to be found.

Police say the incident happened near Tuggeranong Pines in Canberra's south. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

The court also heard officers had uncovered images on a mobile phone of a person pointing a firearm at a sheep while wearing clothing police believe matched those found at Mr Auld's home.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt refused bail, saying the likelihood of Mr Auld reoffending, endangering the wellbeing of others or interfering with evidence was "so great that his detention in custody is currently justified".

"There is … an outstanding firearm that was used in the commission of these offences," she said.

"There was, in my view, some attempts to conceal and some attempts to evade detection by the group, with the firearm being concealed on the CCTV footage and number plates on vehicles being replaced.

"There is also possibly a risk that there may be some interference or communication about the firearm."

Mr Auld was remanded in custody to return to court later this month.

Police are urging anyone with information to provide details via the Crime Stoppers ACT website, quoting 8502989.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.title: Remand centre built for adults to remain open to children over capacity concerns
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.author: Claudia Williams
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

A room at the Wacol Youth Remand Centre, which was designed to hold adults but where children are now accommodated. (Supplied)

Queensland's detention services inspector has released his report into the Wacol Youth Remand Centre, which has held children since April last year.

Anthony Reilly found it would be "beneficial" to continue holding children at the centre due to anticipated impacts of the state's proposed breach bail, go to jail laws.

He said while it was not considered a "suitable facility for the detention of children", it was more suitable than holding children in police watch houses.

A police watch house designed for adults should continue holding Queensland children due to concerns over capacity at youth detention centres under proposed breach bail, go to jail laws, an independent watchdog says.

Queensland detention services inspector Anthony Reilly made the finding in his report into the Wacol Youth Remand Centre.

The centre, originally built for adults, opened in April last year to hold children aged 10 to 18 as a safer alternative to a police watch house while they wait for a room at one of Queensland's three youth detention centres.

The inspector noted in the report the draft consultation had recommended the "institutionalised" centre cease holding children when the state's fourth youth detention centre at Woodford opens.

The hallway outside children’s accommodation pods at the Wacol Youth Remand Centre. (Supplied: Queensland Ombudsman)

However, Mr Reilly said the impact of the proposed laws may mean the state's youth detention centres "do not have sufficient capacity".

"As a consequence, it is possible that children will need to be detained in large numbers and for lengthy periods in watch houses," he said.

Mr Reilly, who is also the state's ombudsman, said in that scenario it would therefore be "beneficial" to continue to accommodate children at the remand centre.

"While we do not consider the centre to be a suitable facility for the detention of children, we consider it to be more suitable than detention in police watch houses," the report states.

David Crisafulli says the government is continuing to invest in more facilities, early intervention and rehabilitation. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

When questioned, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said his government had increased capacity by 20 per cent and would continue to invest in more facilities, early intervention and rehabilitation.

"But faced with the choice of a few extra people in jail and a few less people in your lounge room, I'm on the side of Queensland victims, and I'm choosing the latter," he said.

"We're working across the system, and that's my commitment to people. We're doing what we said we're going to do."

An exercise yard at the Wacol Youth Remand Centre. (Supplied: Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support)

Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the need to keep the centre open showed the "government that has refused to plan for the consequences of their own decisions".

Mr Reilly noted while changes to the centre had been made to help accommodate children, its infrastructure is "institutional" and lacks the space, privacy and natural light children need.

The report made 13 recommendations to the department, including making efforts to soften the centre's environment.

In response, the Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support said it would continue to explore ways to "soften" the environment and prioritise allowing children to access programs and outdoor facilities at other youth detention centres.

A mural outside one of the accommodation pods at Wacol Youth Remand Centre. (Supplied)

In the 12 months to June 20, the average number of children at the centre each day was 32, however, the report states the number has "significantly increased" to 54 as of August 2026.

The inspection report found the increased capacity to hold children is being "diminished" as the number being detained rises.

The average length of a child's stay was 7.1 days, according to data from the first 11 months of the centre.

However, the inspectors found not all children are "moved quickly".

The report also found children identified as being high-risk are being transferred from youth detention centres to the remand centre and, in some cases, staying for more than a month.

Between April 2025 and March this year, 20 children were returned to the centre as a strategy to manage high-risk and complex behaviours, the report states.

Inside a secure admissions holding cell where the centre plans to paint a mural. (Supplied)

This included one child who was held at the centre for a total of 49 days, before being returned to the youth detention centre where they were previously housed.

"We found no records that show the decision-making process or risk assessments that informed the child's continued stay at the centre," the report states.

Similarly, the inspector found no explanation of the decision-making process or risk assessments that informed the child's return to the detention centre.

In response to the inspector's recommendation, the Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support said it had strengthened governance and oversight for "risk-based transfers" to the centre.

Premier David Crisafulli confirmed the legislation, which is set to be introduced into parliament this week, will apply to both youths and adults.

The ombudsman acknowledged children received better support in the centre than they would in a police watch house.

Mr Crisafulli said the government would "keep reducing the amount of time that a child spends in a watch house", and wanted to try "early intervention to stop them going there in the first place".

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.author: Natasha Clark
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

Sandy Spratt rescued his daughter from drowning while visiting Broome. (Supplied: Sandy Spratt)

A young father has been awarded Western Australia's Royal Life Saving Bravery Award for rescuing his toddler from drowning in a backyard pool in Broome.

Sandy Spratt is using the recognition to encourage others to complete a first aid course.

Eighty-four West Australians were recognised at the 2026 awards on Friday.

A Perth man has been recognised at the Royal Lifesaving WA Bravery Awards after saving his daughter's life from drowning.

Sandy Spratt, a 25-year-old father of two young daughters, was holidaying in Broome, 2080 kilometres north of Perth, in August 2025 when he visited a family member's home.

Mr Spratt enjoyed catching up with family as his daughters played safely near a gated pool.

But a sudden silence from his daughters' laughter alarmed him.

He ran straight to the pool and saw his three-year-old daughter Adaleena unconscious, floating with her face down in the water.

He immediately performed CPR, bringing his daughter back to consciousness by the time paramedics arrived.

"I already knew what to do without even thinking about it," Mr Spratt said.

Adaleena made a full recovery after spending time in Broome Hospital.

Sandy Spratt saved his daughter Adaleena's life while holidaying in Broome. (Supplied: Sandy Spratt)

Royal Life Saving WA, which awarded Mr Spratt for his bravery, said unfamiliar pools for children could increase the likelihood of drowning.

"Holidays and unfamiliar aquatic environments can present unexpected risks, making supervision especially important around water," a spokesperson said.

Royal Life Saving WA chief executive Peter Leaversuch said those awarded, such as Mr Spratt, had shown bravery and quick thinking.

"Lifesaving skills are not only for professional lifesavers or emergency responders," he said.

"We hope people never need to use these skills, but the stories recognised through the Bravery Awards show just how valuable they can become when someone needs help."

Mr Spratt is one of 84 West Australians recognised at the 2026 awards on Friday.

Mr Spratt wants the honour to extend beyond his actions of that day.

He had completed first aid training through a past job, which he credited with saving his daughter's life.

Mr Spratt said he wanted to share a message on the importance of completing first aid training, which involved learning CPR.

"Doing a first aid course really does save lives and is worth every bit," he said

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.title: Firmus wobbles have opponents relieved, critics questioning deals
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.author: Selina Bryan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-09/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Firmus has abandoned its ASX float after lacklustre demand, with the news welcomed by Tasmanian opponents of its plans. (Supplied: Firmus Technologies)

The news of data centre builder Firmus' share market float being pulled after lacklustre demand has been met with a mixed reaction.

While there has been disappointment from some investors, for the opponents of Firmus' data centre plans in northern Tasmania, the response has been relief.

The news of data centre operator Firmus's share market float being pulled has been met with disappointment from some investors.

But in one community where Firmus had big plans, the response was relief.

Firmus was attempting to raise cash from investors to fund its data centre plans until this week's development.

A group based in northern Tasmania, called the Environmental Awareness Association, has been campaigning against the company's three projects in the region.

Anti-data centre protesters pictured in August outside George Town Council building, ahead of the vote on whether to approve Firmus' proposed data centre. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Nicholla Thompson from the association lives at Rowella, across the Tamar River from Firmus' proposed Bell Bay site, and said community backlash had contributed to investor concerns.

Nicholla Thompson believes community opposition to Firmus contributed to investor hesitancy. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"The dominoes are starting to fall," she said.

"They wanted it to sneak through and not be seen by people; it was thanks to the little group that we've got that really highlighted what was happening over here."

The opponents' group was relieved by the news, but was not yet celebrating it as a win for their campaign.

"A big company shouldn't be able to come in and change substantially how we choose to live in a beautiful community like this and put an AI factory up in the middle of it and have us have to endure the sound, the diesel fumes and the total destruction of our properties in value and in peace and how we live," Ms Thompson said.

Why Firmus float hangs in the balance (Alicia Barry)

When asked about any impact on its Tasmanian projects, a Firmus spokesperson said nothing had "fundamentally changed" about the business.

Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors.

Sam Baker, from Shadforth Financial Group, said it was hard to tell if the community opposition had contributed to the IPO failing, but it would have been considered by investors.

He said it would be important to watch what Firmus did over the coming weeks and months to see if it could raise the capital.

"Firmus not being able to get this ASX listing off the ground has cast some doubt over the funding of their potential rollout of data centres in northern Tasmania," he said.

Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said the IPO was a matter for Firmus, but the Tasmanian government had been supportive "all the way through" the company's plans in the state.

"That relationship is positive and we look forward to it continuing in a collaborative, positive way," he said.

The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder.

The Tasmanian Greens said the state government should be embarrassed by its support of Firmus, saying investors, academics and communities had been raising concerns for months.

"The big question for Tasmania is why our government was so easily pulled into uncritically supporting this company despite the furiously waving red flags surrounding it," Tabatha Badger, the Greens' information and technology spokeswoman, said.

Ms Badger said the government should pause any planning decisions on Firmus's three proposals in Tasmania.

Firmus was also named a sponsor for Tasmania's NBL team, the JackJumpers. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The Tasmanian-founded company had recently announced sponsorships with the Tasmania Devils AFL club, several cricket teams, including the Hobart Hurricanes, and the JackJumpers and Tasmania Jewels basketball teams.

Dr Andrew Hughes, a political marketing specialist at ANU's College of Business and Economics, said the Firmus IPO falling over was a golden opportunity for the Devils to walk away from the deal.

He said he was surprised the Devils had signed with Firmus, given the club was already exposed to community backlash over the proposed AFL stadium in Hobart.

"There was this big wedge already there, so the community is divided already and then you get a sponsor who already comes from a divided perception as well," he said.

"When they appointed Ken Hinkley as coach, they talked about community and character and care.

"I thought, 'well, hang on, if that's the things you stand for, then that's exactly what you need to look for in the sponsors and partners you grow the club with is exactly those sort of core values as well'.

"And data centres, in the minds of most people, do not say that, so it sets you back."

Premier Jeremy Rockliff has been strong in his support for Firmus' plans for Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Dr Hughes said Firmus would now have a lot of work to do to rebuild trust in its brand.

"Going into a community where it's already a negative perception of that brand and then you build on it by adding some more negative to it … because your IPO, which would have funded those deals, does not go through," he said.

Dr Hughes said if the sponsorship deals with Firmus fell over, it would be harder for the clubs to re-enter the market and find new sponsors.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Weather-roiling El Nino hits record strength, Japan weather agency says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
The El Nino that’s upending weather across South America and Asia has intensified to the strongest on record, according to Japan’s national forecaster, threatening widespread economic disruptions that could linger long after the climate pattern dissipates.

The naturally occurring weather pattern warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.

Sea surface temperatures in a patch of the tropical Pacific Ocean monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency were 4 degrees Celsius above normal as of September, the highest in records going back to 1949, the forecaster said in a bulletin published Friday. The previous record was set in December 1997, when temperatures were 3.7 C above normal, the bureau said.

El Nino has already disrupted weather patterns worldwide. The climate event has led to the weakest Indian monsoon in more than a decade, exacerbated wildfires in Indonesia that have spewed toxic smoke over neighboring Singapore and Malaysia, and threatened sugar and coffee output in Brazil.

The JMA’s outlook comes a day after the World Meteorological Organization said in its latest seasonal forecast that El Nino is set to be the most intense ever. The WMO’s projection is based on the Nino 3.4 region, which overlaps with but lies west of the Nino 3 region tracked by Japan.

The Japanese bureau predicts a 100% chance that El Nino will persist through the Northern Hemisphere winter, in line with the U.S. Climate Prediction Center’s outlook that the weather-roiling phenomenon is certain to last through the January-March period.

Many record-hot years -- including 1998, 2010, 2016, 2023 and 2024 -- followed major El Nino events or developed alongside them.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.summary: The El Nino has already disrupted weather patterns worldwide. The weather-roiling phenomenon is set to be the most intense ever, the World Meteorological Organization says. The Japanese bureau predicts a 100% chance that El Ninos will persist through the Northern Hemisphere winter.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan to launch research study on rapid-response space transport
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jesse Johnson
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Defense Ministry will launch a research study on rapid-response space transportation capabilities to secure the Self-Defense Forces’ stable use of satellites, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Friday.

The move comes as more countries, including China, Russia and Japan’s ally, the United States, continue to bolster their military capabilities in space.

“Currently, the Ministry of Defense and the Self-Defense Forces are working to strengthen their capabilities in the space domain,” Koizumi told a regular news conference. “However, as we move forward with these efforts, it remains a critical national security issue to be able to rapidly restore functionality in the event that some of the satellites we use — including those required during emergencies — are lost.”

Koizumi pointed to the U.S., which is able to conduct on-demand space launches within 24 hours of notification.

“The importance of rapid access to space is growing,” Koizumi said, but noted that the launch capabilities required to achieve a similar goal “cannot be resolved by the Defense Ministry alone.”

With the study, he said, the ministry is soliciting a “broad range of ideas” about space transport capabilities by drawing on the technical expertise of the private sector.

The defense chief also said that one aim of the study is to serve as a catalyst for the emergence of new, Japanese-made internationally competitive systems.

Japan’s growth strategy has noted space and rocket launch sites as a crucial driver for expanding the country’s economy.

But the government has acknowledged that building out Japan’s space capabilities represents a significant challenge as it looks to boost the frequency of launches, improve domestic rocket manufacturing capabilities and develop launch sites and related infrastructure.

“This study aims to clarify the specific requirements for the rapid-response space transportation capabilities needed by the Defense Ministry and the SDF,” Koizumi said. “By demonstrating this demand, we believe it will encourage investment and commercialization by private-sector operators and contribute to strengthening Japan’s space industry infrastructure, including rockets and launch sites.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi says the study will help secure the Self-Defense Forces' stable use of satellites. The study will be launched to help secure Japan's space capabilities, he says. The U.S. is able to conduct on-demand space launches within 24 hours of notification.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Nobel Peace Prize goes to international jurist Navi Pillay
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay for her work as a judge and human rights lawyer, at a time when the committee said international law faces “tremendous pressure” and its institutions are “under attack.”

Pillay, 85, has “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict,” the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement on Friday, calling her “one of the great defenders of international legal principles.”

Pillay is currently serving as a judge at the International Court of Justice, in The Hague, in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide. Last year, she chaired the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which investigated Israel’s retaliatory war in Gaza and concluded that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration had committed genocide against Palestinians, a finding that the Israeli government firmly denounced.

In what appeared to be a swipe at Netanyahu, and some other leaders around the world, including U.S. President Donald Trump, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the committee, spoke of “a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice.”

He told reporters in Oslo that the prize served as “a message that international law and its institutions are the cornerstone of a more peaceful world.”

Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988.

She has served as a judge in South Africa, at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and was U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014.

Her work helped influence the definition of acts that can constitute genocide and crimes against humanity, including rape and sexual violence — and because of it a defendant in Rwanda faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda.

“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the committee said.

Arguably the most prestigious prize in global diplomacy, the Nobel Peace Prize can also stir controversy. Last year, Trump campaigned aggressively, and ultimately unsuccessfully, to obtain the award, which he has long coveted. Earlier this year, the 2025 laureate María Corina Machado gifted her medal to the U.S. president, stunning Norway.

Pillay, who will receive 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) in prize money, wasn’t among the favorites. Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight, trailed closely by Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children’s rights activist.

At the time of Friday’s announcement, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said it had not succeeded in reaching Pillay. She received the news while attending the Nuremberg Forum, a gathering to discuss international law in Nuremburg, Germany, where she got a standing ovation, according to the Associated Press.

“Your applause means a great deal to me,” she was quoted as telling those in attendance. “You know, you don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this.”

She added: “But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Navi Pillay, 85, is a judge at the International Court of Justice, in The Hague, in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide. She has ‘held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict,’

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Japan’s Prudential Life ordered to halt operations for over three months
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
The Financial Services Agency (FSA) on Friday ordered Prudential Life Insurance and Gibraltar Life Insurance, both part of the U.S. Prudential Financial group, to suspend some operations for more than three months over fraud committed by their employees.

The FSA also issued a business improvement order to Prudential Holdings of Japan, the parent company of the two Tokyo-based life insurers, calling for stronger corporate governance.

Under the partial business suspension order, which runs from Tuesday to the end of January 2027, the two insurers will be prohibited from entering into new insurance contracts or selling insurance products, so that they can focus on rebuilding their management and oversight systems.

Prudential Life has voluntarily refrained from making new sales since February, and the FSA’s order will further delay the resumption of its sales activities.

In January, Prudential Life said that more than 100 of its current and former employees had improperly received a total of ¥3.1 billion ($19.6 million) from customers, prompting the resignation of then-President Kan Mabara and an on-site inspection by the FSA.

According to a third-party investigation report released Thursday, the total amount of losses reported by victims exceeded ¥6.1 billion. The report cited a corporate culture that placed excessive emphasis on sales performance as one of the causes of the misconduct.

Prudential Life plans to review its compensation system, which relies heavily on commissions linked to sales performance, and introduce a minimum guaranteed salary. Prudential Life President and CEO Hiromitsu Tokumaru and two executives will voluntarily return 30% of their monthly remuneration for three months.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: The Financial Services Agency orders Prudential Life Insurance and Gibraltar Life Insurance to suspend some operations for more than three months. The two insurers will be prohibited from entering into new insurance contracts or selling insurance products. The FSA also issued a business improvement order to Prudentials Holdings of Japan, the parent company of the two life insurers.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Japan sees record number of workers’ compensation approvals for mental health in fiscal 2025
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jessica Speed
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Japan saw a record number of workers’ compensation approvals for mental health disorders in fiscal 2025, according to health ministry data released Friday.

The figure, published in this year’s white paper on measures to prevent karōshi, or death from overwork, marked a record high for the seventh consecutive year. The report is compiled under legislation enacted in 2014 to prevent deaths, suicides and illnesses caused by excessive workloads and work-related psychological stress.

A total of 4,958 workers filed compensation claims for mental disorders during fiscal 2025, up 1,178 from the previous year and more than three times the figure from a decade earlier. Of those, 1,082 cases were approved for compensation, up 26 from the previous year. Among approved cases, 76 involved suicide or attempted suicide.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Japan saw a record number of workers’ compensation approvals for mental health disorders in fiscal 2025. The figure marked a record high for the seventh consecutive year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Data leaks at travel companies could impact millions of customer records
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Maddie Baker
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Several travel companies in Japan have reported potential data breaches, raising concerns that customers’ personal information might have been compromised amid a series of cyberattacks in the country.

The affected companies include Adventure, which operates the travel booking website Skyticket, travel agency H.I.S. and travel technology company Temairazu.

In the case of Skyticket, up to 14.64 million customer records may be at risk, approximately 4.13 million of which may include members’ login passwords, according to its operator. The company said Friday that data stored on internal servers and in the cloud had been accessed without authorization between Oct. 2 and Oct. 4.

Skyticket’s bus reservation service and business management system were also allegedly affected by unauthorized access between August and October.

The potentially jeopardized information includes customers’ names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses. Passport numbers and credit card information were not leaked, according to the company.

In response, the company said it had blocked the unauthorized access and was investigating the incidents. It also temporarily suspended payments using saved credit cards and warned customers of potential phishing attempts via email, text and phone calls.

The company apologized and pledged to strengthen its security measures to prevent future incidents.

Major travel agency H.I.S., meanwhile, said Wednesday that the passport information of up to 627 people might have been leaked following unauthorized access at its Thailand-based subsidiary, H.I.S. Tours.

H.I.S said the incident took place in December last year and that safety measures had been put in place but that an investigation later revealed passport information, including customers’ dates of birth and passport numbers, could have been compromised.

The company said the announcement was delayed because its manual investigation was complicated by large amounts of unrelated data being mixed in with personal information.

Travel technology company Temairazu also reported unauthorized access to its systems.

On. Sept 28, the company said a third party had accessed its travel booking service on Sept. 21, potentially leading to customers receiving fraudulent text messages seeking their banking details. Temairazu said it had blocked the unauthorized access and restored its services.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Travel companies in Japan have reported potential data breaches. The affected companies include Adventure, Skyticket, travel agency H.I.S. and travel technology company Temairazu. The company said Friday that data stored on internal servers and in the cloud had been accessed without authorization.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: SoftBank seeks $100 billion from Gulf states for AI, FT says
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Min Jeong Lee
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
SoftBank Group seeks to raise as much as $100 billion from Gulf investors to help it amp up its bets on artificial intelligence (AI), the Financial Times (FT) reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Founder Masayoshi Son has held early talks with potential investors including those in the United Arab Emirates, the newspaper said. The proposed fund would buy companies and use AI and machines, including from SoftBank’s robotics arm Roze, to improve operations, the FT said.

Fundraising of that scale would fuel more spending by the tech investment firm, which has invested almost $65 billion in OpenAI ahead of the AI lab’s public debut. The Japanese company is grappling with growing borrowing costs, while the ChatGPT-developer has pushed back its initial public offering. Still, Son has forecast big investment returns from AI advances, including in the realm of machines that manipulate real-world objects.

A SoftBank representative declined to comment. SoftBank shares dropped as much as 7.3% in Tokyo on Friday, weighed by concerns over the pace of OpenAI’s revenue growth.

The SoftBank chief has sought to position himself at the center of the AI industry, and for years had been able to raise billions of dollars at home and abroad to fulfill his vision.

But Son is now trying to get more capital from a region grappling with the threat of economic contraction from the Iran war, now entering its eighth month. In 2017, the entrepreneur obtained commitments of nearly $100 billion for the first Vision Fund, much of which came from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala. That first vehicle’s had a mixed record since, backing winners such as ByteDance but also high-profile flameouts like WeWork.

SoftBank would need to assure investors it can deliver on promises. In 2025, the company announced a $500 billion data center project in the U.S. in partnership with OpenAI, Oracle and Abu Dhabi’s state-backed AI investment firm MGX. That endeavor has yet to yield material progress.

Any fundraising would coincide with OpenAI’s efforts to raise another $30 billion in a new financing at a valuation of around $1.4 trillion. The firm is in talks with investment funds including MGX to help anchor the round.

SoftBank also plans to take Roze public in the U.S. Unit SB Energy, which is tasked with building an 8.8-gigawatt data center facility in Ohio, is also preparing to list on the Nasdaq.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: SoftBank Group seeks to raise as much as $100 billion from Gulf investors to help it amp up its bets on artificial intelligence (AI) Firm has invested almost $65 billion in OpenAI ahead of the AI lab’s public debut.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: Devjyot Ghoshal
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
BANGKOK – Ekniti Nitithanprapas was a young graduate student in the United States when Thailand devalued the baht in 1997, setting off the Asian financial crisis.

A loan from the International Monetary Fund and a raft of recovery measures helped Thailand find a way out of the economic morass.

Almost 30 years on, Bangkok will next week host the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank and Ekniti, now Thailand’s finance minister, is looking to steer the economy through a new challenge: how to escape years of sluggish growth.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: Yayoi Kusama Museum new  exhibit unveils a ‘ladder to heaven’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Zoria Petkoska
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
The first exhibition at the Yayoi Kusama Museum to open since the artist’s death in August begins with an installation titled “Life” in the museum’s first-floor lobby.

The allusion to mortality continues upward, with the fourth floor devoted to a single light installation, “Longing for Heaven.” The exhibition ends with a rooftop installation titled “Ladder to Heaven.”

The show’s title, too, sounds prophetic: “The Light Spreads Out, and Glittering Things Start Appearing All Around Me,” a direct quote from the artist. The museum’s curators say this was not deliberate, as the exhibition is refreshed twice a year and decisions were made months ago. Still, it’s hard not to see the exhibition, which opened Oct. 8, as a possible message from the afterlife.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.summary: The Yayoi Kusama Museum's first exhibition opened Oct. 8. The exhibition is the first since the artist's death in August. The museum's curators say this was not deliberate, as the exhibition is refreshed twice a year.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Walking through flames: Orangutan rescued in Indonesia fires
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
PALANGKARAYA, INDONESIA – The orangutan clings to the top of a mostly leafless tree in Indonesia’s Borneo, as waves of thick smoke from the forest fires burning below waft over her.

Nicknamed Novita, the ape shown in footage released by a conservation group is among dozens that have been rescued from wildfires burning across parts of Sumatra and Borneo in recent months.

They include Bara, a male orangutan plucked from the haze on Thursday, authorities said.

“He was found on top of a tree on razed land. The haze was quite thick in the area because fires were burning around there,” Handi Nasoka, a local natural resources conservation agency official, said on Friday.

“Seeing the condition of the recently burned lands ... we didn’t dare to gamble and assume he’ll survive.”

Bara was “relatively healthy, with minor burn injuries,” Handi added, and will be moved to a nature reserve elsewhere in the Central Kalimantan region where he was rescued.

Wildfires have piled pressure on already endangered orangutans, forcing local groups and authorities to carry out high-stakes rescues of animals suffering smoke inhalation and burns.

Novita, a female estimated to be 3 to 4byears old, remains at the Nyaru Menteng rehabilitation center in Indonesia’s Palangkaraya after being rescued last month.

“Novita is still receiving intensive care,” Andi Muhammad Khadafi, head of the Central Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency, told reporters on Thursday.

“We’ve been told that the burns on her hands and feet are improving, although even after she recovers, she may not return 100% to how she was before she suffered the burns.”

“She had to leave her habitat, and we had to rescue her, primarily because of the flames,” he added.

Novita was rescued by the Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation, which has taken in several apes caught up in forest fires.

She was found clinging to a tree in late September and tranquilized by a rescue team, who administered oxygen and intravenous fluids before moving her to the rehabilitation center.

“We rescued her from an area that was burning. Before we reached her, she had to walk through the fire to get to the tree and climb it, so the soles of her feet and her toes were burned,” said foundation CEO Jamartin Sihite.

Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, which in Borneo typically peaks between July and September.

The fires have intensified this year in part because of the El Nino weather phenomenon, set to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.

El Nino typically brings severe drought to Indonesia, but experts note that slash-and-burn practices and drying of peatlands have made previously resistant landscapes increasingly fire-prone.

Between January and July alone, more than 202,000 hectares were razed by fire, according to government figures that have not been updated since.

The Nusantara Atlas project, which uses satellite monitoring, estimated nearly 896,000 hectares — over five times the size of Greater London — had burned by the end of August.

The fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and also caused regional air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia.

Japan saw the average number of influenza patients jump to 11.35 per clinic for the week through Oct. 4, the health ministry said Friday, causing people to rush to get flu shots as an unusually early season hits the country.

The health ministry figure was about seven times higher than in the same period in 2025, which was 1.56. The latest numbers are up from 7.17 patients per monitored medical institution the week before.

The flu has been spreading rapidly particularly among children, with schools that closed classes rising sixfold week-over-week to 937.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.title: Inside the deadlock at the world’s top climate science body
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.author: Kate Abnett
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.text:
BRUSSELS/SINGAPORE – The decision was expected to take minutes. But after nearly three years of debate, members of the world’s leading authority on climate change still can’t agree on a timeline to publish its next review of the latest science on the warming planet.

Such assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have informed every major United Nations climate agreement for three decades. But the impasse over publication dates could leave countries to decide the next phase of action without consensus on critical issues — including the extent to which some global warming might be reversible — according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former IPCC scientists, government negotiators and meeting observers.

The dispute reflects deep rifts between wealthy industrialized nations, major emerging economies and poorer nations over how to respond to rapidly warming temperatures and how much of that burden should be shouldered by different countries.

On Monday, representatives from the IPCC’s 195 member states will convene in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, for a plenary meeting many see as the last chance to agree publication dates falling before U.N. climate talks in November 2028. That’s when governments are due to assess progress toward goals set out in the landmark agreement reached in Paris in 2015.

The U.N. Environment Program has said repeatedly that global efforts to limit warming are falling short and that faster emissions cuts are needed to avoid more extreme weather and climate-related disasters. Scientists have said climate change fueled wildfires that surged across Europe this summer and likely played a role in landslides and flash floods that killed hundreds in Nepal and China’s Tibet.

The possibility the IPCC’s reports might not be ready in time for the 2028 climate talks has alarmed a coalition of countries pushing for more robust action. Those discussions are intended to guide decisions on climate financing and national targets to bring down greenhouse gas emissions.

“Access to the latest and best available science … enables a just, equitable, evidence-based approach to addressing the greatest challenge of our time, rather than one driven by those whose entrenched interests are at odds with reducing greenhouse gases,” the High Ambition Coalition said in a statement due to be published on Friday.

The statement is signed by more than 30 countries, including European, Latin American and small-island states.

The IPCC does not conduct original research. But its reviews of the world’s existing knowledge on climate change — published every five to seven years — carry weight with governments because they are written by hundreds of international experts and approved by every member state. IPCC findings contributed to a commitment in the Paris Agreement to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Its reports are also used by governments to plan their responses to climate change and have been cited in international court rulings.

Countries including India, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Russia and China are pressing for more time to prepare the IPCC’s next reports to ensure scientists from less-resourced countries can make meaningful contributions. Some struggle to publish new research in time to be included or to take time off from their regular jobs for unpaid IPCC work, they say.

“If you have a process that goes very quickly … it wouldn’t be inclusive,” said Joyce Kimutai, a climate scientist who represents Kenya at the IPCC.

The deadlock — unprecedented in the IPCC’s history — comes as the organization faces increasing pressure from governments critical of climate policies they say hurt industrial competitiveness or restrict the ability of emerging economies to use cheaper, more polluting fuels to meet development needs. The United States, the IPCC’s biggest funder, quit the organization in January.

The IPCC will publish three key reports: one on the extent and causes of climate change, another on vulnerabilities and how countries can adapt, and a third on options to avoid warming getting worse. Scientists chairing groups preparing the reports have proposed a work plan that would see all three approved by September 2028.

Robert Vautard, a French co-chair, said the proposal was based on the anticipated workload rather than the timing of the 2028 U.N. summit. Report timelines are typically approved in “a matter of minutes,” he added.

Opponents of the chairs’ proposal want the second and third reports pushed into 2029, saying the timeline is too short to analyze thousands of studies, agree wording and complete expert and government reviews.

The dispute is sowing discord and distrust in an organization intended to help countries bridge divides by providing a scientific basis for climate negotiations. Observers at five previous IPCC meetings described days of contentious debate.

Participants have traded accusations of politicizing the IPCC’s work.

Some pushing to publish before the 2028 summit note that major oil-producing nations are among the most vocal advocates for more time, accusing them of trying to avoid pressure to reduce carbon dioxide emissions more quickly.

“The elephant in the room is the politics,” said Lisa Schipper, an IPCC editor from Sweden.

Some countries, she said, are using the debate as a “stalling tactic.”

Russia’s economy ministry said framing the debate as a confrontation with oil producers was a “deliberate misrepresentation.”

Attempts to synchronize the assessment cycle with U.N. negotiations “raise serious questions about preserving the IPCC’s independent nature,” the ministry said. “In such circumstances, there is a risk that scientific assessments could be used to advance a predetermined climate policy agenda.”

Thiagarajan Jayaraman, a scientist who represents India at the IPCC, said it was “short-sighted” to suggest the value of the body’s work rests solely on contributing to the 2028 U.N. talks. Representatives from Saudi Arabia and China have made similar arguments at previous meetings. Their governments did not respond to questions for this article.

Developing countries have long argued their perspectives are not sufficiently reflected in IPCC reports because they do not have enough experts involved and because their researchers have fewer resources to publish peer-reviewed studies.

The result, Thiagarajan said, is that issues of “equity and inclusivity” are in some instances “simply ducked.”

He takes issue, for example, with what he says is a lack of consideration of wealthy countries’ historical contributions to global warming and poorer nations’ development needs in models the IPCC uses to evaluate how much temperatures might rise under different emissions scenarios.

India argues countries that got rich through centuries of fossil fuel use should make the biggest emissions cuts. Some industrialized nations want major emerging economies such as India and China, now among the world’s biggest emitters, to also make ambitious cuts.

The IPCC says it is taking steps to make assessments more inclusive. Just over half the lead authors and editors selected for the next review are from developing economies or ones in transition.

The next reports will for the first time include chapters on climate finance and addressing irreversible harm inflicted on some countries, IPCC Chair Jim Skea said in June, issues important to many developing nations.

Jozef Pecho, a climatologist at GoSpace Labs in Slovakia who uses IPCC reports in his work, said he feared “the room for cherry picking and distorting science would grow” if governments don’t have an updated assessment for the 2028 U.N. talks.

Countries pushing for that timeline at the IPCC say negotiators would otherwise have to rely on reports published in 2021-22. Much has changed since then.

In 2024, global temperatures averaged more than 1.5 C above preindustrial levels for the first time. The next reports will attempt to fill knowledge gaps about the overshoot, including the potential consequences of interventions to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Joeri Rogelj, an IPCC author from Belgium, said there was no use in writing such assessments if they aren’t available when policy makers can use them.

“The importance of the IPCC … is that these authoritative assessments of science are being used,” he said.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/environment.summary: The dispute reflects deep rifts between wealthy industrialized nations, major emerging economies and poorer nations over how to respond to rapidly warming temperatures. The deadlock is unprecedented in the IPCC’s history. The next reports will attempt to fill knowledge gaps about the overshoot.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Okinawa resolution calls for revision of U.S. forces pact after murder
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Members of the Okinawa Prefectural Assembly adopted a resolution on Friday calling for revisions to a pact seen as giving the United States military preferential treatment in Japan, following a murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine.

The recent killing of a Japanese woman has triggered outrage in Japan, where any crimes involving U.S. forces have long inflamed criticism of the troops’ presence.

The resolution, which will soon be submitted to the U.S. Embassy, was carried 45 in favor and two against, local media said. The assembly also adopted an opinion statement to the same effect, which will be sent to the Japanese government.

“We are seeing the limitations of the U.S. military’s training program and ability to maintain discipline, and have to say that it is not functioning as an organization,” said Ryotaro Odo, who leads the assembly’s special committee on U.S. military bases.

The assembly called for a fundamental revision of the Japan Status of Forces Agreement, including provisions on the handing over of suspects.

That 1960 pact is often accused of rendering U.S. military bases virtually extraterritorial and immune to Japan’s domestic laws.

The prefectural assembly passed a similar resolution and opinion statement in 2024, following a series of sexual assaults by U.S. servicemen in Okinawa Prefecture, according to Kyodo News.

Police said on Sunday that a U.S. Marine stationed in Okinawa Prefecture had been arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet.

Local media reported the woman was choked to death and that the Marine is denying the allegations.

The U.S. has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly in Okinawa Prefecture.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run incidents and drunk-driving accidents by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests in the prefecture.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Government submits bill on food consumption tax reduction to parliament
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Eric Johnston
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government submitted the food consumption tax reduction bill to parliament Friday, setting the stage for intense discussions next week over its merits and risks to the economy, and whether other measures would be more beneficial.

The government plans to reduce the food and nonalcoholic beverage consumption tax, its signature policy, from 8% to 1% from April before returning it to 8% in 2029 when a new income-linked benefits system is to be introduced.

Next week’s debates will likely see opposition parties pressing the government to offer a clear plan of how it intends to make up lost tax revenue without hurting the larger economy and address concerns about whether it’s the best way to help consumers hit by high prices.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Erling Haaland calls for Manchester City fans to ‘stick together’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
MANCHESTER, ENGLAND – Manchester City striker Erling Haaland urged the embattled club’s supporters to stick together in his first public comments since City was found guilty of more than 100 charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial rules.

City has appealed against the independent commission’s verdict, insisting the judgment contained “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact.”

Asked what his message was to supporters ahead of what should be a combustible Premier League match at Liverpool on Sunday, Haaland called for unity and positivity amid the off-field turmoil.

“We have to stick together,“ the Norway striker told Sky Sports. “We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile.

“So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game.

“We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile.”

The independent commission found that City arranged “sham” contracts with several commercial partners as part of what it described as a “disguised funding scheme” that artificially inflated the club’s revenues and reduced its costs by more than £900 million ($1.19 billion).

The charges spanned nearly a decade.

Haaland, whose father Alf-Inge also played for City, said his connection to the club and the U.K. in general extended beyond playing for Enzo Maresca’s side.

“I care a lot about this place, and the U.K. generally, I care a lot about the fans because I’m a fan myself, and I feel with them as well,” he said.

City takes a three-point lead atop the table to Anfield on Sunday to face an opponent with whom it developed a fierce rivalry during Pep Guardiola’s battles with former Liverpool manager Juergen Klopp.

“It’s always special to play against Liverpool,” Haaland said. “Especially with Pep and Klopp. I remember sitting and watching the games (before signing with City), how much they pushed each other. It’s always special games there.

“I won there, I drew there, I lost. So it’s always special, and every Premier League game is different, and every game against Liverpool is always special.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.summary: Erling Haaland urges Manchester City supporters to stick together ahead of Sunday's clash with Liverpool. City's supporters have been accused of breaches of Premier League financial rules. Haal and his father Alf-Inge also played for City and the U.K.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Tokyo’s palace runners say respect vital as Chiyoda considers new safety measures
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Elizabeth Beattie
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
With views of Edo Period architecture, stunning foliage and the gleaming Marunouchi skyline, the 5-kilometer route that snakes around the Imperial Palace attracts thousands of runners each morning, wearing down the tread of their running shoes and working up a sweat as they keep pace around the beloved running track and mainstay of the Tokyo running scene.

But recently, the circuit, a rarity in the bustling capital given its close proximity to the central business district and long stretches unbroken by traffic lights, has made headlines for the wrong reasons. Angry commenters have argued on social media that runners pose a safety concern, particularly as more tourists congest the pathway.

“The Imperial Palace run — maybe it’s about time we banned it, huh? With more tourists around, and families with kids or elderly folks walking on what’s supposed to be an ordinary sidewalk, it’s pretty dangerous having runners zooming by one after another at a decent clip,” wrote one user on X in a post that has attracted 8,400 likes.

The 5-kilometer route is a rarity in the bustling capital given its close proximity to the central business district.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
BERLIN – Germany’s largest department store in Berlin, Kaufhaus des Westens (KaDeWe), will sell high-end brand rice from Japan on a trial basis for about two weeks this month, sources said Thursday.

The move comes as the Japanese side approached the department store about handling high-grade Japanese rice, at a time when the country aims to expand sales abroad through retail stores and people in Germany are increasingly interested in washoku Japanese cuisine.

Six varieties, including Yumepirika from Hokkaido and Koshihikari from Niigata Prefecture, will be available to purchase during the trial, set to run from Monday through Oct. 24.

Tastings will be available to allow customers to compare the flavors of the different rice varieties and produce from different regions. A leaflet on how to cook rice will also be distributed.

“We want people (in Germany) to find that rice flavors vary by production area, just like wine and olive oil,” an official from the Japanese side said.

The official added that the planned trial is also intended to raise awareness of high-quality Japanese rice as cheap non-Japanese rice is often used at washoku restaurants in Germany.

Between January and August, Japanese rice exports to Germany rose 15% compared to a year earlier to 699 metric tons, the largest among European countries.

MATSUDO, CHIBA PREF. – When Shuji Nishizawa and his wife bought their semi-basement apartment in 2003, the tiled garden terrace was the main draw. On Aug. 13, it became the floodwater’s way in.

Now, pointing to muddy lines that run across the walls 1.8 meters above the floor of his apartment, Nishizawa, 60, explains how the water rapidly rose during the torrential downpour that struck his neighborhood that evening.

Nishizawa, a self-employed web specialist, was in the common area of Sanctus Shinmatsudo, a 10-story apartment complex in Matsudo, Chiba Prefecture, when his wife rushed in to tell him that rainwater had begun gushing down the steps from ground level and pooling on their terrace.
