https://www.dw.com/en/india-cockroach-pa.title: India: Cockroach party denied permission to protest in Delhi, founder Dipke pushes on
https://www.dw.com/en/india-cockroach-pa.text:
Train cancellations have been reported in Delhi ahead of CJP’s protest tomorrow. There is heavy security in the capital. Police have denied permission to protest but CJP's leader has vowed to press on with the plan.

Here are our rolling updates from India on Friday, October 9:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

The recently-built Noida Airport at Jewar will be renamed Narendra Modi International Airport, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath announced on Friday.

Modi inaugurated the airport near Noida, one of Delhi's satellite cities, on March 28.

"The Council of Ministers of Uttar Pradesh expresses its gratitude to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for gifting the state the Noida International Airport at Jewar. The Cabinet has approved a proposal to name it Narendra Modi International Airport, Noida-Jewar," Adityanath, who belongs to Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said.

Uttar Pradesh, where the airport is located, is the most populous state in India and is bound for elections next year.

Leaders from the opposition INDIA bloc are expected to meet President Droupadi Murmu on Friday over their demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.

The reported meeting comes after opposition lawmakers, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, took to the streets in New Delhi's heart of political powerin daily protests this week.

The protests took place amid a heightened deployment of security personnel and led to Gandhi being briefly detained on two successive days, along with his sister and MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, congress workers and other opposition members.

The delegation of opposition leaders is reported to meet Murmu at 8 p.m. local time (1430 UTC).

India's Foreign Ministry said on Friday that steps announced by the United States concerning its Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) "do ​not ‌advance shared ambitions" of New Delhi and Washington.

The statement comes after the US suspended eight companies, including India's Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL, from filing for green cards for their foreign workers. (Scroll down our updates to read more on the US move).

Talent mobility is ​of "tremendous mutual benefit for ⁠the ​two countries and ​our expectation ​is all ‌stakeholders in ​this process ⁠can appreciate this fact," ⁠India's Ministry of External Affairs ​said.

The ministry clarified that the suspension of applications under PERM was distinct from the H-1B visa program.

"The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents, though there could be some impact on the permanent-residency/Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies," it said.

The ministry also appeared to criticize comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Thursday that described H-1B visa workers as "indentured servants".

"Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said.

It added that the "unwarranted" descriptions "ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem."

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abijeet Dipke said on Friday that he was poised to go on with the movement's planned protest in New Delhi on October 10, despite being denied permission by the police.

"Jantar Mantar is a designated protest site; Article 19 gives the fundamental right to protest. So, what is the need to get permission?" Dipke told news agency ANI as he declared that the rally would go ahead.

"Did they take permission before deleting 13 crore (130 million) votes? You want that we should not agitate against those who are rigging elections? This cannot be possible. The country cannot run like this. To save the nation, we will protest," he told ANI.

Protesters are calling for India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to step down over alleged irregularities in voter lists.

Police have not authorized the Cockroach Janta Party's planned demonstrations in New Delhi on Saturday.

The Delhi Police said on Friday that they had received an application from the CJP on October 7 informing them of the protest but it was on "very short notice."

"Our established guidelines require such requests to be submitted 10 days prior to the planned protest, which was not the case here," Joint Commissioner of Delhi Police Nupur Prasad told a press conference.

The official went on to add that CJP's alleged violation of rules during their previous protest was taken into account in denying them permission to protest.

Prasad said that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law was in force in the New Delhi area, barring any form of assembly or protest.

Over 20,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed in the city ahead the planned protest, according to news agency PTI.

Indian Railways has canceled mail and express trains scheduled to arrive at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations between 4 a.m. and 2 p.m. on October 10 amid a protest called by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), Indian media reports said Friday.

The Times of India cited an internal railway order as saying that the decision was made due to "anticipated severe road traffic congestion" around the two major stations in the capital.

Meanwhile, Delhi police have proposed the closure of entry and exit gates at 57 metro stations in the capital and reducing train frequency at the stations, news agency ANI reported, citing an official communication.

India's Cockroach movement leaders have been sounding the bugle for a nationwide march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on October 10 to demand the resignation of the country's top poll official.

In a setback for Indian IT workers, the United States has suspended Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL from its Permanent Labor Certification program.

The certification allows employers to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers.

The Indian companies are on a list of eight major tech firms, including Microsoft, which have been barred from applying for the program under which foreign employees can work permanently in the US.

The Trump administration said an alleged abuse of the program was behind its decision.

"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Thursday.

Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into the companies.

Indian media reports have said that the move could potentially impact thousands of the country's IT professionals.

According to reported figures, Indian applicants secured nearly 70% of all US H-1B visa approvals in the 2025 fiscal year.

News agency ANI on Friday cited a report by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) as saying that the US green card freeze is a warning for the Indian IT sector to prepare for broader restrictions on foreign workers.

The New Delhi-based think tank advised that Indian IT companies should diversify export markets, strengthen delivery from India and expand local hiring in the US where needed, ANI reported.

It also called for more focus on artificial intelligence to reduce the sector's vulnerability to sudden changes in US policy, according to ANI.

As the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ramps up its call for a protest march in New Delhi on October 10 over alleged voter roll manipulation, the youth-led movement has accused India's authorities of mass detentions of its members.

CJP spokesperson Deepak Baliyan and activists from across the country were among those arrested, CJP leaders said in a series of social media posts on Thursday night.

Baliyan was released later in the evening after being arrested by Rajasthan police at his house, CJP Co-Convener Ashutosh Ranka said on X on Friday.

Ranka claimed that at least 10,000 people were detained country-wide on Thursday.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke alleged on X that a group of the movement's volunteers from the state of Telangana were arrested by Madhya Pradesh police onboard a train in Bhopal.

The movement earlier said that a group of students from the western Indian city of Pune who were headed for the planned protest in Delhi were also detained. The CJP said they were being taken on a bus to an unknown location.

There have been no police statements on the alleged detentions so far.

Leaders of the CJP have railed against the alleged mass arrests, likening the situation to a "state of emergency."

"Why not just declare EMERGENCY?", Dipke said as he reacted to a video of the students from Pune purportedly being detained.

The last time an emergency decree was issued in India was under former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were applied by the Congress leader for 21 months, with civil liberties being suspended, most of the opposition being jailed and media censored.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) calls the period  a "dark chapter" in India's history.

Another prominent CJP spokesperson Saurav Das accused the Modi government of being "at war with its own young citizens."

"Hello India. We are under a State of Emergency," Das wrote on X.

Meanwhile, founder 'Cockroach' Dipke has said that he will land in Delhi on Saturday and march to Jantar Mantar.

"This intimidation is not going to work, Modi. The youth of this country are no longer scared of you," Dipke said.

Thousands are expected to converge at the capital's Jantar Mantar protest site on Saturday to participate in CJP's protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Jantar Mantar served as ground-zero for the viral online Cockroach movement's debut protest in July which culminated with the resignation of the then-education minister.

The CJP, opposition parties and their student units have been holding near-daily demonstrations against Kumar.

Around 130 million names have been removed from electoral rolls under an exercise called Special Intensive Revision (SIR).

Opposition leaders and critics say that those struck off the lists include a huge number of minority voters.

They accuse Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains, questioning the independence of the Election Commission of India (ECI), which is overseeing the exercise.

The ECI and the BJP deny the allegations.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily capsule of all the biggest headlines creating a stir in India.

Protests over the deletion of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls have gripped the world's largest democracy.

The bloc of parties opposing Prime Minister Narendra Modi — rallied by Modi's main political adversary Rahul Gandhi —  has been taking to the streets of the Indian capital since Wednesday. In turn, Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were briefly detained on two consecutive days.

Now, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement has accused the Indian authorities of mass detentions ahead of their planned protest in New Delhi tomorrow.

Parts of central Delhi remain under heavy security, with reports saying that thousands of additional paramilitary personnel are being deployed to the capital over the protests.

In other news, Indian IT bigwigs Infosys, Tata, Wipro and  HCL have found themselves among a list of companies suspended from the United States green card program.

Follow along for more.
https://www.dw.com/en/india-cockroach-pa.summary: U.S. suspends Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL from its Permanent Labor Certification program. The certification allows employers to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers.

https://www.dw.com/en/two-german-officia.title: Two German officials shot dead during routine gun inspection in Bavaria; suspect arrested after overnight standoff
https://www.dw.com/en/two-german-officia.text:
A routine inspection of legally owned firearms turned deadly in Bavaria. Police spent hours negotiating with an armed suspect before storming his home. Follow DW for more.

Two local government employees have been shot dead while checking whether legally owned firearms were being correctly stored

Germany's army plans to purchase cruise missiles for mass deployment

German Chancellor Merz has sharply criticized ex-Chancellor Schröder for attending Vladimir Putin's birthday party

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germanyon Friday, October 9, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

The German government paid its tribute to Navi Pillay shortly after the announcement of her award.

Pillay's work fighting against apartheid and for human rights, justice and international law deserves the "highest respect," government spokesman Steffen Meyer said in Berlin.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Pillay "stood for the idea that peace is grounded in justice."

He went on to praise her for her verdicts at the ICJ concerning the genocide in Rwanda and her work as head of the UN human rights commission.

Awarding her the Nobel Peace Prize not only honored her own work, but was also an "important commitment to international criminal justice."

Two local government employees have been shot dead during a routine firearms inspection at a home in southern Germany, police said.

A 60-year-old suspect was arrested early Friday following a standoff lasting more than 12 hours in the Bavarian village of Berngau. (Scroll down for more on the man's arrest)

The victims, a 45-year-old man and a 54-year-old woman, worked for the district administration in Neumarkt in der Oberpfalz.

They had visited the suspect's home on Thursday to conduct a routine inspection of legally owned firearms, including whether the weapons were being stored correctly.

Police believe the suspect opened fire on the two officials during the inspection.

Witnesses reported hearing gunshots at around 2 p.m. local time (1200 GMT), prompting a major police operation.

Officers found the 45-year-old government official dead outside the house. The woman's body was subsequently discovered inside the building.

Police believe both victims died shortly after the shooting.

Germany's chancellor Friedrich Merz has sharply criticized former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder for  attending President Vladimir Putin's birthday bash, a German government spokesperson said on Friday.

"Putin alone" is responsible for the war in Ukraine, and his orders cause "immeasurable suffering, civilian casualties, families torn apart, and deaths and injuries" every day, spokesperson Steffen Meyer said.

For that reason, "the chancellor sees ... it ⁠is downright immoral for Mr. Schröder to ‌attend such a ⁠celebration," he added.

The German Foreign Office and Interior Ministry said they had not been informed of this trip in advance.

Putin celebrated his 74th birthday at his home in Moscow.

According to the Kremlin, the Russian leader learned from the media that Schröder was "in Moscow on business" and invited "his old friend."

The Nobel Peace Prize announcement is always eagerly anticpated, and this year the news had special resonance in one corner of Germany. That's because the laureate, Navi Pillay, received the news in the Bavarian city of Nuremberg.

The South African judge, and former UN human rights chief, is attending the Nuremberg Forum to discuss international law.

And the significance of the location was not lost on Pillay. Nuremberg is where Nazi war criminals went on trial after World War II.

Those trials helped lay the foundation of international law.

"Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me," she said to a standing ovation. "You know, you don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's army has decided to acquire large numbers of low-cost cruise missiles capable of striking targets up to 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) away.

Army chief Lieutenant General Christian Freuding announced the decision at a military gathering in Berlin, saying the weapons would be used to overwhelm enemy air defenses through sheer numbers.

The move reflects lessons from the war in Ukraine, where drones and missiles have been deployed in large numbers to exhaust air defenses. Launching numerous relatively cheap weapons simultaneously can force defenders to expend expensive interceptor missiles, potentially allowing more sophisticated weapons to reach their targets.

Germany plans to combine the cheaper missiles with more powerful weapons designed to strike strategically important targets, including US-made cruise missiles it intends to purchase.

Freuding said the army was considering two commercially available systems, although neither had yet been approved for use by the German armed forces. Initial deliveries could begin in 2027.

US defense company Covenant opened a cruise missile production facility in Leipzig earlier this week. It plans to manufacture 1,000 Anthem missiles in 2027 and 5,000 in 2028.

The company says each missile would cost a six-figure sum, below €860,000 ($1 million), compared with several million dollars for conventional cruise missiles.

Deaths from heart attacks in Germany fell by more than 15% between 2022 and 2025, according to figures released by the Federal Statistical Office.

Deaths from cerebrovascular diseases, including strokes and brain hemorrhages, also declined by 6.3% over the same period.

However, deaths from respiratory diseases rose by around 8% in 2025 compared with the previous year, reaching 81,200.

Overall, Germany recorded around 1.01 million deaths in 2025, virtually unchanged from the previous year. The total was nevertheless 5.6% lower than in 2022.

Despite the decline in heart attack and stroke-related deaths, cardiovascular disease remained Germany's leading cause of death, accounting for 334,100 deaths in 2025.

Heart attack deaths fell among both men and women, with the sharpest decline, 30.6%, among people aged 80 to 85.

It is not clear what is behind the decline. Changes in population size and age structure may have contributed, as the statistics are not adjusted for age.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nearly 65,000 young people left school in Germany without obtaining a basic school-leaving qualification in the 2024/2025 academic year, according to figures from the Federal Statistical Office.

The figure rose from 62,000 the previous year and 56,000 two years earlier, continuing an upward trend that has raised concerns about educational standards and Germany's shortage of skilled workers.

The proportion of students leaving school without at least a Hauptschulabschluss, Germany's basic secondary school qualification, reached 8.4% in 2024/2025.

That compares with 6.6% in 2018/2019 and around 5.5% in 2013/2014.

The latest rate is the highest recorded in 20 years, although it was even higher around the turn of the millennium.

The number of school leavers without qualifications has also risen substantially over the past decade, from around 47,400 in 2014/2015.

Numbers temporarily fell during the COVID-19 pandemic, potentially reflecting relaxed examination requirements, before beginning to climb again.

The figures were obtained by the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), a political party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht.

German police have begun excavating land in the southern state of Bavaria in a renewed search for a woman who disappeared without a trace almost two decades ago.

Investigators say new information suggests that the remains of Kerstin Lee Langley, missing since the summer of 2007, could be buried in a meadow and woodland near the village of Kadenzhofen, north of Neumarkt in der Oberpfalz.

Specialists from Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office and the Regensburg criminal police department are examining an area covering approximately 100 square meters (1,076 square feet).

An excavator is removing soil in layers, which investigators then examine for possible evidence.

Police spokesperson Corinna Wild told public broadcaster BR24 that investigators were following specific information suggesting Langley's body could be buried at the site.

Police told DW they had ruled out any connection between the search and a fatal shooting just a few kilometers away in the village of Berngau, where two local government employees were killed during a routine firearms inspection at around the same time on Thursday afternoon.

Police said a man who opened fire on local government employees in the southern town of Berngau barricaded himself inside his home and contacted their operations center by telephone.

He admitted firing shots, said he had firearms in his possession and warned that he would not surrender without resistance.

Special police units, including a tactical response team with an armored vehicle, were deployed to the village. A police helicopter was also used, while residents were advised to stay indoors or avoid the cordoned-off area.

Negotiators spent hours trying to persuade the suspect to surrender peacefully.

"We always try to achieve a peaceful solution, and that generally happens through communication," a police spokesperson said.

However, at around 2:20 a.m. (0020 GMT/UTC) Friday, officers entered the building using explosives.

Police said officers fired shots during the operation, lightly wounding the suspect in the leg. He was subsequently given medical treatment.

Police have not yet established why the suspect allegedly opened fire on the two officials.

Investigators from the Regensburg criminal police department are expected to question the man in coordination with prosecutors in Nuremberg-Fürth.

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us after what should have been a routine firearms inspection ended with two local government employees dead in a Bavarian village.

The two officials had gone to a home in Berngau on Thursday to check whether legally owned guns were being stored correctly.

Police believe the 60-year-old homeowner shot them both.

Officers responding to reports of gunfire found one of the officials, a 45-year-old man, dead outside the house. The body of his 54-year-old female colleague was later discovered inside.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

Heart attack deaths fell among men and women, with the sharpest decline, 30.6% among people aged 80 to 85. Nearly 65,000 young people left school without a basic school-leaving qualification.

https://www.dw.com/en/90s-art-scene-in-t.title: 90s art scene in the UK: An international, edgy trendsetter
https://www.dw.com/en/90s-art-scene-in-t.text:
The 1990s are remembered for Britpop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the familiar icons.

The 1990s in Britain are often remembered through a haze of nostalgia consisting of rave culture, Britpop and provocative art and fashion by the likes of Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen.

Undeniably, the decade was a time of major change in British society — the long reign of Margaret Thatcher had come to an end and the West entered a period of relative post-Cold War stability.

Meanwhile, British cultural icons like Oasis, the Spice Girls and Vivienne Westwood garnered international fame.

But Tate Britain's new exhibition "The 90s: Art and Fashion," which opens on October 8 and runs through February 14, 2027, urges viewers to look beyond the familiar names and images.

Even though now prominent artists such as Damien Hirst and Juergen Teller are among the show's 70 contributors, the exhibition also aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities which were left out of the mainstream discourse.

After all, says chief curator Edward Enninful in the exhibition's program, "the energy of the 90s was not concentrated in a single movement, but distributed across communities, disciplines and geographies that have not always been equally represented."

For Enninful, the exhibition is personal: The Ghanaian-born British fashion editor, stylist and creative director became the youngest-ever fashion director of i-D Magazine in the 90s at age 18, helping shape the diverse and experimental London fashion scene of the 1990s. He later became editor-in-chief of British Vogue in 2017.

Enninful writes that he and his co-curators aimed to present a body of work which "reflects a broader landscape of practices and voices that shaped the period, many of which operated beyond the structures of visibility at the time." The exhibition pays special attention to artists of color and women whose work was not necessarily showcased as prominently at the time.

Black masculinity became "a site of cultural negotiation" in Britain in the 90s, writes co-curator Helen Little in the program text: "Figures such as Chris Ofili, Steve McQueen, Keith Piper, Koto Bolofo and Ozwald Boateng reimagined the Black masculine, challenging the racist specter of Black men, who had been defined as part of a masculinity crisis linked to post-industrial decline and excluded from the narrative of 'Cool Britannia.'"

Just like "Swinging London" in the 1960s, "Cool Britannia" became a widespread phrase to refer to the 1990s as an era during which British youth culture, pop music, art and political optimism boomed.

The 90s also offered artists plenty of chances to create without waiting for support from traditional gatekeepers. Britain entered the decade in recession, but that economic uncertainty also left artists free to do what they wished.

Empty buildings and industrial spaces were turned into informal venues. A 23-year-old Damien Hirst orchestrated "Freeze," a self-organized student exhibition in 1988 in a disused London warehouse. It became a landmark early art exhibition for the generation of artists known as the "Young British Artists" or YBA.

Artists Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin opened The Shop, a temporary art gallery and social space in 1992, as a place where exhibitions could develop outside established galleries. Lucas and Emin also paved the way for women artists thanks to their deeply personal works and their edgy expressions of female liberation.

While the Spice Girls helped make feminism accessible to a younger generation of Brits in the 90s by popularizing the "girl power" slogan and shaping "identity through agency power and resistance," as Tate curator Helen Little argues, Emin and Lucas meanwhile "presented a new visual language of clothing as art to tackle societal taboos around female sexuality, vulnerability and desire" — from t-shirts with provocative slogans to a grunge look of scuffed Dr. Martens boots with razor blades. Their work "held a mirror up to gender, behavior and identity," Little writes.

At the same time, the British fashion industry came into the international spotlight.

In a feminine sensuality counter to the gender stereotypes dismissed by Emin and Lucas, waif-like Kate Moss came to represent the feminine ideal of the 1990s. Dubbed "heroin-chic," the style was an antithesis to the glamorous, athletic physiques of the supermodels who preceded her. Corinne Day's photographs of the model led to the raw aesthetic to be labelled "grunge" after the anguished style of rock music hailing from Seattle and led by Nirvana.

The trend has undergone significant cultural reexamination since then: "Along with the look also came criticism that the strung-out look of drug or alcohol addiction was glamorized while encouraging serious eating disorders in a generation of young women," points out Alex Farquharson, director of the Tate Gallery in his foreword to the exhibition.

The 1990s were also an exciting era for Britain in haute couture, as legendary designers John Galliano led Dior, while Alexander McQueen started directing Givenchy at the age of 27.

McQueen's runway presentations were more akin to performance art than commercial fashion shows — and they often included historical critiques. Among them was the famous finale of his Fall/Winter 1998 collection at a London warehouse, during which the model stood in a circle of flames. Titled "Joan," the show was a reference to the killing of Joan of Arc.

McQueen designed several other runway shows that reflected on British history, with topics of conquest and punishment repeatedly coming to the forefront. His 1995 presentation "Highland Rape" referenced the history of Scotland's subjugation, with the designer describing it as "England's rape of Scotland."

As co-curator Jessica Vaughan points out in her exhibition text: "Art, fashion and photography were not simply transgressive reactions … but reflected a genuine public unease with Britain's global identity and its past."

In a world that can now feel increasingly mediated by screens, algorithms and established platforms, the artwork of the 90s offers a reminder of the value of physical spaces and fresh DIY creativity of the last smartphone-free decade.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier
https://www.dw.com/en/90s-art-scene-in-t.summary: "The 90s: Art and Fashion" urges viewers to look beyond familiar names and images. The show aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities left out of the mainstream discourse.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.

In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.

Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.

Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.

Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.

During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.

But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.

Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.

Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.

US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.

One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.

Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.

Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."

But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.

On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".

In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".

Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.

This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.

Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwkg.title: Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwkg.text:
Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.

The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.

The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.

Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.

The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.

The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled

"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.

Further details of their recovery were due to be revealed later on Friday.

The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.

Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.

Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August.

France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.

Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours.

They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.

The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

The paintings were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window. Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c862y6.title: Why is it so hard to put out Indonesian fires shrouding the region in toxic smog?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c862y6.text:
Wildfires have been burning throughout parts of Indonesia for weeks, sending smoke across the country and into neighbouring Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.

The BBC’s Gavin Butler explains why the fires are so difficult to battle and produce so much toxic haze.

The municipality building in Baglung was left teetering on an unstable ledge due to floods before it fell into a river.

Days of near continuous downpours have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital.

The BBC is in Inner Mongolia where dozen of Chinese data centres are being constructed, as the country aims to lead the world in artificial intelligence.

Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions.

Verified footage appears to show a cargo ship colliding with a fishing boat near Singapore, with investigators still working to establish exactly when and how the crash happened.

The BBC goes inside a fortified storage facility to view luxury goods seized by police that are now up for auction.

Rescuers are searching for survivors after the vessel travelling from the mainland to a popular tourist destination caught fire.

There are still hundreds of workers trapped in a network of tunnels that run along the Trishuli river.

BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is in Nepal where authorities are trying to begin rebuilding amid the debris.

Galaxy Robot Park is a 16,500-square-meter venue in South Korea, with attractions including humanoid robots dancing to K-pop hits.

The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made using cold water.

Wildfires in Indonesia have destroyed part of the natural habitat of hundreds of orangutans, risking the survival of the species.

The BBC reports from Sano Barkhu, a village overlooking the town of Syfrubesi, which was destroyed by the Nepal flooding.

Rescue dogs searched for flood victims in Tibet while authorities worked through the night at a Nepal power plant where hundreds are missing.

A 17-year-old boy has gone viral for wearing a superhero costume while volunteer firefighting in Indonesia, as the country faces a super El Niño.

Thousands in Nepal are still waiting to be rescued, but unpredictable weather is making such operations increasingly difficult.

Footage of the flash floods have become almost impossible to find on China’s heavily censored internet.

A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator.

The BBC’s Helena Humphrey visited Isha Foundation in the US state of Tennessee, that lost contact with their tour group on the China-Nepal border.

Laura Bicker explains how a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border is raising fears of a second flood.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j9.title: Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6j9.text:
Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.

The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.

It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.

While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.

The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.

But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.

Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".

But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it "deeply wrong" and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.

"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn.

"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."

Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human, reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.

The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.

It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom, it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".

Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.

But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.

It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.

Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.

Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.

When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".

The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools.

Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.

Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn8.title: 'Tropical jungle' of wallabies, porcupines and parrots must move after neighbours complain
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn8.text:
A man who lives in a log cabin and keeps wallabies, mongooses, porcupines, parrots and other rare birds has been told to move.

James Wale relocated to the rural Carmarthenshire site two years ago, having previously run a rare bird business in Pembrokeshire.

Neighbours said the site sounded like a "tropical jungle", especially at night.

Carmarthenshire Council issued Wale with an enforcement notice alleging he had broken planning rules, but he has been given more time to relocate the animals.

Planning agents representing the bird enthusiast said he wanted to create a "major tourism venture", and that his former business in the grounds of Picton Castle ended because the lease was not renewed.

Wale moved to the 17-acre woodland near Llannon and had hoped to set up an owl garden centre, but scaled back his plans to create a private bird welfare home along with some forestry and farming activities.

As well as the exotic animals, Wale also kept horses, goats, chickens and ducks, according to the enforcement appeal.

Documents said the abandoned venture planned to include "reptile, mongoose and several animal enclosures".

A planning application was then prepared for a smaller-scale venture including about 30 bird and animal enclosures, with Wale not intending to live onsite.

Two enforcement notices were issued by the council last year, one of which was withdrawn, and another sent this year which told him to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and stop keeping non-agricultural birds and animals.

During the subsequent appeal, seven objectors expressed concerns about the changes at the land linked to sanitation, stray animals and unusual noises.

One objector said the noises were "not those of native species".

Another claimed the noise "often sounds like a tropical jungle" which, along with the sound of generators and dog-barking, was "particularly troublesome late at night".

A further comment said the site had become waterlogged, turning a "once beautiful forest" into a "fly-tipping incident".

The person submitted a photo of goats and a Labrador to the council and said they had strayed onto their land.

Llannon councillor Llinos Mai Davies claimed the site adversely affected neighbouring properties and had a negative impact on the character of the area.

Photos of the land were submitted showing the boggy conditions and the woodland access track off the A476.

A planning inspector appointed by Welsh ministers has now dismissed the appeal after seeing the cabin during a visit to the land.

"The appellant keeps a few chickens, ducks and horses on site along with a variety of more unusual animals including eagles, falcons, parrots, hornbills, mongooses, skunks, porcupine and wallaby," they said.

The inspector said there was a minor element of forestry and agricultural activity taking place, but that the main operation was of a "fundamentally different character" and unauthorised.

Wale should be given 12 rather than six months to stop using the land to keep non-agricultural animals, remove the enclosures and restore the site to its original condition, the inspector concluded.

"Given the unusual type and mix of the animals, it may well take more time to find a suitable alternative location," they added.

Wale also has 12 months to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and its associated foul drainage.

His agents told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that a planning application would be drawn up in a bid to keep the birds on site.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqn8.summary: James Wale relocated to the rural Carmarthenshire site two years ago. He had previously run a rare bird business in Pembrokeshire. Council issued him with an enforcement notice alleging he had broken planning rules. He has been given more time to relocate the animals, but has been told to move.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8.title: Autism, ADHD and mental health review: What you need to know
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8.text:
It has been called a "generational opportunity" to rethink support for both mental health conditions and ADHD and autism.

The review, commissioned by then-health secretary Wes Streeting 10 months ago after saying young people were being "over-diagnosed" and "written off", could have major implications for NHS services, the benefits system, schools and employment support.

Its 600-plus pages contain a host of conclusions and recommendations. Here are the key takeaways.

The report is clear that there is an increasing risk of over-diagnosis, but only when it comes to ADHD and autism.

Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups.

They gave the example of children aged six to 17 – more than 4% have been diagnosed with autism. That's well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level.

But this comes with a big caveat. There are weaknesses in the data. Evidence about the true level of autism relies on surveys that have not been done for nine years, so the review team have had to estimate what has happened since.

And there are some age groups where these conditions are still being under-diagnosed, and that should not be overlooked.

It is why the review team said it could not yet conclude over-diagnosis was happening "at scale". But there is certainly evidence to suggest we are moving from an era of under-diagnosis to one of over-diagnosis, the experts said.

They warn not every difficulty requires a medical response and there is a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the "normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour".

Where the review team very clearly rejects the idea of over-diagnosis is with mental health. In fact, the chair, Prof Peter Fonagy, has said Streeting was "completely wrong" on that.

He said the increase in mental distress is real – one in four 16 to 24-year-olds are now thought to experience it, up from one in six 30 years ago. He links this to a variety of factors including economic uncertainty, the impact of social media and loss of youth services.

This contrasts with autism and ADHD. While diagnoses have increased, the true level in the whole population (regardless of whether they have come forward or not) has remained broadly stable, according to best estimates.

What is not happening with mental health, though, is an increase in severe mental illness. Population rates of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, for example, have remained stable.

Instead, what is driving the rise is conditions such as anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders.

Where the review experts share, to some extent, Streeting's concerns is on the impact of diagnosis.

They said there was a risk it ends up closing doors to opportunities.

It can, they said, act as a label that defines them by their "difficulties" rather than "strengths and potential".

This then hampers them in education, work and relationships.

Around a third of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (NEET) report their mental health or autism as a factor.

Those diagnosed with ADHD before the age of 17 are four times more likely to be a NEET than those without.

Addressing this, they said, would require better support post-diagnosis. Some of that is down to the NHS, but as important is the approach of schools, workplaces and wider society.

Another area where the review team is united in its view is that the support system is "falling short" of what people need for both mental health and neurological conditions such as ADHD and autism.

Waiting times for assessment are too long. A third of young people referred to mental health services wait more than a year, while of the 900,000 people waiting for ADHD or autism checks, 90% have waited more than three months.

In the lead up to publication of the report, NHS Alliance, which represents health bosses, said the system was in chaos.

But this goes further than the NHS. The report said support across care, education, employment and welfare remains fragmented, with people having to "jump through hoops" and face repeated assessment and conflicting requirements to get support.

No time should be wasted in tackling these challenges, the review says.

On long waits, it says everyone on a waiting list should be reassessed so that those most in need are prioritised for help. There should no longer be a first-come, first-served approach.

Some of those waiting may benefit from non-medical support, advice about sleeping better or getting more physical exercise, for example. That may even lead to some being removed from the waiting list.

There should also be better assessments before people are placed on waiting lists too. Not every problem needs a medical solution, the experts make clear.

Quality and consistency of autism and ADHD assessments must be improved, with the review highlighting concerns about those done by the private sector on behalf of the NHS. Half of ADHD and a third of autism assessments are done by non-NHS providers, such as charities and private firms.

But they are not subject to the same regulation as NHS providers – and this must change.

The experts also said it wanted to see a ban on direct-to-public advertising of assessments.

The review has said it wants to see action over the next 12 to 24 months. The government has promised to act – and is expected to set out more details in its forthcoming mental health strategy which is expected by the end of the year.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8.summary: Review team says there is an increasing risk of over-diagnosis. But only when it comes to ADHD and autism, it says. Government has promised to act – and is expected to set out more details in its forthcoming mental health strategy.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63r.title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63r.text:
Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.

In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.

He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.

Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.

Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.

Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.

He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."

Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".

Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".

It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico and the Financial Times, alongside the Budget on 28 October.

The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.

The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.

He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.

He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.

He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.

He also hinted that the government was looking at ensuring the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.

He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."

"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63r.summary: Andy Burnham says non-compete clauses in employment contracts have "gone too far" He says they have forced workers to leave their jobs and made it harder for firms to hire new staff. He also says there is "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.title: Ex-first minister Mark Drakeford suggests Wales Office should go
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.text:
Former Labour First Minister Mark Drakeford has said it is time to consider scrapping the UK government's Wales Office.

Drakeford said "the time has come" to think about abolishing the department, which was largely stripped of its powers when devolution began in 1999.

Asked on S4C's Y Byd yn ei Le if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that."

But Labour MP Ruth Jones described the suggestion as "foolish", arguing Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock was "fighting the corner for Wales".

The future of the Wales Office has been the subject of regular speculation since devolution, with successive UK governments considering whether its functions could be folded into a single department, also covering Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Earlier this year, then-First Minister Eluned Morgan said there remained "a role" for the Welsh secretary, but argued the post should be "the voice of Wales at the cabinet table" rather than "the UK government's voice in Wales".

Under a previous UK Labour government, Peter Hain combined cabinet responsibility for Wales and Northern Ireland between 2005 and 2007.

Asked if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that.

"Of course, [former Labour prime minister] Tony Blair thought of this too.

"This has been part of discussions in Westminster not only now but for more than a decade."

The post of Welsh secretary, or secretary of state for Wales, was created by Harold Wilson's Labour government in October 1964, with the Welsh Office opening the following April.

In 1999 the Welsh Office's powers over areas including health, education, environment, agriculture and transport were taken over by the Welsh Assembly, now known as the Senedd, and what remained of the UK government department was given the title of Wales Office.

Interviewed on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday, Ruth Jones dismissed the idea of abolishing it.

"I've got tremendous respect for Mark Drakeford but, let's be honest, he's now retired and, therefore, let the politicians who are elected to get on with the job get on with the job," she said.

"In terms of the Wales Office, the only person from Wales actually at the [UK] cabinet table is the secretary of state for Wales, and he is there fighting the corner for Wales.

"So I would say to disband that would be foolish."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.summary: Former Labour First Minister Mark Drakeford says it is time to consider abolishing Wales Office.
