Facing allegations of forced labor, Chinese aquaculture companies have sought help from international seafood quality-assurance outfits to reassure consumers worldwide. Those organizations—Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP) among the most prominent—claim they are independent entities with exacting standards.

Despite the fact Xinjiang has been almost completely closed to independent outside investigation since 2017 and despite the Chinese state not typically allowing unannounced inspections relating to labor, environmental or human-rights abuses, Tianyun has claimed to hold multiple international certifications, including from BAP, according to a 2023 article by Seafood Guide.

Many researchers and ocean-sustainability advocates therefore regard BAP and similar firms as unable or disinclined to root out problems.

In a May 2024 open letter, more than 70 environmental, animal welfare and community organizations accused BAP of “greenwashing,” arguing that certified farms are “rarely, if ever, held to account for adverse outcomes” tied to their operations.

Indeed, with increasing frequency, provincial Chinese agricultural departments have found illegal levels of drugs in the Chinese farmed fish, such as antibiotics at levels that threaten humans and dangerous use of sedatives, such as diazepam, to calm fish during transport.

In response to such criticism, the organization behind the BAP—the Global Seafood Alliance—told The Outlaw Ocean Project that “BAP certification is the most comprehensive certification program for farmed seafood,” and noted the introduction of “additional social responsibility clauses to strengthen human rights requirements.”

The Aquaculture Stewardship Council, the other major global certification body, announced in 2024 that it would withdraw from China. While it cited financial considerations, industry reporting linked the decision to an investigation documenting the widespread use of state-sponsored forced labor, including Uyghur and North Korean workers, in Chinese seafood-processing plants.

Despite the accomplishment of building roughly 250 farms in and around the desert, authorities in Beijing have yet to crack what might be the single greatest challenge to its aquaculture: feeding the fish themselves.

The only commercially viable option at scale remains fishmeal: a pulverized, protein-rich powder made from wild-caught fish. Globally, more than a fifth of all fish harvested ends up as fishmeal or animal feed.

While China’s farms historically relied on forage fish pulled from its own coastal waters, the pressure proved unsustainable.

Of fifteen fish species assessed in a 2019 Frontiers in Marine Science study, eleven were overfished, depleted or outside safe biological limits—five of them forage fish. To ease the strain, China cut its near-shore fleet by roughly 40,000 vessels in 2020 and has increasingly turned to imported fishmeal, especially from Peru. Today, China imports more than 40 percent of the world’s fishmeal, a share projected to rise to 55 percent by 2032.

“China wants food autonomy,” said Philip Chou, a China specialist with the environmental group Oceana. “But to get there, it’s also going to need feed autonomy.” Right now, Chou said, China has neither.

China’s efforts to sell the world on its Xinjiang farmed fish has gone well beyond touting certifications by supposedly independent monitors.

Since 2022, China has carefully controlled media tours for foreign reporters and actively recruited foreign food buffs—called vloggers or “frontier influencers”—to record and post videos and other testimonials about the wonders of growing fish in “The Sea of Death.”

A video from an American vlogger showcased his tour of a fish farm located on the edge of the Taklamakan: “It’s incredible how they have developed such a barren land to this extent.”

But it’s the government itself that frames the industry in the grandest terms.

In a 2025 article published by state media, establishing farms in the forbidding western frontier was declared “a testament to human ingenuity and resilience.”

“Xinjiang’s aquaculture is not merely about producing fish,” the article went on, “it is about reimagining how inland regions can contribute to the nation’s protein security, how technology can redefine agriculture, and how harmony between people and nature can be sustained in the most challenging of environments. From snow-fed rivers to desert oases, Xinjiang has shown that blue dreams can indeed flourish on dry land.”

Beijing presents Xinjiang’s aquaculture boom as proof that technology can conquer geography. For foreign consumers, though, the story of fish raised in one of the most arid places on Earth is about how modern food systems displace their burdens: drawing feed from distant seas, labor from vulnerable populations and trust from consumers asked to believe their meals aren’t harming anyone.

https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.author: Outlaw Ocean Project
https://www.france24.com/en/environment/.text:
On March 6, 2024, Pascal Goumain, the president of Saumon de France, was presenting his company’s salmon pens in Cherbourg as part of France’s food future. In an interview, Goumain described plans to adapt the farm to climate change and pointed to official backing for expansion. “The French Ministry of Agriculture set an objective to farm 20,000 tonnes of salmon in France by 2030,” Goumain said. The promise of fish farming, he argued, is that it is both sustainable and important for food sovereignty. “We should be a leading aquaculture country,” he said, “but we’re falling behind.”

The industry and government pitch of aquaculture in France has been straightforward: People want more seafood, the limit of what can be viably pulled from the wild is quickly being reached, and fish farming is the way to meet the growing demand while slowing the collapse of the oceans. “The quantities caught are not sufficient to feed consumers,” former minister of the sea Annick Girardin said in 2021. The Haut-Commissariat au Plan on fish farming echoed the point in 2023, asserting that in a context of climate change and overfishing, the “responsible development” of aquaculture could expand supply without undermining the fishing sector.

Globally, the ocean-sustainability argument for fish farming – “grow more, so we can catch less” – is one of the reasons that the $313-billion aquaculture industry is currently the fastest-growing food sector, and why half of the seafood eaten around the world is now farm-raised rather than caught at sea.

There is a problem, though. “The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in France – salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream – are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained. Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil, ingredients made by cooking and pulverising wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

The concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, DC. These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, violent protests typically spurred by the horrid stench from fishmeal factories, and escalating geopolitical tensions as countries compete for scarce sources of protein. What economists often call “externalities", these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export. In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, on farms, and in factories. In other countries, like India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labour strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish.

The four-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fishmeal ships at sea. The goal was to chronicle what economists call this industry’s “externalities” – the hidden and displaced social costs of producing this feed that rarely appear on the balance sheets of the seafood companies that depend on it.

The investigation revealed that the fishmeal industry also contributes to geopolitical tensions.

For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity. In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal, after a fisher was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fishmeal boat. Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara, a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various UN resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illegal catch into fishmeal in Western Saharan plants, then exporting it to farms globally labeled as Moroccan. A violent clash over trucks, many of them carrying this fish and fishmeal out of Western Sahara, led to the collapse of a 29-year ceasefire between the countries in 2020. As recently as 2024, a Western Saharan fishmeal plant supplied fish oil to a French importer named S.A.S. Ch. Daudruy Van Cauwenberghe & Fils, which advertises supplements for animal feed on its website, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that maps seafood supply chains. S.A.S. Ch. Daudruy Van Cauwenberghe & Fils did not respond to a request for comment.

READ MORE
The Saya de Malha Bank, a 'forgotten ecosystem' in need of protection

France’s greatest exposure to these problems comes less from home-grown salmon than from the more than €6 billion worth of seafood the country imports annually, including shrimp, trout, tilapia, and other forms of fish that rely heavily on fishmeal and fish oil. For example, shrimp raised on farms in Ecuador and sold at major grocers in France such as E.LeClerc, Cora, and Carrefour is fed fishmeal from plants throughout Latin America that have been tied to at least five worker deaths, 20 cases of illegal fishing, and over a half dozen instances of civil unrest from neighbours protesting the stench from fishmeal factories, the investigation found. Carrefour Group, which also owns Cora, said it was immediately launching an investigation into the issues concerning its supply chain and “will take all necessary measures in the event of confirmed non-compliance", which could include the exclusion of sources of supply “that do not meet our ethical and environmental standards". E.Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment.

More than sixty percent of the salmon eaten in France comes from farms in Norway, which rely heavily on imported fish feed made from wild-caught fish. The feed raising this salmon is linked to a range of documented impacts, including food insecurity in Western Africa, pollution from waste and chemicals, and the spread of parasites and disease to wild fish populations. A 2024 Science Advances review found that about 87 percent of global fishmeal goes to aquaculture, compared with roughly seven percent to pigs and about five percent to poultry.

The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden from the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, in particular as feed for fish, chickens, and pigs. The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets. For example, less than 30 percent of the fleet had publicly available location information, and less than 25 percent had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the vessels in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species. At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths. The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Pauly. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

For most of human history, we ate what ecosystems produced on their own: wild fish, grazing animals, and crops grown for people. Livestock survived largely on grass and agricultural leftovers that humans didn’t eat. Today, we do something different: We grow or catch food that people could eat and feed it to animals instead, especially in industrial livestock and fish farming. These calories are converted before they’re consumed.

READ MORE
Posidonia meadows: Lungs of the seas at risk

This global transformation has rewired the trophic chain, turning farms and oceans into engineered calorie-processing systems. The natural food web, consisting of who eats what and how energy moves from plants to animals to humans, is no longer mainly determined by ecosystems. It’s now shaped by industrial design. Animals have become less like savings accounts that turn waste into food, and more like biological factories steered by globally traded feed commodities such as soy and fishmeal. Roughly 90 percent of the catch used to produce fishmeal globally is edible for humans, according to a 2017 study published in the Fish and Fisheries journal. Most fishmeal plants around the world rely on whole fish rather than processing waste or inedible byproducts, further intensifying local protein scarcity.

The science of animal feed – combining corn, soy, grains, and ingredients like fishmeal to raise livestock faster, more efficiently, and at a larger scale – has been central to the rise of modern civilisation. Techniques of animal husbandry emerged roughly 12,000 years ago in the so-called Fertile Crescent, a region stretching from Mesopotamia to Egypt. Alongside innovations such as irrigation and the plough, the domestication of livestock enabled humans to build stable food systems, settle permanently, and eventually develop cities. As farming shifted from grazing animals on open land to penning them, humans assumed responsibility for providing balanced diets, an early precursor to today’s industrial feed systems.

In her 2021 book The Fishmeal Revolution, Kristin A. Wintersteen traces how the Humboldt Current – a cold, nutrient-rich upwelling system along the Pacific coast of South America – was reimagined as a protein mine. That shift, she argues, turned Peru into a global fishmeal superpower, responsible for roughly a quarter of worldwide production. Fishmeal became a critical input fueling the post-World War II expansion of industrial chicken and hog farming, and later aquaculture, particularly in northern Europe and the United States. Since then, this model spread far beyond Peru, including to West Africa and Southeast Asia.

Modern aquaculture does have benefits. Fish farming provides millions of people with year-round access to affordable protein. In India, for example, aquaculture is a crucial source of jobs, especially for women. In Bangladesh, fish farming has driven an overall decline in the price of fish, making it more accessible for lower-income households. Even accounting for feed ingredients like soy and fishmeal, and transportation to the US, certain farmed fish, including tilapia and Atlantic salmon, emit less greenhouse gas per pound than beef or pork.

READ MORE
Forced labour, disease and conflict: The hidden side of industrial fishing in Saya de Malha

Harvesting bivalves, like clams, oysters, scallops, and mussels, is an especially sustainable type of aquaculture, since these species do not require feed. This kind of farming also has a very low carbon footprint and produces shells that can function as a form of carbon capture, according to a 2020 paper by Nature Food. As of 2022, roughly a third of global aquaculture did not require external feed inputs. France is the European Union’s second-largest producer of farmed seafood by volume, behind Spain, with bivalves accounting for nearly 80 percent of what the country grows.

The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fishmeal and fish oil, and especially on the use of whole fish or fish that people can eat. However, as aquaculture overall grows, so too does demand for fishmeal. The total amount of global fishmeal production is predicted to rise by nearly 10 percent, mostly from trimmings, between 2022 and 2032, according to the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization. Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from IFFO, the international fishmeal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system". She added that her organisation’s “role is not to advise which markets should use fishmeal and fish oil". “Sustainability frameworks won’t work if they ignore real-world economics,” she said, and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat".

France has not only been a consumer of farmed seafood. It has also tried to help find alternatives to fishmeal. In northern France, inside a vast warehouse, millions of mealworm larvae wriggled in stacked trays at Ynsect, a company that promised to mass-produce insect protein as a replacement for fishmeal in livestock and aquaculture feed. When the firm broke ground in 2021 on what was billed as the world’s largest insect farm, France’s agriculture minister hailed it as a symbol of the country’s “reconquest of protein sovereignty". Investors poured more than half a billion dollars into the company.

READ MORE
In the Saya de Malha Bank, sharks are being hunted to extinction for their fins

But the fix proved harder than the pitch. By 2022, Ynsect had suffered more than $105 million in losses, largely because demand from feed buyers remained weak. In 2023, the company said it would shift away from the lower-margin business of feed for fish and farm animals, focusing instead on higher-end pet food markets. Its retreat illustrated a broader problem with alternatives to fishmeal: Even when a substitute looks promising in theory, it frequently struggles with cost, nutrition, and scale. Alternatives often lack the full range of nutrients that support the growth of farmed fish, especially omega-3. Certain “green” options, like insect meal, are expensive, and there has been limited interest among feed companies to pay a premium for them as a result.

Insects, moreover, turned out not to be as circular a solution as advertised. One of the industry’s main selling points was that larvae could be raised on waste. But in the European Union, disease-prevention rules largely bar insect producers from feeding them household food waste, manure, or catering scraps. Instead, most producers must rely on feed-grade crops. As a result, a sector promoted as a way to ease pressure on oceans has, in many cases, ended up competing with people and livestock for the same agricultural resources. The lesson from Ynsect was not that replacing fishmeal is impossible. It was that there is no easy substitute waiting in the wings.

For now, the pattern persists: Wild fish are caught and rendered into feed, while the costs of this production are left elsewhere. And reporting across several continents and oceans showed just how varied those costs can be. In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks while demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal. In Russia, fish processing workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore. “People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.

The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labour and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. In 2025, France imported more than $124 million worth of seafood from China, which is rapidly expanding its aquaculture industry. China now raises more than four times the amount of fish it catches. One of the fastest-growing regions in this boom is China’s mountainous and desert inland west, particularly Tibet and Xinjiang, two regions known for intense political repression.

In Tibet, the Chinese government has relocated roughly half a million Tibetans, leveling villages and monasteries for development projects such as hydroelectric dams and fish farms. This effort often uses coercive tactics, including repeated home visits, threats of criminal prosecution, and warnings that utilities could be cut off for those who refused to move, according to a 2024 Human Rights Watch report. In response to these sorts of policies, at least 169 Tibetans have set themselves on fire, typically on camera, outside police stations, monasteries, or public squares. In Xinjiang, more than a million people have been held in detention camps, and the government has engaged in large-scale land seizures, forced sterilizations, and criminal penalties for speaking native languages or practicing religious and cultural traditions.

The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, much of which is exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States. China’s effort to promote fish farming in Tibet and Xinjiang is partly facilitated by severe state repression, including the widespread appropriation of land, intense police surveillance, and the incarceration of tens of thousands of local residents. The United States bans all goods produced “wholly or in part” by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region on the presumption that they were made with state-sponsored forced labor. No such law exists for Tibet. EU law, which applies in France, does not single out China but prohibits products made with forced labor from being placed or made available on the EU market, including imports.

As the production of seafood has become more globalised, its supply chains have stretched longer, and it has become tougher for consumers to know whether it was harvested sustainably or legally. Most grocers who sell seafood are in the dark as well because tracking is difficult and costly. Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said this is partly because grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. The other reason may be plausible deniability, he added. “Companies can escape blame or the need to fix problems if they’re unaware of them.”

Where government regulators have proven lacking in ensuring that supply chains are free from unsustainable, illegal, or unethical practices, industry-led certification programs have sought to fill the gap. Critics say these programmes serve more as a sustainability smokescreen, giving downstream customers a way to avoid looking deeper into their supply chains. The programmes generally focus on environmental crimes, while mostly overlooking labour abuses on ships. Their biggest weakness, according to researchers, is that they do not actually track seafood fully, which results in false reassurances for consumers.

Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at the strategic litigation non-profit group Corporate Accountability Lab, said that on land – at processing plants or on farms – certification programmes rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the guarantees given by managers at the factories. Instead, the programmes frequently alert companies before inspectors show up, which gives them a chance to clean up the scene so there are no violations. At sea, these programmes also often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors directly visit and check conditions offshore on vessels, where crimes are most common. Certification programmes are rife with conflicts of interest, since they are typically funded by the companies that they are supposed to police, Brudney added.

The various organisations that make up the certification industry emphasize that each plays its own role and cannot be held accountable for others’ responsibilities. For example, Devan Meserve, a spokesperson for The Global Seafood Alliance, which runs a programme called Best Aquaculture Practices, said that her organisation represents the “most comprehensive programme for farmed seafood", partially because it covers the “entire aquaculture production chain". Protecting workers on the fishing vessels that supply feed mills is, however, an “immense challenge", she noted, because audits occur strictly at port and do not witness harvest conditions. Meserve added that her organisation helps the industry counter illegal and overfishing by requiring feed mills to source most of the fish they use in fishmeal or fish oil from fisheries accredited by certification programmes like MarinTrust and Marine Stewardship Council.

Partly bolstered by these certification programmes, seafood companies routinely make marketing claims about the ethics and sustainability of their seafood. Often, these claims fail to reckon with crimes or social concerns further up their supply chains, including on the ships or plants that produce the feed for the fish farms. This disconnect is creating growing legal risk for seafood companies and grocers. Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies across six US jurisdictions. The legal complaints focused on a common pattern: marketing claims that portrayed products as sustainable or ethically sourced, paired with supply chain evidence that suggested otherwise. Plaintiffs challenged language such as “sustainable", “eco-friendly", “all-natural", “wild-caught,” and “from the coast of Maine", as well as claims of superior worker-safety standards.

In at least four cases, the use of fishmeal or fish oil and their link to industrial fishing and ecosystem depletion were central to arguments that the products were not environmentally sustainable. Additional allegations included forced labour on fishing vessels and reliance on harmful pesticides and antibiotics. During this same period, seafood companies have paid more than $2 million in settlement fees to resolve false-advertising cases. The Outlaw Ocean investigation assessed more than 800 seafood companies that made marketing claims comparable to – or stronger than – those cited in the lawsuits and found that over half of the companies had documented crimes or concerns within their supply chains.

Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with the Canadian sustainable seafood group SeaChoice, said many industries have already had to begin reckoning with the human rights and environmental abuses buried in their supply chains. She cited sweatshop garments, blood diamonds, and fair-trade coffee as examples. Seafood, she said, has been slower to face that kind of scrutiny. But as the world searches for more protein and leans further into aquaculture, that may change, particularly if more governments begin restricting imports tied to illegality or unsustainable practices. “That’s when investors will begin to see material, not just reputational, risk,” she said, “and companies will have to adjust".

The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.

The Outlaw Ocean Project is a non-profit journalism organisation based in Washington DC that produces investigative stories about human rights, labour and environmental concerns on the two thirds of the planet covered by water. The organisation is run by Ian Urbina, an award-winning journalist who used to work for The New York Times.

Most of the stories are reported at least partially at sea. In the United States, the group publishes its stories in various news outlets, including the New Yorker, NBC News, The Atlantic and The Washington Post. The reporting is also regularly translated into other languages, particularly French and Spanish, and broadcast in partnership with dozens of foreign newspapers, magazines, radio and television outlets.

https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-coalition-vo.text:
Saudi Arabia and its allied forces in Yemen vowed a "firm response" to Houthi attacks that target civilians. The kingdom's authorities said three Saudi nationals were killed in Thursday's attack on Riyadh airport.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen launched strikes that destroyed targets used by the Houthis, a coalition spokesperson said Friday.

Major General Turki al-Maliki said three rocket launch platforms were destroyed, adding that Houthi attacks on civilians would be met with a "firm response."

The Saudi-Houthi conflict has intensified in recent weeks, with Saudi Arabian authorities having said Friday that Houthi attacks on Riyadh's main international airport on Thursday killed three Saudi citizens and injured several people of "different nationalities."

The King Khalid International Airport was targeted twice on Thursday, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.The first attack aimed at airport facilities and the second targeted an aircraft that belonged to the Saudia airline.

Hundreds of flights were canceled because of Thursday's attacks, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.

The Indian Embassy later said Air India had suspended operations through to Saturday, while the Lufthansa Group said its airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through to October 16.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday recommended airlines not to operate in additional portions of Saudi Airspace in an updated bulletin.

The EASA said recent attacks had demonstrated the ability and the intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital.

On Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthis warned employees at Saudi oil facilities that oil installations remain a target.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Houthis have fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war to reinstate the internationally backed government in Sanaa. Houthi rebels took control of the capital in 2014.

But ever since, the Saudi-led coalition has found it hard to turn the tide of the war that quieted under a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

In the last weeks, the Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast, capturing a wide swath of territory that has given them greater control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

A Saudi-led coalition has pressed a counteroffensive against the Houthis fighters and recaptured several areas along the strait, Yemeni officials have said. But the fighting appears to be far from over.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgk.title: Ex-Deutsche Bank trader jailed for rigging rates has conviction overturned
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgk.text:
Another former banker sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis has had his conviction overturned following a long-running legal battle.

The Court of Appeal has quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who went to prison in 2018 for "manipulating" the benchmark interest rate, Euribor.

It comes after the same UK court overturned five convictions of ex-Barclays bankers in the rate rigging trials earlier this week.

Bittar, who watched proceedings via video link from Switzerland because he was not granted a visa to attend court, told the BBC: "I have waited a very, very long time for this day."

The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.

There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.

The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.

Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.

Eighteen of these have now been acquitted.

Only one former trader in the world now remains convicted: former Barclays trader Peter Johnson, who was also one of the original whistleblowers in the interest rate rigging scandal. He pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance at winning at trial. The court confirmed that he too has now applied to appeal against his conviction.

The news has already prompted lawyers and senior politicians to press for the Bank of England and the Treasury to release all their records about their own roles in interest rate 'rigging' during the financial crisis, amid concerns raised of a cover-up of the role of central banks and governments.

Speaking after his conviction was quashed, Bittar said: "Finally the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised.

"I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it."

His wife, Caroline, who lives in the UK, said their family had lost 15 "valuable years", with their children "growing up with this injustice".

She added they were looking forward to "enjoying life with our family and friends without this shadow hanging over us".

On Wednesday, Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham and Philippe Mouryoussef saw their convictions for 'manipulating' the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor quashed after a 10-year struggle for justice.

They launched fresh appeals against their jail sentences following a Supreme Court ruling last year that acquitted Tom Hayes, the first to be jailed for 'rigging' interest rates in 2015, and Carlo Palombo, jailed in 2019.

Tom Hayes, who was initially sentenced to 14 years, reduced on appeal to 11, is now seeking damages from his former employer UBS.

The traders were among 37 City traders and brokers prosecuted for "manipulating" the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor, which track the cost of borrowing cash between the banks and have been used to set the interest rates on millions of mortgages and commercial loans.

The BBC has uncovered evidence of a much larger, state-led 'rigging' of interest rates, under pressure from central banks and governments across the world. Evidence implicating Downing Street and the Bank of England was suppressed throughout the criminal trials.

Former Conservative cabinet minister David Davis told the BBC the innocent traders had been the victims of a series of miscarriages of justice.

He said the people exonerated this week and before were "the victims of a scapegoating exercise which arose as a result of the government's own misbehaviour in lowballing [falsely understating] Libor interest rates themselves, in order to try and rescue the economy after their own self-induced crash in the late 2000s".

In 2015, during the first trial for interest rate 'rigging', of former UBS trader Hayes, Mr Justice Jeremy Cooke decided as a matter of law that any attempt to influence the rates could not be lawful, and that any rate influenced by commercial interest must automatically be false. Judges in the subsequent eight trials followed suit.

However, in July 2025, the Supreme Court decided that all the judges had erred, misdirecting juries that it was wrong as a matter of law. Instead, whether the requests were right or wrong was properly a matter of fact for the jury to decide, not the judge.

All convictions in the United States were overturned in 2022 after an appeal court ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the traders' requests had broken any rules or laws.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4g.text:
Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.

As first reported by the Financial Times, the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday.

Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one.

Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said "the vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment.

Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs.

To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties.

Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats.

However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels.

More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest.

Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty".

"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said.

One Lib Dem MP said Sir Ed's argument was "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

The Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday. Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.title: Ofsted faces fresh calls to halt graded school inspections in England
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.text:
A second head teachers' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections in England, saying it is "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale" of its members.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) also raised the prospect of potential strike action, saying a new grading system had become an "overbearing mess".

On Friday, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said an independent survey of education providers showed it was "on the right track" with inspections.

The Department for Education (DfE) said ministers were "working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better".

ASCL's announcement comes after another union, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), said changes Ofsted made to inspections just under a year ago had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.

ASCL said it had passed a motion of no confidence in "the ability of Ofsted's leadership to address the damage being done by the new inspection system", adding that it was "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary, said the union did not take the step "lightly", but added Ofsted's "warm words about recognising wellbeing pressures... have not been matched by the action necessary" and that "negotiation [had] hit a brick wall".

"The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed," he said.

ASCL called on the government to pause inspections and review the system, and said it would survey members on whether to hold an informal ballot on industrial action if there was no change.

In response, Ofsted said it had "worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge".

"We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do," a spokesperson added.

England's schools inspectorate introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".

An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.

That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade.

Last month, the NAHT said testimonies from its members, seen by the BBC, suggested some school leaders had faced "intolerable" pressure because of the new inspections, leaving them "overwhelmed" and "anxious".

It warned the system could pose a "risk to life" if changes were not forthcoming.

An independent report, commissioned by Ofsted to evaluate its new framework, concluded this week that leaders were "generally positive" about their inspection experience, and that it was "more collaborative and accounts for context better than previous inspections".

But it also said nearly half (48%) of school leaders who responded to its survey said their staff's mental wellbeing had been negatively affected "a fair amount" or "a lot" by a recent inspection.

The interim report was based on focus groups and nearly 700 responses from school, college and early years leaders who were invited to complete a survey following inspections this year. A full report is due to be published next year.

Sir Martyn said: "The data published today shows that we are on the right track.

"I know that workload and wellbeing in education continue to be challenging, and I don't take that lightly.

"We will keep listening to feedback from professionals and parents alike as we continue to improve what we do."

The DfE said "inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw1m.summary: ASCL says it is "increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale" of its members. The Association of School and College Leaders also raised the prospect of potential strike action. Ofsted chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver says an independent survey shows it is on the right track.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said the lack of clarity over Manchester City’s future after the club was found guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules was causing uncertainty throughout the Premier League.

City remain adamant they have done no wrong and have appealed against the findings of an independent commission announced last week.

The Premier League leaders potentially face a severe points deduction that threatens their place in the English top flight.

Iraola believes the world’s richest league is caught in limbo until there is a definitive outcome.

“I think the worst thing probably is the uncertainty, that no one knows what’s going to happen,” the Spaniard said ahead of City’s first outing since the verdict at Liverpool on Sunday.

“But we have to focus on Liverpool – be the best club we can be, the best team we can be and that’s my challenge.”

Iraola only joined the Reds in June but is looking forward to a red-hot atmosphere at home.

“The atmosphere is going to be big, especially at Anfield,” he said.

“We want to give also our supporters reasons to be with us. When they see the team they want to see on the pitch, we can create an even better atmosphere and we will work for that.”

Liverpool are still unbeaten under Iraola, but three draws in their opening five league games means they start the weekend six points off the top.

Iraola’s options up front are limited after Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo were injured on international duty.

“As a club manager, you are always waiting until the game ends (hoping) the doctor doesn’t call you, doesn’t give you bad news, but in this case we’ve been unlucky with Alex and Cody, both of them,” he said.

“They are injured and they are not going to be involved on Sunday.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: US to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution: Is that legal?​
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Shola Lawal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The Pentagon has said it will livestream the upcoming execution of convicted mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad – a first for the United States.

A Pentagon spokesperson made the announcement on Thursday, drawing uproar from legal quarters as experts and rights groups raised concerns that it could violate US and international laws and, in particular, put minors at risk.

The US military rarely invokes capital punishment, last executing an officer by hanging in 1961. Firing squads are even rarer, and were last used in the military in 1945.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a then-Army major, opened fire at an Army processing centre in Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others.

An Army psychiatrist found he was acting in an effort to stop military deployments to Afghanistan and to halt the killing of fellow Muslims. Hasan was himself scheduled to be deployed later that month.

Following a lengthy military trial in which Hasan made little effort to defend himself, a jury convicted him in July 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of murder, and imposed the death penalty.

Although he said he acted on religious grounds and was found to have corresponded with al-Qaeda-linked elements, Hasan was not convicted of “terrorism” as the US military justice code does not have a stand-alone charge for it.

This week, the Pentagon said US President Donald Trump had given the go-ahead for Hasan to face a firing squad. The military requires presidential approval for executions, and only the president can stipulate a particular method.

On Thursday, a Pentagon official said Hasan was to be executed at the same Fort Hood military base where he killed 13 people in 2009.

The official said the execution would be livestreamed.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle set the execution date for December 3 at 1pm local time (18:00 GMT).

Speaking in a podcast interview this week, Hegseth said the livestream would act as a deterrent.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said during the interview with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec.

He added that the timing of the execution was symbolic. “We’re going to do it at one o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad.”

The rules vary in the 27 US states where death penalties are still in place.

Texas law allows up to five close relatives of the victim, a spiritual guide, justice officials, state-ordained chaplains, a judge, the sheriff, and the media to attend an execution.

All persons, however, must be adults older than 18.

It was on August 14, 1936. Rainey Bethea was publicly hanged in Owensboro, Kentucky, after confessing to the rape and killing of 70-year-old Lishia Edwards.

The US is a signatory to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which bans torture, cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment.

While the convention does not completely ban the death penalty, it does strictly restrict its use to the “most serious crimes” and encourages its abolition.

Washington ratified it in 1992, but it issued reservations and stated that the US would retain the right to impose capital punishment as it sees fit.

Legal experts say the public execution of Hasan could violate the clause against degrading punishment under the convention. A livestream would likely also be recorded and shared widely.

British-American human rights lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented clients on death row in the US and founded the Louisiana Capital Assistance Center in New Orleans in 1993 to represent low-income individuals facing the death penalty, called the move “barbaric”.

He said a public execution broadcast in this manner would violate several laws in the US that prohibit the transmission of obscene, indecent, or graphic material, especially to minors.

There’s no single federal law stipulating who may witness executions, but death penalty states typically prohibit minors.

Likewise, the Army’s justice code (PDF) prohibits minors from witnessing an execution.

“I’ve watched six executions, and I suffer from PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder] to this day,” Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “It’s a nightmare, and you’ll have people who will have traumatic responses to it.”

Smith said several legal challenges are likely, and the Army will likely have to consider several factors if it does go ahead with broadcasting the execution.

Challengers are likely to question how the US military will prevent children from viewing the livestream, and how they will make Hasan’s shooting less ghastly based on the body parts targeted, he said.

Regarding using the public execution as a deterrent, Stafford Smith added the opposite could actually be more likely. He said it could end up “provoking more cases” and that Hasan could be seen as a “martyr” by some.

He added: “This is likely going to Congress. The Democrats will want to stop this. So that will be an interesting battle.”

Democrat Senator Chris Murphy called the move “disgusting” and compared it to executions carried out by the Islamic State (ISIL). “I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions [are] medieval,” he said in an interview with CNN.

Amnesty International Australia said Hegseth’s statements showed an “appalling disregard for human dignity”, and called on Melbourne to intervene.

Meanwhile, New Zealand’s national censor told rights groups urging it to protest that it has no authority to block internet users from viewing the livestream – a sign that governments attempting to restrict access might be hampered.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Nidal Malik Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others. The US military rarely invokes capital punishment, last executing an officer by hanging in 1961. The military requires presidential approval for executions, and only the New Zealand's national censor told rights groups to protest

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea accuse one another of launching war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an “all-out invasion” in a message to the United Nations Security Council, while Eritrea says it is facing a “war of aggression” from its neighbour.

“The all-out invasion of parts of northern Ethiopia by Eritrea is a matter of public record,” said a letter by Ethiopia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Gedion Timothewos, which was shared with news agencies on Friday.

“It is a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence,” added the letter dated Thursday and addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.

Gedion said that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and demanded their withdrawal, just days after the two nations cut diplomatic ties.

Eritrea’s Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel rejected Ethiopia’s claims.

“The Ethiopian regime has been pursuing, in effect, an unprovoked war of aggression against Eritrea for more than three years now,” he said on X.

Yemane said Asmara had shown restraint since landlocked Ethiopia had essentially declared a war against Eritrea when it stated in 2023 that it would gain access to the sea.

Citing statements made by Ethiopian officials, Yemane accused Addis Ababa of using the current conflict ⁠to take Assab, an Eritrean port, in order to restore access to the Red Sea.

Eritrea also denied Ethiopia’s claim that it is backing the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which is part of an alliance of seven armed groups that has been attempting to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government since September.

Over the past week, Ethiopia’s army has pushed back the TPLF and seized the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle.

Witnesses also told the AFP news agency that rebels had lost the Tigrayan cities of Shire and Adigrat. Eritrean troops were reportedly seen in Adigrat before Ethiopian drone strikes hit them, according to several witnesses.

Ethiopia and Eritrea have traded accusations since the reported ⁠incursions by Eritrean troops this week raised fears of outright war in the region, where the two nations have fought previous conflicts.

The stakes have been raised this time around by conflicts in the Horn of Africa region and tensions across the Red Sea.

Diplomatic ties between the two have collapsed amid the escalation: Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country last week. In response, Eritrea announced it was severing ties.

The neighbours have a tumultuous history, as Eritrea won independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and they fought a border war for two years in 1998.

Relations improved slightly in 2018 when Abiy took power in Addis Ababa, and Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.

Eritrea, however, was not part of the peace deal that ended the war, which soured ties soon afterwards.

Tensions are also fuelled by Abiy’s repeated claim that landlocked Ethiopia – which lost its access to the coast when Eritrea secured independence – has a right to sea access, which Eritrea sees as a threat to seize its Red Sea port of Assab.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Bangladesh’s mango diplomacy with India has reached its limits
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Faisal Mahmud
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
For two years, Dhaka has deployed a soft diplomatic arsenal of prized Haribhanga mangoes, hilsa fish, jamdani fabrics, and Tangail sarees to keep its relationship with New Delhi from freezing into permanent estrangement. These gestures kept doors open, preserved public channels, and prevented temporary friction from decaying into absolute hostility.

Yet, as the dust settles, a cold geopolitical reality remains visible. Soft power can create an opening, but it cannot settle the hard politics waiting behind it. There comes an inevitable point in every strained diplomatic relationship when the mangoes have simply done all they can.

Since the mass uprising that began in Bangladesh in July 2024 and toppled Sheikh Hasina’s increasingly authoritarian rule of 15 years, Bangladesh has sought to avoid sharp confrontation with India. The instruments chosen by Dhaka were conspicuously soft.

Cultural programmes, textile exhibitions, hilsa festivals and trade gestures were paired with a determined effort by the Bangladeshi High Commission in New Delhi to keep talking to Indian counterparts, even when the respective governments had little pleasant to say to each other. This campaign was not entirely pointless. It was merely incapable of bearing the political weight eventually demanded of it.

A basket of mangoes can generate a momentary thaw. A saree exhibition can fill a grand room with appreciative visitors. A shipment of the coveted silvery delicacy of hilsa can evoke profound nostalgic warmth in Kolkata. None of these things, however, can determine the fate of Hasina, settle disputes over shared river waters, rebuild shattered political trust, or address the core security anxieties of two tightly interconnected neighbouring states.

That fundamental distinction – between keeping a diplomatic relationship alive and actually repairing its broken core – now defines the delicate balance between Bangladesh and India.

The limits of this approach were demonstrated clearly in 2025. In July, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus’s erstwhile interim administration dispatched 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) of high-grade Haribhanga mangoes to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, alongside additional consignments for senior officials and political leaders across New Delhi.

The gesture was interpreted as a deliberate signal that Dhaka sought normal, functional ties despite the intense bitterness that followed Hasina’s overthrow and her subsequent flight to Indian soil. The mangoes arrived swiftly on schedule. The heavy political problems remained exactly where they were.

Hasina remained in India while authorities in Dhaka pursued her formal extradition. The two capitals argued persistently over border management, transit rights, and the treatment of Bangladeshi citizens. Visa services, long a bellwether of bilateral warmth, were suspended and later resumed after Tarique Rahman’s BNP came to power in February this year. But the number of visas issued has still not returned to pre-2024 levels.

Unresolved questions concerning shared water resources, bilateral trade imbalances, and regional security continued to linger without resolution. Soft diplomacy was, at best, a pleasing sweetener rather than the main course.

Few pursued this softer strategy more visibly than Bangladesh’s outgoing envoy in New Delhi, M Riaz Hamidullah. Under his leadership, the High Commission experimented energetically with cultural outreach. The first jamdani exposition in Delhi, held in September 2025, brought traditional Bangladeshi weaving into an Indian artistic space where shared history was obvious.

In April 2026, the mission mounted another exhibition displaying 300 handloom sarees sourced directly from master weavers in Tangail and Pabna. The response from the Indian capital was positive.

As for cultural diplomacy, the initiative was a success. Indian connoisseurs arrived in droves, designers exchanged ideas, and sarees sold out within 24 hours. The shared Bengali cultural inheritance proved far easier to discuss than shared rivers. There was sound logic behind this tactic: building constituencies within Indian society who did not view Bangladesh strictly through the lens of immediate political quarrels provided a crucial buffer.

The diplomatic mistake lies in confusing access with real influence. A sold-out textile exhibition proves Indian admiration for Bangladeshi craftsmanship; it does not indicate agreement with Dhaka’s strategic posture. Cultural familiarity has never guaranteed political convergence in South Asia.

If it did, Dhaka and Kolkata would have settled every bilateral disagreement over hilsa-laden lunch decades ago. Indeed, even the fabric eventually ran into politics when the Tangail exhibition became entangled in contentious debates over heritage claims and geographical indication status.

Atmospherics inevitably run out of room. Sooner or later, formal political engagement must take over. Nothing illustrates this shift better than the continuing efforts to arrange a visit by Tarique Rahman to New Delhi. India extended invitations for both a direct bilateral visit and attendance at the BRICS summit in his capacity as chair of BIMSTEC.

Rahman did not make the journey. Dhaka noted that a high-level summit required an appropriate environment and mutual respect, while Indian officials publicly underscored that invitations had been extended without producing a visit.

This polite impasse revealed the true state of affairs. A prime ministerial visit requires a substantive agenda, careful political preparation, and deliverable outcomes that both leaders can sell to domestic audiences. India’s high commissioner in Dhaka, Dinesh Trivedi, has repeatedly urged direct top-level dialogue, emphasising that direct contact between leaders is necessary to resolve outstanding issues.

Soft diplomacy operates best when the underlying strategic foundation is already functional. When two governments agree on the fundamentals, cultural affinity adds warmth and colour. When they clash over fundamental interests, soft power can prevent complete rupture, but it cannot negotiate the terms of reconciliation.

India’s previous relationship with Dhaka rested on deep security cooperation, energy links, and established political arrangements. Hasina’s removal dismantled that comfortable architecture.

The leadership in Dhaka now demands a new equilibrium based strictly on sovereignty, reciprocity, and strategic flexibility. New Delhi maintains its own sharp concerns regarding regional security and Dhaka’s shifting external alignments.

These are complex matters involving trade treaties, water allocation, border enforcement, and intelligence cooperation. They cannot be managed by cultural envoys or resolved over dinner menus.

The gestures of the past two years were not failures; they preserved vital space during a turbulent political transition. But symbolism is now yielding diminishing returns. Both capitals understand that the next phase of South Asian geopolitics cannot be stitched together with fabric or negotiated over fruit. The mangoes succeeded in keeping the diplomatic door open. Real political bargaining must now walk through it.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Bangladesh has deployed soft diplomatic arsenal of prized Haribhanga mangoes, hilsa fish, jamdani fabrics, and Tangail sarees. New Delhi maintains its own sharp concerns regarding regional security and Dhaka’s shifting external alignments.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/automa.title: Automattic loses its interim CFO just weeks after boardroom shakeup
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/automa.author: Sarah Perez
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/automa.text:
Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.

The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”

Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit.

He had replaced the former CFO Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean.

Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.

It’s unclear why Klaperman chose to leave Automattic, but sources told TechCrunch that the decision came after he was demoted back to his original role at VIP. (As an interim CFO, he could have been replaced by a permanent hire, but nothing on that front has yet to be announced.) Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure.

When Mullenweg originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/automa.summary: Jeremy Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company. The company confirmed the departure with the following statement.

You’ve built the product. Now you need customers. But when you’re starting from zero, there may be no marketing budget, established brand, or sales team to help you find them. So how do you get the first 1,000 people to take a chance on what you’ve built?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Gamma CEO and co-founder Grant Lee, Engine founder and CEO Elia Wallen, and GV (Google Ventures) general partner Crystal Huang will take the Builders Stage for “The Zero-to-1K Playbook: How to Get Your First 1,000 Customers Without a Marketing Budget.”

They’ll break down how founders are using community building, product-led growth, founder-led sales, strategic outbound, and word of mouth to find those critical early customers.

Still working toward your first 1,000 customers? Secure your Disrupt pass now, save up to $100, and hear how founders are finding early customers when budget, brand, and scale aren’t available yet. Bring a co-founder, colleague, partner, or peer and save 50% on your pass.

Lee knows what it takes to grow well beyond those first customers. Before co-founding Gamma,  he was COO of ClearBrain, which was acquired by Amplitude, and CFO of Optimizely. A Stanford-trained engineer with experience in finance and operations, he spent years creating the slide decks that eventually inspired him to rethink how people create and share ideas.

Gamma has since grown far beyond presentations. TechCrunch reported in March 2026 that the AI-powered visual communication platform was approaching 100 million users after reaching $100 million in annual recurring revenue in 2025. The company has continued expanding into websites, social content, and AI-generated marketing assets.

For an early-stage founder, the interesting part of that story starts well before 100 million users. How do you convince the first people to try a product from a company they’ve never heard of — and turn that early traction into momentum?

Get your ticket to Disrupt and hear Lee’s perspective on what it takes to start building a customer base from zero. Save up to $100 on your pass, and get a second pass at 50% off.

Wallen brings another founder journey to the conversation. He started Travelers Haven in 2008 and bootstrapped it into one of the country’s largest corporate housing companies. He raised Engine’s first outside capital in 2019 and later shifted his full attention to the travel platform.

Today, Engine has served more than 30,000 businesses and one million travelers and is cash-flow positive. Its growth continued in July when Engine acquired Options Travel, a travel management company with more than 30 years in the business, along with its group-flights product, TempoTrip.

Wallen’s experience spans the stages early founders are trying to navigate: starting without an established brand, finding customers, building around what those customers need, and scaling from there.

If your startup needs customers long before it has a large marketing operation, add this Builders Stage session to your Disrupt agenda. Register now and save up to $100, and get a second at 50% off.

Huang brings the investor’s view. As a general partner at GV, she concentrates on SaaS, infrastructure, and AI, with a particular interest in product- and developer-led adoption strategies. Before GV, she invested at NEA and Notable Capital and began her career in technology M&A at Blackstone.

She’ll also be evaluating startups firsthand at Disrupt as one of this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 judges.

Huang adds the investor lens: how early-stage companies approach product-led adoption and build momentum before they have the resources of an established business.

Want to hear how a founder’s early go-to-market strategy looks from both sides of the table? Secure your Disrupt pass and hear from founders who have built customer bases and an investor who evaluates how companies grow. Save up to $100 on your pass, and get a second of the same pass at 50%.

More than 10,000 founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders are expected, along with 250+ speakers and 300+ exhibiting startups.

And for founders trying to find customers, investors, partners, or simply other people who understand the zero-to-one grind, the conversations don’t end when the sessions do. Matchmaking, dealmaking, and ad hoc networking give attendees opportunities to make the connections that can move a young company forward.

https://www.theverge.com/policy/1008677/.title: Trump’s attempt to rename AI is looking awfully artificial
https://www.theverge.com/policy/1008677/.author: Adi Robertson
https://www.theverge.com/policy/1008677/.text:
A ‘super’ new euphemism probably isn’t enough to make Americans forget their concerns about AI.

A ‘super’ new euphemism probably isn’t enough to make Americans forget their concerns about AI.

President Donald Trump has a knack for turning words against his enemies. His first successful presidential run was built on monikers like “Little Marco” and “Crooked Hillary”; he changed “fake news” from a phrase describing scammy media outlets to a derogatory term for the press at large. Over the past few weeks, he’s clearly decided he can work the same magic to promote artificial intelligence — branding a technology he wants to accelerate “super”, while turning “artificial” into his latest go-to pejorative and declaring resisters “THE ENEMY.” Some of the biggest names in AI are going along with him. But he’s picked a tough linguistic battle, and it may not pan out the way he hopes.

A longtime AI booster, Trump has gone into pro-robot overdrive since an industry conversation over “pacing” frontier development last month. His current position is that AI safety risks are overblown and US companies need to speed up development, including by building more data centers, which he insists contrary to polling data will be “very popular.” On top of discouraging industry self-regulation, he’s decided AI needs a rebrand by fiat. Trump declared in a rambling United Nations speech last month that “the use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake” and promised to rename the technology “super intelligence.” He then followed through with an executive order last week, forbidding the use of “AI” wherever possible.

Changes have been swift. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), already a rebrand of the AI Safety Institute, has been renamed the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI).

https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.title: Microsoft barred from sponsoring foreign workers for US residency
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.author: Joe Miller, Financial Times
https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026.text:
The US says Microsoft abused immigration rules; the company disputes the claim.

Donald Trump’s administration has temporarily banned Microsoft, Adobe, and several other tech companies from sponsoring workers for permanent US residency, claiming they abused immigration programs at the expense of American citizens.

Vice-president JD Vance said on Thursday that the H-1B visa programme for highly skilled foreign workers had “become rife with fraud” and that over-reliance on such schemes was “a fundamental insult to the American worker.”

He added that “no company in the US” had “abused this system” more than Microsoft.

Vance’s message to Microsoft that it could not “lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants” triggered an angry reaction from the Indian government.

“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement on Friday.

Referring to Vance’s remarks, it said “such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem.”

Six other IT outsourcing companies—Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini—were also suspended from the Permanent Labor Certification, or Perm, program, which allows US employers to hire foreign workers on a permanent basis.

“Subpoenas have been served, investigations are under way and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Labor Department Inspector-General Anthony D’Esposito.

Microsoft said the “vast majority” of its employees in the US were American, while Tata Consultancy Services, India’s largest outsourcing company, said its strategy was centred on hiring locally in the US and that Perm applications were in “single digits in the last two years.”

Adobe and Tata as well as Cognizant, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini did not respond to requests for comment.

The announcement marks the latest move in the Trump administration’s broad crackdown on immigration. It has previously taken aim at H-1B visas widely used by tech companies and specialist industries.

Last year, the White House attempted to impose a $100,000 fee on new applications, but, in June, a federal judge ruled the fee amounted to an unauthorized tax and infringed on Congress’ authority to raise funds. The Trump administration has appealed against the ruling.

Before the fee increase, the government charged $215 to register for the H-1B visa lottery and a $780 base fee for employers sponsoring visa applicants. More than 400,000 such visas were approved last year.

While Indians have been the biggest recipients of H-1B visas and the new restrictions target many of the largest outsourcing groups, the impact is likely to be small as the route from H-1B to permanent residency has been out of reach for most Indians, given a decades-long backlog.

Nearly 1 million people from India are waiting for employment-based permanent residency as of December last year, according to an August study by the non-profit National Foundation for American Policy.

Nasscom, the Indian IT services lobbying group, said the number of employees transitioning to permanent residency through Perm was “relatively limited” as Indian tech companies had “significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas.”

In his comments on Thursday, Vance said the visas were helping companies undercut US workers. He claimed some H-1B holders were earning between $20,000 and $48,000 less than US citizens hired for similar positions.

Amazon, the biggest user of H-1B visas, was not mentioned in the press conference. But Vance singled out Microsoft, saying it “laid off last year 6,000 American workers at the same time the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards,” referring to US permanent residency.

The White House on Thursday also announced a fraud investigation into the use of J-1 student visas at nine American universities, including Harvard, Yale, and Stanford.

Microsoft, whose shares dropped more than 1 percent following the announcement, said the visa applications mentioned by Vance were largely “to extend or change the status” of existing employees.

“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company said. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings.”

At a separate event on Thursday, the Trump administration gave Microsoft’s Indian-born chief executive, Satya Nadella, the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

He was honored alongside South African-born Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who was born in Taiwan.

Vance said there was no contradiction between the two announcements.

“Our message to Microsoft is: ‘You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.’”

Additional reporting by Michael Stott in New Delhi
