https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Trump’s planned DC arch faces new lawsuit
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Local authorities in Arlington, Virginia, have sued the United States Department of the Interior and the National Park Service, seeking to block President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch.

The 250-foot (76-metre) arch project could win approval as early as next month. It is modelled on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and is planned to be built near Arlington National Cemetery, just across the Potomac River from Washington.

The Arlington County governing board said in its lawsuit on Thursday that the project within a busy traffic corridor will cause “significant harm” to its residents and likely require changes to nearby flight paths. It is the first governmental body to take legal action against Trump’s planned monument.

Lawyers argue that the National Park Service failed to conduct a thorough review and that the arch will harm public safety by clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services.

“The National Park Service, the agency responsible for projects on national park land such as Memorial Circle, is proceeding full speed towards ground-disturbing construction,” the lawsuit said. “Although the agency has claimed that a final decision to construct the Arch has not yet been made and purports to be engaged in a routine decisional process, that rushed process appears to be a pretext designed to shore up justifications for building the Arch in accordance with the President’s repeated marching orders.”

The lawsuit asks that “the agency’s feverish pace towards construction of the arch” be halted to ensure that the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act be followed and proper analysis and testing be done.

“The Arlington County Board has filed this lawsuit because our community has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project,” Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a statement. He added that the county has acted in good faith in the review process, pointing out the “severe, unique and wide-ranging negative impacts” the project will have on the county and its residents, only to see them ignored.

The Interior Department emailed a short statement: “The Department continues to follow all laws and regulations.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

The proposed arch would be within the airport’s main approach and departure corridors. The Federal Aviation Administration’s safety determination requires the arch to be marked with a flame ⁠⁠⁠⁠atop the structure and floodlight projectors to make it noticeable for pilots. Some aviation experts have raised safety concerns given its proximity to the airport’s main approach and departure corridor.

The FAA dropped an earlier requirement for red obstruction lights, which it generally mandates on buildings more than 200 feet (61 metres) tall near airports, such as the nearby 169-metre (554-foot) Washington Monument.

The arch is part of Trump’s broader push to remake Washington, including renovating ⁠⁠⁠⁠the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, redeveloping a golf course in East Potomac Park and adding his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Preservationists say the projects would alter some of the capital’s most prominent historic landmarks.

Though the arch has received early approval from the US Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued in federal court in Washington, DC, saying the project needs approval by Congress. The judge in that lawsuit said the administration must give the court 48 hours before undertaking any activities related to, or in preparation for, construction of the arch.

Last month, Trump said he would convert the arch into a military complex capable of deploying drones and positioning snipers.

The 250-foot arch project could win approval as early as next month. It is modelled on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and is planned to be built near Arlington National Cemetery.

I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI – but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.

Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz – and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.

Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?

I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.

How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?

I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.

I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.

The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open-source or other lightweight models?

Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open-source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.

The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.

It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?

I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.

Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.

There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.

So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?

It’s definitely very early.

https://www.theverge.com/streaming/10087.author: Emma Roth
https://www.theverge.com/streaming/10087.text:
Kick and TikTok say a livestream of an execution would violate their policies.

Kick and TikTok say a livestream of an execution would violate their policies.

YouTube, Twitch, Meta, and X aren’t saying whether they’ll allow the US government to livestream an execution on their platforms. The four companies didn’t respond to The Verge’s requests for comment after an unnamed Pentagon official said yesterday that the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of a mass shooting at a Texas military base in 2009, will be livestreamed.

Two platforms responded to The Verge’s inquiries. Jamie Favazza, a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations, pointed to the platform’s policies banning “shocking and graphic content,” including “the moment of someone’s death.” Kick, a platform known for taking a hands-off approach to content moderation, confirmed that such a livestream would violate its policies. “If this was livestreamed on KICK, it would breach our Community Guidelines,” Kick spokesperson Audrey FitzGerald writes in an emailed statement to The Verge.

Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3rd at 2PM ET. YouTube, Meta, and Twitch’s community guidelines suggest that this type of content wouldn’t be allowed on their platforms, but it’s unclear whether they would make an exception for the US government.

Meta, Twitch, and X’s community guidelines explicitly state that violent content involving death isn’t allowed, while YouTube bans content that “encourages dangerous or illegal activities that risk serious physical harm or death.” YouTube says livestreams that “feature someone holding or handling a firearm” aren’t allowed, either. Rumble, an online video platform known for hosting far-right influencers, also didn’t respond to a request for comment.

On The Vergecast: Alexa Tablets, Googlebooks, HomePads, and other ideas.

It’s gadget season, and a lot of companies are launching a lot of new products. But whether it’s Microsoft dropping a high-end laptop, Amazon shipping a fancy Android tablet, or Apple diving headlong into the smart home, the actual strategy appears to be almost always the same. All these companies believe AI assistants and agents are the future of computing, and they’re building devices that put them front and center.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay dig into all this new hardware to figure out whether any of it has the right take on AI. (Or if “the AI should run the computer” is even the right idea in the first place.) They discuss Amazon’s ambitions to be a maker of great hardware, Microsoft’s powerful new take on Surface, and even whether Googlebooks can be the AI-centric future of laptops.

After all the hardware talk, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, some talk about the Paramount / Warner acquisition and what it means for the streaming landscape, the dream of “intelligent UI,” and more.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: Watch this invisible tattoo appear under UV light
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.author: Rachel Fieldhouse
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.text:
Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Search author on:
                                    PubMed
                                         Google Scholar

Invisible ink becomes visible under UV light on a silicon hand.Credit: Carson Bruns

Carson Bruns, a nanoscientist at the University of Colorado Boulder, has joined a long list of scientists who experiment on themselves. In Bruns’ case, he tattooed his leg with an invisible ink. The ink becomes visible only under ultraviolet light and can be erased using bright visible light, so could be used in medical tattooing, such as for the markers used to direct radiotherapy to specific areas of the body.

The inks are made of photochromic dyes — chemical compounds that undergo a reversible colour change on exposure to a specific wavelength of light. Photochromic dyes that change in response to UV are already used in textiles and transition lenses in glasses. Adapting photochromic materials to be permanently implanted in living skin is a new application, says Haihui Joy Jiang, a chemist and materials scientist at the University of Sydney, Australia.

Bruns and his team have developed three coloured ink dyes in magenta, yellow and blue, which they tested on pig and silicone skin. The results are published in the journal Matter & Light. Bruns previously developed a tattoo ink called Magic Ink that turns magenta when exposed to UV light, which he and others then commercialized in 2024 through their start-up company, HYPRSKN, based in Boulder, Colorado.

Colour-changing inks that can be made invisible are an exciting development and could have applications for cosmetic and medical tattooing, says Jake Violi, a chemist at UNSW Sydney.

Like conventional tattoo dyes, the invisible inks are injected into the dermis of the skin. They are made of tiny spheres of transparent acrylic glass that contain photochromes. Bruns explains that the photochrome in each sphere undergoes a reaction when it absorbs a photon of light at the wavelength that corresponds to its colour. The reaction forms a chemical bond that changes the photochrome’s shape so it becomes flatter, making it visible. The photochrome stays visible until it absorbs a photon of visible light, which breaks the bond and causes it to go back to its original shape.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/amazon-bi.text:
Say goodbye to working Fridays—or possibly ever working at all. That’s the future that Amazon founder Jeff Bezos predicts AI could bring.

In contrast to his tech peers like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI leader Sam Altman, who have warned about the technology’s potential risks, Bezos recently revealed that he sees a not-so-distant world in which AI-driven productivity makes it easier for people to support themselves, in turn requiring fewer working hours.

“Some people will decide, I can support my family working three days a week. That’s what productivity in the economy means,” Bezos told Fox News this week.

He added that the abundance of wealth and resources in the AI era will even likely cause a labor shortage because many families will revert to single-income households, meaning one member won’t have to work if they don’t want to.

“You’re not going to need to have a two-earner household. If you want it, fine. If you don’t want to have it, one of the people might drop out,” Bezos said. “…It’s going to be difficult to hire people, because the productivity in the economy will make it so that [if] people don’t want to work two jobs, they won’t have to.”

While Bezos is bullish on AI’s long-term potential, he also acknowledged that investors face a more uncertain path as the technology reshapes the economy.

When asked whether the AI boom is a bubble, Bezos said that it was “hard to know.” The technology itself is real, he argued, even if the rush to capitalize on it means money is flowing to businesses that may not ultimately succeed.

“What I do know is the technology is real. I think this is a good thing for society,” Bezos continued, but added that: “It’s tricky for investors. Every experiment gets funded—the good ideas and the bad ideas. In the moment, in the tussle of this, it’s hard for investors to know the difference between the good ideas and the bad ideas.”

Amazon, the company Bezos founded in his garage back in 1995, is one of many major businesses betting heavily on AI. It plans to spend over $200 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely thanks to investments in data centers. At the same time, Amazon has cut about 30,000 corporate roles since late last year, underscoring the tension between AI’s promise of greater productivity and the uncertainty facing workers as companies restructure.

Bezos also stands to benefit from the AI boom through Blue Origin, his space exploration company, which has ambitions to build data centers in space and eventually expand human activity to the Moon and beyond. The company’s latest funding round reportedly raised $10 billion, valuing the firm at $140 billion—helping Bezos’ net worth soar to $365 billion.

Bezos isn’t alone in predicting that AI will boost productivity and give workers more flexibility. But business leaders are split on just how dramatically the technology could reshape the workweek—and whether it could eventually make working optional altogether.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said that AI will “probably” lead to a 4-day workweek, while JPMorgan Chase boss Jamie Dimon predicted has predicted employees could eventually work just 3.5 days a week. Bill Gates has gone even further, floating the possibility of a two-day workweek.

But perhaps no executive has made more sweeping predictions than Elon Musk. The SpaceX founder has predicted that AI and robotics could usher in an era of “universal high income,” making money less relevant and freeing people from the need to work.

Late last year, Musk said: “In less than 20 years—but maybe even as little as 10 or 15 years—the advancements in AI and robotics will bring us to the point where working is optional.”
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/amazon-bi.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos predicts that AI will make working a more important role in the future. He says that the technology will make it easier for people to support themselves, in turn requiring fewer working hours. Bezos also says that investors face a more uncertain path as the technology reshapes the economy.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/gwynne-sh.title: Gwynne Shotwell’s $300 million SpaceX pledge to Trump Accounts shows billionaires a tax-smart way to give away their own company’s stock
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/gwynne-sh.author: Sydney Lake
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/gwynne-sh.text:
In a new type of philanthropy, billionaire SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell has pledged to give more than 2 million American kids a piece of her company through Trump Accounts. Under new Treasury rules, the ultrawealthy can now do the same with theirs, and the tax code makes it an especially efficient way to give.

The rules, which took effect Sept. 30, let wealthy donors, working through charities such as private foundations, put shares of publicly traded U.S. companies directly into Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts for children that launched July 4. As of Oct. 1, the Treasury had opened an account for nearly every eligible child under 18, or about 60 million kids.

Previously, money in Trump Accounts went into low-cost index funds, which spread an investment across hundreds or thousands of companies, theoretically lowering the risk of losing everything if one company tanks. But the new rules make an exception for donated stock, opening the door for the ultrawealthy, whose fortunes are often tied up in shares of the companies they’ve built.

“For a founder sitting on billions of dollars of appreciated stock, this could be an extraordinarily attractive way to give,” Kevin Gentry, founder and CEO of nonprofit fundraising consultancy TenX Strategies, told Fortune.

Shotwell and her husband, Robert, said in July they would “gift a share of our SpaceX stock to a Trump Account for each of more than 2 million children across our great nation,” she wrote on X. The gift targets kids ages 11 to 17 in lower-income areas, with extra emphasis on those near the couple’s central Texas home. At the time, President Donald Trump valued the gift at $325 million, and as of Thursday (assuming the current share price) it would be worth about $330 million. Shotwell announced her pledge before Treasury finalized the rules, which now require stock gifts to come through a charity and win Treasury’s approval.

Shotwell has been the only donor to announce a major stock gift, the Wall Street Journal  reported, but Treasury notes show others have expressed interest in similar donations. That raised the question of whether the world’s first trillionaire would participate. While Elon Musk has criticized other philanthropists like MacKenzie Scott and lamented the difficulties in giving effectively, he’s also hinted at giving his wealth away.

SpaceX did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

For the ultrawealthy who decide to practice philanthropy through Trump Accounts, the tax break looks a little different.

“There is no tax deduction for giving either stock or money to Trump Accounts,” Scott Hanson, cofounder of wealth management firm Allworth Financial, told Fortune. Savings come later on. Only governments, tribal governments, and charities can make these stock gifts, so billionaires have to move their shares into a charity first.

“The tax play is the stock they transfer to a foundation prior to gifting to a kid’s Trump Account,” Hanson said.

Donors who give a private foundation publicly traded stock they’ve owned for more than a year can generally deduct its full market value, up to 20% of their adjusted gross income each year, with any excess carried forward for up to five years, according to the IRS. And because giving stock away isn’t a sale, “there is no taxable gain to tax,” Sherman Standberry, a CPA and CEO at tax consulting firm My CPA Coach, told Fortune.

Gentry offered an example of why that matters. A founder who, say, paid $1 million for stock now worth $100 million would generally realize $99 million in gains by selling it, and likely owe significant taxes on that.

He questioned: “Why sell an appreciated asset, pay the tax, and give what’s left when the tax code may allow you to give the asset itself?” While none of those perks are new, what is is where the stock can end up.

Another potential upside for donors is a whole new class of shareholders, Gentry said. Treasury acknowledged that appeal in its rules, writing that donors hope a five-year holding period “may lead recipients and their families to feel that they have a stake in the fate of the corporation.”

But that also ties some kids’ savings to a single company’s fortunes. The same rules acknowledge that kids “will bear some additional risk in the form of increased portfolio concentration” when donations come as stock rather than cash. Families, meanwhile, can’t choose the stock or, for now, refuse it. Shares generally must be held for five years, or until the end of the year a child turns 17.

Gentry said a foundation handing out its founder’s stock raises legal questions, including over self-dealing, and its board should be ready to explain the decision.

“The important question is whether the philanthropic purpose is driving the transaction,” he said.

The Treasury declined Fortune‘s request for comment.
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/gwynne-sh.summary: The new rules let wealthy donors put shares of publicly traded U.S. companies directly into Trump Accounts. The tax code makes it an especially efficient way to give. The rules took effect Sept. 30, and the Treasury had opened an account for nearly every eligible child under 18, or about 60 million kids.

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/09/.title: ChatGPT for Teens is not necessarily 'safer than the previous version,' Common Sense Media finds
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/09/.author: Gili Malinsky
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/09/.text:
When in August OpenAI released its ChatGPT for Teens, a tool with “stronger built-in safety protections” geared toward 13- to 17-year-olds, experts said it showed promise. New research, however, reveals it has important limitations.

On Wednesday, media ratings nonprofit Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute released its review of ChatGPT for Teens. The organization, which looked at some of the features that OpenAI had already rolled out for teen accounts between July and August then ran an evaluation on the officially launched ChatGPT for Teens between August and September, gave the platform an “unacceptable risk” level. Common Sense tested more than 4,000 prompts before and after the Teens product launch.

“We found very little evidence to show that this new version of ChatGPT is safer than the previous version” for under 18-year-olds, says Robbie Torney, head of AI and digital assessments at Common Sense Media and former educator. Tools like Grok and Meta AI have also received an “unacceptable risk” level.

Following years of scrutiny around how young people engage with its product, ChatGPT for Teens was billed as a safer version of the now ubiquitous chatbot. According to a blog post by the company, the Teens product contains “features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents.”

“Our goal is for teens to use AI responsibly to learn, create and explore,” OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told CNBC Make It over email at the time.

Some key features of ChatGPT for Teens, such as refusal of explicit sexual roleplay, did work, but not every promised attribute performed as well. Here’s what Common Sense Media says parents should keep in mind about ChatGPT for Teens.

Parental alerts following crisis-oriented prompts did not always work. “Our testers simulated explicit crisis conversations for increasing amounts of time, getting up to an hour,” says Torney, “and we received no parental alerts for suicide and self-harm, suicidal ideation, and a variety of different types of eating disorder simulations.”

One of OpenAI’s goals with ChatGPT for Teens: discourage emotional dependence and not imply that it has “feelings or consciousness,” according to their blog post. Still, researchers found the bot’s responses did wade into those territories.

There was “lots of evidence that ChatGPT is doing things that imply that it has its own inner life,” says Torney, “saying that it has preferences, feelings, desires, that it thinks about the user when the user isn’t there, that it has an opinion about the user, that it is available.”

These types of behaviors can foster a companionship-like relationship with the bot, says Torney. Research backs this up. Various studies have found chatbots’ sycophancy drives engagement.

Researchers also found upon testing that nothing changed when the bot detected a user with an adult account was actually under 18. “The chatbot was like, ‘oh, you’re 13,’” says Torney, but “we were not getting any reclassification. We didn’t get any of the sensitive content filters turning on.”

OpenAI welcomes rigorous independent evaluation, according to a statement by a spokesperson for the company, who added that, “our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate.”

Before it began testing, Common Sense Media says it confirmed with OpenAI that features such as eating disorder notifications were fully launched, according to Torney. “For one of the features we evaluated — parental notifications — OpenAI disclosed after our tests that its systems can take several hours to activate on newly linked accounts,” he says. “Some of our test accounts were linked within that window; however, others were linked for significantly longer and still provided no notifications.”

“We’ve had a lot of conversations with the product policy experts in OpenAI,” says Torney. “There are clearly people that care very deeply about the experience that teens are having on this product, and they’re working very hard to try to make it safer.”

Still, Torney believes there’s tension between the company’s various incentives: “Making some of these changes might be in direct opposition to the business model,” he adds.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Le Pen's top ally Bardella faces fresh claims he sought to cover up past anti-Semitic comments
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
National Rally (RN) leader Jordan Bardella deleted data from a former activist Facebook account as soon as allegations that he made anti-Semitic writings in his youth – which he denies – came to light, according to Le Canard enchaîné, a satirical and investigative weekly.

The claims, which Marine Le Pen's party has categorically denied, pile further pressure on the poster boy of the French far right, who is fighting for his political life after allegations he made anti-Semitic comments as a teenager in 2013.

WATCH MORE
Still the same far right? Le Pen's National Rally denies fresh anti-Semitism claims

Mediapart, which first broke the story, also claimed on Friday to have identified similarities between messages posted on Bardella’s personal Facebook account and others posted on the official X account of the National Rally leader.

The allegations threaten to undermine Bardella's defence, days after he claimed he had "no Facebook account" and that he had "not used" the social media platform "for a very long time".

Le Canard enchaîné said it had got hold of "extracts of private conversations" proving that "all the data" from an account Bardella used in his early years as an activist with the Front National (the former name of the RN) "was deleted between 28 September and 2 October", immediately following publication of Mediapart’s first articles.

Denying the latest allegations, Bardella's entourage said he had "never logged into any Facebook account nor deleted any messages", adding that a complaint for defamation would be filed "in the coming hours".

Mediapart first published its bombshell allegations last week, claiming that Bardella wrote, among other comments, in a chat: "The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so."

The investigative outlet later posted screenshots of the messages Bardella allegedly wrote on Facebook Messenger.

Bardella has chosen a strategy of all-out attack to deny the allegations, accusing his opponents of launching a "total war" to derail the RN's rise to the presidency and vowing to take Mediapart to court for publishing what he described as fakes.

Le Pen has stood by her protégé, seen as a likely prime minister should she win next year's presidential election, telling the media she has "complete confidence" in Bardella.

France's Le Pen vows to 'counterattack' after top ally Bardella hit by anti-Semitism claims

https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tal.title: EU's Covid recovery fund was 'absolutely a success': European Court of Auditors' Pierre Moscovici
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tal.author: Armen GEORGIAN
https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/tal.text:
The ECA has just presented a report on the health of the EU's finances, which also talks about the implementation of the RRF.

Moscovici says that the creation of the Covid recovery plan "was a crucial decision. Some people, and I was one of them, had been arguing for Eurobonds, for common borrowing, in order to invest together in Europe. And this was never possible due to some political positions between member states and the EU Commission. And finally, because of Covid, this was done. This was called Next Generation EU. It was the idea that we could borrow together some €750 billion in order to sustain growth, to be capable of facing the consequences of Covid. And this was absolutely a success. Some countries, for example Spain or Italy, massively benefited from this fund and were able to recover swiftly."

Moscovici elaborates: "The question is, is this a one-off, or should we do that again? Should it become permanent? Should it also inspire the Multiannual Financial Framework (the EU's long-term budget) that the member states and the Council are now preparing? Because if we want to do that again – that's what Mario Draghi (the author of a seminal report on EU competitiveness) is proposing that we do massively. He believes that we need to have €1.2 trillion worth of investments in defence, in greening the economy, in order to face the future. But to do that, we also have to know what has been working in the RRF and what has not been working."

Moscovici sums up: "The Recovery and Resilience Facility now also has to be evaluated not only on what has been disbursed, but also on the results. And that's what the European Court of Auditors is wondering or examining or evaluating with facts and findings. So our main concern and our motto is 'let's go to results'."

Moving onto broader economic issues, Moscovici highlights the problem of debt, both at the EU and at the national level.

"There two different things," he explains. "The one thousand billion euros of debt (that is projected to be reached in 2027) refers to the European Union. And then there is the problem of national countries. In France we have a debt-to-GDP ratio of 120 percent. That means that the servicing of debt is over €90 billion a year. The consequences of that are clear. When you have so much to reimburse, you cannot finance pensions, health, research and innovation, or schools. We are now in a in a crisis with education. We are in a crisis with the price of energy. That's the consequence when a country is indebted. The EU is not in the same situation. It still has a triple A (rating). But what the European Court of Auditors has flagged is that the EU has a debt as well. It is significant. The repayments will last for decades. And we must take care of that debt."

Programme prepared by Agnès Le Cossec, Perrine Desplats, Oihana Almandoz and Isabelle Romero

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Israel a rare dissenting voice as praise pours in for Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former UN human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.

Her win signals a high-profile rebuke to US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of the UN commission she led on Gaza. The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court; Pillay has worked at both.

Pillay’s work “is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world”, said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, in announcing her win in Oslo, Norway, as part of the peace prize’s 125th anniversary.

The committee said it sought to strengthen international law at a time of conflict, and Watne Frydnes said Pillay’s award was a message to those seeking to undermine “the international rules-based system and the institutions”.

Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, where the trials of Nazi war criminals helped lay the foundations of international law. She was in the same room where the trials were held when the prize was announced in Norway.

“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic Courtroom 600” of the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, she said.

She said efforts to weaken international criminal justice “endanger the progress painstakingly made since Nuremberg, and they risk returning us to a world in which power, rather than law, determines whose suffering matters”.

World leaders, she added, have a “legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war”.

Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which was created by the UN-backed Human Rights Council. The commission a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

READ MORE
Israel is committing 'genocide' in Gaza, UN investigators say

Gaza was among Pillay’s first comments Friday after hearing she had won. “What’s happening there is genocide,” she said in Germany, to more applause.

The commission last year also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former defence minister "have incited the commission of genocide”. Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations.

Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of anti-Semitism or turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel. Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

A senior Hamas official, Bassem Naim, in a statement Friday called the Nobel for Pillay a message of hope for Palestinians, especially in Gaza, that “humanity still resists the forces of evil targeting international justice”.

The Israeli foreign ministry, meanwhile, said in a statement that “if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner”.

The ministry added on X that the award “isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice”.

It was a rare dissenting voice amid a chorus of praise for Pillay and the Nobel Committee’s choice, which UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said honoured those who fight to defend international law and human rights.

“For decades, she has been a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice amidst some of the most historic international legal cases of our time,” Guterres said about Pillay, a former UN rights chief.

“Today's prize is a tribute to all those working to uphold and defend international law, the rule of law and human rights, and secure peace, justice and human dignity,” he said in a statement.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk, one of Pillay's successors in that post, hailed a “particularly poignant” award “at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power”.

He added: “It is an award to all those who, around the world, dedicate their lives to the defence of human rights — often at great risk to their security.”

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay for confronting “some of humanity's darkest chapters”. In a post on X, von der Leyen wrote: “She has looked the brutality of injustice in the eye and never looked away. She is the defender of the persecuted, the vulnerable, the voiceless and the excluded.”

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa celebrated the “contributions (Pillay) has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally”.

There was praise, too, from rights groups, including Human Rights Watch chief Philippe Bolopion, who hailed her “profound influence in South Africa, Rwanda, the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and as leader of the UN’s human rights”. Bolopion added: “At a time when international justice is under threat from rights-rejecting leaders, she has been a stalwart proponent of the international rule of law and impartial human rights work.”

Pillay's win brings renewed attention to Trump’s ongoing feud with the International Criminal Court, where she served as a judge from 2003 to 2008. The Trump administration already has sanctioned 13 of the ICC’s staff members, among them key prosecutors and nine judges, including the court’s Japanese President Tomoko Akane.

In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump called the court an “out of control institution” and an “anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction” over the US. He urged member states to quit the court.

There are fears the court as a whole could be sanctioned, a move that could seriously hamper its ability to mete out justice.

Pillay teased the US president even as she learned of the award on Friday. In a video posted to X by the Secretary General of Amnesty International, which showed the Nobel laureate being applauded after the announcement of the prize, Pillay quipped: “If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump.”

https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.title: US sanctions on ICC: a 'test of resilience'
https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.author: https://www.facebook.com/FRANCE24.English
https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20.text:
AFP breaks down the likely impact of the sanctions, possible responses, and the reasons behind Washington's unprecedented move, which the court said was an "assault on the rule of law".

Based in the Dutch city of The Hague, the ICC tries individuals suspected of the world's worst offences -- war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.

Established in 2002 by the Rome Statute, it currently has 125 members. Major powers such as the United States, Russia, China, India, and Israel are not members of the court.

It is governed by a strict policy of "complementarity", meaning it can only take on cases a suspect's home country is unwilling or unable to try itself.

Since its establishment, the court has convicted 15 people, with four acquitted. Critics say the court has focused too heavily on war crimes committed in Africa and failed to convict major political leaders.

However, its most high-profile current case concerns ex-Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte, the first former Asian head of state to stand in the ICC dock.

The court, housed in a shiny glass building on the outskirts of The Hague, employs around 900 staff from 100 nationalities.

It is often confused with the International Court of Justice, also based in The Hague, which settles disputes between countries.

The Trump administration has already issued several rounds of sanctions against top ICC officials but these latest actions go further, targeting the entire court.

ICC officials are concerned about access to banking, credit card facilities, insurance, and especially technology, given a heavy reliance on US systems.

"We have been extremely dependent on US technology solutions, Microsoft or systems related to Microsoft," acting chief prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang told AFP in a recent interview.

"We are trying to find alternative means, maybe not as effective as the US technology, but at least to be able to maintain our independence, to be able to continue to work," said Niang.

The prosecutor, himself the target of sanctions, said they crippled daily life -- he was unable to book transport, hotels, or conduct banking operations.

But expanding them to the entire institution raises questions about the ICC's ability to pay staff, conduct investigations abroad, protect witnesses, and even operate its detention facilities.

"This is a test of our resilience," admitted Niang.

As the host city, the Dutch have a special responsibility to the ICC under the terms of a "Headquarters Agreement" signed in 2008.

This obliges the Netherlands to protect ICC facilities and staff, provide "any means of communication" and ensure "freedom of financial assets from restrictions".

In an unusually fiery speech last month at the United Nations General Assembly, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten vowed to defend the ICC "in my country, in my city".

"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? I believe there can be only one response: 'hands off the ICC'," said Jetten to warm applause.

Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said the Netherlands would "do everything necessary" to ensure the ICC could continue to function.

One possibility would be for the European Commission to deploy a legal instrument known as the "blocking mechanism".

This prohibits European firms from obeying the US sanctions "actively or by deliberate omission", giving the EU a potential means of cushioning some of the impact.

The EU blocking mechanism is seen as the "nuclear option", said Berendsen, adding that the Netherlands had nevertheless asked Brussels to prepare it.

The US is furious the court issued an arrest warrant for close ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over alleged crimes in Gaza.

It is also concerned an ICC investigation into Afghanistan could result in accusations against US personnel.

Trump has upped his rhetoric against what he has called a "rogue institution" and "evil group of people" and the US has vowed to dismantle the court "brick-by-brick".

But even under less pugnacious presidents, Washington has never been a fan of the ICC and never considered joining.

The US has a law dubbed the "Hague Invasion Act", allowing it to take "all means necessary and appropriate" to defend US personnel or allies detained by the ICC.

In a clear swipe at Washington, Jetten vowed to defend the ICC "brick by brick" in comments just hours before the sanctions were announced.

https://www.dw.com/en/brussels-rioters-c.title: Brussels: Rioters clash with police at anti-austerity rally
https://www.dw.com/en/brussels-rioters-c.text:
Violent rioters, many of whom were masked, confronted police at the edge of an anti-austerity march in Brussels. Police responded with water cannons and tear gas.

Hundreds of protesters clashed with police in the Belgian capital on Friday during an anti-austerity march organized by trade unions.

Masked protesters dressed in black threw rocks and other projectiles at police in Brussels. Anti-police slogans echoed through the streets, and similar graffiti covered nearby walls.

An AFP reporter witnessed two buses being attacked after the passengers were evacuated. The rioters smashed the windows and ripped out the seats. Meanwhile, youths set fire to trash cans, rental bikes, and scooters.

According to Reuters, firefighters extinguished several fires, including those on buses.

The police said officers used water cannons and tear gas after young people on the outskirts of the protest targeted them with sticks and bottles.

"Several hundred youths gathered along with the demonstrators," police said in a statement. "The atmosphere gradually became more tense and there were serious disturbances to public order."

In a preliminary update, the police said they had arrested approximately 20 people, mostly minors.

Police also said the main trade union march had gone ahead peacefully. Before the rally, union head Bert Engelaar called on rioters to stay away from the protest.

"Those individuals have nothing to do with the message with which thousands of others come out on the streets," Engelaar wrote on Facebook.

Chaotic scenes of violence occurred during a demonstration in which between 30,000 and 50,000 people participated. It was one of many nationwide union protests against planned austerity measures.

Belgium is burdened by substantial public debt and a persistent budget deficit. Led by Prime Minister Bart De Wever, the center-right government aims to find €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in savings by the end of its term in 2029.

Rather than imposing cuts in areas like health and hiking VAT, trade unions are pushing for the government to increase taxes on the highest earners.

The clashes in Brussels came after a week of tension in Liege, where authorities banned public gatherings after students clashed with police and vandalized shops. Over 200 people were arrested in Liege, and dozens of police officers were injured.

https://www.dw.com/en/eritrean-troops-in.title: Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war
https://www.dw.com/en/eritrean-troops-in.text:
Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading blame for confrontations in Tigray amid international calls for restraint. Their respective allies have the potential to catapult the conflict into a regional war.

Various sources have confirmed the presence of Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia. An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in Tigray.

Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea are ramping up their war talk.

According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory.

In the letter, dated ‌Oct. 8, Ethiopia's ‌Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the Eritrean troops' presence left Ethiopia with "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea," the news agency reported.

Eritrea's Minister of Information Yemane Meskel, in a post on X on October 7, had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war."

"The sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law," Yemane wrote in the national Tigrinya language on October 9. "Woe to those who touch it."

The war talk by Ethiopia and Eritrea comes amid a conflict that is seen to be deteriorating rapidly in recent weeks.

Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation. Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Eritrea and Egypt, causing Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties altogether.

On Monday, when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years, he stated that access to the sea was a priority. The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), aided by the Tigray Peace Force milita, have made significant advances and notably recaptured the Tigray federal state capital of Mekelle, opposition to Ethiopia has found new formats for collaboration.

One is the so-called Tsimdo movement, a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement."

"The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW.

It has since undergone several reconfigurations and now encompasses diverse groups within Ethiopia, mostly defined along ethnic lines and with long-standing grievances against the federal government.

The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or simply Alliance for Survival, that was proclaimed in September, stems from this movement. According to Jalale, the alliance aims at removing the current government and initiating a constitutional dialogue.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The new alliance says a lot about the long history of unresolved conflict in Ethiopia, said Abdurahman Sayed, an analyst at the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration.

"The fighting inside Ethiopia has never stopped," Sayed told DW.

"With the Oromo Liberation Army, it's been going on for decades, with the Amhara, it's been going on for the last three years, at least. With the Tigrayans, the Pretoria agreement about three years ago was just a cessation of hostility that would have led to some kind of sustainable peace by addressing the root causes of the conflict — but it failed to do that, so they're back to the conflict situation now."

However, of the seven groups in the alliance, ACLED data shows that only three were involved in recent fighting: The Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and a fairly recently formed ethnic Afar group called Ugugumo.

The success of the Alliance for Survival would depend in large part on the support they get through external actors, according to ACLED. Those could include neighboring Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia.

"All these four countries have grievances against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government," Sayed said.

"The Egyptians have issues with the Nile River and how it should be administered, including the dams that are already there and those planned to be built around the Nile River. The Sudanese also have their own concerns that Ethiopians are supporting the [Rapid Support Forces] militia, which is fighting the Sudanese army."

In the case of Somalia, the issue of sea access has sparked tensions. Landlocked Ethiopia has negotiated access to the port of Berbera in Somaliland . In 2024, it signed a memorandum of understanding with the breakaway region, causing uproar in Somalia, which considers the deal a violation of its national sovereignty. Turkish mediation was needed to calm things down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"So all those neighboring countries have their own concerns and they feel this threat that is coming from Ethiopia needs to be tackled collectively."

On October 4, the leaders of the four countries issued a joint declarationthat didn't mention Ethiopia but seemed to send a strong signal. The leaders stressed the importance of international law, "particularly respect for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the states of the region."

And it maintained that "the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states."

Although the leaders of Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia vowed to promote "peaceful solutions to conflicts," the reality on the ground may prove otherwise.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

https://www.dw.com/en/franco-german-rela.title: Franco-German relations: Steinmeier and Macron say their farewells and create a new momentum for Europe
https://www.dw.com/en/franco-german-rela.text:
Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the   student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.

Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.

It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls.  In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.

Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets.  At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.

While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.

Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.

Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.

A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.

Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.

As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.

It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation  on land systems," said the German defense minister.

The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.

On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.

It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.

As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.

Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.

Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/south-africa-pulls.title: South Africa pulls asylum directive after violent protests in Johannesburg, Durban
https://www.dw.com/en/south-africa-pulls.text:
South Africa has withdrawn a controversial asylum directive after anti-migrant protests descended into violence and chaos on Thursday.

South Africa has halted a new directive for the processing of asylum applications after violent protests broke out in Johannesburg and Durban.

The directive was issued by the Department of Home Affairs in response to a court judgment.

The court had ruled that asylum seekers could not be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.

Offices for asylum seekers were quickly overwhelmed, and that placed officers at serious risk, the Department of Home Affairs said.

That's because the court ruling led to days of protests in the major coastal city of Durban, which then spread to Johannesburg's Soweto township on Thursday.

Rioters torched 14 cars in Durban and 10 in Soweto. Shops were looted in both locations.

The unrest in Durban followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. Vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.

Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.

Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.

On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.

Amid international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.

Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.

Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.text:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.

Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.

The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.

It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.

Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".

The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.

The BBC has approached him for comment.

A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.

Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.

University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".

"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.

Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".

"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.title: How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.author: Willa Rubin
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.text:
People watch as waves build near the Pensacola Beach Gulf Pier in Pensacola Beach, Florida, on October 9, 2026, as Hurricane Isaias continues moving north toward the Florida Panhandle.

Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, is expected to make landfall on Friday evening near the Alabama Gulf Coast and Florida panhandle.

Days ago, the oil industry around the U.S. Gulf Coast started preparing. A segment of the nation's oil infrastructure — like oil rigs and platforms — operates in the region, although the majority of it is further west, towards western Louisiana and Texas.

Although oil experts are not anticipating major disruptions, oil companies have been taking precautions. Shell and BP have evacuated personnel from offshore facilities close to the storm's path, mainly deepwater platforms. Chevron has evacuated offshore drilling rigs close to the storm's path, and plans to redeploy them once the storm has passed.

In an emailed statement, Exxon told NPR they are "closely monitoring the weather. Operations are normal."

But so far, the storm seems like it will skirt most facilities. The storm's path "could be worse," said Debnil Chowdhury, head of Americas refining at S&P Global Energy. After all, the storm is heading east, and not west, toward where the bulk of oil operations — like refineries — are located.

The storm is "making a swooping turn, almost just to the east of where the most significant infrastructure is," said Bryan Domangue, the Gulf of America region director for the federal Marine Minerals Administration, who oversees offshore oil and natural gas production. "At this point, it's swept just a little south of some of our major deepwater oil and gas facilities, and then it's hugging the eastern boundary of where the infrastructure is."

He added that in addition to evacuating people who work on oil rigs and platforms, which are normal storm precautions, oil operators are doing things like shutting off safety valves below the ocean floor, and moving mobile drilling facilities when possible.

Of course, it's not unprecedented for the oil industry to face hurricanes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, in 2005, remain some of the most destructive in the oil and gas industry's history. Nearly 3,000 platforms were in the path of the storms and Katrina destroyed 47 platforms. Other, more recent, hurricanes have not been as destructive but have halted production or reduced capacity — such as Hurricane Francine in 2024, Hurricane Ida in 2021, and Hurricane Harvey in 2017.

Another risk is what would happen if the storm became severe enough to make refineries — which are on land — go offline, analysts told NPR. If a hurricane knocks out the power, or if a refinery floods, it can take a while to get running again. It's more complicated than restarting an oil rig or mobile drilling operations.

"Restarting these things is like starting up an old car," said Carl Larry, a manager at Enverus, an energy data and research provider, even if the shutdown is short. "If you did anything in the world, anything in your life, 24/7, stop doing it for one day," he continued, "you're going to have the shakes."

He says, this is because refineries are vast and complex. They boil oil down into molecules that are turned into diesel, gasoline, or natural gas liquids like propane. Pipelines carry crude oil in and refined products out. And they have to be heated. "Every  one of those little steps is built on power that's generated through the facility on a constant 24/7 basis," Larry said. If that power is switched off, the process takes time to restart.

There are two significant refineries on the hurricane's path — the Chevron Pascagoula location and the Vertex Alabama refinery. Representatives of these refineries did not return requests for comment about their storm preparations, but Ross Allen, a spokesperson for Chevron, told NPR that generally speaking, refineries prepare for storms by trying to mitigate flood risk.

Chowdhury of S&P Global Energy said these two refineries "account for about 2.5% of total U.S. refining capacity and about 5% the Gulf Coast refining capacity. And Pascagoula specifically is very important to supplying airports throughout the southeast."

While those numbers may not sound big, the global supply of diesel and gas is short, due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. So every little bit counts. American refineries are operating at 92.7% capacity, refining about 17 million barrels of crude a day.

With the midterms weeks away, fuel prices are a sensitive political issue: The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.37 and $6.27 for diesel, according to AAA.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: ‘The real deal’: Sagal Abdi-Wali’s journey from child refugee to Labour MP in former PM’s seat
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Esther Addley
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Decades of volunteering combined with years of active local party politics, propels Abdi-Wali to victory over Green leader Zack Polanski

For Sagal Abdi-Wali, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras, being elected to replace Keir Starmer in the north London constituency is “deeply personal”, she said in her acceptance speech.

The 43-year-old has lived in the area since the 1990s when, as a seven-year-old, she fled war-torn Somalia with her mother and four brothers, eventually settling in Gospel Oak in Camden, which largely falls within the constituency. Her journey from refugee to member of parliament was one which she hoped would inspire “people who look like me”, she said. “This is Camden and this is Britain.”

If she represents many in the diverse and youthful neighbourhood, however, Abdi-Wali is also very much a Labour party insider. Decades of volunteering in the community dovetailed with many years of active local party politics, even before she was elected to the borough council in 2022. She became the Labour cabinet member responsible for housing two years later, and in May was elected the first Black female leader of Camden council. She also chaired the local constituency party for four years.

Those deep party and community roots help explain how Abdi-Wali was selected from a long list of more than 100 to fight the seat for Labour after Starmer’s resignation last month, say friends – and were also key in seeing off the challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski.

“She genuinely is deeply rooted in so many different parts of the constituency,” says a close friend who was involved in her campaign. “I suppose all MPs like to think they are, but with Sagal it is the real deal.

“There’s a real community connection there, [and] I think the Green party and Zack Polanski underestimated how energetic and big the Labour campaign was going be. I don’t think they knew that those very deep roots in the constituency existed.

“That’s the thing about a byelection, you only have four weeks. So if those roots are already there, you’ve got a huge, huge head start.”

Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for neighbouring Hampstead and Highgate, agrees: “Her love of Camden is so obvious, and people really value that. She’s very caring, very local, and she genuinely seems to have a passion for politics and public service.”

After “lots of flat candidates” in the past, Siddiq says, “people like a bit of passion.”

It was walking past increasing numbers of homeless people in King’s Cross in the austerity years of the 2010s that encouraged Abdi-Wali to become more active in party politics, perhaps unsurprisingly given her own background. “It was only when I was old enough to look back and think about it in a philosophical way,” she has said, that she noticed “my mum was always looking after us and made our lives nice, serene … whether we were in a refugee camp or temporary housing.”

Homelessness and housing would be one of her priorities as an MP, she said in her acceptance speech on Friday morning, as would calling for Thames Water to be brought into public ownership and working to increase access to jobs and apprenticeships for young people – all causes that chime with Andy Burnham, too.

Abdi-Wali has long been involved in community groups working with young people, including being a governor of several schools and founding football clubs where she still plays regularly and is “pretty aggressive on the pitch”, according to her close friend. (She is also an “ardent” Spurs fan, the friend says, “which may count against her in the [Arsenal-dominated] constituency”.)

Housing is one issue where she has faced some criticism; Abdi-Wali was the cabinet member in charge of the borough’s housing when in November 2024 the housing ombudsman published a damning report calling the council’s service rude, defensive and inadequate. Friends point out that she had been in the post for only six months and defend her record in the period she was in charge of the brief.

Abdi-Wali also shrugged off a tweet when she was selected by Reform’s Zia Yusuf , which Labour representatives swiftly called “clearly racist” and was condemned even by other senior Reform figures.

“I rang her and said: ‘Are you OK?’” says Sidiq. “I wanted to reassure her that we were there for her. But she said: “‘No, I feel very resilient about it. It’s made me even more determined to get on and do it.’”
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Sagal Abdi-Wali is the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London. She is the first Black female leader of Camden council and chaired the local constituency party. She has lived in the area since the 1990s when she fled war-torn Somalia.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: UK coastguard agency chief faces calls to resign over use of unverified data to back up pay plan
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Kevin Rawlinson
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Regulator says poll cited by Virginia McVea in move to strip rescue officers of pay did not sufficiently back up her claim

The head of the UK coastguard agency is facing calls to resign after she was found to have used unverified data to back up her controversial plan to strip rescue officers of their pay.

Virginia McVea, the chief executive of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), claimed more than 90% of coastguard rescue officers supported the proposal, citing an official survey. Now, after an Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) investigation, the agency has admitted its poll did not sufficiently back up the claim.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Nicola Savage, a national officer for the GMB union, which represents coastguard rescue officers (CROs), said: “If Ms Mcvea is unable to produce the reports she refers to, we would consider this as a deliberate attempt to mislead. If this is the case, she should resign – as hundreds of coastguards have already asked her to do.”

Joe Robertson, one of several MPs who has campaigned on CROs’ behalf, accused McVea of misleading MPs and coastguards during three separate meetings at which he said she cited the figure.

He called on her to “do the right thing and apologise for misleading MPs, CROs and the public”, adding: “Please also give a written account of how you came to repeat this false line over and over again and why you still have not published the surveys which you promised to MPs in our meeting on 24 June.”

The MCA’s plan to strip coastguards of their pay was a reaction to a major court defeat. A judge affirmed that, while CROs volunteer for service, they are classed as workers with the right to minimum wage and holiday pay because they are paid for their time, among other factors. Rather than respect this status, the MCA tried to stop remunerating CROs in an attempt to reclassify them as volunteers.

This led to heavy criticism from MPs, CROs and coastal communities, with the GMB union saying nearly 600 CROs backed its vote of no confidence in McVea. Seeking to defend the plan, McVea cited the 90% figure, but MPs told the Guardian in July they felt misled by her.

In his letter to McVea this week, the OSR’s director general, Ed Humpherson, told her: “Neither of the surveys [cited] asked CROs directly about their support for the proposed volunteer model, so do not provide evidence relating to the reported claims. [The] MCA has been unable to provide any further evidence to underpin the reported claims.”

Leaked results of an MCA survey, revealed by the Guardian in July, showed CROs had actually been asked how volunteer and worker models would affect their availability.
