after newsletter promotion

The results suggested the MCA had included people who said they would become less able to respond to calls if they were volunteers, as well as those who replied “other”, among those in support of the volunteer model. The agency said at the time that “survey findings were considered alongside a range of operational, legal and practical factors”. But it refused to say how.

The plan was ultimately scrapped by the maritime minister, Keir Mather, as he responded to near-universal criticism. CROs are still waiting to find out what system will be adopted, but it is understood the option of not paying coastguards is no longer on the table.

The MCA has been approached for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Christian Bittar has conviction for rigging interest rates quashed
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Joanna Partridge
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Former City banker becomes eighth to clear their name, just days after five others were acquitted

Former City trader Christian Bittar has become the eighth person to have his conviction for rigging interest rates quashed, just days after five other former bankers also successfully cleared their names.

Christian Bittar, who previously worked for Deutsche Bank, was convicted in 2018 of conspiracy to defraud.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

On Wednesday, the court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, all of whom worked at Barclays.

This week’s acquittals come just over a year after the UK supreme court overturned a decade-old ruling against the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes and former Barclays trader Carlo Palombo. Their victory opened the door for the other traders to challenge their convictions.

Bittar said after his acquittal: “I have waited a very, very long time for this day. Finally, the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it.”

Bittar and the five other former traders were all sentenced to jail on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).

The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.

The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries, that had ultimately “deprived” the men a fair trial.

Friday’s ruling marks a further blow for the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the former traders.

While the SFO did not contest the appeals of the five men acquitted on Wednesday, it did contest Bittar’s appeal, stating his conviction was safe.

Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said: “We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.”

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

Ben Rose of law firm Hickman and Rose, who represented Bittar, said it was a “scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to ensure that these trials are fair”.

Peter Johnson, the ninth former trader who was convicted of rate rigging, also intends to appeal against his conviction. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to manipulate Libor in 2014.

Ellen Gallagher, a partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said: “Peter’s fight to clear his name continues.

“As the court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Gaya Gupta
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional

Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.

Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website.

Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year-long term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers.

Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property.

Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors.

Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations.

In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired.

Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April.

Congress created the Fed to be an independent and nonpartisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy.

Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Insurance model is no substitute for the NHS | Letter
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Susan Jones points out that an NHS-style system does not require either sales costs or shareholder profits

In Dining across the divide (4 October), the young participant, Ted, is quoted as expressing his “desire to abolish the NHS and replace it with a social insurance model. This would still have provision for free treatment at the point of need, but people would pay through insurance systems, and they would choose the level of cover they’ve got. Those models deliver far better outcomes for patients.”

As a retired insurance underwriter, I must disagree profoundly with Ted’s assertion. Let’s concentrate on business fundamentals. Insurance comes in two “flavours”: first, events that become likelier as time goes on – eg, life assurance. The older you get, the more likely you are to die and the more premium is needed to cover the risk; and second, events whose likelihood stays essentially the same over time, eg home insurance – the likelihood of a house burning down is much the same for everyone and the cost is spread evenly between policyholders.

Clearly, medical insurance is flavour one. Premiums need to rise with age. To reduce premiums and keep customers, insurance companies apply ever-increasing “excesses” and “co-pays” and can refuse to cover pre-existing conditions. The more you need medical insurance, the more expensive and difficult it is to get.

There is also the business case. When you buy an insurance policy, premiums are calculated to include the cost of claims (about 60%); administration (about 10%); sales (about 20%); shareholder profits (about 15%); less investment returns (about 5%).

In contrast, an NHS-style system does not require either sales costs or shareholder profits. Of course, there would be no investment return – but nevertheless, it is still about 30% cheaper to operate than an insured healthcare system. Like most sound business ideas, it’s simple arithmetic.
Susan Jones
Biggin Hill, London

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Clashes have erupted near Brussels Central station on the sidelines of a demonstration organised by the country’s socialist trade union against the federal government’s austerity plans.

As thousands of protesters gathered at the station on Friday, a smaller group clashed with the police and threw wooden beams, glass bottles and rubbish bins, The Belgian Times reported.

Police were deployed in large numbers around the stations as officers checked groups of young people not wearing trade union colours.

Police said the main trade union rally went ahead peacefully but “groups of troublemakers were responsible for serious incidents before and after the march.”

Riot police responded to those protesters with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges. Police said those who “cause the problems of public order are not linked” to the rally.

Reporting from Brussels, Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard said damage was caused during Friday morning’s protests with an “acrid smell of burning in the air”, due to fires that were set and the tear gas.

“Police [and] emergency services have been arriving, starting to disperse or clean up and then the protests flare up again. So the day is still early; often these things get worse in the evening in terms of the street violence,” Birchard explained.

“There were some young people who came out, they say they were inspired by what they had seen in France in terms of school protests, and they also wanted to talk about the education environment they’re learning in,” she said, adding that the students felt that they were “not being listened to”.

The clashes came after a week of tension in the city of Liege after authorities banned gatherings as students clashed with police and vandalised shops. More than 200 people were arrested in Liege, and dozens of police were injured.

The ABVV trade union and the Christian ACV, the country’s two biggest unions, organised protests on Friday morning, with protesters marching from Brussels Central station to Brussels South Station under the slogan “stay out of our pockets”.

Police said about 30,000 people attended the demonstrations, while ABVV had earlier estimated attendance at 50,000.

The anger stems from the government’s austerity measures, as officials consider a new budget that opposes potential measures that affect purchasing power, the wage indexation system and value-added tax (VAT), as well as plans to introduce annualised working time.

At the same time, the ACV organised a separate protest involving hundreds of activists at the capital’s headquarters of the governing coalition parties.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Trump launches probe into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
United States President Donald Trump has announced a committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and whether alleged false statements on mortgage documents constitute grounds for her removal under federal law.

The White House announced the new committee on Wednesday, but published the notice on its website on Friday.

The three-member committee, which will be tasked with reviewing evidence and reporting to the president on whether he has sufficient cause to remove her, will include the assistant to the president for economic policy, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the director of the Office of Government Ethics.

The notice says there will be a hearing on November 5, where Cook will be required to appear and answer questions.

Trump began efforts to remove Cook as one of the governors on the US Federal Reserve Board in August 2025 after Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte accused her of misrepresenting two different properties on a 2021 mortgage application before she joined the central bank. She was appointed to the Fed Board in 2022 by then-President Joe Biden. Cook’s term runs until 2038.

Trump announced Cook’s removal amid the allegations, but Cook sued, and a federal judge blocked her firing in September 2025. Cook remained in office while the case continued.

In June, the Supreme Court declined to let Trump remove Cook while the litigation continues.

The case led to the US Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that the president could not remove a Fed governor without adequate cause and needed to follow a clear process to lay out the reasons and provide evidence.

The ruling left Cook in her position, but kicked the case against her back to a federal district court.

The case has been closely watched as Trump has put political pressure on the central bank to cut interest rates, including launching investigations into then-Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, whose term ended in May.

In December 2025, Trump said he would only appoint someone who agreed with him on cutting interest rates. He appointed Kevin Warsh as Powell’s replacement.

Amid ongoing tensions with Iran, pressure on the oil market and rising inflation, the Fed last month raised the benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.75–4 percent, the first hike in three years. With the final rate decision before the midterm elections later this month, CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts that rates will likely remain unchanged.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Israeli settler attacks target Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Israeli settlers have carried out attacks and pogroms disrupting the Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank, while Israeli forces separately detained several Palestinians across the occupied territory.

At least 19 settler attacks were recorded on Friday by the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, a Palestinian government body operating under the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).

The commission said the incidents included attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters, the burning and uprooting of olive trees, and the theft of crops and livestock. Other Palestinians and their vehicles were also targeted.

Settlers set fire to Palestinian-owned groves and stole olives in what is considered the most important season for harvesting the single-seeded stone fruit.

More than 50 olive trees were uprooted by settlers in Qusra, the commission said.

Settlers also assaulted and injured Palestinian farmers involved in the harvest in the Tal, where a Palestinian-owned vehicle was set on fire, it added.

Additionally, olive harvesters were attacked in Jorish, Beita, Naqoura, Birzeit, Deir Bzeih and Farata.

A farmer was injured in reported gunfire in Kafr ad-Dik, and the use of live ammunition was reported during a settler pogrom, backed by Israeli forces, in Deir Ballut.

Elsewhere, an elderly Palestinian woman in Berin, east of Hebron, was injured after settlers set their dogs on farmers while sheep were stolen in Ein Qinya.

A Palestinian man and his child were attacked and their vehicle stolen by settlers in Yabrud. Settler attacks on Palestinian-owned vehicles were also reported in the towns of Sarda and al-Rihan.

Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank said settlers, backed Israeli forces, have grown more brazen in their attacks against Palestinians during the olive harvest despite the presence of foreign activists and observers.

“Palestinians have to go about the harvest in large groups, that include international solidarity activists, to try to stop settler intimidation and attacks,” Ibrahim said, adding that the settlers wait for the groups to start leaving at the end of the harvest, before springing into action.

“It has become a very difficult journey, as the Palestinians try to leave the harvesting areas, Israeli settlers continue to intimidate them under the protection of the Israeli army,” she said.

As Ibrahim reported, a Palestinian family was under attack by Israeli settlers who recently started building an illegal settlement outpost near Ramallah, “using it as a base to attack Palestinians”, she said.

“No one is being spared,” said Ibrahim.

For Palestinians, the olive harvest is supposed to be a joyous season, but instead, they fear settler attacks and intimidation backed by the Israeli forces.

As settler attacks and pogroms continue, the Israeli army arrested 16 Palestinians in raids across the occupied West Bank on Friday, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency and local sources speaking to the Anadolu news agency.

In Hebron, southern West Bank, Israeli forces arrested nine Palestinians after raiding and searching their homes, including Ibrahimi Mosque Director Moataz Abu Sneineh and Hammam Abu Markhiya, an official responsible for the mosque’s custodians, Wafa reported.

In the city of Qalqilya, Israeli forces arrested five Palestinians during a raid, local sources said.

Two other Palestinians were arrested after Israeli forces raided and searched several homes in Beita, south of Nablus, the sources said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into Category 3 storm with US in its sights
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Hurricane Isaias has strengthened into a major Category 3 storm as the Gulf Coast of the United States prepares for potentially “life-threatening” conditions.

The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday that Isaias was packing winds in excess of 193kph (120mph) and was expected to continue strengthening over the course of the day. A Category 3 storm, considered a major hurricane by the NHC, is capable of causing devastating damage.

Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, is expected to make landfall in the US later on Friday or early Saturday between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and Choctawhatchee Bay in Florida, the center said.

When it comes ashore, the storm is forecast to weaken quickly as it moves inland into the southern US. But the NHC urged local governments to quickly prepare for the dangerous conditions that Isaias could bring.

“Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today”, forecasters said. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast”.

Storm surge as high as 2.7 metres (9 feet) could impact an area extending from the Alabama-Florida border to Grayton Beach, Florida, creating “dangerous” conditions for residents who live along the Gulf shoreline. Isaias is projected to produce 10.1 to 20.3cm of rainfall (4 to 8 inches) across the coast, with possible localised totals of up to 38cm (15 inches).

“This is a life-threatening situation”, the center warned. “Persons located within these areas should take all necessary actions to protect life and property from rising water and the potential for other dangerous conditions.”

States of emergency have been issued by governments in parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia. Several coastal counties along the Gulf of Mexico have mandatory evacuation orders.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who has requested an emergency declaration from US President Donald Trump ahead of Isaias’ landfall, warned residents in the state’s panhandle region of potentially significant storm damage.

“But the surge is really what puts a lot of people’s lives in jeopardy if they haven’t heeded evacuation orders, and does the most significant damage from these storms,” DeSantis said. “Everywhere from Pensacola all the way into the Big Bend section of north Florida, you could see storm surge. So please take caution of that.”

“And we always say you hide from the wind, but you run from the water. When the water’s rising and things are happening, it’s a very, very difficult conundrum — and you do not want to be caught in that,” he added.

On Thursday, the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) urged Gulf Coast residents to prepare for the hurricane and said its offices were “fully engaged”.

As of early Friday, the NHC said Isaias was centred about 386km (240 miles) south of Pensacola in Florida and moving north-northeast at 24kph (15 mph).

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/tesla-.title: Tesla renames ‘Full Self-Driving’ to ‘Tesla Assisted Driving’ in Europe
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/tesla-.author: Sean O'Kane
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/tesla-.text:
Tesla has changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving,” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”

It’s a big capitulation from Tesla, which has been using the “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” name for years despite the system requiring humans to pay attention to the road and take over when necessary. But the name change could help Tesla achieve its goal of wider adoption on the continent, which could unlock a potentially massive new revenue stream for the company.

Germany’s transport minister, Steffen Bilger, said earlier this month that calling the software “Full Self-Driving” was somewhat misleading because it doesn’t perform the entire task of driving. He spoke with Tesla last month, and the company suggested the name change, according to an official release from the ministry. Bilger said he will now advocate for approval of Tesla Assisted Driving across Europe ahead of an EU-wide vote that could happen later this year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked Bilger on X this week.

Musk has spent years agitating for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), or FSD, to be approved in Europe. “FSD in Europe will save lives of people in the car, as well as vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, and pets,” he wrote on X in June 2025. “Please let your government know that you want approval.”

In March of this year, he wrote that the “extreme regulatory burden” of the EU “stifles innovation in Europe,” adding that Europe “will love Tesla self-driving!”

Just a few weeks later, the Netherlands became the first European country to approve FSD (Supervised). On Wednesday, Reuters reported that Tesla’s campaign for European approval has been “built on faulty company safety research” and “flawed studies.” The outlet also reported that the Dutch vehicle safety regulator, RDW, faced fierce pressure from Tesla and its legion of online supporters.

Tesla’s software has certainly become more capable over the years. What used to be little more than a mix of lane centering and adaptive cruise control is now a driver assistance system that some owners use for nearly 100% of their daily driving. FSD can pull in and out of parking spots and navigate surface streets and highways. Tesla is so confident in the technology that it recently made it possible for FSD to intervene in a human driver’s control of the vehicle if it senses an oncoming collision — even if FSD is not active.

But FSD has been at the center of federal investigations and civil lawsuits over crashes in which it was allegedly in use. Its less capable predecessor, Autopilot, has been associated with dozens of fatalities. Tesla discontinued Autopilot earlier this year after a judge ruled Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing about the system’s capabilities.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/rememb.title: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/rememb.author: Jagmeet Singh
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/rememb.text:
Orkut, the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection.

In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join.

Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube.

In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote.

“I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added.

This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users.

In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch.

Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch.

An email sent to Orkut seeking comment from Büyükkökten did not elicit a response.

https://www.wired.com/story/the-doj-is-w.title: The DOJ Is Weighing Perjury Charges Against Cassidy Hutchinson
https://www.wired.com/story/the-doj-is-w.author: Hugo Lowell
https://www.wired.com/story/the-doj-is-w.text:
Federal prosecutors have been weighing a perjury and obstruction of justice case against Cassidy Hutchinson, who implicated President Donald Trump in the January 6 Capitol riot in testimony four years ago, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The efforts mark the Justice Department’s intent to proceed against Hutchinson, a former aide to ex-Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, though prosecutors are not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment at least until after the midterms, the sources say.

Hutchinson testified as a star witness to the committee that investigated the riot, recounting that Trump encouraged his supporters to march to the Capitol even though he knew many were armed. She sat for several interviews in addition to her public testimony, where she recalled hearing that Trump had lunged at one of his Secret Service agents after being told he could not join his supporters at the Capitol.

In recent months, prosecutors at the Justice Department have focused on the fact that the former special counsel, Jack Smith, did not corroborate much of Hutchinson’s account to the committee, and the Secret Service’s denial of any altercation in the presidential limo, the sources say.

By comparing the transcripts of Hutchinson’s interviews with the committee and against her testimony to Smith’s team, prosecutors have been trying to construct a case based on how her testimony has changed, the sources say.

Prosecutors have also taken a special interest in Hutchinson’s claim that she had penned a statement on a notecard for Trump to release during the Capitol riot—a claim disputed by former Trump White House counsel Eric Herschmann, who said he had written the note.

It was not immediately clear whether prosecutors intend to ultimately proceed with both perjury and obstruction charges, which have been under consideration for several months. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Hutchinson and her lawyer did not respond to texts and calls seeking comment. Hutchinson, now 29, has kept a low profile since publishing a memoir of her time in Trump’s first administration in 2023 titled “Enough.”

Punchbowl News first reported the Justice Department’s interest in charging Hutchinson.

The grand jury investigation is the latest example of the Justice Department pursuing criminal cases against Trump’s perceived political enemies. Trump fired former Attorney General Pam Bondi in April partly for moving too slowly to bring such cases, sources familiar with the matter said.

Some Justice officials have been skeptical about whether there is a viable criminal case against Hutchinson, in part due to the high bar for successfully prosecuting perjury charges, the sources say. To prove that Hutchinson lied to Congress, prosecutors would need to show beyond a reasonable doubt that Hutchinson lied, that she did so knowingly, and that it materially impacted the investigation, former US Attorney Joyce Vance tells WIRED.

The investigation into Hutchinson became a priority for the DOJ after a criminal referral by Representative Barry Loudermilk, a Georgia Republican who for years has been deeply critical of the January 6 committee investigation. Loudermilk had separately sought to depose Hutchinson until he was blocked by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who was concerned it could surface damaging texts of a sexual nature between lawmakers and Hutchinson.

In an unorthodox move, the referral ended up getting assigned to the Civil Rights Division at the DOJ, as opposed to the US Attorney for the District of Columbia or the Criminal Division, which would usually handle public corruption cases.

Under Justice Department guidelines, the Civil Rights Division is only supposed to take cases with a nexus to a civil rights violation. The division is led by Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump loyalist who has been a reliable advocate for the Trump administration's prosecutorial agenda.

The Justice Department is not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment until after the midterms.

https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.author: Ed Silverman
https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/.text:
The gifts and payments that doctors receive from drugmakers increased inappropriate prescribing and the number of prescriptions written, likely leading to rising health care costs, according to a Cochrane review of dozens of previous studies that have explored the influence the pharmaceutical industry has on medical practice.

In addition, pharmaceutical advertising or education aimed at doctors may also increase inappropriate prescribing, probably increases the number of prescriptions written, and may increase the costs of prescriptions. But conflict-of-interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between companies and doctors probably improved prescribing practices, the analysis found.

However, there was not enough evidence to draw clear conclusions on whether free drug samples and other promotions affect decisions to place specific drugs on hospital formularies. These are the list of medicines approved for use and routinely stocked in a hospital or health system.

https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/09/medi.author: Bob Herman
https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/09/medi.text:
The federal government has released new quality ratings for Medicare Advantage insurers for 2027, with Humana emerging as the biggest winner.

But deep uncertainty remains around Medicare Advantage quality measures, which come with tens of billions of dollars in extra revenue for the highest-performing plans. One health insurance company, Alignment Healthcare, has already threatened to sue the government after its star ratings were downgraded — a now-common occurrence for almost any insurer that is unhappy with its grades.

Nearly 71% of Medicare Advantage enrollees are currently in a plan that will have at least four out of five stars for quality, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Getting at least four stars triggers bonuses, which total $13 billion across the industry annually. Ratings for 2027 lead to bonus payouts in 2028.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/disney-of.title: Disney offered a 13-year-old $2 million to sing in ‘The Lion King.’ His mom took $100K plus royalties instead. He’s still getting paid 34 years later
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/disney-of.author: Orianna Rosa Royle
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/disney-of.text:
Becoming an overnight millionaire is every teenager’s dream. But when Disney offered 13-year-old Jason Weaver $2 million to sing as young Simba in The Lion King—his mom told them no.

“When they offered that deal, it was really just to take this money and go,” Weaver once told VladTV in a 2019 interview that’s currently going viral on social media. “I think they knew and forecasted that they were gonna make a s–t ton of money.”

It was a huge offer for a kid from Chicago. Weaver says his biggest paycheck until then was about $80,000, for playing a young Michael Jackson. “That amount of money to an average middle-class family in Chicago in the early ’90s … That’s something,” he said.

But his mom and manager, Marilyn “Kitty” Haywood, wasn’t dazzled.

Instead, she negotiated for royalties and about $100,000 upfront. And three decades on, the now 47-year-old “I Just Can’t Wait to Be King” singer is still getting paid—and has since made more than the $2 million he rejected.

“If she hadn’t done that, that would have been one of the biggest mistakes of my career,” he added.

As the saying goes, good things come to those who wait. Weaver’s mom said an upfront check could be the last he ever saw from the film. She’d noticed something: Disney kept rereleasing its old classics, decade after decade—a habit that began with the 1944 reissue of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. She’d also taken stock that Disney was on a roll: The casting call came hot off the heels of the success of Aladdin and Beauty and the Beast.

“She was able to see the playing field and go, ‘Wait a minute, this is gonna make a lot of money over time, so what happens when my son turns 40? Is he still gonna be able to get a check from this when they eventually release this?’” Weaver recalled. “And sure enough, she was absolutely right.”

It was a risky ask at the time. Weaver said that Disney wasn’t doing royalty deals for newcomers back then, only for “established huge pop stars.” But Haywood wasn’t new to the entertainment business. She sang with the Chicago group Kitty & the Haywoods, and backed Aretha Franklin—and she knew that the first offer is rarely the last. If Disney was willing to put $2 million on the table straight away, the film was clearly worth far more.

She was right. The film has since been turned into a theme park, dolls, T-shirts, video games, and more. Next to it, Haywood said, $2 million looks small. “[It’s] hundreds of [millions], if not billions of dollars that they made off of this franchise,” as Weaver put it.

Taking the cash upfront would have meant missing out on all of it.

Plus, her gamble didn’t just beat Disney’s first offer. It gave Weaver—who admits that as a teenager, he probably would have blown the millions—an income that’s still paying out. Hand a 13-year-old $2 million, and it could be gone before he’s even old enough to drive. “I wasn’t thinking about a portfolio or diversifying,” Weaver said.

After lending his vocal cords to Disney, Weaver went on to star in two sitcoms, Thea (1993–94) and Smart Guy (1997–99), where he played Marcus Henderson. He also landed film roles in Drumline, The Ladykillers, and ATL, and more recently roles in The Chi and Sistas.

He kept singing, too. His debut album, Love Ambition, came out on Motown in 1995, and in 2004 he was featured on Chingy’s “One Call Away,” which peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Weaver hasn’t disclosed his net worth or how much The Lion King still pays him. But he says the royalties keep coming, whether or not he’s got a job on.

The Lion King has since grossed nearly $1 billion at the box office, and its 2019 remake pulled in more than $1.6 billion. Meanwhile, estimates put Weaver’s worth between $4 million and $7 million. Even at the lower figure, that’s about double the $2 million his mom turned down.

Not only has Weaver, by his own account, made more than what Disney originally offered, but he continues to be shocked by how much it pays years on.

“When I got my first royalty check, me and my mom thought it was a mistake,” he said. And 34 years later, the checks keep coming—and they won’t stop with him, either: Weaver agreed the royalties could be passed down to his kids, and their kids after that.

“Honestly that income, that residual income that I generate—man that is so helpful,” he added. “Even nowadays, when I get a check, it’s like … yes!”

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/elon-musk.title: Elon Musk just lost his trillionaire status again after three days—but he says ‘it’s not like it’s sitting in a bank account’ anyway
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/elon-musk.author: Emma Burleigh
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/elon-musk.text:
In the span of just three days, SpaceX founder Elon Musk ascended to trillionaire status before crashing out of the club in a billion-dollar downturn. And while he remains the richest person in the world by a $600-billion longshot, the entrepreneur says his wealth is always at the whim of his companies’ success.

“Trillionaire represents some percentage ownership in companies that I built, and it’s not sitting in a bank account,” Musk said in an interview with entrepreneur Peter Diamandis earlier this year, about three months before he first became a trillionaire following  SpaceX’s IPO in June.

Musk’s net worth started to fall from its recent high of $1.05 trillion on Tuesday, dropping down to $987 billion on Thursday, according to the Bloomberg Billionaire Index.

His aerospace company’s shares were down 3.5% and trading under $162 yesterday, just as his EV car business Tesla was also down over 2%. Forbes estimates that Musk lost $21 billion Wednesday morning when SpaceX shares fell following a report that the company plans to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips. The strategy could have impacted shares due to potential concerns about the company’s spending needs and debt load, even as it invests heavily in AI infrastructure.

It’s a steep $63 billion loss after he regained his trillionaire status this Monday; SpaceX shares rose nearly 8% at the start of the week, as Morgan Stanley analysts even called the stock “cheap” at the day’s prices. And as Musk owns around 4.76 billion shares of SpaceX—including another 1.3 billion shares of unvested restricted stock—his net worth shot up from $976.9 billion to $1.04 trillion afterward.

Very few people—if any others at all—will ever reach a 13-figure net worth in their lifetimes. But the jaw-dropping number isn’t actually what it seems, Musk has said. And in 10 years, he’s predicted his fortune may mean nothing at all.

“I own a percentage of the companies. The companies are doing lots of useful things, the value of the company grows,” the tech entrepreneur continued. “I own a percentage of the companies, and that sums up to that number, which seems high.”

Musk is just one of the world’s richest entrepreneurs who have watched their net worths dramatically rise and fall with the motions of the stock market.

Oracle founder Larry Ellison dethroned Musk as the richest person in the world briefly last year after his company’s breakout earnings report sent shares soaring by 36%. The now-82-year-old entrepreneur, who owns 40% of Oracle, experienced an eye-watering $101 billion wealth surge. But Ellison’s net worth fell by an estimated $34 billion just two days following Oracle’s stock surge, while Musk enjoyed a $35 billion gain, putting him back on top.

And on the flipside, Michael Dell, who owns 40% of his namesake tech company, gained around $122 billion between September of this year and the same time in 2025—nearly doubling his wealth within the span of that year. Larry Page’s net worth had grown $16.3 billion in the same period, while Jeff Bezos watched his wealth surge $24.5 billion.

But despite the massive wealth surge, Ray Dalio, the billionaire founder of Bridgewater Associates, has also echoed Musk in arguing that paper wealth and spendable money are two different things. Rising asset values can make people wealthier on paper, but they must sell those assets to turn that wealth into money they can actually spend.

“Wealth is not the same as money,” Dalio said on Steven Bartlett’s The Diary of a CEO podcast earlier this year. “You see a lot of people getting wealthy but you can’t spend the wealth. You have to sell the wealth to get money because you can only spend money.”

As billionaires’ fortunes balloon while many workers struggle to keep up with their paychecks, Musk, the richest person on earth—and occasionally, the only trillionaire—believes that monetary wealth will be less meaningful thanks to gains from AI.

In response to how companies would earn returns in the era of AI, Musk told The Economist that “Money won’t matter in 2036.”

The reason, he said, is that AI would take over so much human work that jobs will be voluntary, and cash itself would become irrelevant. Back in 2024, Musk also proposed the idea of “universal high income” to distribute money in a non-working world. The 55-year-old entrepreneur took inspiration from Iain M. Banks’ Culture sci-fi novels, which feature a world filled with intelligent robotic beings and no traditional jobs.

“In those books, money doesn’t exist. It’s kind of interesting,” Musk said in an episode of the Moonshots with Peter Diamandis podcast earlier this year. “And my guess is, if you go out long enough—assuming there’s a continued improvement in AI and robotics, which seems likely—money will stop being relevant.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/verizon-.author: CJ Haddad
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/verizon-.text:
Telecom stocks sank on Friday after Elon Musk’s SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio.

Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T all sold off while SpaceX climbed slightly.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr told CNBC that competition in the spectrum market was “really good news for the American consumers.”

Telecommunications stocks sold off on Friday after Elon Musk’s SpaceX
 announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio, aiming to expand its Starlink internet into mobile service.

Verizon
 was down roughly 7% on the news, and is pacing its worst day since 2002. Shares of T-Mobile
 were down 12% while AT&T
 fell around 10%. SpaceX stock climbed slightly, around 1% for the day.

The deal includes acquiring the spectrum from Grain Management, which SpaceX described as a “license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band,” in a Thursday statement.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whose agency will oversee approval of the deal, said that competition in the spectrum market was “really good news for the American consumers” in a CNBC interview.

“We’re probably going to bring over $100 billion of spectrum into the market over the next two years, so we’re seeing a lot of competition,” Carr told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Friday.

“There’s going to be moves in the market. People are going to try to out-compete, out-innovate, and I think that’s great. We’re going to see how this plays out. It’s not for us ultimately to pick winners and losers,” he added.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: International Criminal Court faces 'test of resilience' as US imposes sweeping sanctions
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
US President Donald Trump's administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court that threaten to cripple its operations and spark fresh transatlantic tension.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts.

READ MORE
Israel a rare dissenting voice as praise pours in for Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay

Here's a look at the likely impact of the sanctions, possible responses, and the reasons behind Washington's unprecedented move, which the court said was an "assault on the rule of law".

Based in the Dutch city of The Hague, the ICC tries individuals suspected of the world's worst offences – war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.

Established in 2002 by the Rome Statute, it currently has 125 members. Major powers such as the United States, Russia, China, India, and Israel are not members of the court.

It is governed by a strict policy of "complementarity", meaning it can only take on cases a suspect's home country is unwilling or unable to try itself.

Since its establishment, the court has convicted 15 people, with four acquitted. Critics say the court has focused too heavily on war crimes committed in Africa and failed to convict major political leaders.

However, its most high-profile current case concerns ex-Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte, the first former Asian head of state to stand in the ICC dock.

The court, housed in a shiny glass building on the outskirts of The Hague, employs around 900 staff from 100 nationalities.

It is often confused with the International Court of Justice, also based in The Hague, which settles disputes between countries.

The Trump administration has already issued several rounds of sanctions against top ICC officials but these latest actions go further, targeting the entire court.

ICC officials are concerned about access to banking, credit card facilities, insurance, and especially technology, given a heavy reliance on US systems.

"We have been extremely dependent on US technology solutions, Microsoft or systems related to Microsoft," acting chief prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang told AFP in a recent interview.

"We are trying to find alternative means, maybe not as effective as the US technology, but at least to be able to maintain our independence, to be able to continue to work," said Niang.

The prosecutor, himself the target of sanctions, said they crippled daily life -- he was unable to book transport, hotels, or conduct banking operations.

But expanding them to the entire institution raises questions about the ICC's ability to pay staff, conduct investigations abroad, protect witnesses, and even operate its detention facilities.

"This is a test of our resilience," admitted Niang.

As the host city, the Dutch have a special responsibility to the ICC under the terms of a "Headquarters Agreement" signed in 2008.

This obliges the Netherlands to protect ICC facilities and staff, provide "any means of communication" and ensure "freedom of financial assets from restrictions".

In an unusually fiery speech last month at the United Nations General Assembly, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten vowed to defend the ICC "in my country, in my city".

"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? I believe there can be only one response: 'hands off the ICC'," said Jetten to warm applause.

READ MORE
EU will 'stand firmly' behind ICC chief as the US levies new sanctions

The European Union on Friday called the US sanctions "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work".

One possibility would be for the European Commission to deploy a legal instrument known as the "blocking mechanism".

This prohibits European firms from obeying the US sanctions "actively or by deliberate omission", giving the EU a potential means of cushioning some of the impact.

The EU blocking mechanism is seen as the "nuclear option", said Berendsen, adding that the Netherlands had nevertheless asked Brussels to prepare it.

The US is furious the court issued an arrest warrant for close ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over alleged crimes in Gaza.

It is also concerned an ICC investigation into Afghanistan could result in accusations against US personnel.

Trump has upped his rhetoric against what he has called a "rogue institution" and "evil group of people" and the US has vowed to dismantle the court "brick-by-brick".

But even under less pugnacious presidents, Washington has never been a fan of the ICC and never considered joining.

The US has a law dubbed the "Hague Invasion Act", allowing it to take "all means necessary and appropriate" to defend US personnel or allies detained by the ICC.

In a clear swipe at Washington, Jetten vowed to defend the ICC "brick by brick" in comments just hours before the sanctions were announced.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.title: Saving for the future is making some investors ‘NISA broke’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Yuko Tamura
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
You may not have noticed any celebrations, but Oct. 4 was 投資の日 (tōshi no hi, Securities Investment Day), which was established in 1996 by the Japan Securities Dealers Association. That’s because the number 10 can be read as “tō” and the number 4 can be read as “shi”: thus tō-shi, 10-4, 投資 (investment).

Although 投資の日 is relatively well known, NISAの日 (Nīsa no hi, NISA Day) on Feb. 13 has yet to receive much attention. NISA stands for Nippon Individual Savings Account, the tax-exempt investment system for residents of Japan.

As 2027 approaches, however, we’re bound to hear the term NISA more frequently. The Japanese government is planning to reintroduce こどもNISA (kodomo nīsa, Kids NISA) at the beginning of next year. Previously known as Junior NISA, こどもNISA will allow those under 18 to invest up to ¥600,000 ($3,800) a year until they hit the maximum holding limit of ¥6 million, without taxes on gains or distributions. It’s meant to help children build assets in the long term, so withdrawals are subject to age restrictions.

According to a poll conducted by Fuji Television, though, 49% said they felt the こどもNISA program might deepen 格差 (kakusa, inequality) between 富裕層 (fuyū-sō, affluent individuals) and 低所得層 (teishotoku-sō, low-income individuals). As one critique put it: こどもNISAを使って投資できるお金持ちの子どもが有利になるばかりだ (Kodomo nīsa o tsukatte tōshi dekiru okanemochi no kodomo ga yūri ni naru bakari da, Kids NISA will only further benefit children from wealthy families who are able to invest through Kids NISA).

The grammatical structure ～ばかりだ (~bakari da) comes at the end of a complete sentence and adds the nuance that what has been stated will continue to get worse. For example, 雨で野菜の値段が上がるばかりだ (Ame de yasai no nedan ga agaru bakari da, Vegetable prices will only keep climbing because of the rain).

Be careful, though. The particle, ばかり (bakari), has a range of meanings. For instance, when it’s used after a noun or in the middle of a sentence, it translates more as “only” or “just,” as in, あの人は仕事の話ばかりしている (Ano hito wa shigoto no hanashi bakari shite-iru, That person only talks about work) or 食べたばかりなのに空腹だ (Tabeta bakari nano ni kūfuku da, I just ate, but I’m still hungry).

If you think that NISAで投資していると自由に使えるお金が減るばかりだ (Nīsa de tōshi shite-iru to jiyū ni tsukaeru okane ga heru bakari da, Investing through NISA only leaves me with less and less money to spend freely), you’re not alone. Over the past few months, we’ve been seeing a new word, NISA貧乏 (Nīsa binbō, NISA broke). Many 投資家 (tōshika, investors) hope their investments will make them rich, but in their day-to-day lives they remain cash poor. This is partly because adult 投資家 based in Japan can invest up to ¥3.6 million ($22,800) per year through NISA, which is six times the こどもNISA limit.

People describing themselves as NISA貧乏 are more likely to cancel parties, travel and even dates because 誘われるたびに飲みに行っていたらお金が減るばかりだ (sasowareru tabi ni nomi ni itte-itara okane ga heru bakari da, if you go out drinking every time you’re invited, you’ll just end up spending all your money).

The discussion around the buzzword became heated online after Abema Times reported on an event called the NISA貧乏バー (Nīsa binbō bā, NISA broke bar) and spoke to a man who confessed that he had broken up with his girlfriend in order to invest the full ¥3.6 million annual allowance.

For such investors, the biggest fear is that 物価高で老後に必要な資金は増えるばかりだ (bukkadaka de rōgo ni hitsuyōna shikin wa fueru bakari da, as inflation keeps pushing prices higher, the amount needed for retirement only keeps growing).

The additional amount needed to invest through こどもNISA could therefore be both an opportunity and a burden for parents. On the other hand, securities companies are eager to get young investors on board. Last week, SBI announced that it would release a new fund named ゼロカン (zerokan), which comes from “zero all-country index fund,” for こどもNISA with a surprisingly low zero trust fee.

An old saying goes, 若い時の苦労は買ってでもせよ (Wakai toki no kurō wa katte demo seyo), which loosely translates to “Hardships in youth are worth paying for.” The idea is that struggles in our younger years can pay off later in life. But these days, young Japanese investors may be taking the saying a little too literally, sacrificing valuable experiences in the present for an unknowable future.

https://www.dw.com/en/macron-and-steinme.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
https://www.dw.com/en/macron-and-steinme.text:
Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the   student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.

Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.

It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls.  In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.

Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets.  At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.

While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.

Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.

Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.

A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.

Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.

Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.

As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.

It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation  on land systems," said the German defense minister.

The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.

On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.

It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.

As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.

Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.

Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.

This article was originally written in German.
https://www.dw.com/en/macron-and-steinme.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest in the role.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj20.title: US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj20.text:
The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), saying it wants to restrict the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.

The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

The announcement comes just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

US President Donald Trump has reacted sourly to the Norwegian prize's choice of winner this year and last, after having expressed a desire to receive it himself. He criticised Pillay for being part of a panel that accused Israel, as well as Hamas, of war crimes during the 7 October conflict.

The US says the ICC has no jurisdiction over it as it never ratified the statute founding it - but the international court has investigated US actions elsewhere.

Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."

The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.

Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.

He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories to "rein in" the institution.

The ICC responded by saying that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".

The Trump administration has repeatedly criticised the court, including over its investigation into the actions of US forces in Afghanistan, a probe it has since deprioritised.

It has also been critical of the ICC issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj20.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said measures were intended to "defend US sovereignty" The measures include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC. ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdx.text:
A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.

The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.

Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes.

Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.

Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.

He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.

That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.

Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018.

He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".

A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1472.title: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1472.author: Gabrielle Emanuel
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1472.text:
A woman wearing a face mask walks past the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, founded in the 1930s to monitor strains of dangerous pathogens.

A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe.

The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more information.

A security person wearing a face mask looks out from the door of an infectious diseases hospital in the town of Shelekhov, where an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute had died.

Russia has insisted this is not a health emergency and stated that its health authorities have not found dangerous pathogens in any of the deceased woman's contacts.

But there are still far more questions than answers.

That uncertainty has global leaders and health experts turning to a law that obligates countries, including Russia, to share exactly this type of information. It's called the International Health Regulations or IHR.

On Wednesday, at a WHO press conference, Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus invoked IHR as the best way to determine current situation in Russia and determine the appropriate response.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," he said. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."

Here are the key things to know about the IHR and how it applies in today's world.

This law requires countries to share health information that could have international implications. It goes way back to the 1850s with cholera outbreaks in Europe, which led to the creation of guidelines for sharing disease information.

"That's very, very long for international law," says Alexandra Phelan, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "Look at the negotiation documents and they're debating: Is cholera caused by a bacteria or miasma [a bad smell]? Like we're really right in the middle of germ theory."

Then, when WHO was founded in 1948, these regulations — then called the International Sanitary Regulations — were adopted. That was one of the organization's first moves. The law has since been amended and updated, most notably after the SARS or Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome outbreak in 2003 and most recently due to COVID-19 pandemic.

A country is supposed to notify WHO if the health event has the potential to cause an international health emergency.

Today, IHR is among the most widely ratified international treaties, with 197 signatories including the U.S. and Russia. (Even though the Trump administration says it has withdrawn from WHO, the U.S. is still bound by the IHR with the exception of some recent amendments.)

One of the core obligations in the law "is that parties or states must notify WHO within 24 hours of detecting a [serious health] event," explains Phelan.

Some events – like a case of smallpox or a new type of influenza — should immediately trigger a notification. For other situations, a checklist helps a country assess whether notification is needed.

Each year, she says, WHO receives thousands of notifications from all over the world and most turn out to be nothing.

Some people fear the Russian woman — who died Oct. 2 — had pneumonic plague. That's one of the diseases "explicitly listed" under IHR, says Phelan, as something to assess and notify the WHO.

However, Russia did not notify WHO about this woman's death. Instead, WHO learned about it through media reports and then, on Oct. 3, went to Russia seeking verification and additional information.

"Russia's response, firstly, was delayed," says Phelan. "But also it wasn't comprehensive."

It took Russia several days to respond. On Oct. 6, health officials told WHO there were no cases of plague in the region and that the woman was hospitalized with severe pneumonia of unknown origin before she died. They also explained that health authorities had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.

WHO asked Russia for more information, including about lab tests conducted, public health measures and the health status of the woman's contacts. However, as with many international laws, there's no mechanism to make countries comply with the law and share information.

Phelan says the next few days and weeks will be key in understanding how much information Russia is going to share. If they aren't fully transparent, she hopes pressure from other countries either convinces Russia to comply with IHR or, at least, helps keep up the norm of other countries respecting IHR and notifying WHO about future health events.

That kind of notification is critical if the world is to be ready to respond and contain future outbreaks, says Lawrence Gostin, who directs the WHO Center on Global Health Law and is a professor at Georgetown University.

"This case shows the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," he says.

"Legally, this is the only thing that's holding Russia to account," Gostin explains. And yet, "you have countries that are hiding the ball."

He believes that the risk to the general population from the current situation in Russia is likely very low. But, for him, the fact that countries can disregard the IHR notification requirements is a "blaring siren about how unprepared we are" to quickly control health threats.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1472.summary: The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague.
