https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Ed Davey faces growing revolt against leadership as senior Lib Dem MP quits
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat leader as party slips in polls

Ed Davey is facing a growing revolt against his leadership of the Liberal Democrats, following the resignation of a senior frontbench figure on Friday.

Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, has handed in his resignation in an attempt to unseat Davey after months of frustration that the party is failing to cut through with voters, the Guardian understands.

Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader, immediately backed Davey, saying he enjoyed the support of the “vast majority of MPs”, who wanted him to lead them into the next election and were “furious at this distraction”.

“We Liberal Democrats are the last line of defence against a Reform UK government, and Ed is determined to lead a strong and united party into the next general election whenever it comes,” Cooper said in a statement.

“As Ed said at conference, we are in the fight of our lives against the right who want to turn our country into their version of Trump’s America.”

Maynard’s resignation, first reported by the Financial Times, came four days after Alison Bennett, the Lib Dem care and carers spokesperson, stood down from the frontbench.

Davey has led the party since 2019, first as acting leader and then officially from August 2020. At the 2024 general election he steered the party to its most successful result in more than 100 years. The party now has 71 MPs, and is the third biggest party in the House of Commons. But the party has slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls behind the Greens and Reform UK, and frustration has mounted over a failure to attract voters in a disparate political landscape.

At the party’s conference in Brighton in September, Davey played down criticism from a Liberal Democrat council leader who questioned whether he was the right person to lead the party. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, said the party was “sleepwalking into irrelevance” and “lacking ambition”.

Davey unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters, which he said would be paid for entirely by increased growth, created through rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.

But his resistance to Labour’s proposals to change the pension triple lock to help pay for a national care service, announced in Andy Burnham’s Labour Party conference speech, was met with opposition by senior and backbench Lib Dems, with one saying his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.summary: Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat Ed Davey. Maynard's resignation came four days after Alison Bennett stood down from the frontbench. The party has slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls behind the Greens and Reform UK.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St Pancras
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Pressure is building on the party leader after byelection defeat, a damaging row over Zionism and polls that show him less popular than Nigel Farage

W
hen Zack Polanski addressed his campaigners flush with victory after the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, he declared: “Labour’s electoral stranglehold is over.” The election of Hannah Spencer as the new Green MP for the Greater Manchester seat was a seismic victory, he continued: “I said we were here to replace Labour and this is what replacing looks like.”

But in the wake of Polanski’s defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on Thursday, and a calamitous row over the party’s stance on Zionism, the debate around what, or who, could be replaced has shifted to Polanski himself.

On Friday the leader of the Green party in England and Wales was defiant after losing to Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, who took 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 33%. Asked what was going wrong in his party, which has fallen from highs of 21% in some polls after the victory in Gorton and Denton to around 10-11%, Polanski, responded: “If things are going wrong by the fact that we just tripled our vote share and had our second best byelection result in Green party history, you know what? I’ll take that.” While emphasising that Green members would ultimately decide who they wanted as leader, he said: “Of course I can carry on.”.

That the last few months have been difficult for the Greens – and Polanski in particular – is beyond doubt. Polanski himself is, according to new polling from More in Common, now less popular with voters than Nigel Farage, and is the least popular major UK party leader, falling by four points to a -28 net approval.

His standing, bruised by a series of controversies over a failure to pay council tax and the sharing of a post criticising police, has been further damaged by a controversial motion that was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton last weekend, equating Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. Polanski’s decision to abstain from the debate and the vote to instead campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, was condemned by his detractors, but also, more significantly, criticised by senior figures in his own party.

The former Green leader Caroline Lucas told BBC Newsnight on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”. Asked if he should stand down, she said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection.” Following his defeat she appeared to temper her position, saying Polanski had “transformed the party” and she hoped he would now “help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures”.

On Friday, pressure mounted, as the leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, called for Polanski to step down, saying it was a “big mistake” for him not to have spoken and voted for amendments stating that any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians, rather than impose a one-state system.

But there was bullishness among the Polanski faithful, with Greens Organise, the leftwing faction that backed his leadership bid, saying he should stay on. A statement from the group said that “not all growth and success is linear, there will be ups and downs; the real test for a political organisation is how we deal with failure”. It added: “We have reshaped the British political landscape. The Green party can still become the ecosocialist party we need. Zack is still the leader who can get us there.”

Green party supporters pointed out that the party achieved a 13-point swing from Labour in Holborn and St Pancras, traditionally a safe Labour seat. The Camden councillor Hamza Chowdhury – who was overlooked as the candidate in the constituency in favour of Polanski – went as far as saying the result was “a huge win for the Green party and the wider movement”.

Polanski cheerleaders point out that since he was elected leader in September 2025, the party has quadrupled its membership to more than 230,000. As well as the winning of its first ever seat in the north of England, he presided over the Greens’ best-ever performance in May’s local and mayoral elections, including gaining their first-ever directly elected mayoralty, in Hackney, east London.

Nonetheless, the result in north London exposed the dual challenge Polanski now faced, said Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. At the same time as the replacement of Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham had brought disillusioned progressives back to Labour, Polanski had become a more polarising figure.

A series of missteps, starting when he shared a social media post critical of police after the Golders Green stabbings, had damaged his popularity with the wider UK public, added Tryl. “It was just one of those moments which gave soft Green supporters pause for thought. Similarly, many people don’t vote directly on something like the Zionism is racism motion, but it adds to that sense of ‘oh, I thought these were nice guys who were focused on the environment’.”

The result in north London was a “good one” for Labour, he added, despite the drop in its majority. While governing parties usually get hit hard in byelections, the drop in Holborn was below the average for defending a seat at byelections in any postwar parliament, he noted.

But Labour hopes of the death of the Green party were likely to have been exaggerated. “I think writing off the Greens is premature,” he said. “Burnham has managed, for now, to unite the left, but a lot of big decisions, including on North Sea oil drilling and, more importantly, the budget, are coming down the line.”

As for Polanski, the path towards rebuilding the popularity that saw him win the support of young voters desperate for hope and change would lie in a return to his original economic messaging around “rip-off Britain” and generational fairness, rather than divisive internal battles, said James Baggaley from UCL’s Policy Lab. “The question for the Greens and Polanski now is: do they want to reassure voters on questions of antisemitism and also get back to what they were actually winning on, which was the economy?”

He is the least popular major UK party leader, falling by four points to a -28 net approval. Holborn drop in Holborn was below the average for defending a seat at byelections in any postwar parliament.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live

US politics live – latest updates

The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.

The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”

Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”

Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.

Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”

Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.

Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.

Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.

The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.

The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.

Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.

Media have sought to televise US executions ⁠in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.

Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.

In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.

Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.

The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.

The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.

Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.

Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.

“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”

Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.

“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press.

Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.

“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”

Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.

It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: U.N. office of human rights chief warns that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution. Critics compare the plan to dictators.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: DHS defends ICE shooting in NYC, says officers believed they were in danger
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
The United States Department of Homeland Security has defended Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) shooting of a man in New York City while his child was present. Federal officials used the incident to criticise sanctuary-city policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

New York officials have condemned the shooting and have called for ICE to end its operations in the city.

The shooting took place on Thursday afternoon when ICE officers attempted to arrest a man identified by New York City police as Oscar Belgal.

Homeland Security officials gave their account of the incident on Friday during a news conference, saying that Belgal refused to exit his car when approached by officers and then accelerated, striking two ICE vehicles.

They said officers then opened fire, grazing Belgal’s neck while his five-year-old child was in the back seat.

According to Homeland Security officials, Belgal received first aid and was taken to hospital before being transferred to a secure detention facility outside New York state. They did not disclose where Belgal is being held.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the agents did not know the child was inside the vehicle when they fired.

ICE senior official Marcos Charles said agents had attempted to arrest Belgal as part of an investigation into suspected gang involvement in an earlier shooting of a US Customs and Border Protection officer.

According to US officials, Belgal is an undocumented migrant from the Dominican Republic who had previously evaded arrest and received a five-year sentence for grand larceny in April 2025.

“[Belgal] was a thug,” Mullin said at the Friday news conference. “The absolute worst of the worst.”

Mullin confirmed that officers were wearing body cameras but the footage has not been made public. New York City police released bodycam footage on Friday of police officers on the scene who had responded to a 911 call about the incident.

In other violent incidents involving federal immigration officers, video evidence has contradicted initial accounts from ICE and Homeland Security officials, including in Minneapolis, where footage of the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good challenged federal officials’ descriptions of the encounters.

The latest shooting prompted protests on Thursday night in the Bronx, where the shooting took place, with demonstrators condemning ICE and calling for the agency to be abolished. Tensions rose after NYPD officers clashed with some of the protesters.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he had called US President Donald Trump to demand an end to ICE enforcement in the city.

Speaking to reporters late on Thursday at the scene of the shooting, Mamdani said he had tried unsuccessfully to secure Belgal’s release in phone calls with Trump and Mullin.

“These actions are making the city less safe,” Mamdani said. “ICE is rotten to its core.”

Mullin accused Mamdani of prioritising politics over public safety and said Trump had offered to transfer Belgal to New York police custody if they pursued charges. Mullin said Mamdani refused this offer.

New York City officials have condemned the shooting and called for ICE to end its operations in the city.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: ‘A Ceuta-style surge is possible’: Border tensions on NATO’s eastern flank
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Agnieszka Pikulicka-Wilczewska
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
Masked and armed men attempted to cross into Latvia from Belarus alongside 20 undocumented migrants on Monday.

“The (masked) escorts of the illegal migrants, who were located on the Belarusian side, were armed, issued threats to … soldiers, and also actively urged and drove the migrant group toward Latvia,” Janis Dombrava, Latvia’s interior minister, said on Tuesday.

The group was stopped by the military.

Later, masked men managed to enter Latvia, destroying an electrical box and stealing surveillance cameras before returning to Belarus – an act of sabotage orchestrated by the country, according to Latvian officials. It was not clear if the second incident involved the same masked men as the first.

“Unlike many previous incidents, this time the provocation was particularly demonstrative and aggressive,” said Dombrava.

Since 2021, Belarus, Russia’s ally, has used migration as a tool to destabilise NATO’s eastern flank. It shares borders with Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia – the latter considered Europe’s weakest link.

“The crisis at the EU [European Union] border with Belarus has been ongoing for five years. The situation in Latvia has been deteriorating since May of this year,” Bartosz Chmielewski, Baltics expert from the Poland-based Centre for Eastern Studies told Al Jazeera. “There has been a steady rise in border violations and the number of people crossing.”

In September and October, “the number of border violations has already reached 12,000, a level equal to the total for the entire previous year”, he said.

According to Olevs Nikers, the Latvian president of the Baltic Security Foundation, “A Ceuta-style surge is physically possible, and we should plan for it.”

He was referring to the recent crossing of tens of thousands of people from Morocco to Spain.

“But sustained low-level pressure may be the more effective strategy. It creates exhaustion, budget pressure and friction between allies. Poland’s renewed controls on its border with Lithuania are already an example of this.”

He noted that Lithuania’s border with Belarus is four times longer than Latvia’s 173km (107 miles), yet pressure has been concentrated in Latvia.

“This looks less like spontaneous migration than a deliberate instrument, adjusted to test the neighbour perceived as most vulnerable,” Nikers said.

Any migration pressure from Belarus may cause bureaucratic chaos. Latvia, with a population of 1.8 million, would struggle with the reception, processing and providing medical aid to potential asylum seekers, he said.

According to the Polish Border Guard, in 2021, almost 40,000 people tried to cross the border from Belarus. Thousands more crossings of undocumented people were never recorded.

Before Russia’s war in Ukraine began in 2022, Belarus built a system – including travel agencies, plane connections and visa programmes – encouraging migrants seeking a better life to cross into the European Union from the east. The scheme targeted people from the Global South, or Latin America, Africa and much of Asia.

According to experts, the system has since been dismantled, but Belarus is still pressing migration when it can.

“A sudden influx of several thousand people into Latgale in winter would become a humanitarian and political problem before it became a border-security problem,” Nikers added.

Out of all of NATO’s eastern flank countries, Latvia seems the least prepared for provocations coming from the east.

“Until now, Latvia remained on the sidelines, as the pressure was primarily focused on Poland and Lithuania. Now it finds itself in the spotlight, partly because it is unprepared, its border infrastructure is inadequate, and the resources of the border guard – even with military support – are dwindling,” Chmielewski said.

“Latvia struggles to execute major infrastructure projects … It shares the shortest border with Belarus, but has been unable to complete the necessary infrastructure there; this is due both to the challenging terrain and the state’s limited operational capacity.”

Other experts said the migration pressure from Belarus might be a response to recent political developments in Latvia.

“The elections in Latvia were won by a coalition led by [Prime Minister] Andris Kulbergs, which seeks to maintain sanctions against Belarus. So Belarus uses both carrots and sticks to show it can destabilise the situation in the Baltics,” said Marta Jaroszewicz, assistant professor at the University of Warsaw’s Centre of Migration Research.

“For the past year, there have been periodic releases of Belarusian political prisoners, a process supported by the US administration. Belarus’s goal is the lifting of sanctions and the ability to transport its raw materials via Baltic ports, including through Poland. The objective is, in fact, the normalisation of trade.”

Russian and Belarusian pressure on the EU has also changed over the years as migration pressure is only one of the tactics employed. Others include disinformation, arson, the recruitment of local citizens and GPS jamming, according to Nikers.

He said that “2026 is increasingly about airspace and infrastructure. The most important change is that Russia has moved from targeting what we believe to targeting what we depend on: cables, grids, navigation and airspace. It is also increasingly operating below the Article 5 threshold.”

Established in the aftermath of World War II, NATO’s collective defence commitment, Article 5, was designed to ensure mutual protection among member states in response to the perceived threat of Soviet expansion, particularly in Eastern Europe during the early stages of the Cold War.

“This is an attempt at intimidation by Russia. And what deters Russia from aggressive actions on the eastern flank is the solidarity of European nations,” Chmielewski said. “That is what Russia fears most: that should it stage a more brazen provocation, solidarity will stretch from Lisbon to Stockholm, and the European Union will act as a united front.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.summary: Masked men attempted to cross into Latvia from Belarus with 20 undocumented migrants. Latvia's interior minister said the group was armed and threatened to drive them to Latvia. Belarus has used migration as a tool to destabilise NATO’s eastern flank.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/lumenu.title: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/lumenu.author: Amanda Silberling
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/lumenu.text:
When Sara Tashakorinia’s husband died in a car accident eight years ago, the last thing she needed was the roughly 570 hours of paperwork it takes, on average, to settle a loved one’s affairs. But for millions of people each year, this is their reality: a crushing loss, followed by a soullessly mundane avalanche of tedious administrative work.

“The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about, trying to navigate something and learn something when you literally have zero information,” Tashakorinia told TechCrunch.

After years of volunteering to help others navigate what she had to learn on her own, it occurred to Tashakorinia that AI might be able to help — not with the complex, messy experience of grieving and healing, but with the least human parts of the process, like finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts.

The result is LumenUs, the grief care platform that Tashakorinia founded last year to relieve grieving families of some of the administrative burden.

“I think going through it, your threshold of pain is so high, and you’re so lost that you don’t really realize, why do people treat you this way? Why was I left with a stack of paperwork, and why was the funeral home charging me a 300% markup on a casket?” Tashakorinia said.

While Tashakorinia hopes LumenUs will eventually support people throughout the lifelong grieving process, the startup will initially focus on people in the immediate aftermath of a death. When people initially join the platform, they go through an onboarding process in which they share information about the nature of their particular situation.

“We are asking very specific questions to understand the legal and financial means, and their state of mind, and this is only to personalize who they are, and then personalizing what happened,” Tashakorinia said.

From there, the platform organizes tasks by urgency, helping users decipher what needs to be done immediately and what can wait. In some cases, this can even help people discover that they’re entitled to money that can help ease the financial burden of death. In fact, billions of dollars in life insurance benefits go unclaimed because people don’t know they’re available.

“We are using AI to automate as much as we can to save time during this process, and give it back to [users],” she said.

Tashakorinia has a background in cybersecurity, which is sure to prove essential for building a product that asks people to share so much sensitive personal and financial information. She is building LumenUs alongside co-founders Sajad Mirzaei, a former engineer at Google and Box, and Larry Keeley, an innovation scientist, professor, and entrepreneur. The team is also consulting with clinicians and social workers while testing the product.

LumenUs, a participant in this year’s upcoming Startup Battlefield 200, TechCrunch’s annual showcase of promising early-stage startups, will launch in early access in October.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/lumenu.summary: Sara Tashakorinia founded LumenUs to help families of a loved one's affairs. The platform will help people navigate the process of finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/danu-r.title: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/danu-r.author: Russell Brandom
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/danu-r.text:
For Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma, the eureka moment came after years of working as a software developer at a London bank. It was the kind of high-touch office that’s typical in finance — but despite all the perks, Ma was alarmed to realize that the building’s recycling bins were being emptied into the trash.

“Even though they have tons of money, there’s all these different recycling bins that just end up in the same place,” Ma told TechCrunch.

The more she dug into the problem, the deeper it seemed to go. It wasn’t just her building. The economics of recycling as a whole often boil down to human beings sorting by hand through streams of waste to pull out different kinds of recyclable material.

“I saw the technology and thought, we can do so much better,” Ma remembers.

Now, she’s making good on that promise with six-year-old, Edinburgh, Scotland-based Danu Robotics, which makes a robot designed to sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. Ma has been working on that idea for six years and is finally bringing her version of the product to market. Her robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors. For example, it picks up items with a pincer claw instead of a suction system. But the bigger difference is the business approach: Danu leverages AI to continuously improve the robot’s software.

The approach is already seeing some traction. Danu has letters of interest from two large customers and $500,000 worth of signed contracts. More notably, more than 200 customers are in its sales pipeline, which gives the company a hook into the $20 billion market for recycling sorting across Europe and North America.

On the back of that promise, Dabnu has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on.

There’s already a robust market for robotic waste-pickers, particularly the suction-based arms offered by competitors like Glacier and RecycleEye. But Ma believes the economics of recycling will make it easy for a new competitor to prove its worth. Because recycling centers make money off the materials they’re able to sort out, there’s an immediate return on investment for a working system. Ma estimates that a working site will earn $485,000 in additional revenue from having the robot on the sorting line, compared with a $160,000 initial investment and $24,000 in maintenance fees each year. That’s significantly cheaper than the competition, and Ma believes the robot will be more efficient, too.

Since those machines are already shipping, Ma’s next goal is to make the robot sturdier, smaller, and more versatile. Once it’s portable enough, it can be used outside dedicated waste facilities, opening up a whole other world of use cases.

“Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Ma told TechCrunch, “and that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste.”
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/danu-r.summary: Danu Robotics is making a robot that can sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. The company has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on. The robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/we-can.title: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/we-can.author: Amanda Silberling
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/we-can.text:
In a tan polo shirt, brown leather belt, and round bolo tie, MIT PhD student Wil Norton kind of looks like a park ranger, leading our tour group through a tropical jungle. We’re not actually on safari, though — we’re at MIT’s Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). But what we’re about to see is even more exotic than a cheetah or a jaguar: a pair of humanoid Unitree robots, each costing about $50,000.

(“They’ll tell you they cost $16,000,” Norton says. “That’s a lie.”)

We usually only see these robots on YouTube when they’re performing a synchronized martial arts routine, or dancing on “America’s Got Talent.” Here, they’re approachable. Even though I know it isn’t sentient, I want to be its friend.

With Norton’s permission, I approach the robot, whose nickname is Gabe. For a moment, I’m not sure how to interact with something that has a LiDAR sensor where its brain should be, but I default to treating it like a person.

“Hello, sir, it’s nice to meet you,” I say, grabbing its gloved, dexterous hand and shaking it.

I think about this interaction later — my instinctive impulse to be friendly to a robot — when I attend Dr. Sherry Turkle‘s “Artificial Intimacy” book launch at MIT Future Fest.

Turkle, who joined the faculty at MIT in 1976, has been researching the relationship between humans and computers perhaps longer than anyone, charting technology’s psychological impact on us from the first home computers to ChatGPT.

“When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us,” Turkle writes in the book. “And we are wired to care for it in return.”

I’m not alone in my tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models (LLMs) — as Turkle notes, it seems to be in our nature. One study found that about 70% of people are polite when interacting with AI, while another showed that users are more likely to say “please” or “thank you” to chatbots once a conversation has progressed past a first prompt-and-response.

“People tend to categorize whether this is the right use or wrong use, but I don’t think that is a clear boundary,” Dr. Pat Pataranutaporn, a colleague of Turkle who founded the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, told TechCrunch. “The question is, who are we becoming when we talk to [AI]?”

There’s no material consequence of my politeness toward Gabe the robot, but as LLMs infiltrate everything from Google searches to customer service interactions, it has become routine for people to interact with these seemingly sentient chatbots. We’re more vulnerable than ever to the flip side of this impulse, which is that some people can ascribe so much legitimacy to the feelings of chatbots — which are programmed to never spark conflict — that they end up favoring them over other humans.

“You can think of it like fantasy and fiction. We go to the cinema even though we know the story is completely fictional, but we want to experience a certain dimension of human experience that maybe our reality cannot give us,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we benefit from that ability to experience other dimensions of human experience without losing it to the fantasy, where you can no longer come back to the reality?”

Pataranutaporn describes himself as a “critical optimist,” and he studies AI’s potential to contribute to human flourishing. But he’s well aware of how dangerous this technology can be in the extremes. He even served as an expert in a wrongful death lawsuit over the suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer, III, whose mother sued the chatbot platform Character.AI, alleging that a chatbot modeled after a “Game of Thrones” character had encouraged her son to end his life.

“It can create a situation where people don’t feel agency in actually creating their own future — like when you say that AI will replace everyone, people ask, what are we gonna do? And these companies are not really responding ethically or responsibly,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we have imagination while still being responsible for the impact of that imagination?”

While Turkle’s book explores the risk of turning to AI for emotional support, rather than other people, she doesn’t think that AI-human interactions are universally harmful.

She recalls a project she advised in which a student created an AI bot to help people practice for job interviews.

“My big metaphor is, stay in your lane, chatbot!” Turkle said at the event. “Coaching for a job interview? That’s a lane. I can do that … A chatbot that says to a three-year-old, ‘I’m your parent, you can talk to me, not your parents,’ is not in a lane.”

But when this technology deviates from its lane even slightly, we become vulnerable to the way it can slowly chip away at our skepticism and make us trust it. It can start with something as simple as a handshake.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/we-can.summary: MIT PhD student Wil Norton meets a robot at MIT's Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab. He says he's not sure how to interact with the robot, but he treats it like a person. He's not alone in his tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models.

Windows is slowly morphing into an agentic OS.

Windows is slowly morphing into an agentic OS.

When Microsoft released Windows 11 five years ago, it felt like an operating system that was still being renovated, a work in progress. You’d think by now that those renovations would be complete, with Microsoft turning its attention to Windows 12. Instead, Windows 11 feels like it’s here to stay, forming the foundation for Microsoft’s next big ambition: transforming Windows into an agentic OS.

At a Windows and Surface event this week, Microsoft laid out its plan to bring AI agents to Windows, including hybrid intelligence that lets Windows take advantage of free local models instead of expensive cloud ones. “I think today is the day we’ll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours,” said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

After trying to sell businesses on a new Copilot last month, Nadella took a similar approach for his vision of agents and hybrid intelligence for Windows. It was so similar that when he mentioned the security, identity, and management aspects of Microsoft’s platform for securing agents, it almost seemed like he was pitching businesses again instead of AI developers, creatives, and just regular Windows users.

After a somewhat dizzying start, Windows chief Pavan Davuluri appeared onstage to try and explain why agents and hybrid intelligence are so important for Windows users. There were demos of GitHub Copilot coding locally without expensive cloud tokens; a long list of models that can now run locally; examples of agents like OpenClaw, Hermes, and Perplexity; and even deeper integration of Copilot in Windows.

I wasn’t fully convinced by any of these demos, though.

The Facebook whistleblower reflects on going public five years ago and inspiring a movie character.

Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen was mostly unfazed watching Oscar-winning actress Mikey Madison play a character named after her in The Social Reckoning, except for one thing: the wrist warmers.

In Aaron Sorkin’s new thriller, the fictional Haugen — who, like her nonfictional counterpart, leaks thousands of documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz — habitually dons the accessories. It’s a character quirk that reflects real life, where they’re a way to deal with the effects of a vasoconstrictive disorder. “I’ve figured out lots of ways to minimize how much of an obstruction this is,” she tells The Verge in an interview. “But having to watch myself wear wrist warmers for two hours, I came out of it being like, ‘Oh my god, this is really disruptive. Like, how have I successfully not thought about this for like seven years?’” With The Social Reckoning appearing in theaters Friday, Haugen hopes Meta’s CEO might watch it and have a similar moment of recognition with his own counterpart: a callous, robotic character played by Jeremy Strong. “I hope Mark Zuckerberg watches the movie and has as much of a knee-jerk emotional response as I had on that regarding, ‘Do I really want to live this life anymore?’”

Strong’s version of Zuckerberg has become sick of taking criticism for content moderation and fact-checking decisions as he prepares for congressional testimony, and waves off concern for design choices that his staff believe will stoke anger on the platform.

What to do about the iPhone Pro Max not fitting the Tesla's built-in wireless charger? And we hear from a listener who -- shockingly -- doesn't care about CarPlay.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/p7-dar.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unseen variant of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit called P7 DarkSword.

"Compared with the variants we usually observe, P7 reduces its on-device footprint, adds on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and adds two way C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure," iVerify said in a new report published Thursday.

The name "P7" is a nod to the threat actor's use of the "p7_" variable prefix in changes made to the original DarkSword code.

DarkSword was first publicly documented earlier this March by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), iVerify, and Lookout, detailing its ability to target iPhones running iOS versions between iOS 18.4 and 18.7. The kit was detected in the wild in November 2025.

The toolkit is engineered to chain multiple iOS vulnerabilities to escape the browser sandbox, escalate to kernel privileges, and inject the main payload into SpringBoard, the iOS process that handles app launches and the home screen. The exploit chain is assessed to be a commercial product that somehow landed in a second-hand market, from where it was acquired by financially motivated operators and other threat actors since late 2025.

The exploit kit has been put to use in attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine by multiple threat actors, including a Turkish commercial surveillance vendor named PARS Defense via a fake Snapchat-themed website and a Russia-aligned threat actor called Star Blizzard (aka COLDRIVER) using fake invitation lures.

In August 2026, attack surface management platform Censys detailed a campaign mounted by an unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor that involved targeting Apple iOS devices with the exploit kit, in addition to serving an Apple ID decoy sign-in page.

As recently as last month, iVerify said it observed "multiple unsuccessful, likely LLM-assisted attempts to update the framework to support iOS 26.x," fueled by the leak of the exploit kit shortly after its public disclosure. These variants, the mobile security company added, are focused on stability, stealth, and quality of stolen data.

P7 DarkSword represents an evolution in these aspects by eliminating debug logging over HTTP requests and syslog and using browser localStorage to prevent re-exploitation. Unlike prior variants that copied and exfiltrated the keychain database to process on the attacker's infrastructure, the new version extracts keychain data into JSON on the phone prior to exfiltration.

"The implant is injected into the SpringBoard process, which handles all communication with the attacker's infrastructure," iVerify said.

The latest iteration is equipped to poll for commands every 15 seconds, send a "heartbeat" message, send a list of installed applications, and transmit iCloud Keychain information and data from applications like Apple Notes, Photos, and cryptocurrency wallets.

The response to the periodic tasking poll contains commands to be executed on the victim's phone. This includes -

The disclosure comes as Censys said it identified open directories on five hosts carrying components related to DarkSword and Coruna, another iOS exploit kit uncovered this year as weaponized in attacks aimed at iPhone models running iOS versions between 13.0 and 17.2.1.

"Coruna is the companion payload kit the same ecosystem distributes," Censys said. "Its stages run inside the victim's browser session after DarkSword's exploit stages land, and its wallet-harvesting modules steal crypto recovery phrases, balances, and keystore data from iOS apps. Operators run DarkSword and Coruna together against their own C2 infrastructure."

The five hosts are listed below -

An analysis of the production server's exploit registry has revealed that the DarkSword exploit kit comprises two CVE identifiers not previously documented -

It's suspected that the open-directory cluster and the 156.239.230[.]120 platform are run by a Chinese-speaking threat actor with an aim to conduct cryptocurrency wallet theft. That said, exactly who is behind is unknown.

"The platform runs a Chinese-speaking exploitation-as-a-service operation," Censys researcher Aidan Holland said. "The admin panel exposes an agent/reseller model, and a copy of the production server recovered 11 victim recovery phrases, 179 device loot directories, and a 75-account control-plane roster."

Censys said it also detected a separate China-based operator running the same kit in the wild against its own C2 server at "66ds[.]lol," while including a new cryptocurrency wallet target (BitKeep) not present in the open-directory set. The findings once again highlight the proliferation of the kit among financially motivated actors.

"The operator behind it sits on Tencent and Shenyang hosting, tied to the operator through a unique self-signed certificate authority," Censys said.

https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/s.title: Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training Too
https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/s.author: Arielle Waldman
https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/s.text:
Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Those closest to executives must match their security postures because the weakest link in a family becomes the entry point for attacks.

An attacker attempts to breach an executive's personal laptop, but effective multifactor authentication (MFA) blocks them. Actually, it was only a deterrent, because the attacker discovers the executive's son did not enable MFA on his gaming console, and uses that access to move laterally, eventually breaking into the corporate network.

Cybercriminals' increasingly brazen techniques have expanded beyond the office walls to target top executives' family members and friends who may not know how to protect themselves— worse yet, they don't even see it coming. While leadership receives ongoing security awareness training on password hygiene, and how to look out for signs of phishing and vishing, that still leaves those closest to them vulnerable, creating a dangerous blind spot for organizations, and artificial intelligence (AI) now offers bad actors new tools to exploit it.

In March, Google Cloud's Office of the CISO warned that personal attacks against executives are on the rise. Authors urged boards to consider how they are supporting executives and their families in implementing effective social media settings, knowing attackers routinely use that avenue for reconnaissance.

Related:Why the CISO-CFO Relationship Is a Key to Cybersecurity Success

Attacks abusing those relationships always start with reconnaissance, due to everyone's enormous digital footprint. Eerily, an attacker can map out a household's relationships, routines, and locations without ever touching a network, warns Brian Hill, field chief information security officer (CISO) of client advisory at BlackCloak.

From there, attacks branch out into three categories: impersonation, compromising the household's devices, and phishing or smishing—a tactic aimed at less technical family members.

However, the consequences aren't just digital, Hill warns. A leaked itinerary or home address can turn into physical surveillance, a break-in, or extortion.

"Even something as harmless as a child's school play on a shared calendar can give an attacker exactly the timing they need for a fraudulent wire request," Hill tells Dark Reading.

The tactic of using executives' confidants to conduct social engineering campaigns, assist with account takeovers, or to provide clues that help an attacker guess passwords is not a new phenomenon.

In 2023, BlackCloak and Ponemon Institute released a study titled, "Understanding the Serious Risks to Executives’ Personal Cybersecurity & Digital Lives" where 42% of respondents said, "their key executives and family members already experienced at least one attack by a cybercriminal."

Related:What We Missed: Google Gemini Joins the AI Escape Party

That same year, Dragos disclosed that it blocked a ransomware attack where a threat actor contacted family members after one of its executives ignored ransom demands. The problem was further highlighted by Mandiant's CTO, Charles Carmakal, at RSA Conference 2024 where he warned that cybercriminals engaged in SIM swapping attacks against executive's children. Attackers used that access to contact executives, adding pressure on ransomware victims to give into payment demands, according to a KnowBe4 blog post.

The latest research from Ponemon and BlackCloak showed that 51% of organizations reported attacks on their business leaders in 2025, up from 43% in 2023, reveals Hill. In the cybersecurity and digital privacy company's own onboarding of new clients, 39% of executives had devices that were already compromised without their knowledge, and 20% had unmonitored, open-access home networks.

"Every one of those gaps is shared with the people they live with," Hill says. Targeting family members “is not only common, it is one of the most predictable paths an attacker will take."

Bad actors have always been opportunistic, and nobody is off the table when it comes to using family or friends to get to a [very important person] VIP, warns Erich Kron, CISO advisor at KnowBe4.

Related:CISA Calls for More Guidance, Less Spin, as Cyber Outages Escalate

Executive-targeted social engineering, known as "whaling", has been around for quite some time, he adds, explaining that threat actors target someone close to the executive to exploit their family's or friend's trust and relationship, while trying to harvest sensitive data.

"Family members and friends tend to be less trained and less protected than high-level executives, therefore it is easier for cybercriminals to earn their trust and perform malicious actions," Kron tells Dark Reading.

AI is compounding the problem, especially when it comes to reconnaissance. Threat actors can scan social media platforms or public records seven times faster versus doing manual reconnaissance. That allows attackers to identify family and friends far easier than before, Kron warns.

NCC Group has tracked the trend over the years, and what is important to remember is that that attackers don’t necessarily view someone's personal and professional lives as separate, reveals Matt Hull, vice president of cyber intelligence and response at NCC Group.

They look for whatever information gives them an opportunity, Hull adds. Details that appear harmless like interests, hobbies, or even fitness and location-based services such as Strava can potentially reveal routines, or patterns of behaviors, he warns.

"NCC Group has previously described how cybercriminals tend to target people based on the information they can gather, rather than beginning with a fixed method of attack," Hull tells Dark Reading.

Although an indirect attack, like compromising an executive's loved one or executive assistant, increases the number of actions that may fail, it actually increases the likelihood of success, explains Jeremy Banon, The Cyber Health Company CEO and founder.

"The last 12 months, we have seen this pick-up significantly," Banon tells Dark Reading.

Addressing the challenge begins by acknowledging the reality, says Banon, adding how important it is for relatives to tighten their security postures because "hopping from vulnerable family member to the eventual target is easier than ever."

While the top advice is to reduce digital footprints, that's nearly impossible these days. But there are steps people can take toward that direction.

Regarding social media accounts, remove legal names from usernames and profile photos. Same is true for WhatsApp, Apple contact cards, and personal emails, adds Banon, who emphasizes that "aliases are your friend."

Excellent password management and MFA adoption means ideally don't use SMS, which attackers can intercept and abuse, and ensure SIM swap protection for the entire family.

Some social media accounts and experts promote the idea of crafting and using family safe words to prove legitimacy, but Banon is skeptical.

"I don't think they're harmful, but I'm pessimistic this works," Banon says. "If you text your safe word once, it's burned. Then you need a new safe word."

Family members must be mindful of podcasts or social videos they create because attackers can abuse just a few seconds to conduct impersonation scams, cloning the voice and calling the spouse with an urgent request, explains Hill.

Less technically inclined family members need to be aware of QR code lures, fake delivery notices, and messages impersonating banks or schools. If attackers control their accounts, they can access family chats, calendars, and email threads that contain travel plans, financial details, and business information.

"Encourage family and friends to learn about scams and how modern cyberattacks work so they can quickly identify and ignore or report social engineering attempts," Kron advises. "In our modern digital world, just knowing someone important can put you on a much more targeted list."

Features Writer, Dark Reading

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.title: Two large asteroids found spinning as fast as a fairground ride
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Jonathan O’Callaghan
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
Large asteroids have been found spinning so fast they should break apart, suggesting they might be stronger than we thought.

Dmitrii Vavilov at the University of Washington in Seattle and his colleagues analysed some of the first data collected by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began a 10-year survey of the sky in June 2026. From a sample of more than 9000 asteroids, they measured the rotation of 260, based on a change in their brightness caused by the spinning asteroids’ irregular shapes.

Of these, 66 were deemed to be super-fast rotators, spinning quickly enough to complete a rotation in less than 2.2 hours, a limit at which asteroids should no longer be able to hold themselves together under their own gravity.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.author: Jo Marchant
https://www.newscientist.com/article/259.text:
A seasonal rise in covid-19 cases in Europe and North America has focused attention on a group of variants called XFG, which has dominated worldwide over the past year. A string of covid-19 variants has arisen since the virus emerged in 2019, but do we need to be concerned every time we hear of a new strain? Or have our past covid-19 infections and vaccinations given us a baseline level of protection?

Six years on from the height of the covid-19 pandemic, “we’re in this weird, uncharted territory”, says Danny Altmann at Imperial College London. “It’s not as good as we hoped, where we would just barely notice it, like the common cold. But it is not as bad as some of my colleagues feared, where we’re brewing the next disaster.”

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/californi.title: ‘Trojan horse’: California’s top 1% pay nearly half the state’s income taxes. Prop 40 opponents warn the billionaire tax could reach everyone else
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/californi.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/californi.text:
California’s revenue is notoriously top heavy, leaving state coffers vulnerable to boom-and-bust cycles as the wealthiest residents see their incomes rise and fall with the stock market.

In recent years, the top 1% of California households have accounted for about 40%-50% of all personal income tax revenue, according to the conservative Hoover Institution.

In fact, the top 1% paid more than $60 billion in California personal income taxes in 2021, when the stock market soared. The flip side is that the state suffers crippling deficits when the market tanks, like during the Great Financial Crisis.

Now, California’s Proposition 40 seeks to tax billionaires’ wealth in addition to their incomes, and opponents have launched a full-court press, calling it a “Trojan horse” that will eventually come for all Californians.

The ballot initiative calls for residents worth more than $1 billion to pay a one-time tax equivalent to 5% of their assets. The union pushing Prop 40, the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, has said the wealth tax could raise $100 billion in revenue and help offset federal cuts to health spending.

Prop 40 includes a provision that says the state legislature could modify it with a two-thirds vote—but only “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.”

Prop 40 backers insist it’s only aimed at billionaires. Still, any changes would be up to state lawmakers, though courts would also weigh in on any attempts to stretch the scope to all taxpayers or to extend it beyond a one-time levy.

According to CalMatters, there have been numerous instances in which the state legislature has amended other ballot measures after they have passed. There have also been times when the courts have upheld the changes and when they have struck them down.

In 1995, the state Supreme Court ruled lawmakers can make changes if they advance voters’ original intent “by any reasonable construction,” the report said. But in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal rejected an attempt to amend the Political Reform Act, saying it “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the law.

Of course, there’s nothing that would prevent another ballot initiative in the future from taxing wealth to fund other spending priorities. And if Prop 40 succeeds, similar initiatives could pop up elsewhere.

A group of Nobel laureate economists who support Prop 40 have said the ballot measure could “kickstart a movement” that spreads well beyond California.

In a letter signed by Daron Acemoglu, Abhijit Banerjee, Peter Diamond, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman, and Joseph Stiglitz, the economists argued that while billionaires have “made important contributions,” they have also been “amply rewarded” and have used loopholes to avoid taxes on capital returns, allowing their wealth to compound further.

“As Californians head to the polls, their vote may well come to be seen as a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy,” the letter added.

Prop 40’s critics have warned the tax is unlikely to be a one-time deal and also raised alarms about the forms of wealth that would be targeted, such as unrealized capital gains and privately held stock that’s key for startups.

Supporters point to the AI boom and say California’s ultra-rich would still be among the world’s wealthiest. And the Nobel laureates contend the tax will not doom Silicon Valley, saying California has attracted 80% of all new venture capital funding in the U.S. since the start of 2026, up from about 50% before 2025.

Prop 40 has split the state’s political and business leaders. Gov. Gavin Newsom is against it, while U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna is for it. But even the congressman has conceded he doesn’t want illiquid stakes or voting shares to be taxed. Some unions have also come out in opposition, saying other areas of state spending should be priorities, too.

Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he’s “perfectly fine” with it, while Google cofounder Sergey Brin contributed over $100 million toward opposing the billionaire tax.

Further complicating the matter is competition from other ballot measures that would nullify Prop 40. Proposition 41 would make any new taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit, while Proposition 42 would prohibit taxes on financial assets and personal property other than real estate.

A recent poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found all three have support from a majority of voters.

“Supporters of Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax initiative, have a lot of work to do,” said Mark Baldassare, the survey’s director, told KQED.
