https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/chick-fil.title: Chick-fil-A is keeping humans at the drive-thru while McDonald’s tests AI ordering and defends a separate pricing algorithm in court
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/chick-fil.author: Tatiana Sataua
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/chick-fil.text:
The fast-food industry has spent decades trying to make ordering a burger faster. Digital menus, mobile apps, self-service kiosks—you name it. Now, artificial intelligence wants a turn at the drive-thru speaker. But at Chick-fil-A, the familiar “my pleasure” still needs to come from a human.

While McDonald’s is testing AI-powered voice ordering at its drive-thrus, Chick-fil-A CEO Andrew Cathy says his restaurants won’t follow suit. The chicken chain isn’t rejecting AI altogether, but it believes some parts of the fast-food experience are better left to humans, even if technology could make them more efficient.

McDonald’s is also defending a different kind of algorithm in court. A new lawsuit alleges its pricing recommendation system helped coordinate higher menu prices, claims the company denies. The two technologies are separate, but both put a spotlight on how much control restaurants are willing to hand over to AI—and how much responsibility remains with the people using it.

Chick-fil-A calls its approach to technology “human plus.” The company is exploring AI behind the scenes but won’t use it to replace drive-thru order-takers, Cathy told CNBC.

“We’re not gonna substitute that interaction with technology, because we feel like that hospitality is so important to create that warm environment for consumers,” he said.

Alex Susskind, a Cornell University professor who studies restaurant operations and hospitality technology, sees the logic. Chick-fil-A’s drive-thrus often have employees standing outside with tablets, taking orders and directing cars through lines that can stretch around the building. Those human interactions, he told Fortune, make the wait more tolerable.

Susskind, a former chef and restaurant operator, isn’t against automation. Technology has an important role in restaurants, he said, particularly when it removes repetitive tasks without sacrificing service. Before adopting it, he said restaurants should ask: “Is this making my customers’ experience better or more meaningful?”

In contrast to Chick-fil-A’s human-centric approach to drive-thru ordering, McDonald’s is testing Archy, an AI-powered system that takes drive-thru orders in English and Spanish, claiming to be accurate more than 90% of the time.

The technology is part of a broader system called ArchIQ, which also includes automated inventory management and equipment monitoring. McDonald’s says these tools are intended to simplify restaurant operations and free employees to spend more time serving customers.

It isn’t the burger giant’s first try. McDonald’s ended an earlier drive-thru voice-ordering test with IBM in 2024 after rolling it out to more than 100 U.S. restaurants, a trial that drew attention for viral videos of botched orders.

Susskind has seen firsthand how quickly an automated ordering system can go wrong. He called a local pizzeria to order one large pizza, half pepperoni and half plain cheese, which seemed simple enough. But on the other end was an AI phone assistant that kept insisting he wanted two pizzas, even after he repeatedly corrected it.

With no easy way to reach a person, Susskind eventually went to the restaurant himself. Employees explained there was a bug in the system, which the restaurant later fixed.

“We only talk about technology when it doesn’t work. We’ve been using AI in a million different ways without even knowing it, or without calling it AI,” he told Fortune, pointing to spell-check as an example.

Restaurants should use technology in ways customers appreciate, he said: “Because if it works well, then it makes their experience easier.”

For customers, the frustration can be as simple as an ordering bot that turns one pizza into two. For employees, it can mean having to clean up mistakes made by technology that was supposed to make their jobs easier.

Keith Spencer, a career expert focused on AI’s impact on workers, said automated ordering could eliminate some repetitive responsibilities for restaurant employees. But fewer tasks don’t necessarily mean less work. Some workers may find themselves handling customer complaints, correcting automated orders, and troubleshooting systems they didn’t choose to implement.

“If AI takes over routine tasks while workers have more opportunity to focus on customer service and problem-solving, it could make shifts more manageable,” Spencer told Fortune. “If the primary goal is simply to reduce labor hours, the impact could look very different.”

McDonald’s is facing a different set of questions about its use of algorithms, this time over whether a pricing-recommendation system could undermine competition between its restaurants.

In a proposed class-action lawsuit filed Oct. 2 in federal court in Chicago, customer Michael Thomas alleges McDonald’s used confidential restaurant sales data and a shared pricing algorithm to coordinate menu prices among independently operated franchises. The complaint further alleges McDonald’s pressured franchisees to follow the system’s recommendations and tracked when they deviated from them. The plaintiff argues those practices reduced competition between restaurants and led customers to pay higher prices.

McDonald’s disputes the allegations.

“The complaint is filled with inaccuracies and we will vigorously defend against this lawsuit,” McDonald’s Corporation said in a statement. “AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do.”

According to McDonald’s, franchisees independently set their prices and may choose whether to use the company’s pricing recommendations. The company also denies using dynamic pricing or changing prices in real time based on individual customers.

David Scupp, an antitrust attorney, said the legal distinction depends partly on whether competing businesses share confidential information through a common pricing tool and whether they retain genuine independence in setting prices.

“In general, having a human making the final pricing decision and being able to reject or accept the pricing recommendation, I think, makes it less of an antitrust problem,” Scupp told Fortune. That alone doesn’t settle it, he added. The underlying data and how the system operates also matter.

The allegations have not been established in court, and McDonald’s pricing recommendation system is separate from its AI drive-thru technology.

For Susskind, the debate isn’t about rejecting AI. It’s about making sure technology improves the experience rather than getting in the way of it.

“Hospitality is a human business,” he said.
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/chick-fil.summary: McDonald's is testing an AI-powered system that takes drive-Thru orders in English and Spanish. The allegations have not been established in court.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/leaky-pip.title: ‘A very leaky pipeline’: 1.7 million trade jobs will open each year through 2035—and experts are scrambling to figure out how to fill them
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/leaky-pip.author: Sasha Rogelberg
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/leaky-pip.text:
Mike Rowe, the host of TV show Dirty Jobs, recently offered a sobering diagnosis of the state of skilled trades jobs today: “For every five tradespeople who retire this year, two replace them.” “Five out, two in,” Rowe said during a Ford Pro Accelerate panel on workforce development. “I don’t care how you vote. I don’t care what your politics are. Math doesn’t care either.”

“How long do you want to wait for your toilet to get fixed?” he added. “How long do you want to wait for the lights to come back on when you flip the switch?”

Now economists are putting a number to just how big this shortage is—and what exactly it takes to fill it. The recent State of America’s Skilled Trades report, published by nonprofits Jobs for the Future and The Burning Glass Institute, found there will be 1.7 million skilled trade job openings every year through 2035, including 600,000 new net positions added in through the same time period.

The surge bucks the trend of slugging job growth and unemployment, which ticked up to 4.2% in September, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Trade job opportunities have exploded in the latest era of technology, in large part a result of the growing AI boom demanding the construction of data centers, as well as increased defense production, and even the growth in demand for affordable housing units. These tradespeople are part of a 18-million strong workforce who added an estimated $3.8 trillion to the U.S. GDP last year.

But these trade industries are facing a two-fold problem, as Rowe alluded to: More tradespeople are retiring, leaving experts and employers scratching their heads about how to recruit enough young people to not just replace this greying workforce, but meet the growing demand for these types of jobs.

“You have to think about this like a bathtub with a faucet and a drain,” Matt Sigelman, president of Burning Glass Institute, told Fortune. “We also have a very leaky pipeline.”

Nearly one-quarter of skilled trade workers are 55 or older, according to the report, and only 11% are under 25. For some trades, like tool and die makers, nearly half of the workforce is over 55.

In the mid-late 20th century, trade jobs were prized. The Baby Boom gave way to around 77 million people added to the U.S. population, many of whom entered the workforce in the 1960s and ‘70s, when public works and suburban housing projects soared in demand. An influx of funding for vocational training in schools helped bolster this workforce. However, manufacturing jobs peaked in 1979, and the rise of a service-based economy in the U.S. coincided with the increasing affordability of college, leading to shrinking opportunities in the trades by the end of the century.

The result is the winding-down workforce that took advantage of the post-war need for housing and infrastructure, and a workforce today that is trained to contribute to the service economy. All the while, the growing need for trade roles across industries has escalated the shortage.

“We have a growing need for tradespeople, and one of the things that we’re studying now is how an array of different national priorities, each of which you know have overlapping demand for the same skill trades,” Sigelman said. “There’s significant overlap in the nature of the tradespeople that are needed for each of these kinds of priorities and many others, and so those shortages can easily compound.”

Tides are beginning to change. Gen Z has become decidedly frustrated with the often prohibitive costs of higher education. Inundated with messaging around AI displacing entry-level, white-college work, many have sought refuge in trade positions. Industry giants are working to meet the growing interest in trade roles. General Motors has invested nearly $200 million in the last year to modernize internal skilled trade careers and manufacturing, engineering, and technician roles. Technicians, on average, can make between $80,000 to $90,000.

“[We need to] really make sure high school students understand this is a great career and frankly maybe a little more AI-proof than some others,” CEO Mary Barra told Fortune last month, “Potentially even higher, depending on how many hours they work.”

But getting young prospective workers interested in skilled trades is only half the battle. While recruitment is crucial for filling increasing trade roles, “part of what exacerbates the need for us to do that work is that so few people who start a program finish,” Sigelman said.

Of 100 people who start an apprenticeship or community college workforce program, Sigelman noted, only about 48 finished. While higher education institutions like four-year colleges also face retention challenges, they have the financial and staff resources to intervene and slow attrition rates. Smaller trade and vocation programs lack these same resources, Sigelman said.

Sligelman noted that one solution to increasing the network of skilled tradespeople is expanding who believes they can have a trade position. A recent study by the Ad Council Research Institute of more than 3,000 high school students and 25,000 parents of high school students found 71% of teens said they would be proud of attending a trade school, but just 9% considered a postgraduate career in trades. The problem, according to Sigelman, is one of exposure: Many people who become plumbers go into the field because their parent or neighbor was a plumber.

“We’ve yet to see the network broaden, even as awareness is rising,” he said. “It’s not an awareness gap; it’s a navigation gap. How do we help people navigate to these fields?”
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/leaky-pip.summary: The State of America’s Skilled Trades report found there will be 1.7 million skilled trade job openings every year through 2035. The surge bucks the trend of slugging job growth and unemployment, which ticked up to 4.2% in September.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/tesla-fu.title: Tesla drops 'Full Self-Driving' brand name in Europe after regulator pushback
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/tesla-fu.author: Lora Kolodny
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/tesla-fu.text:
Tesla changed the brand name for its “Full Self-Driving (Supervised),” or FSD, systems to “Assisted Driving” in Europe under pressure from German regulators.

Elon Musk’s automaker markets the system for $99 per month under its old brand name in the U.S.

In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million “active” FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were subscribed via free trials.

Elon Musk’s automaker Tesla
 has changed the brand name of its “Full Self-Driving (Supervised),” or FSD, system in Europe to “Assisted Driving” after German regulators called the branding “somewhat misleading.”

The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners.

Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year.

On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport, known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla’s brand name “FSD” was “somewhat misleading,” adding that “It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times.”

Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla’s “browbeating” pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company’s technology.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla’s FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions.

In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that “false advertiser” label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing.

In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million “active” FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.

Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

An Omani FlyDubai co-pilot had planned to seize a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight and crash it into a terminal at Israel's Ben Gurion airport on September 30 in a suicide attack before he was thwarted by his fellow pilot, the UAE attorney general said on Friday, according to the state news agency.

The co-pilot had drawn inspiration from al Qaeda's September 11, 2001 attacks on the US, and was seeking to inflict the maximum loss of life possible, public prosecutors said.

Investigators found the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to "familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport", the state news agency WAM reported.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.author: Maddie Nixon and Claire Campbell
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

The US Government says Nidal Hasan's death by firing squad will be live streamed. (AFP: Bell Country Sherriff's Department)

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has said the execution of convicted Fort Hood military base shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed.

Human rights groups and politicians have condemned the plan.

Amnesty International Australia is urging Anthony Albanese to raise the issue with Washington.

The United Nations has condemned a US plan to livestream the execution of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan, labelling it "abhorrent".

United States Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said in a video posted by official Pentagon accounts that Hasan's death by firing squad will be livestreamed.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Mr Hegseth said.

Nidal Hasan shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, while working as a US Army psychiatrist.

The United States's first execution by a military firing squad since World War II will be live streamed, the Pentagon has said.

His execution, set for December 3, will be the first that the US military has carried out by firing squad since World War II.

The move has drawn sharp condemnation from human rights groups and politicians.

"A government executing someone in public or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent," UN spokesperson Stephanie Dujarric said.

In a message sent to AFP,  the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said the livestreaming of an execution "is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".

Mr Hegseth's announcement sparked strong reactions across the political divide in the US.

But President Donald Trump has so far stayed silent on the matter, directing all enquiries to the Pentagon.

Republican Senator Thom Tillis took to social media to say public executions are what oppressive dictatorships do.

Republican Thom Tillis has been a US Senator from North Carolina since 2015. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," he said.

Meanwhile, Democratic senator Chris Murphy accused the Secretary of Defense of "mimicking ISIS" in an interview with CNN.

"I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public execution is medieval. It’s frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups," he said.

The Federal Communications Commission said it would defer to the Pentagon on whether US broadcast networks could air a planned military execution.

Soldiers held a vigil at Hood Stadium on the Fort Hood army post after the fatal shooting. (Jessica Rinaldi: REUTERS)

Former US Army sergeant Alonzo Lunsford was shot seven times during the Fort Hood attack, but survived.

He told the BBC that he agreed with the sentence, but said he was concerned about the execution being livestreamed.

"I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," he said.

Mr Lunsford said he would attend the execution in person to "look him in the eyes".

He added: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief."

Amnesty International Australia has urged the Albanese government to underline the country's "long-standing commitment to the global abolition of the death penalty" to Washington.

"The Albanese Government must uphold that commitment by raising its concerns directly with the United States, urging authorities to halt the execution, commute Hasan’s death sentence and abandon plans to broadcast it,” Kyinzom Dhongdue, Strategic Campaigns and Advocacy Manager at Amnesty International said.

"The suggestion that an execution by firing squad should be live streamed for public viewing is an appalling disregard for human dignity.

"Turning a state-sanctioned killing into a public spectacle only compounds the cruelty of the death penalty."

The planned suicide attack was inspired by the events of September 11 in the US, public prosecutors believe

An ⁠Omani Flydubai ⁠co-pilot had planned to seize a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight and crash it into a terminal at Israel’s Ben ‌Gurion airport on September 30 in a suicide attack before he was thwarted by his fellow pilot, the UAE attorney general said on Friday, according to ⁠the state news agency.

The plan was inspired by ‌the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors ‌believe as a result of their investigation ⁠launched ⁠on October 1, which found the suspect had used ‌two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the ‌flight route ‌and the airport”, the state ‌news agency WAM reported.

The incident caused the ⁠jet to plunge 16,000 feet in 30 seconds.

The attorney ⁠general said the suspect had worked for several airlines in different countries ‌in the ‌past, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining flydubai in January 2026.

https://www.dw.com/en/china-eu-reach-dea.title: China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
https://www.dw.com/en/china-eu-reach-dea.text:
An agreement between the EU and China would reduce exports of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid cars to the 27-member European bloc by up to 50%, according to the EU trade envoy.

European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic announced on Friday that China and the European Union had reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU by more than half.

This announcement followed two-day talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's growing trade deficit with China.

Earlier, Sefcovic said this week's talks were the culmination of three months of intensive work.

According to Sefcovic, the deal would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU."

He added that this opens the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half, based on projections over a four-year period.

"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," Sefcovic said.

Although he did not offer details on how the agreement will be implemented, Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result.

Sevcovic added the two sides also reached an agreement to reduce Chinese import duties on €4 billion ($4.5 billion) worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.

They also agreed to simplify China's process for granting export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets.

The agreement will require approval from the leaders of all 27 EU nations, who will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels on Thursday.

According to UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totaled $560 billion (€500 billion) last year, up from $517 billion in 2023. Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose approximately 10% from a year earlier. Shipments to Hungary increased by 43%.

Meanwhile, China imported $268.3 billion (€240 billion) worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion the previous year. Purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France led the way.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned lawmakers at the European Parliament that the trade gap had reached a tipping point. She said the EU would use all available tools to rebalance the relationship.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68x.title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68x.text:
Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.

Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.

Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.

Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".

Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".

Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.

It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".

The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.

The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.

Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.

Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.

Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".

Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".

Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.

Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.

Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: Labour byelection win shows party starting to win back voters on left
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Sammy Gecsoyler and Peter Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Party now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PM

Labour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% of a relatively low turnout to keep Starmer’s old north London seat for the party, pushing Polanski, who had stood for the party he leads, into second place on 33%.

While the result was broadly as predicted, Labour strategists were buoyed up by the party’s relatively straightforward route to victory in a diverse inner-city area of the sort the Greens have been targeting with recent success.

The result “sends a clear message to those voters who lost faith in Labour in recent years”, said Lucy Powell, who called last month for the party to unite progressive voters under Andy Burnham if it wants to win the next election.

After the byelection win, she told the Guardian: “We hear you, we’ve listened and we know we needed to be clearer about what we stand for and what type of country we want to see, proudly putting our values centre stage. We’re delighted so many of you are backing us once again.”

The byelection came after the Green party voted at their conference last weekend to adopt a hugely controversial policy equating Zionism with racism, and saying Israel should be replaced with a single Palestinian state.

Polanski has been criticised for showing minimal leadership on the most toxic internal debate the Greens have faced in living memory, with the chair of Jewish Greens saying he should resign.

The byelection, called after Starmer resigned his Commons seat shortly after he was ousted by Burnham, saw a low turnout of 38.7%, possibly due to the widespread predictions that Labour was set to win, despite a major campaigning effort from the Greens.

The turnout also suggests Burnham could still face a battle to engage some voters in urban areas, particularly London, where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.

In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.

“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.”

Responding to the defeat, Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, said that while the result showed his party remained a major threat to Labour, many voters had told him they wanted to “give Andy Burnham a chance”.

It was the Greens’ second best-ever byelection result, more evidence of the party’s increased prominence and campaigning power since Polanski became leader 13 months ago.

The best came in February, when the Greens took an equally safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton in Greater Manchester, in a major upset that weakened Starmer’s position. Around the same time, the Greens peaked at 21% in national polling, above Labour. They are now about 11%, more than 15 points behind Burnham’s party.

Polanski’s position has come under scrutiny since the Zionism motion was passed, with critics accusing him of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate to campaign in the byelection, giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.

In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.

On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”

However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.

Speaking shortly before the byelection result was announced, Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, said Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.

Speaking to Newsnight, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”

Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.”

There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Florida execution called off after DeSantis withdraws death warrant for first time
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Governor halts execution of William Lee Thompson, after Christa Pike survived failed lethal injections

Ron DeSantis cancelled a planned execution in the state on Friday, days before a 74-year-old man was due to be killed by lethal injection.

The move – the first time Florida’s governor has withdrawn a death warrant in his nearly eight years in office – comes just over a week after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee.

DeSantis, who has aggressively used the death penalty during his time as governor, signed a letter on Thursday withdrawing the death warrant for William Lee Thompson. The Republican did not give a reason for the withdrawal, which comes at a time of increased national and international scrutiny on the use of the death penalty in the US.

Pike, 50, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. She was taken to a hospital and declared brain dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. On Thursday her lawyer said she was “up and walking” in hospital, but said her arms were severely injured.

Adding to the attention on state executions, this week the Pentagon announced that it would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.

William Lee Thompson, 74, had been scheduled to be killed by the state on Tuesday, for the murder and kidnapping of Sally Ivester in 1976. Lawyers for Thompson said he is suffering from dementia.

A second Florida execution scheduled for Tuesday is still set to take place. In that case, James Robertson, 63, is due to be executed for the first-degree murder of Frank Hart, then a fellow inmate, in 2008. Robertson waived all appeals, and told investigators he killed Hart so he could be moved to death row.

DeSantis did not provide a reason in the letter for withdrawing Thompson’s death warrant, but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Florida prison officials, however, had still been preparing for Thompson’s potential execution next week.

Grace Hanna, executive director of Floridians for alternatives to the death penalty, said Thompson’s attorneys had told DeSantis he was “incompetent for execution due to his dementia”.

“He did not know where he was, stated that ‘Bush’ was the president, and, at times, did not even recognize that he had been sentenced to death,” Hanna said. “In accordance with state law, he underwent an evaluation last week. Officials never released the findings or explained today’s withdrawal.”

Thompson’s attorney, Bri Lacy, said they were relieved by the result.

“Mr Thompson suffers from dementia and his health is failing – both of which were gravely concerning with an impending execution,” Lacy said in an email to Associated Press.

“Now that Mr Thompson is no longer under a death warrant, we hope FDOC [Florida department of corrections] will relocate him to an adequate medical facility and provide the care he needs.”

A spokesperson for DeSantis did not immediately return an email seeking comment. Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future.

Florida carried out 19 executions last year, a record in the state since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida became the first state in nearly a decade to execute two prisoners in one day.

Thompson was due to be executed by lethal injection on Tuesday. He was scheduled to be killed by lethal injections on Tuesday, but his execution was cancelled on Friday.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Multiple hospitalized after Avianca flight from Medellín to New York had to divert to Miami due to strong turbulence

At least eight people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami early on Friday.

Miami-Dade fire rescue said one person was rushed to a trauma center with severe injuries while seven others were taken to area hospitals in ambulances.

The Federal Aviation Administration said the Avianca flight was en route from Medellín, Colombia, to John F Kennedy international airport in New York when the Airbus A320 had to divert to Miami.

Avianca said the unhurt passengers were rebooked on other flights to continue their trip to New York. The airline said “the safety of our customers and employees is, and will remain, the foundation of our operations”.

Serious injuries from in-flight turbulence are rare, but scientists say they may be becoming more common as the climate crisis alters the jet stream. The International Air Transport Association said the number of reports it received about turbulence incidents surged more than 25% last year.

Last summer, 24 people were taken to the hospital after a Delta Air Lines flight encountered turbulence caused by a thunderstorm over Wyoming. The National Transportation Safety Board has said passengers and flight attendants were thrown into the ceiling with enough force to crack some of the interior panels before tossing them back to the floor and then up again. The seatbelt sign was off at the time so some passengers were up and drinks were being served when the plane hit the turbulence.

At least 20 passengers have filed lawsuits against Delta over that incident, arguing the airline could have avoided the severe weather.

The FAA recommends that passengers stay buckled whenever possible to protect against unexpected turbulence.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Andy Burnham is lucky – Polanski, Farage and Badenoch all seem determined to help him | Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Everywhere the PM turns, he finds generous adversaries. They have made his early days in No 10 so much easier

I
don’t know where Andy Burnham found his magic lamp, but I hope he’s taking good care of it. In the early hours of Friday morning, the genie that’s looked so kindly on him these past few months granted him yet another wish, with a byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. It was just the latest gift for a prime minister for whom things keep going right – and who is especially blessed in his choice of opponents.

Let’s start with that win in London, where Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali defeated the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. It’s easy to miss how rare such a victory is. As the veteran psephologist Peter Kellner pointed out, this was a win that “defied history”. If the past half-century were any guide, Labour should have lost, thanks to a “truly dreadful record” defending its own seats when in government and facing a byelection challenge from the left or centre-left, the likes of the Greens or the Lib Dems. The average swing against Labour in such contests had been 24%. “On those figures,” wrote Kellner, “Polanski should have won at a canter.” But he lost.

That reinforces the case Burnham made for why he should replace the previous Holborn and St Pancras MP, one Keir Starmer, as Labour leader: namely, that he was uniquely placed to defeat challenges from both left and right. This latest win over the Greens, coupled with his own success in Makerfield in June, is early vindication of that argument.

Burnham can claim much credit for the London result: it’s his leftward shift that has persuaded many progressive voters that they don’t need to vote Green to get what they want and that they should give Labour another chance. But Burnham really ought to share the credit with Polanski himself, who has proved a most generous adversary.

Yes, Polanski brought an initial surge in energy, enthusiasm and membership to the Greens. But under him the party has steadily dismantled the moral halo it once enjoyed as the UK’s foremost advocate for the planet, reshaping itself into something darker. Thanks to Sunday’s conference vote branding Zionism as racism, which Polanski ducked, the party now demands the destruction of a state founded, and still regarded by most Jews, as an essential refuge, one whose creation was approved by a UN vote. “Destruction” is not metaphorical, by the way. The motion passed says that the change it seeks – a Palestinian state replacing, rather than existing alongside, Israel – must be secured “by all available means”, a phrase clarified in an accompanying booklet produced by the motion’s proposers to include “armed struggle”. Meaning, violence.

Thus have the Greens allowed themselves to become toxified by the kind of cranks and bigots whose manias crowd out anyone who dares hold a moderate or nuanced view, including many longtime, dedicated local activists. A moment like this calls for leadership, but all the Greens have is a quack hypnotherapist who once earned a living promising to make women’s breasts larger and who, when faced with a difficult decision, ran away. (Now, after the event, Polanski says he would not have voted for the Zionism resolution.) Instead of a leader, the Greens are stuck with a charlatan and a coward.

No wonder former leader Caroline Lucas could not say yes, when asked by Newsnight, whether Polanski should stay in his post. Burnham himself would have no such hesitation: the PM might even be quietly pleased that Polanski performed just well enough in Thursday’s byelection to fend off an immediate challenge. The longer Polanski leads the Greens, the better for Labour.

Meanwhile, Burnham’s other opponents seem similarly determined to do him a favour. Of course, there will be stormier times ahead, but the party conference season now concluded was like a warm, extended summer for the prime minister.

Reform UK, for so long Labour’s strongest challenger in the polls, saw its moment in the sun clouded by eve-of-conference revelations that two senior aides to Nigel Farage had been caught on film apparently discussing how they might get around UK electoral law to take a £500,000 donation from a US benefactor. In politics, the scandals that bite hardest are those that confirm suspicions the voters already harbour. In this case, three in four Britons told YouGov back in July that they regarded Farage as sleazy, with 56% describing him as “very sleazy”.

The party’s leading lights tried to make assorted policy announcements, but the only debate that really cut through was the one started by Suella Braverman, with her eccentric and exclusivist insistence that certain minorities, even those born in England into families rooted in the country for several generations, are not truly English – a definition that would exclude Rishi Sunak and a good portion of the England football team. Farage’s army of would-be mavericks and rebels looks increasingly like a rabble of crooks and spivs and – as if to prove the Greens have no monopoly on the demographic – cranks and bigots.

All this has created an opening for the Conservatives to reclaim their place as the dominant party of the right – but here, too, the genie has smiled on Burnham. True, Kemi Badenoch continues to enjoy higher ratings than her party, but that isn’t saying much. True, too, that she has, belatedly, woken up to the fact that victory will not come solely from trying to out-Reform Reform – people will always vote for the real thing – and that she has to appeal to that vast swathe of Middle England seats lost in 2024 to the Lib Dems.

Her conference pitch – promising to abolish inheritance tax on even the most expensive homes, and to extend free childcare to those earning over £100,000 – might conceivably appeal to some of those high earners. But it draws a dividing line with Labour that Burnham could only have dreamed of. Now the Tories have made plain that, in an age of stretched resources, their priority is to help some of the richest people in the land. That is a battle Burnham will be itching to fight.

As for the Lib Dems, the PM will be only too happy to see them muddling along, an inoffensive receptacle for Tory-sceptic voters in parts of the country that would never go to Labour. Though Burnham wants to eat into their vote too, promising that he will, in the next term, deliver on two of their signature issues: Europe and electoral reform.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

He did that in a speech that was the highlight of the conference season, one that showed a politician who understands the importance of making arguments – and is comfortable making them. After Starmer, who was the opposite in both respects, listening to Burnham was like “gulping down oxygen”, one cabinet minister told me.

And yet, everyone at Labour’s top table knows that the weather will change soon enough. The government, and everyone else, is paying too much to borrow money. At some point, the welfare budget will have to be cut: Labour MPs may be applauding now, but they will be less cheerful when asked to vote for reduced benefits, especially as they face re-selection contests in their local parties, a process that gets under way as soon as January.

There’s a hole in defence spending to fill, the full sweep of public services crying out for cash, a US president apparently bent on driving up global oil prices and therefore inflation, and a civil service machine that ministers privately curse as bloated and ineffective. What’s more, the period we’re in right now – the middle of the parliament – is when governments should be focused entirely on delivery, driving through their agenda. Instead, vital time has been spent on the transition from one PM to another – time Labour will not get back.

For now, Burnham is lucky in his opponents, whose choices hurt them and help him. But the skies will eventually darken and, when they do, the prime minister will reach once again for that magic lamp – hoping against hope that it still works.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appeal

B
y holding Holborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. The seat has substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average 19.3-point fall in four byelections under Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance.

The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of a motion declaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski now says he would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend?

He intends to remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But with calls for his resignation growing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March, YouGov put the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling 10% nationally.

As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating has fallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats.

In an interview with the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, who said she wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion.

Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing the controversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinics
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses leaves NHS ‘weaker’, driving patients to seek care elsewhere

Full report | NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds

The NHS is facing an exodus of staff quitting its ADHD and autism services to join private clinics amid huge demand from children and adults to get a diagnosis.

The loss of specialist personnel to the private sector has already forced one NHS trust in England to limit access to its neurodevelopmental service to only the most urgent cases.

The brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists, nurses and other staff are leaving the NHS “weaker” and making it more likely that people will be forced to seek private healthcare.

The NHS care watchdog announced on Friday it will start inspecting private clinics that offer diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism, which are unregulated. The Care Quality Commission’s move follows the publication of the government-commissioned review of mental health and neurodiversity urging ministers to ensure all service providers are properly regulated amid claims of a “wild west” of private firms offering diagnostic tests.

Scores of private clinics have been set up in recent years offering assessments and treatment for ADHD and autism. They have capitalised on the large number of people who have been unable to access NHS care because services have been overwhelmed by an explosion in demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity, creating long waits for help and large backlogs.

Adrian James, the CQC’s interim inspector of mental health care, said: “This new responsibility will … close a significant gap in our oversight, meaning that people receiving these diagnoses can have far greater confidence in the service they are receiving.”

Prof Peter Fonagy’s report – thought to be the biggest inquiry of its kind in the world to date – voiced concern that private firms face the temptation of “financial incentives” to wrongly diagnose and treat patients whose symptoms mean they should not qualify for either.

The CQC already regulates services offering diagnosis and treatment. But the change means non-NHS clinics offering only diagnostic assessments will in future have to register with them.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the tighter regulation means “people can be confident that assessments are high quality and that the NHS is not being overcharged by independent or private providers”. About 810,000 children and adults in England are waiting for an assessment.

The risks to the NHS of losing staff to the private sector was highlighted last week when the Health Service Journal revealed that the Herefordshire and Worcestershire health and care NHS trust had been forced to restrict children and young people’s access to its neurodevelopmental service for that reason.

A paper presented to the trust’s board reported: “Neurodevelopmental staffing is reduced significantly, with the majority of leavers choosing to take up employment with ISP [independent sector providers] and RtC [Right to Choose] providers for ND [neurodiversity].”

Right to Choose gives NHS patients the right to have an NHS-funded ADHD or autism assessment with a private provider to help them receive care more quickly.

The trust responded to the exodus last month by limiting access by under-18s to only those with the most serious symptoms. It will revert to a normal service on Monday. A total of 1,298 people have already waited at least two years for an ADHD or autism assessment with the trust.

Thea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust and a member of the government’s ADHD taskforce, said NHS services suffered when staff joined private operators, as also happens in physiotherapy and child and adolescent mental health services.

She said: “Some staff stay with the NHS part-time when they get a private-sector job, but many will walk away entirely, leaving the health service in a weaker position and under greater pressure.

“Concerning inequalities will widen further if the NHS can’t keep fully staffed teams or expand them to meet increasing demand for ADHD support. If these services continue to haemorrhage staff, some people will get much quicker support if they can afford to pay for private care,” Stein added.

The NHS Alliance, which represents trusts, confirmed the continuing exodus of staff. “We’re increasingly dealing with one ADHD workforce spread across different providers, both in the NHS and private sector,” Rebecca Gray, the director of the alliance’s mental health network, said.

“The significant growth in the private sector market, where people accessing services can often be seen more quickly than in stretched NHS services, will make working in the independent sector attractive to some staff.”

The Independent Healthcare Providers Network (IHPN), a trade body that represents many non-NHS firms, welcomed the CQC’s enhanced new role.

Sean Phillips, the IHPN’s head of policy, said: “While all of IHPN members who deliver ADHD and autism assessments are CQC registered – with 83% rated good or outstanding – we have long called for greater ‘end-to-end’ oversight of neurodevelopmental provision and it’s welcome to see that the CQC have confirmed they will now be regulating all providers of ADHD and autism assessments.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.title: Drone strike kills 30 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/9.text:
At least 30 displaced people, including women and children, have been killed and dozens of others have been wounded following a drone attack in southeastern Sudan.

The governor of Wad al-Mahi province told Al Jazeera on Friday that a drone belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted the centre of the province, killing 26 women and four children.

Governor Mahjoub Al-Sheikh described the attack as “cowardly”. He said the drone was launched from “inside Ethiopia”, according to the AFP news agency.

Al Jazeera Arabic’s Sudan correspondent, Wadah Al-Tahir, explained that the attack was the latest in a wave of drone strikes targeting the Blue Nile region and this time Wad al-Mahi province near the city of Damazin was struck.

Friday’s attack was just outside a displacement camp, near an informal gold mining site, where women earn a daily wage using chemicals and their bare hands to clear gold nuggets from the earth extracted by men.

The latest frontline in the war between the Sudanese army and the RSF is the border region with Ethiopia, which is facing its own internal conflict that threatens to escalate.

Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of harbouring RSF fighters and bases – Ethiopia has denied the allegations.

Local sources say the porous border between the two countries is a key supply line for the paramilitary and its allies, AFP reported.

The RSF launched its offensive towards Damazin but the advance could put the army in a bind, forcing it to defend territory on both the Blue Nile front and in the Kordofan region, where a year of deadly drone strikes has left the two sides deadlocked.

Aid workers estimate that Sudan’s civil war has killed more than 200,000 people since it started in April 2023, creating one of the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.

Nearly 100,000 people have been displaced in Blue Nile state this year alone, according to United Nations figures.

https://www.theverge.com/tech/1008833/am.title: Amazon’s new Kindles appear to have a light leak problem
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1008833/am.author: Terrence O’Brien
https://www.theverge.com/tech/1008833/am.text:
Reddit users are reporting shadows and visible LEDs around screen edge of new Kindles.

Reddit users are reporting shadows and visible LEDs around screen edge of new Kindles.

Some users are reporting that the new Kindles have a light leak issue that is especially apparent when using dark mode. The latest base-model Kindles have a flush bezel that gives them a sleek appearance and looks great… as long as you keep the lights on. But things can change once you turn down the lights and turn up the brightness on the e-reader.

In some cases, users see shadows around the edges of the screen, or even visible LED strips. The issue appears to affect both the plastic and aluminum models in all colors. Some minor glowing around the edges might be a byproduct of the combination of front lighting and a flush screen. But Reddit users say images shared there show something more dramatic that appears to be a defect.

Good e-Reader says that Amazon is aware of the issue and has confirmed that a manufacturing issue may have led to defects in the current batch of Kindles. However, when contacted by The Verge, the company declined to provide an on-the-record statement.

https://www.darkreading.com/identity-acc.title: What We Missed: FBI Strikes Back at ShinyHunters
https://www.darkreading.com/identity-acc.author: Rob Wright, Alexander Culafi
https://www.darkreading.com/identity-acc.text:
Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from the arrest of a suspected ShinyHunters operative to the compromise of a Pentagon-run data center.

After ShinyHunters claimed a breach against the FBI and defaced its website, a suspected member of the cybercrime gang was detained in Jordan.

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with ShinyHunters' supposed breach against the FBI.

The group recently claimed, without evidence, that it obtained data belonging to nearly every FBI employee and job applicant. This purportedly happened as part of a breach of a third-party jobs portal used by the FBI, in which the gang vandalized the site and claimed to have stolen the aforementioned data.

Earlier this month, Jordanian authorities detained a suspected member of ShinyHunters; as first reported by Reuters, the alleged member is apparently cooperating with officials. The FBI has responded aggressively to this recent incident involving the bureau, cooperating with Dutch authorities to arrest another suspected member of the gang last month.

Related:Carbonato Botnet Puts an AI Agent on Hacked Docker Hosts

ShinyHunters, a loose collective of financially motivated threat actors, has claimed a swath of attacks in recent months against entities including ReliaQuest, Instructure, and even fellow threat group Cl0p.

Also discussed on this episode: Hackers gained access to a reportedly unencrypted Defense Manpower Data Center file-sharing system for roughly nine months, from October 2025 until this past July 16, exposing Pentagon records on nearly 2.8 million living people and 294,000 deceased people tied to the US military; and the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) disclosed a hack involving several unidentified zero-day vulnerabilities.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright with Dark Reading.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

DR's Rob Wright: And this is "What We Missed." This is a discussion about some of the recent stories that we did not cover in the pages, pods, or videos of Dark Reading. And first up, Alex, our old friends at ShinyHunters, back again.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yes.

DR's Rob Wright: This is a big one. FBI versus ShinyHunters, back and forth. There's a lot to cover here, so I'll try to zoom through it as quickly as I can. But basically, ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI. I believe the first report on this was from 404 Media. They contacted members of the media, including 404, saying they had breached the FBI and that they had obtained data on every single FBI employee, which is not great. And then the situation developed from there. More recently, there was allegedly a ShinyHunters hacker who was detained in Jordan, of all places. And according to Reuters, the first to report this, they're cooperating with the FBI. And I believe there was another hacker that was also arrested recently that was connected to ShinyHunters, arrested by the Dutch National Police a couple of weeks ago. So, Alex, what do you think is going on here?

Related:Microsoft Disrupts EvilTokens Device Code Phishing Service

DR's Alex Culafi: I think it's interesting, and it seems like there's some validity to the ShinyHunters claim. Data was accessed somewhere. There was that thing where it was one of the FBI sites that they put the Umbreon on it [a Pokemon and alias/symbol of the group member arrested by the Dutch].

DR's Rob Wright: Yes. Mm-hmm.

DR's Alex Culafi: It's a little surprising to me that they're going after the US government in this way because historically (and say what you want about the competency of certain members of this administration), it's generally a bad idea. To target one of the most powerful governments on Earth if you are a financially motivated threat actor, especially if you want to keep making money and you want to stay free? So, OK, maybe you saw an opportunity for this target, but it also seems very ill-advised given how big our military and defense budget is. I don't know. What do you think?

Related:AI Model Evaluator METR Hit by Credential Theft, Probing

DR's Rob Wright: Well, the coverage on this has been pretty interesting. I encourage people to check out 404's coverage. I guess the motive here is that the ShinyHunters members were upset with the way they were being portrayed by the FBI. There was a recent FBI alert that alluded to them engaging in swatting and threats of physical violence, and contacting victims directly and harassing them. And apparently they took umbrage at that, which is neither here nor there. I don't really care why they went after the FBI. I do think it's interesting that they kind of turned around and said, "We're not gonna release the data."

I don't know if you saw the FBI's response to this. They put out a video where Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's cyber division, basically said, "Hey, if you do this again, you're gonna be in real trouble" in so many words — the video is really interesting, and I think on one hand it's good that the authorities are taking a hard line and going after these guys. And I don't know how they got this individual in Jordan so quickly. They must have been investigating this person for a while. It's great that the Jordanian authorities are assisting. But I also kind of wonder: Is this going to be another case where these hackers know that if they, quote unquote, "cooperate," they're probably goget off easy and get a slap on the wrist and maybe even go work for the authorities? So, I'm hoping that is not the case, but I think that these guys, especially hackers associated with the Com, are operating in that way with that sort of confidence that they're gonna get off.

DR's Alex Culafi: And it also raises questions about the provenance of another breach that happened this month.

DR's Rob Wright: Yep. Yes.

DR's Alex Culafi: Rolling right into our next story. Hackers gained access to an unencrypted data center, which is spun up by the Pentagon. It's a file-sharing system that unnamed threat actors had access to through a vulnerability for roughly nine months, from October 2025 until July 2026, when the vulnerability, which we don't know the exact status of, was patched. It exposed records of nearly 2.8 million people living and nearly 300,000 deceased, all tied to the US military in varying degrees.

The exposed information varied, but included Social Security numbers, names, birth dates, contact information, race, sex, and military occupational information. The Pentagon says there's no indication the information has been misused. They're offering free credit monitoring. The officials have not publicly identified the attackers, and the thing that's been coming out is that this data appears to have been unencrypted that they pulled off of the server, which is a really big red flag since this is something tied to the Pentagon and the federal government.

And the reason why I connected this to the FBI case, even though they haven't been publicly connected, is I'm like, what if ShinyHunters attacked this data center too? And then these back-channel conversations that the FBI is having. They're like, “We are gonna be chill about this. You need to do nothing with this data, or we will destroy you.” And that's conspiracy thinking. That's not official information, but it does make me wonder given how close these things happen together.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, no, I had the same thought. I thought maybe this was connected to ShinyHunters or another Com-adjacent group. It definitely seems odd that this happened so close to the FBI breach and that it was also personal data or personnel data. The thing that really bugs me about this is credit monitoring. Are you serious with this? Are you serious with unencrypted data? Are we still doing this?

DR's Alex Culafi: This is very 2006 of them.

DR's Rob Wright: This is so bad. And this is not a third-party system. This is their environment. They should have known about this. They should have been better prepared. And they weren't. And it's a horrendous look for them. So regardless of who did it — the government, the Pentagon, Department of Defense, I'm not gonna call it the other thing — I just think it’s a horrible look. Egg on their face. Big time.

DR's Alex Culafi: Then there's one other question I have. This attack started October 2025. And I'm not saying like the old administration would have done this better or not. I have no idea when the vulnerability started and when a lot of this stuff started. But it does make me wonder about all the budgetary cuts that have happened to US cyber defense since the start of 2025.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah.

DR's Alex Culafi: It does make me wonder how much of this can be tied up or possibly attributed. That's speculation on my part.

DR's Rob Wright: I know. And how can it not? All right. Lastly, we have an interesting story that did not get a lot of play from what I saw out there in the cyber sphere, the news sphere. But apparently the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) was breached recently. They put out an interesting blog post about this that was actually pretty candid. It really went into detail about what happened, but basically, an agentic AI attack used two zero-days in a platform called Zammad, which I guess is an AI-powered support and help desk platform. So this agentic AI attack got in there, got some data, got some employee data from this organization, which DVID is a good organization that's done a lot of interesting research over the years. And used these two zero-days, got in, stole some data. They're still investigating. There are more updates coming, but what do you think, Alex? Sound a little familiar?

DR's Alex Culafi: So, is this a case of rogue AI, or is this a case of threat actors abusing another platform?

DR's Rob Wright: I think it's unclear at this point, but yeah, you're not off-base to ask that question because we keep seeing information about other OpenAI agents or Anthropic agents probing or trying to hack other websites.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yeah. And there's an article that I just wrote about why we should stop calling it "rogue AI," so I need to correct myself. The thing I will say is, if it is a case of, let's say, underscoped, overpermissioned AI causing nonsense, it is the responsibility of the organization that sells that AI to make good on it. And they're the ones who, whichever way, should probably be held accountable. But I don't know if this is one of those cases, so I even feel weird saying that.

DR's Rob Wright: No, you're right. And it could be a threat actor, but again, I don't think you're wrong to suggest that after seeing what we've seen with Hugging Face and with other agentic AI models escaping and doing things that they shouldn't be doing out there, you know, in terms of vulnerability research, finding zero-days, finding information to meet their goals. So, it's certainly a possibility.

DR's Alex Culafi: I guess the thing that is probably true, independent of, let's say, the origin and the intention behind this incident, is that as the agents get more capable, as the vulnerability-hunting gets more widespread, this is gonna be a thing that a lot of small, medium, and large organizations are gonna have to deal with that they wouldn't have had to before, because we have all these very capable non-human identities causing mayhem. And I hope I hope everyone involved takes that seriously.

DR's Rob Wright: No, I know what you mean. Yeah. It's a brave new world, Alex.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yeah, not so new though.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, that's true. Well, thank you for joining me on this episode of "What We Missed." I appreciate the time, Alex.

DR's Alex Culafi: Thanks, Rob.

Senior News Director, Dark Reading

Rob Wright is a longtime reporter with more than 25 years of experience as a technology journalist. Prior to joining Dark Reading as senior news director, he spent more than a decade at TechTarget's SearchSecurity in various roles, including senior news director, executive editor and editorial director. Before that, he worked for several years at CRN, Tom's Hardware Guide, and VARBusiness Magazine covering a variety of technology beats and trends.

Prior to becoming a technology journalist in 2000, he worked as a weekly and daily newspaper reporter in Virginia, where he won three Virginia Press Association awards in 1998 and 1999. At TechTarget and Dark Reading, he has won several Azbee awards, including the 2026 National Silver Award for a series on vibe coding.

At Dark Reading, Rob currently covers security operations, cloud security, and Internet infrastructure. He has a keen interest in malvertising activity and the certificate authority industry, and has written extensively on both topics. He graduated from the University of Richmond in 1997 with a degree in journalism and English. A native of Massachusetts, he lives in the Boston area.
