Speaking about actors who choose to not reveal their sexuality, Evans said you "never know what a person has gone through".

Asked if he thought a gay actor would ever be cast as James Bond, Evans said he was "on the list for Bond for a good decade."

Evans began his career as a theatre actor and later appeared in films including Clash Of The Titans (2010) and the Fast & Furious franchise.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.author: Huo Jingnan
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.text:
Three employees recently fired by OpenAI allege the company punished them for being outspoken about safety. OpenAI disputes the claims and says they were dismissed for mishandling sensitive information.

Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.

OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.

In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."

The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.

"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.

In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."

OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.

OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.

In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.

"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.title: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.text:
The price of a gallon of diesel fuel is shown electronically on a pump at a QuikTrip station Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Greenwood Village, Colo.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.

Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."

"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."

The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.

The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.

The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.

Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said that Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. already in October, and that Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel, as well.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.title: The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.author: Rachel Treisman
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.text:
A huge crowd gathers to witness the public hanging of Rainey Bethea in 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky. Public outrage over the spectacle made Bethea's death the last high-profile public execution in the United States. The Pentagon wants to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter.

The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing squad — a first for the military since World War II.

The Pentagon says Hasan's execution will take place on the afternoon of Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of his shooting rampage. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the proceedings would be available for public viewing.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in a video interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.

The Pentagon confirmed to NPR in a statement Friday that the execution "will be livestreamed," saying details would follow.

But much remains uncertain. Legal experts have said Hasan could delay his execution by years if he decides to file a habeas corpus appeal in federal court. Michael Radelet, a professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies capital punishment, says outside groups could potentially challenge the livestream plans too.

"Hegseth is a rather controversial person," Radelet told NPR. "If he says, 'Do it this way,' it's not at all clear that it will actually be done that way."

If it does come to pass, it would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century — and the first ever to be livestreamed.

"Public executions have typically been held in authoritarian countries to instill fear in the population and to show the power and control of the government," Robin Maher, the executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told NPR. "We're not aware of any regulation or historical precedent for a [U.S.] military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public."

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman — in 1936. The case drew national attention.

Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers had built a gallows near the riverfront, according to NPR station WKMS. People celebrated with "necktie" parties the night before and sipped soft drinks at the scene in what attendees and historians describe as a festive atmosphere.

"They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Colas, and you'd have thought it was a big picnic or something," attendee Bill Shelton recalled in a 2013 oral history interview with the Daviess County Public Library.

The spectacle prompted a public backlash over the perceived barbarity of executions. Kentucky held a "semipublic" hanging in a prison yard the following year, Radelet said, before outlawing public executions altogether in 1938. There haven't been any in the U.S. since.

He said the closest example was the lethal injection of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001. The Justice Department made a closed-circuit telecast available for designated survivors and victims' loved ones to watch remotely; 232 of them gathered in a viewing room in Oklahoma City to do so.

"It's like getting rid of the guillotine — when it's gone, it's gone," Radelet said. "There was no serious discussion about bringing it back."

He said public executions fell out of favor for two main reasons: They are no longer widely believed to be a crime deterrent, and authorities became worried that public executions — especially those that went wrong — would turn people against the death penalty.

In fact, as part of that shift, executions have become less visible over time, Maher said. Initially, she said, states would conduct them in the middle of the night. Now, she said, some states that still carry out the death penalty have limited access for media witnesses.

"We moved away from public executions quite deliberately because they had turned into spectacles. That was not sitting comfortably with people anymore," said Maher. "And I think there was a move away from that sort of circus environment to inside prisons in the middle of the night."

Tennessee's recent botched lethal injection of Christa Pike has reignited debate over the death penalty. Radelet thinks a firing squad execution — especially if it's livestreamed — could further diminish public support for capital punishment, already at a five-decade low.

"There probably wouldn't be too much blood, but enough to make people talk about it over their morning coffee, if they're not sick," Radelet said. "And that discussion might be yet another step towards abolishing the death penalty."

Justin Mazzola, deputy research director at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement that Hegseth's announcement "adds to the display of cruelty" seen recently with Pike's botched execution.

"The U.S. death penalty is irredeemably broken," he said. "It is high time that the U.S. authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all."

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at a Maryland shipyard this week. His plan for livestreaming the execution of the Fort Hood shooter has been met with criticism and calls for reconsideration.

Hegseth's comments were met immediately with questions, concerns and calls for reconsideration. On Friday, Vice President Vance told reporters, "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, released a statement saying a public execution "will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

"In no way can Hassan's [sic] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he wrote.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X that he supports Hasan's death sentence but called a livestream "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," he wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, similarly mused on CNN about whether Hegseth is "mimicking ISIS executions." He called public executions "medieval" regardless of people's feelings about the death penalty itself.

The top Democrats on both the House and Senate Armed Services committees issued statements condemning the Pentagon's plan. Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called it "another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure's repeated failings" and "a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters."

"The Trump Administration should reconsider this abhorrent move, which only gives the shooter what he wants: more attention and more control," Reed wrote.

Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., also called on the Pentagon to revoke its decision, saying, "A country cannot condone livestreaming a man's death for entertainment."

"We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square," she wrote on X. "Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing?"

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1474.title: U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1474.author: Nate Perez
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/g-s1-1474.text:
A detainee boards a deportation flight on GlobalX Air in Minnesota in December 2025.

The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation.

A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties, and respond how it plans to do so.

The administration said it is working "collaboratively" with Soliman's lawyers to find and contact him, and is "beginning the process to facilitate" his return, according to Friday's filings in the case from Timothy Courchaine, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona.

Soliman, who is a gay, had been able to get an order from a U.S. immigration judge to prevent him from being deported to his home country, Egypt, where he could be persecuted for his sexuality.

Instead, the Trump administration deported him earlier this year to Equatorial Guinea, which ranks as one of the least free countries in the world, according to Freedom House, a nonprofit devoted to protecting and growing democracy, and human rights across the globe.

Arizona District Court Judge John Hinderaker, an appointee of President Trump, said that DHS violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment when it removed Soliman to a third country.

"It is unrebutted that he has since been held under armed guard; threatened at gunpoint; and arrested, beaten, and held incommunicado by Equatorial Guinean authorities," Hinderaker wrote in his Oct. 6 order.

The ruling comes even as the U.S. Supreme Court last week allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries where they have no ties, at least for now, while agreeing to take the case up for full oral argument in December.

DHS told NPR in a statement this week that it would comply with lawful court orders and that Soliman would continue to receive due process.

"But the end result will be the same — he will not remain in the U.S. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson added.

Dana Camilleri, one of Soliman's lawyers, said compliance means diplomats in Equatorial Guinea must work to facilitate Soliman's release. She is working to get a similar outcome for another client in the central African country, a gay Brazilian man.

" We're all just really hopeful that this could be the beginning of getting them home," Camilleri said. "Because they're in an awful situation, and our government put them there."

The office of the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea did not respond to a request for comment.

Soliman has been held under armed guard at a decommissioned hotel where he has been threatened at gunpoint, arrested, beaten and been unable to communicate with his family or lawyers, according to court filings.

Soliman emigrated to the U.S. from Egypt when he was a child, grew up in Arizona and became a green card holder. He lost his immigration status after a 2023 drug possession and aggravated assault led to a prison sentence.

That's when an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent to Egypt, where he would most likely be tortured.

The harm Soliman is alleged to have suffered in Equatorial Guinea could put the U.S. in violation of international law, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a  senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The council advocates for a fair process for immigrants in the U.S.

" We are signatories of the UN convention against torture, and domestic law makes it illegal to send someone to a place where they will be persecuted," Reichlin-Melnick said. " All of this really violates a lot of the basic principles of due process and human rights that Americans support," and serves as "a direct rebuke to the Trump administration's broader strategy of third country removals."

The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places where they have no ties or connections as part of the president's immigration crackdown.

Hinderaker's order to return Soliman marks the second time a judge has forced the government to return a third-country migrant from an African nation. A Colorado judge also ordered the return of Brayan Omar Sanchez Servellon, originally from Honduras, who was sent to the Central African Republic earlier this year.

He was ordered to return to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties. The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places they have no ties.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.title: A congressman wants his House colleagues to pledge to accept election results
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.author: Marc Rivers
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.text:
Patrick Jarenwattananon

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill on June 24, 2025.

Two U.S. House members are calling on their colleagues to pledge that they'll accept this fall's election results and oppose any effort to block the seating of fellow members next year.

The pledge concerns an unlikely scenario that's been circulating among Democrats and democracy advocates: that Republicans, spurred on by President Trump, would point to allegations of election fraud and seek to block certain House members from being added to the chamber's roll on Jan. 3, 2027, effectively preventing an incoming Democratic majority from taking power.

Trump sought to overturn his 2020 election loss, leading to the riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., one of the lawmakers behind the pledge, cited Jan. 6 in making his case for the effort.

"Because we've lived through that, because of some of the things the president has done and has said that he's willing to do to stop the will of the people if he doesn't win or if the Republicans don't get what they want, then I think it's really important that we, again, shut down any opportunity for those who want to stop the will of the people," Gottheimer told NPR All Things Considered host Ailsa Chang in an interview.

Trump has long claimed baselessly that Democrats cheat to win elections, and in May said he would do "anything necessary" to make sure the U.S. has "honest" elections.

Gottheimer is joined in the effort by Rep. Don Bacon, a retiring Republican from Nebraska.

"[I]t's important to put down a clear, bipartisan marker that we follow state certifications, seat certified winners and preserve trust in the institution," Bacon told the Wall Street Journal, which first reported on the pledge.

At least two other moderate Republicans — Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Mike Lawler of New York — are signing onto the pledge, their offices confirmed to NPR on Friday.

Here's how Gottheimer described the Jan. 3 concern, in the NPR interview: "There's been some chatter out there … that what will happen is, instead of allowing a name to be added to the rolls and to vote as the members of Congress, that you will have a member actually object, which they can do. And then there can be a vote in the House to say that we're not going to recognize what the state sent us — the state-certified election — and we're going to kick it back for investigation, either in the House or back to the state."

Rick Hasen, a UCLA professor whose election law blog has hosted a lot of the debate about the procedural concern, was asked about the idea on WNYC's On The Media.

"If Democrats have won control of the House of Representatives, and somehow on Jan. 3, somebody tries this kind of maneuver, it's going to provoke such a massive public reaction," he said. "This just seems very far-fetched."

Gottheimer responded to that quotation by saying that the Jan. 6 riot seemed similarly far-fetched ahead of time. He also tied the pledge to voters' faith in the election results, saying the effort is lawmakers' "attempt to make sure people can feel strong confidence in our elections and that the will of the people will find their way on Jan. 3."

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software sent humans to the moon, dies at 90
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.author: Rachel Treisman
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-599.text:
Margaret Hamilton sits in mock-up of Apollo the command module on display at MIT in 1969.

Margaret Hamilton, the computing pioneer whose software put the first NASA astronauts on the moon, has died at age 90.

Hamilton's death — of unspecified causes, on Sept. 30 — was announced Wednesday by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she worked from 1959 until the mid-1970s.

"To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement," said Olivier de Weck, interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. "She not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved."

Hamilton, who grew up in Indiana, earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy from Earlham College in 1958. She moved to Boston the following year — so her husband could pursue his law degree — and took a job in the meteorology department at MIT, working with the professor who discovered chaos theory.

It was her first foray into software engineering. Hamilton then got a programming job in another lab, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system.

"She had so much foresight in thinking through the ways that humans would use computers, and to create reliable systems that could be used even in the highest-risk, life and death kind of environments," said Teasel Muir-Harmony, curator of the Apollo Collection at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.

In 1961, MIT's Instrumentation Lab won the NASA contract to develop software for the Apollo project. Hamilton saw a newspaper advertisement seeking people to develop the software to "send man to the moon," and applied. She was the first female programmer hired for the Apollo missions, starting with uncrewed flights and moving to onboard software.

By 1968, she had worked her way up to assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, leading a crew of over 100 engineers. Hamilton was in her early 30s, as were many of her colleagues in the nascent field of software engineering — a term she herself is credited with coining.

Margaret Hamilton founded two software companies after leaving MIT. She's seen here in her Cambridge, Mass., home and office, in 1986.

"In this period where she was working, this is a brand new field, and she really helped to define it," Muir-Harmony said. "Margaret Hamilton, like many of the people who worked on the Apollo program, helped really develop computing as we know it today."

Hamilton made an impression with her problem-solving and leadership skills. She often brought her daughter, Lauren, then 4, to the lab — resulting in an infamous "Lauren error."

"Her daughter overloaded a system during some kind of a test. And she thought, 'Oh my gosh, this is something that could actually happen in outer space. So I better account for this,'" said Dean Robbins, an author who published a book about Hamilton in 2017. "So her daughter actually played a part in her technical achievements."

Hamilton was known for her focus on "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate and solve errors on its own.

"Her goal wasn't simply to build a system that worked when everything went right," Muir-Harmony said. "It was to build a system that could continue working when things went wrong."

Perhaps the most famous example of that is the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. Just three minutes before the first humans were supposed to touch down on the moon, alarms went off on board, signifying computer overload. Fortunately, Hamilton's team had built a system that could shut down unnecessary background tasks at that moment.

"Mission Control was able to recognize what was happening, able to trust the computer … to prioritize tasks, to know that the astronauts could continue … with the first lunar landing," Muir-Harmony said.

After leaving MIT, Hamilton founded two software engineering companies. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Barack Obama in 2016, and the following year was immortalized in miniature as part of a "women of NASA" Lego set.

Hamilton is also the subject of a black-and-white photo from 1969 that often makes the rounds on social media, showing a young woman with long hair and glasses, smiling as she stands beside a towering stack of notebooks — filled with the code that sent humans to the moon.

President Barack Obama presents the Presidential Medal of Freedom to mathematician and computer scientist Margaret Hamilton in November 2016.

But despite public recognition in her later years, Robbins said Hamilton was "not one to toot her own horn." In fact, she initially shied away from the idea of a biography and only agreed because she thought it would be fun to read with her great-grandchildren. (She is survived by four great-grandchildren, two grandsons, her daughter and son-in-law and three siblings.)

"She really warmed up to explaining what she had done, developing the software," he recalled. "She got very excited about telling me all about the technical aspects of developing this. And she was sending me photos and actual code that she had written, and pictures of the primitive machinery that they'd had to use back in the 1960s."

The entire process was painstaking. Muir-Harmony explained that programs were stored on the Apollo guidance computer by hand-weaving copper wire through magnetized cores ("which basically looked like little donuts"). As the overseer of that process, Hamilton earned the nickname "rope mother" in the lab.

Robbins struggled to simplify all of that for his grade-school audience, until he realized: Hamilton's story was all about problem-solving. And she broke barriers for women in the process.

"There was no playbook for how to use computers to get astronauts to the moon," he said. "She had to come up with it on the fly and under tremendous pressure. And I think she was proud of that in her own modest way."

Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 that from her perspective, the software experience was "at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission."

"Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world," she said. "There was no choice but to be pioneers."

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Hazardous waves are possible as far south as Ecuador and as far north as Mexico, as 13 aftershocks reported

A powerful 7.6 magnitude earthquake has struck Panama and triggered tsunami warnings along the west coast of Central and South America, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).

The quake hit along the southern coast of the country, the USGS said. It was centered near the southern tip of the Central American country, about 14km (9 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, the USGS said.

The Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama said the quake struck at just before 1pm local time near the southern town of Tonosí. The Panamanian institute said that a second 6.0 magnitude earthquake struck soon after, at 1.22pm.

By 1.3opm there had reportedly been 13 aftershocks.

The president, José Raúl Mulino, said he had asked a key minister to call for calm. “What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” Mulino wrote on X.

Local newspaper La Prensa said that across the Central American country, buildings, schools and homes were evacuated as a result of the “powerful movement of the earth”.

Footage published by La Prensa showed severe damage to several buildings in the city of Penonomé, including the St John Baptist Cathedral. Other photos showed a highway to the west of the capital that had been completely sheared in half by the earthquake.

Tremors were felt strongly ​in the ⁠capital of ⁠Panama ​City, ‌according ‌to ‌witnesses who spoke to Reuters. The Associated Press reported that buildings shook and visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.

The USGS said hazardous waves were possible along the coasts of Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico, although the tsunami warning for Chile was cancelled at 4.18pm local time.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, and friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were killed on a surfing trip in 2024

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Mexican judge has convicted three men of the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend in a case that sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.

The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.

Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, traveled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.

“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”

Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ murders as “hell”.

“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.

Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.

“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”

The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv

The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.

Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.

Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.

The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.

“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree.

New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.

Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.

“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.

Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.

The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Prospect of contentious Orange Order march down Garvaghy Road has led to a two-week standoff in Portadown

The Northern Ireland secretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists.

Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

He said he took the decision after advice from Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of the Northern Ireland Police Service, that the parade “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect” across Northern Ireland.

The Parades Commission ruled two weeks ago that a small, circumscribed march could pass along Garvaghy Road – a reversal of 28 years of successive bans. But police prevented the Orangemen from marching after thousands of residents and supporters, including Sinn Féin leaders, blocked the road.

Garvaghy Road residents welcomed the secretary of state’s decision, saying it brought relief and certainty after a tense standoff that revived memories of the 1990s, when Orangemen fought pitched battles with police in an attempt to march the route.

It was the only “sensible, reasonable and logical outcome”, said Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.

The Sinn Féin leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the party’s Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said in a statement that residents had endured fear and anxiety. “There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening.”

The Irish government welcomed the decision and appealed to both sides to seek common ground. “This isn’t a time for triumphalism or claiming victories or anything like that,” said the taoiseach, Micheál Martin. “Those on the unionist, loyalist side will look at this through a different prism. We need to be conscious of that. We need to acknowledge that.”

Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, accused Boutcher and Bryant of bowing to republican agitation and threats of potential violence. “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest. The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters, and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”

Robinson asked the secretary to state to explain what the government will do to “restore confidence in the rule of law”.

after newsletter promotion

The chief constable paved the government’s decision earlier on Friday when he asked Bryant to review the Parade Commission’s determination, made last month, that conditions in Portadown enabled the parade to go ahead.

“I’ve looked at the changing situation in Portadown, the fact that it’s very difficult for that procession to proceed, and I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” said Bryant.

He thanked Portadown’s Orange Lodge for its “peaceful and law-abiding approach” and regretted that both sides could not reach a compromise, leading to a standoff. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”

Boutcher said the dispute had affected relationships within and between communities and the police. “It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long-term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”

The dispute has fuelled angry exchanges at the Stormont assembly and destabilised the executive, with unionists demanding O’Neill step down as first minister for allegedly breaking the law at a Garvaghy Road protest.

Earlier on Friday, the PSNI sent the Sinn Féin deputy leader a letter probing alleged criminal offences relating to her involvement in the protest. O’Neill said she will cooperate with the investigation.

Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer.

Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll.

Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one.

The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed.

In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place.

The investigation into Farage’s gift began after the Guardian revealed in May that the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.

The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members.

They would then have further discussions and call a further hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty. That process can take weeks. The MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more.

If parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, a recall petition could be held, requiring signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over a period of six weeks.

In the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats, and Conservatives are hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister.

But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the byelection against independent candidates including Count Binface by more than 11,000 votes.

He has also recently embarked on a tour of the country, in an attempt to shore up his core support, and a reorganisation of his party HQ. This includes launching a new Reform TV channel to pump out the party’s message direct to voters, hiring a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations.

Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, when he beat the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling. The Conservative had previously won the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate in the seat.

Men found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigation

Two Latvian men have been released on bail after being arrested at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by the US military and Nato.

The two men, aged 32 and 26, were arrested at 2am on Thursday after they were discovered inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations.

An investigation had begun four hours earlier, when military police found an abandoned vehicle near the facility at around 10pm on Wednesday.

Military police, joined by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence, before finding and arresting the two men inside the base.

The suspects, both Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

They have since been released on bail, with strict conditions, as the police continue their investigation.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said they were “very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites”, but that there was nothing from their investigation so far to suggest a connection to an incident near RAF Fairford in September.

“Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence police and Cambridgeshire constabulary on this. A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity,” she added.

Officers have since carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. The abandoned vehicle was also taken to a nearby police location.

Located west of Huntingdon, RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says he picked ‘devoted fan’ Katie Zacharia to be next press secretary
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Shrai Popat in Washington and Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after giving birth to her second child

Donald Trump on Friday announced that he had picked Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary, lining up a conservative commentator he called a “devoted fan” to be his most prominent spokesperson.

Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after the birth to her second child.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia,” the president wrote in a social media post on Truth Social.

“She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump added.

The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia has been selected for the role.

The Guardian has reached out to Zacharia for comment.
 Zacharia’s selection puts her at the heart of the White House’s efforts to shape the public narrative around Trump’s second term, as his approval rating falls to record lows, and his party fights to maintain control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections. Trump has asked supporters to vote like his name is on the ballot, turning the election into a referendum on his presidency amid widespread economic discontent and an unpopular war with Iran.

Zacharia previously worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and now serves as a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns Truth Social, the president’s social network, on which he made the announcement about her selection official.

The appointment came as a something of a surprise in Washington, after weeks of building speculation about who the president might choose to replace Leavitt. Several reports suggested Scott Jennings, the conservative TV pundit was an “an early favorite” for the role, though skeptics noted that his past criticism of the president would likely be an issue.

Zacharia, a California native, has been involved in Republican politics for years.

She attended Pepperdine University and served as president of her school’s College Republican organization. She interned in the White House’s office of political affairs during the second Bush administration as well as at the Republican National Committee.

She obtained her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011.

Prior to joining DHS, Zacharia worked as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative nonprofit focused on “election integrity”. The organization is headed up by Trump ally and diplomat Ric Grenell.

Zacharia was a frequent join Fox News commentator, often promoting or defending the US president’s policies while harshly criticizing Democrats.

She is married to film producer Tyler Zacharia. They have four children.

In his Truth Social post, Trump praised Leavitt, who he said had done a “fantastic job” in the role. On Monday, Fox News announced that Leavitt would join the network as an on-air contributor.

“I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration,” Trump wrote, adding: “Good luck Katie!”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New York City’s Marble Hill residents furious after ICE shooting: ‘Why do this?’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Auzzy Byrdsell in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Locals also express fear after man shot in the neck while his child was in the back of his car

Residents of Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood were furious at federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Friday but also scared after an officer shot their neighbor who had his child in the back of his car.

Orlando Perez had parked his car on the corner of 225th St and Marble Hill Avenue on Thursday night and witnessed ICE arresting Oscar Belgal, 28, after he had been shot in the neck, apparently with an assault-style rifle.

Enter your email to keep reading - for free. It takes just 30 seconds

We’re committed to keeping our quality reporting open. By registering and providing us with insight into your preferences, you’re helping us to engage with you more deeply, and that allows us to keep our journalism free for all.

Not signed in before? Create an account

“I thought I was going to get shot,” he said on Friday. The streets, now calm after protests had broken out the night before, were noticeably quieter than normal despite golden early October sunshine under blue skies.

Perez said he did not see that the agents targeting Belgal were not wearing uniforms and he did not see them wearing identification badges or any gear showing that they belonged to ICE.

However, footage of the aftermath of the shooting shows a man in a high visibility construction-type vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, and carrying an assault-style rifle. Bystanders can be heard on video asking each other: “Is it ICE or not?”
 The car that Belgal had driven appeared to have bullet holes in it, according to Perez. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said in a press conference in Washington DC on Friday morning that federal officers did not know there was a child in the target’s car.

But Perez added that the car had only light tints on the windows and that ICE “had to see that the kid was inside”.

Leading New York City and state politicians and officials have condemned ICE’s action, called for an investigation and demanded violent federal immigration enforcement cease.

Zachary Miller said he heard six gun shots from his apartment on Thursday afternoon, when the shooting occurred around 4pm, just when children were streaming home from school. Federal and city law enforcement have listed prior convictions for Belgal and said he was on probation for felony offenses, with the Trump administration accusing him of having gang affiliations.

Miller said he knew Belgal from being around the neighborhood and said: “He’s a nice kid.

“I don’t see him doing something like this,” he said, referring to the accusations of gang ties and drugs and weapons crimes.

Miller has lived in the Marble Hill neighborhood – which is geographically in the Bronx, but considered part of Manhattan – where the shooting occurred for 20 years and said he had never seen such a violent encounter with law enforcement. 
 “I’m a little upset,” he said. “Why do this to this neighborhood?”

Carlos Martinez, 18, said that he had heard five or six gunshots while he was eating in P & P Gourmet Deli, which sits on the corner directly across from where the shooting and arrest took place.

“I thought the shots came from inside the store, so I was nervous,” he said.
 Coming from a Dominican family, like Belgal, and growing up in the Bronx, he said he longer feels safe at home, despite he and all his family members being US citizens.

“Over here we are all community, but personally I am uncomfortable,” he said. “They want to target the most innocent people.”

The small three-way intersection where Belgal was shot is home to about five apartment complexes and some businesses. New York police on Friday afternoon took away street barricades but yellow crime scene tape was still visible around the scene.

Another longtime resident, Carlos Rodriguez, said he felt “soiled” by ICE’s presence in his neighborhood.

“I need to take a shower and clean off the filth that comes into my ambit of being,” he said.

He said he wished that New York’s progressive Democratic mayor, Zohran Mamdani, would be more outspoken about ICE tensions in New York.

“From my point of view, he can come out stronger and more often about this,” he said, adding that he wanted lawmakers to be more proactive against enforcement agents, especially where they are going to residents’ homes and demanding access to make checks or an arrest.

Mamdani strongly condemned ICE at a hastily arranged press conference on Thursday night, as protesters can be heard chanting in the background, and called for the agency to be abolished.

Meanwhile, several local residents said they had seen ICE officers and vehicles “camped out” in a parking lot nearby that serves a store belonging to the giant retail chain Target.

Rodriguez said he suspected the agents were looking for Belgal.

Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez late on Thursday criticized Target for accommodating ICE.

At a hearing in federal court on Friday afternoon, Belgal’s attorneys said he still had a bullet in his body.

A US justice department prosecutor said Belgal had been booked into the federal Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn, which is newly being used to detain immigrants. He had been temporarily brought to a privately run ICE facility in New Jersey after the shooting, and a federal judge at the hearing on Friday ordered the agency to keep Belgal in the area after his attorneys filed emergency motions requesting his release.

José Olivares contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Residents of Manhattan's Marble Hill neighborhood were furious at ICE on Friday. Orlando Perez had parked his car on the corner of 225th St and Marble Hill Avenue on Thursday night. A federal judge at the hearing on Friday ordered the agency to keep Belgal in the area.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Motorist, reportedly trying to beat a traffic light, barrels through busy intersection and slams into pedestrians

At least one person was killed and nine injured in New York City’s eastern Bronx when a motorist barreled through a busy intersection, slammed into pedestrians and triggered a chain-reaction crash involving several vehicles, according to authorities and media reports.

The horrifying collision happened shortly after 2pm in the Bronx’s Allerton neighborhood, with the driver at the center of the crash reportedly saying he was trying to beat a traffic light.

Sources told the New York Post that four women, ranging in age from 50 to 60, were walking through a crosswalk when the Mercedes struck them.

The victims were transported to Jacobi medical center, where one woman was pronounced dead. Two others were reported to be in critical condition, while the fourth was expected to survive, according to the Post’s sources.

The New York fire department (FDNY) said that emergency medical crews treated nine people in the aftermath of the crash, according to the local outlet News 12.

Surveillance footage obtained by News 12 captured a white Mercedes-Benz hurtling through the intersection, striking a group of pedestrians in the crosswalk before crashing into multiple vehicles waiting at a traffic light.

According to the NYPD’s preliminary findings, the Mercedes rear-ended two vehicles with such force that both cars were pushed into two additional vehicles.

The driver, who suffered minor injuries and remained conscious and alert, reportedly told a witness that he had been attempting to beat the traffic light, the Post said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Prosecutors oppose Luigi Mangione’s push for dismissal of state charges
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Manhattan prosecutors say murder case over 2024 killing can proceed under ‘exception’ to state double jeopardy law

Manhattan prosecutors filed paperwork on Friday opposing Luigi Mangione’s arguments for dismissing his state-level case in the killing of the UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson.

Mangione on 14 August pleaded guilty to federal charges in Thompson’s 4 December 2024 killing outside a Midtown hotel – weeks before his scheduled 8 September New York state murder and weapons trial. The killing prompted an intense manhunt but also sparked an outpouring of rage against the practices of the for-profit US healthcare industry.

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Shortly after he entered his guilty plea to two federal stalking charges, Mangione’s legal team filed a motion to dismiss the state-level murder case against him.

Judge Gregory Carro, who is overseeing Mangione’s state case, subsequently postponed these proceedings, scheduling the next court date for 10 December, according to a 17 August letter. Carro told prosecutors to respond to Mangione’s push for dismissal by 9 October and gave his defense a 30 October deadline to reply.

Mangione’s defense has argued that New York state’s double jeopardy law prohibits him from being prosecuted by the Manhattan district attorney’s office.

New York state law holds that “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”.

Manhattan prosecutors argued in their papers that Mangione’s murder case can proceed “under an exception” to the state double jeopardy law. They insist that elements of the federal stalking and state murder charges do not overlap in a way that would trigger double jeopardy protections.

Mangione has claimed that Manhattan prosecutors cannot pursue weapons charges against him because he had previously faced federal weapons counts. But the federal court dismissed these counts, Manhattan state prosecutors noted.

“Statutory double jeopardy applies only when a defendant has been ‘separately prosecuted’ for the same misconduct, and dismissed federal charges do not constitute a separate prosecution,” they argued.

As for the murder charge, Manhattan prosecutors insist that the federal stalking charges Mangione pleaded guilty to are dramatically different from his state murder case.
