As a campaign of Russian sabotage sweeps across Europe, Estonia is seeing a shift in what targets Moscow chooses to go after, the Baltic nation’s counterintelligence chief told Foreign Policy in an interview on Wednesday.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

“Initially, these attacks were more against symbolic objects,” said Margo Palloson, who has served as the director-general of the Estonian Internal Security Service since 2023. Those attacks included vandalizing Estonian opinion-makers’ cars, burning Ukrainian flags, and carrying out an arson attack on a Ukrainian restaurant.

As a campaign of Russian sabotage sweeps across Europe, Estonia is seeing a shift in what targets Moscow chooses to go after, the Baltic nation’s counterintelligence chief told Foreign Policy in an interview on Wednesday.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

“Initially, these attacks were more against symbolic objects,” said Margo Palloson, who has served as the director-general of the Estonian Internal Security Service since 2023. Those attacks included vandalizing Estonian opinion-makers’ cars, burning Ukrainian flags, and carrying out an arson attack on a Ukrainian restaurant.

An August attack by Russian-directed saboteurs on Estonian robotics firm Milrem, which supplies Ukraine’s military forces, marked a new phase, he said. “Now the game has changed a little bit—we assess the purpose clearly was to disrupt, restrict, or cancel all the supplies” to Ukraine. Reuters reported this week that Russia has targeted defense firms in Denmark, another strong supporter of Ukraine. And then there was the attempted explosive attack in early August on a plane in Germany by Russian intelligence operatives.

The attacks have emerged as a new Kremlin strategy as Ukraine stymies or even pushes back Russia on the battlefield. Danish officials separately said Russia was likely to increase the number of sabotage and other attacks on Europe in the coming months.

These operations increasingly use explosives, Palloson noted, raising the level of danger to civilians. European Union ambassadors recently met to discuss the possibility of a mass-casualty event caused by sabotage or other forms of state-sponsored violence, Politico reported Wednesday.

To combat the threat, Estonia’s government is liaising with the country’s defense sector, including giving companies advice on physical security, Palloson said.

Estonia is also stopping espionage at the border. Since 2025, Estonia has arrested 20 people who traveled to Russia and were then recruited by Russian intelligence, Palloson said. These would-be spies were not in military or intelligence but rather were civilians whom Russia could have later instructed to take jobs useful for intelligence purposes within Estonia, he added.

Russia’s increasing use of criminal groups and amateurs, including Ukrainians recruited through social media, complicates the process for tracking potential saboteurs and spies. Using these networks can obscure Russia’s connection, with as many as seven layers of intermediaries between the saboteur and Russia, Palloson said.

Ukrainians refugees used by Russia, meanwhile, may not even know they’re working for the Kremlin and in some cases may believe they’re working for Ukraine’s own internal security service, he added. Ukraine is much more rarely accused of sabotage in Europe, but Ukrainian military personnel were reportedly behind a 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipelines, which carried Russian gas to Germany.

The use of criminal groups is also adding a commercial dimension to the attacks, with some criminal groups proposing new operations to Russia as a method of generating revenue, Palloson said. “Some groups who commit these attacks realize that this is also an option to earn good money,” he said.

For now, Palloson said he felt comfortable with Estonia’s response to the new wave of saboteur tactics as well as the legal framework at his disposal. However, frustration is growing in some European countries, which he did not name, about the powers available to counterintelligence staff.

The small Baltic country has refashioned the relationship between citizens and the state for
the current moment.

“I have heard from some European colleagues that they feel they don’t have the right legal tools to handle this,” he said. The United Kingdom first arrested and then later released seven individuals suspected of being linked to an Iranian plot targeting a U.S. airbase in England in September.

Despite the attacks, Palloson said he saw no signs that Russian sabotage was weakening support for Ukraine. “[Support] is still very high and higher every day. In Estonian society, there is no fear or panic,” he said.

The nightmare scenario for Estonia, of course, would be a Russian invasion. In the lead-up to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian security services worked hard to lay the groundwork for an easy takeover, sending in assassination squads ahead of time and bribing Ukrainian officials so that they would offer little resistance.

Estonia’s military and intelligence services see little sign of Russia preparing a similar attack on Estonia. Nevertheless, the country is learning from Ukraine’s experience, Palloson said.

“All [intelligence] services in Europe are trying to study how to protect their societies against intelligence activity, influence activity, and sabotage.”

Sam Skove is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @samuelskove

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/09/arc.title: The United States Is Not Ready for the Arctic Age
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/09/arc.author: Bobby Ghosh
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/09/arc.text:
“WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” Donald Trump wrote on TruthSocial in late August, after he announced a fresh round of tariffs on exports from the United States’ northern neighbor. Seen from the lower latitudes, this was just another of the president’s tirades, straining both the caps-lock key and credulity, but in fact, the United States depends a great deal on Canada, to the tune of 4 million barrels of crude oil a day, plus electricity, aluminum, auto parts, and much else besides.

Viewed from the vicinity of the North Pole, the gap between Trump’s rants and reality is wider still: In the northern reaches of the continent they share, the United States needs Canada—desperately. As the melting ice caps uncover a new zone of economic competition in the Arctic, U.S. hopes of success depend on close cooperation with the country that the president is busy antagonizing.

“WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” Donald Trump wrote on TruthSocial in late August, after he announced a fresh round of tariffs on exports from the United States’ northern neighbor. Seen from the lower latitudes, this was just another of the president’s tirades, straining both the caps-lock key and credulity, but in fact, the United States depends a great deal on Canada, to the tune of 4 million barrels of crude oil a day, plus electricity, aluminum, auto parts, and much else besides.

Viewed from the vicinity of the North Pole, the gap between Trump’s rants and reality is wider still: In the northern reaches of the continent they share, the United States needs Canada—desperately. As the melting ice caps uncover a new zone of economic competition in the Arctic, U.S. hopes of success depend on close cooperation with the country that the president is busy antagonizing.

Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, Rana Foroohar, Crown, 272 pp., $33, October 2026

Rana Foroohar’s new book, Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, explains why this is an extraordinary act of self-harm. The Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the planet, and the receding ice is opening access to shipping lanes, fish stocks, energy, minerals, and a sea floor that can house communications cables. The economic opportunity unlocked will run into at least hundreds of billions of dollars; the late Scott Minerd, chief investment officer of Guggenheim Partners, saw potential for $1 trillion in investments in infrastructure alone.

Trump is aware of the economic opportunity, but his response, ranging from musings about annexing Greenland to ordering the construction of 11 icebreakers in no-bid contracts after a golf game, has been as wrong-minded as it is heavy-handed. Those icebreakers, for example, are to be made by a Finnish shipbuilder owned by a British company with—drum roll, please—Canadian roots.

Who needs whom, again?

A truck crosses into the United States from Canada on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, on Sept. 6. Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images

Foroohar, a former correspondent for Time and Newsweek and currently a columnist for the Financial Times, has written an important book about an important place just as the president is giving it the wrong kind of attention. Sea Change provides a much-needed update to post-Cold War scholarship on the Arctic, which has long rested on the twin pillars of Oran Young’s 1993 Arctic Politics and Michael Byers’s 2013 International Law and the Arctic.

Those books were written during a period of so-called “Arctic exceptionalism,” when disputes were mediated and adversaries generally cooperated in science and shipping. Foroohar’s subtitle announces its end: An expansionist Russia, an ambitious China, and a flailing United States have brought great-power competition to the top of the world.

Now back to icebreakers. Foroohar’s story begins in the fall of 2024 when she boards the USCGC Healy at Nome, Alaska, for a voyage into the Arctic Circle. The scientists on the ship test the waters for temperature, salinity, oxygen, and plankton. The crew charts possible shipping passages and monitors foreign ships. The Healy protects commerce and stands ready to rescue sailors in waters cold enough to kill a human being in a matter of minutes. Its missions overlap: Better maps make shipping safer, scientific data informs economic ventures and military operations. In the Arctic, power stems from knowing the water and being able to move through it.

As Foroohar notes, icebreakers are the cornerstone of economic, scientific, research, and military activity in the Arctic, and any country staking a claim to the gold in them thar waters must have a fleet of such ships. Russia has more than 40 icebreakers, many of them nuclear powered, operating in the northern seas; China, which calls itself a “near Arctic state” despite having no territory that far north, has at least five. The Canadian Coast Guard has nine icebreakers. The U.S. Coast Guard has three: The Polar Star, now 50 years old, spends much of each year breaking a channel to McMurdo Station in the Antarctic. Storis is a secondhand oil-industry vessel bought off the commercial market and modified for the job. Which leaves the Healy as the only purpose-built, Arctic-ready U.S. icebreaker in regular service.

The Russian 50 Years of Victory nuclear-powered icebreaker is seen at the North Pole on Aug. 18, 2021. Ekaterina Anisimova/AFP via Getty Images

And sometimes, not even that. The Healy suffered serious fires in 2020 and 2024, and mechanical failure in July. This meant that when she was being repaired, there were long spells during which the United States had no icebreaker in the Arctic. It will be years before the 11 new ships on order are ready for service. In the meantime, the United States will need the help of allies that have icebreakers—no prizes for guessing which one in particular.

Sea Change leaves the ice to examine how the United States reached this sorry state of affairs. Here, Foroohar offers an updated reading of Alfred Thayer Mahan’s seminal 1890 masterwork, The Influence of Sea Power Upon History: 1660-1783, for the new age of industrial policy. For Mahan, national power rested on commerce, ports, ships, productive capacity, and the people able to sustain them. The United States remains the world’s preeminent naval power, but successive administrations have allowed much of that foundation to disappear. At the end of World War II, U.S. shipyards produced more than half the world’s commercial tonnage. Today, the country builds fewer than five commercial ships a year, while naval construction suffers delays, cost overruns, and labor shortages.

Ottawa has announced ambitious military spending plans, including in the sparsely protected Arctic.

This is perilous, not only for U.S. ambitions in the Arctic. As Foroohar puts it, “national security lives downstream from industrial capacity.”

Foroohar’s previous books examined the effects of financialization, monopoly, and offshoring on the U.S. economy. She sees the ruin of shipbuilding as a result of policies that treated the lowest immediate price as the highest economic good. Ships could be built more cheaply abroad, so the work went abroad. Companies shed inventory and redundant suppliers because Wall Street regarded both as waste. The savings to businesses and investors were real, but so too were the costs, borne by workers, communities, and, eventually, the country at large.

On this, Foroohar is persuasive. Shipbuilding is an especially unforgiving demonstration of the limits of market logic. A balance sheet can trace the savings made and profits accrued from buying a cheaper, foreign-built ship, but it can’t register the loss of knowing how to build one. A country could conceivably jerry-rig a shipyard in a time of crisis and provide crash-course training for thousands of workers, but it is impossible to quickly create a supply chain where one has ceased to exist. The Biden administration recognized the problem and began using industrial policy to rebuild strategic industries. Among other things, it signed a pact, known as the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, with Canada and Finland.

The Trump administration, likewise, claims to be seeking self-reliance in critical sectors. But, as its attempts to boost the U.S. icebreaker count shows, the United States can’t go it alone. Yes, three of Trump’s proposed ships will be built by Gulf Copper in Galveston, Texas. But the expertise will be Finnish, and the ownership and British. The president seems to think that U.S. power will come from coercing weaker countries into doing his bidding. Foroohar shows the limits of this approach.

Sea Change is less convincing when Foroohar tries to fit nearly every U.S. economic problem onto the deck of the Healy. Shipbuilding leads her into financial regulation, antitrust, vocational education, national service, defense procurement, and the civic virtues of military life. Together they sometimes make the book feel as crowded as her cabin on an icebreaker.

U.S. President Donald Trump arrives to participate in a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington on Sept. 21.Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

She also spends more time explaining the failures of the old economic order than on the dangers of the one replacing it. Tariffs can preserve an industry, but they can also preserve its inefficiencies. Government support can build capacity or become a permanent subsidy to politically connected companies. If the United States is going to pay more to make essential things at home, it needs better ways to decide which things are truly essential and how much extra it should pay.

But the book’s shortcomings are few, and matter less than the subject to which it draws attention. With Sea Change, Foroohar is encouraging Washington to put the Arctic in the middle of the map.

To tourists or casual observers, Italy might appear to be one giant museum—brimming with beautiful art but somewhat stuck in the past—that plays only a marginal role in global affairs.  A new book by Jason Horowitz, an American journalist who spent much of the last quarter century in Italy, paints a different picture: of a nation that has served as a laboratory for political trends that spread across Europe and the United States.

After learning the ropes of journalism in Rome working for a variety of news outlets, Horowitz married the daughter of an Italian diplomat, then later spent nearly a decade as the New York Times’ Rome bureau chief (when he finally went “native,” as he puts it, becoming an Italian citizen). His memoir, The Italian Job, reads both as a reflection on his personal and professional experiences in the country and on its recent political history.

To tourists or casual observers, Italy might appear to be one giant museum—brimming with beautiful art but somewhat stuck in the past—that plays only a marginal role in global affairs.  A new book by Jason Horowitz, an American journalist who spent much of the last quarter century in Italy, paints a different picture: of a nation that has served as a laboratory for political trends that spread across Europe and the United States.

The Italian Job: A Memoir of an American Reporter in Rome, Jason Horowitz, Celadon, 352 pp., $29.99, October 2026

After learning the ropes of journalism in Rome working for a variety of news outlets, Horowitz married the daughter of an Italian diplomat, then later spent nearly a decade as the New York Times’ Rome bureau chief (when he finally went “native,” as he puts it, becoming an Italian citizen). His memoir, The Italian Job, reads both as a reflection on his personal and professional experiences in the country and on its recent political history.

The book is infused with an evident love for Italy and Italians, yet one of its central arguments is that the country has paved the way for the rise of the modern far right.

A sizable share of the book is devoted to Silvio Berlusconi, a media tycoon who first became prime minister in the mid-1990s and, as the leader of the center-right Forza Italia party, dominated Italy’s political life for 20 years. Berlusconi, who died in 2023, resigned in ignominy in 2011 amid an acute financial crisis that threatened to send the eurozone’s third-largest economy into default—and after facing a scandal stemming from his infamous “bunga bunga” parties.

Horowitz dwells on how Berlusconi served as a model for future U.S. President Donald Trump, and he is hardly the first to draw comparisons between the two leaders—both wealthy businessmen with a penchant for norm-busting behavior. But as an American journalist with experience covering the political scenes of both Rome and Washington, Horowitz is particularly perceptive.

“Berlusconi set the mold for Trump, the Italian original before the American knockoff,” Horowitz writes. He “showed that a weakened political mainstream was vulnerable to takeover by a brand-name businessman with a messianic complex—Italy was broken and only he could fix it—unlimited access to screen time, and a charisma that moved the masses.”

Berlusconi, then Italy’s prime minister, poses in Villa Madama in Rome on Feb. 20, 2002. GABRIEL BOUYS/AFP via Getty Images

The two leaders both faced a long list of legal troubles and responded to them in similar ways: Trump’s tirades about “witch hunts” seem to come out of Berlusconi’s playbook, Horowitz notes. Unsurprisingly, Trump has long been interested in Berlusconi’s political adventure. “Who is this guy?” Trump reportedly asked an associate whom he had dispatched to Italy in 2011, according to the book. “What’s he doing? How’s he doing?”

On top of inspiring the future U.S. president, Berlusconi left another long-lasting mark in Italy and beyond, Horowitz argues: By breaking the firewall around Italy’s far right and repeatedly bringing it into coalition governments, he helped pave the way for its rise, which culminated in Giorgia Meloni’s election as prime minister four years ago and contributed to a broader trend across much of Europe.

According to Horowitz, Berlusconi believed—to some extent correctly—that opening the gates of government to the post-fascist Italian Social Movement, a predecessor of Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party, would accelerate its transformation into a more mainstream conservative force.

While Meloni has pursued a staunchly conservative agenda, curtailing abortion rights, banning surrogacy, and strengthening police powers, most Italians I speak to agree that she does not represent a threat to democratic freedoms. But what Berlusconi failed to foresee, Horowitz writes, was that his coalition partners would eventually take center stage and sideline Forza Italia.

Berlusconi wipes the forehead of Salvini during a joint press conference at the Temple of Hadrian in Rome on March 1, 2018. ALBERTO PIZZOLI/AFP via Getty Images

In 2018, Matteo Salvini—the leader of another far-right party, the League—became interior minister in a coalition government with the anti-establishment Five Star Movement. Italy came to represent a beacon for international right-wing populists, including former White House strategist Steve Bannon, who visited Italy frequently at that time as part of his efforts to build a broad anti-globalist alliance. As Horowitz puts it, Italy was “the place to be for the most eager arsonists of the existing world order.”

After two more coalitions quickly rotated in and out of government, Meloni skyrocketed in the polls and won the 2022 general election, becoming the first far-right head of government in western Europe since the end of World War II—exactly a century after the march on Rome brought Benito Mussolini’s National Fascist Party to power in Italy.

Horowitz suggests the Italian far right’s escape from its cave is being replicated by similar parties across Europe. The Italian Job doesn’t delve deep into other countries’ politics, but it’s worth noting that Italy set a trend: In recent years, populist nationalist parties have backed or become part of governments in Sweden and the Netherlands. In France, National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in next spring’s presidential election. The Reform U.K. party has topped national polls for much of the last year. Last month, the Alternative for Germany party gained significant ground over the conservative Christian Democrats in several state elections.

Alice Weidel, a co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, speaks to supporters at an AfD election campaign rally ahead of state elections, in Neubrandenburg, Germany, on Sept. 18.Sean Gallup/Getty Images

As to whether the far right is destined to grow tamer as it nears power, Horowitz leaves the question open. Italians, he writes, may be tempted by populism, but they are ultimately a nation of moderates with little sympathy for authoritarianism. The Italian political system, with its inherent fragmentation and a strong judiciary, was built from the ashes of World War II with the goal of providing strong checks and balances.

In other political cultures with fewer constitutional ramparts, Horowitz notes, the story may be different. I’d point to the much greater power concentrated in the hands of the executive in France, where President Emmanuel Macron pushed through an extremely controversial pension reform in 2023 that the legislature wasn’t allowed to vote on.

                How an Obscure General Became the Star of Italy’s Far Right            


    
    	Bestselling author Roberto Vannacci is eclipsing Giorgia Meloni, but entering politics could blunt his popularity.

        |
        
    
    Giorgio Ghiglione

Giorgia Meloni wants to be Europe’s top transatlantic leader for the Trump era.

Bestselling author Roberto Vannacci is eclipsing Giorgia Meloni, but entering politics could blunt his popularity.

Horowitz’s book is about more than Italian politics. The Vatican, for one, clearly had an outsized place in his life in Rome, as it appears abundantly in The Italian Job. (The author is not alone: A decade later, when I interned in the same Associated Press bureau where Horowitz took his first professional steps, the job was about 50 percent covering the pope and 50 percent covering Berlusconi.) Horowitz guides readers through three conclaves, which elected the popes Benedict XVI, Francis, and Leo XIV, respectively; describes the power struggles between conservatives and reformists within the church; and takes readers behind the scenes of the many papal trips he covered as part of the Vatican press corps.

Cardinals attend Pope Francis’s inauguration Mass at St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City on March 19, 2013.GABRIEL BOUYSGABRIEL BOUYS/AFP via Getty Images

Prime ministers and popes aside, Horowitz does a good job of capturing Italy’s collective psyche. The book contains an obligatory dose of Italian color, with reckless driving, elaborate swearing, and enthusiasm for food illustrated in its pages. But Horowitz isn’t peddling stereotypes. Even when tackling some of the most Italian cliches, he brings real depth to his observations about what defines the country and its people.

When addressing Italians’ insistence to follow traditional recipes to the letter, for example, Horowitz argues that it may reflect a broader reluctance to embrace change and innovation. I had never thought about it that way, but he may well be right.

In some respects, Horowitz’s experience in the country was hardly comparable to that of the average Italian. As he mentions in the book, his in-laws are connected to some of the most exclusive social circles in Rome. Yet he is lucid when describing the challenges Italians face—not from an academic perspective, but after he and his family were confronted with some of those problems in their everyday lives. The lack of good job opportunities and the low salaries, which prompt large numbers of talented graduates to emigrate, are recurring themes in The Italian Job (at one point, Horowitz’s wife is offered a salary so low that she thought there had been a mistake), as is the aging population, which is putting Italy’s welfare state and family-based model of elder care under strain.

Horowitz’s takes are also influenced by his own political views. The book betrays a certain sympathy for liberal reformers such as former Prime Ministers Matteo Renzi and Mario Draghi, while the Five Star Movement comes across as a bunch of lunatics with a penchant for conspiracy theories—an assessment that overlooks its gradual transition from anti-establishment movement to a more mainstream, moderate, and left-leaning party in recent years.

But no description of a divided country full of contradictions like Italy can be entirely objective, much less one as wide-ranging and personal as this one. If anything, a little bias here and there is proof that Horowitz has truly succeeded in going native.

https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/09/int.title: What Life Was Like for a Jewish Artist in 1930s Berlin
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/09/int.author: Chloe Hadavas and Allison Meakem
https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/10/09/int.text:
This month, we’re reading two tales of artistic daring set in epochal moments, from Napoleonic France to Weimar-era Germany.

Yiyun Li (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 352 pp., $29, October 2026)

This month, we’re reading two tales of artistic daring set in epochal moments, from Napoleonic France to Weimar-era Germany.

Yiyun Li (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 352 pp., $29, October 2026)

You’d be forgiven for not recognizing the name John Field—even more so his wife, Adelaide Percheron, who, as the writer Yiyun Li has pointed out, appears in no more than five paragraphs in a biography of the Irish composer. Field, the inventor of the nocturne, would end up a “footnote in the life of Frédéric Chopin,” who popularized the form. But in her latest novel, Li, a prolific Chinese-born author and creative writing professor at Princeton University, reimagines the life of this “forgotten master” alongside that of Percheron, a musician in her own right.

Music Against the Night, the first installment of a new trilogy, is set at the turn of the 19th century, that era when the “whole globe was a playground for would-be conquerors.” Across decades, Li follows Field and Percheron, known as “Percherette,” as they come of age and discover their prodigious talents: Field in Dublin, and then London, where he trains under a virtuoso and piano manufacturer; and the orphaned Percherette from Pondicherry, a colonial settlement in India, to Paris and the French countryside.

Though we catch glimpses of the couple’s fate—including their estrangement and deaths—through short interludes and codas, the pair do not meet in this volume. Instead, the chapters are filled with their childhood preoccupations: their deeply felt connections with their peers, their fraught ties to their families and guardians, and, of course, their near-maniacal relationship with music, which is variously an albatross and—for both characters—equal to life itself. None of this is to say that the book feels childish. One of Li’s great gifts as a writer is her ability to render the lives of children as entire and worthy in themselves.

The novel’s private dramas are contraposed with the sweep of history. Field and Percherette lived through a time of epochal change, of the French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars that reordered the continent. A sense of contingency, even futility, runs through the narrative. Field “might think someone born with gifts enjoyed some measure of grace, divine favor, as kings do,” Li writes. “But even a king could lose his head, as had happened the year before in France.” In another section, she notes: “A nation’s fate is as treacherous as an artist’s: many things go wrong, leading to disappointment and disillusion. It requires the courage of suspending one’s disbelief to be an artist or a revolutionary.”

If this sounds like bleak reading, know that at the heart of the novel is a child so full of life that, even recognizing the hardship and obscurity that will befall Percherette later in life, you can’t help but feel stirred by her presence on the page or moved by her uncanny ability to “stay enchanted with a disenchanting life; to dream in a world that is keen to judge and punish the dreamers.”—Chloe Hadavas

Rebecca Birrell (Henry Holt and Co., 352 pp., $28.99, October 2026)

Venus, Vanishing should be historical fiction. But at a time of Kennedy Center takeovers and far-right resurgence, Rebecca Birrell’s debut novel reads much more like a cautionary tale about what can happen when hate-driven autocrats try to capture the arts.

Birrell, an art historian at the University of Cambridge, sets Venus, Vanishing in the interwar period in Germany. Protagonist Hannah Sherman escapes the clutches of her traditional Jewish mother to experience the hedonism of Weimar-era Berlin—think Babylon Berlin but with a focus on the visual arts. Trained as a seamstress—her family’s trade—Hannah spends her free time self-studying to become a painter. She also courts several lovers, men and women.

When a wealthy client—Elke—notices Hannah’s artistic talent, she offers to become her patron, providing Hannah eye-popping sums of money so that she can stop working as a seamstress and focus exclusively on painting. Hannah’s specialty is nudes, and Elke soon commissions portraits of herself and her friends: “Italian Renaissance examples except for the backgrounds, which would be German landscapes,” Birrell writes. As Hannah completes these assignments, the two women become “infatuated” with one another, crossing countless boundaries.

Their relationship develops a political dimension, too. Elke’s husband is an important figure in Germany’s culture ministry. When the couple displays Hannah’s paintings at a gallery, they list—without her consent—the artist as a fictional, non-Jewish man: Answald Dietrich. (“In the current market, a German man is far more appealing an investment than a woman,” Elke writes to Hannah as an explanation.) The newly appointed Führer—Birrell never mentions Adolf Hitler by name—takes a liking to “Dietrich’s” paintings, choosing to make them the artistic face of his “new Germany.” Little does he know that “the star of the Great German Art Exhibition is a Jew.”

Thus begins a fast-paced tale of deception, forgery, sex, and escape—all set to the backdrop of rising antisemitism over several years in 1930s Berlin. Much as Hannah resents the fact that her paintings “would help [Elke’s] husband ascend in the government,” she is trapped, for Elke “knew that I was Jewish and my humanity was at stake.” Since moving out of her parents’ house, Hannah had concealed her Jewish background, going by Schmidt rather than Sherman. But Elke is a longtime patron of the Sherman family business and knows Hannah’s secret. Her husband, however, does not. Elke could end up either as Hannah’s protector—or her biggest threat.

As the plot progresses, Hannah’s Jewishness moves from marginal to central to her identity; Germany’s changing politics leaves her no other choice (“a Jew’s a Jew, even a Mischling,” her neighbor tells her). When Hannah marries Saul—a fellow Jewish communist—they only become more marginalized.

Interestingly, at a time of fierce debate over Israel-Palestine within the Jewish community, Birrell explicitly notes that Saul is anti-Zionist; as he and Hannah seek to leave Berlin, Saul rejects some of his friends’ flight to Palestine—instead adhering to his Bundist principles. “Saul insisted [Palestine] was someone else’s homeland that the English had declared was ours,” Hannah says. “We already had a homeland, he said, and we were already living in it.”

Although Venus, Vanishing is a work of fiction, Birrell writes in a “Historical Notes” chapter at the end of the book that Hannah is a “composite figure” of several little-known European Jewish women artists from the interwar period, including Charlotte Salomon, Frania Hart, and Alice Haarburger. The Nazis murdered all three of them. In a literary genre dominated by stories of the Holocaust, Birrell wanted Hannah to offer a “counternarrative,” she writes: “I hoped to write a novel primarily about Jewish life, not Jewish death.”—Allison Meakem

A promising legal theorist at the European Union’s Court of Justice unravels in The Rhyl Poster, a philosophical thriller by Tom McCarthy. Intan Paramaditha’s work of contemporary political horror, Night of a Thousand Hells, is translated from the Indonesian by Stephen Epstein and Tiffany Tsao. Esther Yi probes the absurdities and contradictions of contemporary life in her short-story collection, To God. Benedict Anning makes his debut with Atomic Coffin, a Cold War-era thriller in which a hidden Soviet submarine harbors unexpected terrors. A coming-of-age tale meets folk horror in K-Ming Chang’s Needlemouth.

In Will Maclean’s Secret History-esque Solace House, a decaying English manor is home to dark secrets. Veteran sci-fi stylist M. John Harrison returns with The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic tale set along the English Channel. A detective duo turns to food to help their clients recover lost memories in Hisashi Kashiwai’s A Serving of Hope, translated from the Japanese by Jesse Kirkwood. Cameroonian American novelist Imbolo Mbue’s Every Story Is a Love Story explores the unlikely bonds between those affected by grief and remorse. And in Alexander Maksik’s Passengers, a flight gets endlessly delayed.—CH

1. A protest march began in Pakistan on Sunday to demand the release of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. The march was originally scheduled for late September. Why was it delayed?

Khan called for the protest to be delayed.

Khan had temporarily been moved out of the capital, Islamabad.

The government surged security forces to Islamabad and surrounding regions.

The government offered to negotiate over protesters’ demands.

The march to Islamabad could put pressure on the government to free Khan, who has been imprisoned for more than three years for corruption, FP’s Michael Kugelman writes in South Asia Brief.

2. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called for snap elections, following his government’s failure to pass emergency measures to tackle what issue?

Rising costs of oil and gas

A lack of affordable housing

Nationwide anti-tourism protests

The elections, set for Nov. 29, will be risky, as Sánchez’s party is trailing in most local opinion polls. But the socialist leader has navigated tricky political waters before, Omar G. Encarnación wrote in August.

3. Lithuania’s parliament voted on Tuesday in favor of a constitutional amendment that would lift a ban on what?

Stationing nuclear weapons on the country’s soil

Importing goods directly from Russia and Belarus

Purchasing alcohol after 3 p.m. on Sundays

Transgender individuals serving in the military

FP’s Sam Skove spoke with the president of neighboring Latvia last week to discuss Russia’s increasing appetite for sabotaging Ukraine’s allies.

4. Which East African country reported its first case of Ebola on Tuesday?

The continent’s current Ebola crisis, centered in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

5. North Korea accused the United States of fueling tension in the Taiwan Strait on Wednesday over what?

Offering to sell weapons to China

Sending three nuclear submarines to Japan

Its military support for Taiwan

Washington’s expanded military agreement with the Philippines

Beijing needs Pyongyang as a geopolitical ally and bargaining chip, Deng Yuwen wrote in May.

6. Wednesday marked the three-year anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks in southern Israel. Which armed group perpetrated those attacks?

Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces

Israel’s refusal to abandon convenient assumptions about its national security played a role in the country’s early failings in its war against Hamas, Simon Frankel Pratt and Jamie Levin write.

7. Thousands of Brazilian students marched in downtown Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday to protest what?

Renewed Amazon deforestation for critical mineral mining

The possibility of a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency

The rising cost of living amid wars in Iran and Ukraine

The increasing use of artificial intelligence chatbots in schools

After a first-round presidential election on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro—the son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro—and incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are headed for an Oct. 25 runoff election, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports in Latin America Brief.

8. European Union trade chief Maros Sefcovic began two days of trade talks with China on Thursday with the goal of doing what?

Signing an electric vehicle import deal

Securing access to advanced AI models

Gaining preferential access to some heavy rare earths

Decreasing the bloc’s trade deficit with Beijing

Among the EU’s top priorities are limiting the import of Chinese hybrid vehicles and getting clarification on China’s restrictions on rare-earth exports, FP’s Alexandra Sharp writes in World Brief.

9. Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson was awarded the Nobel Prize in literature on Thursday. One of her more notable works, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, retells which ancient Greek story as a modern tragic teenage love affair?

Heracles’s 10th labor

Perseus’s slaying of Medusa

Carson is the third Canadian-born writer to receive the award, after Alice Munro in 2013 and Saul Bellow in 1976, the New York Times reports.

10. South African lawyer and judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was announced as the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday in recognition of her efforts to do what?

End violence against women in South Africa

Deliver humanitarian aid to conflict zones

Promote peace and international law

Bring visibility to the suffering of Uyghurs in China

Pillay’s work “is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world,” the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee said.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
US President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver another 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.

Trump’s shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia’s energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.

READ MORE
Trump says Ukraine, Russia agree not to hit energy targets

His move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.”

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on November 3.

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reposted the Treasury Department’s announcement on X Friday and said that “Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world”.

The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new US investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The US has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the US was $6.23 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on September 22.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Paris court jails Indian man for leading sadist neo-Nazi cult that tortured girls
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
A Paris court on Friday sentenced a young Indian man to 20 years in prison for leading a masculinist group that forced young girls, many of them minors, to perform sexual acts and in some cases tortured them.

Prosecutors had sought a 30-year jail term for Rohan Rane, a 29-year-old who they described as a neo-Nazi lover of sadism and macabre ultra-violence.

Most of the dozens of victims of the group led by Rane were American girls, the court was told. Many were aged under 15. Other young male members of the masculinist group were from the United States, India, Germany and New Zealand.

Six of the girls, now aged between 18 and 21, made official complaints. About 20 victims were identified but others could not be contacted, prosecutors said.

After five days of hearings, mainly behind closed doors, the court found Rane guilty of offences, notably extortion committed as part of an organised gang, with the aggravating circumstances of acts of torture and barbarity perpetrated on the victims.

Prosecutors said all of the girls were lured by the "CVLT" group that was driven by nihilism, racism, anti-Semitism, Nazi aesthetics and values, and the hatred of feminists and the LGBTQ+ community.

READ MORE
The rise of masculinism: Violence and misogyny online (1/3)

The group became active ahead of the Covid-19 pandemic on the Discord platform with Rane as its leader.

The Indian went to France to study at a commercial school in the southern town of Antibes before becoming a sports coach.

Vulnerable victims were picked out in online forums and persuaded to send nude images. The men threatened to tell their families and school friends if they did not give in to their demands.

According to investigators, many of the girls were black or Jewish and they were forced to engage in sexual acts or to self-harm with knives, including scoring the names of their tormentors or a Nazi swastika into their skin.

The scenes were accompanied by insults and jeers from the men, who called themselves "war lords". One 26-year-old American group member has been jailed in the United States for the 2021 rape of a 12-year-old.

Rane was first arrested in 2021 in France. US authorities passed on information about his leadership in the "CVLT" group and how he had vaunted his desire to fullfil his "sadism".

A US group, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, first rang alarm bells over "CVLT" in 2020 after discovering disturbing images of a 12-year-old online with the name "Rohan" scored into her skin.

The French hearings remained closed following a US request, despite requests from some of the American victims who came forward that a public example be made of Rane's case.

The court was told that threats had been made to the victims, witnesses and even some US prosecutors.

US authorities have indicated that they will seek Rane's extradition once his sentence in France is served.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Powerful 7.6 magnitude quake shakes Panama, triggering tsunami warnings
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
A magnitude-7.7 earthquake jolted Panama on Friday, setting off panic in the capital city and warnings of dangerous tsunami waves.

USGS said the quake was detected at 1756 GMT with an epicenter 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in the south-center of Panama. It initially measured at magnitude 8.

The quake was registered at a shallow depth of 12 kilometers, meaning its impact was likely to be more severe.

It was felt across the country of around 4.5 million people, according to the USGS.

Several large aftershocks, one a magnitude-6 tremor, were recorded.

There were no reports yet of casualties but extensive damage was expected, particularly in the center of the Central American nation.

Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200 kilometers from the epicenter, AFP witnessed.

Tsunami waves up to three meters high could hit the Panama coastline in the coming hours, the US Tsunami Warning System said.

Earthquakes are rare in Panama and when they do occur usually strike in western Chiriqui province.

Haxie Meyers-Belkin is pleased to welcome Rosa Freedman, Professor of Law Conflict and Global Development at the University of Reading. Navi Pillay's career represents a remarkable contribution to international law and human rights, from her pioneering role in post-apartheid South Africa to her work at the United Nations. Yet her legacy also raises difficult questions about political impartiality, particularly in relation to Israel and Gaza. She believes we need to distinguish between the significance of her lifelong achievements and the controversy surrounding the decision to award her the Nobel Peace Prize at this particular moment. More broadly, this debate invites us to examine whether the prize is recognising individual merit or increasingly serving as a vehicle for political messaging. At a time when international law and multilateral institutions face mounting pressure, and serious threats, Freedman asserts that the challenge is to scrutinise their shortcomings without undermining the principles they exist to uphold.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: French students vow to keep up protests as UN voices 'concern' over violence
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Students in France were largely back in the classroom Friday following days of protests demanding better education and school conditions, as the UN voiced "concern" over the sometimes violent clashes.

Tens of thousands have taken to the streets across France since students in late September began blocking entrances to high schools, which led to squads of riot police being deployed.

The students – most aged 15 to 18 – have complained of absent teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.

More than 6,800 people have been detained since the start of the demonstrations, of whom 86 percent are minors, the justice ministry said Friday.

A government source told journalists that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was "at least 30 million euros".

The United Nations said Friday it was watching the events "with concern" and urged people on all sides to remain peaceful.

"We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent," said Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights agency.

READ MORE
France suspends the use of stun grenades after student protester loses hand

While the demonstrations have been largely peaceful, some protesters have started fires and vandalised bus shelters.

In response, police have used tear gas, batons and blast balls, leading to accusations from rights groups and the students themselves of a disproportionate use of force.

Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.

After a 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, the government has suspended the use of the weapon.

The government source said Friday the authorities were seeing a "marked slowdown" in the movement, and told journalists that most of the injured high school students "were not hurt by police action (but were) students who injured themselves accidentally" during the protests.

But many students told AFP they were not relenting. Organisers have called for large-scale demonstrations next week.

"We're saving our energy for next week," said one 16-year-old student in the southwestern city of Toulouse.

Alice, a high school student in the southern port city of Marseille, said the education minister's announcements "are a first step but they're not enough".

On Thursday evening in the capital Paris, police said they had used tear gas in Bastille square to disperse some "high-risk profiles".

In a bid to placate the anger, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.

French government vows to boost teacher numbers in bid to ease school crisis

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has also promised a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October, while Economy Minister Roland Lescure said there was room to address demands for more school resources within the highly constrained 2027 budget.

In the current draft budget, education has the second largest increase in funding – after defence – with a boost of 1.4 percent to €90.9 billion.

Last Friday, some 800 schools had closed due to the protests.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-1.title: Retiring Riverland grape grower says industry support has come too late
https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-1.author: Eliza Berlage
https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-1.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

After more than five decades, Jack Papageorgiou is retiring from farming. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

Green leaves shoot out from budding grapevines, but like many growers in South Australia's Riverland, Jack Papageorgiou's fruit will go unharvested.

For more than five decades, Jack has dedicated himself to caring for this land.

Jack hopes the 2026 vintage was his last. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

He survived the crippling Millennium Drought, when low irrigator allocations drove temporary water prices sky-high.

But the wine industry downturn, which has seen some growers receive prices below the cost of producing their wine grapes, has cost his family too much.

"But we had no choice or else … we would have been hurting even more."

Now, Jack is ready to call it quits.

"I hope I find a buyer before the next vintage, but I'm hoping in the next 12 months I will have the property sold," he said.

Farmers in the country's biggest wine region say they're thinking about walking away from the industry due to grape prices not seen since the 1970s. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

Last month, the South Australian government announced a $109 million package for the struggling wine industry, featuring loans of up to $500,000 to help growers transition to other crops.

But older growers like Jack say the support has come too late.

"I wish they would have looked at the wine industry five years ago."

Jack Papageorgiou has held numerous leadership roles in the agricultural industry and the local community. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

Jack said many growers had "lost faith" with no improvement in sight, reflected in vacant land across towns that were once a sea of vineyards.

"A lot of grape growers made a commercial decision that this is unsustainable," he said.

Athena is never far from Jack Papageorgiou's side. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

Jack migrated to Australia from Greece with his mum and two brothers in 1964, his father joining them the following year, prompted by the search for "a better life".

The family lived in Melbourne for about a decade, where Jack finished his schooling, before moving to Cooltong in South Australia's Riverland.

The three brothers began their 15-year farming partnership with a shared chequebook, and a loan from their parents to run their wine-grape, citrus and dried-fruit property.

Jack and his older brother, Spiro, are two of the three Papageorgiou brothers who farmed together. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

In the years since, the brothers purchased their own properties and moved on to other ventures.

But finding a willing buyer will be difficult, with banks often unwilling to lend money for properties with vineyards and his land unsuitable for subdivision to create housing.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

Jack's life changed when his son Theo died by suicide in 2016.

Jack's only son Theo died by suicide at the age of 27. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

He channelled the experience into mental health support within his community, including weekly coffee catch-ups with his fellow growers.

"It's no good sitting on your own, worrying about it and getting stressed," he said.

Riverland Wine executive officer Andrew Weeks said Jack had been committed and courageous in his contributions to the community.

"Jack's always been very willing to go and stick his hand up and put himself on the line and advocate for growers," he said.

"He's been involved in a number of different hearings or local meetings with different politicians at all sorts of levels and putting his hand up and saying to people: 'This is not good enough.'

Andrew Weeks says Jack has given a lot to the local community and industry. (ABC Riverland: Eliza Berlage)

As for what he will do next, Jack hoped to hit the road to see more of Australia and return to "the old country" — Greece.

But most of all, he wanted to dedicate his energy to his loved ones.

Jack recently celebrated 44 years of marriage with his wife, Poppy. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

"I'm 73, I believe I've still got years to live yet," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/m.title: Shark attack survivor thanks 'legends' who saved him
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/m.author: Brianna Melville and Chris Lewis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt

Mel Ismail thanks the civilian heroes, first responders and medical staff who saved his life. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

After a shark bit off his leg Mel Ismail wants to highlight the locals and trained responders who saved his life.

Mr Ismail has connected with hero surfer Shannan Dunn who risked his own life to rescue him.

Mr Ismail says he will "adapt, improvise and overcome" the challenges of life without his leg.

The West Australian surfer who looked a shark in the eye and survived wants the lasting legacy of his story to be the heroic behaviour of those who helped save his life.

Mel Ismail was surfing north of Geraldton in mid-September when he was bitten.

Three weeks after his harrowing ordeal, the firefighter and part-time teacher is adjusting to life without his lower leg.

But he plans to surf again.

Mr Ismail this week spent time with Shannan Dunn, who raced into the water while the shark was likely close by.

He said his spirits had lifted at the sight of the other man coming towards him.

Mel Ismail and Shannan Dunn have connected over their escape from the shark. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"Your words were, 'I got you mate, we'll get you in. We're gonna get you in,'" Mr Ismail told Mr Dunn.

"Even when I [fell] off the front of the board, you went, 'That's alright, let's get back on, keep going, just keep going.'"

Mr Dunn recalled the chaotic paddle to shore as he struggled to keep Mr Ismail on the board.

"We were both off the board at stages, [then] we were both on there at the same time," he said.

"It was a bit of a mess, but we got there.

"If I was in the same situation, I'd want someone to come and get me."

Shark attack survivor Mal Ismail reunites with one of the men who helped save him. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The two had previously seen each other's faces in the surf while battling for waves, but said the rescue brought them together.

"One day when I get my leg better I'll probably have to throw a few waves his way," Mr Ismail said.

Mr Ismail extended his thanks to other beachgoers who helped save his life.

Chrissy and Rick, who asked to be identified by their first names, helped treat Mr Ismail when he made it to shore.

Teenage cousins Cruz and Clay McDonald and their friend Jasper Hill, surfing during the attack and initially none the wiser, rushed to shore to help.

They fashioned a second tourniquet out of one of their leg ropes, helped load Mr Ismail into Mr Dunn’s four-wheel drive, and kept his spirits high on the bumpy ride to the ambulance.

Paramedics, volunteers, nurses and doctors then provided life-saving care.

Mel Ismail is adjusting to life after the loss of his leg. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"So many people take them for granted. They're heroes," Mr Ismail said.

"What they do, what they see and experience, they save people's lives. We don't hold them up highly enough and say, 'Hey, you're actually legends.'

"That's what I want to put out there as my story."

Mel Ismail is home adjusting to life without his lower leg. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Now back at home in Geraldton, Mr Ismail said the hardest part of his ordeal had been coming to terms with the loss of his right leg.

He said his family and community had flooded him with support, including a friend who had delivered hand-built wheelchair ramps for his house.

"I'm looking at it and trying to think, 'Hey, be positive, move forward,'" he said.

Mel Ismail is trying to stay positive after losing his leg to a shark attack. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"I just can't walk outside anymore and do things. But I will be able to soon, maybe.

"If I want to go out into the garden or mow the lawn, that's sort of finished for a bit."

He has already returned to the gym and plans to eventually get back to work and back on a surfboard.

"I always call it 'adapt, improvise and overcome', so I'm going to go with that motto," he said.

Mel Ismail's broken surfboard on the day he was bitten. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"I got enough friends that want to see me in the water again.

"It might be on a soft top [surfboard] for starters. They might think I'm surfing better than I ever have."

Mr Ismail has not held his surfboard since it was broken during the shark attack and conceded it might bring back memories.

Mel Ismail has returned to the gym and plans to return to work and surfing. (Supplied: Kylie Fleay)

"I'll get my head around that probably in the next couple of weeks," he said.

"I'll see it with some friends around, and we'll work together through that."

He also did not hold resentment towards the shark, which was yet to be identified.

"Sometimes I say 'bloody shark' if I'm feeling down," he said.

He said the fisheries department's inability to identify the animal was not a major factor for him.

"A shark took my leg. It wasn't an elephant, and it wasn't a donkey," he said.

Mel Ismail says he has no interest in finding out the species of shark that attacked him. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The death of Perth man Greg O'Neill in a shark attack at Sorrento Beach four days after Mr Ismail lost his leg has sparked significant debate again around shark mitigation across WA.

It was a discussion Mr Ismail was happy to stay out of.

"Look, I knew the risks of being a surfer for many years and so have my friends," he said.

"What happened to me at Glennies was a random attack. It doesn't happen very often in this area.

"I don't know why [it happened]. Maybe because it's their domain and you are part of the food chain there."

He said people should not let fear stop them from doing what they enjoy.

"A shark attack does put fear into people," he said.

"There are so many car crashes, and we don't put enough fear into people about that. I've attended so many of them.

"Go back and do what you need to do. If you love surfing, surf."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/v.author: James Vyver
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Australia's official histories of wars in the Middle East have yet to be published. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

Australia's official histories of the Afghanistan and Iraq wars have been written for several years but have not been cleared for publication by government.

The Australian War Memorial has joined the RSL and Legacy in calling for the release.

Australia's involvement in Afghanistan will be marked at a national commemorative service on Sunday.

The RSL, Legacy and the Australian War Memorial are calling for the release of overdue official histories covering the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Ex-service organisations have agreed on a "concerted effort" to address the delay, described as having "negative consequences" for veterans.

Era-defining, comprehensive and exhaustive, the histories are the nation's primary record of conflicts fought in the public's name.

The works also allow veterans to understand the full picture of their individual service for the first time.

Iraq veteran Lisa, who lives with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) due her service, said she had "carried the weight" of her actions for two decades.

"Did I put someone in danger because I made a wrong call? Did I jeopardise the safety of some of our sources inadvertently?" the former intelligence officer said.

"These are the questions I still ask myself 20 years later … I think knowing the official history will be really helpful for some of us to understand."

Ex-service organisations say the delay has "negative consequences" for veterans. (File photo: Defence Department)

Commissioned in 2015 and completed in 2023, none of the four Middle East volumes have been published.

"I hear about this a lot from veterans; they're particularly concerned that the government's starting to try and hide something," RSL national president Peter Tinley said.

A former SAS Commander and Afghanistan veteran, Mr Tinley is now calling on the Albanese government to expedite the histories' release.

"Prime minister, veterans of Australia are looking to you now, their families and the families of the fallen veterans," he said.

Australian War Memorial director Matt Anderson agreed the works were overdue.

"Our veterans have waited long enough, and we owe it to them to have these on the public record as soon as possible," he told the ABC in a statement.

Official histories tell the operational, political and social aspects of war. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

The Australian War Memorial facilitates the writing of official histories and publishes the final work in a convention dating back to World War I.

The volumes are written with unique access to government, defence and intelligence documents as well as thousands of interviews with veterans.

The Middle East volumes were commissioned by the Abbott government in 2015 at a cost of almost $13 million.

Two volumes covering Australia's peacekeeping in East Timor were commissioned at the same time, the first of which is now publicly available.

The second has been cleared but not yet published.

Though written at arm's length from the government of the day, completed manuscripts must be cleared before publication.

Of the four Middle East volumes, one has been cleared, two remain with government, while the other is finished but has not been submitted.

One Middle East volume has been cleared, two remain with government, the fourth is completed but has not yet been submitted for security checks. (ABC News: Phil Jaiyawong)

Led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, the defence, diplomatic, intelligence and security departments also review the works.

"I can't say that I'm fully conscious of any reason why it should be proceeding so slowly," Australian War Memorial Council chair Kim Beazley said of the Middle East volumes.

"I guess in the case of a pressed bureaucracy, this doesn't necessarily rate very high in order of importance.

Documents released under Freedom of Information show the director of the Australian War Memorial questioned delays to the clearance process for the East Timor volumes at the highest levels of departmental bureaucracy in 2023.

The correspondence also indicates a "whole-of-government protocol" to complete security clearances within six months was not met.

Craig Stockings is a professor of history at UNSW Canberra and was appointed as official historian by prime minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2016.

Last month, Professor Stockings raised the "remaining challenges" of the official histories project at a Department of Veterans Affairs roundtable.

The official histories are reviewed by defence, diplomatic, intelligence and security departments. (Supplied: Defence Force)

The roundtable comprised of 20 members: senior bureaucrats, veterans' groups and government agencies.

"Professor Stockings stressed the importance and impact of these six official histories on the veteran community, as well as the complexities, sensitivities and negative consequences of the long delays in the clearance process," the meeting's official communique reported.

"Members voiced support for a concerted effort by interested ex-service organisations to advocate for the completion of the project," it concluded.

Professor Stockings declined to comment for this article.

The ABC contacted the prime minister, defence minister and minister for veterans' affairs with an extensive list of questions for this story.

None of those questions were answered.

"Defence continues to support the Australian War Memorial's Official Histories Project," a Defence spokesperson said.

Ex-service organisations say the histories allow veterans to understand the full picture of their individual service for the first time. (ABC News: Margaret Burin)

Mark Lax is the chair of Legacy and a 50-year veteran of the RAAF with a PhD in military history.

Dr Lax authored a series of chapters for the Afghanistan volumes about the air force's involvement.

"It's been held up somewhere, and the question I have is, 'Where and why?'"

Dr Lax said references to classified material were checked by a former spy chief who was part of the official history team.

"A retired major general who had been heavily involved in the intelligence world," Dr Lax said.

Veterans' groups want the public to know the full story of the Middle East conflicts. (ABC: ADF/Janine Fabre)

In 2020, the Brereton Inquiry found "credible information" that Australian special forces were involved in serious crimes in Afghanistan.

Victoria Cross recipient and former Special Air Service Regiment soldier Ben Roberts-Smith is facing five counts of war crime murder, which relate to deployments in Afghanistan in 2009 and 2012.

He has categorically rejected the allegations and said he plans to fight to clear his name in court.

Currently on bail, Mr Roberts-Smith was granted permission by a judge to attend a service in Canberra on Sunday, marking 25 years since Australia entered the Afghanistan conflict.

RSL national president Peter Tinley said the official histories were needed to ensure the full picture of Middle East wars, including humanitarian work carried out by Australian forces, was understood by the public.

"It's got to be bigger than just alleged war crimes," he said.

"The key issue for veterans is they gave service. [Now] they would expect the government of the day to actually honour that service by an official recording of it."

Sarah Hartwig (right) kicked four goals as the Western Bulldogs beat Essendon by 43 points at Whitten Oval. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Western Bulldogs have signalled their potential with a dominant 43-point win over Essendon to crack the AFLW top four.

The home side trailed after two minutes before kicking five unanswered goals to seize control of the game.

Sarah Hartwig kicked a career-high four goals as the Bulldogs earned their seventh win of the season.

The Western Bulldogs have brought a ruthless mentality to Pride Round in thrashing Essendon by 43 points.

Friday night's 10.5 (65) to 2.10 (22) result was the Bulldogs' seventh win for the season and sent a warning to the top eight sides on the cusp of finals.

It came despite their shaky start in front of a home crowd at Whitten Oval.

Essendon came out firing and Emily Gough kicked the first goal inside the first two minutes, spurring the Dons, who played with high pressure and repeatedly locked the ball in their forward half.

The Bulldogs responded with five unanswered goals with the help of an unstoppable Isabelle Pritchard, who had 30 disposals and 10 clearances.

"We weren't playing the style of game that we came to play," Dogs midfielder Jess Fitzgerald said after quarter time.

"We wanted to come into the game with a bit of a ruthless mentality, and we felt like we didn't bring that in the first.

"So, yeah, we turned that on."

Essendon were down by 25 points at half-time but hopes of repeating last week's win over the Giants, a comeback from 24 points down at half-time, were cut short by their inability to find the goals.

After Gough's early major, the Bombers kicked nine points until Sophie Alexander found their second just before three-quarter time.

The Bombers managed one more point in the final term, while the Dogs slotted another three goals.

Star forward Sarah Hartwig had a career-high four goals and helped the Western Bulldogs surpass the 60-point mark for the fifth time since 2025.

"Honestly, it's just that work rate and the pressure that we bring, especially in the forward line. That's what we pride ourselves on," she said.

Despite the win, the Bulldogs still have work to do in the season's run home, Hartwig said.

"We're not looking to finals yet. We've got three tough games coming up, so we're going to focus on that first," she said.

The Dogs will face Carlton, Melbourne and Geelong — all premiership contenders — in the final three games of the season.

Essendon will play North Melbourne, before facing Hawthorn and Collingwood.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/s.author: Monte Bovill
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Student Leila Clarke is running in the university elections. (ABC News: Mark Alexander)

For one week every year, the main concourse at the Australian National University (ANU) is known as "the gauntlet" as students navigate their way past their peers who are vying for votes.

Many turn down offers of pamphlets and how-to-vote cards, but for Leila Clarke, that hasn't deterred her from running in the student elections.

"The university is supposed to serve students; we are here to learn," the third-year law and international relations student said.

"If they are not listening to what we have to say, a lot of the time they get things wrong."

Student Audrey Clementine says student politics is important. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

It is a sentiment shared by fellow candidate Audrey Clementine, who said many students want to contribute to the future of their university.

"I really think that student democracy has an impact," the second-year student said.

Student Seamus Giveen dressed as a beer on campus. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

This year's campaign has featured slick social media videos and eye-catching stunts, which has included some candidates jumping into Canberra's Lake Burley Griffin and the creek that runs through the ANU campus.

One of the candidates, Seamus Giveen, was dressed as a beer to entice students to vote.

The ANU has seen a record number of nominations at its student elections. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

But beyond the colour of student politics, many argue it's a crucial platform for students to air their concerns and to get institutions to act.

At the ANU, a record number of nominations were received this year, which follows a tumultuous time at the institution.

The university had embarked on, and later abandoned, a $250 million cost-cutting endeavour which sparked staff and student protests and badly tarred the university's reputation.

Genevieve Bell stepped down as vice-chancellor in September last year, followed by Julie Bishop resigning as chancellor in May.

ANU Students’ Association president Charley Ellwood says students want failures by university management fixed. (ABC News: Mark Alexander)

The current president of the ANU Students' Association Charley Ellwood said students haven't shied away from being assertive with the university.

"University management will try to do things which seem to be at odds with what students want," he said.

Student Iz Coombs says the union should amplify the voices of students. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The relevance of student elections is often drawn into question, with only about 10 per cent of the student population at the ANU voting.

There is also longstanding criticism that, for some, student politics is just a stepping stone to a career in politics.

"I think the student union should primarily be for the purpose of helping our students and letting their voice be heard."

Some ANU students are spending the week campaigning for votes. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

For Mr Ellwood, having students at the table when the university is making decisions is essential.

"We have seen many examples of where students and student unions have pushed back against things that universities, but also politics in general, have done," he said.

"There have been plenty of times where our input has been disregarded, where I have personally felt quite undermined.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Workplace Accidents and Incidents

Mental health claims to WorkCover have increased by 108 per cent since 2021-2022. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The number of mental health-related claims to Queensland's workers' compensation insurer has more than doubled since 2021.

Unions and lawyers worry the state government may tighten eligibility criteria to offset the trend.

An independent review into the scheme is set to be finalised in the second half of 2026.

Mental health claims to Queensland's state-owned workers' compensation insurer have more than doubled in the past five years.

Unions and lawyers are concerned the government may try to clamp down on eligibility to stifle the trend.

Data from WorkCover's annual report shows 4,110 mental injury claims were accepted in the last financial year marking a 108 per cent increase from 1,974 claims in 2021-2022.

Maurice Blackburn workers' compensation lawyer, Alison Barrett said the climbing figures are not just happening in Queensland, but nationally too.

Alison Barrett, Principal Lawyer, Supervising Principal at Maurice Blackburn Lawyers. (Supplied)

Ms Barrett said mental injury claims can be for diagnoses like post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, adjustment disorders or psychological injuries as a result of a physical injury.

She said there's no one explanation for why they are on the rise but greater awareness may be one element.

"I think it is a very small part of it," she said.

"I think the bigger issue is that there are very real psychosocial hazards in our workplaces; we're seeing things like excessive workloads … occupational violence and aggression … bullying and harassment, exposure to more trauma in the workplace."

Former WorkCover deputy chair, now General Secretary of the Queensland Council of Unions, Jacqueline King, said it was no coincidence mental injury claims were rising, in line with reported assaults of frontline workers.

QCU general secretary Jacqueline King said workers were being exposed to increasing levels of violence and trauma. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

"Certainly, the rise in the psychological claims was being driven out of the public sector … [from] Queensland Health, Education Queensland, Queensland Police Service, Corrective Services, Youth Justice [and] Child Safety," Ms King said.

The annual report stated those who suffer from mental injuries are less likely to return to work, 71.4 per cent, when compared with those who are physically injured, 93.2 per cent.

Mental health claims also resulted in longer periods off work, 123 average annual paid days, compared with 47 days for those with physical injuries.

WorkCover's annual report found those who suffered from mental injuries were less likely to return to work. (ABC News: Stephen Cavenagh)

Mental injuries accounted for $334 million in payouts with an average claim cost of $25,138.

An independent review of the WorkCover scheme is currently underway, to ensure whether it remains fit for purpose.

Part of the review will look at the rise of mental injuries, and whether changes to the scheme are needed to ensure its sustainability.

Topic:
