Topic:
State and Territory Government

But Ms Barrett fears this will lead to less people being able to access compensation for mental injuries.

"We're definitely concerned that the rising psychological injury claims could lead to a policy response that's focused on restricting access to compensation, rather than actually addressing why workers are becoming psychologically injured in the first place," she said.

It's a concern shared by Ms King.

"[These workers could be] forced into the welfare system or alternatively, if they're lucky enough, they can get access to insurance through their superannuation," Ms King said.

Ms King said mental health claims were linked to rising assaults against frontline workers. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Both Ms Barrett and Ms King have called on the government to focus its efforts on treating the cause of psychological injuries, not the symptom.

"The better response is to prevent the injuries, improve workplace safety, provide earlier support rather than taking a knife to compensation entitlements, which we've seen in other states in Australia," Ms Barrett said.

A spokesperson for the Office of Industrial Relations (OIR) said in a statement, "Reducing risks of psychological injuries is just as important as physical ones, and employers have a range of responsibilities as well as resources to support workers."

On the OIR's website, it stated the review is expected to be finalised in the second half of 2026.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Domestic Violence

Fitness influencer Sam Wood was charged with domestic violence offences after he allegedly strangled his wife during a family argument in Noosa. (Supplied: 28 by Sam Wood, Facebook)

As Sam Wood sat in his cell on Thursday afternoon, he leaned forward.

Days earlier, the 46-year-old television personality was charged with assaulting and strangling his wife on a family holiday in Noosa.

Police allege Mr Wood became involved in a family argument in Noosa on Saturday night before he assaulted and strangled his wife.

Instead of flying back to Melbourne with his family, the fitness guru was confined to a police watch house.

After a long preamble, the magistrate delivered news Mr Wood did not want to hear.

His bail application was refused, with the wealthy businessman ordered to remain behind bars.

The alleged incident at the luxury beachside resort spanned a short period with devastating consequences.

In Noosa on Saturday night, police allege Mr Wood threw his wife against a wall and tried to strangle her after an argument.

Snezana Wood and her daughter Eve Markoski-Wood, either side of Sam Wood. (Supplied)

The prosecutor told the court of an incident "of a similar nature" in Victoria a few years ago.

"It involved choking, he also threw her up against a wall and floor and tried to strangle her," sergeant Jeanette Grigoris told the court.

If you need help immediately, call emergency services on Triple Zero.

Magistrate Janelle Boegheim said while no police statement was made, the alleged incident and the "history of the relationship" would be admissible as evidence.

"To be clear, that [Victorian] allegation is no proof of any criminal conduct," Ms Boegheim said.

The court heard Ms Wood's video statement described her husband as "volatile and prone to angry outbursts" and she was "compelled to walk on eggshells around him".

Sam Wood appeared via video link in the Maroochydore Magistrates Court on Thursday. (Supplied: @scottbreton)

The court also heard Mr Wood's bail conditions would involve seeking therapeutic intervention due to a severe depressive disorder.

"He alleges he did not share [this] with his wife or family members to protect them," Ms Boegheim said.

Mr Wood's lawyer told the court his client denied both charges and had never faced the criminal justice system.

In 2015, Samuel James Wood was a personal trainer at his gym in Melbourne's south-east when he was selected as the lead of The Bachelor.

The reality TV dating show was relatively new to Australia and quickly gained a loyal following.

Sam Wood rose to fame after featuring on the reality TV show The Bachelor in 2015. (Supplied: The Bachelor Australia, Facebook)

In the final episode, Sam chose Snezana, a single mother from Perth, as his winner. The couple married in 2018.

The series also provided the platform to launch his next project, 28 by Sam Wood.

The fitness platform targeting women quickly took off, and earned him a fortune.

Mr Wood sold the business to pharma billionaire Dennis Bastas in 2022 for a reported $71 million and acquired a small stake in the larger business.

The former Bachelor star founded a fitness program targeting women called 28 by Sam Wood. (Supplied: 28 by Sam Wood, Facebook)

While he relinquished ownership, he remained the public face of the popular program.

But on Tuesday, the company severed all ties with Mr Wood and scrubbed his face from the platform's website.

The atmosphere outside court on Thursday afternoon was tinged with anticipation.

Dozens of journalists, photographers and cameramen — some who travelled from interstate — crowded the footpath outside Maroochydore Magistrates Court.

Dozens of journalists crowded Maroochydore Magistrates Court on Thursday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Josh Dye)

As journalists filled the foyer waiting for the courtroom to open, a passing police officer said: "What's everyone here for?"

Many members of the media expected he would be granted bail, with plans hatched to capture the moment he would walk out of the watch house, through a throng of reporters and into a waiting vehicle.

When Mr Wood's lawyers arrived, his father Andrew was also in tow.

The 73-year-old was a key part of the bail application, with a mooted plan for Mr Wood to live with his father about 50 kilometres from the family home in Melbourne.

Inside court with a room full of journalists, Andrew Wood cut a lone figure sitting in support of his son, who was beamed into the courtroom via video link.

Sam Wood's father, Andrew Wood, entered the court with Mr Wood's legal team. (ABC News: Nykayla Dux)

The next 90 minutes shocked observers in court one as graphic details about the alleged incident were aired.

By the time the acting magistrate read out her decision to refuse bail, most in the room were unsurprised.

Under Queensland law, strangulation does not have to be prolonged and can last only a few seconds.

The offence, which was only added a decade ago, carries a maximum seven-year jail sentence.

The prosecutor told the court on Thursday that Mr Wood could expect jail time if convicted.

Following the hearing, Mr Wood was transferred to Wacol prison in Brisbane's south-west.

Sam Wood was transferred to the Brisbane Correctional Facility in Wacol. (ABC News: Leonie Mellor)

His legal team is preparing to file a bail application in the Supreme Court, which could be heard as early as next week.

His defence team may again seek to contest the strength of the prosecution's evidence, which solicitor Mathew Cuskelly attempted to do on Thursday.

Fitness influencer Sam Wood will launch a new fight for bail in Queensland's highest court after he was remanded in custody yesterday.

Mr Cuskelly told the court the lack of photographic evidence of Ms Wood's neck area was relevant given the strangulation charge.

"One would assume the investigators would have photographed that area, but they are absent," he told the court.

Mr Cuskelly also said a doctor's opinion should have been sought to comment on Ms Wood's injuries, and that the responding paramedic's evidence should be approached "cautiously".

Pending the outcome of any Supreme Court bail application, Mr Wood will remain in prison ahead of his next court appearance on the Sunshine Coast on November 23.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/e.title: Man fined $10k for illegal dump that left $3m clean-up bill
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/e.author: Elise Kinsella
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Land Pollution

The site in Wollert was filled with 11,000 tonnes of contaminated soil and industrial rubbish. (Supplied: EPA)

A Melbourne man has been fined $10,000 for illegally dumping 11,000 tonnes of waste on land he was renting from the local council.

The City of Whittlesea spent $3 million cleaning up the site.

An environmental law expert says illegal dumping fines are often lower than the cost of legally disposing of waste.

A man has been fined $10,000 for running an illegal tip on land leased from a suburban Melbourne council, but that penalty was a fraction of the $3 million clean-up bill the council was left with.

Mohamad Yassin Yousef Sadek was convicted of environmental offences in August in the Heidelberg Magistrates' Court, where he was also ordered to pay $5,000 to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to cover its costs.

The EPA prosecuted the case, alleging Sadek was a leaseholder on land owned by Whittlesea City Council in 2021 when he did deals with truck drivers to illegally accept industrial waste from their worksites over two months.

The EPA said 11,000 tonnes of contaminated soil and industrial rubbish later had to be cleared from the property in Wollert on Melbourne's northern fringe.

Some of the waste contained asbestos.

The EPA found asbestos in soil tested from a number of locations on the property. (Supplied: EPA)

The clean-up cost local ratepayers $3 million.

Environmental law expert Brad Jessup said Victoria has an illegal dumping problem, and he was concerned small penalties created a financial incentive for polluters.

"This is an example where the fine was likely less than the costs of [lawfully] disposing of the waste," Dr Jessup said.

EPA inspectors first visited the council-owned land in September 2021 following a tip-off that waste was being illegally stored there.

"EPA officers observed built-up areas of mudstone and crushed rock material, textiles, brick fragments, metal, timber and grey fibrous cement materials," the agency said.

It said soil testing detected asbestos at seven locations on the property.

Melbourne councils are struggling to combat the rise of illegal dumping, despite over $21 million of funding from the Victorian state government.

The EPA said Sadek failed to comply with environmental notices it issued over a nearly two-year period.

In July 2023, the EPA ordered the council, as landowner, to remove all industrial waste.

The EPA reported the council had to clear more than 300 truck and trailer loads of contaminated soil and waste from the property, which came with a multi-million-dollar cost.

It took another three years after this for the criminal case against Sadek to be finalised.

In a statement to the ABC, Whittlesea City Council said the scale of environmental damage to its land was significant.

The City of Whittlesea was left with a huge bill to remove rubbish from the Wollert property.  (Supplied: Facebook/City of Whittlesea)

"Council was required by the EPA to undertake remediation works after the head tenant and sub tenants failed to do so," it said.

"With the criminal proceedings against the sub tenants now concluded and majority of the remediation works completed, council is considering all available options to recover the costs incurred."

Dr Jessup said environmental laws had been reformed in recent years, giving prosecutors the power to seek larger fines for polluters and strip them of the proceeds of their offending.

In Sadek's case, neither of those powers were used.

The legal expert said part of the issue was that the EPA preferred to prosecute environmental matters in the magistrates' court.

"The magistrates' court has caps and has limits on the kind of fines it can issue, and there is less willingness to engage with some of the more complex legal topics around sentencing," Dr Jessup said.

"We're not seeing large penalties that deter and we're not seeing recouping of profits."

Brad Jessup says the small fines handed out for illegal dumping are not enough of a deterrent. (Supplied)

A public register of EPA court cases that have been finalised shows 49 cases have gone before the magistrates' court since 2025, with just two cases in the Supreme Court and one in the County Court.

Of the cases listed on the EPA's register, the majority of environmental offences resulted in fines of less than $10,000.

Whereas magistrates have to consider a range of factors in handing down fines, he said laws that came in five years ago allowing prosecutors to recover proceeds of environmental offending were more clear-cut.

However, he said he was unaware of any cases where those laws — which he said were a more powerful deterrent — had been used.

"The law that's not being used is essentially an accounting tool," he said, allowing courts to "just take that [profit] away."

He acknowledged it was more expensive and time-consuming to bring cases in higher courts.

The EPA said it considered the appropriate jurisdiction for every matter and was not driven by budget constraints.

"EPA's enforcement decisions are based on the facts, evidence and legal considerations of each case, including the available sentencing and enforcement outcomes," a spokesperson said.

The ABC could not reach Sadek for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/r.title: Russian couple's home targeted in Melbourne arson attack
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/r.author: Jessica Longbottom
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Cars at the home of Alexei Shishkin and Inessa Shishkina were among those targeted in firebombings across Melbourne this week. (YouTube)

Two cars firebombed during a spate of arson attacks in Melbourne were at the home of Russian Australian  philanthropist Inessa Shishkina and her businessman husband Alexei Shishkin.

Their son, Erik Shishkin, was jailed earlier this year over a Reservoir home invasion.

Police are trying to determine whether more than a dozen car firebombings across the city this week are related.

The property of a Russian Australian philanthropist whose son was jailed over a home invasion was among the targets in a string of arson attacks in Melbourne this week.

The ABC can reveal two cars at the Balwyn North home of Inessa Shishkina and her husband Alexei Shishkin were firebombed early on Wednesday morning.

Mr Shishkin began importing Australian grocery items to Russia in the 1990s and, according to a video featuring his wife, was the first person to open an Australian supermarket in the country before the couple moved to Australia in 2001.

In a subtitled 2020 interview with YouTube channel Foreign Influence, Ms Shishkina said her husband no longer had work ties to Russia but was involved in some construction projects in Australia.

Alexei Shishkin imported Australian groceries to Russia before moving out of the country. (YouTube)

She said she was involved in organising charity events and donating to them, and collected donations for her church's elderly community.

In a written statement to the ABC, Ms Shishkina said she had been deeply affected by Wednesday's firebombing, and it had rocked her "sense of security and confidence in the future".

"Twenty-five years ago, we chose Australia as our home because we believed it was a safe, stable and comfortable country to live in," she said.

"We do not harm anyone, we have no enemies and we pay substantial taxes."

The pair's son, Erik Shishkin, was imprisoned in June for breaking into a Reservoir home with an accomplice in May 2024.

He was found to have brandished a gun at the home’s occupants before he and his co-offender were overpowered and fled.

Erik Shishkin was also charged with possessing a drug of dependence and dealing with the proceeds of crime and was sentenced to three years' jail.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Jessica Longbottom at jessicalongbottom@protonmail.com. If you're sharing sensitive information, read our tips on how to contact us confidentially.

Police are trying to determine whether the 14 car firebombings over five days in Taylors Hill, Keilor, Balwyn North, Maidstone, Reservoir and Oakleigh East are related.

A 13-year-old boy is fighting for life after he was burned in the bombing in Taylors Hill, in Melbourne’s north-west, on Monday morning. He is believed to have been paid to carry out the crime.

Arson Squad detectives work at the Balwyn North home. (ABC News)

On Thursday, Acting Commander Troy Papworth said police believed the rise in arson attacks was linked to organised crime and appeared to be an intimidation tactic.

The ABC has discovered that one of the cars destroyed in Springvale was owned by a now-closed car repairs business in Hoppers Crossing, Vivid Finish Accident Repairs.

When the ABC visited the home on Thursday, the family said it was the second time they had been targeted.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/j.title: Mexican men guilty of murdering brothers Jake and Callum Robinson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/j.author: Brad Ryan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Australian brothers Jake (left) and Callum Robinson were killed while on a surfing trip in Mexico. (Supplied)

A judge has convicted three Mexican men of the murders of Jake and Callum Robinson and Carter Rhoad.

The brothers from Western Australia and their American friend were robbed and shot dead while on a surfing holiday.

The convicted killers will be sentenced on October 16.

Three men have been found guilty of killing Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad while they were camping in Mexico in 2024.

Jesús Gerardo, known as "El Kekas", Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús — whose full names have been withheld for legal reasons — have been on trial in a Mexican court.

A judge today found all three men guilty of aggravated homicide and several related offences.

The three victims were killed during a surfing trip in Mexico's Baja California region, on the Pacific coast, in April 2024.

The brothers' parents, Debra and Martin Robinson, travelled from Western Australia to attend the trial and were in court for the verdict.

Martin and Debra Robinson have attended each day of the trial in Mexico. (Reuters: Enrique Botello)

Ms Robinson cried and embraced an Australian consular representative when it was handed down.

Judge Raul Hernandez Arellano conveyed his condolences to the couple and told them he was ashamed the murders had taken place in his country.

He said he wanted to deliver justice but could only do what the laws in Mexico allowed him to.

A day earlier, Ms Robinson asked the court to hand down maximum prison sentences.

"No sentence can bring Callum and Jake back; nothing can undo what has happened, but accountability matters," she said in a victim impact statement.

Jake Robinson (right) had travelled to America to visit his brother Callum (left). (Supplied: Instagram)

The men will be sentenced on October 16.

The prosecution had told the trial that the victims were murdered during a robbery gone wrong.

The defence had attempted to argue there was not enough evidence to prove the case.

But the judge found several witnesses had given credible and consistent evidence.

Jesús Gerardo, alias El Kekas, had a reputation as a violent hit man, the trial heard.  (Supplied: Mexican police handout)

Ángel Jesús has been in custody in a local jail. (Supplied)

Irineo Francisco has links to the Sinaloa cartel, according to court documents. (Supplied)

They included Ari Gisell, the ex-girlfriend of Jesús Gerardo, who was previously jailed for instigating the robbery that led to the murders.

She told the trial Jesús Gerardo had described to her how he killed the men and joked about how they cried.

He had said the victims had handed over their car keys and wallets and "begged not to be killed", according to her testimony.

Jake, 31, had travelled to California to see Callum, 32, before they travelled south to Mexico.

Both men were originally from Perth.

Jake was a doctor who was due to start a new job at a Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.

Callum was a talented lacrosse player who had moved to the US to pursue the sport.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-1.title: 'Parasitic twinning' could explain calf born with two extra legs
https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-1.author: Kemii Maguire and Brandon Long
https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2026-1.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Veterinary Medicine

The heifer calf was born with four regular legs and two on her head. (Supplied: Pittsworth and District Vet Services)

Experts say "parasitic twinning" or genetic mutations could explain why a calf grew extra limbs in utero.

Veterinarian Megan Smith operated for 90 minutes to remove the extra limbs from the heifer's head.

The calf has made a full recovery and has been returned to her mother.

"Parasitic twinning" could explain why a southern Queensland calf was born with two extra legs growing from its head.

The heifer, nicknamed Spider, made a full recovery after surgery to remove the limbs when she was just over a week old.

A geneticist said it was difficult to determine how common birth anomalies were in cattle, in part due to a lack of research data.

Spider is reunited with her mother. (Supplied: Pittsworth and District Vet Services)

But for the vet who helped reunite Spider with her mother, there was no doubt it was a once-in-a-career operation.

Imke Tammen from the University of Sydney's School of Veterinary Science has studied the inherited traits of livestock for more than 30 years.

Dr Tammen said exactly why Spider was born with extra legs would likely remain a mystery, but abnormalities could happen in the womb.

The rare phenomenon, where an embryo begins developing as twins but stalls, can leave part of the second animal attached to the first.

Dr Tammen said there could be other explanations too.

"Sometimes … something goes wrong in the development of just one animal and that can result in additional legs," she said.

Imke Tammen says researchers need more data on birth abnormalities in cattle. (Supplied: Australian Museum, Emlyn Crockett)

In some cattle, extra limbs can also be linked to inherited genetic conditions.

Scientists have identified genetic mutations responsible for some forms of these abnormalities, meaning DNA testing can sometimes help farmers identify animals carrying the problem.

However, Dr Tammen said there was not enough information to say how common these conditions were in cattle.

She urged farmers who discovered an unusual birth to report it to their veterinarian as collecting information about cases can help researchers understand what causes them.

For Pittsworth veterinarian Megan Smith, the case was unlike anything she had seen in her 20-year career.

The calf's owners, who wished to remain private, were considering putting her down, but the vet offered to attempt the risky surgery at minimal cost.

Megan Smith says the case is unlike anything she has seen in her 20-year career. (Supplied: Pittsworth and District Vet Services)

She and a veterinary nurse anaesthetised the calf, which appeared to have some Angus genetics, and spent more than 90 minutes removing the unusual limbs.

Dr Smith said the case was a rare opportunity for her team and a chance to give the calf a normal life.

"Sometimes you can have these great opportunities and can achieve great things, so it's awesome."

The calf received 28 stitches during the operation. (Supplied: Pittsworth and District Vet Services)

The extra legs could have caused serious problems as the calf grew, including making her head uncomfortable and affecting her balance.

Spider recovered quickly.

Dr Smith said the calf was drinking from a bottle just an hour after waking from the operation before returning to her mother.

Dr Tammen praised the regional vets for taking on the surgical challenge.

"I think that's excellent," she said.

"It's improving the welfare of that calf and is a very appropriate way of ensuring that the calf has a good life."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/s.title: Shop owners ramp up security due to rise in Pokémon card thefts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/s.author: Sharne Wakefield
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Pokémon trading cards were allegedly stolen and a store ceiling was damaged at a Blair Athol store in early September. (Supplied: Benjamin Hill)

Game and collectibles shop owners are bolstering their security because of a rise in Pokémon card thefts.

One card store owner says almost $20,000 worth of Pokémon and other trading cards were allegedly stolen from his shop.

Another trader says these cards have a high resale value.

When Benjamin Hill went to his collectables store one day, he was shocked to find the ceiling smashed through and almost $20,000 worth of Pokémon and other trading cards gone.

"It was pretty confronting to be honest … I was aware this could happen, but you never think it would be you," the shop owner said.

"I was shaking a little bit as well; it took me a few days to get over it."

Mr Hill said the alleged thief had sneaked through the back toilet door and crawled through the ceiling at his Blair Athol shop in early September.

Benjamin Hill's trading card store was allegedly broken into last month. (ABC News: Sharne Wakefield)

He said Pokémon trading cards could have been the target, as they generally cost between 50 cents and $50 but some rare cards were being auctioned for millions of dollars.

Mr Hill said these trading cards were high in value, untraceable and easy to resell.

"It's just a little bit of cardboard that can fit in your pocket. You could have $1,000 in your pocket," he said.

Pokemon trading cards have been the target of thieves because some are of high value. (ABC News: Sharne Wakefield)

SA Police told ABC News a 47-year-old man was this week arrested and charged with serious criminal trespassing, theft and property damage over the alleged break-in at Mr Hill's store.

Mr Hill said he had since upgraded his security and taken all expensive items off site.

In recent months, tens of thousands of dollars' worth of trading cards were stolen from collectables shops in Brisbane, Perth and Melbourne.

SA Police arrested a 29-year-old man who allegedly smashed a glass cabinet at a Noarlunga toy store and stole Pokémon cards last month.

ABC News spoke to several Adelaide shop owners, including one who was spending about $20,000, to bolster security measures such as installing bollards, fog alarms, roller shutters and new CCTV.

Trading cards were allegedly stolen from Benjamin Hill's store. (Supplied: Benjamin Hill)

Card shop owner Hung Nguyen is one of those taking extra precautions.

"What's happening around Melbourne and Queensland, it's just made us think twice about looking into our security a bit more," he said.

"I guess there's nothing stopping us from comparing ourselves to a jewellery shop."

Hung Nguyen has installed bollards and security alarm at his store. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

The Japanese game is 30 years old but Pokémon trading cards have seen a global resurgence in recent years, prompting its government to consider a clampdown on the industry.

Due to a lack of supply, high demand and influx of investors, Pokémon cards are soaring in price, with an American YouTuber selling an ultra-rare card for a record $22.6 million this year.

Recently, these Japanese cards have been outperforming Bitcoin and the S&P 500 on the stock market.

Hung Nguyen says he has increased security at his game store. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

"Like a box that was worth $100 to $200 is now worth $8,000," Mr Nguyen said.

The trader said most of these cards were being resold for more than double their retail price.

"You could say the return on investment is 100 per cent, which is crazy," Mr Nguyen said.

"So for them, it's, 'Why wouldn't I get into it and make a quick flip?'"

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.title: Father's trust in child care shattered by son's shocking injury
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.author: Max Tillman and Genevieve Blandin de Chalain
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Genevieve Blandin de Chalain

A Tamworth father has spoken out after his child broke their femur at day care.  (ABC News Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

A Tamworth father's trust has been shattered after his five-year-old child suffered a broken femur while in care.

Darcy Galliano says emergency services were not contacted and the incident was not reported to authorities.

The NSW Early Learning Commissioner says they will work with Little Kindy to attempt to bring the operation up to standard during an enforced six-month closure.

Putting a child into the care of another requires parents to take a leap of faith.

For Tamworth father Darcy Galliano, that bond of trust was breached when he was called to collect his five-year-old son from childcare.

Staff at the centre told him the boy had a dislocated knee; his instincts as a parent told him otherwise.

"My son was in excruciating pain; it [looked] like he was going to blackout," Mr Galliano said.

"Me being a father, I realised his knee [wasn't] dislocated, but something else was wrong.

"When I lifted him, [the child's mother] could hear him scream from the Woolworths car park across the road."

According to the centres' incident report, medical personal were not contacted, and the incident was not reported to authorities.  (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

According to an incident report from the Little Kindy Childcare Centre seen by the ABC, Mr Galliano's son was attempting to jump over a wooden bench when he slipped and hit his left knee just before 3pm on September 1.

Staff applied an ice pack and contacted his mother.

According to the incident report, medical personnel were not contacted, and the incident was not reported to authorities.

Subsequent medical examinations revealed the child had suffered a spiral fracture to his left femur.

He underwent emergency surgery and will spend six months in a full leg cast.

Little Kindy Early was suspended for at least six months for multiple compliance breaches.  (ABC News: Max Tillman)

Eight days after the incident, the NSW Early Learning Commission (ELC) closed the centre for six months, citing "ongoing non-compliance and child safety risks".

Among the breaches listed in the commission's report were a failure to maintain a safe environment, a failure to report incidents and inadequate child protection practices

NSW Early Learning Commissioner Darryl Currie also highlighted "unclean and hazardous areas presenting significant risks such as inadequate soft-fall surfacing beneath equipment and unstable or unsecured furniture" as well as "non-compliance with record-keeping and restriction of personal devices".

He said the centre was known to the regulator.

"There had been other compliance actions in the past, in this case," Mr Currie said.

"With regards to this matter, it was considered there was an immediate risk to children."

The NSW Early Learning Commission says it will work with Little Kindy to bring the business up to standard over the next six months.  (ABC News: Max Tillman)

Mr Currie said the ELC would be "working with the provider to actually attempt to get them up to what is required to be able to provide a safe service in NSW".

Little Kindy operates three centres across Tamworth, in northern NSW, with its remaining centres in East and West Tamworth still operating.

It operates 24 centres across the country, with 13 in NSW.

Little Kindy has been contacted for comment.

The latest data shows a dramatic increase in the number of NSW centres having their approvals cancelled.

Between April 1 and June 30 this year, 174 services were delisted, compared to 20 in the same period last year.

But the ELC said all but one of those cancellations were due to the operator letting their approval lapse by not providing a service for more than 12 months.

Marg Rogers, an associate professor in early childhood education at the University of New England, said the temporary closure of a childcare centre in a regional town could have lasting effects on the community.

"We live in a childcare desert in all parts of Australia that are regional, remote or rural … [which] means there are at least three families applying for one space," she said.

Marg Rogers says closures can have major ripple effects in close-knit communities.  (ABC News: Max Tillman)

"That means it has an implication on parents' ability to go to work, and to trust services.

"So a closure, even though it may be very justified, can have a huge ripple effect on the community."

Darcy Galliano fears for his son's long-term health and future job prospects due to his injury. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

Mr Galliano said his trust in others to care for his child had been shattered.

"He's a strong kid, and we can deal with it, but what happens if something happened to a six-month-old baby?' he said.

"Every other child and every other parent [enrolled at Little Kindy] has been impacted, and I'm sure there are single parents who have been displaced because of an inability to keep up to standards.

Nic Maddinson, one of a number of Australian cricketers batting out of position, made a 33-ball duck on day one. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

It was Steve Waugh — Mr Mental Disintegration himself — who once said the most emotionally taxing aspect of his time as the most important man in Australian cricket was not the burden of captaincy, nor the concurrent need to keep making big runs, but his role as a national selector.

How long to wait for a treasured teammate's form to come right, when the axe might end his career? Should he be replaced with fresh blood or someone on a second or third chance, as Waugh himself had once been? What was the right balance of talent and personalities?

Overnight in Durban, Waugh's man-management issues seemed trifling compared to the self-inflicted problems of Australia's current selectors. But you'd need a very specific combination of tarot cards and crystals to work out which question of George Bailey's led to the answer "Nic Maddinson".

The final analysis on day one was not entirely disastrous. Australia stumbled to 6-187 before bad light stopped play and there were at least positive signs in a few problematic areas.

One was a solid start from Marnus Labuschagne, whose momentary lapse on the brink of lunch ended a sparkling partnership with Steve Smith. The other was a steady hand from Matt Renshaw, who was undefeated on 46 at the day's premature end.

Matt Renshaw is stranded four runs short of his first Test half-century in nine years as bad light halts play on the first day of the opening Test against South Africa.

There were deeper currents, though. Troubling ones. What stood out was not just the sense of a well-drilled bowling attack reminding the world why South Africa was the reigning world champion, but of Australia, with its makeshift batting order and selection on the fly, presenting as an increasingly confused rabble.

Maddinson's mere selection was contentious enough; he had not played a first-class match in 19 months. The corollary was throwing him to the wolves as opener on a pitch offering lateral movement. That second part was so surprising to most onlookers that the host broadcaster initially had him down as batting at five.

But then, how else could it have played out? Had Cooper Connolly got the nod instead, he probably would have slotted in at five and Renshaw would have moved up to open with Travis Head, himself a world-class number five whose impact in Tests is now being blunted by his ongoing hostage ordeal at the top of the order. Further problems flow from there.

You had to feel for Maddinson. Mark Waugh, who was among the selectors who picked the left-hander for his first three Tests in 2016, has since admitted he had been discarded too quickly. Now he's been brought back almost at random and given this thankless task.

Maddinson's 33-ball duck was awful to watch, but one would hope he's backed to make a slightly better fist of whatever follows.

Another thing Steve Waugh used to do was make it clear to each player in his team what was expected of them in their specific role. It's hard to imagine things being phrased so plainly now. Aside from Labuschagne and Smith, could any current Australian batsman say he's in the right spot for the right reason?

Another cheap dismissal for Travis Head raises questions about his experimental role as opener. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

At 32, Head's identity crisis should, on current evidence, be considered a serious matter for the future of this team.

Right now, we are being asked to accept that Renshaw — an undoubtedly tough and capable player whose Test record is nevertheless modest — needs to bat where he is most comfortable, and that as a result, Head, now in his prime years, needs to play an essentially experimental role that is clearly not suited to him.

It is true that Bailey's job has been made harder by injuries to Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, and a dearth of irresistible opening candidates in the Sheffield Shield. But the strangest aspect of all the pre-tour kvetching over selection was how much of it centered on Labuschagne, who was and remains the logical choice at three.

Far more baffling, in hindsight, was the lack of focus on Bailey's claim that the number-three slot could be just as easily filled by Connolly, who has never made a first-class century, or the since-injured Inglis, neither of whom have batted higher than five for their state.

Even in this era of "false threes" and result pitches, the linchpin positions in the top order should surely not be devalued so casually. Australia is now approaching double digits for opening combinations of the post-Warner era.

Anyway, that is what Australia could have controlled. What it still can't, it seems, is the sideways movement of medium pacers. When this tour was merely on the horizon, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi loomed as the destroyers.

Both are missing in Durban, yet Marco Jansen and Wiaan Mulder caused Australia just as many problems without Jansen ever really hitting their stride.

It made for an absorbing battle, but for Australia things could actually have been far worse. We must now accept a world order in which the combination of the words "Ollie Robinson" and "Ashes hero" are not just plausible but a distinct possibility.

The consolation is that a Test series is never decided on its opening day and can therefore often be taken with a grain of salt, per Merv Hughes's tinder-dry diary entry following the first day of another Test series, three decades ago:

"Back to hotel. Few beers downstairs, then up to room … Have room service. Watch Cape Fear. Quiet night." Thus ended the day Shane Warne bowled the ball of the century.

Nothing so dramatic transpired this time around but, for Australia, you sense the road ahead will be trying.

The longest federal government shutdown in US history has ended (Reuters: John Pryke)

The White House has offered the the new White House press secretary position to Katie Zacharia.

She is a communications adviser for US President Donald Trump's Truth Social platform, and has previously served ‌as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

Karoline Leavitt was the White House press secretary before leaving the job in August.

Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for US President Donald Trump's Truth Social platform, has been offered the position of White House press secretary.

The vacancy was created by Karoline Leavitt's departure from the role in August.

Ms Zacharia did ‌not immediately respond to a request for comment.

If she accepts ‌the role, she would fill ‌a critical role in the Trump administration before next month's midterm congressional elections.

The New York Times first reported the news and it was confirmed by a White House official on Friday, local time.

Ms Zacharia briefly served ‌as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security before departing in March.

Karoline Leavitt, who recently returned from maternity leave, says she has decided to quit as White House press secretary to focus on being a mother.

The conservative commentator is ‌a senior communications adviser ‌for Truth Social and the Trump Media & Technology ‌Group, according to her LinkedIn page.

Ms Zacharia previously worked as a legal ‌adviser for Fix California, a conservative group that aims to address what it describes as "the left’s stranglehold" on state politics.

The group was founded by Richard Grenell, who has served as Mr Trump's envoy to Venezuela ‌and is ‌the interim president and executive director of the Kennedy Center in Washington.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Shincheonji's founder Lee Man-Hee speaking at a bible seminar in Daegu, 2026. (Supplied: Shincheonji)

Eight months ago, the charities watchdog announced it was investigating Christian fringe group Shincheonji amid allegations that members were being subjected to manipulative tactics.

The group remains a registered charity in Australia, with tax concessions.

Advocates are calling for swift action and transparency.

South Korean Christian fringe group Shincheonji remains a registered charity in Australia, eight months after the charities watchdog announced it was investigating the sect.

Following an ABC investigation into Shincheonji's Melbourne chapter earlier this year, the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC) announced a probe into the group's charity status.

Previous ABC reporting uncovered the invasive, highly organised tactics members use to bring in new recruits, motivated by the indoctrinated belief that by recruiting they are doing God's work, and allegations they were brain-washing, financial abusing, and isolating members.

Shincheonji followers believe only those who have heard God's word through the group's founder and Messiah, 95-year-old Lee Man-hee, will be saved from the apocalypse.

Man-hee remains detained in South Korea for allegedly violating the Political Parties Act by orchestrating an illegal scheme for followers to join the conservative People Power Party, according to local media.

In 2021, Man-Hee was found guilty of embezzling the equivalent of $5.5 million and received a three-year suspended sentence in South Korea.

Shincheonji claims to have churches in more than 100 countries and a congregation of more than 300,000 members.

A 2025 Shicheonji Bible seminar in Gwangju. (Supplied: Shincheonji)

As an Australian registered charity, Shincheonji gets tax concessions.

Its charitable purpose, as registered with the ACNC, is "advancing religion".

At the time the ACNC announced its investigation, the regulator said it would "act firmly where vulnerable people or significant charity assets are at risk".

To be registered as a charity, a group must meet certain criteria, including being not-for-profit and having only charitable purposes that are for the public benefit.

While the charity is still registered, it is unclear if any regulatory action has been taken by the ACNC, as some actions, like issuing a warning, are made publicly available while others, such as when a matter is referred to another agency, are not disclosed.

An ACNC spokesperson said they could not speak publicly about the investigation, nor could they confirm if the investigation was ongoing or had concluded.

"Anyone can raise a concern about a charity with the ACNC, and we take all concerns seriously," the spokesperson said.

Shincheonji's Melbourne chapter has been contacted for comment.

The group's leader, Lee Man-hee, was born in 1931 in South Korea. (Supplied)

Maria Esguerra, director of cult survivor support group The Olive Leaf Network, said she continued to get regular requests for support from former or current Shincheonji members in Australia.

"From what we understand, [Shincheonji] has shifted toward hybrid recruitment strategies across social media, Discord, campus clubs, and dating apps," Ms Esguerra said.

"Despite rising awareness on university campuses, these adaptive tactics continue to target university students, international students, and young adults."

Maria Esguerra is worried about children who grow up in Shincheonji. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Ms Esguerra described Shincheonji's retention of their charity status as pointing to a "regulatory gap in public protection and oversight".

"Charity registration signals public trust and credibility; maintaining it provides an unearned badge of legitimacy that obscures risks to vulnerable individuals and families," she said.

She said there was an urgent need to align charitable status with transparency, public benefit and a duty of care.

"While the ACNC operates under procedural fairness and secrecy laws, this structural lag allows Shincheonji to retain tax concessions and public trust," she said.

Dariyn Girton was traumatised by her time as a member of Shincheonji. (ABC News: Scott Jewell)

Former Shincheonji member Dariyn Girton spent three years inside the Melbourne branch of Shincheonji and told her story to the ABC earlier this year.

Ms Girton said during her time in Shincheonji, she was pressured to give money beyond her means and sell her possessions to keep up with payments so she could make it into the "Kingdom of Heaven".

Do you know more? Contact Coco Veldkamp on email cocoveldkamp@proton.me.

Ms Girton said she was "disheartened" that the group was still operating as a charity.

"This organisation has done so much damage to unsuspecting victims across the world and on our own doorstep, with spiritual and financial abuse being just the tip of the iceberg," she said.

Assistant Minister for Charities Andrew Leigh said he could not comment on the investigation and could not confirm if it was ongoing or had closed.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.author: Cam Wilson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Cam Wilson recently came across an AI-generated book (pictured) that looked undeniably similar to the one he co-authored last year. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

A few months back, I was doomscrolling before bed when I received a WhatsApp message from a friend with a link to Amazon.

As someone who has spent years reporting on technology, and now solely on artificial intelligence, it's pretty common to get tips about something weird that was generated with AI.

Unusually, this tip was about me. Sort of.

The listing was for a book entitled Conspiracy Nation Exercises: Redefine Living Through Cam Wilson Teachings.

I couldn't know for sure it was something, and not someone, who'd decided to write a book about me, but there were signs.

The title closely resembled a book of mine that I co-wrote and published last year.

The AI-generated book (left) had a similar title to the original book (right). (ABC News: Scott Preston)

The "author", Leni McAllister, doesn't seem to exist, and the short blurb has the tell-tale signs of AI-generated writing.

Identifying "slop" becomes a sixth sense after you've seen enough of it.

Em dashes. The distinctive tempo. The blurb even had the "it's not X — it's Y" that AI seems to love.

So, I bought the book.

Two days later, it arrived in the mail. I didn't expect it to be so absurdly big. Like A4-sized-big.

I was able to quickly flick through its meagre 89 pages, although even that number gives a misleading impression about its seriousness. The text was double-spaced and printed in a very large size.

The moment my bemusement turned to hurt was when I realised that they had chosen Comic Sans — the most unserious of all fonts, and one more closely associated with primary school projects — as a suitable match for my "teachings".

The AI-generated book was printed double-spaced on huge pages and in the Comic Sans font. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

I'm not a full-time author but, by all accounts, making a living publishing in Australia is extremely gruelling.

I was holding something that probably took longer to leaf through than it did to generate. Filled with things I didn't say, poorly written and bizarrely laid out, it was extremely frustrating.

It felt like the exact opposite of the care and love we poured into our book.

It also felt like a physical slop that existed not to be enjoyed or understood, but to deceive a prospective reader just long enough to convince them to click "buy" online.

Global online marketplace Etsy is known as a home for the handmade, but users are reporting an influx of AI-generated products and, in some cases, copied artistic works.

I then discovered an infestation of other books online using an identical template, just for different authors and books.

One author who'd put out her debut book around the same time as me, Natalie Kyriacou, responded with exasperation when I sent her a link to Nature's Last Dance Exercises: Redefine Living through Natalie Kyriacou Teachings.

It turns out she already knew about this because she'd heard from those who mistakenly bought the fraudulent version of her book off Amazon.

"We have been trying to remove them but they pop up everywhere," she says.

Amazon admitted the listing for the AI book broke its guidelines. (Reuters: Pascal Rossignol)

So I sent Amazon a list of questions. The next day, the listing for "my" book was taken down.

The listing had broken Amazon's guidelines, I was told, although the exact rule that was broken wasn't clear. The company took others down, too.

"We have proactive and reactive methods that help us detect content that violates our guidelines, whether AI generated or not. We invest significant time and resources to ensure our guidelines are followed, and remove books that do not adhere to those guidelines," an Amazon spokesperson said in an email.

But when I asked for any information about who was behind it, the company didn't provide it.

"Looking into this for you," one staff member said.

Others have struggled to get AI books taken down, sometimes books that aren't just about them, but are attributed to them.

Australian Society of Authors chief executive Lucy Hayward says this has become so common as to be unremarkable.

"On the publication day for an author, you'll often see that there's already an AI-generated version of the book that's already been on sale," she says.

Hayward says there are obvious ways it hurts authors: they lose sales to the fakes, they get poor reviews because someone bought the slop and blamed them, it confuses people trying to buy the book, and they give up.

She says jobs many authors have done as side hustles, like copywriting, have been particularly affected by the spread of generative AI, and fraud is contributing to dropping reading rates.

Hayward says there are some simple fixes, such as requiring platforms like Amazon to effectively police these kinds of derivative works and requiring retailers to label AI-generated content so readers don't get tricked.

"Platforms should bear responsibility," she says.

But her remedies go further.

Hayward says AI companies need to do licensing deals with authors to compensate for the books they've taken and to do more to protect their intellectual property.

The leaked plans have sparked backlash from creatives and critics across the political spectrum.

The government has been quietly consulting on two proposed changes to copyright law to facilitate AI training in Australia.

Both plans would make training opt-out for authors and other creatives, meaning that the burden was on the individual, not the company, to stop their work being used to train AI.

AI companies say an opt-out system is necessary to allow legal AI training in Australia, something the federal government explicitly says it hopes will happen.

Haywood and other creators think the onus should be on AI companies to secure approval from creatives to use and protect their work

When I looked this week, I found dozens more AI-generated books still for sale.

It's not just on Amazon, either. Other platforms reportedly have similar issues.

I can't see any more ripoffs targeting me. Perhaps I should be offended; if my book was more popular, surely there'd be more imitations.

But it's telling that of all of the utopian AI futures that we're promised — abundance, the end of disease, happiness — tech executives' blue-sky thinking is still leaving creatives vulnerable.

Even though AI-enabled rip-offs are already happening en masse, authors are hoping there's more that can be done to protect their work in future.

Or, to quote "Leni McAllister" quoting "Cam Wilson": "This is not an ending. It's an invitation."

Nic Maddinson set a new Test record with his 33-ball duck as Steve Smith struggled on his return to South Africa. (Getty Images)

Nic Maddinson's unlikely Test return has ended with a historic duck as Australia's battered floundered despite a South African DRS debacle.

Here are the quick hits from the opening day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

Maddinson was unable to make the most of an early reprieve on day one. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

With almost a decade having passed since the last of his three Test appearances, veteran opener Nic Maddinson could have been forgiven for thinking his days in Australian whites were over.

But after being parachuted into the squad earlier this week, the 34-year-old's sensational return to the Test arena was cemented at the toss in Durban, with Pat Cummins confirming Maddinson would be the replacement for the injured Cameron Green.

In an even bigger surprise, he was in line to open his side's innings, with the also recently recalled Matt Renshaw dropping down the order.

Maddinson did not play at all in the last Sheffield Shield season, with his last First Class appearance having come back in March 2025.

And with Australia winning the toss and batting, he was put to the test immediately.

Maddinson looked both nervy and underdone in his drought-breaking Test knock, unable to get off the mark during his first 32 balls before being dismissed by his 33rd, the New South Welshman chopping onto his stumps off the bowling of Marco Jansen.

Unfortunately for Maddinson, it was a historic return as well as a miserable one, his 33-ball effort setting a new record for the longest duck by an Aussie opener in Test cricket.

Overall, it was the second-longest no score by an Australian in the history of the format, only behind Mark Whitney's 42-ball 0 in 1981.

Nic Maddinson was unable to make the most of an early reprieve. (Fox Cricket)

Only minutes earlier, Maddinson had been gifted a huge slice of luck.

With the opener swinging across the line wildly, a Wiaan Mulder delivery thudded into his front pad. There was a big appeal, but umpire Richard Kettlebrough was unmoved.

South African captain Temba Bavuma indicated Maddinson had gotten some bat on ball and opted against the first review of the series.

And there certainly were two noises but replays showed Maddinson's willow had gotten nowhere near the ball, instead clipping his pad.

The South Africans watched the big screen ruefully as it showed the three reds that would have sent Maddinson back to the pavilion.

It was an unconvincing start for the South Africans as far DRS was concerned, with Bavuma also burning two reviews on appeals that didn't have a whole lot going for them.

First, Marnus Labuschagne survived a referral on a ball that swung too sharply and was projected to be missing leg stump.

Then, the hosts wasted a second review when a steepling Marco Jansen delivery caught Renshaw on the arm. The ball had looped up to wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, who took a simple catch, and the South Africans were convinced it had brushed the Australian's glove.

The replays showed Jansen had found nothing but arm guard and the hosts had just one review remaining.

Labuschagne's innings came to an end on the stroke of lunch. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It was a gut-wrenching end to an innings of serious promise for Labuschagne.

The Queenslander, so desperately in need of a score to get his Test career back on track, reached the final over of the morning session on 37 and with one eye on kicking on after the first break.

He was able to see off the first five balls of the set, but fell on its last.

Angling into the right-hander, Mulder was able to sneak one past Labuschagne's outside edge and into the front pad.

It looked touch and go whether the ball made impact in-line with the stumps, but the umpire's finger was up.

Labuschagne didn't look overly hopeful sending the decision upstairs, but DRS showed how close he was to getting outside the line of off stump, with the Australian only having to leave the field because of the umpire's original call.

It is not the kind of luck you need when you've gone more than three years without a Test century.

Smith couldn't make the most of his start. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

With all that had been made of Steve Smith's return to the country his Test career had so shockingly unravelled eight years earlier, the understated reception he received when entering the game felt at least a little anticlimactic.

There was no chorus of boos from the few spectators in place for the morning session as Smith joined Labuschagne at the crease, tasked with steadying the Australian innings with both Maddinson and Head back in the sheds.

And Smith began his innings like he had so often in the past: fidgety, idiosyncratic and paranoid, but set on getting himself into the game.

After seeing off the opening pace barrage, Smith stamped his authority on the morning with two big sixes back over the head of spinner Keshav Maharaj in the space of four balls.

Smith made it to lunch, but only lasted three balls after the first break.

He was struck on the finger by a rearing Marco Jansen length ball, before edging the very next delivery through to the slips.

Smith was out for 25 and Australia had lost two wickets in four balls either side of the lunch break.

Matt Renshaw was Australia's best on day one. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Coming in at number five, Renshaw was a bright spot in an otherwise dark day for the Australian batters.

The southpaw watched on as South African spearhead Anrich Nortje removed Alex Carey and Beau Webster in the space of three balls, and looked supremely confident in his new home in the middle order.

He made his way to 46 before bad light ended the day with over an hour left of scheduled play and just 65.2 overs bowled.

Renshaw will begin day two four runs away from his first Test 50 in more than 3,500 days, tasked with continuing to rebuild Australia's innings alongside Cummins.

Zach Bates produced a blistering lap to top qualifying at Mount Panorama on Friday. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

The Top 10 Shootout, which sets the first five rows of the grid for the Bathurst 1000, will be held this afternoon.

Zach Bates will be the last driver on Mount Panorama after topping Friday's qualifying session.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

Zach Bates will be hoping to back-up his record breaking efforts from yesterday as he goes into Saturday's Top 10 Shootout as the favourite to secure pole position.

Brodie Kostecki will also be in the shootout trying to set a new Bathurst 1000 record for most consecutive pole positions for the Great Race.

Here is what you need to know ahead of this afternoon's shootout.

The 10 fastest duos from Friday's qualifying session will hit the mountain this afternoon for a shot at pole position in Sunday's Bathurst 1000.

Here is when the shootout begins in your state or territory.

Here are the results of yesterday's qualifying session which was topped by Zach Bates with a 2:03.938, the fastest time set in the current era of Supercars at Bathurst.

Brodie Kostecki was fifth fastest on Friday and keeps alive his chance of becoming the first driver to secure four consecutive pole positions for the Bathurst 1000.

The entry of Cooper Murray/Lochie Dalton has been strong throughout the opening two days, with Murray third fastest yesterday. Murray was fighting for the win in the final laps of last year's Bathurst 1000.

The 10 fastest duos from Friday's qualifying session have one lap to get their car onto pole.

Each team will select one driver to complete the lap. The 10th fastest team on Friday will go first, then the ninth fastest, and so on.

Each team gets one lap and the top 10 positions on the starting grid will be determined by these single laps.

Dave Rennie pictured during his time as Wallabies coach. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

The Wallabies are facing Dave Rennie for the first time since he took over as All Blacks coach.

Rennie coached the Wallabies for three seasons before his contract was terminated in 2023.

ABC Sport will live blog tonight's Bledisloe Cup Test.

It had the potential to be one of the compelling plot lines in the build-up to tonight's first Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.

How does Dave Rennie feel about leading the All Blacks against the Wallabies, the team he coached until he was sacked in 2023?

But for Rennie and his former gold-clad pupils, there is no animosity.

Wallabies skipper Harry Wilson was handed a Test debut under Dave Rennie in 2020. (Getty Images/Nations Championship: Asanka Ratnayake)

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson could not have spoken more highly of Rennie when he addressed the media yesterday.

Wilson made his Test debut under the New Zealander in 2020, when he was thrown into the cauldron-like atmosphere of a Bledisloe Cup Test in Wellington a few months shy of his 21st birthday.

"I really enjoyed playing under Dave," Wilson said at the Wallabies' captain's run at Eden Park.

Confidence may be high, but the Wallabies know talk is cheap if they are to win their first Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park since 1986.

"He gave me my Test debut and I played a few Tests under him. I've always been really appreciative of that."

Wilson added: "I definitely learnt a lot from him … I know he has got a lot of respect from this group.

"He was, I guess, a very loved member of the Wallabies when he was [coach] and it's going to be different going up against him, that's for sure."

Rennie, whose contract as Wallabies coach was terminated in January 2023, was equally glowing in his praise of the players he coached during his time in Australia.

"I know a lot about the [Wallabies] players, obviously," Rennie said on Thursday.

"There's a big number of them who started in 2020 and they've now played 50, or 60 or 70 Tests.

"So what we know is they're a good side. They're experienced and they've played a lot of football together."

Rennie was shown the door by Rugby Australia after returning a 38 per cent win record from 34 Tests in charge between 2020-22.

He was replaced immediately by Eddie Jones, who lasted 10 months in the role before resigning.

Jones coached the Wallabies to their worst showing at a Rugby World Cup in 2023, when they failed to reach the quarterfinals for the first time.

Dave Rennie took charge of the All Blacks earlier this year. (Getty Images/Nations Championship: Morgan Hancock)

Rennie's poor winning percentage was cited among the reasons for his axing.

What must be acknowledged, however, was the fact he inherited a struggling Wallabies program in the wake of their quarterfinal exit at the 2019 Rugby World Cup.

Rennie also had to contend with coaching a squad during the height of the COVID pandemic, although this did affect every international team.

Among the highlights of his tenure was a 24-22 triumph over the All Blacks in Brisbane in 2020, which was the last time the Wallabies tasted victory over their trans-Tasman rivals.

Three years after he was sacked as Wallabies coach, Dave Rennie is put in charge of the All Blacks for the next two seasons.

But inconsistent results proved his downfall, while Jones's availability following his sacking as England coach in late 2022 was also a contributing factor.

The opportunity to coach at the Test level for a second time seemed to have passed Rennie by until Scott Robertson's sudden departure from the All Blacks last January.

Rennie was handed the reins two months later, issued with the assignment of leading the All Blacks through to next year's Rugby World Cup.

Immediately, rugby fans on both sides of the Tasman were looking ahead to the opening Bledisloe Cup Test with added interest.

But at least publicly, Rennie says there are no hard feelings.

"It's not about me," Rennie said on Thursday.

"I've got no regrets. I got to work with some really good people, people I've a lot of time for.

"It's part of a game we're involved in."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.title: A firing squad, a lethal injection, and a 'disturbing' shift in the US
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.author: Brianna Morris-Grant
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Brianna Morris-Grant

Topic:
World Politics

Capital punishment is in the spotlight in the US. (Getty Images: Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg)

Death row inmate Christa Pike was still fighting for life in a Tennessee hospital when the US federal government announced its plans.

Just days after state officials botched the 50-year-old's execution, federal officials were ready to go ahead with another.

On paper, Tennessee's death penalty protocol looks neat. But experts say the drug used in lethal injection risks severe pain and a feeling of drowning.

The US military, the Pentagon said, would conduct its first execution by firing squad since World War II.

By the time Pike, 50, had begun talking again, the Pentagon had made another announcement.

The firing squad execution would be live streamed.

At a time when approval for the death penalty has declined across the US, these high-profile cases raise an unprecedented discussion for Americans, according to Vincent Hurley, a criminologist at Macquarie University.

"Even if they don't vote, [Americans] can't escape the surreal notion that someone has been executed by the state twice, and it's failed," he said.

"We're living in a world of chaos, and nothing should surprise us.

The number of Americans who support the death penalty fell to a five-decade low of 52 per cent in late 2025, according to Washington-based analytics company Gallup.

Support for the practice has been declining since 1994, when it reached a peak of 80 per cent.

The same Gallup poll found 44 per cent of Americans now oppose the death penalty, the highest level of opposition since 1966.

But a separate poll, by the Pew Research Center, found that when it came to people convicted of murder, nearly two-thirds of respondents supported the death penalty.

It found support for the death penalty had jumped six percentage points compared to April 2021.

Over the last two decades, the number of executions had steadily decreased from a 1999 peak of 98 in a single year.

As death row inmate Christa Pike remains in hospital following a failed lethal injection, we take a closer look at the track record for botched executions in the US.

That changed last year.

In 2025, the number of executions rose to 47 in one year, up from a total of 25 in 2024.

That was largely driven by a dramatic increase in executions in Florida, which accounted for 40 per cent of the year's total.

Louisiana joined Alabama in using nitrogen gas to execute prisoners.

South Carolina performed the first firing squad execution nationally in 15 years, with a subsequent autopsy indicating the shooters missed their target, his heart.

At the same time, the US Supreme Court denied every request for a stay of execution throughout the year.

In the final weeks in the role, former president Joe Biden commuted the death sentences of 37 of the 40 prisoners on federal death row.

In January 2025, President Donald Trump issued an order calling capital punishment an "essential tool".

"Our founders knew well that only capital punishment can bring justice and restore order in response to such evil," the order said.

"Yet for too long, politicians and judges who oppose capital punishment have defied and subverted the laws of our country."

The polling by Gallup and Pew was conducted before Christa Pike received two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and kept breathing.

A picture taken on December 4, 2007 shows death row inmate Christa Pike. (Reuters: J Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/USA Today Network)

Hers was the second failed execution attempt in Tennessee in the last six months, and the first recorded case of someone surviving the drug.

As her legal team filed an emergency motion to preserve evidence in and around the execution chamber, Tennessee officials declined to say whether they would try to execute her again.

The "spectacle" of the failed execution "collapsed" what many Americans thought of as a humane method, according to Dr Hurley.

"When you think about the terminology they use around this, things like procedure, protocol, administering, IV lines," he said.

"It sanitises the whole thing.

Many people may lean into a sense of "moral disengagement", he added.

"There's a theory … where people want to avoid feeling guilty about something that's happening," he said.

"So they dehumanise Christa in this case [and] what was really interesting was when she went to trial, her sexual abuse was never disclosed.

"Whether that would have changed the outcome, no one really knows, but no one got a full picture of her life leading up to the murder."

Topic:Law, Crime and Justice

Topic:
Law, Crime and Justice

Pike was sentenced to die in 1996, following the murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer when she was 18 years old, the same year support for capital punishment hit its peak.

Her legal team has argued severe neglect and sexual abuse throughout her life left Pike with brain damage and diminished control over her own actions.

"I think when [people] see that case, the issue of fairness comes up," Dr Hurley said.

"People now realise that behind her … there is a life of disadvantage.

"When people talk about [the death penalty], they ask, 'Is it retribution for what she's done, or is it punishment?'"

Globally in 2025, executions soared to the highest figure recorded by human rights organisation Amnesty International since 1981.

A total of 2,707 people were executed across 17 countries.

The 78 per cent rise was attributed in Amnesty's annual report to "a handful of governments determined to rule by fear".

The main driver was Iran, which executed 2,159 people, more than double its 2024 number.

But the United States also appeared on the list of those leading the global increase, something the report noted as "alarming".

Both Christa Pike's botched execution and the plans for a firing squad execution were "deeply, deeply disturbing", Kyinzom Dhongdue, Amnesty International Australia's spokesperson, told the ABC.

Nidal Malik Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring dozens more at a military base in 2009.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said his execution by military firing squad would be live streamed on December 3.

The United States's first execution by a military firing squad since World War II will be live streamed, the Pentagon has said.

Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Mr Hegseth told a conservative TV outlet: "Don't care."

"Unfortunately it really shows the current US administration's complete disregard for human life, human dignity, really," Ms Dhongdue said.

"Amnesty's position is that we oppose the death penalty in all cases, no exception.

"We consider this as the ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment and a gross violation of the right to life."

The public execution, she added, reflected an "authoritarian" shift in the US government.

"If we look at other authoritarian regimes, these are often the regimes who have turned executions into public events," she said.

"Amnesty reported 17 public executions in 2025, and those happened in very authoritarian environments like Afghanistan and Iran.

"These are very disturbing and they transform this punishment into a spectacle.

"It's almost always [used] to make the state's power visible and to create fear in the population."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.title: She's finally beaten Ledecky, now Pallister wants Olympic gold
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.author: Elizabeth Wright
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

After a tough few years, Lani Pallister is focused on gaining momentum towards gold at the LA Olympics. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Swimming superstar Lani Pallister wasn't meant to be a distance swimmer.

At the beginning of her career, she was focused on the butterfly events.

It was only when Pallister mistakenly selected the 800 metres freestyle on a race program (instead of the 100m butterfly) that her career path would change.

"I ended up swimming it [800m freestyle], qualified for my first junior team, and now I'm on the senior team, and short course world record holder for the event," Pallister told ABC Sport at the Australian Short Course Championships earlier this month.

It's been a packed year for the 24-year-old, but a satisfying one.

Lani Pallister had a breakthrough in August, finally beating Katie Ledecky in the women's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Sean M. Haffey)

Her success at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, where she won gold in the 400m, 800m and 1,500m, saw her become the first woman at the Games to complete the treble.

But her performance at this year's Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in August, less than two weeks after the Glasgow Games, was her most remarkable breakthrough, beating United States powerhouse Katie Ledecky for the first time in the long course 800m freestyle.

"When you achieve a feat like that, you don't believe it until your hands are on the wall," Pallister said.

"It's not as much about just beating the one person in particular, but I think when you have someone as monumental as Katie, that definitely plays into the feelings and the sense of achievement off the back of it."

Pallister puts this success down to a change in coaching, making the shift from Michael Bohl to Dean Boxall over a year ago.

Lani Pallister has switched to legendary coach Dean Boxall, seeing results already in the pool. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"The past 18-month journey with [Dean] has been unbelievable, and I've achieved things in swim times I didn't think possible for myself," Pallister said.

It is a change that could take her to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, earning redemption for the heartbreak she has experienced in the past few years.

It hasn't been an easy journey for Pallister, with illness and mental health taking a toll on her swimming career.

In 2021, she developed an eating disorder and a series of illnesses that saw her miss qualification for the Tokyo Olympics.

After seeing improvement in her times in the lead-up to the Paris Olympics in 2024, COVID struck, causing Pallister to pull out of the 1,500 and 400m races and finish sixth in the 800 metres.

She thought her swimming career could be over at 22.

Katie Ledecky was incredibly supportive of Lani Pallister gold in the women's 800m freestyle at the Pan Pacs. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

But after changing coaches, breaking world records in short course events, and finally claiming her win over Ledecky, Pallister is excited for the future and focusing on LA.

If everything goes right, an individual Olympic medal could finally be on the cards.

"I really wanted to focus on staying humble," Pallister said.

"There's a lot of work and a lot of things that are going to happen between now and the LA Olympics and I think that week over in LA in 2028 is going to be about consistency, repeat performance and just preparing."

Pallister will be 26 years old by the time the LA Games arrive, and 30 when Brisbane rolls around.

Age doesn't worry her though; moving to Boxall's squad has given her a fresh perspective.

"Female distance swimmers are slowly getting a little bit older," Pallister said, referring to Ledecky, who broke her own 800m world record at 28.

Lani Pallister believes the future for women's distance swimming is bright, with new talent Molly Walker rising through the ranks. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Any thought of retirement is far from Pallister's mind, and with a home Games in Brisbane in sight, it is tempting to hold on.

"At the end of the day, swimming's one of those sports, when you know you're done, you'll be done," Pallister said.

"With friends and family, in a city that I grew up swimming [in], it's probably the perfect way to end, and I think there's a lot of athletes that are in my age group that are kind of thinking the same thing."

Before the LA and Brisbane Games, however, Pallister will be continuing her busy year, having qualified for the 2026 World Aquatic Championships in December.

The championships will be held in China, with Pallister returning as the defending champion and short course 800m world record holder.

Lani Pallister is looking to defend her 800m title at the Short Course World Aquatics Championships in Beijing in December. (Getty Images: Mondadori Portfolio)

At the Australian Short Course Championships, she claimed victory in the 200, 400, 800, and 1,500 metres, meaning her World Championships will be busy.

"The biggest goal for me this year is going back to a World Championships and defending my back-to-back title in the 800," Pallister said.

"When you have the opportunity to race on the international stage and get more race practice under the belt, particularly before the next two years going into LA, it is something that's really important."
