https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.title: America reckons with fraternities as rage engulfs Cornell campus
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.author: Phoebe Hosier and Lia Walsh
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

The Chi Phi fraternity has a long history at Cornell, but the fraternity's campus chapter has been closed down. (ABC News: Phoebe Hosier)

On a cool night on a suburban street in upstate New York, a red light glows from inside a towering spire atop a monstrous house.

Red cups and crushed cider cans litter the property, which now stands as a symbol of a national reckoning at Cornell University's Ivy League campus.

"Bro, look, I'm at the Chi Phi frat," a young man in trackpants says to a friend on FaceTime as he walks by.

He passes a sign with Greek letters, stained from a recent egging.

"I know bro. Creepy isn't it?"

A former student alleges she was raped by a group of men in the house when she was 20. (ABC News: Lia Walsh)

Once home to a fraternity dating back more than 150 years, the property now sits dormant.

But it has come to international prominence because of explosive gang-rape allegations against seven of its former residents.

In an upstairs bedroom, a former student alleges she was drugged and raped for seven hours in 2024, when she was 20.

The fact the alleged rape took place at one of America's most elite universities — and allegedly involved seven privileged young men — has ignited a firestorm of debate that has led to calls for fraternities to be banned.

Fraternities are exclusive social clubs for male undergraduate students who typically reside on campus.

Cornell is home to more than 50 fraternities and their female equivalent, sororities. About a third of the university's undergraduates students are part of fraternity or sorority culture, known as "Greek life".

But some students are now protesting the fraternities' existence.

At recent campus demonstrations, "ban the frats" was a popular chant.

Lewis Holland believes fraternities breed a culture of misogyny. (ABC News: Phoebe Hosier)

"There are frats that can be very positive with upstanding people, but that's fighting against the current," student Lewis Holland told the ABC at a protest this week.

"The only way to fix that problem is to get rid of all of them."

The North American Interfraternity Conference, which represents dozens of the country's largest fraternities, says they can provide a sense of belonging and lifelong friendships, while helping students develop accountability and leadership skills.

Fraternities are largely self-governing, with chapters typically run by elected student members, leaving much of the responsibility for discipline and accountability in the hands of students and their national organisations.

Lewis says that is part of the problem.

"They see women as conquests, with this association between sexual degradation and masculine victory."

The university's handling of the gang-rape allegation sparked protests at Cornell. (ABC News: Phoebe Hosier)

College fraternities have produced some of America's most powerful men, including presidents, members of Congress, top judges and business leaders.

Critics like Lewis argue some frat brothers carry the culture of misogyny learned at fraternities into positions of power.

"You see why the Epstein list is so long, you see why there are so many sex scandals from our politics," he said. "It's a cause and effect."

Cornell faces backlash over handling of sexual assault case. (ABC News)

A 2026 report by a Cornell task force said 52 per cent of undergraduate women affiliated with a sorority had reported experiencing sexual assault.

More than 1,200 incidents of sexual assault, dating and domestic violence and stalking were reported to Cornell between 2018 and 2024, according to USA Today, citing data reported to New York state. Fourteen resulted in suspensions and seven in expulsion or dismissal.

One of the leading voices now calling for the closure of fraternities is Melbourne-born academic Kate Manne, an expert in feminist philosophy who has been teaching at Cornell for 13 years.

Australian-born philosopher and writer Kate Manne, who teaches at Cornell, is arguing for fraternities to be closed. (ABC News: Lia Walsh)

She describes fraternities as a "hotbed of misogyny and sexual assault".

"There is a very strong code that exists there that says if one man does something illegal or immoral, you just participate," she said during an interview in her campus office.

"You don't say anything and you don't call it out. Maybe you even ratchet it up."

That "bro code", she said, amounted to a culture of impunity that was reinforced with what she calls "himpathy" — "sympathy and loyalty for the male perpetrator over the female victim".

In the college town of Ithaca, a network of cul-de-sacs lined with sororities and fraternities surround the sprawling Cornell campus.

Some are dilapidated grand homes with battered couches and beer pong tables. Others are gleaming three-storey estates with chandeliers suspended from high ceilings.

There are dozens of fraternities and sororities at Cornell. (ABC News: Lia Walsh)

When we visit, one young man exits a frat house in trackpants and heads for a nearby BMW. Another leaves in a backwards cap, driving over manicured grass before speeding off in a Range Rover.

We doorknocked some of the fraternity houses and spoke to several students in a bid to hear from members of Cornell's fraternities. But many were wary of speaking with media.

"Sorry, I can't with my job," one fraternity member told us, a look of terror flashing across his face at the request.

But online, fierce debate is raging — not only over the alleged gang rape, but also the bystander culture that may have allowed it to happen.

Widely shared screenshots from a group chat, purportedly from the night of the alleged rape, include messages where men described an "open shop" and invited others upstairs to "whip it out".

Court documents say none of the 57 men in the chat intervened as the alleged rape took place.

That evidence has sparked a reckoning that extends beyond current fraternity members to alumni.

Students want more action from the university. (ABC News: Phoebe Hosier)

In one viral video, a former University of Oregon student recounts how frat brothers across the hall from him would regularly have threesomes with intoxicated women. He never asked questions.

"I was ignoring that icky gut feeling, that moral compass, because everyone else was acting like it was fine," said the video's creator, Pavan, who asked that his surname not be shared.

He told the ABC he had since wrestled with his own complicity in possible sexual violence by staying silent.

"A lot of young men are raised to believe that sexual assault is binary — you are either a rapist or you're not.

"But there's an entire spectrum of sexual assault that we are all complicit in to some degree."

Pavan stressed that fraternities were not monolithic and could offer men an important opportunity for connection and community in a time when male loneliness is on the rise.

But Dr Manne argued the dangers of fraternities far outweighed the benefits.

Advocates argue fraternity houses can be beneficial for young men and give them lifetime friendships. (ABC News: Phoebe Hosier)

"Whatever value they might have is completely eclipsed by the harm," she said, not just to women but also to the men who join them.

She believes the case — along with simmering anger over stalled accountability on the Epstein files and a series of roll-backs to women's reproductive rights — is now sparking a "second wave" of the MeToo movement, 20 years after it began.

With a civil lawsuit filed last month over the gang-rape allegation, and a new criminal investigation underway, the debate about campus culture and the future of fraternities is set to remain in the spotlight.

In a video message last week, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff pledged the university would take a "serious look" at fraternities.

He has also agreed to an independent review into how the university handled the allegations.

All seven men accused of rape have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged.

With Lia Walsh in Ithaca, New York

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/e.title: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake hits off coast of Panama
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/e.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

People stand near a collapsed building in the aftermath of an earthquake. (Jonathan Marquinez via Reuters)

A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake has struck off the coast of Panama, damaging homes, cutting power, halting flights and sending residents into the streets, while triggering more than a dozen aftershocks.

The quake happened off the country's southern coast at a 12.6-kilometre depth, according to the United State's Geological Survey.

Television images showed elderly residents in tears in the streets as a series of weaker aftershocks rattled the ​country.

Ricardo Brown, a 74-year-old in Herrera province in southern Panama, said the earthquake damaged a number of homes in his area of Las Minas.

"We're scared. It's just the two of ‌us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we're afraid it could fall on us," Mr Brown said.

The epicentre was close to the rural community of La Pitaloza in a sparsely populated area in the south of the country.

Major earthquakes are rare in Panama.

Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, said the quake was triggered by the Azuero Sona Fault System that has long contained a build-up of pressure.

"It's a system of active faults that occasionally, due to the accumulation of stress, release this amount of energy," he said.

"The seismic signals have travelled throughout the national territory and that is why it ​could ‌be felt everywhere."

A car damaged by falling debris in the earthquake. (Enea Lebrun via Reuters)

The USGS estimated economic ‌losses could amount to between one to 10 per cent of Panama's gross domestic ​product.

A tsunami threat triggered by the ⁠earthquake off Panama has passed, and no further tsunami danger remains, the US Tsunami Warning System said.

The Panama Canal is about 200 kilometres from the epicentre and is operating normally.

About 90 ‌vessels, including bulk carriers, tankers and container ships, were waiting at both ends of the key waterway to transit or dock at berths serving storage ⁠terminals and trans-shipment services, according to monitoring data.

Power was down across six provinces, and the Tocumen International airport, a major regional hub, had suspended flights.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/j.title: Judith Lucy's cancer journey will reveal resilience she didn't know she had
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Judith Lucy announced this week she has been diagnosed with breast cancer and will undergo a double mastectomy. (Supplied: Token)

Welcome, Judith Lucy, to the After Cancer Diagnosis Club.

It's a club no-one wants to join. There are a host of peculiar requirements. And the club remains a mystery to anyone who is not already a member.

Based on her post on Tuesday, Judith has already enjoyed the induction. The shock of diagnosis is all the more shocking because no-one can tell you precisely what the diagnosis is. Surprise!

For many, an initial finding turns out to be the tip of the cancer iceberg, with each step potentially cascading into more possibilities and medical pathways.

Judith Lucy in her natural environment, generating laughs on stage. (Supplied: Nick Robertson/Just For Laughs)

As a lovely breast care nurse explained to me down the phone as I waited for the biopsy result that ensured my entry to the After Cancer Diagnosis Club, you never really get one diagnosis.

But the upside is, that means even the worst news can change!

Judith spoke highly of her delightfully named surgeon, Dr Fun. You will rely on them like no-one you've ever relied on before to meticulously work their way through microscopic layers of skin and tissue and extract the stuff that will kill you.

There are so many decisions to make in those first few days and there is so much information. Who knew there were so many types of cancer? What's the difference between a stage and a grade?

The medical professionals who work in this field are brilliant and in Australia we have remarkable survival rates.

But it's an extraordinary journey, and it's different for everyone.

Judith Lucy announces breast cancer diagnosis (Instagram: @officialjudithlucy)

A few years back, my mammogram and my dental check-up were both due in the same week, but I only had time for one: I picked the scan foolishly thinking it would be the least problematic!

Good choice. That led to a repeat mammogram, which led to a guided biopsy, which led to a complete mastectomy, resulting in an even worse diagnosis.

At that point my oncologist arrived and explained that in a year it would most likely be largely behind me. A year!

She was right, of course.  A year of chemo, radiation and then mostly it was done. But, of course, it wasn't really done.

Just because you're not hooked up to an infusion every week doesn't really signal "the end" of cancer treatment.

Stretching out for years ahead – for me at least – is the Tamoxifen treatment, daily  oral hormone therapy medication that rattles your bones. Then I opted for the reconstruction and a second mastectomy. Judith plans the same. No regrets here, but these are exhausting procedures.

And after the treatment there is the constant vigilance. Too many headaches? Scan for brain metastases!  Strange rash that won't quit? Biopsy for a recurrence!

My gorgeous kids were my anchor. The sound of my eldest tapping away at her homework next to my hospital bed made me feel safe enough to sleep, but it's a cruel thing asking to borrow your children's strength.

And you'll do most of this alone, sorry to say. Even the most willing families and friends will struggle to understand the fear, the aches, the change.

As one of my friends once described it, "done or dead" is what most people can deal with. Best to project positivity at all times. Emphasising the bright side and gags about a free boob job is the safe way to go. But it can make the experience all the lonelier.

Researchers have looked at what happens when breast screening is adjusted depending on your risk.

"I'm fine" is so much easier an answer for others to hear than "I hurt all the time" or "God, the tiredness!".

Bits of my body will never feel the same. You know how amputees talk about phantom pains? I have a phantom itch where my breast tissue used to be, but no amount of scratching can get to it because there is no sensation in the skin.

It's constant reminder of what was there. As if you needed one.

Listen to Judith and get your boobs checked.

And Judith, you're about to be amazed by the people you meet and what you're capable of.

Annie White is an ABC journalist.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: U.S. sanctions ICC after former judge wins  Nobel Peace Prize
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The Trump administration imposed fresh sanctions against the International Criminal Court, signaling its determination to cripple the organization on the same day that a former ICC judge won the Nobel Peace Prize.

The U.S. Treasury Department added the entire court to its Specially Designated Nationals list, a move that would impose financial punishment on any entity that does business with the ICC. That announcement was a step up from past sanctions that targeted top officials on the court but not the body itself.

The White House has long accused the court of unfairly targeting the U.S. and Israel, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio made clear the Trump administration was prepared to go even further.

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted Friday. He added that the court can’t prosecute Americans such as border patrol agents, service members or elected leaders and said that he expects U.S. allies to “rein in” the body.

The symbolism of the move was stark given that it was announced hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has long coveted the prize himself, reposted a social media message saying the Norwegian Nobel Committee had “shamed itself beyond repair” with the decision.

It was not immediately clear if the sanctions were deliberately timed to coincide with the Nobel announcement.

The U.S. decision spurred swift push back from Japan, the European Union and numerous other U.S. allies that support the court. The foreign ministers of a number of ICC member-states issued a statement defending the court, which has about 900 staff members from 100 countries and a 2026 budget of nearly €197 million ($220 million).

“If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families,” said the statement from Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Friday expressed her deep concern over the move.

In a social media post, Takaichi said that the U.S. decision is “incompatible with” Japan’s position.

“Japan has consistently attached great importance to upholding the rule of law in the international community and supports the International Criminal Court,” the prime minister said, adding that she has stated this position in her speech at the U.N. General Assembly and in a policy address in parliament.

“We will continue to reach out to the United States and extend necessary support to the ICC so that the Court can fulfill its role and functions as originally envisaged,” Takaichi said.

At her meeting with Trump last month, Takaichi clarified Japan’s support for the ICC. The two leaders agreed to leave the issue to talks between Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio.

The ICC was established in 2002 to prosecute perpetrators of the most serious crimes, including war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

ICC judges have issued a total of 68 arrest warrants, according to its website, including one against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 for alleged war crimes in Gaza and another for Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2023 over war crimes related to the alleged abduction of children from Ukraine.

The ICC rejected the new sanctions and called on states “to continue taking concrete actions” to ensure it can continue its work. United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned the U.S. action, according to his spokesman Stephane Dujarric. Dujarric said Guterres was “deeply alarmed by the expected impact of today’s sanctions on the International Criminal Court as a whole, and in particular, its continued ability to perform its important mandates.”

The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen both pointed to a six-month window before the measures take effect as a period for “dialogue.”

“The ICC is the cornerstone of the international criminal justice system. It prosecutes individuals responsible for the most serious crimes under international law,” Kallas said on X. “Protecting the ICC remains an EU priority.”

Zacharia, a lawyer who frequently appears on conservative news outlets, is an adviser for the US president’s social media platform

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he has appointed Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for his Truth Social platform, to serve as White House press secretary following Karoline Leavitt’s departure in August.

He said Zacharia ‌has an “unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter”.

“I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The New York Times first reported the news of her appointment.

https://www.dw.com/en/schools-crisis-in-.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
https://www.dw.com/en/schools-crisis-in-.text:
For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly.

Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.

At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.

Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.

The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.

The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.

Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.

Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).

According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.

The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created.

Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray  announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.

These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.

The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.

Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.

The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.

Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.

The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.

France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.

The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.

It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.

Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.

With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.

This article was originally published in German.

The government has said it will recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French students are protesting against the government's budget cuts, says French journalist.

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-putin-agree-.title: Trump, Putin agree on deal to release Russian diesel to US, world markets
https://www.dw.com/en/trump-putin-agree-.text:
Russia will supply diesel to global markets in a bid to lower prices, US President Donald Trump has said. The move reverses years of pressure on the Russian economy following the invasion of Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release Russian diesel to US and global markets.

The move, which aims to address rising fuel costs before the US midterm elections, marks a dramatic turnaround in US policy toward Moscow since the start of the war in Ukraine.

In a social media post, Trump wrote he had made a deal with Putin during a phone call that was supposed to be about a suspected plague outbreak in Russia.

According to Trump, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

Trump wrote that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that.

The US Treasury Department issued a temporary license that will allow Russian diesel to reach global markets through April 2027.

Trump's announcement follows his signing of a broad Russia sanctions law last month. The law is intended to clamp down on Russia’s energy sector and other areas that fuel its war against Ukraine.

Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian presidential envoy, reposted the Treasury Department's announcement on X, saying that "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

Alexander Novak, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister, said that the country was ready to start supplying additional volumes of diesel to the United States and other countries from October.

He also said that Russia's exports are expected to rise further in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.

Later, the Kremlin released a statement from Putin saying that, during their call, he and Trump had also devoted "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and had discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has condemned the agreement, saying that any easing of sanctions without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of "weakness."

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," he wrote on social media.

"Allowing Russia to ⁠sell ​petroleum products ​is an investment in a ​war that ‌must be ended, not prolonged. What ​is needed ⁠is real de-escalation with Russia ⁠on ​a reciprocal basis," the Ukrainian president stressed.

Zelenskyy added that Ukraine hopes the US will have a strong conversation with Russia: "A strong one, not a weak one."

Since its 2022 full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine, Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and its Western partners.

But as the war has continued with no resolution in sight, Washington's commitment has appeared to waver.

Earlier this year, temporary US sanctions waivers that allowed the sale of Russian oil raised concerns because they could hinder efforts to deprive Moscow of funds for its war in Ukraine.

Last month, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring diesel prices, and even publicly told Zelenskyy to stop the attacks.

Trump's announcement on Friday came just as US, Ukrainian, and European officials were meeting in Miami for new diplomatic talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

According to US envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian, European, US and NATO representatives held constructive discussions in Miami, and agreed to continue diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to Ines Pohl, the chief of DW's Washington D.C. bureau, the diesel deal is mainly about domestic politics.

With the midterms only weeks away, Trump is under heavy pressure over high energy prices. The deal allows him to show that he is taking action and appeal to voters who feel the rising cost of fuel directly, while the war in Ukraine seems far away.

Politically, that is significant: Trump is accepting a loosening of sanctions on Russia, even though Washington had actually wanted to increase pressure on Putin.

It also makes one thing crystal clear: when push comes to shove, Trump consistently chooses what benefits him personally over what Congress has decided.

He appears to be betting that, for many Americans, prices at the pump matter more in the end than the geopolitical consequences. Whether the promised deliveries will actually bring noticeable relief, however, remains doubtful.

https://www.dw.com/en/strong-earthquakes.title: Strong earthquakes shake Panama, prompting tsunami alert
https://www.dw.com/en/strong-earthquakes.text:
Tremors were felt in the capital city, triggering a tsunami warning in Central and South America.

A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday morning.

According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake's epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama's southern tip.

The quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles).

The USGS later reported that a second powerful earthquake, measuring 6.6 in magnitude, struck Panama following a series of aftershocks.

Tremors shook Panama City, causing buildings to shake and prompting people to evacuate into the streets.

"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared."

Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino urged calm in a post on X, writing, "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."

There were no immediate reports of fatalities. According to Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service, damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.

Smith reported several injuries, as well as partial collapses and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage to the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.

Meanwhile, local news outlets reported that the colonial-style Church of San Atanasio in Panama’s Los Santos province collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.

The US Tsunami Warning System issued an alert stating that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico within the next three hours.

The system also reported a tsunami threat to Hawaii. The warning was lifted later on Friday afternoon.

Initially, there were no reports of damage to the Panama Canal. The Panama Canal Authority stated that the waterway was operating as usual.

Tocumen International Airport in Panama City briefly suspended operations and activated evacuation protocols before reopening later on Friday afternoon.

Panama is located along the so-called "Ring of Fire," a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, according to the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor.

The statement released on Friday by Attorney General Hamad Saif al Shamsi and published by the state media did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing.

According to the statement, UAE public prosecutors believe that the co-pilot's plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US and aimed at "causing the greatest possible loss of life."

The investigation found that the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the flight route and airport. He had worked for several airlines in different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining Flydubai in January 2026.

The prosecutor's findings also showed that he met the professional and security requirements for employment.

These requirements included holding a pilot's license, providing a certificate of good conduct, and completing the necessary background checks.

"None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," according to the statement.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ly.title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ly.text:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr5.title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr5.text:
Being a Traitor must be a nightmare.

While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night, and even on the weekend.

There is no rest for the wicked, and Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the group did their dirty work for them by killing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw a first faithful, unlucky industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.

And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).

When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.

"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."

Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."

Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless. chaos, regardless. Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."

On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised.

"I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.

"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.

"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."

I guess now we'll never know.

Back at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions.

The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four.

The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry found the heat being turned up on her as the day rolled on.

"I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment."

Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart was one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before.

Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed was a little too trustworthy to be true.

Friday's mission raised more money for charity and also raised spirits, but not in a good way.

It involved the group paying a visit to a graveside haunted cabin to converse with the dead about matters unresolved.

"It's creepy, it's giving murder," noted actress Sharon Rooney on arrival.

Comedian Romesh Ranganathan joked that his mum was going to "absolutely hate this", as the the group gathered in a chant led by the booming voice of big dog actor Michael Sheen.

The spooky task made Ranganathan himself let out a hellish scream and saw Hart come face-to face with a masked hooded creature, before team-player Croft volunteered to go head-first into a stinky old toilet, in scenes resembling ITV's I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

"Guys, it's a little bit of poo," noted hardman Ross Kemp, as all around him gagged. "It's not gonna kill you."

Croft received a protective shield for his troubles, at least. "If I'd have put my hands and head down a toilet for nothing, I would've been fuming," he noted.

The group, with a little help from the undead, had to find a dead child's toys and a deceased's woman's wedding dress and shoes. This later prompted model Jerry Hall to reminisce about her own wedding to Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

"Before I got married to Mick - we'd already been together seven years, had two children - I put on a wedding dress every day until he agreed that we get married," she revealed.

Some rancid wine that tasted like "salty bin juice", according to comedian Joanne McNally, topped off possibly the most revolting task yet.

On the way back to the castle, YouTuber King Kenny raised more suspicions about Fry allowing him to grab a shield. "She held off to make herself look a bit innocent," he told his fellow faithfuls.

Traitor Jama smartly latched on to the growing suspicions around Hesmondhalgh.

Ahead of the roundtable, Fry told producers she knew she would have to fight like her life depended on it - because it did - and try to disguise herself as still being a faithful.

Once discussions were under way, she played the sympathy card, claiming she had been left feeling "vulnerable" as she knew her reputation as a brain box would make her a target.

Mrs Marple aka Hart wasn't going to let her off the hook that easily, however, noting how Fry's argument the previous night had contradicted that of the innocent but now sadly now departed My'la.

In a nice moment of levity in another tense debate, comedian Joe Lycett reminded the traitors - and specifically Hesmondhalgh - that he would "like to be recruited at some stage". He stressed: "I'm still very much available."

Hesmondhalgh laughed about how "going all dry mouthed" while defending herself was not helping her cause.

"It would be a cruel move taking the most trusted member of our group," noted Sheen.

"Cruel but clever," added Hart.

Ranganathan offered: "The person that we nominated as our most trustworthy person, we have now completely flipped on."

The conclusion was to banish Hesmondhalgh, who, in her parting words, said it had been an "immense experience".

"Alas," she continued, confirming her fidelity as tears appeared in eyes around the table: "It may mean I am not a phenomenal actor."

Singer Blunt, who had led the charge against her, appears to have now put himself in the frame.

He told the group: "I'm so sorry, that's my fault."

"He's been wrong about every theory he's came up with," said Rooney.

"So have I," added a frustrated Croft.

Hart declared that "everything is up in the air" now, following Hesmondhalgh's eviction, before King Kenny called it the team's "biggest loss" so far.

But what of the traitors?

First recruit, Acaster's strategy is to continue playing the game as if he is a faithful, he said. Jama is enjoying her time on the dark side while Hanna, it's fair to say, is not.

"You two saved me," Fry told the other two of her stressful day, while back in the turret in their cloaks.

The episode ended not with a murder but a fresh twist - the promise of a deathly game of hide-and-seek for four chosen contestants.

The traitors agreed to stay out of the game themselves, before settling on Kemp, Ranganathan, his comic pal Rob Beckett and Little Mix and solo singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock.

"I think this is gonna mess with everybody's heads," said Fry.

Presenter Claudia Winkleman greeted the four of them outside the castle in the dead of night.

"Have we won?", quipped Romesh Ranganathan.

No, confirmed Claudia, explaining how when they go down to the woods tonight they'll be in for a big surprise: one of them will be killed face-to-face.

Only Pinnock, it was decided, will be immune from murder in the game, though the Traitors aren't to know that.

This much terror and mischief and it's not Halloween for weeks yet.

Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/us/po.author: Jess Bidgood
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/us/po.text:
Adam Hamilton wants to be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there in nearly 100 years.

At the outset of the midterm cycle, I will admit, I did not expect to find myself in Kansas, a ruby red state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

And I really did not expect to find myself as I did this morning: in Kansas, wearing a hard hat, squeezed in a dark and rattly elevator as it dropped 650 feet below ground into a salt mine.

Politics: Full of surprises!

I was in Hutchinson, a city of grain, metal and salt, to write about how Kansas’ Senate election has become so competitive. The race between Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, and Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who has thrilled the state’s Democrats, was in a dead heat in the most recent Times/Siena poll.

Outside groups on both sides are plowing money into the race — including $5 million from Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, The Times learned today. The Republican counterpart has promised $14 million to save the seat.

Part of the reason it’s close is Hamilton himself, who is not your typical Democratic recruit. For one thing, he was a registered Republican until earlier this year. He is the founding pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, a United Methodist congregation with 24,000 members. He speaks in the quick, deep, extemporaneous cadence of a pastor with a podcast, which is what he is (or was — the podcast went on hiatus just before he began running for Senate).

And he was really excited about visiting this salt mine. I jumped at the chance to join his tour, unsure exactly where the mine fit into his campaign but eager for a chance to spend a little bit more time with a figure who is suddenly commanding national attention.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.title: Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.author: Bobby Allyn
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-599.text:
Sean Fern, a former FBI agent, is joining the prediction market platform Kalshi to lead the company's efforts in fighting money laundering.

Kalshi, a leading prediction market company, has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money laundering team as prediction markets come under increasing legal scrutiny by state and federal regulators.

Sean Fern will work closely with law enforcement and regulators and senior staff at Kalshi to keep an eye on suspicious and potentially criminal activity on the platform, which has exploded in growth in the past year.

According to the firm TickerTracker, Kalshi has crossed $260 billion in bets so far this year, already triple the amount traded in all of 2025.

In an interview with NPR, Fern, who worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn before his time at the FBI, said his aim is to build defenses against people trying to use the platform to commit financial crimes.

"I want to make sure it's a hard place to launder money or evade sanctions and commit fraud," Fern told NPR on Friday. "On a day-to-day basis, that involves knowing who our customers are, knowing where their money comes from, and making sure we aren't doing business with sanctioned entities or parties," he said. "And when something looks off or looks suspicious, we can catch it and make referrals to law enforcement."

The announcement echoes what cryptocurrency companies did during that sector's boom times in the early 2020s. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance, for instance, hired former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to beef up its compliance and anti-money laundering divisions. Several years later, Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

Avoiding its own money laundering scandal, Fern said, is the reason Kalshi tapped him.

At the FBI, Fern was a special agent in the bureau's international corruption squad, where he helped lead the investigation into the multibillion-dollar bribery scheme tied to Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, a scandal that became known as 1MDB.

Kalshi hopes adding Fern will lend credibility to the surging platform as it faces mounting scrutiny over insider trading and market manipulation.

Prediction market bettors can place wagers on everything from sports to what politicians say at public events to the outcome of elections. Experts have warned that introducing betting into domains like voting and policy decisions encourages people to monetize insider information.

Federal regulators and law enforcement in Washington have launched criminal investigations into alleged abuse on prediction market platforms. Earlier this year, regulators settled with former U.S. Rep. George Santos over market manipulation. Federal prosecutors have also indicted a former U.S. Army soldier and a former Google employee for allegedly using non-public information to cash out on Polymarket, Kalshi's main rival. In August, President Trump's former teleprompter operator was fined by regulators for using advance notice of the president's speeches to profit on Kalshi's so-called "mention markets."

Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said that as banks, hedge funds and other financial institutions use Kalshi, the need to shore up financial crime safeguards has become apparent. "We are growing up," Diana said.

The company, which PitchBook estimates to be worth around $40 billion, has 250 employees, and it plans to double its headcount over the next six months.

During his time in federal law enforcement, Fern was one of the lead prosecutors in the trial of OneTaste, an "orgasmic meditation" wellness company whose founders were sentenced to prison following convictions for forced labor conspiracy.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight loss drugs, advocates say
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Tess Ikonomou
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight loss medications, advocates say.

The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.

Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain, and hair thinning.

The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.

While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.

Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a UNSW study found in July.

Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.

“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.

Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.

Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.

“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.

“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”

Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.

“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.

GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.

The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.

The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.

The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.

They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.

“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.

“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”

QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.

“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Adams Education editor
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action

Tensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing into a crisis after school leadership unions said they had no confidence in the watchdog and would hold strike ballots unless “significant wellbeing issues” caused by Ofsted’s inspections regime were fixed.

The Association of School and College Leaders​ (ASCL), which includes senior leaders in many secondary schools, described Ofsted’s inspection system as “an overbearing mess” and urged the government to pause inspections to stop teachers leaving the profession.

A spokesperson for ASCL said that “if change is not forthcoming” the union would seek to hold an indicative ballot on industrial action.

The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said it would also consider steps including strike action at a meeting of its leadership next week.

The combative moves come after a survey published by Ofsted showed 88% of schools reported that recent inspections had negatively affected staff wellbeing.

The Guardian reported last week that Lucy Powell, the education secretary, wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” and overhaul the framework introduced last year. The new framework was intended to lower the strain and workload caused by inspections, but many heads say the opposite has happened.

In response to ASCL’s announcement, a spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “Inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face.

“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”

An Ofsted spokesperson said: “We have worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge.

“We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do.”

​Hostility ​towards Ofsted has been heightened since the death of Ruth Perry, a popular headteacher in Reading. In 2023 a coroner found that an Ofsted inspection contributed to Perry’s mental health deterioration and her death. Labour pledged to reform school inspections in its 2024 election manifesto.

But ASCL said it had “seen no meaningful progress on the part of Ofsted to address significant wellbeing issues caused by inspections, and that it is increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members”.

The motion of no confidence in Ofsted passed by ASCL’s executive stated: “We fear that the disproportionate stress and anxiety exerted by the inspection system will lead to school leaders deciding to leave their posts with a consequent impact on schools, children and young people.”

Pepe Di’​Iasio, ​ASCL’s general ​secretary, said: “​Our repeated attempts to resolve our concerns through discussion and negotiation have hit a brick wall … The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed.”

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT, said: “Our deep concerns about this Ofsted framework and the impact it is having on professionals are longstanding. Our executive committee will be meeting at the end of next week and debating the next steps NAHT will take. We fully expect that debate to include the option of pursuing industrial action.”
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.summary: Unions tell government to fix 'overbearing mess' of inspection regime and impact on staff wellbeing. They say they have no confidence in watchdog and would hold strike ballots if it is not fixed. ASCL says it will hold indicative ballot on industrial action if change is not forthcoming.

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.title: Neanderthal wooden tools from Spain found preserved in stone
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.author: Jacek Krywko
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.text:
Dissolved rock precipitated around the tools, which then decayed.

The Stone Age owes its name to tools that survived to our time. The material early humans worked with most, though, was probably wood because it is so much easier to process. Unfortunately, we know very little about Paleolithic woodwork because wood rots relatively quickly. But at Abric Romaní, a rock shelter in Capellades, west of Barcelona, mineral-rich water coated wooden Neanderthal tools in a limestone-like crust. When wood rotted away, it left behind hollow molds that faithfully reflect its shape.

In a recent Science Advances study, a team of Spanish archaeologists has cataloged 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas dating from 62,000 to 40,000 years ago. They found spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club unlike anything seen before, suggesting Neanderthals were likely much more than just Homo sapiens’ dumber cousins.

The oldest wooden artifacts we have are mostly weapons. They include spears from a German town called Schöningen, a spear tip from Clacton-on-Sea in England, and the spear found alongside an elephant skeleton in Lehringen, Germany. Most came from waterlogged sediments, where a lack of oxygen slowed decay.

The spears mostly give us information about how Neanderthals hunted. The findings at Abric Romaní are different because the finds come from a place where Neanderthals lived, slept, cooked, and made tools over the course of some 20,000 years.

“We have a sample of wooden tools for different subsistence activities, not only hunting,” says M. Gema Chacón, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) and co-author of the study. Because wood turns up in level after level, it shows that woodworking was routine for Neanderthals rather than an occasional one-off.

The shelter sits at the foot of a cliff of travertine, a limestone laid down by calcium-rich spring water. As that water dripped across the shelter floor, calcium carbonate settled on anything lying around—logs, leaves, pine cones, and Neanderthal tools. Sealed inside the crust, the wood slowly decomposed, leaving hollow molds. These are perfect negatives of the original objects, sometimes so detailed that the outlines of wood cells are visible under a microscope.

Abric Romaní has been explored continuously since 1983, so the team has had time to develop a method for excavating objects that are essentially empty space. Each find is outlined, mapped, and photographed, and restoration specialists consolidate the fragile crust. “Then we open very carefully one part of the object,” Chacón explains.

In the past, the team filled the hollows with resin or plaster to get a positive cast. “Now all the wooden remains are printed in 3D,” Chacón says. The molds are digitized with 3D scanning and photogrammetry, and the 3D-printed copies are used both for research and museum displays.

Most of the 597 remains turned out to be natural trunks, fallen branches, and lots of firewood, mostly Scots pine. Only 13 objects were made or modified by Neanderthals. “The morphology of these 13 tools is impossible to find in nature,” says Chacón.

Four shallow trays made of juniper bark, the largest 55 by 20 centimeters, were found near hearths. They may have been used to carry food or scoop embers, much like the bark dishes called coolamons used by Aboriginal Australians. Crossed poles over a thick hearth may be the remains of a tripod, possibly for processing food. A branchless pole more than five meters long was found in the innermost part of the shelter.

That pole fits a pattern seen in every level dug so far. Along the back wall, Neanderthals kept a row of small hearths, around 50 centimeters across and spaced a meter or so apart, with almost no debris around them. Chacón suspects these were sleeping hearths. “This gives you illumination and also protects you from possible carnivores or other animals that could attack the group,” she says. The team thinks the pole leaned against the wall to form a windbreak or simple hut, and experiments showed five meters is about the length such a structure needs.

The shelter’s busy end included large, overlapping hearths surrounded by animal bones, stone-knapping debris, and firewood. That’s where food was prepared, tools were made, and, the team thinks, meals were shared.

But there were also weapons.

The team found a pointed stick and two spears lying close to the antlered skulls of red deer. The best-preserved spear is 2.45 meters long. Chacón says a cast of its point shows an impact fracture identical to those on spears used by Aboriginal Australians. That kind of damage happens when a point strikes bone or something similarly hard. The most surprising find, though, was a club.

The club was carved from a single piece of wood, with a 16-centimeter handle and a pointed, roughly triangular head about 14 centimeters tall. Where the two meet, there is an abrupt right-angle step that may have kept the hand from slipping. The only earlier object hypothesized to be a club has been found in Kalambo Falls in Zambia and is roughly 400,000 years old. According to Chacón, nothing quite like the Romaní club has turned up anywhere.

Anthropologists have observed and documented hunter-gatherer groups over the last couple of centuries and found they used similar clubs to kill game at close range, fight, and sometimes as symbols of social standing. “But when it comes to this club it’s true that we are not sure,” Chacón admits. The club was found in a living area, next to bones, stone tools, and a hearth, so the team hypothesizes it’s been used for everyday work rather than ceremony.

The choice of materials suggests Neanderthals knew their wood. Scots pine is easy to work and dries quickly, so tools were cheap to make and replace. Juniper’s fibrous bark suited the trays. Firewood tended to be dry wood, while tools were made from fresh wood. “When they went to look for wood, it was like when they went to look for stone; they knew exactly what they wanted to make,” says Chacón. “This implies not only planning, but a bit of complexity in the brain to organize your activities.”

That fits a broader shift, as evidence has piled up that Neanderthals twisted fibers into cord, made symbolic objects, and interbred with our species. “Neanderthals are no longer perceived as Homo sapiens’ dumb cousins,” Chacón says. She suggested that the Abric Romaní tools may offer a new perspective to interpret finds at other sites.

“To study all these types of tools properly, you need a lot of time and budget,” Chacón says. Neanderthal tools from Abric Romaní were first described in the 1990s, so it took decades for the team to identify and catalog them. This makes her concerned that insufficient time and funds might have cost us missing similar discoveries elsewhere. “I hear from colleagues telling me ‘perhaps we found something that we thought was wood, we excavated it, we took pictures, but we didn’t keep it,’” she says. “Now they say perhaps it could be a tool.”

Science Advances, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh2287
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.summary: Spanish archaeologists have cataloged 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas. They found spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club. The findings are different because the finds come from a place where Neanderthals lived, slept, cooked

https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.title: Ukraine’s drones knock out AI data center belonging to "Russia’s Google"
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.author: Jeremy Hsu
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.text:
One damaged data center has supercomputers used for training Yandex’s AI model.

Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to the Russian tech giant Yandex. The damage has left Yandex, known as “Russia’s Google” because it operates the country’s most popular search engine, struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services.

The Ukrainian drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions of Russia on October 8 and October 9, according to Reuters. Those actions came as a direct response to a Russian drone strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers, which has disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of Ukrainians since late September.

“We continue to respond to Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, and we’re doing so with high precision,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a post on X. “Another data center was hit as well—our symmetrical response.”

The Ukrainian company Firepoint said its FP-1 one-way attack drones were involved in the latest strike on the Kaluga data center that is Yandex’s largest such facility, Reuters reported. The first Ukrainian attack targeted Yandex’s Sasovo data center that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers used for training the company’s YandexGPT AI model.

Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions to some services. Russian users reported problems accessing media websites and popular apps for the Ivi video streaming platform, the digital banking service T-Bank and the state-owned Russian Railways, according to the independent Russian news publication Meduza.

Other impacted Russian services included a dating app, a real estate aggregator, a self-publishing book platform and the website of the most successful professional soccer club in the Russian Premier League, according to Reuters.

Targeting data centers is just the latest example of them becoming wartime targets in 2026. After the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iranian drones knocked out multiple Amazon data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.

But Russia has been regularly launching mass missile and drone attacks against Ukraine’s cities, targeting power grid infrastructure, transportation hubs and even residential apartment buildings since Russian President Vladimir Putin first launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Ukraine has recently been grappling with a shortage of interceptor weapons capable of shooting down Russian missiles and jet-powered drones. But the Ukrainian military has also gradually ramped up its own medium-range and long-range drone strike campaign in response to Russian attacks.

Ukraine’s drone strikes have focused on Russian military bases and supply lines, Russian-linked shipping in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea, and Russian energy infrastructure such as oil refineries. In the summer of 2026, Ukraine also targeted multiple warehouses belonging to the Russian companies Wildberries and Ozon, which are Russia’s Amazon equivalents.

In a sign of the potentially widening war, coordinated aerial and sea drone strikes sank two commercial ships in the Black Sea within the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries Romania and Bulgaria on October 5 and October 6. Ukraine’s president Zelenskyy attributed those attacks to Russia.
