https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.title: A Cray-1 supercomputer replica from 30 "obsolete" Mac Minis
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.author: Nick Indge
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.text:
Stylish upcycling, with a retro flare, at Spain’s Museo de Historia de la Computación.

The Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famous Cray-1 supercomputer from 1976. Instead of sourcing expensive, cutting-edge tech to run the system, the creative team powered the project with 30 2012-era Mac Minis. Developed over 18 months, the project serves as a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple’s founding.

Mac Minis from over a decade ago might not seem like the obvious first choice for building a cluster supercomputer, but when networked together, the developers can orchestrate the 64 active processing cores into a combined 1.3 teraflops of performance in their most recent tests. The museum reportedly achieved 1.5 teraflops previously using all 70 available cores, prior to one node going offline. Benchmarks were obtained using a custom matrix-multiplication Python script. Five PCs are quad-core i7s, and the remaining 25 are dual-core i5 models. Except for two units from 2014, the rest of the array dates to 2012.

The replica is a valuable tool for museum-goers to understand the shifts in computer architecture since 1976. The original Cray-1 used vector processing, applying a single instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously, whereas the replica distributes work across independent processors in a parallel cluster. The peak theoretical performance of the original Cray-1 was approximately 160 megaflops. What was originally a purpose-built research machine has been re-created with consumer hardware that’s vastly more capable than the machine that inspired it.

Rather than opting for a more standard Linux distribution, the team found that macOS Mojave (10.14) met their project needs by harnessing macOS’s built-in support for MPI (Message Passing Interface), the software layer that allows all the nodes in the cluster to pass tasks to one another.

Guests at the Museo de Historia de la Computación can watch in real time as the system runs matrix algorithms, mapping the scale of system performance from a single core to the full suite running in parallel.

Combining 30 consumer PCs into an operational cluster wasn’t the only engineering challenge the team faced. If you’ve ever stepped inside a server room, or, like me, foolishly installed one in your own basement, you know that fan cooling can be loud. The museum team used passive convection cooling via a steel rack chassis and aluminum tray mounts for each Mac Mini. Compared to the roaring thunder of a modern data center, this cluster is nearly inaudible.

The secret to the near-silence comes from vertical mounting. The PCs’ vertical orientation, combined with the steel chassis and aluminum trays, allows the tower to act as a natural thermal chimney. Hot air rises through the structure and out of the top grills without the need for added mechanical fans. According to the museum, the only noticeable noise inside the Cray-1 replica comes from two gigabit Ethernet switches at the base of the unit that register between 30–33 decibels, though the team plans to replace them with silent models. The fully assembled replica is said to make so little audible sound that you have to get right up next to the tower to be able to hear anything. While exact dB  measurements from inside the exhibit weren’t available, each individual PC is stated to produce 12–15 dBA of noise at idle.

To manage this quiet giant, designers built a custom terminal that looks straight out of a Cold War control room. The team combined elements of the DEC VT05 and Processor Technology Sol-20 Terminal Computer designs of the 1970s, even incorporating an analog control panel, with future plans to add original lamps from an IBM System/3. One master Mac Mini resides in the terminal and serves to direct all the other cluster nodes.

The original design had planned for the terminal to feature CRT monitors for added authenticity, but modern flat Samsung displays eliminated the connectivity headaches that come from attempting to bridge different technological eras. Future design plans will see 3.5- and 5.25-inch floppy drives mounted to the underside of the desk, and a 3D-printed shell will encase the keyboard to mimic the look of the classic HP 250 design.

The Cray-1 team hopes to fill the currently empty second half of the tower through a crowdfunding campaign to secure 70–80 additional M4 Mac Minis. The goal: create a cluster capable of ranking on the TOP500 supercomputers list.

The replica is on permanent display in the museum, alongside two unused authentic Cray CX1 systems. The Museo de Historia de la Computación offers guided tours on Saturdays from 11:30 am to 2 pm. Additional project information can be found on the museum website.
https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/.summary: The Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famous Cray-1 supercomputer from 1976. The museum reportedly achieved 1.5 teraflops of performance using all 70 available cores.

https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/na.title: NASA issues long-awaited call to industry for private space stations
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/na.author: Eric Berger
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/na.text:
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit.”

NASA on Friday released a much-anticipated “request” to the US commercial space industry to develop private space stations that, as early as 2030, will succeed the International Space Station as a place for astronauts to live in low-Earth orbit.

In a cover letter accompanying the 360-page “request for proposals,” NASA stated its plan: “This will ensure NASA has a sustained human presence in LEO for crew members to perform science and exploration.” Several private companies that have worked for years on designing and developing such stations have been keen to learn exactly what capabilities NASA is seeking. These new documents finally provide some answers.

NASA’s solicitation can be found here. Industry responses are due back to NASA on December 8. NASA said it plans to select “two or more” contractors in this phase of the competition, and intends to make a final decision in April.

“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement that accompanied the release of the new documents. “We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars. Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”

Bidders for this funding phase will certainly include Axiom Space, Voyager Space, and Vast Space. Blue Origin won an earlier round of funding from NASA, but questions remain about the company’s commitment to the program. SpaceX appears unlikely to bid, at least for now. Phase 1 winners will be guaranteed at least $100 million.

Future phases of the contract will be worth billions. NASA said Phase 2 of this “Commercial LEO Destinations” competition, kicking off next year, will include funding for development and certification of space stations, and Phase 3 will include the purchase of at least four missions for NASA astronauts to the private space stations.

One of the most closely watched elements of the NASA request was its provisions for crewed transportation to the stations. In earlier discussions with potential space station providers, NASA had indicated it may leave acquiring transportation to the contractors—basically saying it was their responsibility to sell an end-to-end service to the space agency.

This is problematic because SpaceX has said it plans to retire the Crew Dragon spacecraft as soon as possible, and almost certainly when the International Space Station is deorbited in 2030 or 2032. SpaceX, which has the only operational US vehicle for such transportation, has not offered to sell seats to private space station operators. This led NASA, two weeks ago, to provide an additional $359 million to support Boeing’s ongoing efforts to certify its Starliner spacecraft for crewed missions to low-Earth orbit.

But in the new request for proposals (RFP), the space agency goes further in support of would-be space station operators. As part of their bids, contractors do not need to provide proof of a signed contract with Boeing (or another transportation provider), or even a letter of intent. NASA is even offering to “furnish” transportation for the first four NASA service missions to the private stations, likely meaning it will help broker deals between the private companies and Boeing.

Notably, in the new documents, NASA assigns an explicit price to crew and cargo missions. For 2030, it estimates a four-seat crew flight will cost $325 million, and a cargo flight $300 million. In offering to furnish these initial flights, NASA is taking a significant burden off private space station providers, which are already undertaking a challenging task in constructing, testing, and flying orbital space stations.

The potential bidders were still reviewing the lengthy proposal on Friday afternoon, but several offered their initial thoughts on the new NASA documents.

“The release of the RFP is an important milestone,” Marshall Smith, the chief executive of Voyager’s Starlab space station, said. “We appreciate that NASA has incorporated both industry and government feedback. We believe Starlab has the strongest business plan and technical solution to be America’s next space station and we look forward to competing.”

Axiom Space said it also welcomed the release of the final RFP.

“Our team is actively reviewing the RFP now and is energized for the next steps in the process,” an Axiom Space spokesperson said. “With years of experience executing human space flight missions and developing orbital hardware, we are confident the proposal we provide NASA will demonstrate that Axiom Space is the clear choice to meet NASA’s objectives in low-Earth orbit.”
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/na.summary: NASA released a much-anticipated “request’s’ to the US commercial space industry to develop private space stations. The International Space Station will succeed the International Space station as a place for astronauts to live in low Earth orbit.

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.title: What's been driving Hawaii's lava fountains?
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.author: John Timmer
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.text:
Before the lava fountains started, the ground was expanding by half a meter a day.

In most cases, hotspot-driven volcanism is relatively sedate, with lava flowing down mountainsides slowly enough that people can walk out of its way. But in a number of locations—Mount Etna, Hawaii, Iceland—lava gets expelled in dramatic fountains that can reach several hundred meters in height.

Right now, we’re not sure what powers them. However, thanks to a recent set of eruptions at the Kilauea volcano, we have some of the best documentation yet of erupting lava fountains. In a recent edition of Science, researchers from the US Geological Survey describe what we’ve seen and compare it with what we might expect based on our best ideas about what powers these fountains of molten rock.

With three active volcanic regions that engage in fountaining, there has been a steady flow of dramatic videos of red-hot molten rock spouting from the Earth. But Kilauea has had only three fountaining episodes since 1823, even though it’s the youngest and most active volcano in Hawaii. That activity has led to intensive study, and we have a good idea of the volcano’s structure. Previous work has identified a couple of lava residues within a few kilometers of the surface, and the volcano had 35 separate data-gathering stations set up on Kilauea, including “seismic, infrasound, geodetic, gas, and visual and thermal cameras.”

Following a major eruption in 2018 that partly drained one of the underground lava reservoirs, there were indications that it was being steadily refilled. Starting in 2019, however, the refill accelerated, and the local peak inflated at a rate of more than 22 cm a year. Then, in 2023, that doubled to 57 cm a year, and spread to a nearby caldera.

In 2024, a large series of earthquakes accompanied the opening of a vent, and a 900-meter-long fissure opened, sending fountains as high as 160 meters into the sky over the course of 13 hours. Less than a day after that subsided, a second eruption followed. As of last month, 52 additional fountain eruptions had occurred, the most violent of which spewed lava over 400 meters into the air.

What have we learned from all of this?

Perhaps the most significant finding was that we could predict when a fountaining eruption was likely to happen. Each eruption caused rapid deflation of the summit of Kilauea and was followed by the relatively slow refilling of the Halemaʻumaʻu magma reservoir.

The USGS recognized that consecutive eruptions occurred when the summit tilt reached similar levels. While the precise tilt that was associated with eruptions tended downward over time, the difference between consecutive eruptions was relatively small. This pattern ultimately helped the organization issue alerts when eruptions were likely to occur, which was especially useful because there were no clear seismic signals immediately before fountains restarted.

What have the eruptions told us about the mechanism that drives fountain formation?

One leading idea is that pressure within a magma reservoir keeps water mixed with other materials until it reaches a shallow enough depth to exit as steam. That fragments the magma, which allows it to ascend more rapidly, which allows more steam to escape, and so on until there’s a jet of material near the surface. The alternative posits that things are driven by the release of carbon dioxide from the magma, which forms a magma/gas “foam” at the roof of the magma chamber. Once this reaches a critical point, the gas escapes, driving magma with it until the supply in the magma chamber is exhausted.

The new data doesn’t provide a clear picture. It clearly doesn’t favor the formation of a carbon dioxide foam, because the levels of the gas remained low throughout the eruption cycle. Sulfur dioxide levels rose during eruptions and dropped afterward, but remained high throughout the entire period. Levels of this chemical are associated with gases escaping from magma, so this implies that more of it goes on during eruptions, but it also occurs continuously between them.

So the evidence leans toward the steam-driven eruption model, but it’s unclear why a process that is occurring throughout the cycle suddenly triggers fountains when it rises a bit.

The other bit of information from the chemistry of the eruption is from magnesium oxide, which provides an indication of the temperature of the magma. It fluctuated throughout the eruption cycle, consistent with a cycle in which eruptions deplete a reservoir, which is then refilled with hot material. In contrast, other oxides rose over time, suggesting that the newly arriving material has a distinct chemical composition.

Despite the wealth of nearby sensors, the researchers acknowledged it would be nice to have more data. Sampling of gas levels is typically done at infrared wavelengths and, as you can probably imagine, there was a lot going on in the infrared during a fountaining eruption. And, because of the height of some of the fountaining, it wasn’t necessarily safe to install more monitoring hardware. One camera notably sacrificed itself in order to bring us images of red-hot, semi-molten rock falling from the sky.

While Kilauea has proven itself as a spectacular lab for studying volcanic activity, it hasn’t yet proven ready to give up all its secrets.

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef2931  (About DOIs).
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.summary: Kilauea volcano has had only three fountaining episodes since 1823, even though it’s the youngest and most active volcano in Hawaii. Scientists have been studying the volcano's structure and its chemical composition.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09102.title: Northern California Community Wants Stronger Oversight of Dangerous Refineries Nearby
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09102.author: By Liza Gross
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/09102.text:
MARTINEZ, Calif.—Scores of people tired of living near accident-prone refineries packed an elementary school auditorium to hear what their government officials were doing to protect them.

Two local refineries, Marathon Martinez Renewables and Martinez Refining Co., have racked up hundreds of air quality violations over the past five years. MRC agreed in February to pay $10 million in fines for 163 violations that included an accident that blanketed residents’ homes with 24 tons of metal-laden dust four years ago on Thanksgiving Day.

The settlement did not cover a similar episode in 2025, when a fireball sent thick clouds of smoke across town, leaving residents wondering, again, if it was safe to go outside or eat from their gardens.

Marathon’s Martinez Renewables, which recently locked out more than 100 workers in a labor dispute, has received more than 100 violations from the air district for flaring and other infractions since 2021.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Such incidents inspired U.S. Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, a Democrat, to meet with his constituents in this small city an hour northeast of San Francisco on Thursday night. DeSaulnier, a former air regulator whose district includes four refineries, stressed the need to balance the economic benefits refineries bring to the region with the risks they pose to workers and communities.

Refineries are among the county’s top property-tax contributors and provide thousands of good-paying jobs, DeSaulnier said. The region needs these refineries as it transitions toward renewable energy, but they need to be safe, he said. “It’s a constant battle.”

Flaring incidents have increased in recent years, spiking to nearly 70 in 2023. Flaring involves the controlled burning of flammable gases to manage a buildup of pressure in equipment and reduce the risk of explosions. It also releases a mixture of toxic chemicals, fine particles and climate pollutants.

Recognizing residents’ concerns about ongoing flaring, county officials at the meeting announced the release of a new public dashboard that allows people to track incidents, something residents like Heidi Taylor have been asking for.

Taylor, who co-founded Healthy Martinez after MRC showered her home with heavy metals, wants the refinery to undergo a new health risk assessment, which hasn’t been done in 36 years, she said.

“We need to know what health risks Martinez residents are facing, when that information will be made public and how quickly any unacceptable risks will be addressed,” Taylor said.

MRC did not respond to a request for comment from Inside Climate News.

These incidents require greater enforcement but the Trump administration is working to undermine federal oversight of refineries, DeSaulnier said.

The administration has repeatedly tried to eliminate the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, an independent federal agency that investigates the root causes of industrial chemical accidents. So far, Congress has continued to fund the agency.

Keeping refinery workers and surrounding communities safe requires real-time accountability measures that trigger automatic investigations or corrective actions after incidents, DeSaulnier argued in a recent op-ed. He suggested following Chemical Safety Board recommendations such as tracking equipment failures, overdue inspections, leaks and failed safety systems.

DeSaulnier has a long history of trying to improve refinery safety, dating back to his days as a Contra Costa County supervisor. The congressman was briefly overcome with emotion during Thursday’s hearing as he recounted the deaths of five men at the Tosco Avon Refinery in the 1990s, when he said the county averaged one refinery-related death or serious injury every year.

“I went to a couple of funerals,” he said, regaining his composure, “and I will never forget hearing about the lives of five individuals who, in my opinion, never should have died.”

The Avon refinery is now operated by Marathon Petroleum as Martinez Renewables, where an explosion in 2023 left Jerome Serrano, an operator with four children, fighting for his life for months. Workers with the United Steelworkers Local 5 blamed understaffing and unsustainable overtime shifts for the accident.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

More than 100 employees went on strike for safer conditions after Marathon refused to give them the same contract it had negotiated with the USW for more than 200 other bargaining units across the petroleum and renewables industry.

The strike turned into a lockout when the company rejected union members’ unconditional return to work offer. Workers have now been out of the plant for 165 days.

Nick Plurkowski, USW Local 5 president, was glad to see so many people show up to learn about refinery safety. The meeting covered current regulations and other important topics in a way “only the congressman can do,” Plurkowski said, referring to his personal connection to the workers who died. “He understands that the worst possible outcome isn’t the refineries paying fines, it’s when someone we know gets hurt or killed.”

“The amount of flaring is concerning to say the least,” said Plurkowski. He filed a complaint with state occupational health and safety regulators, alleging that the workers who replaced the USW Local 5 workers, who he said were illegally locked out, aren’t qualified to operate the plant safely. As a result, he said, the state is investigating Marathon’s training of the workers currently running the plant.

Marathon spokesperson Jamal Kheiry said the company continues to staff the Martinez Renewables facility with highly qualified personnel, including supervisors, engineers and technical experts with extensive experience and training in safe, reliable plant operations.

DeSaulnier, who has visited workers on the picket line six times, thinks Marathon is trying to make an example of its plant in Martinez, where workers have the support of the community, to show they can break a union anywhere in the country.

But he’s not aiming to shut down renewable refineries, which he sees as a vital link in the transition to renewables. “The energy industry accounts for a fifth of the gross national product,” he said. “You can’t just turn that off overnight.”

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

David Sassoon

Liza Gross is a reporter for Inside Climate News based in Northern California. She is the author of The Science Writers’ Investigative Reporting Handbook and a contributor to The Science Writers’ Handbook, both funded by National Association of Science Writers’ Peggy Girshman Idea Grants. She has long covered science, conservation, agriculture, public and environmental health and justice with a focus on the misuse of science for private gain. Prior to joining ICN, she worked as a part-time magazine editor for the open-access journal PLOS Biology, a reporter for the Food & Environment Reporting Network and produced freelance stories for numerous national outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post, Discover and Mother Jones. Her work has won awards from the Association of Health Care Journalists, American Society of Journalists and Authors, Society of Professional Journalists NorCal and Association of Food Journalists.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/-.title: 'FishTok' trend creates fishing boom among young Victorians
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/-.author: Harrison Tippet
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/-.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Fishing and Aquaculture Industry

Teens in Victoria are taking up a new hobby. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

If they were not standing on Geelong's Cunningham Pier, Ivy Renouf, Zane Winterton and Xavier Clair say they would either be hanging out in the shopping centre, playing video games, or scrolling their phones.

Instead, this trio of 16-year-olds are enjoying a day in the sun, as they try to catch some fish.

Ivy Renouf, Xavier Clair and Zane Winterton are a new breed of anglers in Geelong. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"It's just a nice day," Ivy says.

"I didn't want to be in bed at home, or in town because I do that all the time, so I just wanted to get outdoors with my mates."

These Geelong teens are part of a new generation of Victorians getting hooked on fishing, sparking a surge of interest in the recreational activity.

Zane remembers when he was the only kid he knew who was into fishing, regularly heading out on trips with his dad.

The teenagers use an old tackle box, bait and fishing knives. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Now, he has plenty of mates who want to come along.

"When I was in primary school, before COVID, no-one fished," he says.

"It was just me, like, in the whole school.

All three of these teens say more young Victorians have been taking up fishing in the past few years, lured by both the challenge and the urge to get outside with friends.

"It's a good way to get some good memories with your friends, to be honest," Xavier says.

"Getting outside and maybe catching a fish or maybe not but, like, just hanging out with your friends and having a good time."

The trio catch little more than a pufferfish from the pier, before heading to a new spot.

At the foot of the pier they pass a group of six other young teens, who cheer each other along as they reel in a bream.

Teens carrying fishing gear through towns like Geelong has become a common sight. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

It is hard to put a number on the increasing popularity of fishing with younger Victorians.

Victorians under 18 years old do not need a licence, and the handful of fishing clubs the ABC spoke to say they may have seen slightly more younger members signing up, but have few useful statistics to back up a boom.

Instead, they say it is an increase most visible on Victorian waterways.

Teens and young anglers throughout the state are often seen walking around clutching rods or setting up at popular fishing spots.

Anthony McGrath says it is impossible to miss the jump in fishing's popularity with young Victorians. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Anthony McGrath, executive officer at VRFish, the state's peak body for recreational fishing, says the increase in younger Victorians fishing is irrefutable.

"It's been incredible," Mr McGrath says.

"There's definitely been a massive increase in kids fishing."

"We see it here every day. The buses arrive back from schools, and the kids are walking past in school uniforms with fishing rods in hand or sticking out of their bags.

On the other side of the bay, Jet Reef Worsteling has spent much of his 19 years fishing.

He is the son of one of Australia's most famous anglers, Paul Worsteling, and is a big name on social media, counting 2.3 million followers on TikTok alone.

Jet Reef Worsteling is already a big name in fishing, particularly on social media. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"When I was in primary school and then going into high school, fishing was more of, like, was an older person's activity … it just wasn't cool like surfing or skating or any of that," Mr Worsteling says.

"I could never have pictured it in a million years, but I think the last year and a half, two years, fishing is now one of the cool things for young people to go do when they've got free time."

Topic:
Public Housing

Topic:
Mining and Metals Industry

Those in the fishing industry point to a handful of factors behind the activity's increasing popularity with young Victorians: social media, a post-COVID desire to get outdoors, and a program handing out free fishing rods to 180,000 Victorian kids.

Mr Worsteling says there has been a clear increase in younger users getting active on "FishTok" and other platforms.

"There's definitely a lot more kids posting videos, liking videos, reacting with videos, all that sort of stuff," he says.

"I see it on my Instagram when I post a picture of a fish, or put something up, and you'll see the likes coming through, and you can just see it's young fellas, young fellas, young fellas — little grommets as we used to call them."

Mr McGrath agrees the social media boom has coincided with a post-COVID urge for people to get back outside.

"I think there's something in it with these kids, that they were the ones who were locked up when they should have been out playing," he says.

"So now we see them getting out and really engaging in these environmental type activities."

Mr McGrath says the final reason behind fishing's increasing popularity is slightly more controversial.

Victoria's Little Anglers Kits program was announced prior to the 2022 state election and handed out free fishing rods, reels, tackle boxes and information kits to about 180,000 grade 5 students across the state over the past two years.

Former premier Dan Andrews made a series of fishing announcements in the lead-up to the 2022 election. (AAP: James Ross)

But, the state government in August announced it would scrap the program, as it moves to reel in budget savings.

"We know many Victorian kids have enjoyed this program. I love fishing and we encourage Victorians to get outdoors in a range of ways," Treasurer Colin Brooks said at the time.

"Right now, we want to ensure that taxpayer dollars are wisely spent on the things that matter most."

Mr McGrath says axing the program, funded via fishing licence fees, is "cutting into the core of that access for kids to fishing".

"[The program] is us investing in our future, so we're really disappointed that the premier didn't speak to us before cutting the program, because we think it's got some long-reaching negative impacts that are yet to be seen," he says.

The government declined to respond when asked whether the Little Anglers program was considered a success.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/v.title: Verstappen pips Russell to sprint pole at Singapore F1 grand prix
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/v.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Max Verstappen stopped the clock .120 seconds ahead of George Russell to take sprint race pole in Singapore. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Ranjith Kumar)

Max Verstappen will start in pole for the Singapore F1 sprint race, having finished more than a 10th of second clear of rival George Russell.

The first sprint race qualification session was stopped after Sergio Perez hit a barrier.

Australia's Oscar Piastri finished fourth-fastest, ahead of his McLaren teammate Lando Norris.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen will take pole position for the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race ​on Friday, having pipped Mercedes driver George Russell, who will join him on the front row at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Verstappen, who had never previously taken pole or won a race in Singapore, set the fastest time of one minute 31.156 seconds, 0.120 seconds quicker than Russell.

Australia's Oscar Piastri qualified fourth-fastest, just ahead of McLaren teammate Lando Norris.

"It's closer in Singapore. Your lap itself, you're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close ​to the walls in places," Verstappen said.

The starting grid for Saturday's #F1Sprint 👇#F1 #SingaporeGP pic.twitter.com/HLYwRDmAgw

"Once we ‌bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more. But I did not expect this, so, of course, very happy to be first.

"The last few races we've been a lot stronger, but of course this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car. But we ‌managed to drive with them as well as possible."

Verstappen was investigated by the stewards for overtaking Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton under the yellow flags in SQ1. ⁠However, they accepted the Dutchman's explanation that braking could have created an unsafe situation and he had reduced his speed by lifting off the throttle afterwards.

Ferrari's ​Charles Leclerc was third fastest, while Mercedes ‌championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 84 points, was only seventh quickest.

Oscar Piastri is hoping McLaren will be more competitive during the Singapore Grand Prix weekend after a disappointing round last time in Malaysia.

Russell was the fastest in the only practice session earlier on Friday, but his power unit penalty will not affect his position on the grid for Saturday's sprint.

However, the FIA handed the Briton a 40-place grid penalty for Sunday after he incurred a 10-place penalty for each of four additional elements, effectively consigning him to the back of ​the ‌pack.

"We've been competitive all day, from the first laps in FP1. We obviously topped the time sheets there," Russell said.

"We knew Max was fast and he went on a slightly different strategy from us in Q3, just doing the one lap. Who knows what was best, but pretty ⁠satisfied with the P2.

"It's going to be very challenging. The grip left to ‌right here is a big difference. The drivers ‌on the pole side last year had a big advantage, so it's probably going to be trying to maintain P2."

Sergio Perez brought an end to the first sprint qualifying session when he hit a barrier. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

The first sprint qualifying session was ‌red flagged when Cadillac's Sergio Perez crashed into a barrier and attempted to nurse his car back into the pits, leaving behind debris from his front wing that marshals needed to remove.

That effectively gave drivers one lap to ‌advance to SQ2, ​and Verstappen was one of the ⁠last drivers to set a lap time, with the Dutchman topping the time sheets.

A glitch in the systems delayed the start of SQ2, with the FIA saying some lap times had not been registered. But the FIA added that the issue had been resolved and the "current timings are considered correct".

Moreover, "overtake mode" was not available after the red flag period during SQ1. It was then activated for a period ⁠of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.

"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position ‌around the lap," it said.

"The ‌second and third periods of Sprint Qualifying were not affected."

A software bug also caused chaos last weekend. Cars slowed to a crawl on two formation laps that were held after heavy rain at Sepang forced the original start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.title: Cult of the Lamb video game team honours work of original composer
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.author: Gianfranco Di Giovanni
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Gianfranco Di Giovanni

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Narayana Johnson had never made a game before Cult of the Lamb, one of Australia's most successful games developed by Melbourne based studio Massive Monster.

The game, equal parts cute and dark, tasks players with growing their cult of woodland followers, defeating horrifying bosses and creating a base for their flock to live.

Johnson, also known as his stage name River Boy, was the visionary behind the game's music and the sound effects.

Cult of the Lamb is one of the most popular titles produced in Australia, selling more than 7 million copies as of April this year, and its cultural impact has spread globally through fan art, cosplay and artistic performances.

The team was gearing up for the next expansion, Woolhaven, which would extend the story for the millions of players invested in the game.

Then Narayana Johnson died.

Narayana Johnson was the award-winning composer of the Cult of the Lamb soundtrack. (Supplied: Massive Monster)

Massive Monster producer Kelsey Gamble says it was a devastating time for the small team, who had to navigate the loss of one of their beloved coworkers while continuing to make a game of which he was an integral part.

"How could you possibly fathom something like this happening and then just move on?" she tells ABC News.

"The answer was, we couldn't. We stopped, you know, everybody obviously took time off to process."

The studio stopped work on the expansion, instead prototyping small games, before returning to development proper.

The first step was to pick up the pieces already completed, with some tracks and the overall 'sonic identity' of Woolhaven already established.

That included finding Johnson's laptop, and then unlocking it to get the raw files already finished.

Cult of the Lamb blended the chilled-out base-building of the Animal Crossing series with satanic cults and ritual sacrifice, to great success. (ABC News)

Johnson had been working with singer and songwriter Ray Vavasis, who performs as Arrowbird, on a couple of tracks for the expansion at the time of his passing.

Johnson's niece, and one half of his band Willow Beats, Kalyani Ellis also wrote music for the game.

JoJo Zhou, head of narrative at Massive Monster, says Vavasis's existing attachment to the project made a huge difference.

"Ray was an absolute godsend the way that she was able to continue the work that Narayana had started, even though often the rest of us were kind of scrambling about what we were going to do," she says.

Vavasis says while working on a teaser trailer for the game, she and Johnson developed a short snippet of music with vocals that was originally planned to be expanded to a full track.

While that never happened, it did become the foundation of much of the work after.

"When writing for the game I would use bits we hadn't finished yet, to pay homage," she says.

"Naturally that's what I wanted to do but it was also a way to process grief.

"That little snippet I ended up using in a lot of things, lots of different scenes."

"I was committed to this project but I felt like upholding that legacy gave me the strength of two people."

Cult of the Lamb composer Ray Vavasis, aka Arrowbird, and head of narrative JoJo Zhou speaking at High Score 2026 at ACMI in Melbourne. (ABC Arts: Gianfranco Di Giovanni)

At the 2026 High Score conference this week, Massive Monster announced the memorial River Boy Scholarship to support composers to make music for games.

Funding, mentorship, access to co-working desks and studio space would be offered to successful participants Zhou says.

"The River Boy Scholarship is about helping composers make the leap from their discipline, into games," she says.

The River Boy Scholarship will open for applications in 2027.

Header image: A screenshot from the Woolhaven expansion of Cult of the Lamb, with the god of winter Yngya at the centre. (Supplied: Massive Monster)

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.title: Tasmanian EPA says it was not told extent of Firmus data centre generator plans
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.author: Emily Smith
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Firmus has pulled its ASX float plans following poor interest from investors. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Tasmania's environmental watchdog is concerned Firmus plans on using 276 diesel generators far more often than it first disclosed.

The EPA has now applied to join as a party to a TASCAT appeal, where Firmus is seeking to have conditions around its generator use removed.

A Firmus submission to a federal joint select committee on AI reveals new renewable energy infrastructure it promised to power its data centres may "not necessarily" be built within Tasmania.

Tasmania's environmental regulator is urging a tribunal to hear its concerns, after learning the operator of a recently approved AI data centre wants to use hundreds of diesel generators far more often than it originally disclosed.

Earlier this year, the George Town Council approved a Firmus Technologies proposal to build a 288-megawatt data centre in the state's north, after the Tasmanian Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) determined it did not need to make an environmental assessment.

The data centre's approval was subject to conditions, including that Firmus could only run the 276 on-site diesel generators at limited times, such as during emergencies or routine inspections.

Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. (Supplied: Firmus Technologies)

Firmus, however, has appealed that condition through the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (TASCAT), arguing it wanted to use the generators "for limited augmentation of the mains electricity supply to offset curtailment, manage energy security and maintain operational reliability during periods of energy market stress".

Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) board has now applied to TASCAT to join as a party to Firmus's appeal.

In its October 7 submission, seen by the ABC, the board said it was originally told the generators would be used "just for emergency use in the event of a power failure", and would not be used during normal operation other than for scheduled weekly exercise runs of less than two hours, annual load tests, and utility outage events.

The board said Firmus's recent appeal showed it planned on using the generators in more circumstances than it thought.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff (centre) with co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis at the Firmus Technologies site. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

"That variation, if part of the original proposal, would likely have resulted in the Board making a different decision in relation to whether to assess the proposal," the board said.

It pointed out that if Firmus's appeal against the condition around generator use is upheld, it could allow it to subvert EPA processes it likely would have been subjected to "if the proposal had been accurately presented".

"And further, if upheld, the appeal has the potential to permit an activity in circumstances where the environmental risks have not been properly assessed, which may result in environmental harm including nuisance … necessitating the EPA taking enforcement action in respect of it," it said.

Construction underway at Firmus's St Leonards site. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The EPA board said it would not comment on matters currently being considered by TASCAT, and Firmus declined to comment on the matter.

A state government spokesperson said it was supportive of private investments that created jobs and economic benefits but "projects should use resources responsibly and engage transparently with communities".

Greens MP Tabatha Badger said she welcomed the EPA raising concerns and pointing out the potential for the generators to breach acceptable limits and for noise to carry across the river.

Meanwhile, a submission made by Firmus to the current federal joint select committee on AI reveals its Tasmanian data centres may be powered with renewable infrastructure based interstate, rather than locally.

Firmus has long said it will build two megawatts of new renewable energy generation for every 1 megawatt it uses across new data centres planned for Launceston, Long Reach and Wesley Vale.

Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis are the co-CEOs of Firmus Technologies. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Firmus's co-CEO Tim Rosenfield has previously implied that new capacity would be built in Tasmania.

"[Firmus investment] will add net new energy to Tasmania that will end up being able to be exported across Marinus [Link], which is a good thing we feel," he told ABC Mornings in July.

But according to Firmus's recent submission, which it engaged Oxford Economics Australia to prepare, those renewable projects are "not necessarily sited within Tasmania".

Firmus declined to comment.

The company is currently negotiating with Hydro Tasmania to secure 444MW of power for its centres.

A Hydro Tasmania spokesperson said the new renewable projects it was considering as part of its assessment of Firmus's request "are all located in Tasmania, in line with the Tasmanian government's expectations that data centres in Tasmania support new on-island energy generation".

A Tasmanian government spokesperson said it expected developers to unlock new renewable energy generation projects in Tasmania to support their demand.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.title: Baby flying foxes starving in numbers volunteers have never seen
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.author: Charles Rushforth
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Volunteers are encountering hundreds of flying pups born prematurely across the state, weighing as little as 40 grams. (Supplied: Wildlife ARC Society )

Hundreds of grey-headed flying foxes have given birth prematurely across NSW after a suspected mass starvation event.

Wildlife rescue volunteers have received more than 460 reports of malnourished flying foxes since late September.

The federal environment department is investigating whether a mass starvation event prior to the October birthing season is responsible.

Experienced wildlife carers have been overwhelmed by unprecedented rates of flying foxes giving birth to premature pups across New South Wales.

Since late September, wildlife rescue groups in the state have been called to more than 460 reports of malnourished grey-headed flying foxes affected by a suspected starvation event prior to the October birthing season.

Flying foxes born under the healthy weight range have a heightened risk of death.

Volunteer rescue organisation For Australian Wildlife Needing Aid (FAWNA) estimated that about 95 per cent of pups born prematurely will die in care.

Ecologist and wildlife carer on the central coast Kerryn Parry-Jones said she became alarmed after volunteers began encountering hundreds of premature bats, some weighing less than 40 grams.

"People are finding little baby bats on the ground, sometimes with the placenta and umbilical cords still attached," Dr Parry-Jones said.

"I've never seen large numbers of premature babies coming in like this.

Volunteers with Wildlife Rescue South Coast have taken in dozens of premature flying foxes since late September. (Supplied: Wildlife Rescue South Coast)

Co-ordinator with Wildlife Rescue South Coast (WRSC) Trista Thorpe said volunteers began receiving "abnormal" reports of malnourished bats in late September.

"Those calls just kept increasing and increasing, then we began to get aborted babies in," Ms Thorpe said.

By October, Ms Thorpe said volunteers were responding to dozens of calls per day, recovering dead and sick flying foxes and premature pups at roosting sites and residential properties across the Shoalhaven.

"The smallest one I have weighed was only 38 grams; a newborn [pup] should be born at about 80 or 90 grams," she said.

Many of the flying foxes taken into care have been found to be extremely emaciated. (Supplied: Wildlife Rescue South Coast )

FAWNA NSW president Meredith Ryan said the trend had been recorded as far north as Kempsey in recent weeks, where volunteers were encountering dozens of deceased pups daily.

Ms Ryan said that while starvation events and mass fatalities were common in flying fox populations, the recent rate of premature births was unprecedented.

"We've never had this massive amount of pup mortality," Ms Ryan said.

Recent testing by the Australian Registry of Wildlife Health of flying fox cadavers recovered from the Illawarra has confirmed the animals were "severely emaciated" at time of death.

A spokesperson from the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water said the cause of the starvation event and premature births remained a mystery.

"It is believed these cases of emaciated flying foxes could be related to temporary shortfalls in available food, but there's no confirmed cause," the spokesperson said.

The frequency of reports, limited volunteer numbers and long distances between sites has left wildlife rescue groups struggling to confirm the exact number of flying foxes that have died recently.

Due to the high price of the lyssavirus vaccine required to safely handle bats, both FAWNA and WRSC only have approximately 40 volunteers available to respond to callouts.

Rescuers are struggling with the numbers of flying foxes needing care. (Supplied: Wildlife Rescue South Coast)

WRSC volunteers are now caring for 53 flying foxes at their clinic in Nowra while also responding to multiple daily reports of sick bats or deceased bats, sometimes more than an hour away.

Ms Thorpe said she hasn't slept for 48 hours due to the demands of feeding and cleaning required to keep the bats alive.

"Because the babies are coming in so tiny at the moment, they're all on two-hourly feeds, 24 hours a day," she said.

"So we're not getting much sleep in between all of that."

Ecologist Kerryn Parry-Jones said the rates of bats giving birth prematurely were unprecedented over her 30-year career.  (ABC Central Coast: Keira Proust)

Dr Parry-Jones said while the number of flying foxes who have died at colony sites near the central coast could likely be "in the thousands", the exact numbers can't be confirmed until the immediate crisis is over.

"We won't know until the end of the season just how awful it is."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/q.title: Queensland battles dry spring except in far north
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/q.author: Sophie Johnson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Rainy clouds loom over a beach in Far North Queensland during a wet September. (ABC Far North: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

The bureau forecasts wet cool conditions to continue through to the end of spring in Far North Queensland.

This is a stark contrast to the rest of the state battling dry conditions.

Due to above-average sea surface temperatures, the bureau says the far north can expect an above-average rainfall wet season with increased cyclone severity.

Unseasonal wet and cool conditions in the state's far north are expected to continue throughout spring as the rest of the state battles dry conditions.

The north spent September under a blanket of showers, with some areas recording up to six times their average monthly rainfall.

The Bureau of Meteorology said a persistent ridge along the coast brought weeks of showers to the region which kept temperatures down and rainfall well above average for some places.

Senior forecaster Felim Hannify said similar conditions would continue for the rest of the season.

But from December, temperatures are expected to climb as the wet season gathers pace.

Mr Hannify said sea surface temperatures along the Queensland coast were already above average and were expected to rise further over summer.

"Above-average sea temperatures mean the potential for increased rainfall," he said.

Warmer ocean temperatures could also increase the risk of severe tropical cyclones forming, although they do not necessarily mean more cyclones overall.

Mr Hannify said while El Niño typically brought drier conditions, warmer sea surface temperatures could dampen its influence on rainfall in the north.

Rowan Donnacha Byrne, 6, playing with mud in a campsite in Far North Queensland following a wet few weeks. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The cool, wet conditions have slowed production and delayed flowering for some Far North Queensland growers.

Atherton Tablelands farmer Michael Coulston, who grows bananas, avocados and custard apples, said the cooler weather had held back banana production and helped keep prices high.

He said avocado flowering was also running noticeably late.

"Normally by now you're looking at transitioning into daytime sprays, but we're pushing them out just because we're seeing more flowers holding onto the tree that we're just waiting to see what happens, whether they fruit or they just stay a flower," Mr Coulston said.

Passionfruit flowering has been delayed near Innisfail due to wet and cool weather. (ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson)

Innisfail grower Will Darveniza said wet conditions had slowed growth across his mixed horticulture farm, delaying passionfruit flowering and affecting pollination.

"September was pretty wet compared to previous years and that does a lot to hurt our pollination and flower set," he said.

Mr Hannify said the north-east and far north of the state recorded the most rain during September with "little or nothing" in parts of the south-east.

"Some areas around the north-east tropical coast, particularly in Cairns and the Daintree and the wet tropics in general, saw well over three times their monthly average [rainfall] for September."

Cairns Airport recorded just under 97 millimetres for the month; its average is 34mm. Innisfail received up to 300mm, nearly three times the monthly average.

Kowanyama recorded nearly 15mm, close to six times its monthly average of just 2.4mm.

"It was just persistent shower activity … there was very little prolonged dry spells throughout that month, particularly along more coastal areas."

Parts of Innisfail recorded up to three times the monthly rainfall average in September. (Supplied: Joseph Marano)

Mr Hannify said the extensive shower activity brought on the cooler the temperatures.

"We saw some areas record their lowest mean maximum for September, going back for over 20 years as well," he said.

"Looking at Cairns Airport itself, 27.8 [degrees Celsius] was the was the actual official average maximum for the month of September, which was actually its coolest since 1994. Now the average is 28.2."

"Mareeba recorded 26.7 [degrees Celsius], it was equal with its all-time [coolest average maximum temperature] record set back in 2006 as well."

Mr Hannify said the cooler and wetter September in the north was in part driven by El Niño.

"It certainly may have [had] an impact on just the strength of that ridge and just the orientation of that ridge along the east coast as well," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/t.title: Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russia to supply diesel to US
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Donald Trump (right) says he had a "highly successful" phone call with Vladimir Putin over diesel supply.  (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply disel to the US.

Mr Trump signed sweeping sanctions against Russia last month aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues.

Analysts have cast doubt on how much the deal will near-record high diesel prices in the US.

US President Donald Trump says he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, up-ending years of Washington pressuring Moscow over its war with Ukraine.

The price of diesel, used in agriculture, heating homes and trucking, sits near a record high in the US.

Mr Trump said on social media he had a "highly successful" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets.

Analyst warns export ban the most worrying development since the Middle East conflict began.

An envoy for Mr Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised the cooperation between Russia and the US in a post on X shortly after the call.

Mr Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law aimed at clamping down on Russia’s energy revenues and other areas that are fuelling its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the US leader's new stance.

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," he said.

"Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy."

The US Treasury Department issued a general licence on Friday, local time, allowing the importation of Russian diesel until April 7.

Mr Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter".

Even more would follow, Mr Trump said, "based on the condition of their diesel refineries", which have been damaged by Ukrainian attacks.

The week's most important fuel news, analysis and pricing information.

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available.

It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to the US midterm elections on November 3.

Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices.

"I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is," Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, said on X, adding that Russia usually exported much more diesel when its refinery fleet was not under attack.

The 300,000 tonnes to be immediately delivered is equal to about 2.25 million barrels of diesel.

The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.

"It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market," Jim Mitchell, an analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie, said.

Diesel prices, which can drive inflation, are up 70 per cent since the US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing average US diesel prices to $US6.28 a gallon ($2.37 a litre) on Thursday, according to the AAA motorist group.

The price climb is despite Mr Trump's two recent efforts to boost fuel supplies: pressuring allies ‌to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is normally used for farm equipment.

US diesel futures HOc1 fell sharply following news of the deal and were trading at $US4.64 a gallon, down more than 4.8 per cent.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Mr Trump said.

Three industry sources said Mr Trump would in the coming days direct some US department heads to find ways to control diesel prices.

The directive, which they said could take the form of a presidential memo, will push officials to find ways to bypass local and state regulations blocking energy production and use the Cold War-era Defense Production Act (DPA) to increase the output of oil and fuel.

Under the DPA, the president can authorise US-backed loans or loan guarantees to expand domestic manufacturing of critical materials and require companies to prioritise government contracts for essential goods.

Donald Trump says Russia will immediately deliver 300,000 tons of diesel.

The White House has been weighing how to use the DPA to expand refining capacity as the war with Iran has exposed US vulnerability to supply disruptions and price spikes.

Refining executives told administration officials last month that federal money would be better directed ​toward making refineries more efficient or expanding plants rather than financing a new refinery, which would be more costly and ⁠take years to complete.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.title: NT council's China trade mission questioned amid cost-of-living crisis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.author: Matt Garrick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Local Government

The Darwin City Council will lead an Asian trade delegation including about 10 businesses in December. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Darwin lord mayor Peter Styles will lead a delegation of businesses to China and Vietnam later this year, in a bid to help bolster the Top End economy.

The trip comes after rates in the city were raised above inflation, but the council has denied it is a "junket".

It is the first of such overseas delegations led by the city's council since 2023.

Darwin City Council has defended its decision to lead a trade delegation to Asia during a year when the city's rates have been hiked and its annual hard rubbish collection delayed to 2027.

The council has confirmed about $18,000 of ratepayer funding will be spent on the mission, to be led by lord mayor Peter Styles, which aims to open economic doors for the Top End city.

The council's general manager of innovation, Alice Percy, said the delegation would lead about 10 businesses to Guangzhou in China and Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam in December.

Guangzhou, China's third-largest city, will be part of the council-led trade delegation. (Getty Images)

"This is definitely not a junket for the mayor and for the council," she said.

"It's an important economic opportunity for Darwin as a capital city."

Ms Percy said it would be the first time the city's council had led a delegation abroad since 2023.

Alice Percy says the trade mission could be lucrative for the Darwin economy.  (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The delegation comes a year after China Southern Airlines began flying to and from Darwin, with the council voicing its ambition to try and convince more carriers to fly to the city.

While attending businesses will fund their own trips, the council has said it will provide support and facilitate introductions and networking opportunities with businesses in Asia.

Mr Styles is a previous NT government Asian engagement minister, and after he lost his seat in 2016, he held private consultancy businesses in the same field.

Peter Styles will lead the delegation.  (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The council was asked whether it viewed Mr Styles's previous roles as possible conflicts of interest in leading the delegation, but it did not respond by deadline.

Mr Styles was unavailable for an interview.

The council's move to embark on the trip comes six months after it raised rates by 5.5 per cent, above inflation level, and ditched its annual pre-cyclone clean-up for 2026, postponing it until next May.

At the time of the rate hike, Mr Styles said the council was grappling with rising expenses and a large damage bill following a destructive cyclone season.

The trip will also take in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser)

Former Darwin lord mayor Graeme Sawyer said the council risked seeming out of touch with its ratepayers.

"Particularly at a time when cost of living and everything else is so front and centre in people's minds, you're really treading on some rough country here," he said.

Mr Sawyer said he had concerns about a "culture of secrecy" within the Darwin council, where discussed items were routinely being made confidential and unable to be viewed by the public.

Graeme Sawyer says the council should be "open and explicit" with ratepayers about its reasons for ventures like this one. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"If council's not being open and explicit about the benefits and the reasons for these sorts of things, then naturally people are just going to think it's another junket," he said.

The Asian trade delegation was originally made confidential by the council when the resolution was passed earlier this year, but the council has confirmed it has now been made public.

In the community, the ABC asked Darwin residents what they thought of the upcoming trade mission, which will fund two council staff members to travel abroad alongside the lord mayor.

Kathy Carter would like to see the council focus more on rates, roads and rubbish.  (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Darwin resident of more than 40 years, Kathy Carter, said she did not support the initiative.

"I think it's probably not a good idea," she said.

"The rates have just been put up, and we need more interest in rates, roads and rubbish.

"They can do cultural ties and trading things and all that stuff with the [NT] government."

Mike Sproule says the money going towards the delegation could be better spent elsewhere.  (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Resident of The Gardens for more than 30 years, Mike Sproule, said he had "found over the last couple of years the performance of the council seems to be struggling".

"I'm all for cultural ties and growing business, but … it just seems to be a bit of a waste of money, really," he said.

Darwin City Council has said the trade mission will be held between December 8 and 16.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/t.author: Alex Sinnott
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police were called to a fire outside a residence in Taylors Lakes, in suburban Melbourne. (ABC News)

A vehicle fire at Taylors Lakes, in Melbourne's north-western suburbs, has marked the sixth consecutive evening of firebombings across the Victorian capital.

In a separate incident, a man was arrested in Melbourne's south-eastern suburbs following a fire at Oakleigh South.

Deakin University criminologist James Martin says the recent string of firebombings could be related to Victoria's crackdown on the illegal tobacco trade.

Victoria Police are investigating another car fire in Melbourne after six consecutive days of arson attacks across the city.

Firefighters were called to the blaze at a house on Nepean Court in Taylors Lakes just after 11pm yesterday, finding a vehicle on fire in a double garage.

Emergency services said no-one was injured in the blaze, 30 kilometres north-west of central Melbourne.

The fire is being treated as suspicious.

"Firefighters arrived on scene within five minutes to find a car on fire in a double garage attached [to a] double-storey residence," a Fire Rescue Victoria spokesperson said.

"Crews, wearing breathing apparatus, contained the fire to the garage. Firefighters checked for fire extension into the property."

A car and part of a house were extensively damaged in the arson attack. (ABC News)

In a separate incident, protective services officers arrested a man following a fire in Oakleigh South this morning.

Emergency services were called to reports of a factory fire on Valley Street about 3am.

Victoria Police said the fire caused minor damage to the property and there were no injuries.

A 53-year-old man was arrested at Clayton Railway Station a short time later.

A series of vehicle and residential firebombings have occurred across Melbourne in recent weeks, with properties in Springvale, Oakleigh East, Reservoir, Taylors Lakes, Maidstone and Keilor targeted.

Earlier this week, a senior detective said Victoria Police was concerned about the attacks and aware of the community's safety concerns.

Premier Ben Carroll also weighed into the issue, labelling arsonists as "adult imbeciles" and meeting with Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush to discuss the attacks.

Deakin University criminologist James Martin said it could be linked to Victoria's crackdown on the sale of illegal tobacco.

"Criminological research shows pretty consistently that violence tends to increase when you start cracking down on illicit markets," Dr Martin told 774 ABC Melbourne this week.

James Martin says previous examples suggest the illegal tobacco crackdown may be linked to the string of Melbourne firebombings. (ABC News)

"There is a tenuous timing link."

Victoria gave new powers to inspectors and police last month to shutter businesses caught selling illicit tobacco, with 61 stores linked to organised crime since closed for breaches.

Police said this week that in the past four weeks they had seized 2 million cigarettes, more than 40,000 vapes, more than 120 kilograms of loose tobacco and $500,000 in cash.

Dr Martin said enforcement could put pressure on offenders who may want to send a message to people providing information to authorities or who were unwitting participants in a particular trade.

"Or it could be attacks to signal strength or tit-for-tat attacks against rival gangs that might perceive your stores being closed as a potential weakness," he said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: ‘Children Untold’ shines a light on the plight of postwar orphans
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Mark Schilling
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Japan’s defeat in World War II left an estimated 120,000 children orphaned, many of them destitute and abandoned. These children are the subject of Miwa Nishikawa’s latest film “Children Untold,” which she scripted based on her own extensive research.

Told from the perspective of a tenderly raised, musically talented 12-year-old girl, the film is neither as heartbreakingly sad as the 1988 anime masterpiece “Grave of the Fireflies” nor as cheerily upbeat as the hit 1950 musical “Tokyo Kid,” which starred postwar enka icon Hibari Misora as a war orphan with a big heart and voice.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.title: Still-simmering ‘Japanese Ramen Simulator’ is already worth a slurp
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Owen Ziegler
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
I step outside my restaurant, flip the signboard to “open” and pull out my charumera horn to play a tune that echoes throughout the neighborhood — the best fake ramen shop in the world is open for business.

“Japanese Ramen Simulator,” a game developed by Tokyo-based indie studio Wild Dog and launching for ¥1,900 on Oct. 9, does what it says on the tin: You step into the shoes of a chef-owner of a ramen shop. You stock your shop with an increasingly diverse array of ingredients, hire staff, serve customers and gradually expand your business from a single counter to a multistory restaurant.

To those unfamiliar with the simulation genre, where real-world activities are painstakingly rendered into virtual entertainment, watching even 30 seconds of “Japanese Ramen Simulator” will seem ridiculous. You start the day preparing for service based on predetermined recipes — placing orders for ingredients on a laptop at the back of the shop (the ingredients arrive immediately by drone), organizing your kitchen or doing some renovation by adding seats, removing decorations, etc. — and then you open the shop. Customers enter, you take their orders, you make their ramen with variations of toppings and side orders like gyōza (dumplings), chāshū-don (pork rice bowls) and more. And then at 10 p.m., you close up.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.summary: “Japanese Ramen Simulator’s’ is a game developed by Tokyo-based indie studio Wild Dog. It's a game that lets you stock your shop with an increasingly diverse array of ingredients. You start the day preparing for service based on predetermined recipes.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Trump says Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, and his administration temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine.

Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, are near a record and have put Trump’s fellow Republicans at risk ahead of the Nov. 3 congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress. Diesel prices fell after the announcement, but analysts said the deal may not be enough to keep them down.

Trump said on social media he had a “highly successful” discussion with President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The U.S. exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-names-new-pr.title: Trump names new press secretary to succeed Karoline Leavitt
https://www.dw.com/en/trump-names-new-pr.text:
Trump has appointed Katie Zacharia to take over the White House press secretary role vacated by Karoline Leavitt. She assumes the role with Trump struggling with low approval ratings driven by the US war with Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, succeeding Karoline Leavitt.

In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said it was a "great honor" to appoint Zacharia to the role, calling her a "loyal and brilliant supporter" and member of the Make America Great Again movement.

Zacharia, a 42-year-old native of California, had been serving as Senior Communications Advisor to Truth Social. She had also earlier worked as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs at the Department of Homeland Security.

Zacharia, in a post on X, thanked Trump and said "his leadership is a blessing to this country."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our country and communicating to the American people the major wins that the administration is making every single day," Zacharia said. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out."

Zacharia said her predecessor Leavitt was "fabulous" and that she set a "high standard" to meet for the press secretary job.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump had announced that Leavitt would resign in August to spend more time with her young children and family.

Earlier this week, conservative-leaning broadcaster Fox News announced that Leavitt would provide commentary on the network starting from November 1.

Leavitt took a combative approach to questions from the White House press corps during her tenure as press secretary.

In January, she called a White House reporter a "left-wing hack" after a question regarding the fatal US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shooting of American citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis. She also had to defend Trump's controversial handling of the Epstein files and the ongoing Iran war.

Leavitt managed to stay in the role for over 18 months — a long tenure for a high-stress job under a demanding president. During Trump's first term from 2017 to 2021, he had four press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.

Zacharia's tenure comes as Trump faces low approval ratings due to high energy prices amid the Iran war and the looming midterms on November 3, where the opposition Democrats are expected to make major congressional gains.
