https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63d.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63d.text:
If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.

The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.

But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.

Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.

The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).

What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.

Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.

Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.

"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.

A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."

Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".

But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how the easy stores are to navigate.

"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."

Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.

Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.

Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."

The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.

Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.

She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.

Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".

"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."

Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".

"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."

The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.

The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.

It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.

Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.

"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.

While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.

"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.

Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.

But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.

Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.

There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.

For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.

Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63d.summary: Boots is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership this week. New owners Wittington Investments are a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family. New-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5.text:
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.

"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.

"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.

Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.

"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.

The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.

Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.

The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.

The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.

On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.

But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.

Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.

It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.

When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).

"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.

On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.

But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.

"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.

"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."

The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.

So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.

More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.

But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.

A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.

Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.

A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.

"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."

Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.

But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.

"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."

Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.

Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."

The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.

More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.

But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.

The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.

Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.

Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.

Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.

Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.

He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.

Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.

"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.

Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.

She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.

The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.

The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.

This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.

Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.

And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.

What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.

The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.

Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.

She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.

For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.

But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.

"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.

"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."

As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.

A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.

"The canteen is still open."

The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.

Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Tait in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies

US politics – live updates

Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.

Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.

In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.

“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”

He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”

Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.

Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exception to its provisions.

But the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to an “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.

“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal” which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.

“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other.” he said.

Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”

But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone component and ammunition.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.title: Investigators say flydubai pilot's 'drift towards terrorism' started in Australia
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.author: Matthew Doran
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/f.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A flydubai plane was carrying passengers bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates. (AFP: Jack Guez)

The co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv began showing signs of a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" in Australia nearly 10 years ago, investigators say.

United Arab Emirates authorities say the man was trying to take control of the plane to crash it into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport.

The Australian Federal Police is investigating his time in Australia and any links to extremism.

Emirati investigators have revealed the pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv started to "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia.

The man, widely reported as Omani national Al-Hammami, is accused of attacking his co-pilot with an axe in the skies over Saudi Arabia, as they were flying a flydubai plane with more than 170 passengers.

The Indian co-pilot, Smit Machchhar, managed to unlock the cockpit door during the violent attack, which allowed passengers to storm in and wrest back control.

Captain Smit Machchhar has been praised for his actions during the mid-air incident. (X: India in Israel)

A LinkedIn profile seen by multiple media outlets, since deleted, showed Al-Hammami said he studied at Melbourne's RMIT.

The Attorney-General of the United Arab Emirates, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, alleged Al-Hammami was trying to take control of the plane to crash it into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport in a "suicide attack".

The moment the plane lost altitude was captured on camera.

Mr Al Shamsi said the pilot had been inspired by Al Qaeda's September 11 attacks in New York, learning of his leanings during interrogations of the 29-year-old.

"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the UAE's state news agency reported, in comments attributed to the attorney-general.

"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."

It said Al-Hammami had "regularly attended" a mosque during his time studying in Melbourne, and "became acquainted" with an organisation linked to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Known as "My Centre," the news agency reported it was managed by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza".

"[Al-Hammami] also said that he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach," the news agency reported.

Last week, the Australian Federal Police confirmed it had launched an investigation into Al-Hammami's time in Australia and any links to extremism.

The pilot is accused of using the crash axe, stored in the cockpit, to attack his co-pilot during the attack in early October.

"In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution," the Emirati news agency said.

"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim."

Passengers have described the terrifying plummet that saw the jet descend nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds and the cockpit scrum that helped the flydubai flight land safely.

The plane plummeted during the incident, before passengers managed to take back control and a pilot, travelling on the flight, managed to execute an emergency landing in northern Saudi Arabia.

Questions have been raised as to how Al-Hammami was allowed to fly the plane to Tel Aviv, given he had reportedly been sacked by his country's national carrier due to his extremist views.

Israel also has rules banning flight crews from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with it from operating planes in and out of Tel Aviv. Oman falls into that category.

There have been demands in Israel for the country's transport minister to resign, given her department is meant to flag security risks among flight crews.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.title: Oldest Wallaby remembers historic Eden Park win over All Blacks
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.author: Hamish Cole
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/d.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Don Strachan is the oldest living Wallaby, having made his debut in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole/Sharon Gordon)

Don Strachan has accomplished a feat that only a handful of Wallabies still living have achieved — defeating the All Blacks at Eden Park.

In his second test match in 1955, the then-26-year-old prop started in Australia's 8–3 defeat of New Zealand at the iconic ground in Auckland.

The Wallabies have only tasted success against the All Blacks there on three other occasions, the last 40 years ago.

"We were determined to win that [1955] game," Strachan said.

An excerpt from a local newspaper following the game detailed the win as "one of the finest" the Wallabies had produced.

"The Australians gave a magnificent exhibition to outplay the All Blacks," the article said.

Don Strachan featured in the Wallabies 8–3 win over the All Blacks at Eden Park in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Despite the victory, New Zealand retained the Bledisloe Cup following wins in the first and second test matches in Wellington and Dunedin.

The series loss still haunts Strachan all these years later.

He was disallowed a try in his debut game at Carisbrook on the South Island, which the All Blacks won 8–0.

"We were cheated," Strachan said.

Hailing from Orange in the New South Wales Central West, the 97-year-old is the oldest living Australian rugby union player.

"I'm Wallaby number 413, and that means there are 412 of them who are no longer here anymore," he said.

"I wouldn't have wished for anything else. I've been lucky … I've had a great time."

Don Strachan is Wallaby number 413 after making his debut against the All Blacks in Dunedin in 1955. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

His international rugby career almost ended before it began following a motorbike crash in the Blue Mountains while returning from a game in Sydney.

"I had a terrific motor accident. A truck came over the hill on the wrong side of the road," Strachan said.

"[It] hit me head-on. Threw me almost into the front yard of the house next door."

After suffering a compound fracture to his leg, Strachan narrowly avoided having it amputated and spent several months in hospital.

Back on his dad's potato farm near Orange, Strachan began building his strength to return to the footy field.

"I used to lift 1,000 bags of potatoes a day," he said.

"I had a very strong back, legs and shoulders … That stood me in good stead because I had the muscles to support everything else."

As a front rower, Strachan "loved the game" and the physicality that came with it.

Don Strachan remembers his time with the Wallabies fondly. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

"I never got pushed out of a scrum in my life … If they played fair, I played fair," he said.

"If they wanted to do something else, I'd accommodate them.

"I accommodated a few of them."

That love of rugby ultimately saw Strachan captain the Combined NSW Country side for five years, represent the NSW Waratahs and play twice for Australia.

Don Strachan captained the Combined NSW Country side for five years. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

It could have been more after being selected for a seven-month tour of the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada and the United States in 1955, but with a baby on the way with wife Wendy and a farm to help run, he declined the opportunity.

In 1947, the Orange Rugby Club had been travelling to Sydney most winter weekends to take on lifesaving clubs and agricultural schools.

From that team spawned the idea to create a four-team local competition in Orange that would become the Central West Rugby Union tournament in 1956.

The Orange Emus have won 17 first-grade premierships in the Central West Rugby Union competition, winning the Blowes Cup in 2025. (Supplied: Orange Emus)

Given that macropods had been adopted by many clubs across the country, Strachan and his friends turned to the other side of the Australian coat of arms for inspiration. And thus, the Orange Emus Rugby Club was born.

"We had a collection of some of the nicest people you could ever meet," he said.

To fund the construction of an oval and grandstand, the club had to get creative.

"We used to do these rabbit drives," Strachan said.

"We were catching 1,200 rabbits at a time and taking them into the abattoirs and selling them.

"The whole club got together and worked and made this money … eventually we were able to put it together."

The Orange Emus became one of the most successful clubs in the Central West Rugby Union competition, winning 17 first-grade titles.

The Wallabies will play NZ on Saturday afternoon.

https://www.dw.com/en/strong-earthquakes.title: Strong earthquakes shake Panama, buildings damaged
https://www.dw.com/en/strong-earthquakes.text:
Panama's president has declared a "major disaster" after a series of tremors damaged buildings, briefly suspended flights and triggered a tsunami alert in Central and South America.

A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday morning.

According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake's epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama's southern tip.

The quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

The USGS later reported that a second powerful earthquake, measuring 6.6 in magnitude, struck the country following a series of aftershocks.

The tremors were strongly felt in the capital Panama City, causing buildings to shake and sending people rushing into the streets.

"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared."

Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino described the earthquake as a "major disaster" which had destroyed roads near the epicenter.

Mulino did not say whether there were any casualties.

According to Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service, damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.

Smith reported several injuries, as well as partial collapses and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage to the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.

Meanwhile, local news outlets reported that the colonial-style Church of San Atanasio in Panama’s Los Santos province collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.

The US Tsunami Warning System issued an alert stating that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico within the next three hours.

The system also reported a tsunami threat to Hawaii. The warning was lifted later on Friday afternoon.

Initially, there were no reports of damage to the Panama Canal. The Panama Canal Authority stated that the waterway was operating as usual.

Tocumen International Airport in Panama City briefly suspended operations and activated evacuation protocols before reopening later on Friday afternoon.

Panama is located along the so-called "Ring of Fire," a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Karl Sexton

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2d.title: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2d.text:
Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.

The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.

The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand.

Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades.

Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.

But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".

"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.

The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.

The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).

Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.

Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.

CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.

In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.

Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.

"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.

Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.

"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."

The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.

At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.

The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.

But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.

The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.

For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.

Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text:
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.

The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.

That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.

More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.

The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.

The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.

Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.

The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.

His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.

Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.

Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.

Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.

On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.

We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.

However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.

Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.

But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.

Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.

The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.

But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.

It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.

Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.

Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.

Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.

By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.

Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.

He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.

The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.

The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.

Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.

Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.

Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.

"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.

The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.

The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Intercommunal clashes kill 71 people in South Sudan
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Intercommunal clashes have killed 71 people in South Sudan’s town of Rumbek, in Lakes State, the caretaker government said in a statement.

“According to initial security reports, approximately 71 people were reportedly killed,” including four soldiers, the South Sudanese interim Ministry of Information said in a statement on Friday. The exact number of fatalities has yet to be verified.

According to AFP, witnesses said a group of people from outside Rumbek tried to take control of the town and briefly succeeded. The attackers withdrew when police and military reinforcements arrived. Two witnesses said the fighting moved outside the city limits.

The government statement said, “Rumbek town is currently under the control of Government security forces, and efforts are ongoing to restore normalcy”.

The caretaker government strongly condemned the violence and urged all communities to “exercise maximum restraint and refrain from acts of retaliation that could further escalate tensions”.

On September 22, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country’s first election since its independence in 2011. Kiir appointed a caretaker administration as the country prepares for its first-ever national elections.

His decree ended a power-sharing arrangement set up under a 2018 peace deal that halted a five-year civil war in which about 400,000 people were killed.

Intercommunal conflict has continued across South Sudan, resulting in multiple deadly clashes.

On September 17, 26 people were killed, and 82 were injured during days of fighting in a disputed region on the border between South Sudan and Sudan.

In early March, intercommunal violence left at least 169 people dead after dozens of armed men attacked a town.

A Palestinian man has been killed by Israeli forces near Hebron in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

The ministry said 32-year-old Shadi Ahmad Ibrahim Ajarma was shot and killed near the Nabi Yunis junction north of Hebron late on Friday, Wafa news agency reported.

The ministry added that Israeli forces are withholding the victim’s body.

The internationally recognised government of Yemen says it has conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the past 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters.

The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations, which are part of the “Dawn of Yemen” campaign, also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory.

He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans.

The Yemeni government announced on Sunday the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen” to retake Yemeni territory held by the Iran-backed Houthis.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthro.title: Anthropic can’t reliably control its AI agents. It’s cutting off its internal evals from the live internet instead
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthro.author: Tim Fernholz
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthro.text:
Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.

The incidents, disclosed in a blog post, involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, avoided paywalls and anti-bot restrictions, used URL shortening services to smuggle information pass restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police.

Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, underscoring the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior.

Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools.

The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government.

Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before.

However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents.

It’s not clear what that means, but Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers to use, and for the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access.

“You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.”

Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.”

The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations.

Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthro.summary: Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies. The company said it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until it is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents. Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-pu.title: Trump's diesel agreement with Putin accused of contradicting Russia sanctions law
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-pu.author: Kevin Breuninger
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-pu.text:
President Donald Trump announced Russia will supply diesel fuel to the global market.

Trump claimed the move, unveiled with less than a month left in an affordability-focused midterm election, would swiftly bring down record-high diesel prices.

Commentators and critics highlighted contradictions between the new policy and recent efforts by the U.S. to curtail Russian energy exports.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a searing statement that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow “plays into Russia’s hands.”

President Donald Trump’s Friday announcement that Russia will supply diesel fuel to the global market marked an apparent pivot from recent efforts to pressure Moscow to end the Ukraine war by targeting Russian energy exports.

Trump claimed the move, unveiled with less than a month left in an affordability-focused midterm election, would swiftly bring down record-high diesel prices.

But commentators and critics were quick to highlight contradictions between the new policy and prior efforts by the U.S. to clamp down on Russian oil sales.

Those efforts most recently included the enactment of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, empowering Trump to impose tariffs up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas, among other restrictions. Trump signed the bill into law just three weeks ago.

“Congress just passed a law giving Trump the power to impose new tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil & gas,” Scott Lincicome, vice president of the libertarian Cato Institute, said on X after Trump’s Friday announcement.

“Can America tariff America?” he quipped.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, accused Trump’s latest move of being “directly contrary to Congress’s intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill.”

Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown University Law Center’s Institute of International Economic Law, in an X post said that the relaxation of Russian diesel restrictions “pretty much proves the point that the Graham Russia Bill was not going to force the Trump Administration to increase economic pressure on Moscow.”

Some of the criticism crossed party lines.

“Through the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, we gave the president significant authorities and leverage against China and Russia to bring Putin’s war to an end with a negotiated settlement,” Rep. Michael McFaul, R-Texas, said in an X post. “Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin’s war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days,” McFaul said.

The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC’s questions about the diesel agreement with Russia.

Less than a year earlier, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on multiple Russian oil companies in response to what it called “Russia’s lack of serious commitment to a peace process to end the war in Ukraine.”

Trump also had previously slammed NATO allies for continuing to buy Russian oil. In a September 2025 Truth Social post, he wrote, “the purchase of Russian Oil, by some, has been shocking! It greatly weakens your negotiating position, and bargaining power, over Russia.”

Later that month, Trump again harangued world leaders for doing business with Russia.

“They’re funding the war against themselves. Who the hell ever heard of that one?” he said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. “They can’t be doing what they’re doing. They’re buying oil and gas from Russia while they’re fighting Russia.”

Trump announced the diesel deal in a Truth Social post Friday afternoon after what he described as a “highly successful discussion” with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Under the agreement, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then another 500,000 tons in November, followed by 1 million tons “immediately thereafter” and 3 million more depending on refinery conditions, Trump wrote.

The Treasury Department soon after said that Trump directed the Office of Foreign Assets Control to immediately issue a “temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market.” OFAC specified that the sanctioned transactions will be authorized for about six months, until April 7.

Russia seemed to celebrate the move. “Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world,” an X account associated with Putin’s economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev said in response to the announcement.

But Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whose military has started targeting Russian oil refineries, said in a searing statement that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow “plays into Russia’s hands.”

“Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness,” Zelenskyy said. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”

“We count on America’s fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia,” he said.

“A strong one, not a weak one,” he added.

Trump thanked Putin later Friday afternoon for enabling “massive amounts of oil” to come to the U.S.

“We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we’re very happy to get it,” Trump told reporters before heading to Syracuse, New York.

The Trump administration has previously eased some Russian energy sanctions temporarily, though more narrowly than Friday’s announcement.

Earlier this year, in an attempt to stabilize markets after the start of the Iran war, the Trump administration issued limited, 30-day waivers allowing countries to buy sanctioned Russian oil that was already in transit.

But some interpreted the latest move as a more significant step.

“It looks like Trump cut a deal with the devil,” Jeremy Siegel, professor emeritus of finance at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC’s “Closing Bell” Friday afternoon.

“It’s not a permanent solution at all. It’s sort of a short-term Band Aid,” Siegel said. “And cutting back on or eliminating sanctions on Russia for the invasion in Ukraine, I think, is a very unfortunate consequence.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-pu.summary: The move marked an apparent pivot from recent efforts to pressure Moscow to end the Ukraine war. Critics and critics highlighted contradictions between the new policy and recent efforts by the U.S. to curtail Russian energy export.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A 22-year-old man was helped from the River Torrens by SA Police after attempting to evade patrols on Saturday morning. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Police officers have saved a 22-year-old man from drowning when he jumped into the River Torrens to evade them.

A group of men were fighting on Hindley Street in the Adelaide CBD about 5am on Saturday when one of them ran off after patrols arrived.

Officers lost sight of the 22-year-old after a brief chase but he was later spotted on police-monitored cameras leaping into the river.

Police arrived to find the man struggling in the water and calling for help.

Three officers jumped in to save the drowning man, holding him above water before other patrols pulled the group to safety.

The Blair Athol man was taken to hospital in a non-life-threatening condition.

The officers were assessed by paramedics at the scene.

Police continue to investigate the fight.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.title: Kimberley leaders hope jailing of 'evil' Broome bishop exposes more abusers
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.author: Rachel Jackson and Erin Parke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Sexual Offences

Christopher Alan Saunders has been sentenced to six-and-a-half years in prison.   (ABC News: Anne Barnetson)

Albert Wiggan describes the jailing of disgraced bishop Christopher Saunders as like "cutting off the head of a snake".

The Aboriginal community leader describes the Catholic cleric as an "evil predator" and is urging people to call out sex abusers.

"They’ve exposed this bloke for who he is," Mr Wiggan said.

Albert Wiggan says he hopes the court sentence encourages community members to call out sexual abuse. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Mr Wiggan says he knew Saunders since childhood, but had never experienced inappropriate behaviour.

But he feels deeply for those who did, describing a sense of betrayal that is still sinking in.

It is a call for action echoed by current Bishop of Broome Tim Norton, who concedes the Catholic Church has been too slow to act.

"As a church I hope we are learning in this very deep and difficult process," Bishop Norton said.

"I sense we are but it's a slow pace. It needs to be a lot faster."

Broome Bishop Tim Norton says the church needs to act.  (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Once a trusted member of the community, the bishop was sentenced to more than six years prison on Wednesday for sexually assaulting two young men.

The evidence laid bare during a three-week trial was a far cry from the "hero" character Albert Wiggan was once told about as a child.

The former bishop oversaw the baptisms, marriages and funerals of generations of local families.  (ABC News: Shane Gordon)

"There was folklore about him ... we know about him through stories our parents would share," Mr Wiggan said.

He said families in remote Aboriginal communities grew to trust him with the people they loved most.

Saunders first arrived at the Broome Diocese in 1975, where he stayed for five decades.

Saunders in the remote Kimberley parish of Kalumburu in the mid 1980s. (Supplied)

Community leaders like Mr Wiggan says the church should have been faster to act when he started to betray their trust.

It is a sentiment shared by Bishop Norton, who said the church's abuse of power in the Kimberley was "inexcusable".

"Being in a place that is remote and even forgotten about by a lot of Australia ... that has been allowed to go on for too long," he said.

Bishop Norton says the abuse of power by the Catholic Church lasted "too long". (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Despite being found guilty, no action has been taken by the Catholic Church to defrock Saunders, meaning he has kept his honorary titles and the benefits of a retirement package negotiated in 2021.

Human rights advocate and Noongar woman Dr Hannah McGlade said the six-year sentence was a positive outcome, but the church still needed to take responsibility for the harm inflicted.

Dr Hannah McGlade says the lasting impacts of institutional sexual abuse are still evident today. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

The Curtin University Associate Professor said the lasting impacts of institutional abuse continued to impact men, women and children today.

"Without proper healing and intervention, the cycles have unfortunately sometimes continued with men who were once victims becoming perpetrators."

Former bishop Christopher Saunders attending court in Broome. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic )

The Kimberley region has some of the highest rates of suicide and self-harm in Australia, and the highest rates of family violence in the state.

Back in Broome, Bishop Norton said the deep and lasting nature of the case was "tremendous" but he was committed to moving forward with the community.

Tim Norton hoped the Catholic Church would be able to move forward with the community. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

"What I have learned here is people in the Kimberley are certainly bruised and hurt by this whole event, but the resilience I've encountered here is extraordinary," he said.

The church will hold healing and reconciliation sessions in Broome open to everyone in the community, not just members of the church.

Mr Wiggan believes the court sentence "sets a precedent". (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Albert Wiggan said he hoped the court sentence would help to provide more survivors of sexual abuse with the strength to come forward.

"I hope there will be more brave people out there and more people who come out and share their story because it needs to happen."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: China militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan’s east coast, patrol finds
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TAIPEI – A Chinese militia boat was spotted along with two other vessels off Taiwan’s Pacific coast in August, according to a surveillance report reviewed by reporters, the first known sighting of such a craft in the sensitive area.

The report by Taiwan’s Apex Aviation identifies the Minfudingyu 07902 as a fishing boat that doubles as a Chinese militia vessel, which was seen operating with a Chinese coast guard cutter and a research vessel one day in mid-August.

China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.

Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict.

China was “using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment, seeking to expand their scope of operations during a nonconflict scenario to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction,” Taiwan’s Defense Ministry in a statement when asked about the Apex report.

Such actions undermine international order and challenge Taiwan’s maritime rights, the ministry said, adding that the island’s military was using reconnaissance tools to track Chinese activity in coordination with other agencies, including Taiwan’s coast guard.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office and Defense Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

In a practice dating to the 1950s, China’s maritime militia, more commonly observed around South China Sea flashpoints, consists of fishing vessels whose crews receive training and support to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships.

Analysts say the fleet helps Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance.

Taiwan has confirmed that the Minfudingyu, the coast guard cutter 2502 and the research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 03 were operating near Taiwan in mid-August, said two senior Taiwan officials briefed on the matter.

Authorities identified the fishing boat as part of the People’s Liberation Army’s maritime militia fleet, which Taiwan was tracking and which was operating “in coordination with Chinese coast guard maritime harassment drills,” one official said.

“The purpose of militia boats is to conduct substantive harassment,” the official said.

The other official said the three craft were operating “in an area not commonly used by Chinese vessels” and had been “designated for heightened monitoring.”

The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue.

The Apex report says a reconnaissance aircraft the company operates detected a Chinese maritime group more than 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off the coast of Taiwan’s eastern county of Hualien. The company asked that the date of the spotting be withheld, citing safety concerns related to counter-reconnaissance against its operations.

The report uses radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data to document the cluster of vessels.

The patrol by Apex, better known for pilot training and charter flights, reflects Taiwan’s efforts to involve civilian firms in technologies relevant to the government’s “whole of society resilience” initiative, though the company says its patrols are independently run and not carried out for the government.

Chinese warships, coast guard vessels, research ships and some civilian vessels continue to operate in overlapping ways, “creating pressure in the waters surrounding Taiwan,” said Honor Hung, Apex’s defense and security director.

The three Chinese vessels were spread over a roughly 10-nautical-mile radius, Honor said, adding that one surveillance tracking could not determine their missions or any coordination among them.

Apex uses a civilian light aircraft equipped with a powerful U.S.-made radar that allows its patrols to detect objects on the surface as small as 900 square centimeters.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: China has stepped up activity off Taiwan's east coast with regular coast guard patrols. Taiwan says it believes China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. China's military is using reconnaissance tools to track Chinese activity in coordination with other agencies, Taiwan says.

BEIJING – China and the European Union have reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said Friday after talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU’s ballooning trade deficit with China.

The “shared understanding” would “moderate” China’s export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU, and would cut the imports of several million cars over four years, Sefcovic said after the two-day talks, without offering details on how the agreement will be implemented.

Shares of European carmakers, which have slid steadily over the past two years due to U.S. tariffs and soaring Chinese exports, broadly gained on the news.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Israeli drone attack wounds six in Lebanon near Syria border
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
An Israeli drone attack has wounded six people in Lebanon’s Hermel district, close to the Syrian border, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

The ministry said on Friday that the six wounded included five Syrian nationals, two of them women, and one Lebanese.

Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that the drone attack targeted a car.

It added the area has largely been spared such attacks since an Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire was agreed in June.

Israel’s military claimed it struck “a Syrian terrorist” who “operated under the direction of the Iranian regime”, alleging that the man “planned and advanced attacks” against Israeli forces in Syria’s southern territory.

Since the ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes against Syria. It has sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan since 1974, and has carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory, sometimes seizing residents.

Israel has also continued to attack Lebanon since a ceasefire with Hezbollah was agreed in June.

It has vowed to keep troops in so-called security zones along its border in both Syria and Lebanon.

Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa told the UN General Assembly last month: “We reject Israeli attempts to impose a fait accompli. We reject their aggressions, which undermine peace and security.”

He said Israel had carried out “500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and 300 detentions” in Syria.

He also called for Israeli withdrawal from Syrian territory and for the international community to commit to a 1974 agreement that created a UN-supervised separation zone between Israeli and Syrian forces.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/g.title: Champion golfer reflects on lasting legacy in outback WA
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/g.author: Jarrod Lucas and Ivo da Silva
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Ben Eccles, the 2023 WA PGA Championship winner, with 1978 champion Graham Marsh at Kalgoorlie Golf Course.  (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Australian golfing champion Graham Marsh has built almost as many golf courses as the 70 tournament wins he collected over a decorated career.

At last count, it was 65 projects around the world as a golf course architect since 1986, including Secret Harbour, Terrey Hills and The Vines.

Despite turning 82 this year, Marsh's diary remains full, with projects in Queensland and Cyprus.

It was a full-circle moment for Marsh this week when he returned to his birthplace of Kalgoorlie for the WA PGA Championship, getting his hands on a trophy he won in 1978.

While his family left the historic mining city when he was an infant, Marsh's role as the architect of the Kalgoorlie Golf Course has left a lasting legacy.

Graham Marsh has returned to his birthplace at Kalgoorlie for the WA PGA Championship and (inset) in his playing days.   (Main image: Jarrod Lucas, ABC Goldfields. Inset: State Library of WA)

"We don't have this desert form of golf in Australia, this is the first of its kind, and I think that makes it very special," he said.

"There have been attempts, there was something at Alice Springs at one stage, but never with the commitment that this place has had or with the beauty of this place, to be frank.

"Every hole has a dramatically different look, whereas on many golf courses, the look is very much the same."

The arid climate means Kalgoorlie Golf Course is watered with recycled effluent.   (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

After decades of lobbying, the 18-hole course opened in 2010 at a cost of $18.5 million, heavily backed by the state government and the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which manages the course today.

It has faced significant challenges, serving as a lightning rod for criticism from some sections of the community for the cost burden on ratepayers.

Water shortages in a city reliant on a 560-kilometre-long pipeline for its drinking water remain an ongoing challenge, with work progressing to increase the storage capacity of dams at the golf course.

A permanent clubhouse and resort has been promised by multiple developers but is yet to be delivered, with the latest proposal stuck in legal disputes with millions of dollars of ratepayer funds already spent.

Efforts to boost tourism and attract travelling golfers have been stifled by a lack of available accommodation for those willing to make the journey.

A kangaroo at sunset at the Kalgoorlie Golf Course. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Marsh hopes those challenges can be overcome, like some of the unique problems he faced, including transforming the site of a former rubbish tip into the course's driving range.

"The brief was they wanted a golf course that was world-class, that would bring notoriety to the area, especially through Asia but Australia-wide," Marsh said.

"They wanted 36 holes, and that was in the design, until the original developer pulled out, and so things changed because it was all about money at that stage.

"Being involved in a project like this, which had such a rough start, they still allowed us to produce something that is world-class."

A new suburb has emerged from the bushland adjacent to the Kalgoorlie Golf Course since it opened in 2010. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Part of the deal to get the course built included handing over land belonging to Kalgoorlie-Boulder's then three existing golf clubs.

A portion of that land has been used for a new housing estate called GreenView, with about 250 residential lots developed next to the course and more than 2,000 lots planned in in the future.

A retirement village and a short-stay facility have also been built on other parcels of land freed up by old courses.

There are long-term plans for about 2,000 houses at the GreenView Estate in Kalgoorlie-Boulder's north-west.  (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

At the same time, the local game continues to grow, with 620 golf members and a renewed focus on developing junior players.

"The fact we weren't constricted by housing inside the golf course, only on the perimeter, it's what we call in the industry as being 'core golf' and that provides for a very serene and beautiful environment to play the game," Marsh said.

"It is very warming to my heart to see that golf has such a powerful role to play in developing the community."

This week has seen the course enjoying its time in the national spotlight again as the home of the WA PGA Championship.

A 120-strong field teed off on Thursday, hoping to join the ranks of several former WA PGA winners who have gone onto bigger things.

Among them is defending champion Austin Bautista, who is playing in South Africa this week and 2022 winner David Micheluzzi on the European Tour.

David Micheluzzi is sprayed with champagne after winning the 2022 WA PGA Championship at Kalgoorlie.     (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Kalgoorlie has hosted the WA PGA since 2012, and has locked in another five years until 2031, with the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder's sponsorship worth more than $100,000 a year.

Mayor Glenn Wilson said it was money well spent, with the tournament watched by 412,000 viewers on pay television last year and estimates it injected $329,000 into the local economy.

"The benefits that we see from an event of this scale and magnitude go far beyond our city boundaries," he said.

"This course is unique. It's a credit to our staff."

Ben Eccles, Graham Marsh, Glenn Wilson and the PGA's Kim Felton at the Kalgoorlie Golf Course. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Victorian Ben Eccles, the 2023 WA PGA champion, said the red dirt of Kalgoorlie made it a unique and tough course to play.

"It's a world-class golf course, it gets the season off to such an awesome start and I don't think I'd be the only one to say that we all look forward to coming here," he said.

"It's a really special place for me in my career and I'll come back as long as it's held here."

Graham Marsh in 1975. (Supplied: State Library of WA)

And while Marsh says the course "has never looked better", he warned there were challenges on the horizon.

"I think robotics is going to change things, because staffing is a huge problem in this part of the world," he said.

"This course is coming up 17 years old and at 25 years, you're already starting to look at new irrigation systems because they don't last forever … you've got to have the capital, the drive and resolve to put money aside to keep it as a championship golf course.

"The worst thing you can do is sit back and pat yourself on the shoulders and say this is wonderful. If you're not looking 25 years in advance, you're not thinking long-term and that's what this place will need moving forward to keep its notoriety."
