https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A 29-year-old man has been denied bail after allegedly shooting at a car and injuring a teenage passenger. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A 29-year-old man has been denied bail after he allegedly shot at a vehicle and seriously injured a teenage passenger in Canberra's south on Friday night.

Police said four teenagers had been travelling in a red Ford Falcon along Abrahams Crescent and Beaumaris Street in Conder when they encountered a red Hyundai i30 hatchback.

The driver of the Hyundai allegedly followed the Ford along Tom Roberts Avenue to the intersection of Box Hill Avenue and Tharwa Drive and shot at the other vehicle at about 10pm, striking a passenger in the back seat.

The occupants of the Ford called police who told the driver to come to Tuggeranong Police Station.

After establishing a crime scene in Conder, police said they saw a man climb out of a bush on Greaves Place and get into a waiting red Audi at about 11.30pm.

Police said the Audi was found parked outside the 29-year-old man's home in Gordon shortly after.

The man was arrested and faced the ACT Magistrates Court today, charged with using a firearm to endanger human life.

The court heard the accused pursued the Ford before firing two or three shots into the vehicle, seriously injuring one of the passengers.

Magistrate James Lawton refused bail, arguing there was a risk that the man could access the firearm, which had not yet been located by police.

Police said the man was also subject to parole conditions.

The matter will return to court on November 4.

Police are urging anyone who was driving in the area of Conder and Banks about 10pm on Friday night, particularly in the vicinity of Abrahams Crescent, Beaumaris Street, Tom Roberts Avenue, Box Hill Avenue, Tharwa Drive and Pockett Avenue, who saw a red Hyundai i30 or a red Ford Falcon, to contact Crime Stoppers.

Police are also appealing for residents along Beaumaris Street with CCTV to come forward.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.title: Homelessness camp in Perth's south tip of iceberg
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.author: Keane Bourke
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Libby Sweeney has been sleeping rough on Perth's streets for more than two years. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A homelessness camp recently disbanded by authorities in Perth's south is just the tip of the iceberg of a growing challenge.

Just ask those on the frontline.

Brett McCaul, the Salvation Army's outreach team leader in Western Australia, has been working in the sector for six years.

Outreach worker Brett McCaul says homelessness has become more pervasive. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

He says the problem is not just the increasing number of people who need help, but the diversity in demographic groups, including dual-income families.

"We really don't have the resources to be able to accommodate the amount of families that we're seeing," he said.

Social services want the WA government to use its budget surplus to invest in breaking people out of the cycle of homelessness, after it failed to achieve its goal of ending rough sleeping.

"We often see we've got a lot of elderly people that are living in some accommodation services, transitional services, that probably should be in aged care.

It was a problem which was evident among the 45 people who camped along Memorial Drive in Rockingham, before they were moved on at the end of last month.

One of the tents at the now-vacated Rockingham homeless camp (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

It's a similar story in Perth's north, where FIFO worker Josh Chinnery volunteers for Vinnies in Joondalup.

Vinnies WA volunteer Josh Chinnery. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The centre reported a 36 per cent increase in demand over the last year, a figure put down, in part, to challenges like family and domestic violence and higher rents.

"Even the people that have been holding down jobs for 20 or 30 years, they're coming in and they're at the point of becoming homeless because they can't afford just their everyday necessities," Mr Chinnery said.

Support services say they are seeing more people who are finding it harder to make ends meet. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Maija Hildebrand, Vinnies WA’s service development manager, also leads the Joondalup-Wanneroo Ending Homeless Group and said those needing help now included a growing number of couples, people with pets and families trying to send their kids to school.

Ms Hildebrand wants more localised solutions to homelessness. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Although it's not as visible as we might have seen in Memorial Drive, it doesn't mean it's not there," she said.

Data from the City of Wanneroo showed around one-in-three people rough sleeping in the area last financial year were sleeping in their cars.

Neil Clifford-Mills knows all about sleeping in cars — his vehicle was his home until he ended up on a park bench in Inglewood in February.

Neil says more people should help those sleeping rough. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"If it wasn't for the generosity of the people around here to help me through, I'd be in trouble," he said.

The 66-year-old said he was receiving Centrelink payments while managing health issues but was unable to find anywhere to live after he couldn't stay with a friend any longer.

"The housing just isn't there," he said.

Mr Clifford-Mills was offered a reprieve after sharing his story on 102.5 ABC Perth, when a listener offered him somewhere to stay temporarily.

"Help me, please help me" - a homeless man's plea from the bench he calls home

"There are a lot of people that do want to help, but I suppose a lot of people don't really think that they would find themselves in that situation," he said.

Even when housing does become available, it is not always suitable.

Housing is scarce for those sleeping rough, and not always suitable. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Libby Sweeney said she had been without stable accommodation for about two-and-a-half years after her relationship with her daughter broke down.

Her two dogs, Pablo and Yogi, keep her company on the streets, but have also limited her options because not all accommodation allows pets.

Libby Sweeney refuses to give up her dogs, even if it means sleeping rough. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I've had people turn around and say to me, look, you're not going to get accommodation with the animals, you're just not. It'd be much easier if you fostered them out," Ms Sweeney said.

"They're like my children.

Both Mr McCaul and Ms Hildebrand said stronger local support services would go some way towards helping with the homelessness problems, because they would be able to leverage people's existing support networks, rather than forcing them to travel into central Perth.

Service providers like Passages in Perth and Mandurah help hundreds experiencing homelessness.

Asked about the issue, a spokesperson for Homelessness Minister Matthew Swinbourn said this year's state budget included an extra $91.1 million for homelessness services.

"The Department [of Communities] works closely with service providers, local governments and community organisations to identify gaps in service delivery and strengthen place-based responses where they are needed most," they said.

Ms Hildebrand, however, said those investments were yet to make a difference in the northern suburbs, where her teams were seeing the time between needing support and becoming homeless shortening.

Higher rents and the cost of living are driving an increase in homelessness (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"We don't have any crisis accommodation, we don't have any transitional, short-term or medium[-term] accommodation for adults over 25," she said.

Iran has managed to preserve its missile and drone factories despite months of U.S. and Israeli bombing, officials familiar with the matter said, allowing it to replenish its arsenals while President Donald Trump holds off on strikes ahead of the midterm elections.

Tehran still has the capacity to manufacture weapons to rebuild its arsenal, according to the Western officials, who asked not to be identified discussing private assessments. One official said Iran remains well-stocked with ballistic missiles and some anti-ship weapons, and can quickly add more.

The Western official said Russia was providing missiles as well, echoing a separate assessment in June. Russia’s Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment.

PANAMA CITY, PANAMA – A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 kilometers, with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200 km from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.

In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/a.author: Alex Sinnott
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Missing Person

Albert Pisani went missing in October 1986, and his remains were found not far from his hometown. (ABC News - file footage)

Gippsland father Albert Pisani went missing in October 1986 and his body was found in suspicious circumstances in June 1987.

Victoria Police have reopened the cold case with Mr Pisani's family members making a public appeal for information.

A reward of up to $1 million, announced in 2016, will be paid for information leading to the conviction of the person or persons responsible for the death of Mr Pisani.

Family members of Albert Pisani have appealed to the public for information on the fortieth anniversary of the slain Gippsland father's disappearance.

Missing Persons Squad detectives are returning the spotlight on the cold case, exactly four decades on from the 27-year-old's disappearance in Victoria's east, on 10 October 1986.

Victoria Police said Mr Pisani was last seen walking on Moe's Prince Street, and it was understood he was intending to use a bank in Moe's town centre then return home to his partner and five children for lunch.

Albert Pisani was last seen walking along Moe's Prince Street in October 1986. (ABC News)

"Albert would regularly travel for a few days on road trips, so family members were not immediately concerned. He was reported missing to police a few days later on 15 October," a Victoria Police statement read.

"Following extensive searches, Albert's remains were located in bushland in Driffield on 9 June 1987, approximately 20km from where he resided in Moe.

Investigations have taken place over the past 40 years, and police have spoken to Mr Pisani's family, friends and associates to try and determine the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

Police believe Mr Pisani was involved in a dispute at his workplace, the State Electricity Commission (SEC) Briquette Factory in nearby Morwell, before he went missing.

"Albert had a fascination with trucks, developed relationships with local and interstate truck drivers and would regularly hitchhike across Australia," Victoria Police said.

"At this stage, it remains unclear who may have been involved and if there is any possible motivation for causing him harm."

Victoria Police have re-released this headshot image of Albert Pisani on the fortieth anniversary of his 1986 disappearance. (ABC News)

Two of Mr Pisani's sisters, Carol Ward and Karen Pisani, have released public statements reflecting on their brother's disappearance and the impact it had on their family.

"Albert was the eldest of eight siblings, worked at the SEC and had a big passion for trucks," Karen Pisani said.

"Unfortunately, I never got to know my brother and godfather, but his death has had a huge impact on my everyday life.

"Our mother, Mary, died in 2016 after suffering significantly from Albert's murder. It was extremely difficult seeing the extent of my mother's pain as Albert was dearly missed and loved by all.

"Forty years on, I still live in fear of the unknown crime. We need anyone with any information to come forward so we can fully put him to rest."

Mr Pisani had no criminal history and was not known to police prior to his disappearance.

Detective David Dunstan says mystery still shrouds Mr Pisani's disappearance. (ABC News: Rebekah Lowe)

In 2016, at the time of the 30th anniversary of Mr Pisani's disappearance, Victoria Police announced a $1 million reward for information to identify those responsible for the Gippsland father's death.

Missing Persons Squad detective inspector David Dunstan said police did not believe Mr Pisani took his own life.

"We simply don't know what happened to him, and we need help from the public to solve this case," he said.

"His disappearance was out of character. These types of missing persons investigations are never closed and sadly, Albert's killer remains out there.

Police have charged a 29-year-old man with murder a day after finding his twin brother's body in the backyard of their home in a south Perth suburb.

Detective Acting Superintendent Jessica Securo said on Friday police had seized blades from the home which could have been used as weapons.

Police said they had seized blades from the house. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Top management officials of some of the four major beer makers suspected of a price cartel are believed to have been informed of details of shipping price hikes negotiated among the companies, informed sources have said.

The Japan Fair Trade Commission is investigating whether these top officials recognized that the information was a result of negotiations, the sources said Friday.

According to the sources, some officials of the companies — Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Holdings — have admitted to the cartel during the commission’s investigation.

Officials from the companies are believed to have held unofficial talks after industry group meetings to exchange information on the timing and scale of shipping price increases and compile price tables.

On Wednesday, the commission conducted compulsory inspections of the headquarters of the four companies on suspicion of violating the Antimonopoly Act.

Under the act, companies found to have engaged in illegal price fixing can face penalties, including financial surcharges and orders to prevent further violations. Unlike routine administrative inspections, compulsory investigations allow authorities to search premises and seize evidence under court warrants, typically in cases considered particularly serious or damaging to consumers.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
DUBAI – The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv’s international airport, the United Arab Emirates’ top prosecutor said on Friday.

In the aftermath of the incident, people on board — the majority of whom were Israeli — described a sudden plunge in altitude and a fight for control of the aircraft, which was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were repatriated on a second flydubai flight hours later.

The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda’s Sept. 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life,” according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media.

The prosecutor found that the co-pilot had first begun to be radicalized while studying in Australia “through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide attacks.”

He said last week’s flight had been the co-pilot’s third to Tel Aviv, and that he had used the two earlier trips to plan the attack.

During the flight, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.

Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board “noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner,” according to the findings.

After gaining entry, he “intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect.”

The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

Israel and the UAE have become close partners since normalizing ties under the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, and Israel carries out stringent security checks on those traveling to the country.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu previously said that the co-pilot — identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami — must have got around restrictions preventing individuals from nations that do not recognize Israel operating flights to the country.

The UAE prosecutor’s “findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot’s license, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks.”

“However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.”

The co-pilot had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, but media outlets reported after the incident that he had been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.

After the incident, Netanyahu had hailed the passengers and the plane’s captain for their bravery in averting what would have otherwise been a catastrophe.

He later ordered a “thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel” in response to the incident.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vg.title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vg.text:
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida, bringing the threat of life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.

The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.

Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.

Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.

Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.

In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"

Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.

Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.

It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.

The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.

After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.

As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).

The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC.

For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges.

"We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through."

Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding.

More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us.

The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power.

People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning".

Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders.

John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.

"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.

"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,

Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".

A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".

Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.

People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".

One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did.

A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions".

US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead.

Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.

Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.

Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.

While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.

Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.

Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".

It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.

With additional reporting by Simon King.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vg.summary: Isaias has made landfall in Florida, bringing the threat of life-threatening flooding and winds. Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency. The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds.

President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’

Donald Trump complained Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran.

At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.

“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.

“The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget, Norway, that you didn’t give this prize.”

Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.”

Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”.

“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”

“Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.

“Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.title: Key things to know about Hurricane Isaias as millions under evacuation orders
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.text:
The hurricane is first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late season. Here’s what forecasters are saying about where Isaias will hit and how hard

Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall on the US Gulf coast Friday night, was forecast to bring a dangerous storm surge, significant rainfall, flooding and strong winds across the US Gulf coast this weekend. Millions of people across several states, including Florida, Georgia and Alabama, were under evacuation orders as officials prepared for the storm. All three states issued states of emergency.

The hurricane, the first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late 2026 season, made landfall as a category 2 storm, with sustained winds of 105 mph.

The National Weather Service warned that Isaias could produce a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast, which occurs when rising ocean water moves inland from the coastline.

Isaias made landfall along the northern Gulf coast late Friday as a category 2 storm.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned it would bring a “life threatening” storm surge and “devastating winds likely across the Florida panhandle and Alabama coasts”.

Isaias could bring 4-8in of rain, with locally higher totals up to 15in (380mm), across parts of the Gulf coast. Forecasters warned of significant flash and river flooding, especially in southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and south-western Georgia.

Hurricane-force winds were expected to spread inland as far as 100 miles (160km) from the Alabama coast, the NHC said. There were also warnings of possible tornadoes late Friday or Saturday in its outer band of rains.

The NHC said: “Across much of the remainder of the Southeast, rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches are expected. Localized higher amounts up to 10 inches are possible, especially across the Southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.”

Florida, Georgia and Alabama have declared states of emergencies, with mandatory evacuations ordered in some coastal communities. Numerous evacuation shelters have opened across Florida, Louisiana, Alabama and Mississippi, with more than 370 trained American Red Cross (Arc) disaster workers supporting the response. The Arc is also pre-positioning cots, blankets, shelf-stable meals and other emergency supplies across the region.

About 5,000 national guard troops were expected to mobilize in Florida, where at least four school districts cancelled late-week classes.

Before the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

The El Niño climate pattern is a factor in this year’s quieter Atlantic hurricane season. While it warms sea surface temperatures in the Pacific where storm activity has been greater, it also increases wind shear – changes in wind speed and direction with height – over the Atlantic, which can disrupt tropical storms before they strengthen into hurricanes.

The hurricane season begins 1 June and runs up to the end of November with the height of the season usually from the middle of August to the middle of October.

The last hurricane to make landfall in the US was Hurricane Milton, which came ashore near Florida’s Siesta Key on 9 October 2024. It followed Hurricane Helene a month earlier, which killed more than 250 people and was the deadliest hurricane to hit the mainland US since Hurricane Katrina in 20o5.

As a hurricane approaches a coast, the churning winds force ocean water up on to land; atmospheric pressure from the storm also helps squeeze the water ashore. The shallower the continental shelf, the higher the threat of a dangerous surge. The water may take a couple of days to fully subside.

Storm surge was expected from south-east Louisiana to Suwannee, in north-east Florida, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).

Up to 9ft of storm surge is forecast between Dauphin Island, Alabama, and Indian Pass, Florida.

Although state officials have declared their preparedness, Isaias will be a key test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (Fema) ability to respond to a major hurricane after significant staffing cuts and an overhaul of the agency under the Trump administration. About 17% of Fema’s workforce left in fiscal year 2025, following Trump’s push to downsize the agency and shift more responsibility to states.

The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO. “It’s not whether Fema is going to respond. They’re going to respond. It’s more about the depth,” Currie said.

Fema, however, said: “FEMA Incident Management Assistance Teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and FEMA personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. FEMA is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell air force base in Montgomery, Alabama, to supplement state resources if requested.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida with severe effects expected across several states
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida declared states of emergency as a downsized Fema faces first major test

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening, sweeping ashore from the northern Gulf of Mexico as the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) in Miami said the center of the cyclone made landfall at 9.30pm ET as a category 2 hurricane with winds reaching 105 mph (165km/h).

Not signed in before? Create an account

Forecasters had expected Isaias to weaken from its peak earlier on Friday as a major category 3 hurricane due to shifts in wind speed.

But even as a high-end category 2 storm, the NHC said, severe impacts would be felt across a wide stretch of the northern Gulf coast from Louisiana to Florida, and far inland.

They included a “life-threatening” storm surge of up to 7ft (2.1 meters) along the Alabama-Florida line, and powerful wind gusts reaching parts of northern Georgia.

“Weakening will occur after landfall, but sustained hurricane-force winds will likely occur near and along Isaias’s track up to 100 miles inland,” wrote Robbie Berg, an NHC hurricane expert, in a Friday advisory.

In the Florida Panhandle, Isaias’s early impacts also came into view. In Panama city beach, Noaa officials observed a water level 5.4 feet (1.64 meters) above average. About 125 miles west, at the Pensacola city hall, a wind gust up to 102 mph (164km/h) was recorded.

Powerful gusts of wind and heavy rainfall appeared to down the canopy of a Crestview gas station on Friday evening, according to a video captured by meteorologist Nick Stewart. The tattered cover hung on top of a filling station.

“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida govenor Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region”.

The governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida all declared states of emergency ahead of the storm’s arrival, urging some residents of coastal communities to evacuate and many more to prepare for the storm’s likely violent arrival.

Alabama governor Kay Ivey announced shortly before the hurricane made landfall that Donald Trump had approved the emergency declaration for her state. “This will help cut tape for our federal partners to aid in any response,” Ivey said.

The Mobile office of the National Weather Service warned parts of Florida could see “extremely dangerous” tornado-like winds.

By Friday evening, nearly 500,000 customers had lost power across Alabama and Florida, according to PowerOutage.com.

“Things are going to get really, really treacherous,” Jamie Rhome, deputy director for the National Hurricane Center, told the AP.

Florida’s national guard deployed roughly 5,000 soldiers and airmen to aid with the response, the AP reported. Some prisons were also evacuating their incarcerated populations. Most flights were grounded at several airports in Florida’s Panhandle.

The state guard has deployed about 400 soldiers to assess the hurricane’s damage and assist with route clearance, among other duties.

The Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission has readied 10 airboats, 18 shallow-draft boats, nine ATVs and six larger platform vessels in the event of damage or flooding.

Uber has also partnered with the state to offer free-round trips, up to $40 each way, to and from state-approved evacuation shelters.

Isaias is notable as one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.

Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company’s website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm’s severity .

Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.

“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier. “Which is a pretty big deal.”

Associated Press contributed reporting.

The storm is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season. Mississippi, Alabama and Florida all declared states of emergency ahead of the storm’s arrival.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said an immediate resumption of peace talks with Ukraine is unlikely, citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month.

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump on Friday, Putin said Moscow was ready to resume negotiations with Kyiv after the parliamentary elections. However, the drone attacks on the capital made the resumption of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US unlikely.

“By launching a large-scale drone attack on Moscow, other cities and polling stations on the most important day of the elections, and by targeting some people involved in organising the elections, the Kyiv regime has, in reality, interrupted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process,” said Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov about the call with Trump.

“As the president said, we will now assess when these negotiations can resume,” he added regarding the trilateral talks.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that Russia’s war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and the United States will keep working towards a deal to end the war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week that the country was ready to hold trilateral talks with the United States and Russia this month.

Earlier on Friday, Donald Trump announced after the call with Putin that Russia agreed to deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to American and global markets.

The deal was criticised by US lawmakers, Zelenskyy and European allies.

Zelenskyy called the agreement a “gift to Putin”.

“All that money goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us. I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair,” he said in a statement.

In response to the US-Russia diesel deal, a government spokesperson said the United Kingdom would continue to “maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Two Renoir paintings recovered after France museum heist, mayor says
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Two paintings by the French Impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir that were stolen from a museum in southern France a month ago have been recovered, the town’s mayor said.

“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, said on Friday. “Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”

Six people have been arrested in connection with the theft, local authorities said. Masson did not say where the paintings were found or in what condition.

Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum a little before 6am on September 8, cutting through a fence to enter the grounds, smashing a window and using an electric saw to cut the clips securing the frames, Masson said at the time.

He described them as “well equipped” and “well informed”.

The museum alarm sounded at 5:48am, and municipal police arrived five minutes later, forcing the thieves to flee.

They had taken four paintings, valued by the mayor at about nine million euros ($10.5m).

Two of the stolen works – Renoir’s “Portrait of Madame Pichon” and “Coco Reading” – were later found dropped in the museum garden, the prosecutor’s office said at the time.

The two works that remained missing were “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well”, the office said.

Police said last month that the thieves were not first-time offenders and had scoped out the premises.

The Marseille prosecutor opened a theft investigation into an organised gang, and the national office for trafficking in cultural goods joined the probe.

The museum, opened in 1960, is in the painter’s last home, where he died in 1919.

“This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums,” Masson said after the robbery.

The theft came less than a year after jewels worth about $100m were stolen from the Louvre in Paris in a daylight robbery.

The four suspected robbers have been arrested, but the jewels have not been found.

In August, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m that were stolen from a museum in March.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Friday that the planned consumption tax cut for food is expected to reduce household financial burdens by about ¥36,000 per citizen.

“The tax rate cut will basically be reflected in prices,” Takaichi said at a plenary meeting of the Senate, the upper chamber of parliament.

She explained that the ¥36,000 figure was calculated by dividing the total tax revenue loss to the central and local governments from the tax cut by the country’s population.

During the Upper House meeting, Yasue Funayama of the Democratic Party for the People asked the prime minister how her administration will make up for local government revenue losses.

Takaichi vowed to fully cover these revenue losses with state funds, saying, “We’ll properly secure necessary local tax grants.”

The prime minister also said the government is considering measures to support agricultural and fishery businesses, as well as food companies and restaurants whose operations could be affected by the tax cut. “It is necessary to assess circumstances on the ground and respond according to the impact on each sector,” she said.

Meanwhile, Komeito Secretary-General Makoto Nishida called on the government to clarify who would be eligible for a financial aid program for workers that will be introduced alongside the consumption tax cut.

Takaichi indicated that the government will explain the matter during parliamentary deliberations, based on discussions by the suprapartisan National Council on Social Security.

Sanseito leader Sohei Kamiya argued that the consumption tax reduction should apply across the board, not only to food.

Takaichi countered that such a move could affect public services, including pensions, medical care, nursing care and measures to address the declining birthrate.

https://www.dw.com/en/mexico-court-finds.title: Mexico: Court finds three men guilty of murder of Australian, US surfers
https://www.dw.com/en/mexico-court-finds.text:
The 2024 murders of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, shocked Mexico and drew international outrage.

A Mexican court on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery which sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico when they were shot dead in Baja California state.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked during a suspected robbery. Their bodies were found days later, in a well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

The judge on Friday ruled that the three Mexican defendants had acted with premeditation. They are yet to be sentenced for the murders.

The prosecution has asked for an "exemplary sentence" of 210 years for each of the three convicted, even though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.

Debra Robinson, mother to the Australian brothers, burst into tears when the court passed the guilty verdict.

"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them," the convictions marked "an important step towards justice and accountability," their father Martin Robinson said in a statement on behalf of the family.

Case prosecutors described the killings of the three surfers during the closing arguments on Thursday, by recalling the testimony of the girlfriend of one of the main suspects.

She had said that Rhoad had begged for his life while her boyfriend had bragged about "how beautifully" his victims cried before he robbed them.

The triple homicide shocked Mexico and drew international attention when it came to light.

Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, riddled with organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.

US weather authorities are warning of "life-threatening" storm surges on the Gulf Coast due to the Category 2 hurricane. Extreme winds, rising water levels and possible tornadoes are also on the radar.

Hurricane Isaias, a Category 2 storm, has made landfall near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Friday evening. Destin is in the panhandle region of northern Florida.

The NHC warned of "life-threatening storm surge impacting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland."

The weather system is also bringing extreme winds, with a tornado watch issued for parts of Florida and southern Georgia.

The storm is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season and was originally a strong Category 3 storm before making landfall.

Florida, Georgia and Alabama have all declared a State of Emergency due to the extreme weather system.

According to power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, roughly 480,000 customers altogether were without electricity as of Friday evening in Florida, Georgia and Alabama.

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-weighs-lives.title: Trump weighs livestream execution amid bipartisan backlash
https://www.dw.com/en/trump-weighs-lives.text:
Donald Trump said he hasn't decided whether the execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, after the Pentagon announced it would do so. The plan has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan "absolutely" deserves the death penalty by firing squad but told reporters he has yet "to make a determination" on whether it will be livestreamed.

"I don't really care how he goes, as long as he goes," Trump said, referring to Hasan.

Trump's remarks comes a day after the Pentagon said it would livestream the execution of 56-year-old Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured 32 others in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a video shared by the Pentagon regarding the execution, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things."

Hasan is currently being held on death row in Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. His execution is slated for December 3.

He is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair after he was shot by an officer responding to the Fort Hood shooting.

US Vice President JD Vance, speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Friday, also said he doesn't know whether the livestream is "actually going to happen."

"If it is shown publicly," Vance added, "I'm not going to be watching it." Vance is a devout member of the Catholic Church, which opposes the death penalty.

"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," the US vice president said.

The Pentagon's plan to broadcast the execution has been met with a fierce backlash from within Trump's own Republican Party and the opposition Democrats.

"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," said Republican Representative Austin Scott of Georgia.

Public executions are common in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and the so-called Islamic State (IS) also engaged in public beheadings when the group controlled large swathes of Syria and Iraq in the 2010s. Iran is another country that carries out public executions.

Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania said "an execution shouldn't be a livestreamed spectacle."

"The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment," he said in a statement posted on X. "Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."

Democratic Congressman Eugene Vindman of Virginia, who said he oversaw legal proceedings following the Fort Hood attack, said livestreaming Hasan's execution "is what terrorists and authoritarian regimes do. It's un-American."

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Pentagon chief Hegseth is "turning the Fort Hood execution into a gruesome inhumane spectacle."

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) also strongly condemned the ideaof a livestreamed execution, while the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plana "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warns
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Damian Carrington Environment editor
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Changing tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfers

The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.

Analysis of dozens of famous waves in world surfing reserves (WSR) found more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines and shifting sands.

The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador, and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of sea-floor shape, swell direction and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a co-author of the study.

Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.

Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR programme in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”

Almost 200 local experts analysed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.

A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

The researchers want more local surfers to use the tools developed to assess their own breaks and work with local authorities and other groups to protect waves from coastal development and climate change.

Some places already do this, such as the city of Gold Coast in Australia, which has put surf protection in planning law; New Zealand, which designates surf breaks of “national significance”; and Peru’s Ley de rompientes (law of the breakers) that protects listed surf breaks.

“Surfing is a huge driver of local economies,” Hodges said. “So whether you’re a surfer or not, that money supports local businesses, hotels, lodgings and so on.”

In Santa Cruz, surfing brings in about $200m (£151m) a year, he said.

“In the east of El Salvador, you have some of the most perfect point break waves you will find, and the entire economy there is pretty much dependent on surfing,” Hodges added.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/elon-m.title: Elon Musk intensifies attack on Ambani over Starlink India launch delay
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/elon-m.author: Jagmeet Singh
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/elon-m.text:
As SpaceX struggles to launch Starlink in India, Elon Musk has stepped up his attack on billionaire Mukesh Ambani, mockingly calling him the country’s “prime minister” to suggest he wields outsized control over its government and accusing him of blocking the satellite internet service from competing.

On Friday, Musk continued his criticism of the famed Reliance Industries’ chairperson in a post on X, arguing that Starlink could bring internet access to areas that remain unconnected, giving children more opportunities to learn, and helping small businesses reach customers worldwide.

“Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” Musk wrote.

Reliance Jio, Reliance Industries’ telecom arm, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Musk’s latest comments follow his accusations earlier this week that unnamed “oligarchs” were blocking Starlink’s launch in India to protect their business interests. India’s Ministry of Communications rejected the allegations, saying the country’s regulatory framework for satellite communications is “fair and non-discriminatory.” Musk then went further on Thursday, questioning Ambani’s influence in a separate post on X. “Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he asked.

SpaceX has spent years trying to launch Starlink in India. Last year, it even struck distribution agreements with Ambani’s Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel, India’s second-largest telecom operator, to offer the service once it received the necessary approvals. However, Starlink has not yet received the go-ahead from New Delhi to begin commercial operations, despite securing key regulatory clearances.

In its Thursday statement, the Indian communication ministry said Starlink and two other licensed satellite operators are undergoing security assessments that must be completed before they can receive satellite spectrum. The ministry said all three are at “broadly the same regulatory stage,” rejecting Musk’s suggestion that Starlink was being singled out.

Jio and Airtel are also seeking to launch their satellite internet services in India. Jio has a joint venture with Luxembourg-based SES, while Airtel is a major shareholder in Eutelsat OneWeb, which is striving to offer satellite connectivity in the country.

India, the world’s most populous country with over a billion internet users, is a major market for Musk. But expanding there also means dealing with powerful business figures such as Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns India’s largest telecom operator and works with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government on major projects.

Alongside Starlink’s delayed launch, Musk has also faced challenges expanding Tesla in India. The electric carmaker launched in the country last year after years of anticipation but registered just 699 vehicles in its first 12 months of deliveries, according to data cited by Electrek. Steep import duties pushed the Model Y’s launch price in India to nearly twice its U.S. price. Tesla lowered its prices earlier this year, but its cars remain considerably more expensive in India than in the U.S.

Before Musk’s latest attack, Starlink and Ambani’s Reliance Jio clashed over how to allocate satellite spectrum in India. Musk’s company wanted the spectrum to be assigned through an administrative process, while Jio pushed for an auction. Ultimately, New Delhi went ahead with Starlink and decided to allocate the spectrum administratively.

Starlink’s launch in India remains in limbo. India’s telecom minister Jyotiraditya Scindia on Friday pushed back against Musk’s allegations, saying the country “does not allow a monopoly in any sector.”

The billionaire's Reliance Industries chairperson has been accused of blocking the satellite internet service from competing. Musk has also accused Ambani, who owns India’s largest telecom operator, of blocking its launch.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/billionai.title: ‘Are we rich?’ The question billionaire and millionaire parents dread, and what happens when they dodge it
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/billionai.author: Mia Osmonbekov
https://fortune.com/2026/10/09/billionai.text:
There’s a question wealthy parents dread, and it’s not coming from activists asking them about their tax returns.

Jessica McGawley, a consultant who’s worked with high-net-worth families for nearly two decades, told Fortune that she has to explain to clients that their children are not “being greedy or rude” by suddenly asking “Are we rich?” after noticing their family has more than one house.

“How a parent feels comfortable talking about sex and death is also how they feel comfortable with money,” she said.

As the scions of wealthy families anticipate the $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer—the sum Cerulli Associates projects will change hands in the U.S. through 2048—they’re often unprepared to handle their inheritance because their families haven’t talked with them about money and how to manage it. McGawley founded her firm Dallington to address this issue, based on her experience of parents having put together “a watertight paper document that explains everything” but failing to actually talk through it with their kids.

“Successful families are very good at preparing wealth for the children. They are not good at preparing the children for the wealth,” McGawley said. “So if you spend all this time and all this energy preparing your wealth for your children, but don’t prepare them for what they’re receiving and why, you’ve missed the point.”

A Fidelity study last year found the majority of parents age 55 or older with at least $500,000 in investable assets haven’t talked to their kids about inheriting money, with more than half (52%) reporting they haven’t communicated their net worth and 68% reporting they haven’t told their kids what they’ll inherit or if they’ll inherit at all. About a third (35%) said they don’t want their children to know how much they’ll get.

But parents who share completed plans with their kids are more than three times as likely to feel confident in their planning, Fidelity separately found in a 2026 survey of 654 married or partnered adults age 55 or older with a net worth of at least $500,000 and at least one adult child. But only 21% have communicated a completed estate plan to their adult children.

McGawley has worked with more than 150 ultra high net worth individuals, with most of her clients falling into the centimillionaire bucket. She said most parents worry that letting their kids know the extent of their wealth will make them entitled.

“There’s this fear that if your kids know how much money that you have as a family, that they’re going to basically give up studying, give up motivation, won’t be bothered—basically have a meal ticket for the rest of their life,” she said.

She said what “changes things” is heirs learning the upsides and downsides that accompany their wealth and how to build an identity outside of inheriting it.

When the ultra-rich avoid telling their kids how much they’re worth, the kids may find out from outsiders before they’re ready, and the shock can strain family relationships over the long term, according to McGawley.

The teenage daughter of a billionaire family McGawley worked with didn’t know the scale of her wealth until she started college, when her new friends looked her up online and found out her family’s net worth. Half of them asked her to buy them things or to get internships at her dad’s company, and the other half criticized her for “not donating all of her inheritance to Gaza.”

“There’s been no preparation time, and then she’s met with these extreme responses to her wealth, which she hasn’t really even understood,” McGawley said. “So really, what you find is somebody wanting to just stick their head in the sand and shut their door.”

But there can also be more serious consequences, especially when parents don’t involve their kids in succession talks early on. They might pick one sibling to take over the business and leave another feeling disinherited, or refuse to hand over control of the business at all, fracturing family relationships.

“If they are just being handed roles, you’re going to have problems,” McGawley said about heirs. “Money is very emotional.”

She said philanthropy can be “a real hotbed for conflict” because the parents might have donated to the same children’s charity or water aid group for 20 years, but their kids want to donate to one “that feels more pertinent at the age that they’re at,” like a women’s rights group. Fewer than half (47%) of Americans with at least $3 million in investable assets surveyed by Bank of America believe the next generation is ready to take on family philanthropic causes, down from 55% in 2024.

“This idea that we can’t survive differences within family needs to be addressed because if you’re going to be a family that works together, inherits together, you need to be able to make decisions together, and you need to be able to manage difficult conversations,” McGawley said.

But when rich parents do talk to their kids about money and its responsibilities, it can turn out well. David Munson, 67, is a fourth-generation heir of his Texas family’s stock and oil wealth and told Fortune his father talked openly about finances—but also made the kids sell eggs to the neighbors to earn their own money. His father worked as a stockbroker in the 1960s and in the 1970s sold oil and gas leases in western Colorado that he won in the federal government’s lease lottery. He eventually left “several hundred million dollars” to Munson and his siblings.

“He taught us to be sensible and productive, and also think about passing down wealth to our kids,” Munson said.

Munson said that today, his four adult children each get $10,000 a month from their trusts, which lets  them pursue their passions without worrying about working.

“It’s important for parents to both talk to their kids about money, but also encourage them to get some work experience, but not expect them to live a poor life growing up,” Munson said. “There can be a lot of blessings to a kid having enough wealth to do things they want to do instead of having to get a job just because they need the money.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2026-.author: Lauren Roberts
https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2026-.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Health & Wellbeing

Christine La Rose, left, and Margaret Blake, right, both faced delays prior to their bladder cancer diagnosis. (Supplied: Christine La Rose and Margaret Blake)

In Australia, three in four people diagnosed with bladder cancer are men, but the five-year survival rate for women is much lower.

It is common for women to face diagnostic delays, with symptoms easily misdiagnosed as urinary tract infections (UTIs) or perimenopause.

Experts are calling for greater awareness about bladder cancer symptoms, as well of the importance of referrals for women with recurrent bladder infections.

That is how much time passed between when Andrea Harris first presented to her GP with a suspected bladder infection, and when she was diagnosed with advanced, muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Ms Harris went back to the doctor multiple times over these four years, wanting to understand more about the root cause of her symptoms.

At one stage, Ms Harris recalls being "in tears" in the doctor's office, pressing for more extensive testing.

A report investigating the financial and legal impact of cancer in Victoria has found both patients and carers have significant out-of-pocket costs.

"I'd have a seven-day lot of antibiotics, and I'd be good for six or seven weeks and then I'd start to get symptoms again," she said.

By the time she was finally diagnosed in March 2024, Ms Harris's cancer had advanced to stage three.

In Australia, three in four people diagnosed with bladder cancer are men, but experts are concerned about the number of women, like Ms Harris, presenting with late-stage bladder cancer.

Alison Zhang, a medical oncologist at Macquarie University Hospital, said although bladder cancer symptoms, like blood in the urine and a frequent need to wee, were similar in both sexes, they were easy to misdiagnose as urinary tract infections (UTIs) or perimenopause in women.

Alison Zhang wants to improve outcomes for women diagnosed with bladder cancer. (Supplied: Alison Zhang)

About 3,345 cases of bladder cancer were estimated to be diagnosed in Australia last year.

But unlike most other cancers, the five-year survival rate has dropped since 1987.

Women diagnosed with bladder cancer in Australia face about a 50 per cent chance of living five years post-diagnosis, while men have an almost 60 per cent chance.

"Women tend to present later with later-stage disease, which is a real problem," Dr Zhang said.

Magdalena Simonis, a practising GP and women's health expert from the University of Melbourne, said men often had their bladder cancer symptoms — especially blood in the urine — escalated quickly as UTIs were far less common in men, and therefore unlikely to be the cause.

"If a man shows up with microscopic, that is, invisible blood in the urine, or visible blood in the urine, we would immediately advance that person to further investigations," she said.

"When a woman presents with the symptoms of bladder cancer, the symptoms are not dissimilar to those of a UTI; they might have a burning sensation with urination or blood in their urine."

Christine La Rose, a patient and support lead for advocacy group BEAT Bladder Cancer Australia, said there needed to be "more focus, more urgency and awareness" on improving outcomes for women.

An otherwise fit and healthy Christine La Rose was shocked to be diagnosed with bladder cancer at 49. (Supplied: Christine La Rose)

Ms La Rose, a bladder cancer survivor herself, faced a short diagnostic delay after initially being told the blood in her urine had been caused by a UTI.

Other common symptoms of bladder cancer include a sudden change in urine colour, loss of appetite and weight loss.

There are a few things that experts agree will help improve outcomes for women.

The first, Dr Zhang said, was to increase community awareness about the symptoms of bladder cancer.

Shame and stigma mean gynaecological side-effects from cancer treatment — affecting women's sexual, urinary and reproductive health — are under-reported and under-researched.

The second, Dr Simonis said, was that women who presented with recurrent UTIs — more than two within six months or three within a year — needed their symptoms investigated further with additional testing and/or a referral to a urologist.

"Women have traditionally been dismissed if they've got pain or ongoing symptoms," she said.

"Any level of discomfort that is continuous is something that we shouldn't really put up with."

Dr Simonis said GPs needed to consider risk factors of bladder disease, such as smoking and age, when treating female patients presenting with UTI-like symptoms.

"If they're a smoker, and they've got ongoing symptoms and recurrent symptoms, then alarm bells should ring a lot earlier," she said.

Ms La Rose said although bladder cancer was "traditionally seen as an older man's disease", she had met women in their 20s, 30s and 40s who had been diagnosed with it.

"Go back or go and get a second opinion. You really need to advocate for yourself and push for answers."

Margaret Blake was one of the many Australian women who needed to do just that.

Margaret Blake urges women to take bladder changes seriously and speak to a doctor as soon as possible. (Supplied: Margaret Blake)

Ms Blake saw three different GPs within the space of six months, concerned about her frequent need to urinate and finding blood in her urine.

She said her third GP was the first one to take her symptoms seriously, referring her for a series of tests, which eventually led to her bladder cancer diagnosis.

Survivors Ms Harris, Ms La Rose and Ms Blake all live with the ongoing consequences of treatment.

Ms La Rose has a neo-bladder, built by a surgeon using a piece of her intestine, which she is grateful to be able to empty easily and maintains a good quality of life.

"I'm really lucky. And I also know how lucky I am to still be here, given the diagnosis," she said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.title: Old Bendigo gold mine hosts underground piano concert
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.author: Anna McGuinness and Tyrone Dalton
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

This is how a piano gets moved underground

A 300kg piano has been transported 61 metres underground in a 'world-first' piano concert in a Bendigo gold mine.

The concert was held in the mine to celebrate the 175th anniversary of the discovery of gold in the central Victorian city.

Bendigo Fine Music says it's the first time they know of that a concert has been held underground in such a unique venue.

A unique piano concert 61 metres underground in an old gold mine.

That was the brainwave of Bendigo Fine Music chair Thomas Heywood.

And yesterday that brainwave became reality, with a piano descending into the Central Deborah Gold Mine in Bendigo for a one-off evening performance.

The 300kg piano was formerly owned by Mr Heywood's mother, who was a renowned concert pianist.

"It's one of those classic 'don't drop the piano' scenarios," Mr Heywood said.

"We couldn't find any evidence that this has been done before.

"It's really quite emotional; it sounds fantastic in here. It is an amazing room for sound. There's a timber ceiling and hardstone walls, and they're ideal for musical performance."

Thomas Heywood came up with the idea of holding the concert in a gold mine to mark 175 years since gold was discovered in Bendigo. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

The Bendigo Fine Music event celebrated 175 years since gold was first discovered in the central Victorian city.

"We were always taught in school that basically the riches that followed from gold made possible what would have taken 500 years in European history to be achieved in a mere 50 years to Federation."

Friday's concert was limited to 60 attendees, who were allowed to remove their hard hats once in the concert room.

Pianist Yasmin Rowe said performing this rare and unusual concert was exciting.

"I've never played underground before, and this is just so special. When I entered this room, I thought it was so, so beautiful," Ms Rowe said.

"You've got this millions-of-years-old rock there right behind the piano; the light, the colour, the atmosphere is wonderful."

Yasmin Rowe and Ian Munro played before an audience of 60 people. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

Ms Rowe and fellow pianist Ian Munro said the underground concert made playing the piano interesting again.

Mr Munro said the rare and unusual concert brought back the memory of a conversation with his piano teacher at the age of 14, who questioned whether he would continue to love playing the piano as an adult.

"When I was 30 [and still loved playing piano], and now I'm very much older than 30, I'm still very interested; it's still got that magic for me."

The main body of the piano was covered with a blanket to protect from moisture in the tunnels.  (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

The operation to get the instrument underground was a family affair by Joshua McPherson, his wife Jo and son Sam.

Mr McPherson said it was "definitely the most unusual" place he had ever taken a piano.

The disassembled instrument was wheeled on a trolley into a lift and rolled along the rocky tunnels of the mine.

"We were worried about moisture dropping from the ceiling — that was our main concern. [It was] a little bit rough underfoot but nothing scary really," he said.

Nic Hamilton was tasked with making sure the piano stayed in tune.  (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Once in place, it was over to piano technician Nic Hamilton to ensure nothing had gone awry on the journey and to tune the piano before the concert.

"It's a fun thing to do, and it's very typical of Thomas [Heywood] to come up with projects that are interesting and exciting."

The piano is moved into the entrance to Central Deborah Gold Mine. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)
