https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.title: Hanson takes aim at Coalition in fiery pitch to conservative voters
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Political Parties

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson speaking at CPAC.   (ABC: Luke Bowden)

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor addressed a conservative conference in Brisbane, pitching themselves as the conservative alternative to the prime minister.

While reserving her strongest criticism for the Albanese government, Senator Hanson also took sharp aim at the Liberal Party for its previous commitments to climate targets and for creating the eSafety Commissioner.

Among her criticisms, Senator Hanson said she would be willing to work with the Coalition if it meant removing Labour from office.

Pauline Hanson has used a speech at a conservative conference to urge voters to abandon the Coalition, while acknowledging she would work with them if it meant removing Labor from government.

In a speech to the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane, the One Nation leader described Opposition Leader Angus Taylor as a "smarmy management consultant" and said the Liberal Party was responsible for Australia's climate change commitments.

"The Liberals signed us up to Paris and net zero. The Liberals legislated the safeguard mechanism, and Labor locked the targets into law and made them even worse," she said.

"They signed us up to this mess, so why would we trust them to get us out of it?"

Ms Hanson pledged to hold a royal commission into net zero climate targets, should One Nation be elected.

As the three-cornered migration battle continues, Angus Taylor is trying to position his party in the middle of the government and One Nation.

And she further criticised the Coalition for creating the office of the eSafety Commissioner, a position she has pledged to abolish on the grounds it infringes on free speech online.

Both Ms Hanson and Mr Taylor addressed CPAC — a spin-off of conservative conferences held in the US and UK — on Saturday morning, taking aim at the Albanese government and pitching themselves as the conservative alternative.

It was the first time a Coalition leader has addressed the annual forum, although notable Liberal figures like Tony Abbott and Jacinta Nampijinpa Price have addressed it in recent years.

Jacinta Nampijinpa Price speaking at CPAC. (ABC: Luke Bowden)

But while Senator Hanson sharply criticised the Coalition, Mr Taylor made almost no mention of One Nation.

His speech made just one apparent indirect reference to Senator Hanson, referencing her dominance of the One Nation party and brand.

"Good government isn't built around one figure. You need a strong team," he said.

And he opened the speech by referencing a number of "mistakes" the Coalition made in government, acknowledging to the audience that "some of you may have doubts".

He pointed to areas like immigration policy, climate change and government spending during the pandemic as policy failures under Coalition governments.

Angus Taylor speaking at CPAC in Brisbane.    (ABC : Luke Bowden )

"We made the mistake as a government of signing up to net zero — which I detested from the get-go," he said.

"Your frustrations about where we let you down in the recent past are understandable and reasonable. Believe me, I share them."

Both leaders reserved their strongest attacks for the Albanese government — Mr Taylor arguing it was leaving Australians "poorer, weaker, and demoralised", and Senator Hanson calling it "wretched and corrupt".

Despite her strong rhetoric on the Coalition, Senator Hanson made clear that One Nation would work with them if it meant changing the government.

"One Nation will work with the Liberals and Nationals to remove this horrible Labor government and deliver something better," she said.

"That's what you, the people, want. It's the will of the people."

Matt Canavan in a Q&A with Pauline Hanson. (By Luke Bowden)

She referenced her time in prison after a 2003 conviction for electoral fraud, later quashed on appeal, under the Howard government, but said she would put "personal grievances aside".

"Yes, I do have reasons to hold a grudge, but I also have children and grandchildren," she said.

"Their futures and your futures matter more."

In a later speech, Nationals leader Matt Canavan also struck a more conciliatory tone — urging those on the right of politics not to become caught up fighting among themselves.

"My message to you today is, look, we do wear lots of different colours. I get that," he said.

"There's lots of different people here.

"But the one thing we have to do at the next election is all put the Labor Party last. That's what we've got to do."

Noah McFadyen completed an impressive debut for South Australia, taking a return catch as his side beat Victoria. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

South Australia's campaign for a third-straight Sheffield Shield title is off to a winning start with victory over Victoria.

The Redbacks won by an innings and 40 runs at Junction Oval.

Debutant Noah McFadyen, who scored a century in SA's only innings of 508, took the final wicket with a caught-and-bowled to clinch the win.

South Australia has started its Sheffield Shield campaign in the same way it ended the last one, beating Victoria at Junction Oval.

The two-time defending champions wrapped up their dominating start today, beating the home side by an innings and 40 runs.

Fittingly, debutant Noah McFadyen took the last wicket of the game when he had David Moody caught and bowled, after top-scoring with 134 in SA's innings.

McFadyen had hit two sixes to go from 88 to 100, finished with 16 fours and five maximums.

The 23-year-old all-rounder had match figures of 3-65, including Moody's wicket to clinch the game.

Resuming at 7-175 and needing another 89 to bat again, Victoria was dismissed for 224.

Victoria made 244 in its first innings and SA took the game away from them with 508.

Fergus O'Neill top-scored in Victoria's second innings with 62, while Nathan McAndrew and Henry Thornton took three wickets apiece.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: Anthropic cites new AI misbehavior, some on government sites
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
Anthropic said its Claude AI model carried out additional unintended actions on the digital systems of outside organizations, including some U.S. government agencies’ websites, prompting a warning from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration for artificial intelligence companies to secure their systems.

In a report outlining previously undisclosed incidents, Anthropic listed four types of unintended behaviors that the AI has demonstrated, including exploiting basic flaws in software to run commands, submitting forms it should not have and bypassing restrictions to access certain public data.

The company said that some of the cases involved websites run by government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, without specifying the agencies. The report did not name the outside entities involved, which Anthropic said was at the request of some of the affected parties.

Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, have disclosed a spate of incidents in recent months involving their AI models acting in unintended ways, ranging from behaviors like those described in Friday’s report, to hacks of third-party websites. These disclosures have fueled concerns about the security risks of cutting-edge AI.

Anthropic said in the report that it sees the behavior as less severe than some other previous incidents involving its AI. “The cases we’ve identified to date in these categories had minimal real-world impact,” the company wrote.

In one example of the improper behavior it found, Anthropic said Friday that its Claude Haiku 4.5 model submitted a tip to a local police department about a homicide, stating in the form, “I may have information regarding this case,” and “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area,” without filling in the site’s name and contact fields. The Philadelphia Police Department disclosed the incident this morning in a press release, the company said.

Anthropic also said it briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved.

On Friday, Trump administration officials said they were now requiring that AI companies notify affected parties and address security incidents involving their models.

“Earlier today, Anthropic contacted the SI Force to disclose the details of various prior incidents that it discovered in late September involving the unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems,” the White House said in a statement from the Super Intelligence Force, a new government unit tasked by Trump with overseeing AI development and safety.

“The company informed us that these events occurred in the past, the activity has ceased, and there is no ongoing similar activity,” the statement said.

Axios reported on the government requirement earlier.

As a result of these uncovered incidents, Anthropic said Friday that it has restricted some types of internet access for its AI models during the testing phase of its training process.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: Anthropic says its Claude AI model carried out additional unintended actions on the digital systems of outside organizations. The company says some of the cases involved websites run by government agencies. The report did not name the outside entities involved, which Anthropic said was at the request of some of those affected parties.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: U.S. Treasury chief Scott Bessent to skip IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
DOHA – U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will skip next week’s annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand, due to domestic engagements, a U.S. official said on Friday.

The Treasury Department confirmed that Deputy Treasury Secretary Francis Brooke and Under Secretary for International Affairs Erin Browne will lead the U.S. delegation for the department, with many pressing economic issues on the agenda.

Treasury said U.S. officials would work with partners at the meetings to address policies and structural imbalances that have held back growth, while pushing for “more transparency and more effective approaches to sovereign debt.”

Bessent’s absence from the high-profile financial event comes at a critical moment when benchmark Treasury yields have surged to their highest levels in nearly 25 years and the ongoing energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East has set back global growth.

It was not immediately clear what domestic engagements are keeping Bessent at home, but he has been a key spokesman for domestic economic policies as the midterm U.S. elections approach.

The U.S. also leads the Group of 20 major economies this year, and the Treasury chief would normally have chaired a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from around the world. Bessent is expected to attend the G20 leaders summit in Miami, Florida, in December.

It is not unprecedented for top officials to miss occasional meetings due to scheduling issues or other factors, but Bessent’s decision may frustrate top officials from other countries, who generally use the meetings to secure formal and informal bilateral meetings with their U.S. counterpart.

Bessent skipped the G20 meetings in South Africa last year amid objections by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration to the country’s land reforms and other issues.

Treasury said the U.S. delegation would focus on the debt issues so that countries facing debt distress could restore stability and return to growth, while creditors and borrowers are “held to clear and consistent standards.”

The U.S. would also continue to press the International Monetary Fund and World Bank — where it is the biggest shareholder — to focus on their core mandates, operate efficiently, and support policies that promote economic stability, productivity and growth.

“Our engagement in Bangkok will be guided by a clear objective: ensuring that the international financial institutions and the broader international economic system advance U.S. economic and national security interests,” Treasury said in a statement.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.summary: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will skip next week's annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand. Bessen's absence comes at a critical moment when benchmark Treasury yields have surged to their highest levels in nearly 25 years.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-delhi-braces.title: India: Delhi braces for Cockroach protest amid strict curbs
https://www.dw.com/en/india-delhi-braces.text:
The 'Cockroaches' are returning to Delhi to demand the resignation of India's election chief. Police have not authorized the protest, and heavy security arrangements are in place. DW has the latest.

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

The CJP is not the only group calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

India's bloc of opposition parties, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, has been carrying out a sustained campaign against Kumar in recent days with its own protest marches.

The country has seen dramatic visuals emerge from Delhi's key corridor of political power, which showed leading opposition MPs, including Gandhi, being carried away to detention buses by uniformed police officials as they tried to dig their heels in.

The ire against India's election chief —  the head of India's independent Election Commission  —  is turning into one of the biggest public and political challenges for Modi in his three-term rule. Opposition and critics allege that a mass deletion of tens of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls benefits Modi's Prime Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi and this is a special edition of our daily India news blog.

As the early morning hours tick away, a countdown to a rally against India's top poll official over alleged voter list irregularities has begun in the heart of the world's largest democracy.

India's 'Cockroaches' are headed once again for Jantar Mantar —  the same protest site where the online satirical movement sprung to the mainstream as a youth-led pressure group in July after it forced the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's then education minister.

The police have denied the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) permission to hold the demonstration but the group's leaders are heralding people from all over the country to converge at Jantar Mantar, calling the protest a "fundamental right".

A showdown between police and protesters seems imminent.

New Delhi, particularly its central areas, have essentially been turned into a fortress with a heavy security blanket — including thousands of paramilitary personnel —  a rare mobile internet blackout, train cancellations and warnings from the police against any protest assembly.

The security arrangements come as memory is still fresh of a clash between youth demonstrators and police during the July Cockroach protest. Police used batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns to disperse the agitating crowd. Several injuries were reported as the protesters alleged police brutality, while the police said it used force only after the protests stopped being peaceful.

We bring you all this and more. Stay with us as events unfold.

India has deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel in central Delhi and restricted transport in and around the capital ahead of a youth-led protest demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the country’s chief election commissioner.

Saturday’s rally, called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-based political movement, is expected to be the biggest yet in a wave of near-daily protests over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Organisers have billed it as a protest to “Save Democracy”.

Police have not authorised a rally at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which authorities usually designate for protests, because they said the request was not made on time and that the CJP had violated undertakings given during earlier protests.

Police have also warned that protesters will face a forceful law enforcement response if they violate the ban.

Roads to the site are blocked with multiple layers of metal barricades, as authorities shut 57 metro stations from Friday night, cancelled several long-distance trains and suspended mobile internet within 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area until Saturday night, the Indian news agency ANI reported.

India’s Supreme Court said on Friday that some trains must still run and that blanket closure of metro stations is unlikely.

“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on X.

The CJP says at least 10,000 people, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.

“You can detain the people, you cannot detain the movement,” said Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students’ Association, who has emerged as a leading face of the protests.

Protesters want Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to quit over a voter list revision that has removed more than 130 million names.

The Election Commission says the exercise removes duplicate and ineligible voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from voting.

Critics say it has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities.

The protests escalated after the Indian Express reported that Kumar’s two deputies had formally raised concerns at least 14 times in the past 10 months over the revisions.

The Election Commission and the BJP have denied the allegations. The BJP says the opposition is misleading the country because it cannot win elections.

The CJP began online as political satire in May after Chief Justice Surya Kant called unemployed youth “cockroaches”, sparking nationwide outrage. Since then, the CJP has garnered a large following among India’s youth.

The July protests led Modi’s education minister to resign over exam paper leaks. The latest demonstrations come months before a series of state elections in early 2027, including in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, which the BJP governs.

https://www.ft.com/content/4e4ea744-6603.title: Russia targets Ukraine’s bridges as Vladimir Putin expands air war
https://www.ft.com/content/4e4ea744-6603.author: Christopher Miller
https://www.ft.com/content/4e4ea744-6603.text:
Christopher Miller in Kyiv

Published43 MINUTES AGO

Simply sign up to the War in Ukraine myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.

Russia is targeting Ukraine’s bridges as part of its escalating air campaign against civilian infrastructure ahead of the winter.

Russian jet-powered drones have struck three bridges over the river Dnipro during the past week, including two in Kyiv, injuring dozens and disrupting vital transport arteries.

Moscow also hit residential buildings, energy infrastructure and a bus stop during rush hour in several Ukrainian cities, killing at least 64 people in the past few days.

One attack on Kyiv’s North Bridge occurred during the day last Sunday, shortly after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv in a show of support for Ukraine.

A video of the attack showed a Russian drone hurtling towards the bridge, its trajectory visible for only seconds before it exploded into a giant ball of flames.

A Russian drone strikes Kyiv's North Bridge on Sunday

Russian drones struck Kyiv’s South Bridge three times in the days before Merz’s arrival, damaging the road surface and halting traffic and metro services. The North Bridge was also hit multiple times, including in the strike after the German chancellor’s arrival. At least four people were injured in those attacks, which caused severe disruptions and traffic jams.

On Tuesday, Russia struck another bridge over the Dnipro in the south-central city of Zaporizhzhia, where five people were injured and traffic was disrupted according to local authorities.

The attacks mark an expansion in Russia’s air campaign, from strikes aimed primarily at energy infrastructure towards transport links that are harder to replace and central to daily life.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT last week, citing intelligence gathered by his agencies, that Russian President Vladimir Putin had instructed his military leaders to abandon any rules of war, leading to a steep increase in strikes on civilian targets in an attempt to regain the advantage in the war. Deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure is a war crime under international law.

The Ukrainian president said the Russian focus on new targets was meant to crush the economy, wear down morale and make life much more difficult for the country’s war-weary population ahead of what is expected to be another difficult winter.

The strikes on Kyiv’s bridges have exposed how dependent the capital is on a handful of crossings between the city’s riverbanks. Damage to even one bridge can disrupt civilian and military supplies and complicate the movement of emergency services.

A Russian drone strikes the South Bridge in Kyiv as traffic crosses the Dnipro river

For Kyiv’s almost 4mn residents, there are just eight bridges connecting the capital’s eastern and western banks. They carry car commuters, pedestrians, metro and railway passengers, as well as trucks and other vehicles that keep the country moving.

When traffic is diverted, the next crossing over the Dnipro north of capital is the Kyiv Hydroelectric Power Plant, which doubles as a bridge, about 16km from the North Bridge. In the opposite direction, the closest crossing is the Kaniv Hydroelectric Power Plant about 130km from the South Bridge.

The damage to Kyiv’s bridges has so far been limited. Tetiana Gaviuk, an analyst at Acled, a US non-profit mapping war zones, said the damage so far was unlikely to cause the bridges to collapse. However, she added, “sustained direct attacks could eventually compromise bridge structures and lead to more frequent or prolonged closures”.

“Such disruptions could have significant socio-economic consequences, as hundreds of thousands of people rely on the bridges to access work, education, healthcare and other essential services,” she said.

Kyiv has been under relentless missile and drone barrages for the past month. Russia’s ballistic missiles are difficult for Kyiv to shoot down with its critically low supply of US Patriot interceptor missiles.

But, increasingly, Moscow is deploying its new jet-powered drones, for which Ukraine also has limited answers. The drones now attack around the clock, targeting major businesses, data centres, railway infrastructure, medical facilities and densely populated residential neighbourhoods.

The drones used in the bridge attacks were new versions of Russia’s Iran-designed Shahed drones: the Geran-4 and Geran-5, both of which use small jet engines.

Ukraine’s defence intelligence agency, HUR, said the Geran-4 has been adapted recently with systems to improve autonomous navigation and a specialised warhead for striking bridge structures.

Zelenskyy told the FT last week that Ukraine’s air defences were able to intercept just over half of Russia’s jet-powered drones. He said domestic efforts to develop an anti-drone system could hit production lines by the end of October. But a reliable and scalable solution probably remains months away.

Automated machine-gun turrets using AI can be spotted in dozens of locations around Kyiv. Serhii Beskrestnov, a government adviser and electronic warfare expert, said they were meant to provide a last layer of protection for special facilities rather than cover for the entire city.

The bridge attacks have forced the government to consider alternative solutions. One idea being debated is the deployment of pontoon bridges over the Dnipro, which could help to ease traffic but would take weeks to assemble.

Businesses are adapting too, with some planning to let customer-support staff work from home, while offering more flexible start times, carpooling and other alternatives to employees who need to be on site.

While the attacks have sparked public concern and prompted some residents to make contingency plans in case the city’s east and west sides are cut off, some Ukrainians also responded with characteristic levity.

On social media, users circulated AI-generated images of crowds crossing the Dnipro on paddleboards. One of the posts included the caption: “This is a case where a summer hobby suddenly became part of Kyiv’s transport infrastructure.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ai-lawye.title: AI is changing how lawyers work — and putting the billable hour under pressure
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ai-lawye.author: Lindsay Dodgson
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ai-lawye.text:
AI is challenging some of the assumptions on which the legal profession was built, forcing firms to reevaluate how their lawyers spend their time and charge for it.

The billable hour is central to the business model of many law firms, but AI means the economics are no longer so straightforward.

AI is also changing how some lawyers learn their trade, as repetitive tasks traditionally helped junior lawyers learn the building blocks of law.

Artificial intelligence is now used by almost 90% of legal professionals in the U.K. and Ireland, and it’s putting one of the profession’s oldest conventions — the billable hour — under the microscope.

That’s according to legal software company Clio’s U.K. & Ireland Legal Insights Report 2026. It found that among firms using AI, almost 80% said they can handle more work without increasing resources, while over 70% said it cut costs by absorbing administrative work once done by support staff.

As a result, AI is challenging some of the assumptions on which the legal profession was built, forcing firms to reevaluate how their lawyers spend their time, how they charge for it and how new lawyers learn the ropes.

Some of the U.K.’s biggest firms are already putting this into practice. A&O Shearman has worked with legal AI company Harvey to develop artificial intelligence agents for tasks, including reviewing loan agreements and analyzing regulatory filings, which it says can complete in minutes work that previously took several hours. Slaughter and May, meanwhile, has rolled out Harvey across all practice areas this year, including for regulatory research and document analysis.

The billable hour is central to the business model of many law firms, but when AI significantly reduces the time lawyers spend sifting through and drafting documents, the economics are no longer so straightforward.

“You can’t charge 16 hours for something that takes 16 seconds,” Nick Rowles-Davies, founder and CEO of legal finance fund Lexolent, based in London and Dubai, told CNBC.

About one in five firms that have widely adopted AI report difficulty meeting billable-hour targets, according to Clio’s report. Globally, senior legal leaders expect the share of work charged by the hour to fall from 72% to 44% over the next two to three years, according to a Deloitte survey.

Routine work is the most exposed, Rowles-Davies said. “If you’ve got standard documents and you’re just putting in detail, then clearly that’s an automatic process.”

But complex legal work still requires human judgment, he added, particularly when interpreting AI output and determining the right strategy for a client.

Lawyers also need to be able to spot AI hallucinations. “There have been a lot of cases where lawyers have been sanctioned for producing briefs before a court with cases that don’t exist,” Rowles-Davies said.

Mansoor Soomro, who leads the Future of Work Research Unit at Teesside University in Middlesbrough, England, told CNBC the billable hour is certainly not disappearing overnight, but it is getting harder to justify.

AI is also changing how lawyers learn their trade, Soomro added, as repetitive tasks traditionally helped junior lawyers learn the building blocks of law. Reviewing hundreds of documents taught them what matters, writing up contracts honed their drafting skills and researching dozens of cases helped them develop legal reasoning, he added.

As AI takes on more of that work, firms will need to be deliberate about replacing those learning opportunities, according to London-based Jorge Bestard, head of EMEA at Harvey. “A faster route to a draft does not automatically mean a faster route to competence,” he told CNBC.

A&O Shearman is placing more value on “curiosity and entrepreneurship,” said Francesca Bennetts, the firm’s London-based head of legal talent. It is also building career paths in legal engineering, product and AI delivery that “barely existed a few years ago,” she told CNBC.

“The need to develop exceptional lawyers doesn’t go away,” Bennetts said. “They are the partners and experts of the future.”

Soomro expects judgment to become “disproportionately valuable” in the sector, with lawyers spending more time checking and challenging AI’s output and interpreting what it means for a client.

“The future may therefore not belong to the lawyer who knows the most about one narrow area, but to the lawyer who knows how to connect multiple areas to solve a complex client problem,” he said.

Whether AI efficiencies ultimately make lawyers’ working lives better may depend on what firms do with the time they get back. Clio’s report found that 51% of legal professionals work evenings, but only 32% want to, while 22% work weekends compared with 11% who would choose to. Joshua Lenon, Clio’s New York-based lawyer-in-residence, believes some lawyers are already seeing the benefits.

“Lawyers [are] telling us that their day is getting better,” Lenon told CNBC, as AI becomes more commonplace. “People are really looking at these tools and saying, ‘This is making work better.’”

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Science and Technology

Cilia in the airways of a child with rare genetic disorder. (Supplied: Ning Xu)

The winner of a Nikon image and video competition has been disqualified after using AI.

Days after the winner was announced, microscopy experts started to question the accuracy of the clip on social media.

The international competition has since named a new winner.

The winner of an international imagery competition has been disqualified after it was found that they used generative AI.

Nikon said the video broke the rules of the annual Small World In Motion competition that awards the best photos and videos taken through the lens of a microscope.

The video, taken by Ning Xu, an optical engineering researcher at Tsinghua University in China at the time, "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI," Nikon said in a statement.

The decision is based on the video's eligibility and was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions, Nikon said.

Stunning scenes of the world through microscopes have been put on display by the Nikon Small World In Motion competition winners.

Days after the winner was announced, microscopy experts started to question the accuracy of the clip on social media.

The winner's video showed tiny hair-like structures fluttering in the airways of a child with the rare genetic disease, primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD).

Dr Xu's video, magnified to 100 times in size, showed cilia that line airways to clear out mucus.

His video claimed to use a series of complicated light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour, allowing researchers to gain a better understanding of PCD.

A screenshot of a Bluesky poster questioning if the video was real. (ABC: Supplied)

Edward Phelps, an associate professor at Florida University, said the images of nuclei "do not behave as nuclei" and that the cilia "appear from nowhere and do not match the known size", in the comment section of a LinkedIn post made by Nikon.

The post has since been deleted by Nikon.

The microscopy community wrote an open letter to the competition, calling for the winners' work to be externally examined.

"A potentially misleading portrayal of PCD is shaping public understanding of an already poorly understood rare disease," the letter stated.

It called on clinicians and researchers who diagnose and study PCD to sign the letter and push for Nikon to enforce its own rules.

Roundworm and single-celled Dileptus under a microscope. (Supplied: Nam Nhat Nguyen)

Following the controversy, Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat was awarded first place for a video of a microscopic roundworm encountering a single-celled organism called a Dileptus.

The video initially took second place.

In September, the ABC announced the winners of the competition, which first started in 1975.

The video was one of dozens highlighted in the competition, including baby jellyfish in ocean drops and bioluminescent sparkles.

Jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets, magnified 25 times. This video came third in the 2026 Nikon Small World in Motion competition. (Supplied: Benedikt Pleyer)

The winner receives a prize worth US$3,000 ($4,300).

The competition is open to anyone around the world with an interest in film or time-lapse photography through a microscope.

The ABC has reached out to Dr Zu for comment.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.title: In 1975 editor Hilary McPhee changed Australian publishing forever
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/h.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Writer, editor and publisher Hilary McPhee, who died in October. (ABC Conversations: Nicola Harrison)

The name Hilary McPhee is etched in huge and luminous letters on the history of the Australian book world and the memory of her will forever burn with a steady flame.

In 1975, when publishing here was run by men and was largely a reflection of British publishing, Hilary McPhee and Diana Gribble set up their own small operation, calling it simply McPhee Gribble.

Hilary had had broad experience in publishing by this time, some of it at Penguin and some at Heinemann.

McPhee Gribble's first venture was attached to Penguin and was a very successful children's series called Practical Puffins.

When they turned their attention to adult writing the men in the industry warned them of failure, suggesting they confine their product to pornography or books on horses or ballet.

With her energy, tiny physique, steady gaze, swift jaunty step, throaty chuckle, perky tilt of the chin and seductive husky voice, she was a commanding presence.

I often used to think she sounded as if she had a bit of melted chocolate on her tongue.

And yet her encyclopedic knowledge, her sharp mental clarity, sparkling wit, profound understanding and empathy gave her the bright edge of a sort of loving sprite with an assassin's weapon in her pocket.

Hilary McPhee and Diana Gribble were young feminists in Melbourne in the 1970s when they started McPhee Gribble publishing. (Supplied)

That weapon was in fact a 2B pencil with which she, as editor, marked her writers' manuscripts.

The marks were indicators of matters to be discussed, face to face, with the writer. She also had a supply of erasers.

McPhee Gribble published four of my books in the 1980s, and I would go to the old converted sewing factory at 66 Cecil Street, Fitzroy, climb the stairs to Hilary's office and sit on a little couch at a low table with Hilary while we went through the manuscript.

She was, need I say, a brilliant editor. Legendary.

The publishing house lasted from 1975 to 1989 when it was sold to Penguin.

They were 14 glory years in Australian writing, when Hilary and Di published, among many others, the all-time stand-out favourites Helen Garner and Tim Winton.

They were keen to promote the issues and writing of women, as well as the flavour and history of Australia.

McPhee Gribble gained a reputation as a "feminist" publisher. They also broke new ground when, in 1984, they published An Aboriginal Mother Tells of the Old and the New by First Nations woman Elsie Labumore.

Hilary McPhee is being remembered for her contribution to Australian literature. (Supplied: Sophie Cunningham)

After Penguin took over McPhee Gribble, Hilary ran the Picador imprint at Pan Macmillan Australia until 1994 where she published The First Stone by Helen Garner and The Riders by Tim Winton.

While Hilary's rural childhood was particularly characterised by books and reading, her first real contact with editing and publishing was in the early 1960s when she was a history student at the University of Melbourne and was working for the literary journal Meanjin.

In 2015, she was invited to be a guest editor to celebrate its 75th anniversary.

During the intervening years she had achieved many and varied milestones within Australian publishing, and from 1994 to 1997 she became the first woman chair of the Australia Council for the Arts.

From 1997 to 2004 she was inaugural Vice-Chancellor's fellow at the University of Melbourne. And in 2001 she was awarded an Order of Australia for her service to literature and the arts in general.

These are such highly distinguished achievements for the sprite with the 2B pencil, and, having listed them, I rush back to thoughts of the sewing factory in Fitzroy.

One day as Hilary and I were crossing busy Brunswick Street on our way to Cecil Street, she turned to me as we negotiated the traffic and suggested I write a book about writing. From this minute conversation, my book Dear Writer was born.

This was the swiftest publishing contract ever.

They used to throw big Christmas parties in Cecil Street. The hullabaloo of a bewildering cross-section of the literary who's who rose to the heavens on this, one of the most exciting nights of a writer's year.

The publishing partnership of McPhee Gribble became a legend of Australian letters, but it also joined two lives inextricably.

At other times there were gatherings at Hilary's house in Fitzroy and indeed, over time, she became a treasured personal friend.

If the image of the powerful woman publisher suggests a thoroughly tough individual, be assured there were vast other dimensions to her.

I recall an afternoon when she rang me to ask if she could come over to my house. She was in tears. A writer whose novel she had published long ago before the existence of McPhee Gribble had spoken publicly at a literary event in Melbourne, fiercely criticising her editing.

She was inconsolable, so fragile, having had no inkling for years that he harboured these feelings which he took pleasure in parading in public.

In her private life there were, as well as times of great joy, tormenting moments of tears, sorrow, heartache, and even serious illness.

Now that I think about it all, I have realised that courage is a word that comes forward in matters of both her professional and private self.

In 1964, she married Peter Freeman and had two children, Sara and Rupert, and in 1975, she married John Michie and had a son, James. In 2009, her marriage of 1986 to Don Watson ended.

Not until I read her second memoir, Other People's Houses, in 2019 did I know anything about the death of the first child. He was the two day-old son from her first marriage.

About the baby she writes: "I sat by his humidicrib and stroked his little red limbs, and he gripped my finger."

This tragic event was a vivid part of the complex emotional fabric concealed within the polished public exterior.

The title of the memoir echoes that of Other People's Words from 2001. It is interesting that these two personal books seem to point the reader away from the author.

The pioneering editor and author reflects on an unusual chapter in her literary career that took her to Jordan to work with the royal family.

Other People's Words is one of my favourite books, and for one thing it is evidence of the fact that Hilary was a superb writer of a prose that sings in the heart as well as a profoundly serious researcher.

Archaeology was her favourite kind of history, and she sometimes compared writing itself to a kind of archaeology.

She must have known, as an editor, how good her own writing was.

I see her reading it over and smiling as she looks up at the yellow Mermaid roses blooming in her Fitzroy garden.

Early in Other People's Words she tells of how, in the 60s, she started writing a novel, but abandoned it because she could not trust herself to write as herself. She kept imitating things she had read.

The memoir is pure, authentic and mature McPhee. Here she finds, as she says, "the words that ring true for me, which is the best I can do".

In 2025, Melbourne University Press re-issued the book with a new final chapter titled Twenty-five Years On. This fascinating piece might be the last thing Hilary would ever publish.

It is essentially a meditation on the phenomenon of artificial intelligence and its effect on writing, reading, knowing, imagining and being. She writes tenderly of her children and grandchildren, and their world.

Yes, Hilary, publishing today is a long, long way from Cecil Street in 1975. You have left a boundless legacy and a broad, indelible mark on literature and lives.

Carmel Bird is the author of numerous novels and short story collections and the winner of the Patrick White Award.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Taiwan’s leader says increasing defense spending to ‘deter war’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
TAIPEI – Taiwan aims to “deter war” by increasing its defense spending, the democratic island’s leader said on Saturday, as China uses military pressure to assert its territorial claims.

Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex it.

“Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, rather, it is to deter war,” President Lai Ching-te said in speech to celebrate Taiwan’s National Day.

Successive administrations have ramped up military spending as Taiwan improves its fighting abilities to avoid a potential Chinese invasion — and to show the United States it is serious about its own defense.

Lai’s government has earmarked a record 1.1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($34.5 billion) in defense spending for 2027, which accounts for more than 3% of GDP.

“We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others,” Lai said in his annual address in front of the Presidential Office in Taipei where thousands of people, including foreign diplomats, were gathered.

“However, peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” Lai said, noting China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.”

Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China, but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist.”

Government officials in Washington and Taipei have said repeatedly that U.S. policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump, whose remarks have at times jangled nerves.

While the United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, Washington is Taipei’s most important security backer.

Trump’s suggestion in May following a meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing that U.S. arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China set off alarm bells across the world.

Taiwan is waiting for Trump’s signature on $14 billion worth of weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot air defence system.

Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital ahead of Lai’s wide-ranging speech, which also covered housing pressure and the declining population.

“You can really feel the warmth in Taiwanese society,” said Feng Jing-heng, 70, who was in the crowd watching the military parade and dance performances.

Saturday’s celebrations mark the 115th anniversary of the toppling of China’s Qing dynasty and the subsequent founding of the Republic of China.

The current dispute between China and Taiwan dates to a civil war between the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek, who retreated to the island in 1949 after being defeated by Mao Zedong’s communist fighters.

Parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu, who is a senior member of the main opposition party that favours closer ties with China, said “U.S. support is extremely important to Taiwan’s security,” but he noted the historical and cultural links with China.

“The overwhelming majority of Taiwanese compatriots do not want war; they wish to live their lives in peace and hope for peaceful cross-strait exchanges,” Han said at the National Day event.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jesse Johnson
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has again found herself in a tough spot after the U.S., Tokyo’s key security ally, slapped the International Criminal Court with fresh sanctions, months after it targeted the Japanese head of the court with similar measures.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday ordered the Treasury Department to add the entire court to its Specially Designated Nationals list, a move that would impose financial punishment on any entity that does business with the ICC.

The announcement was a step beyond his administration’s targeted sanctions against top court officials, including ICC President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.title: Could Indonesia’s ‘content governor’ rival Prabowo for the presidency in 2029?
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.author: Anand Mathai
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.text:
Dedi Mulyadi’s blend of populist policies and social media savvy has made him one of Indonesia’s most talked-about politicians.

Dressed in his trademark white shirt and traditional Sundanese headcloth, West Java Governor Dedi Mulyadi stood near the barren slopes of Mount Wayang.

Announcing a new initiative to pay hundreds of local farmers to replant its forests and shield the region from flooding, he delivered a line perfectly pitched for the cameras tracking his every step.

“I am a leader who does not want obedience caused by poverty,” he declared on September 26. “I want obedience caused by prosperity.”

A July simulation by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) placed Dedi at 35 per cent in a multi-candidate presidential preference test, leaving Prabowo trailing far behind at 14.5 per cent. A subsequent August survey by Tempo Data Science produced similar results, placing Dedi above 40 per cent and Prabowo around 15 per cent.

The 2029 presidential election is some time away, but analysts say Dedi’s poll numbers have raised an awkward question for Gerindra: could the governor who rose to prominence under its banner eventually become its chairman’s rival for the presidency?

Dedi’s ascent has been propelled by his mastery of social media. His primary YouTube channel has 9.2 million subscribers and generates tens of millions of views every month, earning him the nickname “Gubernor Konten”, or “content governor”.

Rather than broadcasting dry policy speeches, his feed operates more like a populist reality show: he intervenes in neighbourhood disputes, hands out cash to the elderly and recently made headlines by offering a 50-million-rupiah (US$3,200) personal bounty to anyone who could catch pickpockets or muggers.

In a July survey conducted by Lembaga Survei Indonesia (LSI), public satisfaction with Dedi’s performance across West Java reached a staggering 95.4 per cent.

Djayadi Hanan, executive director of LSI, observed that Dedi’s grass roots appeal combined political cultivation spanning a quarter-century, as he climbed from local councillor and two-term regent of Purwakarta to national lawmaker, with an instinctive command of social media that starkly contrasted with the archaic outreach methods of his older peers in the political circle.

Dedi’s “main strength is authenticity”, Djayadi said, a trait he shared with Prabowo’s predecessor, former president Joko Widodo, who also rose from humble origins to national fame by branding himself a man of the people.

“By contrast, you cannot imagine President Prabowo Subianto making social media content hugging a taxi driver or eating at a street vendor without people viewing it as staged,” Djayadi added.

According to Burhanuddin Muhtadi, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute, Dedi’s surging profile outside his home province is not merely a product of his social media activities. His poll numbers also reflected a growing public weariness with the central government, Burhanuddin said.

He added that Dedi’s huge popularity should not be attributed to just his political strengths.

“Part of his rise also reflects negative sentiment towards the Prabowo government. Dedi projects a more down-to-earth, accessible image, whereas Prabowo has a much more high-profile presidential persona.”

With the surge in Dedi’s online presence, his content creation has begun to raise eyebrows within Jakarta’s establishment.

In August, in the wake of a magnitude-7.7 earthquake, Dedi travelled to East Nusa Tenggara to personally deliver relief assistance. While framed as an act of humanitarian solidarity, his excursion beyond West Java’s borders drew intense chatter, with critics questioning why he was leveraging a distant crisis to elevate his national profile.

For some analysts, Dedi’s manoeuvres risk crossing an unwritten line in a political system where institutional loyalty is prized above personal popularity.

While Dedi has earned a reputation as an on-the-spot problem solver, venturing beyond his provincial boundaries risks overstepping his mandate, said Aditya Perdana, a political science lecturer at Universitas Indonesia.

By attempting to intervene in crises outside West Java, Aditya argued, the governor was increasingly playing “offside” in the eyes of party elites by projecting influence where he had no jurisdiction.

His widening ground engagement has likely not gone unnoticed inside Prabowo’s party, which Dedi joined only in 2023 after decamping from Golkar, according to analysts.

“The potential main friction lies in Prabowo’s inner circle in Gerindra, who may perceive Dedi’s activities outside of West Java as his political warm-up agenda for the 2029 election,” said Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political researcher at the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN).

Publicly, Gerindra has dismissed the polling disparity between the two men. After the release of the SMRC report, the party’s daily executive chairman, Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, brushed off pollster’s figures, saying surveys could “fluctuate” from one cycle to the next.

Djayadi has noted Dedi’s “strategic ambiguity” by routinely deflecting questions about his national ambitions and insisting he remains focused on his present position.

“I am currently just thinking about how to be a successful governor,” Dedi told reporters last month when pressed on his 2029 prospects. “Now is not the time for that.”

As for Prabowo, while Gerindra elites have already publicly pushed him to run for a second term, the 75-year-old incumbent has so far refused to commit, stating repeatedly earlier this year that he would not run in 2029 if he felt his administration had underperformed.

Should Prabowo decide to run, Dedi has been touted by some observers as the president’s running mate. But Burhannudin said voter data suggested that such an alliance could fail.

“One complication is the emerging ‘anyone but Prabowo’ sentiment,” Burhanuddin explained.

“If Dedi becomes the running mate of an incumbent whose popularity has been declining significantly ... some voters who currently support Dedi could instead move towards Anies or Gibran,” he added, referring to former Jakarta governor Anies Baswedan and Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, both of whom are also seen as potential 2029 contenders.

“We should not assume that all Dedi supporters would automatically follow him into a Prabowo-Dedi ticket. Some may prefer Dedi precisely because they see him as an alternative to the incumbent.”

Nor can Gerindra sideline Dedi and order him to remain an obedient campaigner on Prabowo’s behalf without consequence, Burhanuddin said.

“The publicly available survey data suggest that, if Dedi is removed from the presidential-choice simulation, Anies and Gibran benefit more than Prabowo,” he added.

Another possibility is that Dedi could leave Gerindra to seek a ticket elsewhere.

This prospect has become plausible following a landmark Constitutional Court ruling last year that abolished the minimum requirement of 20 per cent of the vote for a political party before it could nominate a presidential candidate, which has opened a back door for popular independents to contest in an election for the top job.

“This significantly changes the strategic environment,” Burhanuddin said. “Other parties that lack a sufficiently popular presidential figure of their own may be interested in nominating Dedi for president.”

Dedi, however, faces the daunting task of sustaining his populist aura given the relentless public scrutiny. While his personal approval rating remains sky-high, his governance record is not without blemishes.

In June, the turbulent rollout of West Java’s public school admissions system left thousands of parents frustrated after their children failed to secure places at state schools, prompting Dedi to issue a public apology.

With West Java facing a projected 3.4-trillion-rupiah deficit, Dedi announced last month that he was halting all new provincial projects to avoid taking on massive debt.

The polling landscape, however, remains far from uniform. A nationwide survey conducted in late August by pollster Median offered a counterweight to earlier findings, placing Prabowo in the lead with 32.4 per cent support, followed by Dedi at 20.6 per cent and Anies at 20.5 per cent.

Three years is a long time in Indonesian politics, Burhanuddin warned, and early regional momentum can easily evaporate as the stakes rise.

“His current popularity is real, but sustaining it until 2029 will depend on whether his personal appeal can survive the much harder tests of governing performance, greater national scrutiny and the changing political environment.”
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/.summary: Dedi Mulyadi is one of Indonesia's most talked-about politicians. His primary YouTube channel has 9.2 million subscribers and generates tens of millions of views every month. Indians could choose Anies Baswedan and Gibran Rakabuming Raka as presidential candidates.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm79.title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm79.text:
US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat".

The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start.

In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team".

Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs."

He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat".

"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made.

"We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans.

The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible".

BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.

"We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend."

In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.

Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm79.summary: Ella Langley cancels sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night. Police say they could not find a credible threat at the venue. The 27-year-old singer made the decision two hours before the show was due to start.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgj.title: 'Stain on the country': Trump criticises Norway over Nobel Peace Prize
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgj.text:
US President Donald Trump has once again made complaints that he did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize, calling this year's decision "disgraceful and embarrassing".

The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay on Friday. Hours after the announcement, Donald Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of the "mystery person".

"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway" he said, adding "we will not forget".

Trump has been outspoken about his desire to win the prize, and made similar criticisms in 2025 when it was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.

Last year, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre explained to Trump it was an independent committee based in Norway, not the Norwegian government, which decides who will receive the prize.

Speaking to his supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York, the US president repeated claims that he had settled eight wars and was "about to settle or win two more", without providing evidence.

"The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation," he said.

Pillay, a former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge, was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

The South African's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes.

Shortly afterwards, the 85-year-old reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.

Last year, the president openly expressed his displeasure at missing out on the prize, with the White House accusing the committee of placing "politics over peace".

In January, Machado gifted her medal to Trump during a meeting at the White House, which she said was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.

Trump said on social media that the move was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".

The Nobel committee later clarified that the prize was not transferable.

"Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others," it said in a statement. "The decision is final and stands for all time."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgj.summary: Donald Trump has made similar complaints about the prize in the past. The US president has previously said he was "about to settle or win two more" The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3d.title: Flydubai attacker began a 'drift towards extremism and terrorism' in Australia, UAE says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3d.text:
The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say.

UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack".

He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.

Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification.

According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.

"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.

"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."

The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".

"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.

This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".

More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.

In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".

Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft.

Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.

Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.

He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.

Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3d.summary: UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi says pilot was inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US. He was also said to have been inspired by the 11 September terror attacks in 2001. He is also said in a report by UAE's state news agency Wam.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317.text:
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.

But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".

Both he and his country have denied any involvement.

Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.

There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.

Both have been inoperable ever since.

Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.

They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.

Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.

As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.

Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.

But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.

They went on following the forensic crumbs.

Eventually they led to Ukraine.

The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.

In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.

That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.

He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.

But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.

Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.

By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.

Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.

None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.

But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.

"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."

Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.

That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.

Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.

"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.

The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.

Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.

"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.

Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".

Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.

Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.

He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.

Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.

Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.

He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.

But he is a civilian.

Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.

In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".

As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."

Croatia is a different matter.

The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.

After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.

It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.

It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.

When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".

This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.

"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.

He argued that the Nord Stream pipelines had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed that to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.

"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."

Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.

Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.

Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.

He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.

His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.

They are not saying, though.

And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.

His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.

I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c317.summary: Serhii K will go on trial in Germany next week after his extradition to Germany. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure. Both he and his country have denied any involvement with Germany.
