https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Shaun Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?

Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.

The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.

By September, he had started to feel better and was on another work trip, this time to Poland. Asleep in his Warsaw hotel room, he was again woken by terrifying head pain, even worse than in London. He later described the sensation as “someone standing over me with a baseball bat and just repeatedly hitting me on the head”. It was a nine or 10 on the pain scale, he felt, worse than anything he could remember.

Two hours later, the same feeling returned, and he started to suspect that what was happening might not be an internal process but rather some external attack. He dragged himself off the bed and curled up on the floor, where the intense pain subsided somewhat. That was the last time he had the “attack” sensation, but he went on to suffer chronic nerve pain, fatigue and other severe health problems for years.

Sources described the man in question as a senior CIA officer who had recently been assigned an important job relating to worldwide operations against Russia. At the time, he was only vaguely aware of the stories that had emerged from Cuba two years previously, about US diplomats who believed they may have been attacked with a sonic weapon.

These incidents, in which people reported feeling a variety of unusual sounds, pressure and pain, followed by residual symptoms that could last for years, had acquired the name Havana syndrome, after the city where mass reports of the phenomenon first emerged.

Later, dozens of CIA officers around the world reported Havana syndrome episodes, which in official documents were called anomalous health incidents (AHIs). Many believed AHIs were the result of a Russian intelligence operation to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivered sonic or pulsed microwave energy.

There was sustained pushback against that theory. Some scientists insisted the idea of a portable weapon that could deliver these injuries belonged in the realm of science fiction. They said a whole range of conditions could cause pain, dizziness and cognitive issues.

Various experts suggested AHIs could be down to environmental factors, toxins or even the sound of chirping crickets. One explanation was that the symptoms were psychogenic and the result of “mass hysteria”, while some inside the CIA even accused those involved of faking their injuries in the hope of a medical payout. The disagreements over what was causing Havana syndrome led to bitter arguments and broken friendships at the spy agency.

In 2022, a panel of scientific experts convened by the US government concluded that “the signs and symptoms of AHIs are genuine and compelling” and “could be due to external stimuli”.

But the next year, a long-awaited report delivered the official assessment of the US intelligence community: “The available intelligence consistently points against the involvement of US adversaries in causing the reported incidents,” read an unclassified summary. It was “very unlikely” that a sinister Russian campaign was behind AHIs, it concluded.

Yet the mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die. This summer, the “very unlikely” assessment from 2023 was rescinded by Donald Trump’s outgoing director of national intelligence, who claimed it was based on flawed analysis.

Now, a decade after the first reports emerged from Havana, two CBS journalists who have covered the story from the start are to release a book that sets out the case for Russia being behind at least some of the episodes. It also accuses parts of the US government and intelligence community of covering up the evidence.

This article is based on early access to their findings, as well as on the Guardian’s own interviews with intelligence sources, AHI patients and scientists.

David Relman, the Stanford professor who led the official scientific panel on Havana syndrome in 2022, told the Guardian he believed there was a subset of AHI cases that were “most plausibly explained by exposure to pulsed microwave energy”.

His panel had access to patient records and to more than 1,000 classified documents on the topic. “To any reasonable person looking at all the evidence I was able to see, it inevitably leads to the conclusion that there may have been a cover-up,” he said.

Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados are longstanding producers for the CBS programme 60 Minutes. In an interview at the programme’s studios in midtown Manhattan, the pair recounted how they first came across the story a decade ago.

They covered the Obama administration’s policy of re-establishing diplomatic relations with Cuba in 2015, so when reports emerged the next year of a mysterious new condition afflicting employees at the reopened embassy in Havana, they contacted a senior US diplomat who had been posted there. “I expected him to say: ‘This is all bullshit,’” said Zill. “But he said: ‘Oh no, this is completely true. And I can put you in touch with a bunch of people who were hit.’”

The pair spoke to more than a dozen of them, off the record, but by the time they were ready to put a story together there were new reports of similar cases occurring among US diplomats stationed in China. Then there were whispers about it happening in other locations around the world.

Once the first 60 Minutes episodes devoted to the topic aired, victims started contacting the producers, keen to tell their stories. Many of these new sources were – or had been – undercover operatives for the CIA, meaning they could not speak openly as most details of their work were classified. But people stationed around the world who had not known each other told stories that seemed remarkably similar.

A pattern linked some of the key cases: the alleged victims were working, or had previously worked, on beats where they rubbed up against Russian interests.

In some cases, the location of the supposed hits was notable in itself: allies of Moscow where some part of the elite was looking to improve relations with the west. This was the case in Cuba, where the original cluster of cases had come during the Obama-era thaw in relations with the US, which had irritated hardliners in the Cuban regime and their backers in Moscow.

It was also the case in Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia and Vietnam. Several CIA officers who had been stationed in Kyiv around the time of the 2014 Maidan revolution in Ukraine, decried by the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as a US-backed coup, later suffered AHIs in different locations across the world.

“I went through years of doubts about the story, and all the crazy things we were hearing,” said Zill. But the more source meetings she and Rey had, the more they felt there really was something there. “We’re meeting these highly effective intelligence officers and they’re all telling versions of the same story,” said Rey.

The origins of Havana syndrome go back long before Cuba. A cornerstone case is that of Mike Beck, a counter-intelligence officer at the National Security Agency who got sick while on temporary assignment to an undisclosed location in the 1990s to check a US diplomatic facility for bugs.

Beck developed a rare form of Parkinson’s disease at the age of 45 and died this year. A declassified NSA statement, included in his 2014 workplace compensation claim, noted that “there is intelligence information from 2012 associating the hostile country to which Mr Beck travelled in the late 1990s with a high-powered microwave system weapon that may have the ability to weaken, intimidate or kill an enemy, over time, and without leaving evidence”. The unnamed “hostile country”, sources said, was Russia.

The first known AHIs among the contemporary batch of cases occurred in late 2014, when several US government employees at the consulate in Frankfurt, Germany, became ill. One was found unconscious in a consulate stairwell after feeling sudden, intense pressure on her chest and hearing a “high-pitched squeal”, Rey and Zill reported.

The next year, a researcher at a US defence institute – who asked the Guardian not to use her name – was on a tour of the Balkans, attending meetings with military officers from the host nations alongside US defence attaches. Her itinerary took in Montenegro, which was in the process of applying for Nato membership, and Serbia, a Russian ally that harboured resentments towards the US over the 1999 Nato bombing of Yugoslavia.

On her final evening in Belgrade, as she walked through lively pedestrianised streets to her hotel, the researcher was sure she spotted someone following her. Later, as she approached her hotel room, she felt “a sinking feeling, as though I was in a lift that was descending suddenly”, she recalled in a telephone interview.

Inside her room, she continued to feel odd sensations. “I just had this falling sensation, a feeling of gravity pulling at me, and nausea.” At one point, she turned on her government laptop and found the screen was flickering with blue static. The computer never worked again.

She said she was able to continue her trip, but in the subsequent weeks she felt weak, had difficulty speaking clearly and developed pain that felt “like a drill was going into my eye”. She was unable to focus at work. “I used up all my vacation, then my sick leave, then colleagues donated their leave. Eventually, I had to leave my job,” she said. It was only much later that she connected what had happened to her with reports about Havana syndrome.

The next cohort of AHI patients included people at the heart of a new CIA policy on Russia. In 2017, as Donald Trump took office for the first time, the agency launched a drive to push back against the increasingly brazen global reach of Moscow’s intelligence agencies.

“They wanted us to take the same kind of tactics and spirit we used in the global war on terror to the Russians,” said Marc Polymeropoulos, who was made deputy chief of operations for Europe and Eurasia in 2017. Polymeropoulos, who had spent most of his career in the Middle East, was one of several veterans of the “war on terror” who were moved to senior roles focused on Russia. Even as Trump publicly denied that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, the agency made plans to push back hard against Russian activity.

“Obviously, we didn’t have permission to run lethal operations against the Russians, but we could do things we hadn’t done as much previously, such as enlist the help of multiple friendly services and expose the Russians for what they were doing,” said Polymeropoulos, in an interview at a restaurant just outside Washington.

In early December 2017, Polymeropoulos and another senior CIA executive made a liaison trip to Moscow, to meet their counterparts in Russia’s SVR and FSB intelligence services. The official meetings were ill-tempered and lacking in substance. Late one night, Polymeropoulos woke up suddenly in his hotel room. “I had vertigo and a splitting headache. I thought it was food poisoning at first, I thought I was going to puke and crap my brains out, and I remember being like, holy shit, the room is spinning and my ears are ringing,” he said.

On his return to Washington, Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside, and with superiors who insisted his symptoms were unrelated to other AHIs. He saw a variety of doctors on his own time, but owing to the classified nature of his job he could not share details of where he had been when he became ill.

He left the CIA in 2019 and, frustrated at being stonewalled in his requests for medical assessment, became the first CIA officer to go public with a Havana syndrome story under their real name, telling the journalist Julia Ioffe about what happened in Moscow.

The resulting publicity prompted the CIA to send him to the Walter Reed military medical centre, where he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. In 2023 he was found eligible for compensation under the Havana Act, which authorised payments to “personnel who incur brain injuries from hostilities while on assignment”. The financial payout was modest, but he saw it as a moral victory after years of fighting for recognition.

One early theory was that AHIs could be the result of data collection attempts gone wrong – a machine designed to pull classified data from operatives’ electronic devices that had unfortunate side-effects when turned up too high. That is still seen by some as a possibility, although even if intelligence collection was the initial idea, the damaging health effects would have quickly become apparent to the operators.

Some observers insisted the whole concept of “Havana syndrome” was an invention. They asked why, if Russia possessed a brain-frying weapon, it was not using it on a wider range of its enemies. Why were there not more reports of collateral victims?

The sociologist Robert Bartholomew and the neurologist Robert Baloh co-authored a book that declared the whole story a hoax – “a case study in the social construction of mass psychogenic illness” – borne of high-stress work environments and propagated by excitable journalists.

Douglas Fields, a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claimed in a journal article that the medical studies of patients which showed cognitive changes had used unsound methodology, and that theories of an energy weapon “defy the laws of physics”. Reports of Havana syndrome should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster, he suggested.

Other scientists, including some who had reviewed patients’ medical records, strongly disagreed. “The early scepticism was perfectly appropriate, but over time we started to see an increase in the number of individuals who have gone through clinical evaluations that cannot be faked,” said James Giordano, a professor emeritus of neurology at Georgetown University Medical Center and the forensic neuroscientist on the original cohort of cases from Havana.

“We are talking about objective signs that are presenting with a very distinct pattern,” Giordano said. Key symptoms included “a profound tumbling or falling sensation” as well as pressure in the head, chest and throat, and cognitive effects. It was true that chemical or drug exposure could cause similar symptoms, he said, but this would be visible on blood tests. Another key factor was the sudden onset and the sense of a specific location where the apparent attack felt strongest.

When the Biden administration took office in 2021, the then CIA director, Bill Burns, and the director of national intelligence, Avril Haines, vowed to get to the bottom of the issue. Burns met many of the AHI cohort, including Polymeropoulos, listening carefully to their stories and promising them a full investigation.

Burns also fired the CIA’s chief medical officer, who had infuriated some AHI patients by accusing them of faking their symptoms. The same year, more than 100 CIA operatives and other US government officials reported AHIs in locations around the world. In Vienna, there were so many hits that the work of the CIA station was essentially paralysed and the station chief recalled. A spate of government employees also reported incidents on US soil, including several who claimed to have been hit on the grounds of the White House. Was this an adversary stepping up its campaign, or was the increasing publicity about AHIs leading more people to misidentify other conditions or episodes as Havana syndrome?

Burns and Haines launched two investigations, one to re-examine intelligence on whether a foreign adversary was behind Havana syndrome, and another that convened a panel of scientists and physicians to determine whether it was even possible for a weapon to cause the symptoms.

Relman, a Stanford professor who chaired the scientific panel, said its members were given access to open source and classified scientific studies into pulsed radio frequency energy, which suggested that the science behind there being a “device” that could cause AHI symptoms was plausible. Scientists who disagreed were simply unaware of the research into such technology that had been taking place for decades in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and then Russia, he said.

Regarding the medical results, Relman conceded that plenty – perhaps the vast majority – of AHI claims could be explained by other factors. But there were dozens of cases “that were unusual in the distinctness of their features and the near impossibility of explaining them based on known medical and environmental conditions”. In short: the publicity around AHIs may have prompted a wave of false reporting, but a core subset of cases seemed real.

Determining who may have carried out such attacks was beyond Relman’s purview. That fell to the second expert group, which in 2023 issued the assessment that it was “very unlikely” to be caused by a foreign adversary, dismaying many AHI patients who had hoped to finally receive closure on what caused their health problems.

Even people who have seen the intelligence on Havana syndrome can disagree on what it suggests. Two sources offered the Guardian radically different interpretations of what the classified data shows on possible Russian involvement.

One highlighted the lack of a “smoking gun”; a piece of human intelligence or an intercept that showed Russian operatives discussing a programme to use directed energy against Americans.

“Everyone has seen how strong our collection capabilities on Russia are,” the source said, referencing how US intelligence got hold of Putin’s war plans before his February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “If this was really a large-scale Russian programme, we would have expected to see something in some of these channels, but we didn’t.”

Another former intelligence official disagreed: “If you’re waiting for an intercept of someone saying: ‘My name is Igor and I’m going to press the button on my secret laser’ before you have confidence, that’s probably never going to happen. But for any reasonable person who has access to the intelligence and knows how to read it, the Russian fingerprints are clear.”

If that is the case, it raises the question of why the 2023 intelligence community assessment found it “very unlikely” that a foreign actor was involved. At the end of the Biden administration, a tweaked version said that while five US intelligence agencies still found it “very unlikely”, one agency now believed there was a “roughly even chance” that a foreign actor had used “a novel weapon or prototype device” in a number of attacks.

This summer, both of those Biden-era assessments were rescinded by Trump’s director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in a memo issued just before she left office. Gabbard said the earlier assessments were marred by “selective exclusion of evidence” and “mischaracterisation of sources”, though the statement did not release any new evidence or provide a revised assessment.

While Gabbard had a chequered reputation among the intelligence community, Mark Zaid, a lawyer who represents more than 30 AHI patients, welcomed her memo and said it was a first step to overturning a CIA cover-up. When asked why the CIA might have perpetrated such a cover-up, Zaid suggested it could be to protect its reputation after prior negligence. “This has built up to a level that the agency can’t let the truth get out because it’s going to reflect so poorly on them,” he said.

Burns, in a comment for Rey and Zill’s book, said it was “simply not true that there was a ‘cover-up’ by the CIA” and described the earlier investigation as “a rigorous effort across the entire intelligence community”.

Rey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years. “There’s not a single cigar-filled backroom meeting that led to decisions getting made,” said Rey. “There was a lot of, ‘This is a pain in the ass’ or ‘The president’s not going to want to hear this’. There was bureaucratic dysfunction, careerism and things that just got in the way of proper investigation.”

One example he gave is the fact that the FBI sent criminal investigators, rather than counterintelligence investigators with access to classified information, to Havana after the attacks there. Another is a nascent investigation at CIA headquarters in late 2019 which reportedly found that, in some cases, phones linked to Russian intelligence operatives had been in the vicinity of suspected Havana syndrome incidents. These included the hits that year on the senior CIA officer in London and Warsaw.

In London, a suspicious phone had supposedly been just 10 metres (30ft) away from his hotel room. But when the then CIA director, Gina Haspel, was briefed on these findings, she allegedly complained it was not solid enough to take to the president, given how sensitive he was on Russia-related matters. “The meeting abruptly ended after Haspel shouted that if she took reports like this to President Trump, she would be fired as director,” Rey and Zill write.

Outside the CIA, some have uncovered intriguing leads about possible links between Russian operatives and AHIs. Christo Grozev, a journalist and investigator who has exposed several Russian intelligence operations, claimed leaked travel data suggested at least four potential crossovers between suspected AHIs and travel by officers from Unit 29155 of Russia’s GRU military intelligence, known for its campaign of sabotage and assassinations in western countries. He also said he had traced travel by “members of what appears to be a technical unit adjacent to 29155” to Cuba during the initial attacks.

Perhaps the most significant piece of evidence to emerge recently has been the alleged US government acquisition of a “Havana syndrome-style device” in an undercover operation. First reported by the independent journalist Sasha Ingber this year, two sources confirmed to the Guardian that a device had been acquired and brought to the US in late 2024 for testing, after a purchase from a dark-web seller.

Rey and Zill’s book recounts a meeting with a person who claimed to be part of the undercover team that acquired the device. The source told them the device was “man-portable”, shot non-thermal pulsed microwaves and was acquired from “a complex Russian illicit network”.

It was not believed to have been used in a Havana syndrome incident, but testing on animals has reportedly shown it may cause similar symptoms to AHIs, which could prove that building such a device is scientifically possible.

That would make the case for a weapon being involved in some incidents more plausible, and would also raise new and worrying questions. If such weapons have proliferated to the extent that one can be bought on the dark web, how many devices could be out there and who may have access to them? Could AHIs thus have not one perpetrator, but many? And is there a future in which such weapons become a widespread element of warfare? “We know the technology has reached a level that enables it to be used in weaponisable ways,” said Giordano. “I see that as a clear and present threat.”

For those who have had symptoms for years, the acquisition of the device and the rescinded intelligence assessments provide some hope that, one day, they will receive official confirmation that they were targeted by a foreign adversary. For many of them, the lack of recognition at home has angered them more than the attack itself.

“The Russians are our enemy, I put them in the same bucket as al-Qaida or the Taliban, or any other groups I worked against,” said Polymeropoulos. “Do I want to see them held accountable? Of course. But I’m actually more upset and feel more of a betrayal from my own government.”

The Havana Syndrome by Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados is published by Crown Publishing in the US on 13 October and by WH Allen in the UK on 15 October.

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Create new pre-apprenticeship scheme to close youth unemployment gap, says Milburn
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
Exclusive: Former minister’s review warns that dramatic action is needed over huge drop in youth apprenticeship starts

A national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work, the government is to be told.

Alan Milburn, who is leading a major review into Britain’s youth jobs crisis, will call for a new “national pre-apprenticeship route” to offer young people further education, training and work experience.

Setting out the recommendation from his highly awaited final report – which has been delayed until after this month’s budget – the former Labour cabinet minister warned action was required to address a dramatic plunge in the number of youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.

Against a backdrop of soaring youth unemployment, as few as one in five apprenticeship starts currently go to a 16- to 18-year-old. The number of under-19s enrolling on an apprenticeship has also almost halved in a decade.

The detail comes as Andy Burnham’s government delays Milburn’s full recommendations until at least November, amid concerns in Downing Street that his report could sit uneasily alongside the 28 October budget.

A former minister in Tony Blair’s cabinet, Milburn has signalled that a shake-up of Britain’s benefits system would form a central plank of his report, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships.

In response, ministers are exploring plans for sweeping welfare changes, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have signalled readiness to stem the government’s rising benefits bill. Other senior Labour figures, including the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, have said there is both a moral case and an economic one to overhaul the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.

However, the government is taking a cautious approach to avoid provoking a repeat of the welfare rebellion which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.

Milburn’s review had been scheduled for launch next week.

Sources close to the review confirmed the delay, although downplayed its significance. One said that Downing Street was working to decide how to present the report alongside several other big reviews, including the Timms review into disability benefits, as well as the budget and the prime minister’s 10-year plan for government.

Burnham has promised to tackle the rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million at the top of his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships.

Currently, as few as 2% of people starting apprenticeships were previously Neet.

Presenting the details of his pre-apprenticeship plan, Milburn said his call for a new programme in England would be targeted at young people who lack the qualifications, confidence, workplace experience or routines needed to secure and sustain a full apprenticeship.

Delivered mainly through further education colleges, it would combine English and maths with technical learning and hands-on experience with an employer. The proposal would be similar to a one-year pre-vocational pathway in Austria that is designed to prepare young people for progression into apprenticeships.

Other countries with much lower Neet rates than the UK have placed much greater emphasis on vocational routes, including the Netherlands and Austria, where more than half of 15- to 19-year olds in upper-secondary education enrol in vocational programmes.

This month, the government announced an expansion in local apprenticeship services, backed by £100m of funding, in a programme delivered by regional mayors, across two years, to double the number of areas matching young people with local businesses.

Milburn said young people had been told for years to go and get an apprenticeship. “But for many young people there is a gap between leaving school and being ready for a full apprenticeship,” he added.

“They may need to improve their English or maths or get more experience of a workplace. And employers understandably want to know that someone is ready to turn up, learn the job and stick at it.

“I want a new national pre-apprenticeship route. A course done through colleges, combining English and maths, technical training and proper experience with an employer. Geared towards one thing: getting a young person into work.”

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.title: ‘Would I sit down with Tommy Robinson? It’s not a definite no’: lessons from people who fought the far right in the 70s, 80s and beyond
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.author: Sam Wollaston
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text:
Extremists are on the rise globally – but UK activists have seen them off in the past in everything from football, politics, music and more. How did they do it?

Tariq Mehmood encountered the far right early – at primary school. “When white children surround you in the playground and sing, ‘God made little black people, he made them in the night, he made them in a hurry, and forgot to paint them white’, and the school doesn’t clamp down on that, then you’re living within the far right. It’s not one organisation, it’s a mass movement.”

I think it’s likely those kids used another word for “black people” but I can’t quite find the stomach to ask. Mehmood is speaking to me on a video call from Beirut, where he teaches at the American University. Now 70, he migrated, in 1967, from Pakistan to Bradford, where his grandfather and uncles worked in the textile mills, and immediately experienced racism. “The headmaster would tell us to be grateful to be in England, we were beaten up by white boys on the way to school, there was an intense violence and a feeling of helplessness.”

Until he realised he wasn’t helpless, or alone. “We knew we couldn’t come to school on our own, so we assembled somewhere, got off the bus together and walked together to the classroom.”

Later, when he was himself working in a mill in Otley in the late 70s, Mehmood was one of the founders of the Bradford Asian Youth Movement. The AYMs were a network of anti-racist groups demanding equal rights and a fairer world as well as defending their communities against attacks from groups such as the National Front (NF) and the British Movement (BM).

Following disagreements within the AYM, Mehmood was part of a splinter group, the United Black Youth League, that broke away in 1981. “The police tried to paint that our split was because the UBYL wanted violence, but this is anything but the truth,” he says. “Some wanted to work within the system – one of the founders of the AYM became an MP, something I fundamentally disagreed with then as I do now.”

There were frequent attacks on the south Asian community in Bradford. “Whenever the National Front had a demonstration, you could always bet that after the pubs closed they would attack us, groups of skinheads – five, six, seven of them in a car, going around, seeing what they could do.”

So, as Mehmood had done at school, the UBYL organised themselves. “If you’re not organised, you get picked on. When you’re organised, often they will flee and you don’t have to fight. We couldn’t trust the police; either they were incapable, or they didn’t care, or they harassed us.”

When they learned that a lot of fascists were planning to go to Bradford, they got ready. “We mobilised hundreds, many of them white, walking around, making sure people knew we were out, they didn’t have anything to fear. We said we’d arm ourselves if need be. Some of us made petrol bombs.”

The petrol bombs require some context. “Remember, it was the year of the massacre of the teenagers in London,” he says, referring to the New Cross house fire in which 13 young black people died (even though it was never proved to have been a racist attack). “Members of the UBYL were blocking up their own letter boxes in case someone poured petrol in and set fire to their houses. That was a reality, and we said no, we will defend ourselves.”

In summer 1981, 12 members of the UBYL, including Mehmood, were arrested after a police raid discovered 38 milk bottles filled with petrol. The Bradford 12, as they became known, were charged with conspiracy to cause explosions and endanger lives. They didn’t deny making the molotov cocktails, but said it was a precaution for self-defence.

In jail, awaiting trial, Mehmood discovered another weapon: the pen. He wrote his first novel, Hand on the Sun, about a young immigrant experiencing racism. “Stories make us human. I wanted to share with future generations that we were proud industrial workers, we weren’t just going to have crumbs, we were politically conscious and had hope. I still have that hope.” After an active campaign and a lengthy trial, on 16 June 1982 Mehmood and the rest of the Bradford 12 – who had argued self-defence – were acquitted by a jury.

The situation with the far right is no better today, he says. In fact, the opposite: “The atmosphere is more vicious than it was in the 80s, primarily because we were dealing with old-style racism born out of British colonial history. Today’s Islamophobia is a more violent, virulent form; it has always been there, under the surface, since the Crusades, but not at a scale you see today. The far right at that time were a few thousand demonstrators here and there, not 100,000, half a million. And they’re not just in Britain, but across Europe.”

He sees it as a failure of the left, of the labour and trade union movements, to educate the white working class that “the real enemy is the billionaires at the top”. Plus, the loss of community organisations. Mehmood’s message about what to do about the far right today is to do as they did: organise and fight back. “The most important lesson is that if you believe there is an injustice, then fight against it.”

Tariq Mehmood’s memoir, Rebellion: Self-defence and the Story of the Bradford 12, is published by Daraja Press. A documentary, also titled Rebellion and co-directed by Mehmood, premieres at the BFI London film festival on October 14 and 15

It was half a century ago, the hot summer of 1976, but Red Saunders remembers it clearly. A photographer and at the time also a member of a radical theatre group, he was in a rehearsal at a studio in Soho, London. “Someone came in and said: ‘Have you seen this shit about Eric Clapton?’”

An article in a music magazine said that at a concert in Birmingham, the musician had told his audience to vote for Enoch “rivers of blood” Powell in order to stop Britain from becoming “a black colony”, as well as chanting the NF slogan: Keep Britain White.

“I was a Clapton fan, I’d been to his gigs, had the albums. I couldn’t believe it,” says Saunders, now 80 and talking to me from his Suffolk home. He wrote a letter to the music press, and got some of his like-minded friends, including Roger Huddle and Jo Wreford to sign it. The letter pointed out Clapton’s hypocrisy, that he was “rock music’s biggest colonialist” and that his own music had its roots in blues, R&B, reggae. And it concluded with a rallying call for musicians and fans to rise up: “Keep the faith, black and white unite and fight.” (Clapton later apologised and expressed deep shame for the ouburst.)

With that letter, Rock Against Racism was born. “The idea was that if we harnessed music and politics together, it might be a powerful combination to fight fascism and racism.” Music was the key, to get the youth on board. The first event was a gig with jazz singer Carol Grimes at a pub in Forest Gate, east London. “We chose the Princess Alice because it was in an area where the National Front were getting substantial votes in local elections,” says Saunders. He admits they were anxious about getting attacked by the NF or the violent neo-Nazis of the British Movement, so they got a bunch of dockers in as security.

In the end, it passed off without incident, apart from the usual disagreement with the pub over money. Rock Against Racism grew and grew from there, fighting racism through live music and putting black and white bands on stage throughout the country. Saunders remembers one gig especially, at the Polytechnic of Central London, featuring the reggae band Misty in Roots and the punk band Sham 69, a lot of whose fans were skinheads. In fact, Saunders says, although the band’s frontman Jimmy Pursey was strongly opposed to far-right politics, some people around the band were members of the British Movement.

Saunders remembers the tension backstage. “Misty had a reading of the King James Bible, while getting into the mood of their music and culture. And they played dominoes, in the most theatrically aggressive way, slapping down the dominoes hard, all directed at these fascists and skinheads standing around watching. It was electric, I thought at any second it was going to kick off.” Somehow the gunslinger tactics defused the situation and the gig ended with the two bands on stage together in a show of solidarity.

The gigs grew into full-scale carnivals, most famously one in London’s Victoria Park featuring the Clash, Steel Pulse, the Tom Robinson Band and more; it began as a march from Trafalgar Square and is thought to have been attended by 100,000 people. But the movement was just as much about small, grassroots responses around the country. Saunders remembers hearing from a kid in Aberystwyth. “She said she’d read my letter in the music press, and that one of her teachers was a Nazi, what could she do? I wrote back and said: ‘You are now Rock Against Racism Aberystwyth.’ When we next heard from her, she’d set up a club – all the local punk bands were playing.”

Saunders says the far right today, with their black balaclava brigades, are more frightening than ever. “The hypocrisy – saying they’re looking after women and children, then we find out many have been reported to police for domestic abuse.” His rallying cry is to recognise the far right for what they want and who they are, and to call them out for it. “They’re looking to rid Britain of black and brown people. They’re flat-out, 100% racists.”

You could say that in 1977 the NF and Tottenham Hotspur FC were heading in opposite directions. The NF, led by John Tyndall, was still on the rise, resurgent in elections for the Greater London Council. Spurs, meanwhile, were relegated to the old second division; the terraces at White Hart Lane weren’t a happy place. “When the team is doing bad, the community does bad,” says fan Richard Buckwell, who was in his mid-20s at the time, and is speaking to me today on a video call from Nottingham, where he now lives.

The NF campaigned and recruited in and around football. “I suppose it’s historically the leading leisure activity of white men,” says Buckwell. When Spurs were back on the up and signed the Argentinians Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, there was a lot animosity. Buckwell, who was active with the Anti Nazi League, and a few like-minded supporters, felt the opposite. “We handed out leaflets that said, ‘They’re welcome here’. And that’s what kicked off Spurs Against Nazis.”

It was launched with a public meeting, attended by about 60 people. In October 1978, they organised a five-a-side football tournament. “It was a huge event – we got 47 teams entering. Aswad participated, Bill Oddie played, Peter Cook came down and refereed.” Having the comedian Cook, a high-profile Spurs supporter, involved was helpful when the club initially tried to stop the use of its cockerel logo.

They printed T-shirts, made badges and banners, and handed out leaflets on match days, sometimes as the NF were doing the same. “I remember one day, leafleting outside the ground, suddenly seeing a load of youngsters running towards us. I thought, what on earth is happening? Is this the National Front?” But it was the opposite: they ran past to charge at and chase off the NF, who were campaigning behind. The message was getting across.

And the Football Fans Against Nazis message spread to other clubs: Leyton Orient, West Brom, Everton, Swansea City, Norwich, Arsenal. In all, about 11 clubs formed grassroots anti-fascist groups to counter the far-right infiltration of fanbases. The message even travelled abroad. “Some of our T-shirts got sent to the freedom fighters against white minority rule in what was then Rhodesia.” Buckwell still has a Spurs Against Nazis T-shirt, “for memory’s sake”. We’re joined on the call not by a Zimbabwean freedom fighter but by Buckwell’s wife, Jane, holding up this last surviving shirt. Plus, a nice cartoon of a footballer kicking a skinhead wearing an NF shirt into touch.

Buckwell remembers that when they saw NF graffiti, they used to alter it to read NF = No Fun. He says that anti-fascist campaigning – including by football fans – undoubtedly played a major part in the NF’s decline, though Tyndall and other members took its embers to ignite a new far-right flame in the British National party (BNP). Racism continued to rage, largely unchecked, through the football terraces, throughout the 80s.

And to this day it hasn’t been totally extinguished. “One thing that made a difference recently was taking the knee, which many clubs continued for a long time. And [former England manager] Gareth Southgate had a tremendous influence.” But campaigns, such as Kick It Out and Show Racism the Red Card, are underfunded, and he would like to see more support, from government and – particularly – from the clubs themselves. “They pay lip service. The amount of money swilling around the big clubs, they could do a lot more.”

At 74, Buckwell still fights the far right, working with Stand Up To Racism in Nottingham. He worries about Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (who goes by the name Tommy Robinson) and his lot. “It is frightening at the moment. But I went on the Together Alliance march, which was tremendous. Nottingham is very diverse and multicultural.”

On a summer evening in 1989, at what became known as the Battle of Welling, Matthew Collins changed sides. As a “troubled and troublesome youth” growing up in south-east London, he’d joined the NF as a teenager. “I was horrendously and viciously racist. I didn’t like what I saw around me.” He became the NF’s south London organiser.

In the mid-80s, the NF was becoming splintered and disorganised and Collins was also volunteering with the emerging BNP, rising to become its south London chair. The BNP opened a bookshop in Welling to distribute far-right material, and a group of concerned locals held a meeting at the library to discuss what to do about it.

Forty neo-Nazis – including Collins – stormed the building and attacked them. It was, he remembers, a bloodbath. Nine people were hospitalised. Most people at the meeting were women, of south Asian heritage. “I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence, people assaulting women in a library, and realised I’d been looking in the wrong places – this wasn’t the change I wanted.” Sickened, the following day he phoned the anti-fascist magazine Searchlight, and told them who had been involved. Collins had flipped; he was now an informant.

Over the next two and a half years or so, he continued his far-right activities but reported back to Searchlight, building up intelligence, warning of attacks, identifying people. It was incredibly stressful, and he would have been killed if he’d been found out, “particularly towards the end when Combat 18 [the security wing of the BNP] were around and it was all about shipping guns and drugs”. And he couldn’t tell anyone, not his family, not his girlfriend. “It was impossible, because you still have to live that life as a race hater.”

Collins took part in a World In Action TV exposé of Combat 18, blacked out and with his voice replaced, but because of what he said it still placed him in the firing line. When he got a visit from special branch, telling him they had intel that there was a threat against him, it was time to get out. Collins went to Australia for 10 years, where he worked in the rag trade and got married.

Now 54, Collins is back in the UK, working for Hope Not Hate, the advocacy group that campaigns against fascism and was an offshoot of Searchlight. He’s head of intelligence, meaning he now runs informants inside extreme organisations. He ran Robbie Mullen, the whistleblower who helped bring down extreme rightwing group National Action, a member of which was plotting to kill then Labour MP Rosie Cooper, and the subject of ITV drama The Walk-In (Stephen Graham played Collins).

He’s not going to tell me all the tricks of the trade, but basically they identify people who are disappointed and disaffected. “They have constant schisms and fallouts because the far right in this country is now completely driven by drugs and alcohol. You just pick and choose and you find someone and you put pressure on them.”

Collins wants to smash today’s far right. “Destroy, disorganise and disorientate. And one of the ways I do that is by finding the better-quality people and getting them out. We’re putting better-equipped and better-behaved people back into society.”

He divides the misery caused by the far right into two: “The misery of being in hock to them, ideologically, socially, culturally. And the misery of the people who live in fear of them, because they might get their windows broken or get beaten up.”

In the run-up to the 2010 general election, the far right were moving in on Jen Craft’s patch. “There were these, essentially, fascists not far from my home town and I wanted to do everything I could to stop them.”

Fortunately, she was in a position to do so. Craft (pictured page 23), born and raised in Thurrock in Essex, was working for the Labour MP, now peer, Margaret Hodge at the time, in Barking. The BNP had targeted the east London constituency as somewhere they could win. They’d done well there in the 2005 general election, and gained 12 council seats the following year.

Craft explains there was a lot of frustration in the area over lack of housing, drastically fewer jobs available with Ford in Dagenham, and rapid demographic change – from predominantly white working class to a significantly more mixed population. “It was a proper tinderbox.” A complacent local Labour party and council meant people “didn’t feel they had the ability to contact anyone or that politicians were on their side”.

The BNP were cleverer than the NF before them. “The way they approached people, they didn’t knock on your door and say, ‘You don’t like all these so-and-so people moving in, do you?’ They’d say, ‘That playground in the park looks a bit rundown, we’ll come and paint it. I bet you’ve not seen a politician in years, tell us what’s worrying you.’”

Craft, whose formative years had coincided with a Blair government and who saw herself as significantly left of him, knew what the BNP were all about. She believes they were targeting Hodge personally, “because she’s Jewish, and because she’d just lost her husband. They thought they could capitalise.”

Craft, who was 25 in 2010, ran Hodge’s campaign. “If you’re going to throw everything at defeating the far right, that’s a good time to do it – when you’ve no real responsibilities and can spend 80 hours a week going for it.”

How do you go about it? “If you knock on someone’s door and find they’re voting for the BNP and you say, ‘Did you know they’re a bunch of racists?’, what that person hears is you’re calling them a racist.” Nor did they begin with, “Hi, I’m from Labour … ” because, such was the mistrust, they would often end up with the door slammed in their faces. So they adopted tactics not unlike those of their opponents. “It was, ‘I’m out with your local team, what issues have you got, what can we fix? Not trying to convince them that our way of seeing the world is right, but just to open that door by saying, ‘We’re here, we’re listening, we’re on your side, how can we deliver for you?’” They organised coffee afternoons and street meetings to find out what it was people cared about.

Later, there was a bit of “Do you know who the BNP are?” And that was the approach in recruiting volunteers and building a campaign team. “This is who they are, this is the threat they pose, come and help us, because if they do win here, where are they going to go next? They won’t stop … ”

The BNP didn’t win. Though Labour lost nationally, in Barking Hodge increased her share of the vote, and the BNP were pushed into third place. It was a turning point for their support; the party fragmented, losing members to new parties emerging on the right, such as Ukip. “I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them,” says Craft.

After that, she became a civil servant, and took a break from politics for a while. In 2024, she stood for Labour in Thurrock, and won. Now an MP, we’re talking in her Westminster office. The incumbent Tory was beaten into third place, behind Reform’s candidate.

The same issues – migration, economic uncertainty and insecurity, disaffection with politics – mean that “in my area, those far-right messages are taking hold again”. The difference now is social media. “In Barking, it was analogue – letters, leaflets. We just had to have a faster printer than theirs, more things to put through doors and more boots on the ground. But the advent of social media means people can spread untruths and distortions very, very quickly – like net migration is rising or there are more small boat crossings, when actually it’s the opposite.”

Craft thinks that to fight the far right today, what’s mostly needed is more regulation of social media companies, and their owners. “Elon Musk wants us to turn against and fight one another. The fact we are not regulating against him is stepping away from our duty to keep this country safe.”

That’s going to be more effective than some tactics she sees. “If you go with a placard and shout, ‘Nazis!’, you probably feel good about yourself, but you’ve done nothing to fight them where it counts, which is at the ballot box.”

In the summer of 2024, after the murder of three girls at a dance class in Southport, misinformation and violence spread across the UK. Mobs smashed windows and cars, attempted to set fire to hotels housing asylum seekers and desecrated Muslim graves, while far-right keyboard warriors poured petrol on the flames from their sunloungers abroad.

On the night of 2 August in Liverpool, an angry crowd gathered outside the Abdullah Quilliam mosque, the oldest in the country. Against police advice, Adam Kelwick, one of the imams, crossed the road to talk to them. He took food – burgers and chips – and drinks. “You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach,” Kelwick says, on the phone from his Liverpool  home. There is a famous picture of Kelwick talking to one man in particular. “I spoke to him for five minutes, we connected, built some kind of relationship, call it a friendship if you like, then I gave the guy a hug.”

It takes two to hug. “So he had it inside him. After coming to the mosque to protest, he could reach out and hug me as well – the same people he was manifesting enmity towards.” Later, when it had quietened down and the cameras had gone, Kelwick sneaked him into the mosque. “I took him in, we walked around, and had an interesting conversation.”

Kelwick thinks “the vast majority of people you see at these protests are just genuine, regular people who’ve been dragged into something they might not understand fully”. Which is why conversation is important. “You have to engage, otherwise you’ll go further apart, then it’s easy to hold enmity and hostility.”

Since that time, Kelwick has been devoting energy to building these links. He tells me about a coach trip they had to north Wales soon afterwards – a bunch of families who’d attended the Liverpool Save Our Kids protest, which kicked off violently, along with families from the Muslim community. “We mixed everyone up together on two coaches; you should have seen the looks on the faces of the locals in north Wales when the doors opened and all these scousers got off along with some quite conservative-looking Muslim families. I think the academics call it contact theory – that you’re less likely to have negative feelings towards each other or uphold negative stereotypes if you have in-person interaction.”

The paranoia cuts both ways. “A lot of people in the Muslim community think everyone at these protests wants to hang, draw and quarter them – so I’ve been working with both sides.”

Kelwick travels a lot, and says the narrative – pushed and funded from above by far-right campaigns and individuals – is the same everywhere: “Immigration is bad, it’s an invasion of military-aged men, they don’t integrate, they’re committing all these crimes and raping our girls … it’s the same in the US, France, Germany, all across Europe.”

But Kelwick has faith in people. “We’re all human, bleed the same blood, have the same issues in life. It doesn’t matter how many billions are pumped into this, if you can facilitate genuine interactions between people from different communities, that has the ability to make these hugely funded efforts irrelevant.”

Would he sit down for a chat with Tommy Robinson himself, I wonder? “It’s not a definite no. I almost arranged to visit him when he was in prison. I think that would be the ideal meeting, without cameras, without anything to prove to anybody, just a genuine sit down where we don’t have to pull any publicity stunt – that would be beneficial.”

Discussion rather than debate is the aim. “I don’t like to be the attacker; it pushes people away. The whole purpose of having this interaction is to come closer. When you strip things down to a human level, that’s where beautiful things can happen. You can do that with every single person – even Tommy Robinson.” Over to you, Mr Yaxley-Lennon, the invitation is there. There might even be a hug in it for you.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Taiwan president says defence spending boost aims to ‘deter war’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te has said the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom” in a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office in Taipei.

Lai made the remarks on Saturday before thousands of people, including foreign diplomats.

“We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination,” he said. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war.”

Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital ahead of the speech.

The holiday marks the 115th anniversary of a 1911 uprising that toppled China’s last imperial dynasty and led to the founding of the Republic of China.

Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory, has never renounced the use of force to take it, and calls Lai a “separatist”.

Beijing has rebuffed his offers of talks.

Lai said China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait”.

Grey-zone tactics are actions that stop short of open war. “Peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” he added.

Lai’s government has set aside a record 1.1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($34.5bn) for defence in 2027, more than 3 percent of gross domestic product.

China held war games around the island shortly after Lai’s first National Day speech in 2024, but not last year. Its last drills near Taiwan were in late December, after news of an $11bn arms deal with Washington, the largest ever US weapons package for the island.

Lai said he welcomed talks between the United States and China, but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist”.

He urged democracies in the Indo-Pacific to join forces to preserve peace and stability in the region.

The US switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago but remains Taiwan’s most important security backer.

Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump.

In May, after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, Trump suggested arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, which set off alarm across the world.

Taiwan is now waiting for Trump to sign off on $14bn worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system.

The dispute dates back to China’s civil war, when the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after defeat by Mao Zedong’s communists.

The Republic of China remains the island’s formal name.

Lai made the remarks on Saturday before thousands of people, including foreign diplomats. The holiday marks the 115th anniversary of a 1911 uprising that toppled China’s last imperial dynasty.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to Philadelphia police
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Philadelphia police have revealed that Anthropic’s artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to authorities, an incident disclosed separately by the tech company.

The Philadelphia Police Department said on Friday that the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.

It called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”.

Anthropic mentioned the case in a Friday report detailing unsanctioned manipulation of government websites by Claude models.

It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appeared to communicate a false tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.

Philadelphia police said the tip “was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination”.

The department said it is disclosing the incident ahead of Anthropic’s report “in the interests of full government transparency and accountability”.

Anthropic disclosed the tip as part of a string of incidents involving websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved.

In reference to the tip to the Philadelphia police, the company said, “We shared this finding with the department on October 8 as soon as our technical review was complete.”

It shared more details about the incident: “In one case, tasked with generating example interactions with websites, Claude submitted an invented tip through a police department’s online form.”

The company added, “From the transcript, Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”

The company contrasted this with “the most serious incident from this summer,” in which “Claude’s misleading reasoning was sustained over hours and supported its continued attack”.

In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologised for the breach of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website.

Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ukraine-.title: The world needs Ukraine’s grain. Its farmers are running out of reasons to plant
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ukraine-.author: Jenni Reid
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ukraine-.text:
Ukraine’s harvest is strong, but farmers are being crushed by an export blockade.

The disruption now threatens future production. Farmers are scaling back corn and barley, shifting toward less logistically exposed oilseeds and niche crops.

The global risk runs in both directions: blocked Ukrainian and Russian supplies are supporting world crop prices today, but a ceasefire or reopened Black Sea route could unleash huge cheap stockpiles and swiftly push prices lower.

Ukraine’s harvest season is moving from wheat and barley into corn, soybeans and sunflower, and farmer Oleksandr Chumak has had a strong yield so far. That should be good news.

Instead, after 11 years of growing a range of crops in the Odesa region of southern Ukraine, Chumak has had enough.

Storage facilities across both Ukraine and Russia are filled with millions of tons of produce that would normally be sent to Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Africa — but are instead trapped in the warring countries.

Russian drone and missile hits on Black Sea targets intensified over the summer and into fall, making it impossible to insure commercial ships. Kyiv’s retaliatory attacks mean Russian exports are now also stuck, further squeezing global supply.

And with fatal Black Sea attacks continuing into October, prospects of a ceasefire look slim, even as Turkey ramps up efforts to broker a deal due to the risk to global food security.

Chumak says that around 80% of his grain cannot currently be sold at a profit, and he is out of cash.

A collapse in domestic prices is giving farmers like him little reason to sow for the 2027 crop in the coming months.

“For the farmers, it’s very difficult because we need to pay taxes, we need to pay rent for land, and now we are not able to do this because we are not able to sell anything,” said Andrii Dykun, chairman of the Ukrainian Agri Council.

“The only crops we are able to sell are rapeseeds and sunflower seeds. But still, the volume is not enough... So why should we plant if today we have no profits at all?”

“If our stocks will be full, it makes no sense to do any farm operations in the spring because then it’s just a waste of time and money.”

PrivatBank, Ukraine’s biggest lender, told CNBC that it had disbursed 1.53 billion hryvnia ($34.2 million) in working capital finance to agribusinesses between June and August, more than double the 718 million hryvnia lent in the same period last year. Small and medium-sized producers account for 70% of its agricultural loan book.

“Funds effectively remain tied up in grain inventories, while farms still need to cover their ongoing operating expenses and secure financing for the autumn and spring sowing campaigns,” said Yevhen Zaihraiev, chief corporate and SME business officer at state-owned PrivatBank.

“We are seeing different strategies among our clients. Some agricultural producers are selling their crops sooner, even at less attractive prices, in order to maintain sufficient operating liquidity. Others, particularly those with access to storage capacity, are postponing sales in anticipation of more favorable market prices,” he said by email.

Ukrainian production of grains and oilseeds is forecast to increase to 85 million tonnes from 80 million tonnes this year, but carry-over stocks from the previous season are pressuring Ukraine’s storage infrastructure and logistics, Zaihraiev noted. Those facilities include long plastic silobags snaking across fields and towering metal grain elevators that are themselves increasingly vulnerable to military strikes.

“We are also seeing agricultural producers gradually revise their planting plans for next year in favor of oilseeds and niche crops, whose prices are less dependent on logistics costs,” Zaihraiev added.

Farmer Oleksandr Chumak said he will follow that strategy, significantly scaling back planting for next year, avoiding corn and barley altogether, and instead opt for crops which require less fertilizer — which is also facing a global squeeze following amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Meanwhile, for Ukrainian farmers — those not currently being drafted to serve — the war with Russia is ever-present. “We are living and working in a place where any time you or your circle can be hit by [a] rocket or drone,” Chumak said by phone. “We are sleeping in beds with explosions 300 to 1,000 metres around.”

Ukraine’s agricultural sector has faced farm takeovers, mines and labor shortages ever since Russia’s full-scale assault began in early 2022. International bodies have struggled to preserve its export routes through various agreements, including the collapsed Black Sea initiative and the European Union’s politically contentious “Solidarity Lanes.”

Now, the situation inside the country and the consequences for global food chains are the most severe they have been since the war began.

Between them, Ukraine and Russia supplied the world with more than half of its sunflower oil, nearly a fifth of its barley and 14% of its wheat in the years leading up to the war, according to the UN. Ukraine is also one of the world’s biggest growers of corn, with China and the European Union among its biggest buyers.

Around 90% of Ukraine’s main agricultural exports typically run via the Black Sea. In August this year, its grain and legume exports totalled 981,000 tonnes, down about 58% year on year.

The risk is heightened by weakness elsewhere. Europe is expected to have a particularly poor corn harvest and needs larger imports just as its demand for feed remains high. The United States is also facing a weaker corn crop.

For now, better wheat and barley crops in Canada, Australia and Argentina, along with good harvests in the Middle East and North Africa, are cushioning the blow.

The continued blockage is supporting commodity prices outside of Russia and Ukraine, but the reopening of Black Sea ports would unleash a wave of cheap supply that would “flip the market fast... with little warning,” said Benoit Fayaud, senior manager for grains and oilseeds analysis at Expana.

A deal which restores Ukrainian and Russian exports could see grains prices in other origins decrease by a few dozen dollars, he told CNBC. “They have such big stocks it will be bearish for the market all over the world,” he added.

Prices for Russian and Ukrainian wheat, barley, oilseeds and other products have become so low within the countries that it has intensified the scramble to find alternative routes via rail, road and river, according to Fayaud.

But these alternative routes are “difficult and slow from both countries,” he said.

Ukraine’s Eastern European neighbors such as Poland and Romania are resisting a push to allow grain to transit through them — even temporarily — due to concerns about a glut destroying demand for their own crops.

Another option via the Danube river has been hampered by low water levels; and a key bridge out of Ukraine has been damaged. There are options to export via the Baltic states and through Georgia by land into the Middle East and Central Asia, but this can only cover a small portion of typical flows, Fayaud said.

Andrii Dykun of the Ukrainian Agri Council stressed that there was no alternative to the Black Sea routes when it came to pricing.

“It would always be cheaper for us, even for the farmers on the western border of Ukraine, to sell the grain to other ports from Black Sea ports because it’s much more profitable for the farmers than to sell it via the border to [the] EU,” he said.

“So without Black Sea ports, it will not work for us at all.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ukraine-.summary: Ukraine's harvest season is moving from wheat and barley into corn, soybeans and sunflower. The disruption now threatens future production. The United States is also facing a weaker corn crop.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/b.author: Luke Pentony
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Wallabies are quietly confident they can win their first Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park since 1986, as they take on the All Blacks.

Follow our live blog.

Not sure I've felt more excited for an international rugby game. Different feel about this one.

You're not alone Marlon!

As mentioned, it's been 40 years since the Wallabies tasted success against the All Blacks at Eden Park.

Here's a few thoughts ahead of tonight's Test:

This is the Wallabies best chance in many years. If they can’t break the hoodoo with this team then heaven knows when.

For those old enough, who can remember the last time the Wallabies beat the All Blacks at Eden Park in 1986?

Moments that stick out for me (yes, I'm that old) include:

What a day for Aussie rugby!

With Ruben Love and Richie Mo'unga sidelined, the All Blacks named Damian McKenzie at fly half.

McKenzie shifts from fullback to fly half, allowing Beauden Barrett to start at 15.

It's an indication of the enormous depth All Blacks coach Dave Rennie has at his disposal.

All three Barrett brothers will start against the Wallabies, with ex-captain Scott named at lock and Jordie slotting in the backline at inside centre.

The All Blacks were forced to make changes elsewhere as they play for the first time since losing 3-1 to the Springboks in Rugby's Greatest Rivalry.

The All Blacks' 23 is as follows:

The Wallabies have only made one forced change to their starting XV in the wake of their 42-38 victory over the Springboks in Perth a fortnight ago.

Reds centre Isaac Henry will start at outside centre following Hunter Paisami's suspension.

Len Ikitau, who starred in his preferred position at 13 against the Boks, will play inside centre.

Ikitau (ankle) was under an injury cloud but was passed fit for tonight's match.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss chose not to move Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back to the centres, instead keeping him on the wing.

The Wallabies' match-day squad is as follows:

11. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii

4. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto

2. Brandon Paenga-Amosa

18. Massimo De Lutiis

20. Nick Champion de Crespigny

Welcome to ABC Sport's coverage of the first Bledisloe  Cup Test at Eden Park.

I'm Luke Pentony and it's great to have you on board.

What a match we have ahead of us …

In the blue corner, the All Blacks have won their past 11 Tests against the Wallabies.

The All Blacks' last defeat to their trans-Tasman rival at Eden Park came in 1986, while they haven't been beaten at their spiritual home by any side since 1994.

The All Blacks have also held the Bledisloe Cup for the past 23 years.

In the red corner, the Wallabies are in a confident mood, having dispensed of the world champion Springboks in their last start.

They are unbeaten in their last six Tests and there's a feeling among their long-suffering fans they're about to snap their Eden Park drought.

But … we've been here before.

It's not the first time the Wallabies have run onto Eden Park in a buoyant mood, only to depart with their tails between their legs.

Is tonight the moment that all changes for the Wallabies?

We'll find out soon enough!
