https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Germany eyes joining GCAP fighter jet project with U.K, Italy and Japan
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
BERLIN – Germany is considering joining Japan, Britain and Italy in their joint project to develop a next-generation fighter jet, a government official suggested Friday.

This came after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday that Britain is positive on Germany’s participation in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP).

Steffen Meyer, first deputy spokesperson for the German government, said at a regular news conference Friday that the country took Burnham’s view very favorably.

Meanwhile, Meyer noted that Germany intends to pursue a European way of finding a solution to the development of a next-generation fighter jet, indicating that the country plans to assert its national interest during various discussions.

There has been mounting speculation that the founding GCAP countries could open the door to Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter program collapsed in June.

Burnham said the idea “is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan.”

GCAP has been set up to allow differing levels of involvement and it expanded for the first time in July, when Canada signed on as an observer, which could pave the way for deeper engagement in the future. Saudi Arabia has long been touted as another country interested in joining.

Germany is viewed by some defense experts as a suitable partner given its growing military budget and the fact that it already works on the Eurofighter Typhoon with the U.K. and Italy.

From Britain’s point of view, adding another country at a time when its military budget is under strain would help share the cost burden, but Japan may need convincing. Italy has also said in the past it would be open to new countries joining to help share the cost.

Japan is particularly focused on the 2035 target for the program given the security threat from China and the fact that it is due to start retiring its F-2 fighters in the middle of the next decade.

Some executives have warned that adding new partners could lead to delays. The GCAP is being led by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.

Asked Friday if Germany had inquired about joining GCAP, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi declined to comment, but noted the group’s thinking on the issue.

“To begin with, GCAP itself was developed with a view to fostering cooperation among Japan, the United Kingdom and Italy, as well as allies and partner nations,” Koizumi told a news conference. “Regarding cooperation with third countries, we intend to work in coordination with the U.K. and Italy to ensure that GCAP becomes an even better program.”
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Germany considering joining Japan, Britain and Italy in joint project to develop next-generation fighter jet. British PM Andy Burnham said Thursday that Britain is positive on Germany's participation in the Global Combat Air Program.

https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.title: South Korea: 38 injured as ceiling collapses during Daegu sales event
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.author: The Korea Times
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.text:
Shoppers fled after plaster finishing collapsed on the second floor of the building in the country’s southeast, fire officials said

According to local authorities and fire officials, the incident occurred at around 10.16am on the second floor of a four-storey building in Gwaneum-dong. At the time, a vendor was selling kitchenware and other goods to elderly customers when a section of the ceiling’s finishing material fell down.

All 66 people inside evacuated the building on their own following the collapse. A total of 38 people were reported to have sustained minor injuries, with nine transported to hospitals. None of the injuries are believed to be life-threatening.

Firefighters dispatched 14 vehicles and 60 personnel to conduct a search and implement safety measures at the scene. A thorough search following the evacuation revealed no additional casualties. Police also deployed officers around the site to manage traffic.

Built in 1994, the four-storey building previously housed a grocery store on the first floor, which had suspended operations in September. Authorities plan to investigate the exact cause and circumstances surrounding the collapse.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook also instructed the Ministry of the Interior and Safety and the National Fire Agency to mobilise all available equipment and personnel for rescue efforts. She also called on authorities to identify nearby medical facilities able to take in patients and swiftly transport anyone found injured, to minimise casualties.
https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/east-asia.summary: The incident occurred at around 10.16am on the second floor of a four-storey building in Gwaneum-dong. A vendor was selling kitchenware and other goods to elderly customers when a section of the ceiling’s finishing material fell down.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago -  why are they resuming now?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg.text:
They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.

By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.

That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.

The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.

That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.

The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed.

"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.

"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC.

He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.

"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.

It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in.

With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends".

Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.

The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."

But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"

Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.

Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US.

"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labeled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people."

"I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."

Vice-President JD Vance, a Catholic, has said he would not be watching the execution.

President Donald Trump dodged the question of whether he'd tune in himself - but confirmed he approved the decision to livestream Hasan's death.

"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: ‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Some say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambition

In the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate with Andy Burnham.

Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words in the cloud – and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”.

At a cabinet away day at Chequers on Monday and a meeting for special advisers on Thursday, the idea that the government was doing its best to improve people’s lives – despite the difficult economic backdrop – was a golden thread.

“The public think the only person that can reach those levers is you,” said a government insider. “They justifiably ask, can you do it or not? And if not, they’ll look for an alternative. We have to avoid the sense of things being out of our control.”

A party strategist said: “Voters don’t want us to put our hands up in despair; they want us to roll our sleeves up. They don’t want us to be helpless in the face of global stuff; they want answers.” But will this prime minister be able to provide them?

At conference, Burnham set out his big vision for the future – on social care and the pensions triple lock, the EU and electoral reform. The party faithful lapped it up and polling suggested the “Burnham bounce” had continued.

But while Labour MPs are relieved to have a leader with a clear political direction, many worry that offering big promises for after the next general election will not be enough to scratch the itch for dramatic change.

Downing Street believes part of the answer is what it describes as “everyday fixes” – cost of living measures that might not, on their own, amount to very much, but added up can make a difference and show the government is trying.

Overseen by the No 10 policy unit and the Cabinet Office’s cost of living taskforce, each department has “incubators” where proposals are dreamed up. Many are in the works, such as rules around car-parking apps and unbranded school uniforms.

They might not grab the media headlines, but strategists say they pick up engagement online, with 85m views across all social platforms last week alone. There will be more announced in the two-and-a-bit weeks running up to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.

“We want to show we can tackle the everyday frustrations that people assume are part of life,” one adviser said. But several admitted they had some qualms about the drumbeat of small interventions.

“We risk looking twee, frankly, if we aren’t successfully thinking about how to tie it to the bigger picture of structural change. Public control, tax, that is what we want to be able to point to as well as the everyday things.”

Another added: “We need to tread carefully. We have very small interventions now and huge ambitions for three years’ time. We also need medium-scale changes in the medium term, and that is what is missing at the moment.”

The government faces a difficult budget, with inflation and soaring borrowing costs as a result of the Iran war thought to have blown a £12bn hole in the public finances, forcing the chancellor to consider tax rises and spending cuts to fund plans to ease the cost of living.

The statement, which is expected to be “low key”, will focus on fiscal devolution, with a household support package centred on cutting energy bills and more help for small businesses. Next year’s spending review would require more revenue, sources said, but details would have to wait.

A No 10 aide said: “The budget is a moment of peak attention and potentially peak peril. We’re not able to do everything we want to, so we have to level with people and say we can’t fix everything all at once, but we’re trying.”

But for some MPs, there is a growing nervousness at the low level of ambition at this budget, especially on cost of living measures, which the Burnham government has made its main test.

One said: “If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we are screwed. As things stand, this looks like a Reeves budget with better vibes. I hope this isn’t all there is. But I really fear that actually it is.”

Treasury insiders acknowledge the need to “kickstart” longer-term changes at the budget – and that a “low-key” statement with the big decisions put off until next year may not be enough for the public. “The budget will be our first punch in the face moment,” a government aide said.

There was a “bit of friction” between the prime minister’s office and the Treasury over balancing fiscal responsibility with hope, the source added. “No 10 wants to signal intent: that we won’t get everything immediately, but we’ll get there.”

There were lingering questions about “how this all adds up when we’re under grey skies”, another adviser added. “It’s impossible to see how anyone can square the additional spending we need given the tightness of the fiscal envelope.”

Ministers and advisers are expecting a barrage of attacks from the Tories and Reform UK on welfare. But they believe the Milburn and Timms reviews, which will be published shortly after the budget – will help them fight back.

Downing Street expects the days after the budget to be “bumpy” but is optimistic that Burnham’s communication skills will help to make the case, and that the public will continue – for now – to give him the benefit of the doubt.

A source said: “We’ll take a bit of a hit over the budget. It’s going to be a tough couple of weeks. But then we have a run to the 10-year plan. If we get that right, we can potentially go into next year with people saying: ‘Yes, it’s difficult, but we trust this guy.’”

At the cabinet away day, Burnham told ministers: “Politics has become too suffocating. We need greater ambition. The country is not where it should be and nothing simple gets us out of that. We need to show a journey and a longer-term plan.”

Ministers were presented with polling that showed support for Labour’s social care policy, including adjusting the pensions triple lock, went up by a quarter after voters were shown a video of the prime minister explaining his plan.

A party strategist told them: “On social care and the triple lock we need to continually make the case, time after time. When we make the case we have the power to persuade.”

There is a political axiom that if you’re explaining, you’re losing. But Labour strategists are pushing back on that idea. The prevailing view inside government is that Burnham is the only one who can go out and make the case – on all of his big promises – to the country.

Not everybody inside the party thinks it will work. “I don’t know how convinced I am about giving people essentially the same message as before: we want to do more but we’re constrained,” one insider said.

But ministers hope that by focusing on policies which signal intent, they can get through these difficult months. “We need more time to lean into the big things we can do, like public control, but we need to be honest with voters. We set ourselves a target of tackling the cost of living, but so many things are out of our control.”

No 10 insight work shows that people were still prepared to accept the Iran conflict as an explanation for why things are so tough, rather than viewing it as an excuse. At the away day, Healey told his colleagues: “We are recognising those pressures, being honest about what we can do and taking practical action wherever possible to give people some breathing space at the budget.”

When parliament returns after conference recess on Monday, Burnham will give a statement, updating MPs on the past few weeks and taking questions. Throughout, he will aim to show the public he is on their side.

But one senior Labour figure cautioned: “We all hope that he has a plan for what comes next. The sense that he gets it and that he’ll keep trying won’t last for ever.”

On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. Book tickets here or at guardian.live
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Downing Street expects the days after the budget to be 'bumpy' But Burnham's communication skills will help make the case, they say.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: UK accused of giving people of Gaza false hope over new refugee safe route
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Only ‘very small number’ of people already in Lebanon or Jordan will be referred, says organisation running scheme

The Home Office is facing claims it gave false hope to the people of Gaza after it emerged that a new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced the reopening of a resettlement scheme for refugees at Labour’s annual conference last month. A statement from her department said: “Around one in four referrals will be for Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, fleeing war and persecution.”

But the body administering the scheme has confirmed it would only refer “a very small number of extremely urgent cases”, all of which would be processed in Jordan and Lebanon.

The umbrella alliance Communities for Palestinians (CFP) said this crucial detail was not in Mahmood’s speech or subsequent Home Office statements, giving people in Gaza and their supporters the belief that they could also apply.

Vicky Moller, a co-founder of CFP, said: “The applause at Shabana’s announcement at conference was at the prospect of a resettlement scheme for Palestinians fleeing war and persecution. People understood that would mean rescuing people from Gaza.”

The Home Office has pushed back at the claims, saying the UK resettlement scheme that Mahmood has reopened has always been for people from outside their country of origin.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “To qualify for refugee status under international frameworks, individuals must be outside their country of origin.

“Palestinians who remain in Gaza would not initially be in scope for these routes. However, Palestinians who have fled Gaza could be referred to the UK through the International Refugee Assistance Project [Irap].”

Restrictions on eligibility for the scheme emerged after an exchange of emails between the CFP and Irap, which has been tasked with making referrals.

According to Irap’s website, it will refer “a very small number of extremely urgent humanitarian cases to the UK for consideration for resettlement”, adding: “These cases will be referred to Irap by humanitarian organisations in Jordan and Lebanon and Irap will then hold interviews to determine if these cases can be referred to the UK government.”

The programme focuses on “extremely vulnerable refugees whose lives have become unsustainable in Jordan or Lebanon”.

The non-profit’s website added: “Irap does not know how many people the UK government will accept under the Palestinian resettlement programme. This is ultimately a decision for the UK government and depends on funding as well as local authorities’ capacity.”

Other safe and legal routes administered by the UK have allowed small numbers of people to enter the UK from their country of origin, including previous schemes for Afghan refugees.

Palestinian refugees fall outside the remit of the refugee convention and UNHCR.

Unrwa was instead set up to serve Palestinian refugees who were defined as any person whose “normal place of residence was Palestine during the period 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948 and who lost both home and means of livelihood as a result of the 1948 conflict”.

As a result, Palestinian refugees live in what refugee charities and NGOs refer to as Palestine – in other words, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip – as well as second countries such as Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.

Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said ministers should recognise the particular circumstances that meant Palestinians could be refugees while living in their own country.

“The government is right to commit to safe and legal routes. They provide a vital way for refugees to reach safety without having to put their lives in the hands of smuggling gangs,” he said.

“But the warm words have to be accompanied by ambition, and that means supporting people in the thousands, not the hundreds. They must also recognise the particular circumstances of Palestinian refugees and be accessible to them no matter where they are in the world.”

A renowned expert in asylum systems has said resettlement programmes are usually designed as a solution for people who have already left their own country.

Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the UK government’s safe and legal route was always going to mean taking Palestinians from neighbouring states such as Egypt, Jordan or Lebanon.

“The Syrian scheme worked the same way: the roughly 20,000 people resettled to the UK between 2014 and 2021 all came from countries around Syria, with nobody to my knowledge being flown directly from Syria,” he said.

“Bringing people directly out of Gaza would be a different kind of programme, closer to an emergency evacuation … And crucially, such an emergency evacuation in Gaza would depend on Israel and Egypt letting people leave and on the Home Office finding a way to do security and biometric checks with no visa centre in Gaza.”
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Home Office facing claims it gave false hope to people of Gaza after it emerged new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan. Home Office has pushed back at the claims, saying the UK resettlement scheme has always been for people from outside their country of origin.

https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.title: UK savings: 5% interest rate deals may not last, say experts
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.author: Rupert Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.text:
Competition is hotting up, with National Savings & Investments lifting rates to the highest in years

National Savings and Investments (NS&I) has increased the returns on some of its accounts, with many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.

Competition in the savings market has been growing, leading to some of the highest interest rates for years.

However, in the current climate, attractive deals do not always hang around for long, says Rachel Springall at the financial data website Moneyfactscompare.co.uk. If a provider attracts enough savings cash it will pull a product from sale.

NS&I has upped the rates on its “British savings bonds”, which are rebadged versions of its guaranteed growth bonds and guaranteed income bonds. They offer a fixed interest rate over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.

The deals are available to new customers and those with existing accounts that are maturing. With the growth version, interest is added each year and paid when the bond matures, while with the income version, interest is paid monthly.

Looking at the growth bonds, the new interest rate on the one-year product is 4.99% (up from 4.82%), while the two-year rate has risen to 5.07% (was 4.81%). The three-year rate has gone up from 4.83% to 5.1%, while the five-year rate has been increased to 5.17% (was 4.85%).

Those are pretty competitive rates, though as Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the advice firm AJ Bell, says, “you can still make more money elsewhere”.

At the time of writing, the top-paying one-year fixed-rate bond was paying 5.12%, while the highest-paying five-year fixed bond was offering 5.37%. But getting the very highest rates sometimes means signing up with less-well-known names. The one-year deal is from Union Bank of India (UK), while the five-year version hails from GB Bank.

If you have a very large sum that you need to stash somewhere – for example, the proceeds of a house sale or an inheritance – these NS&I bonds have one big thing in their favour: you can invest up to £1m per person in each bond issue. The minimum investment is £500.

As NS&I says, “most banks only guarantee your savings up to £120,000,” whereas it is backed by the Treasury and is “the only provider that secures 100% of your savings above this amount”.

Also, it means you are putting your money into the government’s savings bank, and “your savings will be invested back into supporting the UK”.

Money invested in NS&I’s British savings bonds cannot be withdrawn before the end of the fixed term.

That will not suit everyone, and it is a good idea to keep some money in a high-paying easy access account to cover things such as unexpected bills. Earlier this month the digital bank Starling announced that people who sign up for its Easy Saver account will enjoy a table-topping 5% interest rate. This account offers unlimited penalty-free withdrawals, but that rate (made up of a 2.5% variable standard rate, plus a 2.5% fixed interest bonus lasting for six months) only applies to those who open, or have opened, a Starling current account on or after 1 October. The rate applies on balances of up to £25,000.

Starling customers who signed up before then can benefit from a 4% rate when opening a new Easy Saver. That includes a 1.5% fixed interest bonus for six months.

Meanwhile, the savings provider Marcus by Goldman Sachs this week upped the interest rate on its one-year fixed-rate savings account from 4.3% to 4.75%.
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.summary: National Savings & Investments has increased the returns on some of its accounts. Many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: US hosts ‘productive’ trilateral talks to end Russia-Ukraine war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
United States, Ukrainian and European officials have met in Miami, Florida, to discuss a proposal for ⁠ending the Russia-Ukraine war, US envoy Steve Witkoff said in a statement posted to X.

Witkoff said on Friday that “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace”.

Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO”.

The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict”, Witkoff said.

He also noted the “productive” talks discussed “Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday the conflict had reached a dangerous “stalemate”, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.

“The other way that stalemates end is through escalation,” Rubio told reporters, warning that the conflict could spread to neighbouring NATO countries.

Earlier on Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin told US President Donald Trump that the resumption of talks with Ukraine is unlikely, citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month.

The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on civilian buses in eastern Ukraine that killed 33 people. Authorities said the attack was the single deadliest attack this year.

The ongoing talks have been overshadowed by the US-Russia diesel deal on Friday. Trump blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for surging diesel prices.

The deal was criticised by US lawmakers, Zelenskyy and European allies.

Zelenskyy called the agreement a “gift to Putin”. Hours after the deal, a Ukrainian drone hit a Russian fuel site.

The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Israel’s economy prospers despite years of war, but prices worry voters
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.author: John Power
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
After three years of Israel’s multi-front war in the Middle East, it would be no surprise if this month’s Knesset elections were taking place against the backdrop of an economy in dire straits.

Instead, Israel’s economy is – by many measures – flourishing.

After slowing sharply in the initial aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel has rebounded to become one of the fastest-growing advanced economies in recent years.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025, picking up from a 1 percent expansion in 2024, and 3.2 percent in the first half of this year, according to government figures.

The Bank of Israel has forecast 4 percent growth for the whole of 2026 and 5.5 percent growth in 2027 – projections that far exceed the outlooks for major economies such as the United States, United Kingdom, France, Canada, and Japan.

Over the past three years, the shekel has strengthened against the US dollar, hitting a three-decade high in May, and Israel’s stock market has surged, with the benchmark TA-125 up more than 110 percent.

Meanwhile, unemployment stands at 2.8 percent, while inflation is modest at 1.5 percent.

Against this relatively rosy economic backdrop, campaigning for the October 27 election has been dominated by national security, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, and retired general Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar, each claiming to be most qualified to keep Israelis safe.

Driving Israel’s striking economic resilience has been a booming tech sector largely insulated from its conflicts spanning Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran and Yemen.

Despite being on a war footing since October 2023, Israel has attracted record levels of investment in tech, the driver of about one-fifth of economic activity, amid the frenetic global rollout of artificial intelligence (AI).

Total direct foreign investment hit a record $26.2bn last year, up 78 percent from 2024, led by US tech giants Alphabet and Palo Alto Networks’ record-breaking acquisitions of Israeli cybersecurity firms Wiz and CyberArk, respectively.

Foreign capital has continued to flood into the country this year, with inflows reaching a quarterly record of $14.1bn in the January-March period, according to government figures.

Along with prospering from the global AI boom, Israel’s tech scene has benefitted from its close ties to the local defence sector, which has ramped up orders from hundreds of startups supplying everything from radar systems to communications platforms and anti-drone technology.

While Israel’s economy has bounced back in part due to robust employment and wage growth, its resilience is primarily an “export-driven story that reflects strong global technology demand, particularly in areas where Israel – and multinational firms operating from Israel – is globally competitive, such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence,” said Keren Uziyel, a senior analyst for the Middle East and Africa at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU).

“Interest in Israel’s technology goods and services is driving high levels of FDI and venture capital fundraising, and boosting the capital markets, which in turn is having significant wealth effects and boosting government revenue,” Uziyel told Al Jazeera.

But Israel’s military campaigns have come at an enormous cost to the public purse.

In March, the Bank of Israel estimated that Israel’s war costs to date had reached approximately 350 billion shekels ($114.6bn) – a figure not including the then recently-launched Iran war.

Military expenditures are on track to rise substantially in the coming years as Israeli leaders double down on “national security”.

Netanyahu, whose right-wing coalition has cast security as “the foundation of everything else”, has pushed to raise the annual defence budget to 183 billion shekels ($60bn), equivalent to roughly 9 percent of GDP.

If passed, the budget would raise military spending by two and a half times what it was before October 7.

Outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid has backed an expanded defence budget, but has clashed with Netanyahu about how to fund it.

Though security has dominated the run-up to the election, opinion polling suggests that Israelis also view the economy as a key concern.

In an opinion poll released by the Israel Democracy Institute last month, 38 percent of Jewish Israelis and 46 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up about 20 percent of the population – chose the economy and the cost of living as the most important or second-most important election issue.

Israel’s high cost of living, in particular, has long been a source of public discontent.

Israel has for years ranked among the most expensive countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a dynamic economists attribute to the country’s limited trade relations with its neighbours and cumbersome regulations.

Though Israel’s overall rate of inflation has been modest, food prices have risen at a faster pace, increasing 8 percent between the start of 2024 and mid-2026, according to consumer advocacy group Lobby 99.

“People are worried about the economy but not so much about the macroeconomic situation, more so on their personal perspectives, especially cost of living,” Ayal Kimhi, vice president of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research in Tel Aviv, told Al Jazeera.

“However, the security situation dominates the public discourse for obvious reasons, so I do not think the economy will play a major role in the vote,” Kimhi said.

“Some parties do not even bother presenting a vision or an agenda,” he added.

“Other parties do not differ much about economic issues.”

While Israel’s headline economic figures are impressive, they come with caveats attached.

Economists note that while Israel’s economy has grown much faster than its peers, GDP has been boosted in part by the country’s usually high population growth, which has averaged nearly 2 percent over the past decade.

Israel’s growth trajectory has also taken a hit despite the expansion, with the Bank of Israel estimating an accumulated loss of output through the end of 2025 equivalent to 8.6 percent of annual GDP.

Joseph Zeira, a professor of economics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said the country’s economic performance has “not been great at all” considering that growth has consistently lagged the pre-conflict trend since late 2023.

“Actual living standards depend on the area,” Zeira told Al Jazeera, adding that Israelis are grappling with “higher prices, or rather lower real wages and incomes”, and deteriorating public services.

“The only improvement is some decline in housing prices due to a vast wave of construction in recent years,” he said.

The long-term health of Israel’s public finances is another concern.

While Israel’s debt-to-GDP ratio of about 68 is far below that of peers such as the US, the UK, France, and Italy, the gap between government revenue and spending has grown rapidly over the past three years.

In its latest annual report, the Bank of Israel said it was “essential” for the government to “restore orderly budgetary processes” and implement “credible measures” to reduce the public debt.

Other long-term challenges include boosting labour participation among ultra-Orthodox Jewish men – whose refusal to do military service has become a major election issue – and Arab women (among Palestinian citizens of Israel), both of whom are employed at much lower rates than the general population.

“The cost of the military campaigns and mobilisation has severely strained public finances,” Omer Moav, a professor of economics at the University of Warwick and at Reichman University, told Al Jazeera.

“Deficits and national debt have expanded significantly, making current spending trajectories unsustainable without fiscal consolidation,” Moav said.

“The next government is facing a huge challenge.”

Regardless of who prevails in the election, economists say, Israel’s economic prospects will in large part hinge on whether conflict in the region escalates or subsides.

“We expect growth to reach around 4 percent in 2026 and to exceed this level in 2027,” said Uziyel, the EIU analyst.

“However, significant downside risks to growth remain should conflicts in Gaza, Iran, or on the Lebanon front resume.”

“The outlook depends greatly on the security situation,” said Kimhi of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research.

“If we are able to put an end to the war and reduce military spending, the future could be bright.”

Nick Dal Santo ended his time as St Kilda's AFLW coach with a win. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

St Kilda gave departing AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo the perfect send-off with a drought-breaking two-point home win over Collingwood.

With the bottom-of-the-table Saints holding a 0-8 record, Dal Santo announced on Friday he was standing down and took charge of the team for the final time in Saturday's game at Moorabbin Oval.

After scoring just one point last week and tallying five behinds in the first half on Saturday, the Saints kicked five second-half goals on their way to a 5.9 (39 ) to 5.7 (37) win.

It came down to the wire 👀

Relive the last two minutes of #AFLWSaintsPies. pic.twitter.com/pHX4RFB7YE

Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw kicked two goals and Tyanna Smith bagged 25 touches and 12 clearances for the Saints, who ended an 11-match losing streak stretching back almost a full year.

Collingwood (1-8) kicked the only two goals of the first half, the first to captain Ruby Schleicher, who later came off the ground with an injury to her right shoulder.

The other major went to Sabrina Frederick in her 100th AFLW game, as Collingwood stretched a two-point lead after a goalless first quarter to 12 at half-time.

The victory was St Kilda's first of the AFLW season. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

With the wind at their backs, the Saints rallied In the third quarter, kicking three straight goals and four for the term to lead by 10 points at the last change.

Ashley Centra, who gathered 25 touches for the Pies, kicked a goal in the final 30 seconds to cut the gap to two points, but the Saints held on.

"I understand this is my last game, but that was a really good game by the girls. I thought we fought really hard," Dal Santo told Fox and Kayo.

"I'm really proud of this group. It's been a delight and I'm really grateful for being a part of their journeys.

"I've loved it. Five years and the time is right," added Dal Santo, who finished with a 23-39 win-loss record.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/o.author: Catherine James, Lucy Thackray, and Samuel O'Brien
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Arts Festivals

Fans celebrate at Narromine’s Dolly Parton Festival

An outback town has traded its 9 to 5 farm tools and workwear for a day of bedazzled country glam and platinum-blonde bouffants inspired by megastar Dolly Parton.

The 3,500-resident town of Narromine in western NSW transformed into "Dollymine" for its annual October festival which celebrates the country music icon, who died in August at the age of 80.

"So this is Dollymine — not Narromine — for the weekend," attendee Juanita Peardon said.

Narromine has tuned into "Dollymine" for the annual festival this weekend. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

A record number of visitors were urged to leave their frown at the updated town sign for this year's event.

Along the streets of "Dollymine", a sea of pink and bejewelled coats of many colours, sweet lovin' friends and wayfaring strangers gathered to say in their own way "I Will Always Love You" to the Queen of Country.

Festival organiser Skye Rush said she has been blown away by the support this year.

"It's been great; locals have come out in force and all the visitors have come out in force as well," she said.

"Our shops are being used, our accommodation is being used, [the event] fills the town with people."

Skye Rush said the event is the largest it has ever been. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

The festival began in 2022, run by a volunteer committee of die-hard Dolly fans.

It faced funding challenges, and was cancelled in 2024, before being rescued by a $150,000 state government grant and a boost from the local council.

Ms Rush said the event has always been about celebrating Parton's legacy, even before she died in August.

"We're a small town and we support our locals."

Aunty Ruth said Dolly Parton had a strong connection to country. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

Narromine Elder Aunty Ruth said Dolly Parton represents a lot to the town.

"Why wouldn't you celebrate such a beautiful person?" she said.

"To me country is country, and to be on the land; if country music's part of the land, that's where we are going to be."

The town is five and a half hours north-west of Sydney, but the remote location has not stopped people from all over the country from coming to celebrate.

Best-dressed judge Dolly Delicious, travelled to the event from Canberra and has attended all five festivals.

He said Dolly Parton's death in August has not put a dampener on celebrations.

"I'm a bit sad but I'm actually really excited to celebrate her ... all her music, all her looks," he said.

Dolly Delicious and Juanita Peardon have been attending the event for many years. (ABC Western Plains: Lucy Thackray)

Sam and Amber Bloem got married last week and sang Parton's 1982 duet Islands in the Stream at their reception instead of a first dance.

"We love Dolly so we had to stop in," Amber said.

"[There's] lots of pink and sparkles ... fantastic music; it' s just lovely."

Sam (left) and Amber Bloem signed their two children Archie and Jack up to Parton's Imagination Library when they were born. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

The Bourke locals said it was especially important to celebrate Dolly's legacy this year, including her efforts to promote literacy in children.

"Our kids were part of her Imagination Library, so they've been getting books sent from her every month since they've been born," Amber said.

Johnny Gilmore says he has loved the community spirit in Narromine. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

For Johnny Gilmore, supporting regional towns like Narromine has also been a motivator.

"We always like to support country towns and we love the music, so we always come out and try to support the town and have some fun," he said.

"I love her music; everything from the 70s and 80s is always wonderful."

The 10-team men's Rugby League World Cup kicks off on Thursday night.  (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

The Rugby League World Cup was officially launched on Saturday with representatives from all 10 men's teams and eight women's teams.

Samoa captain Junior Paulo hopes those in his side who lost last week's NRL Grand Final can use their pain to propel the Toa to a repeat of 2022, when they made the final.

The men's tournament kicks off on Thursday night while the women's edition begins on Friday afternoon.

Junior Paulo knows what it feels like to pull yourself from the depths of grand final misery and glowingly represent your country at a Rugby League World Cup weeks later.

So he is happy to lend a helping hand to his Samoa teammates who are suffering similar heartache.

Parramatta's Paulo had big dreams of winning the NRL grand final in 2022, but they shattered when the forward's side suffered a 28-12 loss to Penrith in the decider.

He had to forge on, and weeks later found himself leading Samoa in a historic World Cup final against Australia.

Paulo will lead Samoa for the second tournament in a row.  (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Paulo will be looking to repeat the dose this time around after the tournament was officially launched at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday.

Samoa are one of 10 men's teams vying for glory, beginning when Australia face New Zealand on Thursday night, while eight teams will make up the women's tournament that starts with the Jillaroos taking on Samoa in Parramatta the following evening.

This year, four of Samoa's players — Newcastle winger Greg Marzhew, prop Pasami Saulo, and second-rowers Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen — will be feeling a similar pain to Paulo's back in 2022.

The Knights quartet lost to the Sydney Roosters in the grand final last Sunday.

"I was in the same shoes, losing to Penrith and then [having to play in the] World Cup," Samoa co-captain Paulo said.

"All you want to do is … be able to turn it around.

"So for them [Manuleleua and McEwen], they're eager to get back out and play some footy. Hopefully it means they bring the physicality that they do.

"It's time for us to bring them up to being ready to represent Samoa, but also making it enjoyable for them."

Regardless, Paulo cannot wait to lead a star-studded Samoan side when they begin their campaign next Friday against France before facing Papua New Guinea and Tonga.

The men's and women's tournaments will kick off next week.  (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

All eyes are sure to be fixed on star half Jarome Luai after a headline-riddled season where he was announced as the first official signing for the PNG Chiefs from 2028 before later being released by Wests Tigers to join Parramatta for 2027.

"He's [been] just a bit misunderstood by many towards the back end of the year. People were very opinionated about him," said Paulo of his co-captain.

"He's locked in, putting his best foot forward and representing Samoa. He enjoys being in these camps, and you can just tell how locked in he is by the first day we got into camp.

"[I] just want to see him evolve as a leader, and grow into the leader he is now. All the boys will be backing him, and luckily, nothing fazes Romey [Luai] too much."

In the lead-up to the tournament, some members of the team also spent some time in Samoa, which Paulo said was an "indescribable" feeling as it reminded the players they are embarking on something for more than themselves.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.title: Hong Kong to expand community recycling after shelving waste-charging scheme
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.author: Cannix Yau
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.text:
Environment chief Tse Chin-wan also pledges review of permitted profit levels of city’s two power companies

Hong Kong will strengthen its community recycling network with measures such as round-the-clock automated collection points after scrapping the waste-charging scheme due to strong public backlash, the environmental chief has said.

Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan on Saturday also pledged to review the permitted profit levels of the city’s two power companies when their control agreements with the government expire in 2033. He added the government would boost clean energy imports from mainland China.

Tse expressed confidence in achieving the four binding goals on environmental protection as outlined in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan unveiled last month.

Under the plan, the government set out goals to reduce carbon intensity, increase the share of zero-carbon energy used to generate power, and improve air and surface water quality.

The government decided to shelve the twice-delayed waste-charging scheme in 2024 even though it had previously said the direction was among the key methods for Hong Kong to attain carbon neutrality as garbage was the city’s third most significant source of emissions.

Tse said the government would instead double down on the city’s recycling efforts.

“We’ve been talking about waste reduction through refuse collection or reduction for decades,” he told a radio programme.

“We once considered imposing municipal waste charging but due to public opposition and backlash, we will strengthen the Green@Community initiative instead.”

Green@Community is a territory-wide community network covering all 18 districts to promote recycling collection.

Together with smart recycling bins, the community recycling network has more than 800 public collection points.

Tse said with the expansion of Green@Community coverage, Hong Kong’s waste volume had decreased by about 1,000 tonnes over the past three to four years.

“We plan to introduce automation to the Green@Community facilities, allowing recycling stations to operate 24 hours a day, which will provide more convenience for the public. There will be greater public participation,” he said.

He added that the Green@Community mobile application currently had 1.2 million registered users.

“By turning waste into energy, we’re confident of achieving the zero landfill target,” he said.

Tse also pledged to review the permitted profit levels of the city’s two power companies when the control agreements with the government expire in 2033, and to increase the import of clean energy from the mainland.

“We also aim to increase the proportion of zero-carbon electricity imported into Hong Kong from the mainland to 60 to 70 per cent, which is believed to help lower local electricity tariffs at that time. We’re now in discussion with some mainland units,” he said.

He said authorities had requested increasing the transmission capacity of the Daya Bay cable, and would also apply for funding from the Legislative Council to construct a large-scale power reception station on the reclaimed land in Tseung Kwan O Area 132, as well as build new transmission cables from the mainland to import large amounts of zero-carbon energy into Hong Kong.

“We’ll set up a working group. The government will conduct a cautious and comprehensive review including each of the roles, the project details and financial arrangements, etc,” he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-cockroach-.title: India's 'Cockroach' leaders detained ahead of major protest
https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-cockroach-.text:
India's 'Cockroach' party says its leaders have been detained ahead of a major protest called by the collective. Protesters are calling for India's chief election commissioner to resign.

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:

Delhi Police said in a statement that around 500 people were detained on Saturday as they arrived for the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party, news agency ANI reported.

"Around 500 people coming in different groups from various locations have been detained," ANI quoted the Delhi Police statement as saying.

The police added that an additional 50 people had been arrested and described them as "anti-social elements with criminal antecedents" who had been taken into custody to ensure that they "did not disturb" public order or "incite trouble."

Visuals aired by Indian news channels earlier showed police in central Delhi chasing young protesters before forcing them into vehicles and taking them away.

Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been detained by Delhi police, Indian media reported, as a preventative measure to block the planned protest against India's election chief in central Delhi.

According to reports by several media outlets, including India Today, authorities detained Dipke on board a flight after he landed in Delhi on Saturday morning. The news outlet quoted Dipke as saying, "I'm not afraid of you," while police officers urged him to cooperate.

The CJP's X handle soon released footage of the detention. "Shame on you Narendra Modi, Amit Shah," the caption read, referring to India's prime minister and home minister, respectively.

Authorities have also detained CJP's co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, as well as the group's legal aid head, Ratna Singh.

Right before being arrested, Dipke posted a video on Instagram, showing tens of Delhi police officers lining up outside his airplane to enter. "Love you, we'll do it together, Inqalab Zindabad," one of Dipke's associate is heard saying in the video's background.

'Inqalab Zindabad', meaning 'long live the revolution,' is a famous slogan used by Indian freedom fighters during their struggle against British rule. It has regularly been used by the Cockroach party against the Modi government.

The preventative arrests are part of a major crackdown on protesters this weekend.

Most of central Delhi, where the government is headquartered, is under an internet blackout and riddled with barricades, which authorities are using to identify and stop potential protesters.

Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) National President Nitin Nabin held a press conference in New Delhi, denouncing the CJP and opposition party protests over voter list irregularities as an attempt to "create a highly dangerous and serious situation in the country."

He described the INDIA bloc of opposition parties and the Cockroach movement as "two anarchic groups."

"Your 'anarchist competition,' vying to see who can create more instability in the country, will not succeed," Nabin said, accusing both groups of "a plot to destabilize the country."

"I want to say that you are undertaking these efforts, driven by your political agendas, at the behest of foreign forces," he said without elaborating on who the foreign forces were.

Popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been detained by the police ahead of the Jantar Mantar protest, according to the CJP and Indian media reports.

"Dhruv Rathee has been detained. The Dictator is TERRIFIED of young people who question its wrongdoings and refuse to stay silent," the CJP wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Modi.

According to reports, Rathee was detained at his home in Gurugam. Earlier this week, the CJP officially launched Rathee as part of its "fight to save democracy" campaign.

The Germany-based YouTuber participated in a CJP protest in the southern Indian city of Bengaluru on Thursday.

CJP legal head Ratna Singh is also reported to have been detained at her home in New Delhi on Saturday.

After India's education minister, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement has Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in its crosshairs.

Here is a ten-point breakdown of the controversy surrounding the top election official:

Police have already detained some protesters who had started gathering at Jantar Mantar for the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest, ANI news agency reported.

On Friday the Delhi Police said that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law had been enforced in the New Delhi area, prohibiting all forms of assembly or protest.

Meanwhile, Indian news agencies reported that police had heightened security across the capital on Saturday, with flag marches and mock drills being conducted at several locations.

Entry and exit gates at several metro stations have also been closed, according to reports.

ANI also reported that spike strips had been deployed to deter protesters from moving through certain areas.

The protest is being dubbed by some as "Season 2" of the Cockroach movement in India. The first wave of protests culminated with the resignation of India's education minister over exam irregularities, a rare concession by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP party.

DW's Shalu Yadav takes a closer look at how the Indian government is preparing for CJP's latest protest call in this report:

The Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) founder, Abhijeet Dipke, was due to land at Delhi's main airport on Saturday morning as the movement plans to hold a mass protest calling for India’s Chief Election Commissioner to step down over sweeping voter roll revisions, despite being denied permission by police.

Police and paramilitary forces, which local media reported numbered around 43,000 personnel, were deployed ahead of the protest. Multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocked the concrete-grey roads leading to the Jantar Mantar protest site.

On Friday, authorities also ordered the closure of more than 50 metro stations and canceled many trains bound for two major railway stations in the capital.

But India's top court later directed the government to not completely halt train services and said there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.

The Supreme Court stressed the "principle of proportionality," urging authorities to allow the transportation services in a regulated manner to avoid public inconvenience.

"Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," legal news website Bar and Bench reported the court as saying.

On Saturday, Dipke denounced the Modi government over extensive restrictions.

"Modi has accepted defeat even before our protest has begun," the CJP chief wrote on X ahead of his arrival in the capital.

"The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength, but of a leader terrified of his own people."

The CJP is not the only group calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

India's bloc of opposition parties, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, has been carrying out a sustained campaign against Kumar in recent days with its own protest marches.

The country has seen dramatic visuals emerge from Delhi's key corridor of political power, which showed leading opposition MPs, including Gandhi, being carried away to detention buses by uniformed police officials as they tried to dig their heels in.

The ire against India's election chief —  the head of India's independent Election Commission  —  is turning into one of the biggest public and political challenges for Modi in his three-term rule. Opposition and critics allege that a mass deletion of tens of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls benefits Modi's Prime Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi and this is a special edition of our daily India news blog.

As the early morning hours tick away, a countdown to a rally against India's top poll official over alleged voter list irregularities has begun in the heart of the world's largest democracy.

India's 'Cockroaches' are headed once again for Jantar Mantar —  the same protest site where the online satirical movement sprung to the mainstream as a youth-led pressure group in July after it forced the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's then education minister.

The police have denied the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) permission to hold the demonstration but the group's leaders are heralding people from all over the country to converge at Jantar Mantar, calling the protest a "fundamental right".

A showdown between police and protesters seems imminent.

New Delhi, particularly its central areas, have essentially been turned into a fortress with a heavy security blanket — including thousands of paramilitary personnel —  a rare mobile internet blackout, train cancellations and warnings from the police against any protest assembly.

The security arrangements come as memory is still fresh of a clash between youth demonstrators and police during the July Cockroach protest. Police used batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns to disperse the agitating crowd. Several injuries were reported as the protesters alleged police brutality, while the police said it used force only after the protests stopped being peaceful.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574.title: Asbestos mystery leaves beloved beach closed
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574.text:
For more than six years, asbestos has been washing up with the tide, turning one of Plymouth's handful of swimming spots into the centre of a growing environmental mystery.

Mount Batten Beach has been fenced off since the summer, and access restricted to two other areas on the peninsula.

It comes after tests in April and July found asbestos fibres in sand samples at levels that could pose a risk to health if inhaled, Plymouth City Council said.

Inhaling the fibres can increase the risk of serious diseases - including lung cancer - decades after exposure.

The first discovery came in 2019 when 500kg (1,100lb) of material containing the toxic substance was removed from the shoreline, which sits on Plymouth Sound in one of the South West's most popular holiday destinations.

In total, more than 1.5 tonnes of material containing asbestos, including both white and the more dangerous blue varieties, has been cleared from the beach and nearby sites.

Residents and experts believe the material may be coming from roofing and construction waste linked to the former RAF Mount Batten base, where coastal erosion is thought to be exposing the buried material.

The closure has left swimmers, business owners and residents wondering when, or even if, the beach will reopen, and how it looks against the backdrop of Plymouth Sound being named the UK's first National Marine Park.

City councillor Grace Stickland, who has been bathing at Mount Batten for several years, said dozens of people regularly gathered for swims throughout the year, with festive dips attracting as many as 80 participants.

"It was a really popular little beach and everybody loved it," she said.

"All the swimmers feel as though they've been evicted from their homes."

Stickland said older swimmers and people with mobility issues particularly valued Mount Batten because of its accessibility, adding that the closure was "breaking up" a community that had grown around the beach.

The National Marine Park in Plymouth Sound has faced a number of challenges in the past, including hundreds of old tyres being discovered on the seabed and sewage spills.

Yet the asbestos contamination problem has proved difficult to solve.

When asbestos was first discovered in 2019, the council temporarily closed the beach and expected the amount of material washing ashore to decrease over time but that has not been the case.

"Our beach collections have shown that the amount of material washing up on the beach hasn't shown any real decline," a council spokesperson said.

Earlier testing suggested the risk was low. Warning signs were installed and visitors were advised to avoid parts of the beach where asbestos fragments had been found.

But council officials described the latest results as a "new and worrying development".

Although two rounds of testing have found no evidence of airborne asbestos on the beach, the discovery of fibres in the sand was enough to trigger the closure.

Professor Steve Maddern, Plymouth's director of public health, said shutting the beach had been a last resort.

"We understand the disappointment this will cause but the latest sand samples are concerning and we must prioritise the safety of the public," he said in July.

While the beach remains closed, attention has turned to the question: Where is the asbestos coming from?

Residents have long suspected the source could be the former RAF Mount Batten site, which occupied the peninsula for much of the 20th Century before closing in 1992.

During its heyday it was one of Britain's most important flying boat bases, with Sunderland aircraft carrying out anti-submarine patrols and sea rescue missions during World War Two.

Today little remains beyond memorials and historic seaplane hangars.

Maritime archaeologist Mallory Haas, director of the Ships Project CIC in Plymouth, said she believed asbestos-containing roofing materials from the RAF base had been buried and were now being exposed through coastal erosion.

"If you look at what's on the beach, and if you also look at the deposits behind the staircases when you walk down to the beach, you can see it eroding out of the land there," she said.

She added: "It's Britain's Ocean City, the UK's first National Marine Park and it's an MPA [Marine Protected Area].

"It should be some of the most protected waters around."

The properties of asbestos made it an ideal material for use in a number of products, including insulation material for buildings, boilers and pipes; car brakes and floor tiles, insulating board to protect buildings and ships against fire; asbestos cement for roofing sheets and pipes.

Due to the risks to health following inhalation exposure to asbestos the importation of blue and brown asbestos has been banned in the UK since 1985.

This ban was extended to include white asbestos in 1999.

Asbestosis is a rare but serious lung condition that affects people exposed to asbestos. It cannot be cured but treatment may improve the symptoms.

It can take 20 to 30 years after being exposed to asbestos before symptoms appear.

There are sometimes no symptoms.

The advice is to visit a GP if you have symptoms of asbestosis and think you have been exposed to asbestos.

Sources: UKHSA and NHS

Local MP Rebecca Smith has been pressing the council for answers; arguing the closure is having a significant impact on sea swimmers, watersports users, businesses and the wider community.

More than 140 people attended a public meeting about the issue, while a petition has been handed to Parliament calling for urgent action to reopen the beach.

The Conservative MP for South West Devon questioned why the problem had still not been resolved more than six years after asbestos was first discovered.

"You can't be the National Marine Park on one side of the peninsula and have a closed beach on the other side of the peninsula," she said.

"I will find it incredibly difficult to stand up in Parliament and talk about the National Marine Park if that beach remains closed."

Smith said the city council had a strong record of securing external funding for major projects and argued it should use those same skills to find the resources needed to resolve the beach closure.

"There's a will, there's a way," she said. "They need to be using that track record and that skill set to get whatever it takes to sort this beach out."

Nearby businesses are beginning to feel the strain as well.

The Bridge restaurant closed in September, citing the beach closure as a significant factor affecting trade.

For now, Mount Batten's future remains unclear.

A council spokesperson said re-opening the beach was a "high priority" but a "complex task" due to the type and location of the contamination, the potential risks to public health and the need to definitively identify the source of the asbestos.

Further tests in other waterfront locations have been taking place to check whether the contamination is confined to the Mount Batten area.

A contractor, which would identify the source of the contamination and provide solutions to re-open the beach, has yet to be appointed.

"This critical work needs to be robust and comprehensive, but our aim is for it to be carried out as rapidly as possible as we fully understand – and share – the frustrations of those who want the beach to re-open as soon as possible," the spokesperson said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8r.title: Chemicals at former fuel depot 'have been removed'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8r.text:
Barrels of chemicals left at an approved development site have been removed and testing carried out, a developer has said.

The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire is a former RAF and Esso fuel storage and transfer facility and has had outline planning permission approved to build residential and affordable homes.

Concerns were raised after campaigners discovered about 40 barrels of firefighting foam liquid, which contains PFAS - a group of chemicals often dubbed forever chemicals, had been left at the site for decades.

Developer, Newcore, said it had already identified the potential contamination and that "this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately."

The depot previously supplied fuel to the former RAF Upper Heyford, around five miles north, which is suspected to be the source of forever chemical, or PFAS, contamination from firefighting foam.

Images show the barrels to be manufactured by Angus Fire Armour, that settled a legal battle out of court with residents in Yorkshire, after claims they had been exposed to PFAS near the company's foam manufacturing plant.

CEO of Newcore, Hugo Llewelyn, who took over the site in 2012, said it plans to regenerate the site with 50% affordable housing and that it was made aware of the barrels "in recent weeks" and had them removed in a "responsible and professional manner".

"Whilst firefighting foam containers were present on site from the MOD's operation back in the 20th Century, we do not believe it was ever deployed; the containers were sealed; and successive surveys have confirmed that there is no "pathway" for it to cause pollution," he added.

Mr Llewelyn disputes the quality of the testing carried out by campaigners.

"A 'pressure group' has trespassed unlawfully to obtain a questionable sample from this site to demonstrate that in the secured area of the site that was purposefully designed to accommodate foam for firefighting purposes, which is likely to contain PFAS, does, according to their findings, contain PFAS.

"I'm not sure there is anything to be surprised about here," he said.

He added that a Phase 1 assessment of the site last year had already identified the potential for contamination and that, "the specification for the Phase 2 investigation has therefore been designed to specifically address this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately".

The Environment Agency's Chemical Compliance team had contacted the site owners to ensure that the drums are properly managed.

Campaigners from Gallos Brook community group, who have been regularly testing for PFAS in the area, took a sample of soil near the storage area which they claimed is "likely the highest level of soil contamination measured anywhere in the UK."

The group said the sample, which was analysed by a UKAS certified laboratory, came back as having 3.74325 micrograms of PFAS per kilo. PFOS - a particular forever chemical - was found in their testing to be 205 times higher than the safe limit for residential land use.

Llewelyn disputed the testing carried out by campaigners and produced his own results which he claimed were taken from the same area, as part of the Phase 2 investigations.

He said these produced a total level of 0.0641micrograms per kilo of PFAS, roughly 98% lower than results by the campaigners, and were "the accurate results of our professional testing."

The BBC has not been presented with the official lab results to verify these independently.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8x2.title: 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8x2.text:
A man living with terminal cancer says his biggest regret is spending decades carrying childhood trauma without realising it was shaping his life.

Rex Mackrill, 65, from Tetbury, Gloucestershire, says being diagnosed with incurable prostate cancer forced him to reflect on what matters most, and one lesson he wished he learned earlier: to relish the joy of every moment.

"I knew there was something wrong. I knew there was a blackness that I was carrying and I didn't know what it was, and I wish I'd known earlier," he said.

With a limited time left ahead of him, Rex has been looking back on his life and considering what advice he would pass on.

Because prostate cancer runs in his family, Rex regularly monitored his PSA levels.

After a raised test result, further investigations confirmed he had incurable stage four prostate cancer.

Rex underwent chemotherapy but said the treatment took a significant physical toll and he now lives with the side effects of hormone treatment, including intense fatigue.

"I stopped doing a job I love as a GP practice manager," he said.

"By the time I went through chemotherapy, I couldn't do the job that was needed."

Leaving work was one of the biggest practical changes brought about by his diagnosis, although he says his priorities remain firmly focused on his family.

"Sarah and I have always had a strong focus on our boys. We structured our lives to give them the best upbringing we could."

But while cancer changed his perspective and future plans, he says one of the most important discoveries of his life came years before.

For much of his adult life, Rex lived with anxiety but could not explain why.

"I knew that I was frightened, but I didn't know why," he said.

He assumed he simply had to cope.

The turning point came at 60 when a life coach noticed he appeared to "shut down" while discussing certain topics.

"He said, 'You've got trauma, dude'," Rex recalled.

He later sought help and was diagnosed with PTSD.

Rex believes the trauma stemmed from abuse suffered in his childhood and says he is still exploring its impact today.

"I wish I'd known I had a trauma earlier," he said.

Research suggests delayed PTSD diagnoses are not uncommon, with symptoms sometimes emerging years after traumatic events.

Around one in 10 people in the UK are expected to experience PTSD at some point in their lives.

At first, Rex said he struggled to accept help.

But Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy gradually transformed the way he experienced life.

"I used to live at 10 out of 10 anxiety and I don't now," he said.

"It influenced all aspects of my life.

"People would say I was calm and collected, but they weren't aware of the stress and anxiety I carried."

Looking back, he says his advice to anyone struggling is straightforward.

"Go get help. Go and see your GP.

"You don't have to live like that or carry it on your own.

"Go to a trusted friend and say there's something blocking you. They can help you find the support you need."

As he comes to terms with terminal cancer, Rex says his priorities have not changed but what has changed is how present he feels.

"I used to have to go to the Lake District to be present," he said.

"Now I can be much more present wherever I am."

Recently, he found himself captivated by a simple moment outside.

"I was watching rooks floating on the wind," he said.

"One rook wanted to move a little bit along a tree branch, but the wind took it somewhere else.

"It had to circle around and land exactly where it wanted to be."

He now spends time writing poetry, donating possessions like his car to charity and trying to make life easier for those he will leave behind.

"I don't want to burden people with my stuff," he said.

Rex has also taken part in sessions at Longfield Hospice in Minchinhampton that help people discuss end-of-life plans and their wishes for care.

Sarah Mimmack, director of care at the hospice, said many families avoid conversations about death because they find them uncomfortable, but planning ahead can remove uncertainty and pressure.

"If you've done this work before you die, it really helps your family and friends," she said.

She added that while around half of people in the UK die in hospital, only a small proportion say that is where they would choose to spend their final days.

For Rex, however, preparing for death has become another way of making the most of the present.

And if there is one lesson he hopes others take from his experience, it is not to wait.

"Enjoy the joy of life and see that this is a beautiful world we live in," he said.

"We're so lucky. We can love every moment of it."
