https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Yemen’s Taiz under siege again as food and fuel prices rise
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: AbdulHakim Helal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Taiz, Yemen – Taiz is under siege, but 37-year-old Iskandar Abdullah already knows what it’s like to live under one.

The city, a major population centre in Yemen’s southwest, endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, as the Iranian-backed group attempted to capture the city from local pro-government forces. The Houthis continued to maintain a partial siege in the following years through their control over other access points into the city.

“They were difficult days,” Abdullah recalls, even as the Houthis begin a new siege on Taiz following their capture of territory to the south of the city, cutting off the main road to government-held territory. “We witnessed the horrors of the siege and experienced the bitterness of life in all its terrifying details.”

“I hope those painful days never return.”

In early September, the Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of Taiz governorate. The group soon established full control over the port city of Mocha and the district of Dhubab, where the Bab al-Mandeb strait – through which 12 percent of global trade passes – is located.

The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen’s populous northwest, including the capital Sanaa, since the country’s war started in 2014, did not stop their military attacks at the Red Sea. Even as government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October and regained some of the territory lost, the Houthis pressed forward in the countryside surrounding Taiz.

The Houthis successfully captured the town of al-Turbah by October 4, severing the only remaining main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.

Taiz residents, like Abdullah, are now worried that the city is about to face a prolonged full-scale siege. Abdullah remembers how difficult life was between 2015 and 2016, when pro-government forces were confined to an enclave in the centre of the city.

Locals endured “horrors, as well as appalling humanitarian and economic conditions unlike anything experienced by any other Yemeni governorate during the war”, according to Abdullah.

“People lacked even the most basic necessities of life, including drinking water, food, fuel and medicine,” he said. “The only exceptions were supplies smuggled across rugged mountain terrain, carried on the backs of people and donkeys, including oxygen cylinders for the sick and wounded.”

The siege was eventually broken in 2016 when pro-government forces recaptured territory south of Taiz city. In 2024, under domestic and international pressure, the Houthis agreed to reopen another important route into the city from the east, connecting it to Sanaa and other Houthi-controlled areas of northern Yemen.

However, with the recent resumption of fighting, the vital crossing has been closed following attempted incursions by Houthi fighters, according to security sources who spoke to Al Jazeera.

The closure has severed a crucial route that had become essential for Taiz residents – much of the city’s food supplies had entered through the crossing.

Nabil Jamil, director-general of the planning and development office in Taiz governorate, said that the current siege on Taiz is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.

“This time, the siege does not only affect the governorate’s main roads, but also most of the secondary roads connecting the rural districts themselves,” Jamil said.

Jamil said that approximately 2.8 million people had been living in government-held areas of Taiz governorate, alongside another 200,000 people who have been recently displaced by the fighting along the coast and rural Taiz.

“All of them will face humanitarian hardship and deteriorating living conditions as a result of the siege,” he said.

Less than a week into the renewed siege, the city’s streets appeared almost deserted because of a fuel shortage, which had previously entered the city through the al-Turbah route from Aden.

On the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol rose from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 Yemeni riyals ($58).

Meanwhile, markets and grocery shops have seen a surge in demand, as residents rush to stock up on food amid fears that supplies would disappear from shelves because of the siege.

Some residents have accused traders of hoarding and monopolising essential goods in the absence of any effective market oversight.

“Food markets in Taiz have witnessed a noticeable increase in the prices of basic commodities, particularly wheat and flour, while the prices of vegetables and fruits have doubled, as the siege has made it difficult to bring these products into the city,” said Wafiq Saleh, a journalist specialising in economic affairs.

“Traders in the city have food stocks sufficient to last several months,” he added. “Nevertheless, some traders began raising prices as soon as the fighting intensified on the outskirts of the city.”

Fighting is continuing in the Taiz countryside, and there is hope among locals that government forces will be able to retake the areas lost to the Houthis in recent days, or continue their forward momentum in areas to the west of Taiz city, and break the siege from that direction.

But for now, the Houthis appear to be on the front foot in the areas to Taiz city’s south.

Salman al-Maqrami, a journalist specialising in Houthi affairs, believes the primary objective of the Taiz siege is to undermine the cohesion of the forces opposed to them in the city, which has long been a hotbed of hostility towards the group.

“Therefore, there is no doubt that [the Houthis] are seeking revenge against this population that opposes them,” he added.

The fall of Taiz would also be symbolic for the Houthis, allowing the group to present itself as being able to threaten any area under government control, even if the population is hostile.

However, Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and the head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization (JRDO), pointed out that the effect of any such battle for Taiz – including a longstanding siege on such a large city – would be detrimental to civilians.

“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” Sharyan said.

He warned of the enormous humanitarian cost of the renewed siege, “particularly for patients, children, women and the elderly, given the difficulties in accessing hospitals, medical services, and medicines”.

“Restrictions on travel and movement will also affect students, patients, employees and families who depend on travelling between different areas of the governorate and beyond,” he added.

Sharyan called on the international community, human rights organisations and humanitarian agencies to take a clear position that “guarantees residents access to their basic needs, ensures that roads and crossings remain open to civilians and goods, and allows patients to reach healthcare services, in a manner that safeguards human dignity and fundamental rights”.

Jamil said that local authorities in Taiz had sent a letter to the United Nations seeking assistance in addressing the crisis and its humanitarian consequences.

Local authorities’ priorities include opening safe roads and corridors for civilians, especially those who need to travel for medical treatment, and allowing medicine and food to reach Taiz.

“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.

The Houthis have been fighting for the city since the country's war started in 2014. Lawyer Nabil Sharyan says the fall of Taiz would be symbolic for the Houthis.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.title: India protest live: ‘Cockroach’ leaders detained; New Delhi in lockdown
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.author: Nadim Asrar,Priyanka Shankar
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.text:
“It’s official… we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi,” Arvind Kejriwal, the leader of the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), has said in a statement.

“Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear.”

In a post on X, the Cockroach Janta Party has condemned the detention of Dipke and other leaders of the satirical political movement.

Naming Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, who controls the police in New Delhi, the CJP said Dipke and two other prominent leaders of the movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were picked up from inside their plane when their flight landed in New Delhi today so they could join the protest.

The protests are centred on India’s Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters, including a large number of Muslims.

The protesters accuse the governing BJP of using the SIR to sway election results, ‌in collusion with its appointees in the Election Commission, including the poll panel’s chief, Gyanesh Kumar.

Last month, an investigation by the Indian Express revealed that Kumar’s deputies had queried and disagreed with him over list revisions that dropped ⁠about 130 million voters. That number exceeds the population of Japan.

Opposition parties have long accused the government of trying to fix voter ⁠lists to its advantage. Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.

Police ⁠have detained the founder of ⁠the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Abhijeet Dipke, ⁠before a protest called by the youth movement demanding the resignation of ‌the country’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Indian TV channels reported earlier that police officers met Dipke at the New Delhi airport ⁠after he arrived ⁠from the financial capital Mumbai and asked him to call ⁠off the protest as authorities ⁠had banned it.

CJP leaders ⁠Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also arrested from their flight ‌upon landing, the movement said in a statement.

Hello, and welcome to our live coverage of India’s youth returning to the streets as anger grows against the election chief and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Stay with us for the latest news and analysis of the planned protest rally called by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other youth groups in the capital New Delhi.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.author: Mya Kordic
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The plane sustained significant damage during the crash. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

A light aircraft plunged into a field north of Perth on Saturday, with the two men on board surviving the crash with non-life-threatening injuries.

Police said the pilot of the single-engine aircraft crashed near the Greenside private airfield, off Brand Highway in Muchea, north-east of Perth, this morning.

Emergency services responded to the incident, during which the aircraft sustained "significant damage", police said.

The two men on board survived the crash with non-life-threatening injuries. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

A man in his 60s and another man in his 30s were on board the aircraft and were treated at the scene.

They were both transported to Royal Perth Hospital at priority one, and St John Ambulance said the two men are believed to have non-life-threatening injuries.

The Greenside Recreational Flyers Club, one of the state's largest, operates at the airfield, according to its website.

The aircraft crashed around 250 metres from the airfield's runway. Its fuselage, wings and tail were badly damaged.

Police said their inquiries are ongoing.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.title: More Japanese firms hit by large-scale data breaches
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/20.text:
More Japanese companies have revealed that they have experienced major customer data breaches due to cyberattacks.

JR East said that about 6.09 million customer accounts may have been compromised, while JR Kyushu said about 1.3 million customer accounts may have been compromised. Both were a result of a ransomware attack on IDC Frontier, a cloud services subsidiary of SoftBank, they said Friday.

Bookoff Group Holdings, a secondhand goods retailer, reported that its subsidiary responsible for managing membership data had suffered unauthorized access, possibly resulting in a data breach affecting up to 6.43 million customers.

Daiichikosho, the operator of the Big Echo karaoke chain, also said personal information on about 8.72 million customers may have been compromised due to unauthorized access to a system managed by an external contractor.

Adventure Inc., the operator of the Skyticket travel booking website, reported a potential breach involving about 14.64 million sets of personal information, following a cyberattack on its servers and the business management system for its booking website.

The potentially affected information includes email addresses at JR East and customer names, dates of birth and telephone numbers at the other three companies. Adventure said it had confirmed that credit card and passport numbers had not leaked.

The companies respectively said that they had found no evidence of unauthorized use of the affected information by third parties. They are urging customers to watch out for suspicious emails and phone calls.

JR Kyushu says about 1.3 million customer account accounts may be compromised. Adventure Inc. says 14.64 million sets of personal information may have also been compromised.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.title: Trump casts doubt on Pentagon plan to live stream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.text:
Bipartisan outrage and UN condemnation have followed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to stream Nidal Hasan’s death sentence

Nidal Hasan’s execution – scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 – is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945.

But Trump, who supports the death penalty in this case, left uncertain whether the execution would be publicly broadcast.

“They are making a determination about that, but he will be killed,” Trump said. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes.”

“This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Vance said, but added that if the execution was broadcast live, “I’m not going to be watching it”.

Representative Austin Scott of Trump’s Republican Party said he supported executing Hasan but “live streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that”.

Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice” but that public executions were “the kind of thing Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?”

Technology firms YouTube, Meta Platforms and X did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether they would allow the execution to be streamed on their platforms.

TikTok directed questions to its policy banning depictions of “graphic incidents and violence” including “the shooting of an individual”.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the plan, saying in a message on Friday that “the live streaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.

Hegseth said it would be the military’s first firing squad execution since World War II.

“People need to understand that … there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said in a video shared on Thursday on official Pentagon social media accounts.

The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.

The Death Penalty Information Centre says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916.

According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 – six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.

Amnesty’s Justin Mazzola said on Friday that the death penalty was “a violation of human rights”, and that streaming Hasan’s execution “would only compound the cruelty”.

Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralysed from the waist down.

Hasan chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges.

He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.

Court-appointed defence lawyers expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaqi, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-s.summary: Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to stream Nidal Hasan's death sentence at Fort Hood. Heg set to be first firing squad execution since 1945 by US military firing squad. UN condemns plan, saying it would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase

The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.

Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.

The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.

The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.

Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.

Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.

They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.

She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.

“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”

A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.

“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.

“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”

A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.

A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.

“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.

Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.

Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.

That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.

The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.

Watson was approached for comment.
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.summary: Tom Watson, of Worcester, is alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account. Account was deactivated shortly after he was named by campaign group Hope Not Hate. Account has a history of racist comments and has been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘I’m supposed to be here’: Angel Reese’s road from ridicule to the WNBA finals
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Bryan Armen Graham at Barclays Center
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
After years of mockery and doubts about her game, Reese has helped carry Atlanta to the WNBA’s biggest stage. Her critics might want to start forming an apology queue

A lot of folks owe Angel Reese an apology after Friday night. They should probably form an orderly queue.

Not that the bad-faith take merchants who have spent three years gleefully circulating her missed layups, likening her occasionally awkward footwork to “Bambi on ice” and marveling at the supposed comic genius of “mebounds” are likely to join it. The right-wing culture warriors who turned one of the WNBA’s most naturally gifted rebounders into a punchline were never particularly interested in an honest assessment of her basketball abilities. But after Friday the punch line has never worn thinner.

Reese’s career has been measured against Caitlin Clark’s almost from the moment the two became household names, their rivalry inflated into a culture-war proxy battle that neither player could fully control. Now Reese has reached the WNBA finals before her more celebrated contemporary, a delicious reversal for those who have spent three seasons insisting she didn’t belong in the same conversation. Not that basketball achievement is require to be a zero-sum proposition.

On Friday in Brooklyn, Reese poured in a team-high 22 points as the Atlanta Dream completed a three-game sweep of the New York Liberty with an 85-83 victory, reaching the WNBA finals for the first time since 2013. The 24-year-old scored 18 points before half-time, including a pair of three-pointers, and helped eliminate the 2024 champions on their home floor.

As it happens, Reese had been expecting this moment.

“I manifested this when I came to Atlanta. I knew what I was getting. The finals. The finals,” she said afterward. “This team has poured so much into me. We poured so much into each other.”

Exactly 364 days earlier, while watching last season’s championship series from the couch, Reese had posted a prediction on social media: “Manifesting the finals.”

“I was watching the finals from home for the last two years and kept saying, just give me one playoff game,” she said. “I manifest a lot of things and think it’s important to speak positively into your life and your team, but this is all God. I’m thankful and blessed to be here and won’t take it for granted.”

The former Chicago Sky forward, who arrived in Atlanta in an offseason trade, has found more than a new basketball home.

“We have a praying group; eight of our twelve players go to chapel, and we take that seriously,” she said. “It’s a blessing to be around the girls in that locker room.”

Reese’s offensive limitations were always real enough. Her finishing around the basket could be erratic, her shooting needed work and her impatience sometimes got the better of her. But there was an enormous difference between acknowledging those weaknesses and insisting they rendered her accomplishments fraudulent.

Friday’s post-game news conference in the bowels of Brooklyn’s Barclays Center offered a revealing glimpse of the work she has put into addressing them.

“For me, it’s really hard for me to not wan to rush success,” Reese admitted.

She recalled a particularly demanding shooting drill under Dream coach Karl Smesko, who stopped the exercise until Reese made the required shot. Her teammates were left waiting, and her frustration mounted.

“I was upset with him that day, for sure,” she said. “Because I didn’t want to let the team down.”

Smesko remembered the episode, explaining that Atlanta had undertaken substantial changes to Reese’s offensive game. He warned her that the adjustments would not feel natural immediately, but that the work would begin to pay off as the season progressed.

For much of her first two seasons, Reese seemed destined to become a Dennis Rodman for the modern WNBA: a generational rebounder, an indefatigable competitor and the sort of complementary piece whose singular gifts could turn a good team into a great one. That was hardly a modest projection. Rodman was a Hall of Famer and one of basketball’s most influential role players.

A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.

after newsletter promotion

But in her third professional season, Reese is making even that comparison look increasingly restrictive. She is no longer merely the sort of player who can elevate a team built around other stars. She’s becoming the sort of player a championship contender can build around.

Her reflections on Friday extended beyond basketball. Reese spoke movingly about her mother, Angel Webb Reese, who raised her and her brother with help from their grandparents and remains her most dependable source of support.

“She’s really proud because she knows the dark moments that I’ve been through,” Reese said. “I can pick up the phone at three in the morning, call her crying, and she’s just been there for me.”

Her mother, she explained, asks for little beyond the opportunity to be present.

“Support me, show up, and love me, and I’ll give you the world,” Reese said. “She’s not very hard on me, but she’s very loving, and she’s very caring.”

It was a reminder of the human being behind the online caricature, and of the private difficulties that cannot be captured in a compilation of missed shots.

Friday’s victory came without injured leading scorer Allisha Gray, whose absence placed additional demands on Reese and Atlanta’s already depleted rotation. Reese said she had promised Gray that she would help finish the job.

“This is what you brought me here for. I got your back. You got my back,” she recalled telling her. “And I’m glad to have her back for the finals.”

Atlanta will face the Golden State Valkyries in the best-of-seven finals beginning on 17 October. For Reese, who spent her first two seasons hoping for even a single playoff appearance, the prospect of playing for a championship remains almost surreal.

“I knew I belonged here and wanted to help this team do whatever it took – not just get out of the first round or semi-finals, but make the finals and win a championship,” she said.

“The job isn’t done. We’re happy, but not satisfied.”
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.summary: Atlanta Dream's Angel Reese has helped carry Atlanta to the WNBA's biggest stage. Reese's career has been measured against Caitlin Clark's almost from the moment the two became household names. Atlanta will face the Golden State Valkyries in the best-of-seven finals beginning on 17 October.

For some sensational reporting on Trump’s second term, look at Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan.

How did the business class learn to love Trump and embrace chaos? Paul Heideman gives a lucid analysis in his recent book Rogue Elephant.

If you want more on the new tech bros of Silicon Valley, here are four recommendations:

- In their book, Klein and Taylor regularly cite Karen Hao’s Empire of AI.

- There’s also The Nerd Reich, just out from Gil Durán.

- If you enjoyed Yanis Varoufakis in our last episode of Radical Thinking, check out his book Technofeudalism.

- As for how AI is imposing a new age of total corporate control, The Rulers by Cecilia Rikap is a must.

https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1007674.title: My brief romance with an AI bird feeder
https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1007674.author: Thomas Ricker
https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1007674.text:
Everything was great until he arrived.

Everything was great until he arrived.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

It started off promising enough. Dozens of tiny, colorful birds were drawn to my garden just a few weeks after I mounted a $350 $269 Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro. “Looks like Great Tit!” read the first AI-driven alert sent to my phone. “Looks like Eurasian Blue Tit!” read another. I chuckled, still waiting for adulthood to kick in.

This went on for days. Hundreds of miniature tits came to snack on expensive sunflower seeds already husked. They’d skulk about in nearby trees before flittering in to grab a single seed to be safely enjoyed in the canopy above.

I took great delight in my new house guests. I admired them in crisp 4K HDR video recordings. I looked for unique markings in the hope of naming my new feral pets. I clicked deeper into the Kiwibit app to read about my visitors’ migration habits, where they nest, and what they like to eat. It was all going swell until he arrived.

“Looks like Common Wood Pigeon!” came the alert. All I saw was a battleship-gray blob obscuring the live camera feed. The winged rat was so fat and imposing that he blocked the lens. Ugh, no, go back to the tourists!

In mild panic, I triggered the feeder’s Nuisance Animal Alarm, a feature typically reserved for squirrels and the like. The pigeon tensed, looked around, but wasn’t deterred by the audible siren that was surely annoying my neighbors. Soon it went back to gorging on the haute cuisine purchased for more refined guests. It ate and ate and ate. For 15 minutes, it ate until I walked outside and shooed it away.

Thereafter, that pigeon, or pigeons (who can tell) moved in. They’d perch for 30 minutes or more, slamming their faces into the seed pile with the clumsy enthusiasm of a tween bobbing for apples. Mice arrived below to feast on the spoils. Admitting defeat, I dismounted the expensive bird feeder and shoved it into a closet.

I’m not mad at Kiwibit. The “Bird Feeder 2 Pro 4K AI Camera with Solar Panel (Lifetime AI Included)” I tested was a joy to use, until it wasn’t. That’s not Kiwibit’s fault.

If you’ve been tempted to buy a smart bird feeder, I’d suggest starting with something simple, inexpensive, and without AI instead of going all in on day one — you can’t return a used feeder just because it attracts pests.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: ‘So safe you could drink it’: Scientists and pesticide victims fear an EU rollback
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: Lara BULLENS
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
For most of his life, José Nadan worked as a professional beekeeper in Morbihan, a coastal area in Brittany known for its medieval towns and fresh seafood. At the start of his career, he recalls a golden age of beekeeping, when each year, and “without much effort”, the number of hives would naturally increase.

But things took a turn for the worse in the 1980s, when the varroa mite made its way to France. A parasite, the mite weakens bees by suppressing their immune system and spreading deadly viruses that can collapse entire colonies. “We improvised trying to kill them with whatever we had until official products made their way onto the market,” Nadan recalls.

Nadan also spent many years keeping an orchard of cider apple trees he treated with a pesticide that, he was told, was organic and had no effect on humans. “The sales reps even said it was so safe you could drink it,” the 69-year-old says. “I never took the slightest precaution, spraying from my tractor as I drove along the rows of trees,” Nadan recalls. “Sometimes, because of the wind, I’d get some on my face. But I wasn’t worried.”

“I later found out it was a product like Roundup [a Monsanto weed killer] and contained glyphosate,” he says, a substance now known to be harmful to human health.

It was only after he retired that Nadan realised the consequences of being exposed to pesticides for all those years. Six years ago, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer.

His illness has officially been recognised as an occupational hazard caused by pesticides by France’s agricultural social security system.

Pesticides are known to cause a range of health issues, including various types of cancer, respiratory diseases, neurodegenerative illnesses like Parkinson’s or Alzheimer's, cardiovascular diseases and infertility. They also impact children more than adults, leading to developmental delays and cognitive impairments.

And they are everywhere. A 2023 study in which hundreds of samples were gathered from different environments across 10 European countries found that pesticides were present in 100% of air, indoor dust and water samples.

READ MORE
Pesticides, cadmium, PFAS: France reckons with the hidden toxins in food (1/2)

Edmond Leduc, a retired doctor living close to the Belgian border in northern France, has lived next to crop fields treated with pesticides for 44 years. “The farmers working the fields practise intensive farming, so there is always a harvest,” he says. “When it’s potato season, they sometimes spray fungicides every two weeks.”

A lover of gardening, Leduc spent a lot of time outside and admits “not being very careful” in the early years. “I didn’t know the products I was inhaling were toxic.”

Leduc discovered he had lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, in 2018, and was diagnosed with prostate cancer in August of this year – two conditions linked to pesticides.

As one of Europe’s biggest agricultural producers, France is also one of its largest consumers of pesticides. And the number of requests by agricultural workers like Nadan, who are in close contact with the toxic substances, has shot up from 318 in 2024 to 975 in 2025.

Yet as the toll of pesticide exposure is becoming clearer, the EU is preparing to vote on a set of legal amendments that could make it harder to ban these harmful products.

Despite having a multi-layered system to assess the risk of pesticides, Europe still sees cases where they cause harm to both the environment and humans. Unlike the US, which uses a risk-based model that factors actual levels of exposure, the EU uses a hazard-based model, meaning it focuses on the inherent toxicological properties of a certain chemical before it’s approved.

But regulatory assessments are often delayed and take time, slowing down the process for pesticides to enter the market. To speed things up and cut red tape, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would overhaul the current system. Known as Omnibus X, it would amend ten existing EU laws that cover pesticides, biocides, food residues, animal feed and official controls.

A key amendment aims to scrap the periodic re-evaluation of pesticides, which often end up causing greater damage than expected after being initially approved.

The EU ensures the move would have “no compromise on food safety or environmental protection”, but critics of the package disagree.

READ MORE
How can you keep yourself safe from forever chemicals and cadmium in food? (Part 2/2)

“New scientific findings need to be taken into account regularly, because there is always a level of uncertainty [about the risk of a pesticide] before it hits the market,” says ecotoxicologist Martina Vijver, who was up in arms when news of the package dropped. “A periodic review is a safety lock, it’s crucial, because we can’t foresee every consequence.”

An insecticide known as chlorpyrifos, for example, was approved for use in the EU back in 2006. Sprayed on crops to control pests or on grains stored in warehouses, the chemical came to be one of the most commonly used pesticides in Europe. Residues of the substance were found in fruit, vegetables, dairy products and drinking water.

When its approval came up for renewal, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) reviewed the evidence and decided in 2019 that no safe exposure level could be set, and that chlorpyrifos didn’t meet the EU’s health requirements. Even in small doses, chlorpyrifos affects the human body’s neurological, reproductive, metabolic and immune systems. The substance was linked to neurodevelopmental disorders in children, including autism.

Even though the entire regulatory process spanned over seven years, once the ruling passed in January 2020, Member States had three months to dispose of all products containing chlorpyrifos.

“All pesticides are aimed at killing something,” Vijver explains. “If a substance is neurotoxic for insects, for example, that same neurotoxicity could apply to humans [...] Which is not so strange, because that’s the intention [of the pesticide].”

Denis Benoit, a former farmer in charge of pruning trees in the winter and applying pesticides from spring through summer, recalls going home with intense symptoms after a day’s work. “I had a fever at night and red patches on my arms,” he says. “It was because of the insecticides we were using, like D6.”

Like Nadan and Leduc, the 65-year-old from western France was also diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2019. “I do feel regret for having worked with those substances, but it was hard to find work at the time, and we were told they were only toxic in large doses,” he says.

For scientists like Vijver, the regular reassessment of pesticides is one of the few safeguards against such long-hidden harms, and it is precisely what the EU’s upcoming omnibus would remove.

Under the current EU system, a pesticide’s approval expires on a set date, and the company producing it has to show again that its product is safe to keep selling. If the approval no longer expires automatically, the product would stay on the market by default, removing the “safety lock” that Vijver refers to. The burden would then fall on the shoulders of regulators such as the EFSA or individual member states to sound the alarm.

“But who triggers the process? Doctors? Scientists? Or the guy who walks his dog and sees all the birds have died? That’s not our job,” says Vijver.

If passed, the legislation package would also increase the maximum grace period for farmers to substitute banned pesticides from 18 months to three years. Conditions for the exceptional use of banned pesticides, including endocrine disruptors, would also be loosened.

Sending a clear message of concern, Vijver took the initiative to write an open letter on September 17 and urged the European Parliament to pause the vote on the legislative package until an independent investigation into its potential health and environmental impacts is carried out. She gathered 573 other signatories from a wide range of disciplines, including environmental protection, medicine and public health – all of whom “have expertise” in the field, Vijver says.

“I’ve never done something like this before,” she admits. “As scientists, we are really worried. I would never have done this if I wasn’t really worried.”

READ MORE
Eco-friendly French winemakers plant hybrid vines to curb pesticide use

The vote on Omnibus X is expected to take place at the end of October.

Cancer victims and farmers marched arm in arm last weekend, flanked by doctors and activists, to protest pesticides. Organised by a handful of non-profits, the march saw 8,000 demonstrators gather outside a factory in northern France owned by Syngenta, the world’s largest pesticide seller.

Amid the crowd was Fleur Breteau, founder of the Cancer Colère collective, who made waves last year when she sparked a nationwide movement to block the reintroduction of the pesticide acetamiprid.

READ MORE
France's top constitutional court rejects return of bee-killing pesticide

Though the reintroduction of acetamiprid was eventually banned last summer, France passed an agricultural law in August this year that would partially reverse the decision.

Holding a placard that read: “Morgan, dead age 36, breast cancer,” Breteau told French daily Le Monde on October 3 that Morgan was her partner on agricultural issues and had passed away in June. “We’re losing peers every week,” she said.

“When I see the state of some of my fellow retirees, how sick and tired they are, I tell myself that all things considered, I am not doing too bad,” says former beekeeper Nadan, who now helps other agricultural workers as a member of a collective to support pesticide victims.

“I went to the funeral of a crop technician I was helping last week. He would go from farm to farm and survey treated fields, and fell ill shortly after retiring,” Nadan says. “He had a form of Parkinson’s that meant he could barely speak and was in a wheelchair. The disease progressed so rapidly that he didn’t have time to finalise his request to have the illness officially recognised as being caused by pesticides.”

For campaigners, cases like this are a stark reminder of what is at stake as Brussels prepares to rewrite its pesticide rules.

French environmental organisation Générations Futures has organised a weekend of protests and canvassing across the country, aimed at informing people about the EU legislative package that could loosen restrictions on pesticides.

“It’s never easy to bring EU issues into the public sphere because they aren’t very enticing. Our aim this weekend is to inform people about the Omnibus, spark debate, get people talking, which is definitely something its supporters want to avoid,” says Andy Battentier, campaign manager for Générations Futures.

“A third of the European Parliament is made up of right-wing and far-right MEPs, who favour scrapping standards [red tape],” says Battentier on the chances the legislative package will pass.

A first-ever “presidential debate” on pesticides organised by the NGO will also take place in Cambrai, northern France, this Saturday, with leftist representatives of presidential candidates for the 2027 election saying they will attend. Three hundred doctors in France have been awaiting a response from former prime minister Gabriel Attal, centre-right Edouard Philippe and Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau to debate “this major public health issue” – but their seats are likely to remain empty.

“23 million people in France suffer from either a chronic illness or cancer,” the doctors wrote in the letter sent on September 28. “Numerous studies have shown a strong link between these conditions and pesticides. As doctors, we work tirelessly to protect the health of our fellow citizens. What is the point of our efforts if we don’t tackle the root cause of the diseases?”

Back in Morbihan, Nadan still thinks about the bees he fought to save from the varroa mite, which weakens its host so slowly that by the time the damage shows, the colony is often beyond saving. Decades later, he and his fellow farmers fear the same may be true of the products they were told would protect them.

“Many farmers feel a sense of shame, especially because they have children who work in conventional farming,” he says, fearing the Omnibus would only “fuel the surge in cancers and other degenerative diseases” for generations to come.

https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.title: India's 'cockroach' movement chief detained ahead of major protest
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific.text:
Indian police detained the head of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online movement on Saturday ahead of a major protest it called against the Election Commission, the party said.

Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital New Delhi, where the demonstration was due to take place, the youth-led CJP said in a social media post.

The protests are the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision by the Election Commission of India (ECI).

READ MORE
India protests grow over Election Commission mistrust

Opposition parties and critics say the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety in the "special intensive revision", saying it was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters.

"It's official... we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi," Arvind Kejriwal of the opposition Aam Aadmi Party said in a statement.

"Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear."

Delhi has been under a strict security clampdown since Friday, with tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed to stop those seeking to reach the main protest site in the heart of the capital.

Authorities have closed dozens of metro stations, cancelled several trains coming to Delhi and shut down mobile internet temporarily around the protest site.

Television images on Saturday showed police chasing down several protesters and hauling them into vehicles in areas around central Delhi.

More than 200 protesters have been detained so far, local media reports said.

The protests are widely seen as a reprise of CJP's mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal.

This time, they are demanding ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar resign from his post.

FRANCE24 with AFP, Reuters

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Matthew Ward Agius

Police attended the Tollgate Motel after an unexplained infant death was reported. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

South Australian Police have attended the Tollgate Motel in Glen Osmond on Saturday morning to investigate a reported infant death.

ABC News understands police and ambulances were called to the Tollgate Motel, adjacent to the South Eastern Freeway, five kilometres south-east of the Adelaide CBD, from 9am.

Some witnesses estimated around 20 officers were present.

Police vehicles attended the scene throughout the morning. (Supplied)

"There were at least four or five police cars here," a nearby resident told the ABC.

"It's a bit concerning that we've got police cars down the end of our quiet cul-de-sac."

Police left the scene by mid-afternoon, after establishing a cordon.

Police have cordoned off a room at the Tollgate Motel.  (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The cause of the child's death is currently undetermined.

Police have confirmed that an investigation is ongoing with the assistance of crime scene investigators and Eastern District Detectives, and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.title: New mechanism to strengthen oversight of renovations after Tai Po fire: minister
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.author: Emily Hung
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.text:
Home affairs minister says mechanism will encourage rational discussion among owners and stop traders exploiting disputes over major renovations.

A three-tier dispute resolution mechanism could help Hong Kong homeowners strengthen oversight of major renovation projects and prevent exploitation by “unscrupulous traders”, according to the home affairs minister.

The city’s building management challenges came under the spotlight after the deadly blaze at Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court in November 2025. The estate was undergoing a HK$330 million renovation when the fire broke out, killing 168 people and displacing nearly 5,000 residents.

An independent committee investigating the blaze earlier uncovered evidence pointing to suspected bid-rigging and connected bidding companies, among other concerns.

Speaking on a radio programme on Saturday, Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen said the proposed mechanism could better handle disputes among property owners and foster a more constructive environment for building management.

“When major renovations are required, if owners can engage in rational discussions throughout the process and listen to different opinions … it will undoubtedly strengthen management and oversight,” she said.

“If property owners cannot unite and work together rationally to resolve disputes, unscrupulous businessmen could easily take advantage of these loopholes. When they see two parties at odds, they could manipulate one side to gain its support while sidelining the other.”

The three-tier mechanism, introduced in last month’s policy address, is among a series of proposed rules designed to plug regulatory gaps exposed by the fire.

Under the first tier, district council members would intervene early to help neighbours resolve disputes through negotiation.

If the issues remain unresolved, the councillors would refer the parties concerned to professional mediation services provided by the Home Affairs Department. The final tier would be to take the case to court.

The mechanism is expected to take effect next year.

Mak said authorities had been providing mediation training to district council members, who are expected to play a bigger role by not only making referrals but also actively facilitating communication among the parties across all three tiers.

Other proposals include requiring a technical briefing before owners vote so that homeowners can ask questions, prohibiting the rescheduling of owners’ meetings without a valid reason and requiring more parties to declare their interests.

All would require amendments to the Building Management Ordinance.

A public consultation on the proposals ended last month.

On youth development, Mak dismissed concerns over the rising youth unemployment rate, saying the problem was not unique to Hong Kong.

“Youth unemployment above the overall rate did not just happen in Hong Kong, but also in many parts of the world,” she said.

Government statistics show the unemployment rate among people aged 20 to 29 rose to 9.1 per cent between June and August, well above the overall rate of 3.8 per cent.

“What we need to do is not just create more jobs to counter unemployment, but equip our young people with the skills they need to meet those challenges through different measures,” she said.

For example, the authorities have worked with the Hong Kong Science Park and Cyberport to provide 200 three-month technology internship places.

Mak said many companies were satisfied with the interns’ performance and had offered them full-time positions.

“Many young people said they did not expect to enter the industry before the internship programme … we will expand the quota, hoping more tech start-ups can provide such opportunities for our youth,” she said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: ‘How can you stop these kids?’ Indian capital on lockdown before protests
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Yashraj Sharma
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
New Delhi, India – Heavy police barricades line the streets around Connaught Place, the colonial-era square near Jantar Mantar, on Saturday morning as police have begun detaining small groups of protesters arriving for planned demonstrations.

They are here in support of the influential Gen-Z movement and Cockroach Janta Party, which have called for the resignation of India’s election chief, amid a bitter dispute over who gets to vote in the world’s most populous democracy.

Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and a rollback of a controversial voter revision exercise which has struck 130 million names from the voter list.

For now, an eerie silence hangs over parts of central New Delhi. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has gone to lengths to turn the city into a fortress, deploying nearly 30,000 personnel onto the streets.

Police ⁠have also detained the founder of ⁠the Cockroach Janta Party, Abhijeet Dipke.

Indian TV channels reported early on Saturday that officers met Dipke at the New Delhi airport ⁠after he arrived ⁠from the financial capital Mumbai and asked him to call ⁠off the protest as authorities ⁠had banned it.

CJP leaders ⁠Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained from their flight ‌upon landing, the movement said in a statement.

On Friday, the government extraordinarily cancelled all trains to New Delhi; locked down more than 50 metro stations; imposed an internet shutdown; and sent personnel to thousands of students in local communities to warn them against participation in the protest.

Several students en route to New Delhi from different states of India were dragged out of trains and buses and detained by the police. Many have been placed under house arrest in cities hundreds of kilometres away from New Delhi.

The Cockroach movement says thousands have been detained across India as Modi’s government intensifies its crackdown. Yet undeterred protesters have pledged to keep returning to the streets.

Current restrictions in the Indian capital and the nationwide crackdown on protesters have evoked memories of the 1975 Emergency, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties, censored the press and jailed political opponents.

“Narendra Modi just made EMERGENCY official,” Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, wrote in a post on X. “This intimidation is not going to work, Modi. The youth of this country are no longer scared of you.”

Neha Bora, the firebrand Gen-Z protest leader and the national president of the left student body All India Students’ Association, equated the Modi government with British colonialist forces that unsuccessfully clamped down on India’s independence movement. She called on the masses to join the protest.

On Saturday morning, young people were trying to respond to her call despite the police restrictions in place.

Santosh Kumar, 29, a street sweeper in the outer circle of Connaught Place, told Al Jazeera he feels frustrated seeing teenagers detained at police barricades.

“How can you stop these kids? They are detaining 10; 50 more are coming. Modi, the dictator’s time is up: He will not even stay until 2029 (the time of the next elections).

“This is the time we turn Delhi into Nepal and Bangladesh – learn from them and take back our country,” he says, referring to youth-led movements in those countries.

Sameer Irshad, 28, an engineer from Gurugram, approached the barricades near Connaught Place while pushing his 57-year-old mother Sheeba Abdi in a wheelchair.

Abdi told us: “This sort of crackdown, where we cannot peacefully express our dissent, is unseen in Delhi. Why has government turned this place into a fortress? Why are they so scared of citizens like me?”

Last month, India was shaken by revelations of divisions within the supposedly autonomous body that is in charge of conducting elections, over controversial policies that critics say have disenfranchised tens of millions of people.

India’s Election Commission chief, Gyanesh Kumar, was accused of overruling concerns raised by the two other election commissioners about the integrity of ongoing changes in the voter database, an investigation by The Indian Express reported.

India is among the few countries to have taken an active approach to enrolling every last voter.

Critics say the ongoing revision of the voter list flips the foundational principle of Indian democracy: Demanding that citizens prove their voting rights, and disproportionately targeting economically weaker sections, minorities and other vulnerable groups in Indian society.

Arif, a 24-year-old district coordinator for the Students’ Federation of India, another left-wing student organisation to have joined the protest call, was locked in his home in Saharanpur, nearly 200km (125 miles) from New Delhi, on Thursday.

“Several police officials started beating my door out of nowhere late at night, asking my parents for details of my whereabouts,” Arif, who did not want to give his full name, told Al Jazeera from his home in Saharanpur, where he is currently ed under the police’s watch around the clock.

“They just want to stop me from going to Delhi for protest. They are threatening to book me under criminal cases and destroy my future,” he said, adding that this is the first time he has been subject to such detention.

“I really wanted to be in Delhi, to fight and reclaim our democracy. The time for Modi is over,” he said.

This week, Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BNP) celebrated his 25 years in office, starting with his years as chief minister of the western state of Gujarat – where he oversaw the infamous 2002 Muslim pogrom – and later as India’s prime minister since 2014.

But Modi has never looked weaker in power than now, analysts and Indian political observers argue.

In July, the Cockroach-led protests choked key New Delhi streets and forced out Modi’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

This time, Modi has taken more extreme measures to prevent protesters from gaining a foothold in central New Delhi, “because he wishes to retain the aura and image of a leader who never yields to public pressure, someone who is invincible”, said Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, an author and biographer of Modi.

“Modi appears at the lowest point [of his political life] in public perception. This is extremely paradoxical because he has some of the most important autonomous institutions, large sections of the bureaucracy, and state wings in tight control and acting at his behest,” Mukhopadhyay told Al Jazeera.

In the face of growing protests, Modi is now “fast losing people’s perception of being a leader who leads them out of livelihood pits”, he said.

Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court and a rights activist who planned to join the protest on Saturday, told Al Jazeera that “Modi’s government looks quite scared of the people.

“People in India are rising and demanding answers. And when the government gets scared, they adopt draconian measures to stay in power,” Bhushan said. “But only more and more people will rise from repression.”

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/us-fracki.title: How U.S. know-how is fracking Australia into a gas boom, from Texas oilmen to Trump’s energy secretary
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/us-fracki.author: Jordan Blum
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/us-fracki.text:
As the U.S. shale oil and gas revolution took off two decades ago, Australia took notice and wondered whether the boom could be replicated down under.

In September, the effort began to pay off, thanks to the arrival of American oilmen. The first commercial natural gas deliveries from the Beetaloo Basin started flowing to the energy-hungry Northern Territory. The potential is far greater, and little-known Tamboran Resources and Daly Waters Energy had to clear years of roadblocks to get here.

Sydney startup Tamboran first hired an American ExxonMobil and Chevron veteran as its CEO in 2013. In 2014, Texas oil legend Scott Sheffield joined the board of Aussie natural gas player Santos. He was intrigued by the prospect of bringing shale drilling and fracking expertise to the outback, particularly the sparsely populated reserve with a peculiar name: the Beetaloo Basin.

Sheffield saw the Beetaloo’s upside, and its similarity to the Appalachia’s Marcellus Shale. He brought it to the attention of his son, Bryan, also a Texas oil CEO. Bryan was interested but too busy taking his company, Parsley Energy, public. A few months later, shale pioneer Aubrey McClendon took a small land position in the Beetaloo and Bryan read about it.

“I just remember feeling deflated,” Bryan Sheffield told Fortune. “He got into the Beetaloo really early and cheap. I remember thinking to myself, ‘He’s just running circles around me.’”

McClendon died in a car accident a year later, and more setbacks would soon befall the basin. Amid the global pushback to fracking, the Northern Territory imposed a moratorium from 2016 to 2018. Santos and others had drilled with limited results but couldn’t replicate the American formula. COVID-19 then tanked global exploration budgets and most companies’ interest in the Beetaloo. Parsley suffered in the pandemic and was sold to Scott’s company, Pioneer Natural Resources, for $4.5 billion. Two years ago, ExxonMobil bought Pioneer for $60 billion, the largest U.S. oil deal of the century.

After the pandemic, Bryan Sheffield’s top geologist from Parsley again raised the Beetaloo. This time, Sheffield, armed with his own startup private equity firm, Formentera Partners, took the lead.

“This play keeps coming up. This is three times,” Bryan Sheffield said. It felt like a sign.

After investing heavily in the small Aussie gas players, Tamboran and Beetaloo Energy, Sheffield also started his own Australian subsidiary, Daly Waters Energy.

Fast forward four years, partners Daly Waters and Tamboran announced the first natural gas sales ever from the Beetaloo in September. The milestone shows the basin can deliver, but it still must prove it can become economic over the long term.

“This is a total gamechanger,” Sheffield said. Five wells are now ramping up. “We created revenue. This whole time, the past five years, we have not had $1 coming back to us.”

The timing matters, both for the money-losing companies and for Australia, which could face natural gas shortfalls in the coming years. The U.S., Australia, and Qatar are by far the top liquefied natural gas exporters. Qatar is largely offline now because of the Iran war, and more of Australia’s offshore gas fields are drying up. The answer may lie onshore, in Beetaloo shale.

Sheffield’s capital influx was critical, but so was recruiting top American oilfield services players with shale expertise. Drilling leader Helmerich & Payne (H&P), tools and services giant Baker Hughes, and fracking leader Liberty Energy—the company cofounded by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright—all took ownership stakes in Tamboran. Beetaloo Energy recently contracted with Halliburton.

“Applying the American [fracking] recipe to another country is the way forward,” Sheffield said. A newly built pipeline and gas processing plant now move the gas. “The big problem was the lack of service companies and infrastructure. Talking the service companies into moving into this play was key to unlocking it.”

“It’s kind of like in that movie, ‘Field of Dreams,” he added. “’If you build it, they will come.’”

A 1979 minerals drilling program triggered an accidental gas blowout in the Beetaloo. That drew the attention of U.S. oil and gas power Amoco, later acquired by BP, which drilled a test well in 1984. It came up dry. Others tried and failed too, despite survey data showing the basin’s gassy potential.

That was still 20 years before U.S. shale operators would crack the code for shale rock with the right mix of horizontal drilling and slickwater fracking. Slickwater uses a mix of water, sand, and thin, friction-reducing chemicals rather than thicker gels to shatter dense shale rock deep underground and free the gas.

In 2008, in Texas, geologist and Petrohawk Energy cofounder Dick Stoneburner—a great name for a shale rock expert—helped pioneer drilling and fracking and led the discovery of the Eagle Ford Shale oil boom in South Texas. Three years later, Australian mining giant BHP bought Petrohawk for $12 billion as its entry into U.S. shale. Stoneburner was contractually required to assist with the transition, which brought him to Australia.

Once free of his BHP obligation, he was recruited to Tamboran’s board in 2014. That was the year Santos drilled its first Beetaloo test well using modified shale techniques. The results were modest and didn’t wow investors, but they remained promising.

“I got intrigued,” Stoneburner told Fortune. “Santos had limited shale experience, really none. They had a big learning curve.”

Stoneburner saw Santos’ flaws and, eventually, so did Bryan Sheffield. The wells needed wider diameters (wider casing) and slickwater fracking, not gelled fluids, to sustain enough pressure to produce ample gas flows. That required equipment available only in the U.S.

“This is when I knew the play was going to work. They just weren’t doing it right,” Sheffield said. They discovered Australian rigs could only accommodate smaller diameters. “That’s when I knew I had to talk a rig company into moving horizontal rigs to Australia.”

The pitch was easier than expected. Coming out of the pandemic, services companies had excess equipment and were eyeing growth. H&P shipped a high-specification rig, Chris Wright’s Liberty brought a fracking fleet, and Baker Hughes supplied tools and services. “It’s not off-the-shelf stuff. So it’s all worked out very, very well,” Stoneburner said.

Sheffield was first impressed by the detailed report on the Beetaloo put together by his former geologist, Tom Layman. After the pandemic, he was put in touch with Stoneburner. They knew of each other but hadn’t met in person. Sheffield then met Tamboran’s CEO at the time, Alabama native Joel Riddle.

Rather than only invest in Tamboran, Sheffield bought stakes in Beetaloo Energy and Falcon Oil & Gas, which was acquired by Tamboran earlier this year. He also formed Daly Waters.

“He was ready to go,” Stoneburner said, surprised by Sheffield’s speed and aggressiveness.

The largest acreage holder in the Beetaloo was Australian utility Origin Energy. It lacked shale experience and had no clear plan for the land. Under investor pressure to decarbonize and avoid fracking, Origin weighed selling.

In 2022, Tamboran, flush with Sheffield’s capital, pounced. The group acquired Origin for just over $40 million, plus a portion of future royalties, and became the basin’s top player. Sheffield and Stoneburner credit Riddle with getting the deal done.

“Origin was a really huge domino to fall,” Stoneburner said.

“We split the deal because it was too much for [Tamboran] to take on alone, and I kind of just paid out of my family office,” Sheffield elaborated. Tamboran and Formentera-backed Daly Waters essentially halved the acreage, and Sheffield forming a joint venture on Tamboran’s operations. Today he controls nearly 10% of Tamboran stock.

Formentera’s usual strategy is “singles and doubles” in mature U.S. shale basins, and Sheffield’s early Australian equity stakes followed that approach. The Origin deal changed that.

“I knew my investors would not like the Beetaloo because there’s a lot of risk,” Sheffield said. “The pension funds and the endowments, they did not invest. It was just too risky for them. The Beetaloo is the home run product, and it’s more tailored toward family offices.”

Since the Origin deal closed, Tamboran and Daly Waters have brought in their services partners to Australia, built a pipeline and processing facility, finished early permitting, and developed the pilot project, Shenandoah South. It is now finally online and poised to ramp up. Daly Waters plans to add a second H&P rig next year.

Japan’s INPEX became a major investor early this year, supporting the eventual gas supply to Australia’s LNG facilities serving Japan and the rest of Asia, especially INPEX’s Ichthys LNG hub in northwestern Australia. Tamboran also is a joint venture partner with Santos, which operates two LNG facilities the Beetaloo could supply: Darwin LNG and Gladstone LNG.

Last year, Tamboran made a change and removed Riddle as CEO, naming Stoneburner interim CEO. Scott Sheffield joined the board at the same time. He had served only three years on Santos’ board. Riddle is rightfully credited with building Tamboran up, but he also clashed with partners.

“I was there to help mend relationships,” Stoneburner said, which led to Tamboran’s Falcon acquisition.

In January, Tamboran hired Houston-based Todd Abbott—a 15-year veteran under Scott Sheffield’s Pioneer and a friend of Stoneburner. Bryan Sheffield also backed the move. “I was trained as an oilman underneath Scott Sheffield and his people, and Todd Abbott is the exact same,” he said. “We come from the same learning curves.”

Abbott read last year’s news of Stoneburner’s interim role and sent a text. “He just replied back, ‘We should talk,’” Abbott told Fortune.

Abbott’s most fun years were the “grow, grow, grow” days of the Permian Basin’s early shale oil boom at Pioneer. Now, he said, U.S. shale is about, “How do I get another penny out of it?” each day. Tamboran offers a chance to build a pioneering position in a basin again, a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.”

“First production is the really big milestone,” Abbott said of the Beetaloo. “But it’s certainly not the finish line. It’s more of the starting line.”

The Beetaloo’s rock closely resembles the Marcellus Shale of Pennsylvania and West Virginia, though the Beetaloo is 1.3 billion years old versus the Marcellus’ nearly 400 million.

Early well results are promising, Abbott said, but more are needed in the coming weeks and months to attract new investors and partners. Tamboran admits it needs a larger partner to keep scaling. Its stock is up more than 25% this year, but a new auditor’s report still flags its financial viability as a “going concern.” It isn’t profitable yet and is only now booking first revenue. “We’re out looking for the right strategic partner for the long term,” Abbott said.

Production is ramping up to 40 million cubic feet of gas per day. The plan is to grow to 100 million in 2028, once a gas-processing expansion is complete. The goal after that is more drilling and another pipeline by 2030. That would supply more Australia domestic gas beyond the Northern Territory and feed LNG exports. Until now, the territory has relied on emergency contracts with LNG exporters for gas-fired electricity.

“Once it’s fully connected, the Beetaloo is multiple times large enough to supply the Australian domestic market. It takes care of the expected shortage,” Abbott said. “But to really get this basin up to the scale, it needs LNG export access.”

Australian entrepreneur Patrick Elliott founded Tamboran in 2009 and remains on the board, but the Beetaloo quickly became an American-Aussie venture. “Seventeen years is a long time, but there was a lot of work to do, and it’s accelerating now,” Abbott said. “It’s an exponential curve, and you’re starting to see real traction.”

Nothing has underscored the Beetaloo’s potential this year more than the Iran war, which has kept Qatar’s LNG exports largely offline. That leaves the the world, especially Asia-Pacific, heavily dependent on U.S. and Australian LNG, and Australia will need more natural gas to ship. “It has focused everyone on the need for diversifying,” Abbott said. “Supply chains are critical, and energy security is national security.” He added that Australia can supply Asia more cheaply than the U.S. because of shorter shipping distances.

About 75% of Australia’s natural gas production is offshore, which limits growth. The rest was onshore coalbed methane, or coal seam gas, and those resources aren’t in growth mode either.

“There are really not a lot of other sources of this scale in the Asia-Pacific that can do it,” Abbott said. “I think it really put eyes on Australia and on the Beetaloo at a pretty critical moment for us.”
