https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/guitar-ce.title: Guitar Center is dropping its ban on playing ‘Stairway to Heaven.’ It’s part of the CEO’s big turnaround plan
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/guitar-ce.author: Phil Wahba
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/guitar-ce.text:
Musicians often see an instrument as a physical extension of themselves and that sort of connection doesn’t always lend itself to the online shopping experience.

“Selecting a musical instrument is a deeply, deeply personal experience,” says Gabe Dalporto, CEO of Guitar Center. It’s something you have to touch and hear and smell for yourself. A guitar that seems appealing on a website might not speak to a player trying it out in real life, Dalporto says.

Dalporto, 56, is a true believer in the need for brick-and-mortar stores, and he’s made them a pillar of his turnaround of Guitar Center, the once-bankrupt music instrument retailer that’s betting big on customers’ desire for an in-person shopping experience, where newbie and veteran musicians alike can tinker with instruments and tap into employees’ know-how.

Guitar Center’s comeback is still a work in progress, but Dalporto, a nuclear engineer by training and bona fide music nerd, wants the retailer to offer the vast inventory of a big-box store while fostering a sense of community usually reserved for independent music retailers. “The No. 1 thing I get from independents is that they personally know their customers,” he says, “and that’s what I want us to get to.”

Guitar Center is just now recovering from its epic, six-year COVID hangover.

During the pandemic, millions of Americans took up new hobbies to pass the time; some baked sourdough loaves, others took up the ukulele or guitar. A surge in online sales was a lifeline for Guitar Center as lockdowns shuttered its stores. Digital sales doubled in 2020 but remained a small percentage of the business.

To keep up with the surge in new hobbyists, Guitar Center made the ill-advised move of doubling down on inexpensive instruments that appealed to beginners at the expense of its core customer, the more serious musician. When sales came back down to earth, Guitar Center had the wrong merchandise on hand, a problem that was hard to remedy as Chinese factory shutdowns caused supply chain chaos.

“Because of all the beginners moving into the market, it just really got us out of position on our inventory, and it took us a long time to get back,” Dalporto says.

On top of store closures and unsold inventory, the company was choking on enormous debt from a private equity buyout in 2014. The music nearly stopped in late 2020, when Guitar Center sought Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

Even after Guitar Center emerged from bankruptcy protection with a smaller debt load, it struggled to find its place in the market. Sweetwater, an online music instruments retailer, had swept in to steal market share with more serious musicians, while mass retailers like Walmart were attracting entry-level guitarists.

It was clear to Dalporto that Guitar Center had to refocus its efforts back on the guitar aficionado. (He was on the board during bankruptcy reorganization and became CEO in 2023.) Nine out of 10 beginner guitarists are not playing one year after picking up the instrument, so catering to those newbies meant a lot of churn, Dalporto says. The retailer had to constantly hunt for new customers, and even when it found them, they were typically buying from Guitar Center’s inventory of cheap guitars, which, Dalporto concluded, took up too much space in stores. “A beginner doesn’t need 200 guitar choices,” he quips. (Dalporto’s most-prized guitar is a 1964 Fender Stratocaster, a gift from his father.)

During COVID, some 75% of Guitar Center’s assortment was aimed at beginners, while 25% was dedicated to the serious musician. Now those percentages are reversed.

The strategy has helped Guitar Center get back on track: it has reported 10 straight quarters of sales growth. Guitar Center generated $2.6 billion in annual revenue in 2025, up 4% from 2024. In recent years, business has also benefited from factors outside the company’s control, like a country music resurgence boosting the sale of acoustic guitars and Taylor Swift inspiring more young women to take up the instrument.

At the same time, overall guitar sales have been in slight but years-long decline so growth has to come at rivals’ expense. On Dalporto’s watch, Guitar Center has leaned into relatively new, faster-growing areas like DJ equipment, keyboards, drums, and recording studio gear. It’s also strengthening its second-hand guitar business.

There are parallels between Guitar Center and two other big-box chains looking to protect their turf from online competitors: Best Buy in electronics and Barnes & Noble in books. All three are aiming to make their chains more like local mom-and-pop stores.

“If all you have is Amazon, you have no local music gear community, and that’s really what we have to be,” Dalporto says.

Dalporto says he sees James Daunt’s vaunted revitalization of Barnes & Noble as a model to replicate, and he finds inspiration from independents like the Chicago Music Exchange, which he admires for its selection, sense of community, and high level of service.

To capture some of that essence, Guitar Center is trying to make its stores a place to hang out for novices and pros alike. It’s launching open mic nights for local musicians and just held a national ‘Drum Off’ competition where 2,600 drummers performed across its stores. It also dropped its unofficial in-store ban on playing Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven,” a favorite of newbies, to foster a more welcoming environment.

Guitar Center wants its staff to match customers’ enthusiasm for music, whatever their skill level.

“I want to be able to profitably put more labor in the stores,” says Dalporto. “Over time, we are going to be able to deliver a much better customer experience and that will drive additional revenue.”
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/guitar-ce.summary: Guitar Center CEO Gabe Dalporto wants to offer big-box stores to customers. Dalporta wants to see more local community. Guitar Centre has reported 10 straight quarters of sales growth.

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: 'Constructive discussions': US, Europe and Ukraine work on joint plan to end war
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
US, Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Friday in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with Washington seeking a way out of the dangerous stalemate.

The talks were overshadowed by US President Donald Trump's announcement of a deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to boost diesel supplies, underscoring how the conflict has become entwined with soaring energy prices.

US envoy Steve Witkoff posted to X after the meeting that the "constructive discussions" tackled "potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace."

Witkoff said the meeting included "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO."

The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and "longer-term arrangements for Ukraine's and Europe's security to prevent future conflict," Witkoff said.

He also noted the "productive" exchange discussed supporting Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession."

Witkoff did not say if the parties would meet on Saturday as originally planned.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Thursday that the conflict had reached a potentially explosive impasse, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.

"The other way that stalemates end is through escalation," Rubio told reporters in Lisbon, warning that the conflict could spread to neighboring NATO countries.

"We do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict," he added.

Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging fuel prices, although the US-Israeli war with Iran has been the principal disruptor of global energy supplies.

Following a telephone call with Putin on Friday, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November.

The US Treasury Department said it was issuing a temporary license to allow Russian diesel to flow to global markets. It was not immediately clear whether Trump and Putin had discussed Ukraine during their call.

The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, a longtime Trump confidant, and Kushner, the president's son-in-law, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.

US negotiators have since been developing fresh proposals with Russian and Ukrainian officials, a source familiar with the discussions told AFP.

With winter approaching, the prospect of continued fighting and attacks on vital infrastructure has added urgency to the search for a settlement.

The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk that killed 30 people.

Trump's repeated attempts to broker an end to the war have foundered over Moscow's sweeping territorial demands, particularly its insistence on controlling all of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, including areas still held by Kyiv.

Zelensky has rejected surrendering Ukrainian-held territory, warning that Russia could use it as a springboard for another attack.

Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

European officials have expressed concern over high energy costs and the wider economic consequences of the conflict, according to the US sources.

Witkoff and Kushner briefed the president on their latest proposals on Thursday at a meeting also attended by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior officials, Axios reported.

The US administration hopes to make diplomatic headway before November's midterm elections, with Washington also seeking to arrange broader talks involving Russia and Ukraine later this month.

The Kremlin has signaled that such three-way negotiations could resume in October, although no date has been announced.

(FRANCE24 with AFP, REUTERS)

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.title: How DNA ‘fingerprinting’ is keeping Malaysia’s green turtles safe from poachers
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.author: Ushar Daniele
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.text:
Decades of conservation have helped Malaysia’s green turtles recover, but tight budgets, fuel costs and poachers threaten progress

As dawn breaks on Mataking Island off Sabah’s east coast, a tiny green turtle crawls across the sand, driven by instinct towards the surf before disappearing into the ocean on a journey that could cover thousands of kilometres.

The hatchling is one of tens of thousands that emerge from Sabah’s beaches each year, as the species continues a remarkable recovery after decades of conservation efforts to reverse its decline.

Today, Mataking Island – a teardrop-shaped outcrop in the Celebes Sea – is a luxury diving retreat. At low tide, a sandbar dubbed “Moses Crossing” connects its smaller islets, where visitors are greeted by green turtles of all sizes grazing on seagrass among the reefs.

Green turtles have staged a miraculous comeback in recent years. In 2025, they were reclassified from ‘endangered’ to ‘least concern’ – becoming the first marine turtle species to move out of the threat categories on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, which tracks the global extinction risk and conservation status of animals, plants and fungi.

Science has played a vital role in protecting these shelled aquatic reptiles. When they hatch, they are just a few inches long and weigh about as much as a single battery – yet as adults, they grow up to 1.2 metres (4ft) in length and weigh a hefty 200kg (440lbs).

“Turtles don’t stay in one place. They cross borders,” marine biologist Juanita Joseph told This Week in Asia, explaining the need for a system to “fingerprint” the reptiles.

Joseph is working at the University of Malaysia Sabah to help build ShellBank, a global DNA database of marine turtle populations.

Every two to four years, mature females return to the exact beaches where they hatched to lay their eggs. But in between, they cross vast stretches of ocean to reach feeding grounds far beyond Malaysia’s borders.

In Sabah’s Turtle Islands Park, conservation efforts date back decades, with more than 20,000 nests recorded annually. Since 1977, Sabah Parks said more than 14 million hatchlings had been released from these islands.

It is a recovery that stands out against a bleaker global backdrop for wildlife. The WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026, published on Thursday, identified a 73 per cent decline in monitored vertebrate wildlife populations between 1970 and 2022.

Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF International, said concerted action is crucial to sustaining these gains, pointing to the green turtle as a rare bright spot.

“If those efforts stop, we can lose recovery,” Sumba said. “Positive tipping points and self-reinforcing feedback loops can help keep recovery on track and sustain it over the long term.”

But major challenges remain to ensure green turtles stay a conservation success story, Sabah Parks director Maklarin Lakim told This Week in Asia.

“These are marine parks and there are no boundaries that we can physically fence off,” he said. “We do not have many staff [and] the assets we have, such as boats, are also limited … costs are high, especially with the price of fuel now.”

Given these constraints, Sabah Parks’ marine protectors are not overly celebrating the green turtle’s improved status on the Red List, pointing to concerns over the much rarer hawksbill turtle.

“Even though we are happy about one species, for another species we are worried,” Maklarin said.

For marine biologists, building a complete picture of the population and habits of a creature on the move for most of its life is a constant challenge.

“If you want to save turtles, it’s not just one particular component at the beach. It’s the whole sea turtle life cycle,” said Gavin Jolis, marine species strategy manager at WWF-Malaysia.

The ShellBank database aims to track the health of nesting populations, their migration paths and how they navigate lives at sea that can span several decades.

Similarly, DNA collected from turtles at feeding grounds, from carcasses or taken from trafficked products can be matched back to their population of origin.

Joseph said her team began collecting genetic samples from Malaysian nesting beaches in 1998 and from feeding grounds in 2011, with those samples now contributing to ShellBank.

But the database remains a work in progress as researchers gather enough samples across nesting populations to fully map the region. Unlike satellite tracking, which follows individual animals and can be costly, genetic profiling enables researchers to map connections across entire populations.

Samples from turtle meat, shells or other products seized across the region can reveal whether they originated from populations in Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines or further afield.

“ShellBank is a tool. It’s only one of the tools that’s gonna help us with [the] conservation of turtles,” Joseph said.

As the sun peeks over the horizon on Mataking, a bale of turtle hatchlings scrambles across the sand, tiny flippers carrying them towards an ocean they will explore for decades to come.

The surviving females will eventually rely on their internal navigation systems to return to these same shores to lay the next generation of eggs – sustaining a cycle that conservationists have spent decades fighting to protect.

“‘Least Concern’ does not mean ‘no concern’,” Jolis said of the IUCN reclassification. “What it does show is that long-term conservation action is working.”

https://www.dw.com/en/indian-police-deta.title: Indian police detain 'Cockroach' movement founder and dozens of protesters in New Delhi. Follow live.
https://www.dw.com/en/indian-police-deta.text:
India's 'Cockroach' party says its leaders have been detained ahead of a major protest called by the collective. Protesters are calling for India's chief election commissioner to resign.

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday accused opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal of "attempting to incite tensions" in the country.

"The Govt of India will deal strictly with the attempts you are making to incite tension, and BJP workers, remaining constantly among the people, will effectively thwart your designs," BJP President Nitin Nabin told news agencies on Saturday morning.

"Your repeated electoral defeats in various states and the resulting desperation suggest that, in some way, you do not wish to see this country move forward peacefully. However, I warn you today that the BJP and the patriotic citizens of this country will give you a fitting and stern response," he said.

Nabin suggested that "foreign forces" were behind the opposition leaders and that the protests were an attempt to "destabilize" India. BJP leaders have made similar claims before without offering proof.

"I issue a clear warning to you today: the foreign forces upon which you rely for your politics up for sale—and the alliances with such forces through which you seek to destabilize India—will never allow your nefarious intentions to succeed," he said.

It's past noon here and Indian news channels are playing visuals of protesters trying to reach central Delhi, despite the mass preventive detentions taking place.

Several groups of young people have been seen running through the streets, trying to dodge police personnel and barricades.

News agency ANI reported, citing police sources, that more 200 people were detained in the key Connaught Place area as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site.

Here's the situation right now:

With this, it is unclear at the moment whether the planned protest will be able to take place.

But the CJP isn't the only group protesting against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star, Neha Bora, have been leading protests in the capital all week.

Also on the ground are the Gandhi siblings, lawmakers Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, who are leading the opposition alliance's protests against the poll body in New Delhi.

Rahul Gandhi is the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament and possibly Prime Minister Modi's biggest challenger in the 2029 elections. According to Indian media reports, Gandhi is scheduled to attend a political meeting in the southern city of Chennai today.

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday reiterated his demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down and critized the Modi government.

"Gyanesh Kumar will go. This government will go. Then the repair of democracy will begin," the Congress leader wrote on X as he shared a video of himself addressing INDIA bloc MPs in the Central Hall of Parliament.

Late on Friday, Gandhi and a delegation of opposition lawmakers met President Droupadi Murmu to submit a four-point memorandum.

The memorandum outlined what Gandhi called Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah's "gross subversion of India's electoral system" and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Delhi Police said in a statement that around 500 people were detained on Saturday as they arrived for the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party, news agency ANI reported.

"Around 500 people coming in different groups from various locations have been detained," ANI quoted the Delhi Police statement as saying.

The police added that an additional 50 people had been arrested and described them as "anti-social elements with criminal antecedents" who had been taken into custody to ensure that they "did not disturb" public order or "incite trouble."

Visuals aired by Indian news channels earlier showed police in central Delhi chasing young protesters before forcing them into vehicles and taking them away.

Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been detained by Delhi police, Indian media reported, as a preventative measure to block the planned protest against India's election chief in central Delhi.

According to reports by several media outlets, including India Today, authorities detained Dipke on board a flight after he landed in Delhi on Saturday morning. The news outlet quoted Dipke as saying, "I'm not afraid of you," while police officers urged him to cooperate.

The CJP's X handle soon released footage of the detention. "Shame on you Narendra Modi, Amit Shah," the caption read, referring to India's prime minister and home minister, respectively.

Authorities have also detained CJP's co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, as well as the group's legal aid head, Ratna Singh.

Right before being arrested, Dipke posted a video on Instagram, showing tens of Delhi police officers lining up outside his airplane to enter. "Love you, we'll do it together, Inqalab Zindabad," one of Dipke's associate is heard saying in the video's background.

'Inqalab Zindabad', meaning 'long live the revolution,' is a famous slogan used by Indian freedom fighters during their struggle against British rule. It has regularly been used by the Cockroach party against the Modi government.

The preventative arrests are part of a major crackdown on protesters this weekend.

Most of central Delhi, where the government is headquartered, is under an internet blackout and riddled with barricades, which authorities are using to identify and stop potential protesters.

Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) National President Nitin Nabin held a press conference in New Delhi, denouncing the CJP and opposition party protests over voter list irregularities as an attempt to "create a highly dangerous and serious situation in the country."

He described the INDIA bloc of opposition parties and the Cockroach movement as "two anarchic groups."

"Your 'anarchist competition,' vying to see who can create more instability in the country, will not succeed," Nabin said, accusing both groups of "a plot to destabilize the country."

"I want to say that you are undertaking these efforts, driven by your political agendas, at the behest of foreign forces," he said without elaborating on who the foreign forces were.

Popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been detained by the police ahead of the Jantar Mantar protest, according to the CJP and Indian media reports.

"Dhruv Rathee has been detained. The Dictator is TERRIFIED of young people who question its wrongdoings and refuse to stay silent," the CJP wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Modi.

According to reports, Rathee was detained at his home in Gurugam. Earlier this week, the CJP officially launched Rathee as part of its "fight to save democracy" campaign.

The Germany-based YouTuber participated in a CJP protest in the southern Indian city of Bengaluru on Thursday.

CJP legal head Ratna Singh is also reported to have been detained at her home in New Delhi on Saturday.

After India's education minister, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement has Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in its crosshairs.

Here is a ten-point breakdown of the controversy surrounding the top election official:

Police have already detained some protesters who had started gathering at Jantar Mantar for the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest, ANI news agency reported.

On Friday the Delhi Police said that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law had been enforced in the New Delhi area, prohibiting all forms of assembly or protest.

Meanwhile, Indian news agencies reported that police had heightened security across the capital on Saturday, with flag marches and mock drills being conducted at several locations.

Entry and exit gates at several metro stations have also been closed, according to reports.

ANI also reported that spike strips had been deployed to deter protesters from moving through certain areas.

The protest is being dubbed by some as "Season 2" of the Cockroach movement in India. The first wave of protests culminated with the resignation of India's education minister over exam irregularities, a rare concession by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP party.

DW's Shalu Yadav takes a closer look at how the Indian government is preparing for CJP's latest protest call in this report:

The Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) founder, Abhijeet Dipke, was due to land at Delhi's main airport on Saturday morning as the movement plans to hold a mass protest calling for India’s Chief Election Commissioner to step down over sweeping voter roll revisions, despite being denied permission by police.

Police and paramilitary forces, which local media reported numbered around 43,000 personnel, were deployed ahead of the protest. Multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocked the concrete-grey roads leading to the Jantar Mantar protest site.

On Friday, authorities also ordered the closure of more than 50 metro stations and canceled many trains bound for two major railway stations in the capital.

But India's top court later directed the government to not completely halt train services and said there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.

The Supreme Court stressed the "principle of proportionality," urging authorities to allow the transportation services in a regulated manner to avoid public inconvenience.

"Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," legal news website Bar and Bench reported the court as saying.

On Saturday, Dipke denounced the Modi government over extensive restrictions.

"Modi has accepted defeat even before our protest has begun," the CJP chief wrote on X ahead of his arrival in the capital.

"The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength, but of a leader terrified of his own people."

The CJP is not the only group calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

India's bloc of opposition parties, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, has been carrying out a sustained campaign against Kumar in recent days, including organizing its own protest marches.

The country has seen dramatic visuals emerge from Delhi's key corridor of political power, showing leading opposition MPs, including Gandhi, being carried away to detention buses by uniformed police officials as they tried to dig their heels in.

The ire against India's election chief, who heads the country's independent Election Commission, is turning into one of the biggest public and political challenges for Modi during his three terms in office.

Opposition leaders and critics allege that a mass deletion of tens of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls benefits Modi's Prime Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi and this is a special edition of our daily India news blog.

As the early morning hours tick away, a countdown to a rally against India's top poll official over alleged voter list irregularities has begun in the heart of the world's largest democracy.

India's "Cockroaches" are once again headed to Jantar Mantar —  the same protest site where the online satirical movement sprung to the mainstream as a youth-led pressure group in July after forcing the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's then education minister.

Police have denied the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) permission to hold the demonstration, but the group's leaders are urging people from across the country to converge on Jantar Mantar, calling the protest a "fundamental right."

A showdown between police and protesters appears imminent.

New Delhi, particularly its central areas, have effectively been turned into a fortress under a heavy security blanket, including thousands of paramilitary personnel, a rare mobile internet blackout, train cancellations and police warnings against any protest gathering.

The security measures come while memory are still fresh of a clashes between youth demonstrators and police during the July Cockroach protest. Police used batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns to disperse the crowd.

Several injuries were reported. Protesters alleged police brutality, while police said force was used only after the demonstration ceased to be peaceful.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of military-linked Myanmar businessman
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
The United States has removed sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the military-installed government.

The US Department of the Treasury removed Theint Win Htet from its sanctions list on Friday, according to its website, after she sued them in July.

The decision followed a Reuters news agency report that said US President Donald Trump’s administration has opened talks with Myanmar’s government, a break from years of US policy that sanctioned the generals responsible for a coup in 2021 against Myanmar’s democratically elected government.

In January 2024, the Treasury Department under former President Joe Biden’s administration targeted the Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies, which was founded by Theint Win Htet’s father, Thein Win Zaw, along with his family.

The department said the company supplied fuel to the military and owned at least 20 firms with close ties to the military leadership.

Theint Win Htet originally requested her removal in a lawsuit filed against the Biden administration. That case was dismissed last year. She then filed a second complaint in July, arguing that she has no role in her father’s business.

The sanctions had blocked her US credit cards, restricted her foreign bank accounts and forced her to abandon her master’s degree at Columbia University in New York. She now lives in Thailand with her mother, who was taken off the US sanctions list last year.

Theint Win Htet’s lawyer, Washington, DC-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the federal court in the US capital on Friday to voluntarily dismiss the lawsuit after her delisting.

The group Justice For Myanmar has condemned the Treasury Department’s decision, saying Myanmar’s military is escalating attacks on civilians.

“It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta’s terror,” the ‌group ‌said.

The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military officers and companies after the 2021 coup, which sparked a civil war that has killed about 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

Washington lifted sanctions in July last year on several other Myanmar nationals and a company accused of aiding the military.

Cristiano Ronaldo returned to club football action on Friday after a controversial international break with Portugal and scored the opening goal as Al-Nassr beat Diriyah 3-0 in the Saudi Pro League.

The victory put the defending champions level on points behind leader Al-Qadsiah on goal difference in the eighth round.

During the international window, the 41-year-old Ronaldo walked out of the Portugal squad, for which he has scored 146 goals in 234 appearances.

In a long statement posted on Tuesday, Ronaldo said Portugal coach Jorge Jesus had not been true to his word about when he would play the striker in the Nations League.

Ronaldo won the Saudi Arabia title in May with Jesus as Al-Nassr coach, and opened the scoring on Friday midway through the first half.

Kingsley Coman’s shot from outside the area was blocked by goalkeeper Waleed Abdullah, and Ronaldo was there to shoot home the rebound from close range for goal number 980 in his career.

Samu Costa added a second for Al-Nassr, coached by former Tottenham Hotspur boss Ange Postecoglou, just before the break, and Coman sealed the win with 13 minutes remaining.

Al-Qadsiah earlier thrashed Al-Kholood 5-0, with Dutch international Tijjani Reijnders opening the scoring and Italy’s Mateo Retegui and Mexico’s Julian Quinones also finding the target.

https://www.zdnet.com/uncategorized/ring.title: Ring’s new smart lock has a manual fallback that can’t lock you out – how it works
https://www.zdnet.com/uncategorized/ring.author: Maria Diaz
https://www.zdnet.com/uncategorized/ring.text:
The brand just announced a smart lock with a manual 'power dial' that charges the device in case it dies.

October 10, 2026, 4:15 am ET

For as much as Ring has carved itself a spot in the home security market, the brand still doesn’t have a smart lock — though that’s about to change. A new Ring Smart Lock was just announced this week, expanding the Ring ecosystem and Alexa devices.

Also: 7  privacy settings I change ASAP on every new phone – here’s why

The Ring Smart Lock attempts to safeguard against power loss with a unique dial that generates electricity by manually turning it. This is useful if your smart lock dies, since you can simply power it long enough to open your door and get inside.

Imagine coming home from an extended vacation, only to find that your smart lock’s battery died while you were gone. Instead of carrying a physical key in an emergency like this, you can turn the dial on the external smart lock body until the pad lights up to enter your PIN or scan your fingerprint. This totals four different ways the lock can be functional: a fingerprint reader, the keypad, the Ring app, or via Alexa.

Once you get inside, you can pop out the lock’s Quick Release Ultra battery pack and recharge it at home without worrying about replacing batteries. As for different ways to unlock, the Ring Smart Lock supports fingerprint scanning, PIN codes (including temporary codes), Alexa commands, and the Ring app.

Also: Still live – Best October Prime Day 2026 TV deals: Most are actually at Best Buy

As a Ring product, it’s expected to work seamlessly within a Ring and/or Amazon Alexa ecosystem. You can connect multiple compatible devices and control them with Alexa or the Ring app for efficiency.

The idea of a smart lock you can still open with a dead battery sounds quite attractive and is something I’d prefer over carrying a backup key. The underlying idea here is that you have a lock that won’t ever be inoperable — if it dies, you can instantly power it up again.

Aside from the fact that I don’t like carrying a physical key, a hand-crank smart lock that you can quickly use if the battery dies is great for kids and family members. My oldest kid likes unlocking the door every day after school, and having a backup they can use to still unlock it if the battery dies is better than me having to rescue them with a key.

Other locks let you use a 9V battery or a portable battery plugged in via a USB-C port, but that can be far from helpful in an emergency. I don’t carry around 9V batteries, and I don’t always have a portable one with a cable.

We’re still missing a lot of information about the Ring Smart Lock, including battery life estimates, Matter compatibility, and third-party integrations. We also don’t know how many turns or how much you need to turn the power dial, but that’s something we’ll test when the lock is available. I’d like to see some of these integrations in the final product.

Though we only know the Ring Smart Lock will launch in early 2027, there isn’t a set date for availability yet. Amazon says it’ll come in three finishes: black, silver, and brass. In terms of pricing, it’ll cost $250. You can sign up to be notified when the smart lock becomes available for purchase.

https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.title: 'All human emotions': French astronaut Sophie Adenot's first words since returning to Earth
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20261.text:
French astronaut Sophie Adenot went through "all human emotions, from the most joyful to the hardest" during her eight months in space, she said back on solid ground on Saturday in Germany.

Adenot splashed down in the Pacific Ocean Thursday off the coast of California in the Dragon capsule that carried Crew-12, having returned to Earth from a mission on the International Space Station (ISS).

She had spent a total of 235 days in space, breaking the record for the longest uninterrupted orbital stay by a European astronaut.

At 400km away from Earth, Adenot could see there are "no divisions, no borders" but "just a precious planet that we all share", she said Saturday on the tarmac of the European Space Agency (ESA) training centre in Cologne, occasionally in tears.

The 44-year-old astronaut looked visibly weakened on her arrival in Germany and was assisted by two ESA physicians.

In space, the body adapts to the absence of gravity, which leads to bone loss, muscle wasting, cardiovascular deconditioning and even visual problems.

Adenot must now begin an intensive recovery program of about three weeks to regain her pre-flight condition.

"It's a cocktail of astonishing emotions, it's incredible. It's great to be back on Earth, but it also comes with its share of challenges, especially physiological ones," she told a press conference.

She also described the "difficult" moment of Thursday's splashdown, when the capsule bringing back the four astronauts on her team had to endure "a lot of waves for 25 minutes".

"And when the commandos pulled me out of the capsule, the first thing I said to them was, 'Send me back to space, please!' It was much easier up there," she added.

During the mission, Adenot became the first French female astronaut to venture outside the space station for a spacewalk. In all, she undertook three spacewalks on August 18 and 25, and September 1.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/b.title: Zach Bates qualifies on pole for Bathurst 1000
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Bates will start from pole position after a stunning drive on Saturday.  (Getty Images: Daniel Kalisz)

Zach Bates has qualified on pole for Sunday's Bathurst 1000, topping the time sheets during the Top 10 Shootout at Mount Panorama.

Qualifying king Brodie Kostecki failed to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions, finishing second.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

Supercars rookie Zach Bates — not qualifying king Brodie Kostecki — will start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position.

Kostecki was on track to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions after laying a mighty lap of two minutes and 4.4912 seconds as the fifth driver in Saturday's top-10 shootout.

Proven race winners Will Brown, David Reynolds and Anton De Pasquale tried, but failed to beat Kostecki's time.

But provisional pole-sitter Bates refused to waver, proving his mettle as the last driver with a searing lap around the famous Mount Panorama track.

Bates denied Kostecki with a scorching lap of Mt Panorama.  (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone )

A day after becoming the fastest Gen3 racer, the 22-year-old clocked 2:04.2062 to deny Kostecki by 0.285 seconds.

Bates had earlier become the first to go below the 2:04 benchmark in the Gen3 era after taking provisional pole with a time of 2:03.9376.

In just his second pursuit of the holy grail of Australian motorsport, Bates is the third rookie to claim pole position after Klaus Ludwig (1987) and Marcos Ambrose (2001).

The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.

His surprise success comes after his mother Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished 10th as part of the Triple Eight Race Engineering wildcard with the great Craig Lowndes.

Team 18 driver De Pasquale will start in the second row with fourth-fastest Cooper Murray, while series leader Matt Payne was 10th.

But Grove Racing star Payne will be far from disheartened, given he had started from 18th en route to last year's epic wet-weather triumph with former co-driver Garth Tander.

Reynolds will start on the grid in eighth after a family of ducks threatened to derail his bid for a second Bathurst 1000 title.

Tickford co-driver Mark Winterbottom was forced to a sudden halt when ducks were spotted crossing the track at Conrod Straight during practice on Friday.

Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

Winterbottom's sudden braking caught out Reynolds' co-driver James Courtney, who locked up and slammed into the rear of the Tickford Ford Mustang.

But both cars were able to return to complete the 60-minute practice session before the shootout.

Defending Supercars champion Chaz Mostert was among the big names to miss out on the top-10 shootout and will start from 16th for the best qualifying result in the Toyota Supra.

Payne's teammate Kai Allen fell agonisingly short in 11th, while title contender Broc Feeney was 12th ahead of Cam Waters in 13th.

Kostecki's rookie teammate Rylan Gray will start from the back row with Ryan Wood after the duo crashed out in separate incidents in Friday's first practice session.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx30.title: Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx30.text:
No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.

Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.

As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.

She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.

He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.

In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.

On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.

"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.

"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."

As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.

Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.

Its name? Stop the Wedding.

It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.

"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used."

What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?

"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"

Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify.

On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships.

"I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity.

"It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system."

The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether.

A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations.

It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music.

After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter.

She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words.

The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career.

Her then-husband was not impressed.

"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'.

"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time."

It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit.

Moral of The Story (key lyric: "you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You.

Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming.

When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month.

"There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now.

"It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her."

In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness.

"I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music."

For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing.

She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records.

Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently.

"You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom.

"There's a real groundedness."

The same can't be said for her new album, Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top.

Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner.

"God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs.

Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line.

It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey.

"We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says.

"It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo."

The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.

"You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings.

Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments.

And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding.

Ashe's album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx30.summary: Ashe Willson's new album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-1476.title: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-1476.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-1476.text:
An armored vehicle with a banner warning citizens against unlawful gathering stands near the venue of a youth protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Manish Swarup)

Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.

Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.

The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators.

Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.

Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.

Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site

Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.

"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.

Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"

The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.

"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.

India's voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns

The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.

The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.

The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.

The commission and the government deny the allegations.

India's youth movement broadens campaign against Modi

For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.

For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: Ada Yonath obituary
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Mick O'Hare
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
Nobel prizewinning biochemist who succeeded against the odds in mapping the ribosome

For years, the crystallographer and biochemist Ada Yonath had to contend with the disdain and sometimes derision of many of her contemporaries after she set herself the challenge of mapping the molecular structure of the ribosome.

Ribosomes are found in all living cells. Effectively they are tiny factories that synthesise proteins, complex molecules that are vital for building and repairing the tissues and organs of animals and plants. Many scientists believed hers was a fruitless endeavour because ribosomes are so small – sometimes only 20 nanometres in diameter – irregular in shape and lacking internal symmetry. James Watson, one of the Nobel prizewinning discoverers of the double-helix structure of DNA, had tried and failed. But Yonath, who has died aged 87, proved her doubters wrong, and was rewarded with the 2009 Nobel prize in chemistry, only the fourth woman to receive it, which she shared with the biologist Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and biochemist Thomas Steitz.

“I was met with disbelief, even ridicule in the international scientific community,” she said later. “I was called a dreamer, a fantasist, even the village idiot. But when I succeeded, it created an overwhelming internal joy and those who once called me crazy or stupid became supporters.”

It was in the late 1970s, while being laid up following a bicycle accident, and indulging in some “easier” reading, that Yonath, then a young scientist based at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, chanced upon the article that would lead to her eventual breakthrough. Reading about the biology of polar bears, she learned that the bears pack their ribosomes in an orderly way in their cells prior to hibernating. “These stay intact and functional for months. So, if polar bears knew how to do it, we could too,” she reasoned.

Yonath surmised that, if she could crystallise an organism, and hence its ribosomes, she would be able to study their internal structure using X-rays and electron microscopy. However, ribosomes are fragile. Unlike other cell parts, they have no outer protective membrane and are easily damaged. Figuring that ribosomes of organisms that live in harsh conditions were likely to be hardier and more able to survive crystallisation, she attempted to crystallise the thermophile bacteria Geobacillus stearothermophilus, found in austere environments around thermal vents and in desert sands.

It took more than 25,000 attempts, but in the mid-80s, Yonath succeeded. She then froze the bacteria at –185°C, to stabilise its internal structure and to protect it from the X-rays, a technique she was an early successful pioneer of, now known as cryo bio-crystallography. Finally, in 2001 and 2002, after almost two decades of research, Yonath’s team succeeded in mapping, in three dimensions, the bacteria’s ribosome.

The significance of this discovery extended beyond pure science. Many antibiotics work by binding to sites on a bacterium’s ribosome, stopping it from reproducing. Previously, making antibiotics was a hit-and-miss process because often they would attack human ribosomes as well as those of the bacteria. But, armed with knowledge of the structure of different ribosomes, scientists could now deduce where on a ribosome an antibiotic would bind and so make the necessary structural alterations to the drug.

Yonath demonstrated how more than 20 antibiotics function, paving the way for new products, and also studied how antibiotic resistance might be overcome. The Nobel committee specifically noted this work in its citation, highlighting the “fundamental and medically important aspects of ribosome function” leading to “the development of novel antibiotic drugs in the ongoing medical struggle against ever emerging drug resistance among bacterial pathogens”.

Born in Jerusalem, into an Orthodox Jewish family, Ada was the elder daughter of parents who had emigrated from Poland to what was then British-mandated Palestine in 1933. Her father, Hillel Lifshitz, a rabbi and grocer, died when she was 11. Her mother, Esther, then moved with her two daughters to Tel Aviv, where she became a clerk. Despite her modest income, she recognised her daughter’s keen intellect and obtained her a place at the fee-paying Tichon Hadash high school, where Ada taught maths lessons in lieu of school fees.

In 1959, after two years of mandatory military service, she returned to Jerusalem to take a degree in chemistry at the Hebrew University, graduating in 1962, then a master’s in biochemistry (1964). Four years later she received a PhD from the Weizmann Institute for studies into the structure of collagen using X-ray crystallography.

She accepted postdoctoral positions in the US, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Carnegie Mellon University, in Pittsburgh, before returning to the Weizmann Institute, where, in 1970, she began her research into ribosomes and where she remained for the rest of her career. Despite the scepticism of many of her peers, she did receive long-term support and funding from Heinz-Günter Wittman at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in Berlin, frequently travelling to Germany to exchange data and compare notes.

In addition to her Nobel prize, Yonath received numerous awards, including the 2007 Wolf prize in chemistry, second only in importance to the Nobel, and was elected as a foreign member of the UK’s Royal Society.

Outside her work, Yonath was politically outspoken and critical of the Israeli government. Most recently, she criticised Israeli judicial reforms as a “genuine peril to democracy” and to Israeli scientific enterprise.

In 2018, when asked what qualities made a good scientist, she said: “Curiosity, first. Second, curiosity. And third, curiosity. Also, one has to love, and not be afraid of, a challenge.”

Her marriage to Moshe Yonath, a schoolteacher, ended in divorce. Her daughter, Hagith, and a granddaughter, Noa, survive her.

Ada Esther Yonath, crystallographer and biochemist, born 22 June 1939; died 31 August 2026

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Isaias weakens after making landfall in US Gulf Coast as hurricane
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Hurricane Isaias has crashed into the United States Gulf Coast before losing speed and turning into a post-tropical storm as it moved over southern Alabama, threatening flash flooding and strong winds farther inland.

The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Saturday that Isaias is about 89km (55 miles) south-southwest of Montgomery, with maximum ⁠sustained winds of 100 kilometres per hour (65 ⁠miles per hour).

When it made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), the agency said.

Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways.

While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.

Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended their emergency response on Friday night because of dangerous conditions.

Parts of southern Alabama were also flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines.

Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.

More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.

One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could reach 0.91-1.52 metres (3-5ft) from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Florida’s Aucilla River, according to the hurricane centre.

The storm grounded most Friday flights at several airports, including all flights in and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport.

Asked about hurricane preparations, President Donald Trump ⁠told reporters outside the White House, “We’re watching it very ⁠closely, the hurricane,” adding that it was “under control”.

Florida’s National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, with search-and-rescue teams ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.

“Emergency declarations have ‌been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X, as residents ‌were urged to take shelter and watch out for hurricane conditions.

Another tropical storm, Rachel, was also expected to bring strong winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

And Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrelled towards Mexico’s coast early on Saturday.

The NHC said Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 225km/h (140mph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane.

Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along the coast of Jalisco and in parts of Michoacan, Colima, and Nayarit.

Forecasters warned of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: West Indies beat India as Hope’s hundred secures record T20 chase
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Shai Hope has hit an unbeaten 102 off only 45 balls as the West Indies have beaten India in their highest successful Twenty20 run chase.

Hope hit nine sixes and six boundaries on Friday in his second T20 hundred as the West Indies finished with 252-4 in reply to India’s 249-5 and won by six wickets in Ranchi, India, with nine balls to spare.

Overall, it was the second highest successful run chase in T20 history. South Africa’s 259-4 was the highest against the West Indies in March.

Sherfane Rutherford played another supporting role to Hope with 84 off 37 balls, including seven sixes and seven fours.

For India, Sanju Samson scored 82 off 41 balls.

The five-match series stands at 1-1. Indore hosts the third T20 on Sunday.

The West Indies brought in left-arm spinner Gudakesh Motie and made India bat.

Samson and Abhishek Sharma scored 42 runs in 24 balls. Ishan Kishan hit a quick-fire 43 off 22 balls, and Samson reached 50 off 21 balls. Overall, he hit four sixes and nine fours.

India took 79-1 in the powerplay and brought up 100 off 8.1 overs. The Kishan-Samson partnership added 97 off only 43 balls.

Roston Chase then bowled Kishan in the 12th over and Shivam Dube two overs later. Chase finished with 3-24 in four overs.

India was down to 162-4 in the 15th over when Samson fell to Shamar Springer.

Shreyas Iyer hit 40 off 18 balls, accompanied by Tilak Varma’s 44 not out off 18 balls as the duo helped India finish on a high after hitting six sixes between them.

Despite their partnership of 83 from 32 balls, India fell shy of 250 but still achieved its eighth highest total in T20s.

Hope then led the West Indies’ charge by smoking 50 off 24 balls while losing three partners in the powerplay.

Mayank Yadav (3-36) bowled opener Kamil Pooran on four and Shimron Hetmyer for a golden duck.

Hope and Rovman Powell (24) resurrected the innings before Yadav got his third and bowled Powell.

That brought Hope and Rutherford together, and they added 120 off 54 balls.

Kuldeep Yadav sent back Rutherford in the 15th over, and the West Indies were still some distance away.

Romario Shepherd hit 34 off 13 balls with three sixes to provide the finishing flourish.

At the other end, Hope reached 100 off 45 balls, his second 50 coming off 21 balls.

It was Hope’s third century against India in four innings across T20s and ODIs.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Liam O'Hare
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
London, United Kingdom – Nearly 200 people packed into Edami, a small Lebanese bakery in east London, to celebrate a decade of Lajee Celtic, a grassroots sports club based in a Palestinian refugee camp in the occupied West Bank.

What began as a football project has grown into an international symbol of solidarity.

In London, the room was filled with Palestinian flags, the aroma of Edami’s freshly baked manousheh, and Lajee Celtic shirts – which have been worn by celebrities, including football icon Eric Cantona and the actor Hannah Einbinder.

Martin, a Lajee Celtic organiser, travelled down from Glasgow for the celebration in September. He first visited Aida Camp, in the occupied West Bank, more than 10 years ago, a trip he described as life-changing.

“I don’t think anyone would really have expected that the project would have been as successful as it’s been,” said Martin, who requested to be identified by his first name. “But Celtic is a unique football club with its foundation, its Irish identity, the diaspora community, its universal support and then the values, which tie so much of that together.”

The relationship between Aida Camp, where Lajee is based, and Celtic supporters developed over years.

Mohammed al-Azzeh, director of the Lajee Centre, which provides services to the youth of the camp, remembers how it all began.

“We’d built up relationships with friends from Scotland and Ireland who had visited Palestine, and then in 2012, I travelled to Glasgow for the first time. We started to have conversations about creating a football academy,” he recalled.

By 2015, the idea was taking shape when a group of footballers from the camp travelled to Belfast to play a game.

Then came the 2016 Champions League draw. Celtic were paired with Israeli side Hapoel Be’er Sheva.

Supporters ignored warnings that displaying Palestinian flags could result in a fine. As the teams emerged, the stadium was transformed into a sea of Palestinian flags, an action led by Celtic ultras, the Green Brigade.

UEFA subsequently fined Celtic.

The Green Brigade responded by launching the Match The Fine For Palestine campaign. Not to pay the fine, but to support Palestinian organisations, including with the formation of a football academy in Aida Camp.

For al-Azzeh, it was a turning point.

“The support and solidarity shown in that game was really a pivotal moment,” he said. “And that’s what ultimately led to Lajee Celtic becoming what it is today.”

The team has brought together young Palestinians from villages around Bethlehem, refugee camps and communities in Hebron and Jerusalem.

“It means a lot, for us as Palestinians, to be in one place and meeting each other,” al-Azzeh said. “It becomes about more than just playing football.”

Lajee Celtic is competing in organised football for the first time. The club had been due to enter the Palestinian league three years ago, but the competition was cancelled when Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza began. Now, despite restrictions on movement between Palestinian cities and the wider disruption to football, the club has entered the Thousand Martyrs Cup, named after the 1,014 athletes killed in Gaza since October 2023.

Bassil Mikdadi, journalist and founder of Football Palestine, said that international reach has given Lajee Celtic a significance beyond the club itself.

“Lajee Celtic is a blueprint for ways in which fans of European clubs can directly support those on the ground in Palestine. It’s connective tissue,” he said.

For Martin, the popular shirts are more than merchandise.

“When people buy these shirts, they do so knowing that the money is funding football, sports and general youth development in Palestine. And then when the same people wear these shirts, whether they’re in Glasgow or London or New York, they’re each making their own individual solidarity action.”

Lajee Celtic created a link between clubs and communities inside Palestine and supporters and campaigners abroad.

“It has this kind of cross-cultural, cross-border solidarity,” he said.

That connection has become increasingly important as Palestinian football has struggled to continue since the genocide in Gaza.

For Mikdadi, the survival of grassroots clubs is essential: They are the groundwork for the national team.

“The success of the Palestinian national team in recent years … the base of that success has always been players provided by clubs in the West Bank and Gaza,” he said.

The club’s ambitions stretch beyond football. It has expanded into sports such as boxing and table tennis, while creating opportunities for young Palestinians across Palestine and the diaspora.

“Fundraising campaigns come and go all the time. But when you create a football club and when you have that sort of tangible idea at the heart of it, then you are creating a journey,” said Martin.

Mohammed al-Azzeh recalled a meaningful memory on a beach in Cape Town, South Africa, where the team played two friendlies in 2025.

Samir al-Amir, a coordinator with Lajee Celtic, had spent more than 19 years in Israeli prisons. When he travelled with the team to South Africa, it was the first time he had been able to leave the walls and checkpoints of the West Bank.

Al-Azzeh remembers watching him on the beach.

“He was acting like a young boy because it was the first time seeing the sea,” he said. “Without Lajee Celtic, I’m not sure Samir would have ever had that opportunity. That illustrates why the project is so important,” he said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Lajee Celtic is a grassroots sports club based in a Palestinian refugee camp in the occupied West Bank. The club has been a symbol of solidarity for the Palestinian community. The team has brought together young Palestinians from villages around Bethlehem, refugee camps and communities in Hebron and Jerusalem.
