https://www.wired.com/story/how-this-tin.title: How This Tiny Startup Built the World’s Safest Bike Helmet
https://www.wired.com/story/how-this-tin.author: Chris Haslam
https://www.wired.com/story/how-this-tin.text:
FOR DECADES, RESEARCHERS judged cycling helmets on how well they protected against direct impacts. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) still does, even though research shows the danger isn't just how hard your head hits the ground, but how violently it twists. That rotational movement can make the brain twist and stretch inside the skull, increasing the risk of concussion and other brain injuries.

Not waiting for the CPSC to catch up, the cycling industry got to work. Multidirectional Impact Protection System, or MIPS, hit the market in 2007 and is now a common feature on premium helmets. At the same time, Virginia Tech turned helmet safety into something of a competition for manufacturers. In 2018, it launched helmet STAR ratings (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk), testing beyond the legal minimum and measuring both linear and rotational impacts.

Only four of the first 30 helmets earned five stars, but by 2025, 167 of 272 achieved five stars, and Virginia Tech had to tighten its grading. That only drove competition and improved helmet technology. Suddenly, hitting the number one spot was good for business and brains.

Sitting comfortably ahead of the competition, with a 4.61 score (10.1 or lower earns a five-star rating; lower is better), is the Pikio Si Oblik road cycling helmet, featuring a new safety system called Oblik. Inspired by the headbanging, concussion-proof woodpecker, this new design has wiped the floor with the competition. For context, Pikio's 4.61 score is 2.21 points lower than the previous best Canyon Deflectr’s 6.82. That’s about 32 percent lower, a massive shift when many of the highest-rated helmets score only between 7 and 10 points.

How has this relatively obscure Vancouver startup gotten it right the first time? As founder Daniel Abram explains, it “comes from 18 years researching impact protection and helmet design.” After studying mechanical engineering, he moved into helmet research at Simon Fraser University, where he helped develop BrainShield, a system designed to reduce rotational forces during impacts. He later founded helmet technology company BiaGuard, before MIPS paid around $1 million for the patents and intellectual property in 2022.

Most bike helmets use a thin plastic shell over expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam, which crushes on impact to absorb energy before it reaches your skull. Oblik takes that familiar foam structure and breaks it into independently mounted sections rather than one continuous block.

Each section attaches to the base EPS layer with flexible connection points, allowing them to move separately or detach if the helmet takes a serious impact. Combined with dual-density foam that absorbs direct impact, the movement helps to minimize the twisting force transmitted to the head. Abram explained how, “Rather than compressing material in one direction, the system is able to deform, deflect, and detach depending on the impact's intensity, location, and direction, helping manage both linear and rotational impact energy.”

Other helmet technologies approach the problem very differently. The now-ubiquitous MIPS remains the dominant commercial system, using a low-friction layer that can move 10 to 15 millimeters during the first 5 to 10 milliseconds of an impact. MIPS Spherical uses two nested liners that rotate relative to each other, while 6D’s Omni-Directional Suspension (ODS) suspends one liner inside another. WaveCel uses an engineered cellular structure that flexes, crumples, and glides under angled impacts.

Pikio's closest rival, the Release Layer System (RLS), featured on Canyon’s Deflectr and the third-placed, 3D-printed Hexr Miden RLS, tackles rotation from the outside, using external shell panels floating on tiny polycarbonate ball bearings that can roll and detach, redirecting rotational energy before it reaches the head.

Lab testing is one thing, but real-world data is something else. If your Pikio helmet is called into serious action, you will need to replace it—as with most EPS foam designs—but the company is offering a 30 percent discount on a replacement if it can get its hands on your damaged helmet.

“So far we’ve had four helmets returned and replaced,” Abram says. “Each has proven invaluable, not least because they’ve done their job and kept riders safe.”

At $379, the Pikio is a premium choice—a cool $219 more expensive than the second-best STAR-tested Canyon Deflectr RLS. Much of the cost stems from a vastly more complicated manufacturing process. Abram says a standard cycling helmet has around eight to 10 parts, but the Pikio Si uses around 80 individual components. The separate foam sections, intricately engineered flexible connection points, and dual-density construction all add to the cost.

It’s a small price to pay if it saves your life, but how does it fare day to day? I’ve been riding with the Si Oblik for the past month and have been impressed by how few compromises there have been in the pursuit of protection.

At 279 grams (in medium size), it's respectably light, though not class-leading, and the dial-to-fit cradle hugs my head neatly without pinch points. It’s a little bulky for a road lid, but is extremely comfortable; the 17 air vents keep my head refreshingly cool, and nobody has laughed at me for wearing it (yet). I would have preferred Pikio to use a magnetic Fidlock fastening under the chin as they’re brilliant, but it is a minor complaint—which Abram quickly quashed: “Fidlock weighs around 13 grams; a buckle is just four grams.”

It’s a great helmet loaded with unique, deliberately safety-first tech. Abram was keen to point out he is not interested in what he called “crown-like cycle helmet” aesthetics, and that “form always follows function.” The Pikio lacks a little of the cool factor you’ll find with a POC or Giro helmet, but it’s certainly not ugly.

For a company most cyclists have never heard of, taking the top spot at Virginia Tech is an extraordinary result. The harder part may be persuading people to trust an unknown name with something as consequential as head protection. MIPS faced a similar problem before turning an independent safety technology into something licensed across much of the helmet industry, and Oblik could conceivably follow the same path.

Whether Pikio becomes a major helmet brand—a second design is due early in the new year—a technology supplier, or both remains to be seen. But for now, it has given the cycling industry a new number to chase.
https://www.wired.com/story/how-this-tin.summary: The Pikio Si Oblik is a $219-a-cool-a. The PikIO Si Oblik is a new safety system called Oblik. The company is offering 30 percent discount on a helmet that can be replaced with a new design.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/gen-z-ric.title: Gen Z is on track to become the richest generation, but risks getting caught in a ‘cycle that is easy to fall into and hard to break alone’
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/gen-z-ric.author: Joshua Hong
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/gen-z-ric.text:
Gen Z could be on track to become the richest generation in history. But for now, they are struggling to pay off their credit card bills.

According to a September study examining the revolving cycle of debt from credit cards by Freedom Debt Relief, a debt settlement company, Gen Z leaned hardest on minimum-only payments (59%) and boomers the least (28%), against 50% of cardholders overall.

And that has caused significant damage to their mental health, based on the report: 51% of Gen Z feel embarrassed or ashamed of how much credit card debt they carry.

“The most common barrier was money, with 37% saying they didn’t earn enough to pay more than the minimum,” the study read. “But the reasons were more personal nearly as often: about 3 in 10 (30%) feel they should handle the debt on their own.”

Of course, Gen Zers are still in the early stages of their careers and have yet to enter their prime earnings years. So they are more likely to have trouble managing their debt.

Still, after digging a deep hole for themselves, Gen Z risks getting stuck, and they are in the dark. Just 20% of Gen Z knew their exact interest rate on their credit debt—the lowest of any generation and well below baby boomers.

“Behind the balances is a cycle that is easy to fall into and hard to break alone,” the report read. “Many cardholders pay down what they owe only for it to climb again, and most carry that stress quietly.”

The findings show a tension at the heart of Gen Z’s economic outlook: the generation’s long-term financial prospects show some hope, but they have to make do with what they have now to cover their bills.

Gen Z’s wealth could amass to $36 trillion by 2030 and $74 trillion by 2040, according to a 2025 Bank of America report.

But the wealth projections also have some caveats. A lot of the anticipated wealth accumulation depends on the “great wealth transfer” from older generations. In addition, the distribution of that wealth is uneven as certain households own substantial property and investment portfolios while others don’t.

A 2024 report from asset and wealth management firm Cerulli Associates estimated up to $124 trillion will be passed down from older generations to the younger ones by 2048.

But more than half of the volume, about $62 trillion, of transfers is expected to come from those who are currently wealthy—which together make up only 2% of all households.

“Eventually, most of the wealth owned by older generations in the U.S. will be either donated or passed down to Gen X or Millennial heirs,” Chayce Horton, senior analyst at Cerulli wrote in the report. “With $85 trillion to be passed down to these generations collectively, providers that can establish relationships with, and adequately address the needs of, these younger investors will be well positioned for success.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.title: In One Historically Black Florida Community, the Drinking Water Is Brown
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.author: By Amy Green
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.text:
WHITTED, Fla.—When Ann Jones runs her kitchen faucet, the water flows clear only some of the time. Sometimes the water is brown. Fill a pitcher, and the water is the color of iced tea.

Jones, 81, is a gentle woman who has lived most of her life in this unincorporated historically Black community of 52 residents southeast of Orlando. She can recall, as a teen, glimpsing the Ku Klux Klan burn crosses not far from her childhood home, as her family drove past.

Through the years the community has held firmly to its heritage and the close bonds its neighbors share, even as the outer bounds of metro Orlando have crept closer. Recently several new developments have sprung up around the outskirts of the tiny neighborhood, all of them connected to the local water system and offering clean drinking water flowing from their taps.

In Whitted, residents rely on well water, and testing they requested from the Florida Department of Health has confirmed at least some of the wells are contaminated with arsenic and PFAS/PFOS, so-called “forever” chemicals associated with cancer, cardiovascular disease, developmental problems in children and infants, diabetes, immune system disruption and neurological damage. A $2.3 million effort to connect the community to the local water system has moved slowly since the funding was announced in 2024, an issue Osceola County Commissioner Ricky Booth, who represents Whitted, acknowledged.

“Those new developments pay for those services to come in,” he said. “Hearing from the residents, my position has been let’s get them hooked up to city water. It seemed like the right thing to do, and that’s why we’ve been fighting so hard to get it done.”

Jones, who lives with her husband in a tidy home painted bright white, does not drink the tap water. Every two weeks two five-gallon jugs of water and three 24-packs of bottled water are delivered to the house, and a neighbor helps lift and empty the jugs into several pitchers the couple uses for drinking and cooking. The couple bathes in the water, but Jones throws in some bleach with the whites to ensure the water does not stain the laundry. She estimates the couple spends about $150 a month on bottled water, a situation she considers a legacy of the segregation and racism that historically characterized this part of central Florida.

“We’re not begging or asking for something that no one else has, that is sacred to the white people,” she said. “We deserve to have clean water. It doesn’t matter what race you are. Everybody deserves clean water, to know that they are safe in drinking their water.”

In the late 1800s, a small group of Black families settled among this region’s agricultural and ranch lands and began working the citrus groves and sugarcane fields. They established the St. Luke Missionary Baptist Church, and eventually the tiny house of worship would serve as a spiritual and social center for generations of Whitted families. The Black children attended their own schools, and residents knew better than to go after dark into nearby St. Cloud, which was known as a “sundown town.”

In 1964, a resident named James Whitted, whose relatives helped establish the community and lent their name to it, agreed to lease three acres of his land to Osceola County for a dollar a year for the construction of a park and recreational space for the community’s children, according to records residents obtained recently. Whitted was elderly at the time, could not read or write and suffered from some mental health problems, said Christian Wells, professor of anthropology and director of the Center for Brownfields Research and Redevelopment at the University of South Florida. Whitted did not understand the lease he signed actually allowed for a landfill.

The park never materialized. Shortly afterward the county dug a hole on the property, and trucks began dumping trash there. The action was undocumented and unregulated, and records are scarce. But based on a lease agreement, the property is believed to have operated as a landfill from 1964 to 1975, according to a 2024 report by the Florida Department of Health.

Whole cars were dumped at the site with no concern about leaching, said Emily Walsh, a master’s student in anthropology and public health at the University of South Florida whose thesis project is on Whitted. After the dumping stopped, the county covered the landfill and the site has remained undeveloped since.

In 1966 the county sanitation director expressed concern to the Board of County Commissioners that the waste at the site could pollute the groundwater, contaminating the wells of nearby residents. The sanitation director requested the county dig a ditch around the property, and the board instructed the county engineer to investigate. There is no evidence any such investigation took place, and no precautions were taken, Wells said.

Homes surrounded the landfill on three sides, some of them only a few dozen feet from the site and without even a fence separating the properties. When the county began preparing the site for the dump, clearing trees and moving dirt, the residents thought construction was getting underway on the park, Jones said. The children got excited.

“This was a way into what we thought would be a heavenly life, a fun life,” she said.

After the dumping began, all kinds of garbage was deposited at the site: clothing, food, furniture, paint, pots and pans, toys, windows. Individuals tossed trash on the property, too. The landfill smelled, and rats and raccoons became a problem for nearby residents. Still, the site became an informal recreational space for the children, who would venture onto the property and play, Jones said. But James Whitted was devastated.

“He said, ‘I didn’t designate that as a landfill. I wanted that for the kids for a park,’” Jones said.

DeAnna Paul, 64, recalls playing as a child with her sister at the dump and scavenging for bikes or anything they could fix up.

“It was just right in the midst of all the houses,” she said. “I could see dump trucks, different types of large trucks coming in. … They would just off-load into this big hole, and then after so much was in there they would cover it up and make another hole.”

Eventually residents living near the landfill began experiencing problems with their water. Jones said the water first turned yellow, then brown and would discolor sinks and tubs. Most residents back then drank the water anyway. The site also flooded when it rained, and the foul water would flow into residents’ backyards. Some of the residents began suffering from unusual health problems such as rare cancers, Wells said.

For Jessica Paul, the water can smell of eggs and have a metallic taste. Paul, 42, lives with her mother and son in Whitted and estimates the family spends nearly $100 a month on bottled water. She characterized the water as “grimy,” with “sandy-type stuff,” and said she gets “cringe” when taking a shower in it, although she avoids washing her hair with the water because she said the water can dry out her hair and cause it to break.

“It’s really emotional. I know that a lot of people in this area ended up getting sick with cancer and stuff like that, and to know that we’re still having to take showers in it, it’s really uneasy,” said Paul, who has lived all her life in Whitted and is DeAnna Paul’s niece. “I know my anxiety is cray because you don’t know what can happen in 10 years or 15 years or 20 years down the road, and then the fact that I have a 12-year-old son.”

DeAnna Paul said she constantly is running up to the local Sam’s Club for five-gallon jugs of water. She said she is hesitant to have family and friends over to her home.

“What danger am I putting them in if they come here and drink some of the water?” she asked.

In response to mounting community pressure, the Florida Department of Health in 2022 collected water samples from 10 of 18 wells within a quarter mile of the former landfill site. The samples were tested for arsenic, metals and trace elements, PFAS and volatile organic compounds. The department also investigated possible soil and groundwater contamination.

The department found that in some wells arsenic and PFOS concentrations “could pose a health risk to residents, if they use the wells for water for drinking and other consumption purposes including cooking and making baby formula,” according to the 2024 report. The department concluded the water, if consumed over a lifetime, could lead to a higher cancer risk and non-cancerous health effects and recommended residents install filters and avoid drinking the water. The department declined to provide a comment to Inside Climate News.

Nonetheless in a January 2026 email the Florida Department of Environmental Protection told residents the water was safe to drink, now that residents had installed filters. The department said future water monitoring was planned to further define the boundaries of the plume of groundwater pollution but that no health monitoring was recommended.

“PFAS are common, and most people have some level of PFAS in their blood,” the email stated. “PFAS blood testing is not a standard procedure offered by your doctor.”

Across the country a legacy of segregation and systemic lack of investment have left communities such as Whitted more vulnerable to environmental degradation and climate impacts such as flooding, and also less equipped to deal with the problems. Multiple studies also have shown these communities tend to have less access to clean drinking water. Local investments in aging water systems are based on the tax base, and that leaves small communities with fewer resources to rely on state and federal support, according to one study.

In fast-growing Osceola County, providing clean drinking water in a community such as Whitted, where there is less economic development than in other areas of the county, is a matter of political will, Wells said.

“There is just this striking correlation between people who don’t have access to clean and safe water and minority status, race and ethnicity,” Wells said. “The vast majority of communities that I have encountered that have water quality problems or water access problems are Black or Hispanic. And it’s urban areas. It’s in rural areas. It’s everywhere, but there is this very striking correlation between the color of your skin and the ability to access clean and safe water.”

In 2024 Whitted received $1.45 million from the state and $850,000 from the federal government to connect residents to the local water system. At the time, Osceola County said the wells did not provide adequate water volumes for firefighting purposes, and that the project also would help reduce insurance costs by addressing the fire risk. But two years later, construction still has not yet begun. The project is scheduled to be completed in 2028.

Whitted residents also report the community has been excluded from other services and amenities such as trash pickup, road upgrades and streetlights.

“What hurts so much is that all of us in this neighborhood have been here for 60 and 70 years. They built all around us like we were nothing,” Jones said. “They built north, south, east and west and left us with nothing but dirty water and no sewage. If you go down the road you have water and sewage. You have sidewalks. You have streetlights. We have none of that. So we’re just a lost generation, I guess.”

Booth, the county commissioner, attributed the slow progress on the project to connect residents to the local water system to government bureaucracy and said it had nothing to do with Whitted’s heritage as a historically Black community.

“The county doesn’t care about what color that community is. The county cares about helping people,” he said. “I would disagree with anybody who says that anything that happened in the last 40 or 50 years has been some sort of segregation or anything like that. It’s not true.”

Residents also want the county to fulfill the dream of James Whitted and turn the former landfill site into a park. Jessica Paul characterized the situation as an example of environmental racism.

“All we want is just clean water,” she said. “We shouldn’t be even fighting for that. It should be free.”

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.author: Interview by Steve Curwood, Living on Earth
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.text:
From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood with veteran Maine journalist Kevin Miller.

The closely watched race for U.S. Senate in Maine is pitting two environmentally concerned candidates against each other.

Not only do they both have fairly similar green and climate views, they are also both from Aroostook County, the sparsely populated and northernmost region in a state that is 90 percent forested.

Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, seeking her sixth term in office, comes from a family that dates back five generations in the lumber business and is a political dynasty. Her father and uncle served multiple terms in the Maine state Senate and both her mother and father were mayors of her hometown, Caribou.

Democratic challenger Troy Jackson grew up in a working-class family of loggers in the Allagash region, deeper in the woods and about 75 miles from Caribou. Jackson entered politics as a prominent labor activist in the logging industry and served six years as the president of the Maine state Senate. He got into this U.S. Senate race late, after the winner of the Democratic primary dropped out.

Kevin Miller is Maine Public Radio’s veteran state house and environmental reporter. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

STEVE CURWOOD: Give me a sense of these two candidates: Susan Collins, the Republican, and Troy Jackson, the Democrat.

KEVIN MILLER: Senator Collins has been in office for 30 years. She is one of the more senior Republican members of the Senate. She is a fairly moderate, centrist Republican. There are some people who will probably be yelling right now, saying she’s not a moderate, but when you look at her in the context of where the Republican Party is today, she’s definitely more to the center, and she also describes herself as a deal maker.

Troy Jackson was a state lawmaker for 20-some years. He’s a logger from far northern Maine, and he’s a fairly progressive candidate. He’s been closely aligned with Bernie Sanders. He became candidate after our last progressive candidate, Graham Platner, his campaign imploded because of rape allegations against him from a former girlfriend of his. But Troy Jackson, he’s had a similar approach to policies as Graham Plattner, so he was able to kind of step in and say, “I’m going to carry Graham Platner’s progressive movement,” which had a lot of momentum in Maine before Platner had to step down.

CURWOOD: At one point, you worked as an environmental reporter, so talk to me about climate and environment as a priority for Maine voters in this race. Where does it fall on the list?

MILLER: Not very high, from what we’re seeing from polls and hearing from voters. Environment and conservation issues are always fairly important in Maine, just because it’s a big natural resource state. So many of our industries are tied to natural resources. But, like we’re seeing in a lot of other places around the country, it’s the other issues. It’s affordability. It’s inflation. It’s gas prices. One of the big concerns headed into the election right now, or at least into winter, is Maine is the most heavily reliant state on heating oil. More than 50 percent of houses in the state use heating oil, and heating oil is diesel, pretty much. When the price of diesel and heating oil are up above $6 a gallon, that’s a big concern for people. Affordability issues are probably top of mind for a lot of people.

CURWOOD: How do these candidates come down on environmental issues? Let’s talk about renewable energy to start with.

MILLER: They’re fairly well aligned in some respects, at least on renewable energy. They’re both known as being fairly prominent supporters of the push to convert Maine and other states to more renewable sources. They’re both supporters of wind energy, especially offshore wind. The Gulf of Maine is a very windy place. There have been proposals that were in the works to build large offshore wind facilities there. They have now been kind of put on hold by the Trump administration, and I think Senator Collins has been critical of that. Troy Jackson has certainly been critical of that.

We do have a significant number of land-based wind resources here, and Troy Jackson actually was key when he was the Senate president, key to greasing the skids to build a large wind farm that would stretch from his area of northern Maine down and would be a major generator. That project’s been stalled for other reasons.

One other issue that I think they’re closely aligned on is biomass energy. Some people don’t regard this as renewable energy, or it’s a more controversial source because of its impact on the climate—you’re burning wood, you’re releasing carbon dioxide. So some environmentalists don’t view this as a truly renewable source, but because we are such a heavily forested state, it’s a big issue up here.

On the broader climate issues, Senator Jackson was very prominently supporting our current Democratic governor’s very ambitious climate agenda. He’s not quite as progressive as some people would like him to be. Senator Collins has also been largely supportive of some of these climate issues, but I think it comes down to which candidate the environmental community feels is going to be a bigger advocate on environmental issues, and in this case, certainly hearing from the environmental groups, it’s Troy Jackson.

CURWOOD: Why is that? Is it because it would be part of flipping the Senate to the Democratic majority, which would have a large impact on environmental policy of the federal government? The Trump administration has rolled back almost everything, gotten out of the climate agreements, and in fact, doesn’t believe that climate’s a problem.

MILLER: I think that’s a key part of it—a lot of the environmental community just looks at the Democrats as being more favorable to achieving their goals, certainly than Republicans, and compared to what the Trump administration has been doing, they see flipping the Senate as key to that.

CURWOOD: Troy Jackson is a fifth-generation logger from Allagash. You can’t go any farther north there in Maine than Allagash. What’s his relationship to the industry?

MILLER: He has a pretty complicated relationship, I’d say. He’s been a logger his entire life, so he grew up in the industry. But he actually got into politics because of that experience. Back about 30 years ago, there was a lot of tension between the forest landowners and the loggers from Maine because they believed that the forest landowners were hiring too many Canadian workers, who they could hire for cheaper. So Troy Jackson and a number of the loggers actually led a blockade of the logging road border crossings with Canada. This got a huge amount of attention, and he said that he was so frustrated with that experience. He didn’t feel like the folks here in Augusta, the state capital, and in Washington were listening to him or the other loggers. That’s how he ran for the state legislature a couple of years later. He works in the industry, but he has always felt that the landowners are not respecting the labor rights of Maine loggers.

CURWOOD: What about the ecology? Some of the land companies up there are clear cutting. How does he feel about that?

MILLER: Troy has been critical of land management in the past in that respect, and he also led the fight to try to ban the aerial spraying of glyphosate, which most folks probably know as Roundup. That is a herbicide that a lot of landowners use to try to eliminate the undergrowth that they don’t want, so that they can encourage the trees that they want, but of course, glyphosate kills a lot of things. Troy Jackson led the effort to pass a bill in the legislature to ban aerial spraying of glyphosate, but that was eventually vetoed by our Democratic governor Janet Mills because of the opposition from the forest industry.

CURWOOD: Susan Collins has been in the Senate for 30 years. What’s her environmental record?

MILLER: Susan Collins is a fairly prominent supporter of the push toward renewable energy. She has also supported or helped pass legislation to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. So she’s looked at by some, or at least has been looked at in the past, as one of the environmental community’s best allies when it comes to environmental issues in the Republican Party.

I think that’s changed to some respect under the Trump administration. Some in the environmental community now view her as not doing enough to push back against the Trump administration, especially on these drastic cuts to some of the programs. I think that’s where we’re seeing that misalignment now between the environmental community and Susan Collins.

CURWOOD: She’s chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations, and between that and the House chair, they sit on money. If you want it, you have to go through her committee. What’s her record on how federal funds are allocated when it does come to environmental protection?

MILLER: She’s only been chairwoman for a couple of years now under the Republican leadership. What we’ve seen in this most recent cycle with President Trump, he actually proposed a 55 percent cut to the EPA. What the Senate Appropriations Committee did under her leadership, and certainly working with Democrats, they actually reduced that to a 5 percent cut in the budget that eventually came out. The committee as a whole was, you know, applauded by some in the environmental community for lessening that impact, but again, there are still some folks on the left who feel like she’s not doing enough to push back against the Trump administration.

CURWOOD: Every year the League of Conservation Voters publishes the National Environmental Scorecard, which tracks and rates how members of Congress vote on environmental and climate issues. What is the LCV saying about Troy Jackson and Susan Collins?

MILLER: It’s interesting because the League of Conservation has actually endorsed Susan Collins in the past, going back to 2014. They endorsed her and called her as one of the leaders in the fight against climate disruption.

This time around, they’re endorsing Troy Jackson because they see him as being a more effective advocate on environmental issues than Senator Collins, and a big part of that is, as we talked about before, Democratic control of Congress. The environmental community sees that as key to being able to get done what they want to do, or at least stopping the Trump administration from doing what they want to do.

But what I think is really interesting is if you go back to that same year, 2014, the League of Conservation Voters actually came out against Troy Jackson when he was running for one of our congressional seats, and I think they paid more than $150,000 in ads against Troy Jackson. He ended up losing that Democratic primary in part because of the pushback from this group and from some of the abortion rights groups. It’s fascinating now to see how even within that one group, the dynamics have changed between these two people.

CURWOOD: Let’s say that Troy Jackson wins, but the Senate doesn’t flip. What does that do to the state of Maine’s position in national politics?

MILLER: That’s a key thing that Senator Collins has been arguing, that Maine would lose that influential voice in Washington, and it’s going to affect the amount of money that’s flowing back to Maine.

Not only would they lose the chairperson of the Senate Appropriations Committee, but they would lose somebody who’s frequently in the center of a lot of these hotly contested issues because, especially when the Senate is so closely divided, she’s frequently a swing vote, which she says allows her to use her influence more than someone else would. That’s a key part of her argument.

Troy Jackson’s argument is: Look, I’m going to be a better advocate overall for the working people of Maine, for the progressive policies that I’ve been pushing and also for these environmental issues, than Susan Collins would be, especially if the Senate was in Democratic hands.

South Korea's ambassador to Ukraine returned home today, Seoul's foreign ministry said, as a diplomatic row deepens over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.

The announcement came days after South Korea said it recalled him following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's disclosure last month of the prisoner transfer, which Seoul said put their families in North Korea at risk.

"We inform you that Park Ki-chang, Ambassador to Ukraine, returned home this morning," Seoul's foreign ministry said in a statement sent to AFP.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has demanded an official apology over the prisoner revelation.

Russian strikes on Ukraine's southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia killed at least eight people, including three children, according to regional authorities.

The strikes came a day after Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

"The death toll from the air strikes on Zaporizhzhia has risen to eight. Among them are three children," said Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Defence Council of the Zaporizhzhia region.

At least 16 people were wounded, he said, and 12 were missing.

Yesterday, US President Donald Trump said he had secured a deal for Russia to boost diesel supplies to global markets, marking a dramatic shift in Washington's approach to Moscow and a move aimed at easing fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP, Reuters)

The Opal Tower apartment complex in Sydney's west has been declared defect-free at a ceremony.

Residents were forced to evacuate the complex on Christmas Eve in 2018 after cracks were found in the building.

The process of fixing the high-rise and securing compensation for owners has involved a class action, two legal cases, and has cost millions of dollars.

A ribbon-cutting ceremony has taken place at the once-plagued Opal Tower in Sydney's west to mark the building officially being declared defect-free.

The celebration brings an end to a saga, spanning close to eight years, that involved a class action, two legal cases, ongoing rectification work and relocations after cracks appeared on level 10 of the complex on Christmas Eve in 2018.

Fearing a collapse, thousands of people were forced to evacuate with the emergency response also shutting down the nearby train station and surrounding roads at Sydney Olympic Park.

Opal Tower was officially declared defect-free on Saturday. (ABC News)

At the time, police said the tower had moved "1 to 2 millimetres".

Days later, more cracks were discovered on other levels of the 36-storey high-rise.

Opal Tower Owners Corporation chairman Shady Eskander has been at the forefront of the fight to get the complex made up of 392 units repaired, and secure compensation for those affected.

"It's fantastic to announce that Opal Tower is defect-free."

Shady Eskander says the impact of the defects has been devastating for residents. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Mr Eskander told the ABC that a lot of work had taken place and millions of dollars had been spent to be able to declare "this building is the safest and best residential building in Australia".

"Everything that was done was done with the consultants, with the builder, with all of those involved in the design and construction of Opal Tower.

"We came alongside each other in a very collaborative manner."

Developer Ecove, backed by Japanese firm Kajina Corporation, engineers WSP, and builder Icon have been the other parties involved in the process.

An engineer's report commissioned by the NSW government concluded in 2019 that the cracks had been caused by a combination of "design and construction matters, in particular changes made after the original design".

In what Mr Eskander described as an Australian-first, the high-rise is now protected by a 20-year structural warranty.

A report concluded the defects were caused by a combination of "design and construction matters". (Supplied)

All owners have been fairly compensated, and all legal matters have been resolved.

"This is the greatest property comeback story in Australian history," Mr Eskander said in a statement.

Nutan Borkar was out of her unit for 11 months after the incident, and was glad there was finally "light at the end of the tunnel after a big struggle".

"It's great because a lot of time has been invested in getting the building back to the way it should've been," she said.

"I love being here. I wouldn't think of being anywhere else but here now. It's home."

Nutan Borkar says she "wouldn't think of being anywhere else". (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Building standards were lifted across the state, with the Coalition government at the time introducing the role of building commissioner and a suite of other reforms.

"The lesson that can be learnt from Opal Tower … is that quality needs to be there so that defects aren't," Mr Eskander said.

"And we need to ensure that defects don't occur in the towers that are being constructed over Sydney because builders and contractors will spend more on fixing the defect than building it right the first time."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Major earthquake hits Panama, injures at least 27
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
PANAMA CITY, PANAMA – A powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least 27 people, with no deaths reported.

The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System.

The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia said that there were no reports of fatalities so far.

In Panama City, about 200 kilometers from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city’s emblematic skyscrapers.

“I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged,” Salomon Andion, 46, said after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks.

“Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking.”

A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall.

Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles traveled across it.

“We are facing a major disaster,” President Jose Raul Mulino said, adding that some roads had “completely collapsed.”

“It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school,” Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, said.

There were 27 people with minor injuries across the country as a result of the quake, according to a statement from the National Civil Protection System.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake struck at 12:56 pm local time with an epicenter 10 kilometers (six miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province.

The USGS initially estimated it to be a magnitude 8.0 quake before revising it down to 7.7.

A tsunami warning was issued for the eastern Pacific but later lifted.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was “closely monitoring” the situation, with his office “rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist,” at the Panamanian government’s request.

The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating “as normal.”

Mulino traveled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response.

Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle as well as Los Santos.

He said the town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off.

“We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it’s impossible by land,” Boyd said.

Panama City’s international airport, a major hub for the region, was temporarily closed.

Several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution, according to the Civil Aeronautics Authority.

The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala all sent messages of solidarity and offers of aid.

Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found “many houses devastated” and “everyone terrified” in the small town square, which was left without power.

His neighbor, David Castillo, said that residents were choosing not to return home because they are “afraid it will happen again.”

Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica.

Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted pictures on Instagram of his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province that collapsed.

A church and a hotel in Penonome also suffered extensive damage, images shared on local media showed.

More than 80 aftershocks, one above magnitude 6.0, were recorded by the local geosciences institute.

Mulino called for calm.

“What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” he wrote on X, adding that he had called for a report on the damage.

The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide.

The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela’s Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.

https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-econ.title: Chinese nickel investors brace for headwinds as Indonesia weighs smelter freeze
https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-econ.author: Ralph Jennings
https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-econ.text:
Jakarta's proposed restrictions could reshape the foreign-backed supply chains feeding critical sectors, from stainless steel to electric vehicle batteries

Chinese investors could face significant disruption if Indonesia imposes a moratorium on new nickel smelters to curb global overproduction and protect local industries across its vast minerals sector, analysts said.

Semi-finished products, including nickel pig iron and nickel matte, make up about 50 to 60 per cent of Indonesia’s total output, Antara reported. The proposed restrictions were part of the energy minister’s efforts to strengthen the country’s industrial structure, it added.

Nickel pig iron is primarily used to make stainless steel, while nickel matte is used in electric vehicle batteries.

Chinese investment accounts for about 75 per cent of Indonesia’s nickel refining industry, according to an estimate by the US-based Centre for Advanced Defense Studies. .

“Chinese investors are likely to be significantly affected because Chinese companies and capital play a major role in Indonesia’s nickel mining and smelting industries,” said Nukila Evanty, an Indonesia-based member of the Asia Centre research institute’s advisory board.

“Chinese investors should reconsider and selectively scale back new smelting capacity, particularly projects producing intermediate nickel products in an already oversupplied market.”

Indonesia held more than half of the global nickel market in 2023, according to a study by Rafi Adis Subarna, an analyst with Jakarta-based political risk consultancy KRA Group.

Jakarta’s six-year-old ban on raw nickel ore exports had spurred the expansion of domestic mining and production, he argued in the study, citing strong global demand for products such as electric vehicle batteries and an influx of investment in smelting facilities.

Chinese investment had “supported” Indonesia’s expansion of nickel processing capacity over the years, Goldman Sachs said in a February commentary. But that growth had contributed to an oversupply, weighing on prices since 2023, it added.

If a moratorium takes effect, Chinese-invested companies planning conventional smelting capacity expansions could face delays or be forced to cancel projects, particularly where profit margins were already narrow, said Siwage Dharma Negara, a principal fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

Jakarta’s “regulatory uncertainty” posed a bigger concern, he added. “If the government frequently changes investment conditions, investors may postpone their expansion or eventually pull back from the country.”

Indonesia should evaluate whether it had the domestic capabilities, technology and equipment to operate its own nickel smelters under a moratorium, said Zhao Xijun, a finance professor at Renmin University in China.

Chinese enterprises had the necessary expertise and would invest in other countries, from Africa to Latin America, if Indonesia made it difficult, he said.

“Then the loss is Indonesia’s,” he added. “The mines would still be there with no one to develop them.”

Evanty from the Asia Centre advisory board said Chinese investors should prioritise improving existing facilities and diversifying into higher-value products, all with “stronger” environmental standards.

The Indonesian energy and mineral resources minister’s team was preparing a recommendation for President Prabowo Subianto to decide which segments of the semi-finished nickel smelting sector would be restricted, Antara said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.

Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.

Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.

But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.

But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said.

Anthropic this week published a report detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.

Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.

The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.

President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups.

Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.

In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.summary: Philadelphia Police Department says fake tip was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation. It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities. It was discovered by the AI agent, developed by Anthropic, who said it had seen someone matching the description.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2.text:
It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.

It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.

The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.

But that is exactly what we have come to find.

After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.

"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."

It doesn't take long.

"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.

Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground.

We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see.

The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too.

Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise.

"It's really now cooking away," Pete says.

"Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this."

The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares – 33 sq km – of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority.

At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire.

Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead.

Now the challenge is different.

The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.

Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water.

For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial.

"We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says.

"So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible."

And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored.

"Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says.

Walking through the forest, the scale of what happened is almost haunting.

Tree trunks are blackened and charred. The acrid smell of fire still hangs around. Large areas of the forest floor have been scorched.

But look closely and there are splashes of colour.

Green shoots are emerging. Fungi is growing. I even spot a small yellow flower shooting up from the blackened ground.

Dr Sarah Henshall, head of conservation at the Cairngorms National Park Authority, says it is too early to know the full ecological impact of the fire.

"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.

"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."

And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.

Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.

Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.

"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.

There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.

Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.

"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.

Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.

Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.

Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.

Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.

Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text:
A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises.

"When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers.

This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'.

So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag.

Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts.

They divide the menstrual cycle into phases, recommending:

So what does the science say?

Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle.

But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence".

"There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says.

A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next.

That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains.

Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception.

"It's not so much about doing certain exercises in certain phases, it's about working with your own individual body and what your needs might be."

Cesci Burgoyne, a nurse based in Sydney, Australia who is also a qualified personal trainer and nutritionist, adjusts her training depending on how she feels in her cycle. She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively.

"In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC. "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier. I like to try and get my long runs in."

Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women.

Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month.

But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play".

Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating.

"The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable".

Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase.

"A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says.

She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs.

McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress. Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life.

Building strength requires consistent, progressively challenging training, she says, and "we don't want to create another barrier by suggesting women train less for almost half the month."

Dr Bate also warns against normalising severe symptoms: if pain, fatigue or mood changes interfere with exercise or daily life, women should seek medical advice rather than assuming it is an inevitable part of their cycle, she says.

While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware".

McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month.

Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules.

In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued.

For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel".

In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules.

Insulin has been used to treat type 1 diabetes for more than a century but now there is a new treatment being rolled out on the NHS that can delay the onset of the disease for years. Alongside, screening is gathering pace, identifying those that could benefit. So, is this the beginning of a new era for type 1 diabetes treatment?

Dima and his mum Elena explain what it was like to be told that he had tested positive for developing type 1 diabetes and what it was like taking part in the trial for this new drug, teplizumab. Parth Narendran, a Professor of Diabetes Medicine at the University of Birmingham, and Consultant Paediatric Endocrinologist Dr Renuka Dias at Birmingham Women's and Children's Hospital, reveal how these changes are transforming treatment.

In July, the NHS announced plans to incentivise us to walk a marathon a month by offering vouchers and discounts. But with scant detail on how the plan will actually work, we ask Joan Costa-i-Font, Professor of Health Economics at London School of Economics, what makes schemes like this succeed or fail.

Plus, why are horse fly bites so painful? Dr Erica McAlister, an entomologist at the Natural History Museum, explains how the flies break into our skin, while consultant dermatologist Dr Alexandra Banner describes what’s happening in our bodies.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.author: Yuki Noguchi
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.text:
Shelley and Todd Engel.

Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.

In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."

The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION, for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.

Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.

More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.

Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.

His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.

In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.

When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it. The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.

The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events. It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.

In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.

Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.

That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.

It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."

Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."

NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)

Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."

Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.

That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.

He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.

"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."

The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.

Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.

"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.

These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.

But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed

"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.

NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.title: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.author: Malaka Gharib
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.text:
Clare Marie Schneider

One clever way to celebrate the season? Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.

Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.

But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest.

Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook, shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup: a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more."

Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days.

Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta.

Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person?
Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them."

If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health.

Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean?

"Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions.)

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste, says interior designer Elaine Griffin.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen.

Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design.

Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month. "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you.

Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit, she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds.

Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing."

Create a home theater. Devika Girish, co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine, explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home.

Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies.

Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto, likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house."

If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks, says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity. If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes.

"It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain.

Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours.

"Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta.

Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move.

Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering. Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon.

Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor.

These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari, a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots.

Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions, shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you.

Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says.

Email us at lifekit@npr.org with your response and full name, and we may feature your story on NPR.

This digital story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter.
