https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Suicide memorial in Chicago signals compassionate shift by Catholic church
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
First US memorial for suicide victims dedicated by Chicago archdiocese earlier this year at Queen of Heaven cemetery

The Chicago archdiocese has recognized the Rev Charles Rubey’s work supporting families whose loved ones died by suicide this year by dedicating in his honor a memorial to the lives lost to suicide and the victims’ surviving families.

In 1979 Rubey founded the Loving Outreach to Survivors of Suicide, a counseling and support program run by Catholic Charities of the archdiocese of Chicago.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

The archdiocese says the memorial, titled At Peace, at the Queen of Heaven Catholic cemetery in Hillside, Illinois, is the first of its kind by any US archdiocese.

The Catholic church historically banned funeral rites and burial on consecrated grounds for those who died by suicide.

To Rubey, the memorial is a sign of the church’s shift toward a more compassionate understanding of suicide.

“They’ve made a complete turnaround embracing families who have lost a loved one to suicide,” Rubey said. “They’re no longer condemned or thought to be in hell.”

Catholic teaching still considers killing oneself a sin, but it acknowledges that mental health problems can lead people to suicide and says salvation is possible for those who take their own lives.

Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV has dedicated some of his monthly prayer intentions to people suffering from mental health problems and suicidal thoughts.

He called on the church to become “a safe space where everyone has a place – a community that accompanies and never excludes, that listens without judging and draws near without fear”.

The memorial is located in a cemetery that is also home to the world’s largest Catholic mausoleum.

“We did not want this memorial hidden away and we were intentional in every detail,” Sullivan said when the memorial was announced. “This is not something we are ashamed of.″

Until a 1917 church law was revised in 1983, those who died by suicide were denied Catholic burials on consecrated grounds.

In recent decades, a greater understanding of mental illness has helped shift the cultural view on suicide and influenced Catholic teaching.

The Rev James Martin, editor at large of the Jesuit magazine America, says the Catholic church’s approach mirrors that of the broader society with more sympathy for all affected by suicide.

“To be able to extend pastoral care to the family members is extremely important, and to not make them feel any sense of shame or isolation, or judgment on them from the church,” he said.

Ed Shoener, whose daughter Katie died by suicide in 2016, co-founded the Association of Catholic Mental Health Ministers to “educate parish communities to break down the stigma around mental illness and to accompany people in the midst of these struggles”.

The global association advocates for the Catholic church to do more to improve mental health care.

In January, Shoener met with Pope Leo to thank him for his interest in mental health and told the pontiff that he hoped the church could issue an in-depth statement about mental health in the form of an apostolic letter or an encyclical.

This month, he returned to the Vatican for an event coinciding with Leo’s monthly prayer intention and World Mental Health Day on Saturday. Religious leaders and health professionals will gather to examine how parishes respond to mental health issues and how to best answer Leo’s call to establish mental health ministries to overcome stigma and discrimination.

That′s also Shoener’s hope. “I’d love to see this become just a fully integrated ministry into the church – that it’s a common ministry in every parish around the world, just like youth ministry.”

In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Chicago archdiocese has dedicated a memorial to the lives lost to suicide and the victims' surviving families. The memorial is the first of its kind by any US archdiociety. Catholic church historically banned funeral rites and burial on consecrated grounds for those who died by suicide.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/ng-int.title: Post-its, homework breaks and karaoke: inside the Women’s Pro Baseball League’s debut season
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/ng-int.author: Photographs and text by Jaclyn Licht
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/ng-int.text:
The first league of its kind in 70 years brought players from all around the world to Illinois for eight weeks, writing a new chapter in the history of women’s sports

On the morning of 14 September, Rocky Henley sat at her rental home’s dining room table amid scattered rulebooks, colorful markers and graph paper. The New York Heights manager drew a chart on a large poster – her method of sketching plays for the evening’s playoff game. Her assistant manager, Jackson, trudged in from the kitchen in flannel pajama pants and a Heights hoodie and watched her work. He also happens to be her son.

Rocky Henley draws out gameplans at her dining room table on the morning of the Heights’ WPBL playoff game. Photograph: Jaclyn Licht

The Women’s Pro Baseball League (WPBL) is the first league of its kind in 70 years. Players hailed from across the US and 11 different countries to play for four teams: the Heights, Boston Hunters, San Francisco Firebells and Los Angeles Queens. While each team’s namesake city was selected for their market value and reputations for sports fandom, the eight-week inaugural season was played in entirety in Springfield, Illinois.

From left to right: Gabrielle Haas, Maïka Dumais and Hyeonah Kim of the Boston Hunters wait in the dugout before their first WPBL game. Photograph: Jaclyn Licht

The inaugural season of the WPBL marked a pivotal moment in the women’s sports history books. The players, coaches and crew fashioned the paper, the pen and the ink to write this new chapter.

The broadcast producer consulted on merchandise stock. Catchers doubled as assistant coaches. The league doctors taught and studied at the local university.

Before her players arrived for games at Robin Roberts Stadium, Rocky Henley would consult a list of adjectives scribbled on a piece of notepad paper, crossing out repetitions and racking her brain for synonyms. Each Heights player received two Post-it notes on their locker: a green Post-it with a mantra they needed to keep in mind during the game – “stamina,” “determination” and “spirit”, to name a few examples – and a pink one to highlight an adjective reflective of their general personalities – such as “comical”, “ridiculous” or “fun!”

Most of the players balanced the WPBL season with schoolwork or second jobs. Days outside of games consisted largely of practice – often at the local YMCA, where many of the players bought memberships for the summer.

Addisyn Baird, the youngest player in the league, is long accustomed to multitasking. Baird, 18, was called up to play with the LA Queens in late August, just weeks before she was set to start her senior fall semester of high school at the Hill School in Pennsylvania. She juggled Queens games with AP Psych assignments, hockey practice, babysitting and being scouted for colleges. She has spent years navigating the typically male-dominated world of baseball; her father Travis was once removed as head coach of the local youth team for allowing his daughter to play alongside the boys.

“I was kind of used to being the only girl,” she says. “But I mean, you get used to the stares, you get used to the eyes on you. At that point, it’s just all the time.”

Addisyn Baird, the only high schooler in the WPBL, works on a school assignment in a hotel room. Photograph: Jaclyn Licht

While young players like Baird were accustomed to game-time pressure and their roles as pioneers of women in sports, adjusting to life alongside dozens of other fellow athletes in a small city was its own unique journey. Many tried to absorb Illinois culture as much as possible. The Hunters’ Ticara Geldenhuis, who normally lives full-time near Sydney, Australia, enjoyed swimming at the local lake, playing with teammates at the local golf course or day tripping to Chicago. On game nights, whether win or lose, players often frequented the bars in town afterward to play pool or sing karaoke.

Firebells players hold balls in the dugout. Photograph: Jaclyn Licht

The Post-It notes and gameplans Henley spent that morning preparing did not deliver a win that night. The LA Queens defeated the Heights 15-11, eliminating New York from the playoffs.

Two days later, the Queens would beat the Fireballs in Game 1 of the WPBL Championship Series, en route to becoming the league’s inaugural champions. Rocky and Jackson were there in the bleachers watching with their players, inspecting every play with sharp attention and already taking notes for next season.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/ng-int.summary: The inaugural season of the Women's Pro Baseball League (WPBL) is the first league of its kind in 70 years. Players hailed from across the US and 11 different countries to play for four teams: the Heights, Boston Hunters, San Francisco Firebells and Los Angeles Queens.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why | Kitty Sayers
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kitty Sayers
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and what the state owes its citizens. The lessons leave their mark

Y
oung British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up in France as a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets.

“To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past.

The lycée protests in the past week have displayed the organisation and bravery of the French students. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost his hand to a police grenade during a blockade. More than 6,000 people have been arrested, many of them under 18. Hundreds of schools across France are either blockaded or closed. These teenagers know the risks and commit to turning up anyway, day after day. I can’t imagine that happening in Britain, so what makes the French so different?

First, there’s the history. France’s republic was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it. French pupils learn that protest, uprising and rioting are the origin story of their freedoms, so these methods are championed in promoting change. We grew up in school with the idea that if you don’t like something, you have the power to change it. The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education. The French Revolution appears in the curriculum twice, for pupils aged 12 and then again at 16; the student protests of 1968 are taught at age 14 and again at 17. Debating is encouraged in schools from as early as collège, or at about 11 years old. Young people are expected to have an opinion and not be afraid to defend it.

Even I, at 11, started to feel patriotic during our moral and civic education classes, despite not having a French passport. Protesting is taught as a legally framed fundamental right and a civic responsibility. Of course, with lycéens not yet being old enough to vote, protest is the next best thing.

In the final year of lycée, pupils study Rousseau’s Du Contrat Social (The Social Contract), which argues that citizens should only surrender their unrestricted natural liberty in exchange for civil and moral freedoms. You give up your individual interests for the volonté générale (general will) – put simply, you pay heavy taxes and in return you expect the country to work. That bargain is how the French understand their relationship with the state. When the government raises the retirement age, lets electricity bills soar or cuts school budgets, that is seen as a breach of the social contract. Protest is the automatic response.

Britons, on the other hand, are subjects of the UK and are characterised more by an American-style individualism and a desire to live and let live. There is less collective spirit. Britain has an extraordinary history of protest, spanning Peterloo, the Chartists, the suffragettes and the poll tax riots, but there is arguably a different cultural relationship to these events. They can be remembered as stand-alone episodes and interruptions to the national story rather than as the story itself. The Thatcher era also did permanent damage to unions, contributing to the British public being a grumbling but compliant one, lacking in organising power.

Because these values are ingrained across French society, and in every generation, the student protesters are emboldened by the firefighters, nurses, lawyers and teachers who have joined them in solidarity. Across social media, you can see these moments of support and unity. A viral video of the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, protecting students from the police is a striking example of this. It’s difficult to imagine British teenagers taking to the streets, because they would be alone.

Parents have joined their children in protesting, and have called on other parents to do the same for the planned general strike on 17 October. (This is also a response to the police brutality witnessed in the past week.) Many parents were themselves lycée students and marched against education reforms and cuts. The anti-Macroniste parents (of whom there are many) don’t treat their children as delinquents, but as citizens exercising their rights.

That does not mean every French parent supports every protest, or that French society is wholly united behind its students. While the French state technically encourages protest through the curriculum, the force and violence with which it has met its students says otherwise. And there is resentment of the protests among some students, particularly those who come from conservative households and believe that the blockades are a leftwing plot.

Students in France are not necessarily more political than their British counterparts – young British people are active, but tend to take part in established and larger movements such as Extinction Rebellion or the Gaza protests rather than initiate protests themselves. The biggest difference lies in the French willingness to take to the streets, suddenly and en-masse. Unlike in the UK, the state is something the French are taught to engage with as citizens, and to challenge when necessary. If anything, the lycéens are just being good students.

Kitty Sayers is a master’s student in journalism

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Shola Lawal
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
It has been one year since United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) brokered a “ceasefire” aimed at eventually ending Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.

However, rather than receiving relief and a chance to rebuild, Palestinians in the enclave continue to face attacks and be uprooted as Israeli forces have expanded control within the territory.

Trump first proposed the BoP in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.

In November, a United Nations Security Council resolution recognised the board as a “transitional administration” in Gaza.

But what has the board achieved? Here’s what we know:

The BoP’s mission was laid out in Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan, as was the “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire began on October 10, 2025.

The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.

It required Israeli forces to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza since October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas led attacks into southern Israel and Israel began the war. The plan proposed reopening border crossings to allow much-needed aid into Gaza.

The peace plan required Hamas to release all Israeli captives. It also proposed a later phase in which the group would disarm and its members would be granted amnesty or a safe exit from Gaza.

The peace plan established the BoP as a transitional governing body until the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, could take over.

An International Stabilization Force (ISF), led by the US, was supposed to take over security in Gaza from withdrawing Israeli forces, the plan stated. It also proposed the reconstruction and redevelopment of Gaza, whose people, it said, “have suffered enough”.

In February, the BoP’s members, who each joined in exchange for a $1bn annual fee, met in Washington, DC, for its first summit, at which member states pledged $7bn in funding although aid agencies said reconstructing Gaza would cost closer to $70bn.

On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, the BoP also unveiled a 66-project recovery plan worth $2.4bn.

The BoP’s achievements are tied to the success of the Gaza peace plan.

Under that, Hamas has released all 168 living captives and Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners.

Hamas has also announced the dissolution of its government in the Gaza Strip although Israel has dismissed that as a “stunt”.

Other goals under the peace plan have been only partially met.

Governance has been hampered. While a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), meant to act as the governing authority in Gaza, was founded, Israel has not granted it entry into the Strip. The NCAG reports directly to the board and is led by Chief Commissioner Ali Shaath and other Palestinian technocrats. It operates from Cairo. Israel has not stated why the committee is not permitted to enter Gaza.

Aid remains restricted. About 227 aid trucks enter the Strip daily when 600 trucks were supposed to, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) hunger monitor.

Israel has classified thousands of basic items, such as tents and essential equipment like ventilators, as “dual use” items, which means they have military and civilian applications, and has restricted their flow into the Strip. About 1.4 million Palestinians – or most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people – will suffer hunger until at least December, the IPC has noted. That is 200,000 more than those who faced hunger in May, suggesting a significantly deteriorating situation.

Observers argued that the BoP has entirely failed to secure the “ceasefire” as Israeli attacks have continued almost daily on the Strip.

Since October 10, 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians, mostly women and children, have been killed. In the three years since the war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and thousands more are missing and presumed dead under the rubble.

Israel says its continuing attacks target Hamas members, but the group vehemently denies the claims.

Israel also now occupies about 60 percent of the Strip, more than the 50 percent agreed in Trump’s peace plan. The “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the area of Gaza under Israeli occupation, has been pushed farther into the Strip, causing further displacement and squeezing Gaza’s population into an ever-shrinking area. Palestinians unknowingly crossing the “Yellow Line” have been shot dead.

In December, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army “will never fully leave” the Strip.

Mohamad Elmasry at the Doha Institute of Graduate Studies told Al Jazeera that Israel is simply continuing a broader policy of “ethnic cleansing” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. “They are making life miserable,” he said, adding: “This is all by design.”

Consequently, the BoP has also failed to ensure Hamas disarms so phase two of the peace plan could begin.

Although Hamas has agreed to hand its weapons over to the NCAG, it rejects the “disarmament” clause because Israel has not ceased its attacks or withdrawn from the Strip as agreed. At the same time, Israel has said it will not move forward with the plan if Hamas does not disarm, leaving the two sides in a standoff.

Meanwhile, no stabilisation force has been deployed. Six countries – Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo and Uganda – have so far committed personnel to form a security force of 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police headed by the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM).

There has been no meaningful reconstruction in Gaza. Palestinians continue to live in tent camps infested with rodents and insects with little to shield them from intense heat, or rain.

The Trump administration and BoP have echoed Israel’s rejection of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA, which has long provided lifesaving humanitarian aid, education, development programmes and social services in Gaza and employs about 11,000 Palestinians.

The BoP said last month that it will not work with UNRWA, essentially sidelining the agency.

A BoP official told The Associated Press news agency that UNRWA could continue working in Gaza if its programmes were deemed relevant but the agency’s “days are over”.

UNRWA said the move was “not logical”.

In June, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to extend UNRWA’s mandate until 2029. The BoP itself is mandated to oversee the peace process until December 2027 when its progress will be reviewed for possible renewal by the UN.

Analysts and rights groups have raised concerns that the BoP could take over all aspects of Gaza’s rebuilding. Countries too, including France and other European nations, have called out any attempts to replace the UN in the Strip.

But Elmasry said no country is willing to take action. “There are a lot of international actors that do not want to cross the US,” he said. That essentially leaves the fate of more than 2 million Palestinians to Trump, he added.

Ultimately, the BoP has “failed”, said Simon Mabon, a professor at Lancaster University.

“The failure to implement its own plan to end the Gaza conflict demonstrates its impotence and the inability to ensure that Israel and, to a lesser extent, Hamas, remain bound by their own commitments [and] has allowed the genocide to continue,” he concluded.

It required Israel to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel. to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Manchester City whistleblower Rui Pinto to remain under police protection
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Computer hacker Rui Pinto, the man behind the Football Leaks website that helped trigger the Premier League probe into Manchester City’s finances, will remain under police protection, Portuguese authorities confirmed.

Pinto obtained private documents that showed City broke league rules from 2009 to 2018. An independent commission found City guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against them over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

His witness protection measures, which were due to end on Saturday, October 10, will now remain in effect pending a new decision, the Ministry of Justice said in a statement.

A previous resolution was nullified because Pinto had not been “duly informed of the reasons for the decision” and had not had the opportunity to challenge it, the statement added on Friday.

Pinto’s lawyers last week denounced irregularities in the proceedings, highlighting the real threats facing their client, who was assaulted in Lisbon last April.

The 37-year-old said he had to move to a secret location “due to the multiple death threats” he had received.

Pinto has been a protected witness since 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest.

Arrested in Hungary, where he was living in January 2019, and extradited to his home country, Portugal, Pinto spent more than a year in pre-trial detention before agreeing to cooperate with authorities by granting them access to the encrypted data in his possession.

Pinto was both a defendant and a protected witness in the Portuguese justice system. He is also cooperating with investigators from other European countries.

During his first trial, the former history student and self-taught computer expert admitted hacking computers to obtain millions of documents, which he began publishing online in late 2015.

Passed on to a consortium of European investigative media outlets, this wealth of information exposed questionable practices involving star football players, clubs and agents, subsequently leading to tax adjustments and judicial investigations in several countries.

A Portuguese court handed Pinto a suspended four-year sentence in September 2023 after he was found guilty on counts of attempted extortion, illegal access to data and breach of correspondence.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.summary: Rui Pinto's witness protection measures will remain in effect pending a new decision. Pinto obtained private documents that showed Manchester City broke league rules from 2009 to 2018. An independent commission found City guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against them.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Suspect killed after 13 kindergarteners taken hostage, beaten in Brazil
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Brazilian police have rescued 13 children who had been taken hostage at a kindergarten in the southern city of Curitiba after killing the suspect, who threatened to set fire to the building, according to officials.

At least one of the children was wounded in Friday’s incident, the commander of the military police special forces unit in Parana state, Alexandre Lopes Dias, told reporters without elaborating on who or what injured the child.

Parana police spokesperson Leticia Martins told journalists outside the kindergarten that the suspect jumped the gate on Friday, broke into a classroom and held 13 children hostage.

He then spread a flammable substance in the room and held a lighter in his hand. He was carrying a knife and also what was initially believed to be a firearm, but later was found to be fake.

“Our negotiating teams were in place but saw no alternative but to neutralise him,” said Martins, who did not specify whether the suspect had expressed a specific reason for his actions.

The incident took place in the neighbourhood of Sao Braz in Curitiba, a city of 1.8 million residents located 400km (250 miles) south of Sao Paulo.

Lopes Dias told reporters the suspect was identified as a man who suffered from schizophrenia, but he did not reveal the man’s identity or how he was killed.

“During the entire negotiation, he stayed with all the children around him and one on his lap,” the police official said.

Talks lasted up to three hours. The children became agitated, and the attacker started hitting them, Lopes Dias told reporters.

“Once we realised that the kids were becoming increasingly upset and that the attacker started assaulting them physically, we opted for a tactical intervention to avoid a greater problem,” he explained.

Local media showed footage of tearful parents outside the school waiting for information as the negotiations between the suspect and police were ongoing. Minutes after what local media described as flash bangs, officers emerged carrying some of the children outside.

“We entered the classroom using a very tactical approach with little risk for the children,” Lopes Dias added.

Curitiba Mayor Eduardo Pimentel wrote on Instagram: “The 13 children are alive and safe! After anguishing and tense moments, this is the news we were all waiting for.”

Brazil in recent years has experienced multiple attacks on schools. In April 2023, a man killed four children with an axe at a day care in Blumenau, also in southern Brazil.

Curitiba City Hall said in a statement that the children and school staffers would receive psychological support.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: 13 children rescued after suspect killed the suspect, who threatened to set fire to the building. Police say the suspect jumped the gate and held 13 children hostage. He was carrying a knife and also what was initially believed to be a firearm, but later was found to be fake.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: A year after the ‘ceasefire’, Gaza’s healthcare is still collapsing
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Sally Saleh
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
When the “ceasefire” was announced on October 10 last year, we knew how much needed repairing. For the first time in a long while, we thought we might have the breathing space to do it.

We thought medicines and equipment could arrive more regularly. Hospitals and clinics could begin to be restored. Patients could leave Gaza for treatment. Emergency medical teams could come from overseas to support Gaza’s exhausted health workers. We could finally look beyond the next crisis and plan how to care for people over the coming months and years.

None of that happened.

Three years into the genocide, there is barely a moment to catch our breath. We’re being asked to do far more than Gaza’s devastated health system can sustain, while regular deliveries of medical supplies and equipment are still restricted and medical evacuations stalled.

People are still arriving at our clinics with traumatic injuries because Israel’s bombardment continues. More than 1,470 people have been killed since the “ceasefire” started. Even reaching a health centre can now put patients at risk. As the security situation has deteriorated, services supported by Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) have had to be suspended in parts of Gaza. Last month, a 65-year-old patient was killed by Israeli military quadcopter fire while seeking treatment at a MAP-supported health centre in Jabalia.

While treating new arrivals with new injuries, we are trying to look after patients whose treatment may take months or years.

Those who have lost limbs need rehabilitation, prosthetics and more surgery, but Israeli authorities heavily restrict the needed supplies. Children who survived acute malnutrition now live with anaemia and stunting, which need treatment, while people with diabetes and high blood pressure struggle to get their medicines. Cancer patients can’t get the radiotherapy they need, and people with kidney failure can’t count on regular dialysis.

Last month, a colleague of mine at MAP in Gaza lost her aunt, Iktimal. In February, Iktimal sensed something was wrong and had a biopsy, but the lab, like so many across Gaza, didn’t have the supplies to test the sample on time. It was more than a month before she learned she had cervical cancer, a disease that is usually curable when found early.

She had surgery in April, but her recovery was slow and painful, and she went on to develop kidney complications that needed specialist treatment unavailable in Gaza. Her family applied for a medical evacuation, but the process was slow, unclear, and bureaucratic. By the time Israeli authorities approved it, her condition was critical. She travelled to Egypt hoping she would finally get the care she needed, but two weeks later, she died.

Iktimal’s case is not unique. According to the World Health Organization, more than 15,000 people in Gaza are still waiting for medical evacuation; if delayed too long, many of these patients could be lost to a preventable death.

We had another tragic case a month ago: A newborn with a serious heart condition died at Assahaba Medical Complex, a hospital MAP supports. The baby needed emergency surgery that isn’t available in Gaza. The doctors knew what was needed but had no way to provide it.

Sometimes we struggle to provide treatment because even basic medical supplies are running short. Hospitals are also short on IV fluids, anaesthetics and surgical supplies. Even oxygen is in short supply.

Staff in many hospitals have to carry cylinders to a central station for refilling. Across Gaza, more than 500 patients rely on oxygen, some of them around the clock: People with cancer, pulmonary fibrosis and heart conditions, and babies and children in intensive care.

In August, the Palestinian Ministry of Health warned that 22 of Gaza’s 34 oxygen stations had stopped working, and only four of 30 machines used to fill oxygen cylinders were still running.

The stations that still function could fail soon. Israeli authorities continue to block the spare parts needed to repair them, classifying them as “dual-use” items. For similar reasons, Gaza has no working MRI machine, and only one or two CT scanners serve about two million people.

Doctors are sometimes left to make decisions without the scans, tests or medicines they would normally rely on.

A cancer that could have been caught early becomes harder to treat. An injury that could have healed with rehabilitation becomes a permanent disability. A child who needed proper food and treatment can be left with chronic malnutrition, stunting and developmental difficulties that may last a lifetime.

We were told the “ceasefire” would give people in Gaza time to heal and rebuild. It hasn’t. The restrictions that stood between Iktimal and her diagnosis, her treatment and her evacuation are still in place, and her story is one of thousands across Gaza in the past year.

Every delay has a cost. Every week a medicine is held back, a scan can’t be done, a patient is refused exit, someone’s condition passes the point where it can be treated.

Iktimal ran out of time. Right now, thousands of people in Gaza are running out of time, too.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: More than 1,470 people have been killed since the “ceasefire’s’ started. More than 15,000 people in Gaza are still waiting for medical evacuation. Children who survived acute malnutrition now live with anaemia and stunting, which need treatment.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Journalist Hamurabi Huesca Manzano killed in Mexico’s Oaxaca
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
A journalist moonlighting as a taxi driver has been shot dead in the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca, the ninth killed in the country this year, according to human rights organisation Article 19.

Hamurabi Huesca Manzano, who owned the news website Pinotepa Comunica, was killed on Friday after an armed group opened fire on him and two others, according to the state prosecutor’s report.

The office said one line of inquiry suggests that a dispute happened between local criminal groups, and that the intended target of the shooting was a man known as “El Dario”.

El Dario, infamous for instigating violence on the Oaxaca coast, was wounded in the shooting and died in hospital hours later. According to prosecutors, Huesca Manzano was working as a taxi driver, waiting to take El Dario somewhere else when the journalist was shot dead.

The prosecutor’s office says the attackers have been “fully identified”, but did not name them or say whether Huesca Manzano’s journalistic work played any role.

Local reports give differing accounts of where the attack happened, as well; a number of them say Huesca Manzano was shot at his home and that a woman was also injured.

Article 19 condemned the killing and said on X: “We demand that the prosecutor’s office treat his journalistic work as a priority in its investigation.”

The mayor of San Miguel Tlacamama, Antonio Olmedo Mendoza, confirmed Manzano’s death and offered condolences in a statement, local media reported.

“With deep sorrow, I regret the passing of Hamurabi Sinclair Huesca Manzano,” he said, adding that he joined the grief of his family, friends and colleagues.

Mexico is notorious for being one of the most dangerous countries for journalists, with more than 150 media workers killed there since 1994, according to Reporters Without Borders.

Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Abigail Bassett

Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.

I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.

The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.

The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.

People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights

Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds.

https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.author: May Jeong
https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.text:
With his new film about a Romanian family’s life in Norway, Cristian Mungiu wants you to consider the limits of your tolerance

With his new film about a Romanian family’s life in Norway, Cristian Mungiu wants you to consider the limits of your tolerance

Cristian Mungiu’s sixth feature, Fjord, concerns a family on trial. They seem like good people, God-fearing. They’ve just moved from Romania to a small hamlet nestled in the fjords of rural Norway. There is Mamma (Renate Reinsve), Tata (a bald and bespectacled Sebastian Stan), and their passel of children. They are an openly religious and proselytizing family. The parents, unfashionably, believe in punitive consequences to actions. They would never be accused of gentle parenting. All ought to be well, only Norway in 2026 is extravagantly suspicious of the devout — their famous tolerance reserved for the secular.

Fjord starts quietly and builds subtly. We are with the family as they are introduced to their places of learning, employment, and worship. A second, Norwegian, family serves as their foil. Sort of. Questions arise, about what counts as discipline, what as punishment. To those wanting answers, objective analysis, which is to say a kind of measured purity, Mungiu says, come down to the mud with us! In the morally complex world of the movie, nothing is spared — a piano chord, a passing remark, hems of clothes — all are cast in a different light. We are all the more enriched for it.

The Verge spoke with Mungiu, who is himself Romanian, about how his early tenure in journalism informs his writing, what it was like living under Nicolae Ceaușescu’s dictatorial reign, Marxist literary theory, and the challenges and pleasures of thinking for oneself.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

I’d like to start with you at Cannes, where you said the question that Fjord raises is: Are there good minorities and bad minorities? I wonder if this question has changed for you since.

https://www.wired.com/gallery/gifts-for-.author: Simon Hill
https://www.wired.com/gallery/gifts-for-.text:

LEGO ISN'T GOING anywhere. Those beloved little bricks won't biodegrade, are machined to incredibly tight tolerances, and—unless your dog chews one up—retain what Lego refers to as their “clutch power” for decades. Their relevance in terms of cultural pastiche isn’t fading on me either. They're as irresistible to me today as they were as a kid.

If you and your loved ones are also obsessed with Lego sets, we have some great gift ideas. For more recommendations, don't forget to check out our other gift guides.

Updated October 2026: I added the Lego Ideas Peanuts: Snoopy's Doghouse, a Lego Batman game, Star Wars Advent Calendar 2026, Star Trek light kit, and Lego Architecture Paris: City of Love.

One of the reasons that Lego sets are so popular is the company's innumerable licensing deals. No matter what you're into, Lego has signed a deal to make a Lego set about it. (And then, in an ouroboros of advertising, the company will then make a movie about the Lego set about the franchise.) Anyway, this is a long and roundabout way of saying that my son and I are obsessed with the Lego Formula 1 sets. I even got to watch the Lego cars hit the track at a Formula 1 race. Ever since then, we've been watching the races and Netflix's Drive to Survive. It's the perfect collaboration because Lego bricks and Formula 1 engineers are on the same page when it comes to precise engineering and tight tolerances. Also, once you're done building, the cars work as toys as well as sets. —Adrienne So

If you’re curious about Lego’s new Smart Play system, the Star Wars Throne Room Duel and A-Wing set is a great way to dip your toe in the water. This fun build enables you to reenact the climax of Return of the Jedi, with Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker duking it out as Emperor Palpatine looks on and a space battle rages outside. Smart Bricks add lightsaber noises, lasers, explosions, heavy breathing, and even a rendition of “The Imperial March.” They also light up, but you’ll have to remember to charge them.

My daughter and my husband love the Lego Botanicals collection. These gorgeous tree and flower sets work well as holiday centerpieces once you're finished building—you can leave them right out on the table, instead of hiding them away in your Lego basement once you're done. My 11-year-old built this lovely rose bouquet, which has articulated heads so you can arrange them in the case. For the winter holidays, we also recommend the Lego poinsettia set ($50), which was our centerpiece last year. —Adrienne So

A superbly loving parody that throws the best of Batman’s movie outings into the blender with a pinch of slapstick comedy and plenty of charm. Gotham is packed with collectibles, puzzles to solve, and an endless supply of thugs to bash. Melee combat is fun, as you counter and dodge to build combos, and there’s plenty of gadgetry to try out. This is the most fun I’ve had with a Lego game in years, and it’s perfect for split-screen couch co-op. If you’re not a Batman fan, there are tons of other great Lego games, based on other worlds, like Star Wars, Ninjago, and Marvel.

Who doesn’t love Snoopy? This set is an easy build and includes Snoopy, his doghouse, and Woodstock. There’s also a typewriter (fans will recognize the line, “It was a dark and stormy night”) and a campfire, with alternative legs if you want Snoopy to stand, hunch over to type, or lie back on the top of his doghouse. The Ideas range from Lego is based on fan creations that have been shared and voted on to become real sets. This one is lovely, but it’s definitely a display set, not something you’d actively play with.

If you have a coworker who likes Lego and would like to gift him or her something tiny and thoughtful, I suggest this little notepad. It's very cute, with 224 pieces of paper, and one side looks like a brick. The notes themselves are about 5 inches long, which is big enough for a pretty substantial note! Chronicle Books has a whole line of Lego books, puzzles, and stationery for your Lego-obsessed friend. You could also throw in a pack of these brick erasers ($36) to make a little care package. —Adrienne So

If you also have an 8- or a 10-year-old, let me recommend a simple life hack—instead of caving to their demands to let them look at your phone while you're out, just always carry a deck of cards in your bag. It's crazy how many times my kids have settled down and waited patiently in a doctor's office or restaurant, as long as they can start a game of Crazy Eights or Go Fish (I do not recommend Speed). These Lego playing cards are beautiful and brightly colored, feel sturdy, and have held up to several rounds of shuffling around a table. The box comes in a pack of two, so your kids can split it. —Adrienne So

With the holidays approaching, this is a great alternative to regular advent calendars. You get a Star Wars–related minifigure or build behind each door, including irresistibly cute Mando and Grogu figures in Christmas jumpers, critters like a Bantha and Dewback, and tiny ships like an X-wing and the Razor Crest.

I wish we were a family that kept treasured family heirlooms all wrapped up in tissue paper, ready to be marveled over at the next year's tree decorating. Unfortunately, every year finds us with some Christmas tree–related disaster or the other. Our new puppy has chewed the stuffed animals that an uncle has sent us; my son has sent a baseball crashing into the ceramic horse head that I got as a kid. We always need new ornaments, so why not new Lego ones? These are very cute, and my son assembled them in a matter of minutes. —Adrienne So

Have all your sets now become disassembled, and do you need some inspiration while looking at the giant wheelbarrow of Lego bricks on your front porch? This is my kids' favorite book for ideas on what to build. It has been a struggle to not “lose” it from the library.

All of the builds are fairly easy, and so far I haven't seen any that require specialized pieces. However, you will probably need more than just 12 red bricks or 14 yellow ones to make many of the builds, so you should make sure your Lego loved one has a substantial collection already. If you want other sources of inspiration, we also like The Art of the Brick ($40), and I would be remiss if I did not include our own Brian Barrett's book, The Art of the Minifigure ($35). —Adrienne So

If you're having relatives over for the holidays, I suggest having a little puzzle like this to whip out while everyone's waiting for you to put the final touches on dinner. It's not one big puzzle, which can feel overwhelming and makes it hard to get off the dinner table—it's four separate little puzzles. Your kids, or parents, or fun uncle ("funcle") can work on each small puzzle separately and attach them together later. Each of the backs is patterned differently, so you can tell the different puzzles apart when you're putting them away or back together again. —Adrienne So

As Lego-branded toys rolled into my house, I do have the caveat that my kids were very confused. ("Why are all these Lego gifts coming in but none of them are Legos?") However, my son was immediately thrilled and delighted with this mug and demands that I wash it every morning for him to drink out of.

There are several faces to choose from if your children don't want to match. It's ceramic and can hold about 17 ounces of liquid—so, pretty big for a 7-year-old but nothing their little hands can't handle. It's dishwasher-safe. We've also received these off-brand Lego mugs ($13) as gifts, but again, the clutch power of off-brand Lego bricks is unsatisfactory and the bricks don't stick on very well. —Adrienne So

https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-smart.title: The Best Smart Scales for Tracking Weight and Body Composition (2026)
https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-smart.author: Christopher Null
https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-smart.text:
AFTER YEARS OF sleepiness, the smart scale world has finally woken up—driven almost certainly by the GLP-1 craze, as millions of consumers find themselves wondering if those weekly jabs are actually working.

What was previously a category occupied by dated gear has abruptly exploded, and for good reason. Today’s smart scales don’t just report on your weight; they do things like measure your heart rate and break down muscle composition, and some can even give you an eye on your heart health, courtesy of technology like integrated ECG systems. Through mobile apps, they can track all of this information over time.

The big shift in the category in the past year has been a flood of new full-body scanners hitting the market from all corners. Essentially bathroom scales with handlebar-based scanners, these don’t just use bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) to measure conductivity (and, thus, body fat percentage) through your feet. They can now scan through your hands, too, giving you a much more holistic (and ostensibly accurate) look at your body metrics than a floor scale will provide. I’ve personally seen body fat percentage numbers swing up to 6 percent between the two types of scales. (Spoiler: The full-body scanner data is always higher.)

Do you really need all that information? I’ve long suggested that it’s really the trend line that matters most, not the absolute numbers, and as long as your metrics are headed in the right direction, it doesn’t matter quite as much whether things are off by a small percentage. Consistent weigh-ins are the most important part of the process, along with tracking that information over time to determine whether your diet and workout regimen (or medication routine) is getting you the results you need.

Mind you, scale prices are headed up, and new full-body scanners can now top $600 for top-tier tech. That’s part of the reason why I still recommend a standard scale for most users, as these devices are considerably less expensive, and the results they offer are likely to be good enough for all but serious athletes.

Either way, this roundup has an option for every type of user.

Updated October 2026: I've added Withings’ BodyScan 2 and new honorable mentions from Runstar, Tanita, and Withings. I've also added scales to avoid and ensured up-to-date prices throughout.

How Do Smart Scales Work?

Smart scales come in two basic flavors: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. The former connects directly to your phone to sync its readings. The latter uses your home’s wireless network to sync readings straight to the cloud, which your phone’s app can then access. Wi-Fi scales are generally more expensive but more versatile. While older scales often featured erratic wireless connections, newer models have many of their kinks worked out—and firmware updates have improved connectivity.

Virtually all smart scales use the same type of system to gauge your additional vitals: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which involves sending a minuscule electric current up one leg and measuring what happens when it comes down the other side. Some mathematical magic converts all of this into any number of derived measurements about things like your body’s percentage of fat, water, and bone; body-mass index (BMI); and, sometimes, arcana like your basal metabolic rate (BMR), which is a measure of your body’s energy consumption at rest. All the scales I tested can sync data with Apple Health and Google's Health Connect, either directly or by passing data via the app.

When Is the Best Time to Weigh Yourself?

Most experts say that the best time to weigh in is first thing in the morning, before you’ve eaten and after you’ve used the restroom. The main reason for this is consistency: Weighing yourself at the same time every day is the best way to ensure that consecutive weigh-ins are taken under conditions that are as controlled as possible. Since eating and drinking will cause your weight to fluctuate considerably, weighing yourself on an empty stomach means you’re getting an apples-to-apples comparison each morning.

As a small bonus, your weight is usually at its lowest right after you wake up, so you potentially stand to give yourself a gentle confidence boost by stepping on the scale then instead of after dinner.

Early Withings scales weren't great, dragged down perhaps by complications related to the company changing ownership a few too many times in the past decade. Now back in the hands of its cofounder, Withings is doing things right again, starting with the Body Comp, a much more advanced version of its earlier Body Cardio scale, which suffered from a few flaws. In contrast, the experience here is quick and painless: Step on the new Wi-Fi–enabled Body Comp and it (very) quickly runs through a series of measurements, starting with your weight and moving on to a variety of biomarkers that include heart rate, various fat and muscle measurements, vascular age, and electrodermal activity—which measures “skin response via sweat gland stimulation in your feet.” Strangely, the scale’s heart rate measurement regularly skews about 10 beats per minute too fast. It also reports the day’s weather and even forecasts air quality in your area. After the crawl of personal data, I’ve come to rely on seeing the weather on the Body Comp’s bright color display first thing each morning.

The company has resolved long-standing issues around the user having to stand in the perfect spot to get readings, and its app has matured impressively over the past few years. That’s good because this scale isn’t cheap. But as an unintentional weight-watcher, I think it’s worth it. The Withings app tracks data for up to eight users seemingly forever; I now have readings on Withings devices going back to 2010 and hope to keep the streak going well into the future.

Etekcity’s smart scale offers a bevy of features you’d normally pay for through the nose, including Wi-Fi connectivity, a bright color display, and long-term tracking of 14 biometrics that are quickly synced to your smartphone via the VeSync app (a kind of do-everything app that works on a broad group of home appliances). The scale, fortunately, doesn’t suffer from being part of this vast environment, offering an easy-to-understand interface that quickly syncs after each session and tracks your vitals by week, month, quarter, and year. It supports multiple users, and a baby mode adds extra flexibility.

The hardware is sleek and clean, and the display is customizable. You select up to nine metrics to showcase. They rotate across the screen after each weigh-in, so you don't need to turn to the app at all, unless you really want to drill down into specifics. It can even connect to Alexa devices if you want to announce your weight loss success to the entire house.

Wyze has built its entire business by offering smart home technology at a fraction of the price of other brands, and its products always manage to be capable and well-made. Its latest scale is the Wyze Scale X, an update of its old, no-frills Wyze Scale. The Bluetooth-only device displays your weight on its LED screen; you’ll need to turn to the Wyze app to get additional metrics—13 in total, including muscle mass, visceral fat, and BMR measurements.

You can share the scale with up to eight users, and there are even modes for babies, pets, and luggage, so you don’t screw up your stats before you go on a trip. As with most Wyze products, it’s an amazing value, as sale events have brought the price to as low as $20.

If two sensors are good, then 12 must be even better, right?

Full-body scanners or body composition scales hit the market a few years ago, initially coming across a bit like a novelty by offering not just a blunt look at your weight and body fat markers but a more in-depth analysis of your health, limb by limb. Electrodes built into a retractable handle send small pulses from your feet to your hands and back in various combinations, ostensibly giving you a much deeper look at your health than a simple scale, which can’t “see” above the waist, can provide.

Early body scanners felt fairly primitive. But with the BodyScan 2, Withings fully kicks out the jams, offering one of the most advanced weigh-in experiences you can find.

The scale offers two types of scans: The daily scan measures weight—hyper-accurately, thanks to a built-in leveling system that forces you to be perfectly balanced before it records the day’s number—fat, muscle, and water percentages, visceral fat, and your heart rate. Once a week, you’re urged to upgrade to the longevity scan, a 90-second experience that totals a massive collection of 60 metrics, including blood oxygen level (courtesy of a thumb-based scanner), nervous system response, and a guesstimate of your heart health. Perhaps most impressive is the inclusion of a six-lead ECG, which can even help suss out AFib situations without a trip to the doctor.

Wi-Fi connectivity beams all results to Withings’ impressive app, usually instantaneously (aside from ECG results, which take up to two days to show up because a cardiologist reviews them first). While the Withings software is extremely busy, it’s actually easy to navigate, letting you fixate endlessly on every aspect of your health.

Also consider the Renpho MorphoScan Nova for $200, the brand's latest high-end scale. It evolves the chunky metallic-pad design of the standard MophoScan (see below) in favor of a much sleeker glass base and a new app, while keeping the original's oversized handlebar-based LCD screen. For an extra $30, it’s an excellent upgrade for the better looks alone. Additional features include voice prompts during your weigh-in (which you may very well hate) and an upgraded BIA sensor that other MorphoScan devices lack. The only legitimate problem I had with the scale was pokey Wi-Fi performance, but it's generally strong enough to get the job done. The app isn’t as intuitive as Withings’, but for a third of the price of the BodyScan 2, the Nova is worth serious consideration.

Renpho MorphoScan for $170: The Renpho MorphoScan full-body scanner looks surprisingly similar to the Runstar FG2015, including a near-identical display attached to the handlebars. Well, spoiler alert: They are basically the same scale. They even use the same app to collect data (you can use both scales simultaneously with the app).

Runstar Smart Body Fat Scale (FG2015) for $140: My former pick for best full-body scanner, this admittedly garish offering tracks 20 metrics and supports 24 users, effectively breaking down information, limb-by-limb, in its Starfit mobile app. USB-C rechargeability is a nice plus, but the price tag—just $140 if you buy it directly from Runstar—is probably its best feature.

Tanita RD-953 InnerScan Pro

Tanita RD-953 InnerScan Pro for $230: One of the few new feet-only smart scales to hit the market this decade, Tanita’s RD-953 is defined by its Cylonesque looks—and its relative simplicity. The costly Bluetooth-only scale scans quickly, though the placement of its display in the center of the scale, right between your feet, can be awkward for those with even a small breadbasket between their head and the floor. I also didn’t love the very high and hopefully overstated body fat reading the scale gave me, but my harshest criticism is directed at the Healthy Edge app (a different app than is used by Tanita’s other scale), which is about as engaging and motivational as a shopping list on a Post-It Note.

Withings BodyFit for $230: The middle child in the Withings family sits comfortably between the no-holds-barred BodyScan 2 and the feet-only Body Comp Smart Scale, offering a pleasant alternative for users who want full-body analysis but don’t need (or want to pay for) the fitness extremism of Withings’s top-tier model. It’s a sleek and demure unit with a small but informative color screen, quick Wi-Fi connectivity, and fast performance—and, of course, it works seamlessly with Withings’s excellent app.

Arboleaf Body Fat Scale CS20W

Arboleaf Body Fat Scale CS20W for $50: This affordable Bluetooth scale isn’t the most eye-catching I’ve tested in light of its big silver electrodes and an oversized display that comes across as a bit garish. While weight is easy to make out, the six additional statistics showcased are difficult to read, all displayed simultaneously. I like the Arboleaf app better than the scale, where five additional metrics are available, each featuring a helpful explanation when tapped. It’s a solid deal at this price, but the upsell to get an “intelligent interpretation report” for an extra $40 per year is probably safe to skip.

Hume Health Body Pod for $229: Hume Health’s Body Pod, another full-body scanner with handles, is heavily advertised—at least to the apps on my phone—and touted (by Hume) as the Next Big Thing in the world of body management. While the app is indeed glossy and inviting, I was shocked to discover how flimsy the hardware felt, that it lacked Wi-Fi, and that some features are locked behind a $100-a-year Hume Plus subscription plan. It works fine enough, but you can get results that are just as good with a cheaper device.

Garmin Index S2 for $200: Five years after its release, the Index S2 is still Garmin’s current model, a surprise for a company otherwise obsessed with fitness. It’s still noteworthy for its lovely color display, which walks you through its six body metrics (for up to 16 users) with each weigh-in. The display also provides your weight trend over time in graphical form and can even display the weather. The scale connects directly to Wi-Fi and Garmin’s cloud-based storage system, so—unlike with Bluetooth-only scales—you don’t need a phone nearby to track your progress. A phone running the Garmin Connect app (Android, iOS) is handy, so you can keep track of everything over time. Unfortunately, as health apps go, Connect is a bit of a bear, so expect a learning curve—especially if you want to make changes to the way the scale works. You can turn its various LCD-screen widgets on or off in the app, but finding everything can be difficult due to the daunting scope of the Garmin ecosystem. The color screen is nice at first, but it ultimately adds little to the package.

Omron BCM-500 for $85: With its large LCD panel, quartet of onboard buttons, and oversize silver electrodes, the Omron BCM-500 is an eye-catching masterwork of brutalist design. If your bathroom is decked out in concrete and wrought iron, this scale will fit right in. The Bluetooth unit syncs with Omron’s HeartAdvisor app (Android, iOS), but it provides all six of its body metrics directly on the scale, cycling through them with each weigh-in (for up to four users). It can be difficult to read the label for each of the data points, in part because the LCD isn’t backlit, but the app is somewhat easier to follow, offering front-page graphs of weight, skeletal muscle, and body fat. On the other hand, the presentation is rather clinical, and the app is surprisingly slow to sync. For a scale without a Wi-Fi connection, it’s also rather expensive.

Renpho MorphoScan Lite

Renpho MorphoScan Lite for $95: This new entry-level offering in the MorphoScan line is specifically designed for new GLP-1 users. It's a simpler device, ditching the handheld display and, critically, Wi-Fi connectivity. It’s also one of the flimsiest scales I’ve tested—too lightweight for you to extend the handlebars without inadvertently dragging the scale across the floor. If this were a mega-bargain in line with foot-only scale pricing, I’d be sold, but the meager savings compared to other MorphoScan scales don’t justify considering it.

Tanita RD-545 InnerScan Pro

Tanita RD-545 InnerScan Pro for $480: This monstrous, industrial scale looks more like it belongs in the mailroom than the bathroom, and its level of complexity only provides more supportive evidence. The Bluetooth-only scale is confusing to set up and difficult to use correctly, and I was only able to get successful measurements by first opening the mobile app and ensuring the scale was connected before carefully stepping onto it. Then, I had to wait for a prompt to pick up the handles (while balanced on the device). Testing feels like it takes forever, and that’s even if you get it right the first time. For $480, the scale is a questionable value at best, despite its 40 measurements offered. No Wi-Fi at this price, really?

https://www.wired.com/story/humans-watch.title: Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
https://www.wired.com/story/humans-watch.author: Jorge Garay
https://www.wired.com/story/humans-watch.text:
ASTRONOMERS HAVE OBTAINED the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed.

Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant. With this resolution, researchers can now see that these filaments are not continuous as they had previously appeared. Instead, they’re shaped more like beads on a string, made up of pearl-like knots of gas of relatively uniform size.

These “cosmic pearls” are, in fact, enormous. According to the study published in The Astrophysical Journal, each bead measures about four light-days in diameter. “The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare,” Ilaria Caiazzo, a coauthor of the study, said in a press release. “The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them.”

How exactly the pearls formed is not yet entirely clear, though it’s assumed they are concentrations of material ejected during the explosion. What’s strange, however, is their regularity. In the aftermath of a supernova, astronomers expected to find much more oddly shaped accumulations, but the knots are similar in size and appear aligned along the filaments. This peculiar order is a new feature that could help researchers gain a deeper understanding of stellar death.

This image, obtained with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, shows that the ejecta from the remnant—with its unmistakable fireworks-like shape—form a cascading structure resembling a knot.

The Pa 30 nebula is also particularly unusual because the central star isn’t exactly dead. Instead, it’s considered a “zombie star.” Typically, a thermonuclear supernova is the violent death of a star, which is completely destroyed in the explosion. But in rare cases, part of the star may survive, and scientists do not yet fully understand how or why this happens. The unusual structures of Pa 30 could help astronomers reconstruct more precisely how these kinds of detonations occur and how zombie stars can live on afterward.

All of this has been discovered because scientists seem to have a bit of a crush on Pa 30. Few astronomical structures connect modern observation so directly with human accounts from more than eight centuries ago. The nebula matches the records left by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1181, who described the appearance of a new star in the sky that remained visible for several months. At the time, it was impossible to know that they were witnessing the aftermath of a massive stellar explosion. Centuries later, scientists linked that event to the supernova that gave rise to Pa 30.

I COME FROM a car family, the kind that always had four or five vehicles in various states of “restoration.” Changing your own oil in my house was not only a rite of passage but a duty—proof that you were self-sufficient and economical, not, as my uncle would say, a “handy-man.” (“I open my wallet and hand over my credit card!” he’d roar.)

Suffice it to say, I changed my own oil for most of my adult life until about eight years ago, when I bought my first new hybrid SUV. Opening the hood for the first time, I saw an arrangement of black plastic rectangles, not the discrete auto parts I recognized. I didn’t know how to change the oil, and I wasn’t sure I wanted to figure it out. I was (and still am) a working parent, and I always appreciate having another chore taken off my plate.

The nearest oil change facility to my house turned out to be a Valvoline Instant Oil Change, and I have been going there ever since, for both that same hybrid SUV and a second one I bought a few years later. Hybrid vehicles require fully synthetic oil, which costs about twice as much per quart as conventional oil, so having the oil changed by a shop is typically worth it when factoring in the labor—especially if you have a Valvoline Instant Oil Change coupon.

Valvoline may be best known for its line of retail automotive products like oil and additives, but it also operates 2,100 US locations of Valvoline Instant Oil Change garages, which perform oil changes at up to 50 percent less than most car dealerships. And faster, too—usually around half an hour in my experience. If you, too, would like to have your oil changed quickly and inexpensively, or get some cash off some quarts of motor oil if you’re still DIY-ing, check out our Valvoline coupons and deals below.

If you have a basic, non-hybrid vehicle driven under normal conditions (infrequent stop-and-go traffic, no towing), you’re in luck—your oil change will already be relatively inexpensive. It will be even cheaper with this $10-off Valvoline coupon, which includes 5 quarts of Valvoline brand motor oil (diesel quarts may vary), a filter, lube and maintenance check, and tax. Print it or save it to your phone so you have it next time you’re out and about. Not valid with other offers or customer-supplied oil (at that point, you may as well do it yourself).

This is the coupon I personally use when I get my oil changed. In fact, I’m printing it out right now! Synthetic and synthetic blend oils are best for hybrid vehicles, luxury vehicles, vehicles subjected to a lot of stop-and-go traffic, trucks that tow, or any car with an engine that needs a little TLC. Because synthetic oil is engineered to be more consistent and uniform, it provides better temperature stability and cleaning power, leading to less wear and tear on an engine. It is also, of course, more expensive than conventional oil, so this Valvoline coupon offers a little more off—$15 as opposed to $10. Like the offer above, this Valvoline coupon is good for up to 5 quarts of Valvoline oil, a filter, lube and maintenance check, and tax.

When you buy more at Valvoline, you save more. One of the easiest ways to save is to buy in bulk, which is especially cost-effective if you have multiple cars or a family with several cars. When you purchase multiple units of motor oil, gear oil, or transmission fluid, you’ll receive a larger discount the more you buy, up to 25% off.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/the-th.title: The Third-Party Agent Problem: Why Security Built for AI You Chose Misses the Agents You Didn't
https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/the-th.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/the-th.text:
In environments studied for the 2026 State of Agent Security Report, roughly 1,280 third-party products now embed AI. About 282 of them sit behind single sign-on. The other thousand are invisible to identity infrastructure by default, not because anyone hid them, but because an identity stack can only govern what authenticates through it, and most agents never do.

That gap is the clearest expression of a shift the security industry is only starting to name. For several years, "AI security" solved a first-party problem: the company decided to use AI, procured licenses, deployed a model behind a gateway, and security pointed controls at the thing the business had chosen. Agents do not arrive that way. They arrive inside software the enterprise already runs, and they arrive without a decision.

Every control in the first-party toolkit assumes a moment exists: model scanning assumes a model was selected, prompt inspection assumes a gateway was deployed, an acceptable-use policy assumes there was an adoption to accept. That moment gave security a review, a surface to instrument, and an owner to name.

Agents skip the moment. Salesforce's Slack Code, launched in August 2026, lets a user tag a coding agent into any conversation; the agent reads the shared context, writes the code, and opens the pull request. The announcement promises agents "inherit Slack's built-in security model, permissions, and admin controls from day one, without any additional IT lift." Read by a security team, that sentence describes an autonomous actor with reach into GitHub and production infrastructure whose governance is a chat tool's channel membership. There was nothing to instrument, because nothing was adopted.

Security leaders tend to sort agents into two buckets: bought and built. There is a third, and it is the largest. Inherited agents ship inside existing platforms via product updates. Configured agents are an enterprise's own prompts and logic running on someone else's runtime, model, and connectors. Built agents are open frameworks on infrastructure the enterprise owns end to end. The first two account for the overwhelming majority of adoption and are growing exponentially as every major application becomes an agent platform. The third is the smallest and slowest growing, and it is the only one with a repo to scan and a build to gate.

The destination is the same regardless of origin. An agent born in a CRM ends up reading a data warehouse and writing to a ticketing system. An agent assembled on a cloud platform ends up holding tokens into Salesforce, Slack, and Drive. The enterprise application layer is where they all execute, and it has no fixed edges.

Every agent has two parts: the model that reasons and the scaffolding around it that turns a model into an actor, deciding what it is wired to, what it may call, and when it acts. Almost none of the risk lives in the model. It lives in the scaffolding and the ecosystem the scaffolding sits inside. Four questions cover it, and none of them ask what the model would do on its own.

What it looks like in practice

Is the agent registered anywhere? Does a named human raise a hand when asked "whose is this?" Or does it silently run as whoever built it?

What is it allowed to do, and is that more than it needs? Whose OAuth scopes and roles did it inherit at creation, and did anyone decide that on purpose?

What can it reach, directly and transitively, through the products, grants, data stores, and other agents it touches? This is the blast-radius question, and it is rarely answerable from the agent's own configuration screen.

What is it actually doing, and is that normal for what it is? Judged by behavior, not by the description in its prompt.

The Connectivity row is where agent security separates from everything the market already sells. A vendor questionnaire, a prompt filter, and a model scanner all evaluate an agent in isolation. Reach is a property of the environment.

Patrick Opet, global CISO of JPMorgan Chase, told the software industry in 2025 that the third-party supply chain had become a systemic risk, citing incidents serious enough that the bank had to isolate compromised suppliers in an open letter to the industry. He has since applied the same scrutiny to agents: ideally, an agent gets an identity but no entitlements by default, and IT confirms who it acts on behalf of before it touches anything outside that boundary. When a buyer of that size names agents as a supply-chain risk, the question shows up in everyone else's security questionnaires within a few quarters.

Regulators are moving on the same assumption. The EU AI Act's obligations phasing in through 2026 presume an enterprise can inventory its AI systems, name their owners, and evidence oversight. An organization that cannot enumerate its agents cannot comply.

The approach that keeps up with fifty agents through spreadsheets and quarterly reviews collapses at five hundred, and five hundred is one product update away from five thousand. What replaces it is a live answer, continuously refreshed, to what is operating, what each agent inherited, what it can reach directly and through chains, what it is doing, and how all of that changed since yesterday.

Some platforms are now built around exactly that map. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission, and agent action into a single live view so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis.

The industry spent a decade building security for the AI enterprises decided to use. The agents they did not decide on are now the larger population. The six-chapter series this analysis draws on, Into the Expanse, covers where they come from, how to govern them, how attackers use them, where runtime belongs, and what to fund first.

Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform.
