https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/anthro.title: Anthropic Cuts Live Internet Access for Internal AI Tests After Claude Exploits Injection Flaws
https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/anthro.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/anthro.text:
Anthropic on Friday said it's cutting off live internet access for all its internal evaluations following the discovery of new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) models exhibited misaligned behavior and targeted real websites.

The AI company said it identified four broad categories of unintended model actions during evaluations and internal use of Claude -

Anthropic said it's opting not to name the organizations involved in these incidents to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, as well as at their request. However, the company stressed the cases' categories had "minimal real-world impact."

Some of the cases targeted websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels, Anthropic said. In one run related to the second category, Claude Haiku 4.5 is said to have accessed a web page referencing an unsolved homicide and which included a tip form run by a police department.

Although the model was explicitly instructed not to enter personal data, create accounts, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, it failed to account for form submissions. This led the model to submit a false homicide tip with the text below -

I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.

It has since emerged that the incident targeted the U.S. Philadelphia Police Department (PPD), and that the incorrect tip was sent through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18, 2026. But it wasn't discovered by Anthropic until September 28, 2026. The department was notified on October 7, 2026.

The tip was flagged as spam, 6abc Action News reported. "The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable," the PPD told 6abc.

These cases, it added, were discovered following a review of transcripts that started in July 2026, when it disclosed three incidents where its models engaged in unsanctioned activity and breached three organizations during cybersecurity testing.

Then, last month, it divulged a fourth incident dating back to January 2026 that involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which breached "third-parties after being unable to abort its task."

"Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these," Anthropic said.

The latest discovery has prompted the AI giant to launch a deeper scan, specifically in environments where Claude has access to the internet. As this investigation continues, Anthropic said it expects to find new instances of unintended behaviors.

The development comes as AI safety concerns have reached a fever pitch in recent months, after it emerged that rogue OpenAI agents broke out of a test environment and breached Hugging Face in July 2026. Since then, a number of cyber incidents have come to light.

As AI model providers showcase increasingly capable and powerful models, their safety practices have come under growing scrutiny, sparking industry-wide warnings about the dangers of models outpacing safety guardrails, calls for a slowdown on AI development, and the need for additional oversight.

Earlier this week, the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said 10 of the leading foundation model developers, including Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI, have made, or committed to make, changes to their data protection policy.

These range from including clearer transparency information to deploying stronger mechanisms for users to exercise their rights and conducting tougher assessments of safeguards.

"AI has huge potential to benefit our society, but that depends on trust and transparency," Richard Nevinson, director of Technology Regulation at the ICO, said. "But as AI systems operate with greater autonomy, robust data protection safeguards become even more critical."

"Our message is clear: the fact [that] AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance. If people are to trust AI innovation, they rightly expect to know how their personal information is being protected."

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/pantone-c.title: Gen Z is rejecting millennial beige and embracing the colorful ‘dopamine decor’ trend. Designers say it’s a coping mechanism
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/pantone-c.author: Steven John
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/pantone-c.text:
On Dec. 4, 2025, Pantone announced its Color of the Year for 2026: a shade of white called Cloud Dancer. It was the first time in the program’s history, which dates to 1999, that Pantone chose a white. The company described Cloud Dancer as “a billowy white imbued with serenity” and “a symbol of calming influence in a society rediscovering the value of quiet reflection.”

It all sounds lovely. It’s also at odds with much of what has actually taken off in design, decor, and style this year.

Pantone pitched its white as a way to “build atmospheres of serenity and spaciousness, providing a refuge of visual cleanliness.” Meanwhile, many Gen Zers and millennials are going maximalist in their homes and wardrobes. Rather than a billowy white, a large cadre of consumers want bold colors, plenty of texture, and lots of layers.

This isn’t the first time maximalism has had a moment; 1970s style leaned that way, too. But today’s trend-conscious younger Americans are thinking beyond looks. They want decor and outfits that boost their sense of well-being, even when the aesthetic is over the top.

“In 2026, we’re going full-on gummy,” according to Pinterest Predicts 2026, the platform’s annual trend forecast. “Gen Z and Millennials are behind this ASMR overload—think bendy phone cases, elastic cheek tints and probiotic treats that have that spring-back bite.” Pinterest also expects rubberized nail art and 3D jewelry to catch on, and it reported searches for “gummy bears aesthetic” up 50%.

Terms like “dopamine decor” and “gummy bear aesthetic” are everywhere lately, and you likely have an innate sense of what they mean. For context, Fortune spoke to two interior designers whose earlier careers in mental health give them an unusual read on how the way we appoint our spaces, and even our outfits, affects how we feel.

Lori Miller is the principal at LGC Interior Design in Melville, N.Y. Before founding her firm, Miller studied social work at Adelphi University and earned a master’s degree in counseling from C.W. Post, a campus of Long Island University now known as LIU Post. She later directed a psychiatric unit at the Rikers Island jail complex and, later, a crime victims’ program for the Queens District Attorney’s office.

What people find calming is highly subjective, Miller says, but most people gravitate toward blues or greens, not white. In fact, more color, depth, and contrast can be more calming than cool, crisp white spaces.

“In our current period of upset, things are very serious, especially with the upcoming generation, the Gen Zs,” Miller says. “They’ve been through COVID, complicated presidencies, upheavals in politics and financial things; there are just so many different things that they’ve been through, and the ‘gummy’ style seems to keep us calm, to give us motivation. It’s uplifting; it’s bright and cheery.”

That tracks with what researchers have found: young adults report rising anxiety and a sense that things are falling apart, and even well-paid millennials and Gen Zers describe constant money anxiety.

Betsy Wentz, principal at Betsy Wentz Interior Design in Sewickley, Pa., and author of Design Happy: Colorful Homes for the Modern Family, worked in counseling for several years before turning to design. She agrees that pops of color can bring feelings of wellness. White on its own can be calming, she says, but it can also have the opposite effect.

“Color is information—your nervous system will scan a room asking: ‘Am I safe here?'” Wentz says. Colors from nature, like a blue sky or green grass, give your eyes less work to do, she explains, so heart rate and cortisol tend to settle when you look at them. That’s why blues and greens are often treated as neutrals. “White can feel serene or sterile depending on whether it reminds you of your grandmother’s house or a cold hospital. I learned in my counseling years that we pair colors with memories.”

A mix of nostalgia and a craving for safety and comfort runs through much of youth culture today, from the retro design boom to Gen Z’s embrace of conspicuous, maximalist spending over quiet luxury. It helps explain why current trends are often the polar opposite of open white rooms.

“I think Gen Z and Millennials are pushing back on years of beige algorithm homes and a world that’s felt very sharp and unpredictable,” Wentz says. “When life feels sharp, you want a home that looks like it can’t hurt you. Gummy is all rounded corners—literally no sharp edges—and saturated color that feels alive. Everything looks tactile and chewy and squeezable.”

That squeezable quality is where ASMR comes in. Short for autonomous sensory meridian response, ASMR describes the pleasant, tingling calm some people feel in response to soft sensory input, like whispering, tapping, or watching something being squished. (The chills you might get from a favorite song are a related but distinct phenomenon called frisson.) For many people, the right visuals and textures can set it off.

“ASMR is that little ‘ahhh’ your body gets from soft sensory input,” says Wentz. “I came to design with a master’s in mental health counseling, so I’m always thinking about how a room makes you feel. That’s my philosophy—what I call ‘Design Happy.’ We don’t just decorate for the eye, we decorate for the hand and the ear…. I encourage clients to touch the fabrics, wallpapers, and other samples in order to find what feels good to them.”

“Gummy bear design feels good before you even think about it; it’s colorful design that looks edible,” she adds. “Your hand wants to touch it, and your brain says: ‘Yum!’ That’s the whole idea; the design creates joy you can feel with your eyes. ‘Gummy bear,’ in design, is a type of dopamine decor. When a room is full of color, pattern, and soft, touchable things, it gives you a little lift every time you walk in.”

That little lift is part of the appeal for a generation that has also been cutting back on spending while chasing small dopamine hits, and color has long carried that kind of cultural weight; just look at the run on Barbie pink.

Still, Wentz says, rich color and texture work best when balanced, and white has a role to play.

“Culturally, we have spent 20 years being taught that white = clean = good = calm. Think Scandinavian design, think Apple Store, think all-white kitchens. We’ve been trained to read an uncluttered white room as: ‘You have your life together, you can relax now.’ So does white pigment itself lower anxiety? No. Does a beautiful, softly textured, sun-filled ‘Cloud Dancer’ room feel calm because we believe it should? Yes, and belief still works. That’s why I’d use [white] as the quiet canvas and then let your gummy bears dance on top of it.”

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/google-pr.title: As companies pour billions into Earth-based AI infrastructure, Google is taking the data center race off-planet
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/google-pr.author: Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/google-pr.text:
The moonshot idea of putting AI data centers into outer space just moved one step closer to reality, despite doubts about its feasibility.

Last week, Google’s Project Suncatcher launched a refrigerator-sized satellite carrying four AI chips into orbit on a SpaceX rocket, in an early test of whether the technology behind today’s power-hungry data centers could someday operate in space.

The satellite, developed in partnership with Planet Labs, took off on Oct. 1 and is operating as expected, according to a Google blog post. The point of the mission is to see how Google’s custom TPU chips handle the intense vibrations of launch as well as the “radiation and thermal extremes of space,” the company said. The satellite will conduct experiments in low Earth orbit for about a year, the New York Times reported.

Google’s satellite is powered by solar panels that harness energy from the sun. Because space makes it difficult to dissipate heat using water or fans, Google’s researchers designed a system of heat pipes and radiators to keep the chips from overheating. Still, the satellite’s cooling capabilities mean Google will run their chips for 15 minutes at a time before shutting them down to cool off, NPR reported.

However early the experiment might be, the launch is a milestone for an emerging technology that has the potential to help meet AI’s growing demand for compute while avoiding the constraints on resources like power, water, and land on Earth. As companies pour billions of dollars into building out terrestrial data centers, and have faced backlash from community members and politicians in the process, building AI infrastructure in space seems increasingly attractive.

The idea of orbital data centers gained mainstream attention in early 2026 when SpaceX, led by perennial tech optimist Elon Musk, filed plans with the Federal Communications Commission to launch a network of up to 1 million data-center satellites in space.

“The lowest-cost place to put AI will be space, and that will be true within two years, maybe three, three at the latest,” Musk said at the World Economic Forum in January.

Jeff Bezos’s space company Blue Origin in March also filed a proposal to deploy 51,600 satellites in a satellite network dubbed Project Sunrise.

Yet, before the concept went mainstream, Google was already working to make it a reality. In November 2025, it launched Project Suncatcher, to explore “how an interconnected network of solar-powered satellites, equipped with our Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) AI chips, could harness the full power of the Sun.”

With its recent launch, it has taken a significant step toward proving out the orbital data center concept even as experts have warned of major obstacles ahead.

For one, operating data centers in space would require massive solar arrays to capture the sun’s rays and turn it into energy. These large and heavy arrays, along with other equipment, would be expensive to transport to space, Jeff Thornburg, the CEO of Portal Space Systems, previously told Fortune. The expensive price tag remains an obstacle, despite SpaceX, which transports the majority of payloads into space, having cut its estimated launch costs by 95% since 2008 to about $1,000 per kilogram, according to research from Cathie Wood’s ARK Invest.

Another factor is the effect of radiation on the chips powering the data centers which can cause errors. This is something Google is studying with its Project Suncatcher satellite. Although Google said it tested its chips on Earth and found they “can survive a radiation total ionizing dose greater than what they would receive during a five-year space mission,” the company acknowledged that solar events and cosmic rays pose a risk.

There’s also the question of repairing equipment, which is much more difficult in space.

Still, Google isn’t the only company already testing AI chips in orbit. Last November, startup Starcloud launched a satellite carrying one of Nvidia’s high-powered H100 chips into space and showed it could use the chip to run Google’s lightweight AI model, Gemma.

Another startup, Cowboy Space Corp., founded by Robinhood cofounder Baiju Bhatt, also launched a satellite aboard the same SpaceX rocket as Google last week.

The satellite, called Reason-1, plans to test sending solar energy down to Earth using a powerful laser. The company has established contact with the satellite and is preparing to demonstrate its technology for the first time in the coming weeks, Bhatt said in an interview with Bloomberg published Thursday. Bhatt also said Cowboy Space’s ultimate ambition is to build a vehicle to put data center payloads into space.

The Oct. 1 launch is just the beginning of Google’s ambitions with orbital data centers.

The company is planning to send two more satellites into space in 2027 to test how they can communicate via lasers, which it said in a blog post requires precision “similar to hitting a coin-size target from miles away while both points are in motion.”

Still, the ultimate dream of putting data centers into space may not come to fruition even in the next few years, James Manyika, Google’s senior vice president for research, told the New York Times.

“Remember how Google was researching for like 15 years, before anything showed up? I think this is going to look like that,” he said.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/big-tech-.title: Big Tech is betting $700 billion on AI. Healthcare will decide whether the bet pays off
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/big-tech-.author: Bill Miller
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/big-tech-.text:
Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are expected to spend more than $700 billion on capital expenditures this year as they expand the infrastructure required to support AI. For spending at that scale to pay off, AI will need to deliver meaningful productivity gains across the economy.

Few industries offer more room to prove it than healthcare. U.S. healthcare spending reached $5.3 trillion in 2024, or 18% of GDP. By some estimates, close to $1 trillion goes toward administration alone.

Demand for care also continues to outpace the available clinical workforce. If AI can lower the cost of delivering care while freeing clinicians to serve more patients, the economic opportunity could be enormous.

Major AI players are already moving deeper into healthcare. Microsoft and Mayo Clinic are developing a frontier AI model designed specifically for healthcare, while Google Cloud and CVS Health have entered a long-term partnership to power CVS’s new Health100 platform with Gemini.

But for healthcare providers, the AI opportunity comes with a clock. As greater efficiency becomes reflected in reimbursement, what creates an advantage today can become the baseline providers are expected to meet tomorrow.

For providers, the economics of AI can be straightforward. Reducing the administrative work required to deliver care lowers the cost of delivering it.  But providers may have a limited window to benefit from those efficiencies before reimbursement catches up.

Medicare already incorporates productivity into payment updates across hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, home health, and other settings. For 2026, CMS brought that logic to physician payment, applying a 2.5% efficiency adjustment to the work component of certain non-time-based services. The adjustment accounts for efficiencies CMS expects to accrue in how those services are delivered over time.

That gives providers a reason to capture AI-driven savings early. Those that use AI to reduce documentation, intake, or coordination costs can lower their cost structures now, before greater efficiency is more fully reflected in how they are paid. On the other hand, those that wait risk facing the same payment pressure without having captured those savings.

Over time, more efficient providers can compound that advantage by reinvesting in staff, capacity, and care.

Healthcare has something many industries lack: a clear place to put the productivity gains AI creates. Demand already exceeds the available clinical workforce, so time freed from documentation, scheduling, or intake doesn’t have to mean fewer people doing the same work. It can mean more patients getting care sooner.

Capturing that value requires starting with the work, not the technology. The best opportunities are often hiding in plain sight: documentation that keeps a clinician at a screen, an intake process that delays access, or a referral that stalls between care settings. Success should be equally concrete. AI should give clinicians meaningful time back, allow them the opportunity to spend more meaningful time with patients, or eliminate unnecessary work rather than simply shifting it somewhere else.

Consider a patient moving from a hospital to post-acute care. A delayed referral or missing information can trigger phone calls and manual follow-up, delay care, and increase the risk of readmission. If AI helps that handoff happen correctly the first time, the value extends beyond a faster referral. It can eliminate downstream work and cost while getting the patient into care sooner. A tool that saves five minutes but adds another login, data silo, or handoff has simply shifted the burden.

Providers also need to decide upfront what they’ll do with the capacity they create. Time returned to clinicians can mean seeing more patients or easing pressure on an already stretched workforce. When those productivity gains lower the cost of delivering care, they can strengthen margins and create more room to invest in staff, expand access, and improve care.

The next phase of the AI boom will be measured less by how much computing capacity gets built than by what businesses can do with it. Healthcare offers an unusually consequential test: can AI take enough cost and friction out of a massive industry to change its economics while expanding the amount of care it can deliver?

Big Tech has already committed hundreds of billions of dollars to building the infrastructure for AI. The harder question is whether that technology can produce productivity at a scale that makes the investment worthwhile. Healthcare may be one of the clearest places to find out.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/world-men.title: From tax to slack: this World Mental Health Day, reclaim cognitive space in the era of machine speed
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/world-men.author: Stephanie Kramer
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/world-men.text:
We challenge you to read this entire article from the top—no AI summaries, no skim-reading headlines.

We are navigating a silent, profound redefinition of what it means to work, lead, and live. In this hyper-accelerated era, we are flooded with endless streams of content, notifications, and automated drafts. We are constantly informed, but are we still thinking?

By trying to match machine speed, we are pushing the human operating system to its absolute limit — a tension I explored while recently moderating a panel with three researchers on the subject. We face a converging storm: overwhelming data volume, always-on intake, the cognitive tax of context-switching, and “AI sycophancy”—where tools are engineered to agree with us rather than push us. To survive this, we crave cognitive counterweights: deliberate synthesis, ruthless prioritization, and active recovery. Staying pace in this environment requires far more than a “moment” for mental health.

The scale of this digital deluge is staggering. Dr. Gloria Mark of UC Irvine, author of Attention Span, found that screen attention spans have plummeted from 2.5 minutes in 2004 to just 47 seconds today. This is not a failure of personal willpower; it is a structural crisis with a measurable cost. Within the Microsoft 365 suite alone, workers are interrupted every two minutes. Microsoft’s Alexia Cambon calls this a constant “consumption tax.” These constant interruptions wear down our goal-oriented minds, forcing us into rapid attention-switching that spikes stress and drives errors.

The risk isn’t the technology itself; it is our desperate pressure to match its speed. Driven by “productivity guilt,” we use AI to churn out highly polished but low-value communications—doing “more” simply because we can. This loop traps us, backfilling saved time with even more low-value complexity rather than freeing up space for deep thinking.

Used well, AI frees us for deeper work, but the courage to make creative leaps must still come from us. Innovation requires creative friction—people disagreeing, debating, and pushing boundaries. This is the exact opposite of an AI engineered to make us feel, as Cambon notes, “nice and comfy and cozy.”

The old innovation playbook of “move fast and break things” is broken. Anne Morriss, co-author of Move Fast and Fix Things, argues that the old way is:

“Not good for people. It’s not actually good for business… [it leads to] more rework, more unhappy customers, fewer people bought in. So, when we talk about how to get this right, we talk about moving fast and fixing things.”

To protect our stamina, leaders must intentionally build a counterweight to modern speed. High-trust, high-functioning organizations deliberately slow down at critical moments. As Morriss observes:

“It’s called good friction… You can go as fast as the amount of trust that you have built… The Navy SEALs have a mantra that I love: slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.”

This distinction is what separates mere management from true leadership. We must set deliberate, not default, priorities and give them our undivided presence. To navigate this acceleration, leadership must shift from rigid hierarchies to horizontal agility—partnering across boundaries to follow the fluid flow of value. Let AI carry the speed of synthesis so humans can bring the depth of judgment.

Furthermore, our most vital qualities—critical thinking, curiosity, creativity, and focus—are products of time and space, not speed. Deep thinking requires “cognitive slack”; without it, we default to pattern recognition instead of original thought. Even Albert Einstein famously sat in quiet rooms for hours staring at the ceiling, knowing his breakthroughs came from stillness, not the rush of the laboratory.

To build intellectual stamina, we must treat our minds like elite athletes, recognizing that peak performance demands deliberate recovery. This requires what Dr. Mark calls yohaku no bi—the Japanese expression for the beauty of empty space:

“To really be able to shine, to do our best work, we have to give ourselves space.”

How we frame this shift matters. Cambon found that mandated “AI-first” processes actually make employees eight times more likely to produce no work at all. The better path treats technology as an invitation to “co-build, co-produce, and co-innovate.” Crucially, Morriss urges leaders to reject an automated, anxious future:

“We have to tell an alternative story — not just the downside and the anxiety of this revolution, but also what could happen…”

For the first time in history, five generations are navigating a workplace transition together. We have a unique opportunity to pair the wonder of youth with the wisdom of experience. True leadership is about consciously preserving the space where original human thought can breathe, connect, and thrive. When managing our work, our teams, our autonomous agents, and our days, we must protect not only the quality of our output, but also the quality of our lives.

As leaders and teammates, we must start with individual actions to reclaim this space. Personally, I have committed to an “analog hour”: handwritten notes, reading on paper, and walking without headphones.

You can also take Anne Morriss’s practical advice:

“Call a friend or loved one on your way to work, or on your way into your home office, and remind yourself who you are outside of that work identity — which… will help you put boundaries around work in a much more productive way.”

Protecting your intellectual stamina is a personal practice, but it also requires collective action. This month, Project Healthy Minds—the leading mental health tech nonprofit expanding access to services across the U.S.—launched the Project Healthy Minds Workforce Lab.

This is a first-of-its-kind coalition of global organizations, scholars, and thought leaders working to expand the evidence base for “what works” in workforce mental health. I am proud to co-chair the Lab alongside Jacqui Canney, Chief People & AI Enablement Officer of ServiceNow.

Together, we are designing the playbook for a future where technology amplifies human potential without exhausting human capacity. We invite you to join us in this critical work—because in an era of machine speed, the ultimate competitive advantage is human depth.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/glp1-drug.title: What a desert lizard teaches us about patents and the GLP-1 revolution
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/glp1-drug.author: Dr. Bowman Heiden
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/glp1-drug.text:
After steadily rising for decades, America’s obesity rate is finally declining. It peaked in 2022, when 39.9% of adults were obese, according to Gallup. This year, that share dipped to 36.4% — in large part thanks to increasingly widespread GLP-1 weight-loss medicines.

About one in every nine adults currently takes Wegovy, Zepbound, or another GLP-1. That’s roughly a ten-fold increase since 2022.

And that share will likely keep rising as the price of these drugs continues to drop. As recently as last year, the weight-loss treatments cost over $1,000 per month. Today, patients can purchase them for as little as $149 a month — because the leading GLP-1 manufacturers have been forced to slash prices to compete for market share.

Americans can thank a desert lizard—and the patent system—for these increasingly ubiquitous, increasingly affordable treatments.

The story begins in 1990, when John Eng, an endocrinologist at the Veterans Administration, isolated a peptide from the venom of Gila monsters, the nearly two-foot-long lizards native to the Southwest. That peptide mimicked the human hormone GLP-1, which prompts the pancreas to release insulin and makes people feel full. But unlike natural GLP-1, which disappears from the body within minutes, this compound remains active for hours.

Dr. Eng patented the peptide. Amylin Pharmaceuticals eventually licensed and developed it into the first GLP-1 medicine. In 2005, the FDA approved it to treat type 2 diabetes.

That 15-year journey — from discovery to drug approval — wouldn’t have been possible without patent protections.

Patents require innovators to publicly disclose their discoveries. In return for this disclosure, inventors — and any companies that license the patents — receive a limited period of time where no rival is able to copy the discovery and sell it as their own.

That gives companies a chance to earn a return on their investment — and makes those risky and expensive investments financially viable in the first place.

Contrary to conventional wisdom, patents don’t stifle competition. They promote it, by forcing companies to invest in developing their own patented products, rather than simply copying a rival’s inventions.

Consider how patients taking that first GLP-1 medicine from Amylin had to inject themselves twice a day within an hour before eating. Researchers at rival companies later developed once-daily and then once-weekly options, followed by a pill version and a drug that acted on two hormone receptors to help patients lose even more weight.

That does not mean every patent is valid or every patent claim is warranted. But the patent system already has established standards and safeguards for addressing those cases. And those few exceptions do not diminish the central role strong, time-limited patents play in turning risky discoveries into approved medicines — or in motivating rivals to develop better ones.

Companies are already competing to develop the next generation of drugs, including treatments that could reduce side effects and better preserve muscle. When rival brand-name drug makers compete for market share, it drives down prices.

And of course, when patents eventually expire, generic manufacturers can copy those discoveries and introduce them at much lower cost. When patent protections for Ozempic and Wegovy expired in India earlier this year, generic manufacturers flooded the market at prices less than $14 a month.

In the United States, at least one earlier GLP-1 has already lost patent protection and gone generic. And the core patents on blockbuster weight-loss drugs like Wegovy will expire in the early 2030s, meaning generic versions will likely hit the market soon after.

That’ll make already cost-effective medicines even more accessible for patients, and more beneficial for society.

Obesity alone costs the healthcare system nearly $173 billion annually. The total economic cost of diabetes — including medical expenses and lost productivity — reaches another $413 billion. By preventing these conditions, GLP-1 drugs promise to reduce future healthcare spending.

And their impact won’t be limited to obesity and diabetes. For example, the FDA has already approved Wegovy to help cut the risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack, and stroke in obese or overweight adults with cardiovascular disease. Researchers are continuing to investigate whether GLP-1s could be effective at combating opioid addiction, osteoarthritis, Alzheimer’s, and even breast cancer.

That translates to lives saved and billions more dollars in potential savings for the healthcare system. And all of that research is only possible because companies have an opportunity to patent their resulting discoveries and earn a return on the time and money they’ve invested.

The Gila monster did not give us GLP-1s. Scientists—and a patent system that encourages companies to continually invest in new research—did. The patent system most often works as intended, delivering new solutions to our toughest health challenges.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/ella-lang.title: Ella Langley spent a record 24 weeks at No. 1. Most U.S. music fans didn’t know her name—signaling a major cultural shift
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/ella-lang.author: Bilin Lin
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/ella-lang.text:
The internet can’t seem to get over one question: How did a country song that so many people say they’ve never heard, by a singer they’ve never heard of either, set the record for the most weeks at No. 1 in the Billboard Hot 100’s 68-year history?

Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” logged 24 weeks atop the chart, passing the 22-week record held by Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” the Christmas staple you can’t escape hearing every winter. The run finally ended on the chart dated Oct. 10, when Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” debuted at No. 1. Carey’s song, which tends to return to No. 1 each December, would need three more weeks at the top to reclaim the record.

Just 24% of U.S. music listeners knew of Ella Langley in the second quarter of 2026, according to entertainment data and research company Luminate, which shared the figures with Fortune. That was up from 13% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and 17% in the first quarter of this year. Her recognition was growing, but it still reached fewer than one in four music listeners.

A No. 1 hit, apparently, can still leave people asking, “Who?” So what happened to monoculture?

For those unfamiliar with the term, monoculture is a shared set of cultural references: the songs, shows, and movies you could assume other people knew, whether they liked them or not. (Lately, the word has also taken on a second, almost opposite meaning, as critics use it to describe how algorithms and AI flatten culture into sameness.)

It was easier to share references when so much of what people watched and heard came through a few television networks, radio stations, and MTV. Industry gatekeepers picked what reached a mass audience. You didn’t have to be a fan to know what everyone was talking about.

That shared audience was never everyone, and it began fragmenting before TikTok. But personalized feeds take the division further: What reaches you increasingly depends on what the system thinks you, specifically, will want to see.

Take TikTok, which touts the personalization of its For You feed. As the company explains, “there’s no one For You feed.”

Has this ever happened to you? You open social media, watch one Olivia Rodrigo concert clip, and suddenly it feels like every fifth video is another one.

TikTok says it takes cues from what you like and share, who you follow, and whether you watch a video to the end. It also looks at the videos themselves: their captions, sounds, and hashtags. Even your language preference, country setting, and device type factor in, though TikTok says those carry less weight. All of that helps the system decide what deserves another few seconds of your attention. TikTok says it also works to keep feeds varied, for example by generally not showing two videos in a row that use the same sound or come from the same creator.

In the U.S., that system is now overseen by the Oracle-backed joint venture that took over TikTok’s American operations in January, which has said it will retrain the recommendation algorithm on U.S. user data.

Keep watching, and the algorithm may keep serving up more of the same. Researchers have observed that feedback loop in action.

A study published in EPJ Data Science in February tested TikTok’s For You feed using automated accounts programmed with different interests. It found that TikTok increasingly recommended videos matching those interests, with that reinforcement typically kicking in within the first 200 videos watched. The feeds kept some variety, but the more strongly an account’s interests were amplified, the fewer different hashtags it tended to encounter. (The researchers ran their experiments in 2024, before TikTok’s U.S. ownership change.)

That helps explain why you think something is taking over the internet, while Joe next door gets a completely different feed and wonders what you’re talking about.

You can also help narrow the selection yourself. Platforms like TikTok offer tools, such as its “Manage Topics” setting, that let you tell the system which topics you want to see more or less of.

The clues used to personalize your feed can even come from outside the app.

Meta announced in June that it would use information other businesses already share with it, like purchases people make on other websites, to personalize users’ feeds and AI responses, not just ads. The company’s own example: Buy a tent online, and you might start seeing more camping Reels. Users can manage this through a setting called “Activity from other businesses.”

What you watch, what you buy—it can all feed into the calculation, shaping your own little corner of the internet. One just for you.

Not everyone is a fan. New Yorker writer Kyle Chayka has a few complaints about that convenience—a whole book’s worth, in fact: “Filterworld: How Algorithms Flattened Culture.”

“These digital platforms and feeds, they kind of promise a great communal experience … but I think they’re actually kind of atomizing our experiences, because we can never tell what other people are seeing in their own feeds,” he told NPR’s Fresh Air in 2024.

That, he argued, takes some of the joy out of art and makes it harder for people to get excited about the same things.

Smarter algorithms may leave us in separate bubbles. But if something doesn’t interest you, do you really want it in your feed just for a shared cultural experience? And if it never reaches you, how would you know whether you’d like it?

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/nvidia-g.title: Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/nvidia-g.author: Jordan Novet
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/nvidia-g.text:
AI labs are spending tens of billions of dollars per year for Nvidia chips that run their models.

The demand has led to the blossoming of an industry that hyperscalers once had to themselves, including lucrative one-off arrangements and asset-light strategies.

Over 300 neoclouds now rent GPUs to businesses, according to a review from researcher SemiAnalysis, up 55% in under 11 months.

Nvidia
 GPUs are the most sought-after processors in AI, and they’re in such demand that the chipmaker’s stock climbed to yet another record this week, lifting its market cap close to $6 trillion.

Customers can now shop around for access to the chips at the giant clouds from Amazon, Microsoft and Google, as well as at so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave. They can also go to various online marketplaces or even buy the costly hardware directly.

For Nvidia, it all adds up to unrelenting growth, as management anticipates $108 billion in revenue for the October quarter, which would mark an 89% year-over-year jump.

But the paradox of choice can be a headache for companies needing computing power yesterday.

While cloud infrastructure providers have ranked at the top of Nvidia’s customer list for several years, the business is diversifying. Five clients accounted for at least 10% of Nvidia’s accounts receivable in July quarter, up from three in January, according to a filing.

Industry research firm SemiAnalysis counted 323 Nvidia GPU providers as of September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier.

“You’re going to see a whole new crop of really, really exciting neoclouds with hundreds of billions of dollars backlog together,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at a Goldman Sachs tech conference in San Francisco last month.

Here’s a rundown of the various options for accessing GPUs, and why each might make sense:

Many big companies spend tens of millions of dollars per year on a smorgasbord of cloud services from Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Since the 2022 launch of ChatGPT, companies have increasingly turned to the hyperscalers for GPUs so they can run generative AI workloads.

The top cloud providers come with a reputation advantage. If a software company relies on Amazon and Microsoft for GPUs and other capabilities, it won’t need to panic about prospective customers questioning its suppliers.

“When you’re talking to enterprises, your subprocessor had better be Azure,” said Bindu Reddy, CEO of AI assistant startup Abacus, referring to Microsoft’s cloud infrastructure.

In the past year, leading AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI have committed to spending over $500 billion between Amazon and Microsoft, which controlled 59% of the cloud infrastructure market in 2025, according to industry researcher Gartner.

“Hyperscalers are in a good position to show trust to the enterprises because of their 10-plus years of full-stack capabilities,” said Gartner analyst Hardeep Singh. But hyperscalers don’t always have as many GPUs as enterprises require, he said.

Andy Jassy, Amazon’s CEO, told analysts in July that the retailer and cloud pioneer won’t be able to serve all the demand it foresees this year.

“I believe this dynamic will also be true in 2027,” he said.

If the hyperscalers were adequate, neoclouds wouldn’t be proliferating.

Modal, a startup operating virtual sandboxes where AI agents work independent of main IT environments, went from running on the hyperscalers to signing up with the major neoclouds, and now it uses 25 of them, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson.

“You can get a few hundred GPUs or maybe a thousand, but at our scale, we needed way more GPUs,” he said.

The hyperscalers themselves are also chasing the neoclouds. Google and Microsoft have started tapping CoreWeave, even as they all compete with one another.

“Some of the hyperscalers have approached us about taking care of customers they’re worried about because they don’t have the ability to service those customers when they need it,” said Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer of Nebius, a Netherlands-based neocloud with operations in the U.S.

Video generation startup Reactor uses GPUs through Nebius and hyperscalers, said CEO Alberto Taiuti. The location of data centers matters, he said, because Reactor wants user-created videos to show up right away. Nebius delivers the specific GPUs Reactor needs, solid customer service and sufficient hardware and software, at a good price, Taiuti said.

The most visible neoclouds can require some upfront payment, and chips might not come online for months, because providers raise funding based on contracts and set up the data center equipment, Bernhardsson said.

It would be difficult for CoreWeave to turn over 10,000 GPUs to a new customer with one day’s notice, said Chen Goldberg, an executive vice president. CoreWeave’s near-term capacity remains essentially sold out, CEO Mike Intrator said on the company’s August earnings call.

If companies want GPUs immediately, they might have to go beyond the name brands. Some neoclouds aren’t household names because they target specific countries, which can be viable in certain cases.

“Capacity right now is tight, and your relationships with your suppliers is actually one of the most closely guarded secrets for companies like ours,” said Zhen Lu, CEO of Runpod.

Specialist neoclouds can offer more flexibility than the larger GPU clouds, which often require upfront payments and long-term commitments. Some sell so-called bare-metal GPUs, which give customers more control but also require them to manage more of the technical work themselves.

Companies using these smaller neoclouds share the same concerns: When can they get the GPUs, and at what price? Sunny Smith, co-founder and technology chief at Massed Compute, said customers are often willing to commit to capacity when they expect prices to rise.

Oracle
, one of the world’s largest cloud providers, is letting clients bring in their own GPUs. The software maker has more debt than Amazon or Microsoft, and its credit rating is lower so it has less flexibility to go on a GPU spending spree. But it’s happy to operate the technology.

“As we’re generally able to preserve and improve margins in the case of things like bring-your-own-hardware, the ROIC for those types of structures will be even higher,” Oracle CFO Hilary Maxson told analysts on a June earnings call, using the acronym for return on invested capital.

Oracle hasn’t disclosed the names of companies that choose this path. John DiFucci, a Guggenheim Securities analyst who recommends buying Oracle shares, said it would make sense for Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia, the top two producers of GPUs, to bring their own to Oracle.

Instead of buying thousands of GPUs, early-stage startups with limited capital can borrow them for hours at a time for less through clouds. And for companies with heavy-duty computing needs, Oracle’s new route might be more attractive than building whole data centers. OpenAI committed to spending over $300 billion with Oracle over five years, but it hasn’t mentioned anything about bringing in GPUs.

OpenAI declined to comment.

The method might make sense for companies that have the capital to purchase AI chips but don’t have enough power, data center space or skilled labor. Like its hyperscaler peers, Oracle works hard to secure all three in healthy quantities.

Another emerging option is to cut large deals with firms that have truckloads of GPUs for rent.

SpaceX arranged to turn over excess capacity in separate deals with hyperscaler Google and open-source startup Reflection.

In April, SpaceX agreed to provide Cursor with GPUs and then bought the AI coding startup outright for $60 billion. And in May, SpaceX landed a deal to rent GPUs to Anthropic for $1.25 billion each month through mid-2029. That’s more than what most startups can afford.

For SpaceX, though, the numbers work out nicely.

“The current economics have translated into a less than one-year payback on our new capital deployments for compute,” Bret Johnsen, the company’s finance chief, told analysts in August.

It’s not only SpaceX. In July CNBC reported that Meta
 was working to form a cloud unit that could sell AI computing power.

Meanwhile, companies continue to install GPU-filled servers in on-premises data centers the old-school way as CEOs work to balance capability with cost control.

Revenue nearly doubled in the enterprise and small and medium business parts of hardware maker Lenovo’s
 Infrastructure Solutions Group during the June quarter. “We’re seeing more and more enterprises now starting to say, ‘How do I bring AI into my four walls?’” said Vlad Rozanovich, a senior vice president.

The hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes.

Collaboration software maker Dropbox
 relies on GPUs in its data centers, CEO Ashraf Alkarmi said.

“If we want to do a lot more, I think our supply chain connections will still be beneficial and a structural advantage,” he said.

Everpure
, which sells data center storage hardware and software, has acquired its own GPUs, to run open-weight AI models for the company’s software engineers, said CEO Charlie Giancarlo.

“In a very dynamic pricing environment, it’s always good to have multiple sources that you can go to,” he said.

https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.title: Greece’s Seafood Problem Starts Elsewhere
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.author: By Johnny Sturgeon, Ian Urbina
https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10102.text:
This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.

In May, the Hellenic Aquaculture Producers Organization gathered in Athens to promote the industry as the future of sustainable food security. Flanked by industry titans, the European commissioner for fisheries and oceans, Costas Kadis, framed aquaculture as a solution to the pressures of climate change, pollution and overfishing. “In the European Union, aquaculture is at the epicenter of our priorities,” he said.

The industry group’s chairman, Apostolos Touralias, went one step further: “Aquaculture is the most sustainable form of animal protein,” he said. “Aquaculture needs less space, less feed, less freshwater. It produces the lowest carbon footprint regarding all other sectors.”

But not everyone agrees with the industry’s assessment of itself.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

“The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular farmed seafood are fed wild fish—the exact livestock aquaculture claims to be saving. That’s accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained.

After the 2011 debt crisis, Greece bet its coastal future on the blue economy by mapping out 25 “Areas of Organized Development.” While many of these zones remain in the final stage of legal approval, the plan earmarked potentially exclusive use of almost 60,000 acres of coast to multinational aquaculture firms. Expanding the industry’s footprint 24-fold came with a simple economic pitch: People want more seafood, the limit of what can be viably pulled from the wild is quickly being reached and fish farming is the way to meet the growing demand while slowing the collapse of the oceans.

From the Ionian Sea in the west to the Euboean Gulf in the east, the Greek farmed finfish industry is now the most valuable in the European Union. It’s also the bloc’s top producer of sea bream and sea bass, producing over 120,000 tons annually.

Now accounting for over two-thirds of the nation’s total seafood production, the sustainability argument for fish farming—“grow more, so we can catch less”—is one of the reasons that the $313 billion industry is the fastest-growing food sector in the world.

Yet two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil—ingredients made by cooking and pulverizing wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a seabass or sea bream at some Mediterranean farms, for instance, eats more than two-and-a-half times its weight in wild-caught fish.

The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, many of them borne by communities far away from Greece or other developed fish-farming economies, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, D.C.

These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths and violent protests typically spurred by the horrid stench from fishmeal factories. These social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed.

Some sea bass and sea bream farmed in Greece in recent years were fed fishmeal tied to more than a dozen environmental enforcement actions in U.S. waters between 2018 and 2025, and humpback whale deaths in the Southern Ocean in 2024, according to The Outlaw Ocean Project’s investigation.

Across five years, The Outlaw Ocean Project carried out an extensive investigation of fishmeal and fish oil. The reporting effort mapped a vast segment of the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries.

The Food for Feed investigation found that the oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden from the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, especially fish feed but also for chickens and pigs.

In Gambia and Mauritania, the series documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export. In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, on farms and in factories. In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish. The team also developed Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.

In Greece, two of the largest aquaculture players have also been sourcing fishmeal from Western Sahara.

Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara, a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various United Nations resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illicit catch into fishmeal in Western Saharan plants, before exporting it to farms globally labeled as Moroccan.

The seafood company Avramar—which controls 70 percent of Greek production and exports to 40 countries—imports raw materials and ingredients from more than a dozen Moroccan companies. Additionally, one of its subsidiary companies, Perseus—which has since been enveloped into Avramar’s larger operations—was receiving shipments of fishmeal from Western Sahara as recently as 2022.

Meanwhile, Irida—Greece’s largest feed manufacturer and a supplier to Avramar—also received raw ingredients from two companies primarily based in Western Sahara in 2024 and 2025 respectively, according to trade and audit records: Copelit and Protein and Oil Industry.

When asked about these issues, none of the companies responded to a request for comment.

Fishing without the permission of the Western Saharan people, the Sahrawis, and importing to EU markets under false Moroccan labels has humanitarian consequences. Some 180,000 Sahrawi people live in refugee camps in Algeria while overfishing undermines local food security.

Greece is not alone; France, Spain, Germany and the Netherlands also source fishmeal from Africa’s last colonial state.

In countries with available data, at least half of the species landed by fishmeal vessels were classified by scientific studies as “overexploited” or worse, The Outlaw Ocean Project’s investigation found.

In fact, most of the vessels in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, types of fishing boats that deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish and routinely haul in non-target species. At least 165 are also bottom trawlers, a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their path and releasing carbon dioxide buried in sediment.

While companies like Avramar claim a “commitment to safeguarding marine biodiversity,” their reliance on overexploited West African sardines, for example, tells a different ecological story.

Avramar—which was recently acquired by the Canadian company Cooke Inc., and rebranded in August to Cooke Hellas—acknowledged a request for comment but did not respond further.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Pauly, with the Sea Around Us initiative. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

Indeed, the global transformation of the food chain has turned farms and oceans into engineered calorie-processing systems. The natural food web, including who eats what, and how energy moves from plants to animals to humans, is no longer mainly determined by ecosystems. It’s now shaped by industrial design.

As Greek aquaculture looks to expand, the disconnect between its sustainability claims and the feed it relies on poses a legal and reputational risk. While the EU is introducing fines for supply chains that fail to independently undertake due diligence, these won’t enter into force until 2028. Until then, the onus will remain on Greece and other European aquaculture giants to untangle the legal and environmental mess in both their own and foreign waters.

Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with SeaChoice, a Canadian sustainable-seafood group, said many products—such as sweatshop garments, “blood diamonds” and coffee—have already had to begin reckoning with the human rights and environmental abuses buried in their supply chains.

Seafood, she said, has been slower to face that kind of scrutiny. But as the world searches for more protein and leans further into aquaculture, that may change.

https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.title: Severe injuries at French student protests draw scrutiny to police tactics
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261.text:
Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a ​broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said.

READ MORE
French students vow to keep up protests as UN voices 'concern' over violence

The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone metres away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A ​second officer then fired a ‌tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face.

"(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency ⁠services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said.

A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. According to the prosecutor’s office, the police officer said that he was seeking to protect himself and his colleagues ‌after the student confronted police. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after ⁠the incident.

The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of student unrest over conditions in schools. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades.

The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other ​European countries and have been repeatedly criticised in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate.

It has also sparked anger among ‌the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated discontent with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election.

READ MORE
French student protests fuel political clash ahead of 2027 presidential vote

Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback.

In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, ‌a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off – likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who paused the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case.

Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our ​primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said.

Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors.

“France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims – we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” ​said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research.

“It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said.

WATCH MORE
French high school students react to education minister’s measures

Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use ​of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades.

Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from ​Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche.

In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was ​hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added.

A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye.

“He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said.

The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets.

The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden.

READ MORE
‘Nothing will stop us’: French student protests show few signs of ending

Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security.

“We must withdraw ⁠the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party told Reuters. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police.

Thierry Clair, a police ⁠union representative, said that serious injuries such as ​Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions.

“How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.”

(FRANCE24 with Reuters)

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Hunger and malnutrition stalk Gazans, a year on from ceasefire
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Every day, Gazan mother Niyaha al-Masri spends six exhausting hours or more queueing at a community kitchen in the hope of getting some food for her family.

It has been a year since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was supposed to allow food to flood into the ruined territory, yet widespread hunger persists there.

Masri has little choice. Without the kitchen run by humanitarian groups, she and her eight children would have "nothing at all", the 35-year-old told AFP.

Each day she sets out early in the morning and returns in the afternoon, this time bringing four containers of rice, lentils and a little chicken, which the family throws itself at.

Among them is her husband, wounded in both legs by an airstrike, meaning he "cannot go and fight with the others" to get food.

This will be the only meal of the day for the family of 10, living in a tent in Khan Yunis. There was no breakfast and they will have no dinner.

What little flour they have, Masri explained, has to be rationed.

In August 2025, a United Nations-backed body, the IPC, declared a state of famine in Gaza, though Israel quickly denounced it as a lie.

By December, the UN had lifted that declaration, saying that the ceasefire had allowed in enough supplies over the course of two months to ease conditions.

COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry organisation responsible for civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, told AFP that the humanitarian situation in Gaza was stable.

But Shaun Hughes, of the UN's World Food Programme, was less sanguine.

The food security situation, he said, "is still extremely serious".

The most recent figures, from July, show that "1.4 million out of the population of about 2.1 million people are acutely food insecure", he said, with 200,000 of them "just one step below famine".

While some food is getting in, a lack of sufficient nutritional variety continues to pose a health threat.

"Dietary diversity is a major food security issue in Gaza," said Hughes.

"You cannot survive on dry goods and wheat flour and bread alone. Particularly children, particularly pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, they need the micronutrients that come with high protein foods, fresh vegetables, fresh fruits," he explained.

Masri said that her children, aged between three and 14, "dream of eating fruit" but the family doesn't have the means to buy any.

She said one of her sons suffered from malnutrition during the 2025 famine, although "little by little, his condition is improving".

Malnutrition isn't only caused by a lack of food, but also essential nutrients. It weakens the immune system of children, making them vulnerable to illnesses and stunting their growth.

"Repeated bouts of acute malnutrition amongst children is something that human beings just don't recover from," said Hughes.

Cognitive and physical impairments "continue into later life", he added.

At Khan Yunis's Nasser hospital, the head of the malnutrition unit, Israa al-Najjar, told AFP she had "observed an increase in syndromes and conditions" linked to malnutrition that affect the immune system.

In a report published on Thursday, the day after the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attack that sparked the Gaza war, Medecins du Monde published a study that found 93 percent of pregnant or breastfeeding women had symptoms of anaemia, which is closely linked to malnutrition.

Just 17 percent had a sufficiently varied diet to meet their nutritional needs, the group found.

All the while, Masri has kept visiting the community kitchen, despite asthma leaving her exhausted.

Her children spend their days collecting "pieces of nylon, bits of cardboard and chunks of foam" to try and reinforce their tent, which is in a poor state.

She said it was "shameful" that her children had to do so.

"I swear to God, this isn't normal."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/r.title: Russian attacks kill at least seven people in Ukraine after Trump-Putin diesel deal
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Rescuers evacuate a wounded resident from an apartment building damaged in a Russian air strike. (Reuters: Stringer)

At least seven people have died after Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.

The strikes came a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, in stark contrast to sanctions he signed last month.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Mr Trump's deal with Russia would allow the war to be prolonged.

Russian strikes have killed at least seven people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, authorities say, as rescuers continue to search for more people under the rubble.

Ukrainian national police said Russia had targeted residential neighbourhoods in the city with "five guided aerial bombs" early Saturday morning, hitting two residential buildings.

At least ten other people were wounded in the attack, said Mykhailo Semikin, head of Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration.

He said rescuers were continuing their search for people under the rubble.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.

Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 55 people over the past four days, including in a bus stop attack that killed 33 people on Thursday.

The latest attacks came a day after United States President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia.

The deal is a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine, and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

At least seven people were killed in the strikes in Zaporizhzhia. (AP Photo: Kateryna Klochko)

Mr Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.

Instead, Mr Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Mr Trump's shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.

In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy."

Russia is not just abducting Ukrainian kids, it is embarking on a campaign of mass indoctrination, as Denys Kostev experienced firsthand.

He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Mr Zelenskyy called it "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners".

Diplomatic efforts mediated by the US to end the war have so far yielded no results.

Mr Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.title: Woman found dead in Carlton apartment identified as 21yo Jayda Allen Bonner
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.author: Kate Ashton and Mikaela Ortolan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Jayda Allen Bonner, 21, was described by her aunt as a "gentle soul with a heart of gold". (Supplied)

A woman found dead in a Melbourne apartment block overnight has been identified by family as 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner.

A homicide investigation is underway; no charges have been laid over the incident, and one person arrested has since been released.

Ms Allen Bonner's aunt told the ABC that the family had been concerned for the young woman's safety and had tried to get help from authorities.

The family of a young woman found dead in a Melbourne apartment block overnight has told the ABC they had serious concerns about her safety and had recently sought help from police.

Twenty-one-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner was described by her aunt as a "gentle soul" with a "heart of gold."

"[She] would do anything to help anybody," Kellie Carter-Bell said on Saturday.

She said Jayda was a Yagera woman with family in Queensland.

Homicide detectives are investigating after police were called to an apartment in the inner-city suburb of Carlton in the early hours of Saturday.

Authorities said they were called to the apartment on Cardigan Street just before 2am and when they arrived, found the body of a woman.

Jayda Allen Bonner's family says they had recently raised concerns with police about her safety. (Supplied)

While investigations are underway and no charges have been laid, Ms Carter-Bell said the family had been so concerned about Jayda's welfare that they had recently sought help from police.

"We begged for their help, and because we were ringing them and not Jayda, their attitude was, 'Well, what do you want us to do?'"

Victoria Police did not respond to the family's claim, with a spokesperson telling the ABC it could not comment while an investigation was underway.

Police said a 60-year-old man was arrested and interviewed nearby after a crime scene was established in Carlton, but has since been released.

Forensic detectives were seen removing evidence from the complex on Saturday.

Ms Carter-Bell said she wanted the community to see Ms Allen Bonner's picture so they could understand her story.

"We are absolutely devastated," she said.

"We need people to know that the system is so broken," she said.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.title: China’s Zhejiang province calls to limit tech giants’ power over online traffic
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.author: Eve Qiao
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.text:
Communist Party authorities in eastern China urge greater oversight of internet platforms, warning that algorithms amplify social divisions

The publicity department of the Zhejiang provincial party committee published the commentary on social media on Thursday, saying traffic could no longer be viewed simply as a data resource.

The department argued that public feed traffic should be treated as a semi-public utility rather than “a private asset owned by tech platforms”.

It accused platforms of prioritising clicks and commercial interests over the public interest.

Online platforms have considerable control over content visibility, deciding which posts and topics receive exposure or are taken down, according to the department.

“Over time, this could weaken the public’s understanding of social realities and reduce attention to and participation in public affairs,” the department said.

The three platforms have hundreds of millions of monthly users each.

The commentary also warned that platforms amplified disputes through traffic recommendations, triggering wider discussion and user-generated content that could potentially deepen social divisions.

Recommendation algorithms select and rank content based on a user’s online activity and preferences, helping platforms generate traffic and keep users engaged.

Because of this, researchers have raised concerns that users might be exposed to a narrower range of views, reinforcing stereotypes and polarisation.

The recommendation processes used by platforms, along with their decisions on account bans and whether to boost or limit content, often “operate as a black box”, the article said.

“The platforms’ social influence is not matched by corresponding accountability,” it added.

The department called for regulators to clarify the boundaries of platforms’ power, strengthen oversight of platform rules and introduce tougher constraints and penalties for promoting low-value content and amplifying disputes.

It also urged platforms to tighten their content management and make their rules more transparent.

More than 60 rounds of crackdowns were carried out between 2021 and August of this year, according to an August article by CAC head Zhuang Rongwen in the Communist Party magazine Dangjian.

Over the past two years, several major platforms, including RedNote and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, have “updated their recommendation algorithms to promote more positive content, give users greater control over their feeds, diversify recommendations and improve algorithm transparency”, according to the CAC.

Several platforms have also introduced rules for managing trending content and accounts, according to company announcements.

Dong Chenyu, an associate professor at Renmin University of China’s school of journalism and communication, said major Chinese platforms had little incentive to pursue gains by promoting attention-grabbing content that drives traffic and engagement at the expense of the public interest.

“The most direct consequence of pursuing such short-term gains is that you can expect to be fined,” Dong said on a podcast posted on Douyin’s official safety and trust centre account.
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics.summary: Communist Party authorities in eastern China urge greater oversight of internet platforms. They say algorithms amplify social divisions and could weaken public's understanding of social realities.
