https://www.dw.com/en/us-midterms-women-.title: US midterms: Women candidates could make history
https://www.dw.com/en/us-midterms-women-.text:
The US is holding Congress and state governors elections. At all levels of US politics, women are underrepresented — but they may win some historic victories in the midterms on November 3.

Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.

There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."

Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.

Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."

The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa.

125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.

"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.

The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.

Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.

According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.

For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.

Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians.

Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.

For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.

Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.

But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.

This article has been translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/us-midterms-women-.summary: Only 28.4% of the US Congress are women, but 152 women are in the House and Senate. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also higher than ever before. Kelly Dittmar doesn't think Lisa DeMuth will win in Minnesota.

https://www.dw.com/en/taiwan-to-boost-mi.title: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
https://www.dw.com/en/taiwan-to-boost-mi.text:
President Lai Ching-te ⁠said in a National Day speech that his country is boosting defense spending to 'deter war' with China. It comes after US President Donald Trump asked Taiwan to pay for US protection.

Taiwan plans to boost defense spending to deter war, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday, as China steps up military pressure to assert its claim over the self-governed island.

Lai's government has allocated a record NT$1.1 trillion ($34.5 billion) for defense spending in 2027, equivalent to more than 3% of GDP.

Taiwan's 23 million people face the threat of a Chinese attack. Beijing claims the island as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring it under its control.

"Our aim in increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, but to deter war," President Lai Ching-te said in a speech marking Taiwan's National Day.

Successive governments have increased military spending as Taiwan strengthens its defenses against a potential Chinese invasion and seeks to demonstrate to the United States its commitment to defending itself.

"We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others," Lai said in his annual address outside the Presidential Office in Taipei, attended by thousands of people, including foreign diplomats.

He warned that peace could not be taken for granted, accusing China of using military and grey-zone activities to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.

Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China but stressed that Beijing must respect "the right of the people of Taiwan to exist."

Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan remains unchanged under President Donald Trump, although some of his remarks have raised concerns in Taipei.

Trump raised concerns in May when he suggested that US arms sales to Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, following their meeting in Beijing.

Taiwan is awaiting Trump's approval of $14 billion in weapons sales, including the US-made Patriot air defense system.

At a high-profile summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in September, trade and artificial intelligence dominated the agenda. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was discussed only behind closed doors.

Ahead of Lai's speech, Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital.

Facing China's much larger military, which continues to expand its arsenal with advanced weapons, including stealth fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a vast array of missiles,  Taiwan is increasing defence spending and modernising its armed forces.

China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lai's speech. Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls Lai a "separatist" and has rejected his offers of talks.

Democratically governed Taiwan faces growing military and political pressure from China, which claims the island as its territory despite strong objections from the government in Taipei.

The United States welcomed Lai's commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A senior US administration official said that, referring to China, "a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions."

The United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, but Washington is Taipei's most important security backer.

Saturday's celebrations marked the 115th anniversary of the 1911 revolution that toppled China's Qing dynasty and paved the way for the founding of the Republic of China.

The dispute between China and Taiwan dates back to the Chinese civil war, when nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek fled to the island in 1949 after his forces were defeated by Mao Zedong's communists.

https://www.dw.com/en/indian-police-crac.title: Indian police crack down on 'Cockroach' protest in Delhi
https://www.dw.com/en/indian-police-crac.text:
Indian authorities have imposed extraordinary security measures to block protesters from joining a planned demonstration called by the Cockroach Janta Party in New Delhi. The main leaders of the party have been detained.

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:

Tens of thousands of security personnel have been deployed and roads barricaded across New Delhi to prevent the latest Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstration.

Police have detained thousands of protesters in a major crackdown. Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital.

Some protesters who turned back from Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site, have been waiting in different parts of central Delhi, determined to hold their ground.

The CJP has urged people who believe they or someone they know has been unlawfully detained to fill out an online form as soon as possible, saying it is collecting information to support affected volunteers and other individuals.

The protest targeted Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over voter list revisions that critics say favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP.

If you're joining us now, here's a helpful reminder about why India's youth are rising up this time.

Read DW's report here.

DW Hindi's Adarsh Sharma, who is on the ground in New Delhi, spoke to protesters as they faced a security crackdown.

He caught up with one protester who managed to avoid detention.

"We were running back and forth. When the police are moving forward, we go back. When they are withdrawing, we are moving forward," the protester told DW.

The protester described the heavy police presence as a "game of perception."

"Where you have 20 protesters and 10 media persons, there are 100 police personnel standing. It seems like a joke, what they are doing with taxpayers' money," the protester said.

Another protester, Jasmine, described how the morning unfolded for the demonstrators.

"We have been playing a game of cat and mouse with the police, trying to stop them from picking us up," she said.

"I don't think we have ever seen something like this happening. Protesting is a fundamental right… it's such a convoluted idea to take permission to protest… you are protesting against a government, will you ask permission from the same government? They are not going to give it," she said.

Ajinkya Shinde, who was handed the responsibility of leading the Cockroach Janta Party's protest following the detentions of its main leaders, has made his first statement — calling for a continued march to Jantar Mantar.

"We appeal to everyone to march towards Jantar Mantar! If Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar," he said in a video post made by the CJP on X.

Indian media outlets, including Scroll and Newslaundry, reported that their journalists had been detained by police while covering the 'Cockroach' party protest. The journalists were later released.

Newslaundry reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports said journalists were physically assaulted.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom and defends journalists' rights worldwide, has called on Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers.

It has also urged police to return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in New Delhi and the police response without interference.

In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), India ranked 157th out of 180 countries, down six places from 2025. Press freedom groups have raised concerns about the use of criminal laws against journalists and the impact of such measures on independent journalism.

Detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother is reported to have died on Saturday.

Indian media reports said that Dipke's paternal grandmother had been suffering from a prolonged illness and had been unwell in recent days. She died in her native village in Maharashtra, reports said.

News agency ANI, citing police sources, reported that the Delhi Police had informed Dipke of his grandmother's death. It was now up to the CJP leader to decide whether to continue his protest while under detention or travel back for the funeral rites.

Dipke was detained aboard his plane after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday morning, ahead of the protest. He was traveling from Mumbai.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has indicated that it will press on with its protest despite its leaders and supporters being detained.

CJP's National Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead the protest at Jantar Mantar until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in detention, the group said in a statement on X.

The CJP also shared a video of Dipke purportedly recorded on Friday night, anticipating a potential detention.

"If you are seeing this video, it means Ashutosh, Saurav and I have been arrested," Dipke says in the video.

"After us, Ajinkya will lead this movement," he says.

In a separate post, the CJP alleged that its three detained leaders had been taken to an undisclosed location, were being denied access to lawyers and had been cut off from "all contact with others."

The formal association of advocates at India's apex court called for urgent intervention by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant after several lawyers were detained by Delhi police.

This comes amid a reported crackdown on protesters attempting to reach the national capital, specifically central Delhi, to protest against India's chief election commissioner over alleged misconduct.

The arrested lawyers include those protesting outside the premises of the Supreme Court of India, as well as lawyers inside their chambers, legal news website, Bar and Bench, reported.

The Supreme Court Bar Association passed a resolution condemning the use of "excessive force against, and detention of, senior and young advocates, particularly women advocates, who were peacefully protesting in the Supreme Court area today."

The advocates' body expressed "grave concern" and requested the CJI to take action to ensure that the "whereabouts and safety of every detained advocate are ascertained."

Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has slammed the measures taken by Indian authorities to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party's protest from going ahead.

He called out a "war-like deployment" of security personnel and said that the suspension of the internet in a key part of Delhi was among the "most regressive" and "repressive" measures.

"A government confident in the fairness of its elections would welcome questions about them, whereas one that turns its capital into a fortress to avoid them only deepens the very suspicions it seeks to suppress. The government should provide answers, not lathis (sticks); expression, not repression," Tharoor wrote on X.

He also called for the release of the protesters who had been detained.

Tharoor said India's Gen Z "deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ," in a play on words.

Leaders of the CJP on Friday likened the clampdown on their planned protest to a "state of emergency."

A state of emergency was declared in India by former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were invoked by the Congress leader for 21 months, during which civil liberties were suspended, much of the opposition was jailed and media was censored.

Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) National Convenor and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal also mounted an emergency-related attack against Modi's government.

"This is worse than the Emergency. It's official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear," he said, referring to the arrests of CJP's three main leaders.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday accused opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal of "attempting to incite tensions" in the country.

"The Govt of India will deal strictly with the attempts you are making to incite tension, and BJP workers, remaining constantly among the people, will effectively thwart your designs," BJP President Nitin Nabin told news agencies on Saturday morning.

"Your repeated electoral defeats in various states and the resulting desperation suggest that, in some way, you do not wish to see this country move forward peacefully. However, I warn you today that the BJP and the patriotic citizens of this country will give you a fitting and stern response," he said.

Nabin suggested that "foreign forces" were behind the opposition leaders and that the protests were an attempt to "destabilize" India. BJP leaders have made similar claims before without offering proof.

"I issue a clear warning to you today: the foreign forces upon which you rely for your politics up for sale—and the alliances with such forces through which you seek to destabilize India—will never allow your nefarious intentions to succeed," he said.

It's past noon here and Indian news channels are playing visuals of protesters trying to reach central Delhi, despite the mass preventive detentions taking place.

Several groups of young people have been seen running through the streets, trying to dodge police personnel and barricades.

News agency ANI reported, citing police sources, that 200 more people were detained in the key Connaught Place area as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site.

Here's the situation right now:

With this, it is unclear at the moment whether the planned protest will be able to take place.

But the CJP isn't the only group protesting against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star, Neha Bora, have been leading protests in the capital all week.

Also on the ground are the Gandhi siblings, lawmakers Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, who are leading the opposition alliance's protests against the poll body in New Delhi.

Rahul Gandhi is the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament and possibly Prime Minister Modi's biggest challenger in the 2029 elections. According to Indian media reports, Gandhi is scheduled to attend a political meeting in the southern city of Chennai today.

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday reiterated his demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down and critized the Modi government.

"Gyanesh Kumar will go. This government will go. Then the repair of democracy will begin," the Congress leader wrote on X as he shared a video of himself addressing INDIA bloc MPs in the Central Hall of Parliament.

Late on Friday, Gandhi and a delegation of opposition lawmakers met President Droupadi Murmu to submit a four-point memorandum.

The memorandum outlined what Gandhi called Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah's "gross subversion of India's electoral system" and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.text:
Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said.

The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning.

Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come".

The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.

Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed.

"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene.

She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.

The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.

Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."

Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war.

"Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on.

Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.

The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties.

On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.

The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.

According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% in the first eight months of this year.

Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex.

This week’s Conservative Party conference saw the Kemi Badenoch further cement her position at the helm of her party. But can her increased personal popularity help a party that is still lagging behind Reform UK in the polls?

The daughter of a GP and a professor of physiology, Kemi Badenoch was born in Wimbledon but grew up in Lagos, Nigeria. At the age of 16, she moved to London where she worked various jobs including at McDonalds. She studied at Sussex University and it was an introduction to identity politics there that she credits with confirming her conservatism.

After graduating, she worked as a software engineer, a systems analyst before embarking on a career in finance. In 2015 she became digital director at the Spectator magazine.

In 2005, aged 25, she joined the Conservative Party and in 2015 she became a member of the London Assembly. At the 2017 snap general election she successfully ran to be Conservative MP for Saffron Waldon in Essex.

After landing a number of ministerial roles under Boris Johnson she unexpectedly stood for Party Leader when he stood down as Prime Minister in 2022. She came fourth in that contest but ultimately won the leadership contest after the Labour landslide General Election result of 2024.

This week she promised to scrap inheritance tax on family homes, proposed a new ‘Britannia Shield’ missile defence system and ruled out a pact with Nigel Farage’s Reform UK But can she overcome the odds and return the Conservative Party to power?

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-598.title: Opinion: Can I keep the baseball I caught?
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-598.author: Scott Simon
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-598.text:
Los Angeles Dodgers third baseman Enrique Hernández bats during the fifth inning in Game 4 of baseball's National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Atlanta.

This week, an ethical question, of all things, intruded into the baseball playoffs.

Tuesday night, Dodgers versus Braves, in Atlanta. A young man in a Dodger jersey caught a foul ball in the stands. As so often happens these days, someone seated nearby captured it on video, and then felt compelled to instruct the man, "Give it to the kid! Give it to the kid!"

And indeed there was a small boy, maybe preschool-aged, a few rows back in a Braves jersey.

But the Dodgers fan looked into the man's camera and told what turned out to be millions of viewers on social media, "I'm sorry, I can't! I'm not giving it to the kid! I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid!"

Some commenters denounced the man for keeping the ball. Some others have inveighed against the little boy for looking disappointed.

Before we criticize anyone's ethics, we ought to ask ourselves: what would we do if a baseball fell into our hands at a playoff game? Keep it, or give it to the nearest child?

Because I am a father, I'm pretty certain I would give it to a child. But also because I'm a father, I know that within a few days, the ball so tenderly bequeathed might have rolled, abandoned, under a bed, surrounded by lost socks and forgotten Labubus.

Also, a foul ball hit by almost any player would be a nice souvenir. But what if it had been a home run struck by, say, Shohei Ohtani? That ball could be as much of an investment as a Picasso!

We sought ethical advice from Nancy Sherman, a Professor of Philosophy at Georgetown University, who told us, "Manners are not morals."

The professor said she was mostly alarmed by the public shaming of both man and boy, who, after all, were not aware that their instinctive, personal reactions would soon be turned into some kind of moral exercise for the digital age.

"The young guy who caught the ball says, 'I'm sorry…I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid'"… says Professor Sherman. "I think that's a healthy, honest response."

So the next time you go to a game - if a fly ball seems to be arcing your way, you might pause before you reach for it to ask yourself, "Do I really want this ethical dilemma?"

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.text:
Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality

They were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In the Peterloo massacre of 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.

A study by Global Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – as Robert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.

As well as looking at Wedderburn’s story, Global Threads’ research looks at the life of Hugh Hornby Birley, the yeomanry commander who led the fatal charge on the crowd at Peterloo. It found Birley’s family fortune was intimately linked with transatlantic enslavement.

Meanwhile, the story of Sir George Philips, also examined in the project, reflects the contradictions of 19th-century liberal politics. While Philips helped fund the Manchester Guardian as a liberal reaction to Peterloo, he was personally invested in the exploitation of enslaved Africans in the Caribbean, as owner of the Success plantation in Hanover, Jamaica.

Birley and Philips were members of the Portico Library, Manchester’s historic members’ library. In the 19th century it was a centre of information exchange for Manchester’s business elite, helping ensure their place at the apex of global capitalism. The Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico, which stands a few yards from where the Peterloo massacre took place.

Introducing the study, Global Threads said: “Drawing together just three of the thousands of threads connecting Peterloo with Africa and the Americas, we can see how the leaders of each wing of Manchester’s elite – Hugh Hornby Birley and Sir George Philips – owed their positions and power to their family and business activities drawing on colonialism and slavery.

“They actively described the system they had created as a transatlantic one. It was not just profit that connected Peterloo … Birley and his reactionary colleagues brought colonial-style coercion more akin to the putting down of uprisings of enslaved people, working people themselves were connected to transatlantic people and places, and slavery hung like a spectre over the Mancunian struggles for justice and equality.”

On 16 August 1819, 60,000 people converged in the centre of Manchester to campaign for political representation. Conditions for those workers were better than those endured by the trafficked and enslaved African workers at the other end of the transatlantic commodity boom, who were classed as property. But Britain’s working class were disenfranchised. Only 10% of men in the country could vote, and while landowners were enriched by the tariffs placed on foreign grain by the Corn Laws, workers could barely afford bread.

The protest at St Peter’s Field ended in tragedy when the yeomanry – a militia of Tory businessmen – charged the crowd. In the aftermath, the authorities blamed protesters. But Wedderburn, a Jamaican-born Unitarian preacher, was quick to challenge the official narrative.

In September 1819, at a meeting at his Soho chapel, he described Peterloo as “an act of murder … committed by the magistrates and yeoman”. In his preaching and writings, Wedderburn had long argued Africans and English labourers were being denied by the same forces.

The backstory of Birley shows how. Ella Sinclair, writing for Global Threads, found Birley’s family’s business financially benefited from the estate of Daniel Backhouse, an enslaver who funded and profited from 103 voyages that set out from Liverpool between 1773 and 1807, trafficking more than 27,000 Africans.

In the late 18th century, three of those voyages exported people to St Lucia, where Backhouse’s company funded and profited from the Rabot sugar estate. Early 19th-century records reveal that workers there included families trafficked from Guinea and Cape Verde.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

After the emancipation of enslaved Africans in the British empire in the 1830s, the Birley family supported the enslaving US confederacy, which was integral to their cotton interests. Birley was closely involved with the development of Manchester institutions, including “the Liverpool and Manchester Railway – designed to more easily transport slave-produced cotton”, Sinclair found.

Wedderburn’s family was also embedded in the plantation economy. His uncle, John Wedderburn, owned the Blackheath, Blackness, Bluecastle and Glen Islay plantations in Westmoreland, Jamaica. Workers on those plantations included people trafficked from Old Calabar, in modern-day Nigeria, to Montego Bay in 1773, on a ship carrying textiles woven in Manchester.

Robert Wedderburn’s mother was an enslaved woman called Rosanne, while his father was the plantation owner who raped her. Raised in Jamaica by his African grandmother, Talky Amee, Wedderburn served in the Royal Navy and sailed to London, settling in multicultural St Giles and became a leading radical.

Global Threads found that the Dreadnought, the ship that trafficked some enslaved workers to Wedderburn plantations, had also trafficked workers to Success, the plantation later owned by Philips.

At the time of Peterloo, Wedderburn was in prison, accused of inciting slaves to kill their masters. He believed in armed struggle against enslavement across the Caribbean, and that a revolution had begun at Peterloo.

Around the same time as Peterloo, hundreds of abolitionists who had escaped slavery were staging raids on plantations in St Catherine, Jamaica. The British governor at the time was, coincidentally, titled the Duke of Manchester.

In a paper on Wedderburn, Global Threads historians write: “In the weeks following the [Peterloo] massacre, Wedderburn gave the most clear contemporary articulation of a transatlantic understanding of liberation and justice. He drew direct parallels for his followers … showing that the oligarchy profiting from the labour of working people in Manchester – while denying their rights to representation and improved working and living conditions – were part of the same elite and system that imposed the violence and coercion of slavery upon enslaved Africans.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review. Experts are alarmed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review.

The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb).

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage.

The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing.

The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “promises kept” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken, injure or kill people.

But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception.

Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science.

“The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues.

“I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added.

The FDA did not respond to a request for comment.

The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”.

Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts.

Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”.

Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity.

Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical.

“They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.”

The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats.

Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample.

Perchlorate reduces the thyroid gland’s ability to absorb iodine, which is a raw material needed to produce the hormone T4, an essential component of proper brain development. Very low levels of perchlorate exposure are linked to lower T4 production, and lower IQ scores for children.

Still, six months after it published its data, the FDA reapproved perchlorate for use in super sacks. Advocates say the agency used flawed science and manipulated the data. The FDA wrote that there was no meaningful increase in perchlorate across all the 250 foods it measured. But critics countered that the problem was not in all the food – the problem was in kids’ cereal.

The FDA largely ignored the cereal findings, and mostly does not consider endocrine system harms when developing regulations, said Tom Neltner, a former scientist with the EDF who is now director of the Unleaded Kids non-profit. He helped lead litigation over perchlorate, which was ultimately dismissed.

“They put their blinders on and approved the exemption based on data that never considered the harms posed by endocrine disruptors,” Neltner said.

Kennedy leads the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement, of which eliminating toxic chemicals from food is a cornerstone. During the run-up to the 2024 US presidential election, he held up the Gras standard as an example of the broken regulatory system that he would take bold steps to fix as he stands up to big food and makes America healthy again. The loophole drew outrage because campaigners say it virtually eliminates regulatory oversight for new ingredients, chemicals and products, allowing food companies to self-certify that substances are safe without alerting the FDA.

The Gras standard does require companies to demonstrate a new food product is safe by making “widely accepted” scientific evidence to support its claim publicly available. But some companies bury the “public” announcement deep in their websites, push the boundaries of “widely accepted” research or hire from a cottage industry of scientists who are paid to declare food products “safe”, advocates say.

A 2026 review of FDA and other federal food records by Maffini and the Environmental Working Group non-profit found at least 111 food chemicals or substances exploited the Gras standard, and they are used across thousands of products. Upon his appointment to oversee Trump’s health agency, the FDA and Kennedy reiterated his promise to “close the loophole”, and in 2026 he appeared to make good on it. He and the FDA stated that they were “closing critical information gaps”.

Critics warned the “closure” was at best a modest loophole tightening that effectively only requires voluntary compliance, and the quiet opening of the TOR exemption counteracted any gains.

Either the White House or the office of management and budget were involved in the Gras rule negotiations, though it is unclear who added the TOR expansion. Regardless, the controversial exemption is consistent with the administration’s philosophy more broadly, Maffini said.

“This administration is not keen on regulating anything,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Six men on how they plan to stand up against rape culture: ‘Boys need to be taught what is appropriate’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Iris Kim
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
While most of the crowd at a Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was mostly women, men of all ages were in attendance too

Tens of thousands of protesters gathered at city halls and college campuses across the country on Thursday to demand an end to sexual violence. The nationwide rallies followed weeks of public outcry over the mishandling of campus sexual assault cases at Cornell University and Louisiana State University.

The protest organizers – including Women’s March, Feminist Generation and Me Too International – demanded justice for Jane Doe, who said she was drugged and gang-raped by seven students at a Cornell frat party; Kendall Francis, who said she was raped by an LSU football player; and all survivors harmed “from the frat house to the White House”. They also called for reform of Title IX, a set of protections for sexual misconduct victims and LGBTQ+ students that the Trump administration has slowly stripped away.

The latest cases have outraged college students and their families over the pervasiveness of rape culture; 81% of women and 43% of men in the US said they have experienced sexual harassment or assault, according to the National Sexual Violence Resource Center. Parents online are questioning how to raise sons who will stand up to sexual violence instead of being bystanders. Women, survivors and longtime advocates say the onus has often been on them to use the momentum in moments like these to educate others and demand concrete change.

While the demographic makeup of the crowd at the Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was majority women, men of all ages were there, too, holding “I Am Jane Doe” signs and yelling to end rape culture. We asked six of them how they are personally taking a stand against rape culture.

Too often, we see that after a big uproar and high-profile news, that the only people standing up and attending protests are women or female-identifying folks. It’s really important for men to step up and say: “Hey, I need to put an end to this in any way that I can in my day-to-day life.” We need to try to make a difference in our own communities, whether that’s speaking up against frat brothers who say something toxic or misogynistic in the chat, or going out and attending events like the Women’s March.

There’s some really important legislation in the New York state legislature to make consent education a mandatory part of the school curriculum. I’m in Democratic party leadership, and we just passed a resolution last week supporting a framework for teaching consent. I actually think that’s the most important thing that we can do.

People are talking about increasing penalties and closing the voluntary intoxication loophole, which is super important. But the reality is that we don’t get [sexual assault] convictions, the police don’t take [sexual assault] seriously and DAs do not prosecute.

We need to be doing a lot more in prevention. After the assault is just too late. There have been really good studies that show that consent education can have a huge impact on reducing the rate of victimization and perpetration, and nobody talks about it at all. It’s a real, real shame.

I know from my own experiences as a man that many boys need to be taught what is appropriate, and when consent means consent. Men need to do more teaching.

It really starts with reconsidering your own position and understanding where it is near you, and in you.

I’m from Italy, and there was a girl from my high school who was killed by her ex. In my home country, there has been a lot of mobilizing around this issue. It’s very evident that [rape culture] is near us, all across the country, in our society.

There were cases in my social life where I wish I had been more present for the women I know. They have felt uncomfortable in social situations with guys being creepy when they were intoxicated. We all have to be very aware of whether someone is feeling uncomfortable or whether you are making someone uncomfortable.

I see rape culture as something that starts from little moments – how people talk, how women are treated. The language that we use when we talk to women or talk about them is objectifying. Those things are normalized, and then that’s what turns into something bigger, like rape. And when rape happens, it’s also not seriously considered. It always turns into victim-blaming. I’ve seen that, and I want to stand against that.

I grew up in the punk rock scene, and when things happened, we took action. You got your head kicked in if you did something bad. I wish that would happen more often. I know that’s not the right thing to say, and I don’t stand for violence. But the violence that [abusers] are doing to us is so much worse.

In my current life, just being in New York, it’s constant. You can’t sit at a bar without overhearing people saying disgusting things about women. I worked in the music industry and the alcohol industry, and I’ve been surrounded by it my entire life. I’ve spent my whole life fighting against this stuff.

The rallies followed weeks of public outcry over the mishandling of campus sexual assault cases at Cornell University and Louisiana State University.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: AI surveillance startup Flock to cut several hundred jobs amid backlash, sources say
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Company, which grown rapidly in recent years, has been under scrutiny as privacy concerns grow

Flock Safety plans to shed about 18% of its employees, people with direct ⁠knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker of AI-powered surveillance cameras and license-plate readers faces mounting opposition to its products from communities and ⁠lawmakers.

The people said the job ⁠cuts came after ​a voluntary buyout program and were expected to affect roughly 270 employees at Flock, a surveillance technology startup that has seen rapid growth in recent ⁠years. Employees will leave the company at the end of the month.

Sources declined to be identified as the company has yet to make the plan public.

Flock declined ⁠to comment.

In September, Flock announced a voluntary separation program, asking employees to apply if they wanted to ​leave the company, as Wired reported. The ‌company has about 1,500 employees.

Flock faces ‌growing scrutiny from regulators, lawmakers and privacy advocates, despite drawing strong investor interest among venture capitalists. A ‌recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Americans are divided on whether Flock cameras are a good idea. About 38% of the country supports the use of Flock cameras in their community, compared with 47% who oppose their use.

Across 49 states, Flock’s network of about 120,000 AI-powered cameras, affixed to streets and highways, automatically read license plates and record vehicles as they pass.

The company, based in Atlanta and founded in ‌2017, has raised more than $950m from venture capital investors, with its latest $275m round in March led by Andreessen Horowitz valuing the company at $7.5bn. The funds have supported a ​new US manufacturing facility and an upcoming push into drone products, according to the company.

Flock provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. The company says its technology helps investigate and solve crimes, but it has come under increasing scrutiny over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing practices.

Public backlash ⁠has grown. In September, Florida banned automated license plate readers from state highways, ​citing privacy risks tied to Flock’s ​cameras.

Home Depot investors recently demanded reviews ​of the retailer’s partnerships with surveillance technology vendors after reports that Flock’s data was used ​in immigration enforcement.

Flock also ‌faces legal challenges, such ​as a privacy ​lawsuit in Virginia alleging that the widespread deployment of its AI-powered cameras constitutes warrantless surveillance.

Together with AI datacenters, Flock cameras have emerged as a flashpoint ahead of November’s midterm elections, with candidates increasingly attacking their opponents by tying them to the technology.

https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.title: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.author: Jacek Krywko
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.text:
Participants meditated inside an MRI tube, with and without psilocybin.

For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”

In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.

Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.

Volunteers went through the same four-part sequence twice, once sober and once on psilocybin. The sequence included putting participants in four different settings or contexts: eight minutes of lying at rest, a guided meditation, an 11-minute curated music playlist, and finally six minutes of eyes-open video of clouds moving across a sky. Each participant did all four inside an MRI scanner about 80 minutes after dosing, and again on EEG about 150 minutes after.

There were no cognitive tasks researchers routinely go for in brain studies, but there was a purpose behind this omission.

“We wanted ecological validity,” Stoliker says. “We wanted to know what the brain was like when somebody was having an authentic, uninterrupted psychedelic experience. If somebody took a psychedelic in a therapeutic setting, you wouldn’t have them completing tasks.” Stoliker also points out that there’s evidence that giving someone a task mid-trip pulls them out of the state—a phenomenon researchers sometimes call grounding. “Once you introduce these sorts of tasks, you’re actually interrupting the very phenomena you are seeking to measure.” And it worked.

Half of the participants ranked their session among the most meaningful experiences of their lives, and 24 put it in their personal top five. Stolkier and his colleagues started analyzing their brain scan data to find out why.

Measuring global functional connectivity—how much influence each patch of cortex exerts over the rest—the team found that, when participants had their eyes closed, sensory regions lost sway while associative regions gained. “It seems like the brain’s ability to construct reality, or imagination, or our associations, our beliefs, our sense of self—these faculties had more dominance over sensory areas,” Stoliker says, stressing that the interpretation is a hypothetical. “This could help explain why people have meaningful, complex imagery experiences, why they have mystical experiences with imagery that is personally relevant to them.”

Another observation the team made was that connections within each brain network weakened, connections between networks strengthened. The brain’s modularity, a parameter that describes how cleanly neurons stay sorted into specialist teams, dropped across all four parts of the experimental sequence.

What’s more, researchers found that, when sober, activity in a brain with its eyes shut looked very different from a brain watching a movie. Under psilocybin, that difference nearly evaporated. In the visual network, the gap between eyes-open and eyes-closed connectivity shrank by 85 percent. The results from the EEG session independently confirmed that, with alpha-band activity (normally a marker of the brain gating visual input) reduced by nearly half.

“When somebody takes a psychedelic and they’re able to close their eyes and see complex imagery, there seems to be less boundary between the internal and external world than we ordinarily experience,” Stoliker says.

Regardless of these details, the results rather accurately reproduced the chaos in the brain so many researchers claimed psychedelics caused. This chaos, though, turned into order when the team processed their data in a slightly unorthodox way.

Scientists usually do two acts of averaging in a standard brain imaging study. The first is averaging over time. An eight-minute brain scan comprises a few hundred successive images of the whole brain. To understand how two specific regions work together, researchers conventionally average all these images down to a single number describing how well the two regions’ activity matched up across the whole eight minutes.

The problem with this analysis is that it runs the risk of missing ordered structures that appear for a brief period and then disappear into chaos.

The second analysis is averaging over people. Having produced one such number per participant, the standard approach then pools all of them into a group average, on the assumption that individual differences are noise that will be canceled out. Stoliker’s study was focused on individual experiences, so he wanted to avoid that.

Instead, the team fed the moment-by-moment activity of 332 brain regions into CEBRA, a machine-learning tool that compressed the data down to its essential structure while preserving the order of events. For each individual, it produced a trajectory—a path traced through a three-dimensional space, one point for each moment of the scan.

“When they’re not under psilocybin, the brain activity is less differentiated by context,” Stoliker says. “But under psilocybin, we see that the activity becomes organized across time and more clearly differentiated by context.” The trajectories separated into four distinct clusters corresponding to rest, meditation, music, and the movie. A classifier could read a moment of brain activity and say which one the person was in.

It turned out the performance of that classifier scaled with how profound the participants described their experience as being.

To find out which parts of the brain were doing the work, the team replaced one network’s psilocybin activity with its sober version and checked how badly the classifier degraded. The default mode network and the visual network each accounted for over 20 percent of the effect. “The default mode network is strongly associated with the sense of self: daydreaming, mind wandering, thinking about yourself. It’s often been called the narrative self,” Stoliker explains. “On the other end of this gradient, more externally oriented, is the visual system.”

Under psilocybin, the two became less differentiated, which the team thinks explains why participants reported a subjective experience of the self and the external world becoming less separate, a state Stoliker calls “embeddedness.”

“Theoretically, we could suggest that psychedelics are temporarily altering the organization of brain networks that ordinarily help maintain this separation that we experience,” he says. “It really challenges the idea of whether the internal world and external world are separate and highlights the idea that the brain may be responsible for constructing both.”

The day after the session, participants rated whether various things had shifted, like sense of connection to themselves, to others, to nature, along with peace, acceptance, and creativity, all on a scale running from –100 to 100. “For the vast majority of our participants, we found they had positive psychological changes the next day,” Stoliker says. The data from the brain reading classifier the team used for discriminating among meditation, rest, the movie, and the music tracked with the size of that shift.

In the future, Stolkier hopes to use this for therapeutic purposes. If context isn’t just mood-setting but is mechanically shaping brain organization, Stolkier argues, then the room, the playlist, and the instructions start to look like clinical variables a clinician could deliberately tune to improve therapeutic outcomes. But there are details the team must work out first.

As of now, the researchers admit that when two people report identical “embeddedness” scores, they can potentially have very different subjective experiences. Also, all the volunteers in Stoliker’s study were healthy individuals, not patients suffering from psychological or psychiatric disorders that potential therapies using psychedelics could be aimed at.

Finally, we still don’t know how exactly variables like music or visuals should be tuned. “That’s a future avenue where we need more research to determine exactly what conditions should be optimized, and for who. It’s quite possible we would want to take different approaches for each individual, or depending on what their diagnosis is,” Stoliker says. “Still, finding this level of organization hidden underneath that disorder and chaos has some really good explanatory value.”

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10910-z
https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/10/.summary: Researchers at Monash University studied the effects of psychedelic drugs on the brain. They used a brain scan to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. The results were published in Nature.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/buffetts.author: Alex Crippen
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/buffetts.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Warren Buffett watches CNBC in the morning, but nearly every evening he “can’t get enough” of watching YouTube clips while sitting on a recliner in front of an “enormous” television in his Omaha home.

A Wall Street Journal article this week quotes friends as saying he’s “hardly ever” looking at anything related to investing or finance, although he is a “fan of Berkshire Hathaway’s own content” and “proud of how it performs on the video platform.”

Instead, it’s things like “Glenn Close clips ... commercials from the 1950s ... Paul Anka videos ... speeches by complete unknowns ... show tunes, railroads, the big-band era, Nebraska and early Frank Sinatra performances from the 1930s.”

He will also go down some “random rabbit holes.”

For example, Buffett might “come into his office, gushing about a moving amateur rendition of ‘My Way.’”

Sharon Osberg, the three-time world bridge champion who has taught Buffett and Bill Gates the finer points of the game, is also Buffett’s “frequent viewing companion,” says the WSJ.

She reports “Warren’s range is broad. It can be the silliest things,” like a “really good documentary on Roy Cohn” or “the Uzbekistan version of America’s got talent.”

Osberg says Buffett has also been watching clips featuring his late friend and business partner, Charlie Munger, including a 2017 appearance at the University of Michigan.

“You feel the bond between the two of them as he watches Charlie. It’s really quite something.”

The WSJ knocks down the idea Buffett’s YouTube habit had anything to do with Berkshire’s big investment in Alphabet
, the platform’s corporate parent.

“He just really likes watching the clips, friends say.”

The article notes that while Buffett, now 96 years old, is notoriously slow to adopt new technologies, in this instance his move to YouTube is in line with an ongoing shift from streaming to video clips that has made the platform the most-watched video provider on TVs in the U.S.

Berkshire Hathaway added another $192.6 million to its bet on homebuilder Lennar late last week.

In an SEC filing Monday, Berkshire reports buying 2.4 million shares of Lennar Class A
 at an average price of $79.65 and 15 thousand shares of Lennar Class B
 at an average price of $78.33 on Thursday, October 1 and Friday, October 2.

Since Berkshire’s stake topped 10% in mid-September, it’s been required by an SEC rule to disclose additional purchases within two business days.

There’s been no filing so far this week, so it appears there wasn’t any new buying through at least Tuesday.

In total, Berkshire has added $595.3 million of Lennar shares on 11 trading days since September 17.

At today’s closing prices, its disclosed 12.2% stake of 29 million shares is valued at $2.2 billion.

At the end of last year, it owned just 7.2 million shares, then worth $742 million.

Over that period, LEN has dropped more than 25% as rising interest rates have made homes less affordable.

Some links may require a subscription:

Warren Buffett talks about the importance of how consumers think about a company.

AUDIENCE MEMBER: Could you explain a little more about what you call the “mind of the consumer” and the “nature of the product?” ...

WARREN BUFFETT: You know, what you really — when you get into consumer products, you’re really interested in finding out — or thinking about — what is in the mind of how many people throughout the world about a product now, and what is likely to be in their mind five or ten or 20 years from now?

Now, virtually every person on the globe — maybe, well, let’s get it down to 75 percent of the people on the globe — have some notion in their mind about Coca-Cola.

They have — the word “Coca-Cola” means something to them. You know, RC Cola doesn’t mean anything to virtually anyone in the world, you know.

It does to the guy who owns RC, you know, but — and the bottler.

But everybody has something in their mind about Coca-Cola. And overwhelmingly, it’s favorable. It’s associated with pleasant experiences.

Now, part of that is by design. I mean, it is where you are happy. It is at Disneyland, at Disney World. And it’s at ballparks. And it’s every place that you’re likely to have a smile on your face, including the Berkshire Hathaway meeting, I might add. (Laughter)

And that position in the mind is pretty firmly established. And it’s established in close to 200 countries around the world with people.

A year from now, it will be established in more minds. And it will have a slightly, slightly, slightly different overall position. In ten years from now, the position can move just a little bit more.

It’s share of mind. It’s not share of market. It’s share of mind that counts.

Disney, same way. Disney means something to billions of people. And if you’re a parent of a couple of young children and you got 50 videos in front of you that you can buy, you’re not going to sit down and preview an hour and a half of each video before deciding what one to stick in front of your kids.

You know, you have got something in your mind about Disney. And you don’t have it about the ABC Video Company. Or you don’t even have it about other — you don’t have it about 20th Century. You know, you don’t have it about Paramount.

So that name, to billions of people, including lots of people outside this country, it has a meaning. And that meaning overwhelmingly is favorable. It’s reinforced by the other activities of the company.

And just think of what somebody would pay if they could actually buy that share of mind, you know, of billions of people around the world. You can’t do it.

You can’t do it by a billion-dollar advertising budget or a $3 billion advertising budget or hiring 20,000 super salesmen.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/from-bjs.title: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/from-bjs.author: Ryan Baker
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/from-bjs.text:
Dollar General, BJ’s Wholesale Club, Lululemon and Under Armour have said in earnings calls that they have already cut or plan to cut assortments.

Analysts said that after trimming product lines, brands may focus on raising prices to get back to healthy growth.

Box retailers can offer thousands of individual brands, so product cuts can help streamline assortments and stabilize their businesses.

Trimming assortments comes with challenges, as retailers risk losing customers and have to answer to investors as their revenue base shrinks in the short term.

Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets.

As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs.

In March, Dollar General
 said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour
 said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ’s Wholesale Club
 said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs. In September, Lululemon
 said it cut North America SKUs by 15%.

Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make.

When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don’t end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems.

“If you have zero discounting, you’re not taking enough fashion risk,” said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. “But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly.”

Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns.

Under Armour’s operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue.

“Today, we’re managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy,” said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company’s fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. “We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price.”

Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power.

Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years.

“Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things,” said Siegel. “Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer.”

Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand.

Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level.

“It’s a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception,” said Siegel.

He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026.

Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is “rebalancing” its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June.

For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ’s, cutting down the assortment doesn’t necessarily give them the ability to raise prices.

Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business.

“When you shrink a box ... and say, I’m going to focus more on curation, you’re getting smaller, but you’re trying to reestablish why someone’s walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn’t necessarily help your bottom line as much,” said Siegel.

BJ’s CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren’t previously offered.

“That is sourcing sales growth as well and sort of giving us the formula where we can cut SKUs, and see sales go up, and see margin dollars go up,” Eddy said on the company’s fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August.

In June 2025, Dollar General said the elimination of 1,000 SKUs from the previous year opened up more shelf space for its best-selling products and added to its top line. By March 2026, the company said, it had reduced up to 1,500 SKUs, providing benefits to the overall supply chain.

“Being more productive there means getting product to the shelf faster and being there for the consumer with the right amount of items and products that she’s looking for as quickly as we possibly can,” Dollar General CEO Todd Vasos said in the company’s fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August. “As we go forward, the team is looking at continued SKU rationalization, albeit probably more surgical in nature.”

Successfully slashing products from shelves is difficult in practice.

Box stores risk losing customers to competitors that offer the products they scrapped. BJ’s, for instance, acknowledged that a previous attempt to cut SKUs was unsuccessful.

“We just cut SKUs which cut sales, and then we added some SKUs back and so really what we’re doing now is removing unnecessary choice,” Eddy said on the company’s earnings call in August. “Think about in traditional soda, we don’t carry cans and one-liters and two-liters of the same product anymore.”

Meanwhile, publicly traded brands that acknowledge sales need to decline in order for the business to grow still have answers to investors in the near term.

“It’s hard for a company ever to say we need to shrink anything, but it’s dramatically harder to say we need to shrink revenues,” said Siegel. “Frequently we find that brands hit a peak, a healthy peak, extend past the peak by forcing it and then find their way back down pretty harshly.”
