https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ai-movie.title: Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ai-movie.author: Stephen Desaulniers,Julia Boorstin
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/ai-movie.text:
Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” opens this weekend as a broader run of films takes on tech leaders and artificial intelligence.

The slate includes portrayals or documentaries involving Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes and Sam Altman.

The new releases land as polling shows high public concern about AI risks and growing unease about data centers.

This weekend marks the kickoff of a slew of films centered on some of the biggest figures in technology and artificial intelligence, as public concern about the industry grows.

Sony Pictures’ “The Social Reckoning” is expected to open to around $7 million domestically this weekend. The scripted film is a follow-up to Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Network” from 2010, which went on to win three Academy Awards. While Sorkin’s first “Social” film focused on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s founding of the company, “The Social Reckoning” follows the 2021 leak by Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, who exposed internal documents from the tech giant.

“It brought back really warm memories for me,” Haugen told CNBC recently about the film. “And so I felt it captured the spirit of that time period.”

The box office this weekend will also see a limited release of Alex Gibney’s nearly four-hour Elon Musk documentary, called “Musk.” Early showings have drawn critical acclaim, but it’s also been criticized by Musk himself on X, saying the film has zero integrity.

“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim via A24 Films, releases on Oct. 16.

Christmas brings “Artificial” from Neon to theaters. The scripted film depicts OpenAI
 CEO Sam Altman and his brief firing from the role in 2023.

“It looks like an awful movie, but I appreciate people’s creativity, and I really do support that,” Altman recently told CNBC. “I get why people have anxiety. And also if they need to, like, project that anxiety onto someone or have a little bit of relief and poke fun at me, it doesn’t bother me.”

Netflix is also joining in. The streamer’s latest installment of its “Instadocs” series will premiere on Monday, highlighting the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and autonomously hacked into the company’s infrastructure.

These films come at a critical time as the public has grown increasingly concerned about the dangers of AI and wary of the data centers that power the technology. A recent Quinnipiac poll showed that 73% of Americans are concerned about AI’s threat to human survival, while a Pew Research survey showed that 54% think data centers are bad for the environment.

The question now is whether these films will push that public perception even further toward the brink.

David Kirby, Cal Poly’s director of Science, Technology & Society, said the public attention on these films is only adding fuel to the fire.

“Movies are incredibly persuasive media,” he said. “Stories are incredibly persuasive. We’ve known this for centuries.”

“I think the people at the top, they’re worried about it partially because they don’t like to look bad. They don’t like people questioning that they know what they’re doing or that they’re not the people who are going to be saving humanity,” he added.

Hollywood has a history of releasing films that researchers and observers have linked to changes in public opinion. The 2004 blockbuster “The Day After Tomorrow” was recognized for drawing attention to climate change, while the 2013 documentary “Blackfish” was credited with changing perceptions of SeaWorld and marine mammal captivity.

Kirby credited films like “Deep Impact” and “Armageddon” from 1998 as forcing governments to spend more money and attention on the topic of asteroids hitting the Earth.

“Was the science right in it? Not really. It’s controversial, but in terms of raising awareness … that’s what you want,” Kirby said. “You need to break into that public attention. You need people to start paying attention to you. Movies, that’s a perfect way to do that.”

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Palestinian president Abbas postpones legislative, presidential elections to September 2027
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday decreed that presidential and legislative elections both be held on September 11, 2027, postponing the previously scheduled legislative polls, according to official Palestinian media.

"Abbas issued a presidential decree on Saturday calling for simultaneous presidential and legislative elections to be held on September 11, 2027," his office said in a statement published by the Wafa news agency.

The legislative polls, which the international community has strongly advocated for, had been due to take place on November 28 this year, while a presidential vote had been expected in early 2027.

READ MORE
Israeli policies threaten 'life and existence' of Palestinians, Abbas tells UN

A day earlier, Israel's foreign minister accused Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas of "fooling the international community" by planning to postpone upcoming legislative polls, as indications of a delay multiplied.

"Mahmoud Abbas is fooling the international community by cancelling once again promised elections," Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar wrote on X.

"They keep deceiving. Consequences? Not for the corrupt PA!" he added.

The last legislative elections in the Palestinian territories were held two decades ago, and holding polls is part of the reforms demanded by the international community, including the European Union.

Palestinian factions including Abbas' Fatah and its rival Hamas have agreed to hold a "national dialogue" before legislative elections in November, with a source telling AFP on Thursday that the factions were seeking to postpone the vote.

Citing a PA source earlier in October, Palestinian official news agency WAFA reported that Israel had refused to allow Palestinian election officials access to east Jerusalem or Gaza ahead of the polls, increasing concerns that the vote will be postponed.

In early September, top Palestinian official Jibril Rajoub told reporters the November elections would not be held on time.

Rajoub, secretary-general of Fatah, said holding presidential elections first "would solve a large part of the problem".

The last legislative elections in the Palestinian territories were held in 2006, when Islamist movement Hamas won.

They defeated Fatah, which dominates the Palestinian Authority.

READ MORE
Palestinian president’s son Yasser Abbas elected to top Fatah post

The ensuring rift set off a round of factional fighting, with Hamas later seizing power in the Gaza Strip and creating a territorial divide between Fatah in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza.

As a result, the Palestinian Legislative Council, which is the PA's parliament, has not met since 2007.

Abbas won the last Palestinian presidential election in 2005, and his term should have expired in 2009, but he has since ruled by decree.

In June, the 90-year-old leader signed a decree providing for a presidential election to be held at the beginning of 2027.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

The last legislative elections in the Palestinian territories were held two decades ago.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/a.title: Russian attacks kill 15 in Ukraine after Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/a.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/a.text:
The diesel deal contrasted a sweeping Russia sanctions law Trump signed last month to clamp down on Russia’s oil and gas revenues

Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said on Saturday. At least 16 people were wounded in the attack.

“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote Saturday on social media.

He said the attacks showed Moscow understood “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities”, adding that “different signals are needed”.

Zelensky said Ukraine was preparing meetings and coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive from the diesel deal. In a post on social media, he said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and said that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s it uses to intercept Shahed drones.

“It is important to continue working together to protect people and limit Russia’s ability to wage this terrible war,” Zelensky said.

Instead, the American leader announced on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.

In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.

“Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.”

“Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He’s got an election coming up soon,” Petrenko said. “So he needs to emphasise to his voters that petrol will be cheap. But it won’t be effective.”

For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise”.

“Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told Associated Press.

Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine.

In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal on Friday, Zelensky said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy”. He framed it as an investment in the war that could prolong it.

“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelensky called it “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners”.

Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelensky said.

https://www.dw.com/en/operations-plan-ge.title: Operations Plan Germany: How the Bundeswehr trains for NATO collective defense
https://www.dw.com/en/operations-plan-ge.text:
How prepared is Germany for national defense? The answer lies in the Operations Plan Germany. Military exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are designed to put these preparations to the test in realistic scenarios.

In a residential district of Hamburg at midnight, the streets are quiet and deserted. Suddenly, the silence is shattered: Several helicopters circle the night sky, and flashing blue lights illuminate the darkness. A long convoy of vehicles moves through the streets. Soldiers stand atop armored Bundeswehr vehicles, their machine guns at the ready. For local residents, it is an unusual, perhaps even unsettling sight in an otherwise peaceful port city.

"Red Storm Charlie" is the name of the exercise that will bring parts of Hamburg, northern Germany's largest city, to a standstill for three days. The Bundeswehr, police, and civilian organizations are jointly testing how well prepared they are to respond in a crisis.

The scenario centers on a deteriorating security situation on NATO's eastern flank. NATO troops, represented in the exercise by Bundeswehr soldiers, arrive at the port of Hamburg, Germany's largest seaport, before moving eastwards through the Hanseatic city.

Acts of sabotage and demonstrations, also included in the scenario, hamper their advance. With around 1,700 participants, including 500 soldiers, the exercise held in late September 2026, was the largest of its kind to date.

"Red Storm Charlie" forms part of a classified strategy known as the "Operationsplan Deutschland" (Operations Plan Germany). Through this document, the Bundeswehr is preparing for the possibility of a Russian attack on NATO territory. The Operations Plan Germany is an integral element of NATO's broader defense planning and is closely aligned with the Alliance's overall defense framework.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the event of war or a major crisis, not only the city of Hamburg but Germany as a whole would assume a pivotal role as a logistics hub for hundreds of thousands of NATO soldiers, weapons, and pieces of heavy equipment. "This is a highly detailed and strictly classified plan that specifies exactly where NATO allies would arrive in Germany, including which ports they would use and which routes would be required for their transit across the country," security expert Aylin Matlé of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) told DW.

The Baltic states are widely regarded as the region where NATO considers a Russian attack most likely. In such a scenario, the alliance would concentrate large troop contingents from its 32 member states there. To reach the region, soldiers from southern and western Europe would need to pass through Germany. "In concrete terms, this means that around 800,000 soldiers and 200,000 vehicles would have to move through our country within six months. Those are the calculations," says Marcel Bohnert, a Bundeswehr officer who contributed to the first version of the Operations Plan.

Speaking to DW in a personal capacity rather than as a representative of the Bundeswehr, Bohnert explained: "We must ensure that soldiers can use our roads and ports safely. That is why we take care of all their needs: We arrange accommodation, provide food, ensure their security, and guide them through our transport network."

The plan also covers transport in the opposite direction, from east to west, including the evacuation of wounded soldiers and civilians fleeing the conflict. Its development was commissioned by Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As Germany's highest-ranking military officer, Breuer is far from alone in his concern that Russia could target additional countries. Germany is already confronting a wide range of Russian hostile activities, from cyberattacks to acts of sabotage directed against the Bundeswehr.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A new dimension of the threat emerged with the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. An explosive-laden drone was deployed there and failed to detonate only through luck. The German government holds Russia responsible. "The threat is becoming more tangible. It is serious, acute, and increasingly visible. This is exactly what the Russian president wants. Moscow is testing our response," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told the Bundestag on September 23.

The Bundeswehr is also addressing this threat through the Operations Plan Germany, which is continuously being refined and updated. Lessons learned from exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are incorporated into the plan. According to Bohnert, the plan also serves as a deterrent: "We hope to discourage Russia from further aggression by demonstrating our strength through the rapid build-up of military capabilities and the highly organized, swift deployment of forces to the borders."

How well prepared is Germany for its role as a military logistics hub? Matlé identifies one major vulnerability in the country's ageing and, in some cases, deteriorating infrastructure. Germany, she argues, must address the maintenance and repair of the bridges, roads, and transport routes required for troop movements "far more quickly and comprehensively." "Some of this infrastructure dates back to the Cold War and was not designed to accommodate heavy loads or military equipment."

A further challenge lies in striking the right balance between confidentiality and public involvement. To guard against acts of sabotage, sensitive details such as the precise transit routes for NATO troops must not fall into Russian hands. At the same time, the plan can only succeed through close cooperation between the Bundeswehr and civilian society, including local and regional authorities, the police, and relief organizations. "Parts of the plan must be publicly accessible because we need support from society, as well as from ministries and governments, to make it work," said Bohnert.

The debate over the confidentiality of the more than 1,000-page document recently resurfaced after the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) emerged as the strongest party in recent elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Security experts expressed concern that the party, which is classified in part as right-wing extremist and is regarded as Russia-friendly, could pass information from the plan to Moscow if it were to assume the office of state premier. The Defense Ministry rejected these concerns, noting that no federal state is given access to the complete document. Instead, the sensitive sections of the Operations Plan are shared only in excerpts and strictly on a need-to-know basis.

According to observers, however, the growing number of hybrid threats is underscoring the need for secrecy. During the "Red Storm Charlie" exercise in Hamburg, accredited journalists were not informed of routes or locations until the very last moment because of concerns over potential disruptions and acts of sabotage.

This article was originally written in German.

The scenario centers on a deteriorating security situation on NATO's eastern flank. The plan can only succeed through close cooperation between the Bundeswehr and civilian society, says Bohnert.

https://www.dw.com/en/indian-authorities.title: Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest in central Delhi. Follow live.
https://www.dw.com/en/indian-authorities.text:
Indian authorities have imposed extraordinary security measures to block protesters from joining a demonstration called by the Cockroach Janta Party in New Delhi. The main leaders of the party have been detained too.

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:

Tens of thousands of security personnel have been deployed and roads barricaded across New Delhi to prevent the latest Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstration.

Police have detained thousands of protesters in a major crackdown. Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital.

Some protesters who turned back from Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site, have been waiting in different parts of central Delhi, determined to hold their ground.

The CJP has urged people who believe they or someone they know has been unlawfully detained to fill out an online form as soon as possible, saying it is collecting information to support affected volunteers and other individuals.

The protest targeted Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over voter list revisions that critics say favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP.

If you're joining us now, here's a helpful reminder about why India's youth are rising up this time.

Read DW's report here.

DW Hindi's Adarsh Sharma, who is on the ground in New Delhi, spoke to protesters as they faced a security crackdown.

He caught up with one protester who managed to avoid detention.

"We were running back and forth. When the police are moving forward, we go back. When they are withdrawing, we are moving forward," the protester told DW.

The protester described the heavy police presence as a "game of perception."

"Where you have 20 protesters and 10 media persons, there are 100 police personnel standing. It seems like a joke, what they are doing with taxpayers' money," the protester said.

Another protester, Jasmine, described how the morning unfolded for the demonstrators.

"We have been playing a game of cat and mouse with the police, trying to stop them from picking us up," she said.

"I don't think we have ever seen something like this happening. Protesting is a fundamental right… it's such a convoluted idea to take permission to protest… you are protesting against a government, will you ask permission from the same government? They are not going to give it," she said.

Ajinkya Shinde, who was handed the responsibility of leading the Cockroach Janta Party's protest following the detentions of its main leaders, has made his first statement — calling for a continued march to Jantar Mantar.

"We appeal to everyone to march towards Jantar Mantar! If Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar," he said in a video post made by the CJP on X.

Indian media outlets, including Scroll and Newslaundry, reported that their journalists had been detained by police while covering the 'Cockroach' party protest. The journalists were later released.

Newslaundry reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports said journalists were physically assaulted.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom and defends journalists' rights worldwide, has called on Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers.

It has also urged police to return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in New Delhi and the police response without interference.

In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), India ranked 157th out of 180 countries, down six places from 2025. Press freedom groups have raised concerns about the use of criminal laws against journalists and the impact of such measures on independent journalism.

Detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother is reported to have died on Saturday.

Indian media reports said that Dipke's paternal grandmother had been suffering from a prolonged illness and had been unwell in recent days. She died in her native village in Maharashtra, reports said.

News agency ANI, citing police sources, reported that the Delhi Police had informed Dipke of his grandmother's death. It was now up to the CJP leader to decide whether to continue his protest while under detention or travel back for the funeral rites.

Dipke was detained aboard his plane after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday morning, ahead of the protest. He was traveling from Mumbai.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has indicated that it will press on with its protest despite its leaders and supporters being detained.

CJP's National Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead the protest at Jantar Mantar until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in detention, the group said in a statement on X.

The CJP also shared a video of Dipke purportedly recorded on Friday night, anticipating a potential detention.

"If you are seeing this video, it means Ashutosh, Saurav and I have been arrested," Dipke says in the video.

"After us, Ajinkya will lead this movement," he says.

In a separate post, the CJP alleged that its three detained leaders had been taken to an undisclosed location, were being denied access to lawyers and had been cut off from "all contact with others."

The formal association of advocates at India's apex court called for urgent intervention by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant after several lawyers were detained by Delhi police.

This comes amid a reported crackdown on protesters attempting to reach the national capital, specifically central Delhi, to protest against India's chief election commissioner over alleged misconduct.

The arrested lawyers include those protesting outside the premises of the Supreme Court of India, as well as lawyers inside their chambers, legal news website, Bar and Bench, reported.

The Supreme Court Bar Association passed a resolution condemning the use of "excessive force against, and detention of, senior and young advocates, particularly women advocates, who were peacefully protesting in the Supreme Court area today."

The advocates' body expressed "grave concern" and requested the CJI to take action to ensure that the "whereabouts and safety of every detained advocate are ascertained."

Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has slammed the measures taken by Indian authorities to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party's protest from going ahead.

He called out a "war-like deployment" of security personnel and said that the suspension of the internet in a key part of Delhi was among the "most regressive" and "repressive" measures.

"A government confident in the fairness of its elections would welcome questions about them, whereas one that turns its capital into a fortress to avoid them only deepens the very suspicions it seeks to suppress. The government should provide answers, not lathis (sticks); expression, not repression," Tharoor wrote on X.

He also called for the release of the protesters who had been detained.

Tharoor said India's Gen Z "deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ," in a play on words.

Leaders of the CJP on Friday likened the clampdown on their planned protest to a "state of emergency."

A state of emergency was declared in India by former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were invoked by the Congress leader for 21 months, during which civil liberties were suspended, much of the opposition was jailed and media was censored.

Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) National Convenor and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal also mounted an emergency-related attack against Modi's government.

"This is worse than the Emergency. It's official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear," he said, referring to the arrests of CJP's three main leaders.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday accused opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal of "attempting to incite tensions" in the country.

"The Govt of India will deal strictly with the attempts you are making to incite tension, and BJP workers, remaining constantly among the people, will effectively thwart your designs," BJP President Nitin Nabin told news agencies on Saturday morning.

"Your repeated electoral defeats in various states and the resulting desperation suggest that, in some way, you do not wish to see this country move forward peacefully. However, I warn you today that the BJP and the patriotic citizens of this country will give you a fitting and stern response," he said.

Nabin suggested that "foreign forces" were behind the opposition leaders and that the protests were an attempt to "destabilize" India. BJP leaders have made similar claims before without offering proof.

"I issue a clear warning to you today: the foreign forces upon which you rely for your politics up for sale—and the alliances with such forces through which you seek to destabilize India—will never allow your nefarious intentions to succeed," he said.

It's past noon here and Indian news channels are playing visuals of protesters trying to reach central Delhi, despite the mass preventive detentions taking place.

Several groups of young people have been seen running through the streets, trying to dodge police personnel and barricades.

News agency ANI reported, citing police sources, that 200 more people were detained in the key Connaught Place area as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site.

Here's the situation right now:

With this, it is unclear at the moment whether the planned protest will be able to take place.

But the CJP isn't the only group protesting against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star, Neha Bora, have been leading protests in the capital all week.

Also on the ground are the Gandhi siblings, lawmakers Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, who are leading the opposition alliance's protests against the poll body in New Delhi.

Rahul Gandhi is the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament and possibly Prime Minister Modi's biggest challenger in the 2029 elections. According to Indian media reports, Gandhi is scheduled to attend a political meeting in the southern city of Chennai today.

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday reiterated his demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down and critized the Modi government.

"Gyanesh Kumar will go. This government will go. Then the repair of democracy will begin," the Congress leader wrote on X as he shared a video of himself addressing INDIA bloc MPs in the Central Hall of Parliament.

Late on Friday, Gandhi and a delegation of opposition lawmakers met President Droupadi Murmu to submit a four-point memorandum.

The memorandum outlined what Gandhi called Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah's "gross subversion of India's electoral system" and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.title: 'Cockroach' group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text:
Hundreds of protesters have reportedly been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over electoral reforms.

The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke, who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches", was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.

Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.

Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.

The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.

It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.

Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.

The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.

The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.

Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."

He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday.

The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.

Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar".

Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line".

The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks.

Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police.

One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained.

"On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said.

She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy".

A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police.

Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night.

Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site.

The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.

Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"

The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.

In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Chelsea ‌attacking midfielder Cole Palmer has ⁠signed a ⁠contract extension that will keep him at Stamford Bridge until 2034, the ⁠Premier League club announced on Saturday.

The 24-year-old England international has become a ⁠key figure since joining Chelsea from Manchester City in 2023, scoring 91 goals in 138 appearances across all competitions.

He was ‌part of the squad that won the Club World Cup in 2025 and the 2024-25 UEFA Conference League.

“Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of ⁠confidence so it was ⁠only right to sign,” Palmer said. “Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions.

“I ⁠feel like we win major trophies here consistently.”

Chelsea have ⁠agreed long-term contracts with several first-team players and emerging talent. Forward Joao Pedro recently signed a deal through 2034, and winger ‌Pedro Neto agreed a six-year contract last month.

Earlier on Friday, Chelsea ⁠manager Xabi ⁠Alonso insisted Palmer ‌remains committed to playing for England after the attacker drew criticism for missing the recent international break due to injury.

Palmer, ⁠left out of England’s World Cup squad this year after a persistent groin injury affected his ⁠form, was called up by Thomas Tuchel for Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia.

However, Palmer was forced to pull out of the squad due ‌to a recurrence of the issue, with Tuchel saying the midfielder “misses too many opportunities” to play in an England shirt.

Asked about Tuchel’s comments, Alonso told reporters: “The most important thing for Cole is to be fully fit, that he ⁠enjoys his game, that he is ⁠feeling OK.

“Whenever he is not, like in the Brentford game, we could see that he was struggling. He’s committed but he needs ⁠to be fully fit to play. We need him – the club and ⁠the national team,” the Spaniard ⁠added.

“Now he’s fine. He’s been feeling better this week. We use the ‌first two weeks for him to recover. It’s a little bit from the pubalgia (groin injury) he had.”

Chelsea, ‌10th ‌in the Premier League standings, host 17th-placed Bournemouth later on Saturday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Why is US turning to Russia for diesel despite sanctions?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Christine Maguire
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
United States President Donald Trump says he has agreed a deal to release stocks of diesel fuel from Russia to try to ease high fuel costs in the US before November’s midterm elections.

However analysts told Al Jazeera that the deal will likely have little effect on easing the global energy crisis while European countries could refuse to buy from Russia altogether.

The agreement comes despite years of sanctions on Russia over its war on Ukraine, the latest of which were announced last month by the US and specifically targeted buyers of Russian oil.

On Friday night, Trump announced on social media that after a “highly successful discussion” with Russian President Vladimir Putin, it had been agreed that Russia would “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global marketplace.

Another 500,000 tonnes would be released in November, and a further 1 million tonnes sometime after that, Trump said. He added that, based on the current condition of its diesel refineries, Russia would then deliver another 3 million tonnes of diesel.

Trump claimed that this move, along with what he described as “total control” by the US of the Strait of Hormuz, would bring down diesel prices in the US and the rest of the world.

“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” he wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Trump later thanked Putin for the deal, telling reporters outside the White House on Friday: “To be honest, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel which is what we want.”

Putin said in a statement on Friday that Russia “confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large”.

Global fuel prices have surged as a result of both the US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine. Tehran has largely closed off the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies had been shipped in peacetime, since the US and Israel first launched strikes on Iran in February.

The recent attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, another key oil export route from the Gulf, as well as attacks by Yemen’s Houthis around the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb strait have compounded supply disruptions.

Meanwhile, oil refineries and energy and port facilities have come under heavy attack in both Russia and Ukraine.

Global fuel inventories have plummeted, and diesel prices reached record highs in both the US and Europe in September.

Last week, the Group of Seven countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of emergency reserves of diesel and crude oil after a US pressure campaign on the European Union in which the Trump administration threatened a US ban on its diesel exports.

Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera last week that the impact of the G7 release “would be short-lived given that this is just a temporary solution to the supply crunch”.

Surging diesel prices in the US saw the national average rise to a record $6.52 a gallon (3.79 litres) in September, more than twice the price from a year earlier. The national average is currently $6.20, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The US is the world’s largest diesel exporter. Its inventories have fallen sharply since the Iran war began and remain below normal levels despite refiners increasing their output.

In September, US lawmakers and Trump floated restricting diesel exports in a bid to lower consumer costs. Trump also called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt attacks on diesel fuel targets, accusing him of causing a shortage after Ukraine ramped up its strikes on Russia’s oil industry this year, aiming to disrupt its energy industry, which it uses to fund its war effort. Trump did not single Russia out for similar treatment over its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

Trump is particularly concerned about bringing down the price of diesel before the US midterm elections. The Iran war is already deeply unpopular and many small-business owners in his MAGA (Make America Great Again) support base rely on diesel being affordable.

Consumers are feeling the effects of rising prices as diesel is used by truckers to transport food and products and by farmers operating machinery. The latest Pew Research Center polling indicated that the economy is the most important issue for 84 percent of registered voters.

States that voted for Trump and typically support candidates from his Republican Party, like Iowa and Kansas, are now seen as battlegrounds in the November 3 elections, putting Trump under pressure to avoid a Republican defeat.

The US banned imports of Russian oil and gas in 2022 under the Biden administration in response to the invasion of Ukraine in February that year.

A sweeping Russian sanctions law passed in Congress last month and signed by Trump also targets countries that buy Russian oil and gas. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 expanded existing sanctions and aimed to pressure Putin by targeting officials, banks and shadow tankers that facilitate the Russian energy trade.

It also gave Trump the power to impose 100 percent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil and natural gas.

After Trump’s announcement on Friday, the US Department of the Treasury said the Office of Foreign Assets Control was “immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market”.

Yes, it is, giving analysts reason to doubt that Russia will be able to release as much diesel as Trump is promising.

Neil Atkinson, former head of the International Energy Agency’s oil industry and markets division, told Al Jazeera that he is sceptical about Russia being able to do this.

“In the very short term, it’s very hard to see how Russia can deliver the volumes that are talked about in the deal other than at the expense of its domestic market,” he said.

Russia was previously the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the US. But Russian diesel and gas exports in the third quarter of this year were at 190,000 barrels per day compared with 690,000 barrels per day in the second quarter and 850,000 barrels per day in the first quarter, explained Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a maritime intelligence analyst with the shipping analytics company Windward, citing data from the commodities tracker Vortexa.

Russia, therefore, banned diesel exports in July in a bid to meet domestic demand and in late September expanded the ban until the end of October.

Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities have also contributed to the fuel crisis in Russia. Putin has admitted that 1 percent of Russia’s gross domestic product has been affected by Ukrainian attacks.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said its air strikes have destroyed more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity. In July, it also struck hundreds of Russian shadow fleet tankers in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, affecting the delivery of gas to Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

Bockmann told Al Jazeera that Russian domestic shortages were “so acute that over the third quarter for the first time we saw Russia import gasoline and diesel and gas oil”.

She added that “as recently as this week”, a ship carrying diesel and gas oil arrived in the port of Vysotsk.

Last week, Russia said it would consider a partial lifting of diesel export restrictions in the case of overproduction. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told the Russian parliament that the domestic market was balanced and “if diesel production exceeds domestic demand, we will consider partially reopening exports.”

Russia typically produces double the diesel needed to meet its domestic needs, according to the International Energy Agency. It has different standards of diesel suitable for different temperatures. Its summer-grade diesel for temperatures over 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) may be released to make way for the winter and Arctic grades needed domestically in the coming months.

Trump’s announcement came as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law,  were meeting with Ukrainian officials and European negotiators in Miami, Florida, to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.

Zelenskyy reacted to the announcement, saying it was “a weak decision by strong partners”.

He said the deal “plays into Russia’s hands,- allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

On Friday, Putin said he was “convinced [the agreement] will have a positive impact on the entire global economy”.

The Russian president also noted that “an agreement was reaffirmed to maintain personal contacts between the presidents of the two countries and to continue cooperation across their respective administrations, security services and agencies.”

Analysts said the agreement will do little to address the global energy crisis, however.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that the Trump-Putin deal to release Russian diesel is a short-term solution and “another classic Trump deal”.

“Announce an ‘agreement’ with an unpleasant dictator with impressive headline numbers and no certainty that any of the objectives will be achieved,” he said. “Even if some of the diesel does make it out of Russia, it is only a short-term solution given the globe’s daily consumption of diesel is around 30 million barrels,” which is roughly the total amount that could be released under the outlines of the deal that Trump announced.

Bockmann also told Al Jazeera that it is unclear how much impact releasing Russian diesel will have on reducing prices and global shortages.

“I’m not sure how effective the issuing of the general licence will be in allowing volumes to be imported at levels that are going to impact the domestic price of diesel in the US,” she said.

Atkinson said the volumes announced by Trump – even if Russia could manage to provide them – “don’t really move the needle very much” on prices because the US uses about 3.7 million barrels of diesel a day.

There are also indications that European countries may not even buy diesel from Russia.

“It’s very hard to see how a European government could, in all morality, buy oil from Russia when the whole point of the last four years is that Europe has been trying to wean itself off Russian oil and gas supplies as soon as practical,” Atkinson said.

A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.

A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.

When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.

The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. It has a more traditional remote shape instead of the curved wand of previous versions. As with all LG TVs, the MRGB95B runs on webOS. It runs quickly, but I find it less intuitive to navigate than Google TV, Apple TV, or Roku. It supports all of the major streaming apps.

Speaking of software, a quick note: LG has recently come under increased scrutiny after a video from Gamers Nexus showed security vulnerabilities and continuous audio recording on its TVs, which LG has denied. When setting up the MRGB95B, it’s only necessary to accept the terms of use and privacy policy if you want to use webOS.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Hayden Field
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.text:
Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.

Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company’s new AI agent Dots — and told the crowd that the company wants to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta’s Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users’ data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw — with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”

In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.

Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”

But though Muse topped the App Store charts and, per Apptopia, gained 600,000 daily active users in the US within weeks, Meta’s promises seem to have fallen short.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/david-aut.title: The economist behind the ‘China shock’ says AI is a paradoxical  ‘skill-disequalizer’ for Gen Z workers
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/david-aut.author: Nick Lichtenberg
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/david-aut.text:
Gen Z was promised that AI would be the great equalizer: a tool that lets a 24-year-old produce work like a veteran’s. David Autor’s latest research suggests it may do the opposite.

In a three-month experiment with patent lawyers, AI improved draft quality across the board. But when researchers took the tool away and tested independent judgment, only the experienced lawyers showed an average improvement. The juniors did not.

“Our results challenge the idea of AI being an automatic skill equalizer,” Autor said in written responses to Fortune. “Our data suggest that it’s a performance equalizer, but a skill-disequalizer, in that only practitioners who already had foundational mental models were able to level up their underlying skill sets.”

The study sorted lawyers by experience, not age. “Senior” meant seven or more years in practice, and the researchers did not study Gen Z as a group. But early-career workers are the people the findings bear on most directly.

Autor is head of MIT’s economics department and a Google Technology and Society Visiting Fellow. He is best known for the “China shock,” developed with economists David Dorn and Gordon Hanson. Their research showed that Chinese import competition did lasting damage to American manufacturing communities, which did not adjust as smoothly as optimistic accounts of globalization predicted. In heavily exposed labor markets, wages and labor-force participation stayed depressed, and unemployment stayed elevated, for at least a decade.

More recently, Autor and Hanson have warned of a “China shock 2.0”: Chinese competition in advanced industries that threatens American technological leadership and the high-wage jobs that come with it. Some prominent economists, including Apollo Global Management’s Torsten Slok, have warned that the “AI shock” could have similarities to the China shock in terms of its impact on the U.S. labor force, with Tufts’ Bhaskar Chakravorti even coining the phrase “the wired belt” as a parallel to the rust belt.

Autor pushed back in an appearance on the Possible podcast hosted by LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, saying AI “will not be, in any sense, a repeat of the China trade shock” because that was experienced by U.S. firms as a “pure negative competitive shock,” but AI will have a “very different texture” in boosting productivity.

The AI debate rests on a version of the assumption the China shock overturned: that once technology takes over routine work, workers will naturally move up to higher-level skills. In his responses to Fortune, Autor said his worry about AI is not mass job loss. “The danger that we may face with AI is not that it eliminates large numbers of jobs in net, but that it eliminates some areas of specialty while creating new ones simultaneously,” he said. “That sounds like a reasonable deal, but the workers losing those old careers are generally not the ones who will be able to take advantage of the new roles that emerge.”

The patent-law experiment looks at a narrower question: whether workers using a powerful new tool are actually building the expertise they need to advance.

Autor and six co-authors published the study as a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, which has not been peer-reviewed. According to the paper, it enrolled 133 lawyers at 11 U.S. intellectual-property law firms that have ongoing patent-drafting relationships with Google. Researchers randomly assigned access to a custom AI patent-drafting assistant, a then-unreleased Google Labs tool. Two-thirds of the lawyers got access. The rest went without until the study ended.

Google’s role went beyond the tool. The paper lists Autor’s six co-authors as Google employees. It also states that Google conducted the study and paid its direct costs, and that MIT’s human-subjects committee determined MIT was not engaged in the research. In an email to Fortune, Google representatives described the paper as independent research Autor did as part of his fellowship.

Lawyers drafted patents from simulated inventor materials after 10 days and again after 90 days. Patent attorneys at an independent law firm graded the work without knowing which lawyers had used AI, according to the paper. They scored enforceability, accuracy, strategic ambiguity, completeness and clarity.

After 90 days, AI access raised drafting scores by 0.38 standard deviations, the paper found. In a Google blog post accompanying the paper, Autor and co-author Tanya Rodchenko described that as an 11-percentile-point gain relative to control scores. The paper says the improvement came from less weak work, not more excellent work.

The harder test came at the end. Lawyers had to mark up a hypothetical patent that, according to the blog post, contained many substantive and stylistic errors. The paper calls this a task patent lawyers “routinely perform unaided.” No AI was allowed.

Senior lawyers who had AI access beat their control-group peers by 0.45 standard deviations, according to the paper. Junior lawyers showed no average gain.

The paper also reports caveats. Only 91 of the 133 lawyers finished the AI-free test. The firms declined a skills test at the outset, so the researchers inferred skill gains from random assignment instead of measuring before and after. The authors also flagged 15 of the 91 markups as possibly AI-assisted despite the ban, and the flags turned up about as often among control lawyers. With those 15 excluded, the paper says, the senior advantage shrinks to 0.39 standard deviations and holds up, though at a looser statistical threshold. The overall effect does not.

The juniors’ scores split, the paper found: significantly more poor scores, fewer mediocre ones, more good ones and no gain at the top. The authors write that AI “served as a springboard for some juniors and a cushion for others.”

The blog post describes how the juniors worked. They tended to go top to bottom, polishing introductory text before reaching the main claims. Some spotted serious flaws but left comments describing them instead of fixing them. Control-group juniors did the same, a pattern the authors call “a baseline junior deficit” that three months of AI access did not fix.

The juniors did notice a difference: they liked the tool. In his responses to Fortune, Autor said AI-assisted junior lawyers reported a surge in task satisfaction, the largest effect in the study. They felt that skipping the “blank page problem” let them step straight into a reviewer role, he said.

“Young professionals need to beware of the illusion of competence,” he said. “The only way you’re really going to know if you’re developing skills is if you do tasks without AI assistance and evaluate your performance.”

According to the blog post, the experienced lawyers described AI in follow-up interviews as a “logic auditor” and not as a finished product. The authors write that it weakened their attachment to existing prose and forced them to spell out the why and how of their structural edits.

“Arguably, you can use AI as a ‘logic auditor’ only if you already know the law well enough to spot when fluent text is legally flawed,” Autor told Fortune. He said he believes offloading baseline drafting freed seniors to focus on strategic scope, “the forest not the trees.”

On the unassisted test, the blog post says, treated seniors skipped low-stakes prose, rebuilt claims from scratch, cut language that could narrow legal protection and tied many of their edits to legal doctrine.

That doesn’t mean juniors should abandon the tool. Autor told Fortune that novices should work like seniors: frame the argument unassisted first, then use AI as a critic to pressure-test the logic. He acknowledged that is a lot to ask. “Most of us don’t have the self-discipline to do things by hand when a readily available, low-effort tool is sitting right there, offering to do it for us,” he said.

For employers, better output creates a temptation to hire fewer juniors. Autor called that short-sighted. “If firms automate away formative practice without replacing it with some kind of guided learning environment, they sever the apprenticeship pipeline that produces tomorrow’s senior partners,” he told Fortune.

He suggested firms decide which tasks can be permanently completed with AI assistance and which judgment tasks require unassisted mastery. They could also pair AI rollouts with regular unassisted skill checks, such as offline redlining exercises, and hold partners accountable for mentoring juniors through the technology’s mistakes. These are ideas, not proven fixes. “It’s early days in this area of research and practice,” Autor said, and few solutions have been robustly proven.

The paper lists other limits. The sample was small and drawn from firms doing ongoing patent work for a single sophisticated client, and three months is brief compared with the years it takes to build patent expertise. The blog post adds that newer models and wider AI familiarity might change the results if the trial were run today. It does not show that AI keeps juniors from becoming experts over a career.

Autor ties the issue back to his China work. Most technological advantage, he told Fortune, comes less from equipment or blueprints than from human know-how, built through slow, laborious mastery. “If we think that AI will relieve us of the burden of mastering expertise, I think we will be sorely disappointed,” he said. “Human intelligence and machine intelligence will be complements for the long term.”
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/david-aut.summary: MIT professor David Autor says his research suggests AI may do the opposite. Autor is head of MIT’s economics department and a Google Technology and Society Visiting Fellow.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/apple-iph.title: A $100 price hike may be all it takes to scare off iPhone buyers in this economy, as Apple reportedly slashes orders
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/apple-iph.author: Fernanda Tronco
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/apple-iph.text:
Apple has told some suppliers to cut production of components for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, Nikkei Asia reported Friday, raising fresh questions about how much more consumers are willing to pay for premium smartphones as memory-chip costs soar.

Citing people familiar with the matter, Nikkei reported that Apple’s October component orders for the two models are at least 15% below what the company originally requested. Demand has been softer than expected from late August into October, according to the report, and Apple has grown more cautious about shipments since early September.

“In October alone, we are seeing orders from Apple reducing by 15% to 20% for both the premium models; we don’t know how things would develop from here,” one executive-level source told the publication.

The cuts will affect some, but not all, suppliers’ October production volumes, depending on their lead times. It remains unclear whether Apple will make further adjustments from November onward.

Apple has not confirmed the reported reductions and did not immediately respond to Fortune‘s request for comment.

The report comes barely a month into John Ternus’s tenure as CEO. Ternus succeeded Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the iPhone 18 Pro lineup is the first flagship launch under his leadership.

Suppliers quoted by Nikkei pointed to price. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max at $1,299, according to Apple’s website—each $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro models they replaced. Apple unveiled the phones on Sept. 9 and began selling them on Sept. 18.

The increases come amid a global memory-chip shortage fueled by the AI boom. Tech giants racing to build AI data centers are gobbling up a growing share of memory supply, leaving less for makers of phones, laptops, and other consumer electronics. Apple had already raised prices on Macs and iPads in June, and on his final earnings call as CEO in July, Cook described memory pricing as a “100-year flood.”

J.P. Morgan Global Research estimates that prices for dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, will have risen more than 400% from the start of 2024 through the end of 2026.

Those costs are rippling through the broader economy. The Consumer Price Index for software and accessories and the Producer Price Index for storage devices have both risen 23% since the end of 2024, while the import price index for computers, peripherals, and parts has climbed 37%, according to J.P. Morgan economist Abiel Reinhart.

The smartphone industry is feeling the squeeze, too. In August, International Data Corporation (IDC) forecast that global smartphone shipments will fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual decline on record. IDC also expects the average selling price of a smartphone to rise 27.6% to $581 as manufacturers pass higher costs on to consumers.

Apple’s launch calendar may also be a factor. This fall, the company introduced only premium models: the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and its first foldable, the $2,000 iPhone Duo. It held back the standard iPhone 18, which is expected to arrive in spring 2027 alongside the lower-cost iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, according to Bloomberg and other reports.

One supply-chain manager told Nikkei that demand isn’t as strong as in previous years, when Apple introduced all of its new models at once. Still, suppliers said the staggered schedule alone doesn’t account for the weaker demand. One source said they expect the iPhone Duo, which goes on sale Oct. 23, could face similar cuts once it ships.

The delay leaves price-sensitive shoppers with fewer new options this fall, although its role in the reported production cuts remains unclear.

Apple isn’t the only phone maker navigating rising component costs. In June, Nikkei Asia reported that three major Chinese smartphone makers, Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo, had cut their 2026 shipment targets by as much as 30%, their second round of reductions this year.

Manufacturers that rely on lower-priced devices have less room to absorb higher costs, while raising prices risks alienating budget-conscious buyers. IDC expects Android phones to absorb nearly all of this year’s shipment decline, as Apple, Samsung, and Huawei lean on their scale to weather the crunch. But Apple’s pricing power doesn’t make it immune to weaker demand.

The reported reductions don’t, on their own, mean Apple is losing market share or facing a broader financial downturn. Supplier orders can shift with demand expectations, inventory levels, and component availability.

Apple’s latest financial results offer some context, though they predate the iPhone 18 launch. For its fiscal third quarter ended June 27, Apple reported revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% from a year earlier and a June-quarter record. iPhone revenue rose nearly 22%, also a June-quarter record. Cook, then CEO, called it Apple’s “strongest June quarter ever,” with double-digit revenue growth across iPhone, Mac, and Services, and in every geographic segment.

But Cook also warned on that call that tight supply would weigh on iPhone, Mac, and iPad sales in the months ahead. That’s a reminder that Apple’s near-term numbers could reflect both what it can build and what shoppers are willing to buy.

The key question is whether the reported cuts reflect a temporary adjustment or a broader pullback in consumers’ willingness to pay for premium smartphones. Apple’s brand and pricing power may help cushion rising costs, but the reported reductions suggest that even the world’s most valuable consumer tech brand faces limits as devices get more expensive.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/a-message.title: A message to my daughters: Don’t get left behind
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/a-message.author: Ali Kashani
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/a-message.text:
By now, you’ve heard from your professors about their AI policies. Perhaps you’ve also heard that AI is destroying the college experience, or that AI might cause the extinction of the human race. Or maybe AI will cure all cancers, end global poverty, and deliver superintelligence for everyone.

It’s no wonder college graduates are booing commencement speakers who talk about AI and doomerism has taken over the news: Everything they have heard about it has convinced them that AI is malignant, or at least dangerously unpredictable.

However, to sit this out and let events take their course could be a lapse of judgment you spend a lifetime regretting. Some of AI’s most outspoken commentators, including Nobel laureates, have also been among the most mistaken.

I run a company that makes autonomous robots, one of the most exciting applications of recent advances in AI, so I have an obvious stake. This also means I see the tradeoffs at street level. Robots are not omniscient beings. They often encounter situations they can’t handle on their own (or they literally run into glass walls).

On the other hand, they enable humans to do more rewarding work. Even though robots may eventually displace some jobs, the track record shows that they also create many new jobs.

Those who embrace new technologies are best placed to shape them and reap their benefits. You are lucky to be living through such a dazzling period of invention. You have the opportunity to help direct these advances toward a better future for yourself and the world at large.

For more than a century, major breakthroughs have sparked widespread fears of job loss, only to be followed by rising productivity and incomes, entirely new categories of work, and sustained growth in GDP.

Yes, technology has brought about many changes in employment. But that’s not so bad. Two hundred years ago, most of us would have been subsistence farmers, like my grandparents. Today, only 2% of Americans work in agriculture. I think most people reading this would not change places with a farmer of 200 years ago.

Farming jobs evaporated as technologies, from fertilizers to combines, enabled greater productivity, automation, and consolidation. If you were a farming family, these were years of great disruption.

On the other hand, hunger declined to historically unprecedented levels, food prices fell, life expectancy rose, and countless new industries emerged to absorb the workers no longer needed in the fields.

Even as 90% of jobs got displaced, the total number of jobs has increased dramatically, from 44 million in the U.S. in 1920 to 167 million in 2024 — faster than the population grew — while unemployment remained remarkably stable through most of the century.

A century ago, only 5% of workers, or about 2 million people, had professional and managerial jobs; today, it’s 35% of the workforce, or almost 60 million people.

Today, 50 million people worldwide earn money as social media influencers, and 6.5 million of them are making $100,000 a year or more. Could my grandparents have imagined working as social media influencers? Could we ourselves have imagined it, 20 years ago?

“This time is different,” the doomers say. But is it?

With AI, we can expect something similar: Some jobs will disappear. Most will be transformed. Many new jobs will emerge, including ones we can’t even imagine today.

Our grandchildren will view the drudgery of many jobs we do today with disbelief, just as we do when we think about lamp lighters, elevator men, or “knocker uppers” (human alarm clocks).

Today, tens of thousands of Americans already work directly in robotics, and many more work in the AI, engineering, manufacturing, maintenance, and operations services that surround the sector. There is always more to do; often more exciting, more rewarding, more fruitful work, thanks to technology.

Consider Charlie Snodgrass, who works as a robotics field technician or “robot wrangler” for our company, Serve Robotics. He saw his work as a delivery driver evaporate, but he was able to find new work and retraining with Serve, supporting our robots in LA. We currently operate more than 2,000 robots across 20 cities. As our robot fleet grows, so does our human workforce, because robots need humans. The jobs we create offer better pay and safer working conditions than the gig work they displace.

So this is the message I want you, and every young person starting out, to hear: Do not let either hype or fear make this choice for you.

Educate yourself on AI. Question it. Learn new ways to use it to solve problems worth solving.

The future of AI is not something that will simply happen to us; it will be built by those who choose to participate. This is your moment to be one of them, and to help make what comes next better than what came before.

https://grist.org/solutions/fifty-billio.title: Fifty billion seedlings: Can Ethiopia replant its ravaged forests?
https://grist.org/solutions/fifty-billio.author: Freddie Clayton, Yale E360
https://grist.org/solutions/fifty-billio.text:
Niku Argane’s farm sits on a steep hillside in central Ethiopia’s semi-mountainous Gurage Zone, where years of flooding have carved deep gullies through the land. Soil that once produced enough barley and potatoes to feed his wife and four children — and left a surplus to sell in the market — has eroded, while drought has made what land remains harder to cultivate.

“We have never stopped farming, but our production declined because of land degradation,” the 32-year-old said from his farm in Ambele Kebele.

Over the last century, Ethiopia nearly eradicated its forests as trees were cleared for farming, grazing, and fuel. The loss of tree cover and tree roots allowed wind and rain to wash away fertile topsoil and contributed to declining crop yields. That vulnerability is now being compounded by climate change. Ethiopia is among the countries most vulnerable to its effects: Heavier downpours are sluicing away depleted soils and triggering landslides, while more intense droughts, combined with the loss of shade that trees once provided, rapidly dry out the land.

Land degradation costs the country an estimated $4.3 billion a year through smaller harvests and lost income to farmers, which also means there is less food to eat. With more than 100 million Ethiopians dependent on agriculture for their livelihoods, the consequences reach far beyond the environment. Climate shocks and crop losses are among the biggest drivers of acute hunger; in 2024, 15.8 million Ethiopians were estimated to need food assistance, roughly 12 percent of the population.

Now the country is trying to reverse this trajectory. Argane planted 80 tree seedlings on his farmland and another 50 in a communal area — a small contribution to a vastly larger effort. In just the last seven years, tens of millions of Ethiopians have planted more than 47 billion seedlings across the country in one of the world’s largest environmental restoration campaigns. Volunteers for the program, which aims to plant 50 billion seedlings by 2030, are planting trees to rebuild native forests and integrating them into farmland. In the process, they are sequestering carbon to help protect future generations from ever more extreme weather.

Such programs often fall short, but Ethiopians are finding hope in the scale of their ambitions. “Reforestation is one of the most difficult things you can imagine,” said Aad Kessler, a researcher at the Netherlands’ Wageningen University. “It almost always fails, but this is so big that even if 30 percent of the trees survive, it’s still huge.”

In the early 20th century, forests covered an estimated 35 to 40 percent of Ethiopia. Its highlands were greener, with forests spanning much of the country’s cool, fertile uplands. But as populations grew and settlements spread, trees were cleared for agriculture, pasture, fuel, and construction. As soils lost their fertility, cultivation moved onto increasingly marginal land, including steep slopes, where tillage and the loss of protective vegetation led to the erosion of fertile topsoil, which washed into rivers and reservoirs. By 1989, forest cover was estimated at less than 3 percent, while Ethiopia’s highlands were losing around 1 billion metric tons of topsoil every year.

After the devastating droughts and famines of the 1970s and 1980s, Ethiopia’s government and international donor organizations began investing heavily in soil and water conservation, excluding livestock from worn-out land, planting trees across the country, and building terraces and check dams — small, low barriers of rocks and logs placed across gullies — to slow the flow of rainwater. By the 2000s, restoration programs were being implemented at increasing scale.
