The government supercharged that effort in 2019 by turning tree-planting into a nationwide campaign with a scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative, which mobilized millions of individuals and groups, including farmers, public servants, schools, and religious organizations, and distributed free seedlings across the country. In 2024, the government established the Green Legacy and Landscape Restoration Special Fund, committing 0.5 percent to 1 percent of the annual federal budget — roughly $73 million to $145 million — to restoring landscapes. It was an unusually large commitment for a low-income country, and the program’s success and ambition, according to development experts, contributed to the selection of Ethiopia as the host of next year’s U.N. climate conference — a prestigious honor that will help the nation showcase its greening efforts.

In August, 26.6 million Ethiopians planted 800 million tree seedlings in a single day, according to government figures, beating the previous year’s tally of 714.7 million. One of the volunteers, Yeshihareg Teferi, traveled at sunrise from her home in Addis Ababa to Tulu Dimtu so she could hunch in the rain to dig holes in the mud. It was Teferi’s fifth year participating in the annual event. Previously she’d planted indigenous species, including African wild olive and African fern pine. This time, she chose juniper. “We have a responsibility to ensure future generations inherit a green and fertile environment, rather than barren land,” she said.

There are already signs the work is having an impact.

The government reports that national forest cover rose from 17.2 percent in 2019 to 23.6 percent in 2023, while studies of restored areas have found substantial reductions in soil erosion. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from more than 350 square miles to around 100 square miles.

Such efforts can also benefit wildlife. In Abijata-Shalla National Park, in the Ethiopian highlands, workers replanted degraded areas and built terraces and contour bunds (small earthen ridges that run across hillsides to slow runoff and allow water to soak into the soil). As trees and native grasses returned, more water infiltrated into the ground, and water levels on lakes in the park began to rise, said Kumera Wakjira, director-general of the Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority. More water spurred the return of fish and fish-eating birds like cormorants and African darters. Grant’s gazelles and wild dogs are also expanding into areas where they were previously scarce, Wakjira said.

But planted trees are not guaranteed to survive. A 2022 study of 176 reforestation projects in Asia found that around half of planted trees did not live five years. And trees alone do not make a forest, said Endalkachew Wolde-Meskel, a soil scientist and senior researcher at the Center for International Forestry Research: That process usually requires the regeneration of grasses and other vegetation, in addition to soil- and water-conservation measures and management by local communities. “The objective is not really ‘plant trees,’” he said. “It is to restore the functioning of the entire landscape.”

Emiru Birhane Hizikias, an Ethiopian restoration ecologist at Norway’s Nord University, said it was a “blessing, politically speaking,” to have the prime minister lead on tree planting but that the scale of the Green Legacy Initiative had outpaced the systems needed to make it work effectively on the ground. Too often, he said, the focus is on getting huge numbers of seedlings into the earth rather than ensuring their survival. You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, he said, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

Abreham Berta Aneseyee, an environmental scientist at Ethiopia’s Wolkite University and an adviser to the Ministry of Agriculture, disputes that characterization, saying the planting campaign is accompanied by practical advice from government experts in forestry and farming. The experts go from farm to farm, advising smallholders on how to plant and care for different types of seedlings, he said, including how deeply to place them in soil and how to conserve soil with structures like bunds. They also advise farmers on managing forests and protecting trees rather than cutting them down.

A 2026 study of more than 44,500 seedlings planted in southern Ethiopia under the Green Legacy Initiative in 2023 found that about 80 percent had survived, with rates significantly higher among older seedlings, wet-season plantings, and seedlings whose planters had received training in best “plantation practices.” In Humbo and Boloso Sore districts in Ethiopia’s southwestern Wolaita Zone, the Green Legacy Initiative has been layered onto longer-running efforts to sustainably manage land, with communities building check dams to stabilize gullies, digging half-moon ditches to trap water and let it soak into the soil, and planting trees alongside grasses and other vegetation.

Ethiopia’s approach has few direct parallels in Africa for its combination of political leadership, funding, public mobilization, and scale, said Kessler of Wageningen University. He compared the effort with China’s restoration of the Loess Plateau, one of the world’s most highly eroded regions. In the 1990s, China launched major restoration efforts on the plateau, including a World Bank-backed watershed rehabilitation project and, starting in 1999, the Grain for Green program, which paid farmers to restrict cultivation and plant trees, shrubs, and grasses. By 2016, more than 11,500 square miles of rain-fed cropland had been converted to more dense forest or grassland, contributing to a 25 percent increase in vegetative cover in a decade.

The comparison has limits, though. China paid farmers to take degraded slopes out of cultivation, while millions of Ethiopian smallholders still depend on the land for food and livelihoods. But Kessler said the two efforts shared a fundamental approach: “Do it massively, and then see where you end up.”

Kessler’s work, which includes a government-backed field project in Ethiopia, takes a more participatory approach, involving farmers and communities in decisions about what to restore and how. “Of course it is better [than top-down action],” he said, “but it takes more time.”

Even as Ethiopia invests in rebuilding forests and soils, climate change is altering the conditions landscapes must withstand. In the arid pastoral regions of Afar and Somali, the Green Legacy Initiative focuses on drought-tolerant species, but it is unclear whether the trees planted today will be able to withstand the conditions they face decades from now.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects more frequent and intense rainfall in East Africa as global temperatures rise. In July 2024, exceptionally heavy rainfall in Ethiopia’s Geze Gofa district, in the southern highlands, triggered two landslides that killed at least 257 people. Recent studies also suggest that climate change is making El Niños more frequent and severe, with consequences for East Africa. This summer, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network linked El Niño to “historically poor” summer rains in parts of Ethiopia, leaving some areas with their driest June and July on record.

For some farmers, the changing climate has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season. Belayneh Mamo, 65, a farmer from Ethiopia’s northern and drought-prone Amhara region, relies on July rainfall for his teff, sorghum, maize, and wheat for bulgur. He also receives government-provided coffee, neem, and gesho seeds, but was unable to plant any crop until August, when the season’s first rains arrived.

“In previous years, September was a period when crops were already developing and food such as bulgur and maize were becoming available for consumption,” he said. “The delays affected the seedlings we plant, our crops, and the availability of animal feed.”

On Argane’s hillside in the Gurage Zone, however, signs of restoration are already visible. Since 2019, he has planted grass, fodder, fenugreek, and fruit trees along the edges of his fields, helping to hold soil in place while providing feed for the four cows, six goats, and three sheep that he keeps for milk and meat. His barley harvest has risen from about 1,800 pounds per acre to roughly 3,200, while the trees and grasses have reduced erosion and slowed the flow of water across his land during heavy rains.

“Restoring degraded land isn’t just about protecting the environment,” Argane said. “It’s also about making life better for my family and community.”

The consumer may be trying to hold onto some of the choices available to him or her amid uncertainty and financial tightening. Nonetheless, it all ultimately boils down to how much money the individual has.

India has multiple income levels and segments and diverse tastes and hence, one product alone cannot be an indicator of the macro status of the economy. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy8.title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy8.text:
A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.

Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.

Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities.

The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.

Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault

Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube.

Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.

They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.

By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.

Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.

Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.

Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.

In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.

"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.

Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.

In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.

Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.

Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".

The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.

The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.

One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.

"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."

Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students.

"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."

Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.

"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.

Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.

"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.

Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.

The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.

NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.

In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.author: Helena Horton and Michael Goodier
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.text:
Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding

When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.

Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England.

But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story.

Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset.

The businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt.

As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs.

And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge.

Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.

The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50.

Bekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room.

He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head.

Hugh Thomas, a food writer from Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.”

Some, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs.

Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomed a cage of endangered red squirrels. But there, too, lay a problem.

The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds.

Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.”

While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds.

People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.

Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”

The worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”. The local authority declared an emergency that evening.

Villagers have also set up a petition against the spraying of pesticides on the Newt’s farmland.

The model and actor Gabriella Wilde, who also lives locally, said: “I was surprised and a little disappointed to learn that they are using such harmful chemicals in their farming operations. That is certainly not the image they project to their guests and local fans. Is it really necessary, especially given how many local farms are making great strides in moving away from old school harmful practices, and towards more nature friendly farming?”

Farmers have been suspicious that new boreholes drilled by the hotel have dried up sections of the River Brue, the stream that Bruton is named after. The cider-maker Oliver Dowding, the nextdoor neighbour of the hotel, has entered negotiations with the Newt via the Environment Agency over his section of the river, which runs through his land. He said, ironically, that the newts which used to live on his land had disappeared.

Though the Newt boasts that its food is “locally produced”, its farms do not have organic certification. John Sykes, who lives nearby, pointed to the severely trimmed hedges around the estate as well as the sterile lawns.

“Look, there are no berries for the birds here. And what bothers me is the land immediately adjacent to our village used to be an organic farm, now they’ve bought it, and it isn’t any more. They are continuing to buy farmland, and I don’t know when they will stop. I don’t want to live somewhere that’s just one man’s estate,” Sykes said.

A spokesperson for the Newt in Somerset said: “Fundamental to our philosophy is a love of gardens, respect for the land and a determination to share that passion with a broad audience. To ensure best practice, we employ experts across our operations, including agronomists, horticulturists, arborists, conservationists, educationalists, beekeepers, nutritionists, livestock and wildlife specialists, alongside our hospitality teams.

“We are equally committed to our local community, maintaining close relationships with local organisations and proudly employing more than 650 people, who are either from or live within the local area.”
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/oc.summary: Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel. He has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues including pesticides on it. Newcastle, Somerset, has been accused of using pesticides on its farmland.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Jane Doe in the Cornell seven case is getting threats | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Every time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without fail

If she really was raped, why didn’t she speak up earlier? Why did she get drunk? Why was she wearing such a short skirt? Why did she walk home by herself?

God, it’s exhausting, isn’t it? Every time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without fail. People accuse the woman of asking for it. They question her motives; they scrutinize her looks; they attack her character. And without fail, she is punished for speaking up.

It happened to Christine Blasey Ford when she accused Brett Kavanaugh, then a supreme court nominee, of assaulting her when they were both teenagers in the 1980s. Ford and her family reportedly had to flee their home because of threats and harassment.

According to her lawyers, her email was hacked and she was impersonated online. Her entire life was turned upside down. Meanwhile, Kavanaugh was praised by Donald Trump and now has a lifetime appointment on the supreme court.

It happened with E Jean Carroll, who accused Trump of sexually assaulting her back in 1996. Trump said Carroll was not his “type” and “totally lying”. His lawyer asked Carroll why she didn’t scream during the alleged attack and why she didn’t go to the police at the time. Carroll’s life was upended and the Trump administration opened a criminal investigation into her.

Now we’re seeing the cycle repeat with the woman known as Jane Doe in the Cornell gang-rape case. According to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, Doe is receiving threats from people who have discovered her identity and is terrified for her safety. Doe was even the victim of a swatting episode this week, a form of harassment where someone places a false call to emergency services with the goal of sending armed officers to the victim’s location. Giuffra told CNN that officers pointed weapons at Doe’s family after a fake tip about someone “killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” Giuffra said.

Nobody ended up dead on that particular occasion, but Doe’s character is systematically being assassinated. “What attracts women to those parties – late at night, like Jane Doe – to walk alone to a fraternity house and take her chances?” Caitlin Flanagan tut-tutted in the Free Press. “What she’s really looking for is a man. And she has no idea how to find a good one.” The underlying message here? She should have known better than to go to a frat party. Silly little girl: she was asking for it.

Rightwing commentator Megyn Kelly, who has been vocal about her experience of sexual harassment at Fox News and should really know better, went even further and attacked Doe’s looks. “No one will even consider the possibility that this woman made a decision to get it on with four men total, not seven, and enjoyed it because, I’m just going to be honest, she’s not the most attractive gal,” Kelly said on a recent episode of her podcast. “She’s extremely beefy in like her arms and her legs. She has a whole video online talking about her cankles. And she possibly enjoyed being admired. This is how women make these mistakes.”

It should go without saying that being raped is not a “mistake”. It should go without saying that a woman should be able to go to a party and have a drink and walk home at night and wear whatever she likes without it being an invitation for men to rape her. And yet it seems that women have to keep saying all this over and over again.

Bernadette Greene Placentia told the Phoenix New Times that she was attacked in August while walking across a parking lot in the middle of the night to fix a damaged campaign sign.

“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson said. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”

“The Pentagon has secretly installed several conservative military veterans with large online followings in government roles … [to] amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s viewpoints,” the Washington Post reported in August. One of these influencers is a retired army colonel called Kurt Schlichter who is, surprise, surprise, a raging misogynist.

This week, Wired highlighted a number of Schlichter’s disturbing writings, including an article for Townhall in which he argues “liberal women” could end western civilization. “These self-righteous crones are a pestilence, a plague upon Western society … whose antics, if unchecked, will inevitably lead to the fall of civilization,” he wrote.

Nearly 22,000 Palestinian children have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza over three years, with more than 71,000 orphaned, according to a report by Gaza’s health ministry summarized by Drop Site news. That number includes 5,444 children under five and 1,125 infants under one year old.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: LeBron James is everything Philadelphia wants. And everything it can’t stand | Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The sports-mad city has embraced its new superstar, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philly was never his first choice

P
hiladelphia has always had an instinctive affinity with athletes who embrace the grind over the glamour. In a place where sports mean a little too much, commitment has traditionally counted for more than celebrity. What it demands above all, sometimes unreasonably, is the sense that they have bought in, that the city and its fortunes matter to them as much as they do to the people who devote their lives to backing its teams.

Few embodied that ethic more completely than Lane Johnson, the Eagles’ revered right tackle and best player for more than a decade, who abruptly announced his retirement Tuesday after 14 seasons, two Super Bowl titles and a career spent neutralizing some of the most freakish physical specimens to walk the earth. Johnson’s quotidian greatness on the offensive line was almost perversely workmanlike. According to Pro Football Focus, he allowed just 10 sacks across close to 7,000 pass-blocking snaps in the last 13 years, going entire seasons without letting his man bring down the quarterback. The Eagles won nearly two-thirds of their games when he played and lost nearly two-thirds when he didn’t.

Surely a first-ballot Hall of Famer when he’s eligible in 2031, he earned a place in the first rank of Philadelphia sporting legends alongside Mike Schmidt, Julius Erving and Bobby Clarke, despite playing a position where success is largely measured by how little anyone notices you. But perhaps the most revealing thing Johnson did was decide when to stop. At 36, he walked away from millions in future earnings to prioritize his mental wellbeing and focus on his parents’ health. For a man who made his living holding the line, there was something fitting about knowing when to let go.

Johnson’s departure comes at a particularly anxious moment on the local sports scene. The ageing Phillies’ desultory wildcard exit against the Atlanta Braves last week marked a fifth consecutive playoff appearance with diminishing returns. The Flyers have opened their season with five straight losses, splashing cold water on the mounting optimism that had surrounded them. The Union have US soccer’s most exciting prospect in generational talent Cavan Sullivan, but they remain a decidedly niche concern in a town dominated by its four traditional major-league teams. And the Eagles, almost comically beset by injury and suddenly without one of their franchise cornerstones as they travel to London this week, appear consigned to a rebuild. Across the city, the sensation is less of a championship window closing than of several slamming shut at once.

All of which has left the new-look 76ers, who debuted their tricked-out starting five on Thursday night in Brooklyn, carrying an almost inordinate share of the city’s sporting hopes. The timing makes for an uncomfortable juxtaposition. Philadelphia is losing an athlete who spent 14 years making the city his own, just as it welcomes the greatest basketball player to ever live, who has given precious little indication that he intends to do the same.

The Philly sporting identity has always been shaped by its uneasy relationship with New York, the northern neighbor that eclipsed it as America’s commercial and cultural capital a long time ago and has spent the intervening centuries reminding it of that fact. That history has bred a peculiar combination of civic pride and insecurity, a conviction that Philadelphia is entitled to better and a gnawing suspicion that deep down it doesn’t even deserve it. The 76ers, third on the NBA’s all-time wins list, haven’t won a championship since 1983, spending more than four decades watching Boston and Los Angeles pile up the sport’s prizes. The city’s athletes are expected to understand that burden, or at least pretend to share it.

James admitted at last month’s media day that Philadelphia had not been his preferred landing spot in free agency. The 41-year-old had dreamed of finishing his career at Madison Square Garden, only to abandon the idea after the Knicks ended their 53-year title drought in June, wary of being perceived as a ring-chaser. For a city that has spent generations bristling at New York’s perceived superiority, the confession carried a particular sting. Nearly a century after WC Fields quipped that he would rather see Paris before he died but Philadelphia would do, the NBA’s most famous star appeared to have reached the same conclusion. Even now, James seems reluctant to commit to the place geographically. Asked where he would live, he answered: “Both. Multiple residences.” That apparently means commuting from New York in a Fanatics-branded helicopter that gets roughly 1.6 miles to the gallon.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The Leonardo AW139, supplied through his sponsorship arrangement with Michael Rubin’s sports merchandising empire, has become James’s preferred mode of transport between the two cities. Publicly available flight-tracking data showed 18 trips between Manhattan and Northeast Philadelphia Airport in the first days of October alone. Never mind that Amtrak’s Acela service connects the cities in about 90 minutes, with comfortable seats, wifi and enough legroom even for a 6ft 9in basketball player.

The environmental optics have raised eyebrows. The AW139, according to a Defector report, is unusually emissions-intensive, even by the standards of private helicopters. But in Philadelphia, the symbolism is as offensive as the carbon footprint. It’s hard to imagine a more exquisitely calibrated insult to the city’s sporting psyche. Philly fans have never cared much where their sporting heroes come from. What matters is whether, somewhere along the way, they come to regard the city as their own. Johnson gave the city 14 years of his body, his loyalty and his labor. James appears determined to give it his working hours.

Which is fine. James isn’t the first gun-for-hire to find himself in an arranged marriage in the winter of his career. Yet the helicopter is merely the latest indignity in James’s increasingly depressing transformation from athlete-activist into walking corporate billboard. Not so long ago, James was helping lead More Than a Vote, the organization he co-founded in 2020 to combat voter suppression, register voters and mobilize Black communities. He leveraged his extraordinary celebrity to encourage civic participation and tell people that their voices mattered. It was a meaningful demonstration of what an athlete with virtually unlimited cultural influence could accomplish. Six years later, he’s hawking online gambling and brown liquor.

His reported $15m-a-year partnership with Polymarket, a prediction-market platform encouraging ordinary marks to wager on everything from basketball to elections to war, is all the more dispiriting. The mainstreaming of prediction markets, and the relentless creep of gambling into news, politics and virtually every corner of society, are one of the bleaker developments in American public life. The same cultural capital that once encouraged people to participate in democracy is now being deployed to encourage them to speculate on it with their disposable income, all so a handful of techno-fascist investors can become obscenely rich. His involvement with Fanatics, with its ever-expanding connections to the gambling industry, makes the whole spectacle even harder to reconcile with his cultivated image as a socially conscious athlete. It’s the kind of corporate exploitation couched in cultural legitimization and the aesthetics of cool that feels ripe for a Spike Lee satire … were the Bamboozled director not appearing in glossy Polymarket ads himself.

Nobody begrudges James the fortune his extraordinary talent and longevity has earned him. Nor should anyone expect professional athletes in his echelon to move like ascetics. His philanthropic work, most notably the I Promise School in Akron, remains meaningful regardless of what and who he chooses to align himself with. But there’s something grotesque about the NBA’s first active billionaire collecting millions more to promote an industry fueling an emerging public-health crisis, while burning extraordinary quantities of fuel to avoid the mild inconvenience of the train.

Johnson spent 14 years protecting Philadelphia’s quarterbacks before deciding there were things more important than football and money. James has accumulated enough wealth to say no to almost anything, yet he keeps finding reasons to say yes. Perhaps that’s the most lamentable part of the spectacle: a man who once seemed determined to change the world now seems more concerned with what it will pay him to fly over it.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.summary: Lane Johnson, the Eagles’ revered right tackle and best player for more than a decade, announced his retirement Tuesday. Johnson’s departure comes at a particularly anxious moment on the local sports scene. The Eagles have opened their season with a new season in Philadelphia.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.title: ‘Anachronism’: Rubio’s civilisational rhetoric prompts pushback from Iran
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.author: Maziar Motamedi
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.text:
Tehran, Iran – A speech by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoking memories of ancient Persia has been met with coldness or disdain across the Iranian political spectrum amid Washington’s ongoing war on Iran.

With the Acropolis in Athens as a backdrop, Rubio presented the United States, founded in the 18th century, as the inheritor of ancient Western civilisation running from Greece to Rome.

During the speech, he argued that modern-day Western countries have lost their confidence, weakened their industries and militaries, and need renewed ambition and power in the future.

Referencing the ancient Greco-Persian Wars, he used the Persian destruction of Athens in 480 BC under King Xerxes I as an example of Western civilisation surviving an external enemy.

“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines and razed the Acropolis to the ground,” Rubio said. He subsequently hailed the return of the Athenians and the construction of the Parthenon under Pericles.

The top US diplomat also directed his rhetoric against Iran’s current leaders, who have been in power since a 1979 Islamic revolution, calling them “fanatics” who run a “death cult” that wields martyrdom as a tool to achieve their political objectives.

“The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity,” Rubio claimed. He boasted that the choice of President Donald Trump’s administration was the “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.

The US and Iran have been at war since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. While fighting between the two sides has subsided, the US has continued a naval blockade on Iran while shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.

Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, and parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf both responded by invoking the Roman Emperor Valerian, who was captured alive by Persian King Shapur I’s forces in battle in 260 AD.

“Anyone who brings history into this must be prepared for its repetition,” Rezaei said.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused Rubio of flattening Greek, Roman, Christian and modern history.

It also accused the secretary of state of incorporating an “America First” narrative to legitimise a military escalation against Iran after a relative decrease in fighting since June when a now-defunct memorandum of understanding was agreed.

“It appears that the US has concluded it is better to justify its policy of coercion and force to the world under the beautiful neon lights of ‘philosophy of history’, instead of naked bullying that uses the language of cowboys,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said in a statement. He added that Rubio was resorting to “anachronism”, rehashing long buried historical events for modern-day legitimacy.

After the 2020 assassination of Qassem Soleimani, a commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Trump threatened to hit 52 Iranian sites “very hard”, including places “important to Iran & the Iranian culture”.

Since February, the US has been criticised for damaging Iranian historical and cultural sites during its bombing of Iran.

Culture Minister Reza Salehi-Amiri urged Western politicians to speak about Iran with a “language of respect” since “it is not an enemy created in a political speech but a living civilisation, a great nation and a lasting reality in world history” that dates back millennia.

Iranian historian Touraj Daryaei told local media on Friday that while Rubio’s account of the sack of Athens was true, he omitted an important fact cited by Greek historian Herodotus and others – a major motivation for the Persian attack was retaliation.

In 498 BC, Athens’ forces burned Sardis, a provincial Persian capital in western Anatolia. For Iranians who feel they were subject to an unprovoked attack by the US and Israel, this event could have modern-day relevance.

Shima, a 26-year-old resident of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that she did not appreciate Rubio’s attempt to use conflicts 2,500 years ago to muster support for the ongoing war with Iran.

“They want to continue the war, and they will say whatever they think will work in the moment,” she said.

During his January 2025 Senate confirmation hearing, Rubio had referred to Iranians as “the people of an ancient civilisation and culture with tremendous pride and advances who take great pride in their Persian heritage and identity”.

“I don’t know of any nation on Earth in which there’s a bigger difference between the people and those who govern them,” he said at the time. “In no way are the clerics who run the country representative of the people and its history and contributions it’s made to humanity.”

But the US war on Iran, its naval blockade of southern Iranian ports and isolating sanctions have not had the worst impact on Iran’s government and leaders but on Iranians themselves and have failed to change the behaviour of the government.

Trump’s comments on the potential “death of a civilisation” in Iran in case of a military escalation have instilled more pessimism among Iranians about the goals of the US war, which was initially cited as an attempt to free the people from their government.

Most Iranians reacted negatively to Rubio’s latest speech although some members of the diaspora or others opposed to the Islamic Republic argued that the US secretary of state is against Iranian authorities, not an entire ancient civilisation.

Iranian state media were quick to slam Rubio for his remarks with the hardline Vatan-e Emrouz newspaper on Saturday publishing a front page image of Rubio in ancient Roman military attire and holding a shield and sword.

“Ancient war” read the headline. The newspaper claimed that Rubio was trying to “create historical-ideological backing for the US war against Iran”.

Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, DC, told Al Jazeera he believes Rubio’s aim was to define a common enemy for the US and Europe to rebuild their relations around.

“He decided that Iran, rather than Islam, which was previously viewed as the civilisational enemy, should play that role to bind the West together,” he said. “It also reflects US frustration that Europe has not played a major role in the war and seeks to paper over deep divisions between the US and Europe on Russia and Ukraine.”

Rubio delivered his speech as Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to sell diesel fuel to the US and global markets despite sanctions on Russia. The US president said the agreement would lower diesel prices, which have risen to record levels due to the Iran war. Nasr said Trump’s announcement and Rubio’s speech together could be a message by the administration that Iran and not Russia is the enemy the West should be focused on.

“I think whether this rhetoric would alienate Iranians was no more a concern than President [George W] Bush’s Islamophobia was a concern alienating Muslims,” Nasr told Al Jazeera. “However, it makes clear that Washington sees no difference between Iranians and Iran as a civilisation and the Islamic Republic.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.summary: Marco Rubio used ancient Persian destruction of Athens as example of Western civilisation surviving an external enemy. He also called Iran's current leaders ‘fanatics’ who run a ‘death cult’ that wields martyrdom as a tool to achieve their political objectives.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Verstappen wins chaotic Singapore GP F1 sprint after Russell crashes
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen won a wet and wild Singapore Grand Prix sprint race on Saturday after George Russell crashed his Mercedes while leading at the end of the opening lap.

Four-time Formula One champion Verstappen held off Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton to win by 2.50 seconds, with Charles Leclerc third as the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri touched and spun on the final lap while in fourth and fifth.

A heavy shower 10 minutes before the scheduled start meant a delay of 30 minutes.

All cars began on intermediate tyres, with some sectors of the Marina Bay Street Circuit much drier than others as the field embarked on two formation laps behind the safety car.

The eventual standing start saw Russell start on the front row alongside pole-sitter Verstappen and it was the Englishman who got away better.

His lead was short-lived as he lost control after touching a treacherous white line on the final bend of the opening lap. He slid sideways into the pit lane wall, bringing out a safety car.

It was another setback in a season of bad luck for Russell, who will start from the back of the grid in Sunday’s Grand Prix because of engine penalties.

“It was a miscalculation,” Russell told Sky Sports. “Came through the corner, had more battery deployment than I thought, pushed me a little bit wider than I hoped and went on to the white line.

“Silly mistake. Big consequences.”

It left Hamilton, who had a brilliant start from sixth on the grid, in second place, having leapfrogged Ferrari teammate Leclerc and the two McLarens.

The big beneficiary of Norris and Piastri’s “papaya spat” on the last lap was championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who inherited fourth place in his Mercedes having started seventh on the grid.

Fifth was RB’s Liam Lawson, sixth was the Haas of Oliver Bearman, seventh was Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg and Norris got going again to limp home in eighth and round out the points scorers.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.summary: Red Bull's Max Verstappen wins Singapore Grand Prix after George Russell crashes his Mercedes. Russell crashed his Mercedes while leading at the end of the opening lap of the race. The Englishman will start from the back of the grid in Sunday's Grand Prix.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders detained; New Delhi in lockdown
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Police in India’s capital New Delhi have detained more than 1,000 protesters, opposition politicians, journalists, student union leaders, lawyers and the founders of the “Cockroach” youth movement in an effort to quash their demonstration demanding the resignation of the election chief.

The satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other youth groups had announced a protest in the subcontinent’s capital for Saturday, aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR).

The protesters accuse the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of using the SIR to sway election results, ‌in collusion with its appointees in the election commission, including Kumar.

Meanwhile, opposition parties say the voter deletions also affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world’s largest democracy.

The CJP had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central Delhi.

But on Saturday, the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.

The Indian capital was also in lockdown with thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed across the city, trains to New Delhi cancelled, mobile internet services suspended and metro stations and markets shuttered, in an effort to stop the protests.

BJP spokesman Sambit Patra has dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements”.

“Their flop show has been completely demolished,” Patra said. “What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance,” he told reporters.

Police detained the founder of ⁠the CJP Abhijeet Dipke, as well as his associates Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, in an aeroplane upon arrival at New Delhi from Mumbai.

Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.”

In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke was seen addressing the other passengers on the flight.

“It was nice to know you all. We can see where the nation is heading,” he said. “This is dictatorship where Delhi police has entered in the flight and trying to arrest us.”

Delhi police also detained other CJP members, YouTuber and Modi critic Dhruv Rathee, Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist), Dipankar Bhattacharya, the general secretary of the party,  Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court, politicians Yogendra Yadav and Mamata Banerjee, among others.

Despite the detentions of the founders of the youth movement, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”.

But journalists trying to cover these protests and people attempting to protest anywhere in the capital were also detained and whisked away in police buses.

Shranaya, a state committee member of the left-wing Students’ Federation of India (SFI), who goes by her first name, told Al Jazeera that their office in New Delhi had been under surveillance for hours, but members inside had managed to escape and protest.

“This is dictatorship live and in front of us, just to protect a bureaucrat who steals elections for the BJP on Modi’s behest. They are murdering democracy in the daylight in the Indian capital,” she said.

“This government is unaware of the power of the people, and that is our upper hand. We do not have weapons, but we have zeal. We will be again on the streets, and we will keep returning,” she added. “We are students. We are unemployed. We are ‘cockroaches’ – and we will return.”

She then climbed a barricade but was dragged away by police and taken away in a bus.

The opposition Congress party’s president, Mallikarjun Kharge slammed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government after the detentions.

“Modi government has turned the ‘Mother of Democracy’ into a ‘Muzzled Democracy’!” he posted on X. “Detentions, arrests, jails, lathis [batons] and pellets cannot deter the people of India. Since the days of our freedom struggle, the youth have been at the forefront of shaping the nation’s destiny,” he added.

Global human rights group Amnesty International warned that the detentions signal the Indian government’s desperate attempts to “supress critical voices”.

“The authorities must immediately and unconditionally release all those who have been detained solely for exercising their right to Freedom of Expression and Right to peaceful assembly,” Aakar Patel, chair of board of Amnesty International India, told Al Jazeera.

The Committee to Protect Journalists urged Indian police to “respect journalists”.

“We call on the Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in Delhi and the police response without interference,” Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia Pacific programme coordinator, told Al Jazeera.

The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls in advance of recent state polls.

The unrest is also coming before a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.

Sanjay Kapoor, editor of Hard News Magazine and a political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is “very strange” to see Modi’s government “so panic-driven and fearful of what the protesters might do”.

“The truth is that the BJP and the centre have been very, very scared of how it will all play out,” he said.

Kapoor noted that most of the people coming to the protests do not want Modi’s BJP to continue to govern.

“Modi’s government has begun to lose a lot of credibility at the moment,” he said. “BJP is afraid that the ground has shifted dramatically against them and they would find it very difficult to come back to power,” he added.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: More than 1,000 protesters detained in New Delhi, India's capital, police say. Protesters accuse governing Bharatiya Janata Party of using the SIR to sway election results. They say voter deletions also affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Child among seven killed by Israel in Gaza on ‘ceasefire’ anniversary
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
At least seven people, including an eight-year-old girl, have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to medical sources, a year after the United States-backed “ceasefire” came into effect – “in name only”.

Shahd Abdul-Razzaq al-Najjar, 8, was killed on Saturday by an Israeli quadcopter drone in the al-Jawazat area of western Gaza City, according to a source in ambulance and emergencies speaking to Al Jazeera.

In the same part of Gaza City, four people were killed and several injured in a separate Israeli bomb attack near Haider Abdel Shafi roundabout, the city’s al-Shifa Hospital said.

One more Palestinian was killed in an Israeli drone attack in the Tuffah neighbourhood of northeastern Gaza City, the hospital said.

In the southern city of Khan Younis, a woman succumbed to injuries sustained in an Israeli attack earlier on Saturday.

Also on Saturday, the enclave’s Ministry of Health said at least 1,481 Palestinians have been killed and 5,254 injured since the so-called ceasefire came into effect on October 10 last year.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,370 people and injured 175, 371 since October 7, 2023, the ministry added.

In the past 24 hours, Israeli attacks killed at least nine people and injured 65, it said, adding that one more person succumbed to injuries sustained in previous Israeli aggression.

Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum reported from Gaza on Saturday that the “ceasefire” has only heightened uncertainty in the enclave.

“The rhythm of the genocide has not changed,” he said. “The danger has not gone away completely, and that’s why people believe that it has more consequences, far beyond the immediate loss of life.”

On Friday, more than 100 humanitarian, human rights and civil society organisations said in a joint statement that the ceasefire in Gaza exists only in name.

“The ceasefire exists in name only, with Israeli forces continuing to kill and injure Palestinians daily, and restrictions on aid, equipment and rebuilding materials preventing families from recovering,” the statement said.

In the occupied West Bank, at least 12 Israeli settler pogroms were recorded on Saturday morning, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.

Israeli settlers assaulted Palestinian farmers through beatings, spraying them with pepper spray, stealing their property and attacking homes, the Wafa news agency reported. They also detained several Palestinians during the attacks with the help of the Israeli military forces.

In the Ramallah and el-Bireh Governorate, settlers, along with the army, forced farmers to leave their lands and threatened them against returning. Two farmers were beaten and pepper-sprayed, as settlers stole a vehicle and their phones.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: At least seven people have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza, medical sources say. The latest attack comes a year after the U.S. backed “ceasefire’s’ in Gaza came into effect.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/supreme-.title: How Supreme Court justices are leaning in major 401(k) case over private funds and underperformance
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/supreme-.author: Cheryl Winokur Munk
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/supreme-.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard a case this week in which a former Intel employee alleged company retirement-plan fiduciaries breached their duty by investing in hedge funds and private equity, pointing in part to the funds’ underperformance.

Lower courts already rejected the claims, ruling underperformance alone is not enough without showing a “meaningful benchmark” for courts to assess performance.

Several justices appeared receptive to Intel’s position during oral arguments. A ruling for Intel could make some retirement plan sponsors more comfortable adding alternative investments to 401(k) plans, though the largest employers may still move slowly.

The Supreme Court heard a major case this week concerning an Intel retirement plan which could result in a decision that influences employers’ appetite for private investments in 401(k)s.

Many plan sponsors are in limbo, awaiting the Supreme Court decision and finalized Labor Department rules covering alternative investments before changing their 401(k) menu, even as the asset management industry is gearing up with new products.

“I think companies want to know what’s going to happen with the proposal and what’s going to happen with the Supreme Court case before they go rushing in to change their investment strategies,” said Elizabeth Hopkins, principal at Hopkins ERISA Law and a former senior trial attorney with the Labor Department, who filed an amicus brief in the Supreme Court case on behalf of former high-ranking DOL officials.

Here’s what employers and employees need to know about forces influencing the market for private investments in 401(k) plans.

Employers have been whipsawed for the past several years by changing government policies on alternative investments in 401(k) plans and a high-profile lawsuit filed in 2019 by a former Intel
 employee. That case, Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee, which the Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Tuesday, Oct. 6, concerns private investments in a defined contribution plan like a 401(k) and the circumstances under which these investments are appropriate.

The case is not challenging whether alternative assets like hedge funds and private equity can be used in a 401(k) plan alongside stocks and bonds. Rather, the question before the court is whether a retirement plan underperformance claim requires alleging a “meaningful benchmark.” The heart of the dispute is how to handle claims by employees that plan sponsors have invested their retirement funds imprudently.

Employees contend that the relatively low returns on Intel’s plans reflect a breach of fiduciary duty. The lower courts disagreed. Their reasoning: claims of underperformance alone are not enough without showing a “meaningful benchmark” for courts to assess performance.

During the arguments, Supreme Court justices seemed skeptical that plan sponsors’ investment choices should provide easy fodder for litigious individuals. Justices frequently turned to a fruit metaphor, with Justice Clarence Thomas summing up his take on the Ninth Circuit’s decision as: “you can’t compare apples and oranges…if you have a fund…that is designed to produce high returns but riskier returns…you can’t compare that to a fund that is to protect against losses.”

Several other justices, including from among the liberal side of the court, seemed to agree with his line of reasoning, Ronald Mann, co-director of the Charles Evans Gerber Transactional Studies Center at Columbia Law School, noted in an analysis on SCOTUSblog. Justice Elena Kagan, for instance, commented, “the thing that you need … is another apple.”

Justice Samuel Alito challenged the employees’ attorney, Matthew Wessler, to clarify whether his position was that one could “state a claim by comparing apples and oranges but supplement that with the suggestion that the strategy was flawed.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett opted for the same metaphor as well.

Meanwhile, Justice Neil Gorsuch asked Wessler to “agree with the general principle that when we’re limited to underperformance claims … a meaningful benchmark of some kind is required, apples, not oranges.”

Wessler did not respond to a request for comment for this article.

The underlying problem for the court seemed to be the lack of a benchmark. Notably, justices explicitly asked Aimee Brown, assistant to the Solicitor General, how much guidance the court should provide in this case.

Brown’s view was that the court should suggest “some parameters” for what a “meaningful benchmark” needs to be. “Prudence is about process and not about performance,” she told the justices.

Attorneys who attended the arguments in person, listened to the recording or read the transcript took the justices’ questions as a sign they were leaning toward siding with Intel and affirming the 9th Circuit. “When the justices are asking opposing counsel to pick and choose among the approaches to use in an opinion, it usually is a safe bet that they are not going to vote for you,” Mann wrote.

On rebuttal, Wessler noted that all of the allegations need to be considered together and holistically. “I think that matters in a case like this, where you have an allegation about an imprudent either strategy or implementation of that strategy that then turns out badly,” he told the court.

Employers are awaiting the court’s ruling, in some cases hoping for guidance that helps temper future litigation. “Private funds can be an effective and entirely appropriate component of 401(k) plan investment options,” Eugene Scalia, partner at Gibson Dunn & Crutcher, said in an email. “A ruling for Intel by the court would affirm that and lend further support to the Labor Department rulemaking,” said the former U.S. Secretary of Labor who submitted an amicus brief on behalf of The American Investment Council and The Managed Funds Association.

“A positive outcome in this case will go a long way toward getting plan sponsors that have wanted to do this for years, but held off, for fear of being sued, feel more confident that they can do this with less fear of being sued,” said Joshua Lichtenstein, partner at Ropes & Gray who heads the firm’s ERISA fiduciary practice and was a co-author of an amicus brief to the court on the Investment Company Institute’s behalf.

The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, or ERISA, doesn’t discuss alternative investments in 401(k)s, but President Trump pushed for their inclusion during his previous administration. Under his watch, the Labor Department issued an Information Letter in June 2020 designed to “help Americans saving for retirement gain access to alternative investments that often provide strong returns,” then-Secretary of Labor Scalia said in a statement.

In December 2021, however, the DOL under the Biden administration issued a supplemental statement, contending that most plan fiduciaries were not suited to evaluate alternative investments, given their complexity and high risk. That had a chilling effect on the market.

The tide shifted, once again, in Trump’s second term. In August 2025, he issued a presidential executive order to democratize access to alternative assets for 401(k) investors. Then, in October 2025, Congressman Troy Downing introduced the Retirement Investment Choice Act to codify the executive order into law. And in March, the Labor Department issued a proposed rule that would ease legal and regulatory barriers against adding alternative investments to retirement plans. Comments were due by June 1.

“The proposal is the clearest guidance the department has ever given on the types of information and process that a plan sponsor should go through when making investment decisions,” Lichtenstein said.

Most large companies do not offer private investments within their 401(k) plans, even though there’s nothing in ERISA saying they can’t, said Kent Mason, partner at Davis & Harman, who filed an amicus brief in the Intel case on behalf of the American Benefits Council and represents major employers, large plans and national vendors of retirement plan services.

The latest developments in court and in the regulatory landscape might not change this. “The largest companies are going to be the slowest to do this,” Mason said, adding that he expects smaller and mid-size companies to start adding private investments to their 401(k) line-up before large companies, who are subject to more litigation risk.

He expects this even if the Supreme Court sides with Intel and Labor Department rules are adopted. “While the rules provide an excellent and helpful framework, the six-factor analysis is still subjective,” he said, referring to recently proposed Labor Department guidance on selecting investment options in plans. “Plaintiffs’ attorneys are still likely to file suit alleging large companies failed to meet their safe-harbor fiduciary obligations.”

Alternative investments are already common in defined benefit plans, even as 401(k)s have been slower to adopt them. But that’s expected to change over time, as investors push for it, more products become available and more companies become comfortable — even if it’s slow out of the gate.

“There’s a clear business case for making sure plans provide employees with a broad base of investment options,” said Harvey Bines, partner at law firm Sullivan & Worcester, whose focus includes investment management law. However, employers will have to take extra care to cover all the legal and fiduciary bases. “The more novel and riskier the options you offer, the more care and oversight you need to incorporate to make and continue the offering,” Bines said.

Momentum is rising. During Trump’s second term, asset managers and plan providers continue to forge partnerships to offer alternative investments within 401(k)s, with announcements from Empower in May 2025 and Voya Financial in July. OneDigital and Principal Financial Group announced similar partnerships in January and August of this year. In September, Constitution Capital Partners announced the Constitution Capital Horizon CIT, a collective investment trust, that launched with more than $50 million in initial assets across 18 retirement plans and near-term commitments bringing total plan assets to more than $1 billion.

“We’re seeing plan sponsors, together with their advisors and consultants, take a closer look at private market investments and begin incorporating them in thoughtful ways,” Amy Vaillancourt, president of retirement at Voya Financial, said in an email. She noted that interest isn’t just coming from employers. Voya’s research found nearly two-thirds of participants want access to private market investments.

“Sponsors want to understand where private markets may benefit their participants’ long-term retirement outcomes,” Brett Fisher, head of investment product strategy at Principal Financial Group, said in an email. At the same time, they “want to make those decisions in a way that aligns with their fiduciary obligations.”

https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/10/.title: I work hard to stay close to my friends. A researcher says it’s good for my well-being—and these 3 habits can help
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/10/.author: Renée Onque
https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2026/10/10/.text:
Not to brag, but without realizing it, I’ve become a model friend — someone my loved ones admire for how well I maintain my relationships. At least, so they tell me.

Last month, my closest friend asked me for pointers on how to stay connected to her community while balancing work, well-being and everything else in her life. It’s no easy feat. Loneliness levels in the U.S. are high, and instead of turning to each other, many people reach for their tech devices, found an American Psychiatric Association poll published on May 12. Eight percent of Americans report having zero close friends, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey of about 5,000 U.S. adults.

Some businesses now offer to facilitate the friendship process, offering summer camps for adults or guidance from friendship coaches that can sometimes cost thousands of dollars. And when you do form friendships, you could grow apart for a number of reasons, says Jessica D. Ayers, an assistant professor of psychological science at Boise State University: classic ones like moving to a different state for a new job or being in different stages of life, or newer ones like trying to keep up with each other on social media and forgetting to keep in touch outside of your smartphones.

Especially if your friends have busy lives or don’t often reach out to make plans, putting in the work to stay in touch may seem like a fundamentally selfless gesture. In fact, making the effort to maintain friendships can benefit you too, says Ayers, who researches the science of friendship and how to maintain connections. Staying in touch with friends can improve well-being, lower levels of depression and loneliness, decrease anxiety, and even “increase our chances of survival after things like major surgery,” she says.

The benefit is mutual for both parties, Ayers says, especially in “long-lasting and sustained relationships.” And a high degree of social fitness contributes to a longer, healthier and more fulfilled life, according to an ongoing 88-year-old Harvard University happiness study. Put simply, your friendships can help you succeed.

Staying in touch can require a lot of hard work, at least on paper. I didn’t fully realize this until I considered just how many strategies I have for keeping in contact with my community. I set up multiple one-on-one hangouts per month with a rotating cast of friends, clear time in my calendar to be present for my loved ones’ birthday celebrations and stay up-to-date in five-plus group chats with friends and family.

In a sense, I was trained to do this: I have five siblings, and growing up in our household, showing up for each other was a non-negotiable. But there’s more to it. Whenever a friend crosses my mind, I reach out to them, just to see how they’re doing or ask when we can hang out in the near future. I host small get-togethers — one of my favorites was an October 2025 party themed around the movie “Coraline.” I travel to visit my friends who live in different states at least once a year, or plan vacations together with them.

Ayers says she approves of my practices. Even the simple act of sending a friend a quick note because you briefly thought about them is “a brilliant practice,” she says, adding: “It is the best thing you can do.”

To keep your friendships healthy and strong, Ayers recommends three things:

Ayers and her best friend live in different states — Idaho and California, respectively — she says. They send each other voice memos throughout the week, ranging from quick check-ins to 15-minute breakdowns of an important update, she says.

But especially with friends who live nearby, you should take your conversations offline whenever you can, Ayers says. Even in group chats, she says, you can write something like: ”‘Hey, I’m going to come see you in person ... We [should] go to this coffee shop and just hang out,’ instead of relying solely on the technology aspect to mediate.”

You can even invite your friends into your regular schedule, without having to find extra time in your calendar. Ask a friend to tag along when you’re running errands, or doing some other low-pressure activity, suggests Ayers. She invites her friends to her children’s sporting events, she says: “We can catch up in between our kids going to bat, or our kids’ time on the soccer field, and it’s a lot less pressure because there’s no expectations there.”

Being a social person has trade-offs. I’m not sure I’ve had a free weekend all year. But knowing I’ve built a community that I can rely on, and vice versa, brings me a worthwhile peace of mind. I’ll sacrifice a day of couch-rotting to watch my favorite show for a night of off-key karaoke or baking brownies at midnight with my homegirls in a heartbeat, time and time again.
