https://www.dw.com/en/ragebait-is-the-20.title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
https://www.dw.com/en/ragebait-is-the-20.text:
Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.

The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.

"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.

Literally translating as "That crazy," it's used by young Germans as a catch-all response — basically an alternative to the simple "ok" or "oh cool" — when they don't necessarily feel like providing a detailed answer. Noting that English keeps having a strong influence on German slang, the jury added that the Youth Word of the Year 2025 "skillfully captures the spirit of the times."

Teens in Germany use the word "aura" to jokingly describe how the rating of a person's charisma can go up and down with "aura points": "I just tripped in front of my crush: minus 50 aura!" or "Wow, I didn't know you could wiggle your ears that way: plus 1000 aura." It was selected as the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

Everyone knows the Walt Disney cartoon anthropomorphic dog who is clumsy and a bit foolish. Young Germans have adopted the term to describe someone who is silly, eccentric or awkward — usually in an affectionate way. It was named German Youth Word of the Year 2023.

The English verb "smash" was chosen as German Youth Word of the Year 2022. It roughly means "starting something with someone," "picking someone up" or "having sex with someone." It comes from the dating game app "Smash or Pass," where potential partners are either accepted as a "smash" by swiping right or rejected as a "pass" by swiping left, inspired by the dating app Tinder.

The English word "cringe" was selected as the German Youth Word of the Year 2021. Just like in English, German teens use it to describe a person or situation they find extremely embarrassing. But the German language also has its own term to express the feeling of being embarrassed because someone else has embarrassed themselves (without noticing): "fremdschämen" — secondhand embarrassment.

The German Youth Word of the Year in 2020 was also an English word, "lost." German teens don't use it in the sense of having lost their way, but to express a lack of perspective, or of not knowing what to do. They might also use the term in a math class for instance as a way of saying "I don't get it."

Man or woman of honor: that's the German Youth Word of the Year for 2018 (no word was selected in 2019). It refers to a person you can always count on and who's loyal to his friends and family. It can also be used ironically as an insult, when someone claims to have strong principles but doesn't apply them in real life. German rappers often use "Ehrenmann" in their lyrics.

To be or not to be? Germany's young people would answer Shakespeare's most famous existential question with "I bims," derived from "Ich bin" — I am. It was chosen as the German Youth Word of the Year in 2017.

When a person is flying high and ready to, say, party all night, German teens will highlight this energy by borrowing from US hip-hop slang, literally saying "you're on fly." In English, "I'm so fly" is a rapper way of saying you're cool. It was embodied by the main character in the film "Super Fly" from 1972, with its famous Curtis Mayfield soundtrack.

Do you check your phone while you're walking and run into things? Then apparently you have something in common with German teens. The 2015 German Youth Word of the Year was "Smombie" — a cross between smartphone and zombie. Walking while checking for a new like, follow or message can be hazardous. Perhaps Germany should adopt this phone lane idea spotted in China.

"Läuft bei dir" basically means "things are going well with you." But as with most of the youth words of the year, this one can also contain traces of irony depending on the context. It's perhaps always a question of perspective: Despite the mud, the heavy metal fans in this picture taken at the Wacken open air festival still seem to think everything rocks.

Who's the leader of the pack among your friends? Chances are, they're the babo: that is, the boss, the ringleader, the head honcho. German rapper Haftbefehl (pictured) may also like to see himself as the babo. In 2013, he released a track called "Chabos know who the babo is." While "chabos" (roughly, guys) is derived from Angloromani, babo comes from Turkish.

In 2012, an English abbreviation won German Youth Word of the Year. YOLO stands for You Only Live Once. In that case, live it up. Maybe that means launching your singing career on YouTube, getting a colorful tattoo or just dancing in the streets with your friends.

It's not surprising that teen speak is heavily influenced by the music scene. Swag was borrowed from the American rap scene and made it over to Germany around 2010, becoming popular thanks to Austrian rapper Money Boy's track "Turn My Swag On." If you've got swag, you radiate coolness.

Ever played limbo? Then you know there's a limit to how far down you can go — even if you're really good. "Niveaulimbo" — literally, limbo level — refers to the ever-sinking quality of something. That could be a TV show, a joke or a party that starts getting out of hand.

"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."

All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.

Around one million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.

"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added. "It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment."

"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.

As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.

"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

This article was originally written in German.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-sticks-to-.title: Germany sticks to Russia sanctions after Trump diesel deal
https://www.dw.com/en/germany-sticks-to-.text:
After Washington announced a sanctions pause on Russian diesel, Germany has said it remains committed to pressuring Moscow and supporting Ukraine. More on DW.

Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 10

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.

"The federal ⁠government ⁠has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.

"The federal government ​remains committed to the decisions on ​sanctions against ‌Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.

Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.

Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.

A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."

"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.

Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.

In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.

The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.

However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.

Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.

"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.

"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.

Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.

The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.

"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel.

Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.

Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.

"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,

Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.

The German government said European sanctions on Russia will continune unabated after the Trump administration paused US sanctions on Russian diesel yesterday.

And Germany's former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder is under fire after attending Vladimir Putin's birthday in Moscow.

Germany's support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing, government says. Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since 2023.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.title: Hundreds protest over data centre plans
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.text:
Hundreds of people have taken part in a protest against plans to build a new data centre because of concerns about its effects on the area.

Developers want to construct a complex on a 101 acre site between Caernarfon and Y Felinheli, in Gwynedd, saying it could create more than 900 jobs during construction and 200 permanent roles.

About 300 gathered for a rally in Caernarfon to highlight their opposition. Almost 15,000 have signed a petition opposing the plan.

Canolfan Ddata Menai has previously said its proposals would "transform and revitalise the long-derelict" site as well as offer significant employment.

But opponent Ernest Dyson, who lives near the proposed site, said it was "basically the destruction of the most beautiful part of the Menai Strait".

"It is quite incredible it should come to this.

"The people of the area are custodians of it. That's what we must think of," he said.

Liz Saville Roberts, the Plaid Cymru MP for Dwyfor Meirionnydd, said: "We know that we need data centres but they have to be the right size, the right technology and in the right places.

"We need proper regulations and we need to make sure that communities benefit from this.

"We have too long a history in Wales of extractive industries that left nothing behind and have little benefit for communities.

"That mustn't happen again in the 21st Century."

Canolfan Ddata Menai said the project would ensure "continued use" of the surrounding area , including Lôn Las Menai cycleway and footpath, and would have "no undue impact" on the Menai Strait and an associated site of special scientific interest (SSSI).
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm78.summary: Developers want to build a new data centre on 101 acre site in Gwynedd. They say it could create more than 900 jobs during construction and 200 permanent roles. Opponent Ernest Dyson says it is "basically the destruction of the most beautiful part of the Menai Strait"

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll

Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.

Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.

The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.

Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.

On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”

Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.

Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.

Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent but few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown. In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.

Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.

In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.

Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.

Buses were used to transport more than 5,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.

Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.

After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”

Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”

Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.

“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”

The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.

The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.

Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.

Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.

This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.

Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.

Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.

“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.

“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: Authorities impose strict lockdown in Delhi to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll. Thousands of protesters were blocked from attending demonstration.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote

The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference.

The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October.

Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote.

“The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028.

“These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.”

In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election.

Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023.

He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.

Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits.

Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Shawn Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening. The closest opponent, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of vote. Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: When streets become a workplace: Gaza workers convert tents into offices
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Khan Younis, Gaza – Dr Mohammed al-Khalidi, a specialist in prosthetics and orthotics, sits in a modest tent in al-Mawasi, southern Gaza. It has been his place of work since his clinic on al-Bahr Street in Rafah was destroyed by Israeli bombing in April 2024. His second and third clinics in Khan Younis’s Old City, southern Gaza, were subsequently destroyed by Israel in May 2025.

After this triple heartbreaking setback, al-Khalidi salvaged whatever medical equipment he could find and moved into his new office, a tent, where he has received patients for the past two years.

This transitory space reflects a new reality in Gaza since Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave began in October 2023. Offices, clinics and shops have been wiped out in waves of Israeli air raids over the past three years, leaving professionals to conduct their work from tents or on the road.

This phenomenon emerged in December 2023 following the displacement of Khan Younis residents to a narrow strip of coastal land between their hometown and Deir el-Balah.

After a ceasefire, repeatedly broken by Israel, was announced for the enclave in October 2025, more of these tent offices, surgeries and shops emerged across Gaza as professionals sought to continue their practices.

Working within these canvas confines presents multiple challenges for al-Khalidi. There is limited space, unreliable electricity, and the intense heat and loud noises to deal with.

The setting bears little resemblance to his previous practice in a bricks-and-mortar office, but he still feels this arrangement is better than suspending services altogether.

There is a massive need for prosthetics in Gaza, where between 5,000 and 6,000 people have undergone amputations between October 2023 and October 2025.

“Working from a temporary space is nothing like working in a fully equipped clinic, but for me, it is better than stopping the service altogether,” al-Khalidi told Al Jazeera.

“Patients who need prosthetic limbs or orthotic devices cannot always wait until conditions return to normal. Some have lost a limb during the war, while others need follow-up care or adjustments to devices they rely on in their daily lives.”

More than four-in-five buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since Israel’s genocidal war began in 2023, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS), creating a real estate crisis.

The lack of office space has seen rental prices reach unaffordable levels for most Gaza professionals. But resilience, necessity, and duty have encouraged Palestinians to find solutions to this situation. Tents are now where lawyers meet clients, doctors treat patients, and traders sell their wares.

After Omar al-Tawashi, a civil engineer and construction auditor, saw his office destroyed in an Israeli air strike in August 2024, he began work from his home in July 2025. But that too met the same fate, so he shifted operations to a tent in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, to continue his work.

“My move to a tent was not a professional choice. It was a direct result of the destruction of the place where I used to work, compounded by the rental crisis, which made finding an alternative office extremely difficult,” he said.

“In some cases, rents have risen to more than 10 times their pre-war levels, making a new office beyond my means”.

The tent is not a suitable environment for his engineering work, but there is no alternative for al-Tawashi.

“There is heat, cold and noise, and none of the privacy needed when discussing projects or reviewing technical files,” Omar said. “But stopping work would mean losing my source of income”.

In the crowded market in Nuseirat camp, central Gaza, accountant Mahmoud Shaheen receives clients inside a small tent amid the sound of neighbouring vendors and passers-by.

Shaheen was once responsible for a Gaza-based company’s accounts, but the office was destroyed in an Israeli air strike in November 2025.

“Moving to a tent was not so much a professional choice as a response to a reality imposed by the war,” he told Al Jazeera.

With the start of the new school year in Gaza last month, tents have been pitched across the country as substitutes for schools destroyed in Israeli air raids or converted into refuges for the displaced.

Teacher Palestine Hussein has been forced to adapt to this new reality. She previously taught English at an educational centre in Bureij in central Gaza, which she had spent years building.

It was destroyed in seconds when an Israeli air raid destroyed the educational facility, so she now teaches children from a tent at al-Balata, a camp for displaced Palestinians in Nuseirat.

There is a lack of seats for the students, ventilation, or protection from the noise and heat. But despite these challenges, Hussein is determined to provide children in the camp with some form of education.

“Although the tent may appear to be a temporary place, to me it represents an attempt to hold on to what remains of my profession and rebuild my dream from scratch, even with the most basic resources,” Hussein told Al Jazeera.

Trader Khalil al-Tahrawi saw his clothing store in Nuseirat destroyed by Israeli bombing in October 2023. After salvaging surviving merchandise from his destroyed shop, he displayed his goods – mostly men’s T-shirts and jeans – at a small tent in the Nuseirat market.

He pays $350 a month in rent for the small patch of pavement to sell the clothing, which he removes every night to protect them from thieves.

“This routine makes the work even more difficult and consumes my time and energy,” al-Tahrawi told Al Jazeera.

Repeated power cuts, unreliable internet and shortages of equipment have complicated efforts by Gaza’s business community to rebuild during this period of a relative decrease in bombing.

Customers, too, are changing their consumption patterns, heading to certain towns or camps for a particular good or service. Often what they find are prices more inflated than during Israel’s siege on Gaza before Israel’s genocidal war.

One customer, Mohammed Zweid, a 24-year-old IT worker, looks through a market in Nuseirat. “Accessing professionals in tents and temporary spaces is better than having no service at all,” he told Al Jazeera. “The transformation has changed not only where services are provided, but also how they are experienced.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.summary: More than four-in-five buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since Israel's genocidal war began in 2023. Repeated power cuts, unreliable internet and shortages of equipment have complicated efforts by Gaza's business community to rebuild.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.author: Aatif Ammad
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longf.text:
In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted.

The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts.

For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras.

He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place.

Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s.

Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh.

“Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842.

“They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added.

Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike.

“Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.”

Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand.

“In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.”

There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs.

Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees).

“We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.”

Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers.

Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago.

Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets.

“When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.”

The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery.

He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options.

“The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.”

The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves.

“India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said.

These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said.

Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver.

India more than doubled its effective import taxes on gold and silver in May. That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years.

High silver prices are now forcing Lucknow’s brides to make tough, sometimes devastating, decisions.

For 28-year-old Lucknow resident Uzma Siddique, who is set to marry in December, owning and wearing a pair of silver nagras on her big day has always topped her wedding wishlist.

“My mother wore silver nagras at her wedding in 1992. So did my grandmother and so did my great-grandmother,” Siddique said. “I always imagined myself wearing them and taking my wedding photographs in them and posting them on Instagram. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.”

But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her.

“A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said.

Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead.

“I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.”

Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option.

“They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said.

But many of her friends have had to go without.

“Some had dreamed of wearing silver nagras on their wedding day, but they had to let go of that dream because they simply couldn’t afford them. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said.

Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. Unlike Siddique, Safiya has not been able to buy silver nagras for her wedding.

From a lower middle-class family, she says soaring prices put upholding that tradition out of reach.

“My entire wedding shopping budget is around $1,250 (120,000 rupees). I simply cannot spend more than half of it on a pair of shoes,” Khan said, noting that she was sad to end the family tradition.

“I think this tradition will end with my generation,” she said. “My mother had a pair of silver nagras, but she had to sell them last year because of financial difficulties. We always believed we would buy another pair for my wedding. Had we known silver prices would rise so dramatically, we would never have sold them.”

She has been shocked by how a distant war has so negatively affected this beloved local tradition.

“I know the recent conflicts have pushed silver prices higher, but I never imagined that a war thousands of km away could take away a tradition so close to my heart,” she said. “I had always dreamed of taking my wedding photographs in silver nagras. Now that dream will never come true.”

Naseem Jahan, a Lucknow resident in her late seventies, still treasures the pair of silver chappals her mother gave her for her wedding in 1972.

“I remember my mother paid around $2.50 (250 rupees) for this pair,” Jahan recalled. “We had to wait nearly seven months after placing the order before it was finally ready. Those were beautiful days.”

More than five decades later, the silver slippers remain one of her most cherished possessions. She has them polished every three years and proudly wears them to weddings and other important family gatherings, as do many of the older women in Lucknow.

“Every time I wear them, people come to admire them and praise their beauty. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile.

But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation.

“Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said.

When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable.

Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision.

“I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. I want them to continue their journey.”

As the only precious keepsake she has preserved from her wedding, Jahan knows how connected brides feel to the shoes.

“I have developed an emotional bond with them. They remind me of my mother, my wedding day and the Lucknow I grew up in. I only wish silver prices would come down again so that more people could experience this tradition.”

Jahan’s decision to part with her silver nagras will keep a pair in her family, but it will not bring new work to the craftsmen who once made the footwear for Lucknow’s brides. In Chowk Bazaar, dwindling demand has left many artisans facing the prospect of a trade that may not survive long enough to serve the next generation.

Jabbar Hussain, 48, a fourth-generation craftsman and shopkeeper who makes nagras and sells them in his shop, sits in his empty store in Lucknow’s Chowk Bazaar, struggling to understand what has happened to a business that once flourished.

Between June and September, Hussain’s shop would normally be crowded with customers placing orders for nagras. But over the past three months, Hussain says, he has not sold a single pair. He blames the unprecedented rise in silver prices for making the handmade footwear a luxury few can now afford.

“A pair that once sold for around $125 (12,000 rupees) now costs between $622 and $778 (60,000 and 75,000 rupees) because silver has become so expensive,” he said. “People still walk into the shop, admire the craftsmanship and ask about the price. But the moment they hear it, they quietly leave. Every customer who walks away feels like another piece of our family's future disappearing.”

Hussain, like others before him, now fears he will be forced to close his shop.

“There were nearly 30 of us not long ago,” he said. “Most have already abandoned the profession because silver has become too expensive and orders have dried up. Those who are still here are also thinking of leaving.”

He is now thinking of taking a loan to open a cafe, which he hopes will provide a steady income. “I need to find another way to earn,” he said.

Hussain had hoped to teach the craft to his sons so they could carry forward the family’s legacy, but now he is advising them to pursue other professions. He no longer sees a future in the silver nagras trade and blames the war in the Middle East.

“We have nothing to do with this war, yet we are paying the price,” he said, frustrated at how a conflict so far away has threatened his livelihood. “I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.”

Still, Hussain clings to the hope that silver prices will decline and orders will return. Economists and market analysts are less optimistic.

Ayyub said silver prices are expected to remain above $2,085 per  (200,000 rupees) kg for the foreseeable future because once precious metal prices rise sharply, they rarely fall significantly enough to return to their previous levels. Historically, the same has been the case with gold.

“Even if prices decline, they are unlikely to return to their earlier levels,” Ayyub said.

Not far from Hussain’s workshop, 40-year-old former silver nagras maker Kuldeep Gautam now spends his days behind the counter of a jewellery shop.

Known for his intricate workmanship, Gautam once earned between $415 and $518 (40,000 and 50,000 rupees) a month making the ornate footwear. But he has not received a single order since January, he says. As orders disappeared and his savings dwindled, Gautam was forced to abandon the craft and take up a job as a salesman.

“I left the craft because I had no other choice,” he said. “Whenever I pass my old workshop, I don’t even look at it. It hurts too much.”

Beyond the loss of income, Kuldeep says he mourns the loss of the identity his craft had given him.

“People knew me for my work and appreciated my craftsmanship. It gave me dignity. Today, I earn only $155 (15,000 rupees) a month, and I struggle to pay my children’s school fees. I never imagined my life would come to this.”

“I still yearn to make nagras, but there are no buyers anymore. The war has destroyed our lives.”

Back in his shop, Azhar Hussain also faces the prospect of abandoning a craft that has carried his family for more than a century. His plan, he says, is to secure a bank loan to buy an electric rickshaw so he can start earning again.

“At least an e-rickshaw will earn me $5 to $7 (500 to 700 rupees) a day,” he said. “I don’t want to leave this craft, but I have no choice.”
