https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/pokemon-.title: Pokémon card values are soaring. What collectors should know before buying or selling
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/pokemon-.author: Bob Woods
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/pokemon-.text:
What is driving interest? Pokémon and other trading-card games are drawing strong collector demand, while sources say high sports-card prices are pushing some buyers toward non-sports cards.

What determines value? Authenticity, condition, graded population, liquidity and verified transaction history can sharply affect what a card sells for.

What is the biggest risk? Counterfeits are rising, especially in Pokémon submissions, making authentication and careful price research critical before buying.

In 2022, a rare Topps 1952 Mickey Mantle baseball card — one of sports-card collectors’ holiest grails — sold for $12.6 million. Wow, you say, that’s a lot of dough for a thin piece of cardboard, slab of bubblegum not included.

Well, what do you say about a 1998 Pikachu Illustrator Pokémon card going for $16.5 million earlier this year? If you’re pro wrestler and social media influencer Logan Paul, seller of the item, you say, Not a bad return on the $5.3 million (plus a trade) I paid for it in 2021.

Those are extreme examples, but a vivid illustration of how TCGs — shorthand for competitive trading card games, led by Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh! — are encroaching on an over-saturated sports-card market as an enticing investment opportunity. Throw in vintage and modern-day non-sports trading cards, depicting historical events and fictional characters ranging from the Civil War to Luke Skywalker, and it’s a whole new ballgame.

The record $16.5 million Pokémon card sale is drawing fresh attention to a collectibles market where grading, scarcity and authentication can determine whether a card is worth dollars or hundreds of thousands.

“It is one of our fastest-growing categories that we’ve seen and one of the largest contributors to [our] growth over the last number of quarters,” said Adam Ireland, vice president and general manager of collectibles at online marketplace eBay
, which also provides authentication and price guides for TCGs and non-sports cards. “From an investment point of view, you start with Pokémon,” he said. “It was the most searchable term within the eBay collectibles environment through the first half of the year.”

Heritage Auctions, which deals in art, jewelry, coins and many other collectibles, launched a dedicated TCG department six years ago. “Now it’s a $50-million category,” said executive vice president Joe Maddalena. “That’s just TCGs. I’m not talking about Star Wars and any of that stuff,” he said, though he added that non-sports stuff contributed around $10 million to Heritage’s overall sales in 2025, which topped $2.1 billion.

While buyers can find myriad non-sports cards for less than $10 — almost like investing in penny stocks in hopes of eventually striking gold — Maddalena and Ireland cited some eye-popping sales on their respective platforms. A first-edition Pokémon Charizard card worth $20,000 pre-Covid is now valued by Heritage at $500,000. A Tyler the Great Warrior Yu-Gi-Oh! card shattered records when it was auctioned on eBay for $311,211, while Magic’s Black Lotus card has gone for $500,000 on the site. Heritage sold a 1977 Luke Skywalker card for $687,500 in May.

Whereas collectability, value and investability of sports cards can rise and fall on the real-world performance of athletes, both trading-card genres share common factors. For instance, rookie cards of superstar athletes are highly coveted; the non-sports counterpart is referred to as first appearance. Especially critical are the authenticity, physical condition, total graded population, liquidity and pricing of specific cards, criteria determined by professional grading services such as PSA and CGC Cards.

PSA (Professional Sports Authenticator), founded in 1991, is the most recognizable grading service. Its process begins when a trained grader examines a card to verify its originality or genuineness, then assesses the quality and condition of the card using PSA’s grading scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most pristine, aka gem mint. There generally are very limited populations of PSA 10s of highly sought-after cards, thus their astronomical values.

PSA has been grading non-sports cards since its inception, “but with more people viewing it as a potential asset class or thing they want to potentially invest in or speculate in, you’re seeing more demand for grading services in the last seven years,” said PSA president Ryan Hoge.

Indeed, PSA graded more than 19 million cards in 2025, up from two million in 2020. The company had already graded more than eight million cards as of last May, with output from January through April up 39% year-over-year. Much of that uptick, Hoge said, is attributable to TCGs. “Collectively, TCGs [account for] 50% of our current business, more than all the sports cards combined.”

To keep up with escalating demand and address mounting complaints of long turnaround times, PSA’s parent company, Collectors — which owns other vertically integrated services, including Beckett, SGC and Card Ladder — is investing $200 million into PSA’s operations, doubling its physical infrastructure, implementing logistics technology and hiring 1,000 new employees, including hundreds of graders.

Trading-card collecting, of all types, is an intriguing and eclectic hobby, dating back more than a century. It’s an increasingly lucrative market, too, but one that’s hard to quantify, especially when it comes to calculating sales of new products versus aftermarket deals.

ICv2, an outlet that covers fandom culture, reported that sales of new TCG products alone reached $2.5 billion in 2025. “For this year, we estimate that it will be close to $5 billion,” said editor-in-chief Milton Griepp, noting fervor surrounding the 30th anniversary of Pokémon. Figures from resale platforms like eBay and TCGplayer are diffuse, he said, “so estimates have air between the data.”

Most familiar are sports cards, which for decades have portrayed past and active players from America’s traditional pastimes — primarily baseball, but also football, basketball and hockey — and their best-known makers, Topps (acquired by Fanatics in 2022), Upper Deck, Fleer and Donruss.

Baby boomers grew up amassing sports card collections, largely for sentimental value — and maybe the bubblegum. But once those boomers started aging, cards not wrecked in bicycle spokes or tossed out by their parents accrued monetary value, creating not only a robust marketplace, but a new breed of investors. Buyers and sellers flocked to specialty card shops and shows, where scores of entrepreneurial dealers hawked vintage and modern products.

There was a significant surge in the sports card market in the early 1990s, driven by rising prices of 1950s and 1960s cards, and another during the Covid-19 pandemic when locked-down consumers, flush with disposable stimulus money, swelled the collector/investor ranks. Today it’s a multi-billion-dollar industry that’s shifted toward rare, iconic vintage cards, high-end inserts and overproduction of modern base sets.

“The sports side of the hobby has gotten so expensive,” said Jeff Copeland, an emeritus professor of English at the University of Northern Iowa and a longtime collector of sports and non-sports cards. “In some cases, cards that sold 10 years ago for $20 are now $1,000. So collectors feeling the pinch in sports cards looked across the aisle at non-sports cards, remembered collecting them in their childhood and saw the value on the prices,” said Copeland, who regularly writes for The Wrapper, a venerable non-sports fanzine.

There’s also new money from investors just coming into the hobby, said Alex Tymchuk, a non-sports card dealer. “Maybe they weren’t really into baseball or basketball [card] collecting, but they can relate to Mickey Mouse, Spider-Man or Captain America.”

Likewise, Kit Young, an esteemed dealer among sports and non-sports card collectors, has seen an influx of “younger folks coming in with money. People think [the cards] are going to go up in value, so they’re buying on the come based on the future.”

TCGs and non-sports cards are considered very distinct categories. Hobbyists undoubtedly recognize certain cards’ escalating values, but nostalgia, camaraderie and the pure fun of collecting are the prime motivators. “I would say that about 95% of those collecting non-sport cards today are not in it for investment,” Copeland said.

Nonetheless, the investment community is gaining prominence — and making money, a lot of it on trading in TCGs. The genre originated in 1993 with Magic and was joined by Pokémon (1996) and Yu-Gi-Oh! (1999) as enduring blockbuster games played with specially designed cards that combine strategic deck-building with collecting. A plethora of TCGs have since come and gone, from American Idol to Game of Thrones, while others have thrived, such as One Piece and Disney’s Lorcana. Speculators are also watching up-and-coming franchises, including Riftbound, Naruto and Dungeon Crawler Carl.

Non-sports trading cards comprise a much more diverse, more relatable universe of subjects and characters. Spider-Man, Batman, Superman, Wolverine and other superheroes evolved from comics to TV to movies, with trading cards at each iteration. A 1966 Donruss Spider-man PSA 9 card valued at $29 in 2013 sold for $175,100 last month.

Topps has produced non-sports sets documenting the Civil War, World War II and Desert Storm. Yet its most acclaimed, and valuable, such set imagined a fictional conflict. Mars Attacks, released in 1962, was a huge hit with kids, though many parents objected to the gruesome artwork of Martians eviscerating Earthlings. Although full 55-card sets even in poor condition can fetch around $1,500, Heritage recently sold a near-mint condition one for $268,400.

Another Topps hit is the Star Wars franchise, which has spun off more than 100 sets since the original film premiered in 1977. That translates to literally hundreds of millions of Star Wars cards in print, so investors can easily find individual cards or complete sets for nominal prices. At the other end of the price spectrum, there was the Heritage sale of a PSA 10 Luke Skywalker card for $687,500 in May. “That card is notoriously hard to find in that grade,” Maddalena said.

As investor interest in non-sports cards and TCGs keeps growing, the market has developed an ecosystem that parallels traditional exchanges, indexes and brokers. Sports card shops and shows attract non-sports buyers and sellers, who rely on grading services for valuations and dealers for guidance and trends. While Heritage and other elite auction houses showcase cards and accept bids online and in-person, hobbyist websites, such as Vintage Non-Sports, Blowout Cards and Fanatics Collect, are doing a brisk auction business.

Collectors’ PSA Vault, where millions of physical cards are stored, has a partnership with eBay, “that allows you to buy and sell very quickly,” Hoge said. “It feels like a Robinhood or a Fidelity type experience.”

A recent phenomenon luring investors is so-called “breaker” platforms where individual sellers live-stream auctions for TCGs, non-sports cards and other products in real time. A seller offers unopened packs of cards, boxes containing multiple packs or entire cases to buyers, who purchase individual spots. The seller breaks open the item, then each buyer receives the card or cards pulled for their spot. Whatnot is the most prominent platform, though Drip Shop Live, Fanatics Live and eBay Live are popular alternatives.

Another aftermarket trend is online gacha game platforms, including Collector Crypt and Courtyard, which bridge physical TCGs with blockchain technology. Tuomas Holmberg, CEO of Collector Crypt, said in a recent ICv2 interview that the company is running at a $50 million per month sales rate. GameStop’s Power Packs gacha game, operated in conjunction with PSA, may be one reason why the company’s collectible sales are surging, Griepp said.

Despite a market infrastructure that in many ways mirrors conventional methods for investing in stocks and bonds, there isn’t a network of brokerages or regulatory guardrails around TCGs and non-sports cards. That puts the onus on buyers and sellers to perform their own due diligence.

“Like any investment, do your homework, know what’s out there, know what the good deals are,” Ireland said. Review online price guides that document the history of verified transactions and population data “so you know the level of scarcity behind any individual card,” he said.

Beware of counterfeits, “a constant issue,” Hoge said. “The technology continues to get better, so we have to stay on our toes to keep ahead of the bad guys.”

PSA reported a more than 45% increase in counterfeit cards flagged by the company last year from submissions compared to 2024. There was a modest 5% rise in counterfeit sports cards, yet a 125% increase in fake Pokémon cards.

Maddalena’s advice is to “buy the best. If you can only afford $1,000, buy the best $1,000 card you can. If you can afford $10,000, buy the best $10,000 card you can,” he said. “If you speculate on a wide swath of stuff, you’re going to get hurt. You’re going to have things that go up, you’re going to have things that become worthless.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/de-extin.title: How de-extincting dire wolves and woolly mammoths may extend human life
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/de-extin.author: Colleen McKown
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/de-extin.text:
Colossal Biosciences is on a mission to revive extinct species.

The company has created three genetically engineered dire wolf pups and is working on the woolly mammoth.

The science of de-extinction has implications for the environment, medicine and research on evolution.

Colossal Biosciences’ efforts to bring back extinct animals like the woolly mammoth and dire wolves have drawn comparisons to Jurassic Park.

CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told CNBC’s Julia Boorstin at the CNBC AI Forum last week that he understands those comparisons.

“I think anyone that saw Jurassic Park in the 90s and didn’t say it was cool, like I don’t think they’re probably very fun at parties,” Lamm joked. “But yes, I saw the movies. I love them. They entertained us. They scared us.”

However, Lamm said, “I constantly have to remind people on X that, you know, they were movies,” he said. “I don’t think Jurassic Park had any conservation or general human benefit models to it, so we’ve tried to take a slightly different perspective.”

Since viable dinosaur DNA is no longer available, bringing back dinosaurs is, in fact, impossible. But what is underway at Colossal, besides the dire wolf and woolly mammoth projects, is work to genetically engineer the dodo bird, the Tasmanian tiger, and a giant bird called a moa, among others.

“It’s highly likely in the next coming year or two, people will continue to see us deliver extinct species back to Earth, and we could even have more dire wolves, too,” Lamm told Boorstin.

The process of creating the wolf pups involved taking genetic material from a skull and a tooth that were tens of hundreds of years old. Using AI models, Colossal used the ancient DNA to reconstruct the dire wolf genome and map it to its closest living relative, the gray wolf. The team then created embryos by editing the cells of modern gray wolves.

Three pups, named Romulus, Remus, and Khaleesi, have been born to domestic dogs used as surrogate mothers.

Skeptics, Boorstin pointed out, say that they didn’t really de-extinct a dire wolf, rather, they created a genetically modified gray wolf.

Lamm called this a “semantic argument” that “misses the forest for the trees.”

“Gray wolves are just genetically modified dire wolves. They were just done by nature or God or however you want to classify it,” he said.

Colossal is undertaking a similar process in their woolly mammoth project  –  that involves genetically modifying an Asian elephant. Lamm told Time in August that the company is aiming to have a woolly mammoth birth in the 2030s.

“We call it a woolly mammoth,” he said. “Because if it looks like a duck, it quacks like a duck, it serves ecological functions of a duck, it’s a duck, in our perspective.”

Lamm became interested in this work after a 2019 meeting with renowned Harvard geneticist George Church, who Lamm called “arguably the father of synthetic biology.”

Church, who initiated the Personal Genome Project, had been dreaming about bringing back the woolly mammoth for decades, he told CNBC in 2021.

However, the vision to revive animals like the woolly mammoth goes far beyond creating a real-life Jurassic Park with previously extinct creatures.

″[Church] had this vision that we could leverage CRISPR and all these tools and technologies to bring back extinct species, use some of those technologies for human healthcare, and then build this programmable life model that we could apply to so many different use cases on Earth,” Lamm said.

Those use cases include those aforementioned conservation-focused benefits that de-extinction promises. For example, the engineered woolly mammoths could help fight climate change by stomping down snow cover in high-altitude arctic regions, which keeps soil frozen, and knocking down trees, thereby converting heat-absorbing forests into grasslands.

But the processes around de-extinction are also opening new doors in genome engineering and developmental biology, Lamm said.

That could have implications on “everything from microbes to plastic in the oceans to gene therapies and targeted delivery for humans to eradicating genetic diseases,” he said. Lamm theorized that these efforts around DNA synthesis could even lead to developing crops or trees that grow faster.

“We’re pushing the bounds of DNA synthesis to synthesize the largest cargos of DNA,” he said. “That will be massively transformative for how we think about programmable life.”

A company spun off from Colossal, called Astromech, is pushing into what Lamm called “convergent evolution,” studying what causes species that are similar in nearly every way to have different immunities or other health issues, such as why elephants get cancer at a fraction of the rate humans do. That research could be leveraged to solve human healthcare challengers or pandemic responses, Lamm said. Astromech was valued at $2 billion in March, according to D Magazine.

“We are in a biodiversity crisis, so we need these tools because we’re going to lose about half of biodiversity in the next 25 years. So, we do need cryopreservation, we need biobanks, we need genetic rescue and these types of tools,” Lamm said. “It opens the gate for us to say, if we take these models and we take these evolutionary trends, what can we learn from it, and how can that apply to other uses cases, and how can we use directed evolution on everything from crops to human healthcare and beyond?”

These efforts to tackle some of the world’s biggest problems have made Colossal Biosciences attractive to investors. In July, the company announced a $200 million Series C round led by TWG Global, bringing its valuation to $10.2 billion. In total, the company has raised more than $435 million since its founding.

But it’s not lost on Lamm that many people are inspired by the idea of bringing animals back from extinction, especially young people. Lamm said that 30% of the company’s investors “come to us from their kids.”

“If we can inspire the next generation and get them excited about science and education and conservation, and then build out a synthetic biology platform that can be leveraged for so many different use cases, that’s the real mission here,” he said. “Our kids, they’re going to inherit our problems, and the decisions on how we solve those.”
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/de-extin.summary: Colossal Biosciences is working on the woolly mammoth and dire wolves. The company has raised more than $435 million since its founding.

https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202610.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202610.text:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended after the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) announced on Saturday that it had opened disciplinary proceedings against the 41-year-old over his decision to walk out on the national team.

Ronaldo apologised to supporters earlier this week while criticising Portugal coach Jorge Jesus and said he would accept any punishment that was imposed.

WATCH MORE
Portugal's Ronaldo walks away amid tensions with coach

"Disciplinary proceedings have been initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo," said the federation in a statement, classifying the case as "urgent" and confirming Ronaldo is currently suspended pending a decision on the final punishment.

Ronaldo left Portugal's squad after first being made to warm up as a substitute against Norway on September 27 and not brought on, and then finding out he would not start against Denmark in the match on October 1.

The former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker is Portugal's all-time top goalscorer and record appearance-maker.

On Tuesday, Ronaldo accused Portugal coach Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time in Nations League matches but said he was not retiring from international duty and would be available to play once any potential punishment was served.

"I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team," Ronaldo said, while accepting his actions must be "punished" by the federation.

Portugal won all four of their Nations League matches and qualified for the quarter-finals with two games to spare.

Ronaldo returned to club action on Friday with Saudi Arabian side Al-Nassr and scored as they won 3-0 against Diriyah in a Saudi Pro League match.

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Yemen says advancing against Houthis around key Bab al-Mandab strait
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Yemeni military sources said on Saturday their forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait but have not yet secured control of the waterway, after the government launched an operation to capture lost territory.

The Saudi-backed government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the pro-Iran group seized Yemen's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.

READ MORE
Yemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city

The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area but they claimed to have repelled the assault.

"Saudi-led forces attempted to advance from the Ras al-Ara area in Lahj governorate towards the area south of Bab al-Mandab," Hizam al-Asad, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, told AFP.

"However, our forces repelled them outside the Bab al-Mandab zone, inflicting heavy losses in personnel and equipment and forcing the survivors to retreat.

"Our forces maintain control over Bab al-Mandab, Mayun Island, and the remaining areas along the country's western coast," he said.

Sources from the military of Yemen's internationally recognised government also said Mayun Island – located in the heart of the strait – remained in Houthi hands as fighting continued.

Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Clashes in western Yemen, specifically around the strait, had killed at least 63 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP on Saturday.

Thirty-five members of government forces had been killed, while 28 Houthis had died, the sources said.

On Friday, a Yemeni military source confirmed to AFP that their forces had launched a "major operation" in the strait region, supported by air power from Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government.

After four years of relative calm, Yemen's civil war reignited in July before the Houthi gains on Yemen's western coastline.

Saudi Arabia leads an international military coalition helping the Yemeni government fight the Houthis.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Early on Saturday, the coalition said it had destroyed more than 130 Houthi targets in a "large-scale operation".

The Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel reported on Saturday that enemy strikes had targeted the Bab al-Mandab area.

It also reported four Saudi strikes on the capital Sanaa's international airport on Saturday, a day after saying two were killed in a Saudi strike on the airport.

In addition to battling Yemeni government forces on the ground, the Houthis have also been firing on targets inside Saudi Arabia, attacking transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian sites with drones and missiles.

READ MORE
Explosions heard in Saudi capital Riyadh after Houthis' deadly attacks on airports

Riyadh said Friday that attacks on the Saudi capital's international airport had killed three people the previous day.

Saudi Arabia has been retaliating with strikes on key Houthi targets inside Yemen.

Houthi media reported on Friday that two people had died in attacks on the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa.

Ordinary civilians have been paying the price for the renewed fighting in one of the world's poorest countries, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.

Houthis claim to have repelled government forces in Bab alMandab area but have not yet secured control of waterway. Saudi-backed government last week announced counter- offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by Houthis.

https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.title: Are Chinese military aircraft already using a new joint air facility in Laos?
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.author: Gabriel Dominguez
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.text:
Recent satellite imagery shows twice as many K-8/JL-8-family trainer aircraft on site as Laos’ air force is thought to possess

Eight of the two-seat trainer and light-attack aircraft were visible at Ban Keun Airport in commercial satellite imagery taken on September 30, according to Reuters, which first reported the images. More than two dozen military and support vehicles were also visible.

Beijing says the jointly maintained and operated centre is intended to strengthen training for Laotian air force pilots.

The Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force is assessed by the IISS Military Balance 2026 to operate about four K-8Ws.

The South China Morning Post could find no public record of Laos acquiring a new batch of K-8-family aircraft.

Possible explanations for the discrepancy include additional Laotian aircraft not reflected in published inventories, aircraft assigned to the new academy or the presence of Chinese military aircraft.

“In my opinion, not only possibly but certainly, since there are eight aircraft to be seen there and Laos itself only owns four,” he said, adding that the imagery could show four Laotian K-8Ws alongside four JL-8s from the PLA Air Force.

Rupprecht also pointed to apparent differences in their colour schemes, noting that Laotian K-8Ws had been seen in camouflage while PLA aircraft of the type commonly use a much lighter-coloured livery.

A satellite imagery expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, was more cautious in his assessment.

The expert said four aircraft were covered by tarpaulins, while the remaining four appeared lighter in colour – possibly consistent with Chinese aircraft – but sunlight reflection prevented a definitive identification.

Timothy Heath, China expert and founder of security research firm Perceptum, called the four-and-four interpretation “very plausible”.

But according to Brian Hart, deputy director of the CSIS China Power Project, even if some of the aircraft were operated by the PLA, their presence would not necessarily signal a significant expansion of Chinese air power in the region.

“These aircraft do not provide China any significant new ability to project air power in the region,” Hart said. “They are primarily trainer aircraft.”

The imagery also shows Ban Keun has the capacity to accommodate considerably more aircraft than Laos’ existing jet-trainer fleet, which Military Balance lists as comprising about four K-8Ws and three Yak-130s.

The satellite imagery expert said the apron appeared to contain about 24 marked parking positions suitable for small aircraft such as the K-8/JL-8. Few other facilities were yet visible, although construction was continuing, and the number of positions could indicate that aircraft would travel to Ban Keun for training, with enough space to accommodate joint training.

More broadly, Ban Keun occupies a distinct place in China’s small overseas military footprint.

Hart said in an interview when the centre opened last month that Ban Keun was China’s first acknowledged overseas military facility centred on air power.

According to official Laotian reporting, cooperation at the centre will include joint training and exercises, personnel development, humanitarian assistance and other areas.

If PLA aircraft were among those visible, their presence would demonstrate actual Chinese military aviation access to Ban Keun, said Isaac Kardon, an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University’s school of advanced international studies.

“Training and a strategically useful military presence can coexist,” Kardon added, saying that the main questions were who operated the aircraft, under whose command and with what permissions.

In January 2024, nine JL-8s from the PLA Air Force’s Red Falcon aerobatic team flew to Laos for celebrations marking the Lao People’s Army’s 75th anniversary, showing that Chinese military aircraft could operate from Laotian territory temporarily.

PLA aircraft have also temporarily used partner airfields in countries including Russia, Pakistan and Thailand for exercises and training.

What would distinguish Ban Keun from those temporary deployments, Kardon said, is whether the PLA had “reliable access” – an arrangement allowing it “to return and use the facility predictably, rather than negotiating each deployment as a separate event”.

He said an enduring PLA operating location would require three elements together: “reliable access, sustained support and a recurring operational role”, including personnel and facilities capable of maintaining, fuelling and supporting Chinese aircraft over time.

Kardon said fuel storage, maintenance facilities and communications would be relevant indicators, although they could also support an ordinary training establishment.

Calling Ban Keun a PLA aviation base would require clearer evidence about its standing mission, command arrangements and China’s control of the facilities, he added.

Hart said the joint facility’s location meant that even if China stationed more capable aircraft there in future, it would not fundamentally change the PLA’s ability to project air power in the region because Chinese aircraft could already reach the area from bases in China.

“Still, operating from there could help China to build experience with overseas basing – a valuable stepping stone if the PLA seeks to open bases farther afield in the future,” he added.

Whatever Ban Keun’s eventual status, the facility’s significance was primarily political and institutional, Heath said.

At the same time, Kardon cautioned that permission to train Laotian pilots did not automatically imply permission for Chinese aircraft to conduct regional intelligence or combat operations.

Ban Keun could represent “an aviation application of the Ream model”, he said, referring to the China-Cambodia Joint Training and Support Centre at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base.

“A standing, jointly supported aviation facility that enables repeated or extended Chinese deployments would be a meaningful development,” Kardon added. “Whether Ban Keun meets that description remains to be established.”
https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military.summary: Beijing says the jointly maintained and operated centre is intended to strengthen training for Laotian air force pilots. The centre is also intended to train Laotians in the air force.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c54g.title: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c54g.text:
A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.

The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.

Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.

It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."

The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".

Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.

She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party.

"Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said.

Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy.

"This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. "

Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version.

However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious".

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation."

He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue.

"They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years," he told BBC Politics Live. "So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position.

Following Polanksi's by-election defeat in Holborn and St Pancras this week, the leader of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said he should resign.

She added it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on the motion or amendments. He left early to campaign for the north London by-election, which Labour won on Thursday with Greens coming second.

Following his defeat, Polanski told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.

He lost out to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c54g.summary: Westminster leader Ellie Chowns says motion is a "significant and damaging policy" Motion was approved at Green Party conference earlier this month. It has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups. Ex-leader Caroline Lucas says motion not being protected from entryism.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Deaths came from falling trees as nearly a million people are without power and rain and flooding remain a concern

Two people have died amid Isaias after it made landfall late on Friday on Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane, according to authorities.

Both of those deaths occurred after trees fell on homes, one in Escambia county, Florida, and another in Birmingham, Alabama, as the storm moved in inland, local officials said.

Meanwhile, though it had weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone, Isaias still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland, forecasters and officials warned.

More than 868,000 customers furthermore were without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on early Saturday as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according to PowerOutage.us.

Although storm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-western Georgia.

“Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.”

Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend.

Across much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday as a potent category 2 hurricane. It was an atypically late-forming first Atlantic hurricane of the season and lashed the US Gulf coast with heavy rain, fierce winds and life-threatening flooding.

The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h), and it was predicted to dissipate on Sunday.

Isaias’s winds were so intense they sounded like “a train whistle”, Tim Mowry told the Associated Press after enduring the storm as his home in Pensacola, Florida.

Mowry described losing power on Friday afternoon but said could rely on a generator. He said his son tried to drive to his home after his place about 15 minutes away lost power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the road.

All things considered, Mowry said he was “really fortunate” with respect to how he fared during Isaias.

Crestview, Florida, resident Ashley Weeks told the news station WEAR that a tree from her backyard fell on top of her house, damaging the the roof near her daughter’s bedroom and turning the ceiling into piles of debris.

It was “just scary – everything, my whole life is in the house”, Weeks said. “We heard a loud … like a bomb went off in the house. It was so loud. And I got up and [saw] the tree through the roof, and it was – freaking out.”

Alabama’s governor, Kay Ivey, warned of “possible spinoff tornadoes” and asked residents to “prepare for the worst”.

“Right now, we are worried about strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes in certain parts of the state,” Ivey said. “As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop. We often hear in emergency management: Hope for the best. Prepare for the worst.

“That is the approach we need with this particular storm system.”

Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, said in an interview with Fox News on Saturday morning that his administration had not received any reports of fatalities yet in the state. He attributed that to likely heightened preparation and previous experience with other tropical storms and hurricanes.

“We’re a peninsula in the middle of a tropical part of the world,” DeSantis said. “We’ve gotta deal with these things,” DeSantis said.

And while the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six.

Isais is one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013.

None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.

The Associated Press contributed reporting
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: More than 868,000 customers without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on Saturday. Storms still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland. Storm is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘People are leaving’: New York City’s EMS workers are struggling to make ends meet
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lok Darjee in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
EMS workers, who make life-or-death decisions in emergencies, are the lowest paid first responders

After 31 years in New York City’s emergency medical services, Oren Barzilay has started giving young New Yorkers advice he never imagined giving when he began his EMS career. “Don’t come here,” he tells them. “You are only going to hurt yourself.”

It is a striking reversal for Barzilay, the recently retired president of FDNY EMS Local 2507. What changed for Barzilay was not his view of work or the value of service. It was what he believes is the New York City failure to pay the people who put their lives at risk to save the lives of others.

“After 31 years, I am stuck at $59,000,” he said.

Barzilay’s reversal comes as New York City’s EMS workforces remain locked in a years-long fight over wages and pay parity. The fight has become an early test of a contradiction facing Mamdani’s young administration.

As a candidate, Mamdani built his political identity in part around organized labor, affordability and demands that employers pay workers more. As mayor, he now sits on the other side of the bargaining table, responsible for a vast municipal workforce and a finite city budget. EMS workers’ years-long campaign for higher wages and pay parity – unfolding as his administration filed a lawsuit to stop $10,000 payments to public-school paraprofessionals in court – is forcing that tension into the open.

For many EMS workers their job is a passionate calling. Natasha Villaruel, a paramedic, has about 20 seconds to make a life-saving decision. When the 36-year-old paramedic receives a 911 call for someone in respiratory distress, the routine begins almost automatically, with precision. “You respond with lights and sirens safely. You try to get there as fast as you can,” said Villaruel over the phone.

By the time she and her fellow paramedic reach the doorway, she is already reading the patient’s vitals.

“You assess the patient from the door to see how they’re breathing, to see the color of their skin,” she said. “The first thing you want to know is if they can speak, because now if they can’t speak, you know this is very, very urgent.”

Villaruel, who was born in Jamaica and moved to Brooklyn at four, described the pressure of those first few seconds. “Within 20 seconds, you have to make a life decision.”

More than 4,500 EMS workers such as Villaruel respond to over 1.9mmedical and fire emergencies each year across New York City’s five boroughs, making life-or-death decisions for a city of more than 8.58 million people. Yet the workers entrusted with those decisions are among the lowest-paid first responders in the city. An FDNY EMT starts at $39,386 a year, barely above New York City’s minimum wage. After five years, an EMT can earn roughly $59,534, but a firefighter with similar years of experience makes as much as $105,146 – nearly double what EMS and EMTs make. Many EMS workers are struggling to make ends meet.

Villaruel said her own household is sustainable largely because her husband is a firefighter. But her colleagues, she said, have struggled far more. “We have people that live in shelters,” she said. “We have people that get vouchers. We have people that get food stamps.”

Meanwhile, the ambulances are taking longer to reach New Yorkers facing life-threatening emergencies. The average ambulance response time rose from 11 minutes and 21 seconds in fiscal year 2025 to 13 minutes and 9 seconds in fiscal year 2026, according to the Mayor’s Management Report. The delay in emergency response comes as the city’s EMS system struggles to keep workers. According to New York State EMS workforce report, the number of active EMS responders fell 17.5% between 2019 and 2022 statewide. Union leaders said lower wages are driving an exodus of EMS workers.

“We have a tremendous attrition problem. People are leaving,” said Anthony Almojera, an FDNY EMS paramedic lieutenant and vice president of Local 3621. Almojera said he remains frustrated with the city council and successive administrations. “I don’t know why, over the years, many administrations have decided they do not want to value us,” said Almojera

For some patients, those minutes can be life-altering. “Time matters a lot,” said Dr Shreya Kashyap, second-year neurology resident at Mount Sinai. For patients suffering an acute stroke, she said, every delay can increase the risk of permanent damage to brain tissue. “There’s this phrase that’s very popular in neurology education,” Kashyap said. “It’s called ‘time is brain.’”

The pay disparity is hardly new to city hall. Sandy Nurse, a Brooklyn councilmember, who has supported efforts to raise EMS compensation, said: “EMS workers, frontline emergency management workers, make very, very low wages.” In 2024, Nurse co-sponsored bills to establish a Department of Emergency Medical Services as its own standalone organization, ensuring better wages for service workers as well as mental healthcare. Her progressive caucus also has won $1m for an EMS mental health pilot program.

Barzilay argues that the decades-long failure to achieve pay parity is not due to a lack of political support. He places much of the blame on city hall, particularly the offices responsible for negotiating labor contracts and determining what the city can afford.

Nearly four years after the last contract, the Mamdani administration says negotiations are now underway but declined to disclose when bargaining sessions have taken place or where negotiations currently stand.

“Contract negotiations are currently underway with the EMS union, and we remain fully committed to good-faith bargaining at the table,” Kenneth Londono, communications director for the mayor’s office of labor relations, said in a statement. “The Mamdani administration values the vital, life-saving work that our EMS members perform for New Yorkers every single day.”

Londono said the administration hopes to reach a “fair and sustainable outcome” that supports EMS workers while “remaining fair to city taxpayers”.

Barzilay remains skeptical. Asked whether he believed there are good-faith negotiations under the new administration, he said: “No. Not as of yet.”

Almojera was more hopeful and believes the administration is making a good-faith effort to address the problems facing EMS.

“Negotiations haven’t formally commenced,” Almojera said. “We’re just talking. You know, just talking back and forth.”

For Almojera, Mamdani’s appointment of Lillian Bonsignore as fire commissioner was an encouraging sign. Bonsignore spent 31 years in FDNY EMS, beginning as an EMT before becoming a paramedic and eventually chief of EMS operations. “Making her commissioner is acknowledging that the Fire Department is mostly EMS,” Almojera said. “She knows exactly what we do. She’s one of us.”

Villaruel was less optimistic: “I feel like politicians are politicians,” she said. “They tell you what you want to hear. And then when it’s time for the work to be put in, everyone is blind and deaf.”

Bonsignore’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

For Villaruel, who has spent more than a decade in EMS, the work itself is not what is pushing people away.

“It’s not like they don’t like the job,” Villaruel said. “It’s the pay that’s the problem.”

“Who doesn’t like saving people?” she asked.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: EMS workers are among the lowest-paid first responders in New York City. EMS workers make life-or-death decisions in emergencies. negotiations currently stand, but the mayor's office says they are committed to good-faith bargaining.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Fighting continues to intensify in Yemen as the internationally recognised government forces push a military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, which controls part of the country.

Speaking at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”.

Government forces are particularly looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital trading chokepoint that has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have all but halted shipping.

At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.

More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in September, the UN’s migration agency (IOM), said.

Fierce battles across several fronts have prompted concerns from rights groups that Yemen has essentially returned to civil war after the relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014.

Amid the US-Iran war, Yemen’s worst fighting in years threatens to destabilise the region further, experts say. Here’s what we know:

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Riyadh has increasingly relied on it for oil exports amid the US-Iran war, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Sunday, the Yemeni government announced the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa.

On Saturday, it said it had conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the previous 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters.

The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory.

He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans.

The Bab al-Mandeb strait emerged as yet another front in the US-Israel war on Iran when the Houthis declared a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia in July.

While the Houthis said that was in retaliation for ongoing Saudi blockades on Yemen, analysts viewed the move as calculated to provide more leverage for Iran amid on-and-off negotiations with the US – a close ally of Riyadh.

Battles are now raging around the strategic southern cities of Mocha and Dubhab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides currently claim control of the shipping lanes.

The Houthis, who have developed sophisticated weapons systems, including ballistic missiles, have also targeted Saudi Arabia with missile and drone attacks. On Friday, Saudi Arabia’s aviation authorities said three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, had been killed and several others wounded in Houthi strikes on the international airport in Riyadh – the first such deaths in the kingdom since fighting resumed. Several airlines suspended flights.

The coalition forces also heavily bombarded Sanaa, on Friday, with several injuries reported, including a child. Both sides are also fighting to control Taiz.

Civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took control of Sanaa and imposed their own government in the capital. The seizure came amid dissatisfaction with the ruling government and following a revolution three years earlier.

A coalition of armed forces and local armed groups backed by Saudi Arabia launched military operations and restored the internationally recognised government in Aden. Fighting resulted in the deaths of between 150,000 and 227,000 people, while millions were displaced.

While the Houthis controlled much of the north, the Yemeni government controlled the southern regions.

A UN-brokered truce in 2022 saw a lull in fighting and allowed aid to reach the deprived population, which has faced famine since 2016.

In 2023, the Houthis, who form part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” alliance of proxy armed groups, began disrupting shipping in the Red Sea in response to Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. In March this year, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel amid the war on Iran, officially entering the US-Israel war with Iran which began in February.

Tensions escalated when the group declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, shattering the relative calm in the country since 2022. It followed the announcement with a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back Yemeni coalition forces from the strategic port city.

In September, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.

On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, leader of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a military offensive to “restore state authority”.

Analysts say the scale of fighting means Yemen has fallen back into civil war as both sides come under scrutiny for targeting civilians.

As the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, declared that the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”, civilians, including women and children, are the ones bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.

The envoy stressed the need for the UNSC to support urgent mediation once more, although analysts have pointed out that recent gains by Yemeni government forces could mean they are more determined to push through the ongoing offensive, rather than agree to a settlement.

But “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now”, Grundberg warned.

Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, said: “It is beginning to resemble the 2015 Saudi-led coalition war on Yemen, when Sanaa and various other provinces were attacked relentlessly around the clock.”

A number of sites in Sanaa have been targeted, he said, including Sanaa International Airport. Several industrial facilities, including a chips factory in the north and a sponge factory in the south, have also been hit.

At least four telecommunications infrastructure sites have been struck in the capital and throughout areas controlled by the Houthi movement. Mount Attan in Sanaa was also hit by 10 air raids.

Mawry reported that, according to Saudi coalition officials, strikes have destroyed 136 military targets in areas under Houthi control, including military sites, launch pads and radars belonging to the Houthi group.

“Meanwhile, the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of targeting public infrastructure and telecommunications facilities, warning that the campaign risks plunging the country back into a humanitarian crisis similar to the one experienced from 2015 to 2022,” Mawry said.

The US, which has previously indicated that it does not want to get involved in the Yemen conflict, nevertheless on Friday called on the Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while demanding that Iran end its support for the group.

Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said Washington was “gravely concerned” by the Houthis’ recent escalation, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and airports.

“The pattern remains unmistakable. The Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians,” Bartos said.

“We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and we demand that Iran cease all support to the Houthis,” he added.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Government forces are looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August.

https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.title: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.author: Terrence O’Brien
https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-i.text:
Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’

Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’

After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed “unintended model actions,” including submitting a false tip regarding an unsolved murder, that led to the decision.

Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these.

The ability to gain access to the live internet, even when models were supposed to be operating in isolation, has been an ongoing issue for AI companies. Many incidents, including the Hugging Face attack, involved agents that were supposed to be denied access to the internet. Yet, in case after case, the agents found creative solutions to bypass those restrictions. Physically removing internet access would certainly improve security around AI testing, but it would also limit its usefulness.

The report also amounts to an admission that Anthropic is often unaware of what its agents are doing and does not have a reliable system for monitoring their behavior. Cutting off internet access is just the latest action the company has taken to try and rein in its agents, including temporarily pausing training its frontier models.

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/vance-mi.title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/vance-mi.author: Marshall Ritzel,Gabriel Cortés
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/vance-mi.text:
The Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from PERM, the Labor Department program that lets employers sponsor foreign workers for green cards.

Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing laid-off American workers with foreign hires.

Data shows two-thirds of Microsoft’s H-1B approvals went to people already working at the company.

Amazon and Meta, the nation’s two largest H-1B work visa sponsors, were not suspended.

As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft, claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas.

The suspension of the Labor Department’s PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn’t affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers.

Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon
 and Meta
 were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended.

The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department’s inspector general, Anthony D’Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad.

All eight suspended companies rank among the nation’s top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe
 is the smallest, at No. 45.

Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals.

The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/vance-mi.summary: The Labor Department suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from PERM, the Labor Department program that lets employers sponsor foreign workers for green cards. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing laid-off American workers with foreign hires.

Saturday’s blast followed ‌attacks earlier ‌this week on Riyadh airport that ‌killed four people

A loud ⁠blast was ⁠heard at the airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday, an eyewitness and people briefed on the matter ‌said, amid an escalation of missile strikes on the kingdom by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group.

The Saudi government’s media office and the Saudi civil aviation authority did not ⁠immediately respond to requests for comment.

King Khalid International Airport ‌urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight ‌status before heading to the airport. Etihad Airways ⁠and ⁠Qatar Airways cancelled multiple flights between their respective hubs ‌and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday.

Saturday’s blast followed ‌attacks earlier ‌this week on Riyadh airport that ‌killed four people, injured several others, damaged a ⁠Saudia aircraft and sent smoke billowing over ⁠the facility.

The strikes prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to ‌the Saudi ‌capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8vg.title: Drone strike by Sudan paramilitary kills 41 near Ethiopian border, rights group says
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8vg.text:
A drone attack by Sudan's paramilitary forces has killed 41 people in the country's Blue Nile region bordering Ethiopia, a rights group has said.

The strike by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a camp for displaced people in the state's Abu Shandi area on Friday, Emergency Lawyers said.

The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it was "appalled by horrifying reports". It said initial reports suggested most of the casualties were women and children.

The Sudanese army and paramilitary forces including the RSF have been locked in a power struggle since 2023, a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million from their homes.

It has also created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with millions of people needing medical help.

The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.

Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks.

Ocha said in a statement that the area reportedly struck on Friday had been "under sustained atttack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to grave harm".

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as ‘thanks’ for Trump diesel deal, Zelenskyy says
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Oliver Holmes
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Ukrainian president says money from fuel sales will intensify war as European leaders reiterate support for Kyiv

Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal cut by Donald Trump with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, accusing Washington of helping fund Moscow’s war.

The Ukrainian president has expressed repeated outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November midterm elections where the cost of fuel is a key voter issue.

The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.

He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 15 people, including three children.

“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.

“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.

There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.

In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.

“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.

The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.

“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.

Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationship with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.

The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.

Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.

Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.

Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.
