https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8e.title: Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8e.text:
A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in the third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.

The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital Warsaw, police have told news agencies PAP and AP.

It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which killed a female caretaker.

A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.

Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition is not life-threatening. Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had come to submit enrolment documents were also injured, the state news agency reported.

Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggest she did not know the three victims.

Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had arrested 76 people after deploying to schools across the country.

"When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.

Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.

A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8e.summary: Woman, 21, arrested after injuring three people in third knife attack at Polish schools this week. Police say she used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in Warsaw. It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw33.title: Saudi capital airport hit again, sparking evacuations, reports say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw33.text:
An international airport in the Saudi capital has been attacked again, reports say, just days after Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed two successful attacks on the hub.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was evacuated after a loud blast was heard on Saturday, two international news agencies have reported.

More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to Reuters, citing an eyewitness. Saudi authorities have not commented, while the airport told passengers to check with their airline before travelling there.

The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, were killed in two attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior.

Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.

They came during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.

The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

But the informal truce began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw33.summary: King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was evacuated after a loud blast was heard on Saturday. The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, were killed in two attacks by the Houthis the day prior. The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A replica of Donald Trump’s Oval Office goes for the gold in Washington DC
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The tourist attraction just unveiled an elaborate, full-scale overhaul to match Trump’s second-term aesthetic

S
itting behind a replica Resolute Desk, nine-year-old Sydney Wright posed for the camera like a future US president. “I love it,” she smiled. And what about the dazzling gold appliqués, gold leaf and gold trim surrounding her? “It’s cool.”

Sydney was among a steady stream of visitors on Thursday to The People’s House: A White House Experience, an interactive museum – with an orientation film narrated by The West Wing star Martin Sheen – at 1700 Pennsylvania Avenue, just 150 yards from the real thing.

Run by the White House Historical Association, the tourist attraction has just unveiled an elaborate overhaul of its full-scale Oval Office to match Donald Trump’s second-term aesthetic, described by the New York Times as a “gilded rococo nightmare”.

Gone is the understated, plain decor of Joe Biden and his predecessors. In its place is a spectacle of two dozen portraits in heavy carved frames, swirling wall onlays, gleaming brass vases and decorative knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface.

Barack Obama had pictures of two former presidents on the wall; Biden put up a total of seven paintings. Trump has stacked the walls with historical figures including George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin. Ronald Reagan appears twice, while there is only one woman on display: former first lady Jackie Kennedy.

A bust of former president Theodore Roosevelt by James Earle Fraser glowers from a bookshelf, flanked by bound volumes of the 26th president’s works. Other books on display include Hawthorne’s Works and Writings of Washington. There are two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence.

But for all the detail, the people’s house cannot recreate the experience of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who reportedly entered the Oval Office one day to find Trump in DIY mode, using superglue in an effort to stick gold ornaments to the fireplace.

Still, for many tourists arriving in the nation’s capital, this is as close as they will get to the heart of presidential power, especially with the White House currently undergoing extensive demolition and construction work.

Sydney’s father, Drew Wright, a 36-year-old firefighter from Athens, Georgia, said he viewed the room’s additions as “paying homage to the people who laid the pathway that we have to raise our children in this great nation”.

Asked about the goldening, Wright, who voted for Trump twice, replied: “There’s always going to be critics. There’s always going to be haters. Just because they’re the loudest ones in the room doesn’t mean they’re right. I don’t know what it looked like before but I think it’s a pretty classic look.”

Cheri Lujan Hamilton, 54, the chief clerk of the New Mexico state senate, also likes what Trump has done with the place. “I’m kind of in awe,” she said. “I was disappointed we couldn’t get into the White House for a tour so this is the next best thing.”

Taking in all the gold, Hamilton remarked: “It’s grand. I like everything that’s grand. I do think all the gold around the doors is maybe a little too much. But I like it on the top.”

Pedro Robles, 50, a police officer from Nashville, Tennessee, called the replica “pretty cool” and disputed the notion that the gilding crosses into bad taste. “I don’t think so,” he said. “I don’t think it looks tacky.”

Such opinions would be music to the ears of Trump who, when asked by Time magazine what he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, answered: “This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office.”

A team of specialised designers visited Trump’s actual office while he was away to ensure authenticity. They used 3D scanning in Indianapolis and crafted hand-carved gold frames in California, while teams in Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces.

The replica transition took one week with more than 25 crew members onsite. They used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls.

Matthew Costello, chief education officer at the White House Historical Association, said in an email: “As we have seen throughout White House history, each president transitions the Oval Office according to his own tastes. It is our hope that through the evolutions of our Oval Office replica, people will be inspired to learn more about and even see themselves in White House history.”

There is, however, one key difference between the real Oval Office and its imitator. While the actual workspace relies on gilded gold leaf, the museum opted for a specialised gold paint solution to protect against chipping or other wear and tear from visitors.

The transformation provides a microcosm of an aggressive campaign by Trump to remake Washington DC in his own image.

Beyond the Oval Office makeover, Trump knocked down the East Wing to build a $400m ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden’s traditional grass lawn to build a white stone patio reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, added a row of presidential portraits that replace Biden with an autopen and constructed a granite helipad on the south lawn.

He also initiated a troubled overhaul of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, proposed a towering 250ft triumphal arch near Arlington national cemetery and threatened to tear down the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts if it does not bear his name.

Washington purists and architecture critics have recoiled at Trump’s ostentatious tastes. But Carl Wilkerson, 73, a retired marine wearing a US Marine Corps T-shirt, offered an impassioned defense of presidential swagger, saying: “We need to have a little bling-bling, man. This is the United States of America. This is the greatest country on the planet, so we need to show it off.”

Drawing on his time overseas, Wilkerson, from Hereford, Arizona, argued that US presidential architecture had fallen behind the competition, saying: “You go over there in the east. He’s walked in their palaces and it’s like, boom. It pops. Their palaces outdid the White House 10 to one. We need to step up our game a little bit. We are the greatest country on the planet. So you need to act like it – and look like it.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: The White House Historical Association has just revealed an elaborate, full-scale Oval Office. Retired marine Carl Wilkerson, 73, offered an impassioned defense of presidential swagger.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: With or without Hamas
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.author: Lorenzo Kamel
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
As we begin the fourth year of a war that has brought the near-total destruction of Gaza, calls for Hamas to surrender administrative authority and evacuate the Strip are intensifying. For Gaza to have any viable future, it is argued, the group’s political and military wings must be dismantled.

While Hamas’s fate is a critical question, charting a meaningful path towards recovery is impossible without addressing the realities that gave rise to it in the first place.

What is happening today in Gaza is directly related to the origins of the Palestinian-Israeli question, which has little to do with any particular armed group.

Hamas did not exist in 1948, when hundreds of Palestinian villages, including Naj and Huj, were depopulated and destroyed during the Nakba – the Palestinian catastrophe that accompanied the creation of the State of Israel – to make way for the establishment of Sderot, Or HaNer and numerous other Israeli cities and villages built upon their ruins.

The group had not yet been established in 1967, when the Arab-Israeli War took place and Israel initiated its military occupation of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, while simultaneously seizing and unilaterally annexing East Jerusalem—actions that actively set the stage for the broader Israeli settlement project.

In the following decades, the occupation profoundly affected Palestinian society. That, combined with growing religious influence—as the number of local mosques tripled from 200 to 600 between 1967 and 1987  — and a vacuum left behind by a fading secular nationalist leadership, prepared the ground for the rise of faith-based nationalist factions. The outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987 was a political turning point that directly triggered the creation of Hamas.

The group was established by a group of Palestinian men, including three prominent figures. Ibrahim al-Yazouri, was born in Bait Daras, near today’s Ashdod, and was just eight years old when soldiers of the Haganah killed members of his family and expelled the survivors to Khan Younis, south of Gaza City.

Another founder, Abdulaziz al-Rantisi, was born in Yibna—a village near Jaffa whose ruins now sit beneath the Israeli city of Yavne. He was only a year old when Israeli forces expelled his family to Khan Younis.

Lastly, Ahmed Yassin, was born in al-Jura, a village near Ashkelon that was razed to the ground by the Israeli military. He was 12 years old, when he and his family had to flee their home and settle in al-Shati refugee camp on the Gaza coast.

Highlighting this history should not be misunderstood as an attempt to downplay Hamas’s responsibilities. However, the group’s actions cannot be separated from the historical context and the role the State of Israel has played throughout this process.

Unlike the self-proclaimed ISIL (ISIS) and other groups that have emerged in recent years—which lack deep roots in local societies and rely on obsolete ideologies—Palestinian factions are deeply intertwined with local society and national identity.

While Hamas’s trajectory is marked by several disastrous decisions—most notably its fatal decision to launch the assault on Israel on October 7, 2023—the group remains, above all, a symptom of a century of suffering, oppression and a relentless struggle for self-determination.

Any proposed solution – with or without Hamas – to the war in Gaza that fails to address these underlying realities is bound to fail. It must be emphasised here that the widespread tendency in the West to frame the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination as a “reward for Hamas” is deeply flawed. It stems from a systemic prejudice that must not be normalised.

The right was enshrined in international law and supported by an overwhelming majority of nations long before Hamas’s attack.

It is also a mistake to equate Hamas’s actions with the will of the Palestinian people. Today, nearly 50 percent of the population of the Gaza Strip is under the age of 18; when Hamas won the elections in 2006, more than half of Gaza’s current residents had not even been born.

Furthermore, in an Arab Barometer survey conducted in the West Bank and Gaza between late September and early October 2023, only 29 percent of Gaza respondents said they trusted the Hamas-led government. The majority blamed poverty on internal factors; 31 percent directly pointed to the Hamas authorities as being responsible for the situation.

Crucially, a majority (54 percent) supported a two-state solution to the conflict; 73 percent favoured a peaceful resolution. Just 20 percent favoured military action.

The presence of Hamas in Gaza cannot justify the Strip’s wholesale destruction and the crimes committed against civilians that have resulted in Israeli officials facing accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Hamas was not present at al-Nasr Hospital in November 2023, when the Israeli army left newborns to die in incubators after forcing their caregivers to evacuate and prevented their return. Hamas was not in the car with Hind Rajab, the young Palestinian girl, when Israeli forces fired 335 bullets into it in January 2024.

Ironically and unsurprisingly, Hamas has long been viewed as useful by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to maintain the argument that there are no moderate Palestinian partners with whom to negotiate.

This strategy aligns closely with the 2017 Subjugation Plan—officially titled “Israel’s Decisive Plan”—a political and ideological framework presented by Israeli far-right politician Bezalel Smotrich in 2017, which explicitly advocated for disregarding Palestinian national aspirations.

This refusal to address the structural roots has frozen the contemporary diplomatic landscape. The Israeli unwillingness to engage in dialogue with Palestinian interlocutors contrasts sharply with the pragmatic realism historically articulated by Israeli General Moshe Dayan, who famously observed that peacemaking requires negotiating with enemies rather than friends.

Today’s diplomatic landscape is defined by a deep imbalance in expectations. For many years, Palestinian factions have faced strict, non-negotiable prerequisites to attain international political legitimacy—such as the explicit recognition of Israel, the renunciation of violence and adherence to past accords.

Conversely, no reciprocal demands have been placed on Israeli authorities, who face no requirement to recognise a sovereign Palestinian state, honour previous treaties, or renounce violence.

In fact, Israel’s own political evolution is intertwined with factions that utilised political violence. Paramilitary organisations such as the Irgun, led by Menachem Begin, and the Lehi, led by Yitzhak Shamir, conducted operations that targeted civilians, yet both leaders eventually transitioned into mainstream politics and became prime ministers.

This power imbalance directly manifests as a diplomatic asymmetry also in recent ceasefire negotiations, which remain deadlocked by Israel’s demand for the complete disarmament of Hamas. By establishing the eradication of the group’s military capabilities as a precondition for a permanent truce, Israel’s leadership sets a political threshold that effectively forecloses a negotiated settlement.

This allows the Israeli government to perpetuate a status quo that yields significant strategic, territorial and political dividends.

Ultimately, doing away with Hamas will not do away with the Palestinian demand for freedom, nor will it satisfy Israel’s and Palestine’s legitimate right to security. The conflict did not begin with the rise of a militant faction and it will never end until all involved parties finally realise that, as Peruvian Indigenous jurist Dionisio Inca Yupanqui warned two centuries ago, “a nation that oppresses another ultimately forges its own chains”.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.summary: Hamas did not exist in 1948, when hundreds of Palestinian villages were depopulated and destroyed during the Nakba. The group had not yet been established in 1967, when the Arab-Israeli War took place. The outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987 was a political turning point that directly triggered the creation of Hamas.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Three injured in third school attack in Poland in less than a week
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Three ‌people have been injured in a stabbing attack at a ⁠further education ⁠college in Warsaw, in the third attack on a school in Poland in less than a week.

The series of incidents has stoked ⁠concerns in Poland about copycat violence among young people, and ushered police to check tens of thousands of schools and detain dozens of people across the country earlier on Saturday.

In the latest attack, a 21-year-old woman used a “dangerous object” on Saturday at about 12:30pm local time (10:30 GMT) to attack a 17-year-old woman, said Jakub Filipiak, a spokesman for Warsaw police.

The suspect also ended up hurting two other people, aged 17 and 24 respectively, he said.

“One person was injured and transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Two other bystanders also sustained injuries but did not require hospitalisation,” Filipiak added.

The police did not identify the educational institution, but said it was open on a Saturday because it is a higher education establishment. The attacker did not know any of the victims, the police said.

National Wyborcza newspaper identified the institution as TEB Edukacja, a school that gives post-secondary education. The suspect studied at this school, according to national media reports.

The attack came after police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools nationwide as part of efforts to prevent further violence following two school attacks earlier in the week.

On Friday, schools across Poland stepped up security, with some suspending classes, many parents keeping children at home and police patrols deployed to educational institutions after two attacks at schools earlier in the week left one person dead and several others wounded, including children.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the Mazovian province in central Poland attacked fellow students, teachers and passersby with a sharp object, injuring nine people before fleeing and being arrested nearby.

The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school custodian and wounded two others in a knife attack at his former school in the same province.

The assaults, both carried out by Polish nationals, shocked a country where school violence by minors is a new phenomenon.

By Thursday night, rumours that the attacks were coordinated and that there would be more on the culmination day dubbed “bloody Friday” were being shared in parents’ online groups and by mainstream media.

Fifty-nine schools pre-emptively suspended classes on Friday across Poland, the majority in the Mazovian district, where the capital Warsaw is located. School directors sent messages announcing stepped-up security measures including extra school staff placed at entrances and voluntary backpack checks.

“There will be no compromise here. The safety of the youth is the most important thing,” Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said.

The government earlier said that it had so far found no evidence that an internet challenge promoting school attacks was ongoing. There is also no official confirmation that any of the attacks are linked.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Three people injured in stabbing attack at a school in Warsaw, Poland. The attack comes after police detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools. The attacks have stoked fears of copycat violence among young people.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Liverpool vs Man City: Premier League – teams, prediction, Haaland, charges
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.author: Manasi Pathak
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Who: Liverpool vs Manchester City
What: Premier League, matchday 6
Where: Anfield, Liverpool, United Kingdom
When: Sunday, October 11, at 4:30pm local time (15:30 GMT)
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up and live updates from 12:30 GMT.

Manchester City will face the full fury of Anfield on Sunday when the Premier League leaders confront old rivals Liverpool in their first game since being found guilty of breaking the competition’s financial rules.

City can expect a hostile reception from Liverpool fans after an independent commission found they arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million ($1.2bn) between 2009 and 2018.

The financial breaches occurred during a period in which City won three Premier League titles and numerous other trophies, with Liverpool struggling to break the Etihad Stadium outfit’s silverware monopoly.

City have appealed against the devastating verdict and manager Enzo Maresca was bullish that they will overturn the original ruling. But the Premier League season is now stuck in stasis awaiting a ruling on the appeal and any potential sanction.

Liverpool supporters have often created a febrile atmosphere for City’s visits since they emerged as title contenders following the takeover by their Abu Dhabi-based owners in 2008.

This weekend’s showdown is likely to set a new standard for vitriol directed at City’s players and fans.

An independent commission found Man City guilty of nearly all of the 115 charges of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules between 2009 and 2018.

The Premier League said the commission found that City used schemes during the affected period to appear to comply with financial rules.

City have continued to protest their innocence and have lodged an appeal, but if the decision is upheld, then points deductions, fines, transfer embargoes and relegation are all possible punishments for the club.

A social media post promoting a “Bus greeting” has urged Liverpool supporters to gather near ‌‌the stadium several hours before kickoff with flags, banners, pyrotechnics and flares ahead of the arrival of the City players’ bus.

Merseyside Police said there would be an appropriate policing operation ⁠⁠in place on the day.

“If they want an understanding of how angry the game is going to be, then Anfield will tell them like you would never believe,” former Manchester United captain and England defender Gary Neville said on The Overlap podcast.

“I suspect there may be banners, there will certainly be chanting. There will be a reception like you have never seen for them at Anfield … it will be a brutal day.”

Over the past 12 years, Liverpool have finished second to City on three occasions. Only one of those, in 2013-14, came during the period under scrutiny in this financial breach controversy.

But City’s rivals believe the wrongdoing in that period built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who stepped down at the end of last season.

Opta’s supercomputer has handed City a 40.7 percent chance of victory on Sunday.

Liverpool have a 34.6 percent probability, while there is a 24.7 percent chance of a draw.

In his pre-match conference on Friday, Man City’s manager Maresca said he has absolute faith the club will win its appeal and rejected any suggestion that City’s haul of silverware over the past 15 years was now tainted.

“I completely trust the club,” said Maresca, who was appointed manager in June but also previously worked at City as part of Guardiola’s coaching staff.

“I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club. … There is not another club in the world where I would like to be.”

His Liverpool counterpart, Andoni Iraola, said the lack of clarity over City’s future is causing uncertainty throughout the Premier League.

“I think the worst thing probably is the uncertainty, that no one knows what’s going to happen,” Iraola said.

“But we have to focus on Liverpool – be the best club we can be, the best team we can be and that’s my challenge.”

While off the field, Man City are embroiled in a huge controversy; on the pitch, they’ve been the best team this season.

City are top of the Premier League’s points table with 15 points, winning all five games so far.

Liverpool are sixth in the standings, having won twice and drawn three times. They are on nine points, six behind City.

Man City and Liverpool last met on April 4 this year in the FA Cup quarterfinals.

Erling Haaland scored a hat-trick and Antoine Semenyo added another goal as City thrashed Liverpool 4-0 at the Etihad.

(Only in the Premier League)

(Last five matches, latest first; only Premier League games)

Liverpool were handed a huge blow ahead of Sunday’s heavyweight clash, with attackers Alex Isak and Cody Gakpo both ruled out.

Both players returned from international duty with injuries. Gakpo picked up an ankle injury playing for the Netherlands against Serbia, while Isak suffered what ⁠⁠Iraola described as a “small” thigh injury with Sweden against Romania.

Isak’s absence is a significant blow after the striker had finally found his form, scoring four goals in the opening five league games.

Neither injury is believed to be long-term, with Gakpo’s availability depending on how he copes with the pain while the club monitors both players day by day.

Haaland’s involvement against Liverpool had been in doubt after the striker came off during Norway’s Nations League loss to Portugal earlier this month.

But that was understood to be a precautionary measure amid an intense run of games during an extended international break.

Maresca has confirmed that Haaland, who has scored 169 goals in 205 games for the club, is available for their trip to Merseyside.

“He’s good. He went to Marbella, [had] two, three days off, played golf, recovery,” the City boss revealed. “Ready for Anfield. He’s good.”

Probable Liverpool XI (4-2-3-1): Alisson; Jeremie Frimpong, Ronald Araujo, Virgil van Dijk, Milos Kerkez; Ryan Gravenberch, Alexis Mac Allister; Victor Munoz, Szoboszlai, Bradley Barcola; Florian Wirtz

Probable Man City XI (4-2-3-1): Gianluigi Donnarumma; Matheus Nunes, Ruben Dias, Marc Guehi, Josko Gvardiol; Enzo Fernandez, Eliott Anderson; Jeremy Doku, Rayan Cherki, Iliman Ndiaye; Erling Haaland

An independent commission found City had arranged ‘sham’ deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million ($1.2bn) between 2009 and 2018. City have appealed against the devastating verdict and manager Enzo Erling Haaland has scored

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/trump-med.title: Trump’s Medicaid cuts strip health coverage from some legal immigrants—including refugees and victims of human trafficking
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/trump-med.author: Mikella Schuettler, Fatima Hussein, The Associated Press
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/trump-med.text:
New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of broader federal changes to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.

The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest Trump administration policy to target foreigners.

The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.

Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to a strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.

Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”

D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.

In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.

The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.

Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.

“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.

Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.

Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.

Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.

Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.

“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.

The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.

Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.

“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.

Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the administration deferred over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.

As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.

In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.

As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.

Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat.

“At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization.

UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months.

“We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said.

The change effective Oct. 1 will be part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers say
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.text:
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.

The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.

She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.

Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition in hospital.

Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.

Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to reschedule Pike's execution.

The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text:
Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".

The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.

The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.

"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.

The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.

The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".

The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.

Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.

Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.

Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".

He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Dozens reported injured in Yemeni Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Saudi authorities yet to confirm strike as government-allied forces in Yemen claim successful offensive to retake Bab al-Mandab strait

Yemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport in Saudi Arabia, with dozens reported wounded and a witness describing panic in the terminal.

Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.

“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told Agence France-Presse. “I saw [gate} 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”

A source at a local hospital told the news agency that five people were in intensive care after being wounded at the airport, and “dozens” more had been injured.

The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.

Witnesses said people were being evacuated from the airport.

Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.

The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.

A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.

“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”

By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”

The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.

An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.

It is thought that as many as 500 Houthis fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.

The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – the poorest country in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.

The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago, and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of the objective.

There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
March is first since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful

Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel.

The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine“ as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.

Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger, and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march.

The Metropolitan police have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.

The Metropolitan police posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.

“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”

The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.

At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”

Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”

Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.

“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.

The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.

A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.

The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.

Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.

The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.

The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.summary: March is first since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position that Israel’'s occupation of West Bank was unlawful. Thousands of people gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians. Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat

Nine people, including children, died in a mass murder on Friday in Erie, Pennsylvania, after a gun-wielding attacker opened fire outside a home and then entered the property, according to authorities.

The suspected attacker was also found dead as police responded to the deadly violence, which triggered a standoff involving Erie police officers and tactical teams.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Police discovered the killings at about 5pm when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities that they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside.

Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered fatal gunshot wounds.

The situation quickly developed into a standoff as police officers and tactical personnel surrounded the residence. More gunshots were heard coming from inside the home, and officers entered the place.

Inside, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding seven additional victims, including children, along with the suspected attacker. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, spoke about the scale of the mass murder, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed.

“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public.”

He added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”

Authorities on Saturday said they were still investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings, with authorities attempting to determine a motive for the violence.

The city of Erie also issued a statement on social media confirming that the suspected shooter had died and that the immediate danger had passed.

The statement described the case as a “terrible tragedy”, although the city’s statement did not provide further information about the events leading up to the shooting.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, has killed two people and left hundreds of thousands of customers without power across the southeastern United States.

The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane before weakening as it moved inland through Alabama overnight.

One person died in Birmingham, Alabama, when a tree fell on a house overnight, according to local emergency officials. A second person was killed in Escambia County, Florida, after a tree fell during the storm, according to local authorities.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said on Saturday that state officials had not confirmed any storm-related fatalities, including the report from Escambia County.

Isaias hit land with sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), bringing powerful gusts and heavy rain to the Florida Panhandle. By Saturday morning, the storm had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone with wind speeds of about 55km/h (35mph).

More than 900,000 electricity customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday morning. That number has since gone down to under 800,000, according to PowerOutage.us.

Fallen trees and downed power lines caused widespread disruption, while flooding forced road closures in parts of southern Alabama, including Houston County. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said on Saturday morning that her team was concerned about “strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes”.

Local officials in Pensacola, Florida reported strong winds that damaged an airport and tore the roof off a hotel. Trees and power lines also came down across the city, leaving some residents without electricity and roads blocked.

Despite the storm’s weakening, officials warned that dangerous conditions could persist. Heavy rainfall threatened flash flooding across parts of the Southeast.

“The flooding story is not over,” DeSantis said on Saturday, warning that saturated ground and continued rainfall could cause dangerous flooding a day or two after the storm passed. He said state search and rescue resources would remain available in case rapidly rising waters required emergency rescues.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to be alert for contractors seeking to exploit storm victims as homeowners begin repairing damaged properties.

https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202610.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/sport/202610.text:
French prodigy Paul ⁠Seixas rode solo ​to claim the first Monument victory of his career ​at the Giro di Lombardia on Saturday, ahead of Spain's Enric Mas and Italy's Giulio Ciccone.

The 20-year-old attacked 19 km from ​the finish ‌in Como (Italy) to claim the title ⁠won by Tadej Pogacar for the last five years.

READ MORE
French teen prodigy Paul Seixas to make Tour de France debut this year

The Slovenian missed the ‌race after crashing at the Vuelta a Espana two ⁠months ago. Seixas won his first Monument – one of the five most prestigious one-day races in professional cycling – ​in his third appearance. He finished seventh ‌in this race last year and second behind Pogacar at the last Liege–Bastogne–Liege.

Seixas, who finished fourth in this year's Tour de ‌France, pulled clear on the Civiglio climb with 19 km to go. Britain's ​Tom Pidcock and Ciccone were the only riders able to follow his wheel.

The Frenchman dropped both rivals a few hundred ​metres later and rode alone over the final 18 ​km to become the youngest Monument winner ​since 1944 and youngest ever winner of the Giro di Lombardia.

The Decathlon–CMA ​CGM rider is the first Frenchman to win a Monument since Julian Alaphilippe at Milan–San Remo in 2019, and the first to triumph at the Giro di Lombardia since Thibaut ⁠Pinot in 2018.

The victory came two weeks after a huge disappointment for ⁠Seixas at ​the World Championships, where he finished 15th after starting among the favourites.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.title: King warns malicious online actors are evolving tactics
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.text:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

The letter from the King to NCSC came after he spoke to AI executives at Dumfries House in Ayrshire last month on how the tech can be used to benefit security.

The meeting followed a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.summary: King Charles III wrote to National Cyber Security Centre to mark 10th anniversary. He spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics" by using automated technologies. He said he was filled with "profound gratitude" for the work done by the agency.

A driver look at his overturned truck in a flooded parking lot on Saturday morning in Tiger Point, Fla., close to where Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday night.

Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed.

Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.

One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.

"The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email.

Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

"We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence."

Hurricane Isaias forced a Waffle House restaurant to shut down when it passed through Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane.

As of 11:50 a.m. ET Saturday, about 780,000 power customers remained without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the monitoring site Poweroutage.us. That figure had been closer to 900,000 earlier Saturday.

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.

The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

An uprooted tree is seen in Gulf Breeze, Fla., on Saturday. The southeastern U.S. faced a high risk of flooding as Isaias, weakened from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, moved northward.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to theNational Hurricane Center. It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county,"tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as theFlorida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger

A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire, police have said.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated shortly after the incident and the site will remain closed on Sunday.

South Yorkshire police said that at 1.35pm it received reports of an individual entering the enclosure at the zoo near Doncaster.

The force said the attack “resulted in serious injury”.

The statement added: “Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time.

“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”

The force earlier said: “We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this distressing footage.”

Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.

It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Pike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical care

Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.

Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”

Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.

But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.

Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.

There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.

Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.

Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.

Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.

After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.

Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation. And the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year, but they continue elsewhere.

For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.
