https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Huge wave’ of carbon storage projects causes alarm in small-town USA as oil firms eye billions in subsidies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Erin McCormick in Cass county, Indiana, with photographs by Kaiti Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Dozens of projects are in development across US despite concerns over environmental and health risks

The plan to bury carbon under remote Indiana farmland is supposed to be a slam dunk for the climate, according to its supporters – all generously funded by US tax dollars.

But as far as Melissa Harrison and some other residents of Clymers, Indiana, are concerned, it just might be the end of their town. “This is our place,” she says. Generations of her family are buried in the cemetery, and she is raising her five grandchildren in one of several dozen white-clapboard homes among cornfields and industrial plants serving the farming industry.

Now a local ethanol plant has spearheaded a project to bury vast stores of carbon deep in the geologic formation that runs under the town and surrounding farms.

The government subsidies for the plan, which is supposed to help prevent global heating, are so generous that companies all over the country have been rushing to get permission for similar projects.

But residents around some of these carbon sequestration projects are organizing to stop them, making Clymers a center of emerging national tensions around these projects.

While international climate monitors say carbon sequestration projects could be secondary tools to help contain global warming, they also say the main focus must be on urgent and deep cuts to fossil fuels. Some environmental groups question the benefits of carbon sequestration and are concerned it could delay the transition to clean energy and pose risks to surrounding communities.

Harrison said the town of Clymers was already overburdened by hazards from industrial agriculture facilities including a fertilizer supplier, a hazardous waste recycling company and the giant ethanol plant that is proposing the project. She said the community faced contaminated well water, a lack of sewage facilities and high poverty rates.

Warmly remembered as once having been a thriving “heartland” community with a beautiful white church, two grocery stores, a Chevy dealer and a diner, the town is now struggling. Its school is closed; the old Methodist church has been demolished and the playground is surrounded by fertilizer tanks on trailers, which the fertilizer company rents to nearby farms.

Harrison, like other residents in the area, received a letter about the project. Some were asked to accept $150 a year in exchange for having the carbon sink under their properties.

“If they make Clymers bad enough that no one wants to live here, they can take over the whole town, real cheap,” she said.

In a statement to the Guardian, the company proposing the project, the Andersons Renewables, said it “is a safe, established technology, with a rigorous permitting, engineering, and monitoring process to protect groundwater, public health, and the surrounding environment”.

“The proposed project would capture carbon dioxide from the ethanol production process, compress it, and then inject it deep underground, more than 3,000 feet, into geologic formations identified for permanent storage,” said the statement.

“We were able to determine the site’s suitability through seismic analysis and by drilling a test well,” it added.

The company, which was partly owned by a subsidiary of Marathon Oil at the time it proposed the project, said in its statement that it understood why residents might be concerned, but it planned to work transparently with the community to allay those worries.

The undertaking is one of dozens of carbon sequestration projects expected to be given the green light for construction in the US by the Environmental Protection Agency and state environmental regulators in the next year – as a flood of corporate permit applications reach the end of their approval processes. Oil industry companies are often sponsors and benefactors of these projects.

Carbon sequestration involves capturing industrial CO2 emissions that would normally be vented to the atmosphere before they can contribute to global heating, and burying them in rock formations thousands of feet underground for what proponents say is permanent storage.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has said carbon capture storage (CCS) is one mitigation option that could help keep global heating in check, assuming it supports deep fossil fuel cuts, but has warned it should not be over-relied on. Both Democratic and Republican presidential administrations have supported such plans in past years. The Biden administration authorized a lucrative tax credit reimbursement program for them as part of the Inflation Reduction Act.

The Trump administration, which has called the climate crisis “a hoax” and canceled funding for many other types of climate projects, continued this tax credit, which often benefits energy companies that are already using underground technology such as fracking. It offers companies $85 in transferable tax credits for each ton of point-source carbon stored – a bounty that has set off what some call “a carbon-capture gold rush”.

Since even the smallest projects expect to store hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon each year, the tax credits could be hugely profitable, said Brad Johnston, an analyst with Enverus, an energy industry market research company and data company that tracks permits for this type of project. Many are proposed for ethanol plants, which emit a nearly pure stream of CO2, making their emissions simpler to capture and put underground.

While only a handful of projects are operating, a “huge wave” is about to be approved, Johnston said.

Experts say the money brought in to these companies by tax credits from these carbon projects can rival the revenues from selling the actual ethanol itself, thereby potentially doubling a plant’s earnings.

Many environmental groups criticize the projects, saying they merely subsidize oil and gas industry companies and don’t reliably cut emissions at scale.

For instance, a small project that sequesters 200,000 metric tons of carbon per year can earn $17m annually through a tax credit called 45Q. Larger projects plan to sequester tens of millions of tons of carbon, said Kerwin Olson, executive director of the Indiana group Citizens Action Coalition, which has helped residents in the state organize against the many projects proposed there.

“You can do the math,” he said. “That is a lot of cash – an enormous amount of cash.”

“You’re talking billions of dollars.”

Environmental experts say the risks of carbon storage include earthquakes, water table contamination and potentially deadly carbon leaks, and point to several cases where carbon has leaked.

In 2024, the nation’s first commercial carbon capture project, under a lake that provides drinking water for large parts of central Illinois, developed two leaks. The state subsequently banned new CCS projects under one of the state’s biggest aquifers.

In 2020, a pipeline carrying carbon dioxide ruptured in rural Mississippi, creating a mass poisoning that resulted in 45 people being hospitalized and 200 evacuated. Emergency responders found people lying on the ground unable to breathe and didn’t know what was happening. “It looked like you were going through the zombie apocalypse,” Jack Willingham, emergency director for the affected county, told NPR.

Charles Harvey, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at MIT, helped to start one of the world’s first companies devoted to sequestering carbon to prevent global heating in the early 2000s. But since then, he has become a staunch opponent of the strategy, and acknowledged experiencing guilt akin to what J Robert Oppenheimer felt over inventing the atomic bomb.

“It’s just the stupidest way to reduce emissions,” said Harvey. Oil companies are lobbying hard for the projects, he said, but he believes CO2 emissions could be best tackled if the money was spent on renewable energy.

“It is loved by the industry because it’s a subsidy for whatever they’re already doing,” he said.

Johnston, the Enverus analyst, said that, given the setbacks caused by the Illinois leaks, his sense was that companies were being extra careful to engineer their projects to avoid any further problems.

“I think any additional setback from a leak or a failure of one of these wells would be pretty detrimental to the CCS industry,” he said. “So I think a lot of these operators are very diligent about doing it right and probably overbuilding a lot of these systems.”

The Clymers project’s sponsoring companies called a meeting of residents and landowners in the area and told them that the carbon storage was perfectly safe and couldn’t leak.

“I said that’s bullcrap. I’m worried about my well,” said farmer Dennis Crume, who refused to sign the form offering him $150 an acre to accept the plan. But Indiana state law essentially strips individual landowners of the right to reject these proposals, experts say.

Crume grows soybeans and corn on several plots of land skirting Clymers, some of which he leases from other owners. He raises a few cows in a grassy field behind his house and tries to grow everything his family eats in his garden. But he worries about the pollution he sees cropping up all around him.

“I’m trying to look out for our grandkids,” said Crume, who has 11 of them living nearby. “We’ve got to do something for the environment.”
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.summary: Dozens of projects are in development across the US despite concerns over environmental and health risks. Environmental groups criticize the projects, saying they merely subsidize oil and gas industry companies.

Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital and returned to a Tennessee women’s prison after surviving the US state’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said on Saturday.

The 50-year-old is back in the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she had been incarcerated for 30 years. She had been in hospital since September 30 when officials administered two doses of pentobarbital in an attempt to execute her.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer.

Her lawyers said she was continuing to receive medical care in prison and that they would monitor her recovery. They also expressed gratitude to the first responders and medical team who treated her.

The failed execution has drawn attention to the US death penalty as a separate controversy unfolds over the military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan. The former army psychiatrist was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. His execution is scheduled for December 3.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement on Thursday of the livestream drew criticism, even from some supporters of capital punishment. Vice President JD Vance questioned on Friday whether it would happen and said he would not watch. In a social media post, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the proposal “beyond disgusting”.

Archbishop Paul S Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, also condemned the plan, calling it “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death”.

In Tennessee, however, Pike’s failed execution has not prompted Republican legislators to reconsider capital punishment. Instead, some have discussed alternative methods, including the electric chair and firing squads.

Support for the death penalty in the US has declined from its peak in the 1990s. Ten states have abolished capital punishment since Pike was sentenced in 1996, but executions continue nationwide.

Thirty people have been executed in the US this year, with eight more scheduled, mostly in Texas and Florida.

A Pew Research Center poll in July found that about two-thirds of US adults considered the death penalty morally justified for people convicted of murder. But roughly six in 10 said it did not deter crime, while about seven in 10 said there was some risk of an innocent person being executed.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Eritrea urges UN to intervene in standoff with Ethiopia
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Eritrea has asked the United Nations to take “deterrent measures” after what it called Ethiopia’s “declaration of war” in the conflict over the Tigray region.

Eritrea’s request comes a day after Addis Ababa, in a letter to the Security Council, accused Asmara of launching an “all-out invasion”, saying Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s Tigray.

In a separate letter to the council on Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh said the claims of an Eritrean incursion were part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression and urged the UN to intervene, invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows measures from sanctions to military action.

The neighbouring countries have accused each other of starting a war over Tigray, where Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing rebels.

An alliance of seven armed groups launched attacks against federal Ethiopian forces in the northern region last month, as they attempt to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.

Eritrean forces have since reportedly intruded into Ethiopian territory, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).

The Ethiopian army pushed TPLF rebels back this week and seized the region’s capital, Mekelle. It also said it launched drone strikes against Eritrean troops in the region.

“Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea … and take the requisite deterrent measures,” Eritrea’s Saleh said in the letter on Saturday.

He said Ethiopia’s action would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.

Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos on Friday accused Eritrea of “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.

Timothewos invoked Ethiopia’s right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, but he did not specify what measures the country was taking.

Faisal Roble, a Horn of Africa specialist, believes both sides are “preparing for the last phase of an open conflict”.

“There is really no doubt that both of them are inching towards an open conflict,” he told Al Jazeera from the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.

“Whatever they write to the United Nations, it is just posturing and making sure that they have some sort of international support on their side,” the analyst added.

In his letter, Saleh called Ethiopia’s actions “deceitful attempts to rationalise its brazen acts of war”, claiming that they were “hollow in substance”.

Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Friday of pursuing aggression against Eritrea through its demands for sovereign access to the Red Sea. Writing on X, he did not explicitly confirm or deny the reported troop crossings.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.

Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, and they fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000.

Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.

Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab.

TPLF fighters battled Ethiopian government forces, then backed by Eritrea, in a devastating 2020-2022 war.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/petra-.title: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/petra-.author: Lucas Ropek
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/petra-.text:
As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power.

Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles.

Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight.

The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.”

Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.”

As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said.

Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department.

Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said.

“Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.”

The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. But Petra’s product has not actually deployed on a live vehicle yet, Goodman clarified. Instead, the fuel cells are in the testing phase, during which the government is deciding whether to move forward, he said.

Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said.

Petra Power was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. You can catch all the action this coming week in downtown San Francisco at Moscone West.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/cloudf.title: Cloudflare acquires Deno to improve its Workers programming model
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/cloudf.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/cloudf.text:
Cloudflare announced Friday that it’s acquiring Deno, the startup behind the programming runtime of the same name.

According to Cloudflare’s Kenton Varda, Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform, which allows customers to build and run software on Cloudflare’s network. (Varda is principal engineer for Cloudflare Workers.)

Deno — which was co-founded by Bert Belder and Node.js creator Ryan Dahl — recently launched celld, an open source implementation of Workers, which Varda wrote “delighted” the Cloudflare team. Varda argued that contrary to “a popular theory” that the company “made Cloudflare Workers work differently from other cloud platforms in order to create ‘lock-in,’” the company believes “being open source and giving people an escape hatch is good business.”

Dahl, meanwhile, wrote that his team is “joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model a mainstream way to build servers.”

The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Deno had raised a total of $26 million, including a Series A led by Sequoia.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/cloudf.summary: Cloudflare is buying Deno, the startup behind the programming runtime of the same name. The company will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform.

A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.

A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.

Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger has confirmed that “one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.”

Photos and videos posted on X and Threads appear to show a small circuit board sandwiched under the screen. The implant allegedly intercepts anything displayed on the screen, including the seed passphrase shown during the initial setup. Using an embedded SIM card, the implant then sends that information back to the attacker, who can then siphon funds from user accounts.

Reports indicate that whoever is behind the hack has stolen over $86 million worth of crypto from hundreds of wallets. There’s no indication that Ledger’s systems have been compromised or that wallets purchased directly from the company have been affected. Instead, the issue appears to be a supply chain attack primarily involving users in Southeast Asia and the CryptoBillis reseller. Ledger has provided guidance on how to check if your wallet has been tampered with.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/anthropic.title: After Anthropic’s Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case, police say ‘cases involve real victims, grieving families’
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/anthropic.author: Mae Anderson, The Associated Press
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/anthropic.text:
An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said.

It’s the latest example of AI models acting in unintended ways and manipulating government and other websites during tests. In a report Friday, Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission.

The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said.

Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site.

Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police.

There are rising concerns about AI companies’ unchecked AI agentsmeddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation.

In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models.

“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the Philadelphia Police Department said in a statement. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”

Anthropic said in its report that most of the reported behaviors are forms of what it calls “persistence” — “in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping.”

The company said it was modifying its training to “reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.”

Anthropic said it briefed the White House on cases that involved U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, and notified each agency involved.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/baby-boom.title: ‘Fantasy economics’: Baby boomer vs. Gen Z tensions hit France as pension costs drive debt crisis and education cuts that fuel student protests
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/baby-boom.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/baby-boom.text:
Bond market turmoil and the simultaneous mass student protests at French schools are not a coincidence and point to the generational tradeoffs made in government spending, according to Nobel laureate Paul Krugman.

In a Substack post on Thursday, the economics professor at the City University of New York’s Graduate Center acknowledged that the high debt and deficits driving up French bond yields lately are not unique to the eurozone’s second largest economy.

In fact, the U.S. is guilty of the same fiscal sins, especially as aging demographics push entitlement spending up faster than revenue comes in.

“But France does stand out, even among fiscally troubled nations, in one main way: its persistent inability to get realistic about retirement,” Krugman added.

That’s as France’s official French retirement age, when workers can collect full benefits, was just 62 in 2023, while the average actual age of retirement was lower than anywhere else in Western Europe at only 60.4 years.

Meanwhile, French students are taking to the streets to protest missing teachers, run-down classrooms, and buildings that aren’t equipped for rising temperatures. Protestors blame years of underinvestment in public education.

Krugman drew a straight line from France’s retirement largesse to the student unrest, highlighting the generational tensions over how to allocate public resources to baby boomers versus the country’s youth.

“Thus the fiscal pressure caused largely by France’s very generous government pension plan has led to cutbacks in other spending, notably on education,” he wrote. “France is effectively handing over large subsidies to older French at the expense of everyone else. Mass national student demonstrations should come as no surprise.”

Of course, U.S. debt is also on an unsustainable trajectory as spending on seniors jumps amid more baby boomer retirements. But even some Republicans have expressed openness to tax hikes to keep Social Security’s trust fund solvent.

For his part, French President Emmanuel Macron attempted to raise the retirement age to 64, but intense political pushback has stalled those efforts.

And the front-runner in France’s presidential election next year, far-right leader Marine Le Pen, has vowed to roll back the official retirement age to 62 and even previously suggested dropping it to as low as 60.

“This would be extremely expensive and is symptomatic of a general unwillingness on the part of France’s rising right to face reality,” Krugman said. “Again, this is hardly unique to France — think of all the false promises and claims Donald Trump has made. But for now, at least, financial markets believe that fantasy economics is an even bigger problem for France than for the rest of us.”

Indeed, markets are pricing in growing odds of a French debt default. Earlier this month, French 10-year bond yields jumped to the highest since 2002, and the premium over equivalent German yields widened to the most since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011.

Those metrics later eased, but France’s fundamentals remain troubling, with anemic GDP growth, a budget deficit estimated at about 5.4% of GDP, and rising debt-service costs as yields jump.

France’s debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to climb to 122% next year from 119% this year, and the government’s latest plan failed to halt the surge in bond yields as investors doubted its credibility.

Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry, global strategists at Macquarie, also drew a connection between the French debt crisis and the student protests.

In a note Wednesday, they warned that the longer the protest go on, the more likely it is that the government will cave and approve more spending, which would make the debt situation worse.

That would drive up yields on French bonds, making borrowing to fund that spending even more expensive—and thus worsen the problem that the rioters are complaining about.

“France is veering toward a full-blown civil crisis because of its political polarization, which heretofore had been manifested mainly in the political realm itself, and at the ballot box only,” they wrote. “And rather than being isolated events, we think a direct and self-reinforcing causal connection can be drawn between the rise in France’s debt yields and the street riots of the past few days.”

https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.title: Convicted murderer Christa Pike leaves hospital, returns to prison after botched execution
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/americas/202.text:
The convicted murderer who survived a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee last week has been discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers said Saturday.

Christa Pike, 50, was administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on September 30 that failed to kill her.

READ MORE
Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after surviving Tennessee execution attempt

She was transported to hospital in critical condition but later regained consciousness, with her lawyers saying this week that she was walking around but in a "foggy" mental state.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her lawyers said in a statement Saturday.

Pike was sentenced to death in Tennessee for murdering a classmate, a crime committed when she was a teenager.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the statement went on.

Pike "is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery", the lawyers said.

The attempted execution came after days of last-minute legal wrangling that ultimately reached the Supreme Court.

Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.

Since the botched execution, her lawyers have repeatedly called on Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.

Lee has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.

Pike's stunning survival renewed focus on the ethical debate surrounding capital punishment in the United States.

That debate has intensified following the Pentagon's announcement this week that it intends to livestream an execution by firing squad later this year.

The move has prompted outrage from a broad array of public figures in the United States, including many Republicans supportive of the death penalty.

Pope Leo, the first American pontiff, posted Saturday on X that "the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person".

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," he said.

The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place.

The federal government instituted a moratorium under president Joe Biden, but President Donald Trump's administration lifted it when he returned to office in 2025.

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-says-ukraine.title: Trump says Ukraine should elect a new president
https://www.dw.com/en/trump-says-ukraine.text:
President Trump has criticized Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not making a deal with Russia to end the Ukraine war. He has also warned Kyiv against targeting Russian oil refineries.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said it's time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting that current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to put an end to Ukraine's war with Russia.

Speaking at the White House, Trump said, "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," adding that ”for some reason (Zelenskyy) never does."

Zelenskyy has "lost 30% of your country and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

The US president also warned Kyiv against targeting Russian oil refineries.

Trump said he had told Zelenskyy to "do what you want" against Russia, but "don't hit refineries."

"He better damn well stop," Trump said.

https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-suspe.title: Saudi Arabia suspends operations at Riyadh airport after an attack causes multiple injuries
https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-suspe.text:
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has already been targeted multiple times this week amid intensified fighting between Yemen-based Houthi rebels and a Saudi-backed coalition.

A number of people were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday, the country's civil aviation authority has confirmed.

"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.

"The attack resulted in a number of injures, which are currently being assessed."

The General Authority of Civil Aviation said operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.

A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.

The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."

Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."

The reports come amid intensified fighting between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.

The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.

Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.

There was no immediate Houthi statement about the reported blast on Saturday.

Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.

The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.

The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-looks-to-ste.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
https://www.dw.com/en/india-looks-to-ste.text:
The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?

In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.

"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.

"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.

For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.

"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."

Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.

At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing.

"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.

She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.

For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.

However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.

"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.

Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".

However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.

"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole.

"India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"

Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.

"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."

BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.

The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.

Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.

"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.

She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.

There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.

Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.

While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.

"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."

Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."

He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.

"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.
https://www.dw.com/en/india-looks-to-ste.summary: The 18th BRICS summit takes place in Delhi this weekend. India is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO. But many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8.title: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.

Zelensky warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war in Ukraine.

Speaking to the media as he left the White House on Saturday, Trump said the Ukrainian president "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.

"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".

Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.

"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," he said.

"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."

Trump confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.

Zelensky reacted by saying the relaxation of the penalties will allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.

On Saturday the EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism, saying suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."

She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.

The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8.summary: US President Donald Trump says Ukraine should get a new president. He says Ukraine's president should stop attacking Russian refineries. Russia and Ukraine have intensified their strikes on energy-generating and transport facilities.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Nine killed in shooting in US state of Pennsylvania, including two children
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Nine people were killed Friday in a shooting in the US state of Pennsylvania, according to Governor Josh Shapiro. Police said the suspected shooter was among the nine dead.

Local media reported that two children were also among those killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, which is 188 kilometres (117 miles) north of Pittsburgh.

Police in the city of Erie were called Friday around 5:00pm local time (21:00 GMT) to reports of shots fired and discovered two women dead in the street, the Erie News Now outlet said.

The attacker barricaded himself inside the home as police surrounded the building and ordered him to exit.

More gunshots were heard during the standoff, Erie News Now reported.

When police eventually entered the building, they found several more victims around the home, including the two children. The deceased attacker had an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, the outlet said, citing police.

Erie News Now said that police officers who responded to the scene were being offered counselling over the horrifying incident.

“I have not seen anything like this in my 28-plus years,” Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah told a local news station on Saturday. “I’m not sure that the city of Erie has ever seen the loss of life and the devastation that we just witnessed.”

Lorah declined to provide more details but said the circumstances of the shooting were “deeply disturbing”.

Shapiro said Saturday he offered his administration’s “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin.

Mass shootings occur frequently in the United States, where guns vastly outnumber the population and efforts to increase firearm restrictions face steep political and legal hurdles.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Police say the suspected shooter was among the nine dead. Two children were also among those killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania. Police say they are being offered counselling over the horrifying incident.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Pope Leo XIV has declared that the death penalty is “inadmissible” while his home country, the United States, announces plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

Marking World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, the pope reiterated the Catholic Church’s teaching on capital punishment, writing on X that it was “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person”.

“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” his post said.

“Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” added the leader of the Catholic Church.

The American Pope’s comments come days after US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan on December 3 will be livestreamed.

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009.

Pope Leo did not specifically refer to the planned execution, or last month’s botched execution attempt on Christa Pike, who survived two doses of the lethal injection in Tennessee.

But his post came hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, told Vatican News that the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution was “unacceptable”.

It was Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, in 2018 who first amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances.

Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church did not exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.”

The planned livestream of Hasan’s execution has sparked outrage across the US political divide. Republican representative Austin Scott said he supported executing Hassan but that “livestreaming executions is what Jihadists do. America is better than that.”

Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice”, but that public executions are “the kind of thing that Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?”

On Thursday, a Pentagon official confirmed the plans, but on Friday, Vice President JD Vance, who is a practising Catholic, expressed doubt on whether the livestream would be going ahead, telling reporters that if it is, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Pope Leo XIV has declared that the death penalty is ‘inadmissible’ while his home country, the United States, announces plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. The American Pope wrote on X that it was ‘an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person’

https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.title: Riyadh airport suspends operations after attack leaves multiple people wounded
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.author: FRANCE 24
https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/.text:
Saudi authorities suspended operations at Riyadh's international airport on Saturday after a fresh attack there left multiple people wounded.

The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency", a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility.

The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen's Houthis.

The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday.

READ MORE
Diplomats take shelter in Saudi capital as Yemen's Houthis target Riyadh airport

A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic.

"I was on gate 403" at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."

A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday.

"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh", with many in critical condition, the source said.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, with officials issuing few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.

The aviation authority said the number of injured from Saturday's attack was still being assessed, adding airport "operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities".

A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with "dozens of people injured" in all.

A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass.

Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport. Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Mecca had been injured while waiting to board their flight.

A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by "a missile around 3:00pm" (1200 GMT).

"Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target," the source said.

The Yemen conflict flared back to life after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle Eastern war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.

The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war in the region.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen's government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour's civil war.

Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.

The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was "aware of attacks" on Riyadh airport on Saturday and called on American citizens to avoid the area.

The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Spain's embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a "new attack... by the Houthis".

A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies "indicated that they had decided to prohibit their staffs' travel to/from Riyadh Airport over the next week as a prudential step". Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station.

READ MORE
Yemen says advancing against Houthis around key Bab al-Mandab strait

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.

The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.

The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area – a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but they claimed to have repelled the assault.

Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Saudi civil aviation authority confirms attack injured several people at King Khalid International Airport. Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/w.title: Billionaires want to colonise the Moon but whether they can is complicated
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/w.author: Tessa Flemming
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

German scientists test newly developed spacesuits as the race to inhabit the Moon speeds up. (AP: Martin Meissner)

The 20th century ignited a space race between the US and USSR.

But in this century, a new race emerges between billionaires and major world powers to control the Moon.

SpaceX's Elon Musk wants to build a self-growing city on the Moon within a decade, a dream researchers have said could be near-impossible due to its lack of water.

Meanwhile, Blue Origin's Jeff Bezos has shared his desire to colonise the Moon.

There are echoes of old Cold War tensions rising between the US and a Russia-China alliance, as reports emerge of a race to build nuclear reactors on the Moon.

It begs the question: Can anyone actually own the Moon?

An artist's impression of a Bezos-owned Blue Origin New Glenn spacecraft, designed to help create settlements on the Moon and in space. (Supplied: Blue Origin)

The 1967 United Nations Outer Space Treaty (OST) arrived at the height of the Cold War, after a USSR rocket carrying a Soviet flag crashed onto the lunar surface in 1959.

It raised concerns in the west about USSR claims of sovereignty over the Moon.

While that never eventuated, it did kickstart the ethos of a free Moon for all.

US President Lyndon B Johnson (far right) sits beside US Secretary of State Dean Rusk as he signs the OST. (Wikimedia Commons: ITU)

One of the OST's key rulings is that the Moon should be "used exclusively for peaceful purposes", prohibiting weapons testing or military use on its surface.

Other key articles related to the Moon are below:

The exploration and use of outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries, irrespective of their degree of economic or scientific development, and shall be the province of all mankind.

Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be free for exploration and use by all States without discrimination of any kind, on a basis of equality and in accordance with international law, and there shall be free access to all areas of celestial bodies.

There shall be freedom of scientific investigation in outer space, including the moon and other celestial bodies, and States shall facilitate and encourage international co-operation in such investigation.

Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means.

The OST was endorsed unanimously by the UN's General Assembly, but in the years since, its limits have also been tested.

The Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle's view of Earth in 1969 after the historic Moon landing. (Reuters: File)

The problem with the OST, as Hussein Badreddine, a specialist in space law at the University of Sydney explains, is that the treaty is "very general and broad".

Notably, the OST has no provisions for mining the Moon.

In 1979, the UN Moon Agreement treaty tried to address this by ruling that "the Moon and its natural resources are the common heritage of mankind".

However, only 18 nations (including Australia) ratified that treaty.

The US and Russia were not among them.

A scientist, an engineer, an archaeologist and a lawyer break down some of the physical, environmental, ethical and legal challenges of mining on the Moon.

Dr Badreddine said the suggestion that nations would need a licence to mine the Moon, with a fee that would then be shared amongst humanity, was seen by some US companies as "trying to socialise the Moon".

Instead, in 2015, an act granted US citizens and private entities the ability to own and sell space resources.

Luxembourg, the UAE and Japan enacted similar legislation.

Fellow space lawyer Cassandra Steer, however, is more optimistic about OST's endurance.

She has previously written about its merits and said she maintained "faith in the long-term endurance of the treaty, because it's most useful to think about as a constitution".

"The 'non-appropriation principle' in Article II is certainly under pressure, but what seems to be happening is a convergence around a new interpretation of the treaty, rather than discarding the treaty."

Actions like those of the US, Luxembourg, the UAE and Japan were "widening the interpretation of what's possible", she said.

The global space industry is on a trajectory to be worth a trillion dollars by 2030, the UN says. (Reuters: NASA/Kim Shiflett)

Rebecca Connolly, Space Law Council of Australia and New Zealand chair, believes "the Moon is becoming the next frontier of geopolitical competition".

She said it was a competition where "being first matters".

"Countries that establish infrastructure and sustained operations on the Moon may gain considerable influence over how future activities are conducted," Dr Connolly said.

Gaps in international law raise concerns about who will control access to the Moon and its resources. (Reuters: NASA/Handout)

Dr Steer said the risk that SpaceX could control access to, and resources on, the Moon was "something that keeps me up at night".

"The US can't get to the Moon without SpaceX, but SpaceX could do it without the US, even without government contracts at this point," she said.

"Even if SpaceX were contracted by the NASA, there is still a possible scenario where SpaceX lands first on resource-rich lunar real-estate, and is able to use AI and robotics to build enough mining infrastructure to deny access to whoever comes second, and that is a real concern."

Already, a SpaceX rocket crash has carved a crater in the Moon. (NASA via AP)

The US is establishing a new non-binding set of guiding principles around lunar exploration.

The NASA-led Artemis Accords hope to reaffirm support for the OST, and build guardrails around space debris and the use of space resources.

Seventy-six nations have signed up so far, but Russia and China rejected them.

The US space agency has outlined plans for a sprawling lunar outpost involving rovers, hopping drones and resource-extraction technology as part of a renewed race to the Moon.

It is why Dr Badreddine prefers a treaty "under the UN umbrella" that specifically addresses military activity, resource extraction and environmental concerns.

"That treaty must be detailed and it should be negotiated under the auspices of the UN rather than outside the UN," he said.

What the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs does have is a working group, which is recommending legal principles for space resources.

Its last round draft recommendations, in April this year, recommended the Moon and its resources could not become property of any state or organisation.

It also reaffirmed the need for peace on the Moon, a message that seems more pertinent than ever.

What started as one small step for man has turned into one giant "what if" for space. (Supplied: NASA)

Last week, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans for weapons innovation, pointing to the need to dominate "any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon".

It comes after the US confirmed for the first time it had deployed weapons in space.

Unlike the Moon, space does not have the same guardrails for peace.

But any battles on the Moon would be a "flagrant" breach of the OST's principles, Dr Steer said.

"It would also probably be in breach of the UN Charter," she said.

"But none of that matters to the current administration.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.title: Author Trent Dalton's diary scrawls sent singer Katie Noonan a lifeline
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.author: Leisa Scott and Vanessa Gorman
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Katie Noonan's marriage heartbreak inspired her most vulnerable album to date. (Australian Story)

As ARIA award-winning singer Katie Noonan sat in the audience watching author Trent Dalton's book Love Stories coming to life on stage, her own love story was falling apart.

That day, Katie found out that the 26-year partnership with her jazz saxophonist husband and father of her two children was all but over.

"I remember that day so vividly," Katie, 49, tells Australian Story. "It was quite intense actually, watching that play and the searing honesty of how hard [it is] in the trenches, being married and being artists."

After the show, Katie bumped into Trent, the author of the international bestseller Boy Swallows Universe, and his wife and co-writer of the play, Fiona Franzmann.

Katie Noonan and Trent Dalton, who first met 25 years ago, have joined creative forces. (Australian Story: Vanessa Gorman)

Katie and Trent had known each other since 2001, when they were enthusiastic young creatives from Brisbane; he was a fledgling journalist who had come to interview her, the breakout star with the ethereal voice from the indie pop rock band named george.

Now, as they caught up over a drink, Katie told Trent how much the play had touched her. How beautiful the writing was and how real it felt.

And that her own marriage was in serious trouble.

"She really let me know she was going through one of the toughest times in her life," Trent recalls. "And that was where my relationship with Katie kind of got a bit more poignant."

Katie Noonan is adjusting to a new pace of life at her Sunshine Coast home with Saffy her loyal staffy by her side. (Australian Story)

Six weeks later, Katie was out of the family home and living alone in a new place on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

"There have been days that were catastrophically hard and dark and lonely and depressed and all those things," Katie says.

But music has always been her best friend, and so she turned to it.

Exploring different music genres is a hallmark of Katie's career. One of her projects is the Australian Vocal Ensemble [AVE], an a capella quartet that celebrates the work of Australian writers such as Tim Winton and the late David Malouf.

Katie Noonan finds solace in music, especially in difficult times. (Australian Story: Marc Smith)

She knew Trent and his writing would be perfect as AVE's next muse. "I reached out to him and said, 'Do you have any words?'"

He had plenty. He had 153 pages of thoughts, lyrics and dreams he wrote as a lovesick young man falling for Fiona. He said Katie could have them.

The result was not just a new piece for AVE but an album about love — the wonder and the heartache — and a creative outlet that has helped Katie on the road to healing.

Recorded live in Katie Noonan's lounge room, the album Alone but all one features her vocals and piano accompanied by a string quartet. (Supplied: Katie Noonan)

Growing up, music filled the Noonan household. Katie's mother, Maggie, was an acclaimed opera singer and singing teacher and her late journalist dad, Brian, had been a crooner on shows such as Bandstand.

"One of my fondest memories," Katie says, "[is] sitting in bed with Dad Saturday mornings, listening to ABC Radio, listening to The Goons and the Jazz Show while Mum was teaching."

Katie Noonan's childhood was filled with music. (Supplied: Katie Noonan)

After leaving school, Katie studied opera at the Queensland Conservatorium of Music (often called The Con) while living in a house "full of thespians, actors and musicians and incense and patchouli oil and a lot of djembes and fire twirling and crystals".

This potent mix led to the formation of the band george (sporting a lower-case g), with Katie's older brother Tyrone on keyboards and guitar.

Polyserena by george was one of the biggest Australian albums of 2002. (Supplied: Festival Mushroom Records)

As Katie explored her musical options, switching to jazz at The Con, the band started touring and building a loyal following.

The 2002 debut album Polyserena reached number one and stayed in the charts for 15 weeks, buoyed by the support of radio stations such as the ABC's triple j and Brisbane community radio station 4ZZZ.

"We were sort of the seven-year overnight success because we'd been touring and touring and touring," Katie says.

By then, Katie had met the man who would become her husband.

"I adored and was madly in love with him," she says.

Within 18 months of marriage, they had two boys, and although Katie's husband played in her next band, Elixir, Katie had the capacity to earn the most.

She became the primary breadwinner, touring widely with a range of bands and different musical genres, while he stayed home to look after the kids.

"As a wife and mother and making so many sacrifices to be the breadwinner, it puts a lot of pressure," Katie's mother Maggie says.

Katie Noonan with her parents Maggie and Brian Noonan. (Supplied: Katie Noonan)

From the outset, Katie was determined to do music her way, without surrendering to commercial interests. When a record company executive told her to lose weight early in her career, she told them "no" in a rather colourful manner.

"I've never been afraid to have an opinion," she says. "I'm always going to speak up for things that matter to me."

Having artistic control in such a fickle industry was so important to Katie that 15 years ago, she started her independent label, an "act of bravery and lunacy in a lot of ways".

Elixir was a folk jazz trio that collaborated with cartoonist Michael Leunig (far left). (Supplied: Michelle G Hunder)

It's a tough way to make a living. Albums don't sell in big numbers anymore, she says. And the streaming service Spotify gives very little, if anything, back to artists, a subject Katie has often spoken out about.

So the answer is to tour — and keep touring. "I will play anywhere," she says. "I love playing little, tiny halls … and then I get to play the Opera House."

But when COVID hit, everything went belly-up. Katie was three dates into a 25-day solo tour when the plug was pulled on live gigs. "The financial pressure was staggering," Katie says.

"I put on a lot of weight during COVID … plus a bit of perimenopause rage thrown in," she says. "And, you know, also drinking too much."

There were problems in the marriage before the pandemic, Katie admits, but "COVID broke us".

Now, as Katie pulls her solo life together, she acknowledges that separating was the best option, even though she would not have made that decision.

Today was a day I gave my new address and my solo Medicare number

I was one of four for so long, but never again

Now I am alone, but all one

Now I am alone, but all one

Today was a day, I got asked for my next of kin

I stood frozen as the tears bloomed out as I realised I didn't have one anymore

Today was a day like that moment weeks ago — where he blew my world apart with a letter from the law and angry silent apathy

She's desperate for her relationship with her now-adult sons to get back on an even footing but accepts they need time.

"I've stuffed up, I've overshared way too much with them emotionally," she says. "I wish I hadn't in retrospect.

"Being largely estranged from my children has been a sorrow that I wouldn't wish upon anyone, but … they know I love them."

There have been times, Katie says, when she felt she wouldn't get through the day.

On other days, songs just "fell out", demanding to be written. The result was one half of her new album titled Alone but all one.

"It was an album that I never intended to write," she says. "[It] just fell out from a place of deep sadness and sorrow and loss and grief and not knowing who I was anymore."

Katie Noonan says her latest songs just "fell out of her", spawned from a place of grief and sorrow. (Australian Story: Marc Smith)

Amid that torment, she received Trent's 153 pages, his words celebrating "the wonderment" of new love — and a sliver of light entered.

"That was a great gift for me that I needed because I couldn't write those," Katie says. "I was deep in the other world."

Trent Dalton's writings conveyed the feeling of falling in love. (Supplied)

Katie is at her piano, singing When the Heart Falls Apart, one of the songs on the new album, while Trent watches on.

Under his elbow is one of his dog-eared notebooks, the pages into which a 20-something Trent poured his joy at having found Fiona — and the pages from which Katie found the words that helped her navigate her marriage breakdown.

Katie Noonan and Trent Dalton collaborated on Katie's new album. (Australian Story)

The juxtaposition of the joy of love, seen through Trent's eyes, and Katie's heartbreak at its loss is the essence of the album.

It's a thrill for Trent that his "really revealing, really embarrassing" words have found a life outside these pages more than a quarter of a century after writing them.

He's even more chuffed that Katie "took all of that and just turned it into something that might get somewhere close to her feeling better".

"All that gushing I was doing, I think somehow reminded her of the truth — that it was true love," says Trent of Katie's love story with her husband.

Trent Dalton flicks through some of the 153 pages of notes he gifted to Katie Noonan. (Australian Story)

"Like any story, the ending shouldn't be the definition of the entire story," he says. "You are allowed to look back on beginnings and middles and go, 'That was amazing.'"

Katie says while the past two years have been the most challenging of her life, she's now at a point of gratitude — for the life she is building and the love she shared with her husband.

"I'll always love him because he's the father of my children and he is a beautiful human and an amazing musician," Katie says.

"I'm so grateful that he allowed me to be an artist because he decided to be a stay-at-home dad. I couldn't have been an artist without him."

Katie Noonan's 30th studio album explores love in all its stages. (Supplied: Katie Noonan)

Music is her constant. It has been "my succour, my panacea" throughout her heartbreak, she says, and she's immersing herself in it.

For Katie's Australian Vocal Ensemble, a 13-piece song cycle called Just for Dreaming has been created, with music by Jessica Wells and lyrics based on Trent's notebook musings about his hope for a better life after a messy, troubled childhood.

She's heavily involved with the Eumundi School of Music, the "legacy project" she and friends began 10 years ago, providing professional music lessons and scholarships to budding school-age musos.

And Katie Noonan is touring again, singing the songs from the album she never intended to write but, with a little help from a friend, is the one she needed to bring to life.
