https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.title: Union says cruise ship crews still open to exploitation under legal loophole
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.author: Jasper Wells
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A decades-old exemption to Australian labour law for cruise ships has been extended with some new protections for workers. (ABC News: Jasper Wells)

A legal exemption for cruise ships from Australian labour law has been altered to allow some new protections for crew.

Critics say the legal loophole that left them vulnerable shouldn't have existed in the first place and allows for worker exploitation.

The exemption was due to expire at the end of the year but has been extended to 2028.

The union that represents cruise ship workers has warned that the exploitation of staff will become "embedded" in the industry after the federal government extended a decades-old exemption that allowed cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour law.

The government has announced new protections for cruise workers following an ABC News investigation that revealed allegations of shocking conditions among the crew on some Carnival Cruise vessels.

It includes the ability to collectively bargain and make complaints to the maritime safety regulator.

Passengers boarding a Carnival cruise ship are promised a world of endless food, relaxation and oceanic luxury. But for the crew, life is vastly different.

But the government has decided to continue the practice of allowing cruise ships an exemption to labour laws, extending the long-standing exemption until 2028.

The ABC revealed in August that workers were accusing the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations.

Transport Minister Catherine King called the allegations "horrifying".

Catherine King said the new conditions on the exemption would help draw tourists as well as protect workers. (ABC News)

In response to the investigation Australia's anti-slavery commissioner said: "I think some change in this area is long overdue."

Maritime Union of Australia national secretary Jake Field said the exemption should never have existed in the first place and did so at the expense of Australian jobs.

Introduced in 1998, the exemption lets cruise ships avoid Australian labour law and instead follow the looser international Maritime Labour Convention.

The new obligations are the first time cruise operators have had conditions attached to their exemption.

Originally expiring at the end of this year, it was extended until 2028 with the new conditions that ship operators cannot restrict crews rights to collective bargaining, and complaints about working conditions must to be reported to the maritime regulator, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority.

Under the new conditions, cruise operators can no longer restrict crews' rights to collective bargaining.

The ABC has seen letters from Carnival that warned crew against the presence of Maritime Union of Australia representatives at ports and reminded staff that they were under no obligation to stop.

Carnival corporation operates over 90 ships globally, with around 100,000 crew on their ships at any one time. (ABC New: Pete Garnish)

Transport Minister Catherine King said in a statement that the changes would protect workers while supporting Australia's maritime industry.

Carnival and Royal Caribbean Cruises did not comment when asked if they would begin bargaining with crews. Carnival said it was considering the details of the announcement.

Carnival operates three ships full-time in Australia: Adventure, Encounter and Splendor. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The changes also mean that all crew complaints regarding the Maritime Labor Convention must be reported to the Australian regulator.

It is intended to give the government a better understanding of the types of complaints being made about conditions and how they are managed.

The government has said it will be the last time the exemption is renewed and it is considering a review of the laws, the findings of which are not yet public.

Carnival operates three ships full-time from Australia, with roughly 1,000 crew on each, mostly flown in from South-East Asian and African countries.

In a previous statement to the ABC, Carnival rejected the allegations made by crew and said the maritime authority had carried out "surprise inspections of our three ships in recent weeks and cleared Carnival on each occasion".

It said that the company followed international standards.

The Maritime Union argued the changes do not go far enough.

Jake Field said the exemption should not exist in the first place and it would "further embed an industry built on exploitation at the expense of foreign seafarers".

Some crew members allege the company would not treat them when they were sick, and that they had to buy their own food and water when the ship was in port. (ABC News: Jasper Wells)

Almost 1.5 million Australians went on cruises last year, according to the Cruise Lines International Association.

Ms King said that cruises were a vital economic driver for port towns across Australia and a draw for international tourists.

Mr Field said the union had been telling Carnival that their employees wanted to bargain with them, to no avail.

"They've responded to that by not allowing New South Wales [SafeWork] to access the vessel," he said.

"That's how serious they take the rights of workers."

Carnival previously said in a statement: "SafeWork NSW has no regulatory role covering international seafaring."

https://www.dw.com/en/trump-slams-zelens.title: Trump slams Zelenskyy, says Ukraine should elect new president
https://www.dw.com/en/trump-slams-zelens.text:
President Trump has criticized Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not making a deal with Russia to end the Ukraine war. Trump also warned Kyiv against targeting Russian oil refineries that will supply the US with diesel fuel.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said it's time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting that current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to put an end to Ukraine's war with Russia.

Speaking at the White House, Trump said, "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a [peace] deal," adding that ”for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does."

Speaking to Ukrainian citizens, Trump claimed Zelenskyy has "lost 30% of your country and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

Independent estimates put the percentage of Ukrainian territory under Russian control at 20%, with British defense officials recently stating that about half a million Russian soldiers had been killed in the war and that there were no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians had died.

The US president also warned Kyiv against targeting Russian oil refineries.

Trump said he had told Zelenskyy to "do what you want" against Russia, but "don't hit refineries."

"He better damn well stop," Trump added.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3y0.title: Expedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote island
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3y0.text:
A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart's plane.

The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance.

The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate.

The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.

Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938.

The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel.

They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country.

When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef created by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.

"Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said.

Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.

From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.

But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.

Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference.

The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earheart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel.

While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered.

One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.

Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.

But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's.

Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water.

"I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said.

The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory.

But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago.

Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.

In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.

Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

They are currently halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard a ship. The group are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island by Monday in the Pacific Ocean. The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.title: The Kennedy Center names new artistic director, amid concerns
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.author: Anastasia Tsioulcas
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-599.text:
The blocked-off entrance to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Oct. 1. The center has been shut to the public since September.

The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. His appointment came despite complaints from staff about his business practices as a consultant for the arts institution.

According to an email obtained by NPR sent to high-level staff Thursday, Matt Floca, the center's executive director and chief operating officer, announced that Canny would be the center's new artistic director. Canny has served as a consultant to the Kennedy Center since shortly after President Trump became the institution's chairman in February 2025.

Floca has no background in arts administration, programming or fundraising, in contrast to chief administrators at similar performing arts venues around the country. He was previously head of facilities at the Kennedy Center before being promoted in March, and holds a degree in construction management.

Floca wrote: "Rick will advise me and the broader leadership team on artistic strategy, business practices, presenting and talent curation, ticketing and pricing models, media opportunities, and programming sponsorships."

Floca also wrote: "Since April 2025, Rick has worked with the Center as a consultant through his firm, Favor the Artist, including serving as creative lead for the Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize. He will continue in this capacity while serving as the Center's Artistic Director."

The Kennedy Center is mostly closed, but it says it will maintain a small amount of public and educational programming, while the entire closure is being contested in federal court. The previous head of programming came and left within two weeks in January.

Arts administrators around the country have told NPR that booking performances for performing arts centers is done years in advance.

The Kennedy Center did not respond to NPR's requests for comment on Canny's appointment, but confirmed the contents of the email. Canny also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Favor the Artist's website does not include any information about its client roster or about the firm's history. The published lists of his professional background indicate that Canny has little experience in programming the kinds of performers more typically booked at a venue such as the Kennedy Center, including marquee contemporary solo performers and groups, orchestras, and dance and theater troupes.

NPR has obtained an internal memo written in March by the center's then-senior director of music programming, Sammy Miller, raising concerns about fees and expenses charged by Canny. NPR has reached out to Miller for comment, but did not receive a reply.

In that memo, sent to Floca and the Kennedy Center's human resources department, Miller said that during one month in early 2026, Canny had charged the center $30,000 in consulting fees. And in another month, Canny had charged over $28,000 in fees and travel expenses, including two first-class round-trip flights between Los Angeles and Washington, D.C.

The Kennedy Center did not reply to NPR's request for comment regarding staff concerns about Canny. In a statement to The New York Times on Friday, the center said that the $30,000 fee "did not reflect Mr. Canny's current agreement," but did not provide specifics. The institution also told the Times that Canny's travel expenses had been reviewed.

Miller wrote that he had previously tried to resolve his concerns through the center's general counsel and its finance office, but "both offices appear to be protecting Mr. Canny."

In its recent public statements and court filings, the Kennedy Center has repeatedly claimed to be on the verge of bankruptcy. Last month, Trump said that the arts institution has lost "hundreds of millions" of dollars. Trump has not offered evidence to support that claim.

The Kennedy Center remains shut to the public while Trump and the center's board, most of whom were hand-selected by the president, fight in a federal court to shutter the institution for two years for a large-scale renovation. Last month, Trump threatened to tear down the center if his name is not prominently displayed on the building.

https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.title: Photos: Thousands march across Europe to demand end to Israel’s war on Gaza
https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.text:
Several thousand pro-Palestinian protesters have marched through European capitals, demanding an end to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

In London, demonstrators moved past the British parliament carrying placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine”.

“We are here today to mark three years of the ongoing genocide in Gaza,” Aimee Shalan, director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, told the AFP news agency, calling for “full sanctions on Israel”.

A so-called ceasefire took effect a year ago, but Israel continues to strike Gaza on a near-daily basis. The attacks have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the truce began, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

London’s Metropolitan Police said they made “several arrests”, including a man and a woman holding placards supporting Palestine Action, a group banned under UK law.

Officers had also warned they would use public order powers to compel anyone wearing face coverings to remove them, pledging “zero tolerance” for hate crimes.

In Berlin, about 3,500 people joined a march organised by United for Palestine, police said, setting off from a square between the chancellery and parliament. Many condemned Germany’s arms exports and longstanding military support for Israel.

Similar marches were held in Warsaw and Rome, where protesters denounced ongoing Israeli bombardment and their governments’ ties with Israel, echoing calls for an immediate and lasting ceasefire.

Israel’s genocide has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,200 Palestinians since October 2023.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Attack on airport in Saudi capital, Riyadh, leaves several injured
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
The latest attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital has injured several people, according to the country’s Civil Aviation Authority.

Operations at the airport in Riyadh were temporarily suspended after the attack on Saturday afternoon, said the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). Its statement added that officials were assessing the damage and determining the exact number of injuries.

On Thursday, at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in Houthi attacks at the airport, according to GACA.

Those attacks were launched by Yemen’s Houthi group, which is at war with Riyadh and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in Aden.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen on Saturday, said the Houthis have yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack.

But the Iran-backed group has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target.

Earlier on Saturday, King Khalid airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic. The airport did not specify the cause of the disruptions in its initial advisory.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also instructed Saudi citizens travelling to the kingdom to contact local embassies if their travel itineraries have been disrupted following the attack.

Following reports of the latest attack, President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether the United States planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the ⁠⁠⁠⁠recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.

At the same time, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in the kingdom.

The US mission said it was “aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh” and “strongly recommends” all US citizens avoid the airport and surrounding areas.

The British and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”.

Japan’s embassy “strongly” condemned Houthi attacks on airports and other Saudi civilian facilities.

Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights because the airport had closed due to a “security situation”.

On Thursday, the Houthi military spokesperson said that the Yemeni armed group had launched a ballistic missile towards the airport in Riyadh, claiming that the missile successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.

Days earlier, alleged Houthi attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports killed three civilians and injured 36 others.

At least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in Houthi attacks at the Airport on Thursday. The Houthi group has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/christa-p.title: Christa Pike is discharged from a hospital and back in prison after becoming the first person to survive lethal-injection drugs during an execution
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/christa-p.author: The Associated Press
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/christa-p.text:
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, her attorneys said Saturday.

Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her attorneys said in a written statement.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the statement said.

Pike had been hospitalized since surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point she was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance.

The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed.”

The failed execution brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of what went wrong. The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution

As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

Pike was hospitalized since surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her. She was hospitalized after surviving two dose of pentobital.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/trump-us-.title: Trump says he’s evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi Arabia’s fight against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen after fresh attacks on Riyadh
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/trump-us-.author: Samy Magdy, Cara Anna, The Associated Press
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/trump-us-.text:
The airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, was attacked again Saturday and evacuated, two regional officials said, just days after three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war.

President Donald Trump told reporters he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen who have claimed this week’s attacks on King Khalid International Airport as well as other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure.

“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

In the latest attack, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights at the Riyadh airport and many people were wounded, one of the regional officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Ambulances were seen rushing there.

The surge in attacks has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate Houthi statement Saturday.

Saudi civil aviation authorities said operations at the airport had been suspended and the number of wounded and damage were being assessed. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.

Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.

The attacks on airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, has rattled markets and the region.

Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces in an attempt to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.

The rebels’ gains gave them better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that’s a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign ended that.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Officials said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive.

The Saudi and Omani foreign ministers spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region, the kingdom said Saturday. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.

Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.”

This week, the Houthis warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

At least 225 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.

Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines have been among the airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for the next few days.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.”

The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.

In Thursday’s attack, the Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/g.title: New Australian comedy horror asks if we can still laugh at Nazis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/g.author: Velvet Winter and Yasmin Jeffery
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/g.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

British actor Asa Butterfield plays a police officer with a very unique problem in Gnomes. (Supplied: Stan)

After spending ten years developing her horror-comedy series Gnomes, co-writer Tegan Higginbotham had a concern plaguing her mind.

Can we still laugh at Nazis?

"We grew up on Mel Brook's comedies where Nazis are funny," she says.

Created by Joel Kohn (The Mirror), Higginbotham co-wrote the series with her husband Paul F Verhoeven, as well as pulling double duty as one half of a ditzy police duo, the other half being fellow comedian Matt Okine.

Gnomes might be set in a small Australian township but its set-up hinges on a deadly but petrified European gnome queen who was stolen by the Nazis in the final whiffs of WWII as Hitler's last-ditch attempt to regain power.

"We really enjoyed playing into genre and have the bad guy Nazis, and we wanted to evoke that straight from the get-go," Higginbotham says.

The killer gnomes that plague Nompton can be traced back to some very dim Nazi officers. (Supplied: Stan)

Hitler's bumbling Nazi guards fail to activate the gnome queen's power, inadvertently tipping the first domino that results in a plague of killer gnomes terrorising the tiny fictional town of Nompton.

"There is also, of course, that very known history that Hitler had that side where he's interested in the occult and would try to capture artefacts," Higginbotham says.

"And, you know what? I still want to exist in a world where Nazis are funny. It's really concerning me that we're back to a place where they're being taken seriously."

Tegan Higginbotham and Gnomes creator Joel Kohn. (Supplied: Stan)

From Resident Evil's box office smash to Widow's Bay's near clean sweep of the Emmys, horror-comedy is having a moment in 2026.

It was the heady combination of genuine over-the-top, B-movie horror and smart, quippy comedy in Gnomes which secured its leading man, British actor Asa Butterfield.

"What attracted me to the project was the writing and comedy, and the sort of absurdity of it. There were great characters, some great gags, and some really funny references to some classic horror movies," Butterfield says.

Arnold's team gets the bad news about their precinct just before gnome havoc is unleashed. (Supplied: Stan)

The Sex Education star plays Senior Sergeant Arnold Kipps who is having one of the worst days in his career.

His ex-partner and former flame Ellie (Megan Smart) has long moved up in the police ranks but suddenly returns to Nompton's minuscule station to break the news that the town is just too darn boring to justify a full police staff.

The powers that be are closing up shop and Arnold and his sergeants are most likely getting the can.

Newcomer Widow's Bay has pulled off a near-clean sweep at the 78th annual Emmy Awards, winning Outstanding Series, Writing, Directing, Lead Actor, Supporting Actor and Supporting Actress in the comedy categories.

As if this isn't enough to deal with, Arnold is stuck babysitting the aforementioned gnome queen, the star attraction at Nompton's Gnome-a-palooza festival.

An unfortunate accident involving Arnold reawakens the queen who animates all the garden gnomes in town to do her deadly bidding.

"It's been really fun to empower these gnomes with genuine fear and terror, but also knowing they are just garden gnomes," Butterfield says.

Creating the army of gnomes was a challenge for the production team, which brought the cursed creatures to life with a mix of puppetry and special effects.

"We had a great SFX team building hundreds of gnomes, some made of foam, some that could smash, some that can run," Butterfield says.

"Having natural puppets to react to really helps because you don't only have to imagine it. Like there's a vampire gnome there, it's stalking you on the top of a dresser. Or a wizard gnome shooting actual fire out its wand.

"It's the sort of a thing which, honestly, brings out the big kid inside me."

Luke McGregor's video store clerk is one of the Nompton residents who has an unfortunate run in with a possessed gnome. (Supplied: Stan)

Higginbotham is still shocked that the movie star agreed to sign onto a tiny Australian show about killer gnomes.

"I can't believe he said yes. When they first mentioned that Asa was even considering the role and reading the script I was like, 'That's great. But this is never going to happen,'" she says.

"I've never quite worked with a performer like him. This is somebody who's been doing this since he's a kid. He's just a class above.

"The way he conducts himself on set, the love that he has for every single person on set and for their craft and what they individually do. I mean, I've never seen the man do a bad take.

"He's truly a remarkable actor and we've been so lucky to have him."

"Asa is heaven, he really is. He brings this positivity to set that really bolsters everyone around, and it's such a nice energy on set," Megan Smart told ABC of her Gnomes co-star. (Supplied: Stan)

While Butterfield might have been able to micro-dose a Melbourne lifestyle (read: get very into coffee) in his seven weeks filming the series, what impressed him most during his time in Australia was the quality of the local screen industry.

"We moved incredibly quickly, which is credit to the crew and the team to be able to pull off a show that's this ambitious. You couldn't do that back home or in the US, there's no way," he says.

"You would have thought that in doing that people would be more stressed. And yes, it's stressful. But everyone always has a smile on their face, which I really appreciate.

"Everyone says, 'Yeah, we can do that.' I wish our crews back home had a bit more of that energy."

It might have taken 10 years for Higginbotham to get anyone to jump on board with Gnomes, but for the writer the wait was worth it.

"I know 20-something-year-old me, who wanted it all to happen right away, wouldn't agree with me saying this, but I do believe that things happen when they're meant to," she says.

"It's the right time for this sort of entertainment. It was meant to be now. For whatever reason the universe wanted me to have that lesson, for all of us to have to be patient."

Gnomes is streaming on Stan now.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/l.title: Archie the flying fox joined Richard Morecroft behind the news desk
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/l.author: Shannon Corvo
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Media Industry

Late presenter Richard Morecroft fostered baby Archie. (ABC News)

Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft is best known for his decades of news reading, but unbeknownst to viewers, he was sometimes joined at the desk by a furry companion.

Morecroft, who died this week aged 70, was a familiar presence as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS.

But if you were to peek under his shirt as he read particular news bulletins in late 1987, you would find another passion.

Wrapped inside a handkerchief was a baby grey-headed flying fox.

Morecroft adjusting Archie before presenting the NSW 7PM news bulletin. (ABC News)

Archie was considered well-versed in current affairs. (ABC News)

Morecroft originally thought it was a boy and named it Archie.

"I think probably of its species, that little flying fox ... was probably the best educated in terms of knowledge of news and current affairs," he said in late December, 2001.

"Thousands of people watching at home wouldn't have known that there was a small furry animal wrapped in a handkerchief stuffed inside my shirt."

The presenter said the handkerchief was used to keep the pup warm.

Morecroft getting his makeup done with Archie. (ABC News)

Morecroft fostered two-week-old Archie, who he believed belonged to the Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park colony, after completing a Wildlife Information and Rescue Service (WIRES) training course in the late 1980s.

Archie and Morecroft recorded their journey together in a 30-minute Wildscreen episode with ABC TV's natural history unit, titled Raising Archie.

"This is a young grey-headed flying fox which came from a colony not very far from Sydney," he explained during the program.

"His mother died and so I'm the new foster parent for a few months.

"What we're hoping is that eventually he will be able to rejoin the colony and get back into the wild."

Morecroft encouraging Archie to fly. (ABC News)

He said pups needed lots of attention.

"They have to have nappies changed, their fur cleaned and be wrapped up as they would be in their mother's wings."

At one point, Morecroft encouraged an older Archie to fly.

The documentary also highlighted threats facing colonies, including overdevelopment and the impact of flying foxes raiding orchards.

Morecroft also interviewed iconic naturalist, David Attenborough, with an older bat named Gollum.

David Attenborough and Richard Morecroft with a bat called Gollum. (ABC News)

A letter Morecroft sent to his trainer in November 1987 reveals more about how he cared for Archie.

"It's been a delight (and occasionally quite a challenge) to have the opportunity to raise a young flying fox," he wrote.

"According to weight and forearm measurements (90 grams and 60 millimetres) a couple of days after receiving her, she must have been very young when orphaned.

"However, she seems to be progressing well (now 107g and forearm 71mm) and is enjoying exercise sessions."

Baby Archie, the grey-headed flying fox. (ABC News)

He said Archie "took particular delight" in being groomed.

"Warm, damp cotton buds are great for the armpits and the 'hip pits!'" the letter read.

"And a soft baby's toothbrush grooming the fur produces either a relaxed ecstasy or a vigorous cooperative effort with tongue and one foot."

John George, whose late wife Helen trained hundreds of people to care for native animals, including Morecroft, said the presenter was "totally committed".

"She loved it, loved him and she could rely on him totally," he said.

Morecroft was an active member of the wildlife rescue, as seen here with the founder Mikla Lewis (centre) at the 1991 Christmas party. (Supplied: WIRES)

WIRES founder Mikla Lewis still remembers being surprised by Morecroft's call.

"One day I picked up the phone and this voice on the other end said, 'Hello, I'm Richard Morecroft and I'd like to join'," she said.

"I definitely knew who he was."

She said he was "really besotted" with Archie.

Morecroft talking about types of bats in the documentary Raising Archie.

WIRES bat unit coordinator Storm Stanford said bats these days did not stay with carers as long, and incubators were used for warmth to reduce disease risks.

"Back when Richard was doing it, we didn't know about lyssavirus or, I think it just came in the year after or a few months after he was doing the caring," Ms Stanford said.

Archie was fostered at two weeks old. (ABC News)

She said the disease was spread by saliva through a cut or a bite, which could cause a fever, fatigue and seizures.

There is a vaccine, but people are told not to handle bats, even while wearing gloves.

Ms Stanford said caring for a pup could take at least four or five hours a day.

Archie was eventually sent to a creche to socialise with other bats away from their carers, before being released back into the colony.

Morecroft died earlier this week on the south coast of NSW after being diagnosed with cancer earlier this year.

https://www.dw.com/en/eritrea-urges-un-d.text:
Eritrea has officially requested UN Security Council assistance over the conflict in Tigray. Both Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of fueling regional instability.

In the ongoing struggle for control of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, both Ethiopia and Eritrea have appealed to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) for assistance.

On Friday, citing Article 51 of the UN Charter, Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said his country was making use of its right to exercise self-defense measures against Eritrea.

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units in recent weeks and supporting, financing, arming and directing insurgent groups.

On Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, who rejected Ethiopia's accusations, responded in a letter, writing, "Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia's deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea... and take the requisite deterrent measures," asking the international body to invoke Chapter VII of ​the ⁠UN Charter, which allows measures ⁠from ​sanctions to military action.

Saleh said Ethiopia's actions could cause, "huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilize the region."

Last month, Tigrayan rebel groups announced they had joined forces to oust Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, swiftly launching major attacks on Ethiopian government forces and seizing regional airports.

Since then, Ethiopian troops have driven back Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) militants and taken control of large parts of the region, including the capital, Mekelle.

Recent fighting, which broke a 2022 peace agreement, and this weekend's exchange of accusations only deepen the growing rift between Ethiopia and Eritrea, who were allies in a bloody 2020-2022 border war that saw them team up against TPLF rebels.

The developments also come as Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed reiterates his landlocked country's need for access to the Red Sea — a demand he repeated on Monday — and which Eritrea regards as a direct threat to its sovereignty.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Hanson seems more and more like the de facto opposition leader. At CPAC, Angus Taylor warmed the seat for her
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Josh Butler
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Cooperation between One Nation and the Liberals ‘up to Angus Taylor’, Pauline Hanson says at conservative conference. How would that work?

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The annual Conservative Political Action Conference billed itself as a chance for the leaders of the three main conservative parties – Liberals, Nationals and One Nation – to make their pitch and compete for rightwing voters.

The reception they received in Brisbane on Saturday suggests Pauline Hanson is effectively the preferred opposition leader, with Angus Taylor relegated to leading a minor party.

But how would they work together, if the opportunity arose? While Hanson repeatedly criticised the Coalition, to laughter from the audience, the One Nation leader is keeping the door open to some kind of arrangement to defeat Labor.

Discussion of how to “unite the right” echoed around the Brisbane convention centre.

It was always a risk for Taylor, still leader of the second-largest bloc in parliament, to agree to equal billing on the conference lineup with Hanson, who leads a party room of five others. The Liberal leader was the first guest speaker, with his office calling his opening address a “keynote”, but CPAC had effectively advertised all three leaders – Taylor, Hanson and Matt Canavan – as co-headliners.

This framing would be remarkable in itself, if Hanson hadn’t already been operating as de facto opposition leader through 2026, while filling a void left by Taylor who has struggled for mainstream cut-through and political oxygen. Hanson followed Taylor on the schedule, but it’s the first time in a while – Taylor has been following her lead all year.

That Hanson literally took a seat Taylor had just vacated as they conducted back-to-back interviews with Karl Stefanovic, the One Nation leader nestling herself into a spot Taylor had just warmed up for her, was a moment that felt symbolic.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Taylor was always up against it, in front of a CPAC crowd which leans more conservative than the centre-right. Beginning with a mea culpa for Liberal governments past – apologising for his role in immigration increases, pandemic spending and net zero – Taylor admitted his side “made mistakes” but were now “unashamedly on the right”. His speech favoured conservative talking points, including “big government”, “climate bureaucracy”, “NDIS fraud”, and no less than six mocking references to “socialism”.

While CPAC usually finds speaking slots for half the Coalition frontbench each year, Taylor is the first sitting Liberal leader to feature. It’s interesting that he felt the need to, or wanted to, front a convention where the demographic is somewhat outside the voters the Coalition must win back – those in the centre.

This audience represents a very activated, politically engaged conservative base. But with the Coalition vote still cratering eight months from Sussan Ley’s dumping, and One Nation’s rise carving off voters on the right, trying to win back some of that base makes sense for the Liberal leader.

It was a valiant effort to reclaim the Coalition’s mantle as “the most credible alternative government”, but not even Taylor’s newly announced immigration crackdown – confirmed, coincidentally or otherwise, just days before CPAC – could save him from heckles from those more partial to Hanson. A handful booed as he said net overseas migration would rise from 100,000 to 160,000 under the Coalition plan; more booed when he dodged questions from Stefanovic about why he wasn’t trying harder to work with Hanson.

This is where the problem lies for Taylor, presenting a vexed conundrum with no easy solution. While the Liberal leader’s speech ran through a list of relatively well explained Coalition policies – cutting taxes, indexing tax brackets, instant asset write-offs – and philosophical markers for how the Coalition would intellectually approach government, it was clear that much of the crowd wasn’t really buying what he was selling. The biggest claps Taylor got were when he railed against socialism and big government, not for talking up fiscal discipline.

Sign up to Politics, really

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

after newsletter promotion

Hanson, by contrast, got a standing ovation from most of the room before even walking on stage, with a hype video – set to Vanessa Amorosi’s Amazing – playing her on. More scripted than usual, Hanson’s speech went to economic pain, anger at climate policies and “mass migration”, and criticism of “elitists”. Nearly every line received enthusiastic applause.

Despite claiming Australians don’t want a “smarmy management consultant” replacing Anthony Albanese, and questioning how conservatives could “trust” the Coalition, Hanson repeatedly signalled her keenness for rightwing parties to cooperate in some way.

In a press conference, she wouldn’t say exactly how that would work. Hanson said she didn’t want ministry positions for One Nation in a Coalition government, nor would she accept Coalition ministers in a One Nation government, appearing to rule out a formal agreement.

But asked if One Nation would continue playing hardball and beating up the Liberals, or if cooperation might emerge, she said it was “up to Angus Taylor”.

After seeing how his message went across to the Brisbane convention room, compared to Hanson’s, Taylor may have a lot to think about.

Josh Butler is a Guardian Australia political reporter and chief of staff in Canberra

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Albanese wants universal childcare to be his legacy. But paying for it isn’t as easy as ABC
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Krishani Dhanji
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Labor is running out of time to make its case to Australian families about how they are going to make childcare accessible and affordable for all

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Rachel Hill, a mother of two from Sydney, explains the maths of family planning.

The not-for-profit worker recently bumped up her workload from two days a week to full-time to try to cover ever-rising costs. Instead, the additional money has been swallowed by childcare fees.

“I did not want to go back full-time, it was purely because of the cost of living,” she says.

“We went from paying around $175 a week for four days of care … to now paying $536 a week for five days, so any increase I got in my salary I’m basically now paying in day care.”

Hill says her husband always wanted a bigger family. If raising children were more affordable, they may have considered having a third. But with only a small village around them, she says “it’s just not working”.

“If our circumstances were different I might have had more reason to pursue more children, but financially it just wasn’t ever going to work for us.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, wants universal childcare to be his political legacy, his entry to the Labor hall of fame alongside Medicare and the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It should, he says, be “as natural as public school”.

But the sector has been rocked by widespread allegations of child abuse and safety breaches, damaging public trust and forcing the government to tighten standards – all while trying to figure out what a universal system might look like and how to pay for it.

It is working against a ticking clock: the 2026 intergenerational report, released last month, showed deaths would outnumber births in Australia by the 2060s. Australia needs more babies, and Labor says universal childcare is key to making that happen.

While many might presume universal childcare means free childcare – akin to public schools for older children – the government has defined it as care that is “available, quality and affordable”. Overseas examples point to provinces in Canada which offer $10 a day capped care, or Estonia, where fees are capped at low weekly or monthly rates tied to the minimum wage. Labor won’t yet say which model it would choose, but have indicated it is likely to be means-tested.

It has commissioned two consulting firms to produce separate work outlining the scope of the challenge. The biggest report is by Deloitte and aims to set out the cost of delivering childcare services in any part of the country – metropolitan, outer-suburban, regional or remote.

The work requires the cooperation of about 1,000 childcare centres across that geographic spread, but they have not been forthcoming. The low turnout of volunteers has led to the government compelling service providers to hand over the centres’ financial data. Deloitte is due to hand the report to government by the end of the year.

The cabinet is also currently mulling over a report by KPMG which outlined the business case for the government owning and leasing childcare centres. The work – which the government has refused to release, citing cabinet in confidence rules – centres around the $1bn building early education fund, which provides for state governments and not-for-profits to set up centres in childcare deserts.

The first grant round from that fund was announced this month, with $17.3m split between three not-for-profit providers to build four childcare centres in outer metropolitan and regional areas. Dozens more are yet to be announced.

It gives us a clear hint of where Labor believes it can make a mark. The government wants to see not-for-profits making up a bigger share of the childcare sector, with 70% of the sector currently privately run.

“Outer suburbs and regions where there are growing families, but not enough childcare places, we want to build more quality, not-for-profit early learning in those places that need it the most, and it is part of our journey towards universal early education,” the childcare minister, Jess Walsh, told Guardian Australia.

That shift is already starting to happen. In August, the for-profit provider Edge Early Learning went into administration, while competitor G8 has closed dozens of under-enrolled and underperforming centres. This week, Goodstart Early Learning, a not-for-profit provider and one of the recipients of the building early education fund, signed an agreement to investigate the potential take over of up to 31 of Edge Early Learning’s 64 centres.

Goodstart’s head of advocacy, John Cherry, says there is “certainly an opportunity there for the not-for-profit sector to expand, but at the moment, not-for-profit providers around the country are running on very thin margins and very challenged by operational conditions”.

after newsletter promotion

Not-for-profit childcare providers are not necessarily cheaper for parents – comparison website childcare estimator says fees are about 8% cheaper at some not-for-profits – but they consistently have higher quality and safety ratings.

Any reform would also have to tackle the childcare subsidy.

Currently, a family with one child and a household income of up to $88,520 receives a government subsidy covering 90% of childcare fees. That subsidy tapers off at a rate of 1% per additional $5,000 of income, running down to nothing when the household income reaches $538,520.

Labor has consistently raised these subsidies since it came to power in 2022 and says a family with a household income of $168,000, with one child in care for 30 hours a week, is $7,440 a year better off than they would be without the higher subsidies. But the fees themselves have been rising quickly, jumping 7.3% in the 12 months to August – more than twice the inflation rate.

The childcare subsidy was projected to cost the budget about $16.2bn last financial year and is slated to rise to $18.4bn by 2028-29.

The government already has a blueprint for universal childcare sitting on its desk. In June 2024, the productivity commission looked at three options: the recommended option was free childcare for families with a household income under $90,000, then progressively dropping the subsidy down from 100% towards zero with every $5,000 increase in household income, tapering off at $580,000. For a household income of $168,000, mentioned above, that would be an 85% subsidy.

The productivity commission also modelled a flat $10 a day or 90% subsidy option for all families, but said the cost to the budget would be much higher and the benefit would disproportionately go to wealthier households.

Parents have to wait until their children turn three to get further relief, when additional subsidies offered by state governments for preschool kick in. But preschools run on school terms and typically offer 15 hours a week, leaving considerable gaps for parents working full-time.

The fees currently faced by parents are comparable to private school fees, says Eshanee Collins, a Sydney-based mortgage broker. She says returning to work was part of her identity after having children, but the cost of care made it a tough decision.

“I work full-time, and in all honesty, our household would probably be better off if I didn’t work and [did] not pay that [childcare] money,” she says.

Childcare is likely to become a key election battleground, with the Coalition looking at both the design of the childcare subsidy and paid parental leave settings, while One Nation has promoted income splitting and other policies that incentivise one parent staying home.

The Greens, meanwhile, have commissioned parliamentary budget office modelling on the cost of providing 50 hours a week of free childcare, which could cost $127bn over a decade.

Whichever way it’s sliced, childcare is expensive to run and public buy-in is essential. Labor is running out of time to decide what model of universal care they want to pursue – and how to get voters on board.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Falling international student numbers create ‘massive problems’ for Australian universities, expert warns
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Krishani Dhanji
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Immigration debate and visa uncertainty is putting students off and increasing pressure on budgets

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

University leaders warn they’re struggling to fill international student places due to visa uncertainty and heated political debate on immigration, with regional areas hit the hardest and concern that financial deficits could affect domestic students.

The latest numbers from the Department of Education in October show on average universities are filling just two-thirds of their allocated places, and just five public universities have reached more than 80% capacity, all in capital cities.

Not signed in before? Create an account

Mike Ferguson, pro vice-chancellor of international students at Charles Sturt University, which has campuses across regional New South Wales, said his institution has filled just 40% of its cap this year.

“At the moment, we’re around 35% down on where we were last year, and we had expected to grow from last year. Currently we only have 20% of the international student volume we had prior to the pandemic,” Ferguson said.

Charles Sturt has estimated the gap between international student recruitments pre-Covid and now is costing $35m, and the university has announced job cuts and restructuring in response.

Ferguson attributed the fall to government policy, including hiking visa applications to $2,500, high refusal rates, and growing uncertainty from announcements by the Coalition and One Nation targeting international students.

He said regional universities primarily recruited students from south Asian countries, which were experiencing higher visa refusal rates of about 53%.

“It’s not only resulting in us losing what we believe to be largely genuine students … but it’s also creating a large deterrent from new students to come in and apply, knowing they’re having to pay world record visa fees with only a one in two chance of actually getting a visa,” Ferguson said.

But he said the university does support Labor’s decision to crack down on onshore student transfers and visa hopping to improve integrity in the system.

Prof Andrew Norton, an expert in higher education, said the declining numbers were affecting all public universities because they cross-subsidise their teaching and research with international student fees.

“It creates massive problems because international students are basically the only profitable aspect of university operations,” he said.

Duncan Bentley, vice-chancellor of Federation University in regional Victoria, said he too supported those measures but that his university was also facing significant pressures with far fewer international students enrolling this year.

The university has pushed the government for a special regional skills student visa that would prioritise international students wanting to do courses in critical areas such as allied health or teaching.

“We endorse, and have been asking for a long time for, the 12-month ban on course hopping, apart from exceptional and genuine circumstances,” Bentley said.

“The criteria for this regional visa would be any overseas student who wants to come and study in a regional university can have access to a special visa … the course should be on a regional skills shortage list, based on the premise that domestic regional graduates can’t meet the demand.”

Western Sydney University vice-chancellor, George Williams, said his university had also experienced significant declines in overseas students and warned the financial deficits could have an impact on domestic students.

“It has an enormous impact on our budget and it means universities across the sector are asking where they can save money, where they can pull back,” Williams said.

“In our case, international students heavily subsidise domestic students, and it puts real pressure on the services we can offer to domestic students.”

Williams also said international students were being deterred by the heated political debate, “which would lead people to wonder whether they would be welcome in Australia”.

Adelaide University told the ABC in September it had only reached 60% of its international student capacity, after its merger with the University of South Australia, creating a potential $90m revenue shortfall.

The government’s 2026 planning level for international students was set at 295,000, and so far it’s tracking towards 250,000, which is just above the Coalition’s proposed level of 240,000.

Labor will also reduce the number of international students eligible to bring family to Australia while they study, while the Coalition has promised to abolish temporary graduate visas.

Phil Honeywood, chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), said diminishing international student numbers in regional areas could also lead to critical skills shortages.

“The high non-refundable visa cost makes the system more like a lottery ticket,” Honeywood said.

“There’s not enough nurses, childcare workers, aged care workers or engineers in regional communities … so basically if you have diminishing numbers of international students in these regional areas and they’re not able to stay past their degrees, that creates a cascading skill shortage.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: José Olivares
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
ICE official, who was sleeping on man’s lawn and appeared ‘intoxicated’, faces felony charges, California police say

A 72-year-old man shot an off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official in California early on Friday morning after the “intoxicated and agitated” official assaulted him and his daughter on their property, local authorities allege.

The Fresno police department said that the ICE official was receiving medical care after being shot in the midsection. The official, identified as David Gonzalez, is facing felony charges for assaulting the father-daughter duo, Fresno police said.

It was not immediately clear for how Gonzalez had been with ICE and what exactly he did for ICE. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, referred all questions about Gonzalez to Fresno police.

According to Fresno police, at about 3am, a woman found Gonzalez sleeping on her and her father’s front lawn. She told her 72-year-old father, who was inside, and then attempted to shoo Gonzalez off their property.

But when Gonzalez was awakened, “he appeared intoxicated and agitated” and physically assaulted the 72-year-old father, forcing him to the ground, police said. When the father’s daughter tried to intervene, Gonzalez physically attacked and took her to the ground as well, police said.

The father feared for his and his daughter’s physical safety and shot Gonzalez once, police said. Shortly thereafter, the daughter’s boyfriend, an off-duty police officer, arrived and placed handcuffs on Gonzalez.

“It is unknown at this time why Gonzalez was in the area at the time of the [shooting], but it has been confirmed he was off-duty and alone,” local authorities said.

Fresno police on Friday said the investigation into the shooting was continuing while Gonzalez was in custody and receiving medical treatment. He was booked with battery likely to cause great bodily injury, felony vandalism and battery.

The father and daughter were not booked with any crimes as they recovered from injuries of their own, police said.

The confrontation that led to Gonzalez’s shooting is one of the latest cases in which federal ICE officials have fallen under scrutiny for alleged criminal behavior. ICE has also been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second term for the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.

Lawmakers have also criticized ICE’s hiring practices amid the agency’s rush to bring on more officials to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda. In August 2025, an ICE supervisor filed a whistleblower complaint to the DHS office of inspector general alleging that the agency was skirting basic vetting and violating federal rules during its hiring spree.

In July, an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian immigrant in Biddeford, Maine. The ICE officer in question had reportedly been a recent hire by the agency despite an alleged history of violence and mental health problems.

Meanwhile, in April, a longtime ICE officer in Cincinnati was arrested after allegedly lying to DHS about domestic violence allegations against him. Local news reports say police had been called more than 20 times in the past to years to the home he shared with his girlfriend.

The Ohio Immigrant Alliance, a pro-immigrant group, released a report in August documenting more than 150 federal immigration officials accused of abuse and crimes. One of the latest entries in their report cited allegations that an ICE official reportedly broke into an ex-girlfriend’s apartment in south-east Louisiana.

https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.title: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.author: Terrence O’Brien
https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/1.text:
Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid removing their songs.

Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid removing their songs.

Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” Artists are saying that their non-AI works are being caught up in the purge, however.

Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation.

DistroKid also makes it exceedingly difficult to contact them. McGwire first had to have a “lengthy circular conversation” with a bot before getting hold of a live agent. One of the songs removed was a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” which he claims to have had a proper license for. Another track used a beat he purchased through a marketplace, which others had also licensed.

Most infuriating for McGwire was a song removed for an uncleared sample. The song he allegedly sampled was released two years after his track.

Much of the frustration from artists stems from the lack of communication and recourse. Nerdcore rapper Insane Ian posted that he “had an original song taken down with no warning, and they wouldn’t tell me why either.”

Rapper King Chase also struggled to get through to a person at DistroKid.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/20.text:
Two people diagnosed with depression can experience vastly different symptoms. One might struggle with persistent anxiety and repetitive negative thoughts, while another may experience trauma related symptoms or substance abuse. But do these differences also appear in the way their brains function?

Researchers at the University of Helsinki investigated this question and uncovered a striking finding: people with the same depression diagnosis can have dramatically different patterns of brain activity. In some cases, communication between brain regions was unusually strong, while in others, it was weaker than normal.

Depression is a major global health concern. According to the World Health Organization (WHO, 2025), approximately 332 million (5.2%) adults worldwide are affected. In Finland, depression is the leading individual cause of both extended sick leave and disability pensions.

Brain Study Reveals Five Distinct Depression Profiles

To investigate the biological differences associated with depression, researchers examined brain activity in 263 people diagnosed with major depressive disorder and 75 healthy participants who served as a comparison group.

The analysis revealed five distinct groups based on differences in functional connectivity, a measure of how closely activity in different brain regions is coordinated. When two regions show synchronized activity, it suggests they are working together as part of a larger brain network. However, stronger connectivity does not necessarily mean the brain is functioning better.

"What was particularly interesting was the contrasting patterns of brain activity found under the umbrella of the same depression diagnoses. In some individuals, the functional connectivity between brain regions was stronger than usual, while in others it was weaker," says Director Satu Palva of the Neuroscience Center, University of Helsinki.

These differences were also associated with particular symptoms. Participants in one group showed especially strong connections between brain regions, along with more pronounced substance abuse problems. Another group displayed weaker connections and a greater prominence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms.

The contrasting results could help explain why earlier studies examining the brains of people with depression have sometimes reached conflicting conclusions. If researchers study different combinations of patients, they may observe very different patterns, even though everyone involved has received the same diagnosis.

The findings add to growing evidence that depression may not have a single, consistent biological signature. Instead, the condition could involve several distinct patterns of brain function.

The Five Brain Patterns Linked to Depression

The researchers classified participants with depression into five groups based on how strongly different brain areas communicated and the frequencies at which their activity was coordinated.

Each group had a characteristic pattern of brain connectivity and associated symptoms:

Group 1: Strong connectivity and severe symptoms

Participants generally showed relatively strong connections between brain regions. This profile was associated with more severe symptoms across several areas, including depression, anxiety, rumination, and reduced ability to function in daily life. Rumination refers to repeatedly dwelling on distressing thoughts, worries, or negative experiences.

Group 2: Weaker connectivity and milder depression

This group was characterized by relatively weak communication between brain regions. Compared with the other groups, participants generally experienced milder symptoms.

Group 3: Widespread weak connectivity and trauma symptoms

People in this group showed reduced connectivity across substantial portions of the brain. Symptoms associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were particularly prominent.

Group 4: Mixed connectivity and multiple challenges

This profile combined unusually strong connections in some brain regions with weaker connections in others. Participants tended to experience more severe depression, greater substance abuse problems, and lower overall well-being.

Group 5: The strongest connectivity and substance abuse symptoms

Participants in the fifth group had the strongest connections between brain regions of any group identified in the study. Substance abuse was a particularly prominent issue, while trauma related symptoms were less pronounced than in the other groups.

Importantly, all five groups also showed differences from the healthy participants. These distinctions extended beyond whether brain connections were strong or weak. The groups also differed in which brain regions were involved and the frequencies at which their activity was synchronized.

Together, the patterns suggest that people diagnosed with depression may experience substantially different changes in how their brain networks operate.

Measuring Brain Activity With Millisecond Precision

To capture these differences, the scientists used magnetoencephalography (MEG), a brain imaging technique that detects extremely faint magnetic fields produced by electrical activity in the brain.

Unlike methods that track slower changes associated with brain activity, MEG can follow electrical signals as they unfold over extremely short periods. This makes it particularly useful for investigating the timing and coordination of communication between brain regions.

Using MEG, the researchers recorded brain activity in all 263 participants with depression and the 75 healthy control subjects.

"MEG enabled us to monitor electrical brain activity with millisecond precision, helping us get closer to what actually happens in the brain at any given moment. Previously, depression phenotypes have been studied using methods with slower responses," Palva notes.

This high level of temporal precision allowed the team to examine rapid changes in brain activity that might be difficult to distinguish using slower measurement techniques.

By studying these fast signals, the researchers were able to identify differences not only in the strength of connectivity but also in the frequencies at which brain regions appeared to work together.

Could Brain Activity Lead to More Personalized Depression Treatments?

The discovery raises an important possibility for the future of mental health care: treatments might eventually be selected partly according to a person's individual pattern of brain activity.

Today, finding an effective depression treatment can involve trying different medications or therapies and evaluating how well each works. Because patients can respond differently to the same treatment, identifying the most suitable approach is not always straightforward.

Brain activity measurements could eventually provide additional information to help guide these decisions. However, the researchers emphasize that their findings are not yet ready for clinical use.

"We're not yet at the point where brain measurements can be used to choose the right treatment for patients, but the study does show one possible route," Palva says.

A major long-term goal is to better understand how particular symptoms relate to the way brain networks function. Connecting these biological patterns with patients' experiences could help researchers develop more precise ways to identify and characterize depression.

Eventually, such knowledge might allow doctors to determine which therapies are most likely to help individual patients, potentially reducing the amount of trial and error involved in treatment.

For now, the five brain profiles offer a different way to understand depression. Rather than assuming that one diagnosis corresponds to one underlying pattern of brain activity, the findings suggest that depression can involve markedly different biological changes, sometimes even in opposite directions.

The research was carried out in collaboration with Aalto University and Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (HUS).
