https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/m.title: Retracing the steps of Mark Dennis, 'brilliant' barrister with a dark side
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/m.author: Charlotte Grieve, Kyle Taylor, and Daryna Zadvirna
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Mark Dennis built a reputation defending accused criminals before he himself became the accused. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide.

There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling.

"I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange".

The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd".

But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years.

"All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said.

In some photos, Loxsom said Dennis was hugging shirtless children.

Loxsom shared his suspicions with an electrician.

"His gut was this guy was doing something bad with kids as well," he said.

The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed.

But, like Loxsom, what really alarmed him was the sheer volume of photographs in almost every room, even the kitchen.

"It was just disturbing. Like, these kids weren't happy," he said.

Dennis was found dead in his home in Sydney's inner west in February. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

Eventually, Loxsom decided to make a report with the child protection hotline.

"I didn't do it straight away, which now I regret," he said.

In January, Dennis came onto the police's radar again when he was searched at Sydney Airport as he returned from a trip to Cambodia.

What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing".

Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home.

Last week, Background Briefing and ABC Investigations revealed his death did not bring the police investigation to an end.

Codenamed Operation Queenstown, Cambodian and Australian national police have been quietly probing Dennis's network and links to famous children's charity Sunrise Cambodia all year.

The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children.

In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching.

Listen to Dark Menace, a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts.

The claims raise important questions for all children's charities that must balance the need to fundraise with child safety, as multiple former Sunrise staff say they saw Dennis's bad behaviour but felt they could not report it.

"They saw this," one former staff member told the ABC through a translator. "But they could not do anything because he's a big sponsor."

A spokesperson for Sunrise said they were never aware of any complaints about Dennis and police had told them no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of his victims.

The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first.

Dennis grew up in a large family on Sydney's northern beaches, and by 2001, was a criminal defence barrister with a room at the prestigious Forbes Chambers.

"You don't get to go to Forbes unless you are absolutely brilliant," says one solicitor who briefed Dennis.

"He was one of those people who was married to the profession."

His nickname was "Dark Menace" — a play on words that several acquaintances said reflected his personality and black sense of humour, exemplified by his "WASNTME" personalised number plate.

Across his career, Dennis was known to have mentored junior lawyers and published papers under provocative titles and on topics like defending accused paedophiles and cross-examining child witnesses.

Some of the legal papers authored by Dennis. (ABC News / supplied)

"You need to watch the child witness carefully and assess matters such as intelligence, level of vocabulary and articulation, degree of self-confidence, general demeanour," he wrote in 2017.

One lawyer who knew Dennis for more than a decade said he was "not shocked" by the charges because he had a reputation for sexual harassment and aggression towards women.

"It's one of those situations where, and I know I'm not the only person who's thought about this, I think a lot of us in retrospect are like, 'This was actually f***ing obvious,'" he said.

Three lawyers told the ABC about an incident where Dennis was intoxicated at the 2012 Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS) Christmas party in Sydney, when he lunged at a woman with an open fist.

He was then banned from ALS Christmas parties.

Barrister Charles Waterstreet, who worked at Forbes alongside Dennis for more than a decade until facing his own sexual misconduct allegations, described his former colleague as "very ambitious" but "an oddball".

"He loved a drink, especially on Friday nights," he said. "He sort of became another personality."

Forbes Chambers is on the eleventh floor of a building overlooking Sydney's Hyde Park. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

In 2011, Dennis began hosting legal conferences to raise funds for his charity, Reasonable Cause, that pledged to help "disadvantaged young Cambodians to further their education".

Tickets cost $450, and the guest list included magistrates, silks and politicians, according to the 2024 invitation.

In interviews with more than 20 sitting Forbes barristers, some were quick to defend their late colleague — insinuating the evidence was thin, based on industry rumours, and one said they did not think his charity work should be "smeared".

"It did such good work. I don't think it was connected … to some sexual interest," they said.

However, despite some celebrating his work and attending his legal conferences, many could not name the charity the money went to.

The largest recipient of Dennis's fundraising was Sunrise Cambodia — a high-profile children's charity founded by Adelaide-born Geraldine Cox.

Cox has spent decades crisscrossing the globe, and according to her 2011 report, delivering speeches to company executives in the United Arab Emirates, government officials in Australia, private schools, and lawyers like Dennis.

"I flew to Sydney to address a group of lawyers at an event arranged by sponsor Mark Dennis, where over $14,000 was raised. Who said lawyers do not have hearts!" Cox wrote.

Her work has been celebrated internationally. She has won awards, been praised by Australian media and rubbed shoulders with Hollywood celebrities and Australian prime ministers.

Geraldine Cox's work has brought her into contact with the likes of Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt and Anthony Albanese. (ABC News / supplied)

Starting in 2008, Dennis personally sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise whom he visited in the orphanages each year. Over time, he backed the whole organisation — raising at least $340,000 in seven years through the legal conferences.

In 2010, he also began funding and attending Sunrise's annual beach holidays to Sihanoukville, a once-sleepy Cambodian coastal town now filled with scam compounds and casinos.

Itineraries for these trips obtained by the ABC show the children played football, shared meals, performed concerts and socialised with sponsors, including Dennis.

Photographs from these trips show Dennis on the beach, and hugging and playing with young children at the hotel. There is no suggestion the photographs are sexual.

Dennis playing with children during one of the Sunrise trips to Sihanoukville. (ABC News / supplied)

A spokesperson for Sunrise said sponsors were not permitted to initiate contact with children.

"However, if a child comes running at a sponsor for a hug, the sponsor is not expected to push them away as this can be very emotionally damaging to a kid who may actually feel safe for the first time in his/her life," they said.

A former Sunrise employee told the ABC it was during one of these beach trips that Dennis was swimming when he went under the water and touched her leg in a sexual manner.

"I felt really afraid," she said. "I kicked Mark off. I was very terrified. He apologised later."

A Sunrise spokesperson said the charity did not know about this allegation and was "very sorry to hear this".

"Had they reported this, we could and would have dealt with it at the time," the spokesperson said.

The woman did not complain formally, but said staff were concerned about Dennis's behaviour and agreed they needed to be "careful" around him to "protect the kids".

Geraldine Cox (second from left) and Dennis (seated with arms crossed) on a beach at Sihanoukville. (Supplied)

The same former employee said she was also concerned about Dennis's behaviour towards an autistic teenage girl living in Sunrise, whom he regularly tried to come close to, and touched her breasts.

She said she saw Dennis entering the girls' and boys' bedrooms at Sunrise, but staff felt there was nothing they could do "because he's a big sponsor" and therefore did not report this.

Eng Sopheak, who lived at Sunrise from the age of five and then worked as Cox's personal driver, also said he witnessed Dennis regularly entering the girls' dormitories.

"I was personally worried," he said, because men were typically not allowed to enter the dormitories.

Eng Sopheak became Cox's personal driver after living at Sunrise as a child. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Sopheak said there needed to be greater separation between sponsors and children.

"My recommendation to sponsors is just that they donate the money, but they don't need to have a relationship with the child," he said.

"So I'd want it to stop."

A spokesperson for Sunrise said dormitories were private areas and as of last year, sponsors were no longer invited to Sihanoukville. They said they had plans to phase out individual child sponsorship but did not specify when.

However, Sunrise's website still allows sponsors to preference the age and gender of children whom they can visit for $50 per month.

By 2018, Dennis was appointed chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered Australian charity managing donations for Sunrise at the time.

In this role, Dennis was involved in almost every aspect of Sunrise's operations — managing redundancies, approving wages, signing off on hiring policies and even becoming a 49 per cent shareholder of Sunrise's Sihanoukville property, which was valued at more than $US3 million in 2017.

"He was the big boss," said Yi Soksan, who held senior positions at Sunrise between 2011 and 2018.

Soksan said staff were told by Cox to "just trust" Dennis because he was a donor and lawyer, and recalls her saying: "He's my friend, he's one of the big donors and sponsors. He loves Sunrise."

Yi Soksan says he knew Dennis as "the big boss". (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

"She advised us, 'He's also the lawyer, so he understands, you know, the rules, the laws. So, just trust him.'"

Cox said she had no recollection of discussing Dennis with staff. While she considered him a friend, she said she had no knowledge of his personal life and never witnessed any bad behaviour.

While chairman, Dennis wielded power over Cox. In an email sent in November 2019, Cox asked for his approval for Sunrise to cover personal expenses.

"Since I offered to reduce my salary … around the time you took over, Mark, I am finding it increasingly difficult to have any sort of normal life," she wrote.

While their relationship was financial and social, it was also fractious.

Emails show Dennis privately described Cox as an "unreliable historian" and "something of a compulsive spender" — descriptions Cox said she could not comment on.

Dennis was granted access to Sunrise's bank accounts in 2018, allowing him to use Sunrise's money to make purchases for children.

A note from Dennis acknowledging receipt of $US4,000 for the purchase of two motorbikes and a computer. (Supplied)

Sunrise said this was normal practice, and its current policy permitted donors to purchase gifts for individual children on special occasions like birthdays, capped at $20 per year.

Maggie Eno, who runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang, was critical of everything from sponsors attending beach holidays to giving gifts to children.

"Individual purchasing … it's grooming," Eno says. "It's horrifying."

Maggie Eno runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang.  (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Eno, who did not want to comment on Sunrise specifically, said sponsors should never have access to children because criminals were "sophisticated" and "always" had the goal of getting "direct access to the children".

"Paedophiles or child sex offenders don't just groom the child, they groom the family of the child, and they groom the organisation taking care of the child," she said.

"The majority of people are good, kind people, but there is always a risk."

A spokesperson for Sunrise said work was underway to distance relationships between sponsors and children.

Former Sunrise resident Sok San, now aged 28, was among the children Dennis bought gifts for and socialised with on the beach trips.

He first learned that Dennis was charged and had died when contacted by the ABC, and said he cried.

"He promised to buy me an iPad," San said in June, adding Dennis wanted him to download Facebook on the device.

Former Sunrise resident Sok San says he kept in touch with Dennis after leaving the orphanage. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

San said his mother died when he was young, there was violence in his childhood, and he started living in Sunrise at around 10 years old.

He first met Dennis in the orphanage as a child and said Dennis bought him a small watch and gave "toys, books and cookies" to other children.

"He's a good person, and he also came to watch a traditional dance," San said.

He called Dennis "godfather" and said they kept in touch outside Sunrise when he became an adult. They met for ice cream in Siem Reap, and Dennis made promises, like paying for his university studies in America, he said.

Dennis also continued relationships with other children outside Sunrise after his chairmanship ended in 2020.

Two boys told the ABC that Dennis took groups of former Sunrise children to dinners at a restaurant in the high-end part of Phnom Penh where alcohol was served. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Facebook messages obtained by the ABC show Dennis maintained direct contact online with children he met through Sunrise.

"I am incredibly proud of you," Dennis wrote to one boy in September 2024.

"Thank you for your support all the years," the boy responded.

Behind Sunrise's gates, emails show staff had been concerned about these relationships for years.

One email shows an employee contacted Sunrise's former operations manager, Rob Madsen, in 2020 for help when he learned Dennis was sending money to a 17-year-old outside Sunrise.

"He has been still supported by Mak [sic] Dennis," the email said. "Many kids living outside [Sunrise] have been supported/sponsored by him secretly."

"Kids requested me to keep it secret as he doesn't want [Sunrise's] managers to know about his support. He buys motorbikes for all kids, school fees, etc."

Sunrise said it had no record of this. They said all children were trained on the dangers of maintaining contact with sponsors after leaving the orphanage, but Sunrise did not have the power or resources to monitor what graduates did.

Dennis flew to Cambodia for one final trip in January this year, where he visited Cox's personal residence, a wooden villa on the grounds of Sunrise.

He was in Cambodia on a golfing trip, Cox said, and saw her as a "concerned friend" after hearing she was bedridden following a fall.

Little did she know, this would be Dennis's last visit to Sunrise.

02 Dark Menace | What Happened At Sunrise

When he returned to Sydney, he was intercepted by Australian Border Force officers at the airport who searched his devices and allegedly discovered child abuse material.

Documents released to the ABC under Freedom of Information laws reveal Dennis was communicating this material between 2023 and 2025 to two people, including an account with an Australian number and username "Kanje".

Dennis denied possessing child abuse material in a police interview, but never entered a formal plea.

In a bail hearing the following day, prosecutors said they had discovered an image of a boy aged between six and 10 on his phone, and chat logs where he expressed a desire to rape a 16-year-old.

Commonwealth prosecutor Jon Kisch described the material on Dennis's phone as "disturbing" and "very serious offending", which, if proven, would attract a long jail sentence.

The judge allowed Dennis to be released under strict conditions. Less than three weeks later, he was found dead, leaving behind many unanswered questions.

"I want to know what happened," said one young woman Dennis met through Sunrise.

“I want to know [if] this is true or not. I want to know why. I want to know what happened to him.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.author: Al Newstead

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The Avalanches mine magic from ad jingles and obsolete tech on their new album. (Supplied: Dean Podmore)

A few familiar notes – the startup sound of an old computer, an antique advertising jingle – and suddenly you're teleported to the past.

The Avalanches know this power intimately. And their new album weaponises it.

"Everybody has a commercial they hear, a cereal or soft drink tune from 30 years ago, and it just transports them," Avalanches co-founder Robbie Chater tells Double J's Karen Leng.

"It's phenomenal how it sticks with you over so long. You think you've forgotten it and then it hits."

Nostalgia has been crucial to the Australian group since 2000's Since I Left You, their groundbreaking debut constructed from thousands of obscure analogue samples, made them unlikely stars.

It took 16 mythical years, and losing four members, to make a sequel: the warm, psychedelic Wildflower and its panoply of not just samples but rappers and singers.

We Will Always Love You in 2020 was a cosmic masterpiece inspired by the star-crossed romance of scientists Carl Sagan and Ann Druyan.

Now a trio – co-founders Chater, Tony Di Blasi and new member Andy Szekeres – they find inspiration in the past on new album No Bad Memories, mining sounds from outdated technology and advertising and their ability to trigger emotional impact.

"It's a special power," says Szekeres. "A sound that can instantly take millions of people back to this intense feeling of emotion that's separate from the product."

Even the album's title is sampled, from a 1980s ad for an obsolete medium most under 30 wouldn't recognise: floppy disks.

"It's spruiking the quality of their data storage," says Chater. "Really clever [and] funny. It was a working title [but] began to take on another meaning."

Spanning 31 tracks, No Bad Memories has everything fans love about The Avalanches. A dense fantasia that's joyful, funky, soulful yet capable of tugging on the heartstrings and boasting another all-star cast of guests.

From returning collaborators Jamie xx, Karen O and Rivers Cuomo to in-demand producers Barry Can't Swim, Tunisia's Khadija Al Hanafi, Japanese music legend Haruomi Hosono and Ryoji Ikeda's sensory-testing experiments.

An overlooked bridge from Carly Simon's Make Me Feel Something becomes the sparkling centrepiece of One More Fantasy, an Avalanches specialty.

Lead single Together unites electronic acts Nikki Nair, Jessy Lanza and viral musician Prentiss with video game-y synths and a children's chorus liberated from a '70s TV adaptation of Enid Blyton's The Famous Five.

Its fizzy rhythm is threaded with mouse clicks, loading data, camera shutters and jingles for Nokia and Toshiba.

It's a kaleidoscopic album where legacy acts and emerging talent co-mingle with forgotten jingles and the physical clicking, whirring and static of antiquated devices.

"The sounds our generation knows," notes Chater, "also, when it goes wrong."

Szekeres adds: "I still have trauma … Like, a zip disk drive plugged into a sampler that stopped working. It's a very distinct sound."

The dreaded Windows error and malfunctioning hardware are among the record's numerous Easter eggs.

Where The Avalanches once dug through op-shop vinyl crates for inspiration, No Bad Memories sent them down YouTube rabbit holes.

"So much fun! We need to be excited to give us the energy to make a project because obviously it's lots of archival work; very time-consuming," says Chater.

The Avalanches's Robbie Chater, Andy Szekeres and Tony Di Blasi modelling fictional products for the album's marketing. (Facebook: The Avalanches)

The resulting tapestry thrives in whimsy, melancholy and imagination. A bittersweet soundtrack that both critiques and celebrates how consumer culture sells emotion, not just product.

"You're growing up and its capitalism coming at you. You don't have a choice of whether you absorb all this messaging or not," says Chater.

"But then also a lot of the ads are really beautiful – the photography, that saturated colour – and the jingles stick in your mind.

The three estimate they "probably made more [ads] than we sampled".

With visual artist Jonathan Zawada, they conjured Takumi Digital Archives, a fictional company behind walkmans, cameras, shampoo, magazines, you name it.

They built an interactive website, cast The Sixth Sense star Haley Joel Osment as a Takumi employee for promotional videos and made physical prototypes to market the album.

"You can really go off on a tangent. 'Maybe we're going to start actually making these products,'" Szekeres recalls. "Then you stop and go, 'actually, what are we doing here?'"

Stitching together commercials, real and imagined, was a challenge but a crucial "part of the record's DNA", says Chater.

A big influence was Suzanne Ciani, a 1970s electronic music pioneer known for pinball game sounds and brand audio idents.

"One of our heroes, [she] wrote amazing jingles for Coke and Atari on a modular synth," says Chater of Ciani, who features on the track Our Love Is Alive.

The trailblazing "Diva of the Diode", Suzanne Ciani established herself amid the male-dominated electronic music scene.   (Suzanne Ciani: Bob L/Metrograph Pictures)

Another milestone was enlisting Mike Patton, the "phenomenal voice" out front of Faith No More and Mr Bungle.

A long-time fan, Patton narrates commercials for the "Superfun!" game system, emulating the '90s "console wars" between Sega and Nintendo.

"Always fighting with each other [through] very bro-y, frat-testosterone ads. Mike was perfect for that. Some of the stuff he sent through was just wild."

Initially, The Avalanches planned a swift follow-up to their last album.

"Eight to 10 songs, no concept. [Just] this great, feel-good party record," explains Chater. "We're like, 'We'll knock it out in six months!"

Those plans fell by the wayside as their tendency for painstaking detail emerged.

"It's difficult. I definitely know if something's not right and I'll be frustrated and push and push and push until it's working for me," says Chater. "We don't want to take too long making records.

"We love having a deadline now and trying to hit it. Even if we didn't hit it exactly.

"You certainly get better at letting go and relaxing a bit."

Chater says Di Blasi acts a welcome counterpoint.

"We can get a bit cerebral," he confesses.

"He's like, 'Sometimes guys, I don't want to have a f***ing instruction manual to understand the record. I just want to have a good time.'"

No Bad Memories manages to have its cake and eat it too.

Feel-good dance music and joyous pop rubs shoulders with experimental sound collage, like a house party featuring museum exhibits as breakout rooms.

You can switch off and enjoy the ride, or dig in and admire the artistic alchemy, flipping obsolete formats and overlooked sounds into collaborations subverting memory, loss and nostalgia.

No Bad Memories proves looking backward isn't just escapism; it's about reclaiming agency.

"That's been a big part of this whole project, thinking about that we're all participants in this crazy, late-stage capitalism system," Chater says.

"Our music's on Spotify, we're on Instagram that's owned by Meta, probably not the most ethical companies in the world.

"It's really important for each of us to think about how we participate in that system and where we're comfortable and what lines we want to draw."

No Bad Memories is out October 16. The Avalanches Australian tour kicks off in Perth on February 27.

Jessica Skinner is just the second female coach to lead the Jillaroos. (ABC Sport: Dan Irvine)

Jessica Skinner is standing beside the silverware she hopes to lift at the Women's Rugby League World Cup final in Brisbane next month.

But when asked what raising the trophy would mean, her answer isn't about winning.

"I feel like I'm lifting my people, Australians, my community in Trangie (regional NSW), my family," she tells ABC Sport.

Skinner is a proud Barkindji and Māori woman, who is preparing for her first World Cup as head coach of the Jillaroos, Australia's national women's rugby league team.

The World Cup is the pinnacle of the women's game, and Australia has enjoyed over a decade of dominance, winning the last three tournaments.

Skinner admits the pressure is there to secure a fourth at the 2026 tournament, which will be co-hosted across Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

"To know that you're stepping into big shoes, and there's an expectation that we win a World Cup, or that we win all the time, especially in the green and gold, it's nerve racking," she says.

"But [I'm] really excited as well."

Skinner says she knows she's stepping into big shoes, with a fourth title on the line. (ABC Sport: Dan Irvine)

Skinner rarely talks about herself, even when discussing one of the biggest moments of her career. For her, this tournament is just as much about others.

It shows in her unique coaching style, where she strives to always put the person before the player.

"I want to be known as a coach, who, when people leave my environments, they feel valued, seen and cared for," Skinner says.

It's this philosophy that has helped her rise to the top.

Skinner hails from Trangie, a town of about 1,000 people in the central west of New South Wales.

She lives there with her son, 16, and daughter, 13, surrounded by what she calls her village.

"I love that I get to represent the bush," she says.

"I love the female game, the Indigenous, the Māori.

"I carry that responsibility and I'm proud to do so. What you can't see, you can't be."

For a long time, Skinner didn't think her coaching style was 'elite', because she believes in putting the person before the player.   (Supplied: NRL Photos)

Skinner was a school teacher before anything else, and fell into coaching women's football at the grassroots when there was nobody else to do it.

The initial plan wasn't to go professional.

"It started out with wanting to be involved in my community, and [have] a sense of belonging," Skinner says.

"To [now] having a seat at the table I suppose in the women's game, and with the Jillaroos, it's massive."

But it hasn't been quick, with Skinner working away in the shadows for a while.

Her elite coaching career began in 2019 as assistant coach of the Prime Minister's XIII.

It led to other coaching roles with the Newcastle Knights NRLW side, the NRL Indigenous Women's Academy, the Women's Indigenous All Stars and First Nations Gems.

Jess Skinner led the Indigenous Women's All Stars to victory over the Maori Women's All Stars in 2024. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Skinner was assistant coach to Brad Donald at the 2021 World Cup, which was played in 2022, because of COVID-19.

"[He's] a great mentor and someone who's really passionate about bringing women through," Skinner says.

The natural progression to head coach came after Donald resigned last year.

"It feels like a massive jump, but it's been 16 years in the making," she says.

"I've done my craft; I've done my trade and my apprenticeship and [I'm] ready to take it on."

Skinner first stepped into the role for last year's historic Test against England in Las Vegas, where the Jillaroos won 90 — 4.

Eight months later, she led the team to the 2025 Pacific Cup Crown.

Jess Skinner was appointed as interim Jillaroos coach for the 2025 Las Vegas Test Match against England. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

The call-up to be head coach arrived during a period of grief. Skinner's mother had just passed away.

"I lost her three days before I got a call from the CEO, Andrew Abdo," she says.

"So, it's been quite a hard time."

There were multiple times when Skinner could have changed paths, but she had the courage to persevere.

"It hasn't been the easiest ride," she says.

Skinner says she's been up against it in a male dominated space. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

She says one of the biggest challenges has been the lack of women coaching at the elite level.

"You have to have resilience, grit and thick skin through this journey," she says.

There's also the sacrifice of time away from her children.

"I'm on my own with my two children, so I'm relying on my village to help me, and my parents have been a part of that," she says.

Then there's the fact her nearest NRLW team is almost 500 kilometres away.

"If I want to go outside of the Jillaroos program, go to NRLW, that means a relocation, and as an Aboriginal woman on country, that means a lot to me [to stay]," Skinner says.

Skinner takes great pride in connecting with her culture, and paving the way for other Indigenous women to play, or work in rugby league.   (Supplied: Chloe Davies)

"It's all helped me be a better version [of myself] and to grow, [but] it has been a lot."

A lot, that has been worth it.

"I feel like I've got the best of both worlds, my community obligations, being a mum and being able to lead this team," Skinner says.

She is moved when speaking about her parents and what it means personally when she pulls on the Jillaroos jersey.

It's a stirring topic for someone so humble.

"You don't ever think about you in the jersey, it's always about others," Skinner says.

A Proud Barkindji woman, Jess Skinner has a deep connection to community and country.   (Supplied: THRIV3)

"[But] for me, and I feel a bit emotional about it, it's representing my parents. My mum as an Aboriginal woman in this country and my dad as a Māori man coming to this country. And then my sisters and brothers.

"It's my community, the students, every team that I've coached, every male or female that's invested in me to continue to be the best version of myself.

"I think when I get into this campaign and hopefully if it is us [holding] the trophy up, I'm holding them with me."

Skinner believes the intuition she brings to the table is her superpower.

"I've got this human radar to recognise when our women are not themselves and I can action it to get the support they need.

"That genuine care that I've carried from my grassroots journey to now in the World Cup, I think that's something that's missing in coaching, particularly in the elite space."

Skinner is a prominent member of the community in Trangie, being involved in growing the game from the grassroots up.   (Supplied: THRIV3)

Skinner will be the only female head coach at the upcoming World Cup, and is one of three women coaching rugby league internationally.

Roosters assistant coach Melissa Spero is leading Nigeria and former Jillaroo Meg Ward currently coaches Tonga.

Out of this year's 12 NRLW teams, Gold Coast Titans coach Karyn Murphy was the sole female head coach.

Skinner says the main things that have helped her get to where she is today are her village in Trangie, and her network of mentors.

She lists a number of male mentors, who have helped her along the way.

"We talk about women elevating women, but we actually have a lot of great men that are elevating woman and investing in us," Skinner says.

There's also her solid network of female coaches.

"It's a small little crew and we help keep each other on track and motivated to keep pushing through," she says.

Beyond earning another trophy, Skinner says a successful World Cup campaign would result in more full-time female staff within elite rugby league, particularly NRLW.

"We've got female coaches, performance staff, physios, doctors coming through our programme and I'd loved to be able to see post World Cup, more female head coaches, head of performance, full-time within the game," she says.

"I take a large amount of pride when I'm coming through that I'm bringing others with me."

Skinner wants every one of her players to feel valued. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

Jessica Skinner's identity as a coach can be distilled into one idea — that the person comes before the player.

"If people leave my environments and they're not feeling that sense of belonging, that hurts me more than a loss," she says.

"For a long time, I felt like [my style of coaching] wasn't elite because I had those values."

Skinner is not only out to build great rugby league players, but great women.

"Bringing your whole self to the team is why you're selected and is our superpower," she says.

And when asked what the most important part of coaching is for her, Skinner brings it back to being about others.

"I [also] hope that I show that women, mothers, Indigenous, Māori [and] coloured people can be at the elite level.

"I hope I get the opportunity to succeed this year, and stay in the role long term to keep proving that it can be done."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.title: Shipping companies offering sailors 'crazy money' to transit Strait of Hormuz
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.author: Lucia Stein and Som Patidar
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Before the US-Israel attacks on Iran, well over 100 commercial ships passed through the strait each day.   (Reuters)

Oil tanker captains in the Persian Gulf are being paid up to $US100,000 (about $143,000) a month to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, industry insiders and maritime unions say, as Iran and the United States continue to impose separate blockades of the critical waterway.

Gulf oil producers are increasingly desperate to get their oil out of the region and onto market after a recent step-up in attacks from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on tankers attempting to pass the dangerous choke-point.

The new wave of assaults on vessels followed reports last month that crude shipments were edging back toward prewar levels, indicating Middle Eastern oil exports were recovering.

Facebook ads seen by the ABC show some seafarers in Asia have been offered double or triple their pay as well as "danger money" bonuses worth tens of thousands to work in the Gulf.

The vast sums of money are being used to persuade them to stay on vessels and continue running the strait despite the risk of attack.

"Right now [the captains] are getting paid crazy," Indian marine engineer Harshal Singh told a podcast in late September.

"A ship captain usually get 15 lakh Rupees per month (about $22,000). Right now in Strait of Hormuz they can make 1 crore rupees (about $143,000) in a month."

The commercial tankers struck as they transited the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks were "highly, highly targeted", according to marine traffic watchers.

Captains receive pay increases while they are in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Oman, and again during each Hormuz transit, according to Indian union representatives.

But the journeys come with substantial risk, with at least 24 seafarers killed in 100 confirmed incidents since the war began, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.

In this month alone, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has recorded nine incidents of attacks on tankers within the Strait of Hormuz.

For many shipowners, the risks are being outweighed by revenues reaching levels rarely seen in the industry's recent history.

"They are offering [seafarers] double, sometimes even five times the wages they will get during the transit of Hormuz," Manoj Yadav, the general secretary of the Mumbai-based Forward Seamen's Union of India, told the ABC.

In India, where the vast majority of the world's seafarers are from, the salary bump is a huge draw.

But unions have warned seafarers are at risk of being exploited and some have very little choice in performing a job that could cost them their lives.

The strait's significance has been in the spotlight since Iran placed an effective chokehold on the shipping route, used for 20 per cent of the world's oil and gas trade, at the end of February.

After months of gridlock, the US responded by implementing its own blockade on Iranian shipments through the critical energy artery.

Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war. (Reuters)

Sailing into the Gulf, loading and coming out again now carries great risk.

While the US intercepts vessels attempting to trade with Iran, the IRGC targets ships sailing in the strait and harasses them, including through drone overflights and surveillance, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center said last weekend.

It means fewer operators are willing to make the voyage, and transit remains below typical prewar traffic levels, when more than 100 commercial vessels crossed the strait each day.

"I think the issue is less [to do with] insurance and more availability of crews that are willing to make that hazardous transit because of a significant amount of attacks," former Australian naval officer Jennifer Parker told the ABC.

An increasing number of ships have attempted to get around Iranian controls by taking the south corridor route, which hugs the Omani coast, rather than the north corridor route, which sails close to Iran.

Ships navigating the strait also take "dark journeys" by travelling at night with their GPS signalling equipment switched off.

Marine intelligence companies previously told the ABC some of these dark transits have occurred with the knowledge and permission of Iran via diplomatic-level negotiations. Others have not.

Kpler data shows that in late September transits through the Strait of Hormuz were starting to climb back to the prewar baseline, raising questions about Iran's continued ability to choke off oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.

In mid-August US President Donald Trump declared the US Navy had removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz, clearing one impediment to vessels navigating the area.

The US Navy had also begun offering assistance and coverage to ships sailing via the route close to the Omani coast.

"The US are also employing uncrewed service vessels in the Strait of Hormuz for intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance."

Reports on the number of ships being guided out by American forces vary greatly. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran has "lost complete control" of the strait.

"There's almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began," he said on Wednesday.

But the IRGC has denied seaborne crude flows in the strait are rebounding. Adviser Majid Mirahmadi said a daily average of just 10 ships were transiting the waterway in October against an average of 125 before the war.

Analysis by Laura Tingle

In one Facebook ad found by the ABC, a professional vessel management company was seen offering prospective seafarers the market rate plus a double-pay bonus to work on a crude oil tanker sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Another shipping owner offered second and third officers who signed with them a $US1,500 bonus to work in the Gulf.

Commercial ship company Sinokor is believed to be offering some of the highest bonuses and incentives, with Bloomberg reporting it was advertising six months' extra salary if seafarers made a return voyage in the area. The journey would take a month, it said.

Mr Yadav said while some owners were offering double pay and bonuses to seafarers, not everyone was making money from the war.

The union leader said some unwilling crews were being pressured to sail under threat they would be replaced if they refused and charged the cost of their repatriation.

"There are two types of offers," he concluded.

Iran's proposal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week, according to its Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, but Donald Trump has already rejected the deal.

India is one of the world's largest suppliers of seafarers, alongside the Philippines and China, with more than 4,500 workers currently stationed on commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf, according to India's External Affairs ministry.

RP Veettil, president of the Sailors Union of India, said companies should provide hazard pay to workers operating in dangerous conditions and not expect them to join vessels passing through the Hormuz "warlike area".

"The seafaring job is very dangerous," he told the ABC.

"Putting blame on the seafarer that they are going by their own choice and getting killed … is not a good idea."

Ms Parker said it was unfortunate that innocent people from countries unrelated to the war were being drawn into this conflict.

https://www.dw.com/en/money-networks-and.title: Money, networks and bias: Why women struggle to win seats in US politics
https://www.dw.com/en/money-networks-and.text:
The US is holding Congress and state governors elections. At all levels of US politics, women are underrepresented — but they may win some historic victories in the midterms on November 3.

Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.

There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."

Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.

Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."

The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa.

125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.

"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.

The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.

Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.

According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.

For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.

Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians.

Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.

For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.

Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.

But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.

This article has been translated from German.
https://www.dw.com/en/money-networks-and.summary: Only 28.4% of the US Congress are women, but 152 women are in the House and Senate. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also higher than ever before. Kelly Dittmar doesn't think Lisa DeMuth will win in Minnesota.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmje.title: Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmje.text:
Four people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain.

Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed after trees fell on their houses.

At least 600,000 people were without power in several states as of Saturday afternoon, according to poweroutage.us.

Isaias made landfall in Florida on late Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (168 km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone.

The storm felled trees and damaged houses. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people.

Two deaths were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed after a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said.

Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them.

"I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet.

Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital.

Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that were submerged by flood waters. In a post on X, the Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation".

In neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash.

"Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.

She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain.

"As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said.

In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m).

"After dark, floodwater is much harder to see, and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said in a post on Facebook.

The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) warned the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall.

In addition to Isaias, Tropical Storm Rachel is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday, and Hurricane Simon will hit the Pacific coast of Mexico on Sunday.

Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.

Two deaths reported in Florida and Alabama, including a woman who died after a tree fell on her house. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation"

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
United States President Donald Trump says Ukraine should replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a new leader, lashing out at him for Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said at the White House on Saturday, adding that “for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does.”

Trump said that under Zelenskyy, Ukraine has “lost 30 percent of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never have started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Following the remarks, Ukraine’s foreign minister defended Zelenskyy. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Andriy Sybiga said in a post on X. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”

Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices ahead of the US midterms, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.

He has also sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

Trump suggested on Saturday that if he had been US president in 2022 “that war would have never started”.

“There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence,” he said.

The remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, according to Ukrainian officials.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed at least 60 people over the past four days.

On Friday, Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine.

He said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional three million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he added.

The move drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy. After Russia’s strikes on Saturday, he wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia”.

Zelenskyy said the attacks show Moscow understands “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities.”

The president said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.

He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s used to intercept Shahed drones.

Ukraine’s European allies have expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.

Trump’s announcement about the deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine.

Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Trump says Ukraine should replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a new leader. He says Ukraine has lost 30% of its population and 2 million people killed. Trump says he has been urging Zelensyy for weeks to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Barcelona beat Getafe as Gordon scores his first goal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
Anthony Gordon scored his first goal for Barcelona as the Spanish champions extended their perfect start in La Liga with a 3-0 win over Getafe on Saturday.

England international Gordon opened the scoring in the second minute, and Gabriel Jesus added another after half an hour for the league leaders, who have won every match they have played this season.

French defender Jules Kounde tucked home the third from Lamine Yamal’s cross to cap Barca’s solid win against Jose Bordalas’s side at Camp Nou.

Barca moved five points clear of second-placed Atletico Madrid, who won 2-1 at Alaves earlier, and lead Real Madrid, fourth, by nine points before Los Blancos host Villarreal later on.

Barca were without their top scorer Raphinha, who sustained a hamstring problem during the international break with Brazil.

Flick replaced him with former Arsenal striker and Selecao compatriot Jesus, and his side came roaring out of the blocks.

Gordon, who has impressed since joining before this season, grabbed his first Barca goal with a low deflected effort after bundling his way past three players.

The winger was Barca’s brightest spark in the first half, continuing his fine goalscoring form for England in the recent Nations League matches.

Barca defender Eric Garcia forced a save from Getafe goalkeeper David Soria with a drive from distance as Flick’s side controlled the game.

Getafe defender Zaid Romero gave the ball away in his own box for Barca’s second, passing it straight to Jesus, who stroked into the bottom corner.

Soria denied Olmo before Yamal teed up Kounde for the third.

The defender, making a record 194th appearance for Barca for a French player, overtaking Eric Abidal, was on hand to turn home from close range from teenage star Yamal’s cross.

Barca, who also won their Champions League opener, have nine victories from nine matches across all competitions.
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.summary: Barca beat Getafe 3-0 in La Liga on Saturday to extend their perfect start in La La Liga. Anthony Gordon scored his first goal for the Spanish champions. Gabriel Jesus added another after half an hour for the champions. Jules Kounde scored the third for Barca.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.title: Ronaldo suspended by Portugal FA after leaving camp and criticising coach
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/10.text:
After saying he deserved to be ‌disciplined, Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo got what he asked for Saturday as he was provisionally suspended by ⁠his national team.

The Portuguese Football Federation opened disciplinary proceedings against the team captain after he walked out of camp during the just-completed international break following a ⁠miscommunication with head coach Jorge Jesus.

In a letter that was revealed this week, Ronaldo said he was told by Jesus he would be used as a substitute ⁠in a Nations League match against Norway. Ronaldo warmed up along the sideline, but did not see playing time.

Before the following match against Denmark, the 41-year-old striker departed camp after notifying the federation he was leaving.

“Disciplinary proceedings have been initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, ‌following a decision by the Non-Professional Section on October 9, 2026,” the Portuguese Football Federation said in a statement.

Ronaldo has already returned to his club team, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia, and scored a goal in a 3-0 victory over Diriyah on Friday.

In his explanation of his actions, Ronaldo admitted that his decision to leave camp was not the best way to handle the situation. But he ⁠added that Jesus “broke his word” on more than one ⁠occasion.

“I owe my national team teammates an apology for leaving the training camp,” Ronaldo said. “Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach’s word, as anyone who witnessed our conversations can testify, I should not have ⁠done it. The responsibility is exclusively mine.”

After just participating in his sixth World Cup for Portugal this year, Ronaldo said ⁠he is open to discipline. According to reports, the ⁠federation’s regulations call for a suspension of anywhere from a month to six months for a player who “abandons” national team activity.

“The consequence of my actions should be assessed and punished by the [federation],” Ronaldo said. “The punishment should ‌not have any mitigating circumstances. I am not just any player; I am the captain of the team, and that constitutes an aggravating factor.”

After playing in 234 matches for ‌his ‌national team and scoring 146 goals, Ronaldo said he still has the desire to play for Portugal in the future. Portugal has Nations League matches scheduled against Denmark and Wales next month.

https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/apple-.title: Apple discloses deal to hire team and license tech from personalized podcast startup Huxe
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/apple-.author: Anthony Ha
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/apple-.text:
Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal.

As first reported in MacRumors, Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.”

Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.”)

In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook). But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down, with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data.

“The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said. It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.”

On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal.

The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted. Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans.

Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own, so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app. Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree.
https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/10/apple-.summary: Apple has agreed to make employment offers to Huxe AI employees. The company also announced it would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.title: South Melbourne stuns Melbourne Victory to claim Australia Cup
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

After a dramatic late equaliser, South Melbourne beat Melbourne Victory in a shootout to win the Australia Cup final. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

South Melbourne have made history, becoming the first NPL side to win the Australia Cup, beating Melbourne Victory in the final.

South Melbourne and Victory were 0-0 after 90 minutes, then 1-1 after extra time.

Victory missed two of their penalties in the shootout, as South Melbourne clinched the Cup 4-3.

A-League aspirants South Melbourne have become the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup after beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotion-charged blockbuster final.

In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic soccer history, former NSL powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at AAMI Park.

South Melbourne, who have long craved an A-League licence, only strengthened their bid for that with a win that capped off an extraordinary evening.

Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.

In the penalty shootout, South goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.

Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line, but then saved the re-take too.

South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.

In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, Sinisa Cohadzic's South succeed where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.

With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.

The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.

South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.

A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of AAMI Park, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskas and John Margaritis.

The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.

On the field, South Melbourne attacking pair Juach and Yuki Uchida gave the Victory defence headaches all night.

Lopez made several great saves while Victory counterpart Jack Duncan was called into action on multiple occasions in regular time.

Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Guillermo May squared the ball to Santos but the Brazilian's poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.

Denis Genreau's hooked volley hit the crossbar and bounced in, but Victory could not hold onto the lead. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.

Juach spurned a couple of great chances to equalise and the game appeared lost for South.

Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.

AAMI Park erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Oscar Piastri shrugged off the sprint crash before qualifying seventh for Sunday's main race. (Getty Images: Steven Tee/LAT Images)

McLaren teammates Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have collided on the last lap of the sprint race at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix.

Australian Piastri was knocked out of the race, while Norris limped to eighth.

The main race will be held from 11pm AEDT on Sunday, with Norris qualifying fifth fastest and Piastri seventh.

World champion Lando Norris has apologised to his McLaren team after a final-lap collision with stablemate Oscar Piastri wrecked their ​pursuit of a podium finish at a chaotic Singapore Grand Prix sprint race.

The McLaren duo were chasing Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who was struggling with his tyres in the dying stages of ​the 20-lap sprint, ‌when disaster struck on the final lap.

Norris, running fifth behind Piastri in fourth, attempted to overtake his teammate but clipped the Australian's rear tyre with his front wheel, ‌sending both cars spinning and handing Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli fourth ⁠place.

Norris and Piastri collide 💥

Here's the moment 👇#F1Sprint #SingaporeGP pic.twitter.com/jVetu3oSOs

"Sorry about that. Obviously, I didn't want that to happen, ‌but I thought I was ​fully alongside. I just ‌ran out of space at the apex, but I was there," Norris said over the team radio.

While Norris limped home to eighth place to claim the final point available, Piastri was forced to retire as he ​became ‌one of nine cars that did not finish — a record number of retirements for a Formula 1 sprint race.

"I'd rather just go back ⁠and review it," Norris told Sky Sports.

"I ‌apologised to them that one ‌of the cars is out but, like I said, the rest of it we'll ‌go review."

Elsewhere Norris suggested he was entitled "to go for a big gap" because everyone should be fighting for places in a competitive race.

"What's the title of the race?" he asked an interviewer who implied his move on the inside was "unnecessary".

"What's after 'sprint'?"

When the interviewer replied "race", he laughed and sarcastically said: "Wow, good job".

Piastri said he had not seen the incident properly to comment but downplayed its significance as they were not ‌in high ​points scoring positions.

"From ⁠where I sit, it's for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I'm not that bothered either way," Piastri said.

"Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars ⁠fixed [ahead of qualifying for Sunday's race]. Just a shame for the team."

Both McLaren drivers were summoned to ‌the stewards ‌after the collision.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the sprint and ​the Dutchman leapfrogged Norris to climb to fifth in the world championship standings.

Verstappen also took pole for the main race in Singapore ahead of Leclerc, with Norris fifth and Piastri seventh.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid Airport on Thursday after an attack by the Houthi rebel group. (Reuters)

The airport in the Saudi capital has been attacked a second time.

Separately, Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks on Saturday.

Palestinian legislative elections due next month have been postponed until September 2027 by President Mahmoud Abbas.

The airport in the Saudi capital has been attacked a second time, two days after three Saudi citizens were killed at the same airport in a strike conducted by the Houthi rebel group.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh have now been suspended according to the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority, who also stated an unknown number of people had been injured

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, but it comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis against Saudi Arabia.

King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times this week, since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the earlier attacks, including a strike on Wednesday that killed a Sudanese national.

On Thursday, at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in another attack at the airport according to the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation.

The Houthi group are yet to release a statement about Saturday's strike.

The Saudi government-run Center for International Communication, which oversees foreign media in the kingdom, did not respond to a request for comment.

The airport issued an alert telling passengers to check their flight status with airlines before heading to the airport.

At least 225 flights at the airport had been cancelled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.

On Saturday, flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled.

In Yemen, its Transport Ministry said the rebels attacked Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early on Wednesday, local time.

Aden Airport in Yemen was attacked by Houthi rebels on Wednesday.   (Reuters: Fawaz Salman)

Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces in an attempt to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.

On Friday as he left the White House, US President Donald Trump was asked about the attacks on the Riyadh airport and told reporters, "It's not good" and "I'm not happy".

There has been no immediate sign of US military support to respond to the attacks.

Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability".

Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks on Saturday, according to health officials.

Medics said an Israeli strike killed four people near Panda Mall in Gaza City, while another killed one person in the Tuffah neighbourhood further south of the city.

The Israeli military said the two strikes targeted militants, without giving further information.

Some of the rubble that lines streets in Gaza. (ABC News)

Israel has stepped up strikes against Hamas in recent weeks, saying the Palestinian militant group has been rearming and carrying out attacks in violation of the ceasefire.

Hamas denies rebuilding its arsenal or planning attacks and accuses Israel of undermining the US-brokered ceasefire which was issued and agreed upon a year ago.

On Saturday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections due next month, until September 11, 2027.

Mr Abbas called for a presidential poll for the same date, blaming Israel and security Palestinian territories for the delay.

Mahmoud Abbas has postponed legislative elections until 2027. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

Mr Abbas's decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections", the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.

The decree called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to vote.

There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian vote would go ahead next month. Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Mr Abbas's rival, the Islamist group ​Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.

Mr Abbas has ruled by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.

The Palestinian Authority held municipal elections in April in the West Bank and in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, the only city in the enclave to participate. The vote was the first election held in Gaza since 2006.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Man with gun kills one Philadelphia police officer and injures another
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press and Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
10-year police veteran Shane Seiber was killed after responding to a report of a man with a gun

A Philadelphia police officer was fatally shot and another was wounded on Saturday after responding to a report of a man with a gun, authorities said.

Shane Seiber, 40, was killed early on Saturday morning in West Philadelphia, according to the city’s police commissioner, Kevin Bethel.

Seiber, a 10-year veteran of the Philadelphia police department, and the other officer were transported to the Penn Presbyterian medical center, where the surviving officer underwent surgery. He was listed in stable condition, Bethel said.

Bethel also said a suspect was in custody.

Citing law enforcements sources, the Philadelphia Inquirer identified that suspect as Eric Lewis. The Inquirer also reported that Lewis, 35, was employed by Philadelphia’s municipal water department.

Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, said he ordered flags to fly at half-mast for Seiber. He is survived by his wife and two children: a boy, age seven, and a girl, three.

Seiber was at least the 376th Philadelphia police department officer to die in the line of duty since 1851, according to the Officer Down Memorial Page, which honors US law enforcement personnel who died while on the job. He was the 129th of those officers to die from gunfire, the memorial page said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/video/inside-s.text:
Washington’s sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court (ICC) came hours after one of its former judges, Navi Pillay, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday.

The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

It has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

The US has denounced the court in the past, especially after it issued the arrest warrants for Israeli officials.

Washington has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges, but the latest move seeks to cripple the operations of the court, according to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Why is the US so against the ICC? And will Europe defy Washington and defend the court?

Presenter: Sami Zeidan

Reed Brody – International human rights lawyer and member of the International Commission of Jurists, who participated in the 1998 Rome conference that created the ICC and has helped prosecute some of the world’s high-profile defendants

Nathalie Tocci – Professor of practice at Johns Hopkins SAIS Europe and a former special adviser to EU High Representatives Federica Mogherini and Josep Borrell

Suhail Khan – Republican political analyst, former senior political appointee with the Bush administration and a former policy adviser and counsel on Capitol Hill
