Hundreds of doctors have gathered outside the World Medical Association (WMA) summit in the Netherlands, calling for the suspension of the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) from the grouping of physicians.

On Saturday, 81 healthcare workers removed their scrubs and hung them in a line facing the WMA assembly in Rotterdam, each bearing the name of a Palestinian healthcare worker currently held in illegal Israeli detention.

It was part of a protest against the continued membership of the Israeli association in the WMA, “despite them breaching almost every ethical principle in the WMA’s Code of Medical Ethics”, the IMA Out! coalition that organised the demonstration said in a statement.

“These scrubs should not be empty. Our colleagues belong with their patients, not in Israeli prisons. Today, we literally placed their names at the WMA’s doorstep,” said Mejrem Ahmetaj, a general practitioner and member of IMA Out!.

Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 1,700 Palestinian healthcare workers and destroyed nearly all the hospitals and healthcare facilities in the enclave.

The campaign accused the Israeli medical association of remaining silent as Palestinian healthcare has been systematically destroyed.

“The IMA is not a bystander. It defends these attacks and blocks international condemnation while Palestinian healthcare is being destroyed. That is not medical neutrality. That is complicity,” added Ahmetaj.

At a meeting of international doctors, medical leaders and human rights activists during the WMA summit on Thursday, the destruction of Palestinian healthcare and the responsibility of the international medical community were discussed, the campaign said.

“Our Palestinian colleagues are being killed and imprisoned, where they are starved and tortured. Their hospitals have been destroyed and patients driven out or murdered. The IMA has said and done nothing about these war crimes against health workers, patients and hospitals,” said a statement by Jonathan Fluxman on behalf of IMA OUT!.

“Thirty years of WMA dialogue with the IMA has done nothing but give the IMA a sense of impunity … It is time for national medical associations and the WMA to speak out and take action. Break your ties with the IMA and suspend the IMA from the WMA now,” he added.

The IMA OUT! campaign said it delivered a petition calling for the IMA’s suspension, signed by more than 6,500 health workers from around the world.

They also demanded accountability for the complicity of Israeli doctors in the starvation, torture and medical neglect of Palestinian prisoners.

Among those held by Israel is Dr Hussam Abu Safia, head of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, whose unlawful detention has prompted an international outcry.

He was briefly held at the notorious Sde Teiman detention camp and has been subject to torture and medical neglect. Doctors protesting in Rotterdam held up placards demanding his release.

Abu Safia’s son Elyas, addressing a meeting organised by the campaign, said, “My father and all Palestinian detainees must be treated in accordance with medical ethics, and doctors must abide by the Hippocratic oath they have taken. Care cannot be given based on whose life is deemed worthy.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Hurricane Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast, packing winds of up to 241km/h (150mph) as it threatens to bring destructive winds, storm surges and life-threatening flooding to southwestern Mexico.

The US National Hurricane Center said that Simon was expected to approach or move just inland of Mexico’s west-central coast late on Saturday or early Sunday. The storm was about 115 miles (185km) south-southwest of Manzanillo, with further strengthening possible before landfall.

The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25 to 51cm) of rain to parts of southwestern Mexico through Sunday.

“This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the agency warned, urging residents to complete preparations to protect lives and property.

Authorities issued a hurricane warning for parts of the Pacific coast south of the resort city of Puerto Vallarta, including the area around Manzanillo, the country’s largest Pacific port. A tropical storm watch was in effect farther south towards Lazaro Cardenas.

Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas. Officials also urged hotels and other tourism businesses in Puerto Vallarta to ensure workers and visitors had access to shelters or safe locations.

Businesses in the popular tourist destination boarded up windows and placed sandbags at entrances as the storm approached.

The hurricane centre also warned of a dangerous storm surge and large and destructive waves near where Simon makes landfall.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is the latest tech executive to offer lengthy thoughts on how AI safety might be improved.

In a Saturday morning post on X, Nadella wrote that it’s time “to step back and assess the trust architecture” of AI.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” Nadella wrote, using the Trump administration’s preferred term for AI.

As outlined by Nadella, this approach “means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work,” as well as “externalizing controls and safeguards.” He also called for “every meaningful model action” to be documented with “tamper-proof human readable evidence,” and for systems where “an authorized person” always has the ability “to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”

“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he said. “Think of it like an emergency brake.”

Nadella’s comments come as leading AI companies acknowledge more and more incidents where they seemed to lose control of their models, and after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a plan for more cautious AI development.

https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/us-debt-g.title: CBO chief warns it’s ‘probably not plausible’ that a strong economy alone can steady U.S. debt as 5%-6% growth is needed—more than Bessent’s 3% view
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/us-debt-g.author: Jason Ma
https://fortune.com/2026/10/10/us-debt-g.text:
Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel said faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check, even if GDP expands at more than double its current pace.

Gross debt is now $40 trillion, and publicly held debt is 100% of GDP. Just keeping that ratio flat, let alone bringing it down, would require a massive, sustained boom. For now, CBO see the debt-to-GDP ratio soaring to 120% by 2036.

During a Minneapolis Fed conference on Thursday, Swagel said stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, but it’s not that simple.

Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs.

“So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” Swagel added. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are inherently political choices.”

Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari asked if AI can help supercharge economic growth, and he replied that CBO has detected an increase in total factor productivity, which measures the efficiency of labor, capital, and other inputs.

The CBO’s next batch of economic forecasts due early next year will incorporate its views on AI, Swagel said, adding that future growth will be stronger. Still, the budget deficit is so deep that even the extra AI-powered growth won’t be enough, he warned.

Kashkari then asked how much faster growth would have to be in order to stabilize the debt. Swagel cautioned against doing arithmetic on the fly but offered some back-of-the-envelope numbers.

Assuming interest rates of 4%-5%, he estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8% and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6%.

That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%.

The rough numbers from the CBO chief also far exceed what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said would be needed to overcome the debt.

“With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.”

Meanwhile, other estimates fall somewhere in between. According to the Penn Wharton Budget Model, growth would have to average 3.5%-4% over a decade to maintain the debt-to-GDP ratio.

Swagel also noted that an economic shock that sends interest rates up suddenly would set off a vicious fiscal cycle.

“So there’s almost like a turbocharger,” he explained. “An interest rate shock feeds into the deficit, feeds into the debt, feeds back into interest rates.”

So far, the bond market is absorbing all the debt the U.S. Treasury is issuing to fund the budget deficit, but long-term yields have surged to the highest levels in 24 years.

Some of that is due to the strong economy, expectations for Fed rate hikes, high oil prices keeping inflation high, and the flood of AI hyperscaler debt competing for bond market demand.

But the enormous scale of U.S. debt is also a factor. Swagel said it’s small now, with a 1-percentage-point increase in the debt ratio leading to a 0.015-percentage-point hike on long-term interest rates.

“So it’s modest, but the fiscal trajectory is really quite challenging,” he added. “It adds up, and of course there’s that turbocharger type effect that I mentioned where it feeds back into deficits.”

https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/microsof.author: Greg Iacurci
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/10/microsof.text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said advanced AI systems should include containment, independent controls and an “emergency brake.”

Other AI and tech industry leaders have called for stronger safeguards and, in several cases, pacing frontier development.

President Donald Trump opposes slowing U.S. AI development, while his administration has launched a safety-focused task force.

Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an “emergency brake” that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task.

“We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient,” Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X.

“Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system,” he said.

Nadella’s comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft
 co-founder Bill Gates, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX
 CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast.

An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of “gambling with our lives.” Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there’s a greater than 10% chance that the technology could “kill all humans” within the next decade.

Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new “AI Force,” led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors.

Microsoft’s Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around “principles of observability.”

They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model’s actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote.

“The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most,” he wrote. “It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/o.author: Hamish Cole
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/o.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Molly Ticehurst was murdered by her former partner Daniel Billings in her Forbes home in April 2024. (Supplied)

The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions will not appeal the 28-year sentence of murderer Daniel Billings.

The 31-year-old stabbed his former partner Molly Ticehurst to death in her Forbes home in 2024.

Billings will be eligible for parole in 2044.

The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) will not appeal the 28-year sentence handed down to murderer Daniel Billings in the Orange Supreme Court.

Warning: This article includes descriptions of domestic violence and murder.

Billings, 31, pleaded guilty to stabbing his former partner and childcare worker Molly Ticehurst to death in her Forbes home in April 2024.

Judge Natalie Adams sentenced him to 28 years in prison with a non-parole period of 20 years, sparking outrage from politicians and friends of Ms Ticehurst.

In a statement, the ODPP said it would not challenge the judgement.

"Having carefully considered the sentence imposed and the circumstances of this case, the ODPP has determined not to institute an appeal against Mr Billing's sentence," the spokesperson said.

"This decision was made in accordance with the prosecution guidelines."

The ODPP had 28 days following the sentencing to appeal.

Daniel Billings pleaded guilty to murdering Molly Ticehurst. (Supplied)

The independent member for Orange Phil Donato, who previously worked as a police prosecutor, said he was "disappointed" by the ODPP's decision.

"This is a matter that drew nationwide condemnation in relation to domestic violence.

"[It] is a gross injustice."

Phil Donato says murderer Daniel Billings deserves a life sentence for killing his former partner, Molly Ticehurst.  (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Billings was out on bail at the time of the murder for offences alleged to have been committed against Ms Ticehurst, including sexual assault, which he denies.

The court heard during a hearing in the Orange Supreme Court in September, that Billings broke through Ms Ticehurst's bedroom window at 11:27pm, stabbed her multiple times with a hunting knife and left the home less than a minute later.

At a press conference on September 16, NSW Premier Chris Minns described Billings as a "bastard" and said the sentence was inadequate.

"I just feel terrible for the family who are decent, honest, hard-working people who've lost their daughter at the hands of a complete bastard."

Speaking outside court after the sentence was handed down on September 11, Ms Ticehurst's childhood friend Aidan Clark said life imprisonment for Billings was the outcome her friends and family wanted.

"There's nothing that will bring Molly back and no time was ever going to be enough," he said.

The total sentence Justice Adams handed down was 35 years, which was discounted to 28 years due to Billings's guilty plea.

Justice Natalie Adams sentenced Billings to 28 years behind bars, with a non-parole period of 20 years.  (ABC News)

While handing down her judgement, Justice Adams said her considerations included Billings mental state and level of remorse shown after the murder.

In 2024, a review was announced by the NSW government into the contact Ms Ticehurst had with government agencies and domestic violence services after reporting Billings to police.

Ms Ticehurst's mother Kate Shaw called for the review's release following the conclusion of the sentencing hearing. The premier committed to do so once the appeal process had finished.

"The NSW government will make as much information as possible about the outcomes of the review available to the family of Molly Ticehurst and the people of NSW as soon as it is able to," a government spokesperson said.

Mr Donato said the review needs to be released immediately.

"The family of Molly deserves to know what's in that report and if there were failings in the system," he said.

"There needs to be accountability and transparency around it.

"There is no reason now why it should not be released."

Bail reforms were introduced in NSW following a campaign sparked by Ms Ticehurst's murder.

The reforms included people accused of serious domestic violence offences being required to wear electronic monitoring devices when granted bail.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.title: Race to stop rice-sized bee from a silent extinction
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.author: Justin Huntsdale
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Nikolas Johnston, Tegan Edwards and James Dorey have studied a rare, tiny bee they say faces extinction. (Supplied: University of Wollongong)

The population of a tiny bee first described in 2024 has declined by 99 per cent in the last 150 years and should be classed as critically endangered, scientists say.

The Hylaeus navai bee in Fiji is an example of a bee that could have become extinct before being discovered.

Scientists want students in the South Pacific to take on more research to better understand what lives in the region.

A tiny Fijian bee species has only just been discovered by scientists but it is already the precipice of extinction.

Scientist Tegan Edwards spent a month in Fiji battling humidity, heat and rain while wrangling a 9-metre pole with a net as she searched for a bee smaller than a grain of rice that almost no-one has heard of.

Such is the work of trying to save a creature at risk of becoming extinct before its existence is even known.

"It's a pretty common situation, especially with insects," Ms Edwards said.

"It's hard to catalogue them because they're so diverse and it's hard to see them before they go, especially in areas that are more under-studied."

The masked bee, Hylaeus navai, was first formally described in 2024.

But it is at risk of what ecologists like David Attenborough have called "silent extinction".

Researchers believe the species has suffered a 99 per cent population collapse in the last 150 years. Their findings were published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Ecology and Evolution this week.

Ms Edwards said European insects were extremely well researched, but experts still had a lot to discover about what lived on Australia's neighbours in the Pacific Islands.

A female example of the bee, as found and documented by scientist James Dorey. (Supplied: James Dorey)

That is what led her and fellow University of Wollongong (UOW) colleague James Dorey to Fiji to begin their search.

Dr Dorey, an evolutionary biologist, first found a single Hylaeus navai on a trip to Fiji in 2016, and then "a whole bunch more" on two visits in 2019.

He said that not only was insect was difficult, it was hard to kill it in order to correctly record and describe it.

James Dorey says a bee's history can be accurately tracked via an analysis of its genome. (Supplied: University of Wollongong)

Dr Dorey said scientific analysis indicated the bees were critically endangered.

"We see mutations in the bee's genome," he said.

"You can look at the frequency of the mutations to say something about when they arose, but also make predictions about how maybe 100 years ago the population was this size and now it's this size, and see how things have changed."

Dr Dorey said the population collapse aligned with colonisation in Fiji, which brought habitat destruction and potential pesticide use.

Along with natural events such as cyclones damaging habitats, he said another potential threat was that the bees were attracted to red flowering plants such as the African tulip, which is poisonous to a variety of bees.

Tegan Edwards had to develop the strength and skill to wield the 9-metre pole and net to catch the rare bees. (Supplied: University of Wollongong)

Bees are responsible for pollinating the plants that form a huge part of human and animal diets.

They are essential to the health, reproduction and survival of entire ecosystems.

Ms Edwards wants to find and help them before they become extinct — and for people to care, regardless of how tiny they are.

Tegan Edwards says knowledge helps keep pollinators safe. (Supplied: University of Wollongong)

"Pollinators underpin all of our systems, so we need to look towards conserving our pollinators," she said.

"What we don't know, we can't conserve.

"So if we don't know they're there, we can't find the threats they're facing and try and help them.

"More research into the pollinators that underpin our food and medicine systems is really worthwhile."

The research team have not revisited Fiji to check on populations of the masked bee since 2024.

"It's challenging to monitor because it takes a lot of skill and strength to wield the nets and catch them," Dr Dorey said.

"We also need people on the ground in Fiji to do the work and monitor these insects."

The UOW research into the bee has been funded by a federal government grant, which has allowed the scientists to form a partnership with the University of the South Pacific.

Dr Dorey hopes that partnership will help train Fijian students to research the rare bee year-round.

The jewel in the crown of the Supercars season is here, as 54 drivers prepare to tackle Mount Panorama for the Bathurst 1000.

Zach Bates lit up the Top 10 Shootout last night to put him and teammate Aaron Seton on pole in the number 10 Matt Stone Racing Chevrolet car.

Follow all the live action from the Bathurst 1000 throughout the day from lights out to the chequered flag on the blog below.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/l.title: Being vision impaired made me feel unlovable, then I met Jed
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
People With Disability

Chanelle has a rare vision condition that affects both eyes. (Supplied)

Chanelle Morris thought she was going to be "alone forever" after many deflating and hurtful dating experiences because of her vision impairment.

The 27-year-old had all but given up on finding love when she caught the eye of Jed on a social outing at a driving range.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Chanelle and Jed's words.

Chanelle: I have a type of chorioretinal dystrophy, a rare vision condition which impacts my peripheral vision and ability to notice detail.

I'm legally blind in one eye and the other one is not that much better.

I thought no-one would love me because of my condition.

Chanelle says having a vision impairment made dating difficult. (Supplied)

I thought that I was too much for people. I feel like a lot of people with disability experience that.

Something that really rocked my confidence was when I would speak to someone, it would appear that my eyes were focused behind them, not on them.

So I stopped approaching people in public settings.

I used to get anxious in the lead-up to meeting someone from a dating app because I chose not to disclose my vision condition. It led to some people not believing me when I told them, or worse, being the subject of blind jokes that were disrespectful.

Once I included my condition in my dating profile, I got fewer matches, but they were more authentic, genuine and open.

I just didn't think that anyone would accept my vision impairment because most people didn't understand it and there was a lot of fear around it.

Chanelle: I was hosting a women's golf event at a driving range on the Gold Coast and Jed just happened to be there that day.

Our meet-cute is a funny story because he was checking me out, but I couldn't see that.

One of the ladies I was there with noticed and actually went over to Jed to see if he was single and was interested in me.

She came charging over to me and said, "Go right now, he's interested."

I wrote my number on a drink coaster and went straight over, and I can't remember what I said, I just remember the adrenaline. I gave him my number and then I left because it was at the end of the event.

But I left my golf clubs behind because I was so nervous.

So I sent one of my friends back to get them because I was like, "I'm not going back in there."

Chanelle and Jed's meet-cute was at a driving range. (Supplied)

I remember Jed texted me that day to organise a date two days later.

I was so nervous, I couldn't eat.

But he was so sweet and texted me specific instructions on where he was sitting at the restaurant so I could find him.

I'd never had anyone do that for me before.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

Jed: When I went to the driving range, I thought I'd go hit some golf balls on my day off. Little did I know I'd find the love of my life.

Jed says Chanelle's vision impairment was never a barrier to them dating. (Supplied)

I was definitely checking Chanelle out.

The first thing her friend said to me was, "She's keen on you but she has an eye condition."

So I knew about her vision impairment straight away.

But it wasn't something that was going to change my mind or affect my decision to see her.

I was pretty nervous before our date, but it couldn't have gone any better, the conversation flowed so well.

I just love how caring and supportive she is.

Jed: I have type 1 diabetes and Chanelle will get me some sugar if I need it because my sugar's low or she carries my insulin pen for me in her purse.

I think that's why we get on so well, because we know what it's like to need support and help.

I've always admired her selflessness.

She has so much time for other people, including me.

She goes to conferences for motivational speaking and I am so proud and impressed by that.

I'll come home, and she's got some sort of little surprise for me.

I've never felt so at ease before in my life.

Chanelle and Jed say the support they show one another has deepened their love. (Supplied)

Chanelle: He shows up for me in a way that I didn't even know was possible and he says to me that I do the same for him.

The main thing I can't do with my vision impairment is drive, so Jed drives me a lot, which is great.

Every time we go to a restaurant or a cafe, he reads the menu without me even asking or helps me read labels at the grocery store.

He's like my eyes for anything, even helping me find the bathroom when we're out, which is a big anxiety for people with low vision.

Jed's my caddy at my golf competitions now, so he's literally my eyes.

We'll practise at the golf range now and as soon as he's not looking, I can't hit the ball.

I need him to help me play.

I can really be myself and I love that.

He makes me feel like a whole person and I'm more than enough for him.

My heart is healing in ways I never expected, and I could not be more grateful.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/m.title: Butter knives, kitchen scissors among items surrendered to machete bins
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/m.author: Rachel Eddie
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/m.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
State and Territory Government

The machete amnesty bins were rolled out as the Victorian government moved to ban the weapons last year. (Supplied/ABC News: Cordelia Brown)

Victoria's machete bins collected more than 12,000 machetes and "other knives" after a statewide ban on the weapons was instituted.

The bins were manufactured at a South Australian prison before being installed at police stations around the state.

The government says the machete amnesty program came in at half the projected total cost, but has not revealed where the money was spent.

Machete bins manufactured by South Australian prisoners were trucked off to Victoria in three batches over two weeks last year, before butter knives were counted among the weapons dumped inside them.

The bins were rolled out to dozens of police stations when machetes were banned in September 2025, so that Victorians could safely surrender the blades while the government attempted to crack down on violent knife crime.

But the government was widely criticised for being opaque with the details of its $13 million program, with the opposition making wild claims about its cost and usefulness despite having called for the ban.

The ABC has confirmed the amnesty actually came in at half the projected total cost, at $6.55 million.

Documents released to the ABC under Freedom of Information laws colour in further details, revealing inmates at the privately run Mount Gambier Prison, operated by G4S, constructed the 75 blue bins at the facility's metal fabrication workshop.

The government paid G4S $925,000 to manufacture the bins and install them outside police stations. The contract also covered collecting, transporting, cataloguing and destroying the surrendered weapons.

The bins were manufactured at a South Australian prison before being shipped to Victoria. (Supplied: Victorian government)

A sample catalogue of items disposed in the bins shows that butter knives were among the dumped items, along with "anomalous content" like kitchen scissors.

Guns and axes were also surrendered, images and records released to the ABC show.

The Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS) said 12,357 machetes and "other knives" — including butter knives — were surrendered to the bins.

Retailers handed in another 5,674 machetes after being prohibited from selling them, taking the haul to 18,031 weapons.

The 75 bins were made in three batches over 30 days, departmental documents show, and trucked over to Melbourne in lots.

G4S had expected to place the bins at 58 stations, but this was reduced to 45. Surplus bins were swapped in and out once they were damaged or full.

Under pressure for not being forthcoming with the details, the government has previously put the cost of each bin at $2,400.

An early breakdown of estimated costs — buried among the documents — said manufacturing the bins would cost a total of $139,000, including a one-off charge for other "non-technical equipment".

This would have amounted to $1,854 per bin, but the ABC has been told design changes and GST pushed the cost up.

The machete disposal bins were placed at dozens of police stations across Victoria. (AAP: Joel Carett)

G4S further expected it would need to spend $600,000 in labour, $260,000 for an operations manager, and $240,000 for vehicle costs including hiring two vehicles.

The contractor's proposal estimated the total cost of its work would be between $865,500 and $1.2 million, depending on whether work could be stepped up or down.

The bins ultimately cost taxpayers $925,000.

Another $884,000 contract went towards "creative services" for "editorial and design and graphic and fine art services".

Market research to support public messaging cost another $123,000, according to public tenders.

The government has not previously explained how the remaining budget was spent, however it included a multilingual public awareness campaign to ensure machetes were handed in.

A DJCS spokesperson said the amnesty was delivered on time and under budget, "with the remaining unspent funds redirected to additional police and Protective Services Officers (PSO) in shopping centres to keep Victorians safe".

Victoria Police had advised the government that if its machete ban included an amnesty, infrastructure such as surrender bins had to be installed.

"Surrender bins prevent individuals walking into police station reception areas with machetes and other edged weapons, which creates significant safety risk and public alarm," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

"The machete surrender bins allow for proactive disposal of these blades by members of the community in a safe and controlled way."

Victoria will ban the sale of machetes from today. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Victoria Police said its officers had since seized more than 11,200 knives, machetes and other illegal blades so far in 2026.

Despite criticising the government's machete ban, the opposition itself had previously called for it.

Premier Ben Carroll has since introduced further anti-knife crime measures, including by borrowing another Coalition commitment to give police greater search powers.

It is a sign that knife crime continues to haunt the government heading into the state election, and that it was not resolved by the machete bins.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/j.title: Jenny Woodward honoured at Queensland journalism awards after 40 years presenting
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/j.author: Ned Hammond
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Awards and Prizes

Jenny Woodward has spent 40 years explaining the weather to the ABC's Queensland audience. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

After 40 years talking Queenslanders through rain, wind and shine, ABC News Queensland weather presenter Jenny Woodward has been given the state's Most Outstanding Contribution to Journalism award.

The prize honours what has been a remarkable career in broadcast journalism, which has built Woodward into one of the country's most trusted and respected voices.

Woodward was presented with the award at the Queensland Clarion Awards in Brisbane last night.

A Brisbane native, Woodward's career in journalism began at commercial TV station Channel 10/4/5a in Toowoomba in the 1970s, where she worked on kids' and special event television.

Jenny Woodward began presenting the weather in 1975 at a Toowoomba local TV station. (Supplied: Jenny Woodward)

Presenting came early, with news and weather reading part of her responsibilities at the regional station.

"As humans we all love stories and I am taking scientific data, lots of specific weather terms which can be a little dry," Woodward said.

"So I want the audience to understand what's happening, but not overwhelm them with the detail."

After a brief stint at Channel 7 in Brisbane, Woodward brought her burgeoning ability to the national broadcaster in 1986.

David Mackay, Rod Young and Jenny Woodward at the ABC in 1987. (ABC News: Jenny Woodward)

By 1987, she was presenting the ABC News weather alongside news presenter Rod Young and sports presenter David Mackay.

In those days, the job would require a dash into the city to pick up charts from the Bureau of Meteorology and a chat with a forecaster, before racing back to the studio to go to air.

"There were three camera operators in the studio and a floor manager to give us our cues," Woodward said.

Fashion and hairstyles changed a lot over 40 years and Jenny Woodward has had viewers write in to give her advice on her styling. (Supplied: Jenny Woodward)

The fax machine soon made things easier, and the technological advancements did not stop there.

"Now the cameras are robotic, and we take our cues through an earpiece," she said.

Along the way, it has become standard to send weather presenters to all sorts of locations — a development that has seen Woodward become the queen of the Ekka.

The Brisbane Ekka has very much become Jenny Woodward's annual stomping ground. (Supplied: Jenny Woodward)

"It's chaotic, unpredictable, very noisy and fun. I know the audience is just waiting to see if the animal is going to bite me or pee on me," she said.

"Often they do both."

Nowadays, Woodward stands by a graphical map developed by a company and projected with a green screen, walking audiences through forecasts that have widened in scope and tightened in accuracy.

Her curation of audience-submitted photographs of stunning weather formations and beautiful Queensland landscapes has become a staple of her presentation.

"I look at every photo that comes in and I love seeing what takes people's interest," she said.

Jenny Woodward was awarded an Order of Australia for her service to broadcast media. (Supplied)

It's storytelling, as Woodward says, not statistics — and "weather is a constantly changing, evolving story".

"I really believe that as a reporter, if you are not engaged with your material then you can't expect the audience to be either. Although in this story, we all have a personal interest," she said.

"And it's always about the audience. We are nothing without them."

The way the weather is done has changed dramatically, and Jenny Woodward has certainly kept up. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

Woodward is no stranger to awards, having been handed a Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) in 2024 for her service to broadcast media.

Meanwhile, the ABC's Scott Kyle received The John Bean Memorial Award for Television Camerawork.

Antonia O'Flaherty was recognised for her radio reporting on the Caboolture Hospital medical scan bungle.

Angelica Silva took the gong in multicultural reporting for I Feel Scared Like Never Before: Inside the Moments That Reshaped Fear Among Indian Australians, and Grace Tobin and Kirsten Robb were recognised for their reporting on the IVF mix-up.

Grace Nakamura from the ABC's Toowoomba bureau was recognised for her regional and community coverage. Owen Jaques from the Sunshine Coast bureau took out the gong in sports journalism.

Dark Reality of Australia’s AI Dream Factory, by Josh Robertson, Justine Landis-Hanley and the Background Briefing team came out top in the business and podcast categories. Josh Robertson, Maddison Connaughton and the Background Briefing team were also recognised for The Road to Bondi.

The ABC's Story Lab team won the award for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Issues Reporting for Deep Time: Tell Me a Story and a second for Innovation for Deep Time: Time, Place and Topic Views.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/b.title: Drying wetlands create genetic risk for southern Australia's brolgas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/b.author: Sam Bradbrook
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Brolgas are known for their distinctive mating dance, which shows their impressive height and wingspan. (Supplied: Warren Chad)

Brolgas are listed as endangered in Victoria as drying wetlands put their homes under threat.

A new study has found genetic variation among Victorian brolgas has declined and become distinct from northern populations.

Wetland restoration projects across south-west Victoria and south-east South Australia have shown promising signs for the species.

Declining wetlands are behind a genetic rift placing south-eastern Australia's vulnerable brolga population at further risk.

The birds, which can grow up to 1.5 metres tall, with a wingspan of up to 2.5m, are known for finding a breeding pair for life, and have an elaborate mating dance.

Brolgas can be found in all mainland Australian states and the Northern Territory, but a closer look at their populations tells a differing story.

Brolgas form mating pairs for life and give birth to one chick a year if the breeding season is successful. (Supplied: Leanne Hall)

In northern Australia, brolga numbers are stable, but in Victoria, where they are listed as endangered, numbers are as low as 1,000 in the state.

A new Macquarie University study into their genetic makeup has found differences between the northern and southern populations, confirming beliefs the two groups had become distinct.

There was little genetic variation among individual birds in Victoria, pointing to increased vulnerability into the future as traits that aid survival become limited.

"One individual could have that genetic makeup that's really good for surviving an event, an extreme event, and can help that population to survive," lead researcher Abby Bryce said.

Abby Bryce says she fell in love with brolgas while studying in Australia. (Supplied: Abby Bryce)

"If there's less of those individuals and less of that genetic diversity, there's not as much of that diversity to have one or two that could give that slight edge for that population down the line."

Ms Bryce said the reduction of wetland habitat for brolgas to breed and feed was driving the reduction of numbers in Victoria and south-east South Australia.

The loss of wetlands also meant the birds roamed across a smaller area, exacerbating genetic concerns.

"All of these factors, wetland loss, degradation and climate change are all playing a factor and limiting the habitats and conditions brolgas are having to live with."

Brolgas hold a special place for Gunditjmara people. They have long shared a home together in south-west Victoria.

Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation's Damein Bell, a Gunditjmara man, says kurout, as they are known in the Gunditjmara language, is a totem for his ancestors.

Damein Bell has worked on projects to protect brolgas. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"They're such a protector of their own family," he said.

"There's a series of pretty well-known photographs of brolgas protecting their nests from swans and from foxes, a very physical protector."

Brolga were once spread throughout swampy wetland areas, but as land was drained for farming activities, their numbers declined.

"For an indicator of country health, our brolgas are very important for down here on Gunditjmara country," he said.

Tae Rak (Lake Condah), near Heywood, is now welcoming brolgas for the first time in decades. (Supplied: Annette Ruzicka)

Gundtij Mirring has led water restoration projects at Tae Rak (Lake Condah), which have seen brolgas return to a site used by Gunditjmara people for centuries.

"The landscape has been changed so much that it is expected that our rare and threatened species are not going to be doing so well," Budj Bim Indigenous Protection Area manager Evelyn Nicholson said.

"But what is within our power to do, we will do to support them."

Evelyn Nicholson and Damein Bell say the return of brolgas to Tae Rak is a promising sign. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

The Nature Glenelg Trust is involved in wetland restoration projects across south-east SA and south-west Victoria.

Director Mark Bachmann said conservation efforts had shown real promise.

Green Swamp, a restored wetland in the Southern Grampians region, had recorded up to 250 birds flocking there at one time.

Mark Bachmann has led wetland restoration projects in Victoria and SA. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

"Whenever we restore a wetland that may have been drained historically and if it has the right attributes for brolga to utilise, then the birds find those wetlands," he said.

"That shows us that when those birds that have gathered and flocked up each year, then dispersed around the landscape, they're actually pretty good at finding a restored wetland in the landscape."

Mr Bachmann said each wetland restored "to the way it was" made a difference.

Brolgas at Green Swamp in the Southern Grampians in 2024, one of the wetlands the Nature Glenelg Trust worked to restore. (Supplied: Mark Bachmann)

"We can make sure that they're here for our kids and our grandkids to continue to enjoy and see in the landscape."

The Suns had plenty to celebrate once again after they sealed a sixth-straight win in the AFLW.   (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Ian Hitchcock)

Gold Coast Suns have consolidated their spot in the top-four with a 22-point win over flag contenders Melbourne in Mackay.

Geelong beat GWS by 63 points to go top of the ladder, while Adelaide downed Richmond by 32 points in Melbourne.

North Melbourne can re-take top spot if they beat Fremantle on Sunday.

Gold Coast have rubber-stamped their AFLW top-four credentials with a historic 22-point victory over Melbourne.

The Suns posted their sixth straight win on Saturday night, faring better in sweltering heat at Mackay's Great Barrier Reef Arena to down the Demons 9.7 (61) to 5.9 (39).

Gold Coast had not beaten Melbourne in their four previous clashes since the Suns entered the women's competition in 2020.

"It's been a long few years for us and we've been slowly building every year," Suns co-captain Lucy Single told Fox Footy after the landmark triumph.

"So to kind of get that win under our belt has been so awesome and I think that's really boosted our confidence."

The Suns find themselves sitting pretty with three rounds left before finals, drawing level with Melbourne at 7-2.

Melbourne took a three-point lead into quarter-time, but Gold Coast kicked away in the second term and did not look back.

Midfielder Charlie Rowbottom had a game-high 33 possessions and six clearances as Ava Usher, Mikayla Nurse and Havana Harris (two goals apiece) all fired up forward.

Despite the mercury hovering in the mid-20s, Usher said the Suns were not fazed by the conditions.

"We knew it was going to be a really tough arm-wrestle and in the end we just got over the line in really hot conditions," the first-year Sun said.

"We're pretty used to it."

Adelaide had too much firepower for Richmond in the earlier game, winning 9.8 (62) to 4.6 (30) at Melbourne's Princes Park.

The 32-point victory put the Crows back in the finals hunt at 4-5, although they remain just outside the eight with three games of round nine to play.

Prolific ball-winner Ebony Marinoff collected 40 disposals, 13 tackles and a goal.

It's been an AFLW season to forget for St Kilda, but Saturday's win over Collingwood has given departing Saints coach Nick Dal Santo a perfect send-off.

The 40-possession game was one shy of her career-best mark.

The Crows captain said it had been a tough week following a 14-point Showdown loss to Port Adelaide.

"I'd be lying [to say] we didn't know what was on the line tonight," Marinoff said.

"But really proud of the girls' efforts just to really start well … because we hadn't over the last fortnight."

Earlier in the day, Geelong took top spot — at least for now — with a 63-point win over GWS at Kardinia Park, with Jacqueline Parry and Aishling Moloney each kicking four goals.

The Cats will fall back to second, however, if North Melbourne beats Fremantle on Sunday.

The other early game saw St Kilda win their first game for the season, with a two-point win over Collingwood at Moorabbin.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

A Korean barbecue restaurant on Springvale Road was set alight just after midnight. (ABC News)

A 15-year-old boy is being treated for burns after allegedly torching a Korean barbecue restaurant in Springvale.

Police are searching for another male believed to be involved.

It is the seventh straight day of arson attacks across Melbourne.

A teenager is being treated for burns in hospital and another male is on the run after allegedly setting fire to a restaurant in Melbourne's south-east.

Just after midnight, Protectice Services Officers (PSO) patrolling Springvale Station were told that two males had broken into a Korean barbecue restaurant on Springvale Road.

Shortly after, black smoke could be seen coming from the building and firefighters were called.

Nobody was inside at the time.

The pair is believed to have fled in a vehicle before police received reports that a teenage boy with burns was at a nearby fast food restaurant on Warrigal Road in Heatherton.

The 15-year-old boy was taken to hospital under police guard and the investigation remains ongoing as officers search for the other male believed to be involved.

A jerry can was located by police near the restaurant and taken as evidence.  (ABC News)

It is the seventh straight day of arson attacks across the city.

In a botched firebombing of two vehicles in Taylors Hill, in Melbourne's north-west, on Monday morning, a 13-year-old boy suffered severe burns to 90 per cent of his body.

He remains in a critical condition and is fighting for his life.

On Friday, his sister urged other Victorian children not to accept money in exchange for carrying out crimes.

It came after it was revealed the group of youth involved in the Taylors Hill attack had been tasked with lighting the fire by middlemen on WhatsApp.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/y.title: 'Trouble coming' as hundreds at Darwin shelter moved 100km to tiny town
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/y.author: Felicity James
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/y.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Yvonne Dunn is worried YiSSA's closure will unfairly impact women and children fleeing domestic violence. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Yvonne Dunn fears it will be women and children left most at risk, as Darwin's largest short-stay accommodation facility is forced to close this weekend with no city-based replacement.

The 400-bed YiSSA shelter, which has been operating at capacity with a waiting list, is closing after the Northern Territory government rejected a financial rescue offer from the federal government to keep it operating.

Instead, the NT government has asked YiSSA residents to move 100 kilometres away from Darwin and its services, to the outskirts of an outback town.

The tiny town of Batchelor, with a population of about 370, has one general store and no access to public transport.

The new YiSSA accommodation site in Batchelor was under construction last week. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Dunn, a caseworker for women fleeing violence, is among those pleading with the NT government to accept the federal government's offer, or at least push out the closure date beyond the Top End wet season.

"My concern is what will happen to the children and the mothers and the grandmothers and the aunties?," Ms Dunn said.

"Because as we all know, in Indigenous society, child-rearing is a shared responsibility."

Ms Dunn warned "trouble is coming", as women who move to Batchelor will be unable to access domestic violence legal services, court and appointments.

"They'll never get their children back, because they can't meet the requirements of the reunification plan with the Department of Children and Families," Ms Dunn said.

Yvonne Dunn says YiSSA residents escaping domestic violence may "never get their children back" if they move to Batchelor. (ABC News: Felicity James)

"They won't be able to exercise their legal rights and get restraining orders."

She said the NT government's handling of the YiSSA negotiations and the hasty closure of the shelter was "worse than the 2007 Intervention".

"At least with the Intervention you had resources attached to it," Ms Dunn said.

The move has also cut residents off from Darwin's Aboriginal health service, Danila Dilba.

"We're concerned about the 250 clients that we have, who have their address registered at YiSSA," Danila Dilba's chief executive Rob McPhee said.

Rob McPhee says Danila Dilba cannot travel to Batchelor and hundreds of patients could be left without support. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"They will no longer be able to access our services from Batchelor, we do not provide transport down there.

"That includes women and children who are escaping violence or domestic violence situations — we had 34 individual clients that our family and domestic violence service was supporting at YiSSA over the last 12 months."

Mr McPhee said an early intervention program called Early Steps Together, which has supported women at risk of family violence, was among the services they would no longer be able to provide.

The NT government has not responded to questions about what supports will be available in Batchelor for families fleeing domestic violence, including transport options for residents who do not have cars.

YiSSA has been used by remote Aboriginal community residents in town for medical treatment or other appointments, the city's homeless population, and families fleeing violence.

There remains confusion about what has motivated the closure.

In a statement to the ABC, an NT government spokesperson said "long-standing concerns" about YiSSA from residents in nearby suburbs had fed into the decision.

NT Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill has distanced herself from that reasoning, citing an unworkable proposal from the federal government.

Rob McPhee says YiSSA's closure will put pressure on Darwin families and suburbs, with overcrowding already occurring in some areas. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Mr McPhee said Danila Dilba's clients had told staff they "will not go" to Batchelor because it was too far away from Darwin-based services.

"So people are going to continue to come to Darwin and they're going to need somewhere to stay," he said.

"People are going to be living rough or they're going to be putting pressure on family households, and we know that pressure is already starting to be seen in suburbs like Karama and Malak."

Mr McPhee said people staying at YiSSA were there because they had no other safe accommodation options.

Rob McPhee says "the homeless issue is in Darwin", not Batchelor. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"There's access to schools, there's access to support services, there's access to healthcare like our clinics [in Darwin]," he said.

"That all goes when that facility is closed and it's going to be replaced with whatever supports are in Batchelor, which we know are very few."

"The homeless issue is in Darwin, we need short-stay accommodation here — the Northern Territory is in a housing crisis and Darwin has a homelessness crisis."

Fiona Dhawunymymurruwuy is one of many former YiSSA residents who have described the shelter as a welcoming and secure place, where women, children and medically vulnerable people felt safe and respected.

Fiona Dhawunymymurruwuy says YiSSA "looked after us" and she felt connected to the people there. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"YiSSA was like home to me, where there was a lot of Aboriginal people and a lot of people that I know, relatives in YiSSA — it was like a community to me," she said.

"I felt connected, like they were my countrymen, my people.

"The security there, they protect the adults and the kids — no one goes out unless there's adults for the kids."

Ms Dhawunymymurruwuy lived at YiSSA for one year, after coming to Darwin from Arnhem Land's Milingimbi community for dialysis, which she requires several times a week.

During that time, she secured herself a job assisting with Yolŋu language at a local primary school but became too unwell to continue.

YiSSA's residents have been asked to move to a new site 100 kilometres away from Darwin and its services. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

She is currently in hospital rehabilitation after requiring a leg amputation and is due to be discharged later this month.

"They said to me, 'If we discharge you, where do you have to go?,'" Ms Dhawunymymurruwuy said

"I said, 'I don't have a house, I don't have a home because YiSSA, where I stay, it's closing and there's no choice for me'.

Fiona Dhawunymymurruwuy doesn't know where she will stay when she is discharged from hospital, after previously spending a year at YiSSA. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The NT government has said that "medically vulnerable" people will not be shifted to Batchelor and that correspondence recently provided to the ABC about its exploration of dialysis options in Batchelor was a "miscommunication".

The ABC has made several requests to the NT government for information about where YiSSA residents who need dialysis will be accommodated, and has been told "no resident who needs medical care will be left without a way to reach it".

At a recent press conference, the NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro was asked directly where medically vulnerable residents would be accommodated, but did not provide details.

"We on a number of occasions have to provide emergency care to people in Darwin and so these plans are already stood up, we did it all through the flood and cyclone events, it's a very normal practice for government," Ms Finocchiaro said.

For the other remaining residents, Ms Finocchiaro said: "People who are homeless, who would like to continue to receive homeless services, will move out to that facility — if they don't, that's really a matter for them".

The government has previously said dialysis patients would not be moved to Batchelor, 100 kilometres from Darwin.

Mr McPhee said he had concerns about last-minute arrangements being made for dialysis patients and other unwell residents at facilities like Darwin hotels.

"They need to access dialysis three times a week to stay healthy and if they don't access those services, they become unwell, and that's going to put more pressure on the hospital system," he said.

"Dialysis patients are high risk — if we've got people living rough or living in overcrowded situations here in Darwin, their risk of getting some type of infection, ending up in hospital or dying increases significantly."

The federal government's YiSSA rescue offer included a condition that Aboriginal corporation Yilli Rreung Housing, which has been managing the YiSSA shelter, be awarded a long-term contract to continue its operation.

Yilli Rreung Housing has not had its contract renewed, and Mission Australia, which the NT government said would be providing "wraparound services" at Batchelor, told the ABC on Wednesday it was still in negotiations about a "potential service agreement" for the smaller 150-bed site.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.title: SES volunteers change in front of others at 'embarrassing' regional HQ
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.author: Grace Marshall and Sarah Buchecker
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Mildura-Swan Hill

Topic:
Emergency Services

The cramped storage area for uniforms at SES Mildura. (ABC News: Grace Marshall)

The Mildura SES Unit is lobbying the state government for $1 million to upgrade its outdated Mildura headquarters.

The proposed redevelopment would provide improved training facilities, climate-controlled offices, better amenities and a wellness area for volunteers.

The Coalition has committed $1 million for the redevelopment if successful at the November election.

The carpet is green, the walls are wood-panelled and there is a hole in the ceiling of the Mildura SES headquarters.

It is a building unit controller Elliot Matotek's grandfather helped build 43 years ago, and one he may not have expected to still be in service; a time capsule of a facility.

That was a time when jobs were run out of volunteers' homes and recovery equipment stored in their garages and back sheds.

But now, generations of volunteers later, the building is deteriorating.

"I'm sure when my grandfather built it back in the day, in 1983, it was probably very nice," Mr Matotek said of the headquarters in Victoria's north-west.

Mr Matotek is pushing for the state Labor government to match the Coalition's election promise to spend $1 million and upgrade the facilities.

"It's almost embarrassing when we have to do open nights to try and recruit volunteers, and we show them the facility that we're in," he said.

Elliot Matotek's grandfather helped build the Mildura SES facilities in 1983. (ABC News: Grace Marshall)

Currently, volunteers have to change in the two single toilets or in front of others.

"If you're contaminated, if we've done a search in the river and you need to have a shower, we don't have a shower here. You have to go home," Mr Matotek said.

If they come back from a large deployment or a fatal accident, there is nowhere for the volunteers to decompress.

The only place to take a moment is two small couches between the vehicle bay and an open shared space.

Mildura SES responded to more than 1,100 incidents across the four financial years from 2022 to 2026, including 188 road crash rescues.

Earlier this year, Mildura experienced its wettest March day on record, making the unit the busiest in the state with almost 200 requests for help over two days.

SES volunteers from across the state travelled to Mildura to help, but the unit's small office space meant they had to move to a different building.

Damage to the Mildura SES unit's roof. (ABC News: Grace Marshall)

Designs for the SES building redevelopment have already been costed, and include new operational spaces, two private offices, a meeting room and training spaces.

Private change rooms, disability toilets and laundry facilities are also included.

Mr Matotek said he would not be surprised if, over the years, the unit had lost volunteers due to the poor facilities.

Two years ago, in stage 1 of the redevelopment, the Mildura SES Unit built a new shed for its vehicles through a combination of government funding and community donations.

Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

This week, Emergency Services Minister Paul Edbrooke said he would continue monitoring "demand, volunteer capacity and facility needs", but would not promise funding for stage 2 of development.

It came after the state opposition announced $1 million towards the project if it wins the election.

Nationals member for Mildura Jade Benham said the unit deserved the money.

Stage 1 of the project was a new shed to house SES vehicles. (ABC News: Grace Marshall)

Greens candidate for Mildura Katie Clements also backed the unit's call for funding and said it was wrong for regional communities to bear the cost of climate change through "increases in insurance premiums and emergency repair".

Ms Clements said coal and gas corporations need to pay their "fair share" toward the cost of emergency work in Victoria.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.title: Tasmanians expressed doubts about AI firm Firmus, now so have investors
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.author: Ashleigh Barraclough
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Ashleigh Barraclough

Firmus has been trying to win over communities in Tasmania, where it wants to build three AI data centres. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

Firmus Technologies has been the talk of the town after it was forced on Friday to pull the pin on its highly anticipated debut on the Australian Securities Exchange due to lacklustre demand.

At the start of the year, not many people knew about the company quietly building an AI data centre in Launceston, in northern Tasmania.

Fast forward to June, Tasmania's energy minister, after questions in parliament, revealed Firmus wanted to build two more AI data centres in Tasmania.

A firestorm of anti-AI data centre sentiment erupts in the community and suddenly every Tasmanian has something to say about Firmus.

The company hits hitch after hitch as it races to get its three Tasmanian projects up and running to cash in on the AI boom.

Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors.

Come September and Firmus is a sponsor of not one, but three sporting bodies in Tasmania — the fabled Tasmania Devils AFL club, the JackJumpers and Jewels basketball teams, and Cricket Tasmania. Many see it as an attempt to build a social licence.

Despite these efforts, EMRS polling conducted in September found the majority of Tasmanians aren't keen on AI data centres setting up shop in the state. Women and younger people are leading the push against them.

Regardless of these sentiments, AI data centres are needed to power tools like ChatGPT and Claude which Australians are increasingly taking up.

Firmus claims its facilities can produce AI tokens much cheaper than its competitors, and its innovative cooling technology means they won't use much water.

But Firmus hasn't established much of a track record yet. It only has one operational AI data centre in Australia, which is in Melbourne.

About 80 people gathered ahead of the George Town Council meeting, urging councillors to vote Firmus's proposal down. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

The company wants 444 megawatts to power its three Tasmanian facilities, which would make it the state's biggest power user. We don't yet know where all that power will come from.

It seems investors, like Tasmanian communities, aren't yet convinced by what Firmus is selling.

What was meant to be the biggest initial public offering since Telstra  — aiming to raise $7 billion to fund its AI data centre rollout — has been cancelled, with the company saying it will look to raise funds privately instead.

When neighbouring communities found out about Firmus's Bell Bay project, they were furious at what they saw as a lack of community consultation.

Firmus responded to the backlash by hosting community drop-in sessions and fronting the media to address questions, but trust was already low.

Firmus co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis fronted the media to address community concerns. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The local council, George Town, ended up approving the data centre — it didn't see how it could say no under the planning laws.

It was a win for Firmus, but the company still appealed. It wasn't happy with a condition imposed by the council that would limit its use of backup diesel generators to during power failures, emergencies, maintenance and testing.

That caught the Environment Protection Authority by surprise. It's made a submission to the appeal saying it had understood the generators would only be used very infrequently, and had it known otherwise, it would have assessed the application differently.

A render showing what the Bell Bay Firmus project could look like. (Supplied)

Firmus's other new Tasmanian proposal, at Wesley Vale in the north-west, has faced even bigger hurdles.

The company accidentally revealed it wanted to use farmers' irrigation water to cool the facility — something state-owned Tasmanian Irrigation said it wasn't legally able to do. While Firmus only wanted a small amount of water, farmers were annoyed the company didn't talk to them about it.

In the end, Firmus said it would just use rainwater and water it trucks in. But the problems weren't over yet.

The local council, Latrobe, decided it didn't want to determine the project's fate. It says the planning laws aren't up to scratch to make a decision on projects of this scale. Instead, it would rather the state government assess it as a major project, where broader questions, such as Firmus' monumental energy needs for the three projects, can be considered.

The project attracted more attention last month when Latrobe Council said Firmus may have started development work at Wesley Vale without approval.

Firmus says it was simply doing site maintenance permitted under its forest practices plan. Nonetheless, it's agreed to pause work while the council investigates — a process that remains ongoing.

Latrobe Council is investigating the work at Firmus's Wesley Vale site. (Supplied: Erin Woodcock)

Firmus's most progressed Tasmanian facility in Launceston is also tracking behind schedule. It was initially slated to be operational in the first half of this year, but that's been delayed to early 2027.

A government document states Aboriginal relics were found at the site, and construction was paused while Firmus sought approval to relocate them.

Amidst last week's chaos with the initial public offering, Firmus pulled out of its scheduled Thursday appearance at a federal parliament AI inquiry taking place in Melbourne.

A detail in Firmus's submission to the inquiry raised eyebrows. The company has publicised its commitment to underwrite double the amount of renewable energy that it uses, and has implied that would be in Tasmania. But its inquiry submission states the new developments could be interstate.

The Tasmanian government has been all aboard with Firmus since the beginning.

In the lead up to the state election in July last year, the Liberals announced a "world-first AI factory zone" in northern Tasmania where Firmus was building an AI data centre.

It wasn't a funding promise, but a political commitment to Firmus and its ambitions.

The Greens have led criticism of Firmus and the Tasmanian government's unwavering support for the company.

To them, Friday's news the company had to pull its initial public offering was not surprising. They say it's reflective of questions and concerns raised about Firmus's projects that haven't been adequately addressed.

Jeremy Rockliff's government has supported Firmus since it announced its Launceston AI data centre. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Questions are now being asked about what the cancellation of the share market float means for Firmus's announced projects.

Firmus says its plans haven't changed. It says it has the money to go ahead with its projects, including in Tasmania.

But the company has a long road ahead to convince investors and the public it can be trusted, and is worth embracing.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/q.title: Planning under pressure to tackle rising heat risk
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/q.author: Baz Ruddick
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/q.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Climate Change

Conservationists are calling for extreme heat to be recognised as a hazard in state planning.

Heatwaves kill more people than natural disasters, according to government research.

The Planning Institute of Australia's head of policy, Nicole Bennetts, says there are a lack of legislative mandates for developers to mitigate heat.

When Chris Kahler moved into his home in Townsville two decades ago, it was a very different environment than it is today.

"I was sitting in the kitchen trying to shelter from the heat and I was just dripping sweat, it was terrible. It was hot, still, horrid," Mr Kahler said.

A large mango tree provides a shady refuge from the heat at Mr Kahler's Townsville home.  (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

In a bid to make his home cooler, the botanist has since modified it by enlarging windows and removing walls to encourage cross breezes, planted out his yard and painted his roof white to reflect heat.

It has allowed him to survive the sweltering conditions without running an air conditioner, despite the sometimes oppressive north Queensland humidity.

Heatwaves are Australia's deadliest natural hazard, and according to the Queensland Government's heatwave risk assessment, are responsible for more deaths than any other natural hazard combined.

As the climate warms, and many urban environments become more densely developed, there is growing concern about how heat is impacting communities.

Crystal Falknau, from the North Queensland Conservation Council, said she wants to see changes in how suburbs are planned and developed.

Mr Kahler worked with a builder to open up his home so breezes could pass through to cool it. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"We see these small brick houses that are built to be lived in with air conditioning," Ms Falknau said.

"If you don't have access to rooftop solar, and if the power goes out, it means that you're stuck in basically a brick oven, and that's what can kill people."

Crystal Falknau, coordinator of the North Queensland Conservation Council, says heat can be particularly dangerous in high humidity environments. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The organisation was part of a group which petitioned the state government to include heat as a natural hazard in its planning policy.

"Something like a cyclone or a flood, it's a big disruption and it's treated as an emergency. When you have a heatwave, it's a silent killer," she said.

According to government reporting, Queensland's yearly average temperature has warmed by 1.5 degrees since records began in 1910, while the National Climate Risk Assessment projected heat-related mortality would increase significantly if temperatures increased by 2 and 3 degrees.

More people die from the effects of extreme heat than other natural hazards.  (ABC News: Pete Mullins)

Nicole Bennetts is the head of policy and advocacy with the Planning Institute of Australia.

Nicole Bennetts says that unlike flood and bushfire risk which can be mapped, heat hazards can be difficult to plan for. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

She said while mapping for natural disasters like floods and bushfires in planning schemes can be relatively straightforward, it is difficult to plan for heat.

"A flood has devastating impacts on property you can see. Heat is invisible, it is something that creeps up on us," Ms Bennetts said.

She said extreme heat is often exacerbated during heatwaves where there are repeated hot days.

"Concrete, our roofs, our walls of buildings, they all trap heat," she said.

Dense housing estates can restrict cooling cross breezes and exacerbate the "urban heat island" effect. (ABC News)

"You can have an air temperature of 35 degrees but an urban environment feeling more like 40 or 40 plus because of the cumulative days of heat being trapped."

The new draft State Planning Policy, which is now open for consultation, identifies the reduction of "urban heat islands" as a key planning priority.

Ms Bennetts said the Planning Institute would like to see requirements on developments to reduce the heat of urban environments.

"We need to be designing and planning our cities for the climate that they will be accommodating in decades from today, not the climate that they were designed for maybe 20 years ago," she said.

In a statement, Minister of State Development Jarrod Bleijie said Queensland's State Planning Policy had not been reviewed since 2016 and previously not mentioned heat at all.

James Davidson is an architect who specialises in climate resilient design.

His firm publishes guides for councils around adaptation and resilience against flood, fire, heat and other hazards.

Architect James Davidson says construction codes need to be more flexible. (ABC News: Hannah Ross)

He believes that the National Construction Code rather than planning policies, need to adapt to allow more innovative design.

"I think we're at risk of building the same old stuff over and over and over until these construction codes and our Australian standards come up to speed essentially," he said.

"Realistically, what we're designing for today will still be there in 20, 30, 40 or 50 years' time."

Australian suburbs are becoming denser with larger building footprints on smaller lots.  (ABC News: John Gunn)

He said air conditioning systems can often struggle in high temperatures and electricity grids fail under the extreme loads put on them on hot days.

"One of the most critical things to do is to look at passive systems, things that don't need to be activated if if you lose power," he said.

"Better design doesn't necessarily have to cost more money. It just is a different way of thinking about arranging space and utilising certain types of materials as well.

Botanist Chris Kahler has modified his home. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

For Mr Kahler, a better quality of life was found by allowing nature into his home.

"Letting the garden almost into the house, occasionally birds and butterflies will be wafting though the kitchen as I'm cooking — I just love it," he said.

"The breeze kind of funnels through that green, cooled garden and then into the house."

He said he is frustrated when he sees urban sprawl which doesn't take into account heat, especially in the face of climate change.

Mr Kahler says trees and plants not only shade, but also cool the air through photosynthesis and transpiration.  (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"It's a problem we can't solve but we can certainly ameliorate or dampen the effect, but we don't seem to have the interest."

Header image: Botanist Chris Kahler has modified his home in a bid to make it cooler in Townsville's hot climate. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)
