https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.title: 'Cockroach Party' protesters vow to return after hundreds detained in Delhi
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.author: Karishma Vyas
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Security personnel seen detaining a protester during the demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party. (AP: Manish Swarup)

India's police have detained hundreds of "Cockroach Party" protesters in New Delhi during demonstrations against the country's Election Commission.

It comes after the Commission's move to drop some 130 million names from their voter list.

The protesters have vowed to return even after Cockroach Janta Party founder was taken into custody.

Chaos erupted in India's capital New Delhi on Saturday as police detained hundreds of protesters, journalists and lawyers during demonstrations targeting the Election Commission's move to drop some 130 million names from the voter list.

Police and paramilitary forces enforced a lockdown in much of the city with at least 45 metro stations closed and more than 240 trains to New Delhi and Nizamuddin railway stations cancelled.

Internet was cut around the Jantar Mantar protest site and demonstrators reported that anyone attempting to reach the location was detained or turned away.

India's youth "cockroach" movement was set to hold fresh protests prior to Abhijeet Dipke being arrested.

"I along with my friends left in the morning to protest against the election commissioner. There was no way to reach Jantar Mantar, so we decided to assemble around Gurdwara Bangla Sahib," Aditi Subramanian told the ABC.

"The police with no accompanied female officers detained all of us and threw us in the bus violently … with no internet connectivity. It has been so difficult to verify who has been taken where," she said.

Social media and television footage showed unarmed protesters being carried by their arms and legs into police buses and journalists being violently detained despite showing their press credentials.

Demonstrators, organised by the "Cockroach" youth movement, were demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of the voter list that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Policewomen are seen detaining and carrying a protester during the demonstration. (AP: Manish Swarup)

"We are concerned by reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today's large-scale demonstrations in Delhi," UN Human Rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement.

The statement called on Indian authorities to "ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled".

It also called for "utmost restraint in response to peaceful protesters" and for those "arbitrarily detained" to be "immediately and unconditionally released".

About 130 million voters were kicked off the registrar, which is more than four times the population of Australia.

"I came last night from Haryana (state) to demand Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. We will not let him fool the people anymore. We will come again tomorrow," protester Pramod Kumar told the ABC after being detained by police.

"If you go anywhere in Delhi today you will see police everywhere, carrying sticks and batons and detaining anyone of us who goes close to Jantar Mantar.

"The situation is very tense," he said.

At New Delhi airport, police also detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka after their flight from Mumbai landed, the group said in a statement.

"If you think that by threatening us with jail, you can stop us, then that is not going to happen. We are ready to go to the jail," Mr Dipke said as officers moved through the plane to take him into custody.

"But we will fight to save the democracy of this country. And we will make sure Gyanesh Kumar resigns as he has deleted more than 130 million votes and has snatched the voting rights of the people."

Detained protesters seen shouting slogans as police drive them away in a van. (AP: Manish Swarup)

Delhi police did not return the ABC's calls but in a statement they said that protesters had not secured the required permission.

"Delhi Police has to look after well-being of citizens and economic interests alongside the interests of those who want to protest."

Public anger towards the revised voter list has been growing since the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two election commissioners had questioned and disagreed with Mr Kumar over removing millions of names from records.

Mr Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.

The commission said the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

A Delhi police officer seen inside a police van at the site of a protest. (AP: Manish Swarup)

BJP national spokesman and MP Sambit Patra in a statement said the anarchists had failed.

"We have been seeing that a few anarchist forces have been spreading anarchy in a corner of Delhi for the past few days," the statement said.

"But today the anarchists have failed.

"The flop show of anarchist elements has completely collapsed."

Opposition parties say the voter deletions affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world's largest democracy.

"We are going to defend our Constitution. We are going to protect the voice of the Indian people. And we are going to ensure that what was done to India over the last 10-15 years will never, ever be done again," Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi posted on X.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.title: Trump lashes out at Zelenskyy over rising diesel prices in the US
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/t.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
World Politics

Donald Trump has blamed Volodymyr Zelenskyy for skyrocketing diesel prices.  (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service via Reuters)

US President Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for sky-rocketing diesel prices in America.

Mr Trump's comments come after he said he had brokered a new diesel supply deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin despite signing sanctions against Moscow last month.

European allies have expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.

US President Donald Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in America.

The US president, who earlier this week struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, has been urging Mr Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

He has also sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

"He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Mr Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters.

Ukrainian and European officials reacted to Mr Trump's diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war efforts.

Diesel prices have skyrocketed due to a collision of events, including the difficulty of getting oil out of the Middle East since the start of the Iran war, which has raised the price of all oil products.

Mr Trump also suggested that if he had been US president in 2022, "that war would have never started".

"There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence."

Mr Trump said the Ukrainian president had "lost 30 per cent" of the country in a "war that should have never started".

"I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

Funeral workers carry the coffins of family members who were killed in a missile strike on a residential building in Ukraine on October 7. (AP Photo/Dan Bashakov)

Independent estimates are that about 20 per cent of Ukraine's territory is under Russian control.

British defence officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers had been killed in the war. There are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died.

Mr Trump's extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said on Saturday, local time.

Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. At least 18 people were wounded.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.

Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.

A rescue worker next to a residential building destroyed in a Russian missile strike on Pryluky, Ukraine, on October 7. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka)

"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.

He said every additional billion dollars Russia earned from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.

The strikes came a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel.

Mr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia would receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.

Former vice-president Mike Pence joined the chorus of western leaders condemning Mr Trump's deal with Russia saying it would fuel "Putin's war machine".

In a post on X, Mr Pence said: "President Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian fuel amidst Putin's ongoing and brutal attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine makes no sense and is a betrayal of the legacy and leadership of the late Senator Lindsey Graham."

Mr Trump announced on Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.

"Trump has once again shown his true face," Oleksandr Petrenko, 26, said.

"He didn't care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he's interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay."

For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement "didn't really come as a surprise".

"Trump has been working with Putin for a long time," she told The Associated Press.

Ukraine's European allies also expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, "as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest," and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex.

The German government "remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine "remains unwavering".

In an apparent reversal of Washington's campaign to squeeze Russian fuel revenue powering the war in Ukraine, Donald Trump says Moscow will supply diesel to the US.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all.

Citing his embassy's reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and "serious sources" saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia's refining capacity, he asked on X: "So where will the surpluses for export come from?"

Mr Trump's announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.

He announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.

Speaking about Friday's announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to discuss the issue publicly, said the diesel deal announcement was not tied to anything under discussion in Florida.

He confirmed the Ukrainian delegation had left Florida and was on its way back to Ukraine.

Ukranian ambassador to Australia and New Zealand Vasyl Myroshnychenko told Weekend Breakfast that Mr Trump's recent comments calling for an new president were not being taken seriously in Ukraine.

"There is a general consensus in Ukraine, among even opposition leaders, that there is no way how we can hold elections at the moment," he said.

Mr Myroshnychenko said ongoing security threats due to strikes contributed to that feeling.

"We cannot guarantee that those people who are at the front lines can vote, including those people who are outside of Ukraine," he added.

Mr Myroshnychenko echoed similar sentiments over the diesel supply deal, saying it was not going to help end the war in Ukraine.

"Out of the sales of diesel or other petroleum products, they will continue funding this war," he said.

"And the only way how we can actually bring Russia to a ceasefire or to actually negotiate in good faith, we need to demonstrate that the price of waging this war will continue increasing."

Mr Myroshnychenko also thanked Australia for the ongoing support.

"Two weeks ago, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and President Zelenskyy have signed a bilateral security agreement in New York," he said.

The Australian government has recently announced a $60 million package, including military, humanitarian and energy assistance, for the Ukrainian war effort.

"I'm grateful to the Australian government for their support," Mr Myroshnychenko said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.title: At CPAC, Angus Taylor faced the reality of Pauline Hanson's growing appeal
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.author: Clare Armstrong
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Government and Politics

Angus Taylor spoke at the 2026 Australian Conservative Political Action Conference this weekend. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

When Angus Taylor finished speaking to a room of conservative faithful in Brisbane this weekend, about 50 people stood to applaud him.

A few minutes later, hundreds rose to their feet to give Pauline Hanson a standing ovation simply because the One Nation leader had walked out onto the stage.

Such was the contrast in reception, that anyone might reasonably question why Mr Taylor had bothered to attend this year's Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) at all.

Pauline Hanson urges voters to abandon the Coalition, while acknowledging she would work with them to remove Labor from government.

No sitting Liberal leader before him had attended CPAC, a gathering once viewed as too far to the right of the Coalition's mainstream.

But as the Liberals and Nationals have adopted more of the populist conservative policies championed at the conference, the distance between them has narrowed.

Mr Taylor's address hit many of the same points as the speech delivered by Ms Hanson, but it was clear the audience was giving all the credit to the latter.

The opposition leader also pulled his punches when it came to One Nation despite the party's surge in the polls correlating with the Coalition's decline.

Pauline Hanson received a standing ovation as she took the stage. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Ms Hanson showed no such qualms, delivering a sharp jab in Mr Taylor's direction as she noted while voters did not want Anthony Albanese as prime minister, neither were they keen on a "smarmy management consultant".

When speaking to the media later in the afternoon Ms Hanson denied her words were aimed at Mr Taylor, but she may as well have winked as she said so.

Mr Taylor may not have won hearts and minds, but his willingness to participate had a notable effect on the tenor of the proceedings.

Protesters were seen outside the conference. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The line to get into CPAC snaked outside the Brisbane venue on Saturday morning as hundreds of attendees arrived early, eager to get a good position for the headline speeches.

Inside, the lights cast an eerie red glow over the crowd, while posters featuring giants of conservative politics adorn the walls.

Under the stern gazes of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, the audience sat through an introductory video urging them to back "Angus", "Pauline", and "Matt" (Nationals leader Matt Canavan).

The organisers made no secret of their desire to emphasise what united the three parties rather than what divided them.

As the three-cornered migration battle continues, Angus Taylor is trying to position his party in the middle of the government and One Nation.

Mr Taylor's presence made that possible, even if Ms Hanson remained the undisputed favourite.

Throughout the day the audience oscillated between rapt attention and listlessness with heckles generally targeted not at the speakers, but the subjects of their shared ire.

Net zero, eSafety commissioner Julie Inman Grant (the "Karen of the internet" according to Ms Hanson), Anthony Albanese, "woke" school curriculums and Welcome to Country were among the topics most likely to elicit a boo.

And nothing revived a fading crowd more than a dig at Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen, whose name came up so often he was probably owed an appearance fee.

CPAC chair Warren Mundine revealed Mr Bowen's name alone gave him "chills" and recounted his visceral reaction when the pair once crossed paths in the street.

"My mate had to grab me to say, 'It doesn't go well on your CV if you murder a federal minister,'" Mr Mundine quipped.

Matt Canavan also attended the conference. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

But a shared opposition to Labor does not entirely resolve the Coalition's electoral woes.

The question hanging over the conference was whether the Liberals were witnessing the consolidation of a broader conservative movement or the gradual erosion of their own place at the centre of it.

One unsurprising absence from the CPAC line-up was Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie.

Rather than compete with One Nation on its own turf, Mr Hastie has increasingly sought to make the conservative case to voters beyond the Coalition's traditional base.

A cap reading "Australia First" left at the conference. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Last week, he appeared on a live episode of the Brine & Biff, a podcast billed as a place for thoughtful political debate, albeit where one host is portrayed as a cartoon gherkin.

Mr Hastie cracked out the sales pitch for the Coalition's plan to slash migration but also argued "chasing One Nation down the rabbit hole" was not going to win his side government.

His willingness to confront One Nation, rather than accommodate it, puts him at odds with the political future CPAC's organisers are trying to build.

The Australian event's founder Andrew Cooper closed day one by painting a vision for a future "Coalition of the willing" between the country's three conservative political parties.

In the furious debate about migration policy, figures and justifications get easily lost.

In the meantime, he urged the Liberals, Nationals and One Nation to "share" preferences at the next election.

He warned "ego" and infighting over "minor differences" would only "hand power" back to Labor.

And thanked the audience for showing "respect" to every speaker and thus starving the "noisy rabble outside" — including the media — of the ability to spin a narrative about "division" in the conservative ranks.

But the media was not outside, we were in the building wearing bright red lanyards emblazoned with the tagline "fake news".

They're standard issue at every CPAC, where the ambition to become part of the political mainstream has apparently not extended to retiring jokes from its fringe days.

Matt Renshaw's brilliant 190 gave Australia the momentum in Durban and showed how the tourists should go about it. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

Like many great plans, it was deceptively simple. Stillness. Balance. Patience. Concentration. No frills, no fast moves and no undue risks, just decisive action when needed.

Not for the first time at Test level, a burly Queenslander, a three-pound cleft of willow and a healthy dose of self-confidence was the difference between Australian success and failure.

That Matt Renshaw resurrected an Australian first innings which teetered near oblivion at 6-124 was the first point of order.

Of consequences further-reaching, the left-hander resurrected his entire Test career overnight in Durban, sweeping, clipping and crashing his way to 190 from 397 deliveries across 465 minutes of life-affirming Test batting.

Numerous records fell or threatened to. Renshaw's epic was the highest score by an Australian in Durban, the fourth highest overall by an Aussie against South Africa, and the best by a number-five of any nation at Kingsmead.

It was also a new Test personal best for Renshaw, usurping the 184 he made nine years ago as a boyish tyro against Pakistan in Sydney, back when the world was at his feet.

Renshaw is 30 now — a husband, a father of two children and an entirely different cricketer. He knows his own mind and understands his place in the scheme of things.

For a nation which has been crying out for big, important runs by someone not named Smith or Head, his Daddy hundred here was one for the ages.

Practically speaking, Renshaw helped Australia to a first-innings total of 390, which was at least 150 more than had seemed optimistic when he first took guard.

On a deeper level, it restored belief in the value of grinding out an innings of depth and character. It was the real deal — the proper Test match batting the Australian cricketing public has been craving.

No mistake should be made about the high degree of difficulty, either. When Renshaw began shepherding the tail a day earlier, Australia was at the mercy of a vigorous and versatile South African pace attack jagging the ball all over the place.

Waiting in the wings were the Proteas' twin spin options of Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, with 1700+ first-class wickets between them.

Australia has struggled against left-arm spin in recent times. Last time they played a Test in Durban, Maharaj took nine wickets. And Australia's selection for this match — four left handers in the top six — was said to favour right-arm off-spinner Harmer even more.

Matt Renshaw blunted South Africa's spin attack with judicious use of the sweep and reverse sweep in Durban. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

So much for that, in the end. Renshaw swept, reverse-swept and paddled Maharaj into irrelevance and by the time Harmer finally removed the top-scorer for spin's first wicket of the game, the horse had well and truly bolted.

As it turned out, the sterner challenge was curbing the influence of the quicks, who'd posed constant difficulties for the rest of Australia's batters.

A microcosm came when Renshaw was on 130, yet still not able to relax. He was struck a scary blow to the grille of his helmet from an absolute snorter by Anrich Nortje, who bowled with genuine pace and accuracy in short, sharp spells.

Handling the wily and indefatigable Wiaan Mulder was no cinch either. Early on day two, the all-rounder scythed through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc and threatened to blow the game open.

Wiaan Mulder (centre) took two wickets on day two and proved hard to play for Australia's batters. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

That he didn't was not exclusively a matter of Renshaw's dominance but of the rearguard partnerships which have so often saved Australia's bacon in recent times.

Renshaw shared stands of 86 across 32 overs with Pat Cummins and a monumental and possibly series-shaping 134 from 47 overs with Nathan Lyon.

Australia will not be looking too far ahead, but there was a blueprint here, not just of personnel but of general batting philosophy: know your game, make them bowl to you, stick around and wear them down.

Australia's total was the most obvious metric of success, but its innings duration of 137.2 overs will surely please Andrew McDonald and his analysts just as much.

In Australia's 35 Test innings in the two years before this match, they'd batted past the 100-over mark only six times, compared with 13 times in the 42 innings of the two-year period preceding.

That downward trend has, of course, coincided with a proliferation of the result pitches which characterise the World Test Championship era.

Concurrently, it is agreed by most involved in the Australian domestic scene, it has been difficult for Test batting candidates to put their best feet forward, or get in the habit of playing long innings, when the primary bloc of red-ball cricket occurs in spring, when Sheffield Shield pitches sometimes resemble Monty Don's perennial beds.

Without peering too far into the future or wishing disruption on a player who's just delivered something so special, one awkward talking point that will be aired soon enough is if and when Renshaw might move up to his normal position of opener.

The theory going into this game was that in batting down the order, he could blunt the influence of the spinners, which he assuredly did. But he would surely be just as assured against the new ball as he was here against the second new ball.

And yet, who'd be an opener these days? Late on day two, Ryan Rickelton provided a study in contrasts for the Proteas.

Having spent the better part of two days chasing leather in the field, and perhaps daydreaming that he was in Renshaw's shoes, he lasted only three deliveries before chasing Josh Hazlewood outside his off-stump and sending an edge to the cordon.

The more telling image of day two arrived an hour earlier, on the stroke of tea, when an exhausted Renshaw removed his helmet and trudged off for refreshments.

Appearing on the balcony of the player's area, Australian skipper Cummins peered down on the centurion with something like a look of love on his face.

Ray Illingworth once said a captain needs the patience of a saint, the diplomacy of an ambassador, the compassion of a social worker and the skin of a rhino. Colleagues who can bat for eight hours help, too.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.author: Olivia Mason
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Joshua Prosso lived in state care for eight years. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )

Joshua Prosso lived in state care for nearly a decade as a child, but believes he was never equipped with essential skills to succeed in adulthood.

He says initiatives to support employment, housing access, income, mobility and essential life skills would assist wards of the state once they turn 18.

A report by the Guardian for Children and Young People has made seven recommendations to improve the state's foster care system.

Joshua Prosso spends his free time visiting the graves of relatives he never had the chance to meet.

The 19-year-old describes himself as an "amateur genealogist", a fascination born out separation from his family under state guardianship.

"It was a whole lot of despair when I realised that there was this whole branch of my close family that had only passed away a few years ago that I'd never heard of, that I never got to meet, and in a way it was because the Department hadn't helped," he said.

Mr Prosso spent about eight years in Department for Child Protection (DCP) residential care, much of it in group homes with other young people facing their own trauma.

As an adult, Joshua Prosso visits graves of family members who he never knew while being in state care. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )

"In a way it felt like psychological torture being in the department, because it felt like I was just locked in a room for years, just banging constantly on my door, yelling at my door," he said.

Now, he is advocating for others transitioning out of care, when turning 18 means the end of state guardianship.

While Mr Prosso was supported to find a subsidised rental property, he said he does not have the same skills as most of his peers.

He said the department did not provide him with enough driving lessons for him to get his licence and only received limited schooling.

"I went twice a week for a few hours," he said.

Joshua Prosso has participated in an inquiry by the Guardian for Children and Young People. (Supplied: Office of the Guardian for Children and Young People)

Now, he is calling on the government to do more to set young people like him up for independence and success.

"Making sure they're left with a job, a stable form of income, a capacity to get to places … that they're able to cook, clean, that sort of stuff," Mr Prosso said.

A recent inquiry by the Guardian for Children and Young People in conjunction with a group with lived experience in state care, including Mr Prosso, made seven recommendations for improvement.

Among them were better housing certainty, a clear transition to adulthood framework, continuity of trusted relationships, and support until at least 21 years of age.

"I think we have to be really much clearer about if the state is the parent, then what are the services, what are the offerings that the state are willing to provide?" Acting Guardian Sue Macdonald said.

Ms Macdonald said during the inquiry, young people described feeling "a sense of helplessness and hopelessness", like they were "falling off of a cliff edge" when they turned 18.

"If you feel like every relationship you've ever had has let you down, it is really difficult to know where to go for help or know how to accept it when it is available," she said.

"Young people stay home longer because they can't afford housing, they do rely on the supports of their parents more, but the population of young people in care, that hasn't translated for them.

"They are still expected to stand on their own two feet at 18 with very limited support."

She added that investing in better support systems would translate into better outcomes for the entire community.

"Less presentations to emergency departments, less interactions with the justice system, more goal-directed behaviour in terms of getting a job and education," she said.

Sue Macdonald says young people leaving state care have limited support when they exit the system at 18. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In a statement, DCP chief executive Jackie Bray said the government had invested in a range of transition and post-care initiatives and was working to further strengthen support.

"Supported Independent Living Services provide accommodation and individually-tailored packages to build practical living skills, confidence and independence," the statement read.

The statement said the program included support with things like "housing, education, training, employment, health and disability services.

"Young people's voices are critical for driving child protection system improvements and informing our daily efforts to ensure our services are meeting their needs."

Mr Prosso says change cannot come soon enough.

Meanwhile, he said alongside his advocacy work, the research into his ancestry has given him purpose.

"I sort of hold a bit more of an admiration for my family, looking at intergenerational trauma patterns," he said.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Christa Pike in 2023 before her failed execution attempt. (AP Photos: Texas Department of Corrections)

Death row inmate Christa Pike has been returned to prison after a stint in hospital recovering from a botched execution.

Ms Pike had been recovering in hospital after surviving two lethal injections during an attempted execution by the state of Tennessee last month.

Tennessee's governor has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigations into the botched execution continue.

Christa Pike has been released from a US hospital and sent back to prison after surviving Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection.

Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre, where she had been housed for more than 30 years, her attorneys said in a joint statement.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the statement read.

"She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."

Christa Pike cries during her sentencing hearing in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. (Reuters)

Pike was sentenced to death for the murder and torture of a classmate, a crime she committed in 1995, when she was 18-years-old.

Convicted killer Christa Pike awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital this week, with her first words being: "Where am I?"

On September 30, local time, Pike had been taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and ‌with severe arm injuries after two pentobarbital injections failed to kill her.

At one point she was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive.

The botched execution of Christa Pike exposes the fallacy of lethal injections being the most humane method of execution.

She awoke "angry and confused" in the hospital this week her lawyers said, with a long recuperation ahead after surviving the attempted execution.

The Death Penalty Information Center said Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.

The state's prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution.

A Tennessee judge this week ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to their failed attempt to execute her, a development one of her lawyers called the "first of many steps to preserve and enforce her constitutional rights."

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look in to the botched execution of Pike and a similar failure involving Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous ​lines.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Small Businesses

Mr Barbaro says that annually his company pays about $150,000 in merchant fees. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

NSW small businesses are looking at how to cover the cost of merchant fees after the ban on card payment surcharges took effect on October 1.

Some owners have increased the price of items, while others have opted to absorb the cost.

The consumer watchdog says businesses have the option of offering "discounts to consumers, who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID."

Small businesses across New South Wales are grappling with how they will cover the cost of merchant fees.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) last week introduced a ban on business owners adding extra fees for credit or debit card payments on EFTPOS, Mastercard, Visa and American Express.

The changes, according to the RBA, are in the "public interest", and designed to make the system more transparent and less confusing for both businesses and customers.

The Reserve Bank of Australia says the changes are in the "public interest". (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Sydney cafe owner Philip Barbaro said he had been forced to put prices up for some items, as his fees to the bank must still be paid for the use of cards.

Mr Barbaro said the cafe business was tough in the Sydney market.

"In my very competitive market in the city we have not touched the price of our coffee, but there were other items on the menu we had to increase this week, to offset the bank surcharge."

Specialist baker and owner of the Jamaican Patty Bakehouse in Sydney's inner west, Chris Skuce, said he opened his shop a year ago as a nod to his Jamaican heritage.

Mr Skuce says he will, at some stage, have to increase prices.   (ABC News: Simon Amery )

Mr Skuce said he had been absorbing the cost of the bank fee in order to keep making the patties that were part of his childhood.

"I haven't passed the cost on yet, but I will increase my prices at some stage probably in the new year," he said.

Executive director of advocacy group Business Sydney, Paul Nicolaou, said people were struggling.

"There have been rising interest rates, energy costs and the subsequent drop in discretionary spending affecting both households and business," he said.

Price rises were now being introduced across the board, he added.

"Business owners need to cover their costs, and unfortunately someone has to pay, and it is going to be the consumer."

The unintended consequence of the Reserve Bank's card surcharge ban, which was intended to lower prices for consumers.

Mr Nicolaou said the banks should be doing something about merchant fees, along with other payment platforms.

"It is all electronic now, does it require a fee?"

A spokesperson for the Australian Competition & Consumer Commission (ACCC) said that while businesses were able to build the fee into their pricing structure, they "must not mislead consumers about their prices or the reasons for any price changes".

"Businesses can also offer discounts to consumers, who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID," the spokesperson added in a statement.

"Where a business offers a discount for a particular payment method, this should be clearly disclosed before consumers choose to book, order or pay.

"Businesses should not display only the discounted price or make the discounted price more prominent than the full price."

Mr Barbaro said he was now looking at alternatives for customers.

The removal of card payment surcharges took effect on October 1.  (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Mr Barbaro said that could be an incentive.

"There is the old saying that cash is king."

Mr Skuce said, however, he was not looking at cash discounts.

"Most people want to pay by card. It is just a hassle to handle cash."

Mr Skuce said he did not see any net benefits to the consumer, as prices would increase.

"I am befuddled with the change. Another hit to the bottom line and completely unnecessary in my opinion."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/k.title: Island horses take centre stage in movie project
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/k.author: Olivia Nunes-Malek
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/k.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Olivia Nunes-Malek

The community project explores the relationship between a horse and its rider on the frontline during World War I. (Supplied: Pluggas Studios)

A Fraser Coast resident has created a short film focused on the wild horses from K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, that were sent to Middle East during World War I.

The breed was chosen by the military for its light frame and unique hoof pattern.

The film will be screened at select cinemas later this month.

For as long as she can remember, Violet Whitaker has been passionate about horses.

As president of the 5th Light Horse Regiment in Hervey Bay, about 280 kilometres north of Brisbane, her focus is preserving the region's equine history for future generations.

When she learnt some of the horses on K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, were involved in Australia's military efforts during World War I, she knew it was the perfect backdrop for a short film.

"[It's an] insight into the intimate bond between war horses and their riders," Ms Whitaker said.

Clydesdale horses were introduced to K'gari and bred to bolster the Indian Army's steed supply in the late 1800s, according to Queensland's Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI).

Loggers also used the herd during this time to haul timber across the island.

The Clydesdale horse and the Arab thoroughbreds eventually bred to form the wild horses previously seen on K'gari. (Supplied: Violet Whitaker)

Maryborough RSL sub-branch president Christopher Nelson said the Clydesdale breed worked best for these two purposes.

"They were large, heavily boned and very muscular," he said.

Mr Nelson said Arabic thoroughbreds were later brought to the island to meet the growing demands for horses needed for the Boer War.

The leftover stock eventually interbred to create the brumby population, which were considered ideal creatures for World War I.

Christopher Nelson say the broad hooves of K'gari's wild horses made them ideal candidates for World War I. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

"[They had] broad hooves which were beneficial for desert environments, and light-muscled which would have given them manoeuvrability," Mr Nelson said.

Australia sent more than 120,000 horses overseas during the war.

Those taken from K'gari were among the 39,000 sent to the Middle East between 1914 and 1916, according to the Australian War Memorial.

But the total number taken from the island was not known, Mr Nelson said.

After leaving the island, the horses were sent for training at military camps across Australia.

The horses taken from K'gari undertook training at different military camps across Australia. (Supplied: Violet Whitaker)

Mr Nelson said the process involved "breaking in" the horses to feel comfortable with different tasks, including wearing a saddle or hearing loud explosions.

"Because of their strength they were used to pull artillery, they sourced water and carried soldiers into conflict," he said.

Military historian Jean Bou said after the training, handlers transferred the horses to Australian ports to be shipped to Egypt and Palestine.

Dr Bou said the horses needed about six months to acclimatise to their new surroundings.

Jean Bou says it took roughly six months for the wild horses to get used to their new environments. (Supplied: Jean Bou)

"They had a long period of getting used to the new climate, whatever the local food sources were and then exercised to make sure their fitness was sufficient," he said.

Most of the horses that Australia exported died during the war, but Dr Bou said the surviving horses faced different fates.

"The older horses were destroyed and the younger horses were absorbed into the imperial remount system in the Middle East," he said.

Only one horse, Major General Sir William Bridges's charge named Sandy, returned to home soil in Sydney.

Roughly 39,000 horses shipped from Australia were used on the frontlines in Egypt and Palestine. (Supplied: Violet Whitaker)

"He lived a life of luxury, in a paddock, well fed, well attended to, and he was retired and he was famous," Mr Nelson said.

"I think he got a lot of attention by the early newspapers and by photographers and everything else."

The Forgotten Horses of Fraser (K'gari), which Ms Whitaker wrote and filmed on Queensland's Fraser Coast, follows the fictitious journey of a brumby from the island chosen to be one of thousands of steeds to serve in the Middle East.

The filmmaker said viewers would experience the war from a unique perspective.

Violet Whitaker says the feedback she has received about the upcoming film has been "overwhelming". (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

"It will be narrated by a horse, to show the huge sacrifice horses did for the war," she said.

The project was created over nearly 12 months on a "shoestring budget" of $20,000 from community donations and Ms Whitaker's savings.

She said the ongoing support from residents was "overwhelming".

Mr Nelson said the film, in its final post-production, encapsulated the "strong attachment" between a rider and their mount.

The 40-minute project was filmed at multiple locations across the Fraser Coast region. (Supplied: Pluggas Studios)

"They were your partner, your war comrade, your friend and lifesaver," he said.

The 40-minute film will have a limited release at select cinemas across the Fraser Coast later this month.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.title: Win friends and influence people with nori ‘caviar’
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.author: Simon Daly
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2026/1.text:
Cheap ways to impress a crowd never fall out of fashion, and describing a dish as containing “caviar” is a particularly cost-effective way — whether it’s really caviar we’re talking about or not.

Of course, real-deal caviar is salt-cured roe farmed exclusively from sturgeon. But there are plenty of other gourmet aquatic ova, especially in Japan: ever-popular ikura (salmon roe), tarako (cod roe) and even tobiko (flying fish roe).

Beyond the realm of fish eggs, “caviar” is also a term used in molecular gastronomy to describe the products of spherification, a technique that encapsulates oils and other liquids into miniature balls. This method is mainly aesthetic, with flavor profiles that usually veer away from anything approaching authentic caviar’s salty and creamy characteristics.

A recent conversation with cookbook author Emiko Davies turned to nori production in Japan and how its commercial success after World War II can be largely traced back to the groundbreaking work of British phycologist Kathleen Drew-Baker. Her research into the life cycle of edible seaweeds uncovered overlooked steps that, once implemented in Japan, made artificial seeding of nori possible. The industry boomed and earned her the moniker “mother of the sea,” especially in Kumamoto, where her research was first implemented on a commercial scale.

Dry and crispy nori, well-known as the outer layer of maki-zushi (sushi rolls) and onigiri (rice balls), is also added as a topping to meals such as ramen as a mouthwatering morsel. Rather than chemically created caviar, the gelling action of chia can be added to make a plant-based simulacram.

Nori is rich in glutamate (the umami molecule) and rich oceanic flavors, which are amplified as red algae is processed to become the dark green sheets we know so well. Nori is usually a flavor accent, but mixed with chia seeds and seasoned with soy, it is a vegan umami bomb, fit to top any amuse-bouche or canape.

Cook time: 5 minutes, plus 30 minutes to rest

2 sheets nori (around 6 grams)

25 milliliters extra virgin olive oil

Optional: 2 1/2 milliliters fish sauce

Roughly rip up the nori sheets, then place everything in a spice mill or coffee grinder and pulse until powdered. Feel free to start with kizami nori (presliced nori) or powdered aonori (green dried seaweed) if you have it.

Add the powdered nori to a small mixing bowl or jar, then mix in your chia seeds and all liquids until smooth. Taste a dab to check the flavor, then add optional fish sauce if you think it needs to be punchier.

Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes or overnight. When the chia has soaked up the liquids and swelled, the mixture will be ready for the next step.

Wet the smallest spoon you own and drag it across the surface of the chia mix to create tiny scoops. You can also use a second spoon to make classic quenelles.

Serve as high- or lowbrow as you like. Buckwheat blini and pancakes with creme fraiche work on the fancy end, though it also works with potato chips and sour cream dip. I went with a middle ground: toasted bagel crisps and cream cheese.

https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/a.title: Tiger kills man who entered big cat enclosure at UK wildlife park
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/a.author: Associated Press
https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/a.text:
The animal was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident

A man died on Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said.

Emergency medical personnel responded to the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster after the incident was reported at about 1.35pm, but the victim died at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said in a statement.

The tiger was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident, the force said.

The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack and officers remained at the scene Saturday night as they investigated.

https://www.dw.com/en/storm-isaias-leave.title: Storm Isaias leaves 4 dead as it moves across southern US
https://www.dw.com/en/storm-isaias-leave.text:
The storm, which is now a post-tropical cyclone, had made landfall near Destin, Florida on Friday evening. The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerful winds and has caused mass power outages in Florida and Alabama.

Storm Isaias has left four people dead as it moves across the southern United States, officials said Saturday.

Two of the deaths were in Florida, while the other two were in Alabama.

The storm originally made landfall on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida. It is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.

Florida, Alabama and Georgia have all declared states of emergency due to the storm. According to PowerOutage.com, over 500,000 customers are without power in Florida and Alabama.

The Florida Division of Emergency Management said approximately 5,000 Florida National Guard soldiers and airmen have been "activated to support impacted communities."

The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerfall winds, bringing the risks of flooding and tornadoes. It has ripped the roofs off buildings and downed trees in its wake.

The storm has weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and is moving over the southern US states of Tennessee and Kentucky into West Virginia, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

In its latest update, the NHC warned of possible flash and urban flooding and said "landslides are possible across the Southern Appalachians." It also warned of wind gusts along with additional power outages and downed trees.

In addition, swells from Isaias will continue to impact much of the Gulf coasts of the US, Mexico and western Cuba, and are "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions." NHC said a couple of tornadoes are also possible across eastern Georgia and the Carolinas.

Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon has hit Category 4 strength as it barrels towards Mexico's Pacific coast, where it is expected to make landfall on Sunday. The storm is expected to impact Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for American tourists.

https://www.dw.com/en/palestinian-presid.title: Palestinian president postpones elections until late 2027
https://www.dw.com/en/palestinian-presid.text:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas previously committed to holding legislative elections in November 2026. He said that due to "obstacles ⁠posed by Israeli measures" the vote would be pushed back until late next year.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has postponed legislative elections for almost another year, according to a decree issued on Friday.

Abbas had previously scheduled legislative elections for November 28, and presidential elections for early next year. Now both elections have been pushed back to September 11, 2027.

They would be the first Palestinian elections in more than 20 years.

In his decree, Abbas cited "obstacles ⁠posed by Israeli measures" as the reason for the postponement of "free, fair and inclusive elections."

He pointed to Israeli settler violence, military attacks and restrictions of movent in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as Israel's continued withholding of tax revenue.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Gaza, where Israeli strikes continue after three years of war, the decree cited "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions," the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces and a lack of progress towards reconstruction, among other issues.

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded to the news on X, calling the decree "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability."

Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that elections would be held as part of France's recognition of the State of Palestine last year.

The delay comes just weeks after Abbas reaffirmed this commitment to hold elections in November when he delivered a video address to the UN General Assembly.

Abbas has governed by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.

https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-12-ki.title: Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh airport attack
https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-12-ki.text:
Officials said at least 12 people were killed in a strike on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. The airport had already been targeted multiple times this week.

At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.

"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.

Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.

At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."

Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.

The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."

Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."

The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.

However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.

In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."

When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.

The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.

Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.

Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.

The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.

The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9rk.title: Three friends on their student debt: one paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9rk.text:
When Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte met as freshers in 2012, their main responsibility was making it to lectures on time after early morning sports practice.

Their student debt, growing with interest from the day they took out their loans, was the last thing on their minds.

"The conversation was just so much less relevant at that time," says Charlotte. "As our careers have gone on and our paths have diverged more and more... those conversations start to come more to the forefront."

The friends, now in their early 30s, went to the University of Newcastle in the same year tuition fees tripled to £9,000 a year in England and Wales, and new loans called Plan 2 were introduced. Each borrowed about £37,500 to cover three years of tuition and living costs.

This year marks a decade since the first students in their year started repaying.

They may have started out in the same position, but over that time their career trajectories, life choices and earnings have shaped how much they've repaid, how much interest they've racked up, and how much they owe - with very different outcomes.

Student loans have come under scrutiny this year and there's been a particular backlash over Plan 2 loans. The government has said it wants to make the whole system fairer and campaigners are waiting to see what, if anything, changes in this month's Budget.

The anger about Plan 2 grew after the government announced updated terms in November. The income at which graduates start repaying is set to be frozen for three years, meaning graduates would start making payments sooner and pay more each month.

But it has also been brewing because the interest rate is higher than most other student loan plans, and many have seen their debts rise despite making monthly repayments.

"Since April this year, I've paid off in the region of £450 and I've accrued over £500 in interest," says Charlotte, a physiotherapist in Bristol.

She did a master's degree after uni and worked in the NHS before moving to the private sector. She earns about £50,000, but her loan is still going up.

"It makes me angry... it's just disheartening."

All three friends earn above the national average of £39,039. But research from the Institute for Fiscal Studies in February suggests Plan 2 graduates need to earn about £63,000 or more for a loan balance of £50,000 to start going down.

"I just had no concept that the debt was going to go up," says Libby, who remembers being in tears when her first student loan letter came through after graduating.

Now a project manager in a housing association and living in Worcester, she earns £72,000 and says her student loan balance has hovered at about £47,000 for a number of years. But she is currently on maternity leave and knows the interest will continue to accrue while her earnings - and therefore monthly repayments - drop.

"It feels like I will never pay it off, so it's something that I'm kind of just sucking up until the loan is written off," she says.

Her partner did the same course, starting a year before her and before tuition fees near tripled with the introduction of Plan 2 loans.

She says it is "so frustrating" that she has to pay out thousands of pounds a year more on her student debt.

Current and former students have different student loan plans depending on where they live in the UK and when they went to university. Plan 2 loans were given out in England for a little more than a decade from 2012 and are still issued in Wales.

The debt is written off after 30 years.

Lizzy, who studied economics and now works in financial services and lives in Bristol, is the highest paid of the friends, who bonded over rowing at university. She earns £85,000 a year and decided last year to clear her student debt by borrowing money from her family instead.

She had estimated that, based on her current earnings trajectory, she would repay her loan in 11 years. By paying off her debt in full early she has accrued less interest and hopes to repay her family in four years - saving about £20,000.

The amount graduates are voluntarily repaying towards their student loans has been growing. MoneySavingExpert.com founder Martin Lewis has warned that only higher earners could benefit from making voluntary repayments and most should not be "panicked into overpaying".

Finance journalist Holly Mead told the BBC it could make sense for those who are confident they will clear the debt and can make "a really significant overpayment" of tens of thousands of pounds, like Lizzy.

But smaller voluntary repayments could mean "you're just voluntarily paying more interest that you don't need to pay", she added.

Lizzy says she knows there are many "scenarios in which it doesn't pay off" for people to repay it early.

"I made a gamble on my future self to actually repay it," she says. "I'm in a very privileged position to be able to do that... Buying your way out of the system or not being in at all is in itself a luxury. It buys you freedom."

She and Libby finished their A-levels in 2011 but took a year out before going to university - Libby on a gap year, and Lizzy to resit economics after missing the grade she'd hoped for by a single mark.

Lizzy says she knew the delay would mean her fees would be higher, but "it was never explained" that the repayment terms would "look and feel very different".

"I think that's something that took me probably the best part of 10 years to understand," she adds, noting that her twin sister did start university in 2011 and had less debt as a result.

"Whether you went to uni in 2012 or 2011 actually financially has a huge impact, and it shouldn't," she says.

There's been lots of discussion about what teenagers were told about Plan 2 loans before they took them out. In March, a BBC investigation found the Department for Education (DfE) had compared monthly repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts in presentations at schools in England a decade ago.

An inquiry by MPs then concluded that this amounted to "mis-selling" because it was inaccurate for higher earners.

Last month, the government said university applicants in England would be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out.

All three friends follow the Rethink Repayment campaign on social media. It was set up by Oliver Gardner, who says the first Plan 2 borrowers are grappling with competing financial pressures such as getting on the property ladder and starting families.

"Maybe in your 20s, you can get away without saving as much, potentially. But now people are like, 'we need the savings to do these big things that we want to do with our lives'," he says.

The campaign wants a lower Plan 2 interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse that decision to freeze the threshold at £29,385 in England for three years from 2027 - which, while it is not the first freeze, sparked this year's debate.

Gardner said the government was "engaging much more openly and honestly" but the "the onus is very much on them in the upcoming October budget to take this by the reins" because graduates would not accept "minor tinkering around the edges".

The DfE said it was "taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university" by increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants and having "raised the repayment threshold for Plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021".

"We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way," it said.

Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte feel grateful they met back in 2012, and say that if they had their time again they would go back to university.

"I still wouldn't change my university experience," says Charlotte, "but would go back and do something different in the sense of my course and my career trajectory? Probably."

https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-1476.title: Attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more, Saudi authorities say
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-1476.author: The Associated Press
https://www.npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-1476.text:
This image from video obtained and verified by AP shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (UGC via AP)

CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition.

The attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi-backed government forces there.

The statement, which did not assign blame for the attack, said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.

The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport that killed four people — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.

Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis. "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. The rebels at times take days to claim responsibility.

Riyadh airport operations were suspended

Saudi civil aviation authorities earlier said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.

Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. Statements later turned to condolences.

Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and a Houthi-launched ballistic missile had been intercepted in Al-Kharj governorate, southeast of Riyadh.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.

Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.

Earlier Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of "supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions" in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.

Flight disruptions are growing

The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."

The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.

Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.

Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."

Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Oklahoma stun No 1 Texas as Sandell’s last-second kick seals Red River upset
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Sandell’s 47-yard kick seals 27-24 upset in Dallas

Sooners overcome offensive struggles to stun Texas

Manning throws three TDs but two costly picks

Tate Sandell kicked a 47-yard field goal on the final play and Oklahoma overcame their continued offensive ineptitude with touchdowns on special teams and defense in a 27-24 win over No 1 Texas in the Red River rivalry game on Saturday.

The Sooners (3-2, 1-1 Southeastern Conference) beat a No 1 team for the first time since a 38-17 win over Missouri in 2007. They had been 0-4-1 when facing a top-ranked Texas team.

Arch Manning threw three touchdowns for the Longhorns (4-1, 1-1), but both of his interceptions were costly.

Texas had two late chances, but Gianni Spetic was wide right on a 53-yard field-goal attempt with 1:55 left. After the Sooners went three-and-out for the seventh time in the game, Manning’s last pass was intercepted by Omarion Robinson with 19 seconds left.

That set up the Sooners at their own 39-yard line, and John Mateer completed passes of 13 and 20 yards to Isaiah Sategna on opposite sides of the field, both upheld on replay review.

Oklahoma then ran a play to set up the kick by Sandell, who had made a 53-yarder and missed another from the same distance.
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.summary: Oklahoma beat Texas 27-24 in Red River rivalry game on Saturday. Sooners beat No 1 team for first time since 2007 win over Missouri. Arch Manning threw three touchdowns for the Longhorns.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Police arrived at the house within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter, which identified gunshots. (Reuters: Greg Wohlford/USA Today)

Nine people, including a male suspect, have been killed after a shooting at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania.

Officers were alerted to the incident via a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots.

District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continued.

A pregnant woman, children and other relatives are among eight victims gunned down by a man at a home in Pennsylvania.

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman.

Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two "distressed" women arrived and began pounding on the door shortly before 5pm on Friday, local time, Mr Lorah said.

The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.

Police arrived to find the two women dead outside.

Bystanders gather near a house where nine people were confirmed dead. (Reuters: Greg Wohlford/USA Today)

After deploying a drone and robot, police went inside the home and found the bodies of a five-year-old boy; a one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.

"Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home," Mr Lorah said at a news conference.

"But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole."

Mr Lorah declined to discuss motive but said investigators would talk to other relatives and examine the mobile phones of the women who were killed outside the home.

"We have to figure out what that is."

Mr Lorah said officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter, a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots.

No additional shots were fired after that.

"Sounds that may have been mistaken for gunfire came from flashbang devices, chemical munitions, used by SWAT officers," he said.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration's "full support" to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin, who spoke directly to the victims' families during the news conference.

"I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier," she said.

"But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we're grieving with you. And we are here to support you."

District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continued.

Erie is about 190 kilometres north of Pittsburgh.

Speaking at a campaign rally outside Philadelphia, Mr Shapiro mentioned both the Erie killings and the shooting of two Philadelphia police officers early Saturday.

"Today has been a dark day across this commonwealth," he said.
