Passengers with a life raft retrieved from a French aircraft drop. (Supplied: John Tua)

A Solomons Islands ferry was travelling between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro when its engine failed on Friday, about 100 nautical miles from its destination.

Aircraft from Australia and New Caledonia have dropped supplies and equipment for the boat with more than 70 passengers onboard.

A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached the ferry on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food.

More than 70 passengers have been stranded aboard a drifting ferry in Solomon Islands waters since Friday, as an international operation scrambles to get supplies to the vessel.

The ferry was sailing between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro in Temotu Province when its engine failed on Friday, leaving it adrift at sea.

A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached MV Awka on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food, passenger John Tua said.

Mr Tua, a nurse with the provincial government, said the engine was overheating when it broke down about 100 nautical miles from its destination.

While the seas have been mostly calm, Mr Tua said the ship had also experienced rough swells.

A distress call was issued on Friday, with the Solomon Islands enlisting help from the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) and New Caledonian government.

John Tua with communication equipment dropped from an Australian aircraft. (Supplied: John Tua)

An AMSA spokesperson said its Cairns-based rescue jet made several drops of critical items including food, water, medical supplies and communications equipment.

A French aircraft from New Caledonia was first on the scene on Saturday, dropping life rafts and desalination equipment.

"The urgent need was water. We've run out of water onboard … the ship's water supply was used to cool the engine down when it was heating up," Mr Tua said.

"We have lots of brown coconuts on board to drink, but our water is finished."

On Sunday morning, the Panama-registered bulk carrier Sunnine 3 reached the vessel early and began transferring water and food, which was lifestreamed online by Mr Tua.

Passengers have stayed in touch with families using the ship's Starlink internet, while Mr Tua has been the main source of news for worried relatives.

Temotu Premier Stanley Tehiahua said a police patrol boat was on its way from Honiara.

"To all relatives, families and friends anxiously awaiting news of their loved ones, we recognise the emotional distress and uncertainty you are experiencing," he said in a statement.

The ABC has requested comment from the Solomon Islands Maritime Safety Administration and the country's Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.

The incident comes three weeks after the inter-island ferry MV Matui sank in rough seas in neighbouring Vanuatu with more than 50 people onboard. More than 30 people from the MV Matui are still missing.

There have been calls for Australia and New Zealand to invest more in maritime safety, including from Peter Nuttall, a sustainable researcher at the University of the South Pacific, who told the ABC after the Matui sinking that Australia could easily invest in better vessels for the Pacific.

"We could have built 40 to 60 safe, brand new, low-carbon ferries for the same budget as we've spent on 20-something patrol boats, several which have already been scrapped," Dr Nuttall said.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.title: Nao-Cola Yamazaki is your favorite writer’s favorite writer
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.author: Kris Kosaka
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/202.text:
Your favorite writer’s favorite writer is someone the world hasn’t discovered yet: Nao-Cola Yamazaki, a name cited in interviews with Japanese authors and literary translators as someone who deserves more international recognition.

More than 20 years after Yamazaki’s Japanese-language debut, two of the author’s books have finally appeared in English translation for the first time.

“Don’t Laugh at Other People’s Sex Lives,” translated by Polly Barton, and “Beautiful Distance,” translated by Charlotte Goff, hit bookstores Sept. 29, both hand-selected by actress and book-lover Sarah Jessica Parker for her own imprint, SJP Lit.

Yamazaki, 48, who uses they/them pronouns, often writes about relationships that bridge or challenge the divides within the rigid constraints of society.

Their first book, “Don’t Laugh at Other People’s Sex Lives,” was an instant success upon its publication in 2004. It was nominated for the Akutagawa Prize — Yamazaki would go on to have four other nominations for the coveted prize for emerging novelists — and although it didn’t win, it earned the Bungei Prize and was adapted into a popular film in 2008.

Writing from the perspective of a male first-person protagonist, Yamazaki transforms a potentially problematic premise — an extramarital affair between a university art student and his much older teacher — into a quietly profound narrative on humanity’s sometimes baffling and often humorous struggle for physical and emotional connection.

Yamazaki was only 26 when their first book was published. For someone who gained success at a young age,they say they are excited and grateful for this fresh chance at connecting with new readers, even if they are no longer among the youngest cohort of writers. “Sometimes I think I should change my name to Nao-Cognac or Nao-Coffee,” they joke. Yamazaki adopted the pen name “Nao-Cola” as a nod to their favorite soda and a means to separate themselves from the many others in their generation named Naoko, their given name.

Their second recently translated novella “Beautiful Distance,” originally published in 2016, won the Shibata Renzaburo Award and became a critically acclaimed bestseller. The poignant story follows a Japanese salaryman in his daily routine, juggling work duties and navigating mundane healthcare bureaucracy while caring for his terminally ill wife.

Although published more than 10 years apart, the two books both offer universally relatable stories depicting a male narrator coming to terms with his strong emotions amid the pressures of societal expectations.

“Both novellas are, in a sense, love stories,” says Yamazaki. “As a writer, I actually had quite a lot of ambition in writing them. I thought, ‘If I’m going to write novels, I want to take on love.’”

They cite two favorite works of classical literature, Murasaki Shikibu’s “The Tale of Genji” and Emily Bronte’s “Wuthering Heights,” as famous examples of love stories that also reveal deep hierarchical divisions within society.

Similarly, Yamazaki’s characters often struggle to forge relationships within the constraints of Japanese culture.

While Yamazaki identifies as nonbinary and has recently started writing a series of essays on the topic, the decision to write from a male perspective wasn’t originally meant to be a political statement.

“Wiithout thinking deeply about it, I wrote the male protagonist in my debut using ‘ore wa’ — ‘I’ in the masculine first-person form in Japanese,” Yamazaki says. “I found it incredibly pleasurable and fun, so I just kept writing that way.”

At the time, Yamazaki was surprised at the “huge reaction,” realizing that “readers pay a lot of attention to the author’s gender and age. But for me, I don’t think those things are all that important.”

Labels, boundaries and borders of all kinds are porous to the author, and it shows in their writing style. Yamazaki writes from male, female and nonbinary perspectives, experimenting frequently with language to subvert or reconfigure expectations for gender or class.

Apart from literary fiction, Yamazaki has also written numerous essays, short stories and children’s books. Their engaging vignettes on nontraditional family life, serialized in Nishinippon Shimbun, were published in 2015 as an essay collection titled “Cute Husband.” Yamazaki discusses marriage with their bookstore clerk husband and how the two of them reject rigid societal norms for a more “gentle” relationship: For instance, the essay “Winning and Losing” depicts the real-life, thoughtful negotiations between two partners working full time with caregiving responsibilities. The essay collection remains one of their most top-selling works.

Through all their writings, Yamazaki deliberately amplifies the voices of those on the margins of society.

“When people are divided along lines such as gender or … disability, I want my work to be on the side of the minority,” they say. Yamazaki finds inspiration in the human determination to find connection despite the boundaries in place to keep people apart by labeling them as “other.”

Their bold writing style also speaks to an open perspective on what constitutes literature itself.

“A single sentence casually posted on social media can be incredibly literary or interesting,” Yamazaki says. “Or even a random conversation. When I follow the line of the mountains with my eyes, I feel the same kind of pleasure I get from reading a book. Maybe this is also a sentence; maybe a mountain range is also part of a book.”

Yamazaki is well-connected within the writing community in Japan through friendships with other authors including Sayaka Murata and Asako Yuzuki, both of whom have internationally bestselling works. Yamazaki says that their collective works on the bookshelf have been a catalyst for “changing perceptions” about Japanese women.

“Sometimes Japan can be perceived overseas as somewhat backward when it comes to gender discrimination. Although I don’t identify simply as a woman, there are many authors thinking and writing about gender in Japan,” says Yamazaki, adding that the current popularity in Japanese literature widens the path for more diverse perspectives to be read.

“Writer friends and I often discuss how our job isn’t just to write our own books,” Yamazaki says. “It’s also our work to create a larger bookshelf.”

Yamazaki is now finding opportunities to speak directly to readers abroad, having recently participated in the Edinburgh Book Festival in August and gearing up for a publicity tour across the U.K. later this month.

“When I saw how the book festival was so welcomed by everyone in Edinburgh — rather than just being a separate location where only book lovers gathered — I really felt hopeful,” the author says, adding that they wish Japan could host something similar.

Ultimately, what’s important to Yamazaki is being represented on and reading from that global bookshelf.

“Reading books by all kinds of writers, from all periods and all parts of the world, is invaluable. Even one book might be able to widen the world’s perspective.”

The 48-year-old author's first book, ‘Don’t Laugh at Other People’s Sex Lives, was an instant success upon its publication in 2004.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.title: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680.text:
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.

But Zaw Min has no choice.

"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.

"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."

Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.

According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.

Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.

Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.

The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.

Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.

"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.

The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.

They said they had no comment on the matter.

With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.

The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.

International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.

In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.

Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.

"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.

Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.

"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."

Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.

"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."

Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.

The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.

In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.

U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.

When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.

But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.

"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.

"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.

"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."

In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.

The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.

She does not know where her husband is now.

Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.

Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.

"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."

In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.

The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.

BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.

"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.

"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."

While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.

So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.

Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".

But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.

It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.

The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".

In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.

Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.

As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjzx.title: Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjzx.text:
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?

That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.

The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.

The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.

The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.

Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.

With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.

The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".

Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.

"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.

Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".

Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.

"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced).

Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.

"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.

"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.

"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."

The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.

In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".

"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".

In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.

That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.

Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.

"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.

"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."

The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.

When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.

But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.

"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."

As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.

"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.

"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.

"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."

The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.

In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.

At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.

Kim says that began to change as they filmed.

"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."

Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.

She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.

On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.

"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.

"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."

Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.

"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.

The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.

"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.

"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."

In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.

"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.

"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.

"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.

"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Deceased were all members of the same family, officials say, and one of victims placed the initial emergency call

Five people were shot and killed in an apparent murder-suicide at a residence in Georgia on Friday, authorities say.

The deceased were family members who lived at the home in Douglas, a city in south Georgia.

Officers responded to reports of an active shooter later on Friday, Brannen Pruette, the Douglas police chief, said at a Saturday news conference. One of the victims placed the initial emergency call.

Responding officers found four deceased adults inside the home. A fifth individual was transported to a hospital, where they were later pronounced dead.

Details around how the tragedy unfolded remain unclear, including who opened fire.

Hours before the deadly shooting, a female victim called police to complain that her husband was “killing her” with his smoking. EMS transported her to a local medical center.

Police did not offer additional information, citing the ongoing investigation.

“We recognize the profound impact this loss has on those closest to the victims in our community. We ask everyone to respect the privacy of the family and allow them the time and space they need to grieve,” Pruette said.

Charlie Davis, the Douglas city manager, said it was the area’s second murder-suicide incident in three months.

“Domestic violence doesn’t know race. It doesn’t know religion. It doesn’t know geographic location,” Davis said. “We encourage everyone to refrain from speculation and allow the family the space, dignity and compassion they deserve during this time.”

In a similar episode of violence, a man in Pennsylvania fatally shot several family members on Friday, before killing himself.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.title: Iran war live: 12 killed in Riyadh, US weighs joining fight against Houthis
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.author: Mahmoud Sayed,Kristina Harazim
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/.text:
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it has redirected 135 and disabled four commercial vessels since the resumption of the US naval blockade against Iran on July 14.

CENTCOM’s statement on Saturday updates the number of redirected vessels to 135, from 133, since its latest update.

“US forces have destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ multibillion-dollar shadow network over the same period”, the statement read.

⁠The ⁠⁠Saudi Arabia-backed chairman of ⁠⁠Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, ⁠⁠Rashad al-Alimi, has expressed condolences and solidarity with Saudi Arabia following the attack on the King Khalid airport in a post on his X account.

“This criminal assault reflects the terrorist nature that governs the behavior of the militias and their recklessness with the lives of civilians and the interests of the Yemeni people, at a time when the Kingdom continues its noble fraternal stances in support of the Yemeni economy and alleviating the suffering of our citizens,” he said.

He went on to say that aggression against Saudi Arabia was “aggression against our security, our interests, and future of our generations”.

Al-Alimi added that the Yemeni government army and forces loyal to it would move forward with operation “Dawn of Yemen” to end the Houthi threat and restore state institutions “whatever the sacrifices that may entail”.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and later imposed their own government. Most recently, the group swept through the western coast of Yemen on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.

The Houthis have not claimed the latest attack on Riyadh.

US President Donald Trump has commented on the deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport, telling reporters “I think it’s terrible”.

“The Saudis are good fighters but I think the attack was a terrible thing”, the US president remarked.

The Saudi-led military has accused Yemen’s Houthis of conducting the attack on Saturday which killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300.

Flight tracking data show no inbound flights to Riyadh as of shortly after 3am local time on Sunday.

Almost all of the flights scheduled to arrive in Riyadh on Sunday are shown as cancelled on the tracking website Flight Radar24.

Saudi’s General Authority of Civil Aviation had said on Saturday that operations were temporarily suspended at Khalid International Airport in Riyadh following an attack that killed 12 people and injured 309 others.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the alleged Houthi attack constitutes a “full-blown war crime.”

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it has “disabled” a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman.

CENTCOM said in a statement on Saturday “the ship’s crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran.” The US military claims the operation was carried out “without harming the crew”.

“A U.S. military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition,” the statement read.

CENTCOM said the vessel was “attempting to transit regional waters after having previously departed an Iranian port.”

The Saudi-led coalition has said it intercepted and destroyed a drone in eastern Saudi Arabia, according to a post by coalition forces spokesperson Turki al-Maliki on X.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington “strongly condemns” Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the Saturday attack on King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, which the Houthis have not claimed responsibility for.

“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Rubio said in a social media post on Saturday.

Saudi authorities said the Saturday attack killed 12 people, including one US national. Rubio confirmed that the attack killed an American.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.title: Pro surfer swaps California waves for life in the outback
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.author: Abbey Halter and Zara Margolis
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/s.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Caio Ibelli has a new home in outback Queensland. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Last month, Brazilian professional surfer Caio Ibelli was riding barrelling waves at the Surfing Champions Trophy in the Maldives.

Today, he's at home, in the outback, almost 1,000 kilometres from the east coast.

The 32-year-old is one of Mount Isa's newest residents, swapping surf and sand for the red dirt plains of north-west Queensland.

Caio Ibelli's days are now spent wrangling his toddler in the outback town of Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Originally from Brazil, Ibelli moved to Australia after a stint in California.

First picking up a surfboard when he was three years old, he said by the time he was seven, his talent was being noticed.

Caio Ibelli was three years old when he started surfing in Brazil. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

By 23, Ibelli had qualified for the World Surf League tour, kicking off a nine-year professional career.

"After that, I kind of retired … I wanted to have kids and a family," he said.

Ibelli said although a move to the outback wasn't always planned, he was proud to be raising his son in the city, despite knowing little about what to expect.

One-year-old Thomas Ibelli is spending his first years in the outback, despite his dad's professional surfing career. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"It is getting a little bit too hot. It's about 38 degrees right now, and I heard it goes all the way to 46 … I've never felt that in my life," he said.

It was his wife's career that brought the family, including their one-year-old son, Thomas, to the region after completing her medical degree.

"Every time I speak with my friends in the hospital and say that my husband is a professional surfer, everybody has the same reaction… 'Oh, how?'" Talie Ibelli laughed.

"We actually love it here. We love the community, and it's a great opportunity for my son to be raised here … this is the real Australia."

Caio Ibelli won the World Surfing Championships in the Maldives last month. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

The family have only been to the beach about six times since moving to the bush, which makes his recent win in the Maldives all the more impressive.

He said muscle memory along with his new-found "outback attitude" helped him snag the overall win.

"The event was cool. Winning it was amazing, it was awesome," he said.

Caio Ibelli spent about a decade travelling the world surfing circuit.  (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

"Seeing my son playing on the blue water, watching the sharks all day, it was just super special."

Mount Isa has its fair share of athletic prowess, with tennis star Pat Rafter, golfer Greg Norman and AFL player Charlie Cameron all born in the city.

It's unclear yet whether Caio Ibelli's son, Thomas, will follow in his father's footsteps. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Ibelli said it was a privilege to be among the mining city's claims to fame, including perhaps being its most famous surfer.

"After I won the contest in the Maldives, coming back to Mount Isa, I've been going around in places, and people are like, 'Are you the surfer?' And I'm like, 'Yeah', and people are kind of tripping," he said.

The Ibelli family have found a home in north-west Queensland, living in the mining city of Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I feel so fortunate to be here, Australia is such a good place, and Mount Isa is amazing."

Even with the positives, he admits it is tough to be a surfer with no surf.

"I'm really missing some kind of water, so sometimes I go to swim, or I'm just hoping Mount Isa Council will build us a wave pool sometime soon," he laughed.

Ibelli's next dream is teaching bush kids how to surf.

Caio and Talie Ibelli plan on raising Thomas as an "Aussie kid". (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I'm so grateful for being here with my family, and I feel like the least I could do is like giving back, and I would love to some day take local people to the beach and surf," he said.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.author: Ewa Staszewska
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Federal Government

Angus Taylor tells Insiders he needs "every good leader" heading into the next federal election.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he would welcome back former colleague Josh Frydenberg to the Liberals, if he were to contest a seat at the next federal election.

Mr Taylor has also defended the Coalition's proposed cuts to migration, arguing that more skilled migrants with a higher average income would achieve budget neutrality.

The Coalition says it will release more details of its migration plan closer to the election.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he would welcome the return of former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg to politics, as he continues to defend the Coalition's newly released migration policy.

On Saturday, Mr Frydenberg released excerpts of his upcoming memoir A Grateful Son, published in The Australian, which included details of his election defeat four years ago.

The former Kooyong MP, who was a leadership frontrunner, fuelled speculation he may contest a seat in the next election as he outlined his vision for Australia.

He urged the Liberal Party to "reclaim" the centre of politics, arguing there was a lack of political courage in Canberra.

Mr Frydenberg proposed several policy changes across energy and AI and a pitch to leverage a portion of state GST revenue based on how many homes were built.

Josh Frydenberg says Canberra lacks political courage. (AAP: James Ross)

When asked whether he would welcome or fear his former colleague's return, Mr Taylor said he needed "every good leader" heading into the next federal election.

"People will play different roles … whether it's just liking Facebook and Instagram posts all the way through to being a candidate," he told Insiders on Sunday.

"But we've all got to mobilise, and I welcome Josh playing whatever role he's able to play."

The Coalition would cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for two years.

Mr Taylor immediately added that the Coalition would not adopt Mr Frydenberg's suggestion of raising the GST.

"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis. That we won't do," he said.

"We'll put Australia and Australians first, but we won't be raising taxes.

"I'm a fiscal conservative. I believe in lower taxes, and that's why we'll be giving the tax-back guarantee, lower income taxes for Australians without raising the GST."

Despite economic concerns raised by the business, aged care, education and construction sectors about the Coalition's migration policy, the opposition leader maintained it would be "budget neutral".

Mr Taylor said the policy had not been officially costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office, due to "constraints".

"In terms of analysis, there are limitations on what the parliamentary office can do because of its legislation. It cannot model directly Labor's policies so we had to give it assumptions to work with," he said.

"That is a constraint, but as we approach the election, we won't have that constraint."

The policy proposes slashing temporary migration by 650,000 places over four years and offsetting the lost tax revenue with 100,000 additional skilled migrants, who would be higher-paid and therefore pay more tax.

One Nation wants negative migration in its first years, the Coalition has promised to more than halve it, while Labor has announced measures to ensure migration actually falls to its target of 225,000.

He reiterated that aged care, which heavily relies on temporary visas, would be subject to a transitional arrangement that allowed these workers to stay on existing visas for a longer period of time.

"If you cut numbers and raise standards, you can maintain budget neutrality. And you can strengthen the economy because the average income, the average productivity of the person coming into this country rises," he said.

"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone."

Australia's net overseas migration, or NOM, fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, with Labor pursuing a target of 245,000 for this financial year and 225,000 the year after.

SA Police said the incident was not random and the men were known to each other. (ABC News file image: Will Hunter)

SA Police are investigating an incident in the Barossa Valley hinterland after a 30-year-old man sustained multiple stab wounds yesterday evening.

Police said emergency crews were called to a private property on Pine Creek Road at Bethel.

The victim, who is from Kapunda, was flown to hospital in a critical condition.

"His condition is now considered stable," police said in a statement.

"A 22-year-old Nuriootpa man was arrested at the scene by police without incident."

Police said the 22-year-old was charged with attempted murder and refused police bail.

"Police wish to reassure the local community that this was not a random incident and the men involved are known to each other," police said.

The man is expected to appear in court on Monday.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident and has not yet spoken to police to contact Crime Stoppers.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/b.author: Eliza Bidstrup
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/b.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt

Topic:
Travel and Tourism

The 11.5-metre sculpture of WA's Carnaby's cockatoos sits in Apex Park in Moora. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

An 11.5-metre sculpture of two endangered Carnaby's cockatoos has been unveiled in the WA town of Moora.

The project has been seven years in the making, with the Kerkhoff Carnaby Group first floating the idea in 2019.

It is hoped the sculptures will inspire conservation work, ensuring the longevity of the species.

From the Big Pineapple in Queensland to the Big Prawn in New South Wales, the next "big thing" will be unveiled in the West Australian town of Moora.

A group of conservationists has worked tirelessly for seven years to launch two 11.5-metre Carnaby's cockatoos in the wheatbelt town, 180 kilometres north of Perth.

Those spearheading the project say they hope the sculptures will be a tourism drawcard and bring awareness to the endangered icon of the region.

The Kerkhoff Carnaby Group came up with the idea in 2019 in an effort to put Moora on the map and highlight the town as an important place for the cockatoos' conservation.

The group's namesake, 84-year-old Moora conservationist Wally Kerkhoff, has built and installed nesting hollows for the local Carnaby's population throughout the area for more than 40 years.

The critically endangered birds are found in Moora between July and February, when they breed in the hollows of old salmon gums and wandoo trees.

Carnaby's cockatoos landed on the sculptures on the day of installation, giving their tick of approval. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

Moore Catchment Council community landcare officer Rachel Walmsley has worked alongside Mr Kerkhoff for 14 years and described the conservationist as a "legend".

"If it wasn't for Wally, we wouldn't have Carnaby's in Moora anymore," she said.

Ms Walmsley said she hoped the new installation would inspire the next generation of Carnaby's cockatoo conservers.

"Wally has done his job. He won't be around forever," she said.

"We need to carry on the fight to keep these birds alive and thriving."

Fittingly, the Kerkhoff Group voted to name the male Carnaby figure Wally, with Mr Kerkhoff given the rights to pick a name for his female counterpart, settling on Mrs Carnaby.

The COVID-19 pandemic and rising fuel prices made completing the project challenging.

The project cost $540,000, with 74 per cent from community donations.

There are 240 named donors, many of whom live in Moora and surrounding towns.

Kerkhoff Carnaby Group secretary Topsy De Vries said the community support behind the project meant the giant birds belonged to the residents.

"As we would encounter more roadblocks, say we needed more money to bring the project to life, I would have neighbours come over wanting to give what they described as 'a bit of money', then handing over cheques of $10,000," she said.

"We did feel like giving up a couple of times, but we couldn't because people trusted us.

"People really believed in us."

Erich Juhren volunteered his time to travel to Queensland and back to retrieve the cockatoos. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

One of those residents who went "above and beyond" was retired truck driver Erich Juhren.

Mr Juhren drove the sculptures, in sections, several thousand kilometres from Queensland to their new home, where they were put together piece by piece and "perched" on a branch.

Official measuring of the sculpture by manufacturer Natureworks Australia confirm the birds stand as tall as the Big Tractor in the nearby town of Carnamah.

The Big Carnaby's Cockatoo project was a collaboration between the Kerkhoff Carnaby Group, Moore Catchment Council and the Shire of Moora. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

"People have asked us, 'Why so big?' And I always say, 'It's no good building a small, big thing,'" Ms De Vries said.

Ms De Vries said there was an air of disbelief that the day of the unveiling had arrived.

"My family have seen me go through this for the past seven years and they can't believe it's nearly over," she said.

Ms De Vries said the sculptures had already lured tourists from around the state to watch them being erected and the finishing touches being applied.

"One of the local cafes is already benefiting because we now have to wait 30 minutes for our morning coffee," she said.

Moora Shire President Ken Seymour said the local government welcomed the new attraction.

"I look forward to seeing these sculptures attracting more people to the regions, getting people out of the city and enjoying what we have to offer," he said.

Ownership and maintenance of the Carnaby's cockatoo sculptures will be transferred to the Shire of Moora as of the launch day.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Prosper Heri Ngorora
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Beni, Democratic Republic of Congo – The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has spread to another health zone in the east, while a fatal imported case in Kenya has underscored the risk of cross-border transmission.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said in an October 8 update that Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu province had reported cases for the first time. As of October 6, four confirmed cases, including two deaths, had been recorded there.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola virus. According to the WHO, cases had been reported in 64 health zones across seven provinces in the DRC. Ituri remained the worst-affected province in cumulative cases, while North Kivu was accounting for a growing share of newly confirmed infections.

As of October 6, the WHO had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 confirmed deaths in the DRC. A further 2,269 people had recovered, and the crude case fatality ratio stood at 48.2 percent.

Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease on October 6, according to the WHO. The patient, a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the DRC, fell ill there and received treatment at several health facilities before travelling to Kenya through Uganda.

The patient travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda, before flying to Nairobi, arriving on October 3. The patient was isolated in hospital and tested positive for the virus. Despite supportive treatment, the patient died on October 5, the WHO said.

Kenyan authorities identified 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers. The WHO also reported efforts to trace passengers and crew members from the flight to Nairobi.

Public health measures have been initiated in Kenya and Uganda, including contact tracing and enhanced surveillance.

On October 8, preliminary laboratory results for a suspected Ebola case in Kenya’s Wajir County came back negative, according to the county governor. The result eased concerns about a possible second case, although monitoring continued.

The imported infection has underscored the importance of surveillance and coordination between neighbouring countries. Identifying exposed people and monitoring them for symptoms are central to detecting infections early and interrupting further transmission.

In the DRC, the response is facing mounting pressure from limited treatment capacity, insecurity and difficulties securing cooperation from some communities.

Daniel Makasi Levergénois, founder of Watoto Radio, said insecurity and misinformation were undermining efforts to contain the outbreak. In Beni and Butembo, both in North Kivu, rumours and misconceptions about Ebola had contributed to reluctance among some residents to cooperate with response teams, he said.

In an October 5 update, medical charity Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said North Kivu accounted for nearly 40 percent of newly confirmed cases nationwide, up from 24 percent at the end of August.

MSF also reported that, as of September 28, 34 percent of confirmed Ebola patients were being treated in non-specialised health facilities. Dedicated treatment centres lacked sufficient beds, while delays in diagnosis meant some patients were being treated outside facilities equipped to manage Ebola.

The organisation warned that many of these facilities lacked the resources and expertise needed to manage the disease, increasing the risk of transmission among patients and healthcare workers.

“For weeks, treatment capacity has stretched to its limit,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator of MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in Butembo.

“Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment. This is extremely concerning.”

Alberto Lusenge, a community leader in Beni, said the failure to stop transmission early in Ituri province, followed by new cases and attacks on response workers in Beni and Butembo, had deepened public concern.

Lusenge warned that mistrust could discourage residents from reporting symptoms or cooperating with health workers. He said North Kivu could become a greater focus of the outbreak if authorities failed to secure stronger cooperation from local communities.

The WHO said response teams were following up 23,741 of the 29,535 identified contacts as of October 4, equivalent to 80.4 percent – below the response target of at least 85 percent.

Contact tracing allows health authorities to identify people who may have been exposed, monitor them for symptoms and detect infections early. Gaps in follow-up can make it harder to identify and interrupt chains of transmission.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for a community-centred response, including active case finding, systematic contact tracing, daily follow-up of exposed people and sustained engagement with local communities.

The DRC’s 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak, caused by a different virus species, killed nearly 2,300 people. The current outbreak presents distinct challenges: According to the WHO, there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease.

Early detection, supportive care and infection prevention therefore remain central to the response. But as infections spread into additional health zones and treatment facilities struggle to accommodate patients, health authorities face the dual challenge of containing transmission and maintaining public trust.

Jean Kaseya, director-general of Africa CDC, has stressed the importance of rapidly identifying and monitoring people exposed to the virus.

“To bring this outbreak under control, we need to know where every contact is, track them and quickly identify anyone showing symptoms before they pass the virus on to their family, their community or across borders. We will only bring this outbreak under control once the last chain of transmission has been broken,” Kaseya said in a news release seen by Al Jazeera.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.title: Pre-COP push leaves Australia's remotest territory feeling forgotten
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.author: Kimberley Putland
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Climate Change

Residents of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Australia's most isolated inhabited territory, are facing significant challenges from climate change. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

A delegation from the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has been denied the opportunity to attend COP31 after their application was not selected by the federal government.

A contingent of federal ministers, including the prime minister, has wrapped up pre-COP talks in Tuvalu.

UWA's Oceans Institute says despite the setback, it remains committed to working alongside the Cocos (Keeling) Islands community.

Residents of Australia's remotest territory say they feel forgotten by the government's global climate change efforts ahead of the major COP31 forum in Türkiye.

The federal government hosted pre-COP meetings in Tuvalu and Fiji this week in a bid to raise the voices of Pacific Island nations.

But on the far opposite side of Australia's recognised territory, and 8,900km from this week's Pacific meetings, residents of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands (CKI) feel they have been left in the lurch.

Tuvalu (pictured) and Cocos (Keeling) Islands face similar climate threats like flooding and coastal erosion. (Supplied)

Faced with coastal erosion, flooding and other climate-driven issues mirroring those of Pacific nations, the Cocos Islanders made a bid to be represented at COP31.

Their application was approved by the United Nations, but not selected for funding by the Australian government, with the delegation informed they had been unsuccessful just before this week's talks.

Their panel proposal, submitted by the University of Western Australia's Oceans Institute, would have featured the challenges faced by the Cocos (Keeling) Islands as a low-lying island community.

The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are facing coastal erosion and flooding, like their Pacific Island counterparts. (Supplied: Chris Bray)

Home Island resident Luluk Sloan said COP31 presented an opportunity to bring global awareness to the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

With a coastal hazard management plan suggesting retreat slammed by the islands' residents, they had hoped attendance would have allowed them to learn how other island communities were dealing with climate-driven challenges.

"A council delegation was actually looking at visiting the Pacific Islands just to see what sort of mitigation they've got planned in terms of not retreating," she said.

"I think it's a disappointment that we don't have that link; we can't really tell our story globally."

Luluk Sloan lives on Home Island. (Supplied: Luluk Sloan)

Ms Sloan said it felt like the islands were being left behind.

West Island resident Rose Cummins also would have attended the conference.

"I certainly applaud the Pacific Islands. I think they've done an incredible job in raising the profile of climate change and how it's directly impacting them," Ms Cummins said.

"I guess we would just like the same opportunity."

Rose Cummins lives on West Island. (Supplied: Rose Cummins)

A spokesperson for the Department of Climate Change, Energy and Water acknowledged the impact climate change was having on the Islands.

But the department rejected suggestions that the focus on the Pacific came at the expense of Australian communities.

"Engagement with Pacific partners complements, rather than replaces, our support for Australian communities facing climate risks," the spokesperson said.

The Oceans Institute said it remained committed to working with the islands' community to help address the ongoing challenges posed by climate change.

Residents say there has been a lack of meaningful consultation on the plan to manage the islands' ongoing coastal risks.

"I think a lot of people felt that it's another consultation," Ms Sloan said.

"What are they going to do about it? Possibly, probably, nothing."

Cocos (Keeling) Islands residents say they have seen metres of shoreline vanish. (Supplied: Luluk Sloan)

Ms Cummins said expressions of interest for a community reference group, promised since the start of the year, were only issued last month.

"There's no decision-making abilities; it won't affect any policy or anything like that," she said.

"That will still be done by experts who don't live here."

The Climate Change Department spokesperson said the Coastal Hazard Risk Management and Adaptation Plan (CHRMAP) was a key step in supporting CKI to respond and adapt to climate change.

"The [plan] gives us a clear picture of the coastal hazards facing the islands and will help guide the work we do together to strengthen preparedness and improve community safety," the spokesperson said.

But Ms Sloan remained sceptical.

"I think people are slowly realising that … the delivery of services is on the decline," she said.

"And that's probably because they're thinking: 'Oh yeah, 50 years from now, the islands are going to go under.'"

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Houthi attack on Saudi airport kills 12, over 300 wounded
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
RIYADH – The third attack in a week on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday left at least 12 people dead and more than 300 wounded, Saudi authorities said, as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.

The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the U.S., Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, officials said, 309 were wounded.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.

Saturday’s attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia’s threat warning system. Last week’s two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

The deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

A Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond to the attack.

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children. Reporters could not independently verify those claims.

All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had “shut down Riyadh international airport.” The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Oct. 5.

U.S. President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, saying they “demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life.”

One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing toward the facility. A video verified by reporters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveler said they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh said it was “aware of attacks” and “strongly recommends all U.S. citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas.”

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.

The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ceasefire unraveled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive last week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country’s third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organizers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.title: Call to protect nesting birds from the cars on SA's Goolwa Beach
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.author: Caroline Horn
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/c.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Environmental Impacts

Cedric Varcoe is a prominent Ngarrindjeri Elder and artist. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Ngarrindjeri elder Cedric Varcoe would like vehicle access to Goolwa Beach to be restricted to protect birds and the environment.

Drivers can currently access the beach at Goolwa and drive along a 12-kilometre stretch to the mouth of the Murray River.

Ngarrindjeri rangers will continue to work with Birdlife Australia to help monitor and protect nesting birds on the stretch of South Australian coast.

A Ngarrindjeri elder says keeping vehicles off Goolwa Beach could help to protect endangered birds as rangers and volunteers work to try and save as many chicks as possible.

Cedric Varcoe welcomed the birds in a ceremony at the Coorong last week, marking the breeding season for some and the return to South Australia of others from as far away as the Arctic.

The birds of the Coorong are some of the Ngarrindjeri community's Ngartji (totems), and Mr Varcoe said it was the community's role to fight to preserve them and protect their habitat.

"In our culture they're our friend, our spiritual guide, our protectors, and when they're not here, or when they're no longer here, our spirit is no longer alive and strong as well," he said.

There is a lack of data around the number of vehicles using Goolwa Beach. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The Coorong welcome ceremony coincided with the fledging of three hooded plover chicks from the Coorong Beach, a more remote site on the other side of the mouth of the Murray River from Goolwa Beach.

Birdlife Australia has been working with Ngarrindjeri rangers to improve bird survival under the federally funded Shorebird and Wetland Habitat program.

The three hooded plover fledglings on Coorong Ocean Beach were watched over by Ngarrindjeri rangers and Birdlife Australia. (Supplied: Birdlife Australia)

The charity's director of coastal, wetland and marine programs, Grainne Maguire, said the area was important for both resident and migratory shorebirds.

"They fatten up and they rest and they get all that energy which determines the journey back, but also if they breed successfully when they go back."

Signage placed on Coorong Beach, on the other side of the Murray Mouth from Goolwa Beach. (Supplied: Birdlife Australia)

One of the resident birds being watched is the fairy tern, considered to be at high risk of extinction in the wild, with 1,000 remaining in South Australia across 10 breeding sites.

Two of those sites are in the Coorong, where the terns lay their eggs in a shallow and often difficult to see nest above the high tide mark.

A 12-kilometre stretch of beach between Goolwa and the mouth of the Murray River is open to four-wheel drives and popular with fishers and families.

This photo from New Years Day on 2022 shows how busy the beach can get during peak periods. (Supplied)

The beach at Goolwa attracts a high number of tourists, where the local council has responsibility for the access ramp.

While a permit system has been discussed in the past there is not currently one in place.

Hindmarsh Island resident Wayde Eldridge regularly drives on the beach, setting up his jetski and shade for himself and his dogs Little and Notso.

Wayde Eldridge of Hindmarsh Island with his dogs Little and Notso. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

He thought people driving on the beach were responsible and a ban would be unpopular.

Adelaide University associate professor Craig Styan has been looking at how the beach is used and has surveyed a number of beachgoers.

He said while there was no level of driving on the beach that had zero environmental impact, it posed a difficult management question.

"It's almost a paradox … the reason for going is because it's a natural environment, but you being there potentially impacts on some of those natural values," he said.

A fairy tern in its nest on a Coorong beach. (Supplied: Birdlife Australia)

Dr Styan said many beach drivers were unaware of the impact their cars were having.

SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke said the government would "continue to work with relevant agencies and local councils on matters affecting the safety and protection of our beaches and coastal environments".

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.title: People-loving Autumn is ready for a new home
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/community/2.text:
As the days grown noticeably shorter and there’s a chill in the air that can’t be ignored, along comes Autumn.

He’s a very sweet beagle, a colorful chap with a penchant for play. And, he’ll warm your heart no matter what the temperature.

Autumn just arrived at ARK as a result of his family having to deal with a dramatic lifestyle upheaval, one that very sadly allowed no room for this happy, friendly fellow. His zest for exercise keeps him a trim 11 kilograms and you’ll notice his whole body shiver with delight when he sees a leash coming his way.

Autumn loves people, all people, and if you walk away without spending some quality time with him, he’ll look very perplexed. “What? We’re friends, aren’t we?!” Autumn also loves to “talk” so you’ll never feel alone.

Food is another of his loves and he doesn’t waste even the smallest morsel. He’s almost 14 and a bit gray around the muzzle, but Autumn is very full of life and he’s a darn good-looking dog. All in all, he’s a doll, a wonderful dog, and quite a star.

Don’t miss out on the chance to welcome Autumn into your home.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Ronaldo suspended by Portugal FA after leaving camp, criticizing coach
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
After saying he deserved to be disciplined, Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo got what he asked for Saturday when he was provisionally suspended by his national team.

The Portuguese Football Federation opened disciplinary proceedings against the team captain after he walked out of camp during the just-completed international break following a miscommunication with head coach Jorge Jesus.

In a letter that was revealed this week, Ronaldo said he was told by Jesus he would be used as a substitute in a Nations League match against Norway. Ronaldo warmed up along the sideline but did not see playing time.

Before the following match against Denmark, the 41-year-old striker departed camp after notifying the federation he was leaving.

“Disciplinary proceedings have been initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, following a decision by the Non-Professional Section on October 9, 2026,” the Portuguese Football Federation said in a statement.

Ronaldo has already returned to his club team, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia, and scored a goal in a 3-0 victory over Diriyah on Friday.

In his explanation of his actions, Ronaldo admitted that his decision to leave camp was not the best way to handle the situation. But he added that Jesus “broke his word” on more than one occasion.

“I owe my national team teammates an apology for leaving the training camp,” Ronaldo said. “Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach’s word, as anyone who witnessed our conversations can testify, I should not have done it. The responsibility is exclusively mine.”

After just participating in his sixth World Cup for Portugal this past summer, Ronaldo said he is open to discipline. According to reports, the federation’s regulations call for a suspension of anywhere from a month to six months for a player who “abandons” national team activity.

“The consequence of my actions should be assessed and punished by the (federation),” Ronaldo said. “The punishment should not have any mitigating circumstances. I am not just any player; I am the captain of the team, and that constitutes an aggravating factor.”

After playing in 234 matches for his national team, while scoring 146 goals, Ronaldo said he still has the desire to play for Portugal in the future. Portugal has Nations League matches scheduled against Denmark and Wales next month.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NEW DELHI – Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the “Cockroach” youth movement in Delhi on Saturday as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India’s election chief.

Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as ​authorities moved to stop a demonstration organized by the Cockroach movement.

The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics ‌say disproportionately benefits ‌Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, ​but the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.

A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said more than 2,000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India’s financial hub, Mumbai.

There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions.

The United Nations human rights office expressed concerns over ⁠mass detentions before and during the protests.

“We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” U.N. human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in ⁠a statement.

He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.

The Indian mission to the U.N. in Geneva, however, called the U.N.’s concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India.”

It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution. “As ​in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions ⁠in the interest of public order,” the statement added.

Police detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement.

Television footage showed Dipke challenging ⁠officers who approached him on board the ​aircraft.

“I have come to be arrested, arrest me. ... I am not afraid of you guys,” he said.

“No, this ​is not an arrest,” one officer replied. “Please cooperate.”

The movement condemned what it called the “authoritarian detention” of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting.

“We ​will continue our protest ‌tomorrow, day after ... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets,” CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters.

CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders’ whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke’s grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral.

Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also ‌detained, TV channels showed.

Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.

Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes.

The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter ​rolls ​ahead of recent state polls.

Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar’s voter-list revisions that ​removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.

Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.

The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s ⁠economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation.

The near daily protests come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit.

The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.

Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi’s opponents would not back down.

A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been “weaponized” by rivals due to ​election defeats.

Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world’s largest democracy.

Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died.

The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enroll.

Demonstrations were aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists. The U.N. human rights office expressed concerns over ⁠mass detentions
