U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace its leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, a day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia that drew a sharp rebuke from Zelenskyy.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Zelenskyy, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House, blasted Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, which comes as soaring energy prices have become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party ahead of next month’s midterm elections. The Russian government said on Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports with immediate effect.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
A man has died after entering a tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and being attacked by one of the animals, police said.

South Yorkshire Police said officers and emergency medical staff were called to Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35pm on Saturday (12:35 GMT) after receiving reports that a man had entered the enclosure.

He died at the scene. It was not immediately clear how he got in.

The tiger was not injured and stayed inside the enclosure during the incident, police said, adding that there was no wider risk to the public.

The park was evacuated, and officers remained at the scene on Saturday night.

“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time,” police said in a statement.

Police also confirmed they were aware of footage circulating on social media that appeared to show the man inside the enclosure shortly before the attack, urging members of the public not to share the distressing video.

The park said it had closed after a serious incident involving the tiger enclosure and would remain closed until Sunday.

“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,” the park said in a statement on its website.

“The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operating in 2009, and its Land of the Tigers attraction –  a purpose-built 0.4-hectare (2-acre) reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers – opened in 2011.

A raised walkway, 300 metres (985 feet) long, lets visitors watch the tigers roam through woodland and grassland and play in a waterfall pool, the park said.
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.summary: Man died after entering tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster, England. Police say he was attacked by one of the animals, who was not injured. The park was evacuated and officers remained at the scene on Saturday night.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/p.title: Game developer explores colonialism through the eyes of a penguin
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/p.author: Francisco Dominguez
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By Francisco Dominguez

Naphtali Faulker is a Ngāi Te Rangi game developer who is setting the template for the next generation of Indigenous designers. ( Supplied: Origame Digital)

1939. A harsh wind howls over the Antarctic. Scattered Nazi polar exploration camps are in turmoil, corrupted by the eldritch forces their expeditions sought out deep into the tundra. Oblivious to it all, a solitary penguin glides belly first along the ice before flying into an airborne spin reminiscent of Nintendo character Mario.

Origame Digital's "weird fiction" game Penguin Colony explores colonial myth-making and the eldritch horrors of HP Lovecraft through an unusual perspective; that of a carefree penguin.

Naphtali Faulkner, a Ngāi Te Rangi game developer based in Melbourne, sees no issue with the tonal dissonance here.

Each of the penguins who call Antarctica home are playable: baby penguins able to slip into narrow crevices, a teleporting penguin, or any number of waddling adults, all of them indifferent to the horrors inflicted on the fascist humans around them.

In Naphtali Faulker's game cute, waddly penguins became the central metaphor for a Lovecraftian interrogation of colonialism.  (Supplied: Origame Digital)

Penguin Colony addresses revisionist histories at the heart of settler movements.

Faulkner cites the example of Celtic New Zealand, a pseudoscientific alternate history that claims Anglo settlers predate Māori populations.

In the game's Antarctic setting, Nazis' search for relics that support Aryan race myth-making leads them to the unknowable monsters from Lovecraft's 1930s novella At the Mountains of Madness, who they foolishly mistake for an ancient Aryan king.

"They just make that [history] up. The game's story is about exploring how they do this and the tools and mechanisms that allow this colonial myth-making to happen," Faulkner says.

He sees the same myth-making applied to Australia's origin story.

Drawing on the writing of HP Lovecraft in a game critiquing racist pseudo-histories seems paradoxical.

The American author, best known for creating the monstrous Cthulhu, was a notorious racist. Adaptations of his work historically dodge the issue, but Faulkner sees it as inseparable from Lovecraft's stories, the way his unknowable monsters colonise the world, and his overtly xenophobic depictions of Indigenous populations and subservient slave races, such as the giant amoeba-like Shoggoths that appear across his bibliography.

"Most adaptations are trying to scare you with gore or tentacles or otherworldly looking stuff. That's not the scariest thing about Lovecraft," Faulkner says. "The scariest thing about Lovecraft is how it makes assumptions about things and all the white characters just nod along with it."

Faulkner's previous game, Umurangi Generation, is a cyberpunk photography simulation set in Tauranga Aotearoa during a climate crisis.  (Supplied: Origame Digital)

Faulkner describes the dominant mode of "human-centred Silicon Valley design" in video games as a flawed, complacent approach that spoonfeeds unchallenging "content" to players.

Citing Wiradjuri professor Norman Sheehan's framework of "respectful design", which underpins his approach to game design, Faulkner states: "Indigenous knowledge says human beings don't create knowledge between their ears: the thing between their ears is a sponge that sees things out in the world and absorbs them."

The story of Penguin Colony, delivered through narrative vignettes, is fragmentary, opaque, and — most shockingly of all — partly missable.

Game objects, often called "collectibles", are usually clearly marked and precisely quantified. Here, they're not so easily discovered, although your direction is always implied by the direction of the wind, a deliberate move to recreate the mystery the medium once held pre-social media.

"When players realise that their playthrough didn't give them everything, but it did give someone something else, I think they're going to view the world [as] a little bit bigger than they thought it was before."

Gentoo penguin colony at Neko Harbour. The penguin colony is in the foreground, the background is a cracking glacier. Gentoo penguins are foraging generalists (they can switch from eating krill to fish and viceversa). They are the least ice-tolerant and they are expanding across the Antarctic Peninsula in relation to the warmer conditions across the Antarctic Peninsula. (Supplied: Ignacio Juarez Martinez)

Faulkner recalls playing Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas in 2004. Enterprising players around the world suspected Bigfoot was in the game. They were wrong, but that didn't stop players searching every corner of its 36 square kilometre map to follow what proved to be a delusional breadcrumb trail.

"It's a very Lovecraftian idea," Faulkner says. "Most Lovecraftian stories are an academic or a researcher finding an eldritch truth and trying to come to terms with whatever the hell it is. The only way you can do that is by telling players to go and role-play that outside of the game. If you tried to gamify that with stats and numbers, you would never get the same emotional feeling."

Faulkner was inspired by the work of the Japanese game studio FromSoftware which, through action games such as Elden Ring and the Dark Souls series, have used difficulty, complexity and deliberately obscure storytelling to make communities work together to decipher their games.

Faulkner, who describes himself as "an old Souls-head", hopes his game can challenge players and inspire similarly enduring debates — without the infamous difficulty of FromSoftware games.

He sees Penguin Colony as testing players in ways they're not used to experiencing.

For him, video games are an emerging art form yet to live up to its full potential, captured by a commercially driven American design sensibility.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/r.title: Running legend Kipchoge sets race record at Melbourne Marathon
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Eliud Kipchoge (centre) beat Thomas Do Canto (right) and Reece Edwards (left) to the finish of the Melbourne Marathon at the MCG. (ABC News: Rudy de Santis)

Dual Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge has put on a show, breaking the race record for the Melbourne Marathon.

The Kenyan superstar kicked clear in the last 10 kilometres of the race, to finish in 2 hours 9 minutes and 10 seconds.

Kipchoge beat Australians Thomas Do Canto and Reece Edwards, while New Zealand runner Camille French won the women's race.

Eliud Kipchoge has lived up to his star billing at the Melbourne Marathon with a race-record performance.

Kenya's two-time Olympic champion and former world record holder has delighted several thousand fans at the MCG on Sunday morning with a dominating run.

Kipchoge broke away inside the last 10 kilometres of the 42.2km race and won in 2 hours 9 minutes 10 seconds — 2 seconds inside the previous race best.

He would have finished a few seconds quicker, but was waving to the crowd on the half-lap inside the MCG to the finish.

Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 while fellow Australian Reece Edwards came third in 2:15:57.

In the women's race, New Zealand's Camille French was first to the tape in 2:28:25. Australia's Sinead Diver was 23 seconds back in second place, with Irish runner Nichola Sheridan a further 24 seconds back in third.

The 42km journey took participants down St Kilda Road, past Flinders Street Station, around Albert Park Lake, before a finish inside the MCG.

Kipchoge, 41, last won a marathon in 2023. He looked at the finish like it had been an easy training run, spending several minutes with fans alongside the MCG boundary line.

Kipchoge said it was a great feeling to finish at the famous stadium that also hosted the start and finish of the marathon at the 1956 Olympics — 70 years ago.

"So I come here to celebrate the 70 years and tell the people of Melbourne, 'Let us run together here at the MCG' so it was a beautiful time for me, happy to enter this stadium," Kipchoge said after the race.

This is only his second visit to Australia and his Melbourne Marathon debut.

It is part of Kipchoge's world tour, featuring a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Rubio cites ‘necessity’ of U.S. sanctions on ICC in call with Japanese counterpart
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jesse Johnson
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio “raised the necessity of U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court” during a telephone call with his Japanese counterpart over the weekend — further highlighting the allies’ conflicting views.

Rubio told Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi that U.S. sanctions on the ICC were needed “as a result of the Court’s rogue actions that threaten American sovereignty,” according to a State Department readout of their meeting.

A Japanese readout released late Saturday by the Foreign Ministry said Motegi had “conveyed the Japanese government’s position on the recent U.S. institutional sanctions,” with the two top diplomats agreeing “to maintain close communication.”

Before his talks with Rubio, Motegi also spoke over the phone with ICC President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, with the two exchanging views “on the current situation surrounding the ICC,” according to the Foreign Ministry.

Both calls lasted about 15 minutes.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday ordered the Treasury Department to add the entire court to its Specially Designated Nationals list, a move that would impose financial punishment on any entity that does business with the ICC.

The announcement was a step beyond his administration’s targeted sanctions against top court officials, including Akane.

The Trump administration in August imposed sanctions on Akane and a senior ICC trial lawyer as part of a campaign to “systematically disable” the Hague-based tribunal. The measures freeze assets under U.S. jurisdiction and largely bar U.S. individuals and companies from transactions with them.

Because most internationally active banks have ties to the U.S. financial system, the sanctions effectively shut targeted individuals and organizations out of the global financial system.

On Saturday, the court’s Assembly of States Parties, its management oversight and legislative body, called for “the immediate revocation” of the sanctions, urging “the international community to stand firm in defence of the Court in the face of these unprecedented measures, and to demonstrate their collective resolve to safeguard the integrity of the international rule of law.”

The sanctions push has put Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a tough spot as she looks to balance Japan’s key security alliance with Tokyo’s support for multilateral organizations.

Takaichi said immediately after the announcement of the measures late Friday that Japan was “deeply concerned” over the move to sanction the entire ICC. In a social media post, she called the U.S. decision “incompatible with” Japan’s position.

“Japan has consistently attached great importance to upholding the rule of law in the international community and supports the International Criminal Court,” Takaichi wrote on X, adding that she has stated this position in her speech at the U.N. General Assembly and in a policy address before parliament.

“We will continue to reach out to the United States and extend necessary support to the ICC so that the Court can fulfill its role and functions as originally envisaged,” she said.

Japan is the largest financial contributor to the ICC. The U.S. is not a state party to the Rome Statute, which founded the ICC in 2002.

The Trump administration has unleashed a campaign to dismantle the ICC — though it has put in place a six-month grace period before the latest measures are implemented.

The period is “intended to provide time for States Parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental U.S. concerns regarding the ICC,” according to the State Department.

“We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court,” Rubio said Friday.

“If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”

The Trump administration’s embrace of legal liability to enforce artificial intelligence safety sets the stage for future conflicts over who foots the bill when AI models go rogue: the companies that design the systems or the people that deploy the technology.

Holding AI developers financially responsible for the safety of their products has won support from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former White House AI czar David Sacks, who argue that existing liability laws would be more effective than new rules. President Donald Trump, in spurning new AI safeguards, has taken it a step further, saying the Justice Department should intervene if models get out of hand.

https://www.dw.com/en/shooter-kills-8-pe.title: Shooter kills 8 people and himself in Pennsylvania — police
https://www.dw.com/en/shooter-kills-8-pe.text:
The 45-year-old shooter, who is yet to be identified, carried out the killings at his home in Erie. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro offered support as the lakeside city grieves.

A man killed eight people and himself during a mass shooting at a house in Erie, Pennsylvania, local police said Saturday.

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said seven of the eight victims were related to the shooter, with the eighth person being a family friend. The shooter had died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound before authorities arrived at the scene.

Among the victims was a 1-year-old girl and 5-year-old boy, with a pregnant woman also dead in the shooting.

"Some scenes stay with you long after you leave them. This is one of those tragic scenes," Lorah said, describing an "eerie silence" when police arrived at the home.

The identity of the 45-year-old shooter has not yet been revealed by authorities. The motive for the massacre is also still unclear, with police pursuing an investigation.

At a press conference, Erie Mayor Daria Devlin addressed the families of the victims.

"I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier," she said. "But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we're grieving with you. And we are here to support you."

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro spoke with Devlin by phone and offered his support to Erie.

"I've spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my administration's full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians," Shapiro said in a statement post on X.

Shapiro said his "heart breaks for this family" and added that he and his wife Lori Shapiro "are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community."

Shapiro, a Democrat, has pushed for gun control bills in his state and signed an executive order in 2024 to reestablish the Pennsylvania Office of Gun Violence Prevention.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh International Airport this week.

The victims on Saturday included four Saudis, two people from ⁠Bangladesh and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The attack was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

It came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

Here’s a round of the global reaction:

US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, soon. He also said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.

“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.

“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.

Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.

“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.

The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.

It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the Kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.

Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.title: Commemoration marks 25 years since Australia joined Afghanistan conflict
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.author: Penny Travers and Niki Burnside
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/a.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Unrest, Conflict and War

Opposition leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese lay wreaths at the Stone of Remembrance.  (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The ceremony to mark 25 years of Australia's service in Afghanistan was attended by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Governor-General Sam Mostyn and former prime minister John Howard, among others.

Janny Poate, whose son Robert was killed in the war, spoke about her grief and the struggle of families back home.

A wreath-laying ceremony was followed by the Ode of Remembrance, Last Post, a minute's silence and the flyover of a Chinook helicopter.

Thousands of Australians who served in Afghanistan have been commemorated during a 25th anniversary service at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra.

Among those in attendance were Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Afghanistan veteran Ben Roberts-Smith, who is facing five counts of war crime murder, but was granted permission by the court to travel to Canberra for the ceremony.

Australian forces were deployed to Afghanistan in 2001 under Operation Slipper, as part of a multinational mission to combat terrorism following the September 11 attacks in the United States.

Over the next two decades, more than 35,000 Australians served in Afghanistan or in support roles in the Middle East.

Forty-seven Australian Defence Force (ADF) personnel died and 263 were wounded as a result of their service in the country.

Private Robert Poate was killed by a rogue Afghan army officer in 2012. (ABC: ADF)

Private Robert Poate was one of those soldiers killed during the conflict, and his mother, Janny Poate, spoke at today's service of the families that "formed part of the story".

"Families hoped every day that their partner, parent, child or sibling would return safely," she said.

"We remember those families and loved ones who experienced the overwhelming loss of a family member who never came home and those who have suffered loss since.

Janny Poate, whose son Robert was killed in Afghanistan, spoke of her grief during the service. (ABC News)

Today's pre-service included video recordings of past and present ADF members sharing their experiences of serving in Afghanistan, which became Australia's longest war.

"Every person who served there experienced a different Afghanistan," Australian War Memorial director Matt Anderson said.

"Some of you saw the very worst of war, others saw friendship, humanity, humour and moments of extraordinary courage and kindness.

"And some carried experiences home that they would find difficult to put into words."

Those in attendance included Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his predecessors Scott Morrison, Tony Abbot and John Howard. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

He said it was worth reflecting on the words of Chaplain Rob Sutherland, who once said that "perhaps we will measure success in Afghanistan differently".

"Whatever conclusions are ultimately drawn by history about the campaign itself, there's one part of the Afghanistan story that to me is already clear: the great success of Afghanistan is the men and women who served there," he said.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn began her address by paying her condolences to the family of Corporal Brendan Hannam, who was killed last week during a training exercise in the Northern Territory.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn speaking at the ceremony in Canberra. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

"Corporal Hannam served in Afghanistan, and his loss is felt well beyond Australia, well beyond these shores," she said.

"I'm grateful to the Chief of the Defence Force who shared with me a message of condolence sent to him from the chairman of the NATO Military Committee, who wrote the following:

"Training to keep our forces ready is never without risk. Those who accept that risk every day deserve our deepest respect and gratitude."

John Howard attended the service to mark 25 years since the start of Australia's service in Afghanistan.  (AAP: Lukas Coch)

Also in attendance at today's service were former prime ministers Tony Abbott, Scott Morrison, and John Howard — who was in office when the decision to send Australian troops to Afghanistan was made.

During his address, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese quoted Mr Howard in explaining Australia's motivation to join the conflict.

Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith was also among the attendees, having been granted a granted a variation to his bail conditions by the New South Wales Local Court.

Ben Roberts-Smith attended the Afghanistan commemoration service at the Australian War Memorial. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The former Special Air Service Regiment (SASR) soldier is facing five counts of war crime murder, which relate to his deployments in Afghanistan.

He has categorically rejected the allegations and said he planned to fight to clear his name in court.

A wreath-laying ceremony was followed by the Ode of Remembrance, Last Post, and a minute's silence.

The service concluded with a flyover of a Chinook helicopter.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/j.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Media Industry

Donald Trump frequently clashes with reporters during encounters with the press. (Reuters: Al Drago)

The US Justice Department is investigating whether five news networks violated federal antitrust laws.

The department launched the investigation in response to all five major US television networks suspending White House coverage in solidarity with reporters who had their credentials pulled.

The department said ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News were under investigation.

US television networks are under investigation for potentially violating federal antitrust laws over decisions to boycott covering the White House following its decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organisations.

The US Justice Department said the networks under investigation include ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

"Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," a Justice Department spokesperson said.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."

Donald Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news". (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations.

Cable networks CNN and MS NOW and newsletter publisher Politico have been banned from the White House, effective immediately, with more to follow, US President Donald Trump says.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and frequently clashed with reporters.

The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.

The networks did not immediately respond to requests from Reuters for comment.

The New York Times was first to report about the probe.

The investigation comes after weeks of tension between the White House and the press.

On September 19, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from entering the building, revoking their credentials.

The White House said covering the president was a "privilege — not a right".

The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.

CNN is one of the five news organisations — along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC — that make up the primary White House television pool.

A federal judge has ordered US President Donald Trump to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

All of the five television networks that cover the White House suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.

The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" their access.

However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued afterward.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: 26% in Japan see U.S. as biggest threat to world peace: survey
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
A media association survey has found that the proportion of people in Japan who think the United States is the biggest threat to world peace came to 26.8%, the second highest after China, cited by 32.5%.

The rate for the United States rose 9.3 percentage points from the previous fiscal 2025 survey. The figure stood at 6.6% in fiscal 2024.

In the Japan Press Research Institute’s latest fiscal 2026 survey, released Saturday, participants were asked to pick one of the eight choices, including Russia and North Korea, as the country that they think poses the greatest threat to world peace.

China was up from second place, with its share rising 8.2 points.

Selected by 18.3%, Russia fell to third after ranking top in preceding surveys.

North Korea remained fourth, with 9.1%, while Iran, which has been in a military conflict with the United States, was chosen by 1.9%.

An official of the institute said that “the recognition that the United States poses a threat to the world is gradually expanding” due to the unpredictability of actions by U.S. President Donald Trump.

In the survey, a total of 82.5% of respondents said that Trump is having a negative impact on the world, including those who somewhat think so, up 3.1 points. The share of respondents who think Trump is having a good impact came to 13.2%.

The survey also showed that 76.7% have a sense of crisis very much or somewhat about a potential Taiwan contingency.

The survey was conducted between July 17 and Aug. 16, covering 5,000 people age 18 or over across Japan. Valid responses were received from 2,676.

China is second highest after China, cited by 32.5% of respondents. The rate for the United State rose 9.3 percentage points from the previous fiscal 2025 survey.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Trust in science falls as COVID-era confidence fades, global survey finds
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: Jason Gale
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
The COVID-era surge in public trust in science has largely faded, with the steepest drop among people struggling financially, according to one of the largest global surveys of attitudes toward science.

Across countries surveyed before, during and after the pandemic, 72% of people expressed at least some trust in science in 2025, down from 80% in 2020 and 77% in 2018. Strong trust in scientists also dropped below its pre-pandemic level, according to the Wellcome Global Monitor, which surveyed more than 140,000 adults worldwide.

The retreat has potentially far-reaching consequences for public health as vaccination rates decline and preventable diseases resurge. The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in three decades, with almost 3,900 cases this year, while childhood vaccination rates have fallen below levels needed to prevent outbreaks in many communities.

The findings come as misinformation and conspiracy theories complicate responses to health threats, and scientific institutions in some countries face growing political and funding pressures.

The survey doesn’t establish what caused the decline, though the politicization of science during the pandemic probably contributed, said John-Arne Rottingen, chief executive officer of Wellcome, a London-based health research foundation. Vaccines, masks and public-health measures became politically contested, he said.

“Politics has made some of science more political and that has led to the polarization and maybe a lack of trust,” Rottingen said in an interview from Berlin.

The decline was particularly pronounced among people experiencing financial hardship. In 2025, 39% of those who said they were living comfortably reported a lot of trust in science, compared with 20% among those who find it difficult to get by.

That divide has widened since the pandemic. Strong trust fell 16 percentage points among those struggling financially between 2020 and 2025, compared with 10 points among those living comfortably. Countries with greater economic inequality also tended to have lower trust in science, as did places where people had less confidence in public institutions or perceived greater corruption.

People struggling financially may see science as part of a broader system that isn’t working for them, Rottingen said. “Science is seen as one of those institutions that are not delivering,” he said.

Scientists also need to do a better job of reaching such communities, he said. “We haven’t been good enough at explaining and engaging with those groups and those communities on how science is benefiting them.”

Experiences with healthcare were also closely associated with trust. While 26% globally said they had a lot of trust in science, that rose to 43% among people with a lot of confidence in their country’s hospitals and health clinics.

The survey, produced by Wellcome with Gallup and Ipsos, points to a connection between trust and vaccinations. When respondents were asked what they do when a doctor or nurse recommends a vaccine, 34% said they wanted it immediately, 48% preferred to think about it and 15% said they didn’t get vaccines at all.

Those who wanted a recommended vaccine immediately were twice as likely to express a lot of trust in science as those who didn’t vaccinate — 36% versus 18% — though Wellcome cautioned that other factors also shape vaccine decisions.

Falling vaccination coverage shows how mistrust can have consequences beyond the individual because vaccines also protect people in the wider community who can’t be vaccinated or don’t mount a strong immune response, Rottingen said.

“I am worried” about rising measles cases in the U.S. and Europe, he said. Public willingness to use new vaccines and other technologies will also be crucial in future health emergencies, he said. “The power of science can only be fully realized if people trust the science and trust the technologies coming from science.”

Politics also appears to shape Americans’ views of science. The share saying science benefits most people rose to 57% in 2025 from 48% in 2018, bucking a global decline.

Yet views were sharply divided along political lines. Among Americans who disapproved of their country’s leader, 74% said science benefited people like them “a lot,” compared with 44% among those who approved. The survey was conducted after Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election but while Joe Biden was still president.

Scientists nevertheless remain more trusted than governments and journalists, according to the survey. The proportion expressing a lot of trust in scientists rose to 43% during the pandemic from 34% in 2018, before falling to 32% in 2025.

The decline needs to be kept in perspective, Rottingen said. About seven in 10 people globally still trust science.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author

OSAKA – Two people were killed while participating in traditional local festivals featuring danjiri floats in two cities in Osaka Prefecture on Saturday.

The victims, both men, were crushed under floats that overturned when traveling on the road, according to the Osaka Prefectural Police department.

Both are believed to have lost their balance during a yarimawashi performance — a highlight of the festival in which a float pulled by a team of participants turns a corner at a high speed. The two men were standing on the side of the floats to prevent them from overturning.

The danjiri is about 4 meters tall and weighs roughly 4 tons. The police department is investigating the accidents.

In the city of Izumisano, a danjiri toppled over when it was turning right at an intersection around 10:55 a.m., leading to the death of a 51-year-old company executive from the city. Seven other male participants were injured, some seriously.

In Izumiotsu, a danjiri overturned after turning right at an intersection around 1:20 p.m., killing a 48-year-old corporate worker from the neighboring city of Izumi. Nine male participants suffered non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

No spectators were hurt in the two incidents, police said.

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/soci.text:
Firm awarded new contract to supply services at six pools despite failing to provide required staffing on seven occasions previously

A controversial decision by Hong Kong authorities to award a HK$122 million (US$15.6 million) lifeguard and first aid services contract to a company previously found to have failed to provide the required staffing at swimming pools has sparked concerns over whether public funds are being used prudently.

The department outsourced services at six public swimming pools in September 2024 in a trial scheme to tackle long-standing lifeguard shortages, awarding two contracts worth a total of HK$75.9 million to Spotlight Enterprises for two years of services.

The pools were Island East, Tai Kok Tsui, Lam Tin, Tung Cheong Street, Tsing Yi Southwest and Ping Shan Tin Shui Wai.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/w.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Colin Hanssen, who lives with cerebral palsy, has burgeoned into a prolific artist in the last six months. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

A West Australian artist who lives with cerebral palsy has caught the attention of art curators across the state.

Colin Hanssen combines painting with performance to express his lived experience.

The 31-year-old is preparing his first collection to be featured in Perth galleries.

On a quiet country road on Western Australia's south coast, Colin Hanssen is wrapping up his first exhibition.

Despite being a newcomer to the world of painting, there's been plenty to see on the walls, and floor, of the artist's rural Albany studio.

For Hanssen, who was born with cerebral palsy and is largely non-verbal, art has become a vital form of self expression.

The 31-year-old uses his wheelchair and right hand to blend colourful and earthy tones, combining performance with paint to create his abstract pieces.

Colin Hanssen's work is displayed in his Redmond studio, on the outskirts of Albany.  (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

His mother Wendy Hanssen said the unique skill was realised just six months ago in an art therapy class.

"That was when it was brought home that actually this could be an outlet for Colin," she said.

Wendy Hanssen says painting is an outlet for her son, who is largely non-verbal.  (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

His recent selection for this year's Southern Art and Craft Trail, an event which highlights talent across the region, shows just how much he has exceeded expectations, according to Ms Hanssen.

"We went and saw a neurosurgeon who told us to love Colin while we've got him, because he wasn't going to make it to his first birthday," she said.

"Colin's first birthday came and went, and we knew that we were clearly on the right track.

Colin Hanssen's paintings blend vibrant and earthy tones. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Art therapist Serena McLaughlan has worked with Hanssen since he first started painting, and helped to curate the exhibition's collection.

"They [visitors] come in and they're just drawn to the work," she said.

"They're really interested in the story and fascinated by the process."

Serena McLaughlan is an art therapist based in the Great Southern. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

She said much of Hanssen's work draws from his time living in Africa.

"Engaging with vast expanses of landscape is a lived experience that comes through in the painting," she said.

"It's the power of art to talk of his lived experience and his stories over words.

Serena McLaughlan says many of Colin's paintings draw on his lived experiences. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

With the Art Trail completed, the team now have their sights set on the city.

"We've had two people, two artists from different galleries in Perth, asking if Colin will exhibit with them," Ms Hanssen said.

"We're going to look at getting a series done."

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/n.title: Gravel cycling championship brings global audience to tiny town
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/n.author: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet and Georgia Loney
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/n.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The race stretches across more than 100 kilometres in South West WA. (Supplied: SWPIx)

Thousands of cyclists and spectators have flooded into Nannup, in southern Western Australia, for the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships.

Just under 1,000 cyclists took to the track over the weekend through the Blackwood Valley around Nannup.

Local leaders say it has brought the town and its picturesque surrounds to a potential global audience of 130 million people.

A tiny town in southern Western Australia has become the first location outside Europe to hold an elite gravel cycling world championship.

Nannup, about 268 kilometres south of Perth, hosted thousands of cyclists and spectators this weekend for the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships.

It was a major coup for the historic timber town, which is building its reputation as a mountain biking destination.

Crowds line the streets of Nannup for the Gravel World Championships. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

With the event expected to draw a global audience of up to 130 million people, Shire of Nannup Deputy President Vicki Hansen said securing it had taken years of work.

"Now, Nannup, Western Australia is across the world."

Vicki Hansen says it took years of work to secure the event. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

The hills and forests surrounding the town have proven the ideal terrain for mountain biking, with Ms Hansen hopeful the event would showcase the local trails.

The event attracted almost 1,000 competitors from all over the world. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We want all these international riders, who didn't qualify, but have seen the event, to come on over," Ms Hansen said.

Competitors raced over two days, traversing courses of up to 144km through the Blackwood Valley.

Close to 1,000 cyclists are racing through the Blackwood Valley. (Supplied: SWPix)

"Nannup itself is only 70 metres above sea level but within a kilometre or less than that it suddenly increases to 300 metres above sea level," Shire President Tony Dean said.

"In that elevation … we've got the gravel itself."

Dutch cyclist Marianne Vos is the first person to win the gravel world championships twice. (Supplied: SWPix)

Dutch cyclist Marianne Vos took out the elite women's title in 4 hours and 30 minutes, followed by Germany's Rose Kloser and the Netherlands' Larisa Hartog.

It was the second championship victory for the two-time Olympic medallist.

This year will be the fifth UCI Gravel World Championships event held, with previous events taking place in Italy and Belgium.

Wendy Oosterwoud, who travelled almost 30 hours from the Netherlands to compete in Nannup, said it was her first time outside of Europe.

"I think the flight was 21 hours, the drive to Amsterdam was almost two hours, [and] from Perth to Nannup was almost three," she said.

"I'm really happy to see this part of the world."

Wendy Oosterwoud says travelling to the Nannup gravel races was her first time outside Europe. (Supplied: Wendy Oosterwoud)

The Dutch cyclist has claimed seven podium titles, including winning the women's elite at a gravel world series in Poland this year.

She said the Nannup course was broader than those overseas.

"Here in Nannup, it's wide gravel roads," she said.

"But in the Netherlands … you have, I think, 200 corners, left right, left right."

Nils Lageman says the race is the most significant of its kind in the world. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

German cyclist Nils Lageman made the journey from his home near Cologne to compete in the 35-39 age group.

"The world championships were calling, and I just had to respond, wherever it is," he said.

"It looks great because of the nature."

US cyclists Tim Borsetti, Mark Litrell and John Steward had never heard of Nannup until the the event (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Many international cyclists said they had never heard of Nannup, until the event, including US cyclist Tim Borsetti.

"I targeted this because I knew it would be an awesome event, because you guys have big wide roads like we do in the States," he said.

With a regular population of about 1,000 people, accommodation in Nannup has been fully booked for the event.

Mr Dean said a tent city, and visitors staying in other nearby towns, had helped share the load.

Nannup welcomed the visiting cyclists and spectators with open arms. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We're spreading the love between Nannup and the rest of the South West," he said.

"With that many visitors, they're going to have to commute, unfortunately."

It has proven a win for some local businesses, with cafe owner Hayley Rubery registering one of the busiest days she could remember.

Tents and accommodation in surrounding communities helped Nannup handle the bumper crowds. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We had a 700 per cent increase in revenue to a normal Friday. It's insane," she said.

"We sold five days' worth of milk in one day, and we've never made more toasties in our entire lives."

Hayley Rubery says the event brought a 700 per cent jump in business. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

With the town's previous events leaning towards smaller-scale arts and culture festivals, Ms Rubery said they had been unsure what to expect.

"We prepped anyway and thank God we did."

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: Tomoka Nishiyama earns right to become shogi’s first female kishi player
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
KANAZAWA, ISHIKAWA PREF. – In what could amount to breaking shogi’s glass ceiling, female professional Tomoka Nishiyama obtained the right to become a kishi and compete in the open category of professional shogi, on Saturday when she won the Hakurei title for the fifth time.

Nishiyama, 31, who holds four titles in the joryu kishi system for women, would become the first female kishi if she exercises her right.

Kishi and joryu kishi operate under different professional systems. While joryu kishi is a status for only women, both men and women can become kishi.

In June 2025, the Japan Shogi Association introduced a new system under which a woman who wins the elite Hakurei title five times is given the right to become a kishi of a fourth dan rank or higher.

In the fifth match of the best-of-seven Hakurei title series on Saturday, Nishiyama beat challenger Kana Fukuma, 34, who also holds four joryu kishi titles, in 118 moves, winning the series with a 4-1 record.

After the match, held in Kanazawa, Ishikawa Prefecture, Nishiyama said, “I can’t give an answer right now,” when asked if she will exercise her right to become a kishi. She is slated to announce her decision within two weeks.

At a news conference later, Nishiyama said that gaining the right, a development that has the potential to revive women’s shogi, gave her “a renewed sense of resolve.”

“This isn’t an issue only for me, so I’d like to consider it calmly,” she added, indicating that she would decide whether to exercise the right after consulting people around her.

Before the introduction of the new system, there were already two other ways for a joryu kishi to become a kishi. One is to perform well in a competition series among third-dan players at Shoreikai, a professional shogi training institution, and the other is to pass a transfer exam.

After joining Shoreikai in 2010 at the age of 14, Nishiyama narrowly missed a chance to become a kishi. She left Shoreikai in 2021 at age 25.

Nishiyama also failed in a transfer exam, held between September 2024 and January 2025, recording two wins and three losses against five fourth-dan players.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Tomoka Nishiyama won the Hakurei title for the fifth time on Saturday. Nishiyamas would become the first female kishi if she exercises her right to become a kishi. Nishyama holds four titles in the joryu kishi system for women.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: The Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Investigation launched after five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after CNN, MS Now and Politico were barred from White House

The US Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of the US president, Donald Trump, last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.

A spokesperson for the department said group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” they said.

The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.

Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC.

The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports – a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.

Last month’s developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.

On 19 September, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico and MS Now from entering the building, ​revoking their credentials. The White House said covering the president was a “privilege – not a right”.

CNN, MS Now and Politico sued over the days-long ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organisations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.

Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed. They broadcasters in the pool share the costs of covering the president, take ​turns organizing coverage and share ​the footage with outlets around the country.

Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration’s decision to investigate.

“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Williams fans 12 as Cleveland win decisive Game 5

Ramírez’s two-run homer provides only scoring

Guardians to face Rays for place in World Series

Gavin Williams struck out 12, José Ramírez homered on a pitch just above home plate and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 2-0 on Saturday night to complete a comeback from a 2-0 deficit in their best-of-five American League Division Series.

Cleveland open the American League Championship Series at Tampa Bay on Monday night, seeking their first World Series appearance since 2016. The Guardians/Indians franchise have not won the title since 1948, the longest drought among MLB teams.

It'll take just a moment

Not signed in before? Create a free account

Guardians pitchers struck out 21, the most in a nine-inning postseason game. The White Sox managed just three hits, putting only nine balls in play, and struck out 75 times over the series.

Two days after getting the save in Game 4, Williams became just the third pitcher in postseason history to get the last out of a game and start the following game when his team faced elimination in both.

He did not allow a hit until Kyle Teel looped a knuckle-curve into right field with two outs in the sixth, two innings after Ramírez homered for the second straight game, a two-run drive off Sean Burke.

After a walk loaded the bases, Erik Sabrowski relieved Williams and struck out Munetaka Murakami.

Williams’s 12 strikeouts tied Cleveland’s record for a postseason game. He got 22 swings and misses, and his 24 strikeouts over three games tied for the second most in a best-of-five postseason series.

Hunter Gaddis followed Sabrowski and got four outs. Cade Smith finished for his first career five-out save, striking out the side in the ninth. He blew a fastball by Tristan Peters for the final out, setting off a celebration at Progressive Field.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/l.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

The man was allegedly stabbed in the chest at a Brisbane house about 4am on Saturday.  (Supplied)

A Logan man has been charged with the stabbing murder of a 32-year-old who died in hospital overnight.

The Brisbane man was wounded in the chest early Saturday morning at a house on Barcelona Street at Wishart.

He was taken to Princess Alexandra Hospital where he died from his injuries.

His alleged attacker, also 32, faces one charge of murder, and is also charged with contravening an order about information necessary to access information stored electronically.

Forensic officers at the house where the 32-year-old Wishart man was allegedly stabbed.  (Supplied)

Police said the two men knew each other.

Forensic officers were still at the two-storey house on Sunday, where they could be seen dusting for prints.

The accused is due to face Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday.

He was initially charged with grievous bodily harm but the charge was upgraded to murder after his alleged victim's death.

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/p.title: Palestinian supporters mark Global Day for Gaza
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/p.author: Monty Jacka and Keely Johnson
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/p.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic:
Demonstrations

Hundreds of people turned out for the rally in Hobart. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

Pro-Palestinian supporters are gathering across Australia as part of the Global Day for Gaza.

Protesters carrying Palestinian flags and wearing keffiyehs are calling for an end to Australia's arms trade with Israel.

They are also calling for "true peace in Gaza" and the West Bank.

Pro-Palestinian rallies are taking place across the country to mark the lives lost in the three years of Israel's retaliatory campaign in Gaza following the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack.

As part of the Global Day for Gaza, protesters are gathering in capital cities and various regional locations.

In Hobart, hundreds of people marched along the waterfront, with many waving Palestinian flags, holding placards and chanting "the West Bank will be free".

People in Hobart began gathering about 11am. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

The group began congregating from about 11am and later made their way to the Tasmanian Parliament where they heard from speakers including the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre's Nala Mansell, and Feras Shaheen, from the Tasmanian Palestine Advocacy Network.

Mr Shaheen urged protesters to ramp up their advocacy, saying new measures were needed to end the war in Gaza.

About 100 people attended an event at Newcastle's Civic Park in NSW. (ABC News: Keely Johnson)

According to the Gaza health ministry, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and more than 175,000 injured.

The UN estimates 1.9 million people have been displaced.

Hunter Valley woman Lynn Benn, from environmental group the Knitting Nannas, was among the protesters at Newcastle's Civic Park.

Ms Benn says she wants to see “true peace” in Gaza and the West Bank. (ABC News)

She told the ABC that many had turned out because they were angry about the ongoing situation in Gaza.

"Food supplies are restricted, critical medical supplies are restricted, and there are thousands and thousands of children in there," she said.

Ms Benn said she wanted to see “true peace” in Gaza and the West Bank.

Dr Leka is calling on the Australian government to pay heed to the requirements of international law. (ABC News)

Niko Leka, from Palestine Action Group Muloobinba, said while today was a globally significant day, he and many other Novocastrians have been turning up to protest the war for years.

“Showing up here is another intervention, a peaceful intervention,” Dr Leka said.

“The action that is required is for the Australian government to pay heed to the requirements of international law.

"No more arms trade with Israel, no more investment, stopping our relationships with their universities until they start obeying international law.”

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: Eliud Kipchoge wins first marathon since 2023
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
MELBOURNE – Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge won his first marathon in three years on Sunday when the Kenyan great cruised to victory in Melbourne.

The most-decorated marathoner in history crossed the finish line in 2 hours, 9 minutes, 10 seconds, two seconds inside the race record.

It was his first victory over the distance since Berlin in 2023 and part of his “World Tour” to raise funds for causes he believes in.

The 41-year-old former world record-holder announced in 2025 he planned complete marathons on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.

Melbourne was the third stop after South Africa and Brazil.

He broke away inside the last 10 kilometers on a course raced partly on the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and which finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground.

“On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering and shouting my name,” Kipchoge said, looking fresh at the finish.

He would have gone faster, but slowed down inside the MCG while waving to fans.

“It was actually different — running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground,” he added.

“It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne.”

Australian Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 while New Zealand’s Camille French came first in the women’s race in 2:28:25.

https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.title: Chinese retiree devotes life to photography after tumour shrinks post-bucket-list trip
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.author: Alice Yan
https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture.text:
Driven by a new-found motivation to live, Wang has spent her pension on advanced gear, travelled to 30 countries to pursue bird photography

After spending all her savings on a month-long trip to Antarctica following a cancer diagnosis, a woman from southwestern China discovered that her tumour had shrunk.

Wang Ying, 67, is an amateur wildlife photographer who has photographed more than 1,200 bird species.

In 2013, as she was preparing to retire from her job as an administrator at a school in Kunming, the capital of southwestern China’s Yunnan province, Wang was diagnosed with a form of thyroid cancer. Doctors urged her to undergo surgery immediately, the Shanghai Morning Post reported.

The diagnosis was a crushing blow. “If I were to die, I wished to die somewhere far away. I absolutely did not want to have surgery,” she recalled.

Wang then decided to travel to Antarctica to photograph penguins. She had been an enthusiastic bird photographer for decades.

Her savings were not enough to cover the month-long trip, which cost 150,000 yuan (US$22,000), so Wang’s mother helped pay the difference.

In Antarctica, Wang most wanted to photograph a mother penguin feeding her chick, she said.

While other tourists left the icy land, Wang stayed outside for a long time despite the harsh conditions: temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius, gale-force winds and heavy snowfall.

At last, she captured the moment a mother penguin returned from fishing and fed her chick.

“I took pictures of this precious moment. I was so happy! Seeing them walk together and look for their home, I felt very touched,” Wang was quoted as saying.

After returning from Antarctica, Wang went to hospital for a check-up. To her surprise, she found that the tumour had shrunk since her previous examination a month earlier. Doctors told her that she did not need surgery for the time being, but should continue to monitor her condition closely.

Wang said the experience had rekindled her hope and given her great motivation to live.

Since then, she has devoted her time and money to bird photography. She has visited more than 30 countries, spending her entire pension on advanced photography equipment.

Wang plans to visit the US, Peru and several African countries this year and next.

“After travelling to many places and seeing a variety of things, I have come to terms with changes in life. I won’t make a fuss about some issues now,” Wang said.

Wang’s story has attracted widespread interest on Chinese social media.

“This case again shows that physical health is related to mood. A good mood and a good rest can improve immunity, leading to the destruction of tumour cells,” one internet user commented.

Another person noted: “Thyroid cancer is not very aggressive and has a high survival rate. But after all, it is good to see her get better in such a short time.”

She has spent her pension on advanced gear, travelled to 30 countries to pursue bird photography. Wang's mother helped pay the difference to pay for the month-long trip to Antarctica.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘My body is still peaking’: Eliud Kipchoge wins first marathon in three years
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Australian Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Kenyan breaks Melbourne Marathon record by two seconds

‘I’m happy to run with the gen Zs,’ 41-year-old says

Marathon’s greatest competitor, Eliud Kipchoge, has sent a message to the next generation declaring that he’s not done yet.

The 41-year-old Kenyan revelled in his Melbourne Marathon debut on Sunday, breaking the race record and delighting thousands of fans at the MCG finish.

Beating the old race mark by two seconds, his two hours nine minutes and 10 seconds over a new course gave Kipchoge his first marathon win in three years.

Jimmy Whelan, a former Australian professional cyclist, was with the two-time Olympic champion and former world record-holder until about 30km. Then Kipchoge went up a gear and dominated to the finish.

Looking as though he has just done a training run, Kipchoge then spent well over half an hour celebrating with fans along the MCG boundary fence.

He was mobbed by media at the finish and took the chaos in his stride.

“The crowd is so wonderful – I’ve never seen a crowd like this,” he said. “Melbourne is really, really a sporting city.

“I believe that my body is still peaking – still able to compete with the next generation. The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the gen Zs.”

“I [increased] the pace after 30km, to see whether I can run well and beat the [race record]. My plan went well.”

Kipchoge had said repeatedly over the last few days that his Melbourne visit was more than just another race. It is the third leg in his world tour, where he will run a marathon on each continent, including Antarctica.

He has also done some community work while in Melbourne and is acutely aware of the city’s rich sporting heritage.

“The experience is awesome – the culture of Melbourne is wonderful,” he said.

“The last four days, I’ve seen myself, sport can do wonder. It was four-in-one – with the tennis, finishing at the cricket, the Olympics were here in 1956, running on the Formula One track.

“I will come back to Melbourne to watch the tennis, the Formula One next year, to see people of Melbourne playing cricket. This is the best track ever.”

Kipchoge could have finished a few seconds quicker but was waving to the crowd on the half-lap inside the MCG to the finish.

This is his second visit to Australia. The Kenyan finished ninth in the 2025 Sydney Marathon.

Australia’s Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 and Whelan was fifth. New Zealand’s Camille French won the women’s race in 2:28:25, with Australia’s Sinead Diver next in 2:28.49.

The Australian Seth O’Donnell and the New Zealander Georgie Gregec won the half-marathon titles.

Earlier on Sunday, a woman was taken to hospital after she was struck by a car near Flinders Street station, about 200 metres from the marathon route.

Reports suggest police officers in the vicinity drew their weapons after the car, which was seen driving erratically, hit the woman about 10.45am, before performing a U-turn and driving away.

The woman was taken to Royal Melbourne hospital and her condition is not known.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”.

Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.

It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.

Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.

It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.

It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.

“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.

The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.

Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.

The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.

The renewed siege took shape in early October.

The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.

Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.

Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.

He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.

Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).

“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.

The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.

“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.title: US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.author: Al Jazeera Staff
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text:
United States forces have disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew “ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran”, according to US Central Command (CENTCOM).

A US military fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday, “fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew”, CENTCOM said in a statement. The vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after “having previously departed an Iranian port”.

CENTCOM said its forces resumed their blockade against all ships “entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14”, disabling four commercial vessels and turning around 135 ships during “three months of strict enforcement”.

US forces also destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC’s) “multibillion-dollar shadow network” over the same period, CENTCOM said.

Meanwhile, Iran’s IRGC said it struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz for attempting to take an “illegal route”, as Tehran seeks to enforce its own blockade on the vital waterway.

In a statement carried by official Iranian media, the IRGC claimed Iranian forces “have taken control of the administration of the strait”.

“In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck,” the statement said.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Sunday that an outbound tanker in the strait was struck on the port side by an unknown projectile, causing a fire on board. The UK agency said crew members were reported safe, while the damage and environmental impact remained unknown at the time of the report.

Tehran has attempted to enforce control over the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran, insisting that ships obtain permission to cross via its preferred routes. However, vessels have increasingly risked taking an alternative route hugging the strait’s southern coast.

The UKMTO said on Thursday that a vessel sailing 94km (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, off the north coast of Qatar, was struck by multiple projectiles, resulting in a number of casualties.

The agency did not specify the origin of the ship or the number of people killed or injured, adding that authorities were investigating the incident amid a recent rise in attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.

Ships in the Gulf attempting to cross the strait, which is the sole maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region, have faced repeated attacks since the US and Israel began the war in late February.

The Strait of Hormuz remains vital to the global economy, with about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the passage before the war began.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.title: NASCAR and IndyCar look to generate Formula One-type growth overseas
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/sports/2026.text:
NASCAR and IndyCar are looking to add races outside their U.S. home bases, according to people familiar with the matter.

IndyCar has focused specifically on Barcelona, with the city not on Formula One’s 2027 calendar, according to one of the people who wasn’t authorized to speak publicly about the plans. NASCAR has been in talks with potential partners, including in Mexico and Canada, a person familiar said.

The US-based leagues have seen F1, owned by Liberty Media, expand more outside its European base in recent years, helping boost its popularity. That’s included adding races in the U.S. that have lured new fans and media attention. F1 revenue this year is projected by analysts to gain about 9% to $4.2 billion, nearly double from five years ago.

IndyCar and NASCAR are privately held entities and don’t regularly disclose results. But court filings showed Nascar’s revenue was $1.7 billion in 2024, according to BlackBook Motorsport.

“We’re talking to different potential partners globally,” said Adam Layton, senior vice president for NASCAR International. The scope of the search includes Europe and other parts of the world, he said.

IndyCar is always evaluating new opportunities, a spokesperson for the circuit said, while declining to comment on specific destinations like Barcelona.

NASCAR Chief Executive Officer Steve O’Donnell, who took on the role in April, has talked about his desire to expand beyond the U.S. In August, he told the podcast Racin’ With the Boys that “plopping a race in Europe” is the next move.

The time has come for the American-based racing competitions to ramp up internationally, according to Mark Howell, a motorsports historian and professor at Northwestern Michigan College.

“Europe would be the next big step,” Howell said.

NASCAR does have a presence in other parts of the world through competitions such as the Euro Series and Canada Series. But the NASCAR Cup Series, its flagship competition, is held in the United States.

IndyCar tried to add Mexico City to its 2026 schedule, but it didn’t materialize because of timing conflicts with the men’s soccer World Cup. Plans for an exhibition event in Argentina in 2024 were also shelved.

Mark Miles, CEO of IndyCar parent Penske Entertainment, said in a 2024 interview with BlackBook Motorsport that while he was open to the idea of expanding further internationally, the core series would remain closer to home.

“IndyCar has and will continue to be a North American series,” he said.

https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.title: Unsung turtle conservation heroes in Malaysia’s Sabah unite to fight poachers
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.author: Ushar Daniele
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.text:
A group of volunteers is helping to stem the illegal trade of protected turtles by monitoring the movements of poachers

Roziah Jelali has a tip or two on catching a turtle poacher: carrying a pair of binoculars and having patience in spades are key to doing the job well.

The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah tracking a man whom she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles. Once thriving off the azure seas of Omadal Island in the Malaysian state, many turtles had been hunted down, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts.

Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands.

“Every day after my patrol, I would sit near my house with my binoculars and watch him. He was initially operating on Bum Bum Island, then he came to Omadal,” Roziah told This Week in Asia.
https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/health-en.summary: Roziah Jelali spent three months tracking a man who she suspected of illegally capturing turtles. She would carry binoculars and write detailed notes on her target's movements at her stilted home.
