https://www.dw.com/en/us-justice-departm.title: US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott for antitrust violation
https://www.dw.com/en/us-justice-departm.text:
The Department of Justice is investigating whether the five news organizations violated antitrust laws when they suspended their coverage of Trump in protest. The networks under probe are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

The US Department of Justice announced on Saturday that it is investigating whether the White House press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month, violated the nation's anti trust law.

Group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law, spokesperson Emily Covington said.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said.

The networks under the scrutiny are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate.

"The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access," Zamora said on X. "The public's right to know depends on that access."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On September 21, a pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage after the Trump administration barred news networks CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying covering the president was a "privilege, not a right."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As a result, the five television networks suspended coverage in protest and refused to provide replacement program.

The news outlets also sued the administration, accusing it of violating free speech and free press rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and pursuing retaliation over their coverage.

On September 24, the White House reinstated their press credentials after a US district Judge ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.

The president has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and clashed with reporters during interviews.

The White House press pool is a roating group of news outlets which cover the president and accompany him on official duties.

CNN is one of the five news organizations, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBS, that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the cost of covering the president and take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

The White House press pool has now become a proxy for a fight over press freedom.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘I get really upset when I visit’: the harsh reality of life in a high-security hospital in England
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Diane Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
When the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana was transferred from a category A prison to Broadmoor hospital, many observers complained that he was getting off lightly. But these places are anything but ‘cushy’, says the mother of one patient

R
ampton high-security hospital in Nottinghamshire was built in 1912. Everything about the bleak, remote facility for mentally ill people is forbidding, says Jan Neate. “I get really upset going there,” she says. “Even though I really want to see Jake, visiting is an ordeal.”

Jake, 45, is Neate’s son. He has been held at Rampton for eight years. In 2017, many years after being diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, he killed his partner, Suzanne Brown, and was deemed mentally unfit to stand trial.

When Neate visits him, her fingerprints and biometrics are taken before she is escorted in. Jake is searched when he is brought into the room and searched again when he leaves. Mother and son are permitted a hug, which is often distressing. “Both of us usually cry when we hug,” says Neate. “It reminds me of what our lives were like before and I think it reminds Jake of that, too.”

England has three high-security hospitals – Rampton, Ashworth in Merseyside and Broadmoor in Berkshire. According to the NHS trust that manages Rampton, secure hospitals are for people with severe mental health disorders who pose grave or immediate danger to themselves or to the public. They have accommodated some of the country’s most abhorred criminals, including Peter Sutcliffe, Ronnie Kray, Ian Brady, Ian Huntley and Beverley Allitt. Valdo Calocane, who was convicted of killing three people in 2023 and diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, has spent time in Rampton.

These high-security hospitals have been in the spotlight this year, after it was reported that Axel Rudakubana – who murdered three young girls at a dance class in Southport in 2024 – had been moved from Belmarsh, a category A high-security prison, to Broadmoor, which has security equivalent to a category B prison. Officials said the move was due to the deterioration of his mental health and the fact he could no longer be safely managed in prison. The plan is to return Rudakubana to Belmarsh after treatment.

Throughout its history, Broadmoor has had a reputation for being tough, even menacing, given the notoriety of various people housed within its walls. Nonetheless, some saw this move as the start of a “cushier” life for Rudakubana and an attempt by him to manipulate the system. Mark Fairhurst, the chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said the move would afford him freedoms not available in a high-security prison.

Relatives of those incarcerated in high-security hospitals are usually unwilling to speak out because of the understandable stigma attached to the violent acts committed by those inside. But while Jake did something terrible, Neate is keen for people to understand the reality of this form of incarceration.

What happens inside high-security hospitals raises important questions about how we treat people who have committed extreme violence but who are also vulnerable themselves. These are difficult, emotive questions about mental health, retribution and rehabilitation.

Jake is sometimes placed in a form of segregation known as seclusion; Neate knows of at least two periods of seclusion so far this year. In both cases, she believes the seclusion lasted several days. She is given very little information about what happens to him during these periods, which she says is terrifying: “I dread the phone ringing one day and staff telling me that something terrible has happened to him.”

If Jake refuses his medication, his doctors have permission to administer it via injection.

He has been having seizures and injuring himself. “On one occasion, he fell and injured his shoulder when he was having a seizure,” says Neate. “On another occasion, also when he was thought to be having a seizure, he fell and injured his head.”

Jake was taken to an ordinary hospital after receiving these injuries, but Neate wasn’t given any information about where he was. Whenever she calls Rampton, to see how Jake is, she gets the briefest of replies – confirmation that he is eating, drinking and sleeping, but nothing else. “Anyone who thinks Rampton is an easy option for someone like Jake really doesn’t understand how things are,” she says.

Inspections of Rampton carried out by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) between July 2019 and June 2023 identified a number of failings, including a shortage of staff. Some therapy staff were used on wards to plug the gaps, leading to a reduction in patients’ therapeutic programmes. Concerns were also raised about overnight lock-ups in patients’ rooms being extended due to staff shortages, along with periods of “confinement” during the day. Poor medicine management was identified and there were repeated issues with the safeguarding of patients.

A focused review of Rampton by the CQC in March 2024 said staffing levels had improved and the use of confinement had decreased, but there remained a “culture of relying on therapy and education staff to cover nursing gaps”. While medicine management had also improved, staff did not always follow the correct procedure, “which could constitute an assault and trespass against the person”. The review added: “While we observed staff providing person-centred care, we remain concerned that people in long-term segregation were not always treated with dignity, compassion and respect.”

In a May 2025 CQC report, the hospital had its rating upgraded from “inadequate” to “requires improvement”. It was found that the trust still had work to do to address staff shortages and to support staff.

A
s a boy, Jake was happy and playful, says Neate: “We went on loads of outings like swimming, football and visits to museums. He was a really nice boy.” When he was 17, he started to get ill. “He became paranoid and was admitted to hospital for two weeks as a voluntary patient. The doctors said if he stopped smoking skunk, he would recover.”

He went on to study geography at the University of Birmingham, but left when he was headhunted by a bank in Canary Wharf, London. Then, at 20, he was diagnosed with schizophrenia. He had to leave his job, but he built up a window-cleaning round where he lived in Essex and he was popular with his customers. To treat his schizophrenia, he was put on the drug clozapine and he gave up recreational drugs, living successfully in the community. At that point, says Neate, Jake had an illness, but he also had a life.

In 2007, Jake and Suzanne met at a disco in Harlow. “He was 26 and she was 23,” says Neate. Suzanne, who was known as Sue, worked as a nursery nurse. “Sue had such a sweet, kind nature. Whenever she came to my house, she would always bring a homemade cake with her. She really looked after Jake, made sure he took his medication and went to all his appointments with him. She was a very giving person. I miss her.”

At this stage, “Jake had dreams and ambitions and he loved Sue to pieces”, says Neate. “His schizophrenia then was nothing like it is now. He was never violent. I don’t think he and Sue even argued with each other.” When they bought their first flat together, in Braintree, they had a new kitchen fitted and were full of plans for the future.

Jake had received excellent care and support from the NHS mental health trust in Harlow, but their move meant Jake’s care was transferred to a new trust. For 10 years, clozapine had kept him stable. But in 2017, after he started to experience physical side-effects – severe constipation, urine retention and an inability to eat or sleep – the drug was stopped suddenly.

Withdrawal from clozapine is supposed to be closely monitored, but Jake, Sue and Neate were unaware of this. “None of us had any idea what could happen as a result of him being taken off clozapine,” says Neate. “Sue and Jake really trusted their clinical team. I thought that the worst that might happen would be that Jake might have a row with Sue. I had no concept of the gravity and severity of it all. It’s a heavy-duty drug and taking him off it should have been treated as a medical emergency.”

Jake began to experience psychosis and repeatedly tried to seek help, but little was forthcoming. Jake wrote to his doctors, listing the symptoms he was experiencing after being taken off clozapine, but he didn’t receive a response. Neate says she made dozens of phone calls and sent numerous emails during this period, trying to get help for Jake, but this didn’t result in any interventions. She believes that, had there been effective responses to the pleas she, Sue and Jake were making, the horror that followed could have been avoided.

In texts to his mother in this period, Jake said he had been researching private hospitals. “I feel a bit angry that no one told me of the implications of going on to this drug,” he wrote. “I would like to be an inpatient to deal with all the issues.”

His condition worsened. On 15 December 2017, a mental health worker visited the couple’s flat and said telephone support would be put in place and a home visit organised for the following week. That evening, Neate received a call from Sue, “screaming and hysterical”. She said Jake was hurting her. Neate told her to get out of the flat and immediately called the police.

Three hours after that call, police officers arrived at the flat. By then, it was far too late. Jake had stabbed Suzanne 173 times.

Neate says she didn’t understand the severity of what was happening until the police called her and said: “‘We’ve taken the dead woman from the flat.’ All I could say was: ‘Oh my God, what do you mean?’ … I am always asking myself if I could have prevented this happening if I had been close by.”

Jake was initially charged with murder, but was found to be unfit to stand trial. He said he had been hearing voices coming out of the TV urging him to kill Sue and was having terrible thoughts about God, the devil and the battle between good and evil.

When a person is deemed mentally unfit to stand trial, a trial of the facts takes place. Rather than deciding on a defendant’s criminal guilt or innocence, this determines whether the defendant carried out the alleged acts. The trial found that Jake had killed Sue. The jury heard that Sue was devoted to Jake and that she had looked after him when he was unwell with “the patience of a saint”.

“I miss Sue so much,” says Neate. “I miss her lovely sunny nature … We used to go on outings together, to spas and to the cinema. I feel so lonely. I don’t have Jake as he was and I don’t have Sue. Jake was a perpetrator, but I believe he was also a victim of the system.”

A report on mental health services after Sue’s killing identified eight failings and made seven recommendations for change. It found that an up-to-date risk assessment was not carried out after the sudden cessation of clozapine and that there was neither appropriate professional monitoring nor guidance for Jake and his family. It also found that clinical information was not communicated consistently within and between teams.

An investigation for the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) found that the police response was delayed because it was initially miscategorised by the call handler. The IOPC did not identify any misconduct, but found that two members of staff in the control room “had not met expected standards”.

When Jake was sent to Rampton, it was supposed to be temporary. Neate was told that when he was more stable he could be moved to a medium-security unit with a less restrictive regime. Jake is held at Rampton on what is known as a section 37 order; the Home Office has to give permission for the release of those held under this type of indefinite hospital order.

In a letter to Neate on 28 July 2026, Jake’s doctor at Rampton wrote: “In recent years we have seen several episodes of decline in his condition, but overall he is making progress.” He also described Jake as having a serious mental health disorder that is “very resistant to treatment”.

A spokesperson for Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS foundation trust said: “While we cannot comment on the care of individual patients, we fully understand that families want the very best for their loved ones and we recognise how difficult it can be when progress feels slow. We always welcome families raising concerns with us and are committed to working with them openly.

“Decisions about moving a patient to a lower level of security are made carefully, taking account of their recovery and wellbeing alongside wider safety considerations. For many patients at Rampton these decisions also involve the Ministry of Justice and the receiving service, which can mean the process takes time.”

Neate firmly believes Jake is deteriorating at Rampton. “Jake says he is fighting a battle between good and evil and says he has to rescue Sue,” she says. “He isn’t the same person he used to be … I don’t think he’s always treated as a human being, as a person. Everything is so clinical there. They talk about his presentation, as if he’s a thing, rather than a human with a heart.

“I feel like I’m banging my head against a wall trying to help him. All I want for Jake is a life that’s reasonable, with some hope in it. People who are mentally ill are entitled to a bit of care. But I don’t believe Jake’s getting that. It’s not at all cushy or luxurious for him in Rampton, very far from it.”

https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/r.title: Trump factor could help Democrats win Republican strongholds at midterms
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/r.author: Lauren Day and Bradley McLennan
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-11/r.text:
BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Daniel DeGarmo sells items ranging from trinkets to houses in his work as an auctioneer. (ABC News: Lauren Day)

Pastor and auctioneer Daniel DeGarmo has a gift for persuasion.

In his church, he can move a congregation. On the auction floor, he can move just about anything else.

This unlikely combination of professions gives him a unique view of his community of Chillicothe, in rural Ohio.

"Everyone in the community, whether it's in church or the auction house, we're feeling the strain of things being more expensive," he says.

"Some people are going to blame politics; they're going to blame the government; they are going to blame Trump. Other people are going to blame the previous government and the previous president."

The father of eight voted for Donald Trump in both 2016 and 2024. He was happy with Mr Trump's first term, but this time is different.

Chillicothe, Ohio, has voted Republican in recent years but some locals sense change on the way. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

He has been particularly upset by the Trump administration's treatment of immigrants and the failure to bring down the cost of living.

That is why he is carefully weighing what to do at the November midterm elections, which will determine the makeup of Congress for the second half of Mr Trump's presidency.

For years, Chillicothe was a bellwether town in a bellwether state, meaning local election results mirrored the national mood.

More recently, both the town and the state have been Republican strongholds. But this year, Ohio is one of several previously reliably "red", or Republican, states that have suddenly and unexpectedly come into play.

Polls are now suggesting the midterms could bring a "blue wave" — or even a tsunami — and see Democrats win in areas once viewed as almost unwinnable.

Cook Political Report founder Charlie Cook told ABC America last month that a Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives was a "done deal".

He rated the party's chances of taking control of the Senate as "very realistic".

Campaigning is in full swing in Ohio ahead of the midterms on November 3. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

To win a Senate majority, Democrats need to gain four Republican-held seats while also holding onto their own seats, which new polling suggests is increasingly possible.

In North Carolina, the party appears on track to flip a Republican seat. In Maine, the Senate race is considered a toss-up.

And a New York Times/Siena poll last week found Democrats were also performing strongly in five reliably Republican states: Texas, Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown leads incumbent Republican John Husted 49 to 46.

Mr DeGarmo says he will not be backing either candidate put up by the major parties.

"Right now I'm stuck in the middle, and I'm not really sure if I'll even vote, quite frankly," he says.

"If I do, it'll be the first time I would ever vote for an independent candidate."

Earlier this month, Mr Trump visited Ohio as part of a weeks-long midterms campaign blitz and repeated his plea to voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot".

Some voters say they will — which could prove a problem for him.

Donald Trump's approval rating is at dire lows. But he has deliberately tied his party's fortunes to his own popularity, and "Trump-a-palooza" showed his tactics are not changing.

"What we're seeing is definitely a lot more of a referendum on Trump than it is a referendum on the Democratic Party," says Boston University political science professor David Hopkins.

"The Democratic Party has not really become more popular over the last few years, but it's just the Republicans have become less popular."

This dynamic has given rise to a new term many are now using to predict November's outcome.

Rather than a "blue wave" of voters enthusiastically endorsing the Democratic message, some are now describing a "red undertow" where Republicans are sucked into the backwash of their leader's unpopularity.

Polls consistently rank rising living costs, which Mr Trump promised to lower, as a major source of voter anger.

Chillicothe voter Chad Beatty, who owns a landscaping and lawn care business, says fuel prices are "killing" his business to the point "it's almost not worth working".

Chad Beatty says Donald Trump has delivered on none of his promises. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

He voted Democrat at the last election and believes the party will win a Senate seat in Ohio this year.

"[Trump] hasn't delivered on nothing he said he's gonna do and finally, I think people are catching onto his game and know that he's not for them," he says.

As well as a political bellwether, Chillicothe has been a bellwether of America's economic story, too.

Last year, the local paper mill closed, and about 800 people lost their jobs. Now, a controversial data centre is proposed for the site.

Hairdresser Lacey Powell used to be a Democrat when her father worked at the mill. But she feels like the party no longer cares about blue-collar or working-class voters.

Lacey Powell voted for Trump because she believed he would help small business. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

She voted for Trump in 2024 because she thought he would support small businesses like hers, but she is disappointed in what she has seen.

Like Mr DeGarmo, she is unsure if she will vote in the midterms.

"We were told about tariffs: it would be hard at first, and then we'd see relief — and you know, I just haven't seen that as a taxpayer, as a consumer," she says.

"Things that have been promised aren't happening, and I'm worried. I'm worried about my clients; I'm worrying about my kids."

Professor Hopkins says a generation ago, blue-collar workers typically backed the Democrats.

But with the decline of manufacturing and the rise of the culture war, those voters gravitated towards the Republican Party during the Trump era.

"Those are the kinds of people who are also especially being hit by the rise in inflation, the rise in gas prices and diesel prices over the last couple of years," he says.

That is why he believes the swing away from Republicans has been bigger in states with large populations of blue-collar workers like Ohio.

The closure of Chillicothe's paper mill was a major blow for the local timber industry. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

While it is often difficult to draw a direct link between the White House and people's personal financial situations, Professor Hopkins says voters this cycle are able to see the clear impact of Mr Trump's policies on tariffs and the war with Iran.

"That's made it difficult for Republican candidates to articulate their vision of what to do to solve people's economic problems," he says.

"They're faced with this choice of either endorsing Trump and Trump's policies, which voters don't like, or separating themselves from Trump and risking that Trump himself will be enraged by their disloyalty."

Two Carlton AFL football players have been hospitalised in Melbourne on Sunday, the club says.

The club confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward were admitted to hospital under separate circumstances.

"Cowan received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later," it said. 

Will Hayward experienced a minor cut to the head after a fall, and admitted himself to hospital, where he received stitches before being discharged.

Will Hayward of the Blues. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Chris Hyde)

Ambulance Victoria said advanced life-support paramedics responded to reports of an incident in South Yarra about 5:15am today.

"A man in his 20s was transported by road ambulance to The Alfred Hospital with upper body injuries in a stable condition," it said.

It is unclear which player Ambulance Victoria was referring to.

https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.title: India detains thousands and locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.author: No Author
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.text:
NEW DELHI – Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the “Cockroach” youth movement in Delhi on Saturday as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India’s election chief.

Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as ​authorities moved to stop a demonstration organized by the Cockroach movement.

The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics ‌say disproportionately benefits ‌Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, ​but the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.

A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said more than 2,000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India’s financial hub, Mumbai.

There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions.

The United Nations human rights office expressed concerns over ⁠mass detentions before and during the protests.

“We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” U.N. human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in ⁠a statement.

He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.

The Indian mission to the U.N. in Geneva, however, called the U.N.’s concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India.”

It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution. “As ​in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions ⁠in the interest of public order,” the statement added.

Police detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement.

Television footage showed Dipke challenging ⁠officers who approached him on board the ​aircraft.

“I have come to be arrested, arrest me. ... I am not afraid of you guys,” he said.

“No, this ​is not an arrest,” one officer replied. “Please cooperate.”

The movement condemned what it called the “authoritarian detention” of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting.

“We ​will continue our protest ‌tomorrow, day after ... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets,” CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters.

CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders’ whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke’s grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral.

Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also ‌detained, TV channels showed.

Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.

Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes.

The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter ​rolls ​ahead of recent state polls.

Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar’s voter-list revisions that ​removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.

Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.

The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s ⁠economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation.

The near daily protests come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit.

The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.

Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi’s opponents would not back down.

A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been “weaponized” by rivals due to ​election defeats.

Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world’s largest democracy.

Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died.

The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enroll.
https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/1.summary: Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the “Cockroach’s’ youth movement in Delhi. Demonstrations were aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists. The U.N. human rights office expressed concerns over ⁠mass detentions

https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.title: Hong Kong finance chief highlights 4 priorities ahead of Apec meeting this month
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.author: Matthew Cheng
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.text:
Meeting will focus on areas that play to city’s strengths, such as fiscal policies that support livelihoods, digital infrastructure and young talent

The Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong this month will focus on fiscal policies that support livelihoods, digital infrastructure financing, inclusive finance and young financial talent, underlining the city’s role as an international financial centre, the finance chief said.

“These four priorities are areas of strength for Hong Kong and fields in which we can make an active contribution,” Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday.

“Hosting the finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong highlights the central government’s strong support for the city and reflects the city’s status as an important international financial centre in the region.”

About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from Apec’s 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21 at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. It will be the first time Hong Kong is hosting the event.

He outlined Hong Kong’s efforts and strengths in the four areas set out in the meeting’s agenda, noting that the city had been training students and young professionals in green finance, asset and wealth management and fintech. It provided internships and educational courses to help the younger generation better understand regional markets and emerging businesses.

Chan added that more than 150 young volunteers had been recruited to help at the Apec meeting, offering them a valuable learning experience outside the classroom while allowing visiting guests to feel the enthusiasm and hospitality of the city’s youth.

On green finance, Chan emphasised the city’s role in connecting regional projects seeking funding with investors who look for transparency through green bonds, transition finance, project certification and professional services. He noted that Hong Kong had issued about US$38 billion in green and sustainable bonds in 2025, the highest value in the Asian market for the eighth consecutive year.

Chan also highlighted the city’s efforts to advance inclusive finance, citing the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Commercial Data Interchange programme, which allows small and medium-sized enterprises to authorise banks in advance to access operational data from different sources, improving the efficiency of loan approvals and easing financing difficulties.

The finance chief also said Hong Kong could foster deeper exchange and collaboration among Apec governments, financial institutions, investors and tech companies, allowing public resources to play a guiding role and mobilising more market capital to support the development of the regional digital economy and artificial intelligence.

Beyond the four priorities, Chan said Hong Kong would also showcase its strength as an international insurance and risk-management hub, which could help facilitate regional collaboration amid increasing climate risks.

“Our insurance-linked securities services, captive insurance companies and ‘Marine Specialty Risk Pool’ can cooperate with regional partners. Catastrophe bonds and speciality underwriting can provide additional protection and financing tools for regional infrastructure investment and climate-risk response,” he said.

“These open up broader markets for Hong Kong’s financial, insurance and professional services sectors.”

He added that he expected dignitaries attending the meetings to learn about Hong Kong’s latest developments in innovation, technology and urban construction, while experiencing the city’s cultural and artistic vitality and charm.

Mainland China is the host of this year’s Apec meetings, with the annual Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting to be held in Shenzhen in November.
https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/hong.summary: Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong this month will focus on fiscal policies that support livelihoods, digital infrastructure and young talent. The finance chief said the city's four priorities are areas of strength for Hong Kong and fields in which we can make an active contribution.
